docs.title: Logarithmic Functions
docs.text:
A professor's notebook — rigorous, honest, alive.

References: Stewart, Calculus (§1.6, §3.6, §7.1); MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus (supplementary notes on exponentials and logarithms)

docs.title: 0. Motivation — Why Should We Care?
docs.text:
Before the machinery, a word of honesty: logarithms are not a trick. They are the inverse of the most natural function in analysis — the exponential — and they appear wherever growth, decay, entropy, or information lives.

In 1614, John Napier introduced logarithms to turn multiplication into addition (a computational miracle before computers). Today they appear in:

  • Information theory: Shannon entropy \(H = -\sum p_i \log p_i\)
  • Signal processing: decibels, Fourier analysis
  • Physics: thermodynamic entropy \(S = k_B \ln \Omega\)
  • Machine learning / deep learning: cross-entropy loss, log-likelihood, softmax, log-sum-exp trick — we will return to all of these

docs.title: 1. Definition — The Right One
docs.text: There are two equivalent entry points. I prefer the integral definition because it requires no prior knowledge of \(e\) and makes differentiability immediate.

docs.title: 1.1 The Natural Logarithm via an Integral
docs.text:
\[\boxed{\ln x ;:=; \int_1^x \frac{1}{t},dt, \qquad x > 0}\]

Why is this a good definition?

We want a function \(L\) satisfying \(L'(x) = 1/x\) with \(L(1) = 0\). The First Fundamental Theorem of Calculus hands us exactly that. Every property of \(\ln\) — its domain, sign, monotonicity, the logarithm laws — follows from this integral and from properties of Riemann integrals.

Geometric picture. \(\ln x\) is the signed area under the hyperbola \(y = 1/t\) from \(t=1\) to \(t=x\).

  • \(x > 1\): area is positive, so \(\ln x > 0\).
  • \(x = 1\): zero-width strip, so \(\ln 1 = 0\).
  • \(0 < x < 1\): we integrate backwards, so \(\ln x < 0\).
y = 1/t
│
│ ██████
│ ████████
│ ███████████
│_________________________
0    1        x        t

Shaded area = ln x  (for x > 1)

docs.title: 1.2 The Number \(e\) — Emerging from the Definition
docs.text:
Define \(e\) as the unique number satisfying \(\ln e = 1\), i.e.,

\[\int_1^e \frac{1}{t},dt = 1.\]

It can be shown this number exists (by IVT: \(\ln\) is continuous, \(\ln 1 = 0\), \(\ln\) is unbounded above) and is unique (strict monotonicity). Numerically, \(e \approx 2.71828\ldots\)

docs.title: 2. Fundamental Properties
docs.text: All of the following follow from the integral definition. I will prove each.

docs.title: 2.1 Domain and Range
docs.text:
\(\ln : (0, \infty) \to \mathbb{R}\) is a bijection.

  • Domain \((0,\infty)\): \(1/t\) is only integrable on intervals avoiding \(t=0\).
  • Range \(\mathbb{R}\):
    • \(\ln x \to +\infty\) as \(x \to \infty\) (compare with \(\int_1^x \frac{1}{t},dt \geq \int_1^x \frac{1}{x},dt = \frac{x-1}{x}\)... or use the harmonic series argument).
    • \(\ln x \to -\infty\) as \(x \to 0^+\) (substitute \(u = 1/t\)).

docs.title: 2.2 Logarithm Laws
docs.text:
Theorem. For \(a, b > 0\) and \(r \in \mathbb{Q}\):

\[\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b \tag{L1}$$ $$\ln!\left(\tfrac{a}{b}\right) = \ln a - \ln b \tag{L2}$$ $$\ln(a^r) = r\ln a \tag{L3}\]

Proof of (L1). Fix \(a > 0\) and let \(f(x) = \ln(ax)\). Then $\(f'(x) = \frac{a}{ax} = \frac{1}{x} = (\ln x)'.\)$ So \(f(x) = \ln x + C\) for some constant. Setting \(x=1\): \(f(1) = \ln a = \ln 1 + C = C\). Therefore \(\ln(ax) = \ln x + \ln a\). Setting \(x = b\) gives (L1). \(\blacksquare\)

(L2) follows from (L1): \(\ln(a/b) + \ln b = \ln!\left(\frac{a}{b} \cdot b\right) = \ln a\).

(L3) for integer \(r\) follows by induction from (L1); the rational and real cases require a bit more care.

docs.title: 2.3 Derivative and Monotonicity
docs.text:
\[\frac{d}{dx}\ln x = \frac{1}{x} > 0 \quad\text{for all } x > 0.\]

So \(\ln\) is strictly increasing. Also, \(\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\ln x = -1/x^2 < 0\), so \(\ln\) is strictly concave on \((0,\infty)\).

Remark (concavity matters in ML). The strict concavity of \(\ln\) is exactly why Jensen's inequality gives \(\ln(\mathbb{E}[X]) \geq \mathbb{E}[\ln X]\) — a fact that underlies the EM algorithm and variational inference.

docs.title: 2.4 The Chain Rule with \(\ln\)
docs.text:
\[\frac{d}{dx}\ln|u(x)| = \frac{u'(x)}{u(x)}\]

This is the workhorse for integration: \(\int \frac{u'}{u},dx = \ln|u| + C\).

Example. \(\int \frac{2x}{x^2+1},dx = \ln(x^2+1) + C\). (Here \(u = x^2+1 > 0\), so no absolute value needed.)

docs.title: 3.1 Change of Base
docs.text:
For any base \(b > 0\), \(b \neq 1\), define:

\[\log_b x := \frac{\ln x}{\ln b}\]

This is not a separate function — it is a rescaled natural logarithm. The base \(b=10\) gives \(\log_{10}\) (common log), and \(b=e\) gives \(\ln\) itself.

Derivative: $\(\frac{d}{dx}\log_b x = \frac{1}{x \ln b}\)$

In practice: unless forced otherwise, always work in base \(e\). The extra factor of \(\ln b\) in denominators is noise.

docs.title: 3.2 The Exponential Function — The Inverse
docs.text:
Since \(\ln:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}\) is a bijection, its inverse \(\exp = \ln^{-1}: \mathbb{R} \to (0,\infty)\) exists. We denote \(\exp(x) = e^x\). From inverse function differentiation:

\[\frac{d}{dx}e^x = e^x.\]

The mutual inverse relationship: $\(\ln(e^x) = x \quad \forall x \in \mathbb{R}, \qquad e^{\ln x} = x \quad \forall x > 0.\)$

docs.title: 4. Asymptotic Behavior — Two Important Limits
docs.text:
These are indispensable and constantly appear in analysis and ML.

Theorem. $\(\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\ln x}{x^p} = 0 \quad \text{for any } p > 0 \tag{A1}\)$ $\(\lim_{x \to 0^+} x^p \ln x = 0 \quad \text{for any } p > 0 \tag{A2}\)$

Proof of (A1). For \(x > 1\): $\(\ln x = \int_1^x \frac{dt}{t} \leq \int_1^x t^{p/2 - 1},dt = \frac{2}{p}\left(x^{p/2}-1\right) \leq \frac{2}{p} x^{p/2}.\)$ So \(0 \leq \frac{\ln x}{x^p} \leq \frac{2}{p} x^{-p/2} \to 0\). \(\blacksquare\)

Verbal summary: Logarithms grow more slowly than any positive power of \(x\). Any power of \(x\) damps out \(|\ln x|\) at the origin.

Growth rate hierarchy (slowest to fastest):
ln(ln x) ≪ ln x ≪ x^ε ≪ x ≪ x^2 ≪ e^x ≪ e^(e^x)
for any fixed ε > 0.

docs.title: 5.1 The Fundamental Antiderivative
docs.text:
\[\int \frac{1}{x},dx = \ln|x| + C\]

The absolute value handles \(x < 0\): for \(x < 0\), let \(u = -x\), then \(du = -dx\) and \(\int \frac{1}{x}dx = \int \frac{-du}{u} = -\ln u = \ln|x|\).

docs.title: 5.2 Integration by Parts: \(\int \ln x, dx\)
docs.text:
\[\int \ln x, dx = x\ln x - x + C\]

Proof. Set \(u = \ln x\), \(dv = dx\). Then \(du = \frac{1}{x}dx\), \(v = x\). $\(\int \ln x, dx = x\ln x - \int x \cdot \frac{1}{x}, dx = x\ln x - x + C. \qquad \blacksquare\)$

docs.title: 5.3 Logarithmic Integration Pattern
docs.text:
\[\int \frac{f'(x)}{f(x)},dx = \ln|f(x)| + C\]

Example. \(\displaystyle\int \tan x, dx = \int \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}, dx = -\ln|\cos x| + C = \ln|\sec x| + C\).

docs.title: 6. Logarithmic Differentiation
docs.text:
A technique for differentiating products, quotients, or functions with variable exponents.

Strategy: Take \(\ln\) of both sides, differentiate implicitly, solve for \(y'\).

Example 1. Let \(y = x^x\) for \(x > 0\). $\(\ln y = x \ln x \implies \frac{y'}{y} = \ln x + 1 \implies y' = x^x(\ln x + 1).\)$

Example 2. Let \(y = \dfrac{x^2 \sqrt{x+1}}{(2x-1)^3}\).

\[\ln y = 2\ln x + \tfrac{1}{2}\ln(x+1) - 3\ln(2x-1)$$ $$\frac{y'}{y} = \frac{2}{x} + \frac{1}{2(x+1)} - \frac{6}{2x-1}\]

Multiply through by \(y\) to get \(y'\). Much cleaner than the quotient rule.

docs.title: 7. Taylor Series and Approximations
docs.text:
Near \(x = 0\):

\[\ln(1+x) = x - \frac{x^2}{2} + \frac{x^3}{3} - \cdots = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n} x^n, \qquad |x| \leq 1,; x \neq -1\]

Proof sketch. We know \(\frac{d}{dx}\ln(1+x) = \frac{1}{1+x} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty (-1)^n x^n\) for \(|x| < 1\). Integrating term by term and using \(\ln(1) = 0\) gives the series.

First-order approximation: For small \(x\), $\(\ln(1+x) \approx x.\)$ This is everywhere in ML. The log-likelihood gradient, the natural gradient, the derivation of KL divergence — all lean on this.

docs.title: 8. Connections to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: This is where the abstract machinery becomes viscerally useful. I want to show why logarithms, specifically, appear — not just that they do.

docs.title: 8.1 Cross-Entropy Loss
docs.text:
In a \(K\)-class classification problem, let \(\mathbf{p} = (p_1, \ldots, p_K)\) be the true distribution (a one-hot vector in practice) and \(\hat{\mathbf{p}} = (\hat{p}_1,\ldots,\hat{p}_K)\) be the model's predicted probabilities (output of a softmax). The cross-entropy loss is:

\[\mathcal{L} = -\sum_{k=1}^K p_k \ln \hat{p}_k\]

For a one-hot label where \(p_c = 1\) for correct class \(c\):

\[\mathcal{L} = -\ln \hat{p}_c\]

Why \(\ln\)? Because we are doing maximum likelihood estimation. The likelihood of data \({x_i, y_i}_{i=1}^N\) under the model is: $\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{MLE}} = \prod_{i=1}^N \hat{p}_{y_i}(x_i).\)$ Maximizing this is equivalent to minimizing \(-\ln \mathcal{L}_{\text{MLE}} = -\sum_i \ln \hat{p}_{y_i}(x_i)\). The product became a sum because of property (L1). This is why gradient descent on the cross-entropy loss is maximum likelihood.

Key calculus here. \(\frac{\partial}{\partial z_c}(-\ln \hat{p}_c) = \hat{p}_c - 1\) (after passing through the softmax — a beautiful calculation involving \(\frac{d}{dx}\ln\) and the chain rule). This is why the gradient of cross-entropy + softmax is so clean.

docs.title: 8.2 The Log-Sum-Exp Trick — Numerical Stability
docs.text:
The softmax is: $\(\hat{p}_k = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{j} e^{z_j}}\)$

For large logits \(z_k\) (e.g., \(z_k = 1000\)), \(e^{z_k}\) overflows to inf on a computer. The fix: use the identity

\[\ln!\sum_j e^{z_j} = c + \ln!\sum_j e^{z_j - c}\]

(follows from (L1): \(\ln(e^c \cdot \sum e^{z_j - c}) = c + \ln\sum e^{z_j-c}\)). Choose \(c = \max_j z_j\). Now the largest term inside the sum is \(e^0 = 1\), and everything is numerically safe.

This is applied logarithm arithmetic — property (L1) saves numerical computation.

docs.title: 8.3 KL Divergence
docs.text:
The Kullback–Leibler divergence from distribution \(q\) to \(p\):

\[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p | q) = \sum_k p_k \ln \frac{p_k}{q_k} = \sum_k p_k(\ln p_k - \ln q_k)\]

Properties:

  • \(D_{\mathrm{KL}} \geq 0\) always (Gibbs' inequality, proved using concavity of \(\ln\) and Jensen's inequality: \(-\ln\) is convex, so \(-\mathbb{E}_p[\ln(q/p)] \geq -\ln\mathbb{E}_p[q/p] = 0\)).
  • \(D_{\mathrm{KL}} = 0\) iff \(p = q\).
  • Not symmetric — it is not a metric, but it measures "information lost when using \(q\) to approximate \(p\)."

In variational autoencoders (VAEs), the loss is ELBO = reconstruction loss + \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_\phi(z|x) | p(z))\). The KL term regularizes the latent space toward the prior. Its gradient is computable exactly when both distributions are Gaussian, using the formula for Gaussian KL — which requires \(\ln\) of the determinants of covariance matrices.

docs.title: 8.4 Entropy and Information
docs.text:
Shannon entropy: \(H(p) = -\sum_k p_k \ln p_k\)

This measures the average uncertainty (or information content) in a distribution. The \(\ln\) makes it additive for independent events (from (L1)): \(H(p \otimes q) = H(p) + H(q)\).

In decision tree learning (CART, ID3), splitting criteria use information gain \(= H(\text{parent}) - \sum H(\text{children})\). The logarithm is not cosmetic — it is the unique (up to scalar) function making information additive. (Shannon's theorem.)

docs.title: 8.5 Log-Likelihood and Gradient Descent
docs.text:
Training a neural network by gradient descent on negative log-likelihood:

\[ heta^* = \arg\min_ heta \left[-\sum_{i=1}^N \ln p_ heta(y_i | x_i) ight]\]

The gradient is:

\[ abla_ heta \left[-\ln p_ heta(y|x) ight] = - abla_ heta \ln p_ heta(y|x) = - rac{ abla_ heta p_ heta(y|x)}{p_ heta(y|x)}\]

(by the chain rule: \( rac{d}{dx}\ln f(x) = rac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\))

This score function \( abla_ heta \ln p_ heta\) appears in policy gradient methods (REINFORCE), the Fisher information matrix, and natural gradient descent. Every one of these rests on the single formula \((\ln f)' = f'/f\).

docs.title: 8.6 Logarithmic Learning Rate Schedules
docs.text:
Practitioners use schedules like: $\(\eta_t = \eta_0 / \ln(t+2)\)$

This decays very slowly (slower than \(1/t\), faster than constant) — precisely because \(\ln t\) grows slowly (recall (A1)). The asymptotic hierarchy of §4 is not academic — it tells you which schedule converges, and how fast.

docs.title: Example 9.1 — Differentiate \(f(x) = \ln(\sin^2 x + 1)\)
docs.text:
\[f'(x) = \frac{2\sin x \cos x}{\sin^2 x + 1} = \frac{\sin 2x}{\sin^2 x + 1}\]

(Chain rule: outer derivative \(1/u\), inner derivative \(2\sin x\cos x = \sin 2x\).)

docs.title: Example 9.2 — Evaluate \(\int_0^1 \frac{x}{x^2+1},dx\)
docs.text: Let \(u = x^2+1\), \(du = 2x,dx\): $\(\int_0^1 \frac{x}{x^2+1}dx = \frac{1}{2}\int_1^2 \frac{du}{u} = \frac{1}{2}\left[\ln u\right]_1^2 = \frac{\ln 2}{2}.\)$

docs.title: Example 9.4 — A Limit Using L'Hôpital
docs.text:
\[\lim_{x \to 0^+} x \ln x\]

Form \(0 \cdot (-\infty)\). Rewrite as \(\frac{\ln x}{1/x}\), form \(\frac{-\infty}{\infty}\). Apply L'Hôpital:

\[\lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{\ln x}{1/x} = \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{1/x}{-1/x^2} = \lim_{x \to 0^+} (-x) = 0.\]

(Consistent with (A2): \(p=1\) there.)

docs.title: Example 9.5 — Cross-Entropy Gradient (ML Application)
docs.text:
Suppose \(\hat{p} = \sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})\) (sigmoid, binary classification). Loss: \(\mathcal{L} = -y\ln\hat{p} - (1-y)\ln(1-\hat{p})\). Compute \(\partial \mathcal{L}/\partial z\):

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z} = -\frac{y}{\hat{p}}\hat{p}' + \frac{1-y}{1-\hat{p}}\hat{p}'\]

where \(\hat{p}' = \hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\) (standard sigmoid derivative). Substituting:

\[= -y(1-\hat{p}) + (1-y)\hat{p} = \hat{p} - y.\]

The loss gradient is simply prediction minus label — a beautiful fact enabled entirely by \(\frac{d}{dx}\ln x = 1/x\) eating the denominator.

docs.title: 10. Visualization Reference
docs.text:
Graph of y = ln(x):

y
│
 2│                               ·
  │                          ·
 1│                    ·(e,1)
  │               ·
 0│──────────────·────────────────── x
  │         ·   1
-1│     ·
  │  ·
-2│·
  │
  (defined only for x > 0)

Key points: ln(1)=0, ln(e)≈1, ln(e²)=2, ln(1/e)=-1
Tangent at x=1 has slope 1 (since (ln x)'|_{x=1} = 1)
Concave down everywhere (second derivative < 0)

Comparison of growth rates:

         x=10     x=100    x=1000
─────────────────────────────────
ln(x)   2.30     4.61     6.91
√x      3.16     10.0     31.6
x       10       100      1000
x²      100      10000    10⁶
eˣ      22026    10^43    10^434

ln grows far more slowly than any power of x.

docs.title: 11. Summary — The Essential Facts
docs.text: Fact Formula Definition \(\ln x = \int_1^x \frac{1}{t},dt\) Derivative \(\frac{d}{dx}\ln x = \frac{1}{x}\) Product rule \(\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b\) Power rule \(\ln(a^r) = r\ln a\) Antiderivative $\int \frac{1}{x},dx = \ln IBP result \(\int \ln x,dx = x\ln x - x + C\) Asymptotics \(\ln x / x^p \to 0\) as \(x\to\infty\), any \(p>0\) Taylor series \(\ln(1+x) = x - x^2/2 + x^3/3 - \cdots\) Change of base \(\log_b x = \ln x / \ln b\)

docs.title: 12. Personal Marginalia
docs.text:
Why is the natural log "natural"? Because \(\frac{d}{dx}\ln_b x = \frac{1}{x \ln b}\), and only \(b = e\) gives the clean coefficient \(1\). Any other base clutters every derivative and integral with a constant factor. Nature (and mathematicians) despise clutter.

The logarithm is the original data scientist's transform. Raw data spanning orders of magnitude — incomes, earthquake energies, neural firing rates, word frequencies (Zipf's law) — becomes Gaussian-ish after a log transform. Why? Because many natural phenomena are log-normally distributed: their logarithm is normal. The moment you take a log, you're doing exponential-family statistics.

Jensen's inequality + concavity of \(\ln\) = half of modern probabilistic machine learning. The ELBO in variational inference, the EM algorithm, contrastive learning bounds — all are applications of \(\ln(\mathbb{E}[X]) \geq \mathbb{E}[\ln X]\) combined with the definition of KL divergence. One concavity fact, infinite consequences.

References:

  • Stewart, J. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, §1.6 (Inverse Functions and Logarithms), §3.6 (Derivatives of Logarithmic Functions), §7.1 (Integration by Parts)
  • MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus — Supplementary Notes on Exponentials and Logarithms
  • Shannon, C.E. A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)
  • Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville. Deep Learning, Ch. 3 (Probability and Information Theory)

docs.title: Transformation of Functions
docs.text:
A professor's notebook — rigorous, geometric, and alive.

References: Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals §1.3; MIT 18.02 Supplementary Notes on Functions and Graphs

docs.title: 0. Motivation — Why Transformations?
docs.text:
Every function you will ever encounter in analysis, geometry, signal processing, or machine learning is, at its core, a transformed version of something simpler. The Gaussian \(e^{-(x-\mu)^2/2\sigma^2}\) is a shifted, scaled, and compressed version of \(e^{-x^2}\). The ReLU applied to a linear layer is a shifted threshold function. A convolutional filter is a translated version of a kernel.

The central insight is this: you do not need to relearn a function from scratch when it is transformed. You need to understand how the transformation acts on the graph.

There are exactly four elementary transformations — translations, reflections, stretches/compressions — and every sophisticated transformation in analysis is a composition of these four. Learn them once, deeply, and you have a universal toolkit.

docs.title: 1. The Setup — Precise Language
docs.text:
Let \(f: D \subseteq \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) be a function with graph

\[\Gamma_f = {(x, f(x)) : x \in D} \subset \mathbb{R}^2.\]

A transformation is a map \(T: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2\) that sends the graph \(\Gamma_f\) to a new graph \(\Gamma_g\). The question is always: given \(f\), what is \(g\)?

We classify transformations according to whether they act on the input (horizontal, affects \(x\)) or the output (vertical, affects \(y = f(x)\)). This distinction is the single most important conceptual divide.

\[g(x) = \underbrace{a \cdot f(\underbrace{bx + c}_{\text{input transformation}}) + d}_{\text{output transformation}}\]

Every transformation we study is a special case of this general form.

docs.title: 2.1 Definition
docs.text:
\[g(x) = f(x) + d, \qquad d \in \mathbb{R}\]

The graph of \(g\) is the graph of \(f\) shifted vertically by \(d\) units.

  • \(d > 0\): shift up.
  • \(d < 0\): shift down.

docs.title: 2.2 Why? — Precise Argument
docs.text: For each \(x\), the output value changes from \(f(x)\) to \(f(x) + d\). The \(x\)-coordinate of every point is unchanged; the \(y\)-coordinate increases by \(d\). The transformation on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is \((x, y) \mapsto (x, y+d)\) — a pure vertical translation.

docs.title: 2.3 Effect on Domain and Range
docs.text:
• Domain: unchanged.
  • Range: shifted by \(d\). If \(\text{ran}(f) = [m, M]\), then \(\text{ran}(g) = [m+d, M+d]\).

docs.title: 2.4 Example
docs.text:
Let \(f(x) = x^2\). Then \(g(x) = x^2 + 3\) is the parabola shifted up 3 units. The vertex moves from \((0,0)\) to \((0,3)\).

        g(x) = x² + 3
y       │    *
        │   * *
   3────│──*───*──
        │ *     *
   0────┼─────────── x
        f(x) = x²

docs.title: 3.1 Definition
docs.text:
\[g(x) = f(x - c), \qquad c \in \mathbb{R}\]

The graph of \(g\) is the graph of \(f\) shifted horizontally by \(c\) units.

  • \(c > 0\): shift right.
  • \(c < 0\): shift left.

docs.title: 3.2 The Crucial Subtlety — Sign Reversal
docs.text:
This is where students stumble. The intuition says: replacing \(x\) with \(x - c\) should shift left (subtracting makes things smaller). It does the opposite.

Rigorous explanation. The graph of \(f\) passes through \((x_0, f(x_0))\). The graph of \(g(x) = f(x-c)\) passes through the point where \(g(x) = f(x_0)\), i.e., where \(x - c = x_0\), i.e., where \(x = x_0 + c\). So the point \((x_0, f(x_0))\) on \(\Gamma_f\) corresponds to the point \((x_0 + c, f(x_0))\) on \(\Gamma_g\). The shift is right by \(c\).

Mnemonic. Think of it as a delay: \(f(x-c)\) "waits" until \(x = c\) before it starts behaving like \(f\) does at \(x=0\). It is delayed to the right.

docs.title: 3.3 Example
docs.text:
\(f(x) = \sqrt{x}\), domain \([0, \infty)\).

  • \(g(x) = \sqrt{x-2}\): domain \([2,\infty)\), shifted right 2.
  • \(h(x) = \sqrt{x+3}\): domain \([-3,\infty)\), shifted left 3.
h(x)=√(x+3)    f(x)=√x    g(x)=√(x-2)
     ↗               ↗              ↗
─────────────────────────────────────── x
    -3           0         2

docs.title: 4.1 Definition
docs.text:
\[g(x) = a \cdot f(x), \qquad a > 0\]
  • \(a > 1\): vertical stretch by factor \(a\) (graph pulled away from \(x\)-axis).
  • \(0 < a < 1\): vertical compression by factor \(a\) (graph pushed toward \(x\)-axis).

docs.title: 4.2 Precise Geometry
docs.text: Every \(y\)-coordinate is multiplied by \(a\). The \(x\)-intercepts (where \(f(x) = 0\)) are fixed points of this transformation — they do not move. The transformation on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is \((x,y) \mapsto (x, ay)\).

docs.title: 4.3 Example
docs.text:
\(f(x) = \sin x\).

  • \(g(x) = 3\sin x\): amplitude 3, stretched vertically.
  • \(h(x) = \tfrac{1}{2}\sin x\): amplitude \(\tfrac{1}{2}\), compressed.
y
 3│   *               g(x) = 3sin(x)
  │  * *
 1│ *   *             f(x) = sin(x)
  │*     *
──┼────────────────────────────────── x
  │       *     *
-1│        *   *
  │         * *
-3│          *

docs.title: 5.1 Definition
docs.text:
\[g(x) = f(bx), \qquad b > 0\]
  • \(b > 1\): horizontal compression by factor \(1/b\) (graph squeezed toward \(y\)-axis).
  • \(0 < b < 1\): horizontal stretch by factor \(1/b\) (graph pulled away from \(y\)-axis).

docs.title: 5.2 The Sign Paradox — Again
docs.text:
The horizontal case is always "backwards" from vertical:

  • Multiplying \(x\) by \(b > 1\) compresses horizontally (counterintuitive but correct).

Proof. The feature of \(f\) at \(x = x_0\) now occurs when \(bx = x_0\), i.e., at \(x = x_0/b\). Since \(b > 1\), \(x_0/b < x_0\) — the feature moved closer to the origin. Compression.

docs.title: 5.3 Example — Sinusoidal Period
docs.text:
\(f(x) = \sin x\) has period \(2\pi\).

  • \(g(x) = \sin(2x)\): period \(2\pi/2 = \pi\) — compressed.
  • \(h(x) = \sin(x/2)\): period \(2\pi/(1/2) = 4\pi\) — stretched.

General rule: If \(f\) has period \(T\), then \(f(bx)\) has period \(T/b\).

f(x) = sin(x):     one full wave over [0, 2π]
g(x) = sin(2x):    two full waves over [0, 2π]  ← compressed
h(x) = sin(x/2):   half wave over [0, 2π]       ← stretched

docs.title: 6.1 Reflection in the \(x\)-axis (Vertical Flip)
docs.text:
\[g(x) = -f(x)\]

Every \(y\)-coordinate is negated. The graph flips over the \(x\)-axis. The transformation on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is \((x,y) \mapsto (x,-y)\).

Fixed points: the \(x\)-intercepts of \(f\).

docs.title: 6.2 Reflection in the \(y\)-axis (Horizontal Flip)
docs.text:
\[g(x) = f(-x)\]

Every \(x\)-coordinate is negated. The graph flips over the \(y\)-axis. The transformation on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is \((x,y) \mapsto (-x,y)\).

Fixed points: points on the \(y\)-axis (where \(x=0\)).

Effect on domain: if \(D = [a,b]\), the new domain is \([-b,-a]\).

docs.title: 6.3 Reflection in Both Axes
docs.text:
\[g(x) = -f(-x)\]

This is equivalent to a \(180°\) rotation about the origin. Note: if \(f\) is an odd function (\(f(-x) = -f(x)\)), then \(g = f\) — the graph is symmetric under this rotation.

docs.title: 6.4 Example
docs.text:
\(f(x) = \sqrt{x}\), domain \([0,\infty)\).

  • \(-f(x) = -\sqrt{x}\): reflected over \(x\)-axis, domain unchanged.
  • \(f(-x) = \sqrt{-x}\): reflected over \(y\)-axis, domain \((-\infty, 0]\).
f(-x)=√(-x)   │    f(x)=√x
     ↗         │         ↗
───────────────┼─────────────── x
               │
    -f(-x)     │   -f(x)
     ↘         │        ↘

docs.title: 7. The General Form — Composing All Four
docs.text:
\[\boxed{g(x) = a \cdot f(b(x - h)) + k}\]

where:

Parameter Type Effect \(h\) Horizontal translation Shift right by \(h\) \(k\) Vertical translation Shift up by \(k\) \(\|b\|\) Horizontal scale Compress by \(\|b\|\) if \(\|b\|>1\), stretch if \(\|b\|<1\) \(\|a\|\) Vertical scale Stretch by \(\|a\|\) if \(\|a\|>1\), compress if \(\|a\|<1\) \(a < 0\) Reflection Flip over \(x\)-axis \(b < 0\) Reflection Flip over \(y\)-axis

docs.title: 7.1 Order of Operations Matters
docs.text:
To graph \(g(x) = a \cdot f(b(x-h)) + k\) from \(f\), apply transformations in this order:

  1. Horizontal shift: replace \(x\) with \(x - h\).
  2. Horizontal scale/reflect: replace \(x\) with \(bx\).
  3. Vertical scale/reflect: multiply outputs by \(a\).
  4. Vertical shift: add \(k\).

Warning. Many textbooks write \(f(bx + c)\) rather than \(f(b(x-h))\). These are equivalent with \(h = -c/b\), but the factored form \(b(x-h)\) makes the shift explicit. Always factor out \(b\) before reading off the horizontal shift.

docs.title: 7.2 Example — Full Analysis
docs.text:
Analyze \(g(x) = 2\sin(3x - \pi) + 1\).

Step 1: Factor. \(g(x) = 2\sin!\left(3!\left(x - \tfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\right) + 1\).

Now read off:

  • \(f(x) = \sin x\) (base function)
  • \(b = 3\): horizontal compression, period \(= 2\pi/3\)
  • \(h = \pi/3\): shift right by \(\pi/3\)
  • \(a = 2\): vertical stretch, amplitude \(= 2\)
  • \(k = 1\): shift up by \(1\)

Key features of \(g\):

  • Midline: \(y = 1\)
  • Amplitude: \(2\) (oscillates between \(-1\) and \(3\))
  • Period: \(2\pi/3\)
  • Phase shift: right \(\pi/3\)
y
 3│    *
  │   * *
 1│──*──────*──────── midline y=1
  │ *        *
-1│*          *
  │
  └──────────────────── x
     π/3   π/3+π/3
     (peak at x = π/3 + π/6 = π/2)

docs.title: 8.1 \(g(x) = |f(x)|\) — Reflect negative parts upward
docs.text:
The portions of the graph below the \(x\)-axis are reflected up. Points where \(f(x) \geq 0\) are unchanged.

Formally: \(|f(x)| = f(x)\) when \(f(x) \geq 0\), and \(|f(x)| = -f(x)\) when \(f(x) < 0\).

Example. \(f(x) = \sin x\). Then \(|\sin x|\) takes all the negative half-arches and flips them up — the result has period \(\pi\) instead of \(2\pi\).

docs.title: 8.2 \(g(x) = f(|x|)\) — Mirror right half onto left
docs.text:
The graph for \(x \geq 0\) is kept; the graph for \(x < 0\) is replaced by a mirror image of the right half.

Formally: \(f(|x|) = f(x)\) for \(x \geq 0\), and \(f(|x|) = f(-x)\) for \(x < 0\). The result is always an even function: \(g(-x) = f(|-x|) = f(|x|) = g(x)\).

Example. \(f(x) = e^x\). Then \(f(|x|) = e^{|x|}\), which is V-shaped on a log scale and symmetric about the \(y\)-axis.

docs.title: 9. Even and Odd Functions — Symmetry as Transformation
9.1 Even Functions
docs.text:
\(f(-x) = f(x)\) for all \(x\) in the domain.

Geometric meaning: the graph is symmetric about the \(y\)-axis. Applying the transformation \(g(x) = f(-x)\) gives back \(f\) — the graph is invariant under reflection in the \(y\)-axis.

Examples: \(x^2\), \(\cos x\), \(|x|\), \(x^4 - 3x^2\).

docs.title: 9.2 Odd Functions
docs.text:
\(f(-x) = -f(x)\) for all \(x\).

Geometric meaning: the graph is symmetric about the origin (invariant under \(180°\) rotation). Applying \(g(x) = -f(-x)\) gives back \(f\).

Examples: \(x\), \(x^3\), \(\sin x\), \(\tan x\).

docs.title: 9.3 Decomposition Theorem
docs.text:
Every function \(f\) defined on a symmetric domain can be uniquely written as:

\[f(x) = \underbrace{\frac{f(x) + f(-x)}{2}}_{\text{even part}} + \underbrace{\frac{f(x) - f(-x)}{2}}_{\text{odd part}}\]

Proof. Let \(E(x) = \frac{f(x)+f(-x)}{2}\) and \(O(x) = \frac{f(x)-f(-x)}{2}\). Then \(E(-x) = E(x)\) ✓, \(O(-x) = -O(x)\) ✓, and \(E(x)+O(x) = f(x)\) ✓. Uniqueness follows from the fact that the only function that is both even and odd is the zero function.

This decomposition matters in signal processing. Every signal can be written as the sum of its even and odd parts — this is the real-variable analog of writing a complex exponential as cosine plus \(i\) times sine.

docs.title: 10. Inverse Functions as Reflections
docs.text:
The graph of \(f^{-1}\) (when it exists) is obtained by reflecting \(\Gamma_f\) over the line \(y = x\).

Proof. \((a, b) \in \Gamma_f \iff f(a) = b \iff a = f^{-1}(b) \iff (b, a) \in \Gamma_{f^{-1}}\). The map \((a,b) \mapsto (b,a)\) is exactly reflection over \(y = x\). \(\blacksquare\)

y = x
  ↗
│   * (b,a) on f⁻¹
│  /
│ * (a,b) on f
│/
└──────────────────── x

This means: a function and its inverse are mirror images across the diagonal. Visually: if \(f\) is increasing and concave up, then \(f^{-1}\) is increasing and concave down (since curvature reflects over the line \(y=x\)).

Example. \(f(x) = e^x\) and \(f^{-1}(x) = \ln x\) are reflections of each other over \(y = x\). Both are increasing; \(e^x\) is convex (cups upward) and \(\ln x\) is concave (cups downward).

docs.title: 11. Composition of Transformations — The Formal View
docs.text:
It is worth recording the transformations as maps on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) so we can compose them algebraically.

Transformation Map on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) Vertical shift up \(k\) \((x,y) \mapsto (x, y+k)\) Horizontal shift right \(h\) \((x,y) \mapsto (x+h, y)\) Vertical stretch by \(a > 0\) \((x,y) \mapsto (x, ay)\) Horizontal compress by \(b > 0\) \((x,y) \mapsto (x/b, y)\) Reflect over \(x\)-axis \((x,y) \mapsto (x,-y)\) Reflect over \(y\)-axis \((x,y) \mapsto (-x,y)\) Reflect over \(y=x\) \((x,y) \mapsto (y,x)\)

These are all affine maps (linear maps plus translation). Their composition is again affine. This is the language of linear algebra — and it foreshadows why neural networks apply affine transformations before nonlinearities.

docs.title: 12. Connections to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
12.1 Neural Networks as Function Compositions
docs.text:
A single layer of a neural network computes:

\[\mathbf{h} = \sigma(W\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b})\]

Break this down:

  • \(W\mathbf{x}\): a linear transformation — rotates and stretches the input space.
  • \(+ \mathbf{b}\): a translation — shifts the origin.
  • \(\sigma(\cdot)\): a nonlinear transformation applied elementwise (ReLU, sigmoid, tanh).

The whole network is a composition of affine transformations and nonlinearities. Understanding function transformations is literally understanding what a neural network computes at each layer.

docs.title: 12.2 Activation Functions as Shifted/Scaled Versions of Each Other
docs.text:
Consider the logistic sigmoid: \(\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\).

Tanh is a rescaled, shifted sigmoid: $\(\tanh(x) = 2\sigma(2x) - 1\)$

This is a vertical stretch by 2, horizontal compression by 2, and vertical shift down by 1 applied to \(\sigma\). The two functions have the same shape; only their range differs (\([0,1]\) vs \([-1,1]\)). In practice, tanh is preferred in some contexts precisely because it is zero-centered — a consequence of the vertical shift.

docs.title: 12.3 Data Normalization — Affine Transformation of Inputs
docs.text:
Standardization (z-score normalization) transforms data \(x\) to:

\[\tilde{x} = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\]

This is a horizontal shift by \(\mu\) followed by a horizontal compression by \(\sigma\) — but since \(x\) is the input, in function terms:

\[f!\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)\]

is \(f\) shifted right by \(\mu\) and stretched horizontally by \(\sigma\). Standardization ensures the input distribution has mean 0 and variance 1, making gradient descent converge faster (the loss landscape is better conditioned). This is entirely a consequence of the transformation of functions.

docs.title: 12.4 Batch Normalization — Adaptive Affine Rescaling
docs.text:
Batch normalization in deep learning normalizes the activations of each layer and then applies a learned affine transformation:

\[\hat{z} = \gamma \cdot \frac{z - \mu_B}{\sigma_B} + \beta\]
  • \(\frac{z-\mu_B}{\sigma_B}\): normalize (shift and compress).
  • \(\gamma\): learned vertical stretch.
  • \(\beta\): learned vertical shift.

The network learns the optimal affine transformation for each layer's activations. The parameters \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\) are exactly the \(a\) and \(k\) from \(g(x) = a \cdot f(x) + k\).

docs.title: 12.5 The ReLU and Its Translations
docs.text:
The Rectified Linear Unit is \(\text{ReLU}(x) = \max(0, x)\). Notice:

\[\text{ReLU}(x - c) = \max(0, x-c)\]

This is ReLU shifted right by \(c\) — it "activates" at \(x = c\) instead of \(x = 0\). The leaky ReLU \(\max(\alpha x, x)\) is a piecewise rescaling (vertical compression for \(x < 0\)). The ELU approximates a smooth version. All are transformations of the same underlying threshold idea.

docs.title: 12.6 Convolutional Neural Networks — Translation as a Core Operation
docs.text:
A convolution is:

\[(f * g)(x) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(t), g(x - t), dt\]

The term \(g(x-t)\) is exactly \(g\) translated by \(t\). A convolutional neural network learns a filter \(g\) and applies it at every translation \(t\) — the fundamental operation is horizontal translation of a function. The property that makes convolutions powerful — translation equivariance — is precisely the statement that shifting the input by \(c\) shifts the output by \(c\):

\[\text{Conv}[f(x-c)](https://claude.ai/chat/x) = (f*g)(x-c).\]

This is not a coincidence. It is the algebraic consequence of the convolution using \(g(x-t)\) (a translate of \(g\)) rather than \(g(x+t)\).

docs.title: 12.7 Positional Encoding in Transformers
docs.text:
In the Transformer architecture, positional encodings use:

\[PE(pos, 2i) = \sin!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right), \quad PE(pos, 2i+1) = \cos!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right)\]

Each encoding is a sinusoid with a different horizontal compression (\(b = 1/10000^{2i/d}\)). Different dimensions of the encoding correspond to different frequencies. The model can learn to identify position by the phase — which is exactly a horizontal translation of the sinusoid.

docs.title: Example 13.1 — Identify All Transformations
docs.text:
Given \(g(x) = -3\sqrt{2x + 6} + 1\), express relative to \(f(x) = \sqrt{x}\) and describe all transformations.

Step 1: Factor the inside. $\(g(x) = -3\sqrt{2(x+3)} + 1\)$

Step 2: Read off parameters from \(g(x) = a \cdot f(b(x-h)) + k\):

  • \(a = -3\): vertical stretch by 3, reflect over \(x\)-axis
  • \(b = 2\): horizontal compression by \(1/2\)
  • \(h = -3\): horizontal shift left by 3
  • \(k = 1\): vertical shift up 1

Step 3: Key points. \(f\) has the point \((0,0)\). Applying transformations:

  • Shift left 3: \((-3, 0)\)
  • Compress horizontally by \(1/2\): \((-3/2, 0)\)... wait — the shift happens after factoring, so apply in order: first compress (applied to the factored form), then shift.

Actually, using \(b(x-h)\): point \((x_0, f(x_0))\) on \(f\) maps to \((x_0/b + h,; a\cdot f(x_0) + k)\).

Point on \(f\) Point on \(g\) \((0, 0)\) \((0/2 + (-3),; -3 \cdot 0 + 1) = (-3, 1)\) \((1, 1)\) \((1/2 - 3,; -3 + 1) = (-5/2, -2)\) \((4, 2)\) \((2 - 3,; -6+1) = (-1, -5)\)

docs.title: Example 13.2 — From Graph to Formula
docs.text:
A function \(g\) has the graph of \(f(x) = x^2\) shifted left 2, compressed vertically by \(1/3\), reflected over the \(x\)-axis, and shifted down 4. Find \(g(x)\).

Apply in order:

  1. Left 2: \(f(x+2) = (x+2)^2\)
  2. Compress vertically by \(1/3\): \(\frac{1}{3}(x+2)^2\)
  3. Reflect over \(x\)-axis: \(-\frac{1}{3}(x+2)^2\)
  4. Shift down 4: \(g(x) = -\frac{1}{3}(x+2)^2 - 4\)

docs.title: Example 13.3 — Even/Odd Decomposition
docs.text:
Decompose \(f(x) = e^x\) into even and odd parts.

\[E(x) = \frac{e^x + e^{-x}}{2} = \cosh x$$ $$O(x) = \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{2} = \sinh x\]

So \(e^x = \cosh x + \sinh x\). This is the hyperbolic function decomposition — and it is exactly the real-axis version of Euler's formula \(e^{ix} = \cos x + i\sin x\).

docs.title: Example 13.4 — Sinusoidal Model (Applied)
docs.text:
Model the temperature \(T\) (°C) in a city: it oscillates between 10°C and 30°C with a period of 12 hours, reaching its maximum at \(t=2\) pm (taken as \(t=14\)).

Parameters:

  • Amplitude \(= (30-10)/2 = 10\)
  • Midline \(= (30+10)/2 = 20\)
  • Period \(= 12 \Rightarrow b = 2\pi/12 = \pi/6\)
  • Maximum at \(t = 14\): use cosine (max at \(t=0\) for cosine), shift right 14.
\[T(t) = 10\cos!\left(\frac{\pi}{6}(t - 14)\right) + 20\]

This is \(f(t) = \cos t\) with \(b = \pi/6\) (stretch), \(h = 14\) (shift right), \(a=10\) (stretch), \(k=20\) (shift up).

docs.title: 14. Visualization Reference
docs.text:
SUMMARY OF TRANSFORMATIONS ON y = f(x):

Transformation    Formula          Effect on Graph
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Shift up k        f(x) + k         Move up k units
Shift down k      f(x) - k         Move down k units
Shift right h     f(x - h)         Move right h units
Shift left h      f(x + h)         Move left h units
Vert. stretch a   a·f(x), a>1      Pull away from x-axis
Vert. compress    a·f(x), 0<a<1    Push toward x-axis
Horiz. compress   f(bx), b>1       Squeeze toward y-axis
Horiz. stretch    f(bx), 0<b<1     Pull from y-axis
Reflect x-axis    -f(x)            Flip over x-axis
Reflect y-axis    f(-x)            Flip over y-axis
Reflect y=x       f⁻¹(x)           Swap x and y roles
|output|          |f(x)|           Reflect neg. parts up
|input|           f(|x|)           Mirror right half left

HORIZONTAL vs VERTICAL — The Key Asymmetry:

Vertical changes act DIRECTLY on y:
  y → ay + k   (what you see is what you get)

Horizontal changes act INVERSELY on x:
  f(bx + c) = f(b(x + c/b))
  ↑ compress by b, THEN shift LEFT by c/b

Always factor the horizontal part first.

docs.title: 15. Summary Table
docs.text: Operation Formula Domain Effect Range Effect Shift up \(k\) \(f(x)+k\) none \(+k\) to every value Shift right \(h\) \(f(x-h)\) \(+h\) to every \(x\) none Vert. stretch \(a\) \(a,f(x)\) none multiply by \(a\) Horiz. compress \(b\) \(f(bx)\) divide by \(b\) none Reflect \(x\)-axis \(-f(x)\) none negate Reflect \(y\)-axis \(f(-x)\) negate none Inverse \(f^{-1}(x)\) becomes range of \(f\) becomes domain of \(f\)

docs.title: 16. Personal Marginalia
docs.text:
The horizontal/vertical asymmetry is deep, not superficial. In the formula \(g(x) = f(bx+c)\), the input transformation \(x \mapsto bx+c\) acts before \(f\) sees it. You are changing what you feed to \(f\), not what \(f\) produces. So naturally, a large \(b\) means you are feeding \(f\) inputs that are "already large" — \(f\) completes its oscillation sooner, hence compression. Vertical changes act after \(f\) finishes — they modify the output directly.

Every deep learning architecture is a transformation story. ResNets add \(f(x) + x\) — the identity is a skip connection, and the whole block is a perturbation of the identity transformation. Attention is a dynamic weighting of translated/scaled value vectors. Normalizing flows are stacks of invertible transformations (diffeomorphisms) applied to a simple base distribution. If you understand what transformation does to a graph, you are halfway to understanding what an architecture does to a distribution.

The even/odd decomposition is not a curiosity. It is the \(\mathbb{R}\)-version of Fourier analysis. Every \(L^2\) function on \([-L,L]\) decomposes into cosines (even) and sines (odd) — a decomposition into symmetric and antisymmetric pieces. The same logic, generalized.

References:

  • Stewart, J. Calculus: Early Transcendentals §1.3 (New Functions from Old Functions)
  • MIT 18.02 Supplementary Notes — Functions, Graphs, and Transformations
  • Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville. Deep Learning, Ch. 6 (Deep Feedforward Networks), Ch. 9 (Convolutional Networks)
  • Vaswani et al. Attention Is All You Need (2017) — Positional Encoding
  • Ioffe & Szegedy. Batch Normalization (2015)

docs.title: Combinations of Functions
docs.text: "The power of mathematics lies not just in individual objects, but in how they interact."

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text: Field Value Course Calculus I / Multivariable Calculus References Stewart §1.3; MIT 18.02 Notes Prerequisites Sets, domain/range, basic function notation Tags #calculus #functions #composition #ML #deeplearning

docs.title: 0. Motivation — Why Combine Functions?
docs.text: In practice, almost no interesting quantity is computed by a single primitive rule. A neural network applies a linear map, then a nonlinearity, then another linear map — that is already three functions composed. Understanding precisely how functions interact is therefore not bookkeeping; it is the substrate on which all of modern machine learning is built.

docs.title: 1. Algebraic Combinations
docs.text: Let \(f\) and \(g\) be functions with domains \(D_f, D_g \subseteq \mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: 1.1 Pointwise Operations
docs.text:
For every \(x \in D_f \cap D_g\), define:

\[ (f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x) $$ $$ (f - g)(x) = f(x) - g(x) $$ $$ (fg)(x) = f(x),g(x) $$ $$ \left(\frac{f}{g}\right)(x) = \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}, \quad g(x) \neq 0 \]

Domain rule. The natural domain of any algebraic combination is \(D_f \cap D_g\) (with the additional constraint \(g(x)\neq 0\) for division). This intersection can be strictly smaller than either factor — always check.

docs.title: 1.2 Worked Example
docs.text:
Let \(f(x) = \sqrt{x}\) and \(g(x) = \sqrt{4 - x^2}\).

\[ D_f = [0, \infty), \qquad D_g = [-2, 2] \] \[ D_f \cap D_g = [0, 2] \]

So \((f + g)(x) = \sqrt{x} + \sqrt{4-x^2}\) is only defined on \([0,2]\).

 f(x) = √x          g(x) = √(4−x²)        (f+g)(x)

 |        /          |  ╭───╮              |  ╭──
 |      /            | /     \             | /    \
 |    /              |/       \            |/      
 |  /                0    2   -2           0   2
 0

Notice how the combined domain is the intersection.

docs.title: 2.1 Definition
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{(f \circ g)(x) = f\bigl(g(x)\bigr)} \]

The output of \(g\) is fed as input to \(f\). Formally:

\[ \text{dom}(f \circ g) = {x \in D_g : g(x) \in D_f} \]

Order matters. \(f \circ g \neq g \circ f\) in general. This is the non-commutativity of composition — crucial in deep learning where layer order is everything.

docs.title: 2.2 Schematic
docs.text:
g              f
   x ──────────► g(x) ──────────► f(g(x))

   Input      Intermediate      Final output

docs.title: 2.3 Three-Function Composition
docs.text:
For three functions \(f\), \(g\), \(h\):

\[ (f \circ g \circ h)(x) = f(g(h(x))) \]

This is how a 3-layer network works: input \(\to\) hidden\(_1\) \(\to\) hidden\(_2\) \(\to\) output.

docs.title: 2.4 Decomposition — The Reverse Problem
docs.text:
Given a complicated function, identify "outer" and "inner":

Composite \(F(x)\) Outer \(f\) Inner \(g\) \(\sin(x^2)\) \(\sin(u)\) \(x^2\) \(e^{-x^2}\) \(e^u\) \(-x^2\) \(\sqrt{\ln x}\) \(\sqrt{u}\) \(\ln x\) \(\ln(\sin x)\) \(\ln u\) \(\sin x\) \((3x^2+1)^{10}\) \(u^{10}\) \(3x^2+1\)

Why bother? Because the Chain Rule says \(\frac{d}{dx}f(g(x)) = f'(g(x))\cdot g'(x)\). Decomposition is the prerequisite to differentiation.

docs.title: 2.5 Domain of Composition — Careful Example
docs.text:
Let \(f(u) = \sqrt{u}\) and \(g(x) = x - 1\).

\[ (f \circ g)(x) = \sqrt{x-1}, \qquad \text{dom} = {x : x - 1 \geq 0} = [1,\infty) \]

Now the other way: \(g(f(x)) = \sqrt{x} - 1\), which requires \(x \geq 0\), so \(\text{dom}(g \circ f) = [0,\infty)\).

Completely different domains. Order is not cosmetic.

docs.title: 3. Visualization of Composition
docs.text:
Think of the number line mapping:

  f ∘ g pipeline:

  ℝ ────g────► ℝ ────f────► ℝ
  x     ──►   g(x)   ──►   f(g(x))

  Example: f(u)=u², g(x)=cos(x)

  x=0  ──► cos(0)=1 ──► 1²=1
  x=π/2──► cos(π/2)=0 ──► 0²=0
  x=π  ──► cos(π)=-1 ──► (-1)²=1

Notice that \(f(g(x)) = \cos^2(x)\) collapses the negative outputs of cosine because squaring makes them positive.

docs.title: 4. Scalar Multiples and Vertical/Horizontal Transformations
docs.text:
These are special algebraic combinations worth naming explicitly.

Let \(c > 0\). Starting from \(y = f(x)\):

Combination Effect \(y = f(x) + c\) Shift up by \(c\) \(y = f(x) - c\) Shift down by \(c\) \(y = f(x + c)\) Shift left by \(c\) \(y = f(x - c)\) Shift right by \(c\) \(y = c,f(x)\) Vertical stretch/shrink \(y = f(cx)\) Horizontal shrink/stretch \(y = -f(x)\) Reflect over \(x\)-axis \(y = f(-x)\) Reflect over \(y\)-axis

Note. \(f(cx)\) for \(c>1\) compresses horizontally — input argument reaches the same value faster. In signal processing, this is time compression; in ML, this relates to feature scaling.

docs.title: 5. Even and Odd Symmetry Under Combinations
docs.text:
A useful structural result:

\(f\) \(g\) \(f + g\) \(fg\) even even even even odd odd odd even even odd neither in general odd

Proof sketch (product, odd × odd): \((fg)(-x) = f(-x)g(-x) = (-f(x))(-g(x)) = f(x)g(x) = (fg)(x)\). So the product is even. \(\square\)

This is used in Fourier analysis and in understanding symmetry of activation functions in neural networks.

docs.title: 6. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
docs.text: This section is why everything above actually matters beyond the exam.

docs.title: 6.1 A Neural Network Is a Composition of Functions
docs.text:
A feedforward neural network with \(L\) layers computes:

\[ \hat{y} = (f_L \circ f_{L-1} \circ \cdots \circ f_1)(x) \]

where each layer function is:

\[ f_\ell(z) = \sigma(W_\ell z + b_\ell) \]

Here \(W_\ell z + b_\ell\) is an algebraic combination (affine map), and \(\sigma\) is a fixed nonlinearity. Composition stacks these layers.

  Input x
     │
     ▼
  ┌──────────────────┐
  │  f₁(x) = σ(W₁x+b₁) │  ← affine + nonlinearity
  └──────────────────┘
     │
     ▼
  ┌──────────────────┐
  │  f₂(z) = σ(W₂z+b₂) │
  └──────────────────┘
     │
     ▼
  ┌──────────────────┐
  │  f₃(z) = W₃z+b₃    │  ← output (no activation on last layer for regression)
  └──────────────────┘
     │
     ▼
  Output ŷ

docs.title: 6.2 The Chain Rule = Backpropagation
docs.text:
Because the network is a composition, differentiating it requires the chain rule applied repeatedly:

\[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial W_\ell} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial f_L} \cdot \frac{\partial f_L}{\partial f_{L-1}} \cdots \frac{\partial f_{\ell+1}}{\partial f_\ell} \cdot \frac{\partial f_\ell}{\partial W_\ell} \]

This is backpropagation. It is the chain rule for composed functions, applied to a computational graph. Understanding \(f \circ g\) and its derivative is the entire theoretical basis for training neural networks.

docs.title: 6.3 Activation Functions Are the Nonlinear Piece
docs.text:
Without a nonlinear activation, the composition of linear maps is still linear:

\[ W_2(W_1 x + b_1) + b_2 = (W_2 W_1)x + (W_2 b_1 + b_2) \]

This is just one affine map — no depth is gained. The activation function \(\sigma\) breaks linearity. Common choices:

Name Formula Domain Notes ReLU \(\max(0, x)\) \(\mathbb{R}\) Not differentiable at 0; dominant in practice Sigmoid \(\dfrac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\) \(\mathbb{R}\) Output in \((0,1)\); used in binary classification Tanh \(\tanh(x)\) \(\mathbb{R}\) Output in \((-1,1)\); odd function GELU \(x \cdot \Phi(x)\) \(\mathbb{R}\) Used in Transformers/BERT

All of these are combinations of elementary functions (exponentials, polynomials, products).

docs.title: 6.4 Feature Engineering as Algebraic Combination
docs.text:
Before deep learning, practitioners manually built new features by algebraically combining raw inputs:

\[ x_{\text{new}} = \frac{x_1}{x_2}, \quad x_{\text{new}} = \sqrt{x_1^2 + x_2^2}, \quad x_{\text{new}} = \ln(1 + x_1) \]

Deep networks learn these combinations. The network is discovering useful algebraic and composed transformations of the input automatically — which is why representation learning works.

docs.title: 6.5 Loss Functions Are Algebraic Combinations of Outputs and Labels
docs.text:
The cross-entropy loss:

\[ \mathcal{L} = -\sum_{i} y_i \log \hat{y}_i \]

is a product and sum applied to \(\log \circ \hat{f}\) — a composed and then algebraically combined function.

docs.title: 7. Multivariable Setting (MIT 18.02 Preview)
docs.text:
In higher dimensions, functions map \(\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m\). Algebraic combinations extend naturally. Composition becomes:

\[ (f \circ g)(\mathbf{x}) = f(g(\mathbf{x})), \quad g: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^k, \quad f: \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^m \]

The chain rule for composed multivariate functions involves the Jacobian matrix:

\[ D(f \circ g)(\mathbf{x}) = Df(g(\mathbf{x})) \cdot Dg(\mathbf{x}) \]

where \(\cdot\) denotes matrix multiplication. This is the foundation of automatic differentiation (autograd) in PyTorch and JAX.

docs.title: 8. Summary Table
docs.text: Operation Notation Key Constraint Sum \((f+g)(x)\) \(x \in D_f \cap D_g\) Difference \((f-g)(x)\) \(x \in D_f \cap D_g\) Product \((fg)(x)\) \(x \in D_f \cap D_g\) Quotient \((f/g)(x)\) \(x \in D_f \cap D_g\), \(g(x)\neq 0\) Composition \((f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))\) \(x \in D_g\) and \(g(x) \in D_f\) Scalar multiple \(cf(x)\) \(x \in D_f\)

docs.title: 9. Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1. Let \(f(x) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x-1}}\) and \(g(x) = \ln(x)\). Find the domain of \(f \circ g\).

Hint: You need \(g(x) \in D_f\), which means \(g(x) > 1\).

Exercise 2. Show by direct computation that \((f \circ g)(x) \neq (g \circ f)(x)\) for \(f(x) = e^x\) and \(g(x) = x^2\).

Exercise 3. Decompose \(F(x) = \sin^3(\ln x)\) into three functions \(f, g, h\) such that \(F = f \circ g \circ h\).

Exercise 4. If \(f\) is even and \(g\) is odd, is \(f \circ g\) even, odd, or neither? Prove your answer.

Answer: \((f \circ g)(-x) = f(g(-x)) = f(-g(x)) = f(g(x))\) since \(f\) is even. So \(f \circ g\) is even.

Exercise 5 (ML flavour). Consider a 2-layer network: $$ \hat{y} = W_2 \cdot \text{ReLU}(W_1 x + b_1) + b_2 $$ Write this as an explicit composition \(f \circ g\) and identify the domain of \(f\) and \(g\). What happens to the domain if we replace ReLU with sigmoid?

docs.title: 10. References
docs.text:
1. Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §1.3 — New Functions from Old Functions.
  2. MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus Lecture Notes — Functions of Several Variables and the Chain Rule.
  3. Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville. Deep Learning, MIT Press. Chapter 6 — Deep Feedforward Networks.

docs.title: Inverse Functions and Logarithms
docs.text: "An inverse function is not a formula trick — it is a question of whether a process can be undone."

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text: Field Value Course Calculus I / Multivariable Calculus References Stewart §1.5–1.6; MIT 18.02 Notes Prerequisites Combinations of functions, domain/range, composition Tags #calculus #inverse #logarithm #exponential #ML #deeplearning

docs.title: 0. Motivation
docs.text: The exponential \(e^x\) encodes growth. Its inverse — the logarithm — decodes it: given the result of growth, how long did it run? In machine learning, log-likelihoods, cross-entropy, softmax, and the entire information-theoretic foundation of learning are built on logarithms. Inverse functions more broadly appear whenever we ask: can we recover the input from the output? This note answers that question rigorously.

docs.title: 1.1 Definition
docs.text:
A function \(f\) is one-to-one (injective) if distinct inputs produce distinct outputs:

\[ \boxed{x_1 \neq x_2 \implies f(x_1) \neq f(x_2)} \]

Equivalently (contrapositive):

\[ f(x_1) = f(x_2) \implies x_1 = x_2 \]

docs.title: 1.2 The Horizontal Line Test
docs.text:
\(f\) is one-to-one if and only if every horizontal line \(y = c\) intersects the graph of \(f\) at most once.

  One-to-one ✓              NOT one-to-one ✗

  y │    /                  y │    ∩
    │   /                     │   / \
 ───┼──/──── y=c           ───┼──/───\── y=c (hits twice!)
    │ /                       │ /     \
    │/                        │/       \
    └────── x                 └────────── x

    f(x) = x³                 f(x) = x²

docs.title: 1.3 Strictly Monotone ⟹ One-to-One
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(f\) is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing on an interval \(I\), then \(f\) is one-to-one on \(I\).

Proof. Suppose \(f\) is strictly increasing and \(x_1 \neq x_2\). WLOG \(x_1 < x_2\). Then \(f(x_1) < f(x_2)\), so \(f(x_1) \neq f(x_2)\). \(\square\)

This is why restricting domain restores injectivity. \(f(x) = x^2\) is not injective on \(\mathbb{R}\), but is strictly increasing on \([0,\infty)\), hence injective there.

docs.title: 2.1 Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f: A \to B\) be one-to-one and onto (bijective onto its range). The inverse function \(f^{-1}: B \to A\) is defined by:

\[ \boxed{f^{-1}(y) = x \iff f(x) = y} \]

The domain of \(f^{-1}\) is the range of \(f\), and the range of \(f^{-1}\) is the domain of \(f\).

Notation warning. \(f^{-1}(x) \neq \dfrac{1}{f(x)}\). The superscript \(-1\) denotes the inverse function, not the reciprocal. The reciprocal is written \([f(x)]^{-1}\).

docs.title: 2.2 The Cancellation Identities
docs.text:
For all \(x\) in the appropriate domain:

\[ f^{-1}(f(x)) = x \qquad \text{(for all } x \in D_f\text{)} $$ $$ f(f^{-1}(x)) = x \qquad \text{(for all } x \in D_{f^{-1}}\text{)} \]

These say: applying \(f\) then \(f^{-1}\) (or vice versa) returns to the original input.

docs.title: 2.3 How to Find \(f^{-1}\) Explicitly
docs.text:
Algorithm:

  1. Write \(y = f(x)\).
  2. Solve for \(x\) in terms of \(y\).
  3. Swap \(x \leftrightarrow y\) (by convention, we want \(y = f^{-1}(x)\)).
  4. State the domain of \(f^{-1}\) (= range of \(f\)).

Example. \(f(x) = 2x + 3\).

\[ y = 2x + 3 \implies x = \frac{y-3}{2} \implies f^{-1}(x) = \frac{x-3}{2} \]

Example. \(f(x) = x^3 + 1\).

\[ y = x^3 + 1 \implies x = (y-1)^{1/3} \implies f^{-1}(x) = (x-1)^{1/3} \]

Example (domain restriction). \(f(x) = x^2\) on \([0, \infty)\).

\[ y = x^2, ; x \geq 0 \implies x = \sqrt{y} \implies f^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{x}, \quad x \geq 0 \]

Without the restriction, the inverse would not be a function (two \(x\) values map to the same \(y\)).

docs.title: 2.4 Graph of \(f^{-1}\)
docs.text:
The graph of \(f^{-1}\) is the reflection of the graph of \(f\) across the line \(y = x\).

  y │         /  f(x)
    │     ╱  /
    │   ╱  ·/·
    │ ╱  ·/ · (reflected points)
    │╱  /  ╱  f⁻¹(x)
  ──┼──/──╱──────── x
    │ / ╱
    │/╱

    Points (a,b) on f  ↔  points (b,a) on f⁻¹

Proof. If \((a, b)\) is on the graph of \(f\), then \(f(a) = b\), so \(f^{-1}(b) = a\), meaning \((b, a)\) is on the graph of \(f^{-1}\). Swapping coordinates \((a,b) \mapsto (b,a)\) is exactly reflection across \(y = x\). \(\square\)

docs.title: 2.5 Derivative of the Inverse (Preview to Chapter 3)
docs.text:
If \(f\) is differentiable and one-to-one, then:

\[ \boxed{(f^{-1})'(a) = \frac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(a))}} \]

Intuition. Differentiate the cancellation identity \(f(f^{-1}(x)) = x\) using the chain rule:

\[ f'(f^{-1}(x)) \cdot (f^{-1})'(x) = 1 \implies (f^{-1})'(x) = \frac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(x))} \]

Geometrically: if \(f\) has slope \(m\) at a point, \(f^{-1}\) has slope \(1/m\) at the reflected point. Steep \(f\) gives shallow \(f^{-1}\), and vice versa.

docs.title: 3.1 Definition and Properties
docs.text:
For \(a > 0\), \(a \neq 1\), the exponential function \(f(x) = a^x\) satisfies:

\[ a^{x+y} = a^x \cdot a^y, \qquad (a^x)^y = a^{xy}, \qquad a^0 = 1 \]

It is strictly monotone (increasing if \(a>1\), decreasing if \(0 < a < 1\)), hence injective on all of \(\mathbb{R}\).

The natural exponential \(f(x) = e^x\), where \(e = 2.71828\ldots\), is the unique exponential whose derivative equals itself:

\[ \frac{d}{dx} e^x = e^x \] 
  y │        e^x
    │       /
    │      /
    │     /
    │   _/
    │__/
  ──┼──────────── x
    │

  Domain: ℝ,  Range: (0, ∞)
  Horizontal asymptote: y = 0 as x → -∞

docs.title: 4.1 Definition
docs.text:
Since \(f(x) = a^x\) is one-to-one, it has an inverse. The logarithm base \(a\) is:

\[ \boxed{\log_a x = y \iff a^y = x} \]

Domain: \((0, \infty)\). Range: \(\mathbb{R}\). This is the answer to: "To what power must I raise \(a\) to get \(x\)?"

docs.title: 4.2 The Natural Logarithm
docs.text:
The inverse of \(e^x\) is the natural logarithm:

\[ \ln x = y \iff e^y = x \]

This is the most important logarithm in analysis. All other logarithms are scalar multiples of it:

\[ \log_a x = \frac{\ln x}{\ln a} \]

docs.title: 4.3 Graph
docs.text:
y │        ln(x)
    │       /
    │     _/
    │   _/
    │__/
  ──┼──│──────────── x
    │  1  (passes through (1,0))
    │

  Domain: (0,∞),  Range: ℝ
  Vertical asymptote: x = 0

  Reflection of e^x across y=x:

  y │     /  e^x
    │   ·/·
    │ ·/  ·    ←── y=x
    │/  ·  ·
    │     · ·  ln(x)
  ──┼──────────────── x

docs.title: 4.4 Laws of Logarithms
docs.text:
Let \(x, y > 0\) and \(r \in \mathbb{R}\):

\[ \ln(xy) = \ln x + \ln y $$ $$ \ln!\left(\frac{x}{y}\right) = \ln x - \ln y $$ $$ \ln(x^r) = r \ln x \]

Proof of the first law. Let \(a = \ln x\) and \(b = \ln y\), so \(x = e^a\) and \(y = e^b\). Then:

\[ \ln(xy) = \ln(e^a \cdot e^b) = \ln(e^{a+b}) = a + b = \ln x + \ln y \quad \square \]

The other two follow similarly.

docs.title: 4.5 Cancellation Identities for \(\ln\) and \(e^x\)
docs.text:
\[ e^{\ln x} = x \qquad (x > 0) $$ $$ \ln(e^x) = x \qquad (x \in \mathbb{R}) \]

These are just the general cancellation identities for \(f\) and \(f^{-1}\) specialized to \(e^x\) and \(\ln\).

docs.title: 4.6 The Derivative
docs.text:
\[ \frac{d}{dx} \ln x = \frac{1}{x}, \qquad x > 0 \]

Proof via inverse function derivative. We know \(e^{\ln x} = x\). Differentiate both sides:

\[ e^{\ln x} \cdot \frac{d}{dx}\ln x = 1 \implies x \cdot \frac{d}{dx}\ln x = 1 \implies \frac{d}{dx}\ln x = \frac{1}{x} \quad \square \]

More generally: \(\dfrac{d}{dx} \ln|x| = \dfrac{1}{x}\) for \(x \neq 0\).

docs.title: 5.1 Arcsine
docs.text:
\(\sin x\) is not injective on \(\mathbb{R}\). Restricting to \([-\pi/2, \pi/2]\) makes it strictly increasing, hence invertible.

\[ \arcsin(x) = \sin^{-1}(x) = y \iff \sin(y) = x \text{ and } y \in \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right] \]

Domain: \([-1, 1]\). Range: \([-\pi/2, \pi/2]\).

  y │  π/2 ─────────────·
    │              ·
    │          ·
  ──┼─────·────────────── x
    │  ·         -1   1
    │·
  -π/2

  Cancellation: sin(arcsin x) = x  for x ∈ [-1,1]
               arcsin(sin x) = x  for x ∈ [-π/2, π/2]

Derivative:

\[ \frac{d}{dx}\arcsin(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}, \quad |x| < 1 \]

Proof. Let \(y = \arcsin x\), so \(\sin y = x\). Differentiate: \(\cos y \cdot y' = 1\), so \(y' = \dfrac{1}{\cos y} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \sin^2 y}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\). \(\square\)

docs.title: 5.2 Arctangent
docs.text:
\(\tan x\) restricted to \((-\pi/2, \pi/2)\):

\[ \arctan(x) = y \iff \tan(y) = x \text{ and } y \in \left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \]

Domain: \(\mathbb{R}\). Range: \((-\pi/2, \pi/2)\).

\[ \lim_{x \to \infty} \arctan x = \frac{\pi}{2}, \qquad \lim_{x \to -\infty} \arctan x = -\frac{\pi}{2} \] 
  y │  π/2 ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ (asymptote)
    │          ___──────
    │    ___───
  ──┼───────────────────── x
    │     ───___
    │ ─────
  -π/2 ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ (asymptote)

Derivative:

\[ \frac{d}{dx}\arctan(x) = \frac{1}{1+x^2} \]

Proof. Let \(y = \arctan x\), so \(\tan y = x\). Differentiate: \(\sec^2 y \cdot y' = 1\), so \(y' = \cos^2 y = \dfrac{1}{1+\tan^2 y} = \dfrac{1}{1+x^2}\). \(\square\)

docs.title: 5.3 Summary of Inverse Trig Derivatives
docs.text:
Function Domain Derivative \(\arcsin x\) \((-1,1)\) \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\) \(\arccos x\) \((-1,1)\) \(-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\) \(\arctan x\) \(\mathbb{R}\) \(\dfrac{1}{1+x^2}\)

Note: \(\arcsin x + \arccos x = \pi/2\) (complementary), so their derivatives sum to zero.

docs.title: 6.1 Strategy
docs.text:
• To isolate an exponential: take \(\ln\) of both sides.
  • To isolate a logarithm: exponentiate both sides.

Example. Solve \(3e^{2x} = 15\):

\[ e^{2x} = 5 \implies 2x = \ln 5 \implies x = \frac{\ln 5}{2} \]

Example. Solve \(\ln(x+1) + \ln(x-1) = 1\):

\[ \ln((x+1)(x-1)) = 1 \implies x^2 - 1 = e \implies x = \sqrt{e+1} \]

(Reject \(-\sqrt{e+1}\) since \(x > 1\) required for domain.)

docs.title: 7. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
7.1 The Sigmoid as an Inverse of Logit
docs.text:
The sigmoid function used in logistic regression and neural network output layers is:

\[ \sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}} \]

Its inverse is the logit (log-odds):

\[ \sigma^{-1}(p) = \ln!\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) \]

Sigmoid maps \(\mathbb{R} \to (0,1)\) — converting any real score into a probability. Its inverse maps probabilities back to log-odds. The fact that \(\sigma\) and logit are mutual inverses is why logistic regression and binary cross-entropy form a natural pair.

  Sigmoid:                         Logit (inverse):

  y  1 ─ ─ ─ ─────────────        y  │         /
     │      ___/                      │        /
     │   __/                          │       /
  0.5│  /                          ───┼──────/────── x
     │ /                              │    /       0.5  1
     │/                               │   /
  ───┼──────────── x               (−∞)│  /

  Domain: ℝ → (0,1)               Domain: (0,1) → ℝ

docs.title: 7.2 Log-Likelihood and Cross-Entropy
docs.text:
Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) — the theoretical basis for training — maximizes:

\[ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} p_\theta(x_i) \]

Because this product is numerically unstable and hard to differentiate, we take the log:

\[ \ell(\theta) = \ln \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \ln p_\theta(x_i) \]

The logarithm converts a product into a sum — this is the third law of logarithms at work. Maximizing \(\ell(\theta)\) is equivalent to maximizing \(\mathcal{L}(\theta)\) because \(\ln\) is strictly increasing (a consequence of it being a one-to-one function). This is the entire theoretical justification.

Cross-entropy loss (minimized in classification):

\[ H(y, \hat{y}) = -\sum_{c} y_c \ln \hat{y}_c \]

The \(\ln\) here comes directly from log-likelihood. Training a classifier with cross-entropy is MLE.

docs.title: 7.3 Softmax Is a Multi-Class Generalization of Sigmoid
docs.text:
The softmax function maps a vector \(\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^K\) to a probability distribution:

\[ \text{softmax}(\mathbf{z})_k = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{j=1}^K e^{z_j}} \]

Its inverse is the log-softmax:

\[ \ln \text{softmax}(\mathbf{z})_k = z_k - \ln!\left(\sum_j e^{z_j}\right) \]

Log-softmax is more numerically stable to compute directly than softmax followed by \(\ln\). This is why torch.nn.LogSoftmax exists as a separate primitive in PyTorch.

docs.title: 7.4 Entropy and Information Theory
docs.text:
The entropy of a distribution \(p\) is:

\[ H(p) = -\sum_x p(x) \ln p(x) = \mathbb{E}[-\ln p(X)] \]

The \(\ln\) here quantifies surprise: low-probability events have high \(-\ln p\) (lots of information). High-probability events carry little information. The logarithm is the unique function that converts multiplicative independence into additive information:

\[ \text{if } p(A \cap B) = p(A)p(B), \text{ then } -\ln p(A \cap B) = -\ln p(A) - \ln p(B) \]

This additive property — the logarithm law — is why information is measured in log-units (bits or nats).

docs.title: 7.5 Numerical Stability: The Log-Sum-Exp Trick
docs.text:
Softmax involves \(\sum_j e^{z_j}\). For large \(z_j\), this overflows. The trick:

\[ \ln!\left(\sum_j e^{z_j}\right) = c + \ln!\left(\sum_j e^{z_j - c}\right), \quad c = \max_j z_j \]

This works because \(\ln(e^c \cdot X) = c + \ln X\). The cancellation identity for \(\ln\) and \(e^x\) makes this manipulation exact. Every modern deep learning framework uses this.

docs.title: 7.6 Learning Rate Schedules and Log-Scale
docs.text: Hyperparameter search over learning rates is done on a log scale. Searching \(\eta \in [10^{-5}, 10^{-1}]\) uniformly in log-space means sampling \(\log_{10}\eta \in [-5, -1]\) uniformly. This reflects that the learning rate's effect on training is multiplicative, not additive — the natural domain for a logarithm.

docs.title: 7.7 Invertibility and Autoencoders
docs.text: In an autoencoder, the encoder \(f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^k\) (with \(k \ll n\)) compresses input to a latent code, and the decoder \(g: \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^n\) reconstructs. The goal is for \(g \approx f^{-1}\), i.e., the decoder approximates the inverse of the encoder. The theory of whether a map can have a left-inverse is precisely the theory of injective (one-to-one) functions. A non-injective encoder cannot have a true inverse — information is irreversibly lost.

docs.title: 7.8 Normalizing Flows — Exact Invertibility
docs.text:
Normalizing flows are generative models that require the transformation \(f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n\) to be exactly invertible. The change-of-variables formula for densities involves the Jacobian determinant:

\[ p_X(x) = p_Z(f^{-1}(x)) \cdot \left|\det J_{f^{-1}}(x)\right| \]

This requires \(f\) to be a bijection. The entire architecture of a normalizing flow (RealNVP, Glow, etc.) is engineered so that \(f^{-1}\) can be computed efficiently. Invertibility is not a convenience — it is the structural requirement.

docs.title: 8. Summary
docs.text:
Core Chain:

  a^x  ──────────────────►  Strictly monotone
  (a>1, strictly increasing)       │
                                   ▼
                           One-to-one (injective)
                                   │
                                   ▼
                           Inverse exists: log_a(x)
                                   │
                                   ▼
                    Cancellations: a^(log_a x) = x
                                   log_a(a^x) = x
Concept Key Property ML Relevance One-to-one \(f(x_1)=f(x_2)\Rightarrow x_1=x_2\) Invertible encoders, normalizing flows Inverse function \(f^{-1}(f(x))=x\) Decoder \(\approx\) encoder\(^{-1}\); logit is sigmoid\(^{-1}\) Natural log \(\ln(e^x)=x\); \(\frac{d}{dx}\ln x = 1/x\) Log-likelihood, cross-entropy, info theory Log laws Product \(\to\) sum MLE \(\to\) sum of log-likelihoods \(\arctan\) Maps \(\mathbb{R}\to(-\pi/2,\pi/2)\) Bounded activation, gradient stability Log-sum-exp Algebraic identity Numerical stability in softmax

docs.title: 9. Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1. Prove that \(f(x) = x^3 + x\) is one-to-one on \(\mathbb{R}\) without computing its inverse explicitly. (Hint: show it is strictly increasing.)

Exercise 2. Find the inverse of \(f(x) = \dfrac{e^x - e^{-x}}{2}\) (this is \(\sinh x\)). State its domain.

Answer: \(f^{-1}(x) = \ln(x + \sqrt{x^2+1})\), domain \(\mathbb{R}\).

Exercise 3. Use the inverse function derivative formula to find \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\arctan(x)\) from scratch, without memorizing the formula.

Exercise 4. Simplify: \(\ln(e^{3x} \cdot e^{-x}) - 2\ln(e^x)\).

Answer: \(3x - x - 2x = 0\).

Exercise 5. Solve for \(x\): \(;2^x = 3^{x-1}\).

Hint: Take \(\ln\) of both sides and use \(\ln(a^b) = b\ln a\).

Exercise 6 (ML flavour). The sigmoid satisfies \(\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\).

  • (a) Show that \(\sigma(-x) = 1 - \sigma(x)\).
  • (b) Find \(\sigma^{-1}(p)\) explicitly.
  • © Show that \(\sigma'(x) = \sigma(x)(1 - \sigma(x))\). (This identity is used in the backprop update rule for logistic output neurons.)

Exercise 7. Let \(f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^k\) with \(k < n\). Explain rigorously why \(f\) cannot be injective, and therefore cannot have a left inverse. (Hint: dimension / rank argument.)

docs.title: The Tangent Problem
docs.text: "The problem of finding the tangent line to a curve is the fundamental problem of differential calculus — and secretly, the fundamental problem of intelligence itself."

docs.title: §1. The Classical Geometric Question
docs.text:
Let \(C\) be a curve in the plane, and let \(P\) be a point on \(C\).

Naïve attempt: A tangent line at \(P\) is a line that "touches" \(C\) at \(P\) without "crossing" it. This Euclidean intuition (inherited from the tangent to a circle) is wrong in general.

Why it fails: The parabola \(y = x^2\) at the origin. The \(x\)-axis touches the curve at exactly one point and doesn't "cross" it — yet every introductory student correctly names \(y = 0\) as the tangent. But the cubic \(y = x^3\) at the origin: the \(x\)-axis does cross the curve, yet it is also the tangent line. The geometric intuition of "not crossing" is not the right criterion.

The correct approach is limiting. We must escape statics and enter dynamics.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Let \(f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) be a function. Fix a point \(P = (a, f(a))\) on the graph.

Take a second point \(Q = (a + h, f(a+h))\) on the graph, with \(h \neq 0\).

The line through \(P\) and \(Q\) is called a secant line. Its slope is:

\[m_{PQ} = \frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}\]

This is the difference quotient — the single most important formula in all of calculus.

docs.title: The Tangent Line
docs.text:
\[\boxed{m_{\text{tan}} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}}\]

The tangent line at \(P = (a, f(a))\) is the line through \(P\) with slope \(m_{\text{tan}}\):

\[y - f(a) = m_{\text{tan}}(x - a)\]

This limit, when it exists, is defined to be the derivative \(f'(a)\).

docs.title: Example 1 — The Parabola \(f(x) = x^2\)
docs.text:
Find the tangent line at \(P = (1, 1)\).

\[m = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{(1+h)^2 - 1^2}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{1 + 2h + h^2 - 1}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{2h + h^2}{h}\] \[= \lim_{h \to 0} (2 + h) = 2\]

Tangent line: \(y - 1 = 2(x - 1)\), i.e., \(y = 2x - 1\).

Notice: we cannot simply substitute \(h=0\) into \((2h+h^2)/h\) — it's \(0/0\). The algebraic cancellation of \(h\) is not a trick; it is the rigorous resolution of the indeterminate form. This is why limits are necessary.

docs.title: Example 2 — The Square Root \(f(x) = \sqrt{x}\)
docs.text:
Find \(f'(a)\) for \(a > 0\).

\[m = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\sqrt{a+h} - \sqrt{a}}{h}\]

Rationalize by multiplying by \(\dfrac{\sqrt{a+h}+\sqrt{a}}{\sqrt{a+h}+\sqrt{a}}\):

\[= \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{(a+h) - a}{h(\sqrt{a+h}+\sqrt{a})} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{1}{\sqrt{a+h}+\sqrt{a}} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{a}}\]

So \(f'(a) = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{a}}\). The tangent slope decreases as \(a\) grows — the curve flattens.

docs.title: Example 3 — Where the Limit Fails: \(f(x) = |x|\) at \(x = 0\)
docs.text:
\[\lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{|h| - 0}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{h}{h} = 1\] \[\lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{|h| - 0}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{-h}{h} = -1\]

The one-sided limits disagree. The derivative does not exist at \(x = 0\). The graph has a corner, and no unique tangent line can be assigned.

This is a canonical example of a continuous-but-not-differentiable point. Continuity is necessary but not sufficient for differentiability.

docs.title: The Secant-to-Tangent Process
docs.text:
f(x) = x²,  approaching tangent at P = (1,1)

  y
  |          . curve
  |        /
  |      /  ← secant through P and Q (h large)
  |    * Q
  |   /
  |  * P  ← as Q → P, secant → tangent
  | /
  |/_____________________ x
     0    1    2

  h=1:  m_PQ = (4-1)/1 = 3
  h=0.5: m_PQ = (2.25-1)/0.5 = 2.5
  h=0.1: m_PQ = (1.21-1)/0.1 = 2.1
  h=0.01: m_PQ = 2.01
  h→0:  m_tan = 2   ← exact tangent slope

docs.title: Slope as a Function
docs.text:
Once we compute \(f'(a)\) for every \(a\), we obtain a new function — the derivative function \(f'(x)\). This is the profound insight: differentiating a function produces another function encoding the entire landscape of slopes.

\(f(x)\) \(f'(x)\) Geometric meaning \(x^2\) \(2x\) Slope grows linearly; steeper as \(x\) increases \(\sqrt{x}\) \(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\) Slope always positive but decreasing \(\sin x\) \(\cos x\) Slope oscillates; zero at peaks/troughs \(e^x\) \(e^x\) Slope equals height — exponential's hallmark

docs.title: §5. The Formal Definition (Rigorous Statement)
docs.text:
Definition (Stewart §2.7; MIT 18.02). Let \(f\) be defined on an open interval containing \(a\). The derivative of \(f\) at \(a\) is

\[f'(a) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}\]

provided the limit exists. If it does, \(f\) is said to be differentiable at \(a\).

Alternative form (using \(x \to a\) instead of \(h \to 0\)):

\[f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}\]

These are identical; the substitution \(x = a + h\) converts one to the other.

Theorem. Differentiability implies continuity. If \(f'(a)\) exists, then \(f\) is continuous at \(a\).

Proof sketch: $\(\lim_{h \to 0} [f(a+h) - f(a)] = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h} \cdot h = f'(a) \cdot 0 = 0\)$

Hence \(\lim_{h\to 0} f(a+h) = f(a)\). \(\blacksquare\)

The converse fails: \(|x|\) is continuous at 0 but not differentiable.

docs.title: §6. Velocity as the Same Limit
docs.text:
The tangent problem is isomorphic to the velocity problem. If \(s(t)\) is the position of a particle at time \(t\), then:

\[v(a) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{s(a+h) - s(a)}{h} = s'(a)\]

The difference quotient \(\frac{s(a+h)-s(a)}{h}\) is the average velocity over \([a, a+h]\). The derivative is the instantaneous velocity — the limit of average velocities over shrinking intervals.

This dual interpretation (geometric slope / physical rate of change) is why the derivative is the central object of calculus. It encodes how fast things change.

docs.title: §7. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: Everything that follows is a direct descendant of the difference quotient.

docs.title: 7.1 The Loss Landscape
docs.text:
In supervised learning, we have a model parameterized by weights \(\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) and a loss function \(\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w})\) measuring prediction error. Training means finding:

\[\mathbf{w}^* = \arg\min_{\mathbf{w}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w})\]

To minimize \(\mathcal{L}\), we need to know its slope — that is, we need its gradient \(\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} \mathcal{L}\). Each partial derivative \(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w_i}\) is exactly the tangent problem applied to \(\mathcal{L}\) in the \(w_i\)-direction.

docs.title: 7.2 Gradient Descent
docs.text:
The update rule for gradient descent is:

\[\mathbf{w}^{(t+1)} = \mathbf{w}^{(t)} - \eta \nabla_{\mathbf{w}} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}^{(t)})\]

where \(\eta > 0\) is the learning rate. The gradient \(\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} \mathcal{L}\) tells us the direction of steepest ascent; we step in the opposite direction to descend.

This is the tangent problem, iterated over millions of parameters.

Loss landscape (1D illustration):

  L(w)
  |
  |    *                        *
  |  *   *                    *   *
  | *      *        *        *     *
  |*         *    *   *    *         *
  |             **       **
  |___________________________________________ w
              ↑                   ↑
           local min           global min

  At each w, the tangent slope = ∂L/∂w tells us 
  which direction to move. Gradient descent follows 
  the tangent lines downhill.

docs.title: 7.3 Backpropagation is the Chain Rule
docs.text:
A deep neural network is a composition of functions:

\[\hat{y} = f_L \circ f_{L-1} \circ \cdots \circ f_1(\mathbf{x})\]

To compute \(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{w}_k}\) for layer \(k\), we apply the chain rule (itself a theorem about tangent lines of composite functions):

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{w}_k} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{y}} \cdot \frac{\partial \hat{y}}{\partial f_{L-1}} \cdots \frac{\partial f_{k+1}}{\partial f_k} \cdot \frac{\partial f_k}{\partial \mathbf{w}_k}\]

Backpropagation is just the chain rule applied systematically from output to input. Every tensor flowing backwards in a neural network is a derivative — a generalized tangent slope.

docs.title: 7.4 Numerical Differentiation (Finite Differences)
docs.text:
Before automatic differentiation existed, ML practitioners would approximate derivatives using the definition directly:

\[f'(a) \approx \frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h} \quad \text{(forward difference)}\] \[f'(a) \approx \frac{f(a+h) - f(a-h)}{2h} \quad \text{(central difference, more accurate)}\]

The central difference is \(O(h^2)\) error vs \(O(h)\) for forward difference — this comes from Taylor expansion. This is still used today to gradient-check neural network implementations: verify that autodiff gradients match finite difference approximations.

docs.title: 7.5 Activation Functions and Non-Differentiability
docs.text:
The ReLU activation \(\sigma(x) = \max(0, x)\) is not differentiable at \(x = 0\) — exactly like \(|x|\) at 0. In practice, training proceeds anyway because:

  • The set \({x = 0}\) has measure zero (the network almost never lands exactly there).
  • A subgradient (a generalization of derivative) is used: \(\partial\sigma(0) = [0,1]\).

The Leaky ReLU and smooth approximations (Swish, GELU) were invented precisely to fix this non-differentiability while preserving the computational advantages of ReLU.

docs.title: 7.6 Summary Table
docs.text: Calculus concept ML/DL counterpart Derivative \(f'(a)\) Gradient component \(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w_i}\) Tangent line Local linear approximation of loss surface Chain rule Backpropagation Difference quotient Finite difference / gradient check Non-differentiability ReLU kink; handled by subgradients Gradient descent Iterative tangent-following to minimize loss Second derivative Hessian; used in second-order optimizers (Adam approximates it)

docs.title: §8. A Note on Notation
docs.text:
Various notations you will encounter, all meaning the same thing:

\[f'(a) = \frac{df}{dx}\bigg|_{x=a} = \frac{d}{dx}f(x)\bigg|_{x=a} = Df(a) = \dot{f}(a) \text{ (physics, time derivative)}\]

Leibniz notation \(\frac{df}{dx}\) is suggestive: it "looks like" the ratio \(\frac{\Delta f}{\Delta x}\) in the limit. This is not coincidence — it is why Leibniz notation is so powerful for the chain rule:

\[\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du} \cdot \frac{du}{dx}\]

The \(du\)'s "cancel" (not rigorously, but the notation encodes the chain rule's content).

docs.title: §9. What Comes Next
docs.text:
The tangent problem motivates everything that follows:

  1. Differentiation rules — product, quotient, chain rule: so we never have to return to the limit definition.
  2. Linear approximation — \(f(x) \approx f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)\): the tangent line as the best local approximation.
  3. Taylor series — approximation by polynomials to arbitrary order.
  4. Partial derivatives and gradients — tangent lines in higher-dimensional spaces.
  5. Optimization — critical points where \(f'(a) = 0\); second derivative test.
  6. Differential equations — equations involving \(f'\), encoding physical and biological laws.

Every one of these threads pulls on the same knot: the limit of the difference quotient. Learn this well and the rest of calculus is commentary.

docs.text:
1. Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §§2.6–2.7. (Tangent and velocity problems; the derivative as a function.)
  2. MIT OpenCourseWare, 18.02 Multivariable Calculus. Lecture Notes. (Generalization to gradients and directional derivatives.)
