docs.title: Precise Definition of a Limit
docs.text: "Before this definition, calculus was a powerful but philosophically embarrassing machine. After it, calculus became mathematics." — The spirit of Weierstrass, ~1861

docs.title: §0. Historical Motivation — Why We Needed Precision
docs.text:
Newton and Leibniz invented calculus in the 1660s–1680s. They spoke of "infinitely small quantities" — quantities that are nonzero when you divide by them, but vanish when you're done. Bishop Berkeley famously mocked these as "the ghosts of departed quantities."

For nearly 200 years, calculus worked brilliantly in practice but rested on a philosophical swamp. The precise \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) definition was the work of Augustin-Louis Cauchy (1820s) and Karl Weierstrass (1850s–1860s). It banished infinity from the definition and replaced it with a game between two real numbers.

This is that definition.

docs.title: §1. Intuition First — The Approach Game
docs.text:
Before the symbols, the idea.

Saying \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L\) means:

You can force \(f(x)\) arbitrarily close to \(L\) by keeping \(x\) sufficiently close to \(a\) (but not equal to \(a\)).

Think of it as a two-player game:

  • Player \(\varepsilon\) (the Challenger): Names a tolerance. "I want \(f(x)\) within \(\varepsilon\) of \(L\)." They're trying to make the task hard by choosing \(\varepsilon\) very small.
  • Player \(\delta\) (the Defender): Must respond with a radius. "Stay within \(\delta\) of \(a\), and I guarantee \(f(x)\) is within \(\varepsilon\) of \(L\)."

The limit exists \(\iff\) the Defender can always win — no matter how small \(\varepsilon\) the Challenger names, a valid \(\delta\) exists.

                 ε-band around L
              ┌─────────────────┐
    L + ε ────│─────────────────│────
              │    f(x) must    │
    L   ──────│──── land here ──│────
              │                 │
    L - ε ────│─────────────────│────
              └─────────────────┘
                   ↑         ↑
              a - δ         a + δ
              └─────────────┘
               δ-neighborhood
               (x lives here,
                x ≠ a)

If every x in (a-δ, a+δ), x≠a maps into (L-ε, L+ε),
the Defender wins for this ε.
The limit exists iff the Defender wins for ALL ε > 0.

docs.title: §2. The Formal Definition
docs.text:
Definition (Stewart §2.4 / MIT 18.02). Let \(f\) be a function defined on some open interval containing \(a\), except possibly at \(a\) itself. We write $\(\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L\)$ and say "the limit of \(f(x)\) as \(x\) approaches \(a\) equals \(L\)" if:

\[\forall, \varepsilon > 0,\quad \exists, \delta > 0 \text{ such that } \quad 0 < |x - a| < \delta \implies |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon.\]

Every symbol earns its place. Let's dissect.

docs.title: §3. Anatomy of the Definition — Symbol by Symbol
\(\forall, \varepsilon > 0\) — "For every epsilon greater than zero"
docs.text:
• \(\varepsilon\) (epsilon) measures closeness in the output — how close \(f(x)\) must be to \(L\).
  • The quantifier \(\forall\) means the Defender must handle every challenge, including \(\varepsilon = 0.001\), \(\varepsilon = 10^{-100}\), and \(\varepsilon = 10^{-10^{10}}\).
  • We require \(\varepsilon > 0\) because \(\varepsilon = 0\) would demand exact equality — impossible for a limit that's only approached, not attained.

docs.title: \(\exists, \delta > 0\) — "There exists a delta greater than zero"
docs.text:
• \(\delta\) (delta) measures closeness in the input — how close \(x\) must be to \(a\).
  • Crucially, \(\delta\) is allowed to depend on \(\varepsilon\). For a smaller \(\varepsilon\), you may need a smaller \(\delta\). This is not a defect — it's the whole point.
  • \(\delta > 0\) ensures we're looking at a genuine (non-degenerate) neighborhood.

docs.title: \(0 < |x - a| < \delta\) — The punctured neighborhood
docs.text:
• \(|x - a| < \delta\) says \(x\) is within \(\delta\) of \(a\).
  • \(0 < |x - a|\) says \(x \neq a\). This is the puncture. We are taking a limit as \(x\) approaches \(a\), not at \(a\).

This single condition is why limits and function values are independent.

Whether \(f(a)\) is defined, undefined, or even \(f(a) \neq L\) is completely irrelevant. The limit is a statement about the approach, not the arrival.

docs.title: \(\implies |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon\) — The guarantee
docs.text:
• \(|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon\) says \(f(x)\) is within \(\varepsilon\) of \(L\).
  • The implication \(\implies\) means: every \(x\) in the punctured \(\delta\)-neighborhood must produce an \(f(x)\) in the \(\varepsilon\)-neighborhood of \(L\).

docs.title: §4. The Logical Structure — Unpacked
docs.text:
The full statement is a nested quantifier:

\[\underbrace{\forall, \varepsilon > 0}_{\text{Challenger picks}},\quad \underbrace{\exists, \delta > 0}_{\text{Defender responds}},\quad \underbrace{\forall, x}_{\text{for all inputs}}\colon \underbrace{0 < |x-a| < \delta}_{\text{in the punctured neighborhood}} \implies \underbrace{|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon}_{\text{output is controlled}}\]

The order of quantifiers is non-negotiable. Swapping \(\forall\varepsilon\) and \(\exists\delta\) would produce a meaningless or different statement. In mathematics, quantifier order is everything.

Compare:

  • \(\forall \varepsilon > 0,; \exists \delta > 0: \ldots\) — \(\delta\) may depend on \(\varepsilon\) ✓ (this is the definition)
  • \(\exists \delta > 0,; \forall \varepsilon > 0: \ldots\) — one \(\delta\) works for all \(\varepsilon\) — this would be much stronger and almost never true.

docs.title: §5. Three Worked \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) Proofs
docs.text:
The proof strategy is always the same:

  1. Scratch work (not part of the proof): manipulate \(|f(x)-L|\) to find what \(\delta\) should be.
  2. Formal proof: Given \(\varepsilon > 0\), state your \(\delta\), then verify the implication holds.

docs.title: Proof 1 — Linear Function
docs.text:
Claim: \(\lim_{x \to 3}(2x - 1) = 5\).

Scratch work. We need \(|(2x-1) - 5| < \varepsilon\), i.e., \(|2x - 6| < \varepsilon\), i.e., \(2|x-3| < \varepsilon\), i.e., \(|x-3| < \varepsilon/2\). So choose \(\delta = \varepsilon/2\).

Proof. Given \(\varepsilon > 0\), let \(\delta = \varepsilon/2\). Suppose \(0 < |x-3| < \delta\). Then: $\(|(2x-1) - 5| = |2x - 6| = 2|x-3| < 2\delta = 2 \cdot \frac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon. \qquad \blacksquare\)$

docs.title: Proof 2 — Quadratic (Requires Bounding)
docs.text:
Claim: \(\lim_{x \to 2} x^2 = 4\).

Scratch work. We need \(|x^2 - 4| < \varepsilon\). Factor: \(|x^2-4| = |x-2||x+2|\). We control \(|x-2|\) (it's \(< \delta\)), but \(|x+2|\) floats.

Bound \(|x+2|\): Restrict \(\delta \leq 1\) initially. Then \(|x-2|<1 \implies 1 < x < 3 \implies 3 < x+2 < 5 \implies |x+2| < 5\).

So \(|x^2 - 4| < 5|x-2| < 5\delta\). We want \(5\delta \leq \varepsilon\), so \(\delta \leq \varepsilon/5\).

Take \(\delta = \min(1, \varepsilon/5)\) to satisfy both constraints simultaneously.

Proof. Given \(\varepsilon > 0\), let \(\delta = \min(1, \varepsilon/5)\). Suppose \(0 < |x-2| < \delta\).

Since \(\delta \leq 1\), we have \(|x-2| < 1\), so \(1 < x < 3\), hence \(|x+2| < 5\).

Therefore: $\(|x^2 - 4| = |x-2||x+2| < \delta \cdot 5 \leq \frac{\varepsilon}{5} \cdot 5 = \varepsilon. \qquad \blacksquare\)$

The \(\min\) trick appears again. Whenever we need \(\delta\) to satisfy two simultaneous conditions, we take the minimum. This is the standard move in analysis.

docs.title: Proof 3 — Limit Does Not Exist (\(\lim_{x \to 0} \sin(1/x)\))
docs.text:
Sometimes the most instructive proof is a disproof.

Claim: \(\lim_{x \to 0} \sin(1/x)\) does not exist.

Proof (by negating the definition). The negation of \(\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = L\) is:

\[\exists, \varepsilon_0 > 0 \text{ such that } \forall, \delta > 0,; \exists, x \text{ with } 0 < |x| < \delta \text{ and } |f(x) - L| \geq \varepsilon_0.\]

For any proposed limit \(L\), choose \(\varepsilon_0 = 1/2\).

For any \(\delta > 0\), we can find \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\) large enough so that: $\(x_1 = \frac{1}{2\pi n + \pi/2} \quad \text{and} \quad x_2 = \frac{1}{2\pi n + 3\pi/2}\)$ both lie in \((0, \delta)\), with \(f(x_1) = \sin(2\pi n + \pi/2) = 1\) and \(f(x_2) = \sin(2\pi n + 3\pi/2) = -1\).

Since \(f\) takes values \(1\) and \(-1\) in every punctured neighborhood of \(0\), it cannot be within \(1/2\) of any single value \(L\) for all such \(x\). Hence no limit exists. \(\blacksquare\)

   1 ─ · · · · · · ·  ·  ·   ·    ·     ·
       ↑ oscillates between +1 and -1

   0 ────────────────────────────────────── x
                                        → 0

  -1 ─ · · · · · · ·  ·  ·   ·    ·     ·

  The oscillations become infinitely rapid as x → 0.
  No single L can be "approached."

docs.title: §6. What "Except Possibly at \(a\)" Really Means
docs.text:
The definition requires \(f\) to be defined on a punctured neighborhood of \(a\) — some interval \((a-r, a+r) \setminus {a}\) — but explicitly not at \(a\) itself.

This handles three cases uniformly:

Case \(f(a)\) \(\lim_{x\to a} f(x)\) Example Defined, matches limit \(= L\) \(= L\) \(f(x) = x^2\) at \(a=2\) Defined, doesn't match \(\neq L\) \(= L\) \(g(x) = \begin{cases}x^2 & x\neq 2\ 99 & x=2\end{cases}\) Undefined at \(a\) DNE \(= L\) \(\frac{\sin x}{x}\) at \(a=0\)

In all three cases, \(\lim_{x\to 2}\) or \(\lim_{x\to 0}\) may still equal \(L\). The limit is blind to \(f(a)\).

docs.title: §7. One-Sided Limits — Modifying the Definition
docs.text:
The two-sided limit requires control from both sides. We modify the punctured neighborhood:

Right-hand limit: $\(\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = L \iff \forall,\varepsilon>0,;\exists,\delta>0: \mathbf{0 < x - a < \delta} \implies |f(x)-L|<\varepsilon\)$

Left-hand limit: $\(\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = L \iff \forall,\varepsilon>0,;\exists,\delta>0: \mathbf{-\delta < x - a < 0} \implies |f(x)-L|<\varepsilon\)$

Theorem. \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L \iff \lim_{x\to a^-}f(x) = L ;\text{ and }; \lim_{x \to a^+}f(x) = L\).

docs.title: §8. Infinite Limits and Limits at Infinity — The Same Idea, New Neighborhoods
Infinite Limit: \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = +\infty\)
docs.text:
\[\forall, M > 0,;\exists,\delta>0: 0 < |x-a|<\delta \implies f(x) > M\]

The role of \(\varepsilon\) is now played by \(M\) — the Challenger names a height, the Defender finds a neighborhood where \(f\) exceeds it.

docs.title: Limit at Infinity: \(\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = L\)
docs.text:
\[\forall,\varepsilon>0,;\exists, N>0: x > N \implies |f(x)-L|<\varepsilon\]

Here \(\delta\) is replaced by \(N\) — instead of a neighborhood around a point, the Defender gives a threshold beyond which \(f(x)\) is controlled.

All four combinations (\(a\) finite/infinite, \(L\) finite/infinite) have analogous definitions — the pattern is always: replace the relevant neighborhood with the appropriate notion of "close" or "large."

docs.title: §9. Uniqueness of Limits
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L\) and \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = M\), then \(L = M\).

Proof. Suppose \(L \neq M\); WLOG \(L < M\). Let \(\varepsilon = (M-L)/2 > 0\).

By the definition applied to \(L\): \(\exists,\delta_1\) such that \(0<|x-a|<\delta_1 \implies |f(x)-L|<\varepsilon\), i.e., \(f(x) < L+\varepsilon\).

By the definition applied to \(M\): \(\exists,\delta_2\) such that \(0<|x-a|<\delta_2 \implies |f(x)-M|<\varepsilon\), i.e., \(f(x) > M-\varepsilon\).

But \(L + \varepsilon = L + \frac{M-L}{2} = \frac{L+M}{2}\) and \(M - \varepsilon = \frac{L+M}{2}\).

So for \(0 < |x-a| < \min(\delta_1,\delta_2)\): \(f(x) < \frac{L+M}{2}\) and \(f(x) > \frac{L+M}{2}\) simultaneously — contradiction. \(\blacksquare\)

Why this matters: Uniqueness is the reason we can write \(\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = L\) with an equals sign. The limit is a function from (function, point) pairs to real numbers — it must be single-valued.

docs.title: §10. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
10.1 The Definition Lives Inside Every Derivative
docs.text:
The weight update in gradient descent is: $\(w \leftarrow w - \eta \cdot \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w}\)$

That partial derivative is, by definition: $\(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\mathcal{L}(w+h) - \mathcal{L}(w)}{h}\)$

Every time a GPU computes a backward pass, it is numerically approximating this limit. The \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) definition is what guarantees the limit exists (and thus the derivative is well-defined) for the smooth loss functions used in practice.

Numerical differentiation (finite differences) is literally choosing a small \(h = \delta\) and hoping the resulting \(f(x+h) - f(x))/h\) is within \(\varepsilon\) of the true derivative. The precision-stability tradeoff in choosing \(h\) is the \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) game made computational.

docs.title: 10.2 The Puncture Condition and \(0/0\) in Softmax / Cross-Entropy
docs.text:
The cross-entropy loss is \(\mathcal{L} = -\log(\hat{p}_y)\) where \(\hat{p}_y\) is the softmax probability of the true class. When \(\hat{p}_y \to 0^+\), \(\mathcal{L} \to +\infty\). This is an infinite limit: $\(\lim_{\hat{p} \to 0^+} (-\log \hat{p}) = +\infty\)$

The puncture (\(\hat{p} \neq 0\) required) corresponds to the practical need for numerical clipping: \(\hat{p} = \max(\hat{p}, \varepsilon_{\text{clip}})\) for some small \(\varepsilon_{\text{clip}} > 0\) — exactly choosing a \(\delta > 0\) to stay away from the problematic point.

docs.title: 10.3 Convergence Proofs in Optimization
docs.text:
When theoreticians prove that stochastic gradient descent converges, they must show: $\(\lim_{t \to \infty} \mathbb{E}[|\nabla \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}_t)|^2] = 0\)$

This is the \(\varepsilon\)-\(N\) definition: for every desired precision \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists a number of steps \(N\) such that after \(N\) steps, the expected gradient norm is below \(\varepsilon\). The entire convergence theory of deep learning is the \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) framework applied to sequences.

docs.title: 10.4 Quantifier Order and Uniform vs. Pointwise Convergence
docs.text:
In deep learning theory, one distinguishes:

  • Pointwise convergence of a sequence of models \(f_n \to f\): for each input \(x\), \(\lim_{n\to\infty}f_n(x) = f(x)\).
  • Uniform convergence: \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_x|f_n(x)-f(x)| = 0\).

The difference is exactly quantifier order:

\[\text{Pointwise: }\forall x,;\forall\varepsilon>0,;\exists N: n>N \implies |f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$$ $$\text{Uniform: }\forall\varepsilon>0,;\exists N,;\forall x: n>N \implies |f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon\]

Uniform convergence (where \(N\) doesn't depend on \(x\)) is what PAC-learning theory and generalization bounds require. This distinction — invisible without the precise definition — is foundational to statistical learning theory.

docs.title: §11. The Negation — When Limits Fail
docs.text:
The precise definition makes it possible to rigorously prove a limit does not exist. Negate the statement:

\[\lim_{x \to a} f(x) \neq L \iff \exists,\varepsilon_0 > 0 \text{ such that } \forall,\delta>0,;\exists, x: 0<|x-a|<\delta ;\text{ and }; |f(x)-L|\geq\varepsilon_0\]

And the limit fails to exist for any \(L\) iff this holds for every candidate \(L \in \mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: §12. Summary — The Definition, Every Piece
docs.text: \[\boxed{\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L \iff \forall,\varepsilon>0,;\exists,\delta>0: 0 < |x-a|<\delta \implies |f(x)-L|<\varepsilon}\] Piece Measures Role \(\varepsilon > 0\) Output tolerance The Challenger's demand \(\delta > 0\) Input radius The Defender's response \(0 < \|x-a\| < \delta\) Punctured \(\delta\)-neighborhood Where \(x\) lives (never \(= a\)) \(\|f(x)-L\| < \varepsilon\) Output control What must be guaranteed \(\delta\) depends on \(\varepsilon\) — Fundamental flexibility of the definition \(f(a)\) irrelevant — Limit \(\perp\) function value at \(a\)

docs.title: §13. Problems
docs.text:
Computational \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) Proofs:

  1. Prove \(\lim_{x \to 4}(3x+1) = 13\) from the definition.
  2. Prove \(\lim_{x \to 1} x^2 = 1\) from the definition.
  3. Prove \(\lim_{x \to 2} \frac{1}{x} = \frac{1}{2}\) from the definition. (Hint: bound \(1/|x|\) from above by restricting \(\delta \leq 1\).)

Conceptual: 4. Write out the precise negation of \(\lim_{x\to 0^+}\sqrt{x} = 0\). Then explain why the negation is false (i.e., prove the limit does equal \(0\)). 5. Why can two functions \(f \neq g\) (differing only at \(x = a\)) have the same limit at \(a\)? What does this say about the limit operator?

Proof: 6. Prove: if \(\lim_{x\to a}f(x) = L\) and \(L > 0\), then there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that \(f(x) > 0\) for all \(x\) in the punctured \(\delta\)-neighborhood of \(a\). (This is the "sign-preservation" lemma — used constantly in analysis.)

docs.text:

docs.title: Continuity
docs.text: "The limit exists; the function arrives at its destination."

docs.title: §1. Motivation — Why Continuity?
docs.text:
Calculus is, at its heart, the study of change. But for the machinery of derivatives and integrals to work, we need a prior guarantee: that functions don't teleport. A function that jumps arbitrarily makes differentiation meaningless and integration treacherous.

Continuity is that guarantee. It is the precise mathematical way of saying: small changes in input produce small changes in output. Before Stewart ever writes \(f'(a)\), continuity is doing silent structural work.

docs.title: §2. The Formal Definition
docs.text:
Definition (Continuity at a point). A function \(f\) is continuous at \(a\) if: $\(\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a)\)$

This deceptively simple equation packs three simultaneous requirements:

Requirement What It Demands \(f(a)\) is defined \(a\) is in the domain \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x)\) exists left and right limits agree The two are equal the function actually arrives where the limit points

Fail any one of these and continuity breaks.

docs.title: The \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) Formulation
docs.text:
The limit definition hides the real muscle. Unpacking it:

\(f\) is continuous at \(a\) if: for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that $\(|x - a| < \delta \implies |f(x) - f(a)| < \varepsilon\)$

Reading this carefully: You hand me any tolerance \(\varepsilon\) — how close you want \(f(x)\) to \(f(a)\) — and I can always find a neighborhood of \(a\) (radius \(\delta\)) inside which \(f\) cooperates. This is a uniform challenge-response game that \(f\) must win for every \(\varepsilon\).

docs.title: §3. A Taxonomy of Discontinuities
docs.text: Understanding continuity is inseparable from cataloguing its failures.

docs.title: 3.1 Removable Discontinuity
docs.text:
\[f(x) = \frac{x^2 - 1}{x - 1} = x + 1 \quad (x \neq 1)\]

The limit \(\lim_{x \to 1} f(x) = 2\) exists, but \(f(1)\) is undefined (or perhaps defined as something else). The graph has a hole. Surgery: redefine \(f(1) = 2\) and continuity is restored.

 y
 3|        ●
 2|      ○       ← hole at (1, 2)
 1|    /
  +--+--+-- x
     1

docs.title: 3.2 Jump Discontinuity
docs.text:
\[f(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & x < 0 \ 2 & x \geq 0 \end{cases}\]

Left and right limits exist but are unequal: \(\lim_{x \to 0^-} f(x) = 1 \neq 2 = \lim_{x \to 0^+} f(x)\). The function jumps. No redefinition fixes this.

 y
 2|          ●────────
 1|────────○
  +--------+-------- x
           0

docs.title: 3.3 Infinite (Essential) Discontinuity
docs.text:
\[f(x) = \frac{1}{x} \quad \text{at } x = 0\]

The limit doesn't exist (it diverges). The function explodes.

docs.title: 3.4 Oscillatory Discontinuity
docs.text:
\[f(x) = \sin!\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) \quad \text{at } x = 0\]

The function oscillates infinitely fast near 0. No limit exists. The function neither jumps nor blows up — it simply refuses to settle.

docs.title: §4. Continuity on Intervals
docs.text:
Definition. \(f\) is continuous on \((a, b)\) if it is continuous at every point therein.

\(f\) is continuous on \([a, b]\) if it is continuous on \((a, b)\), and:

  • \(\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = f(a)\) (right-continuous at \(a\))
  • \(\lim_{x \to b^-} f(x) = f(b)\) (left-continuous at \(b\))

Polynomials, \(\sin\), \(\cos\), \(e^x\), \(\ln x\) (on \((0,\infty)\)) — these are all continuous on their natural domains. They are the smooth citizens of analysis.

docs.title: §5. The Algebra of Continuous Functions
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(f\) and \(g\) are continuous at \(a\), then so are:

  • \(f + g\), \(f - g\), \(f \cdot g\)
  • \(f/g\) (provided \(g(a) \neq 0\))
  • \(f \circ g\) (composition), provided \(g\) is continuous at \(a\) and \(f\) is continuous at \(g(a)\)

The composition rule is particularly important. It says: continuous functions compose to continuous functions. This is the structural backbone that lets us treat \(e^{\sin x}\) or \(\ln(1 + x^2)\) as continuous without hesitation.

docs.title: §6. The Great Theorems
docs.text: These are the theorems that make calculus work. Continuity is their hypothesis.

docs.title: 6.1 Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT)
docs.text:
Theorem (IVT). If \(f\) is continuous on \([a, b]\) and \(N\) is any number between \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\), then there exists \(c \in (a, b)\) such that \(f(c) = N\).

Geometric reading: A continuous curve connecting two points cannot avoid any height in between. It must cross every horizontal level.

Canonical application: Proving roots exist.

Example. Show \(p(x) = x^3 - x - 2\) has a root in \((1, 2)\).

\[p(1) = 1 - 1 - 2 = -2 < 0$$ $$p(2) = 8 - 2 - 2 = 4 > 0\]

\(p\) is continuous (polynomial), \(0\) lies between \(-2\) and \(4\), so IVT guarantees a \(c \in (1, 2)\) with \(p(c) = 0\). \(\blacksquare\)

Note: IVT is an existence theorem. It tells you the root is there; it doesn't find it.

docs.title: 6.2 Extreme Value Theorem (EVT)
docs.text:
Theorem (EVT). If \(f\) is continuous on \([a, b]\), then \(f\) attains both its maximum and minimum values on \([a, b]\).

This seems obvious but is shockingly delicate. Remove either hypothesis — lose the closed endpoint, or lose continuity — and the theorem fails.

Failure with open interval: \(f(x) = x\) on \((0,1)\) never attains its supremum 1.

Failure with discontinuity: \(f(x) = 1/x\) on \([0,1]\) has no maximum.

docs.title: §7. Continuity in Higher Dimensions (18.02 Perspective)
docs.text:
In multivariable calculus, the definition extends naturally:

Definition. \(f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) is continuous at \(\mathbf{a}\) if: $\(\lim_{\mathbf{x} \to \mathbf{a}} f(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{a})\)$

But the topology is richer. In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), a limit requires \(f(\mathbf{x}) \to L\) along every possible path to \(\mathbf{a}\). This makes discontinuities harder to detect and easier to miss.

Classic trap:

\[f(x,y) = \frac{xy}{x^2 + y^2}, \quad f(0,0) = 0\]

Along \(y = 0\): limit is 0. Along \(y = x\): limit is \(\frac{x^2}{2x^2} = \frac{1}{2}\). The limits differ — \(f\) is discontinuous at the origin despite being continuous along every coordinate axis.

Lesson: In \(\mathbb{R}^n\), checking limits along axes is not sufficient. You must check all paths, or find a single contradicting path.

docs.title: Partial Continuity ≠ Continuity
docs.text: A function can be continuous in each variable separately while failing to be jointly continuous. This is a genuine pathology of multivariable analysis and should disturb you the first time you see it. Good. It should.

docs.title: §8. Uniform Continuity
docs.text:
Standard continuity at a point is local — the \(\delta\) may depend on both \(\varepsilon\) and \(a\). Uniform continuity removes the dependence on \(a\):

Definition. \(f\) is uniformly continuous on a set \(S\) if: for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that for all \(x, y \in S\): $\(|x - y| < \delta \implies |f(x) - f(y)| < \varepsilon\)$

Why it matters: \(f(x) = x^2\) is continuous on \(\mathbb{R}\) but not uniformly continuous — as \(x \to \infty\), the function steepens and any fixed \(\delta\) becomes insufficient. But \(f(x) = x^2\) on \([0, 1]\) is uniformly continuous (it's continuous on a compact set — see below).

Theorem (Heine-Cantor). If \(f\) is continuous on a compact set \(K\) (closed and bounded in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)), then \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \(K\).

docs.title: §9. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: This is where the abstract becomes engineering.

docs.title: 9.1 Loss Landscape Continuity
docs.text:
In supervised learning, you minimize a loss function \(\mathcal{L}(\theta)\) where \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}^n\) are model parameters. Gradient descent requires:

\[\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta)\]

This only makes sense if \(\mathcal{L}\) is continuous (and differentiable). If \(\mathcal{L}\) had jump discontinuities, gradient information would be meaningless — the gradient wouldn't tell you which direction to move.

Deep networks use activation functions like ReLU (\(\max(0, x)\)), sigmoid, tanh — all chosen to be continuous (even if not everywhere differentiable). The continuity of the loss landscape is what makes optimization tractable.

docs.title: 9.2 The Universal Approximation Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem (Cybenko, 1989; Hornik, 1991). A feedforward neural network with a single hidden layer containing sufficiently many neurons can approximate any continuous function \(f: [a,b]^n \to \mathbb{R}\) to arbitrary precision.

The hypothesis is continuity of the target function. Neural networks are themselves continuous (compositions of continuous functions). They approximate within the class of continuous functions. If your target function is discontinuous, the theorem gives no guarantee.

This is IVT and EVT whispering inside your neural architecture.

docs.title: 9.3 Lipschitz Continuity in Deep Learning
docs.text:
A function \(f\) is Lipschitz continuous with constant \(L\) if:

\[|f(x) - f(y)| \leq L,|x - y| \quad \forall, x, y\]

This is uniform continuity with a linear modulus. In deep learning:

  • Wasserstein GANs (WGANs) require the discriminator to be 1-Lipschitz. The gradient penalty term enforces this.
  • Spectral normalization constrains weight matrices to ensure Lipschitz bounds, stabilizing training.
  • Gradient clipping is an informal way to enforce approximate Lipschitz behavior.

Lipschitz continuity is the practitioner's version of uniform continuity — with a quantitative constant that can be constrained and regularized.

docs.title: 9.4 Continuity of the Activation Function
docs.text:
Activation Continuous? Differentiable at 0? Notes Sigmoid Yes Yes Saturates; vanishing gradient Tanh Yes Yes Zero-centered; still saturates ReLU Yes No (at 0) Subgradient used; sparse activations Leaky ReLU Yes No (at 0) Fixes dying ReLU problem Softplus Yes Yes Smooth ReLU approximation Step function No — Not used; gradient is zero almost everywhere

The step function was used in early perceptrons. Its discontinuity made gradient-based learning impossible. The switch to continuous activations (sigmoid, then ReLU) was what made backpropagation viable.

docs.title: 9.5 Continuity in Reinforcement Learning
docs.text:
In continuous control (robotics, locomotion), the policy \(\pi_\theta(a | s)\) and value function \(V^\pi(s)\) must be continuous in the state \(s\) for smooth control. Discontinuous policies cause jerky, unstable behavior in physical systems.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) explicitly enforce continuity and differentiability of learned solutions to PDEs — continuity is a hard constraint, not just a hope.

docs.title: §10. Summary Table
docs.text: Concept Key Content Continuity at \(a\) \(\lim_{x\to a} f(x) = f(a)\); \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) formulation Types of discontinuity Removable, jump, infinite, oscillatory Continuity on \([a,b]\) Pointwise continuity + one-sided at endpoints Algebra of continuity Sums, products, quotients, compositions preserve continuity IVT Continuous \(f\) on \([a,b]\) hits every intermediate value EVT Continuous \(f\) on \([a,b]\) attains max and min Multivariable Path-independence required; partial continuity insufficient Uniform continuity \(\delta\) independent of basepoint; compact \(\Rightarrow\) uniform ML connection Loss landscapes, UAT, Lipschitz bounds, activation design

docs.title: Example 1 — Three-Part Check
docs.text:
Is \(f\) continuous at \(x = 2\)?

\[f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 - 2 & x \neq 2 \ 1 & x = 2 \end{cases}\]
  1. \(f(2) = 1\) ✓ (defined)
  2. \(\lim_{x \to 2} (x^2 - 2) = 4 - 2 = 2\) ✓ (limit exists)
  3. \(f(2) = 1 \neq 2\) ✗ (mismatch)

Conclusion: \(f\) is discontinuous at \(x = 2\). Removable discontinuity — redefine \(f(2) = 2\) to repair.

docs.title: Example 2 — Using IVT to Locate a Root
docs.text:
Show \(\cos x = x\) has a solution.

Let \(g(x) = \cos x - x\). Then:

  • \(g(0) = 1 - 0 = 1 > 0\)
  • \(g(\pi/2) = 0 - \pi/2 < 0\)

\(g\) is continuous (difference of continuous functions), and \(0\) is between \(g(0)\) and \(g(\pi/2)\). IVT gives \(c \in (0, \pi/2)\) with \(g(c) = 0\), i.e., \(\cos c = c\). \(\blacksquare\)

(This fixed point \(c \approx 0.739\) is called the Dottie number.)

docs.title: Example 3 — Multivariable Failure
docs.text:
Show \(f(x, y) = \dfrac{x^2 y}{x^4 + y^2}\), \(f(0,0) = 0\) is discontinuous at the origin.

Along the parabolic path \(y = x^2\):

\[f(x, x^2) = \frac{x^2 \cdot x^2}{x^4 + x^4} = \frac{x^4}{2x^4} = \frac{1}{2}\]

So \(\lim_{x \to 0} f(x, x^2) = \frac{1}{2} \neq 0 = f(0,0)\).

The limit doesn't equal the function value. Discontinuous. \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: §12. Things Worth Losing Sleep Over
docs.text:
• Is the composition of two discontinuous functions ever continuous? (Yes. Take $f = g = $ Dirichlet function. Then \(f \circ g \equiv 0\).)
  • A function can be continuous at exactly one point and discontinuous everywhere else. (Classic: \(f(x) = x\) if \(x \in \mathbb{Q}\), \(f(x) = 0\) if \(x \notin \mathbb{Q}\). Continuous only at \(x = 0\).)
  • Uniform continuity on \((a,b)\) + continuity implies unique continuous extension to \([a,b]\).
  • Every continuous function on \([a,b]\) is Riemann integrable — the proof runs through uniform continuity.

docs.text:
1. Stewart, J. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. — §2.5 (Continuity), §3.1 (Derivatives and Continuity), §4.1 (EVT)
  2. MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus — Lecture notes on limits and continuity in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), path-dependence of limits
  3. Cybenko, G. (1989). "Approximation by superpositions of a sigmoidal function." Mathematics of Control, Signals and Systems.
  4. Arjovsky, M. et al. (2017). "Wasserstein GAN." arXiv:1701.07875. — Lipschitz constraint in GANs

Next: [[Differentiability]] — where continuity is necessary but not sufficient. See also: [[Limits]], [[Compactness]], [[Uniform Convergence]]

docs.title: Limits at Infinity
docs.text: "Infinity is not a place the function goes — it is a direction the input travels, and we ask what the output approaches."

docs.title: §1. Motivation
docs.text:
Limits at a point ask: what does \(f(x)\) approach as \(x\) gets close to \(a\)?

Limits at infinity ask something geometrically different: what does \(f(x)\) approach as \(x\) grows without bound? We are not plugging in \(\infty\) — that is not a number. We are describing the long-run behavior of a function, its eventual tendency as the input escapes toward the horizon.

This is the language of asymptotes, of steady states, of what a neural network's loss converges to after thousands of epochs.

docs.title: §2. The Formal Definition
docs.text:
Definition. We write \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = L\) if: for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists \(M > 0\) such that $\(x > M \implies |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon\)$

Compare this with the \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) definition of a finite limit. The role of \(\delta\) (a small radius around \(a\)) is now played by \(M\) (a large threshold past which \(x\) must lie). Instead of proximity to a point, we have escape to the right.

Similarly:

\(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) = L\) if: for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists \(M\) such that \(x < M \implies |f(x) - L| < \varepsilon\)

docs.title: Geometric Reading: Horizontal Asymptotes
docs.text:
When \(\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = L\), the line \(y = L\) is a horizontal asymptote as \(x \to +\infty\).

 y
 L ·····●·············●·············●·········  ← f(x) hugging y = L
   |        /
   |      /
   |    /
   +--+--+--+--+--+--+--+--+--+-- x
      M

A function can have at most two horizontal asymptotes (one as \(x \to +\infty\), one as \(x \to -\infty\)), and they need not be the same.

Example. \(f(x) = \arctan(x)\): $\(\lim_{x \to +\infty} \arctan(x) = \frac{\pi}{2}, \qquad \lim_{x \to -\infty} \arctan(x) = -\frac{\pi}{2}\)$

Two distinct horizontal asymptotes.

docs.title: §3. Infinite Limits at Infinity
docs.text:
We must distinguish carefully between two distinct phenomena:

Notation Meaning \(\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = L\) \(f(x)\) approaches a finite value \(L\) \(\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = \infty\) \(f(x)\) grows without bound

The second is not a limit in the strict sense — the limit does not exist (no real number is approached). It is a useful notation for the manner of divergence.

Definition. \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = \infty\) means: for every \(N > 0\), there exists \(M\) such that \(x > M \implies f(x) > N\).

You challenge me with any height \(N\); I find a point past which \(f\) stays above it. Similarly defined for \(-\infty\).

docs.title: §4. Computing Limits at Infinity — The Core Techniques
4.1 The Fundamental Fact
docs.text:
\[\lim_{x \to \pm\infty} \frac{1}{x^r} = 0 \quad \text{for any } r > 0\]

This is the anchor. Every algebraic technique for limits at infinity reduces to this.

docs.title: 4.2 Rational Functions: Divide by Dominant Power
docs.text:
For a rational function \(\dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)}\), divide numerator and denominator by \(x^n\) where \(n = \deg(q)\).

Three cases by degree comparison:

Case 1: \(\deg(p) < \deg(q)\) — limit is \(0\).

\[\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{3x^2 + 1}{x^3 - 5} = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{3/x + 1/x^3}{1 - 5/x^3} = \frac{0}{1} = 0\]

Case 2: \(\deg(p) = \deg(q)\) — limit is ratio of leading coefficients.

\[\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{4x^3 - 2x}{7x^3 + x^2} = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{4 - 2/x^2}{7 + 1/x} = \frac{4}{7}\]

Case 3: \(\deg(p) > \deg(q)\) — limit is \(\pm\infty\) (diverges).

\[\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x^3 + 1}{x^2 - 3} = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x + 1/x^2}{1 - 3/x^2} = \infty\]

Mnemonic: Bottom heavy → 0. Equal degree → leading ratio. Top heavy → ∞.

docs.title: 4.3 Expressions Involving Radicals
docs.text:
Radical expressions require more care. The technique: multiply by the conjugate or factor out the dominant term.

Example. Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} \left(\sqrt{x^2 + x} - x\right)\).

Naively: \(\infty - \infty\), indeterminate. Multiply by conjugate:

\[\sqrt{x^2+x} - x = \frac{(\sqrt{x^2+x} - x)(\sqrt{x^2+x}+x)}{\sqrt{x^2+x}+x} = \frac{x^2 + x - x^2}{\sqrt{x^2+x}+x} = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+x}+x}\]

Now divide numerator and denominator by \(x\) (valid for \(x > 0\)):

\[= \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + 1/x} + 1} \xrightarrow{x\to\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1} + 1} = \frac{1}{2}\]

Warning: For \(x \to -\infty\), \(\sqrt{x^2} = |x| = -x\). Sign errors here are extremely common.

Example. \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to -\infty} \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}\).

Factor: \(\sqrt{x^2+1} = \sqrt{x^2}\sqrt{1+1/x^2} = |x|\sqrt{1+1/x^2} = -x\sqrt{1+1/x^2}\) (since \(x < 0\)).

\[\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}} = \frac{x}{-x\sqrt{1+1/x^2}} = \frac{-1}{\sqrt{1+1/x^2}} \to -1\]

docs.title: 4.4 Exponentials and Logarithms
docs.text:
Hierarchy of growth rates (fastest to slowest):

\[e^x \gg x^n \gg \ln x \quad \text{as } x \to \infty\]

More precisely:

\[\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x^n}{e^x} = 0 \quad \text{(exponential beats any polynomial)}$$ $$\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\ln x}{x^r} = 0 \quad \text{for any } r > 0 \text{ (power beats log)}\]

These are proved via L'Hôpital's rule.

Example. \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} x^{100} e^{-x} = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x^{100}}{e^x} = 0\).

No matter how large the polynomial degree, exponential decay wins.

docs.title: §5. L'Hôpital's Rule at Infinity
docs.text:
Theorem (L'Hôpital). If \(\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = \lim_{x \to \infty} g(x) = 0\) or \(\pm\infty\), and \(g'(x) \neq 0\) for large \(x\), then: $\(\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}\)$ provided the right-hand limit exists (or is \(\pm\infty\)).

The rule applies to the indeterminate forms \(0/0\) and \(\infty/\infty\). Other indeterminate forms must be converted:

Form Conversion \(\infty - \infty\) Algebraic manipulation (common denominator, conjugate) \(0 \cdot \infty\) Write as \(f/(1/g)\) to get \(0/0\) or \(\infty/\infty\) \(1^\infty\), \(0^0\), \(\infty^0\) Take logarithm: \(\lim e^{g \ln f}\)

Example. \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} x e^{-x}\) — form \(\infty \cdot 0\).

Rewrite: \(\dfrac{x}{e^x}\) — form \(\infty/\infty\). Apply L'Hôpital:

\[\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x}{e^x} = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{1}{e^x} = 0\]

Example. \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} \left(1 + \frac{1}{x}\right)^x\) — form \(1^\infty\).

Let $L = $ the limit. Then:

\[\ln L = \lim_{x \to \infty} x \ln!\left(1 + \frac{1}{x}\right) = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\ln(1+1/x)}{1/x}\]

Form \(0/0\). L'Hôpital:

\[= \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\frac{-1/x^2}{1+1/x}}{-1/x^2} = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{1}{1 + 1/x} = 1\]

So \(\ln L = 1\), hence \(L = e\). The definition of \(e\), recovered.

docs.title: §6. Limits at Infinity for Trigonometric Functions
docs.text:
\(\sin x\) and \(\cos x\) oscillate between \(-1\) and \(1\) forever. They have no limit as \(x \to \infty\).

But bounded oscillation combined with decay is a different story:

\[\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 0 \quad \text{(Squeeze Theorem: } -\frac{1}{x} \leq \frac{\sin x}{x} \leq \frac{1}{x}\text{)}\]

The Squeeze Theorem at infinity. If \(g(x) \leq f(x) \leq h(x)\) for all large \(x\), and \(\lim_{x\to\infty} g(x) = \lim_{x\to\infty} h(x) = L\), then \(\lim_{x\to\infty} f(x) = L\).

This shows up constantly: any bounded function multiplied by something decaying to 0 has limit 0.

docs.title: §7. The Limit \(\lim_{x \to \infty}\left(1 + \frac{r}{x}\right)^x = e^r\)
docs.text:
This generalization of the definition of \(e\) deserves its own entry. It is the continuous-compounding formula from finance, and it appears in the theory of differential equations, probability, and information theory.

Proof sketch. Let \(y = x/r\). Then as \(x \to \infty\), \(y \to \infty\), and:

\[\left(1+\frac{r}{x}\right)^x = \left[\left(1+\frac{1}{y}\right)^y\right]^r \to e^r\]

Application: Continuous compounding. If principal \(P\) is compounded \(n\) times per year at rate \(r\):

\[A = P\left(1+\frac{r}{n}\right)^{n} \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} Pe^r\]

docs.title: §8. Asymptotic Notation and Rate Comparison
docs.text:
When limits at infinity are taken seriously as a comparative tool, we get asymptotic analysis.

Definition. We write \(f(x) = O(g(x))\) as \(x \to \infty\) if \(\lim_{x \to \infty} \left|\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)}\right| < \infty\) (bounded ratio).

We write \(f(x) \sim g(x)\) if \(\lim_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)} = 1\) (asymptotically equal).

Examples:

  • \(3x^2 + 5x \sim 3x^2\) as \(x \to \infty\)
  • \(\ln(x^2 + 1) \sim 2\ln x\) as \(x \to \infty\)
  • \(e^x + x^{100} \sim e^x\) as \(x \to \infty\)

This is the language of algorithm complexity (\(O(n \log n)\), \(O(n^2)\), etc.) and of asymptotic analysis in probability and statistics.

docs.title: §9. Oblique (Slant) Asymptotes
docs.text:
When \(\deg(p) = \deg(q) + 1\), a rational function has neither a horizontal asymptote nor pure divergence. It approaches a line \(y = mx + b\).

Finding the oblique asymptote: Perform polynomial long division.

\[f(x) = \frac{x^2 + 3x + 1}{x + 1}\]

Long division: \(x^2 + 3x + 1 = (x+1)(x+2) - 1\), so:

\[f(x) = x + 2 - \frac{1}{x+1}\]

As \(x \to \infty\), \(\dfrac{1}{x+1} \to 0\), so \(f(x) \to x + 2\). The oblique asymptote is \(y = x + 2\).

        y
        |         /  ← y = x + 2 (asymptote)
        |       / ·
        |     /·
        |   /·
        | /·
 -------+------------ x
       /|
      / |

docs.title: §10. Limits at Infinity in Multiple Variables (18.02)
docs.text:
For \(f: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\), the statement \(\lim_{|\mathbf{x}| \to \infty} f(\mathbf{x}) = L\) means \(f\) approaches \(L\) as the input point recedes to infinity in any direction.

This requires agreement along all rays and all paths — the same pathological subtleties as finite multivariable limits.

Example. Does \(f(x,y) = \dfrac{xy}{x^2 + y^2}\) have a limit as \((x,y) \to \infty\)?

Along \(y = x\): \(f = \dfrac{x^2}{2x^2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

Along \(y = 0\): \(f = 0\).

Different limits along different paths — no limit at infinity.

Example. \(f(x,y) = \dfrac{1}{x^2 + y^2}\). As \((x,y) \to \infty\) along any path, \(x^2 + y^2 \to \infty\), so \(f \to 0\). Limit exists and equals \(0\).

docs.title: §11. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
11.1 Convergence of Training: The Limit That Matters Most
docs.text:
Training a neural network is iteratively minimizing \(\mathcal{L}(\theta_t)\). The question of convergence is precisely:

\[\lim_{t \to \infty} \mathcal{L}(\theta_t) = ?\]

Does this limit exist? Does it equal the global minimum? For convex losses (logistic regression, linear regression), convergence to the global minimum is guaranteed under mild conditions. For non-convex losses (deep networks), the limit may be a local minimum or saddle point — and proving convergence at all requires careful analysis.

Learning rate schedules (cosine annealing, exponential decay) are designed to ensure this limit exists and is "good": $\(\eta_t = \eta_0 \cdot e^{-\lambda t} \to 0 \quad \text{(ensures the steps shrink to zero)}\)$

The intuition is: if step sizes don't go to zero, the optimizer keeps bouncing around even after reaching a minimum.

docs.title: 11.2 Activation Functions and Their Asymptotic Behavior
docs.text:
The asymptotic behavior of activations as inputs go to \(\pm\infty\) directly determines gradient flow and the vanishing gradient problem.

Activation \(\lim_{x \to +\infty}\) \(\lim_{x \to -\infty}\) Consequence Sigmoid \(\sigma(x)\) \(1\) \(0\) Saturates; \(\sigma'(x) \to 0\) — vanishing gradient Tanh \(1\) \(-1\) Saturates; same issue ReLU \(\infty\) \(0\) No saturation for \(x > 0\); dead neurons for \(x < 0\) Leaky ReLU \(\infty\) \(-\infty\) (slope \(\alpha\)) No dead neurons Softplus \(\ln(1+e^x)\) \(\infty\) \(0\) Smooth ReLU; same asymptotic behavior ELU \(\infty\) \(-1\) Bounded below; smooth

The vanishing gradient problem is a limit statement: \(\sigma'(x) = \sigma(x)(1-\sigma(x)) \to 0\) as \(|x| \to \infty\). When activations saturate, gradients die, and early layers of deep networks stop learning.

ReLU was a breakthrough because \(\lim_{x \to \infty} \text{ReLU}'(x) = 1 \neq 0\): no saturation in the positive half.

docs.title: 11.3 Softmax and the Winner-Take-All Limit
docs.text:
The softmax function:

\[\text{softmax}(\mathbf{z})_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}\]

Consider scaling the logits: \(\text{softmax}(z/T)\) where \(T > 0\) is temperature.

\[\lim_{T \to 0^+} \text{softmax}(\mathbf{z}/T) = \mathbf{e}_{\arg\max_i z_i}\]

In the limit of zero temperature, softmax becomes the argmax — a one-hot vector. This is used in knowledge distillation (large \(T\) softens the distribution, transferring more information) and in reinforcement learning (temperature controls exploration vs. exploitation).

This is a genuine limit at infinity (\(1/T \to \infty\)) giving a discontinuous function as its limit — the argmax.

docs.title: 11.4 Batch Size and the \(n \to \infty\) Limit
docs.text:
Stochastic gradient descent with batch size \(B\) uses a noisy estimate of the gradient:

\[\hat{ abla}\mathcal{L} = rac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B} abla \mathcal{L}( heta; x_i)\]

By the Law of Large Numbers:

\[\lim_{B o \infty} \hat{ abla}\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}[ abla\mathcal{L}( heta; x)] = abla\mathcal{L}( heta)\]

Full-batch gradient descent is the limit \(B o \infty\). Finite batch sizes introduce beneficial noise that helps escape sharp minima — a deliberate departure from the limit.

docs.title: 11.5 Neural Tangent Kernel — The Infinite Width Limit
docs.text:
For an \(L\)-layer network with width \(n\):

\[\lim_{n \to \infty} f_\theta(\mathbf{x}) \approx \text{(linear model in function space)}\]

In the infinite-width limit, training a neural network becomes equivalent to kernel regression with the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK). This is one of the deepest results in modern deep learning theory (Jacot et al., 2018) — and it is a statement about a limit at infinity in the width parameter.

docs.title: 11.6 Asymptotic Complexity in Algorithm Design
docs.text:
The \(O(\cdot)\) notation used in algorithm analysis is directly the asymptotic notation from §8:

\[T(n) = O(n^2) \iff \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{T(n)}{n^2} < \infty\]

Choosing between \(O(n \log n)\) and \(O(n^2)\) sorting is a statement about what happens as \(n \to \infty\) — a limit at infinity comparing growth rates.

docs.title: §12. Summary of Key Limits
docs.text: \[\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{1}{x^r} = 0 \quad (r > 0)\] \[\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{p(x)}{q(x)} = \begin{cases} 0 & \deg p < \deg q \ \frac{a_n}{b_m} & \deg p = \deg q \ \pm\infty & \deg p > \deg q \end{cases}\] \[\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x^n}{e^x} = 0, \qquad \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\ln x}{x^r} = 0\] \[\lim_{x \to \infty} \left(1+\frac{r}{x}\right)^x = e^r\] \[\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 0 \quad \text{(but } \lim_{x\to\infty}\sin x \text{ does not exist)}\]

docs.title: §13. Things Worth Losing Sleep Over
docs.text:
• \(\lim_{x \to \infty} \sin(x)/x = 0\) but \(\lim_{x \to \infty} \sin(x)\) does not exist. The limit of a product is not always the product of the limits when one factor diverges.
  • A function can oscillate between two values and still have a limit at infinity — if the oscillation amplitude decays. But if it doesn't decay, the limit fails to exist even if the function stays bounded.
  • Horizontal asymptote is a statement about limit. A function can cross its horizontal asymptote finitely or even infinitely many times and still have that asymptote. (Example: \(\sin(x)/x\) crosses \(y = 0\) infinitely often.)
  • \(L\)'Hôpital's rule requires the hypotheses \(0/0\) or \(\infty/\infty\). Applying it to \(\dfrac{x + \sin x}{x}\) (which is NOT of that form) gives the wrong answer. Always check the form first.
  • Two functions with the same limit at infinity can differ arbitrarily on any bounded interval. The limit at infinity tells you nothing about local behavior.

docs.title: Example 2 — Indeterminate \(\infty - \infty\) with Radical
docs.text:
\[\lim_{x \to \infty} \left(\sqrt{4x^2 + 3x} - 2x\right)\]

Multiply by conjugate:

\[= \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{4x^2 + 3x - 4x^2}{\sqrt{4x^2+3x}+2x} = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{3x}{\sqrt{4x^2+3x}+2x}\]

Divide by \(x\):

\[= \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{3}{\sqrt{4 + 3/x}+2} = \frac{3}{\sqrt{4}+2} = \frac{3}{4}\]

docs.title: Example 3 — \(1^\infty\) Form
docs.text:
\[\lim_{x \to \infty} \left(\frac{x+3}{x-1}\right)^x\]

Write \(\dfrac{x+3}{x-1} = 1 + \dfrac{4}{x-1}\). Let \(u = x - 1 \to \infty\):

\[= \lim_{u \to \infty} \left(1 + \frac{4}{u}\right)^{u+1} = \lim_{u \to \infty} \left(1+\frac{4}{u}\right)^u \cdot \underbrace{\left(1+\frac{4}{u}\right)}_{\to 1} = e^4 \cdot 1 = e^4\]

docs.title: Example 4 — L'Hôpital
docs.text:
\[\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\ln x}{\sqrt{x}}\]

Form \(\infty/\infty\). L'Hôpital:

\[= \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{1/x}{1/(2\sqrt{x})} = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{2\sqrt{x}}{x} = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{2}{\sqrt{x}} = 0\]

docs.text:

  3. Jacot, A., Gabriel, F., Hongler, C. (2018). "Neural Tangent Kernel: Convergence and Generalization in Neural Networks." NeurIPS 2018.

docs.title: Derivatives and Rate of Change
docs.text: "The derivative is the instantaneous rate of change — a limit that collapses an interval to a point, and in doing so, extracts the geometry of the function at that point."

docs.title: §1. Motivation — The Two Problems That Built Calculus
docs.text:
Newton and Leibniz arrived at the derivative from two directions that turn out to be the same thing.

The tangent problem. Given a curve \(y = f(x)\) and a point \(P = (a, f(a))\), find the slope of the line tangent to the curve at \(P\). A tangent line touches the curve at one point and captures its instantaneous direction.

The velocity problem. Given a position function \(s(t)\), find the instantaneous velocity at time \(t = a\). Average velocity over \([a, a+h]\) is \(\Delta s / \Delta t\); but what happens as the time interval collapses?

Both reduce to the same limiting process. The derivative is their common answer.

docs.title: 2.1 The Difference Quotient
docs.text:
The average rate of change of \(f\) over \([a, a+h]\) is the slope of the secant line through \((a, f(a))\) and \((a+h, f(a+h))\):

\[\frac{\Delta f}{\Delta x} = \frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}\] 
 y
 |               ● (a+h, f(a+h))
 |             /
 |           /  ← secant line, slope = Δf/Δx
 |         /
 |       ● (a, f(a))
 |
 +---+---+---+------- x
     a   a+h

As \(h \to 0\), the second point slides toward \((a, f(a))\), and the secant line rotates toward the tangent line.

docs.title: 2.2 The Derivative
docs.text:
Definition. The derivative of \(f\) at \(a\) is: $\(f'(a) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}\)$ provided this limit exists. If it does, \(f\) is differentiable at \(a\).

Equivalent formulation (substituting \(x = a + h\)):

\[f'(a) = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}\]

Both forms appear constantly. Know both.

docs.title: 2.3 The Derivative as a Function
docs.text:
If \(f\) is differentiable at every point in its domain, we get the derivative function:

\[f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}\]

This is itself a function — it assigns to each \(x\) the slope of the tangent to \(f\) at \(x\).

docs.title: 2.4 Notation
docs.text:
All of the following mean the same thing:

\[f'(x) = y' = \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{df}{dx} = Df(x) = \dot{y} \text{ (physics)}\]

Leibniz notation \(dy/dx\) is not a fraction — it is a single symbol, the limit of \(\Delta y / \Delta x\). But it behaves like a fraction in chain rule and in differentials, which is one of its great virtues.

docs.title: §3. Differentiability and Continuity
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(f\) is differentiable at \(a\), then \(f\) is continuous at \(a\).

Proof. We want \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a)\). Write:

\[f(x) - f(a) = \frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a} \cdot (x - a)\]

Taking limits:

\[\lim_{x \to a} [f(x) - f(a)] = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x)-f(a)}{x-a} \cdot \lim_{x \to a}(x-a) = f'(a) \cdot 0 = 0\]

So \(\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a)\). \(\blacksquare\)

The converse is false. Continuity does not imply differentiability.

Canonical counterexample: \(f(x) = |x|\) at \(x = 0\).

\(f\) is continuous at \(0\), but:

\[\lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{|h| - 0}{h} = 1, \qquad \lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{|h| - 0}{h} = -1\]

Left and right derivatives disagree. The limit does not exist. \(f'(0)\) does not exist — there is a corner.

docs.title: Geometric Picture of Non-Differentiability
docs.text:
Corner (|x|)         Cusp (x^{2/3})       Vertical Tangent (x^{1/3})
 y                    y                     y
  \  /                  |                   |/
   \/                   |                   |
   0      x           --+---  x           --+--  x
                                            |
slope: +1/-1 disagree   slope → ∞          slope = ∞

Three ways differentiability fails: corners, cusps, vertical tangents (and discontinuities).

docs.title: §4. The Differentiation Rules
docs.text: Computing derivatives from the definition every time is untenable. The differentiation rules are theorems — each provable from the limit definition.

docs.title: 4.1 Basic Rules
docs.text: Rule Formula Constant \((c)' = 0\) Power \((x^n)' = nx^{n-1}\) Constant multiple \((cf)' = cf'\) Sum/Difference \((f \pm g)' = f' \pm g'\) Product \((fg)' = f'g + fg'\) Quotient \(\left(\dfrac{f}{g}\right)' = \dfrac{f'g - fg'}{g^2}\) Chain Rule \((f \circ g)'(x) = f'(g(x)) \cdot g'(x)\)

docs.title: 4.2 The Product Rule — Intuition
docs.text:
Why is \((fg)' = f'g + fg'\) and not \(f'g'\)? Think of \(f\) and \(g\) as side lengths of a rectangle with area \(A = f(x)g(x)\).

        g + Δg
   +----------+----+
   |          |    |
 f |  f·g     |f·Δg|
   |          |    |
   +----------+----+
   |    g·Δf  | ε  |  ← second-order small, vanishes
   +----------+----+
      g           Δg

\(\Delta A = f \cdot \Delta g + g \cdot \Delta f + \Delta f \cdot \Delta g\)

Dividing by \(\Delta x\) and taking \(\Delta x \to 0\): the last term is \((\Delta f / \Delta x) \cdot \Delta g \to f' \cdot 0 = 0\).

So \(\dfrac{dA}{dx} = f \cdot g' + g \cdot f'\). \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: 4.3 The Chain Rule — The Most Important Rule
docs.text:
If \(y = f(u)\) and \(u = g(x)\), then: $\(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du} \cdot \frac{du}{dx}\)$

In function notation: \((f \circ g)'(x) = f'(g(x)) \cdot g'(x)\).

Reading: differentiate the outside (leaving the inside alone), then multiply by the derivative of the inside.

Example. \(y = \sin(x^2)\).

  • Outside: \(\sin(\square)\), derivative \(\cos(\square)\)
  • Inside: \(x^2\), derivative \(2x\)
\[y' = \cos(x^2) \cdot 2x\]

Example. \(y = e^{-x^2/2}\) (the Gaussian).

\[y' = e^{-x^2/2} \cdot (-x) = -xe^{-x^2/2}\]

The chain rule chains: \(y = f(g(h(x)))\) gives \(y' = f'(g(h(x))) \cdot g'(h(x)) \cdot h'(x)\).

docs.title: 4.4 Derivatives of Elementary Functions
docs.text:
\[\frac{d}{dx} x^n = nx^{n-1} \qquad \frac{d}{dx} e^x = e^x \qquad \frac{d}{dx} \ln x = \frac{1}{x}\] \[\frac{d}{dx} \sin x = \cos x \qquad \frac{d}{dx} \cos x = -\sin x \qquad \frac{d}{dx} \tan x = \sec^2 x\] \[\frac{d}{dx} \arcsin x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} \qquad \frac{d}{dx} \arctan x = \frac{1}{1+x^2}\]

The derivative of \(e^x\) equals itself — this is the defining property of the exponential. It is why exponential functions appear everywhere dynamics are modeled.

docs.title: §5. Higher-Order Derivatives
docs.text:
The derivative \(f'\) is itself a function; we can differentiate it again.

\[f''(x) = (f')'(x) = \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} \qquad f^{(n)}(x) = \frac{d^n y}{dx^n}\]

Interpretations:

  • \(f'(x)\): instantaneous rate of change, slope of tangent
  • \(f''(x)\): rate of change of slope — concavity
  • \(f'''(x)\): rate of change of concavity — jerk in physics

Physics chain: $\(s(t) \xrightarrow{;\frac{d}{dt};} v(t) \xrightarrow{;\frac{d}{dt};} a(t) \xrightarrow{;\frac{d}{dt};} j(t)\)$ position \(\to\) velocity \(\to\) acceleration \(\to\) jerk

Newton's second law \(F = ma\) is a statement about the second derivative of position.

Concavity:

  • \(f'' > 0\) on \((a,b)\): \(f\) is concave up (bowl facing up, slope increasing)
  • \(f'' < 0\) on \((a,b)\): \(f\) is concave down (bowl facing down, slope decreasing)
Concave up (f'' > 0)        Concave down (f'' < 0)
        ___                   ‾‾‾
      /     \               /       \
tangent lines below        tangent lines above

docs.title: §6. Implicit Differentiation
docs.text:
Not every curve is expressible as \(y = f(x)\). When \(x\) and \(y\) are related implicitly (e.g., \(x^2 + y^2 = r^2\)), differentiate both sides with respect to \(x\), treating \(y\) as a function of \(x\) and applying the chain rule.

Example. Differentiate \(x^2 + y^2 = 25\):

\[2x + 2y\frac{dy}{dx} = 0 \implies \frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{x}{y}\]

At \((3, 4)\): slope \(= -3/4\).

Example. Differentiate \(x^3 + y^3 = 6xy\) (folium of Descartes):

\[3x^2 + 3y^2 y' = 6y + 6xy' \implies y'(3y^2 - 6x) = 6y - 3x^2 \implies y' = \frac{6y - 3x^2}{3y^2 - 6x} = \frac{2y - x^2}{y^2 - 2x}\]

docs.title: Logarithmic Differentiation
docs.text:
For products, quotients, and powers of functions, take \(\ln\) first.

Example. \(y = \dfrac{x^3 \sqrt{x+1}}{(2x-1)^4}\)

\[\ln y = 3\ln x + \frac{1}{2}\ln(x+1) - 4\ln(2x-1)\] \[\frac{y'}{y} = \frac{3}{x} + \frac{1}{2(x+1)} - \frac{8}{2x-1}\] \[y' = y \cdot \left[\frac{3}{x} + \frac{1}{2(x+1)} - \frac{8}{2x-1}\right]\]

This is far cleaner than the quotient and product rules applied directly.

docs.title: §7. The Mean Value Theorem
docs.text:
The MVT is the central theorem of differential calculus. Everything about the connection between derivatives and function behavior flows from it.

Theorem (MVT). If \(f\) is continuous on \([a, b]\) and differentiable on \((a, b)\), then there exists \(c \in (a, b)\) such that: $\(f'(c) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}\)$

Geometric reading: There is a point where the instantaneous slope equals the average slope over the interval. The tangent at \(c\) is parallel to the secant from \(a\) to \(b\).

 y
 |                    ● (b, f(b))
 |              ·  ·/
 |           · /· /   ← tangent at c parallel to secant
 |          /●/
 |        /  c
 |  (a, f(a))●
 +---+-------+------- x
     a       b

Consequences:

  • \(f' = 0\) everywhere on \((a,b)\) \(\implies\) \(f\) is constant
  • \(f' > 0\) everywhere \(\implies\) \(f\) is strictly increasing
  • \(f' < 0\) everywhere \(\implies\) \(f\) is strictly decreasing

These seem obvious but require proof — and the proof uses MVT.

Rolle's Theorem (special case): if \(f(a) = f(b)\), then \(f'(c) = 0\) for some \(c \in (a, b)\). Between two equal values, the derivative vanishes somewhere.

docs.title: §8. Linear Approximation and Differentials
docs.text:
Near \(x = a\), a differentiable function looks like a line:

\[f(x) \approx f(a) + f'(a)(x - a) \quad \text{for } x \text{ near } a\]

This is the tangent line approximation (or linearization). It is the first-order Taylor polynomial.

Example. Approximate \(\sqrt{4.02}\).

Let \(f(x) = \sqrt{x}\), \(a = 4\), \(f'(x) = 1/(2\sqrt{x})\), \(f'(4) = 1/4\).

\[\sqrt{4.02} \approx \sqrt{4} + \frac{1}{4}(4.02 - 4) = 2 + \frac{0.02}{4} = 2.005\]

(Exact: \(2.00499...\))

docs.title: Differentials
docs.text:
Write \(dy = f'(x), dx\) where \(dx = \Delta x\) is a small change in \(x\) and \(dy\) is the corresponding change in the tangent line (approximating \(\Delta y = f(x + \Delta x) - f(x)\)).

This notation makes the chain rule transparently a cancellation of differentials:

\[\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy}{du} \cdot \frac{du}{dx}\]

and justifies the substitution rule in integration.

docs.title: 9.1 Related Rates
docs.text:
When two quantities both depend on time \(t\), differentiating an equation relating them gives a relationship between their rates.

Example. A ladder 10 m long leans against a wall. The base slides away at \(2\) m/s. How fast is the top sliding down when the base is 6 m from the wall?

Let \(x\) = distance of base from wall, \(y\) = height of top. \(x^2 + y^2 = 100\).

Differentiate with respect to \(t\):

\[2x\frac{dx}{dt} + 2y\frac{dy}{dt} = 0\]

When \(x = 6\): \(y = \sqrt{100 - 36} = 8\). Given \(dx/dt = 2\):

\[2(6)(2) + 2(8)\frac{dy}{dt} = 0 \implies \frac{dy}{dt} = -\frac{24}{16} = -\frac{3}{2} \text{ m/s}\]

The top slides down at \(3/2\) m/s.

docs.title: 9.2 Optimization
docs.text:
At a local extremum, \(f'(c) = 0\) (critical point) or \(f'(c)\) does not exist.

First Derivative Test: \(f'\) changes sign at \(c\).

  • \(+ \to -\): local maximum
  • \(- \to +\): local minimum

Second Derivative Test: At critical point \(c\) with \(f'(c) = 0\):

  • \(f''(c) > 0\): local minimum (concave up)
  • \(f''(c) < 0\): local maximum (concave down)
  • \(f''(c) = 0\): inconclusive

docs.title: §10. Partial Derivatives (18.02 Perspective)
docs.text:
For \(f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\), the partial derivative with respect to \(x_i\) holds all other variables fixed:

\[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(\mathbf{a}) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(\mathbf{a} + h\mathbf{e}_i) - f(\mathbf{a})}{h}\]

where \(\mathbf{e}_i\) is the \(i\)-th standard basis vector.

Geometric reading: \(\partial f / \partial x\) is the slope of the slice of the surface \(z = f(x,y)\) cut by a plane of constant \(y\).

docs.title: The Gradient
docs.text:
\[\nabla f = \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}, \ldots, \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n}\right)\]

The gradient is the vector of all partial derivatives. Its geometric meaning: it points in the direction of steepest ascent of \(f\), and its magnitude is the rate of steepest ascent.

\(\nabla f(\mathbf{a})\) is perpendicular to the level set \({f = f(\mathbf{a})}\) at \(\mathbf{a}\).

This is the most important geometric fact in multivariable calculus.

docs.title: Differentiability in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)
docs.text:
In higher dimensions, existence of partial derivatives does not imply differentiability (unlike in \(\mathbb{R}\)). The function must be well-approximated by a linear map near \(\mathbf{a}\):

\[f(\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{h}) = f(\mathbf{a}) + \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{h} + o(|\mathbf{h}|)\]

If partial derivatives exist and are continuous near \(\mathbf{a}\), then \(f\) is differentiable at \(\mathbf{a}\). (Sufficient, not necessary.)

docs.title: §11. The Jacobian
docs.text:
For \(\mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m\), the derivative generalizes to the Jacobian matrix:

\[J_\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{pmatrix} \partial f_1/\partial x_1 & \cdots & \partial f_1/\partial x_n \ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \ \partial f_m/\partial x_1 & \cdots & \partial f_m/\partial x_n \end{pmatrix}\]

This is the best linear approximation to \(\mathbf{f}\) near \(\mathbf{x}\):

\[\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{h}) \approx \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}) + J_\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}),\mathbf{h}\]

The chain rule in multiple dimensions: if \(\mathbf{h} = \mathbf{g} \circ \mathbf{f}\), then:

\[J_\mathbf{h} = J_\mathbf{g} \cdot J_\mathbf{f}\]

Matrix multiplication of Jacobians.

docs.title: §12. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: This is not analogy — derivatives are the literal computational object underlying all of modern machine learning.

docs.title: 12.1 Gradient Descent is Differentiation Applied
docs.text:
To minimize a loss \(\mathcal{L}(\theta)\), gradient descent takes steps in the direction of steepest descent:

\[\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta)\]

The gradient \(\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}\) is a vector of partial derivatives — one per parameter. A neural network with \(10^9\) parameters has a gradient in \(\mathbb{R}^{10^9}\).

The fundamental insight: the gradient tells you, for each parameter \(\theta_i\), how much a small increase in \(\theta_i\) increases the loss. Move opposite that direction.

docs.title: 12.2 Backpropagation is the Chain Rule
docs.text:
Training a neural network requires computing \(\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}\) where \(\mathcal{L}\) is a composition of many functions (layers). This is precisely the chain rule applied to the computational graph.

For a network \(\hat{y} = f_L \circ f_{L-1} \circ \cdots \circ f_1(\mathbf{x})\):

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta^{(k)}} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{y}} \cdot \frac{\partial \hat{y}}{\partial f_{L-1}} \cdot \frac{\partial f_{L-1}}{\partial f_{L-2}} \cdots \frac{\partial f_k}{\partial \theta^{(k)}}\]

Backpropagation is the chain rule evaluated efficiently via dynamic programming — computing the product from right to left, reusing intermediate values.

In matrix form, the chain rule for Jacobians is:

\[J_{\mathcal{L}, \theta^{(k)}} = J_{\mathcal{L}, f_L} \cdot J_{f_L, f_{L-1}} \cdots J_{f_k, \theta^{(k)}}\]

Every backward pass through a layer is a Jacobian-vector product.

docs.title: 12.3 Automatic Differentiation
docs.text:
Modern frameworks (PyTorch, JAX, TensorFlow) implement automatic differentiation (autograd) — not numerical differentiation (finite differences) nor symbolic differentiation, but exact differentiation via the chain rule on the computational graph.

Two modes:

  • Forward mode: propagate \(\dot{x}\) (tangent vector) forward through the graph. Efficient when \(n \ll m\) (few inputs, many outputs).
  • Reverse mode (backprop): propagate \(\bar{y}\) (adjoint/gradient) backward through the graph. Efficient when \(m \ll n\) (few outputs — as in scalar loss — many inputs). This is why backprop is used.

The derivative you write in calculus class — the limit of a difference quotient — is what autograd computes, exactly, for every parameter simultaneously.

docs.title: 12.4 Second Derivatives: Curvature and Optimization
docs.text:
The Hessian \(H = \nabla^2 \mathcal{L}\) is the matrix of second partial derivatives:

\[H_{ij} = \frac{\partial^2 \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta_i \partial \theta_j}\]

Newton's method uses the Hessian to take curvature-aware steps:

\[\theta \leftarrow \theta - H^{-1} \nabla \mathcal{L}\]

This converges much faster than gradient descent near a minimum (quadratic vs. linear convergence). But computing and inverting an \(n \times n\) Hessian for \(n = 10^9\) is catastrophically expensive.

Quasi-Newton methods (L-BFGS, Adam) approximate \(H^{-1}\) cheaply:

  • Adam uses running estimates of the gradient mean (first moment) and gradient squared (second moment — diagonal Hessian approximation) to adapt step sizes per parameter.

The second derivative test from single-variable calculus — \(f''(c) > 0\) at a critical point means local min — generalizes to: \(H\) is positive definite at a critical point means local min. This is what determines whether gradient descent has found a true minimum.

docs.title: 12.5 Directional Derivative and the Gradient
docs.text:
The directional derivative in direction \(\mathbf{u}\) (unit vector):

\[D_\mathbf{u} f(\mathbf{a}) = abla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{u} = | abla f| \cos heta\]

This is maximized when \(\mathbf{u} = abla f / | abla f|\) — the gradient direction. Gradient descent moves in this direction (with a sign flip for minimization).

In deep learning, understanding which direction to move in parameter space is exactly this computation.

docs.title: 12.6 The Jacobian in Neural Networks
docs.text:
For a layer \(\mathbf{z} = W\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}\) followed by activation \(\mathbf{h} = \sigma(\mathbf{z})\):

\[J_{\mathbf{h}, \mathbf{a}} = \text{diag}(\sigma'(\mathbf{z})) \cdot W\]

During backprop, the gradient is pre-multiplied by this Jacobian. If \(\sigma'(\mathbf{z})\) is near zero (sigmoid saturation), the Jacobian has small entries and the gradient is crushed — the vanishing gradient problem, now expressed as a Jacobian becoming nearly zero.

Batch normalization, residual connections (ResNets), and careful weight initialization all address this by keeping Jacobians well-conditioned through the depth of the network.

docs.title: 12.7 Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs)
docs.text:
PINNs encode physical laws (ODEs/PDEs) as constraints on the neural network's derivatives. The loss function penalizes violations of the differential equation:

\[\mathcal{L} = \underbrace{\mathcal{L}_{\text{data}}}_{\text{fit data}} + \underbrace{\lambda,\mathcal{L}_{\text{PDE}}}_{\text{derivatives must satisfy PDE}}\]

where \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{PDE}}\) involves the actual partial derivatives of the network output (computed via autograd). The derivative — the calculus object — appears inside the loss being minimized.

docs.title: §13. Summary Table
docs.text: Concept Key Content Derivative at \(a\) \(\lim_{h\to 0} \frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}\); slope of tangent Differentiability Implies continuity; converse false Failures Corners, cusps, vertical tangents, discontinuities Chain rule \((f\circ g)' = f'(g)\cdot g'\); most-used rule Product rule \((fg)' = f'g + fg'\); rectangle area argument Higher derivatives \(f''\): concavity; \(f'''\): jerk MVT Instantaneous slope equals average slope somewhere Linear approximation \(f(x) \approx f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)\) Gradient \(\nabla f\) Vector of partials; direction of steepest ascent Jacobian \(J_\mathbf{f}\) Matrix derivative for \(\mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m\) Backpropagation Chain rule on computational graph (reverse mode AD) Hessian \(\nabla^2 \mathcal{L}\) Second-order info; used in Newton/quasi-Newton methods

docs.title: §14. Things Worth Losing Sleep Over
docs.text:
• A function with \(f'(c) = 0\) need not have a local extremum there. (\(f(x) = x^3\) at \(x = 0\): inflection point, not extremum.)
  • Partial derivatives can exist everywhere while the function is not differentiable. (The partial derivatives exist but the linear approximation fails.)
  • \(\partial^2 f / \partial x \partial y = \partial^2 f / \partial y \partial x\) (Clairaut's theorem) requires continuity of the mixed partials — it is not automatic.
  • The Jacobian of a composition is the product of Jacobians — this is the chain rule, the product rule, and matrix multiplication unified into one theorem.
  • Weierstrass constructed a function that is continuous everywhere but differentiable nowhere. It looks like noise at every scale. This shattered the 19th-century intuition that continuity implied differentiability "almost everywhere."

docs.title: Example 1 — From Definition
docs.text:
Find \(f'(x)\) for \(f(x) = x^2\) using the definition.

\[f'(x) = \lim_{h\to 0} \frac{(x+h)^2 - x^2}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0} \frac{2xh + h^2}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0}(2x + h) = 2x\]

docs.title: Example 2 — Chain Rule (nested)
docs.text:
Differentiate \(y = \ln(\sin(e^x))\).

\[y' = \frac{1}{\sin(e^x)} \cdot \cos(e^x) \cdot e^x = \frac{e^x \cos(e^x)}{\sin(e^x)} = e^x \cot(e^x)\]

docs.title: Example 3 — Implicit Differentiation
docs.text:
Find \(y'\) for \(e^{xy} = x + y\).

Differentiate both sides w.r.t. \(x\):

\[e^{xy}(y + xy') = 1 + y'\] \[y e^{xy} + xy' e^{xy} = 1 + y'\] \[y'(xe^{xy} - 1) = 1 - ye^{xy}\] \[y' = \frac{1 - ye^{xy}}{xe^{xy} - 1}\]

docs.text:

  2. MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus — Partial derivatives, gradient, directional derivatives, Jacobian, chain rule in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)
  3. Goodfellow, I., Bengio, Y., Courville, A. Deep Learning (2016), Ch. 4 (Numerical Computation), Ch. 6 (Backpropagation)
  4. Baydin, A.G. et al. (2018). "Automatic Differentiation in Machine Learning: a Survey." JMLR 18(153).
