docs.title: § 0 — Motivation: Why Should You Care?
docs.text:
Before we define anything, a confession: the name "hyperbolic" is not an accident, and these are not just "the sinh/cosh things you memorize for an exam." They appear naturally in:

  • The shape of a hanging cable (catenary): \(y = a\cosh(x/a)\)
  • Special relativity: Lorentz boosts are hyperbolic rotations
  • Solutions to the heat equation and wave equation
  • The backpropagation algorithm in deep learning (\(\tanh\) is one of the most classical activation functions)
  • Geodesics on the hyperbolic plane (differential geometry)

They also make many integrals tractable that would otherwise require painful trigonometric substitutions.

docs.title: § 1 — Definitions: Exponential Heart
docs.text:
Everything comes from two combinations of \(e^x\):

\[\boxed{\sinh x = \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{2}, \qquad \cosh x = \frac{e^x + e^{-x}}{2}}\]

Think of \(e^x = \cosh x + \sinh x\) as splitting the exponential into its even part (\(\cosh\)) and odd part (\(\sinh\)).

The remaining four follow exactly as in trigonometry:

\[\tanh x = \frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x} = \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{e^x + e^{-x}}\] \[\operatorname{csch} x = \frac{1}{\sinh x}, \quad \operatorname{sech} x = \frac{1}{\cosh x}, \quad \coth x = \frac{1}{\tanh x}\]

Personal note: I always re-derive \(\tanh\) from scratch instead of memorizing it. If you know the two boxed formulas above, you know everything.

docs.title: § 2 — The Hyperbola Connection (Why "Hyperbolic"?)
docs.text:
Recall that \((\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\) parametrizes the unit circle \(x^2 + y^2 = 1\).

Claim: \((\cosh t, \sinh t)\) parametrizes the right branch of the unit hyperbola \(x^2 - y^2 = 1\).

Proof: $\(\cosh^2 t - \sinh^2 t = \left(\frac{e^t+e^{-t}}{2}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{e^t-e^{-t}}{2}\right)^2\)$

\[= \frac{(e^t+e^{-t})^2 - (e^t-e^{-t})^2}{4} = \frac{4e^t e^{-t}}{4} = \frac{4}{4} = 1 \qquad \square\]

This is the fundamental identity:

\[\boxed{\cosh^2 x - \sinh^2 x = 1}\]

The parameter \(t\) is twice the area of the hyperbolic sector (analogous to how \(\theta/2\) is the area of a circular sector). This geometric fact is why \(t\) is called the hyperbolic angle.

Circular:                        Hyperbolic:
   ┌──────────────┐                 ┌──────────────┐
   │     *        │                 │      *       │
   │  *     *     │                 │   *          │
   │ *       *    │                 │  *           │
   │  *     *     │                 │   *          │
   │     *        │                 │      *       │
   └──────────────┘                 └──────────────┘
  (cos θ, sin θ) on circle         (cosh t, sinh t) on hyperbola
  x² + y² = 1                      x² - y² = 1

docs.title: § 3 — Identities: The Rosetta Stone
docs.text:
Every trigonometric identity has a hyperbolic analogue, with one sign twist (Osborn's Rule: replace every product of two sines with its negative).

Circular Hyperbolic \(\cos^2 x + \sin^2 x = 1\) \(\cosh^2 x - \sinh^2 x = 1\) \(1 + \tan^2 x = \sec^2 x\) \(1 - \tanh^2 x = \operatorname{sech}^2 x\) \(\sin(x+y) = \sin x \cos y + \cos x \sin y\) \(\sinh(x+y) = \sinh x \cosh y + \cosh x \sinh y\) \(\cos(x+y) = \cos x \cos y - \sin x \sin y\) \(\cosh(x+y) = \cosh x \cosh y + \sinh x \sinh y\) \(\cos 2x = 2\cos^2 x - 1\) \(\cosh 2x = 2\cosh^2 x - 1\) \(\sin 2x = 2\sin x \cos x\) \(\sinh 2x = 2\sinh x \cosh x\)

Proof of \(1 - \tanh^2 x = \operatorname{sech}^2 x\):

Divide \(\cosh^2 x - \sinh^2 x = 1\) through by \(\cosh^2 x\):

\[1 - \frac{\sinh^2 x}{\cosh^2 x} = \frac{1}{\cosh^2 x} \implies 1 - \tanh^2 x = \operatorname{sech}^2 x \qquad \square\]

docs.title: \(\sinh x\): Odd, unbounded
docs.text:
\[\sinh(-x) = \frac{e^{-x}-e^{x}}{2} = -\sinh x\]
  • Domain: \(\mathbb{R}\), Range: \(\mathbb{R}\)
  • \(\sinh(0) = 0\)
  • Strictly increasing, one-to-one
  • Looks like \(x\) near origin, then grows like \(e^x/2\)
     ↑ sinh x
  4  │                    *
  3  │                *
  2  │            *
  1  │        *
  0  │────────────────────→ x
 -1  │    *
 -2  │*
     -2  -1   0   1   2

docs.title: \(\cosh x\): Even, minimum at 1
docs.text:
\[\cosh(-x) = \cosh x, \quad \cosh(0) = 1\]
  • Domain: \(\mathbb{R}\), Range: \([1, \infty)\)
  • Convex, resembles a parabola near origin but grows exponentially
  • This is the catenary (shape of a hanging chain)

docs.title: \(\tanh x\): The S-curve
docs.text:
\[\tanh(-x) = -\tanh x, \quad \tanh(0) = 0\] \[\lim_{x\to+\infty}\tanh x = 1, \quad \lim_{x\to-\infty}\tanh x = -1\]
  • Domain: \(\mathbb{R}\), Range: \((-1, 1)\)
  • Strictly increasing, one-to-one
  • Squashes all of \(\mathbb{R}\) into \((-1,1)\) — this is why it's invaluable in neural networks
     ↑ tanh x
  1  │─────────────────────────── (asymptote)
     │               ****
     │          ****
     │       ***
  0  │────────────────────────→ x
     │   ***
     │****
 -1  │─────────────────────────── (asymptote)
     -3  -2  -1   0   1   2   3

docs.title: § 5 — Derivatives
docs.text:
Theorem. The derivatives of the hyperbolic functions are:

\[\frac{d}{dx}\sinh x = \cosh x, \qquad \frac{d}{dx}\cosh x = \sinh x\]

Proof (both at once):

\[\frac{d}{dx}\sinh x = \frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{2}\right) = \frac{e^x + e^{-x}}{2} = \cosh x\] \[\frac{d}{dx}\cosh x = \frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{e^x + e^{-x}}{2}\right) = \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{2} = \sinh x \qquad \square\]

Contrast with trig: \(\frac{d}{dx}\cos x = -\sin x\), but \(\frac{d}{dx}\cosh x = +\sinh x\). The minus sign is missing — this is the same sign twist from Osborn's Rule.

The full table:

\(f(x)\) \(f'(x)\) \(\sinh x\) \(\cosh x\) \(\cosh x\) \(\sinh x\) \(\tanh x\) \(\operatorname{sech}^2 x\) \(\operatorname{csch} x\) \(-\operatorname{csch} x \coth x\) \(\operatorname{sech} x\) \(-\operatorname{sech} x \tanh x\) \(\coth x\) \(-\operatorname{csch}^2 x\)

Proof for \(\tanh x\) (quotient rule):

\[\frac{d}{dx}\tanh x = \frac{\cosh x \cdot \cosh x - \sinh x \cdot \sinh x}{\cosh^2 x} = \frac{\cosh^2 x - \sinh^2 x}{\cosh^2 x} = \frac{1}{\cosh^2 x} = \operatorname{sech}^2 x \qquad \square\]

docs.title: § 6 — Inverse Hyperbolic Functions
docs.text:
Since \(\sinh\) and \(\tanh\) are strictly monotone on \(\mathbb{R}\), and \(\cosh\) is monotone on \([0,\infty)\), the inverses exist.

Crucial fact: The inverses can be expressed in closed form via logarithms:

\[\sinh^{-1} x = \ln!\left(x + \sqrt{x^2+1}\right), \quad x \in \mathbb{R}\] \[\cosh^{-1} x = \ln!\left(x + \sqrt{x^2-1}\right), \quad x \geq 1\] \[\tanh^{-1} x = \frac{1}{2}\ln!\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right), \quad |x| < 1\]

Proof of the \(\sinh^{-1}\) formula: Let \(y = \sinh^{-1} x\), so \(\sinh y = x\):

\[\frac{e^y - e^{-y}}{2} = x \implies e^y - e^{-y} = 2x \implies e^{2y} - 2xe^y - 1 = 0\]

This is a quadratic in \(e^y\). By the quadratic formula:

\[e^y = \frac{2x \pm \sqrt{4x^2 + 4}}{2} = x \pm \sqrt{x^2+1}\]

Since \(e^y > 0\) and \(\sqrt{x^2+1} > |x|\), we must take the \(+\) sign:

\[y = \ln!\left(x + \sqrt{x^2+1}\right) \qquad \square\]

docs.title: Derivatives of Inverses
docs.text:
\[\frac{d}{dx}\sinh^{-1} x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}, \quad \frac{d}{dx}\cosh^{-1} x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2-1}}, \quad \frac{d}{dx}\tanh^{-1} x = \frac{1}{1-x^2}\]

Proof of the first (implicit differentiation): If \(\sinh y = x\), then \(\cosh y \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} = 1\), so

\[\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{\cosh y} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + \sinh^2 y}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^2}} \qquad \square\]

docs.title: § 7 — Integration Formulas
docs.text:
The derivatives immediately give antiderivatives:

\[\int \cosh x , dx = \sinh x + C, \quad \int \sinh x , dx = \cosh x + C\] \[\int \operatorname{sech}^2 x , dx = \tanh x + C\]

The real power comes from recognizing when a substitution reduces to these:

\[\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}} = \sinh^{-1}!\left(\frac{x}{a}\right) + C = \ln!\left(x + \sqrt{x^2+a^2}\right) + C\] \[\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2-a^2}} = \cosh^{-1}!\left(\frac{x}{a}\right) + C \quad (x > a > 0)\] \[\int \frac{dx}{a^2-x^2} = \frac{1}{a}\tanh^{-1}!\left(\frac{x}{a}\right) + C \quad (|x|<a)\]

docs.title: Example: Hyperbolic Substitution
docs.text:
Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int \sqrt{x^2+1}, dx\).

Let \(x = \sinh t\), so \(dx = \cosh t , dt\) and \(\sqrt{x^2+1} = \sqrt{\sinh^2 t + 1} = \cosh t\).

\[\int \cosh t \cdot \cosh t , dt = \int \cosh^2 t , dt = \int \frac{1 + \cosh 2t}{2}, dt = \frac{t}{2} + \frac{\sinh 2t}{4} + C\]

Back-substituting (\(t = \sinh^{-1} x\), \(\sinh 2t = 2\sinh t \cosh t = 2x\sqrt{x^2+1}\)):

\[= \frac{1}{2}\sinh^{-1} x + \frac{x\sqrt{x^2+1}}{2} + C\]

Compare the trigonometric route (\(x = \tan\theta\)) — it's messier. Hyperbolic substitution is cleaner for \(\sqrt{x^2 + a^2}\) integrands.

docs.title: § 8 — Taylor Series and Asymptotic Behavior
docs.text:
From the Taylor series of \(e^x\):

\[\cosh x = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{x^{2n}}{(2n)!} = 1 + \frac{x^2}{2!} + \frac{x^4}{4!} + \cdots\] \[\sinh x = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{x^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!} = x + \frac{x^3}{3!} + \frac{x^5}{5!} + \cdots\] \[\tanh x = x - \frac{x^3}{3} + \frac{2x^5}{15} - \cdots \quad (|x| < \pi/2)\]

These are exactly the circular Taylor series but without the alternating signs (another instance of the Osborn sign flip).

Asymptotics: For large \(x\):

\[\sinh x \approx \cosh x \approx \frac{e^x}{2}, \qquad \tanh x \approx 1 - 2e^{-2x}\]

docs.title: § 9 — Connection to AI, Machine Learning, Deep Learning
docs.text: This is where the abstract becomes immediately applicable.

docs.title: 9.1 — \(\tanh\) as an Activation Function
docs.text:
In a neural network, a neuron computes \(\sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b)\) where \(\sigma\) is the activation function. The \(\tanh\) function was one of the first standard choices:

\[\tanh(z) = \frac{e^z - e^{-z}}{e^z + e^{-z}} \in (-1, 1)\]

Why \(\tanh\)?

  1. Zero-centered output. The output range \((-1,1)\) means the mean activation is near 0. This matters because if activations are all positive (as with the sigmoid \(\sigma = 1/(1+e^{-x}) \in (0,1)\)), gradients in backpropagation always have the same sign, causing inefficient zig-zag updates.

  2. Saturating nonlinearity. It introduces the nonlinearity without which a deep network collapses to a linear map (\(\because\) composition of linear maps is linear).

  3. Smooth and differentiable. Gradient-based optimization (SGD, Adam) requires \(\frac{d}{dz}\tanh z = \operatorname{sech}^2 z = 1 - \tanh^2 z\). Notice: if you've already computed \(\tanh(z)\), the derivative costs almost nothing to compute — a single multiplication and subtraction. This is computationally elegant.

The vanishing gradient problem: \(\operatorname{sech}^2 z \leq 1\) and \(\operatorname{sech}^2(z) \to 0\) as \(|z| \to \infty\). In deep networks, gradients are products of many such terms. When neurons saturate (large \(|z|\)), \(\operatorname{sech}^2(z) \approx 0\), and the gradient signal vanishes through the chain rule. This is one reason ReLU (\(\max(0,x)\)) became popular — it doesn't saturate for \(x>0\).

Backpropagation chain rule:

∂L/∂w₁ = (∂L/∂a_n) · (∏ sech²(zᵢ)) · (∂a₁/∂w₁)
                          i=2..n

If n is large and neurons saturate → product → 0 (vanishing gradient)

docs.title: 9.2 — \(\sinh^{-1}\) and Data Preprocessing
docs.text: In some ML pipelines, the transformation \(x \mapsto \sinh^{-1}(x) = \ln(x + \sqrt{x^2+1})\) is used as a variance-stabilizing transform for heavy-tailed data. Unlike \(\log(x)\) (defined only for \(x>0\)), \(\sinh^{-1}\) is defined on all of \(\mathbb{R}\) and behaves like \(\ln(2x)\) for large \(x\) and like \(x\) near 0. It is used in financial data preprocessing where returns can be negative.

docs.title: 9.3 — \(\cosh\) in the Loss Function Landscape
docs.text:
The log-cosh loss is a smooth approximation to the mean absolute error:

\[L(y, \hat{y}) = \sum_i \ln\cosh(y_i - \hat{y}_i)\]

Since \(\ln\cosh(x) \approx \frac{x^2}{2}\) for small \(x\) (MSE behavior) and \(\approx |x| - \ln 2\) for large \(x\) (MAE behavior), it inherits robustness to outliers from MAE while remaining twice-differentiable everywhere. This matters for optimization since MSE is sensitive to outliers and Huber loss has a non-smooth kink at the transition point.

docs.title: 9.4 — \(\tanh\) in Recurrent Neural Networks (LSTMs)
docs.text:
In Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997), both \(\tanh\) and the sigmoid \(\sigma\) appear in the core update equations:

\[\tilde{C}_t = \tanh(W_c \cdot [h_{t-1}, x_t] + b_c) \quad \text{(candidate cell state)}$$ $$h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(C_t) \quad \text{(output/hidden state)}\]

The role of \(\tanh\) here: squash the cell state into \((-1, 1)\) before it becomes the hidden state. It keeps magnitudes bounded over long sequences, partially mitigating the exploding gradient problem.

docs.title: 9.5 — Summary Table for AI
docs.text:
Function Where it appears Why \(\tanh\) Hidden layer activations, LSTM gates Zero-centered, smooth nonlinearity \(\operatorname{sech}^2 = \tanh'\) Backpropagation through \(\tanh\) Derivative needed for gradient flow \(\ln\cosh\) Loss function (log-cosh loss) Smooth robust regression \(\sinh^{-1}\) Data preprocessing Variance-stabilizing transform \(\cosh, \sinh\) Hyperbolic geometry, manifold learning Hyperbolic embeddings (Poincaré disk)

Deep cut: The Poincaré embedding model (Nickel & Kiela, 2017) embeds hierarchical data (like WordNet) in hyperbolic space rather than Euclidean space, because hyperbolic space can represent tree-like structures with exponentially growing neighborhoods more efficiently. The metric on the Poincaré disk is defined using \(\cosh\) of a certain distance.

docs.title: § 10 — The Catenary: A Classical Application
docs.text:
Problem. A flexible inextensible cable of uniform linear density \(\rho\) hangs under gravity between two supports. Find the shape.

Let the lowest point be the origin. Let \(T_0\) be the tension there (horizontal). At arc length \(s\) from the lowest point, the tension \(T\) acts tangentially, and \(\rho g s\) is the weight of the hanging segment. Force balance:

\[T\cos\theta = T_0, \qquad T\sin\theta = \rho g s\]

Dividing: \(\tan\theta = \frac{\rho g s}{T_0}\). Since \(\tan\theta = y'\) and \(s = \int_0^x \sqrt{1+(y')^2}, dx'\), differentiating both sides in \(x\):

\[y'' = \frac{\rho g}{T_0}\sqrt{1+(y')^2}\]

Let \(a = T_0/(\rho g)\) and \(p = y'\). Then \(p' = \frac{1}{a}\sqrt{1+p^2}\), which separates:

\[\int \frac{dp}{\sqrt{1+p^2}} = \int \frac{dx}{a} \implies \sinh^{-1}(p) = \frac{x}{a} + C\]

With \(p(0) = y'(0) = 0 \Rightarrow C = 0\). So \(y' = \sinh(x/a)\). Integrating:

\[\boxed{y = a\cosh!\left(\frac{x}{a}\right) + C}\]

The catenary. The constant \(C\) is fixed by the height at the lowest point.

docs.title: § 11 — Quick Reference Card
docs.text: \[\sinh x = \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{2}, \quad \cosh x = \frac{e^x + e^{-x}}{2}, \quad \tanh x = \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{e^x + e^{-x}}\] \[\cosh^2 x - \sinh^2 x = 1, \quad 1 - \tanh^2 x = \operatorname{sech}^2 x\] \[(\sinh x)' = \cosh x, \quad (\cosh x)' = \sinh x, \quad (\tanh x)' = \operatorname{sech}^2 x\] \[\sinh^{-1} x = \ln(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}), \quad \tanh^{-1} x = \frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{1+x}{1-x}\] \[(\sinh^{-1} x)' = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}, \quad (\tanh^{-1} x)' = \frac{1}{1-x^2}\]

docs.title: § 12 — Exercises
docs.text:
1. (Identity) Prove \(\cosh(x+y) = \cosh x \cosh y + \sinh x \sinh y\) directly from the exponential definitions.

2. (Derivative) Compute \(\frac{d}{dx}[\tanh(\ln x)]\) and simplify. (Hint: what is \(\tanh(\ln x)\) explicitly?)

3. (Integral) Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^1 \tanh x , dx\). (Express as \(\ln\cosh(1)\), then think about what that is numerically.)

4. (Inverse) Verify the formula \(\tanh^{-1} x = \frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{1+x}{1-x}\) by showing \(\tanh(\tanh^{-1} x) = x\).

5. (Application) Show that the arc length of \(y = \cosh x\) from \(x = 0\) to \(x = a\) equals \(\sinh a\).

6. (ML) The derivative of the sigmoid \(\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\) satisfies \(\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))\). Show that \(\tanh(z) = 2\sigma(2z) - 1\), and use this to express \((\tanh z)'\) in terms of \(\sigma\).

7. (Challenging) Prove that \(\displaystyle\int \operatorname{sech} x , dx = \arctan(\sinh x) + C = 2\arctan(e^x) + C\). (This result bridges hyperbolic and circular functions in a surprising way.)

End of note.

docs.title: Inverse Hyperbolic Functions
docs.text:
A Professor's Personal Notebook

References: Stewart, Calculus §3.11, §6.7; MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus Prerequisite: [[Hyperbolic Functions]]

docs.title: § 0 — Why Bother With Inverses?
docs.text:
The honest answer: integrals.

The forms \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}\), \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2-1}}\), \(\dfrac{1}{1-x^2}\) appear constantly in calculus, physics, and machine learning. Without inverse hyperbolic functions, you are forced into trigonometric substitution — doable, but slower and more error-prone.

With inverse hyperbolic functions, these integrals become one-line antiderivatives.

A second reason: inverse hyperbolic functions are not transcendental mysteries — they collapse to logarithms. Every one of them is expressible in closed form. This makes them simultaneously computable, differentiable, and elegant.

docs.title: § 1 — Existence of Inverses
docs.text:
Recall from [[Hyperbolic Functions]]:

Function Domain Range Monotone? Inverse exists? \(\sinh x\) \(\mathbb{R}\) \(\mathbb{R}\) Strictly increasing ✓ on all of \(\mathbb{R}\) \(\cosh x\) \(\mathbb{R}\) \([1, \infty)\) Neither (even function) ✓ only on \([0, \infty)\) \(\tanh x\) \(\mathbb{R}\) \((-1, 1)\) Strictly increasing ✓ on all of \(\mathbb{R}\) \(\operatorname{sech} x\) \(\mathbb{R}\) \((0, 1]\) Neither (even function) ✓ only on \([0, \infty)\) \(\operatorname{csch} x\) \(\mathbb{R}\setminus{0}\) \(\mathbb{R}\setminus{0}\) Strictly decreasing on each branch ✓ (separately on each branch) \(\coth x\) \(\mathbb{R}\setminus{0}\) \((-\infty,-1)\cup(1,\infty)\) Strictly decreasing on each branch ✓ (separately on each branch)

Personal note: The restriction of \(\cosh\) to \([0,\infty)\) is the standard convention, analogous to restricting \(\cos\) to \([0,\pi]\) to define \(\arccos\).

docs.title: § 2 — Logarithmic Closed Forms
docs.text: This is the core theorem. Every inverse hyperbolic function reduces to a logarithm.

docs.title: Theorem 2.1
docs.text:
\[\boxed{\sinh^{-1} x = \ln!\left(x + \sqrt{x^2 + 1}\right), \quad x \in \mathbb{R}}\]

Proof. Let \(y = \sinh^{-1} x\), so \(\sinh y = x\):

\[\frac{e^y - e^{-y}}{2} = x \implies e^y - e^{-y} = 2x\]

Multiply through by \(e^y\):

\[e^{2y} - 2x e^y - 1 = 0\]

This is a quadratic in \(e^y\). Quadratic formula:

\[e^y = \frac{2x \pm \sqrt{4x^2 + 4}}{2} = x \pm \sqrt{x^2 + 1}\]

Since \(e^y > 0\) for all \(y\), and \(\sqrt{x^2+1} > |x|\), the expression \(x - \sqrt{x^2+1} < 0\) always. So we must take \(+\):

\[e^y = x + \sqrt{x^2+1} \implies y = \ln!\left(x + \sqrt{x^2 + 1}\right) \qquad \square\]

docs.title: Theorem 2.2
docs.text:
\[\boxed{\cosh^{-1} x = \ln!\left(x + \sqrt{x^2 - 1}\right), \quad x \geq 1}\]

Proof. Let \(y = \cosh^{-1} x \geq 0\), so \(\cosh y = x\):

\[\frac{e^y + e^{-y}}{2} = x \implies e^{2y} - 2xe^y + 1 = 0\]

Quadratic formula:

\[e^y = \frac{2x \pm \sqrt{4x^2 - 4}}{2} = x \pm \sqrt{x^2 - 1}\]

Both roots are positive when \(x \geq 1\), but they correspond to \(y \geq 0\) and \(y \leq 0\) respectively. Since we restrict \(\cosh^{-1}\) to the branch \(y \geq 0\), we need \(e^y \geq 1\), which requires \(e^y = x + \sqrt{x^2-1}\):

\[y = \ln!\left(x + \sqrt{x^2-1}\right) \qquad \square\]

Sanity check: At \(x = 1\): \(\cosh^{-1}(1) = \ln(1 + 0) = 0\). ✓

docs.title: Theorem 2.3
docs.text:
\[\boxed{\tanh^{-1} x = \frac{1}{2}\ln!\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right), \quad |x| < 1}\]

Proof. Let \(y = \tanh^{-1} x\), so \(\tanh y = x\):

\[\frac{e^y - e^{-y}}{e^y + e^{-y}} = x\]

Cross-multiply: \(e^y - e^{-y} = x(e^y + e^{-y})\). Rearrange:

\[e^y(1 - x) = e^{-y}(1 + x) \implies e^{2y} = \frac{1+x}{1-x}\]

Take logarithm:

\[2y = \ln!\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right) \implies y = \frac{1}{2}\ln!\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right) \qquad \square\]

Observe: The argument \(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\) must be positive, which requires \(|x| < 1\) — consistent with \(\tanh: \mathbb{R} \to (-1,1)\).

docs.title: The Remaining Three
docs.text:
By analogous quadratic arguments (left as exercises):

\[\coth^{-1} x = \frac{1}{2}\ln!\left(\frac{x+1}{x-1}\right), \quad |x| > 1\] \[\operatorname{sech}^{-1} x = \ln!\left(\frac{1 + \sqrt{1-x^2}}{x}\right), \quad 0 < x \leq 1\] \[\operatorname{csch}^{-1} x = \ln!\left(\frac{1}{x} + \frac{\sqrt{1+x^2}}{|x|}\right), \quad x \neq 0\]

docs.title: § 3 — Graphs and Geometric Intuition
docs.text: The graphs of the inverses are obtained by reflecting the hyperbolic graphs across \(y = x\).

docs.title: \(\sinh^{-1} x\)
docs.text:
↑ y = sinh⁻¹ x
  2  │           *
  1  │       *
  0  │───*───────────────→ x
 -1  │   *
 -2  │*
     -3  -1   0   1   3

Domain: ℝ,  Range: ℝ
Looks like: ln(2x) for large x, like x near origin
  • Passes through \((0, 0)\)
  • Odd function: \(\sinh^{-1}(-x) = -\sinh^{-1}(x)\)
  • Grows without bound, but slowly (logarithmically)

docs.title: \(\cosh^{-1} x\)
docs.text:
↑ y = cosh⁻¹ x
  3  │                    *
  2  │               *
  1  │          *
  0  │──────────*──────────→ x
               1    2    3

Domain: [1, ∞),  Range: [0, ∞)
Starts at (1, 0), increasing, concave down

docs.title: \(\tanh^{-1} x\)
docs.text:
↑ y = tanh⁻¹ x
     │
  2  │                *
  1  │           *
  0  │───────────────────→ x
 -1  │   *
 -2  │*
     -1          0    1
      (asymptotes at x = ±1)

Domain: (-1, 1),  Range: ℝ
Vertical asymptotes at x = ±1
  • \(\tanh^{-1}\) is the reflection of \(\tanh\) across \(y = x\)
  • Where \(\tanh\) has horizontal asymptotes at \(y = \pm 1\), \(\tanh^{-1}\) has vertical asymptotes at \(x = \pm 1\)

docs.title: § 4 — Derivatives: The Algebraic Computation
docs.text: These are among the most useful derivatives in calculus.

docs.title: Theorem 4.1 (Derivatives of Inverse Hyperbolics)
docs.text:
\[\frac{d}{dx}\sinh^{-1} x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}\] \[\frac{d}{dx}\cosh^{-1} x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2-1}}, \quad x > 1\] \[\frac{d}{dx}\tanh^{-1} x = \frac{1}{1-x^2}, \quad |x| < 1\] \[\frac{d}{dx}\operatorname{sech}^{-1} x = \frac{-1}{x\sqrt{1-x^2}}, \quad 0 < x < 1\] \[\frac{d}{dx}\operatorname{csch}^{-1} x = \frac{-1}{|x|\sqrt{1+x^2}}, \quad x \neq 0\] \[\frac{d}{dx}\coth^{-1} x = \frac{1}{1-x^2}, \quad |x| > 1\]

Striking observation: \(\tanh^{-1}\) and \(\coth^{-1}\) have the same formal derivative \(\frac{1}{1-x^2}\), but on disjoint domains (\(|x|<1\) vs \(|x|>1\)). Together they provide the complete antiderivative of \(\frac{1}{1-x^2}\) on \(\mathbb{R}\setminus{\pm 1}\).

docs.title: Full Proof: Three Methods for \((\sinh^{-1} x)'\)
docs.text:
Method 1: Implicit Differentiation (cleanest)

Let \(y = \sinh^{-1} x\), so \(\sinh y = x\). Differentiate both sides with respect to \(x\):

\[\cosh y \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} = 1 \implies \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{\cosh y}\]

Now use the fundamental identity \(\cosh^2 y - \sinh^2 y = 1\):

\[\cosh y = \sqrt{1 + \sinh^2 y} = \sqrt{1 + x^2}\]

(positive square root since \(\cosh y > 0\) always). Therefore:

\[\frac{d}{dx}\sinh^{-1} x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^2}} \qquad \square\]

Method 2: Differentiate the Logarithm Directly (confirms the formula)

\[\frac{d}{dx}\ln!\left(x + \sqrt{x^2+1}\right) = \frac{1}{x + \sqrt{x^2+1}} \cdot \frac{d}{dx}!\left(x + \sqrt{x^2+1}\right)\]

The inner derivative:

\[\frac{d}{dx}!\left(x + \sqrt{x^2+1}\right) = 1 + \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}} = \frac{\sqrt{x^2+1} + x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}\]

So:

\[\frac{d}{dx}\sinh^{-1} x = \frac{1}{x+\sqrt{x^2+1}} \cdot \frac{x + \sqrt{x^2+1}}{\sqrt{x^2+1}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+1}} \qquad \square\]

Method 3: Inverse Function Theorem (most general)

If \(f\) is differentiable and bijective, \((f^{-1})'(x) = \dfrac{1}{f'(f^{-1}(x))}\).

Here \(f = \sinh\), \(f' = \cosh\), \(f^{-1} = \sinh^{-1}\):

\[(\sinh^{-1})'(x) = \frac{1}{\cosh(\sinh^{-1} x)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^2}} \qquad \square\]

docs.title: Proof for \((\cosh^{-1} x)'\)
docs.text:
Let \(y = \cosh^{-1} x \geq 0\), so \(\cosh y = x\). Implicit differentiation:

\[\sinh y \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} = 1 \implies \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{\sinh y}\]

From the identity: \(\sinh y = \sqrt{\cosh^2 y - 1} = \sqrt{x^2-1}\) (positive root since \(y \geq 0 \Rightarrow \sinh y \geq 0\)):

\[\frac{d}{dx}\cosh^{-1} x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2-1}}, \quad x > 1 \qquad \square\]

docs.title: Proof for \((\tanh^{-1} x)'\)
docs.text:
Let \(y = \tanh^{-1} x\), so \(\tanh y = x\). Implicit differentiation:

\[\operatorname{sech}^2 y \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} = 1 \implies \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{\operatorname{sech}^2 y} = \cosh^2 y\]

Use \(1 - \tanh^2 y = \operatorname{sech}^2 y\):

\[\operatorname{sech}^2 y = 1 - x^2 \implies \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{1-x^2} \qquad \square\]

docs.title: § 5 — Integration: The Payoff
docs.text: The derivatives immediately give antiderivatives. These are the standard integral forms that appear throughout calculus.

docs.title: Standard Forms
docs.text:
\[\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}} = \sinh^{-1}!\left(\frac{x}{a}\right) + C = \ln!\left(x + \sqrt{x^2+a^2}\right) + C, \quad a > 0\] \[\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2-a^2}} = \cosh^{-1}!\left(\frac{x}{a}\right) + C = \ln!\left(x + \sqrt{x^2-a^2}\right) + C, \quad x > a > 0\] \[\int \frac{dx}{a^2-x^2} = \frac{1}{a}\tanh^{-1}!\left(\frac{x}{a}\right) + C, \quad |x| < a\] \[\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}} = \sin^{-1}!\left(\frac{x}{a}\right) + C \quad \text{(circular, for contrast)}\]

The pattern: \(\sqrt{x^2 + a^2}\) → use \(\sinh^{-1}\). \(\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}\) → use \(\cosh^{-1}\). \(a^2 - x^2\) in denominator → use \(\tanh^{-1}\).

Proof of the first form. Let \(u = x/a\):

\[\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}} = \int \frac{a, du}{\sqrt{a^2 u^2 + a^2}} = \int \frac{a, du}{a\sqrt{u^2+1}} = \int \frac{du}{\sqrt{u^2+1}} = \sinh^{-1}(u) + C \qquad \square\]

docs.title: Worked Examples
docs.text:
Example 5.1. Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^2 \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+4}}\).

\[= \left[\sinh^{-1}!\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\right]_0^2 = \sinh^{-1}(1) - \sinh^{-1}(0) = \ln(1+\sqrt{2}) - 0 = \ln(1+\sqrt{2})\]

Numerically: \(\approx 0.8814\).

Example 5.2. Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{4-x^2}\).

Here \(a = 2\), \(|x| < 2\):

\[= \frac{1}{2}\tanh^{-1}!\left(\frac{x}{2}\right) + C = \frac{1}{4}\ln!\left(\frac{2+x}{2-x}\right) + C\]

Double-check by partial fractions:

\[\frac{1}{4-x^2} = \frac{1}{(2-x)(2+x)} = \frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{1}{2-x} + \frac{1}{2+x}\right)\]

Integrating: \(\frac{1}{4}\left(-\ln|2-x| + \ln|2+x|\right) + C = \frac{1}{4}\ln\frac{2+x}{2-x} + C\). ✓

Example 5.3. Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int \frac{x, dx}{\sqrt{x^4+1}}\).

Let \(u = x^2\), \(du = 2x, dx\):

\[= \frac{1}{2}\int \frac{du}{\sqrt{u^2+1}} = \frac{1}{2}\sinh^{-1}(x^2) + C = \frac{1}{2}\ln!\left(x^2 + \sqrt{x^4+1}\right) + C\]

Example 5.4. (Completing the square) Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2 - 4x + 5}}\).

Complete the square: \(x^2 - 4x + 5 = (x-2)^2 + 1\). Let \(u = x - 2\):

\[= \int \frac{du}{\sqrt{u^2+1}} = \sinh^{-1}(u) + C = \sinh^{-1}(x-2) + C = \ln!\left((x-2) + \sqrt{x^2-4x+5}\right) + C\]

docs.title: Reflection Identities
docs.text: \[\sinh^{-1}(-x) = -\sinh^{-1}(x) \quad \text{(odd)}\] \[\tanh^{-1}(-x) = -\tanh^{-1}(x) \quad \text{(odd)}\] \[\cosh^{-1}(x) \geq 0 \quad \text{(not odd — domain is } [1,\infty)\text{)}\]

docs.title: Reciprocal Relations
docs.text:
\[\operatorname{csch}^{-1} x = \sinh^{-1}!\left(\frac{1}{x}\right), \quad x \neq 0\] \[\operatorname{sech}^{-1} x = \cosh^{-1}!\left(\frac{1}{x}\right), \quad 0 < x \leq 1\] \[\coth^{-1} x = \tanh^{-1}!\left(\frac{1}{x}\right), \quad |x| > 1\]

Proof of the first: Let \(y = \operatorname{csch}^{-1} x\), so \(\operatorname{csch} y = x\), i.e., \(\sinh y = 1/x\). This means \(y = \sinh^{-1}(1/x)\). \(\square\)

docs.title: Linking \(\tanh^{-1}\) to \(\coth^{-1}\)
docs.text:
Note \(\tanh^{-1}\) and \(\coth^{-1}\) share the derivative \(\frac{1}{1-x^2}\) on complementary domains. Together:

\[\int \frac{dx}{1-x^2} = \begin{cases} \tanh^{-1} x + C & |x| < 1 \ \coth^{-1} x + C & |x| > 1 \end{cases} = \frac{1}{2}\ln\left|\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right| + C\]

The last form is valid on all of \(\mathbb{R} \setminus {\pm 1}\) and unifies both cases.

docs.title: § 7 — Taylor Series of Inverse Hyperbolic Functions
docs.text:
For \(|x| < 1\):

\[\sinh^{-1} x = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n (2n)!}{4^n (n!)^2 (2n+1)} x^{2n+1} = x - \frac{x^3}{6} + \frac{3x^5}{40} - \frac{15x^7}{336} + \cdots\]

This follows from the binomial series applied to \((1+x^2)^{-1/2}\), then integrated term by term:

\[\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^2}} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \binom{-1/2}{n} x^{2n} = 1 - \frac{x^2}{2} + \frac{3x^4}{8} - \cdots\]

Integrating:

\[\sinh^{-1} x = \int_0^x \frac{dt}{\sqrt{1+t^2}} = x - \frac{x^3}{6} + \frac{3x^5}{40} - \cdots\]

For \(|x| < 1\):

\[\tanh^{-1} x = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{x^{2n+1}}{2n+1} = x + \frac{x^3}{3} + \frac{x^5}{5} + \cdots\]

Proof (from the logarithm form):

\[\tanh^{-1} x = \frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{1+x}{1-x} = \frac{1}{2}\left[\ln(1+x) - \ln(1-x)\right]\]

Using \(\ln(1+u) = u - u^2/2 + u^3/3 - \cdots\):

\[= \frac{1}{2}\left[\left(x - \frac{x^2}{2} + \frac{x^3}{3} - \cdots\right) - \left(-x - \frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{x^3}{3} - \cdots\right)\right] = x + \frac{x^3}{3} + \frac{x^5}{5} + \cdots \qquad \square\]

Personal note: This is the Leibniz-Gregory series for \(\pi/4\): setting \(x = 1\) (formally, as the series converges at the boundary) gives \(\tanh^{-1}(1)\)... but \(\tanh^{-1}(1) = +\infty\). The analogous identity for \(\arctan\) gives \(\pi/4 = 1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - \cdots\) — note the alternating signs, reflecting the circular vs. hyperbolic difference.

docs.title: § 8 — Comparison: Circular vs. Hyperbolic Inverses
docs.text:
Property \(\arcsin x\) \(\sinh^{-1} x\) Domain \([-1, 1]\) \(\mathbb{R}\) Range \([-\pi/2, \pi/2]\) \(\mathbb{R}\) Derivative \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\) \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\) Closed form Not a logarithm \(\ln(x+\sqrt{x^2+1})\) Property \(\arctan x\) \(\tanh^{-1} x\) Domain \(\mathbb{R}\) \((-1, 1)\) Range \((-\pi/2, \pi/2)\) \(\mathbb{R}\) Derivative \(\frac{1}{1+x^2}\) \(\frac{1}{1-x^2}\) Horizontal asymptotes \(\pm \pi/2\) None (\(\to \pm\infty\))

The sign flip \(1 - x^2\) vs. \(1 + x^2\) in the denominators mirrors the \(-1\) vs. \(+1\) in \(\cos^2 + \sin^2 = 1\) vs. \(\cosh^2 - \sinh^2 = 1\).

docs.title: § 9 — Connection to AI, Machine Learning, Deep Learning
9.1 — Inverse \(\tanh\) in Policy Optimization (Reinforcement Learning)
docs.text:
In reinforcement learning, particularly Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) and similar algorithms, the agent's policy must output actions in a bounded range, say \([-1, 1]\). A common trick:

  1. Sample \(z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\) (Gaussian, unbounded)
  2. Apply \(a = \tanh(z)\) to squash to \((-1, 1)\)

But training requires computing the log-probability of \(a\) under the original distribution. By the change-of-variables formula:

\[\log p(a) = \log p(z) - \sum_i \log!\left|\frac{d(\tanh z_i)}{dz_i}\right| = \log p(z) - \sum_i \log(1 - \tanh^2 z_i)\]

During inference, given observed action \(a\), we need \(z = \tanh^{-1}(a)\) — the inverse! This is numerically computed as:

\[z = \tanh^{-1}(a) = \frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{1+a}{1-a}\]

Implementation note: near \(|a| = 1\), this is numerically unstable. In practice:

# PyTorch / JAX safe implementation
def atanh_safe(x, eps=1e-6):
    x_clipped = x.clamp(-1 + eps, 1 - eps)
    return 0.5 * (torch.log1p(x_clipped) - torch.log1p(-x_clipped))

docs.title: 9.2 — \(\sinh^{-1}\) as a Variance-Stabilizing Transform
docs.text:
In financial machine learning and regression with heavy-tailed targets, the transform:

\[\tilde{y} = \sinh^{-1}(y) = \ln!\left(y + \sqrt{y^2+1}\right)\]

is preferred over \(\log(y)\) because:

  • Defined for all reals (returns can be negative)
  • Behaves like \(\ln(2y)\) for large \(y\) — compresses scale
  • Behaves like \(y\) near zero — preserves small values

This is used in Kaggle competitions involving financial targets, where the evaluation metric is often computed on transformed values.

docs.title: 9.3 — \(\tanh^{-1}\) and Fisher's Z-Transformation
docs.text:
In statistics (which underpins all of ML evaluation), Fisher's Z-transformation of a correlation coefficient \(r \in (-1, 1)\) is:

\[Z = \tanh^{-1}(r) = \frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{1+r}{1-r}\]

This stabilizes the variance of the sample correlation, making it approximately normally distributed. Used in:

  • Hypothesis testing for correlations
  • Confidence intervals for model performance metrics
  • Comparing feature correlations across datasets in exploratory data analysis

docs.title: 9.4 — Gradient Flow Through \(\sinh^{-1}\) Activations
docs.text:
Recently (2020s), \(\sinh^{-1}\) (arcsinh) has been proposed as an activation function in neural networks. Its derivative is:

\[\frac{d}{dx}\sinh^{-1}(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}\]

Key properties as an activation:

  • Not bounded (unlike \(\tanh\)) — avoids saturation and vanishing gradients
  • Sublinear growth — gradient \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+1}} \to 0\) slowly as \(|x| \to \infty\) — does not explode like ReLU for large inputs
  • Smooth and odd — zero-centered, differentiable everywhere (unlike ReLU)

Compared to popular activations:

| Activation | Range | Gradient at large \(|x|\) | Smooth? | |---|---|---|---| | ReLU | \([0, \infty)\) | 0 or 1 | No (kink at 0) | | \(\tanh\) | \((-1,1)\) | \(\to 0\) (saturates) | Yes | | GELU | \(\approx \mathbb{R}\) | \(\to 1\) | Yes | | \(\sinh^{-1}\) (arcsinh) | \(\mathbb{R}\) | \(\to 0\) slowly | Yes |

docs.title: 9.5 — Hyperbolic Geometry in Representation Learning
docs.text:
The Poincaré disk model of hyperbolic geometry uses the metric:

\[ds^2 = \frac{4(dx^2 + dy^2)}{(1-|x|^2)^2}\]

Distances in this space involve \(\cosh^{-1}\):

\[d(u, v) = \cosh^{-1}!\left(1 + 2\frac{|u-v|^2}{(1-|u|^2)(1-|v|^2)}\right)\]

Why does ML care? Hyperbolic space has exponentially growing volume — perfect for embedding trees and hierarchies. The number of nodes at depth \(d\) in a tree grows as \(b^d\); hyperbolic space can accommodate this exponential branching with low distortion.

Poincaré embeddings (Nickel & Kiela, NeurIPS 2017) use \(\cosh^{-1}\) in the loss function to embed WordNet noun hierarchy with far fewer dimensions than Euclidean embeddings require.

Euclidean space:  volume grows as r^n  (polynomial)
Hyperbolic space: volume grows as e^r  (exponential)
Trees:            nodes grow as b^d    (exponential)
→ Hyperbolic space is the natural home for hierarchical data

docs.title: § 10 — A Subtlety: Two Antiderivative Conventions
docs.text:
Consider \(\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{1-x^2}\).

Via partial fractions:

\[\frac{1}{1-x^2} = \frac{1}{(1-x)(1+x)} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{1+x} + \frac{1}{1-x}\right)\] \[\int \frac{dx}{1-x^2} = \frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{1+x}{1-x} + C = \frac{1}{2}\ln!\left|\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right| + C\]

Via inverse hyperbolic: On \(|x| < 1\): \(= \tanh^{-1}(x) + C\). On \(|x| > 1\): \(= \coth^{-1}(x) + C\).

Both are correct — they differ by a constant on each connected component of the domain. The absolute value version is the most general single formula.

Personal note: This subtlety trips up many students. The issue is that \(\ln\) requires a positive argument, but \(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\) is negative when \(|x| > 1\). The absolute value fixes this while keeping the formula unified. Always specify the domain when writing antiderivatives of \(\frac{1}{1-x^2}\).

docs.title: Logarithmic Forms
docs.text: \[\sinh^{-1} x = \ln(x+\sqrt{x^2+1}), \quad x\in\mathbb{R}$$ $$\cosh^{-1} x = \ln(x+\sqrt{x^2-1}), \quad x\geq 1$$ $$\tanh^{-1} x = \tfrac{1}{2}\ln\tfrac{1+x}{1-x}, \quad |x|<1\]

docs.title: Integral Forms
docs.text: \[\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}} = \sinh^{-1}!\tfrac{x}{a}+C, \quad \int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2-a^2}} = \cosh^{-1}!\tfrac{x}{a}+C, \quad \int\frac{dx}{a^2-x^2}=\tfrac{1}{a}\tanh^{-1}!\tfrac{x}{a}+C\]

docs.title: § 12 — Exercises
docs.text:
1. (Logarithm derivation) Derive \(\operatorname{sech}^{-1} x = \ln!\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{1-x^2}}{x}\right)\) from the definition, following the method of §2.

2. (Derivative) Differentiate \(f(x) = x\sinh^{-1}(x/3) - \sqrt{x^2+9}\) and simplify. (The answer should be surprisingly clean.)

3. (Integral) Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^{1/2} \frac{dx}{1-x^2}\). Express as a logarithm and verify with \(\tanh^{-1}\).

4. (Completing the square) Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+6x+5}}\) by completing the square and using an inverse hyperbolic antiderivative.

5. (Taylor series) Use the series \(\tanh^{-1} x = x + x^3/3 + x^5/5 + \cdots\) to compute \(\int_0^{0.5} \tanh^{-1}(x), dx\) approximately. How many terms do you need for 4-decimal accuracy?

6. (ML) Show that the log-probability correction term in the SAC reparametrization trick, \(\log(1 - \tanh^2(z))\), equals \(-2\log\cosh(z) + \text{const}\). (Hint: \(\operatorname{sech}^2(z) = 1 - \tanh^2(z)\).)

7. (Challenging) Prove the identity \(\sinh^{-1}(\tan\theta) = \ln|\sec\theta + \tan\theta|\) for \(|\theta| < \pi/2\). This connects inverse hyperbolic and circular functions through the Gudermannian function.

8. (Theory) Verify directly from the chain rule that \(\frac{d}{dx}\coth^{-1}(x) = \frac{d}{dx}\tanh^{-1}(1/x)\) equals \(\frac{1}{1-x^2}\) for \(|x|>1\).

End of note.

docs.title: Minimum and Maximum Values
docs.text:
"Nature is thrifty in all her actions." — Pierre Louis Maupertuis

Personal note: Every optimization algorithm in machine learning — gradient descent, Adam, RMSProp — is, at its core, a machine trying to do what we're about to describe rigorously. Understanding this chapter is understanding the soul of modern AI.

docs.title: §1. The Absolute Extrema — Definitions
docs.text:
Let \(f\) be a function defined on a domain \(D \subseteq \mathbb{R}\).

Definition 1.1 (Absolute Maximum). A value \(f(c)\) is the absolute maximum of \(f\) on \(D\) if $\(f(c) \geq f(x) \quad \text{for all } x \in D.\)$

Definition 1.2 (Absolute Minimum). A value \(f(c)\) is the absolute minimum of \(f\) on \(D\) if $\(f(c) \leq f(x) \quad \text{for all } x \in D.\)$

The absolute maximum and minimum are collectively called extreme values or absolute extrema.

Remark. Existence is not guaranteed in general. Consider:

  • \(f(x) = x\) on \((0,1)\): no maximum, no minimum — the interval is open.
  • \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x}\) on \((0, \infty)\): no minimum.
  • \(f(x) = \sin(x)\) on \(\mathbb{R}\): maximum value \(1\) achieved at infinitely many points, but the set of maxima is well-defined.

This motivates the fundamental existence theorem.

docs.title: §2. The Extreme Value Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem 2.1 (Extreme Value Theorem — EVT). If \(f\) is continuous on a closed, bounded interval \([a, b]\), then \(f\) attains both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on \([a, b]\).

That is, there exist \(c, d \in [a, b]\) such that $\(f(c) \leq f(x) \leq f(d) \quad \text{for all } x \in [a, b].\)$

Why both conditions are necessary:

Condition dropped Counterexample What fails Continuity \(f(x) = \begin{cases} x & x \in (0,1] \ 2 & x=0 \end{cases}\) on \([0,1]\) Min not attained Closed interval \(f(x) = x\) on \((0,1)\) Neither attained Bounded interval \(f(x) = x\) on \([0, \infty)\) No max

Proof sketch. The proof uses two deep facts from real analysis:

  1. A continuous image of a compact set is compact (Heine–Cantor).
  2. A compact subset of \(\mathbb{R}\) is closed and bounded, hence contains its supremum and infimum.

Since \([a,b]\) is compact and \(f\) is continuous, \(f([a,b])\) is compact, so \(\sup f([a,b])\) and \(\inf f([a,b])\) are attained. \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: §3. Local Extrema
docs.text:
Global search is hard. We begin locally.

Definition 3.1 (Local Maximum). \(f\) has a local maximum at \(c\) if there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that $\(f(c) \geq f(x) \quad \text{for all } x \in (c-\delta, c+\delta) \cap D.\)$

Definition 3.2 (Local Minimum). \(f\) has a local minimum at \(c\) if there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that $\(f(c) \leq f(x) \quad \text{for all } x \in (c-\delta, c+\delta) \cap D.\)$

Intuition. A local max is the highest point in its neighborhood — it doesn't need to beat everyone, just its neighbors. This is critical in optimization: most algorithms find local extrema, and global optimization is generally NP-hard.

docs.title: §4. Fermat's Theorem — The Critical Point Condition
docs.text:
Theorem 4.1 (Fermat's Theorem). If \(f\) has a local extremum at \(c\) and \(f'(c)\) exists, then $\(f'(c) = 0.\)$

Proof. Suppose \(f\) has a local maximum at \(c\). Then for all \(x\) sufficiently close to \(c\): $\(f(x) - f(c) \leq 0.\)$

Case 1: \(x > c\). Then \(\dfrac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c} \leq 0\), so taking \(x \to c^+\): $\(f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c^+} \frac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c} \leq 0.\)$

Case 2: \(x < c\). Then \(\dfrac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c} \geq 0\), so taking \(x \to c^-\): $\(f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c^-} \frac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c} \geq 0.\)$

Since \(f'(c)\) exists and satisfies both \(f'(c) \leq 0\) and \(f'(c) \geq 0\), we conclude \(f'(c) = 0\). The local minimum case is symmetric. \(\blacksquare\)

Warning (Converse is FALSE). \(f'(c) = 0\) does not imply \(c\) is an extremum.

Example: \(f(x) = x^3\). Then \(f'(0) = 0\), but \(x=0\) is an inflection point, not an extremum. The function changes sign of its derivative here — it's increasing on both sides of \(0\).

docs.title: §5. Critical Numbers
docs.text:
Definition 5.1. A number \(c\) in the domain of \(f\) is a critical number (or critical point) if either:

  1. \(f'(c) = 0\), or
  2. \(f'(c)\) does not exist.

Why include non-differentiable points? Fermat's theorem requires \(f'(c)\) to exist. But extrema can occur where the derivative fails to exist.

Example: \(f(x) = |x|\) on \([-1, 1]\). The minimum is at \(x = 0\), but \(f'(0)\) doesn't exist (corner point). So \(0\) is a critical number.

Example: \(f(x) = x^{1/3}\). Then \(f'(x) = \frac{1}{3}x^{-2/3}\), which doesn't exist at \(x = 0\). The point \(x=0\) is a critical number (it's an inflection point here, but could be an extremum in other examples).

Corollary 5.1. If \(f\) has a local extremum at \(c\), then \(c\) is a critical number of \(f\).

This is the contrapositive of Fermat's theorem combined with the observation about non-differentiable points.

docs.title: §6. The Closed Interval Method
docs.text:
The EVT guarantees extrema exist on \([a,b]\). The Closed Interval Method finds them:

Algorithm 6.1 (Closed Interval Method). To find the absolute extrema of a continuous \(f\) on \([a,b]\):

  1. Find all critical numbers of \(f\) in \((a, b)\).
  2. Evaluate \(f\) at each critical number.
  3. Evaluate \(f\) at the endpoints: \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\).
  4. The largest value is the absolute maximum; the smallest is the absolute minimum.

Why does this work? By EVT, the absolute extrema exist. By Corollary 5.1, any interior extremum must be a critical point. The endpoints are candidates by default (boundary of the domain). Exhausting all candidates and comparing gives the answer.

docs.title: Example 7.2 — With Non-differentiable Point
docs.text:
Find the absolute extrema of \(f(x) = |x^2 - 1|\) on \([-2, 2]\).

\(f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 - 1 & |x| \geq 1 \ 1 - x^2 & |x| < 1 \end{cases}\)

\(f'(x) = \begin{cases} 2x & |x| > 1 \ -2x & |x| < 1 \ \text{DNE} & x = \pm 1 \end{cases}\)

Critical numbers: \(x = 0\) (where \(f' = 0\)), \(x = \pm 1\) (where \(f'\) DNE).

\(x\) \(f(x)\) \(-2\) \(3\) \(-1\) \(0\) \(0\) \(1\) \(1\) \(0\) \(2\) \(3\)

Absolute maximum: \(f(\pm 2) = 3\). Absolute minimum: \(f(\pm 1) = 0\).

docs.title: 8.1 Anatomy of a Function on \([a, b]\)
docs.text:
f(x)
  │                                    * abs max (endpoint)
  │                *                  /
  │               / \                /
  │    loc max   /   \    loc min   /
  │     *       /     \    *       /
  │    / \     /       \  / \     /
  │   /   \   /         \/   \   /
  │  /     \ /                \_/
  │ /       *   saddle (f'=0,
  │/         inflection)
  ├──────────────────────────────────── x
  a    c₁    c₂    c₃    c₄    c₅    b
       ↑      ↑     ↑     ↑
    loc max  f'=0  loc  loc
             not   min  min
             extr

Legend:

  • * = critical point (either \(f' = 0\) or \(f'\) DNE)
  • The absolute extremum can occur at a critical point or at an endpoint
  • A critical point with \(f'=0\) is NOT necessarily an extremum (see \(c_2\) above — inflection)

docs.title: 8.2 Sign Chart for Derivative Analysis
docs.text:
For \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 1\):

f'(x) = 3x(x-2)

x:     -∞    0    +∞
       ──────┼──────┼──────
f'(x): + + + 0 - - - 0 + + +
              ↑           ↑
           loc max      loc min

Reading the chart:

  • \(f' > 0 \Rightarrow f\) is increasing
  • \(f' < 0 \Rightarrow f\) is decreasing
  • Sign change \(+ \to -\) at \(x=0\): local max
  • Sign change \(- \to +\) at \(x=2\): local min

docs.title: 8.3 Multi-variable Preview (Loss Surface)
docs.text:
In 2D, a loss function \(\mathcal{L}(\theta_1, \theta_2)\) looks like a surface. The contour plot below is conceptual:

    θ₂
    │      saddle
    │       ×
    │   ∗           ∗
    │  local       local
    │  min          min
    │
    │       ∗
    │    global
    │      min
    └─────────────────── θ₁

Gradient descent follows \(-\nabla \mathcal{L}\) — the steepest descent direction — which is exactly the generalization of \(f'(c) = 0\) to multiple dimensions.

docs.title: §9. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: This is not a digression. This entire chapter IS the theoretical foundation of machine learning.

docs.title: 9.1 Loss Minimization as the Core Problem
docs.text:
In supervised learning, we train a model with parameters \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}^n\) by minimizing a loss function: $\(\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \ell(f_\theta(x^{(i)}), y^{(i)})\)$

where \(\ell\) is a pointwise loss (e.g., squared error, cross-entropy). Finding optimal \(\theta^*\) is exactly an absolute minimum problem.

The critical point condition becomes: $\(\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta^*) = \mathbf{0} \quad \text{(gradient is the zero vector)}\)$

This is Fermat's theorem in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

docs.title: 9.2 Gradient Descent — Iterative Fermat
docs.text:
Since \(\mathcal{L}\) is typically non-convex and high-dimensional (GPT-4 has ~\(10^{12}\) parameters), we can't solve \( abla \mathcal{L} = 0\) analytically. Instead:

\[ heta_{t+1} = heta_t - \eta abla_ heta \mathcal{L}( heta_t)\]

where \(\eta > 0\) is the learning rate. This is a discrete approximation to following the steepest descent path toward a local minimum. The fixed points of this update (\( heta_{t+1} = heta_t\)) are exactly the critical points.

Variants:

  • SGD (Stochastic Gradient Descent): Uses a minibatch to approximate \( abla \mathcal{L}\)
  • Adam: Adapts the learning rate per parameter using first and second moment estimates
  • RMSProp: Divides by running average of squared gradients

All seek the same thing: a point where \( abla \mathcal{L} \approx \mathbf{0}\).

docs.title: 9.3 The Local vs Global Minimum Problem
docs.text:
A deep neural network's loss landscape is non-convex, so gradient descent finds local minima, not necessarily global ones. This is the direct multi-dimensional generalization of our observation that \(f'(c) = 0\) does not guarantee a global minimum.

Surprising empirical finding (2014–present): In practice, local minima of large neural networks tend to have similar loss values to the global minimum. The more dangerous critical points are saddle points — where \(\nabla \mathcal{L} = 0\) but the Hessian \(H\) is indefinite (some eigenvalues positive, some negative). These are the analog of \(f(x) = x^3\) at \(x=0\).

Theorem (informal, Dauphin et al., 2014). In high dimensions, most critical points with high loss are saddle points, not local minima. True local minima with high loss are exponentially rare.

docs.title: 9.4 Second-Order Methods and the Hessian
docs.text:
The second derivative test in 1D:

  • \(f''(c) > 0\) at a critical point \(\Rightarrow\) local min
  • \(f''(c) < 0 \Rightarrow\) local max
  • \(f''(c) = 0 \Rightarrow\) inconclusive

In \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the Hessian matrix \(H = \nabla^2 \mathcal{L}\) plays this role:

  • \(H\) positive definite \(\Rightarrow\) local min
  • \(H\) negative definite \(\Rightarrow\) local max
  • \(H\) indefinite \(\Rightarrow\) saddle point

Newton's method for optimization uses the full Hessian: $\(\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - H^{-1} \nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta_t)\)$

This converges quadratically near a minimum but costs \(O(n^3)\) to invert \(H\) — infeasible for large networks. Quasi-Newton methods (L-BFGS) approximate \(H^{-1}\) cheaply.

docs.title: 9.5 Convex Optimization — When Local = Global
docs.text:
If \(\mathcal{L}\) is convex (e.g., linear regression with MSE loss, logistic regression), then: $\(\text{every local minimum is a global minimum}\)$

This is the analog of: a function with \(f'' > 0\) everywhere on an interval has at most one local (= global) minimum. Convexity is defined by: $\(\mathcal{L}(\lambda \theta_1 + (1-\lambda)\theta_2) \leq \lambda \mathcal{L}(\theta_1) + (1-\lambda)\mathcal{L}(\theta_2), \quad \lambda \in [0,1]\)$

Support Vector Machines and linear models exploit convexity to guarantee finding the global minimum. This is why they have convergence guarantees that deep networks lack.

docs.title: 9.6 Regularization as a Constraint
docs.text:
L2 regularization (weight decay) solves: $\(\min_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta) + \frac{\lambda}{2}|\theta|^2\)$

This is equivalent to finding the minimum of the unconstrained loss subject to \(|\theta| \leq R\) for some \(R\) — a constrained optimization problem. The method of Lagrange multipliers (multivariable calculus) formalizes this connection, and the critical point condition becomes the KKT conditions in convex optimization.

docs.title: 9.7 Summary Table
docs.text: Calculus Concept ML/DL Analogue Local minimum of \(f\) Converged weights in gradient descent \(f'(c) = 0\) \(\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L} = 0\) (training complete) Saddle point The main obstruction in deep net training Second derivative test Hessian analysis, curvature of loss landscape Closed interval method Grid search / hyperparameter search Absolute minimum on \([a,b]\) Global optimum (convex problems only) Convex function Convex loss (linear/logistic regression) Gradient descent Iterative approximation to critical points

docs.title: §10. The Second Derivative Test (Preview)
docs.text:
Full treatment in the next section, but the setup:

If \(f'(c) = 0\), how do we classify \(c\)?

Theorem 10.1 (Second Derivative Test). Suppose \(f''\) is continuous near \(c\) and \(f'(c) = 0\):

  • If \(f''(c) > 0\): \(c\) is a local minimum (\(f\) is concave up)
  • If \(f''(c) < 0\): \(c\) is a local maximum (\(f\) is concave down)
  • If \(f''(c) = 0\): inconclusive (need higher derivatives or sign analysis)

Intuition. Near a local min, the graph looks like a upward parabola — \(f'' > 0\) means concave up, i.e., the function curves away from the tangent line upward. This is exactly why gradient descent converges: near a true minimum, the loss surface curves upward in all directions.

docs.title: §11. Key Theorems — Reference Card
docs.text: Theorem Statement Conditions EVT Continuous \(f\) on \([a,b]\) attains abs. max and min \(f\) continuous, \([a,b]\) closed & bounded Fermat Local extremum at \(c\), \(f'(c)\) exists \(\Rightarrow\) \(f'(c) = 0\) \(f\) differentiable at \(c\) Closed Interval Method Check critical pts + endpoints for absolute extrema \(f\) continuous on \([a,b]\) 2<sup>nd</sup> Deriv. Test \(f'(c)=0\), \(f''(c)\neq 0\) classifies \(c\) \(f''\) continuous near \(c\)

docs.title: §12. Common Mistakes and Traps
docs.text:
Trap 1. Assuming \(f'(c) = 0\) implies \(c\) is an extremum. Counterexample: \(f(x) = x^3\) at \(x=0\). Always check sign change of \(f'\).

Trap 2. Forgetting to check endpoints on closed intervals. The absolute max/min can occur at \(a\) or \(b\).

Trap 3. Applying EVT to open intervals or discontinuous functions. The theorem's conclusion is false without both hypotheses.

Trap 4. In ML: confusing "gradient is zero" with "global minimum found." In non-convex problems, \(\nabla \mathcal{L} = 0\) only guarantees a critical point.

Trap 5. Using the second derivative test when \(f''(c) = 0\). The test is inconclusive. Use first derivative sign analysis instead.

docs.text:
1. Stewart, J. — Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. Chapter 4.1: Maximum and Minimum Values.
  2. MIT 18.02 — Multivariable Calculus (Denis Auroux). Lectures on optimization, critical points, second derivative test in several variables.
  3. Dauphin, Y. et al. — Identifying and attacking the saddle point problem in high-dimensional non-convex optimization. NeurIPS 2014.
  4. Boyd, S. & Vandenberghe, L. — Convex Optimization. Cambridge University Press. (For the connection between calculus extrema and modern ML optimization theory.)

— End of Note —
