docs.title: Fermat's Theorem
docs.text:
"To find the maxima and minima of a quantity, one takes the ordinary derivative and sets it equal to zero." — Pierre de Fermat, c. 1638 (paraphrase)

Personal note: Fermat wrote this before calculus existed — before Newton, before Leibniz. He was computing what we now call derivatives using an ad-hoc "method of adequality." The theorem bearing his name is the rigorous formalization of his geometric intuition: at a peak or valley, the tangent line must be horizontal.

docs.title: §1. Motivation — What Does Extremum Mean Geometrically?
docs.text:
Stand on a smooth hill. At the very top, the ground beneath your feet is flat — the slope is zero in every direction. If you're in a valley, same thing. The tangent plane is horizontal.

In one dimension: if \(f\) has a local max at \(c\), then just to the left of \(c\) the function is increasing (\(f' > 0\)), and just to the right it is decreasing (\(f' < 0\)). At the transition point itself, \(f'(c) = 0\).

        f(c) ← local max
       /     \
      /        \       f' changes + → −
─────              ─────
    f' > 0   f'=0   f' < 0

Fermat's Theorem makes this intuition a theorem — rigorous, with clear hypotheses.

docs.title: §2. Statement of the Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem (Fermat's Theorem). Let \(f\) be defined on an open interval containing \(c\). Suppose:

  1. \(f\) has a local extremum at \(c\) (either a local max or local min), and
  2. \(f\) is differentiable at \(c\).

Then \(f'(c) = 0\).

Logically: $\(\bigl(f \text{ has local extremum at } c\bigr) ;\wedge; \bigl(f'(c) \text{ exists}\bigr) ;\implies; f'(c) = 0\)$

docs.title: §3. Complete Proof
docs.text:
We prove the local maximum case. The local minimum case is symmetric (or apply the result to \(-f\)).

Setup. Suppose \(f\) has a local maximum at \(c\). By definition, there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that: $\(f(x) \leq f(c) \quad \text{for all } x \in (c - \delta,; c + \delta). \tag{\)*\(}\)$

We are given that \(f'(c)\) exists, so the limit $\(f'(c) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(c+h) - f(c)}{h}\)$ exists (as a finite real number). Since the two-sided limit exists, the one-sided limits both exist and equal \(f'(c)\).

Case 1: Right-hand limit (\(h \to 0^+\), i.e., \(h > 0\) small).

For \(0 < h < \delta\), we have \(c + h \in (c - \delta, c + \delta)\), so by \((*)\): $\(f(c + h) - f(c) \leq 0.\)$

Since \(h > 0\): $\(\frac{f(c+h) - f(c)}{h} \leq 0.\)$

Taking the limit as \(h \to 0^+\) (the inequality is preserved under limits): $\(f'(c) = \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{f(c+h)-f(c)}{h} \leq 0. \tag{1}\)$

Case 2: Left-hand limit (\(h \to 0^-\), i.e., \(h < 0\) small).

For \(-\delta < h < 0\), we have \(c + h \in (c - \delta, c + \delta)\), so by \((*)\): $\(f(c+h) - f(c) \leq 0.\)$

But now \(h < 0\), so dividing reverses the inequality: $\(\frac{f(c+h) - f(c)}{h} \geq 0.\)$

Taking the limit as \(h \to 0^-\): $\(f'(c) = \lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{f(c+h)-f(c)}{h} \geq 0. \tag{2}\)$

Conclusion. From (1) and (2): $\(f'(c) \leq 0 \quad \text{and} \quad f'(c) \geq 0 \implies \boxed{f'(c) = 0.}\)$

For the local minimum case: the inequality \((*)\) reverses to \(f(x) \geq f(c)\), which flips the signs in Cases 1 and 2, and we again conclude \(f'(c) = 0\). \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: §4. The Converse is FALSE — This is Critical
docs.text:
\(f'(c) = 0\) does NOT imply \(c\) is an extremum.

This is one of the most common errors. Fermat's theorem is a one-way implication only.

docs.title: Counterexample: \(f(x) = x^3\) at \(c = 0\)
docs.text:
\[f'(x) = 3x^2 \implies f'(0) = 0.\]

Yet \(f\) is strictly increasing on all of \(\mathbb{R}\): for \(x > 0\), \(f(x) > 0 = f(0)\), and for \(x < 0\), \(f(x) < 0 = f(0)\). So \(x = 0\) is neither a local max nor a local min — it is an inflection point.

  f(x) = x³

       │      /
       │     /
       │    /
  ─────┼───────── x
       │  /
       │ /
       │/
         ↑
    f'(0) = 0, but NOT an extremum
    (function strictly increasing through 0)

docs.title: Summary of Logical Structure
docs.text:
Statement True? Local extremum at \(c\) + differentiable \(\Rightarrow\) \(f'(c)=0\) ✓ Fermat's Theorem \(f'(c) = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) local extremum at \(c\) ✗ FALSE (\(x^3\) counterexample) \(f'(c) = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(c\) is a critical number ✓ (by definition) Local extremum at \(c\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(c\) is a critical number ✓ (Fermat + non-diff. case)

The correct chain is: $\(\text{local extremum} \implies \text{critical number} \centernot\impliedby \text{critical number}\)$

docs.title: §5. Why the Hypothesis "Differentiable at \(c\)" is Essential
docs.text: Fermat's theorem requires \(f'(c)\) to exist. Drop this and the conclusion fails.

docs.title: Example: \(f(x) = |x|\) at \(c = 0\)
docs.text:
\(f\) has an absolute (and local) minimum at \(c = 0\). But: $\(f'(0) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{|h| - 0}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{|h|}{h}\)$

The right limit is \(+1\), the left limit is \(-1\) — they disagree. So \(f'(0)\) does not exist.

The minimum occurs at a corner, not a smooth point. There is no horizontal tangent — there is no tangent line at all.

  f(x) = |x|

   \   /
    \ /
     *  ← global min, f'(0) DNE
     |
─────┼───── x

This is why the definition of critical number includes both \(f'(c) = 0\) and \(f'(c)\) DNE — to capture all possible extrema locations.

docs.title: The Full Picture: Where Can Extrema Occur?
docs.text:
\[\text{local extremum at } c \implies c \text{ is a critical number}\] \[c \text{ is a critical number} \iff f'(c) = 0 ;\text{ or }; f'(c) \text{ does not exist}\]

Fermat's theorem handles the differentiable case. The non-differentiable case is separate (but the conclusion — that \(c\) is a critical number — holds trivially).

docs.title: §6. Why the Hypothesis "Open Interval" is Essential
docs.text:
The theorem requires \(f\) to be defined on an open interval containing \(c\) (not just at \(c\), and not on a closed interval where \(c\) is an endpoint).

Why? The proof uses the limit from both sides of \(c\). If \(c = a\) is the left endpoint of \([a,b]\), only the right-hand limit is available:

\[f'(a^+) \leq 0\]

But we can't conclude \(f'(a) \geq 0\) from the left (there is no left side). So we can't squeeze to \(f'(a) = 0\).

Example. \(f(x) = x\) on \([0, 1]\). The absolute minimum is at \(x = 0\) and the absolute maximum at \(x = 1\). But \(f'(x) = 1 \neq 0\) everywhere — including at the endpoints. Fermat's theorem simply doesn't apply here, because \(0\) and \(1\) are not interior to the domain.

Consequence. This is precisely why the Closed Interval Method must check endpoints separately — Fermat doesn't cover them.

docs.title: §7. Visualization: The Full Taxonomy
docs.text:
All points c in domain of f
│
├── f'(c) exists
│   ├── f'(c) = 0  ──────────────────→ CRITICAL NUMBER
│   │   ├── sign of f' changes + → −  → local MAX    ← Fermat applies
│   │   ├── sign of f' changes − → +  → local MIN    ← Fermat applies
│   │   └── sign of f' doesn't change → INFLECTION (e.g. x³ at 0)
│   │
│   └── f'(c) ≠ 0  → NOT a critical number
│                     (cannot be an interior extremum by Fermat)
│
├── f'(c) does not exist
│   ├── corner (e.g. |x| at 0)  ──→ CRITICAL NUMBER (may be extremum)
│   ├── cusp (e.g. x^{2/3} at 0) → CRITICAL NUMBER (may be extremum)
│   └── vertical tangent         → CRITICAL NUMBER (may be extremum)
│
└── c is an ENDPOINT of [a,b]
    └── Fermat does NOT apply → check separately

docs.title: Example 8.1 — Polynomial, All Cases
docs.text:
\[f(x) = x^4 - 4x^3\] \[f'(x) = 4x^3 - 12x^2 = 4x^2(x - 3)\]

Critical numbers: \(f'(x) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0\) or \(x = 3\).

Classify \(x = 0\):

Sign of \(f'(x) = 4x^2(x-3)\) near \(x=0\):

  • For \(x\) slightly \(< 0\): \(4x^2 > 0\), \((x-3) < 0\) → \(f'(x) < 0\)
  • For \(x\) slightly \(> 0\): \(4x^2 > 0\), \((x-3) < 0\) → \(f'(x) < 0\)

Sign does not change → \(x = 0\) is not an extremum (inflection point). \(f'(0) = 0\), Fermat's conclusion holds, but the converse is false.

Classify \(x = 3\):

  • For \(x < 3\): \(4x^2 > 0\), \((x-3) < 0\) → \(f'(x) < 0\)
  • For \(x > 3\): \(4x^2 > 0\), \((x-3) > 0\) → \(f'(x) > 0\)

Sign changes \(- \to +\) → \(x = 3\) is a local minimum.

f'(x) sign chart:
      − − − 0 − − − 0 + + +
      ──────┼───────┼──────
            0       3
         inflec.  loc min

docs.title: Example 8.2 — Non-differentiable Extremum
docs.text:
\[f(x) = \begin{cases} -x + 1 & x < 0 \ x^2 + 1 & x \geq 0 \end{cases}\]

At \(c = 0\): $\(\lim_{h\to 0^-} \frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0^-} \frac{(-h+1)-1}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0^-} \frac{-h}{h} = -1\)$ $\(\lim_{h\to 0^+} \frac{f(h)-f(0)}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0^+} \frac{h^2+1-1}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0^+} h = 0\)$

One-sided limits disagree: \(f'(0)\) DNE. Fermat's theorem does not apply. Yet \(f(0) = 1\) is a local minimum (approaching from left, \(f \to 1^+\); from right, \(f \to 1^+\) through \(x^2+1 \geq 1\)).

docs.title: Example 8.3 — Verifying Fermat Directly
docs.text:
\[f(x) = \sin x, \quad c = \frac{\pi}{2}\]

\(f'(x) = \cos x\), so \(f'(\pi/2) = \cos(\pi/2) = 0\). ✓

\(f(\pi/2) = 1\) is a local (and global) maximum on any interval containing \(\pi/2\). Fermat's theorem confirms \(f'(\pi/2) = 0\), consistent.

docs.title: §9. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, Deep Learning
docs.text: Fermat's Theorem is the theoretical certificate that gradient descent is doing the right thing — and also explains why it can get stuck.

docs.title: 9.1 The Training Objective
docs.text:
In machine learning, we minimize a loss: $\(\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m \ell(f_\theta(x^{(i)}), y^{(i)}), \quad \theta \in \mathbb{R}^n\)$

At any interior local minimizer \(\theta^_\) where \(\mathcal{L}\) is differentiable, Fermat's theorem (in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)) gives: $\(\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta^_) = \mathbf{0}\)$

This is the necessary condition gradient descent tries to satisfy. Every weight update moves toward making this gradient zero.

docs.title: 9.2 The Converse Failure = The Saddle Point Problem
docs.text:
The converse of Fermat's theorem fails in 1D with \(x^3\). In high-dimensional ML it fails catastrophically at saddle points.

A saddle point \(\theta^_\) satisfies \(\nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta^_) = \mathbf{0}\) but is neither a max nor a min — it's a max in some directions and a min in others. In \(\mathbb{R}^n\) for large \(n\), saddle points are exponentially more common than local minima.

  Saddle point in 2D:

    θ₂
    │    ╲   ╱   ← increasing in θ₂ direction (local max)
    │     ╲ ╱
    │      ×  ← ∇L = 0 here, but saddle
    │     ╱ ╲
    │    ╱   ╲   ← decreasing in θ₁ direction (local min)
    └──────────── θ₁

Consequence for training: Gradient descent near a saddle point has gradient \(\approx \mathbf{0}\), so updates become tiny — training stalls. This is a major practical problem in deep learning.

Solutions used in practice:

  • Momentum (SGD with momentum): carries velocity through saddle regions
  • Adam: uses second moment estimates to escape flat regions
  • Noise in SGD (from random minibatches): perturbs away from saddle points

All of these are engineering responses to the failure of the converse of Fermat's theorem.

docs.title: 9.3 ReLU and Non-differentiable Points in Neural Networks
docs.text:
The ReLU activation \(\sigma(x) = \max(0, x)\) is not differentiable at \(x = 0\): $\(\sigma'(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & x > 0 \ 0 & x < 0 \ \text{undefined} & x = 0 \end{cases}\)$

This is the neural network version of \(|x|\) — a corner. In practice, we use the subgradient (set \(\sigma'(0) = 0\) or \(0.5\) by convention). Fermat's theorem doesn't directly apply at these points, but the critical number concept extends to the non-smooth setting via subdifferential calculus.

The entire field of non-smooth optimization — used when training networks with \(\ell_1\) regularization, ReLU activations, max-pooling — is a generalization of the observation that extrema can occur where \(f'\) fails to exist.

docs.title: 9.4 Fermat's Theorem in Convex Optimization
docs.text:
For convex loss functions (e.g., logistic regression, ridge regression), Fermat's theorem becomes if and only if:

\(\theta^_\) is a global minimum \(\iff\) \(\nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta^_) = \mathbf{0}\)

This is because for convex differentiable functions, every critical point is a global minimum (there are no saddle points, no local-but-not-global minima). This is the reason logistic regression and linear SVM have convergence guarantees — gradient descent provably reaches the global minimum.

For non-convex deep networks, only the \(\Rightarrow\) direction holds (Fermat), not \(\Leftarrow\).

docs.title: 9.5 Summary
docs.text: Fermat's Theorem Concept Machine Learning Meaning Local extremum \(\Rightarrow\) \(f'(c)=0\) Optimal weights have zero gradient \(f'(c)=0 \centernot\Rightarrow\) extremum Zero gradient ≠ trained model (saddle points!) Non-differentiable extremum ($ x Open interval hypothesis Interior optimum (not boundary of param space) Convex case: \(f'(c)=0 \iff\) global min Logistic regression, linear models Inflection point (\(x^3\) at 0) Saddle point in loss landscape

docs.title: §10. The Contrapositive — A Useful Form
docs.text:
Fermat's theorem by contrapositive:

\[f'(c) eq 0 \implies c ext{ is NOT a local extremum (for interior points).}\]

This is algorithmically useful. If you're doing gradient descent and \(| abla \mathcal{L}( heta)| > \varepsilon\), you can certify: \( heta\) is not (approximately) a local minimum. Training should continue.

Conversely, \(| abla \mathcal{L}( heta)| \approx 0\) is a necessary condition for convergence — but not sufficient (saddle point!). This is why modern optimizers also monitor the loss value and validation metrics, not just the gradient norm.

docs.title: §11. Connections Within Calculus
docs.text:
Fermat's Theorem
        │
        ├──→ Definition of Critical Numbers
        │           │
        │           ├──→ Closed Interval Method (absolute extrema)
        │           └──→ First Derivative Test (local extrema)
        │
        ├──→ Second Derivative Test
        │     (f'(c)=0 + f''(c)>0 → local min; classifies critical pts)
        │
        ├──→ Rolle's Theorem
        │     (f(a)=f(b) → ∃c: f'(c)=0; uses Fermat in proof)
        │
        └──→ Mean Value Theorem
              (follows from Rolle's; one of the deepest theorems in calculus)

Rolle's Theorem proof sketch using Fermat. If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), differentiable on \((a,b)\), and \(f(a) = f(b)\): by EVT, \(f\) attains its max and min on \([a,b]\). If both occur at endpoints, \(f\) is constant and \(f' \equiv 0\) (any \(c\) works). Otherwise, an extremum occurs at some interior \(c \in (a,b)\), and by Fermat, \(f'(c) = 0\). \(\blacksquare\)

Fermat's theorem is thus the seed from which Rolle's and the MVT grow.

docs.title: §12. Key Points — Professor's Summary
docs.text:
1. The theorem: differentiable local extremum \(\Rightarrow\) zero derivative. The tangent is horizontal.

  2. The proof idea: squeeze the derivative between \(\leq 0\) (from the right) and \(\geq 0\) (from the left). Both sides of the derivative limit must agree, forcing \(f'(c)=0\).

  3. The converse is false. \(f'(c)=0\) only gives a candidate. Test the sign of \(f'\) around \(c\), or use the second derivative test.

  4. Two hypotheses matter: differentiability at \(c\) (corners can be extrema without \(f'=0\)), and \(c\) being interior (endpoints escape Fermat).

  5. In ML: this theorem is why \(\nabla \mathcal{L} = \mathbf{0}\) is the training convergence condition — and why convergence to zero gradient is necessary but not sufficient for a good model.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Stewart, J. — Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed., §4.1. Theorem 4 (Fermat's Theorem), proof and discussion of critical numbers.
  2. MIT 18.02 — Multivariable Calculus (Auroux). Extension of Fermat's condition to \(\nabla f = \mathbf{0}\) for functions of several variables; saddle points in 2D.
  3. Dauphin, Y. et al. — Identifying and attacking the saddle point problem in high-dimensional non-convex optimization. NeurIPS 2014. (Empirical and theoretical analysis of why saddle points dominate in deep networks.)
  4. Rudin, W. — Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., Theorem 5.8. (Analysis-level proof of Fermat's theorem.)

— End of Note —

Logical chain: Fermat's Theorem → Critical Numbers → Closed Interval Method → Rolle's Theorem → Mean Value Theorem. Every theorem in the next sections rests on this one.

docs.title: The Mean Value Theorem
docs.text: "The Mean Value Theorem is the midwife of calculus — it delivers the deep connection between a function's local behavior and its global change." — Personal marginal note

docs.title: §1. Motivation — Why Should We Care?
docs.text:
Before the theorem, a question:

If you drive from Dhaka to Chattogram — a distance of roughly 250 km — in 3 hours, must there have been some instant when your speedometer read exactly \(\frac{250}{3} \approx 83.3 \text{ km/h}\)?

Intuitively: yes. You can't average 83.3 km/h without ever hitting that speed.

The Mean Value Theorem is precisely the theorem that makes this rigorous. It is, at its core, a theorem about the relationship between average rate of change (slope of a secant) and instantaneous rate of change (slope of a tangent).

docs.title: §2. Prerequisites
docs.text: Before the MVT, we need two foundational results. I'll state them and prove the first in full.

docs.title: 2.1 Rolle's Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem (Rolle, 1691). Let \(f\) be a function satisfying:

  1. \(f\) is continuous on \([a, b]\)
  2. \(f\) is differentiable on \((a, b)\)
  3. \(f(a) = f(b)\)

Then there exists at least one \(c \in (a,b)\) such that \(f'(c) = 0\).

Proof.

Since \(f\) is continuous on the closed bounded interval \([a,b]\), by the Extreme Value Theorem (Stewart §4.1), \(f\) attains both an absolute maximum \(M\) and an absolute minimum \(m\) on \([a,b]\).

Case 1: \(M = m\). Then \(f\) is constant on \([a,b]\), so \(f'(x) = 0\) for all \(x \in (a,b)\). Any \(c \in (a,b)\) works. \(\checkmark\)

Case 2: \(M \neq m\). Since \(f(a) = f(b)\), at least one of \(M\) or \(m\) must be attained at an interior point \(c \in (a,b)\) (not just at the endpoints).

At such a \(c\), \(f\) has a local extremum. Since \(f\) is differentiable at \(c\), by Fermat's Theorem (Stewart §4.1): $\(f'(c) = 0\)$

\(\square\)

Geometric picture:

    f(a) = f(b)
      *-----------*
     /  horizontal \
    /   tangent     \
   /        *        \
  /        (c, f(c))  \
 a                    b

Somewhere between \(a\) and \(b\), the curve must "turn around," and at that turning point the tangent is horizontal.

docs.title: 2.2 The Mean Value Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem (Lagrange's MVT). Let \(f\) be a function satisfying:

  1. \(f\) is continuous on \([a, b]\)
  2. \(f\) is differentiable on \((a, b)\)

Then there exists at least one \(c \in (a,b)\) such that: $\(\boxed{f'(c) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}}\)$

This is the theorem. Elegant. The right-hand side is the slope of the secant line through \((a, f(a))\) and \((b, f(b))\). The theorem asserts: the tangent line at \(c\) is parallel to this secant.

docs.title: §3. Proof of the MVT
docs.text:
The proof is a beautiful reduction to Rolle's Theorem. The key idea: subtract the secant line from \(f\) to create a new function that satisfies Rolle's hypotheses.

Construction. Define the secant line through \((a, f(a))\) and \((b, f(b))\): $\(L(x) = f(a) + \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}(x - a)\)$

Now define: $\(g(x) = f(x) - L(x) = f(x) - f(a) - \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}(x-a)\)$

Verify Rolle's conditions:

  1. \(g\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) — yes, \(f\) is continuous and \(L\) is a polynomial (hence continuous). ✓
  2. \(g\) is differentiable on \((a,b)\) — yes, \(f\) is differentiable and \(L'(x) = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}\) exists. ✓
  3. Check endpoints: $\(g(a) = f(a) - f(a) - 0 = 0\)$ $\(g(b) = f(b) - f(a) - \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}(b-a) = f(b) - f(a) - (f(b)-f(a)) = 0\)$

So \(g(a) = g(b) = 0\). ✓

Apply Rolle's Theorem: \(\exists, c \in (a,b)\) such that \(g'(c) = 0\).

Compute \(g'\): $\(g'(x) = f'(x) - \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}\)$

Setting \(g'(c) = 0\): $\(f'(c) - \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a} = 0 \implies f'(c) = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}\)$

\(\square\)

The geometric story of the proof:

         f(b)
          *
         /|  ← secant line L(x)
        / |
   f(c)/  |
  ....*.  |   ← tangent parallel to secant
      /   |
     /    |
f(a)*     |
    a  c  b

\(g(x)\) measures the vertical gap between \(f\) and the secant. At both endpoints this gap is 0. So somewhere in between, the gap must reach a maximum or minimum — and Rolle tells us \(g'(c) = 0\) there, which is exactly \(f'(c) =\) slope of secant.

docs.title: Example 1 — The Driving Analogy Made Rigorous
docs.text:
Let \(s(t)\) = position (km) at time \(t\) (hours), with \(s(0) = 0\), \(s(3) = 250\).

Assume \(s\) is continuous on \([0,3]\) and differentiable on \((0,3)\) (reasonable physical assumption).

By MVT: \(\exists, c \in (0,3)\) such that: $\(s'(c) = \frac{s(3)-s(0)}{3-0} = \frac{250}{3} \approx 83.3 \text{ km/h}\)$

Since \(s'(t)\) is velocity, the speedometer must have read exactly 83.3 km/h at some moment \(t = c\).

This is not just intuition anymore — it's a theorem.

docs.title: Example 2 — A Polynomial
docs.text:
Let \(f(x) = x^3 - x\) on \([0, 2]\).

Secant slope: \(\dfrac{f(2)-f(0)}{2-0} = \dfrac{(8-2)-0}{2} = \dfrac{6}{2} = 3\)

MVT guarantees \(\exists, c \in (0,2)\) with \(f'(c) = 3\).

\(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 1\). Solve: $\(3c^2 - 1 = 3 \implies 3c^2 = 4 \implies c = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3} \approx 1.155\)$

Indeed \(c \approx 1.155 \in (0,2)\). ✓

Note: MVT guarantees existence — it doesn't say \(c\) is unique. Here it happens to be unique in \((0,2)\), but for other functions there could be multiple such \(c\).

docs.title: Example 3 — Using MVT to Prove an Inequality
docs.text:
Claim: \(|\sin b - \sin a| \leq |b - a|\) for all \(a, b \in \mathbb{R}\).

Proof. If \(a = b\) this is trivial. Assume WLOG \(a < b\).

\(f(x) = \sin x\) is differentiable everywhere. By MVT, \(\exists, c \in (a,b)\): $\(\sin b - \sin a = f'(c)(b-a) = \cos(c) \cdot (b-a)\)$

Taking absolute values: $\(|\sin b - \sin a| = |\cos c| \cdot |b-a| \leq 1 \cdot |b-a| = |b-a|\)$

since \(|\cos c| \leq 1\) always. \(\square\)

This is the power of MVT for inequalities: you convert a statement about a function's values into a statement about its derivative, which is often easier to bound.

docs.title: Example 4 — Uniqueness of Solutions
docs.text:
Claim: The equation \(x^3 + x = 2\) has exactly one real solution.

Existence: \(f(x) = x^3 + x - 2\) has \(f(0) = -2 < 0\) and \(f(1) = 0\). So \(x = 1\) is a solution.

Uniqueness (by MVT / Rolle): Suppose there were two solutions \(a < b\) with \(f(a) = f(b) = 0\). By Rolle's Theorem, \(\exists, c \in (a,b)\) with \(f'(c) = 0\).

But \(f'(x) = 3x^2 + 1 \geq 1 > 0\) for all \(x\). Contradiction. ✗

Therefore \(x = 1\) is the unique solution. \(\square\)

docs.title: §5. Important Corollaries
docs.text: These follow quickly from MVT and are used constantly.

docs.title: Corollary 1 — Zero Derivative Implies Constant
docs.text:
If \(f'(x) = 0\) for all \(x \in (a,b)\), then \(f\) is constant on \((a,b)\).

Proof. Take any \(x_1, x_2 \in (a,b)\) with \(x_1 < x_2\). By MVT: $\(f(x_2) - f(x_1) = f'(c)(x_2 - x_1) = 0\)$

So \(f(x_1) = f(x_2)\). Since \(x_1, x_2\) were arbitrary, \(f\) is constant. \(\square\)

docs.title: Corollary 2 — Equal Derivatives Imply Functions Differ by a Constant
docs.text:
If \(f'(x) = g'(x)\) for all \(x \in (a,b)\), then \(f(x) = g(x) + C\) for some constant \(C\).

Proof. Apply Corollary 1 to \(h(x) = f(x) - g(x)\). \(\square\)

This is the reason antiderivatives are defined up to a constant — a fact that underlies all of integral calculus.

docs.title: Corollary 3 — Monotonicity
docs.text:
• If \(f'(x) > 0\) on \((a,b)\), then \(f\) is strictly increasing on \([a,b]\).
  • If \(f'(x) < 0\) on \((a,b)\), then \(f\) is strictly decreasing on \([a,b]\).

Proof (increasing case). Take \(x_1 < x_2\) in \([a,b]\). By MVT, \(\exists, c\) with: $\(f(x_2) - f(x_1) = f'(c)(x_2 - x_1) > 0\)$

since \(f'(c) > 0\) and \(x_2 - x_1 > 0\). So \(f(x_2) > f(x_1)\). \(\square\)

docs.title: §6. The Generalized (Cauchy) MVT
docs.text:
Theorem (Cauchy's MVT). Let \(f, g\) be continuous on \([a,b]\), differentiable on \((a,b)\), and \(g'(x) \neq 0\) on \((a,b)\). Then \(\exists, c \in (a,b)\): $\(\frac{f'(c)}{g'(c)} = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{g(b)-g(a)}\)$

Taking \(g(x) = x\) recovers Lagrange's MVT.

This is the key lemma behind L'Hôpital's Rule. When computing \(\lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\) of the form \(\frac{0}{0}\), Cauchy's MVT provides the justification for replacing the ratio of functions with the ratio of derivatives.

docs.title: §7. MVT in Higher Dimensions — A Glimpse (MIT 18.02)
docs.text:
In multivariable calculus, the MVT generalizes but requires care. For a function \(f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\):

MVT for scalar fields. If \(f\) is differentiable, then for points \(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^n\): $\(f(\mathbf{b}) - f(\mathbf{a}) = \nabla f(\mathbf{c}) \cdot (\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a})\)$ for some \(\mathbf{c}\) on the segment joining \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\).

This is a direct generalization: the gradient \(\nabla f\) replaces \(f'\), and the dot product replaces ordinary multiplication.

For vector-valued \(\mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m\), the exact MVT fails in general (there need not exist a single \(c\)). Instead, one uses the MVT inequality: $\(|\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{b}) - \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{a})| \leq \sup_{\mathbf{c} \in \overline{ab}} |D\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{c})| \cdot |\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}|\)$

where \(D\mathbf{f}\) is the Jacobian matrix. This inequality is fundamental in numerical analysis and functional analysis.

docs.title: §8. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: This is where the theorem stops being "pure math" and starts running your GPU.

docs.title: 8.1 Gradient Descent — The MVT Beneath Every Update
docs.text:
The backbone of training neural networks is gradient descent. Given a loss function \(\mathcal{L}( heta)\) where \( heta \in \mathbb{R}^p\) are the parameters:

\[ heta_{t+1} = heta_t - \eta abla_ heta \mathcal{L}( heta_t)\]

Why does this work? MVT tells us exactly:

\[\mathcal{L}( heta_{t+1}) - \mathcal{L}( heta_t) = abla \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{c}) \cdot ( heta_{t+1} - heta_t)\]

for some \(\mathbf{c}\) between \( heta_t\) and \( heta_{t+1}\).

When the step is small, \( abla \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{c}) \approx abla \mathcal{L}( heta_t)\), so: $\(\mathcal{L}( heta_{t+1}) - \mathcal{L}( heta_t) \approx abla \mathcal{L}( heta_t) \cdot (-\eta abla \mathcal{L}( heta_t)) = -\eta | abla \mathcal{L}( heta_t)|^2 \leq 0\)$

The loss decreases. The MVT is the mathematical reason gradient descent works — it licenses the approximation that a small step in the negative gradient direction reduces the objective.

docs.title: 8.2 Learning Rate and the Lipschitz Condition
docs.text:
The MVT motivates one of the most important practical choices in deep learning: choosing the learning rate \(\eta\).

If \( abla \mathcal{L}\) is Lipschitz continuous with constant \(L\): $\(| abla \mathcal{L}( heta) - abla \mathcal{L}(\phi)| \leq L| heta - \phi|\)$

Then by MVT-type reasoning, one can show: $\(\mathcal{L}( heta_{t+1}) \leq \mathcal{L}( heta_t) - \left(\eta - rac{L\eta^2}{2} ight)| abla \mathcal{L}( heta_t)|^2\)$

The right-hand side is decreasing only when \(\eta < rac{2}{L}\).

Practical implication: If your learning rate is too large (bigger than \( rac{2}{L}\)), gradient descent is theoretically not guaranteed to converge. This is why learning rate schedules and adaptive methods (Adam, RMSProp) exist — they are heuristic attempts to stay in the MVT-safe zone.

docs.title: 8.3 Backpropagation and the Chain Rule
docs.text:
The chain rule — the engine of backpropagation — is proved using the MVT. Recall:

\[\frac{d}{dx}[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x)) \cdot g'(x)\]

One rigorous proof of this fact proceeds by writing: $\(\frac{f(g(x+h)) - f(g(x))}{h} = \frac{f(g(x+h)) - f(g(x))}{g(x+h)-g(x)} \cdot \frac{g(x+h)-g(x)}{h}\)$

and applying MVT to control the first factor as \(h \to 0\).

In deep learning, every layer's gradient computation is an application of this chain rule. The entire backpropagation algorithm is the chain rule applied recursively — and the chain rule's proof leans on MVT.

docs.title: 8.4 Loss Landscape Analysis
docs.text:
Modern deep learning theory studies the loss landscape \(\mathcal{L}: \mathbb{R}^p o \mathbb{R}\) of neural networks. Questions like:

  • Are there saddle points? Local minima? (Answered using critical point theory — \( abla \mathcal{L} = 0\), directly from MVT corollaries.)
  • How "flat" are the minima? (Studied via the Hessian \(H = abla^2 \mathcal{L}\), which is the second-order MVT — Taylor's theorem.)

The second-order MVT (Taylor with remainder): $\(\mathcal{L}( heta + \delta) = \mathcal{L}( heta) + abla \mathcal{L}( heta)^ op \delta + rac{1}{2}\delta^ op H(\mathbf{c})\delta\)$

is used in the analysis of Newton's method, natural gradient descent, and second-order optimizers like K-FAC.

docs.title: 8.5 Generalization and Lipschitz Neural Networks
docs.text:
In learning theory, the generalization gap (difference between training and test error) can be bounded using the Lipschitz constant of the network. By MVT:

\[|f_\theta(x) - f_\theta(x')| \leq \text{Lip}(f_\theta) \cdot |x - x'|\]

Networks with small Lipschitz constants generalize better — this is the theoretical motivation behind spectral normalization (used in GANs) and gradient penalty methods. All of these bound or control the Lipschitz constant, which is defined via MVT.

docs.title: §9. Summary Table
docs.text: Concept Statement Key Use Rolle's Theorem \(f(a)=f(b) \Rightarrow \exists, c: f'(c)=0\) Proof engine for MVT Lagrange's MVT \(\exists, c: f'(c) = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}\) The core theorem Cauchy's MVT \(\frac{f'(c)}{g'(c)} = \frac{\Delta f}{\Delta g}\) L'Hôpital's Rule Corollary 1 \(f'=0 \Rightarrow f=\text{const}\) Integration theory Corollary 3 \(f'>0 \Rightarrow f\) increasing Optimization Multivariate MVT \(\Delta f = \nabla f(\mathbf{c}) \cdot \Delta \mathbf{x}\) Gradient descent analysis

docs.title: §10. Hypotheses Are Not Optional
docs.text:
A common exam trap — and a deep conceptual point.

The MVT requires both continuity on \([a,b]\) and differentiability on \((a,b)\).

Counterexample 1 — Continuity fails: $\(f(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x \in [0,1) \ 1 & x = 1 \end{cases}\)$ \(\frac{f(1)-f(0)}{1-0} = 1\), but \(f'(x) = 0\) wherever it exists. No \(c\) works.

Counterexample 2 — Differentiability fails: $\(f(x) = |x| \text{ on } [-1, 1]\)$ \(\frac{f(1)-f(-1)}{2} = 0\), but \(f'(x) = \pm 1 \neq 0\) everywhere \(f'\) is defined; \(f'(0)\) doesn't exist.

The hypotheses in theorems are not bureaucratic formalities — they are load-bearing walls.

docs.title: How Derivatives Affect the Graph
docs.text: "The derivative does not merely describe the function — it is the function's autobiography. Every rise, fall, bend, and inflection is written in \(f'\) and \(f''\)."

docs.title: §1. The Central Philosophy
docs.text:
A function \(f\) is a static object — it just is. Its derivative \(f'\) is dynamic — it tells you how \(f\) is moving at each point. The second derivative \(f''\) tells you how that movement is itself changing.

This hierarchy:

\[f \xrightarrow{\text{differentiate}} f' \xrightarrow{\text{differentiate}} f''\]

corresponds to:

\[\text{height} \xrightarrow{} \text{slope} \xrightarrow{} \text{curvature}\]

Everything about the shape of a graph — its rises and falls, its peaks and valleys, its bends and straightenings — is encoded in these two derived functions.

docs.title: §2. The First Derivative — Increasing and Decreasing
2.1 The Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem (Increasing/Decreasing Test). Let \(f\) be differentiable on an open interval \(I\).

  • If \(f'(x) > 0\) for all \(x \in I\), then \(f\) is strictly increasing on \(I\).
  • If \(f'(x) < 0\) for all \(x \in I\), then \(f\) is strictly decreasing on \(I\).
  • If \(f'(x) = 0\) for all \(x \in I\), then \(f\) is constant on \(I\).

Proof of the increasing case.

Take any \(x_1 < x_2\) in \(I\). By the Mean Value Theorem, \(\exists, c \in (x_1, x_2)\): $\(f(x_2) - f(x_1) = f'(c)(x_2 - x_1)\)$

Since \(f'(c) > 0\) and \(x_2 - x_1 > 0\), we get \(f(x_2) - f(x_1) > 0\), i.e., \(f(x_2) > f(x_1)\). \(\square\)

(The MVT is doing all the real work here — this is why MVT is called the "workhorse of differential calculus.")

docs.title: 2.2 Finding Intervals — The Method
docs.text:
To determine where \(f\) increases/decreases:

  1. Find all critical numbers: points where \(f'(x) = 0\) or \(f'(x)\) does not exist.
  2. These critical numbers partition the real line into open intervals.
  3. Pick a test value in each interval; evaluate \(f'\).
  4. Sign of \(f'\) → increasing or decreasing on that interval.

Example. \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 4\)

\(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x - 9 = 3(x^2 - 2x - 3) = 3(x-3)(x+1)\)

Critical numbers: \(x = -1, ; x = 3\)

Interval Test value \(f'\) Behavior \((-\infty, -1)\) \(x = -2\) \(3(-5)(-1) = 15 > 0\) Increasing ↑ \((-1, 3)\) \(x = 0\) \(3(-3)(1) = -9 < 0\) Decreasing ↓ \((3, \infty)\) \(x = 4\) \(3(1)(5) = 15 > 0\) Increasing ↑ 
        ↑           ↓           ↑
  ------+---\-------+-------/---+------
       -1    \             /    3
              \           /
               \_________/

docs.title: 3.1 Definitions
docs.text:
Definition. A number \(c\) in the domain of \(f\) is a critical number if either \(f'(c) = 0\) or \(f'(c)\) does not exist.

Fermat's Theorem. If \(f\) has a local maximum or minimum at \(c\), then \(c\) is a critical number of \(f\).

Important converse failure: A critical number need not yield a local extremum. The canonical example: \(f(x) = x^3\) has \(f'(0) = 0\) but \(x = 0\) is neither a maximum nor a minimum — it's an inflection point.

f(x) = x³

        |  /
        | /
        |/
--------+--------
       /|
      / |
     /  |

f'(0) = 0, but no extremum at x = 0.

docs.title: 3.2 The First Derivative Test
docs.text:
First Derivative Test. Suppose \(c\) is a critical number of a continuous function \(f\).

  • If \(f'\) changes positive → negative at \(c\): local maximum at \(c\).
  • If \(f'\) changes negative → positive at \(c\): local minimum at \(c\).
  • If \(f'\) does not change sign at \(c\): no local extremum (inflection).

Visual mnemonic:

LOCAL MAX:         LOCAL MIN:         NO EXTREMUM:
    *                                     
   / \               ___              ___/
  /   \             /   \            /
 /     \           /     \         __
         \/                \/
f'>0  f'<0         f'<0  f'>0      f'>0  f'>0

Continuing the example \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 4\):

  • At \(x = -1\): \(f'\) goes \(+ \to -\) → local max, \(f(-1) = 1 - 3 + 9 + 4 = 9\)
  • At \(x = 3\): \(f'\) goes \(- \to +\) → local min, \(f(3) = 27 - 27 - 27 + 4 = -23\)

docs.title: 4.1 Concavity Defined
docs.text:
Definition. A differentiable function \(f\) is:

  • Concave upward on \(I\) if \(f'\) is increasing on \(I\).
  • Concave downward on \(I\) if \(f'\) is decreasing on \(I\).

Equivalently (when \(f''\) exists):

Concavity Test.

  • \(f''(x) > 0\) on \(I\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(f\) is concave up on \(I\) (holds water ∪)
  • \(f''(x) < 0\) on \(I\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(f\) is concave down on \(I\) (spills water ∩)

Geometric intuition. Concave up means the tangent lines lie below the curve. Concave down means they lie above. This is not a cosmetic property — it determines how well linear approximations (tangent lines) over- or under-estimate the function.

CONCAVE UP (∪)          CONCAVE DOWN (∩)
   f'' > 0                  f'' < 0

    curve                  curve
   /      \               /      \
  /        \             /        \
 / tangents \           / tangents \
     below                 above

tangent UNDERESTIMATES   tangent OVERESTIMATES

docs.title: 4.2 Inflection Points
docs.text:
Definition. A point \((c, f(c))\) is an inflection point of \(f\) if \(f\) is continuous at \(c\) and the concavity of \(f\) changes at \(c\).

Necessary condition: If \(f''(c)\) exists and \((c, f(c))\) is an inflection point, then \(f''(c) = 0\).

Warning: \(f''(c) = 0\) does NOT guarantee an inflection point. Again, \(f(x) = x^4\): \(f''(0) = 0\) but concavity does not change at \(0\) (it's concave up everywhere).

Example. \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 4\)

\(f''(x) = 6x - 6 = 6(x-1)\)

\(f''(x) = 0\) at \(x = 1\).

  • \(x < 1\): \(f''(x) < 0\) → concave down
  • \(x > 1\): \(f''(x) > 0\) → concave up

Concavity changes at \(x = 1\) → inflection point at \((1, f(1)) = (1, -8)\).

Full shape of f(x) = x³ - 3x² - 9x + 4:

      local max (−1, 9)
         *
        / \
       /   \         ← concave down
      /     \
     /  IP   \
    /  (1,−8) \
   /            *    ← inflection
                 \
                  \  ← concave up
                   *
            local min (3, −23)

docs.title: §5. The Second Derivative Test for Local Extrema
docs.text:
Second Derivative Test. Suppose \(f''\) is continuous near \(c\) and \(f'(c) = 0\).

  • If \(f''(c) > 0\): local minimum at \(c\).
  • If \(f''(c) < 0\): local maximum at \(c\).
  • If \(f''(c) = 0\): inconclusive — use the first derivative test.

Why does this work?

If \(f'(c) = 0\) and \(f''(c) > 0\), then \(f'\) is increasing through \(0\) at \(c\). So \(f'\) goes from negative (before \(c\)) to positive (after \(c\)) — exactly the first derivative test's condition for a local minimum.

Proof sketch.

\(f''(c) > 0\) means, by definition of derivative: $\(f''(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f'(x) - f'(c)}{x - c} = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f'(x)}{x-c} > 0\)$

For \(x\) near \(c\): \(f'(x)\) and \((x-c)\) have the same sign. So:

  • \(x < c \Rightarrow f'(x) < 0\)
  • \(x > c \Rightarrow f'(x) > 0\)

This is exactly a local minimum by the first derivative test. \(\square\)

The inconclusive case — three behaviors are possible:

Function \(f'(0)\) \(f''(0)\) Behavior at 0 \(f(x) = x^4\) 0 0 Local min \(f(x) = -x^4\) 0 0 Local max \(f(x) = x^3\) 0 0 Inflection

When the second derivative test fails, go back to the first derivative test. It never fails (as long as \(f'\) is defined nearby).

docs.title: §6. Asymptotes — Behavior at the Boundary
docs.text: Shape analysis is incomplete without understanding what happens as \(x \to \pm\infty\) or as \(x\) approaches a discontinuity.

docs.title: 6.1 Horizontal Asymptotes
docs.text:
\[\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = L \quad \text{or} \quad \lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) = L\]

implies \(y = L\) is a horizontal asymptote.

docs.title: 6.2 Vertical Asymptotes
docs.text:
\[\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = \pm\infty \quad \text{or} \quad \lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = \pm\infty\]

implies \(x = a\) is a vertical asymptote. These arise at zeros of denominators, logarithm arguments going to zero, etc.

docs.title: 6.3 Slant (Oblique) Asymptotes
docs.text:
When \(\deg(\text{numerator}) = \deg(\text{denominator}) + 1\), polynomial long division yields: $\(f(x) = (mx + b) + \frac{r(x)}{q(x)}\)$

where \(\frac{r(x)}{q(x)} \to 0\) as \(x \to \infty\). The line \(y = mx + b\) is the slant asymptote.

docs.title: §7. A Systematic Curve-Sketching Algorithm
docs.text:
This is the full synthesis — a procedure that transforms \(f\) into a picture using everything above.

Algorithm (Stewart §4.5):

  1. Domain — Where is \(f\) defined?
  2. Intercepts — \(y\)-intercept at \(f(0)\); \(x\)-intercepts where \(f(x) = 0\).
  3. Symmetry — Even (\(f(-x)=f(x)\))? Odd (\(f(-x)=-f(x)\))? Periodic?
  4. Asymptotes — Horizontal, vertical, slant.
  5. Intervals of increase/decrease — Find \(f'\), critical numbers, sign chart.
  6. Local extrema — Apply first or second derivative test.
  7. Concavity and inflection points — Find \(f''\), solve \(f''=0\), sign chart.
  8. Sketch — Plot key points, connect with appropriate shape.

Full worked example. \(f(x) = \dfrac{x^2}{x^2 - 1}\)

Domain: \(x \neq \pm 1\), so \((-\infty,-1) \cup (-1,1) \cup (1,\infty)\).

Symmetry: \(f(-x) = \frac{x^2}{x^2-1} = f(x)\) → even function, symmetric about \(y\)-axis.

Intercepts: \(f(0) = 0\) → \(y\)-intercept \((0,0)\); \(f(x) = 0\) gives \(x = 0\) → \(x\)-intercept \((0,0)\).

Asymptotes:

  • \(x \to \pm 1\): denominator \(\to 0\), numerator \(\to 1\) → vertical asymptotes \(x = \pm 1\)
  • \(x \to \pm\infty\): \(\frac{x^2}{x^2-1} = \frac{1}{1-1/x^2} \to 1\) → horizontal asymptote \(y = 1\)

First derivative: $\(f'(x) = \frac{2x(x^2-1) - x^2(2x)}{(x^2-1)^2} = \frac{2x^3 - 2x - 2x^3}{(x^2-1)^2} = \frac{-2x}{(x^2-1)^2}\)$

Critical number: \(x = 0\) (denominator never \(0\) in domain).

Sign chart for \(f'(x) = \frac{-2x}{(x^2-1)^2}\): denominator always positive; sign determined by \(-2x\).

Interval Sign of \(-2x\) \(f'\) Behavior \((-\infty,-1)\) \(+\) \(+\) Increasing \((-1,0)\) \(+\) \(+\) Increasing \((0,1)\) \(-\) \(-\) Decreasing \((1,\infty)\) \(-\) \(-\) Decreasing

At \(x=0\): \(f'\) goes \(+ \to -\) → local max, \(f(0) = 0\).

Second derivative (after computation): $\(f''(x) = \frac{6x^2+2}{(x^2-1)^3}\)$

Numerator \(6x^2+2 > 0\) always. Sign of \(f''\) determined by \((x^2-1)^3\):

  • \(|x| > 1\): \((x^2-1)^3 > 0\) → \(f'' > 0\) → concave up
  • \(|x| < 1\): \((x^2-1)^3 < 0\) → \(f'' < 0\) → concave down

\(f'' \neq 0\) in domain → no inflection points.

Final sketch:

y
|           |           |
|   \       |     /     |
... *-------+-------* ...   y = 1 (asymptote)
|    \      |(0,0) /    |
|     \     *     /     |
|      \   / \   /      |
|       \_/   \_/       |
|      local max at 0   |
        x=-1       x=1   (vertical asymptotes)

docs.title: §8. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
8.1 Loss Landscape Topology
docs.text:
In training a neural network, the loss function \(\mathcal{L}: \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}\) (over millions of parameters) has a shape — a high-dimensional analog of the curves we've been analyzing. Every concept from this note has a direct counterpart:

Calculus concept ML/DL counterpart Increasing/decreasing Loss going up/down during training Critical point (\(f'=0\)) Stationary point — where gradient descent stops Local minimum A solution the optimizer converged to Saddle point Critical point that is a min in some directions, max in others — a major obstacle in deep learning Concave up region (\(f''>0\)) "Sharp" minimum — bad for generalization Concave down region (\(f''<0\)) Descent away from a local max Inflection point Transition in curvature of the loss curve

docs.title: 8.2 Saddle Points — The Deep Learning Problem
docs.text:
In \(\mathbb{R}^1\), a critical point is either a max, min, or inflection point. In \(\mathbb{R}^p\) (high-dimensional parameter space), there is a fourth type: saddle points — points where \(\nabla \mathcal{L} = \mathbf{0}\) but the Hessian \(H = \nabla^2 \mathcal{L}\) has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

Saddle point in ℝ²:
f(x,y) = x² - y²

        ↑ y
        |
  \     |     /     ← concave down in y
   \    |    /
----\---+---/----→ x
   / \  |  / \
  /   \ | /   \    ← concave up in x
        |

At the origin: \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 0\), \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 0\), but it's neither a max nor a min.

Why this matters: Early deep learning theory (Dauphin et al., 2014) suggested that saddle points — not local minima — are the primary obstacle for gradient-based optimizers. In high dimensions, most critical points are saddle points (the probability that all eigenvalues of the Hessian are positive is exponentially small in the dimension).

SGD and Adam navigate these saddle points through noise and momentum — but the underlying geometry is exactly the second derivative / concavity analysis from §4.

docs.title: 8.3 Sharp vs. Flat Minima and Generalization
docs.text:
The concavity at a minimum predicts generalization:

  • Sharp minimum (\(f''\) very large): The loss surface curves steeply. A small perturbation of \(\theta\) causes a large increase in training loss — and even larger increases in test loss (since train and test distributions differ slightly). Poor generalization.

  • Flat minimum (\(f''\) small): The loss surface is nearly flat. Small perturbations don't hurt much. Better generalization.

Sharp minimum:          Flat minimum:
     |                  _____________
     *                 /             \
    /|\               /               \
   / | \             /                 \
  /  |  \           /                   \

  Bad for test        Good for test

This is the theoretical foundation behind:

  • Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) — explicitly seeks flat minima by perturbing weights and minimizing the worst-case loss in a neighborhood
  • Weight averaging methods (SWA, EWA) — average iterates to land in flatter regions
  • Batch size effects — large batch sizes tend to find sharper minima (Keskar et al., 2017)

All of this is concavity / second derivative analysis, lifted to high dimensions.

docs.title: 8.4 Learning Rate Schedules and Curvature
docs.text:
The optimal learning rate at a point is inversely proportional to the curvature (\(f''\)) there:

\[\eta_{\text{optimal}} \propto \frac{1}{f''(c)}\]

This is Newton's method: \(\theta \leftarrow \theta - \frac{f'(\theta)}{f''(\theta)}\).

In high dimensions, this becomes \(\theta \leftarrow \theta - H^{-1}\nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta)\).

Adaptive optimizers (Adam, RMSProp, Adagrad) approximate this by maintaining running estimates of the second moment of the gradient — a cheap surrogate for curvature. The reason they work better than vanilla SGD is exactly that they adapt the step size to local curvature:

  • High curvature region (\(f''\) large) → small step
  • Low curvature region (\(f''\) small) → large step

This is the geometric insight from §4 operationalized in code.

docs.title: 8.5 Activation Functions and Concavity
docs.text:
The choice of activation function in a neural network is, in part, a choice about concavity:

Activation Concavity Consequence Sigmoid \(\sigma(x)\) Concave up for \(x<0\), down for \(x>0\) Vanishing gradients; inflection at \(x=0\) ReLU \(\max(0,x)\) Linear (no concavity) No vanishing gradient; not differentiable at 0 GELU, Swish Smooth, with inflection Empirically superior; behaves like ReLU but differentiable Softplus \(\log(1+e^x)\) Always concave up Smooth ReLU approximation

The inflection point of the sigmoid at \(x=0\) is the reason sigmoid saturates and causes vanishing gradients in deep networks — the concavity flips, and \(\sigma''\) changes sign there. ReLU eliminates this by having no curvature at all (above zero). The entire history of activation function design is an applied study in concavity.

docs.title: §9. The Full Picture — Derivative Dictionary
docs.text:
FUNCTION f(x)
│
├─── f'(x) > 0  →  f is INCREASING   (graph rises left to right)
├─── f'(x) < 0  →  f is DECREASING   (graph falls left to right)
├─── f'(x) = 0  →  CRITICAL POINT    (horizontal tangent)
│         │
│         ├── f' changes + → −  →  LOCAL MAX
│         ├── f' changes − → +  →  LOCAL MIN
│         └── f' doesn't change sign  →  INFLECTION (if f''=0 too)
│
└─── f''(x) > 0  →  CONCAVE UP    ∪  (tangents below curve)
     f''(x) < 0  →  CONCAVE DOWN  ∩  (tangents above curve)
     f''(x) = 0  →  POSSIBLE INFLECTION POINT
           │
           └── concavity changes?  →  YES: INFLECTION POINT
                                       NO:  not an inflection point

docs.title: §10. Why the Hypotheses Matter
docs.text:
The differentiability hypothesis is essential. Consider \(f(x) = |x|\) on \([-1, 1]\):

  • \(f'(x) = -1\) for \(x < 0\) and \(f'(x) = +1\) for \(x > 0\)
  • \(f'(0)\) does not exist
  • \(f\) has a global minimum at \(x = 0\) — but Fermat's Theorem still holds! (\(x=0\) is a critical number because \(f'(0)\) DNE)

The theorems in this note require differentiability, but the extrema can still occur at non-differentiable points — they just can't be detected by \(f' = 0\) there. Always check where \(f'\) fails to exist, not just where \(f' = 0\).

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. Cengage Learning. — §4.3 (How Derivatives Affect the Shape of a Graph), §4.5 (Summary of Curve Sketching).
  2. MIT OpenCourseWare 18.02 — Multivariable Calculus. Gradient, Hessian, and multivariable second derivative test.

docs.title: Local Extreme Values
docs.text: "An extremum is not merely where the derivative vanishes — it is where the function hesitates, reverses its testimony, and commits to a new direction. Understanding why requires the full weight of the Mean Value Theorem."

docs.title: §1. The Central Question
docs.text:
Given a function \(f\), we want to know: where does \(f\) achieve its highest or lowest values locally?

This is not just a geometric curiosity. The same question — phrased in higher dimensions — is exactly what gradient descent answers during neural network training. Every parameter update in backpropagation is navigating the local geometry of a loss surface. The theory begins here, with a single real variable.

docs.title: 2.1 Absolute (Global) Extrema
docs.text:
Definition. A function \(f\) has an absolute maximum at \(c\) if \(f(c) \geq f(x)\) for all \(x\) in the domain of \(f\). Similarly, \(f\) has an absolute minimum at \(c\) if \(f(c) \leq f(x)\) for all \(x\) in the domain.

These are the global champions — no point anywhere does better.

docs.title: 2.2 Local (Relative) Extrema
docs.text:
Definition. A function \(f\) has a local maximum at \(c\) if there exists an open interval \((a, b)\) containing \(c\) such that \(f(c) \geq f(x)\) for all \(x \in (a, b)\).

Definition. A function \(f\) has a local minimum at \(c\) if there exists an open interval \((a, b)\) containing \(c\) such that \(f(c) \leq f(x)\) for all \(x \in (a, b)\).

Key point: Local extrema are neighborhood champions — \(f(c)\) beats all nearby competitors, but not necessarily the whole field.

Absolute vs. Local:

          absolute max
               *
              / \
 local max   /   \
     *       /     \
    / \     /       \
   /   \___/         \
  /    local min      \______ → x
 /
absolute min is at x → -∞ (if it exists)

Every absolute extremum is also a local extremum.
The converse is FALSE.

docs.title: 2.3 Why the Distinction Matters
docs.text: In optimization, we often want the absolute minimum of the loss function, but gradient-based methods can only guarantee finding a local minimum. The relationship between local and global minima — and whether they coincide — is a deep question in both calculus and machine learning.

docs.title: 3.1 Statement
docs.text: Theorem (Fermat). If \(f\) has a local maximum or local minimum at \(c\), and if \(f'(c)\) exists, then \(f'(c) = 0\).

docs.title: 3.2 Full Proof
docs.text:
Proof (local maximum case).

Suppose \(f\) has a local maximum at \(c\). Then \(\exists, \delta > 0\) such that: $\(f(c) \geq f(x) \quad \text{for all } x \in (c - \delta,, c + \delta)\)$

Consider the difference quotient approaching from the right. For \(0 < h < \delta\): $\(f(c + h) \leq f(c) \implies f(c + h) - f(c) \leq 0 \implies \frac{f(c+h) - f(c)}{h} \leq 0\)$

Taking the limit as \(h \to 0^+\): $\(f'(c) = \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{f(c+h) - f(c)}{h} \leq 0 \quad \cdots (1)\)$

Now approach from the left. For \(-\delta < h < 0\): $\(f(c + h) \leq f(c) \implies f(c + h) - f(c) \leq 0\)$

But now \(h < 0\), so dividing flips the inequality: $\(\frac{f(c+h) - f(c)}{h} \geq 0\)$

Taking the limit as \(h \to 0^-\): $\(f'(c) = \lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{f(c+h) - f(c)}{h} \geq 0 \quad \cdots (2)\)$

Since \(f'(c)\) exists (by hypothesis), both one-sided limits equal \(f'(c)\). From \((1)\) and \((2)\): $\(f'(c) \leq 0 \quad \text{and} \quad f'(c) \geq 0\)$

Therefore \(f'(c) = 0\). \(\square\)

(The local minimum proof is identical with all inequalities reversed.)

docs.title: 3.3 The Critical Converse Failure
docs.text:
Fermat's theorem is NOT reversible. \(f'(c) = 0\) does not imply a local extremum at \(c\).

Canonical counterexample: \(f(x) = x^3\)

\[f'(x) = 3x^2 \implies f'(0) = 0\]

But \(f\) is strictly increasing everywhere — \(x = 0\) is an inflection point, not an extremum.

f(x) = x³         f'(x) = 3x²

     |  /              |
     | /               |   ___
     |/                |  /
-----+-----        ----+------
    /|                 |
   / |               (always ≥ 0)
  /  |

f'(0) = 0 but no extremum.    f' never changes sign through 0.

Second canonical counterexample: \(f(x) = x^{1/3}\)

\[f'(x) = \frac{1}{3}x^{-2/3} \quad \text{— undefined at } x = 0\]

Yet \(f\) has a local (and absolute) minimum at \(x = 0\). Extrema can occur where \(f'\) fails to exist.

This motivates the following:

docs.title: §4. Critical Numbers
docs.text:
Definition. A number \(c\) in the domain of \(f\) is a critical number (or critical point) of \(f\) if either:

  1. \(f'(c) = 0\), or
  2. \(f'(c)\) does not exist.

Fermat's Theorem restated: If \(f\) has a local extremum at \(c\), then \(c\) is a critical number.

Critical numbers are necessary but not sufficient for local extrema.

The task is then to classify each critical number: is it a local max, local min, or neither? Two tools exist for this: the First Derivative Test and the Second Derivative Test.

docs.title: §5. The Extreme Value Theorem (Existence)
docs.text:
Before classifying extrema, a theorem guarantees they exist on closed intervals:

Theorem (Extreme Value Theorem). If \(f\) is continuous on a closed interval \([a, b]\), then \(f\) attains both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on \([a, b]\).

The closed interval method for finding absolute extrema:

  1. Find all critical numbers \(c\) in \((a, b)\).
  2. Evaluate \(f\) at each critical number and at both endpoints \(a\), \(b\).
  3. The largest value is the absolute maximum; the smallest is the absolute minimum.

Why endpoints matter: Local extrema detected by \(f' = 0\) live in the interior. But absolute extrema can occur at the boundary of the domain — and the derivative says nothing there.

Closed interval [a, b]:

        interior max             endpoint max
              *                         *
             / \                       /
            /   \     *               /
           /     \___/ \             /
          /             \___________/
         a                          b

Interior critical pts + endpoints = candidates for absolute extrema.

docs.title: 6.1 Statement
docs.text:
First Derivative Test. Suppose \(c\) is a critical number of a continuous function \(f\).

  • If \(f'\) changes from positive to negative at \(c\): \(f\) has a local maximum at \(c\).
  • If \(f'\) changes from negative to positive at \(c\): \(f\) has a local minimum at \(c\).
  • If \(f'\) does not change sign at \(c\): \(f\) has no local extremum at \(c\).

docs.title: 6.2 Why This Works — Proof Sketch
docs.text:
Local maximum case. Suppose \(f'\) changes \(+ \to -\) at \(c\). Then:

  • On \((c - \delta, c)\): \(f'(x) > 0 \implies f\) is increasing toward \(c\).
  • On \((c, c + \delta)\): \(f'(x) < 0 \implies f\) is decreasing away from \(c\).

So \(f\) rises to \(c\) then falls — this is exactly a local maximum. \(\square\)

(Formally this uses the Increasing/Decreasing Test, which in turn uses the Mean Value Theorem — see the previous note. So the MVT is, once again, the load-bearing structure.)

docs.title: 6.3 How to Apply It — The Sign Chart Method
docs.text:
Algorithm:

  1. Find all critical numbers of \(f\).
  2. Plot them on a number line, creating open intervals between them.
  3. Choose a test value in each interval.
  4. Evaluate \(f'\) at the test value — record only the sign.
  5. Read off the behavior from the sign changes.

Example. \(f(x) = x^4 - 8x^2 + 3\)

\[f'(x) = 4x^3 - 16x = 4x(x^2 - 4) = 4x(x-2)(x+2)\]

Critical numbers: \(x = -2, ; 0, ; 2\).

Sign chart for \(f'(x) = 4x(x-2)(x+2)\):

Interval Test pt Sign of \(4x\) Sign of \((x-2)\) Sign of \((x+2)\) \(f'\) \(f\) \((-\infty, -2)\) \(-3\) \(-\) \(-\) \(-\) \(-\) \(\searrow\) \((-2, 0)\) \(-1\) \(-\) \(-\) \(+\) \(+\) \(\nearrow\) \((0, 2)\) \(1\) \(+\) \(-\) \(+\) \(-\) \(\searrow\) \((2, \infty)\) \(3\) \(+\) \(+\) \(+\) \(+\) \(\nearrow\)

Sign transitions:

  • \(x = -2\): \(f'\) goes \(- \to +\) → local minimum, \(f(-2) = 16 - 32 + 3 = -13\)
  • \(x = 0\): \(f'\) goes \(+ \to -\) → local maximum, \(f(0) = 3\)
  • \(x = 2\): \(f'\) goes \(- \to +\) → local minimum, \(f(2) = 16 - 32 + 3 = -13\)
f(x) = x⁴ − 8x² + 3:

  f' < 0      f' > 0     f' < 0      f' > 0
       \       /  \       /
        \     /    \     /
    ↓    \   / ↑    \   /  ↑
          \ /        \ /
           *          *
        (-2,−13)   (2,−13)    ← local min (equal by symmetry)

              (0,3)
              *                ← local max
             / \

Note on symmetry: \(f(-x) = f(x)\) (even function), so the graph is symmetric about the \(y\)-axis, which explains why the two minima have equal value. Always exploit symmetry — it halves the work and is a consistency check.

docs.title: 6.4 The First Derivative Test Never Fails
docs.text:
Unlike the Second Derivative Test (§7), the First Derivative Test:

  • Works when \(f''\) does not exist.
  • Works when \(f''(c) = 0\) (the inconclusive case for the second test).
  • Applies to non-differentiable critical numbers (where \(f'\) DNE).

It is the gold standard. The second derivative test is a shortcut that sometimes breaks down.

docs.title: 7.1 Statement
docs.text:
Second Derivative Test. Suppose \(f''\) is continuous near \(c\), and \(f'(c) = 0\).

  • If \(f''(c) > 0\): \(f\) has a local minimum at \(c\).
  • If \(f''(c) < 0\): \(f\) has a local maximum at \(c\).
  • If \(f''(c) = 0\): inconclusive — the test says nothing. Use the first derivative test.

docs.title: 7.2 Full Proof
docs.text:
Local minimum case: \(f'(c) = 0\), \(f''(c) > 0\).

By definition of the derivative: $\(f''(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f'(x) - f'(c)}{x - c} = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f'(x)}{x - c} > 0\)$

(using \(f'(c) = 0\)). Since this limit is positive, there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that for all \(x \in (c - \delta, c + \delta) \setminus {c}\):

\[\frac{f'(x)}{x - c} > 0\]

This means \(f'(x)\) and \((x - c)\) have the same sign:

  • \(x \in (c - \delta, c)\): \(x - c < 0 \implies f'(x) < 0\)
  • \(x \in (c, c + \delta)\): \(x - c > 0 \implies f'(x) > 0\)

So \(f'\) changes from negative to positive at \(c\). By the First Derivative Test: local minimum. \(\square\)

The local maximum case is identical with \(f''(c) < 0\) and all signs reversed.

docs.title: 7.3 Geometric Interpretation
docs.text:
The second derivative test is really the First Derivative Test applied one level up:

  • \(f''(c) > 0\) means \(f'\) is increasing through \(0\) at \(c\).
  • An increasing function that passes through \(0\) goes from negative to positive.
  • Negative to positive in \(f'\) means local minimum in \(f\).
f''(c) > 0 → f' increasing:        f''(c) < 0 → f' decreasing:

  f'                                  f'
   |     /                             |\ 
   |    /                              | \
   |   /                              0|  \
---0--/--------→ x                 ---+---\---→ x
   | /     c                         c     \
   |/                                       \

f' goes −→+ at c: LOCAL MIN        f' goes +→− at c: LOCAL MAX

docs.title: 7.4 The Inconclusive Case — All Three Behaviors Possible
docs.text:
When \(f'(c) = 0\) and \(f''(c) = 0\), anything can happen:

Function \(f'(0)\) \(f''(0)\) Behavior at \(0\) \(f(x) = x^4\) \(0\) \(0\) Local (and absolute) min \(f(x) = -x^4\) \(0\) \(0\) Local (and absolute) max \(f(x) = x^3\) \(0\) \(0\) Inflection — neither 
x⁴ (local min):     -x⁴ (local max):     x³ (neither):

      ___                                    /
     /   \              \_____/            /
    /     \                               /
---*-------              ---*---         ---*---
   0                        0               0

f''(0)=0 in all three cases. Test fails to distinguish them.

Rule: When \(f''(c) = 0\), abandon the second derivative test and fall back to the first derivative test. Always.

docs.title: 7.5 Comparison: First vs. Second Derivative Test
docs.text:
Feature First Derivative Test Second Derivative Test Requires \(f\) continuous at \(c\), \(f'\) defined nearby \(f''\) continuous near \(c\) Works when \(f''(c) = 0\) ✓ Yes ✗ No (inconclusive) Works when \(f'\) DNE at \(c\) ✓ Yes ✗ No Computational cost Sign chart required Single evaluation \(f''(c)\) Can it fail? No Yes (when \(f''(c) = 0\))

Practical note: Use the second derivative test when \(f''\) is easy to compute and you already have \(f''\) from concavity analysis. Fall back to the first derivative test when the second test is inconclusive or when \(f''\) is tedious.

docs.title: §8. A Complete Worked Example
docs.text:
Find and classify all local extrema of \(f(x) = x^2 e^{-x}\).

Step 1: Domain. All of \(\mathbb{R}\).

Step 2: Find \(f'\).

\[f'(x) = 2x e^{-x} + x^2(-e^{-x}) = e^{-x}(2x - x^2) = x(2-x)e^{-x}\]

Note: \(e^{-x} > 0\) always, so the sign of \(f'\) is determined entirely by \(x(2-x)\).

Step 3: Critical numbers.

\(f'(x) = 0 \iff x(2-x) = 0 \iff x = 0 \text{ or } x = 2\)

\(f'\) exists everywhere (product of smooth functions).

Step 4: Sign chart.

Interval Sign of \(x\) Sign of \((2-x)\) Sign of \(f'\) \(f\) \((-\infty, 0)\) \(-\) \(+\) \(-\) \(\searrow\) \((0, 2)\) \(+\) \(+\) \(+\) \(\nearrow\) \((2, \infty)\) \(+\) \(-\) \(-\) \(\searrow\)

Step 5: Apply First Derivative Test.

  • \(x = 0\): \(f'\) goes \(- \to +\) → local minimum, \(f(0) = 0 \cdot e^0 = 0\).
  • \(x = 2\): \(f'\) goes \(+ \to -\) → local maximum, \(f(2) = 4e^{-2} \approx 0.541\).

Verification via Second Derivative Test:

\[f''(x) = \frac{d}{dx}\left[x(2-x)e^{-x}\right] = e^{-x}(2 - 4x + x^2)\]
  • \(f''(0) = e^0(2) = 2 > 0\) → local minimum ✓
  • \(f''(2) = e^{-2}(2 - 8 + 4) = -2e^{-2} < 0\) → local maximum ✓

Step 6: Asymptotic behavior.

As \(x \to +\infty\): \(e^{-x} \to 0\) faster than any polynomial grows, so \(f(x) \to 0\). As \(x \to -\infty\): \(e^{-x} \to +\infty\), so \(f(x) \to +\infty\).

f(x) = x²e^{-x}:

      ↑ f
      |
   ↗  |
  /   |             local max (2, 4e⁻²)
 /    |               *
/     |              / \
      |             /   \______________→ 0
      |            /
------*-----------*-----------------------→ x
      0           2
   local min     local max

f(0)=0 (local min), f(2)≈0.541 (local max), f→0 as x→+∞

docs.title: §9. Extrema at Non-Differentiable Points
docs.text: Fermat's theorem only addresses the case where \(f'(c)\) exists. But extrema can live precisely where \(f'\) breaks down. Three common scenarios:

docs.title: 9.1 Corner Points
docs.text:
\(f(x) = |x|\) has a global (and local) minimum at \(x = 0\), where \(f'(0)\) does not exist (left derivative \(= -1\), right derivative \(= +1\)).

The first derivative test still works: \(f'\) changes from \(-1\) (negative) to \(+1\) (positive) — this is a sign change from negative to positive, so it is a local minimum.

docs.title: 9.2 Cusp Points
docs.text: \(f(x) = x^{2/3}\) has a global minimum at \(x = 0\). Here \(f'(x) = \frac{2}{3}x^{-1/3} \to \pm\infty\) as \(x \to 0^\pm\) — the derivative blows up rather than being undefined. Still a critical number, still a local minimum.

docs.title: 9.3 Endpoints (on closed intervals)
docs.text:
On \([a, b]\), the endpoints \(a\) and \(b\) are automatically critical in the sense that the Extreme Value Theorem mandates checking them. The derivative is one-sided at endpoints; Fermat's theorem does not apply.

Corner:         Cusp:           Endpoint:
  /\              |               ___
 /  \            / \             /   |
/    \          /   \           /    |
      (0)      (0)              a    b

f'(0) DNE     f'(0) DNE       f'(a) is one-sided
All three are critical numbers and can be extrema.

docs.title: §10. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
10.1 The Loss Landscape as a High-Dimensional Cousin
docs.text:
In training a neural network with parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^p\) (where \(p\) can be billions), we minimize the loss function \(\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\). The local extreme value theory of one variable is the seed from which the entire theory grows:

One-variable calculus Neural network training Local minimum at \(c\) Converged parameter vector \(\boldsymbol{\theta}^*\) \(f'(c) = 0\) \(\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{L} = \mathbf{0}\) (zero gradient) Critical number Stationary point of \(\mathcal{L}\) Local max / min / saddle Determined by eigenvalues of Hessian \(H = \nabla^2 \mathcal{L}\) \(f''(c) > 0\) → local min All eigenvalues of \(H\) positive → local min \(f''(c) < 0\) → local max All eigenvalues of \(H\) negative → local max \(f''(c) = 0\) → inconclusive Zero eigenvalue → degenerate direction Mixed signs in \(f''\) → impossible in \(\mathbb{R}^1\) Mixed eigenvalues → saddle point (common in \(\mathbb{R}^p\)!)

The Second Derivative Test generalizes to the multivariable second derivative test using the Hessian matrix, which is precisely what MIT 18.02 develops.

docs.title: 10.2 Why Local Minima Are Acceptable in Deep Learning
docs.text:
A profound insight from modern ML theory: not all local minima are created equal, but in overparameterized neural networks, most local minima are acceptable.

The intuition from one-variable calculus: if a function has many local minima but they all have nearly the same function value, then finding any local minimum is as good as finding the global one.

In neural networks:

  • The loss landscape in high dimensions has exponentially many local minima.
  • Empirically, these local minima tend to have similar test performance.
  • The real enemies are saddle points (which do not exist in \(\mathbb{R}^1\)) — gradient descent can stall near them because the gradient is small even though the point is not a minimum.

docs.title: 10.3 Saddle Points — The High-Dimensional Surprise
docs.text:
In \(\mathbb{R}^1\), a critical point with \(f'(c) = 0\) is either a local max, local min, or an inflection point (where \(f'\) doesn't change sign). There is no "saddle point" in one variable in the usual sense.

In \(\mathbb{R}^p\), a saddle point is a stationary point where the Hessian has both positive and negative eigenvalues — it is a minimum in some directions and a maximum in others.

Saddle point of f(x,y) = x² − y²:

      ↑ y
       \   ↑ concave down in y direction
        \  |
    \    \ |   /
     -----*-----→ x
    /     |    \
          | ↑ concave up in x direction

∂f/∂x = 0, ∂f/∂y = 0 at origin.
Hessian = diag(2, −2): one positive, one negative eigenvalue.
→ Saddle point. Neither a max nor a min.

Dauphin et al. (2014) showed that in high-dimensional loss surfaces, saddle points are far more common than local minima: the probability that a random critical point is a local minimum (all Hessian eigenvalues positive) decreases exponentially with dimension. In practice, gradient descent spends most of its time escaping saddle points, not climbing out of local minima.

This is why SGD with noise (stochastic gradient descent) is better than pure gradient descent — the noise provides random perturbations that help escape the flat regions near saddle points.

docs.title: 10.4 The First Derivative Test as Gradient Descent
docs.text:
The First Derivative Test says: follow the sign of \(f'\) to find a local minimum. If \(f' > 0\), decrease \(x\). If \(f' < 0\), increase \(x\). Keep moving until \(f' = 0\).

This is exactly gradient descent: $\(\theta_{n+1} = \theta_n - \eta \cdot f'(\theta_n)\)$

The learning rate \(\eta\) controls how large each step is. The algorithm traces the sign chart we drew in §6 — it follows \(f'\), crossing the \(x\)-axis (critical point) to find the minimum.

Gradient Descent as First Derivative Test:

f'(x) > 0: move left (decrease θ)    f'(x) < 0: move right (increase θ)

         f'(x) > 0     f'(x) < 0
         ←←←←←←←←     →→→→→→→→→
              *         *
        local max    local min ←  gradient descent converges here

The algorithm IS the first derivative test, animated.

docs.title: 10.5 The Second Derivative Test as Newton's Method
docs.text:
The Second Derivative Test is: at a critical point, the sign of \(f''\) determines the type of extremum. Operationally, this corresponds to Newton's method for optimization:

\[\theta_{n+1} = \theta_n - \frac{f'(\theta_n)}{f''(\theta_n)}\]

Newton's method uses the curvature (\(f''\)) to scale the step size. Near a local minimum where \(f''(c) > 0\), the step \(\frac{f'(\theta)}{f''(\theta)}\) points in the right direction and has the right magnitude. This is exactly using the Second Derivative Test to navigate toward the minimum.

In high dimensions, Newton's method becomes: $\(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{n+1} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_n - H^{-1} \nabla \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_n)\)$

where \(H\) is the Hessian. This is the high-dimensional Second Derivative Test applied as an algorithm.

Why don't we use Newton's method in deep learning? Because computing and inverting \(H \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times p}\) costs \(O(p^3)\) operations — with \(p = 10^9\) parameters, this is completely infeasible. Adaptive optimizers (Adam, RMSProp) approximate the diagonal of \(H^{-1}\) cheaply using running averages of squared gradients.

docs.title: 10.6 Critical Points in Loss Curves During Training
docs.text:
When practitioners plot the training loss over time:

Training loss:

 ℒ
 |
 |\ 
 | \        ← rapidly decreasing (f' < 0, steep slope)
 |  \
 |   \___   ← plateau (near a saddle point? f' ≈ 0)
 |       \
 |        \___________   ← convergence (approaching local min)
 |
 +----------------------→ epochs

Each "plateau" corresponds to a region near a critical point.
Escaping plateaus is the hard problem.

The rapid decrease corresponds to being far from any critical point (large \(|f'|\)). Plateaus correspond to being near a saddle point or a "flat" region where \(f'\) is small but not zero. Final convergence is approaching a local minimum where \(f' \approx 0\) and \(f'' > 0\).

docs.title: §11. The Full Logical Architecture
docs.text:
The theorems of this section form a strict logical hierarchy:

MEAN VALUE THEOREM
        |
        ↓
INCREASING/DECREASING TEST
(f' > 0 ⟹ f increasing)
        |
        ↓
FIRST DERIVATIVE TEST
(sign change in f' ⟹ local extremum)
        |
        ↓
SECOND DERIVATIVE TEST
(sign of f''(c) when f'(c)=0 ⟹ type of extremum)

Each lower result depends on the one above it.
MVT is the root of the entire tree.

The Second Derivative Test is not an independent theorem — it is a corollary of the First Derivative Test applied to \(f'\) (using the fact that \(f'' > 0\) implies \(f'\) is increasing, which combined with \(f'(c) = 0\) gives the sign change the First Derivative Test needs).

docs.title: §12. Summary Table
docs.text: Situation Conclusion \(f'(c) = 0\) or DNE \(c\) is a critical number — candidate for extremum \(f\) has local extremum at \(c\), \(f'(c)\) exists \(f'(c) = 0\) (Fermat) \(f'\) changes \(+ \to -\) at \(c\) Local maximum at \(c\) \(f'\) changes \(- \to +\) at \(c\) Local minimum at \(c\) \(f'\) doesn't change sign at \(c\) No extremum at \(c\) \(f'(c) = 0\), \(f''(c) > 0\) Local minimum at \(c\) \(f'(c) = 0\), \(f''(c) < 0\) Local maximum at \(c\) \(f'(c) = 0\), \(f''(c) = 0\) Inconclusive — use First Derivative Test \(f\) continuous on \([a,b]\) Absolute extrema exist (EVT)

docs.title: §13. Why the Hypotheses Matter — Edge Cases
docs.text:
Continuity is essential in the First Derivative Test. If \(f\) is discontinuous at \(c\), the sign change of \(f'\) does not guarantee an extremum. Consider:

\[f(x) = \begin{cases} x & x < 0 \ x + 2 & x \geq 0 \end{cases}\]

\(f'(x) = 1\) everywhere it exists — no sign change, no critical number. But this is a jump discontinuity, not an extremum example. More pathologically, one can construct functions where \(f'\) changes sign but \(f\) jumps over the "extremum."

Fermat's theorem requires \(f'(c)\) to exist. When \(f'(c)\) DNE, Fermat says nothing — but \(c\) is still a critical number and must still be checked for extrema (by the definition of critical number, not by Fermat).

The Second Derivative Test requires \(f''\) to be continuous near \(c\). If \(f''\) is discontinuous, the proof that \(f'\) changes sign breaks down.

These hypotheses are not bureaucratic fine print — they are load-bearing walls. Every calculus proof is only as strong as the hypotheses it rests on.
