docs.title: What Does f'' Say About f'
docs.text: "The second derivative is the derivative of the derivative — but it speaks a deeper language: it tells you how fast the slope itself is changing." — Personal note, drawn from Stewart §4.3 and MIT 18.02

docs.title: 0. Setup & Notation
docs.text:
Let \(f : I \to \mathbb{R}\) be twice differentiable on an open interval \(I\). Define:

\[f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}, \qquad f''(x) = (f')'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f'(x+h) - f'(x)}{h}\]

The question is: what does knowing \(f''\) tell us about \(f'\)?

The answer operates on two levels:

  1. Analytical: \(f''\) is the rate of change of \(f'\) — just as \(f'\) is the rate of change of \(f\).
  2. Geometric: \(f''\) controls the concavity of \(f\), i.e., whether the slope \(f'\) is increasing or decreasing.

docs.title: 1. The Fundamental Relationship: \(f''\) as the Rate of Change of \(f'\)
Theorem 1.1 (Sign of \(f''\) and Monotonicity of \(f'\))
docs.text:
Let \(f\) be twice differentiable on \((a, b)\).

  • If \(f''(x) > 0\) for all \(x \in (a, b)\), then \(f'\) is strictly increasing on \((a, b)\).
  • If \(f''(x) < 0\) for all \(x \in (a, b)\), then \(f'\) is strictly decreasing on \((a, b)\).
  • If \(f''(x) = 0\) for all \(x \in (a, b)\), then \(f'\) is constant on \((a, b)\) (i.e., \(f\) is linear).

Proof. Apply the First Derivative Test to \(f'\): since \((f')' = f''\), the sign of \(f''\) determines whether \(f'\) is monotone, by the standard theorem that a positive derivative implies a strictly increasing function. \(\blacksquare\)

This is the core insight. Everything else follows from this.

docs.title: Definition 2.1 (Concavity)
docs.text:
\(f\) is concave up on \((a, b)\) if for all \(x, y \in (a,b)\) and \(t \in (0,1)\): $\(f(tx + (1-t)y) \leq t f(x) + (1-t)f(y)\)$

Geometrically: the chord lies above the curve. The tangent lines lie below the curve.

\(f\) is concave down if the reverse inequality holds.

docs.title: Theorem 2.2 (Second Derivative Test for Concavity) (Stewart §4.3)
docs.text:
• \(f''(x) > 0\) on \((a,b)\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(f\) is concave up on \((a,b)\).
  • \(f''(x) < 0\) on \((a,b)\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(f\) is concave down on \((a,b)\).

Proof sketch. Fix \(c \in (a,b)\). The tangent line at \(c\) is \(L(x) = f(c) + f'(c)(x-c)\). Define \(g(x) = f(x) - L(x)\). Then \(g(c) = 0\), \(g'(c) = 0\), and \(g''(x) = f''(x) > 0\). By Theorem 1.1, \(g'\) is increasing near \(c\). Since \(g'(c) = 0\): \(g'(x) < 0\) for \(x < c\) and \(g'(x) > 0\) for \(x > c\) near \(c\). So \(g\) has a local minimum at \(c\), hence \(g(x) \geq g(c) = 0\). This means \(f(x) \geq L(x)\): the tangent line lies below \(f\). \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: Visualization
docs.text:
Concave Up (f'' > 0):          Concave Down (f'' < 0):
f' is INCREASING                f' is DECREASING

     *                           *       *
   *   *                           *   *
  *     *                            *
 *       *

slope gets steeper ↗            slope gets flatter ↘
tangent lines rotate CCW        tangent lines rotate CW

ASCII slope arrows along \(f(x) = x^2\) (concave up everywhere):

x = -2: slope = -4  ↘ steep
x = -1: slope = -2  ↘ mild
x =  0: slope =  0  →
x =  1: slope =  2  ↗ mild
x =  2: slope =  4  ↗ steep

The slopes are increasing \((-4, -2, 0, 2, 4)\) — exactly what \(f'' = 2 > 0\) predicts.

docs.title: Definition 3.1 (Inflection Point)
docs.text:
A point \(c\) is an inflection point of \(f\) if:

  1. \(f\) is continuous at \(c\), and
  2. \(f''\) changes sign at \(c\) (concavity reverses).

Critical nuance: \(f''(c) = 0\) is necessary but not sufficient for an inflection point.

docs.title: Example 3.2 (The Classic Failure)
docs.text:
\[f(x) = x^4, \quad f''(x) = 12x^2\]

\(f''(0) = 0\), yet \(f''\) does not change sign at \(0\) — it remains \(\geq 0\) everywhere. So \(x = 0\) is not an inflection point. The curve is concave up on all of \(\mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: Example 3.3 (Genuine Inflection)
docs.text:
\[f(x) = x^3, \quad f'(x) = 3x^2, \quad f''(x) = 6x\]
  • \(f''(x) < 0\) for \(x < 0\): concave down, \(f'\) is decreasing.
  • \(f''(0) = 0\): inflection point.
  • \(f''(x) > 0\) for \(x > 0\): concave up, \(f'\) is increasing.

The slope \(f'(x) = 3x^2\) reaches its minimum at \(x = 0\) (it decreases then increases), consistent with \(f''\) changing from \(-\) to \(+\).

docs.title: 4. The Second Derivative Test for Local Extrema
docs.text: This is perhaps the most used consequence. It exploits \(f''\)'s information about \(f'\) near a critical point.

docs.title: Theorem 4.1 (Second Derivative Test) (Stewart §4.3)
docs.text:
Suppose \(f'(c) = 0\) and \(f''(c)\) exists.

  • If \(f''(c) > 0\): \(f\) has a local minimum at \(c\).
  • If \(f''(c) < 0\): \(f\) has a local maximum at \(c\).
  • If \(f''(c) = 0\): the test is inconclusive.

Proof. If \(f'(c) = 0\) and \(f''(c) > 0\): by continuity of \(f''\), there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that \(f''(x) > 0\) on \((c - \delta, c + \delta)\). By Theorem 1.1, \(f'\) is increasing on this interval. Since \(f'(c) = 0\):

  • For \(x \in (c-\delta, c)\): \(f'(x) < f'(c) = 0\), so \(f\) is decreasing.
  • For \(x \in (c, c+\delta)\): \(f'(x) > f'(c) = 0\), so \(f\) is increasing.

Hence \(f(c)\) is a local minimum. \(\blacksquare\)

Why the test fails when \(f''(c) = 0\): Consider \(f(x) = x^4\) (local min at 0), \(g(x) = -x^4\) (local max at 0), \(h(x) = x^3\) (saddle/inflection at 0). All have \(f''(0) = 0\).

docs.title: 5. A Summary Table
docs.text: Condition \(f'\) behavior \(f\) shape Language \(f'' > 0\) on \((a,b)\) \(f'\) increasing Concave up "Bowl" shape \(f'' < 0\) on \((a,b)\) \(f'\) decreasing Concave down "Cap" shape \(f'' = 0\) everywhere \(f'\) constant Linear Straight line \(f''\) changes sign at \(c\) \(f'\) has local extremum at \(c\) Inflection point Slope reversal \(f'(c)=0\), \(f''(c)>0\) \(f'\) crosses zero upward at \(c\) Local minimum of \(f\) \(f'(c)=0\), \(f''(c)<0\) \(f'\) crosses zero downward at \(c\) Local maximum of \(f\)

docs.title: 6. Worked Example: Complete Analysis of \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x\)
docs.text:
(This is the standard example from Stewart §4.3 and MIT 18.02)

\[f(x) = x^3 - 3x$$ $$f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 = 3(x-1)(x+1)$$ $$f''(x) = 6x\]

Step 1. Critical points: \(f'(x) = 0 \Rightarrow x = \pm 1\).

Step 2. Apply Second Derivative Test:

  • \(f''(-1) = -6 < 0\): local maximum at \(x = -1\), value \(f(-1) = 2\).
  • \(f''(1) = 6 > 0\): local minimum at \(x = 1\), value \(f(1) = -2\).

Step 3. Concavity and inflection:

  • \(f''(x) < 0\) for \(x < 0\): concave down (slope decreasing).
  • \(f''(0) = 0\) and sign change: inflection point at \(x = 0\).
  • \(f''(x) > 0\) for \(x > 0\): concave up (slope increasing).

Sketch of \(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3\) alongside \(f''(x) = 6x\):

f'(x):                     f''(x):
      *           *                   /
       *         *              -----/-----
        *       *              /
         *     *          (f'' = 0 at origin)
          *   *
           * *
            *   ← minimum of f' at x=0
                  (where f'' changes sign)

The minimum of \(f'\) occurs at \(x = 0\), which is precisely where \(f'' = 0\) and changes sign. This is the inflection point of \(f\). Perfect consistency.

docs.title: 7. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: This is not a detour — this is where the second derivative becomes genuinely powerful in modern computational mathematics.

docs.title: 7.1 Gradient Descent and the Role of \(f''\)
docs.text:
In machine learning, we minimize a loss function \(\mathcal{L}(\theta)\) over parameters \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}^n\). The standard update rule is:

\[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta_t)\]

This uses only \(\nabla \mathcal{L}\) (the first derivative). But the curvature — governed by \(f''\) — critically affects convergence:

  • If \(f'' \gg 0\) (high curvature): a fixed learning rate \(\eta\) causes oscillation or divergence.
  • If \(f'' \approx 0\) (flat region): gradient descent moves painfully slowly.

The ideal step size at each point is \(\eta \approx \frac{1}{f''(x)}\) — larger curvature demands a smaller step.

docs.title: 7.2 Newton's Method: Explicitly Using \(f''\)
docs.text:
Newton's method for optimization is:

\[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \frac{f'(\theta_t)}{f''(\theta_t)}\]

In higher dimensions, this becomes: $\(\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - H^{-1} \nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta_t)\)$

where \(H = \nabla^2 \mathcal{L}\) is the Hessian matrix — the multivariable analogue of \(f''\). Each entry \(H_{ij} = \frac{\partial^2 \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta_i \partial \theta_j}\) describes how the gradient in direction \(i\) changes as you move in direction \(j\).

Newton's method converges quadratically (vs. linearly for gradient descent) because it accounts for curvature. The cost: computing and inverting \(H\) for a network with \(n\) parameters is \(O(n^2)\) storage and \(O(n^3)\) inversion — infeasible for modern deep networks with \(n \sim 10^9\).

docs.title: 7.3 Saddle Points in Deep Learning
docs.text:
A critical point where \(f'(c) = 0\) but \(f''(c) = 0\) is called a saddle point in higher dimensions (or inflection-type point in 1D). In the loss landscapes of deep neural networks:

  • Local minima are relatively rare in high dimensions.
  • Saddle points are ubiquitous — the gradient vanishes, the Hessian has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

Standard gradient descent can get stuck near saddle points because the gradient becomes tiny. This is one reason why momentum methods (Adam, RMSProp) were developed — they use accumulated gradient history to escape flat regions.

The sign of \(f''\) (or eigenvalues of the Hessian) determines whether a critical point is:

  • A minimum: all eigenvalues \(> 0\) (positive definite Hessian — \(f''\)-analogue)
  • A maximum: all eigenvalues \(< 0\)
  • A saddle: mixed signs

docs.title: 7.4 Convexity and Loss Landscapes
docs.text:
A function \(\mathcal{L}\) is convex if and only if \(f''(\theta) \geq 0\) everywhere (in 1D). Convexity guarantees:

  • Every local minimum is a global minimum.
  • Gradient descent converges to the global optimum.

Deep neural network loss functions are highly non-convex — \(f''\) changes sign constantly, creating a rugged landscape of hills, valleys, and saddle points. Understanding where \(f'' > 0\) vs. \(f'' < 0\) in parameter space is an active research problem (loss landscape geometry).

docs.title: 7.5 Second-Order Optimization Methods in Practice
docs.text:
Method Uses \(f'\)? Uses \(f''\) (Hessian)? Notes Gradient Descent ✓ ✗ Slow, simple Momentum / Adam ✓ Approximate Most common in deep learning Newton's Method ✓ ✓ (exact) Fast convergence, expensive L-BFGS ✓ ✓ (approximate) Used in small-scale ML, scipy Natural Gradient ✓ ✓ (Fisher info) Theoretically principled

The tension between using \(f''\) for faster convergence vs. the computational cost of computing it is a central theme of modern optimization.

docs.title: 8. Rigorous Note: The Converse and Edge Cases
docs.text:
Remark 8.1. The converse of Theorem 2.2 is false: a function can be concave up at a point where \(f''(c) = 0\). Example: \(f(x) = x^4\) is concave up on all of \(\mathbb{R}\), yet \(f''(0) = 0\).

Remark 8.2. A function can have an inflection point where \(f''\) fails to exist. Example: \(f(x) = x^{1/3}\) has an inflection at \(x = 0\) but \(f''(0)\) does not exist.

Remark 8.3. The condition "\(f''\) changes sign" is the correct definition of inflection — not merely "\(f''(c) = 0\)". Always verify sign change.

docs.title: L'Hopital's Rule
docs.text: "An indeterminate form is not a number — it is a competition. Two tendencies fight each other, and the limit is the outcome of that fight. L'Hôpital's rule is the referee." — Personal note, drawn from Stewart §4.4 and MIT 18.02

docs.title: 0. Motivation: Why "0/0" Is Not Zero
docs.text:
Consider the innocent-looking limit: $\(\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x}\)$

If you naively substitute \(x = 0\): you get \(\frac{0}{0}\). This is not the number zero. It is not \(1\). It is not undefined in the sense of "no limit exists." It is indeterminate — the symbol \(\frac{0}{0}\) carries no information about the actual limiting value. The answer could be anything: \(1\), \(5\), \(\infty\), or the limit may not exist.

Indeed, \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1\), while \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{5x}{x} = 5\), and \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{x^2}{x} = 0\) — all of the form \(\frac{0}{0}\).

The form itself tells you nothing. That is the point.

docs.title: 1. The Complete Taxonomy of Indeterminate Forms
docs.text:
There are seven indeterminate forms. All others reduce to one of these.

Form Symbol Intuition Quotient \(\dfrac{0}{0}\) Small over small — race to zero Quotient \(\dfrac{\infty}{\infty}\) Large over large — race to infinity Product \(0 \cdot \infty\) Tiny times huge — who wins? Difference \(\infty - \infty\) Two infinities cancel — how much? Power \(0^0\) Zero base, zero exponent Power \(1^\infty\) Base approaching 1, exponent exploding Power \(\infty^0\) Infinite base, vanishing exponent

Non-indeterminate forms (these have definite values):

Form Value \(\frac{0}{\infty}\) \(0\) (tiny over huge = zero) \(\frac{\infty}{0}\) \(\infty\) (huge over tiny = blow up) \(0^\infty\) \(0\) \(\infty^\infty\) \(\infty\) \(\infty + \infty\) \(\infty\)

Memorize this distinction. The non-indeterminate forms require no tools — just logic.

docs.title: 2. L'Hôpital's Rule: Statement and Proof Sketch
Theorem 2.1 (L'Hôpital's Rule) (Stewart §4.4)
docs.text:
Suppose \(f\) and \(g\) are differentiable on an open interval containing \(a\) (except possibly at \(a\) itself), and \(g'(x) \neq 0\) near \(a\). If $\(\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \lim_{x \to a} g(x) = 0\)$ or $\(\lim_{x \to a} |f(x)| = \infty \quad \text{and} \quad \lim_{x \to a} |g(x)| = \infty\)$ then: $\(\lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}\)$ provided the right-hand limit exists (or is \(\pm\infty\)). The theorem holds equally for one-sided limits and for \(a = \pm\infty\).

The rule applies only to \(\frac{0}{0}\) and \(\frac{\infty}{\infty}\) directly. All other indeterminate forms must first be algebraically converted to one of these two.

docs.title: Proof Sketch (for \(\frac{0}{0}\), \(a\) finite)
docs.text:
Extend \(f\) and \(g\) by setting \(f(a) = g(a) = 0\), making them continuous at \(a\). Apply the Cauchy Mean Value Theorem: for any \(x \neq a\), there exists \(c\) between \(x\) and \(a\) such that:

\[\frac{f(x) - f(a)}{g(x) - g(a)} = \frac{f'(c)}{g'(c)}\]

Since \(f(a) = g(a) = 0\), this gives \(\dfrac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \dfrac{f'(c)}{g'(c)}\).

As \(x \to a\), \(c \to a\) (it is squeezed between \(x\) and \(a\)), so: $\(\lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{c \to a} \frac{f'(c)}{g'(c)} = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)} \qquad \blacksquare\)$

Key insight: L'Hôpital's rule is not "differentiate the fraction." It is "differentiate numerator and denominator separately and form a new fraction." This is not the quotient rule.

docs.title: 3. Applying the Rule: The Two Direct Forms
3.1 The \(\frac{0}{0}\) Form
docs.text:
Example 3.1. \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x}\)

Check: \(\sin 0 = 0\), \(0 = 0\). Form is \(\frac{0}{0}\). ✓

\[\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} \overset{H}{=} \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\cos x}{1} = \cos 0 = \boxed{1}\]

Example 3.2. \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 1} \frac{x^3 - 1}{x - 1}\)

Form \(\frac{0}{0}\): $\(\overset{H}{=} \lim_{x \to 1} \frac{3x^2}{1} = 3\)$

(Cross-check: factor as \((x-1)(x^2+x+1)/(x-1) = x^2+x+1 \to 3\). Consistent.)

Example 3.3 (Apply twice). \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^x - 1 - x}{x^2}\)

Form \(\frac{0}{0}\): $\(\overset{H}{=} \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^x - 1}{2x} \quad \left(\frac{0}{0}\text{ again}\right) \overset{H}{=} \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^x}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\)$

This is deeply related to the Taylor expansion: \(e^x = 1 + x + \frac{x^2}{2} + \cdots\), so \(\frac{e^x - 1 - x}{x^2} \to \frac{1}{2}\).

docs.title: 3.2 The \(\frac{\infty}{\infty}\) Form
docs.text:
Example 3.4. \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\ln x}{x}\)

Form \(\frac{\infty}{\infty}\): $\(\overset{H}{=} \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{1/x}{1} = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{1}{x} = 0\)$

Conclusion: logarithms grow slower than any positive power of \(x\). This is a fundamental fact in analysis and algorithm theory.

Example 3.5. \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{e^x}{x^n}\) for any fixed \(n \in \mathbb{N}\)

Apply L'Hôpital \(n\) times: $\(\frac{e^x}{x^n} \to \frac{e^x}{nx^{n-1}} \to \frac{e^x}{n(n-1)x^{n-2}} \to \cdots \to \frac{e^x}{n!} \to \infty\)$

Conclusion: \(e^x\) grows faster than any polynomial. Every time you differentiate, you get another \(e^x\) on top — the exponential is inexhaustible.

docs.title: Hierarchy of Growth Rates (from these examples)
docs.text:
\[\ln x \ll x^a \ll e^x \ll e^{x^2} \qquad \text{as } x \to \infty\]

for any \(a > 0\). This ordering is provable entirely via L'Hôpital applied to \(\frac{\infty}{\infty}\) forms.

docs.title: 4. Converting the Other Five Forms
docs.text: The remaining five indeterminate forms must be rewritten into \(\frac{0}{0}\) or \(\frac{\infty}{\infty}\) before applying the rule.

docs.title: 4.1 Form \(0 \cdot \infty\): Rewrite as a Fraction
docs.text:
If \(\lim f = 0\) and \(\lim g = \infty\): $\(f \cdot g = \frac{f}{1/g} \quad \left(\frac{0}{0}\right) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f \cdot g = \frac{g}{1/f} \quad \left(\frac{\infty}{\infty}\right)\)$

Choose whichever gives a cleaner derivative.

Example 4.1. \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0^+} x \ln x\)

Form \(0 \cdot (-\infty)\). Write \(x \ln x = \dfrac{\ln x}{1/x}\), form \(\frac{-\infty}{\infty}\):

\[\overset{H}{=} \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{1/x}{-1/x^2} = \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{1/x \cdot x^2}{-1} = \lim_{x \to 0^+} (-x) = 0\]

So \(x \ln x \to 0\) as \(x \to 0^+\). The zero "wins" over the logarithm.

This means \(f(x) = x \ln x\) extends continuously to \(f(0) = 0\) — a useful fact in entropy calculations.

docs.title: 4.2 Form \(\infty - \infty\): Combine into a Single Fraction
docs.text:
Example 4.2. \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \left(\frac{1}{\sin x} - \frac{1}{x}\right)\)

Form \(\infty - \infty\). Combine: $\(= \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{x - \sin x}{x \sin x} \quad \left(\frac{0}{0}\right)\)$

\[\overset{H}{=} \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1 - \cos x}{\sin x + x \cos x} \quad \left(\frac{0}{0}\right)\] \[\overset{H}{=} \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{2\cos x - x \sin x} = \frac{0}{2} = 0\]

docs.title: 4.3 Power Forms \(0^0\), \(1^\infty\), \(\infty^0\): Take the Logarithm
docs.text:
Strategy: If \(L = \lim f(x)^{g(x)}\), then \(\ln L = \lim g(x) \ln f(x)\), which is a \(0 \cdot \infty\) form — handled by §4.1.

Example 4.3 (\(1^\infty\)). \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} (1 + x)^{1/x}\)

Let \(L = \lim_{x \to 0}(1+x)^{1/x}\). Then: $\(\ln L = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\ln(1+x)}{x} \quad \left(\frac{0}{0}\right) \overset{H}{=} \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1/(1+x)}{1} = 1\)$

So \(\ln L = 1\), hence \(L = e^1 = e\). This is the definition of \(e\) as a limit.

Example 4.4 (\(0^0\)). \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0^+} x^x\)

\[\ln L = \lim_{x \to 0^+} x \ln x = 0 \quad \text{(from Example 4.1)}\]

So \(L = e^0 = 1\).

Example 4.5 (\(\infty^0\)). \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} x^{1/x}\)

\[\ln L = \lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\ln x}{x} = 0 \quad \text{(from Example 3.4)}\]

So \(L = e^0 = 1\).

docs.title: Warning 5.1: Check the Form First
docs.text:
L'Hôpital's rule applies only when the limit is genuinely indeterminate. Never apply it otherwise.

Wrong: $\(\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x + x}{x + 2} \overset{???}{=} \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\cos x + 1}{1} = 2\)$

The original limit: substitute \(x = 0\): \(\frac{0 + 0}{0 + 2} = \frac{0}{2} = 0\). Not indeterminate. The correct answer is \(0\), not \(2\). L'Hôpital gave the wrong answer here.

docs.title: Warning 5.2: Circular Reasoning for \(\frac{\sin x}{x}\)
docs.text: The proof that \(\frac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x\) uses \(\lim_{x\to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1\). Using L'Hôpital to prove that same limit is circular. The limit \(\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1\) must be established geometrically first (squeeze theorem), then used to derive the derivative of \(\sin x\).

docs.title: Warning 5.3: The New Limit Must Exist
docs.text:
The theorem states: apply L'Hôpital if \(\lim \frac{f'}{g'}\) exists. If it does not exist, this does not mean the original limit fails to exist — the original might still converge.

Example 5.3. \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{x + \sin x}{x}\)

Form \(\frac{\infty}{\infty}\). Attempting L'Hôpital: \(\frac{1 + \cos x}{1}\), which oscillates — no limit. Yet the original: \(\frac{x + \sin x}{x} = 1 + \frac{\sin x}{x} \to 1\). The original limit exists even though L'Hôpital fails. The rule's hypothesis was not satisfied (the derivative ratio has no limit), so the rule simply does not apply — this is not a contradiction.

docs.title: Warning 5.4: Don't Loop Forever
docs.text:
Sometimes repeated application of L'Hôpital cycles back to the original form. Recognize this and use algebra instead.

Example 5.4. \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{e^x + e^{-x}}{e^x - e^{-x}}\)

Applying L'Hôpital: \(\frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{e^x + e^{-x}}\) — the numerator and denominator have swapped. The rule will cycle indefinitely. Instead, divide numerator and denominator by \(e^x\): $\(\frac{1 + e^{-2x}}{1 - e^{-2x}} \to \frac{1 + 0}{1 - 0} = 1\)$

docs.title: 6. Visualization: The \(\frac{0}{0}\) Race
docs.text:
Think of \(\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\) with \(f(0) = g(0) = 0\) as asking: which function reaches zero faster?

Both start at 0 when x = 0.

f(x) = x²:    ●━━━━━━━━━━━━━━○   (reaches 0 quadratically — fast)
g(x) = x:     ●━━━━━━━━━━━━━━○   (reaches 0 linearly — slow)

Ratio x²/x = x → 0:   f reaches 0 much faster, so the ratio → 0.

f(x) = x:     ●━━━━━━━━━━━━━━○   (linear)
g(x) = x:     ●━━━━━━━━━━━━━━○   (same speed)

Ratio x/x = 1 → 1:    Dead heat.

f(x) = x:     ●━━━━━━━━━━━━━━○   (linear — slow)
g(x) = x³:   ●━━━━━━━━━━━━━━○   (cubic — fast)

Ratio x/x³ = 1/x² → ∞:  g reaches 0 far faster, ratio blows up.

L'Hôpital measures this "speed comparison" via the ratio of instantaneous rates at the collision point.

docs.title: 7. Connection to Taylor Series: The Deep Reason L'Hôpital Works
docs.text:
L'Hôpital's rule is, at its core, a corollary of first-order Taylor approximation.

Near \(x = a\): $\(f(x) \approx f(a) + f'(a)(x-a), \qquad g(x) \approx g(a) + g'(a)(x-a)\)$

If \(f(a) = g(a) = 0\): $\(\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} \approx \frac{f'(a)(x-a)}{g'(a)(x-a)} = \frac{f'(a)}{g'(a)}\)$

This is exactly L'Hôpital evaluated at \(a\). The \((x - a)\) factors cancel, which is the algebraic reason the rule works.

When \(f'(a) = g'(a) = 0\) too: you need second-order terms — apply L'Hôpital again. Each application peels off one order of the Taylor expansion.

Example 7.1. \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{1 - \cos x}{x^2}\)

Taylor: \(1 - \cos x = \frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{x^4}{24} + \cdots\)

\[\frac{1 - \cos x}{x^2} \approx \frac{x^2/2}{x^2} = \frac{1}{2}\]

Via L'Hôpital twice: \(\frac{\sin x}{2x} \to \frac{\cos x}{2} \to \frac{1}{2}\). ✓

docs.title: 8. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: Indeterminate forms appear throughout the mathematics of ML — often invisibly, inside definitions and derivations that practitioners take for granted.

docs.title: 8.1 Entropy and the \(0 \cdot \ln 0 = 0\) Convention
docs.text:
In information theory, the entropy of a discrete distribution \(p = (p_1, \ldots, p_n)\) is: $\(H(p) = -\sum_{i=1}^n p_i \ln p_i\)$

When \(p_i = 0\), the term \(0 \cdot \ln 0\) is the indeterminate form \(0 \cdot (-\infty)\).

Using Example 4.1: \(\lim_{p \to 0^+} p \ln p = 0\). So the convention \(0 \ln 0 := 0\) is not arbitrary — it is the exact limit, ensuring entropy is continuous at zero probabilities.

This matters in:

  • Cross-entropy loss: \(\mathcal{L} = -\sum_i y_i \log \hat{p}_i\) — if the model outputs \(\hat{p}_i = 0\) for a true class (\(y_i = 1\)), the loss is \(\infty\). This is why softmax outputs are numerically clipped or log-sum-exp stabilized.
  • KL divergence: \(D_{KL}(P | Q) = \sum_i P_i \ln \frac{P_i}{Q_i)}\). The form \(0/0\) under the log requires the convention \(0 \ln(0/0) = 0\).

docs.title: 8.2 Softmax and the \(\frac{\infty}{\infty}\) Form
docs.text:
The softmax function is: $\(\sigma_i(\mathbf{z}) = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}\)$

When logits \(z_i \to \infty\), this is the \(\frac{\infty}{\infty}\) form. L'Hôpital's intuition (the dominant term "wins") justifies the fact that softmax converges to a one-hot distribution as logits become extreme. More rigorously, after dividing numerator and denominator by \(e^{\max_j z_j}\), the form resolves — exactly the algebraic technique of §5.4.

Numerical overflow in softmax is a practical manifestation of \(\frac{\infty}{\infty}\): computing \(e^{700}\) overflows float32. The standard fix — subtracting \(\max z_j\) — is precisely the algebraic manipulation that resolves the indeterminate form before evaluating numerically.

docs.title: 8.3 The \(\frac{0}{0}\) Form in Gradient Derivations
docs.text:
Many activation function gradients are defined as limits that hide \(\frac{0}{0}\) forms:

Sinc activation: \(\text{sinc}(x) = \frac{\sin x}{x}\), defined as \(1\) at \(x = 0\) by taking the limit (Example 3.1).

Derivative of ReLU at 0: \(\text{ReLU}(x) = \max(0, x)\) is not differentiable at \(0\) — the left and right derivatives disagree (\(0\) vs \(1\)). In practice, subgradient methods assign \(0\) or \(1\) arbitrarily. The reason we cannot resolve this via L'Hôpital is that the limit \(\lim_{h\to 0} \frac{\text{ReLU}(h) - \text{ReLU}(0)}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{h}{h} = 1 \neq \lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{0}{h} = 0\) — the one-sided limits disagree. Not an indeterminate form problem; a genuine discontinuity in the derivative.

docs.title: 8.4 L'Hôpital-Type Reasoning in Neural Scaling Laws
docs.text:
The empirical neural scaling laws (Kaplan et al., OpenAI) describe how loss \(\mathcal{L}\) behaves as compute \(C \to \infty\): $\(\mathcal{L}(C) \sim C^{-\alpha}\)$

Comparing growth rates of different architectures involves limits of the form \(\frac{C^{-\alpha}}{C^{-\beta}}\) as \(C \to \infty\) — \(\frac{0}{0}\) forms. L'Hôpital (equivalently, the growth hierarchy from §3) resolves these: the architecture with larger \(\alpha\) dominates (loses slower = better). The mathematical structure is identical to Example 3.4.

docs.title: 8.5 The Gumbel-Softmax and \(0^0\)
docs.text:
The Gumbel-Softmax trick (for differentiable discrete sampling) involves: $\(y_i = \frac{e^{(\log p_i + g_i)/\tau}}{\sum_j e^{(\log p_j + g_j)/\tau}}\)$

As temperature \(\tau \to 0\), this approaches a one-hot sample. The limiting form involves \(e^{z/\tau}\) as \(\tau \to 0^+\) — an \(e^\infty = \infty^1\) competition — and the analysis reduces to comparing exponential growth rates, exactly the \(\frac{\infty}{\infty}\) framework.

docs.title: 9. Summary
docs.text:
Form Strategy Key example \(\frac{0}{0}\) Direct L'Hôpital \(\frac{\sin x}{x} \to 1\) \(\frac{\infty}{\infty}\) Direct L'Hôpital \(\frac{\ln x}{x} \to 0\) \(0 \cdot \infty\) Write as \(\frac{f}{1/g}\) \(x \ln x \to 0\) \(\infty - \infty\) Combine into fraction \(\frac{1}{\sin x} - \frac{1}{x} \to 0\) \(0^0, 1^\infty, \infty^0\) Take \(\ln\), reduce to \(0 \cdot \infty\) \((1+x)^{1/x} \to e\)

The golden rule: L'Hôpital applies only when the form is genuinely \(\frac{0}{0}\) or \(\frac{\infty}{\infty}\). Everything else is algebra first, limit second.

The deep reason it works: Taylor expansion. Each application of L'Hôpital peels one order off the Taylor series, revealing the dominant term.

docs.title: 10. References
docs.text:
1. James Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. — §4.4 "Indeterminate Forms and L'Hôpital's Rule" (primary source for all seven forms, theorem statement, and worked examples)
  2. MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus — Lecture notes on limits, Taylor approximations, and indeterminate forms in higher dimensions

docs.title: Curve Sketching
docs.text: "A picture is worth a thousand symbols — but only if you know what to look for."

docs.title: Preface: Why Bother Sketching?
docs.text:
Before numerical solvers and plotting libraries existed, mathematicians had to understand a function before they could draw it. Curve sketching is the discipline of extracting the complete qualitative story of \(f(x)\) from its formula alone — without evaluating hundreds of points. It is, at its heart, a systematic interrogation of a function.

This note follows the classical treatment of Stewart §4.5 and the spirit of MIT 18.02, building up the full algorithmic pipeline from domain analysis to asymptotic behavior to the precise shape of local extrema.

docs.title: The Seven-Step Protocol
docs.text:
Given \(f: D \subseteq \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\), a complete sketch requires answering these questions in order:

Step Question Tool 1 Where is \(f\) defined? Domain analysis 2 Does \(f\) have symmetry? Even/odd test 3 Where does \(f\) cross the axes? Intercepts 4 What happens at the boundary of \(D\)? Asymptotes 5 Where is \(f\) increasing/decreasing? Sign of \(f'\) 6 Where are the peaks and valleys? Critical points + 1st/2nd derivative test 7 Where does \(f\) bend? Sign of \(f''\), inflection points

Work through all seven before committing a single curve to paper.

docs.title: Step 1 — Domain
docs.text:
The domain \(D\) is the maximal subset of \(\mathbb{R}\) on which \(f(x)\) is defined. Standard obstructions:

  • Division by zero: \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x-2}\) excludes \(x = 2\).
  • Even roots of negatives: \(f(x) = \sqrt{x^2-1}\) requires \(|x| \geq 1\).
  • Logarithms: \(f(x) = \ln(x)\) requires \(x > 0\).

Principle. Determine the domain first. Every subsequent step is restricted to \(D\).

docs.title: Step 2 — Symmetry
docs.text:
Definition. A function \(f\) is:

  • Even if \(f(-x) = f(x)\) for all \(x \in D\) (symmetric about the \(y\)-axis).
  • Odd if \(f(-x) = -f(x)\) for all \(x \in D\) (symmetric about the origin).

Exploiting symmetry reduces the domain you need to analyze by half — sketch on \([0, \infty)\), then reflect.

Examples:

  • \(f(x) = x^4 - 3x^2 + 1\) is even (all even powers).
  • \(f(x) = x^3 - x\) is odd (all odd powers).
  • \(f(x) = x^3 + x^2\) is neither.

docs.title: Step 3 — Intercepts
docs.text:
\(y\)-intercept: Set \(x = 0\), compute \(f(0)\) (only if \(0 \in D\)).

\(x\)-intercepts (zeros): Solve \(f(x) = 0\). This can be hard in general; use what algebra allows.

Remark. Do not spend excessive time hunting zeros unless they are obvious. The shape of the curve matters more than precise root locations for a sketch.

docs.title: 4.1 Vertical Asymptotes
docs.text:
\(x = a\) is a vertical asymptote if \(\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = \pm\infty\) or \(\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = \pm\infty\).

Candidates: points where the denominator vanishes and the numerator does not.

Example. \(f(x) = \frac{x}{x^2-1}\). The denominator vanishes at \(x = \pm 1\).

\[\lim_{x \to 1^+} \frac{x}{x^2-1} = +\infty, \qquad \lim_{x \to 1^-} \frac{x}{x^2-1} = -\infty\]

So \(x = 1\) is a vertical asymptote (similarly \(x = -1\)).

docs.title: 4.2 Horizontal Asymptotes
docs.text:
\(y = L\) is a horizontal asymptote if \(\lim_{x \to \pm\infty} f(x) = L\).

Rational function rule: $\(f(x) = \frac{a_n x^n + \cdots}{b_m x^m + \cdots} \implies \begin{cases} y = 0 & n < m \ y = a_n/b_m & n = m \ \text{no H.A.} & n > m \end{cases}\)$

docs.title: 4.3 Oblique (Slant) Asymptotes
docs.text:
When the degree of the numerator exceeds the denominator by exactly 1, divide:

\[f(x) = \frac{x^2 + 1}{x - 1} = x + 1 + \frac{2}{x-1}\]

The line \(y = x + 1\) is an oblique asymptote as \(x \to \pm\infty\).

docs.title: Step 5 — Intervals of Increase and Decrease
docs.text:
Theorem (Monotonicity Test). Let \(f\) be differentiable on \((a,b)\).

  • If \(f'(x) > 0\) on \((a,b)\), then \(f\) is strictly increasing on \([a,b]\).
  • If \(f'(x) < 0\) on \((a,b)\), then \(f\) is strictly decreasing on \([a,b]\).

Procedure:

  1. Compute \(f'(x)\).
  2. Find all critical numbers \(c\) where \(f'(c) = 0\) or \(f'(c)\) does not exist.
  3. Use these to partition \(D\) into intervals.
  4. Test the sign of \(f'\) on each interval (pick any sample point).

docs.title: Step 6 — Local Extrema
docs.text: Definition. \(f\) has a local maximum at \(c\) if \(f(c) \geq f(x)\) for all \(x\) near \(c\), and a local minimum if \(f(c) \leq f(x)\) for all \(x\) near \(c\).

docs.title: First Derivative Test
docs.text:
Suppose \(c\) is a critical number of \(f\).

  • If \(f'\) changes from \(+\) to \(-\) at \(c\): local max.
  • If \(f'\) changes from \(-\) to \(+\) at \(c\): local min.
  • If \(f'\) does not change sign: neither (saddle).

docs.title: Second Derivative Test
docs.text:
Suppose \(f'(c) = 0\) and \(f''(c)\) exists.

  • \(f''(c) > 0 \Rightarrow\) local minimum (curve is concave up, so \(c\) is the bottom of a bowl).
  • \(f''(c) < 0 \Rightarrow\) local maximum (curve is concave down, so \(c\) is the top of a hill).
  • \(f''(c) = 0 \Rightarrow\) inconclusive (must revert to first derivative test).

Mnemonic. A smiley face \(\cup\) is concave up (\(f'' > 0\)); a frowny face \(\cap\) is concave down (\(f'' < 0\)).

docs.title: Step 7 — Concavity and Inflection Points
docs.text:
Definition. \(f\) is concave up on \((a,b)\) if \(f''(x) > 0\) there; concave down if \(f''(x) < 0\) there.

Definition. \(c\) is an inflection point if \(f\) is continuous at \(c\) and the concavity changes at \(c\).

Warning. \(f''(c) = 0\) is necessary but not sufficient for an inflection point. Check that concavity actually changes.

Example. \(f(x) = x^4\): \(f''(x) = 12x^2\), so \(f''(0) = 0\), but concavity is up on both sides — \(x = 0\) is not an inflection point.

docs.title: Step 1: Domain
docs.text: Denominator \(= 0\) when \(x = \pm 2\). So \(D = \mathbb{R} \setminus {-2, 2}\).

docs.title: Step 2: Symmetry
docs.text: \(f(-x) = \frac{(-x)^2-1}{(-x)^2-4} = f(x)\). Even function — sketch for \(x \geq 0\) and reflect.

docs.title: Step 3: Intercepts
docs.text:
• \(y\)-intercept: \(f(0) = \frac{-1}{-4} = \frac{1}{4}\).
  • \(x\)-intercepts: \(x^2 - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow x = \pm 1\).

docs.title: Step 4: Asymptotes
docs.text:
Vertical: \(x = \pm 2\).

Check signs near \(x = 2\): $\(\lim_{x \to 2^+} \frac{x^2-1}{x^2-4}: \quad \text{numerator} \to 3 > 0, \quad \text{denominator} \to 0^+ \Rightarrow +\infty\)$ $\(\lim_{x \to 2^-} \frac{x^2-1}{x^2-4}: \quad \text{denominator} \to 0^- \Rightarrow -\infty\)$

Horizontal: $\(\lim_{x \to \pm\infty} \frac{x^2-1}{x^2-4} = \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{1 - 1/x^2}{1 - 4/x^2} = 1\)$ So \(y = 1\) is a horizontal asymptote.

docs.title: Step 5: Monotonicity
docs.text:
\[f'(x) = \frac{2x(x^2-4) - (x^2-1)(2x)}{(x^2-4)^2} = \frac{2x[(x^2-4)-(x^2-1)]}{(x^2-4)^2} = \frac{-6x}{(x^2-4)^2}\]

Critical point: \(f'(x) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0\).

Sign analysis of \(f'(x) = \frac{-6x}{(x^2-4)^2}\) (denominator always \(\geq 0\), denominator \(=0\) excluded):

Interval Sign of \(-6x\) \(f'\) Behavior \((-\infty,-2)\) \(+\) \(+\) increasing \((-2,0)\) \(+\) \(+\) increasing \((0,2)\) \(-\) \(-\) decreasing \((2,\infty)\) \(-\) \(-\) decreasing

docs.title: Step 6: Extrema
docs.text:
\(f'\) changes from \(+\) to \(-\) at \(x = 0\): local maximum at \((0, 1/4)\).

Confirm: \(f''(0)\) — or just note the sign change.

docs.title: Step 7: Concavity
docs.text:
\[f''(x) = \frac{-6(x^2-4)^2 - (-6x) \cdot 2(x^2-4)(2x)}{(x^2-4)^4} = \frac{-6(x^2-4) + 24x^2}{(x^2-4)^3} = \frac{18x^2 + 24}{(x^2-4)^3}\]

The numerator \(18x^2 + 24 > 0\) always. So the sign of \(f''\) is the sign of \((x^2-4)^3 = (x-2)^3(x+2)^3\):

Region \((x^2-4)^3\) Concavity $ x > 2$ $ x < 2$

No inflection points (concavity doesn't change within a continuous piece of the domain).

docs.title: Sketch Summary
docs.text:
y
    |       *         *
  --|--  *  |  *   *  |  *  -- y=1 (asymptote)
    |  *    |    *    |    *
  1/4 -----+--------- --------
    | *     |         |     *
    |*      |         |      *
 ---+-------+---------+--------> x
   -2  -1   0    1    2

Vertical asymptotes at x=±2
Horizontal asymptote y=1
Local max at (0, 1/4)
Crosses x-axis at x=±1

docs.title: Visualization: Reading the Derivative Portrait
docs.text:
One of the most powerful mental models in curve sketching is the derivative portrait — aligning \(f\), \(f'\), and \(f''\) visually.

f(x):  rises /    peaks ⌒    falls \    valley ⌣    rises /
f'(x): positive    zero      negative     zero      positive
f''(x): ?         negative    ?          positive      ?

Wherever \(f''\) switches sign, that's an inflection point — the graph transitions from bending left to bending right (or vice versa). In practice, when sketching by hand, draw the \(f'\) sign chart and \(f''\) sign chart on the same number line as \(f\) to keep track.

docs.title: Example 1: Polynomial — \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x\)
docs.text:
Feature Value Domain \(\mathbb{R}\) Symmetry Odd Zeros \(x = 0, \pm\sqrt{3}\) \(f'(x)\) \(3x^2 - 3 = 3(x-1)(x+1)\) Critical pts \(x = \pm 1\) Local max \((-1, 2)\) Local min \((1, -2)\) \(f''(x)\) \(6x\) Inflection \((0, 0)\)

The graph is an S-curve through the origin, rising steeply on both ends, with a local max on the left and local min on the right.

docs.title: Example 2: Rational with Hole — \(f(x) = \frac{x^2 - 4}{x - 2}\)
docs.text:
\[f(x) = \frac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2} = x + 2, \quad x \neq 2\]

This is a line with a hole (removable discontinuity) at \((2, 4)\). No asymptote — merely a gap. The sketch is a straight line with an open circle at \(x = 2\).

This example is a reminder: factor before jumping to conclusions about asymptotes.

docs.title: Example 3: \(f(x) = xe^{-x}\)
docs.text:
\[f'(x) = e^{-x} - xe^{-x} = e^{-x}(1-x)\]

Critical point: \(x = 1\) (local max since \(f'\) changes \(+ \to -\)). \(f(1) = e^{-1} \approx 0.368\).

\[f''(x) = e^{-x}(x-2)\]

Inflection at \(x = 2\): \(f(2) = 2e^{-2} \approx 0.271\).

As \(x \to +\infty\): \(f(x) \to 0\) (exponential beats polynomial). As \(x \to -\infty\): \(f(x) \to -\infty\).

This curve starts from \(-\infty\) on the left, rises through the origin, peaks at \((1, e^{-1})\), inflects at \((2, 2e^{-2})\), then decays to \(0\) — a beautiful unimodal shape that appears constantly in probability (it's related to the Gamma distribution) and in ML.

docs.title: Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: This is not a detour — it is the whole point of why any of this matters.

docs.title: 1. Loss Landscapes and Gradient Descent
docs.text:
The central problem in training a neural network is minimizing a loss function \(\mathcal{L}(\theta)\) over a high-dimensional parameter space \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}^n\). In 1D, this is exactly curve sketching.

Gradient descent updates: $\(\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \cdot \mathcal{L}'(\theta_t)\)$

This is navigating the curve \(\mathcal{L}\) by following \(-f'\). The algorithm:

  • follows \(f'\) to find descent directions (Step 5 above)
  • gets stuck at \(f'(c)=0\) — which can be a minimum, maximum, or saddle point (Step 6 above)
  • uses \(f''\) (curvature) in second-order methods like Newton's method and natural gradient descent

The entire theory of optimization in ML is the multivariable generalization of Steps 5–7.

docs.title: 2. The Sigmoid and Its Derivative
docs.text:
The sigmoid function: $\(\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}\)$

is one of the most important activation functions. Its curve-sketching analysis:

  • Domain: \(\mathbb{R}\)
  • Range: \((0,1)\)
  • Horizontal asymptotes: \(y = 0\) as \(x \to -\infty\), \(y = 1\) as \(x \to +\infty\)
  • Inflection point at \(x = 0\) (where \(\sigma(0) = 1/2\))
  • \(\sigma'(x) = \sigma(x)(1-\sigma(x))\), which peaks at \(x=0\) with value \(1/4\)

The vanishing gradient problem in deep networks is visible directly from the sketch: away from \(x = 0\), \(\sigma'(x) \to 0\). When gradients are multiplied across many layers, this near-zero derivative causes the gradient signal to vanish. This is why ReLU (\(f(x) = \max(0,x)\), with \(f'(x) = 1\) for \(x > 0\)) replaced sigmoid in deep networks — its derivative does not decay.

docs.title: 3. Convexity and Optimization Guarantees
docs.text:
Definition. \(f\) is convex if for all \(x, y\) in the domain and \(\lambda \in [0,1]\): $\(f(\lambda x + (1-\lambda)y) \leq \lambda f(x) + (1-\lambda)f(y)\)$

Equivalently (for twice-differentiable \(f\)): \(f'' \geq 0\) everywhere.

Why it matters in ML: If \(\mathcal{L}\) is convex, every local minimum is a global minimum, and gradient descent is guaranteed to converge. Logistic regression and SVMs have convex losses. Deep neural networks do not — their loss landscapes are highly non-convex, which is why training requires careful initialization, momentum, and learning rate scheduling.

Understanding convexity is Step 7 of curve sketching applied to loss functions.

docs.title: 4. Newton's Method — The Second-Derivative Optimizer
docs.text:
Newton's method for finding zeros of \(f'\) (i.e., critical points of \(f\)): $\(\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \frac{f'(\theta_t)}{f''(\theta_t)}\)$

In \(n\) dimensions, this becomes: $\(\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - H^{-1} \nabla \mathcal{L}\)$

where \(H\) is the Hessian (matrix of second derivatives). This is the basis of quasi-Newton methods (L-BFGS), natural gradient methods, and Fisher information in deep learning — all of which use curvature information (\(f''\)) to take smarter steps than vanilla gradient descent.

docs.title: 5. Activation Function Design
docs.text:
Every nonlinear activation function in deep learning is designed with curve-sketching principles:

Activation \(f(x)\) Key feature Curve Property Sigmoid \(1/(1+e^{-x})\) Bounded, smooth Inflection at 0 Tanh \((e^x - e^{-x})/(e^x + e^{-x})\) Bounded, zero-mean Inflection at 0, odd ReLU \(\max(0,x)\) No vanishing gradient Non-differentiable at 0 GELU \(x\Phi(x)\) Smooth ReLU-like Slight dip near \(x = -0.17\) Softplus \(\ln(1+e^x)\) Smooth approximation to ReLU \(f'' > 0\) everywhere (convex)

Each design decision traces back to understanding what the curve looks like — its range, its derivative behavior, its inflection structure.

docs.title: 6. Fourier Analysis and Neural Networks (a bridge)
docs.text: MIT 18.02 motivates much of its analysis through the idea that complex curves can be decomposed into simpler components. Modern deep networks approximate arbitrary functions by composing simple nonlinearities — a continuous analog of the same idea. Universal approximation theorems guarantee that sufficiently wide networks with non-polynomial activations can approximate any continuous function on a compact set — but the quality of that approximation depends on the smoothness structure of the target function, which is precisely the language of curve sketching.

docs.title: The Derivative Sign Chart: A Practical Tool
docs.text:
For any function, maintain a sign chart as you work:

x:         -∞    -2    -1     0     1     2    +∞
f'(x):           +++   +++   ---   ---  
f''(x):          ---   +++   +++   ---   
f:          ↗     ↗     ↘     ↘
concavity:   ∩     ∪     ∪     ∩

This single diagram encodes the entire qualitative behavior of the function before you draw a single point.

docs.title: Summary: The Checklist
docs.text:
• Domain — where is \(f\) defined?
  • Symmetry — even, odd, or neither?
  • Intercepts — \(f(0)\) and zeros of \(f\)
  • Vertical asymptotes — zeros of denominator
  • Horizontal/oblique asymptotes — limits at \(\pm\infty\)
  • \(f'(x)\) — compute, find critical numbers, sign chart
  • Local extrema — first or second derivative test
  • \(f''(x)\) — compute, find inflection candidates, sign chart
  • Inflection points — confirm sign change of \(f''\)
  • Sketch — place all features, connect with smooth curve

docs.text:
1. Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §4.5 "Summary of Curve Sketching." Cengage Learning.
  2. MIT OpenCourseWare. 18.02 Multivariable Calculus. Lecture notes on functions, derivatives, and critical point analysis. https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-02sc-multivariable-calculus-fall-2010/
  3. Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville. Deep Learning, Chapter 4 "Numerical Computation." MIT Press, 2016. — For the connection between calculus and optimization.

docs.title: Graphing with Calculus
docs.text: "Calculus does not merely help you draw a curve — it tells you what the curve is trying to say."

docs.title: Preface: Beyond Plotting Points
docs.text:
Point-by-point plotting is computationally brute force and geometrically blind. You might miss a narrow local maximum, misread an asymptote, or connect two branches that belong to different sheets of a discontinuous function.

Calculus gives you a structural understanding: the derivative is the curve's velocity (how fast it's rising or falling), the second derivative is its steering (which way it bends). Together they give you a complete qualitative portrait — the exact shape, not just a cloud of dots.

This note is the natural continuation of the [[Curve Sketching]] note. Where that note gave you the protocol, this note goes deeper into the geometric meaning of each step, the pathological cases that break naive intuition, and the rigorous theorems that justify every claim.

docs.title: Foundational Theorems
docs.text: These are the theorems that make graphing with calculus rigorous, not just heuristic. Every claim in a sketch ultimately rests on one of these.

docs.title: Extreme Value Theorem (EVT)
docs.text:
Theorem (Stewart §4.1). If \(f\) is continuous on a closed interval \([a,b]\), then \(f\) attains both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on \([a,b]\).

This guarantees that extrema exist before we go hunting for them. Note the hypotheses: continuous and closed. Both matter.

  • \(f(x) = x\) on \((0,1)\): no maximum (open interval fails).
  • \(f(x) = 1/x\) on \([0,1]\): no maximum (not continuous at 0).

docs.title: Fermat's Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(f\) has a local extremum at \(c\) and \(f'(c)\) exists, then \(f'(c) = 0\).

Proof sketch. Suppose \(f\) has a local maximum at \(c\). For small \(h > 0\): $\(\frac{f(c+h) - f(c)}{h} \leq 0 \implies f'(c) \leq 0 \quad (\text{right-side limit})\)$ $\(\frac{f(c+h) - f(c)}{h} \geq 0 \text{ for } h < 0 \implies f'(c) \geq 0 \quad (\text{left-side limit})\)$ Since both limits must equal \(f'(c)\), we get \(f'(c) = 0\). \(\square\)

Warning. The converse is FALSE. \(f'(c) = 0\) does not imply a local extremum. Example: \(f(x) = x^3\) at \(x = 0\).

docs.title: Rolle's Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), differentiable on \((a,b)\), and \(f(a) = f(b)\), then there exists \(c \in (a,b)\) such that \(f'(c) = 0\).

Geometrically: if a smooth curve starts and ends at the same height, it must have at least one horizontal tangent somewhere in between.

docs.title: Mean Value Theorem (MVT)
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and differentiable on \((a,b)\), then there exists \(c \in (a,b)\) such that: $\(f'(c) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}\)$

The MVT is the engine behind the monotonicity test. If \(f' > 0\) on \((a,b)\), then for any \(x_1 < x_2\) in \((a,b)\): $\(f(x_2) - f(x_1) = f'(c)(x_2 - x_1) > 0\)$ so \(f\) is strictly increasing. This is the rigorous proof of what the derivative sign tells us.

docs.title: Tangent Lines and Local Linearity
docs.text:
The derivative \(f'(a)\) is the slope of the tangent line to \(f\) at \(x = a\): $\(L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)\)$

Near \(x = a\), the function looks like this line — this is local linearity, the central geometric idea of differential calculus. The curve and its tangent agree to first order.

This has a profound consequence for sketching: wherever \(f'(a) > 0\), the curve is locally going uphill to the right. The sign of \(f'\) is the direction of travel.

docs.title: The Derivative as a New Function
docs.text:
When sketching \(f\), it is often illuminating to also sketch \(f'\) (and \(f''\)) directly. The relationships:

Property of \(f\) Property of \(f'\) Local maximum at \(c\) Zero crossing: \(+ \to -\) Local minimum at \(c\) Zero crossing: \(- \to +\) Inflection point at \(c\) Local extremum of \(f'\) Concave up \(f'\) is increasing Concave down \(f'\) is decreasing \(f\) linear \(f'\) constant \(f\) quadratic \(f'\) linear

If you can sketch \(f'\) from \(f\), you understand the curve.

docs.title: Definition and Characterization
docs.text:
Definition. \(f\) is concave up on \((a,b)\) if \(f'\) is increasing on \((a,b)\), equivalently if \(f''(x) > 0\) for all \(x \in (a,b)\).

\(f\) is concave down if \(f'\) is decreasing, equivalently \(f''(x) < 0\).

Geometric meaning: A concave-up function lies above all its tangent lines. A concave-down function lies below all its tangent lines.

Proof of the tangent-line characterization (concave up case): By the MVT applied on \([a, x]\), for any \(x > a\): $\(f(x) - f(a) = f'(c)(x-a) \quad \text{for some } c \in (a,x)\)$ Since \(f'\) is increasing and \(c > a\), \(f'(c) > f'(a)\), so: $\(f(x) > f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) = L(x)\)$ The curve lies strictly above the tangent. \(\square\)

docs.title: Second Derivative Test — Full Statement and Proof
docs.text:
Theorem. Let \(f'(c) = 0\).

  • If \(f''(c) > 0\): \(f\) has a local minimum at \(c\).
  • If \(f''(c) < 0\): \(f\) has a local maximum at \(c\).
  • If \(f''(c) = 0\): inconclusive.

Proof (minimum case). Since \(f''(c) > 0\) and \(f''\) is the derivative of \(f'\), and \(f'(c) = 0\), by the definition of the derivative: $\(\lim_{x \to c} \frac{f'(x) - f'(c)}{x - c} = f''(c) > 0\)$ This means for \(x\) near \(c\): \(\frac{f'(x)}{x-c} > 0\), so \(f'(x)\) has the same sign as \(x - c\).

  • For \(x < c\): \(f'(x) < 0\) (decreasing to the left).
  • For \(x > c\): \(f'(x) > 0\) (increasing to the right). By the First Derivative Test, \(c\) is a local minimum. \(\square\)

docs.title: Why \(f''(c) = 0\) is Inconclusive
docs.text:
Function \(f''(0)\) Behavior at 0 \(f(x) = x^4\) \(0\) Local min \(f(x) = -x^4\) \(0\) Local max \(f(x) = x^3\) \(0\) Neither (saddle) \(f(x) = x^5\) \(0\) Neither

When \(f''(c) = 0\), look at the sign of \(f'\) on both sides, or examine higher derivatives (\(f'''(c) \neq 0\) implies inflection; \(f^{(4)}(c) > 0\) with \(f'(c) = f''(c) = f'''(c) = 0\) implies local min).

docs.title: Inflection Points: Rigorous Treatment
docs.text: Definition. A point \((c, f(c))\) is an inflection point if \(f\) is continuous at \(c\) and there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that \(f\) is concave up on \((c-\delta, c)\) and concave down on \((c, c+\delta)\), or vice versa.

docs.title: Necessary Condition
docs.text:
If \((c, f(c))\) is an inflection point and \(f''(c)\) exists, then \(f''(c) = 0\).

This is the analog of Fermat's theorem, one derivative up.

docs.title: Sufficient Conditions for Inflection
docs.text:
Condition 1. If \(f''(c) = 0\) and \(f'''(c) \neq 0\), then \(c\) is an inflection point.

Why: \(f'''(c) \neq 0\) means \(f''\) is not flat at \(c\) — it is genuinely crossing zero, so \(f''\) changes sign.

Condition 2. If \(f''\) changes sign at \(c\) (regardless of whether \(f''(c)\) exists), then \(c\) is an inflection point.

Example. \(f(x) = x^{1/3}\): \(f''(x) = -\frac{2}{9} x^{-5/3}\), which does not exist at \(x = 0\). Yet concavity changes (from concave up on \((-\infty,0)\) to concave down on \((0,\infty)\)... actually let's check: \(f''(x) < 0\) for \(x > 0\) and \(f''(x) > 0\) for \(x < 0\)). So \(x=0\) is an inflection point even though \(f''(0)\) doesn't exist.

docs.title: Vertical Asymptotes — Four Cases
docs.text:
At \(x = a\) where \(f\) is undefined, there are four possible one-sided behaviors:

\[\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = +\infty, \quad \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = -\infty$$ $$\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = +\infty, \quad \lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = -\infty\]

These can occur in any combination independently. Sketch all four near the asymptote.

Example. \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x(x-1)}\).

Near \(x = 0\): numerator \(\to 1 > 0\), \((x-1) \to -1 < 0\), so sign depends on \(x\):

  • \(x \to 0^+\): denominator \(\to 0^+(-1) = 0^-\), so \(f \to -\infty\).
  • \(x \to 0^-\): denominator \(\to 0^-(-1) = 0^+\), so \(f \to +\infty\).

Near \(x = 1\): numerator \(\to 1\), \(x \to 1\), so sign depends on \((x-1)\):

  • \(x \to 1^+\): \(f \to +\infty\).
  • \(x \to 1^-\): \(f \to -\infty\).

docs.title: Oblique Asymptotes — Why They Occur
docs.text:
Oblique asymptotes arise when a rational function has the numerator degree exceeding the denominator by exactly 1. The quotient in polynomial long division gives the asymptote.

General formula. If \(f(x) = Q(x) + R(x)/D(x)\) where \(\deg R < \deg D\), then \(y = Q(x)\) is an asymptote as \(|x| \to \infty\) (it need not be linear if \(Q\) is quadratic, etc. — but those are called curvilinear asymptotes).

Example. \(f(x) = \frac{x^3}{x^2 + 1}\).

\[f(x) = x - \frac{x}{x^2+1}\]

Asymptote: \(y = x\) (oblique). The correction term \(-x/(x^2+1) \to 0\) as \(x \to \pm\infty\).

As \(x \to +\infty\): \(-x/(x^2+1) < 0\), so \(f\) approaches \(y = x\) from below. As \(x \to -\infty\): \(-x/(x^2+1) > 0\), so \(f\) approaches \(y = x\) from above.

Note. A curve can cross a horizontal or oblique asymptote — the asymptote describes behavior at \(\infty\), not a barrier.

docs.title: Graphing Rational Functions: Complete Algorithm
docs.text: For \(f(x) = P(x)/Q(x)\) with \(\gcd(P,Q) = 1\):

docs.title: 1. Factor completely
docs.text: \[f(x) = \frac{a(x-r_1)^{m_1}\cdots(x-r_k)^{m_k}}{b(x-s_1)^{n_1}\cdots(x-s_j)^{n_j}}\]

docs.title: 2. Identify zeros and poles
docs.text:
• Zeros of \(f\): \(x = r_i\) (with multiplicity \(m_i\))
  • Poles (vertical asymptotes): \(x = s_i\) (with multiplicity \(n_i\))

docs.title: 3. Behavior at zeros
docs.text:
At a zero \(x = r\) of multiplicity \(m\):

  • \(m\) odd: graph crosses the \(x\)-axis (sign change)
  • \(m\) even: graph touches the \(x\)-axis (no sign change, bounces back)

docs.title: 4. Behavior at poles
docs.text:
At a pole \(x = s\) of multiplicity \(n\):

  • \(n\) odd: graph goes to \(+\infty\) on one side, \(-\infty\) on the other (opposite signs)
  • \(n\) even: graph goes to \(+\infty\) (or \(-\infty\)) on both sides (same sign)

docs.title: 5. Determine end behavior
docs.text: Compare degrees of \(P\) and \(Q\) as in the asymptote section above.

docs.title: 6. Sign chart of \(f(x)\)
docs.text:
The sign of \(f\) changes at each zero of odd multiplicity and at each pole of odd multiplicity. It does not change at even-multiplicity zeros or poles.

Pick a test point in each interval and determine \(+/-\).

docs.title: Domain
docs.text: \(D = \mathbb{R} \setminus {1}\)

docs.title: Symmetry
docs.text: Neither even nor odd (mixed powers, asymmetric denominator).

docs.title: Intercepts
docs.text:
• \(y\)-intercept: \(f(0) = 0\)
  • \(x\)-intercepts: \(x = 0\) (multiplicity 2, bounce) and \(x = -2\) (multiplicity 1, cross)

docs.title: Asymptotes
docs.text:
Vertical: \(x = 1\) (pole of order 2 → same sign on both sides).

Near \(x = 1\): numerator \(\to 1^2 \cdot 3 = 3 > 0\), denominator \(\to 0^+\) on both sides. $\(\lim_{x \to 1^\pm} f(x) = +\infty\)$

Horizontal/Oblique: \(\deg P = 3\), \(\deg Q = 2\), degree difference is 1 → oblique asymptote.

\[\frac{x^2(x+2)}{(x-1)^2} = \frac{x^3 + 2x^2}{x^2 - 2x + 1}\]

Long division: $\(= x + 4 + \frac{7x - 4}{(x-1)^2}\)$

Oblique asymptote: \(y = x + 4\).

As \(x \to +\infty\): remainder \(\frac{7x-4}{(x-1)^2} \to 0^+\), so \(f\) approaches from above. As \(x \to -\infty\): remainder \(\to 0^-\), so \(f\) approaches from below.

docs.title: Sketch Summary
docs.text:
y
        |          /  (oblique asymptote y=x+4)
        |        /
     32/3+     *           ← local min at (4, 32/3)
        |    /    .....
        |   / ....
        | /...
    ----|--+-----|------+----------> x
        | -2    0       1     4
       1/4 ← local min at x=-1
         \  /
          \/
   curve bounces at x=0
   crosses at x=-2

docs.title: Exponential and Logarithmic
docs.text:
Key features of \(f(x) = e^x\):

  • \(f'(x) = e^x > 0\) always → strictly increasing
  • \(f''(x) = e^x > 0\) always → always concave up
  • No zeros, no extrema, no inflection points
  • Horizontal asymptote \(y = 0\) as \(x \to -\infty\)

Key features of \(f(x) = \ln x\):

  • Domain \((0,\infty)\)
  • \(f'(x) = 1/x > 0\) → strictly increasing
  • \(f''(x) = -1/x^2 < 0\) → always concave down
  • Zero at \(x = 1\)
  • Vertical asymptote \(x = 0^+\) (\(f \to -\infty\))

docs.title: Trigonometric Functions
docs.text:
\(f(x) = \sin x\):

  • \(f' = \cos x\): zero at \(x = \pi/2 + n\pi\)
  • \(f'' = -\sin x\): zero at \(x = n\pi\) (inflection points at the zeros of \(\sin\))
  • Local maxima at \(x = \pi/2 + 2n\pi\), local minima at \(x = -\pi/2 + 2n\pi\)

\(f(x) = \tan x\):

  • Domain: \(\mathbb{R} \setminus {\pi/2 + n\pi}\)
  • \(f' = \sec^2 x > 0\) always → strictly increasing on each branch
  • \(f'' = 2\sec^2 x \tan x\): changes sign at \(x = n\pi\) (inflection)

docs.title: Mixed Functions: \(f(x) = x^n e^{-x}\), \(n \geq 1\)
docs.text:
This family is fundamental in statistics (Gamma distributions) and ML.

\[f'(x) = x^{n-1}e^{-x}(n - x)\]
  • Critical point at \(x = n\) (local/global max on \((0,\infty)\), since \(f \to 0\) at both ends)
  • \(f(n) = n^n e^{-n}\)
  • Inflection points at \(x = n \pm \sqrt{n}\) (from \(f'' = 0\), approximately)

As \(n\) increases, the peak moves right and sharpens — the function becomes more concentrated. This is exactly how Gamma distributions behave.

docs.title: Graphing in Parametric Form
docs.text:
When a curve is given as \(x = x(t)\), \(y = y(t)\), the calculus of sketching generalizes naturally.

Slope of tangent: $\(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt}\)$

Concavity: $\(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{d(dy/dx)/dt}{dx/dt}\)$

Critical points: \(dy/dt = 0\) with \(dx/dt \neq 0\) (horizontal tangent); \(dx/dt = 0\) with \(dy/dt \neq 0\) (vertical tangent).

Example. The cycloid \(x = t - \sin t\), \(y = 1 - \cos t\):

\[\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\sin t}{1 - \cos t}\]

Cusp at \(t = 0\) (both derivatives \(= 0\)). As \(t \to 0\):

\[\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\sin t}{1-\cos t} = \frac{2\sin(t/2)\cos(t/2)}{2\sin^2(t/2)} = \cot(t/2) \to \infty\]

Vertical tangent at each cusp.

docs.title: Graphing in Polar Form
docs.text:
For \(r = f(\theta)\) (MIT 18.02 emphasis):

The Cartesian coordinates are \(x = r\cos\theta\), \(y = r\sin\theta\).

Slope: $\(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{r'(\theta)\sin\theta + r(\theta)\cos\theta}{r'(\theta)\cos\theta - r(\theta)\sin\theta}\)$

Key features to identify:

  • Loops: values of \(\theta\) where \(r = 0\)
  • Maximum radius: maximize \(r(\theta)\)
  • Symmetry: \(f(-\theta) = f(\theta)\) (symmetric about polar axis); \(f(\pi - \theta) = f(\theta)\) (symmetric about \(\theta = \pi/2\))

Example. Cardioid \(r = 1 + \cos\theta\):

  • \(r = 0\) when \(\theta = \pi\)
  • Maximum \(r = 2\) at \(\theta = 0\)
  • Symmetric about polar axis
  • Cusp at origin (since \(r = 0\) and \(r'(\pi) = \sin\pi = 0\))

Example. Rose curve \(r = \cos(n\theta)\):

  • \(n\) petals if \(n\) is odd; \(2n\) petals if \(n\) is even
  • Each petal is traced as \(\theta\) sweeps an interval of length \(\pi/n\)

docs.title: Pathological Cases and What They Teach
Case 1: Cusps
docs.text:
\(f(x) = x^{2/3}\): \(f'(x) = \frac{2}{3}x^{-1/3}\), which \(\to \pm\infty\) as \(x \to 0^\pm\).

The graph has a cusp at the origin — both tangent slopes blow up but from opposite signs. Not a corner (which has two finite different slopes), not a smooth point. The EVT still applies on \([-1,1]\): the minimum \(f(0) = 0\) is achieved even though \(f'(0)\) doesn't exist.

docs.title: Case 2: Corners
docs.text: \(f(x) = |x|\): \(f'(0^+) = 1\), \(f'(0^-) = -1\). A corner — both one-sided derivatives exist and are finite, but unequal. Not differentiable, but still a local minimum.

docs.title: Case 3: Vertical Tangent Without Asymptote
docs.text: \(f(x) = x^{1/3}\): \(f'(0) = +\infty\) (in the limit sense). The graph passes through the origin with a vertical tangent. This is distinct from a vertical asymptote (where the graph does not pass through).

docs.title: Case 4: Oscillation
docs.text: \(f(x) = x \sin(1/x)\) for \(x \neq 0\), \(f(0) = 0\). The function is continuous at 0 (by squeeze theorem: \(|f(x)| \leq |x| \to 0\)), but oscillates infinitely often near 0. The derivative does not exist at 0. Classic example showing continuity \(\not\Rightarrow\) differentiability (especially dramatically near a point of accumulation of oscillations).

docs.title: Optimization: Graphing in Service of Extrema
Closed Interval Method (Absolute Extrema)
docs.text:
To find the absolute maximum and minimum of a continuous \(f\) on \([a,b]\):

  1. Find all critical numbers \(c\) in \((a,b)\).
  2. Evaluate \(f\) at each \(c\) and at the endpoints \(a\), \(b\).
  3. The largest value is the absolute max; the smallest is the absolute min.

Example. \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x + 1\) on \([-2, 2]\).

\(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 3 = 0 \Rightarrow x = \pm 1\).

\(x\) \(f(x)\) \(-2\) \(-8+6+1 = -1\) \(-1\) \(-1+3+1 = 3\) \(1\) \(1-3+1 = -1\) \(2\) \(8-6+1 = 3\)

Absolute maximum: \(3\) at \(x = \pm 1\) and... wait: \(f(-1) = 3\) and \(f(2) = 3\). Two absolute maxima. Absolute minimum: \(-1\) at \(x = -2\) and \(x = 1\).

docs.title: Unbounded Domains
docs.text:
On \((-\infty, \infty)\) or half-lines, check:

  • All critical points
  • Behavior as \(x \to \pm\infty\)

If \(f(x) \to \infty\) at both ends and has a unique critical point, that point is the absolute minimum (no EVT guarantee needed — analyze directly).

docs.title: The Derivative Portrait: Reading Graphs of \(f'\)
docs.text:
Given a graph of \(f'\) (not \(f\)), recover the graph of \(f\):

Feature of \(f'\) graph Implication for \(f\) \(f'(x) > 0\) \(f\) increasing \(f'(x) < 0\) \(f\) decreasing \(f'(x) = 0\) (zero crossing \(+ \to -\)) local max of \(f\) \(f'(x) = 0\) (zero crossing \(- \to +\)) local min of \(f\) \(f'\) has local max or min at \(c\) inflection point of \(f\) at \(c\) \(f'\) is increasing \(f\) concave up \(f'\) is decreasing \(f\) concave down

This skill is tested heavily in both Stewart and MIT 18.02 problem sets, and is exactly the skill that appears in understanding loss landscapes in ML.

docs.title: Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
1. Activation Functions as Transcendental Curve Sketching
docs.text:
Every activation function is a curve sketching problem. The design of activation functions in deep learning is guided by exactly the features studied in this note:

ReLU: \(f(x) = \max(0,x)\)

Derivative: \(f'(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x < 0 \ 1 & x > 0 \end{cases}\) (undefined at 0)

  • Corner at origin (Step 3 above: pathological case)
  • Concavity: \(f''(x) = 0\) everywhere except \(x = 0\) (linear on both sides)
  • Problem: \(f'(x) = 0\) for \(x < 0\) → dead neurons: gradient is zero, no learning signal flows back through inactive neurons

Leaky ReLU: \(f(x) = \max(\alpha x, x)\), \(0 < \alpha < 1\)

Fixes dying neurons by giving a small nonzero slope on the negative side.

GELU (Gaussian Error Linear Unit): \(f(x) = x \Phi(x)\) where \(\Phi\) is the CDF of \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\).

  • Smooth approximation to ReLU
  • Has a local minimum near \(x \approx -0.17\) (a slight dip)
  • \(f'(x) = \Phi(x) + x\phi(x)\) where \(\phi\) is the standard normal PDF
  • Used in BERT, GPT, and most modern transformers

The choice between activations is exactly the question: which curve has the right derivative behavior (no vanishing, no dying, smooth, bounded)?

docs.title: 2. Convex vs. Non-Convex Loss Landscapes
docs.text:
A function is convex iff \(f'' \geq 0\) everywhere. In higher dimensions, the analog is: the Hessian matrix \(H\) is positive semidefinite everywhere.

Convex losses (e.g., logistic regression, SVM):

  • Every local minimum is a global minimum (consequence of concavity analysis)
  • Gradient descent converges
  • The loss curve looks like a parabola (or higher-dimensional bowl)

Non-convex losses (deep neural networks):

  • \(f''\) changes sign in many places → many inflection points in the loss landscape
  • Multiple local minima, saddle points, and flat regions
  • Saddle points are critical: \(\nabla \mathcal{L} = 0\) but the Hessian has both positive and negative eigenvalues (indefinite)

The geometry of saddle points is: \(f''(c) = 0\), \(f'''(c) \neq 0\) (or in higher dimensions, the Hessian is indefinite). Gradient descent near a saddle point slows to a crawl — the gradient is small but the point is not a minimum. This is why momentum-based optimizers (Adam, RMSProp) are essential for deep learning.

docs.title: 3. Second-Order Methods and the Hessian
docs.text:
The Newton step for optimization is:

\[\theta \leftarrow \theta - H^{-1} \nabla f\]

where \(H = \nabla^2 f\) is the Hessian. In 1D, this is \(\theta \leftarrow \theta - f'(\theta)/f''(\theta)\).

Geometrically: Newton's method uses the local quadratic approximation (Taylor expansion to second order) to jump directly to the minimum of the parabola. This works perfectly for convex quadratics and very well near the minimum of any smooth strongly convex function.

The problem: inverting \(H\) costs \(O(n^3)\) for \(n\) parameters. A GPT-3 has \(n \sim 175 \times 10^9\). Inverting that matrix is impossible. Hence:

  • L-BFGS: approximates \(H^{-1}\) using finite-difference estimates
  • Adam: uses diagonal approximation to \(H\) (i.e., only tracks \(\partial^2 f / \partial \theta_i^2\))
  • Shampoo, K-FAC: use structured approximations to the Hessian

All of these are curve-sketching (using \(f''\)) in disguise.

docs.title: 4. The Bias-Variance Tradeoff as Overfitting Geometry
docs.text:
A polynomial of degree \(n\) fitted to data is a curve. The curve-sketching question: how many oscillations does it have?

A degree-\(n\) polynomial has at most \(n-1\) local extrema. Fitting high-degree polynomials to a small dataset produces a wildly oscillating curve — overfitting. Regularization (L2 = weight decay) penalizes large coefficients, pulling the curve back toward a smoother, flatter shape.

This is concavity control applied to the model, not the loss.

docs.title: 5. Taylor Expansion and Approximation Theory
docs.text:
The Taylor polynomial of \(f\) at \(a\):

\[f(x) \approx f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + \frac{f''(a)}{2}(x-a)^2 + \cdots\]

This is the local curve of \(f\) near \(a\) expressed in terms of derivatives. Neural networks can be understood as building global approximations using local (layer-by-layer) Taylor-like approximations. The expressiveness of a network with ReLU activations comes precisely from its ability to produce piecewise-linear approximations to curved functions — with more layers, the approximation is finer, the effective number of linear pieces grows exponentially with depth.
