docs.title: The Midpoint Rule
docs.text: "The midpoint rule is not merely a better rectangle. It is the first hint that the geometry of approximation has a deeper structure — one that will eventually lead to Gaussian quadrature, spectral methods, and the numerical backbone of scientific computing."

docs.title: 0. Motivation: Why Not Just Use Left or Right Endpoints?
docs.text:
From [[The Definite Integral]], we know:

\[\int_a^b f(x), dx = \lim_{n\to\infty} \sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i^*), \Delta x\]

The choice of sample point \(x_i^*\) is free. Left endpoints (\(L_n\)) and right endpoints (\(R_n\)) are the obvious first choices — but they are systematically biased.

For an increasing function:

  • \(L_n\) always underestimates (samples the low end of each strip)
  • \(R_n\) always overestimates (samples the high end)

The errors do not cancel within each strip; they only cancel when averaged: \(T_n = (L_n + R_n)/2\) — the Trapezoid Rule.

But there is a smarter single-point choice: the midpoint \(\bar{x}_i = \dfrac{x_{i-1} + x_i}{2}\).

The Midpoint Rule is not just "splitting the difference." Its superiority over \(L_n\) and \(R_n\) has a precise algebraic reason — and it is second-order accurate, not first-order. Understanding why is the point of this note.

docs.title: 1. The Rule: Definition
docs.text:
Definition (Midpoint Rule — Stewart §7.7). Let \([a,b]\) be partitioned into \(n\) equal subintervals of width \(\Delta x = (b-a)/n\). The midpoint of the \(i\)-th subinterval \([x_{i-1}, x_i]\) is:

\[\bar{x}_i = \frac{x_{i-1} + x_i}{2} = a + \left(i - \frac{1}{2}\right)\Delta x\]

The Midpoint Rule approximation is:

\[\boxed{M_n = \sum_{i=1}^n f(\bar{x}_i), \Delta x = \Delta x\left[f(\bar{x}_1) + f(\bar{x}_2) + \cdots + f(\bar{x}_n)\right]}\]

Geometrically: erect a rectangle of height \(f(\bar{x}_i)\) over each subinterval. Sum the areas.

docs.title: 2. Geometric Interpretation
docs.text:
f(x)
  |
  |        ___________
  |       |     *     |        ← height = f(x̄ᵢ) at midpoint
  |       |   *   *   |
  |       |  *     *  |
  |       | *       * |
  |_______|___________|______> x
         x_{i-1}  x_i
              ↑
             x̄ᵢ (midpoint)

The rectangle's height is set at the exact center of the interval. For a curve that is concave up (like \(x^2\)), the midpoint rectangle slices through the curve — part of the rectangle pokes above the curve, part sits below. These local errors partially cancel.

Contrast with \(L_n\):

Left endpoint:             Midpoint:
  |                          |
  |**                        |    **
  |  **                      |  **  **
  |    **                    |**      **
  |____**____                |__________
  x₀        x₁              x̄ᵢ
  [systematically low]    [errors partially cancel]

docs.title: 3. Worked Example from First Principles
docs.text:
Compute \(\displaystyle\int_1^2 \frac{1}{x}, dx\) using \(M_5\).

Setup: \([a,b] = [1,2]\), \(n = 5\), \(\Delta x = 1/5 = 0.2\).

Midpoints: \(\bar{x}_i = 1 + (i - 1/2)(0.2)\) for \(i = 1, \ldots, 5\).

\(i\) \(\bar{x}_i\) \(f(\bar{x}_i) = 1/\bar{x}_i\) 1 1.1 0.909091 2 1.3 0.769231 3 1.5 0.666667 4 1.7 0.588235 5 1.9 0.526316 Sum 3.459540 \[M_5 = 0.2 \times 3.459540 = 0.691908\]

True value: \(\displaystyle\int_1^2 \frac{1}{x}, dx = \ln 2 \approx 0.693147\).

Error: \(|0.693147 - 0.691908| = 0.001239\).

Compare with \(n = 5\) Trapezoid Rule on the same problem:

\[T_5 \approx 0.695635, \quad \text{error} = 0.002488\]

The Midpoint Rule error is about half the Trapezoid error. This is not a coincidence — it is a theorem (see §5).

docs.title: 4. Another Example: \(\int_0^1 e^{x^2}, dx\)
docs.text:
This integral has no elementary antiderivative. We must use numerical methods.

With \(n = 4\), \(\Delta x = 0.25\), midpoints: \(0.125, 0.375, 0.625, 0.875\).

\(\bar{x}_i\) \(e^{\bar{x}_i^2}\) 0.125 \(e^{0.015625} \approx 1.01575\) 0.375 \(e^{0.140625} \approx 1.15091\) 0.625 \(e^{0.390625} \approx 1.47784\) 0.875 \(e^{0.765625} \approx 2.15027\) Sum 5.79477 \[M_4 = 0.25 \times 5.79477 \approx 1.44869\]

True value \(\approx 1.46265\). Error \(\approx 0.01396\).

This is the kind of integral that appears constantly in probability theory (related to the normal distribution). Numerical integration is not a fallback — it is the standard tool.

docs.title: 5. Error Analysis: Why Midpoint is Better Than Trapezoid
docs.text:
This is the heart of the note. The claim:

\[|E_M| \leq \frac{(b-a)^3}{24n^2} K, \quad |E_T| \leq \frac{(b-a)^3}{12n^2} K, \quad K = \max_{a \leq x \leq b} |f''(x)|\]

So \(|E_M| \leq \frac{1}{2}|E_T|\). The Midpoint Rule is twice as accurate as the Trapezoid Rule, at the same cost (both use \(n\) function evaluations).

docs.title: 5.1 Where the Error Formula Comes From
docs.text:
Proof (one subinterval, then scale). On a single subinterval \([x_{i-1}, x_i]\) with midpoint \(\bar{x} = (x_{i-1}+x_i)/2\) and half-width \(h = \Delta x / 2\), expand \(f\) in a Taylor series about \(\bar{x}\):

\[f(x) = f(\bar{x}) + f'(\bar{x})(x - \bar{x}) + \frac{f''(\bar{x})}{2}(x-\bar{x})^2 + \frac{f'''(\bar{x})}{6}(x-\bar{x})^3 + O((x-\bar{x})^4)\]

Integrate over \([x_{i-1}, x_i] = [\bar{x}-h, \bar{x}+h]\):

\[\int_{\bar{x}-h}^{\bar{x}+h} f(x), dx = 2h, f(\bar{x}) + f'(\bar{x})\underbrace{\int_{-h}^{h} u, du}_{=,0} + \frac{f''(\bar{x})}{2}\underbrace{\int_{-h}^{h} u^2, du}_{=,2h^3/3} + \frac{f'''(\bar{x})}{6}\underbrace{\int_{-h}^{h} u^3, du}_{=,0} + \cdots\]

(The odd-power integrals vanish by symmetry of \([\bar{x}-h, \bar{x}+h]\).)

\[= 2h, f(\bar{x}) + \frac{f''(\bar{x})}{3}h^3 + O(h^5)\]

The Midpoint Rule approximation for this strip is \(f(\bar{x}) \cdot 2h\). So the local error is:

\[e_i = \int_{\bar{x}-h}^{\bar{x}+h} f, dx - f(\bar{x}) \cdot 2h = \frac{f''(\bar{x})}{3}h^3 + O(h^5)\]

Since \(h = \Delta x / 2 = (b-a)/(2n)\):

\[|e_i| \leq \frac{K}{3} \cdot \frac{(b-a)^3}{8n^3}\]

Summing over \(n\) subintervals:

\[|E_M| = \left|\sum_{i=1}^n e_i\right| \leq n \cdot \frac{K}{3} \cdot \frac{(b-a)^3}{8n^3} = \frac{K(b-a)^3}{24n^2}\]

\(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: 5.2 Why the First-Order Error Vanishes: The Symmetry Argument
docs.text:
The key insight: expanding about the midpoint makes \(\int_{-h}^{h} u, du = 0\) by odd symmetry. The first-order error term cancels exactly — not approximately.

For left/right endpoints, there is no such symmetry. Expanding about \(x_{i-1}\) (left endpoint):

\[\int_{x_{i-1}}^{x_i} f, dx = f(x_{i-1})\Delta x + \frac{f'(x_{i-1})}{2}(\Delta x)^2 + O((\Delta x)^3)\]

Local error \(\sim C(\Delta x)^2\), total error \(\sim C(b-a)\Delta x = O(1/n)\). First order.

For midpoint: local error \(\sim C(\Delta x)^3\), total error \(\sim Cn \cdot (\Delta x)^3 = O(1/n^2)\). Second order.

The midpoint is special precisely because it is the center of symmetry of the interval. Symmetry kills the linear error term. This is the same reason Gaussian quadrature is so powerful — it chooses nodes to kill even higher-order error terms.

docs.title: 6. Comparison of Methods
docs.text:
Method Error Order Formula Notes Left \(L_n\) \(O(1/n)\) \(\Delta x\sum f(x_{i-1})\) Biased for monotone \(f\) Right \(R_n\) \(O(1/n)\) \(\Delta x\sum f(x_i)\) Biased opposite direction Midpoint \(M_n\) \(O(1/n^2)\) \(\Delta x\sum f(\bar{x}_i)\) Best single-point rule Trapezoid \(T_n\) \(O(1/n^2)\) \(\frac{\Delta x}{2}[f(x_0)+2f(x_1)+\cdots+f(x_n)]\) \(n+1\) evaluations Simpson \(S_n\) \(O(1/n^4)\) \(\frac{\Delta x}{3}[f(x_0)+4f(x_1)+2f(x_2)+\cdots+f(x_n)]\) Combines \(M\) and \(T\)

Observe: Simpson's Rule = \(\frac{2}{3}M_n + \frac{1}{3}T_n\). This is not a coincidence — it is a Richardson extrapolation, combining two second-order methods to cancel their leading error terms and achieve fourth order.

docs.title: Error Bounds for the Example \(\int_1^2 1/x, dx\)
7. Choosing \(n\): Solving for Required Accuracy
docs.text:
Problem. How large must \(n\) be to guarantee \(|E_M| \leq 10^{-4}\) for \(\int_1^2 \frac{1}{x}, dx\)?

Use the error bound \(|E_M| \leq \frac{K(b-a)^3}{24n^2}\) with \(K = 2\), \(b-a = 1\):

\[\frac{2}{24n^2} \leq 10^{-4} \implies n^2 \geq \frac{2}{24 \times 10^{-4}} = \frac{2}{0.0024} \approx 833.3\] \[n \geq \sqrt{833.3} \approx 28.9 \implies \boxed{n = 29}\]

For the Trapezoid Rule with the same tolerance: \(n \geq \sqrt{1666.7} \approx 41\). The Midpoint Rule reaches the same accuracy with 29% fewer function evaluations.

docs.title: 8. Visualization: Error Cancellation in Action
docs.text:
Concave-up curve (f'' > 0), one subinterval [x_{i-1}, x_i]:

         true curve
            /‾‾‾\
           /     \
  ________/  (+)  \________
  |       \       /        |
  |    (–) \_____/ (–)     |   ← Midpoint rectangle
  |_________________________|
  x_{i-1}      x̄ᵢ       xᵢ

  (+) region: rectangle ABOVE curve (overestimates here)
  (–) region: rectangle BELOW curve (underestimates here)

  For concave-up f: the (–) regions at the tails are EXACTLY
  equal by symmetry → first-order errors cancel.
  Residual error is third-order in h.

For a concave-up function (\(f'' > 0\)):

  • Midpoint Rule underestimates (the rectangle is below the chord)
  • Trapezoid Rule overestimates (the trapezoid is above the curve)

This means \(M_n \leq \int_a^b f \leq T_n\) when \(f\) is concave up — giving a guaranteed enclosure of the true value.

docs.title: 9. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
9.1 Numerical Integration in Probabilistic Models
docs.text:
In Bayesian deep learning and probabilistic ML, we regularly need:

\[\mathbb{E}_{z \sim p(z)}[f(z)] = \int f(z), p(z), dz\]

When \(p\) is Gaussian and \(f\) is a neural network output, this is intractable analytically. The Gauss-Hermite quadrature (a higher-order analog of the Midpoint Rule optimized for Gaussian measure) is used to approximate it. Understanding why the midpoint outperforms endpoints — symmetry cancels error — is the conceptual foundation of quadrature theory.

docs.title: 9.2 The Midpoint Method as a Time Integrator
docs.text:
In continuous-time RL and Neural ODEs, we integrate the ODE:

\[\dot{x} = f(x, t), \quad x(0) = x_0\]

The explicit midpoint method (a Runge-Kutta 2 scheme):

\[k_1 = f(x_n, t_n)$$ $$k_2 = f!\left(x_n + \frac{h}{2}k_1,; t_n + \frac{h}{2}\right)$$ $$x_{n+1} = x_n + h, k_2\]

This is exactly the Midpoint Rule applied to the integral \(x(t_{n+1}) = x_n + \int_{t_n}^{t_{n+1}} f(x(t), t), dt\). Evaluating \(f\) at the estimated midpoint of the time step — rather than the left endpoint (Euler's method) — doubles the convergence order from \(O(h)\) to \(O(h^2)\). Neural ODE solvers (like torchdiffeq) use exactly this principle, extended to higher-order Runge-Kutta schemes.

docs.title: 9.3 Mini-Batch Gradient Estimation as Midpoint Sampling
docs.text:
When we estimate \(\nabla_\theta R(\theta) = \int \nabla_\theta \ell, d\mathcal{D}\) using a mini-batch, the choice of which data points to include is analogous to the choice of quadrature node.

  • Random sampling (SGD) \(\approx\) random Riemann sum (high variance)
  • Stratified sampling: divide the dataset into strata and sample one from each — this is conceptually the Midpoint Rule (sample the "center" of each stratum)
  • Quasi-random sequences (Halton, Sobol) place sample points more uniformly, achieving \(O(1/n^2)\) or better convergence — exactly the gain from midpoint vs. left endpoint

The variance reduction in stratified sampling for gradient estimation is the direct ML analog of the accuracy gain in the Midpoint Rule.

docs.title: 9.4 Symmetry in Initialization
docs.text: The reason the midpoint is optimal on \([x_{i-1}, x_i]\) is the same reason symmetric weight initialization is preferred in neural networks. Kaiming and Xavier initializations are designed so that the forward and backward passes have symmetric variance — odd-order moments cancel, just as the \(\int u, du = 0\) term vanished in our Taylor expansion. The underlying mathematical principle is identical: exploit symmetry to cancel leading-order error terms.

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text: Midpoint Rule Concept ML/DL Analog Midpoint \(\bar{x}_i\) = center of interval Stratified mini-batch center Symmetry kills linear error term Symmetric initialization kills gradient bias \(O(1/n^2)\) vs. \(O(1/n)\) for \(L_n\), \(R_n\) Variance reduction from stratification Explicit midpoint ODE integrator Runge-Kutta-2 in Neural ODE solvers Gauss quadrature (generalized midpoint) Gauss-Hermite for Bayesian inference Richardson extrapolation → Simpson Ensemble averaging → bias cancellation

docs.title: 10. Quick-Reference Cheatsheet
docs.text: \[M_n = \Delta x \sum_{i=1}^n f(\bar{x}_i), \quad \bar{x}_i = a + \left(i - \tfrac{1}{2}\right)\Delta x, \quad \Delta x = \frac{b-a}{n}\] \[|E_M| \leq \frac{K(b-a)^3}{24n^2}, \quad K = \max_{[a,b]}|f''(x)|\] \[|E_T| \leq \frac{K(b-a)^3}{12n^2} = 2|E_M|_{\max}\] \[\text{For required tolerance } \varepsilon: \quad n \geq \sqrt{\frac{K(b-a)^3}{24\varepsilon}}\] \[\text{Key identity: } S_{2n} = \frac{2}{3}M_n + \frac{1}{3}T_n \quad \text{(Simpson from Midpoint + Trapezoid)}\]

docs.title: Area Functions
docs.text: "The area function is the moment calculus becomes self-aware. We stop asking 'what is the area under this curve?' and start asking 'what function does the process of accumulating area produce?' The answer — that accumulation undoes differentiation — is the deepest theorem in elementary mathematics."

docs.title: 0. The Central Question
docs.text:
We know how to compute \(\int_a^b f(t), dt\) when \(a\) and \(b\) are fixed numbers. It gives a single real number.

Now ask something different: what if the upper limit is allowed to vary?

Fix \(a\). For each \(x \in [a, b]\), define:

\[g(x) = \int_a^x f(t), dt\]

This is no longer a number — it is a function of \(x\). It measures the accumulated signed area under \(f\) from the fixed left endpoint \(a\) to the moving right endpoint \(x\).

This function \(g\) is called an area function (or accumulation function). The question is: what are its properties? Is it differentiable? If so, what is \(g'(x)\)?

The answer is the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 1 — and it is not obvious.

docs.title: 1. Building Intuition: A Concrete Example
docs.text:
Let \(f(t) = t\) (a simple ramp) and \(a = 0\). Define:

\[g(x) = \int_0^x t, dt\]

For each \(x\), \(g(x)\) is the area of a right triangle with base \(x\) and height \(x\):

\[g(x) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot x \cdot x = \frac{x^2}{2}\]

Now observe:

\[g'(x) = \frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{x^2}{2}\right) = x = f(x)\]

The derivative of the area function equals the original function. This is not a coincidence.

docs.title: Another Example
docs.text:
Let \(f(t) = \cos t\), \(a = 0\):

\[g(x) = \int_0^x \cos t, dt = [\sin t]_0^x = \sin x\]

Then \(g'(x) = \cos x = f(x)\). Again.

docs.title: And One More
docs.text:
Let \(f(t) = e^t\), \(a = 0\):

\[g(x) = \int_0^x e^t, dt = [e^t]_0^x = e^x - 1\]

Then \(g'(x) = e^x = f(x)\). Every time.

The pattern is undeniable. The derivative of \(\int_a^x f(t), dt\) is \(f(x)\).

docs.title: 2. Visualization: The Area Function as a Running Total
docs.text:
Think of \(f(t)\) as a rate — say, water flowing into a tank at rate \(f(t)\) liters/second.

\[g(x) = \int_0^x f(t), dt = \text{total water in tank at time } x\]

The rate of change of the total at time \(x\) is... the current flow rate — which is \(f(x)\).

This is obvious physically. The FTC says it is also mathematically rigorous.

f(t):  rate of accumulation
  |
  |   ****
  |  *    *
  | *      *
  |*        *
  +-----------> t
  0          x

g(x) = ∫₀ˣ f(t) dt: total accumulated so far
  |                    *
  |                  **
  |               ***
  |           ****
  |      *****
  |******
  +-----------> x
  0

At any point \(x\): the slope of \(g\) equals the height of \(f\).

  • Where \(f > 0\): \(g\) is increasing
  • Where \(f < 0\): \(g\) is decreasing
  • Where \(f = 0\): \(g\) has a horizontal tangent
  • Where \(f\) has a maximum: \(g\) has an inflection point

docs.title: 3. The Theorem: FTC Part 1
docs.text:
Theorem (Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 1 — Stewart §5.3).

Let \(f\) be continuous on \([a, b]\). Define the area function:

\[g(x) = \int_a^x f(t), dt, \quad x \in [a, b]\]

Then \(g\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), differentiable on \((a,b)\), and:

\[\boxed{g'(x) = f(x)}\]

In Leibniz notation:

\[\frac{d}{dx} \int_a^x f(t), dt = f(x)\]

docs.title: Proof
docs.text:
By the definition of the derivative:

\[g'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{g(x+h) - g(x)}{h}\]

Compute the numerator using additivity of the integral:

\[g(x+h) - g(x) = \int_a^{x+h} f(t), dt - \int_a^x f(t), dt = \int_x^{x+h} f(t), dt\]

So:

\[g'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{1}{h} \int_x^{x+h} f(t), dt\]

Since \(f\) is continuous on \([x, x+h]\) (assuming \(h > 0\) small), the Mean Value Theorem for Integrals guarantees \(\exists, c_h \in [x, x+h]\) such that:

\[\int_x^{x+h} f(t), dt = f(c_h) \cdot h\]

Therefore:

\[g'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(c_h) \cdot h}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0} f(c_h)\]

As \(h \to 0\), \(c_h \in [x, x+h]\) forces \(c_h \to x\). By continuity of \(f\):

\[\lim_{h \to 0} f(c_h) = f(x)\]

Therefore \(g'(x) = f(x)\). The case \(h < 0\) is analogous. \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: What the Proof Reveals
docs.text:
The proof uses two major theorems:

  1. MVT for Integrals — the average value of \(f\) on \([x, x+h]\) is achieved somewhere inside
  2. Continuity of \(f\) — as the interval shrinks to a point, the average value converges to \(f(x)\)

Continuity is essential. If \(f\) has a jump discontinuity at \(x_0\), then \(g\) is still continuous at \(x_0\) but not differentiable there. The area function is always at least one derivative smoother than the integrand.

docs.title: 4. The Area Function is an Antiderivative
docs.text:
Corollary. \(g(x) = \int_a^x f(t), dt\) is an antiderivative of \(f\) on \([a, b]\).

This is a profound statement. It says:

Every continuous function has an antiderivative.

Before FTC, there was no guarantee that \(\int_0^x e^{-t^2}, dt\) was the derivative of anything. FTC Part 1 guarantees it is — it is the derivative of itself, in the sense that:

\[\frac{d}{dx} \int_0^x e^{-t^2}, dt = e^{-x^2}\]

The function \(g(x) = \int_0^x e^{-t^2}, dt\) is called the error function (up to scaling), written \(\text{erf}(x)\). It has no elementary closed form — but it exists, it is differentiable, and FTC tells us its derivative exactly.

docs.title: 5. Changing the Lower Limit
docs.text:
The lower limit \(a\) affects \(g\) only by a constant. If we change \(a\) to \(b\):

\[\int_b^x f(t), dt = \int_a^x f(t), dt - \int_a^b f(t), dt = g(x) - C\]

So \(\frac{d}{dx}\int_b^x f(t), dt = g'(x) = f(x)\) regardless of the lower limit.

The lower limit shifts the area function vertically — it does not change its derivative.

\[\frac{d}{dx}\int_c^x f(t), dt = f(x) \quad \text{for any constant } c \in [a,b]\]

docs.title: 6. The Chain Rule Extension
docs.text:
What if the upper limit is not \(x\) but \(u(x)\)?

\[\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^{u(x)} f(t), dt = f(u(x)) \cdot u'(x)\]

This follows immediately from the Chain Rule applied to \(g(u(x))\):

\[\frac{d}{dx}[g(u(x))] = g'(u(x)) \cdot u'(x) = f(u(x)) \cdot u'(x)\]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Example 1.

\[\frac{d}{dx}\int_1^{x^3} \sin(t^2), dt = \sin(x^6) \cdot 3x^2\]

Example 2.

\[\frac{d}{dx}\int_x^{x^2} e^{t^3}, dt\]

Split at any convenient constant \(c\) (say \(c = 0\)):

\[= \frac{d}{dx}\int_0^{x^2} e^{t^3}, dt - \frac{d}{dx}\int_0^{x} e^{t^3}, dt = e^{x^6} \cdot 2x - e^{x^3}\]

Example 3. (Both limits variable)

\[\frac{d}{dx}\int_{\sin x}^{\cos x} \sqrt{1+t^4}, dt = \sqrt{1+\cos^4 x}\cdot(-\sin x) - \sqrt{1+\sin^4 x}\cdot\cos x\]

The general rule: differentiate the upper limit contribution minus the lower limit contribution, each evaluated at the limit and multiplied by its derivative.

docs.title: 7. Reading \(g\) from \(f\): A Graphical Analysis
docs.text: Given the graph of \(f\), we can sketch \(g(x) = \int_a^x f(t), dt\) without computing anything.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text: Property of \(f\) on \((p, q)\) Consequence for \(g\) \(f(x) > 0\) \(g\) is increasing \(f(x) < 0\) \(g\) is decreasing \(f(x) = 0\) (and sign change) \(g\) has a local extremum \(f\) increasing (\(f' > 0\)) \(g\) is concave up \(f\) decreasing (\(f' < 0\)) \(g\) is concave down \(f\) has a local max/min \(g\) has an inflection point \(f\) crosses \(x\)-axis from \(+\) to \(-\) \(g\) has a local maximum \(f\) crosses \(x\)-axis from \(-\) to \(+\) \(g\) has a local minimum

docs.title: Example: Sketch \(g\) from \(f\)
docs.text:
Suppose \(f\) looks like this on \([0, 6]\):

f(t)
  |
 2|   ****
  |  *    *
  | *      *
  |*        *
--+----------*--------*----> t
  0    1    2    3   4*  5  6
                        *
                    -1|  ****

\(f > 0\) on \((0, 3)\): \(g\) increases. \(f = 0\) at \(t = 3\): \(g\) has a local max. \(f < 0\) on \((3, 6)\): \(g\) decreases. \(f\) increases on \((0,1)\): \(g\) concave up. \(f\) decreases on \((1,3)\): \(g\) concave down. Inflection of \(g\) at \(t = 1\) (where \(f\) has its max).

g(x) = ∫₀ˣ f(t) dt
  |
  |         *  ← local max
  |       **  **
  |      *      *
  |    **        *
  |  **           *
  |**              **
  +-------------------> x
  0   1   2   3   4   5   6
      ↑
   inflection point
   (where f' = 0, i.e., f has its max)

docs.title: Problem 1
docs.text:
Find \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\displaystyle\int_0^x \frac{\sin t}{t}, dt\).

The integrand \(\frac{\sin t}{t}\) has a removable discontinuity at \(t = 0\) (define it as \(1\) there), so \(f\) is continuous. By FTC Part 1:

\[\frac{d}{dx}\int_0^x \frac{\sin t}{t}, dt = \frac{\sin x}{x}\]

This function, \(\text{Si}(x) = \int_0^x \frac{\sin t}{t}, dt\), is called the sine integral — important in signal processing and optics. Its existence and differentiability are guaranteed by FTC.

docs.title: Problem 2
docs.text:
Let \(h(x) = \displaystyle\int_1^{e^x} \ln t, dt\). Find \(h'(x)\).

Chain rule: \(u(x) = e^x\), \(f(t) = \ln t\).

\[h'(x) = \ln(e^x) \cdot \frac{d}{dx}(e^x) = x \cdot e^x\]

docs.title: Problem 3
docs.text:
Find the inflection points of \(g(x) = \displaystyle\int_0^x (t^2 - t - 2), dt\).

\(g'(x) = x^2 - x - 2 = (x-2)(x+1)\)

\(g''(x) = 2x - 1\)

\(g''(x) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 1/2\). Check sign change: \(g'' < 0\) for \(x < 1/2\), \(g'' > 0\) for \(x > 1/2\).

Inflection point at \(x = 1/2\).

(Note: \(g'(1/2) = (1/4) - (1/2) - 2 = -9/4 \neq 0\), so this is genuinely an inflection, not an extremum.)

Also: \(g'(x) = 0\) at \(x = 2\) and \(x = -1\) — local extrema of \(g\).

docs.title: Problem 4 (Tricky)
docs.text:
Find \(\lim_{x \to 0} \dfrac{\displaystyle\int_0^x \sin(t^2), dt}{x^3}\).

Direct substitution gives \(0/0\) — L'Hôpital:

\[= \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(x^2)}{3x^2} = \lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin(x^2)}{3x^2} = \frac{1}{3}\]

(using \(\lim_{u\to 0} \frac{\sin u}{u} = 1\) with \(u = x^2\).)

Key: FTC Part 1 let us differentiate the numerator immediately: \(\frac{d}{dx}\int_0^x \sin(t^2), dt = \sin(x^2)\).

docs.title: 9. Why the Dummy Variable \(t\) Matters
docs.text:
A subtle but important point. In \(g(x) = \int_a^x f(t), dt\), the variable \(t\) is a dummy variable — it disappears after integration. We could write \(\int_a^x f(u), du\) or \(\int_a^x f(s), ds\) and get the same \(g(x)\).

We cannot write \(\int_a^x f(x), dx\) — this is a category error. The upper limit \(x\) and the integration variable \(x\) cannot share a name, because inside the integral, the integration variable ranges over \([a, x]\); the \(x\) in the upper limit is fixed relative to that sweep.

\[\int_a^x f(x), dx \quad \leftarrow \text{ILLEGAL NOTATION}\] \[\int_a^x f(t), dt \quad \leftarrow \text{correct}\]

This is not pedantry. Confusing bound and free variables is the source of many errors in both calculus and programming.

docs.title: 10. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
10.1 Accumulation Functions in Recurrent Networks
docs.text:
A recurrent neural network (RNN) computes a hidden state:

\[h_t = \sigma(W_h h_{t-1} + W_x x_t + b)\]

In the continuous limit (as the time step \(\Delta t \to 0\)), this becomes:

\[\frac{dh}{dt} = -h(t) + \sigma(W_x x(t) + b)\]

The hidden state \(h(T)\) is an area function:

\[h(T) = h(0) + \int_0^T \left[-h(t) + \sigma(W_x x(t) + b)\right] dt\]

The hidden state is literally accumulating area under the transformed input signal. FTC Part 1 tells us that \(\frac{dh}{dt}\) at any moment equals the current integrand — the network's current "velocity" of state change. This is precisely the continuous-time RNN (CT-RNN) formulation.

docs.title: 10.2 Neural ODEs: Area Functions as Forward Passes
docs.text:
In a Neural ODE (Chen et al., 2018):

\[z(T) = z(0) + \int_0^T f_\theta(z(t), t), dt\]

The output \(z(T)\) is an area function with integrand \(f_\theta\) — a neural network. The forward pass is numerical integration; the backward pass uses the adjoint method, which is itself derived by differentiating an area function.

By FTC Part 1:

\[\frac{dz}{dt} = f_\theta(z(t), t)\]

The "derivative of the area function equals the integrand" — this is the ODE that the network implicitly defines. FTC is the theorem that makes Neural ODEs well-posed.

docs.title: 10.3 Cumulative Distribution Functions
docs.text:
In probabilistic ML, every probability density \(p(x)\) defines a cumulative distribution function:

\[F(x) = \int_{-\infty}^x p(t), dt\]

\(F\) is exactly an area function. FTC Part 1 gives:

\[F'(x) = p(x)\]

This is the foundational identity of probability theory: the density is the derivative of the CDF. When we use the reparameterization trick in VAEs, or when we compute quantile functions in quantile regression, we are working directly with area functions and their derivatives.

docs.title: 10.4 Gradient of a Loss Integral Over Time
docs.text:
In reinforcement learning, the return is:

\[G_t = \int_t^\infty r(s), e^{-\gamma(s-t)}, ds\]

(continuous-time discounted return). This is an area function of \(t\) (with a moving lower limit). Differentiating:

\[\frac{dG_t}{dt} = -r(t) + \gamma G_t\]

By FTC Part 1 (with lower limit \(t\) instead of upper):

\[\frac{d}{dt}\int_t^\infty r(s)e^{-\gamma(s-t)}, ds = -r(t) + \gamma \int_t^\infty r(s)e^{-\gamma(s-t)}, ds\]

This is the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation in disguise — the fundamental equation of optimal control and RL. It follows directly from differentiating an area function.

docs.title: 10.5 Activation Functions as Area Functions
docs.text:
The softplus activation:

\[\text{softplus}(x) = \log(1 + e^x) = \int_{-\infty}^x \sigma(t), dt\]

where \(\sigma(t) = 1/(1+e^{-t})\) is the sigmoid. By FTC:

\[\frac{d}{dx}\text{softplus}(x) = \sigma(x)\]

The sigmoid is the derivative of softplus — and both are area functions of each other. The entire zoo of smooth activation functions is organized by this differentiation-integration relationship.

docs.text: Area Function Concept ML/DL Analog \(g(x) = \int_a^x f(t), dt\) Hidden state in CT-RNN / Neural ODE \(g'(x) = f(x)\) (FTC Part 1) \(\dot{z}(t) = f_\theta(z,t)\) (ODE definition) CDF \(F(x) = \int_{-\infty}^x p(t), dt\) Probabilistic model CDF; reparameterization trick \(\frac{d}{dt}\int_t^\infty r, ds\) Bellman equation / HJB in RL Chain rule for area: \(\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^{u(x)} f\) Backprop through ODE solver (adjoint method) Softplus = \(\int \sigma, dt\) Activation function hierarchy via integration Dummy variable \(t\) ≠ free variable \(x\) Bound vs. free variables in computation graphs

docs.text: \[g(x) = \int_a^x f(t), dt \implies g'(x) = f(x) \quad \text{(FTC Part 1)}\] \[\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^{u(x)} f(t), dt = f(u(x))\cdot u'(x) \quad \text{(Chain Rule)}\] \[\frac{d}{dx}\int_{v(x)}^{u(x)} f(t), dt = f(u(x))\cdot u'(x) - f(v(x))\cdot v'(x)\] \[g(a) = \int_a^a f(t), dt = 0 \quad \text{(area function starts at zero)}\] \[g \text{ increasing} \iff f > 0; \quad g \text{ concave up} \iff f \text{ increasing}\] \[F'(x) = p(x) \quad \text{(CDF is area function of density)}\]

docs.title: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
docs.text: "The Fundamental Theorem is not a computational trick. It is a declaration that two operations — differentiation and integration — which were invented to solve completely different problems, are in fact inverse processes. This is one of the most surprising facts in all of mathematics."

docs.title: 0. The Two Problems, and Why Their Connection is Miraculous
docs.text:
Calculus was born from two entirely separate questions:

The Tangent Problem (Fermat, Descartes, ~1630s):

Given a curve \(y = f(x)\), what is the slope of the tangent line at a point? This led to the derivative \(f'(x)\).

The Area Problem (Archimedes, Cavalieri, ~250 BC – 1630s):

Given a curve \(y = f(x)\), what is the area under it between two points? This led to the definite integral \(\int_a^b f(x), dx\).

These are geometrically opposite questions — one is local (what is \(f\) doing right here?), the other is global (what has \(f\) accumulated over an interval?). There is no obvious reason they should be related.

The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (FTC) says they are not merely related — they are inverse operations, as opposite as multiplication and division.

This is the theorem. Everything else is commentary.

docs.title: FTC Part 1 — Differentiation Undoes Integration
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), then the area function

\[g(x) = \int_a^x f(t), dt\]

is differentiable on \((a,b)\) and:

\[\boxed{\frac{d}{dx} \int_a^x f(t), dt = f(x)}\]

This says: if you integrate \(f\) and then differentiate, you get \(f\) back.

docs.title: FTC Part 2 — Integration Undoes Differentiation
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and \(F\) is any antiderivative of \(f\) (i.e., \(F' = f\)), then:

\[\boxed{\int_a^b f(x), dx = F(b) - F(a)}\]

This says: if you differentiate \(F\) to get \(f\), then integrating \(f\) recovers the net change in \(F\).

docs.title: The Compact Picture
docs.text: \[\text{Differentiation} \underset{\text{FTC 2}}{\overset{\text{FTC 1}}{\rightleftharpoons}} \text{Integration}\] \[\frac{d}{dx}\left[\int_a^x f(t), dt\right] = f(x) \tag{FTC 1}\] \[\int_a^b \left[\frac{d}{dx}F(x)\right] dx = F(b) - F(a) \tag{FTC 2}\]

docs.title: 2. Proof of FTC Part 1
docs.text:
Setup. Let \(f\) be continuous on \([a,b]\), and define \(g(x) = \int_a^x f(t), dt\).

Step 1: Compute \(g(x+h) - g(x)\).

By additivity of the integral:

\[g(x+h) - g(x) = \int_a^{x+h} f(t), dt - \int_a^x f(t), dt = \int_x^{x+h} f(t), dt\]

Step 2: Apply the Mean Value Theorem for Integrals.

Since \(f\) is continuous on \([x, x+h]\) (for small \(h > 0\)), \(\exists, c_h \in (x, x+h)\) such that:

\[\int_x^{x+h} f(t), dt = f(c_h) \cdot h\]

Step 3: Take the limit.

\[g'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{g(x+h) - g(x)}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(c_h) \cdot h}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0} f(c_h)\]

Since \(c_h \in (x, x+h)\), as \(h \to 0\) we have \(c_h \to x\). By continuity of \(f\):

\[\lim_{h \to 0} f(c_h) = f(x)\]

Therefore \(g'(x) = f(x)\). \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: What Continuity Actually Does
docs.text:
The proof depends on continuity in a precise way. If \(f\) has a jump discontinuity at \(x_0\):

\[f(x_0^-) \neq f(x_0^+)\]

then as \(h \to 0^+\), \(f(c_h) \to f(x_0^+)\) and as \(h \to 0^-\), $f(c_h) \to f(x_0^-) $. The left and right limits of the difference quotient disagree. So \(g\) is not differentiable at \(x_0\) — even though \(g\) is still continuous there (integration smooths out jump discontinuities by one degree of regularity).

docs.title: 3. Proof of FTC Part 2
docs.text:
Setup. \(f\) continuous on \([a,b]\), \(F\) any antiderivative (\(F' = f\)).

Step 1: Invoke FTC Part 1.

We know \(g(x) = \int_a^x f(t), dt\) satisfies \(g'(x) = f(x)\).

So both \(F\) and \(g\) are antiderivatives of \(f\).

Step 2: Antiderivatives differ by a constant.

If \(F'(x) = g'(x) = f(x)\) on \((a,b)\), then \((F - g)'(x) = 0\) on \((a,b)\).

By the Mean Value Theorem: if a function has zero derivative everywhere on an interval, it is constant. So:

\[F(x) - g(x) = C \quad \text{for some constant } C \in \mathbb{R}\]

Step 3: Determine \(C\) and evaluate.

At \(x = a\): \(g(a) = \int_a^a f(t), dt = 0\). So:

\[F(a) - 0 = C \implies C = F(a)\]

Therefore \(g(x) = F(x) - F(a)\) for all \(x \in [a,b]\).

At \(x = b\):

\[\int_a^b f(t), dt = g(b) = F(b) - F(a)\]

\(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
We write \(F(b) - F(a)\) as:

\[\Big[F(x)\Big]_a^b \quad \text{or} \quad F(x)\Big|_a^b\]

docs.title: The MVT is Load-Bearing
docs.text: The step "antiderivatives differ by a constant" is not obvious — it requires the MVT for derivatives. Specifically: if \(h' = 0\) on \((a,b)\), pick any \(x \in (a,b)\); by MVT applied to \([a,x]\), \(h(x) - h(a) = h'(c)(x-a) = 0\). So \(h(x) = h(a)\) for all \(x\). Without MVT, we cannot conclude \(F - g = \text{const}\).

docs.title: 4. The Net Change Theorem
docs.text:
FTC Part 2 has an important physical restatement:

\[\int_a^b F'(x), dx = F(b) - F(a)\]

The integral of a rate of change equals the net change.

\(F(t)\) \(F'(t)\) \(\int_a^b F', dt = F(b) - F(a)\) Position Velocity Net displacement Velocity Acceleration Net change in velocity Population \(P(t)\) Growth rate \(P'(t)\) Net population change Mass \(m(x)\) Linear density \(\rho(x)\) Total mass Charge \(Q(t)\) Current \(I(t)\) Net charge transferred Loss \(\mathcal{L}(\theta)\) \(\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L} \cdot \dot\theta\) Net change in loss

The last row is from ML — we return to it in §8.

docs.title: 5. Computing with FTC Part 2: Worked Examples
Example 1: Polynomial
docs.text:
\[\int_1^3 (x^2 - 4x + 3), dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3} - 2x^2 + 3x\right]_1^3\]

At \(x=3\): \(9 - 18 + 9 = 0\). At \(x=1\): \(\frac{1}{3} - 2 + 3 = \frac{4}{3}\).

\[= 0 - \frac{4}{3} = -\frac{4}{3}\]

The negative value means the region below the \(x\)-axis dominates.

docs.title: Example 4: Rational (requires recognizing antiderivative)
docs.text: \[\int_1^e \frac{1}{x}, dx = \Big[\ln|x|\Big]_1^e = \ln e - \ln 1 = 1 - 0 = 1\]

docs.title: Example 5: FTC Part 1 with Chain Rule
docs.text:
\[\frac{d}{dx}\int_{x^2}^{x^3} \sqrt{1+t^4}, dt\]

Split: let \(g(x) = \int_0^{x^3}\sqrt{1+t^4},dt - \int_0^{x^2}\sqrt{1+t^4},dt\).

\[= \sqrt{1+x^{12}} \cdot 3x^2 - \sqrt{1+x^8} \cdot 2x\]

docs.title: Example 6: FTC + L'Hôpital
docs.text:
Evaluate \(\displaystyle\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\int_0^x (e^{t^2} - 1), dt}{x^2}\).

Form \(0/0\). Apply L'Hôpital — differentiate numerator via FTC Part 1:

\[= \lim_{x\to 0} \frac{e^{x^2} - 1}{2x} \overset{0/0}{=} \lim_{x\to 0}\frac{2x e^{x^2}}{2} = 0\]

docs.title: 6. Why Any Antiderivative Works
docs.text:
FTC Part 2 says \(\int_a^b f = F(b) - F(a)\) for any antiderivative \(F\). Why doesn't the choice matter?

Suppose \(F\) and \(G\) are both antiderivatives of \(f\): \(F' = G' = f\).

Then \((F - G)' = 0\) so \(F(x) = G(x) + C\) for some constant.

\[G(b) - G(a) = [F(b) - C] - [F(a) - C] = F(b) - F(a)\]

The constant cancels. This is why we can write \(\int x^2, dx = \frac{x^3}{3} + C\) and use any particular \(C\) when evaluating a definite integral.

docs.title: 7. Visualization: The Geometric Heart of FTC
FTC Part 1 — Geometric Proof Sketch
docs.text:
Fix \(x\). The difference \(g(x+h) - g(x) = \int_x^{x+h} f(t), dt\) is the area of a thin vertical strip:

f(t)
  |
  |    *
  |   * *
f(x)|--*---*--
  |  *     *
  |         *
  +----|----|----> t
       x   x+h
       |←h→|
       thin strip ≈ f(x)·h

As \(h \to 0\), the strip becomes a rectangle of height \(f(x)\) and width \(h\). So:

\[g'(x) = \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{\text{area of strip}}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(x)\cdot h + O(h^2)}{h} = f(x)\]

docs.title: FTC Part 2 — Telescoping Visualization
docs.text:
Partition \([a,b]\) into \(n\) subintervals. By MVT for derivatives, on each \([x_{i-1}, x_i]\):

\[F(x_i) - F(x_{i-1}) = F'(c_i),\Delta x = f(c_i),\Delta x\]

Sum over all subintervals — the differences telescope:

\[F(b) - F(a) = \sum_{i=1}^n [F(x_i) - F(x_{i-1})] = \sum_{i=1}^n f(c_i),\Delta x\]

The right side is a Riemann sum for \(\int_a^b f\). As \(n \to \infty\):

\[F(b) - F(a) = \int_a^b f(x), dx \quad \blacksquare\]

This is arguably the most transparent proof of FTC Part 2 — it shows the integral as a telescoping sum of infinitesimal changes in \(F\).

F(b) - F(a) = [F(x₁)-F(x₀)] + [F(x₂)-F(x₁)] + ··· + [F(xₙ)-F(xₙ₋₁)]
                    ≈f(c₁)Δx       ≈f(c₂)Δx              ≈f(cₙ)Δx
            = Σ f(cᵢ)Δx
            → ∫ₐᵇ f(x)dx

docs.title: 8. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
docs.text: The FTC is not background mathematics for ML — it is operationally present in the core algorithms.

docs.title: 8.1 Backpropagation is FTC Part 2
docs.text:
Consider a scalar loss \(\mathcal{L}\) as a function of parameters \( heta(t)\) evolving along a path. By the chain rule (which is the infinitesimal form of FTC Part 2):

\[\mathcal{L}( heta(T)) - \mathcal{L}( heta(0)) = \int_0^T rac{d\mathcal{L}}{dt}, dt = \int_0^T abla_ heta \mathcal{L} \cdot \dot heta, dt\]

In discrete gradient descent with steps \( heta_{k+1} = heta_k - \eta abla \mathcal{L}( heta_k)\):

\[\mathcal{L}( heta_K) - \mathcal{L}( heta_0) \approx \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} abla_ heta\mathcal{L}( heta_k) \cdot ( heta_{k+1} - heta_k) = -\eta\sum_{k=0}^K | abla\mathcal{L}|^2\]

This is a Riemann sum for \(\int_0^T abla\mathcal{L}\cdot\dot heta,dt\) — FTC Part 2 in discrete form. Backpropagation computes this derivative so we can integrate it via gradient descent. The entire training loop is:

\[\underbrace{ ext{forward pass}}_{ ext{evaluate } \mathcal{L}} o \underbrace{ ext{backprop}}_{ ext{compute } F' = abla\mathcal{L}} o \underbrace{ ext{gradient step}}_{ ext{integrate: } \Delta heta = -\eta F'}\]

FTC Part 2: integrate the derivative to get net change.

docs.title: 8.2 The Adjoint Method in Neural ODEs is FTC Part 1
docs.text:
In a Neural ODE, the forward pass computes:

\[z(T) = z(0) + \int_0^T f_\theta(z(t), t), dt\]

To train, we need \(\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\theta}\). The adjoint state \(a(t) = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z(t)}\) satisfies:

\[\frac{da}{dt} = -a(t)^\top \frac{\partial f_\theta}{\partial z}\]

This ODE is derived by differentiating the area function \(\mathcal{L}(z(T)) = \mathcal{L}!\left(z(0) + \int_0^T f_\theta, dt\right)\) with respect to \(z(t)\) — applying FTC Part 1 inside the gradient computation. The entire backward pass of a Neural ODE is FTC Part 1 applied to a functional.

docs.title: 8.3 Score Functions and the Log-Derivative Trick
docs.text:
In policy gradient RL and variational inference, we need:

\[ abla_ heta \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_ heta}[f(x)] = abla_ heta \int f(x), p_ heta(x), dx\]

Passing \( abla_ heta\) under the integral (valid by dominated convergence):

\[= \int f(x), abla_ heta p_ heta(x), dx = \int f(x), p_ heta(x), rac{ abla_ heta p_ heta(x)}{p_ heta(x)}, dx = \mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_ heta}[f(x), abla_ heta \log p_ heta(x)]\]

This is differentiating under the integral sign — FTC Part 1 applied to a parameter-dependent integral. The result is the REINFORCE / score function estimator, the foundation of policy gradient methods in RL.

docs.title: 8.4 Normalizing Flows: FTC as Change of Variables
docs.text:
A normalizing flow transforms a simple density \(p_z(z)\) to a complex density \(p_x(x)\) via an invertible map \(x = g(z)\). The change-of-variables formula:

\[p_x(x) = p_z(g^{-1}(x))\left|\det\frac{\partial g^{-1}}{\partial x}\right|\]

In 1D, this is just:

\[p_x(x) = p_z(z)\left|\frac{dz}{dx}\right| = \frac{p_z(g^{-1}(x))}{|g'(g^{-1}(x))|}\]

which is the 1D FTC: \(\int_a^b p_z(g^{-1}(x))|dg^{-1}/dx|,dx = \int_{g^{-1}(a)}^{g^{-1}(b)} p_z(z),dz\). Normalizing flows are architecturally built on FTC as a change-of-variables identity.

docs.title: 8.5 Continuous-Time Bellman Equation
docs.text:
In continuous-time RL with value function \(V(s,t)\) and reward \(r(s,t)\):

\[V(s,t) = \int_t^T r(s(\tau), \tau), e^{-\gamma(\tau-t)}, d\tau + e^{-\gamma(T-t)}V(s(T), T)\]

\(V\) is an area function of \(t\) (with lower limit \(t\)). Differentiating via FTC:

\[\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} + \mathcal{H}\left(s, \nabla_s V\right) = \gamma V\]

This is the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation — the central equation of optimal control. It is obtained by applying FTC Part 1 to the value function integral. Every RL algorithm (Q-learning, actor-critic, PPO) is, at the continuous-time limit, solving this PDE — which is a consequence of the FTC.

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text: FTC Concept ML/DL Analog \(\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^x f = f(x)\) (FTC 1) Adjoint method in Neural ODEs \(\int_a^b F' = F(b)-F(a)\) (FTC 2) Backprop: total loss change = integral of gradient Net Change Theorem Training loss decrease = integrated gradient norm Telescoping sum proof Discrete gradient descent as Riemann sum Differentiating under the integral REINFORCE / score function estimator in RL Change of variables (FTC in substitution) Normalizing flows density transformation Area function \(g(x) = \int_a^x f\) Value function \(V(s,t)\) in continuous-time RL HJB: derivative of area function Bellman equation: \(\partial_t V + \mathcal{H} = \gamma V\) Any antiderivative works (constant cancels) Gauge freedom in value function baselines

docs.title: 9. Common Errors and How to Avoid Them
Error 1: Forgetting the Chain Rule in FTC Part 1
docs.text:
\[\frac{d}{dx}\int_1^{x^2} e^{t^3}, dt \neq e^{x^6}\]

Correct: \(= e^{(x^2)^3} \cdot 2x = e^{x^6} \cdot 2x\).

The upper limit is \(u(x) = x^2\), so multiply by \(u'(x) = 2x\).

docs.title: Error 2: Mixing the Integration Variable with the Limit
docs.text:
\[\int_1^x x^2, dx \quad \leftarrow \text{ILLEGAL}\]

The integration variable and the limit cannot share a name. Write \(\int_1^x t^2, dt = \frac{x^3}{3} - \frac{1}{3}\).

docs.title: Error 3: Using FTC Part 2 Across a Discontinuity
docs.text:
\[\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{1}{x^2}, dx \neq \left[-\frac{1}{x}\right]_{-1}^{1} = -1-1 = -2\]

\(f(x) = 1/x^2\) has a non-integrable singularity at \(x = 0\). The function is not continuous on \([-1,1]\), so FTC Part 2 does not apply. (The correct answer is \(+\infty\) — the integral diverges.)

Always verify continuity on \([a,b]\) before applying FTC Part 2.

docs.title: Error 4: Sign Errors When Differentiating a Lower Limit
docs.text:
\[\frac{d}{dx}\int_x^b f(t), dt = \frac{d}{dx}\left(-\int_b^x f(t), dt\right) = -f(x)\]

Not \(+f(x)\). Flip the integral, pick up a minus sign.

docs.title: 10. The Bigger Picture: FTC in the Landscape of Mathematics
docs.text:
The FTC is not an isolated result. It is the \(n=1\) case of a family of theorems connecting derivatives to integrals across dimensions:

Theorem Domain Statement FTC \([a,b] \subset \mathbb{R}^1\) \(\int_a^b f', dx = f(b) - f(a)\) Green's Theorem Region \(D \subset \mathbb{R}^2\) \(\iint_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right) dA = \oint_{\partial D} P, dx + Q, dy\) Stokes' Theorem Surface \(S \subset \mathbb{R}^3\) \(\iint_S (\nabla \times \mathbf{F})\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \oint_{\partial S} \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r}\) Divergence Theorem Volume \(V \subset \mathbb{R}^3\) \(\iiint_V (\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}), dV = \oiint_{\partial V} \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S}\) Generalized Stokes \(n\)-manifold \(M\) \(\int_M d\omega = \int_{\partial M} \omega\)

All of these say the same thing: the integral of a derivative over a region equals the integral of the original over the boundary. The FTC is the 1D baby case. The generalized Stokes' theorem (differential geometry) is the full adult.

This is why the FTC matters beyond calculus — it is a special case of one of the most general theorems in mathematics.

docs.title: 11. Quick-Reference Cheatsheet
docs.text: \[\textbf{FTC Part 1:} \quad \frac{d}{dx}\int_a^x f(t), dt = f(x)\] \[\textbf{Chain Rule Form:} \quad \frac{d}{dx}\int_a^{u(x)} f(t), dt = f(u(x))\cdot u'(x)\] \[\textbf{Both Limits Variable:} \quad \frac{d}{dx}\int_{v(x)}^{u(x)} f(t), dt = f(u(x))u'(x) - f(v(x))v'(x)\] \[\textbf{FTC Part 2:} \quad \int_a^b f(x), dx = F(b) - F(a), \quad F' = f\] \[\textbf{Net Change:} \quad \int_a^b F'(x), dx = F(b) - F(a)\] \[\textbf{Checklist before FTC 2:}$$ $$\quad 1.\ f \text{ continuous on } [a,b]? \checkmark$$ $$\quad 2.\ F \text{ is antiderivative of } f \text{ on all of } [a,b]? \checkmark$$ $$\quad 3.\ \text{No singularities hidden inside } (a,b)? \checkmark\]

docs.title: The Fresnel Function
docs.text: "The Fresnel integrals are the canonical example of a function that exists perfectly — continuous, differentiable, with known Taylor series and asymptotic behavior — yet resists every attempt to write it in closed form. They are what mathematics looks like when FTC Part 1 is the end of the road, not the beginning."

docs.title: 0. The Setup: A Function Defined by Integration
docs.text:
From [[Fundamental Theorem of Calculus]], we know that if \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), then the area function

\[g(x) = \int_a^x f(t), dt\]

is guaranteed to exist and satisfy \(g'(x) = f(x)\) — even if \(f\) has no elementary antiderivative.

The Fresnel sine function is precisely such an object:

\[\boxed{S(x) = \int_0^x \sin(t^2), dt}\]

The integrand \(\sin(t^2)\) is continuous everywhere. Its antiderivative exists (guaranteed by FTC Part 1). But that antiderivative cannot be written using polynomials, exponentials, logarithms, trigonometric functions, or any finite combination thereof.

\(S(x)\) is not a formula. It is a function defined by the act of integration itself.

This is not a failure. It is the normal state of affairs — most functions do not have elementary antiderivatives. The Fresnel functions are simply the most famous members of this class, arising naturally in physics and engineering.

docs.title: 1. Definitions
docs.text:
There are two Fresnel functions, arising as a pair:

\[\boxed{S(x) = \int_0^x \sin(t^2), dt}\] \[\boxed{C(x) = \int_0^x \cos(t^2), dt}\]

They appear together because \(\sin\) and \(\cos\) are always companions — they are the imaginary and real parts of \(e^{it}\), and \(S(x) + iC(x) = \int_0^x e^{it^2}, dt\) (up to conventions).

docs.title: Alternate Normalization (Physics / Engineering)
docs.text:
In many physics texts (optics, diffraction theory), the Fresnel integrals are normalized differently:

\[S_{\text{phys}}(u) = \int_0^u \sin!\left(\frac{\pi t^2}{2}\right) dt, \qquad C_{\text{phys}}(u) = \int_0^u \cos!\left(\frac{\pi t^2}{2}\right) dt\]

The substitution \(t^2 = \pi s^2/2\) converts between conventions. We use the Stewart convention \(S(x) = \int_0^x \sin(t^2), dt\) throughout.

docs.title: 2. Immediate Properties from FTC
docs.text:
By [[Fundamental Theorem of Calculus]] Part 1, since \(\sin(t^2)\) and \(\cos(t^2)\) are continuous everywhere:

\[S'(x) = \sin(x^2), \qquad C'(x) = \cos(x^2)\]

This is the complete answer to "what is the derivative?" — and it follows in one line from FTC, no computation required.

From these derivatives, we can read off everything about the shape of \(S\) and \(C\):

docs.title: Critical Points of \(S(x)\)
docs.text:
\(S'(x) = \sin(x^2) = 0\) when \(x^2 = n\pi\) for integer \(n \geq 0\):

\[x = \sqrt{n\pi}, \quad n = 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots\] \[x = 0,\ \sqrt{\pi},\ \sqrt{2\pi},\ \sqrt{3\pi},\ \sqrt{4\pi},\ \ldots\] \[\approx 0,\ 1.772,\ 2.507,\ 3.070,\ 3.545,\ \ldots\]

At each \(x = \sqrt{n\pi}\), \(S\) has a local extremum:

  • \(n\) odd: \(\sin(x^2) = \sin(n\pi) = 0\), and changes sign \(+ \to -\): local maximum
  • \(n\) even (nonzero): changes sign \(- \to +\): local minimum

docs.title: Concavity of \(S(x)\)
docs.text:
\[S''(x) = 2x\cos(x^2)\]

Inflection points where \(S''(x) = 0\):

  • \(x = 0\)
  • \(x^2 = \frac{\pi}{2} + n\pi\), i.e. \(x = \sqrt{\frac{(2n+1)\pi}{2}}\) for \(n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\)

The concavity oscillates with increasing frequency as \(x\) grows.

docs.title: Near the origin: \(S(x) \approx x^3/3\)
docs.text:
For small \(x\), \(\sin(t^2) \approx t^2\), so:

\[S(x) \approx \int_0^x t^2, dt = \frac{x^3}{3}\]

More precisely, using the Taylor series \(\sin u = u - u^3/6 + \cdots\) with \(u = t^2\):

\[\sin(t^2) = t^2 - \frac{t^6}{6} + \frac{t^{10}}{120} - \cdots\]

Integrating term by term (valid by [[Fundamental Theorem of Calculus]]):

\[S(x) = \frac{x^3}{3} - \frac{x^7}{7 \cdot 6} + \frac{x^{11}}{11 \cdot 120} - \cdots = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n x^{4n+3}}{(2n+1)!,(4n+3)}\]

This series converges for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) (by ratio test — the factorial in the denominator dominates any power of \(x\)). So we can compute \(S(x)\) to arbitrary precision for any \(x\).

Similarly:

\[C(x) = x - \frac{x^5}{5 \cdot 2!} + \frac{x^9}{9 \cdot 4!} - \cdots = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n x^{4n+1}}{(2n)!,(4n+1)}\]

docs.title: 4. Behavior as \(x \to \infty\): The Cornu Spiral Limit
docs.text:
The most remarkable property of the Fresnel functions is their limiting behavior:

\[\lim_{x \to \infty} S(x) = \lim_{x \to \infty} C(x) = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{4} \cdot \sqrt{2} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}\]

More precisely:

\[\int_0^\infty \sin(t^2), dt = \int_0^\infty \cos(t^2), dt = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}} \approx 0.6267\]

This is a non-trivial result — the integrals converge even though \(\sin(t^2)\) does not \(\to 0\) as \(t \to \infty\) in the usual sense (it keeps oscillating). The convergence is conditional, via cancellation of the increasingly rapid oscillations.

Proof sketch (for the curious). Use the substitution \(u = t^2\), \(du = 2t, dt\), \(dt = \frac{du}{2\sqrt{u}}\):

\[\int_0^\infty \sin(t^2), dt = \int_0^\infty \sin(u)\frac{du}{2\sqrt{u}} = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^\infty u^{-1/2}\sin(u), du\]

This is a Mellin transform evaluated at \(s = 1/2\), and equals \(\frac{1}{2}\cdot\Gamma(1/2)\cdot\sin(\pi/4) = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\sqrt{\pi}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}}\). \(\blacksquare\)

The fact that the integral converges to a finite value is a consequence of the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma — rapidly oscillating functions average out.

docs.text:
S(x) = ∫₀ˣ sin(t²) dt

 S(x)
 0.7|                    ·  ·  ·  ·  (→ √(π/8) ≈ 0.627)
    |               ****

    |        ***            ***
 0.3|      **                   **
    |    **
 0.1|  **
    | *
 0.0|*_________________________ __> x

Key landmarks:
  x = 0:       S = 0
  x = √π ≈ 1.77:  first local max ≈ 0.625
  x = √(2π) ≈ 2.51: first local min
  x = √(3π) ≈ 3.07: second local max
  x → ∞:      S → √(π/8) ≈ 0.627

The function oscillates with increasing frequency and decreasing amplitude of oscillation, converging to its limiting value from alternating sides.

docs.title: 5.2 The Cornu Spiral (Euler's Spiral)
docs.text:
Parametrize the curve \((C(x), S(x))\) in the plane as \(x\) runs from \(-\infty\) to \(+\infty\):

S(x)
  |              · ·
 0.6|          ·      ·          ← approaches (√(π/8), √(π/8))
  |        ·     ⊕    ·              as x → +∞
 0.4|      ·             ·
  |     ·                ·
 0.2|    ·                  ·
  |   ·                        ·
  |  ·                              ·  ·  ·
  |·_________________________ ___________> C(x)
-0.6  -0.4  -0.2   0   0.2   0.4   0.6

⊕ = (√(π/8), √(π/8)) ≈ (0.627, 0.627): right eye of spiral
⊗ = (-√(π/8), -√(π/8)): left eye of spiral

The curve spirals inward toward \((+\sqrt{\pi/8}, +\sqrt{\pi/8})\) as \(x \to +\infty\) and toward \((-\sqrt{\pi/8}, -\sqrt{\pi/8})\) as \(x \to -\infty\) (by oddness of \(S\) and \(C\)).

Key geometric property: The tangent angle of the Cornu spiral at arc-length parameter \(x\) is exactly \(x^2\) radians. This is the defining property used in optics.

The curvature at point \(x\) is \(\kappa(x) = 2x\) — it increases linearly with arc length, making the Cornu spiral the unique curve of linearly increasing curvature.

docs.title: 6. Symmetry Properties
docs.text:
Since \(\sin((-t)^2) = \sin(t^2)\) and \(\cos((-t)^2) = \cos(t^2)\), the integrands are even functions of \(t\). Therefore:

\[S(-x) = \int_0^{-x}\sin(t^2), dt = -\int_0^x \sin(t^2), dt = -S(x)\] \[C(-x) = -C(x)\]

Both \(S\) and \(C\) are odd functions. The Cornu spiral is symmetric under \(180°\) rotation about the origin.

docs.title: 7. The Stewart Example: Reading \(S(x)\) from \(S'(x) = \sin(x^2)\)
docs.text:
Stewart uses \(S(x)\) as a paradigmatic example of FTC Part 1 in action (§5.3). The exercise is: given only that \(S'(x) = \sin(x^2)\) and \(S(0) = 0\), determine the behavior of \(S\).

Where is \(S\) increasing?

\(S'(x) = \sin(x^2) > 0\) when \(x^2 \in (2k\pi, (2k+1)\pi)\) for integer \(k \geq 0\), i.e.:

\[x \in \left(\sqrt{2k\pi},\ \sqrt{(2k+1)\pi}\right), \quad k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\]

The first increasing interval is \((0, \sqrt{\pi}) \approx (0, 1.772)\).

Where is \(S\) concave up?

\(S''(x) = 2x\cos(x^2) > 0\) when \(\cos(x^2) > 0\) (for \(x > 0\)), i.e., \(x^2 \in [0, \pi/2) \cup (3\pi/2, 5\pi/2) \cup \ldots\)

The first local maximum:

At \(x = \sqrt{\pi}\): \(S(\sqrt{\pi}) = \int_0^{\sqrt{\pi}}\sin(t^2), dt \approx 0.6247\).

This can be estimated with \(M_n\) or \(T_n\). Using the Taylor series with enough terms gives the value to any desired precision.

docs.title: 8. Numerical Computation of \(S(x)\)
docs.text: Since there is no closed form, we compute \(S(x)\) numerically.

docs.title: Method 1: Taylor Series (small \(x\))
docs.text:
\[S(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{N} \frac{(-1)^n x^{4n+3}}{(2n+1)!,(4n+3)}\]

For \(x = 1\), taking 4 terms:

\[S(1) \approx \frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{42} + \frac{1}{1320} - \frac{1}{75600} \approx 0.3333 - 0.0238 + 0.000758 - 0.0000132 \approx 0.3103\]

True value: \(S(1) \approx 0.3103\). \(\checkmark\)

For large \(x\), the Taylor series converges slowly (large terms that nearly cancel). Switch to asymptotic expansion or numerical quadrature.

docs.title: Method 3: Asymptotic Expansion (large \(x\))
docs.text:
For \(x \gg 1\), integration by parts gives:

\[S(x) \approx \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}} - \frac{\cos(x^2)}{2x} - \frac{\sin(x^2)}{4x^3} + \cdots\]

This is an asymptotic series — it does not converge, but for large \(x\), the first few terms give excellent approximations.

docs.title: 9. Why This Function Matters: Fresnel Diffraction
docs.text:
The Fresnel functions were introduced by Augustin-Jean Fresnel (~1818) in his wave theory of light.

When a plane wave passes through a narrow slit, the intensity at a point on the screen is:

\[I \propto \left[C(u_2) - C(u_1)\right]^2 + \left[S(u_2) - S(u_1)\right]^2\]

where \(u_1, u_2\) are parameters determined by the geometry. The diffraction pattern — the alternating bright and dark bands — is encoded in how \(C\) and \(S\) vary.

The Cornu spiral is the direct visual representation of this: the chord length between two points on the spiral gives the amplitude, and the chord squared gives the intensity.

This is not a contrived application. The Fresnel functions are the exact, non-approximated solution to the diffraction problem for arbitrary screen geometry.

docs.title: 10. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
10.1 The Error Function: Fresnel's Cousin in ML
docs.text:
The Gaussian integral \(\int_0^x e^{-t^2}, dt\) is the error function \(\text{erf}(x)\) (up to scaling) — structurally identical to \(S(x)\): a continuous integrand with no elementary antiderivative, defined as an area function via FTC.

In ML, \(\text{erf}\) appears everywhere:

  • Normal CDF: \(\Phi(x) = \frac{1}{2}\left[1 + \text{erf}!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\right]\)
  • GELU activation: \(\text{GELU}(x) = x,\Phi(x) = \frac{x}{2}\left[1 + \text{erf}!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\right]\)
  • Probit models: logistic regression with Gaussian noise uses \(\Phi^{-1}\)

The GELU (Gaussian Error Linear Unit) is the default activation in BERT, GPT-2, GPT-3, and most modern transformers. It is defined via the error function — which is defined via FTC Part 1. Every forward pass through a transformer computes an area function.

docs.title: 10.2 Fresnel-Type Integrals in Quantum ML
docs.text:
In quantum machine learning and path integral formulations:

\[Z = \int \mathcal{D}[\phi], e^{iS[\phi]}\]

where \(S[\phi]\) is the action — a Fresnel-type oscillatory integral in infinite dimensions. The Fresnel integral \(\int e^{it^2} dt\) is the 1D baby case of the Feynman path integral. Approximating \(Z\) numerically is one of the central computational challenges, and all the issues we saw — rapid oscillation, conditional convergence, need for asymptotic methods — appear in full force.

docs.title: 10.3 Fourier Analysis: Chirp Signals and Fresnel Transforms
docs.text:
A chirp signal is \(f(t) = e^{i\alpha t^2}\) — a sinusoid whose frequency increases linearly with time. In radar, sonar, and MRI:

\[\hat{f}(\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{i\alpha t^2} e^{-i\omega t}, dt\]

This integral evaluates to a Gaussian times a phase factor — by completing the square and using the Fresnel integral \(\int e^{it^2}, dt = \sqrt{\pi/2}, e^{i\pi/4}\). Matched filtering in radar signal processing — how a receiver recognizes a transmitted chirp — is built on this Fresnel integral identity.

In ML: linear attention and random Fourier features (Rahimi & Recht, 2007) approximate kernel functions using exactly these oscillatory integrals.

docs.title: 10.4 Numerical Integration of Oscillatory Integrands
docs.text:
The challenge of computing \(S(x)\) for large \(x\) is representative of a general problem in scientific ML:

\[\int_a^b f(t)\sin(\omega t^2), dt, \quad \omega \gg 1\]

Standard quadrature (Midpoint, Trapezoid, Simpson) fails badly because the integrand oscillates faster than the grid can resolve. The solutions are:

  • Levin's method: reformulate as an ODE, avoid oscillation entirely
  • Filon quadrature: exploit the oscillatory structure analytically
  • Numerical steepest descent: deform the contour into the complex plane where the integrand decays

These are active research areas in scientific computing and appear in Monte Carlo simulation for neural network training with oscillatory loss landscapes.

docs.title: 10.5 Taylor Series as Feature Expansion
docs.text:
The Taylor expansion of \(S(x)\):

\[S(x) = \frac{x^3}{3} - \frac{x^7}{42} + \frac{x^{11}}{1320} - \cdots\]

is a polynomial feature expansion — exactly what kernel methods and polynomial regression use. The fact that we can represent \(S(x)\) to arbitrary precision with a polynomial of high enough degree is the mathematical foundation of the universal approximation theorem: continuous functions on compact sets can be approximated arbitrarily well by polynomials (Weierstrass), and by neural networks (Cybenko, Hornik).

\(S(x)\) is the canonical example that functions can be perfectly well-defined and smooth while requiring infinite series — never a finite formula. Neural networks are doing the same thing: approximating a target function (which may have no closed form) with a finite parametric family.

docs.title: Differentiation and Integration as Inverses
docs.text: "To say that differentiation and integration are inverses is to say something far deeper than 'they undo each other.' It is to say that the local and the global are not separate — that knowing how fast something changes at every point is the same as knowing how much it accumulates over every interval. This equivalence is not obvious. It is a theorem. And it is the reason calculus works."

docs.title: 0. The Philosophical Starting Point
docs.text:
Two operations. Two completely different origins.

Differentiation asks: what is \(f\) doing right now? It is local — it examines \(f\) in an infinitesimal neighborhood of a single point and extracts the instantaneous rate of change.

Integration asks: what has \(f\) done over an interval? It is global — it surveys \(f\) across an entire region and accumulates all contributions.

There is no a priori reason these should be related. A geographer measuring the slope of a hillside at a single rock is doing something completely different from a hydrologist measuring the total rainfall over a watershed. The FTC says: these two people are, in a precise mathematical sense, doing inverse operations of each other.

This note asks: what exactly does "inverse" mean here? How complete is the inversion? Where does it fail? And what is the algebraic structure underneath?

docs.title: 1. Two Operators, Precisely Defined
docs.text:
Let us be precise about what we are inverting.

The Differentiation Operator \(D\).

\[D: f \mapsto f', \qquad (Df)(x) = \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}\]

\(D\) acts on differentiable functions and produces functions (their derivatives). It is a linear operator:

\[D(\alpha f + \beta g) = \alpha Df + \beta Dg\]

The Indefinite Integration Operator \(J\).

\[J: f \mapsto F + C, \qquad (Jf)(x) = \int f(x), dx = F(x) + C, \quad F' = f\]

\(J\) is also linear, but its output is not unique — it produces a family of functions differing by a constant.

The Definite Integration Operator \(I_a\) (fix left endpoint \(a\)):

\[(I_a f)(x) = \int_a^x f(t), dt\]

\(I_a f\) is a single, well-defined function (not a family).

The FTC says \(D\) and \(I_a\) are mutual inverses — in a sense we now make precise.

docs.title: 2. FTC Part 1: \(D \circ I_a = \text{Id}\)
docs.text:
Theorem (FTC Part 1). If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\):

\[D(I_a f)(x) = \frac{d}{dx}\int_a^x f(t), dt = f(x)\]

In operator notation: \(D \circ I_a = \text{Id}\) on the space of continuous functions.

What this says: Integrate first, then differentiate — you get back to where you started. The area function \(\int_a^x f(t), dt\) is an antiderivative of \(f\), and differentiating it recovers \(f\) exactly.

docs.title: The Proof in One Diagram
docs.text:
integrate
   f(t)  ─────────────────►  g(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt
     ▲                              │
     │  D∘Iₐ = Id                  │  differentiate
     │                              │
     └──────────────────────────────┘
              g'(x) = f(x)  ✓

The round trip — integrate then differentiate — brings you back to \(f\).

Proof.

\[g'(x) = \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{g(x+h)-g(x)}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{1}{h}\int_x^{x+h}f(t),dt = \lim_{h\to 0}f(c_h) = f(x)\]

where \(c_h \in (x, x+h)\) by the MVT for integrals, and \(c_h \to x\) forces \(f(c_h) \to f(x)\) by continuity. \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: 3. FTC Part 2: $I_a \circ D = $ Net Change
docs.text:
Theorem (FTC Part 2). If \(F\) is differentiable on \([a,b]\) with continuous derivative \(F'\):

\[I_a(DF)(b) = \int_a^b F'(x), dx = F(b) - F(a)\]

In operator notation: \(I_a \circ D \neq \text{Id}\), but rather:

\[(I_a \circ D \circ F)(b) = F(b) - F(a)\]

What this says: Differentiate first, then integrate — you do not get back to \(F(x)\). You get the net change \(F(b) - F(a)\).

The round trip — differentiate then integrate — loses the starting value \(F(a)\).

docs.title: Why It Is Not a Perfect Inverse
docs.text:
differentiate
   F(x)  ─────────────────►  f(x) = F'(x)
     ▲                              │
     │  I∘D ≠ Id                   │  integrate from a to b
     │                              │
     └──────────────────────────────┘
       F(b) - F(a), not F(x)  ✗ (loses F(a))

Differentiation destroys the constant. If \(F(x) = x^2 + 7\) and \(G(x) = x^2 + 13\), then \(F' = G' = 2x\). Integration recovers \(2x\) but cannot reconstruct whether the constant was \(7\) or \(13\).

The information lost by \(D\) is exactly the initial value \(F(a)\).

docs.title: 4. The Precise Algebraic Relationship
docs.text:
Let us organize what we know into a clean statement.

Setting: Let \(\mathcal{C}[a,b]\) be the space of continuous functions on \([a,b]\), and \(\mathcal{C}^1[a,b]\) the space of continuously differentiable functions.

\[D: \mathcal{C}^1[a,b] \to \mathcal{C}[a,b], \qquad I_a: \mathcal{C}[a,b] \to \mathcal{C}^1[a,b]\]

Result 1 (FTC Part 1): \(D \circ I_a = \text{Id}_{\mathcal{C}[a,b]}\)

\[\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^x f(t), dt = f(x) \quad \text{for all } f \in \mathcal{C}[a,b]\]

Result 2 (FTC Part 2): \(I_a \circ D \neq \text{Id}_{\mathcal{C}^1[a,b]}\), but:

\[\int_a^x F'(t), dt = F(x) - F(a) \quad \text{for all } F \in \mathcal{C}^1[a,b]\]

So \(I_a \circ D\) recovers \(F\) up to the lost constant \(F(a)\):

\[(I_a \circ D)(F)(x) = F(x) - F(a)\]

Recovery formula: \(F(x) = (I_a \circ D)(F)(x) + F(a)\).

docs.title: The Kernel of \(D\)
docs.text:
The failure of \(I \circ D = \text{Id}\) is quantified by the kernel of \(D\):

\[\ker(D) = {F \in \mathcal{C}^1[a,b] : DF = 0} = {\text{constant functions}}\]

Differentiation kills constants. Integration cannot reconstruct them. The information lost is exactly a real number — the value \(F(a)\).

This is the algebraic content of "\(+C\)" in indefinite integration.

docs.title: 5. The Indefinite Integral Resolves the Asymmetry
docs.text:
The indefinite integral \(\int f(x), dx = F(x) + C\) is designed to represent the entire family of antiderivatives — recovering all the information that \(D\) could have destroyed.

If we define:

\[J: f \mapsto {F + C : C \in \mathbb{R}}\]

then \(D \circ J = \text{Id}\) and \(J \circ D(F) = F + C\) — the full family containing \(F\), not the specific function. The constant \(C\) encodes the "missing" information.

The definite integral \(I_a\) makes a choice: fix \(C\) by requiring \(g(a) = 0\). That pins down exactly one antiderivative.

   | *   *     *                   |    * *
   |*     *   * *                  |   *   *
---+-------*-*----> x           ---+--*-----*----> x
   |        *                      |*         *
  -1|                              0|

I extracts accumulation from     (area under f, net signed)
the rate. g rises when f > 0,
falls when f < 0.

docs.title: 6.3 The Asymmetry in Pictures
docs.text:
Differentiate then integrate:

\[F(x) = x^2 + 5 \xrightarrow{D} 2x \xrightarrow{I_0} x^2\]

We get \(x^2\), not \(x^2 + 5\). The constant \(5\) was annihilated by \(D\).

Integrate then differentiate:

\[f(x) = 2x \xrightarrow{I_0} x^2 \xrightarrow{D} 2x\]

We get \(2x\) back exactly. The round trip is perfect.

This asymmetry is fundamental. \(D\) is like erasing a digit: you can erase \(5\) to get \(_\), and writing it back in (specifying \(+C\)) restores full information. But once you hand me \(_\) without telling me what was erased, I cannot recover it.

docs.title: 7. The Telescope: Why FTC Part 2 Works
docs.text:
The cleanest proof of FTC Part 2 reveals the mechanism of partial inversion.

Partition \([a,b]\) into \(n\) subintervals. On each \([x_{i-1}, x_i]\), the MVT for derivatives gives \(c_i\) with:

\[F(x_i) - F(x_{i-1}) = F'(c_i),\Delta x\]

Sum:

\[\sum_{i=1}^n [F(x_i) - F(x_{i-1})] = \sum_{i=1}^n F'(c_i),\Delta x\]

Left side telescopes to \(F(b) - F(a)\). Right side is a Riemann sum for \(\int_a^b F'\). As \(n\to\infty\):

\[F(b) - F(a) = \int_a^b F'(x), dx\]

The telescope is the mechanism. Integration sums up all the local increments \(F'(c_i)\Delta x\), and they perfectly reconstruct the net global change \(F(b)-F(a)\) — but only the net change, not the starting point.

F(b) - F(a)
= [F(x₁)-F(x₀)] + [F(x₂)-F(x₁)] + ··· + [F(xₙ)-F(xₙ₋₁)]   ← telescopes
≈ F'(c₁)Δx    +  F'(c₂)Δx    + ··· +  F'(cₙ)Δx              ← MVT
→ ∫ₐᵇ F'(x) dx                                                ← n→∞

The telescope metaphor: Each term \(F(x_i) - F(x_{i-1})\) is a piece of the story. Integration is the act of reading all the pieces together. The story it recovers is the total change — not the initial chapter.

docs.title: 8. The Full Inverse Relationship: A Precise Summary
docs.text:
\[\boxed{ \begin{aligned} &\textbf{FTC Part 1 (Perfect inversion):}\ &\quad \frac{d}{dx}\int_a^x f(t), dt = f(x) \quad &&\text{if } f \text{ continuous}\[8pt] &\textbf{FTC Part 2 (Imperfect: loses initial value):}\ &\quad \int_a^b F'(x), dx = F(b) - F(a) \quad &&\text{if } F' \text{ continuous}\[8pt] &\textbf{Recovery (complete inversion using initial condition):}\ &\quad F(x) = F(a) + \int_a^x F'(t), dt \quad &&\text{(ODE initial value problem)} \end{aligned} }\]

The third line is the key insight: FTC Part 2 becomes a perfect inverse once you supply the initial value \(F(a)\). This is the fundamental theorem of ODEs — knowing \(F'\) everywhere and \(F\) at one point completely determines \(F\) everywhere.

docs.title: 9. Analogy: Summation and Differencing
docs.text:
The discrete analogs sharpen the intuition.

Let \((a_n)\) be a sequence. Define:

  • Forward difference operator: \(\Delta a_n = a_{n+1} - a_n\) (discrete derivative)
  • Summation operator: \(\Sigma_k^n a_i = \sum_{i=k}^n a_i\) (discrete integral)

Then:

\[\sum_{i=k}^{n} \Delta a_i = \sum_{i=k}^n (a_{i+1} - a_i) = a_{n+1} - a_k \quad \text{(telescoping = discrete FTC Part 2)}\] \[\Delta \left(\sum_{i=k}^n a_i\right) = a_{n+1} \quad \text{(discrete FTC Part 1)}\]

The discrete FTC is the telescoping sum. The continuous FTC is the limiting form of this same fact.

Discrete Continuous Sequence \(a_n\) Function \(F(x)\) Difference \(\Delta a_n = a_{n+1}-a_n\) Derivative \(F'(x)\) Telescoping sum \(\sum \Delta a_i = a_n - a_0\) \(\int_a^b F', dx = F(b)-F(a)\) Summation then difference = Id Integration then differentiation = Id Difference then summation = net change Differentiation then integration = net change

docs.title: 10. Where the Inversion Fails
docs.text: The FTC requires hypotheses. Each hypothesis failure breaks the inversion in a specific way.

docs.title: Failure 1: Discontinuity of \(f\)
docs.text:
If \(f\) has a jump at \(x_0\), then \(g(x) = \int_a^x f\) is continuous but not differentiable at \(x_0\). FTC Part 1 fails at the discontinuity:

\[g'(x_0) \text{ does not exist}\] \[\text{Example: } f(x) = \begin{cases}0 & x < 0 \ 1 & x \geq 0\end{cases}, \quad g(x) = \int_{-1}^x f(t),dt = \max(0, x)\]

\(g\) is the ramp function — continuous but not differentiable at \(0\).

docs.title: Failure 2: Non-integrable singularity
docs.text:
\[\int_{-1}^1 \frac{1}{x^2}, dx \neq \left[-\frac{1}{x}\right]_{-1}^1\]

\(F(x) = -1/x\) is an antiderivative of \(1/x^2\) on \((-\infty,0)\) and on \((0,\infty)\) separately, but not across the singularity at \(0\). The integral diverges. FTC Part 2 requires \(F'\) continuous on the entire closed interval — no exceptions.

docs.title: Failure 3: Volterra's function (pathological)
docs.text: There exist functions \(F\) that are differentiable everywhere with \(F'\) bounded, yet \(F'\) is not Riemann integrable. For such \(F\), FTC Part 2 fails in the Riemann sense (though it holds for the Lebesgue integral). This is why Lebesgue integration is the right framework for a fully general FTC.

docs.title: Failure 4: Complex analysis — a happy failure
docs.text: In complex analysis, \(f(z) = 1/z\) has no antiderivative on any domain containing the origin. The integral \(\oint_{|z|=1} \frac{1}{z}, dz = 2\pi i \neq 0\) — the round trip does not return to zero. This "failure" of the FTC is Cauchy's theorem in disguise, and is the foundation of complex analysis and residue theory.

docs.title: 11. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
docs.text: The inversion relationship between \(D\) and \(I\) is operationally present throughout modern ML.

docs.title: 11.1 Forward Pass and Backward Pass
docs.text:
The entire training loop of a neural network is organized around this inversion:

Direction Operation Mathematical Role Forward pass Compute \(\mathcal{L}(\theta)\) Evaluate \(F\) Backward pass (backprop) Compute \(\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}\) Apply \(D\) to \(F\) Gradient step \(\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\nabla\mathcal{L}\) Apply \(I\) to \(DF\) Net result \(\Delta\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{new}} - \mathcal{L}_{\text{old}}\) \(I \circ D\) = net change

The forward-backward-update cycle is one instance of "differentiate, then integrate" — FTC Part 2 applied to the loss landscape. The gradient step never recovers the full loss function; it only moves along it by a net change.

docs.title: 11.2 Neural ODEs: The Inversion Made Explicit
docs.text:
A Neural ODE directly instantiates $I \circ D = $ net change:

\[z(T) = z(0) + \underbrace{\int_0^T f_\theta(z(t), t), dt}_{I \circ D \text{ applied to } z}\]

The forward pass is \(I\). The defining ODE \(\dot{z} = f_\theta\) is \(D\). Training requires computing \(\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\theta}\) — differentiating through the integral — which is exactly \(D \circ I\) applied to a loss functional.

The adjoint method exploits FTC Part 1 (\(D \circ I = \text{Id}\)) to avoid storing intermediate states: instead of backpropagating through every integration step, it solves a new ODE backward in time. The correctness of this trick rests entirely on FTC Part 1.

docs.title: 11.3 Score-Based Generative Models (Diffusion)
docs.text:
A diffusion model corrupts data via a forward SDE:

\[dx = -\frac{1}{2}\beta(t)x, dt + \sqrt{\beta(t)}, dW\]

and learns to reverse it. The score function \(s_\theta(x,t) \approx \nabla_x \log p_t(x)\) is the gradient (differentiation) of the log-density. The reverse SDE integrates this score:

\[dx = \left[-\frac{1}{2}\beta(t)x - \beta(t)s_\theta(x,t)\right]dt + \sqrt{\beta(t)}, d\bar{W}\]

The entire generative process is: learn the derivative (score) of the log-density, then integrate to generate samples. This is \(I \circ D\) — imperfect inversion that recovers the distribution up to the initial noise (the "lost constant").

docs.title: 11.4 Continuous Normalizing Flows
docs.text:
An CNF models a density via the change of variables formula. If \(z(t)\) evolves by \(\dot{z} = f_\theta(z,t)\), the log-density evolves by:

\[\frac{d\log p(z(t))}{dt} = -\text{tr}!\left(\frac{\partial f_\theta}{\partial z}\right)\]

This is \(D\) applied to the log-density along the flow. The log-likelihood at \(t=1\) is:

\[\log p(z(1)) = \log p(z(0)) - \int_0^1 \text{tr}!\left(\frac{\partial f_\theta}{\partial z}\right) dt\]

This is FTC Part 2: integrate the derivative (\(D\) applied to log \(p\)) to get the net change in log-density. The initial value \(\log p(z(0))\) must be specified separately — exactly the "lost constant" of \(I \circ D\).

docs.title: 11.5 The Fundamental Inversion in Optimization Theory
docs.text:
In convex optimization, if \(f\) is convex and \(x^* = \arg\min f\), then:

\[f(x) - f(x^_) = \int_0^1 \langle \nabla f(x^_ + t(x-x^_)),\ x - x^_\rangle, dt\]

This is FTC Part 2 — the excess loss \(f(x) - f(x^_)\) equals the integral of the gradient along a line. Convergence proofs for gradient descent (showing \(f(x_k) \to f(x^_)\)) use this identity.

The Polyak-Łojasiewicz inequality, the gradient dominance condition, and smoothness bounds are all forms of controlling the relationship between \(D\) (gradient) and \(I\) (accumulated loss change).

docs.title: 11.6 Residual Networks as Discrete FTC
docs.text:
A ResNet computes:

\[x_{k+1} = x_k + f_\theta(x_k)\]

This is the Euler method for integrating \(\dot{x} = f_\theta(x)\). The output \(x_K\) satisfies:

\[x_K = x_0 + \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} f_\theta(x_k) \approx x_0 + \int_0^T f_\theta(x(t)), dt\]

This is the discrete FTC: sum of increments (\(\approx\) derivatives) equals net change. A ResNet is a telescoping sum — literally the discrete version of \(I \circ D\).

The skip connections are what make ResNets equivalent to numerical ODE integrators. Remove the skip connections and you lose the telescoping structure — this is part of why plain deep networks are harder to train.

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text: Inversion Concept ML/DL Analog \(D \circ I_a = \text{Id}\) (perfect) Adjoint method: backprop through ODE avoids redundant computation $I \circ D = $ net change (imperfect) Training step: loss decreases by \(\int \|\nabla\mathcal{L}\|^2, dt\) Lost constant = initial value \(F(a)\) Initial hidden state \(h_0\); initial noise \(z_0\) in diffusion Recovery: \(F(x) = F(a) + \int_a^x F'\) ODE initial value problem; score-based generation Kernel of \(D\) = constants Gauge freedom in value functions (RL baselines) Discrete FTC = telescope ResNet skip connections = Euler ODE integrator \(D\) then \(I\) applied to log \(p\) Normalizing flows / CNF log-likelihood computation Failure at discontinuity Non-smooth activations (ReLU): subgradient needed

docs.title: 12. The Wider World: \(D\) and \(I\) in Other Settings
docs.text: The inversion relationship extends far beyond single-variable calculus:

docs.title: Multivariable Calculus (MIT 18.02)
docs.text:
The gradient \(\nabla F\) is the multivariable derivative. Line integration is the multivariable integral. Their relationship:

\[\int_C \nabla F \cdot d\mathbf{r} = F(\mathbf{b}) - F(\mathbf{a})\]

This is the gradient theorem — FTC for line integrals. Perfect analog: integrate the derivative along a path, get net change. Path-independence of conservative fields follows directly.

docs.title: Differential Equations
docs.text:
The ODE \(F' = f\), \(F(a) = F_0\) has unique solution:

\[F(x) = F_0 + \int_a^x f(t), dt\]

This is the complete inversion: supply both \(f\) (the derivative) and \(F_0\) (the lost constant), and FTC Part 2 reconstructs \(F\) exactly. The initial condition restores the information \(D\) destroyed.

docs.title: Functional Analysis
docs.text: On \(L^2[a,b]\), differentiation \(D\) and integration \(I_a\) are adjoints in a suitable sense. The theory of Sobolev spaces, weak derivatives, and PDEs is built on making this adjoint relationship precise for non-smooth functions.

docs.title: 13. Quick-Reference Cheatsheet
docs.text: \[\boxed{D \circ I_a = \text{Id}}: \quad \frac{d}{dx}\int_a^x f(t),dt = f(x)\] \[\boxed{I_a \circ D = \text{net change}}: \quad \int_a^b F'(x),dx = F(b) - F(a)\] \[\boxed{\text{Complete inversion}}: \quad F(x) = F(a) + \int_a^x F'(t),dt\] \[\ker(D) = {\text{constants}} \implies \text{indefinite integral} = F + C\] \[\text{Discrete analog}: \quad \sum_{i=k}^{n}\Delta a_i = a_{n+1} - a_k \quad \text{(telescoping)}\] \[\text{Fails when}: \begin{cases} f \text{ has jump} & \Rightarrow g = I_a f \text{ not differentiable there} \ F' \text{ has singularity in } [a,b] & \Rightarrow \text{FTC Part 2 inapplicable} \end{cases}\] \[\text{ResNet: } x_K = x_0 + \sum_{k=0}^{K-1}f_\theta(x_k) \approx x_0 + \int_0^T f_\theta,dt \quad \text{(discrete FTC)}\]

docs.text:

  2. MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus. Units 4–6 — FTC in one and several variables; gradient theorem; Green's and Stokes' theorems as higher-dimensional inversions.
  3. Spivak, Michael. Calculus, 4th ed. Ch. 13–14 — rigorous treatment of \(D\) and \(I\) as operators; kernel; failure cases.
  4. Chen, R.T.Q. et al. "Neural Ordinary Differential Equations." NeurIPS 2018 — \(D \circ I = \text{Id}\) via adjoint method.

  6. He et al. "Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition." CVPR 2016 — ResNets as discrete FTC / Euler integration.
