docs.title: Indefinite Integrals
docs.text: "The indefinite integral is not a number, not a function — it is a family. The \(+C\) is not sloppiness or convention. It is the precise record of what differentiation destroyed and integration cannot recover without additional information."

docs.title: 0. From Definite to Indefinite
docs.text:
From [[Fundamental Theorem of Calculus]], we know:

\[\int_a^b f(x), dx = F(b) - F(a), \quad \text{where } F' = f\]

The definite integral is a number. It depends on both \(a\) and \(b\).

Now strip away the bounds entirely. Ask not "what is the accumulated area?" but simply:

What function, when differentiated, gives \(f(x)\)?

This is the antidifferentiation problem, and its answer is the indefinite integral:

\[\int f(x), dx = F(x) + C\]

where \(F'(x) = f(x)\) and \(C \in \mathbb{R}\) is an arbitrary constant.

The indefinite integral is not a single function. It is the complete family of antiderivatives of \(f\) — one for each value of \(C\).

docs.title: 1. Definition and Notation
docs.text:
Definition. If \(F'(x) = f(x)\), then \(F\) is an antiderivative of \(f\). The indefinite integral of \(f\) is:

\[\int f(x), dx = F(x) + C, \qquad C \in \mathbb{R}\]

docs.title: Notation Decoded
docs.text:
\[\underbrace{\int}_{\text{integral sign}} \underbrace{f(x)}_{\text{integrand}} \underbrace{dx}_{\text{``with respect to } x\text{''}} = \underbrace{F(x) + C}_{\text{family of antiderivatives}}\]

The \(dx\) specifies the variable of integration — essential when the integrand involves multiple symbols.

The integral sign \(\int\) is an elongated S, from the Latin summa — a reminder that the definite integral is a sum, and the indefinite integral is the tool that evaluates it.

docs.title: Why \(+C\) is Necessary and Sufficient
docs.text:
Necessary: If \(F\) is one antiderivative of \(f\), then \(G = F + C\) is another, since \(G' = F' = f\). Without \(+C\), we omit infinitely many valid answers.

Sufficient: If \(F\) and \(G\) are both antiderivatives of \(f\) on an interval, then \((F - G)' = 0\), so by the Mean Value Theorem, \(F - G = C\) (constant). Every antiderivative is captured by \(F + C\) for some \(C\).

Proof. Let \(H = F - G\). Then \(H' = 0\) on \((a,b)\). Pick any \(x \in (a,b)\). By MVT applied to \([a,x]\): \(H(x) - H(a) = H'(c)(x-a) = 0\). So \(H(x) = H(a)\) for all \(x\) — \(H\) is constant. \(\blacksquare\)

The \(+C\) is not vagueness. It is the exact parameterization of all solutions.

docs.title: 2. The Table of Standard Indefinite Integrals
docs.text: Every differentiation formula, read backwards, gives an integration formula. These are derived directly from the known derivatives.

docs.title: Power Functions
docs.text: \[\int x^n, dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C, \qquad n \neq -1\] \[\int x^{-1}, dx = \int \frac{1}{x}, dx = \ln|x| + C\] \[\int \sqrt{x}, dx = \frac{2}{3}x^{3/2} + C\] \[\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}, dx = 2\sqrt{x} + C\]

docs.title: Exponential and Logarithmic
docs.text: \[\int e^x, dx = e^x + C\] \[\int a^x, dx = \frac{a^x}{\ln a} + C, \qquad a > 0,\ a \neq 1\] \[\int \ln x, dx = x\ln x - x + C\]

docs.title: Trigonometric
docs.text: \[\int \sin x, dx = -\cos x + C\] \[\int \cos x, dx = \sin x + C\] \[\int \sec^2 x, dx = \tan x + C\] \[\int \csc^2 x, dx = -\cot x + C\] \[\int \sec x \tan x, dx = \sec x + C\] \[\int \csc x \cot x, dx = -\csc x + C\]

docs.title: Inverse Trigonometric
docs.text: \[\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}, dx = \arcsin x + C\] \[\int \frac{1}{1+x^2}, dx = \arctan x + C\] \[\int \frac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^2-1}}, dx = \text{arcsec}, x + C\]

docs.title: Verification Protocol
docs.text:
Every indefinite integral can be self-verified by differentiation:

\[\frac{d}{dx}\left[\int f(x), dx\right] = f(x)\]

Example: verify \(\int x^3, dx = \frac{x^4}{4} + C\):

\[\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{x^4}{4} + C\right) = x^3 \checkmark\]

This is the gold standard. Always differentiate your answer.

docs.title: 3. Properties: Linearity of the Indefinite Integral
docs.text:
The indefinite integral is a linear operator:

\[\int [f(x) \pm g(x)], dx = \int f(x), dx \pm \int g(x), dx \tag{Sum Rule}\] \[\int c\cdot f(x), dx = c\int f(x), dx \tag{Constant Multiple}\]

Proof of Sum Rule. Let \(F' = f\), \(G' = g\). Then \((F+G)' = f+g\). So \(F + G\) is an antiderivative of \(f + g\):

\[\int [f+g], dx = F + G + C = \int f, dx + \int g, dx \quad \blacksquare\]

(Technically each \(\int\) carries its own \(+C\), but their sum is absorbed into a single constant.)

What is NOT linear:

\[\int f(x)\cdot g(x), dx \neq \left(\int f, dx\right)\cdot\left(\int g, dx\right)\] \[\int \frac{f(x)}{g(x)}, dx \neq \frac{\int f, dx}{\int g, dx}\]

Integration does not distribute over products or quotients. This is why we need techniques like substitution, parts, and partial fractions.

docs.title: Example 1: Polynomial
docs.text:
\[\int (3x^4 - 5x^2 + 7x - 2), dx\]

Apply linearity and power rule term by term:

\[= \frac{3x^5}{5} - \frac{5x^3}{3} + \frac{7x^2}{2} - 2x + C\]

Verify: differentiate to recover \(3x^4 - 5x^2 + 7x - 2\). \(\checkmark\)

docs.title: Example 2: Rewrite Before Integrating
docs.text:
\[\int \frac{x^3 + 2x - 1}{x}, dx = \int\left(x^2 + 2 - \frac{1}{x}\right)dx = \frac{x^3}{3} + 2x - \ln|x| + C\]

Key habit: simplify algebraically before reaching for a technique.

docs.title: Example 4: Trigonometric Rewrite
docs.text:
\[\int \tan^2 x, dx = \int(\sec^2 x - 1), dx = \tan x - x + C\]

The identity \(\tan^2 x = \sec^2 x - 1\) converts to a form in the standard table.

docs.title: Example 5: Separating a Fraction
docs.text: \[\int \frac{1 + \cos^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta}, d\theta = \int\left(\sec^2\theta + 1\right)d\theta = \tan\theta + \theta + C\]

docs.title: Example 6: Initial Value Problem (Pinning the Constant)
docs.text:
Find \(F(x)\) given \(F'(x) = 3x^2 - 2x + 5\) and \(F(1) = 4\).

Step 1: Integrate.

\[F(x) = \int(3x^2 - 2x + 5), dx = x^3 - x^2 + 5x + C\]

Step 2: Apply the initial condition.

\[F(1) = 1 - 1 + 5 + C = 5 + C = 4 \implies C = -1\] \[\boxed{F(x) = x^3 - x^2 + 5x - 1}\]

The initial condition is the additional information that pins down a unique antiderivative from the infinite family. This is exactly the "lost constant" discussed in [[Differentiation and Integration as Inverse Processes]].

docs.title: 5. The Initial Value Problem (IVP): Antiderivatives with Constraints
docs.text:
The general pattern:

\[\text{Given: } F'(x) = f(x),\ F(a) = F_0 \implies F(x) = F_0 + \int_a^x f(t), dt\]

This is the fundamental theorem applied as a recovery formula — the indefinite integral parameterizes all solutions; the initial condition selects the unique one.

docs.title: Physics Example: Recovering Position from Acceleration
docs.text:
Given: \(a(t) = -9.8\) m/s² (gravity), \(v(0) = 20\) m/s (initial velocity upward), \(s(0) = 0\) (ground level).

Step 1: Integrate acceleration to get velocity.

\[v(t) = \int (-9.8), dt = -9.8t + C_1\]

Apply \(v(0) = 20\): \(C_1 = 20\).

\[v(t) = -9.8t + 20\]

Step 2: Integrate velocity to get position.

\[s(t) = \int(-9.8t + 20), dt = -4.9t^2 + 20t + C_2\]

Apply \(s(0) = 0\): \(C_2 = 0\).

\[\boxed{s(t) = -4.9t^2 + 20t}\]

Maximum height: \(v(t) = 0 \Rightarrow t = 20/9.8 \approx 2.04\) s. \(s(2.04) \approx 20.4\) m.

Each integration introduces one \(C\); each initial condition eliminates one \(C\). The system is determined when the number of conditions equals the number of integrations.

docs.title: 6. Antiderivatives of Piecewise Functions
docs.text: If \(f\) is defined piecewise, the antiderivative is piecewise — with a separate constant on each piece, plus continuity constraints at the junctions.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
\[f(x) = \begin{cases} x & x < 0 \ \cos x & x \geq 0 \end{cases}\]

Integrate on each piece:

\[F(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{x^2}{2} + C_1 & x < 0 \ \sin x + C_2 & x \geq 0 \end{cases}\]

Require continuity at \(x = 0\): \(\lim_{x\to 0^-} F(x) = \lim_{x\to 0^+} F(x)\):

\[\frac{0}{2} + C_1 = \sin 0 + C_2 \implies C_1 = C_2\]

One free constant remains (as expected — there is still a family of antiderivatives). If we add \(F(0) = 3\): \(C_2 = 3\), \(C_1 = 3\).

docs.title: 7. What Integration Cannot Do: Non-Elementary Antiderivatives
docs.text:
Some perfectly continuous functions have no antiderivative expressible in elementary functions (polynomials, exponentials, logs, trig, and their compositions). The indefinite integral "exists" in the sense of FTC Part 1, but cannot be written with our usual symbols.

Famous examples:

Integrand "Antiderivative" Name \(e^{-x^2}\) \(\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}\text{erf}(x) + C\) Error function \(\sin(x^2)\) \(S(x) + C\) Fresnel \(S\) (see [[Fresnel Function]]) \(\cos(x^2)\) \(C(x) + C\) Fresnel \(C\) \(\frac{\sin x}{x}\) \(\text{Si}(x) + C\) Sine integral \(\frac{1}{\ln x}\) \(\text{li}(x) + C\) Logarithmic integral \(\sqrt{1 - k^2\sin^2 x}\) \(E(x,k) + C\) Elliptic integral

These functions are perfectly well-defined — the Riemann integral of each integrand exists. What fails is the ability to express the antiderivative in closed elementary form. This is a theorem (Liouville, 1835; made rigorous by Risch, 1969): there is a decision procedure to determine whether an elementary antiderivative exists, and it says "no" for all of the above.

Risch Algorithm: The algorithmic version of Liouville's theorem. CAS systems (Mathematica, SymPy, Maple) implement it. When your CAS returns an integral unevaluated, it is not confused — it has determined no elementary form exists.

docs.title: 8. Visualization: The Family of Antiderivatives
docs.text:
The indefinite integral \(\int f(x), dx = F(x) + C\) is a family of curves — vertical translates of one another.

f(x) = 2x           ∫ 2x dx = x² + C

F(x) = x² + C for various C:

y

  |            **           **
  |    C = 0: *_______       *
  |          *         *
  |         *    C=-2:  *__*___
  |        *           *       *
  +---------*-----------*-------> x
           -2           2

All curves have the same shape (same derivative = 2x).
They differ only by vertical translation.
At each x, the slope of every curve = 2x. ← this is f(x).

The initial condition \(F(a) = F_0\) picks exactly one curve from this family — the one that passes through the point \((a, F_0)\).

docs.title: 9. Indefinite vs. Definite: The Precise Relationship
docs.text:
The connection is FTC Part 2:

\[\int_a^b f(x), dx = \left[F(x) + C\right]_a^b = (F(b) + C) - (F(a) + C) = F(b) - F(a)\]

The constant \(C\) cancels in a definite integral. This is why we can use any antiderivative — the choice of \(C\) is irrelevant for definite integrals.

Feature Indefinite \(\int f, dx\) Definite \(\int_a^b f, dx\) Result Family of functions \(F(x)+C\) A real number Depends on \(a\), \(b\) No Yes Contains \(+C\) Yes No (cancels) Role Antidifferentiation Area / accumulation Requires FTC to evaluate No — direct antidifferentiation Yes (or Riemann sums)

docs.title: 10. The Net Change Theorem (Restatement)
docs.text:
From [[Fundamental Theorem of Calculus]], the net change theorem:

\[F(b) - F(a) = \int_a^b F'(x), dx\]

reads directly as: the definite integral of the rate of change is the net change in quantity. The indefinite integral is what allows us to compute the left-hand side: find \(F\) such that \(F' = f\), then evaluate \(F(b) - F(a)\).

The indefinite integral is the computational workhorse that makes FTC Part 2 usable.

docs.title: 11. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
11.1 Antiderivatives as Potential Functions
docs.text:
In physics-informed ML and conservative dynamics, a vector field \(\mathbf{F} = -\nabla V\) is conservative (force = negative gradient of potential). Finding \(V\) given \(\mathbf{F}\) is the multivariable antidifferentiation problem:

\[V(x) = -\int F(x), dx + C\]

The constant \(C\) is a gauge freedom — physics depends only on differences in potential, not absolute values. In Hamiltonian neural networks (Greydanus et al., 2019), networks are designed to learn a scalar Hamiltonian \(H\) such that dynamics follow \(\dot{p} = -\partial H/\partial q\), \(\dot{q} = \partial H/\partial p\). The antiderivative of the learned energy gradient is never computed explicitly — but the \(+C\) gauge freedom is baked in by design.

docs.title: 11.2 The \(+C\) as a Baseline in Reinforcement Learning
docs.text:
In RL, the value function \(V^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}[\sum_t \gamma^t r_t | s_0 = s]\) is defined up to a constant. Adding a constant baseline \(C\) to rewards:

\[r'_t = r_t - C\]

does not change the optimal policy (the gradient of the expected return is unchanged) but reduces variance in policy gradient estimates. This is the RL analog of \(+C\): an undetermined constant that can be chosen optimally (typically \(C = V^\pi(s_t)\) — the value function baseline itself).

docs.title: 11.3 Weight Initialization as Initial Condition
docs.text:
Training a neural network is solving a high-dimensional IVP:

\[ rac{d heta}{dt} = - abla_ heta \mathcal{L}( heta), \qquad heta(0) = heta_{ ext{init}}\]

The "antiderivative" is \( heta(t) = heta(0) - \int_0^t abla_ heta \mathcal{L}, d au\). The indefinite integral (without initial condition) gives a family of parameter trajectories — one for each starting point \( heta(0)\). The initial condition \( heta(0) = heta_{ ext{init}}\) selects a unique trajectory.

Why initialization matters: Different \( heta_{ ext{init}}\) correspond to different members of the antiderivative family. The loss landscape has many local minima (different particular solutions to \(\dot heta = - abla\mathcal{L}\)); initialization chooses which one gradient descent converges to. The "\(+C\)" freedom in the antiderivative family is exactly the sensitivity to initialization in neural network training.

docs.title: 11.4 Symbolic Integration in ML Systems
docs.text:
The Risch algorithm (the decision procedure for elementary antiderivatives, §7) is a canonical example of symbolic AI — a rule-based system that manipulates mathematical expressions exactly. CAS systems (SymPy, Mathematica) implement it.

Modern ML has a parallel: neural integration (Lample & Charton, 2019) — a transformer trained to compute symbolic integrals, outperforming rule-based CAS on many benchmarks. The training data is pairs \((f, \int f, dx)\) generated by differentiating known functions. The network learns the inverse (integration) from the forward (differentiation) by pattern recognition across millions of examples.

This is the ML version of "read the derivative table backwards" — but at scale, with a neural network discovering the patterns rather than a human encoding them.

docs.title: 11.5 Score Functions as Antiderivatives of Potentials
docs.text:
In energy-based models and score matching:

\[p_ heta(x) = rac{1}{Z( heta)} e^{-E_ heta(x)}\]

The score is \( abla_x \log p_ heta(x) = - abla_x E_ heta(x)\).

The energy \(E_ heta\) is the antiderivative (potential) of the negative score field. In score-based diffusion models (DDPM, Score-SDE), we learn the score \(s_ heta(x,t) \approx abla_x \log p_t(x)\) directly, never computing \(E_ heta\) explicitly — because (in high dimensions) the antiderivative may not be a simple scalar function. The \(+C\) ambiguity in the potential corresponds to the normalization constant \(Z( heta)\) — which is intractable to compute and is exactly what score matching avoids.

docs.title: 11.6 Antiderivatives in Numerical ODE Solvers
docs.text:
Every numerical ODE solver is approximating an antiderivative. Given \(\dot{x} = f(x,t)\):

\[x(T) = x(0) + \int_0^T f(x(t), t), dt\]

The indefinite integral \(\int f, dt\) is what we seek. Euler, Runge-Kutta, and Adams methods are progressively more accurate approximations to this antiderivative. The initial condition \(x(0) = x_0\) is what pins the particular solution.

In Neural ODEs (Chen et al., 2018), the function \(f_\theta\) is a neural network. The ODE solver computes the antiderivative of \(f_\theta\) numerically, and backpropagation through this computation (via the adjoint method) is the training algorithm. The whole architecture is: parameterize an integrand (\(f_\theta\)), integrate it (ODE solver), evaluate loss, differentiate through the integration (adjoint = FTC Part 1), update parameters.

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text: Indefinite Integral Concept ML / DL Analog \(\int f, dx = F + C\) (family) Parameter trajectory family; depends on init Initial condition pins \(C\) \(\theta(0) = \theta_{\text{init}}\) selects one trajectory \(+C\) gauge freedom RL baseline; energy model normalization \(Z(\theta)\) Non-elementary antiderivatives Intractable posteriors in Bayesian ML (require variational/MCMC) Risch algorithm (symbolic) Neural integration (Lample & Charton, 2019) Piecewise antiderivatives + continuity Piecewise-linear activations (ReLU) with matching at kinks \(\int F', dx = F + C\) (recover \(F\) up to constant) Score matching: recover energy up to \(\log Z\) Antiderivative of ODE RHS Neural ODE forward pass via numerical integration

docs.title: Error 1: Forgetting \(+C\)
docs.text:
\[\int 3x^2, dx = x^3 \quad \leftarrow \text{WRONG}$$ $$\int 3x^2, dx = x^3 + C \quad \leftarrow \text{correct}\]

In a definite integral, \(C\) cancels. In an indefinite integral, omitting \(C\) means giving one answer when infinitely many are correct.

docs.title: Error 2: Integrating Through a Singularity
docs.text:
\[\int_{-1}^{2} \frac{1}{x}, dx \neq [\ln|x|]_{-1}^2 = \ln 2 - \ln 1 = \ln 2\]

\(1/x\) has a non-integrable singularity at \(x = 0 \in [-1,2]\). The integral diverges. Check for singularities in \([a,b]\) before applying FTC Part 2.

docs.title: Error 3: \(n = -1\) in Power Rule
docs.text:
\[\int x^{-1}, dx \neq \frac{x^0}{0} + C \quad \leftarrow \text{UNDEFINED}$$ $$\int x^{-1}, dx = \ln|x| + C \quad \leftarrow \text{correct}\]

The power rule fails at \(n = -1\). This is a separate entry in the table.

docs.title: Error 4: Constant Multiple vs. Function Multiple
docs.text:
\[\int 2f(x), dx = 2\int f(x), dx \quad \leftarrow \text{correct (constant multiple)}$$ $$\int x \cdot f(x), dx \neq x\int f(x), dx \quad \leftarrow \text{WRONG (function multiple — use integration by parts)}\]

Only constants pull out of the integral.

docs.title: Error 5: Misidentifying the Standard Form
docs.text:
\[\int \frac{1}{x^2 + 4}, dx \neq \ln(x^2+4) + C\]

Note \(\frac{1}{x^2+4} = \frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{1}{(x/2)^2+1}\). This requires the \(\arctan\) form:

\[= \frac{1}{2}\arctan!\left(\frac{x}{2}\right) + C\]

Always check whether a rational integrand matches an inverse trig form before trying other techniques.

docs.title: 13. Quick-Reference Cheatsheet
docs.text: \[\int f(x), dx = F(x) + C \iff F'(x) = f(x)\] \[\textbf{Linearity:}\quad \int[\alpha f + \beta g],dx = \alpha\int f,dx + \beta\int g,dx\] \[\textbf{Power Rule:}\quad \int x^n,dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+C,\quad n\neq -1\] \[\int x^{-1},dx = \ln|x|+C\] \[\int e^x,dx = e^x+C \qquad \int a^x,dx = \frac{a^x}{\ln a}+C\] \[\int \sin x,dx = -\cos x+C \qquad \int \cos x,dx = \sin x+C\] \[\int \sec^2 x,dx = \tan x+C \qquad \int \csc^2 x,dx = -\cot x+C\] \[\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} = \arcsin x+C \qquad \int \frac{dx}{1+x^2} = \arctan x+C\] \[\textbf{IVP:}\quad F'=f,\ F(a)=F_0 \implies F(x) = F_0 + \int_a^x f(t),dt\] \[\textbf{Verify:}\quad \frac{d}{dx}\left[\int f(x),dx\right] = f(x) \quad \text{always check!}\]

docs.title: Net Change Theorem
docs.text: "The integral of a rate of change is the net change." — Stewart, Calculus §5.4

docs.title: § 0 — Why This Theorem Deserves Its Own Page
docs.text:
Most students encounter the Net Change Theorem as a footnote to FTC Part 2, barely a sentence long. But pause here. This is the theorem that turns the abstract machinery of integration into a physical interpreter. It says: if you integrate a derivative, you recover displacement, not distance. That distinction will haunt you through ODEs, physics, and eventually backpropagation in neural networks.

The theorem is not new mathematics — it is FTC Part 2 read with the right emphasis.

docs.title: § 1 — Statement
docs.text:
Let \(F\) be differentiable on \([a, b]\) with \(F' = f\) integrable on \([a, b]\). Then:

\[\boxed{\int_a^b f(x),dx = F(b) - F(a)}\]

Equivalently, stated in the language of rates:

The integral of a rate of change of a quantity over \([a,b]\) equals the net change of that quantity over \([a,b]\).

This is FTC Part 2 (Stewart §5.3) reinterpreted. The new content is entirely in the reading of it.

docs.title: § 2 — Proof (Rigorous)
docs.text:
Setup. Let \(f\) be integrable on \([a,b]\) and let \(F\) be any antiderivative of \(f\), i.e., \(F'(x) = f(x)\) for all \(x \in (a,b)\), continuous on \([a,b]\).

Proof. Partition \([a,b]\) with \(a = x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_n = b\). By the Mean Value Theorem, on each subinterval \([x_{i-1}, x_i]\) there exists \(c_i \in (x_{i-1}, x_i)\) such that:

\[F(x_i) - F(x_{i-1}) = F'(c_i)(x_i - x_{i-1}) = f(c_i),\Delta x_i\]

Summing over all subintervals (a telescoping sum on the left):

\[F(b) - F(a) = \sum_{i=1}^n [F(x_i) - F(x_{i-1})] = \sum_{i=1}^n f(c_i),\Delta x_i\]

The right-hand side is a Riemann sum for \(f\) on \([a,b]\). Since \(f\) is integrable, as \(|\Delta| \to 0\):

\[\sum_{i=1}^n f(c_i),\Delta x_i ;\longrightarrow; \int_a^b f(x),dx\]

Therefore:

\[\int_a^b f(x),dx = F(b) - F(a) \qquad \square\]

Remark. The key move is MVT on each subinterval — this is what "connects" \(F'\) to the Riemann sum of \(f\). The telescoping collapse of \(F(b) - F(a)\) from \(n\) local increments is the geometric soul of the argument.

docs.title: § 3 — The Semantic Content: Net vs. Total
docs.text:
This is the philosophical core.

Quantity Formula Meaning Net displacement \(\displaystyle\int_a^b v(t),dt\) Final position minus initial position Total distance \(\displaystyle\int_a^b \|v(t)\|,dt\) Accumulated odometer reading

These are equal only when \(v(t) \geq 0\) throughout (motion in one direction).

Example. A particle moves with velocity \(v(t) = t^2 - 4t + 3 = (t-1)(t-3)\) on \([0,4]\).

  • Net displacement: $\(\int_0^4 (t^2 - 4t + 3),dt = \left[\frac{t^3}{3} - 2t^2 + 3t\right]_0^4 = \frac{64}{3} - 32 + 12 - 0 = \frac{4}{3}\)$

  • Total distance: note \(v(t) < 0\) on \((1,3)\), so split the integral: $\(\int_0^1 v,dt + \left|\int_1^3 v,dt\right| + \int_3^4 v,dt\)$

Compute each: $\(\int_0^1 (t^2-4t+3),dt = \left[\frac{t^3}{3}-2t^2+3t\right]_0^1 = \frac{1}{3}-2+3 = \frac{4}{3}\)$ $\(\int_1^3 (t^2-4t+3),dt = \left[\frac{27}{3}-18+9\right] - \left[\frac{1}{3}-2+3\right] = 0 - \frac{4}{3} = -\frac{4}{3}\)$ $\(\int_3^4 (t^2-4t+3),dt = \left[\frac{64}{3}-32+12\right] - [9-18+9] = \frac{4}{3} - 0 = \frac{4}{3}\)$

Total distance \(= \dfrac{4}{3} + \dfrac{4}{3} + \dfrac{4}{3} = 4\), but net displacement \(= \dfrac{4}{3}\).

The particle wandered backward and almost returned to where it started.

docs.title: § 4 — Visualization
docs.text:
v(t) = t² - 4t + 3  on [0, 4]

v(t)
 3 |  *                               *
   |    *                           *
 1 |------*-----------*-----------*--------→ t
   |        1    *       *    3    4
-1 |               * velocity negative *
   |                   * here *

   [+area]  [−area cancel] [+area]

Net displacement = shaded areas with sign = 4/3
Total distance   = all areas as positive = 4

Timeline of the particle:
                        ←  moves back
  0 ————————→ 1 ←———— 2 ←———— 3 ————→ 4

  start=0   at x=4/3   at x=−2/3  at x=4/3 (net)

docs.title: § 5 — Physical Instances of the Theorem
docs.text:
The theorem is a template. Recognize it everywhere:

\(f(t) = F'(t)\) \(F(t)\) Net Change \(\int_a^b f,dt\) Velocity \(v(t)\) Position \(x(t)\) Displacement \(\Delta x\) Acceleration \(a(t)\) Velocity \(v(t)\) Change in velocity \(\Delta v\) Power \(P(t)\) [watts] Energy \(E(t)\) [joules] Work done \(\Delta E\) Current \(I(t)\) [amps] Charge \(Q(t)\) [coulombs] Net charge flow \(\Delta Q\) Birth rate \(-\) Death rate Population \(N(t)\) Net population change Marginal cost \(C'(q)\) Total cost \(C(q)\) Added cost from producing \(q_1\) to \(q_2\) units

docs.title: § 6 — Connection to MIT 18.02 (Multivariable Extension)
docs.text:
In 18.02, the Net Change Theorem is the 1D ancestor of the Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals (also called the Gradient Theorem):

\[\int_C abla F \cdot d\mathbf{r} = F(\mathbf{b}) - F(\mathbf{a})\]

Here the "rate of change" is \( abla F\), the path is a curve \(C\) from \(\mathbf{a}\) to \(\mathbf{b}\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and the net change is still just endpoint values. The analog of "net vs. total" becomes path-independence vs. path-dependence (conservative vs. non-conservative fields).

Further generalizations follow the same logic:

  • Stokes' Theorem: \(\iint_S ( abla imes \mathbf{F}) \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \oint_{\partial S} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}\)
  • Divergence Theorem: \(\iiint_V ( abla \cdot \mathbf{F}),dV = \oiint_{\partial V} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}\)

All of these say: integrate a derivative over a region = evaluate something on its boundary. The Net Change Theorem is the simplest member of this family.

docs.title: § 7 — Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
docs.text: This is where calculus stops being "pure" and starts paying rent.

docs.title: 7.1 — Gradient Descent as Accumulated Net Change
docs.text:
In gradient descent, parameter \( heta\) evolves by discrete steps:

\[ heta_{t+1} = heta_t - \eta abla_ heta \mathcal{L}( heta_t)\]

In the continuous (idealized) limit, this is the ODE:

\[ rac{d heta}{dt} = - abla_ heta \mathcal{L}( heta)\]

By the Net Change Theorem, the total displacement of parameters over training time \([0, T]\) is:

\[ heta(T) - heta(0) = \int_0^T rac{d heta}{dt},dt = -\int_0^T abla_ heta \mathcal{L}( heta(t)),dt\]

The net change in \( heta\) is the integral of its rate of change (the gradient). Understanding whether the optimizer has truly moved the parameters far from initialization requires thinking about net movement (trajectory integral), not step-by-step snapshots.

docs.title: 7.2 — Backpropagation: The Chain Rule is a Net Change Machine
docs.text:
In a deep network, the output loss \(\mathcal{L}\) depends on the input \(x\) through a composition \(f_n \circ \cdots \circ f_1(x)\). Backpropagation computes \(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w_{ij}}\) for every weight.

When activations are viewed continuously (as in neural ODEs), the gradient flowing back through the network satisfies an adjoint ODE. By the Net Change Theorem applied to this adjoint:

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} = \int_0^T \mathbf{a}(t)^\top \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta}(z(t), \theta),dt\]

where \(\mathbf{a}(t)\) is the adjoint (costate) variable. This is the continuous backpropagation formula used in Neural ODEs (Chen et al., 2018). It is literally the Net Change Theorem applied to the adjoint system.

docs.title: 7.3 — Cumulative Loss and Learning Curves
docs.text:
When you plot a training loss curve and compute the area under the curve (AUC), you are computing:

\[\text{Cumulative Loss} = \int_0^T \mathcal{L}(t),dt\]

This is the net accumulated loss, not the instantaneous value. Practitioners use this to compare learning schedules: two optimizers with the same final loss but different AUC curves have very different sample efficiency.

docs.title: 7.4 — Neural ODEs — The Continuous Limit of ResNets
docs.text:
A ResNet layer performs: $\(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} = \mathbf{h}_t + f(\mathbf{h}_t, \theta_t)\)$

This is a discrete Euler step for the ODE: $\(\frac{d\mathbf{h}}{dt} = f(\mathbf{h}(t), \theta)\)$

By the Net Change Theorem, the output of the network is: $\(\mathbf{h}(T) = \mathbf{h}(0) + \int_0^T f(\mathbf{h}(t), \theta),dt\)$

The network output is the initial hidden state plus the net change accumulated by integrating the learned vector field \(f\). ResNets literally compute a net change integral. When depth → ∞, this is exact.

docs.title: 7.5 — Reward in Reinforcement Learning
docs.text:
In RL, the return (cumulative discounted reward) is:

\[G_t = \int_t^\infty e^{-\lambda(s-t)} r(s),ds \quad \text{(continuous time)}\]

or in discrete form \(G_t = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \gamma^k r_{t+k}\). This is the net change in "value" from time \(t\) forward, accumulated through the reward rate \(r(s)\). Policy gradient methods optimize precisely this net change, using its gradient with respect to policy parameters.

docs.title: § 8 — Common Mistakes and Edge Cases
docs.text:
Mistake 1: Confusing net displacement with total distance. $\(\int_a^b v(t),dt \neq \int_a^b |v(t)|,dt \quad \text{(in general)}\)$ Net displacement can be zero even if the particle traveled far.

Mistake 2: Forgetting units. If \(v\) is in m/s and \(t\) in seconds, then \(\int v,dt\) is in meters. The integral inherits units: \([f] \cdot [x]\).

Mistake 3: The theorem applies to net change, not absolute value. \(\int_a^b f,dx = F(b) - F(a)\) can be negative. This means \(F\) decreased over \([a,b]\).

Mistake 4: Assuming the antiderivative is unique. \(F\) is unique only up to a constant. But \(F(b) - F(a)\) is constant-independent, so the net change is well-defined regardless of which antiderivative you choose.

docs.title: § 9 — A Note on the "Net" Language
docs.text:
Why "net"? The word comes from accounting: net profit = revenue − expenses. In calculus, positive and negative contributions to the Riemann sum cancel each other. What remains after cancellation is the net contribution. The theorem says: all that survives the cancellation is the difference in endpoint values of \(F\). Everything in between washes out.

This is profound: no matter how wild the path \(F\) takes between \(a\) and \(b\), the integral of its derivative sees only the endpoints. The path is invisible to the Net Change Theorem.

docs.title: § 10 — Summary
docs.text: \[\int_a^b F'(x),dx = F(b) - F(a)\] Aspect Content What it says Integral of rate = net change in quantity Proof key step MVT on each subinterval + telescoping + Riemann sum limit Net ≠ Total Sign matters; total distance requires \(\int\|v\|\) 1D → nD Gradient Theorem in 18.02 is the multivariable version ML connection Gradient descent ODE, Neural ODEs, backprop adjoint, RL returns

docs.title: The Substitution Rule
docs.text: "The substitution rule is the integral counterpart of the chain rule — and just as the chain rule is the most-used differentiation tool, substitution is the most-used integration tool."

docs.title: § 0 — Motivation: Why Substitution Exists
docs.text:
Direct antidifferentiation works for \(\int x^2,dx\). It fails immediately for \(\int 2x\sqrt{1+x^2},dx\). The integrand is a composition — a function of a function — and the chain rule is what created it. Substitution is how we undo the chain rule under an integral sign.

The idea is conceptually simple: rename part of the integrand as a new variable \(u\), transforming a hard integral into a recognizable one. The rigor lies in understanding why this renaming is valid — it is not a notational trick, it is a theorem.

docs.title: § 1 — The Substitution Rule for Indefinite Integrals
Theorem (Substitution Rule — Indefinite)
docs.text:
Let \(g\) be a differentiable function on an interval \(I\), and let \(f\) be continuous on the range of \(g\). Then:

\[\boxed{\int f(g(x)),g'(x),dx = \int f(u),du}\]

where \(u = g(x)\).

docs.title: Proof
docs.text:
Let \(F\) be an antiderivative of \(f\), so \(F' = f\). By the Chain Rule:

\[\frac{d}{dx}\bigl[F(g(x))\bigr] = F'(g(x))\cdot g'(x) = f(g(x))\cdot g'(x)\]

Therefore \(F(g(x))\) is an antiderivative of \(f(g(x))\cdot g'(x)\), so:

\[\int f(g(x)),g'(x),dx = F(g(x)) + C\]

On the other hand:

\[\int f(u),du = F(u) + C = F(g(x)) + C\]

The two sides are equal. \(\square\)

Key insight. The substitution rule is the Chain Rule read backwards. Differentiation creates \(f(g(x))\cdot g'(x)\) from \(F(g(x))\); substitution recovers \(F(g(x))\) from \(f(g(x))\cdot g'(x)\).

docs.title: Differential Notation
docs.text:
Write \(u = g(x)\), then \(du = g'(x),dx\). This is the mnemonic:

\[\int f(\underbrace{g(x)}_{u})\underbrace{g'(x),dx}_{du} = \int f(u),du\]

The \(dx\) is not being cancelled like a fraction — but the differential notation is designed so that the algebra behaves as if it were, a consequence of the proof above.

docs.title: § 2 — The Substitution Rule for Definite Integrals
Theorem (Substitution Rule — Definite)
docs.text:
Let \(g'\) be continuous on \([a,b]\), and let \(f\) be continuous on the range of \(g\). Then:

\[\boxed{\int_a^b f(g(x)),g'(x),dx = \int_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f(u),du}\]

docs.title: Proof
docs.text:
Let \(F' = f\). By FTC Part 2 applied to the left side:

\[\int_a^b f(g(x)),g'(x),dx = \Bigl[F(g(x))\Bigr]_a^b = F(g(b)) - F(g(a))\]

By FTC Part 2 applied to the right side:

\[\int_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f(u),du = \Bigl[F(u)\Bigr]_{g(a)}^{g(b)} = F(g(b)) - F(g(a))\]

The two sides are identical. \(\square\)

Critical remark. The limits of integration change: \(x = a \Rightarrow u = g(a)\) and \(x = b \Rightarrow u = g(b)\). This is not optional. Forgetting to transform the limits — and then substituting \(u\) back to \(x\) — are the two most common errors.

docs.title: Example 1 — Direct Recognition
docs.text:
\[\int 2x\sqrt{1+x^2},dx\]

Let \(u = 1 + x^2\), so \(du = 2x,dx\):

\[\int \sqrt{u},du = \frac{2}{3}u^{3/2} + C = \frac{2}{3}(1+x^2)^{3/2} + C\]

Check by differentiating: \(\frac{d}{dx}\left[\frac{2}{3}(1+x^2)^{3/2}\right] = \frac{2}{3} \cdot \frac{3}{2}(1+x^2)^{1/2} \cdot 2x = 2x\sqrt{1+x^2}\). ✓

docs.title: Example 2 — Adjusting for a Missing Constant
Example 3 — Definite Integral (Transform Limits)
docs.text:
\[\int_0^1 \frac{x}{(1+x^2)^3},dx\]

Let \(u = 1+x^2\), \(du = 2x,dx\). Limits: \(x=0 \Rightarrow u=1\); \(x=1 \Rightarrow u=2\).

\[\frac{1}{2}\int_1^2 u^{-3},du = \frac{1}{2}\left[-\frac{1}{2u^2}\right]_1^2 = \frac{1}{2}\left(-\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{3}{8} = \frac{3}{16}\]

docs.title: Example 4 — Trigonometric Substitution Setup
docs.text:
\[\int \cos^5 x \sin x,dx\]

Let \(u = \cos x\), \(du = -\sin x,dx\):

\[-\int u^5,du = -\frac{u^6}{6} + C = -\frac{\cos^6 x}{6} + C\]

docs.title: Example 5 — Subtle: The Substitution is Non-Obvious
docs.text:
\[\int \frac{\ln x}{x},dx\]

Let \(u = \ln x\), \(du = \frac{1}{x}dx\):

\[\int u,du = \frac{u^2}{2} + C = \frac{(\ln x)^2}{2} + C\]

docs.title: Example 6 — Definite Integral with Symmetry
docs.text:
\[\int_{-2}^{2} x^3 \cos(x^2),dx\]

The integrand \(f(x) = x^3\cos(x^2)\): note \(x^3\) is odd, \(\cos(x^2)\) is even, so their product is odd. For any odd function \(f\) on \([-a,a]\):

\[\int_{-a}^a f(x),dx = 0\]

Therefore the answer is \(0\) — no computation needed. Substitution is sometimes best avoided.

docs.title: The Geometry of Substitution
docs.text:
Original integral: area under f(g(x))·g'(x) from a to b
                   in the x-coordinate system

         f(g(x))·g'(x)
          |   ████
          |  ██████
          | █████████
          |___________→ x
          a           b

After substitution u = g(x):
Area is preserved, redrawn in u-coordinates

         f(u)
          |     ██
          |   ██████
          |  █████████
          |____________→ u
         g(a)         g(b)

The substitution is a change of coordinates. If \(g\) is increasing and convex, the \(u\)-axis is a "stretched" version of the \(x\)-axis. The factor \(g'(x)\) in the integrand is precisely the Jacobian of the coordinate change — it corrects for the stretching so that area is preserved.

docs.title: The Chain Rule / Substitution Duality
docs.text:
DIFFERENTIATION (Chain Rule):
  F(g(x)) ——d/dx——→ f(g(x)) · g'(x)

INTEGRATION (Substitution):
  f(g(x)) · g'(x) ——∫dx——→ F(g(x)) + C

These are exact reverses of each other.
Substitution is the chain rule run in reverse.

docs.title: Substitution as a Reparametrization
docs.text:
x-space:   [a ————————————————————— b]
              curves according to g
u-space:   [g(a) ————————————————— g(b)]
              straightened out

The differential du = g'(x)dx is the
"local magnification factor" at each point.

docs.title: § 5 — Symmetry Theorems (Bonus Tools via Substitution)
docs.text: These follow directly from substitution with \(u = -x\):

docs.title: Theorem (Odd/Even Symmetry)
docs.text:
Let \(f\) be integrable on \([-a, a]\).

  1. If \(f\) is even (\(f(-x) = f(x)\)): \(\displaystyle\int_{-a}^a f(x),dx = 2\int_0^a f(x),dx\)

  2. If \(f\) is odd (\(f(-x) = -f(x)\)): \(\displaystyle\int_{-a}^a f(x),dx = 0\)

Proof of (2). Split: \(\int_{-a}^a = \int_{-a}^0 + \int_0^a\). In the first piece, let \(u = -x\), \(du = -dx\):

\[\int_{-a}^0 f(x),dx = \int_a^0 f(-u)(-du) = \int_0^a f(-u),du = \int_0^a -f(u),du = -\int_0^a f(x),dx\]

Adding: \(\int_{-a}^a f,dx = -\int_0^a f,dx + \int_0^a f,dx = 0\). \(\square\)

docs.title: § 6 — Common Mistakes and How to Catch Them
docs.text:
Mistake 1: Forgetting to transform \(dx\). If \(u = x^2\), then \(du = 2x,dx\), not \(du = dx\). The \(dx\) must be fully replaced.

Mistake 2: Forgetting to transform limits in definite integrals. If you use limits of \(x\) with the \(u\)-integrand, you get a wrong answer. Either transform limits (preferred) or back-substitute before evaluating.

Mistake 3: The \(g'(x)\) factor is not present. \(\int \sqrt{1+x^2},dx\) cannot be done by the substitution \(u = 1+x^2\) because \(du = 2x,dx\) and there is no \(x\) in the integrand to absorb. A different technique (trig substitution) is needed.

Mistake 4: Losing the constant of proportionality. \(\int e^{3x},dx\): Let \(u = 3x\), \(du = 3,dx\), so \(dx = \frac{1}{3}du\). Answer: \(\frac{1}{3}e^{3x}+C\). Forgetting the \(\frac{1}{3}\) is the most common arithmetic error.

Mistake 5: Applying substitution where symmetry gives zero instantly. Always check odd/even symmetry on symmetric intervals before computing.

docs.title: § 7 — Connection to MIT 18.02 (Multivariable Extension)
docs.text:
In 18.02, the substitution rule generalizes to change of variables in multiple integrals.

For a transformation \((x,y) = \mathbf{g}(u,v)\):

\[\iint_R f(x,y),dA = \iint_S f(\mathbf{g}(u,v)),\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|,du,dv\]

The scalar \(g'(x)\) in 1D becomes the Jacobian determinant \(\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|\) in 2D — it measures how the transformation stretches area. This is exactly the same correction factor, now in matrix form.

Classic 18.02 examples:

  • Polar coordinates: \(x = r\cos\theta\), \(y = r\sin\theta\), Jacobian \(= r\), giving \(dA = r,dr,d\theta\)
  • Spherical coordinates: \(dV = \rho^2\sin\phi,d\rho,d\phi,d\theta\)

Every change of variables in multivariable calculus is a higher-dimensional substitution.

docs.title: § 8 — Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
8.1 — The Reparametrization Trick (VAEs)
docs.text:
This is perhaps the most direct and famous use of substitution in deep learning.

In a Variational Autoencoder (VAE), we want to compute:

\[\nabla_\phi ,\mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi(z|x)}[\mathcal{L}(z)]\]

The gradient is with respect to \(\phi\) (the encoder parameters), but \(z\) is sampled from a distribution that depends on \(\phi\). Naively differentiating through a sampling operation is undefined.

The fix is substitution. Write \(z = \mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \cdot \epsilon\) where \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\) (independent of \(\phi\)). Then:

\[\mathbb{E}_{z \sim q_\phi}[\mathcal{L}(z)] = \mathbb{E}_{\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)}[\mathcal{L}(\mu_\phi + \sigma_\phi \epsilon)]\]

This is a substitution \(z = g_\phi(\epsilon)\) that moves the \(\phi\)-dependence out of the distribution and into the integrand, where \(\nabla_\phi\) can act. The Jacobian factor here is absorbed into the change of variable.

In integral notation:

\[\int \mathcal{L}(z),q_\phi(z),dz = \int \mathcal{L}(g_\phi(\epsilon)),p(\epsilon),d\epsilon\]

This is literally the substitution theorem.

docs.title: 8.2 — Normalizing Flows
docs.text:
A normalizing flow transforms a simple distribution \(p_\epsilon(\epsilon)\) into a complex one \(p_x(x)\) via an invertible map \(x = f(\epsilon)\). The change of variables formula for probability densities is:

\[p_x(x) = p_\epsilon(f^{-1}(x)),\left|\det\frac{\partial f^{-1}}{\partial x}\right|\]

This is the substitution rule in \(\mathbb{R}^n\): the Jacobian determinant corrects for how the map \(f\) stretches probability mass. The entire architecture of normalizing flows is built on applying the substitution theorem iteratively through a sequence of invertible layers.

docs.title: 8.3 — Feature Map Integrals (Kernel Methods)
docs.text:
In kernel methods, the kernel function is:

\[k(x, x') = \int \phi(x, \omega),\phi(x', \omega),p(\omega),d\omega\]

Random Fourier Features (Rahimi & Recht, 2007) approximate this by Monte Carlo. The substitution \(\omega = g(z)\) for some base distribution \(p(z)\) allows sampling from complex spectral distributions by transforming samples from simple ones. Again: substitution theorem, now inside an expectation over a feature space.

docs.title: 8.4 — Change of Variables in Loss Functions
docs.text:
When training with custom noise schedules (e.g., in diffusion models like DDPM or score-based models), the forward process adds noise according to a schedule \(\alpha(t)\). The loss involves:

\[\mathcal{L} = \int_0^T w(t),\mathbb{E}\left[|\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t) - \epsilon|^2\right]dt\]

Changing time variable \(t \to \lambda = \log\frac{\alpha(t)}{1-\alpha(t)}\) (log-SNR) simplifies the geometry of the loss. This is substitution — the weight function \(w(t)\) transforms into \(w(g^{-1}(\lambda))\cdot |{(g^{-1})}'(\lambda)|\), i.e., exactly \(f(g(x))\cdot g'(x)\) under a new name.

docs.title: 8.5 — Integration by Substitution in Numerical Quadrature
docs.text:
Neural networks are often evaluated by integrating over their input space (e.g., computing expectations, partition functions, or marginal likelihoods). Substitution is used to:

  • Map unbounded domains \((-\infty, \infty)\) to \((-1, 1)\) for Gaussian quadrature
  • Importance sampling: \(\int f(x),p(x),dx = \int f(x)\frac{p(x)}{q(x)},q(x),dx\), which is substitution of the measure

Importance sampling, which underlies MCMC, policy gradient (REINFORCE), and off-policy RL, is the substitution theorem applied to probability measures.

docs.title: § 9 — The Substitution Rule in the Bigger Picture
docs.text:
DIFFERENTIATION RULES          INTEGRATION COUNTERPARTS
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Power Rule                  ←→  Power Rule for integrals
Chain Rule                  ←→  Substitution Rule        ← (this note)
Product Rule                ←→  Integration by Parts
Quotient Rule               ←→  Partial Fractions

Every differentiation rule has an integration counterpart. Substitution is the most fundamental because the Chain Rule governs all composite functions, and almost every interesting function is a composition.

docs.title: § 10 — Summary
docs.text: \[\int f(g(x)),g'(x),dx = \int f(u),du, \qquad u = g(x)\] \[\int_a^b f(g(x)),g'(x),dx = \int_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f(u),du\] Aspect Content Theorem basis Chain Rule run in reverse Proof mechanism \(\frac{d}{dx}[F(g(x))] = f(g(x))g'(x)\) + FTC Key requirement The factor \(g'(x)\) must be present (up to a constant) Definite integrals Transform limits: \(x: [a,b] \to u: [g(a), g(b)]\) Symmetry Odd function on \([-a,a]\) → 0; even function → double half-interval 18.02 extension Jacobian determinant replaces \(g'(x)\) in multiple integrals ML applications Reparametrization trick (VAE), normalizing flows, diffusion model noise schedules, importance sampling

docs.text:
1. Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §5.5 (The Substitution Rule). Cengage Learning.
  2. MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus — Lecture Notes on Change of Variables, Jacobians. ocw.mit.edu
  3. Kingma, D. P. & Welling, M. Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes. ICLR 2014. — Reparametrization trick.
  4. Rezende, D. & Mohamed, S. Variational Inference with Normalizing Flows. ICML 2015. — Change of variables in generative models.
  5. Rahimi, A. & Recht, B. Random Features for Large-Scale Kernel Machines. NeurIPS 2007.

docs.title: Integrals of Symmetric Functions
docs.text: "Symmetry is one of the most powerful problem-solving tools in mathematics. When a function has it, the integral often collapses to something trivial — or doubles into something clean. Learning to see symmetry before computing is the mark of a mature analyst."

docs.title: § 0 — The Core Idea
docs.text:
Before you touch an antiderivative, ask: does this integrand have symmetry?

If the interval of integration is symmetric about the origin, \([-a, a]\), and the function is either purely even or purely odd, the integral either vanishes immediately or halves. This is not an approximation. It is an exact theorem, and it saves enormous computation.

The result is elementary but its reach is surprisingly wide — from trigonometric integrals to Fourier analysis to the symmetry arguments underlying quantum mechanics and neural network weight initialization.

docs.title: § 1 — Even and Odd Functions: Definitions and Geometry
Definitions
docs.text:
A function \(f\) defined on a symmetric interval \([-a, a]\) (or all of \(\mathbb{R}\)) is:

  • Even if \(f(-x) = f(x)\) for all \(x\) in the domain
  • Odd if \(f(-x) = -f(x)\) for all \(x\) in the domain

docs.title: Geometric Meaning
docs.text:
EVEN FUNCTION: f(-x) = f(x)          ODD FUNCTION: f(-x) = -f(x)

   f(x)                                  f(x)
    │     ╭───╮                           │           ╱
    │    ╱     ╲                          │          ╱
    │   ╱       ╲                         │         ╱
────┼──╱─────────╲──→ x               ───┼────────╱─────→ x
    │              ╲  ╱                   │       ╱
    │               ╲╱                    │      ╱
                                          │     ╱
   Mirror symmetry                        │    ╱
   about the y-axis.                   Rotational symmetry
   Graph folds onto                    about the origin.
   itself.                             Graph maps to itself
                                       under 180° rotation.

docs.title: Standard Examples
docs.text:
Even Odd \(x^{2n}\) (even powers) \(x^{2n+1}\) (odd powers) \(\cos x\) \(\sin x\) \(\cosh x\) \(\sinh x\) \(\|x\|\) \(x^3 - x\) \(e^{x^2}\) \(x e^{-x^2}\) \(f(x) + f(-x)\) (symmetrization) \(f(x) - f(-x)\) (antisymmetrization)

Remark. Most functions are neither even nor odd. But every function with a symmetric domain decomposes uniquely as a sum of an even and an odd part: $\(f(x) = \underbrace{\frac{f(x)+f(-x)}{2}}_{\text{even part}} + \underbrace{\frac{f(x)-f(-x)}{2}}_{\text{odd part}}\)$ This decomposition is used heavily in Fourier analysis.

docs.title: Theorem (Integrals of Symmetric Functions)
docs.text:
Let \(f\) be integrable on \([-a, a]\).

Part (i) — Odd function: $\(f \text{ odd} \implies \int_{-a}^a f(x),dx = 0\)$

Part (ii) — Even function: $\(f \text{ even} \implies \int_{-a}^a f(x),dx = 2\int_0^a f(x),dx\)$

docs.title: Proof of Both Parts
docs.text:
Split the integral at \(0\):

\[\int_{-a}^a f(x),dx = \int_{-a}^0 f(x),dx + \int_0^a f(x),dx\]

In the first integral, substitute \(x = -t\), so \(dx = -dt\). When \(x = -a\), \(t = a\); when \(x = 0\), \(t = 0\):

\[\int_{-a}^0 f(x),dx = \int_a^0 f(-t)(-dt) = \int_0^a f(-t),dt\]

Therefore:

\[\int_{-a}^a f(x),dx = \int_0^a f(-t),dt + \int_0^a f(t),dt = \int_0^a \bigl[f(-t) + f(t)\bigr],dt\]

Case (i): \(f\) odd. Then \(f(-t) = -f(t)\), so \(f(-t) + f(t) = 0\): $\(\int_{-a}^a f(x),dx = \int_0^a 0,dt = 0 \qquad \square\)$

Case (ii): \(f\) even. Then \(f(-t) = f(t)\), so \(f(-t) + f(t) = 2f(t)\): $\(\int_{-a}^a f(x),dx = \int_0^a 2f(t),dt = 2\int_0^a f(x),dx \qquad \square\)$

Proof anatomy. The entire argument rests on a single substitution \(x = -t\) plus the definition of symmetry. This substitution "folds" the left half \([-a, 0]\) onto the right half \([0, a]\), and the symmetry condition tells you what happens when the two halves meet.

docs.title: § 3 — Visualization of the Theorem
docs.text:
ODD FUNCTION on [-a, a]:

     f(x)
      │     ╭──────╮  ← positive area = A
      │    ╱        ╲
──────┼───╱──────────╲────→ x
  -a  │  ╱  0         a
      │              ╭──────────╮
      │              │ negative area = -A

  Net area = A + (-A) = 0 ✓
  The two halves are mirror images with opposite sign.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

EVEN FUNCTION on [-a, a]:

     f(x)
      │  ╭────╮    ╭────╮
      │ ╱      ╲  ╱      ╲
      │╱        ╲╱        ╲
──────┼────────────────────╲──→ x
  -a        0               a
      │← area A →│← area A →│

  Total area = A + A = 2A = 2∫₀ᵃ f(x)dx ✓
  The two halves are identical.

docs.title: Example 1 — Vanishing by Oddness
docs.text:
\[\int_{-3}^{3} \left(x^5 - 4x^3 + \sin x\right)dx\]

Check each term: \(x^5\) is odd, \(4x^3\) is odd, \(\sin x\) is odd. Their sum is odd. On \([-3, 3]\):

\[\int_{-3}^{3} \left(x^5 - 4x^3 + \sin x\right)dx = 0\]

No computation required.

docs.title: Example 2 — Doubling by Evenness
docs.text:
\[\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \cos^2 x,dx\]

\(\cos^2(-x) = \cos^2(x)\), so \(\cos^2 x\) is even:

\[= 2\int_0^{\pi} \cos^2 x,dx = 2\int_0^{\pi} \frac{1 + \cos 2x}{2},dx = \int_0^{\pi}(1+\cos 2x),dx\] \[= \left[x + \frac{\sin 2x}{2}\right]_0^{\pi} = \pi\]

docs.title: Example 3 — Splitting a Mixed Integrand
docs.text:
\[\int_{-2}^{2} \left(x^4 + x^3 + 3\right)dx\]

Split by symmetry type: \(x^4 + 3\) is even, \(x^3\) is odd.

\[= \int_{-2}^{2}(x^4 + 3),dx + \underbrace{\int_{-2}^{2} x^3,dx}_{=,0} = 2\int_0^2(x^4 + 3),dx\] \[= 2\left[\frac{x^5}{5} + 3x\right]_0^2 = 2\left(\frac{32}{5} + 6\right) = 2 \cdot \frac{62}{5} = \frac{124}{5}\]

docs.title: Example 4 — A Non-Obvious Odd Function
docs.text:
\[\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{x^3 + x}{1 + x^2 + x^4},dx\]

Let \(f(x) = \dfrac{x^3 + x}{1 + x^2 + x^4}\). Check:

\[f(-x) = \frac{-x^3 - x}{1 + x^2 + x^4} = -f(x)\]

\(f\) is odd. Therefore:

\[\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{x^3 + x}{1 + x^2 + x^4},dx = 0\]

The antiderivative of this rational function would be genuinely painful. Symmetry gives the answer in two lines.

docs.title: Example 5 — Trigonometric Integral (Odd \(\times\) Even)
docs.text:
\[\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \sin^3 x \cos^2 x,dx\]

\(\sin^3 x\) is odd, \(\cos^2 x\) is even. The product of an odd and an even function is odd. Therefore:

\[\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \sin^3 x \cos^2 x,dx = 0\]

Parity multiplication rules. odd \(\times\) even \(=\) odd. odd \(\times\) odd \(=\) even. even \(\times\) even \(=\) even. This mirrors the sign algebra of \({+1, -1}\) under multiplication.

docs.title: Example 6 — The Sigmoid
docs.text:
\[\int_{-1}^{1} \frac{e^x}{1 + e^x},dx\]

Let \(\sigma(x) = \dfrac{e^x}{1+e^x}\). Note that \(\sigma(x) + \sigma(-x) = 1\), so:

\[\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{2} + \underbrace{\left(\sigma(x) - \frac{1}{2}\right)}_{\text{odd part}}\]

The odd part integrates to zero on \([-1,1]\); the constant \(\frac{1}{2}\) integrates to \(1\):

\[\int_{-1}^{1}\sigma(x),dx = 1\]

docs.title: § 5 — The Algebra of Even and Odd Functions
docs.text:
Operation Result even \(+\) even even odd \(+\) odd odd even \(+\) odd neither (in general) even \(\times\) even even odd \(\times\) odd even even \(\times\) odd odd \(\frac{d}{dx}\)(even) odd \(\frac{d}{dx}\)(odd) even \(\int_0^x\)(even \(dt\)) odd (with zero constant) \(\int_0^x\)(odd \(dt\)) even

The derivative/integral rows follow from FTC. If \(f\) is even and \(g(x) = \int_0^x f(t),dt\), then substituting \(t = -s\):

\[g(-x) = \int_0^{-x} f(t),dt = -\int_0^x f(-s),ds = -\int_0^x f(s),ds = -g(x)\]

So \(g\) is odd. \(\square\)

Deep pattern. Even functions \(\leftrightarrow\) cosines; odd functions \(\leftrightarrow\) sines. This is Fourier's insight: every periodic function decomposes into even (cosine) and odd (sine) components. The integral theorem above is the seed of the orthogonality relations in Fourier analysis.

docs.title: § 6 — Extension: Symmetry About \(x = c\)
docs.text: The theorem requires \([-a, a]\) (symmetric about \(0\)). For an interval symmetric about \(c\), shift first.

docs.title: Theorem (Symmetry About \(x = c\))
docs.text:
Let the interval be \([c - a, c + a]\). Substitute \(t = x - c\):

\[\int_{c-a}^{c+a} f(x),dx = \int_{-a}^{a} f(t+c),dt\]

Now apply the odd/even theorem to \(\tilde{f}(t) = f(t+c)\).

Example. \(\displaystyle\int_1^5 (x-3)^3,dx\). Let \(t = x-3\), interval becomes \([-2, 2]\):

\[\int_{-2}^{2} t^3,dt = 0 \quad (\text{odd function on symmetric interval})\]

Example. \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi} \sin x,dx\). Let \(t = x - \pi/2\):

\[\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \cos t,dt = 2\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos t,dt = 2[\sin t]_0^{\pi/2} = 2 \checkmark\]

docs.title: § 7 — Connection to MIT 18.02
docs.text: In multivariable calculus, symmetry arguments become even more powerful.

docs.title: Double Integrals over Symmetric Regions
docs.text:
If \(D\) is symmetric about the \(y\)-axis and \(f(-x, y) = -f(x, y)\) (odd in \(x\)):

\[\iint_D f(x, y),dA = 0\]

Example. \(\iint_D xy,dA\) where \(D\) is the unit disk. The integrand \(xy\) is odd in \(x\), and the disk is symmetric about the \(y\)-axis:

\[\iint_D xy,dA = 0\]

No Jacobian, no polar conversion, no computation.

docs.title: Trigonometric Orthogonality
docs.text:
The integrals \(\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\sin\theta,d\theta = 0\) and \(\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\cos\theta,d\theta = 0\) appear constantly in polar and spherical coordinate calculations. More precisely, for integers \(m \neq n\):

\[\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sin(mx)\cos(nx),dx = 0\]

because \(\sin(mx)\cos(nx)\) is odd (odd \(\times\) even). This is the symmetry theorem. Every such orthogonality relation in Fourier series for mixed sin-cos terms reduces to this one observation.

docs.title: § 8 — Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
8.1 — Weight Initialization and Symmetry Breaking
docs.text:
With all weights initialized to zero, neurons at the same layer compute identical outputs — the symmetry problem. With symmetric (zero-mean) weight distributions, for any odd activation \(\phi\) (e.g., \(\tanh\)):

\[\mathbb{E}_{w \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)}[\phi(wx)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\phi(wx)\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}e^{-w^2/2\sigma^2},dw = 0\]

The integrand is odd in \(w\) (odd \(\times\) even), the domain is symmetric, so the integral vanishes. The expected output of a \(\tanh\) neuron under symmetric random weights is exactly zero. He and Xavier initialization introduce careful scaling of variance, not to destroy this symmetry, but to ensure gradients neither explode nor vanish despite it.

docs.title: 8.2 — Fourier Features and Attention
docs.text:
Random Fourier feature methods (Rahimi & Recht) and positional encodings in transformers rely on the orthogonality of sinusoids. The identity:

\[\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sin(mx)\cos(nx),dx = 0 \quad \text{for all } m, n\]

holds because the integrand is odd. Positional encodings use alternating \(\sin\) and \(\cos\) features at different frequencies; the orthogonality (which is the symmetry theorem) guarantees these features carry independent information.

docs.title: 8.3 — Batch Normalization and Odd Activations
docs.text:
After batch normalization, pre-activations are approximately \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\). For any odd activation \(\phi\):

\[\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}[\phi(z)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\phi(z)\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2},dz = 0\]

Odd activations (\(\tanh\), \(\text{erf}\), \(\sinh\)) have zero mean output after batch norm — a statistically clean property. ReLU, which is neither even nor odd, has mean output \(\approx 0.5\) under \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\), introducing a positive bias that must be handled. This asymmetry is one reason batch norm is more critical for ReLU networks.

docs.title: 8.4 — The Sigmoid's Even-Odd Decomposition
docs.text:
From Example 6 in general: since \(\sigma(x) - \frac{1}{2}\) is odd:

\[\int_{-a}^{a}\sigma(x),dx = a\]

This has a direct interpretation: under zero-mean inputs, the sigmoid neuron has expected output \(\frac{1}{2}\) — a constant positive bias. This saturation at \(\frac{1}{2}\) is one reason \(\tanh\) (which is odd, with zero mean) is often preferred over sigmoid in symmetric architectures.

docs.title: 8.5 — Score Matching and Stein's Identity
docs.text:
In score-based generative models (DDPM, score matching), the Stein identity states:

\[\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p}\left[\nabla_x \log p(x) \cdot \phi(x)\right] = -\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p}[\nabla_x \phi(x)]\]

When \(p\) is symmetric (e.g., Gaussian) and \(\phi\) is odd, both sides vanish — one by the symmetry theorem, the other by FTC on an odd function. This gives a zero-value sanity check for score network implementations: certain test expectations should be exactly zero under symmetric data.

docs.title: 8.6 — \(L^2\) and \(L^1\) Regularization
docs.text: The \(L^2\) regularizer \(R(\theta) = \sum_i \theta_i^2\) is even in each \(\theta_i\). Its gradient \(\nabla_\theta R = 2\theta\) is odd — it always pushes symmetrically toward zero, with no directional bias. The \(L^1\) regularizer \(\sum_i |\theta_i|\) is also even; its subgradient \(\text{sgn}(\theta_i)\) is odd. The symmetry of both regularizers about \(\theta = 0\) is what makes them geometrically unbiased: they penalize deviation from zero equally in both directions.

docs.title: § 9 — Common Mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake 1: Non-symmetric interval. \(\int_0^3 x^3,dx \neq 0\). The interval \([0, 3]\) is not symmetric about \(0\). Oddness only kills the integral on \([-a, a]\).

Mistake 2: Not checking the condition. Always verify \(f(-x) = \pm f(x)\) explicitly. Many functions look symmetric but are not. \(e^x\) is neither even nor odd.

Mistake 3: odd \(\times\) odd = even, not odd. \(\int_{-a}^a x \cdot \sin x,dx \neq 0\). The product \(x \cdot \sin x\) is even (odd \(\times\) odd), so the integral doubles: \(= 2\int_0^a x\sin x,dx\).

Mistake 4: Singularities on the interval. \(f(x) = 1/x\) is odd, but \(\int_{-1}^{1} 1/x,dx\) does not exist in the Riemann sense. The theorem requires integrability. (The Cauchy principal value is zero, but this is a separate concept.)

Mistake 5: Not decomposing a mixed function. For \(\int_{-2}^{2}(e^x + x^2),dx\): write \(e^x = \cosh x + \sinh x\). The odd part \(\sinh x\) integrates to zero; the even part \(\cosh x\) doubles. Always decompose before integrating.

docs.title: § 10 — Summary
docs.text: \[f \text{ odd on } [-a,a]: \quad \int_{-a}^a f(x),dx = 0\] \[f \text{ even on } [-a,a]: \quad \int_{-a}^a f(x),dx = 2\int_0^a f(x),dx\] Concept Content Proof key step Substitute \(x = -t\), fold \([-a,0]\) onto \([0,a]\), use \(f(-t) \pm f(t)\) Parity of products odd\(\times\)even = odd; odd\(\times\)odd = even; even\(\times\)even = even Unique decomposition \(f = \frac{f(x)+f(-x)}{2} + \frac{f(x)-f(-x)}{2}\) Symmetry about \(c\) Shift \(t = x-c\), then apply theorem to \(f(t+c)\) 18.02 extension Odd integrand over symmetric domain → double integral vanishes; Fourier orthogonality ML applications Weight initialization, batch norm, sigmoid bias, score function testing, regularizer geometry

docs.title: Area Between Curves
docs.text: "The area between two curves is conceptually the simplest application of the definite integral — and yet it is where students first learn to read geometry carefully before writing symbols. The formula is trivial; finding the limits and handling sign changes is where the real work lives."

docs.title: § 0 — From Single Curve to Two Curves
docs.text:
In the definite integral, we measured the signed area between \(f(x)\) and the \(x\)-axis. The \(x\)-axis is just the function \(g(x) = 0\). The natural generalization: what is the area between two arbitrary curves \(f\) and \(g\)?

The idea is unchanged — Riemann rectangles, now with height \(f(x_i^_) - g(x_i^_)\) instead of \(f(x_i^*)\) alone.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Let \(f\) and \(g\) be continuous on \([a, b]\) with \(f(x) \ge g(x)\) for all \(x \in [a, b]\).

The area of the region bounded above by \(f\) and below by \(g\) on \([a, b]\) is:

\[\boxed{A = \int_a^b \bigl[f(x) - g(x)\bigr],dx}\]

docs.title: Derivation from Riemann Sums
docs.text:
Partition \([a,b]\) with sample points \(x_i^*\). Each rectangle has:

  • Width: \(\Delta x_i\)
  • Height: \(f(x_i^_) - g(x_i^_)\) (top curve minus bottom curve)
  • Area: \([f(x_i^_) - g(x_i^_)],\Delta x_i \ge 0\)

Summing and taking the limit:

\[A = \lim_{|P|\to 0}\sum_{i=1}^n [f(x_i^_) - g(x_i^_)],\Delta x_i = \int_a^b [f(x) - g(x)],dx\]

By linearity of the integral, this equals \(\int_a^b f,dx - \int_a^b g,dx\) — the area under \(f\) minus the area under \(g\).

     y
     │        f(x) ← top curve
     │    ╭───────────╮
     │   ╱  shaded     ╲
     │  ╱   region      ╲
     │ ╱  ╭──────────╮   ╲
     │╱   │  g(x)     │    ╲
     │────────────────────────→ x
          a            b

  Height of each rectangle = f(x*) − g(x*)
  Area = ∫ₐᵇ [f(x) − g(x)] dx

docs.title: Why the Condition \(f \ge g\) Matters
docs.text: Without it, \(f(x) - g(x)\) can be negative, and the integral gives a signed area (positive where \(f > g\), negative where \(g > f\)), not the geometric area. When the curves cross, we must split.

docs.title: § 2 — When Curves Cross: Handling Sign Changes
docs.text: If \(f\) and \(g\) intersect within \((a, b)\), the formula must be adapted.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Find all intersection points by solving \(f(x) = g(x)\) on \([a, b]\). Call them \(c_1 < c_2 < \cdots < c_{k}\).
  2. On each subinterval between consecutive intersection points, determine which function is on top.
  3. Integrate \(|f(x) - g(x)|\) on each subinterval (using whichever sign makes the integrand positive):
\[A = \int_a^{c_1}|f - g|,dx + \int_{c_1}^{c_2}|f - g|,dx + \cdots\]

More precisely:

\[\boxed{A = \int_a^b |f(x) - g(x)|,dx}\]

This is always correct, but the absolute value requires splitting at zeros of \(f - g\).

     y
     │        ╭──── f(x)
     │    ╭───╯  ╲
     │   ╱  A₁    ╲  ╭── g(x)
     │──╱───────────╲╱─────────→ x
     │              │╲    A₂  ╱
     │              │  ╲    ╱
     │              c₁  ╲──╱  c₂

  A = A₁ + A₂ = ∫ₐᶜ¹[f−g]dx + ∫ᶜ¹ᶜ²[g−f]dx
  (switch the order in the second integral because g > f there)

docs.title: § 3 — Integration with Respect to \(y\)
docs.text: Sometimes the natural variable is \(y\), not \(x\). When curves are expressed as \(x = f(y)\) and \(x = g(y)\), and the region is bounded horizontally, integrate with respect to \(y\).

docs.title: Formula
docs.text:
Let \(f(y) \ge g(y)\) on \([c, d]\) (right curve minus left curve):

\[\boxed{A = \int_c^d \bigl[f(y) - g(y)\bigr],dy}\] 
   y
   │
 d─┤    ╭──── x = f(y) (right)
   │   ╱│████████
   │  ╱ │████████
   │ ╱  │████████
 c─┤╱   │
   │    │
   └────┴──────────→ x
     g(y)  f(y)

  Width of each strip = f(y*) − g(y*)
  Area = ∫ᶜᵈ [f(y) − g(y)] dy

docs.title: When to Integrate in \(y\)
docs.text:
• When curves are given as \(x = h(y)\) directly.
  • When integrating in \(x\) requires splitting into multiple integrals but \(y\) gives a single clean integral.
  • When the region is easier to describe by horizontal strips than vertical ones.

docs.title: § 4 — Finding Limits of Integration
docs.text: The limits come from the intersection points of the bounding curves, or from explicitly stated boundaries.

docs.title: Solving for Intersections
docs.text:
Set \(f(x) = g(x)\) and solve. Always:

  1. Find all solutions in the relevant domain.
  2. Verify which function is on top between each pair of consecutive solutions (plug in a test point).
  3. Sketch before integrating — even a rough sketch prevents sign errors.

Personal note. The single most common error in area problems is not the integration itself — it is setting up the wrong limits or forgetting to check which curve is on top. Sketch first, always.

docs.title: Example 1 — Area Between a Parabola and a Line
docs.text:
Find the area between \(f(x) = x^2\) and \(g(x) = x + 2\).

Step 1: Find intersections. $\(x^2 = x + 2 \implies x^2 - x - 2 = 0 \implies (x-2)(x+1) = 0\)$ So \(x = -1\) and \(x = 2\).

Step 2: Determine which is on top. Test \(x = 0\): \(f(0) = 0\), \(g(0) = 2\). So \(g \ge f\) on \([-1, 2]\).

Step 3: Integrate. $\(A = \int_{-1}^{2}(x + 2 - x^2),dx = \left[\frac{x^2}{2} + 2x - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-1}^{2}\)$

\[= \left(2 + 4 - \frac{8}{3}\right) - \left(\frac{1}{2} - 2 + \frac{1}{3}\right) = \frac{10}{3} - \left(-\frac{7}{6}\right) = \frac{10}{3} + \frac{7}{6} = \frac{27}{6} = \frac{9}{2}\] 
     y
     │        ╭──── g(x) = x+2
   4─┤       ╱██
     │      ╱████╲
   2─┤     ╱██████╲──── f(x) = x²
     │    ╱████████╲  ╱
     │───╱──────────╲╱────→ x
        -1           2

  Shaded area = 9/2

docs.title: Example 2 — Curves That Cross
docs.text:
Find the area enclosed by \(f(x) = \sin x\) and \(g(x) = \cos x\) on \([0, \pi]\).

Step 1: Find intersections on \([0, \pi]\). \(\sin x = \cos x \implies \tan x = 1 \implies x = \pi/4\).

Step 2: Determine which is on top on each piece.

  • On \([0, \pi/4]\): test \(x = 0\): \(\sin 0 = 0 < \cos 0 = 1\), so \(\cos \ge \sin\).
  • On \([\pi/4, \pi]\): test \(x = \pi/2\): \(\sin(\pi/2) = 1 > \cos(\pi/2) = 0\), so \(\sin \ge \cos\).

Step 3: Integrate. $\(A = \int_0^{\pi/4}(\cos x - \sin x),dx + \int_{\pi/4}^{\pi}(\sin x - \cos x),dx\)$

First integral: $\([\sin x + \cos x]_0^{\pi/4} = \left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) - (0+1) = \sqrt{2} - 1\)$

Second integral: $\([-\cos x - \sin x]_{\pi/4}^{\pi} = (-(-1) - 0) - \left(-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) = 1 + \sqrt{2}\)$

\[A = (\sqrt{2}-1) + (1+\sqrt{2}) = 2\sqrt{2}\]

docs.title: Example 3 — Integrating in \(y\)
docs.text:
Find the area of the region bounded by \(x = y^2\) and \(x = y + 2\).

In \(x\): the parabola opens rightward — solving for the two \(x\)-branches is messy. In \(y\), this is clean.

Step 1: Intersections. \(y^2 = y + 2 \implies y^2 - y - 2 = 0 \implies (y-2)(y+1) = 0\), so \(y = -1, 2\).

Step 2: Which is on the right? Test \(y = 0\): \(x = y^2 = 0\) vs \(x = y+2 = 2\). So \(x = y+2\) is the right curve.

Step 3: Integrate. $\(A = \int_{-1}^{2}\bigl[(y+2) - y^2\bigr],dy = \left[\frac{y^2}{2} + 2y - \frac{y^3}{3}\right]_{-1}^{2}\)$

\[= \left(2 + 4 - \frac{8}{3}\right) - \left(\frac{1}{2} - 2 + \frac{1}{3}\right) = \frac{9}{2}\]

The same numerical answer as Example 1 — because the region is the same, just described with a different variable.

docs.title: Example 4 — Three Bounding Curves
docs.text:
Find the area of the region bounded by \(y = x^2\), \(y = 2x\), and \(y = 0\).

Step 1: Find all pairwise intersections.

  • \(x^2 = 2x \implies x = 0, 2\)
  • \(x^2 = 0 \implies x = 0\)
  • \(2x = 0 \implies x = 0\)

The region has vertices at \((0,0)\) and \((2,4)\).

Step 2: Determine the geometry. On \([0, 2]\): \(2x \ge x^2 \ge 0\). The region is between \(y = 2x\) (top) and \(y = x^2\) (bottom):

\[A = \int_0^2 (2x - x^2),dx = \left[x^2 - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2 = 4 - \frac{8}{3} = \frac{4}{3}\]

docs.title: Example 5 — Area Requiring Both \(x\) and \(y\) Integration
docs.text:
Find the area between \(y = \sqrt{x}\) and \(y = x^2\) on \([0, 1]\).

Intersections: \(\sqrt{x} = x^2 \implies x = 0, 1\).

On \((0,1)\): test \(x = 1/4\): \(\sqrt{1/4} = 1/2\), \((1/4)^2 = 1/16\). So \(\sqrt{x} \ge x^2\).

\[A = \int_0^1\left(\sqrt{x} - x^2\right)dx = \left[\frac{2}{3}x^{3/2} - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{3}\]

docs.title: § 6 — Visualization: The Full Geometry
docs.text:
VERTICAL STRIPS (integrate in x):

   y │    f(x) ← top                  
     │  ╭────────────╮                
     │ ╱│████│████│███╲               
     │╱ │████│████│████╲              
     │  │████│████│█████│             
     │──┼────┼────┼─────┼──→ x        
        a   x₁   x₂    b             

   Each vertical strip has width dx
   and height f(x) − g(x).

────────────────────────────────────────

HORIZONTAL STRIPS (integrate in y):

   y                                    
   d─┤      ────── x = f(y) (right)    
     │  ╭───┤████████                  
     │  │   │████████                  
     │  │   │████████                  
   c─┤  ╰───┤                          
     │  x=g(y)                         
     └──────────────────→ x            

   Each horizontal strip has height dy
   and width f(y) − g(y).

────────────────────────────────────────

WHEN CURVES CROSS:

   y                                    
     │   f above g      g above f      
     │ ┌───────────┐  ┌─────────────┐  
     │ │    A₁     │  │     A₂      │  
     │─┴───────────┴──┴─────────────┴─→x
       a           c₁               b  

   Total area = A₁ + A₂
   NEVER: ∫ₐᵇ (f−g)dx (this cancels the areas)
   ALWAYS split at each crossing point c₁

docs.title: § 7 — Connection to MIT 18.02
docs.text:
In 18.02, the area between curves becomes the foundation for double integrals over general regions.

The area of a region \(D\) in the plane is:

\[A = \iint_D dA\]

When \(D\) is described as \({(x,y) : a \le x \le b,\ g(x) \le y \le f(x)}\):

\[A = \int_a^b \int_{g(x)}^{f(x)} dy,dx = \int_a^b [f(x) - g(x)],dx\]

The inner integral \(\int_{g(x)}^{f(x)}dy = f(x) - g(x)\) recovers exactly the area-between-curves formula. So area between curves is the 1D cross-section of a 2D double integral — the limits of the inner integral are the bounding curves.

This connection is crucial: in 18.02, setting up double integrals over non-rectangular regions requires exactly the same skill as finding limits for area-between-curves problems.

docs.title: Type I and Type II Regions (18.02 Language)
docs.text:
Type Description Integral form Type I \(a \le x \le b\), \(g(x) \le y \le f(x)\) \(\int_a^b\int_{g(x)}^{f(x)} h,dy,dx\) Type II \(c \le y \le d\), \(g(y) \le x \le f(y)\) \(\int_c^d\int_{g(y)}^{f(y)} h,dx,dy\)

The choice between Type I and Type II is exactly the choice between integrating in \(x\) or \(y\) in the area problem.

docs.title: § 8 — Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
8.1 — ROC Curves and AUC
docs.text:
The Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) is the single most used model evaluation metric in binary classification. The ROC curve plots True Positive Rate (TPR) against False Positive Rate (FPR) as the classification threshold varies.

Mathematically, AUC is the area under a parametric curve:

\[\text{AUC} = \int_0^1 \text{TPR}(\text{FPR}),d(\text{FPR})\]

When comparing two classifiers A and B, the difference in performance is:

\[\Delta\text{AUC} = \int_0^1 [\text{TPR}_A(t) - \text{TPR}_B(t)],dt\]

This is exactly the area between two curves. A classifier dominates another if this integral is positive — if its ROC curve lies above the other's everywhere. The area between their ROC curves quantifies by how much.

TPR
 1│         ╭──── Classifier A
  │     ╭───╯████
  │    ╱████████╲
  │   ╱██████████╲─── Classifier B
  │  ╱████████████╲
  │ ╱██████████████╲
  │╱────────────────╲──→ FPR
 0                   1

  Shaded area = ΔAUC = advantage of A over B

docs.title: 8.2 — Precision-Recall AUC
docs.text:
The Precision-Recall curve similarly defines an area metric:

\[\text{AP} = \int_0^1 P(R),dR\]

where \(P\) is precision and \(R\) is recall. The area between two precision-recall curves compares models — a direct area-between-curves computation over \([0,1]\).

docs.title: 8.3 — Wasserstein Distance as Area Between CDFs
docs.text:
For one-dimensional distributions, the Wasserstein-1 distance (Earth Mover's Distance) equals the area between cumulative distribution functions:

\[W_1(p, q) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|F_p(x) - F_q(x)|,dx\]

This is the area between two curves \(F_p\) and \(F_q\). The absolute value means it splits at crossings — exactly the procedure in § 2. This metric is used in Wasserstein GANs and optimal transport based losses.

CDF
 1│              ╭──── F_q(x)
  │         ╭───╯
  │     ╭───╯ ████████
  │ ╭───╯████████╲
  │ │████████████ ╲─── F_p(x)
  │─┼─────────────────────→ x

  W₁ = shaded area between the two CDFs

docs.title: 8.4 — Learning Curves and Sample Efficiency
docs.text:
When plotting validation loss against training steps for two models, the area between the learning curves measures cumulative sample efficiency:

\[\Delta = \int_0^T [\mathcal{L}_A(t) - \mathcal{L}_B(t)],dt\]

If model A has lower loss throughout training, \(\Delta > 0\) and A is more sample efficient. This integral accounts for the full trajectory, not just the endpoint — a model that trains faster but converges to the same loss may have a substantially smaller \(\Delta\).

docs.title: 8.5 — Gain Curves in Ranking Models
docs.text:
In information retrieval and recommendation systems, Cumulative Gain curves measure ranking quality:

\[\text{DCG}@k = \sum_{i=1}^k \frac{\text{rel}_i}{\log_2(i+1)}\]

The continuous analog is an area under a gain curve. The area between the gain curve of a learned ranker and the random baseline quantifies the model's lift — how much better than chance the ranking is. This is the area-between-curves formula applied to ranked retrieval evaluation.

docs.title: 8.6 — Calibration and the Area Between Reliability Curves
docs.text:
A well-calibrated model has predicted probabilities that match empirical frequencies. The reliability diagram plots empirical accuracy vs. predicted confidence. The area between this curve and the diagonal \(y = x\) (perfect calibration) is the Expected Calibration Error (ECE):

\[\text{ECE} \approx \int_0^1 |f(p) - p|,dp\]

where \(f(p)\) is the empirical accuracy at predicted confidence \(p\). This is the area between the calibration curve and the line \(y = x\) — the splitting at crossings (§ 2) handles over- and under-confidence regions separately.

docs.title: § 9 — Common Mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake 1: Not finding all intersection points. Solve \(f(x) = g(x)\) completely. Quadratics have two roots, trig equations have infinitely many — restrict to the domain and find all of them.

Mistake 2: Wrong sign (not checking which curve is on top). \(\int_a^b (g - f)\) instead of \(\int_a^b (f - g)\) gives the right magnitude but wrong interpretation. Always plug in a test point between the limits.

Mistake 3: Not splitting when curves cross. \(\int_{-1}^{1}(x^3 - x),dx = 0\) suggests the area is zero — but the curves cross at \(x = 0\), and the enclosed regions have equal area on each side. The actual area is \(\int_{-1}^{0}(x^3 - x),dx + \int_0^1(x - x^3),dx = 1/2\).

Mistake 4: Integrating in \(x\) when \(y\) is far cleaner. When a region is bounded by \(x = y^2 + 1\) and \(x = 3 - y^2\), integrating in \(x\) requires inverting and splitting. In \(y\), it is a single integral. Recognize horizontal strip regions.

Mistake 5: Using the net signed area formula for a geometric area problem. \(\int_a^b [f(x) - g(x)],dx\) gives signed area. For the geometric area (always positive), use \(\int_a^b |f(x) - g(x)|,dx\), splitting at every crossing.

docs.title: § 10 — Summary
docs.text: \[A = \int_a^b [f(x) - g(x)],dx \quad (f \ge g \text{ on } [a,b])\] \[A = \int_a^b |f(x) - g(x)|,dx \quad (\text{general, split at crossings})\] \[A = \int_c^d [f(y) - g(y)],dy \quad (\text{integrate in } y: \text{ right} - \text{left})\] Concept Content Formula Top minus bottom (or right minus left in \(y\)), integrated over the interval Limits Intersection points of the bounding curves Crossing curves Split at each crossing; integrate \(\|f-g\|\) on each piece Choice of variable Use whichever gives a single integral over a simply-described domain 18.02 connection Area between curves = inner integral of a double integral over a Type I/II region ML applications AUC/ROC comparison, Wasserstein distance, learning curve efficiency, ECE calibration
