docs.title: Integration by Parts
docs.text:
A professor's personal notebook · Stewart §7.1 · MIT 18.02

Personal note: IBP is not a formula to memorise — it is the product rule read backwards. Once you see it that way, every step becomes inevitable rather than magical. The real skill is not the algebra; it is choosing \(u\) and \(dv\) so the resulting integral is simpler than the one you started with. That choice is an art, and this note is about developing that art.

docs.title: §1 · The Derivation — Not a Formula, a Theorem
docs.text:
Start from the product rule. For differentiable functions \(u(x)\) and \(v(x)\):

\[\frac{d}{dx}[u(x)v(x)] = u'(x)v(x) + u(x)v'(x)\]

Integrate both sides over \([a,b]\):

\[\int_a^b \frac{d}{dx}[uv],dx = \int_a^b u'v,dx + \int_a^b uv',dx\]

The left side is just \([u(x)v(x)]_a^b\) by FTC. Rearrange:

\[\boxed{\int_a^b u,v',dx = \big[uv\big]_a^b - \int_a^b v,u',dx}\]

In indefinite form, writing \(dv = v'(x),dx\) and \(du = u'(x),dx\):

\[\boxed{\int u,dv = uv - \int v,du}\]

Observation: The formula trades \(\int u,dv\) for \(\int v,du\). This is only useful if \(\int v,du\) is easier than \(\int u,dv\). Your entire job is to make that true.

docs.title: §2 · The LIATE Rule — A Heuristic, Not a Law
docs.text:
When faced with a product \(f(x)\cdot g(x)\), assign \(u\) to whichever function appears earlier in this list:

Priority Class Examples 1st **L**ogarithm \(\ln x,\ \log_a x,\ \ln(x^2+1)\) 2nd **I**nverse trig \(\arcsin x,\ \arctan x,\ \text{arcsec},x\) 3rd **A**lgebraic (polynomial) \(x^n,\ \sqrt{x},\ x^{3/2}\) 4th **T**rigonometric \(\sin x,\ \cos x,\ \tan x\) 5th **E**xponential \(e^x,\ a^x,\ e^{3x}\)

Why this order works:

  • L and I first: their derivatives simplify (\((\ln x)' = 1/x\), \((\arctan x)' = 1/(1+x^2)\)) but their integrals are messy. So make them \(u\) (differentiate them).
  • E last: \(e^x\) integrates to itself — it doesn't simplify things to let it be \(u\).
  • A in the middle: polynomials reduce degree when differentiated, eventually becoming constants.

LIATE is a heuristic. There are cases where it fails or where the "wrong" assignment is actually correct. The real test is always: does \(\int v,du\) look simpler?

docs.title: 3.1 Polynomial × Exponential: \(\int xe^x,dx\)
docs.text:
Assignment (LIATE: A before E): \(u = x\), \(dv = e^x,dx\)

\[du = dx, \qquad v = e^x\] \[\int xe^x,dx = xe^x - \int e^x,dx = xe^x - e^x + C = e^x(x-1) + C\]

Verification: \(\frac{d}{dx}[e^x(x-1)] = e^x(x-1) + e^x = xe^x\) ✓

docs.title: 3.2 Polynomial × Exponential (repeated): \(\int x^2 e^x,dx\)
docs.text:
Assignment: \(u = x^2\), \(dv = e^x,dx\)

\[du = 2x,dx, \qquad v = e^x\] \[\int x^2 e^x,dx = x^2 e^x - \int 2xe^x,dx = x^2 e^x - 2\int xe^x,dx\]

Now apply the result from 3.1:

\[= x^2 e^x - 2e^x(x-1) + C = e^x(x^2 - 2x + 2) + C\]

Pattern: \(\int x^n e^x,dx\) requires IBP exactly \(n\) times. The general result is:

\[\int x^n e^x,dx = e^x\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^{n-k}\frac{n!}{k!}x^k + C\]

docs.title: 3.3 Logarithm alone: \(\int \ln x,dx\)
docs.text:
Trick: write \(\ln x = \ln x \cdot 1\). Assign \(u = \ln x\), \(dv = dx\).

\[du = \frac{1}{x}dx, \qquad v = x\] \[\int \ln x,dx = x\ln x - \int x \cdot \frac{1}{x},dx = x\ln x - \int 1,dx = x\ln x - x + C\]

This is the prototype for all "lone L or I" integrals. The trick is always: pair with \(1\) and assign \(dv = dx\).

docs.title: 3.4 Inverse trig alone: \(\int \arctan x,dx\)
docs.text:
Same trick: \(u = \arctan x\), \(dv = dx\)

\[du = \frac{1}{1+x^2}dx, \qquad v = x\] \[\int \arctan x,dx = x\arctan x - \int \frac{x}{1+x^2},dx\]

For the remaining integral, \(u\)-sub with \(w = 1+x^2\):

\[\int \frac{x}{1+x^2},dx = \frac{1}{2}\ln(1+x^2)\] \[\int \arctan x,dx = x\arctan x - \frac{1}{2}\ln(1+x^2) + C\]

Similarly: $\(\int \arcsin x,dx = x\arcsin x + \sqrt{1-x^2} + C\)$ $\(\int \arccos x,dx = x\arccos x - \sqrt{1-x^2} + C\)$

docs.title: 3.5 Cyclic IBP: \(\int e^x \sin x,dx\)
docs.text:
This is the most structurally important case. Let \(I = \int e^x\sin x,dx\).

First IBP: \(u = \sin x\), \(dv = e^x dx\)

\[du = \cos x,dx, \qquad v = e^x\] \[I = e^x\sin x - \int e^x\cos x,dx\]

Second IBP on \(\int e^x\cos x,dx\): \(u = \cos x\), \(dv = e^x dx\)

\[du = -\sin x,dx, \qquad v = e^x\] \[\int e^x\cos x,dx = e^x\cos x - \int e^x(-\sin x),dx = e^x\cos x + I\]

Substituting back:

\[I = e^x\sin x - (e^x\cos x + I) = e^x\sin x - e^x\cos x - I\] \[2I = e^x(\sin x - \cos x)\] \[\boxed{I = \frac{e^x(\sin x - \cos x)}{2} + C}\]

Critical observation: The key was that applying IBP twice with consistent assignment (always making the trig function \(u\)) reproduced \(I\) on the right-hand side. This creates an algebraic equation in \(I\) which we solve directly. Never switch the roles of \(u\) and \(dv\) between the two applications, or you will undo your work and get \(0 = 0\).

Similarly: $\(\int e^{ax}\sin bx,dx = \frac{e^{ax}(a\sin bx - b\cos bx)}{a^2+b^2} + C\)$ $\(\int e^{ax}\cos bx,dx = \frac{e^{ax}(a\cos bx + b\sin bx)}{a^2+b^2} + C\)$

docs.title: §4 · Reduction Formulae — IBP Iterated Systematically
docs.text: A reduction formula expresses \(\int f^n\) in terms of \(\int f^{n-1}\) (or \(\int f^{n-2}\)). These are derived by IBP and are extremely useful when \(n\) is large.

docs.title: 4.1 \(\int \sin^n x,dx\)
docs.text:
Write \(\sin^n x = \sin^{n-1}x \cdot \sin x\).

Assignment: \(u = \sin^{n-1}x\), \(dv = \sin x,dx\)

\[du = (n-1)\sin^{n-2}x\cos x,dx, \qquad v = -\cos x\] \[\int\sin^n x,dx = -\sin^{n-1}x\cos x + (n-1)\int\sin^{n-2}x\cos^2 x,dx\]

Replace \(\cos^2 x = 1 - \sin^2 x\):

\[= -\sin^{n-1}x\cos x + (n-1)\int\sin^{n-2}x,dx - (n-1)\int\sin^n x,dx\]

Let \(I_n = \int\sin^n x,dx\), rearrange:

\[\boxed{I_n = -\frac{\sin^{n-1}x\cos x}{n} + \frac{n-1}{n}I_{n-2}}\]

Base cases: \(I_0 = x+C\), \(I_1 = -\cos x + C\).

Example — \(\int\sin^4 x,dx\):

\[I_4 = -\frac{\sin^3 x\cos x}{4} + \frac{3}{4}I_2\] \[I_2 = -\frac{\sin x\cos x}{2}+\frac{1}{2}I_0 = -\frac{\sin x\cos x}{2}+\frac{x}{2}\] \[I_4 = -\frac{\sin^3 x\cos x}{4} + \frac{3}{4}\left(-\frac{\sin x\cos x}{2}+\frac{x}{2}\right) = -\frac{\sin^3 x\cos x}{4} - \frac{3\sin x\cos x}{8} + \frac{3x}{8} + C\]

docs.title: 4.2 \(\int x^n e^{ax},dx\)
docs.text: \[\int x^n e^{ax},dx = \frac{x^n e^{ax}}{a} - \frac{n}{a}\int x^{n-1}e^{ax},dx\]

docs.title: 4.3 \(\int (\ln x)^n,dx\)
docs.text: \[\int(\ln x)^n,dx = x(\ln x)^n - n\int(\ln x)^{n-1},dx\]

docs.title: 4.4 \(\int \sec^n x,dx\)
docs.text: \[\int\sec^n x,dx = \frac{\sec^{n-2}x\tan x}{n-1} + \frac{n-2}{n-1}\int\sec^{n-2}x,dx, \quad n \geq 2\]

docs.title: §5 · Definite Integrals — IBP with Limits
docs.text:
\[\int_a^b u,dv = \big[uv\big]_a^b - \int_a^b v,du\]

Example:

\[\int_0^1 xe^x,dx = \big[xe^x\big]_0^1 - \int_0^1 e^x,dx = e - \big[e^x\big]_0^1 = e - (e-1) = 1\]

Wallis Integral via reduction formula:

Using \(I_n = \frac{n-1}{n}I_{n-2}\) with \(\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^n x,dx\):

\[I_{2n} = \frac{(2n-1)!!}{(2n)!!}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}, \qquad I_{2n+1} = \frac{(2n)!!}{(2n+1)!!}\]

Wallis product (taking the limit of \(I_{2n}/I_{2n+1}\) as \(n\to\infty\)):

\[\frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{2}{1}\cdot\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{4}{3}\cdot\frac{4}{5}\cdot\frac{6}{5}\cdot\frac{6}{7}\cdots\]

docs.title: §6 · Tabular Integration — IBP at Scale
docs.text:
When \(u\) is a polynomial (eventually reduces to 0) and \(dv\) is easy to integrate repeatedly:

\(\int x^3 e^{2x},dx\):

Sign Differentiate (\(u\) column) Integrate (\(dv\) column) \(+\) \(x^3\) \(e^{2x}\) \(-\) \(3x^2\) \(\frac{1}{2}e^{2x}\) \(+\) \(6x\) \(\frac{1}{4}e^{2x}\) \(-\) \(6\) \(\frac{1}{8}e^{2x}\) \(+\) \(0\) \(\frac{1}{16}e^{2x}\)

Multiply diagonals, apply signs:

\[= x^3\cdot\frac{e^{2x}}{2} - 3x^2\cdot\frac{e^{2x}}{4} + 6x\cdot\frac{e^{2x}}{8} - 6\cdot\frac{e^{2x}}{16} + C\] \[= e^{2x}\left(\frac{x^3}{2} - \frac{3x^2}{4} + \frac{3x}{4} - \frac{3}{8}\right) + C\]

Rule: Stop when the \(u\)-column reaches 0. The last entry in the \(dv\)-column is not used.

docs.title: §7 · The Tricky Cases — Where Intuition Breaks
7.1 When IBP produces a useful equation
docs.text:
We already saw the cyclic case. Another: \(\int\sqrt{1-x^2},dx\)

\(u = \sqrt{1-x^2}\), \(dv = dx\)

\[du = \frac{-x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}dx, \qquad v = x\] \[\int\sqrt{1-x^2},dx = x\sqrt{1-x^2} + \int\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{1-x^2}},dx\]

Now write \(x^2 = 1-(1-x^2)\) in the numerator:

\[\int\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{1-x^2}},dx = \int\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}},dx - \int\sqrt{1-x^2},dx = \arcsin x - I\]

So: $\(I = x\sqrt{1-x^2} + \arcsin x - I\)$ $\(2I = x\sqrt{1-x^2} + \arcsin x\)$ $\(\int\sqrt{1-x^2},dx = \frac{x\sqrt{1-x^2}}{2} + \frac{\arcsin x}{2} + C\)$

This is the area formula for a semicircle — check: \(\int_{-1}^1\sqrt{1-x^2},dx = \pi/2\). ✓

docs.title: 7.2 When \(u\)-substitution is needed inside IBP
docs.text:
\(\int x^3\sqrt{x^2+1},dx\): try \(u = x^2+1\) first, giving \(\int \frac{(u-1)}{2}\sqrt{u},du = \frac{1}{2}\int(u^{3/2}-u^{1/2}),du\), which is just power rule. IBP is not needed here — recognise when \(u\)-sub is cleaner.

Important: IBP is not always the right tool even when you see a product. \(\int xe^{x^2},dx\) yields immediately to \(u = x^2\), not IBP.

docs.title: 7.3 Integration by Parts in two variables (MIT 18.02)
docs.text:
For operators on functions, IBP generalises. If \(u, v\) are functions on \([a,b]\):

\[\int_a^b u,v'',dx = \big[uv'\big]_a^b - \int_a^b u'v',dx\]

Apply IBP again on the right:

\[\int_a^b u,v'',dx = \big[uv'\big]_a^b - \big[u'v\big]_a^b + \int_a^b u''v,dx\]

This is the adjoint identity — it says \(\langle u, Lv\rangle = \langle Lu, v\rangle + \text{boundary terms}\) for \(L = d^2/dx^2\), which makes \(L\) self-adjoint when the boundary terms vanish.

docs.title: §8 · Visualisation — What IBP Is Geometrically
docs.text:
Consider two increasing functions \(u(x)\) and \(v(x)\) parametrised by \(x \in [a,b]\).

The point \((u(x), v(x))\) traces a curve in the \(uv\)-plane from \((u(a),v(a))\) to \((u(b),v(b))\).

v
^
|         * (u(b),v(b))
|        /
|       / curve (u(x),v(x))
|      /
|*----+
(u(a),v(a))
+-----------> u

The rectangle \([u(a),u(b)] \times [v(a),v(b)]\) is divided into two regions by this curve:

  • Area to the left of curve \(= \int_{v(a)}^{v(b)} u,dv\)
  • Area below curve \(= \int_{u(a)}^{u(b)} v,du\)

The two together make up the full rectangle:

\[\int_{v(a)}^{v(b)} u,dv + \int_{u(a)}^{u(b)} v,du = \big[u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a)\big]\]

This is exactly IBP. The formula \(\int u,dv = uv - \int v,du\) is the statement that the two shaded areas sum to the rectangle.

v(b) ┤ · · · · ·*
     │ · · · ·/  |
     │ · · ·/    |  ← Region A = ∫u dv
     │ · ·/      |
v(a) ┤ ·/────────┤
     │  ↑        |
     │  Region B = ∫v du
     └───┬────────┬──→ u
       u(a)     u(b)

Area(A) + Area(B) = Area of full rectangle = \(u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a)\)

docs.title: 9.1 Backpropagation is Discrete IBP
docs.text:
In a neural network with loss \(\mathcal{L}\) and a layer computing \(z = \sigma(Wx+b)\):

The chain rule \(\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial W} = \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial z}\cdot\frac{\partial z}{\partial W}\) is the discrete product rule.

Backpropagation sums these over the network depth — which is the discrete analogue of:

\[\int_a^b (uv)',dx = \int_a^b u'v,dx + \int_a^b uv',dx\]

The reverse-mode automatic differentiation algorithm is literally the continuous IBP identity applied layer by layer.

docs.title: 9.2 The Adjoint Method — Neural ODEs
docs.text:
A Neural ODE defines the hidden state by: $\(\frac{dh}{dt} = f_\theta(h(t), t), \quad h(t_0) = h_0\)$

To compute \(\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\theta}\) without storing all intermediate states, define the adjoint \(a(t) = \frac{d\mathcal{L}}{dh(t)}\).

The adjoint satisfies: $\(\frac{da}{dt} = -a(t)^T \frac{\partial f_\theta}{\partial h}\)$

This ODE for \(a(t)\) is derived by IBP on the functional: $\(\mathcal{L} = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} \langle a(t),\ \dot{h}(t) - f_\theta(h(t),t)\rangle,dt\)$

Applying IBP to \(\int a,\dot{h},dt = [ah]_{t_0}^{t_1} - \int \dot{a},h,dt\) produces the adjoint equation. This is the IBP formula at the level of functionals — the foundation of optimal control and variational methods in ML.

docs.title: 9.3 Integration by Parts in Loss Regularisation
docs.text:
Score matching (the objective behind diffusion models and energy-based models) asks:

\[\mathcal{J}( heta) = rac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{p_{data}}\left[\left| abla_x\ln p_ heta(x) - abla_x\ln p_{data}(x) ight|^2 ight]\]

Expanding the square and applying IBP to the cross term:

\[\int p_{data}(x)\langle abla_x\ln p_ heta, abla_x\ln p_{data} angle,dx = -\int p_{data}(x),\Delta_x\ln p_ heta(x),dx\]

where \(\Delta\) is the Laplacian. (IBP: \(\int abla u\cdot abla v = -\int u,\Delta v\) when boundary terms vanish.)

This gives the tractable objective: $\(\mathcal{J}( heta) = \mathbb{E}_{p_{data}}\left[ ext{tr}( abla_x^2\ln p_ heta(x)) + rac{1}{2}| abla_x\ln p_ heta(x)|^2 ight] + ext{const}\)$

No knowledge of \(p_{data}\) needed — IBP removed it. This is why DDPM, score-based models (Song & Ermon, 2019) are tractable.

docs.title: 9.4 Fisher Information and IBP
docs.text:
The Fisher information is:

\[\mathcal{I}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\ln p(x;\theta)\right)^2\right]\]

Under regularity conditions, IBP on \(\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\int p(x;\theta),dx = 0\) gives the identity:

\[\mathcal{I}(\theta) = -\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\ln p(x;\theta)\right]\]

This is why the Hessian of the log-likelihood (the observed Fisher information) is used in natural gradient descent and second-order optimisation methods like K-FAC.

docs.title: 9.5 Entropy and the Gibbs Inequality
docs.text:
The differential entropy \(H(p) = -\int p(x)\ln p(x),dx\).

To show the normal distribution maximises entropy among fixed-variance distributions, one sets up a variational problem and applies IBP to the Euler-Lagrange equation. The result is that the optimal \(p^*(x) \propto e^{-\lambda x^2}\), i.e., Gaussian.

This underpins the rate-distortion theory behind variational autoencoders (VAEs): the Gaussian prior is not arbitrary — it is information-theoretically optimal, proven via an argument that is IBP at its core.

docs.title: §10 · Summary Table — IBP Pattern Recognition
docs.text: Integrand form Assignment Result type \(x^n e^{ax}\) \(u=x^n\), \(dv=e^{ax}dx\) Repeat \(n\) times; use tabular \(x^n\sin ax\) \(u=x^n\), \(dv=\sin ax,dx\) Repeat \(n\) times \(x^n\cos ax\) \(u=x^n\), \(dv=\cos ax,dx\) Repeat \(n\) times \(x^n\ln x\) \(u=\ln x\), \(dv=x^n dx\) Single IBP \(\ln x\) \(u=\ln x\), \(dv=dx\) Single IBP \(\arctan x\), \(\arcsin x\) \(u=\text{inv.trig}\), \(dv=dx\) Single IBP + u-sub \(e^{ax}\sin bx\) Either choice consistently Cyclic; solve for \(I\) \(e^{ax}\cos bx\) Either choice consistently Cyclic; solve for \(I\) \(\sin^n x\), \(\cos^n x\) \(u=\sin^{n-1}x\), \(dv=\sin x,dx\) Reduction formula \(\sec^n x\) \(u=\sec^{n-2}x\), \(dv=\sec^2 x,dx\) Reduction formula

docs.title: §11 · Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
docs.text:
Mistake 1 — Switching \(u\)/\(dv\) roles between IBP applications. In cyclic IBP, always assign the same type of function to \(u\) in both applications. Switching undoes the work: you get \(I = I\), i.e., \(0 = 0\).

Mistake 2 — Forgetting \(+C\) when computing \(v\). When integrating \(dv\) to get \(v\), you technically get \(v + C_0\). It turns out adding \(C_0\) is harmless (it cancels), but students sometimes propagate it incorrectly.

Mistake 3 — Using IBP when \(u\)-sub is simpler. \(\int xe^{x^2}dx\): do NOT set \(u=x\). Recognise \(x,dx = \frac{1}{2}d(x^2)\) and substitute directly.

Mistake 4 — Wrong sign in the reduction formula. The reduction formula for \(\sin^n\) has a subtle sign: \(I_n = -\frac{\sin^{n-1}x\cos x}{n} + \frac{n-1}{n}I_{n-2}\). Derive it fresh rather than memorising.

Mistake 5 — Not verifying. IBP answers are easy to verify: differentiate the result. Algebraic errors are common; always check.

docs.title: Trigonometric Integrals
docs.text:
A professor's personal notebook · Stewart §7.2 · MIT 18.02

Personal note: Trigonometric integrals are not a collection of tricks — they are a systematic exploitation of three identities. Every technique in this chapter reduces to one of: the Pythagorean identity, a half-angle identity, or a product-to-sum identity. Once you see which identity is needed and why, the method is obvious. My goal here is to make the "why" so clear that you never need to memorise a case — you can reconstruct every strategy from scratch.

docs.title: §1 · The Three Master Identities
docs.text: Everything in this chapter flows from these. Know them cold.

docs.title: Pythagorean Identities
docs.text: \[\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1 \tag{P1}$$ $$\tan^2 x + 1 = \sec^2 x \tag{P2}$$ $$\cot^2 x + 1 = \csc^2 x \tag{P3}\]

docs.title: Half-Angle (Power-Reduction) Identities
docs.text: \[\sin^2 x = \frac{1 - \cos 2x}{2} \tag{H1}$$ $$\cos^2 x = \frac{1 + \cos 2x}{2} \tag{H2}\]

docs.title: Product-to-Sum Identities
docs.text:
\[\sin mx \cos nx = \frac{1}{2}[\sin(m+n)x + \sin(m-n)x] \tag{Q1}$$ $$\sin mx \sin nx = \frac{1}{2}[\cos(m-n)x - \cos(m+n)x] \tag{Q2}$$ $$\cos mx \cos nx = \frac{1}{2}[\cos(m-n)x + \cos(m+n)x] \tag{Q3}\]

Why three families? Because \(\sin^m x \cos^n x\), \(\tan^m x \sec^n x\), and \(\sin mx \cos nx\) each require a different structural attack. The Pythagorean identities handle the first two families; the product-to-sum identities handle the third. The half-angle identities are the fallback for even powers in the first family.

docs.title: §2 · Family I — Integrals of the Form \(\int \sin^m x \cos^n x,dx\)
docs.text: The strategy depends entirely on the parity (odd or even) of \(m\) and \(n\).

docs.title: Case A — At least one exponent is odd
docs.text:
Strategy: Factor out one copy of the odd-powered function, use (P1) to convert the rest to the other function, then \(u\)-substitute.

Why it works: If \(m\) is odd, write \(\sin^m x = \sin^{m-1}x\cdot\sin x\). Since \(m-1\) is even, \(\sin^{m-1}x = (1-\cos^2 x)^{(m-1)/2}\) by (P1). Now set \(u = \cos x\), \(du = -\sin x,dx\) — the leftover \(\sin x,dx\) is exactly \(-du\).

Example 1: \(\displaystyle\int \sin^3 x\cos^2 x,dx\)

\(m=3\) (odd), \(n=2\) (even). Factor from \(\sin\):

\[= \int \sin^2 x \cdot \cos^2 x \cdot \sin x,dx = \int (1-\cos^2 x)\cos^2 x\sin x,dx\]

Let \(u = \cos x\), \(du = -\sin x,dx\):

\[= -\int(1-u^2)u^2,du = -\int(u^2 - u^4),du = -\frac{u^3}{3}+\frac{u^5}{5}+C\] \[= \boxed{-\frac{\cos^3 x}{3}+\frac{\cos^5 x}{5}+C}\]

Verification: \(\frac{d}{dx}\left[-\frac{\cos^3 x}{3}+\frac{\cos^5 x}{5}\right] = \cos^2 x\sin x - \cos^4 x\sin x = \sin x\cos^2 x(1-\cos^2 x) = \sin^3 x\cos^2 x\) ✓

Example 2: \(\displaystyle\int \sin^2 x\cos^5 x,dx\)

\(n=5\) (odd). Factor from \(\cos\):

\[= \int\sin^2 x\cos^4 x\cdot\cos x,dx = \int\sin^2 x(1-\sin^2 x)^2\cos x,dx\]

Let \(u=\sin x\), \(du=\cos x,dx\):

\[= \int u^2(1-u^2)^2,du = \int u^2(1-2u^2+u^4),du = \int(u^2-2u^4+u^6),du\] \[= \frac{u^3}{3}-\frac{2u^5}{5}+\frac{u^7}{7}+C = \boxed{\frac{\sin^3 x}{3}-\frac{2\sin^5 x}{5}+\frac{\sin^7 x}{7}+C}\]

Example 3: \(\displaystyle\int\cos^5 x,dx\)

Both exponents: \(m=0\) (even), \(n=5\) (odd). Factor one \(\cos x\):

\[= \int\cos^4 x\cdot\cos x,dx = \int(1-\sin^2 x)^2\cos x,dx\]

Let \(u=\sin x\):

\[= \int(1-u^2)^2,du = \int(1-2u^2+u^4),du = u - \frac{2u^3}{3}+\frac{u^5}{5}+C\] \[= \boxed{\sin x - \frac{2\sin^3 x}{3}+\frac{\sin^5 x}{5}+C}\]

docs.title: Case B — Both exponents are even
docs.text:
Strategy: Apply half-angle identities (H1) and (H2) to reduce powers. Repeat until all powers are odd or the integral is elementary.

Why it works: (H1) and (H2) literally halve the exponent. Apply them repeatedly: \(\sin^{2k} x \to \sin^{2(k-1)} x + \text{double-angle terms} \to \cdots\). Eventually all terms have exponent 0 or 1.

Example 4: \(\displaystyle\int\sin^2 x,dx\)

\[= \int\frac{1-\cos 2x}{2},dx = \frac{x}{2}-\frac{\sin 2x}{4}+C\]

Example 5: \(\displaystyle\int\cos^2 x,dx\)

\[= \int\frac{1+\cos 2x}{2},dx = \frac{x}{2}+\frac{\sin 2x}{4}+C\]

Example 6: \(\displaystyle\int\sin^4 x,dx\)

\[= \int\left(\frac{1-\cos 2x}{2}\right)^2 dx = \frac{1}{4}\int(1-2\cos 2x+\cos^2 2x),dx\]

Apply (H2) to \(\cos^2 2x = \frac{1+\cos 4x}{2}\):

\[= \frac{1}{4}\int\left(1-2\cos 2x+\frac{1+\cos 4x}{2}\right)dx = \frac{1}{4}\left[\frac{3x}{2}-\sin 2x+\frac{\sin 4x}{8}\right]+C\] \[= \boxed{\frac{3x}{8}-\frac{\sin 2x}{4}+\frac{\sin 4x}{32}+C}\]

Example 7: \(\displaystyle\int\sin^2 x\cos^2 x,dx\)

Use both half-angle identities together, or notice:

\[\sin^2 x\cos^2 x = \frac{1}{4}\sin^2 2x = \frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{1-\cos 4x}{2} = \frac{1-\cos 4x}{8}\] \[\int\sin^2 x\cos^2 x,dx = \frac{x}{8}-\frac{\sin 4x}{32}+C\]

docs.title: Summary Table — \(\int\sin^m x\cos^n x,dx\)
docs.text:
m odd?  → Factor sin x, let u = cos x
n odd?  → Factor cos x, let u = sin x
Both odd? → Either works (choose smaller exponent for simplicity)
Both even? → Half-angle identities, reduce, repeat

docs.title: §3 · Family II — Integrals of the Form \(\int\tan^m x\sec^n x,dx\)
docs.text:
The key identity is (P2): \(\tan^2 x = \sec^2 x - 1\).

The key derivatives: \((\tan x)' = \sec^2 x\) and \((\sec x)' = \sec x\tan x\).

So: to use \(u = \tan x\), you need \(\sec^2 x,dx\) left over; to use \(u = \sec x\), you need \(\sec x\tan x,dx\).

docs.title: Case A — \(n\) is even (the \(\sec\) exponent is even)
docs.text:
Strategy: Factor out \(\sec^2 x\) (for the \(du\) in \(u=\tan x\) substitution). Convert the remaining even power of \(\sec\) to \(\tan\) via \(\sec^2 x = 1+\tan^2 x\). Let \(u=\tan x\).

Example 8: \(\displaystyle\int\tan^3 x\sec^4 x,dx\)

Factor \(\sec^2 x\): \(= \int\tan^3 x\sec^2 x\cdot\sec^2 x,dx\)

Convert: \(\sec^2 x = 1+\tan^2 x\). Let \(u=\tan x\), \(du=\sec^2 x,dx\):

\[= \int u^3(1+u^2),du = \int(u^3+u^5),du = \frac{u^4}{4}+\frac{u^6}{6}+C = \boxed{\frac{\tan^4 x}{4}+\frac{\tan^6 x}{6}+C}\]

docs.title: Case B — \(m\) is odd (the \(\tan\) exponent is odd)
docs.text:
Strategy: Factor out \(\sec x\tan x\) (for the \(du\) in \(u=\sec x\) substitution). Convert the remaining even power of \(\tan\) to \(\sec\) via \(\tan^2 x = \sec^2 x - 1\). Let \(u=\sec x\).

Example 9: \(\displaystyle\int\tan^3 x\sec^3 x,dx\)

Factor \(\sec x\tan x\): \(= \int\tan^2 x\sec^2 x\cdot\sec x\tan x,dx\)

Convert: \(\tan^2 x = \sec^2 x-1\). Let \(u=\sec x\), \(du=\sec x\tan x,dx\):

\[= \int(u^2-1)u^2,du = \int(u^4-u^2),du = \frac{u^5}{5}-\frac{u^3}{3}+C = \boxed{\frac{\sec^5 x}{5}-\frac{\sec^3 x}{3}+C}\]

docs.title: Case C — \(m\) even, \(n\) odd (the hard case)
docs.text:
Strategy: No clean substitution exists. Convert everything to \(\sec\) via \(\tan^2 x = \sec^2 x - 1\), then use the reduction formula for \(\int\sec^n x,dx\).

Example 10: \(\displaystyle\int\tan^2 x\sec x,dx\)

\[= \int(\sec^2 x-1)\sec x,dx = \int\sec^3 x,dx - \int\sec x,dx\]

These are both known: $\(\int\sec^3 x,dx = \frac{\sec x\tan x}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\ln|\sec x+\tan x|+C \quad \text{(derived below)}\)$ $\(\int\sec x,dx = \ln|\sec x+\tan x|+C\)$

\[= \frac{\sec x\tan x}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\ln|\sec x+\tan x|+C\]

docs.title: Derivation of \(\int\sec^3 x,dx\) ⚑
docs.text:
This is important enough to prove carefully. Use IBP with \(u=\sec x\), \(dv=\sec^2 x,dx\):

\[du = \sec x\tan x,dx, \qquad v = \tan x\] \[\int\sec^3 x,dx = \sec x\tan x - \int\sec x\tan^2 x,dx\] \[= \sec x\tan x - \int\sec x(\sec^2 x-1),dx\] \[= \sec x\tan x - \int\sec^3 x,dx + \int\sec x,dx\]

Let \(I = \int\sec^3 x,dx\): $\(I = \sec x\tan x - I + \ln|\sec x+\tan x|\)$ $\(2I = \sec x\tan x + \ln|\sec x+\tan x|\)$

\[\boxed{\int\sec^3 x,dx = \frac{\sec x\tan x}{2}+\frac{\ln|\sec x+\tan x|}{2}+C}\]

docs.title: Reduction Formula for \(\int\sec^n x,dx\)
docs.text:
\[\int\sec^n x,dx = \frac{\sec^{n-2}x\tan x}{n-1}+\frac{n-2}{n-1}\int\sec^{n-2}x,dx, \quad n\geq 2\]

Derivation: IBP with \(u=\sec^{n-2}x\), \(dv=\sec^2 x,dx\). Identical structure to the \(\sec^3\) derivation above.

docs.title: Summary Table — \(\int\tan^m x\sec^n x,dx\)
docs.text:
n even? → Factor sec²x, u = tan x, convert remaining sec² → 1+tan²
m odd?  → Factor sec x tan x, u = sec x, convert remaining tan² → sec²-1
Both conditions? → Either works
m even, n odd → Convert tan² → sec²-1, use sec reduction formula

docs.title: Analogous: \(\int\cot^m x\csc^n x,dx\)
docs.text: Identical structure, using \(\cot^2 x = \csc^2 x-1\), \((\cot x)' = -\csc^2 x\), \((\csc x)' = -\csc x\cot x\).

docs.title: §4 · Family III — Products of Sines and Cosines with Different Arguments
docs.text:
For \(\int\sin mx\cos nx,dx\), \(\int\sin mx\sin nx,dx\), \(\int\cos mx\cos nx,dx\): use product-to-sum identities (Q1)–(Q3) directly.

Example 11: \(\displaystyle\int\sin 5x\cos 3x,dx\)

Apply (Q1): \(\sin 5x\cos 3x = \frac{1}{2}[\sin 8x+\sin 2x]\)

\[= \frac{1}{2}\int(\sin 8x+\sin 2x),dx = -\frac{\cos 8x}{16}-\frac{\cos 2x}{4}+C\]

Example 12: \(\displaystyle\int\cos 3x\cos 5x,dx\)

Apply (Q3): \(\cos 3x\cos 5x = \frac{1}{2}[\cos(-2x)+\cos 8x] = \frac{1}{2}[\cos 2x+\cos 8x]\)

\[= \frac{\sin 2x}{4}+\frac{\sin 8x}{16}+C\]

Example 13: \(\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sin mx\sin nx,dx\), \(m\neq n\) integers

Apply (Q2): \(\sin mx\sin nx = \frac{1}{2}[\cos(m-n)x - \cos(m+n)x]\)

\[= \frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{\sin(m-n)x}{m-n}-\frac{\sin(m+n)x}{m+n}\right]_{-\pi}^{\pi} = 0\]

Since \(\sin(k\pi) = 0\) for any integer \(k\).

When \(m=n\): $\(\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sin^2 mx,dx = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{1-\cos 2mx}{2},dx = \pi\)$

This is the orthogonality of sine functions — the cornerstone of Fourier series. See §7.

docs.title: §5 · Powers of \(\tan x\) Alone and \(\cot x\) Alone
\(\int\tan^n x,dx\)
docs.text:
Use the reduction \(\tan^n x = \tan^{n-2}x\cdot\tan^2 x = \tan^{n-2}x(\sec^2 x-1)\):

\[\int\tan^n x,dx = \int\tan^{n-2}x\sec^2 x,dx - \int\tan^{n-2}x,dx = \frac{\tan^{n-1}x}{n-1} - \int\tan^{n-2}x,dx\]

Reduction formula: $\(\int\tan^n x,dx = \frac{\tan^{n-1}x}{n-1} - \int\tan^{n-2}x,dx, \quad n\neq 1\)$

Chain from base cases \(\int\tan^0 x = x\) and \(\int\tan x = \ln|\sec x|\):

\[\int\tan^2 x,dx = \tan x - x + C$$ $$\int\tan^3 x,dx = \frac{\tan^2 x}{2} - \ln|\sec x| + C$$ $$\int\tan^4 x,dx = \frac{\tan^3 x}{3} - \tan x + x + C\]

docs.title: \(\int\cot^n x,dx\)
docs.text:
\[\int\cot^n x,dx = -\frac{\cot^{n-1}x}{n-1} - \int\cot^{n-2}x,dx, \quad n\neq 1\]

Base cases: \(\int\cot x,dx = \ln|\sin x|+C\), \(\int\cot^2 x,dx = -\cot x - x + C\).

docs.title: §6 · Definite Integrals — The Wallis Formulas
docs.text:
Using the reduction formula for \(\int\sin^n x,dx\) with definite limits on \([0,\pi/2]\):

\[W_n = \int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^n x,dx = \int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^n x,dx\]

The reduction gives: \(W_n = \frac{n-1}{n}W_{n-2}\), with \(W_0 = \pi/2\), \(W_1 = 1\).

Explicit formulas:

\[W_{2n} = \frac{(2n-1)!!}{(2n)!!}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{1\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdots(2n-1)}{2\cdot 4\cdot 6\cdots(2n)}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}\] \[W_{2n+1} = \frac{(2n)!!}{(2n+1)!!} = \frac{2\cdot 4\cdot 6\cdots(2n)}{1\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdots(2n+1)}\]

First several values:

\(n\) \(W_n\) 0 \(\pi/2\) 1 \(1\) 2 \(\pi/4\) 3 \(2/3\) 4 \(3\pi/16\) 5 \(8/15\) 6 \(5\pi/32\)

Wallis's product (from \(W_{2n}/W_{2n+1} \to \pi/2\) as \(n\to\infty\)):

\[\frac{\pi}{2} = \prod_{k=1}^\infty\frac{(2k)(2k)}{(2k-1)(2k+1)} = \frac{2}{1}\cdot\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{4}{3}\cdot\frac{4}{5}\cdot\frac{6}{5}\cdot\frac{6}{7}\cdots\]

docs.title: §7 · Orthogonality — The Deepest Result in This Chapter
docs.text:
Theorem (Orthogonality of trigonometric functions on \([-\pi,\pi]\)):

\[\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sin mx\sin nx,dx = \pi,\delta_{mn}\] \[\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos mx\cos nx,dx = \pi,\delta_{mn} \quad (m,n \geq 1)\] \[\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sin mx\cos nx,dx = 0 \quad \text{for all integers } m,n\] \[\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos^2 0,dx = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}1,dx = 2\pi\]

where \(\delta_{mn} = 1\) if \(m=n\), \(0\) otherwise (Kronecker delta).

Proof of the first (m ≠ n case): Apply product-to-sum (Q2):

\[\sin mx\sin nx = \frac{1}{2}[\cos(m-n)x-\cos(m+n)x]\] \[\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sin mx\sin nx,dx = \frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{\sin(m-n)x}{m-n}-\frac{\sin(m+n)x}{m+n}\right]_{-\pi}^{\pi} = 0\]

since \(\sin(k\pi) = 0\) for all integers \(k\).

Proof of the m = n case: Apply (H1):

\[\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\sin^2 nx,dx = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\frac{1-\cos 2nx}{2},dx = \pi - \frac{\sin 2n\pi}{2n}\bigg|_{-\pi}^{\pi} = \pi\]

Why orthogonality is the right word: Define the inner product \(\langle f,g\rangle = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}f(x)g(x),dx\). The set \({1, \cos x, \sin x, \cos 2x, \sin 2x, \ldots}\) is an orthogonal basis of \(L^2([-\pi,\pi])\) under this inner product — exactly as the standard basis vectors \(\mathbf{e}_i\) are orthogonal under the dot product.

Fourier coefficients follow immediately:

\[f(x) = \frac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^\infty(a_n\cos nx + b_n\sin nx)\]

Multiply both sides by \(\cos mx\) and integrate over \([-\pi,\pi]\). By orthogonality, every term vanishes except \(n=m\):

\[a_m = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}f(x)\cos mx,dx, \qquad b_m = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}f(x)\sin mx,dx\]

The integrals from this chapter compute every Fourier coefficient.

docs.title: 10.1 Orthogonality → Fourier Features in ML
docs.text:
The orthogonality relations in §7 are the foundation of Random Fourier Features (RFF) — a technique for approximating kernel machines at scale.

The RBF kernel can be written as: $\(K(x,x') = e^{-|x-x'|^2/2\sigma^2} = \mathbb{E}_{\omega\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{-2}I)}\left[\cos(\omega^Tx)\cos(\omega^Tx')+\sin(\omega^Tx)\sin(\omega^Tx')\right]\)$

This is Bochner's theorem — a kernel is shift-invariant if and only if it is the Fourier transform of a non-negative measure. The trig integrals of §4 (and the orthogonality of §7) are what make the Fourier transform of \(e^{-x^2}\) itself a Gaussian.

Rahimi & Recht (2007) — Random Fourier Features: approximate \(K(x,x') \approx z(x)^Tz(x')\) where \(z(x) = \sqrt{2/D}[\cos(\omega_1^Tx+b_1),\ldots,\cos(\omega_D^Tx+b_D)]\). This converts an \(O(n^2)\) kernel computation to \(O(nD)\) using the integrals \(\int\cos(ax)\cos(bx),dx\) — exactly §4.

docs.title: 10.2 Fourier Series → Convolutional Neural Networks
docs.text:
A 1D CNN layer with filter \(w\) computes: $\((w * f)(x) = \int w(x-y)f(y),dy\)$

In frequency space (Fourier domain), convolution becomes multiplication: $\(\widehat{w*f}(\xi) = \hat{w}(\xi)\cdot\hat{f}(\xi)\)$

Computing \(\hat{f}(\xi) = \int f(x)e^{-2\pi i\xi x},dx\) reduces — via Euler's formula \(e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta+i\sin\theta\) — to exactly the integrals \(\int f(x)\cos(2\pi\xi x),dx\) and \(\int f(x)\sin(2\pi\xi x),dx\) from this chapter.

The FFT computes these at all frequencies simultaneously in \(O(n\log n)\), but the integrals themselves — and why they converge, why they are well-defined, why orthogonality holds — are the trig integrals of §7.

docs.title: 10.3 Positional Encodings — Transformers
docs.text:
The positional encoding in the original Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017):

\[PE(pos, 2i) = \sin!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right), \quad PE(pos, 2i+1) = \cos!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right)\]

The key property needed: for any fixed offset \(k\), \(PE(pos+k)\) is a linear function of \(PE(pos)\). This follows from the addition formula:

\[\sin(a+b) = \sin a\cos b+\cos a\sin b, \quad \cos(a+b) = \cos a\cos b - \sin a\sin b\]

These addition formulas — which are algebraic consequences of the product-to-sum identities (Q1)–(Q3) — are exactly why sine and cosine were chosen. Any relative positional relationship can be expressed as a matrix multiplication in embedding space.

docs.title: 10.4 Activation Function Analysis
docs.text:
The Fourier spectrum of activation functions determines which frequencies a neural network can represent at a given layer.

For a ReLU network, \(\text{ReLU}(x) = \max(0,x)\). Its Fourier coefficients on \([-\pi,\pi]\):

\[b_n = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\text{ReLU}(x)\sin nx,dx = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{\pi}x\sin nx,dx\]

This is IBP + trig integrals. The result determines the spectral bias of ReLU networks — they preferentially learn low-frequency components first (Rahaman et al., 2019, NeurIPS). This is a fundamental limitation explaining why neural networks generalise in the way they do.

Similarly, for \(\tanh(x)\): $\(a_n = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\tanh(x)\cos nx,dx\)$

The decay rate of these coefficients governs how well depth-\(L\) networks approximate smooth functions — tying trig integrals to universal approximation theory.

docs.title: 10.5 Signal Processing in Audio/Speech Models
docs.text:
Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs), used as features in almost every pre-deep-learning speech recognition system (and as baselines today):

\[c_n = \sqrt{\frac{2}{N}}\sum_{k=1}^N\log S_k\cos!\left[\frac{\pi n(k-1/2)}{N}\right]\]

This is a discrete cosine transform (DCT) — the discretisation of \(\int f(x)\cos(n\pi x/L),dx\), one of the central integrals of this chapter.

In Whisper (OpenAI, 2022) and wav2vec (Meta), the front-end computes a log-mel spectrogram, which involves:

  1. STFT → \(\int f(t)e^{-i\omega t},dt\) — trig integrals at every frequency
  2. Mel filterbank (weighted sums of spectral energy)
  3. Log compression

All three steps have trig integrals at their analytic foundation.

docs.title: 10.6 Normalisation Constants in Circular Distributions
docs.text:
Von Mises distribution (the "normal distribution on the circle") used in directional statistics and in modelling protein backbone angles for AlphaFold:

\[p(\theta;\mu,\kappa) = \frac{e^{\kappa\cos(\theta-\mu)}}{2\pi I_0(\kappa)}\]

where \(I_0(\kappa) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}e^{\kappa\cos\theta},d\theta\) is the modified Bessel function of order 0.

Computing \(I_0(\kappa)\) analytically requires the series expansion: $\(e^{\kappa\cos\theta} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{(\kappa\cos\theta)^n}{n!}\)$

and then \(\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^n\theta,d\theta\) — the even-power cosine integrals from §2, Case B.

This integral is at the heart of AlphaFold's learned distributions over torsion angles in protein structure prediction.

docs.title: §11 · Non-Obvious Worked Examples for Exam Practice
docs.text:
Example 14: \(\displaystyle\int\frac{\sin^3 x}{\cos^{3/2}x},dx\)

Write as \(\int\sin^3 x\cos^{-3/2}x,dx\). \(m=3\) (odd). Factor \(\sin x\):

\[= \int(1-\cos^2 x)\cos^{-3/2}x\sin x,dx\]

Let \(u=\cos x\):

\[= -\int(1-u^2)u^{-3/2},du = -\int(u^{-3/2}-u^{1/2}),du = 2u^{-1/2}+\frac{2u^{3/2}}{3}+C\] \[= \frac{2}{\sqrt{\cos x}}+\frac{2\cos^{3/2}x}{3}+C\]

Example 15: \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\sin^4 x\cos^2 x,dx\)

Both even. Use \(\sin^4 x\cos^2 x = (\sin x\cos x)^2\sin^2 x = \frac{\sin^2 2x}{4}\cdot\frac{1-\cos 2x}{2}\):

\[= \frac{1}{8}\int_0^{\pi}\sin^2 2x(1-\cos 2x),dx = \frac{1}{8}\int_0^\pi\sin^2 2x,dx - \frac{1}{8}\int_0^\pi\sin^2 2x\cos 2x,dx\]

First: \(\int_0^\pi\frac{1-\cos 4x}{2},dx = \pi/2\).

Second: let \(u=\sin 2x\), \(du=2\cos 2x,dx\); \(u(0)=u(\pi)=0\), so \(= 0\).

\[= \frac{1}{8}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2} - 0 = \frac{\pi}{16}\]

Example 16: \(\displaystyle\int\frac{\cos x - \sin x}{\cos x+\sin x},dx\)

Observe the numerator is \((\cos x+\sin x)'\) (up to sign — actually \((\sin x+\cos x)' = \cos x-\sin x\)). This is a \(u\)-sub in disguise:

Let \(u = \cos x+\sin x\), \(du = (-\sin x+\cos x),dx = (\cos x-\sin x),dx\):

\[= \int\frac{du}{u} = \ln|\cos x+\sin x|+C\]

Example 17 (MIT 18.02 style): \(\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}|\sin x|,dx\)

\(|\sin x|\) is non-negative. Split at \(\pi\) (where \(\sin x\) changes sign):

\[= \int_0^\pi\sin x,dx + \int_\pi^{2\pi}(-\sin x),dx = [-\cos x]_0^\pi + [\cos x]_\pi^{2\pi}\] \[= (1+1)+(1+1) = 4\]

docs.title: §12 · Common Mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake 1 — Applying the wrong case. Seeing \(\int\sin^4 x\cos^3 x,dx\) and treating it as "both even" because you notice \(4\) first. Check both exponents: \(\cos\) has exponent \(3\) (odd). Factor from \(\cos\), use \(u=\sin x\).

Mistake 2 — Forgetting the Jacobian in substitution. When \(u=\tan x\), \(du=\sec^2 x,dx\). You must have exactly \(\sec^2 x,dx\) leftover after factoring, or the substitution doesn't close.

Mistake 3 — Half-angle with wrong sign. \(\sin^2 x = \frac{1-\cos 2x}{2}\), \(\cos^2 x = \frac{1+\cos 2x}{2}\). The minus sign is for \(\sin\), plus for \(\cos\). Mixing these up gives answers off by \(x/2\).

Mistake 4 — Not simplifying \(\sin^2 x\cos^2 x\) first. This equals \(\frac{1}{4}\sin^2 2x\), which reduces the work dramatically. Students who blindly apply (H1) and (H2) separately get a messier path to the same answer.

Mistake 5 — Cyclic reduction with wrong signs in \(\tan^n\). The reduction \(\int\tan^n x = \frac{\tan^{n-1}x}{n-1}-\int\tan^{n-2}x\) has a minus sign between the two integrals. This is because \(\tan^2 x = \sec^2 x-1\), and the \(-1\) term gives \(-\int\tan^{n-2}x\).

docs.title: Trigonometric Substitution
docs.text:
A professor's personal notebook · Stewart §7.3 · MIT 18.02

Personal note: Trigonometric substitution is geometry in disguise. Every one of the three cases is a right triangle — you are literally naming the sides of a triangle and using the Pythagorean theorem to collapse a square root into a single trig function. Once you draw the triangle, the algebra becomes inevitable. The student who skips the triangle drawing is the student who makes sign errors and forgets to back-substitute. Draw the triangle. Always.

docs.title: §1 · The Core Idea — Why Trig Substitution Works
docs.text:
We want to integrate expressions involving \(\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}\), \(\sqrt{a^2 + x^2}\), or \(\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}\).

These square roots resist every technique seen so far — they are not derivatives of simple functions, and \(u\)-substitution leaves the radical intact.

The key insight: the Pythagorean theorem eliminates square roots of quadratics. Specifically:

\[1 - \sin^2\theta = \cos^2\theta \implies \sqrt{a^2 - a^2\sin^2\theta} = a\cos\theta\] \[1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta \implies \sqrt{a^2 + a^2\tan^2\theta} = a\sec\theta\] \[\sec^2\theta - 1 = \tan^2\theta \implies \sqrt{a^2\sec^2\theta - a^2} = a\tan\theta\]

We introduce \(x = a\cdot(\text{trig function of }\theta)\) to force the radicand into a perfect square.

This is the substitution \(u = g(\theta)\) running in reverse: we substitute \(x\) as a function of \(\theta\), integrate in \(\theta\), then back-substitute to express the answer in \(x\). The triangle is the back-substitution machine.

docs.title: §2 · The Three Cases — Substitution Table
docs.text:
Radical form Substitution Range Identity used Simplified radical \(\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}\) \(x = a\sin\theta\) \(-\dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) \(1-\sin^2\theta = \cos^2\theta\) \(a\cos\theta\) \(\sqrt{a^2 + x^2}\) \(x = a\tan\theta\) \(-\dfrac{\pi}{2} < \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) \(1+\tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta\) \(a\sec\theta\) \(\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}\) \(x = a\sec\theta\) \(0 \leq \theta < \dfrac{\pi}{2}\) or \(\pi \leq \theta < \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\) \(\sec^2\theta-1 = \tan^2\theta\) \(a\tan\theta\)

Why these specific ranges?

For \(x = a\sin\theta\): we need \(\cos\theta \geq 0\) so that \(\sqrt{a^2-x^2} = a\cos\theta\) (not \(-a\cos\theta\)). This holds on \([-\pi/2, \pi/2]\).

For \(x = a\tan\theta\): we need \(\sec\theta > 0\), which holds on \((-\pi/2, \pi/2)\).

For \(x = a\sec\theta\): \(\tan\theta \geq 0\) on \([0, \pi/2)\); if \(x < -a\), use \([\pi, 3\pi/2)\).

The range restriction is not bureaucracy — it ensures the substitution is a bijection (invertible) on that domain, which is required for \(u\)-substitution to be valid. Ignoring the range leads to subtle sign errors in back-substitution.

docs.title: §3 · The Reference Triangles
docs.text: Draw these triangles before doing any algebra. They encode all back-substitution automatically.

docs.title: Case 1: \(x = a\sin\theta\)
docs.text:
hypotenuse = a
       /|
      / |
     /  |  opposite = x
    /   |
   / θ  |
  /_____|
adjacent = √(a²-x²)
\[\sin\theta = \frac{x}{a}, \quad \cos\theta = \frac{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}{a}, \quad \tan\theta = \frac{x}{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}\]

docs.title: Case 2: \(x = a\tan\theta\)
docs.text:
hypotenuse = √(a²+x²)
       /|
      / |
     /  |  opposite = x
    /   |
   / θ  |
  /_____|
adjacent = a
\[\sin\theta = \frac{x}{\sqrt{a^2+x^2}}, \quad \cos\theta = \frac{a}{\sqrt{a^2+x^2}}, \quad \tan\theta = \frac{x}{a}\]

docs.title: Case 3: \(x = a\sec\theta\)
docs.text:
hypotenuse = x
       /|
      / |
     /  |  opposite = √(x²-a²)
    /   |
   / θ  |
  /_____|
adjacent = a
\[\sin\theta = \frac{\sqrt{x^2-a^2}}{x}, \quad \cos\theta = \frac{a}{x}, \quad \tan\theta = \frac{\sqrt{x^2-a^2}}{a}\]

Rule: Label the triangle with the two sides you know from the substitution. The third side follows from the Pythagorean theorem. All trig ratios are then read directly from the triangle — no algebra required.

docs.title: Worked Example 1: \(\displaystyle\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{4-x^2}}\) (recovering arcsin)
docs.text:
Let \(x = 2\sin\theta\), \(dx = 2\cos\theta,d\theta\), \(\sqrt{4-x^2} = 2\cos\theta\).

\[\int\frac{2\cos\theta,d\theta}{2\cos\theta} = \int d\theta = \theta + C\]

Back-substitute from triangle: \(\sin\theta = x/2\), so \(\theta = \arcsin(x/2)\).

\[= \arcsin\frac{x}{2} + C\]

This recovers the arcsin formula. Trig sub is the proof that formula is correct.

docs.title: Worked Example 2: \(\displaystyle\int\sqrt{9-x^2},dx\)
docs.text:
Let \(x = 3\sin\theta\), \(dx = 3\cos\theta,d\theta\), \(\sqrt{9-x^2} = 3\cos\theta\).

\[= \int 3\cos\theta \cdot 3\cos\theta,d\theta = 9\int\cos^2\theta,d\theta = 9\int\frac{1+\cos 2\theta}{2},d\theta\] \[= \frac{9}{2}\left(\theta + \frac{\sin 2\theta}{2}\right) + C = \frac{9}{2}\theta + \frac{9\sin 2\theta}{4} + C\]

Now \(\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta\). From triangle: \(\sin\theta = x/3\), \(\cos\theta = \sqrt{9-x^2}/3\).

\[\sin 2\theta = 2\cdot\frac{x}{3}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{9-x^2}}{3} = \frac{2x\sqrt{9-x^2}}{9}\] \[= \frac{9}{2}\arcsin\frac{x}{3} + \frac{9}{4}\cdot\frac{2x\sqrt{9-x^2}}{9} + C = \boxed{\frac{9}{2}\arcsin\frac{x}{3} + \frac{x\sqrt{9-x^2}}{2} + C}\]

Geometric interpretation: \(\int_{-3}^3\sqrt{9-x^2},dx = 9\pi/2\) is the area of a semicircle of radius 3. ✓ (since \(\pi r^2/2 = 9\pi/2\).)

docs.title: Worked Example 3: \(\displaystyle\int\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{9-x^2}},dx\)
docs.text:
Let \(x = 3\sin\theta\), \(dx = 3\cos\theta,d\theta\), \(\sqrt{9-x^2} = 3\cos\theta\), \(x^2 = 9\sin^2\theta\).

\[= \int\frac{9\sin^2\theta}{3\cos\theta}\cdot 3\cos\theta,d\theta = 9\int\sin^2\theta,d\theta = \frac{9}{2}\int(1-\cos 2\theta),d\theta\] \[= \frac{9}{2}\left(\theta - \frac{\sin 2\theta}{2}\right) + C = \frac{9}{2}\theta - \frac{9\sin 2\theta}{4} + C\]

From triangle: \(\theta = \arcsin(x/3)\), \(\sin 2\theta = 2x\sqrt{9-x^2}/9\).

\[= \boxed{\frac{9}{2}\arcsin\frac{x}{3} - \frac{x\sqrt{9-x^2}}{2} + C}\]

docs.title: Worked Example 4 (definite): \(\displaystyle\int_0^{3/2}\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{9-x^2}},dx\)
docs.text:
Method 1 — back-substitute, then apply limits. Use the antiderivative from Example 3: $\(\left[\frac{9}{2}\arcsin\frac{x}{3} - \frac{x\sqrt{9-x^2}}{2}\right]_0^{3/2}\)$ $\(= \frac{9}{2}\arcsin\frac{1}{2} - \frac{(3/2)\sqrt{9-9/4}}{2} - 0 = \frac{9}{2}\cdot\frac{\pi}{6} - \frac{(3/2)(3\sqrt{3}/2)}{2} = \frac{3\pi}{4} - \frac{9\sqrt{3}}{8}\)$

Method 2 — change limits to \(\theta\). When \(x=0\): \(\sin\theta=0\), so \(\theta=0\). When \(x=3/2\): \(\sin\theta=1/2\), so \(\theta=\pi/6\).

\[9\int_0^{\pi/6}\sin^2\theta,d\theta = \frac{9}{2}\left[\theta-\frac{\sin 2\theta}{2}\right]_0^{\pi/6} = \frac{9}{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{6}-\frac{\sin(\pi/3)}{2}\right) = \frac{9}{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{6}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\right) = \frac{3\pi}{4}-\frac{9\sqrt{3}}{8}\]

Both methods agree. ✓

docs.title: Worked Example 5: \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+4}}\)
docs.text:
Let \(x = 2\tan\theta\), \(dx = 2\sec^2\theta,d\theta\), \(\sqrt{x^2+4} = 2\sec\theta\).

\[= \int\frac{2\sec^2\theta,d\theta}{2\sec\theta} = \int\sec\theta,d\theta = \ln|\sec\theta+\tan\theta|+C\]

From triangle: \(\tan\theta = x/2\), \(\sec\theta = \sqrt{x^2+4}/2\).

\[= \ln\left|\frac{\sqrt{x^2+4}}{2}+\frac{x}{2}\right|+C = \ln\left|x+\sqrt{x^2+4}\right|+C\]

(absorbed the \(\ln(1/2)\) into \(C\).)

\[= \boxed{\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+4}\right)+C}\]

This equals \(\sinh^{-1}(x/2)+C\) — connecting to the inverse hyperbolic forms.

docs.title: Worked Example 6: \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+4)^{3/2}}\)
docs.text:
Let \(x = 2\tan\theta\), \(dx = 2\sec^2\theta,d\theta\), \((x^2+4)^{3/2} = 8\sec^3\theta\).

\[= \int\frac{2\sec^2\theta,d\theta}{8\sec^3\theta} = \frac{1}{4}\int\frac{d\theta}{\sec\theta} = \frac{1}{4}\int\cos\theta,d\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{4}+C\]

From triangle: \(\sin\theta = x/\sqrt{x^2+4}\).

\[= \boxed{\frac{x}{4\sqrt{x^2+4}}+C}\]

Verification: \(\frac{d}{dx}\left[\frac{x}{4\sqrt{x^2+4}}\right] = \frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{x^2+4}-x\cdot\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+4}}}{x^2+4} = \frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{4}{(x^2+4)^{3/2}} = \frac{1}{(x^2+4)^{3/2}}\) ✓

docs.title: Worked Example 7: \(\displaystyle\int x^3\sqrt{x^2+9},dx\)
docs.text:
Note: Before jumping to trig sub, check if \(u\)-sub works. Let \(u = x^2+9\), \(du = 2x,dx\), \(x^2 = u-9\):

\[= \int(u-9)\sqrt{u}\cdot\frac{du}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\int(u^{3/2}-9u^{1/2}),du = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{2u^{5/2}}{5}-\frac{18u^{3/2}}{3}\right)+C\] \[= \frac{(x^2+9)^{5/2}}{5}-3(x^2+9)^{3/2}+C\]

Lesson: Trig sub is not always the best tool even when a radical is present. When \(x^{\text{odd}}\cdot\sqrt{x^2+a^2}\) appears, try \(u = x^2+a^2\) first — it is often cleaner.

docs.title: Worked Example 8: \(\displaystyle\int\sqrt{x^2+4},dx\)
docs.text:
Let \(x=2\tan\theta\), \(dx=2\sec^2\theta,d\theta\), \(\sqrt{x^2+4}=2\sec\theta\).

\[= \int 2\sec\theta\cdot 2\sec^2\theta,d\theta = 4\int\sec^3\theta,d\theta\]

Using the result from the Trigonometric Integrals note:

\[= 4\cdot\frac{\sec\theta\tan\theta+\ln|\sec\theta+\tan\theta|}{2}+C = 2\sec\theta\tan\theta+2\ln|\sec\theta+\tan\theta|+C\]

From triangle: \(\sec\theta = \sqrt{x^2+4}/2\), \(\tan\theta = x/2\).

\[= 2\cdot\frac{\sqrt{x^2+4}}{2}\cdot\frac{x}{2}+2\ln\left|\frac{\sqrt{x^2+4}}{2}+\frac{x}{2}\right|+C\] \[= \boxed{\frac{x\sqrt{x^2+4}}{2}+2\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+4}\right)+C}\]

(absorbed \(\ln(1/2)\) into \(C\).)

docs.title: §6 · Case 3 — \(\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}\): Substitution \(x = a\sec\theta\)
docs.text: This case requires the most care because \(|x| \geq a\), and the domain splits into \(x \geq a\) and \(x \leq -a\).

docs.title: Worked Example 9: \(\displaystyle\int\frac{\sqrt{x^2-9}}{x},dx\)
docs.text:
Let \(x = 3\sec\theta\), \(dx = 3\sec\theta\tan\theta,d\theta\), \(\sqrt{x^2-9} = 3\tan\theta\).

\[= \int\frac{3\tan\theta}{3\sec\theta}\cdot 3\sec\theta\tan\theta,d\theta = 3\int\tan^2\theta,d\theta = 3\int(\sec^2\theta-1),d\theta\] \[= 3(\tan\theta - \theta)+C\]

From triangle: \(\tan\theta = \sqrt{x^2-9}/3\), \(\sec\theta = x/3\) so \(\theta = \text{arcsec}(x/3)\).

\[= \boxed{\sqrt{x^2-9} - 3,\text{arcsec}\frac{x}{3}+C}\]

docs.title: Worked Example 10: \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x^2\sqrt{x^2-25}}\)
docs.text:
Let \(x = 5\sec\theta\), \(dx = 5\sec\theta\tan\theta,d\theta\), \(\sqrt{x^2-25}=5\tan\theta\), \(x^2=25\sec^2\theta\).

\[= \int\frac{5\sec\theta\tan\theta,d\theta}{25\sec^2\theta\cdot 5\tan\theta} = \frac{1}{25}\int\frac{d\theta}{\sec\theta} = \frac{1}{25}\int\cos\theta,d\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{25}+C\]

From triangle: \(\sin\theta = \sqrt{x^2-25}/x\).

\[= \boxed{\frac{\sqrt{x^2-25}}{25x}+C}\]

docs.title: §7 · Completing the Square — Extending Trig Sub to General Quadratics
docs.text:
When the expression under the radical is \(ax^2+bx+c\) (with \(a\neq 1\) or \(b\neq 0\)), complete the square first to reduce to one of the three standard forms.

Algorithm: $\(ax^2+bx+c = a\left[\left(x+\frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 + \frac{c}{a}-\frac{b^2}{4a^2}\right]\)$

Let \(u = x + b/(2a)\), which shifts the variable. Then the form under the radical becomes \(A(u^2\pm k^2)\) or \(A(k^2-u^2)\), and the appropriate substitution applies.

docs.title: Worked Example 11: \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2-6x+13}}\)
docs.text:
Complete the square: \(x^2-6x+13 = (x-3)^2+4\).

Let \(u = x-3\), \(du = dx\):

\[= \int\frac{du}{\sqrt{u^2+4}}\]

This is Example 5 with \(a=2\)! From that result:

\[= \ln\left|u+\sqrt{u^2+4}\right|+C = \boxed{\ln\left|(x-3)+\sqrt{x^2-6x+13}\right|+C}\]

docs.title: Worked Example 12: \(\displaystyle\int\frac{2x+1}{\sqrt{-x^2+4x+5}},dx\)
docs.text:
Complete the square: \(-x^2+4x+5 = -(x^2-4x)+5 = -[(x-2)^2-4]+5 = 9-(x-2)^2\).

Let \(u = x-2\), \(x = u+2\), \(dx = du\), \(2x+1 = 2(u+2)+1 = 2u+5\):

\[= \int\frac{2u+5}{\sqrt{9-u^2}},du = \int\frac{2u}{\sqrt{9-u^2}},du + 5\int\frac{du}{\sqrt{9-u^2}}\]

First integral: let \(w = 9-u^2\), \(dw = -2u,du\): $\(\int\frac{2u}{\sqrt{9-u^2}},du = -\int w^{-1/2},dw = -2\sqrt{w} = -2\sqrt{9-u^2}\)$

Second integral: standard form #22: $\(5\int\frac{du}{\sqrt{9-u^2}} = 5\arcsin\frac{u}{3}\)$

\[= -2\sqrt{9-(x-2)^2}+5\arcsin\frac{x-2}{3}+C = \boxed{-2\sqrt{-x^2+4x+5}+5\arcsin\frac{x-2}{3}+C}\]

docs.title: Worked Example 13 (the hardest type): \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{(5+4x-x^2)^{3/2}}\)
docs.text:
Complete the square: \(5+4x-x^2 = -(x^2-4x-5) = -[(x-2)^2-9] = 9-(x-2)^2\).

So \((5+4x-x^2)^{3/2} = (9-(x-2)^2)^{3/2}\).

Let \(u=x-2\):

\[= \int\frac{du}{(9-u^2)^{3/2}}\]

Now \(u = 3\sin\theta\), \(du = 3\cos\theta,d\theta\), \((9-u^2)^{3/2} = 27\cos^3\theta\):

\[= \int\frac{3\cos\theta,d\theta}{27\cos^3\theta} = \frac{1}{9}\int\sec^2\theta,d\theta = \frac{\tan\theta}{9}+C\]

From triangle: \(\sin\theta = u/3\), so \(\cos\theta = \sqrt{9-u^2}/3\), \(\tan\theta = u/\sqrt{9-u^2}\).

\[= \frac{u}{9\sqrt{9-u^2}}+C = \boxed{\frac{x-2}{9\sqrt{5+4x-x^2}}+C}\]

docs.title: §8 · Visualisation — The Three Triangles Side by Side
docs.text:
CASE 1: x = a sinθ          CASE 2: x = a tanθ         CASE 3: x = a secθ
  √(a²−x²) is adjacent        a is adjacent               a is adjacent

        a                    √(a²+x²)                        x
       /|                       /|                           /|
      / |                      / |                          / |
     /  | x                   /  | x                       /  | √(x²−a²)
    /   |                    /   |                         /   |
   / θ  |                   / θ  |                        / θ  |
  /_____|                  /_____|                        /_____|
  √(a²−x²)                    a                              a

sinθ = x/a               tanθ = x/a               secθ = x/a
cosθ = √(a²−x²)/a        secθ = √(a²+x²)/a        tanθ = √(x²−a²)/a

Mnemonic for which case:

  • \(a^2 - x^2\): the \(a\) is the hypotenuse → use \(\sin\) (opposite/hypotenuse \(= x/a\))
  • \(a^2 + x^2\): the \(\sqrt{\phantom{x}}\) is the hypotenuse → use \(\tan\) (opposite/adjacent \(= x/a\))
  • \(x^2 - a^2\): \(x\) is the hypotenuse → use \(\sec\) (hypotenuse/adjacent \(= x/a\))

docs.title: §9 · Strategy — When to Use Trig Sub vs. Other Methods
docs.text:
Expression involves √(a²−x²), √(a²+x²), or √(x²−a²)?
│
├─ Is there an odd power of x outside the radical?
│   Example: x³√(x²+4), x√(9−x²)
│   → Try u = (expression under radical) FIRST
│      If u-sub closes → done. If not → trig sub.
│
├─ Is it purely the radical alone, or radical with even powers?
│   Example: ∫√(a²−x²)dx, ∫x²/√(a²−x²)dx
│   → Trig sub directly
│
├─ Is the quadratic not in standard form?
│   Example: √(x²−6x+13), √(5+4x−x²)
│   → Complete the square first → standard form → trig sub
│
└─ Is the integrand rational in √(a²±x²) after substitution?
    Example: ∫dx/(x²√(x²−25))
    → Trig sub → result is trig integral (usually just ∫cosθ or ∫sinθ)

The five-step procedure:

  1. Identify the radical form and the value of \(a\).
  2. Make the substitution from the table in §2.
  3. Draw the triangle and label all three sides.
  4. Convert entirely to \(\theta\): radical, \(dx\), any remaining \(x\) terms.
  5. Integrate in \(\theta\), then back-substitute using the triangle.

docs.title: §10 · Connection to Inverse Hyperbolic Functions
docs.text:
The results of trig sub are often rewritable using inverse hyperbolic functions (which arise naturally from the \(x = a\tan\theta\) and \(x = a\sec\theta\) substitutions):

\[\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}} = \ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+a^2}\right)+C = \sinh^{-1}\frac{x}{a}+C\] \[\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2-a^2}} = \ln\left|x+\sqrt{x^2-a^2}\right|+C = \cosh^{-1}\frac{x}{a}+C, \quad x>a\] \[\int\frac{dx}{a^2-x^2} = \frac{1}{a}\tanh^{-1}\frac{x}{a}+C = \frac{1}{2a}\ln\left|\frac{a+x}{a-x}\right|+C, \quad |x|<a\]

The equivalence \(\ln(x+\sqrt{x^2+a^2}) = \sinh^{-1}(x/a)\) follows from the definition \(\sinh^{-1}(t) = \ln(t+\sqrt{t^2+1})\). Both forms appear in tables; know that they are equal.

docs.title: Worked Example 14: \(\displaystyle\int\frac{\sqrt{4x^2-9}}{x^2},dx\), \(x > 3/2\)
docs.text:
Factor: \(\sqrt{4x^2-9} = \sqrt{4(x^2-9/4)} = 2\sqrt{x^2-(3/2)^2}\).

Let \(a = 3/2\), \(x = \frac{3}{2}\sec\theta\), \(dx = \frac{3}{2}\sec\theta\tan\theta,d\theta\), \(\sqrt{x^2-9/4} = \frac{3}{2}\tan\theta\).

\[= \int\frac{2\cdot\frac{3}{2}\tan\theta}{\frac{9}{4}\sec^2\theta}\cdot\frac{3}{2}\sec\theta\tan\theta,d\theta = \int\frac{3\tan\theta\cdot\frac{3}{2}\sec\theta\tan\theta}{\frac{9}{4}\sec^2\theta},d\theta = \int\frac{\frac{9}{2}\sec\theta\tan^2\theta}{\frac{9}{4}\sec^2\theta},d\theta\] \[= 2\int\frac{\tan^2\theta}{\sec\theta},d\theta = 2\int\sin\theta\tan\theta,d\theta = 2\int\frac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta},d\theta\] \[= 2\int\frac{1-\cos^2\theta}{\cos\theta},d\theta = 2\int(\sec\theta-\cos\theta),d\theta = 2\ln|\sec\theta+\tan\theta|-2\sin\theta+C\]

From triangle (\(x = \frac{3}{2}\sec\theta\)): \(\sec\theta = \frac{2x}{3}\), \(\tan\theta = \frac{\sqrt{4x^2-9}}{3}\), \(\sin\theta = \frac{\sqrt{4x^2-9}}{2x}\).

\[= \boxed{2\ln\left|\frac{2x}{3}+\frac{\sqrt{4x^2-9}}{3}\right|-\frac{\sqrt{4x^2-9}}{x}+C}\]

docs.title: Worked Example 15: \(\displaystyle\int_0^2\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{4-x^2}^3},dx\)
docs.text:
Let \(x = 2\sin\theta\). Limits: \(x=0\Rightarrow\theta=0\); \(x=2\Rightarrow\theta=\pi/2\).

\((4-x^2)^{3/2} = 8\cos^3\theta\), \(x^2 = 4\sin^2\theta\), \(dx = 2\cos\theta,d\theta\).

\[= \int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{4\sin^2\theta\cdot 2\cos\theta,d\theta}{8\cos^3\theta} = \int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta},d\theta = \int_0^{\pi/2}\tan^2\theta,d\theta\] \[= \int_0^{\pi/2}(\sec^2\theta-1),d\theta = [\tan\theta-\theta]_0^{\pi/2}\]

But \(\tan(\pi/2) = \infty\)! The integral diverges — this is an improper integral. Verify: near \(x=2\), \((4-x^2)^{3/2}\to 0\) faster than \(x^2\to 4\), so the integrand blows up. ✓

docs.title: 12.1 The Gaussian Integral — Foundation of All Probabilistic ML
docs.text:
The most important integral in machine learning is:

\[\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2},dx = \sqrt{\pi}\]

Its multivariable proof (MIT 18.02) uses polar coordinate substitution — which is trig sub in disguise. The key step:

\[\left(\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2},dx\right)^2 = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2},r,dr,d\theta\]

The substitution \(x = r\cos\theta\), \(y = r\sin\theta\) is trig substitution in 2D. Every normal distribution, every Gaussian process, every VAE, every diffusion model is normalised by this integral.

The generalisation to \(d\) dimensions:

\[\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{-|x|^2/(2\sigma^2)},dx = (2\pi\sigma^2)^{d/2}\]

is proved by \(d\) sequential trig substitutions (or one spherical coordinate substitution — the \(d\)-dimensional analogue).

docs.title: 12.2 Normalisation Constants in Kernel Methods
docs.text:
Gaussian RBF kernel: \(K(x,x') = e^{-|x-x'|^2/(2\sigma^2)}\)

The fact that this kernel is positive-definite (required for a valid SVM kernel) is proved via Bochner's theorem: \(K\) is the Fourier transform of \(p(\omega) = (2\pi\sigma^2)^{-d/2}e^{-\sigma^2|\omega|^2/2}\), which requires the integral

\[\hat{K}(\omega) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} K(x)e^{-i\omega^Tx},dx\]

This is a \(d\)-dimensional trig integral, evaluated by completing the square in the exponent and using the Gaussian integral result — whose proof is the polar trig substitution above.

docs.title: 12.3 Computing the Partition Function in Energy-Based Models
docs.text:
In statistical mechanics and energy-based models (EBMs), the normalisation constant (partition function) is:

\[Z = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{-E(x)/T},dx\]

For a quadratic energy \(E(x) = \frac{1}{2}x^T A x\) (multivariate Gaussian):

\[Z = \int e^{-\frac{1}{2}x^TAx},dx = \frac{(2\pi)^{d/2}}{\sqrt{\det A}}\]

This is proved by:

  1. Diagonalise \(A = Q\Lambda Q^T\) (change of variables \(u = Q^Tx\), Jacobian = 1)
  2. Each dimension separates: \(\prod_{i=1}^d \int e^{-\lambda_i u_i^2/2},du_i = \prod_i\sqrt{2\pi/\lambda_i}\)
  3. Each factor uses the Gaussian integral, proved via trig substitution in polar form

The result \(Z = (2\pi)^{d/2}/\sqrt{\det A}\) appears in every Gaussian process, every Bayesian linear regression, and every Laplace approximation in deep learning.

docs.title: 12.4 Arc Length and Geodesics in Latent Space
docs.text:
In variational autoencoders and Riemannian manifold learning, one computes arc lengths along curves in a learned latent space. The arc length of a parametric curve \(\gamma(t) = (x(t), y(t))\) is:

\[L = \int_a^b\sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2},dt\]

For the unit circle \(x = \cos t\), \(y = \sin t\): \(L = \int_0^{2\pi} 1,dt = 2\pi\) — trivial. But for an ellipse \(x = a\cos t\), \(y = b\sin t\):

\[L = \int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{a^2\sin^2 t + b^2\cos^2 t},dt\]

This is an elliptic integral — not expressible in closed form — but it is reduced to standard form via trig substitution. Geodesic distance in learned latent manifolds (used in disentangled representation learning) requires exactly this arc-length computation.

docs.title: 12.5 Attention Score Normalisation — The \(\sqrt{d_k}\) Factor
docs.text:
The scaled dot-product attention in Transformers:

\[\text{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax}!\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\]

The \(\sqrt{d_k}\) in the denominator is explained as follows. If \(q_i, k_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\) independently, then \(q_i \cdot k_j = \sum_{l=1}^{d_k} q_{il}k_{jl}\) has variance \(d_k\).

The standard deviation of \(q\cdot k\) is \(\sqrt{d_k}\), computed via:

\[\text{Var}\left[\sum_{l=1}^{d_k} q_l k_l\right] = \sum_{l=1}^{d_k}\text{Var}[q_l k_l] = d_k\]

where \(\text{Var}[q_l k_l] = \mathbb{E}[q_l^2 k_l^2] = \mathbb{E}[q_l^2]\mathbb{E}[k_l^2] = 1\) (computed using the Gaussian integral \(\int x^2 e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi},dx = 1\), which again uses the trig-based Gaussian integral at its core).

docs.title: 12.6 Normalising Flows — The Jacobian Determinant
docs.text:
In normalising flows (RealNVP, Glow, Neural Spline Flows), we learn an invertible map \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^d\) and the log-likelihood is:

\[\log p_X(x) = \log p_Z(f(x)) + \log\left|\det\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right|\]

For radial flows \(f(z) = z + \beta h(\alpha,r)(z-z_0)\) where \(r = |z-z_0|\), computing \(\det\partial f/\partial z\) requires evaluating:

\[\int_S h(\alpha, r),dS\]

over a sphere — a surface integral evaluated via spherical trig substitution. The residual stream geometry of transformer circuits is analysed using exactly these integrals.

docs.title: §13 · Common Mistakes
docs.text:
Mistake 1 — Wrong case. Seeing \(\sqrt{x^2+9}\) and substituting \(x = 3\sin\theta\) (Case 1) instead of \(x = 3\tan\theta\) (Case 2). The sine substitution gives \(\sqrt{9-9\sin^2\theta+9} = \sqrt{18-9\sin^2\theta}\), which is not simpler. Always match the form to the table.

Mistake 2 — Forgetting \(dx\). Writing \(x = a\sin\theta\) but forgetting to replace \(dx = a\cos\theta,d\theta\). This is the most common error — the \(d\theta\) substitution must be applied to \(dx\) as well.

Mistake 3 — Sign errors from the range. \(\sqrt{a^2-a^2\sin^2\theta} = a|\cos\theta|\). On \([-\pi/2,\pi/2]\), \(\cos\theta \geq 0\), so \(|\cos\theta| = \cos\theta\). If you accidentally use \(\theta\) outside this range, you get a sign flip.

Mistake 4 — Not completing the square first. Attempting trig sub on \(\sqrt{x^2-4x+8}\) directly. The correct first step is completing the square: \(x^2-4x+8=(x-2)^2+4\), then substituting \(u=x-2\).

Mistake 5 — Incorrect back-substitution. Writing \(\sin\theta = x/a\) then guessing \(\cos\theta = \sqrt{1-x^2/a^2}\) from memory, with an error in the sign or the structure. Draw the triangle every time — it prevents all back-substitution errors.

Mistake 6 — Using trig sub when \(u\)-sub suffices. \(\int x\sqrt{a^2-x^2},dx\): let \(u=a^2-x^2\), \(du=-2x,dx\). This gives \(-\frac{1}{2}\int u^{1/2},du = -\frac{u^{3/2}}{3}+C = -\frac{(a^2-x^2)^{3/2}}{3}+C\). No trig needed.
