docs.title: Prelude — Probability IS Integration
docs.text:
There is a profound unity lurking here:

Every quantity in continuous probability theory is an integral.

Probability itself is an integral. Expected value is an integral. Variance is an integral. Information entropy is an integral. The KL divergence is an integral. The evidence lower bound (ELBO) in VAEs is an integral. The likelihood in a Gaussian process is an integral of an integral.

This is not a coincidence — it is the Kolmogorov foundation: probability is a measure, and computing probabilities of continuous events is Lebesgue integration. For us, working at the level of Riemann integration, the statement is:

\[\boxed{P(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f_X(x), dx}\]

Every formula in this note is a specialization or composition of this single idea.

The Dictionary:

Probability concept Integration concept Probability of an event Area under the PDF Expected value Weighted area (\(\int x, f(x), dx\)) Variance Second central moment integral Independence Product structure of the joint PDF Conditioning Slice of the joint, renormalized Entropy \(-\int f \ln f, dx\) Generating functions Laplace/Fourier transform of the PDF

docs.title: 1. Probability Density Functions — The Central Definition
Definition (Rigorous)
docs.text:
A function \(f_X: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) is a probability density function (PDF) for a continuous random variable \(X\) if:

(i) Non-negativity: \(f_X(x) \ge 0\) for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\)

(ii) Normalization: $\(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_X(x), dx = 1\)$

(iii) Probability via integration: $\(P(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f_X(x), dx\)$

Critical remark: \(f_X(x)\) is not a probability. It is a density — analogous to mass per unit length. The probability requires integrating over an interval. \(P(X = a) = \int_a^a f_X(x), dx = 0\) for any single point. This is conceptually sharp: continuous random variables have probability zero of taking any exact value.

docs.title: Example 1.1 — Verifying a PDF
docs.text:
Claim: \(f(x) = ce^{-3x}\) for \(x \ge 0\) (and \(0\) otherwise) is a valid PDF for some \(c\). Find \(c\).

Normalization condition: $\(\int_0^\infty ce^{-3x}, dx = 1 \implies c\left[-\frac{e^{-3x}}{3}\right]_0^\infty = 1 \implies \frac{c}{3} = 1 \implies \boxed{c = 3}\)$

Verify: \(f(x) = 3e^{-3x}\) for \(x \ge 0\). This is the Exponential distribution with parameter \(\lambda = 3\).

docs.title: Example 1.2 — Computing a Probability
docs.text:
Setup: \(f_X(x) = \frac{3}{8}x^2\) for \(0 \le x \le 2\). Find \(P(1 \le X \le 2)\).

Step 1 — Verify normalization: $\(\int_0^2 \frac{3}{8}x^2, dx = \frac{3}{8} \cdot \frac{x^3}{3}\Bigg|_0^2 = \frac{1}{8}(8) = 1 \quad \checkmark\)$

Step 2 — Compute: $\(P(1 \le X \le 2) = \int_1^2 \frac{3}{8}x^2, dx = \frac{3}{8} \cdot \frac{x^3}{3}\Bigg|_1^2 = \frac{1}{8}(8-1) = \boxed{\frac{7}{8}}\)$

docs.title: Definition & Fundamental Theorem Connection
docs.text:
\[\boxed{F_X(x) = P(X \le x) = \int_{-\infty}^x f_X(t), dt}\]

Properties (all derived from the integral):

  • \(F\) is non-decreasing (since \(f \ge 0\), adding more area cannot decrease \(F\))
  • \(\lim_{x\to-\infty} F(x) = 0\), \(\lim_{x\to\infty} F(x) = 1\)
  • \(F\) is right-continuous
  • \(P(a < X \le b) = F(b) - F(a)\) — this is the FTC for probability

FTC gives back the PDF: $\(f_X(x) = F_X'(x) \quad \text{(almost everywhere)}\)$

The CDF and PDF are a FTC pair. PDF is the derivative of CDF; CDF is the integral of PDF.

docs.title: Example 2.1 — CDF of a Power Distribution
docs.text:
Setup: \(f(x) = 3x^2\) for \(0 \le x \le 1\).

\[F(x) = \int_0^x 3t^2, dt = t^3\Big|_0^x = x^3, \quad 0 \le x \le 1\]

Find the median \(m\): \(F(m) = 0.5 \implies m^3 = 0.5 \implies m = (0.5)^{1/3} \approx 0.794\).

Find the 90th percentile \(p_{0.9}\): \(p_{0.9}^3 = 0.9 \implies p_{0.9} = 0.9^{1/3} \approx 0.965\).

Connection to §9 (Survival/Biology note): The survival function \(S(x) = 1 - F(x) = 1 - x^3\) gives the probability of exceeding \(x\). Every concept in survival analysis is the CDF or its complement, computed via integration.

docs.title: Example 2.2 — CDF from a Piecewise PDF
docs.text:
Setup: $\(f(x) = \begin{cases} x & 0 \le x \le 1 \ 2-x & 1 < x \le 2 \ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\)$

(Triangular distribution — note: \(\int_0^1 x, dx + \int_1^2 (2-x), dx = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} = 1\) ✓)

CDF for \(0 \le x \le 1\): $\(F(x) = \int_0^x t, dt = \frac{x^2}{2}\)$

CDF for \(1 < x \le 2\): $\(F(x) = F(1) + \int_1^x (2-t), dt = \frac{1}{2} + \left[2t - \frac{t^2}{2}\right]_1^x = \frac{1}{2} + \left(2x - \frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{3}{2}\right) = 2x - \frac{x^2}{2} - 1\)$

Check: \(F(2) = 4 - 2 - 1 = 1\). ✓

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a continuous random variable \(X\) with PDF \(f_X\):

\[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x, f_X(x), dx}\]

Existence: This integral must converge absolutely — i.e., \(\int_{-\infty}^\infty |x|, f_X(x), dx < \infty\). Some distributions (e.g., Cauchy) have no finite mean because this integral diverges.

Interpretation: \(\mathbb{E}[X]\) is the center of mass of the distribution — the balance point of the PDF curve. This is literally the same formula as the center of mass integral from the physics note, with \(f_X(x)\) playing the role of linear density \(\rho(x)\).

docs.title: Example 3.1 — Expected Value of Power Distribution
docs.text:
Setup: \(f(x) = (n+1)x^n\) for \(0 \le x \le 1\).

\[\mathbb{E}[X] = \int_0^1 x \cdot (n+1)x^n, dx = (n+1)\int_0^1 x^{n+1}, dx = (n+1) \cdot \frac{1}{n+2} = \boxed{\frac{n+1}{n+2}}\]

Sanity check: As \(n \to \infty\), the distribution concentrates near \(x = 1\), and \(\mathbb{E}[X] \to 1\). As \(n = 0\) (uniform), \(\mathbb{E}[X] = \frac{1}{2}\). Both are correct. ✓

docs.title: Example 3.2 — Cauchy Distribution Has No Mean
docs.text:
PDF: \(f(x) = \frac{1}{\pi(1+x^2)}\), \(x \in \mathbb{R}\).

Attempt to compute \(\mathbb{E}[X]\): $\(\int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{x}{\pi(1+x^2)}, dx = \frac{1}{\pi} \cdot \frac{1}{2}\ln(1+x^2)\Bigg|_{-\infty}^\infty\)$

This integral diverges (both tails diverge to \(\pm\infty\)). The Cauchy distribution has no finite expected value despite being symmetric about \(0\).

This is not a mere technicality. In finance, the Cauchy distribution models fat-tailed returns where "the average return" literally does not exist — the empirical mean of samples from a Cauchy distribution never converges, no matter how much data you collect. The divergence of the integral is the mathematics of this phenomenon.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
\(n\)-th moment about the origin: $\(\mu_n' = \mathbb{E}[X^n] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x^n, f_X(x), dx\)$

\(n\)-th central moment: $\(\mu_n = \mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^n] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty (x-\mu)^n, f_X(x), dx\)$

Variance (\(n=2\)): $\(\boxed{\text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2] = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2}\)$

Proof of the shortcut formula: $\(\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2] = \int (x-\mu)^2 f(x), dx = \int (x^2 - 2\mu x + \mu^2)f(x), dx\)$ $\(= \mathbb{E}[X^2] - 2\mu \mathbb{E}[X] + \mu^2 = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - 2\mu^2 + \mu^2 = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - \mu^2 \quad \blacksquare\)$

Skewness (\(n=3\) central moment, normalized): \(\gamma_1 = \frac{\mu_3}{\sigma^3}\) — measures asymmetry.

Kurtosis (\(n=4\)): \(\gamma_2 = \frac{\mu_4}{\sigma^4} - 3\) — measures tail heaviness relative to Gaussian.

docs.title: Example 4.1 — Variance of Triangular Distribution
docs.text:
For the triangular distribution from Example 2.2 with PDF \(f(x) = x\) on \([0,1]\) and \(f(x) = 2-x\) on \([1,2]\):

\(\mathbb{E}[X]\) (by symmetry about \(x=1\)): \(\mathbb{E}[X] = 1\).

\(\mathbb{E}[X^2]\): $\(= \int_0^1 x^2 \cdot x, dx + \int_1^2 x^2(2-x), dx = \int_0^1 x^3, dx + \int_1^2 (2x^2 - x^3), dx\)$ $\(= \frac{1}{4} + \left[\frac{2x^3}{3} - \frac{x^4}{4}\right]_1^2 = \frac{1}{4} + \left(\frac{16}{3} - 4\right) - \left(\frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{4}\right)\)$ $\(= \frac{1}{4} + \frac{4}{3} - \frac{5}{12} = \frac{3 + 16 - 5}{12} = \frac{14}{12} = \frac{7}{6}\)$

\[\text{Var}(X) = \frac{7}{6} - 1^2 = \frac{1}{6}, \qquad \sigma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \approx 0.408 \quad \blacksquare\]

docs.title: Part II — The Great Distributions, Derived Rigorously
5. Uniform Distribution
docs.text:
PDF: \(f(x) = \frac{1}{b-a}\) for \(x \in [a,b]\).

Verification: \(\int_a^b \frac{1}{b-a}, dx = 1\). ✓

Mean: $\(\mathbb{E}[X] = \int_a^b \frac{x}{b-a}, dx = \frac{1}{b-a} \cdot \frac{b^2-a^2}{2} = \frac{(b-a)(b+a)}{2(b-a)} = \boxed{\frac{a+b}{2}}\)$

Variance: $\(\mathbb{E}[X^2] = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b x^2, dx = \frac{b^3-a^3}{3(b-a)} = \frac{a^2+ab+b^2}{3}\)$ $\(\text{Var}(X) = \frac{a^2+ab+b^2}{3} - \frac{(a+b)^2}{4} = \frac{4(a^2+ab+b^2) - 3(a+b)^2}{12} = \boxed{\frac{(b-a)^2}{12}}\)$

docs.title: 6. Exponential Distribution
docs.text:
PDF: \(f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}\) for \(x \ge 0\), \(\lambda > 0\).

Normalization: \(\int_0^\infty \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, dx = \lambda \cdot \frac{1}{\lambda} = 1\). ✓

Mean (integration by parts: \(u=x\), \(dv = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}dx\)): $\(\mathbb{E}[X] = \int_0^\infty x \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, dx = \left[-xe^{-\lambda x}\right]_0^\infty + \int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda x}, dx = 0 + \frac{1}{\lambda} = \boxed{\frac{1}{\lambda}}\)$

Second moment (two integrations by parts): $\(\mathbb{E}[X^2] = \int_0^\infty x^2 \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, dx = \frac{2}{\lambda^2}\)$

\[\text{Var}(X) = \frac{2}{\lambda^2} - \frac{1}{\lambda^2} = \boxed{\frac{1}{\lambda^2}}\]

Memoryless property (unique to exponential): $\(P(X > s+t \mid X > s) = P(X > t)\)$

Proof via integration: $\(P(X > s+t \mid X > s) = \frac{P(X > s+t)}{P(X > s)} = \frac{\int_{s+t}^\infty \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, dx}{\int_s^\infty \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, dx} = \frac{e^{-\lambda(s+t)}}{e^{-\lambda s}} = e^{-\lambda t} = P(X > t) \quad \blacksquare\)$

docs.title: 7. The Gaussian — Derived from First Principles
The Gaussian Integral: Full Proof
docs.text:
Claim: $\(\boxed{\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2}, dx = \sqrt{\pi}}\)$

Proof (MIT 18.02 polar coordinate method):

Let \(I = \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2}, dx\). Consider \(I^2\):

\[I^2 = \left(\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2}, dx\right)\left(\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-y^2}, dy\right) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-(x^2+y^2)}, dx, dy\]

Convert to polar: \(x = r\cos\theta\), \(y = r\sin\theta\), \(dA = r, dr, d\theta\):

\[I^2 = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2} r, dr, d\theta = 2\pi \int_0^\infty r e^{-r^2}, dr\]

Substitution \(u = r^2\), \(du = 2r, dr\):

\[= 2\pi \int_0^\infty \frac{1}{2} e^{-u}, du = 2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \pi\]

Therefore \(I = \sqrt{\pi}\). \(\blacksquare\)

Corollary: With substitution \(x = t/(\sigma\sqrt{2})\): $\(\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-t^2/(2\sigma^2)}, dt = \sigma\sqrt{2}\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2}, dx = \sigma\sqrt{2\pi}\)$

docs.title: The Normal Distribution
docs.text:
PDF: For \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\):

\[\boxed{f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}}\]

The normalization constant \(\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\) is exactly \(\left(\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}, dx\right)^{-1} = (\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1}\), derived above.

Mean: $\(\mathbb{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{x}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}, dx\)$

Substitute \(u = (x-\mu)/\sigma\): $\(= \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{\sigma u + \mu}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-u^2/2} \sigma, du = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\underbrace{\int_{-\infty}^\infty u e^{-u^2/2}, du}_{=0 \text{ (odd)}} + \mu\underbrace{\int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-u^2/2}, du}_{=1} = \boxed{\mu}\)$

Variance: $\(\text{Var}(X) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{(x-\mu)^2}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}, dx\)$

Substitute \(u = (x-\mu)/\sigma\): $\(= \sigma^2 \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^\infty u^2 e^{-u^2/2}, du\)$

Integration by parts: \(v = u\), \(dw = u e^{-u^2/2}, du\): $\(\int_{-\infty}^\infty u^2 e^{-u^2/2}, du = \left[-u e^{-u^2/2}\right]_{-\infty}^\infty + \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-u^2/2}, du = 0 + \sqrt{2\pi}\)$

\[\text{Var}(X) = \sigma^2 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{2\pi}}{\sqrt{2\pi}} = \boxed{\sigma^2}\]

docs.title: Example 7.1 — The 68-95-99.7 Rule (Exact Integrals)
docs.text:
For \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\), using the error function \(\text{erf}(z) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}\int_0^z e^{-t^2}, dt\):

\[P(-k\sigma \le X \le k\sigma) = \text{erf}\left(\frac{k}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\] \(k\) \(P(\mu - k\sigma \le X \le \mu + k\sigma)\) Exact Integral 1 \(\approx 0.6827\) \(\text{erf}(1/\sqrt{2})\) 2 \(\approx 0.9545\) \(\text{erf}(\sqrt{2})\) 3 \(\approx 0.9973\) \(\text{erf}(3/\sqrt{2})\)

These cannot be expressed in elementary closed form — they require the error function, a non-elementary antiderivative defined by the integral. The Gaussian is the canonical example of a function whose integral is non-elementary but profoundly important.

docs.title: The Gamma Function: An Improper Integral
docs.text:
Definition: $\(\boxed{\Gamma(n) = \int_0^\infty t^{n-1} e^{-t}, dt, \quad n > 0}\)$

Key properties derived from integration:

(i) Recursion: \(\Gamma(n) = (n-1)\Gamma(n-1)\)

Proof: Integration by parts, \(u = t^{n-1}\), \(dv = e^{-t}, dt\): $\(\Gamma(n) = \left[-t^{n-1}e^{-t}\right]_0^\infty + (n-1)\int_0^\infty t^{n-2}e^{-t}, dt = 0 + (n-1)\Gamma(n-1) \quad \blacksquare\)$

(ii) Integer values: \(\Gamma(n) = (n-1)!\) for \(n \in \mathbb{N}\)

(iii) Half-integer: \(\Gamma(1/2) = \sqrt{\pi}\)

Proof: \(\Gamma(1/2) = \int_0^\infty t^{-1/2}e^{-t}, dt\). Let \(t = u^2\): $\(= \int_0^\infty u^{-1} e^{-u^2} \cdot 2u, du = 2\int_0^\infty e^{-u^2}, du = \sqrt{\pi} \quad \blacksquare\)$

docs.title: Gamma Distribution PDF
docs.text:
PDF: \(X \sim \text{Gamma}(\alpha, \beta)\):

\[f(x) = \frac{x^{\alpha-1} e^{-x/\beta}}{\beta^\alpha, \Gamma(\alpha)}, \quad x > 0\]

Normalization (substitution \(t = x/\beta\)): $\(\int_0^\infty \frac{x^{\alpha-1}e^{-x/\beta}}{\beta^\alpha\Gamma(\alpha)}, dx = \frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_0^\infty t^{\alpha-1}e^{-t}, dt = \frac{\Gamma(\alpha)}{\Gamma(\alpha)} = 1 \quad \blacksquare\)$

Mean: $\(\mathbb{E}[X] = \frac{1}{\beta^\alpha\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_0^\infty x^\alpha e^{-x/\beta}, dx = \frac{\beta^{\alpha+1}\Gamma(\alpha+1)}{\beta^\alpha\Gamma(\alpha)} = \beta \cdot \alpha = \boxed{\alpha\beta}\)$

Variance: \(\text{Var}(X) = \alpha\beta^2\).

Special cases:

  • \(\alpha = 1\): Exponential distribution (§6)
  • \(\alpha = n/2\), \(\beta = 2\): Chi-squared distribution with \(n\) degrees of freedom (\(\chi^2_n\)) — fundamental in statistics and ML regularization

docs.title: 9. Beta Distribution
docs.text:
PDF: \(X \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta)\) on \([0,1]\):

\[f(x) = \frac{x^{\alpha-1}(1-x)^{\beta-1}}{B(\alpha,\beta)}, \quad x \in [0,1]\]

where the Beta function is defined by requiring normalization:

\[B(\alpha,\beta) = \int_0^1 x^{\alpha-1}(1-x)^{\beta-1}, dx\]

Key identity (proven via Gamma functions): $\(B(\alpha,\beta) = \frac{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)}\)$

Mean: $\(\mathbb{E}[X] = \frac{B(\alpha+1,\beta)}{B(\alpha,\beta)} = \frac{\Gamma(\alpha+1)\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\alpha+\beta+1)} = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}\)$

Variance: \(\text{Var}(X) = \frac{\alpha\beta}{(\alpha+\beta)^2(\alpha+\beta+1)}\)

Why Beta matters for ML: The Beta distribution is the conjugate prior for a Bernoulli/binomial likelihood. In Bayesian deep learning, Beta distributions appear in variational dropout, uncertainty quantification, and Thompson sampling.

docs.title: Example 9.1 — Bayesian Update via Integration
docs.text:
Setup: A classifier's accuracy \(\theta \sim \text{Beta}(2,2)\) (prior: slightly centered at 0.5). We observe 7 successes out of 10 trials. Find the posterior.

Posterior \(\propto\) Likelihood × Prior: $\(p(\theta | \text{data}) \propto \theta^7(1-\theta)^3 \cdot \theta^{2-1}(1-\theta)^{2-1} = \theta^8(1-\theta)^4\)$

This is proportional to \(\text{Beta}(9, 5)\).

Posterior mean (normalizing constant found by integration): $\(\mathbb{E}[\theta | \text{data}] = \frac{9}{9+5} = \frac{9}{14} \approx 0.643\)$

The normalization requires \(B(9,5) = \int_0^1 \theta^8(1-\theta)^4, d\theta = \frac{\Gamma(9)\Gamma(5)}{\Gamma(14)} = \frac{8! \cdot 4!}{13!} = \frac{40320 \times 24}{6227020800} = \frac{1}{6435}\).

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
For jointly distributed \((X, Y)\) with joint PDF \(f_{X,Y}(x,y)\):

\[P((X,Y) \in A) = \iint_A f_{X,Y}(x,y), dA\]

Marginal PDFs: $\(\boxed{f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f_{X,Y}(x,y), dy, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx}\)$

Independence: \(X \perp Y\) iff \(f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_X(x), f_Y(y)\) for all \((x,y)\).

Covariance: $\(\text{Cov}(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}[XY] - \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y] = \iint xy, f_{X,Y}(x,y), dA - \mu_X \mu_Y\)$

docs.title: Example 10.1 — Joint Distribution on a Triangle
docs.text:
Setup: \((X,Y)\) has joint PDF \(f(x,y) = 8xy\) on the region \(0 \le y \le x \le 1\) (a triangle).

Verify normalization: $\(\int_0^1 \int_0^x 8xy, dy, dx = \int_0^1 8x \cdot \frac{x^2}{2}, dx = \int_0^1 4x^3, dx = [x^4]_0^1 = 1 \quad \checkmark\)$

Marginal of \(X\): $\(f_X(x) = \int_0^x 8xy, dy = 8x \cdot \frac{x^2}{2} = 4x^3, \quad 0 \le x \le 1\)$

Marginal of \(Y\): $\(f_Y(y) = \int_y^1 8xy, dx = 8y \cdot \frac{1-y^2}{2} = 4y(1-y^2), \quad 0 \le y \le 1\)$

\(\mathbb{E}[X]\), \(\mathbb{E}[Y]\): $\(\mathbb{E}[X] = \int_0^1 x \cdot 4x^3, dx = \frac{4}{5}, \qquad \mathbb{E}[Y] = \int_0^1 y \cdot 4y(1-y^2), dy = \int_0^1 (4y^2 - 4y^4), dy = \frac{4}{3} - \frac{4}{5} = \frac{8}{15}\)$

\(\mathbb{E}[XY]\): $\(\mathbb{E}[XY] = \int_0^1\int_0^x 8x^2y^2, dy, dx = \int_0^1 \frac{8x^5}{3}, dx = \frac{8}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{6} = \frac{4}{9}\)$

\[\text{Cov}(X,Y) = \frac{4}{9} - \frac{4}{5}\cdot\frac{8}{15} = \frac{4}{9} - \frac{32}{75} = \frac{100 - 96}{225} = \frac{4}{225} > 0\]

Positive covariance makes sense: the triangle constraint \(Y \le X\) means larger \(X\) tends to come with larger \(Y\).

docs.title: Part III — Key Theorems That Need Integrals
Theorem
docs.text:
If \(Y = g(X)\) and \(X\) has PDF \(f_X\), then: $\(\boxed{\mathbb{E}[g(X)] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty g(x), f_X(x), dx}\)$

You do not need the PDF of \(Y\) to compute \(\mathbb{E}[Y]\) — you compute directly using \(f_X\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
\[\boxed{M_X(t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{tX}] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{tx}, f_X(x), dx}\]

Why it's powerful: \(M_X(t)\) encodes all moments: $\(\mathbb{E}[X^n] = M_X^{(n)}(0) = \left.\frac{d^n}{dt^n}M_X(t)\right|_{t=0}\)$

Proof: \(M_X(t) = \int e^{tx} f(x), dx = \int \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(tx)^n}{n!} f(x), dx = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{t^n}{n!}\mathbb{E}[X^n]\). Differentiating \(n\) times and setting \(t=0\) extracts \(\mathbb{E}[X^n]\). \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: Example 12.1 — MGF of the Normal Distribution
docs.text:
For \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\):

\[M_X(t) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{tx} \cdot \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}, dx\]

Complete the square in the exponent: $\(tx - \frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} = -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\left[x^2 - 2(\mu+\sigma^2 t)x + \mu^2\right]\)$ $\(= -\frac{(x-(\mu+\sigma^2 t))^2}{2\sigma^2} + \mu t + \frac{\sigma^2 t^2}{2}\)$

Therefore: $\(M_X(t) = e^{\mu t + \sigma^2 t^2/2} \cdot \underbrace{\int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(x-(\mu+\sigma^2 t))^2/(2\sigma^2)}, dx}_{=1 \text{ (Normal PDF integrates to 1)}}\)$

\[\boxed{M_X(t) = e^{\mu t + \sigma^2 t^2 / 2}}\]

Extract moments: $\(M_X'(t) = (\mu + \sigma^2 t), e^{\mu t + \sigma^2 t^2/2} \implies M_X'(0) = \mu = \mathbb{E}[X] \quad \checkmark\)$ $\(M_X''(t) = (\sigma^2 + (\mu+\sigma^2 t)^2), e^{\mu t+\sigma^2t^2/2} \implies M_X''(0) = \sigma^2 + \mu^2 = \mathbb{E}[X^2] \quad \checkmark\)$

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent with PDFs \(f_X\) and \(f_Y\), then \(Z = X + Y\) has PDF:

\[\boxed{f_Z(z) = (f_X * f_Y)(z) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f_X(t), f_Y(z-t), dt}\]

Proof: The joint PDF of \((X,Y)\) is \(f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_X(x)f_Y(y)\) (by independence). The CDF of \(Z = X+Y\): $\(F_Z(z) = P(X+Y \le z) = \iint_{x+y \le z} f_X(x)f_Y(y), dx, dy = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f_X(x)\left(\int_{-\infty}^{z-x}f_Y(y), dy\right)dx\)$

Differentiate with respect to \(z\) (FTC): $\(f_Z(z) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f_X(x), f_Y(z-x), dx = (f_X * f_Y)(z) \quad \blacksquare\)$

This is the same convolution integral as signal processing (§8 of the physics note) — the mathematical structure is identical. The sum of independent random variables is the convolution of their distributions.

docs.title: Example 13.1 — Sum of Two Exponentials
docs.text:
Setup: \(X, Y \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)\) independent. Find the PDF of \(Z = X+Y\).

\[f_Z(z) = \int_0^z \lambda e^{-\lambda t} \cdot \lambda e^{-\lambda(z-t)}, dt = \lambda^2 e^{-\lambda z} \int_0^z dt = \lambda^2 z e^{-\lambda z}, \quad z \ge 0\]

This is the Gamma(2, \(1/\lambda\)) distribution. ✓

More generally: sum of \(n\) independent \(\text{Exp}(\lambda)\) → \(\text{Gamma}(n, 1/\lambda)\). The convolution integral, when applied \(n\) times, accumulates the factor from \(\frac{z^0}{0!}\) to \(\frac{\lambda^n z^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} e^{-\lambda z}\).

docs.title: Example 13.2 — Sum of Two Normals is Normal
docs.text:
Setup: \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_1, \sigma_1^2)\), \(Y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_2, \sigma_2^2)\) independent. Show \(Z = X+Y\) is normal.

Via MGFs (much cleaner than direct convolution): $\(M_Z(t) = M_X(t) \cdot M_Y(t) = e^{\mu_1 t + \sigma_1^2 t^2/2} \cdot e^{\mu_2 t + \sigma_2^2 t^2/2} = e^{(\mu_1+\mu_2)t + (\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)t^2/2}\)$

This is the MGF of \(\mathcal{N}(\mu_1+\mu_2,, \sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)\). Since MGFs uniquely determine distributions: $\(\boxed{Z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_1+\mu_2,, \sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)} \quad \blacksquare\)$

The convolution integral in closed form would require the Gaussian integral machinery — the MGF approach works because the completing-the-square calculation (Example 12.1) was done once.

docs.title: Theorem (1D)
docs.text:
If \(Y = g(X)\) is monotone and differentiable, and \(X\) has PDF \(f_X\):

\[\boxed{f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y)) \cdot \left|\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)\right|}\]

Derivation: \(F_Y(y) = P(Y \le y) = P(g(X) \le y)\). If \(g\) is increasing: \(= P(X \le g^{-1}(y)) = F_X(g^{-1}(y))\). Differentiate via chain rule: \(f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y)) \cdot (g^{-1})'(y)\). \(\blacksquare\)

2D Theorem (MIT 18.02 L26): If \((U, V) = \mathbf{g}(X, Y)\): $\(f_{U,V}(u,v) = f_{X,Y}(x(u,v),, y(u,v)) \cdot |J|\)$ where the Jacobian: $\(J = \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} = \begin{vmatrix} \partial x/\partial u & \partial x/\partial v \ \partial y/\partial u & \partial y/\partial v \end{vmatrix}\)$

docs.title: Example 14.1 — Lognormal Distribution
docs.text:
Setup: \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\). Find the PDF of \(Y = e^X\) (lognormal).

\(g(x) = e^x \implies g^{-1}(y) = \ln y \implies (g^{-1})'(y) = 1/y\).

\[f_Y(y) = f_X(\ln y) \cdot \frac{1}{y} = \frac{1}{y\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-(\ln y - \mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}, \quad y > 0\]

Mean of lognormal (requires the MGF of the normal evaluated at \(t=1\)): $\(\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mathbb{E}[e^X] = M_X(1) = e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}\)$

The \(e^{\sigma^2/2}\) factor shows that the mean exceeds \(e^\mu\) — the log-normal is right-skewed. Used in: stock price models (Black-Scholes), income distributions, rainfall data.

docs.title: Example 14.2 — Box-Muller Transform (How Computers Sample Gaussians)
docs.text:
Setup: \(U_1, U_2 \sim \text{Uniform}[0,1]\) independent. Define: $\(Z_1 = \sqrt{-2\ln U_1}\cos(2\pi U_2), \quad Z_2 = \sqrt{-2\ln U_1}\sin(2\pi U_2)\)$

Claim: \(Z_1, Z_2 \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\) independent.

Proof via Jacobian: Let \(R = \sqrt{-2\ln U_1}\), \(\Theta = 2\pi U_2\). Then \(R^2 \sim \text{Exp}(1/2)\) (Chi-squared with 2 df) and \(\Theta \sim \text{Uniform}[0,2\pi]\).

Joint PDF of \((R,\Theta)\): $\(f_{R,\Theta}(r,\theta) = f_R(r) \cdot f_\Theta(\theta) = \frac{r}{1} e^{-r^2/2} \cdot \frac{1}{2\pi} = \frac{r}{2\pi}e^{-r^2/2}\)$

Converting to \((Z_1, Z_2) = (r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\) — polar to Cartesian: Jacobian \(= 1/r\) (inverse of Cartesian-to-polar Jacobian \(= r\)):

\[f_{Z_1,Z_2}(z_1,z_2) = \frac{r}{2\pi}e^{-r^2/2} \cdot \frac{1}{r} = \frac{1}{2\pi}e^{-(z_1^2+z_2^2)/2} = \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z_1^2/2}}_{f_{Z_1}} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z_2^2/2}}_{f_{Z_2}}\]

The joint PDF factors → \(Z_1, Z_2\) are independent \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\). \(\blacksquare\)

This is how every numerical library (NumPy, PyTorch, TensorFlow) generates Gaussian random numbers. Every torch.randn() call uses a variant of this Jacobian calculation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Conditional PDF of \(Y\) given \(X = x\): $\(f_{Y|X}(y|x) = \frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_X(x)}\)$

Conditional expectation: $\(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty y, f_{Y|X}(y|x), dy\)$

Law of Total Expectation: $\(\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mathbb{E}_X[\mathbb{E}[Y|X]] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \mathbb{E}[Y|X=x], f_X(x), dx\)$

This is a double integral — first integrate out \(Y\) at fixed \(x\), then integrate over \(x\). It is Fubini's theorem in probabilistic clothing.

docs.title: Example 15.1 — Regression Function
docs.text:
Setup: Joint PDF \(f(x,y) = 6xy^2\) on \(0 \le x \le 1\), \(0 \le y \le 1\).

Marginal of \(X\): \(f_X(x) = \int_0^1 6xy^2, dy = 6x \cdot \frac{1}{3} = 2x\)

Conditional PDF of \(Y|X=x\): $\(f_{Y|X}(y|x) = \frac{6xy^2}{2x} = 3y^2, \quad 0 \le y \le 1\)$

(Independent of \(x\) — \(Y\) and \(X\) are independent here.)

Conditional expectation: $\(\mathbb{E}[Y|X=x] = \int_0^1 y \cdot 3y^2, dy = \frac{3}{4}\)$

The regression function is constant — as expected when \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent.

docs.title: Part IV — ML & Deep Learning: Probability Integrals Everywhere
docs.text: This section makes explicit what every deep learning textbook leaves implicit: the integral is the foundation.

docs.title: ML.1 — Maximum Likelihood Estimation Is Integral Optimization
docs.text:
For i.i.d. data \({x_i}_{i=1}^n\) from distribution \(p_\theta\), the log-likelihood:

\[\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \log p_\theta(x_i) \approx n \int \log p_\theta(x), p_{\text{true}}(x), dx\]

This is an expected value integral under the true distribution. MLE maximizes the expected log-likelihood — the integral over data space. For continuous models (e.g., VAEs), this expectation cannot be computed exactly and is approximated by Monte Carlo (sample average), just as in §2/§3 above.

docs.title: ML.2 — Information Entropy
docs.text:
Shannon entropy for a continuous distribution:

\[\boxed{H(X) = -\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)\log f(x), dx}\]

Gaussian entropy (derived from integration):

\[H(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)) = -\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)\log f(x), dx\] \[= -\mathbb{E}\left[-\frac{(X-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} - \frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2)\right] = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) = \frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi e\sigma^2)\]

(Used \(\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^2] = \sigma^2\).)

Theorem: Among all continuous distributions on \(\mathbb{R}\) with fixed mean and variance, the Gaussian maximizes entropy — proven by calculus of variations on the entropy integral. This is why the Gaussian is the "most uncertain" distribution given second-moment constraints — a fact at the heart of maximum entropy models.

docs.title: ML.3 — KL Divergence: The Distance Between Distributions
docs.text:
\[\boxed{D_{KL}(P | Q) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}, dx}\]

Non-negativity (Gibbs' inequality) — proven by Jensen's inequality applied to the integral:

\[D_{KL}(P|Q) = -\int p(x)\log\frac{q(x)}{p(x)}, dx \ge -\log\int p(x)\cdot\frac{q(x)}{p(x)}, dx = -\log 1 = 0\]

KL between two Gaussians (closed form from evaluating the integral):

\[D_{KL}(\mathcal{N}(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2)| \mathcal{N}(\mu_2,\sigma_2^2)) = \log\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1} + \frac{\sigma_1^2 + (\mu_1-\mu_2)^2}{2\sigma_2^2} - \frac{1}{2}\]

This appears in VAE loss functions as the regularization term, forcing the encoder to match a standard Gaussian prior. The entire VAE training objective is:

\[\mathcal{L} = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z|x)}[\log p_\theta(x|z)]}_{\text{reconstruction: } \int \log p_\theta \cdot q_\phi, dz} - \underbrace{D_{KL}(q_\phi(z|x) | p(z))}_{\text{two Gaussian integrals}}\]

Both terms are integrals.

docs.title: ML.4 — The Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) is an Integral
docs.text:
In Variational Inference, we want \(\log p(x)\) but it requires an intractable integral:

\[\log p(x) = \log \int p(x|z), p(z), dz\]

We lower bound it (Jensen's inequality on the integral):

\[\log p(x) \ge \int q(z)\log\frac{p(x,z)}{q(z)}, dz =: \text{ELBO}(q)\]

The ELBO is a functional of \(q\) — optimizing over it is variational calculus applied to integrals. This is the mathematical core of:

  • Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
  • Bayesian Neural Networks
  • Diffusion Models (score matching is related)

docs.title: ML.5 — Monte Carlo Integration: SGD as Approximate Integration
docs.text:
Problem: \(I = \int_\mathcal{X} f(x), p(x), dx = \mathbb{E}_p[f(X)]\)

Monte Carlo estimate: \(\hat{I}_n = rac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i)\), \(x_i \sim p\).

Strong Law: \(\hat{I}_n o I\) almost surely (law of large numbers).

Rate of convergence (Central Limit Theorem): $\(\sqrt{n}(\hat{I}_n - I) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, ext{Var}_p[f(X)])\)$

Error \(\sim O(1/\sqrt{n})\), independent of dimension. This is why Monte Carlo is preferred over numerical quadrature in high dimensions (quadrature error degrades exponentially with dimension — the "curse of dimensionality").

SGD is mini-batch Monte Carlo integration of the gradient:

\[ abla_ heta \mathcal{L} = \int abla_ heta \ell(f_ heta(x), y), p(x,y), dx, dy \approx rac{1}{B}\sum_{i \in ext{batch}} abla_ heta \ell(f_ heta(x_i), y_i)\]

Every SGD step is an unbiased Monte Carlo estimate of the true gradient integral.

docs.title: ML.6 — The Reparameterization Trick: Differentiating Through an Integral
docs.text:
Problem: In a VAE, the encoder outputs \(q_\phi(z|x) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_\phi, \sigma_\phi^2)\) and we need:

\[ abla_\phi \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}[f(z)] = abla_\phi \int f(z), q_\phi(z|x), dz\]

Naive Monte Carlo can't differentiate through the sampling step.

Reparameterization: Write \(z = \mu_\phi + \sigma_\phi \varepsilon\), \(\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\):

\[\int f(z), q_\phi(z|x), dz = \int f(\mu_\phi + \sigma_\phi \varepsilon), \phi(\varepsilon), d\varepsilon\]

Now \(\phi(\varepsilon)\) is independent of \(\phi\), so we can move \( abla_\phi\) inside the integral:

\[ abla_\phi \int f(\mu_\phi + \sigma_\phi \varepsilon), \phi(\varepsilon), d\varepsilon = \int abla_\phi f(\mu_\phi + \sigma_\phi \varepsilon), \phi(\varepsilon), d\varepsilon\]

This is the Leibniz rule (differentiation under the integral sign), applied to make backpropagation through stochastic layers possible. Without this, VAEs cannot be trained.

Leibniz Rule (used here): $\( rac{d}{d\alpha}\int_a^b f(x, \alpha), dx = \int_a^b rac{\partial f}{\partial \alpha}(x, \alpha), dx\)$

(valid when \(\partial f/\partial\alpha\) is continuous and bounds \(a,b\) are independent of \(\alpha\).)

docs.title: ML.7 — Score Function & Fisher Information
docs.text:
The score function is: $\(s(x; heta) = abla_ heta \log p_ heta(x)\)$

Fisher Information Matrix: $\(\mathcal{I}( heta) = \mathbb{E}[s(x; heta) s(x; heta)^T] = \int abla_ heta \log p_ heta(x), ( abla_ heta \log p_ heta(x))^T, p_ heta(x), dx\)$

This is an integral of an outer product — a matrix-valued integral. It appears in:

  • Natural Gradient descent (K-FAC optimizer)
  • Score matching (diffusion models)
  • Cramér-Rao bound (fundamental lower bound on variance of any estimator)

Cramér-Rao Bound: $\( ext{Var}(\hat heta) \ge \mathcal{I}( heta)^{-1}\)$

The bound is an integral inequality — proven by applying Cauchy-Schwarz to the integral \(\int s(x; heta), p_ heta(x), dx\).

docs.title: Master Formula Sheet
docs.text:
\[\text{(PDF normalization)}\quad \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x), dx = 1\] \[\text{(Probability)}\quad P(a \le X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x), dx\] \[\text{(CDF)}\quad F(x) = \int_{-\infty}^x f(t), dt, \qquad f(x) = F'(x)\] \[\text{(Mean)}\quad \mu = \mathbb{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x, f(x), dx\] \[\text{(LOTUS)}\quad \mathbb{E}[g(X)] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty g(x), f(x), dx\] \[\text{(Variance)}\quad \sigma^2 = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - \mu^2 = \int x^2 f(x), dx - \left(\int x, f(x), dx\right)^2\] \[\text{(Joint → Marginal)}\quad f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f_{X,Y}(x,y), dy\] \[\text{(Convolution)}\quad f_{X+Y}(z) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f_X(t), f_Y(z-t), dt\] \[\text{(Change of variables)}\quad f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y))\left|\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)\right|\] \[\text{(MGF)}\quad M_X(t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{tX}] = \int e^{tx} f(x), dx\] \[\text{(Entropy)}\quad H(X) = -\int f(x)\log f(x), dx\] \[\text{(KL divergence)}\quad D_{KL}(P|Q) = \int p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}, dx\] \[\text{(Gaussian integral)}\quad \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2}, dx = \sqrt{\pi}, \qquad \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}, dx = \sigma\sqrt{2\pi}\] \[\text{(Gamma function)}\quad \Gamma(n) = \int_0^\infty t^{n-1}e^{-t}, dt = (n-1)!, \qquad \Gamma(1/2) = \sqrt{\pi}\] \[\text{(Leibniz rule)}\quad \frac{d}{d\alpha}\int_a^b f(x,\alpha), dx = \int_a^b \frac{\partial f}{\partial\alpha}(x,\alpha), dx\]

A professor's working notebook — rigorous, honest, and a little opinionated.

docs.title: 0. Why This Matters Before We Begin
docs.text: Population models are the pedagogical spine of first-order ODEs. They are also, quietly, the conceptual skeleton of a surprising slice of modern machine learning — activation functions, learning-rate schedules, neural population codes, epidemic-spread on graphs. The mathematics here is not a warm-up act; it is the act.

docs.title: 1.1 Derivation from First Principles
docs.text:
Let \(P(t)\) denote population at time \(t\). The Malthusian hypothesis is that the instantaneous rate of change is proportional to current population:

\[ \frac{dP}{dt} = kP, \qquad P(0) = P_0 \]

where \(k \in \mathbb{R}\) is the intrinsic growth rate (births minus deaths per individual per unit time).

Solving by separation of variables:

\[ \frac{dP}{P} = k,dt \implies \int_{P_0}^{P} \frac{du}{u} = \int_0^t k,ds \implies \ln!\left(\frac{P}{P_0}\right) = kt \] \[ \boxed{P(t) = P_0, e^{kt}} \]
  • \(k > 0\): unbounded exponential growth.
  • \(k < 0\): exponential decay (radioactive decay, drug clearance — same equation).
  • \(k = 0\): \(P(t) = P_0\), a fixed point (trivially stable).

docs.title: 1.2 The Fixed Point and Stability
docs.text:
The ODE \(\dot{P} = kP\) has a single equilibrium: \(P^* = 0\).

The linearisation around \(P^*\) is trivial — the equation is linear. Stability:

  • \(k < 0\): \(P^* = 0\) is stable (all trajectories decay to it).
  • \(k > 0\): \(P^* = 0\) is unstable (trajectories flee from it).

docs.title: 1.3 Phase Line
docs.text:
k > 0:          k < 0:

P                P
↑    →  →  →    ↑   ←  ←  ←
|                |
0                0

All trajectories on the real line either all flow away from (or toward) the origin. No complexity here — that comes next.

docs.title: 1.4 Concrete Example
docs.text:
World population (crude estimate): In 1800, \(P_0 \approx 10^9\). Suppose \(k = 0.014\) yr\(^{-1}\) (roughly 1.4% annual growth). Predict population in 1900.

\[ P(100) = 10^9 \cdot e^{0.014 \times 100} = 10^9 \cdot e^{1.4} \approx 10^9 \times 4.055 \approx 4.05 \times 10^9 \]

Historical reality: ~1.6 billion in 1900. The model overshoots drastically — because \(k\) isn't constant, and resources are finite. This failure motivates §2.

docs.title: 2.1 The Key Insight: Carrying Capacity
docs.text:
Verhulst (1838) proposed that \(k\) is not constant but decreases linearly with population — as \(P\) grows, competition for resources reduces the effective per-capita growth rate:

\[ \text{effective rate} = r\left(1 - \frac{P}{K}\right) \]

where:

  • \(r > 0\): intrinsic (maximum) growth rate,
  • \(K > 0\): carrying capacity (environmental ceiling).

This yields the logistic equation:

\[ \boxed{\frac{dP}{dt} = rP\left(1 - \frac{P}{K}\right)} \]

docs.title: 2.2 Qualitative Analysis Before Solving
docs.text:
Fixed points: Set \(\dot{P} = 0\): $$ P^* = 0 \quad \text{(trivial, unstable)} \qquad \text{and} \qquad P^* = K \quad \text{(non-trivial)} $$

Phase line analysis:

Region Sign of \(\dot{P}\) Direction \(P < 0\) negative (biologically meaningless) — \(0 < P < K\) positive \(P\) increases \(P = K\) zero equilibrium \(P > K\) negative \(P\) decreases

So \(K\) is a stable equilibrium (globally attracting for \(P > 0\)). \(P^* = 0\) is unstable.

Phase line:

←  (0)  →  →  →  →  [K]  ←  ←  ←

docs.title: 2.3 Exact Solution
docs.text:
Separate variables:

\[ \frac{dP}{P(1 - P/K)} = r,dt \]

Use partial fractions on the left:

\[ \frac{1}{P(1-P/K)} = \frac{1}{P} + \frac{1/K}{1-P/K} \]

Integrate both sides:

\[ \ln P - \ln!\left(1 - \frac{P}{K}\right) = rt + C \] \[ \ln!\left(\frac{P}{K - P}\right) = rt + C \]

Apply initial condition \(P(0) = P_0\), so \(C = \ln!\left(\frac{P_0}{K-P_0}\right)\). Exponentiate and solve for \(P\):

\[ \boxed{P(t) = \frac{K P_0}{P_0 + (K - P_0),e^{-rt}}} \]

This is the logistic function — an S-shaped (sigmoidal) curve.

docs.title: 2.4 Asymptotic Behavior
docs.text:
\[ \lim_{t \to \infty} P(t) = K \qquad (\text{regardless of } P_0 \in (0, K]) \] \[ \lim_{t \to -\infty} P(t) = 0 \]

The inflection point (where growth is fastest, \(\ddot{P} = 0\)) occurs at \(P = K/2\).

Proof of inflection: Differentiate \(\dot{P} = rP(1-P/K)\) with respect to \(t\):

\[ \ddot{P} = r\dot{P}\left(1 - \frac{2P}{K}\right) = r^2 P!\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right)!\left(1 - \frac{2P}{K}\right) \]

Setting \(\ddot{P} = 0\) (with \(P > 0\), \(P \neq K\)) gives \(P = K/2\). \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: 2.5 Visualization: The S-Curve
docs.text:
P(t)
 K  ──────────────────────────── (asymptote)
    |                   /‾‾‾‾‾‾‾
K/2 |................../  ← inflection (fastest growth)
    |              /
    |           /
    |        /
    |     /
    |  /
    |/
    0──────────────────────────── t
  • Below \(K/2\): growth is accelerating (convex).
  • Above \(K/2\): growth is decelerating (concave).
  • The curve is symmetric about the inflection point in log-odds space.

docs.title: 2.6 Concrete Example
docs.text: U.S. population: Stewart uses \(P_0 = 3.9 \times 10^6\) (1790), \(K \approx 197 \times 10^6\), and fits \(r\) to historical data. At \(t = 0\) (1790): rapid growth. By 1900, growth slows — logistic fits better than exponential.

docs.title: 3. The Harvesting Extension (Brief)
docs.text:
A natural perturbation: suppose we remove \(h\) individuals per unit time (fishing, hunting):

\[ \frac{dP}{dt} = rP!\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right) - h \]

The equilibria satisfy a quadratic. For \(h < rK/4\) (below the maximum sustainable yield), two equilibria exist; above it, population collapses. MSY is achieved at \(P = K/2\) — the same inflection point, not a coincidence.

\[ h_{\max} = \frac{rK}{4} \]

docs.title: 4. Comparison Table
docs.text: Feature Exponential Logistic ODE \(\dot{P} = kP\) \(\dot{P} = rP(1-P/K)\) Fixed points \(P^*=0\) \(P^_=0\) (unstable), \(P^_=K\) (stable) Solution \(P_0 e^{kt}\) Sigmoidal formula Long-run behavior \(\infty\) or \(0\) Converges to \(K\) Shape J-curve S-curve Realistic? Short-term only Better for bounded resources

docs.title: 5. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: This is the part most textbooks skip. Don't.

docs.title: 5.1 The Logistic Function Is the Sigmoid
docs.text:
Rewrite the logistic solution. Let \(P_0 = K/2\) (starting at inflection), \(u = rt\):

\[ P(t) = \frac{K}{1 + e^{-rt}} = K \cdot \sigma(rt) \]

where \(\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\) is the sigmoid (logistic) activation function in neural networks.

This is not a notational coincidence. The sigmoid activation was originally motivated by biological neuron firing rates — neurons saturate at maximum firing (analogous to \(K\)) and have a threshold below which they barely fire. The logistic ODE describes exactly this saturation dynamic.

In practice: every time a neural network applies \(\sigma(w^\top x + b)\), it is evaluating the logistic function — the solution to a population ODE.

docs.title: 5.2 Logistic Regression
docs.text:
Binary classification via logistic regression models the probability that output \(y=1\):

\[ P(y=1 \mid x) = \sigma(w^\top x + b) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(w^\top x + b)}} \]

The cross-entropy loss is the negative log-likelihood of this model. Training via gradient descent is literally fitting the parameters of a logistic (population-growth) curve to data.

docs.title: 5.3 Neural ODE and Continuous-Depth Networks
docs.text:
In the 2018 Neural ODE framework (Chen et al.), the hidden state \(h(t)\) of a network satisfies:

\[ \frac{dh}{dt} = f_\theta(h(t), t) \]

where \(f_\theta\) is a neural network. This is a learned ODE. The logistic equation is the simplest non-trivial case of such a system with a single hidden unit.

Euler discretization of \(\dot{h} = f_\theta(h)\) with step \(\Delta t = 1\) gives exactly a ResNet layer:

\[ h_{t+1} = h_t + f_\theta(h_t) \]

Understanding population ODEs qualitatively — fixed points, stability, phase lines — is the conceptual prerequisite for reasoning about the dynamics of deep networks.

docs.title: 5.4 Epidemic/Information Diffusion (SIR Model)
docs.text:
The spread of information, memes, or viruses in a network follows the SIR model:

\[ \frac{dS}{dt} = -\beta SI, \qquad \frac{dI}{dt} = \beta SI - \gamma I, \qquad \frac{dR}{dt} = \gamma I \]

This is a direct generalization of population ODEs to a 3-compartment system. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) trained on epidemiological or social data are learning to approximate the solutions to ODE systems like this one.

docs.title: 5.5 Learning Rate Schedules
docs.text:
Many modern optimizers use exponential decay of the learning rate:

\[ \eta(t) = \eta_0, e^{-\lambda t} \]

This is the solution to \(\dot{\eta} = -\lambda \eta\) — a population decay ODE applied to an optimization hyperparameter. "Cosine annealing" is a smooth perturbation of this.

docs.title: 5.6 Summary of ML Connections
docs.text: Population Model ML/DL Analogue Logistic function \(\sigma\) Sigmoid activation, logistic regression Exponential growth/decay Learning rate schedules, weight decay Carrying capacity \(K\) Saturation, vanishing gradient in deep nets Phase-line stability analysis Loss landscape fixed-point analysis Logistic ODE Continuous-depth networks (Neural ODEs) SIR generalization Epidemic GNNs, diffusion on graphs

docs.title: 6.1 Existence and Uniqueness (Picard–Lindelöf)
docs.text:
The right-hand side \(f(t, P) = rP(1-P/K)\) is a polynomial in \(P\), hence continuously differentiable (Lipschitz in \(P\) on any compact set). By the Picard–Lindelöf theorem, the IVP has a unique solution on some interval around \(t_0\).

For the logistic equation, the explicit formula shows the solution exists for all \(t \in \mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: 6.2 Global Stability of \(K\) (Lyapunov Argument)
docs.text:
Define the Lyapunov function \(V(P) = (P - K)^2\) for \(P > 0\).

\[ \dot{V} = 2(P-K)\dot{P} = 2(P-K) \cdot rP\left(1-\frac{P}{K}\right) \]

Note \(1 - P/K = -(P-K)/K\), so:

\[ \dot{V} = 2(P-K) \cdot rP \cdot \left(-\frac{P-K}{K}\right) = -\frac{2rP}{K}(P-K)^2 \leq 0 \]

with equality only when \(P = K\) or \(P = 0\). Since \(P > 0\), \(\dot{V} < 0\) whenever \(P \neq K\). So \(K\) is Lyapunov stable and the trajectory converges to it. \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: 7. Quick-Reference Formulas
docs.text: \[ P_{\text{exp}}(t) = P_0 e^{kt} \] \[ P_{\text{logistic}}(t) = \frac{KP_0}{P_0 + (K-P_0)e^{-rt}} \] \[ P_{\text{inflection}} = \frac{K}{2}, \qquad t_{\text{inflection}} = \frac{1}{r}\ln!\left(\frac{K - P_0}{P_0}\right) \] \[ h_{\max} = \frac{rK}{4} \quad \text{(maximum sustainable yield)} \] \[ \sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}} = P_{\text{logistic}}(x)\big|_{K=1,, P_0=1/2} \]

docs.title: 8. Exercises (Self-Check)
docs.text:
1. Doubling time. Show that for exponential growth, the doubling time is \(T_2 = \frac{\ln 2}{k}\), independent of \(P_0\).

  2. Logistic — large \(K\). Show that if \(P_0 \ll K\), the logistic solution approximates exponential growth for small \(t\). (Hint: expand \(e^{-rt}\) or take \(K \to \infty\).)

  3. Harvesting. For \(\dot{P} = rP(1-P/K) - h\) with \(h < rK/4\), find both equilibria and determine their stability via linearisation.

  4. Sigmoid. Starting from \(\frac{d\sigma}{dx} = \sigma(1-\sigma)\), derive this directly from the logistic ODE. What is the biological interpretation?

  5. Neural ODE. Euler-discretize \(\dot{h} = \tanh(Wh)\) with step 1. Compare to a one-layer RNN update rule.

docs.title: Spring Motion Models
docs.text:
A professor's working notebook — rigorous, honest, and a little opinionated.

Tags: #calculus #ODE #mechanics #oscillations #ML-connection References: Stewart §17.1, §17.3 · MIT 18.02 (vector fields, phase plane) Date: 2026-04-18

docs.title: 0. Why This Is the Most Important ODE in Physics
docs.text:
The spring — specifically, the second-order linear ODE it produces — is arguably the single most recurring equation in all of science and engineering. It governs sound, light, electrical circuits (RLC), quantum harmonic oscillators, climate oscillations, and the small-oscillation limit of every potential well in classical mechanics. If you understand the spring, you understand oscillations universally.

And, quietly, it underlies recurrent neural networks, attention mechanisms with positional encodings, and second-order optimizers in ML. We will get there.

docs.title: 1.1 Physical Setup
docs.text:
A mass \(m > 0\) hangs (or slides) on a spring with spring constant \(k > 0\). Let \(x(t)\) denote displacement from the natural equilibrium position (so \(x = 0\) is already the rest position with gravity balanced by the spring's static extension, if vertical).

Forces acting on \(m\):

Force Expression Direction Spring restoring \(-kx\) Always toward \(x=0\) Damping (friction/resistance) \(-c\dot{x}\), \(c \geq 0\) Opposes velocity External driving \(F(t)\) Prescribed

By Newton's second law, \(\sum F = ma = m\ddot{x}\):

\[ \boxed{m\ddot{x} + c\dot{x} + kx = F(t)} \]

This is the master equation for all cases below. Divide through by \(m\):

\[ \ddot{x} + \frac{c}{m}\dot{x} + \frac{k}{m}x = \frac{F(t)}{m} \]

Define the standard parameters: $$ \omega_0 = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} \quad \text{(natural angular frequency)}, \qquad \gamma = \frac{c}{2m} \quad \text{(damping coefficient)} $$

The equation becomes:

\[ \ddot{x} + 2\gamma\dot{x} + \omega_0^2, x = \frac{F(t)}{m} \]

docs.title: 2. Case I — Simple Harmonic Motion (Undamped, Unforced)
2.1 Characteristic Equation and General Solution
docs.text:
Substitute \(x = e^{rt}\):

\[ r^2 + \omega_0^2 = 0 \implies r = \pm, i\omega_0 \]

Complex roots \(\Rightarrow\) general solution:

\[ \boxed{x(t) = C_1\cos(\omega_0 t) + C_2\sin(\omega_0 t)} \]

Equivalently, using amplitude-phase form:

\[ x(t) = A\cos(\omega_0 t - \phi) \]

where \(A = \sqrt{C_1^2 + C_2^2}\) is the amplitude and \(\phi = \arctan(C_2/C_1)\) is the phase angle.

docs.title: 2.2 Initial Conditions
docs.text:
Given \(x(0) = x_0\), \(\dot{x}(0) = v_0\):

\[ C_1 = x_0, \qquad C_2 = \frac{v_0}{\omega_0} \] \[ A = \sqrt{x_0^2 + \frac{v_0^2}{\omega_0^2}}, \qquad \phi = \arctan!\left(\frac{v_0}{\omega_0 x_0}\right) \]

docs.title: 2.3 Energy Conservation
docs.text:
Kinetic + Potential energy is conserved:

\[ E = \frac{1}{2}m\dot{x}^2 + \frac{1}{2}kx^2 = \frac{1}{2}kA^2 = \text{const} \]

Verification: \(\dot{E} = m\dot{x}\ddot{x} + kx\dot{x} = \dot{x}(m\ddot{x} + kx) = \dot{x} \cdot 0 = 0\). \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: 2.4 Phase Plane: An Ellipse
docs.text:
Let \(v = \dot{x}\). The system becomes:

\[ \dot{x} = v, \qquad \dot{v} = -\omega_0^2 x \]

Eliminating \(t\): \(\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{-\omega_0^2 x}{v}\), so \(v,dv = -\omega_0^2 x,dx\), giving:

\[ \frac{v^2}{\omega_0^2} + x^2 = A^2 \qquad \text{(family of ellipses)} \] 
  v = ẋ
  ↑
  |    ·  ·  ·
  |  ·         ·        ← closed orbits (ellipses)
  | ·             ·        means periodic, no energy loss
  |·               ·
  +────────────────→ x
  |·               ·
  | ·             ·
  |  ·         ·
  |    ·  ·  ·

Every trajectory is a closed ellipse — the system is conservative. No fixed points other than the origin (a center).

docs.title: 3. Case II — Damped Free Oscillation
docs.text:
Set \(F(t) = 0\), \(c > 0\):

\[ \ddot{x} + 2\gamma\dot{x} + \omega_0^2, x = 0 \]

docs.title: 3.1 Characteristic Equation
docs.text:
\[ r^2 + 2\gamma r + \omega_0^2 = 0 \implies r = -\gamma \pm \sqrt{\gamma^2 - \omega_0^2} \]

The discriminant \(\Delta = \gamma^2 - \omega_0^2\) governs the qualitative behavior.

docs.title: 3.2 Subcase: Underdamping (\(\gamma < \omega_0\), i.e., \(\Delta < 0\))
docs.text:
\[ r = -\gamma \pm i\omega_d, \qquad \omega_d = \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - \gamma^2} \quad \text{(damped frequency)} \]

General solution:

\[ \boxed{x(t) = e^{-\gamma t}!\left[C_1\cos(\omega_d t) + C_2\sin(\omega_d t)\right] = A e^{-\gamma t}\cos(\omega_d t - \phi)} \]

The system oscillates but the amplitude decays exponentially. The factor \(e^{-\gamma t}\) is an envelope squeezing the oscillation to zero.

x(t)
  |   /\        /\
  |  /  \      /  \
  | /    \    /    \      ← decaying oscillation
  |/      \  /      \
  +─────────────────────→ t
  |        \/        \/
             ↑
       envelope: ±Ae^{-γt}

docs.title: 3.3 Subcase: Overdamping (\(\gamma > \omega_0\), i.e., \(\Delta > 0\))
docs.text:
Two distinct negative real roots \(r_1, r_2 < 0\):

\[ \boxed{x(t) = C_1 e^{r_1 t} + C_2 e^{r_2 t}} \]

No oscillation — the system creeps back to equilibrium. Think of a door closer in a thick oil: it closes, but slowly and without bouncing.

docs.title: 3.4 Subcase: Critical Damping (\(\gamma = \omega_0\), i.e., \(\Delta = 0\))
docs.text:
Repeated root \(r = -\gamma\):

\[ \boxed{x(t) = (C_1 + C_2 t),e^{-\gamma t}} \]

Critical damping returns to equilibrium as fast as possible without oscillating. This is why car shock absorbers and galvanometers are tuned to near-critical damping.

Why the extra \(t\)? When the characteristic equation has a repeated root \(r_0\), the two linearly independent solutions are \(e^{r_0 t}\) and \(t e^{r_0 t}\). Their Wronskian is \(e^{2r_0 t} \neq 0\), confirming independence. \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: 3.5 Comparison of Damping Regimes
docs.text:
x(t)
  |
  |  \   ← overdamped (slow, no bounce)
  |   \·
  |    ·\  ← critical (fastest return, no bounce)
  |    · \/‾
  |   /\      ·  ← underdamped (oscillates, decays)
  |  /  \  /\  \/
  | /    \/   \/
  |/
  +───────────────────→ t

docs.title: 3.6 Phase Plane: Spiral vs. Node
docs.text:
Regime Phase portrait Underdamped Stable spiral (inward, clockwise) Critically damped Stable node (degenerate) Overdamped Stable node

All three: trajectories converge to origin. The origin is a stable fixed point for all \(c > 0\).

docs.title: 4. Case III — Forced Oscillations and Resonance
docs.text:
Now \(F(t) = F_0\cos(\omega t)\), a periodic driving force at frequency \(\omega\):

\[ m\ddot{x} + c\dot{x} + kx = F_0\cos(\omega t) \]

docs.title: 4.1 Method of Undetermined Coefficients
docs.text:
The general solution is:

\[ x(t) = x_h(t) + x_p(t) \]

where \(x_h\) is the (decaying) homogeneous solution and \(x_p\) is a particular solution we seek.

Try \(x_p = D\cos(\omega t) + E\sin(\omega t)\). Substitute and match coefficients:

\[ D = \frac{F_0/m,(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)}{(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)^2 + 4\gamma^2\omega^2}, \qquad E = \frac{2\gamma\omega, F_0/m}{(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)^2 + 4\gamma^2\omega^2} \]

The amplitude of the steady-state response is:

\[ \boxed{A_p(\omega) = \frac{F_0/m}{\sqrt{(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)^2 + 4\gamma^2\omega^2}}} \]

docs.title: 4.2 Resonance
docs.text:
As \(\omega \to \omega_0\) with \(\gamma \to 0\) (undamped), the denominator \(\to 0\), so \(A_p \to \infty\).

Pure resonance (\(c = 0\), \(\omega = \omega_0\)): The method of undetermined coefficients fails (forcing frequency equals natural frequency). Use variation of parameters or the standard resonance ansatz \(x_p = t(D\cos\omega_0 t + E\sin\omega_0 t)\):

\[ \boxed{x_p(t) = \frac{F_0}{2m\omega_0},t\sin(\omega_0 t)} \]

The amplitude grows linearly in time — unbounded oscillation. This is the Tacoma Narrows Bridge phenomenon (1940), and why soldiers break step when crossing bridges.

docs.title: 4.3 Amplitude–Frequency Response Curve
docs.text:
A_p(ω)
  ↑
  |          ← γ small: sharp peak near ω₀
  |         /\
  |        /  \
  |       /    \___
  |  ____/          ‾‾‾‾‾‾‾   ← γ large: broad, low peak
  |
  +──────────────────────────→ ω
              ↑ ω₀
         resonance peak

The resonant frequency (for damped system) where \(A_p\) is maximized:

\[ \omega_{\text{res}} = \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - 2\gamma^2} \]

(Only exists when \(\gamma < \omega_0/\sqrt{2}\); otherwise the peak is at \(\omega = 0\).)

docs.title: 5. The RLC Circuit — Same Equation
docs.text:
The series RLC circuit (resistor \(R\), inductor \(L\), capacitor \(C\)) with EMF \(E(t)\) satisfies:

\[ L\ddot{q} + R\dot{q} + \frac{1}{C}q = E(t) \]

Identify: \(L \leftrightarrow m\), \(R \leftrightarrow c\), \(1/C \leftrightarrow k\), \(q \leftrightarrow x\). Identical ODE. Every result about mechanical oscillators translates immediately to electrical circuits. This is mathematical universality — a single equation ruling two different physical worlds.

Mechanical Electrical Mass \(m\) Inductance \(L\) Damping \(c\) Resistance \(R\) Spring constant \(k\) \(1/C\) Displacement \(x\) Charge \(q\) Velocity \(\dot{x}\) Current \(\dot{q} = I\) Driving force \(F(t)\) EMF \(E(t)\)

docs.title: 6. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: Here the spring stops being a toy and becomes a lens.

docs.title: 6.1 Sinusoidal Positional Encodings (Transformers)
docs.text:
The Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017 — Attention Is All You Need) encodes position \(pos\) in a sequence using:

\[ PE_{(pos, 2i)} = \sin!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right), \qquad PE_{(pos, 2i+1)} = \cos!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right) \]

These are exactly the solutions to \(\ddot{x} + \omega_i^2 x = 0\) — undamped simple harmonic motion at frequency \(\omega_i = 10000^{-2i/d}\). Each "dimension" of the positional encoding is an independent oscillator. The Transformer's ability to represent relative position relies on the trigonometric identities \(\cos(\alpha - \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta\) — which are addition formulas for SHM solutions.

The recently proposed RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding, Su et al. 2021) used in LLaMA, GPT-NeoX, and many modern LLMs encodes position via a rotation matrix — again, the rotation group underlying SHM in the phase plane.

docs.title: 6.2 Recurrent Neural Networks as Discretized Oscillators
docs.text:
A second-order ODE \(\ddot{x} + 2\gamma\dot{x} + \omega_0^2 x = 0\) written as a first-order system:

\[ \frac{d}{dt}\begin{pmatrix}x \ v\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1 \ -\omega_0^2 & -2\gamma\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x \ v\end{pmatrix} \]

Euler discretize with step \(\Delta t\):

\[ \begin{pmatrix}x_{t+1} \ v_{t+1}\end{pmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}1 & \Delta t \ -\omega_0^2\Delta t & 1-2\gamma\Delta t\end{pmatrix}}_{W}\begin{pmatrix}x_t \ v_t\end{pmatrix} \]

This is a linear RNN update \(h_{t+1} = Wh_t\). The eigenvalues of \(W\) determine stability — exactly as in the damping regimes. Underdamped \(\leftrightarrow\) complex eigenvalues (oscillatory hidden state), overdamped \(\leftrightarrow\) real eigenvalues (monotone forgetting).

The vanishing gradient problem in RNNs is the overdamped regime: if \(|eigenvalues(W)| < 1\), gradients decay exponentially through time — information is damped away. LSTMs and GRUs are engineered specifically to stay near the critically damped or marginally stable boundary.

docs.title: 6.3 Second-Order Optimization (Heavy Ball, Momentum)
docs.text:
Standard SGD: \( heta_{t+1} = heta_t - \eta abla L( heta_t)\) — Euler discretization of gradient flow \(\dot{ heta} = - abla L\).

SGD with momentum (Polyak's Heavy Ball method):

\[ v_{t+1} = eta v_t - \eta abla L( heta_t), \qquad heta_{t+1} = heta_t + v_{t+1} \]

This is the discretization of the damped oscillator equation:

\[ m\ddot{ heta} + c\dot{ heta} = - abla L( heta) \]

where \(m \sim \eta/(1- eta)\) and \(c \sim 1- eta\). Momentum "accumulates" velocity like a mass, helping escape shallow minima and accelerating convergence in narrow valleys — exactly the behavior of an underdamped spring released near a potential minimum.

Nesterov Accelerated Gradient is the critically-damped version of this, achieving the optimal convergence rate \(O(1/t^2)\) for convex \(L\) — a consequence of tuning to the equivalent of critical damping.

docs.title: 6.4 Neural ODEs Revisited
docs.text:
In the Neural ODE framework, the second-order spring can be cast as a learned system:

\[ \frac{d}{dt}\begin{pmatrix}x \ v\end{pmatrix} = f_\theta!\left(\begin{pmatrix}x \ v\end{pmatrix}, t\right) \]

where \(f_\theta\) is a neural network. The network learns to mimic (or generalize) spring-like dynamics from data. Hamiltonian Neural Networks (Greydanus et al., 2019) and Lagrangian Neural Networks enforce conservation of the energy \(E = \frac{1}{2}v^2 + \frac{1}{2}\omega_0^2 x^2\) as a structural prior — the phase-plane ellipses become the invariant set the network is constrained to respect.

docs.title: 6.5 Summary of ML Connections
docs.text: Spring Concept ML/DL Analogue \(\cos(\omega t)\), \(\sin(\omega t)\) solutions Transformer positional encodings (PE, RoPE) Phase-plane rotation Rotary embeddings (LLaMA, GPT-NeoX) Damping regimes Vanishing/exploding gradients in RNNs Critical damping LSTM/GRU gating; Nesterov optimizer Spring ODE as first-order system Linear RNN hidden state update Second-order ODE for \(\theta\) SGD with momentum (Heavy Ball) Energy-conserving phase ellipse Hamiltonian Neural Networks Resonance Overfitting to periodic patterns in time series

docs.title: 7.1 Linear Independence of Solutions (Wronskian)
docs.text:
For the underdamped case, solutions \(x_1 = e^{-\gamma t}\cos\omega_d t\) and \(x_2 = e^{-\gamma t}\sin\omega_d t\):

\[ W(x_1, x_2) = \begin{vmatrix} x_1 & x_2 \ \dot{x}_1 & \dot{x}_2 \end{vmatrix} \]

Computing: $$ W = e^{-\gamma t}\cos\omega_d t \cdot e^{-\gamma t}(-\gamma\sin\omega_d t + \omega_d\cos\omega_d t) - e^{-\gamma t}\sin\omega_d t \cdot e^{-\gamma t}(-\gamma\cos\omega_d t - \omega_d\sin\omega_d t) $$

\[ = e^{-2\gamma t}\left[\omega_d\cos^2\omega_d t + \omega_d\sin^2\omega_d t\right] = \omega_d, e^{-2\gamma t} \neq 0 \]

So \({x_1, x_2}\) forms a fundamental set of solutions. \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: 7.2 Abel's Identity (Why the Wronskian Decays)
docs.text:
For \(\ddot{x} + p(t)\dot{x} + q(t)x = 0\), Abel's theorem gives:

\[ W(t) = W(t_0)\exp!\left(-\int_{t_0}^t p(s),ds\right) \]

For our equation, \(p = 2\gamma\), so \(W(t) = W_0 e^{-2\gamma t}\) — confirming the calculation above.

docs.title: 7.3 Stability via Characteristic Roots
docs.text:
The origin \((x, v) = (0,0)\) is asymptotically stable if and only if all characteristic roots have negative real parts.

For \(r = -\gamma \pm \sqrt{\gamma^2 - \omega_0^2}\): since \(\gamma > 0\) and \(\omega_0 > 0\):

  • Real parts are \(-\gamma \pm \text{Re}!\left(\sqrt{\gamma^2 - \omega_0^2}\right)\).
  • If \(\gamma \geq \omega_0\): both roots real and \(< 0\). ✓
  • If \(\gamma < \omega_0\): roots are \(-\gamma \pm i\omega_d\), real part \(= -\gamma < 0\). ✓

So for any \(\gamma > 0\), the equilibrium is asymptotically stable. \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: 8. Quick-Reference Formulas
docs.text: \[ \omega_0 = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}, \qquad \gamma = \frac{c}{2m}, \qquad \omega_d = \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - \gamma^2} \] \[ \text{Underdamped } (\gamma < \omega_0): \quad x(t) = Ae^{-\gamma t}\cos(\omega_d t - \phi) \] \[ \text{Critically damped } (\gamma = \omega_0): \quad x(t) = (C_1 + C_2 t)e^{-\gamma t} \] \[ \text{Overdamped } (\gamma > \omega_0): \quad x(t) = C_1 e^{r_1 t} + C_2 e^{r_2 t}, \quad r_{1,2} = -\gamma \pm \sqrt{\gamma^2 - \omega_0^2} \] \[ \text{Resonance amplitude}: \quad A_p(\omega) = \frac{F_0/m}{\sqrt{(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)^2 + 4\gamma^2\omega^2}} \] \[ \text{Pure resonance particular solution}: \quad x_p(t) = \frac{F_0}{2m\omega_0},t\sin(\omega_0 t) \] \[ \text{Energy (SHM)}: \quad E = \frac{1}{2}m\dot{x}^2 + \frac{1}{2}kx^2 = \frac{1}{2}kA^2 \]

docs.title: 9. Exercises (Self-Check)
docs.text:
1. Period and frequency. A spring with \(k = 4\) N/m and \(m = 1\) kg is released from \(x_0 = 0.5\) m with \(v_0 = 0\). Write the explicit solution and compute the period.

  2. Damping classification. For \(m = 1\), \(k = 9\), classify the motion for \(c = 2\), \(c = 6\), \(c = 10\). Find \(x(t)\) in each case for \(x(0) = 1\), \(\dot{x}(0) = 0\).

  3. Wronskian. Verify Abel's identity directly for the overdamped case.

  4. Resonance growth. For \(m=1\), \(c=0\), \(k=\omega_0^2\), \(F(t) = F_0\cos(\omega_0 t)\), use variation of parameters to derive \(x_p = \frac{F_0}{2\omega_0}t\sin(\omega_0 t)\).

  5. Momentum as damped spring. Take the loss \(L(\theta) = \frac{1}{2}\theta^2\) (quadratic). Write the SGD-with-momentum update as a second-order ODE in the continuous limit. Find the condition on \(\beta\), \(\eta\) for underdamped vs overdamped optimization.

  6. Transformer PE. Verify that if \(f(t) = \cos(\omega t)\) and \(g(t) = \sin(\omega t)\), then \(\cos(\omega(t+k))\) and \(\sin(\omega(t+k))\) can be written as a linear (rotation) transformation of \(f(t)\) and \(g(t)\). This is why the Transformer can represent relative position from absolute PEs.

docs.title: 0. Orientation
docs.text:
A differential equation is a constraint on a function expressed through its own rates of change. Nature tends to know rates — not states. It knows how fast a population grows, how fast heat diffuses, how fast a voltage changes. The differential equation is the mathematical language in which nature speaks; our job is to decode it into explicit functions.

This note builds the full architecture: classification → existence/uniqueness → first-order methods → second-order theory → systems → qualitative analysis → the ML thread running through all of it.

docs.title: 1. What Is a Differential Equation?
docs.text:
A differential equation (DE) is an equation involving an unknown function and one or more of its derivatives.

General implicit form:

\[ F!\left(x,, y,, y',, y'',, \ldots,, y^{(n)}\right) = 0 \]

where \(y = y(x)\) is the unknown, \(x\) is the independent variable.

A solution is any function \(y = \phi(x)\) defined on some interval \(I\) such that substituting \(\phi\) and its derivatives into the equation produces a true identity for all \(x \in I\).

docs.title: 2. Classification
docs.text: Every DE should be classified along four axes before attempting a solution. Classification determines which tools apply.

docs.title: 2.1 Ordinary vs. Partial
docs.text:
Type Unknown depends on Derivatives Notation ODE one variable \(x\) ordinary \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) \(y' = f(x,y)\) PDE multiple variables \(x,t,\ldots\) partial \(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\) \(u_t = \alpha u_{xx}\)

All of §3–§7 concern ODEs. PDEs appear briefly in §8.

docs.title: 2.2 Order
docs.text:
The order is the highest derivative present.

\[ y'' + y = 0 \quad \text{(order 2)}, \qquad \frac{dy}{dx} = y^2 \quad \text{(order 1)}, \qquad y''' = e^x \quad \text{(order 3)} \]

docs.title: 2.3 Linearity
docs.text:
An ODE of order \(n\) is linear if it has the form:

\[ a_n(x),y^{(n)} + a_{n-1}(x),y^{(n-1)} + \cdots + a_1(x),y' + a_0(x),y = g(x) \]

Key requirements:

  • The unknown \(y\) and each derivative \(y^{(k)}\) appear to the first power.
  • No products like \(y \cdot y'\) or functions like \(\sin(y)\), \(e^y\).

If these fail, the ODE is nonlinear.

ODE Linear? Reason \(y'' - 3y' + 2y = e^x\) ✓ Yes Coefficients depend only on \(x\) \(y' = y^2\) ✗ No \(y^2\) is nonlinear \(y' + (\sin x)y = 0\) ✓ Yes \(\sin x\) is a coefficient, not involving \(y\) \(yy'' = 1\) ✗ No Product \(yy''\) \(y'' + \sin(y) = 0\) ✗ No Pendulum equation — \(\sin(y)\) nonlinear

docs.title: 2.4 Homogeneity (for Linear ODEs)
docs.text:
A linear ODE is:

  • Homogeneous if \(g(x) = 0\): \(\quad a_n y^{(n)} + \cdots + a_0 y = 0\)
  • Non-homogeneous (inhomogeneous) if \(g(x) \neq 0\)

Warning: "Homogeneous" has a different (unrelated) meaning for first-order nonlinear ODEs — see §4.4.

docs.title: 3. Existence and Uniqueness
docs.text: Before solving, we ask: does a solution exist, and is it unique? These are not pedantic questions — they tell you whether your model is well-posed.

docs.title: 3.1 First-Order IVP (Picard–Lindelöf Theorem)
docs.text:
Theorem (Picard–Lindelöf). Consider the initial value problem:

\[ \frac{dy}{dx} = f(x, y), \qquad y(x_0) = y_0 \]

If \(f\) is continuous in a rectangle \(R = {|x - x_0| \leq a,; |y - y_0| \leq b}\) and \(\partial f / \partial y\) is continuous (equivalently, \(f\) is Lipschitz in \(y\)) on \(R\), then:

  1. A solution exists on some interval \(|x - x_0| < h\).
  2. The solution is unique on that interval.

Lipschitz condition (precise): \(\exists, L > 0\) such that \(|f(x,y_1) - f(x,y_2)| \leq L|y_1 - y_2|\) for all \((x,y_1),(x,y_2) \in R\).

The Lipschitz constant \(L\) controls how fast nearby solutions can diverge — it is the local "sensitivity" of the ODE.

docs.title: 3.2 Failure of Uniqueness: A Classic Example
docs.text:
\[ \frac{dy}{dx} = y^{1/3}, \qquad y(0) = 0 \]

Here \(\partial f/\partial y = \frac{1}{3}y^{-2/3}\) blows up at \(y = 0\) — Lipschitz fails. Two distinct solutions pass through \((0,0)\):

\[ y_1(x) = 0 \qquad \text{and} \qquad y_2(x) = \left(\frac{2x}{3}\right)^{3/2} \]

Both satisfy the ODE and initial condition. Uniqueness fails exactly where Lipschitz fails. \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: 3.3 Second-Order IVP
docs.text:
Theorem. For \(y'' + P(x)y' + Q(x)y = G(x)\) with \(P, Q, G\) continuous on interval \(I\) and \((x_0, y_0, y_0') \in I \times \mathbb{R}^2\), there exists a unique solution on all of \(I\).

Note: the solution interval is the entire interval of continuity of the coefficients — much stronger than the first-order result.

docs.title: 4.1 Separable Equations
docs.text:
Form: \(\frac{dy}{dx} = g(x),h(y)\)

Method: Separate and integrate.

\[ \frac{dy}{h(y)} = g(x),dx \implies \int \frac{dy}{h(y)} = \int g(x),dx \]

Example: \(\frac{dy}{dx} = xy\)

\[ \frac{dy}{y} = x,dx \implies \ln|y| = \frac{x^2}{2} + C \implies y = Ae^{x^2/2} \]

This is the Gaussian! It appears as the fundamental solution to the heat equation and as the normal distribution in probability — the solution to the "most entropic" separable ODE.

docs.title: 4.2 Linear First-Order: Integrating Factor
docs.text:
Form: \(\frac{dy}{dx} + P(x)y = Q(x)\)

Integrating factor: \(\mu(x) = e^{\int P(x),dx}\)

Multiply both sides by \(\mu\):

\[ \frac{d}{dx}[\mu(x),y] = \mu(x),Q(x) \]

Integrate:

\[ \boxed{y = \frac{1}{\mu(x)}\left[\int \mu(x),Q(x),dx + C\right]} \]

Why does this work? We are manufacturing a perfect derivative on the left. The product rule gives \(\frac{d}{dx}[\mu y] = \mu y' + \mu' y\). For this to equal \(\mu(y' + Py)\), we need \(\mu' = \mu P\), i.e., \(\mu = e^{\int P,dx}\). \(\blacksquare\)

Example: \(y' + \frac{2}{x}y = x^2\), \(\quad x > 0\)

\[ \mu = e^{\int 2/x, dx} = e^{2\ln x} = x^2 \] \[ \frac{d}{dx}[x^2 y] = x^4 \implies x^2 y = \frac{x^5}{5} + C \implies y = \frac{x^3}{5} + \frac{C}{x^2} \]

docs.title: 4.3 Exact Equations
docs.text:
Form: \(M(x,y),dx + N(x,y),dy = 0\)

Exactness condition: \(\frac{\partial M}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial N}{\partial x}\)

If exact, there exists \(F(x,y)\) with \(F_x = M\), \(F_y = N\), and the solution is \(F(x,y) = C\) (a family of level curves).

Finding \(F\):

\[ F = \int M,dx + g(y) \quad \text{then solve } F_y = N \text{ for } g'(y) \]

Example: \((2xy + 3),dx + (x^2 - 4y^3),dy = 0\)

Check: \(M_y = 2x\), \(N_x = 2x\). ✓ Exact.

\[ F = \int (2xy+3),dx = x^2 y + 3x + g(y) $$ $$ F_y = x^2 + g'(y) = x^2 - 4y^3 \implies g'(y) = -4y^3 \implies g(y) = -y^4 \]

Solution: \(x^2 y + 3x - y^4 = C\)

docs.title: 4.4 Homogeneous First-Order (Substitution \(v = y/x\))
docs.text:
Form: \(\frac{dy}{dx} = F!\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)\)

Substitution: \(v = y/x\), so \(y = vx\), \(y' = v + xv'\):

\[ v + xv' = F(v) \implies \frac{dv}{F(v) - v} = \frac{dx}{x} \]

Now separable. Solve for \(v(x)\), then \(y = vx\).

docs.title: 4.5 Bernoulli Equation
docs.text:
Form: \(y' + P(x)y = Q(x)y^n\), \(n \neq 0, 1\)

Substitution: \(w = y^{1-n}\), which linearizes the equation:

\[ w' + (1-n)P(x)w = (1-n)Q(x) \]

Now a linear first-order ODE — solve by integrating factor.

docs.title: 4.6 Summary Table of First-Order Methods
docs.text: Type Recognizer Method Separable \(y' = g(x)h(y)\) Separate and integrate Linear \(y' + P(x)y = Q(x)\) Integrating factor \(e^{\int P,dx}\) Exact \(M,dx + N,dy=0\), \(M_y=N_x\) Find potential \(F\) Homogeneous \(y' = F(y/x)\) \(v = y/x\) Bernoulli \(y' + Py = Qy^n\) \(w = y^{1-n}\) Logistic \(y' = ry(1-y/K)\) Partial fractions (see [[Models for Population Growth]])

docs.title: 5.1 Structure Theorem
docs.text:
The complete general solution of the non-homogeneous linear ODE:

\[ y'' + P(x)y' + Q(x)y = G(x) \]

is:

\[ \boxed{y = y_h + y_p} \]

where:

  • \(y_h = C_1 y_1 + C_2 y_2\) is the general homogeneous solution (\(y_1, y_2\) linearly independent solutions of the homogeneous equation),
  • \(y_p\) is any particular solution of the full non-homogeneous equation.

Proof sketch: If \(y\) is any solution, then \(y - y_p\) satisfies the homogeneous equation (by linearity), so \(y - y_p \in \text{span}{y_1, y_2}\). \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: 5.2 Constant Coefficients: The Characteristic Equation
docs.text:
For \(ay'' + by' + cy = 0\), try \(y = e^{rx}\):

\[ ar^2 + br + c = 0 \implies r = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a} \]

The discriminant \(\Delta = b^2 - 4ac\) governs the three cases:

Case 1: \(\Delta > 0\) (two distinct real roots \(r_1 \neq r_2\))

\[ y_h = C_1 e^{r_1 x} + C_2 e^{r_2 x} \]

Case 2: \(\Delta = 0\) (repeated root \(r_1 = r_2 = r\))

\[ y_h = (C_1 + C_2 x),e^{rx} \]

Why \(xe^{rx}\)? We need two linearly independent solutions. Since \(e^{rx}\) is already one, we use reduction of order: assume \(y_2 = v(x)e^{rx}\), substitute, and solve for \(v(x) = x\). \(\blacksquare\)

Case 3: \(\Delta < 0\) (complex conjugate roots \(r = \alpha \pm i\beta\))

\[ y_h = e^{\alpha x}(C_1\cos\beta x + C_2\sin\beta x) \]

Euler's formula \(e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta\) converts complex exponentials to real sinusoids.

docs.title: 5.3 The Wronskian and Linear Independence
docs.text:
For two solutions \(y_1, y_2\), the Wronskian is:

\[ W(y_1, y_2)(x) = \begin{vmatrix} y_1 & y_2 \ y_1' & y_2' \end{vmatrix} = y_1 y_2' - y_2 y_1' \]

Theorem (Abel): \(W(x) = W(x_0),\exp!\left(-\int_{x_0}^x P(t),dt\right)\)

Consequence: \(W\) is either identically zero (dependent) or never zero (independent) on \(I\). There is no middle ground.

\(y_1, y_2\) form a fundamental set of solutions \(\iff\) \(W(y_1, y_2) \neq 0\) on \(I\).

docs.title: 5.4 Finding \(y_p\): Method of Undetermined Coefficients
docs.text:
Applies when coefficients are constant and \(G(x)\) is of a "nice" type. Guess \(y_p\) based on the form of \(G(x)\):

\(G(x)\) Trial \(y_p\) \(P_n(x)\) (polynomial degree \(n\)) \(x^s(A_n x^n + \cdots + A_0)\) \(e^{\alpha x}\) \(x^s A e^{\alpha x}\) \(\cos\beta x\) or \(\sin\beta x\) \(x^s(A\cos\beta x + B\sin\beta x)\) \(e^{\alpha x}\cos\beta x\) \(x^s e^{\alpha x}(A\cos\beta x + B\sin\beta x)\) Sum of above Sum of corresponding trials

The modification rule: \(s = 0\) normally; \(s = 1\) if the trial solution duplicates a term in \(y_h\); \(s = 2\) if the duplication is with a repeated root.

Example: \(y'' - 3y' + 2y = e^x\)

Homogeneous: \(r^2 - 3r + 2 = 0 \Rightarrow r = 1, 2\), so \(y_h = C_1 e^x + C_2 e^{2x}\).

\(G = e^x\) and \(e^x\) already appears in \(y_h\) (with \(r=1\)), so use \(y_p = Axe^x\) (\(s=1\)):

\[ y_p' = Ae^x + Axe^x, \quad y_p'' = 2Ae^x + Axe^x \]

Substitute: \((2Ae^x + Axe^x) - 3(Ae^x + Axe^x) + 2Axe^x = -Ae^x = e^x\)

So \(A = -1\), giving \(y_p = -xe^x\).

docs.title: 5.5 Finding \(y_p\): Variation of Parameters
docs.text:
Works for any \(G(x)\) (including non-elementary). Given \(y_h = C_1 y_1 + C_2 y_2\), assume:

\[ y_p = u_1(x),y_1(x) + u_2(x),y_2(x) \]

Impose the auxiliary condition \(u_1' y_1 + u_2' y_2 = 0\) (suppresses second derivatives of \(u\)). Then substituting into the ODE gives:

\[ u_1' y_1' + u_2' y_2' = G(x) \]

Solving this \(2 \times 2\) linear system via Cramer's rule:

\[ \boxed{u_1' = -\frac{y_2, G}{W}, \qquad u_2' = \frac{y_1, G}{W}} \]

Integrate to get \(u_1, u_2\).

Why this works: We have two unknowns \(u_1', u_2'\) and two equations (the auxiliary condition + the ODE). The Wronskian \(W \neq 0\) guarantees the system is non-singular. \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: 6. Systems of ODEs and Phase Plane Analysis
6.1 Converting to First-Order Systems
docs.text:
Any \(n\)-th order ODE can be converted to a system of \(n\) first-order ODEs. For \(y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = g(x)\), let \(y_1 = y\), \(y_2 = y'\):

\[ \dot{y}_1 = y_2, \qquad \dot{y}_2 = g - py_2 - qy_1 \]

In vector form: \(\dot{\mathbf{y}} = A\mathbf{y} + \mathbf{b}\) (if linear), or \(\dot{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{y})\) (general).

This is the standard form for numerical solvers (Euler, Runge–Kutta) and for Neural ODEs.

docs.title: 6.2 Linear Autonomous Systems
docs.text:
\[ \dot{\mathbf{x}} = A\mathbf{x}, \qquad A \in \mathbb{R}^{2\times 2} \]

The solution is \(\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At}\mathbf{x}_0\), where \(e^{At} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(At)^n}{n!}\) (matrix exponential).

The qualitative behavior depends entirely on the eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \lambda_2\) of \(A\):

docs.title: 6.3 Classification of Fixed Points (2D)
docs.text:
Let \(\tau = \text{tr}(A) = \lambda_1 + \lambda_2\) and \(\Delta = \det(A) = \lambda_1\lambda_2\).

Condition Eigenvalues Fixed Point Type Stable? \(\Delta < 0\) Real, opposite signs Saddle Unstable \(\Delta > 0\), \(\tau^2 > 4\Delta\), \(\tau < 0\) Real, both \(< 0\) Stable node ✓ \(\Delta > 0\), \(\tau^2 > 4\Delta\), \(\tau > 0\) Real, both \(> 0\) Unstable node ✗ \(\Delta > 0\), \(\tau^2 < 4\Delta\), \(\tau < 0\) Complex, \(\text{Re}<0\) Stable spiral ✓ \(\Delta > 0\), \(\tau^2 < 4\Delta\), \(\tau > 0\) Complex, \(\text{Re}>0\) Unstable spiral ✗ \(\Delta > 0\), \(\tau = 0\) Pure imaginary Center Neutrally stable
