docs.title: 6.5 Stability: The Lyapunov Framework
docs.text:
Definition. The fixed point \(\mathbf{x}^*\) is:

  • Stable (Lyapunov): \(\forall \varepsilon > 0\), \(\exists \delta > 0\) s.t. \(|\mathbf{x}(0) - \mathbf{x}^_| < \delta \implies |\mathbf{x}(t) - \mathbf{x}^_| < \varepsilon\) for all \(t > 0\).
  • Asymptotically stable: Stable and \(\mathbf{x}(t) \to \mathbf{x}^*\) as \(t \to \infty\).
  • Unstable: Not stable.

Lyapunov's Direct Method. If there exists \(V: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) with:

  1. \(V(\mathbf{x}^_) = 0\) and \(V(\mathbf{x}) > 0\) for \(\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{x}^_\),
  2. \(\dot{V}(\mathbf{x}) = \nabla V \cdot \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}) \leq 0\),

then \(\mathbf{x}^*\) is stable. If \(\dot{V} < 0\) (strictly), it is asymptotically stable.

\(V\) is a "generalized energy" that the system dissipates. Finding \(V\) is an art — for quadratic systems, \(V = \mathbf{x}^\top P \mathbf{x}\) with \(P\) the solution to the Lyapunov matrix equation \(A^\top P + PA = -Q\).

docs.title: 7. Numerical Methods: The Bridge to Computation
docs.text: Analytic solutions are the exception. Numerical methods are the rule.

docs.title: 7.1 Euler's Method
docs.text:
For \(y' = f(x,y)\), \(y(x_0) = y_0\), with step \(h\):

\[ y_{n+1} = y_n + h,f(x_n, y_n) \]

This is a first-order Taylor approximation: \(y(x+h) \approx y(x) + hy'(x)\).

Local truncation error: \(O(h^2)\). Global error: \(O(h)\).

docs.title: 7.2 Improved Euler (Heun's Method)
docs.text:
A predictor-corrector scheme:

\[ \tilde{y}_{n+1} = y_n + h,f(x_n, y_n) \qquad \text{(predict)} $$ $$ y_{n+1} = y_n + \frac{h}{2}\left[f(x_n, y_n) + f(x_{n+1}, \tilde{y}_{n+1})\right] \qquad \text{(correct)} \]

Global error: \(O(h^2)\).

docs.title: 7.3 Runge–Kutta (RK4)
docs.text:
The workhorse of scientific computing. Four slope evaluations per step:

\[ k_1 = f(x_n,, y_n) $$ $$ k_2 = f!\left(x_n + \tfrac{h}{2},, y_n + \tfrac{h}{2}k_1\right) $$ $$ k_3 = f!\left(x_n + \tfrac{h}{2},, y_n + \tfrac{h}{2}k_2\right) $$ $$ k_4 = f!\left(x_n + h,, y_n + h,k_3\right) $$ $$ \boxed{y_{n+1} = y_n + \frac{h}{6}\left(k_1 + 2k_2 + 2k_3 + k_4\right)} \]

Global error: \(O(h^4)\). The weighted average \(\frac{1}{6}(k_1 + 2k_2 + 2k_3 + k_4)\) is a Simpson's rule approximation to the integral \(\int_0^h f,dt\).

docs.title: 7.4 Comparison
docs.text:
Method          | Order | Evaluations/step | Use when
─────────────────|───────|──────────────────|──────────────────
Euler           |   1   |        1         | Teaching only
Improved Euler  |   2   |        2         | Quick estimates
RK4             |   4   |        4         | Most problems
RK45 (adaptive) |  4–5  |       6–7        | Production (scipy)

docs.title: 8. A Brief Look at PDEs
docs.text: The most important PDEs in science all arise from ODE-like local balance laws.

docs.title: 8.1 The Big Three
docs.text:
Heat (diffusion) equation: $$ \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \alpha \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} $$ Models heat conduction, diffusion of particles, probability density evolution (Fokker–Planck).

Wave equation: $$ \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = c^2 \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} $$ Models sound, light, vibrating strings. Second-order in both \(t\) and \(x\) — the spring ODE extended to a continuum.

Laplace/Poisson equation: $$ \nabla^2 u = 0 \quad \text{(Laplace)}, \qquad \nabla^2 u = f \quad \text{(Poisson)} $$ Models steady-state heat, electrostatics, fluid potential. Solutions are harmonic functions.

docs.title: 8.2 Separation of Variables for PDEs
docs.text:
The standard technique: assume \(u(x,t) = X(x)T(t)\). For the heat equation:

\[ \frac{T'}{T} = \alpha\frac{X''}{X} = -\lambda \quad \text{(separation constant)} \]

This yields two ODEs: $$ T' = -\lambda T \implies T(t) = e^{-\lambda t} $$ $$ X'' = -\frac{\lambda}{\alpha}X \implies X(x) = A\cos(\mu x) + B\sin(\mu x), \quad \mu = \sqrt{\lambda/\alpha} $$

Boundary conditions on \(X\) force \(\lambda\) to take discrete values — eigenvalues — and the solution is a Fourier series. The PDE reduces to infinitely many decoupled ODEs.

docs.title: 9. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: The ODE is not a detour from ML — it is ML's hidden foundation.

docs.title: 9.1 Every Gradient Flow Is an ODE
docs.text:
Training a neural network by gradient descent on loss \(L(\theta)\) is, in the continuous limit, solving:

\[ \frac{d\theta}{dt} = -\nabla_\theta L(\theta) \]

This is a first-order autonomous ODE — a gradient flow. The minima of \(L\) are exactly the stable fixed points of this ODE. Saddle points are unstable fixed points. The entire theory of §6 (stability, phase portraits, Lyapunov functions) applies to understanding optimization.

docs.title: 9.2 Neural ODEs (Chen et al., 2018)
docs.text:
A ResNet layer: \(h_{t+1} = h_t + f_\theta(h_t)\) is Euler's method with \(h=1\) applied to \(\dot{h} = f_\theta(h)\).

The Neural ODE takes the continuous limit: define the hidden state by the IVP:

\[ \frac{dh}{dt} = f_\theta(h(t), t), \qquad h(0) = x \]

The network "depth" becomes a continuous time variable. Output is \(h(T)\), computed by any ODE solver (e.g., RK45). Backpropagation through the solver uses the adjoint method — a classical ODE technique for sensitivity analysis.

The adjoint \(\mathbf{a}(t) = \partial L / \partial h(t)\) satisfies a backward ODE:

\[ \frac{d\mathbf{a}}{dt} = -\mathbf{a}^\top \frac{\partial f_\theta}{\partial h} \]

This is variation of parameters / the transpose of the linearized forward equation.

docs.title: 9.3 Stability ↔ Generalization
docs.text:
The damping theory of §5 (Spring note) and the stability theory of §6 both say: negative real parts of eigenvalues \(\Rightarrow\) convergence to a fixed point.

In neural networks:

  • The Jacobian \(J = \partial f_\theta / \partial h\) at a fixed point plays the role of the matrix \(A\).
  • If all eigenvalues of \(J\) have negative real parts: the network's representation is stable — small input perturbations don't explode. This is related to robustness and adversarial stability.
  • If eigenvalues have positive real parts: exploding activations or sensitivity to inputs.

docs.title: 9.4 Diffusion Models (Score-Based Generative Models)
docs.text:
The forward process of a diffusion model (DDPM, score matching) is the stochastic differential equation:

\[ dx = -\frac{1}{2}\beta(t),x,dt + \sqrt{\beta(t)},dW_t \]

This is the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process — a damped linear ODE with noise. Specifically:

  • The deterministic part \(-\frac{1}{2}\beta(t)x\) is an exponentially decaying ODE (overdamped spring with time-varying \(k\)).
  • The noise \(dW_t\) is Brownian motion.

The reverse process (generation = denoising) solves a backward SDE derived from the score function \(\nabla_x \log p_t(x)\). Learning this score is exactly learning the drift of an ODE.

Without understanding the forward/backward ODE, diffusion models are a black box. With it, they become a natural extension of the framework we've built.

docs.title: 9.5 Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs)
docs.text:
PINNs solve PDEs by embedding the equation as a loss term. For PDE \(\mathcal{N}[u] = 0\):

\[ L(\theta) = \underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_i |u_\theta(x_i, t_i) - u_{\text{data}}(x_i, t_i)|^2}_{\text{data loss}} + \underbrace{\frac{1}{M}\sum_j |\mathcal{N}[u_\theta](x_j, t_j)|^2}_{\text{physics loss}} \]

The neural network \(u_\theta\) is trained to satisfy both data and the differential equation simultaneously. The network is the approximate solution to the PDE, and the ODE/PDE theory determines whether the solution is physically reasonable.

docs.title: 9.6 Numerical Solvers Inside ML
docs.text: Modern ML frameworks (JAX, PyTorch) include differentiable ODE solvers (torchdiffeq, diffrax). These compute \(\frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}\int_0^T f_\theta(h,t),dt\) using the adjoint method. Every concept from §7 (Euler, RK4, step size, stability) is directly relevant to training speed and numerical accuracy.

docs.title: 10. The Existence–Methods–Qualitative Trinity
docs.text:
The most important meta-lesson of this subject:

                    DIFFERENTIAL EQUATION
                           │
           ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐
           │               │               │
     EXISTENCE &      ANALYTIC         QUALITATIVE
     UNIQUENESS       SOLUTIONS        ANALYSIS
     (Picard–        (separation,      (phase plane,
      Lindelöf)       integrating       fixed points,
                      factor,           Lyapunov,
                      char. eq.,        stability)
                      var. params.)
           │               │               │
           └───────────────┴───────────────┘
                           │
                    NUMERICAL METHODS
                    (Euler, RK4, etc.)
                    when analytic fails

Many ODEs have no closed-form solution. Qualitative and numerical methods are not fallbacks — they are the primary tools for most real-world problems. Analytic solutions, when they exist, provide exact benchmarks and structural insight.

docs.title: 11. Quick-Reference: Solution Forms
docs.text:
First-order: $$ y' = ky \implies y = Ce^{kx} $$ $$ y' + P(x)y = Q(x) \implies y = e^{-\int P,dx}!\left[\int Q,e^{\int P,dx},dx + C\right] $$

Second-order, constant coefficients \(ay''+by'+cy=0\):

Discriminant Roots Solution \(b^2-4ac>0\) \(r_1\neq r_2\) real \(C_1e^{r_1 x}+C_2 e^{r_2 x}\) \(b^2-4ac=0\) \(r\) repeated \((C_1+C_2 x)e^{rx}\) \(b^2-4ac<0\) \(\alpha\pm i\beta\) \(e^{\alpha x}(C_1\cos\beta x+C_2\sin\beta x)\)

Variation of parameters: $$ u_1' = -\frac{y_2 G}{W}, \qquad u_2' = \frac{y_1 G}{W}, \qquad W = y_1 y_2' - y_2 y_1' $$

Matrix exponential (linear system \(\dot{\mathbf{x}}=A\mathbf{x}\)): $$ \mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At}\mathbf{x}_0, \qquad e^{At} = P,\text{diag}(e^{\lambda_i t}),P^{-1} \quad \text{(when } A \text{ diagonalizable)} $$

docs.title: 12. Exercises (Self-Check)
docs.text:
1. Classification. Classify each as order/linear/homogeneous: (a) \(y'' + (\sin x)y = e^x\), (b) \(yy' = x\), © \(y''' - y = 0\), (d) \(y' + y^2 = 1\).

  2. Non-uniqueness. Verify that both \(y=0\) and \(y=(x/2)^2\) solve \(y' = \sqrt{y}\), \(y(0)=0\). Where does Picard–Lindelöf fail?

  3. Integrating factor. Solve \(y' + (\cot x)y = \cos x\). (Hint: \(\int\cot x,dx = \ln|\sin x|\).)

  4. Exact equation. Show \((e^x\sin y + 2x)dx + (e^x\cos y + 2y)dy = 0\) is exact and find the general solution.

  5. Wronskian. For \(y'' - y = 0\) with solutions \(y_1 = e^x\), \(y_2 = e^{-x}\): compute \(W\), verify Abel's theorem, and confirm the discriminant of the characteristic equation matches.

  6. Variation of parameters. Solve \(y'' + y = \sec x\) using variation of parameters. (The method of undetermined coefficients fails here — why?)

  7. Phase portrait. For \(\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 2 \ 0 & -3 \end{pmatrix}\mathbf{x}\): find eigenvalues, classify the fixed point, sketch the phase portrait.

  8. Neural ODE. Write the spring equation \(\ddot{x} + 2\gamma\dot{x} + \omega_0^2 x = 0\) as a first-order system. Apply Euler's method with step \(h\). For what values of \(h\) does the discrete system remain stable? (Compare \(|\lambda h| \leq 2\) for Euler stability.)

  9. Gradient flow. For \(L(\theta) = \frac{1}{2}(\theta - \theta^_)^2\), solve the gradient flow ODE \(\dot{\theta} = -L'(\theta)\) explicitly. Show it is an integrating-factor problem. At what rate does \(\theta(t) \to \theta^_\)?

  10. Diffusion intuition. The forward diffusion SDE has deterministic part \(\dot{x} = -\frac{\beta}{2}x\). Solve this ODE. What does the solution say about the long-term fate of any initial data point? Why is this desirable for a generative model?

docs.title: Direction Fields
docs.text:
A professor's working notebook — rigorous, honest, and a little opinionated.

Tags: #ODE #direction-fields #qualitative-analysis #calculus #ML-connection References: Stewart §9.2 · MIT 18.02 · Strogatz Ch. 2 Date: 2026-04-18 Related notes: [[General Differential Equations]] · [[Models for Population Growth]] · [[Models for the Motion of a Spring]]

docs.title: 0. The Central Idea
docs.text:
Most ODEs cannot be solved explicitly. Yet we can see the solution without solving anything.

The direction field (also called a slope field) is a picture of the ODE itself — before any solving. At every point \((x, y)\) in the plane, the ODE \(y' = f(x, y)\) tells us the slope a solution curve must have if it passes through that point. Draw a tiny line segment with that slope at each point, and the plane fills with arrows that guide solution curves like a river guides a boat.

Epistemological point worth internalizing: A direction field is not an approximation. It is an exact graphical representation of the ODE. The solution curves are the unique curves that are everywhere tangent to the field.

docs.title: 1. Definition
docs.text:
Let \(y' = f(x, y)\) be a first-order ODE. The direction field (slope field) is the assignment:

\[ (x, y) ;\longmapsto; \text{line segment through } (x,y) \text{ with slope } f(x,y) \]

defined at every point in the domain of \(f\).

A solution curve (integral curve) is a curve \(y = \phi(x)\) such that at every point on the curve, the tangent line coincides exactly with the direction field segment at that point:

\[ \phi'(x) = f(x, \phi(x)) \quad \text{for all } x \text{ in the domain.} \]

docs.title: 2. How to Sketch a Direction Field by Hand
2.1 The Isocline Method
docs.text:
An isocline is the set of points where the slope takes a fixed value \(c\):

\[ \mathcal{I}_c = {(x, y) : f(x, y) = c} \]

Along each isocline, all direction-field segments have the same slope \(c\). This makes sketching systematic:

Procedure:

  1. Choose several values \(c \in {-2, -1, 0, 1, 2, \ldots}\).
  2. Plot the curve \(f(x,y) = c\) (the isocline) for each \(c\).
  3. Along each isocline, draw parallel line segments of slope \(c\).
  4. Fill in between by interpolation.

docs.title: 2.2 Special Case: The Nullcline
docs.text:
The isocline \(c = 0\) is called the nullcline: \(f(x,y) = 0\).

Along the nullcline, all segments are horizontal (\(y' = 0\)). Solution curves have local extrema exactly where they cross the nullcline. This is often the most informative single curve to draw first.

docs.title: 2.3 Worked Example 1 — Autonomous ODE: \(y' = y(1-y)\)
docs.text:
(The logistic equation with \(r = K = 1\).)

Isoclines: \(y(1-y) = c\), i.e., horizontal lines in \(y\) (since \(f\) doesn't depend on \(x\)!):

\(c\) Isocline \(y(1-y) = c\) Slope of segments \(0\) \(y = 0\) or \(y = 1\) (nullclines) horizontal — \(1/4\) \(y = 1/2\) (vertex of parabola) slope \(1/4\) ↗ \(-1\) \(y \approx -0.618\) or \(y \approx 1.618\) slope \(-1\) ↘

Sketch:

y
 2  ─────────────────────────────────  (slope < 0 here: y decreasing)
    ↘   ↘   ↘   ↘   ↘   ↘   ↘   ↘
 1  ─────────────────────────────────  ← nullcline y=1 (stable equilibrium)
    ↗   ↗   ↗   ↗   ↗   ↗   ↗   ↗
1/2 · · · · · · · · · · · · · · · · · ← max slope here
    ↗   ↗   ↗   ↗   ↗   ↗   ↗   ↗
 0  ─────────────────────────────────  ← nullcline y=0 (unstable equilibrium)
    ↘   ↘   ↘   ↘   ↘   ↘   ↘   ↘
-1  ─────────────────────────────────  (slope < 0: y continues falling)
    ──────────────────────────────→ x

Reading the field:

  • For \(0 < y < 1\): \(f > 0\), arrows point up-right. Solutions rise toward \(y = 1\).
  • For \(y > 1\): \(f < 0\), arrows point down-right. Solutions fall toward \(y = 1\).
  • For \(y < 0\): \(f < 0\), arrows fall away. Solutions fall to \(-\infty\).
  • \(y = 1\): stable equilibrium. \(y = 0\): unstable equilibrium.

Without solving, we see the full story of the logistic equation.

docs.title: 2.4 Worked Example 2 — Non-Autonomous: \(y' = x - y\)
docs.text:
Nullcline: \(x - y = 0\), i.e., the line \(y = x\). Horizontal segments here.

Isoclines: \(x - y = c \Rightarrow y = x - c\) — a family of parallel lines of slope 1.

Isocline \(y = x - c\) Slope of segments \(y = x\) (i.e., \(c=0\)) \(0\) — \(y = x - 1\) (i.e., \(c=1\)) \(1\) ↗ \(y = x + 1\) (i.e., \(c=-1\)) \(-1\) ↘ \(y = x - 2\) \(2\) ↗↗

Sketch:

y
 3|  ↘  ↘  ↘  ↘
  |    ↘  ↘  ↘  ↘
 2|  —  —  ↘  ↘  ↘
  |  ↗  —  —  ↘  ↘
 1|  ↗  ↗  —  —  ↘
  |  ↗  ↗  ↗  —  —
 0|  ↗  ↗  ↗  ↗  —
  |─────────────────→ x
    0   1   2   3

Nullcline: diagonal y = x
Solutions curve toward y = x - 1 (the particular solution)

The exact solution is \(y = x - 1 + Ce^{-x}\). As \(x \to \infty\), \(e^{-x} \to 0\) and all solutions converge to \(y = x - 1\). The direction field shows this funnel without any algebra.

docs.title: 3.1 Definition
docs.text:
An ODE \(y' = f(y)\) is autonomous if \(f\) does not explicitly depend on \(x\). The direction field has a special structure: all segments on a given horizontal line \(y = c\) have the same slope \(f(c)\).

This means the direction field is translation-invariant in \(x\) — horizontally shifting a solution gives another solution.

docs.title: 3.2 The Phase Line
docs.text:
For autonomous \(y' = f(y)\), the full qualitative story is captured on a 1D phase line — just the \(y\)-axis:

Procedure:

  1. Find equilibria: \(f(y^*) = 0\).
  2. Determine the sign of \(f(y)\) in each interval between equilibria.
  3. Draw arrows: \(\uparrow\) where \(f > 0\) (solutions increase), \(\downarrow\) where \(f < 0\) (solutions decrease).
  4. Classify each equilibrium:
    • Stable: arrows point toward \(y^*\) from both sides.
    • Unstable: arrows point away from \(y^*\) on both sides.
    • Semi-stable: arrows on one side point toward, the other away.

Example: \(y' = y(1-y)(2-y)\)

Equilibria: \(y^* = 0, 1, 2\).

Sign of \(f\):

  • \(y < 0\): \(f = (-)((+))(+) < 0\) ↓
  • \(0 < y < 1\): \(f = (+)((+))(+) > 0\) ↑ ... wait, \((1-y) > 0\), \((2-y) > 0\), \(y > 0\): \(f > 0\) ↑
  • \(1 < y < 2\): \(f = (+)((-))( +) < 0\) ↓
  • \(y > 2\): \(f = (+)((-))(-) > 0\) ↑

Phase line:

y
↑  ↑  ↑
2  ●  ←── unstable (arrows away below, away above... wait)
↓  ↓  ↓     actually: ↓ below, ↑ above → unstable
1  ●  ←── stable (↑ below, ↓ above)
↑  ↑  ↑
0  ●  ←── unstable (↓ below, ↑ above)
↓  ↓  ↓

Wait — re-examine at \(y=2\): below \(y=2\) (i.e., \(1<y<2\)): \(f < 0\) ↓; above \(y=2\) (i.e., \(y>2\)): \(f > 0\) ↑. So arrows diverge from \(y=2\): unstable. At \(y=1\): below \(↑\), above \(↓\): stable. At \(y=0\): below \(↓\), above \(↑\): unstable.

     ↑ (y > 2: rising)
 2 ──●── unstable
     ↓ (1 < y < 2: falling)
 1 ──●── stable  ← global attractor for 0 < y < 2
     ↑ (0 < y < 1: rising)
 0 ──●── unstable
     ↓ (y < 0: falling)

The direction field in the \((x,y)\)-plane is the "extrusion" of this phase line horizontally — the same arrow pattern repeated at every \(x\).

docs.title: 4. Reading Qualitative Information from Direction Fields
docs.text:
A direction field lets you answer the following questions without solving:

Question How to read from the field Where are equilibria? Horizontal rows of horizontal segments (autonomous) Is an equilibrium stable? Do nearby segments point toward or away from it? Do solutions blow up? Do slopes steepen and curve sharply upward/downward? Are solutions bounded? Do all arrows funnel into a bounded band? What is the long-run behavior? Follow arrows from any initial condition forward Do solutions have inflection points? Where the slope \(f(x,y)\) itself is neither increasing nor decreasing along trajectories

docs.title: 4.1 Funnel and Spout
docs.text:
• Funnel: A region in the direction field where all solutions entering it converge to a single curve. Indicates a stable attractor.
  • Spout (anti-funnel): A region where solutions diverge. Indicates an unstable trajectory.

For \(y' = x - y\) above: the line \(y = x - 1\) is a funnel — all solutions flow toward it as \(x \to \infty\).

docs.title: 5. From Direction Field to Euler's Method
docs.text:
Direction fields are not just pictures — they are the geometric soul of Euler's method.

Recall Euler's method for \(y' = f(x,y)\), \(y(x_0) = y_0\), step \(h\):

\[ y_{n+1} = y_n + h \cdot f(x_n, y_n) \]

Geometric interpretation: Start at \((x_0, y_0)\). The direction field gives slope \(f(x_0, y_0)\). Walk along that segment for horizontal distance \(h\) to reach \((x_1, y_1)\). Repeat.

y
 |        ___true solution curve
 |      _/·
 |    _/ ··   ← Euler polygonal path
 |  _/  ·
 |_/  ·
 | ↗·
 |/·
 +──────────────→ x
  x₀  x₁  x₂  x₃

Each arrow = one direction-field segment walked for distance h.

Euler's method is literally following the direction field one step at a time. The error at each step arises because the field changes direction before we correct our heading — the smaller \(h\), the more frequently we re-consult the field, the more accurate the path.

This geometric picture explains:

  • Why Euler's method underestimates when the solution is concave-up (the slope is rising, but we're using the old slope too long).
  • Why RK4 is better: it samples the field at multiple points within each step, computing a weighted average slope — a more faithful reading of the field.

docs.title: 6. Existence, Uniqueness, and the Direction Field
docs.text:
Picard–Lindelöf guarantees (under continuity + Lipschitz) that exactly one solution curve passes through each point. This has a direct visual consequence:

Theorem (Non-Crossing). If the conditions of Picard–Lindelöf hold, then distinct solution curves of \(y' = f(x,y)\) cannot intersect.

Proof. Suppose two distinct solutions \(\phi_1\) and \(\phi_2\) both pass through \((x_0, y_0)\): \(\phi_1(x_0) = \phi_2(x_0) = y_0\). By uniqueness, \(\phi_1 \equiv \phi_2\) on the interval — contradiction. \(\blacksquare\)

Visual corollary: In a well-posed direction field, the solution curves form non-intersecting, non-crossing families that foliate the plane. Like streamlines of a fluid — they never cross.

Where uniqueness fails: At points where \(f\) or \(\partial f/\partial y\) is discontinuous, the non-crossing guarantee breaks, and multiple solution curves can pass through a single point (as in the \(y' = y^{1/3}\) example).

docs.title: 7.1 Example: \(y' = y^2 - x\)
docs.text:
Nullcline: \(y^2 = x\), i.e., \(x = y^2\) (a rightward parabola). Horizontal segments here.

Sign analysis:

  • Left of parabola (\(x > y^2\)): \(y' = y^2 - x < 0\) → segments slope downward ↘
  • Right of parabola (\(x < y^2\)): \(y' = y^2 - x > 0\) → segments slope upward ↗

Isoclines: \(y^2 - x = c\) → \(x = y^2 - c\) (parabolas shifted left by \(c\)).

y
 2|  ↗  ↗  ↗|↘  ↘  ↘
  |         |
 1|  ↗  ↗  ↗|↘  ↘  ↘
  |         |
 0|  ↗  ↗  ↗|↘  ↘  ↘
  |         |
-1|  ↗  ↗  ↗|↘  ↘  ↘
  |─────────|───────────→ x
  0         ← nullcline x = y²

Solutions starting far right (large \(x\)) have negative slopes and bend toward the nullcline. Solutions that cross the nullcline begin rising again. This ODE has no simple analytic solution — the direction field is essential.

docs.title: 7.2 Example: \(y' = \sin(y)\) (Autonomous)
docs.text:
Equilibria: \(\sin(y^_) = 0 \Rightarrow y^_ = n\pi\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).

Sign pattern: \(\sin(y) > 0\) for \(y \in (0, \pi)\); \(\sin(y) < 0\) for \(y \in (\pi, 2\pi)\); etc.

Stability:

  • \(y^* = 2k\pi\): \(\frac{d}{dy}\sin(y)\big|_{y^*} = \cos(2k\pi) = 1 > 0\) → unstable (derivative test)
  • \(y^* = (2k+1)\pi\): \(\cos((2k+1)\pi) = -1 < 0\) → stable

Linearization stability test: For autonomous \(y' = f(y)\), equilibrium \(y^*\) is:

  • Stable if \(f'(y^*) < 0\) (slope of \(f\) is negative at the fixed point)
  • Unstable if \(f'(y^*) > 0\)

This is the 1D version of the eigenvalue stability criterion from [[General Differential Equations]] §6.

Phase line for \(y' = \sin y\):

     ↑ (rising: sin > 0)
 π ──●── stable
     ↓ (falling: sin < 0)
 0 ──●── unstable
     ↑ (rising: sin > 0)  ... wait, sin(y) < 0 for y ∈ (-π, 0)
-π ──●── stable
     ↑

Correcting: for \(y \in (-\pi, 0)\): \(\sin y < 0\) ↓; for \(y \in (0, \pi)\): \(\sin y > 0\) ↑.

     ↑ (0 < y < π)
 π ──●── stable   (↑ below, ↓ above)
     ↓ (π < y < 2π)
2π ──●── unstable (↓ below, ↑ above)

The direction field is a horizontal striped pattern: bands of rising and falling, alternating at each multiple of \(\pi\).

docs.title: 8. The Geometry of \(y' = f(x, y)\): Deeper Structure
8.1 Level Sets of \(f\) Are Isoclines
docs.text: The isoclines \(f(x,y) = c\) are the level curves of \(f\) viewed as a function of two variables. Sketching isoclines is exactly the same skill as sketching level curves from MIT 18.02 — the direction field connects ODE theory to multivariable calculus.

docs.title: 8.2 The Direction Field as a Line Field
docs.text:
Formally, a direction field is a line field on the plane: at each point \((x,y)\), we assign a 1-dimensional linear subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) — the tangent line of slope \(f(x,y)\). This is a section of the projectivized tangent bundle \(PT\mathbb{R}^2\).

A solution curve is a horizontal section — a curve whose tangent direction is everywhere in the assigned line. This is the beginning of the geometric theory of ODEs (Lie, Cartan, Frobenius), which generalizes to PDEs and differential geometry.

docs.title: 8.3 Integral Curves as Trajectories
docs.text:
The direction field of \(y' = f(x,y)\) can be written as the vector field:

\[ \mathbf{v}(x,y) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \ f(x,y) \end{pmatrix} \]

(We always move at speed 1 in the \(x\)-direction.) The integral curves of \(\mathbf{v}\) — curves everywhere tangent to \(\mathbf{v}\) — are exactly the solution curves. This is the MIT 18.02 viewpoint: solving an ODE = finding integral curves of a vector field.

docs.title: 9. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
9.1 Loss Landscape as a Direction Field
docs.text:
In optimization, the gradient flow \(\dot{\theta} = -\nabla L(\theta)\) defines a vector field (direction field) on the parameter space. The direction field of this ODE is the negative gradient field — the arrows point in the direction of steepest descent.

Gradient descent is Euler's method on this direction field. Every insight from §5 applies directly:

  • Large learning rate \(h\): coarse reading of the field → possible overshoot.
  • Small learning rate: fine reading → slow but accurate.
  • The loss landscape's basins, ridges, and saddles are the direction field's funnels, spouts, and saddle trajectories.

Visualizing the direction field of \(\dot{\theta} = -\nabla L(\theta)\) for a simple model (say, 2D parameter space) is literally the same exercise as drawing the direction field of a first-order ODE.

docs.title: 9.2 Neural ODE Vector Fields
docs.text:
In a Neural ODE, the network \(f_\theta(h, t)\) defines a direction field in the hidden-state space \(\mathbb{R}^d\). Training the network is training the direction field itself — adjusting \(\theta\) to make the integral curves of the field match the desired input-output mapping.

The direction field picture makes certain properties immediately visible:

  • If the field is convergent (funneling), the network is robust to perturbations.
  • If the field has spirals, the hidden state oscillates — potentially useful for time-series.
  • If the field has saddles, nearby trajectories diverge exponentially — dangerous for stability.

docs.title: 9.3 Score Functions in Diffusion Models
docs.text:
The score function \(\nabla_x \log p_t(x)\) in a diffusion model is exactly the direction field for the reverse-time SDE. At each point \(x\) in data space at time \(t\), the score tells you the direction (slope) in which \(p_t\) increases most rapidly. The reverse diffusion process follows this direction field from noise back to data — it is an integral curve problem.

Learning the score is learning the direction field of the reverse process.

docs.title: 9.4 Continuous Normalizing Flows
docs.text:
A normalizing flow transforms a simple distribution (e.g., Gaussian) into a complex one via a learned diffeomorphism. The continuous version (CNF) defines this transformation as the flow of an ODE:

\[ \frac{dz}{dt} = f_\theta(z, t), \qquad z(0) \sim p_0 \]

The direction field of \(f_\theta\) determines the transformation. The Jacobian of the flow — needed to compute the change-of-variables formula for the log-likelihood — is computed via the instantaneous change of variables formula:

\[ \frac{d\log p(z(t))}{dt} = -\text{tr}!\left(\frac{\partial f_\theta}{\partial z}\right) \]

This is a consequence of Liouville's theorem from classical mechanics: the divergence of the direction field governs the expansion/compression of probability mass.

docs.title: 9.5 Summary
docs.text:
Direction Field Concept ML/DL Analogue Direction field / slope field Gradient field \(-
abla L(	heta)\) in parameter space Integral curve / solution curve Gradient descent trajectory Euler's method on field SGD with fixed learning rate Nullcline (zero-slope locus) Stationary points of loss (\(
abla L = 0\)) Stable equilibrium (funnel) Loss minimum, attractor Unstable equilibrium (spout) Saddle point, loss maximum Non-crossing of integral curves Uniqueness of gradient trajectories (Picard–Lindelöf) Neural ODE direction field Learned vector field \(f_	heta(h,t)\) in hidden space Score function \(
abla\log p_t\) Direction field of reverse diffusion SDE Liouville / flow divergence Log-likelihood in continuous normalizing flows

docs.title: 10. Formal Summary: What a Direction Field Encodes
docs.text:
Given \(y' = f(x,y)\):

\[ \text{Direction field} ;\longleftrightarrow; \begin{cases} \text{Geometry of all solutions simultaneously} \ \text{Location and stability of equilibria (autonomous)} \ \text{Long-run behavior without solving} \ \text{Initial value dependence (non-crossing foliation)} \ \text{Numerical method geometry (Euler, RK4)} \end{cases} \]

The direction field is the qualitative theory of the ODE made visual.

docs.title: 11. Quick-Reference
docs.text:
Isocline: \(f(x,y) = c\) — curve along which all segments have slope \(c\).

Nullcline: \(f(x,y) = 0\) — horizontal segments, location of extrema.

Autonomous ODE \(y' = f(y)\):

  • Equilibria at \(f(y^*) = 0\)
  • Stable if \(f'(y^_) < 0\); unstable if \(f'(y^_) > 0\)
  • Phase line = 1D direction field on \(y\)-axis

Non-crossing theorem: Under Picard–Lindelöf, distinct solution curves never intersect.

Euler's method = walking along direction field with step \(h\).

Stability test (linearization): Eigenvalue of \(f'(y^_)\) determines stability in 1D; eigenvalues of Jacobian \(Df(\mathbf{x}^_)\) in 2D.

docs.title: 12. Exercises
docs.text:
1. Isoclines. For \(y' = x^2 + y^2\): write the isoclines, describe their geometry, and sketch the direction field for \(-2 \leq x,y \leq 2\). Can solutions decrease? Are there equilibria?

  2. Autonomous phase line. For \(y' = y^2 - 4\): find all equilibria, classify them (stable/unstable), draw the phase line, and describe the fate of solutions starting at \(y(0) = 0\), \(y(0) = 3\), \(y(0) = -3\).

  3. Non-crossing. The ODE \(y' = 2y\) has solutions \(y = Ce^{2x}\). Verify that distinct members of this family never intersect. Now consider \(y' = 2y^{1/2}\): find two solutions through \((0,0)\), and identify exactly where the non-crossing guarantee fails.

  4. Direction field and Euler. For \(y' = y - x\), \(y(0) = 0.5\): sketch the direction field. Perform 3 steps of Euler's method with \(h = 0.5\). The exact solution is \(y = (x+1) + Ce^x\); find \(C\) from the initial condition and compute the error at \(x = 1.5\).

  5. Stability via linearization. For \(y' = \sin(\pi y)\): find all equilibria in \([-2, 2]\), compute \(f'(y^*)\) at each, classify as stable or unstable, and draw the phase line.

  6. Funnel. For \(y' = -y + \sin x\): the particular solution is \(y_p = \frac{1}{2}(\sin x - \cos x)\). Using the direction field, argue (without solving) that all solutions converge to \(y_p\) as \(x \to \infty\). What does this say about the direction field far from \(y_p\)?

  7. Neural ODE connection. Consider the direction field \(\dot{h} = -h + \tanh(wh)\) for \(h \in \mathbb{R}\), \(w > 0\). Find all equilibria (as a function of \(w\)). Show that for \(w \leq 1\) there is only one equilibrium, but for \(w > 1\) there are three — a bifurcation. Sketch the phase line for each case and relate this to the expressivity of a Neural ODE unit.

docs.title: Euler's Method
docs.text:
A professor's working notebook — rigorous, honest, and a little opinionated.

Tags: #ODE #numerical-methods #calculus #approximation #ML-connection References: Stewart §9.2 · MIT 18.02 · Burden & Faires Numerical Analysis Date: 2026-04-18 Related notes: [[Direction Fields]] · [[General Differential Equations]] · [[Models for Population Growth]]

docs.title: 0. Orientation
docs.text:
Euler's method is simultaneously the simplest numerical ODE solver, the geometric act of walking a direction field, the conceptual ancestor of every modern integrator, and — as we will see — the exact mathematical operation performed by a residual neural network at each layer.

It is tempting to dismiss Euler's method as a toy. Resist that temptation. Its errors are instructive, its geometry is exact, and understanding why it fails is the prerequisite for understanding why RK4, adaptive solvers, and implicit methods work.

docs.title: 1. The Setup
docs.text:
We want to approximate the solution to the initial value problem (IVP):

\[ \frac{dy}{dx} = f(x, y), \qquad y(x_0) = y_0 \]

We cannot (or choose not to) find the exact solution analytically. Instead, we approximate \(y(x)\) at a discrete sequence of points:

\[ x_0,; x_1 = x_0 + h,; x_2 = x_0 + 2h,; \ldots,; x_n = x_0 + nh \]

where \(h > 0\) is the step size.

docs.title: 2. Derivation: Three Equivalent Viewpoints
docs.text: The formula is the same from all three angles. Understanding all three is what separates a user of Euler's method from someone who truly knows it.

docs.title: 2.1 Taylor Series
docs.text:
Expand \(y(x + h)\) around \(x\):

\[ y(x+h) = y(x) + h,y'(x) + \frac{h^2}{2},y''(x) + \frac{h^3}{6},y'''(x) + \cdots \]

We know \(y'(x) = f(x, y(x))\) from the ODE. Drop all terms of order \(h^2\) and higher:

\[ y(x+h) \approx y(x) + h,f(x,,y(x)) \]

This is Euler's method. The dropped terms constitute the local truncation error.

docs.title: 2.2 Geometric / Direction Field
docs.text:
At the current point \((x_n, y_n)\), the ODE tells us the slope: \(f(x_n, y_n)\). Walk along the tangent line for horizontal distance \(h\):

\[ y_{n+1} = y_n + h \cdot \underbrace{f(x_n, y_n)}_{\text{slope at current point}} \]

We are navigating by the direction field — reading the compass at \((x_n, y_n)\) and walking in that direction until \(x_{n+1}\), then re-reading.

docs.title: 2.3 Integral Approximation (Rectangle Rule)
docs.text:
Integrate the ODE from \(x_n\) to \(x_{n+1}\):

\[ y(x_{n+1}) = y(x_n) + \int_{x_n}^{x_{n+1}} f(x, y(x)),dx \]

Approximate the integral using the left-endpoint rectangle rule:

\[ \int_{x_n}^{x_{n+1}} f(x, y(x)),dx \approx h \cdot f(x_n, y_n) \]

This gives exactly the Euler update. The error in Euler's method is precisely the error in the rectangle rule — and we can control it by shrinking \(h\).

The master formula:

\[ \boxed{y_{n+1} = y_n + h,f(x_n, y_n), \qquad n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots} \]

docs.title: 3. Geometric Picture
docs.text:
y
 |
 |                    * ← true solution y(x_{n+2})
 |              *  · ↗
 |         *  ·  ↗  ← Euler step 2 (wrong slope again)
 |    *  ·  ↗ ← y_{n+2} (Euler)
 |  · ↗  ↗ ← Euler step 1 (tangent line at (x_n, y_n))
 |↗  ← y_{n+1} (Euler)
 ●──────────────────────────→ x
(x_n, y_n)    x_{n+1}   x_{n+2}

· · · = true solution curve
──── = Euler polygonal path (piecewise linear)

The key geometric defect: After taking a step, we are no longer on the true solution curve. We restart from the wrong point \((x_{n+1}, y_{n+1})\) and read the direction field there — but since \(y_{n+1} \neq y(x_{n+1})\), we are reading the field at the wrong height. Each step compounds the error from all previous steps.

docs.title: 4.1 Local Truncation Error (LTE)
docs.text:
The local truncation error is the error made in a single step, assuming we start exactly on the true solution (\(y_n = y(x_n)\)).

From the Taylor expansion:

\[ y(x_{n+1}) = y(x_n) + h,y'(x_n) + \frac{h^2}{2},y''(x_n) + O(h^3) \]

Euler gives \(y_{n+1} = y(x_n) + h,f(x_n, y(x_n)) = y(x_n) + h,y'(x_n)\).

Therefore:

\[ \text{LTE} = y(x_{n+1}) - y_{n+1} = \frac{h^2}{2},y''(x_n) + O(h^3) = O(h^2) \]

LTE is second order in \(h\).

docs.title: 4.2 Global Truncation Error (GTE)
docs.text:
The global truncation error at \(x_N = x_0 + Nh\) is the accumulated error over all \(N\) steps.

Taking \(N\) steps of size \(h\) to reach a fixed point \(x_N\): there are \(N = (x_N - x_0)/h\) steps. Each contributes LTE \(\approx Ch^2\), so:

\[ \text{GTE} \approx N \cdot Ch^2 = \frac{x_N - x_0}{h} \cdot Ch^2 = C(x_N - x_0),h = O(h) \]

Euler's method is a first-order method: halving \(h\) halves the global error.

docs.title: 4.3 The Error Constant
docs.text:
More precisely, if \(|y''(x)| \leq M\) on \([x_0, x_N]\), then:

\[ |y(x_N) - y_N| \leq \frac{Mh}{2L}\left(e^{L(x_N - x_0)} - 1\right) \]

where \(L\) is the Lipschitz constant of \(f\) in \(y\). The exponential factor \(e^{L(x_N-x_0)}\) is the error amplification — errors grow exponentially over long intervals, making Euler's method unreliable for large integration windows unless \(h\) is very small.

docs.title: 4.4 Geometric Interpretation of Error
docs.text:
Euler underestimates or overestimates depending on the concavity of the solution:

Concave-up (y'' > 0):         Concave-down (y'' < 0):

  true ___                        true
      /                    ___---
Euler/  ← underestimates   Euler   ← overestimates
   /                             \
  • If \(y'' > 0\) (solution bends upward): Euler's tangent-line approximation lies below the curve → underestimate.
  • If \(y'' < 0\) (solution bends downward): tangent lies above → overestimate.

The second derivative \(y''\) is exactly what the LTE formula \(\frac{h^2}{2}y''\) captures.

docs.title: 5.2 Example 2 — Logistic Equation
docs.text:
IVP: \(y' = y(1-y)\), \(y(0) = 0.1\). Exact solution: \(y(x) = \frac{1}{1 + 9e^{-x}}\).

Apply Euler with \(h = 0.5\) on \([0, 3]\):

\(n\) \(x_n\) \(y_n\) \(f = y_n(1-y_n)\) \(y_{\text{exact}}\) Error 0 0.0 0.1000 0.0900 0.1000 0.0000 1 0.5 0.1450 0.1240 0.1480 0.0030 2 1.0 0.2070 0.1642 0.2142 0.0072 3 1.5 0.2891 0.2057 0.3100 0.0209 4 2.0 0.3920 0.2384 0.4378 0.0458 5 2.5 0.5112 0.2497 0.5750 0.0638 6 3.0 0.6361 — 0.7109 0.0748

The Euler path follows the S-curve but lags behind — it consistently underestimates because the logistic curve is concave up in its initial phase (below the inflection point \(y = 0.5\)).

docs.title: 5.3 Example 3 — A Cautionary Case: Stiff ODE
docs.text:
IVP: \(y' = -100y\), \(y(0) = 1\). Exact solution: \(y = e^{-100x}\) (decays to 0 very fast).

Euler: \(y_{n+1} = y_n + h(-100y_n) = y_n(1 - 100h)\).

  • If \(h = 0.015\): \(1 - 100(0.015) = -0.5\). Each step multiplies by \(-0.5\): \(1, -0.5, 0.25, -0.125, \ldots\) — oscillating but decaying. ✓ (barely stable)
  • If \(h = 0.025\): \(1 - 100(0.025) = -1.5\). Each step multiplies by \(-1.5\): \(1, -1.5, 2.25, -3.375, \ldots\) — diverging. ✗

The exact solution is essentially 0 after \(x = 0.1\), yet Euler explodes for step sizes that seem small. This is stiffness — Euler's method requires \(h < 2/100 = 0.02\) for stability, which may be far smaller than accuracy requires. This motivates implicit methods.

docs.title: 6.1 The Test Equation
docs.text:
The standard stability analysis uses the test equation (Dahlquist's test problem):

\[ y' = \lambda y, \qquad \lambda \in \mathbb{C}, \quad y(0) = 1 \]

Exact solution: \(y = e^{\lambda x}\). For \(\text{Re}(\lambda) < 0\), the solution decays — and we want the numerical method to also decay.

Euler's method on the test equation:

\[ y_{n+1} = y_n + h\lambda y_n = (1 + h\lambda)y_n \]

So \(y_n = (1 + h\lambda)^n\). This decays to 0 iff \(|1 + h\lambda| < 1\).

docs.title: 6.2 Region of Absolute Stability
docs.text:
The region of absolute stability is:

\[ \mathcal{S}_{\text{Euler}} = {z \in \mathbb{C} : |1 + z| < 1} \]

where \(z = h\lambda\). This is a disk of radius 1 centered at \(z = -1\) in the complex plane.

Im(z)
  ↑
1 ─ ┤      · · ·
    ┤    ·       ·
    ┤   ·    ●    ·     ← stability region (disk)
    ┤   ·  (-1,0)  ·      center: (-1,0), radius: 1
    ┤    ·       ·
-1 ─ ┤      · · ·
    ─┼──────────────→ Re(z)
   -2    -1    0

Note: the right half-plane (Re(z) > 0) is entirely OUTSIDE.
For real λ < 0: need hλ ∈ (-2, 0), i.e., h < 2/|λ|.

Consequence for stiff ODEs: If \(\lambda \ll 0\) (large negative, rapid decay), the stability condition \(h < 2/|\lambda|\) forces extremely small step sizes — even though accuracy doesn't require them. This is the stiffness problem.

docs.title: 6.3 Comparison with Other Methods
docs.text:
Method Stability region contains... Order Euler (explicit) Disk of radius 1 at \((-1,0)\) 1 Trapezoidal (implicit) Entire left half-plane 2 Backward Euler (implicit) Complement of unit disk at \((1,0)\) 1 RK4 Much larger region (extends to \(\approx -2.8\) on real axis) 4

Backward Euler (\(y_{n+1} = y_n + hf(x_{n+1}, y_{n+1})\)) uses the slope at the next point — it is unconditionally stable for the test equation (\(A\)-stable). The cost: solving an implicit equation at each step.

docs.title: 7.1 Improved Euler (Heun's Method)
docs.text:
The central flaw of Euler: it uses the slope only at the left endpoint. Heun's method averages the slopes at both endpoints:

\[ \tilde{y}_{n+1} = y_n + h,f(x_n, y_n) \qquad \text{(predictor: Euler)} $$ $$ y_{n+1} = y_n + \frac{h}{2}!\left[f(x_n, y_n) + f(x_{n+1}, \tilde{y}_{n+1})\right] \qquad \text{(corrector: trapezoid)} \]

LTE: \(O(h^3)\). GTE: \(O(h^2)\). Second-order method — same cost as two Euler steps, but far more accurate.

Geometric interpretation: use the average of the field at the current and predicted next point — a more faithful reading of the direction field.

docs.title: 7.2 Midpoint Method
docs.text:
\[ y_{n+1} = y_n + h,f!\left(x_n + \frac{h}{2},; y_n + \frac{h}{2}f(x_n, y_n)\right) \]

Evaluate the slope at the midpoint of the interval. Also second-order. Geometrically: take a half-step of Euler to estimate the midpoint, read the field there, then use that slope for the full step.

docs.title: 7.3 The Runge–Kutta Family
docs.text: All Runge–Kutta methods are refinements of Euler: evaluate \(f\) at multiple intermediate points, then take a weighted average. Euler is RK1 — one evaluation, weight 1. See [[General Differential Equations]] §7 for RK4.

docs.title: 7.4 The Euler Family Tree
docs.text:
Euler (RK1, explicit)
                   h·f(xₙ, yₙ)
                         │
          ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
          │                             │
    Midpoint method              Heun's method
    (evaluate at midpoint)       (average of two slopes)
          │                             │
          └──────────┬──────────────────┘
                     │
              Runge–Kutta RK4
           (weighted 4-point average)
                     │
              Adaptive RK45
           (variable step size,
            error control)

docs.title: 8. Euler's Method for Systems
docs.text:
First-order systems \(\dot{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{f}(x, \mathbf{y})\), \(\mathbf{y}(x_0) = \mathbf{y}_0\) (where \(\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n\)):

\[ \boxed{\mathbf{y}_{n+1} = \mathbf{y}_n + h,\mathbf{f}(x_n, \mathbf{y}_n)} \]

Identical formula, vectorized. Every component is updated simultaneously using the current values of all components.

Example (spring, from [[Models for the Motion of a Spring]]):

\(\ddot{x} + \omega_0^2 x = 0\) written as system: \(y_1 = x\), \(y_2 = \dot{x}\):

\[ \begin{pmatrix}y_1 \ y_2\end{pmatrix}_{n+1} = \begin{pmatrix}y_1 \ y_2\end{pmatrix}_n + h\begin{pmatrix}y_2 \ -\omega_0^2 y_1\end{pmatrix}_n = \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}1 & h \ -\omega_0^2 h & 1\end{pmatrix}}_{M}\begin{pmatrix}y_1 \ y_2\end{pmatrix}_n \]

The update is a linear map \(M\). The eigenvalues of \(M\) are \(1 \pm ih\omega_0\) — magnitude \(\sqrt{1 + h^2\omega_0^2} > 1\).

The Euler method for a conservative oscillator always grows the amplitude. Each step the state spirals outward:

y₂ (velocity)
  ↑
  |      /‾‾‾→ Euler spirals outward!
  |     /  ↗
  |    /  ↗
  |   ·  ●  ← true orbit: closed ellipse
  |    ↖  ↘
  |     ↖  ↘
  +───────────→ y₁ (position)

Euler: outward spiral (energy grows)
True:  closed ellipse (energy conserved)

This energy drift is a fundamental flaw of Euler for conservative systems — it creates numerical dissipation in the wrong direction. Symplectic integrators (e.g., symplectic Euler, Störmer–Verlet) fix this by preserving a discrete energy-like quantity.

docs.title: 9. Step-Size Control and Adaptive Methods
docs.text:
In practice, we don't use fixed \(h\). Adaptive solvers (RK45, Dormand–Prince) estimate the local error at each step and adjust \(h\) accordingly:

  • Error too large: reduce \(h\), repeat step.
  • Error small enough: accept step, possibly increase \(h\) next step.

The error estimate uses two approximations of different orders (e.g., RK4 and RK5) and takes their difference as a proxy for the true error.

Why Euler's analysis matters here: The step-size selection formula in adaptive solvers is derived from the same Taylor-expansion argument as the LTE. If target tolerance is \(\varepsilon\) and current error estimate is \(e\), the new step size satisfies:

\[ h_{\text{new}} = h_{\text{old}}\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{e}\right)^{1/(p+1)} \]

where \(p\) is the method order. For Euler (\(p=1\)): \(h_{\text{new}} = h_{\text{old}}\sqrt{\varepsilon/e}\).

docs.title: 10. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: This section is not an analogy. It is a mathematical identity.

docs.title: 10.1 ResNets Are Euler's Method
docs.text:
A ResNet (He et al., 2016) layer performs:

\[ h_{n+1} = h_n + \mathcal{F}_\theta(h_n) \]

where \(\mathcal{F}_\theta\) is a neural network block (convolutions + batch norm + ReLU). Compare with Euler:

\[ y_{n+1} = y_n + h,f(x_n, y_n) \]

They are identical with \(h = 1\) and \(f_\theta \equiv \mathcal{F}_\theta\). The residual connection \(h_n \to h_{n+1}\) is not a heuristic engineering trick — it is Euler's method applied to the ODE \(\dot{h} = f_\theta(h)\).

This correspondence (formalized in Neural ODEs, Chen et al. 2018) means:

  • Network depth = number of Euler steps.
  • Layer width = dimensionality of the state space \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
  • Skip connections = the \(y_n\) term in Euler's update.
  • Step size \(h\) = implicit; can be absorbed into the parameterization of \(\mathcal{F}_\theta\).

docs.title: 10.2 Gradient Descent Is Euler on the Gradient Flow
docs.text:
The gradient flow ODE is \(\dot{ heta} = - abla L( heta)\). Euler's method on this:

\[ heta_{n+1} = heta_n + h,(- abla L( heta_n)) = heta_n - \eta, abla L( heta_n) \]

This is exactly stochastic gradient descent with learning rate \(\eta = h\).

Every property of Euler's method translates:

Euler Property SGD Property Step size \(h\) Learning rate \(\eta\) LTE \(\propto h^2\) Gradient noise \(\propto \eta^2\) in loss landscape Stability requires small \(h\) SGD diverges for large \(\eta\) \(O(h)\) global error Suboptimal convergence rate \(O(1/\sqrt{T})\) Euler spirals for oscillators SGD oscillates in narrow loss valleys Stiffness \(\Rightarrow\) tiny \(h\) Ill-conditioned loss \(\Rightarrow\) tiny \(\eta\)

docs.title: 10.3 Implicit Euler and Proximal Methods
docs.text:
The proximal gradient method in optimization is backward (implicit) Euler on gradient flow:

\[ \theta_{n+1} = \arg\min_\theta\left[L(\theta) + \frac{1}{2\eta}|\theta - \theta_n|^2\right] \]

The first-order condition gives \(\theta_{n+1} = \theta_n - \eta\nabla L(\theta_{n+1})\) — implicit Euler. The proximal step is unconditionally stable (large \(\eta\) allowed), just as backward Euler is \(A\)-stable.

Proximal algorithms (ISTA, ADMM, proximal gradient descent) are the optimization analogues of implicit ODE integrators.

docs.title: 10.4 Euler Instability ↔ Training Instability
docs.text:
For the test equation \(y' = \lambda y\), Euler is stable iff \(|1 + h\lambda| < 1\). For a neural network trained on a loss with Hessian eigenvalue \(\Lambda_{\max}\) (the curvature), the gradient flow has \(\lambda \approx -\Lambda_{\max}\), and SGD (= Euler) is stable iff:

\[ \eta < \frac{2}{\Lambda_{\max}} \]

This is exactly the spectral radius condition for gradient descent convergence derived in convex optimization. It is the same stability criterion as Euler's method on the test equation — not a coincidence, but the same theorem.

When training explodes for large learning rates, it is not mysterious: Euler's method has left its stability region.

docs.title: 10.5 Higher-Order Methods in ML
docs.text:
If Euler = ResNet = SGD, what are the higher-order methods?

Numerical Method ML Analogue Euler (RK1) SGD, 1-layer ResNet Midpoint / Heun 2-stage ResNet blocks RK4 Multi-step ResNets / dense connections Adaptive RK45 Neural ODEs with adaptive depth Implicit / symplectic Euler Proximal methods, Hamiltonian NNs Symplectic integrators Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC)

Symplectic integrators preserve the discrete energy (the Hamiltonian), just as HMC preserves volume in phase space — the same mathematical structure underlies both.

docs.title: 10.6 Euler Discretization and the Diffusion Model Timestep
docs.text:
In DDPM (Ho et al., 2020), the forward noising process is the SDE:

\[ dx = -\frac{\beta(t)}{2}x,dt + \sqrt{\beta(t)},dW_t \]

The discrete forward process is Euler–Maruyama discretization of this SDE:

\[ x_{t+1} = x_t - \frac{\beta_t}{2}x_t\Delta t + \sqrt{\beta_t \Delta t},\varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) \]

The number of diffusion timesteps \(T\) is the number of Euler steps; the noise schedule \(\beta_t\) is the step-size sequence. The reverse (denoising) process is a numerical solver running the reverse SDE — and the quality vs. speed tradeoff of diffusion sampling is literally the accuracy vs. cost tradeoff of ODE/SDE solvers, with DDIM (Song et al., 2020) corresponding to higher-order solvers.

docs.title: 10.7 Summary Table
docs.text: Euler Concept ML/DL Analogue Euler update \(y_{n+1} = y_n + hf\) ResNet layer \(h_{n+1} = h_n + \mathcal{F}_\theta(h_n)\) Euler on gradient flow SGD with learning rate \(\eta = h\) Step size \(h\) Learning rate \(\eta\) LTE \(O(h^2)\), GTE \(O(h)\) Discretization noise in training Stability condition $h < 2/ \lambda Euler spirals for oscillator SGD oscillates in narrow loss valleys Implicit Euler Proximal gradient descent Stiffness Ill-conditioned loss landscape Heun / midpoint (RK2) 2-stage ResNet / improved gradient estimates Adaptive step-size Adaptive learning rate (Adam, RMSProp) Symplectic Euler Hamiltonian Monte Carlo Euler–Maruyama DDPM forward/reverse diffusion timestep

docs.title: 11. Quick-Reference
docs.text:
The update: $$ y_{n+1} = y_n + h,f(x_n, y_n) $$

LTE: \(\tau_n = \frac{h^2}{2}y''(x_n) + O(h^3) = O(h^2)\)

GTE: \(O(h)\) — first-order method.

Error bound (exact): $$ |y(x_N) - y_N| \leq \frac{Mh}{2L}!\left(e^{L(x_N - x_0)} - 1\right), \qquad M = \max|y''|,; L = \text{Lipschitz const.} $$

Stability (test equation \(y' = \lambda y\)): Stable iff \(|1 + h\lambda| < 1\) (disk of radius 1 at \(z=-1\) in \(z = h\lambda\) plane).

Real \(\lambda < 0\): stable iff \(h < 2/|\lambda|\).

Vectorized (systems): $$ \mathbf{y}_{n+1} = \mathbf{y}_n + h,\mathbf{f}(x_n, \mathbf{y}_n) $$

Defect for conservative systems: Euler grows energy. Use symplectic Euler instead: $$ p_{n+1} = p_n - h,\nabla_q H(q_n, p_n), \qquad q_{n+1} = q_n + h,\nabla_p H(q_n, p_{n+1}) $$

docs.title: 12. Exercises
docs.text:
1. By hand. Apply Euler's method with \(h = 0.2\) to \(y' = x + y\), \(y(0) = 1\) on \([0, 1]\). The exact solution is \(y = 2e^x - x - 1\). Fill a table and compute the global error at \(x = 1\).

  2. Order verification. For the same IVP, run Euler with \(h = 0.1\) and \(h = 0.05\). Show numerically that halving \(h\) approximately halves the error — confirming \(O(h)\) convergence.

  3. LTE derivation. Derive the LTE for Heun's method (improved Euler) by Taylor expansion. Show it is \(O(h^3)\), confirming second-order accuracy.

  4. Stability. For \(y' = -50y\), \(y(0) = 1\): find the largest \(h\) for which Euler is stable. Then apply Euler with \(h = 0.05\) (stable) and \(h = 0.045\) (just inside boundary) and observe the difference.

  5. Concavity and error. For \(y' = y\), \(y(0) = 1\) (exact: \(e^x\)): show analytically that \(y'' > 0\) everywhere, and deduce that Euler always underestimates. Verify with your table from Example 5.1.

  6. Spring system. Apply Euler with \(h = 0.1\) to \(\ddot{x} + x = 0\), \(x(0) = 1\), \(\dot{x}(0) = 0\) (exact: \(x = \cos t\)) on \([0, 2\pi]\). Compute the amplitude \(\sqrt{x_n^2 + v_n^2}\) at each step and show it grows — confirming the energy drift analysis in §8.

  7. SGD as Euler. Consider \(L(\theta) = \frac{1}{2}(\theta - 3)^2\). Write the gradient flow ODE and solve it. Apply Euler with \(h = 0.5, 1.0, 2.5\) (the last is outside the stability region). What happens in each case? Relate to the stability condition \(h < 2/\Lambda_{\max}\).

  8. ResNet depth. A Neural ODE defined by \(\dot{h} = \tanh(h)\), \(h(0) = 0.5\). Simulate this using Euler's method with \(h = 0.5\) for \(T = 4\) (so 8 Euler steps). Each step is a ResNet layer. What is the fixed point of the ODE? Does the Euler approximation converge to it?

docs.title: Separable DEs
docs.text: "The art of mathematics is asking the right question — and for ODEs, the right question is often: can I tear this apart?"

docs.title: Tags
docs.text: #calculus #ODE #differential-equations #machine-learning #deep-learning

docs.title: 1. What Is a Separable Equation?
docs.text:
A first-order ODE of the form

\[\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x, y)\]

is called separable if \(f\) factors as a product of a function of \(x\) alone and a function of \(y\) alone:

\[\frac{dy}{dx} = g(x) \cdot h(y)\]

The key insight: we can algebraically separate all \(y\)-dependence to one side and all \(x\)-dependence to the other, then integrate both sides independently.

Ref: Stewart §9.3 — "Separable Equations"; MIT 18.02 Lecture Notes on ODEs.

docs.title: 2.1 Formal Statement
docs.text:
Let \(g : I \to \mathbb{R}\) and \(h : J \to \mathbb{R}\) be continuous on open intervals \(I, J \subseteq \mathbb{R}\), with \(h(y) \neq 0\) on \(J\). Consider

\[\frac{dy}{dx} = g(x), h(y). \tag{1}\]

Claim: Any solution \(y = \phi(x)\) satisfying \(\phi(x_0) = y_0\) (for some \((x_0, y_0) \in I \times J\)) is implicitly defined by

\[H(y) = G(x) + C, \tag{2}\]

where \(H(y) = \displaystyle\int \frac{dy}{h(y)}\) and \(G(x) = \displaystyle\int g(x), dx\).

docs.title: 2.2 The Method (Leibniz Notation — Rigorous Justification)
docs.text:
We formally write:

\[\frac{1}{h(y)}, dy = g(x), dx\]

This notation is shorthand for the following rigorous argument:

Proof. Suppose \(y = \phi(x)\) is a differentiable solution of (1) on some interval. Define

\[F(x) = H(\phi(x)) - G(x),\]

where \(H' = \frac{1}{h}\) and \(G' = g\). By the chain rule:

\[F'(x) = H'(\phi(x)) \cdot \phi'(x) - G'(x) = \frac{\phi'(x)}{h(\phi(x))} - g(x).\]

Since \(\phi\) solves (1), \(\phi'(x) = g(x), h(\phi(x))\), so:

\[F'(x) = \frac{g(x), h(\phi(x))}{h(\phi(x))} - g(x) = g(x) - g(x) = 0.\]

Therefore \(F(x) = C\) for some constant \(C\), i.e., \(H(\phi(x)) = G(x) + C\). \(\blacksquare\)

Existence & uniqueness of the solution is then guaranteed by the Picard–Lindelöf theorem (provided \(g\) and \(h\) satisfy a Lipschitz condition), which tells us this implicit equation does define a unique local solution through any point \((x_0, y_0)\).

docs.title: 3. The Method — Step by Step
docs.text:
Given \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = g(x), h(y)\):

  1. Separate: Write \(\dfrac{dy}{h(y)} = g(x), dx\) (valid when \(h(y) \neq 0\)).
  2. Integrate both sides: \(\displaystyle\int \frac{dy}{h(y)} = \int g(x), dx + C\).
  3. Solve for \(y\) (explicitly if possible, implicitly if not).
  4. Check singular solutions where \(h(y) = 0\) — these are constant solutions \(y = y_0\) with \(h(y_0) = 0\), and they may or may not be captured by the general solution at specific values of \(C\).

docs.title: Example 1 — Exponential Growth/Decay
docs.text:
\[\frac{dy}{dx} = ky, \quad k \in \mathbb{R}\]

Separate (assuming \(y \neq 0\)):

\[\frac{dy}{y} = k, dx\]

Integrate:

\[\ln|y| = kx + C_1 \implies |y| = e^{C_1} e^{kx} \implies y = A e^{kx}, \quad A \in \mathbb{R} \setminus {0}.\]

Check \(y = 0\): Substituting back, \(0 = k \cdot 0\) ✓. So \(y = 0\) is also a solution, recovered by \(A = 0\).

General solution:

\[\boxed{y = Ae^{kx}, \quad A \in \mathbb{R}}\]

This is the backbone of radioactive decay (\(k < 0\)), population growth (\(k > 0\)), and — critically — gradient descent convergence analysis in ML.

docs.title: Example 2 — Logistic Equation
docs.text:
\[\frac{dy}{dx} = ry\left(1 - \frac{y}{K}\right), \quad r, K > 0\]

This is separable: \(g(x) = r\), \(h(y) = y(1 - y/K)\).

Separate:

\[\frac{dy}{y(1 - y/K)} = r, dx\]

Partial fractions on the left (\(\frac{K}{y(K-y)} = \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{K-y}\)):

\[\int \left(\frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{K - y}\right) dy = \int r, dx\] \[\ln|y| - \ln|K - y| = rx + C_1\] \[\ln\left|\frac{y}{K - y}\right| = rx + C_1 \implies \frac{y}{K - y} = Ae^{rx}\]

Solving for \(y\):

\[\boxed{y(x) = \frac{K}{1 + Be^{-rx}}, \quad B = \frac{K - y_0}{y_0}}\]

where \(y(0) = y_0\).

The sigmoid / logistic function \(\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}\) is the special case \(K = 1, r = 1, B = 1\). It is literally the solution to a separable ODE, and it is the activation function used in logistic regression and as a neuron model in neural networks.

docs.title: Example 3 — Separable but Implicit Solution
docs.text:
\[\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x^2}{1 - y^2}\]

Separate:

\[(1 - y^2), dy = x^2, dx\]

Integrate:

\[y - \frac{y^3}{3} = \frac{x^3}{3} + C\]

This cannot be solved explicitly for \(y\) in general — the solution curve is defined implicitly. This is perfectly fine; the implicit relation still defines \(y\) as a function of \(x\) near any point where the implicit function theorem applies (i.e., where \(\partial/\partial y,(y - y^3/3 - x^3/3 - C) = 1 - y^2 \neq 0\)).

docs.title: Example 4 — Singular Solutions
docs.text:
\[\frac{dy}{dx} = y^{1/3}\]

Separate (\(y \neq 0\)):

\[y^{-1/3}, dy = dx \implies \frac{3}{2} y^{2/3} = x + C \implies y = \left(\frac{2(x+C)}{3}\right)^{3/2}\]

Singular solution: \(y \equiv 0\) satisfies the ODE (since \(0^{1/3} = 0\)), but it is not recovered from the general solution for any finite \(C\).

Note: \(h(y) = y^{1/3}\) is not Lipschitz at \(y = 0\), so Picard–Lindelöf does not guarantee uniqueness there — consistent with having two solutions through \((x_0, 0)\).

docs.title: Phase Line for \(\dot{y} = ry(1 - y/K)\) (Logistic)
docs.text:
dy/dx > 0        dy/dx = 0     dy/dx < 0
                     ↓
←————[unstable: y=0]————→————[stable: y=K]←————
      ↑                              ↑
   repeller                       attractor

Solution curves in the \((x, y)\)-plane:

y
K ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─────────────────────────  ← asymptote y = K
           /
          /   ← S-shaped growth
         /
────────/──────────────────────────────→ x
0 ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─  ← asymptote y = 0

The inflection point occurs at \(y = K/2\), i.e., \(x = \frac{1}{r}\ln B\).

docs.title: Slope Field Intuition
docs.text:
For a separable equation \(\frac{dy}{dx} = g(x)h(y)\), the slope at \((x, y)\) factors. This means:

  • Along any horizontal line \(y = c\): the slope is \(g(x) \cdot h(c)\), scaling only with \(x\).
  • Along any vertical line \(x = a\): the slope is \(g(a) \cdot h(y)\), scaling only with \(y\).

The level curves of \(H(y) - G(x) = C\) are the solution curves.

docs.title: 6. Connection to AI, Machine Learning & Deep Learning
docs.text: This is where separable equations stop being "just calculus" and become the mathematical substrate of modern AI.

docs.title: 6.1 The Sigmoid is the Solution to a Separable ODE
docs.text:
As shown in Example 2, the logistic equation

\[\frac{d\sigma}{dx} = r\sigma(1 - \sigma)\]

has the solution \(\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-rx}}\).

In neural networks, \(\sigma\) is used as an activation function — every forward pass through a sigmoid neuron is evaluating the closed-form solution to a separable ODE.

docs.title: 6.2 Exponential Learning Rate Decay
docs.text:
In training neural networks, a common scheduler decays the learning rate \(\eta(t)\) as:

\[\frac{d\eta}{dt} = -k\eta \implies \eta(t) = \eta_0 e^{-kt}\]

This is the exponential decay ODE (Example 1) — a separable equation. The choice of \(k\) directly controls convergence speed vs. stability of gradient descent.

docs.title: 6.3 Neural ODEs — Continuous-Depth Networks
docs.text:
"What if a neural network were an ODE?" — Chen et al., NeurIPS 2018

Neural ODEs replace the discrete layer update

\[\mathbf{h}_{t+1} = \mathbf{h}_t + f(\mathbf{h}_t, \theta)\]

with a continuous-time ODE:

\[\frac{d\mathbf{h}}{dt} = f(\mathbf{h}(t), t, \theta)\]

where \(\mathbf{h}(t) \in \mathbb{R}^n\) is the hidden state and \(f\) is a neural network parameterized by \(\theta\).

When \(f(\mathbf{h}, t) = g(t) \cdot \tilde{f}(\mathbf{h})\), this ODE is separable, and the solution structure we've studied applies directly. Training such a model involves solving an ODE at each forward pass (via Runge-Kutta solvers) and computing gradients via the adjoint method — a continuous analogue of backpropagation rooted in the theory of ODEs.

docs.title: 6.4 Diffusion Models (Score-Based Generative Models)
docs.text:
Modern image generators (Stable Diffusion, DALL-E) are built on stochastic differential equations (SDEs) of the form

\[d\mathbf{x} = f(\mathbf{x}, t), dt + g(t), d\mathbf{W}\]

The probability flow ODE (the deterministic skeleton of this SDE) is:

\[\frac{d\mathbf{x}}{dt} = f(\mathbf{x}, t) - \frac{1}{2} g(t)^2 \nabla_\mathbf{x} \log p_t(\mathbf{x})\]

When the score function \(\nabla_\mathbf{x} \log p_t(\mathbf{x})\) depends only on \(t\) (not \(\mathbf{x}\)), this collapses to a separable ODE. Understanding separability is the first step toward understanding why these models can run both forward (adding noise) and backward (denoising = generating) in time.

docs.title: 6.5 Gradient Flow and Loss Dynamics
docs.text:
In continuous-time gradient descent (gradient flow), the parameters \(\theta(t)\) evolve as:

\[\frac{d\theta}{dt} = -\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta)\]

For certain simple loss landscapes (e.g., quadratic loss \(\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \frac{1}{2}\lambda \theta^2\)), this is separable:

\[\frac{d\theta}{dt} = -\lambda\theta \implies \theta(t) = \theta_0 e^{-\lambda t}\]

The convergence rate to the minimum is controlled by the eigenvalues \(\lambda\) of the Hessian of \(\mathcal{L}\) — a fact directly read off from the separable ODE solution.

docs.title: 7. Summary Table
docs.text: Equation Form Solution ML/DL Appearance \(\frac{dy}{dx} = ky\) Separable \(y = Ae^{kx}\) Learning rate decay, population/activation dynamics \(\frac{dy}{dx} = ry(1-y/K)\) Separable \(y = \frac{K}{1+Be^{-rx}}\) Sigmoid activation, logistic regression \(\frac{d\theta}{dt} = -\lambda\theta\) Separable \(\theta(t) = \theta_0 e^{-\lambda t}\) Gradient flow, loss convergence \(\frac{d\mathbf{h}}{dt} = g(t)\tilde{f}(\mathbf{h})\) Separable ODE in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) Implicit / numerical Neural ODEs (Chen et al. 2018)

docs.title: 8. Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Dividing by \(h(y) = 0\): Always check for constant solutions (singular solutions) separately.
  2. Losing the \(\pm\) in \(\ln|y|\): The absolute value matters — it's why \(A\) can be any real number.
  3. Forgetting \(+C\) on one side: The integration constant appears once; don't write it on both sides.
  4. Assuming an explicit solution always exists: Many separable equations yield only implicit solutions (Example 3). That's not failure — it's the nature of the problem.
  5. Checking the domain of validity: The solution \(y(x)\) may only be valid on a subinterval of \(\mathbb{R}\), determined by where the implicit function theorem applies.

docs.text:
1. James Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. — §9.3 "Separable Equations."
  2. MIT 18.02 — Multivariable Calculus Lecture Notes on ODEs and slope fields.
  3. Ricky T.Q. Chen et al., "Neural Ordinary Differential Equations," NeurIPS 2018. arXiv:1806.07366
  4. Yang Song et al., "Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations," ICLR 2021.

docs.title: Orthogonal Trajectories
docs.text: "Two families of curves, each one cutting every member of the other at a perfect right angle. Nature loves this — and so does the mathematician."

docs.title: Tags
docs.text: #calculus #ODE #differential-equations #orthogonal-trajectories #geometry #machine-learning

docs.title: Links
docs.text: [[Separable Equations]] | [[Exact Equations]] | [[Gradient and Directional Derivatives]]

docs.title: 1. The Central Idea
docs.text:
Suppose you have a one-parameter family of curves

\[F(x, y, C) = 0, \quad C \in \mathbb{R}.\]

A second family of curves is called the orthogonal trajectories of the first if every curve in the second family intersects every curve in the first family at a right angle — i.e., their tangent lines are perpendicular at each point of intersection.

The mechanism is purely slope-based:

If one curve has slope \(m\) at a point, the orthogonal trajectory through that point has slope \(-\dfrac{1}{m}\).

This is because two lines with slopes \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) are perpendicular if and only if

\[m_1 \cdot m_2 = -1 \implies m_2 = -\frac{1}{m_1}.\]

docs.title: Step 1 — Eliminate the Parameter
docs.text:
Given a family \(F(x, y, C) = 0\), differentiate implicitly with respect to \(x\) to get a relation involving \(x\), \(y\), and \(y' = dy/dx\). Then eliminate \(C\) between this and the original equation to obtain the ODE of the given family:

\[\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x, y). \tag{1}\]

docs.title: Step 2 — Write the ODE of the Orthogonal Family
docs.text:
Replace \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) with \(-\dfrac{1}{dy/dx}\):

\[\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{1}{f(x, y)}. \tag{2}\]

docs.title: Step 3 — Solve the New ODE
docs.text: Solve (2) — often it is separable — to find the orthogonal family \(G(x, y, K) = 0\).

docs.title: 3. Rigorous Justification
docs.text:
Let \(\gamma_1\) be a curve in the original family and \(\gamma_2\) a curve in the orthogonal family, intersecting at a point \(P = (x_0, y_0)\).

At \(P\), the tangent vector to \(\gamma_1\) is \((1, f(x_0, y_0))\) (in direction \((dx, dy)\) with \(dy/dx = f\)).

The tangent vector to \(\gamma_2\) is \((1, -1/f(x_0, y_0))\).

Their dot product:

\[\langle 1,, f \rangle \cdot \left\langle 1,, -\frac{1}{f} \right\rangle = 1 \cdot 1 + f \cdot \left(-\frac{1}{f}\right) = 1 - 1 = 0. \quad \checkmark\]

So the construction is geometrically exact: the dot product vanishes at every intersection point, confirming perpendicularity. \(\blacksquare\)

Note on vertical tangents: If \(f(x, y) \to \infty\) at some point (vertical tangent in the original family), the orthogonal trajectory has slope \(0\) there — a horizontal tangent. The reciprocal-negation rule still holds in the limit.

docs.title: Example 1 — Concentric Circles and Lines Through the Origin
docs.text:
Given family: Concentric circles centered at the origin,

\[x^2 + y^2 = C^2, \quad C > 0.\]

Step 1 — Find the ODE.

Differentiate: \(2x + 2y,y' = 0 \implies y' = -\dfrac{x}{y}.\)

(No \(C\) appears — no elimination needed here.)

Step 2 — Orthogonal ODE.

\[\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{1}{-x/y} = \frac{y}{x}.\]

Step 3 — Solve.

This is separable:

\[\frac{dy}{y} = \frac{dx}{x} \implies \ln|y| = \ln|x| + K_1 \implies y = Kx, \quad K \in \mathbb{R}.\]

Orthogonal family: All lines through the origin, \(y = Kx\).

        y
        |     /
        |    / (lines y = Kx)
   ○ ○  |   /
  ○   ○ |  /
 ○     ○|/
─○──────+──────○─ x
 ○     ○|\
  ○   ○ | \
   ○ ○  |  \
        |   \
        |

Every line through the origin cuts every concentric circle at a right angle — precisely what radii do. This is the geometric content of the gradient being perpendicular to level sets.

docs.title: Example 2 — Parabolas and Ellipses
docs.text:
Given family: Parabolas \(y = Cx^2\).

Step 1 — Find the ODE.

Differentiate: \(y' = 2Cx\). Eliminate \(C = y/x^2\):

\[y' = 2 \cdot \frac{y}{x^2} \cdot x = \frac{2y}{x}.\]

Step 2 — Orthogonal ODE.

\[\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{x}{2y}.\]

Step 3 — Solve (separable):

\[2y, dy = -x, dx \implies y^2 = -\frac{x^2}{2} + K \implies \frac{x^2}{2K} + \frac{y^2}{K} = 1.\]

This is the family of ellipses \(\dfrac{x^2}{2K} + \dfrac{y^2}{K} = 1\) (centered at the origin, semi-axes ratio \(\sqrt{2}:1\)).

         y
         |
     ·   |   ·       ← ellipses (orthogonal family)
  ·  \   |   /  ·
 ·    \  |  /    ·
·      \ | /      ·
─·──────\|/──────·── x
·       /|\       ·
 ·     / | \     ·
  ·   /  |  \   ·
     /   |   \

The parabolas \(y = Cx^2\) (opening up/down) cross each ellipse at 90°.

docs.title: Example 3 — Exponential Family
docs.text:
Given family: \(y = Ce^x\).

Step 1 — ODE.

\(y' = Ce^x = y\) (since \(C = ye^{-x}\)). So \(y' = y\).

Step 2 — Orthogonal ODE.

\[\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{1}{y}.\]

Step 3 — Solve (separable):

\[y, dy = -dx \implies \frac{y^2}{2} = -x + K \implies y^2 = -2x + K.\]

Orthogonal family: Parabolas \(y^2 = K - 2x\) (opening leftward).

These are the level curves of the potential function associated with the vector field \(\mathbf{F} = (1, -y)\) — an electrostatics analogy.

docs.title: Example 4 — Family Requiring Implicit Differentiation
docs.text:
Given family: \(x^2 + y^2 = 2Cx\) (circles tangent to the \(y\)-axis at the origin).

Step 1 — ODE.

Differentiate implicitly: \(2x + 2y,y' = 2C\). Eliminate \(C\) using \(C = \dfrac{x^2 + y^2}{2x}\):

\[2x + 2y,y' = \frac{x^2 + y^2}{x}\] \[2x^2 + 2xy,y' = x^2 + y^2\] \[y' = \frac{y^2 - x^2}{2xy}.\]

Step 2 — Orthogonal ODE.

\[\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{2xy}{y^2 - x^2} = \frac{2xy}{x^2 - y^2}.\]

Step 3 — Solve.

This is a homogeneous ODE (substitute \(v = y/x\), i.e., \(y = vx\)):

\[v + x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{2v}{1 - v^2}\] \[x\frac{dv}{dx} = \frac{2v}{1-v^2} - v = \frac{2v - v(1-v^2)}{1-v^2} = \frac{v(1+v^2)}{1-v^2}\]

Separate:

\[\frac{1-v^2}{v(1+v^2)}, dv = \frac{dx}{x}.\]

Partial fractions on the left:

\[\frac{1-v^2}{v(1+v^2)} = \frac{1}{v} - \frac{2v}{1+v^2}\]

Integrate:

\[\ln|v| - \ln(1+v^2) = \ln|x| + \text{const}\] \[\ln\left(\frac{|v|}{1+v^2}\right) = \ln|x| + \text{const} \implies \frac{v}{1+v^2} = Kx\]

Substitute \(v = y/x\):

\[\frac{y/x}{1 + y^2/x^2} = Kx \implies \frac{xy}{x^2+y^2} = Kx \implies x^2 + y^2 = \frac{y}{K}\] \[\boxed{x^2 + y^2 = 2Ky}\]

Orthogonal family: Circles tangent to the \(x\)-axis at the origin — perpendicular to the original family, as expected by symmetry.

docs.title: 5. Visualization — The Big Picture
docs.text:
The orthogonal trajectories picture is always this:

Family 1 (level curves of U):         Family 2 (∇U field lines):

    ──── C₁ ────                           │  ↗  │
   ──── C₂ ────      ⊥ at every cross →  │ ↗   │
  ──── C₃ ────                            │↗    │

The two families tile the plane like curvilinear coordinate systems — one family gives the "latitudes," the other the "longitudes."

docs.title: 6. The Gradient Connection — Why This Is Deep
docs.text:
Let \(U(x,y) = C\) define the given family (level curves of \(U\)). The gradient \( abla U = (U_x, U_y)\) is perpendicular to the level curves at every point (this is the fundamental theorem of gradients).

The orthogonal trajectories are precisely the integral curves of \( abla U\), i.e., the curves \(\mathbf{r}(t)\) satisfying

\[ rac{d\mathbf{r}}{dt} = abla U(\mathbf{r}(t)).\]

This is the gradient flow of \(U\). Slopes confirm it:

  • Level curve slope: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{U_x}{U_y}\) (implicit differentiation of \(U = C\)).
  • Gradient direction slope: \(\dfrac{U_y}{U_x}\).
  • Product: \(\left(-\dfrac{U_x}{U_y} ight)\left(\dfrac{U_y}{U_x} ight) = -1\). \(\checkmark\)

docs.title: 7. Connection to AI, Machine Learning & Deep Learning
7.1 Gradient Descent IS Orthogonal to Loss Contours
docs.text:
In training a neural network with parameters \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}^n\) and loss \(\mathcal{L}(\theta)\):

  • The level sets \(\mathcal{L}(\theta) = C\) are the loss contours (constant-loss hypersurfaces).
  • The gradient descent path \(\dot{\theta} = -\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}\) follows the negative gradient.

By the exact geometric argument above, the gradient direction is orthogonal to every loss contour it crosses. This means:

Gradient descent is, by construction, the orthogonal trajectory family of the loss contours.

When the loss is quadratic (e.g., linear regression with MSE), the contours are ellipses and the gradient paths are the ellipses' orthogonal trajectories — which curve inward toward the minimum. This is the geometric reason gradient descent "aims at the bottom."

Loss contours (ellipses):        Gradient descent paths:

  ───────────────────               ↓   ↓
    ─────────────                    ↘ ↙
      ──────────       ⊥ at every   → ★ ←   (minimum)
        ──────         crossing      ↗ ↖
          ──                        ↑   ↑

docs.title: 7.2 Natural Gradient — When Orthogonality Gets Curved
docs.text:
Standard gradient descent uses Euclidean orthogonality (the flat metric on \(\mathbb{R}^n\)). But parameter spaces of probabilistic models have curved geometry (Fisher information metric). The natural gradient (Amari, 1998) replaces:

\[\dot{\theta} = -\nabla \mathcal{L} \quad \longrightarrow \quad \dot{\theta} = -F(\theta)^{-1} \nabla \mathcal{L}\]

where \(F(\theta)\) is the Fisher information matrix. This is the orthogonal trajectory family of the loss contours in the curved Riemannian metric of the model's parameter manifold — a deep generalization of the Euclidean orthogonal trajectory construction we have done here.

docs.title: 7.3 Electric Field Lines and Attention in Transformers
docs.text:
The self-attention mechanism in transformers computes weighted sums that can be understood as a potential field \(U\) over token positions. The "attention flow" — which tokens attend strongly to which — follows the gradient of \(U\), forming the orthogonal trajectories of the constant-attention contours.

This is an active research area: interpreting attention as a physical potential flow (with orthogonal equipotentials and field lines) gives geometric intuitions for attention head specialization and information routing.

docs.title: 7.4 Normalizing Flows and Coordinate Grids
docs.text:
A normalizing flow transforms a simple distribution (e.g., Gaussian) into a complex one by a diffeomorphism \(T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n\). A well-designed flow preserves the orthogonal trajectory structure of the source distribution's level sets — the image curves form a curvilinear coordinate system where the two families remain orthogonal.

This is used in conformal normalizing flows, where the map \(T\) is angle-preserving (conformal), ensuring orthogonality is preserved exactly. The mathematical foundation is the Cauchy-Riemann equations — the classical source of orthogonal trajectories in complex analysis.

docs.title: 7.5 Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs)
docs.text:
In PINNs, a neural network \(u_\theta(x, y)\) is trained to satisfy a PDE. Many PDEs have orthogonality constraints baked in:

  • Laplace equation \(\nabla^2 u = 0\): the level curves of \(u\) (equipotentials) and its gradient field lines are orthogonal trajectories of each other.
  • Heat equation: isotherms (level sets of temperature) are orthogonal to heat flux lines.

PINNs must implicitly learn to produce solutions that respect these orthogonality conditions — and failure to do so is a sign of poor training or insufficient network expressiveness.

docs.title: 8. Summary Table
docs.text: Given Family ODE of Family Orthogonal ODE Orthogonal Family \(x^2 + y^2 = C^2\) \(y' = -x/y\) \(y' = y/x\) \(y = Kx\) (lines through origin) \(y = Cx^2\) \(y' = 2y/x\) \(y' = -x/(2y)\) \(x^2/2 + y^2 = K\) (ellipses) \(y = Ce^x\) \(y' = y\) \(y' = -1/y\) \(y^2 + 2x = K\) (parabolas) \(x^2 + y^2 = 2Cx\) \(y' = (y^2-x^2)/(2xy)\) \(y' = 2xy/(x^2-y^2)\) \(x^2 + y^2 = 2Ky\) (circles)

docs.title: 9. Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Not eliminating \(C\) completely: The ODE of the family must be free of the parameter — otherwise you haven't captured the whole family, only one curve.
  2. Forgetting \(h(y) = 0\) cases (vertical tangents): When \(f(x,y) \to \infty\), the orthogonal slope is \(0\) (horizontal). These are consistent limit cases, not failures.
  3. Using \(m_2 = 1/m_1\) instead of \(-1/m_1\): Perpendicularity requires the negative reciprocal. \(m_2 = 1/m_1\) gives parallel tangents (same slope family), not orthogonal.
  4. Confusing level curves with gradient curves: The gradient \(\nabla U\) is perpendicular to the level sets \(U = C\); the gradient flow is the orthogonal family. Don't mix them.
  5. Applying to polar families: In polar coordinates \(r = f(\theta, C)\), the orthogonal trajectory condition becomes \(\dfrac{dr}{d\theta} = -\dfrac{r}{dr_{\text{original}}/d\theta}\) (derivable from the polar slope formula). The Cartesian rule does not directly apply.

docs.title: 10. Polar Coordinates — Bonus
docs.text:
For families given in polar form \(r = f(\theta, C)\), the ODE of the given family involves \(\dfrac{dr}{d\theta}\). The orthogonal trajectory condition in polar coordinates is:

\[\left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)_{\perp} = -\frac{r^2}{\left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)_{\text{original}}}\]

Example: \(r = Ce^\theta\) (equiangular spirals, \(dr/d\theta = r\)).

Orthogonal ODE: \(dr/d\theta = -r^2/r = -r\).

Solve: \(dr/r = -d\theta \implies r = Ke^{-\theta}\).

The orthogonal trajectories to equiangular spirals winding outward are equiangular spirals winding inward — an elegant self-referential symmetry.

docs.title: 11. References
docs.text:
1. James Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. — §9.3, Exercises on orthogonal trajectories.
  2. MIT 18.02 — Problem sets on gradient fields and orthogonal families.
  3. Shun-ichi Amari, "Natural Gradient Works Efficiently in Learning," Neural Computation, 1998. (§7.2 above)
  4. Ricky T.Q. Chen et al., "Neural Ordinary Differential Equations," NeurIPS 2018. (background for §7.3)
  5. George F. Simmons, Differential Equations with Applications and Historical Notes, 2nd ed. — Ch. 2, for the classical geometric theory.
