docs.title: Mixing Problems
docs.text: "A tank, a pipe in, a pipe out — and hidden inside this mundane setup is the entire theory of first-order linear ODEs, compartmental models, and the mathematics of how information decays and concentrates in neural networks."

docs.title: Tags
docs.text: #calculus #ODE #differential-equations #mixing-problems #first-order-linear #machine-learning #deep-learning

docs.title: Links
docs.text: [[Separable Equations]] | [[Orthogonal Trajectories]] | [[First-Order Linear ODEs]]

docs.title: 1. The Physical Setup
docs.text:
A tank contains a solution (fluid + dissolved substance). Two processes happen simultaneously:

  • Inflow: Solution enters at rate \(r_{in}\) (volume/time) with concentration \(c_{in}\) (substance/volume).
  • Outflow: Well-mixed solution leaves at rate \(r_{out}\) (volume/time).

We want to track \(Q(t)\) = amount of substance in the tank at time \(t\).

The governing principle is a balance law (conservation):

\[\frac{dQ}{dt} = \text{Rate in} - \text{Rate out}\] \[\boxed{\frac{dQ}{dt} = r_{in} \cdot c_{in} - r_{out} \cdot \frac{Q(t)}{V(t)}}\]

where \(V(t)\) is the volume of solution in the tank at time \(t\).

The term \(\frac{Q(t)}{V(t)}\) is the concentration in the tank at time \(t\) — the "well-mixed" assumption means the outflow carries whatever concentration is currently in the tank.

docs.title: 2. The Volume Function \(V(t)\)
docs.text:
\[V(t) = V_0 + (r_{in} - r_{out}),t\]

where \(V_0 = V(0)\) is the initial volume.

Three cases:

Condition Effect ODE type \(r_{in} = r_{out}\) \(V(t) = V_0\) (constant) Linear, constant coefficients \(r_{in} > r_{out}\) Tank fills Linear, variable coefficients \(r_{in} < r_{out}\) Tank drains Linear, variable coefficients (finite time blow-up possible)

docs.title: 3. The ODE — First-Order Linear
docs.text:
Substituting \(V(t) = V_0 + (r_{in} - r_{out})t\):

\[\frac{dQ}{dt} + \underbrace{\frac{r_{out}}{V_0 + (r_{in} - r_{out})t}}_{P(t)} Q = \underbrace{r_{in} \cdot c_{in}}_{f(t)} \tag{1}\]

This is a first-order linear ODE in standard form \(Q' + P(t)Q = f(t)\).

docs.title: Integrating Factor Method
docs.text:
Multiply both sides by the integrating factor

\[\mu(t) = e^{\int P(t), dt},\]

so that the left side becomes an exact derivative:

\[\frac{d}{dt}\left[\mu(t), Q(t)\right] = \mu(t), f(t).\]

Integrate both sides:

\[\mu(t), Q(t) = \int \mu(t), f(t), dt + C.\]

Solve for \(Q(t)\) and apply the initial condition \(Q(0) = Q_0\).

docs.title: 4. Rigorous Derivation of the Integrating Factor
docs.text:
Claim: If \(\mu(t) = e^{\int P(t),dt}\), then \(\mu(t)(Q' + P(t)Q) = \frac{d}{dt}(\mu Q)\).

Proof:

\[\frac{d}{dt}(\mu Q) = \mu' Q + \mu Q'.\]

Since \(\mu = e^{\int P,dt}\), we have \(\mu' = P(t),\mu\). Therefore:

\[\frac{d}{dt}(\mu Q) = P\mu Q + \mu Q' = \mu(Q' + PQ). \quad \blacksquare\]

So multiplying the ODE by \(\mu\) converts the left side to a perfect derivative, which we can integrate directly.

docs.title: Example 1 — Constant Volume (Equal Flow Rates)
docs.text:
Setup: A 500 L tank initially contains 10 kg of salt dissolved in water. Brine containing 0.05 kg/L flows in at 10 L/min. Well-mixed solution drains at 10 L/min.

Parameters:

  • \(V_0 = 500\) L, \(r_{in} = r_{out} = 10\) L/min (so \(V(t) = 500\))
  • \(c_{in} = 0.05\) kg/L, \(Q_0 = 10\) kg

ODE:

\[\frac{dQ}{dt} = 10 \cdot 0.05 - 10 \cdot \frac{Q}{500} = 0.5 - \frac{Q}{50}\] \[\frac{dQ}{dt} + \frac{1}{50}Q = 0.5 \tag{2}\]

Integrating factor: \(\mu = e^{t/50}\).

\[\frac{d}{dt}\left(e^{t/50} Q\right) = 0.5, e^{t/50}\]

Integrate:

\[e^{t/50} Q = 0.5 \cdot 50, e^{t/50} + C = 25, e^{t/50} + C\] \[Q(t) = 25 + Ce^{-t/50}\]

Apply \(Q(0) = 10\): \(10 = 25 + C \implies C = -15\).

\[\boxed{Q(t) = 25 - 15e^{-t/50} \text{ kg}}\]

Interpretation:

  • As \(t \to \infty\): \(Q(t) \to 25\) kg. The equilibrium concentration is \(c_{in} = 0.05\) kg/L applied to 500 L, giving \(25\) kg. ✓
  • The system forgets its initial condition exponentially, with time constant \(\tau = 50\) min.
  • At \(t = 50\) min (one time constant): \(Q(50) = 25 - 15e^{-1} \approx 19.48\) kg.
Q(t)
25 ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ────────────────  ← equilibrium

10 ──/

docs.title: Example 2 — Draining Tank (Variable Volume)
docs.text:
Setup: A 200 L tank initially contains 50 kg of salt. Pure water (\(c_{in} = 0\)) flows in at 4 L/min. Mixed solution drains at 6 L/min.

Parameters:

  • \(V(t) = 200 + (4-6)t = 200 - 2t\) (tank empties at \(t = 100\) min)
  • \(Q_0 = 50\) kg, \(c_{in} = 0\)

ODE:

\[\frac{dQ}{dt} = 0 - 6 \cdot \frac{Q}{200 - 2t} = -\frac{6Q}{200 - 2t} = -\frac{3Q}{100 - t}\] \[\frac{dQ}{dt} + \frac{3}{100 - t} Q = 0 \tag{3}\]

This is actually separable (it's homogeneous linear):

\[\frac{dQ}{Q} = -\frac{3, dt}{100 - t}\] \[\ln|Q| = 3\ln|100 - t| + C_1\] \[Q(t) = K(100 - t)^3\]

Apply \(Q(0) = 50\): \(50 = K \cdot 100^3 \implies K = 50/10^6 = 5 \times 10^{-5}\).

\[\boxed{Q(t) = 50\left(\frac{100 - t}{100}\right)^3 = 50\left(1 - \frac{t}{100}\right)^3 \text{ kg}}\]

Check: \(Q(100) = 0\) — tank is empty and contains no salt. ✓

The concentration in the tank:

\[c(t) = \frac{Q(t)}{V(t)} = \frac{50(1 - t/100)^3}{200 - 2t} = \frac{50(1-t/100)^3}{200(1 - t/100)} = \frac{50}{200}(1-t/100)^2 = \frac{1}{4}\left(1-\frac{t}{100}\right)^2\]

At \(t = 0\): \(c(0) = 1/4\) kg/L. At \(t = 100\): \(c(100) = 0\) kg/L. The tank dilutes to zero as it drains.

docs.title: Example 3 — Two-Tank Cascade (System of ODEs)
docs.text:
Setup: Tank 1 (100 L) and Tank 2 (200 L) are connected. Brine at 0.1 kg/L flows into Tank 1 at 5 L/min. The outflow of Tank 1 (5 L/min) feeds into Tank 2. Tank 2 drains at 5 L/min. Initially both tanks contain pure water.

Let \(Q_1(t)\), \(Q_2(t)\) = salt in tanks 1 and 2.

System:

\[\frac{dQ_1}{dt} = 5 \cdot 0.1 - 5 \cdot \frac{Q_1}{100} = 0.5 - \frac{Q_1}{20}\] \[\frac{dQ_2}{dt} = 5 \cdot \frac{Q_1}{100} - 5 \cdot \frac{Q_2}{200} = \frac{Q_1}{20} - \frac{Q_2}{40}\]

Solve Tank 1 first (same structure as Example 1):

\[Q_1(t) = 10(1 - e^{-t/20})\]

Substitute into Tank 2's ODE:

\[\frac{dQ_2}{dt} + \frac{Q_2}{40} = \frac{Q_1}{20} = \frac{10(1-e^{-t/20})}{20} = \frac{1}{2}(1-e^{-t/20})\]

Integrating factor \(\mu = e^{t/40}\):

\[\frac{d}{dt}(e^{t/40} Q_2) = \frac{1}{2}e^{t/40}(1 - e^{-t/20}) = \frac{1}{2}e^{t/40} - \frac{1}{2}e^{-t/40}\]

Integrate:

\[e^{t/40} Q_2 = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 40, e^{t/40} - \frac{1}{2} \cdot (-40), e^{-t/40} + C = 20e^{t/40} + 20e^{-t/40} + C\] \[Q_2(t) = 20 + 20e^{-t/20} + Ce^{-t/40}\]

Apply \(Q_2(0) = 0\): \(0 = 20 + 20 + C \implies C = -40\).

\[\boxed{Q_2(t) = 20 - 40e^{-t/40} + 20e^{-t/20}}\]

As \(t \to \infty\): \(Q_2 \to 20\) kg = \(0.1\) kg/L \(\times\) 200 L. ✓

Key structure: The two-tank cascade is a compartmental model — the output of one ODE drives the next. This is the architecture of recurrent and feedforward systems in both biology and machine learning.

docs.title: 7. The Equilibrium and Time Constant
docs.text:
For the constant-volume case \(Q' + \frac{r}{V}Q = r \cdot c_{in}\), the solution always takes the form:

\[Q(t) = Q_{eq} + (Q_0 - Q_{eq}),e^{-t/\tau}\]

where:

  • \(Q_{eq} = c_{in} \cdot V\) — the equilibrium amount (what the tank converges to)
  • \(\tau = V/r\) — the time constant (how fast it gets there)

At \(t = \tau\): the gap \(|Q(t) - Q_{eq}|\) has decayed to \(e^{-1} \approx 36.8%\) of its initial value.

At \(t = 5\tau\): gap is \(e^{-5} \approx 0.67%\) — effectively at equilibrium.

The time constant \(\tau\) has a clean physical meaning: it is the time it takes to flush one full tank volume through the system (\(\tau = V/r\)).

docs.title: 8. Connection to AI, Machine Learning & Deep Learning
docs.text: The mixing problem is not merely a physics exercise. Its mathematical structure — a first-order linear ODE with a source term and a decay term — is the fundamental equation of memory, forgetting, and information blending in machine learning.

docs.title: 8.1 Exponential Moving Average — The Discrete Mixing Problem
docs.text:
In optimization and statistics, the exponential moving average (EMA) of a quantity \(x_t\) is:

\[S_t = \beta S_{t-1} + (1-\beta) x_t, \quad \beta \in (0,1).\]

This is the discrete-time version of the mixing ODE. To see why, write it as:

\[S_t - S_{t-1} = -(1-\beta)(S_{t-1} - x_t)\] \[\Delta S = -(1-\beta)(S - x_t)\]

In continuous time with step \(\Delta t \to 0\), setting \(\beta = 1 - r\Delta t / V\):

\[\frac{dS}{dt} = -\frac{r}{V}(S - c_{in}) = \frac{r}{V}c_{in} - \frac{r}{V}S\]

This is exactly the constant-volume mixing ODE. The EMA is the mixing problem in disguise, with:

  • \(\beta\) controlling the time constant (memory length)
  • \(x_t\) playing the role of inflow concentration
  • \(S_t\) being the amount in the tank

docs.title: 8.2 Momentum in Gradient Descent (Heavy Ball / Adam)
docs.text:
The momentum update in SGD is:

\[v_t = eta v_{t-1} + (1- eta) abla \mathcal{L}( heta_t)\] \[ heta_{t+1} = heta_t - \eta v_t\]

The velocity \(v_t\) obeys a mixing ODE: it is a running average of past gradients, with old gradients "rinsing out" exponentially. The time constant is \( au = 1/(1- eta)\) steps.

  • \( eta = 0.9\): memory of \( au = 10\) steps.
  • \( eta = 0.99\): memory of \( au = 100\) steps.

Adam uses two mixing ODEs simultaneously:

$\(m_t = eta_1 m_{t-1} + (1- eta_1) abla \mathcal{L}\)$ (first moment — gradient EMA) $\(v_t = eta_2 v_{t-1} + (1- eta_2)( abla \mathcal{L})^2\)$ (second moment — squared gradient EMA)

Both are mixing problems running in parallel, one tracking the "mean tank" and one tracking the "variance tank."

docs.title: 8.3 Batch Normalization — Mixing Running Statistics
docs.text:
During inference, batch normalization uses running estimates of mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\):

\[\mu_{\text{run}} \leftarrow (1-\alpha),\mu_{\text{run}} + \alpha,\mu_{\text{batch}}\]

This is a mixing ODE with time constant \(\tau = 1/\alpha\). The running mean is the "amount of substance" in a tank being continuously flushed with the batch statistics.

Choosing \(\alpha\) too large = the tank is too reactive (noisy estimates). Too small = too sluggish (doesn't track distribution shift). This is exactly the tradeoff between \(\tau\) being too short or too long in Example 1.

docs.title: 8.4 Leaky Integrator Neurons — The Neural Mixing Tank
docs.text:
The standard model of a biological neuron's membrane potential \(V(t)\) is:

\[\tau_m \frac{dV}{dt} = -V(t) + R_m I(t)\] \[\frac{dV}{dt} + \frac{V}{\tau_m} = \frac{R_m}{\tau_m} I(t)\]

This is precisely the mixing ODE with:

  • \(Q \leftrightarrow V\) (membrane potential ↔ amount of substance)
  • \(r/V \leftrightarrow 1/\tau_m\) (leak rate)
  • \(r \cdot c_{in} \leftrightarrow R_m I(t)/\tau_m\) (input current ↔ inflow)

The neuron integrates its input and leaks — it is a mixing tank. The Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neuron used in spiking neural networks is built directly on this ODE.

In deep learning, Liquid State Machines and Echo State Networks (reservoir computing) generalize this to high-dimensional networks of leaky integrators — tanks coupled into a cascade, exactly like Example 3.

docs.title: 8.5 LSTM Forget Gate — Controlled Mixing
docs.text:
The LSTM cell state update:

\[C_t = f_t \odot C_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde{C}_t\]

where \(f_t \in (0,1)\) is the forget gate and \(i_t\) is the input gate.

Compare with the mixing ODE solution:

\[Q(t + \Delta t) = e^{-\Delta t/\tau} Q(t) + (1 - e^{-\Delta t/\tau}) Q_{eq}\]

The forget gate \(f_t\) plays the role of \(e^{-\Delta t/\tau}\) — the "fraction remaining in the tank." The input gate \(i_t \odot \tilde{C}_t\) is the new inflow. The LSTM learns to set its own time constant adaptively, solving a parameterized family of mixing problems at each timestep.

The entire architecture of LSTMs is a learnable, input-dependent version of the mixing ODE. Grokking one gives you the geometric intuition for the other.

docs.title: 8.6 Compartmental Models in Epidemiology and Federated Learning
docs.text:
The two-tank cascade (Example 3) generalizes to compartmental models: systems of ODEs where substance flows between compartments. In ML:

  • SIR/SEIR epidemic models (used in federated learning to model data infection/spread across nodes) are compartmental mixing systems.
  • Graph Neural Networks can be understood as compartmental mixing problems on graphs, where "substance" (feature information) diffuses between nodes according to the graph Laplacian — a high-dimensional mixing ODE.

docs.title: 9. Summary Table
docs.text: Scenario ODE Solution Form ML Analogue Constant volume \(Q' + \frac{r}{V}Q = rc_{in}\) \(Q_{eq} + (Q_0 - Q_{eq})e^{-t/\tau}\) EMA, momentum, batch norm Variable volume \(Q' + \frac{r_{out}}{V_0 + \Delta r \cdot t}Q = r_{in}c_{in}\) Power-law or integrating factor Annealed learning rate schedules Two-tank cascade System of 2 linear ODEs Sum of exponentials Multi-layer RNNs, reservoir computing Leaky neuron \(\tau_m V' + V = R_m I(t)\) Convolution of \(I\) with \(e^{-t/\tau_m}\) LIF neurons, LSTMs

docs.title: 10. Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Using \(Q/V_0\) instead of \(Q/V(t)\) in variable-volume problems. The concentration uses the current volume — a common and fatal error.
  2. Forgetting the units. Rate in is (L/min) × (kg/L) = kg/min. Rate out is (L/min) × (kg/L) = kg/min. \(dQ/dt\) must have units kg/min.
  3. Not checking the domain. If \(r_{out} > r_{in}\), \(V(t)\) reaches zero in finite time \(t^* = V_0/(r_{out} - r_{in})\). The solution is only valid on \([0, t^*)\).
  4. Confusing \(Q(t)\) with \(c(t)\). \(Q\) is amount (kg); \(c = Q/V\) is concentration (kg/L). The problem statement specifies which one is given and which is sought.
  5. Wrong equilibrium. The equilibrium is \(Q_{eq} = c_{in} \cdot V\) (concentration × volume), not \(c_{in}\) alone.

docs.title: 11. References
docs.text:
1. James Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. — §9.3, "Separable Equations" (mixing problems as applications); §9.5 "Linear Equations."
  2. MIT 18.02 — Lecture notes on first-order linear ODEs and applications.
  3. Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, "Long Short-Term Memory," Neural Computation 9(8), 1997. (§8.5 above)
  4. Diederik P. Kingma & Jimmy Ba, "Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization," ICLR 2015. (§8.2 above)
  5. W. Maass, T. Natschläger, H. Markram, "Real-Time Computing Without Stable States: A New Framework for Neural Computation Based on Perturbations," Neural Computation, 2002. (Liquid State Machines, §8.4)

docs.title: Natural Growth and Decay
docs.text: "The simplest ODE in existence. One equation. And yet it is the heartbeat of compound interest, radioactive decay, population dynamics, and the gradient flow of every neural network ever trained."

docs.title: Tags
docs.text: #calculus #ODE #differential-equations #exponential-growth #natural-growth #machine-learning #deep-learning

docs.title: Links
docs.text: [[Separable Equations]] | [[Mixing Problems]] | [[Orthogonal Trajectories]] | [[First-Order Linear ODEs]]

docs.title: 1. The Governing Principle
docs.text:
The Law of Natural Growth (or Decay) asserts:

The rate of change of a quantity is proportional to the quantity itself.

Mathematically:

\[\frac{dP}{dt} = kP, \quad k \in \mathbb{R} \tag{1}\]

where:

  • \(P(t)\) is the quantity at time \(t\)
  • \(k\) is the proportionality constant (the growth/decay rate)
  • \(k > 0\): growth; \(\quad k < 0\): decay

This is the simplest separable ODE, and it has a unique, explicit, beautiful solution.

docs.title: 2.1 Separation of Variables
docs.text:
Assuming \(P(t) \neq 0\), separate:

\[\frac{dP}{P} = k, dt\]

Integrate both sides:

\[\int \frac{dP}{P} = \int k, dt\] \[\ln|P| = kt + C_1, \quad C_1 \in \mathbb{R}\]

Exponentiate:

\[|P(t)| = e^{C_1} e^{kt}\] \[P(t) = \pm e^{C_1} e^{kt} = A e^{kt}, \quad A \in \mathbb{R} \setminus {0}.\]

Check \(P = 0\): Substituting into (1): \(0 = k \cdot 0\) ✓. Recovered by \(A = 0\).

General solution:

\[\boxed{P(t) = A e^{kt}, \quad A \in \mathbb{R}} \tag{2}\]

docs.title: 2.2 Applying the Initial Condition
docs.text:
Given \(P(0) = P_0\):

\[P_0 = A e^{0} = A \implies A = P_0\] \[\boxed{P(t) = P_0, e^{kt}} \tag{3}\]

docs.title: 2.3 Uniqueness
docs.text: By Picard–Lindelöf: \(f(t, P) = kP\) is Lipschitz in \(P\) (with constant \(|k|\)) on any rectangle, so there exists a unique solution through any initial condition \((t_0, P_0)\). The family (2) is therefore the complete solution — no singular solutions exist.

docs.title: 3. The Constant \(k\) — What It Means
docs.text:
Rewrite (3) as:

\[\frac{P(t)}{P_0} = e^{kt}\]

Taking logarithm:

\[k = \frac{1}{t} \ln\frac{P(t)}{P_0}\]

So \(k\) is the instantaneous fractional growth rate per unit time. Concretely:

  • In time \(\Delta t\), the quantity changes by the factor \(e^{k\Delta t}\).
  • For small \(k\Delta t\): \(e^{k\Delta t} \approx 1 + k\Delta t\) — a growth of approximately \(k \cdot 100%\) per unit time.

docs.title: Doubling Time (\(k > 0\))
docs.text:
The time \(T_2\) for \(P\) to double:

\[2P_0 = P_0 e^{kT_2} \implies T_2 = \frac{\ln 2}{k} \approx \frac{0.693}{k}\]

The famous Rule of 70: for a growth rate of \(k \times 100%\) per year, doubling time \(\approx 70/(\text{percent rate})\) years.

docs.title: Half-Life (\(k < 0\), write \(k = -\lambda\), \(\lambda > 0\))
docs.text:
The time \(t_{1/2}\) for \(P\) to halve:

\[\frac{P_0}{2} = P_0 e^{-\lambda t_{1/2}} \implies t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}\]

Key fact: Half-life is independent of \(P_0\). No matter how much substance you start with, it always takes the same time to halve.

docs.title: Example 1 — Radioactive Decay: Carbon-14
docs.text:
Carbon-14 decays with half-life \(t_{1/2} = 5730\) years.

Find \(k\):

\[k = -\frac{\ln 2}{5730} \approx -1.2097 \times 10^{-4} \text{ yr}^{-1}\]

Model: \(P(t) = P_0, e^{-1.2097 \times 10^{-4}, t}\)

Radiocarbon dating: A bone fragment has \(72%\) of original C-14. How old is it?

\[0.72 P_0 = P_0, e^{kt} \implies t = \frac{\ln 0.72}{k} = \frac{\ln 0.72}{-1.2097 \times 10^{-4}} \approx 2694 \text{ years}\] 
P/P₀
1.0 ●
    │\
0.5 │ \●─────────── ← half-life at t = 5730
    │   \
0.25│    \●────────── ← t = 11460 (two half-lives)
    │     \
0.125      \●──────── ← t = 17190
    └──────────────────→ t (years)
       5730 11460 17190

docs.title: Example 2 — Population Growth: Malthusian Model
docs.text:
A bacterial population of 500 doubles every 3 hours.

Find \(k\):

\[T_2 = 3 \implies k = \frac{\ln 2}{3} \approx 0.2310 \text{ hr}^{-1}\]

Model: \(P(t) = 500, e^{0.2310, t}\)

Question: How many bacteria after 24 hours?

\[P(24) = 500, e^{0.2310 \times 24} = 500, e^{5.545} \approx 500 \times 256 = 128{,}000\]

(Exactly \(500 \times 2^8\) — 8 doublings in 24 hours. \(\checkmark\))

Question: When does the population reach 1 million?

\[10^6 = 500, e^{0.2310, t} \implies t = \frac{\ln(2000)}{0.2310} \approx \frac{7.601}{0.2310} \approx 32.9 \text{ hours}\]

docs.title: Example 3 — Newton's Law of Cooling (Shifted Natural Decay)
docs.text:
Newton's Law of Cooling states that the rate of change of temperature \(T(t)\) of an object is proportional to the difference between \(T\) and the ambient temperature \(T_a\):

\[\frac{dT}{dt} = k(T - T_a), \quad k < 0\]

Substitution: Let \(u(t) = T(t) - T_a\). Then \(u' = T'\), so:

\[\frac{du}{dt} = ku\]

This is the natural decay equation! Solution: \(u(t) = u_0, e^{kt}\), i.e.:

\[\boxed{T(t) = T_a + (T_0 - T_a), e^{kt}}\]

Example: Coffee at \(90°C\) in a \(20°C\) room. After 10 min, coffee is \(70°C\). Find \(T(30)\).

Find \(k\):

\[70 = 20 + (90 - 20)e^{10k} \implies 50 = 70 e^{10k} \implies k = \frac{1}{10}\ln\frac{5}{7} \approx -0.03365 \text{ min}^{-1}\]

At \(t = 30\):

\[T(30) = 20 + 70, e^{-0.03365 \times 30} = 20 + 70, e^{-1.0094} \approx 20 + 70(0.3644) \approx 45.5°C\] 
T(t) °C
 90 ●
    │\
 70 │ ●
    │  \
 45 │   \  ●
    │    \   \
 20 ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─  ← T_a = 20°C (asymptote)
    └──────────────────────────→ t
     0    10    20    30  (min)

docs.title: Example 4 — Compound Interest
docs.text:
A bank offers continuous compounding at annual rate \(r\). Principal \(P_0\) dollars.

\[\frac{dP}{dt} = rP \implies P(t) = P_0, e^{rt}\]

Comparison with discrete compounding \(n\) times/year:

\[P_n(t) = P_0\left(1 + \frac{r}{n}\right)^{nt}\]

As \(n \to \infty\):

\[\lim_{n \to \infty} P_0\left(1 + \frac{r}{n}\right)^{nt} = P_0, e^{rt}\]

This is one of the most important limit definitions of \(e\) — the natural growth ODE is the continuous limit of compound interest.

docs.title: Example 5 — Two Measurements, No Initial Condition Given
docs.text:
Setup: A radioactive substance measures 8 g at \(t = 0\) and 5 g at \(t = 1\) year. When will 1 g remain?

Find \(k\) (no need for half-life):

\[5 = 8, e^{k \cdot 1} \implies k = \ln\frac{5}{8} \approx -0.4700 \text{ yr}^{-1}\]

Model: \(P(t) = 8, e^{-0.4700, t}\)

When is \(P = 1\)?

\[1 = 8, e^{-0.4700, t} \implies t = \frac{\ln(1/8)}{-0.4700} = \frac{3\ln 2}{0.4700} \approx 4.42 \text{ years}\]

docs.title: Growth vs. Decay — Family of Solutions
Phase Line
docs.text:
For \(P' = kP\):

k > 0:     ←──── 0 ────→          (0 is unstable equilibrium)
            decay  growth

k < 0:     ────→ 0 ←────          (0 is stable equilibrium)

The only equilibrium is \(P^* = 0\). Its stability depends entirely on the sign of \(k\).

docs.title: 7. The Exponential Function IS the Solution
docs.text:
The natural growth ODE \(y' = ky\) can be taken as the defining property of the exponential function:

\(e^{kt}\) is the unique function equal to \(k\) times its own derivative, with value 1 at \(t = 0\).

This is why \(e\) appears everywhere in calculus — it is the base that makes the derivative of \(e^x\) exactly \(e^x\) (i.e., \(k = 1\)). Every other base \(a^x = e^{x \ln a}\) satisfies \(\frac{d}{dx}a^x = (\ln a), a^x\) — scaling the rate by \(\ln a\).

docs.title: 8. Connection to AI, Machine Learning & Deep Learning
docs.text: The natural growth/decay law is not a background fact in ML — it is the structural skeleton of training dynamics, weight behavior, and information propagation.

docs.title: 8.1 Gradient Flow — Parameters Decay to Minimum
docs.text:
For a quadratic loss \(\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \frac{\lambda}{2}\theta^2\) (L2-regularized), gradient flow gives:

\[\frac{d\theta}{dt} = -\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L} = -\lambda\theta\]

This is natural decay with rate \(k = -\lambda\):

\[\theta(t) = \theta_0, e^{-\lambda t}\]

The parameter decays exponentially toward zero at rate \(\lambda\) — the regularization strength is literally the decay constant. This is why L2 regularization is also called weight decay.

More generally, near a local minimum \(\theta^_\), the Hessian \(H = \nabla^2 \mathcal{L}(\theta^_)\) governs the linearized dynamics. Each eigenmode \(v_i\) of \(H\) (with eigenvalue \(\lambda_i > 0\)) decays independently as \(e^{-\lambda_i t}\). Directions with large curvature (\(\lambda_i\) large) decay fast; flat directions (\(\lambda_i\) small) decay slowly.

docs.title: 8.2 Vanishing and Exploding Gradients — Natural Growth in Backpropagation
docs.text:
In a deep network with \(L\) layers, the gradient of the loss with respect to layer \(\ell\) involves a product of Jacobians:

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{h}_\ell} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{h}_L} \cdot \prod_{i=\ell}^{L-1} \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_{i+1}}{\partial \mathbf{h}_i}\]

If each Jacobian has spectral norm \(\rho\) (dominant eigenvalue), this product behaves as \(\rho^{L - \ell}\):

\[\left|\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{h}_\ell}\right| \approx \left|\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{h}_L}\right| \cdot \rho^{L - \ell}\]

This is discrete natural growth/decay in depth \(L - \ell\) (playing the role of time):

  • \(\rho < 1\): vanishing gradients — exponential decay in depth.
  • \(\rho > 1\): exploding gradients — exponential growth in depth.
  • \(\rho = 1\): neutral propagation — why residual connections (ResNets) and careful weight initialization (Xavier, He) aim for \(\rho \approx 1\).

The law of natural growth is precisely why deep networks are hard to train without architectural care.

docs.title: 8.3 Learning Rate Decay Schedules
docs.text:
The most common learning rate schedule is exponential decay:

\[\eta(t) = \eta_0, e^{-\lambda t}\]

This solves \(\frac{d\eta}{dt} = -\lambda \eta\) — natural decay applied to the learning rate itself. The intuition:

  • Early training (\(t\) small): large \(\eta\) for fast progress.
  • Late training (\(t\) large): small \(\eta\) for fine-grained convergence.

The decay constant \(\lambda\) controls the tradeoff. In practice, the discrete version is:

\[\eta_t = \eta_0 \cdot \gamma^{t/T}, \quad \gamma \in (0,1)\]

which is \(e^{-(t/T)\ln(1/\gamma)}\) — exactly \(P_0 e^{kt}\) with \(k = -\frac{\ln(1/\gamma)}{T}\).

docs.title: 8.4 Weight Decay IS Natural Decay
docs.text:
The L2-regularized SGD update:

\[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta_t) - \eta \lambda \theta_t = (1 - \eta\lambda)\theta_t - \eta \nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta_t)\]

The factor \((1 - \eta\lambda)\) multiplied at each step is the discrete natural decay: after \(T\) steps with no gradient signal,

\[\theta_T = (1 - \eta\lambda)^T \theta_0 \approx e^{-\eta\lambda T} \theta_0\]

(using \((1-x)^n \approx e^{-nx}\) for small \(x\)). Weight decay is natural decay in discrete time — parameter values shrink exponentially toward zero unless gradients push back.

docs.title: 8.5 Dropout as Stochastic Decay
docs.text:
At each forward pass, dropout retains each neuron with probability \(p\) and zeroes it with probability \(1-p\). Over \(T\) training steps, the expected magnitude of a weight that receives no useful gradient signal decays as:

\[\mathbb{E}[\text{effective weight}] \sim p^T \cdot w_0 = e^{T \ln p} \cdot w_0\]

Since \(\ln p < 0\) for \(p \in (0,1)\), this is natural decay in \(T\) — dropout induces an effective exponential shrinkage of "useless" weights.

docs.title: 8.6 Attention Score Softmax — Natural Growth Normalizing
docs.text:
The softmax function in attention:

\[\text{softmax}(z_i) = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}\]

The numerator \(e^{z_i}\) is the natural growth function evaluated at the attention logit. The softmax is not merely a convenient normalization — it is the Boltzmann distribution arising from entropy maximization, and the exponential is there because the entropy-maximizing distribution over energies \(z_i\) takes the form \(e^{z_i / T}\) (here temperature \(T = 1\)). The law of natural growth is the generating mechanism behind every attention score in every transformer.

docs.title: 8.7 Information-Theoretic Interpretation — KL Divergence and Exponential Families
docs.text:
The natural growth solution \(P(t) = P_0 e^{kt}\) belongs to the exponential family of distributions — the most important parametric family in statistics and machine learning:

\[p(x; \eta) = h(x)\exp(\eta \cdot T(x) - A(\eta))\]

Every distribution used in deep learning (Gaussian, Bernoulli, Categorical, Poisson) is an exponential family member. Their canonical form is precisely the natural growth function in the sufficient statistic \(T(x)\) — which is why the cross-entropy loss (used to train virtually every classifier) takes logarithmic form: \(\log p = \eta \cdot T(x) - A(\eta) + \log h(x)\), recovering \(kt\) from \(e^{kt}\).

docs.title: 9. Summary Table
docs.text: Phenomenon \(k\) \(P(t)\) Time Scale C-14 radioactive decay \(-1.21 \times 10^{-4}\) yr\(^{-1}\) \(P_0 e^{-1.21 \times 10^{-4} t}\) \(t_{1/2} = 5730\) yr Bacterial growth \(+0.231\) hr\(^{-1}\) \(P_0 e^{0.231 t}\) \(T_2 = 3\) hr Continuous compound interest \(r\) (annual rate) \(P_0 e^{rt}\) \(T_2 = \ln 2 / r\) Weight decay (L2 reg.) \(-\lambda\) \(\theta_0 e^{-\lambda t}\) \(\tau = 1/\lambda\) Gradient vanishing (per layer) \(\ln \rho < 0\) \(g_0 \rho^L\) Layers to vanish: $1/ Exponential LR schedule \(-\lambda\) \(\eta_0 e^{-\lambda t}\) \(\tau = 1/\lambda\)

docs.title: 10. Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Confusing \(k\) and \(t_{1/2}\) or \(T_2\). The growth rate is \(k = \ln 2 / T_2 = -\ln 2 / t_{1/2}\). Always derive \(k\) explicitly before writing the solution.
  2. Using base 2 or base 10 instead of \(e\). The ODE \(P' = kP\) forces base \(e\). If the problem states doubling time \(T_2\), write \(P(t) = P_0 \cdot 2^{t/T_2} = P_0 e^{(t/T_2)\ln 2}\) — both are equivalent, but the ODE derivation always produces the \(e\)-form.
  3. Forgetting to check \(P = 0\). The separation step assumes \(P \neq 0\); verify that \(P = 0\) is also a solution (it is, trivially).
  4. Newton's cooling — not applying the shift. Set \(u = T - T_a\) first; then it becomes natural decay. Working directly on \(T' = k(T - T_a)\) without substitution is error-prone.
  5. Assuming \(k\) is always negative for "decay." \(k\) is negative for decay, positive for growth. The sign is determined by the physics/problem statement, not by convention.

docs.title: Logistic Model
docs.text: "Malthus said populations grow forever. Verhulst said: no — the world pushes back. That pushback, encoded as a single quadratic term, gives us one of the most consequential ODEs in all of science."

docs.title: 1.1 The Malthusian Model (Too Simple)
docs.text:
The simplest population model assumes growth proportional to current population:

\[\frac{dP}{dt} = kP, \quad k > 0\]

Solution: \(P(t) = P_0 e^{kt}\) — unbounded exponential growth. This is biologically absurd for large \(t\): no environment has infinite resources.

docs.title: 1.2 The Logistic Correction (Pierre François Verhulst, 1838)
docs.text:
Verhulst's insight: the per-capita growth rate \(\frac{1}{P}\frac{dP}{dt}\) should not be constant — it should decrease linearly as \(P\) approaches the carrying capacity \(K\) of the environment:

\[\frac{1}{P}\frac{dP}{dt} = r\left(1 - \frac{P}{K}\right)\]

This gives the logistic equation:

\[\boxed{\frac{dP}{dt} = rP\left(1 - \frac{P}{K}\right)} \tag{1}\]

Parameters:

  • \(r > 0\): intrinsic growth rate (units: \(1/\text{time}\))
  • \(K > 0\): carrying capacity (units: population)
  • \(P_0 = P(0)\): initial population

Qualitative behavior before solving:

  • If \(P \ll K\): \(1 - P/K \approx 1\), so \(dP/dt \approx rP\) — exponential growth.
  • If \(P = K\): \(dP/dt = 0\) — equilibrium.
  • If \(P > K\): \(dP/dt < 0\) — population declines back toward \(K\).

docs.title: 2. Solving the Logistic ODE — Full Derivation
docs.text: Equation (1) is separable: \(g(t) = r\), \(h(P) = P(1 - P/K)\).

docs.title: Step 1 — Separate
docs.text: \[\frac{dP}{P(1 - P/K)} = r, dt \tag{2}\]

docs.title: Step 2 — Partial Fractions
docs.text:
Decompose the left side. Write \(1 - P/K = (K-P)/K\):

\[\frac{1}{P \cdot (K-P)/K} = \frac{K}{P(K-P)}\]

Partial fractions:

\[\frac{K}{P(K-P)} = \frac{A}{P} + \frac{B}{K-P}\] \[K = A(K-P) + BP\]
  • Set \(P = 0\): \(K = AK \implies A = 1\).
  • Set \(P = K\): \(K = BK \implies B = 1\).

So:

\[\frac{K}{P(K-P)} = \frac{1}{P} + \frac{1}{K-P}\]

docs.title: Step 3 — Integrate Both Sides
docs.text: \[\int \left(\frac{1}{P} + \frac{1}{K-P}\right) dP = \int r, dt\] \[\ln|P| - \ln|K - P| = rt + C_1\] \[\ln\left|\frac{P}{K-P}\right| = rt + C_1\] \[\frac{P}{K-P} = Ae^{rt}, \quad A = e^{C_1} > 0 \tag{3}\]

docs.title: Step 4 — Solve for \(P\)
docs.text:
From (3): \(P = Ae^{rt}(K - P)\):

\[P = KAe^{rt} - PAe^{rt}\] \[P(1 + Ae^{rt}) = KAe^{rt}\] \[P(t) = \frac{KAe^{rt}}{1 + Ae^{rt}} = \frac{K}{1 + A^{-1}e^{-rt}}\]

docs.title: Step 5 — Apply Initial Condition
docs.text:
At \(t = 0\): \(P(0) = P_0\):

\[P_0 = \frac{K}{1 + A^{-1}} \implies 1 + A^{-1} = \frac{K}{P_0} \implies A^{-1} = \frac{K - P_0}{P_0}\]

Let \(B = A^{-1} = \frac{K - P_0}{P_0}\). The general solution is:

\[\boxed{P(t) = \frac{K}{1 + \left(\dfrac{K - P_0}{P_0}\right)e^{-rt}}} \tag{4}\]

docs.title: Step 6 — Singular Solutions
docs.text:
Setting \(h(P) = 0\):

  • \(P \equiv 0\): trivially satisfies (1) (extinct population). Recovered from (4) as \(P_0 = 0\).
  • \(P \equiv K\): also satisfies (1). Recovered from (4) as \(P_0 = K\) (giving \(B = 0\)).

Both are unstable/stable equilibria respectively (see §4).

docs.title: 3.1 The S-Curve (Sigmoid Shape)
docs.text:
The logistic function is the archetypal S-shaped curve (sigmoidal):

P(t)
 K  ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ──────────────────  ← stable equilibrium
                        ___/
K/2 ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ────/── ← inflection point
                  ___/
               __/
P₀ ──────────/
     │
     0              t*             → t
                    ↑
            t* = (1/r) ln((K-P₀)/P₀)

docs.title: 3.2 The Inflection Point
docs.text:
Where is growth fastest? Differentiate (1):

\[\frac{d^2P}{dt^2} = r\frac{dP}{dt}\left(1 - \frac{P}{K}\right) + rP\left(-\frac{1}{K}\frac{dP}{dt}\right) = r\frac{dP}{dt}\left(1 - \frac{2P}{K}\right)\]

Setting \(d^2P/dt^2 = 0\) (and \(dP/dt \neq 0\)):

\[1 - \frac{2P}{K} = 0 \implies \boxed{P^* = \frac{K}{2}}\]

The inflection point — where the population grows fastest — occurs exactly at half the carrying capacity. This is a structural feature independent of \(r\) and \(P_0\).

The time \(t^_\) at which \(P(t^_) = K/2\):

\[\frac{K}{2} = \frac{K}{1 + Be^{-rt^_}} \implies 1 + Be^{-rt^_} = 2 \implies e^{-rt^*} = \frac{1}{B}\] \[t^* = \frac{1}{r}\ln B = \frac{1}{r}\ln\frac{K - P_0}{P_0}\]

docs.title: 3.3 Limiting Behavior
docs.text: \[\lim_{t \to \infty} P(t) = K \qquad \text{(approaches carrying capacity)}$$ $$\lim_{t \to -\infty} P(t) = 0 \qquad \text{(approached zero in the past)}\]

docs.title: 4. Phase Line Analysis — Qualitative Theory
docs.text: The logistic ODE \(\dot{P} = rP(1 - P/K)\) is autonomous: the right side depends only on \(P\), not \(t\) explicitly.

docs.title: Equilibria
docs.text: Set \(\dot{P} = 0\): $\(rP\left(1 - \frac{P}{K}\right) = 0 \implies P^* = 0 \quad \text{or} \quad P^* = K\)$

docs.title: Stability via \(\frac{d}{dP}[rP(1-P/K)]\)
docs.text:
Let \(f(P) = rP(1 - P/K)\). Then \(f'(P) = r(1 - 2P/K)\).

  • At \(P^* = 0\): \(f'(0) = r > 0\) → unstable equilibrium (small perturbations grow).
  • At \(P^* = K\): \(f'(K) = r(1 - 2) = -r < 0\) → stable equilibrium (small perturbations decay).

docs.title: Phase Line
docs.text:
f(P) = dP/dt

      ↑ f(P)
      │         ╭──────╮
      │        /        \
      │       /          \
──────┼──────/────────────\──────── P
      0                   K
   unstable            stable

Sign of dP/dt:
  P ∈ (0, K):  dP/dt > 0  →  P increases toward K
  P ∈ (K, ∞):  dP/dt < 0  →  P decreases toward K
  P < 0:  biologically invalid

All solutions with \(P_0 > 0\) converge to \(K\) as \(t \to \infty\). The carrying capacity is a global attractor on \((0, \infty)\).

docs.title: 5. The Logistic Function as a Special Case
docs.text:
Setting \(K = 1\), \(r = 1\), \(P_0 = 1/2\) (so \(B = 1\)):

\[\sigma(t) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-t}}\]

This is the standard logistic / sigmoid function. Its derivative:

\[\sigma'(t) = \sigma(t)(1 - \sigma(t))\]

This is exactly the logistic ODE evaluated at \(K = 1\): \(\dot{P} = P(1-P)\).

The sigmoid is not just a convenient S-shape — it is the explicit solution to the logistic ODE, evaluated at \(K = 1\).

Its key analytic properties:

Property Value \(\sigma(0)\) \(1/2\) (inflection point) \(\lim_{t\to\infty}\sigma(t)\) \(1\) \(\lim_{t\to-\infty}\sigma(t)\) \(0\) \(\sigma'(t)\) \(\sigma(t)(1-\sigma(t)) \leq 1/4\) Maximum of \(\sigma'\) \(1/4\), attained at \(t = 0\) \(\sigma(-t)\) \(1 - \sigma(t)\) (antisymmetry about \((0, 1/2)\))

docs.title: Family of Logistic Curves (varying \(P_0\), fixed \(r, K\))
Phase Portrait
docs.text:
dP/dt
  ↑
r·K/4─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ╭──╮  ← maximum growth rate at P = K/2
  │                /    \
  │               /      \
  │              /        \
──┼─────────────/──────────\──────────── P
  0            K/2          K
           ↑                ↑
       inflection         equilibrium

docs.title: 7.1 Logistic with Harvesting
docs.text:
\[\frac{dP}{dt} = rP\left(1 - \frac{P}{K}\right) - H\]

where \(H > 0\) is a constant harvesting rate. The equilibria shift; for \(H > rK/4\) (the maximum of \(rP(1-P/K)\)) there are no equilibria and the population collapses to zero in finite time. The threshold \(H^* = rK/4\) is the maximum sustainable yield.

docs.title: 7.2 Gompertz Model
docs.text:
\[\frac{dP}{dt} = rP\ln\frac{K}{P}\]

Used in tumor growth modeling and sometimes ML (Gompertz activation). The per-capita rate \(r\ln(K/P)\) decays logarithmically rather than linearly. More pessimistic than logistic for large \(P\).

docs.title: 7.3 Allee Effect
docs.text:
\[\frac{dP}{dt} = rP\left(1 - \frac{P}{K}\right)\left(\frac{P}{A} - 1\right), \quad 0 < A < K\]

Introduces a minimum viable population \(A\): populations below \(A\) decline to extinction. Three equilibria: \(0\) (stable), \(A\) (unstable), \(K\) (stable).

docs.title: 8. Connection to AI, Machine Learning & Deep Learning
docs.text: The logistic model is not background material for ML — it is ML, in several precise senses.

docs.title: 8.1 Logistic Regression — The Static Logistic Model
docs.text:
In binary classification, given features \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d\), logistic regression models:

\[P(y = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}) = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b)}}\]

The sigmoid here is the logistic solution at a fixed "time" \(t = \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b\). The model is literally evaluating the logistic ODE solution on a linear projection of the input.

Training minimizes the cross-entropy loss:

\[\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \left[y_i \ln \hat{p}_i + (1-y_i)\ln(1-\hat{p}_i)\right]\]

The gradient:

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{w}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{p}_i - y_i)\mathbf{x}_i\]

uses \(\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))\) — the logistic ODE identity — to simplify the chain rule derivative cleanly.

docs.title: 8.2 Sigmoid Activation — Every Neuron Solves a Logistic ODE
docs.text:
A sigmoid neuron computes \(\sigma(z)\) where \(z = \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b\). The value \(\sigma(z)\) is the solution to \(\dot{P} = P(1-P)\) evaluated at \(t = z\).

The vanishing gradient problem in deep networks has an ODE interpretation: for large \(|z|\), \(\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z)) \to 0\) — the logistic curve flattens at both ends. Gradients flowing through many sigmoid layers multiply these near-zero derivatives, causing exponential decay of gradient signal (vanishing) or, in certain architectures, exponential growth (exploding).

This is why ReLU (which does not saturate) largely replaced sigmoid in hidden layers — it does not suffer from the saturation inherent in the logistic ODE's asymptotic approach to \(0\) and \(1\).

docs.title: 8.3 Softmax — The Multiclass Logistic Model
docs.text:
Softmax generalizes the sigmoid to \(C\) classes:

\[\text{softmax}(\mathbf{z})_c = \frac{e^{z_c}}{\sum_{j=1}^C e^{z_j}}\]

For \(C = 2\): \(\text{softmax}(\mathbf{z})_1 = \frac{e^{z_1}}{e^{z_1} + e^{z_2}} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(z_1 - z_2)}} = \sigma(z_1 - z_2)\).

Softmax is the multivariate generalization of the logistic solution — the carrying capacity \(K\) becomes a normalization constraint forcing probabilities to sum to 1.

docs.title: 8.4 Neural ODEs and the Logistic Vector Field
docs.text:
A Neural ODE (Chen et al., 2018) defines the hidden state dynamics as:

\[\frac{d\mathbf{h}}{dt} = f_\theta(\mathbf{h}(t), t)\]

The logistic ODE is the simplest nontrivial choice: \(f_\theta(h) = rh(1-h)\) (component-wise, with \(K=1\)). The residual network (ResNet) layer:

\[\mathbf{h}_{t+1} = \mathbf{h}_t + f(\mathbf{h}_t)\]

is the Euler discretization of a Neural ODE with step size \(\Delta t = 1\). As the number of layers \(\to \infty\) and step size \(\to 0\), the ResNet converges to a Neural ODE. The logistic model is the prototype for understanding what these continuous-depth networks are computing.

docs.title: 8.5 Population Dynamics of SGD — Loss Landscape as Carrying Capacity
docs.text:
There is a striking analogy between the logistic model and stochastic gradient descent (SGD) convergence:

Logistic model SGD convergence Population \(P(t)\) Model performance (e.g. accuracy) Carrying capacity \(K\) Optimal achievable accuracy Growth rate \(r\) Learning rate \(\eta\) \(1 - P/K\) (saturation) Diminishing returns near optimum Inflection at \(K/2\) Fastest learning at intermediate performance \(t \to \infty: P \to K\) Training convergence

Under certain loss landscape assumptions, the training accuracy \(a(t)\) satisfies approximately:

\[\frac{da}{dt} \approx \eta \cdot a \cdot (1 - a)\]

— a logistic ODE with \(K = 1\). The S-shaped learning curve (fast initial progress, slowing near perfect accuracy) is the logistic curve. This model motivates learning rate warmup (matching the low-growth phase near \(P_0\)) and learning rate decay (near saturation at \(K\)).

docs.title: 8.6 Diffusion Models — Logistic Noise Schedules
docs.text:
In DDPM (denoising diffusion probabilistic models), the noise schedule \(\bar\alpha_t\) (fraction of signal remaining at timestep \(t\)) is often chosen as a cosine schedule which closely approximates the logistic curve run in reverse:

\[\bar\alpha_t = \frac{\sigma(s)}{\sigma(0)} \cdot \frac{\sigma(1 - t/T + s)}{\sigma(s)}, \quad s = 0.008\]

The logistic shape ensures the signal-to-noise ratio degrades smoothly — neither too fast (poor sample quality) nor too slow (poor training) — mirroring the inflection point structure of the logistic ODE.

docs.title: 8.7 Grokking — Delayed Generalization as Logistic Dynamics
docs.text:
Grokking (Power et al., 2022) refers to the phenomenon where a neural network first memorizes training data (loss on train \(\to 0\)), then — after a long delay — suddenly generalizes (test loss \(\to 0\)).

The generalization dynamics follow a near-perfect logistic curve: a long near-zero plateau, then rapid S-shaped improvement, then saturation at high accuracy. The "carrying capacity" is set by the model's capacity and the task's algorithmic structure. The logistic ODE is the minimal model that captures this behavior.

docs.title: 9. The Logistic Map — Discrete Chaos
docs.text:
The discrete-time logistic model is:

\[P_{n+1} = rP_n\left(1 - P_n\right), \quad r \in (0, 4]\]

(Euler discretization of \(\dot{P} = rP(1-P)\) with step size 1, \(K=1\).)

Its dynamics are radically different from the continuous ODE:

\(r\) range Behavior \(0 < r < 1\) \(P_n \to 0\) \(1 < r < 3\) \(P_n \to\) fixed point \(1 - 1/r\) \(3 < r < 3.57\) Period doubling (2, 4, 8, 16, ...) \(r > 3.57\) Chaos \(r = 4\) Full chaos on \([0,1]\)

The logistic map is the canonical example of deterministic chaos — a simple, deterministic, one-dimensional rule generating unpredictable trajectories. It demonstrates how discretization (Euler with too large a step) can destroy the stability guaranteed by the continuous ODE.

In ML, this is a warning: discretizing a Neural ODE with too large a time step can destabilize training, turning smooth convergent dynamics into chaotic parameter oscillations.

docs.title: 10. Summary
docs.text: Feature Value / Formula ODE \(\dot{P} = rP(1 - P/K)\) Solution \(P(t) = \frac{K}{1 + \frac{K-P_0}{P_0}e^{-rt}}\) Equilibria \(P^* = 0\) (unstable), \(P^* = K\) (stable) Inflection point \(P = K/2\) at \(t^* = \frac{1}{r}\ln\frac{K-P_0}{P_0}\) Max growth rate $\frac{dP}{dt}\big Special case (\(K=1\)) Sigmoid \(\sigma(t) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-t}}\) \(\sigma'(t)\) \(\sigma(t)(1-\sigma(t))\) Discrete analogue Logistic map \(P_{n+1} = rP_n(1-P_n)\) — can be chaotic

docs.title: 11. Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Confusing \(r\) and \(K\). \(r\) sets the speed of growth; \(K\) sets the ceiling. They are independent parameters with different units (\(r\): time\(^{-1}\); \(K\): population).
  2. Forgetting the \(P > K\) case. If \(P_0 > K\), the solution still exists and decreases monotonically to \(K\). The formula (4) handles this: \(B < 0\), but the solution remains valid and positive.
  3. Assuming the inflection is at \(t = 0\). The inflection is at \(P = K/2\), which occurs at \(t^* = \frac{1}{r}\ln\frac{K-P_0}{P_0}\). Only when \(P_0 = K/2\) is \(t^* = 0\).
  4. Linearizing too aggressively. Near \(P = 0\), \(\dot{P} \approx rP\) (exponential). Near \(P = K\), letting \(u = K - P\) gives \(\dot{u} = -ru + O(u^2)\) (exponential decay). The global S-shape is not captured by either local linearization alone.
  5. Applying the logistic to non-bounded phenomena. The model assumes a fixed carrying capacity \(K\). If \(K\) itself changes over time (e.g., technology shifts the food supply), you need the non-autonomous logistic \(\dot{P} = r(t)P(1 - P/K(t))\), which is generally not separable.

docs.title: Natural vs Logistic
docs.text: "The exponential model asks: what happens when growth is unchecked? The logistic model asks: what happens when the world pushes back? Between these two questions lies most of mathematical biology, economics, and the theory of learning in machines."

docs.title: 1. The Two Models at a Glance
docs.text:
Both models govern a population \(P(t)\) (or any growing quantity). They differ in one fundamental assumption: whether the per-capita growth rate is constant or declines as \(P\) grows.

Natural Growth Logistic Growth ODE \(\dfrac{dP}{dt} = kP\) \(\dfrac{dP}{dt} = rP!\left(1 - \dfrac{P}{K}\right)\) Per-capita rate \(\dfrac{1}{P}\dfrac{dP}{dt} = k\) (constant) \(\dfrac{1}{P}\dfrac{dP}{dt} = r!\left(1 - \dfrac{P}{K}\right)\) (decreasing) Solution \(P(t) = P_0 e^{kt}\) \(P(t) = \dfrac{K}{1 + \left(\frac{K-P_0}{P_0}\right)e^{-rt}}\) Long-run behavior \(P \to \infty\) (if \(k>0\)) \(P \to K\) Type of ODE Separable, linear Separable, nonlinear Parameters \(k\) (growth rate), \(P_0\) \(r\) (intrinsic rate), \(K\) (carrying capacity), \(P_0\)

docs.title: 2.1 The ODE and Its Meaning
docs.text:
\[\frac{dP}{dt} = kP, \quad P(0) = P_0 \tag{1}\]

Verbal reading: the rate of change of population is proportional to the current population. Every individual reproduces at the same rate \(k\), regardless of how crowded the environment is.

\(k > 0\): growth. \(k < 0\): decay (same equation models radioactive decay, drug clearance, etc.).

docs.title: 2.2 Derivation of the Solution
docs.text:
Separate variables (\(P \neq 0\)):

\[\frac{dP}{P} = k,dt \implies \ln|P| = kt + C_1 \implies P(t) = Ae^{kt}.\]

Apply \(P(0) = P_0\): \(A = P_0\).

\[\boxed{P(t) = P_0 e^{kt}}\]

The singular solution \(P \equiv 0\) is the extinction equilibrium — unstable for \(k > 0\), stable for \(k < 0\).

docs.title: 2.3 Key Properties
docs.text:
Doubling time (for \(k > 0\)): Solve \(P_0 e^{kt_d} = 2P_0\):

\[t_d = \frac{\ln 2}{k} \approx \frac{0.693}{k}\]

Half-life (for \(k < 0\)): \(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{|k|}\).

Scale invariance: \(\dfrac{P(t+s)}{P(t)} = e^{ks}\) depends only on the elapsed time \(s\), not on \(t\). The model has no memory of when it started — it looks the same at every moment.

Phase line:

k > 0:
         dP/dt > 0       dP/dt > 0
────────────[P=0]────────────────────→  P
          unstable      (unbounded growth)

k < 0:
         dP/dt < 0       dP/dt < 0
←────────────[P=0]────────────────────  P
                        stable

docs.title: 2.4 When Is It Valid?
docs.text:
Natural growth is a local approximation — valid when \(P \ll K\) (far below the carrying capacity). It is exact for:

  • Radioactive decay
  • Continuous compounding of interest
  • Early-phase epidemic spread (before herd effects)
  • First few generations of a bacterial colony

docs.title: 3.1 The ODE and Its Meaning
docs.text:
\[\frac{dP}{dt} = rP\left(1 - \frac{P}{K}\right), \quad P(0) = P_0 \tag{2}\]

Verbal reading: growth rate is \(rP\) (Malthusian) multiplied by a saturation factor \((1 - P/K)\) that decreases linearly from \(1\) (when \(P = 0\), no competition) to \(0\) (when \(P = K\), fully saturated).

  • \(r > 0\): intrinsic growth rate (what the rate would be with no crowding)
  • \(K > 0\): carrying capacity — the population the environment can sustain
  • The factor \((1 - P/K)\) encodes intraspecific competition: each individual slightly reduces everyone else's growth rate

docs.title: 3.2 Derivation of the Solution
docs.text:
Separate variables:

\[\frac{dP}{P(1 - P/K)} = r,dt\]

Partial fractions (multiply numerator and denominator by \(K\)):

\[\frac{K}{P(K - P)} = \frac{1}{P} + \frac{1}{K - P}\]

So:

\[\int \left(\frac{1}{P} + \frac{1}{K-P}\right)dP = \int r,dt\] \[\ln|P| - \ln|K - P| = rt + C_1\] \[\ln\left|\frac{P}{K-P}\right| = rt + C_1 \implies \frac{P}{K-P} = Ae^{rt}\]

Solve for \(P\):

\[P = Ae^{rt}(K - P) \implies P(1 + Ae^{rt}) = KAe^{rt} \implies P = \frac{KAe^{rt}}{1 + Ae^{rt}} = \frac{K}{1 + A^{-1}e^{-rt}}\]

Apply \(P(0) = P_0\): \(A = \dfrac{P_0}{K - P_0}\), so \(A^{-1} = \dfrac{K - P_0}{P_0}\).

\[\boxed{P(t) = \frac{K}{1 + \left(\dfrac{K - P_0}{P_0}\right)e^{-rt}}}\]

docs.title: 3.3 Key Properties
docs.text:
Equilibria: Set \(dP/dt = 0\):

  • \(P^* = 0\) — unstable (for \(r > 0\)): any perturbation above 0 grows
  • \(P^* = K\) — stable: all solutions with \(P_0 > 0\) converge to \(K\)

Inflection point: The growth rate \(dP/dt = rP(1 - P/K)\) is a downward parabola in \(P\), maximized at:

\[P = \frac{K}{2}, \quad \text{where} \quad \frac{dP}{dt}\bigg|_{\max} = \frac{rK}{4}\]

The inflection point of \(P(t)\) occurs at \(t^* = \dfrac{1}{r}\ln!\left(\dfrac{K-P_0}{P_0}\right)\) (when \(P_0 < K/2\)).

S-shaped (sigmoid) curve: \(P(t)\) starts concave up (accelerating), inflects at \(P = K/2\), then concave down (decelerating) toward \(K\).

Phase line:

dP/dt
  │         ▲
  │       /   \
  │      /     \
  │     /       \
  │    /         \
  │   /           \
──┼──/─────────────\────→ P
  0               K

  ←────[P=0]──────────[P=K]────→  P
      unstable         stable
         ○ ─────────────── ●

docs.title: 3.4 The Linearization Near Equilibria
docs.text:
__Near \(P^_ = K\):_* Let \(P = K - u\) where \(u \ll K\) (small perturbation below \(K\)):

\[\frac{du}{dt} = -\frac{dP}{dt} = -r(K-u)\frac{u}{K} \approx -ru \quad \text{(linearized)}\]

So \(u(t) \approx u_0 e^{-rt}\) — the approach to \(K\) is exponential with rate \(r\). This is a key asymptotic result: the logistic model converges to carrying capacity at the same exponential rate \(r\) it would have grown at if unconstrained.

docs.title: 4.1 The Per-Capita Growth Rate
docs.text:
This is the most illuminating comparison. Define \(g(P) = \dfrac{1}{P}\dfrac{dP}{dt}\):

Model \(g(P)\) Behavior Natural growth \(k\) Horizontal line — constant Logistic \(r(1 - P/K)\) Decreasing line — hits 0 at \(P = K\) 
g(P) = (1/P)(dP/dt)

k ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─   ← Natural growth (constant)
  \
   \
    \
     \
      \
       \─────────────────────────── → P
       K                            ← Logistic (linear decline)

The logistic model's \(g(P)\) is the most natural first correction to the Malthusian model: if resources are finite, the per-capita rate must decrease as population increases. The linear decrease in \(g\) is the simplest possible such correction.

docs.title: 4.2 Solution Curves on the Same Axes
docs.text:
P(t)
K ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─────────────────────────  ← logistic asymptote
                  /
               __/
            __/      ← logistic (S-curve)
         __/
K/2 ──__/────────────────────────────────────  ← inflection point
      /
     /
    /  ↗ ↗ ↗ ← natural growth (exponential, P₀ small)
   /↗↗↗
──/──────────────────────────────────────────→ t
P₀       t*

(Both curves coincide near t=0 when P₀ ≪ K)

For small \(t\) and \(P_0 \ll K\): \(1 - P/K \approx 1\), so logistic \(\approx\) natural growth. The two models are indistinguishable early on — this is why Malthus's model appeared correct before populations hit resource limits.

docs.title: 4.3 Structural Comparison Table
docs.text: Property Natural Growth Logistic ODE order 1<sup>st</sup> 1<sup>st</sup> Linearity Linear Nonlinear Equilibria One: \(P=0\) Two: \(P=0\) (unstable), \(P=K\) (stable) Solution curve shape Pure exponential Sigmoid (S-curve) Long-run behavior \(\infty\) \(K\) Inflection point None \(P = K/2\) Parameters 2: \(k, P_0\) 3: \(r, K, P_0\) Solvable in closed form Yes (trivially) Yes (partial fractions) Biologically realistic Only for \(P \ll K\) For all \(P \in (0, K)\) Self-correction None Yes — growth slows as \(P \to K\)

docs.title: 5. Phase Portrait Analysis
docs.text:
The phase portrait plots \(\dot{P} = dP/dt\) against \(P\).

Natural growth: \(\dot{P} = kP\) — a line through the origin. No equilibrium except \(P = 0\).

Logistic: \(\dot{P} = rP(1 - P/K)\) — a downward-opening parabola with roots at \(P = 0\) and \(P = K\).

dP/dt
  │
rK/4─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─●─ ─ ─ ─ ─           ← maximum growth rate
  │              /   \
  │             /     \
  │            /       \
  │           /         \
──┼──────────/───────────\──────────→ P
  │         /             \
  0        /               K
           ↑               ↑
       unstable          stable
       equilibrium      equilibrium

The area under the parabola (from \(0\) to \(K\)) represents total growth over the population's history — a finite quantity, unlike the exponential case.

docs.title: 6. The Sigmoid Connection and the Logistic Function
docs.text:
Setting \(K = 1\), \(r = 1\), \(P_0 = 1/2\) (so \(A^{-1} = 1\)):

\[P(t) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-t}} =: \sigma(t)\]

This is the standard logistic (sigmoid) function. It satisfies:

\[\sigma'(t) = \sigma(t)(1 - \sigma(t))\]

which is exactly the logistic ODE with \(K = 1\), \(r = 1\). The sigmoid is not just an activation function chosen for computational convenience — it is the exact closed-form solution of the logistic growth ODE, and inherits all of the qualitative properties above.

docs.title: 7. Connection to AI, Machine Learning & Deep Learning
7.1 Sigmoid Activation — The Logistic Solution in Every Neuron
docs.text:
As shown above, every forward pass through a sigmoid neuron evaluates \(\sigma(x) = (1 + e^{-x})^{-1}\), which is the logistic solution with \(K = 1\). The properties that make logistic growth biologically sensible are exactly the properties that make sigmoid activations useful:

  • Bounded output (\(0 < \sigma < 1\)): prevents unbounded activation, analogous to \(P\) bounded by \(K\).
  • Soft saturation near 0 and 1: gradient nearly zero far from the inflection — the activation is "decided."
  • Linear near the inflection (\(\sigma \approx 1/2\), i.e., \(x \approx 0\)): maximum sensitivity, analogous to maximum growth rate at \(P = K/2\).

The vanishing gradient problem in deep networks is the biological carrying-capacity effect in disguise: when \(P \approx K\) (neuron saturated), \(dP/dt \approx 0\) — the gradient through a saturated sigmoid neuron is nearly zero, slowing or stopping learning.

docs.title: 7.2 Logistic Regression — Modeling Class Probability
docs.text:
In binary classification, logistic regression models:

\[P(Y=1 \mid \mathbf{x}) = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b)}}\]

The logistic curve is chosen precisely because:

  • It maps \(\mathbb{R} \to (0,1)\) (valid probability)
  • It is the maximum entropy model for binary outcomes with linear constraints on the log-odds
  • Its derivative \(\sigma'(\cdot) = \sigma(\cdot)(1 - \sigma(\cdot))\) is clean and makes the cross-entropy gradient tractable

The logistic regression model is the logistic ODE evaluated at \(t = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b\).

docs.title: 7.3 Neural Scaling Laws — Logistic vs. Power Law Growth
docs.text:
Empirical scaling laws (Kaplan et al., 2020) show that test loss \(\mathcal{L}\) of large language models decreases as a power law in compute \(C\):

\[\mathcal{L}(C) \sim C^{-\alpha}\]

But for a fixed task, performance (e.g., accuracy \(A\)) often follows a logistic curve in log-compute:

\[A(\log C) = \frac{A_{\max}}{1 + Be^{-r\log C}}\]

The carrying capacity \(A_{\max}\) is the task ceiling — analogous to \(K\). The model improves rapidly at first (exponential phase), then saturates as it approaches the ceiling. The inflection point \(A = A_{\max}/2\) corresponds to the "half-compute" point — the sweet spot of maximum marginal gain per FLOP.

docs.title: 7.4 Training Dynamics — Loss Curves as Logistic Decay
docs.text:
The training loss of a neural network often follows a curve qualitatively similar to the logistic solution reflected: starting flat, then dropping steeply, then flattening again as it approaches the minimum. Near a local minimum, the linearized gradient flow gives:

\[\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{dt} = -\lambda \mathcal{L} \implies \mathcal{L}(t) = \mathcal{L}_{\min} + (\mathcal{L}_0 - \mathcal{L}_{\min})e^{-\lambda t}\]

which is the natural growth/decay equation. So early training (far from minimum) is logistic-like; late training (near minimum) is Malthusian (exponential) in the loss gap. The crossover between regimes is the inflection point of the loss curve.

docs.title: 7.5 Population-Based Optimization — Evolutionary Algorithms
docs.text:
In genetic algorithms and evolutionary strategies, the frequency of a fit genotype in a population follows the logistic equation exactly (Fisher's fundamental theorem of natural selection, 1930). The carrying capacity \(K = 1\) (the genotype eventually fixes at 100% frequency), and \(r\) is determined by the fitness differential.

Evolutionary optimization algorithms explicitly simulate logistic dynamics among candidate solutions — and the logistic model's inflection point corresponds to the phase transition from exploration (many diverse solutions) to exploitation (converging to the best).

docs.title: 7.6 Epidemic Models and Federated Learning
docs.text:
The SIR epidemic model contains a logistic subsystem:

\[\frac{dI}{dt} = \beta SI - \gamma I = I(\beta S - \gamma)\]

Early in the epidemic (\(S \approx S_0 \approx N\)), this is natural growth with rate \(\beta S_0 - \gamma\). As \(S\) depletes, growth slows and reverses — qualitatively logistic. The basic reproduction number \(R_0 = \beta N / \gamma\) is the logistic \(K/P_0\) analogue: \(R_0 > 1\) means the "infection population" grows, \(R_0 < 1\) means decay.

In federated learning, privacy-noise injection and client dropout create epidemic-like dynamics: information (gradient signal) "infects" aggregation rounds logistically, with \(K\) set by the privacy budget.

docs.title: 8. Modified Growth Models — Beyond the Two Classics
docs.text: Once we understand natural and logistic growth, we can classify modifications:

docs.title: 8.1 Gompertz Model
docs.text:
\[\frac{dP}{dt} = rP\ln!\left(\frac{K}{P}\right)\]

Per-capita rate: \(g(P) = r\ln(K/P)\) — logarithmic decline instead of linear. Used for tumor growth (cells divide faster than they die when small; slowdown is faster than logistic near \(K\)).

Solution: \(P(t) = K\exp!\left(-e^{-rt + c}\right)\) where \(c = \ln\ln(K/P_0)\).

docs.title: 8.2 Allee Effect — Minimum Viable Population
docs.text:
\[\frac{dP}{dt} = rP\left(1 - \frac{P}{K}\right)\left(\frac{P}{A} - 1\right), \quad 0 < A < K\]

Three equilibria: \(0\) (stable), \(A\) (unstable — the Allee threshold), \(K\) (stable). If \(P < A\), the population collapses to extinction. Used in conservation biology and — in ML — models the loss barrier phenomenon where optimization gets stuck near a saddle before finding the basin of attraction.

docs.title: 8.3 Harvesting Models
docs.text:
\[\frac{dP}{dt} = rP\left(1 - \frac{P}{K}\right) - H\]

With constant harvesting \(H\). If \(H < rK/4\) (below the maximum growth rate), two equilibria exist; if \(H > rK/4\), population collapses. The maximum sustainable yield is \(H^* = rK/4\), achieved at \(P = K/2\) — the inflection point again.

│                          /──────────

docs.title: 10. Summary — The Core Insight
docs.text:
Question Natural Growth Logistic What drives growth? \(P\) itself \(P\) and available "room" \((1 - P/K)\) What stops growth? Nothing (in the model) Carrying capacity \(K\) What is the long run? Infinity \(K\) When is it valid? \(P \ll K\), short time All \(P \in [0, K]\), all time What does it miss? Everything about limits Allee effects, stochastic fluctuations

The deepest insight: the logistic model is the natural growth model plus a feedback term \(-rP^2/K\) that represents competition. This feedback is what makes the model self-correcting and bounded. In ML, this is precisely the role of regularization: adding a term that penalizes large weights (analogous to large \(P\)), preventing the unbounded growth that unconstrained optimization would produce.

docs.title: Other Population Models
docs.text: "The logistic model is elegant but rigid — it assumes a fixed carrying capacity, symmetric growth, and no memory. The real world is messier. Each modification of the logistic equation is a lesson in how a single extra parameter can shatter simplicity and birth entirely new phenomena."

docs.title: 1. The Zoo of Growth Models — Overview
docs.text:
All population models specify the per-capita growth rate \(\frac{1}{P}\frac{dP}{dt}\). The models differ in how this rate depends on \(P\):

Model Per-capita rate \(\frac{1}{P}\dot{P}\) ODE Malthus (exponential) \(r\) (constant) \(\dot{P} = rP\) Logistic (Verhulst) \(r(1 - P/K)\) (linear decay) \(\dot{P} = rP(1-P/K)\) Gompertz \(r\ln(K/P)\) (log decay) \(\dot{P} = rP\ln(K/P)\) Allee effect \(r(1-P/K)(P/A - 1)\) \(\dot{P} = rP(1-P/K)(P/A-1)\) Theta-logistic \(r(1-(P/K)^\theta)\) \(\dot{P} = rP(1-(P/K)^\theta)\) Doomsday \(rP^{1+\epsilon}\) \(\dot{P} = rP^{1+\epsilon}\) Harvesting \(r(1-P/K) - H/P\) \(\dot{P} = rP(1-P/K) - H\)

Each model is a separable first-order ODE (or reducible to one). The solution techniques are the same; the qualitative behavior is radically different.

docs.title: 2.1 Setup
docs.text:
Proposed by Benjamin Gompertz (1825), originally for mortality curves. The per-capita growth rate decays logarithmically rather than linearly:

\[\frac{dP}{dt} = rP\ln\frac{K}{P} \tag{1}\]

Note: \(\ln(K/P) = \ln K - \ln P > 0\) when \(P < K\), and \(< 0\) when \(P > K\). So the qualitative behavior is similar to the logistic, but the approach to \(K\) is asymmetric — slower from below, faster from above.

docs.title: 2.2 Solving the Gompertz ODE
docs.text:
Rewrite: \(\ln(K/P) = \ln K - \ln P\).

Separate:

\[\frac{dP}{P\ln(K/P)} = r, dt\]

Substitution: Let \(u = \ln(K/P)\). Then:

\[\frac{du}{dP} = -\frac{1}{P} \implies du = -\frac{dP}{P}\]

So \(\frac{dP}{P\ln(K/P)} = \frac{-du}{u}\). The ODE becomes:

\[-\frac{du}{u} = r, dt \implies \frac{du}{u} = -r, dt\] \[\ln|u| = -rt + C_1 \implies u = Ae^{-rt}\]

Back-substitute \(u = \ln(K/P)\):

\[\ln\frac{K}{P} = Ae^{-rt}\] \[\frac{K}{P} = e^{Ae^{-rt}}\] \[\boxed{P(t) = K, e^{-Ae^{-rt}}} \tag{2}\]

Apply \(P(0) = P_0\):

\[P_0 = Ke^{-A} \implies A = \ln\frac{K}{P_0}\] \[P(t) = K\exp!\left(-\ln!\tfrac{K}{P_0}\cdot e^{-rt}\right) = K\left(\frac{P_0}{K}\right)^{e^{-rt}} \tag{3}\]

docs.title: 2.3 Key Properties
docs.text:
• Equilibria: \(P^* = 0\) (unstable), \(P^* = K\) (stable) — same as logistic.
  • Inflection point: Set \(d^2P/dt^2 = 0\).

From \(\dot{P} = rP\ln(K/P)\):

\[\ddot{P} = r\dot{P}\ln\frac{K}{P} + rP \cdot \frac{-\dot{P}}{P} = r\dot{P}\left(\ln\frac{K}{P} - 1\right)\]

Setting \(\ddot{P} = 0\) (with \(\dot{P} \neq 0\)):

\[\ln\frac{K}{P} = 1 \implies P^* = \frac{K}{e} \approx 0.368K\]

The inflection is at \(P = K/e\) — lower than the logistic's \(K/2\). The Gompertz curve is skewed: it rises steeply early and tails off slowly into \(K\).

P(t)
 K  ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ────────────────────  ← K
                    ___/ ← Gompertz (slow tail)
K/2 ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─/─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─
K/e ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ── ←inflection (Gompertz)
               __/ ← logistic inflection at K/2
              /
─────────────/──────────────────────────────
     0                                   → t

docs.title: 2.4 Applications
docs.text:
• Tumor growth: Gompertz fits the growth of solid tumors better than logistic — they slow down more gradually as they approach their maximum size.
  • Mortality tables: Gompertz's original use — human mortality rate increases exponentially with age.
  • Technology adoption: Product adoption curves often fit Gompertz better than logistic (asymmetric S-curve).

docs.title: 3.1 Motivation
docs.text:
The logistic model assumes: more individuals → slower growth (crowding). The Allee effect (Warder Clyde Allee, 1931) adds: too few individuals → slower growth too (difficulty finding mates, reduced cooperative defense, inbreeding).

This creates a minimum viable population \(A\) below which the population declines to extinction.

docs.title: 3.2 The ODE
docs.text:
\[\frac{dP}{dt} = rP\left(1 - \frac{P}{K}\right)\left(\frac{P}{A} - 1\right), \quad 0 < A < K \tag{4}\]

Equilibria: \(P^* = 0\), \(P^* = A\), \(P^* = K\).

Stability analysis — let \(f(P) = rP(1-P/K)(P/A - 1)\):

  • \(f'(0)\): near \(P=0\), \(f(P) \approx rP(1)(0/A - 1) = -rP < 0\) → __\(P^_ = 0\) is stable_* (extinction attractor).
  • \(P^* = A\): unstable (the tipping point).
  • \(P^* = K\): stable (the survival attractor).

docs.title: 3.3 Phase Line
docs.text:
f(P) = dP/dt

      ↑
      │
   ───┼──────────────────────────────── P
      0    A              K
      │    ↑              ↑
   ←──│──→   ←───────────   ←──────────
  (-)│(+)       (-)             (+)... wait:

Sign of f(P) on each interval:
  P ∈ (0, A):   f < 0  →  P decreases to 0  (extinction)
  P ∈ (A, K):   f > 0  →  P increases to K  (survival)
  P ∈ (K, ∞):   f < 0  →  P decreases to K

Phase line:

  0 ←───── A ─────→ K ←─────
 (stable) (unstable) (stable)

The Allee threshold \(A\) is a separatrix: populations above \(A\) survive; below \(A\) they go extinct. This is called the strong Allee effect.

docs.title: 3.4 Solving the Allee ODE
docs.text: The ODE (4) is separable. Partial fractions on \(\frac{1}{P(1-P/K)(P/A - 1)}\) are messy but tractable. The solution is implicitly defined, and the key qualitative feature is the existence of the threshold \(A\) — the exact formula is less important than the phase line.

docs.title: 3.5 Applications
docs.text:
• Conservation biology: Minimum viable population estimates for endangered species.
  • Epidemiology: Below a critical infectious population, an epidemic dies out (Allee-like threshold = herd immunity complement).
  • Invasive species: A newly introduced population must exceed \(A\) to establish.

docs.title: 4.1 The ODE
docs.text:
\[\frac{dP}{dt} = rP\left[1 - \left(\frac{P}{K}\right)^\theta\right], \quad \theta > 0 \tag{5}\]

The parameter \(\theta\) controls the shape of density dependence:

  • \(\theta = 1\): standard logistic.
  • \(\theta < 1\): density dependence kicks in early (when \(P\) is still small). Concave per-capita rate.
  • \(\theta > 1\): density dependence kicks in late (population grows almost freely until near \(K\)). Convex per-capita rate.

docs.title: 4.2 Inflection Point
docs.text:
Setting \(\ddot{P} = 0\) (similar calculation as before):

\[P^* = K\left(\frac{1}{1+\theta}\right)^{1/\theta}\]
  • \(\theta = 1\): \(P^* = K/2\) ✓ (logistic)
  • \(\theta \to 0^+\): \(P^* \to K/e\) (approaches Gompertz inflection)
  • \(\theta \to \infty\): \(P^* \to K\) (inflection pushed to the top — nearly J-shaped)

The theta-logistic is a one-parameter family interpolating between all major growth curves.

docs.title: 4.3 Solving
docs.text:
The ODE is separable:

\[\frac{dP}{P[1-(P/K)^\theta]} = r, dt\]

Substitute \(u = (P/K)^\theta\):

\[du = \theta(P/K)^{\theta-1} \cdot \frac{1}{K}, dP = \frac{\theta}{P}(P/K)^\theta, dP = \frac{\theta u}{P}, dP\]

So \(dP/P = du/(\theta u)\):

\[\int \frac{du/(\theta u)}{1 - u} = rt + C\] \[\frac{1}{\theta}\int \frac{du}{u(1-u)} = rt + C\] \[\frac{1}{\theta}\left[\ln u - \ln(1-u)\right] = rt + C\] \[\frac{1}{\theta}\ln\frac{(P/K)^\theta}{1-(P/K)^\theta} = rt + C\]

This defines \(P(t)\) implicitly. For \(\theta = 1\) it reduces exactly to the logistic solution.

docs.title: 5.1 The ODE
docs.text:
\[\frac{dP}{dt} = kP^{1+\epsilon}, \quad k > 0,, \epsilon > 0 \tag{6}\]

The per-capita rate \(kP^\epsilon\) increases with \(P\) — no carrying capacity, the population accelerates itself.

docs.title: 5.2 Solving (Separable)
docs.text:
\[P^{-(1+\epsilon)}, dP = k, dt\] \[\int P^{-(1+\epsilon)}, dP = kt + C\] \[\frac{P^{-\epsilon}}{-\epsilon} = kt + C\] \[P^{-\epsilon} = -\epsilon kt + C_0\]

Apply \(P(0) = P_0\): \(C_0 = P_0^{-\epsilon}\):

\[P(t) = \left(P_0^{-\epsilon} - \epsilon k t\right)^{-1/\epsilon} \tag{7}\]

docs.title: 5.3 Finite-Time Blow-Up
docs.text:
The solution \(P(t) \to \infty\) in finite time \(t^* = \frac{P_0^{-\epsilon}}{\epsilon k} = \frac{1}{\epsilon k P_0^\epsilon}\).

This is called a doomsday singularity — the population grows so fast it becomes infinite in finite time. Obviously unphysical past some point, but the model fits certain superexponential growth phases (e.g., global human population from 1 AD to 1970, which von Foerster et al. famously fit with \(\epsilon \approx 1\) and \(t^* \approx 2026\)... an eerie coincidence with the present date).

P(t)
 ∞  ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─│  ← blow-up at t*
                                      │
                                     /│
                                    / │
                                  _/  │
                              ___/    │
P₀ ──────────────────────────        │
     0                       t*    → t

docs.title: 6.1 Constant Harvesting
docs.text:
\[\frac{dP}{dt} = rP\left(1 - \frac{P}{K}\right) - H, \quad H > 0 \tag{8}\]

Equilibria: Set \(\dot{P} = 0\):

\[rP\left(1 - \frac{P}{K}\right) = H \implies \frac{r}{K}P^2 - rP + H = 0\] \[P^* = \frac{rK \pm \sqrt{r^2K^2 - 4rKH}}{2r} = \frac{K}{2}\left(1 \pm \sqrt{1 - \frac{4H}{rK}}\right)\]

Three regimes:

Condition Equilibria Behavior \(H < \frac{rK}{4}\) Two real equilibria \(P_-^* < P_+^*\) \(P_+^_\) stable, \(P_-^_\) unstable \(H = \frac{rK}{4}\) One equilibrium \(P^* = K/2\) Saddle-node bifurcation \(H > \frac{rK}{4}\) No real equilibria \(\dot{P} < 0\) always — extinction

Maximum sustainable yield (MSY): \(H^* = rK/4\), achieved at \(P = K/2\).

dP/dt
  ↑         logistic curve rP(1-P/K)
  │        ╭──────╮
rK/4 ─ ─ ─│─ ─ ─╮│─ ─ ─ ─ ─  ← H = rK/4 (tangent: MSY)
  │       /    H₂ \\
  H₁ ─ ─/─ ─ ─ ─ ─\─ ─ ─ ─ ─  ← H₁ < rK/4 (two crossings: two equil.)
  │     /            \
──┼────/──────────────\──────── P
  0   P*₋             P*₊   K

docs.title: 6.2 Proportional Harvesting (Threshold Policy)
docs.text:
\[\frac{dP}{dt} = rP\left(1 - \frac{P}{K}\right) - EP, \quad E > 0\] \[= P\left[r\left(1 - \frac{P}{K}\right) - E\right] = P\left[(r-E) - \frac{r}{K}P\right]\]

This is still a logistic equation with modified growth rate \(\tilde{r} = r - E\) and modified carrying capacity \(\tilde{K} = K(1 - E/r)\) (for \(E < r\)). Proportional harvesting preserves the logistic structure; constant harvesting does not.

docs.title: Per-Capita Rate vs. Population
docs.text:
(1/P)(dP/dt)
    ↑
  r │─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─ ─  ← Malthus (constant)
    │\
    │ \  ← Logistic (linear)
    │  \
    │   \  ← Theta-logistic θ>1 (convex)
    │    \___
    │  ___\  ← Theta-logistic θ<1 (concave) / Gompertz
    │ /    \
    │/      \
────┼─────────\──────────────────  P
    0          K

Phase line comparison (all with K=1):

Malthus:    0 ───────────────────────→ ∞  (no ceiling)

Logistic:   0 → → → → K ← ← ←  (symmetric)

Gompertz:   0 → → → K ← ←  (skewed left: slow tail)

Allee:      0 ← A → → K ← ←  (threshold at A)

Doomsday:   0 ─────────────────────→ ∞ in FINITE time

docs.title: 8. Connection to AI, Machine Learning & Deep Learning
8.1 Gompertz Activation and Loss Curves
docs.text:
The Gompertz curve appears in ML as a model for training loss dynamics. Loss curves are almost never symmetric S-curves — they drop rapidly early, then tail off extremely slowly. The Gompertz ODE's inflection at \(K/e \approx 0.37K\) (lower than logistic's \(K/2\)) means the fastest learning happens early, matching observed neural network training.

The Gompertz activation function:

\[G(x) = e^{-e^{-x}}\]

has been proposed as an alternative to sigmoid. It is the Gompertz solution evaluated at \(t = x\) with \(K = 1\), \(A = 1\). Unlike sigmoid, it is asymmetric: slower to saturate at 1 than at 0, which can be beneficial for modeling asymmetric distributions.

docs.title: 8.2 Allee Effect and Rare Event Learning
docs.text:
The Allee threshold has a direct analogue in few-shot and zero-shot learning: a model trained on fewer than \(A\) examples of a class fails to learn it (collapses to "extinction" — random guessing); above \(A\) examples it generalizes successfully.

More precisely, in memorization vs. generalization (grokking): the model first memorizes (population at \(P_0 \ll A\)), then — after enough weight norm regularization acts like environment pressure — crosses the Allee threshold and "generalizes" (escapes to the \(K\)-attractor). The Allee model is a minimal ODE that exhibits this threshold-crossing behavior.

docs.title: 8.3 Doomsday and Superexponential Scaling Laws
docs.text:
The neural scaling laws (Kaplan et al., 2020) show that language model performance scales as a power law with compute:

\[\mathcal{L}(C) \sim C^{-\alpha}, \quad \alpha \approx 0.05\]

Equivalently, capability \(P \sim C^{\alpha}\) grows as a power law in compute \(C\). If compute itself grows superexponentially (as it has historically), \(C(t) \sim e^{\beta t^\gamma}\), then \(P(t)\) grows superexponentially too — a doomsday-type trajectory in capability space.

The finite-time blow-up in the doomsday model is a mathematical caricature of the intelligence explosion hypothesis: if capability growth rate \(\sim P^\epsilon\) (smarter systems build better systems faster), the system reaches infinite capability in finite time \(t^*\).

docs.title: 8.4 Theta-Logistic and Learning Rate Schedules
docs.text:
The theta-logistic's parameter \(\theta\) controls when density dependence (saturation) kicks in. In deep learning:

  • \(\theta < 1\) regime (early saturation): analogous to aggressive learning rate decay — the model slows down early, converging cautiously but potentially to a sharper minimum.
  • \(\theta > 1\) regime (late saturation): analogous to warmup schedules — the model grows nearly freely until close to convergence, then slows.

The cosine annealing schedule (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017) has a theta-logistic-like shape with \(\theta > 1\): it keeps the learning rate high for most of training, then decays sharply at the end.

docs.title: 8.5 Harvesting and Dropout / Regularization
docs.text:
Dropout removes a fraction \(H\) of activations at each forward pass. The effect on a single layer's output is analogous to constant harvesting:

\[\text{effective output} = f(\mathbf{x}) - H\]

For small \(H\) (low dropout rate), two stable regimes exist: high activation (analogous to \(P_+^*\), the learned representation) and zero activation (analogous to \(P = 0\), dead neurons). For \(H\) above the MSY threshold, all activations collapse to zero — neuron death, the analogue of population collapse past the harvesting threshold.

This geometric analogy explains why too-high dropout rates cause training failure: they push the system past the bifurcation point where no stable "alive" equilibrium exists.

docs.title: 8.6 Compartmental Population Models and Graph Neural Networks
docs.text:
Multi-species population models (Lotka-Volterra predator-prey, SIR epidemics) are compartmental systems of ODEs:

\[\frac{d\mathbf{P}}{dt} = F(\mathbf{P}), \quad \mathbf{P} \in \mathbb{R}^n\]

These are the continuous-time substrate of message-passing in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). The GNN update:

\[\mathbf{h}_v^{(k+1)} = \phi\left(\mathbf{h}_v^{(k)},\ \bigoplus_{u \in \mathcal{N}(v)} \psi(\mathbf{h}_u^{(k)})\right)\]

is an Euler step of a compartmental ODE on the graph, where each node \(v\) is a "species" exchanging "population" (features) with neighbors. The stability theory of population ODEs — equilibria, Jacobian eigenvalues, limit cycles — directly informs the over-smoothing problem in deep GNNs (features converging to a uniform fixed point, like all populations reaching the same carrying capacity).

docs.title: 9. Summary — The Hierarchy of Models
docs.text:
Malthus: dP/dt = rP
    ↓  (add ceiling K)
Logistic: dP/dt = rP(1 - P/K)
    ↓  (change linear → log saturation)     ↓  (add shape parameter θ)
Gompertz: rP ln(K/P)              Theta-logistic: rP[1-(P/K)^θ]
    ↓  (add minimum viable population A)
Allee: rP(1-P/K)(P/A - 1)
    ↓  (add external removal)
Harvesting: rP(1-P/K) - H
    ↑  (remove ceiling, add acceleration)
Doomsday: kP^{1+ε}  →  blow-up in finite time t*

docs.title: 10. Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Treating all models as separable without checking. All models in this note are separable (or reducible to separable via substitution). But multi-species models (Lotka-Volterra) are generally not separable — they require phase plane or linearization methods.
  2. Confusing Allee effect stability. In the strong Allee effect, \(P^* = 0\) is stable (extinction is an attractor). Students often expect \(0\) to be unstable as in the logistic. It is not — small populations go extinct.
  3. Forgetting \(\theta\)'s effect on units. In the theta-logistic, \((P/K)^\theta\) is dimensionless for any \(\theta\), so \(r\) always has units \(1/\text{time}\) regardless of \(\theta\).
  4. Missing the MSY bifurcation. In the harvesting model, the transition at \(H = rK/4\) is a saddle-node bifurcation — two equilibria collide and annihilate. This is not a smooth transition; it is a sudden collapse. Fishing industries that ignore this threshold have historically caused stock collapses.
  5. Applying the Doomsday model globally. The doomsday ODE fits data over a finite interval. Extrapolation to \(t \to t^*\) is physically meaningless — the model breaks down long before blow-up (as Malthus himself understood about food limits).

docs.title: 11. References
docs.text:
1. James Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. — §9.4 "Models for Population Growth" (logistic, harvesting).
  2. MIT 18.02 — Autonomous ODEs, phase lines, bifurcations.
  3. Benjamin Gompertz, "On the Nature of the Function Expressive of the Law of Human Mortality," Phil. Trans. Royal Soc., 1825.
  4. Warder C. Allee, Animal Aggregations: A Study in General Sociology, 1931.
  5. Heinz von Foerster, Patricia Mora, Lawrence Amiot, "Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026," Science 132, 1960.
  6. Jared Kaplan et al., "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models," arXiv:2001.08361, 2020. (§8.3)
  7. Robert M. May, "Simple mathematical models with very complicated dynamics," Nature 261, 1976. (logistic map, period doubling)
  8. Ilya Loshchilov & Frank Hutter, "SGDR: Stochastic Gradient Descent with Warm Restarts," ICLR 2017. (§8.4)
