docs.title: Linear Equations
docs.text: "The art of mathematics is asking the right questions. Linear equations are where every question first becomes precise." — Personal margin note, Stewart §1.1

docs.title: 0. Preliminary Remarks
docs.text:
This note is organized the way I actually think about linear equations — not as a drill on slope-intercept form, but as the foundational skeleton of analysis, geometry, and learning theory. Every deep idea in applied mathematics (optimization, neural networks, least squares) eventually reduces to asking: when does a linear system have a solution, and how do we find it?

We begin with the simplest case (one variable, one equation) and build upward with full rigor.

docs.title: 1. Definition: Linear Equation in One Variable
docs.text:
Definition 1.1. A linear equation in one variable \(x\) is any equation of the form $\(ax = b, \quad a, b \in \mathbb{R},\ a eq 0.\)$

The qualifier \(a eq 0\) is not cosmetic — it is the exact condition that guarantees existence and uniqueness of a solution.

Proof of Existence and Uniqueness. Suppose \(ax = b\) with \(a eq 0\). Since \(a \in \mathbb{R}^{ imes}\) (the multiplicative group of nonzero reals), its multiplicative inverse \(a^{-1}\) exists. Multiply both sides on the left by \(a^{-1}\): $\(a^{-1}(ax) = a^{-1}b \implies (a^{-1}a)x = a^{-1}b \implies 1 \cdot x = rac{b}{a} \implies x = rac{b}{a}.\)$ Existence: \(x_0 = b/a\) is a solution. Uniqueness: Suppose \(x_1\) is another solution, so \(ax_1 = b = ax_0\). Multiply by \(a^{-1}\): \(x_1 = x_0\). \( lacksquare\)

Remark. If \(a = 0\): the equation becomes \(0 = b\). If \(b eq 0\), there is no solution. If \(b = 0\), every \(x \in \mathbb{R}\) is a solution. The trichotomy {no solution, unique solution, infinitely many solutions} already appears here and persists into systems of any dimension.

docs.title: 2. Linear Equations in Two Variables
docs.text:
Definition 2.1. A linear equation in two variables \(x, y\) is any equation of the form $\(ax + by = c, \quad (a, b) \neq (0, 0),\ a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}.\)$

The solution set is a line in \(\mathbb{R}^2\).

Why is it a line? The equation defines a level set of the linear functional \(L(x,y) = ax + by\). Level sets of linear maps on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) are affine subspaces of dimension 1 — i.e., lines. (We'll return to this language in §5.)

docs.title: 2.1 Standard Forms
docs.text:
Form Equation When to use Standard \(ax + by = c\) Systems, dot-product geometry Slope-intercept \(y = mx + k\) Reading off slope/intercept Point-slope \(y - y_0 = m(x - x_0)\) Building from a point + slope Parametric \((x,y) = (x_0, y_0) + t(d_1, d_2)\) Vectors, direction, ML feature paths

Conversion Example. Given \(3x - 2y = 6\):

  • Slope-intercept: \(y = \tfrac{3}{2}x - 3\), so slope \(m = 3/2\), \(y\)-intercept \(= -3\).
  • Parametric: take \(t=x\), then \((x, y) = t(1, 3/2) + (0, -3)\).

docs.title: 2.2 Geometric Intuition
docs.text:
y
        |          / slope = 3/2
    1   |         /
        |        /  3x - 2y = 6
   -3 --+-------/---------- x
        |      / (0,-3)
        |     /
        |    * (2,0)  ← x-intercept

The line \(3x - 2y = 6\) crosses:

  • \(x\)-axis at \((2, 0)\): set \(y=0 \Rightarrow x = 2\)
  • \(y\)-axis at \((0, -3)\): set \(x=0 \Rightarrow y = -3\)

docs.title: 2.3 The Normal Vector Perspective
docs.text:
The equation \(ax + by = c\) can be written as the dot product: $\(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} = c, \quad \mathbf{n} = \begin{pmatrix} a \ b \end{pmatrix},\ \mathbf{x} = \begin{pmatrix} x \ y \end{pmatrix}.\)$

The vector \(\mathbf{n}\) is perpendicular to the line. This is not a coincidence — it is the geometric definition of a hyperplane.

Lemma 2.2. \(\mathbf{n}\) is orthogonal to every direction vector of the line \(ax + by = c\).

Proof. A direction vector \(\mathbf{d} = (d_1, d_2)\) satisfies \(\mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{x}_0 + t\mathbf{d}) = c\) for all \(t\). Expanding: \(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x}_0 + t(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}) = c\). Since \(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x}_0 = c\), we get \(t(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}) = 0\) for all \(t\), hence \(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d} = 0\). \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: 3. Systems of Linear Equations
docs.text: Definition 3.1. A system of \(m\) linear equations in \(n\) unknowns is a collection $\(\sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{ij} x_j = b_i, \quad i = 1, \ldots, m.\)$ In matrix form: \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\), where \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\), \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n\), \(\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^m\).

docs.title: 3.1 The Fundamental Trichotomy (Theorem)
docs.text:
Theorem 3.2 (Existence and Uniqueness for Linear Systems). For the system \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\), exactly one of the following holds:

  1. No solution — the system is inconsistent.
  2. Exactly one solution — the system is consistent and the solution is unique.
  3. Infinitely many solutions — the system is consistent with a free-parameter family.

Proof sketch. By Gaussian elimination, \(A\) row-reduces to a row echelon form \(R\). The system \(R\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{c}\) (transformed RHS) is inconsistent iff a row of the form \([0\ 0\ \cdots\ 0\ |\ c]\) with \(c \neq 0\) appears (case 1). Otherwise: if every column of \(R\) has a pivot, the solution is unique (case 2); if there are free variables (columns without pivots), infinitely many solutions exist (case 3). \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: 3.2 \(2 \times 2\) Case — Geometric Picture
docs.text:
Two lines in \(\mathbb{R}^2\):

  • Intersect at one point → unique solution
  • Parallel (distinct) → no solution
  • Identical → infinitely many solutions
Case 1: Unique          Case 2: No Solution      Case 3: Infinite
  y  /  /                  y  //                   y  
    X ← solution             ||  ← parallel           same line
   / /                      ||

docs.title: 3.3 Worked Example
docs.text:
Solve: $\(\begin{cases} 2x + y = 5 \ x - y = 1 \end{cases}\)$

Elimination method: Add the equations: \(3x = 6 \Rightarrow x = 2\). Substitute: \(2 - y = 1 \Rightarrow y = 1\). Solution: \((x, y) = (2, 1)\).

Matrix form: $\(\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \ y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \ 1 \end{pmatrix}\)$

\(\det(A) = 2(-1) - 1(1) = -3 \neq 0\), so the unique solution exists. By Cramer's rule: $\(x = \frac{\det\begin{pmatrix}5&1\1&-1\end{pmatrix}}{-3} = \frac{-6}{-3} = 2, \quad y = \frac{\det\begin{pmatrix}2&5\1&1\end{pmatrix}}{-3} = \frac{-3}{-3} = 1.\)$

docs.title: 4. Linear Functions vs. Affine Functions
docs.text:
This distinction matters enormously in machine learning.

Definition 4.1. A function \(f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) is linear if:

  1. \(f(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = f(\mathbf{u}) + f(\mathbf{v})\) for all \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}\)
  2. \(f(c\mathbf{u}) = c f(\mathbf{u})\) for all \(c \in \mathbb{R}\)

Definition 4.2. A function \(f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) is affine if \(f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b\) for some \(\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^n\), \(b \in \mathbb{R}\).

Remark. Every linear function is affine (with \(b=0\)), but not vice versa. The equation \(y = 3x + 5\) defines an affine function, not a linear one in the strict algebraic sense, since \(f(0) = 5 \neq 0\). In casual usage (and in Stewart), "linear equation" allows a nonzero constant term. In linear algebra, we must be precise.

docs.title: 5. Hyperplanes: Generalization to \(\mathbb{R}^n\)
docs.text:
Definition 5.1. A hyperplane in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is the solution set of a single linear equation: $\(H = {\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n : \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} = b}.\)$

Dimension of \(H\) as an affine subspace: \(n - 1\).

\(n\) Hyperplane 1 Point 2 Line 3 Plane \(n\) \((n-1)\)-dimensional flat

The vector \(\mathbf{w}\) is the normal to \(H\). The scalar \(b\) shifts \(H\) away from the origin.

docs.title: 6. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
docs.text: This is where the theory stops being "abstract" and starts being the engine underneath every model you will ever train.

docs.title: 6.1 Linear Regression
docs.text:
Setup. Given data \({(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^N\) with \(\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^n\), fit: $\(\hat{y} = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b.\)$

The optimal parameters solve the normal equations — a linear system: $\(A^T A \mathbf{w} = A^T \mathbf{y}, \quad A = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{x}_1^T \ \vdots \ \mathbf{x}_N^T \end{pmatrix}.\)$

This is literally solving a linear equation. The entire field of least squares is built on the existence/uniqueness theorem for \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\).

Geometric insight: \(\hat{\mathbf{y}} = A\mathbf{w}\) is the orthogonal projection of \(\mathbf{y}\) onto the column space of \(A\). The residual \(\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}\) is orthogonal to every column of \(A\) — this is exactly the normal equation \(A^T(\mathbf{y} - A\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{0}\).

docs.title: 6.2 Perceptron and Support Vector Machines
docs.text:
A perceptron classifies input \(\mathbf{x}\) as: $\(\hat{y} = \text{sign}(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b).\)$

The decision boundary \(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b = 0\) is exactly a hyperplane (Definition 5.1). The weights \(\mathbf{w}\) are the normal vector; \(b\) is the bias that shifts it.

An SVM finds the hyperplane that maximizes the margin between two classes — a quadratic program whose solution is determined by solving a linear system at its dual.

docs.title: 6.3 Neural Networks: Linear Layers
docs.text:
Every fully connected (dense) layer computes: $\(\mathbf{z} = W\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}, \quad W \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n},\ \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n,\ \mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^m.\)$

This is a system of \(m\) linear equations applied simultaneously. Without nonlinear activations (ReLU, sigmoid, etc.), a composition of linear layers collapses to a single linear map: $\(W_L \cdots W_2 W_1 \mathbf{x} = W_{\text{eff}} \mathbf{x}.\)$

A 100-layer fully linear network has identical expressive power to a single linear layer. Depth only helps because of nonlinearity. Nonlinearity is the entire point of deep learning, and linear algebra is the scaffolding it runs on.

docs.title: 6.4 Gradient Descent and Linear Systems
docs.text:
Training a neural network minimizes a loss \(\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w})\). At convergence, \( abla_\mathbf{w} \mathcal{L} = \mathbf{0}\) — a (generally nonlinear) system of equations. For a quadratic loss (as in linear regression), this reduces to: $\( abla \mathcal{L} = 2A^T(A\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{0} \iff A^T A \mathbf{w} = A^T \mathbf{y}.\)$

A linear system again.

Gradient descent iterates \(\mathbf{w}_{k+1} = \mathbf{w}_k - \eta abla \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}_k)\). Its convergence rate is governed by the condition number \(\kappa(A^T A) = \lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}\) — a quantity from the spectral theory of linear operators.

docs.title: 6.5 Summary Diagram
docs.text:
Linear Equation  ──────────────►  Hyperplane in ℝⁿ
       │                                │
       │                                │
       ▼                                ▼
  Linear System                   Decision Boundary
  Aₓ = b                         (SVM, Perceptron)
       │
       │ Overdetermined (m > n)
       ▼
  Least Squares (A^T A w = A^T y)
       │
       ├──────────────► Linear Regression
       │
       └──────────────► Each layer of a Neural Network
                        z = Wx + b

docs.title: Example 7.1 — Unique Solution
docs.text: $\(3x - 2y = 4,\quad x + y = 3.\)$ From the second: \(x = 3 - y\). Substitute: \(3(3-y) - 2y = 4 \Rightarrow 9 - 5y = 4 \Rightarrow y = 1,\ x = 2\).

docs.title: Example 7.2 — No Solution
docs.text: $\(2x + 4y = 6,\quad x + 2y = 4.\)$ Divide first by 2: \(x + 2y = 3\). But second says \(x + 2y = 4\). Contradiction. \(\emptyset\).

docs.title: Example 7.3 — Infinitely Many Solutions
docs.text: $\(2x + 4y = 6,\quad x + 2y = 3.\)$ Both reduce to \(x + 2y = 3\). Free variable \(y = t \in \mathbb{R}\): solution set \({(3 - 2t,\ t) : t \in \mathbb{R}}\).

docs.title: Example 7.4 — ML Context
docs.text: Suppose two data points: \((x_1, y_1) = (1, 2)\) and \((x_2, y_2) = (3, 4)\). Fit \(y = wx + b\): $\(\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1 \ 3 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}w \ b\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}2 \ 4\end{pmatrix}.\)$ \(\det = 1\cdot1 - 3\cdot1 = -2 \neq 0\). Unique solution: \(w = 1,\ b = 1\). Model: \(\hat{y} = x + 1\).

docs.title: 8. Key Theorems — Summary
docs.text: Theorem Statement Existence & Uniqueness (1 var) \(ax = b,\ a\neq 0 \Rightarrow\) unique solution \(x = b/a\) Fundamental Trichotomy Any linear system has 0, 1, or \(\infty\) solutions Normal Vector Theorem \(\mathbf{n} = (a,b)\) is \(\perp\) to the line \(ax + by = c\) Linear Layer Collapse Composition of linear maps is linear; nonlinearity is essential for depth Normal Equations Least squares \(\Leftrightarrow\) solving \(A^TA\mathbf{w} = A^T\mathbf{y}\)

docs.title: 9. Things to Prove Yourself
docs.text:
1. Show that the solution set of \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) (when consistent) is a coset of the null space \(\ker(A)\).
  2. Verify that \(\mathbf{n} = (a,b)\) is perpendicular to the line \(ax + by = c\) using vectors. (Lemma 2.2 done in full detail.)
  3. Prove that a composition of two affine maps \(f(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{a}\) and \(g(\mathbf{x}) = B\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{b}\) is again affine. What is its linear part?
  4. Derive the normal equations \(A^TA\mathbf{w} = A^T\mathbf{y}\) by minimizing \(|A\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{y}|^2\) via calculus.
  5. Show that a network of \(L\) linear layers (no activations) is equivalent to a single linear transformation.

docs.text:

  • MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus — Lecture Notes on Vectors and Linear Equations.
  • Strang, G. Introduction to Linear Algebra, 5th ed. Ch. 1–3.
  • Goodfellow, I., Bengio, Y., Courville, A. Deep Learning. Ch. 2 (Linear Algebra), Ch. 6 (Deep Feedforward Networks).

docs.title: Electric Circuits
docs.text:
"Every circuit is a linear system in disguise. Kirchhoff didn't invent new mathematics — he read the physics and wrote down the equations that were already there." — Personal margin note, Stewart §7.3 / MIT 18.02

See also: [[Linear Equations]] (foundations, trichotomy theorem, matrix form)

docs.title: 0. Preliminary Remarks
docs.text:
Electric circuits are one of the most natural and historically important applications of linear systems. The key insight — due to Kirchhoff in 1845 — is that the physical laws governing current and voltage are linear constraints. Every node and every loop contributes one linear equation. The circuit becomes a matrix. Solving it is Gaussian elimination.

This note builds from physical laws → linear equations → full matrix system → worked examples → connection to ML (circuit simulation in neural networks and analog computing).

docs.title: 1.1 Ohm's Law
docs.text:
Law 1.1 (Ohm). For a resistor with resistance \(R > 0\) (in ohms, \(\Omega\)), if current \(I\) (amperes) flows through it, the voltage drop across it is: $\(V = IR.\)$

This is the fundamental linear relation between voltage and current. It is a single linear equation in two unknowns — one constraint.

Remark. Ohm's Law is an empirical approximation valid for resistors at constant temperature. It fails for diodes, transistors, and nonlinear elements — which is precisely where circuit analysis becomes nonlinear and requires numerical methods.

docs.title: 1.2 Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL)
docs.text:
Law 1.2 (KCL). At every node (junction) of a circuit, the algebraic sum of currents is zero: $\(\sum_{k} I_k = 0,\)$ where currents entering the node are positive and currents leaving are negative (or vice versa — pick a convention and be consistent).

Physical meaning: Charge is conserved. No charge accumulates at a node.

Mathematical character: KCL gives one linear equation per node in the unknown currents.

docs.title: 1.3 Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL)
docs.text:
Law 1.3 (KVL). Around every closed loop in a circuit, the algebraic sum of voltage drops is zero: $\(\sum_{k} V_k = 0.\)$ Voltage rises (across sources) are counted positive; voltage drops (across resistors) are counted negative.

Physical meaning: The electric potential is a well-defined function on the circuit graph. Its line integral around any closed path vanishes — this is the statement that the electric field is conservative (\(\nabla \times \mathbf{E} = 0\) in the static case).

Mathematical character: KVL gives one linear equation per independent loop.

Key observation. Substituting Ohm's Law (\(V_k = I_k R_k\)) into KVL converts voltage equations into current equations. Every equation is linear in the unknown currents. The entire circuit is a linear system.

docs.title: 2.1 Circuit Vocabulary
docs.text: Term Meaning Node Junction where two or more wires meet Branch A single element (resistor, source) between two nodes Loop Any closed path through the circuit Mesh A loop that encloses no other loop (minimal loop) Reference node One node chosen as "ground" (\(V = 0\))

docs.title: 2.2 Two Systematic Methods
docs.text:
Method Unknowns Equations from Best when Node voltage Node voltages \(V_i\) KCL at each node Many nodes, few meshes Mesh current Mesh currents \(I_m\) KVL around each mesh Planar circuits, many meshes

Both methods produce a square linear system \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\).

docs.title: Circuit Description
docs.text:
A voltage source \(\mathcal{E}\) in series with two resistors \(R_1\) and \(R_2\). One loop, one unknown current \(I\).

     ┌────R₁────┬────R₂────┐
     │          │          │
    [ε]         │          │
     │          │          │
     └──────────┴──────────┘
          (ground)

docs.title: Applying KVL
docs.text:
Traverse the loop clockwise. Voltage rises across the source, drops across resistors: $\(\mathcal{E} - IR_1 - IR_2 = 0.\)$

Rearranging: $\(I(R_1 + R_2) = \mathcal{E}.\)$

This is a linear equation in one unknown \(I\).

Solution: $\(I = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{R_1 + R_2}.\)$

Existence and uniqueness follow from Definition 1.1 of [[Linear Equations]], since \(R_1 + R_2 > 0\).

Concrete example. \(\mathcal{E} = 12,\text{V}\), \(R_1 = 2,\Omega\), \(R_2 = 4,\Omega\): $\(I = \frac{12}{2+4} = 2,\text{A}, \quad V_{R_1} = 2 \cdot 2 = 4,\text{V}, \quad V_{R_2} = 2 \cdot 4 = 8,\text{V}.\)$

Check KVL: \(12 - 4 - 8 = 0\). \(\checkmark\)

docs.title: Circuit Description
docs.text:
R₁          R₂
   ┌────/\/\/────┬────/\/\/────┐
   │             │             │
  [ε₁]          R₃           [ε₂]
   │             │             │
   └─────────────┴─────────────┘
         (ground node)

Two meshes. Assign mesh currents \(I_1\) (left loop, clockwise) and \(I_2\) (right loop, clockwise).

docs.title: Applying KVL to Each Mesh
docs.text:
Mesh 1 (left loop):

Voltage rise across \(\mathcal{E}_1\), drop across \(R_1\) (carries \(I_1\)), drop across \(R_3\) (carries \(I_1 - I_2\), since \(I_2\) flows opposite through \(R_3\)): $\(\mathcal{E}_1 - I_1 R_1 - (I_1 - I_2)R_3 = 0\)$ $\(\mathcal{E}_1 = I_1(R_1 + R_3) - I_2 R_3. \tag{1}\)$

Mesh 2 (right loop):

Voltage rise across \(\mathcal{E}_2\), drop across \(R_2\) (carries \(I_2\)), drop across \(R_3\) (carries \(I_2 - I_1\)): $\(\mathcal{E}_2 - I_2 R_2 - (I_2 - I_1)R_3 = 0\)$ $\(\mathcal{E}_2 = -I_1 R_3 + I_2(R_2 + R_3). \tag{2}\)$

docs.title: Matrix Form
docs.text:
\[\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} R_1 + R_3 & -R_3 \ -R_3 & R_2 + R_3 \end{pmatrix}}_{A} \begin{pmatrix} I_1 \ I_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathcal{E}_1 \ \mathcal{E}_2 \end{pmatrix}\]

Observation. The matrix \(A\) is symmetric and has a special structure: diagonal entries are sums of resistances in each mesh; off-diagonal entries are the negative of shared resistances. This is the mesh resistance matrix — it arises from the topology of the circuit, not from the specific values.

docs.title: Solvability
docs.text:
\(\det(A) = (R_1+R_3)(R_2+R_3) - R_3^2 = R_1 R_2 + R_1 R_3 + R_2 R_3 > 0\) (since all \(R_i > 0\)).

Therefore \(A\) is invertible and the solution is unique: $\(\begin{pmatrix} I_1 \ I_2 \end{pmatrix} = A^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} \mathcal{E}_1 \ \mathcal{E}_2 \end{pmatrix}.\)$

Theorem 4.1. For any circuit of \(n\) independent meshes with positive resistances, the mesh resistance matrix \(A\) is symmetric positive definite (SPD), hence always invertible. The linear system \(A\mathbf{I} = \boldsymbol{\mathcal{E}}\) always has a unique solution.

Proof sketch. \(A\) is symmetric by construction (shared resistances appear symmetrically). For any nonzero \(\mathbf{x}\): $\(\mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x} = \sum_{\text{branches}} R_b \left(\sum_{\text{meshes}\ni b} \pm x_m\right)^2 > 0,\)$ since each term is a squared current times a positive resistance, and at least one term is nonzero. Hence \(A\) is SPD \(\Rightarrow\) \(\det(A) > 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) unique solution. \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: Concrete Numerical Example
docs.text:
\(R_1 = 1,\Omega,\ R_2 = 2,\Omega,\ R_3 = 3,\Omega,\ \mathcal{E}_1 = 10,\text{V},\ \mathcal{E}_2 = 5,\text{V}\):

\[A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & -3 \ -3 & 5 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{b} = \begin{pmatrix} 10 \ 5 \end{pmatrix}.\]

\(\det(A) = 20 - 9 = 11\).

By Cramer's rule: $\(I_1 = \frac{\det\begin{pmatrix}10&-3\5&5\end{pmatrix}}{11} = \frac{50+15}{11} = \frac{65}{11} \approx 5.91,\text{A}.\)$ $\(I_2 = \frac{\det\begin{pmatrix}4&10\-3&5\end{pmatrix}}{11} = \frac{20+30}{11} = \frac{50}{11} \approx 4.55,\text{A}.\)$

Current through \(R_3\): \(I_1 - I_2 = 15/11 \approx 1.36,\text{A}\).

docs.title: 5. General Circuit — The Node Voltage Method
docs.text: For a circuit with \(n+1\) nodes (label one as ground, \(V_0 = 0\)), the \(n\) remaining node voltages \(V_1, \ldots, V_n\) are the unknowns.

docs.title: KCL at Node \(i\)
docs.text:
By KCL, the sum of currents leaving node \(i\) equals zero. The current from node \(i\) to node \(j\) through resistance \(R_{ij}\) is: $\(I_{ij} = \frac{V_i - V_j}{R_{ij}}.\)$

Summing over all neighbors \(j\) of node \(i\): $\(\sum_{j \sim i} \frac{V_i - V_j}{R_{ij}} = I_{\text{ext},i},\)$

where \(I_{\text{ext},i}\) is external current injected at node \(i\) by current sources.

Rearranging: $\(\left(\sum_{j \sim i} \frac{1}{R_{ij}}\right) V_i - \sum_{j \sim i} \frac{1}{R_{ij}} V_j = I_{\text{ext},i}.\)$

docs.title: The Conductance Matrix (Laplacian)
docs.text:
Define conductance \(G_{ij} = 1/R_{ij}\). The system in matrix form is:

\[\underbrace{L}_{n \times n} \mathbf{V} = \mathbf{I}_{\text{ext}},\]

where \(L\) is the graph Laplacian of the circuit: $\(L_{ii} = \sum_{j \sim i} G_{ij}, \qquad L_{ij} = -G_{ij}\ (i \neq j).\)$

Theorem 5.1 (Laplacian Structure). The conductance matrix \(L\) satisfies:

  1. \(L\) is symmetric: \(L_{ij} = L_{ji}\).
  2. All diagonal entries are positive.
  3. All off-diagonal entries are \(\leq 0\).
  4. Each row sums to zero: \(\sum_j L_{ij} = 0\).
  5. \(L\) is positive **semi**definite. After fixing ground (\(V_0 = 0\)), the reduced matrix \(\tilde{L}\) is SPD, hence invertible.

Proof of row-sum zero: \(\sum_j L_{ij} = L_{ii} + \sum_{j \neq i} L_{ij} = \sum_{j\sim i} G_{ij} - \sum_{j\sim i} G_{ij} = 0\). \(\blacksquare\)

This means \(L\) itself has a null space spanned by \((1, 1, \ldots, 1)^T\) (constant potentials correspond to zero current — you can shift all potentials by the same constant). Grounding one node removes this degeneracy and makes the system uniquely solvable.

docs.title: Circuit
docs.text:
Node 1 ──── R₁₂ = 2Ω ──── Node 2
        │                          │
       R₁₃ = 4Ω               R₂₃ = 1Ω
        │                          │
     Node 3 ──────────────────── (ground)

External: current source pushes I_s = 3A into Node 1.
          current source pulls I_s = 3A out of Node 2.

Unknowns: \(V_1, V_2\) (Node 3 is ground: \(V_3 = 0\)).

docs.title: Matrix System
docs.text:
\[\begin{pmatrix} 3/4 & -1/2 \ -1/2 & 3/2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} V_1 \ V_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \ -3 \end{pmatrix}\]

\(\det = \frac{3}{4} \cdot \frac{3}{2} - \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{9}{8} - \frac{1}{4} = \frac{7}{8}\).

\[V_1 = \frac{1}{\det}\det\begin{pmatrix}3&-1/2\-3&3/2\end{pmatrix} = \frac{8}{7}\left(\frac{9}{2} - \frac{3}{2}\right) = \frac{8}{7} \cdot 3 = \frac{24}{7} \approx 3.43,\text{V}.\] \[V_2 = \frac{1}{\det}\det\begin{pmatrix}3/4&3\-1/2&-3\end{pmatrix} = \frac{8}{7}\left(-\frac{9}{4} + \frac{3}{2}\right) = \frac{8}{7} \cdot \left(-\frac{3}{4}\right) = -\frac{6}{7} \approx -0.86,\text{V}.\]

Currents: $\(I_{12} = G_{12}(V_1 - V_2) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{30}{7} = \frac{15}{7},\text{A}.\)$ $\(I_{13} = G_{13} \cdot V_1 = \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{24}{7} = \frac{6}{7},\text{A}.\)$ $\(I_{23} = G_{23} \cdot V_2 = 1 \cdot \left(-\frac{6}{7}\right) = -\frac{6}{7},\text{A}\ \text{(flows from ground to Node 2)}.\)$

docs.title: 7. Superposition — The Linearity Principle
docs.text:
Theorem 7.1 (Superposition). In a linear circuit, the response (current or voltage anywhere) due to multiple independent sources equals the sum of responses due to each source acting alone (all others replaced by their internal resistances: voltage sources \(\to\) short circuit, current sources \(\to\) open circuit).

Proof. The node voltage system is \(L\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{I}_{\text{ext}}\). If \(\mathbf{I}_{\text{ext}} = \mathbf{I}^{(1)} + \mathbf{I}^{(2)}\) (two sources), then: $\(L\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{I}^{(1)} + \mathbf{I}^{(2)} \implies \mathbf{V} = L^{-1}\mathbf{I}^{(1)} + L^{-1}\mathbf{I}^{(2)} = \mathbf{V}^{(1)} + \mathbf{V}^{(2)}.\)$

This is exactly linearity of the map \(\mathbf{I}_{\text{ext}} \mapsto \mathbf{V} = L^{-1}\mathbf{I}_{\text{ext}}\). \(\blacksquare\)

Remark. Superposition fails for power (since \(P = V^2/R\) is quadratic, not linear). This is a critical practical note — never superpose power directly.

docs.title: 8. Thévenin's Theorem — Existence of a Canonical Form
docs.text:
Theorem 8.1 (Thévenin). Any linear circuit with two output terminals can be replaced by a single voltage source \(V_{\text{th}}\) in series with a single resistance \(R_{\text{th}}\).

Proof sketch. The terminal voltage \(V\) and current \(I\) satisfy a relation of the form \(V = V_{\text{th}} - I R_{\text{th}}\) (a linear equation!) — this follows from the fact that the open-circuit voltage is \(V_{\text{th}} = V|_{I=0}\) and the short-circuit current is \(I_{sc} = V_{\text{th}}/R_{\text{th}}\). The linear relationship between \(V\) and \(I\) is guaranteed by the linearity of the underlying system. \(\blacksquare\)

How to find \(V_{\text{th}}\) and \(R_{\text{th}}\):

  1. \(V_{\text{th}}\) = open-circuit voltage at terminals (solve the linear system with \(I = 0\)).
  2. \(R_{\text{th}}\) = resistance seen from terminals with all independent sources killed.

Example. Circuit: \(\mathcal{E} = 10,\text{V}\), \(R_1 = 6,\Omega\) in series, \(R_2 = 3,\Omega\) in parallel with terminals.

\[V_{\text{th}} = \mathcal{E} \cdot \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} = 10 \cdot \frac{3}{9} = \frac{10}{3},\text{V}.$$ $$R_{\text{th}} = R_1 \parallel R_2 = \frac{6 \cdot 3}{6 + 3} = 2,\Omega.\]

This two-parameter description encodes the entire linear circuit for any load.

docs.title: Series Circuit
docs.text:
┌────[ε]────R₁────R₂────┐
  │                        │
  └────────────────────────┘
  One loop → one linear equation

docs.title: Parallel Resistors
docs.text:
┌───R₁───┐
  A ─────┤        ├───── B
         └───R₂───┘

  Equivalent: 1/R_eq = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂
  → Linear equation in conductances

docs.title: Wheatstone Bridge
docs.text:
┌───R₁───C───R₂───┐
  A ─────┤                  ├───── B
         └───R₃───D───R₄───┘
              Galvanometer C─D

  Bridge balanced (I_G = 0) iff R₁/R₂ = R₃/R₄
  → One linear constraint among resistances

docs.title: General \(n\)-Node Circuit
docs.text:
Node 1 ─G₁₂─ Node 2 ─G₂₃─ Node 3
     │                           │
     G₁₃ ─────────────────────G₃(gnd)

  KCL at each non-ground node → n linear equations
  Matrix form: LV = I_ext

docs.title: 10. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
10.1 Circuit Simulation as Linear Algebra
docs.text:
SPICE (the industry-standard circuit simulator) solves the node voltage system \(L\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{I}\) at its core. The matrix \(L\) is sparse (most entries zero — each node connects to few others). Efficient sparse linear solvers (LU factorization with fill-reducing orderings) are the computational heart of every circuit simulator.

The same sparse linear algebra appears in:

  • Graph neural networks (GNNs): message passing on a graph is exactly the Laplacian operator \(L\) applied to node features.
  • Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs): enforce circuit equations as loss terms.

docs.title: 10.2 Resistor Networks as Neural Networks
docs.text:
A resistor network is mathematically equivalent to a linear neural network:

  • Node voltages \(\leftrightarrow\) neuron activations
  • Conductances \(G_{ij}\) \(\leftrightarrow\) weights \(w_{ij}\)
  • KCL \(\leftrightarrow\) the linear combination at each neuron: \(V_i = \frac{\sum_j G_{ij} V_j}{\sum_j G_{ij}}\)

This is not a metaphor. Hopfield (1984) showed that analog circuits with resistors and capacitors perform associative memory — a precursor to modern attention mechanisms.

docs.title: 10.3 Equilibrium Propagation (Modern ML)
docs.text: The Equilibrium Propagation algorithm (Scellier & Bengio, 2017) trains neural networks by nudging the circuit toward a target state and measuring how the equilibrium \(L\mathbf{V} = \mathbf{I}\) changes. The gradient of the loss is encoded in the difference between two linear system solutions. This is a biologically plausible alternative to backpropagation.

docs.title: 10.4 Power Systems and Grid ML
docs.text:
Power grids are large-scale circuit systems. The DC power flow equations are a linear approximation: $\(B\boldsymbol{\theta} = \mathbf{P},\)$

where \(B\) is the susceptance matrix (a Laplacian), \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) are bus voltage angles, and \(\mathbf{P}\) are power injections. Machine learning models for grid optimization (e.g., optimal power flow) are trained on solutions to this linear system.

docs.title: 10.5 Connection Map
docs.text:
Kirchhoff's Laws
       │
       │ → KCL + Ohm's Law
       ▼
  Linear System  LV = I  (Node Voltage)
       │              ╲
       │               ╲─────► Graph Laplacian
       │                           │
       │                           ▼
       │                   Graph Neural Networks
       │                   (message passing = LV)
       │
       ├──► Sparse LU Factorization ──► SPICE, Circuit Simulators
       │
       ├──► Resistor Network = Linear Neural Net
       │         │
       │         └──► Hopfield Networks, Associative Memory
       │
       └──► Equilibrium Propagation ──► Bio-plausible ML Training

docs.title: 11. Key Theorems — Summary
docs.text: Theorem Statement Ohm's Law \(V = IR\) — linear relation, one equation per element KCL \(\sum I_k = 0\) at each node — one linear equation per node KVL \(\sum V_k = 0\) per loop — one linear equation per loop Mesh Matrix SPD Mesh resistance matrix is always SPD → unique solution Laplacian Structure Conductance matrix is symmetric, row sums zero, SPD after grounding Superposition Response is linear in sources — follows from \(L^{-1}\) being linear Thévenin Any linear circuit seen from two terminals = \(V_{th}\) + \(R_{th}\) in series

docs.title: 12. Things to Prove Yourself
docs.text:
1. Prove that the mesh resistance matrix \(A\) for any planar resistive circuit with \(n\) meshes is symmetric positive definite. (Hint: express \(\mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x}\) as a sum over branches.)
  2. Derive the \(\pi\)-to-Y (delta-to-star) transformation for three resistors. Show it reduces to solving a \(3 \times 3\) linear system.
  3. Prove Superposition rigorously from the linearity of \(L^{-1}\).
  4. Show that if all resistances in a circuit are scaled by a constant \(\lambda > 0\), then all currents scale by \(1/\lambda\) and all voltages remain unchanged (when driven by voltage sources). What does this say about the condition number of \(L\)?
  5. Formulate a \(4\)-node circuit of your choice as a node-voltage system, solve it by Gaussian elimination, and verify each KCL equation in the solution.
  6. Relate the graph Laplacian \(L\) of a resistor network to the adjacency matrix \(A\) of the underlying graph. When is \(L = D - A\) exactly (where \(D\) is the degree matrix)?

docs.title: Predator-Prey Systems
docs.text:
"Nature does not solve differential equations — she simply satisfies them. Our job is to listen carefully enough to write them down." — Personal margin note, Stewart §9.6

See also: [[Linear Equations]] · [[Application to Electric Circuits]]

docs.title: 0. Preliminary Remarks
docs.text:
The predator–prey system is one of the great examples of applied mathematics: simple equations, profound behavior, no closed-form solution — yet completely tractable by qualitative analysis. It sits at the intersection of differential equations, dynamical systems, linear algebra (linearization), and nonlinear analysis.

This note builds the theory from scratch: model derivation → equilibria → linearization → phase plane → full qualitative picture → extensions → connections to ML.

The mathematics here lives in ODE theory and dynamical systems, but the tools are exactly those of [[Linear Equations]] — applied locally near equilibria via the Jacobian.

docs.title: 1. Model Derivation — From Biology to Equations
1.1 The Two Species
docs.text:
Let:

  • \(x(t) \geq 0\) = population of prey (e.g., rabbits) at time \(t\)
  • \(y(t) \geq 0\) = population of predators (e.g., foxes) at time \(t\)

docs.title: 1.2 Modelling Assumptions
docs.text:
Assumption Mathematical consequence Prey grow exponentially without predators \(\dot{x} = ax\) for some \(a > 0\) Each predator-prey encounter reduces prey at rate proportional to both populations \(-bxy\) term in \(\dot{x}\) Predators die exponentially without prey \(-cy\) term in \(\dot{y}\) Each encounter increases predator population \(+dxy\) term in \(\dot{y}\)

The term \(xy\) is the law of mass action: encounters occur at rate proportional to the product of both populations (like molecules colliding in a gas).

docs.title: 1.3 The Lotka–Volterra Equations
docs.text:
Definition 1.1 (Lotka–Volterra System). The predator–prey system with parameters \(a, b, c, d > 0\) is: $\(\boxed{\dot{x} = ax - bxy, \qquad \dot{y} = -cy + dxy.}\)$ Equivalently, with \(\mathbf{u} = (x, y)^T\): $\(\dot{\mathbf{u}} = \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{u}) = \begin{pmatrix} ax - bxy \ -cy + dxy \end{pmatrix}.\)$

Historical note. Vito Volterra derived these equations in 1926 to explain oscillations in Adriatic fish populations following World War I. Alfred Lotka independently derived them in 1910 in a chemical context. The mathematics predates the biology.

Factored form (useful for finding equilibria): $\(\dot{x} = x(a - by), \qquad \dot{y} = y(-c + dx).\)$

docs.title: 2. Equilibria
docs.text:
Definition 2.1. A point \(\mathbf{u}^* = (x^_, y^_)\) is an equilibrium (fixed point) of the system if \(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{u}^*) = \mathbf{0}\), i.e., the population does not change.

Setting \(\dot{x} = 0\) and \(\dot{y} = 0\):

\[x(a - by) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad y(-c + dx) = 0.\]

Case 1: \(x = 0\) and \(y = 0\). Equilibrium at the origin \(E_0 = (0, 0)\).

Case 2: \(x \neq 0\) and \(y \neq 0\). Then \(a - by = 0 \Rightarrow y^* = a/b\), and \(-c + dx = 0 \Rightarrow x^* = c/d\).

Equilibrium at the coexistence point: $\(\boxed{E^* = \left(\frac{c}{d},\ \frac{a}{b}\right).}\)$

Remark. There are exactly two equilibria in the first quadrant (the biologically relevant region \(x \geq 0, y \geq 0\)). The entire qualitative theory will determine what happens near each.

docs.title: 3. Linearization — The Jacobian
docs.text:
The key tool for understanding behavior near equilibria is linearization: approximate the nonlinear system by its best linear approximation at the equilibrium point. This is exactly the multivariable Taylor theorem.

Definition 3.1 (Jacobian). The Jacobian matrix of \(\mathbf{F} = (F_1, F_2)\) at a point \((x_0, y_0)\) is: $\(J(x_0, y_0) = \begin{pmatrix} \partial F_1/\partial x & \partial F_1/\partial y \ \partial F_2/\partial x & \partial F_2/\partial y \end{pmatrix}.\)$

For the Lotka–Volterra system: $\(J(x, y) = \begin{pmatrix} a - by & -bx \ dy & -c + dx \end{pmatrix}.\)$

Theorem 3.2 (Hartman–Grobman). Near a hyperbolic equilibrium \(\mathbf{u}^_\) (one where \(J(\mathbf{u}^_)\) has no eigenvalues with zero real part), the nonlinear system is topologically conjugate to its linearization \(\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}} = J(\mathbf{u}^*)\boldsymbol{\xi}\).

In plain language: the eigenvalues of \(J\) at an equilibrium determine the local qualitative behavior of the full nonlinear system.

docs.title: 3.1 Linearization at \(E_0 = (0, 0)\)
docs.text:
\[J(0,0) = \begin{pmatrix} a & 0 \ 0 & -c \end{pmatrix}.\]

Eigenvalues: \(\lambda_1 = a > 0\), \(\lambda_2 = -c < 0\).

Since eigenvalues have opposite signs, \(E_0\) is a saddle point — unstable. Solutions starting near the origin move away (except along the \(y\)-axis, which is the stable manifold).

Biological meaning: If both populations are near zero, prey grow (positive eigenvalue in \(x\)-direction) and predators die (negative eigenvalue in \(y\)-direction). The extinction state is unstable: any small prey population recovers.

docs.title: 3.2 Linearization at \(E^* = (c/d, a/b)\)
docs.text:
\[J!\left(\frac{c}{d}, \frac{a}{b}\right) = \begin{pmatrix} a - b\cdot\frac{a}{b} & -b\cdot\frac{c}{d} \ d\cdot\frac{a}{b} & -c + d\cdot\frac{c}{d} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -\frac{bc}{d} \ \frac{ad}{b} & 0 \end{pmatrix}.\]

Characteristic equation: $\(\det(J - \lambda I) = \lambda^2 + \frac{bc}{d} \cdot \frac{ad}{b} = \lambda^2 + ac = 0.\)$

Eigenvalues: $\(\lambda = \pm i\sqrt{ac}.\)$

Pure imaginary eigenvalues! The linearization gives a center.

Warning. Here Hartman–Grobman does NOT apply — \(E^*\) is not hyperbolic (eigenvalues have zero real part). The linearization says "center," but the nonlinear system could be a center, a stable spiral, or an unstable spiral. We need a different tool: a conserved quantity.

docs.title: 4. The Conserved Quantity — Proof of Periodic Orbits
docs.text:
Theorem 4.1. The function $\(H(x, y) = d,x - c\ln x + b,y - a\ln y\)$ is a first integral of the Lotka–Volterra system: \(\frac{d}{dt}H(x(t), y(t)) = 0\) along every solution with \(x, y > 0\).

Proof. Compute \(\dot{H}\) along solutions: $\(\frac{dH}{dt} = \frac{\partial H}{\partial x}\dot{x} + \frac{\partial H}{\partial y}\dot{y} = \left(d - \frac{c}{x}\right)(ax - bxy) + \left(b - \frac{a}{y}\right)(-cy + dxy).\)$

Expand each term: $\(\left(d - \frac{c}{x}\right)(ax - bxy) = adx - bdxy - ac + bcy,\)$ $\(\left(b - \frac{a}{y}\right)(-cy + dxy) = -bcy + bdxy + ac - adx.\)$

Sum: $\(\dot{H} = (adx - bdxy - ac + bcy) + (-bcy + bdxy + ac - adx) = 0. \quad \blacksquare\)$

Corollary 4.2. Every solution with \(x(0), y(0) > 0\) is a closed orbit (periodic solution). The period and amplitude depend on the initial condition.

Proof. \(H\) is constant along each trajectory. The level sets \({H(x,y) = k}\) are closed curves in the first quadrant (one verifies this by analyzing \(H\)'s critical points — its unique minimum in the first quadrant is at \(E^*\)). Since trajectories follow level sets, they are closed. \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: 5.1 Nullclines
docs.text:
Definition 5.1. The \(x\)-nullcline is \({(x,y) : \dot{x} = 0}\). The \(y\)-nullcline is \({(x,y) : \dot{y} = 0}\).

For Lotka–Volterra:

  • \(x\)-nullclines: \(x = 0\) (the \(y\)-axis) and \(y = a/b\) (horizontal line)
  • \(y\)-nullclines: \(y = 0\) (the \(x\)-axis) and \(x = c/d\) (vertical line)

The equilibria are exactly the intersections of \(x\)- and \(y\)-nullclines.

docs.title: 5.2 Direction Field — Four Quadrant Analysis
docs.text:
The nullclines divide the first quadrant into four regions. In each, determine signs of \(\dot{x}\) and \(\dot{y}\):

         y
         │
    a/b ─┼────────────────────────────────
         │  II           │   I
         │  ẋ < 0        │   ẋ > 0
         │  ẏ > 0        │   ẏ > 0
         │  (prey ↓,     │   (prey ↑,
         │  pred ↑)      │   pred ↑)
         │               │
         │               E* = (c/d, a/b)
         │               │
         │  III          │   IV
         │  ẋ < 0        │   ẋ > 0
         │  ẏ < 0        │   ẏ < 0
         │  (prey ↓,     │   (prey ↑,
         │  pred ↓)      │   pred ↓)
         │               │
    ─────┼───────────────┼──────────────── x
         0              c/d

Reading the orbit direction counterclockwise: I → II → III → IV → I.

Mnemonic. When prey are plentiful and predators few (Quadrant IV), predators thrive and prey decline → Quadrant I. When predators are many and prey scarce (Quadrant II), predators starve → Quadrant III. The system perpetually chases its tail.

docs.title: 5.3 Time Series — Oscillations with Phase Lag
docs.text:
The populations oscillate periodically. The predator population lags the prey population by approximately a quarter period:

Population
    │
    │    ╭─── Prey x(t)
    │   ╱ ╲              ╭──
    │  ╱   ╲            ╱
    │ ╱     ╲    ╭─── Predator y(t)
    │╱       ╲  ╱  ╲
    │         ╲╱    ╲
    │               ╲   ╭──
    │                ╲ ╱
    ├─────────────────────────── t
         T/4   T/2  3T/4   T

Phase lag: y peaks after x peaks.

Why the lag? Prey grow → more food for predators → predators grow → prey decline → predators decline → prey recover. Each step takes time. The quarter-period lag is a signature of the \(\pm i\sqrt{ac}\) eigenvalues (phase angle = \(\pi/2\)).

docs.title: 6.1 Shape of Level Sets of \(H\)
docs.text:
At the coexistence equilibrium \(E^* = (c/d, a/b)\), compute \(H\): $\(H^* = H(E^*) = d\cdot\frac{c}{d} - c\ln\frac{c}{d} + b\cdot\frac{a}{b} - a\ln\frac{a}{b} = c + a - c\ln\frac{c}{d} - a\ln\frac{a}{b}.\)$

For any other initial condition \((x_0, y_0)\), \(H(x_0, y_0) > H^_\) (since \(E^_\) is the global minimum of \(H\) in the first quadrant — proven below), and the orbit is a closed curve enclosing \(E^*\).

Lemma 6.1. \(E^*\) is the unique global minimum of \(H\) in \(\mathbb{R}_{>0}^2\).

Proof. \(\partial H/\partial x = d - c/x = 0 \Rightarrow x = c/d\), \(\partial H/\partial y = b - a/y = 0 \Rightarrow y = a/b\). So \(E^_\) is the unique critical point. The Hessian: $\(\nabla^2 H = \begin{pmatrix} c/x^2 & 0 \ 0 & a/y^2 \end{pmatrix}\Bigg|_{E^_} = \begin{pmatrix} d^2/c & 0 \ 0 & b^2/a \end{pmatrix},\)$ which is positive definite (diagonal with positive entries). So \(E^*\) is a strict local minimum. Since \(H \to +\infty\) as \(x \to 0^+\), \(x \to +\infty\), \(y \to 0^+\), or \(y \to +\infty\), it is the global minimum. \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: 6.2 Average Populations Over One Period
docs.text:
Theorem 6.2. The time-average of \(x(t)\) over one period \(T\) is \(\bar{x} = c/d\). The time-average of \(y(t)\) over one period is \(\bar{y} = a/b\).

Proof. Integrate \(\dot{x}/x = a - by\) over one period: $\(\int_0^T \frac{\dot{x}}{x},dt = \int_0^T (a - by),dt = aT - b\int_0^T y,dt.\)$

The left side is \([\ln x]_0^T = 0\) (periodic). So \(b\int_0^T y,dt = aT\), giving \(\bar{y} = a/b\). Similarly for \(\bar{x} = c/d\). \(\blacksquare\)

Corollary (Volterra's Principle). The time-averaged populations equal the equilibrium values regardless of amplitude. Uniform harvesting of prey shifts the equilibrium and thus the average predator population — a counterintuitive consequence.

docs.title: 7. Stability Analysis — Summary
docs.text:
Equilibrium Jacobian eigenvalues Type Stability \(E_0 = (0,0)\) \(\lambda = a > 0,\ \lambda = -c < 0\) Saddle Unstable \(E^* = (c/d, a/b)\) \(\lambda = \pm i\sqrt{ac}\) Center (nonlinear) Neutrally stable (Lyapunov stable, not asymptotically stable)

Definition 7.1. An equilibrium is Lyapunov stable if solutions starting close remain close for all time, but do not necessarily converge to it. It is asymptotically stable if solutions also converge to it as \(t \to \infty\).

\(E^*\) is Lyapunov stable (orbits stay on their level curve of \(H\)) but not asymptotically stable (no convergence — the orbit is periodic).

docs.title: 8.1 Logistic Prey (More Realistic)
docs.text:
Replace exponential prey growth with logistic growth: $\(\dot{x} = ax\left(1 - \frac{x}{K}\right) - bxy, \qquad \dot{y} = -cy + dxy.\)$

The carrying capacity \(K\) limits prey growth. The coexistence equilibrium becomes: $\(x^* = \frac{c}{d}, \quad y^* = \frac{a}{b}\left(1 - \frac{c}{dK}\right).\)$

(Exists only if \(c/d < K\), i.e., predators can survive before prey hit carrying capacity.)

The Jacobian at \(E^*\) now has eigenvalues with negative real part — the equilibrium becomes asymptotically stable. Orbits spiral inward: populations don't oscillate forever, they settle to coexistence. This is the Poincaré–Bendixson picture.

docs.title: 8.2 Holling Type II Functional Response
docs.text: Real predators don't hunt indefinitely faster as prey increase — they saturate (handling time). Replace \(bxy\) with: $\(\frac{bxy}{1 + bh,x},\)$ where \(h\) is handling time per prey. This is Holling Type II and introduces a new equilibrium branch and can generate limit cycles (Hopf bifurcation).

docs.title: 8.3 The General Form
docs.text:
\[\dot{x} = x,f(x,y), \qquad \dot{y} = y,g(x,y).\]

Both \(f\) and \(g\) are general functions. Lotka–Volterra is the case \(f = a - by\), \(g = -c + dx\) — both linear in \((x,y)\). The entire rich theory of predator–prey models generalizes from this observation.

docs.title: 9. Numerical Example — Concrete Computation
docs.text:
Parameters: \(a = 1,\ b = 0.1,\ c = 1.5,\ d = 0.075\).

Equilibrium: $\(E^* = \left(\frac{1.5}{0.075},\ \frac{1}{0.1}\right) = (20,\ 10).\)$

Jacobian at \(E^*\): $\(J(20,10) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -0.1 \cdot 20 \ 0.075 \cdot 10 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -2 \ 0.75 & 0 \end{pmatrix}.\)$

Eigenvalues: $\(\lambda^2 + 2 \cdot 0.75 = 0 \implies \lambda^2 = -1.5 \implies \lambda = \pm i\sqrt{1.5} \approx \pm 1.225i.\)$

Period of linearized oscillation: $\(T \approx \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{ac}} = \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1 \cdot 1.5}} \approx 5.13\ \text{time units}.\)$

Initial condition: \((x_0, y_0) = (25, 10)\). Prey start above equilibrium, predators at equilibrium.

Conservation value: $\(H(25, 10) = 0.075 \cdot 25 - 1.5\ln 25 + 0.1 \cdot 10 - 1\ln 10 \approx 1.875 - 4.832 + 1 - 2.303 = -4.26.\)$

Compare with \(H(E^*) = 0.075 \cdot 20 - 1.5\ln 20 + 0.1 \cdot 10 - 1\ln 10 \approx 1.5 - 4.497 + 1 - 2.303 = -4.30\).

Since \(H(x_0, y_0) > H(E^*)\) (less negative), the orbit is outside the equilibrium — a closed curve slightly larger.

docs.title: 11. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
11.1 Lotka–Volterra as a Dynamical System — Neural ODE
docs.text:
The Lotka–Volterra equations are an autonomous ODE: \(\dot{\mathbf{u}} = \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{u})\). This is exactly the structure of a Neural ODE (Chen et al., NeurIPS 2018):

Definition. A Neural ODE parameterizes the vector field \(\mathbf{F}\) by a neural network \(f_\theta\): $\(\dot{\mathbf{h}}(t) = f_\theta(\mathbf{h}(t), t), \qquad \mathbf{h}(t_1) = \text{ODESolve}(f_\theta, \mathbf{h}(t_0), t_0, t_1).\)$

One trains \(\theta\) to fit observed trajectories. If the true dynamics are Lotka–Volterra, a Neural ODE should discover the vector field \(\mathbf{F}(x,y) = (x(a-by),\ y(-c+dx))\).

The conservation law \(H\) is a first integral — a Neural ODE with a Hamiltonian structure (Hamiltonian Neural Network, Greydanus et al., 2019) can be constrained to discover and preserve \(H\) exactly.

docs.title: 11.2 Predator–Prey Dynamics in GANs
docs.text:
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) pit a generator \(G\) against a discriminator \(D\) in a minimax game: $\(\min_G \max_D\ \mathbb{E}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}[\log(1 - D(G(z)))].\)$

The training dynamics of GANs are notoriously oscillatory and unstable — reminiscent of predator–prey orbits around the Nash equilibrium \((G^_, D^_)\). This is not a coincidence:

Theorem (informal). Near a Nash equilibrium, simultaneous gradient descent on a two-player zero-sum game has eigenvalues \(\pm i\omega\) — exactly the pure imaginary eigenvalues of the Lotka–Volterra linearization. Training oscillates; it does not converge.

This is why GAN training is hard and why techniques like gradient penalty, spectral normalization, and unrolled optimization are needed — they add damping (negative real part to eigenvalues) converting the center to a stable spiral.

docs.title: 11.3 Competitive Dynamics in Resource Allocation (RL)
docs.text:
In multi-agent reinforcement learning, agents compete for resources. Their populations evolve under replicator dynamics: $\(\dot{x}_i = x_i\left(f_i(\mathbf{x}) - \bar{f}(\mathbf{x})\right),\)$

where \(f_i\) is agent \(i\)'s fitness and \(\bar{f}\) is the population average. This is a generalization of Lotka–Volterra to \(n\) competing strategies. The game-theoretic equilibria correspond to Nash equilibria; their stability is analyzed via the Jacobian — exactly as in §3.

docs.title: 11.4 Ecological Modeling with ML
docs.text:
Modern approaches use ML to learn predator–prey dynamics from data:

  1. SINDy (Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics): Given time series \((x(t), y(t))\), compute \(\dot{x}\) and \(\dot{y}\) numerically, then regress \(\dot{\mathbf{u}}\) against a library of candidate terms \({x, y, xy, x^2, \ldots}\) using sparse linear regression (\(L^1\) regularization). If the true model is Lotka–Volterra, SINDy recovers \(\dot{x} = ax - bxy\) exactly.

  2. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs): Train a neural network \(\hat{x}(t), \hat{y}(t)\) to satisfy the Lotka–Volterra ODEs as a penalty in the loss: $\(\mathcal{L} = \underbrace{|\hat{x}(t_i) - x_i|^2}_{\text{data fit}} + \lambda \underbrace{|\dot{\hat{x}} - \hat{x}(a - b\hat{y})|^2}_{\text{ODE residual}}.\)$

  3. Conservation-aware learning: Enforce \(H(x(t), y(t)) = \text{const}\) as a hard constraint. This dramatically reduces the hypothesis space and improves generalization.

docs.title: 11.5 Summary Diagram
docs.text:
Lotka–Volterra ODE
  ẋ = x(a - by)
  ẏ = y(-c + dx)
        │
        ├── Equilibria + Jacobian ──► Linear stability theory
        │         (§3)               (eigenvalues ±i√ac)
        │
        ├── Conservation law H ─────► Periodic orbits, Lyapunov stability
        │         (§4)
        │
        ├── Neural ODE ─────────────► Learn F from data (NeurIPS 2018)
        │
        ├── GAN training ───────────► Oscillatory dynamics near Nash equilibrium
        │   (discriminator vs.       Eigenvalues ±iω → need damping tricks
        │    generator)
        │
        ├── Multi-agent RL ──────────► Replicator dynamics, n-species LV
        │
        └── SINDy / PINNs ──────────► Discover/enforce ODE structure from data

docs.title: 12. Key Theorems — Summary
docs.text: Theorem Statement Equilibria \(E_0 = (0,0)\) and \(E^* = (c/d, a/b)\) Saddle at origin \(J(0,0)\) has eigenvalues \(+a, -c\): saddle point, unstable Center at \(E^*\) \(J(E^*)\) has eigenvalues \(\pm i\sqrt{ac}\): linearized center Conservation (Thm 4.1) \(H = dx - c\ln x + by - a\ln y\) is constant along orbits Periodic orbits (Cor 4.2) All orbits in \(\mathbb{R}_{>0}^2\) are closed (periodic) \(E^*\) is global min of \(H\) (Lemma 6.1) Hessian of \(H\) at \(E^*\) is positive definite Volterra's Principle (Thm 6.2) Time averages: \(\bar{x} = c/d\), \(\bar{y} = a/b\) GAN analogy Simultaneous gradient descent near Nash \(\Leftrightarrow\) LV near \(E^*\): eigenvalues \(\pm i\omega\)

docs.title: 13. Things to Prove Yourself
docs.text:
1. Verify by direct computation that \(\dot{H} = 0\) along solutions of the Lotka–Volterra system (fill in all algebra from Theorem 4.1).
  2. Prove Volterra's Principle (Theorem 6.2) for \(\bar{x} = c/d\) by integrating \(\dot{y}/y\) over one period.
  3. For the logistic-prey system (\(\dot{x} = ax(1 - x/K) - bxy\), \(\dot{y} = -cy + dxy\)): find the coexistence equilibrium and compute its Jacobian. Show the eigenvalues have negative real part when \(c/d < K\), confirming asymptotic stability.
  4. Show that the linearization \(\dot{\boldsymbol{\xi}} = J(E^_)\boldsymbol{\xi}\) with \(J(E^_) = \begin{pmatrix}0 & -bc/d \ ad/b & 0\end{pmatrix}\) gives solutions of the form \(\boldsymbol{\xi}(t) = e^{i\sqrt{ac},t}\mathbf{v}\) and write out \(\mathbf{v}\) explicitly.
  5. Prove that the function \(g(s) = s - 1 - \ln s\) satisfies \(g(s) \geq 0\) for all \(s > 0\) with equality iff \(s = 1\). Use this to show \(H(x,y) \geq H(E^_)\) for all \(x, y > 0\). (This gives a clean proof that \(E^_\) is the global minimum.)
  6. SINDy exercise. If you were given noisy data \((x(t_i), y(t_i))\) and had to recover the LV equations using sparse regression, what library of basis functions would you include? What is the minimum number of data points needed in principle?

docs.title: Parametric Curves
docs.text:
"A curve is not just a set of points — it is a journey. The parametric viewpoint remembers the traveller, not just the road." — Personal margin note, Stewart §10.1

See also: [[Linear Equations]] · [[Application to Electric Circuits]] · [[Predator–Prey System]]

docs.title: 0. Preliminary Remarks
docs.text:
Every curve you have ever drawn — a circle, a parabola, a spiral, a cycloid — can be described in two fundamentally different ways: as a relation between \(x\) and \(y\) (implicit or explicit), or as the image of a path traced by a moving point. The second description is parametric, and it is strictly more powerful.

Parametric equations remember direction, speed, and how many times a curve is traversed. They are the natural language for kinematics, differential geometry, computer graphics, and — as we shall see — the geometry of neural network training.

This note builds the full theory: definitions → calculus (tangents, arc length, area) → curvature → classical curves → connection to ML.

docs.title: 1. Definitions
docs.text:
Definition 1.1 (Parametric Curve). A parametric curve in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is a continuous map $\(\gamma: I \to \mathbb{R}^2, \quad t \mapsto (x(t),, y(t)),\)$ where \(I \subseteq \mathbb{R}\) is an interval (open, closed, or all of \(\mathbb{R}\)), and \(x, y: I \to \mathbb{R}\) are continuous functions called the coordinate functions or parametric equations.

The variable \(t\) is the parameter. It often represents time, but it need not — it is simply a bookkeeping variable for tracing the curve.

Definition 1.2 (Smooth Curve). A parametric curve \(\gamma\) is smooth on \(I\) if \(x\) and \(y\) are differentiable and the velocity vector $\(\dot{\gamma}(t) = (x'(t),, y'(t)) \neq (0, 0) \quad \text{for all } t \in I.\)$ The condition \(\dot{\gamma}(t) \neq \mathbf{0}\) rules out cusps (points where the curve momentarily stops and reverses).

Definition 1.3 (Simple and Closed Curves).

  • \(\gamma\) is simple if it does not cross itself: \(\gamma(t_1) = \gamma(t_2) \Rightarrow t_1 = t_2\) (except possibly at endpoints).
  • \(\gamma\) is closed if \(\gamma(a) = \gamma(b)\) for a compact interval \([a,b]\).
  • A simple closed curve is a Jordan curve.

Jordan Curve Theorem (stated without proof). Every Jordan curve in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) divides the plane into exactly two regions — a bounded interior and an unbounded exterior.

docs.title: 2. Eliminating the Parameter
docs.text:
Given \((x(t), y(t))\), one can sometimes solve for \(t\) from one equation and substitute into the other, obtaining an implicit or explicit Cartesian equation \(F(x,y) = 0\).

Warning. Elimination loses information: it discards direction, speed, and multiplicity. Two parametrizations can give the same Cartesian curve.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Example 2.1. \(x = t^2,\ y = t^3\), \(t \in \mathbb{R}\).

From the first: \(t = x^{1/2}\) (for \(t \geq 0\)) or \(t = -x^{1/2}\) (for \(t \leq 0\)). Substituting into \(y = t^3\): $\(y^2 = t^6 = (t^2)^3 = x^3 \implies y^2 = x^3.\)$

This is a cuspidal cubic (semicubical parabola). At \(t = 0\): \((x,y) = (0,0)\), and \(\dot{\gamma}(0) = (0, 0)\) — a cusp, which the Cartesian equation displays as a singularity (\(y^2 = x^3\) is not smooth at the origin).

Example 2.2. \(x = \cos t,\ y = \sin t\), \(t \in [0, 2\pi]\).

\(x^2 + y^2 = \cos^2 t + \sin^2 t = 1\). The unit circle. The parametrization traverses it counterclockwise, once.

Example 2.3. \(x = \cos 2t,\ y = \sin 2t\), \(t \in [0, 2\pi]\).

Same Cartesian curve \(x^2 + y^2 = 1\), but traversed twice as fast, twice in total. Elimination cannot see this.

Example 2.4 (no elimination possible). \(x = t - \sin t,\ y = 1 - \cos t\) (the cycloid). There is no closed-form Cartesian equation. Parametric is the only natural description.

docs.title: 3.1 Tangent Lines and \(dy/dx\)
docs.text:
Theorem 3.1. If \(\gamma(t) = (x(t), y(t))\) is smooth at \(t = t_0\) and \(x'(t_0) \neq 0\), then the slope of the tangent line to \(\gamma\) at \(t_0\) is: $\(\frac{dy}{dx}\Bigg|_{t=t_0} = \frac{y'(t_0)}{x'(t_0)}.\)$

Proof. By the chain rule, if \(y\) is a differentiable function of \(x\) (guaranteed locally by the Inverse Function Theorem when \(x'(t_0) \neq 0\)): $\(\frac{dy}{dt} = \frac{dy}{dx} \cdot \frac{dx}{dt} \implies \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} = \frac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}. \quad \blacksquare\)$

Theorem 3.2 (Second Derivative). The second derivative of \(y\) with respect to \(x\) along the parametric curve is: $\(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{\frac{d}{dt}!\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}{x'(t)} = \frac{\frac{d}{dt}!\left(\frac{y'}{x'}\right)}{x'(t)}.\)$

Proof. Apply Theorem 3.1 with \(dy/dx\) in place of \(y\): $\(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{d}{dx}!\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right) = \frac{\frac{d}{dt}!\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\frac{dx}{dt}}. \quad \blacksquare\)$

Example. For \(x = t^2,\ y = t^3\): $\(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{3t^2}{2t} = \frac{3t}{2}, \quad \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{3/2}{2t} = \frac{3}{4t}.\)$

At \(t = 1\): slope \(= 3/2\), concave up (\(d^2y/dx^2 = 3/4 > 0\)).

docs.title: 3.2 Horizontal and Vertical Tangents
docs.text:
Condition Tangent \(y'(t_0) = 0\), \(x'(t_0) eq 0\) Horizontal tangent at \(\gamma(t_0)\) \(x'(t_0) = 0\), \(y'(t_0) eq 0\) Vertical tangent at \(\gamma(t_0)\) \(x'(t_0) = y'(t_0) = 0\) Need higher-order analysis (possible cusp)

Example. Cycloid \(x = t - \sin t\), \(y = 1 - \cos t\): $\(x'(t) = 1 - \cos t, \quad y'(t) = \sin t.\)$

Horizontal tangents: \(\sin t = 0\) and \(1 - \cos t eq 0 \Rightarrow t = \pi + 2k\pi\). At these \(t\): \((x,y) = (\pi + 2k\pi, 2)\) — tops of the arches.

Vertical tangents (cusps): \(1 - \cos t = 0 \Rightarrow t = 2k\pi\), and \(\sin(2k\pi) = 0\) also. Both vanish — these are cusps at \(t = 2k\pi\), corresponding to \((x,y) = (2k\pi, 0)\) — the touching points on the ground.

docs.title: 3.3 Arc Length
docs.text:
Theorem 3.3 (Arc Length). If \(\gamma: [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^2\) is smooth, the arc length of \(\gamma\) is: $\(L = \int_a^b |\dot{\gamma}(t)|,dt = \int_a^b \sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2},dt.\)$

Proof. Partition \([a,b]\) into \(n\) subintervals with \(\Delta t = (b-a)/n\). The polygonal approximation has length: $\(L_n = \sum_{k=1}^n \sqrt{(\Delta x_k)^2 + (\Delta y_k)^2} = \sum_{k=1}^n \sqrt{\left(\frac{\Delta x_k}{\Delta t}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\Delta y_k}{\Delta t}\right)^2},\Delta t.\)$

By the Mean Value Theorem, \(\Delta x_k = x'(\xi_k)\Delta t\) and \(\Delta y_k = y'(\eta_k)\Delta t\) for some \(\xi_k, \eta_k\) in the \(k\)-th subinterval. As \(n \to \infty\) (and since \(x', y'\) are continuous), \(L_n \to \int_a^b \sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2},dt\). \(\blacksquare\)

Example — Circumference of a circle. \(x = r\cos t\), \(y = r\sin t\), \(t \in [0, 2\pi]\): $\(L = \int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{r^2\sin^2 t + r^2\cos^2 t},dt = \int_0^{2\pi} r,dt = 2\pi r. \quad \checkmark\)$

Example — Length of one cycloid arch. \(x = t - \sin t\), \(y = 1 - \cos t\), \(t \in [0, 2\pi]\): $\(x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2 = (1-\cos t)^2 + \sin^2 t = 1 - 2\cos t + \cos^2 t + \sin^2 t = 2 - 2\cos t = 4\sin^2\frac{t}{2}.\)$ $\(L = \int_0^{2\pi} 2\left|\sin\frac{t}{2}\right|dt = 2\int_0^{2\pi}\sin\frac{t}{2},dt = 2\left[-2\cos\frac{t}{2}\right]_0^{2\pi} = 2(2+2) = 8.\)$

One cycloid arch has length \(8r\) (here \(r=1\)) — exactly 8 times the radius. A beautiful result.

docs.title: 3.4 Area Under a Parametric Curve
docs.text:
Theorem 3.4 (Area). If \(\gamma: [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^2\) traces a curve from left to right (i.e., \(x'(t) > 0\)), the area under the curve and above the \(x\)-axis is: $\(A = \int_\alpha^\beta y,dx = \int_a^b y(t),x'(t),dt.\)$

Proof. Standard substitution \(x = x(t)\), \(dx = x'(t),dt\). \(\blacksquare\)

Example — Area enclosed by a cycloid arch and the \(x\)-axis: $\(A = \int_0^{2\pi} (1 - \cos t)(1 - \cos t),dt = \int_0^{2\pi}(1 - \cos t)^2,dt.\)$ $\(= \int_0^{2\pi}\left(1 - 2\cos t + \cos^2 t\right)dt = 2\pi - 0 + \pi = 3\pi.\)$

The cycloid arch encloses exactly \(3\pi\) — three times the area of the rolling circle (\(\pi r^2 = \pi\)).

docs.title: 4. Curvature
docs.text:
Definition 4.1 (Curvature). The curvature of a smooth curve \(\gamma\) at \(t\) is: $\(\kappa(t) = \frac{|x'y'' - y'x''|}{(x'^2 + y'^2)^{3/2}},\)$ where primes denote \(d/dt\).

Derivation. Curvature measures the rate of change of the unit tangent vector \(\mathbf{T} = \dot{\gamma}/|\dot{\gamma}|\) with respect to arc length \(s\): \(\kappa = |d\mathbf{T}/ds|\). One computes \(d\mathbf{T}/ds = (d\mathbf{T}/dt)/(ds/dt)\) and takes the norm, arriving at the formula above.

Geometric meaning:

  • \(\kappa = 0\): straight line (no bending)
  • \(\kappa = 1/r\): circle of radius \(r\) (constant curvature)
  • Large \(\kappa\): sharp bend; small \(\kappa\): gentle curve

Radius of curvature: \(R = 1/\kappa\) — the radius of the osculating circle (the best-fit circle at that point).

Example — Curvature of \(x = t^2,\ y = t^3\): $\(x' = 2t,\ y' = 3t^2,\ x'' = 2,\ y'' = 6t.\)$ $\(\kappa = \frac{|2t\cdot 6t - 3t^2\cdot 2|}{(4t^2 + 9t^4)^{3/2}} = \frac{|12t^2 - 6t^2|}{t^3(4 + 9t^2)^{3/2}} = \frac{6t^2}{t^3(4+9t^2)^{3/2}} = \frac{6}{t(4+9t^2)^{3/2}}.\)$

As \(t \to 0^+\), \(\kappa \to \infty\) — infinite curvature at the cusp. \(\checkmark\)

docs.title: 5.1 The Cycloid
docs.text:
Rolling circle of radius \(r\): the path traced by a point on the rim.

\[x = r(t - \sin t), \qquad y = r(1 - \cos t), \quad t \in \mathbb{R}.\] 
  y
2r │        ╭────╮             ╭────╮
   │       ╱      ╲           ╱      ╲
   │      ╱        ╲         ╱        ╲
r  │     ╱          ╲       ╱          ╲
   │    ╱            ╲     ╱            ╲
   │───╱──────────────╲───╱──────────────╲──── x
  0  2πr            4πr               6πr
   cusps at x = 2kπr (touching points)

Tautochrone property: A bead slides to the bottom of a cycloid arch in the same time regardless of starting position (Huygens, 1659). The period is \(T = \pi\sqrt{r/g}\) — independent of amplitude.

Brachistochrone property: The cycloid is the curve of fastest descent under gravity between two points (Johann Bernoulli, 1696) — the first variational problem in history.

docs.title: 5.2 Lissajous Figures
docs.text:
\[x = A\sin(\omega_x t + \delta), \qquad y = B\sin(\omega_y t).\]

The shape depends on the frequency ratio \(\omega_x/\omega_y\):

ω_x/ω_y = 1, δ = π/2    ω_x/ω_y = 2, δ = 0     ω_x/ω_y = 3, δ = π/2

Used in electrical engineering (oscilloscope): the ratio \(\omega_x/\omega_y\) can be read from the number of loops.

docs.title: 5.3 Epicycloids and Hypocycloids
docs.text:
A circle of radius \(r\) rolling outside (epicycloid) or inside (hypocycloid) a circle of radius \(R\):

Epicycloid: $\(x = (R+r)\cos t - r\cos!\left(\frac{R+r}{r}t\right), \quad y = (R+r)\sin t - r\sin!\left(\frac{R+r}{r}t\right).\)$

Hypocycloid (rolling inside): $\(x = (R-r)\cos t + r\cos!\left(\frac{R-r}{r}t\right), \quad y = (R-r)\sin t - r\sin!\left(\frac{R-r}{r}t\right).\)$

Special case \(R = 4r\) (hypocycloid): the astroid \(x = R\cos^3 t\), \(y = R\sin^3 t\), whose Cartesian equation is \(x^{2/3} + y^{2/3} = R^{2/3}\).

  Astroid (R=4r):
      y
   R  │     *
      │   *   *
      │  *     *
    ──┼──*──────*──── x
      │  *     *
      │   *   *
  -R  │     *

  Four cusps at (±R, 0), (0, ±R)

docs.title: 5.4 The Archimedean Spiral (Polar → Parametric)
docs.text:
In polar coordinates: \(r = a\theta\). Converting: \(x = a\theta\cos\theta\), \(y = a\theta\sin\theta\), \(\theta \geq 0\).

  Spiral of Archimedes (a=1):
  y
  │      ╭──*
  │    *╱     ╲
  │   ╱   ╭──╮ *
  │  *   ╱ 0 ╲  │
  │──╲───╲────╱──*────── x
  │   *   ╰──╯  ╱
  │    ╲      ╱*
  │     *────*

Arc length: \(L = \int_0^\alpha \sqrt{a^2 + a^2\theta^2},a,d\theta = a^2\int_0^\alpha\sqrt{1+\theta^2},d\theta\).

docs.title: 6. Parametric Curves in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)
docs.text:
The definition extends immediately:

Definition 6.1. A parametric curve in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a map \(\gamma: I \to \mathbb{R}^n\), \(t \mapsto (x_1(t), \ldots, x_n(t))\).

All the calculus of §3 generalizes. The arc length formula becomes: $\(L = \int_a^b |\dot{\gamma}(t)|,dt = \int_a^b \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i'(t)^2},dt.\)$

This is the setting for curves in parameter space — the key bridge to machine learning.

docs.title: 7. Reparametrization and Arc-Length Parametrization
docs.text:
Definition 7.1 (Reparametrization). Given \(\gamma: I \to \mathbb{R}^2\) and a diffeomorphism \(\phi: J \to I\) (bijective, smooth, with smooth inverse), the curve \(\tilde{\gamma} = \gamma \circ \phi: J \to \mathbb{R}^2\) is a reparametrization of \(\gamma\).

Reparametrizations trace the same image at different speeds. The arc-length parametrization is the canonical one:

Definition 7.2. The arc-length parameter is \(s(t) = \int_{t_0}^t |\dot{\gamma}(\tau)|,d\tau\). The curve reparametrized by \(s\) satisfies \(|\gamma'(s)| = 1\) — unit speed.

Why it matters: In the arc-length parametrization, curvature takes the simplest form \(\kappa = |\gamma''(s)|\), and the Frenet–Serret formulas hold. It is the "natural" parametrization intrinsic to the curve.

docs.title: 8. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
8.1 Training Trajectories as Parametric Curves
docs.text:
During gradient descent, the model parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}(t) \in \mathbb{R}^n\) evolve in time. This is a parametric curve in parameter space: $\(t \mapsto \boldsymbol{\theta}(t) = (\theta_1(t), \theta_2(t), \ldots, \theta_n(t)).\)$

For a neural network with \(n = 10^9\) parameters, this is a curve in a billion-dimensional space. Every concept from §3 and §6 applies:

  • Velocity \(\dot{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(t) = -\eta,\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}(t))\): gradient descent is literally the derivative of this curve.
  • Arc length of the training trajectory: measures total parameter movement. Regularization (weight decay, gradient clipping) controls this arc length.
  • Curvature of the loss landscape along \(\boldsymbol{\theta}(t)\): related to the Hessian \(\nabla^2 \mathcal{L}\), governs convergence speed.

docs.title: 8.2 Loss Landscape Curves and the Saddle Point Problem
docs.text: The function \(\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) defines a surface in \(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\). A gradient descent trajectory \(t \mapsto (\boldsymbol{\theta}(t), \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}(t)))\) is a parametric curve on this surface. The curvature of this curve at a saddle point is related to the eigenvalues of the Hessian — exactly the Jacobian/linearization analysis from [[Predator–Prey System]] §3.

docs.title: 8.3 Bezier Curves — Parametric Curves in Computer Graphics and ML
docs.text:
Definition 8.1 (Bézier Curve). A Bézier curve of degree \(n\) with control points \(\mathbf{P}_0, \ldots, \mathbf{P}_n \in \mathbb{R}^2\) is: $\(\gamma(t) = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}(1-t)^{n-k}t^k,\mathbf{P}_k, \quad t \in [0,1].\)$

This is a parametric curve: \(t \mapsto (x(t), y(t))\) where \(x\) and \(y\) are Bernstein polynomials in \(t\).

In ML: Bézier curves model smooth interpolation between checkpoints in training (learning rate schedules as Bézier curves), trajectory planning in robotics, and font design (TrueType fonts use quadratic Bézier curves).

Cubic Bézier example: \(\mathbf{P}_0 = (0,0)\), \(\mathbf{P}_1 = (1,2)\), \(\mathbf{P}_2 = (2,2)\), \(\mathbf{P}_3 = (3,0)\): $\(\gamma(t) = (1-t)^3(0,0) + 3(1-t)^2 t(1,2) + 3(1-t)t^2(2,2) + t^3(3,0).\)$ $\(x(t) = 3t(1-t)^2\cdot 1 + 3(1-t)t^2\cdot 2 + t^3\cdot 3 = 3t, \quad y(t) = 6t(1-t)^2 + 6(1-t)t^2 = 6t(1-t).\)$

  y
2 │         * P₁        P₂ *
  │       ╭────────────────╮
  │      ╱                  ╲
  │     ╱                    ╲
0 │────*───────────────────────*──── x
     P₀=0                    P₃=3

  Curve peaks at t=0.5: (1.5, 1.5)

docs.title: 8.4 Neural ODEs — Parametric Curves as Hidden State Trajectories
docs.text:
A Neural ODE (Chen et al., NeurIPS 2018) defines the hidden state \(\mathbf{h}(t)\) as a parametric curve: $\(\frac{d\mathbf{h}}{dt} = f_\theta(\mathbf{h}(t), t), \qquad \mathbf{h}(t_1) = \mathbf{h}(t_0) + \int_{t_0}^{t_1} f_\theta(\mathbf{h}(t), t),dt.\)$

The arc length of this curve \(\int_{t_0}^{t_1}|f_\theta|,dt\) measures the total computational "work" done by the network. Minimizing it is a form of regularization by path length.

The curvature of \(\mathbf{h}(t)\) determines how much the trajectory bends — high curvature signals rapid feature transformation at that layer-depth.

docs.title: 8.5 Generative Models — Latent Space Curves
docs.text:
In a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) or diffusion model, the latent space \(\mathcal{Z} \subset \mathbb{R}^k\) is a continuous manifold. Interpolation between two latent codes \(\mathbf{z}_0\) and \(\mathbf{z}_1\) is a parametric curve:

\[\gamma: [0,1] \to \mathcal{Z}, \quad \gamma(t) = (1-t)\mathbf{z}_0 + t\mathbf{z}_1 \quad \text{(linear — bad)}.\]

Linear interpolation in latent space is naive. Geodesic interpolation finds the shortest curve \(\gamma\) on the data manifold (minimizing arc length with respect to the metric induced by the decoder). This is the arc-length minimization problem — a direct application of §3.3.

The decoded images \(\text{Decoder}(\gamma(t))\) then interpolate smoothly along the data manifold rather than cutting through empty space.

docs.title: 8.6 Reparametrization Trick in VAEs
docs.text:
The reparametrization trick is literally Definition 7.1:

\[\mathbf{z} = \boldsymbol{\mu} + \boldsymbol{\sigma} \odot \boldsymbol{\epsilon}, \quad \boldsymbol{\epsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I).\]

One reparametrizes the random variable \(\mathbf{z}\) (a point on a stochastic curve) so that the randomness flows through \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\) rather than \(\mathbf{z}\) itself. This makes the map \((\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\sigma}) \mapsto \mathbf{z}\) differentiable — enabling backpropagation through sampling.

This is a reparametrization in the exact sense of Definition 7.1: same point, different parameter. The Jacobian of the reparametrization is what backprop computes.

            dh/dt = f_θ(h,t)               Arc length = computational work

docs.title: 9. Key Theorems — Summary
docs.text: Theorem Statement Tangent slope (Thm 3.1) \(dy/dx = y'(t)/x'(t)\) when \(x'(t) \neq 0\) Second derivative (Thm 3.2) \(d^2y/dx^2 = \frac{d}{dt}(y'/x'),/,x'(t)\) Arc length (Thm 3.3) \(L = \int_a^b\sqrt{x'^2 + y'^2},dt\) Cycloid arch length \(L = 8r\) (eight times the radius) Cycloid arch area \(A = 3\pi r^2\) (three times the circle's area) Curvature formula $\kappa = Jordan Curve Theorem Simple closed curve divides \(\mathbb{R}^2\) into exactly 2 regions Arc-length reparametrization \(\|\gamma'(s)\| = 1\); curvature simplifies to \(\kappa = \|\gamma''(s)\|\)

docs.title: 10. Things to Prove Yourself
docs.text:
1. Prove the arc length formula (Theorem 3.3) rigorously using the MVT and the definition of the Riemann integral.
  2. Compute the curvature of the unit circle \(x = \cos t\), \(y = \sin t\) using the formula in Definition 4.1. Verify \(\kappa = 1\) everywhere.
  3. Show that the astroid \(x = R\cos^3 t\), \(y = R\sin^3 t\) satisfies the Cartesian equation \(x^{2/3} + y^{2/3} = R^{2/3}\). Find all four cusps and verify \(\dot{\gamma} = \mathbf{0}\) at each.
  4. Prove that the area enclosed by a closed parametric curve \(\gamma: [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^2\) (traversed counterclockwise) is: $\(A = \frac{1}{2}\int_a^b (x,y' - y,x'),dt.\)$ (Hint: Green's Theorem with \(P = -y/2\), \(Q = x/2\).)
  5. Derive the curvature formula \(\kappa = |x'y'' - y'x''|/(x'^2+y'^2)^{3/2}\) from \(\kappa = |d\mathbf{T}/ds|\) where \(\mathbf{T} = \dot{\gamma}/|\dot{\gamma}|\).
  6. Compute the arc length of one arch of the cycloid and verify \(L = 8r\). (The key identity is \((1-\cos t)^2 + \sin^2 t = 2(1-\cos t)\).)
  7. For the Bézier curve in §8.3, verify that \(\gamma(0) = \mathbf{P}_0\) and \(\gamma(1) = \mathbf{P}_n\) (endpoints are interpolated). Show that \(\gamma'(0)\) is parallel to \(\mathbf{P}_1 - \mathbf{P}_0\) (tangent at start points toward first control point).
