docs.title: §6 — The Shoelace Formula Connection
docs.text:
The discrete analog of the Green's Theorem area formula is the Shoelace Formula for a polygon with vertices \((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n)\):

\[ A = \frac{1}{2}\left|\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_i)\right| \]

This is literally the Riemann sum approximation to \(\dfrac{1}{2}\displaystyle\oint(x,dy - y,dx)\). The parametric area formula is the continuous limit of the Shoelace Formula as the polygon is refined to a smooth curve.

docs.title: §7 — Rigorous Summary
docs.text:
Theorem (Area Under Parametric Curve). Let \(x = f(t),, y = g(t)\), \(t \in [\alpha,\beta]\), with \(f,g\) continuous and \(f\) differentiable. If \(f'(t)\) does not change sign, then the area bounded by the curve, the \(x\)-axis, and the lines \(x = f(\alpha),, x = f(\beta)\) is: $\(A = \left|\int_\alpha^\beta g(t),f'(t),dt\right|\)$

Theorem (Enclosed Area via Green's Theorem). Let \(C\) be a positively oriented (CCW), simple, closed, piecewise-smooth parametric curve \(x=f(t),,y=g(t)\), \(t\in[\alpha,\beta]\), with \(f(\alpha)=f(\beta)\), \(g(\alpha)=g(\beta)\). Then the area enclosed is: $\(A = \frac{1}{2}\int_\alpha^\beta \bigl[f(t),g'(t) - g(t),f'(t)\bigr],dt\)$

docs.title: §8 — Connection to AI, Machine Learning & Deep Learning
8.1 The Shoelace Formula in Polygon-Based Neural Networks
docs.text:
In PolyWorld and PolygonRNN (polygon-prediction networks for image segmentation), the model predicts a sequence of vertices \((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n)\) tracing the boundary of an object. The area of the predicted polygon is computed via the Shoelace Formula — the discrete parametric area formula — and used as part of the loss function to enforce area constraints.

The differentiability of the Shoelace formula w.r.t. vertex coordinates is what makes this end-to-end trainable via backpropagation: $$ \frac{\partial A}{\partial x_i} = \frac{1}{2}(y_{i+1} - y_{i-1}), \quad \frac{\partial A}{\partial y_i} = \frac{1}{2}(x_{i-1} - x_{i+1}) $$

docs.title: 8.2 ROC Curve Area (AUC) as Parametric Area
docs.text:
The ROC (Receiver Operating Characteristic) curve is a parametric curve: $$ \text{TPR} = g(\tau),\quad \text{FPR} = f(\tau),\quad \tau \in [0, 1] $$

where \(\tau\) is the classification threshold. The AUC (Area Under the Curve) is:

\[ \text{AUC} = \int_0^1 \text{TPR}, d(\text{FPR}) = \int_0^1 g(\tau), f'(\tau), d\tau \]

This is exactly the parametric area formula \(\displaystyle\int g(t),f'(t),dt\). Every time you compute AUC to evaluate a classifier, you are computing a parametric area integral.

docs.title: 8.3 Precision-Recall Area (AP)
docs.text: Similarly, Average Precision (AP) — the area under the Precision-Recall curve — is a parametric area integral where the parameter is the confidence threshold. It is the standard evaluation metric for object detection (COCO, Pascal VOC benchmarks).

docs.title: 8.4 Normalizing Flows and Change of Variables
docs.text:
Normalizing flows transform a simple density \(p_z(z)\) into a complex density \(p_x(x)\) via a differentiable bijection \(x = f(z)\). The fundamental formula is:

\[ p_x(x) = p_z(f^{-1}(x))\left|\det\frac{\partial f^{-1}}{\partial x}\right| \]

The Jacobian determinant \(|\det \partial f^{-1}/\partial x|\) is the multi-dimensional generalization of \(|f'(t)|\) in the change-of-variables formula for parametric area. In 2D, the area element transforms as:

\[ dA_x = |f'(t)|, dA_t \]

which is precisely what we use when converting from \(dx\) to \(f'(t),dt\). The Jacobian is the generalization of \(f'(t)\) to higher dimensions.

docs.title: 8.5 Contour Integration in Signal Processing
docs.text: In complex neural networks and signal processing layers, integrals over parametric contours in the complex plane arise naturally. The area enclosed by such contours, computed via Green's Theorem, determines winding numbers — which govern how many times a learned representation wraps around a singularity, with implications for phase-based neural representations.

docs.title: 8.6 Attention as Area Under a Curve
docs.text:
In soft attention mechanisms, the attention weight \(\alpha_t\) integrates over a continuous time axis. In continuous attention models (e.g., Luong, monotonic attention), the attended context is:

\[ c = \int_0^T \alpha(t), h(t), dt \]

where \(\alpha(t)\) defines a probability distribution over a parametric trajectory \(t \mapsto h(t)\). This is a parametric integral — the weights \(\alpha(t)\) play the role of \(f'(t)\) (the measure), and \(h(t)\) plays the role of \(g(t)\) (the height).

docs.title: §9 — Quick Reference Card
docs.text: Situation Formula Area under parametric curve \(A = \displaystyle\int_\alpha^\beta g(t),f'(t),dt\) Geometric area (no cancellation) \(A = \displaystyle\int_\alpha^\beta \|g(t)\|,\|f'(t)\|,dt\) Enclosed area (CCW closed curve) \(A = \dfrac{1}{2}\displaystyle\int_\alpha^\beta [f(t)g'(t) - g(t)f'(t)],dt\) Polar area (special case) \(A = \dfrac{1}{2}\displaystyle\int_\alpha^\beta r(\theta)^2,d\theta\) Cycloid arch \(3\pi r^2\) Ellipse \(\pi ab\) Astroid \(\dfrac{3}{8}\pi a^2\)

docs.title: §10 — Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Sign of \(f'(t)\): Always determine whether \(x\) is increasing or decreasing. A curve traversed right-to-left gives a negative integral for a positive region.

  2. Closed curve orientation: CCW → positive area. CW → formula gives \(-A\). Check by parameterization: does \(x\) increase when \(y > 0\) (CCW) or decrease (CW)?

  3. Self-intersecting curves: The formula counts areas with multiplicity. For a figure-eight, the two lobes may cancel. Split at self-intersection points.

  4. \(d^2y/dx^2 \neq g''/f''\) (from the tangents note): analogously, area is NOT \(\int g(t),f(t),dt\) — it is \(\int g(t),f'(t),dt\). The derivative \(f'(t)\) comes from the change of variable \(dx = f'(t),dt\).

  5. Confusing arc length with area: Area uses \(g(t),f'(t)\); arc length uses \(\sqrt{f'(t)^2 + g'(t)^2}\). They come from entirely different geometric ideas.

docs.title: Arc Length
docs.text: "Distance is not a gift the curve gives you — it must be earned, infinitesimal by infinitesimal."

docs.title: §0 — Motivation
docs.text:
In Cartesian calculus, arc length of \(y = F(x)\) from \(x=a\) to \(x=b\) is:

\[ L = \int_a^b \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2}, dx \]

But this formula secretly assumes \(x\) increases monotonically along the curve. The moment the curve doubles back, spirals, or loops — as virtually every interesting curve in science and engineering does — this formula breaks down entirely.

The parametric formulation fixes this. Instead of describing the curve as a graph, we describe it as a trajectory: a particle moving through the plane, its position \((x(t), y(t))\) varying with time \(t\). Arc length becomes the total distance traveled — and that is a concept that makes sense regardless of how the curve bends, reverses, or loops.

docs.title: 1.1 Polygonal Approximation
docs.text:
Partition \([\alpha, \beta]\) into \(n\) subintervals by \(\alpha = t_0 < t_1 < \cdots < t_n = \beta\). The curve is approximated by the inscribed polygon with vertices at \((f(t_i), g(t_i))\).

The length of the \(i\)-th chord is:

\[ \ell_i = \sqrt{(f(t_i) - f(t_{i-1}))^2 + (g(t_i) - g(t_{i-1}))^2} \]

By the Mean Value Theorem, applied to \(f\) and \(g\) separately on \([t_{i-1}, t_i]\): there exist \(t_i^*, t_i^{**} \in (t_{i-1}, t_i)\) such that

\[ f(t_i) - f(t_{i-1}) = f'(t_i^*),\Delta t_i, \qquad g(t_i) - g(t_{i-1}) = g'(t_i^{**}),\Delta t_i \]

So:

\[ \ell_i = \sqrt{f'(t_i^*)^2 + g'(t_i^{**})^2},\Delta t_i \]

Summing:

\[ L \approx \sum_{i=1}^n \sqrt{f'(t_i^*)^2 + g'(t_i^{**})^2},\Delta t_i \]

Subtlety. \(t_i^*\) and \(t_i^{**}\) are generally different sample points — so this is not quite a Riemann sum for \(\sqrt{f'^2 + g'^2}\). The rigorous argument uses the fact that if \(f'\) and \(g'\) are continuous, then as \(|\Delta| \to 0\), both sample points converge to the same limiting behavior, and the sum converges to the integral below. This is the content of the arc length theorem in real analysis.

Taking \(n \to \infty\) (and \(|\Delta| \to 0\)):

\[ \boxed{L = \int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}, dt = \int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{f'(t)^2 + g'(t)^2}, dt} \]

docs.title: 1.2 The Infinitesimal Arc Element
docs.text:
Define the arc length element \(ds\):

\[ ds = \sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}, dt = |\mathbf{r}'(t)|, dt \]

This is the speed of the particle times the time increment: \(ds = |\mathbf{v}(t)|,dt\). Arc length is just the integral of speed over time — total distance traveled.

\[ L = \int_\alpha^\beta |\mathbf{r}'(t)|, dt = \int_\alpha^\beta |\mathbf{v}(t)|, dt \]

This is the fundamental formula of kinematics, reinterpreted as geometry.

docs.title: §2 — The Speed Vector Perspective
docs.text:
Let \(\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle f(t), g(t) \rangle\). Then:

  • Velocity vector: \(\mathbf{v}(t) = \mathbf{r}'(t) = \langle f'(t), g'(t) \rangle\)
  • Speed (scalar): \(|\mathbf{v}(t)| = \sqrt{f'(t)^2 + g'(t)^2}\)
  • Arc length: \(L = \int_\alpha^\beta |\mathbf{v}(t)|, dt\)

The speed \(|\mathbf{v}(t)|\) is independent of how the curve is parametrized — it depends on both the curve's shape and the rate of traversal. This is why two different parametrizations of the same geometric curve can give the same \(L\) but different integrands.

docs.title: 2.1 Natural (Arc Length) Parametrization
docs.text:
Define the arc length function from a base point \(t = \alpha\):

\[ s(t) = \int_\alpha^t \sqrt{f'(u)^2 + g'(u)^2}, du \]

Then \(\dfrac{ds}{dt} = \sqrt{f'(t)^2 + g'(t)^2} = |\mathbf{r}'(t)|\).

If we reparametrize the curve by \(s\) (arc length), we get \(\mathbf{r}(s)\) with the remarkable property:

\[ \left|\frac{d\mathbf{r}}{ds}\right| = 1 \quad \text{for all } s \]

The unit tangent vector is then simply \(\hat{\mathbf{T}} = \dfrac{d\mathbf{r}}{ds}\). This is the natural parametrization — the curve traversed at unit speed — and it is the foundation of differential geometry (curvature, Frenet–Serret frames, etc.).

Remark. In practice, \(s(t)\) is rarely expressible in closed form, so reparametrizing explicitly is often impossible. But the existence of arc length parametrization is conceptually essential.

docs.title: §3 — Relation to the Cartesian Formula
docs.text:
Suppose \(y = F(x)\), i.e., \(x = t\), \(y = F(t)\). Then \(f'(t) = 1\), \(g'(t) = F'(t)\), and:

\[ L = \int_a^b \sqrt{1 + F'(t)^2}, dt = \int_a^b \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2}, dx \]

The Cartesian formula is a special case of the parametric formula — with the trivial parametrization \(x = t\).

docs.title: Example 1 — Circumference of a Circle
docs.text:
\[ x = r\cos t, \quad y = r\sin t, \quad t \in [0, 2\pi] \] \[ f'(t) = -r\sin t, \quad g'(t) = r\cos t \] \[ L = \int_0^{2\pi} \sqrt{r^2\sin^2 t + r^2\cos^2 t}, dt = \int_0^{2\pi} r, dt = 2\pi r \checkmark \]

A sanity check: the parametric formula recovers the most ancient result in geometry.

docs.title: Example 2 — Arc Length of One Arch of the Cycloid
docs.text:
\[ x = r(t - \sin t),\quad y = r(1-\cos t),\quad t\in[0,2\pi] \] \[ f'(t) = r(1-\cos t),\quad g'(t) = r\sin t \] \[ f'(t)^2 + g'(t)^2 = r^2\bigl[(1-\cos t)^2 + \sin^2 t\bigr] = r^2\bigl[1 - 2\cos t + \cos^2 t + \sin^2 t\bigr] = r^2[2 - 2\cos t] \]

Using the half-angle identity \(1 - \cos t = 2\sin^2(t/2)\):

\[ = 2r^2(1 - \cos t) = 4r^2\sin^2!\left(\frac{t}{2}\right) \]

Therefore \(\sqrt{f'^2 + g'^2} = 2r\left|\sin(t/2)\right| = 2r\sin(t/2)\) (since \(\sin(t/2) \geq 0\) for \(t \in [0,2\pi]\)).

\[ L = \int_0^{2\pi} 2r\sin!\left(\frac{t}{2}\right) dt = 2r\left[-2\cos!\left(\frac{t}{2}\right)\right]_0^{2\pi} = 2r\bigl[-2\cos\pi + 2\cos 0\bigr] = 2r(2 + 2) = 8r \] \[ \boxed{L = 8r} \]

The arc length of one cycloid arch is exactly 8 radii of the rolling circle — a beautiful, clean answer from what looked like a messy integral.

docs.title: Example 3 — The Astroid
docs.text:
\[ x = a\cos^3 t,\quad y = a\sin^3 t,\quad t\in[0,2\pi] \] \[ f'(t) = -3a\cos^2 t\sin t,\quad g'(t) = 3a\sin^2 t\cos t \] \[ f'^2 + g'^2 = 9a^2\cos^4 t\sin^2 t + 9a^2\sin^4 t\cos^2 t = 9a^2\sin^2 t\cos^2 t(\cos^2 t + \sin^2 t) = 9a^2\sin^2 t\cos^2 t \] \[ \sqrt{f'^2 + g'^2} = 3a|\sin t\cos t| = \frac{3a}{2}|\sin 2t| \]

By symmetry across the four quadrants:

\[ L = 4\int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{3a}{2}\sin 2t, dt = 6a\left[-\frac{\cos 2t}{2}\right]_0^{\pi/2} = 6a\left[\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\right] = 6a \] \[ \boxed{L = 6a} \]

The astroid's perimeter is \(6a\) — exactly \(\dfrac{6}{\pi}\) times the circumference of its circumscribed circle. Remarkably clean.

docs.title: Example 4 — Logarithmic Spiral
docs.text:
\[ x = e^t\cos t,\quad y = e^t\sin t,\quad t\in[0,T] \] \[ f'(t) = e^t(\cos t - \sin t),\quad g'(t) = e^t(\sin t + \cos t) \] \[ f'^2 + g'^2 = e^{2t}[(\cos t-\sin t)^2 + (\sin t+\cos t)^2] = e^{2t}[2\cos^2 t + 2\sin^2 t] = 2e^{2t} \] \[ L = \int_0^T \sqrt{2},e^t, dt = \sqrt{2}(e^T - 1) \]

The logarithmic spiral has finite arc length to any finite \(T\), and it grows exponentially with \(T\).

docs.title: §6 — Surface Area of Revolution (Extension)
docs.text:
When the parametric curve is revolved around the \(x\)-axis, the surface area is:

\[ S = \int_\alpha^\beta 2\pi, |g(t)|, \sqrt{f'(t)^2 + g'(t)^2}, dt = \int_\alpha^\beta 2\pi, |y|, ds \]

Around the \(y\)-axis:

\[ S = \int_\alpha^\beta 2\pi, |f(t)|, \sqrt{f'(t)^2 + g'(t)^2}, dt = \int_\alpha^\beta 2\pi, |x|, ds \]

The integrand \(2\pi |y|, ds\) has a clear geometric meaning: each infinitesimal arc element \(ds\) sweeps out a thin band of circumference \(2\pi|y|\) — a "ring" of area \(2\pi|y|,ds\).

Example. Sphere from semicircle \(x = r\cos t,, y = r\sin t,, t\in[0,\pi]\), revolved around \(x\)-axis:

\[ S = \int_0^\pi 2\pi r\sin t \cdot r, dt = 2\pi r^2 \int_0^\pi \sin t, dt = 2\pi r^2 \cdot 2 = 4\pi r^2 \checkmark \]

docs.title: §7 — Why Most Arc Length Integrals Are Non-Elementary
docs.text:
The integrand \(\sqrt{f'(t)^2 + g'(t)^2}\) involves a square root of a sum of squares. For most natural choices of \(f\) and \(g\), this does not integrate in closed form. Specifically:

  • Ellipse \(x = a\cos t,, y = b\sin t\): the integrand becomes \(\sqrt{a^2\sin^2 t + b^2\cos^2 t}\), which integrates to an elliptic integral — a transcendental function not expressible in elementary terms. This is why the perimeter of an ellipse has no simple formula.
  • Parabola, sine curve, most polynomials: similar non-elementary integrands.

The fact that the circle (\(a = b = r\)), the cycloid, and the astroid do yield clean answers is remarkable — and is why these curves appeared repeatedly in 17th–19th century mathematics.

This is not a failure of technique. Liouville's theorem in differential algebra proves that such integrals are genuinely non-elementary for most curves.

docs.title: §8 — Rigorous Summary
docs.text:
Theorem (Parametric Arc Length). Let \(\mathbf{r}(t) = (f(t), g(t))\) where \(f'\) and \(g'\) are continuous on \([\alpha, \beta]\). Then the arc length of the curve from \(t = \alpha\) to \(t = \beta\) is: $\(L = \int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{f'(t)^2 + g'(t)^2}, dt\)$

Theorem (Parametrization Independence). If \(\mathbf{r}(t)\) and \(\mathbf{R}(u)\) are two smooth parametrizations of the same oriented curve, related by a smooth bijection \(t = \phi(u)\) with \(\phi'(u) > 0\), then both give the same arc length \(L\).

Proof sketch. Substituting \(t = \phi(u)\), \(dt = \phi'(u),du\), and \(f'(t) = \frac{df}{du}\cdot\frac{1}{\phi'(u)}\) — the \(\phi'(u)\) factors cancel, leaving the same integrand in \(u\). \(\square\)

Corollary. Arc length is an intrinsic geometric property of the curve, independent of parametrization.

docs.title: §9 — Connection to AI, Machine Learning & Deep Learning
9.1 Gradient Descent Trajectory Length
docs.text:
Training dynamics in neural networks define a parametric curve \(\theta(t)\) in weight space \(\mathbb{R}^n\). The total path length of the optimization trajectory is:

\[ L = \int_0^T |\theta'(t)|, dt = \int_0^T |\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta(t))|\cdot\eta, dt \]

(in continuous gradient flow). This is the arc length of the loss descent curve. Research has shown that flatter loss landscapes (small \(|\nabla \mathcal{L}|\), i.e., low speed along the trajectory) correlate with better generalization — and the total trajectory length is a measure of how much the optimizer "traveled" to reach a solution.

docs.title: 9.2 Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) and Path Length
docs.text:
In continual learning, EWC penalizes large moves in weight space between tasks. The penalty is related to the squared \(\ell_2\) distance traveled:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{EWC}} = \mathcal{L}_B(\theta) + \frac{\lambda}{2}\sum_i F_i(\theta_i - \theta_{A,i}^*)^2 \]

where \(F_i\) approximates the local metric (Fisher information). This is a discretization of arc length in a Riemannian metric on weight space — the Fisher metric. The arc length integral \(\int |\mathbf{r}'(t)|,dt\) generalizes to \(\int \sqrt{\mathbf{r}'(t)^T \mathbf{F}(\theta(t)), \mathbf{r}'(t)},dt\) in the Fisher geometry.

docs.title: 9.3 Natural Parametrization and Positional Encodings
docs.text:
In Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) — used in LLaMA, Mistral, and most modern LLMs — the position encoding rotates token embeddings by an angle proportional to position:

\[ \mathbf{q}_m = R_{\Theta,m},\mathbf{q}_m \]

where \(R_{\Theta,m}\) is a block-diagonal rotation matrix. The positions \(m\) are the arc length parameter of a curve on the unit circle in each frequency subspace. The choice of unit-speed parametrization (equal angular increments per position) is precisely the natural (arc length) parametrization of the circular trajectory — ensuring uniform spacing in the embedding space.

docs.title: 9.4 Curve Length as a Regularizer in Shape Models
docs.text:
In active contour models (Snakes, used in medical image segmentation), the energy functional to minimize includes an arc length regularization term:

\[ E[\mathbf{r}] = \int_0^1 \left[\alpha|\mathbf{r}'(s)|^2 + \beta|\mathbf{r}''(s)|^2\right] ds + E_{\text{image}}[\mathbf{r}] \]

The first term \(\alpha\int|\mathbf{r}'|^2,ds\) penalizes long contours (arc length proxy). The second penalizes high curvature (bending). This is a calculus of variations problem over parametric curves — and modern deep learning versions (DeepSnake, E2EC) learn to minimize similar energies via neural networks.

docs.title: 9.5 Riemannian Geometry and Geodesics in Latent Space
docs.text:
In VAEs and generative models, the latent space carries a non-Euclidean geometry induced by the decoder. The geodesic (shortest path) between two latent points \(z_0\) and \(z_1\) is the curve \(\gamma(t)\) minimizing:

\[ L[\gamma] = \int_0^1 \sqrt{\gamma'(t)^T \mathbf{G}(\gamma(t)),\gamma'(t)}, dt \]

where \(\mathbf{G}(z)\) is the pullback metric (Riemannian metric induced by the decoder Jacobian). This is the parametric arc length formula in a curved space — the direct generalization of \(\int\sqrt{f'^2+g'^2},dt\) to a Riemannian manifold. Interpolating in latent space along geodesics (instead of straight lines) produces semantically smoother interpolations between generated images.

docs.title: 9.6 Sequence Length and Attention Complexity
docs.text: In transformers, the sequence length \(n\) is treated as a discrete arc length — the number of tokens is the number of steps along the "curve" of a document. The quadratic \(O(n^2)\) complexity of self-attention comes from computing all pairwise interactions along this sequence. Efficient transformers (Longformer, Big Bird) approximate this by attending only to nearby positions — mimicking the local nature of the arc length element \(ds\), which only sees infinitesimal neighborhoods.

docs.title: §10 — Quick Reference Card
docs.text: Quantity Formula Arc length (parametric) \(L = \displaystyle\int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{f'(t)^2 + g'(t)^2}, dt\) Arc length element $ds = \sqrt{f'(t)^2 + g'(t)^2}, dt = Arc length function \(s(t) = \displaystyle\int_\alpha^t \sqrt{f'(u)^2 + g'(u)^2},du\) Cartesian case (\(x=t\)) \(L = \displaystyle\int_a^b \sqrt{1 + F'(x)^2},dx\) Surface of revolution (\(x\)-axis) $S = \displaystyle\int_\alpha^\beta 2\pi Circle \(2\pi r\) Cycloid arch \(8r\) Astroid \(6a\)

docs.title: §11 — Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Forgetting the square root is of a sum, not a sum of square roots. \(\sqrt{f'^2 + g'^2} \neq |f'| + |g'|\).

  2. Assuming the formula gives displacement. Arc length is total distance traveled, not \(|\mathbf{r}(\beta) - \mathbf{r}(\alpha)|\). A curve that loops back still accumulates length on the return trip.

  3. Missing absolute values in \(|\sin(t/2)|\). In the cycloid derivation, \(\sin(t/2) \geq 0\) on \([0, 2\pi]\), so it's fine — but on extended intervals, check the sign.

  4. Confusing arc length with area. Area: \(\int g(t),f'(t),dt\). Arc length: \(\int\sqrt{f'^2 + g'^2},dt\). The geometric content is completely different.

  5. Parametrization independence. Two different parametrizations of the same curve give the same \(L\). The integrand changes, but the integral does not.

docs.title: Surface Area
docs.text: "Arc length measures how far you travel. Surface area measures the skin of the world you sweep out as you travel."

docs.title: §0 — Motivation & The Core Idea
docs.text:
When a parametric curve is revolved about an axis, it sweeps out a surface of revolution. Computing the area of that surface is the central problem of this note.

The key geometric insight: as a tiny arc element \(ds\) of the curve sweeps around an axis, it traces out a thin band (a frustum of a cone). The area of that band is:

\[ dS = 2\pi \cdot (\text{radius}) \cdot ds \]

where \(ds\) is the arc length element and "radius" is the perpendicular distance from the curve to the axis of revolution.

Everything else is careful bookkeeping of what \(ds\) looks like in parametric form.

docs.title: §1 — The Arc Length Element
docs.text:
Before surface area, we need \(ds\) for a parametric curve \(x = f(t),, y = g(t)\).

A small displacement along the curve: $$ ds = \sqrt{(dx)^2 + (dy)^2} = \sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}, dt = \sqrt{f'(t)^2 + g'(t)^2}, dt $$

This is the speed of the parametric point times \(dt\): $$ ds = |\mathbf{r}'(t)|, dt, \quad \text{where } \mathbf{r}'(t) = \langle f'(t), g'(t)\rangle $$

docs.title: §2 — Surface Area Formula: Revolution About the \(x\)-axis
2.1 Derivation
docs.text:
Revolve the curve about the \(x\)-axis. The radius of revolution at parameter \(t\) is the \(y\)-coordinate: \(\text{radius} = y = g(t)\) (assuming \(g(t) \geq 0\)).

Each arc element \(ds\) sweeps out a band of area: $$ dS = 2\pi, g(t), ds = 2\pi, g(t),\sqrt{f'(t)^2 + g'(t)^2}, dt $$

Integrating:

\[ \boxed{S = 2\pi\int_\alpha^\beta g(t),\sqrt{f'(t)^2 + g'(t)^2}; dt} \]

Condition: \(g(t) \geq 0\) on \([\alpha, \beta]\) (the curve must be on or above the \(x\)-axis, so the radius is non-negative).

docs.title: 2.2 Derivation via Frustum Approximation
docs.text:
More rigorously: partition \([\alpha, \beta]\) into \(n\) subintervals. On each subinterval, the curve is approximated by a line segment of length \(\Delta s_k\). Revolving it about the \(x\)-axis gives a frustum (truncated cone) with average radius \(\bar{y}_k\) and slant height \(\Delta s_k\):

\[ \Delta S_k = 2\pi, \bar{y}_k, \Delta s_k \]

Summing and taking \(n \to \infty\): $$ S = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^n 2\pi,\bar{y}k,\Delta s_k = 2\pi\int\alpha^\beta g(t),\sqrt{f'(t)^2 + g'(t)^2}; dt $$

This is a Riemann sum for the integral — the passage to the limit is justified by the continuity of \(g\) and \(\sqrt{f'^2 + g'^2}\).

docs.title: §3 — Surface Area Formula: Revolution About the \(y\)-axis
docs.text:
Revolve about the \(y\)-axis. Now the radius of revolution is the \(x\)-coordinate: \(\text{radius} = x = f(t)\) (assuming \(f(t) \geq 0\)).

\[ \boxed{S = 2\pi\int_\alpha^\beta f(t),\sqrt{f'(t)^2 + g'(t)^2}; dt} \]

Mnemonic. The formula is always \(2\pi \cdot (\text{distance to axis}) \cdot ds\). Identify your axis, identify your distance, write \(ds\) in parametric form.

docs.title: §4 — Special Case: Cartesian Curve \(y = F(x)\)
docs.text:
When \(x = t,, y = F(t)\), then \(f'(t) = 1,, g'(t) = F'(t)\). The surface area about the \(x\)-axis becomes:

\[ S = 2\pi\int_a^b F(x),\sqrt{1 + F'(x)^2}; dx \]

The parametric formula reduces to the standard Cartesian formula. Good. ✓

docs.title: Example 1 — Sphere from a Semicircle
docs.text:
Revolve the semicircle \(x = r\cos t,, y = r\sin t,, t \in [0, \pi]\) about the \(x\)-axis.

\[ f'(t) = -r\sin t,\quad g'(t) = r\cos t $$ $$ \sqrt{f'^2 + g'^2} = \sqrt{r^2\sin^2 t + r^2\cos^2 t} = r \] \[ S = 2\pi\int_0^\pi r\sin t \cdot r, dt = 2\pi r^2 \int_0^\pi \sin t, dt = 2\pi r^2 \cdot [-\cos t]_0^\pi = 2\pi r^2 \cdot 2 \] \[ \boxed{S = 4\pi r^2} \]

The surface area of a sphere. The parametric derivation is cleaner than any Cartesian approach — no awkward \(\sqrt{1 - x^2/r^2}\) denominators to wrestle with.

docs.title: Example 2 — Surface of Revolution of the Cycloid
docs.text:
Revolve one arch of the cycloid \(x = r(t - \sin t),, y = r(1 - \cos t),, t \in [0, 2\pi]\) about the \(x\)-axis.

\[ f'(t) = r(1 - \cos t),\quad g'(t) = r\sin t \] \[ f'^2 + g'^2 = r^2(1-\cos t)^2 + r^2\sin^2 t = r^2(1 - 2\cos t + \cos^2 t + \sin^2 t) = r^2(2 - 2\cos t) \]

Using the half-angle identity \(1 - \cos t = 2\sin^2(t/2)\):

\[ \sqrt{f'^2 + g'^2} = r\sqrt{2 \cdot 2\sin^2(t/2)} = 2r\sin(t/2) \quad (t \in [0,2\pi],\ \sin(t/2) \geq 0) \] \[ S = 2\pi\int_0^{2\pi} r(1-\cos t)\cdot 2r\sin(t/2), dt = 2\pi\int_0^{2\pi} r \cdot 2\sin^2!\frac{t}{2} \cdot 2r\sin\frac{t}{2}, dt \] \[ = 8\pi r^2\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^3!\frac{t}{2}, dt \]

Substitute \(u = t/2\), \(du = dt/2\):

\[ = 16\pi r^2\int_0^{\pi}\sin^3 u, du \]

Using \(\displaystyle\int_0^\pi \sin^3 u, du = \frac{4}{3}\):

\[ \boxed{S = 16\pi r^2 \cdot \frac{4}{3} = \frac{64\pi r^2}{3}} \]

docs.title: Example 3 — Astroid Revolved About the \(x\)-axis
docs.text:
$$ x = a\cos^3 t,\quad y = a\sin^3 t,\quad t \in [0, \pi/2] $$ (use one quarter and multiply by 2 for the upper half, which generates the full surface)

\[ f'(t) = -3a\cos^2 t\sin t,\quad g'(t) = 3a\sin^2 t\cos t \] \[ f'^2 + g'^2 = 9a^2\cos^4 t\sin^2 t + 9a^2\sin^4 t\cos^2 t = 9a^2\sin^2 t\cos^2 t(\cos^2 t + \sin^2 t) = 9a^2\sin^2 t\cos^2 t \] \[ \sqrt{f'^2 + g'^2} = 3a\sin t\cos t = \frac{3a}{2}\sin 2t \]

By symmetry (revolve the upper half \(t \in [0,\pi]\), use \(t\in[0,\pi/2]\) doubled):

\[ S = 2\pi \cdot 2\int_0^{\pi/2} a\sin^3 t \cdot 3a\sin t\cos t, dt = 12\pi a^2\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^4 t\cos t, dt \] \[ = 12\pi a^2 \cdot \left[\frac{\sin^5 t}{5}\right]_0^{\pi/2} = 12\pi a^2 \cdot \frac{1}{5} \] \[ \boxed{S = \frac{12\pi a^2}{5}} \]

docs.title: Example 4 — Cone from a Line Segment (Sanity Check)
docs.text:
Revolve the line segment \(x = t,, y = mt,, t\in[0,h]\) (slope \(m > 0\)) about the \(x\)-axis. This should give a cone.

\[ \sqrt{f'^2 + g'^2} = \sqrt{1 + m^2} \] \[ S = 2\pi\int_0^h mt \cdot \sqrt{1+m^2}, dt = 2\pi m\sqrt{1+m^2}\cdot\frac{h^2}{2} = \pi m h^2\sqrt{1+m^2} \]

The base radius is \(R = mh\) and slant height is \(\ell = h\sqrt{1+m^2}\), so:

\[ S = \pi R \ell \quad \checkmark \]

The parametric formula recovers the elementary cone lateral-area formula.

docs.title: §6 — Visualization
docs.text:
Revolution about x-axis: each point traces a circle of radius y

Curve in xy-plane:              Surface of revolution:

|*       *                           |    \     /
|________________________ x          |________________________ x

Each arc element ds                  Frustum: area = 2π·ȳ·Δs
↓                                    ↓
integrate → S = 2π∫y ds             exact area as n→∞

Sphere from semicircle (r=1):

Semicircle: x=cos(t), y=sin(t), t∈[0,π]

→ S = 2π∫₀^π sin(t)·1 dt = 4π ✓

Frustum approximation (the Riemann sum intuition):

        y_k+1 ___________

As partition refines → exact integral

docs.title: §7 — The Speed Factor and Why It's Not Just \(\int g(t),dt\)
docs.text:
A conceptual trap: why isn't surface area just \(2\pi\int g(t),dt\)?

Because \(t\) is not arc length. The parameter \(t\) might make the curve move fast in some regions and slow in others. The factor \(\sqrt{f'^2+g'^2}\) is the speed — it converts "parameter time" into "geometric length". Without it, we'd be weighting fast-moving portions of the curve the same as slow-moving portions, which gives the wrong answer.

Example of the trap. Reparametrize the sphere semicircle as \(x = r\cos(t^3),, y = r\sin(t^3),, t\in[0, \pi^{1/3}]\). Now \(f'(t) = -3rt^2\sin(t^3),, g'(t) = 3rt^2\cos(t^3)\), and \(\sqrt{f'^2+g'^2} = 3rt^2\). The integral:

\[ 2\pi\int_0^{\pi^{1/3}} r\sin(t^3)\cdot 3rt^2, dt \]

Substitute \(u = t^3\): recovers exactly \(2\pi r^2\int_0^\pi \sin u, du = 4\pi r^2\) ✓

Surface area is parametrization-independent — a property guaranteed by the \(ds\) factor.

This is the geometric content of the formula: \(ds\) is intrinsic to the curve, not to the parametrization.

docs.title: §8 — Surfaces in 3D: The Full Generalization
docs.text:
For completeness (and connection to multivariable calculus / deep learning), the surface area formula generalizes to a parametric surface \(\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \langle x(u,v), y(u,v), z(u,v) \rangle\):

\[ S = \iint_D \left|\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial u} \times \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial v}\right|, du, dv \]

The cross product \(\partial\mathbf{r}/\partial u \times \partial\mathbf{r}/\partial v\) is the normal vector to the surface, and its magnitude is the area element \(dS\). This is the MIT 18.02 generalization — the 2D surface area formula is the 1D special case when the surface is a surface of revolution.

The surface of revolution formula follows from this with \(u = t\), \(v = \theta\) (the revolution angle), and explicit computation of the cross product.

docs.title: §9 — Connection to AI, Machine Learning & Deep Learning
9.1 Mesh Surface Area in 3D Deep Learning
docs.text:
In 3D shape learning — PointNet, MeshCNN, Neural Implicit Surfaces — a learned 3D shape is often represented as a mesh (a collection of triangular faces). The surface area of the mesh is computed as:

\[ S = \sum_{\text{triangles}} \frac{1}{2}\left|\mathbf{e}_1 \times \mathbf{e}_2\right| \]

where \(\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2\) are two edge vectors of each triangle. This is the discrete version of \(|\partial\mathbf{r}/\partial u \times \partial\mathbf{r}/\partial v|, du, dv\) — the parametric surface area formula with a triangular parametrization.

This is differentiable with respect to vertex positions, enabling surface-area regularization losses in 3D generative models.

docs.title: 9.2 Neural Implicit Surfaces and the Eikonal Equation
docs.text:
NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) and NeuS represent surfaces implicitly as zero level sets of a learned function \(F: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}\). The surface area element at a point is:

\[ dS = \frac{|\nabla F|}{\left|\partial F/\partial n\right|} \]

Training includes a loss term enforcing \(|\nabla F| = 1\) (the Eikonal equation), which ensures the level set is a properly-normalized surface — directly analogous to ensuring \(|\mathbf{r}'(t)| = 1\) (arc-length parametrization) in 1D curves. The surface area formula requires the curve/surface to be metrically honest; the Eikonal constraint enforces this in neural implicit representations.

docs.title: 9.3 Isoperimetric Constraints in Generative Models
docs.text:
The isoperimetric inequality states: $$ 4\pi A \leq S^2 $$

for a surface of area \(S\) enclosing volume \(A\) (with equality for spheres). In 3D shape generation and GANs for 3D objects, regularization losses enforcing near-spherical geometry or bounding surface area are related to this inequality. Minimizing surface area subject to fixed volume is a classical variational problem — and its discrete, differentiable version appears in shape optimization layers.

docs.title: 9.4 Riemannian Geometry in Latent Spaces
docs.text:
Modern latent space geometry (Arvanitidis et al., 2018 — "Latent Space Oddity") treats the latent space of a VAE as a Riemannian manifold. The metric tensor is:

\[ G(z) = J(z)^\top J(z) + \sigma^2 I \]

where \(J(z)\) is the Jacobian of the decoder. The surface area of a region in latent space, measured under this metric, is:

\[ S = \int!\sqrt{\det G(z)}, dz \]

This is exactly \(\int|\partial\mathbf{r}/\partial u \times \partial\mathbf{r}/\partial v|,du,dv\) with \(\sqrt{\det G}\) playing the role of the cross-product magnitude. Geodesic interpolation in this Riemannian latent space is used to generate smoother, more semantically meaningful interpolations than straight-line Euclidean interpolation.

docs.title: 9.5 Speed Normalization and Batch Normalization
docs.text: The parametrization-independence of surface area (\(ds\) absorbs speed, not parameter values) has a deep parallel in normalization in neural networks. Batch normalization, layer normalization, and weight normalization all enforce a kind of "unit speed" on the network's internal representations — ensuring that the magnitude of activations or weights doesn't distort the geometry of the learned manifold. The surface area formula teaches: measure geometry intrinsically, not via arbitrary parametrizations.

docs.title: 9.6 Differentiable Rendering
docs.text:
In differentiable rendering (used in inverse graphics and 3D-aware GANs), the rendered image depends on the surface area and orientation of mesh faces. Gradients of the rendered loss with respect to vertex positions flow through the surface area formula:

\[ \frac{\partial S}{\partial \mathbf{v}_i} = \sum_{\text{triangles adjacent to } \mathbf{v}_i} \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{v}_i}\left(\frac{1}{2}|\mathbf{e}_1 \times \mathbf{e}_2|\right) \]

This is the discrete gradient of the parametric surface area integral — the fundamental quantity that allows 3D shape learning from 2D image supervision.

docs.title: §10 — Rigorous Summary
docs.text:
Theorem (Surface Area of Revolution). Let \(x = f(t),, y = g(t)\), \(t\in[\alpha,\beta]\), where \(f, g\) are continuously differentiable and \(g(t) \geq 0\). Assume the curve does not cross itself. Then the area of the surface generated by revolving the curve about the \(x\)-axis is: $\(S = 2\pi\int_\alpha^\beta g(t),\sqrt{f'(t)^2 + g'(t)^2}; dt\)$ This formula is independent of the choice of parametrization (reparametrization-invariant).

Corollary. For revolution about the \(y\)-axis (with \(f(t) \geq 0\)): $\(S = 2\pi\int_\alpha^\beta f(t),\sqrt{f'(t)^2 + g'(t)^2}; dt\)$

docs.title: §11 — Quick Reference Card
docs.text: Revolution Axis Formula Radius used \(x\)-axis \(2\pi\displaystyle\int_\alpha^\beta g(t)\sqrt{f'^2+g'^2},dt\) \(y = g(t)\) \(y\)-axis \(2\pi\displaystyle\int_\alpha^\beta f(t)\sqrt{f'^2+g'^2},dt\) \(x = f(t)\) Cartesian, \(x\)-axis \(2\pi\displaystyle\int_a^b y\sqrt{1+y'^2},dx\) \(y\) Curve Revolve about Surface Area Semicircle radius \(r\) \(x\)-axis \(4\pi r^2\) (sphere) Cycloid arch \(x\)-axis \(\frac{64\pi r^2}{3}\) Astroid (half) \(x\)-axis \(\frac{12\pi a^2}{5}\) Line segment (slope \(m\), length \(h\)) \(x\)-axis \(\pi R\ell\) (cone)

docs.title: §12 — Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Forgetting \(\sqrt{f'^2+g'^2}\): Surface area is \(2\pi\int y,ds\), not \(2\pi\int y,dt\). The speed factor is non-negotiable.

  2. Wrong axis, wrong radius: Revolving about the \(x\)-axis → radius is \(y\). About the \(y\)-axis → radius is \(x\). Confusing these is the most common error.

  3. Negative \(g(t)\): If the curve dips below the \(x\)-axis, the formula breaks (negative radius). Either restrict the interval or use \(|g(t)|\).

  4. Confusing surface area with volume: Surface area of revolution is \(2\pi\int y,ds\). Volume of revolution (disk/washer method) is \(\pi\int y^2, dx\). Different powers, different geometric meanings.

  5. Confusing surface area with arc length: Arc length is \(\int\sqrt{f'^2+g'^2},dt\) (no \(2\pi g(t)\) factor). Surface area wraps arc length around an axis.

docs.title: Bezier Curves
docs.text: "de Casteljau's algorithm is one of those rare things in mathematics: a construction so natural that the theorem proves itself as you draw it."

docs.title: §0 — Historical Prelude
docs.text:
Pierre Bézier (Renault, 1962) and Paul de Casteljau (Citroën, 1959) independently discovered these curves while designing automobile body panels — a problem where you need smooth, controllable curves that an engineer can adjust by pulling on "handles."

De Casteljau's algorithm came first but was classified by Citroën. Bézier published, got his name on the curves. The algorithm remains de Casteljau's.

The setting: we want a curve in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) (or \(\mathbb{R}^n\)) that:

  1. Passes through two endpoints (interpolates boundary data)
  2. Is "attracted to" intermediate control points (approximates, not interpolates)
  3. Is smooth (infinitely differentiable, in fact polynomial)
  4. Is easy to compute, subdivide, and reason about geometrically

docs.title: §1 — Linear Bézier: The Foundation
docs.text:
The simplest case: two control points \(\mathbf{P}_0, \mathbf{P}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^2\).

\[ \mathbf{B}(t) = (1-t),\mathbf{P}_0 + t,\mathbf{P}_1, \quad t \in [0,1] \]

This is just linear interpolation (lerp). As \(t\) goes from \(0\) to \(1\):

  • \(t=0\): \(\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{P}_0\)
  • \(t=1\): \(\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{P}_1\)
  • \(t=1/2\): \(\mathbf{B} = \frac{\mathbf{P}_0 + \mathbf{P}_1}{2}\) (midpoint)

The curve is a straight line segment. This is the atomic building block of everything that follows.

Notation: Write \(\text{lerp}(\mathbf{P}, \mathbf{Q}, t) = (1-t)\mathbf{P} + t\mathbf{Q}\).

docs.title: §2 — Quadratic Bézier: Three Control Points
docs.text: Three points \(\mathbf{P}_0, \mathbf{P}_1, \mathbf{P}_2\).

docs.title: 2.1 de Casteljau's Construction
docs.text:
At parameter \(t\):

Step 1 — Lerp between adjacent pairs: $$ \mathbf{Q}_0(t) = (1-t)\mathbf{P}_0 + t\mathbf{P}_1, \qquad \mathbf{Q}_1(t) = (1-t)\mathbf{P}_1 + t\mathbf{P}_2 $$

Step 2 — Lerp between the results: $$ \mathbf{B}(t) = (1-t)\mathbf{Q}_0(t) + t\mathbf{Q}_1(t) $$

docs.title: 2.2 Explicit Formula
docs.text:
Substitute Step 1 into Step 2: $$ \mathbf{B}(t) = (1-t)^2\mathbf{P}_0 + 2t(1-t)\mathbf{P}_1 + t^2\mathbf{P}_2 $$

Recognize: these are the binomial coefficients \(\binom{2}{0}, \binom{2}{1}, \binom{2}{2}\) weighted by \((1-t)^{2-k}t^k\).

de Casteljau at t = 0.5:

P0 -----Q0----- P1
         \
          B(t)       ← the curve point
         /
P1 -----Q1----- P2

docs.title: §3 — Cubic Bézier: Four Control Points
docs.text: The workhorse of computer graphics. Four points \(\mathbf{P}_0, \mathbf{P}_1, \mathbf{P}_2, \mathbf{P}_3\).

docs.title: 3.1 de Casteljau's Algorithm
docs.text:
Level 1 (3 points): $$ \mathbf{Q}i(t) = (1-t)\mathbf{P}_i + t\mathbf{P}, \quad i = 0,1,2 $$

Level 2 (2 points): $$ \mathbf{R}i(t) = (1-t)\mathbf{Q}_i(t) + t\mathbf{Q}(t), \quad i = 0,1 $$

Level 3 (1 point — the curve): $$ \mathbf{B}(t) = (1-t)\mathbf{R}_0(t) + t\mathbf{R}_1(t) $$

docs.title: 3.2 Explicit Formula
docs.text: \[ \boxed{\mathbf{B}(t) = (1-t)^3\mathbf{P}_0 + 3t(1-t)^2\mathbf{P}_1 + 3t^2(1-t)\mathbf{P}_2 + t^3\mathbf{P}_3} \]

docs.title: 3.3 Matrix Form
docs.text:
Write \(\mathbf{B}(t) = \mathbf{T},M_{\text{Bézier}},\mathbf{P}\):

\[ \mathbf{B}(t) = \begin{bmatrix}1 & t & t^2 & t^3\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \ -3 & 3 & 0 & 0 \ 3 & -6 & 3 & 0 \ -1 & 3 & -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{P}_0 \ \mathbf{P}_1 \ \mathbf{P}_2 \ \mathbf{P}_3\end{bmatrix} \]

This matrix form is used in GPU shader programs for fast evaluation.

docs.title: 4.1 Bernstein Polynomials
docs.text:
Define the Bernstein basis polynomials of degree \(n\):

\[ B_{k,n}(t) = \binom{n}{k}t^k(1-t)^{n-k}, \quad k = 0, 1, \ldots, n \]

Key properties:

  • \(B_{k,n}(t) \geq 0\) for \(t \in [0,1]\) → non-negativity
  • \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^n B_{k,n}(t) = 1\) for all \(t\) → partition of unity (follows from the Binomial Theorem: \([(1-t)+t]^n = 1\))
  • \(B_{k,n}(t)\) peaks near \(t = k/n\) → localization

docs.title: 4.2 The Bézier Curve
docs.text:
Given control points \(\mathbf{P}_0, \ldots, \mathbf{P}_n \in \mathbb{R}^d\):

\[ \boxed{\mathbf{B}(t) = \sum_{k=0}^n B_{k,n}(t),\mathbf{P}_k = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}(1-t)^{n-k}t^k,\mathbf{P}_k, \quad t \in [0,1]} \]

This is a weighted average of the control points — the weights \(B_{k,n}(t)\) sum to 1 (partition of unity) and are all non-negative. The curve is always inside the convex hull of the control points.

docs.title: 5.1 Endpoint Interpolation
docs.text:
Claim: \(\mathbf{B}(0) = \mathbf{P}_0\) and \(\mathbf{B}(1) = \mathbf{P}_n\).

Proof. At \(t=0\): \(B_{k,n}(0) = \binom{n}{k}0^k\cdot 1^{n-k} = 0\) for \(k \geq 1\), and \(B_{0,n}(0) = 1\). So \(\mathbf{B}(0) = \mathbf{P}_0\). Similarly at \(t=1\). \(\square\)

docs.title: 5.2 Convex Hull Property
docs.text:
Claim: \(\mathbf{B}(t)\) lies in the convex hull of \({\mathbf{P}_0, \ldots, \mathbf{P}_n}\) for all \(t \in [0,1]\).

Proof. The \(B_{k,n}(t)\) are non-negative and sum to 1, so \(\mathbf{B}(t)\) is a convex combination of the control points. \(\square\)

Consequence. This is the fundamental containment guarantee — the curve can never escape the convex hull of its control points. Essential for collision detection in graphics.

docs.title: 5.3 Tangent at Endpoints
docs.text:
Claim: \(\mathbf{B}'(0) = n(\mathbf{P}_1 - \mathbf{P}_0)\) and \(\mathbf{B}'(1) = n(\mathbf{P}_n - \mathbf{P}_{n-1})\).

Proof (for \(t=0\)). Differentiate \(B_{k,n}(t) = \binom{n}{k}t^k(1-t)^{n-k}\): $$ B_{k,n}'(t) = \binom{n}{k}\left[kt{k-1}(1-t) - (n-k)tk(1-t)\right] $$ At \(t=0\): only the \(k=1\) term survives (all \(k \geq 2\) terms have \(t^{k-1}\) with \(k-1\geq 1\), so vanish; the \(k=0\) term has \(-n(1-t)^{n-1}\) which at \(t=0\) gives \(-n\)): $$ B_{0,n}'(0) = -n,\quad B_{1,n}'(0) = n, \quad B_{k,n}'(0) = 0 \text{ for } k \geq 2 $$ Therefore: $$ \mathbf{B}'(0) = -n\mathbf{P}_0 + n\mathbf{P}_1 = n(\mathbf{P}_1 - \mathbf{P}_0). \quad \square $$

Geometric meaning: The tangent at \(\mathbf{P}_0\) points directly toward \(\mathbf{P}_1\). Moving \(\mathbf{P}_1\) steers the curve's initial direction.

docs.title: 5.4 Affine Invariance
docs.text:
Claim: Applying any affine map \(\phi(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}\) to the control points gives the transformed curve: \(\phi(\mathbf{B}(t)) = \text{Bézier}(\phi(\mathbf{P}_0), \ldots, \phi(\mathbf{P}_n))(t)\).

Proof. Affine maps commute with convex combinations (partition of unity): $$ \phi(\mathbf{B}(t)) = \phi!\left(\sum_k B_{k,n}(t)\mathbf{P}k\right) = A\sum_k B}(t)\mathbf{Pk + \mathbf{b} = \sum_k B}(t)(A\mathbf{Pk + \mathbf{b}) = \sum_k B_k). \quad \square $$}(t)\phi(\mathbf{P

Consequence. To rotate/translate/scale a Bézier curve, just transform the control points. You don't need to re-evaluate the curve. This is why Bézier curves dominate computer graphics.

docs.title: 5.5 Variation Diminishing Property
docs.text: A Bézier curve crosses any line no more times than its control polygon does. Intuitively: the curve is "smoother" than the jagged polygon.

docs.title: §6 — de Casteljau's Algorithm: The Full Picture
docs.text:
For degree \(n\) with control points \(\mathbf{P}_0^{(0)}, \ldots, \mathbf{P}_n^{(0)}\), define the triangular array:

\[ \mathbf{P}_i^{(r)}(t) = (1-t),\mathbf{P}_i^{(r-1)} + t,\mathbf{P}_{i+1}^{(r-1)}, \quad r = 1, \ldots, n,\quad i = 0, \ldots, n-r \]

The curve point at parameter \(t\) is: $$ \mathbf{B}(t) = \mathbf{P}_0^{(n)}(t) $$

For cubic (\(n=3\)), the full triangle:

Level 0 (given):   P0    P1    P2    P3
                     \   / \   / \   /
Level 1:            Q0    Q1    Q2
                      \   / \   /
Level 2:              R0    R1
                        \   /
Level 3 (curve pt):      B(t)

Each step is a lerp. The algorithm uses \(\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\) lerp operations total.

docs.title: 6.1 Subdivision Property ⭐
docs.text:
The most important algorithmic property. Evaluating \(\mathbf{B}(t_0)\) via de Casteljau also gives the control points of the two sub-curves:

  • Left sub-curve \([0, t_0]\): control points are the left edge of the triangle: \(\mathbf{P}_0^{(0)}, \mathbf{P}_0^{(1)}, \mathbf{P}_0^{(2)}, \ldots, \mathbf{P}_0^{(n)}\)
  • Right sub-curve \([t_0, 1]\): control points are the right edge: \(\mathbf{P}_0^{(n)}, \mathbf{P}_1^{(n-1)}, \ldots, \mathbf{P}_n^{(0)}\)

This is the basis of adaptive subdivision — the key algorithm in font rendering, path clipping, and intersection testing.

docs.title: 7.1 Derivative Formula
docs.text:
The derivative of a degree-\(n\) Bézier is a degree-\((n-1)\) Bézier:

\[ \mathbf{B}'(t) = n\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} B_{k,n-1}(t),(\mathbf{P}_{k+1} - \mathbf{P}_k) \]

Proof sketch. Differentiate \(B_{k,n}(t)\) and use the identity \(B_{k,n}'(t) = n[B_{k-1,n-1}(t) - B_{k,n-1}(t)]\).

Let \(\Delta\mathbf{P}_k = \mathbf{P}_{k+1} - \mathbf{P}_k\) (forward differences). Then:

\[ \mathbf{B}'(t) = n,\mathbf{B}_{\Delta}(t) \]

where \(\mathbf{B}_\Delta\) is the Bézier curve with control points \(\Delta\mathbf{P}_0, \ldots, \Delta\mathbf{P}_{n-1}\).

docs.title: 7.2 Curvature at Endpoints
docs.text:
At \(t = 0\), for a cubic:

\[ \kappa(0) = \frac{|\mathbf{B}'(0) \times \mathbf{B}''(0)|}{|\mathbf{B}'(0)|^3} \]

where \(\times\) denotes the 2D "cross product" (scalar: \(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v} = u_x v_y - u_y v_x\)), and:

\[ \mathbf{B}'(0) = 3(\mathbf{P}_1 - \mathbf{P}_0), \qquad \mathbf{B}''(0) = 6(\mathbf{P}_0 - 2\mathbf{P}_1 + \mathbf{P}_2) \]

docs.title: §8 — Joining Bézier Curves: Continuity Conditions
docs.text:
A single cubic Bézier has limited shape vocabulary. Complex shapes (fonts, paths) are built from piecewise Bézier splines — sequences of cubic segments joined end-to-end.

Let segment 1 end at \(\mathbf{P}_3\) with last handle \(\mathbf{P}_2\), and segment 2 start at \(\mathbf{Q}_0 = \mathbf{P}_3\) with first handle \(\mathbf{Q}_1\).

Continuity Class Condition Geometric Meaning \(C^0\) \(\mathbf{P}_3 = \mathbf{Q}_0\) Curves share an endpoint — no gap \(G^1\) \(\mathbf{Q}_1 - \mathbf{P}_3\) parallel to \(\mathbf{P}_3 - \mathbf{P}_2\) Same tangent direction — no kink \(C^1\) \(\mathbf{Q}_1 - \mathbf{P}_3 = \mathbf{P}_3 - \mathbf{P}_2\) Same tangent direction and speed \(C^2\) \(C^1\) + second derivative matches Matching curvature — the join is invisible

Design implication (Illustrator, Figma). When you drag a "smooth" handle in a vector editor, you're enforcing \(G^1\). When you hold a modifier key to enforce equal handle lengths, you're enforcing \(C^1\). The editor is managing these conditions for you.

G¹ join (smooth, different handle lengths):

    P2    P3=Q0    Q1
     o----●--------o
          ↑
      tangent direction continuous,
      speeds may differ (‖P3-P2‖ ≠ ‖Q1-Q0‖)

C¹ join (equal handle lengths):

    P2    P3=Q0    Q1
     o----●----o
          ↑
      P3 - P2 = Q1 - P3 (exact reflection)

docs.title: §9 — Rational Bézier Curves and Conics
docs.text:
Standard Bézier curves cannot represent a circle arc exactly — they are polynomials, and circle arcs are algebraic of a different kind. The fix: rational Bézier curves.

Attach a weight \(w_k > 0\) to each control point:

\[ \mathbf{B}(t) = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^n w_k B_{k,n}(t),\mathbf{P}_k}{\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^n w_k B_{k,n}(t)} \]

This is a projective generalization. For \(n=2\) with weights \((1, w, 1)\):

  • \(w = 1\): parabola arc
  • \(w < 1\): ellipse arc
  • \(w = \cos(\theta/2)\) for arc subtending angle \(\theta\): exact circle arc
  • \(w > 1\): hyperbola arc

NURBS (Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines) — the industry standard in CAD (SolidWorks, CATIA, Rhino) — are piecewise rational Bézier curves with a knot vector controlling the join structure.

docs.title: §11 — Bézier Curves in AI, Machine Learning & Deep Learning
11.1 Font Rendering and OCR
docs.text:
TrueType fonts store every glyph as piecewise quadratic Bézier curves; PostScript/PDF uses cubic Bézier curves. The entire Latin alphabet, CJK character sets, Arabic script — everything is Bézier control points.

OCR neural networks (Tesseract 4+, TrOCR) must decode these curves. Training data for OCR is generated by rendering Bézier-encoded fonts. Understanding what the network "sees" requires understanding how Bézier curves are rasterized.

docs.title: 11.2 Trajectory Planning in Reinforcement Learning
docs.text:
In robot learning and autonomous driving, smooth reference trajectories are represented as Bézier curves. A policy network predicts control points \(\mathbf{P}_0, \ldots, \mathbf{P}_n\) rather than a sequence of waypoints, because:

  • The convex hull property guarantees the trajectory stays within a safe region
  • The tangent conditions enforce smooth acceleration/deceleration
  • Subdivision allows adaptive refinement at high-curvature regions
  • The entire trajectory is represented by \(4(n+1)\) numbers (compact)

Example. In Waymo's motion forecasting, predicted agent trajectories are parametrized as cubic Bézier curves. The loss function penalizes deviation between predicted and ground-truth control points.

docs.title: 11.3 Bézier Curves as Learnable Parameters
docs.text:
BézierFormer and related models directly output Bézier control points from attention-based decoders:

\[ \hat{\mathbf{P}}_0, \ldots, \hat{\mathbf{P}}_n = \text{Decoder}(\text{image features}) \]

The predicted curve is \(\hat{\mathbf{B}}(t) = \sum_k B_{k,n}(t)\hat{\mathbf{P}}_k\). The loss is:

\[ \mathcal{L} = \int_0^1 |\hat{\mathbf{B}}(t) - \mathbf{B}^_(t)|^2, dt \approx \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N |\hat{\mathbf{B}}(t_j) - \mathbf{B}^_(t_j)|^2 \]

This integral loss is differentiable with respect to the control points \(\hat{\mathbf{P}}_k\) because \(B_{k,n}(t)\) is a smooth function of \(t\), and the chain rule flows through:

\[ \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \hat{\mathbf{P}}_k} = \frac{2}{N}\sum_j B_{k,n}(t_j),(\hat{\mathbf{B}}(t_j) - \mathbf{B}^*(t_j)) \]

docs.title: 11.4 Text Detection: Scene Text in the Wild
docs.text: ABCNet and TextBPN use Bézier curves to detect arbitrarily curved text in natural images (menus, storefronts, logos). The network predicts control points of a Bézier curve that traces the text baseline, enabling recognition of text that cannot be enclosed in a simple bounding box.

docs.title: 11.5 Neural Architecture: Bézier Activation Functions
docs.text:
Some recent work uses learnable Bézier activation functions:

\[ \sigma(x) = \sum_{k=0}^n B_{k,n}!\left(\frac{x - x_{\min}}{x_{\max} - x_{\min}}\right) w_k \]

where the weights \(w_k\) are learned. This subsumes ReLU, sigmoid, tanh, and GELU as special cases, with the shape learned from data. The partition of unity property ensures \(\sigma\) is a well-normalized blending of the weights.

docs.title: 11.6 Latent Space Interpolation
docs.text:
In GANs and VAEs, interpolating between two latent codes \(\mathbf{z}_0\) and \(\mathbf{z}_1\) via a straight line often crosses low-density regions (producing blurry or out-of-distribution images). Bézier interpolation with control points placed in high-density regions:

\[ \mathbf{z}(t) = (1-t)^2\mathbf{z}_0 + 2t(1-t)\mathbf{z}_c + t^2\mathbf{z}_1 \]

where \(\mathbf{z}_c\) is chosen to stay near the data manifold, produces semantically smoother interpolations. The convex hull property keeps the path in the convex hull of \({\mathbf{z}_0, \mathbf{z}_c, \mathbf{z}_1}\) — a region more likely to be in-distribution.

docs.title: 11.7 Attention Weight Smoothing and Positional Encodings
docs.text:
The Bernstein basis functions \(B_{k,n}(t)\) are a smooth partition of unity — they sum to 1, are non-negative, and have compact support on \([0,1]\). This is exactly the property required of attention weights (softmax output). Some continuous attention models replace the softmax with a Bernstein mixture:

\[ \alpha_k = \frac{B_{k,n}(\tau)}{\sum_j B_{j,n}(\tau)} \]

where \(\tau\) is a learned "focus" parameter. This gives smooth, controllable attention as a function of position.

docs.title: 11.8 Diffusion Model Trajectory Parametrization
docs.text:
In diffusion models, the noising/denoising path \(\mathbf{x}(t)\) for \(t \in [0,1]\) is typically linear (DDPM) or follows a learned schedule. Emerging work (2024) parametrizes the denoising trajectory as a Bézier curve in data space:

\[ \mathbf{x}(t) = \sum_{k=0}^n B_{k,n}(t),\mathbf{C}_k \]

where \(\mathbf{C}_0 = \mathbf{x}_{\text{noise}}\), \(\mathbf{C}_n = \mathbf{x}_{\text{data}}\), and intermediate control points \(\mathbf{C}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{C}_{n-1}\) are predicted by the network. The subdivision property allows adaptive step sizing; the convex hull property bounds the trajectory.

docs.title: §12 — Rigorous Summary
docs.text:
Definition. The Bézier curve of degree \(n\) with control points \(\mathbf{P}_0, \ldots, \mathbf{P}_n \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is: $\(\mathbf{B}: [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}^d, \qquad \mathbf{B}(t) = \sum_{k=0}^n \binom{n}{k}(1-t)^{n-k}t^k,\mathbf{P}_k\)$

Theorem (Properties). \(\mathbf{B}\) satisfies:

  1. (Endpoint interpolation) \(\mathbf{B}(0) = \mathbf{P}_0\), \(\mathbf{B}(1) = \mathbf{P}_n\)
  2. (Convex hull) \(\mathbf{B}(t) \in \text{conv}(\mathbf{P}_0,\ldots,\mathbf{P}_n)\) for all \(t \in [0,1]\)
  3. (Tangents) \(\mathbf{B}'(0) = n(\mathbf{P}_1-\mathbf{P}_0)\), \(\mathbf{B}'(1) = n(\mathbf{P}_n - \mathbf{P}_{n-1})\)
  4. (Affine invariance) For any affine \(\phi\): \(\phi(\mathbf{B}(t)) = \text{Bézier}(\phi(\mathbf{P}_0),\ldots,\phi(\mathbf{P}_n))(t)\)
  5. (Smoothness) \(\mathbf{B} \in C^\infty([0,1])\); in fact \(\mathbf{B}\) is a polynomial of degree \(\leq n\)
  6. (Subdivision) de Casteljau at \(t_0\) splits \(\mathbf{B}\) into two Bézier sub-curves with explicitly computable control points

docs.title: §13 — Quick Reference
docs.text: Degree Points Formula 1 (linear) \(\mathbf{P}_0, \mathbf{P}_1\) \((1-t)\mathbf{P}_0 + t\mathbf{P}_1\) 2 (quadratic) \(\mathbf{P}_0, \mathbf{P}_1, \mathbf{P}_2\) \((1-t)^2\mathbf{P}_0 + 2t(1-t)\mathbf{P}_1 + t^2\mathbf{P}_2\) 3 (cubic) \(\mathbf{P}_0,\ldots,\mathbf{P}_3\) \((1-t)^3\mathbf{P}_0 + 3t(1-t)^2\mathbf{P}_1 + 3t^2(1-t)\mathbf{P}_2 + t^3\mathbf{P}_3\) \(n\) (general) \(\mathbf{P}_0,\ldots,\mathbf{P}_n\) \(\sum_{k=0}^n\binom{n}{k}(1-t)^{n-k}t^k\mathbf{P}_k\) Property Condition \(C^0\) join \(\mathbf{P}_3^{(1)} = \mathbf{P}_0^{(2)}\) \(G^1\) join handles collinear across join \(C^1\) join handles equidistant and collinear Tangent direction \(\mathbf{B}'(0)\) points toward \(\mathbf{P}_1\) Exact circle arc rational Bézier, \(w_1 = \cos(\theta/2)\)

docs.title: Polar Coordinates
docs.text: "Cartesian coordinates ask: how far right, how far up? Polar coordinates ask: how far, and in which direction? The second question is often the more natural one."

docs.title: §0 — Motivation
docs.text:
Cartesian coordinates \((x, y)\) are adapted to translation symmetry — grids, rectangles, straight lines. But many natural phenomena have rotational symmetry: planetary orbits, sound waves, electromagnetic fields, the receptive fields of visual neurons. For these, insisting on \((x, y)\) is like measuring angles with a ruler.

Polar coordinates are the natural language of rotational geometry.

docs.title: §1 — Definition
docs.text:
A point \(P\) in the plane is specified by:

\[ (r,, \theta) \]

where:

  • \(r\) = radial distance from the origin (the pole) to \(P\)
  • \(\theta\) = polar angle measured counterclockwise from the positive \(x\)-axis (the polar axis) to the ray \(OP\)
                y
                |
                |  * P = (r, θ)
                | /
                |/ θ
   _____________|_____________ x
              origin
              (pole)

  r = distance OP
  θ = angle from positive x-axis (CCW positive)

docs.title: 1.1 Conversion Formulas
docs.text:
Polar → Cartesian: $$ x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta $$

Cartesian → Polar: $$ r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}, \qquad \theta = \arctan!\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) \quad \text{(adjusted for quadrant)} $$

Quadrant adjustment. \(\arctan(y/x)\) only gives \(\theta \in (-\pi/2, \pi/2)\). Use \(\text{atan2}(y, x)\) (the two-argument arctangent) for the correct quadrant: $\(\theta = \begin{cases} \arctan(y/x) & x > 0 \ \arctan(y/x) + \pi & x < 0,\ y \geq 0 \ \arctan(y/x) - \pi & x < 0,\ y < 0 \ +\pi/2 & x = 0,\ y > 0 \ -\pi/2 & x = 0,\ y < 0 \end{cases}\)$

docs.title: 1.2 Non-Uniqueness — A Feature, Not a Bug
docs.text:
Unlike Cartesian coordinates, polar representation is not unique:

\[ (r, \theta) \equiv (r, \theta + 2\pi k) \quad \text{for any integer } k $$ $$ (r, \theta) \equiv (-r, \theta + \pi) \]

The same point is represented by infinitely many polar pairs. This matters when:

  • Finding intersections of polar curves (a point may lie on both curves but with different \((r, \theta)\) values)
  • Integrating over a region (must avoid double-counting)

docs.title: 2.1 Coordinate Curves
docs.text:
In Cartesian coordinates, \(x = c\) (vertical line) and \(y = c\) (horizontal line) are the coordinate curves.

In polar coordinates:

  • \(r = c\) (constant): a circle of radius \(c\) centered at the origin
  • \(\theta = c\) (constant): a ray from the origin at angle \(c\)
r = 1     r = 2     r = 3          θ = π/4       θ = π/2
  O——————————————————              |              |
       circles                    \              |
                                   \     rays    |

docs.title: 2.2 The Polar Area Element
docs.text:
This is crucial for integration. In Cartesian: \(dA = dx,dy\).

In polar, a small "polar rectangle" with sides \(dr\) and \(r,d\theta\) has area:

\[ dA = r, dr, d\theta \]

The factor of \(r\) arises because the arc length of a circular arc of radius \(r\) and angle \(d\theta\) is \(r,d\theta\), not \(d\theta\).

        r+dr ____
            /    \   ← arc length = r·dθ
           /      \
         r/___dθ___\

  Area of this sector ≈ r·dr·dθ
  (area of annular sector, exact in the limit)

Proof via Jacobian. The change of variables \((x,y) \mapsto (r,\theta)\) has Jacobian:

\[ \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(r,\theta)} = \begin{vmatrix} \cos\theta & -r\sin\theta \ \sin\theta & r\cos\theta \end{vmatrix} = r\cos^2\theta + r\sin^2\theta = r \]

So \(dx,dy = |J|,dr,d\theta = r,dr,d\theta\). ✓

docs.title: §3 — Polar Curves
docs.text: A polar curve is defined by \(r = h(\theta)\) for \(\theta \in [\alpha, \beta]\).

docs.title: 3.1 A Gallery of Standard Curves
docs.text:
Circle through origin: $$ r = 2a\cos\theta \quad \text{(circle of radius } |a|, \text{ centered at } (a, 0)) $$ $$ r = 2a\sin\theta \quad \text{(circle of radius } |a|, \text{ centered at } (0, a)) $$

Limaçon: \(r = a + b\cos\theta\)

  • \(|a| > |b|\): no inner loop (dimpled or convex)
  • \(|a| = |b|\): cardioid \(r = a(1 + \cos\theta)\)
  • \(|a| < |b|\): inner loop

Rose curves: \(r = a\cos(n\theta)\) or \(r = a\sin(n\theta)\)

  • \(n\) odd: \(n\) petals
  • \(n\) even: \(2n\) petals
  • Petal length: \(a\)

Lemniscate of Bernoulli: \(r^2 = a^2\cos(2\theta)\)

  • Figure-eight shape, \(r\) real only when \(\cos(2\theta) \geq 0\)

Archimedean spiral: \(r = a\theta\) — constant increase in \(r\) per revolution

Logarithmic spiral: \(r = ae^{b\theta}\) — constant angle between tangent and radial direction

docs.title: 3.2 Symmetry Tests
docs.text:
Symmetry Test (sufficient, not necessary) About \(x\)-axis (\(\theta = 0\)) \(h(-\theta) = h(\theta)\) About \(y\)-axis (\(\theta = \pi/2\)) \(h(\pi - \theta) = h(\theta)\) About origin \(h(\theta + \pi) = h(\theta)\) or \(h(-\theta) = -h(\theta)\)

Caution. Due to non-uniqueness of polar coordinates, a curve can be symmetric even if none of these tests pass. Always plot to verify.

docs.title: 4.1 Tangent Lines to Polar Curves
docs.text:
A polar curve \(r = h(\theta)\) is a parametric curve with \(\theta\) as parameter:

\[ x = h(\theta)\cos\theta, \quad y = h(\theta)\sin\theta \]

By the product rule: $$ \frac{dx}{d\theta} = h'(\theta)\cos\theta - h(\theta)\sin\theta $$ $$ \frac{dy}{d\theta} = h'(\theta)\sin\theta + h(\theta)\cos\theta $$

Tangent slope (from our parametric tangent formula — see [[Tangents of Parametric Curves]]):

\[ \boxed{\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{h'(\theta)\sin\theta + h(\theta)\cos\theta}{h'(\theta)\cos\theta - h(\theta)\sin\theta}} \]

Horizontal tangents: numerator \(= 0\), denominator \(\neq 0\)

Vertical tangents: denominator \(= 0\), numerator \(\neq 0\)

docs.title: 4.2 Area Enclosed by a Polar Curve
docs.text:
As derived in [[Area of Parametric Curves]] (§4 there), the polar area formula is a theorem — it follows from the parametric area formula + Green's Theorem. For \(r = h(\theta)\), \(\theta \in [\alpha, \beta]\):

\[ \boxed{A = \frac{1}{2}\int_\alpha^\beta \bigl[h(\theta)\bigr]^2, d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\int_\alpha^\beta r^2, d\theta} \]

Intuition. A thin sector of angle \(d\theta\) and radius \(r\) has area \(\frac{1}{2}r^2,d\theta\) (like a triangle with base \(r,d\theta\) and height \(r\)). Sum infinitely many such sectors.

         * r=h(θ)
        /|
       / |
      /  |  thin sector: dA = ½r²dθ
     /dθ |
    /    |
   O_____|

Area between two curves \(r_1(\theta) \leq r_2(\theta)\) on \([\alpha, \beta]\):

\[ A = \frac{1}{2}\int_\alpha^\beta \left[r_2(\theta)^2 - r_1(\theta)^2\right] d\theta \]

docs.title: 4.3 Arc Length of a Polar Curve
docs.text:
From the parametric arc length formula with \(x = h(\theta)\cos\theta\), \(y = h(\theta)\sin\theta\):

\[ L = \int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{d\theta}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dy}{d\theta}\right)^2}, d\theta \]

After expanding using product rule and simplifying (the cross terms cancel via \(\sin^2+\cos^2=1\)):

\[ \boxed{L = \int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2}, d\theta = \int_\alpha^\beta\sqrt{h(\theta)^2 + h'(\theta)^2}, d\theta} \]

docs.title: 4.4 Surface Area (Revolution About the Polar Axis)
docs.text:
Revolve \(r = h(\theta)\), \(\theta \in [\alpha, \beta]\) about the polar axis (\(x\)-axis). Radius from the axis is \(y = r\sin\theta\):

\[ S = 2\pi\int_\alpha^\beta h(\theta)\sin\theta\cdot\sqrt{h(\theta)^2 + h'(\theta)^2}; d\theta \]

docs.title: Example 1 — Area of a Cardioid
docs.text: \[ r = a(1 + \cos\theta), \quad \theta \in [0, 2\pi] \] \[ A = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^{2\pi} a^2(1+\cos\theta)^2, d\theta = \frac{a^2}{2}\int_0^{2\pi}(1 + 2\cos\theta + \cos^2\theta), d\theta \] \[ = \frac{a^2}{2}\left[2\pi + 0 + \pi\right] = \frac{3\pi a^2}{2} \] \[ \boxed{A = \frac{3\pi a^2}{2}} \]

docs.title: Example 2 — Area of One Rose Petal
docs.text:
\[ r = \cos(2\theta) \quad \text{(4-petaled rose)} \]

One petal occupies \(\theta \in [-\pi/4, \pi/4]\) (where \(r \geq 0\)):

\[ A_{\text{petal}} = \frac{1}{2}\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\cos^2(2\theta), d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\frac{1+\cos(4\theta)}{2}, d\theta \] \[ = \frac{1}{4}\left[\theta + \frac{\sin(4\theta)}{4}\right]_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} = \frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{\pi}{8} \]

Total area (4 petals): \(4 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{8} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

docs.title: Example 3 — Area Between Two Curves
docs.text:
Find the area inside \(r = 3\sin\theta\) and outside \(r = 1 + \sin\theta\).

Step 1. Find intersections: \(3\sin\theta = 1 + \sin\theta \Rightarrow \sin\theta = 1/2 \Rightarrow \theta = \pi/6,, 5\pi/6\).

Step 2. On \([\pi/6, 5\pi/6]\): \(3\sin\theta \geq 1 + \sin\theta\) (check at \(\theta = \pi/2\): \(3 \geq 2\) ✓).

\[ A = \frac{1}{2}\int_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}\left[(3\sin\theta)^2 - (1+\sin\theta)^2\right]d\theta \] \[ = \frac{1}{2}\int_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}\left[9\sin^2\theta - 1 - 2\sin\theta - \sin^2\theta\right]d\theta \] \[ = \frac{1}{2}\int_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}\left[8\sin^2\theta - 2\sin\theta - 1\right]d\theta \]

Using \(8\sin^2\theta = 4(1-\cos 2\theta)\):

\[ = \frac{1}{2}\int_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}\left[4 - 4\cos 2\theta - 2\sin\theta - 1\right]d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\int_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}\left[3 - 4\cos 2\theta - 2\sin\theta\right]d\theta \] \[ = \frac{1}{2}\left[3\theta - 2\sin 2\theta + 2\cos\theta\right]_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6} = \pi \] \[ \boxed{A = \pi} \]

docs.title: Example 4 — Arc Length of the Cardioid
docs.text:
\(r = a(1+\cos\theta)\), \(h'(\theta) = -a\sin\theta\):

\[ r^2 + \left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2 = a^2(1+\cos\theta)^2 + a^2\sin^2\theta = a^2(2 + 2\cos\theta) = 4a^2\cos^2!\frac{\theta}{2} \] \[ L = \int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{4a^2\cos^2!\frac{\theta}{2}}, d\theta = 2a\int_0^{2\pi}\left|\cos\frac{\theta}{2}\right|d\theta = 2a\cdot 2\int_0^{\pi}\cos\frac{\theta}{2}, d\theta = 4a\left[2\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\right]_0^{\pi} \] \[ \boxed{L = 8a} \]

The Cardioid: r = 1 + cos(θ)

                At θ=0: r = 2 (rightmost point)

Area = 3π/2 a²

  (2, π/4) = (2, π/4 + 2π) = (-2, π/4 + π)

  All three pairs name the SAME point.

  Implication: two polar curves can intersect at a point
  that satisfies DIFFERENT (r,θ) pairs on each curve.
  Always check separately if both curves pass through origin!

docs.title: §7 — Intersection of Polar Curves: A Subtle Problem
docs.text:
Finding intersections of \(r = f(\theta)\) and \(r = g(\theta)\):

Step 1. Solve \(f(\theta) = g(\theta)\) — gives intersection points with the same \((r, \theta)\).

Step 2. Check if both curves pass through the origin (pole). The origin is on \(r = f(\theta)\) if \(f(\theta) = 0\) for some \(\theta_1\), and on \(r = g(\theta)\) if \(g(\theta) = 0\) for some \(\theta_2\) (not necessarily the same \(\theta\)!).

Step 3. Use the periodicity/sign equivalence to check for missed intersections.

Example. \(r = \sin\theta\) and \(r = \cos\theta\):

  • \(\sin\theta = \cos\theta \Rightarrow \theta = \pi/4\): intersection at \((1/\sqrt{2},, \pi/4)\) ✓
  • \(r = \sin\theta = 0\) at \(\theta = 0\); \(r = \cos\theta = 0\) at \(\theta = \pi/2\): both pass through origin, so origin is another intersection ✓
  • Total: two intersection points.

docs.title: 8.1 Cylindrical Coordinates \((r, \theta, z)\)
docs.text: $$ x = r\cos\theta,\quad y = r\sin\theta,\quad z = z $$ Volume element: \(dV = r, dr, d\theta, dz\)

docs.title: 8.2 Spherical Coordinates \((\rho, \phi, \theta)\)
docs.text:
$$ x = \rho\sin\phi\cos\theta,\quad y = \rho\sin\phi\sin\theta,\quad z = \rho\cos\phi $$ Volume element: \(dV = \rho^2\sin\phi, d\rho, d\phi, d\theta\)

Both are the MIT 18.02 generalizations of 2D polar coordinates. The \(r\) in polar becomes the factor in the Jacobian determinant in all cases.

docs.title: §9 — Rigorous Summary
docs.text:
Theorem (Polar Area). Let \(r = h(\theta)\) be continuous on \([\alpha, \beta]\) with \(\beta - \alpha \leq 2\pi\). The area of the region bounded by the curve and the rays \(\theta = \alpha\), \(\theta = \beta\) is: $\(A = \frac{1}{2}\int_\alpha^\beta h(\theta)^2, d\theta\)$

Theorem (Polar Arc Length). If \(h\) is continuously differentiable on \([\alpha, \beta]\), the arc length of \(r = h(\theta)\) is: $\(L = \int_\alpha^\beta\sqrt{h(\theta)^2 + h'(\theta)^2}, d\theta\)$

Theorem (Polar Jacobian). The change of variables \((x,y) = (r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\) has Jacobian \(|\partial(x,y)/\partial(r,\theta)| = r\), so \(dx,dy = r,dr,d\theta\).

docs.title: §10 — Connection to AI, Machine Learning & Deep Learning
10.1 \(\text{atan2}\) Is Everywhere in Geometry-Aware Networks
docs.text:
The two-argument arctangent \(\text{atan2}(y, x)\) — the correct quadrant-aware polar angle — is used in:

  • Optical flow networks: flow vectors are often decomposed into magnitude and angle
  • Oriented bounding boxes in object detection (rotated RoI pooling)
  • Phase computation in complex-valued neural networks
  • SE(2)-equivariant networks (rotation + translation equivariance)

The derivative \(\partial,\text{atan2}(y,x)/\partial x = -y/(x^2+y^2)\), \(\partial/\partial y = x/(x^2+y^2)\) flows through backpropagation without issue. The polar angle is a differentiable operation on features.

docs.title: 10.2 Rotational Equivariance via Polar Coordinates
docs.text:
Group equivariant CNNs (Cohen & Welling, 2016; Weiler et al., 2019) design filters that are equivariant to rotations. A core technique: represent filters in polar coordinates \((r, \theta)\) and decompose the angular part in a Fourier basis:

\[ f(r, \theta) = \sum_k a_k(r), e^{ik\theta} \]

Because \(e^{ik\theta}\) transforms predictably under rotation (\(\theta \to \theta + \phi\) gives factor \(e^{ik\phi}\)), filters written this way are automatically equivariant. The polar coordinate system is the natural basis for rotation equivariance.

docs.title: 10.3 Polar Representation in Radar / Lidar Processing
docs.text: Autonomous driving perception networks often receive data from lidar sensors, which output point clouds in polar / spherical coordinates \((r, \theta, \phi)\) naturally. Networks like PolarNet, RangeNet++, and Cylinder3D operate directly in polar/cylindrical coordinate grids rather than converting to Cartesian — exploiting the natural symmetries of the sensor geometry. The polar area element \(r,dr,d\theta\) determines how to properly normalize features in these coordinate grids.

docs.title: 10.4 Complex Numbers, Polar Form, and Attention
docs.text:
Every complex number \(z = x + iy\) has polar form \(z = re^{i\theta}\). In complex-valued neural networks and in Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) — used in modern LLMs including LLaMA, Mistral, and GPT-4 — the attention mechanism encodes position as a rotation in the complex plane:

\[ \text{RoPE}(x, m) = x \cdot e^{im\theta} \]

This is polar multiplication: rotate the query/key vector by angle \(m\theta\) in each 2D subspace. The relative position between tokens \(m\) and \(n\) appears as a phase difference \(e^{i(m-n)\theta}\) in the dot product — a purely polar-coordinate phenomenon. Every modern LLM using RoPE is doing polar coordinate arithmetic in its attention layers.

docs.title: 10.5 Fourier Transform as Polar Integration
docs.text:
The 2D Discrete Fourier Transform (used in CNNs via the convolution theorem, in spectral graph networks, and in physics-informed neural networks) can be written in polar coordinates in frequency space:

\[ \hat{f}(\xi_1, \xi_2) = \int_0^\infty\int_0^{2\pi} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta), e^{-2\pi i r(\xi_1\cos\theta + \xi_2\sin\theta)}, r, dr, d\theta \]

The \(r,dr,d\theta\) area element is the polar Jacobian. The Radon transform (used in CT scans and some neural network architectures) is a line integral in polar coordinates. These are the analytical foundations of frequency-domain learning.

docs.title: 10.6 Gaussian Integrals — The Foundation of Probabilistic ML
docs.text:
The most important integral in all of machine learning:

\[ \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2}, dx = \sqrt{\pi} \]

The standard proof uses polar coordinates:

\[ \left(\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2}, dx\right)^2 = \int_{-\infty}^\infty\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-(x^2+y^2)}, dx, dy = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}, r, dr, d\theta = \pi \]

Every Gaussian distribution, every normal distribution likelihood, every Bayesian posterior involving Gaussians, every variational autoencoder's KL divergence — all rest on this polar coordinate computation. The factor of \(r\) in \(r,dr,d\theta\) is literally what makes Gaussian integrals tractable.

docs.title: 10.7 Loss Landscapes and Angular Geometry
docs.text:
In cosine similarity — used in contrastive learning (SimCLR, MoCo, CLIP), metric learning, and attention:

\[ \text{sim}(u, v) = \frac{u \cdot v}{|u||v|} = \cos\theta_{uv} \]

This is exactly the polar coordinate inner product. The angular distance \(\theta_{uv}\) is the polar angle between the two vectors. Contrastive losses minimize angular distance between positive pairs and maximize it between negative pairs — they are polar coordinate optimization problems in high-dimensional embedding space.

ArcFace (face recognition) explicitly adds an angular margin \(m\) to the polar angle:

\[ \mathcal{L} = -\log\frac{e^{s\cos(\theta_{y_i} + m)}}{e^{s\cos(\theta_{y_i}+m)} + \sum_{j\neq y_i}e^{s\cos\theta_j}} \]

This is purely polar geometry — the entire loss is written in terms of \(r\) (the norm, scaled by \(s\)) and \(\theta\) (the angle between feature and weight vectors).

docs.title: §11 — Quick Reference Card
docs.text: Concept Formula Polar → Cartesian \(x = r\cos\theta,\ y = r\sin\theta\) Cartesian → Polar \(r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2},\ \theta = \text{atan2}(y,x)\) Area element \(dA = r,dr,d\theta\) Polar area \(A = \frac{1}{2}\int_\alpha^\beta r^2,d\theta\) Area between curves \(A = \frac{1}{2}\int_\alpha^\beta (r_2^2 - r_1^2),d\theta\) Arc length \(L = \int_\alpha^\beta\sqrt{r^2 + (dr/d\theta)^2},d\theta\) Tangent slope \(dy/dx = (r'\sin\theta + r\cos\theta)/(r'\cos\theta - r\sin\theta)\) Jacobian $ Curve Polar Equation Notes Circle (centered at origin) \(r = a\) Circle (through origin) \(r = 2a\cos\theta\) center \((a,0)\) Cardioid \(r = a(1+\cos\theta)\) area \(= 3\pi a^2/2\) \(n\)-petal rose (odd \(n\)) \(r = a\cos(n\theta)\) \(n\) petals \(2n\)-petal rose (even \(n\)) \(r = a\cos(n\theta)\) \(2n\) petals Lemniscate \(r^2 = a^2\cos(2\theta)\) figure-eight Archimedean spiral \(r = a\theta\) Logarithmic spiral \(r = ae^{b\theta}\)

docs.title: §12 — Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Missing the Jacobian factor \(r\): The area element is \(r,dr,d\theta\), not \(dr,d\theta\). Forgetting \(r\) is the most common integration error in polar coordinates.

  2. Wrong quadrant for \(\theta\): \(\arctan(y/x)\) is not \(\text{atan2}(y,x)\). Always adjust for the correct quadrant.

  3. Double-counting in closed curves: If a curve is traced twice as \(\theta\) goes from \(0\) to \(2\pi\), the area integral counts it twice. Check how many times the curve is traversed.

  4. Missing intersections at the origin: Two curves can meet at the origin with completely different \(\theta\) values. Always check the origin separately.

  5. Rose petal count: \(r = \cos(n\theta)\) has \(n\) petals if \(n\) is odd, \(2n\) petals if \(n\) is even. It is not always \(n\) petals.

  6. Confusing \(r < 0\): When \(h(\theta) < 0\), the point \((h(\theta), \theta)\) is plotted in the opposite direction — at \((|h(\theta)|, \theta + \pi)\). This is valid but counterintuitive.
