docs.title: Polar Curves
docs.text: "The choice of coordinate system is not a matter of taste — it is a matter of what the geometry is trying to tell you."

docs.title: 0. Why Bother? A Motivating Remark
docs.text:
Cartesian coordinates encode a point as a displacement from an origin: how far right, how far up. This is natural when geometry is built from rectangles and grids. But many curves — spirals, roses, cardioids, limaçons — are intrinsically radial: they are defined by how far you are from a fixed center, and in which direction. For such curves, the Cartesian description is grotesque while the polar description is one line.

In machine learning, the same philosophy recurs constantly: the right representation collapses complexity. A kernel function, an attention mechanism, a Fourier feature map — all are attempts to find coordinates in which the problem becomes simple.

docs.title: 1. The Polar Coordinate System
docs.text:
Definition. A point \(P\) in the plane is assigned polar coordinates \((r, \theta)\) where:

  • \(r\) = the radial distance from the pole (origin) \(O\) to \(P\)
  • \(\theta\) = the polar angle measured counter-clockwise from the polar axis (positive \(x\)-axis)

The conversion identities are exact:

\[x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta\] \[r^2 = x^2 + y^2, \qquad \tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}\]

Remark on uniqueness. Unlike Cartesian coordinates, polar representations are not unique:

\[\left(r,, \theta\right) = \left(r,, \theta + 2\pi k\right) \quad \text{for any } k \in \mathbb{Z}\] \[\left(r,, \theta\right) = \left(-r,, \theta + \pi\right)\]

This non-uniqueness is not a bug — it is the source of the richness we exploit when finding intersections of polar curves.

docs.title: 2. Polar Curves: Definition and Graphing
docs.text: A polar curve is the set of points whose polar coordinates satisfy an equation \(r = f(\theta)\), or more generally \(F(r, \theta) = 0\).

docs.title: 2.1 Standard Toolkit of Polar Curves
docs.text: Curve Equation Description Circle (centered at pole) \(r = a\) Radius \(a\) Line through pole \(\theta = \alpha\) Angle \(\alpha\) Circle passing through pole \(r = 2a\cos\theta\) Diameter \(2a\), center \((a, 0)\) Cardioid \(r = a(1 + \cos\theta)\) Heart-shaped, passes through pole Limaçon \(r = b + a\cos\theta\), \(b \neq a\) Inner loop if \(b < a\) Rose curve \(r = a\cos(n\theta)\) \(n\) petals (\(n\) odd), \(2n\) petals (\(n\) even) Lemniscate of Bernoulli \(r^2 = a^2\cos(2\theta)\) Figure-eight Archimedean spiral \(r = a\theta\) Uniform radial expansion Logarithmic spiral \(r = ae^{b\theta}\) Self-similar, appears in nature

docs.title: 2.2 Worked Example — The Cardioid \(r = 1 + \cos\theta\)
docs.text:
Build the table of values:

\(\theta\) \(\cos\theta\) \(r\) \(0\) \(1\) \(2\) \(\pi/3\) \(1/2\) \(3/2\) \(\pi/2\) \(0\) \(1\) \(2\pi/3\) \(-1/2\) \(1/2\) \(\pi\) \(-1\) \(0\) \(4\pi/3\) \(-1/2\) \(1/2\) \(3\pi/2\) \(0\) \(1\) \(2\pi\) \(1\) \(2\)

The curve passes through the pole (\(r=0\)) when \(\theta = \pi\). It reaches maximum radius \(r = 2\) at \(\theta = 0\).

Symmetry test: \(f(-\theta) = 1 + \cos(-\theta) = 1 + \cos\theta = f(\theta)\), so the cardioid is symmetric about the polar axis (the \(x\)-axis). ✓

Polar Sketch: r = 1 + cos(θ)   (Cardioid)

         θ=π/2
          |
    r=1   |   r=3/2
          |
θ=π ------O----------> θ=0  (r=2)
  (r=0)   |
          |
         θ=3π/2

The curve looks like a heart rotated 90°.
Widest point: r=2 on the right (θ=0)
Cusp at origin: θ=π

docs.title: 2.3 Worked Example — Rose Curve \(r = \cos(2\theta)\)
docs.text:
This has \(n = 2\) (even), so it produces \(2 \times 2 = 4\) petals. The petals appear along the lines \(\theta = 0, \pi/2, \pi, 3\pi/2\).

Petal tips occur where \(|r| = 1\):

  • \(\theta = 0\): \(r = 1\) → petal along positive \(x\)-axis
  • \(\theta = \pi/2\): \(r = \cos(\pi) = -1\) → \(r < 0\) means the point plots in the direction \(\theta = \pi/2 + \pi = 3\pi/2\) … actually let's be careful.

At \(\theta = \pi/4\): \(r = \cos(\pi/2) = 0\) → crosses the pole (start/end of petal).

Rose: r = cos(2θ)

        petal
         ↑
petal ←--O--→ petal
         ↓
        petal

4 equal petals at 90° intervals.
Each petal has length r=1.

docs.title: 3.1 Derivation
docs.text:
Given \(r = f(\theta)\), the Cartesian parametrization is:

\[x(\theta) = f(\theta)\cos\theta, \qquad y(\theta) = f(\theta)\sin\theta\]

By the chain rule:

\[\frac{dy}{d\theta} = f'(\theta)\sin\theta + f(\theta)\cos\theta\] \[\frac{dx}{d\theta} = f'(\theta)\cos\theta - f(\theta)\sin\theta\]

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at a point is:

\[\boxed{\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{f'(\theta)\sin\theta + f(\theta)\cos\theta}{f'(\theta)\cos\theta - f(\theta)\sin\theta}}\]

docs.title: 3.2 Horizontal and Vertical Tangents
docs.text:
• Horizontal tangent: \(\dfrac{dy}{d\theta} = 0\) and \(\dfrac{dx}{d\theta} \neq 0\)
  • Vertical tangent: \(\dfrac{dx}{d\theta} = 0\) and \(\dfrac{dy}{d\theta} \neq 0\)

Example. For the cardioid \(r = 1 + \cos\theta\), find horizontal tangents.

\(f(\theta) = 1 + \cos\theta\), \(f'(\theta) = -\sin\theta\).

\[\frac{dy}{d\theta} = -\sin\theta \cdot \sin\theta + (1+\cos\theta)\cos\theta = -\sin^2\theta + \cos\theta + \cos^2\theta\] \[= \cos(2\theta) + \cos\theta = 2\cos^2\theta - 1 + \cos\theta\]

Setting equal to zero: \(2\cos^2\theta + \cos\theta - 1 = 0\), which factors as \((2\cos\theta - 1)(\cos\theta + 1) = 0\).

So \(\cos\theta = 1/2 \Rightarrow \theta = \pi/3, 5\pi/3\) and \(\cos\theta = -1 \Rightarrow \theta = \pi\) (the pole — needs separate analysis).

At \(\theta = \pi/3\): \(r = 3/2\), giving the Cartesian point \((3/4, 3\sqrt{3}/4)\). ✓

docs.title: 4.1 The Sector Formula
docs.text:
The key idea: a thin "wedge" of angle \(d\theta\) and radius \(r\) has area \(\approx \frac{1}{2}r^2, d\theta\) (the area of a circular sector with angle \(d\theta\) and radius \(r\)).

Theorem (Area in Polar Coordinates). The area enclosed by \(r = f(\theta)\) between \(\theta = \alpha\) and \(\theta = \beta\) is:

\[\boxed{A = \frac{1}{2}\int_\alpha^\beta r^2, d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\int_\alpha^\beta [f(\theta)]^2, d\theta}\]

Proof sketch. Partition \([\alpha, \beta]\) into \(n\) subintervals. On the \(i\)-th subinterval \([\theta_{i-1}, \theta_i]\), approximate the region by a circular sector of radius \(f(\theta_i^_)\) and angle \(\Delta\theta_i\). Its area is \(\frac{1}{2}[f(\theta_i^_)]^2 \Delta\theta_i\). Summing and taking \(n \to \infty\) gives the integral. \(\square\)

docs.title: 4.2 Example: Area Inside the Cardioid \(r = 1 + \cos\theta\)
docs.text:
By symmetry (symmetric about \(x\)-axis), compute the upper half and double:

\[A = 2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \int_0^\pi (1 + \cos\theta)^2, d\theta = \int_0^\pi (1 + 2\cos\theta + \cos^2\theta), d\theta\]

Use \(\cos^2\theta = \frac{1 + \cos(2\theta)}{2}\):

\[= \int_0^\pi \left(1 + 2\cos\theta + \frac{1}{2} + \frac{\cos(2\theta)}{2}\right)d\theta = \int_0^\pi \left(\frac{3}{2} + 2\cos\theta + \frac{\cos(2\theta)}{2}\right)d\theta\] \[= \left[\frac{3\theta}{2} + 2\sin\theta + \frac{\sin(2\theta)}{4}\right]_0^\pi = \frac{3\pi}{2} + 0 + 0 = \frac{3\pi}{2}\]

docs.title: 4.3 Area Between Two Polar Curves
docs.text:
If \(f(\theta) \geq g(\theta) \geq 0\) on \([\alpha, \beta]\), the area between \(r = f(\theta)\) (outer) and \(r = g(\theta)\) (inner) is:

\[A = \frac{1}{2}\int_\alpha^\beta \left([f(\theta)]^2 - [g(\theta)]^2\right)d\theta\]

Example. Area inside \(r = 3\sin\theta\) and outside \(r = 1 + \sin\theta\).

First, find intersections: \(3\sin\theta = 1 + \sin\theta \Rightarrow \sin\theta = 1/2 \Rightarrow \theta = \pi/6, 5\pi/6\).

On \([\pi/6, 5\pi/6]\), \(3\sin\theta \geq 1 + \sin\theta\). By symmetry:

\[A = 2 \cdot \frac{1}{2}\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}\left[(3\sin\theta)^2 - (1+\sin\theta)^2\right]d\theta\] \[= \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}\left[9\sin^2\theta - 1 - 2\sin\theta - \sin^2\theta\right]d\theta = \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}\left[8\sin^2\theta - 2\sin\theta - 1\right]d\theta\]

Expand \(8\sin^2\theta = 4(1-\cos 2\theta)\):

\[= \int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}[3 - 4\cos(2\theta) - 2\sin\theta], d\theta = \left[3\theta - 2\sin(2\theta) + 2\cos\theta\right]_{\pi/6}^{\pi/2}\] \[= \left(\frac{3\pi}{2} - 0 + 0\right) - \left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \sqrt{3} + \sqrt{3}\right) = \pi\]

docs.title: 5. Arc Length of a Polar Curve
5.1 Formula
docs.text:
Starting from the general arc-length formula \(L = \int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{d\theta}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dy}{d\theta}\right)^2}, d\theta\), compute:

\[\left(\frac{dx}{d\theta}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dy}{d\theta}\right)^2 = (f')^2\cos^2\theta - 2ff'\sin\theta\cos\theta + f^2\sin^2\theta$$ $$\quad + (f')^2\sin^2\theta + 2ff'\sin\theta\cos\theta + f^2\cos^2\theta$$ $$= (f')^2 + f^2\]

Therefore:

\[\boxed{L = \int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2}, d\theta}\]

Example. Arc length of the cardioid \(r = a(1 + \cos\theta)\):

\(dr/d\theta = -a\sin\theta\).

\[r^2 + \left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2 = a^2(1+\cos\theta)^2 + a^2\sin^2\theta = a^2(1 + 2\cos\theta + \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta)$$ $$= a^2(2 + 2\cos\theta) = 4a^2\cos^2(\theta/2)\]

using the half-angle identity \(1 + \cos\theta = 2\cos^2(\theta/2)\).

\[L = \int_0^{2\pi} 2a\left|\cos(\theta/2)\right|, d\theta = 4a\int_0^\pi \cos(\theta/2), d\theta = 4a\left[2\sin(\theta/2)\right]_0^\pi = 8a\]

docs.title: 6. Intersection of Polar Curves
docs.text:
This is where most students get burned. The issue is non-uniqueness of representation.

To find all intersections of \(r = f( heta)\) and \(r = g( heta)\):

Step 1. Solve \(f( heta) = g( heta)\) simultaneously. These give "genuine" intersections.

Step 2. Check whether the pole lies on both curves: \(f( heta_1) = 0\) for some \( heta_1\), and \(g( heta_2) = 0\) for some \( heta_2\). If so, the pole is an intersection point (even if \( heta_1 eq heta_2\)).

Step 3. Check equivalent representations. If \(r = f( heta)\), also check \(r = f( heta + 2\pi k)\) and \(-r = f( heta + \pi)\) against \(g\).

Example. Find all intersections of \(r = \cos heta\) and \(r = 1 - \cos heta\).

Step 1: \(\cos heta = 1 - \cos heta \Rightarrow 2\cos heta = 1 \Rightarrow heta = \pi/3, 5\pi/3\).

Points: \(r = 1/2\) at \( heta = \pi/3\): Cartesian \((1/4, \sqrt{3}/4)\) and at \( heta = 5\pi/3\): \((1/4, -\sqrt{3}/4)\).

Step 2: \(r = \cos heta = 0\) when \( heta = \pi/2\). \(r = 1 - \cos(\pi/2) = 1 eq 0\). But \(r = 1 - \cos heta = 0\) when \( heta = 0\), and \(r = \cos(0) = 1 eq 0\). The pole is NOT on \(r = 1 - \cos heta\)... actually wait: \(1 - \cos heta = 0 \Rightarrow heta = 0\), so the pole lies on \(r = 1 - \cos heta\) (at \( heta = 0\)). And \(r = \cos(\pi/2) = 0\), so the pole lies on \(r = \cos heta\) (at \( heta = \pi/2\)). Hence the pole is also an intersection.

Total: 3 intersection points.

docs.title: 8. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
docs.text: Polar coordinates and polar curve theory connect to modern ML in several deep and concrete ways. This is not superficial analogy — these are genuine mathematical bridges.

docs.title: 8.1 Radial Basis Functions (RBFs) and Kernel Methods
docs.text:
A radial basis function \(\phi(x) = \phi(|x|)\) depends only on the distance from a center — it is constant on spheres, which are the "circles" of Euclidean space. This is exactly the polar symmetry \(r = \text{const}\).

The Gaussian RBF kernel \(k(x, x') = e^{-|x - x'|^2 / 2\sigma^2}\) is radially symmetric. In polar-like coordinates centered at \(x'\), it becomes \(k = e^{-r^2/2\sigma^2}\), a function of \(r\) alone — identical in structure to polar curves like \(r = e^{-a\theta^2}\).

SVM with RBF kernels implicitly map data into an infinite-dimensional feature space where linearly inseparable data (a donut-shaped class, say) becomes separable. The donut has polar equation \(r_1 \leq r \leq r_2\) — it is a polar region.

docs.title: 8.2 Fourier Features and Periodic Representations
docs.text:
The rose curve \(r = \cos(n\theta)\) is built from \(\cos(n\theta)\) — a Fourier basis function. In Random Fourier Features (Rahimi & Recht, 2007), RBF kernels are approximated by random projections of the form \(z(x) = \cos(\omega^T x + b)\) where \(\omega\) is sampled from a specific distribution. These feature maps live naturally in polar/angular space.

Positional encodings in Transformers (e.g., \(\sin(k / 10000^{2i/d})\), \(\cos(k / 10000^{2i/d})\)) are essentially polar angle encodings applied to the token index \(k\). The self-attention mechanism computes \(Q K^T\), and the quality of this dot product depends critically on how angles are preserved — RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding) makes this explicit by applying a rotation matrix in 2D blocks, i.e., a rotation in polar coordinates.

docs.title: 8.3 Loss Landscape Geometry and Angular Structure
docs.text:
The loss landscape \(\mathcal{L}(\theta)\) of a neural network is a high-dimensional scalar field. Understanding its critical points (saddles, minima) requires analyzing the directional behavior of \(\mathcal{L}\) — in polar coordinates centered at a critical point, this means studying \(\mathcal{L}(r, \hat{\theta})\) as \(r \to 0\) from different directions \(\hat{\theta}\).

The sharpness of a minimum (related to the Hessian's largest eigenvalue) corresponds to the maximum of \(\partial^2\mathcal{L}/\partial r^2\) over all directions \(\hat{\theta}\). Flat minima (small sharpness) generalize better — this is the content of SAM (Sharpness-Aware Minimization).

docs.title: 8.4 Circular/Torus Data Manifolds
docs.text:
In data with periodic structure — time-of-day features, molecular bond angles, protein dihedral angles, directions in 2D space — the natural representation is angular: the data lives on a circle \(S^1\) or torus \(S^1 \times S^1\), described by polar/toroidal coordinates.

von Mises distribution is the analogue of the Gaussian for circular data: \(p(\theta) \propto e^{\kappa \cos(\theta - \mu)}\). Neural networks for protein structure prediction (AlphaFold) must handle such circular outputs — a naive MSE loss on angles is metrically wrong (the angle 359° is close to 1°, but their difference is 358°).

docs.title: 8.5 Equivariant Networks and Rotational Symmetry
docs.text: A CNN that must be equivariant to rotation is most naturally designed in polar coordinates. Steerable CNNs and E(2)-equivariant networks decompose feature maps into irreducible representations of SO(2) — i.e., into Fourier modes \(e^{in\theta}\), the complex version of polar rose harmonics. The \(n\)-petal rose \(r = \cos(n\theta)\) is the real part of the \(n\)-th Fourier mode.

docs.title: 8.6 Summary Table
docs.text: ML Concept Polar Connection RBF Kernel / SVM Radial symmetry \(r = f(\|x\|)\) Random Fourier Features Cosine modes \(\cos(n\theta)\) Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE) 2D rotation in polar form Protein angle regression Circular statistics on \(S^1\) Sharpness-Aware Minimization Directional Hessian in polar coords E(2)-equivariant CNNs SO(2) Fourier decomposition

docs.title: 9. Summary of Key Formulas
docs.text: Quantity Formula Cartesian from polar \(x = r\cos\theta,; y = r\sin\theta\) Polar from Cartesian \(r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2},; \tan\theta = y/x\) Slope of tangent \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{r'\sin\theta + r\cos\theta}{r'\cos\theta - r\sin\theta}\) Area \(A = \dfrac{1}{2}\displaystyle\int_\alpha^\beta r^2, d\theta\) Area between curves \(A = \dfrac{1}{2}\displaystyle\int_\alpha^\beta(r_{\text{out}}^2 - r_{\text{in}}^2), d\theta\) Arc length \(L = \displaystyle\int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{r^2 + (r')^2}, d\theta\)

docs.title: 10. Exercises Worth Doing
docs.text:
1. (Stewart §10.3) Sketch \(r = 2\sin(3\theta)\) and determine the number of petals and the area of one petal.

  2. (MIT 18.02) Find the area of the region inside \(r = 2\) and inside \(r = 2(1 + \cos\theta)\). Hint: sketch first — both curves together.

  3. (Tangent lines) Find all tangent lines to \(r = 1 + \sin\theta\) that are horizontal or vertical.

  4. (Arc length) Compute the arc length of one petal of \(r = \cos(2\theta)\).

  5. (Intersections) Find all intersections of \(r = 1\) and \(r = 2\cos\theta\). Account for intersections arising from different parametrizations.

  6. (ML connection) Let \(\phi: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\) be defined by \(\phi(r, \theta) = e^{-r^2}\). Show that \(\phi\) is a radial function and compute \(\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} \phi, dA\) using polar area elements.

docs.title: Symmetry
docs.text: "Symmetry is not decoration — it is a theorem waiting to be used. Every symmetry you detect is half an integral you don't have to compute."

docs.title: 0. Why Symmetry Deserves Its Own Note
docs.text:
In Cartesian coordinates, symmetry tests are almost trivial: replace \(x \to -x\) or \(y \to -y\) and check if the equation is unchanged. In polar coordinates, the situation is genuinely more subtle — and more interesting. Because the polar representation of a point is non-unique, the failure of a symmetry test does not mean the symmetry is absent. A curve can possess a symmetry that no algebraic substitution reveals directly.

This is not a quirk to be swept under the rug. It is a precise mathematical phenomenon, and understanding it forces you to think carefully about the difference between a curve (a set of points) and its equation (a representation).

docs.title: 2. The Three Standard Symmetries
docs.text:
There are three symmetries that appear naturally in polar curve analysis, corresponding to the three fundamental reflections of the plane.

          y-axis (θ = π/2)
               |
               |
  ─────────────O─────────────  x-axis (polar axis)
               |
               |

  Three symmetry axes in polar geometry:
  1. About the polar axis (x-axis):      reflection (r, θ) ↦ (r, -θ)
  2. About the line θ = π/2 (y-axis):    reflection (r, θ) ↦ (r, π - θ)
  3. About the pole (origin):            reflection (r, θ) ↦ (-r, θ) or (r, θ + π)

docs.title: 3. Symmetry Tests: The Sufficient Conditions
docs.text: For each symmetry, there is a sufficient algebraic test. These are conditions on the equation \(r = f(\theta)\) that guarantee the symmetry. Crucially, failing the test does not rule out the symmetry.

docs.title: 3.1 Symmetry About the Polar Axis (x-axis)
docs.text:
Geometric meaning. The curve is unchanged under the reflection \((x, y) \mapsto (x, -y)\).

In polar terms: the reflection of \((r, \theta)\) is \((r, -\theta)\). Equivalently (using the non-uniqueness), \((-r, \pi - \theta)\).

Sufficient Test.

\[\text{If } f(-\theta) = f(\theta), \text{ then the curve } r = f(\theta) \text{ is symmetric about the polar axis.}\]

Proof. If \((r_0, \theta_0)\) lies on the curve, then \(r_0 = f(\theta_0)\). We need the reflected point \((r_0, -\theta_0)\) to also lie on the curve. Indeed: \(f(-\theta_0) = f(\theta_0) = r_0\). So \((r_0, -\theta_0)\) satisfies \(r = f(\theta)\). \(\square\)

Secondary test (using non-uniqueness): If replacing \((r, \theta)\) with \((-r, \pi - \theta)\) leaves the equation unchanged, the curve is also symmetric about the polar axis.

Example. \(r = 1 + \cos\theta\).

\(f(-\theta) = 1 + \cos(-\theta) = 1 + \cos\theta = f(\theta)\). ✓ Symmetric about polar axis.

Example. \(r = \cos(2\theta)\).

\(f(-\theta) = \cos(-2\theta) = \cos(2\theta) = f(\theta)\). ✓ Symmetric about polar axis.

docs.title: 3.2 Symmetry About the Line \(\theta = \pi/2\) (y-axis)
docs.text:
Geometric meaning. The curve is unchanged under the reflection \((x, y) \mapsto (-x, y)\).

In polar terms: the reflection of \((r, \theta)\) is \((r, \pi - \theta)\). Equivalently, \((-r, -\theta)\).

Sufficient Test.

\[\text{If } f(\pi - \theta) = f(\theta), \text{ then the curve is symmetric about } \theta = \pi/2.\]

Proof. If \((r_0, \theta_0)\) is on the curve, we need \((r_0, \pi - \theta_0)\) on the curve. \(f(\pi - \theta_0) = f(\theta_0) = r_0\). \(\square\)

Secondary test: replacing \((r, \theta)\) with \((-r, -\theta)\) leaves the equation unchanged.

Example. \(r = 1 + \sin\theta\).

\(f(\pi - \theta) = 1 + \sin(\pi - \theta) = 1 + \sin\theta = f(\theta)\). ✓ Symmetric about \(\theta = \pi/2\).

  Cardioid r = 1 + sinθ         Cardioid r = 1 + cosθ
  (opens upward, symmetric       (opens rightward, symmetric
   about y-axis)                  about x-axis)

         ♥                              ♥ rotated 90°
         |                           ────
    ─────O                              O

docs.title: 3.3 Symmetry About the Pole (Origin)
docs.text:
Geometric meaning. The curve is unchanged under the map \((x, y) \mapsto (-x, -y)\), i.e., rotation by \(\pi\).

In polar terms: the reflection of \((r, \theta)\) through the pole is \((-r, \theta)\), which is the same point as \((r, \theta + \pi)\).

Sufficient Test.

\[\text{If } f(\theta + \pi) = f(\theta), \text{ then the curve is symmetric about the pole.}\]

Or equivalently: if replacing \(r\) with \(-r\) leaves the equation unchanged (i.e., \(f(-\theta)\) ... actually: if \(-r = f(\theta)\) implies \(r = f(\theta)\), i.e., the equation is even in \(r\)).

More precisely:

\[\text{If } f(\theta + \pi) = f(\theta) \text{ for all } \theta, \quad \text{OR} \quad \text{if replacing } (r,\theta) \text{ with } (-r, \theta) \text{ leaves } F(r,\theta)=0 \text{ unchanged.}\]

Proof. Under \(f(\theta + \pi) = f(\theta)\): if \((r_0, \theta_0)\) is on the curve, then \((r_0, \theta_0 + \pi)\) represents the point diametrically opposite. \(f(\theta_0 + \pi) = f(\theta_0) = r_0\), so this opposite point is also on the curve. \(\square\)

Example. \(r^2 = \cos(2\theta)\) (lemniscate of Bernoulli).

Replace \(r\) with \(-r\): \((-r)^2 = r^2 = \cos(2\theta)\). Equation unchanged. ✓ Symmetric about the pole.

Example. \(r = \cos(3\theta)\) (3-petal rose).

\(f(\theta + \pi) = \cos(3\theta + 3\pi) = \cos(3\theta)\cos(3\pi) - \sin(3\theta)\sin(3\pi) = -\cos(3\theta) \neq f(\theta)\) in general.

So the sufficient test fails. But the curve still has... wait. Let's check: the 3-petal rose has 3 petals at \(120°\) apart. It is symmetric about the polar axis (check: \(f(-\theta) = \cos(-3\theta) = \cos(3\theta)\) ✓), and about \(\theta = \pi/3\) and \(\theta = 2\pi/3\)... but NOT about the pole. A 3-petal rose does not have 180° rotational symmetry — rotating by \(\pi\) maps petal to gap.

docs.title: 4. The Critical Subtlety: Sufficient ≠ Necessary
docs.text: This is the heart of the matter. The three tests above are sufficient conditions. A curve can fail all three tests and still possess a symmetry, because the same geometric curve can be represented by multiple equations.

docs.title: 4.1 A Canonical Example
docs.text:
Consider \(r = \sin(2\theta)\) (a 4-petal rose).

Test for symmetry about the pole: \(f(\theta + \pi) = \sin(2(\theta+\pi)) = \sin(2\theta + 2\pi) = \sin(2\theta) = f(\theta)\). ✓ Passes.

Test for symmetry about polar axis: \(f(-\theta) = \sin(-2\theta) = -\sin(2\theta) \neq f(\theta)\) in general. ✗ Fails.

Yet clearly \(r = \sin(2\theta)\) is symmetric about the polar axis — the graph is a symmetric 4-petal rose. Why does the test fail?

Because when \(\theta\) is replaced by \(-\theta\), we get \(r = -\sin(2\theta)\). This is not the same equation as \(r = \sin(2\theta)\). However, the point \((-\sin(2\theta), \theta)\) in polar coordinates is the same geometric point as \((\sin(2\theta), \theta + \pi)\). And \(\sin(2(\theta + \pi)) = \sin(2\theta)\). So the reflected point does lie on the curve — but you need the alternative representation to see it.

The correct procedure for \(r = \sin(2\theta)\) and polar axis symmetry:

The reflection of \((r, \theta)\) is \((r, -\theta)\). But equivalently it is \((-r, \pi - \theta)\).

Check the second form: does \(r = -\sin(2(\pi - \theta))\)... actually let's be systematic.

The reflected point \((r_0, \theta_0)\) through the polar axis is \((r_0, -\theta_0)\). For this to lie on the curve we need \(r_0 = \sin(-2\theta_0) = -\sin(2\theta_0)\). But \(r_0 = \sin(2\theta_0)\). So we need \(\sin(2\theta_0) = -\sin(2\theta_0)\), i.e., \(\sin(2\theta_0) = 0\). This is not always true.

But! The point \((r_0, -\theta_0)\) can also be written as \((-r_0, \pi - \theta_0)\). Does \((-r_0, \pi - \theta_0)\) lie on \(r = \sin(2\theta)\)?

We need \(-r_0 = \sin(2(\pi - \theta_0)) = \sin(2\pi - 2\theta_0) = -\sin(2\theta_0) = -r_0\). ✓

Yes! So the reflected point, in its alternative representation, satisfies the equation. The symmetry is real; the naïve test just didn't catch it because it only tried one representation.

Summary of what can happen:

  Algebraic test passes  →  Symmetry is definitely present. ✓
  Algebraic test fails   →  Symmetry may STILL be present.
                            Must check alternative representations.

docs.title: 5. Complete Decision Procedure
docs.text:
To rigorously determine whether \(r = f(\theta)\) is symmetric about the polar axis, you should check both forms:

About polar axis: symmetric if either

  1. \(f(-\theta) = f(\theta)\) (primary), or
  2. Replacing \((r, \theta)\) by \((-r, \pi - \theta)\) leaves the equation unchanged: \(-r = f(\pi - \theta)\) is equivalent to the original.

About \(\theta = \pi/2\): symmetric if either

  1. \(f(\pi - \theta) = f(\theta)\) (primary), or
  2. Replacing \((r, \theta)\) by \((-r, -\theta)\): \(-r = f(-\theta)\) is equivalent to the original.

About the pole: symmetric if either

  1. \(f(\theta + \pi) = f(\theta)\) (primary), or
  2. Replacing \(r\) by \(-r\) leaves the equation unchanged: \(-r = f(\theta)\) implies \(r = f(\theta)\).

docs.title: 6. Important Logical Consequence
docs.text:
Proposition. If a curve has any two of the three symmetries, it automatically has the third.

Proof. Let \(S_1\) = symmetry about polar axis, \(S_2\) = symmetry about \(\theta = \pi/2\), \(S_3\) = symmetry about pole.

\(S_3\) = (rotation by \(\pi\)) = (reflection in \(x\)-axis) \(\circ\) (reflection in \(y\)-axis) = \(S_1 \circ S_2\).

So: \(S_1\) and \(S_2 \Rightarrow S_3\). Similarly, \(S_1\) and \(S_3 \Rightarrow S_2\), and \(S_2\) and \(S_3 \Rightarrow S_1\). \(\square\)

Practical use. If you establish polar axis symmetry and \(\theta = \pi/2\) symmetry, you get symmetry about the pole for free.

docs.title: 7. Symmetry and Integration: The Payoff
docs.text:
The real value of symmetry in calculus is halving (or quartering) integrals.

Theorem. If \(r = f(\theta)\) is symmetric about the polar axis, then the area enclosed is:

\[A = 2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \int_0^\pi [f(\theta)]^2, d\theta = \int_0^\pi [f(\theta)]^2, d\theta\]

instead of integrating over \([0, 2\pi]\).

General principle. If the curve has an \(n\)-fold rotational symmetry (e.g., a \(2n\)-petal rose), integrate over \(1/n\)-th of the full period and multiply by \(n\).

docs.title: 7.1 Example: Area of \(r = \cos(2\theta)\) (4-petal rose)
docs.text:
The rose \(r = \cos(2\theta)\) has 4-fold symmetry (symmetric about both axes and the pole). Compute the area of one petal, then multiply by 4.

One petal exists for \(\theta \in [-\pi/4, \pi/4]\) (where \(r \geq 0\)):

\[A_{\text{petal}} = \frac{1}{2}\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} \cos^2(2\theta), d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} \frac{1 + \cos(4\theta)}{2}, d\theta\] \[= \frac{1}{4}\left[\theta + \frac{\sin(4\theta)}{4}\right]_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} = \frac{1}{4}\left[\frac{\pi}{4} + 0 - \left(-\frac{\pi}{4} + 0\right)\right] = \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{\pi}{8}\]

Total area \(= 4 \cdot \frac{\pi}{8} = \frac{\pi}{2}\).

Without symmetry, you would integrate over \([0, 2\pi]\) and carefully subtract the \(r < 0\) contributions — far more error-prone.

docs.title: 7.2 Example: Area of a Limaçon \(r = 2 + \cos\theta\)
docs.text:
Symmetric about polar axis (\(f(-\theta) = 2 + \cos(-\theta) = 2 + \cos\theta\)):

\[A = \int_0^\pi (2 + \cos\theta)^2, d\theta = \int_0^\pi (4 + 4\cos\theta + \cos^2\theta), d\theta\] \[= \int_0^\pi \left(4 + 4\cos\theta + \frac{1 + \cos(2\theta)}{2}\right)d\theta = \left[4\theta + 4\sin\theta + \frac{\theta}{2} + \frac{\sin(2\theta)}{4}\right]_0^\pi\] \[= 4\pi + 0 + \frac{\pi}{2} + 0 = \frac{9\pi}{2}\]

docs.title: 8. Symmetry in Named Curves: A Complete Table
docs.text:
Curve Equation Polar Axis \(\theta = \pi/2\) Pole Notes Circle \(r = a\) ✓ ✓ ✓ All symmetries Cardioid (right) \(r = a(1+\cos\theta)\) ✓ ✗ ✗ Opens right Cardioid (up) \(r = a(1+\sin\theta)\) ✗ ✓ ✗ Opens up Limaçon \(r = b + a\cos\theta\) ✓ ✗ ✗ 3-petal rose \(r = \cos(3\theta)\) ✓ ✗ ✗ 3-fold, not 2-fold 4-petal rose \(r = \cos(2\theta)\) ✓ ✓ ✓ All three 4-petal rose \(r = \sin(2\theta)\) ✓* ✓* ✓ *Test fails but symmetry holds Lemniscate \(r^2 = a^2\cos(2\theta)\) ✓ ✗ ✓ Lemniscate \(r^2 = a^2\sin(2\theta)\) ✗ ✓* ✓ Archimedean spiral \(r = a\theta\) ✗ ✗ ✗ No symmetry Log spiral \(r = ae^{b\theta}\) ✗ ✗ ✗ Self-similar only

*Symmetry present but not detected by primary sufficient test alone.

docs.title: 9. \(n\)-fold Rotational Symmetry of Rose Curves
docs.text:
This deserves special treatment. The curve \(r = \cos(n\theta)\) has a rotational symmetry of order \(n\) (if \(n\) is odd) or \(2n\) (if \(n\) is even):

Odd \(n\): \(r = \cos(n\theta)\) has \(n\) petals. It has \(n\)-fold symmetry (invariant under rotation by \(2\pi/n\)). It passes through the pole \(n\) times (once per petal).

Even \(n\): \(r = \cos(n\theta)\) has \(2n\) petals. It has \(2n\)-fold symmetry. The extra petals arise because when \(r < 0\), the point plots on the opposite side.

Why does even \(n\) double the petals?

At \(\theta \in [0, 2\pi]\), the function \(\cos(n\theta)\) takes both positive and negative values. When \(\cos(n\theta) < 0\), we have \(r < 0\), which plots the point in the direction \(\theta + \pi\). So the "negative" values of \(r\) trace petals that the "positive" values didn't. For even \(n\), these negative petals fall in the gaps between the positive petals, yielding \(2n\) total. For odd \(n\), the negative petals overlap with the positive petals (same directions), yielding only \(n\) total.

r = cos(2θ): 4 petals          r = cos(3θ): 3 petals

     ✿                               ❧
  (even n)                        (odd n)
  negative r fills the gaps      negative r overlaps

docs.title: 11. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
docs.text: Symmetry in polar curves is not merely an analytic convenience. It is a special case of the pervasive principle of equivariance and invariance that structures modern deep learning.

docs.title: 11.1 Symmetry as a Form of Prior Knowledge
docs.text:
When we observe that \(r = f(-\theta) = f(\theta)\) (polar axis symmetry), we are encoding that the function does not depend on the sign of the angle — only the magnitude. This is a constraint on the function space. In ML terms:

A model is invariant to a transformation \(T\) if \(f(T(x)) = f(x)\). A model is equivariant to \(T\) if \(f(T(x)) = T'(f(x))\) for some related transformation \(T'\).

The polar axis symmetry of a loss function \(\mathcal{L}(\theta)\) (say, as a function of a 2D parameter) means the loss has the same value at conjugate angles — the optimizer can exploit this to reduce search space.

docs.title: 11.2 Symmetry and Data Augmentation
docs.text:
If the true data-generating distribution has polar axis symmetry (e.g., a physical system that is symmetric about a fixed axis), then data augmentation by reflection is valid and provably optimal. The augmented training set is the orbit of the data under the symmetry group.

This is exactly what is done in image classification: horizontal flips (axis symmetry), 90° rotations (4-fold symmetry), etc. The theory is: if the distribution has symmetry \(G\), a model that is \(G\)-invariant requires exponentially less data than a generic model (Vapnik-Chervonenkis theory with symmetry constraints).

docs.title: 11.3 Symmetric Kernels
docs.text:
A kernel \(k(x, x')\) that depends only on \(|x - x'|\) is radially symmetric — it is symmetric about every axis through the origin in the difference space. The Gram matrix \(K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j)\) inherits this symmetry: it is symmetric (\(K = K^T\)), which is why SVMs and Gaussian Processes are PSD (positive semidefinite) by construction.

In polar terms: a kernel \(k(r)\) that is a function of \(r = |x - x'|\) alone is invariant under all rotations — the maximal possible symmetry in polar coordinates.

docs.title: 11.4 Even/Odd Decomposition and Neural Activation Functions
docs.text:
Any function can be decomposed into its even and odd parts:

\[f(\theta) = \underbrace{\frac{f(\theta) + f(-\theta)}{2}}_{\text{even part}} + \underbrace{\frac{f(\theta) - f(-\theta)}{2}}_{\text{odd part}}\]

The even part has polar axis symmetry; the odd part is anti-symmetric.

This decomposition appears directly in activation function analysis:

  • ReLU: \(\text{ReLU}(x) = \frac{x + |x|}{2}\). The even part is \(|x|/2\), the odd part is \(x/2\). ReLU is neither even nor odd.
  • Tanh: an odd function (\(\tanh(-x) = -\tanh(x)\)). This means networks with tanh activations can represent odd functions exactly with one layer, but need extra width for even functions.
  • GELU and Swish: approximately odd near zero, breaking symmetry away from origin.

The Fourier features \(\cos(n\theta)\) (even, polar axis symmetric) and \(\sin(n\theta)\) (odd, anti-symmetric) form the complete basis for \(L^2([0, 2\pi])\) — and their even/odd nature is exactly why they are mutually orthogonal.

docs.title: 11.5 Equivariant Neural Networks for Molecular Data
docs.text:
In molecular property prediction (drug discovery, materials science), molecules are described by 3D atomic coordinates. The energy of a molecule is invariant under rotation and reflection — it has full SO(3) \(\times\) \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) symmetry (the symmetry group of a sphere in polar coordinates).

Models like SchNet, DimeNet, and SE(3)-Transformers are architecturally constrained to respect this symmetry. In spherical coordinates \((r, \theta, \phi)\), the angular part decomposes into spherical harmonics \(Y_\ell^m(\theta, \phi)\) — the 3D generalization of the polar rose curves \(r = \cos(n\theta)\). An equivariant network maps spherical harmonic features to spherical harmonic features, preserving the symmetry exactly.

docs.title: 11.6 Summary
docs.text: Polar Symmetry Concept ML / DL Analogue \(f(-\theta) = f(\theta)\) (even function) Even activation, symmetric kernel \(f(\pi - \theta) = f(\theta)\) (axis symmetry) Equivariant to reflection \(f(\theta + \pi) = f(\theta)\) (pole symmetry) Invariant to 180° rotation \(n\)-fold rose symmetry \(\mathbb{Z}_n\)-equivariant network Sufficient test fails but symmetry holds Implicit symmetry from representation Symmetry → halved integral Symmetry → halved sample complexity Spherical harmonics = 3D polar modes SE(3)-equivariant GNNs (SchNet, DimeNet)

docs.title: 12. Worked Problem Bank
docs.text:
Problem 1. Determine all symmetries of \(r = 3 - 3\sin heta\).

Polar axis: \(f(- heta) = 3 - 3\sin(- heta) = 3 + 3\sin heta eq f( heta)\). Secondary: \(-r = f(\pi - heta)\)? \(3 - 3\sin(\pi - heta) = 3 - 3\sin heta = f( heta)\). That's not \(-r = f(\pi- heta)\)... Let's just test: is \((r, \pi - heta)\) on the curve when \((r, heta)\) is? We need \(r = 3 - 3\sin(\pi - heta) = 3 - 3\sin heta\) ✓. So symmetric about \( heta = \pi/2\).

\( heta = \pi/2\): \(f(\pi - heta) = 3 - 3\sin(\pi - heta) = 3 - 3\sin heta = f( heta)\). ✓ Symmetric about \( heta = \pi/2\).

Pole: \(f( heta + \pi) = 3 - 3\sin( heta + \pi) = 3 + 3\sin heta eq f( heta)\). No.

Answer: Symmetric about \( heta = \pi/2\) only (it is the upward-opening cardioid).

Problem 2. \(r^2 = 4\sin(2 heta)\). Find all symmetries.

Polar axis: Replace \( heta o - heta\): \(r^2 = 4\sin(-2 heta) = -4\sin(2 heta)\). Since \(r^2 \geq 0\) and \(-4\sin(2 heta)\) can be negative, this is not the same. Secondary: replace \((r, heta) o (-r, \pi - heta)\): \((-r)^2 = 4\sin(2(\pi - heta)) = 4\sin(2\pi - 2 heta) = -4\sin(2 heta)\). Still not the same. ✗

\( heta = \pi/2\): \(f(\pi - heta)\): \(r^2 = 4\sin(2(\pi- heta)) = 4\sin(2\pi - 2 heta) = -4\sin(2 heta)\). ✗ Primary fails. Secondary \((-r, - heta)\): \(r^2 = 4\sin(-2 heta) = -4\sin(2 heta)\). ✗

Pole: Replace \(r o -r\): \((-r)^2 = r^2\). Equation unchanged. ✓ Symmetric about pole.

Answer: Symmetric about the pole only. (This lemniscate is tilted 45° relative to the standard one.)

Problem 3. Compute the total area enclosed by \(r = \sin(3 heta)\) using symmetry.

The 3-petal rose. Check: \(f(- heta) = \sin(-3 heta) = -\sin(3 heta) eq f( heta)\). Secondary: \(-r = f(\pi - heta)\): \(-r = \sin(3\pi - 3 heta) = \sin(3\pi)\cos(3 heta) - \cos(3\pi)\sin(3 heta) = 0 + \sin(3 heta)\). So \(-r = \sin(3 heta)\), i.e., the reflected point \((-r, \pi - heta)\) satisfies the equation \(r = \sin(3 heta)\) ✓ (since \((-r, \pi- heta)\) means \(r' = -r = \sin(3 heta)\) when we rename \(r' o r\)... this requires care).

Actually let's just note: \(\sin(3 heta) = 0\) at \( heta = 0, \pi/3, 2\pi/3, \pi, \ldots\). Petals lie on \( heta = \pi/6, \pi/2, 5\pi/6\). The curve is symmetric about the \(y\)-axis (the test via \((-r, - heta)\): \(r = \sin(3 heta)\) and the reflected point \((-r, - heta)\): does \(-r = \sin(-3 heta) = -\sin(3 heta)\), i.e., \(r = \sin(3 heta)\) ✓). So symmetric about polar axis via this secondary form.

By symmetry, all 3 petals have equal area. Compute one petal on \([0, \pi/3]\) (where \(r \geq 0\)):

\[A_{ ext{petal}} = rac{1}{2}\int_0^{\pi/3}\sin^2(3 heta), d heta = rac{1}{4}\int_0^{\pi/3}(1 - \cos(6 heta)), d heta\] \[= rac{1}{4}\left[ heta - rac{\sin(6 heta)}{6} ight]_0^{\pi/3} = rac{1}{4}\left[ rac{\pi}{3} - 0 ight] = rac{\pi}{12}\]

Total \(= 3 \cdot rac{\pi}{12} = rac{\pi}{4}\).

docs.title: 13. Summary
docs.text:
THREE SYMMETRIES IN POLAR COORDINATES:

  1. About polar axis (x-axis):
       Primary test:    f(-θ) = f(θ)
       Secondary test:  replacing (r,θ) with (-r, π-θ) preserves equation

  2. About θ = π/2 (y-axis):
       Primary test:    f(π-θ) = f(θ)
       Secondary test:  replacing (r,θ) with (-r, -θ) preserves equation

  3. About pole (origin):
       Primary test:    f(θ+π) = f(θ)  OR  replacing r with -r preserves equation

  KEY LOGICAL FACTS:
    • Any 2 of the 3 symmetries imply the 3rd
    • Failing primary test ≠ no symmetry (non-uniqueness of polar representation)
    • Always try both primary and secondary tests before concluding

  INTEGRATION PAYOFF:
    • 1 symmetry  →  integrate over half the domain, ×2
    • 2 symmetries →  integrate over quarter domain, ×4
    • n-fold rose  →  integrate one petal, ×n

docs.title: Tangents to Polar
docs.text: "The derivative in polar coordinates is not a polar object — it is a Cartesian slope computed via a parametric detour. Understanding this detour is understanding the geometry."

docs.title: 0. The Central Idea
docs.text:
A polar curve \(r = f(\theta)\) is not given as \(y = g(x)\). So "the slope of the tangent" is not immediately meaningful in polar language. The strategy:

  1. Reparametrize. Treat \(\theta\) as the parameter, writing \(x(\theta) = f(\theta)\cos\theta\) and \(y(\theta) = f(\theta)\sin\theta\).
  2. Apply parametric differentiation. The slope of the tangent is \(dy/dx = (dy/d\theta)/(dx/d\theta)\).
  3. Interpret geometrically. Horizontal tangents, vertical tangents, and the behavior at the pole all have clean geometric meanings.

Everything reduces to parametric curve theory — which means every theorem you proved for parametric curves applies here immediately.

docs.title: 1. Derivation of the Slope Formula
docs.text:
Let \(r = f(\theta)\), where \(f\) is differentiable. The Cartesian parametrization is:

\[x(\theta) = f(\theta)\cos\theta, \qquad y(\theta) = f(\theta)\sin\theta\]

Differentiate both with respect to \(\theta\) using the product rule:

\[\frac{dx}{d\theta} = f'(\theta)\cos\theta - f(\theta)\sin\theta\] \[\frac{dy}{d\theta} = f'(\theta)\sin\theta + f(\theta)\cos\theta\]

By the parametric chain rule \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/d\theta}{dx/d\theta}\):

\[\boxed{\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{f'(\theta)\sin\theta + f(\theta)\cos\theta}{f'(\theta)\cos\theta - f(\theta)\sin\theta}}\]

or equivalently, writing \(r\) for \(f(\theta)\) and \(r'\) for \(f'(\theta)\):

\[\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{r'\sin\theta + r\cos\theta}{r'\cos\theta - r\sin\theta}\]

This is valid whenever the denominator is nonzero. Points where both numerator and denominator vanish require separate analysis (they correspond to singular points or the pole).

docs.title: 1.1 Verification Against Cartesian
docs.text:
For the horizontal line \(\theta = \pi/4\) (i.e., \(y = x\)), we can write \(r = C/(\cos\theta - \sin\theta)^{-1}\)... this is awkward. Instead verify on a circle: \(r = a\) (constant), so \(f'(\theta) = 0\).

\[\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{0 \cdot \sin\theta + a\cos\theta}{0 \cdot \cos\theta - a\sin\theta} = \frac{a\cos\theta}{-a\sin\theta} = -\cot\theta\]

For the circle \(x^2 + y^2 = a^2\), implicit differentiation gives \(2x + 2yy' = 0 \Rightarrow y' = -x/y = -(a\cos\theta)/(a\sin\theta) = -\cot\theta\). ✓

docs.title: 2. Horizontal Tangents
docs.text:
A horizontal tangent occurs where \(dy/dx = 0\), i.e., the numerator vanishes while the denominator does not.

\[\frac{dy}{d\theta} = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{dx}{d\theta} \neq 0\] \[\Updownarrow\] \[r'\sin\theta + r\cos\theta = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad r'\cos\theta - r\sin\theta \neq 0\]

Geometric meaning. The tangent line is parallel to the \(x\)-axis (polar axis). The curve has a local extremum in the \(y\)-direction.

docs.title: 3. Vertical Tangents
docs.text:
A vertical tangent occurs where \(dy/dx\) is undefined with a nonzero numerator:

\[\frac{dx}{d\theta} = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{dy}{d\theta} \neq 0\] \[\Updownarrow\] \[r'\cos\theta - r\sin\theta = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad r'\sin\theta + r\cos\theta \neq 0\]

Geometric meaning. The tangent line is parallel to the \(y\)-axis. The curve has a local extremum in the \(x\)-direction.

docs.title: 4. Worked Example: Cardioid \(r = 1 + \cos\theta\)
docs.text:
This is the central example. We find all horizontal and vertical tangents and determine the tangent at the pole.

\(f(\theta) = 1 + \cos\theta\), \(\quad f'(\theta) = -\sin\theta\).

\[\frac{dy}{d\theta} = -\sin\theta \cdot \sin\theta + (1 + \cos\theta)\cos\theta = -\sin^2\theta + \cos\theta + \cos^2\theta\] \[= \cos(2\theta) + \cos\theta\]

Using \(\cos(2\theta) = 2\cos^2\theta - 1\):

\[\frac{dy}{d\theta} = 2\cos^2\theta + \cos\theta - 1 = (2\cos\theta - 1)(\cos\theta + 1)\] \[\frac{dx}{d\theta} = -\sin\theta\cos\theta - (1+\cos\theta)\sin\theta = -\sin\theta(\cos\theta + 1 + \cos\theta) = -\sin\theta(1 + 2\cos\theta)\]

docs.title: 4.1 Horizontal Tangents
docs.text:
Set \(\frac{dy}{d\theta} = 0\): \((2\cos\theta - 1)(\cos\theta + 1) = 0\).

Case 1: \(\cos\theta = 1/2 \Rightarrow \theta = \pi/3\) or \(\theta = 5\pi/3\).

  • \(\theta = \pi/3\): \(r = 1 + 1/2 = 3/2\). Check \(dx/d\theta = -(\sqrt{3}/2)(1 + 1) = -\sqrt{3} \neq 0\). ✓
    • Cartesian: \(x = (3/2)\cos(\pi/3) = 3/4\), \(y = (3/2)\sin(\pi/3) = 3\sqrt{3}/4\).
  • \(\theta = 5\pi/3\): \(r = 3/2\). By symmetry: \((3/4, -3\sqrt{3}/4)\).

Case 2: \(\cos\theta = -1 \Rightarrow \theta = \pi\).

  • \(r = 1 + (-1) = 0\). The curve is at the pole. Check: \(dx/d\theta = -\sin(\pi)(1 + 2(-1)) = 0\). Both vanish — this is a singular point at the pole. Handle separately (see §6).

Horizontal tangents: at \((3/4, \pm 3\sqrt{3}/4)\).

docs.title: 4.2 Vertical Tangents
docs.text:
Set \(\frac{dx}{d\theta} = 0\): \(-\sin\theta(1 + 2\cos\theta) = 0\).

Case 1: \(\sin\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \theta = 0\) or \(\theta = \pi\).

  • \(\theta = 0\): \(r = 2\). Check \(dy/d\theta = (2(1) - 1)(1 + 1) = 1 \cdot 2 = 2 \neq 0\). ✓
    • Cartesian: \((2, 0)\).
  • \(\theta = \pi\): \(r = 0\). Both \(dy/d\theta\) and \(dx/d\theta\) vanish — singular point again.

Case 2: \(1 + 2\cos\theta = 0 \Rightarrow \cos\theta = -1/2 \Rightarrow \theta = 2\pi/3\) or \(\theta = 4\pi/3\).

  • \(\theta = 2\pi/3\): \(r = 1 - 1/2 = 1/2\). Check \(dy/d\theta = (2(-1/2)-1)(-1/2+1) = (-2)(1/2) = -1 \neq 0\). ✓
    • Cartesian: \(x = (1/2)(-1/2) = -1/4\), \(y = (1/2)(\sqrt{3}/2) = \sqrt{3}/4\).
  • \(\theta = 4\pi/3\): \(r = 1/2\). By symmetry: \((-1/4, -\sqrt{3}/4)\).

Vertical tangents: at \((2, 0)\) and \((-1/4, \pm\sqrt{3}/4)\).

Cardioid r = 1 + cosθ with tangent points marked:

              (3/4, 3√3/4)  ← horizontal tangent
                   •
                  / \
    VT •─────── /   \ ─────• (2,0) ← vertical tangent
  (-1/4, √3/4)  \   /
                  \ /
                   • ← cusp at pole (θ = π)
              (3/4,-3√3/4) ← horizontal tangent

docs.title: 5. Worked Example: Rose Curve \(r = \cos(2\theta)\)
docs.text:
\(f(\theta) = \cos(2\theta)\), \(\quad f'(\theta) = -2\sin(2\theta)\).

\[\frac{dy}{d\theta} = -2\sin(2\theta)\sin\theta + \cos(2\theta)\cos\theta\] \[\frac{dx}{d\theta} = -2\sin(2\theta)\cos\theta - \cos(2\theta)\sin\theta\]

Finding horizontal tangents on the first petal (\(\theta \in [-\pi/4, \pi/4]\)):

Use double-angle identities \(\sin(2\theta) = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta\), \(\cos(2\theta) = 1 - 2\sin^2\theta\):

\[\frac{dy}{d\theta} = -4\sin\theta\cos\theta\sin\theta + (1-2\sin^2\theta)\cos\theta = \cos\theta(-4\sin^2\theta + 1 - 2\sin^2\theta)\] \[= \cos\theta(1 - 6\sin^2\theta)\]

Setting to zero on \((-\pi/4, \pi/4)\): either \(\cos\theta = 0\) (not in range) or \(\sin^2\theta = 1/6\), so \(\sin\theta = \pm 1/\sqrt{6}\), giving \(\theta = \pm\arcsin(1/\sqrt{6})\).

At \(\theta = \arcsin(1/\sqrt{6})\): \(r = \cos(2\theta) = 1 - 2/6 = 2/3\).

The tip of the petal is at \(\theta = 0\): \(r = 1\), and \(dy/d\theta = \cos(0)(1 - 0) = 1 \neq 0\), \(dx/d\theta = 0 - \sin(0) = 0\). So the petal tip has a vertical tangent, as expected by symmetry.

docs.title: 6. Tangents at the Pole
docs.text:
The pole (\(r = 0\)) requires special treatment. When \(r = 0\) and \(f'( heta) eq 0\), both \(x( heta)\) and \(y( heta)\) equal zero, and the formula for \(dy/dx\) becomes \(0/0\).

However, we can evaluate the limit:

\[\lim_{ heta o heta_0} rac{dy/d heta}{dx/d heta} = \lim_{ heta o heta_0} rac{f'( heta)\sin heta + f( heta)\cos heta}{f'( heta)\cos heta - f( heta)\sin heta}\]

At \( heta = heta_0\) where \(f( heta_0) = 0\) and \(f'( heta_0) eq 0\):

\[= rac{f'( heta_0)\sin heta_0 + 0}{f'( heta_0)\cos heta_0 - 0} = rac{\sin heta_0}{\cos heta_0} = an heta_0\]

Theorem. If \(f( heta_0) = 0\) and \(f'( heta_0) eq 0\), then the curve \(r = f( heta)\) passes through the pole with tangent direction \( heta = heta_0\).

Geometric interpretation. The tangent line at the pole is simply the ray at angle \( heta_0\). The curve departs the pole along the ray \( heta = heta_0\) and returns along \( heta = heta_0 + \pi\) (if it passes through the pole again).

Corollary. If \(f( heta_0) = f( heta_1) = 0\) for two distinct values \( heta_0, heta_1 \in [0, 2\pi)\), and \(f'( heta_0), f'( heta_1) eq 0\), then the curve crosses itself at the pole and the two tangent directions are \( heta_0\) and \( heta_1\).

docs.title: 6.1 Example: Rose \(r = \sin(2\theta)\)
docs.text:
The curve passes through the pole at \(\theta = 0, \pi/2, \pi, 3\pi/2\).

\(f'(\theta) = 2\cos(2\theta)\).

  • \(\theta = 0\): \(f'(0) = 2 \neq 0\). Tangent direction \(\theta = 0\) (positive \(x\)-axis).
  • \(\theta = \pi/2\): \(f'(\pi/2) = 2\cos(\pi) = -2 \neq 0\). Tangent direction \(\theta = \pi/2\) (positive \(y\)-axis).
  • \(\theta = \pi\): tangent direction \(\theta = \pi\).
  • \(\theta = 3\pi/2\): tangent direction \(\theta = 3\pi/2\).

The four tangent lines at the pole are the coordinate axes — and they are mutually perpendicular, reflecting the 4-fold symmetry of the rose. ✓

docs.title: 6.2 Example: Cardioid \(r = 1 + \cos\theta\) at the Pole
docs.text:
\(f(\pi) = 0\), \(f'(\pi) = -\sin(\pi) = 0\). Both vanish! The cardioid is not smooth at the pole — it has a cusp. This is the characteristic shape of the cardioid's pointed bottom.

To analyze the cusp, higher-order terms are needed (expand \(f(\theta)\) around \(\theta = \pi\)).

Smooth crossing at pole:              Cusp at pole:
  r = sin(2θ)                           r = 1 + cosθ

    \  |  /                                  |
     \ | /                                  /|\
      \|/     ← four tangent lines          / | \
  ────●────                              ───●───   (pole)
      /|\                                   |
     / | \                              tangent undefined
    /  |  \

docs.title: 7. The Angle \(\psi\) Between the Radius Vector and the Tangent
docs.text:
This is an elegant result not always covered in introductory courses, but it appears naturally and is worth knowing.

Definition. Let \(\psi\) be the angle from the radius vector \(\overrightarrow{OP}\) (the ray at angle \(\theta\)) to the tangent line at \(P\), measured counter-clockwise.

Theorem.

\[\tan\psi = \frac{r}{dr/d\theta} = \frac{r}{r'}\]

Proof. The radius vector makes angle \(\theta\) with the polar axis. The tangent makes angle \(\phi\) with the polar axis, where \(\tan\phi = dy/dx\). So \(\psi = \phi - \theta\).

\[\tan\psi = \tan(\phi - \theta) = \frac{\tan\phi - \tan\theta}{1 + \tan\phi\tan\theta}\]

Substituting \(\tan\phi = \frac{r'\sin\theta + r\cos\theta}{r'\cos\theta - r\sin\theta}\) and \(\tan\theta = \sin\theta/\cos\theta\), after simplification:

\[\tan\psi = \frac{r}{r'} \qquad \square\]

Geometric consequences:

  • If \(r' = 0\) at a point, then \(\tan\psi \to \infty\), i.e., \(\psi = \pi/2\): the tangent is perpendicular to the radius. This occurs at the tip of a rose petal (where \(r\) is maximum).
  • If \(r = 0\) (at the pole), \(\tan\psi = 0\), i.e., \(\psi = 0\): the tangent coincides with the radius vector — confirming the theorem of §6.
  • For the equiangular (logarithmic) spiral \(r = ae^{b\theta}\): \(r' = abe^{b\theta} = br\), so \(\tan\psi = r/(br) = 1/b = \text{const}\). The angle \(\psi\) is constant for all points on the spiral — this is the defining property of the logarithmic spiral.
The angle ψ:

         tangent line
        /
       /  ← ψ (angle between radius and tangent)
      /ψ
─────●──────────────→ radius vector (angle θ)
     P

For log spiral r = ae^{bθ}: ψ = arctan(1/b) everywhere.
Self-similar: the spiral "looks the same" from every point.

docs.title: 8. Second Derivative and Concavity
docs.text:
For completeness: the second derivative \(d^2y/dx^2\) in polar coordinates. Since \(dy/dx\) is itself a function of \(\theta\):

\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right) = \frac{\frac{d}{d\theta}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)}{\frac{dx}{d\theta}}\]

Let \(Q(\theta) = dy/dx\) (computed by the formula in §1). Then:

\[\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{Q'(\theta)}{dx/d\theta} = \frac{Q'(\theta)}{r'\cos\theta - r\sin\theta}\]

This is rarely needed in introductory work but appears in curvature calculations.

Curvature formula in polar. The signed curvature of \(r = f(\theta)\) is:

\[\kappa = \frac{r^2 + 2(r')^2 - rr''}{[r^2 + (r')^2]^{3/2}}\]

This follows from the parametric curvature formula \(\kappa = (x'y'' - y'x'')/[(x')^2 + (y')^2]^{3/2}\) applied to the polar parametrization.

docs.title: 9. Complete Worked Example: Limaçon \(r = 1 + 2\sin\theta\)
docs.text:
This limaçon has an inner loop (since \(|2| > |1|\)). Let's find all tangents and understand the inner loop geometrically.

\(f(\theta) = 1 + 2\sin\theta\), \(\quad f'(\theta) = 2\cos\theta\).

\[\frac{dy}{d\theta} = 2\cos\theta\sin\theta + (1+2\sin\theta)\cos\theta = \cos\theta(2\sin\theta + 1 + 2\sin\theta) = \cos\theta(1 + 4\sin\theta)\] \[\frac{dx}{d\theta} = 2\cos\theta\cos\theta - (1+2\sin\theta)\sin\theta = 2\cos^2\theta - \sin\theta - 2\sin^2\theta\] \[= 2(\cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta) - \sin\theta = 2\cos(2\theta) - \sin\theta\]

Horizontal tangents: \(\cos\theta(1 + 4\sin\theta) = 0\).

  • \(\cos\theta = 0\): \(\theta = \pi/2\) or \(3\pi/2\).
    • \(\theta = \pi/2\): \(r = 1 + 2 = 3\). Check \(dx/d\theta = 2(-1) - 1 = -3 \neq 0\). ✓ Point: \((0, 3)\).
    • \(\theta = 3\pi/2\): \(r = 1 - 2 = -1\). \(r < 0\): actual point is at distance 1 in direction \(3\pi/2 + \pi = \pi/2\), so \((0, 1)\). Check \(dx/d\theta = 2(-1) - (-1) = -1 \neq 0\). ✓
  • \(\sin\theta = -1/4\): \(\theta = \pi + \arcsin(1/4)\) or \(\theta = -\arcsin(1/4)\) (i.e., \(2\pi - \arcsin(1/4)\)).
    • At \(\theta = -\arcsin(1/4)\): \(r = 1 + 2(-1/4) = 1/2\).
    • At \(\theta = \pi + \arcsin(1/4)\): \(r = 1 + 2(-1/4) = 1/2\).

Inner loop. The inner loop forms when \(r < 0\), which occurs when \(1 + 2\sin\theta < 0\), i.e., \(\sin\theta < -1/2\), i.e., \(\theta \in (7\pi/6, 11\pi/6)\).

The inner loop passes through the pole at \(\theta = 7\pi/6\) and \(\theta = 11\pi/6\).

Tangent at pole for \(\theta = 7\pi/6\): direction \(7\pi/6\) (i.e., \(210°\)). Tangent at pole for \(\theta = 11\pi/6\): direction \(11\pi/6\) (i.e., \(330°\)).

These two tangent lines cross at the pole at angle \(|330° - 210°| = 120°\) to each other — the inner loop self-intersects at the pole with a \(120°\) crossing angle.

Limaçon r = 1 + 2sinθ:

      (0,3) ← horizontal tangent
        •
       / \       outer loop
      /   \
─────●─────● ← (r=0 crossings, pole)
      \   /
       \_/   ← inner loop

The inner loop lives where r < 0 (θ ∈ (7π/6, 11π/6))
Self-intersection at pole, crossing angle = 120°

docs.title: 11. Visualization
docs.text:
TANGENT VECTOR GEOMETRY IN POLAR:

      y
      |       P = (r, θ)
      |      •  ← tangent direction (slope = dy/dx)
      |     /|
      |    / |         The slope dy/dx is a Cartesian quantity,
      |   /  |         computed via the parametric chain rule.
      |  / ψ |
      | /    |
      |/ θ   |
      O──────────────→ x

      ψ = angle from radius OP to tangent at P
      θ = angle of radius OP from polar axis
      φ = θ + ψ = angle of tangent from polar axis

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

TANGENT AT THE POLE:

  If r = f(θ₀) = 0, f'(θ₀) ≠ 0:

        tangent = ray at angle θ₀
       /
      /  θ₀
  ───O──────────────→ polar axis
  (pole)

  The curve ENTERS the pole along θ₀ and DEPARTS along θ₀ + π.

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

THREE SCENARIOS AT r = 0:

  f(θ₀) = 0, f'(θ₀) ≠ 0  →  smooth pass through pole
  f(θ₀) = 0, f'(θ₀) = 0  →  CUSP (e.g., cardioid tip)
  f(θ₀) = f(θ₁) = 0      →  SELF-INTERSECTION at pole

docs.title: 12. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
docs.text: The mathematics of tangent lines in polar coordinates connects to ML in ways that are structural, not cosmetic.

docs.title: 12.1 Gradient as a Tangent Object
docs.text:
In machine learning, the gradient \(\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}\) is the tangent direction of steepest ascent of the loss \(\mathcal{L}\) as a function of model parameters \(\theta\). When the parameter space is naturally polar (e.g., phase angles in complex-valued networks, or directions in weight space), the formula for \(dy/dx\) in polar coordinates is literally the expression for how the loss changes as you move tangentially along a polar curve in parameter space.

More precisely: if the loss landscape restricted to a 2D subspace of parameter space is described by a polar curve \(r = f(\phi)\) (level set or gradient flow curve), then:

\[\frac{d\mathcal{L}}{d\phi}\bigg|_{\text{tangent}} = \frac{dy/d\phi}{dx/d\phi} \cdot \cos\alpha - \sin\alpha\]

where \(\alpha\) encodes the parameterization choice. This is exactly the polar tangent formula in a different notation.

docs.title: 12.2 Loss Surface Curvature and \(\kappa\)
docs.text:
The curvature formula \(\kappa = \frac{r^2 + 2(r')^2 - rr''}{[r^2+(r')^2]^{3/2}}\) measures how rapidly the tangent direction rotates. In the loss landscape:

  • High curvature = sharp minimum = poor generalization (the Hessian has large eigenvalues).
  • Low curvature = flat minimum = better generalization.

SAM (Sharpness-Aware Minimization) explicitly seeks minima with small \(\kappa\) along all directions — i.e., it minimizes the maximum curvature of the loss surface, exactly the quantity \(\kappa\) measures in polar parametrizations of 2D cross-sections.

docs.title: 12.3 Logarithmic Spiral and Adam Optimizer
docs.text:
The logarithmic spiral \(r = ae^{b\theta}\) has constant \(\psi = \arctan(1/b)\) — the tangent makes a fixed angle with the radius at every point. This self-similar structure means the spiral "looks the same" at every scale.

The Adam optimizer update has a similar self-similar property: by normalizing the gradient by its running second moment, Adam implicitly adapts the step length to be proportional to the "radius" in parameter space from the initialization. The effective trajectory of Adam in a quadratic loss is approximately a logarithmic spiral toward the minimum — the angle \(\psi\) is governed by the ratio of the learning rate to the second-moment estimate.

docs.title: 12.4 Tangents and Decision Boundaries
docs.text:
A classification decision boundary \(f(x) = 0\) in 2D can often be expressed in polar coordinates, especially for radially-structured data. The tangent to the decision boundary at a point \(P\) determines the local geometry of the margin.

For an SVM with RBF kernel, the decision boundary in polar coordinates near the support vectors behaves like a smooth polar curve. The condition for a support vector is that the margin is exactly 1 — geometrically, the tangent to the decision boundary at the support vector is perpendicular to the weight vector \(\mathbf{w}\). In polar terms: \(\psi = \pi/2\), i.e., \(r' = 0\) (a petal tip condition).

docs.title: 12.5 Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK)
docs.text:
The Neural Tangent Kernel \(\Theta(x, x') = abla_W f_W(x) \cdot abla_W f_W(x')\) measures the inner product of gradients (tangent vectors) in parameter space. In the infinite-width limit, training a neural network is equivalent to kernel regression with kernel \(\Theta\).

The tangent vector \( abla_W f_W(x)\) at input \(x\) is precisely the derivative of the output with respect to parameters — the "tangent direction" of the output function as the network moves through parameter space. The polar tangent formula computes the same object in a 2D parametric setting.

docs.title: 12.6 Summary Table
docs.text: Polar Tangent Concept ML / DL Analogue \(dy/dx\) via parametric chain rule Gradient via chain rule (backprop) Horizontal tangent: \(dy/d\theta = 0\) Gradient zero in output direction Vertical tangent: \(dx/d\theta = 0\) Gradient zero in input direction Cusp at pole: \(f = f' = 0\) Non-smooth loss (ReLU kink) \(\tan\psi = r/r'\) (equiangular spiral) Adam's self-similar parameter updates Curvature \(\kappa\) Sharpness of loss minimum (SAM) Neural Tangent Kernel Inner product of polar tangent vectors

docs.title: 13. Exercises
docs.text:
1. (Stewart §10.3) Find the slope of the tangent to \(r = 2\sin\theta\) at \(\theta = \pi/6\). Verify by converting to Cartesian form and differentiating implicitly.

  2. Find all horizontal and vertical tangents to \(r = 2 + 2\sin\theta\) (cardioid opening upward). Classify the tangent at the pole.

  3. (Rose) For \(r = \cos(3\theta)\), find the tangent direction at the pole for each passage through the origin. How many distinct tangent directions are there, and what angles do they make?

  4. (Angle \(\psi\)) Show that for the Archimedean spiral \(r = a\theta\) (\(a > 0\)), \(\tan\psi = \theta\). Describe geometrically what happens to \(\psi\) as \(\theta \to \infty\).

  5. (Lemniscate) For \(r^2 = a^2\cos(2\theta)\), find \(dr/d\theta\) implicitly, then compute \(dy/dx\) at \(\theta = \pi/6\). What happens as \(\theta \to \pi/4\)?

  6. (Curvature) Compute the curvature \(\kappa\) of the circle \(r = 2a\cos\theta\) at an arbitrary point and verify it equals \(1/(a)\) (radius of circle = \(a\), curvature = \(1/a\)).

  7. (ML-flavored) A 2D loss landscape restricted to a ray from the origin is described by \(r = 1 - e^{-\theta^2}\) (a curve that starts at the pole and approaches \(r = 1\)). Compute \(\tan\psi\) as \(\theta \to 0^+\) and \(\theta \to \infty\). Interpret: is the gradient direction aligned with or transverse to the radial direction at initialization (\(\theta \approx 0\))?
