docs.title: Graphing Polar
docs.text: "Before you integrate, before you differentiate — you must see. A polar curve that you cannot sketch from its equation is a curve you do not yet understand."

docs.title: 0. The Philosophy of Polar Graphing
docs.text:
In Cartesian coordinates, graphing \(y = f(x)\) is mechanical: sweep \(x\) left to right, plot height \(f(x)\). The geometry is transparent because the axes are the geometry.

In polar coordinates, graphing \(r = f(\theta)\) is genuinely different. As \(\theta\) increases, you rotate around the origin, and the curve is traced by a point at distance \(r(\theta)\) from the pole. When \(r < 0\), the point appears on the opposite side of the pole. The curve can cross itself, loop back, retrace, and produce far more intricate shapes than the equation suggests.

The discipline required: You must think simultaneously about angle (direction) and radius (distance), and you must track the sign of \(r\) carefully. The reward is that a one-line equation like \(r = \cos(2\theta)\) produces a four-petalled rose — and once you understand why, no memorization is needed.

docs.title: 1. The Systematic Graphing Procedure
docs.text:
Here is the procedure I always follow, in order. Do not skip steps.

Step 1 — Check symmetry. Apply the three symmetry tests. Every symmetry you establish halves (or quarters) the work. (See: [[Symmetry in Polar Curves]])

Step 2 — Find zeros and maximum \(|r|\). Solve \(f(\theta) = 0\) — these are the angles where the curve passes through the pole. Find \(\theta\) where \(|f(\theta)|\) is maximum — these are the farthest points from the pole.

Step 3 — Find where \(r\) changes sign. Between consecutive zeros of \(f\), determine the sign of \(r\). When \(r > 0\), the point is in the direction \(\theta\). When \(r < 0\), it is in the direction \(\theta + \pi\).

Step 4 — Build a table of key values. Evaluate \(r\) at \(\theta = 0, \pi/6, \pi/4, \pi/3, \pi/2, 2\pi/3, 3\pi/4, 5\pi/6, \pi\) and by symmetry fill in the rest. Add any special angles from Steps 2–3.

Step 5 — Plot the key points in polar form. Mark them on a polar grid (concentric circles at \(r = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\) and rays at multiples of \(\pi/6\) or \(\pi/4\)).

Step 6 — Connect smoothly. Join the points with a smooth curve, respecting the direction of increasing \(\theta\). Note where the curve is approaching or leaving the pole.

Step 7 — Verify with Cartesian conversion (optional). Convert special points to \((x, y)\) and check they lie in the expected position.

docs.title: 2. Polar Graph Paper: The Mental Model
docs.text:
POLAR GRID (mental reference — commit this to memory):

              π/2 (90°)
               |
         2π/3  |  π/3
              \|/
    5π/6  ────•────  π/6
              /|\
        π ──•─O─•── 0 = 2π   ← polar axis
              \|/
    7π/6  ────•────  11π/6
              /|\
         4π/3  |  5π/3
               |
             3π/2 (270°)

Concentric circles: r = 1, 2, 3, ...
Rays at multiples of π/6 (30°) and π/4 (45°).

KEY QUADRANT FACTS:
  θ ∈ [0, π/2]:      1st quadrant  (r > 0 → upper right)
  θ ∈ [π/2, π]:      2nd quadrant  (r > 0 → upper left)
  θ ∈ [π, 3π/2]:     3rd quadrant  (r > 0 → lower left)
  θ ∈ [3π/2, 2π]:    4th quadrant  (r > 0 → lower right)

  r < 0 at angle θ → plots in OPPOSITE quadrant

docs.title: 3. Graphing Circles and Lines
docs.text: These are the base cases — understand them completely before moving to more complex curves.

docs.title: 3.1 Circle \(r = a\)
docs.text:
All points at distance \(|a|\) from the pole. This is the circle \(x^2 + y^2 = a^2\).

r = 2:

      ╭───╮
     │  O  │   radius 2, centered at pole
      ╰───╯

docs.title: 3.2 Circle \(r = 2a\cos\theta\)
docs.text:
Convert: \(r^2 = 2ar\cos\theta \Rightarrow x^2 + y^2 = 2ax \Rightarrow (x-a)^2 + y^2 = a^2\).

Circle of radius \(|a|\), centered at \((a, 0)\). Passes through the pole (since \(r = 0\) when \(\theta = \pi/2\)).

r = 2cosθ  (a = 1):

       ╭──╮
      │    │
   ─O─╯    ╰   center at (1, 0), radius 1

Traced once as θ goes from -π/2 to π/2.
At θ = π/2 or -π/2: r = 0 (at the pole).
At θ = 0: r = 2 (rightmost point).

docs.title: 3.3 Circle \(r = 2a\sin\theta\)
docs.text: Similarly: \((x)^2 + (y-a)^2 = a^2\). Circle centered at \((0, a)\), passes through pole.

docs.title: 3.4 Line \(\theta = \alpha\)
docs.text: All points at angle \(\alpha\) from the polar axis, for any \(r\) (including \(r < 0\), giving the opposite ray). This is the full line through the pole at angle \(\alpha\).

docs.title: 3.5 Line \(r = \frac{d}{\cos(\theta - \alpha)}\)
docs.text: A line at perpendicular distance \(d\) from the pole, with the perpendicular foot in direction \(\alpha\).

docs.title: 4. Graphing Limaçons: \(r = b \pm a\cos\theta\) or \(r = b \pm a\sin\theta\)
docs.text:
The limaçon family is controlled by the ratio \(k = a/b\):

Condition Shape \(k < 1\) (i.e., \(a < b\)) Convex limaçon (no dimple, no loop) \(k = 1\) (i.e., \(a = b\)) Cardioid \(1 < k < 2\) Limaçon with inner dimple \(k \geq 2\) (i.e., \(a \geq 2b\)) Limaçon with inner loop

docs.title: 4.1 Full Analysis: Cardioid \(r = 1 + \cos\theta\)
docs.text:
Symmetry: \(f(-\theta) = 1 + \cos\theta = f(\theta)\) → symmetric about polar axis.

Zeros: \(r = 0\) when \(\cos\theta = -1\), i.e., \(\theta = \pi\). Passes through pole once.

Maximum: \(r = 2\) at \(\theta = 0\).

Key values (upper half only, by symmetry):

\(\theta\) \(r = 1 + \cos\theta\) Approx Cartesian \((x, y)\) \(0\) \(2\) \(2.00\) \((2, 0)\) \(\pi/6\) \(1 + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) \(1.87\) \((1.62, 0.93)\) \(\pi/3\) \(3/2\) \(1.50\) \((0.75, 1.30)\) \(\pi/2\) \(1\) \(1.00\) \((0, 1)\) \(2\pi/3\) \(1/2\) \(0.50\) \((-0.25, 0.43)\) \(5\pi/6\) \(1 - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) \(0.13\) \((-0.11, 0.07)\) \(\pi\) \(0\) \(0\) \((0, 0)\) ← pole

Graphing narrative:

  • Start at \(\theta = 0\): point \((2, 0)\), the rightmost tip.
  • As \(\theta\) increases from \(0\) to \(\pi\): \(r\) decreases from \(2\) to \(0\). The point spirals inward counter-clockwise, tracing the upper half of the cardioid.
  • At \(\theta = \pi\): arrives at the pole, forming a cusp (since \(f'(\pi) = -\sin(\pi) = 0\)).
  • From \(\theta = \pi\) to \(2\pi\): by symmetry with the upper half, the lower half is traced.
Cardioid r = 1 + cosθ:

            (0,1)
             •
           /   \
         /       \
(-.25,.43)•      •(2,0)    ← maximum radius
         \       /
           \   /
             •
           (pole, cusp)

Shape: like a heart, cusp pointing LEFT,
       maximum extent to the RIGHT.

docs.title: 4.2 Full Analysis: Limaçon with Inner Loop \(r = 1 + 2\cos\theta\)
docs.text:
Here \(a/b = 2 > 1\), so there is an inner loop.

Zeros: \(r = 0\) when \(\cos\theta = -1/2\), i.e., \(\theta = 2\pi/3\) and \(\theta = 4\pi/3\).

Sign of \(r\):

  • \(\theta \in [0, 2\pi/3)\): \(\cos\theta > -1/2\), so \(r > 0\).
  • \(\theta \in (2\pi/3, 4\pi/3)\): \(\cos\theta < -1/2\), so \(r < 0\) → inner loop (points reflect through pole).
  • \(\theta \in (4\pi/3, 2\pi]\): \(r > 0\) again.

Maximum: \(r = 3\) at \(\theta = 0\). Inner loop maximum: \(|r| = 1\) at \(\theta = \pi\) (\(r = -1\), so \(|r| = 1\)).

\(\theta\) \(r\) Sign Direction plotted \(0\) \(3\) \(+\) \(\theta = 0\) \(\pi/3\) \(2\) \(+\) \(\theta = \pi/3\) \(\pi/2\) \(1\) \(+\) \(\theta = \pi/2\) \(2\pi/3\) \(0\) — pole \(5\pi/6\) \(-\sqrt{3}+1 \approx -0.73\) \(-\) \(\theta = 5\pi/6 + \pi = 11\pi/6\) \(\pi\) \(-1\) \(-\) \(\theta = 0\) (inner loop on pos. \(x\)-axis) \(7\pi/6\) \(-\sqrt{3}+1\) \(-\) \(\theta = \pi/6\) \(4\pi/3\) \(0\) — pole

Inner loop narrative:

When \(\theta \in (2\pi/3, 4\pi/3)\), we have \(r < 0\). The point plots at angle \(\theta + \pi\), with distance \(|r|\) from the pole. So:

  • At \(\theta = \pi\): \(r = -1\), point at \((-(-1), \pi + \pi) = (1, 0)\) in polar → the Cartesian point \((1, 0)\). This is inside the outer loop.

The inner loop is traced as \(\theta\) sweeps from \(2\pi/3\) to \(4\pi/3\), but the actual point moves in the angular range \([2\pi/3 + \pi, 4\pi/3 + \pi] = [5\pi/3, 7\pi/3]\), i.e., back around the right side of the plane.

Limaçon r = 1 + 2cosθ:

         outer loop
        ╭────────╮
       │           │
  ─────●─────────────●────  (r=3)
       │   ╭───╮   │
        ╰──│   │──╯
           ╰───╯
           inner loop
           (traced when r < 0)

Outer loop: r > 0, θ ∈ [0,2π/3] ∪ [4π/3, 2π]
Inner loop: r < 0, θ ∈ [2π/3, 4π/3]

docs.title: 5. Graphing Rose Curves: \(r = a\cos(n\theta)\) and \(r = a\sin(n\theta)\)
docs.text:
The petal count rule:

  • \(n\) odd: \(n\) petals.
  • \(n\) even: \(2n\) petals.

Why? (See the rigorous argument in [[Symmetry in Polar Curves]].)

For odd \(n\): when \(r < 0\) during \(\theta \in (\pi/(2n), 3\pi/(2n))\) etc., the negative-\(r\) portions retrace petals that were already drawn with \(r > 0\), just approached from the opposite direction.

For even \(n\): the negative-\(r\) portions draw new petals in the gaps, doubling the count.

docs.title: 5.1 Full Analysis: 4-Petal Rose \(r = \cos(2\theta)\)
docs.text:
Symmetry: \(f(-\theta) = \cos(-2\theta) = \cos(2\theta)\) → about polar axis. \(f(\pi - \theta) = \cos(2\pi - 2\theta) = \cos(2\theta)\) → about \(\theta = \pi/2\). By the proposition (any two → all three): also about the pole.

Zeros: \(\cos(2\theta) = 0 \Rightarrow 2\theta = \pi/2 + k\pi \Rightarrow \theta = \pi/4, 3\pi/4, 5\pi/4, 7\pi/4\). Four zeros → four passages through the pole.

Maxima: \(r = \pm 1\) at \(\theta = 0, \pi/2, \pi, 3\pi/2\).

Sign analysis over \([0, 2\pi]\):

\(\theta\) interval \(2\theta\) interval \(\cos(2\theta)\) \(r\) sign Petal \([0, \pi/4]\) \([0, \pi/2]\) \(+\) \(+\) Petal 1 (right) \([\pi/4, 3\pi/4]\) \([\pi/2, 3\pi/2]\) \(-\) \(-\) Petal 2* (upper, via \(r<0\)) \([3\pi/4, 5\pi/4]\) \([3\pi/2, 5\pi/2]\) \(+\) \(+\) Petal 3 (left) \([5\pi/4, 7\pi/4]\) \([5\pi/2, 7\pi/2]\) \(-\) \(-\) Petal 4* (lower, via \(r<0\)) \([7\pi/4, 2\pi]\) \([7\pi/2, 4\pi]\) \(+\) \(+\) Returns to Petal 1

*Petals 2 and 4 are drawn with \(r < 0\). At \(\theta = \pi/2\), \(r = \cos(\pi) = -1\), so the point is at distance 1 in direction \(\pi/2 + \pi = 3\pi/2\) — the downward direction. But by the full sign table, the upper petal (\(r < 0\), \(\theta \in [\pi/4, 3\pi/4]\)) actually traces upward since the reflected direction points upward.

Let me be explicit. At \(\theta = \pi/2\): \(r = -1\). Point: distance 1, direction \(\pi/2 + \pi = 3\pi/2\). That is \((0, -1)\) in Cartesian — downward, not upward. So the petal drawn during \(\theta \in [\pi/4, 3\pi/4]\) with \(r < 0\) is actually the downward petal (Petal 4), not the upper one.

Wait — let's redo this carefully.

At \(\theta = \pi/2\): \(r = \cos(\pi) = -1\) → point at \((|r|, \theta + \pi) = (1, 3\pi/2)\) → Cartesian \((0, -1)\).

So during \(\theta \in [\pi/4, 3\pi/4]\): \(r < 0\), actual direction = \(\theta + \pi \in [5\pi/4, 7\pi/4]\) — the lower half. This draws the bottom two petals.

The full tracing order:

  1. \(\theta \in [0, \pi/4]\): Right petal traced outward.
  2. \(\theta \in [\pi/4, 3\pi/4]\): \(r < 0\) → bottom two petals partially traced.
  3. \(\theta \in [3\pi/4, 5\pi/4]\): Left petal.
  4. \(\theta \in [5\pi/4, 7\pi/4]\): \(r < 0\) → top two petals partially traced.
  5. \(\theta \in [7\pi/4, 2\pi]\): Back to right petal start.

The standard description (right, top, left, bottom petals at \(\theta = 0, \pi/2, \pi, 3\pi/2\)) is correct; it's the order of tracing that requires care.

4-petal rose r = cos(2θ):

         top petal
            •
            |
left  •──── O ────•  right
  petal     |      petal
            •
         bottom petal

Petal tips at θ = 0 (right), π/2 (top? — check!),
π (left), 3π/2 (bottom).

At θ = π/2: r = cos(π) = -1 → point at (1, 3π/2) = (0,-1).
So the petal at θ = π/2 is actually the BOTTOM petal (via r < 0).
The TOP petal is traced at θ = 3π/2: r = cos(3π) = -1 → (1, π/2) = (0,1). ✓

docs.title: 5.2 Full Analysis: 3-Petal Rose \(r = \cos(3\theta)\)
docs.text:
Zeros: \(3\theta = \pi/2 + k\pi \Rightarrow \theta = \pi/6, \pi/2, 5\pi/6, 7\pi/6, 3\pi/2, 11\pi/6\).

Six passages through the pole during \([0, 2\pi]\).

Sign over \([0, \pi]\) (then check if lower half retraces):

\(\theta\) \(r = \cos(3\theta)\) Sign \([0, \pi/6]\) positive \(+\) → Petal 1 (right) \([\pi/6, \pi/2]\) negative \(-\) → points in \([\pi/6+\pi, \pi/2+\pi] = [7\pi/6, 3\pi/2]\) \([\pi/2, 5\pi/6]\) positive \(+\) → Petal 2 (upper left) \([5\pi/6, \pi]\) negative \(-\) → points in \([5\pi/6+\pi, 2\pi] = [11\pi/6, 2\pi]\)

During \(\theta \in [\pi/6, \pi/2]\) with \(r < 0\): actual direction \(\in [7\pi/6, 3\pi/2]\) (lower left to downward). This traces the lower left petal (Petal 3's bottom half).

For odd \(n = 3\): petals lie at \(\theta = 0, 2\pi/3, 4\pi/3\) (where \(r = 1\)). The three petals are equally spaced at \(120°\). The \(r < 0\) segments retrace each petal from the other side, not creating new petals.

3-petal rose r = cos(3θ):

      Petal 2 ↗
         •
        / \
       /   \
   ───O─────•──  Petal 1 (θ=0, r=1, point at (1,0))
       \   /
        \ /
         •
      Petal 3 ↘

Petals at angles 0°, 120°, 240°.
Each petal has length r = 1.
Odd n → n petals (the r<0 portions retrace existing petals).

docs.title: 5.3 The General Rose \(r = a\cos(n\theta)\): Key Facts Summary
docs.text:
ROSE CURVE FACTS:

  r = a·cos(nθ):                                  
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  n odd:  n petals, each of length a         │
  │          Petals at θ = 0, 2π/n, 4π/n, ...  │
  │          Symmetric about polar axis         │
  │                                             │
  │  n even: 2n petals, each of length a        │
  │          Petals at θ = 0, π/n, 2π/n, ...   │
  │          Symmetric about BOTH axes + pole   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  r = a·sin(nθ):  same counts, but ROTATED by π/(2n)

  Area of ONE petal = πa²/(4n)   [derive via ½∫r²dθ]
  Total area:
    n odd:  n · πa²/(4n) = πa²/4
    n even: 2n · πa²/(4n) = πa²/2

docs.title: 6. Graphing the Lemniscate: \(r^2 = a^2\cos(2\theta)\)
docs.text:
This is qualitatively different — \(r^2\) rather than \(r\), so \(r\) is only defined where \(\cos(2\theta) \geq 0\).

Domain: \(\cos(2\theta) \geq 0 \Leftrightarrow 2\theta \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2] \cup [3\pi/2, 5\pi/2] \Leftrightarrow \theta \in [-\pi/4, \pi/4] \cup [3\pi/4, 5\pi/4]\).

The curve simply does not exist for \(\theta \in (\pi/4, 3\pi/4) \cup (5\pi/4, 7\pi/4)\).

Graphing:

  • At \(\theta = 0\): \(r = a\). Rightmost point \((a, 0)\).
  • As \(\theta \to \pi/4\): \(r \to 0\). Arrives at pole.
  • The curve traces the right lobe for \(\theta \in [-\pi/4, \pi/4]\).
  • For \(\theta \in [3\pi/4, 5\pi/4]\): traces the left lobe.
Lemniscate r² = a²cos(2θ):

        does not     does not
        exist here   exist here
          ↓               ↓
  ←──────── (π/4 to 3π/4: no curve) ────────→

Left lobe:  •────────────O────────────•  Right lobe
  (traced                             (traced
  θ∈[3π/4,5π/4])                    θ∈[-π/4, π/4])

Figure-eight shape. Each lobe is a closed curve
passing through the pole.
Resembles the symbol ∞.

Cartesian form: \(r^4 = a^2 r^2 \cos(2\theta) = a^2(r^2\cos^2\theta - r^2\sin^2\theta) = a^2(x^2 - y^2)\). Since \(r^2 = x^2 + y^2\): \((x^2 + y^2)^2 = a^2(x^2 - y^2)\).

docs.title: 7.1 Archimedean Spiral \(r = a\theta\), \(\theta \geq 0\)
docs.text:
• \(r\) increases linearly with \(\theta\). Each full revolution (\(\Delta\theta = 2\pi\)) increases \(r\) by \(2\pi a\).
  • The spacing between successive arms is constant: \(\Delta r = 2\pi a\).
Archimedean spiral r = θ (a=1):

         r increases by 2π per revolution

         ╭──────╮
        ╱    ╭──╯
       │    ╱
       ╰───O──────→

Arms equally spaced: Δr = 2π between adjacent arms.
No symmetry (r ≠ f(-θ) since θ ≥ 0 changes domain).

docs.title: 7.2 Logarithmic Spiral \(r = ae^{b\theta}\)
docs.text:
• For \(b > 0\): expands outward.
  • For \(b < 0\): contracts toward the pole.
  • Self-similar: \(\tan\psi = 1/b\) is constant — the curve cuts every ray at the same angle.
  • As \(\theta \to -\infty\) (for \(b > 0\)): \(r \to 0\), spiraling into the pole infinitely.
Log spiral r = e^{0.1θ}:

Arms get farther apart exponentially.
Same shape at every scale (self-similar).

        ╭────────╮
       ╱    ╭───╯
      │   ╭─╯
      ╰──O

The golden spiral (nautilus shell) is a log spiral.

docs.title: 8. A Systematic Graphing Example: \(r = 2\sin(3\theta)\)
docs.text:
This is a 3-petal rose (odd \(n = 3\)), using sine instead of cosine, so it is rotated.

Step 1 — Symmetry.

\(f(\pi - \theta) = 2\sin(3\pi - 3\theta) = 2\sin(3\pi)\cos(3\theta) - 2\cos(3\pi)\sin(3\theta) = 0 + 2\sin(3\theta) = f(\theta)\). ✓ Symmetric about \(\theta = \pi/2\).

Step 2 — Zeros. \(2\sin(3\theta) = 0 \Rightarrow 3\theta = k\pi \Rightarrow \theta = 0, \pi/3, 2\pi/3, \pi, 4\pi/3, 5\pi/3\).

Step 3 — Sign.

\(\theta\) interval \(\sin(3\theta)\) \(r\) Actual direction \((0, \pi/3)\) \(+\) \(> 0\) Same as \(\theta\) \((\pi/3, 2\pi/3)\) \(-\) \(< 0\) \(\theta + \pi\) \((2\pi/3, \pi)\) \(+\) \(> 0\) Same as \(\theta\) \((\pi, 4\pi/3)\) \(-\) \(< 0\) \(\theta + \pi\) \((4\pi/3, 5\pi/3)\) \(+\) \(> 0\) Same as \(\theta\) \((5\pi/3, 2\pi)\) \(-\) \(< 0\) \(\theta + \pi\)

For odd \(n\): positive-\(r\) intervals trace petals; negative-\(r\) intervals retrace those same petals from the other direction. Only 3 distinct petals.

Step 4 — Maximum \(r = 2\) at \(3\theta = \pi/2, 5\pi/2, 9\pi/2\), i.e., \(\theta = \pi/6, 5\pi/6, 3\pi/2\).

Petal tips: \((\pi/6, 2)\), \((5\pi/6, 2)\), \((3\pi/2, 2)\).

In Cartesian:

  • \(\theta = \pi/6\): \((2\cos(\pi/6), 2\sin(\pi/6)) = (\sqrt{3}, 1)\).
  • \(\theta = 5\pi/6\): \((-\sqrt{3}, 1)\).
  • \(\theta = 3\pi/2\): \((0, -2)\).

Step 5 — Key values table:

\(\theta\) \(r\) \(0\) \(0\) \(\pi/6\) \(2\) \(\pi/3\) \(0\) \(\pi/2\) \(-2\) (i.e., actual point \((0, 2)\) — wait: \(r = 2\sin(3\pi/2) = 2(-1) = -2\); point at direction \(\pi/2 + \pi = 3\pi/2\), distance 2 → \((0, -2)\)) \(2\pi/3\) \(0\) \(5\pi/6\) \(2\) \(\pi\) \(0\)

Step 6 — Sketch:

3-petal rose r = 2sin(3θ):

         • (-√3, 1)    • (√3, 1)
          \           /
      petal 2       petal 1
            \       /
             ──O──
                |
             petal 3
                •
              (0, -2)

Symmetry: about θ = π/2 (y-axis). ✓
Petals are at 30°, 150°, 270° (tilted vs r = cos(3θ) which has petals at 0°, 120°, 240°).

docs.title: 9. Recognizing Curve Type from Equation: A Quick Reference
docs.text:
Before graphing, identify the curve type from the equation's structure:

EQUATION RECOGNITION GUIDE:

  r = a                         → Circle (center at pole)
  r = 2a·cosθ or r = 2a·sinθ   → Circle (through pole)
  r = a ± b·cosθ (or sinθ)     → Limaçon family:
       a = b  →  Cardioid
       a > b  →  Convex/dimpled limaçon
       a < b  →  Limaçon with inner loop
  r = a·cos(nθ) or a·sin(nθ)   → Rose curve:
       n odd  →  n petals
       n even →  2n petals
  r² = a²·cos(2θ)               → Lemniscate (figure-eight)
  r² = a²·sin(2θ)               → Lemniscate (rotated 45°)
  r = aθ                        → Archimedean spiral
  r = ae^{bθ}                   → Logarithmic spiral
  r·cosθ = a  (i.e., x = a)    → Vertical line
  r·sinθ = b  (i.e., y = b)    → Horizontal line

docs.title: 10. Common Graphing Errors and How to Avoid Them
docs.text:
Error 1: Ignoring \(r < 0\).

The most common mistake. When \(r < 0\), the point is NOT at \((\text{negative distance}, \theta)\) — it is at \((|r|, \theta + \pi)\). Always check the sign of \(r\) in each interval.

Fix: In your sign table, explicitly write the "actual direction" column as in §8.

Error 2: Wrong petal count on rose curves.

Students often say "\(r = \cos(4\theta)\) has 4 petals" when it has 8.

Fix: Memorize the rule — even \(n\) gives \(2n\) petals. Alternatively, find all zeros of \(r\) in \([0, 2\pi]\) and count: \(r = \cos(n\theta) = 0\) at \(2n\) values of \(\theta\), and consecutive zeros bound one petal each.

Error 3: Conflating the parameter interval with the full curve.

For \(r = \cos(2\theta)\), the full curve is traced as \(\theta \in [0, 2\pi]\). For \(r = \cos\theta\), the full circle is traced in \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\) (the second half retraces).

Fix: Find the period of \(r = f(\theta)\). For \(f(\theta) = \cos(n\theta)\), the period is \(2\pi/n\). Trace over \([0, 2\pi]\) but note when retracing begins.

Error 4: Missing the symmetry → overworking.

Students compute all of \([0, 2\pi]\) when they could exploit symmetry to do half.

Fix: Always run the symmetry check first. Symmetric about polar axis → compute \([0, \pi]\) and reflect.

Error 5: Incorrect orientation of rotated curves.

\(r = a\cos\theta\) → circle on the right of the pole. \(r = a\sin\theta\) → circle on top. \(r = a\cos(n\theta)\) → first petal along positive \(x\)-axis. \(r = a\sin(n\theta)\) → first petal rotated by \(\pi/(2n)\).

Fix: The cos-version always has a feature on the polar axis. The sin-version is the cos-version rotated by \(\pi/(2n)\) (for rose) or \(\pi/2\) (for cardioid).

docs.title: 12. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
12.1 Polar Graphs as Visualization Tools in ML
docs.text: In ML model evaluation, radar charts (also called spider charts or polar charts) are direct applications of polar graphing: each metric (accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC) is assigned an angular direction, and performance is plotted as a polar curve. Comparing two models is equivalent to asking which polar region is larger — the area formula \(A = \frac{1}{2}\int r^2, d\theta\) quantifies this.

docs.title: 12.2 Feature Map Visualization via Rose Patterns
docs.text:
In convolutional neural networks, filters in the first layer learn oriented features — edges at various angles. Visualizing the orientation tuning of a neuron as a polar plot (response \(r\) as a function of angle \(\theta\) of the input edge) produces a rose-like curve. A neuron tuned to a single orientation produces a 2-petal rose (\(r = \cos^2\theta\) roughly); a neuron with broader tuning produces a more circular plot.

This is not metaphor — it is literally how orientation tuning curves are displayed in computational neuroscience and CNN interpretability research.

docs.title: 12.3 Limaçon-Shaped Decision Boundaries
docs.text: A linear classifier has a straight-line decision boundary. A kernel SVM or a neural network can produce curved boundaries. In polar coordinates centered at a cluster center, a smooth convex boundary looks like a limaçon (cardioid when the boundary passes through the origin; convex limaçon when it doesn't). Classifiers that produce boundaries with inner loops effectively create "islands" of one class inside the other — the inner loop encloses a pocket of the positive class inside the negative class.

docs.title: 12.4 Lemniscate and Information Geometry
docs.text: The lemniscate \(r^2 = a^2\cos(2\theta)\) satisfies \((x^2 + y^2)^2 = a^2(x^2 - y^2)\). In information geometry, the Fisher information metric on a family of probability distributions can produce level curves with this shape near saddle points of the KL divergence. The lemniscate's figure-eight form means there are two "basins" of nearby distributions, meeting at a point (the pole) — a geometric picture of bimodal model families.

docs.title: 12.5 Spiral Dynamics in Gradient Descent
docs.text:
The trajectory of gradient descent with momentum in a 2D quadratic loss \(\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}) = \frac{1}{2}(\lambda_1 w_1^2 + \lambda_2 w_2^2)\) with \(\lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2\) is an inward spiral. In polar coordinates centered at the minimum, this trajectory approximates a logarithmic spiral \(r = ae^{-b\theta}\) (contracting, \(b > 0\)). The spiral's winding is tighter when the condition number \(\lambda_2/\lambda_1\) is large — an ill-conditioned loss makes the spiral oscillate widely before converging. This is precisely why ill-conditioned problems are hard: the log spiral has many turns before \(r \approx 0\).

Preconditioning (used in Adam, AdaGrad, natural gradient) effectively makes \(\lambda_1 \approx \lambda_2\), converting the tight spiral into a nearly radial path — the angle \(\psi \approx \pi/2\) everywhere (perpendicular to the level curves), which is the steepest descent direction.

docs.title: 12.6 Sinusoidal Positional Encodings as Polar Plots
docs.text:
The positional encoding in the original Transformer (\(\text{PE}_{k,2i} = \sin(k/10000^{2i/d})\), \(\text{PE}_{k,2i+1} = \cos(k/10000^{2i/d})\)) can be read as: for each frequency band \(i\), the 2D vector \((\cos(\omega_i k), \sin(\omega_i k))\) traces a circle (the polar curve \(r = 1\)) as \(k\) increases. Different frequency bands trace this circle at different angular rates \(\omega_i\). The full positional encoding is a stack of these circular traces — a multi-frequency polar representation of position.

RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding) makes this exact: it applies a rotation by \(\omega_i k\) to each 2D subspace of the embedding, which is literally multiplication by the rotation matrix in polar form \(e^{i\omega_i k}\). The polar curve \(r = 1\) (unit circle) is the geometry underlying RoPE.

docs.title: 12.7 Summary Table
docs.text: Polar Graphing Concept ML / DL Analogue Radar/polar chart of metrics Model evaluation across multiple axes Rose curve = orientation tuning CNN filter visualization, V1 neurons Limaçon with inner loop Decision boundary with interior pocket Lemniscate (figure-eight) Bimodal information geometry Log spiral = grad. descent path GD with momentum in ill-conditioned loss \(r = 1\) (unit circle) Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) Petal count (odd/even \(n\)) Symmetry of learned representations

docs.title: 13. Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1. Sketch \(r = 3\cos\theta\) by identifying it as a circle. Find its center and radius. Verify: at what value of \(\theta\) does the curve pass through the pole?

Exercise 2. Sketch \(r = 2 - 2\sin\theta\). Classify (cardioid/dimpled/inner loop), determine symmetry, find the maximum \(r\), and identify where the cusp lies.

Exercise 3. (Stewart §10.3) For \(r = \cos(4\theta)\): how many petals? In which directions do the petal tips point? Compute the area of one petal.

Exercise 4. For \(r = 2 + 3\cos\theta\): find the values of \(\theta\) where \(r = 0\). Trace the inner loop carefully — what range of \(\theta\) produces the inner loop, and in what angular region of the plane does the inner loop lie?

Exercise 5. (Lemniscate) For \(r^2 = 9\sin(2\theta)\): determine the domain (which \(\theta\) give real \(r\)?), the symmetry, and sketch the curve.

Exercise 6. (MIT 18.02 flavored) A curve is defined by \(r = 1 - 2\sin(2\theta)\). This is NOT a standard limaçon. Analyze it: find all zeros and maxima of \(r\), determine all symmetries, identify how many times the curve passes through the pole and with what tangent directions, and produce a careful sketch.

Exercise 7. (Comparison) Sketch both \(r = \sin(2\theta)\) and \(r = \cos(2\theta)\) on the same polar axes. By what angle is one the rotation of the other? Verify using the identity \(\cos(2\theta) = \sin(2\theta + \pi/2)\).

Exercise 8. (ML-flavored) Consider the radar chart of two models A and B:

  • Model A: accuracy = 0.9, precision = 0.8, recall = 0.7, F1 = 0.74 (metrics at \(\theta = 0, \pi/2, \pi, 3\pi/2\)).
  • Model B: accuracy = 0.7, precision = 0.9, recall = 0.95, F1 = 0.92.

Treating the metrics as \(r\) values at equally spaced angles and connecting them as a polar curve, estimate which model has greater enclosed area. Which model would you prefer for a medical diagnosis task (where recall matters most)?

docs.title: Arc Length in Polar
docs.text: "Length is the most primitive geometric quantity. Before area, before curvature — you must be able to measure how long a curve is. In polar coordinates, this requires genuinely more work than in Cartesian, and the reward is a formula of surprising elegance."

docs.title: 0. Motivation and Setup
docs.text:
The arc length of a curve is defined as the limit of the total length of inscribed polygonal approximations as the segments become infinitesimally fine. In Cartesian coordinates, this produces the familiar formula \(L = \int_a^b \sqrt{1 + (y')^2}, dx\). In polar coordinates, we re-derive everything from the parametric viewpoint — and the derivation is the understanding.

A polar curve \(r = f(\theta)\) is a parametric curve with parameter \(\theta\):

\[x(\theta) = f(\theta)\cos\theta, \qquad y(\theta) = f(\theta)\sin\theta\]

The parametric arc length formula is:

\[L = \int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{d\theta}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dy}{d\theta}\right)^2}, d\theta\]

Everything reduces to computing the integrand.

docs.title: 1. Derivation of the Polar Arc Length Formula
docs.text:
From the polar parametrization, compute the derivatives using the product rule:

\[\frac{dx}{d\theta} = f'(\theta)\cos\theta - f(\theta)\sin\theta\] \[\frac{dy}{d\theta} = f'(\theta)\sin\theta + f(\theta)\cos\theta\]

Now square and add:

\[\left(\frac{dx}{d\theta}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dy}{d\theta}\right)^2\] \[= \bigl[f'(\theta)\cos\theta - f(\theta)\sin\theta\bigr]^2 + \bigl[f'(\theta)\sin\theta + f(\theta)\cos\theta\bigr]^2\]

Expand each square:

\[= [f'(\theta)]^2\cos^2\theta - 2f'(\theta)f(\theta)\sin\theta\cos\theta + [f(\theta)]^2\sin^2\theta$$ $$\quad + [f'(\theta)]^2\sin^2\theta + 2f'(\theta)f(\theta)\sin\theta\cos\theta + [f(\theta)]^2\cos^2\theta\]

The cross terms cancel. Collect:

\[= [f'(\theta)]^2(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta) + [f(\theta)]^2(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta)\] \[= [f'(\theta)]^2 + [f(\theta)]^2\]

Therefore:

\[\boxed{L = \int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2}, d\theta}\]

where \(r = f(\theta)\) and \(dr/d\theta = f'(\theta)\).

The cross-term cancellation is the key algebraic miracle. It is exactly the same identity that makes \(|e^{i\theta}|^2 = \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1\): the Pythagorean theorem absorbs all the mixed terms.

docs.title: 2. The Infinitesimal Arc Length Element
docs.text:
The integrand has a clean geometric interpretation. Define the arc length element in polar coordinates:

\[ds = \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2}, d\theta\]

This can be understood via a polar coordinate version of the Pythagorean theorem. Consider a small change \(d\theta\):

  • The point moves along the circle \(r = \text{const}\) by arc \(r, d\theta\) (tangential component).
  • The radius changes by \(dr = (dr/d\theta), d\theta\) (radial component).

These two infinitesimal displacements are perpendicular (the radial direction and the tangential direction on a circle are orthogonal). So by the Pythagorean theorem:

\[ds^2 = (r, d\theta)^2 + (dr)^2 = r^2, d\theta^2 + \left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2 d\theta^2 = \left[r^2 + \left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2\right]d\theta^2\] \[\Rightarrow ds = \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2}, d\theta\] 
INFINITESIMAL ARC LENGTH GEOMETRY:

                  ds (arc element)
                 /
                / ← hypotenuse
               /
  r·dθ ───── / ────────
  (tangential|          r·dθ = arc along circle
  component) |
             | dr (radial component)
             |
             O

  ds² = (r dθ)² + (dr)²

  The radial and tangential displacements are perpendicular.
  This perpendicularity is the geometric heart of the formula.

docs.title: 3. Comparison with Cartesian and Parametric Formulas
docs.text:
Setting Arc Length Formula Cartesian \(y = g(x)\) \(\displaystyle L = \int_a^b \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2}, dx\) Parametric \(x(t), y(t)\) \(\displaystyle L = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sqrt{\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2}, dt\) Polar \(r = f(\theta)\) \(\displaystyle L = \int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2}, d\theta\) Complex \(z(\theta) = re^{i\theta}\) $\displaystyle L = \int_\alpha^\beta

All four are instances of the same idea: integrate the magnitude of the velocity vector along the curve.

docs.title: 4. Important Caution: Retracing
docs.text:
The arc length formula measures the total length of the path traced, including any retracing. If the curve \(r = f(\theta)\) retraces itself as \(\theta\) varies over \([\alpha, \beta]\), the formula overcounts the geometric length of the curve.

Example. The circle \(r = \cos\theta\) is fully traced for \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\) (since \(r(0) = 1\), \(r(\pi/2) = 0\), \(r(\pi) = -1\) → same as \(r = 1\) at \(\theta = 0\) via alternative representation). If you integrate over \([0, 2\pi]\), you traverse the circle twice, getting \(L = 2\pi\) instead of the correct circumference \(\pi\).

Rule: Always identify the minimal period over which the curve is traced exactly once, and integrate over that interval.

For \(r = \cos\theta\) (circle): integrate over \([0, \pi]\). For \(r = \cos(n\theta)\) (one petal): integrate over \([0, \pi/(2n)]\) (where \(r\) goes from 0 to 1 and back to 0... actually, let's be careful below).

docs.title: 5. Worked Example 1: Circumference of the Circle \(r = a\)
docs.text:
\(r = a\) (constant), \(dr/d\theta = 0\).

\[L = \int_0^{2\pi} \sqrt{a^2 + 0}, d\theta = a \cdot 2\pi = 2\pi a\]

Trivially correct — the circumference of a circle of radius \(a\). ✓

docs.title: 6. Worked Example 2: Arc Length of the Cardioid \(r = a(1 + \cos\theta)\)
docs.text:
This is the canonical non-trivial example. It requires a half-angle identity.

\(r = a(1 + \cos\theta)\), \(\quad \dfrac{dr}{d\theta} = -a\sin\theta\).

Compute \(r^2 + (dr/d\theta)^2\):

\[r^2 + \left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2 = a^2(1+\cos\theta)^2 + a^2\sin^2\theta\] \[= a^2\bigl[1 + 2\cos\theta + \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta\bigr]\] \[= a^2\bigl[2 + 2\cos\theta\bigr] = 2a^2(1 + \cos\theta)\]

Now apply the half-angle identity: \(1 + \cos\theta = 2\cos^2(\theta/2)\).

\[r^2 + \left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2 = 4a^2\cos^2!\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\]

Therefore:

\[L = \int_0^{2\pi} \sqrt{4a^2\cos^2!\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}, d\theta = \int_0^{2\pi} 2a\left|\cos!\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\right|, d\theta\]

For \(\theta \in [0, 2\pi]\): \(\theta/2 \in [0, \pi]\), and \(\cos(\theta/2) \geq 0\) on \([0, \pi]\). So \(|\cos(\theta/2)| = \cos(\theta/2)\) throughout. No absolute value issue here.

\[L = 2a\int_0^{2\pi}\cos!\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)d\theta = 2a\left[2\sin!\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\right]_0^{2\pi} = 4a[\sin(\pi) - \sin(0)] = 4a \cdot 1 = 4a \cdot 1\]

Wait: \(\sin(\pi) = 0\). Let me recheck:

\[2a\int_0^{2\pi}\cos!\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)d\theta = 2a \cdot \left[2\sin!\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\right]_0^{2\pi} = 4a\left[\sin(\pi) - \sin(0)\right] = 4a[0 - 0]= 0?\]

That cannot be right. Recheck the antiderivative: \(\int \cos(\theta/2), d\theta = 2\sin(\theta/2) + C\). So:

\[L = 2a\left[2\sin!\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\right]_0^{2\pi} = 4a!\left[\sin(\pi) - \sin(0)\right] = 4a[0 - 0] = 0\]

This is wrong because \(\sin(\pi) = 0\), not \(1\). Let me redo more carefully.

\(\int_0^{2\pi} \cos(\theta/2), d\theta = \left[2\sin(\theta/2)\right]_0^{2\pi} = 2\sin(\pi) - 2\sin(0) = 0 - 0 = 0\).

This is wrong because cosine is not always positive on \([0, 2\pi]\) after the substitution... but we said \(|\cos(\theta/2)| = \cos(\theta/2)\) since \(\theta/2 \in [0, \pi]\) and \(\cos\) is not always non-negative there.

Careful: \(\cos(\theta/2) \geq 0\) iff \(\theta/2 \in [0, \pi/2]\), i.e., \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\). For \(\theta \in (\pi, 2\pi]\): \(\theta/2 \in (\pi/2, \pi]\), so \(\cos(\theta/2) \leq 0\).

Therefore \(|\cos(\theta/2)| \neq \cos(\theta/2)\) everywhere. We must split the integral:

\[L = 2a\int_0^{2\pi}\left|\cos!\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\right|d\theta = 2a\int_0^{\pi}\cos!\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)d\theta + 2a\int_\pi^{2\pi}\left(-\cos!\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\right)d\theta\]

By symmetry of \(|\cos(\theta/2)|\) about \(\theta = \pi\):

\[= 2 \cdot 2a\int_0^{\pi}\cos!\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)d\theta = 4a\left[2\sin!\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)\right]_0^{\pi} = 4a\bigl[2\sin(\pi/2) - 2\sin(0)\bigr] = 4a[2 \cdot 1] = 8a\] \[\boxed{L_{\text{cardioid}} = 8a}\]

Sanity check. For \(a = 1\): the cardioid fits inside a circle of radius 2. Its perimeter \(8\) is less than \(2\pi \cdot 2 \approx 12.57\). Plausible. ✓

CARDIOID ARC LENGTH:

  r = a(1 + cosθ)

  Key identity used:  1 + cosθ = 2cos²(θ/2)

  Key issue:  |cos(θ/2)| requires splitting at θ = π
              (cos(θ/2) ≥ 0 for θ ∈ [0, π])
              (cos(θ/2) ≤ 0 for θ ∈ [π, 2π])

  Without splitting → get 0 (catastrophic cancellation!)
  With splitting    → get 8a ✓

  Total length = 8a regardless of orientation.

docs.title: 7. Worked Example 3: Arc Length of One Petal of \(r = \cos(2\theta)\)
docs.text:
One petal of the 4-petal rose lies over \(\theta \in [-\pi/4, \pi/4]\) (where \(r \geq 0\)).

\(\dfrac{dr}{d\theta} = -2\sin(2\theta)\).

\[r^2 + \left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2 = \cos^2(2\theta) + 4\sin^2(2\theta) = \cos^2(2\theta) + 4(1 - \cos^2(2\theta))\] \[= 4 - 3\cos^2(2\theta)\] \[L_{\text{petal}} = \int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\sqrt{4 - 3\cos^2(2\theta)}, d\theta = 2\int_0^{\pi/4}\sqrt{4 - 3\cos^2(2\theta)}, d\theta\]

(used symmetry about \(\theta = 0\)). This integral does not reduce to elementary functions — it is an elliptic integral of the second kind.

Specifically, with the substitution \(u = 2\theta\):

\[L_{\text{petal}} = \int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{4 - 3\cos^2 u}, du = 2\int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{1 - \frac{3}{4}\cos^2 u}, du\] \[= 2\int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{1 - \frac{3}{4}(1 - \sin^2 u)}, du = 2\int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{\frac{1}{4} + \frac{3}{4}\sin^2 u}, du\]

This is \(2E(k)\) for a specific modulus \(k\) — an elliptic integral. The numerical value is approximately \(L_{\text{petal}} \approx 1.211\).

The lesson: most polar arc length integrals are not elementary. The cardioid is special because the half-angle identity collapses the integrand to a pure absolute value of cosine. Rose curves generically lead to elliptic integrals.

docs.title: 8. Worked Example 4: Arc Length of the Logarithmic Spiral \(r = ae^{b\theta}\), \(\theta \in [0, \Theta]\)
docs.text:
\(\dfrac{dr}{d\theta} = abe^{b\theta} = br\).

\[r^2 + \left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2 = r^2 + b^2r^2 = r^2(1 + b^2) = a^2e^{2b\theta}(1+b^2)\] \[L = \int_0^\Theta \sqrt{a^2 e^{2b\theta}(1+b^2)}, d\theta = a\sqrt{1+b^2}\int_0^\Theta e^{b\theta}, d\theta\] \[= a\sqrt{1+b^2} \cdot \frac{1}{b}\left[e^{b\theta}\right]_0^\Theta = \frac{a\sqrt{1+b^2}}{b}\left(e^{b\Theta} - 1\right)\] \[\boxed{L = \frac{a\sqrt{1+b^2}}{b}(e^{b\Theta} - 1)}\]

Geometric interpretation. Note \(r(\Theta) - r(0) = ae^{b\Theta} - a = a(e^{b\Theta} - 1)\). So:

\[L = \frac{\sqrt{1+b^2}}{b}\bigl(r(\Theta) - r(0)\bigr)\]

The arc length is proportional to the change in radius. Since \(\tan\psi = 1/b\) (the angle between the tangent and radius is constant), the factor \(\sqrt{1+b^2}/b = \sec\psi / \tan\psi = \csc\psi\)... actually: \(\tan\psi = 1/b\), so \(\sec^2\psi = 1 + \tan^2\psi = 1 + 1/b^2\), and \(\sec\psi = \sqrt{1+1/b^2}\). Hmm — let me restate cleanly.

Since \(\psi = \arctan(1/b)\): the radial displacement when moving along the curve by arc length \(ds\) is \(dr = ds \cdot \cos\psi\) (the radial component of the arc). So \(ds = dr/\cos\psi = dr \cdot \sec\psi\), and:

\[L = \sec\psi \cdot (r(\Theta) - r(0))\]

This is the simplest possible relationship: the arc length is just the radial increment scaled by \(\sec\psi\).

docs.title: 9. Worked Example 5: Arc Length of the Archimedean Spiral \(r = a\theta\), \(\theta \in [0, \Theta]\)
docs.text:
\(\dfrac{dr}{d\theta} = a\).

\[r^2 + \left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2 = a^2\theta^2 + a^2 = a^2(1 + \theta^2)\] \[L = a\int_0^\Theta\sqrt{1+\theta^2}, d\theta\]

This requires the standard integral \(\int\sqrt{1+\theta^2}, d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\left[\theta\sqrt{1+\theta^2} + \ln\left(\theta + \sqrt{1+\theta^2}\right)\right] + C\), derived by trigonometric (or hyperbolic) substitution \(\theta = \tan u\) or \(\theta = \sinh u\).

\[L = \frac{a}{2}\left[\Theta\sqrt{1+\Theta^2} + \ln\left(\Theta + \sqrt{1+\Theta^2}\right)\right]\]

For large \(\Theta\): \(\sqrt{1+\Theta^2} \approx \Theta\), so \(L \approx \frac{a}{2}[\Theta^2 + \ln(2\Theta)] \approx \frac{a\Theta^2}{2}\). The arc length grows quadratically in \(\Theta\) — each additional revolution (increasing \(\Theta\) by \(2\pi\)) adds more length than the previous one, because the spiral is further from the origin.

docs.title: 10. Surface Area of Revolution (Extension)
docs.text:
When a polar curve \(r = f(\theta)\) is revolved around the polar axis (the \(x\)-axis), it sweeps out a surface. The surface area element is \(dS = 2\pi y, ds\), giving:

\[S = 2\pi\int_\alpha^\beta y, ds = 2\pi\int_\alpha^\beta f(\theta)\sin\theta \cdot \sqrt{[f(\theta)]^2 + [f'(\theta)]^2}, d\theta\]

(Valid when \(y = r\sin\theta \geq 0\) throughout \([\alpha, \beta]\), i.e., \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\).)

Example. Surface area of the sphere generated by revolving \(r = a\) (semicircle, \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\)) around the polar axis:

\[S = 2\pi\int_0^\pi a\sin\theta \cdot \sqrt{a^2 + 0}, d\theta = 2\pi a^2\int_0^\pi\sin\theta, d\theta = 2\pi a^2[-\cos\theta]_0^\pi = 2\pi a^2 \cdot 2 = 4\pi a^2\]

The surface area of a sphere of radius \(a\) is \(4\pi a^2\). ✓

docs.title: 11. The Role of the Half-Angle Identity: A Pattern
docs.text:
The cardioid calculation succeeds because \(r^2 + (r')^2\) collapses to \(4a^2\cos^2(\theta/2)\) — a perfect square. This happens because the half-angle identity \(1 + \cos\theta = 2\cos^2(\theta/2)\) removes the square root.

When does this pattern occur? For limaçons \(r = a + b\cos\theta\):

\[r^2 + (r')^2 = (a + b\cos\theta)^2 + b^2\sin^2\theta = a^2 + 2ab\cos\theta + b^2\]

This is a perfect square only when \(a = b\) (the cardioid), giving \((a + a\cos\theta)^2 + a^2\sin^2\theta = a^2(2 + 2\cos\theta) = 4a^2\cos^2(\theta/2)\).

For \(a \neq b\): \(r^2 + (r')^2 = a^2 + b^2 + 2ab\cos\theta\). This is NOT a perfect square in general, and the integral becomes an elliptic integral. The cardioid is the unique limaçon whose arc length is expressible in elementary functions.

WHEN DOES POLAR ARC LENGTH HAVE A CLOSED FORM?

  Curve             r² + (r')²              Integrable?
  ─────────────     ──────────────────────  ────────────
  Circle r = a      a²                      Yes (trivial)
  Cardioid          4a²cos²(θ/2)            Yes (half-angle)
  Log spiral        r²(1 + b²)              Yes (exponential)
  Archimedean       a²(1 + θ²)             Yes (trig sub)
  Rose r=cos(nθ)    4-3cos²(2θ) etc.        No (elliptic)
  Gen. limaçon      a²+b²+2ab cosθ          No (elliptic)

docs.title: 12. Numerical Arc Length
docs.text:
When a closed form is unavailable (rose curves, general limaçons), numerical integration applies directly.

Simpson's Rule for \(L = \int_\alpha^\beta g(\theta), d\theta\) where \(g(\theta) = \sqrt{r^2 + (r')^2}\):

Partition \([\alpha, \beta]\) into \(n\) (even) subintervals of width \(h = (\beta - \alpha)/n\):

\[L \approx \frac{h}{3}\bigl[g(\theta_0) + 4g(\theta_1) + 2g(\theta_2) + 4g(\theta_3) + \cdots + 4g(\theta_{n-1}) + g(\theta_n)\bigr]\]

Error bound: \(|E_S| \leq \frac{(\beta - \alpha)^5}{180n^4} \max_{\theta \in [\alpha,\beta]} |g^{(4)}(\theta)|\).

For most polar curves, \(n = 100\) gives arc length accurate to 5+ decimal places.

docs.title: 13. Summary of Key Formulas
docs.text: \[\boxed{L = \int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2}, d\theta}\] \[ds = \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2}, d\theta \qquad \text{(arc length element)}\] \[ds^2 = dr^2 + r^2, d\theta^2 \qquad \text{(metric in polar coordinates)}\] Curve Arc Length Circle \(r = a\) \(2\pi a\) Cardioid \(r = a(1+\cos\theta)\) \(8a\) Log spiral \(r = ae^{b\theta}\), \(\theta \in [0, \Theta]\) \(\dfrac{a\sqrt{1+b^2}}{b}(e^{b\Theta}-1)\) Archimedean spiral \(r = a\theta\), \(\theta \in [0, \Theta]\) \(\dfrac{a}{2}\left[\Theta\sqrt{1+\Theta^2} + \sinh^{-1}(\Theta)\right]\)

docs.title: 15. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
15.1 Arc Length as a Regularizer
docs.text:
The arc length of a curve measures its total variation — how much it "wiggles." In machine learning, regularization is the practice of penalizing overly complex models. The arc length integral is one of the oldest regularizers.

In 1D regression, if you want a function \(y = g(x)\) that is both close to data and smooth, you might minimize:

\[\mathcal{L}(g) = \sum_{i}(y_i - g(x_i))^2 + \lambda \int \sqrt{1 + (g'(x))^2}, dx\]

The second term is exactly the arc length of the graph of \(g\). This is a total variation regularizer — it penalizes length, not just curvature or derivative magnitude. The polar analogue \(\int \sqrt{r^2 + (r')^2}, d\theta\) would regularize a polar function \(r = f(\theta)\) by its arc length.

docs.title: 15.2 Geodesics and Riemannian Metrics
docs.text:
The arc length element \(ds^2 = dr^2 + r^2, d\theta^2\) is the Riemannian metric of the Euclidean plane in polar coordinates. Minimizing arc length between two points gives the geodesic — which in Euclidean space is just a straight line, but in curved spaces (manifolds) is genuinely complex.

In Riemannian optimization (used in training models on curved parameter spaces — e.g., networks with orthogonal weight matrices, probabilistic models on the simplex, or transformers with unit-norm attention heads), the geodesic distance is the correct notion of "how far apart" two parameter settings are. The natural gradient descent algorithm follows geodesics in the Fisher information metric, which on the probability simplex produces arc length integrals of the form \(\int \sqrt{\sum_i (\dot{p}_i)^2 / p_i}, dt\) — a curved-space generalization of the polar arc length formula.

docs.title: 15.3 Curve Length in Latent Space
docs.text:
In Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and other generative models, the latent space has a learned metric. Interpolating between two latent codes \(z_0\) and \(z_1\) along the straight line \(z(t) = (1-t)z_0 + tz_1\) is not the same as interpolating along the geodesic — the straight line may pass through low-probability regions of latent space where the decoder produces poor outputs.

The correct interpolation minimizes the arc length in the pullback metric: the metric on latent space induced by the decoder map. Computing this arc length requires integrating \(\sqrt{g_{ij}(z(t))\dot{z}^i(t)\dot{z}^j(t)}, dt\) along the path — exactly the structure of \(\int \sqrt{r^2 + (r')^2}, d\theta\) in polar coordinates. VAE papers (Arvanitidis et al., 2018) compute these geodesics to produce better interpolations.

docs.title: 15.4 Path Length in Reinforcement Learning
docs.text:
In reinforcement learning, the agent's trajectory through state space is a curve. The total path length influences sample efficiency: a policy that reaches the goal via a shorter path has explored less of the state space and tends to generalize better (shorter description length ↔ lower complexity). Intrinsic motivation methods like curiosity-driven exploration (Pathak et al., 2017) implicitly reward shorter arc length paths to novel states.

In continuous control (robotics, physics simulations), the arc length of the agent's trajectory in polar coordinates (for circular motion tasks like orbit stabilization or wheel control) is the relevant cost function. Minimizing \(\int \sqrt{r^2 + (r')^2}, d\theta\) is literally the control objective.

docs.title: 15.5 The Metric Tensor and Transformer Geometry
docs.text:
The polar arc length element \(ds^2 = dr^2 + r^2, d\theta^2\) is written in matrix form as:

\[ds^2 = \begin{pmatrix} dr & d\theta \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & r^2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} dr \ d\theta \end{pmatrix}\]

The matrix \(G = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & r^2 \end{pmatrix}\) is the metric tensor in polar coordinates. It encodes how distance is measured — and it depends on position (specifically on \(r\)).

The attention matrix \(A = \text{softmax}(QK^T/\sqrt{d})\) in a Transformer can be interpreted as an approximation to the metric tensor of the input data manifold. In this view, the attention mechanism computes a position-dependent inner product — exactly the role played by \(G(r, \theta)\) in the polar metric. The arc length of a sequence of tokens through the attention geometry is \(\int \sqrt{v^T A v}, dt\) where \(v\) is the token velocity — the metric-weighted arc length formula.

docs.title: 15.6 Summary Table
docs.text: Polar Arc Length Concept ML / DL Analogue \(L = \int \sqrt{r^2 + (r')^2}, d\theta\) Total variation regularization \(ds^2 = dr^2 + r^2 d\theta^2\) (metric) Riemannian metric on parameter space Geodesic = arc-length minimizer Natural gradient / geodesic interpolation in VAE Log spiral: \(L \propto \Delta r\) Adam: step size ∝ radial distance Elliptic integrals for rose curves Non-closed-form geometry in deep nets Metric tensor \(G\) in polar Attention matrix as position-dependent metric Arc length regularizer Smooth policy in RL, total variation loss

docs.title: 16. Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1. (Warm-up) Compute the arc length of the circle \(r = 4\sin\theta\) over a full tracing. What is the minimal interval for a single tracing? What goes wrong if you integrate over \([0, 2\pi]\)?

Exercise 2. Compute the total arc length of the cardioid \(r = 3(1 - \sin\theta)\). (Hint: use the identity \(1 - \sin\theta = 1 - \cos(\theta - \pi/2)\) to reduce to the standard cardioid, or redo the computation directly with the analogous half-angle identity \(1 - \sin\theta = ?\).)

Exercise 3. (Stewart §10.4) Find the arc length of \(r = e^{2\theta}\) for \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\).

Exercise 4. Set up (but do not evaluate) the arc length integral for one petal of \(r = \sin(2\theta)\). Show that the integrand simplifies to \(\sqrt{4 - 3\sin^2(2\theta)}\) (or similar), and identify this as an elliptic integral.

Exercise 5. (Archimedean spiral) For \(r = 2\theta\), \(\theta \in [0, 2\pi]\): set up the arc length integral and evaluate it using the formula from §9. What is the arc length of the first complete revolution?

Exercise 6. (Surface area) The curve \(r = a\sin\theta\), \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\), is a circle of radius \(a/2\). Revolving it about the polar axis generates a sphere of radius \(a/2\). Verify this by computing the surface area using the polar surface area formula and confirming you get \(4\pi(a/2)^2 = \pi a^2\).

Exercise 7. (Half-angle identity challenge) For \(r = a(1 - \cos\theta)\) (cardioid opening left), compute \(r^2 + (r')^2\) and simplify using the identity \(1 - \cos\theta = 2\sin^2(\theta/2)\). What absolute value issue arises, and where must you split the integral?

Exercise 8. (ML-flavored) A gradient descent trajectory in a 2D loss landscape (in polar coordinates centered at the minimum) follows \(r(\theta) = r_0 e^{-0.05\theta}\) (a contracting log spiral) for \(\theta \in [0, 10\pi]\) (5 full revolutions). Compute the total path length traveled by the optimizer. How does this compare to the straight-line distance \(r_0\) from initialization to minimum?

docs.title: Area in Polar
docs.text: A region bounded by a polar curve has a shape no Cartesian rectangle can cleanly tile. We need a new slicing strategy — and the geometry of circular sectors gives it to us.

docs.title: 1. Why Cartesian Integration Breaks Down
docs.text:
In Cartesian coordinates, we integrate by slicing a region into thin vertical rectangles of width \(dx\) and height \(f(x)\). The key geometric fact exploited is:

\[\text{Area of a thin strip} \approx f(x),dx\]

A polar curve \(r = f(\theta)\) sweeps out its region by rotation, not translation. The natural "thin piece" is not a rectangle — it is a thin circular sector swept out by a small angular increment \(d\theta\).

docs.title: 2. The Geometric Engine: Area of a Circular Sector
docs.text:
Lemma. A circular sector of radius \(r\) subtending angle \(\Delta\theta\) (in radians) has area

\[A_{\text{sector}} = \frac{1}{2}r^2,\Delta\theta.\]

Proof. A full disk of radius \(r\) has area \(\pi r^2\) and subtends \(2\pi\) radians. By proportionality,

\[A_{\text{sector}} = \frac{\Delta\theta}{2\pi}\cdot\pi r^2 = \frac{1}{2}r^2,\Delta\theta. \qquad \square\]

This is the exact geometric fact that drives everything that follows.

docs.title: 3. Setting Up the Riemann Sum
docs.text:
Let \(r = f(\theta)\) be a continuous, non-negative function on \([\alpha,\beta]\), where \(0 < \beta - \alpha \leq 2\pi\). Consider the region \(\mathcal{R}\) bounded by the curve and the two rays \(\theta = \alpha\), \(\theta = \beta\).

Partition \([\alpha, \beta]\): choose \(\alpha = \theta_0 < \theta_1 < \cdots < \theta_n = \beta\), with \(\Delta\theta_i = \theta_i - \theta_{i-1}\).

Approximate the \(i\)-th sub-region by a circular sector with:

  • radius \(= f(\theta_i^_)\) for some sample point \(\theta_i^_ \in [\theta_{i-1}, \theta_i]\),
  • angle \(= \Delta\theta_i\).

The area of this approximating sector is \(\tfrac{1}{2}[f(\theta_i^*)]^2,\Delta\theta_i\).

Sum: \(\displaystyle A \approx \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{2}[f(\theta_i^*)]^2,\Delta\theta_i\)

This is a Riemann sum for \(\tfrac{1}{2}[f(\theta)]^2\) over \([\alpha, \beta]\).

docs.title: 4. The Main Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem (Area in Polar Coordinates). If \(f\) is continuous and \(f(\theta) \geq 0\) on \([\alpha, \beta]\), then the area of the region bounded by the polar curve \(r = f(\theta)\) and the rays \(\theta = \alpha\), \(\theta = \beta\) is

\[\boxed{A = \frac{1}{2}\int_\alpha^\beta [f(\theta)]^2,d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\int_\alpha^\beta r^2,d\theta}\]

Proof. Since \(f\) is continuous on a closed interval, \([f(\theta)]^2\) is also continuous, hence Riemann integrable. The Riemann sums above converge to the integral as \(|\text{partition}| \to 0\). \(\square\)

Remark. The integrand is \(\tfrac{1}{2}r^2\), not \(r\) — this is a quadratic functional in the radius, reflecting the fact that sectors grow in area quadratically with radius (just as disk area grows as \(r^2\)).

docs.title: Example 1: Full Rose — \(r = \cos(2\theta)\) (Four-Petal Rose)
docs.text:
The curve \(r = \cos(2\theta)\) traces four petals. One petal lies over \(\theta \in [-\pi/4,, \pi/4]\) (where \(r \geq 0\)).

\[A_{\text{one petal}} = \frac{1}{2}\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\cos^2(2\theta),d\theta\]

Use \(\cos^2(u) = \frac{1+\cos(2u)}{2}\):

\[= \frac{1}{2}\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\frac{1+\cos(4\theta)}{2},d\theta = \frac{1}{4}\left[\theta + \frac{\sin(4\theta)}{4}\right]_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\] \[= \frac{1}{4}\left[\frac{\pi}{4} + 0 - \left(-\frac{\pi}{4} + 0\right)\right] = \frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{\pi}{8}\]

Total area of all four petals: \(4 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{8} = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\).

docs.title: Example 2: Cardioid — \(r = 1 + \cos\theta\)
docs.text:
The cardioid \(r = 1 + \cos\theta\) traces a complete, closed curve as \(\theta\) ranges over \([0, 2\pi]\).

\[A = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^{2\pi}(1+\cos\theta)^2,d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^{2\pi}(1 + 2\cos\theta + \cos^2\theta),d\theta\]

Over a full period: \(\int_0^{2\pi}\cos\theta,d\theta = 0\) and \(\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2\theta,d\theta = \pi\).

\[A = \frac{1}{2}\left[2\pi + 0 + \pi\right] = \frac{3\pi}{2}\]

docs.title: Example 3: Area Between Two Curves
docs.text:
Setup. Given two polar curves \(r = f(\theta)\) (outer) and \(r = g(\theta)\) (inner), with \(f(\theta) \geq g(\theta) \geq 0\) on \([\alpha, \beta]\), the area between them is:

\[A = \frac{1}{2}\int_\alpha^\beta \left([f(\theta)]^2 - [g(\theta)]^2\right)d\theta\]

Example. Find the area inside \(r = 3\sin\theta\) and outside \(r = 1 + \sin\theta\).

Find intersections: \(3\sin\theta = 1 + \sin\theta \Rightarrow 2\sin\theta = 1 \Rightarrow \sin\theta = \tfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow \theta = \tfrac{\pi}{6}, \tfrac{5\pi}{6}\).

On \([\pi/6, 5\pi/6]\), \(3\sin\theta \geq 1 + \sin\theta\).

\[A = \frac{1}{2}\int_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}\left[(3\sin\theta)^2 - (1+\sin\theta)^2\right]d\theta\] \[= \frac{1}{2}\int_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}\left[9\sin^2\theta - 1 - 2\sin\theta - \sin^2\theta\right]d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\int_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}\left[8\sin^2\theta - 2\sin\theta - 1\right]d\theta\]

Using \(8\sin^2\theta = 4(1-\cos 2\theta) = 4 - 4\cos 2\theta\):

\[= \frac{1}{2}\int_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}\left[3 - 4\cos 2\theta - 2\sin\theta\right]d\theta\] \[= \frac{1}{2}\left[3\theta - 2\sin 2\theta + 2\cos\theta\right]_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6} = \pi\]

docs.title: 7. Common Pitfalls and Subtleties
docs.text:
Pitfall 1: Curve traced multiple times. The lemniscate \(r^2 = \cos(2\theta)\) is only real when \(\cos(2\theta) \geq 0\), i.e., \(\theta \in [-\pi/4, \pi/4] \cup [3\pi/4, 5\pi/4]\). Integrating over \([0, 2\pi]\) naively would double-count the area. Always sketch the curve and identify the correct angular range for one complete tracing.

Pitfall 2: Negative \(r\) values. If \(f(\theta) < 0\) on part of \([\alpha, \beta]\), the formula still makes sense geometrically because \([f(\theta)]^2 \geq 0\). However, the curve is reflected through the pole. Be careful about which region you are actually computing.

Pitfall 3: Finding intersection angles. Polar intersections are subtle. Two curves can intersect at the pole with different \(\theta\) values (since both reach \(r = 0\) at different angles). Always check whether the pole is an intersection separately.

docs.title: 8. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: Polar coordinates and the area formula appear — sometimes overtly, often structurally — in several corners of modern ML.

docs.title: 8.1 Radial Basis Functions (RBFs) and Kernel Methods
docs.text:
Support Vector Machines and kernel methods frequently use radial kernels of the form

\[K(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \phi(|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}|)\]

The effective receptive area of such a kernel — how much of feature space it "sees" — is computed as an integral in polar/spherical coordinates. In 2D, this is exactly the polar area integral. For the Gaussian kernel \(\phi(r) = e^{-r^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), the normalization constant requires:

\[\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2/(2\sigma^2)} r,dr\]

which emerges from writing \(\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} K,dA = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2/(2\sigma^2)},r,dr,d\theta = 2\pi\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2/(2\sigma^2)},r,dr\).

The factor of \(r\) (the Jacobian) is the polar-coordinate remnant of the sector area element \(r,dr,d\theta\) — directly analogous to \(\tfrac{1}{2}r^2,d\theta\) in our formula.

docs.title: 8.2 Polar Decomposition and Neural Network Geometry
docs.text:
The geometry of weight spaces in neural networks is often studied in polar/spherical coordinates. The unit hypersphere \(\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\) is parameterized angularly, and integration over weight vectors decomposes as:

\[\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(\mathbf{w}),d\mathbf{w} = \int_0^\infty \int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}} f(r,\boldsymbol{\omega}),r^{n-1},dS(\boldsymbol{\omega}),dr\]

The angular integral over \(\mathbb{S}^{n-1}\) is the higher-dimensional generalization of our \(\int_\alpha^\beta r^2,d\theta\) formula. Understanding the geometry of parameter space — how much "volume" of weight space corresponds to good solutions — uses exactly this machinery.

docs.title: 8.3 Fourier Features and Directional Statistics
docs.text:
Random Fourier Features (Rahimi & Recht, 2007) approximate shift-invariant kernels by sampling frequencies \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\) from a spectral distribution. The spectral density of a radial kernel is itself a radial function, and sampling from it efficiently uses the polar decomposition: sample angle \(\theta \sim \text{Uniform}[0, 2\pi]\) independently from the radial component \(r \sim p_r\).

Directional statistics (von Mises distribution, wrapped Cauchy) model data on circles and spheres. Computing normalizing constants and expected values under these distributions requires polar area integrals. This appears in:

  • orientation estimation in computer vision,
  • molecule conformation prediction (AlphaFold-style models),
  • circular embeddings for temporal/angular data.

docs.title: 8.4 Activation Function Analysis and Angular Regions
docs.text:
In a two-layer ReLU network, the decision boundary of a single neuron is a hyperplane, but the activation region (where the neuron fires) is a half-space. In 2D, this corresponds to a wedge — an angular sector — and the probability that a random Gaussian input activates a neuron is:

\[P(\text{neuron fires}) = \frac{\Delta\theta}{2\pi}\]

where \(\Delta\theta\) is the angular measure of the sector. Computing the expected number of active neurons, or the measure of the activation region, reduces to polar area calculations.

docs.title: 8.5 Diffusion Models and Score Functions
docs.text:
Modern generative models (score-based diffusion models) define a noising process on \(\mathbb{R}^n\). The score function \(\nabla_\mathbf{x}\log p_t(\mathbf{x})\) points radially inward toward regions of high probability. The normalization of the forward process uses Gaussian integrals in \(n\)-dimensional polar coordinates. Specifically,

\[\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} |\mathbf{x}|^2,e^{-|\mathbf{x}|^2/(2\sigma^2)},d\mathbf{x} = n\sigma^2(2\pi\sigma^2)^{n/2}\]

derived by switching to polar coordinates — the 2D version of this is our \(\int r^2,d\theta\) formula elevated to \(n\) dimensions.

docs.title: 9. Summary Table
docs.text: Concept Cartesian Analog Polar Form Area element \(dx,dy\) \(r,dr,d\theta\) (double integral) Area under curve \(\int_a^b f(x),dx\) \(\frac{1}{2}\int_\alpha^\beta r^2,d\theta\) Area between curves \(\int_a^b (f-g),dx\) \(\frac{1}{2}\int_\alpha^\beta (r_{\text{out}}^2 - r_{\text{in}}^2),d\theta\) Key approximation Rectangle: \(f(x),\Delta x\) Sector: \(\frac{1}{2}f(\theta)^2,\Delta\theta\)

docs.title: 10. Key Formulas at a Glance
docs.text: \[\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2}\int_\alpha^\beta r^2,d\theta\] \[\text{Area between curves} = \frac{1}{2}\int_\alpha^\beta \left(r_{\text{outer}}^2 - r_{\text{inner}}^2\right)d\theta\] \[\text{Arc length} = \int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{r^2 + \left(\frac{dr}{d\theta}\right)^2},d\theta \quad \text{(for reference)}\]

docs.title: Parabola
docs.text: Every parabola is the same parabola — just scaled and rotated. This single geometric fact, once internalized, unlocks the whole theory.

docs.title: 1. The Geometric Definition (Start Here, Always)
docs.text:
Definition. A parabola is the set of all points in the plane equidistant from a fixed point \(F\) (the focus) and a fixed line \(\ell\) (the directrix).

\[\text{Parabola} = {, P \in \mathbb{R}^2 : |PF| = d(P, \ell) ,}\]

This is the true definition — not "\(y = x^2\)". The algebraic form is a consequence.

The vertex is the unique point on the parabola closest to both focus and directrix simultaneously. By symmetry it lies exactly halfway between them.

          Focus F
            *
            |  ← p (focal distance)
            |
  ──────────V────────── ← Vertex
            |
            |  ← p
  ──────────────────── ← Directrix ℓ

The distance \(p > 0\) from vertex to focus (= vertex to directrix) is called the focal parameter or focal length.

docs.title: 2. Deriving the Equation from the Definition
docs.text:
Place the vertex at the origin, focus at \(F = (0, p)\), directrix \(y = -p\).

Let \(P = (x, y)\) be any point on the parabola. Then:

\[|PF| = d(P, \ell)\] \[\sqrt{x^2 + (y-p)^2} = |y + p|\]

Square both sides (both sides non-negative for \(y \geq -p\)):

\[x^2 + (y-p)^2 = (y+p)^2\] \[x^2 + y^2 - 2py + p^2 = y^2 + 2py + p^2\] \[x^2 = 4py\] \[\boxed{x^2 = 4py}\]

This is the standard form. Every coefficient is geometrically meaningful: \(4p\) encodes the focal length.

Four standard orientations:

Opens Equation Focus Directrix Up \(x^2 = 4py\), \(p>0\) \((0, p)\) \(y = -p\) Down \(x^2 = -4py\), \(p>0\) \((0, -p)\) \(y = p\) Right \(y^2 = 4px\), \(p>0\) \((p, 0)\) \(x = -p\) Left \(y^2 = -4px\), \(p>0\) \((-p, 0)\) \(x = p\)

docs.title: 3. The General Second-Degree Parabola
docs.text:
The general conic:

\[Ax^2 + Bxy + Cy^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0\]

is a parabola when the discriminant \(B^2 - 4AC = 0\).

When \(B = 0\) (axis-aligned), the conditions reduce to: exactly one of \(A, C\) is zero.

Completing the square reduces any axis-aligned parabola to standard form. Example:

\[y = 2x^2 - 8x + 5\] \[= 2(x^2 - 4x) + 5 = 2(x^2 - 4x + 4 - 4) + 5 = 2(x-2)^2 - 3\]

Vertex at \((2, -3)\), opens up, \(4p = \tfrac{1}{2} \Rightarrow p = \tfrac{1}{8}\).

docs.title: 4.1 The Latus Rectum
docs.text:
The latus rectum is the chord through the focus perpendicular to the axis of symmetry. For \(x^2 = 4py\):

At \(y = p\): \(x^2 = 4p^2 \Rightarrow x = \pm 2p\).

\[\text{Length of latus rectum} = 4p\]

This is the natural "width" of the parabola at focus level — a clean intrinsic measurement.

docs.title: 4.2 Reflective Property
docs.text:
Theorem. Any ray parallel to the axis of a parabola, upon reflection off the parabola, passes through the focus.

Proof sketch. At a point \(P = (x_0, y_0)\) on \(x^2 = 4py\), the tangent line has slope \(\frac{dy}{dx}\big|_{x_0} = \frac{x_0}{2p}\). The normal bisects the angle between the incoming ray (parallel to the \(y\)-axis) and the line \(PF\). One verifies by direct computation that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection with respect to this normal. \(\square\)

This is why parabolic mirrors focus parallel light rays (telescopes, satellite dishes) and parabolic reflectors broadcast a point source as parallel rays (flashlights, headlights).

  Incoming rays (parallel to axis)
   ↓  ↓  ↓  ↓  ↓
   ↘  ↘  ↘  ↘  ↘
    \  \  |  /  /       ← parabola
     \  \ | / /
      \   F   /         ← all rays converge at F

docs.title: 4.3 Tangent Line at \((x_0, y_0)\)
docs.text:
For \(x^2 = 4py\), differentiating implicitly: \(2x = 4py' \Rightarrow y' = \frac{x}{2p}\).

Tangent at \((x_0, y_0)\):

\[y - y_0 = \frac{x_0}{2p}(x - x_0)\]

Since \(x_0^2 = 4py_0\), this simplifies to:

\[xx_0 = 2p(y + y_0)\]

A beautiful symmetric form — \(x\) and \(x_0\) appear symmetrically on the left.

docs.title: 5. Parabola as a Conic Section
docs.text:
A parabola arises when a plane cuts a (double-napped) cone parallel to exactly one generator (ruling line).

        /\
       /  \
      / ·· \     ← plane cuts parallel to one side
     /  ··  \
    /___··___\
       (parabola)

The three conic sections and their discriminant conditions (\(B^2 - 4AC\)):

Conic Discriminant Eccentricity Ellipse (incl. circle) \(< 0\) \(e < 1\) Parabola \(= 0\) \(e = 1\) Hyperbola \(> 0\) \(e > 1\)

The parabola is the boundary case \(e = 1\): one focus, one directrix, and the definition of distance-from-focus \(=\) distance-from-directrix is exactly eccentricity \(1\).

docs.title: 6. Parametric Form
docs.text:
The natural parametrization of \(x^2 = 4py\):

\[x = 2pt, \quad y = pt^2, \quad t \in \mathbb{R}\]

Verify: \((2pt)^2 = 4p^2t^2 = 4p(pt^2)\). ✓

Velocity vector: \(\dot{\mathbf{r}} = (2p,, 2pt)\). At \(t=0\) (vertex), \(\dot{\mathbf{r}} = (2p, 0)\) — horizontal tangent, as expected.

Curvature at the vertex (\(t = 0\)):

\[\kappa = \frac{|\dot{x}\ddot{y} - \dot{y}\ddot{x}|}{(\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2)^{3/2}} = \frac{|2p \cdot 2p - 0|}{(4p^2)^{3/2}} = \frac{4p^2}{8p^3} = \frac{1}{2p}\]

So the radius of curvature at the vertex is \(\rho = 2p\) — the diameter of the osculating circle equals the latus rectum length. Another clean intrinsic fact.

docs.title: Example 1: Find Focus and Directrix
docs.text:
Given \(y = -\frac{1}{12}x^2 + 3\).

Rewrite: \(x^2 = -12(y - 3)\).

Compare with \(x^2 = -4p(y - k)\): \(4p = 12 \Rightarrow p = 3\).

  • Vertex: \((0, 3)\)
  • Opens down
  • Focus: \((0, 3 - 3) = (0, 0)\)
  • Directrix: \(y = 3 + 3 = 6\)

docs.title: Example 2: Find the Equation
docs.text:
Focus \(F = (2, 3)\), directrix \(x = -4\).

The axis is horizontal (focus and directrix are separated horizontally). Vertex is halfway: \(x_V = \frac{2 + (-4)}{2} = -1\), \(y_V = 3\).

Focal length \(p = 2 - (-1) = 3\) (opens right).

\[\boxed{(y - 3)^2 = 12(x + 1)}\]

docs.title: Example 3: Arc Length of \(y = x^2\) from \(x=0\) to \(x=1\)
docs.text:
\[L = \int_0^1 \sqrt{1 + (y')^2},dx = \int_0^1\sqrt{1 + 4x^2},dx\]

Let \(x = \frac{1}{2}\sinh t\), \(dx = \frac{1}{2}\cosh t,dt\), \(\sqrt{1+4x^2} = \cosh t\):

\[L = \int_0^{\sinh^{-1}(2)}\cosh^2 t,\frac{dt}{2} = \frac{1}{4}\left[\sinh t\cosh t + t\right]_0^{\sinh^{-1}(2)}\]

Numerically: \(L \approx 1.4789\).

docs.title: 9. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
9.1 Quadratic Loss and Parabolic Geometry
docs.text:
The mean squared error (MSE) loss for a single parameter \(w\):

\[\mathcal{L}(w) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - wx_i)^2\]

is a parabola (or paraboloid in higher dimensions) in \(w\). This is not a coincidence — the square loss is the unique loss (up to scaling) whose level sets are spheres and whose geometry is Euclidean. The vertex of the parabola is the global minimum, and gradient descent on a parabola converges in one step with the right learning rate.

For the 1D case with exact solution \(w^* = \frac{\sum x_i y_i}{\sum x_i^2}\), the loss surface is:

\[\mathcal{L}(w) = \mathcal{L}(w^_) + \frac{\sum x_i^2}{n}(w - w^_)^2\]

Literally a parabola with vertex at the optimum. The coefficient \(\frac{\sum x_i^2}{n}\) (the curvature) determines how sharply the loss rises away from the minimum — this is the Hessian in 1D.

docs.title: 9.2 The Hessian and Paraboloid Approximations
docs.text:
The second-order Taylor approximation of any smooth loss \(\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w})\) around a point \(\mathbf{w}_0\) is:

\[\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}) \approx \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}_0) + abla\mathcal{L}^ op\Delta\mathbf{w} + rac{1}{2}\Delta\mathbf{w}^ op H,\Delta\mathbf{w}\]

where \(H = abla^2\mathcal{L}\) is the Hessian. The last term is a paraboloid — the \(n\)-dimensional analog of a parabola. Newton's method exploits this: it finds the vertex of the local paraboloid approximation in one step:

\[\mathbf{w}_{ ext{new}} = \mathbf{w}_0 - H^{-1} abla\mathcal{L}\]

All second-order optimization methods (L-BFGS, natural gradient, Adam to some degree) are approximations to navigating parabolic loss geometry.

docs.title: 9.3 SVM and Quadratic Programming
docs.text:
The hard-margin Support Vector Machine dual problem is:

\[\max_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} \sum_i \alpha_i - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_j y_i y_j K(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j)\]

subject to \(\alpha_i \geq 0\), \(\sum_i \alpha_i y_i = 0\).

The objective is a quadratic (paraboloid) in \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}\). The feasible set is a convex polytope. Finding the SVM solution means finding the vertex of a paraboloid above a polytope — a quadratic programming problem. The geometry of the parabola (unique minimum, no local minima) guarantees the solution is unique.

docs.title: 9.4 Parabolic Activation Functions and Squaring Operations
docs.text:
The squared activation \(\sigma(x) = x^2\) (and related monomials) appears in:

  • Polynomial networks and tensor decomposition
  • Attention mechanisms: the dot-product \(\mathbf{q}^\top\mathbf{k}\) is linear, but before softmax it creates a quadratic scoring surface
  • Quadratic neurons (recent research): neurons computing \((\mathbf{w}_1^\top\mathbf{x})(\mathbf{w}_2^\top\mathbf{x})\) whose composition creates parabolic response surfaces

The variance of activations: \(\text{Var}(wx) = w^2\text{Var}(x)\) — the dependence on \(w^2\) (not \(w\)) means weight initialization schemes (He, Xavier) must account for the squaring. The safe initialization radius in weight space is the focus of a related parabola in the variance-vs-depth relationship.

docs.title: 9.5 Parabolic Learning Rate Schedules
docs.text:
Several learning rate annealing strategies follow parabolic curves. The cosine annealing with warm restarts is approximately parabolic near its minima. The polynomial decay schedule:

\[\eta_t = \eta_0\left(1 - \frac{t}{T}\right)^k\]

with \(k=2\) is literally parabolic decay. The rationale: the loss surface near the optimum is parabolic (as in §9.1), so a learning rate that decays quadratically matches the curvature of the landscape near convergence.

docs.title: 9.6 Paraboloids in Gaussian Processes
docs.text: A Gaussian process with squared-exponential kernel has log-likelihood whose dependence on the length-scale hyperparameter \(\ell\) is approximately parabolic near its optimum. Marginal likelihood maximization (type-II maximum likelihood) thus looks like finding the vertex of a paraboloid in hyperparameter space — again a parabolic optimization problem.

docs.title: 10. Summary of Key Facts
docs.text: Property Formula Standard form (vertex at origin) \(x^2 = 4py\) General vertex \((h,k)\) \((x-h)^2 = 4p(y-k)\) Focus \((h, k+p)\) Directrix \(y = k - p\) Latus rectum length \(4p\) Curvature at vertex \(\kappa = \frac{1}{2p}\) Eccentricity \(e = 1\) Discriminant condition \(B^2 - 4AC = 0\) Parametrization \((2pt, pt^2)\)

docs.title: Parabola Formulas
docs.text: A quick-reference sheet. Every formula here is a consequence of one definition: \(|PF| = d(P,\ell)\).

docs.title: 1. Standard Forms (Vertex at Origin)
docs.text: Orientation Equation Focus Directrix Axis Opens up \(x^2 = 4py,\ p>0\) \((0,,p)\) \(y = -p\) \(x = 0\) Opens down \(x^2 = -4py,\ p>0\) \((0,,-p)\) \(y = p\) \(x = 0\) Opens right \(y^2 = 4px,\ p>0\) \((p,,0)\) \(x = -p\) \(y = 0\) Opens left \(y^2 = -4px,\ p>0\) \((-p,,0)\) \(x = p\) \(y = 0\)

docs.title: 2. Standard Forms (Vertex at \((h,k)\))
docs.text:
Orientation Equation Opens up \((x-h)^2 = 4p(y-k)\) Opens down \((x-h)^2 = -4p(y-k)\) Opens right \((y-k)^2 = 4p(x-h)\) Opens left \((y-k)^2 = -4p(x-h)\)

For all cases: $\(\text{Focus} = \text{vertex} + p\cdot(\text{unit vector along axis, toward opening})\)$ $\(\text{Vertex} = \text{midpoint of (focus, foot on directrix)}\)$

docs.title: 3. Slope–Intercept ↔ Standard Form
docs.text:
\[y = ax^2 + bx + c \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad (x-h)^2 = \frac{1}{a}(y-k) \cdot \text{sign}(a) \cdot 4p\]

More directly:

\[y = a(x-h)^2 + k \quad \Longrightarrow \quad 4p = \frac{1}{|a|}, \quad p = \frac{1}{4|a|}\]
  • \(a > 0\): opens up; \(\quad a < 0\): opens down
  • Vertex: \((h,,k)\)
  • Focus: \(\left(h,;k + \dfrac{1}{4a}\right)\)
  • Directrix: \(y = k - \dfrac{1}{4a}\)

docs.title: 4. Key Measurements
docs.text: \[\text{Focal length (vertex to focus)} = p\] \[\text{Latus rectum length} = 4p\] \[\text{Focal chord length through focus at angle } \theta = \frac{4p}{\sin^2\theta}\] \[\text{Eccentricity} = e = 1\]

docs.title: 5. Tangent and Normal Lines
docs.text:
For \(x^2 = 4py\) at point \(P_0 = (x_0, y_0)\):

\[\text{Tangent:} \quad xx_0 = 2p(y + y_0)\] \[\text{Slope of tangent:} \quad m = \frac{x_0}{2p}\] \[\text{Normal:} \quad y - y_0 = -\frac{2p}{x_0}(x - x_0)\]

Tangent in slope form (tangent with slope \(m\)):

\[y = mx - pm^2\]

(Touches \(x^2 = 4py\) at \((2pm,, pm^2)\))

docs.title: 6. Parametric Equations
docs.text:
For \(x^2 = 4py\):

\[x = 2pt, \quad y = pt^2, \quad t \in \mathbb{R}\]

For \(y^2 = 4px\):

\[x = pt^2, \quad y = 2pt, \quad t \in \mathbb{R}\]

Tangent at parameter \(t\):

\[ty = x + pt^2 \quad \text{(for } y^2 = 4px\text{)}\]

docs.title: 7. Curvature
docs.text:
\[\kappa(t) = \frac{1}{2p(1+t^2)^{3/2}}\] \[\kappa\big|_{\text{vertex}} = \frac{1}{2p} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \text{Radius of curvature at vertex} = 2p\]

(The osculating circle at the vertex has diameter equal to the latus rectum.)

docs.title: 8. Arc Length
docs.text:
For \(y = \frac{x^2}{4p}\) from \(x = 0\) to \(x = a\):

\[L = \int_0^a \sqrt{1 + \frac{x^2}{4p^2}},dx = \frac{a}{2}\sqrt{1+\frac{a^2}{4p^2}} + p\ln!\left(\frac{a}{2p} + \sqrt{1+\frac{a^2}{4p^2}}\right)\]

docs.title: 9. Area Under a Parabolic Arc
docs.text:
Area between \(y = ax^2\) and the horizontal line \(y = h\) (archimedes):

\[A = \frac{4}{3} \cdot (\text{base}) \cdot (\text{height}) \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \frac{2}{3},bh\]

where \(b = 2\sqrt{h/a}\) is the base width. (Archimedes' result: area \(= \tfrac{2}{3}\) of the circumscribed rectangle.)

General area between \(y = ax^2 + bx + c\) and \(y = dx + e\) (intersecting at \(x_1, x_2\)):

\[A = \frac{|a|}{6}(x_2 - x_1)^3\]

docs.title: 10. Reflective (Optical) Property
docs.text:
Any ray parallel to the axis reflects through the focus.

Any ray through the focus reflects parallel to the axis.

Formally, at point \(P_0\) on the parabola: $\(\angle(\text{incoming ray}, \text{normal}) = \angle(\text{normal}, \overrightarrow{P_0F})\)$

docs.title: 11. Polar Form
docs.text:
With focus at the pole, directrix perpendicular to polar axis:

\[r = \frac{ed}{1 - e\cos\theta} \quad (e=1, \text{ directrix left of focus})\] \[r = \frac{p}{1 - \cos\theta} \quad \text{(standard: directrix } x = -p\text{)}\]

All four orientations:

Directrix Equation \(x = -p\) (left) \(r = \dfrac{p}{1 - \cos\theta}\) \(x = p\) (right) \(r = \dfrac{p}{1 + \cos\theta}\) \(y = -p\) (below) \(r = \dfrac{p}{1 - \sin\theta}\) \(y = p\) (above) \(r = \dfrac{p}{1 + \sin\theta}\)

docs.title: 12. Discriminant Condition (General Conic)
docs.text: \[Ax^2 + Bxy + Cy^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0 \text{ is a parabola} \iff B^2 - 4AC = 0\]

docs.title: 13. Quick Identification Cheat Sheet
docs.text:
Given \(y = ax^2 + bx + c\):

\[\text{Vertex: } \left(-\frac{b}{2a},; c - \frac{b^2}{4a}\right)\] \[\text{Focus: } \left(-\frac{b}{2a},; c - \frac{b^2-1}{4a}\right) = \left(-\frac{b}{2a},; \frac{4ac - b^2 + 1}{4a}\right)\] \[\text{Directrix: } y = c - \frac{b^2+1}{4a}\] \[\text{Axis of symmetry: } x = -\frac{b}{2a}\] \[p = \frac{1}{4|a|}\]
