docs.title: Example 1 — Earth's Orbit
docs.text:
Earth: \(a = 1\) AU \(= 1.496 \times 10^{11}\) m, \(e \approx 0.0167\).

Period check: \(T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM_\odot} a^3\)

With \(GM_\odot = 1.327 \times 10^{20}\) m³/s²:

\[T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{a^3}{GM_\odot}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{(1.496\times10^{11})^3}{1.327\times10^{20}}} \approx 3.156\times10^7 \text{ s} \approx 365.25 \text{ days} \checkmark\]

Perihelion and aphelion: $\(r_{\min} = a(1-e) = 0.9833 \text{ AU}, \qquad r_{\max} = a(1+e) = 1.0167 \text{ AU}\)$

About 3.3% variation in Earth-Sun distance. Not why we have seasons.

docs.title: Example 2 — Halley's Comet
docs.text:
\(T = 75.3\) years, \(e = 0.967\).

Semi-major axis: $\(a = \left(\frac{GM_\odot T^2}{4\pi^2}\right)^{1/3}\)$

In astronomical units: \(a^3 = T^2\) (when \(T\) in years, \(a\) in AU) gives \(a = 75.3^{2/3} \approx 17.8\) AU.

Perihelion distance: \(r_{\min} = a(1-e) = 17.8(0.033) \approx 0.587\) AU (inside Venus's orbit).

Aphelion distance: \(r_{\max} = a(1+e) = 17.8(1.967) \approx 35\) AU (beyond Neptune).

Polar equation (Sun at focus, periapsis at \(\theta = 0\)): $\(\ell = a(1-e^2) = 17.8(1 - 0.967^2) \approx 1.15 \text{ AU}\)$ $\(r = \frac{1.15}{1 + 0.967\cos\theta} \text{ AU}\)$

docs.title: Example 3 — Geostationary Orbit
docs.text:
A satellite in geostationary orbit (\(T = 24\) h) around Earth. Find the orbital radius.

\[r^3 = \frac{GM_\oplus T^2}{4\pi^2}\]

With \(GM_\oplus = 3.986 \times 10^{14}\) m³/s² and \(T = 86400\) s:

\[r = \left(\frac{3.986\times10^{14} \cdot (86400)^2}{4\pi^2}\right)^{1/3} \approx 4.22 \times 10^7 \text{ m} \approx 42{,}200 \text{ km}\]

This is about 6.6 Earth radii from the center, or 35,800 km above the surface.

docs.title: Example 4 — Interplanetary Transfer (Hohmann Transfer)
docs.text:
To travel from Earth (\(a_1 = 1\) AU) to Mars (\(a_2 = 1.524\) AU) on a Hohmann transfer ellipse:

  • Transfer orbit semi-major axis: \(a_t = (a_1 + a_2)/2 = 1.262\) AU
  • Transfer time (half-period): \(t = T_t/2 = \pi\sqrt{a_t^3/GM_\odot}\)
\[t = \pi\sqrt{\frac{(1.262)^3}{1}} \approx \pi \cdot 1.418 \approx 4.454 \text{ years}/\text{(2π)} \approx 259 \text{ days}\]

This is the minimum energy trajectory — the one that uses least fuel. It follows an ellipse with perihelion at Earth's orbit and aphelion at Mars's orbit.

docs.title: Connection to AI / ML / Deep Learning
docs.text: The connections here go deeper than might be expected.

docs.title: 1. Inverse Problems & Orbital Mechanics in ML
docs.text:
Given noisy observations of a planet's position \((r_i, \theta_i)\), recover the orbital parameters \((e, \ell)\) — this is a nonlinear least squares problem:

\[\min_{e,\ell} \sum_i \left(r_i - \frac{\ell}{1 + e\cos\theta_i}\right)^2\]

Modern approaches use Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to solve orbital mechanics problems, where the Kepler equations are embedded as constraints or regularizers in the loss function. The network must learn solutions consistent with Kepler's laws.

docs.title: 2. Hamiltonian Neural Networks — Learning Conservation Laws
docs.text:
Kepler's Second Law is conservation of angular momentum: \(L = r^2\dot\theta = h\). Kepler's Third Law encodes conservation of energy: \(E = -GM/(2a)\).

Hamiltonian Neural Networks (Greydanus et al., 2019) learn to respect these conservation laws by parameterizing dynamics through the Hamiltonian \(\mathcal{H}(q, p)\):

\[\dot{q} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{H}}{\partial p}, \qquad \dot{p} = -\frac{\partial \mathcal{H}}{\partial q}\]

Trained on trajectory data, they provably conserve energy — unlike standard neural ODEs which drift. The orbital mechanics case (2-body problem) is the canonical benchmark.

The Hamiltonian for the Kepler problem is \(\mathcal{H} = p_r^2/2 + p_\theta^2/(2r^2) - GM/r\). The \(p_\theta = h = \text{const}\) is Law II; the value of \(\mathcal{H} = E = \text{const}\) plus the orbit equation gives Law I; Law III follows from integrating Law II over a full period.

docs.title: 3. Neural ODEs and Symplectic Integrators
docs.text:
The equations of orbital motion form a Hamiltonian system. Numerically integrating them requires symplectic integrators (Störmer-Verlet, leapfrog) that preserve phase-space volume (Liouville's theorem) and the symplectic structure.

Neural ODEs use neural networks as the vector field: $\(\frac{dz}{dt} = f_\theta(z, t)\)$

When applied to physical systems like orbital mechanics, vanilla Neural ODEs violate conservation laws over long integration. Symplectic Neural ODEs and Lagrangian Neural Networks are architectures specifically designed to respect these geometric structures.

Kepler orbits are the most-studied test case — if your "physics-aware" architecture can't reproduce elliptical orbits and the \(T^2 \propto a^3\) relation, it's wrong.

docs.title: 4. Symmetry and Equivariant Neural Networks
docs.text:
Kepler's laws are consequences of symmetries:

  • Rotational symmetry of gravity → conservation of angular momentum (Law II) via Noether's theorem
  • Time-translation symmetry → conservation of energy (Law I, orbit is fixed)
  • Hidden SO(4) symmetry (Laplace-Runge-Lenz vector) → closed elliptical orbits specifically (only for \(1/r^2\)!)

Equivariant neural networks (SE(3)-equivariant, E(n)-equivariant) are architectures that bake in these symmetries by design. They appear in:

  • AlphaFold 2 — SE(3)-equivariant attention for protein structure
  • NequIP, MACE — equivariant graph networks for molecular dynamics
  • Orbital mechanics simulators — SO(3)-equivariant networks for n-body problems

The lesson: knowing the symmetry group of your problem → better inductive bias → more data-efficient learning.

docs.title: 5. Areal Velocity = Cross Product = Attention Mechanism?
docs.text:
The areal velocity \(dA/dt = \frac{1}{2}|r \times v|\) is a cross product in 2D — equivalently, the determinant of a \(2 \times 2\) matrix:

\[h = \left|\begin{matrix} r_x & r_y \ v_x & v_y \end{matrix}\right|\]

In the attention mechanism of transformers:

\[\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\]

The \(QK^T\) matrix is a matrix of inner products between queries and keys. The softmax produces a probability distribution that "selects" values — it's an angular weighting, related to projections. The connection is loose but real: both are fundamentally about inner-product geometry and selective integration over a space, with the dot product playing the role of the angular velocity in determining how much "area" (attention) is swept.

docs.title: 6. Orbital Mechanics in Satellite Scheduling — Combinatorial Optimization
docs.text:
Modern ML uses Kepler's laws extensively in:

  • Satellite imagery scheduling (what can a satellite see and when, given its orbit)
  • Collision avoidance (predicting conjunction events)
  • Starlink/satellite constellation optimization — large-scale combinatorial problems where Keplerian propagation is the dynamics model and RL/evolutionary algorithms search for optimal configurations

The orbital propagator (numerical integration of Kepler's equations) is literally called thousands of times per second in reinforcement learning training loops for these applications.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Law Mathematical Content Physical Content Requires I Orbit \(r = \ell/(1 + e\cos\theta)\) is a conic Planets move on ellipses, Sun at focus \(F \propto 1/r^2\) II \(dA/dt = h/2 = \text{const}\) Equal areas in equal times Any central force III \(T^2 = (4\pi^2/GM)a^3\) Period² ∝ (semi-major axis)³ \(F \propto 1/r^2\)

Key quantities:

\[h = r^2\dot\theta \quad \text{(specific angular momentum, conserved)}\] \[E = \frac{1}{2}v^2 - \frac{GM}{r} = -\frac{GM}{2a} \quad \text{(specific energy, conserved)}\] \[\ell = \frac{h^2}{GM} = a(1-e^2) \quad \text{(semi-latus rectum)}\] \[e = \sqrt{1 + \frac{2Eh^2}{G^2M^2}} \quad \text{(eccentricity from energy and momentum)}\]

docs.title: Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Derive the polar orbit equation \(r = \ell/(1 + e\cos\theta)\) from the Binet equation. Show every step carefully.

  2. Saturn's orbital period is 29.46 years. Find its semi-major axis in AU.

  3. A spacecraft is placed in an elliptical orbit with periapsis 6600 km and apoapsis 42,000 km from Earth's center. Find \(e\), \(a\), \(T\), and \(h\).

  4. Using Law II, explain qualitatively why a comet with \(e = 0.99\) spends almost all its time far from the Sun.

  5. (Harder) Prove that for an elliptical orbit, the speed at periapsis and apoapsis satisfies: $\(v_p r_p = v_a r_a = h\)$ and use this to find \(v_p/v_a = r_a/r_p = (1+e)/(1-e)\).

  6. (ML connection) A Hamiltonian Neural Network is trained on 2-body orbital data. What two scalar quantities should it conserve, and how would you verify this numerically after training?

docs.title: Definition & Notation
docs.text:
Definition. A sequence is a function \(a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}\) (or \(\mathbb{C}\), or a metric space). We write its values as \(a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots\) and denote the sequence \({a_n}_{n=1}^{\infty}\), or simply \({a_n}\).

The domain is the natural numbers — the sequence is ordered and countably infinite by definition. This is the essential difference from a set.

Examples of sequences:

Name Formula First few terms Reciprocals \(a_n = 1/n\) \(1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, \ldots\) Powers of \(r\) \(a_n = r^n\) \(r, r^2, r^3, \ldots\) Alternating \(a_n = (-1)^n/n\) \(-1, 1/2, -1/3, 1/4, \ldots\) Factorial growth \(a_n = n!\) \(1, 2, 6, 24, 120, \ldots\) Fibonacci \(F_1=1, F_2=1, F_n = F_{n-1}+F_{n-2}\) \(1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, \ldots\) Recursion \(a_1 = 2,\ a_{n+1} = \frac{1}{2}!\left(a_n + \frac{2}{a_n}\right)\) \(2, 1.5, 1.4167, \ldots \to \sqrt{2}\)

Note. The last example is Newton's method for \(\sqrt{2}\). We will return to this — it is the prototype of iterative algorithms in optimization, which is the heartbeat of modern ML.

docs.title: Limit of a Sequence
docs.text:
Definition (Informal). We say \(\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = L\) if \(a_n\) gets arbitrarily close to \(L\) as \(n\) gets large.

This is fine for intuition. But "arbitrarily close" and "gets large" need precision.

docs.title: Rigorous Definition: The ε-N Criterion
docs.text:
Definition (Formal). We say \(\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = L\) if:

\[\forall \varepsilon > 0,\ \exists N \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } n > N \implies |a_n - L| < \varepsilon\]

Unpacking the logic:

  • You give me any tolerance \(\varepsilon > 0\) (no matter how small).
  • I must produce a threshold \(N\) (depending on \(\varepsilon\)).
  • For all \(n\) beyond \(N\), the sequence is within \(\varepsilon\) of \(L\).

The order of quantifiers is everything: \(\forall \varepsilon\ \exists N\), not \(\exists N\ \forall \varepsilon\).

Personal note. This definition is the foundation of all of analysis. Once you truly internalize it — not just "know" it — limits of functions, derivatives, integrals, and infinite series all fall into place. Every subsequent \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) argument is this definition in costume.

Terminology. If such \(L\) exists, we say \({a_n}\) converges to \(L\). Otherwise it diverges.

docs.title: Proof Template: \(a_n = 1/n \to 0\)
docs.text:
Claim. \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \dfrac{1}{n} = 0\).

Proof. Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) be given. Choose \(N \in \mathbb{N}\) with \(N > 1/\varepsilon\) (such \(N\) exists by the Archimedean property of \(\mathbb{R}\)). Then for all \(n > N\):

\[\left|\frac{1}{n} - 0\right| = \frac{1}{n} < \frac{1}{N} < \varepsilon\]

\(\square\)

Note. The key move: we need \(1/n < \varepsilon\), i.e., \(n > 1/\varepsilon\). So set \(N = \lceil 1/\varepsilon \rceil\). The work in every \(\varepsilon\)-\(N\) proof is: rearrange the target inequality to find what \(N\) must be.

docs.title: Proof Template: \(a_n = r^n \to 0\) for \(|r| < 1\)
docs.text:
Claim. If \(|r| < 1\), then \(\lim_{n\to\infty} r^n = 0\).

Proof. Let \(\varepsilon > 0\). We need \(|r^n - 0| = |r|^n < \varepsilon\). Taking logarithms: $\(n \ln|r| < \ln\varepsilon \implies n > \frac{\ln\varepsilon}{\ln|r|}\)$

(Note: \(\ln|r| < 0\) since \(|r| < 1\), so the inequality flips.) Choose \(N > \dfrac{\ln\varepsilon}{\ln|r|}\). Then for all \(n > N\): \(|r|^n < \varepsilon\). \(\square\)

docs.title: Proof Template: Geometric Sequence Limit
docs.text:
Claim. \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \dfrac{n}{n+1} = 1\).

Proof. \(\left|\dfrac{n}{n+1} - 1\right| = \dfrac{1}{n+1} < \dfrac{1}{n}\). Given \(\varepsilon > 0\), choose \(N > 1/\varepsilon\). Then \(n > N \Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{n+1} < \dfrac{1}{n} < \varepsilon\). \(\square\)

docs.title: Limit Laws for Sequences
docs.text:
Theorem (Limit Laws). Suppose \(\lim a_n = L\) and \(\lim b_n = M\). Then:

  1. \(\lim(a_n \pm b_n) = L \pm M\)
  2. \(\lim(a_n \cdot b_n) = LM\)
  3. \(\lim(a_n / b_n) = L/M\) provided \(M \neq 0\)
  4. \(\lim c \cdot a_n = cL\) for constant \(c\)
  5. \(\lim a_n^p = L^p\) for \(p > 0\) and \(L > 0\)

These are proved by \(\varepsilon\)-\(N\) arguments using the triangle inequality.

Key tool in proofs:

\[|a_n b_n - LM| = |a_n b_n - a_n M + a_n M - LM| \leq |a_n||b_n - M| + |M||a_n - L|\]

Since \({a_n}\) converges it is bounded (\(|a_n| \leq B\) for all \(n\)), giving:

\[\leq B|b_n - M| + |M||a_n - L| < B \cdot \frac{\varepsilon}{2B} + |M| \cdot \frac{\varepsilon}{2|M|} = \varepsilon\]

with the right choice of \(N\).

docs.title: Squeeze Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem (Squeeze / Sandwich). Suppose \(a_n \leq b_n \leq c_n\) for all \(n \geq N_0\), and \(\lim a_n = \lim c_n = L\). Then \(\lim b_n = L\).

Proof. Let \(\varepsilon > 0\). Since \(a_n \to L\), \(\exists N_1\) s.t. \(n > N_1 \Rightarrow |a_n - L| < \varepsilon \Rightarrow L - \varepsilon < a_n\). Since \(c_n \to L\), \(\exists N_2\) s.t. \(n > N_2 \Rightarrow c_n < L + \varepsilon\). For \(n > \max(N_0, N_1, N_2)\):

\[L - \varepsilon < a_n \leq b_n \leq c_n < L + \varepsilon \implies |b_n - L| < \varepsilon \qquad \square\]

Classic application. \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \dfrac{\cos n}{n} = 0\), since \(-\dfrac{1}{n} \leq \dfrac{\cos n}{n} \leq \dfrac{1}{n} \to 0\).

docs.title: Monotone Convergence Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem (MCT). Every bounded monotone sequence converges.

  • If \({a_n}\) is increasing (\(a_n \leq a_{n+1}\)) and bounded above, it converges to \(\sup_n a_n\).
  • If \({a_n}\) is decreasing (\(a_n \geq a_{n+1}\)) and bounded below, it converges to \(\inf_n a_n\).

Proof (increasing case). Let \(L = \sup{a_n : n \in \mathbb{N}}\) (exists since the sequence is bounded above; this uses the Completeness Axiom of \(\mathbb{R}\)). By definition of supremum, for any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists some \(a_N > L - \varepsilon\). Since the sequence is increasing, for all \(n > N\):

\[L - \varepsilon < a_N \leq a_n \leq L < L + \varepsilon\]

Hence \(|a_n - L| < \varepsilon\). \(\square\)

This theorem is deep. It is equivalent to the Completeness Axiom of \(\mathbb{R}\) — you cannot prove it in \(\mathbb{Q}\). The sequence \(a_n = \lfloor n\sqrt{2} \rfloor / n\) is increasing and bounded above by \(\sqrt{2}\), but \(\sqrt{2} \notin \mathbb{Q}\).

docs.title: Bolzano–Weierstrass Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem (Bolzano–Weierstrass). Every bounded sequence in \(\mathbb{R}\) has a convergent subsequence.

Proof sketch. Let \({a_n} \subset [a,b]\). Bisect \([a,b]\): at least one half contains infinitely many terms; call it \(I_1\). Bisect \(I_1\): at least one half has infinitely many terms; call it \(I_2\). Continue. By the Nested Interval Property, \(\bigcap I_k = {L}\) for some \(L\). The subsequence of selected terms converges to \(L\). \(\square\)

Significance. This theorem is used to prove the existence of extreme values (Extreme Value Theorem), convergence of optimization algorithms, and is the beating heart of compactness arguments in analysis.

docs.title: Subsequences
docs.text:
Definition. A subsequence of \({a_n}\) is \({a_{n_k}}\) where \(n_1 < n_2 < n_3 < \cdots\).

Theorem. If \(\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = L\), then every subsequence also converges to \(L\).

Theorem (Contrapositive). If two subsequences converge to different limits, the original sequence diverges.

Classic example. \(a_n = (-1)^n\). The subsequence \(a_{2k} = 1 \to 1\) and \(a_{2k-1} = -1 \to -1\). Since the limits differ, \({(-1)^n}\) diverges.

docs.title: Special Sequences & Their Limits
docs.text:
These should be memorized. They recur constantly.

\[\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{n^p} = 0 \quad (p > 0)\] \[\lim_{n\to\infty} r^n = 0 \quad (|r| < 1), \quad = 1 \quad (r = 1), \quad \text{diverges} \quad (|r| > 1)\] \[\lim_{n\to\infty} n^{1/n} = 1\] \[\lim_{n\to\infty} \left(1 + \frac{x}{n}\right)^n = e^x\] \[\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{x^n}{n!} = 0 \quad \text{for any fixed } x\] \[\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{\ln n}{n} = 0\] \[\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{n^k}{a^n} = 0 \quad (a > 1, k \text{ fixed}) \quad \text{[exponential beats polynomial]}\] \[\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{a^n}{n!} = 0 \quad \text{[factorial beats exponential]}\]

Hierarchy of growth rates (slowest to fastest): $\(\ln n \ll n^p \ll a^n \ll n! \ll n^n\)$

docs.title: Proof: \(\lim n^{1/n} = 1\)
docs.text:
Let \(a_n = n^{1/n} - 1 \geq 0\). By Bernoulli's inequality, for integer \(n \geq 1\):

\[n = (1 + a_n)^n \geq 1 + na_n + \frac{n(n-1)}{2}a_n^2 \geq \frac{n(n-1)}{2}a_n^2\]

So \(a_n^2 \leq \dfrac{2}{n-1}\), giving \(0 \leq a_n \leq \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{n-1}} \to 0\). By Squeeze, \(a_n \to 0\), hence \(n^{1/n} \to 1\). \(\square\)

docs.title: Proof: \(\lim (1 + x/n)^n = e^x\)
docs.text:
Let \(a_n = n \ln(1 + x/n)\). As \(n \to \infty\), set \(h = x/n \to 0\):

\[a_n = \frac{\ln(1+h)}{h} \cdot x \to 1 \cdot x = x\]

using \(\lim_{h\to 0} \ln(1+h)/h = 1\) (L'Hôpital or Taylor). Since \(\exp\) is continuous:

\[\left(1 + \frac{x}{n}\right)^n = e^{a_n} \to e^x \qquad \square\]

docs.title: Example 1 — Limit Laws
docs.text:
\[\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{3n^2 - 2n + 1}{5n^2 + n - 4}\]

Divide numerator and denominator by \(n^2\) (the leading power):

\[= \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{3 - 2/n + 1/n^2}{5 + 1/n - 4/n^2} = \frac{3 - 0 + 0}{5 + 0 - 0} = \frac{3}{5}\]

docs.title: Example 2 — Exponential vs Polynomial
docs.text:
\[\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{2^n}{n^{100}}\]

Use the fact that \(\lim x^n/n! = 0\) to show \(\lim r^n/n^k = \infty\) for \(r > 1\):

By AM-GM or by writing \(2^n = e^{n\ln 2}\) and comparing growth rates: \(n\ln 2 \gg 100\ln n\). The limit is \(+\infty\).

docs.title: Example 3 — Recursive Sequence via MCT
docs.text:
Define \(a_1 = 1\), \(a_{n+1} = \sqrt{2 + a_n}\). Does it converge?

Step 1 — Bounded above. Claim \(a_n \leq 2\) for all \(n\).

  • Base: \(a_1 = 1 \leq 2\). ✓
  • Inductive step: \(a_{n+1} = \sqrt{2 + a_n} \leq \sqrt{2+2} = 2\). ✓

Step 2 — Increasing. \(a_2 = \sqrt{3} > 1 = a_1\). Suppose \(a_n > a_{n-1}\). Then \(a_{n+1} = \sqrt{2+a_n} > \sqrt{2+a_{n-1}} = a_n\).

Step 3 — Conclude. By MCT, \(L = \lim a_n\) exists. Taking limits on both sides: $\(L = \sqrt{2 + L} \implies L^2 = 2 + L \implies L^2 - L - 2 = 0 \implies (L-2)(L+1) = 0\)$

Since \(a_n > 0\) for all \(n\), \(L = 2\).

docs.title: Example 4 — Classic \(\varepsilon\)-\(N\) Proof
docs.text:
Claim. \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \dfrac{2n+3}{n+1} = 2\).

Scratch work. \(\left|\dfrac{2n+3}{n+1} - 2\right| = \left|\dfrac{2n+3 - 2n-2}{n+1}\right| = \dfrac{1}{n+1} < \dfrac{1}{n}\). We need this \(< \varepsilon\): take \(N > 1/\varepsilon\).

Proof. Let \(\varepsilon > 0\). Choose \(N \in \mathbb{N}\) with \(N > 1/\varepsilon\). For all \(n > N\): $\(\left|\frac{2n+3}{n+1} - 2\right| = \frac{1}{n+1} < \frac{1}{n} < \frac{1}{N} < \varepsilon \qquad \square\)$

docs.title: Example 5 — The Number \(e\)
docs.text:
The sequence \(a_n = \left(1 + \dfrac{1}{n}\right)^n\) is:

  • Increasing (can be shown via AM-GM)
  • Bounded above by 3 (by Binomial Theorem: \(a_n < \sum_{k=0}^n \frac{1}{k!} < \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{1}{k!} < 3\))

By MCT, it converges. Its limit is defined as \(e \approx 2.71828\ldots\)

This is one of the most important sequences in mathematics.

docs.title: Connection to Series
docs.text:
Every infinite series \(\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k\) is defined through sequences — specifically, the sequence of partial sums:

\[S_n = \sum_{k=1}^n a_k\]

We say the series converges iff \({S_n}\) converges:

\[\sum_{k=1}^\infty a_k = \lim_{n\to\infty} S_n\]

So the entire theory of infinite series — geometric series, Taylor series, Fourier series — is secretly the theory of sequences. See: [[Series]].

Key necessary condition. If \(\sum a_k\) converges, then \(a_k \to 0\). Proof: \(a_n = S_n - S_{n-1} \to L - L = 0\). The converse fails: \(\sum 1/n\) diverges despite \(1/n \to 0\).

docs.title: Connection to AI / ML / Deep Learning
docs.text: This is where the abstraction pays off. Nearly everything in modern ML is a sequence — and understanding convergence is understanding whether and why algorithms work.

docs.title: 1. Gradient Descent IS a Sequence
docs.text:
Define the parameter sequence:

\[\theta_{n+1} = \theta_n - \eta \nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta_n)\]

This is a recursively defined sequence in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) (or millions of dimensions). The central question of optimization theory is:

\[\text{Does } {\theta_n} \text{ converge, and to what?}\]

The tools are exactly the ones in this note:

  • MCT analog: If the loss is bounded below and decreasing along the sequence, we need a monotone convergence argument (in \(\mathbb{R}^d\), this requires convexity).
  • Cauchy criterion: Convergence without knowing the limit — useful when the true minimum is unknown.
  • Subsequences: Stochastic gradient descent produces a random sequence; convergence is shown for subsequences with probability 1 (almost sure convergence).

For strongly convex loss with Lipschitz gradient and step size \(\eta < 2/L\):

\[|\theta_n - \theta^_| \leq \left(1 - \eta\mu\right)^n |\theta_0 - \theta^_|\]

This is geometric convergence — the sequence \(r^n\) with \(r = 1 - \eta\mu < 1\).

docs.title: 2. Learning Rate Schedules — Convergence Conditions
docs.text:
The Robbins-Monro conditions for SGD convergence require the learning rate sequence \({\eta_n}\) to satisfy:

\[\sum_{n=1}^\infty \eta_n = \infty \qquad \text{and} \qquad \sum_{n=1}^\infty \eta_n^2 < \infty\]

These are series convergence conditions on sequences. A common choice: \(\eta_n = c/n\), for which \(\sum 1/n = \infty\) (harmonic series diverges) and \(\sum 1/n^2 < \infty\) (p-series, \(p = 2 > 1\)). Both conditions satisfied.

The first condition ensures the algorithm can "travel far enough" to reach the minimum; the second ensures the noise eventually dies out. This is rigorous sequence analysis applied directly to algorithm design.

docs.title: 3. Recurrent Neural Networks — Sequences as Input
docs.text:
RNNs process sequences \({x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_T}\) by maintaining a hidden state:

\[h_t = f(W_h h_{t-1} + W_x x_t + b)\]

This is a time-varying recursion — a sequence of hidden states. The question of whether information at time \(t=1\) affects \(h_T\) as \(T \to \infty\) is a question about the convergence/divergence of this recursion.

Vanishing gradients correspond to the sequence \({|\partial h_T/\partial h_1|}\) converging to 0 (like \(r^n \to 0\) for \(|r| < 1\)). Exploding gradients correspond to divergence (like \(r^n \to \infty\) for \(|r| > 1\)). LSTMs and GRUs are architectural fixes for this sequence convergence problem.

docs.title: 4. Attention & Positional Encoding
docs.text:
The transformer's positional encoding is defined as a sequence of vectors:

\[\text{PE}(n, 2i) = \sin!\left(\frac{n}{10000^{2i/d}}\right), \quad \text{PE}(n, 2i+1) = \cos!\left(\frac{n}{10000^{2i/d}}\right)\]

This is a family of sequences in \(n\) (position), parameterized by frequency \(1/10000^{2i/d}\). The design choice ensures that relative positions can be expressed as linear transformations — a property that depends on the identities \(\sin(n+k) = \sin n \cos k + \cos n \sin k\), i.e., the algebraic properties of these sequences.

docs.title: 5. Convergence of Neural Network Training — Loss Sequences
docs.text:
The loss sequence \({\mathcal{L}(\theta_n)}\) is a sequence of non-negative real numbers. We want it to converge. Tools from sequence analysis:

  • Bounded below (loss \(\geq 0\)) + decreasing (with correct step size) → by MCT, \(\mathcal{L}(\theta_n)\) converges to some \(L^*\).
  • But does \(\theta_n\) converge? Not necessarily — the loss can flatten while parameters wander (flat minima, manifold of solutions).
  • Cauchy sequences in parameter space: If \({\theta_n}\) is Cauchy, then \(\theta_n \to \theta^*\). This is what "converging weights" actually means.

The theory of convergence for Adam, RMSProp, etc. is active research, and it is precisely: proving that the parameter sequence \({\theta_n}\) is Cauchy under appropriate conditions.

docs.title: 6. Fixed-Point Iterations — Banach Contraction
docs.text:
Many algorithms are fixed-point iterations: \(x_{n+1} = f(x_n)\), seeking \(x^* = f(x^*)\).

Banach Fixed-Point Theorem. If \(f: X \to X\) is a contraction (\(|f(x) - f(y)| \leq c|x-y|\), \(c < 1\)) on a complete metric space, then the sequence \(x_{n+1} = f(x_n)\) converges to the unique fixed point \(x^_\), and: $\(|x_n - x^_| \leq \frac{c^n}{1-c}|x_1 - x_0|\)$

This is a geometric sequence bound \(\propto c^n\). Applications in ML:

  • Value iteration in reinforcement learning (Bellman operator is a \(\gamma\)-contraction)
  • Newton's method for training (quadratic convergence near solution)
  • Normalizing flows — invertible neural networks as fixed-point iterations

RL note. The Bellman optimality operator \(\mathcal{T}\): $\((\mathcal{T}V)(s) = \max_a \left[R(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a)V(s')\right]\)$ is a \(\gamma\)-contraction in the \(\ell^\infty\) norm (where \(\gamma < 1\) is the discount factor). Therefore the sequence \(V_{n+1} = \mathcal{T}V_n\) converges to \(V^*\) by the Banach theorem. This is the theoretical guarantee behind value iteration.

docs.title: 7. Cauchy Sequences in Deep Learning Numerics
docs.text:
In floating-point arithmetic, exact limits don't exist — we work with Cauchy-like stopping criteria:

\[|\theta_{n+1} - \theta_n| < \delta \quad \text{(parameter change small)}$$ $$|\mathcal{L}_{n+1} - \mathcal{L}_n| < \delta \quad \text{(loss change small)}\]

These are practical implementations of the Cauchy criterion: the sequence has "essentially stopped moving." The relationship between these two criteria (loss converging ≠ parameters converging in non-convex landscapes) is a deep practical issue in training large models.

docs.title: Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. \(\varepsilon\)-\(N\) proof. Prove from the definition that \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \dfrac{n^2 + 1}{2n^2 - 3} = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

  2. Squeeze. Prove \(\lim_{n\to\infty} \dfrac{\sin(n^2)}{n} = 0\).

  3. MCT. Let \(a_1 = \sqrt{2}\) and \(a_{n+1} = \sqrt{2 a_n}\). Prove the sequence converges and find its limit.

  4. Subsequence. Show that \(a_n = \sin(n\pi/2)\) diverges by finding two subsequences with different limits.

  5. Growth rates. Order the following by rate of growth: \(\ln n,\ n^{0.01},\ 1.001^n,\ n!,\ n^n / n!\).

  6. Recursive limit. Define \(a_1 = 0\), \(a_{n+1} = \frac{a_n + 2}{a_n + 3}\). Assuming the limit \(L\) exists, find it. Then prove the sequence converges using MCT.

  7. ML connection. The gradient descent sequence satisfies \(|\theta_n - \theta^_| \leq (1 - \eta\mu)^n |\theta_0 - \theta^_|\). Given \(\mu = 0.1\), \(\eta = 5\), \(|\theta_0 - \theta^_| = 100\), find the smallest \(n\) such that \(|\theta_n - \theta^_| < 0.001\).

docs.title: Monotonic Sequence Theorem
docs.text: "Every bounded monotone sequence converges. This theorem is not trivial — it is equivalent to the completeness of the real numbers."

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
Consider the sequence defined recursively:

\[a_1 = 1, \qquad a_{n+1} = \frac{1}{2}\left(a_n + \frac{2}{a_n}\right)\]

Does this converge? To what? You might suspect \(\sqrt{2}\) — and you'd be right — but proving it converges requires more than intuition. The Monotonic Sequence Theorem (MST) gives you a two-step proof structure:

  1. Show the sequence is monotone (increasing or decreasing).
  2. Show it is bounded (above or below, as appropriate).

Conclusion: it converges. Then you find the limit by setting \(L = \lim_{n\to\infty} a_n\) and solving the resulting equation.

Personal note: The MST is one of the workhorses of analysis. It proves the existence of limits without ever exhibiting the limit explicitly. This "existence before computation" pattern recurs constantly — in fixed-point theorems, in the intermediate value theorem, in the convergence of optimization algorithms.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
Definition. A sequence \({a_n}\) is:

  • Increasing if \(a_{n+1} > a_n\) for all \(n \geq 1\)
  • Nondecreasing if \(a_{n+1} \geq a_n\) for all \(n \geq 1\)
  • Decreasing if \(a_{n+1} < a_n\) for all \(n \geq 1\)
  • Nonincreasing if \(a_{n+1} \leq a_n\) for all \(n \geq 1\)
  • Monotone if it is nondecreasing or nonincreasing

Definition. A sequence \({a_n}\) is:

  • Bounded above if \(\exists M \in \mathbb{R}\) such that \(a_n \leq M\) for all \(n\)
  • Bounded below if \(\exists m \in \mathbb{R}\) such that \(a_n \geq m\) for all \(n\)
  • Bounded if it is both bounded above and below

Definition (Supremum). The least upper bound (supremum) of a set \(S \subseteq \mathbb{R}\), written \(\sup S\), is the smallest \(M\) such that \(s \leq M\) for all \(s \in S\). It need not be an element of \(S\).

docs.title: The Theorem — Statement and Proof
docs.text:
Theorem (Monotonic Sequence Theorem). Every bounded monotone sequence of real numbers converges.

More precisely:

  • If \({a_n}\) is nondecreasing and bounded above, then \(\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = \sup{a_n : n \geq 1}\).
  • If \({a_n}\) is nonincreasing and bounded below, then \(\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = \inf{a_n : n \geq 1}\).

Proof (nondecreasing case).

Let \(S = {a_n : n \geq 1}\). Since \({a_n}\) is bounded above, \(S\) is a nonempty subset of \(\mathbb{R}\) bounded above, so by the Completeness Axiom of \(\mathbb{R}\), the supremum \(L = \sup S\) exists.

We claim \(\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = L\).

Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) be arbitrary. Since \(L = \sup S\), \(L - \varepsilon\) is not an upper bound for \(S\). Therefore there exists \(N\) such that:

\[a_N > L - \varepsilon\]

Since \({a_n}\) is nondecreasing, for all \(n \geq N\):

\[L - \varepsilon < a_N \leq a_n \leq L < L + \varepsilon\]

Therefore \(|a_n - L| < \varepsilon\) for all \(n \geq N\).

Since \(\varepsilon > 0\) was arbitrary, \(\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = L\). \(\square\)

Proof (nonincreasing case).

Let \(b_n = -a_n\). Then \({b_n}\) is nondecreasing and bounded above (by \(-\inf{a_n}\)). By the first case, \(b_n \to L'\), so \(a_n = -b_n \to -L' = \inf{a_n}\). \(\square\)

Remark on necessity. Both conditions are necessary:

  • \(a_n = n\) is monotone but not bounded → diverges to \(\infty\).
  • \(a_n = (-1)^n\) is bounded but not monotone → diverges (oscillates).

docs.title: The Completeness Axiom — What's Really Going On
docs.text:
The proof invokes the Completeness Axiom (also called the Least Upper Bound Property):

Axiom. Every nonempty subset of \(\mathbb{R}\) that is bounded above has a supremum in \(\mathbb{R}\).

This is what distinguishes \(\mathbb{R}\) from \(\mathbb{Q}\). Consider:

\[S = {q \in \mathbb{Q} : q^2 < 2}\]

\(S\) is a nonempty subset of \(\mathbb{Q}\), bounded above (by 2). But \(\sup S = \sqrt{2} \notin \mathbb{Q}\). The rationals have a "hole" at \(\sqrt{2}\).

The Monotonic Sequence Theorem would fail over \(\mathbb{Q}\): the sequence of rational approximations to \(\sqrt{2}\),

\[1,\ 1.4,\ 1.41,\ 1.414,\ 1.4142,\ \ldots\]

is nondecreasing and bounded above (by 2) in \(\mathbb{Q}\), but converges to \(\sqrt{2} \notin \mathbb{Q}\) — i.e., it does not converge in \(\mathbb{Q}\).

The MST is logically equivalent to the Completeness Axiom. You can take either one as the fundamental axiom of \(\mathbb{R}\) and derive the other. Other equivalent formulations: the Cauchy completeness criterion, the Nested Interval Theorem, the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem.

docs.title: Corollaries and Variants
docs.text:
Corollary 1. A nondecreasing sequence either converges or diverges to \(+\infty\).

Proof. If bounded above, MST gives convergence. If not bounded above, for every \(M\) there exists \(N\) with \(a_N > M\), and since the sequence is nondecreasing, \(a_n \geq a_N > M\) for all \(n \geq N\). So \(a_n \to +\infty\). \(\square\)

Corollary 2. A sequence defined by \(a_{n+1} = f(a_n)\) converges if: (i) \(f\) is continuous, (ii) the sequence is monotone, (iii) the sequence is bounded. Moreover, the limit \(L\) satisfies \(L = f(L)\) (it is a fixed point of \(f\)).

Proof. MST gives \(a_n \to L\). By continuity of \(f\): \(L = \lim a_{n+1} = \lim f(a_n) = f(\lim a_n) = f(L)\). \(\square\)

Corollary 3 (Ratio test for sequences). If \(a_n > 0\) and \(a_{n+1}/a_n \leq r < 1\) for all large \(n\), then \(a_n \to 0\).

Proof. The sequence is eventually decreasing (geometric comparison). It is bounded below by 0. MST gives convergence; the fixed-point equation forces the limit to be 0. \(\square\)

docs.title: Example 1 — The Sequence \(a_n = \left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)^n\)
docs.text:
This defines \(e\). We show it is increasing and bounded above by 3.

Monotone: By the AM-GM inequality applied to \((n+1)\) numbers — one copy of \(1\) and \(n\) copies of \((1 + 1/n)\):

\[\left(\frac{1 + n(1 + 1/n)}{n+1}\right)^{n+1} \geq 1 \cdot \left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)^n\] \[\left(\frac{2n+1}{n+1}\right)^{n+1} \geq \left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)^n\] \[\left(1 + \frac{1}{n+1}\right)^{n+1} \geq \left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)^n\]

So \(a_{n+1} \geq a_n\): the sequence is nondecreasing. ✓

Bounded: By the binomial theorem:

\[a_n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} \frac{1}{n^k} = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{1}{k!}\cdot\frac{n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)}{n^k} \leq \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{1}{k!} \leq \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k!}\]

Now \(k! \geq 2^{k-1}\) for \(k \geq 1\), so:

\[a_n \leq 1 + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{2^{k-1}} = 1 + 2 = 3\]

By MST, \(\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n\) exists. We call it \(e \approx 2.71828\). ✓

docs.title: Example 2 — Newton's Method for \(\sqrt{c}\)
docs.text:
\[a_1 = c > 1, \qquad a_{n+1} = \frac{1}{2}\left(a_n + \frac{c}{a_n}\right)\]

Bounded below by \(\sqrt{c}\): By AM-GM, \(a_{n+1} = \frac{1}{2}(a_n + c/a_n) \geq \sqrt{a_n \cdot c/a_n} = \sqrt{c}\). So \(a_n \geq \sqrt{c}\) for all \(n \geq 2\). ✓

Decreasing (for \(n \geq 2\)):

\[a_{n+1} - a_n = \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{c}{a_n} - a_n\right) = \frac{c - a_n^2}{2a_n} \leq 0\]

since \(a_n \geq \sqrt{c} \Rightarrow a_n^2 \geq c\). ✓

By MST, \(L = \lim a_n\) exists. Setting \(L = \frac{1}{2}(L + c/L)\) gives \(L^2 = c\), so \(L = \sqrt{c}\).

This is Newton's method in disguise — and the proof of convergence is the MST applied to a recursively defined sequence.

docs.title: Example 3 — A Decreasing Bounded Sequence
docs.text:
\[a_n = \frac{n+1}{n} = 1 + \frac{1}{n}\]

Decreasing: \(a_{n+1} = 1 + 1/(n+1) < 1 + 1/n = a_n\). ✓

Bounded below by 1: \(a_n = 1 + 1/n > 1\) for all \(n\). ✓

By MST, \(\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = \inf{1 + 1/n} = 1\).

docs.title: Example 4 — Fibonacci Ratios
docs.text:
Let \(F_n\) be the Fibonacci sequence: \(F_1 = F_2 = 1\), \(F_{n+1} = F_n + F_{n-1}\). Define \(r_n = F_{n+1}/F_n\).

Claim: \(r_n\) converges to the golden ratio \(\phi = (1+\sqrt5)/2\).

One approach: show the even-indexed terms are decreasing and bounded below, odd-indexed terms are increasing and bounded above, and both bounds squeeze to the same value. Alternatively:

Assume \(r_n \to L\). Then dividing \(F_{n+2} = F_{n+1} + F_n\) by \(F_{n+1}\): $\(r_{n+1} = 1 + \frac{1}{r_n} \to 1 + \frac{1}{L}\)$

So \(L = 1 + 1/L\), giving \(L^2 - L - 1 = 0\), hence \(L = \phi\). (MST supplies the existence; then we solve for \(L\).)

docs.title: The Theorem in Action — Finding Limits
docs.text:
The standard proof pattern using MST:

Step 1 — Show monotone. Use induction. For \(a_{n+1} = f(a_n)\), show \(a_2 \geq a_1\), then assume \(a_{k+1} \geq a_k\) and prove \(a_{k+2} \geq a_{k+1}\) (by applying \(f\) and using monotonicity of \(f\)).

Step 2 — Show bounded. Use induction again. Show \(a_1 \leq M\); assume \(a_k \leq M\); show \(f(a_k) \leq M\).

Step 3 — Invoke MST. Conclude \(L = \lim a_n\) exists.

Step 4 — Find \(L\). Take limits on both sides of \(a_{n+1} = f(a_n)\): \(L = f(L)\). Solve.

Example. \(a_1 = 2\), \(a_{n+1} = \frac{1}{4}(a_n^2 + 3)\).

Step 1 (decreasing): \(a_{n+1} - a_n = \frac{1}{4}(a_n^2 + 3) - a_n = \frac{1}{4}(a_n - 1)^2 - 0\)... Actually let's check: \(a_2 = (4+3)/4 = 7/4 < 2 = a_1\). Assume \(1 < a_n \leq 2\); then \(a_{n+1} = (a_n^2 + 3)/4 \leq (4+3)/4 = 7/4 < 2\). And \(a_{n+1} - 1 = (a_n^2 - 1)/4 > 0\). So \(a_n\) is decreasing and bounded below by 1.

Step 3: MST gives \(L = \lim a_n\) exists.

Step 4: \(L = (L^2 + 3)/4 \Rightarrow 4L = L^2 + 3 \Rightarrow L^2 - 4L + 3 = 0 \Rightarrow (L-1)(L-3) = 0\).

Since \(L \geq 1\) and \(L \leq 2\), we have \(L = 1\).

docs.title: Connection to AI / ML / Deep Learning
docs.text: The Monotonic Sequence Theorem is not merely background mathematics — it is the conceptual ancestor of convergence proofs throughout optimization and machine learning.

docs.title: 1. Gradient Descent — Monotone Decrease of Loss
docs.text:
In standard gradient descent:

\[w_{n+1} = w_n - \eta \nabla \mathcal{L}(w_n)\]

For a convex loss \(\mathcal{L}\) with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, choosing step size \(\eta \leq 1/L\) gives:

\[\mathcal{L}(w_{n+1}) \leq \mathcal{L}(w_n) - \frac{\eta}{2}|\nabla \mathcal{L}(w_n)|^2\]

So the loss sequence \({\mathcal{L}(w_n)}\) is nonincreasing. It is also bounded below by \(\mathcal{L}^* = \min_w \mathcal{L}(w) \geq 0\). By the MST, \(\mathcal{L}(w_n)\) converges.

This is literally the MST applied to the loss sequence. The convergence proof for gradient descent is the MST in disguise.

The bound \(\eta \leq 1/L\) is the Lipschitz condition ensuring the loss sequence is actually monotone. Violating it (learning rate too large) breaks monotonicity → oscillation → divergence. This is why learning rate tuning matters.

docs.title: 2. EM Algorithm — Monotone Likelihood
docs.text:
The Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm for fitting latent variable models (Gaussian mixtures, HMMs, etc.) produces iterates \(\theta^{(n)}\) satisfying:

\[\mathcal{L}(\theta^{(n+1)}) \geq \mathcal{L}(\theta^{(n)})\]

where \(\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \log p(\text{data} \mid \theta)\) is the log-likelihood. The log-likelihood is bounded above (by 0 for a proper probability model).

By the MST: \(\mathcal{L}(\theta^{(n)})\) converges.

The proof of the EM inequality uses Jensen's inequality on the E-step and optimality on the M-step — but the conclusion of convergence is the MST.

Caveat: The MST gives convergence of the values \(\mathcal{L}(\theta^{(n)})\). Convergence of the parameter sequence \(\theta^{(n)}\) itself is a separate (harder) question requiring additional assumptions on the likelihood surface.

docs.title: 3. Value Iteration in Reinforcement Learning
docs.text:
In dynamic programming / reinforcement learning, the value iteration algorithm updates:

\[V_{n+1}(s) = \max_a \left[R(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a) V_n(s')\right]\]

This is the application of the Bellman optimality operator \(\mathcal{T}\): \(V_{n+1} = \mathcal{T}V_n\).

Convergence proof:

  1. \(\mathcal{T}\) is a contraction mapping with constant \(\gamma < 1\) (discount factor) in the \(\ell^\infty\) norm.
  2. Therefore \({|\mathcal{T}^n V_0 - V^*|}\) is a geometrically decreasing sequence.
  3. A geometrically decreasing positive sequence is monotone and bounded below by 0 → MST gives convergence to 0.
  4. Hence \(V_n \to V^*\) (optimal value function).

The Banach Fixed-Point Theorem (contraction mapping theorem) is a generalization of the MST to complete metric spaces — it says "a sequence defined by a contraction converges to a unique fixed point." The proof is the MST in a metric space.

docs.title: 4. Convergence of Neural Network Training — ELBO Monotonicity
docs.text:
In Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), the training objective is the ELBO (Evidence Lower BOund):

\[\text{ELBO}(\phi, \theta) = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z|x)}[\log p_\theta(x|z)] - \text{KL}(q_\phi(z|x) | p(z))\]

Coordinate ascent variational inference (CAVI), used in mean-field VI, updates each variational parameter to maximize the ELBO holding others fixed. Each update monotonically increases the ELBO:

\[\text{ELBO}^{(n+1)} \geq \text{ELBO}^{(n)}\]

The ELBO is bounded above by \(\log p_\theta(x)\). By the MST: ELBO converges.

This is the same structure as the EM algorithm (and EM is a special case of VI).

docs.title: 5. AdaGrad / RMSProp — Accumulated Squared Gradients
docs.text:
In AdaGrad, the accumulated sum of squared gradients:

\[G_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} g_k^2\]

is nondecreasing (each term \(g_k^2 \geq 0\)). In AdaGrad this is unbounded — which causes the effective learning rate \(\eta/\sqrt{G_n}\) to decay to zero (can be too aggressive). RMSProp replaces this with an exponential moving average:

\[G_n = \beta G_{n-1} + (1-\beta)g_n^2, \qquad \beta \in (0,1)\]

This is bounded above (by \(\max g_k^2\)) and nondecreasing when \(g_n^2 \geq G_{n-1}\)... actually it oscillates. The MST perspective explains why AdaGrad can be ill-behaved (the monotone unbounded sequence \(G_n \to \infty\)) and why RMSProp fixes it (introducing a forgetting factor).

docs.title: 6. Convergence of MCMC — Monotone Coupling
docs.text:
In Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods (Gibbs sampling, Metropolis-Hastings), convergence to the stationary distribution \(\pi\) is sometimes proved via monotone coupling:

Given two chains \(X_n\) and \(Y_n\) started at different initial states, construct a coupling such that once they meet, they stay together. The probability of not yet having met, \(P(\text{not coupled by time } n)\), is a nonincreasing sequence bounded below by 0. By the MST, it converges — and one shows the limit must be 0.

This is a probabilistic MST, but the structure is identical.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Condition Conclusion Nondecreasing + bounded above Converges to \(\sup{a_n}\) Nonincreasing + bounded below Converges to \(\inf{a_n}\) Monotone + unbounded Diverges to \(\pm\infty\) Bounded + not monotone No conclusion (may or may not converge)

The proof recipe for recursive sequences: $\(a_{n+1} = f(a_n) \xrightarrow{\text{(1) monotone, (2) bounded}} \xrightarrow{\text{MST}} L \text{ exists} \xrightarrow{L = f(L)} \text{find } L\)$

The logical backbone:

\[\text{Completeness of } \mathbb{R} \iff \text{MST} \iff \text{Cauchy criterion} \iff \text{Bolzano-Weierstrass} \iff \text{Nested Interval Theorem}\]

All four are equivalent — different faces of the same fundamental property that distinguishes \(\mathbb{R}\) from \(\mathbb{Q}\).

docs.title: Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Prove the MST for the nonincreasing case directly (without reducing to the nondecreasing case).

  2. Let \(a_1 = 1\) and \(a_{n+1} = \sqrt{2 + a_n}\). Prove by induction that \({a_n}\) is increasing and bounded above by 2. Find the limit.

  3. Let \(a_n = \sum_{k=1}^n \frac{1}{k^2}\). Show this sequence converges by applying the MST. (Bound it above using a telescoping comparison.)

  4. Give an example of a bounded sequence that does not converge. Why doesn't the MST apply?

  5. Give an example of an unbounded monotone sequence. What does Corollary 1 say about it?

  6. (Completeness) Exhibit a nondecreasing sequence in \(\mathbb{Q}\) that is bounded above in \(\mathbb{Q}\) but whose supremum is irrational. What does this say about applying the MST over \(\mathbb{Q}\)?

  7. (ML connection) Suppose \(\mathcal{L}(w_n)\) is a nonincreasing sequence of loss values bounded below by 0. By the MST, \(\mathcal{L}(w_n) \to L^*\). Does this imply \(w_n\) converges? Construct a counterexample or give conditions under which it does.

docs.title: Logistic Map
docs.text:
"Boundless complexity from utter simplicity."

A single quadratic recurrence. One parameter. And hidden inside it: the entire zoo of dynamical behaviours — fixed points, period-doubling, chaos, universality. This is one of the most important equations in all of applied mathematics.

docs.title: The Equation
docs.text:
\[\boxed{x_{n+1} = r, x_n (1 - x_n), \qquad x_0 \in (0,1),\quad r \in (0,4]}\]

That is the entire object of study. One quadratic map on \([0,1]\). The parameter \(r\) controls the behaviour, and the range of behaviour as \(r\) varies is extraordinary.

Personal note: Pierre François Verhulst introduced the logistic differential equation in 1838 as a model of population growth with a carrying capacity. The discrete analogue — the logistic map — was popularised by Robert May in his landmark 1976 Nature paper, which introduced it to biologists and arguably birthed the modern study of chaos. Read that paper. It is three pages and changed everything.

docs.title: The Malthusian (Unconstrained) Model
docs.text:
Start simple. If a population \(x_n\) grows by a factor \(r\) each generation:

\[x_{n+1} = r x_n\]

Solution: \(x_n = r^n x_0\). Exponential growth — unbounded. Unrealistic.

docs.title: The Logistic Correction
docs.text:
Introduce a carrying capacity. Normalize so the maximum population is 1. The growth rate is penalized as \(x_n \to 1\):

\[x_{n+1} = r x_n \underbrace{(1 - x_n)}_{\text{penalty term}}\]
  • When \(x_n \approx 0\): nearly unconstrained, \(x_{n+1} \approx r x_n\).
  • When \(x_n \approx 1\): population at carrying capacity, \(x_{n+1} \approx 0\).
  • The factor \((1 - x_n)\) is the fraction of unused capacity.

This is the logistic map. The full behaviour as \(r\) varies from 0 to 4 spans fixed points, cycles, and chaos.

docs.title: Fixed Points & Stability — The Full Analysis
Finding Fixed Points
docs.text:
A fixed point \(x^_\) satisfies \(f(x^_) = x^*\) where \(f(x) = rx(1-x)\):

\[rx^_(1 - x^_) = x^*\] \[x^_[r(1-x^_) - 1] = 0\]

Two fixed points:

\[\boxed{x^* = 0} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \boxed{x^* = \frac{r-1}{r}} \quad (r > 1)\]

The second fixed point only lies in \((0,1)\) when \(r > 1\).

docs.title: Stability Analysis
docs.text:
A fixed point \(x^_\) is stable (attracting) if \(|f'(x^_)| < 1\), and unstable (repelling) if \(|f'(x^*)| > 1\).

Compute the derivative:

\[f'(x) = r(1 - 2x)\]

__At \(x^_ = 0\):_*

\[f'(0) = r\]
  • Stable when \(r < 1\).
  • Unstable when \(r > 1\).

__At \(x^_ = (r-1)/r\):_*

\[f'!\left(\frac{r-1}{r}\right) = r\left(1 - \frac{2(r-1)}{r}\right) = 2 - r\]
  • Stable when \(|2 - r| < 1\), i.e., \(1 < r < 3\).
  • At \(r = 3\): \(|f'(x^*)| = 1\) — bifurcation point.
  • Unstable when \(r > 3\).

docs.title: Stability Summary
docs.text: \(r\) range Attracting fixed point Long-term behaviour \(0 < r < 1\) \(x^* = 0\) Population dies out \(1 < r < 3\) \(x^* = (r-1)/r\) Convergence to equilibrium \(r = 3\) Bifurcation Marginal — period-2 born \(3 < r < 1+\sqrt{6} \approx 3.449\) None (2-cycle) Period-2 oscillation \(r \approx 3.449\) — Period-4 bifurcation \(r \approx 3.570\) — Onset of chaos \(3.570 < r \leq 4\) — Chaos (with periodic windows)

docs.title: What is a Bifurcation?
docs.text: At \(r = 3\), the fixed point \(x^* = (r-1)/r\) loses stability — it transitions from attracting to repelling. Simultaneously, a 2-cycle is born: two points \(x_a, x_b\) with \(f(x_a) = x_b\) and \(f(x_b) = x_a\).

docs.title: Finding the 2-Cycle
docs.text:
The 2-cycle points satisfy \(f(f(x)) = x\) but \(f(x) \neq x\). Factoring out the fixed points from \(f^2(x) - x = 0\), the 2-cycle points are:

\[x_{a,b} = \frac{(r+1) \pm \sqrt{(r+1)(r-3)}}{2r}\]

These are real only when \(r \geq 3\) — the 2-cycle is born exactly at the bifurcation \(r = 3\).

docs.title: Stability of the 2-Cycle
docs.text:
By the chain rule: $\(\frac{d}{dx} f^2(x)\bigg|_{x=x_a} = f'(x_b) \cdot f'(x_a) = (2 - r)^2 + \text{(correction)}\)$

Working through the algebra: the 2-cycle is stable for \(3 < r < 1 + \sqrt{6} \approx 3.4495\).

docs.title: The Period-Doubling Cascade
docs.text:
At each subsequent \(r_k\), the \(2^{k-1}\)-cycle loses stability and a \(2^k\)-cycle is born:

Bifurcation \(k\) \(r_k\) (approx) New period 1 \(3.000000\) 2 2 \(3.449490\) 4 3 \(3.544090\) 8 4 \(3.564407\) 16 5 \(3.568759\) 32 \(\infty\) \(3.569946\ldots\) \(\infty\) (onset of chaos)

docs.title: The Bifurcation Diagram
docs.text:
For each \(r\), iterate the map many times (discarding transient), then plot the remaining \(x_n\) values as \(r\) varies. The result:

 x

  │                              ·:·
  │                         ·:·
  │                    ┌──┐ ·
  │               ┌──┐ ┤  ├──
  │    ──────────┬┘  └─┘  └──────── ...
  │              │
  │              │
 0└──────────────────────────────────────── r
  0    1    2    3   3.45 3.54  3.57   4
            ↑    ↑    ↑    ↑     ↑
       equil- bif  per- per-  chaos
       ibrium   1   2    4    onset

Diagram is self-similar: zoom into any chaotic region
and find periodic windows, each a miniature copy of the whole.

docs.title: Chaos: Sensitive Dependence on Initial Conditions
Definition (Devaney)
docs.text:
The logistic map at \(r > r_\infty\) is chaotic in the sense of:

  1. Sensitive dependence: \(\exists, \delta > 0\) such that for any \(x_0\) and any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists \(y_0\) with \(|x_0 - y_0| < \varepsilon\) yet \(|x_n - y_n| > \delta\) for some \(n\).
  2. Topological transitivity: There exists an orbit dense in \([0,1]\).
  3. Dense periodic orbits: Periodic points are dense.

docs.title: Conjugacy at \(r = 4\)
docs.text:
At \(r = 4\) the logistic map is topologically conjugate to the tent/doubling map via \(x_n = \sin^2(\pi\theta_n)\):

\[\theta_{n+1} = 2\theta_n \pmod{1}\]

This is the doubling map: it shifts binary digits of \(\theta_0\). Any uncertainty in the last bit of \(\theta_0\) propagates to the first bit after \(n\) steps. The Lyapunov exponent at \(r = 4\) is exactly \(\lambda = \ln 2\).

docs.title: Feigenbaum's Universality Constant
docs.text:
In 1975, Mitchell Feigenbaum computed ratios of successive bifurcation intervals:

\[\delta = \lim_{k\to\infty} \frac{r_k - r_{k-1}}{r_{k+1} - r_k}\] \(k\) \(\delta_k\) 1 \(\approx 4.751\) 2 \(\approx 4.656\) 3 \(\approx 4.668\) \(\infty\) \(\mathbf{4.669201609\ldots}\) \[\boxed{\delta = 4.669201609\ldots}\]

This constant is universal: it appears in the period-doubling cascade of any unimodal map with a smooth quadratic maximum — sine map, Hénon map restricted to 1D, and many others. The specific equation doesn't matter; only the local shape of the maximum matters.

Feigenbaum proved this using renormalization group ideas borrowed from quantum field theory — the same mathematical structure that governs phase transitions in statistical mechanics.

The Feigenbaum constant is transcendental and has no known closed form in terms of \(\pi\), \(e\), or other classical constants. It is a genuinely new mathematical constant.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
\[\lambda = \lim_{N \to \infty} \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \ln |f'(x_n)| = \lim_{N\to\infty} \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \ln|r(1 - 2x_n)|\]

Interpretation:

  • \(\lambda < 0\): attracting periodic orbit
  • \(\lambda = 0\): bifurcation point (marginal stability)
  • \(\lambda > 0\): chaos — exponential separation of nearby orbits

docs.title: Exact Value at \(r = 4\)
docs.text:
Using the invariant measure \(\rho(x) = 1/(\pi\sqrt{x(1-x)})\) (arcsine distribution):

\[\lambda = \int_0^1 \ln|f'(x)|, \rho(x), dx = \ln 2\]

docs.title: Lyapunov Exponent vs \(r\) (schematic)
docs.text:
λ
  │
 +│                    ████ ██ █████████  (chaotic, λ > 0)
  │
 0├──────────────────··················   bifurcation pts
  │
 -│  ────────────────  (stable regime, λ < 0)
  │
  └──────────────────────────────────── r
  0        1       2       3    3.57   4

  λ < 0 throughout stable regime; λ > 0 in chaos;
  periodic windows inside chaos give dips back below 0.

docs.title: The Connection to the Logistic Function (Sigmoid)
docs.text:
The logistic function (sigmoid):

\[\sigma(t) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-t}}\]

is the solution to the continuous logistic ODE \(dp/dt = rp(1-p)\):

\[p(t) = \sigma!\left(rt + \ln\frac{p_0}{1-p_0}\right)\]

The logistic map is the Euler discretization of this ODE with step size 1:

\[p_{n+1} \approx p_n + r p_n(1-p_n)\]

which is a logistic map with parameter \(1 + r\). The sigmoid is the equilibrium of the continuous flow; the logistic map iterates the discrete approximation and discovers the rich bifurcation structure that the smooth ODE solution conceals.

Key algebraic link. The derivative of \(\sigma\):

\[\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1 - \sigma(z))\]

is exactly the logistic map expression \(x(1-x)\) evaluated at \(x = \sigma(z)\). This is not a coincidence — it is why the logistic function is the canonical activation for binary classification, and why backpropagation through sigmoid layers involves the logistic map's own derivative structure.

docs.title: Connection to AI / ML / Deep Learning
1. The Sigmoid Neuron and the Vanishing Gradient Problem
docs.text:
The activation \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})\) maps \(\mathbb{R} \to (0,1)\). Its gradient \(\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z)) \leq 1/4\) — saturating to 0 when \(|z|\) is large.

In a deep network of \(L\) sigmoid layers, backpropagation multiplies gradients:

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial w_1} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial x_L} \cdot \prod_{k=1}^{L} \sigma'(z_k) \cdot W_k\]

Each \(\sigma'(z_k) \leq 1/4\), so \(\prod_{k=1}^{L}\sigma'(z_k) \leq (1/4)^L \to 0\) exponentially. This is the vanishing gradient problem — directly caused by the logistic map's derivative being bounded away from 1 at its fixed points. ReLU (\(f'(z) = 1\) in the active region) was introduced precisely to escape this.

docs.title: 2. Bifurcations in RNNs — Exploding and Vanishing Gradients
docs.text:
A vanilla RNN updates:

\[h_{n+1} = \tanh(Wh_n + Ux_n + b)\]

The Jacobian of this map is \(J_n = W \cdot \text{diag}(1 - h_n^2)\). Backpropagating through time multiplies these Jacobians:

\[\frac{\partial h_T}{\partial h_0} = \prod_{n=0}^{T-1} J_n\]

If \(\rho(W) > 1\): eigenvalues of the product grow — exploding gradients (chaos regime of logistic map). If \(\rho(W) < 1\): eigenvalues shrink — vanishing gradients (stable fixed point regime).

The LSTM's gating mechanism is a learned bifurcation controller: the forget gate \(f_t = \sigma(W_f h_{t-1} + U_f x_t)\) adaptively scales the recurrent eigenvalues to stay near 1 — precisely the \(r \approx 3\) boundary between stability and chaos.

docs.title: 3. Echo State Networks — Edge of Chaos
docs.text:
Reservoir Computing (Echo State Networks) designs a fixed random RNN and trains only the readout. The design principle is the edge of chaos: spectral radius \(\rho(W) \approx 1\).

This is exactly the logistic map at \(r \approx 3\):

  • \(\rho < 1\) (stable): reservoir forgets inputs, poor memory
  • \(\rho > 1\) (chaotic): sensitive dependence, unreliable computation
  • \(\rho \approx 1\) (edge): maximum memory capacity and computational richness

This is a theorem in reservoir computing (Jaeger 2001), and it is Feigenbaum's story rewritten in \(N \times N\) matrix language.

docs.title: 4. Neural ODEs — Discretization Chaos
docs.text:
A Neural ODE learns \(dz/dt = f_\theta(z, t)\) and integrates it numerically. The Euler method with step \(h\):

\[z_{n+1} = z_n + h f_\theta(z_n)\]

applied to the logistic ODE \(dp/dt = p(1-p)\) gives:

\[p_{n+1} = p_n(1 + h - h p_n)\]

a logistic map with effective \(r = 1 + h\). For \(h\) small: stable fixed point (correct). For \(h\) large (say \(h = 2.5\)): \(r = 3.5\) — period-4 oscillations from a smooth ODE whose exact solution has no oscillation at all.

Lesson: naive large-step discretization of physics can produce spurious chaos. This motivates adaptive solvers (Dormand-Prince, Runge-Kutta ⅘) inside Neural ODE training, where step size is controlled to keep the effective \(r\) safely below the bifurcation threshold.

docs.title: 5. SGD at the Edge of Stability
docs.text:
For learning rate \(\eta\) on a loss with sharpness \(\lambda_{\max}(\nabla^2 \mathcal{L})\), the linearized gradient descent update is:

\[w_{n+1} = w_n - \eta \nabla \mathcal{L}(w_n)\]

Stability requires \(\eta \lambda_{\max} < 2\) — directly analogous to requiring \(r < 3\) in the logistic map. Recent work (Cohen et al., ICLR 2021) shows that Adam and SGD with large \(\eta\) operate in the Edge of Stability regime where \(\eta \lambda_{\max} \approx 2\) throughout training — the network self-organises to the bifurcation boundary, similar to how some dynamical systems are attracted to the edge of chaos.

docs.title: 6. The Logistic Loss — Why It Cancels the Sigmoid Derivative
docs.text:
For binary classification with sigmoid output \(\hat y = \sigma(z)\), the squared error loss is:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{sq}} = \frac{1}{2}(\sigma(z) - y)^2 \implies \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{sq}}}{\partial z} = (\sigma(z) - y) \cdot \sigma'(z)\]

When \(\sigma(z) \approx 0\) or \(1\) (confident but wrong), \(\sigma'(z) \approx 0\) — the gradient vanishes. The cross-entropy (logistic) loss:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}} = -y\log\sigma(z) - (1-y)\log(1-\sigma(z)) \implies \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}}{\partial z} = \sigma(z) - y\]

The sigmoid derivative cancels because \(\partial(-\log\sigma)/\partial z = 1 - \sigma = (1-\sigma)\), and combined they give \(\sigma - y\) directly. The logistic loss is the unique loss that cancels the saturation of the logistic activation — a deep compatibility between the loss and activation rooted in the exponential family structure of the Bernoulli distribution.

docs.title: 7. Chaos and Generalization — Lyapunov Exponents of Training
docs.text: Recent theory links generalization to the Lyapunov exponent of the SGD trajectory in parameter space. Models that generalise well tend to reside near broad, flat minima (negative Lyapunov exponent — attracting fixed points of the loss landscape dynamics). Models that overfit tend to converge to sharp, narrow minima (borderline unstable, analogous to \(r \approx 3\)). This is an active research area (2022–present) directly inspired by dynamical systems theory of the logistic map.

docs.title: Example 2 — Period-2 Cycle (\(r = 3.2\))
docs.text:
Fixed point: \(x^* = 2.2/3.2 = 0.6875\). Stability: \(|2 - 3.2| = 1.2 > 1\) — unstable.

2-cycle points: $\(x_{a,b} = \frac{4.2 \pm \sqrt{4.2 \cdot 0.2}}{6.4} = \frac{4.2 \pm 0.917}{6.4} \implies x_a \approx 0.799, \quad x_b \approx 0.513\)$

After transient, orbit: \(\ldots, 0.513, 0.799, 0.513, 0.799, \ldots\)

docs.title: Example 3 — Chaos and Sensitive Dependence (\(r = 3.9\))
docs.text:
Two starts: \(x_0 = 0.500000\), \(y_0 = 0.500001\).

| \(n\) | \(|x_n - y_n|\) | |---|---| | 0 | \(10^{-6}\) | | 10 | \(\approx 7.5 \times 10^{-3}\) | | 20 | \(\approx 0.17\) | | 25 | \(\approx 0.36\) |

Lyapunov exponent \(\lambda \approx 0.49\) nats/step. Predicted amplification after 25 steps: \(10^{-6} \cdot e^{0.49 \times 25} \approx 2 \times 10^5 \times 10^{-6} = 0.2\) — consistent with observation.

docs.title: Practice Problems
docs.text:
1. Show \(x^* = (r-1)/r\) is stable for \(1 < r < 3\) by showing \(|f'(x^*)| = |2 - r| < 1\) directly.

  2. For \(r = 2\), make the substitution \(x_n = \frac{1}{2}(1 - y_n)\) and find the recurrence for \(y_n\). Solve it in closed form.

  3. Verify that the 2-cycle points \((x_a, x_b)\) found in Example 2 satisfy \(f(x_a) = x_b\) and \(f(x_b) = x_a\) for \(r = 3.2\).

  4. Prove that at \(r = 4\), the substitution \(x_n = \sin^2(\pi\theta_n)\) transforms the logistic map into the doubling map \(\theta_{n+1} = 2\theta_n \pmod 1\).

  5. Using \(r_1 = 3\), \(r_2 = 3.4495\), \(r_3 = 3.5441\), \(r_4 = 3.5644\), compute \(\delta_1\), \(\delta_2\), \(\delta_3\) and compare to \(\delta = 4.669\).

  6. (ML connection) Show that the logistic loss \(\mathcal{L} = -y\log\sigma(z) - (1-y)\log(1-\sigma(z))\) has gradient \(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial z = \sigma(z) - y\). Explain why this is superior to squared error for sigmoid-activated neurons from a gradient-flow perspective.

  7. (Hard) Prove that the period-3 window implies chaos: if \(f\) has a period-3 orbit, then by Sharkovskii's Theorem, it has orbits of all periods. What does this imply about the logistic map for \(r\) in the period-3 window near \(r \approx 3.83\)?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
\(r\) Attractor \(\lambda\) Behaviour \((0,1)\) \({0}\) \(\ln r < 0\) Extinction \((1,3)\) \({(r-1)/r}\) $\ln 2-r \((3, 3.449)\) 2-cycle \(< 0\) Period doubling begins \((3.449, 3.544)\) 4-cycle \(< 0\) Further doubling \(\vdots\) \(\vdots\) \(\vdots\) \(\vdots\) \((3.570, 4]\) Fractal-like \(> 0\) Chaos (+ windows) \(4\) \([0,1]\) \(\ln 2\) Fully chaotic

The logistic map teaches:

  • Period-doubling route to chaos
  • Universality via the Feigenbaum constant \(\delta = 4.669\ldots\)
  • How sigmoid / logistic functions arise as equilibria of continuous dynamics
  • Why RNNs explode, why LSTM gates help, why cross-entropy loss beats MSE, and why large learning rates create instability
