docs.title: Direction Angles
docs.text: "The direction of a vector is the soul of its geometry. Angles make that soul legible." — personal note, §12.3 philosophy

docs.title: 0. Motivation — Why Should We Care?
docs.text:
When you write \(\mathbf{v} = \langle 3, -1, 2 \rangle\), you know the components. But what is its orientation in space? How does it tilt relative to each axis?

Direction angles answer this precisely. Direction cosines encode orientation in a form that is invariant under scaling, deeply connected to dot products, and — as we will see — absolutely central to how neural networks and SVMs work.

docs.title: 1. Setup & Notation
docs.text:
Let \(\mathbf{a} = \langle a_1, a_2, a_3 \rangle \in \mathbb{R}^3\) be a nonzero vector.

\[|\mathbf{a}| = \sqrt{a_1^2 + a_2^2 + a_3^2}\]

Denote the standard basis vectors \(\mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{k}\) (i.e., \(\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2, \mathbf{e}_3\)).

docs.title: 2. Definition: Direction Angles
docs.text:
Definition. The direction angles \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\) of \(\mathbf{a}\) are the angles it makes with the positive \(x\)-, \(y\)-, \(z\)-axes respectively:

\[\alpha = \angle(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{i}), \quad \beta = \angle(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{j}), \quad \gamma = \angle(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{k})\]

with each angle in \([0, \pi]\).

These are not Euler angles — they are the three separate angles the vector makes with the coordinate axes, one at a time.

docs.title: 2.1 Derivation via the Dot Product
docs.text:
Recall the fundamental formula: \(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = |\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta\).

Applying this to \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{i} = \langle 1,0,0 \rangle\):

\[\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{i} = a_1\] \[|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{i}|\cos\alpha = |\mathbf{a}| \cdot 1 \cdot \cos\alpha\]

Therefore:

\[\boxed{\cos\alpha = \frac{a_1}{|\mathbf{a}|}, \quad \cos\beta = \frac{a_2}{|\mathbf{a}|}, \quad \cos\gamma = \frac{a_3}{|\mathbf{a}|}}\]

docs.title: 3. Definition: Direction Cosines
docs.text:
Definition. The three quantities \(\cos\alpha, \cos\beta, \cos\gamma\) are called the direction cosines of \(\mathbf{a}\).

They are simply the components of the unit vector in the direction of \(\mathbf{a}\):

\[\hat{\mathbf{a}} = \frac{\mathbf{a}}{|\mathbf{a}|} = \langle \cos\alpha,, \cos\beta,, \cos\gamma \rangle\]

This is both conceptually clean and computationally useful.

docs.title: 4. The Fundamental Identity
docs.text:
Theorem. For any nonzero \(\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^3\):

\[\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1\]

Proof. Since \(\hat{\mathbf{a}}\) is a unit vector:

\[|\hat{\mathbf{a}}|^2 = \cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1 \qquad \square\]

⚠️ Key insight. Not every triple \((\cos\alpha, \cos\beta, \cos\gamma)\) is freely choosable — this identity is a constraint surface (a sphere of radius 1 in direction-cosine space). This is the 2-sphere \(S^2\).

docs.title: Example 1 — Explicit Computation
docs.text:
Let \(\mathbf{a} = \langle 1, 2, 3 \rangle\).

Step 1. Compute the magnitude: $\(|\mathbf{a}| = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 9} = \sqrt{14}\)$

Step 2. Direction cosines: $\(\cos\alpha = \frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}, \quad \cos\beta = \frac{2}{\sqrt{14}}, \quad \cos\gamma = \frac{3}{\sqrt{14}}\)$

Step 3. Direction angles (in radians, approx): $\(\alpha \approx 1.301, \quad \beta \approx 1.006, \quad \gamma \approx 0.641\)$

Verification: $\(\frac{1}{14} + \frac{4}{14} + \frac{9}{14} = \frac{14}{14} = 1 \checkmark\)$

docs.title: Example 2 — Axis-aligned vector
docs.text:
Let \(\mathbf{a} = \langle 0, 0, 5 \rangle\) (pointing straight up).

\[|\mathbf{a}| = 5, \quad \cos\alpha = 0, \quad \cos\beta = 0, \quad \cos\gamma = 1\]

So \(\alpha = \beta = \frac{\pi}{2}\), \(\gamma = 0\).

This makes perfect sense: the vector is perpendicular to \(x\) and \(y\), and perfectly aligned with \(z\).

docs.title: Example 3 — Symmetric direction
docs.text:
Let \(\mathbf{a} = \langle 1, 1, 1 \rangle\).

\[|\mathbf{a}| = \sqrt{3}, \quad \cos\alpha = \cos\beta = \cos\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\]

All direction angles are equal: \(\alpha = \beta = \gamma = \arccos!\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \approx 54.74°\).

The "body diagonal" of the unit cube — a beautifully symmetric case.

docs.title: 6. Geometric Visualization
docs.text:
z
         |   /  ← a
         |  /
  γ      | /
(angle)  |/________ y
        /|
       / |   β = angle to y-axis
      /  |
     x   α = angle to x-axis

Each direction angle is measured from its axis to the vector a.
The unit vector â = (cos α, cos β, cos γ) lies on the unit sphere S².

ASCII picture of direction cosine space:

All valid (cos α, cos β, cos γ) triples live on this sphere:

        cos γ
          |
    1 ----+---- 1
   /      |      \
  /       |       \
 cos α ---+------- cos β
          |
         -1

Constraint: cos²α + cos²β + cos²γ = 1  (the unit sphere)

docs.title: 7. Extension to \(\mathbb{R}^n\)
docs.text:
The concept generalizes immediately. For \(\mathbf{v} = \langle v_1, \ldots, v_n \rangle \in \mathbb{R}^n\):

\[\cos\theta_i = \frac{v_i}{|\mathbf{v}|}, \quad \sum_{i=1}^{n} \cos^2\theta_i = 1\]

The direction cosines are still just the components of the unit vector \(\hat{\mathbf{v}}\), now living on \(S^{n-1}\).

This is the natural habitat of machine learning.

docs.title: 8. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
docs.text: This section is where the abstraction pays off. Direction cosines are not just geometry — they are the backbone of how modern ML models measure similarity, learn representations, and make decisions.

docs.title: 8.1 Cosine Similarity
docs.text:
The cosine similarity between two vectors \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) is:

\[\text{sim}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|} = \hat{\mathbf{u}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{v}} = \cos\theta\]

where \(\theta\) is the angle between the two vectors.

This is precisely the dot product of their direction-cosine vectors. It measures angular proximity, ignoring magnitude.

Why this matters in NLP: Word embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe) represent words as high-dimensional vectors. "king" and "queen" have high cosine similarity. "cat" and "refrigerator" do not. The cosine of the direction angles between their respective unit vectors is what is being compared.

\[\text{king} - \text{man} + \text{woman} \approx \text{queen} \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \text{direction angles tell the story}\]

docs.title: 8.2 Weight Vectors and Decision Boundaries in SVMs
docs.text:
A Support Vector Machine constructs a hyperplane

\[\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + b = 0\]

The vector \(\mathbf{w}\) is the normal to this hyperplane. The direction cosines of \(\mathbf{w}\) determine the orientation of the decision boundary in feature space.

The signed distance from a point \(\mathbf{x}_0\) to the hyperplane is:

\[d = \frac{\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_0 + b}{|\mathbf{w}|} = \hat{\mathbf{w}} \cdot \mathbf{x}_0 + \frac{b}{|\mathbf{w}|}\]

Here \(\hat{\mathbf{w}} = \langle \cos\alpha_1, \ldots, \cos\alpha_n \rangle\) — the direction cosines of the weight vector — directly project each feature onto the axis of decision.

docs.title: 8.3 Attention Mechanisms (Transformers)
docs.text:
In the scaled dot-product attention:

\[\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\]

The raw score \(QK^\top\) computes \(q_i \cdot k_j = |q_i||k_j|\cos\theta_{ij}\).

The direction of the query and key vectors — encoded in their direction cosines — determines which values get attended to. The \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalization factor is precisely to control the magnitude effect, making the angular alignment (direction cosines) the dominant factor.

docs.title: 8.4 Normalized Embeddings and Contrastive Learning
docs.text:
In contrastive learning (e.g., SimCLR, CLIP), embeddings are typically \(L^2\)-normalized before computing loss:

\[\hat{\mathbf{z}}_i = \frac{\mathbf{z}_i}{|\mathbf{z}_i|}\]

After normalization, \(\hat{\mathbf{z}}_i\) is exactly the direction-cosine vector of \(\mathbf{z}_i\). The loss function then works entirely on the unit sphere \(S^{n-1}\) — a space defined by the constraint we proved in §4.

The model learns to align directions, not magnitudes. The geometry is entirely in direction angles.

docs.title: 8.5 Gradient Descent and Direction Cosines
docs.text:
The gradient \(\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}\) points in the direction of steepest ascent. The direction cosines of the gradient tell you which parameters \(\theta_i\) the loss is most sensitive to:

\[\cos\alpha_i = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}/\partial \theta_i}{|\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}|}\]

A large \(|\cos\alpha_i|\) means \(\theta_i\) is almost aligned with the gradient — a small nudge there produces the most change.

docs.title: 9. Summary Table
docs.text: Quantity Formula Geometric Meaning Direction angle \(\alpha_i\) \(\arccos!\left(\tfrac{a_i}{\|\mathbf{a}\|}\right)\) Angle between \(\mathbf{a}\) and axis \(i\) Direction cosine \(\cos\alpha_i\) \(\tfrac{a_i}{\|\mathbf{a}\|}\) \(i\)-th component of \(\hat{\mathbf{a}}\) Unit vector \(\hat{\mathbf{a}}\) \(\tfrac{\mathbf{a}}{\|\mathbf{a}\|}\) Vector of all direction cosines Fundamental identity \(\sum \cos^2\alpha_i = 1\) \(\hat{\mathbf{a}}\) lives on \(S^{n-1}\) Cosine similarity \(\hat{\mathbf{u}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{v}}\) Angle between two directions

docs.title: 10. Exercises
docs.text:
1. (Warm-up) Find the direction angles of \(\mathbf{a} = \langle 2, -1, 2 \rangle\). Verify the identity.

  2. (Theoretical) Prove that there is no vector in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) with all three direction angles equal to \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). What is the minimum possible common value?

  3. (Converse) Given that \(\cos\alpha = \frac{1}{2}\) and \(\cos\beta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), find all possible values of \(\cos\gamma\).

  4. (ML connection) Two word embeddings have \(\mathbf{u} = \langle 3, 1, -2, 0 \rangle\) and \(\mathbf{v} = \langle -1, 2, 1, 4 \rangle\). Compute the cosine similarity. What does a value near \(0\) mean geometrically?

  5. (Higher dimensions) A vector in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) makes equal angles with all coordinate axes. Show that \(\cos\alpha_i = \pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\) for all \(i\).

docs.title: 11. References
docs.text:
• Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §12.3 — "The Dot Product." The definition, dot product formula, and worked examples draw from this section.
  • MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus (OCW). Lecture notes on vectors, dot product, and direction cosines. The geometric perspective and \(\mathbb{R}^3\) setup follow this course's treatment.

docs.title: Projections
docs.text: "Projection is the art of seeing one vector through the eyes of another."

docs.title: 0. Motivation
docs.text:
You have two vectors \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\). A natural question: how much of \(\mathbf{b}\) points in the direction of \(\mathbf{a}\)?

This is not a vague question — it has a precise, unique, geometric answer. The projection extracts the "shadow" of \(\mathbf{b}\) cast along \(\mathbf{a}\), and the remainder is the part of \(\mathbf{b}\) that is purely perpendicular to \(\mathbf{a}\).

Everything in applied mathematics — least squares, attention mechanisms, PCA, Gram-Schmidt — rests on this one idea.

docs.title: 1. Scalar Projection
docs.text:
Definition. The scalar projection (or component) of \(\mathbf{b}\) onto \(\mathbf{a}\) is:

\[\text{comp}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b} = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}|}\]

Derivation. Drop a perpendicular from the tip of \(\mathbf{b}\) onto the line through \(\mathbf{a}\). The foot of that perpendicular is at signed distance \(|\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta\) from the origin along \(\hat{\mathbf{a}}\).

From the dot product formula \(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = |\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta\):

\[|\mathbf{b}|\cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}|}\]

Note this is a signed scalar — negative when \(\theta > \frac{\pi}{2}\).

Equivalently, using the unit vector \(\hat{\mathbf{a}} = \frac{\mathbf{a}}{|\mathbf{a}|}\):

\[\text{comp}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b} = \hat{\mathbf{a}} \cdot \mathbf{b}\]

The scalar projection is the dot product of \(\mathbf{b}\) with the unit vector in the target direction. Clean.

docs.title: 2. Vector Projection
docs.text:
Definition. The vector projection of \(\mathbf{b}\) onto \(\mathbf{a}\) is:

\[\text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b} = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}|^2},\mathbf{a} = \left(\hat{\mathbf{a}} \cdot \mathbf{b}\right)\hat{\mathbf{a}}\]

Derivation. We want a vector parallel to \(\mathbf{a}\), with signed length equal to \(\text{comp}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b}\):

\[\text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b} = (\text{comp}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b}),\hat{\mathbf{a}} = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}|}\cdot\frac{\mathbf{a}}{|\mathbf{a}|} = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}|^2},\mathbf{a}\]

Write this more compactly using the outer product notation:

\[\text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b} = \frac{\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}^\top}{|\mathbf{a}|^2},\mathbf{b} = \hat{\mathbf{a}}\hat{\mathbf{a}}^\top,\mathbf{b}\]

The matrix \(P = \hat{\mathbf{a}}\hat{\mathbf{a}}^\top\) is the projection matrix onto \(\text{span}{\mathbf{a}}\).

docs.title: 3. The Orthogonal Decomposition
docs.text:
Theorem. Any vector \(\mathbf{b}\) decomposes uniquely as:

\[\mathbf{b} = \underbrace{\text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b}}_{\parallel,\mathbf{a}} + \underbrace{(\mathbf{b} - \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b})}_{\perp,\mathbf{a}}\]

Proof of orthogonality. Let \(\mathbf{b}_\perp = \mathbf{b} - \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b}\). Then:

\[\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}_\perp = \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a} \cdot \left(\frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}|^2},\mathbf{a}\right) = \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} - \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}|^2}|\mathbf{a}|^2 = 0 \quad \square\]

Proof of uniqueness. Suppose \(\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{q}\) with \(\mathbf{p} \parallel \mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{q} \perp \mathbf{a}\). Then \(\mathbf{p} = c\mathbf{a}\) for some scalar \(c\), and \(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{q} = 0\). Taking the dot product of \(\mathbf{b} = c\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{q}\) with \(\mathbf{a}\):

\[\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = c|\mathbf{a}|^2 \implies c = \frac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}|^2}\]

uniquely determined. \(\quad\square\)

docs.title: 4. Geometric Visualization
docs.text:
b
                 /|
                / |
               /  |  b_⊥  (perpendicular component)
              /   |
             / θ  |
            /_____|_________
           O   proj_a(b)    a →

  |proj_a(b)| = |b| cos θ  (the "shadow" of b on a)
  b_⊥ = b - proj_a(b)      (the "lift" off the line)
  b_⊥ ⊥ a  by construction

  Special cases:

  θ = 0:   b ∥ a  →  proj_a(b) = b,   b_⊥ = 0
  θ = π/2: b ⊥ a  →  proj_a(b) = 0,   b_⊥ = b
  θ = π:   b anti-∥ a → proj = -|b|â  (negative shadow)

docs.title: 5. Projection as a Linear Map — The Projection Matrix
docs.text:
Let \(\hat{\mathbf{a}} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) be a unit vector. Define:

\[P = \hat{\mathbf{a}}\hat{\mathbf{a}}^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\]

Then \(\text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b} = P\mathbf{b}\) for all \(\mathbf{b}\).

Properties:

Property Formula Meaning Idempotent \(P^2 = P\) Projecting twice = projecting once Symmetric \(P^\top = P\) Orthogonal projection Rank \(\text{rank}(P) = 1\) Projects onto a line Eigenvalues \({0, 1}\) Vectors parallel: eigenvalue 1; perpendicular: eigenvalue 0

Proof of idempotency: $\(P^2 = (\hat{\mathbf{a}}\hat{\mathbf{a}}^\top)(\hat{\mathbf{a}}\hat{\mathbf{a}}^\top) = \hat{\mathbf{a}}(\hat{\mathbf{a}}^\top\hat{\mathbf{a}})\hat{\mathbf{a}}^\top = \hat{\mathbf{a}} \cdot 1 \cdot \hat{\mathbf{a}}^\top = P \quad \square\)$

The complementary projection (onto the orthogonal complement) is \(I - P\).

docs.title: 6. Projection onto a Subspace
docs.text:
More generally, suppose \(W = \text{span}{\mathbf{u}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_k}\) where \(\mathbf{u}_i\) are orthonormal. Then:

\[\text{proj}_W \mathbf{b} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} (\mathbf{u}_i \cdot \mathbf{b}),\mathbf{u}_i = UU^\top \mathbf{b}\]

where \(U = [\mathbf{u}_1 \mid \cdots \mid \mathbf{u}_k]\).

If the columns of \(A\) span \(W\) but are not orthonormal, the projection formula becomes:

\[\text{proj}_W \mathbf{b} = A(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top \mathbf{b}\]

This is the normal equations formula — the exact solution to the least squares problem.

docs.title: Example 1 — Standard vector projection
docs.text:
Let \(\mathbf{b} = \langle 1, 2, 3 \rangle\), \(\mathbf{a} = \langle 1, 1, 0 \rangle\).

Step 1. Dot product: \(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 1 + 2 + 0 = 3\)

Step 2. \(|\mathbf{a}|^2 = 1 + 1 + 0 = 2\)

Step 3. Vector projection: $\(\text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b} = \frac{3}{2}\langle 1,1,0 \rangle = \left\langle \frac{3}{2}, \frac{3}{2}, 0 \right\rangle\)$

Step 4. Perpendicular component: $\(\mathbf{b}_\perp = \langle 1,2,3 \rangle - \left\langle \frac{3}{2}, \frac{3}{2}, 0 \right\rangle = \left\langle -\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}, 3 \right\rangle\)$

Verification: \(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}_\perp = 1\cdot(-\frac{1}{2}) + 1\cdot\frac{1}{2} + 0 = 0 \checkmark\)

docs.title: Example 2 — Work done by a force
docs.text:
A force \(\mathbf{F} = \langle 3, 4, 0 \rangle\) is applied to move an object along \(\mathbf{d} = \langle 5, 0, 0 \rangle\).

The work done is the force in the direction of motion, times the distance:

\[W = \mathbf{F} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{d}} \cdot |\mathbf{d}| = \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{d} = 15\]

The scalar projection \(\text{comp}_{\mathbf{d}},\mathbf{F} = \frac{15}{5} = 3\) is the effective component of force. The component \(4\hat{\mathbf{j}}\) does zero work — it is perpendicular to displacement.

docs.title: Example 3 — Projection matrix explicitly
docs.text:
Let \(\hat{\mathbf{a}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\langle 1, 1 \rangle\). Then:

\[P = \hat{\mathbf{a}}\hat{\mathbf{a}}^\top = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1\1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\]

Apply to \(\mathbf{b} = \langle 3, 1 \rangle\):

\[P\mathbf{b} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}4\4\end{pmatrix} = \langle 2, 2 \rangle\]

Check: \(\langle 2,2 \rangle\) is indeed parallel to \(\langle 1,1 \rangle\). And \(P^2 = P\):

\[P^2 = \frac{1}{4}\begin{pmatrix}2&2\2&2\end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\1&1\end{pmatrix} = P \checkmark\]

docs.title: 8. Connection to Direction Cosines
docs.text:
The scalar projection onto \(\mathbf{e}_i\) (the \(i\)-th standard basis vector) is simply:

\[\text{comp}_{\mathbf{e}_i},\mathbf{a} = \frac{\mathbf{e}_i \cdot \mathbf{a}}{|\mathbf{e}_i|} = a_i\]

The direction cosine \(\cos\alpha_i = \frac{a_i}{|\mathbf{a}|}\) is the scalar projection of \(\hat{\mathbf{a}}\) onto \(\mathbf{e}_i\).

In other words: the direction cosines are the projections of the unit vector onto the coordinate axes. The fundamental identity \(\sum \cos^2\alpha_i = 1\) is just \(|\hat{\mathbf{a}}|^2 = 1\) in disguise.

docs.title: 9. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
9.1 Least Squares — The Core of Linear Regression
docs.text:
Given data matrix \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}\) and labels \(\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n\), linear regression solves:

\[\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}} |\mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol{\beta}|^2\]

The solution is:

\[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top \mathbf{y}\]

and the fitted values are:

\[\hat{\mathbf{y}} = X\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \underbrace{X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top}_{\text{hat matrix } H},\mathbf{y} = \text{proj}_{\text{col}(X)},\mathbf{y}\]

Linear regression is exactly the orthogonal projection of \(\mathbf{y}\) onto the column space of \(X\). The residual \(\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}\) is perpendicular to every column of \(X\) — that is the normal equations.

\[X^\top(\mathbf{y} - X\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}) = \mathbf{0}\]

This is the orthogonality condition from §3, generalized.

docs.title: 9.2 Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
docs.text:
PCA finds directions \(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k\) (principal components) that maximize variance. Each data point \(\mathbf{x}_i\) is projected onto these directions:

\[z_{ij} = \mathbf{v}_j \cdot \mathbf{x}_i = \text{scalar projection of } \mathbf{x}_i \text{ onto } \mathbf{v}_j\]

The matrix of projected coordinates \(Z = XV\) is exactly the projection of the data onto the subspace spanned by the principal components. The reconstruction \(\hat{X} = ZV^\top = XV V^\top\) uses the projection matrix \(P = VV^\top\) (since columns of \(V\) are orthonormal).

Dimensionality reduction is projection. The information discarded is \(\mathbf{x} - P\mathbf{x}\), the part perpendicular to the subspace.

docs.title: 9.3 Gram-Schmidt and Orthogonalization in Neural Networks
docs.text:
The Gram-Schmidt process builds an orthonormal basis by iteratively removing projections:

\[\mathbf{u}_k = \mathbf{v}_k - \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} \text{proj}_{\mathbf{u}_j},\mathbf{v}_k\]

This is used in:

  • QR decomposition (backbone of many numerical solvers)
  • Orthogonal weight initialization in RNNs and deep nets, to preserve gradient norms
  • Spectral normalization layers, which project weight matrices to have unit spectral norm

docs.title: 9.4 Attention as Projection
docs.text:
In the Transformer, the query \(\mathbf{q}\) and key \(\mathbf{k}\) interact via:

\[\text{score}(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{k}) = \frac{\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{k}}{\sqrt{d_k}} = \frac{|\mathbf{q}||\mathbf{k}|}{\sqrt{d_k}}\cos\theta\]

The scalar projection of \(\mathbf{k}\) onto \(\mathbf{q}\) is \(\text{comp}_{\mathbf{q}},\mathbf{k} = \frac{\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k}}{|\mathbf{q}|}\). The attention score is a rescaled version of this. The softmax then selects values proportional to how much each key "projects" onto the current query.

The learned weight matrices \(W_Q, W_K, W_V\) are projection matrices into query/key/value subspaces.

docs.title: 9.5 Residual Connections and Orthogonal Decomposition
docs.text:
In ResNets, the residual block computes:

\[\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x} + \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x})\]

Viewed through the lens of projection: \(\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x})\) learns the component of the desired output that is not already captured by the identity map — the orthogonal complement of what \(\mathbf{x}\) already represents. This is the same spirit as \(\mathbf{b}_\perp = \mathbf{b} - \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b}\). The network learns the residual, not the full transformation.

docs.title: 10. Summary
docs.text: \[\boxed{ \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b} = \frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{|\mathbf{a}|^2},\mathbf{a}, \qquad \mathbf{b} = \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b} + \mathbf{b}_\perp, \qquad \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}_\perp = 0 }\] Concept Formula Key Property Scalar projection \(\hat{\mathbf{a}}\cdot\mathbf{b}\) Signed length Vector projection \((\hat{\mathbf{a}}\cdot\mathbf{b})\hat{\mathbf{a}}\) Parallel to \(\mathbf{a}\) Projection matrix \(P = \hat{\mathbf{a}}\hat{\mathbf{a}}^\top\) \(P^2 = P\), \(P^\top = P\) Orthogonal complement \(\mathbf{b} - P\mathbf{b}\) Perpendicular to \(\mathbf{a}\) Subspace projection \(A(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top\mathbf{b}\) Normal equations

docs.title: 11. Exercises
docs.text:
1. (Warm-up) Compute \(\text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b}\) and \(\mathbf{b}_\perp\) for \(\mathbf{a} = \langle 2, 1, -1 \rangle\), \(\mathbf{b} = \langle 4, 0, 3 \rangle\). Verify orthogonality.

  2. (Projection matrix) Write out the \(3\times 3\) projection matrix \(P\) onto \(\hat{\mathbf{a}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\langle 1,1,1\rangle\). Verify \(P^2 = P\) and find all eigenvalues.

  3. (Theoretical) Show that \(|{}\text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}},\mathbf{b}| \leq |\mathbf{b}|\), with equality iff \(\mathbf{b} \parallel \mathbf{a}\). What classical inequality does this imply?

  4. (Least squares) Three data points \((1,2), (2,3), (3,5)\). Set up the matrix \(X\) and compute \(\hat{\mathbf{y}} = Hy\) explicitly. Verify the residual \(\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}\) is orthogonal to the columns of \(X\).

  5. (ML connection) In PCA on centered data \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times p}\), the first PC \(\mathbf{v}_1\) is the eigenvector of \(X^\top X\) with the largest eigenvalue. Show that the projected variance along \(\mathbf{v}_1\) equals \(\lambda_1/n\), where \(\lambda_1\) is that eigenvalue.

docs.title: Triple Products
docs.text: "The scalar triple product is the determinant in geometric clothing. The vector triple product is the identity that separates the masters from the beginners." — personal note, §12.4–12.5 philosophy

docs.title: 0. Motivation
docs.text:
We have the dot product \(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}\) (scalar) and the cross product \(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}\) (vector). What happens when we combine three vectors?

There are exactly two natural ways:

Name Expression Output Scalar triple product \(\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})\) scalar Vector triple product \(\mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})\) vector

Both appear constantly in physics, geometry, and ML. Let's build them carefully.

docs.title: 1.1 Definition
docs.text:
Definition. For \(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3\), the scalar triple product is

\[\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) \in \mathbb{R}\]

docs.title: 1.2 Determinant Formula
docs.text:
Write \(\mathbf{a} = \langle a_1, a_2, a_3 \rangle\), \(\mathbf{b} = \langle b_1, b_2, b_3 \rangle\), \(\mathbf{c} = \langle c_1, c_2, c_3 \rangle\).

Recall \(\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c} = \langle b_2 c_3 - b_3 c_2,; b_3 c_1 - b_1 c_3,; b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1 \rangle\).

Then:

\[\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = a_1(b_2 c_3 - b_3 c_2) - a_2(b_1 c_3 - b_3 c_1) + a_3(b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1)\]

This is exactly the expansion of a \(3 \times 3\) determinant along the first row:

\[\boxed{\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \ c_1 & c_2 & c_3 \end{vmatrix}}\]

The rows are \(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}\) in that order. This is not a coincidence — it is the definition.

docs.title: 1.3 Geometric Meaning: Volume of a Parallelepiped
docs.text:
Theorem. \(|\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})|\) equals the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by \(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}\).

Proof.

  • \(\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}\) is perpendicular to both \(\mathbf{b}\) and \(\mathbf{c}\), with magnitude $|\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}| = $ area of base parallelogram.
  • Let \(\theta\) be the angle between \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}\).
  • The height of the parallelepiped is \(h = |\mathbf{a}||\cos\theta|\).

Therefore:

\[V = \text{base area} \times h = |\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}| \cdot |\mathbf{a}||\cos\theta| = |\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})| \qquad \square\] 
ASCII diagram of the parallelepiped:

        a·(b×c) > 0: a is on the same side as b×c (right-hand orientation)
        a·(b×c) < 0: a is on the opposite side (left-hand orientation)
        a·(b×c) = 0: a lies in the plane of b and c  →  V = 0

              *---------*
             /|  ^      /|
            / |  | b×c / |  ← height = |a|cosθ
           *---------*   |
           |  |      |   |
       a → |  *------|---*
           | /  c    |  /
           |/        | /  ← base = parallelogram spanned by b, c
           *---------*
                b

Corollary. \(\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = 0\) if and only if \(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}\) are coplanar.

docs.title: 1.4 Cyclic Symmetry
docs.text:
Using determinant row-swap properties (each swap flips sign):

\[\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{b} \cdot (\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{c} \cdot (\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})\]

These are cyclic permutations — rotating \((\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}) \to (\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c},\mathbf{a}) \to (\mathbf{c},\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})\) preserves the determinant.

An anticyclic permutation flips the sign:

\[\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = -\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{b})\]

Compact notation: \([\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}]\) or \((\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c})\) for the scalar triple product.

docs.title: 1.5 Dot and Cross Are Interchangeable
docs.text:
\[\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = (\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \cdot \mathbf{c}\]

Proof. Both equal the same determinant — this follows from the cyclic property above. Specifically, the right side is \(\mathbf{c} \cdot (\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})\), which is a cyclic permutation of the left side. \(\square\)

This is why the dot and cross in the scalar triple product are sometimes written interchangeably: the result is the same either way.

docs.title: 1.6 Worked Example
docs.text:
Let \(\mathbf{a} = \langle 1, 4, -7 \rangle\), \(\mathbf{b} = \langle 2, -1, 4 \rangle\), \(\mathbf{c} = \langle 0, -9, 18 \rangle\).

\[\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 4 & -7 \ 2 & -1 & 4 \ 0 & -9 & 18 \end{vmatrix}\]

Expanding along the first row:

\[= 1\begin{vmatrix} -1 & 4 \ -9 & 18 \end{vmatrix} - 4\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 4 \ 0 & 18 \end{vmatrix} + (-7)\begin{vmatrix} 2 & -1 \ 0 & -9 \end{vmatrix}\] \[= 1(-18 + 36) - 4(36 - 0) - 7(-18 - 0)\] \[= 18 - 144 + 126 = 0\]

So the three vectors are coplanar. (Indeed, one can verify \(\mathbf{c} = -\frac{9}{2}\mathbf{b} + \ldots\) — they lie in a common plane through the origin.)

docs.title: 2.1 Definition
docs.text:
Definition. The vector triple product of \(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3\) is

\[\mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) \in \mathbb{R}^3\]

Note the parentheses matter: \(\mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) \neq (\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \times \mathbf{c}\) in general.

docs.title: 2.2 The BAC–CAB Identity
docs.text:
Theorem (BAC–CAB rule).

\[\mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{c}) - \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b})\]

Mnemonic: \(\mathbf{A} \times (\mathbf{B} \times \mathbf{C}) = \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{C}) - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B})\). Read: "BAC minus CAB."

Proof (direct computation).

Let \(\mathbf{a} = \langle a_1, a_2, a_3 \rangle\), etc. Compute \(\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}\) first:

\[\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c} = \langle b_2 c_3 - b_3 c_2,; b_3 c_1 - b_1 c_3,; b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1 \rangle\]

Now compute \(\mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})\) — take the first component as representative:

\[[\mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})]_1 = a_2(b_1 c_2 - b_2 c_1) - a_3(b_3 c_1 - b_1 c_3)\] \[= a_2 b_1 c_2 - a_2 b_2 c_1 - a_3 b_3 c_1 + a_3 b_1 c_3\] \[= b_1(a_2 c_2 + a_3 c_3) - c_1(a_2 b_2 + a_3 b_3)\]

Add and subtract \(b_1 a_1 c_1 - c_1 a_1 b_1 = 0\):

\[= b_1(a_1 c_1 + a_2 c_2 + a_3 c_3) - c_1(a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + a_3 b_3)\] \[= b_1(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{c}) - c_1(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b})\]

This is exactly the first component of \(\mathbf{b}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c}) - \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b})\). The other two components follow identically. \(\square\)

docs.title: 2.3 Geometric Meaning
docs.text:
Claim. \(\mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})\) lies in the plane spanned by \(\mathbf{b}\) and \(\mathbf{c}\).

Proof. By BAC–CAB, the result is \(\mathbf{b}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c}) - \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b})\), which is a linear combination of \(\mathbf{b}\) and \(\mathbf{c}\). \(\square\)

This makes sense: \(\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}\) is perpendicular to the \(\mathbf{b}\)-\(\mathbf{c}\) plane; crossing anything with it brings you back into that plane.

        b×c  ↑  (perpendicular to the b-c plane)
              |
   ___________↑__________
  /           |          /   ← plane of b and c
 /  b         |   c     /
/__________________________/

  a × (b×c) lives inside this plane.
  It is a linear combination of b and c — the "projection" effect.

docs.title: 2.4 The Other Parenthesization
docs.text:
\[(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \times \mathbf{c} = -\mathbf{c} \times (\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) = -[\mathbf{a}(\mathbf{c}\cdot\mathbf{b}) - \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{c}\cdot\mathbf{a})]\] \[= \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c}) - \mathbf{a}(\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{c})\]

Compare with \(\mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c}) - \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b})\).

They differ unless \(\mathbf{a}(\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b})\), confirming that the cross product is not associative.

docs.title: 2.5 Worked Example
docs.text:
Let \(\mathbf{a} = \langle 1,2,3 \rangle\), \(\mathbf{b} = \langle 0,1,0 \rangle\), \(\mathbf{c} = \langle 1,0,1 \rangle\).

Via BAC–CAB:

\[\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{c} = 1 + 0 + 3 = 4, \qquad \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 0 + 2 + 0 = 2\] \[\mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = 4\mathbf{b} - 2\mathbf{c} = 4\langle 0,1,0 \rangle - 2\langle 1,0,1 \rangle = \langle -2, 4, -2 \rangle\]

Verify directly:

\[\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c} = \begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \ 0 & 1 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} = \langle 1\cdot1 - 0\cdot0,; 0\cdot1 - 0\cdot1,; 0\cdot0 - 1\cdot1 \rangle = \langle 1, 0, -1 \rangle\] \[\mathbf{a} \times \langle 1,0,-1 \rangle = \begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \ 1 & 2 & 3 \ 1 & 0 & -1\end{vmatrix} = \langle (2)(-1)-(3)(0),; (3)(1)-(1)(-1),; (1)(0)-(2)(1) \rangle\] \[= \langle -2, 4, -2 \rangle \checkmark\]

docs.title: 3. Summary of All Identities
docs.text: Identity Expression Scalar triple product = determinant \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) = \det[\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}]\) Volume of parallelepiped $V = Cyclic symmetry \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{b}\cdot(\mathbf{c}\times\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{c}\cdot(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\) Dot-cross swap \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) = (\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\cdot\mathbf{c}\) BAC–CAB \(\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{c}) - \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b})\) Non-associativity \(\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) \neq (\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\times\mathbf{c}\) in general Coplanarity test \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) = 0 \iff \mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}\) coplanar

docs.title: 4. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
4.1 Volume Forms and Change of Variables in Generative Models
docs.text:
The scalar triple product is the \(3 \times 3\) determinant. In normalizing flows and variational autoencoders, transformations \(f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n\) preserve probability mass via the change-of-variables formula:

\[p_X(\mathbf{x}) = p_Z(f^{-1}(\mathbf{x})) \left|\det J_f(\mathbf{x})\right|^{-1}\]

The Jacobian determinant \(\det J_f\) is the \(n\)-dimensional generalization of the scalar triple product. For \(n = 3\), the Jacobian determinant of a linear map \(f(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}\) with rows \(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}\) is exactly \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})\).

Understanding the triple product = understanding the volume scaling of a linear transformation = understanding how generative models warp probability distributions.

docs.title: 4.2 The BAC–CAB Rule in Backpropagation Through Cross Products
docs.text:
Certain physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and 3D geometry models (e.g., PointNet, mesh CNNs) compute cross products as part of the forward pass — to get surface normals, angular momentum, torque.

When backpropagating through \(\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}\), the gradient with respect to \(\mathbf{b}\) involves:

\[\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{b}}[\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})] = \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{c}\]

This uses exactly the dot-cross swap identity from §1.5. The BAC–CAB rule then appears in higher-order derivatives through cross product layers.

docs.title: 4.3 Coplanarity → Linear Dependence → Rank Deficiency
docs.text:
The condition \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) = 0\) is coplanarity, which is exactly \(\det[\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}] = 0\), i.e., linear dependence.

In ML:

  • A feature matrix with linearly dependent columns has a singular (rank-deficient) Gram matrix \(X^\top X\). This breaks ordinary least squares and causes the normal equations to have no unique solution.
  • Regularization (Ridge, Lasso) is the practical fix — but the geometry is precisely the parallelepiped collapsing to zero volume.
  • A neural network with redundant neurons has weight vectors that are coplanar → the corresponding rows of the weight matrix are dependent → the layer is not full rank → information is being wasted.

docs.title: 4.4 Quaternions and 3D Rotation in Deep Learning
docs.text:
Quaternion multiplication for \(\mathbf{p} = (p_0, \mathbf{p})\) and \(\mathbf{q} = (q_0, \mathbf{q})\):

\[\mathbf{p}\mathbf{q} = (p_0 q_0 - \mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q},; p_0\mathbf{q} + q_0\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{p}\times\mathbf{q})\]

The vector part of the product involves \(\mathbf{p} \times \mathbf{q}\). When composing rotations or computing the double cover \(SO(3) \cong S^3/{\pm 1}\), the BAC–CAB identity underlies the Rodrigues' rotation formula:

\[R_{\hat{n},\theta}(\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{v}\cos\theta + (\hat{n}\times\mathbf{v})\sin\theta + \hat{n}(\hat{n}\cdot\mathbf{v})(1-\cos\theta)\]

Expanding \(\hat{n} \times (\hat{n} \times \mathbf{v})\) via BAC–CAB gives \(\hat{n}(\hat{n}\cdot\mathbf{v}) - \mathbf{v}\), which is exactly the third term.

This rotation formula is used in 3D pose estimation networks (e.g., in robotics, human pose, and NeRF-based models where camera orientations must be parameterized).

docs.title: 4.5 Geometric Algebra and Attention Over 3D Structures
docs.text:
In equivariant neural networks (e.g., SE(3)-Transformers, Equiformer), layers must be equivariant to rotations and reflections. The scalar triple product \(\mathbf{a}\cdot(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})\) is a pseudoscalar — it is invariant under rotations but flips sign under reflections.

Networks that operate on molecular geometry (AlphaFold2, DiffDock) need to decide whether to use true scalars or pseudoscalars as features, because this determines how the model transforms under orientation reversal. Getting this wrong breaks equivariance.

docs.title: 5. Exercises
docs.text:
1. (Volume) Find the volume of the parallelepiped with edges \(\mathbf{a} = \langle 2,3,4 \rangle\), \(\mathbf{b} = \langle 1,0,-1 \rangle\), \(\mathbf{c} = \langle 0,1,2 \rangle\).

  2. (Coplanarity) For which value of \(k\) are \(\mathbf{a} = \langle 1,2,k \rangle\), \(\mathbf{b} = \langle 3,1,0 \rangle\), \(\mathbf{c} = \langle 1,-1,2 \rangle\) coplanar?

  3. (BAC–CAB proof check) Verify the BAC–CAB identity for the second and third components of the example in §2.5.

  4. (Non-associativity) With \(\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{i}\), \(\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{j}\), \(\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{k}\), compute both \(\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c})\) and \((\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b})\times\mathbf{c}\) explicitly. Confirm they differ.

  5. (Theoretical) Prove that \(\mathbf{a}\times(\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}) + \mathbf{b}\times(\mathbf{c}\times\mathbf{a}) + \mathbf{c}\times(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}) = \mathbf{0}\). (This is the Jacobi identity for the cross product.)

  6. (ML) A \(3 \times 3\) weight matrix \(W\) in a neural network has rows \(\mathbf{w}_1, \mathbf{w}_2, \mathbf{w}_3\). Show that \(\det(W) = \mathbf{w}_1 \cdot (\mathbf{w}_2 \times \mathbf{w}_3)\), and explain what \(\det(W) = 0\) means for the network's expressive power.

docs.title: 6. References
docs.text:
• Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §12.4 "The Cross Product" and §12.5 extensions. The determinant formula, parallelepiped volume, and worked examples follow this treatment.
  • MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus (OCW). Lecture notes §1–3 on vectors and determinants; the geometric interpretation of the scalar triple product as a signed volume is developed there.

docs.title: Torques
docs.text: "Torque is the rotational analogue of force — but the geometry hidden inside the cross product is where the real story lives."

docs.title: §1. Motivation — Why Torque?
docs.text:
Consider trying to open a heavy door. You instinctively push at the edge, not near the hinge. You push perpendicular to the door, not parallel to it. Both of these intuitions are encoded, simultaneously and elegantly, in a single mathematical object: the torque vector.

Torque answers the question: given a force applied at a position in space, how much does it tend to rotate a body about some axis?

docs.title: §2. Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\mathbf{r}\) be the position vector from the pivot point (origin of rotation) to the point where force is applied, and let \(\mathbf{F}\) be the applied force. Then the torque is:

\[\boxed{\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}}\]

This is a cross product — so torque is a vector, not a scalar.

docs.title: 2.1 Unpacking the Cross Product
docs.text:
Recall that for \(\mathbf{r} = \langle r_1, r_2, r_3 \rangle\) and \(\mathbf{F} = \langle F_1, F_2, F_3 \rangle\):

\[\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \ r_1 & r_2 & r_3 \ F_1 & F_2 & F_3 \end{vmatrix}\] \[= \mathbf{i}(r_2 F_3 - r_3 F_2) - \mathbf{j}(r_1 F_3 - r_3 F_1) + \mathbf{k}(r_1 F_2 - r_2 F_1)\]

docs.title: 2.2 Magnitude and Geometric Interpretation
docs.text:
\[|\boldsymbol{\tau}| = |\mathbf{r}||\mathbf{F}|\sin\theta\]

where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\mathbf{r}\) and \(\mathbf{F}\).

Key insight: Torque is maximised when \(\mathbf{r} \perp \mathbf{F}\) (i.e., \(\theta = 90°\)), and zero when \(\mathbf{r} \parallel \mathbf{F}\) (force points directly toward or away from the pivot — no rotation).

docs.title: 2.3 Direction — The Right-Hand Rule
docs.text:
The direction of \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}\) follows the right-hand rule:

  • Point fingers of your right hand along \(\mathbf{r}\)
  • Curl them toward \(\mathbf{F}\)
  • Your thumb points in the direction of \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\)
         τ (out of page ⊙)
         ↑
         |
    r    |        F
  ───────●─────────→
       pivot

In 2D (rotation in the \(xy\)-plane), torque is purely in the \(\hat{k}\) direction:

\[\boldsymbol{\tau} = (r_1 F_2 - r_2 F_1),\hat{k}\]

A positive \(\tau_z\) means counterclockwise rotation; negative means clockwise.

docs.title: Example 1 — Wrench on a Bolt (2D)
docs.text:
A force \(\mathbf{F} = \langle 0, 10, 0 \rangle\) N is applied at position \(\mathbf{r} = \langle 0.3, 0, 0 \rangle\) m (a wrench of length 0.3 m pointing along the \(x\)-axis).

\[\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \ 0.3 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 10 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = \mathbf{k}(0.3 \cdot 10 - 0 \cdot 0) = 3,\hat{k} \text{ N·m}\]

\(\boldsymbol{\tau} = 3,\hat{k}\) N·m — rotation is counterclockwise about the \(z\)-axis.

Visualisation:

    F = 10ĵ
    ↑
    |
    ●────────────→  r = 0.3î
  pivot

  Rotation: counterclockwise ↺
  τ = 3k̂ (pointing out of the page ⊙)

docs.title: Example 2 — Force at an Angle
docs.text:
Force \(\mathbf{F} = \langle 5, 5, 0 \rangle\) N applied at \(\mathbf{r} = \langle 2, 0, 0 \rangle\) m.

\[\boldsymbol{\tau} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \ 2 & 0 & 0 \ 5 & 5 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{k}(2 \cdot 5 - 0 \cdot 5) = 10,\hat{k} \text{ N·m}\]

Notice: only the perpendicular component of \(\mathbf{F}\) (the \(\hat{j}\) part) contributes to torque! The radial component (along \(\hat{i}\)) is wasted — it pushes toward the pivot and creates no rotation.

docs.title: Example 3 — Full 3D Torque
docs.text:
\(\mathbf{r} = \langle 1, 2, 0 \rangle\), \(\mathbf{F} = \langle 0, 3, -1 \rangle\):

\[\boldsymbol{\tau} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \ 1 & 2 & 0 \ 0 & 3 & -1 \end{vmatrix} = \mathbf{i}(2 \cdot(-1) - 0 \cdot 3) - \mathbf{j}(1 \cdot(-1) - 0 \cdot 0) + \mathbf{k}(1 \cdot 3 - 2 \cdot 0)\] \[= \mathbf{i}(-2) - \mathbf{j}(-1) + \mathbf{k}(3) = \langle -2, 1, 3 \rangle \text{ N·m}\]

docs.title: §4. Torque as a Signed Scalar (2D Special Case)
docs.text:
In planar problems (forces and positions in the \(xy\)-plane), it's common to work with the scalar torque:

\[\tau = r_x F_y - r_y F_x = |\mathbf{r}||\mathbf{F}|\sin\theta\]

This is exactly the \(z\)-component of \(\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}\).

This is also the signed area of the parallelogram spanned by \(\mathbf{r}\) and \(\mathbf{F}\) — a lovely geometric fact.

          F
         ↗ 
        /  |  ← area = |τ|
       /   |
      /    |
     ●─────┘
     r

docs.title: §5. Newton's Second Law for Rotation
docs.text:
Just as \(\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}\) governs linear dynamics, torque governs rotational dynamics:

\[\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{net}} = I,\boldsymbol{\alpha}\]

where:

  • \(I\) = moment of inertia (rotational analogue of mass, depends on mass distribution)
  • \(\boldsymbol{\alpha} = \dot{\boldsymbol{\omega}}\) = angular acceleration

And the angular momentum \(\mathbf{L} = I\boldsymbol{\omega}\) satisfies:

\[\boldsymbol{\tau} = \frac{d\mathbf{L}}{dt}\]

This is the rotational analogue of \(\mathbf{F} = \frac{d\mathbf{p}}{dt}\).

docs.title: §6. Equilibrium and Static Torque
docs.text:
A rigid body is in rotational equilibrium iff:

\[\sum_i \boldsymbol{\tau}_i = \mathbf{0}\]

That is, all torques about any chosen pivot must sum to zero.

Example — Seesaw:

       m₁g↓        m₂g↓
         |            |
   ──────●────────────●──── plank
         |←   r₁  →|←  r₂  →|
                  △
                pivot

Equilibrium: \(m_1 g r_1 = m_2 g r_2\) (torques balance about the pivot).

docs.title: §7. Connection to the Cross Product — A Deeper Look
docs.text:
The torque \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}\) is fundamentally an antisymmetric operation:

\[\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F} = -\mathbf{F} \times \mathbf{r}\]

This reflects the physical fact that the order matters: the same force applied at the same point creates torques in opposite senses depending on the reference direction.

docs.title: Decomposition
docs.text:
Any force \(\mathbf{F}\) can be split into components:

\[\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{F}_\perp + \mathbf{F}_\parallel\]

where \(\mathbf{F}_\parallel\) is along \(\mathbf{r}\) and \(\mathbf{F}_\perp\) is perpendicular to \(\mathbf{r}\).

Then: $\(\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}_\perp + \underbrace{\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}_\parallel}_{= \mathbf{0}} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}_\perp\)$

Only the perpendicular component produces torque. The parallel component is rotational dead weight.

docs.title: §8. Moment Arm — An Equivalent Formulation
docs.text:
The moment arm \(d\) is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of \(\mathbf{F}\).

\[|\boldsymbol{\tau}| = |\mathbf{F}| \cdot d\]

This is equivalent to \(|\mathbf{r}||\mathbf{F}|\sin\theta\) since \(d = |\mathbf{r}|\sin\theta\).

           ←────── line of action of F ────→  →F
                          ↕ d (moment arm)
           ●─────────────────────────────────────
         pivot        r

This formulation is often cleaner for problems where the line of action is easy to identify geometrically.

docs.title: §9. Torques and Differential Forms (Preview)
docs.text:
For the advanced reader: torque is naturally expressed using the exterior product \(\wedge\). In 3D, \(\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}\) is dual (via the Hodge star) to the 2-form \(r \wedge F\), which represents an oriented area element.

This is why torque is sometimes called a pseudovector (or axial vector) — it behaves differently from a polar vector under reflections. In even dimensions, the cross product doesn't exist, but the exterior product always does.

docs.title: §10. Torque in AI, Machine Learning & Deep Learning
docs.text: This is where classical mechanics and modern computation collide in surprising ways.

docs.title: 10.1 Gradient Descent as a "Torque" Analogy
docs.text:
In gradient descent, the gradient \(\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}\) plays the role of a force that "pushes" parameters. The learning rate \(\eta\) scales the step — analogous to the moment arm scaling the torque. The update:

\[\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta,\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}\]

is structurally similar to angular impulse: a force applied at a lever arm produces a rotation. The further the parameters are from a minimum (longer lever arm), the larger the induced rotation in parameter space.

docs.title: 10.2 Rigid Body Simulation in Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs)
docs.text:
Physics-Informed Neural Networks often embed torque equations directly as constraints in the loss function. When simulating articulated bodies (robot arms, molecular dynamics):

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{physics}} = \left|\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{net}} - I\boldsymbol{\alpha}\right|^2\]

The network is penalised for predicting motions that violate \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = I\boldsymbol{\alpha}\).

docs.title: 10.3 Robotics and Reinforcement Learning
docs.text:
In robot manipulation (a central problem in deep RL), the policy \(\pi_\theta(a | s)\) outputs joint torques directly as actions. The agent must learn:

  • Which joint to torque
  • By how much
  • In which direction

Algorithms like PPO and SAC are routinely benchmarked on torque-controlled MuJoCo environments (e.g., HalfCheetah-v4, Ant-v4).

State s_t ──→ π_θ ──→ [τ₁, τ₂, ..., τₙ] (joint torques)
                              ↓
                     Physics Simulator
                              ↓
                    Next state s_{t+1}, reward r_t

docs.title: 10.4 Attention Mechanism — A Structural Analogy
docs.text:
In transformer self-attention, the output is a weighted combination:

\[\text{Attention}(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V}) = \text{softmax}!\left(\frac{\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)\mathbf{V}\]

The \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_k}}\) scaling factor plays the role of a moment arm — it controls how strongly the "rotational effect" (attention) of each query-key pair is expressed. Without this scaling, large \(d_k\) causes dot products to grow large, driving softmax into saturation (tiny gradients, no effective learning) — analogous to applying force directly through the pivot.

docs.title: 10.5 Angular Momentum in Optimisers
docs.text:
The momentum term in SGD with momentum:

\[\mathbf{v}_{t+1} = \beta,\mathbf{v}_t + \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}$$ $$\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta,\mathbf{v}_{t+1}\]

is precisely angular momentum carried forward in time. Just as \(\mathbf{L} = I\boldsymbol{\omega}\) persists unless acted on by torque, the velocity \(\mathbf{v}_t\) persists and accumulates — enabling the optimiser to "coast" through flat loss landscapes.

Adam extends this further by normalising by the second moment of gradients — adaptive torque control, in effect.

docs.title: 10.6 Graph Neural Networks and Equivariance
docs.text: SE(3)-equivariant GNNs (e.g., SchNet, DimeNet, NequIP) are designed for molecular property prediction. They must handle torques and angular forces correctly — the network output must transform as a pseudovector under rotations and reflections of the input molecule. Torque's status as an axial vector is not a curiosity; it is an architectural constraint.

docs.title: §11. Summary Table
docs.text: Concept Linear Analogue Rotational (Torque) Cause of change Force \(\mathbf{F}\) Torque \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}\) Newton's 2<sup>nd</sup> Law \(\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}\) \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = I\boldsymbol{\alpha}\) Momentum \(\mathbf{p} = m\mathbf{v}\) \(\mathbf{L} = I\boldsymbol{\omega}\) Impulse-momentum \(\mathbf{F} = \dot{\mathbf{p}}\) \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = \dot{\mathbf{L}}\) Equilibrium \(\sum \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{0}\) \(\sum \boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{0}\) Work done \(W = \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{d}\) \(W = \boldsymbol{\tau} \cdot \boldsymbol{\theta}\)

docs.title: §12. Quick-Reference Formulae
docs.text: \[\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}$$ $$|\boldsymbol{\tau}| = |\mathbf{r}||\mathbf{F}|\sin\theta = |\mathbf{F}| \cdot d$$ $$\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{net}} = I\boldsymbol{\alpha} = \frac{d\mathbf{L}}{dt}$$ $$\text{Equilibrium: } \sum \boldsymbol{\tau}_i = \mathbf{0}\]

docs.title: Tetrahedron
docs.text: "The tetrahedron is the atom of geometry — the irreducible simplex from which all of three-dimensional space can be built."

docs.title: §1. What Is a Tetrahedron?
docs.text:
A tetrahedron is a polyhedron with 4 triangular faces, 4 vertices, 6 edges. It is the 3-dimensional simplex \(\Delta^3\) — the simplest convex solid that fully encloses a volume in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).

Euler's formula check: $\(V - E + F = 4 - 6 + 4 = 2 \checkmark\)$

The tetrahedron is self-dual: its dual polyhedron is another tetrahedron (swap vertices \(\leftrightarrow\) faces).

docs.title: 2.1 General Tetrahedron
docs.text: Given four vertices \(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3\), all other geometric quantities derive from these positions.

docs.title: 2.2 The Regular Tetrahedron — Canonical Coordinates
docs.text:
The most natural embedding of a regular tetrahedron (all edges equal) is obtained by placing vertices at alternating corners of a unit cube:

\[\mathbf{v}_1 = (1,1,1), \quad \mathbf{v}_2 = (1,-1,-1), \quad \mathbf{v}_3 = (-1,1,-1), \quad \mathbf{v}_4 = (-1,-1,1)\]

Verify edge length: $\(|\mathbf{v}_1 - \mathbf{v}_2| = |(0,2,2)| = \sqrt{0+4+4} = 2\sqrt{2}\)$

All \(\binom{4}{2} = 6\) pairs give the same length \(2\sqrt{2}\). ✓

         v₁ (1,1,1)
         /|\
        / | \
       /  |  \
    v₂───────v₃
      \   |  /
       \  | /
        \ |/
         v₄ (-1,-1,1)

Centroid: \(\mathbf{G} = \frac{1}{4}(\mathbf{v}_1 + \mathbf{v}_2 + \mathbf{v}_3 + \mathbf{v}_4) = \frac{1}{4}(0,0,0) = \mathbf{0}\) ✓ (centred at origin)

docs.title: 3.1 The Scalar Triple Product Formula
docs.text:
For a tetrahedron with one vertex at \(\mathbf{a}\) and the other three at \(\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{d}\), define edge vectors from \(\mathbf{a}\):

\[\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}, \quad \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{a}, \quad \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{d} - \mathbf{a}\]

Then:

\[\boxed{V = \frac{1}{6}\left|\mathbf{u} \cdot (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{w})\right|}\]

Why ⅙? The parallelepiped spanned by \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}\) has volume \(|\mathbf{u} \cdot (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{w})|\). A pyramid is \(\frac{1}{3}\) of the prism with the same base and height; the tetrahedron is \(\frac{1}{2}\) of that pyramid — so overall \(\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{6}\).

docs.title: 3.2 The Determinant Form
docs.text:
Equivalently, since \(\mathbf{u} \cdot (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{w}) = \det[\mathbf{u}\ \mathbf{v}\ \mathbf{w}]\):

\[V = \frac{1}{6}\left|\det\begin{pmatrix} u_1 & v_1 & w_1 \ u_2 & v_2 & w_2 \ u_3 & v_3 & w_3 \end{pmatrix}\right|\]

Or equivalently, using all four vertices directly:

\[V = \frac{1}{6}\left|\det\begin{pmatrix} b_1 - a_1 & c_1 - a_1 & d_1 - a_1 \ b_2 - a_2 & c_2 - a_2 & d_2 - a_2 \ b_3 - a_3 & c_3 - a_3 & d_3 - a_3 \end{pmatrix}\right|\]

Geometric meaning of the determinant: It is the signed volume of the parallelepiped — positive if \((\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w})\) form a right-handed system, negative otherwise.

docs.title: 3.3 Worked Example
docs.text:
Let \(\mathbf{a} = (0,0,0)\), \(\mathbf{b} = (1,0,0)\), \(\mathbf{c} = (0,1,0)\), \(\mathbf{d} = (0,0,1)\) (the unit tetrahedron).

\[\mathbf{u} = (1,0,0),\quad \mathbf{v} = (0,1,0),\quad \mathbf{w} = (0,0,1)\] \[\det\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\0&1&0\0&0&1\end{pmatrix} = 1\] \[V = \frac{1}{6} \cdot |1| = \frac{1}{6}\]

This is \(\frac{1}{6}\) of the unit cube — exactly one sixth, since the cube decomposes into exactly 6 congruent tetrahedra.

         (0,0,1)
           |  \
           |    \
           |      \
         (0,0,0)──(0,1,0)
          / \    /
         /   \  /
       (1,0,0)

docs.title: 4.1 Area of One Triangular Face
docs.text:
For a face with vertices \(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}, \mathbf{r}\):

\[\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2}|(\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{p}) \times (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{p})|\]

The cross product \((\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{p}) \times (\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{p})\) is the outward normal to that face (up to sign).

docs.title: 4.2 Outward Face Normals
docs.text:
For each face, the outward unit normal \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}_i\) points away from the opposite vertex. This is used in surface integrals, flux computations, and mesh rendering.

Convention: For face opposite vertex \(\mathbf{d}\), the normal should satisfy \(\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot (\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{d}) < 0\) (points away from \(\mathbf{d}\)).

docs.title: 4.3 Total Surface Area — Regular Tetrahedron
docs.text:
Each face is an equilateral triangle with side \(a\), area \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a^2\). Four faces:

\[S = 4 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a^2 = \sqrt{3},a^2\]

docs.title: §5. Key Metric Properties — Regular Tetrahedron
docs.text: Let edge length be \(a\). All proofs below use the canonical cube embedding scaled so edge \(= a\).

docs.title: 5.1 Circumradius \(R\) (circumscribed sphere)
docs.text:
The circumsphere passes through all 4 vertices. By symmetry its centre is the centroid \(\mathbf{G}\).

\[R = |\mathbf{v}_1 - \mathbf{G}| = \frac{a\sqrt{6}}{4}\]

docs.title: 5.2 Inradius \(r\) (inscribed sphere)
docs.text:
The insphere is tangent to all 4 faces from inside. It satisfies:

\[r = \frac{3V}{S} = \frac{3 \cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{12}a^3}{\sqrt{3},a^2} = \frac{a}{2\sqrt{6}} = \frac{a\sqrt{6}}{12}\]

Key ratio: \(\frac{R}{r} = \frac{a\sqrt{6}/4}{a\sqrt{6}/12} = 3\)

So the circumradius is always exactly 3 times the inradius for a regular tetrahedron. This is a characterisation of tetrahedra among the Platonic solids.

docs.title: 5.3 Height \(h\) (apex to base)
docs.text:
\[h = a\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\]

Note: \(R + r = h\) for the regular tetrahedron (centroid divides the altitude in ratio \(3:1\)).

docs.title: Summary Table — Regular Tetrahedron (edge \(a\))
docs.text: Quantity Formula Approx (\(a=1\)) Volume \(V\) \(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{12}a^3\) \(0.1178\) Surface area \(S\) \(\sqrt{3},a^2\) \(1.7321\) Circumradius \(R\) \(\dfrac{a\sqrt{6}}{4}\) \(0.6124\) Inradius \(r\) \(\dfrac{a\sqrt{6}}{12}\) \(0.2041\) Height \(h\) \(a\sqrt{2/3}\) \(0.8165\) \(R/r\) \(3\) \(3\)

docs.title: 6.1 Centroid
docs.text:
\[\mathbf{G} = \frac{\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{c} + \mathbf{d}}{4}\]

The centroid divides each median (vertex to centroid of opposite face) in ratio \(3:1\) from the vertex.

docs.title: 6.2 Barycentric Coordinates
docs.text:
Any point \(\mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3\) can be written as:

\[\mathbf{p} = \lambda_1 \mathbf{a} + \lambda_2 \mathbf{b} + \lambda_3 \mathbf{c} + \lambda_4 \mathbf{d}, \qquad \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \lambda_3 + \lambda_4 = 1\]

The \(\lambda_i\) are the barycentric coordinates of \(\mathbf{p}\).

Geometric meaning of \(\lambda_i\): \(\lambda_i = \frac{V_i}{V}\) where \(V_i\) is the volume of the sub-tetrahedron formed by \(\mathbf{p}\) and the face opposite vertex \(i\).

\(\mathbf{p}\) is inside the tetrahedron \(\iff\) all \(\lambda_i > 0\).

Interior point P:
                  a
                 /|\
                / | \
               /  P  \      P = λ₁a + λ₂b + λ₃c + λ₄d
              /  / \  \     all λᵢ > 0
             / /     \ \
            b──────────c
              \      /
               \    /
                \  /
                 d

To solve for barycentric coordinates of \(\mathbf{p}\): set up the \(4\times 4\) linear system

\[\begin{pmatrix} a_1 & b_1 & c_1 & d_1 \ a_2 & b_2 & c_2 & d_2 \ a_3 & b_3 & c_3 & d_3 \ 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}\lambda_1\\lambda_2\\lambda_3\\lambda_4\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}p_1\p_2\p_3\1\end{pmatrix}\]

docs.title: §7. Dihedral Angles
docs.text:
The dihedral angle along an edge is the angle between the two faces sharing that edge.

For the regular tetrahedron, all 6 edges have the same dihedral angle:

\[\theta_{\text{dihedral}} = \arccos!\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) \approx 70.53°\]

Derivation: Let the edge be \(\mathbf{v}_1\mathbf{v}_2\). The normals to the two adjacent faces are:

  • \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{123} \propto (\mathbf{v}_2-\mathbf{v}_1)\times(\mathbf{v}_3-\mathbf{v}_1)\)
  • \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{124} \propto (\mathbf{v}_2-\mathbf{v}_1)\times(\mathbf{v}_4-\mathbf{v}_1)\)

The dihedral angle satisfies \(\cos\theta = \hat{\mathbf{n}}_{123}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{124}\). By the canonical coordinates this evaluates to \(\frac{1}{3}\), so:

\[\theta = \arccos!\left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right)\]

Note: The supplement \(\pi - \arccos(1/3) \approx 109.47°\) is the tetrahedral bond angle in chemistry (e.g., methane CH₄).

        Face 1
          /\
         /  \
        /    \    ← dihedral angle ≈ 70.53°
  ─────/──────\─────  edge
        \    /
         \  /
          \/
        Face 2

docs.title: §8. The Solid Angle at Each Vertex
docs.text:
The solid angle \(\Omega\) subtended at each vertex of a regular tetrahedron (the amount of the unit sphere "seen" from that vertex):

\[\Omega = \arccos!\left(\frac{23}{27}\right) \approx 0.55\text{ sr}\]

The total solid angle over all 4 vertices is \(4\Omega \approx 2.2\) sr (less than \(4\pi \approx 12.57\) sr — the full sphere — reflecting the open space between faces).

docs.title: 9.1 The Tetrahedron as a Simplex
docs.text:
The tetrahedron is the 3-simplex \(\Delta^3\):

\[\Delta^3 = \left{(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3,\lambda_4) \in \mathbb{R}^4 ;\middle|; \sum_{i=1}^4 \lambda_i = 1,\ \lambda_i \geq 0\right}\]

This is a 3-dimensional object living in a 3-dimensional affine subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^4\).

Its faces correspond to subsets where some \(\lambda_i = 0\):

  • 4 triangular faces: one \(\lambda_i = 0\)
  • 6 edges: two \(\lambda_i = 0\)
  • 4 vertices: three \(\lambda_i = 0\)

docs.title: 9.2 Decomposition of the Cube
docs.text:
The unit cube \([0,1]^3\) decomposes into exactly 5 tetrahedra (non-overlapping, filling the cube):

Cube → 5 tetrahedra:
  1 central regular tetrahedron
+ 4 corner tetrahedra (right-angle type)

Alternatively, into 6 congruent tetrahedra (all sharing the main diagonal).

This decomposition is exploited in finite element methods and mesh generation.

docs.title: §10. The Cayley–Menger Determinant
docs.text:
The volume of a tetrahedron with vertices at mutual distances \(d_{ij} = |\mathbf{v}_i - \mathbf{v}_j|\) can be computed without coordinates via:

\[288,V^2 = \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \ 1 & 0 & d_{12}^2 & d_{13}^2 & d_{14}^2 \ 1 & d_{12}^2 & 0 & d_{23}^2 & d_{24}^2 \ 1 & d_{13}^2 & d_{23}^2 & 0 & d_{34}^2 \ 1 & d_{14}^2 & d_{24}^2 & d_{34}^2 & 0 \end{vmatrix}\]

This is the Cayley–Menger determinant. It is purely metric — only pairwise distances enter.

Consequence: The shape of a tetrahedron (up to rigid motion and reflection) is completely determined by its 6 edge lengths.

Check for regular tetrahedron (all \(d_{ij} = a\)): All off-diagonal entries \(= a^2\), giving \(288V^2 = 2a^6\), so \(V = \frac{a^3}{12\sqrt{2}} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{12}a^3\). ✓

docs.title: §11. Connection to AI, Machine Learning & Deep Learning
docs.text: The tetrahedron is not merely a topic in solid geometry — it appears, often unexpectedly, at the foundations of modern ML.

docs.title: 11.1 Simplices and Probability Simplices
docs.text:
The probability simplex \(\Delta^{n-1} = {\mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^n : p_i \geq 0, \sum p_i = 1}\) is the direct generalisation of the tetrahedron.

For \(n=4\): the set of all probability distributions over 4 classes is a 3-simplex — a tetrahedron. Each vertex is a one-hot distribution (total certainty about one class); interior points are mixed distributions.

        p₁=1                    "Class 1 certain"
         ▲
        /|\
       / | \
      /  |  \
     ▼───┼───▼
   p₂=1  |  p₃=1
         ▼
        p₄=1

   Interior = all mixed distributions
   over 4 classes

Softmax maps logits \(\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) to the interior of \(\Delta^{n-1}\):

\[\text{softmax}(\mathbf{z})_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}} \in \Delta^{n-1}\]

Every classification head of a neural network outputs a point in a probability simplex.

docs.title: 11.2 Barycentric Interpolation in Neural Rendering and Graphics
docs.text:
NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) and rasterization-based rendering pipelines use barycentric coordinates constantly — every fragment shader interpolates vertex attributes (colour, normal, UV) using the \(\lambda_i\) of the pixel's position within the triangle/tetrahedron.

The barycentric coordinate formula from §6.2 is the engine behind every real-time 3D renderer and neural rendering pipeline.

docs.title: 11.3 Tetrahedral Meshes in Physics-Informed Neural Networks
docs.text:
FEM (Finite Element Method) discretises a 3D domain into tetrahedra. The volume formula (§3) and barycentric coordinates (§6) determine the element stiffness matrices. PINNs that operate on unstructured 3D grids inherit exactly this tetrahedral structure.

The quality of a tetrahedral mesh — measured by the aspect ratio \(R/r = 3\) for a regular tetrahedron — directly controls numerical conditioning of the resulting linear systems that neural solvers aim to bypass or approximate.

docs.title: 11.4 Simplex Methods in Optimisation
docs.text:
The Nelder-Mead simplex algorithm (used in hyperparameter tuning before gradient-based methods dominated) maintains a tetrahedron (in 3D) or \(n\)-simplex (in \(n\)D) in parameter space, and iteratively reflects, expands, or contracts it toward a minimum.

The operations — reflection through the face centroid, expansion along the axis — are exactly the affine operations on barycentric coordinates.

docs.title: 11.5 Tetrahedral Geometry in Molecular ML
docs.text:
Graph neural networks for molecular property prediction (e.g., SchNet, DimeNet++, GemNet) must represent 3D molecular geometry. Tetrahedral carbon (\(sp^3\)) is the fundamental structural motif. The dihedral angle \(\approx 109.47°\) (§7) is a hard geometric constraint that symmetry-aware GNNs must respect.

SE(3)-equivariant networks (e.g., NequIP, SEGNN) encode both edge vectors and face normals of local tetrahedral environments as features — directly using the cross product structure of §4.

docs.title: 11.6 Convex Hull and Support Vector Machines
docs.text:
The minimum enclosing simplex problem — find the smallest simplex containing a set of points — is equivalent to finding the convex hull and relates to the maximum margin problem in SVMs.

A hard-margin SVM in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) with 4 support vectors defines a tetrahedral margin geometry. The decision boundary is the hyperplane equidistant from two tetrahedrally arranged point clouds.

docs.title: 11.7 Topology in Deep Learning — Simplicial Complexes
docs.text:
Topological Data Analysis (TDA) and simplicial neural networks (e.g., SNN, SAT) use simplicial complexes — collections of vertices, edges, triangles, tetrahedra — to model higher-order interactions in data.

The tetrahedron \(\Delta^3\) is the basic 3-cell. Simplicial homology counts "holes" of different dimensions; in a simplicial complex built from data points, a 3-cycle involving tetrahedra detects 3D voids, e.g., protein pockets or topological features of latent spaces.

docs.title: Regular Tetrahedron — Orthographic Projections
docs.text:
Top view (looking down \(z\)-axis):

        v₁
        / \
       /   \
      /     \
    v₂───────v₃
      \     /
       \   /
        \ /
         v₄  (behind centre)

Face-on view (looking at one face):

      v₁
     /  \
    /    \
   /      \
  v₂──────v₃

Exploded view (4 triangular faces pulled apart):

     △         △
  (face 1)  (face 2)

     △         △
  (face 3)  (face 4)

  → fold along edges to assemble

docs.title: §13. Summary of Key Formulas
docs.text: \[V = \frac{1}{6}|\mathbf{u}\cdot(\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{w})| = \frac{1}{6}|\det[\mathbf{u}\ \mathbf{v}\ \mathbf{w}]|\] \[V_{\text{reg}} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{12}a^3, \quad S_{\text{reg}} = \sqrt{3},a^2\] \[R = \frac{a\sqrt{6}}{4}, \quad r = \frac{a\sqrt{6}}{12}, \quad \frac{R}{r} = 3\] \[\theta_{\text{dihedral}} = \arccos!\left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right) \approx 70.53°, \quad \theta_{\text{bond}} = \pi - \arccos!\left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right) \approx 109.47°\] \[288,V^2 = \text{Cayley-Menger det}(d_{ij})\] \[\text{Barycentric: } \mathbf{p} = \sum \lambda_i \mathbf{v}_i,\quad \sum \lambda_i = 1,\quad \lambda_i > 0 \iff \mathbf{p} \text{ interior}\]
