docs.title: Functions of Two Variables
docs.text: "A function of one variable is a curve. A function of two variables is a landscape — it has hills, valleys, ridges, and saddle points. Learning to read that landscape is the entire project of multivariable calculus."

docs.title: 0. Motivation
docs.text:
In single-variable calculus, we study \(f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\). But the real world is rarely one-dimensional:

  • Temperature in a room depends on position \((x, y)\) on the floor.
  • The pressure of a gas depends on volume \(V\) and temperature \(T\).
  • The loss of a neural network depends on millions of parameters \((\theta_1, \theta_2, \ldots, \theta_p)\).

The step from one variable to two is not merely an added variable — it is a qualitative leap in richness. New phenomena appear: partial derivatives, mixed partials, level curves, saddle points, constrained extrema. Understanding the two-variable case deeply is the prerequisite for everything that follows.

docs.title: Formal Definition
docs.text:
A function of two variables is a rule \(f\) that assigns to each ordered pair \((x, y)\) in a set \(D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2\) a unique real number \(z = f(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}\):

\[f: D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad (x,y) \mapsto f(x,y)\]
  • \(D\) is the domain of \(f\) — the set of valid inputs.
  • The range is \({f(x,y) : (x,y) \in D} \subseteq \mathbb{R}\).
  • \(z = f(x,y)\) is the dependent variable; \(x, y\) are independent variables.

docs.title: Natural Domain
docs.text:
Unless stated otherwise, the domain of \(f\) is the largest subset of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) for which the expression \(f(x,y)\) makes sense (real-valued, defined). This requires excluding:

  • Points where denominators vanish.
  • Points where expressions under even roots are negative.
  • Points where logarithms receive non-positive arguments.

Example: \(f(x,y) = \dfrac{\sqrt{y - x^2}}{1 - x^2 - y^2}\)

  • Need \(y - x^2 \geq 0\): above or on the parabola \(y = x^2\).
  • Need \(1 - x^2 - y^2 \neq 0\): outside the unit circle.

Domain: \({(x,y) : y \geq x^2} \setminus {(x,y): x^2+y^2 = 1}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The graph of \(f: D \to \mathbb{R}\) is the set of all points \((x,y,z) \in \mathbb{R}^3\) such that \(z = f(x,y)\) and \((x,y) \in D\):

\[\text{graph}(f) = {(x, y, f(x,y)) : (x,y) \in D} \subset \mathbb{R}^3\]

Geometrically: a surface in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) lying above (or below) the \(xy\)-plane.

docs.title: Visualization
docs.text:
Think of the \(xy\)-plane as a map. The value \(f(x,y)\) is the elevation at location \((x,y)\). The graph is the terrain — the topographic surface.

        z
        │        *  surface z = f(x,y)
        │      * *  *
        │    *       *
        │  *           *
        │*               *
        └──────────────────── y
       /
      /
     x

For each (x,y) in the domain, there is exactly one height z = f(x,y).

docs.title: Key Surfaces to Know
docs.text: Function Surface \(z = ax + by + c\) Plane \(z = x^2 + y^2\) Circular paraboloid (bowl) \(z = x^2 - y^2\) Hyperbolic paraboloid (saddle) \(z = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\) Cone \(z = \sqrt{1 - x^2 - y^2}\) Upper hemisphere of unit sphere \(z = e^{-(x^2+y^2)}\) Gaussian bell surface

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The level curve (or contour) of \(f\) at height \(c \in \mathbb{R}\) is the set:

\[L_c = {(x,y) \in D : f(x,y) = c}\]

It is the horizontal cross-section of the graph at height \(z = c\), projected down to the \(xy\)-plane.

Crucially: A point \((x,y)\) lies on the level curve \(L_c\) if and only if the surface passes through height \(c\) directly above it.

docs.title: The Contour Map
docs.text:
A contour map (contour plot) is the collection of level curves \({L_c}\) for various values of \(c\), drawn in the \(xy\)-plane. Every topographic map you have ever read is a contour map.

Reading a contour map:

  • Closely spaced contours: Steep terrain (rapid change in \(f\)).
  • Widely spaced contours: Gentle terrain (slow change in \(f\)).
  • Closed contours: Peaks, valleys, or saddle points.
  • Contours never cross: If \(L_c\) and \(L_{c'}\) crossed at a point \((x_0, y_0)\), then \(f(x_0,y_0) = c\) and \(f(x_0,y_0) = c'\) simultaneously — impossible for \(c \neq c'\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
\(f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2\): Level curves \(c = x^2 + y^2\) are circles of radius \(\sqrt{c}\) centered at the origin. The surface is a paraboloid. Contours are evenly spaced circles — but the paraboloid gets steeper as \(r\) increases, so equal spacing in \(c\) gives circles that pack closer together.

\(f(x,y) = x^2 - y^2\): Level curves \(c = x^2 - y^2\) are hyperbolas (for \(c \neq 0\)) and the two lines \(y = \pm x\) (for \(c = 0\)). This is the saddle surface — its contour map looks like a topographic pass between two mountains.

\(f(x,y) = xy\): Level curves \(xy = c\) are rectangular hyperbolas with asymptotes along the axes.

Contour map of z = x² + y²:       Contour map of z = x² - y² (saddle):

    y                                   y
    │   (3)  (2)  (1)                   │
    │  ╭──╮╭──╮╭──╮                    │  ╲ ╱ ╲ ╱
    │  │  ││  ││  │                     │   ╳   ╳
    │  ╰──╯╰──╯╰──╯                    │  ╱ ╲ ╱ ╲
    └──────────────── x                 └──────────────── x

  circles = level curves               hyperbolas = level curves
  (bowl shape)                         (saddle shape)

docs.title: The Core Difficulty
docs.text: In \(\mathbb{R}\), approaching a point \(a\) means coming from the left or right — only two paths. In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), approaching \((a,b)\) means coming from infinitely many directions and along infinitely many curved paths. For a limit to exist, the function must approach the same value along every possible path.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
\[\lim_{(x,y)\to(a,b)} f(x,y) = L\]

means: for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that:

\[0 < \sqrt{(x-a)^2 + (y-b)^2} < \delta \implies |f(x,y) - L| < \varepsilon\]

docs.title: The Two-Path Test (Nonexistence)
docs.text:
To show a limit does not exist: find two paths to \((a,b)\) along which \(f\) approaches different values.

Example: Show \(\displaystyle\lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}\frac{x^2 - y^2}{x^2 + y^2}\) does not exist.

  • Along \(y = 0\): \(f(x,0) = x^2/x^2 = 1 \to 1\).
  • Along \(x = 0\): \(f(0,y) = -y^2/y^2 = -1 \to -1\).

Since \(1 \neq -1\), the limit does not exist. \(\square\)

Example (subtler): Show \(\displaystyle\lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}\frac{xy^2}{x^2+y^4}\) does not exist.

  • Along \(y = 0\): \(f \to 0\).
  • Along \(x = y^2\): \(f = \frac{y^2\cdot y^2}{y^4 + y^4} = \frac{1}{2} \to \frac{1}{2}\).

Limit does not exist. Note: along any straight line \(y = mx\), the limit is \(0\) — only a parabolic path reveals the failure. This shows why the two-path test must consider curves, not just lines.

docs.title: Continuity
docs.text:
\(f\) is continuous at \((a,b)\) if:

  1. \(f(a,b)\) is defined.
  2. \(\displaystyle\lim_{(x,y)\to(a,b)} f(x,y)\) exists.
  3. \(\displaystyle\lim_{(x,y)\to(a,b)} f(x,y) = f(a,b)\).

Theorem: Polynomials in \(x,y\) are continuous on all of \(\mathbb{R}^2\). Rational functions are continuous on their domains. Compositions of continuous functions are continuous.

Consequence: For nice functions (polynomials, rationals away from singularities, exponentials, trig), you can evaluate limits by direct substitution. The challenge is only at boundary points of the domain or suspected discontinuities.

docs.title: 5. Partial Derivatives (First Pass)
docs.text:
Full treatment in the next note. Here, the idea.

The partial derivative \(\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(a,b)\) is the derivative of \(f\) in the \(x\)-direction, holding \(y = b\) fixed:

\[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(a,b) = \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(a+h,b) - f(a,b)}{h}\]

Geometrically: it is the slope of the curve obtained by slicing the surface \(z = f(x,y)\) with the vertical plane \(y = b\).

Similarly for \(\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\): hold \(x = a\) fixed, differentiate in \(y\).

Rule: To compute \(\partial f/\partial x\), treat \(y\) as a constant and differentiate in \(x\) using all single-variable rules.

docs.title: Example 1: Domain
docs.text:
Find the domain of \(f(x,y) = \ln(x + y - 1)\).

Need \(x + y - 1 > 0\), i.e., \(x + y > 1\).

Domain: the open half-plane above the line \(x + y = 1\). The boundary line is excluded (log of zero is undefined).

docs.title: Example 2: Level Curves of a Gaussian
docs.text:
Let \(f(x,y) = e^{-(x^2 + y^2)}\).

Level curve at height \(c\) (where \(0 < c \leq 1\)): $\(e^{-(x^2+y^2)} = c \implies x^2 + y^2 = -\ln c\)$

For \(0 < c < 1\): \(-\ln c > 0\), so these are circles of radius \(\sqrt{-\ln c}\). As \(c \to 1^-\): radius \(\to 0\) (peak at origin). As \(c \to 0^+\): radius \(\to \infty\) (function decays to zero far from origin).

The contour map is a family of concentric circles — and the circles get farther apart as \(c\) decreases (the Gaussian decays rapidly near origin, then flattens out).

docs.title: Example 3: A Subtle Limit
docs.text:
Show \(\displaystyle\lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}\frac{x^2 y}{x^2+y^2} = 0\).

Use the Squeeze Theorem. Observe: $\(\left|\frac{x^2 y}{x^2+y^2}\right| \leq \frac{x^2 |y|}{x^2+y^2} \leq |y|\)$

since \(x^2 \leq x^2 + y^2\). As \((x,y) \to (0,0)\), \(|y| \to 0\). By squeeze, the limit is \(0\).

Note: To confirm, convert to polar: \(x = r\cos\theta\), \(y = r\sin\theta\): $\(\frac{r^2\cos^2\theta \cdot r\sin\theta}{r^2} = r\cos^2\theta\sin\theta \to 0 \text{ as } r\to 0\)$

since \(|\cos^2\theta\sin\theta| \leq 1\) for all \(\theta\). The polar method works when the bound is independent of \(\theta\).

docs.title: Example 4: Discontinuity
docs.text:
Let \(f(x,y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{2xy}{x^2+y^2} & (x,y)\neq(0,0) \ 0 & (x,y) = (0,0)\end{cases}\)

Is \(f\) continuous at \((0,0)\)?

Along \(y = mx\): \(f(x,mx) = \dfrac{2mx^2}{x^2(1+m^2)} = \dfrac{2m}{1+m^2}\), which depends on \(m\).

For \(m = 1\): limit is \(1\). For \(m = 0\): limit is \(0\). The limit does not exist, so \(f\) is not continuous at \((0,0)\), regardless of how we define \(f(0,0)\).

docs.title: Reading a Surface from Its Contours
docs.text:
Close contours = steep         Sparse contours = gentle

  ════════════                   ══════════════════
  ══════════════                 ══════════════════
  ════════════════               ══════════════════

  Think: cliff face              Think: gentle meadow

docs.title: Identifying Features from Contour Maps
docs.text:
Peak:              Valley:            Saddle:
  ╭───╮              ╭───╮             ╲   ╱
  │ ╭─╯              │ ╭─╯              ╲ ╱
  │ │                │ │                 ╳
  ╰─╯                ╰─╯                ╱╲
                                       ╱  ╲
  Concentric closed   Concentric closed   Hyperbolas;
  contours,           contours,           two "uphill"
  values increase     values decrease     and two "downhill"
  inward              inward              directions

docs.title: The "Slicing" Interpretation
docs.text:
The surface \(z = f(x,y)\) is simultaneously:

  • The set of all level curves stacked at their respective heights.
  • The set of all "traces" — curves obtained by fixing \(x\) or \(y\) to a constant.
Fix y = b:  curve z = f(x, b) in the plane y = b  →  slope = ∂f/∂x
Fix x = a:  curve z = f(a, y) in the plane x = a  →  slope = ∂f/∂y

docs.title: 8. Functions of Three or More Variables
docs.text:
The definitions extend naturally:

\[f: D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad (x_1, \ldots, x_n) \mapsto f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\]

We can no longer visualize the graph (it lives in \(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\)). Instead, we study level sets:

\[L_c = {(x_1,\ldots,x_n) : f(x_1,\ldots,x_n) = c}\]

which are \((n-1)\)-dimensional hypersurfaces in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

For \(n = 3\): \(f(x,y,z) = c\) defines a level surface in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) — e.g., \(x^2+y^2+z^2 = r^2\) (sphere), \(x^2/a^2+y^2/b^2+z^2/c^2 = 1\) (ellipsoid).

All the theory — limits, continuity, partial derivatives, gradients — extends verbatim to \(n\) variables. The geometry is harder to visualize but the algebra is identical.

docs.title: 9. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
9.1 The Loss Function Is a Function of Millions of Variables
docs.text:
The most important function in all of machine learning is the loss function:

\[\mathcal{L}: \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad \boldsymbol{\theta} \mapsto \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\]

where \(p\) is the number of parameters (GPT-4: \(p \sim 10^{12}\)). This is exactly a function of \(p\) variables — the direct generalization of \(f(x,y)\) to \(p\) dimensions.

Everything we study for \(f(x,y)\) has a direct ML analog:

\(f(x,y)\) concept ML analog Domain \(D \subset \mathbb{R}^2\) Parameter space \(\mathbb{R}^p\) Graph \(z = f(x,y)\) Loss landscape (unvisualizable for \(p \gg 2\)) Level curve \(f(x,y) = c\) Loss contour \(\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol\theta) = c\) — iso-loss surface in parameter space Continuity Smoothness of \(\mathcal{L}\) (required for gradient methods to work) Partial derivative \(\partial f/\partial x\) Gradient component \(\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\theta_i\) — used in backpropagation

docs.title: 9.2 Level Curves as Decision Boundaries
docs.text:
For a binary classifier \(f: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\), the decision boundary is the level curve \(f(x,y) = 0.5\) (or \(f = 0\) for logistic regression). The classifier outputs:

  • Class 1 if \(f(x,y) > 0.5\)
  • Class 0 if \(f(x,y) < 0.5\)

A linear classifier produces straight-line decision boundaries (level curves of a linear \(f\)). A neural network can produce arbitrarily complex level curves — this is the Universal Approximation Theorem in geometric form: a neural network can approximate any continuous function \(f: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\), hence any level curve as a decision boundary.

docs.title: 9.3 Continuity and the Vanishing Gradient Problem
docs.text:
The continuity of the loss function near a region of parameter space is directly connected to gradient flow. At a discontinuity or near a point where the gradient is zero but the function is not at a minimum (a flat region or plateau), gradient descent stalls — the optimization analogue of a function with zero partial derivatives everywhere in a region.

The Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) activation \(\text{ReLU}(x) = \max(0,x)\) makes networks that are continuous but not differentiable at \(x = 0\). The composed function \(\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol\theta)\) for a ReLU network is a piecewise linear function of \(\boldsymbol\theta\) — continuous everywhere, differentiable almost everywhere.

docs.title: 9.4 Gaussian Functions and Radial Basis Networks
docs.text:
The function \(f(x,y) = e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2\sigma^2}\) (Example 2 above) is the 2D Gaussian. Its level curves are concentric circles. In ML:

  • Kernel methods (SVMs with RBF kernel): The kernel \(K(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = e^{-|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}'|^2/2\sigma^2}\) measures similarity as a Gaussian of distance.
  • Radial Basis Function (RBF) networks: Hidden units compute \(\phi(\mathbf{x}) = e^{-|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c}_i|^2/2\sigma_i^2}\) — exactly the two-variable Gaussian, with centers \(\mathbf{c}_i\).
  • Gaussian Processes: The covariance function is a Gaussian of the input distance — level curves of this covariance are ellipses in input space.

docs.title: 9.5 Latent Space and Feature Maps
docs.text:
In a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) or diffusion model, data is mapped to a 2D (or low-dimensional) latent space. The decoder then defines a function \(f: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^d\) (going from 2 latent variables to a high-dimensional output — the reverse direction of what we study here, but the domain is \(\mathbb{R}^2\)).

The latent space interpolation — walking along a straight line or curve in the \((z_1, z_2)\) plane — is exactly choosing a path in the domain \(D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2\) of the decoder function. The continuity of \(f\) ensures nearby latent points decode to nearby outputs.

docs.title: 9.6 Two-Variable Functions as Neural Network Layers
docs.text:
A single neuron with two inputs computes:

\[z = \sigma(w_1 x + w_2 y + b)\]

This is a function \(f(x,y) = \sigma(w_1 x + w_2 y + b)\). Its level curves are:

\[w_1 x + w_2 y + b = \sigma^{-1}(c) = \text{const}\]

which are straight lines (linear decision boundaries). Stacking neurons allows the level curves of the composed function to become arbitrarily curved — the geometric meaning of expressiveness.

docs.title: 9.7 Domain and Data Manifold
docs.text: In practice, input data does not fill all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Natural images, for instance, occupy a low-dimensional manifold \(\mathcal{M} \subset \mathbb{R}^n\) (the manifold hypothesis). The effective domain of the learned function \(f\) is this manifold — points off the manifold are out-of-distribution. This is the geometric basis for why neural networks hallucinate and fail on adversarial examples: the function is evaluated outside its meaningful domain \(D\).

docs.title: 10. Summary
docs.text:
A function of two variables \(f: D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\) is a surface in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), studied through:

Domain: Largest set where \(f(x,y)\) makes sense — exclude division by zero, square roots of negatives, logs of non-positives.

Graph: The surface \(z = f(x,y)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) — the geometric object we analyze.

Level curves: \(f(x,y) = c\) — horizontal slices of the graph, contour lines on a map. They never cross; dense packing means steep terrain.

Limits: Must agree along every path to \((a,b)\), not just along lines. Two-path test proves nonexistence; polar coordinates and squeeze theorem prove existence.

Continuity: Defined exactly as in one variable, but the limit condition is harder to verify due to the infinity of approach paths.

The entire theory extends to \(n\) variables. In machine learning, the loss landscape \(\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol\theta)\) is a function of millions of variables — but every concept introduced here (domain, level sets, continuity, partial derivatives) applies directly, at scale.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. Sections 14.1–14.2. — Primary source: definitions, domain, level curves, limits, continuity, worked examples.
  2. MIT OpenCourseWare 18.02. Multivariable Calculus (Auroux). Lectures on functions of several variables and their graphs. — The contour map perspective and polar coordinate limit technique.
  3. Goodfellow, I., Bengio, Y., Courville, A. Deep Learning. MIT Press (2016). Ch. 4–6. — Loss landscapes, activation functions, and the geometric view of neural networks.
  4. Kingma, D. & Welling, M. "Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes." ICLR (2014). — Latent space as a two-variable domain.

docs.title: Functions of Three+ Variables
docs.text: "When a function depends on two variables, we can still draw it — a surface hovering over a plane. When it depends on three, we lose that luxury. The graph lives in \(\mathbb{R}^4\), invisible to us. And yet the calculus generalizes perfectly. This is the point where you learn to think analytically rather than geometrically — a skill that will serve you in every dimension you ever encounter."

docs.title: 0. Motivation: Why More Variables?
docs.text:
Almost nothing in the real world depends on fewer than three quantities simultaneously.

  • Temperature in a room: \(T(x, y, z)\) — three spatial coordinates.
  • Pressure in a fluid: \(P(x, y, z, t)\) — three space + one time.
  • Gravitational potential: \(\phi(x,y,z) = -GM/\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}\).
  • A neural network layer: output \(f(\mathbf{x}) : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m\) where \(n\) can be millions.
  • The loss function of a model: \(\mathcal{L}(\theta_1, \theta_2, \ldots, \theta_p)\) where \(p \sim 10^{10}\).

The theory of functions of two variables (surfaces, level curves, partial derivatives) extends to three or more variables with essentially no new difficulty — just new notation and a willingness to stop asking "what does this look like?"

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A function of three variables is a rule that assigns a unique real number to each point in some domain \(D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3\):

\[f : D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad (x,y,z) \mapsto f(x,y,z)\]

Domain \(D\): the set of all \((x,y,z)\) for which the expression is defined. Range: the set of all values \(f(x,y,z)\) as \((x,y,z)\) varies over \(D\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Example 1. \(f(x,y,z) = \sqrt{1 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2}\)

Domain: \({(x,y,z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 : x^2 + y^2 + z^2 \leq 1}\) — the closed unit ball \(\overline{B}(0,1)\). Range: \([0,1]\).

Example 2. \(f(x,y,z) = \ln(z - x^2 - y^2)\)

Domain: \({(x,y,z) : z > x^2 + y^2}\) — the open region above the paraboloid \(z = x^2 + y^2\). Range: \(\mathbb{R}\) (since \(\ln\) achieves all real values on \((0,\infty)\)).

Example 3. \(f(x,y,z) = \dfrac{xyz}{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}\)

Domain: \(\mathbb{R}^3 \setminus {(0,0,0)}\) — all of \(\mathbb{R}^3\) except the origin.

Example 4 (Physics). Gravitational potential: $\(\phi(x,y,z) = -\frac{GM}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}}\)$

Domain: \(\mathbb{R}^3\setminus{(0,0,0)}\). The force field is \(\mathbf{F} = -\nabla\phi\) — the gradient of a scalar function.

docs.title: 2. Level Surfaces
docs.text: For a function \(f(x,y,z)\), we cannot draw its graph (that would live in \(\mathbb{R}^4\)). The geometric substitute is the level surface.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The level surface of \(f\) at value \(c\) is:

\[S_c = {(x,y,z) \in D : f(x,y,z) = c}\]

This is a surface in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) — the set of all points where \(f\) takes the value \(c\).

Level surfaces are the three-variable analog of level curves. They replace the graph as the primary geometric object.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
\(f(x,y,z) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2\): Level surfaces are spheres \(x^2+y^2+z^2 = c\) (for \(c > 0\)), a point (for \(c=0\)), empty (for \(c < 0\)). These are the "shells" at constant distance from the origin.

\(f(x,y,z) = x^2 + y^2 - z^2\):

  • \(c > 0\): Hyperboloid of one sheet
  • \(c = 0\): Double cone \(x^2+y^2 = z^2\)
  • \(c < 0\): Hyperboloid of two sheets

\(f(x,y,z) = ax + by + cz\): Level surfaces are planes \(ax + by + cz = k\). All parallel, normal to \((a,b,c)\).

Gravitational potential \(\phi = -GM/r\): Level surfaces are spheres $r = $ const. — points of constant potential energy ("equipotential surfaces").

docs.title: Visualization: Nested Level Surfaces
docs.text:
f = 3  ← outer shell
    ╭───────────────╮
    │   f = 2       │
    │  ╭─────────╮  │
    │  │  f = 1  │  │
    │  │  ╭───╮  │  │
    │  │  │f=0│  │  │
    │  │  ╰───╯  │  │
    │  ╰─────────╯  │
    ╰───────────────╯

Example: f(x,y,z) = x²+y²+z²
Level surfaces are concentric spheres.
Moving outward = increasing f.

The gradient \(\nabla f\) at any point is perpendicular to the level surface through that point and points in the direction of fastest increase. (This will be proved when we study gradients.)

docs.title: The General Definition
docs.text:
For \(n \geq 1\), a function of \(n\) variables is:

\[f : D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad \mathbf{x} = (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n) \mapsto f(\mathbf{x})\]

The domain \(D\) is a subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\); the range is a subset of \(\mathbb{R}\).

Notation conventions:

Notation Usage \(f(x,y,z)\) Emphasize individual variables (3 vars) \(f(\mathbf{x})\) Vector input (any \(n\)) \(f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) Index notation (general \(n\))

docs.title: Level Sets in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)
docs.text:
For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), the level set at \(c\) is: $\(S_c = {{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n : f(\mathbf{x}) = c}}\)$

Generically, this is an \((n-1)\)-dimensional hypersurface in \(\mathbb{R}^n\):

\(n\) Level set Name 2 1D curve Level curve 3 2D surface Level surface 4 3D hypersurface Level hypersurface \(n\) \((n-1)\)D manifold Level hypersurface

docs.title: The \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f: D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) and let \(\mathbf{a}\) be a limit point of \(D\). We say:

\[\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{a}} f(\mathbf{x}) = L\]

if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that:

\[0 < |\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}| < \delta \implies |f(\mathbf{x}) - L| < \varepsilon\]

where \(|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}| = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - a_i)^2}\) is the Euclidean distance in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

This is identical to the two-variable definition — the Euclidean norm generalizes seamlessly.

docs.title: Continuity
docs.text:
\(f\) is continuous at \(\mathbf{a}\) if: $\(\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{a}} f(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{a})\)$

\(f\) is continuous on \(D\) if it is continuous at every point of \(D\).

docs.title: The Subtlety: Paths in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)
docs.text:
For the limit \(\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{a}}f(\mathbf{x})\) to exist, \(f(\mathbf{x})\) must approach \(L\) along every possible path to \(\mathbf{a}\) — and in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(n \geq 2\), there are uncountably many paths.

Standard technique to prove a limit does NOT exist: Find two paths giving different limits.

Example. Show \(\lim_{(x,y,z)\to(0,0,0)}\dfrac{xyz}{x^2+y^2+z^2}\) does not exist.

Path 1: \(x=t, y=t, z=t\) as \(t\to 0\): $\(f = \frac{t^3}{3t^2} = \frac{t}{3} \to 0\)$

Path 2: \(x=t, y=t, z=0\): $\(f = \frac{0}{2t^2} = 0 \to 0\)$

Path 3: \(x=t, y=t, z=t^{1/2}\) (approaching along a curved path) gives a more complex expression. Let us instead try a cleaner example:

Example. \(g(x,y,z) = \dfrac{x^2 y z}{x^4 + y^2 + z^2}\) at the origin.

Path: \(x = t, y = t^2, z = t^2\): $\(g = \frac{t^2 \cdot t^2 \cdot t^2}{t^4 + t^4 + t^4} = \frac{t^6}{3t^4} = \frac{t^2}{3} \to 0\)$

Path: \(x = t, y = t^2, z = 0\): $\(g = \frac{0}{t^4 + t^4} = 0 \to 0\)$

Path: \(x = t, y = t^2, z = t^2\) at the limit \(y = x^2\): $\(g\big|_{y=x^2, z=x^2} = \frac{x^2\cdot x^2 \cdot x^2}{x^4 + x^4 + x^4} = \frac{x^6}{3x^4} = \frac{x^2}{3}\to 0\)$

But along \(y = x^2, z = x^2\): actually the limit is \(0\) here. The function \(g\) actually goes to \(0\) along all polynomial paths — but may not if we allow more exotic approach directions.

Remark (the Curse of Paths): In \(\mathbb{R}^n\), \(n \geq 2\), showing a limit exists requires either a squeeze or estimating with the Euclidean norm. Showing it doesn't exist requires two paths. The squeezing technique is: $\(|f(\mathbf{x}) - L| \leq g(|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}|) \to 0 \text{ as } |\mathbf{x}|\to|\mathbf{a}|\)$

docs.title: 5. Partial Derivatives of Functions of Several Variables
Definition
docs.text:
For \(f(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\), the partial derivative with respect to \(x_i\) at a point \(\mathbf{a}\) is:

\[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(\mathbf{a}) = \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(a_1,\ldots, a_i+h,\ldots,a_n) - f(a_1,\ldots,a_i,\ldots,a_n)}{h}\]

Computationally: treat all variables except \(x_i\) as constants, differentiate with respect to \(x_i\).

docs.title: For Three Variables Explicitly
docs.text:
For \(f(x,y,z)\):

\[f_x = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}: \text{ differentiate w.r.t. } x, \text{ treating } y,z \text{ as constants}\] \[f_y = \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}: \text{ differentiate w.r.t. } y, \text{ treating } x,z \text{ as constants}\] \[f_z = \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}: \text{ differentiate w.r.t. } z, \text{ treating } x,y \text{ as constants}\]

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
\(f(x,y,z) = x^3 y - y^2 z + e^{xz}\sin y\)

\[f_x = 3x^2 y + ze^{xz}\sin y\] \[f_y = x^3 - 2yz + e^{xz}\cos y\] \[f_z = -y^2 + xe^{xz}\sin y\]

docs.title: The Gradient
docs.text:
The gradient of \(f:\mathbb{R}^n o\mathbb{R}\) is the vector of all partial derivatives:

\[ abla f(\mathbf{x}) = \left\langle rac{\partial f}{\partial x_1},, rac{\partial f}{\partial x_2},, \ldots,, rac{\partial f}{\partial x_n} ight angle\]

For three variables: $\( abla f(x,y,z) = \langle f_x, f_y, f_z angle\)$

The gradient is the generalization of the derivative to higher dimensions. Its key properties:

  • \( abla f(\mathbf{a})\) points in the direction of steepest increase of \(f\) at \(\mathbf{a}\).
  • \(| abla f(\mathbf{a})|\) is the rate of steepest ascent.
  • \( abla f(\mathbf{a})\) is perpendicular to the level surface \(f = f(\mathbf{a})\) at \(\mathbf{a}\).

Proof of the last point: Let \(\mathbf{r}(t)\) be any curve lying in the level surface \(f(\mathbf{x}) = c\), so \(f(\mathbf{r}(t)) = c\) for all \(t\). By the chain rule: $\( rac{d}{dt}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) = abla f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot\mathbf{r}'(t) = 0\)$

So \( abla f \perp \mathbf{r}'(t)\) for every curve in the level surface — hence \( abla f\) is perpendicular to the level surface. \(\square\)

docs.title: 6. The Chain Rule in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)
docs.text:
Suppose \(f(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\) and each \(x_i = x_i(t_1, \ldots, t_m)\). Then:

\[\frac{\partial f}{\partial t_j} = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}\cdot\frac{\partial x_i}{\partial t_j}\]

In matrix/vector form, if \(\mathbf{x}: \mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\):

\[\frac{\partial f}{\partial \mathbf{t}} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial \mathbf{x}}\cdot\frac{\partial \mathbf{x}}{\partial \mathbf{t}} = \nabla_\mathbf{x} f \cdot J_\mathbf{x}\]

where \(J_\mathbf{x} = \partial\mathbf{x}/\partial\mathbf{t}\) is the Jacobian matrix.

Example (three variables, two parameters): \(f(x,y,z)\) where \(x=s^2t\), \(y=st^2\), \(z=e^{st}\):

\[\frac{\partial f}{\partial s} = f_x\cdot 2st + f_y\cdot t^2 + f_z\cdot te^{st}\] \[\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} = f_x\cdot s^2 + f_y\cdot 2st + f_z\cdot se^{st}\]

docs.title: 7. Directional Derivatives
docs.text:
For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n o\mathbb{R}\) and a unit vector \(\hat{\mathbf{u}} = (u_1,\ldots,u_n)\), the directional derivative of \(f\) at \(\mathbf{a}\) in direction \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}\) is:

\[D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}}f(\mathbf{a}) = \lim_{h o 0} rac{f(\mathbf{a}+h\hat{\mathbf{u}}) - f(\mathbf{a})}{h} = abla f(\mathbf{a})\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}\]

Proof: Define \(g(h) = f(\mathbf{a}+h\hat{\mathbf{u}})\). Then \(g'(0)\) is the directional derivative, and by the chain rule: $\(g'(h) = abla f(\mathbf{a}+h\hat{\mathbf{u}})\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}} \implies g'(0) = abla f(\mathbf{a})\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}. \quad\square\)$

Maximum directional derivative: By Cauchy–Schwarz: $\(D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}}f(\mathbf{a}) = abla f(\mathbf{a})\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}} \leq | abla f(\mathbf{a})|\)$

with equality when \(\hat{\mathbf{u}} = abla f(\mathbf{a})/| abla f(\mathbf{a})|\). The gradient points in the direction of maximum rate of increase.

docs.title: Second Partial Derivatives
docs.text:
For \(f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\), we can take partial derivatives of partial derivatives:

\[f_{x_i x_j} = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_j,\partial x_i} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x_j}\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}\right)\]

Note the order convention: \(\partial x_j,\partial x_i\) means differentiate first w.r.t. \(x_i\), then \(x_j\).

docs.title: Clairaut's Theorem (Symmetry of Mixed Partials)
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(f\) is defined near \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(f_{x_i x_j}\), \(f_{x_j x_i}\) are both continuous at \(\mathbf{a}\), then: $\(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_j,\partial x_i}(\mathbf{a}) = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i,\partial x_j}(\mathbf{a})\)$

Consequence: For smooth functions, the order of differentiation doesn't matter. For \(f(x,y,z)\):

\[f_{xy} = f_{yx}, \quad f_{xz} = f_{zx}, \quad f_{yz} = f_{zy}, \quad f_{xyz} = f_{xzy} = f_{yxz} = \cdots\]

For a function of \(n\) variables with all mixed partials of order \(k\) continuous, all \(k!\) orderings give the same result.

docs.title: The Hessian Matrix
docs.text:
The Hessian of \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is the \(n\times n\) matrix of all second partials:

\[H_f(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{pmatrix} f_{x_1x_1} & f_{x_1x_2} & \cdots & f_{x_1x_n} \ f_{x_2x_1} & f_{x_2x_2} & \cdots & f_{x_2x_n} \ \vdots & & \ddots & \vdots \ f_{x_nx_1} & f_{x_nx_2} & \cdots & f_{x_nx_n} \end{pmatrix}\]

By Clairaut, \(H_f\) is symmetric: \(H_f = H_f^T\).

The Hessian generalizes the second derivative to higher dimensions and controls:

  • Local convexity/concavity of \(f\)
  • Classification of critical points
  • Second-order Taylor expansion

docs.title: 9. The Taylor Expansion in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)
docs.text:
For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) smooth near \(\mathbf{a}\), the second-order Taylor expansion at \(\mathbf{a}\) is:

\[f(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{h}) = f(\mathbf{a}) + \nabla f(\mathbf{a})\cdot\mathbf{h} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{h}^T H_f(\mathbf{a}),\mathbf{h} + O(|\mathbf{h}|^3)\]

This is the master approximation formula. Each term has a name:

  • \(f(\mathbf{a})\): zeroth-order (value)
  • \(\nabla f(\mathbf{a})\cdot\mathbf{h}\): first-order (linear/gradient term)
  • \(\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{h}^T H_f,\mathbf{h}\): second-order (quadratic/curvature term)

For \(n=3\) with \(\mathbf{h} = (h_1, h_2, h_3)\):

\[f(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{h}) \approx f(\mathbf{a}) + f_x h_1 + f_y h_2 + f_z h_3 + \tfrac{1}{2}(f_{xx}h_1^2 + f_{yy}h_2^2 + f_{zz}h_3^2 + 2f_{xy}h_1h_2 + 2f_{xz}h_1h_3 + 2f_{yz}h_2h_3)\]

docs.title: 10. Critical Points and the Second Derivative Test in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)
Critical Points
docs.text: \(\mathbf{a}\) is a critical point of \(f\) if \(\nabla f(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{0}\), i.e., all partial derivatives vanish simultaneously.

docs.title: Classification via the Hessian
docs.text:
At a critical point \(\mathbf{a}\), the behavior of \(f\) near \(\mathbf{a}\) is determined by \(H_f(\mathbf{a})\):

From the Taylor expansion: \(f(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{h}) - f(\mathbf{a}) \approx \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{h}^T H_f(\mathbf{a}),\mathbf{h}\)

The sign of the quadratic form \(\mathbf{h}^T H_f,\mathbf{h}\) determines the type:

\(H_f(\mathbf{a})\) Type Meaning Positive definite (all eigenvalues \(> 0\)) Local minimum \(f\) increases in all directions Negative definite (all eigenvalues \(< 0\)) Local maximum \(f\) decreases in all directions Indefinite (mixed eigenvalue signs) Saddle point Increases some directions, decreases others Positive/negative semidefinite Degenerate Test inconclusive

For \(n = 2\) (two-variable case): \(D = f_{xx}f_{yy} - f_{xy}^2 = \det H_f\)

  • \(D > 0, f_{xx} > 0\): local min
  • \(D > 0, f_{xx} < 0\): local max
  • \(D < 0\): saddle
  • \(D = 0\): inconclusive

For \(n \geq 3\): Check eigenvalues of \(H_f\) (or use Sylvester's criterion for positive definiteness).

docs.title: Example 1: Domain and Level Surfaces
docs.text:
\(f(x,y,z) = \ln(4 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2)\)

Domain: Need \(4 - x^2 - y^2 - z^2 > 0\), i.e., \(x^2+y^2+z^2 < 4\) — the open ball of radius \(2\).

Level surfaces: \(\ln(4-x^2-y^2-z^2) = c \iff x^2+y^2+z^2 = 4 - e^c\)

Valid when \(4-e^c > 0\), i.e., \(c < \ln 4\). The level surfaces are concentric spheres of radius \(\sqrt{4-e^c}\) centered at the origin, ranging from radius \(0\) (as \(c\to\ln 4^-\)) to radius \(2\) (as \(c\to-\infty\)).

docs.title: Example 2: Partial Derivatives of a Physical Function
docs.text:
The ideal gas law: \(PV = nRT\), so \(P(V,T) = nRT/V\).

For a gas with \(n=1\) mole, \(R = 8.314\) J/(mol·K):

\[P(V,T) = \frac{RT}{V}\] \[\frac{\partial P}{\partial T} = \frac{R}{V} > 0 \quad\text{(pressure increases with temperature at fixed volume)}\] \[\frac{\partial P}{\partial V} = -\frac{RT}{V^2} < 0 \quad\text{(pressure decreases as volume increases at fixed temperature)}\] \[\frac{\partial^2 P}{\partial V^2} = \frac{2RT}{V^3} > 0 \quad\text{(convex in } V\text{)}\]

docs.title: Example 3: Critical Points in \(\mathbb{R}^3\)
docs.text:
\(f(x,y,z) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 2x + 4y - 6z + 14\)

Find critical points: $\(f_x = 2x - 2 = 0 \implies x = 1\)$ $\(f_y = 2y + 4 = 0 \implies y = -2\)$ $\(f_z = 2z - 6 = 0 \implies z = 3\)$

One critical point: \((1, -2, 3)\).

Hessian: $\(H_f = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 2 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = 2I\)$

Positive definite (all eigenvalues \(= 2 > 0\)). So \((1,-2,3)\) is a global minimum.

\(f(1,-2,3) = 1 + 4 + 9 - 2 - 8 - 18 + 14 = 0\).

We can verify: \(f(x,y,z) = (x-1)^2 + (y+2)^2 + (z-3)^2 \geq 0\). ✓

docs.title: Example 4: Limit via Squeeze
docs.text:
Show \(\displaystyle\lim_{(x,y,z)\to(0,0,0)}\frac{x^2 y z}{x^2 + y^2 + z^2} = 0\).

Squeeze: By AM-GM, \(x^2 \leq x^2 + y^2 + z^2\), so \(\dfrac{x^2}{x^2+y^2+z^2} \leq 1\). Also:

\[\left|\frac{x^2 yz}{x^2+y^2+z^2}\right| = \frac{x^2}{x^2+y^2+z^2}\cdot|y|\cdot|z| \leq |y||z| \leq \frac{y^2+z^2}{2} \leq \frac{x^2+y^2+z^2}{2} = \frac{r^2}{2}\]

where \(r = |(x,y,z)|\). As \((x,y,z)\to(0,0,0)\), \(r\to 0\), so the expression \(\to 0\). \(\square\)

docs.title: 12. Visualization Strategies (Since We Can't Draw the Graph)
docs.text:
When you can't visualize the graph of \(f:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}\), use:

1. Level surfaces — fix \(c\) and draw/describe \(f(x,y,z) = c\).

2. Restriction to lower-dimensional slices:

  • Fix \(z = z_0\): get a function of two variables \(f(x,y,z_0)\) — draw its level curves.
  • Fix \(y = 0, z = 0\): get \(f(x,0,0)\) — a standard one-variable graph.

3. The gradient field: \(\nabla f(x,y,z)\) is a vector field in \(\mathbb{R}^3\). Its arrows show direction of fastest increase.

4. Color-coded cross-sections: In computational tools (Python, Mathematica), one plots \(f(x,y,z_0)\) as a heatmap for several values of \(z_0\).

Strategy for understanding f(x,y,z):

  Full function                Slice at z = z₀
  (invisible in ℝ⁴)  →→→     f(x,y,z₀): a surface in ℝ³
                      →→→     Level curves of f(x,y,z₀): curves in ℝ²

  Level surfaces of f  →→→    Nested shells in ℝ³
  ∇f field             →→→    Arrows ⊥ to level surfaces

docs.title: 13. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: Functions of many variables are not a generalization of interest only to physicists. They are the central object of study in machine learning — almost every concept in this section reappears, at billion-dimensional scale.

docs.title: 13.1 The Loss Function Is a Function of Billions of Variables
docs.text:
A neural network with parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_p) \in \mathbb{R}^p\) defines a loss function:

\[\mathcal{L} : \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \ell(f_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf{x}_i), y_i)\]

This is literally a function of \(p\) variables — with \(p \sim 10^{10}\) for GPT-scale models. Everything in this note applies:

  • Domain: The set of \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) for which the network is defined (all of \(\mathbb{R}^p\), typically).
  • Level sets: \({\boldsymbol{\theta} : \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = c}\) — the set of parameters achieving loss \(c\). Modern theory shows these level sets are extremely complex, high-dimensional manifolds.
  • Gradient: \(\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L}\) — the direction of steepest ascent, whose negative gives the gradient descent direction. Computed by backpropagation, which is an efficient algorithm for the chain rule in \(\mathbb{R}^p\).
  • Hessian: \(H_\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol\theta)\) — a \(p\times p\) matrix. For \(p = 10^{10}\), this has \(10^{20}\) entries — cannot be stored. This is why second-order optimization methods are approximated (L-BFGS, K-FAC, Shampoo).
  • Critical points: \(\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L} = \mathbf{0}\) — the training algorithm tries to find these, but in high dimensions most critical points are saddle points, not local minima (Dauphin et al., 2014).

docs.title: 13.2 Backpropagation = Chain Rule in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)
docs.text:
The chain rule in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is the mathematical foundation of deep learning. Given a neural network \(f = f_L \circ f_{L-1} \circ \cdots \circ f_1\):

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \boldsymbol{\theta}_l} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{h}_L}\cdot\frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_L}{\partial \mathbf{h}_{L-1}}\cdots\frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_{l+1}}{\partial \mathbf{h}_l}\cdot\frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_l}{\partial \boldsymbol{\theta}_l}\]

Each factor \(\partial\mathbf{h}_{k+1}/\partial\mathbf{h}_k\) is a Jacobian matrix. Backpropagation is the efficient right-to-left evaluation of this chain of matrix products — exactly the multi-variable chain rule, structured to avoid redundant computation.

docs.title: 13.3 Level Sets as "Weight Space Symmetries"
docs.text:
The level sets \({\boldsymbol\theta : \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol\theta) = c}\) for small \(c\) are the "good parameter regions." Recent work shows:

  • For overparameterized networks (\(p \gg N\)), the global minimum level set is a high-dimensional connected manifold.
  • Neuron permutation symmetry: Swapping two hidden neurons gives a different \(\boldsymbol\theta\) on the same level set — the level set has a large discrete symmetry group of size \(\prod_l (n_l!)\).
  • Mode connectivity (Garipov et al., 2018): Two independently trained minima \(\boldsymbol\theta^__1, \boldsymbol\theta^__2\) are often connected by a path of low loss — they lie on the same level-set component.

docs.title: 13.4 The Hessian in Deep Learning
docs.text:
The Hessian \(H_\mathcal{L}\) at a minimum encodes:

  • Sharpness: \(\lambda_{\max}(H_\mathcal{L})\) — the largest eigenvalue. Sharp minima (large \(\lambda_{\max}\)) generalize poorly; flat minima generalize well. This is the theoretical basis for SAM (Sharpness-Aware Minimization) (Foret et al., 2021).
  • Learning rate stability: Gradient descent is stable only when \(\eta < 2/\lambda_{\max}\) — a direct consequence of the quadratic Taylor approximation.
  • Natural gradient: The Fisher information matrix \(F_\theta\) is the expected Hessian of the log-likelihood. The natural gradient \(F_\theta^{-1}\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L}\) accounts for the Riemannian geometry of the model manifold (Amari, 1998).

docs.title: 13.5 Directional Derivatives and Sensitivity Analysis
docs.text:
The directional derivative \(D_{\hat\mathbf{u}}\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol\theta) = \nabla\mathcal{L}\cdot\hat\mathbf{u}\) answers: "if I perturb the parameters in direction \(\hat\mathbf{u}\), how does the loss change?"

Applications:

  • Adversarial examples (Goodfellow et al., 2014): Find \(\hat\mathbf{u}\) (in input space) that maximizes \(D_{\hat\mathbf{u}}f\) — the direction that fools the classifier. The FGSM attack is literally \(\mathbf{x}^{\text{adv}} = \mathbf{x} + \varepsilon\cdot\text{sign}(\nabla_\mathbf{x}\mathcal{L})\) — a step in the gradient direction in input space.
  • Influence functions: How does the loss on a test point change if we perturb the training data? Answered by directional derivatives in function space.
  • Saliency maps: \(\partial f/\partial x_i\) for each input pixel \(x_i\) — a partial derivative of the network output with respect to inputs, used for interpretability.

docs.title: 13.6 Functions of Many Variables in Attention
docs.text:
A transformer attention head computes:

\[\text{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\]

The softmax output \(A_{ij}\) is a function of all entries of \(Q\) and \(K\) simultaneously. The partial derivatives \(\partial A_{ij}/\partial Q_{kl}\) and \(\partial A_{ij}/\partial K_{kl}\) are the components of the Jacobian computed during backpropagation. Each attention head is a function from \((Q,K,V) \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times d_k}\times\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_k}\times\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_v}\) to \(\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_v}\) — a function of hundreds of thousands of variables, differentiated billions of times per second during training.

docs.title: 13.7 Gaussian Processes and Functions of Infinitely Many Variables
docs.text: A Gaussian Process (GP) is a probability distribution over functions \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\). The GP can be viewed as the limit of a Bayesian neural network as the width \(\to\infty\) (Neal, 1994; Lee et al., 2018). In this limit, the "function of parameters" becomes a "function of infinitely many variables" — and the calculus of variations and functional derivatives generalize the partial derivative framework of this note to infinite dimensions.

docs.title: 14. Summary
docs.text:
Concept Two Variables Three Variables \(n\) Variables Graph Surface in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) Hypersurface in \(\mathbb{R}^4\) (invisible) — Level set Curve in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) Surface in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) \((n-1)\)-manifold Partial derivatives \(f_x, f_y\) \(f_x, f_y, f_z\) \(\partial f/\partial x_i\), \(i=1,\ldots,n\) Gradient \(\langle f_x, f_y angle \in \mathbb{R}^2\) \(\langle f_x,f_y,f_z angle\in\mathbb{R}^3\) \( abla f\in\mathbb{R}^n\) Hessian \(2 imes 2\) matrix \(3 imes 3\) matrix \(n imes n\) symmetric matrix Taylor degree 2 polynomial in 2 vars degree 2 in 3 vars \(f(\mathbf{a})+ abla f\cdot\mathbf{h}+ frac{1}{2}\mathbf{h}^TH\mathbf{h}+\cdots\) Critical point test \(\det H\), sign of \(f_{xx}\) eigenvalues of \(H\) eigenvalues of \(H\)

The key geometric principle: What level curves do for \(f:\mathbb{R}^2 o\mathbb{R}\), level surfaces do for \(f:\mathbb{R}^3 o\mathbb{R}\), and level hypersurfaces do for \(f:\mathbb{R}^n o\mathbb{R}\). The gradient is always perpendicular to these, always points toward steepest increase, and always satisfies \(D_{\hat\mathbf{u}}f = abla f\cdot\hat\mathbf{u}\).

In machine learning, every one of these concepts operates at scale — the domain is \(\mathbb{R}^{10^{10}}\), the level sets are high-dimensional manifolds, the gradient is computed by backpropagation, and the Hessian is approximated rather than stored.

docs.text:

  2. MIT OpenCourseWare 18.02. Multivariable Calculus (Auroux). Lectures 8–13: partial derivatives, gradient, level surfaces, chain rule in higher dimensions.
  3. Dauphin, Y. et al. "Identifying and attacking the saddle point problem in high-dimensional non-convex optimization." NeurIPS (2014). — Critical point geometry of neural network loss landscapes.
  4. Goodfellow, I. et al. "Explaining and Harnessing Adversarial Examples." ICLR (2015). — Directional derivatives in input space; FGSM attack.
  5. Foret, P. et al. "Sharpness-Aware Minimization for Efficiently Improving Generalization." ICLR (2021). — Hessian eigenvalues and generalization.
  6. Amari, S. "Natural Gradient Works Efficiently in Learning." Neural Computation (1998). — Fisher information, Riemannian geometry of parameter space.
  7. Garipov, T. et al. "Loss Surfaces, Mode Connectivity, and Fast Ensembling of DNNs." NeurIPS (2018). — Level set connectivity of neural network minima.

docs.title: Limits and Continuity
docs.text: "In single-variable calculus, a point on the real line has exactly two sides — you approach from the left or from the right. In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), a point is surrounded by an entire circle of directions. In \(\mathbb{R}^n\), by an \((n-1)\)-sphere. The definition of limit must survive all of them simultaneously — and that one requirement changes everything."

docs.title: 0. Why This Topic Is Genuinely Hard
docs.text:
In single-variable calculus, \(\lim_{x\to a}f(x) = L\) is geometrically clear: the graph approaches a single height from two directions. Pathological behavior (jump discontinuities, removable singularities) is easy to detect visually.

In two or more variables, the graph is a surface (or worse, invisible). A point \((a,b)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) can be approached along:

  • Horizontal and vertical lines
  • Diagonal lines at any angle
  • Parabolas, cubics, spirals, any curve whatsoever

A limit exists only if every single path gives the same value \(L\). This is what makes multivariable limits subtle: confirming existence requires a global argument (typically a norm bound or squeeze), while disproving existence requires finding only two paths that disagree.

This asymmetry — two paths to disprove, a norm bound to prove — is the organizing principle of the entire subject.

docs.title: 1. Open and Closed Sets in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)
docs.text: Before defining limits, we need the correct topological language.

docs.title: Balls and Neighborhoods
docs.text:
The open ball of radius \(r > 0\) centered at \(\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n\):

\[B(\mathbf{a}, r) = {\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n : |\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}| < r}\]

The deleted (punctured) ball (excludes the center):

\[B'(\mathbf{a}, r) = {\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n : 0 < |\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}| < r}\]

Here \(|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}| = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i - a_i)^2}\) is the Euclidean norm.

docs.title: Interior, Boundary, Open, Closed
docs.text:
Let \(D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\).

  • Interior point: \(\mathbf{a}\) is an interior point of \(D\) if \(\exists r > 0\) such that \(B(\mathbf{a},r) \subseteq D\).
  • Boundary point: \(\mathbf{a}\) is a boundary point of \(D\) if every ball \(B(\mathbf{a},r)\) contains points both in \(D\) and in \(D^c\).
  • Open set: \(D\) is open if every point of \(D\) is an interior point.
  • Closed set: \(D\) is closed if it contains all its boundary points.
  • Bounded set: \(D\) is bounded if \(\exists M > 0\) such that \(D \subseteq B(\mathbf{0}, M)\).
  • Compact set: \(D\) is compact if it is closed and bounded (in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), by Heine–Borel).

Examples in \(\mathbb{R}^2\):

Set Open? Closed? Bounded? \({(x,y): x^2+y^2 < 1}\) ✓ ✗ ✓ \({(x,y): x^2+y^2 \leq 1}\) ✗ ✓ ✓ \({(x,y): x^2+y^2 = 1}\) ✗ ✓ ✓ \({(x,y): x > 0}\) ✓ ✗ ✗ \(\mathbb{R}^2\) ✓ ✓ ✗

Note: \(\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\emptyset\) are simultaneously open and closed — the only such sets in a connected space.

docs.title: Definition (\(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\))
docs.text:
Let \(f: D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) and let \(\mathbf{a}\) be a limit point of \(D\) (every deleted ball around \(\mathbf{a}\) meets \(D\)). We write:

\[\lim_{\mathbf{x} \to \mathbf{a}} f(\mathbf{x}) = L\]

if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that:

\[\mathbf{x} \in D \text{ and } 0 < |\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}| < \delta \implies |f(\mathbf{x}) - L| < \varepsilon\]

For two variables \((x,y) \to (a,b)\): the condition \(0 < |\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a}| < \delta\) becomes \(0 < \sqrt{(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2} < \delta\).

docs.title: Unpacking the Definition
docs.text:
The definition says: no matter how small a tolerance \(\varepsilon\) you demand around \(L\), I can find a punctured ball of radius \(\delta\) around \(\mathbf{a}\) such that \(f\) maps every point in that punctured ball to within \(\varepsilon\) of \(L\).

Crucially:

  • The center \(\mathbf{a}\) itself plays no role (the punctured ball excludes it).
  • \(f\) need not even be defined at \(\mathbf{a}\).
  • \(\delta\) may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(\mathbf{x}\) — the same \(\delta\) works for all \(\mathbf{x}\) in the punctured ball.

docs.title: 3. Limit Laws
docs.text:
The standard limit laws extend verbatim to \(\mathbb{R}^n\). If \(\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{a}}f(\mathbf{x}) = L\) and \(\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{a}}g(\mathbf{x}) = M\), then:

\[\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{a}}[f(\mathbf{x})+g(\mathbf{x})] = L+M\] \[\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{a}}[f(\mathbf{x})\cdot g(\mathbf{x})] = L\cdot M\] \[\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{a}}\frac{f(\mathbf{x})}{g(\mathbf{x})} = \frac{L}{M} \quad (M\neq 0)\] \[\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{a}}[f(\mathbf{x})]^p = L^p \quad (p \in \mathbb{Z}^+)\]

Proofs: All proofs carry over from the single-variable case, replacing \(|x-a|\) with \(|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a}|\).

docs.title: The Squeeze Theorem (Multivariable)
docs.text:
If \(g(\mathbf{x}) \leq f(\mathbf{x}) \leq h(\mathbf{x})\) near \(\mathbf{a}\), and \(\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{a}}g(\mathbf{x}) = \lim_{\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{a}}h(\mathbf{x}) = L\), then \(\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{a}}f(\mathbf{x}) = L\).

This is the workhorse for proving limits exist when direct substitution fails.

docs.title: Technique 1: Proving a Limit Does NOT Exist — The Two-Path Test
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(f(\mathbf{x})\) approaches different values \(L_1 \neq L_2\) along two different paths to \(\mathbf{a}\), then \(\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{a}}f(\mathbf{x})\) does not exist.

Warning: If two paths give the same value, that proves nothing — the limit may still fail to exist along some other path.

Strategy for choosing paths: Try simple ones first.

  1. Along axes: \(y = 0\) then \(x = 0\)
  2. Along \(y = mx\) for various slopes \(m\)
  3. Along \(y = x^k\) (parabolic/power paths) — useful when \(y = mx\) all give the same value
  4. Along \(y = x\sin(1/x)\) or similar — for highly oscillatory functions

docs.title: Technique 2: Proving a Limit EXISTS — Norm Bound (Squeeze)
docs.text:
Convert to polar coordinates or bound \(|f(\mathbf{x}) - L|\) in terms of \(r = |\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}|\). If:

\[|f(\mathbf{x}) - L| \leq C \cdot r^k \quad (k > 0, C > 0 \text{ constant})\]

then as \(r = |\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}| \to 0\), we get \(|f(\mathbf{x}) - L| \to 0\), so \(\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{a}}f(\mathbf{x}) = L\).

Key inequalities for bounding (WLOG, limit at origin):

\[|x| \leq \sqrt{x^2+y^2} = r, \qquad |y| \leq r\] \[x^2 \leq r^2, \qquad y^2 \leq r^2, \qquad x^2+y^2 = r^2\] \[|xy| \leq \frac{x^2+y^2}{2} = \frac{r^2}{2} \quad\text{(AM-GM)}\] \[\frac{x^2}{x^2+y^2} \leq 1, \quad \frac{y^2}{x^2+y^2} \leq 1 \quad\text{(key for rational functions)}\]

docs.title: 5. Polar Coordinates for Limits at the Origin
docs.text:
For limits \((x,y) \to (0,0)\), the substitution \(x = r\cos\theta\), \(y = r\sin\theta\) converts the two-variable limit into a one-variable limit as \(r \to 0^+\), provided the result is independent of \(\theta\).

\[\lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)} f(x,y) = \lim_{r\to 0^+} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\]

Critical caveat: If the resulting expression in \(r\) and \(\theta\) depends on \(\theta\), this does NOT immediately show the limit fails — it shows polar coordinates are insufficient. The limit fails only if for some \(\theta\) (i.e., some specific path), the one-sided limit differs from others.

Example where polar works cleanly: \(f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^2 y}{x^2+y^2}\)

\[f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) = \frac{r^2\cos^2\theta\cdot r\sin\theta}{r^2} = r\cos^2\theta\sin\theta\]

Since \(|r\cos^2\theta\sin\theta| \leq r \to 0\) as \(r\to 0\), we have \(\lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}f = 0\).

Example where polar reveals nonexistence: \(f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^2 - y^2}{x^2+y^2}\)

\[f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta) = \frac{r^2\cos^2\theta - r^2\sin^2\theta}{r^2} = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta = \cos 2\theta\]

This is independent of \(r\) — so as \(r\to 0\), \(f\) stays at \(\cos 2\theta\), which depends on the direction. Along \(\theta = 0\) (the \(x\)-axis): \(f = 1\). Along \(\theta = \pi/2\) (the \(y\)-axis): \(f = -1\). Limit does not exist.

docs.title: Example 1: Limit Exists — Squeeze
docs.text:
\[\lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)} \frac{x^3 + y^3}{x^2+y^2}\]

Bound: Using \(|x|^3 \leq |x|\cdot r^2\) (since \(|x| \leq r\)) and similarly for \(y\):

\[\left|\frac{x^3+y^3}{x^2+y^2}\right| \leq \frac{|x|^3 + |y|^3}{r^2} \leq \frac{r^3 + r^3}{r^2} = 2r \to 0\]

Therefore the limit is \(\mathbf{0}\).

docs.title: Example 2: Limit Does Not Exist — Linear Paths Differ
docs.text:
\[\lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)} \frac{xy}{x^2+y^2}\]

Path 1: \(y = 0\) (the \(x\)-axis, \(x \neq 0\)): $\(f(x,0) = \frac{x\cdot 0}{x^2+0} = 0 \to 0\)$

Path 2: \(y = x\): $\(f(x,x) = \frac{x\cdot x}{x^2+x^2} = \frac{x^2}{2x^2} = \frac{1}{2} \to \frac{1}{2}\)$

Two paths give \(0 \neq \frac{1}{2}\). Limit does not exist. \(\square\)

In polar: \(f = \frac{r^2\cos\theta\sin\theta}{r^2} = \frac{\sin 2\theta}{2}\) — angle-dependent. Confirms nonexistence.

docs.title: Example 3: Limit Does Not Exist — Linear Paths All Agree, But Parabolic Path Differs
docs.text:
\[\lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}\frac{x^2 y}{x^4 + y^2}\]

Along \(y = mx\) (all linear paths through origin): $\(f(x,mx) = \frac{x^2\cdot mx}{x^4 + m^2x^2} = \frac{mx^3}{x^2(x^2+m^2)} = \frac{mx}{x^2+m^2} \to 0\)$

Every linear path gives limit \(0\) — naively one might conclude the limit is \(0\).

Along \(y = x^2\) (parabolic path): $\(f(x,x^2) = \frac{x^2\cdot x^2}{x^4 + x^4} = \frac{x^4}{2x^4} = \frac{1}{2} \to \frac{1}{2}\)$

So the linear paths all give \(0\), but the parabolic path gives \(\frac{1}{2}\). Limit does not exist. \(\square\)

Moral: Checking only linear paths is never sufficient. Always think about which curves might "fit" the singularity structure of the denominator.

docs.title: Example 4: Limit Exists — Trigonometric Bound
docs.text:
\[\lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)} (x^2+y^2)\sin!\left(\frac{1}{x^2+y^2}\right)\]

Bound: Since \(|\sin(\theta)| \leq 1\) for all \(\theta\):

\[\left|(x^2+y^2)\sin!\left(\frac{1}{x^2+y^2}\right)\right| \leq x^2+y^2 = r^2 \to 0\]

Limit is \(0\). Notice the function is not even defined at the origin, but the limit exists.

docs.title: Example 5: Three Variables
docs.text:
\[\lim_{(x,y,z)\to(0,0,0)}\frac{x^2 y^2 z^2}{x^2+y^2+z^2}\]

Let \(r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}\). Then:

\[\frac{x^2 y^2 z^2}{x^2+y^2+z^2} \leq \frac{x^2 y^2 z^2}{???}\]

Better: use AM-GM. We have \(x^2 \leq r^2\), \(y^2 \leq r^2\), \(z^2 \leq r^2\), so:

\[0 \leq \frac{x^2 y^2 z^2}{r^2} \leq \frac{r^2\cdot r^2\cdot r^2}{r^2} = r^4 \to 0\]

Limit is \(0\).

docs.title: Example 6: \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) Proof Explicitly
docs.text:
Claim: \(\displaystyle\lim_{(x,y)\to(1,2)}(3x - y + 1) = 2\).

Proof. Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) be given. We need \(\delta > 0\) such that \(\sqrt{(x-1)^2+(y-2)^2} < \delta\) implies \(|(3x-y+1) - 2| < \varepsilon\).

Compute: $\(|(3x-y+1)-2| = |3(x-1)-(y-2)| \leq 3|x-1| + |y-2|\)$

Now \(|x-1| \leq \sqrt{(x-1)^2+(y-2)^2} < \delta\) and \(|y-2| \leq \sqrt{(x-1)^2+(y-2)^2} < \delta\). So:

\[|(3x-y+1)-2| \leq 3\delta + \delta = 4\delta\]

Choose \(\delta = \varepsilon/4\). Then \(\sqrt{(x-1)^2+(y-2)^2} < \delta\) implies \(|(3x-y+1)-2| \leq 4\delta = \varepsilon\). \(\square\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A function \(f: D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) is continuous at \(\mathbf{a} \in D\) if:

\[\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{a}}f(\mathbf{x}) = f(\mathbf{a})\]

This requires three things simultaneously:

  1. \(f(\mathbf{a})\) is defined.
  2. \(\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{a}}f(\mathbf{x})\) exists.
  3. They are equal.

\(f\) is continuous on \(D\) if it is continuous at every \(\mathbf{a} \in D\).

docs.title: Sequential Characterization
docs.text:
Equivalent formulation (often more useful for proofs):

\(f\) is continuous at \(\mathbf{a}\) \(\iff\) for every sequence \({\mathbf{x}_k}\) in \(D\) with \(\mathbf{x}_k \to \mathbf{a}\), we have \(f(\mathbf{x}_k) \to f(\mathbf{a})\).

docs.title: Continuity Preserved by Operations
docs.text:
If \(f\) and \(g\) are continuous at \(\mathbf{a}\), then:

  • \(f + g\), \(f - g\), \(f \cdot g\) are continuous at \(\mathbf{a}\)
  • \(f/g\) is continuous at \(\mathbf{a}\) if \(g(\mathbf{a}) \neq 0\)
  • \(|f|\) is continuous at \(\mathbf{a}\)

docs.title: Composition
docs.text:
If \(g: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) is continuous at \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(h: \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous at \(g(\mathbf{a})\), then \(h \circ g\) is continuous at \(\mathbf{a}\).

Consequence: All elementary functions (polynomials, rationals where denominator \(\neq 0\), \(\sin\), \(\cos\), \(\exp\), \(\ln\) on its domain, etc.) composed with continuous functions of several variables are continuous. Most functions you write down are continuous on their natural domain.

docs.title: 8. Types of Discontinuity in Higher Dimensions
docs.text: Unlike the one-variable case (jump, removable, infinite, oscillatory), higher-dimensional discontinuities can be more complex. The key types:

docs.title: Removable Discontinuity
docs.text: \(f\) is not defined at \(\mathbf{a}\) (or defined with the wrong value), but \(\lim_{\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{a}}f(\mathbf{x}) = L\) exists. Redefining \(f(\mathbf{a}) = L\) makes \(f\) continuous. These limits can be computed via squeeze or polar coordinates.

docs.title: Essential Discontinuity (Limit Does Not Exist)
docs.text: The limit fails to exist — different paths give different values. Examples 2 and 3 above are of this type. There is no way to "fix" the function at the point.

docs.title: Unbounded Discontinuity
docs.text: \(|f(\mathbf{x})| \to \infty\) as \(\mathbf{x} \to \mathbf{a}\). Example: \(f(x,y) = 1/(x^2+y^2)\) near the origin.

docs.title: Extreme Value Theorem (Generalization)
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(f: D \to \mathbb{R}\) is continuous and \(D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) is compact (closed and bounded), then \(f\) attains its maximum and minimum on \(D\).

That is, there exist \(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q} \in D\) such that \(f(\mathbf{p}) \leq f(\mathbf{x}) \leq f(\mathbf{q})\) for all \(\mathbf{x} \in D\).

This theorem guarantees optimization problems have solutions — a fact used constantly in ML (loss minimization over compact parameter spaces, though in practice parameter spaces are rarely compact).

docs.title: Intermediate Value Theorem (Generalization)
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(f: D \to \mathbb{R}\) is continuous, \(D\) is connected, and \(f(\mathbf{a}) = A\), \(f(\mathbf{b}) = B\) with \(A < B\), then for every \(c \in (A,B)\), there exists \(\mathbf{p} \in D\) with \(f(\mathbf{p}) = c\).

Geometric consequence: the image of a connected set under a continuous map is connected — hence an interval.

docs.title: Continuity and Level Sets
docs.text:
If \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous, then:

  • Every level set \({f = c}\) is closed (preimage of a closed set under a continuous map).
  • Every superlevel set \({f > c}\) is open.
  • Every sublevel set \({f < c}\) is open.

These facts are foundational in optimization — sublevel sets of continuous functions on compact domains are compact, guaranteeing minima exist.

docs.title: 10. Uniform Continuity
docs.text:
\(f: D\to\mathbb{R}\) is uniformly continuous on \(D\) if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists \(\delta > 0\) such that:

\[\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in D \text{ and } |\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}| < \delta \implies |f(\mathbf{x})-f(\mathbf{y})| < \varepsilon\]

The difference from ordinary continuity: \(\delta\) depends only on \(\varepsilon\), not on the particular point \(\mathbf{x}\).

Theorem (Heine-Cantor). If \(f\) is continuous on a compact set \(D\), then \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \(D\).

docs.title: 11. Differentiability vs. Continuity: The Subtle Hierarchy
docs.text:
This is where multivariable calculus diverges sharply from single-variable. We have the following strict hierarchy of conditions:

Differentiable  ⟹  Continuous  ⟹  (merely) Limit exists at each point
      ⟸ NOT                ⟸ NOT

Continuous partial derivatives  ⟹  Differentiable
      ⟸ NOT

Partial derivatives exist  ⟹ / ⟹  Continuous

The shocking fact: A function can have all partial derivatives exist at a point and yet be discontinuous there.

Example. Define: $\(f(x,y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{xy}{x^2+y^2} & (x,y)\neq(0,0) \ 0 & (x,y) = (0,0) \end{cases}\)$

At \((0,0)\): $\(f_x(0,0) = \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{f(h,0)-f(0,0)}{h} = \lim_{h\to 0}\frac{0}{h} = 0\)$

Similarly \(f_y(0,0) = 0\). Both partial derivatives exist.

But as shown in Example 2, \(\lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}f(x,y)\) does not exist (along \(y=x\) the limit is \(1/2\)). So \(f\) is not continuous at the origin, despite having partial derivatives everywhere.

Why? Partial derivatives only probe \(f\) along the two coordinate axes. They say nothing about behavior along diagonal or curved paths.

The correct condition for differentiability (to be treated in detail in [[Partial Derivatives]]): \(f\) is differentiable at \(\mathbf{a}\) if there exists a linear map \(L:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) such that:

\[\lim_{\mathbf{h}\to\mathbf{0}}\frac{f(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{h}) - f(\mathbf{a}) - L(\mathbf{h})}{|\mathbf{h}|} = 0\]

Differentiability implies continuity. Existence of partial derivatives does not.

docs.title: Paths to a Point in \(\mathbb{R}^2\)
docs.text:
y
            │       ← spiral approach
            │      ↗ parabola y = x²
            │    ↗  diagonal y = x
            │  ↗
            │↗  ← axis approach
────────────•────────────── x
           (0,0)
            ↑
            │ axis approach

A limit exists iff ALL paths give the same value L.

docs.title: Continuity: No "Tears" in the Surface
docs.text:
Continuous at (a,b):         Discontinuous at (a,b):
                                      ●  ← value at (a,b)
   ╭──────────╮                ╭──────╯
   │  smooth  │                │   jump or hole
   ╰──────────╯                ╰──────╮
                                      ╰──────
   lim = f(a,b)             lim ≠ f(a,b) or doesn't exist

docs.title: 13. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: Limits and continuity in multivariable calculus are not abstract tools — they are the mathematical bedrock on which the guarantees of modern machine learning rest. Every theorem about optimization, generalization, and convergence ultimately assumes or proves continuity of something.

docs.title: 13.1 Continuity of Neural Networks
docs.text:
A feedforward neural network \(f_\theta: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m\) is a composition of affine maps and activation functions:

\[f_\theta = \sigma_L \circ W_L \circ \cdots \circ \sigma_1 \circ W_1\]

Since affine maps and standard activations (ReLU, sigmoid, tanh, GELU) are continuous, compositions of continuous functions are continuous, so \(f_\theta\) is continuous in its inputs \(\mathbf{x}\) for any fixed \(\theta\).

But continuity in \(\theta\) also matters: the map \(\theta \mapsto f_\theta(\mathbf{x})\) is continuous (even smooth) for smooth activations, and continuous for ReLU networks (though not differentiable everywhere in \(\theta\)). This continuity guarantees that small perturbations to parameters produce small changes in output — essential for gradient-based training to make sense.

docs.title: 13.2 Continuity of the Loss Function
docs.text:
The loss function \(\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}[\ell(f_\theta(\mathbf{x}), y)]\) is continuous in \(\theta\) under mild conditions. This matters because:

  • Gradient descent requires continuity: If \(\mathcal{L}\) had jump discontinuities in \(\theta\), gradients would be meaningless near those jumps.
  • The Extreme Value Theorem guarantees that \(\mathcal{L}\) attains a minimum on any compact subset of parameter space — a theoretical existence guarantee for optimal parameters.
  • Level sets \({\theta : \mathcal{L}(\theta) \leq c}\) are closed (and bounded for coercive losses), hence compact — so training within a sublevel set is bounded.

docs.title: 13.3 The Two-Path Problem in Optimization Landscapes
docs.text:
The multivariable two-path test for nonexistence of limits has a direct analog in optimization landscape analysis. Consider the question: does gradient flow from initialization \(\theta_0\) converge to the same minimum regardless of path taken?

  • If the loss landscape has a unique minimum: All gradient flow paths converge to the same point — analogous to a limit existing along all paths.
  • If there are multiple local minima: Different paths (initializations) lead to different endpoints — analogous to different paths giving different limits.

The study of loss landscape connectivity (Draxler et al., 2018; Garipov et al., 2018) is precisely an analysis of path-dependence in high-dimensional parameter space.

docs.title: 13.4 ReLU Discontinuity of Gradients
docs.text:
ReLU: \(\sigma(x) = \max(0,x)\) is continuous but not differentiable at \(x = 0\).

In a ReLU network, the gradient \(\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L}\) may not exist at certain parameter values (where any pre-activation hits exactly \(0\)). This means:

  • The loss surface has kinks (gradient discontinuities) — codimension-1 hyperplanes in \(\theta\)-space where the gradient jumps.
  • In practice, these measure zero and can be ignored; training works because gradient descent never lands exactly on a kink (almost surely).
  • Subgradient methods extend the gradient concept to continuous but non-differentiable functions — continuity is the key requirement, not differentiability.

The Clarke subdifferential generalizes the gradient to Lipschitz-continuous (hence continuous) functions. ReLU networks satisfy Lipschitz continuity: \(|f_\theta(\mathbf{x}) - f_\theta(\mathbf{y})| \leq C|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}|\) — a quantitative form of continuity.

docs.title: 13.5 Lipschitz Continuity and Generalization
docs.text:
A function \(f: \mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is \(K\)-Lipschitz if:

\[|f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{y})| \leq K|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}| \quad\forall,\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\]

This is uniform continuity with an explicit modulus: \(\delta = \varepsilon/K\).

In deep learning, Lipschitz continuity appears everywhere:

  • Spectral normalization (Miyato et al., 2018): Constrains each layer's spectral norm so the network is globally Lipschitz — used in GANs for training stability.
  • Wasserstein GANs (Arjovsky et al., 2017): The discriminator must be \(1\)-Lipschitz — enforced via gradient penalty (penalizing \(|\nabla f| > 1\), exactly the gradient of a Lipschitz bound).
  • Robustness guarantees: A network with Lipschitz constant \(K\) satisfies \(|f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{x}+\boldsymbol\delta)| \leq K|\boldsymbol\delta|\) — the perturbation bound for adversarial robustness.
  • PAC-Bayes generalization bounds often depend on the Lipschitz constant of the loss as a function of parameters.

docs.title: 13.6 Limits in Infinite-Dimensional Spaces: Function Spaces
docs.text:
The framework of limits and continuity generalizes to infinite-dimensional spaces — and this is where modern deep learning theory lives.

A functional is a map \(F: \mathcal{F} \to \mathbb{R}\) from a space of functions to the reals. For example:

\[F[f] = \int_\Omega |f(\mathbf{x})|^2,d\mathbf{x} \qquad\text{(the $L^2$ norm squared)}\]

Limits in function spaces use norms like \(|f - g|_{L^2}\), \(|f-g|_{\infty}\), etc. Continuity of \(F\) with respect to these norms is the analog of our \(\varepsilon\)-\(\delta\) definition. Neural networks as function approximators are studied in this setting — convergence theorems (universal approximation, NTK theory) are statements about limits in function spaces.

docs.title: 13.7 Automatic Differentiation and Continuity
docs.text:
Automatic differentiation (autograd) in PyTorch/JAX computes gradients by tracing operations. Its correctness relies on:

  1. Continuity of composed operations: Chain rule is valid only for differentiable (hence continuous) functions.
  2. Handling of discontinuities: At points of non-differentiability (ReLU at 0), frameworks return a subgradient (typically \(0\) or left/right derivative). This is mathematically valid only because ReLU is still continuous there.
  3. The limit definition of derivative: Autograd builds a computational graph that computes \(\lim_{h\to 0}(f(\mathbf{x}+h\mathbf{e}_i)-f(\mathbf{x}))/h\) symbolically, not numerically — exploiting the limit laws and chain rule.

docs.title: Summary Table: ML Concepts Rooted in Continuity
docs.text: ML Concept Continuity Role Gradient descent convergence Continuity of \(\mathcal{L}(\theta)\) ensures gradients make sense Loss landscape connectivity Path-independence ↔ limit exists along all paths ReLU networks Continuous but non-differentiable; subgradient valid Spectral normalization / W-GAN Lipschitz = quantitative continuity Adversarial robustness bounds Lipschitz constant controls sensitivity Neural ODEs Continuity of vector field guarantees ODE solution exists Universal approximation Convergence of \(f_\theta \to f^*\) in \(L^2\) or \(\sup\) norm = continuity in function space Extreme Value Theorem Existence of loss minimizers on compact sets

docs.title: 14. Summary
docs.text:
The core of this note in one diagram:

WANT: lim f(x,y) = L as (x,y) → (a,b)
         (x,y)→(a,b)

To PROVE it exists:                  To PROVE it does NOT exist:
  ┌────────────────────────┐           ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ Find bound:            │           │ Find two paths with       │
  │ |f - L| ≤ C·rᵏ, k>0   │           │ different limits:         │
  │                        │           │  Path 1: L₁              │
  │ OR use polar coords    │           │  Path 2: L₂ ≠ L₁         │
  │ and show →0 for all θ  │           └──────────────────────────┘
  └────────────────────────┘

Key inequalities to memorize:

\[|x|, |y| \leq r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}, \quad |xy| \leq \frac{r^2}{2}, \quad \frac{x^2}{x^2+y^2}\leq 1\]

Continuity = limit equals function value. Preserved under \(+,-,\times,\div,\circ\).

The crucial hierarchy: $\(\text{Cont. partial derivatives} \Rightarrow \text{Differentiable} \Rightarrow \text{Continuous} \Rightarrow \text{Limit exists}\)$

None of these arrows reverses. In particular: partial derivatives existing does not imply continuity.

In machine learning, continuity is the minimum regularity needed for optimization to function. Lipschitz continuity — a uniform, quantitative version — underpins generalization bounds, GAN training stability, and robustness guarantees.

docs.text:

  2. MIT OpenCourseWare 18.02. Multivariable Calculus (Auroux). Lectures on limits in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), continuity, the squeeze technique.
  3. Rudin, Walter. Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed. Chapter 4 — Continuity. Rigorous sequential characterization, Heine–Cantor theorem.
