docs.title: PDEs
docs.text: "A PDE is a constraint on a function of several variables — an equation that relates the function to its own partial derivatives. The universe writes its laws in this language."

docs.title: Tags
docs.text: #calculus #PDE #multivariable #wave-equation #heat-equation #Laplace #separation-of-variables #machine-learning #physics-informed-neural-networks #MIT-18.02 #Stewart

docs.title: 0. What Is a PDE?
docs.text:
An ordinary differential equation (ODE) involves a function of one variable and its derivatives:

\[\frac{d^2 y}{dx^2} + \omega^2 y = 0\]

A partial differential equation (PDE) involves a function of several variables and its partial derivatives:

\[\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = c^2 \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}\]

Here \(u = u(x,t)\) depends on both space \(x\) and time \(t\). The equation relates \(u\) to its own partial derivatives — it is a constraint that \(u\) must satisfy everywhere on its domain.

The fundamental shift in difficulty: In an ODE, specifying \(y(0)\) and \(y'(0)\) (two numbers) determines the solution. In a PDE, we must specify \(u\) on an entire boundary — a function — and the solution fills in the rest of the domain. The space of solutions is infinite-dimensional.

docs.title: 1.1 Order
docs.text:
The order of a PDE is the order of the highest partial derivative appearing.

  • \(u_t = ku_{xx}\): second order (in \(x\)), first order (in \(t\)) — conventionally called second order overall.
  • \(u_{tt} = c^2 u_{xx}\): second order.
  • \(u_{xxx} + u_{yy} = 0\): third order.

docs.title: 1.2 Linearity
docs.text:
A PDE in \(u\) is linear if it is linear in \(u\) and all its derivatives — no products like \(u \cdot u_x\), no nonlinear terms like \(u^2\).

\[\underbrace{a(x,t)u_{xx} + b(x,t)u_{xt} + c(x,t)u_{tt}}_{\text{linear in } u \text{ and its derivatives}} + d(x,t)u_x + e(x,t)u_t + f(x,t)u = g(x,t)\]
  • Homogeneous: \(g = 0\).
  • Inhomogeneous: \(g \neq 0\) (source/forcing term).

docs.title: 1.3 The Classification of Second-Order Linear PDEs
docs.text:
For the general second-order linear PDE in two variables:

\[Au_{xx} + Bu_{xy} + Cu_{yy} + Du_x + Eu_y + Fu = G\]

Define the discriminant \(\Delta = B^2 - 4AC\) (analogous to a conic section):

\(\Delta < 0\) \(\Delta = 0\) \(\Delta > 0\) Elliptic Parabolic Hyperbolic Laplace, Poisson Heat/Diffusion Wave equation Steady-state Irreversible diffusion Wave propagation Boundary value problem Initial + boundary Initial + boundary

Why this matters: The type determines the mathematical character of solutions and the correct type of conditions to impose:

  • Elliptic: need boundary conditions all around the domain.
  • Parabolic: need initial condition + boundary conditions.
  • Hyperbolic: need initial conditions (\(u\) and \(u_t\)) + boundary conditions.
CLASSIFICATION TRIANGLE

          ELLIPTIC                PARABOLIC               HYPERBOLIC
        (Δ = B²-4AC < 0)       (Δ = B²-4AC = 0)       (Δ = B²-4AC > 0)

       ∇²u = 0                  u_t = k u_xx             u_tt = c² u_xx
        │                          │                          │
        ▼                          ▼                          ▼
   Smooth solutions           Smooth for t > 0          Finite speed
   Max principle              Diffuses singularities    of propagation
   No time evolution          Irreversible              Reversible

docs.title: 2. The Three Fundamental PDEs
docs.text: These are the canonical equations of mathematical physics. Every PDE course orbits around them. Every ML application connects back to them.

docs.title: 2.1 The Heat Equation (Parabolic)
docs.text:
\[ oxed{u_t = k, abla^2 u = k(u_{xx} + u_{yy} + \cdots)}\]

Physical meaning: \(u(\mathbf{x}, t)\) = temperature at position \(\mathbf{x}\), time \(t\). \(k > 0\) = thermal diffusivity.

Derivation sketch. Consider a small region \(\Omega\). The rate of change of heat energy is:

\[ rac{d}{dt}\int_\Omega u,dV = k \oint_{\partial\Omega} abla u \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}},dS = k\int_\Omega abla^2 u,dV\]

(The last step uses the Divergence Theorem.) Since \(\Omega\) is arbitrary: \(u_t = k abla^2 u\).

Key properties:

  • Solutions are immediately \(C^\infty\) for \(t > 0\), even if initial data is discontinuous. The heat equation has an infinite speed of propagation — a local disturbance is felt everywhere instantly (unphysical but useful).
  • Maximum principle: The maximum of \(u\) over a closed domain occurs on the boundary or at \(t=0\) — never in the interior. Temperature cannot exceed its boundary values.
  • Irreversibility: Running time backward (\(t o -t\)) gives \(u_t = -k abla^2 u\) — a backward heat equation that amplifies high-frequency noise catastrophically. Heat diffusion is fundamentally irreversible.

In 1D on \([0, L]\) with \(u(0,t) = u(L,t) = 0\), \(u(x,0) = f(x)\):

\[u(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} B_n \sin!\left( rac{n\pi x}{L} ight) e^{-k(n\pi/L)^2 t}\]

where \(B_n = rac{2}{L}\int_0^L f(x)\sin!\left( rac{n\pi x}{L} ight)dx\) — the Fourier sine coefficients of \(f\).

Observation: Each mode \(\sin(n\pi x/L)\) decays exponentially in time with rate \(k(n\pi/L)^2\). High-frequency modes decay faster — the heat equation smooths out detail. This is the mathematics of why hot objects cool and why signals lose high-frequency information over time.

docs.title: 2.2 The Wave Equation (Hyperbolic)
docs.text:
\[\boxed{u_{tt} = c^2,\nabla^2 u}\]

Physical meaning: \(u(\mathbf{x},t)\) = displacement of a vibrating medium (string, membrane, sound pressure). \(c > 0\) = wave speed.

Derivation sketch (1D string). A small segment of a string under tension \(T\), with mass density \(\rho\), obeys Newton's second law. For small displacements:

\[\rho,\Delta x, u_{tt} = T, u_x(x+\Delta x) - T, u_x(x) \approx T, u_{xx}, \Delta x\]

Dividing: \(u_{tt} = \frac{T}{\rho} u_{xx} = c^2 u_{xx}\) with \(c = \sqrt{T/\rho}\).

D'Alembert's Solution (1D, infinite domain):

Given \(u(x,0) = f(x)\) (initial displacement) and \(u_t(x,0) = g(x)\) (initial velocity):

\[\boxed{u(x,t) = \frac{f(x+ct) + f(x-ct)}{2} + \frac{1}{2c}\int_{x-ct}^{x+ct} g(s),ds}\]

Interpretation: The solution is a superposition of two waves — one traveling right at speed \(c\) and one traveling left at speed \(c\).

t=0:        f(x)
            /\
           /  \
          /    \
---------/------\---------  x

t=T:    left wave    right wave
        \  f(x+cT)   f(x-cT) /
         \          /
---------  --------  --------  x

Both halves travel away from the source at speed c.

Key properties:

  • Finite speed of propagation: A disturbance at \(x=0\) reaches position \(x\) only after time \(t = |x|/c\). This is causality.
  • Reversibility: The wave equation is time-reversible (\(t \to -t\) gives the same equation).
  • Conservation: The total energy (kinetic + potential) is conserved.

In 1D on \([0,L]\) with fixed endpoints \(u(0,t) = u(L,t) = 0\):

\[u(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \sin!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)!\left[A_n \cos!\left(\frac{n\pi c}{L}t\right) + B_n \sin!\left(\frac{n\pi c}{L}t\right)\right]\]

The frequencies \(\omega_n = \frac{n\pi c}{L}\) are the natural frequencies of the string — overtones of the fundamental \(\omega_1 = \pi c/L\). This is the mathematics of musical instruments.

docs.title: 2.3 Laplace's Equation and Poisson's Equation (Elliptic)
3. Boundary and Initial Conditions
docs.text: A PDE alone does not determine a unique solution. We need additional conditions.

docs.title: Types of Boundary Conditions
docs.text: Type Form Physical meaning Dirichlet \(u = g\) on \(\partial\Omega\) Prescribed value (temperature fixed at boundary) Neumann \(\nabla u \cdot \hat{n} = h\) on \(\partial\Omega\) Prescribed flux (insulated boundary: \(h=0\)) Robin \(\alpha u + \beta \nabla u \cdot \hat{n} = g\) Convective boundary (mixed)

docs.title: Well-Posedness (Hadamard)
docs.text:
A PDE problem is well-posed if:

  1. A solution exists.
  2. The solution is unique.
  3. The solution depends continuously on the data (stability).

Ill-posed problems arise frequently in inverse problems and have deep connections to machine learning regularization.

docs.title: 4. Method of Separation of Variables
docs.text: This is the primary analytical method for linear homogeneous PDEs on simple domains. The idea: assume the solution factors as a product of functions, each depending on only one variable.

docs.title: 4.1 Heat Equation — Full Solution
docs.text:
Problem: \(u_t = k,u_{xx}\), \(x \in [0,L]\), \(t > 0\)

BCs: \(u(0,t) = 0\), \(u(L,t) = 0\)

IC: \(u(x,0) = f(x)\)

Step 1 — Assume: \(u(x,t) = X(x),T(t)\)

Substituting:

\[X(x),T'(t) = k,X''(x),T(t)\] \[\frac{T'(t)}{kT(t)} = \frac{X''(x)}{X(x)} = -\lambda\]

Since the left side depends only on \(t\) and the right side only on \(x\), both must equal the same constant \(-\lambda\).

Step 2 — Solve the spatial ODE:

\[X'' + \lambda X = 0, \quad X(0) = X(L) = 0\]

This is an eigenvalue problem (Sturm-Liouville). Non-trivial solutions exist only for:

\[\lambda_n = \left(\frac{n\pi}{L}\right)^2, \quad X_n(x) = \sin!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right), \quad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\]

The \(\lambda_n\) are the eigenvalues; the \(X_n\) are the eigenfunctions.

Step 3 — Solve the temporal ODE:

\[T_n'(t) = -k\lambda_n T_n(t) \implies T_n(t) = e^{-k\lambda_n t} = e^{-k(n\pi/L)^2 t}\]

Step 4 — Superposition: (Linearity allows summing all solutions)

\[u(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} B_n,X_n(x),T_n(t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} B_n \sin!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right) e^{-k(n\pi/L)^2 t}\]

Step 5 — Apply initial condition:

\[u(x,0) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} B_n \sin!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right) = f(x)\]

By Fourier series orthogonality (\(\int_0^L \sin\frac{m\pi x}{L}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L},dx = \frac{L}{2}\delta_{mn}\)):

\[B_n = \frac{2}{L}\int_0^L f(x)\sin!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)dx\]

This is why Fourier series exist: they are the natural language of the heat equation. Separation of variables creates Fourier series.

docs.title: 4.2 Wave Equation — Vibrating String
docs.text:
Problem: \(u_{tt} = c^2 u_{xx}\), \(x \in [0,L]\), with \(u(0,t) = u(L,t) = 0\)

ICs: \(u(x,0) = f(x)\), \(u_t(x,0) = g(x)\)

Same spatial eigenfunctions \(X_n = \sin(n\pi x/L)\), but now the temporal ODE is:

\[T_n'' + c^2\lambda_n T_n = 0 \implies T_n(t) = A_n\cos(\omega_n t) + B_n\sin(\omega_n t)\]

where \(\omega_n = cn\pi/L\) is the \(n\)-th angular frequency.

\[u(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\sin!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)!\left[A_n\cos(\omega_n t) + B_n\sin(\omega_n t)\right]\]

Apply ICs:

\[A_n = \frac{2}{L}\int_0^L f(x)\sin!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)dx, \quad B_n = \frac{2}{L\omega_n}\int_0^L g(x)\sin!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)dx\]

docs.title: 4.3 Laplace's Equation on a Rectangle
docs.text:
Problem: \(u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 0\) on \([0,a]\times[0,b]\), with three zero BCs and \(u(x,b) = f(x)\).

Assume \(u = X(x)Y(y)\), leading to:

\[\frac{X''}{X} = -\frac{Y''}{Y} = -\lambda\]

Spatial: \(X_n = \sin(n\pi x/a)\) (to satisfy \(X(0) = X(a) = 0\)).

Vertical: \(Y'' - \lambda_n Y = 0 \implies Y_n(y) = \sinh!\left(\frac{n\pi y}{a}\right)\) (choosing the combination that satisfies \(Y(0) = 0\)).

\[u(x,y) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} C_n \sin!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{a}\right)\sinh!\left(\frac{n\pi y}{a}\right)\]

The \(\sinh\) (rather than exponential) appears because the boundary conditions couple both ends. This reflects the elliptic character of Laplace's equation.

docs.title: 5. The Fundamental Solution and Green's Functions
5.1 Heat Kernel
docs.text:
The fundamental solution of the heat equation on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is:

\[\Phi(\mathbf{x}, t) = \frac{1}{(4\pi kt)^{n/2}} \exp!\left(-\frac{|\mathbf{x}|^2}{4kt}\right), \quad t > 0\]

This is a Gaussian centered at the origin that spreads out over time. The solution to the heat equation with initial condition \(u(\mathbf{x},0) = f(\mathbf{x})\) is:

\[u(\mathbf{x},t) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \Phi(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y},t),f(\mathbf{y}),d\mathbf{y} = (\Phi(\cdot,t) * f)(\mathbf{x})\]

Interpretation: The solution is a convolution of the initial data with the Gaussian kernel. The heat equation performs Gaussian smoothing — this is exactly the operation used in image processing. With variance \(\sigma^2 = 2kt\) at time \(t\), larger \(t\) means more smoothing.

f(x) initial data:          Φ(x,t₁):              u(x,t₁) = Φ * f:

  /\/\  sharp features      _____                    /‾‾\
 /    \                    /     \                  /    \  smoothed
/      \                  /       \                /      \

docs.title: 5.2 Fundamental Solution of Laplace's Equation
docs.text:
In \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the fundamental solution is the potential of a point source at the origin:

\[\Phi(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} -\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\ln|\mathbf{x}| & n = 2 \ \dfrac{1}{(n-2)\omega_n |\mathbf{x}|^{n-2}} & n \geq 3 \end{cases}\]

where \(\omega_n\) = surface area of the unit sphere in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

The Poisson equation \(-\nabla^2 u = f\) has solution \(u = \Phi * f\).

This is the Green's function of \(-\nabla^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\). It is the inverse of the Laplacian — in the same way that \(\frac{1}{k}\) is the inverse of multiplication by \(k\).

docs.title: 6. Superposition and Linearity
docs.text:
The superposition principle is the central tool for linear PDEs.

Theorem: If \(u_1\) and \(u_2\) both satisfy a linear homogeneous PDE \(\mathcal{L}[u] = 0\), then \(c_1 u_1 + c_2 u_2\) also satisfies it, for any constants \(c_1, c_2\).

This is what makes Fourier series work: we build the solution as an infinite superposition of eigenfunctions, each of which individually satisfies the PDE and the boundary conditions. The initial condition then determines the coefficients.

For inhomogeneous problems \(\mathcal{L}[u] = f\): Decompose into particular + homogeneous:

\[u = u_p + u_h, \quad \mathcal{L}[u_p] = f, \quad \mathcal{L}[u_h] = 0\]

This mirrors the ODE strategy exactly.

docs.title: Example 7.1 — Verifying a Solution
docs.text:
Verify that \(u(x,t) = e^{-4\pi^2 t}\sin(\pi x) + 3e^{-\pi^2 t}\sin(2\pi x)\) satisfies \(u_t = u_{xx}\) with appropriate BCs.

Computing \(u_t\):

\[u_t = -4\pi^2 e^{-4\pi^2 t}\sin(\pi x) + 3(-\pi^2)e^{-\pi^2 t}\sin(2\pi x)\]

Wait — recalculate. Let \(k=1\), \(L = 1\). The \(n=1\) mode has \(\lambda_1 = \pi^2\); the \(n=2\) mode has \(\lambda_2 = 4\pi^2\).

\[u_t = -4\pi^2 e^{-4\pi^2 t}\sin(\pi x) - 3\pi^2 e^{-\pi^2 t}\sin(2\pi x)\]

Computing \(u_{xx}\):

\[u_{xx} = -\pi^2 e^{-4\pi^2 t}\sin(\pi x) \cdot (-1)\]

Actually let us be precise. \(\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}\sin(\pi x) = -\pi^2 \sin(\pi x)\) and \(\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}\sin(2\pi x) = -4\pi^2\sin(2\pi x)\).

\[u_{xx} = -\pi^2 e^{-4\pi^2 t}\sin(\pi x) - 3\cdot 4\pi^2 e^{-\pi^2 t}\sin(2\pi x)\]

Hmm — \(u_t \neq u_{xx}\) with the given formula. Let me use the correct form. With \(B_1 = 1\), \(B_2 = 3\) and \(\lambda_n = (n\pi)^2\):

\[u = e^{-\pi^2 t}\sin(\pi x) + 3e^{-4\pi^2 t}\sin(2\pi x)\] \[u_t = -\pi^2 e^{-\pi^2 t}\sin(\pi x) - 12\pi^2 e^{-4\pi^2 t}\sin(2\pi x)\] \[u_{xx} = -\pi^2 e^{-\pi^2 t}\sin(\pi x) - 3\cdot 4\pi^2 e^{-4\pi^2 t}\sin(2\pi x) = -\pi^2 e^{-\pi^2 t}\sin(\pi x) - 12\pi^2 e^{-4\pi^2 t}\sin(2\pi x)\]

\(u_t = u_{xx}\) ✓. The boundary conditions \(u(0,t) = u(1,t) = 0\) hold since \(\sin(0) = \sin(\pi) = 0\) ✓.

docs.title: Example 7.2 — Applying D'Alembert's Formula
docs.text:
Wave equation: \(u_{tt} = 4u_{xx}\) (so \(c = 2\)) on \(\mathbb{R}\)

ICs: \(u(x,0) = \sin x\), \(u_t(x,0) = 0\)

D'Alembert:

\[u(x,t) = \frac{\sin(x+2t) + \sin(x-2t)}{2} + \frac{1}{4}\int_{x-2t}^{x+2t}0,ds\] \[= \frac{\sin(x+2t) + \sin(x-2t)}{2} = \sin x\cos(2t)\]

(using the sum-to-product identity). This is a standing wave: the spatial pattern \(\sin x\) oscillates in time with frequency \(\omega = 2\). The crests and troughs don't travel — they oscillate in place.

docs.title: Example 7.3 — Laplace on a Disk (Polar Coordinates)
docs.text:
Problem: \( abla^2 u = 0\) inside the unit disk \(r < 1\), with \(u(1, heta) = \cos heta\).

In polar coordinates: \( abla^2 u = u_{rr} + rac{1}{r}u_r + rac{1}{r^2}u_{ heta heta} = 0\).

Separate: \(u = R(r)\Theta( heta)\). The angular equation gives \(\Theta = \cos(n heta)\) or \(\sin(n heta)\), and the radial equation gives \(R = r^n\) (regular at \(r=0\)).

For \(n=1\) (matching our BC \(\cos heta\)): \(u(r, heta) = r\cos heta = x\).

Verification: \( abla^2(x) = 0\) ✓. At \(r=1\): \(u = \cos heta\) ✓. Beautiful.

The Poisson integral formula gives the general solution:

\[u(r, heta) = rac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} rac{(1-r^2)}{1 - 2r\cos( heta - \phi) + r^2},f(\phi),d\phi\]

This is the Green's function solution for the disk — the Poisson kernel in the numerator is a sum of all the radial eigenmodes, exhibiting the same structure as the 1D Fourier solution but in polar coordinates.

docs.title: 8. Nonlinear PDEs — A Glimpse
docs.text: Most PDEs arising in nature are nonlinear. Superposition fails. Solutions can develop shocks (discontinuities in finite time) even from smooth initial data.

docs.title: 8.1 Burgers' Equation
docs.text:
\[u_t + u,u_x = u, u_{xx}\]

The \(u,u_x\) term is nonlinear (advection speed depends on \(u\) itself). With \( u = 0\) (inviscid Burgers): waves steepen and break into shocks. With \( u > 0\): diffusion competes with steepening.

Burgers' equation appears in turbulence, traffic flow, and as a test case for numerical PDE solvers.

docs.title: 8.2 Navier-Stokes Equations
docs.text:
\[ ho!\left( rac{\partial \mathbf{v}}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{v}\cdot abla)\mathbf{v} ight) = - abla p + \mu abla^2\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{f}\]

The \((\mathbf{v}\cdot abla)\mathbf{v}\) is the nonlinear inertia term (convective acceleration). Whether smooth solutions exist for all time in 3D is one of the Millennium Prize Problems (Clay Mathematics Institute, $1,000,000).

docs.title: 9. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: PDEs and deep learning are colliding in one of the most active frontiers of applied mathematics.

docs.title: 9.1 Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs)
docs.text:
The problem: Solve a PDE \(\mathcal{L}[u] = f\) in domain \(\Omega\) with boundary condition \(u|_{\partial\Omega} = g\).

The idea (Raissi, Perdikaris, Karniadakis, 2019): Approximate \(u(\mathbf{x})\) by a neural network \(u_\theta(\mathbf{x})\). Define the loss:

\[\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \underbrace{\frac{1}{N_r}\sum_{i=1}^{N_r}\bigl|\mathcal{L}[u_\theta](https://claude.ai/chat/%5Cmathbf%7Bx%7D_i%5Er) - f(\mathbf{x}_i^r)\bigr|^2}_{\text{residual loss}} + \underbrace{\frac{1}{N_b}\sum_{j=1}^{N_b}\bigl|u_\theta(\mathbf{x}_j^b) - g(\mathbf{x}_j^b)\bigr|^2}_{\text{boundary loss}}\]

where \(\mathbf{x}_i^r\) are collocation points in the interior and \(\mathbf{x}_j^b\) are points on the boundary.

Minimizing this loss forces \(u_\theta\) to approximately satisfy the PDE and the boundary conditions. No mesh required — this is a meshless method.

The terms \(\frac{\partial u_\theta}{\partial x}\), \(\frac{\partial^2 u_\theta}{\partial x^2}\) are computed via automatic differentiation through the network graph. Computing second derivatives requires differentiating through the backward pass — this is why PINNs need \(C^2\) activation functions (Tanh, GELU, Swish; ReLU's second derivative is zero almost everywhere).

         Collocation points · in interior         Boundary points × on ∂Ω

         ×  ×  ×  ×  ×  ×
         ×  ·  ·  ·  ·  ×
         ×  ·  ·  ·  ·  ×      u_θ must satisfy:
         ×  ·  ·  ·  ·  ×      · Lu_θ = f   at interior points
         ×  ·  ·  ·  ·  ×      × u_θ = g   at boundary points
         ×  ×  ×  ×  ×  ×

Strengths: Handles complex geometries, inverse problems (identify PDE coefficients from data), incorporates noisy observations.

Weaknesses: Training is slow; fails on problems with sharp gradients or shocks; hard to enforce causality in time-dependent PDEs.

docs.title: 9.2 Neural Operators — Learning Solution Maps
docs.text:
Key insight: A PDE defines a map from initial/boundary conditions to solutions. Instead of solving one PDE, can we learn this map?

Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) (Li et al., 2020): Learn the solution operator \(\mathcal{G}: f \mapsto u\) where \(u\) solves \(\mathcal{L}[u] = f\). The network operates in Fourier space — literally using the Fourier modes that appear in separation of variables. Once trained, FNO evaluates new solutions in milliseconds vs. hours for traditional solvers.

DeepONet (Lu et al., 2021): A neural network that learns operators using the universal approximation theorem for operators, which is itself a generalization of the standard UAT.

docs.title: 9.3 Diffusion Models — The Heat Equation in Reverse
docs.text:
Score-based generative models (DDPM, score matching) are literally built on the heat equation.

Forward process: Starting from data \(\mathbf{x}_0 \sim p_{\text{data}}\), add Gaussian noise incrementally:

\[\mathbf{x}_t = \sqrt{1 - \beta t},\mathbf{x}_0 + \sqrt{\beta t},\boldsymbol{\epsilon}, \quad \boldsymbol{\epsilon} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\]

In the continuous limit, this follows the forward SDE:

\[d\mathbf{x} = -\frac{\beta}{2}\mathbf{x},dt + \sqrt{\beta},d\mathbf{W}\]

The marginal density \(p_t(\mathbf{x})\) satisfies the Fokker-Planck equation — a PDE of the form:

\[\frac{\partial p_t}{\partial t} = \frac{\beta}{2}\nabla\cdot(\mathbf{x}p_t) + \frac{\beta}{2}\nabla^2 p_t\]

This is a convection-diffusion equation. As \(t \to \infty\), \(p_t \to \mathcal{N}(0,I)\) — pure noise. The data distribution has been smoothed into a Gaussian by running the heat equation.

Reverse process (generation): Run the PDE backwards using the reverse-time SDE (Anderson, 1982):

\[d\mathbf{x} = \left[-\frac{\beta}{2}\mathbf{x} - \beta,\nabla_\mathbf{x}\log p_t(\mathbf{x})\right]dt + \sqrt{\beta},d\overline{\mathbf{W}}\]

The term \(\nabla_\mathbf{x}\log p_t(\mathbf{x})\) is the score function — the neural network learns to estimate it. Once known, we can reverse the diffusion and generate data from noise.

DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, Sora — all of these are learned reverse diffusions. They are the heat equation run backward, guided by a neural approximation to the score function.

  DATA                    →   Heat Equation   →              NOISE
  p_data(x)               →   (forward SDE)   →          N(0, I)

  GENERATED SAMPLES       ←   Neural Network  ←          NOISE
  p_data(x)               ←  (reverse SDE)    ←          N(0, I)
                               learns score ∇ log p_t

docs.title: 9.4 The Connection Between Optimization and PDEs
docs.text:
Hamilton-Jacobi equation: The optimal value function \(V(\mathbf{x}, t)\) in continuous-time optimal control satisfies:

\[-V_t = \min_u \bigl[L(\mathbf{x}, u) + \nabla V \cdot f(\mathbf{x}, u)\bigr]\]

This is a first-order nonlinear PDE (Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman). Reinforcement learning is the discrete, approximate version of solving this PDE. Deep RL methods (SAC, PPO, TD3) implicitly approximate the solution to an HJB equation.

docs.title: 9.5 Graph Neural Networks and Discrete Laplacians
docs.text:
The graph Laplacian \(L = D - A\) (where \(D\) is degree matrix, \(A\) is adjacency matrix) is the discrete analogue of \(-\nabla^2\). Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) perform operations that are discrete approximations of:

\[\frac{\partial \mathbf{H}}{\partial t} = -L\mathbf{H}\]

— the heat equation on graphs. Running the forward pass of a GCN is running discrete diffusion on the graph. The deeper the network, the more the node features diffuse — the discrete heat equation "over-smoothing" problem.

docs.title: 10. Connections Across the Three PDEs
docs.text:
THE BIG PICTURE

   u_t = k∇²u          u_tt = c²∇²u         ∇²u = 0
   HEAT / DIFFUSION     WAVE / VIBRATION      LAPLACE / STEADY-STATE

   ↕                    ↕                     ↕
   Parabolic            Hyperbolic             Elliptic
   (B²-4AC < 0)        (B²-4AC > 0)          (B²-4AC < 0... = 0)

   ↕                    ↕                     ↕
   Gaussian kernel      D'Alembert formula    Poisson integral
   convolution          traveling waves       harmonic functions

   ↕                    ↕                     ↕
   Irreversible         Reversible            No time, no memory
   smoothing            energy conserved      mean value property

   ↕                    ↕                     ↕
   Diffusion models     FNO (wave solvers)    GCNs, Laplacian reg.
   Score matching       PINNs                 PINNs (Poisson)
   Image smoothing      Acoustics ML          Electrostatics ML

docs.title: 11. Key Formulas — Reference
docs.text: \[\textbf{Heat: } u_t = k u_{xx} \implies u(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty B_n \sin!\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)e^{-k(n\pi/L)^2 t}\] \[\textbf{Wave: } u_{tt} = c^2 u_{xx} \implies u(x,t) = \frac{f(x+ct)+f(x-ct)}{2} + \frac{1}{2c}\int_{x-ct}^{x+ct}g(s),ds\] \[\textbf{Fundamental solution (heat): } \Phi(x,t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi kt}}e^{-x^2/4kt}\] \[\textbf{Laplace (polar, disk): } u(r,\theta) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty r^n(A_n\cos n\theta + B_n\sin n\theta)\] \[\textbf{Poisson kernel: } u(r,\theta) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{1-r^2}{1-2r\cos(\theta-\phi)+r^2}f(\phi),d\phi\] \[\textbf{Classification: } \Delta = B^2 - 4AC \begin{cases} < 0 & \text{elliptic} \ = 0 & \text{parabolic} \ > 0 & \text{hyperbolic} \end{cases}\]

docs.title: 12. Summary Map
docs.text:
PARTIAL DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS
│
├─ CLASSIFICATION
│   ├─ Order (highest derivative)
│   ├─ Linearity (linear / nonlinear)
│   └─ Type: elliptic / parabolic / hyperbolic
│
├─ THREE CANONICAL PDEs
│   ├─ Heat: u_t = k∇²u  (diffusion, smoothing, irreversible)
│   ├─ Wave: u_tt = c²∇²u  (propagation, reversible, causality)
│   └─ Laplace: ∇²u = 0  (steady-state, harmonic, mean value)
│
├─ SOLUTION METHODS
│   ├─ Separation of variables → Fourier series / eigenfunctions

docs.title: Cobb-Douglas
docs.text: "Economics gave us the question. Calculus gave us the answer. The Cobb-Douglas function sits exactly at that intersection — simple enough to differentiate in closed form, rich enough to model an entire economy."

docs.title: Tags
docs.text: #calculus #multivariable #economics #partial-derivatives #optimization #elasticity #machine-learning #MIT-18.02 #Stewart

docs.title: 0. Origins and Context
docs.text:
In 1927, mathematician Charles Cobb and economist Paul Douglas fit a simple power-law model to U.S. manufacturing data from 1899–1922. They asked: given observed inputs of capital \(K\) and labor \(L\), can we predict total output \(Q\)?

The function they proposed:

\[Q = AK^\alpha L^\beta\]

fit the data remarkably well. More importantly, it had mathematical properties that aligned almost perfectly with economic intuition — constant returns to scale, diminishing marginal products, and tractable closed-form solutions for optimization. It remains, nearly a century later, the workhorse model of production theory in economics and appears throughout machine learning theory as well.

This note treats the Cobb-Douglas function with full mathematical rigor, using it as a sustained application of multivariable calculus.

docs.title: Standard Form
docs.text:
\[Q(K, L) = A K^\alpha L^\beta\]

where:

Symbol Name Domain Interpretation \(Q\) Output \(\mathbb{R}_{>0}\) Total production (goods, revenue, GDP) \(K\) Capital \(\mathbb{R}_{>0}\) Machines, buildings, equipment \(L\) Labor \(\mathbb{R}_{>0}\) Worker-hours, headcount \(A\) Total Factor Productivity (TFP) \(\mathbb{R}_{>0}\) Technology, efficiency, institutional quality \(\alpha\) Capital elasticity \((0,1)\) typically Capital's output share \(\beta\) Labor elasticity \((0,1)\) typically Labor's output share

The domain of \(Q\) is \((K,L) \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}^2\). The function is not defined at \(K=0\) or \(L=0\) (no output without both inputs — a modeling assumption).

docs.title: The Three Regimes
docs.text:
The relationship between \(\alpha + \beta\) and \(1\) defines the returns-to-scale behavior (see §4):

Condition Regime Economic meaning \(\alpha + \beta = 1\) Constant Returns to Scale (CRS) Doubling inputs doubles output \(\alpha + \beta > 1\) Increasing Returns to Scale (IRS) Doubling inputs more than doubles output \(\alpha + \beta < 1\) Decreasing Returns to Scale (DRS) Doubling inputs less than doubles output

The original Cobb-Douglas paper estimated \(\alpha \approx 0.25\), \(\beta \approx 0.75\) for U.S. manufacturing — CRS, approximately.

docs.title: 2. Partial Derivatives — Marginal Products
docs.text: The first partial derivatives of \(Q\) with respect to each input are the marginal products — the additional output from one more unit of an input, holding the other fixed.

docs.title: Marginal Product of Capital (MPK)
docs.text: \[\frac{\partial Q}{\partial K} = A \cdot \alpha K^{\alpha - 1} L^\beta = \alpha \cdot \frac{AK^\alpha L^\beta}{K} = \frac{\alpha Q}{K}\]

docs.title: Marginal Product of Labor (MPL)
docs.text: \[\frac{\partial Q}{\partial L} = A K^\alpha \cdot \beta L^{\beta - 1} = \beta \cdot \frac{AK^\alpha L^\beta}{L} = \frac{\beta Q}{L}\]

docs.title: Key Observations
docs.text:
1. The marginal products are proportional to average products:

\[\text{MPK} = \alpha \cdot \frac{Q}{K} = \alpha \cdot \text{APK}, \qquad \text{MPL} = \beta \cdot \frac{Q}{L} = \beta \cdot \text{APL}\]

This elegant identity — that marginal products are constant fractions of average products — is a special property of the Cobb-Douglas form.

2. Diminishing marginal products (for \(0 < \alpha, \beta < 1\)):

\[\frac{\partial^2 Q}{\partial K^2} = \alpha(\alpha-1)AK^{\alpha-2}L^\beta < 0 \quad \text{since } \alpha - 1 < 0\] \[\frac{\partial^2 Q}{\partial L^2} = \beta(\beta-1)AK^\alpha L^{\beta-2} < 0 \quad \text{since } \beta - 1 < 0\]

Each additional unit of capital (or labor) adds less output than the previous unit, when the other input is held fixed. The surface is concave along each coordinate direction.

3. Marginal products are strictly positive:

\[\frac{\partial Q}{\partial K} > 0, \quad \frac{\partial Q}{\partial L} > 0 \quad \text{for all } K, L > 0\]

More inputs always produce more output — a basic monotonicity assumption.

docs.title: Example 2.1 — Numerical
docs.text:
Let \(A = 1\), \(\alpha = 0.3\), \(\beta = 0.7\). At \((K, L) = (100, 200)\):

\[Q = 100^{0.3} \cdot 200^{0.7} = e^{0.3\ln 100 + 0.7\ln 200}\] \[= e^{0.3(4.605) + 0.7(5.298)} = e^{1.3815 + 3.7086} = e^{5.09} \approx 162.8\] \[\text{MPK} = \frac{0.3 \times 162.8}{100} \approx 0.488 \quad \text{(units of output per unit of capital)}\] \[\text{MPL} = \frac{0.7 \times 162.8}{200} \approx 0.570 \quad \text{(units of output per unit of labor)}\]

Interpretation: at this operating point, an additional unit of labor is slightly more productive than an additional unit of capital.

docs.title: 3. The Gradient and Economic Sensitivity
docs.text:
The gradient of \(Q\) packages both marginal products:

\[ abla Q(K,L) = \left( rac{\partial Q}{\partial K},, rac{\partial Q}{\partial L} ight) = \left( rac{\alpha Q}{K},, rac{ eta Q}{L} ight)\]

Direction of steepest ascent: \( abla Q\) points in the direction of maximum output growth from \((K,L)\). A firm seeking to maximally increase production with one unit of additional expenditure should allocate resources in the direction of \( abla Q\) (weighted by input prices — see §6).

Total differential: For small changes \(dK\) and \(dL\):

\[dQ = rac{\partial Q}{\partial K}dK + rac{\partial Q}{\partial L}dL = rac{\alpha Q}{K}dK + rac{ eta Q}{L}dL\]

Dividing by \(Q\):

\[ rac{dQ}{Q} = \alpha rac{dK}{K} + eta rac{dL}{L}\]

This is the fundamental identity of the Cobb-Douglas: the proportional change in output equals \(\alpha\) times the proportional change in capital plus \( eta\) times the proportional change in labor. This will be recognized as the elasticity interpretation (§5).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A function \(f(K,L)\) is homogeneous of degree \(r\) if for all \(\lambda > 0\):

\[f(\lambda K, \lambda L) = \lambda^r f(K, L)\]

docs.title: Theorem — Cobb-Douglas is Homogeneous of Degree \(\alpha + \beta\)
docs.text:
Proof:

\[Q(\lambda K, \lambda L) = A(\lambda K)^\alpha (\lambda L)^\beta = A \lambda^\alpha K^\alpha \lambda^\beta L^\beta = \lambda^{\alpha+\beta} A K^\alpha L^\beta = \lambda^{\alpha+\beta} Q(K,L) \quad \blacksquare\]

docs.title: Euler's Theorem for Homogeneous Functions
docs.text:
Theorem (Euler): If \(f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) is homogeneous of degree \(r\) and differentiable, then: $\(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i} = r \cdot f(\mathbf{x})\)$

Proof: Differentiate \(f(\lambda \mathbf{x}) = \lambda^r f(\mathbf{x})\) with respect to \(\lambda\) using the chain rule:

\[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i \frac{\partial f}{\partial (\lambda x_i)} = r\lambda^{r-1} f(\mathbf{x})\]

Set \(\lambda = 1\):

\[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i} = r f(\mathbf{x}) \quad \blacksquare\]

docs.title: Application to Cobb-Douglas
docs.text:
Applying Euler's theorem to \(Q = AK^\alpha L^\beta\):

\[K \frac{\partial Q}{\partial K} + L \frac{\partial Q}{\partial L} = (\alpha + \beta) Q\]

Substituting the marginal products:

\[K \cdot \frac{\alpha Q}{K} + L \cdot \frac{\beta Q}{L} = \alpha Q + \beta Q = (\alpha+\beta)Q \checkmark\]

docs.title: Economic Interpretation of Euler's Theorem (CRS Case)
docs.text:
When \(\alpha + \beta = 1\):

\[K \cdot \text{MPK} + L \cdot \text{MPL} = Q\]

If each input is paid its marginal product (the competitive equilibrium condition), and if returns to scale are constant, then total payments to inputs exactly exhaust total output — no surplus, no deficit. This is the mathematical foundation of the factor exhaustion theorem in economics.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The output elasticity of input \(x_i\) is:

\[\varepsilon_i = \frac{\partial \ln Q}{\partial \ln x_i} = \frac{x_i}{Q}\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x_i}\]

It measures the percentage change in output per 1% change in input \(x_i\), all else fixed.

docs.title: Theorem — Elasticities of Cobb-Douglas are Constant
docs.text:
\[\varepsilon_K = \frac{K}{Q}\cdot\frac{\alpha Q}{K} = \alpha\] \[\varepsilon_L = \frac{L}{Q}\cdot\frac{\beta Q}{L} = \beta\]

The parameters \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are the elasticities — constant everywhere on the domain. This is the defining property of the Cobb-Douglas function; it is the unique production function with constant output elasticities.

docs.title: The Log-Linear Transformation
docs.text:
Taking logarithms:

\[\ln Q = \ln A + \alpha \ln K + \beta \ln L\]

This is linear in \(\ln A\), \(\ln K\), \(\ln L\). Setting \(q = \ln Q\), \(a = \ln A\), \(k = \ln K\), \(l = \ln L\):

\[q = a + \alpha k + \beta l\]

This is a linear regression model in log-space. This is precisely why Cobb and Douglas could fit the model with simple linear regression on log-transformed data — and why Cobb-Douglas production functions are so tractable in empirical work.

The partial derivatives in log-space:

\[\frac{\partial q}{\partial k} = \alpha, \qquad \frac{\partial q}{\partial l} = \beta\]

Constant. The slopes in log-log space are the elasticities. Plotting \(\ln Q\) vs \(\ln K\) (with \(L\) fixed) gives a straight line of slope \(\alpha\).

docs.title: 6. Isoquants and the Marginal Rate of Technical Substitution
Isoquants
docs.text:
An isoquant is a level curve of \(Q\):

\[{(K,L) : AK^\alpha L^\beta = \bar{Q}} \quad \text{for fixed } \bar{Q} > 0\]

Solving for \(L\):

\[L = \left(\frac{\bar{Q}}{A}\right)^{1/\beta} K^{-\alpha/\beta}\]

This is a decreasing, convex curve in the \((K,L)\) plane — the familiar downward-sloping, bowed-inward isoquant of economics textbooks.

  L (Labor)
  |
  |·
  | ·
  |  ·
  |   ·
  |    ··
  |      ···         Q = Q₃
  |         ····     Q = Q₂
  |             ···· Q = Q₁ (Q₁ < Q₂ < Q₃)
  +------------------→ K (Capital)

  Each curve: AK^α L^β = const
  Convex to origin → diminishing MRTS

docs.title: Marginal Rate of Technical Substitution (MRTS)
docs.text:
The MRTS is the rate at which labor can be substituted for capital (or vice versa) while keeping output constant — the slope of the isoquant (in magnitude).

Using implicit differentiation on \(AK^\alpha L^\beta = \bar{Q}\):

Differentiate with respect to \(K\) (treating \(L = L(K)\)):

\[\alpha A K^{\alpha-1}L^\beta + A K^\alpha \beta L^{\beta-1}\frac{dL}{dK} = 0\] \[\frac{dL}{dK} = -\frac{\alpha A K^{\alpha-1} L^\beta}{\beta A K^\alpha L^{\beta - 1}} = -\frac{\alpha L}{\beta K}\]

Therefore:

\[\text{MRTS}_{KL} = -\frac{dL}{dK} = \frac{\alpha L}{\beta K} = \frac{\text{MPK}}{\text{MPL}}\]

Interpretation: The slope of the isoquant equals the ratio of marginal products. To substitute one unit of capital out while staying on the same isoquant, you must add \(\text{MPK}/\text{MPL}\) units of labor.

Diminishing MRTS: As \(K\) increases along an isoquant (and \(L\) falls correspondingly):

\[\frac{d(\text{MRTS})}{dK} < 0\]

(Can be verified; requires second-order implicit differentiation.) The isoquant gets flatter — capital becomes progressively less substitutable for labor. This is the mathematical statement of the bowed-in shape of isoquants.

docs.title: 7. Firm Optimization — Cost Minimization
docs.text:
A firm wants to produce output \(\bar{Q}\) at minimum cost. Input prices: capital costs \(r\) per unit, labor costs \(w\) per unit. The problem:

\[\min_{K,L > 0} ; rK + wL \quad \text{subject to} \quad AK^\alpha L^\beta = \bar{Q}\]

docs.title: Method: Lagrange Multipliers
docs.text:
Form the Lagrangian:

\[\mathcal{L}(K, L, \lambda) = rK + wL - \lambda\left(AK^\alpha L^\beta - \bar{Q}\right)\]

First-order conditions:

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial K} = r - \lambda \alpha A K^{\alpha-1} L^\beta = 0 \implies r = \lambda \cdot \text{MPK} = \lambda \cdot \frac{\alpha Q}{K}\] \[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial L} = w - \lambda \beta A K^\alpha L^{\beta-1} = 0 \implies w = \lambda \cdot \text{MPL} = \lambda \cdot \frac{\beta Q}{L}\] \[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \lambda} = -(AK^\alpha L^\beta - \bar{Q}) = 0 \implies AK^\alpha L^\beta = \bar{Q}\]

Divide the first two conditions:

\[\frac{r}{w} = \frac{\lambda \alpha Q/K}{\lambda \beta Q/L} = \frac{\alpha L}{\beta K} = \text{MRTS}_{KL}\]

The optimality condition: at the cost-minimizing input mix, the MRTS equals the input price ratio.

Geometrically: the isoquant is tangent to the isocost line \(rK + wL = C\).

docs.title: Solving for Optimal Inputs
docs.text:
From \(\frac{r}{w} = \frac{\alpha L}{\beta K}\):

\[L = \frac{\beta r}{\alpha w} K\]

Substitute into the constraint \(AK^\alpha L^\beta = \bar{Q}\):

\[AK^\alpha \left(\frac{\beta r}{\alpha w}\right)^\beta K^\beta = \bar{Q}\] \[A \left(\frac{\beta r}{\alpha w}\right)^\beta K^{\alpha+\beta} = \bar{Q}\] \[K^* = \left[\frac{\bar{Q}}{A}\left(\frac{\alpha w}{\beta r}\right)^\beta\right]^{1/(\alpha+\beta)}\] \[L^* = \left[\frac{\bar{Q}}{A}\left(\frac{\beta r}{\alpha w}\right)^\alpha\right]^{1/(\alpha+\beta)}\]

docs.title: The Cost Function
docs.text:
The minimum cost:

\[C^* = rK^* + wL^* = \bar{Q}^{1/(\alpha+\beta)} \cdot A^{-1/(\alpha+\beta)} \cdot B(r,w,\alpha,\beta)\]

where \(B\) is a function of prices and parameters.

For CRS (\(\alpha+\beta=1\)): \(C^* = \bar{Q} \cdot c(r,w)\) — cost is linear in output. Doubling output exactly doubles cost. This is the mathematical statement of constant returns: no cost advantage to scale.

The Lagrange multiplier \(\lambda\): From the first-order conditions:

\[\lambda = \frac{r}{\text{MPK}} = \frac{w}{\text{MPL}} = \frac{\partial C^*}{\partial \bar{Q}}\]

The multiplier equals the marginal cost — the rate at which minimum cost increases as the output target rises. The envelope theorem makes this precise.

docs.title: Computing the Full Hessian
docs.text:
\[\frac{\partial^2 Q}{\partial K^2} = \alpha(\alpha-1)AK^{\alpha-2}L^\beta = \frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)Q}{K^2}\] \[\frac{\partial^2 Q}{\partial L^2} = \beta(\beta-1)AK^\alpha L^{\beta-2} = \frac{\beta(\beta-1)Q}{L^2}\] \[\frac{\partial^2 Q}{\partial K \partial L} = \alpha\beta AK^{\alpha-1}L^{\beta-1} = \frac{\alpha\beta Q}{KL}\]

So the Hessian is:

\[H_Q = \frac{Q}{K^2 L^2}\begin{pmatrix} \alpha(\alpha-1)L^2 & \alpha\beta KL \ \alpha\beta KL & \beta(\beta-1)K^2 \end{pmatrix}\]

docs.title: Is \(Q\) Concave?
docs.text:
Compute \(\det(H_Q)\):

\[\det(H_Q) = \frac{Q^2}{K^4L^4}\left[\alpha(\alpha-1)\beta(\beta-1)K^2L^4 - \alpha^2\beta^2K^2L^2 \cdot \frac{L^2}{L^2}\right]\]

Let me compute directly:

\[\det(H_Q) = \frac{Q^2}{K^4 L^4} \cdot K^2 L^2 \left[\alpha(\alpha-1)\beta(\beta-1)L^2 - \alpha^2\beta^2 K^2 \cdot \frac{K^2}{K^2}\right]\]

More cleanly, from the entries:

\[\det(H_Q) = \left(\frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)Q}{K^2}\right)!\left(\frac{\beta(\beta-1)Q}{L^2}\right) - \left(\frac{\alpha\beta Q}{KL}\right)^2\] \[= \frac{Q^2}{K^2 L^2}\left[\alpha(\alpha-1)\beta(\beta-1) - \alpha^2\beta^2\right]\] \[= \frac{Q^2 \alpha\beta}{K^2 L^2}\left[(\alpha-1)(\beta-1) - \alpha\beta\right]\] \[= \frac{Q^2 \alpha\beta}{K^2 L^2}\left[\alpha\beta - \alpha - \beta + 1 - \alpha\beta\right]\] \[= \frac{Q^2 \alpha\beta}{K^2 L^2}(1 - \alpha - \beta)\]

Cases:

  • \(\alpha + \beta < 1\) (DRS): \(\det(H_Q) > 0\) and \(Q_{KK} < 0\) → \(H_Q\) negative definite → \(Q\) is strictly concave.

  • \(\alpha + \beta = 1\) (CRS): \(\det(H_Q) = 0\) → \(H_Q\) is negative **semi**definite → \(Q\) is concave but not strictly so.

  • \(\alpha + \beta > 1\) (IRS): \(\det(H_Q) < 0\) → \(H_Q\) is indefinite → \(Q\) is neither concave nor convex globally.

Economic significance: Strict concavity of \(Q\) (DRS case) implies that the set \({(K,L) : Q(K,L) \geq \bar{Q}}\) is convex — the "upper contour set" is convex. This guarantees that the cost minimization problem has a unique solution and that the isoquants are strictly convex to the origin.

docs.title: 9. Multi-Factor Generalization
docs.text:
The Cobb-Douglas generalizes naturally to \(n\) inputs:

\[Q(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n) = A \prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{\alpha_i}\]

Partial derivative (marginal product of input \(i\)):

\[\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x_i} = \frac{\alpha_i Q}{x_i}\]

Output elasticity of \(x_i\): \(\varepsilon_i = \alpha_i\) (still constant).

Homogeneity: \(Q(\lambda \mathbf{x}) = \lambda^{\sum \alpha_i} Q(\mathbf{x})\) (homogeneous of degree \(\sum \alpha_i\)).

Euler's theorem:

\[\sum_{i=1}^n x_i \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x_i} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i\right) Q\]

Log-linear form:

\[\ln Q = \ln A + \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i \ln x_i\]

This is a multivariate linear regression in log-space — the empirical foundation of all Cobb-Douglas estimation.

docs.title: 10. Taylor Expansion Near an Operating Point
docs.text:
Suppose a firm operates at \((K_0, L_0)\) and considers small deviations. Using the multivariable Taylor expansion:

\[Q(K_0 + \Delta K,, L_0 + \Delta L) \approx Q_0 + \frac{\alpha Q_0}{K_0}\Delta K + \frac{\beta Q_0}{L_0}\Delta L$$ $$+ \frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)Q_0}{K_0^2}(\Delta K)^2 + \frac{2\alpha\beta Q_0}{K_0 L_0}\Delta K \Delta L + \frac{\beta(\beta-1)Q_0}{L_0^2}(\Delta L)^2\right] + O(|\mathbf{\Delta}|^3)\]

Proportional form (divide by \(Q_0\)):

\[\frac{\Delta Q}{Q_0} \approx \alpha\frac{\Delta K}{K_0} + \beta\frac{\Delta L}{L_0} + \frac{1}{2}\left[\alpha(\alpha-1)\left(\frac{\Delta K}{K_0}\right)^2 + 2\alpha\beta\frac{\Delta K}{K_0}\frac{\Delta L}{L_0} + \beta(\beta-1)\left(\frac{\Delta L}{L_0}\right)^2\right]\]

The first-order term recovers the elasticity formula from §5. The second-order term contains the curvature corrections — negative (for \(\alpha,\beta < 1\)) since \(\alpha - 1 < 0\) and \(\beta - 1 < 0\), confirming diminishing returns.

docs.title: 11. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
11.1 Cobb-Douglas as a Scalable Systems Model
docs.text:
In ML infrastructure and systems research, the throughput of distributed training runs is often modeled with Cobb-Douglas-like functions:

\[\text{Throughput} = A \cdot (\text{Compute})^\alpha \cdot (\text{Bandwidth})^\beta \cdot (\text{Memory})^\gamma\]

The partial derivatives give bottleneck analysis: which resource has the highest marginal product? Allocate budget toward the input with the highest \(\frac{\partial \text{Throughput}}{\partial \text{Resource}} / \text{Resource price}\).

docs.title: 11.2 Neural Scaling Laws — A Cobb-Douglas Structure
docs.text:
The empirical scaling laws of large language models (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022) relate loss to compute \(C\), data \(D\), and parameters \(N\):

\[\mathcal{L} \approx A \cdot N^{-\alpha} + B \cdot D^{-\beta} + \text{irreducible loss}\]

This is not exactly Cobb-Douglas, but the analysis of optimal allocation — given a fixed compute budget \(C = 6ND\) (FLOPs ≈ \(6 \times\) parameters \(\times\) training tokens), how to split between \(N\) and \(D\) to minimize \(\mathcal{L}\) — is formally identical to the cost minimization problem in §7.

The Chinchilla result (Hoffmann et al.): at fixed compute, the optimal model size and token count satisfy \(N^* \propto C^{0.5}\), \(D^* \propto C^{0.5}\) — meaning parameters and data should scale equally. This was derived by minimizing the scaling law subject to the compute constraint, using exactly the Lagrange multiplier technique of §7.

docs.title: 11.3 The Log-Linear Form as a Neural Network Layer
docs.text:
Recall the log-linear form:

\[\ln Q = \ln A + \alpha \ln K + \beta \ln L\]

This is a linear layer applied to log-inputs. In a neural network processing economic or physical data on exponential scales, applying \(\log\) before a linear layer exactly learns Cobb-Douglas relationships. This is the theoretical foundation for using log-transforms in regression networks on economic data.

docs.title: 11.4 Constant Elasticity of Substitution (CES) — Generalization
docs.text:
Cobb-Douglas is the limiting case of the CES production function as substitution elasticity \(\sigma \to 1\):

\[Q = A\left[\alpha K^{(\sigma-1)/\sigma} + (1-\alpha)L^{(\sigma-1)/\sigma}\right]^{\sigma/(\sigma-1)}\]

As \(\sigma \to 1\): \(Q \to AK^\alpha L^{1-\alpha}\) (Cobb-Douglas with \(\beta = 1-\alpha\)).

In ML, CES-like aggregation functions appear in mixture-of-experts models and attention mechanisms, where the elasticity parameter \(\sigma\) controls how "hard" or "soft" the aggregation is. \(\sigma \to \infty\) gives linear (perfect substitution); \(\sigma \to 0\) gives Leontief (perfect complements, like an AND gate).

docs.title: 11.5 Lagrange Multipliers → Constrained Optimization in ML
docs.text:
The cost minimization problem (§7) is formally identical to:

Minimize \(rK + wL\) subject to \(AK^\alpha L^\beta = \bar{Q}\)

and the training problem:

Minimize \(\mathcal{L}(\theta)\) subject to \(|\theta| \leq C\) (L2 regularization / weight decay as a constraint)

Both are solved by Lagrange multipliers. The KKT conditions in constrained ML optimization are the direct generalization. The Lagrange multiplier \(\lambda\) becomes the regularization strength — exactly the marginal cost interpretation: \(\lambda = \partial \mathcal{L}^*/\partial C\) tells you how much the minimum loss decreases per unit increase in the weight budget.

docs.title: 12. Level Curves, Gradient, and Geometric Picture
Gradient of \(Q\)
docs.text:
\[\nabla Q = \left(\frac{\alpha Q}{K},, \frac{\beta Q}{L}\right)\]

The gradient is always positive in both components — \(Q\) is strictly increasing in each input. The gradient points "uphill" on the production surface, perpendicular to the isoquants.

docs.title: Normal to Isoquant
docs.text:
The isoquant \(AK^\alpha L^\beta = \bar{Q}\) is a level curve of \(Q\). The gradient \(\nabla Q\) is perpendicular to this level curve at every point.

At the cost-minimizing point, the isocost line \(rK + wL = C^*\) is tangent to the isoquant. Its normal vector is \((r, w)\). Tangency requires:

\[\nabla Q \parallel (r, w) \implies \frac{\alpha Q / K}{\beta Q / L} = \frac{r}{w} \implies \text{MRTS} = \frac{r}{w}\]

This recovers the optimality condition of §7 from a purely geometric argument. The gradient being parallel to the price vector is the multivariable calculus statement of the tangency condition.

  L
  |
  |·
  | ·     ← isoquant AK^α L^β = Q̄
  |  ·  
  |   * ← optimal (K*, L*)
  |    \   ← isocost rK + wL = C*
  |     \
  |      \
  +-------\---→ K

  At *: ∇Q ∥ (r, w) — gradient perpendicular to isocost
  MRTS = r/w — slopes match

docs.title: 13. Summary — The Calculus of Cobb-Douglas
docs.text:
Q(K,L) = AK^α L^β
│
├─ FIRST PARTIALS (Marginal Products)
│   ├─ ∂Q/∂K = αQ/K  (MPK — diminishing for α < 1)
│   └─ ∂Q/∂L = βQ/L  (MPL — diminishing for β < 1)
│
├─ GRADIENT
│   └─ ∇Q = (αQ/K, βQ/L) — perpendicular to isoquants
│
├─ HOMOGENEITY
│   ├─ Q(λK, λL) = λ^{α+β} Q(K,L)
│   └─ Euler: K·MPK + L·MPL = (α+β)Q
│
├─ ELASTICITIES
│   ├─ ε_K = α, ε_L = β  (constant — defining property)
│   └─ ln Q = ln A + α ln K + β ln L  (log-linear)
│
├─ ISOQUANTS
│   ├─ Level curves of Q — convex, downward sloping
│   └─ MRTS = αL/βK = MPK/MPL
│
├─ OPTIMIZATION (Cost Minimization)
│   ├─ Lagrange: MRTS = r/w at optimum
│   ├─ K* = [...], L* = [...]  (closed form)
│   └─ λ = marginal cost = ∂C*/∂Q̄
│
├─ HESSIAN (Concavity)
│   ├─ det(H) = Q²αβ(1-α-β)/(K²L²)
│   ├─ α+β < 1 → H negative definite → Q strictly concave
│   └─ α+β = 1 → H negative semidefinite → Q concave
│
└─ IN ML/AI
    ├─ Scaling laws → same optimization structure
    ├─ Log-linear form → linear layer on log-inputs
    ├─ Lagrange multipliers → regularized training
    └─ CES generalization → mixture-of-experts, attention

docs.text:

  2. MIT OCW 18.02 — Denis Auroux, Lecture 13 (level curves, gradient, tangency). The geometric derivation of the optimality condition.

docs.title: Tangent Planes
docs.text: "A function is differentiable at a point if and only if it can be well-approximated by a linear map near that point. The tangent plane is that linear map, made geometric."

docs.title: §1. Motivation — From Tangent Lines to Tangent Planes
docs.text:
In single-variable calculus, given \(f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) differentiable at \(x = a\), the tangent line is:

\[L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)\]

This is the best linear approximation to \(f\) near \(a\). It touches the curve and shares its slope.

Now let \(f: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\), i.e., \(z = f(x, y)\). The graph is a surface in \(\mathbb{R}^3\). The natural question: what plays the role of the tangent line?

The answer is a plane — the tangent plane — and it is the unique plane that:

  1. Passes through the point \((a, b, f(a,b))\) on the surface
  2. Has the "correct" slope in every direction through that point

The existence of such a plane is not automatic. It requires differentiability, which in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is a strictly stronger condition than the existence of partial derivatives.

docs.title: §2. Partial Derivatives — The Two Obvious Slopes
docs.text:
Fix a point \((a, b)\) in the domain of \(f\).

Definition. The partial derivatives of \(f\) at \((a,b)\) are:

\[f_x(a,b) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a+h,, b) - f(a,b)}{h}\] \[f_y(a,b) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a,, b+k) - f(a,b)}{k}\]

Geometrically: \(f_x\) is the slope of the curve obtained by slicing the surface with the plane \(y = b\); similarly \(f_y\) with \(x = a\).

Key warning. Existence of \(f_x\) and \(f_y\) does not guarantee differentiability. The classical counterexample:

\[f(x,y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{xy}{x^2 + y^2} & (x,y) \neq (0,0) \ 0 & (x,y) = (0,0) \end{cases}\]

has \(f_x(0,0) = f_y(0,0) = 0\), but \(f\) is not even continuous at \((0,0)\) (approach along \(y = x\): limit is \(\frac{1}{2}\)). So no tangent plane exists there.

docs.title: §3. Differentiability — The Right Definition
docs.text:
Definition (Stewart §14.4, MIT 18.02 Notes). \(f\) is differentiable at \((a,b)\) if there exist constants \(A, B\) such that:

\[\lim_{(h,k) \to (0,0)} \frac{f(a+h,, b+k) - f(a,b) - Ah - Bk}{\sqrt{h^2 + k^2}} = 0\]

When this holds, one can show \(A = f_x(a,b)\) and \(B = f_y(a,b)\).

Interpretation. The error in approximating \(f(a+h, b+k)\) by \(f(a,b) + Ah + Bk\) vanishes faster than the distance \(\sqrt{h^2+k^2}\) to the base point. This is exactly what it means for a linear map to be "tangent."

Sufficient condition (very useful in practice). If \(f_x\) and \(f_y\) exist in a neighborhood of \((a,b)\) and are continuous at \((a,b)\), then \(f\) is differentiable at \((a,b)\).

Most functions encountered in practice (\(C^1\) functions) satisfy this automatically.

docs.title: §4. The Tangent Plane — Definition and Equation
docs.text:
Definition. If \(f\) is differentiable at \((a, b)\), the tangent plane to the surface \(z = f(x,y)\) at the point \(P = (a, b, f(a,b))\) is:

\[\boxed{z = f(a,b) + f_x(a,b)(x - a) + f_y(a,b)(y - b)}\]

Why is this a plane? Rewrite as:

\[z - f(a,b) = f_x(a,b)(x-a) + f_y(a,b)(y-b)\]

This is of the form \(\mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0) = 0\) with normal vector \(\mathbf{n} = \langle f_x(a,b),, f_y(a,b),, -1 \rangle\).

Uniqueness. The tangent plane is the unique plane through \(P\) such that every curve on the surface through \(P\) has its tangent line lying in the plane. This is what "tangent" means geometrically for surfaces.

docs.title: §5. The Linear Approximation (Linearization)
docs.text:
The tangent plane gives the linearization of \(f\) near \((a,b)\):

\[L(x,y) = f(a,b) + f_x(a,b)(x-a) + f_y(a,b)(y-b)\]

For \((x,y)\) near \((a,b)\):

\[f(x,y) \approx L(x,y)\]

The error is \(o(|(x-a, y-b)|)\), i.e., it goes to zero faster than the distance.

Total differential. Writing \(\Delta x = x - a\), \(\Delta y = y - b\), and \(\Delta z = f(x,y) - f(a,b)\):

\[\Delta z \approx dz = f_x, dx + f_y, dy\]

This is the total differential — an infinitesimal version of the tangent plane approximation, and arguably the single most important formula in multivariable differential calculus.

docs.title: Example 1 — Explicit Computation
docs.text:
Let \(f(x,y) = x^2 y + \sin(\pi y)\). Find the tangent plane at \((1, 1)\).

Step 1. Evaluate: \(f(1,1) = 1 \cdot 1 + \sin(\pi) = 1\).

Step 2. Partial derivatives: $\(f_x = 2xy \implies f_x(1,1) = 2\)$ $\(f_y = x^2 + \pi\cos(\pi y) \implies f_y(1,1) = 1 + \pi\cos(\pi) = 1 - \pi\)$

Step 3. Tangent plane: $\(z = 1 + 2(x-1) + (1-\pi)(y-1)\)$

Step 4. Check: at \((1,1)\), \(z = 1\). ✓

docs.title: Example 3 — Error Estimation via Total Differential
docs.text:
A cylindrical can has radius \(r = 5,\text{cm}\) and height \(h = 10,\text{cm}\), with measurement errors \(dr = 0.05,\text{cm}\), \(dh = 0.1,\text{cm}\). Estimate the error in the volume \(V = \pi r^2 h\).

\[dV = \frac{\partial V}{\partial r},dr + \frac{\partial V}{\partial h},dh = 2\pi r h, dr + \pi r^2, dh$$ $$= 2\pi(5)(10)(0.05) + \pi(25)(0.1) = 5\pi + 2.5\pi = 7.5\pi \approx 23.6,\text{cm}^3\]

docs.title: §7. Geometric Visualization
docs.text:
z
          |      ← surface z = f(x,y)
          |   /~~~~/
          |  /~~~~/ ← tangent plane at P
          | /  P·
          |/__________ y
         /
        x

Think of it this way: place a flat board tangent to a curved hill at a point \(P\). The board sits flush against the hill at \(P\) — touching it, matching the slope in both the east-west and north-south directions. That board is the tangent plane.

The normal vector to the plane is \(\mathbf{n} = \langle f_x(a,b),, f_y(a,b),, -1 \rangle\). It points "away" from the surface in the direction of steepest local tilt.

Implicit surfaces. For a surface defined by \(F(x,y,z) = 0\), the tangent plane at \((a,b,c)\) is:

\[F_x(a,b,c)(x-a) + F_y(a,b,c)(y-b) + F_z(a,b,c)(z-c) = 0\]

with normal \(\nabla F = \langle F_x, F_y, F_z \rangle\). This is the gradient theorem: the gradient is always normal to level sets/surfaces.

docs.title: §8. Connection to the Gradient and Directional Derivatives
docs.text:
The tangent plane formula can be written as:

\[z - f(a,b) = abla f(a,b) \cdot \langle x-a,, y-b angle\]

where \( abla f = \langle f_x, f_y angle\) is the gradient.

The directional derivative in direction \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}\) is:

\[D_{\hat{u}} f = abla f \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}}\]

This is the slope of the tangent plane in direction \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}\). The tangent plane encodes all directional derivatives simultaneously — it is the gradient's geometric incarnation.

Maximum slope occurs in direction \(\hat{\mathbf{u}} = rac{ abla f}{| abla f|}\), with value \(| abla f|\).

docs.title: §9. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: This is where the tangent plane stops being pure mathematics and becomes the engine of modern AI.

docs.title: 9.1 — Loss Landscapes and Local Linearization
docs.text:
In machine learning, we have a loss function \(\mathcal{L}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) where \(n\) can be billions (the number of parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) of a neural network). The tangent plane at any point \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0\) in parameter space is:

\[\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \approx \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0) + \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)^{\top}(\boldsymbol{\theta} - \boldsymbol{\theta}_0)\]

This is exactly the \(n\)-dimensional tangent hyperplane. Gradient descent moves along this plane to find the steepest downhill direction:

\[\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_t - \eta, \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)\]

Every gradient descent step is an implicit invocation of the tangent plane: we linearize the loss locally and take a step in the direction of steepest descent on that linearization.

docs.title: 9.2 — Backpropagation is Repeated Chain Rule on Tangent Planes
docs.text:
Consider a neural network \(f = f_L \circ f_{L-1} \circ \cdots \circ f_1\) where each \(f_i\) is a layer. Backpropagation computes \(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \boldsymbol{\theta}}\) via the chain rule:

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \boldsymbol{\theta}_i} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial f_L} \cdot \frac{\partial f_L}{\partial f_{L-1}} \cdots \frac{\partial f_{i+1}}{\partial f_i} \cdot \frac{\partial f_i}{\partial \boldsymbol{\theta}_i}\]

Each factor \(\frac{\partial f_k}{\partial f_{k-1}}\) is a Jacobian matrix — the multivariable generalization of the derivative, which is precisely the linear map whose graph is the tangent plane (or tangent hyperplane) of \(f_k\). Backpropagation is a recursive computation of tangent hyperplanes through the network.

docs.title: 9.3 — The Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK)
docs.text:
In the infinite-width limit, training a neural network is equivalent to kernel regression with the Neural Tangent Kernel:

\[K(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} f(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\theta})^{\top} \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} f(\mathbf{x}'; \boldsymbol{\theta})\]

This kernel measures the inner product of the tangent vectors (gradients) of the output with respect to parameters. In this regime, the network dynamics are entirely governed by local linearization — the network behaves like its own tangent plane around initialization, and the loss evolves linearly. This is one of the deepest theoretical results in deep learning (Jacot et al., 2018).

docs.title: 9.4 — Second-Order Methods and the Hessian
docs.text:
The tangent plane is a first-order (linear) approximation. A second-order approximation uses the Hessian \(H = \nabla^2 \mathcal{L}\):

\[\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \approx \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0) + \nabla \mathcal{L}^{\top}\delta\boldsymbol{\theta} + \frac{1}{2}\delta\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top} H, \delta\boldsymbol{\theta}\]

This is a quadratic approximation — a paraboloid tangent to the loss surface. Methods like Newton's method and natural gradient descent exploit this. The tangent plane is the zeroth-order piece of this expansion; understanding it is prerequisite to understanding curvature.

docs.title: 9.5 — Feature Space Geometry
docs.text: In classification, a linear classifier defines a hyperplane (tangent-plane-like object) in feature space. Support Vector Machines find the optimal separating hyperplane. When the data is nonlinear, a kernel maps data to a high-dimensional space where it becomes linearly separable — one is finding a tangent plane in the lifted space. Deep networks can be understood as learning a feature map \(\phi\) such that \(\mathcal{L}(\phi(\mathbf{x}))\) has a tractable tangent structure.

docs.title: §11. Theorems to Know Cold
docs.text:
Theorem 1 (Differentiability \(\Rightarrow\) Continuity). If \(f\) is differentiable at \((a,b)\), then \(f\) is continuous at \((a,b)\).

Theorem 2 (Sufficient Conditions for Differentiability). If \(f_x\) and \(f_y\) exist in an open disk about \((a,b)\) and are continuous at \((a,b)\), then \(f\) is differentiable at \((a,b)\).

Theorem 3 (Gradient and Level Curves). \( abla f(a,b)\) is perpendicular to the level curve \(f(x,y) = c\) at \((a,b)\).

Theorem 4 (Tangent Plane for Implicit Surfaces). If \(F(x,y,z) = 0\) defines a surface and \(F\) is differentiable with \( abla F eq \mathbf{0}\), the tangent plane at \((a,b,c)\) is \( abla F(a,b,c) \cdot \langle x-a, y-b, z-c angle = 0\).

Theorem 5 (Chain Rule, Gradient Form). If \(\mathbf{r}(t) = (x(t), y(t))\) is a smooth curve and \(f\) is differentiable: $\( rac{d}{dt} f(\mathbf{r}(t)) = abla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t)\)$

docs.title: §12. Things That Will Trip You Up
docs.text:
Partial derivatives exist \( ot\Rightarrow\) Differentiable. The pathological example above (\(f = xy/(x^2+y^2)\) at origin) is the canonical counterexample. Always cite it on exams.

The tangent plane only makes sense when \(f\) is differentiable. Do not write the tangent plane formula for a point of non-differentiability.

The gradient \( abla f \in \mathbb{R}^2\), not \(\mathbb{R}^3\). The normal to the tangent plane is \(\langle f_x, f_y, -1 angle\), which includes the \(-1\) from the \(-z\) term.

Linearization \( eq\) exact. \(L(x,y)\) is an approximation; the quality depends on second derivatives (curvature of the surface).
