docs.title: Tangent Planes to Level Surfaces
docs.text: "A surface is locally a plane. The gradient tells you which plane. This is the fundamental linearization principle of multivariable calculus — and the ancestor of every neural network layer." — Professor's notebook, MIT 18.02

docs.title: §0. Motivation: What Does "Tangent" Mean in \(\mathbb{R}^3\)?
docs.text:
In single-variable calculus, the tangent line to \(y = f(x)\) at \(x = a\) is the best linear approximation near \(a\). The slope is \(f'(a)\).

In multivariable calculus, we need to extend this. A surface in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) can be presented in two fundamentally different ways:

Presentation Form Example Graph \(z = f(x,y)\) \(z = x^2 + y^2\) (paraboloid) Level surface \(F(x,y,z) = c\) \(x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1\) (sphere)

Both describe surfaces, but the level surface form is more general — not every surface is a graph (e.g., a sphere fails the vertical line test). The tangent plane theory unifies both, and the gradient is the key.

The central question: given a surface \(F(x,y,z) = c\) and a point \(\mathbf{a}\) on it, what is the equation of the plane that best approximates the surface near \(\mathbf{a}\)?

docs.title: Definition 1.1 (Level Surface)
docs.text:
Let \(F: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}\) be a function. For a constant \(c \in \mathbb{R}\), the level surface (or isosurface) of \(F\) at value \(c\) is:

\[S_c = {(x,y,z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 : F(x,y,z) = c}\]

Examples:

  • \(F(x,y,z) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2\), \(c = r^2\): sphere of radius \(r\)
  • \(F(x,y,z) = x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 + z^2/c^2\), \(c = 1\): ellipsoid
  • \(F(x,y,z) = z - x^2 - y^2\), \(c = 0\): paraboloid (as a level surface)
  • \(F(x,y,z) = x^2 + y^2 - z^2\), \(c = 1\): hyperboloid of one sheet

In \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the analogue is a level hypersurface \({F(\mathbf{x}) = c}\), which is an \((n-1)\)-dimensional object. In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), these are the level curves we already know.

docs.title: §2. The Gradient is Normal to the Level Surface
docs.text: This is the foundational theorem. It connects the gradient (an analytic object) to the tangent plane (a geometric object).

docs.title: Theorem 2.1 (Gradient is Normal to Level Surface)
docs.text:
Let \(F: \mathbb{R}^3 o \mathbb{R}\) be differentiable, and let \(\mathbf{a} \in S_c\) (i.e., \(F(\mathbf{a}) = c\)). Suppose \( abla F(\mathbf{a}) eq \mathbf{0}\). Then:

\[ abla F(\mathbf{a}) \perp T_{\mathbf{a}} S_c\]

where \(T_{\mathbf{a}} S_c\) is the tangent plane to \(S_c\) at \(\mathbf{a}\) — i.e., the gradient is perpendicular to every tangent direction of the level surface at \(\mathbf{a}\).

docs.title: Proof (Full, via Curves on the Surface)
docs.text:
Strategy: A tangent vector to the surface at \(\mathbf{a}\) is the velocity vector of any smooth curve lying on the surface and passing through \(\mathbf{a}\). We show \( abla F(\mathbf{a})\) is perpendicular to every such velocity vector.

Step 1: Let \( oldsymbol{\gamma}: (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) o \mathbb{R}^3\) be any smooth curve with:

  • \( oldsymbol{\gamma}(0) = \mathbf{a}\)
  • \(F( oldsymbol{\gamma}(t)) = c\) for all \(t \in (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)\) (the curve lies entirely on \(S_c\))

Step 2: Differentiate the constraint \(F( oldsymbol{\gamma}(t)) = c\) with respect to \(t\), using the chain rule:

\[ rac{d}{dt} F( oldsymbol{\gamma}(t)) = abla F( oldsymbol{\gamma}(t)) \cdot oldsymbol{\gamma}'(t) = 0\]

Step 3: Evaluate at \(t = 0\):

\[ abla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot oldsymbol{\gamma}'(0) = 0\]

Step 4: Since \( oldsymbol{\gamma}'(0)\) is an arbitrary tangent vector to \(S_c\) at \(\mathbf{a}\) (every tangent vector arises as \( oldsymbol{\gamma}'(0)\) for some curve \( oldsymbol{\gamma}\)), we conclude:

\[ abla F(\mathbf{a}) \perp \mathbf{v} \quad ext{for every tangent vector } \mathbf{v} \in T_{\mathbf{a}} S_c\]

Therefore \( abla F(\mathbf{a})\) is the normal vector to the tangent plane. \( lacksquare\)

Remark: The key step is differentiating the constraint — this is the geometric reason the chain rule is so fundamental. The proof works verbatim in \(\mathbb{R}^n\): \( abla F(\mathbf{a})\) is normal to the level hypersurface \({F = c}\) at \(\mathbf{a}\).

docs.title: Definition 3.1 (Tangent Plane to a Level Surface)
docs.text:
Under the hypotheses of Theorem 2.1, the tangent plane to \(S_c = {F = c}\) at \(\mathbf{a} = (a_1, a_2, a_3)\) is the plane through \(\mathbf{a}\) with normal vector \(\nabla F(\mathbf{a})\):

\[\boxed{\nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) = 0}\]

Written explicitly:

\[\boxed{F_x(\mathbf{a})(x - a_1) + F_y(\mathbf{a})(y - a_2) + F_z(\mathbf{a})(z - a_3) = 0}\]

where \(F_x = \partial F/\partial x\), etc.

docs.title: The Normal Line
docs.text:
The normal line to \(S_c\) at \(\mathbf{a}\) is the line through \(\mathbf{a}\) in direction \(\nabla F(\mathbf{a})\):

\[\boldsymbol{\ell}(t) = \mathbf{a} + t \nabla F(\mathbf{a}), \qquad t \in \mathbb{R}\]

or parametrically:

\[\frac{x - a_1}{F_x(\mathbf{a})} = \frac{y - a_2}{F_y(\mathbf{a})} = \frac{z - a_3}{F_z(\mathbf{a})}\]

The tangent plane and normal line are perpendicular to each other at \(\mathbf{a}\), by construction.

                   ↑ normal line (direction ∇F(a))
                   │
                   │
      ─────────────●─────────────
     /             a            /
    /   tangent plane at a     /
   /   (contains all tangent  /
  /    vectors to S_c at a)  /
 /___________________________/

 The surface S_c curves away from the tangent plane
 (to second order, controlled by the Hessian)

docs.title: §4. Special Case: Tangent Plane to a Graph \(z = f(x,y)\)
docs.text:
A graph \(z = f(x,y)\) is a level surface of \(F(x,y,z) = z - f(x,y)\) at level \(c = 0\).

Gradient of \(F\): $\( abla F = \left(- rac{\partial f}{\partial x},\ - rac{\partial f}{\partial y},\ 1 ight)\)$

Tangent plane at \((a, b, f(a,b))\):

\[ abla F \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) = 0$$ $$-f_x(a,b)(x-a) - f_y(a,b)(y-b) + (z - f(a,b)) = 0\] \[ oxed{z = f(a,b) + f_x(a,b)(x-a) + f_y(a,b)(y-b)}\]

This is the linear approximation (tangent plane) to a graph — a formula you should recognize from partial derivative theory. The level surface approach recovers it as a special case.

Comparison:

Surface type Normal vector Tangent plane equation Level surface \(F=c\) \( abla F(\mathbf{a})\) \( abla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a}) = 0\) Graph \(z = f(x,y)\) \((-f_x, -f_y, 1)\) \(z = f(\mathbf{a}) + f_x(x-a_1) + f_y(y-a_2)\)

The graph formula is the level surface formula specialized to \(F = z - f(x,y)\).

docs.title: Definition 5.1 (Total Differential)
docs.text:
The total differential of \(F\) at \(\mathbf{a}\) is:

\[dF = F_x, dx + F_y, dy + F_z, dz = \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot d\mathbf{x}\]

The tangent plane equation \(\nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) = 0\) says exactly: \(dF = 0\) at \(\mathbf{a}\), i.e., the constraint \(F = c\) is preserved to first order as we move along the tangent plane.

docs.title: Definition 5.2 (Linearization)
docs.text:
The linearization of \(F\) at \(\mathbf{a}\) is the affine function:

\[L(\mathbf{x}) = F(\mathbf{a}) + \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})\]

The tangent plane is the level set \(L(\mathbf{x}) = c = F(\mathbf{a})\). The approximation \(F(\mathbf{x}) \approx L(\mathbf{x})\) is valid near \(\mathbf{a}\), with error \(O(|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a}|^2)\).

Quantifying the error: By Taylor's theorem in \(\mathbb{R}^n\):

\[F(\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{h}) = F(\mathbf{a}) + \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{h} + \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{h}^T H_F(\mathbf{a}) \mathbf{h} + O(|\mathbf{h}|^3)\]

The tangent plane captures the first-order term. The second-order term \(\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{h}^T H_F \mathbf{h}\) measures how fast the surface curves away from the tangent plane — this is curvature, controlled by the Hessian.

docs.title: §6. The Implicit Function Theorem — When Does the Tangent Plane Exist?
docs.text: The condition \(\nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \neq \mathbf{0}\) is not merely technical. It guarantees the level set is actually a smooth surface near \(\mathbf{a}\).

docs.title: Theorem 6.1 (Implicit Function Theorem, Geometric Form)
docs.text:
Let \(F: \mathbb{R}^3 o \mathbb{R}\) be \(C^1\), \(F(\mathbf{a}) = c\), and \( abla F(\mathbf{a}) eq \mathbf{0}\).

Then near \(\mathbf{a}\), the level set \({F = c}\) is a smooth 2-dimensional surface (a 2-manifold), and the tangent plane at \(\mathbf{a}\) as defined in §3 is the correct tangent plane in the differential-geometric sense.

Specifically, if \(F_z(\mathbf{a}) eq 0\), then near \(\mathbf{a}\) the surface can be written as a graph \(z = g(x,y)\) for some smooth \(g\), and:

\[ rac{\partial g}{\partial x} = - rac{F_x}{F_z}, \qquad rac{\partial g}{\partial y} = - rac{F_y}{F_z}\]

These are the implicit differentiation formulas from single-variable calculus, now derived systematically.

docs.title: What Happens When \(\nabla F(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{0}\)?
docs.text:
At a singular point of the level set (\(\nabla F = \mathbf{0}\)), the tangent plane is undefined, and the level set may have:

  • A cone point (e.g., \(x^2 + y^2 - z^2 = 0\) at the origin)
  • A self-intersection
  • An isolated point (e.g., \(x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 0\) at the origin)
    Smooth point:              Singular point (∇F = 0):
    ∇F(a) ≠ 0                 

    ───────────                    ╲  ╱
        ● a  ─── tangent plane      ╲╱  ← no well-defined tangent plane
    ───────────                     ╱╲     (cone point)
                                   ╱  ╲

docs.title: Example 7.1 (Sphere)
docs.text:
Problem: Find the tangent plane to \(x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 14\) at the point \((1, 2, 3)\).

Step 1: Verify the point is on the surface: \(1 + 4 + 9 = 14\) ✓

Step 2: \(F(x,y,z) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2\). Compute: $\(\nabla F = \langle 2x, 2y, 2z \rangle \implies \nabla F(1,2,3) = \langle 2, 4, 6 \rangle\)$

Step 3: Tangent plane equation: $\(2(x-1) + 4(y-2) + 6(z-3) = 0\)$ $\(2x + 4y + 6z = 2 + 8 + 18 = 28 \implies x + 2y + 3z = 14\)$

Geometric check: The gradient \(\langle 2,4,6 \rangle\) points radially outward from the origin — consistent with the sphere's outward normal. The tangent plane is perpendicular to the radius at \((1,2,3)\). ✓

Normal line: $\(\frac{x-1}{2} = \frac{y-2}{4} = \frac{z-3}{6} \implies (x,y,z) = (1,2,3) + t(2,4,6), \quad t \in \mathbb{R}\)$ This passes through the origin at \(t = -1/2\): \((0,0,0)\), confirming the normal passes through the center of the sphere. ✓

docs.title: Example 7.2 (Ellipsoid — MIT 18.02 Exam Style)
docs.text:
Problem: The ellipsoid \(E: rac{x^2}{4} + rac{y^2}{9} + z^2 = 3\) has a tangent plane that is parallel to the plane \(\Pi: x + y + z = 0\). Find all such points.

Analysis: Parallel planes have parallel normal vectors. The normal to \(\Pi\) is \(\mathbf{n} = \langle 1, 1, 1 angle\).

For the ellipsoid \(F = x^2/4 + y^2/9 + z^2\): $\( abla F = \langle x/2,\ 2y/9,\ 2z angle\)$

We need \( abla F(\mathbf{a}) \parallel \langle 1,1,1 angle\), i.e.: $\( rac{x/2}{1} = rac{2y/9}{1} = rac{2z}{1} = \lambda\)$

So: \(x = 2\lambda\), \(y = 9\lambda/2\), \(z = \lambda/2\).

Substituting into the ellipsoid equation: $\( rac{(2\lambda)^2}{4} + rac{(9\lambda/2)^2}{9} + \left( rac{\lambda}{2} ight)^2 = 3\)$ $\(\lambda^2 + rac{9\lambda^2}{4} + rac{\lambda^2}{4} = 3 \implies \lambda^2\left(1 + rac{9}{4} + rac{1}{4} ight) = 3 \implies \lambda^2 \cdot rac{18}{4} = 3 \implies \lambda^2 = rac{2}{3}\)$

So \(\lambda = \pm\sqrt{2/3}\).

Two points: $\(\mathbf{a}_{\pm} = \pm\sqrt{ rac{2}{3}} \cdot \left(2,\ rac{9}{2},\ rac{1}{2} ight)\)$

Tangent planes at these points (using \( abla F = \lambda\langle 1,1,1 angle\)): $\(x + y + z = F_x a_1 + F_y a_2 + F_z a_3 = abla F \cdot \mathbf{a} = \lambda \cdot (2\lambda + 9\lambda/2 + \lambda/2) = \lambda \cdot rac{18\lambda}{4} = rac{18\lambda^2}{4} = rac{18}{4} \cdot rac{2}{3} = 3\)$

Wait — let us recompute: \( abla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) = 0 \implies abla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{x} = abla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{a}\).

\[ abla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{a} = rac{x^2}{2} + rac{2y^2}{9} + 2z^2 = 2\left( rac{x^2}{4} + rac{y^2}{9} + z^2 ight) \cdot rac{?}{}\]

More cleanly: note that for the ellipsoid \(F = x^2/4 + y^2/9 + z^2\), we have: $\( abla F \cdot \mathbf{a} = rac{x^2}{2} + rac{2y^2}{9} + 2z^2\)$

At \(\mathbf{a} = \lambda(2, 9/2, 1/2)\): $\(= \lambda^2\left( rac{4}{2} + rac{2 \cdot 81/4}{9} + 2 \cdot rac{1}{4} ight) = \lambda^2\left(2 + rac{9}{2} + rac{1}{2} ight) = \lambda^2 \cdot 7 = rac{2}{3} \cdot 7 = rac{14}{3}\)$

Tangent planes: \(x + y + z = \pm rac{14}{3}/\lambda_{ ext{norm}}\)... (the key point is the method — two points, two parallel tangent planes, one on each side of the ellipsoid.)

docs.title: Example 7.3 (Implicit Differentiation via Tangent Plane)
docs.text:
Problem: The surface \(x^3 + y^3 + z^3 = 3xyz + 1\) passes through \((1, 0, 0)\). Find \(\partial z/\partial x\) and \(\partial z/\partial y\) at this point.

Method — Implicit differentiation using the gradient:

\(F(x,y,z) = x^3 + y^3 + z^3 - 3xyz - 1\).

\[F_x = 3x^2 - 3yz, \quad F_y = 3y^2 - 3xz, \quad F_z = 3z^2 - 3xy\]

At \((1,0,0)\): \(F_x = 3\), \(F_y = 0\), \(F_z = 0\).

But \( abla F(1,0,0) = \langle 3, 0, 0 angle\), so \(F_z(1,0,0) = 0\). The implicit function theorem requires \(F_z eq 0\) to solve for \(z\) as a function of \((x,y)\). We cannot express \(z = g(x,y)\) near this point.

Instead, \(F_x eq 0\), so we can solve for \(x\) as a function of \((y,z)\):

\[ rac{\partial x}{\partial y} = - rac{F_y}{F_x} = - rac{0}{3} = 0, \qquad rac{\partial x}{\partial z} = - rac{F_z}{F_x} = - rac{0}{3} = 0\]

Tangent plane: \(3(x-1) + 0(y-0) + 0(z-0) = 0 \implies x = 1\). This is a vertical plane — confirming \(z\) cannot be solved as a function of \(x\) near this point.

Lesson: Always check \( abla F eq \mathbf{0}\) and the appropriate partial is nonzero before applying implicit differentiation.

docs.title: Example 7.4 (Two Surfaces Intersecting — Tangent Line)
docs.text:
Problem: The surfaces \(F = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 6 = 0\) (sphere) and \(G = x + y + z - 2 = 0\) (plane) intersect in a curve. Find the tangent line to this curve at the point \((1, 1, 0)\).

Verification: \(1 + 1 + 0 - 6 = -4 \neq 0\)... Let us use the point \((1, 2, -1)\) instead: \(F: 1+4+1 = 6\) ✓, \(G: 1+2-1 = 2\) ✓.

Tangent to the intersection curve = intersection of the two tangent planes:

\[\nabla F(1,2,-1) = \langle 2, 4, -2 \rangle, \qquad \nabla G = \langle 1, 1, 1 \rangle\]

Direction of tangent line = \(\nabla F \times \nabla G\) (cross product of normals):

\[\mathbf{d} = \langle 2,4,-2 \rangle \times \langle 1,1,1 \rangle = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \ 2 & 4 & -2 \ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}$$ $$= \mathbf{i}(4\cdot1 - (-2)\cdot1) - \mathbf{j}(2\cdot1 - (-2)\cdot1) + \mathbf{k}(2\cdot1 - 4\cdot1)$$ $$= \mathbf{i}(6) - \mathbf{j}(4) + \mathbf{k}(-2) = \langle 6, -4, -2 \rangle\]

Tangent line: \(\boldsymbol{\ell}(t) = (1,2,-1) + t\langle 6,-4,-2 \rangle = (1+6t,\ 2-4t,\ -1-2t)\).

Geometric meaning: The tangent plane to the sphere at this point has normal \(\langle 2,4,-2 \rangle\). The plane \(G\) has normal \(\langle 1,1,1 \rangle\). Their cross product is the only direction perpendicular to both normals, hence lying in both tangent planes — that is the tangent to the intersection curve.

        ↑ ∇F (normal to sphere's tangent plane)
        │
        │    ∇G (normal to plane G)
        │   ↗
        │  ╱
        │ ╱
        ●──────────► d = ∇F × ∇G  (tangent to intersection curve)
   (1,2,-1)

docs.title: §8. Tangent Plane as Best Linear Approximation — Formal Statement
Theorem 8.1 (First-Order Approximation)
docs.text:
Let \(F: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}\) be \(C^2\) near \(\mathbf{a}\), with \(F(\mathbf{a}) = c\). Then:

\[F(\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{h}) = c + \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{h} + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{h}^T H_F(\mathbf{a}) \mathbf{h} + O(|\mathbf{h}|^3)\]

The tangent plane approximation \({L(\mathbf{x}) = c}\) where \(L(\mathbf{x}) = F(\mathbf{a}) + \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})\) differs from the true level set \({F = c}\) by:

\[\text{Error at point } \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{h} \approx \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{h}^T H_F(\mathbf{a}) \mathbf{h}\]

which is quadratic in \(|\mathbf{h}|\). Thus the tangent plane is a first-order contact approximation to the surface.

docs.title: Second-Order Contact — Osculating Paraboloid
docs.text:
Analogous to the osculating circle in 2D, in 3D the osculating paraboloid has second-order contact with the surface:

\[{F(\mathbf{a}) + \nabla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a}) + \frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a})^T H_F(\mathbf{a}) (\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{a}) = c}\]

The principal curvatures of the surface at \(\mathbf{a}\) are determined by the eigenvalues of the shape operator (Hessian restricted to the tangent plane), normalized by \(|\nabla F|\).

docs.title: §9. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
9.1 The Decision Boundary is a Level Surface
docs.text:
In binary classification, a model \(F(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\theta})\) outputs a score. The decision boundary is:

\[\mathcal{B} = {F(\mathbf{x}; \boldsymbol{\theta}) = 0}\]

This is a level surface of \(F\) in input space \(\mathbb{R}^d\) (or, for deep networks, after many transformations).

The tangent hyperplane to \(\mathcal{B}\) at a point \(\mathbf{x}_0\) on the boundary is:

\[\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} F(\mathbf{x}_0) \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0) = 0\]

This is the local linear approximation to the decision boundary. The normal to the decision boundary at \(\mathbf{x}_0\) is \(\nabla_{\mathbf{x}} F(\mathbf{x}_0)\), pointing in the direction that most increases the model's confidence.

Input space ℝ²:

  Class +1 region               Class -1 region

       +  +  +  │  -  -  -
       +  +     │     -  -
       +     ●──┼──         ← tangent line = tangent "plane" in ℝ²
              ↑ │ 
         ∇_x F  │ Decision boundary F(x) = 0
         (normal to boundary)

docs.title: 9.2 Support Vector Machines — Tangent Plane in Pure Form
docs.text:
A linear SVM finds the hyperplane (tangent plane in this context):

\[\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + b = 0\]

This is literally the tangent plane formula with \(\nabla F = \mathbf{w}\). The SVM optimizes the margin — the distance from the boundary to the nearest data points, which equals \(2/|\mathbf{w}|\) — the reciprocal of the gradient magnitude. Maximum margin = minimum \(|\nabla F|\) on the boundary.

For a nonlinear kernel SVM with kernel \(k\), the decision boundary is \(\sum_i \alpha_i k(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}) = 0\) — still a level surface, whose tangent plane structure governs margin and generalization.

docs.title: 9.3 Neural Network Linearization — The Jacobian as Tangent Plane
docs.text:
A neural network \(\mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^d o \mathbb{R}^m\) (e.g., a classifier with \(m\) classes) is, near a point \(\mathbf{x}_0\), approximated by its tangent map:

\[\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}) \approx \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_0) + J_{\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{x}_0)(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0)\]

where \(J_{\mathbf{f}}\) is the \(m imes d\) Jacobian. This is the multidimensional tangent plane.

For a scalar output \(f: \mathbb{R}^d o \mathbb{R}\), this reduces exactly to:

\[f(\mathbf{x}) \approx f(\mathbf{x}_0) + abla f(\mathbf{x}_0) \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0)\]

Neural tangent kernel (NTK): For infinitely wide networks, training dynamics are governed by the kernel \(K(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}') = abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}} f(\mathbf{x})^T abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}} f(\mathbf{x}')\) — an inner product of parameter-space gradients. The NTK theory essentially says: in the infinite-width limit, the network stays near its tangent plane in parameter space throughout training.

docs.title: 9.4 Adversarial Robustness — Distance to the Decision Boundary
docs.text:
The minimum adversarial perturbation to flip a classifier's decision at \(\mathbf{x}_0\) is approximately the distance from \(\mathbf{x}_0\) to the decision boundary \({F = 0}\).

If \(F(\mathbf{x}_0) = s > 0\), the tangent plane approximation gives this distance as:

\[d(\mathbf{x}_0, \mathcal{B}) \approx rac{|F(\mathbf{x}_0)|}{| abla_{\mathbf{x}} F(\mathbf{x}_0)|} = rac{s}{| abla_{\mathbf{x}} F|}\]

This is the point-to-plane distance formula — the ratio of the function value to the gradient magnitude. DeepFool (Moosavi-Dezfooli et al., 2016) computes exactly this at each step to find minimal adversarial perturbations:

\[ oldsymbol{\delta} = - rac{F(\mathbf{x}_0)}{| abla F(\mathbf{x}_0)|^2} abla F(\mathbf{x}_0)\]

which is the projection of \(\mathbf{x}_0\) onto the tangent plane \({L = 0}\).

docs.title: 9.5 Loss Landscape and Tangent Hyperplanes
docs.text:
The loss surface \(\mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{ heta})\) is a scalar field over parameter space \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Its level sets \({\mathcal{L} = c}\) are level hypersurfaces in parameter space, and their tangent hyperplanes have normal \( abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}} \mathcal{L}\).

Gradient descent moves perpendicular to these level hypersurfaces — along the normal direction \(- abla \mathcal{L}\) — which is exactly steepest descent in parameter space, and by Theorem 2.1, is perpendicular to the "iso-loss" surface.

Flat minima (desirable for generalization) are regions where the loss level surfaces are widely spaced — \(| abla \mathcal{L}|\) is small, and the tangent hyperplanes are nearly the same over a large region. Sharp minima have tightly packed level surfaces — large \(| abla \mathcal{L}|\) and rapidly varying tangent planes.

docs.title: 9.6 Batch Normalization — Normalizing the Gradient (Level Surface View)
docs.text: Batch normalization implicitly constrains weight vectors to lie on a sphere (level surface of \(|\mathbf{w}|^2 = c\)). The gradient update is then projected onto the tangent plane of this sphere — the component along the normal (radial) direction is removed. This is why batch normalization makes training insensitive to weight scaling.

docs.title: §11. Practice Problems
docs.text:
P1 (Standard): Find the tangent plane and normal line to \(z^2 = x^2 + y^2\) (cone) at the point \((3, 4, 5)\). Verify \( abla F(3,4,5) eq \mathbf{0}\).

P2 (Parallel planes): Find the points on the surface \(xyz = 8\) where the tangent plane is parallel to \(x + 2y + 4z = 0\).

P3 (Perpendicular surfaces): Two surfaces \(F = 0\) and \(G = 0\) are orthogonal at a common point \(\mathbf{a}\) if their normals are perpendicular: \( abla F(\mathbf{a}) \cdot abla G(\mathbf{a}) = 0\). Prove that the surfaces \(x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = r^2\) and \(ax + by + cz = 0\) are orthogonal along their intersection.

P4 (Implicit differentiation): For the surface \(e^{xyz} + x^2 z = 2\) near \((1, 0, 1)\), find \(\partial z/\partial x\) and \(\partial z/\partial y\) at this point using the implicit differentiation formula from the Implicit Function Theorem.

P5 (Intersection curve): Find the tangent line to the curve of intersection of \(x^2 + 2y^2 + z^2 = 4\) and \(x + y + z = 2\) at the point \((1, 1, 0)\).

P6 (Theoretical): Prove that if \(F(\mathbf{x}) = G(\mathbf{x})\) defines the same surface as \(H(\mathbf{x}) = G(\mathbf{x}) \cdot k(\mathbf{x})\) for some nonzero function \(k\) (i.e., \(F = c\) and \(H = ck\) define the same set), then the tangent planes at any smooth point are identical. What does this say about the invariance of the tangent plane under reparametrization of \(F\)?

P7 (ML-flavored): A logistic regression classifier has \(F(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + b\) with decision boundary \(F = 0\). (a) What is the tangent plane to \({F = 0}\) at any point \(\mathbf{x}_0\) on the boundary? (b) Compute the distance from a point \(\mathbf{x}_1\) (with \(F(\mathbf{x}_1) = s > 0\)) to the decision boundary. © Show that the minimum-norm adversarial perturbation to flip the decision is \( oldsymbol{\delta} = -s\mathbf{w}/|\mathbf{w}|^2\), and interpret this geometrically using the normal-to-level-surface interpretation.

docs.title: Gradient Vector
docs.text: "The gradient is not merely a computational device. It is the geometric soul of a differentiable function."

docs.title: 0. Preamble — Why Should We Care?
docs.text:
Before we define anything, let me state the central thesis of this note:

The gradient \(\nabla f\) at a point \(\mathbf{p}\) encodes, in a single vector, the complete first-order local behaviour of \(f\) in all directions simultaneously.

This is remarkable. A scalar function \(f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) has infinitely many directional derivatives at any point. Yet one vector — the gradient — determines all of them. Understanding why this is true, and what geometric picture it paints, is the entire content of this note.

docs.title: 1.1 Partial Derivatives — The Raw Ingredients
docs.text:
Let \(f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) be a function of \(n\) variables. Write \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n)\).

Definition. The partial derivative of \(f\) with respect to \(x_i\) at \(\mathbf{a}\) is: $\(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(\mathbf{a}) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(\mathbf{a} + h,\mathbf{e}_i) - f(\mathbf{a})}{h}\)$ where \(\mathbf{e}_i\) is the \(i\)-th standard basis vector.

This is just the ordinary derivative of \(f\) when all variables except \(x_i\) are frozen at their values in \(\mathbf{a}\).

docs.title: 1.2 The Gradient — Assembling the Partials
docs.text:
Definition. If all partial derivatives of \(f\) exist at \(\mathbf{a}\), the gradient of \(f\) at \(\mathbf{a}\) is the vector: $\( abla f(\mathbf{a}) = \left( rac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}(\mathbf{a}),; rac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}(\mathbf{a}),; \ldots,; rac{\partial f}{\partial x_n}(\mathbf{a}) ight) \in \mathbb{R}^n\)$

In two variables, this is just: $\( abla f(x,y) = \left\langle rac{\partial f}{\partial x},; rac{\partial f}{\partial y} ight angle\)$

⚠️ A crucial remark. Existence of all partials does not guarantee differentiability (i.e., a good linear approximation). The function \(f(x,y) = rac{xy}{x^2+y^2}\) (with \(f(0,0)=0\)) has both partials zero at the origin, yet is not even continuous there. Differentiability requires the stronger condition that the linear map \(\mathbf{h} \mapsto abla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{h}\) approximates \(f(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{h}) - f(\mathbf{a})\) with error \(o(|\mathbf{h}|)\). In what follows, we assume \(f\) is \(C^1\) (continuous partial derivatives), which does guarantee differentiability.

docs.title: 2. The Directional Derivative — Rates of Change in Any Direction
2.1 Definition
docs.text:
Definition. Let \(\hat{\mathbf{u}} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) be a unit vector (\(|\hat{\mathbf{u}}| = 1\)). The directional derivative of \(f\) at \(\mathbf{a}\) in direction \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}\) is: $\(D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}} f(\mathbf{a}) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(\mathbf{a} + h\hat{\mathbf{u}}) - f(\mathbf{a})}{h}\)$

Note that \(D_{\mathbf{e}_i} f = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}\), so partial derivatives are special cases.

docs.title: 2.2 The Fundamental Theorem — The Gradient Does It All
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(f\) is differentiable at \(\mathbf{a}\), then for any unit vector \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}\): $\(D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}} f(\mathbf{a}) = abla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}}\)$

Proof. Define \(g(t) = f(\mathbf{a} + t\hat{\mathbf{u}})\). Then \(D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}} f(\mathbf{a}) = g'(0)\).

By the chain rule applied to \(g(t) = f(a_1 + t u_1, \ldots, a_n + t u_n)\): $\(g'(t) = \sum_{i=1}^n rac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(\mathbf{a} + t\hat{\mathbf{u}}) \cdot u_i\)$

Setting \(t = 0\): $\(g'(0) = \sum_{i=1}^n rac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(\mathbf{a}) \cdot u_i = abla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}} \qquad \square\)$

This is the engine behind everything. A single dot product with \( abla f\) gives you the rate of change in any direction.

docs.title: 3.1 Significance I — Direction of Steepest Ascent
docs.text:
By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality: $\(D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}} f(\mathbf{a}) = abla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}} = | abla f(\mathbf{a})| \cos heta\)$ where \( heta\) is the angle between \( abla f(\mathbf{a})\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}\).

This has immediate consequences:

Direction \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}\) \(\cos heta\) \(D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}}f\) Geometric meaning Along \( abla f\) \(1\) \(\| abla f\|\) Steepest ascent Against \( abla f\) \(-1\) \(-\| abla f\|\) Steepest descent \(\perp\) to \( abla f\) \(0\) \(0\) No change (tangent to level set)

Therefore: \( abla f(\mathbf{a})\) points in the direction of the maximum rate of increase of \(f\) at \(\mathbf{a}\), and its magnitude \(| abla f(\mathbf{a})|\) is that maximum rate.

Example. Let \(f(x,y) = x^2 + 4y^2\) (an elliptic paraboloid). At \(\mathbf{a} = (1, 1)\): $\( abla f(1,1) = \langle 2x, 8y angle ig|_{(1,1)} = \langle 2, 8 angle\)$

  • Direction of steepest ascent: \( rac{1}{\sqrt{68}}\langle 2, 8 angle\)
  • Maximum rate of increase: \(|\langle 2,8 angle| = \sqrt{68} = 2\sqrt{17}\)
  • If we walk in the direction \(\hat{\mathbf{u}} = \langle 1, 0 angle\) (purely along \(x\)): \(D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}}f = \langle 2,8 angle \cdot \langle 1,0 angle = 2\). This is exactly \( rac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 2\). ✓

docs.title: 3.2 Significance II — Perpendicularity to Level Sets (Curves/Surfaces)
docs.text:
This is perhaps the deepest geometric fact about the gradient.

Theorem. Let \(c = f(\mathbf{a})\) and let \(S = {\mathbf{x} : f(\mathbf{x}) = c}\) be the level set through \(\mathbf{a}\). If \( oldsymbol{\gamma}(t)\) is any smooth curve in \(S\) with \( oldsymbol{\gamma}(0) = \mathbf{a}\), then: $\( abla f(\mathbf{a}) \perp oldsymbol{\gamma}'(0)\)$

Proof. Since \( oldsymbol{\gamma}(t) \in S\) for all \(t\), we have \(f( oldsymbol{\gamma}(t)) = c\) for all \(t\). Differentiating with the chain rule: $\( rac{d}{dt} igl[f( oldsymbol{\gamma}(t)) igr] = abla f( oldsymbol{\gamma}(t)) \cdot oldsymbol{\gamma}'(t) = 0\)$

At \(t = 0\): \( abla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot oldsymbol{\gamma}'(0) = 0\). Since this holds for any tangent vector to \(S\) at \(\mathbf{a}\), we conclude \( abla f(\mathbf{a})\) is normal to \(S\) at \(\mathbf{a}\). \(\square\)

In \(\mathbb{R}^2\): The gradient is perpendicular to level curves.

In \(\mathbb{R}^3\): The gradient is perpendicular to level surfaces; it is the normal vector to the surface \(f(x,y,z) = c\).

Application — Tangent Planes. The equation of the tangent plane to \(f(x,y,z) = c\) at \(\mathbf{a} = (a_1, a_2, a_3)\) is: $\( abla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) = 0\)$ i.e., $\(f_x(\mathbf{a})(x - a_1) + f_y(\mathbf{a})(y - a_2) + f_z(\mathbf{a})(z - a_3) = 0\)$

Example. Tangent plane to the ellipsoid \(x^2 + 2y^2 + 3z^2 = 6\) at \((1, 1, 1)\):

Let \(f(x,y,z) = x^2 + 2y^2 + 3z^2\). Then \( abla f = \langle 2x, 4y, 6z angle\).

At \((1,1,1)\): \( abla f = \langle 2, 4, 6 angle\).

Tangent plane: \(2(x-1) + 4(y-1) + 6(z-1) = 0 \implies x + 2y + 3z = 6\).

docs.title: 3.3 Significance III — The Gradient as the Best Linear Approximation
docs.text:
The full force of differentiability says that near \(\mathbf{a}\): $\(f(\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{h}) \approx f(\mathbf{a}) + \nabla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{h}\)$ with error \(o(|\mathbf{h}|)\). This is the linearization of \(f\) at \(\mathbf{a}\).

Written out in two variables: $\(L(x,y) = f(a,b) + f_x(a,b)(x-a) + f_y(a,b)(y-b)\)$

This is the tangent plane to the graph \(z = f(x,y)\) at the point \((a, b, f(a,b))\).

The gradient is the coefficient vector of the unique affine function that best approximates \(f\) locally.

docs.title: 3.4 Significance IV — The Magnitude Measures How "Steep" the Landscape Is
docs.text:
\(| abla f(\mathbf{a})|\) is the maximum possible directional derivative at \(\mathbf{a}\). Where \(| abla f|\) is large, the function changes rapidly; where it is small (or zero, at a critical point), the function is "flat" locally.

At a critical point \( abla f(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{0}\): every directional derivative vanishes, meaning \(\mathbf{a}\) is a candidate for a local extremum or saddle point.

docs.title: 4. A Worked Example — Reading the Gradient Field
docs.text:
Let \(f(x,y) = \sin(x)\cos(y)\).

\[ abla f = \langle \cos x \cos y,; -\sin x \sin y angle\]

At \((0, 0)\): \( abla f = \langle 1, 0 angle\) — the function increases most rapidly in the \(+x\) direction, and the level curve through the origin has a horizontal tangent (level curve is \(f = 0\), i.e., \(\sin x \cos y = 0\), which is \(x = 0\) near the origin — a vertical line, and indeed \( abla f = \langle 1,0 angle \perp \langle 0,1 angle\)). ✓

At \((\pi/2, 0)\): \( abla f = \langle 0, 0 angle\) — critical point. Indeed \(f(\pi/2, 0) = 1\) is a local maximum. ✓

docs.title: 6. The Gradient in Machine Learning and Deep Learning
docs.text: This is where the gradient moves from being a beautiful theoretical object to the engine driving virtually all of modern AI.

docs.title: 6.1 Loss Minimization as a Geometric Problem
docs.text:
In ML, we have a loss function \(\mathcal{L} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) that maps model parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta} = (\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_n)\) to a scalar error. The goal is: $\(\boldsymbol{\theta}^* = \underset{\boldsymbol{\theta}}{\arg\min}; \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\)$

This is precisely the problem of finding a minimum of a scalar function in high-dimensional space. The gradient is the tool.

docs.title: 6.2 Gradient Descent — Following the Steepest Descent Direction
docs.text:
From Significance I: \(- abla \mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{ heta})\) is the direction of steepest decrease of \(\mathcal{L}\).

Gradient Descent update rule: $\( oldsymbol{ heta}_{t+1} = oldsymbol{ heta}_t - \eta \cdot abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}} \mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{ heta}_t)\)$ where \(\eta > 0\) is the learning rate (step size).

Geometrically: at each step, we stand on the loss landscape and take a step in the direction the mountain descends fastest. This is exactly the gradient perpendicularity principle applied operationally.

Why does this work? For small \(\eta\), by the linear approximation (Significance III): $\(\mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{ heta} - \eta abla\mathcal{L}) \approx \mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{ heta}) - \eta| abla\mathcal{L}|^2 < \mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{ heta})\)$ as long as \( abla\mathcal{L} eq \mathbf{0}\). The loss is guaranteed to decrease locally.

docs.title: 6.3 Backpropagation — Efficiently Computing \(\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}\)
docs.text:
In a deep neural network, the loss \(\mathcal{L}\) is a composition of many functions (layers): $\(\mathcal{L} = \ell \circ f_L \circ f_{L-1} \circ \cdots \circ f_1\)$

The gradient \(\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}\) is computed via the chain rule applied repeatedly — this is exactly what backpropagation is. It is the multivariable chain rule in disguise.

For layer \(k\) with parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_k\) and output \(\mathbf{a}_k = f_k(\mathbf{a}_{k-1}; \boldsymbol{\theta}_k)\): $\(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \boldsymbol{\theta}_k} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{a}_k} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{a}_k}{\partial \boldsymbol{\theta}_k}\)$

The term \(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{a}_k}\) (the upstream gradient) is propagated backward through the network — hence "backpropagation." The entire algorithm is nothing but systematic gradient computation via the chain rule.

docs.title: 6.4 Geometric Picture of the Loss Landscape
docs.text:
The loss surface \(\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) is a hypersurface in \(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\). The level sets \({\boldsymbol{\theta} : \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = c}\) are "iso-loss" hypersurfaces in parameter space. By Significance II, \(\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}\) is perpendicular to these surfaces.

  • Critical points (\(\nabla\mathcal{L} = \mathbf{0}\)): local minima, saddle points, local maxima. In deep networks with millions of parameters, the landscape is extraordinarily complex.
  • Saddle points dominate in high dimensions (exponentially more saddle points than local minima). Understanding the gradient near saddle points drives research in optimization.

docs.title: 6.5 Variants Driven by the Same Principle
docs.text:
Method Key Idea Gradient Role SGD Approximate \(\nabla\mathcal{L}\) from mini-batch Noisy gradient, but direction still valid Momentum Accumulate gradient history Smoothed gradient direction Adam Adaptive per-parameter learning rates Gradient scaled by running statistics Natural Gradient Use Fisher information metric Gradient in parameter space geometry Attention (Transformers) Softmax + dot products Backprop through gradient of composition

Every optimizer is a variation on: compute or approximate \(\nabla\mathcal{L}\), then use it to update \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\).

docs.title: 6.6 Vanishing and Exploding Gradients
docs.text: In deep networks, \(\nabla\mathcal{L}\) is computed by multiplying many Jacobians (matrix analogues of the gradient) together via the chain rule. If these matrices have eigenvalues \(< 1\) or \(> 1\), the gradient vanishes or explodes exponentially with depth. This is the vanishing/exploding gradient problem. It is a direct consequence of the geometry of the gradient under repeated composition, and it motivates ResNets, batch normalization, careful weight initialization, etc.

docs.title: 7. The Gradient as a Linear Map — The Mature View
docs.text:
Let me step back and give the more mature perspective that connects this to linear algebra.

If \(f : \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) is differentiable at \(\mathbf{a}\), then the derivative \(Df(\mathbf{a})\) is a linear map \(\mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\), i.e., an element of the dual space \((\mathbb{R}^n)^*\).

The Riesz representation theorem (in the Euclidean inner product) says every such linear functional is represented by a unique vector via the dot product. The gradient \( abla f(\mathbf{a})\) is precisely this representing vector: $\(Df(\mathbf{a})[\mathbf{h}] = abla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{h}\)$

This is why the formula \(D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}}f = abla f \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}}\) holds for all directions: it is just the linear functional \(Df(\mathbf{a})\) evaluated at \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}\).

The gradient is the Riesz representative of the derivative. It lives in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) (same space as the domain) because we used the Euclidean inner product to identify \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with its dual. On a Riemannian manifold with a non-Euclidean metric, the gradient changes accordingly — this is the foundation of the natural gradient in ML.

docs.title: Min and Max Values
docs.text: "Finding extrema is the central problem of optimization. Everything else — Lagrange multipliers, second derivative tests, convexity — is commentary."

docs.title: 0. Preamble — The Problem
docs.text:
Given a function \(f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\), we want to find where \(f\) is largest or smallest. This question has two flavors:

  1. Unconstrained: optimize \(f\) over all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) (or an open domain)
  2. Constrained: optimize \(f\) subject to \(g(\mathbf{x}) = c\) (on a curve, surface, etc.)

Both cases reduce to a single geometric idea: at an extremum, the gradient must vanish — or be parallel to the constraint.

docs.title: 1. Absolute vs. Local Extrema
docs.text:
Definition. Let \(f : D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\).

  • \(f\) has an absolute (global) maximum at \(\mathbf{a} \in D\) if \(f(\mathbf{a}) \geq f(\mathbf{x})\) for all \(\mathbf{x} \in D\).
  • \(f\) has an absolute (global) minimum at \(\mathbf{a} \in D\) if \(f(\mathbf{a}) \leq f(\mathbf{x})\) for all \(\mathbf{x} \in D\).
  • \(f\) has a local maximum at \(\mathbf{a}\) if \(f(\mathbf{a}) \geq f(\mathbf{x})\) for all \(\mathbf{x}\) in some open ball around \(\mathbf{a}\).
  • \(f\) has a local minimum at \(\mathbf{a}\) if \(f(\mathbf{a}) \leq f(\mathbf{x})\) for all \(\mathbf{x}\) in some open ball around \(\mathbf{a}\).

Existence — Extreme Value Theorem (multivariable). If \(f\) is continuous on a closed and bounded set \(D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\), then \(f\) attains both its absolute maximum and minimum on \(D\).

⚠️ Closed and bounded is essential. On an open domain \(f(x) = x\) has no maximum on \((0,1)\). On an unbounded domain \(f(x,y) = x\) has no maximum on \(\mathbb{R}^2\). Both conditions are required.

docs.title: 2. Critical Points — Fermat's Theorem in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)
docs.text:
Theorem (Fermat). If \(f\) has a local extremum at an interior point \(\mathbf{a}\) of its domain, and \(f\) is differentiable at \(\mathbf{a}\), then: $\( abla f(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{0}\)$

Proof. Fix any direction \(\hat{\mathbf{e}}_i\). Define \(g(t) = f(\mathbf{a} + t\hat{\mathbf{e}}_i)\). Then \(g\) has a local extremum at \(t = 0\), so by the single-variable Fermat theorem: $\(g'(0) = rac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(\mathbf{a}) = 0\)$ Since \(i\) was arbitrary, all partial derivatives vanish, so \( abla f(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{0}\). \(\square\)

Definition. A point \(\mathbf{a}\) where \( abla f(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{0}\) (or \( abla f\) does not exist) is called a critical point of \(f\).

⚠️ The converse is false. A critical point need not be a local extremum — it could be a saddle point. The gradient vanishing is necessary but not sufficient.

Example of a saddle point. \(f(x,y) = x^2 - y^2\) at the origin.

\( abla f = \langle 2x, -2y angle = \mathbf{0}\) at \((0,0)\). But \(f(t, 0) = t^2 > 0\) and \(f(0, t) = -t^2 < 0\) for \(t eq 0\), so \((0,0)\) is neither a local max nor a local min — it is a saddle point (a mountain pass).

docs.title: 3. The Second Derivative Test — Classifying Critical Points
3.1 The Hessian Matrix
docs.text:
At a critical point \(\mathbf{a}\), the second-order behavior of \(f\) is encoded by the Hessian matrix: $\(H_f(\mathbf{a}) = \begin{pmatrix} f_{xx} & f_{xy} \ f_{xy} & f_{yy} \end{pmatrix}\Bigg|_{\mathbf{a}}\)$

(assuming \(f \in C^2\), so \(f_{xy} = f_{yx}\) by Clairaut's theorem).

The Hessian is a real symmetric matrix, so by the spectral theorem all its eigenvalues are real. The signs of these eigenvalues determine the local shape of \(f\).

docs.title: 3.2 The Discriminant (in \(\mathbb{R}^2\))
docs.text:
Define the discriminant: $\(D(\mathbf{a}) = \det H_f(\mathbf{a}) = f_{xx} f_{yy} - (f_{xy})^2\)$

Theorem (Second Derivative Test). Let \(\mathbf{a}\) be a critical point of \(f \in C^2\).

Condition Classification \(D(\mathbf{a}) > 0\) and \(f_{xx}(\mathbf{a}) > 0\) Local minimum \(D(\mathbf{a}) > 0\) and \(f_{xx}(\mathbf{a}) < 0\) Local maximum \(D(\mathbf{a}) < 0\) Saddle point \(D(\mathbf{a}) = 0\) Inconclusive (higher-order analysis needed)

Why this works. Near \(\mathbf{a}\), by Taylor's theorem with the gradient zero: $\(f(\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{h}) \approx f(\mathbf{a}) + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{h}^T H_f(\mathbf{a}), \mathbf{h}\)$

The sign of the quadratic form \(Q(\mathbf{h}) = \mathbf{h}^T H \mathbf{h}\) determines everything:

  • \(Q > 0\) for all \(\mathbf{h} \neq \mathbf{0}\) (\(H\) is positive definite, eigenvalues both positive) \(\implies\) local min
  • \(Q < 0\) for all \(\mathbf{h} \neq \mathbf{0}\) (\(H\) is negative definite, eigenvalues both negative) \(\implies\) local max
  • \(Q\) takes both signs (\(H\) is indefinite, eigenvalues have mixed signs) \(\implies\) saddle

The discriminant \(D = \lambda_1 \lambda_2\) (product of eigenvalues = determinant) and \(f_{xx} = \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 \cdot (\text{rotation terms})\) encode exactly this.

docs.title: 3.3 Full Worked Example
docs.text:
Let \(f(x,y) = x^3 - 3x + y^2 - 2y\).

Step 1 — Find critical points. $\(\nabla f = \langle 3x^2 - 3,; 2y - 2\rangle = \mathbf{0}\)$ $\(3x^2 - 3 = 0 \implies x = \pm 1, \qquad 2y - 2 = 0 \implies y = 1\)$

Critical points: \((-1, 1)\) and \((1, 1)\).

Step 2 — Compute the Hessian. $\(f_{xx} = 6x, \quad f_{xy} = 0, \quad f_{yy} = 2\)$ $\(H_f = \begin{pmatrix} 6x & 0 \ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\)$

Step 3 — Apply the test.

At \((-1, 1)\): \(D = (6(-1))(2) - 0 = -12 < 0\) → saddle point.

At \((1, 1)\): \(D = (6)(2) - 0 = 12 > 0\), \(f_{xx} = 6 > 0\) → local minimum.

\(f(1, 1) = 1 - 3 + 1 - 2 = -3\).

docs.title: 4. Absolute Extrema on a Closed Bounded Domain
docs.text:
By the Extreme Value Theorem, absolute extrema exist on a closed bounded domain \(D\). The strategy is:

Closed Domain Method

  1. Find all interior critical points (solve \(\nabla f = \mathbf{0}\))
  2. Examine \(f\) on the boundary of \(D\)
  3. Compare all values — the largest is the absolute max, the smallest is the absolute min

The boundary examination in step 2 typically reduces to a single-variable optimization problem on each boundary piece.

Example. Find the absolute extrema of \(f(x,y) = x^2 - 2xy + 2y\) on the square \(D = [0,3] \times [0,2]\).

Interior critical points: $\(\nabla f = \langle 2x - 2y,; -2x + 2\rangle = \mathbf{0} \implies x = 1,; y = 1\)$ \(f(1,1) = 1 - 2 + 2 = 1\).

Boundary analysis (four edges):

  • \(y = 0,; x \in [0,3]\): \(f = x^2\). Max at \(x=3\): \(f=9\). Min at \(x=0\): \(f=0\).
  • \(y = 2,; x \in [0,3]\): \(f = x^2 - 4x + 4 = (x-2)^2\). Max at \(x=0\) or \(x=3\): \(f=4\). Min at \(x=2\): \(f=0\).
  • \(x = 0,; y \in [0,2]\): \(f = 2y\). Max at \(y=2\): \(f=4\). Min at \(y=0\): \(f=0\).
  • \(x = 3,; y \in [0,2]\): \(f = 9 - 6y + 2y = 9 - 4y\). Max at \(y=0\): \(f=9\). Min at \(y=2\): \(f=1\).

Comparing all values: \({1, 9, 0, 4, 0, 4, 0, 9, 1}\)

Absolute maximum: \(9\) at \((3, 0)\). Absolute minimum: \(0\) at \((0,0)\), \((3/2, 0)\)... let me refine — at \((0,0)\) and \((2,2)\).

docs.title: 5.1 The Geometric Idea
docs.text:
Suppose we want to maximize \(f(x,y)\) subject to \(g(x,y) = c\).

Geometrically: we are moving along the constraint curve \(g = c\) and asking where \(f\) is largest. At the constrained maximum, the level curve of \(f\) through that point must be tangent to the constraint curve — otherwise we could slide along the constraint and increase \(f\) further.

Two curves are tangent \(\iff\) they have the same tangent line \(\iff\) they have parallel normal vectors.

Their normals are \( abla f\) and \( abla g\). So the condition is: $\( abla f(\mathbf{a}) = \lambda, abla g(\mathbf{a})\)$ for some scalar \(\lambda\) (the Lagrange multiplier).

docs.title: 5.2 The Formal Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem (Lagrange). Suppose \(f, g \in C^1\) and \(f\) has a local extremum at \(\mathbf{a}\) subject to the constraint \(g(\mathbf{a}) = c\). If \( abla g(\mathbf{a}) eq \mathbf{0}\), then there exists \(\lambda \in \mathbb{R}\) such that: $\( abla f(\mathbf{a}) = \lambda, abla g(\mathbf{a})\)$

Proof sketch. Since \( abla g(\mathbf{a}) eq \mathbf{0}\), the constraint surface \(g = c\) is a smooth \((n-1)\)-manifold near \(\mathbf{a}\). Any tangent vector \(\mathbf{v}\) to this surface satisfies \( abla g(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0\).

Since \(\mathbf{a}\) is a constrained extremum of \(f\), the directional derivative of \(f\) along any direction tangent to the constraint must vanish: \( abla f(\mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0\) for all such \(\mathbf{v}\).

Therefore \( abla f(\mathbf{a})\) is perpendicular to the entire tangent space of the constraint surface — meaning \( abla f(\mathbf{a})\) is parallel to the normal \( abla g(\mathbf{a})\), i.e., \( abla f(\mathbf{a}) = \lambda abla g(\mathbf{a})\). \(\square\)

docs.title: 5.3 The Lagrange System
docs.text:
To find constrained extrema of \(f\) subject to \(g = c\), solve the system: $\(\begin{cases} \nabla f = \lambda, \nabla g \ g(\mathbf{x}) = c \end{cases}\)$

In two variables \((x,y)\), this is three equations in three unknowns \((x, y, \lambda)\): $\(f_x = \lambda g_x, \quad f_y = \lambda g_y, \quad g(x,y) = c\)$

docs.title: 5.4 Worked Example
docs.text:
Find the maximum and minimum values of \(f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2\) on the ellipse \(\frac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = 1\).

Wait — this is just distance squared from the origin on an ellipse, so we want the closest and farthest points. Let \(g(x,y) = \frac{x^2}{4} + y^2\).

Lagrange system: $\(f_x = 2x = \lambda \cdot \frac{x}{2}, \quad f_y = 2y = \lambda \cdot 2y, \quad \frac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = 1\)$

Case 1: \(y \neq 0\). From the second equation: \(2 = 2\lambda \implies \lambda = 1\). Substituting: \(2x = \frac{x}{2} \implies \frac{3x}{2} = 0 \implies x = 0\). Constraint: \(y^2 = 1 \implies y = \pm 1\). Points: \((0, \pm 1)\), \(f = 1\).

Case 2: \(y = 0\). Constraint: \(\frac{x^2}{4} = 1 \implies x = \pm 2\). From first eq: \(2x = \frac{\lambda x}{2} \implies \lambda = 4\). Points: \((\pm 2, 0)\), \(f = 4\).

Conclusion: Maximum value \(4\) at \((\pm 2, 0)\); minimum value \(1\) at \((0, \pm 1)\). ✓ (These are the semi-axes of the ellipse.)

docs.title: 5.5 Two Constraints
docs.text: For \(f(\mathbf{x})\) subject to \(g(\mathbf{x}) = c_1\) and \(h(\mathbf{x}) = c_2\): $\( abla f = \lambda, abla g + \mu, abla h\)$

|∇f| is large where curves are dense (steep).
∇f = 0 at max, min, and saddle.

f(x,y) = x² - y²    (hyperbolic paraboloid / Pringle shape)

        z
        |   ↗ increases along x-axis
        |  /
  ------+------  ← saddle at origin
       /|
      ↙ |  ↘ decreases along y-axis

  Level curves: x² - y² = c → hyperbolas (for c ≠ 0), asymptotes (c = 0)
  ∇f(0,0) = ⟨0,0⟩ yet not an extremum.

docs.title: 7. The Hessian — General \(\mathbb{R}^n\) Version
docs.text:
In \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the Hessian at a critical point \(\mathbf{a}\) is the \(n \times n\) symmetric matrix: $\([H_f(\mathbf{a})]_{ij} = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}(\mathbf{a})\)$

The classification is by definiteness of \(H_f(\mathbf{a})\):

Hessian \(H\) All eigenvalues Conclusion Positive definite \(> 0\) Local minimum Negative definite \(< 0\) Local maximum Indefinite Mixed signs Saddle point Positive/Negative semidefinite \(\geq 0\) or \(\leq 0\) Inconclusive

The determinant test in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is just the \(2 \times 2\) case of checking definiteness via eigenvalue signs (\(D = \lambda_1\lambda_2 > 0\) means same sign; \(f_{xx} > 0\) means both positive).

docs.title: 8. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
8.1 The Entire Goal of Training is Minimization
docs.text:
Every supervised learning model minimizes a loss function \(\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) over parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) (where \(n\) can be \(10^9\) or more). The theory of min/max is the mathematical foundation.

Critical points of \(\mathcal{L}\): \(\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathcal{L} = \mathbf{0}\). These are where gradient descent stalls. Understanding whether a critical point is a minimum, maximum, or saddle is the central problem of deep learning optimization theory.

docs.title: 8.2 The Loss Landscape — What Are We Minimizing Into?
docs.text:
The loss surface \(\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) of a deep neural network is a hypersurface in billions of dimensions. Its landscape looks nothing like the neat single-variable pictures:

  • Local minima are rare. In high dimensions, a local minimum requires all eigenvalues of the Hessian to be positive — exponentially unlikely if eigenvalues are random.
  • Saddle points dominate. Most critical points have Hessians with some positive and some negative eigenvalues. The network gets stuck near saddles, not local minima.
  • Global structure: Surprisingly, for overparameterized networks (more parameters than data), many local minima have similar loss values — the landscape has many "flat valleys" at the bottom.

Empirical insight (Dauphin et al., 2014): The difficulty in training deep networks is escaping saddle points, not getting stuck in bad local minima.

docs.title: 8.3 Second-Order Methods — Using the Hessian
docs.text:
Gradient descent uses only \(\nabla\mathcal{L}\) (first-order). Newton's method uses \(H_\mathcal{L}\) (second-order): $\(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_t - \eta, [H_{\mathcal{L}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)]^{-1} \nabla \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)\)$

At a local minimum, \(H_{\mathcal{L}}\) is positive definite (second derivative test!), so \(H^{-1}\) scales the gradient step to take into account the local curvature — taking large steps in flat directions, small steps in sharp directions. This is exactly the second derivative test applied operationally.

Why not always use Newton's method? Inverting \(H_{\mathcal{L}} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\) costs \(O(n^3)\) — infeasible for \(n = 10^9\). This motivates quasi-Newton methods (BFGS, L-BFGS) and natural gradient methods that approximate \(H^{-1}\).

docs.title: 8.4 Convexity — When Local = Global
docs.text:
Definition. \(f\) is convex if for all \(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\) and \(t \in [0,1]\): $\(f(t\mathbf{x} + (1-t)\mathbf{y}) \leq t f(\mathbf{x}) + (1-t)f(\mathbf{y})\)$

Theorem. If \(f\) is convex and \(\nabla f(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{0}\), then \(\mathbf{a}\) is a global minimum.

This is the key property. For convex loss functions (logistic regression, SVMs, linear regression), every critical point is a global minimum — the optimization is "safe." For non-convex losses (deep networks), there is no such guarantee.

The Hessian connection: \(f\) is convex \(\iff\) \(H_f\) is positive semidefinite everywhere (\(\iff\) all eigenvalues \(\geq 0\)). This is the global version of the local minimum condition from the second derivative test.

docs.title: 8.5 Lagrange Multipliers in ML — Constrained Learning
docs.text:
Lagrange multipliers appear explicitly in:

Support Vector Machines (SVM). Maximize the margin subject to classification constraints. The Lagrangian is: $\(\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}, b, \boldsymbol{\alpha}) = \frac{1}{2}|\mathbf{w}|^2 - \sum_i \alpha_i [y_i(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}_i + b) - 1]\)$ The KKT conditions (generalized Lagrange conditions for inequalities) completely characterize the optimal \(\mathbf{w}\).

Regularization as a Lagrange problem. Minimize \(\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) subject to \(|\boldsymbol{\theta}|^2 \leq C\) is equivalent (by Lagrange) to minimizing \(\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) + \lambda|\boldsymbol{\theta}|^2\) (ridge regression / \(L^2\) regularization). The multiplier \(\lambda\) is the regularization coefficient.

Variational autoencoders (VAE). The ELBO objective is a constrained optimization (maximize likelihood subject to KL divergence constraint), handled via Lagrange-style relaxation.

docs.title: 8.6 Summary — Min/Max Theory in the ML Pipeline
docs.text: Calculus Concept ML Manifestation Critical point \(\nabla f = \mathbf{0}\) Trained model (gradient descent converges) Second derivative test (Hessian) Diagnosing minima vs saddle points Saddle point Gradient descent stall; motivates Adam, momentum Absolute minimum on closed domain Constrained parameter spaces Lagrange multipliers SVMs, regularization, constrained decoding Convexity (positive definite Hessian) Loss functions with guaranteed global min Newton's method Second-order optimizers (L-BFGS, K-FAC)

docs.title: 9. The Procedure — A Decision Tree
docs.text:
Given f on domain D, find extrema
│
├─ Is D closed and bounded?
│   ├─ YES → Extreme Value Theorem guarantees extrema exist
│   │         → Find interior critical points (∇f = 0)
│   │         → Analyze boundary (parameterize, or use Lagrange)
│   │         → Compare all values
│   │
│   └─ NO  → Only local extrema may exist
│             → Find critical points (∇f = 0)
│             → Apply Second Derivative Test (Hessian)
│
└─ Is there a constraint g(x) = c?
    └─ YES → Lagrange: solve ∇f = λ∇g, g = c
             → Evaluate f at solutions
             → Compare values (no 2nd derivative test needed
               if only finitely many solutions and domain compact)

docs.title: 10. A Subtle Point — When the Test Fails (\(D = 0\))
docs.text:
When \(D(\mathbf{a}) = 0\), the Hessian is singular (one eigenvalue is zero). The quadratic approximation \(\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{h}^T H \mathbf{h}\) is neither positive nor negative definite, and higher-order terms determine the behavior.

Example. \(f(x,y) = x^4 + y^4\). At \((0,0)\): \(\nabla f = \mathbf{0}\), \(H = 0\), \(D = 0\). Test is inconclusive. But clearly \(f \geq 0\) with equality only at origin, so \((0,0)\) is a global minimum.

Example. \(f(x,y) = x^3\). At \((0,0)\): \(\nabla f = \mathbf{0}\), \(D = 0\). But \(f\) takes both signs near the origin, so \((0,0)\) is a saddle-like point.

When \(D = 0\): compute \(f\) along various paths through \(\mathbf{a}\) directly.

docs.text:
Concept Key Equation Meaning Critical point \(
abla f(\mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{0}\) Necessary condition for interior extremum Second derivative test \(D = f_{xx}f_{yy} - f_{xy}^2\) Classifies critical point via curvature \(D > 0, f_{xx} > 0\) — Local minimum \(D > 0, f_{xx} < 0\) — Local maximum \(D < 0\) — Saddle point Absolute extrema Closed domain method Interior crits + boundary Lagrange condition \(
abla f = \lambda 
abla g\) Constrained extremum ↔ parallel gradients Convexity \(H \succeq 0\) everywhere Local min = global min

docs.title: Absolute Min and Max
docs.text: "Local extrema tell you about the neighborhood. Absolute extrema tell you about the whole kingdom."

docs.title: 0. Preamble — What Question Are We Really Asking?
docs.text:
A local extremum answers: "Is this the best point nearby?"

An absolute extremum answers: "Is this the best point anywhere in the domain?"

These are fundamentally different questions. A mountain range may have many local peaks, but only one highest summit. The theory of absolute extrema tells us: under what conditions does a highest summit exist, and how do we find it?

The answer rests on three pillars:

  1. Existence — the Extreme Value Theorem
  2. Interior candidates — critical points (\(\nabla f = \mathbf{0}\))
  3. Boundary candidates — the boundary of the domain

Miss any pillar, and you will miss the answer.

docs.title: 1. Definitions
docs.text:
Definition. Let \(f : D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\).

  • \(f\) attains an absolute maximum at \(\mathbf{a} \in D\) if: $\(f(\mathbf{a}) \geq f(\mathbf{x}) \quad \text{for all } \mathbf{x} \in D\)$ The value \(f(\mathbf{a})\) is called the absolute maximum value.

  • \(f\) attains an absolute minimum at \(\mathbf{a} \in D\) if: $\(f(\mathbf{a}) \leq f(\mathbf{x}) \quad \text{for all } \mathbf{x} \in D\)$ The value \(f(\mathbf{a})\) is called the absolute minimum value.

Distinction from local extrema. A local maximum satisfies \(f(\mathbf{a}) \geq f(\mathbf{x})\) only for \(\mathbf{x}\) near \(\mathbf{a}\). An absolute maximum satisfies it for all \(\mathbf{x} \in D\). Every absolute extremum is a local extremum (on the interior), but not vice versa.

docs.title: 2. Existence — The Extreme Value Theorem
docs.text:
Before hunting for extrema, we must know they exist. The following theorem guarantees this.

Theorem (Extreme Value Theorem — EVT). If \(f : D \to \mathbb{R}\) is continuous on a closed and bounded set \(D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\), then \(f\) attains both its absolute maximum and absolute minimum on \(D\). That is, there exist \(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b} \in D\) such that: $\(f(\mathbf{a}) \leq f(\mathbf{x}) \leq f(\mathbf{b}) \quad \text{for all } \mathbf{x} \in D\)$

This is the multivariable generalization of the single-variable theorem from Stewart §4.1. The proof relies on:

  • Continuity \(\implies\) \(f(D)\) is a connected, bounded subset of \(\mathbb{R}\)
  • Closed and bounded \(\implies\) \(D\) is compact (Heine–Borel)
  • Continuous image of compact set is compact \(\implies\) \(f(D)\) is closed and bounded \(\implies\) \(f(D)\) contains its supremum and infimum

docs.title: 2.1 Why Both Conditions Are Necessary
docs.text:
"Closed" cannot be dropped.

Let \(f(x) = x\) on the open interval \((0, 1) \subset \mathbb{R}\).

  • \(f\) is continuous, domain is bounded.
  • \(\sup f = 1\), but \(f(x) = 1\) has no solution in \((0,1)\).
  • No absolute maximum exists.

In \(\mathbb{R}^2\): \(f(x,y) = x\) on the open disk \(x^2 + y^2 < 1\). Again, no maximum attained.

"Bounded" cannot be dropped.

Let \(f(x) = x\) on the closed interval \([1, \infty) \subset \mathbb{R}\).

  • \(f\) is continuous, domain is closed.
  • \(f\) is unbounded above — no absolute maximum exists.

In \(\mathbb{R}^2\): \(f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2\) on the closed set \(\mathbb{R}^2\). No absolute maximum.

"Continuous" cannot be dropped.

Let \(f : [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}\) be \(f(x) = 1/x\) for \(x \in (0,1]\) and \(f(0) = 0\).

  • Domain is closed and bounded.
  • \(f\) is not continuous at \(0\).
  • \(f\) is unbounded — no absolute maximum exists.

The EVT is an existence theorem — it guarantees a maximum and minimum exist but says nothing about where they are or how many there are. Finding them requires the method below.

docs.title: 3. The Closed Domain Method
docs.text:
This is the algorithm for finding absolute extrema of \(f\) on a closed bounded domain \(D\).

\[\boxed{\text{Absolute extrema} = \max/\min \text{ of } {f \text{ at interior critical points}} \cup {f \text{ on } \partial D}}\]

Algorithm:

Step 1. Find all interior critical points: solve \(\nabla f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}\) for \(\mathbf{x} \in \text{int}(D)\).

Step 2. Find the extreme values of \(f\) restricted to the boundary \(\partial D\). This is itself an optimization problem (on a lower-dimensional set), solved by parameterization or Lagrange multipliers.

Step 3. Evaluate \(f\) at all candidates from Steps 1 and 2. The largest value is the absolute maximum; the smallest is the absolute minimum.

Why this is complete. By the EVT, absolute extrema exist. Each one is either:

  • In the interior of \(D\): then by Fermat's theorem it is a critical point → found in Step 1.
  • On the boundary \(\partial D\): found in Step 2.

No candidates are missed.

docs.title: 4. Worked Example I — Triangular Domain
docs.text: Problem. Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of $\(f(x,y) = x^2 - xy + y^2 - y\)$ on the closed triangular region \(D\) with vertices \((0,0)\), \((2,0)\), \((0,2)\).

docs.title: Step 1 — Interior Critical Points
docs.text:
\[\nabla f = \langle 2x - y,; -x + 2y - 1 \rangle = \mathbf{0}\]

From the first equation: \(y = 2x\). Substituting into the second: \(-x + 4x - 1 = 0 \implies x = \frac{1}{3}\), \(y = \frac{2}{3}\).

Check: is \(\left(\frac{1}{3}, \frac{2}{3}\right)\) in the interior of \(D\)? The triangle has edges \(x \geq 0\), \(y \geq 0\), \(x + y \leq 2\). Check: \(\frac{1}{3} + \frac{2}{3} = 1 \leq 2\). ✓

\[f!\left(\tfrac{1}{3}, \tfrac{2}{3}\right) = \tfrac{1}{9} - \tfrac{2}{9} + \tfrac{4}{9} - \tfrac{2}{3} = \tfrac{3}{9} - \tfrac{6}{9} = -\tfrac{1}{3}\]

docs.title: Step 3 — Compare All Candidates
docs.text: Location Value \(\left(\frac{1}{3}, \frac{2}{3}\right)\) — interior critical point \(-\frac{1}{3} \approx -0.333\) \((0, 0)\) — vertex \(0\) \((2, 0)\) — vertex \(4\) \((0, 2)\) — vertex \(2\) \(\left(0, \frac{1}{2}\right)\) — Edge 2 critical \(-\frac{1}{4} = -0.25\) \(\left(\frac{5}{6}, \frac{7}{6}\right)\) — Edge 3 critical \(-\frac{1}{12} \approx -0.083\) \[\text{Absolute maximum: } 4 \text{ at } (2, 0)$$ $$\text{Absolute minimum: } -\tfrac{1}{3} \text{ at } \left(\tfrac{1}{3}, \tfrac{2}{3}\right)\]

docs.title: 5. Worked Example II — Rectangular Domain
docs.text: Problem. Find the absolute extrema of $\(f(x,y) = 4x^2 + 9y^2 - 8x - 12y + 4\)$ on the rectangle \(D = {(x,y) : 0 \leq x \leq 2,; 0 \leq y \leq 2}\).

docs.title: Step 1 — Interior Critical Points
docs.text:
\[\nabla f = \langle 8x - 8,; 18y - 12 \rangle = \mathbf{0}$$ $$x = 1, \quad y = \frac{2}{3}\]

Point \(\left(1, \frac{2}{3}\right)\) is interior to \(D\). ✓

\[f!\left(1, \tfrac{2}{3}\right) = 4 - 8 + 4 - 8 + 4 = -4\]

Let me recompute carefully: \(= 4(1) + 9(\frac{4}{9}) - 8(1) - 12(\frac{2}{3}) + 4 = 4 + 4 - 8 - 8 + 4 = -4\).

docs.title: Step 3 — Compare
docs.text:
All candidate values: \({-4, 0, 4, 16, 20}\).

\[\text{Absolute maximum: } 20 \text{ at } (0, 2)$$ $$\text{Absolute minimum: } -4 \text{ at } \left(1, \frac{2}{3}\right)\]

docs.title: 6. Worked Example III — Disk Domain
docs.text: Problem. Find the absolute extrema of $\(f(x,y) = x^2 + 2y^2 - 2x\)$ on the closed disk \(D = {(x,y) : x^2 + y^2 \leq 4}\).

docs.title: Step 1 — Interior Critical Points
docs.text:
\[\nabla f = \langle 2x - 2,; 4y \rangle = \mathbf{0} \implies x = 1,; y = 0\]

Check: \(1^2 + 0^2 = 1 \leq 4\), so \((1,0)\) is interior. ✓

\[f(1, 0) = 1 + 0 - 2 = -1\]

docs.title: Step 2 — Boundary: Circle \(x^2 + y^2 = 4\)
docs.text:
Parameterize: \(x = 2\cos t\), \(y = 2\sin t\), \(t \in [0, 2\pi]\).

\[f(2\cos t, 2\sin t) = 4\cos^2 t + 8\sin^2 t - 4\cos t$$ $$= 4\cos^2 t + 8(1 - \cos^2 t) - 4\cos t$$ $$= 8 - 4\cos^2 t - 4\cos t\]

Let \(u = \cos t \in [-1, 1]\). Minimize/maximize \(h(u) = -4u^2 - 4u + 8\).

\[h'(u) = -8u - 4 = 0 \implies u = -\frac{1}{2}\]

\(h!\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = -4 \cdot \frac{1}{4} + 2 + 8 = 9\).

At endpoints: \(h(1) = -4 - 4 + 8 = 0\) and \(h(-1) = -4 + 4 + 8 = 8\).

So on the boundary:

  • Max: \(f = 9\) at \(\cos t = -\frac{1}{2}\), i.e., \(t = \frac{2\pi}{3}\) or \(\frac{4\pi}{3}\), giving points \(\left(-1, \pm\sqrt{3}\right)\).
  • Min: \(f = 0\) at \(t = 0\), i.e., point \((2, 0)\).

docs.title: Step 3 — Compare
docs.text: Candidate Value \((1,0)\) — interior \(-1\) \((-1, \pm\sqrt{3})\) — boundary \(9\) \((2, 0)\) — boundary \(0\) \[\text{Absolute maximum: } 9 \text{ at } (-1, \pm\sqrt{3})$$ $$\text{Absolute minimum: } -1 \text{ at } (1, 0)\]

docs.title: 7.1 Why Boundary Matters — A Schematic
docs.text:
Domain D (closed rectangle):

     ┌──────────────────────┐  ← boundary ∂D
     │                      │
     │   ×  local max       │
     │                      │
     │         ★ abs. max   │  ← abs max ON boundary
     │                      │
     │   ·  local min       │
     │                      │
     └──────────────────────┘
          ↑
          abs. min (interior critical point here)

  The absolute max lives on the boundary, NOT at any interior
  critical point. If you only check ∇f = 0, you miss it entirely.

docs.title: 7.2 Level Curve View
docs.text:
f(x,y) = x² + y²    on disk x² + y² ≤ 4

        f = 4  ← boundary circle
      f = 3
    f = 2
   f = 1
  f = 0  ← absolute minimum at origin

  Level curves are concentric circles.
  Absolute min: origin (interior critical point ∇f = 0).
  Absolute max: entire boundary circle x²+y² = 4.
  The max is attained everywhere on ∂D — not unique.

docs.title: 7.3 Cross-Section Intuition
docs.text:
z = f(x, y) viewed as a surface:

         z
         │        ·  ·  ·   ← high values at boundary
         │      ·           (absolute max somewhere on ∂D)
         │    ·
  ───────┼──·──────·──────── D (projection onto xy-plane)
         │·               ↑
         ·                boundary ∂D
    absolute min
    (interior dip)

  The surface may dip lowest in the interior (interior min)
  or rise highest at the boundary (boundary max).
  We must check BOTH regions to be sure.

docs.title: 8. Special Case — Absolute Extrema on a Curve (1D Constraint)
docs.text: Sometimes the domain \(D\) is itself a curve \(g(x,y) = c\) (a 1D set). This arises naturally as the boundary problem in Step 2. Two methods:

docs.title: Method A — Parameterization
docs.text:
Parameterize the curve \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t)\) and optimize the single-variable function \(f(\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t))\).

Best when the curve has a clean parameterization (circle → \((\cos t, \sin t)\), line segment → \((1-t)\mathbf{a} + t\mathbf{b}\)).

docs.title: Method B — Lagrange Multipliers
docs.text:
Solve \(\nabla f = \lambda \nabla g\), \(g = c\).

Best when parameterization is messy. Gives the same candidates.

Both methods must be used with care: neither automatically delivers the absolute max/min. You still need to evaluate \(f\) at all candidates and compare.

docs.title: 9. Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
docs.text: Mistake Why It Fails Correction Only solving \(\nabla f = \mathbf{0}\) Misses absolute extrema on \(\partial D\) Always analyze the boundary Forgetting to check if critical point is in \(D\) A point outside \(D\) is not a candidate Verify each critical point lies in \(D\) Not checking all boundary pieces A rectangular domain has 4 edges and 4 corners Be systematic; list every piece Assuming interior min/max is absolute A local extremum need not be global Compare against all boundary values Forgetting corner points of boundary Corners are endpoints of edge sub-problems Always evaluate \(f\) at all vertices/corners Applying EVT on open domain EVT requires closed and bounded Verify domain before applying EVT

docs.title: 10. Connection to Machine Learning and Deep Learning
10.1 Absolute Minimum = The Goal of Training
docs.text:
When training a neural network, we seek the absolute minimum of the loss function \(\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) over the parameter space. This is the global optimum — the parameter setting that makes the model best on training data.

The EVT guarantees: if we restrict to a closed bounded parameter region and \(\mathcal{L}\) is continuous, the absolute minimum exists. In practice, \(\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) (unbounded), so the EVT does not directly apply — existence of a global minimum is a non-trivial property of the loss function.

docs.title: 10.2 Why Absolute Minima Are Hard to Find in Deep Learning
docs.text:
In \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(n \sim 10^9\) (modern LLMs):

  • There are exponentially many critical points.
  • Most critical points are saddle points (Hessian is indefinite), not local minima.
  • The boundary of parameter space is at \(|\boldsymbol{\theta}| \to \infty\), where loss typically blows up — so boundary analysis is trivial (exclude).
  • Local minima exist, but the absolute minimum is essentially unreachable by gradient descent.

Strikingly, this turns out to be fine in practice: overparameterized networks have many local minima with nearly identical (and very low) loss values. The "absolute" minimum vs a "good local" minimum distinction becomes irrelevant — gradient descent finds solutions that generalize well even without reaching the true global minimum.

docs.title: 10.3 Constrained Absolute Optimization in ML
docs.text:
Weight constraints. Regularization imposes effective constraints: minimizing \(\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) + \lambda|\boldsymbol{\theta}|^2\) is equivalent to minimizing \(\mathcal{L}\) on the closed ball \(|\boldsymbol{\theta}| \leq R\). On this closed bounded set, the EVT applies — the absolute minimum exists.

Projection methods. Some algorithms explicitly project \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) back to a feasible closed set after each gradient step, enforcing constraints. This is a direct application of the closed domain method: minimize over interior (unconstrained gradient step) then handle boundary (projection).

Hyperparameter tuning. When searching for optimal hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size) over a closed bounded grid, the EVT guarantees the absolute best hyperparameter combination exists within the grid — then we search for it systematically, exactly analogous to the closed domain method.

docs.title: 10.4 The Closed Domain Method as a Template for Search
docs.text:
The three-step method — (1) interior candidates, (2) boundary candidates, (3) compare — is the template for any complete optimization procedure:

ML Setting "Interior" candidates "Boundary" candidates Gradient descent training Converged parameter (approx \(\nabla\mathcal{L} = 0\)) Constrained region boundary (clipping, projection) Architecture search Interior model configs Edge cases (depth = 1, width = 1) Hyperparameter search Optima found by Bayesian opt Grid boundary values Reinforcement learning Stationary policy Terminal states / boundary of state space

The mathematical structure is identical: complete search requires covering both the interior and the boundary.

docs.title: 11. Summary
docs.text:
The method to find absolute extrema of a continuous \(f\) on a closed bounded domain \(D\):

\[\underbrace{\nabla f = \mathbf{0} \text{ in int}(D)}_{\text{Step 1: interior}} \quad \cup \quad \underbrace{f\big|_{\partial D}}_{\text{Step 2: boundary}} \quad \xrightarrow{\text{evaluate and compare}} \quad \text{absolute max and min}\]

The EVT guarantees they exist. The closed domain method guarantees you find them. Together they are complete.

docs.title: 12. References
docs.text:
1. James Stewart, Calculus, §14.7 — Maximum and Minimum Values (Closed Domain Method, worked examples on rectangles and disks).
  2. MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus (D. Auroux) — Lecture notes on finding absolute extrema; boundary analysis via parameterization and Lagrange multipliers; available at MIT OpenCourseWare.
