docs.title: Volumes and Double Integrals
docs.text: "The single integral measures length swept into area. The double integral measures area swept into volume. The pattern continues — and so does the wonder."

docs.title: 0. Preamble — Motivation
docs.text:
The definite integral \(\int_a^b f(x),dx\) computes the signed area between \(y = f(x)\) and the \(x\)-axis. Now we have a function \(f(x,y)\) of two variables — its graph is a surface \(z = f(x,y)\) floating above the \(xy\)-plane.

The question: What is the volume of the solid between this surface and the \(xy\)-plane, over a region \(D\)?

The answer is the double integral \(\iint_D f(x,y),dA\), and building it from scratch — through the same limiting process as the single integral — is what this note is about.

docs.title: 1.1 Setting Up the Approximation
docs.text:
Let \(f : D \to \mathbb{R}\) be defined on a closed rectangle \(R = [a,b] \times [c,d]\). Divide:

  • \([a,b]\) into \(m\) subintervals of width \(\Delta x = \frac{b-a}{m}\), with partition points \(x_0 = a < x_1 < \cdots < x_m = b\)
  • \([c,d]\) into \(n\) subintervals of width \(\Delta y = \frac{d-c}{n}\), with partition points \(y_0 = c < y_1 < \cdots < y_n = d\)

This creates \(mn\) sub-rectangles \(R_{ij} = [x_{i-1}, x_i] \times [y_{j-1}, y_j]\), each with area: $\(\Delta A = \Delta x \cdot \Delta y\)$

docs.title: 1.2 The Sample Points
docs.text: In each \(R_{ij}\), choose a sample point \((x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_)\). The value \(f(x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_)\) is the height of the surface at that point. The volume of the thin box (column) over \(R_{ij}\) is approximately: $\(\text{Volume of box}_{ij} \approx f(x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_) \cdot \Delta A\)$

docs.title: 1.3 The Double Riemann Sum
docs.text:
Summing over all sub-rectangles: $\(V \approx \sum_{i=1}^{m} \sum_{j=1}^{n} f(x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_),\Delta A\)$

This is the double Riemann sum. As \(m, n \to \infty\) (boxes get thinner), the approximation becomes exact.

docs.title: 1.4 The Double Integral — Definition
docs.text:
Definition. If the limit exists and is the same regardless of choice of sample points, then \(f\) is integrable over \(R\) and: $\(\iint_R f(x,y),dA = \lim_{m,n \to \infty} \sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n} f(x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_),\Delta A\)$

Theorem. If \(f\) is continuous on \(R\), then \(f\) is integrable over \(R\).

Geometric meaning when \(f \geq 0\): \(\iint_R f(x,y),dA\) is the volume of the solid between the surface \(z = f(x,y)\) and the rectangle \(R\) in the \(xy\)-plane.

When \(f\) takes negative values: Like the single integral, the double integral computes signed volume — regions where \(f < 0\) contribute negatively.

docs.title: 2. Fubini's Theorem — How to Actually Compute
docs.text: The definition via limits is impractical. Fubini's theorem converts a double integral into two successive single integrals.

docs.title: 2.1 The Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem (Fubini). If \(f\) is continuous on the rectangle \(R = [a,b] \times [c,d]\), then: $\(\iint_R f(x,y),dA = \int_a^b \int_c^d f(x,y),dy,dx = \int_c^d \int_a^b f(x,y),dx,dy\)$

Both iterated integrals give the same answer. The order of integration can be swapped freely (when \(f\) is continuous).

docs.title: 2.2 The Idea Behind Fubini — Cavalieri's Principle
docs.text:
Fix \(x \in [a,b]\). The cross-sectional area of the solid at position \(x\) is: $\(A(x) = \int_c^d f(x,y),dy\)$ (treat \(x\) as a constant, integrate over \(y\)).

The volume is then: $\(V = \int_a^b A(x),dx = \int_a^b \left[\int_c^d f(x,y),dy\right] dx\)$

This is Cavalieri's principle: volume = integral of cross-sectional areas. Fubini's theorem is the rigorous version.

docs.title: 2.3 Notation
docs.text:
The iterated integral is written: $\(\int_a^b \int_c^d f(x,y),dy,dx\)$

Read from the inside out:

  1. Inner integral: \(\int_c^d f(x,y),dy\) — integrate with respect to \(y\), treating \(x\) as a constant. Result is a function of \(x\).
  2. Outer integral: \(\int_a^b [\cdots],dx\) — integrate the result with respect to \(x\).

docs.title: 2.4 Worked Example — Rectangle
docs.text:
Compute \(\iint_R (x^2 + 2xy),dA\) where \(R = [0,2] \times [1,3]\).

Method (integrate \(y\) first, then \(x\)):

\[\int_0^2 \int_1^3 (x^2 + 2xy),dy,dx\]

Inner integral (\(x\) fixed): $\(\int_1^3 (x^2 + 2xy),dy = \left[x^2 y + xy^2\right]_1^3 = (3x^2 + 9x) - (x^2 + x) = 2x^2 + 8x\)$

Outer integral: $\(\int_0^2 (2x^2 + 8x),dx = \left[\frac{2x^3}{3} + 4x^2\right]_0^2 = \frac{16}{3} + 16 = \frac{64}{3}\)$

Verify by reversing order (integrate \(x\) first, then \(y\)):

\[\int_1^3 \int_0^2 (x^2 + 2xy),dx,dy\]

Inner integral (\(y\) fixed): $\(\int_0^2 (x^2 + 2xy),dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{3} + x^2 y\right]_0^2 = \frac{8}{3} + 4y\)$

Outer integral: $\(\int_1^3 \left(\frac{8}{3} + 4y\right)dy = \left[\frac{8y}{3} + 2y^2\right]_1^3 = \left(8 + 18\right) - \left(\frac{8}{3} + 2\right) = 26 - \frac{14}{3} = \frac{64}{3} \checkmark\)$

docs.title: 3. Double Integrals Over General Regions
docs.text: Most domains of interest are not rectangles. We integrate over general regions by describing the boundary carefully.

docs.title: 3.1 Type I Regions (vertical slices)
docs.text:
Definition. \(D\) is a Type I region if: $\(D = {(x,y) : a \leq x \leq b,; g_1(x) \leq y \leq g_2(x)}\)$

The \(y\)-limits depend on \(x\) — the region lies between two curves \(y = g_1(x)\) (bottom) and \(y = g_2(x)\) (top).

\[\iint_D f(x,y),dA = \int_a^b \int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x,y),dy,dx\]

Example. The region bounded by \(y = x^2\) and \(y = 2x\) is Type I with \(a = 0\), \(b = 2\) (intersection points: \(x^2 = 2x \implies x = 0, 2\)), \(g_1(x) = x^2\), \(g_2(x) = 2x\).

\[\iint_D f,dA = \int_0^2 \int_{x^2}^{2x} f(x,y),dy,dx\]

docs.title: 3.2 Type II Regions (horizontal slices)
docs.text:
Definition. \(D\) is a Type II region if: $\(D = {(x,y) : c \leq y \leq d,; h_1(y) \leq x \leq h_2(y)}\)$

The \(x\)-limits depend on \(y\) — the region lies between \(x = h_1(y)\) (left) and \(x = h_2(y)\) (right).

\[\iint_D f(x,y),dA = \int_c^d \int_{h_1(y)}^{h_2(y)} f(x,y),dx,dy\]

docs.title: 3.3 Choosing the Order of Integration
docs.text:
Some integrals are impossible (or very hard) in one order but elementary in the other. The strategy is:

Sketch the region \(D\). Identify which description (Type I or Type II) produces integrable limits. Try the other order if the inner integral cannot be evaluated in closed form.

Example of switching order. Consider \(\int_0^1 \int_x^1 e^{y^2},dy,dx\).

\(e^{y^2}\) has no elementary antiderivative in \(y\) — we cannot evaluate the inner integral directly.

Switch order. The region is \({0 \leq x \leq y,; 0 \leq y \leq 1}\). As a Type II region: \(0 \leq y \leq 1\), \(0 \leq x \leq y\).

\[\int_0^1 \int_0^y e^{y^2},dx,dy = \int_0^1 \left[xe^{y^2}\right]_0^y dy = \int_0^1 y e^{y^2},dy = \left[\frac{e^{y^2}}{2}\right]_0^1 = \frac{e-1}{2}\]

docs.title: 4. Volume as a Double Integral
docs.text:
The volume of the solid bounded above by \(z = f(x,y) \geq 0\) and below by the region \(D\) in the \(xy\)-plane is:

\[V = \iint_D f(x,y),dA\]

This is the defining geometric interpretation.

docs.title: 4.1 Volume Between Two Surfaces
docs.text: If \(f(x,y) \geq g(x,y)\) on \(D\), the volume between the two surfaces \(z = f(x,y)\) (top) and \(z = g(x,y)\) (bottom) is: $\(V = \iint_D [f(x,y) - g(x,y)],dA\)$

docs.title: 4.2 Full Worked Example — Volume Under a Paraboloid
docs.text:
Problem. Find the volume of the solid bounded above by \(z = 4 - x^2 - y^2\) and below by the \(xy\)-plane, over the region where \(z \geq 0\).

The surface meets the \(xy\)-plane where \(4 - x^2 - y^2 = 0\), i.e., on the circle \(x^2 + y^2 = 4\). So \(D = {x^2 + y^2 \leq 4}\).

\[V = \iint_D (4 - x^2 - y^2),dA\]

Describe \(D\) as Type I: \(-2 \leq x \leq 2\), \(-\sqrt{4-x^2} \leq y \leq \sqrt{4-x^2}\).

\[V = \int_{-2}^{2} \int_{-\sqrt{4-x^2}}^{\sqrt{4-x^2}} (4 - x^2 - y^2),dy,dx\]

Inner integral: $\(\int_{-\sqrt{4-x^2}}^{\sqrt{4-x^2}} (4 - x^2 - y^2),dy = \left[(4-x^2)y - \frac{y^3}{3}\right]_{-\sqrt{4-x^2}}^{\sqrt{4-x^2}}\)$

Let \(r^2 = 4 - x^2\). By symmetry in \(y\): $\(= 2\left[(4-x^2)\sqrt{4-x^2} - \frac{(4-x^2)^{3/2}}{3}\right] = 2(4-x^2)^{3/2}\left[1 - \frac{1}{3}\right] = \frac{4}{3}(4-x^2)^{3/2}\)$

Outer integral: $\(V = \int_{-2}^{2} \frac{4}{3}(4-x^2)^{3/2},dx\)$

Substitute \(x = 2\sin\theta\), \(dx = 2\cos\theta,d\theta\), \(\sqrt{4-x^2} = 2\cos\theta\), limits \(\theta \in [-\pi/2, \pi/2]\):

\[V = \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \frac{4}{3}(2\cos\theta)^3 \cdot 2\cos\theta,d\theta = \frac{4}{3} \cdot 16 \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \cos^4\theta,d\theta\]

Using \(\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos^4\theta,d\theta = \frac{3\pi}{8}\):

\[V = \frac{64}{3} \cdot \frac{3\pi}{8} = 8\pi\]

(This result is more elegantly obtained using polar coordinates — see §6.)

docs.title: 5. Properties of the Double Integral
docs.text:
These mirror the single-variable properties exactly:

Linearity: $\(\iint_D [f + g],dA = \iint_D f,dA + \iint_D g,dA, \qquad \iint_D cf,dA = c\iint_D f,dA\)$

Additivity over regions: If \(D = D_1 \cup D_2\) with \(D_1 \cap D_2\) having zero area: $\(\iint_D f,dA = \iint_{D_1} f,dA + \iint_{D_2} f,dA\)$

Monotonicity: If \(f \geq g\) on \(D\), then \(\iint_D f,dA \geq \iint_D g,dA\).

Area formula: If \(f \equiv 1\): $\(\iint_D 1,dA = \text{Area}(D)\)$

Average value: $\(\bar{f} = \frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\iint_D f(x,y),dA\)$

docs.title: 6. Double Integrals in Polar Coordinates
docs.text:
When \(D\) is a disk, annulus, or sector — or when \(f\) involves \(x^2 + y^2\) — polar coordinates simplify the integral dramatically.

Transformation: \(x = r\cos\theta\), \(y = r\sin\theta\), with the crucial factor: $\(dA = r,dr,d\theta\)$

⚠️ The factor \(r\) is not optional. It arises from the Jacobian of the transformation: \(\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(r,\theta)} = r\). A polar area element is a thin wedge of area \(r,dr,d\theta\), not \(dr,d\theta\).

Formula: $\(\iint_D f(x,y),dA = \int_\alpha^\beta \int_{r_1(\theta)}^{r_2(\theta)} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\cdot r,dr,d\theta\)$

docs.title: 6.1 Common Polar Regions
docs.text: Region Polar Description Disk \(x^2+y^2 \leq a^2\) \(0 \leq r \leq a\), \(0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi\) Upper half-disk \(0 \leq r \leq a\), \(0 \leq \theta \leq \pi\) Annulus \(a^2 \leq x^2+y^2 \leq b^2\) \(a \leq r \leq b\), \(0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi\) Sector, angle \(\alpha\) to \(\beta\) \(0 \leq r \leq a\), \(\alpha \leq \theta \leq \beta\)

docs.title: 6.2 Revisiting the Paraboloid Volume
docs.text:
\[V = \iint_{x^2+y^2 \leq 4} (4 - x^2 - y^2),dA = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2 (4 - r^2),r,dr,d\theta\] \[= \int_0^{2\pi}d\theta \cdot \int_0^2 (4r - r^3),dr = 2\pi \left[2r^2 - \frac{r^4}{4}\right]_0^2 = 2\pi\left(8 - 4\right) = 8\pi \checkmark\]

Far cleaner than Cartesian.

docs.title: 6.3 The Gaussian Integral — A Famous Application
docs.text:
Double integrals in polar coordinates give one of the most celebrated results in all of mathematics:

\[\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2},dx\right)^2 = \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} e^{-(x^2+y^2)},dA = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2} r,dr,d\theta = 2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \pi\]

Therefore: $\(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2},dx = \sqrt{\pi}\)$

This integral is the backbone of probability theory (it normalizes the Gaussian distribution) and appears throughout physics and ML.

docs.title: 7.1 Riemann Sum Geometry
docs.text:
z = f(x,y) surface
       ↑ z
       │    . . . . 
       │  .  ╔══╗  .
       │ .   ║  ║   .    ← thin rectangular column
       │.    ║  ║    .      height = f(xᵢⱼ*, yᵢⱼ*)
       │     ╚══╝           base area = Δx · Δy
       └─────────────── x
      /
     / y

    Volume ≈ Σᵢ Σⱼ f(xᵢⱼ*, yᵢⱼ*) · Δx · Δy

  As mesh → 0: columns become infinitely thin,
  sum → exact volume ∬_R f dA

docs.title: 7.2 Iterated Integral as Cross-Sections (Cavalieri)
docs.text:
Cross-section at fixed x:
  ↑ z                      A(x) = ∫_{g₁(x)}^{g₂(x)} f(x,y) dy
  │  /‾‾‾‾‾‾‾\
  │ /    ↑    \
  │/   A(x)   \            Volume = ∫_a^b A(x) dx
  └────┼────────── x
  a   x   b                "Stacking" cross-sections like bread slices

docs.title: 7.3 Type I vs Type II Regions
docs.text:
Type I (vertical slices):      Type II (horizontal slices):

  y = g₂(x) ─╮                  d ──╮
              │  D                   │  D
  y = g₁(x) ─╯                  c ──╯
              a     b           x=h₁(y)  x=h₂(y)

  Fix x, sweep y from            Fix y, sweep x from
  g₁(x) to g₂(x).               h₁(y) to h₂(y).

docs.title: 7.4 Polar Area Element
docs.text:
Polar area element dA = r dr dθ:

       θ + dθ
      /
     / ← arc length r·dθ
    /______
   |  dA  |  ← width dr
    \______/
     \
      θ

  dA ≈ (r dθ)(dr) = r dr dθ

  NOT dr dθ — the extra r accounts for
  the "stretching" as r grows.

docs.title: 8. Changing the Order of Integration — Strategy Guide
docs.text:
Step 1. Identify the region \(D\) from the given limits:

  • Inner limits of \(y\): \(y\) goes from \(\phi_1(x)\) to \(\phi_2(x)\)
  • Outer limits of \(x\): \(x\) goes from \(a\) to \(b\)
  • Sketch the region \(D\).

Step 2. Re-describe \(D\) with the roles of \(x\) and \(y\) swapped:

  • New \(y\) range (outer): read off the global \(y\) extent from the sketch
  • New \(x\) range (inner): express \(x\) bounds as functions of \(y\)

Step 3. Write the new iterated integral and evaluate.

Example. Reverse the order: \(\int_0^1 \int_{y}^{1} \frac{\sin x}{x},dx,dy\).

Region: \({0 \leq y \leq x,; 0 \leq x \leq 1}\) (triangle below \(y=x\)).

As Type I: \(0 \leq x \leq 1\), \(0 \leq y \leq x\).

\[\int_0^1 \int_0^x \frac{\sin x}{x},dy,dx = \int_0^1 \frac{\sin x}{x} \cdot x,dx = \int_0^1 \sin x,dx = [-\cos x]_0^1 = 1 - \cos 1\]

docs.title: 9. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
9.1 Probability Distributions — The Core Application
docs.text:
In ML, every probabilistic model involves a probability density function (pdf) \(p(\mathbf{x})\), which satisfies \(p \geq 0\) and: $\(\iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} p(x,y),dx,dy = 1\)$

This normalization condition is a double integral. The Gaussian (normal) distribution in 2D is: $\(p(x,y) = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma_1\sigma_2} \exp!\left(-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma_1^2} - \frac{y^2}{2\sigma_2^2}\right)\)$

That this integrates to 1 is precisely a consequence of the Gaussian integral \(\int e^{-x^2},dx = \sqrt{\pi}\) proved via polar coordinates in §6.3.

Expected values. If \(X, Y\) are continuous random variables with joint density \(p(x,y)\): $\(\mathbb{E}[f(X,Y)] = \iint f(x,y),p(x,y),dx,dy\)$

Every expectation in probabilistic ML — expected loss, expected reward in RL, variational lower bound in VAEs — is a (high-dimensional) integral of this form.

docs.title: 9.2 The Loss Function as an Expected Double Integral
docs.text:
In supervised learning, the population risk (expected loss over the true data distribution \(p(x,y)\)) is: $\(\mathcal{R}(f) = \mathbb{E}_{(x,y) \sim p},[\ell(f(x), y)] = \iint \ell(f(x), y),p(x,y),dx,dy\)$

Training minimizes the empirical version (a Riemann sum approximation!): $\(\hat{\mathcal{R}}(f) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \ell(f(x_i), y_i) \approx \mathcal{R}(f)\)$

The law of large numbers says the empirical risk converges to the true integral as \(n \to \infty\). The double Riemann sum is not just an approximation scheme for volumes — it is the mathematical model for how a training set approximates the underlying data distribution.

docs.title: 9.3 Monte Carlo Integration — The ML Workhorse
docs.text:
In high dimensions (\(n \gg 2\)), iterated integrals are computationally infeasible — the cost grows as \(N^n\) for a grid of \(N\) points per dimension. ML uses Monte Carlo integration instead:

\[\iint f(x,y),p(x,y),dx,dy \approx \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N f(x_i, y_i), \quad (x_i, y_i) \sim p\]

This is a stochastic Riemann sum: sample points from \(p\), evaluate \(f\), average. Error scales as \(1/\sqrt{N}\) regardless of dimension — this dimension-independence is why Monte Carlo is used universally in ML (MCMC, variational inference, policy gradient in RL).

The whole theory — why MC works, its variance, importance sampling — rests on the definition of the integral as a limit of Riemann sums.

docs.title: 9.4 Convolutional Neural Networks — Convolution as an Integral
docs.text:
The convolution operation (which gives CNNs their name) is, in continuous form: $\((f * g)(x) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x - t),g(t),dt\)$

In 2D (image processing): $\((f * g)(x,y) = \iint f(x - s,, y - t),g(s,t),ds,dt\)$

A convolutional layer computes a discrete approximation of this — a double Riemann sum. Every convolution in deep learning is a double integral in disguise.

docs.title: 9.5 The Marginal Distribution — Integrating Out Variables
docs.text:
Given a joint distribution \(p(x,y)\), the marginal over \(x\) is: $\(p(x) = \int p(x,y),dy\)$

This is the fundamental operation in latent variable models (VAEs, GMMs, hidden Markov models): to compute the probability of observed data \(x\), integrate out the latent variables \(y\). The integral is usually intractable in closed form — approximating it is the central challenge of variational inference, which replaces the integral with an optimization problem.

docs.title: 9.6 Summary Table
docs.text: Calculus Concept ML Manifestation Double integral \(\iint f,dA\) Expected value \(\mathbb{E}[f(X,Y)]\) Normalization \(\iint p = 1\) Valid probability density Riemann sum approximation Empirical risk / mini-batch gradient Monte Carlo = stochastic Riemann sum MCMC, variational inference, policy gradient 2D convolution integral Convolutional layer in CNN Marginal \(\int p(x,y),dy\) Latent variable integration in generative models Gaussian integral via polar Normalization of the Gaussian distribution Change of variables / Jacobian Normalizing flows, change of representation

docs.title: 10. Summary of Techniques
docs.text: Situation Method Rectangular domain, continuous \(f\) Fubini: either order, pick simpler General domain, vertical slices Type I: \(\int_a^b \int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f,dy,dx\) General domain, horizontal slices Type II: \(\int_c^d \int_{h_1(y)}^{h_2(y)} f,dx,dy\) Inner integral has no antiderivative Switch order of integration \(D\) is a disk/annulus/sector, or \(f = f(x^2+y^2)\) Polar: \(\iint f,dA = \int!\int f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\cdot r,dr,d\theta\) Volume between two surfaces \(V = \iint_D [f_\text{top} - f_\text{bottom}],dA\)

docs.title: Midpoint Rule
docs.text: "When the exact integral is out of reach, the midpoint rule gives you the best possible rectangular approximation — and tells you precisely how wrong you are."

docs.title: 0. Preamble — Why Approximate?
docs.text:
The machinery of Fubini's theorem computes \(\iint_D f(x,y),dA\) exactly — but only when \(f\) has a closed-form antiderivative. In practice:

  • \(f(x,y)\) may be given only as tabular data (sensor readings, simulation outputs)
  • The antiderivative of \(f\) may not exist in closed form (e.g., \(f = e^{-x^2 - y^2}\) over a square)
  • The domain \(D\) may be geometrically irregular

In all these cases, we need a numerical method. The midpoint rule is the simplest and most natural — it is the double Riemann sum with a specific, optimal choice of sample points.

docs.title: 1. Recall — The Single-Variable Midpoint Rule
docs.text:
For \(\int_a^b f(x),dx\), divide \([a,b]\) into \(n\) subintervals of width \(\Delta x = \frac{b-a}{n}\), with midpoints \(\bar{x}_i = a + \left(i - \frac{1}{2}\right)\Delta x\):

\[M_n = \sum_{i=1}^n f(\bar{x}_i),\Delta x \approx \int_a^b f(x),dx\]

The midpoint is the optimal sample point for a rectangle because it cancels the leading error term (the linear part of \(f\) over the subinterval integrates to zero when sampled at the center).

docs.title: 2. The Midpoint Rule for Double Integrals — Setup
2.1 Partition the Rectangle
docs.text:
Let \(R = [a,b] \times [c,d]\). Divide:

  • \([a,b]\) into \(m\) equal subintervals of width \(\Delta x = \frac{b-a}{m}\)
  • \([c,d]\) into \(n\) equal subintervals of width \(\Delta y = \frac{d-c}{n}\)

This produces \(mn\) sub-rectangles \(R_{ij} = [x_{i-1}, x_i] \times [y_{j-1}, y_j]\), each with area: $\(\Delta A = \Delta x \cdot \Delta y\)$

docs.title: 2.2 The Midpoints
docs.text:
The midpoint of the subinterval \([x_{i-1}, x_i]\) is: $\(\bar{x}_i = \frac{x_{i-1} + x_i}{2} = a + \left(i - \frac{1}{2}\right)\Delta x, \qquad i = 1, \ldots, m\)$

The midpoint of the subinterval \([y_{j-1}, y_j]\) is: $\(\bar{y}_j = \frac{y_{j-1} + y_j}{2} = c + \left(j - \frac{1}{2}\right)\Delta y, \qquad j = 1, \ldots, n\)$

The center of the sub-rectangle \(R_{ij}\) is \((\bar{x}_i, \bar{y}_j)\).

docs.title: 2.3 The Midpoint Rule
docs.text:
Definition (Midpoint Rule for Double Integrals). The midpoint rule approximation is:

\[\boxed{M_{mn} = \sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n} f(\bar{x}_i, \bar{y}_j),\Delta A}\]

where \(\Delta A = \Delta x \cdot \Delta y\), and \((\bar{x}_i, \bar{y}_j)\) is the center of the sub-rectangle \(R_{ij}\).

Geometric meaning. Over each sub-rectangle \(R_{ij}\), we build a rectangular column (box) whose height is the value of \(f\) at the center of the base. The midpoint rule sums the volumes of all these columns.

  z
  │       ┌─────┐   ← height = f(x̄ᵢ, ȳⱼ)
  │       │     │
  │       │     │
  └───────┴─────┴────── xy-plane
          R_{ij}
          ↑ center = (x̄ᵢ, ȳⱼ)

docs.title: 3.1 Intuition from 1D
docs.text:
Over a single subinterval \([x_{i-1}, x_i]\), expand \(f\) in a Taylor series about the midpoint \(\bar{x}_i\): $\(f(x) = f(\bar{x}_i) + f'(\bar{x}_i)(x - \bar{x}_i) + \frac{f''(\bar{x}_i)}{2}(x - \bar{x}_i)^2 + \cdots\)$

Integrating over \([x_{i-1}, x_i]\): $\(\int_{x_{i-1}}^{x_i} f(x),dx = f(\bar{x}_i)\Delta x + f'(\bar{x}_i)\underbrace{\int_{x_{i-1}}^{x_i}(x - \bar{x}_i),dx}_{=,0\text{ (odd, symmetric)}} + O((\Delta x)^3)\)$

The linear error term vanishes because \((x - \bar{x}_i)\) is an odd function on \([x_{i-1}, x_i]\) centered at \(\bar{x}_i\). This is why the midpoint is better than an endpoint: it kills the \(O((\Delta x)^2)\) error per interval, leaving only \(O((\Delta x)^3)\) per interval.

The same cancellation happens in 2D over each \(R_{ij}\).

docs.title: 3.2 Error Bound for the Midpoint Rule
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(|f_{xx}|, |f_{yy}| \leq K\) on \(R = [a,b]\times[c,d]\), then the error in the midpoint rule satisfies: $\(|E_M| = \left|\iint_R f,dA - M_{mn}\right| \leq \frac{K(b-a)^3(d-c)}{24m^2} + \frac{K(b-a)(d-c)^3}{24n^2}\)$

Key observations:

  • Error \(\sim O!\left(\frac{1}{m^2}\right) + O!\left(\frac{1}{n^2}\right)\) — doubling \(m\) and \(n\) reduces error by factor of \(4\).
  • Error \(\to 0\) as \(m, n \to \infty\) — the rule is consistent.
  • The bound depends on second derivatives of \(f\), not first — confirming the cancellation of linear error.

Compare with the naive left/right endpoint rule, whose error is \(O(1/m) + O(1/n)\) — the midpoint rule converges an order faster.

docs.title: 4. Worked Example I — Direct Computation
docs.text: Problem. Use the midpoint rule with \(m = 2\), \(n = 2\) to approximate \(\iint_R \sqrt{x + 2y},dA\) where \(R = [0,2]\times[0,1]\).

docs.title: 5. Worked Example II — Function Given as a Table
docs.text:
This is the scenario where the midpoint rule is indispensable: \(f\) is known only at discrete points.

Problem. The temperature \(T(x,y)\) (in °C) at the center of each sub-rectangle in the grid \([0,4]\times[0,2]\) (with \(m=2\), \(n=2\), so \(\Delta x = 2\), \(\Delta y = 1\), \(\Delta A = 2\)) is measured as:

\(\bar{y}_1 = 0.5\) \(\bar{y}_2 = 1.5\) \(\bar{x}_1 = 1\) \(T = 12\) \(T = 18\) \(\bar{x}_2 = 3\) \(T = 20\) \(T = 25\)

Estimate the total heat content \(\iint_R T(x,y),dA\).

\[M_{22} = (12 + 18 + 20 + 25) \times 2 = 75 \times 2 = 150\]

The average temperature over \(R\) is \(\bar{T} = \frac{150}{8} = 18.75,^\circ\text{C}\) (area of \(R\) is \(4 \times 2 = 8\)).

docs.title: 6.2 Why Midpoint Beats Endpoints (1D Analogy Extended to 2D)
docs.text:
Over one sub-rectangle R_{ij}:

  Exact integral:        f   f + f_y·Δy + ...
                        ┌───────────────────┐
                    f + │   (curved surface) │
                  f_y·Δ │                   │
                        └───────────────────┘

  Left corner approx:   f(x_{i-1}, y_{j-1}) ← systematically low if f increasing
  Right corner approx:  f(x_i, y_j)         ← systematically high if f increasing
  Midpoint approx:      f(x̄_i, ȳ_j)        ← linear errors cancel (symmetric)

docs.title: 7. The Midpoint Rule on General Regions
docs.text:
If \(D\) is not a rectangle, a standard approach is:

  1. Enclose \(D\) in a rectangle \(R\).
  2. Extend \(f\) to \(R\) by setting \(f = 0\) outside \(D\).
  3. Apply the midpoint rule to \(R\).

The sub-rectangles \(R_{ij}\) that lie entirely outside \(D\) contribute zero. Sub-rectangles that straddle the boundary contribute an approximation error, but this boundary error \(\to 0\) as the grid refines (assuming \(D\) has a reasonable boundary).

Alternative: Use the midpoint rule over each boundary-aligned sub-region after decomposing \(D\) into Type I or Type II strips.

docs.title: 8. Comparison with Other Rules
docs.text:
Rule Sample point in \(R_{ij}\) Error order (per dimension) Notes Left endpoint \((x_{i-1}, y_{j-1})\) \(O(1/m) + O(1/n)\) Simplest; systematic error Right endpoint \((x_i, y_j)\) \(O(1/m) + O(1/n)\) Systematic error (opposite sign) Midpoint \((\bar{x}_i, \bar{y}_j)\) \(O(1/m^2) + O(1/n^2)\) Best among 1-point rules Trapezoidal (2D) Average of 4 corners \(O(1/m^2) + O(1/n^2)\) Same order as midpoint Simpson's (2D) Weighted combo \(O(1/m^4) + O(1/n^4)\) Higher order; needs even subdivisions

Key takeaway. The midpoint rule achieves the same asymptotic error order as the trapezoidal rule (both \(O(h^2)\)), but with half the function evaluations — one per sub-rectangle instead of four corner evaluations.

docs.title: 9. Connection to Machine Learning and Deep Learning
9.1 Mini-Batch SGD as a Midpoint Rule
docs.text:
In machine learning, the true objective is the expected loss: $\(\mathcal{R}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \iint \ell(\boldsymbol{\theta}; x, y),p(x,y),dx,dy\)$

This integral is approximated by sampling. When we use a mini-batch of \(B\) samples drawn uniformly from the dataset: $\(\hat{\mathcal{R}}_B(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \ell(\boldsymbol{\theta}; x_b, y_b)\)$

If the data space is partitioned into \(B\) equal cells and one sample is drawn from near the center of each cell, this is structurally identical to the midpoint rule. The "midpoint" philosophy — sample the center of each region — is why stratified sampling (a structured variant of this) reduces variance in Monte Carlo integration.

The key analogy:

Midpoint Rule Mini-batch SGD Partition \(R\) into \(mn\) sub-rectangles Partition dataset into \(B\) mini-batches Sample \(f\) at center \((\bar{x}_i, \bar{y}_j)\) Evaluate loss at batch samples \(\frac{1}{mn}\sum_{ij} f(\bar{x}_i,\bar{y}_j)\) \(\frac{1}{B}\sum_b \ell(\boldsymbol{\theta}; x_b, y_b)\) Error \(\to 0\) as \(mn \to \infty\) Gradient estimate improves as \(B \to \infty\)

docs.title: 9.2 Numerical Integration in Bayesian ML
docs.text:
Bayesian inference requires computing integrals of the form: $\(p(y \mid x) = \int p(y \mid x, \boldsymbol{\theta}),p(\boldsymbol{\theta} \mid \mathcal{D}),d\boldsymbol{\theta}\)$

For low-dimensional \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\), the midpoint rule (or more sophisticated quadrature) is applied directly. For high-dimensional \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\), Monte Carlo methods (MCMC, variational inference) take over — but they are conceptually grid-free versions of the same Riemann sum philosophy.

docs.title: 9.3 Quadrature in Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs)
docs.text:
Physics-Informed Neural Networks minimize residuals of PDEs over a domain: $\(\mathcal{L} = \iint_D \left[\mathcal{N}[u](https://claude.ai/chat/x,y)\right]^2 dA\)$

where \(\mathcal{N}[u]\) is a PDE operator applied to the network output \(u\). This integral is approximated by the midpoint rule (or Gaussian quadrature) over a set of collocation points — the midpoints of a partition of \(D\). The quality of the approximation directly controls training quality.

docs.title: 9.4 Gaussian Quadrature — The "Optimal Midpoint" Generalization
docs.text: The midpoint rule uses one evaluation at the center of each sub-rectangle. Gaussian quadrature asks: what are the optimal evaluation points and weights for a given number of function evaluations? The answer (Gauss–Legendre points) generalizes the midpoint idea — place sample points where they eliminate the most error. This is used in high-performance numerical integration throughout scientific ML and finite element methods.

docs.title: 10. Full Procedure Summary
docs.text:
Given \(\iint_R f(x,y),dA\) over \(R = [a,b]\times[c,d]\), approximate with \(m \times n\) grid:

\[\Delta x = \frac{b-a}{m}, \quad \Delta y = \frac{d-c}{n}, \quad \Delta A = \Delta x \cdot \Delta y\] \[\bar{x}_i = a + \left(i - \tfrac{1}{2}\right)\Delta x \quad (i = 1,\ldots,m)\] \[\bar{y}_j = c + \left(j - \tfrac{1}{2}\right)\Delta y \quad (j = 1,\ldots,n)\] \[M_{mn} = \Delta A \sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n} f(\bar{x}_i, \bar{y}_j)\]

To improve accuracy: increase \(m\) and \(n\). Error decreases as \(O(1/m^2) + O(1/n^2)\).

docs.title: 11. References
docs.text:
1. James Stewart, Calculus, §15.1 — Double integrals over rectangles; midpoint rule approximation and examples.
  2. MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus (D. Auroux) — Lecture notes on Riemann sums, numerical approximation of double integrals; available at MIT OpenCourseWare.

docs.title: Fubini's Theorem
docs.text: "The ability to switch the order of integration is one of the most quietly powerful facts in all of analysis. Use it without ceremony — but never without understanding."

docs.title: § 0 — Why This Theorem Exists
docs.text:
Before we state anything, let us ask: what problem does Fubini solve?

Suppose you want to compute

\[\iint_R f(x,y), dA\]

over some rectangle \(R = [a,b] \times [c,d]\). The double integral is defined as a limit of Riemann sums over 2D partitions — conceptually clean, computationally brutal. What we want to do is reduce this to two ordinary 1D integrals, nested inside each other:

\[\int_a^b \left( \int_c^d f(x,y), dy \right) dx \quad \text{or} \quad \int_c^d \left( \int_a^b f(x,y), dx \right) dy\]

These are called iterated integrals. But why should they equal the double integral? And why should the two orderings give the same answer?

That is precisely what Fubini's Theorem guarantees — under the right conditions.

docs.title: § 1 — Setup and Notation
docs.text:
Definition (Double Integral over a Rectangle). Let \(R = [a,b] \times [c,d] \subset \mathbb{R}^2\). Partition \([a,b]\) into \(m\) subintervals and \([c,d]\) into \(n\) subintervals, forming \(mn\) subrectangles \(R_{ij}\) each of area \(\Delta A_{ij} = \Delta x_i \cdot \Delta y_j\). Pick sample points \((x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_)\) in each. The double integral is:

\[\iint_R f(x,y), dA = \lim_{|P| \to 0} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \sum_{j=1}^{n} f(x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_), \Delta A_{ij}\]

where \(|P|\) is the norm of the partition (diameter of the largest subrectangle).

Definition (Iterated Integral). For fixed \(x\), define \(g(x) = \int_c^d f(x,y), dy\) (integrate in \(y\) first). The iterated integral integrating \(y\) first is:

\[\int_a^b \int_c^d f(x,y), dy, dx = \int_a^b g(x), dx\]

Similarly, integrating \(x\) first:

\[\int_c^d \int_a^b f(x,y), dx, dy\]

docs.title: Theorem (Fubini, rectangle version)
docs.text:
Let \(f\) be continuous on the rectangle \(R = [a,b] \times [c,d]\). Then:

\[\iint_R f(x,y), dA = \int_a^b \int_c^d f(x,y), dy, dx = \int_c^d \int_a^b f(x,y), dx, dy\]

Two things are being asserted simultaneously:

  1. The double integral equals each iterated integral (reducing 2D to nested 1D)
  2. The two orderings are equal (order of integration can be swapped freely)

Remark (continuity is sufficient, not necessary). Continuity is the condition Stewart emphasizes, and it is the right condition for a first encounter. The theorem holds under weaker hypotheses (Fubini's full theorem in measure theory requires only that \(f\) be integrable in the Lebesgue sense — see § 6 for the general statement). Continuity on a closed rectangle is more than enough.

docs.title: § 3 — Proof Sketch (the honest version)
docs.text:
A full measure-theoretic proof belongs to a real analysis course. But let us trace the argument to see why it is true.

Step 1: Continuity implies uniform continuity. Since \(f\) is continuous on the compact set \(R\), it is uniformly continuous. This ensures that for any \(\varepsilon > 0\), the iterated integrals are well-approximated by Riemann sums simultaneously in both variables.

Step 2: The inner integral defines a continuous function. Define

\[A(x) = \int_c^d f(x,y), dy\]

Since \(f\) is continuous jointly in \((x,y)\), for fixed \(x\) the function \(y \mapsto f(x,y)\) is continuous (hence integrable), and \(A(x)\) is well-defined. Moreover, uniform continuity of \(f\) implies \(A(x)\) is continuous in \(x\).

Step 3: Both equal the double integral. We use the uniform continuity to show that the Riemann sum approximations for \(\int_a^b A(x), dx\) and for \(\iint_R f, dA\) can be made to agree within \(\varepsilon\). The key identity is:

\[\sum_i \sum_j f(x_i^_, y_j^_), \Delta x_i, \Delta y_j \approx \sum_i \left( \int_c^d f(x_i^*, y), dy \right) \Delta x_i \approx \int_a^b A(x), dx\]

Both approximation steps use uniform continuity. Taking \(|P| \to 0\) gives the result. \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: Example 1 — Polynomial integrand (warm-up)
docs.text:
\[\iint_R (x^2 + 2xy), dA, \quad R = [0,1] \times [1,2]\]

Integrating \(y\) first:

\[\int_0^1 \int_1^2 (x^2 + 2xy), dy, dx\]

Inner integral (treat \(x\) as constant):

\[\int_1^2 (x^2 + 2xy), dy = \left[ x^2 y + xy^2 \right]_1^2 = (2x^2 + 4x) - (x^2 + x) = x^2 + 3x\]

Outer integral:

\[\int_0^1 (x^2 + 3x), dx = \left[ \frac{x^3}{3} + \frac{3x^2}{2} \right]_0^1 = \frac{1}{3} + \frac{3}{2} = \frac{11}{6}\]

Verify by switching order:

\[\int_1^2 \int_0^1 (x^2 + 2xy), dx, dy\]

Inner integral:

\[\int_0^1 (x^2 + 2xy), dx = \left[ \frac{x^3}{3} + x^2 y \right]_0^1 = \frac{1}{3} + y\]

Outer integral:

\[\int_1^2 \left( \frac{1}{3} + y \right) dy = \left[ \frac{y}{3} + \frac{y^2}{2} \right]_1^2 = \left(\frac{2}{3} + 2\right) - \left(\frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{3} + \frac{3}{2} = \frac{11}{6} \checkmark\]

docs.title: Example 2 — Separable functions (the cleanest case)
docs.text:
Suppose \(f(x,y) = g(x)\cdot h(y)\) on \(R = [a,b]\times[c,d]\). Then:

\[\iint_R g(x)h(y), dA = \left(\int_a^b g(x), dx\right)\left(\int_c^d h(y), dy\right)\]

Proof:

\[\int_a^b \int_c^d g(x)h(y), dy, dx = \int_a^b g(x) \left(\int_c^d h(y), dy\right) dx = \left(\int_c^d h(y), dy\right)\int_a^b g(x), dx\]

The inner integral is a constant with respect to \(x\), so it factors out. This is an extremely useful pattern — memorize it.

Concrete instance: \(\iint_{[0,\pi]\times[0,1]} \sin(x) \cdot e^y, dA = \int_0^\pi \sin x, dx \cdot \int_0^1 e^y, dy = 2 \cdot (e-1)\).

docs.title: Example 3 — Switching order rescues a computation
docs.text:
Sometimes one iterated order is tractable and the other is not.

\[\int_0^1 \int_x^1 e^{y^2}, dy, dx\]

Integrating \(y\) first (as written) requires evaluating \(\int e^{y^2}, dy\) — a non-elementary integral. Stuck.

Switch the order. The region of integration is \({(x,y) : 0 \le x \le 1,, x \le y \le 1}\), i.e., the triangle below the diagonal \(y = x\) in \([0,1]^2\).

Describing this region with \(y\) as the outer variable: \(0 \le y \le 1\), \(0 \le x \le y\).

\[\int_0^1 \int_0^y e^{y^2}, dx, dy = \int_0^1 e^{y^2} \cdot y, dy\]

Now substitute \(u = y^2\), \(du = 2y, dy\):

\[= \frac{1}{2}\int_0^1 e^u, du = \frac{1}{2}(e - 1)\]

Lesson: Fubini does not just tell you that you can switch order — it gives you the freedom to switch when one order makes the problem tractable.

docs.title: § 5 — Extension to General Regions
docs.text:
The theorem extends beyond rectangles. For a Type I region \(D = {(x,y) : a \le x \le b,, g_1(x) \le y \le g_2(x)}\):

\[\iint_D f(x,y), dA = \int_a^b \int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x,y), dy, dx\]

For a Type II region \(D = {(x,y) : c \le y \le d,, h_1(y) \le x \le h_2(y)}\):

\[\iint_D f(x,y), dA = \int_c^d \int_{h_1(y)}^{h_2(y)} f(x,y), dx, dy\]

The strategy is always: describe the region, identify which variable has fixed limits (the outer integral), and determine how the other variable's bounds depend on the outer.

docs.title: § 6 — The Full Theorem (Measure-Theoretic Statement)
docs.text:
Fubini's Theorem (general). Let \((X, \mathcal{M}, \mu)\) and \((Y, \mathcal{N}, u)\) be \(\sigma\)-finite measure spaces, and let \(f : X imes Y o \mathbb{R}\) be measurable. If

\[\int_{X imes Y} |f|, d(\mu imes u) < \infty\]

(i.e., \(f \in L^1(\mu imes u)\)), then:

\[\int_{X imes Y} f, d(\mu imes u) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f(x,y), d u(y) ight) d\mu(x) = \int_Y \left(\int_X f(x,y), d\mu(x) ight) d u(y)\]

The Tonelli variant (for non-negative measurable \(f\), no integrability hypothesis needed — equality holds though both sides may be \(+\infty\)) is often used to check the integrability hypothesis before invoking Fubini.

docs.title: The Classic Counterexample
docs.text:
Without the absolute integrability condition, Fubini fails. Consider \([0,1]^2\) with:

\[f(x,y) = \frac{x^2 - y^2}{(x^2 + y^2)^2}\]

One can verify: \(\int_0^1 \int_0^1 f, dy, dx = \frac{\pi}{4}\) but \(\int_0^1 \int_0^1 f, dx, dy = -\frac{\pi}{4}\).

The two iterated integrals disagree because \(\int \int |f|, dA = \infty\). Fubini's hypothesis is violated, and it shows.

docs.title: 7.1 — The Geometric Interpretation
docs.text:
y
|
d |-----+-----+-----+
  |  f  |  f  |  f  |   ← fix y = y₀: integrate across x  →  A(y₀)
c |-----+-----+-----+
  a           b        x

∫_c^d A(y) dy  =  ∫_a^b B(x) dx  =  Volume under surface z = f(x,y)

The double integral computes the volume under the surface \(z = f(x,y)\) above the region \(R\). Fubini says: slice the volume with planes \(x = \text{const}\) to get cross-sectional area \(A(y)\) (or \(B(x)\)), then integrate those areas.

docs.title: 7.2 — Cross-Section Mental Model
docs.text:
Imagine the solid \({(x,y,z) : (x,y) \in R,, 0 \le z \le f(x,y)}\).

  • Fix \(x = x_0\). The cross-section is a 2D region in the \(yz\)-plane with area \(\int_c^d f(x_0, y), dy\).
  • Slide \(x_0\) from \(a\) to \(b\). Integrating those cross-sectional areas gives the volume.

This is Cavalieri's Principle in disguise. Fubini is the analytic rigorous version of: the volume is the integral of the cross-sectional areas.

|  /  cross  \

|/_______________\ y
x = x₀  (fixed)

Area of slice = ∫_c^d f(x₀, y) dy

docs.title: § 8 — Fubini in AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: This is not a digression. Fubini is everywhere in modern ML.

docs.title: 8.1 — Expectation and Joint Distributions
docs.text:
The expected value of a function \(\phi(X, Y)\) under a joint distribution \(p(x,y)\) is:

\[\mathbb{E}[\phi(X,Y)] = \iint \phi(x,y), p(x,y), dx, dy\]

Fubini lets us marginalize in any order:

\[= \int \left(\int \phi(x,y), p(x|y), dx\right) p(y), dy = \int \left(\int \phi(x,y), p(y|x), dy\right) p(x), dx\]

Every time you condition on a variable and integrate out another, you are invoking Fubini.

docs.title: 8.2 — The ELBO in Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
docs.text:
The Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) involves:

\[\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{q(z|x)}\left[\log p(x|z)\right] - \text{KL}(q(z|x) | p(z))\]

The KL divergence term requires switching integration and differentiation in a way that is only valid because the integrands are sufficiently well-behaved — Fubini-type arguments underlie the interchange.

docs.title: 8.3 — Gradient of Expectations (REINFORCE, Score Function Estimator)
docs.text:
In reinforcement learning and variational inference, one needs:

\[ abla_ heta \mathbb{E}_{p_ heta(x)}[f(x)] = abla_ heta \int f(x), p_ heta(x), dx = \int f(x), abla_ heta p_ heta(x), dx\]

Interchanging the gradient and the integral is justified by the Leibniz integral rule — a direct corollary of Fubini applied to a product measure (treating \( heta\) as one coordinate, \(x\) as another). The score function trick \( abla_ heta \log p_ heta(x) = rac{ abla_ heta p_ heta(x)}{p_ heta(x)}\) is the payoff.

docs.title: 8.4 — Kernel Methods and Integral Operators
docs.text:
In kernel machines and Gaussian Processes, the kernel matrix entry is:

\[K(x, x') = \int \phi(x, \omega), \phi(x', \omega), p(\omega), d\omega\]

(Random Fourier Features, Bochner's theorem). Manipulating such integrals — bounding generalization error, computing posterior means — routinely requires switching integration order.

docs.title: 8.5 — Convolutional Neural Networks
docs.text:
The convolution operation at layer \(l\):

\[(f * g)(x) = \int f(x - y), g(y), dy\]

is itself an integral transform. Properties like associativity of convolution — essential to understanding deep network composition — follow from Fubini:

\[\int \int f(x - y), g(y - z), h(z), dy, dz = \int h(z) \left(\int f(x-y), g(y-z), dy\right) dz\]

The inner integral is a convolution; rearranging the order is Fubini.

docs.title: 8.6 — Normalizing Flows and Change of Variables
docs.text:
In normalizing flows, one models a complex distribution by a sequence of invertible transformations. The change of variables formula in multiple dimensions:

\[p_X(x) = p_Z(f^{-1}(x)) \left|\det J_{f^{-1}}(x)\right|\]

requires that the Jacobian determinant integrates correctly under the joint distribution — which is again a Fubini-type argument ensuring the integral of \(p_X\) over \(\mathbb{R}^n\) equals 1.

docs.title: § 9 — Summary and Working Rules
docs.text:
Situation What to do Rectangle, \(f\) continuous Apply Fubini freely in either order Non-rectangular region Sketch the region; decide Type I or Type II; set up limits carefully One order leads to non-elementary integral Switch the order of integration Verifying integrability (general \(f\)) Check \(\iint \|f\| < \infty\) first (Tonelli), then invoke Fubini Counterexample risk Remember: switching order without absolute integrability can give wrong answers

The working habit: Always sketch the region before setting up any iterated integral. Getting the limits wrong is far more common than misapplying the theorem itself.

docs.title: § 10 — References
docs.text:
1. Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §§ 15.2–15.3. — The standard presentation; excellent for building computational fluency and geometric intuition.

  2. MIT 18.02: Multivariable Calculus (Auroux et al.) — Lecture notes on double integrals and iterated integrals; particularly clear on region description and switching order.

  3. Rudin, Walter. Real and Complex Analysis, 3rd ed. Chapter 8. — The definitive rigorous treatment of Fubini–Tonelli in the Lebesgue setting.

  4. Folland, Gerald. Real Analysis, 2nd ed. §2.5. — Careful proof with full measure-theoretic detail; the counterexample is treated explicitly.

docs.title: Average Values
docs.text: "The average is the single number that, spread uniformly over the region, produces the same total. Everything else is bookkeeping."

docs.title: § 0 — Motivation: From 1D to 2D
docs.text:
Recall the average value of a function \(f(x)\) on \([a,b]\) from single-variable calculus:

\[f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{b-a} \int_a^b f(x), dx\]

The denominator \(b-a\) is the measure (length) of the domain. The integral is the total accumulation. Their ratio is the average.

In two dimensions, nothing changes philosophically. The domain now has area instead of length, and we integrate over a region \(D \subset \mathbb{R}^2\) instead of an interval. The formula becomes:

\[\boxed{f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{A(D)} \iint_D f(x,y), dA}\]

where \(A(D) = \iint_D dA\) is the area of \(D\).

Intuition: Imagine pouring water whose depth at \((x,y)\) is \(f(x,y)\) into a flat-bottomed container of the same footprint \(D\). The water redistributes to a uniform depth \(f_{\text{avg}}\). The total volume is conserved:

\[f_{\text{avg}} \cdot A(D) = \iint_D f(x,y), dA\]

docs.title: § 1 — Formal Definition
docs.text:
Definition. Let \(f\) be integrable on a bounded region \(D \subset \mathbb{R}^2\) with area \(A(D) > 0\). The average value of \(f\) over \(D\) is:

\[f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{A(D)} \iint_D f(x,y), dA\]

Remarks:

  • \(A(D)\) is itself a double integral: \(A(D) = \iint_D 1, dA\).
  • If \(f\) is continuous and \(D\) is connected, the Mean Value Theorem for Double Integrals guarantees existence of a point \((x_0, y_0) \in D\) with \(f(x_0, y_0) = f_{\text{avg}}\) (see § 4).
  • The definition extends immediately to \(\mathbb{R}^n\): replace area with \(n\)-dimensional volume.

docs.title: § 2 — Mean Value Theorem for Double Integrals
Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(f\) be continuous on a closed, bounded, connected region \(D\). Then there exists at least one point \((x_0, y_0) \in D\) such that:

\[f(x_0, y_0) = \frac{1}{A(D)} \iint_D f(x,y), dA = f_{\text{avg}}\]

docs.title: Proof
docs.text:
Since \(f\) is continuous on compact \(D\), it attains its minimum \(m\) and maximum \(M\):

\[m \le f(x,y) \le M \quad \forall, (x,y) \in D\]

Integrating over \(D\):

\[m \cdot A(D) \le \iint_D f, dA \le M \cdot A(D)\]

Dividing by \(A(D)\):

\[m \le \underbrace{\frac{1}{A(D)} \iint_D f, dA}_{f_{\text{avg}}} \le M\]

So \(f_{\text{avg}} \in [m, M]\). Since \(f\) is continuous on connected \(D\), by the Intermediate Value Theorem, \(f\) takes every value between \(m\) and \(M\). In particular, there exists \((x_0, y_0) \in D\) with \(f(x_0, y_0) = f_{\text{avg}}\). \(\blacksquare\)

Note: The MVT guarantees existence of such a point, but not uniqueness. There may be many such points, or (for non-connected \(D\)) none at all.

docs.title: Example 1 — Average of a polynomial over a rectangle
docs.text:
Problem. Find the average value of \(f(x,y) = x^2 y + 3y^2\) over \(R = [0,2] \times [0,1]\).

Step 1: Area.

\[A(R) = (2-0)(1-0) = 2\]

Step 2: Double integral.

\[\iint_R (x^2 y + 3y^2), dA = \int_0^2 \int_0^1 (x^2 y + 3y^2), dy, dx\]

Inner integral (\(x\) fixed):

\[\int_0^1 (x^2 y + 3y^2), dy = \left[\frac{x^2 y^2}{2} + y^3\right]_0^1 = \frac{x^2}{2} + 1\]

Outer integral:

\[\int_0^2 \left(\frac{x^2}{2} + 1\right) dx = \left[\frac{x^3}{6} + x\right]_0^2 = \frac{8}{6} + 2 = \frac{4}{3} + 2 = \frac{10}{3}\]

Step 3: Average.

\[f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{10}{3} = \frac{5}{3}\]

docs.title: Example 2 — Average temperature over a triangular region
docs.text:
Problem. The temperature at \((x,y)\) is \(T(x,y) = 4x + 2y\) (in °C). Find the average temperature over the triangle \(D\) with vertices \((0,0)\), \((2,0)\), \((0,4)\).

Step 1: Describe \(D\).

The hypotenuse has equation \(\frac{x}{2} + \frac{y}{4} = 1\), i.e., \(y = 4 - 2x\). So:

\[D = {(x,y) : 0 \le x \le 2,; 0 \le y \le 4 - 2x}\]

Step 2: Area.

\[A(D) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \text{base} \cdot \text{height} = \frac{1}{2}(2)(4) = 4\]

(Or via integration: \(\int_0^2 (4-2x), dx = [4x - x^2]_0^2 = 4\).)

Step 3: Double integral.

\[\iint_D (4x + 2y), dA = \int_0^2 \int_0^{4-2x} (4x + 2y), dy, dx\]

Inner integral:

\[\int_0^{4-2x} (4x + 2y), dy = \left[4xy + y^2\right]_0^{4-2x} = 4x(4-2x) + (4-2x)^2\] \[= (4-2x)\left[4x + (4-2x)\right] = (4-2x)(4+2x) = 16 - 4x^2\]

Outer integral:

\[\int_0^2 (16 - 4x^2), dx = \left[16x - \frac{4x^3}{3}\right]_0^2 = 32 - \frac{32}{3} = \frac{64}{3}\]

Step 4: Average.

\[T_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{64}{3} = \frac{16}{3} \approx 5.33^\circ\text{C}\]

docs.title: Example 3 — Average over a disk (polar coordinates)
docs.text:
Problem. Find the average value of \(f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2\) over the disk \(D: x^2 + y^2 \le R^2\).

Step 1: Area.

\[A(D) = \pi R^2\]

Step 2: Switch to polar. \(x^2 + y^2 = r^2\), \(dA = r, dr, d\theta\).

\[\iint_D (x^2 + y^2), dA = \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^R r^2 \cdot r, dr, d\theta = \int_0^{2\pi} d\theta \int_0^R r^3, dr\] \[= 2\pi \cdot \frac{R^4}{4} = \frac{\pi R^4}{2}\]

Step 3: Average.

\[f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{\pi R^2} \cdot \frac{\pi R^4}{2} = \frac{R^2}{2}\]

Sanity check: \(f = r^2\) ranges from \(0\) (center) to \(R^2\) (boundary). The average \(R^2/2\) lies strictly between them. ✓

Geometric insight: The average is NOT \(R^2/2\) because of a naive "midpoint" argument — it is \(R^2/2\) because points near the boundary carry more area weight (circumference \(2\pi r\) grows with \(r\)), pulling the average above the naive midpoint \(R^2/2\)... wait, here the naive midpoint is \(R^2/2\). But in general, the area-weighted average shifts the answer. For \(f = r\) over the disk: \(f_{\text{avg}} = 2R/3 \ne R/2\) — the boundary-heavy weighting pulls the average toward the rim.

docs.title: 4.2 — Locating the Mean Value Point
docs.text: For Example 2 (\(T = 4x + 2y\) over the triangle), the average was \(16/3\). The MVT guarantees a point with \(4x_0 + 2y_0 = 16/3\) inside \(D\). This is a line segment; any point on it inside \(D\) works. The theorem asserts existence — it does not pinpoint a unique location.

docs.title: 4.3 — Effect of Region Shape on the Average
docs.text:
For \(f(x,y) = x\) (temperature increasing left-to-right):

Region \(D\) \(A(D)\) \(\iint x, dA\) \(f_{\text{avg}}\) Square \([0,1]^2\) \(1\) \(1/2\) \(1/2\) Triangle: vertices \((0,0),(1,0),(0,1)\) \(1/2\) \(1/6\) \(1/3\) Triangle: vertices \((0,0),(1,0),(1,1)\) \(1/2\) \(5/12\) \(5/6\)

The shape of \(D\) shifts the average by changing how much area lies near large vs. small values of \(f\) — the geometric analogue of a weighted average.

docs.title: § 5 — Weighted Average and Probability Density
docs.text:
When the region carries a weight function \(w(x,y) \ge 0\) (a probability density, mass density, etc.), the weighted average is:

\[\langle f \rangle_w = \frac{\iint_D f(x,y), w(x,y), dA}{\iint_D w(x,y), dA}\]

The standard average is the special case \(w \equiv 1\).

Center of mass is a weighted average of position:

\[\bar{x} = \frac{\iint_D x, \rho(x,y), dA}{\iint_D \rho(x,y), dA}, \qquad \bar{y} = \frac{\iint_D y, \rho(x,y), dA}{\iint_D \rho(x,y), dA}\]

where \(\rho\) is the surface mass density.

docs.title: § 6 — Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
6.1 — Expected Value IS a Weighted Average Integral
docs.text:
The expected value of a function \(\phi(x,y)\) under a joint density \(p(x,y)\):

\[\mathbb{E}_{(X,Y) \sim p}[\phi(X,Y)] = \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} \phi(x,y), p(x,y), dx, dy\]

is precisely a weighted average with weight \(w = p\). The denominator \(\iint p, dA = 1\) (probability axiom). Every time you compute an expectation in ML, you are computing the weighted average value of a function over its domain.

docs.title: 6.2 — Loss Function as Average Loss
docs.text:
The empirical risk (training loss) in ML is a discrete average:

\[\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \ell(\hat{y}_i, y_i)\]

Its continuous population analogue is exactly the average value integral:

\[\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \iint \ell(f_\theta(x), y), p(x, y), dx, dy\]

The difference between training loss (sample average) and population loss (integral average) is generalization error — and bounding it requires understanding how well discrete sums approximate double integrals (uniform laws of large numbers, VC theory).

docs.title: 6.3 — Batch Normalization
docs.text:
Batch normalization computes the mean and variance of activations over the spatial dimensions of a feature map. For a \(H \times W\) feature map \(F\):

\[\mu = \frac{1}{HW} \sum_{i=1}^H \sum_{j=1}^W F_{ij}\]

This is a discrete double average — the exact discretization of \(\frac{1}{A} \iint F(x,y), dA\) over the spatial domain. The continuous formulation is used when deriving the theory of spatial statistics and analyzing convolutional architectures.

docs.title: 6.4 — Gaussian Process Posterior Mean
docs.text:
In a Gaussian Process, the posterior mean function is:

\[\mu^*(x) = \int k(x, x'), \alpha(x'), dx'\]

where \(k\) is the kernel and \(\alpha\) encodes the training data. Over a 2D input space \((x_1, x_2)\), this is a weighted average value of \(\alpha\) with weight kernel \(k\) — a double integral of exactly the form § 5 above.

docs.title: 6.5 — Spatial Pooling in CNNs
docs.text:
Global Average Pooling (GAP) — common in modern architectures (ResNet, GoogLeNet) — replaces the final fully-connected layer with:

\[\text{GAP}(F^{(c)}) = \frac{1}{H \cdot W} \sum_{i,j} F^{(c)}_{ij}\]

for channel \(c\). This is literally the discrete average value of the feature map over the spatial domain. The motivation: compute the average activation of each feature detector across the entire image. The continuous limit is \(f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{A} \iint F^{(c)}(x,y), dA\).

GAP reduces a 3D tensor to a vector while being translation-invariant — a property that follows from the invariance of the average value under rearrangement of the domain (Fubini + change of variables).

docs.title: 6.6 — Monte Carlo Integration
docs.text:
The average value formula is the basis of Monte Carlo integration. To compute \(\iint_D f, dA\):

  1. Sample \(N\) points \((x_i, y_i)\) uniformly from \(D\).
  2. Estimate: \(\iint_D f, dA \approx A(D) \cdot \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N f(x_i, y_i)\)

Because the sample mean \(\frac{1}{N}\sum f(x_i, y_i)\) is an unbiased estimator of \(f_{\text{avg}} = \frac{1}{A(D)}\iint f, dA\), by the Law of Large Numbers.

Monte Carlo integration is the workhorse of:

  • Bayesian posterior approximation (MCMC sampling)
  • Policy gradient methods in RL (estimating \(\mathbb{E}_\pi[R]\))
  • Training diffusion models (DDPM, score matching objectives)
  • Dropout (averaging over random subnetworks at test time)

The error scales as \(O(1/\sqrt{N})\) regardless of dimension — this dimension-independence is why MC dominates for high-dimensional integrals, while deterministic quadrature degrades exponentially (the curse of dimensionality).

docs.title: § 7 — Summary
docs.text:
Concept Formula Average value over \(D\) \(f_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{1}{A(D)} \iint_D f, dA\) Area of \(D\) \(A(D) = \iint_D 1, dA\) Reconstruction identity \(\iint_D f, dA = f_{\text{avg}} \cdot A(D)\) Weighted average \(\langle f \rangle_w = \dfrac{\iint f, w, dA}{\iint w, dA}\) MVT guarantee \(\exists,(x_0,y_0)\in D\) s.t. \(f(x_0,y_0) = f_{\text{avg}}\) (f cts, D connected)

The workflow for every problem:

1. Sketch D
2. Compute A(D)  [geometry or integration]
3. Set up ∬_D f dA  [choose order, set variable limits]
4. Evaluate the iterated integral
5. Divide by A(D)

docs.title: § 8 — References
docs.text:
1. Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. § 15.3 — Average Value of a Function. The worked examples and the MVT statement follow Stewart's treatment closely.

  2. MIT 18.02: Multivariable Calculus (Auroux) — Lecture notes on double integrals; the "flatten the solid" geometric interpretation is developed there.

  3. Bishop, Christopher. Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, § 1.2 — Probability densities and expectations as weighted averages.

docs.title: Double Integrals over General Regions
docs.text: "The art of integration is the art of finding the right order." — a recurring theme in 18.02

docs.title: §0 — Personal Preamble
docs.text:
When we first define \(\iint_R f,dA\) over a rectangle, life is pleasant: both limits are constants and Fubini's theorem is almost a triviality. The interesting mathematics begins the moment the region \(D\) stops being a box. This note develops the full rigorous theory, catalogues the practical techniques, supplies worked examples, and — because it cannot be avoided — explains why this machinery is exactly what gradient descent and the study of probability distributions secretly rely on.

All references are to Stewart, Calculus (8e) (§§15.2–15.3) and MIT 18.02 lecture notes.

docs.title: §1 — Motivation: Why Leave the Rectangle?
docs.text:
In applications the domain of integration is almost never a rectangle.

  • A probability density \(p(x,y)\) is integrated over the region \({(x,y): x^2 + y^2 \le 1}\).
  • A neural network's weight space carries a prior supported on a simplex.
  • A fluid-dynamics calculation integrates pressure over the cross-section of a pipe.

We need a definition of \(\iint_D f,dA\) that handles arbitrary bounded regions \(D \subset \mathbb{R}^2\).

docs.title: §2 — The Rigorous Definition (Extension by Zero)
docs.text:
Setup. Let \(D \subset \mathbb{R}^2\) be a bounded region and \(f : D \to \mathbb{R}\) bounded. Enclose \(D\) in a rectangle \(R = [a,b]\times[c,d]\).

Define the extended function:

\[ F(x,y) = \begin{cases} f(x,y) & \text{if } (x,y) \in D \ 0 & \text{if } (x,y) \in R \setminus D \end{cases} \]

Definition (Stewart §15.2). If \(F\) is integrable over \(R\), we set

\[ \boxed{\iint_D f,dA ;:=; \iint_R F,dA} \]

Remark. The value is independent of which rectangle \(R\) we choose (since \(F = 0\) outside \(D\)). The non-trivial part is proving \(F\) is integrable — this requires the boundary \(\partial D\) to have measure zero (e.g., \(\partial D\) is a piecewise-smooth curve), which covers every region we encounter in practice.

docs.title: §3 — Type I and Type II Regions
docs.text: The payoff of the abstract definition is the following concrete evaluation theorem. We isolate two archetypal shapes.

docs.title: 3.1 Type I Region
docs.text:
\[ D = {(x,y) : a \le x \le b,; g_1(x) \le y \le g_2(x)} \] 
y
│      g₂(x)
│    ╭──────╮
│   /        \
│  /  D       \
│  \          /
│   ╰──────╯
│      g₁(x)
│
└───────────────── x
    a           b

Theorem (Fubini, Type I). If \(f\) is continuous on \(D\):

\[ \iint_D f(x,y),dA = \int_a^b \int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x,y),dy,dx \]

Proof sketch. The extension-by-zero \(F\) equals \(f\) when \(g_1(x) \le y \le g_2(x)\) and \(0\) elsewhere. By Fubini on the rectangle:

\[ \iint_R F,dA = \int_a^b \left[\int_c^d F(x,y),dy\right]dx = \int_a^b \left[\int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x,y),dy\right]dx \qquad \square \]

docs.title: 3.2 Type II Region
docs.text:
\[ D = {(x,y) : c \le y \le d,; h_1(y) \le x \le h_2(y)} \] 
y
d ─────────────────╮
│                   │
│      D            │
│                   │
c ─────────────────╯
│  h₁(y)      h₂(y)
└──────────────────── x

Theorem (Fubini, Type II). If \(f\) is continuous on \(D\):

\[ \iint_D f(x,y),dA = \int_c^d \int_{h_1(y)}^{h_2(y)} f(x,y),dx,dy \]

docs.title: §4 — Properties (The Algebra of Double Integrals)
docs.text:
Let \(D, D_1, D_2\) be regions and \(f, g\) integrable.

Property Statement Linearity \(\iint_D (\alpha f + \beta g),dA = \alpha\iint_D f,dA + \beta\iint_D g,dA\) Additivity If \(D = D_1 \cup D_2\), \(D_1 \cap D_2\) has area 0: \(\iint_D f,dA = \iint_{D_1} f,dA + \iint_{D_2} f,dA\) Monotonicity \(f \le g\) on \(D \Rightarrow \iint_D f,dA \le \iint_D g,dA\) Area formula \(\iint_D 1,dA = \text{Area}(D)\) Estimation \(m\cdot\text{Area}(D) \le \iint_D f,dA \le M\cdot\text{Area}(D)\) when \(m \le f \le M\)

docs.title: Example 1 — Triangle (Type I)
docs.text:
Compute \(\displaystyle\iint_D x,dA\) where \(D\) is the triangle with vertices \((0,0)\), \((1,0)\), \((1,1)\).

Setting up the region. The boundary lines are \(x=1\), \(y=0\), and \(y=x\). As a Type I region:

\[ D = {(x,y) : 0 \le x \le 1,; 0 \le y \le x} \] 
y
1 ─        ╱│
│         ╱ │
│        ╱  │
│       ╱ D │
│      ╱    │
0 ────╱─────┤── x
     0      1

Evaluation.

\[ \iint_D x,dA = \int_0^1 \int_0^x x,dy,dx = \int_0^1 x\cdot[y]_0^x,dx = \int_0^1 x^2,dx = \frac{1}{3} \]

Check via Type II. Rewrite as \(D = {0 \le y \le 1,; y \le x \le 1}\):

\[ \int_0^1 \int_y^1 x,dx,dy = \int_0^1 \frac{1-y^2}{2},dy = \frac{1}{2}\left[y - \frac{y^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = \frac{1}{3} \checkmark \]

docs.title: Example 2 — Reversing the Order of Integration
docs.text:
Compute \(\displaystyle\int_0^1 \int_x^1 e^{y^2},dy,dx\).

The inner integral \(\int_x^1 e^{y^2},dy\) has no closed form in this order. Reverse order.

The region. The original order (Type I) describes:

\[ D = {(x,y) : 0 \le x \le 1,; x \le y \le 1} \]

As Type II:

\[ D = {(x,y) : 0 \le y \le 1,; 0 \le x \le y} \] 
y
1 ─╮
│╲ │
│ ╲│ D
│  ╲
│   ╲
0 ───╲─── x
0     1

Evaluation.

\[ \int_0^1 \int_0^y e^{y^2},dx,dy = \int_0^1 y,e^{y^2},dy = \frac{1}{2}\left[e^{y^2}\right]_0^1 = \frac{e-1}{2} \]

Key lesson. Switching the order of integration is not a trick — it is a rigorous operation guaranteed by Fubini's theorem. The limits change precisely because the same region \(D\) is described in two different orders.

docs.title: Example 3 — Parabolic Region
docs.text:
Compute \(\displaystyle\iint_D (x+y),dA\) where \(D = {(x,y) : 0 \le x \le 1,; x^2 \le y \le \sqrt{x}}\).

Note \(y = x^2\) and \(y = \sqrt{x}\) intersect at \((0,0)\) and \((1,1)\), and \(x^2 \le \sqrt{x}\) on \([0,1]\).

y
1 ─────────────────╮  ← y = √x
│          ╭───╯
│       ╭──╯   D
│    ╭──╯
│ ╭──╯  ← y = x²
0 ─────────────────── x
  0                 1
\[ \iint_D (x+y),dA = \int_0^1\int_{x^2}^{\sqrt{x}}(x+y),dy,dx \]

Inner integral:

\[ \int_{x^2}^{\sqrt{x}}(x+y),dy = \left[xy + \frac{y^2}{2}\right]_{x^2}^{\sqrt{x}} = \left(x^{3/2} + \frac{x}{2}\right) - \left(x^3 + \frac{x^4}{2}\right) \]

Outer integral:

\[ \int_0^1\left(x^{3/2} + \frac{x}{2} - x^3 - \frac{x^4}{2}\right)dx = \frac{2}{5} + \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{10} = \frac{3}{10} \]

docs.title: Example 4 — Non-elementary Region via Additivity
docs.text:
Compute the area of the region enclosed between \(y = \sin x\) and \(y = \cos x\) on \([0, \pi]\).

The curves cross at \(x = \pi/4\). Split \(D = D_1 \cup D_2\):

\[ \text{Area} = \int_0^{\pi/4}(\cos x - \sin x),dx + \int_{\pi/4}^{\pi}(\sin x - \cos x),dx \] \[ = [\sin x + \cos x]_0^{\pi/4} + [-\cos x - \sin x]_{\pi/4}^\pi = (\sqrt{2}-1) + (1+\sqrt{2}) = 2\sqrt{2} \]

docs.title: §6 — The Non-Obvious Subtlety: When Fubini Fails
docs.text:
Fubini's theorem requires absolute integrability: \(\iint_D |f|,dA < \infty\).

Counterexample (Sierpiński-type). Define

\[ f(x,y) = \frac{x^2 - y^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}, \quad D = [0,1]^2 \]

One can verify:

\[ \int_0^1\left(\int_0^1 f,dy\right)dx = \frac{\pi}{4}, \qquad \int_0^1\left(\int_0^1 f,dx\right)dy = -\frac{\pi}{4} \]

The iterated integrals are unequal because \(\iint_D |f|,dA = \infty\). This is the canonical warning that order cannot be swapped carelessly.

docs.title: §7 — Connection to Probability Theory
docs.text:
Let \((X, Y)\) be a jointly continuous random vector with density \(p(x,y) \ge 0\).

The marginal density of \(X\) is:

\[ p_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty p(x,y),dy \]

This is precisely the inner integral of a double integral over the strip \({X = x}\). Computing \(\mathbb{E}[g(X,Y)]\) is:

\[ \mathbb{E}[g(X,Y)] = \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} g(x,y),p(x,y),dA \]

Fubini's theorem is invoked every time we compute a marginal or compute an expectation by iterated integration.

docs.title: §8 — Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
docs.text: This is not decorative. Double integrals over general regions are structurally embedded in modern ML.

docs.title: 8.1 Continuous Normalizing Flows (CNFs)
docs.text:
A normalizing flow maps a simple distribution \(p_Z\) to a complex distribution \(p_X\) via an invertible map \(\phi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d\). The probability of \(X \in D\) is:

\[ \Pr(X \in D) = \iint_D p_X(x,y),dA = \iint_{\phi^{-1}(D)} p_Z(z_1,z_2),|\det J_\phi|,dA \]

The change of variables — a multivariable generalization of substitution in double integrals — is the mathematical core of this technique. The region \(\phi^{-1}(D)\) is typically not a rectangle: it is a general region determined by the geometry of the flow.

docs.title: 8.2 Gaussian Processes and Kernel Machines
docs.text:
The covariance operator in a Gaussian Process is:

\[ (Kf)(x) = \int_D k(x, x') f(x'),dx' \]

For 2D spatial data (images, spatial predictions), this becomes:

\[ (Kf)(x_1, x_2) = \iint_D k!\left((x_1,x_2),(x_1',x_2')\right) f(x_1',x_2'),dx_1',dx_2' \]

The domain \(D\) is the support of the data — often a non-rectangular region like a geographic boundary or an image mask.

docs.title: 8.3 Variational Inference and the ELBO
docs.text:
The Evidence Lower Bound in variational autoencoders is:

\[ \mathcal{L}(q) = \mathbb{E}_{q(z)}!\left[\log p(x \mid z)\right] - \mathrm{KL}(q(z) | p(z)) \]

Both terms involve integrals of the form \(\iint q(z) \log[\cdot],dz\). In practice, the variational family \(q\) is a Gaussian, and the reparameterisation trick converts this into a double integral over a rectangle in the \((\mu, \sigma)\) parameter space — but the original problem lives over a general latent region.

docs.title: 8.4 Monte Carlo Integration: Numerical Double Integrals
docs.text:
When the region \(D\) is complex (e.g., the feasible region of a constrained optimisation), double integrals are estimated by:

\[ \iint_D f,dA \approx \frac{\text{Area}(D)}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N f(x_i, y_i), \quad (x_i, y_i) \sim \text{Uniform}(D) \]

Sampling uniformly from a general region \(D\) — not a rectangle — is a non-trivial computational geometry problem, and the correctness of the estimator rests on the theory of this section.

docs.title: 8.5 Convolutional Neural Networks (CNFs) — Continuous Limit
docs.text:
A 2D convolution is:

\[ (f * g)(x, y) = \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} f(x - x', y - y'),g(x', y'),dA \]

In the continuous limit of a CNN, the "receptive field" of a neuron is a bounded, possibly non-rectangular region \(D\), and the activation is \(\iint_D f(x-x', y-y'),g(x',y'),dA\). Understanding how varying \(D\) changes the integral is precisely the theory developed here.

docs.title: 9.1 The Key Mantra for Setting Limits
docs.text:
For a Type I integral ∫∫_D f dA:

STEP 1:  Sketch D.
STEP 2:  Draw a vertical strip at position x.
          ─ Its bottom is y = g₁(x)
          ─ Its top    is y = g₂(x)
          These become the y-limits.
STEP 3:  The strip sweeps from x = a to x = b.
          These become the x-limits.

∫_a^b  ∫_{g₁(x)}^{g₂(x)}  f(x,y) dy dx
outer  ←────────────────────────────────
        inner

For Type II: draw a horizontal strip, read off \(x\)-limits as functions of \(y\).

docs.title: 9.2 Region Classification Flowchart
docs.text:
Is D a rectangle?
                   │
         ┌─── Yes ──┘── No ───┐
         │                    │
    Use constant         Can D be described as
    limits directly.     x ∈ [a,b], g₁(x) ≤ y ≤ g₂(x)?
                                │
                     ┌─── Yes ──┘── No ───┐
                     │                    │
                Type I            y ∈ [c,d], h₁(y) ≤ x ≤ h₂(y)?
                                          │
                               ┌─── Yes ──┘── No ────────────┐
                               │                              │
                           Type II              Split into Type I + Type II
                                                  or use change of variables
                                                  (polar, etc.)

docs.title: 9.3 Switching Order — The Geometric Key
docs.text:
Original (dy dx):              Reversed (dx dy):

y                              y
│    ┌────┐ ← y = g₂(x)       d ──────────────╮
│    │    │                    │               │
│    │ D  │                    │     D         │
│    │    │                    │               │
│    └────┘ ← y = g₁(x)       c ──────────────╯
└────┴────┴──── x              └──┬────────────── x
     a    b                       h₁(y)    h₂(y)

Fix x, sweep y.                Fix y, sweep x.
Outer integral: x.             Outer integral: y.

docs.title: §10 — Theoretical Depth: Measure-Theoretic Footnotes
docs.text:
(For the reader who wants the full story.)

Why does \(\partial D\) having measure zero matter? The Riemann integral on \(R\) exists iff the set of discontinuities of \(F\) has Lebesgue measure zero (Lebesgue's theorem on Riemann integrability). The discontinuities of \(F\) are precisely the points of \(\partial D\) where \(f \ne 0\), so if \(\partial D\) has measure zero, \(F\) is Riemann integrable.

Lebesgue's criterion. \(F : R \to \mathbb{R}\) is Riemann integrable \(\iff\) \(F\) is bounded and the set of its discontinuities has Lebesgue measure zero.

This is why any region bounded by finitely many smooth curves is legal: a smooth curve in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) has 2D Lebesgue measure zero.

Fubini–Tonelli. In Lebesgue theory, for \(f \ge 0\) measurable (Tonelli) or \(\int\int |f|,dA < \infty\) (Fubini):

\[ \int_D f,d(m_1 \times m_2) = \int_a^b \left[\int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x,y),dm_1(y)\right]dm_1(x) \]

The Riemann version we use is a special case.

docs.title: §11 — Common Mistakes and Pathologies
docs.text: Mistake What Goes Wrong Remedy Swapping limits without re-drawing Describes a different region or the empty set Always re-derive limits from a fresh sketch Forgetting to check \(g_1 \le g_2\) Negative area contribution Verify inequality holds on the entire \(x\)-interval Splitting at the wrong \(x\)-value Region mis-described Find intersections of boundary curves first Applying Fubini when $\int\int f = \infty$ Treating a non-Type-I region as Type I Variable limits depend on \(y\), not \(x\) Check: are the top/bottom bounds functions of \(x\) only?

docs.title: §12 — Summary Theorem Sheet
docs.text:
Theorem 1 (Fubini, Type I). If \(f\) is continuous on \(D = {a \le x \le b,; g_1(x) \le y \le g_2(x)}\): $\(\iint_D f,dA = \int_a^b\int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x,y),dy,dx\)$

Theorem 2 (Fubini, Type II). If \(f\) is continuous on \(D = {c \le y \le d,; h_1(y) \le x \le h_2(y)}\): $\(\iint_D f,dA = \int_c^d\int_{h_1(y)}^{h_2(y)} f(x,y),dx,dy\)$

Theorem 3 (Additivity). If \(D = D_1 \cup D_2\) and \(D_1 \cap D_2\) has area zero: $\(\iint_D f,dA = \iint_{D_1} f,dA + \iint_{D_2} f,dA\)$

Theorem 4 (Area). \(\text{Area}(D) = \iint_D 1,dA\)
