docs.title: Properties
docs.text: "Properties are not bureaucratic formalities — each one is a theorem that earns its proof."

docs.title: §0 — Preamble
docs.text:
Single-variable integration has a clean list of properties: linearity, additivity, monotonicity, the triangle inequality. Double integrals inherit every one of these, and add a few of their own born from the two-dimensional domain. This note proves each property rigorously from the definition, supplies geometric intuition, catalogues the failure modes, and traces the properties into their machine learning incarnations — because every identity here gets used implicitly in probabilistic modelling and numerical integration.

Convention throughout. \(D \subset \mathbb{R}^2\) is a bounded region whose boundary has measure zero. All functions are assumed bounded and continuous unless otherwise stated, ensuring Riemann integrability.

docs.title: §1 — The Definition We Are Working From
docs.text:
Recall: enclose \(D\) in a rectangle \(R\). Partition \(R\) into sub-rectangles \(R_{ij}\) of area \(\Delta A_{ij} = \Delta x_i \Delta y_j\). Choose sample points \((x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_)\). The double integral is the limit of the Riemann sum:

\[ \iint_D f,dA := \lim_{|P| \to 0} \sum_{i,j} f(x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_),\Delta A_{ij} \]

where the sum ranges only over sub-rectangles that intersect \(D\), and \(|P|\) is the mesh (largest diagonal of any sub-rectangle).

Every property below follows from manipulating this sum and taking limits.

docs.title: 2.1 Homogeneity
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\iint_D c,f(x,y),dA = c\iint_D f(x,y),dA, \quad c \in \mathbb{R}} \]

Proof. At the level of Riemann sums:

\[ \sum_{i,j} [c,f(x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_)],\Delta A_{ij} = c\sum_{i,j} f(x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_),\Delta A_{ij} \]

Taking \(|P| \to 0\) and using the linearity of limits gives the result. \(\square\)

docs.title: 2.2 Additivity of Integrand
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\iint_D [f(x,y) + g(x,y)],dA = \iint_D f(x,y),dA + \iint_D g(x,y),dA} \]

Proof. Identical: the Riemann sum of a sum is the sum of Riemann sums, and limits distribute over finite sums. \(\square\)

docs.title: 2.3 Combined Linearity
docs.text:
Combining 2.1 and 2.2: for \(\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{R}\),

\[ \iint_D [\alpha f + \beta g],dA = \alpha\iint_D f,dA + \beta\iint_D g,dA \]

Geometric reading. \(\iint_D f,dA\) is the signed volume under \(z = f(x,y)\) over \(D\). Scaling \(f\) by \(c\) scales the volume by \(c\); stacking two surfaces \(f\) and \(g\) yields the sum of their volumes.

z
│       f+g
│      ╱╲
│     ╱  ╲   ← volume under f+g = vol(f) + vol(g)
│    ╱  f  ╲
│   ╱────────╲
│  ╱    g     ╲
└──────────────── xy-plane (D)

ML connection. The expected value operator \(\mathbb{E}\) is a double integral (when the state space is \(\mathbb{R}^2\)):

\[ \mathbb{E}[\alpha f(X,Y) + \beta g(X,Y)] = \alpha,\mathbb{E}[f(X,Y)] + \beta,\mathbb{E}[g(X,Y)] \]

This is exactly linearity of the double integral against the density \(p(x,y)\). Every linearity argument in a derivation involving expected values — loss function decomposition, bias-variance tradeoff, ELBO manipulation — is an invocation of this property.

docs.title: §3 — Property II: Domain Additivity
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\iint_D f,dA = \iint_{D_1} f,dA + \iint_{D_2} f,dA} \]

whenever \(D = D_1 \cup D_2\) and \(D_1 \cap D_2\) has area zero (e.g., they share only a boundary curve).

Proof. The extension-by-zero functions \(F_1, F_2\) (of \(f\) onto a common rectangle \(R\)) satisfy \(F_1 + F_2 = F\) pointwise a.e. (they agree except on the shared boundary, which has measure zero). Linearity of the integral over \(R\) gives the result. \(\square\)

Geometric reading.

         D₁        │        D₂
  ╭───────────╮    │    ╭───────────╮
  │           │    │    │           │
  │  ∫∫f dA  │ ───┼─── │  ∫∫f dA  │
  │   D₁      │    │    │   D₂      │
  ╰───────────╯    │    ╰───────────╯
                   ↑ shared boundary = measure zero

Corollary. For any finite decomposition \(D = D_1 \cup \cdots \cup D_n\) (pairwise overlapping only on boundaries):

\[ \iint_D f,dA = \sum_{k=1}^n \iint_{D_k} f,dA \]

ML connection. In mixture models, the joint density is \(p(x,y) = \sum_k \pi_k p_k(x,y)\) with \(\sum_k \pi_k = 1\). Computing the marginal:

\[ p_X(x) = \int p(x,y),dy = \sum_k \pi_k \int p_k(x,y),dy = \sum_k \pi_k p_{k,X}(x) \]

The interchange of sum and integral is domain additivity (plus linearity) applied to the decomposition of the support into mixture components.

docs.title: §4 — Property III: Monotonicity
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{f(x,y) \le g(x,y) \text{ on } D \implies \iint_D f,dA \le \iint_D g,dA} \]

Proof. Since \(f \le g\) on \(D\), for every partition and every sample point:

\[ \sum_{i,j} f(x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_),\Delta A_{ij} \le \sum_{i,j} g(x_{ij}^_, y_{ij}^_),\Delta A_{ij} \]

Taking limits preserves the inequality. \(\square\)

Corollary (Positivity). \(f \ge 0\) on \(D \implies \iint_D f,dA \ge 0\).

Proof. Apply monotonicity with \(g \equiv 0\). \(\square\)

Geometric reading. If the surface \(z = f\) lies entirely below \(z = g\) over \(D\), then the volume under \(f\) cannot exceed the volume under \(g\).

z
│    z = g(x,y)  ←  upper surface
│   ╭──────────╮
│  ╭╯          ╰╮  z = f(x,y)  ← lower surface
│  │     D      │
└──┴────────────┴── xy
    vol(f) ≤ vol(g)

docs.title: §5 — Property IV: Estimation (Bounding)
docs.text:
Let \(m \le f(x,y) \le M\) for all \((x,y) \in D\). Then:

\[ \boxed{m \cdot \text{Area}(D) \le \iint_D f(x,y),dA \le M \cdot \text{Area}(D)} \]

Proof. Apply monotonicity to the chain \(m \le f \le M\) and use:

\[ \iint_D m,dA = m\cdot\text{Area}(D), \qquad \iint_D M,dA = M\cdot\text{Area}(D) \qquad \square \]

Geometric reading.

z = M ─────────────────────  ← top slab, volume = M · Area(D)
         ╭──────╮
z = f ───╯  D   ╰────────    ← actual surface, volume in between
z = m ─────────────────────  ← bottom slab, volume = m · Area(D)

The integral is "sandwiched" between two box-volumes.

ML connection. In Bayesian inference, when the likelihood \(\mathcal{L}(\theta \mid x,y) \le M\) is bounded, the normalising constant (evidence) satisfies:

\[ m \cdot \text{Vol}(\Theta) \le \int_\Theta \mathcal{L}(\theta),\pi(\theta),d\theta \le M \cdot \text{Vol}(\Theta) \]

These bounds are used to check the sanity of variational approximations and to set hyperparameters in variational inference without computing the evidence exactly.

docs.title: §6 — Property V: The Area Formula
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\iint_D 1,dA = \text{Area}(D)} \]

Proof. The Riemann sum for \(f \equiv 1\) is \(\sum_{i,j} 1 \cdot \Delta A_{ij}\), which is the total area of all sub-rectangles intersecting \(D\). In the limit \(|P| \to 0\) this converges to \(\text{Area}(D)\) (since \(\partial D\) has measure zero). \(\square\)

This is not a definition — it is a theorem that the double integral recovers area, validating the geometric interpretation.

Example. Area of the unit disk \(D = {x^2 + y^2 \le 1}\):

\[ \iint_D 1,dA = \pi(1)^2 = \pi \]

(verified directly via polar coordinates: \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 r,dr,d\theta = \pi\)).

docs.title: §7 — Property VI: Absolute Value Inequality (Triangle Inequality)
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\left|\iint_D f,dA\right| \le \iint_D |f|,dA} \]

Proof. Since \(-|f| \le f \le |f|\), monotonicity gives:

\[ -\iint_D |f|,dA \le \iint_D f,dA \le \iint_D |f|,dA \]

which is the two-sided inequality. \(\square\)

Why it matters. This is the 2D analogue of \(|\int f| \le \int |f|\). In functional analysis it is the key estimate for showing that integration defines a bounded linear functional on \(L^1(D)\).

ML connection. In generalisation bounds (e.g., PAC learning theory), the difference in expected risk between two models \(f\) and \(g\) is bounded:

\[ \left|\mathbb{E}[\ell(f)] - \mathbb{E}[\ell(g)]\right| = \left|\iint [\ell(f) - \ell(g)],p,dA\right| \le \iint |\ell(f) - \ell(g)|,p,dA \]

This is precisely the triangle inequality for double integrals. Rademacher complexity bounds and uniform convergence arguments all rely on it.

docs.title: §8 — Property VII: Mean Value Theorem for Double Integrals
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\iint_D f,dA = f(x_0, y_0)\cdot\text{Area}(D)} \]

for some \((x_0, y_0) \in D\), provided \(f\) is continuous and \(D\) is connected and compact.

Proof. Since \(D\) is compact and \(f\) continuous, \(f\) attains its minimum \(m\) and maximum \(M\) on \(D\). By the estimation property:

\[ m \le \frac{\iint_D f,dA}{\text{Area}(D)} \le M \]

By the Intermediate Value Theorem (since \(D\) is connected and \(f\) is continuous), \(f\) takes every value between \(m\) and \(M\). In particular, there exists \((x_0, y_0) \in D\) such that:

\[ f(x_0, y_0) = \frac{\iint_D f,dA}{\text{Area}(D)} \qquad \square \]

The point \((x_0, y_0)\) is called the mean value point — it is the spatial location at which the function exactly equals its average value over \(D\).

Geometric reading. The volume under \(z = f\) over \(D\) equals the volume of a flat box of height \(f(x_0, y_0)\) and base \(D\).

z
│   ┌─────────────────┐  ← z = f(x₀,y₀)  (the average height)
│   │                 │
│   │  same volume!   │
│   │                 │
└───┴─────────────────┴── D
    Area(D) × f(x₀,y₀) = ∫∫f dA

ML connection. The average activation of a feature map in a CNN over a spatial region \(D\) (Global Average Pooling) is:

\[ \bar{f} = \frac{1}{\text{Area}(D)}\iint_D f(x,y),dA = f(x_0, y_0) \]

The MVT guarantees that this average is attained somewhere — it is not merely an abstract number but a realised value of the function.

docs.title: §9 — Property VIII: Comparison with Integral Over Subdomain
docs.text:
If \(D_1 \subseteq D_2\) and \(f \ge 0\) on \(D_2\):

\[ \boxed{\iint_{D_1} f,dA \le \iint_{D_2} f,dA} \]

Proof. Write \(D_2 = D_1 \cup (D_2 \setminus D_1)\) (essentially disjoint). By domain additivity and positivity:

\[ \iint_{D_2} f,dA = \iint_{D_1} f,dA + \underbrace{\iint_{D_2 \setminus D_1} f,dA}_{\ge 0} \ge \iint_{D_1} f,dA \qquad \square \]

Remark. The hypothesis \(f \ge 0\) is essential. For signed \(f\), enlarging the domain can decrease the integral.

docs.title: §10 — Property IX: Symmetry Reduction
docs.text: These properties dramatically simplify computation when the domain has geometric symmetry.

docs.title: 10.1 Odd Function on Symmetric Domain
docs.text:
If \(D\) is symmetric about the \(y\)-axis (i.e., \((x,y) \in D \Rightarrow (-x,y) \in D\)) and \(f\) is odd in \(x\) (\(f(-x,y) = -f(x,y)\)):

\[ \boxed{\iint_D f(x,y),dA = 0} \]

Proof. Split \(D = D^+ \cup D^-\) where \(D^+ = D \cap {x \ge 0}\). Map \(D^+\) to \(D^-\) via \((x,y) \mapsto (-x,y)\):

\[ \iint_{D^-} f,dA = \iint_{D^+} f(-x,y),dA = -\iint_{D^+} f(x,y),dA \]

So \(\iint_D f,dA = \iint_{D^+} f,dA + \iint_{D^-} f,dA = 0\). \(\square\)

docs.title: 10.2 Even Function on Symmetric Domain
docs.text:
If \(D\) is symmetric about the \(y\)-axis and \(f\) is even in \(x\) (\(f(-x,y) = f(x,y)\)):

\[ \boxed{\iint_D f(x,y),dA = 2\iint_{D^+} f(x,y),dA} \]

Analogues. Replace "\(y\)-axis / odd in \(x\)" with "\(x\)-axis / odd in \(y\)", "\(x=y\) / odd under swap", etc. Full symmetry (both axes) and odd function \(\Rightarrow\) integral is zero.

Example. \(\iint_D xy,dA\) where \(D = {x^2 + y^2 \le 1}\).

\(D\) is symmetric about both axes. \(f(x,y) = xy\) is odd in \(x\) (and in \(y\)). Immediate conclusion: \(\iint_D xy,dA = 0\).

ML connection. In neural network weight initialisation, symmetry arguments like this explain why certain initialisations (e.g., all-zeros) cause symmetry breaking failure: the gradient \(\nabla_W \mathcal{L}\) — an integral over the data distribution — vanishes by a symmetry argument analogous to the above, trapping all neurons in identical states.

docs.title: §11 — Property X: Separability
docs.text:
If \(f(x,y) = g(x)\cdot h(y)\) and \(D = [a,b]\times[c,d]\) is a rectangle:

\[ \boxed{\iint_D g(x),h(y),dA = \left(\int_a^b g(x),dx\right)!\left(\int_c^d h(y),dy\right)} \]

Proof. By Fubini:

\[ \iint_D g(x),h(y),dA = \int_a^b g(x)\left[\int_c^d h(y),dy\right]dx = \left(\int_c^d h(y),dy\right)\int_a^b g(x),dx \qquad \square \]

Warning. Separability requires \(D\) to be a rectangle. On a general domain, \(\iint_D g(x)h(y),dA\) does not factor, because the limits of the inner integral depend on \(x\).

ML connection. In probabilistic graphical models, if \(X \perp Y\) (independence), then \(p(x,y) = p_X(x),p_Y(y)\). The joint expectation factors:

\[ \mathbb{E}[g(X)h(Y)] = \iint g(x)h(y),p_X(x),p_Y(y),dA = \mathbb{E}[g(X)]\cdot\mathbb{E}[h(Y)] \]

This is separability of the double integral. The breakdown of separability when \(X \not\perp Y\) is precisely the reason correlation matters.

docs.title: §12 — The Symmetry of the Properties: A Summary Table
docs.text: # Property Hypothesis Statement I Linearity \(f, g\) integrable \(\iint_D (\alpha f + \beta g),dA = \alpha\iint f + \beta\iint g\) II Domain Additivity \(D = D_1 \cup D_2\), overlap measure 0 \(\iint_D f = \iint_{D_1} f + \iint_{D_2} f\) III Monotonicity \(f \le g\) on \(D\) \(\iint_D f \le \iint_D g\) IV Estimation \(m \le f \le M\) on \(D\) \(m\cdot A(D) \le \iint_D f \le M\cdot A(D)\) V Area \(f \equiv 1\) \(\iint_D 1,dA = \text{Area}(D)\) VI Triangle Ineq. \(f\) integrable $ VII Mean Value Thm \(f\) continuous, \(D\) compact connected \(\exists(x_0,y_0)\in D: \iint_D f = f(x_0,y_0)\cdot A(D)\) VIII Subdomain \(D_1 \subseteq D_2\), \(f \ge 0\) \(\iint_{D_1} f \le \iint_{D_2} f\) IX Symmetry Symmetric \(D\), odd/even \(f\) \(\iint_D f = 0\) or \(= 2\iint_{D^+} f\) X Separability \(f = g(x)h(y)\), \(D\) rectangle \(\iint_D f = (\int g)(\int h)\)

docs.title: Example 1 — Symmetry Kills the Integral
docs.text:
Compute \(\displaystyle\iint_D (x^3 + \sin y + 4),dA\) where \(D = {(x,y): x^2 + y^2 \le 9}\).

Strategy. Use linearity to split, then symmetry.

\[ \iint_D (x^3 + \sin y + 4),dA = \underbrace{\iint_D x^3,dA}_{=0,\ \text{odd in }x} + \underbrace{\iint_D \sin y,dA}_{=0,\ \text{odd in }y} + \iint_D 4,dA \]

\(D\) is a disk of radius \(3\): \(\text{Area}(D) = 9\pi\). Therefore:

\[ = 0 + 0 + 4\cdot 9\pi = 36\pi \]

docs.title: Example 2 — Estimation Without Computing
docs.text:
Show that \(\displaystyle\iint_D e^{x^2 + y^2},dA \le e^2\pi\) where \(D = {x^2 + y^2 \le 1}\).

On \(D\): \(0 \le x^2 + y^2 \le 1\), so \(e^0 \le e^{x^2+y^2} \le e^1\).

By estimation:

\[ \iint_D e^{x^2+y^2},dA \le e\cdot\text{Area}(D) = e\cdot\pi \lt e^2\pi \qquad \checkmark \]

In fact the sharp upper bound is \(e\pi\), but \(e^2\pi\) follows immediately from the estimation property.

docs.title: Example 3 — Separability
docs.text:
Compute \(\displaystyle\iint_{[0,1]^2} e^x \cos y,dA\).

\(f(x,y) = e^x \cos y = g(x)h(y)\) and \(D\) is a rectangle. By separability:

\[ = \left(\int_0^1 e^x,dx\right)!\left(\int_0^1 \cos y,dy\right) = (e - 1)(\sin 1) \]

docs.title: Example 4 — Mean Value Theorem Applied
docs.text:
Find a point \((x_0, y_0)\) in \(D = [0,1]^2\) such that \(\iint_D (x + y),dA = (x_0 + y_0)\cdot\text{Area}(D)\).

Compute:

\[ \iint_D (x+y),dA = \int_0^1\int_0^1(x+y),dy,dx = \int_0^1\left(x + \frac{1}{2}\right)dx = 1 \]

\(\text{Area}(D) = 1\), so we need \(x_0 + y_0 = 1\). Any point on the segment \({x + y = 1} \cap [0,1]^2\) works — e.g., \((x_0, y_0) = (1/2, 1/2)\). (The MVT guarantees existence; it does not specify uniqueness.)

docs.title: 14.1 Linearity Does Not Extend to Infinite Sums
docs.text:
\[ \iint_D \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x,y),dA \ne \sum_{n=1}^\infty \iint_D f_n(x,y),dA \quad \text{in general} \]

Swapping infinite sums and integrals requires uniform convergence (or dominated convergence in the Lebesgue sense). This failure is the core obstruction in many analysis problems.

docs.title: 14.2 Domain Additivity Requires Measure-Zero Overlap
docs.text:
If \(D_1 \cap D_2\) has positive area, the formula \(\iint_D f = \iint_{D_1} f + \iint_{D_2} f\) overcounts the overlap region. The correct formula is inclusion-exclusion:

\[ \iint_{D_1 \cup D_2} f = \iint_{D_1} f + \iint_{D_2} f - \iint_{D_1 \cap D_2} f \]

docs.title: 14.3 Symmetry Requires the Domain to Be Symmetric
docs.text:
\(\iint_D x,dA = 0\) only if \(D\) is symmetric about the \(y\)-axis. If \(D = [0,1]^2\) (not symmetric), then:

\[ \iint_D x,dA = \int_0^1\int_0^1 x,dy,dx = \frac{1}{2} \ne 0 \]

docs.title: 14.4 Separability Fails on Non-Rectangular Domains
docs.text:
On the triangle \(D = {0 \le x \le 1, 0 \le y \le x}\):

\[ \iint_D xy,dA = \int_0^1 x\int_0^x y,dy,dx = \int_0^1 x\cdot\frac{x^2}{2},dx = \frac{1}{8} \]

But \(\left(\int_0^1 x,dx\right)!\left(\int_0^1 y,dy\right) = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{4} \ne \frac{1}{8}\).

docs.title: §15 — Measure-Theoretic Perspective
docs.text:
(For the reader who wants to see behind the curtain.)

In Lebesgue theory, the double integral is \(\int_D f,d(m_1 \times m_2)\) where \(m_1 \times m_2\) is the product measure on \(\mathbb{R}^2\). The properties become:

Riemann Property Measure-Theoretic Basis Linearity Linearity of the Lebesgue integral Domain Additivity Countable additivity of measure Monotonicity Monotonicity of the Lebesgue integral Estimation \(m \cdot \mu(D) \le \int_D f \le M \cdot \mu(D)\) Area formula \(m_1 \times m_2(D) = \text{Area}(D)\) Triangle inequality \(L^1\) norm satisfies $|f|_1 = \int

The MVT is a theorem about continuous functions on compact connected sets — it is not a purely measure-theoretic statement (it uses topology).

Why this matters for ML. Deep learning theory increasingly uses measure theory directly:

  • The Wasserstein distance (used in Wasserstein GANs) is defined via an infimum of integrals over coupling measures.
  • Neural ODEs and continuous normalizing flows work with push-forward measures.
  • The Neural Tangent Kernel convergence proofs use dominated convergence (the measure-theoretic version of swapping limits and integrals).

All of these require the properties above, in their full Lebesgue generality.

docs.title: §16 — Summary: The Dependency Graph of Properties
docs.text:
Definition (Riemann Sum)
        │
        ├──→ Linearity (I)
        │         │
        │         ├──→ Domain Additivity (II)
        │         │         │
        │         │         └──→ Subdomain Monotonicity (VIII)
        │         │
        │         └──→ Separability (X)
        │
        ├──→ Monotonicity (III)
        │         │
        │         ├──→ Estimation (IV)
        │         │         │
        │         │         └──→ Mean Value Theorem (VII)
        │         │
        │         └──→ Triangle Inequality (VI)
        │
        └──→ Area Formula (V)
                  │
                  └──→ Estimation (IV) [via m·Area, M·Area]

        Symmetry (IX) ← Linearity + Domain Additivity + Change of Variables

docs.title: Applications
docs.text: "The integral does not care whether you are weighing a lamina, locating a centroid, or training a neural network. It is always the same operation — accumulate, then normalize."

docs.title: § 0 — The Unifying Idea
docs.text:
Every application in this note follows the same template:

\[\text{Global quantity} = \iint_D (\text{local density of that quantity}), dA\]

The "local density" changes — mass density, charge density, probability density, squared-distance density — but the machinery is identical. Master the pattern once; apply it everywhere.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text: A lamina is a thin flat plate occupying region \(D \subset \mathbb{R}^2\). Its surface mass density \(\rho(x,y)\) (units: kg/m²) describes how mass is distributed: a small patch \(dA\) near \((x,y)\) has mass \(\approx \rho(x,y), dA\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
\[M = \iint_D \rho(x,y), dA\]

If \(\rho\) is constant (uniform lamina), then \(M = \rho \cdot A(D)\) — consistent with the elementary formula.

docs.title: Example 1 — Variable density lamina
docs.text:
A triangular lamina occupies \(D = {(x,y) : 0 \le x \le 1,, 0 \le y \le x}\) with density \(\rho(x,y) = x + y\).

Sketch of \(D\): the region below the line \(y = x\) in the unit square; a right triangle with legs along the axes.

Mass:

\[M = \int_0^1 \int_0^x (x+y), dy, dx\]

Inner integral:

\[\int_0^x (x+y), dy = \left[xy + \frac{y^2}{2}\right]_0^x = x^2 + \frac{x^2}{2} = \frac{3x^2}{2}\]

Outer integral:

\[M = \int_0^1 \frac{3x^2}{2}, dx = \frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{3} = \frac{1}{2}\]

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text: The center of mass \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\) is the point at which the lamina would balance on a pin. It is the density-weighted average position.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
The first moments about the coordinate axes:

\[M_y = \iint_D x, \rho(x,y), dA \qquad \text{(moment about the } y\text{-axis)}\] \[M_x = \iint_D y, \rho(x,y), dA \qquad \text{(moment about the } x\text{-axis)}\]

The center of mass:

\[\bar{x} = \frac{M_y}{M} = \frac{\iint_D x, \rho, dA}{\iint_D \rho, dA}, \qquad \bar{y} = \frac{M_x}{M} = \frac{\iint_D y, \rho, dA}{\iint_D \rho, dA}\]

Why \(M_y\) uses \(x\)? The moment about the \(y\)-axis measures tendency to rotate around the \(y\)-axis — driven by perpendicular distance, which is the \(x\)-coordinate.

docs.title: Special case: uniform density
docs.text:
When $\rho = $ const, it cancels:

\[\bar{x} = \frac{\iint_D x, dA}{A(D)}, \qquad \bar{y} = \frac{\iint_D y, dA}{A(D)}\]

This is the centroid — purely geometric, depending only on the shape of \(D\).

docs.title: Example 2 — Center of mass of Example 1's lamina
docs.text:
Continuing with \(D = {0 \le x \le 1, 0 \le y \le x}\), \(\rho = x+y\), \(M = 1/2\).

Compute \(M_y\):

\[M_y = \int_0^1 \int_0^x x(x+y), dy, dx\]

Inner: \(\int_0^x (x^2 + xy), dy = x^2 y + \frac{xy^2}{2}\Big|_0^x = x^3 + \frac{x^3}{2} = \frac{3x^3}{2}\)

Outer: \(\int_0^1 \frac{3x^3}{2}, dx = \frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{8}\)

Compute \(M_x\):

\[M_x = \int_0^1 \int_0^x y(x+y), dy, dx\]

Inner: \(\int_0^x (xy + y^2), dy = \frac{xy^2}{2} + \frac{y^3}{3}\Big|_0^x = \frac{x^3}{2} + \frac{x^3}{3} = \frac{5x^3}{6}\)

Outer: \(\int_0^1 \frac{5x^3}{6}, dx = \frac{5}{6} \cdot \frac{1}{4} = \frac{5}{24}\)

Center of mass:

\[\bar{x} = \frac{M_y}{M} = \frac{3/8}{1/2} = \frac{3}{4}, \qquad \bar{y} = \frac{M_x}{M} = \frac{5/24}{1/2} = \frac{5}{12}\]

Sanity check: The lamina lives in \(0 \le y \le x \le 1\). The density \(\rho = x+y\) is heavier toward the corner \((1,1)\). So \(\bar{x}\) should be above \(1/2\), and \(\bar{y}\) should be above the geometric centroid \(y = 1/3\) of the region. Both are: \(\bar{x} = 3/4\) ✓, \(\bar{y} = 5/12 > 1/3\) ✓.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
While the center of mass governs translational balance, the moment of inertia governs rotational inertia — resistance to angular acceleration. It is the rotational analogue of mass.

For a point mass \(m\) at distance \(r\) from the axis: \(I = mr^2\). For a distributed mass, integrate.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
Second moments (moments of inertia):

\[I_x = \iint_D y^2, \rho(x,y), dA \qquad \text{(about the }x\text{-axis, distance = }|y|\text{)}\] \[I_y = \iint_D x^2, \rho(x,y), dA \qquad \text{(about the }y\text{-axis, distance = }|x|\text{)}\] \[I_0 = \iint_D (x^2 + y^2), \rho(x,y), dA \qquad \text{(about the origin/}z\text{-axis)}\]

Note: \(I_0 = I_x + I_y\) (the perpendicular axis theorem).

Radius of gyration \(\tilde{x}\) about the \(y\)-axis:

\[\tilde{x} = \sqrt{\frac{I_y}{M}}\]

\(\tilde{x}\) is the distance from the axis at which all the mass, if concentrated, would give the same \(I_y\).

docs.title: Example 3 — Disk with uniform density
docs.text:
Disk \(D: x^2 + y^2 \le R^2\), uniform density \(\rho\).

By symmetry \(I_x = I_y\), so compute \(I_0 = \iint_D r^2 \rho, dA\) in polar:

\[I_0 = \rho \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^R r^2 \cdot r, dr, d\theta = \rho \cdot 2\pi \cdot \frac{R^4}{4} = \frac{\pi \rho R^4}{2}\]

Since \(M = \rho \pi R^2\):

\[I_0 = \frac{MR^2}{2}, \qquad I_x = I_y = \frac{MR^2}{4}\]

These are the standard formulas used throughout engineering mechanics.

docs.title: Example 4 — Rectangle, uniform density
docs.text:
Rectangle \([0,a] \times [0,b]\), uniform \(\rho\). Mass \(M = \rho ab\).

\[I_x = \rho \int_0^a \int_0^b y^2, dy, dx = \rho \cdot a \cdot \frac{b^3}{3} = \frac{\rho a b^3}{3} = \frac{M b^2}{3}\] \[I_y = \frac{M a^2}{3}\]

Why engineers care: \(I\) appears in \(\tau = I\alpha\) (torque = moment of inertia × angular acceleration) and in the deflection of beams under load. A wide, flat beam resists bending better — that is \(I_x \propto b^3\): doubling height multiplies bending resistance by 8.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
A function \(f(x,y) \ge 0\) is a joint probability density function (PDF) for continuous random variables \(X, Y\) if:

\[\iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} f(x,y), dA = 1\]

The probability that \((X,Y)\) falls in a region \(D\):

\[P\big((X,Y) \in D\big) = \iint_D f(x,y), dA\]

docs.title: Marginal Densities
docs.text:
Integrate out one variable to get the marginal:

\[f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y), dy, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y), dx\]

docs.title: Independence
docs.text: \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent if and only if \(f(x,y) = f_X(x) \cdot f_Y(y)\) — the joint PDF factors.

docs.title: Example 5 — Verifying a PDF and computing probability
docs.text:
Let \(f(x,y) = 6xy^2\) on \(D = {0 \le x \le 1,, 0 \le y \le 1}\), zero elsewhere.

Verify: \(\int_0^1 \int_0^1 6xy^2, dy, dx = 6 \int_0^1 x, dx \int_0^1 y^2, dy = 6 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{3} = 1\) ✓

Compute \(P(X > Y)\): the region is \({0 \le y \le x \le 1}\).

\[P(X > Y) = \int_0^1 \int_0^x 6xy^2, dy, dx = \int_0^1 6x \cdot \frac{x^3}{3}, dx = \int_0^1 2x^4, dx = \frac{2}{5}\]

docs.title: Example 6 — Bivariate normal (the fundamental distribution in ML)
docs.text:
The bivariate normal with independent components \(\sigma_X = \sigma_Y = \sigma\), means \(\mu_X = \mu_Y = 0\):

\[f(x,y) = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma^2} \exp!\left(-\frac{x^2+y^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\]

This factors as \(f_X(x) \cdot f_Y(y)\) — confirming independence. To verify \(\iint f = 1\), switch to polar:

\[\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma^2} e^{-r^2/2\sigma^2} r, dr, d\theta = \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\int_0^\infty r, e^{-r^2/2\sigma^2}, dr\]

Substitute \(u = r^2/2\sigma^2\): integral \(= \sigma^2 \int_0^\infty e^{-u}, du = \sigma^2\). So \(\frac{1}{\sigma^2} \cdot \sigma^2 = 1\) ✓

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
For random variables \((X,Y)\) with joint PDF \(f\):

\[\mathbb{E}[X] = \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} x, f(x,y), dA = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x, f_X(x), dx\] \[\mathbb{E}[Y] = \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} y, f(x,y), dA\] \[\mathbb{E}[g(X,Y)] = \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} g(x,y), f(x,y), dA\]

Variance:

\[\text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X])^2] = \iint (x - \mu_X)^2 f(x,y), dA\]

Covariance:

\[\text{Cov}(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}[(X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y)] = \iint (x-\mu_X)(y-\mu_Y), f(x,y), dA\]

Structural observation: Compare with § 2.

Physics Probability Mass density \(\rho(x,y)\) Probability density \(f(x,y)\) Total mass \(M = \iint \rho, dA\) Total probability \(= 1\) First moment \(M_y = \iint x\rho, dA\) \(\mathbb{E}[X] = \iint xf, dA\) Moment of inertia \(I_y = \iint x^2\rho, dA\) \(\mathbb{E}[X^2] = \iint x^2 f, dA\) \(I_y/M = \tilde{x}^2\) \(\mathbb{E}[X^2] - \mu_X^2 = \text{Var}(X)\)

The physics and probability are the same mathematical structure with different interpretations of the weight function.

docs.title: Example 7 — Expected value and variance
docs.text:
Using \(f(x,y) = 6xy^2\) from Example 5:

\(\mathbb{E}[X]\): (use marginal \(f_X(x) = \int_0^1 6xy^2, dy = 2x\))

\[\mathbb{E}[X] = \int_0^1 x \cdot 2x, dx = 2\int_0^1 x^2, dx = \frac{2}{3}\]

\(\mathbb{E}[Y]\): (marginal \(f_Y(y) = \int_0^1 6xy^2, dx = 3y^2\))

\[\mathbb{E}[Y] = \int_0^1 y \cdot 3y^2, dy = 3\int_0^1 y^3, dy = \frac{3}{4}\]

\(\text{Var}(X)\): \(\mathbb{E}[X^2] = \int_0^1 x^2 \cdot 2x, dx = \frac{1}{2}\), so \(\text{Var}(X) = \frac{1}{2} - \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{4}{9} = \frac{1}{18}\)

docs.text:

docs.title: 6.2 — Center of Mass vs. Centroid
docs.text:
Uniform ρ (centroid):           Non-uniform ρ (center of mass):

████████     center

★ = (x̄, ȳ) = geometric center  ★ = weighted average position

docs.title: 6.3 — Moment of Inertia: Why Distance Squared?
docs.text:
Axis of rotation (y-axis)

Contribution to I_y = x² dm

Doubling x quadruples resistance to rotation.
This is why mass near the rim of a flywheel matters more.

docs.title: § 7 — Applications in AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
7.1 — The Loss Function is a Moment Integral
docs.text:
The population risk (true loss) is:

\[\mathcal{R}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim p}[\ell(f_\theta(x), y)] = \iint \ell(f_\theta(x), y), p(x,y), dx, dy\]

This is the first moment of the loss function under the data distribution. Minimizing \(\mathcal{R}(\theta)\) is the theoretical objective; empirical risk minimization (ERM) approximates this integral by a sample mean — a Monte Carlo estimate of the double integral.

docs.title: 7.2 — Variance and Bias-Variance Tradeoff
docs.text:
The bias-variance decomposition involves:

\[\mathbb{E}[(f_\theta(x) - y)^2] = \text{Bias}^2 + \text{Variance} + \sigma^2_{\text{noise}}\]

Each term is an integral of the form \(\iint (\cdot)^2, p(x,y), dx, dy\) — a second moment, exactly as \(I_y = \iint x^2 \rho, dA\). The parallel is not a metaphor; the mathematics is identical.

docs.title: 7.3 — Covariance and Feature Correlation
docs.text:
The covariance matrix \(\Sigma\) of a feature vector \((X_1, \ldots, X_d)\) has entries:

\[\Sigma_{ij} = \text{Cov}(X_i, X_j) = \iint (x_i - \mu_i)(x_j - \mu_j), p(\mathbf{x}), d\mathbf{x}\]

In 2D: \(\text{Cov}(X,Y) = \iint (x-\mu_X)(y-\mu_Y), f(x,y), dA\).

PCA finds the eigenvectors of \(\Sigma\), which requires computing these double (or higher-dimensional) integrals from data. The empirical covariance matrix \(\hat{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})(x_i - \bar{x})^T\) is the Monte Carlo estimate of this integral.

docs.title: 7.4 — Gaussian Distributions are Everywhere
docs.text:
The multivariate Gaussian \(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma)\) with density:

\[f(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2}|\Sigma|^{1/2}} \exp!\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\mu)^T \Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\mu)\right)\]

is defined by the condition \(\iint \cdots \int f, d\mathbf{x} = 1\). Verifying this uses the polar-coordinates trick from Example 6, generalized to \(d\) dimensions. Every forward pass through a Bayesian neural network, every Gaussian Process prediction, and every VAE latent space manipulation involves this integral implicitly.

docs.title: 7.5 — Center of Mass in Attention Mechanisms
docs.text:
The attention mechanism in Transformers computes:

\[\text{Attn}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}!\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V\]

The softmax produces a probability distribution (the weights), and the output is their weighted average of the values \(V\). In the continuous limit (over a sequence modeled as a density), this is:

\[\text{output}(q) = \int \alpha(q, k), v(k), dk, \qquad \int \alpha(q,k), dk = 1\]

This is precisely a center of mass computation: the output is the \(\alpha\)-weighted average of the values \(v\) — the continuous analogue of \(\bar{x} = \frac{1}{M}\iint x\rho, dA\).

docs.title: 7.6 — Moment of Inertia and Regularization
docs.text:
Weight regularization (L2/ridge) adds \(\lambda |\theta|^2\) to the loss:

\[\mathcal{L}(\theta) + \lambda \sum_i \theta_i^2\]

The sum \(\sum \theta_i^2\) is a discrete second moment — the analogue of moment of inertia \(I = \sum m_i r_i^2\). Regularization is the assertion: keep the parameter "mass" close to the origin. The continuous limit is \(\lambda \int \theta^2, p(\theta), d\theta\) — a 1D (or higher) moment of inertia.

docs.title: 7.7 — Probability Density Estimation
docs.text:
Kernel Density Estimation (KDE):

\[\hat{f}(x,y) = \frac{1}{Nh^2} \sum_{i=1}^N K!\left(\frac{x-x_i}{h}, \frac{y-y_i}{h}\right)\]

estimates \(f(x,y)\) from data. The kernel \(K\) must satisfy \(\iint K = 1\) — a double integral normalization condition. Evaluating probabilities under \(\hat{f}\) over regions requires \(\iint_D \hat{f}, dA\), switching the double integral and the sum via Fubini.

docs.title: 7.8 — Score-Based Diffusion Models
docs.text:
Modern diffusion models (DDPM, score matching) learn \(\nabla_x \log p(x)\), the score function of the data density. The training objective involves:

\[\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p, \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}}\left[|s_\theta(x + \sigma\epsilon) - \nabla_x \log p_\sigma(x)|^2\right]\]

Every expectation here is a double (or higher-dimensional) integral. The entire theoretical foundation — existence of scores, denoising score matching equivalence, probability flow ODEs — rests on properties of these integrals: their existence, Fubini-type interchanges, and moments of the Gaussian kernel.

docs.title: § 8 — Summary Table
docs.text: Quantity Formula Analogue in Probability Mass \(M = \iint \rho, dA\) Total probability \(= 1\) First moment (about \(y\)-axis) \(M_y = \iint x\rho, dA\) \(\mathbb{E}[X] = \iint xf, dA\) First moment (about \(x\)-axis) \(M_x = \iint y\rho, dA\) \(\mathbb{E}[Y] = \iint yf, dA\) Center of mass \(\bar{x} = M_y/M\) \(\mu_X = \mathbb{E}[X]\) Moment of inertia (\(y\)-axis) \(I_y = \iint x^2\rho, dA\) \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]\) Moment of inertia (\(x\)-axis) \(I_x = \iint y^2\rho, dA\) \(\mathbb{E}[Y^2]\) Polar moment \(I_0 = I_x + I_y\) \(\mathbb{E}[X^2 + Y^2] = \mathbb{E}[r^2]\) Radius of gyration \(\tilde{x} = \sqrt{I_y/M}\) $\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[X^2]} = $ RMS of \(X\) — — \(\text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - \mu_X^2\) — — \(\text{Cov}(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}[(X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y)]\)

docs.title: § 9 — References
docs.text:
1. Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §§ 15.4–15.5. — Mass, moments, centers of mass, and probability. The notation and problem types follow Stewart throughout.

  2. MIT 18.02: Multivariable Calculus (Auroux) — Lecture notes on applications of double integrals; center of mass derivations.

  3. Casella & Berger. Statistical Inference, 2nd ed. Chapter 4. — Joint densities, marginals, expectations, and moments in full generality.

docs.title: Polar Coordinates
docs.text: "Cartesian coordinates are honest but often unkind. Polar coordinates reward those who see the geometry."

docs.title: §0 — Preamble
docs.text:
There is a class of double integrals that is technically legitimate in Cartesian form but computationally brutal — integrands involving \(x^2 + y^2\), domains that are disks or sectors or annuli. Forcing these into the \(dx,dy\) framework is like trying to describe a circle with a ruler: possible in principle, ugly in practice.

Polar coordinates exist precisely for this class of problems. The passage from \((x,y)\) to \((r,\theta)\) is not merely a substitution — it is a change of measure, and the appearance of the Jacobian factor \(r\) is the theorem's most important output. This note proves the transformation rigorously, develops the geometric intuition, catalogues the standard domain types, supplies worked examples (including the famous Gaussian integral), and traces polar integration into deep learning and probability.

References: Stewart §15.3; MIT 18.02 Sessions 55–56.

docs.title: 1.1 The Archetypal Hard Integral
docs.text:
\[ \iint_D e^{-(x^2+y^2)},dA, \quad D = {x^2 + y^2 \le R^2} \]

In Cartesian form:

\[ \int_{-R}^{R}\int_{-\sqrt{R^2-x^2}}^{\sqrt{R^2-x^2}} e^{-(x^2+y^2)},dy,dx \]

The inner integral \(\int e^{-(x^2+y^2)},dy\) has no closed form in elementary functions. The limits involve square roots. This is a disaster.

In polar form, the same integral becomes \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^R e^{-r^2},r,dr,d\theta\) — a product of two elementary integrals.

docs.title: 1.2 The Diagnostic Test
docs.text:
Use polar coordinates when:

  • The integrand contains \(x^2 + y^2\), \(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\), \(x^2 - y^2\), \(\arctan(y/x)\), or \(xy/(x^2+y^2)\)
  • The domain is a disk, annulus, sector, or wedge
  • The domain boundary is described by \(r = f(\theta)\)

docs.title: 2.1 The Transformation
docs.text:
The polar coordinate map \(\Phi: (r,\theta) \mapsto (x,y)\) is:

\[ x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta \]

with inverse (on \(\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus {(0,0)}\)):

\[ r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}, \qquad \theta = \arctan!\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) \quad \text{(with quadrant correction)} \]

Convention. We always take \(r \ge 0\) and \(\theta \in [0, 2\pi)\) (or \((-\pi, \pi]\) when convenient). Negative \(r\) is defined by \((-r, \theta) = (r, \theta + \pi)\), but we never need it here.

docs.title: 2.2 Polar Grid Geometry
docs.text:
The two families of coordinate curves are:

  • Circles \(r = c\): centred at the origin
  • Rays \(\theta = \alpha\): emanating from the origin
θ = π/2
      │
      │
      │    r = 2
      │  ╭───╮
      │ ╭╯   ╰╮   r = 1
      │╭╯ ╭──╮╰╮
      ││  │  │  │
──────┼╯  │  │  ╰┼──── θ = 0
      │╰╮ ╰──╯ ╭╯│
      │ ╰╮   ╭╯  │
      │  ╰───╯   │
      │
θ = 3π/2

A "polar rectangle" \([r_1, r_2] \times [\theta_1, \theta_2]\) is a curved wedge — an annular sector.

docs.title: §3 — The Jacobian: The Central Theorem
docs.text:
This is the heart of the matter. The change-of-variables formula for double integrals says:

\[ \iint_D f(x,y),dA = \iint_{D^*} f(r\cos\theta,, r\sin\theta),|\det J_\Phi|,dr,d\theta \]

where \(D^*\) is the pre-image of \(D\) in the \((r,\theta)\)-plane, and \(J_\Phi\) is the Jacobian matrix of \(\Phi\).

docs.title: 3.1 Computing the Jacobian
docs.text:
\[ J_\Phi = \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(r,\theta)} = \begin{pmatrix} \partial x/\partial r & \partial x/\partial\theta \ \partial y/\partial r & \partial y/\partial\theta \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -r\sin\theta \ \sin\theta & r\cos\theta \end{pmatrix} \] \[ \det J_\Phi = \cos\theta \cdot r\cos\theta - (-r\sin\theta)\cdot\sin\theta = r\cos^2\theta + r\sin^2\theta = r \]

Since \(r \ge 0\): \(|\det J_\Phi| = r\).

docs.title: 3.2 The Main Formula
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{\iint_D f(x,y),dA = \iint_{D^*} f(r\cos\theta,, r\sin\theta);r;dr,d\theta} \]

The \(r\) is not optional. It is the Jacobian determinant, encoding the geometric fact that a polar area element is not \(dr,d\theta\) but \(r,dr,d\theta\).

docs.title: 3.3 Geometric Proof of the \(r\) Factor
docs.text:
Consider a small polar rectangle: \(r \in [r, r+\Delta r]\), \(\theta \in [\theta, \theta + \Delta\theta]\).

           ╭────╮  ← arc of radius r + Δr, length (r+Δr)Δθ
          ╱      ╲
    Δr   ╱  ΔA    ╲
        ╱    ≈ r   ╲
       ╰────╯        ← arc of radius r, length rΔθ
       ←  rΔθ  →

The area of this curved wedge is:

\[ \Delta A = \frac{1}{2}(r+\Delta r)^2\Delta\theta - \frac{1}{2}r^2\Delta\theta = r,\Delta r,\Delta\theta + \frac{1}{2}(\Delta r)^2\Delta\theta \]

In the limit \(\Delta r, \Delta\theta \to 0\):

\[ dA = r,dr,d\theta \]

The \(r\) factor is the ratio of arc length to radius — it compensates for the fact that arcs at larger \(r\) subtend more area per unit angle than arcs near the origin.

docs.title: 4.1 Type I Polar Region (Fixed \(r\)-bounds)
docs.text:
\[ D^* = {(\theta, r) : \alpha \le \theta \le \beta,; 0 \le r \le R} \]

Examples: Full disk (\(\alpha=0, \beta=2\pi\)), half-disk, sector.

\[ \iint_D f,dA = \int_\alpha^\beta \int_0^R f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta),r,dr,d\theta \]

docs.title: 4.2 Type II Polar Region (\(r\)-bounds depend on \(\theta\))
docs.text:
\[ D^* = {(\theta, r) : \alpha \le \theta \le \beta,; r_1(\theta) \le r \le r_2(\theta)} \]

Examples: Regions bounded by polar curves like \(r = 1 + \cos\theta\) (cardioid), \(r = \cos(2\theta)\) (rose).

\[ \iint_D f,dA = \int_\alpha^\beta \int_{r_1(\theta)}^{r_2(\theta)} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta),r,dr,d\theta \]

docs.title: Example 1 — Area of a Disk (Verification)
docs.text:
Compute \(\text{Area}(D)\) where \(D = {x^2 + y^2 \le R^2}\).

\[ \text{Area}(D) = \iint_D 1,dA = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^R r,dr,d\theta = \int_0^{2\pi}\frac{R^2}{2},d\theta = \pi R^2 \checkmark \]

docs.title: Example 2 — The Gaussian Integral (The Most Important Integral in Probability)
docs.text:
Compute \(I = \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2},dx\).

The trick. Consider \(I^2\):

\[ I^2 = \left(\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2},dx\right)!\left(\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-y^2},dy\right) = \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} e^{-(x^2+y^2)},dA \]

The second equality uses separability (the domain is all of \(\mathbb{R}^2\), a "rectangle" in the extended sense).

Switch to polar. Let \(D_R = {r \le R}\). By exhaustion (\(D_R \nearrow \mathbb{R}^2\) as \(R \to \infty\)):

\[ I^2 = \lim_{R\to\infty}\iint_{D_R} e^{-r^2},r,dr,d\theta = \lim_{R\to\infty}\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^R e^{-r^2},r,dr,d\theta \]

Inner integral: let \(u = r^2\), \(du = 2r,dr\):

\[ \int_0^R e^{-r^2},r,dr = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^{R^2}e^{-u},du = \frac{1}{2}(1-e^{-R^2}) \]

Therefore:

\[ I^2 = \lim_{R\to\infty}\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{1}{2}(1-e^{-R^2}),d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\pi\cdot 1 = \pi \] \[ \boxed{I = \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2},dx = \sqrt{\pi}} \]

This is the most elegant application of polar integration. Every Gaussian in probability and deep learning traces back to this computation.

docs.title: Example 3 — Integrand with \(x^2 + y^2\)
docs.text:
Compute \(\displaystyle\iint_D (x^2 + y^2)^{3/2},dA\) where \(D = {1 \le x^2 + y^2 \le 4}\) (annulus).

In polar: \(x^2 + y^2 = r^2\), so \((x^2+y^2)^{3/2} = r^3\). Domain: \(r \in [1,2]\), \(\theta \in [0,2\pi]\).

\[ = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_1^2 r^3 \cdot r,dr,d\theta = 2\pi\int_1^2 r^4,dr = 2\pi\cdot\frac{r^5}{5}\Bigg|_1^2 = 2\pi\cdot\frac{31}{5} = \frac{62\pi}{5} \]

docs.title: Example 4 — Sector Region
docs.text:
Compute \(\displaystyle\iint_D xy,dA\) where \(D\) is the region in the first quadrant between the circles \(r=1\) and \(r=3\).

\(D\): \(r \in [1,3]\), \(\theta \in [0,\pi/2]\). In polar: \(xy = r\cos\theta \cdot r\sin\theta = r^2\sin\theta\cos\theta = \frac{r^2}{2}\sin(2\theta)\).

\[ = \int_0^{\pi/2}\int_1^3 \frac{r^2}{2}\sin(2\theta)\cdot r,dr,d\theta = \frac{1}{2}\left(\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin(2\theta),d\theta\right)!\left(\int_1^3 r^3,dr\right) \] \[ = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\left[-\frac{\cos(2\theta)}{2}\right]_0^{\pi/2}\cdot\frac{r^4}{4}\Bigg|_1^3 = \frac{1}{2}\cdot 1 \cdot 20 = 10 \]

docs.title: Example 5 — Non-standard Limits: Region Described by a Polar Curve
docs.text:
Compute the area enclosed by one petal of the rose \(r = \cos(2\theta)\).

One petal lies in \(\theta \in [-\pi/4, \pi/4]\) (where \(\cos(2\theta) \ge 0\)).

\[ \text{Area} = \int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\int_0^{\cos(2\theta)} r,dr,d\theta = \int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\frac{\cos^2(2\theta)}{2},d\theta \]

Using \(\cos^2(u) = \frac{1+\cos(2u)}{2}\):

\[ = \frac{1}{2}\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\frac{1+\cos(4\theta)}{2},d\theta = \frac{1}{4}\left[\theta + \frac{\sin(4\theta)}{4}\right]_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} = \frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{\pi}{8} \]

docs.title: Example 6 — Converting a Cartesian Integral to Polar
docs.text:
Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^1\int_0^{\sqrt{1-x^2}} e^{x^2+y^2},dy,dx\).

Identify the region. This is the quarter-disk in the first quadrant: \(x^2 + y^2 \le 1\), \(x \ge 0\), \(y \ge 0\).

Polar translation: \(r \in [0,1]\), \(\theta \in [0, \pi/2]\). Integrand: \(e^{r^2}\).

\[ = \int_0^{\pi/2}\int_0^1 e^{r^2},r,dr,d\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\left[e^{r^2}\right]_0^1 = \frac{\pi}{4}(e-1) \]

docs.title: §6 — The Change of Variables Theorem (Full Generality)
docs.text:
The polar substitution is a special case of the general Change of Variables theorem. This section states the general theorem so that polar is properly contextualised.

Theorem (Change of Variables). Let \(\Phi: D^* \to D\) be a \(C^1\) bijection (except possibly on a set of measure zero), where \(D^*, D \subset \mathbb{R}^2\). Then:

\[ \iint_D f(x,y),dA = \iint_{D^*} f(\Phi(u,v)),\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|,du,dv \]

where \(\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right| = |\det J_\Phi|\) is the absolute Jacobian determinant.

For polar coordinates: \(\Phi(r,\theta) = (r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\), \(|\det J_\Phi| = r\).

Geometric meaning of the Jacobian. \(|\det J_\Phi|\) measures the local area magnification of \(\Phi\): a small region near \((u,v)\) of area \(\delta A\) in the \((u,v)\)-plane maps to a region of area \(\approx |\det J_\Phi|\cdot\delta A\) in the \((x,y)\)-plane. The Jacobian is the correction factor ensuring areas are correctly accounted for.

(r,θ)-plane                    (x,y)-plane
                    Φ
  ┌──────┐   ─────────────→   ╭──────╮
  │ Δr Δθ│                   ╱  r·Δr·Δθ ╲
  └──────┘                  ╱            ╲
  area = ΔrΔθ               ╰────────────╯
                              area = r·ΔrΔθ

  magnification factor = r = |det J_Φ|

docs.title: Error 1 — Forgetting the \(r\) Factor
docs.text:
\[ \iint_D f,dA \ne \int_\alpha^\beta\int_{r_1}^{r_2} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta),dr,d\theta \]

The correct formula always has \(r,dr,d\theta\). Forgetting \(r\) produces a systematically wrong answer with no warning sign.

Mnemonic. \(dA = dx,dy = r,dr,d\theta\). The area element on the left is the same object expressed in two coordinate systems.

docs.title: Error 2 — Wrong \(\theta\)-Range for a Full Circle
docs.text: A full circle requires \(\theta \in [0, 2\pi]\), not \([0, \pi]\). The interval \([0,\pi]\) gives a half-disk.

docs.title: Error 3 — Origin Included When \(r_1 = 0\)
docs.text: When \(r_1 = 0\), \(\Phi\) is not injective at the origin (every \(\theta\) maps to \((0,0)\)). This is legal because \({r=0}\) has measure zero in the \((r,\theta)\)-plane — the change-of-variables theorem allows failures on measure-zero sets.

docs.title: Error 4 — Applying Polar to a Non-Circular Domain
docs.text: Polar coordinates are optimal for circular geometry. For ellipses \(\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}\le 1\), use the elliptic substitution \(x = ar\cos\theta\), \(y = br\sin\theta\) (Jacobian: \(abr\)), not standard polar.

docs.title: Error 5 — Sign of \(r\)
docs.text: Always \(r \ge 0\) in our convention. If a polar curve formula gives \(r < 0\) for some \(\theta\), the curve traces a reflected point — handle by restricting \(\theta\) or using \(|r|\).

docs.title: §8 — Symmetry in Polar Coordinates
docs.text:
Symmetry is easier to exploit in polar form.

Symmetry Condition Simplification About \(x\)-axis \(f(r,-\theta) = f(r,\theta)\) and \(D\) symmetric \(\int_0^{2\pi} \to 2\int_0^\pi\) About \(y\)-axis \(f(r,\pi-\theta) = f(r,\theta)\) and \(D\) symmetric \(\int_0^{2\pi} \to 2\int_0^\pi\) Full rotational \(f\) depends only on \(r\) \(\int_0^{2\pi}d\theta = 2\pi\) factors out \(n\)-fold rotational \(f(r,\theta+2\pi/n) = f(r,\theta)\) \(\int_0^{2\pi} = n\int_0^{2\pi/n}\)

Key example. If \(f(x,y) = g(r)\) depends only on \(r\) (radially symmetric):

\[ \iint_D g(r),dA = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^R g(r),r,dr,d\theta = 2\pi\int_0^R g(r),r,dr \]

docs.title: §9 — The Polar Coordinate Machine: Step-by-Step Protocol
docs.text:
GIVEN: ∫∫_D f(x,y) dA

STEP 1.  Does the domain D have circular/radial structure?
         └── No → stay Cartesian (or use other substitution)
         └── Yes → proceed

STEP 2.  Describe D in polar:
         Find α, β (θ-range) and r₁(θ), r₂(θ) (r-bounds at each θ).
         Draw the region. Label all boundary curves in polar form.

STEP 3.  Substitute:
         x = r cosθ,  y = r sinθ
         Replace all occurrences of x²+y² with r².

STEP 4.  Write the integral:
         ∫_α^β ∫_{r₁(θ)}^{r₂(θ)}  f(rcosθ, rsinθ) · r  dr dθ
                                                        ↑
                                               NEVER FORGET THIS

STEP 5.  Evaluate inner integral (in r), then outer (in θ).

STEP 6.  Check dimensional sanity: Area integrals should give [length]².

docs.title: §10 — Connection to Probability and Machine Learning
10.1 The Gaussian Distribution — Its Very Existence Depends on This
docs.text:
The univariate normal distribution \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) has density \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/2}\). The normalisation constant \(\sqrt{2\pi}\) comes from:

\[ \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2/2},dx = \sqrt{2\pi} \]

Proof: Substitute \(x = t/\sqrt{2}\) to get \(\sqrt{2}\int e^{-t^2/2},dt\)... which reduces to our Gaussian integral. So the very fact that the standard normal density integrates to 1 is a consequence of polar coordinates applied to a double integral. Without this calculation, the Gaussian distribution is not well-defined.

docs.title: 10.2 Multivariate Gaussian
docs.text:
For \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^2\) with covariance \(\Sigma = \sigma^2 I\):

\[ p(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma^2}e^{-|\mathbf{x}|^2/(2\sigma^2)} \]

Normalisation check:

\[ \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} p(x,y),dA = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma^2}\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2/(2\sigma^2)},r,dr,d\theta = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma^2}\cdot 2\pi\cdot\sigma^2 = 1 \]

This is exactly the polar double integral computation, and it must equal 1 for \(p\) to be a valid density.

docs.title: 10.3 Reparameterisation Trick in VAEs (Radial Decomposition)
docs.text:
In Variational Autoencoders, the latent space prior is \(\mathcal{N}(0, I)\). Sampling from this prior and computing expectations uses the identity:

\[ \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)}[f(\mathbf{z})] = \iint f(x,y),\frac{e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2}}{2\pi},dA = \int_0^\infty\int_0^{2\pi} f(r,\theta),\frac{e^{-r^2/2}}{2\pi},r,d\theta,dr \]

Decomposing into radial and angular components (polar coordinates) underlies the radial basis function interpretation of the latent space and the geometry of the latent manifold.

docs.title: 10.4 Attention Mechanisms — Radial Decay
docs.text:
In some spatial attention architectures (e.g., for point clouds or 2D feature maps), attention weights decay radially:

\[ \alpha(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{k}) = \exp!\left(-\frac{|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{k}|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \]

Computing the total attention mass over a spatial region \(D\) is:

\[ \int_D \alpha(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{k}),dA = \iint_D e^{-r^2/(2\sigma^2)},r,dr,d\theta \]

(centring at \(\mathbf{q}\)). This is a polar integral, and its closed form informs how to set \(\sigma\) for a desired effective receptive field size.

docs.title: 10.5 Score-Based Generative Models (Diffusion)
docs.text:
The score function \(\nabla_\mathbf{x}\log p(\mathbf{x})\) for a radially symmetric density \(p(\mathbf{x}) \propto e^{-V(r)}\) is:

\[ \nabla_\mathbf{x}\log p = -V'(r),\hat{r} = -V'(r),\frac{\mathbf{x}}{r} \]

Computing normalisation constants and partition functions for such densities requires polar integration. Diffusion model theory (DDPM, Score SDE) extensively uses radially-symmetric reference distributions whose analysis is pure polar calculus.

docs.title: §11 — Extended Example: Normalising an Unnormalised Density
docs.text:
Problem. The function \(f(x,y) = C e^{-(x^2+y^2)}(1 + x^2 + y^2)\) is a probability density on \(\mathbb{R}^2\). Find \(C\).

We need \(\iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} f,dA = 1\), so \(C^{-1} = \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} e^{-(x^2+y^2)}(1+x^2+y^2),dA\).

Polar form. \(r \in [0,\infty)\), \(\theta \in [0,2\pi]\), integrand \(= e^{-r^2}(1+r^2)\):

\[ C^{-1} = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}(1+r^2),r,dr,d\theta = 2\pi\int_0^\infty (re^{-r^2} + r^3 e^{-r^2}),dr \]

Compute each piece using \(\int_0^\infty r^{2k+1}e^{-r^2},dr = \frac{k!}{2}\):

  • \(\int_0^\infty re^{-r^2},dr = \frac{0!}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\)
  • \(\int_0^\infty r^3 e^{-r^2},dr = \frac{1!}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\)
\[ C^{-1} = 2\pi\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\right) = 2\pi \implies \boxed{C = \frac{1}{2\pi}} \]

This is a non-trivial unnormalised density that arises in practice (it is related to the Chi-squared distribution), and polar coordinates make the normalisation tractable.

docs.title: §12 — Connections to Other Coordinate Systems
docs.text:
Polar coordinates in 2D are the first member of a family:

Dimension Coordinates Jacobian Area/Volume Element 2D Polar \((r, \theta)\) \(r\) \(r,dr,d\theta\) 3D (cylinder) Cylindrical \((r,\theta,z)\) \(r\) \(r,dr,d\theta,dz\) 3D (sphere) Spherical \((\rho,\phi,\theta)\) \(\rho^2\sin\phi\) \(\rho^2\sin\phi,d\rho,d\phi,d\theta\) General \((u_1,\ldots,u_n)\) $ \det J

The Jacobian \(r\) (polar) generalises to \(r\) (cylindrical) and \(\rho^2\sin\phi\) (spherical). In all cases, it is the determinant of the coordinate transformation's Jacobian matrix.

docs.title: §13 — Summary Theorem Sheet
docs.text:
Main Formula:

\[ \iint_D f(x,y),dA = \int_\alpha^\beta\int_{r_1(\theta)}^{r_2(\theta)} f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta);r;dr,d\theta \]

Key substitutions:

\[ x = r\cos\theta, \quad y = r\sin\theta, \quad x^2+y^2 = r^2, \quad dA = r,dr,d\theta \]

Jacobian: \(\det\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(r,\theta)} = r\)

Gaussian integral (consequence): \(\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2},dx = \sqrt{\pi}\)

Radially symmetric integrand: \(\displaystyle\iint_D g(r),dA = 2\pi\int_0^R g(r),r,dr\) (for full disk of radius \(R\))

docs.title: §14 — References
docs.text:
1. Stewart, J. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. Cengage, 2016. §15.3 — Double Integrals in Polar Coordinates; §15.9 — Change of Variables.
  2. MIT OpenCourseWare. 18.02SC Multivariable Calculus, Fall 2010. Sessions 55–56. https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-02sc-multivariable-calculus-fall-2010/
  3. Apostol, T. Mathematical Analysis, 2nd ed. Addison-Wesley, 1974. §11.7 — Change of Variables.
  4. Bishop, C.M. Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning. Springer, 2006. §2.3 — Gaussian distribution and normalisation.
  5. Song, Y. & Ermon, S. "Generative Modeling by Estimating Gradients of the Data Distribution." NeurIPS 2019. (Score-based models using Gaussian reference densities.)
  6. Kingma, D. & Welling, M. "Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes." ICLR 2014. (VAE latent space geometry.)

docs.title: Surface Area
docs.text: "Area is the shadow that curvature casts on the flat world."

docs.title: §0 — Preamble
docs.text:
The length of a curve is computed by straightening infinitesimal arcs. The area of a surface is computed by flattening infinitesimal patches. Both operations involve a Jacobian-like correction factor — the arc length element \(ds = \sqrt{1 + (f')^2},dx\) in 1D becomes the surface area element \(dS = \sqrt{1 + f_x^2 + f_y^2},dA\) in 2D. The derivation of this element is a theorem, not a definition, and its proof requires understanding how a tangent plane approximates a curved surface locally.

This note builds the theory from scratch: the geometric motivation, the rigorous derivation of \(dS\), parametric surfaces and their general area formula, the role of the cross product, worked examples, and — because the machinery is identical — the appearance of surface area in neural rendering and implicit surface learning.

References: Stewart §15.5 (surface area), §16.6 (parametric surfaces); MIT 18.02 Sessions 70–72.

docs.title: §1 — Motivation: Why \(dA\) Alone Is Wrong
docs.text:
Suppose \(z = f(x,y)\) defines a surface \(S\) over a domain \(D \subset \mathbb{R}^2\). A naive attempt at the area is \(\iint_D dA\) — but this gives the area of the shadow (the projection of \(S\) onto the \(xy\)-plane), not the area of \(S\) itself. The two agree only when \(S\) is flat (i.e., \(f\) is constant).

z
│        ╱╲    ← surface S (tilted)
│       ╱  ╲
│      ╱    ╲
│     ╱  S   ╲
│    ╱──────────  ← shadow on xy-plane (area = ∫∫ dA, WRONG)
└─────────────── xy

Tilted patch has MORE area than its shadow.
Correction factor = sec(γ) where γ = angle between patch and horizontal.

A tilted planar patch of area \(\Delta S\) projects to a horizontal patch of area \(\Delta A = \Delta S \cos\gamma\), where \(\gamma\) is the angle between the patch and the \(xy\)-plane. So \(\Delta S = \Delta A / \cos\gamma = \Delta A \cdot \sec\gamma\).

The whole theory is about computing \(\sec\gamma\) in terms of \(f_x\) and \(f_y\).

docs.title: §2 — The Surface Area Element: Rigorous Derivation
2.1 Setup
docs.text:
Let \(S\) be the surface \(z = f(x,y)\) over a domain \(D\). Assume \(f \in C^1(D)\).

Partition \(D\) into small rectangles \(R_{ij}\) of dimensions \(\Delta x \times \Delta y\). Above each \(R_{ij}\), the surface \(S\) has a small curved patch \(S_{ij}\). We approximate \(S_{ij}\) by its tangent plane at a corner point \((x_i, y_j, f(x_i, y_j))\).

docs.title: 2.2 The Tangent Plane Patch
docs.text:
At \((x_0, y_0, z_0) = (x_0, y_0, f(x_0,y_0))\), the tangent plane to \(z = f(x,y)\) is:

\[ z - z_0 = f_x(x_0,y_0)(x-x_0) + f_y(x_0,y_0)(y-y_0) \]

Two vectors lying in this tangent plane, corresponding to steps \(\Delta x\) and \(\Delta y\) in the domain, are:

\[ \mathbf{a} = \langle \Delta x,; 0,; f_x,\Delta x \rangle = \Delta x,\langle 1, 0, f_x \rangle \] \[ \mathbf{b} = \langle 0,; \Delta y,; f_y,\Delta y \rangle = \Delta y,\langle 0, 1, f_y \rangle \]

docs.title: 2.3 Area of the Tangent Patch
docs.text:
The area of the parallelogram spanned by \(\mathbf{a}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) is \(|\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}|\).

\[ \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \Delta x,\Delta y;\begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \ 1 & 0 & f_x \ 0 & 1 & f_y \end{vmatrix} = \Delta x,\Delta y;\langle -f_x,;-f_y,;1\rangle \] \[ |\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}| = \Delta x,\Delta y;\sqrt{f_x^2 + f_y^2 + 1} \]

docs.title: 2.4 The Surface Area Formula
docs.text:
Summing over all patches and taking the limit:

\[ \boxed{A(S) = \iint_D \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right)^2};dA} \]

The integrand \(dS = \sqrt{1 + f_x^2 + f_y^2},dA\) is the surface area element.

docs.title: 2.5 The \(\sec\gamma\) Interpretation
docs.text:
The unit normal to the surface is \(\hat{n} = \frac{\langle -f_x, -f_y, 1\rangle}{\sqrt{1+f_x^2+f_y^2}}\).

The angle \(\gamma\) between the surface and the \(xy\)-plane satisfies:

\[ \cos\gamma = \hat{n}\cdot\hat{k} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+f_x^2+f_y^2}} \]

So \(\sqrt{1+f_x^2+f_y^2} = \sec\gamma\), and:

\[ A(S) = \iint_D \sec\gamma,dA \]

This confirms the geometric intuition: each infinitesimal area element \(dA\) in the domain is inflated by the secant of the tilt angle to give the true surface area.

docs.title: 3.1 Definition
docs.text:
A parametric surface is a map \(\mathbf{r}: D^* \subset \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^3\):

\[ \mathbf{r}(u,v) = \langle x(u,v),; y(u,v),; z(u,v) \rangle, \quad (u,v) \in D^* \]

The surface \(z = f(x,y)\) is the special case \(\mathbf{r}(x,y) = \langle x, y, f(x,y)\rangle\).

Other examples:

  • Sphere: \(\mathbf{r}(\phi,\theta) = \langle R\sin\phi\cos\theta,, R\sin\phi\sin\theta,, R\cos\phi\rangle\)
  • Cylinder: \(\mathbf{r}(\theta, z) = \langle R\cos\theta,, R\sin\theta,, z\rangle\)
  • Torus: \(\mathbf{r}(\theta,\phi) = \langle (R+r\cos\phi)\cos\theta,, (R+r\cos\phi)\sin\theta,, r\sin\phi\rangle\)

docs.title: 3.2 The Tangent Vectors
docs.text:
The partial derivatives of \(\mathbf{r}\) give tangent vectors to the surface:

\[ \mathbf{r}_u = \frac{\partial\mathbf{r}}{\partial u} = \left\langle \frac{\partial x}{\partial u},;\frac{\partial y}{\partial u},;\frac{\partial z}{\partial u}\right\rangle \] \[ \mathbf{r}_v = \frac{\partial\mathbf{r}}{\partial v} = \left\langle \frac{\partial x}{\partial v},;\frac{\partial y}{\partial v},;\frac{\partial z}{\partial v}\right\rangle \]

\(\mathbf{r}_u\) is tangent to the \(u\)-parameter curve (holding \(v\) fixed); \(\mathbf{r}_v\) similarly.

docs.title: 3.3 The Surface Area Element for Parametric Surfaces
docs.text:
A small patch \([u, u+du]\times[v, v+dv]\) maps to a parallelogram spanned by \(\mathbf{r}_u,du\) and \(\mathbf{r}_v,dv\). Its area is:

\[ dS = |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|,du,dv \]

General Surface Area Formula:

\[ \boxed{A(S) = \iint_{D^*} |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|,du,dv} \]

docs.title: 3.4 Recovering the Graph Formula
docs.text:
For \(\mathbf{r}(x,y) = \langle x, y, f(x,y)\rangle\):

\[ \mathbf{r}_x = \langle 1, 0, f_x\rangle, \qquad \mathbf{r}_y = \langle 0, 1, f_y\rangle \] \[ \mathbf{r}_x\times\mathbf{r}_y = \langle -f_x,;-f_y,;1\rangle, \qquad |\mathbf{r}_x\times\mathbf{r}_y| = \sqrt{1+f_x^2+f_y^2} \]

Recovering \(dS = \sqrt{1+f_x^2+f_y^2},dA\). \(\square\)

docs.title: §4 — The Cross Product \(\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v\): What It Encodes
docs.text:
\[ \mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \ \partial x/\partial u & \partial y/\partial u & \partial z/\partial u \ \partial x/\partial v & \partial y/\partial v & \partial z/\partial v \end{vmatrix} \]

Expanding:

\[ = \left\langle \frac{\partial(y,z)}{\partial(u,v)},; \frac{\partial(z,x)}{\partial(u,v)},; \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} \right\rangle \]

where \(\frac{\partial(y,z)}{\partial(u,v)} = \det\begin{pmatrix}y_u & z_u \ y_v & z_v\end{pmatrix}\) is a \(2\times 2\) Jacobian.

So:

\[ |\mathbf{r}_u\times\mathbf{r}_v|^2 = \left(\frac{\partial(y,z)}{\partial(u,v)}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial(z,x)}{\partial(u,v)}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right)^2 \]

This is the 2D analogue of the arc-length formula: just as \(ds = \sqrt{(dx/dt)^2+(dy/dt)^2+(dz/dt)^2},dt\) in 1D, here the "speed" of the surface parameterisation in 2D is \(|\mathbf{r}_u\times\mathbf{r}_v|\).

1D curve:   r(t)          →   ds = |r'(t)| dt       (speed × time)
2D surface: r(u,v)        →   dS = |r_u × r_v| du dv (area magnification)

The cross product magnitude is the area magnification factor of the parametrisation \(\mathbf{r}\) — it is the surface analogue of the Jacobian determinant.

docs.title: Example 1 — Surface Area of a Sphere
docs.text:
Claim: \(A(S^2_R) = 4\pi R^2\).

Parametrisation. Use spherical angles \(\phi \in [0,\pi]\) (polar), \(\theta \in [0, 2\pi]\) (azimuthal):

\[ \mathbf{r}(\phi,\theta) = \langle R\sin\phi\cos\theta,; R\sin\phi\sin\theta,; R\cos\phi\rangle \]

Compute tangent vectors:

\[ \mathbf{r}_\phi = \langle R\cos\phi\cos\theta,; R\cos\phi\sin\theta,; -R\sin\phi\rangle \] \[ \mathbf{r}_\theta = \langle -R\sin\phi\sin\theta,; R\sin\phi\cos\theta,; 0\rangle \]

Cross product:

\[ \mathbf{r}_\phi\times\mathbf{r}_\theta = R^2\langle -\sin^2\phi\cos\theta,; -\sin^2\phi\sin\theta,; -\sin\phi\cos\phi\rangle \] \[ |\mathbf{r}_\phi\times\mathbf{r}_\theta| = R^2\sin\phi\sqrt{\sin^2\phi\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\phi\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\phi} = R^2\sin\phi \]

(using \(\sin^2\phi(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta) + \cos^2\phi = \sin^2\phi + \cos^2\phi = 1\)).

Area:

\[ A = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi R^2\sin\phi,d\phi,d\theta = R^2\int_0^{2\pi}d\theta\int_0^\pi\sin\phi,d\phi = R^2\cdot 2\pi\cdot[-\cos\phi]_0^\pi = 4\pi R^2 \checkmark \]

docs.title: Example 2 — Surface Area of a Cone
docs.text:
Find the surface area of the cone \(z = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) over the disk \(D = {x^2+y^2\le R^2}\).

Compute partials:

\[ f_x = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}, \qquad f_y = \frac{y}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}} \] \[ f_x^2 + f_y^2 = \frac{x^2+y^2}{x^2+y^2} = 1 \] \[ \sqrt{1+f_x^2+f_y^2} = \sqrt{2} \]

Area:

\[ A = \iint_D \sqrt{2},dA = \sqrt{2}\cdot\text{Area}(D) = \sqrt{2}\cdot\pi R^2 \]

Verification. The cone \(z = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) has half-angle \(45°\). The slant height is \(R\sqrt{2}\). The lateral surface area is \(\pi R \cdot (R\sqrt{2}) = \pi R^2\sqrt{2}\). \(\checkmark\)

docs.title: Example 3 — Surface Area of a Paraboloid
docs.text:
Find the area of \(z = x^2 + y^2\) over \(D = {x^2+y^2\le 1}\).

\[ f_x = 2x, \quad f_y = 2y, \quad \sqrt{1+f_x^2+f_y^2} = \sqrt{1+4(x^2+y^2)} \]

Switch to polar (\(r^2 = x^2+y^2\)):

\[ A = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 \sqrt{1+4r^2},r,dr,d\theta = 2\pi\int_0^1 r\sqrt{1+4r^2},dr \]

Let \(u = 1+4r^2\), \(du = 8r,dr\):

\[ = 2\pi\cdot\frac{1}{8}\int_1^5\sqrt{u},du = \frac{\pi}{4}\cdot\frac{2}{3}\left[u^{3/2}\right]_1^5 = \frac{\pi}{6}(5\sqrt{5}-1) \]

docs.title: Example 4 — Cylinder (Parametric)
docs.text:
Find the area of the lateral surface of \(x^2 + y^2 = R^2\), \(0 \le z \le H\).

Parametrisation: \(\mathbf{r}(\theta, z) = \langle R\cos\theta,; R\sin\theta,; z\rangle\), \(\theta\in[0,2\pi]\), \(z\in[0,H]\).

\[ \mathbf{r}_\theta = \langle -R\sin\theta,; R\cos\theta,; 0\rangle, \qquad \mathbf{r}_z = \langle 0,; 0,; 1\rangle \] \[ \mathbf{r}_\theta\times\mathbf{r}_z = \langle R\cos\theta,; R\sin\theta,; 0\rangle, \qquad |\mathbf{r}_\theta\times\mathbf{r}_z| = R \] \[ A = \int_0^H\int_0^{2\pi} R,d\theta,dz = 2\pi R H \checkmark \]

docs.title: Example 5 — A Tricky Graph: \(z = xy\) Over a Triangle
docs.text:
Find the area of \(z = xy\) over \(D = {0\le x\le 1,; 0\le y\le x}\).

\[ f_x = y,\quad f_y = x,\quad \sqrt{1+x^2+y^2} \] \[ A = \int_0^1\int_0^x\sqrt{1+x^2+y^2},dy,dx \]

The inner integral does not have a pleasant closed form in general, but we can note:

\[ \sqrt{1+x^2+y^2} \ge 1 \implies A \ge \text{Area}(D) = \frac{1}{2} \] \[ \text{On }D:; x^2+y^2\le 2x^2\le 2 \implies \sqrt{1+x^2+y^2}\le\sqrt{3} \implies A\le \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \]

The Estimation property bounds \(A \in \left[\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right]\) without computing the integral. Numerically, \(A\approx 0.603\).

docs.title: 6.1 Flat Surfaces
docs.text: \(z = c\) (constant): \(f_x = f_y = 0\), so \(dS = dA\). Area \(= \text{Area}(D)\).

docs.title: 6.2 Constant-Slope Planes
docs.text:
\(z = ax + by + c\): \(f_x = a\), \(f_y = b\), so \(dS = \sqrt{1+a^2+b^2},dA\).

\[ A = \sqrt{1+a^2+b^2}\cdot\text{Area}(D) \]

The magnification factor \(\sqrt{1+a^2+b^2} = \sec\gamma\) is constant — the plane is uniformly tilted.

docs.title: 6.3 Surfaces of Revolution
docs.text:
Rotate \(y = g(x) \ge 0\), \(a\le x\le b\), about the \(x\)-axis. Parametrise:

\[ \mathbf{r}(x,\theta) = \langle x,; g(x)\cos\theta,; g(x)\sin\theta\rangle \] \[ |\mathbf{r}_x\times\mathbf{r}_\theta| = g(x)\sqrt{1+[g'(x)]^2} \] \[ \boxed{A = 2\pi\int_a^b g(x)\sqrt{1+[g'(x)]^2},dx} \]

This is the familiar surface of revolution formula from single-variable calculus — it is a special case of the parametric surface area formula.

Example: Sphere of radius \(R\). Rotate \(y = \sqrt{R^2-x^2}\), \(x\in[-R,R]\):

\[ g'(x) = \frac{-x}{\sqrt{R^2-x^2}}, \quad 1+[g'(x)]^2 = \frac{R^2}{R^2-x^2}, \quad g(x)\sqrt{1+[g'(x)]^2} = R \] \[ A = 2\pi\int_{-R}^R R,dx = 4\pi R^2 \checkmark \]

docs.title: §7 — The First Fundamental Form (Differential Geometry Preview)
docs.text:
For a parametric surface \(\mathbf{r}(u,v)\), define the metric coefficients:

\[ E = \mathbf{r}_u\cdot\mathbf{r}_u = |\mathbf{r}_u|^2, \qquad F = \mathbf{r}_u\cdot\mathbf{r}_v, \qquad G = \mathbf{r}_v\cdot\mathbf{r}_v = |\mathbf{r}_v|^2 \]

The First Fundamental Form is the matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}E & F \ F & G\end{pmatrix}\).

Key identity:

\[ |\mathbf{r}_u\times\mathbf{r}_v|^2 = |\mathbf{r}_u|^2|\mathbf{r}_v|^2 - (\mathbf{r}_u\cdot\mathbf{r}_v)^2 = EG - F^2 \]

(by the Lagrange identity \(|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}|^2 = |\mathbf{a}|^2|\mathbf{b}|^2 - (\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b})^2\)).

Therefore:

\[ dS = \sqrt{EG-F^2},du,dv \]

Coordinate systems. For orthogonal parametrisations (\(F = \mathbf{r}_u\cdot\mathbf{r}_v = 0\)):

\[ dS = \sqrt{EG},du,dv = |\mathbf{r}_u||\mathbf{r}_v|,du,dv \] Surface \(E\) \(F\) \(G\) \(dS\) Sphere \((\phi,\theta)\) \(R^2\) \(0\) \(R^2\sin^2\phi\) \(R^2\sin\phi,d\phi,d\theta\) Cylinder \((\theta,z)\) \(R^2\) \(0\) \(1\) \(R,d\theta,dz\) Graph \(z=f(x,y)\) \(1+f_x^2\) \(f_xf_y\) \(1+f_y^2\) \(\sqrt{1+f_x^2+f_y^2},dx,dy\)

The First Fundamental Form is the object that intrinsic geometry lives in — lengths, angles, and areas on the surface are all determined by \(E, F, G\). It is the bridge between multivariable calculus and Riemannian geometry.

docs.title: §8 — Comparison: Arc Length vs Surface Area
docs.text:
It is worth pausing to see the exact structural parallel:

Object Parametrisation Differential Total measure Curve in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) \(\mathbf{r}(t)\), \(t\in[a,b]\) $ds = \mathbf{r}'(t) Graph \(y=f(x)\) — \(ds = \sqrt{1+(f')^2},dx\) \(\int_a^b\sqrt{1+(f')^2},dx\) Surface in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) \(\mathbf{r}(u,v)\), \((u,v)\in D^*\) $dS = \mathbf{r}_u\times\mathbf{r}_v Graph \(z=f(x,y)\) — \(dS = \sqrt{1+f_x^2+f_y^2},dA\) \(\iint_D\sqrt{1+f_x^2+f_y^2},dA\)

In each case: parametrise → differentiate → take magnitude → integrate.

The 1D magnitude is a vector norm; the 2D magnitude is a cross-product norm. Both are Jacobian-type correction factors.

docs.title: §9 — Common Errors and Pitfalls
docs.text: Error What Goes Wrong Remedy Writing \(A = \iint_D dA\) Computes shadow area, not surface area Always include \(\sqrt{1+f_x^2+f_y^2}\) Wrong order \(\mathbf{r}_u\times\mathbf{r}_v\) vs \(\mathbf{r}_v\times\mathbf{r}_u\) Sign change in normal, but $ \cdot Forgetting \(r,dr,d\theta\) when converting to polar See §3 of polar notes The \(\sqrt{1+f_x^2+f_y^2}\) and the polar \(r\) are two separate factors Using \((u,v)\) with \(\mathbf{r}_u\parallel\mathbf{r}_v\) Cross product \(= 0\), parametrisation degenerate Choose \((u,v)\) so tangent vectors are non-parallel Forgetting \(\sin\phi\) factor for sphere $ \mathbf{r}\phi\times\mathbf{r}\theta

docs.title: §10 — Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
10.1 Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and Surface Rendering
docs.text:
NeRF represents a scene as a continuous function \((x,y,z,\theta,\phi) \mapsto (\text{colour}, \sigma)\) where \(\sigma\) is volume density. The rendered colour along a ray integrates:

\[ C(\mathbf{r}) = \int_0^\infty T(t),\sigma(\mathbf{r}(t)),\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}(t),\mathbf{d}),dt \]

The surface of an object is the level set \({\sigma = \sigma_{\text{threshold}}}\). Computing the area of this implicit surface uses the coarea formula — a generalisation of the surface area integral. The training loss in some NeRF variants explicitly penalises surface area (to encourage thin, sharp surfaces), making the surface area integral a component of the optimisation objective.

docs.title: 10.2 Implicit Neural Representations (INR) and the Eikonal Equation
docs.text:
Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) represent surfaces as zero level sets of a function \(\Phi: \mathbb{R}^3 o \mathbb{R}\). The surface is \(S = {\Phi(\mathbf{x}) = 0}\).

The coarea formula gives:

\[ ext{Area}(S) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} | abla\Phi(\mathbf{x})|,\delta(\Phi(\mathbf{x})),d\mathbf{x} \]

When \(\Phi\) is a true SDF, \(| abla\Phi| = 1\) everywhere (eikonal condition). The loss function in IGR (Implicit Geometric Regularisation) and NeuS includes:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{ ext{eikonal}} = \iint_{\mathbb{R}^3}(| abla\Phi(\mathbf{x})| - 1)^2,d\mathbf{x} \]

This is the \(L^2\) error of the gradient magnitude — enforcing the surface to be a valid SDF. Its derivation uses exactly the parametric surface area machinery developed here.

docs.title: 10.3 Geometric Deep Learning and Surface Meshing
docs.text:
In mesh-based shape generation (e.g., Pixel2Mesh, DeepMesh), the model outputs a triangulated surface. The loss often includes a surface area regulariser:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{area}} = \sum_{\text{triangles}} \text{Area}(\triangle_i) \]

where \(\text{Area}(\triangle_i) = \frac{1}{2}|(\mathbf{v}_2-\mathbf{v}_1)\times(\mathbf{v}_3-\mathbf{v}_1)|\) is exactly the cross-product formula for the area of the parallelogram spanned by two edge vectors — the discrete version of \(|\mathbf{r}_u\times\mathbf{r}_v|\).

The gradient of this loss with respect to vertex positions \(\mathbf{v}_i\) drives shape towards smooth, minimal-area surfaces.

docs.title: 10.4 Riemannian Geometry and Transformer Attention
docs.text:
The attention mechanism in a Transformer computes scores between tokens living in a high-dimensional space. When this space is given a Riemannian metric \(G = (g_{ij})\), the "volume" of attention neighbourhoods is:

\[ \text{Vol}(\mathcal{N}) = \int_{\mathcal{N}} \sqrt{\det G},du,dv \]

The factor \(\sqrt{\det G}\) is exactly \(\sqrt{EG-F^2}\) (for 2D manifolds) — the same quantity that appears in the First Fundamental Form. Recent work on hyperbolic and spherical transformers explicitly computes this volume element to normalise attention weights.

docs.title: 10.5 Diffusion on Surfaces (Graph Neural Networks)
docs.text:
Geometric diffusion — used in protein structure prediction (AlphaFold), molecular property prediction, and 3D shape analysis — involves the Laplace–Beltrami operator on a surface. The heat kernel and eigenfunctions of this operator are defined through integrals of the form:

\[ \langle f, g \rangle_S = \iint_S f,g,dS \]

where \(dS\) is exactly the surface area element. The entire spectral theory of signals on surfaces — used by spectral GNNs — lives in the Hilbert space \(L^2(S, dS)\), whose inner product is the surface integral.

docs.title: §11 — The Protocol: Setting Up Any Surface Area Integral
docs.text:
GIVEN: A surface S

STEP 1. How is S described?
        ├── As a graph z = f(x,y) over domain D
        │       → use A = ∫∫_D √(1 + f_x² + f_y²) dA
        │       → identify D, compute partials, simplify radical
        │
        └── Parametrically r(u,v) over D*
                → compute r_u and r_v
                → compute r_u × r_v  (3×3 determinant)
                → compute |r_u × r_v|  (simplify!)
                → integrate: A = ∫∫_{D*} |r_u × r_v| du dv

STEP 2. Is the domain circular?
        └── Yes → switch to polar before integrating
            (remember: dA = r dr dθ is SEPARATE from √(1+f_x²+f_y²))

STEP 3. Simplify the radical FIRST.
        Look for:
        - f_x² + f_y² = constant  (cone, plane)  → √ pulls out
        - f_x² + f_y² = g(r²)     (paraboloid)   → polar substitution

STEP 4. Check with dimension: area has units [length]².

docs.title: §12 — Summary Formula Sheet
docs.text:
Graph \(z = f(x,y)\):

\[ A(S) = \iint_D\sqrt{1 + f_x^2 + f_y^2},dA \]

Parametric surface \(\mathbf{r}(u,v)\):

\[ A(S) = \iint_{D^_}|\mathbf{r}_u\times\mathbf{r}_v|,du,dv = \iint_{D^_}\sqrt{EG-F^2},du,dv \]

Surface of revolution (\(y = g(x)\ge 0\) rotated about \(x\)-axis):

\[ A = 2\pi\int_a^b g(x)\sqrt{1+[g'(x)]^2},dx \]

Key area elements:

Surface \(dS\) Plane \(z = ax+by+c\) \(\sqrt{1+a^2+b^2},dA\) Cone \(z = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) \(\sqrt{2},dA\) Sphere \(r = R\) \(R^2\sin\phi,d\phi,d\theta\) Cylinder \(r = R\) \(R,d\theta,dz\) Paraboloid \(z=x^2+y^2\) \(\sqrt{1+4r^2},r,dr,d\theta\)

docs.text:

  2. MIT OpenCourseWare. 18.02SC Multivariable Calculus, Fall 2010. Sessions 70–72. https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-02sc-multivariable-calculus-fall-2010/
