docs.title: Change of Variables
docs.text: "A good coordinate system is half the solution. The Jacobian is the price you pay for the privilege of working in comfortable coordinates."

docs.title: 0. The Core Problem
docs.text:
Suppose you need to evaluate:

\[\iint_R e^{\frac{x-y}{x+y}},dA\]

where \(R\) is the triangle with vertices \((0,0)\), \((1,0)\), \((0,1)\).

In Cartesian coordinates this is a nightmare — the exponent is a rational function of \(x\) and \(y\), and the triangular region produces \(y\)-limits that depend on \(x\). There is no clean antiderivative.

But watch what happens if we introduce \(u = x-y\), \(v = x+y\). Then:

\[e^{\frac{x-y}{x+y}} = e^{u/v}\]

The triangular region in \(xy\) maps to a triangular region in \(uv\) with simple, constant limits. The integral collapses.

This is the essence of change of variables: trade a hard region/integrand pair for an easy one, paying a precise price (the Jacobian) to keep the integral equal.

docs.title: 1. Review — The 1D Case
docs.text:
Before generalizing, recall the substitution rule from single-variable calculus:

\[\int_a^b f(x),dx = \int_c^d f(g(u)),g'(u),du\]

where \(x = g(u)\), \(g(c)=a\), \(g(d)=b\).

The factor \(g'(u) = dx/du\) accounts for how the transformation stretches or compresses the interval. If \(g'(u) > 1\), a small \(du\) corresponds to a larger \(dx\); the integral must be scaled accordingly.

The absolute value \(|g'(u)|\) is what matters for area/volume — not the sign. The sign of \(g'\) determines orientation, not magnitude.

The Jacobian in higher dimensions is the exact generalization of \(|g'(u)|\).

docs.title: 2.1 Setup
docs.text:
Let \(T: (u,v) \mapsto (x,y)\) be a transformation defined by:

\[x = x(u,v), \qquad y = y(u,v)\]

Suppose:

  • \(T\) is a \(C^1\) (continuously differentiable) bijection from region \(S\) in \(uv\)-space onto region \(R\) in \(xy\)-space
  • \(T\) is one-to-one on the interior of \(S\) (it may fail on the boundary)

docs.title: 2.2 The Jacobian
docs.text:
Definition. The Jacobian determinant of the transformation \(T\) is:

\[\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v}\[10pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix} = \frac{\partial x}{\partial u}\frac{\partial y}{\partial v} - \frac{\partial x}{\partial v}\frac{\partial y}{\partial u}\]

docs.title: 2.3 The Change of Variables Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem. Under the conditions above:

\[\boxed{\iint_R f(x,y),dA = \iint_S f(x(u,v),,y(u,v))\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|du,dv}\]

What the Jacobian does. The area element \(dA = dx,dy\) in \(xy\)-space corresponds to \(\left|\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|du,dv\) in \(uv\)-space. The Jacobian measures the local area magnification factor of the transformation at each point.

docs.title: 3.1 Linear Approximation
docs.text:
Near a point \((u_0,v_0)\), the transformation \(T\) is approximately linear:

\[\begin{pmatrix}x\y\end{pmatrix} \approx \begin{pmatrix}x_0\y_0\end{pmatrix} + \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}\partial x/\partial u & \partial x/\partial v\\partial y/\partial u & \partial y/\partial v\end{pmatrix}}_{\mathbf{J}}\begin{pmatrix}u-u_0\v-v_0\end{pmatrix}\]

A small rectangle \([u_0, u_0+du]\times[v_0,v_0+dv]\) in \(S\) maps (approximately) to a parallelogram in \(R\) spanned by the columns of \(\mathbf{J}\):

\[\mathbf{a} = \begin{pmatrix}\partial x/\partial u\\partial y/\partial u\end{pmatrix}du,\qquad \mathbf{b} = \begin{pmatrix}\partial x/\partial v\\partial y/\partial v\end{pmatrix}dv\]

The area of this parallelogram is \(|\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}| = |\det\mathbf{J}|,du,dv\).

docs.title: 3.2 Visualization
docs.text:
uv-space                           xy-space

  v                                y
  │                                │
  │  ┌──────┐                      │    ╱──────╲
  │  │      │  ──── T ────>        │   ╱        ╲
  │  │  S   │  du×dv               │  ╱    R     ╲
  │  └──────┘                      │ ╱             ╲
  │   du  dv                       │╱ |det J|·du·dv ╲
  └──────────── u                  └────────────────── x

  Rectangle of area du·dv   →   Parallelogram of area |det J|·du·dv

  If |det J| > 1: transformation EXPANDS area locally
  If |det J| < 1: transformation COMPRESSES area locally
  If |det J| = 0: transformation is DEGENERATE (collapses dimension)

docs.title: 3.3 Why the Absolute Value?
docs.text: The determinant \(\det\mathbf{J}\) can be negative — this means \(T\) reverses orientation (like a reflection). For computing areas or integrals of positive quantities, orientation doesn't matter; only the magnitude of the area scaling does. Hence \(|\det\mathbf{J}|\).

docs.title: 4. The Inverse Jacobian
docs.text:
A useful identity: if \(T: (u,v)\mapsto(x,y)\) has Jacobian \(\partial(x,y)/\partial(u,v)\), then the inverse transformation \(T^{-1}: (x,y)\mapsto(u,v)\) satisfies:

\[\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)} = \left(\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right)^{-1}\]

Proof. By the chain rule:

\[\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\cdot\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)} = \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(x,y)} = \det(I) = 1\]

Practical use. Sometimes it's easier to define \(T^{-1}\) (i.e., express \(u,v\) in terms of \(x,y\)) and compute \(\partial(u,v)/\partial(x,y)\), then take its reciprocal to get \(\partial(x,y)/\partial(u,v)\).

docs.title: 5. The 3D Change of Variables Formula
docs.text:
The extension to three dimensions is direct. Let \(T: (u,v,w)\mapsto(x,y,z)\).

Jacobian:

\[\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)} = \begin{vmatrix} \partial x/\partial u & \partial x/\partial v & \partial x/\partial w\ \partial y/\partial u & \partial y/\partial v & \partial y/\partial w\ \partial z/\partial u & \partial z/\partial v & \partial z/\partial w \end{vmatrix}\]

Formula:

\[\boxed{\iiint_E f(x,y,z),dV = \iiint_{E^*} f(T(u,v,w))\left|\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)}\right|du,dv,dw}\]

The Jacobian now measures the local volume magnification factor of the transformation.

docs.title: 6. Standard Coordinate Systems as Change of Variables
docs.text: Every special coordinate system is a change of variables with a known Jacobian. Let's re-derive them.

docs.title: 6.1 Polar Coordinates (\(\mathbb{R}^2\))
docs.text: \[x = r\cos\theta,\qquad y = r\sin\theta\] \[\mathbf{J} = \begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta & -r\sin\theta\\sin\theta & r\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}\] \[\det\mathbf{J} = r\cos^2\theta + r\sin^2\theta = r\] \[dA = r,dr,d\theta\]

docs.title: 6.2 Cylindrical Coordinates (\(\mathbb{R}^3\))
docs.text: \[x = r\cos\theta,\qquad y = r\sin\theta,\qquad z = z\] \[\mathbf{J} = \begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta & -r\sin\theta & 0\\sin\theta & r\cos\theta & 0\0 & 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}\] \[\det\mathbf{J} = r\quad(\text{same as polar, z-row is trivial})\] \[dV = r,dr,d\theta,dz\]

docs.title: 6.3 Spherical Coordinates (\(\mathbb{R}^3\))
docs.text:
\[x = \rho\sin\phi\cos\theta,\qquad y = \rho\sin\phi\sin\theta,\qquad z = \rho\cos\phi\] \[\mathbf{J} = \begin{pmatrix} \sin\phi\cos\theta & \rho\cos\phi\cos\theta & -\rho\sin\phi\sin\theta\ \sin\phi\sin\theta & \rho\cos\phi\sin\theta & \rho\sin\phi\cos\theta\ \cos\phi & -\rho\sin\phi & 0 \end{pmatrix}\]

Expanding along the third row:

\[\det\mathbf{J} = \rho^2\sin\phi\] \[dV = \rho^2\sin\phi,d\rho,d\phi,d\theta\]

Pattern. All three standard coordinate Jacobians are non-negative (for \(r\ge0\), \(0\le\phi\le\pi\)), so the absolute value is automatic.

docs.title: Example 7.1 — Linear Transformation (Parallelogram Region)
docs.text:
Problem. Evaluate \(\displaystyle\iint_R (x+y),dA\) where \(R\) is the parallelogram with vertices \((0,0)\), \((2,1)\), \((3,3)\), \((1,2)\).

Step 1: Identify the transformation. The sides of the parallelogram are parallel to \(\mathbf{a} = (2,1)\) and \(\mathbf{b} = (1,2)\). Set:

\[x = 2u + v,\qquad y = u + 2v,\qquad (u,v)\in[0,1]\times[0,1]\]

Verify corners: \((u,v) = (0,0)\to(0,0)\); \((1,0)\to(2,1)\); \((0,1)\to(1,2)\); \((1,1)\to(3,3)\). ✓

Step 2: Jacobian.

\[\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} = \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1\1 & 2\end{vmatrix} = 4 - 1 = 3\]

Step 3: Transform integrand. \(x + y = (2u+v) + (u+2v) = 3u + 3v\)

Step 4: Integrate.

\[\iint_R(x+y),dA = \int_0^1\int_0^1(3u+3v)\cdot 3,du,dv = 9\int_0^1\int_0^1(u+v),du,dv\] \[= 9\int_0^1\left[\frac{1}{2}+v\right]dv = 9\left[\frac{v}{2}+\frac{v^2}{2}\right]_0^1 = 9\cdot 1 = \boxed{9}\]

docs.title: Example 7.2 — The Opening Problem
docs.text:
Problem. Evaluate \(\displaystyle\iint_R e^{\frac{x-y}{x+y}},dA\) where \(R\) is the triangle with vertices \((0,0)\), \((1,0)\), \((0,1)\).

Step 1: Choose substitution. Let \(u = x - y\), \(v = x + y\).

Step 2: Find the inverse Jacobian (easier to compute \(\partial(u,v)/\partial(x,y)\) first):

\[\frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)} = \begin{vmatrix}1 & -1\1 & 1\end{vmatrix} = 1+1 = 2\]

Therefore:

\[\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} = \frac{1}{2}\]

Step 3: Map the region. In terms of \(x,y\):

  • Edge \(y=0\), \(0\le x\le 1\): \(u = x\), \(v = x \Rightarrow u = v\)
  • Edge \(x=0\), \(0\le y\le 1\): \(u = -y\), \(v = y \Rightarrow u = -v\)
  • Edge \(x+y=1\): \(v = 1\) (constant!)

So \(S\) in \(uv\)-space: bounded by \(u=v\), \(u=-v\), \(v=1\), i.e., \(0\le v\le 1\), \(-v\le u\le v\).

Step 4: Integrate.

\[\iint_R e^{u/v}\cdot\frac{1}{2},du,dv = \frac{1}{2}\int_0^1\int_{-v}^v e^{u/v},du,dv\]

Inner (\(u\)):

\[\int_{-v}^v e^{u/v},du = v\cdot e^{u/v}\Big|_{-v}^v = v(e^1 - e^{-1}) = v(e-e^{-1})\]

Outer (\(v\)):

\[\frac{1}{2}\int_0^1 v(e-e^{-1}),dv = \frac{e-e^{-1}}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2} = \boxed{\frac{e-e^{-1}}{4}}\]

docs.title: Example 7.3 — Elliptic Region
docs.text:
Problem. Find the area of the ellipse \(\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}\le 1\).

Substitution. \(x = au\), \(y = bv\). Then the ellipse maps to the unit disk \(u^2+v^2\le 1\).

Jacobian:

\[\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} = \begin{vmatrix}a & 0\0 & b\end{vmatrix} = ab\]

Integrate:

\[A = \iint_{\text{ellipse}}dA = \iint_{u^2+v^2\le 1} ab,du,dv = ab\cdot\pi(1)^2 = \boxed{\pi ab}\]

This is a one-line derivation of the ellipse area formula. No elliptic integrals required.

docs.title: Example 7.4 — General Ellipsoid Volume (3D)
docs.text:
Problem. Find the volume of \(\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}+\dfrac{z^2}{c^2}\le 1\).

Substitution. \(x=au\), \(y=bv\), \(z=cw\). Maps ellipsoid to unit ball \(u^2+v^2+w^2\le 1\).

Jacobian:

\[\frac{\partial(x,y,z)}{\partial(u,v,w)} = \begin{vmatrix}a&0&0\0&b&0\0&0&c\end{vmatrix} = abc\]

Integrate:

\[V = \iiint_{\text{ellipsoid}}dV = abc\cdot\iiint_{u^2+v^2+w^2\le 1}du,dv,dw = abc\cdot\frac{4\pi}{3} = \boxed{\frac{4\pi abc}{3}}\]

docs.title: Example 7.5 — Non-Obvious Substitution
docs.text:
Problem. Evaluate \(\displaystyle\iint_R (x^2-xy+y^2),dA\) where \(R: 1\le x^2-xy+y^2\le 4\).

Observation. The region boundaries are level curves of the integrand. Let:

\[u = x^2 - xy + y^2 \quad\text{(this defines level curves)}\]

But we need a two-variable substitution. Notice \(x^2-xy+y^2\) is a quadratic form. Complete the square-style rotation: let \(x = r\cos\theta\), \(y = r\sin\theta\)... actually, let's use the substitution:

\[x = \sqrt{u}\cdot f(\theta), \quad y = \sqrt{u}\cdot g(\theta)\]

for the right \(f, g\). Instead, a cleaner approach: introduce \(u,\theta\) via:

\[x = \sqrt{u},\frac{\cos\theta - \sin\theta/\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt[4]{3/4}}, \quad y = \sqrt{u},\frac{2\sin\theta/\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt[4]{3/4}}\]

This is getting complex — let's use the clean version:

The form \(x^2-xy+y^2 = u\) with the substitution \(x = u^{1/2}\cdot p\), \(y = u^{1/2}\cdot q\) where \(p^2-pq+q^2 = 1\) (the unit level curve). By the theory of quadratic forms, \(x^2-xy+y^2\) can be diagonalized via rotation by \(\theta = \pi/4\):

\[x = \frac{r\cos\theta - s\sin\theta}{\sqrt{\lambda_1}},\quad y = \frac{r\sin\theta + s\cos\theta}{\sqrt{\lambda_2}}\]

Simpler direct approach: use \(x^2-xy+y^2 = u\) and \(y/x = t\), then \(x^2(1 - t + t^2) = u \Rightarrow x = \sqrt{u/(1-t+t^2)}\).

Jacobian computation is involved; the key result via polar-type rescaling gives \(|\mathbf{J}| = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) (constant!).

\[\iint_R u\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}},du,d\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\int_0^{2\pi}\int_1^4 u,du,d\theta = \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot\frac{15}{2} = \boxed{\frac{15\pi}{\sqrt{3}} = 5\pi\sqrt{3}}\]

docs.title: Example 7.6 — Spherical Coordinates Derived from Scratch
docs.text:
Rather than memorizing the spherical Jacobian, derive it:

\[x = \rho\sin\phi\cos\theta,\quad y = \rho\sin\phi\sin\theta,\quad z = \rho\cos\phi\] \[\mathbf{J} = \begin{pmatrix} \sin\phi\cos\theta & \rho\cos\phi\cos\theta & -\rho\sin\phi\sin\theta\ \sin\phi\sin\theta & \rho\cos\phi\sin\theta & \rho\sin\phi\cos\theta\ \cos\phi & -\rho\sin\phi & 0 \end{pmatrix}\]

Expand along row 3:

\[\det\mathbf{J} = \cos\phi\begin{vmatrix}\rho\cos\phi\cos\theta & -\rho\sin\phi\sin\theta\\rho\cos\phi\sin\theta & \rho\sin\phi\cos\theta\end{vmatrix} - (-\rho\sin\phi)\begin{vmatrix}\sin\phi\cos\theta & -\rho\sin\phi\sin\theta\\sin\phi\sin\theta & \rho\sin\phi\cos\theta\end{vmatrix}\]

First minor: $\(= \rho^2\cos\phi\cos\theta\sin\phi\cos\theta + \rho^2\sin\phi\sin\theta\cos\phi\sin\theta = \rho^2\cos\phi\sin\phi(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta) = \rho^2\cos\phi\sin\phi\)$

Second minor: $\(= \rho\sin^2\phi\cos^2\theta + \rho\sin^2\phi\sin^2\theta = \rho\sin^2\phi\)$

Therefore: $\(\det\mathbf{J} = \cos\phi\cdot\rho^2\cos\phi\sin\phi + \rho\sin\phi\cdot\rho\sin^2\phi = \rho^2\sin\phi\cos^2\phi + \rho^2\sin^3\phi = \rho^2\sin\phi\)$

\[\boxed{dV = \rho^2\sin\phi,d\rho,d\phi,d\theta}\]

docs.title: 8. How to Choose a Substitution
docs.text: There is no algorithm, but there are heuristics:

docs.title: 8.1 The Region Is the Guide
docs.text: Shape of \(R\) Try Parallelogram Linear map aligning sides with coordinate axes Ellipse \(\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}\le 1\) \(x=au\), \(y=bv\) (maps to disk) Region bounded by \(xy=c_1\), \(xy=c_2\), \(y/x=c_3\), \(y/x=c_4\) \(u=xy\), \(v=y/x\) Region bounded by \(x+y=c\) \(u=x+y\), \(v=x-y\) or \(v=x\) Circular or radial symmetry Polar or cylindrical Spherical symmetry Spherical coordinates

docs.title: 8.2 The Integrand Is the Guide
docs.text: If the integrand contains an expression like \(g(x,y)\), setting \(u = g(x,y)\) is often productive. Then choose \(v\) to make the Jacobian nonzero.

docs.title: 8.3 Match Boundaries to Coordinate Lines
docs.text: The ideal substitution makes each boundary of \(R\) correspond to \(u = \text{const}\) or \(v = \text{const}\). This gives rectangular limits \([u_1,u_2]\times[v_1,v_2]\) in \(uv\)-space — the simplest possible.

docs.title: 9. The Jacobian in Full Generality — A Linear Algebra View
9.1 The Jacobian as the Derivative
docs.text:
For a differentiable map \(T: \mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), the total derivative at a point \(\mathbf{p}\) is the \(n\times n\) matrix \(DT(\mathbf{p})\) of all partial derivatives — precisely the Jacobian matrix \(\mathbf{J}\).

Locally, \(T\) acts like the linear map \(\mathbf{J}\). A unit cube in the domain maps to a parallelepiped in the range with volume \(|\det\mathbf{J}|\).

docs.title: 9.2 Singular Jacobians
docs.text:
If \(\det\mathbf{J} = 0\) at some point, the transformation collapses a region of positive area/volume to zero. The change-of-variables formula requires \(\det\mathbf{J} \ne 0\) on the interior of \(S\) (one-to-one condition).

Example: polar coordinates have \(\det\mathbf{J} = r = 0\) at the origin. This is a single point (measure zero), so the formula still holds.

docs.title: 9.3 The Chain Rule for Jacobians
docs.text:
If \(T_1: (u,v)\mapsto(s,t)\) and \(T_2: (s,t)\mapsto(x,y)\), then \(T_2\circ T_1\) has:

\[\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} = \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}\cdot\frac{\partial(s,t)}{\partial(u,v)}\]

This is the chain rule for Jacobians — it mirrors \(\det(AB) = \det(A)\det(B)\).

docs.title: 10. Proof Sketch of the Change of Variables Theorem
docs.text:
For the rigorous mind — here's why the theorem is true.

Step 1. For a linear transformation \(T(\mathbf{u}) = A\mathbf{u}\) (constant matrix \(A\)), a rectangle in \(\mathbf{u}\)-space maps to a parallelogram in \(\mathbf{x}\)-space. The area of the parallelogram equals \(|\det A|\) times the area of the rectangle. This is the geometric content of the determinant.

Step 2. For a nonlinear \(T\), partition \(S\) into small rectangles \(S_{ij}\). On each \(S_{ij}\), approximate \(T\) by its linearization \(DT(\mathbf{p}_{ij})\) at the center point. By Step 1, each small piece maps to area \(|\det DT(\mathbf{p}_{ij})|,\Delta u,\Delta v\).

Step 3. The Riemann sum:

\[\sum_{i,j} f(T(\mathbf{p}_{ij})),|\det DT(\mathbf{p}_{ij})|,\Delta u,\Delta v \to \iint_S f(T(\mathbf{u})),|\det DT(\mathbf{u})|,du,dv\]

as the partition is refined. This equals \(\iint_R f(\mathbf{x}),dA\) by the definition of the integral (since \(T\) maps \(S\) to \(R\) bijectively).

Step 4. The error in the linear approximation (Step 2) is \(O(\Delta u^2 + \Delta v^2)\) per rectangle, which vanishes in the limit because there are \(O(1/(\Delta u,\Delta v))\) rectangles — the error is \(O(\Delta u + \Delta v) \to 0\). \(\square\)

docs.title: 11. Connection to AI, Machine Learning & Deep Learning
11.1 Normalizing Flows — The Jacobian as the Core Operation
docs.text:
Normalizing flows are a class of deep generative models that learn to transform a simple distribution (e.g., Gaussian) into a complex data distribution using a sequence of invertible transformations.

If \(\mathbf{z} \sim p_Z(\mathbf{z})\) (simple base distribution) and \(\mathbf{x} = f(\mathbf{z})\) (invertible transformation), then the density of \(\mathbf{x}\) is:

\[p_X(\mathbf{x}) = p_Z(f^{-1}(\mathbf{x}))\left|\det\frac{\partial f^{-1}}{\partial \mathbf{x}}\right| = p_Z(f^{-1}(\mathbf{x}))\left|\det\frac{\partial f}{\partial \mathbf{z}}\right|^{-1}\]

This is precisely the change of variables formula applied to probability densities. The Jacobian determinant \(\left|\det\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial \mathbf{z}}\right|\) accounts for how \(f\) stretches or compresses probability mass.

Design challenge: Computing \(\det\mathbf{J}\) for a general \(n\times n\) matrix costs \(O(n^3)\). For neural networks with millions of parameters, this is infeasible. The main research in normalizing flows is designing architectures where \(\det\mathbf{J}\) is cheap to compute (e.g., triangular Jacobians → \(O(n)\); coupling layers in RealNVP, Glow).

Training a normalizing flow:

  z ~ N(0,I)  →  [f₁]  →  [f₂]  →  ... →  [fₖ]  →  x ≈ data

  Log-likelihood: log p(x) = log p_Z(z) - Σᵢ log|det J_fᵢ|

  Each |det J_fᵢ| IS the Jacobian determinant from change of variables.

  Triangular architecture → det J = product of diagonal entries → O(n)

docs.title: 11.2 The Reparameterization Trick — Gradient Through a Stochastic Node
docs.text:
In Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), the encoder outputs \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\), and we sample:

\[\mathbf{z} = \mu + \sigma\odot\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\qquad \boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)\]

This is a change of variables: \(\mathbf{z} = T(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}; \mu, \sigma)\). The Jacobian of \(T\) with respect to \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\) is diagonal (since \(z_i = \mu_i + \sigma_i\epsilon_i\)):

\[\det\mathbf{J} = \prod_i \sigma_i\]

This allows gradients to flow through the sampling operation — which is why the reparameterization trick works mathematically: it replaces a stochastic node with a deterministic transformation of a fixed noise distribution.

docs.title: 11.3 Score Matching and Diffusion Models
docs.text:
Diffusion models (DDPM, score-based models) define a forward process that gradually adds noise:

\[\mathbf{x}_t = \sqrt{ ar\alpha_t},\mathbf{x}_0 + \sqrt{1- ar\alpha_t}, oldsymbol{\epsilon}\]

This is a change of variables (linear transformation) from \((\mathbf{x}_0, oldsymbol{\epsilon})\) to \(\mathbf{x}_t\). The Jacobian of this transformation is \(\sqrt{ ar\alpha_t}^n\) (for \(n\)-dimensional data) — a scalar scaling of the volume element.

The probability flow ODE in continuous diffusion models is:

\[d\mathbf{x} = \left[\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x},t) - rac{1}{2}g(t)^2 abla_\mathbf{x}\log p_t(\mathbf{x}) ight]dt\]

The change in log-probability along trajectories involves the instantaneous change of variables formula (Liouville's equation):

\[ rac{d\log p(\mathbf{x}(t))}{dt} = - abla_\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x},t)\]

where \( abla_\mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{v}\) is the divergence — the infinitesimal Jacobian. This is the continuous-time generalization of the discrete change-of-variables theorem.

docs.title: 11.4 The Jacobian in Backpropagation
docs.text:
Every layer \(l\) in a neural network computes \(\mathbf{h}^{(l)} = f^{(l)}(\mathbf{h}^{(l-1)})\). The backpropagation algorithm computes:

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{h}^{(l-1)}} = \mathbf{J}_{f^{(l)}}^T\cdot\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\mathbf{h}^{(l)}}\]

where \(\mathbf{J}_{f^{(l)}} = \dfrac{\partial\mathbf{h}^{(l)}}{\partial\mathbf{h}^{(l-1)}}\) is the Jacobian matrix of the layer. For an \(n\)-neuron layer, this is an \(n\times n\) matrix — the same object as our change-of-variables Jacobian, now used not for area scaling but for gradient propagation.

Batch normalization, layer normalization, and spectral normalization all control the singular values of this Jacobian matrix — keeping them near 1 prevents vanishing/exploding gradients.

docs.title: 11.5 Computing Jacobians in Code
docs.text:
import torch

# Define a transformation T: R^2 -> R^2
# x = r*cos(theta), y = r*sin(theta)  (polar coords)
def polar_to_cartesian(r_theta):
    r, theta = r_theta[:, 0:1], r_theta[:, 1:2]
    x = r * torch.cos(theta)
    y = r * torch.sin(theta)
    return torch.cat([x, y], dim=1)

# Compute Jacobian at a point using torch.autograd.functional.jacobian
from torch.autograd.functional import jacobian

point = torch.tensor([[2.0, torch.pi / 3]], requires_grad=True)
J = jacobian(polar_to_cartesian, point)  # shape: (1,2,1,2)
J_matrix = J[0, :, 0, :]  # extract 2x2 Jacobian

print("Jacobian matrix:\n", J_matrix)
print("det(J) =", torch.det(J_matrix).item())
print("Expected r =", point[0, 0].item())  # should equal r = 2.0

Output:

Jacobian matrix:
 tensor([[ 0.5000, -1.7321],
         [ 0.8660,  1.0000]])
det(J) = 2.0000
Expected r = 2.0  ✓

The determinant equals \(r = 2\) — exactly the polar coordinate Jacobian.

docs.title: 12. Summary
docs.text:
Dimension Formula Key object 1D $\int_a^b f(x),dx = \int_c^d f(g(u)) g'(u) 2D $\iint_R f,dA = \iint_S f\circ T\cdot \partial(x,y)/\partial(u,v) 3D $\iiint_E f,dV = \iiint_{E^*} f\circ T\cdot \partial(x,y,z)/\partial(u,v,w) \(n\)D Same pattern, \(n\times n\) det $

The Jacobian determinant \(|\det\mathbf{J}|\) is the local volume scaling factor of the transformation — it is the single most important object in the theory of change of variables, and it reappears throughout modern machine learning as the fundamental bookkeeping device for how transformations distort probability mass.

docs.title: 1. Motivation — Why Vector Fields?
docs.text:
In single-variable calculus we asked: how does a single quantity change? In multivariable calculus, the natural next question is: how does a direction-and-magnitude quantity vary across space?

Physical phenomena that demand this language:

  • Wind velocity at each point in the atmosphere
  • Electric and magnetic force at each point in space
  • Fluid flow inside a pipe
  • The force exerted on a charged particle moving through a field

The moment you say "at every point \((x,y,z)\) there is a force vector", you are talking about a vector field. Almost every fundamental law in physics — Maxwell's equations, Navier–Stokes, Newton's law of gravity — is written in the language of vector fields.

docs.title: 2. Definition
docs.text:
Definition. Let \(D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) be an open set. A vector field on \(D\) is a function $\(\mathbf{F} : D \to \mathbb{R}^n\)$ that assigns to each point \(\mathbf{x} \in D\) a vector \(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}) \in \mathbb{R}^n\).

In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) we write: $\(\mathbf{F}(x,y) = P(x,y),\mathbf{i} + Q(x,y),\mathbf{j} = \langle P(x,y),, Q(x,y)\rangle\)$

In \(\mathbb{R}^3\): $\(\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = P(x,y,z),\mathbf{i} + Q(x,y,z),\mathbf{j} + R(x,y,z),\mathbf{k}\)$

Component functions \(P, Q, R\) are scalar-valued; the vector field is the tuple of them.

Smoothness. We say \(\mathbf{F}\) is of class \(C^k\) if each component function has continuous partial derivatives up to order \(k\). Almost everything in this note assumes at least \(C^1\).

docs.title: Example 1 — Constant Field (trivial but important)
docs.text: $\(\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \langle 1, 0 \rangle\)$ Every arrow points in the \(+x\) direction with unit length. This is what a uniform horizontal wind looks like.

docs.title: Example 2 — Radial (outward) Field
docs.text:
$\(\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \langle x, y \rangle = x,\mathbf{i} + y,\mathbf{j}\)$ At each point \((x,y)\), the vector points directly away from the origin and has magnitude \(\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) — proportional to distance.

Think: a source pumping fluid radially outward from the origin.

docs.title: Example 3 — Rotating Field
docs.text: $\(\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \langle -y, x \rangle\)$ At \((1,0)\): \(\mathbf{F} = \langle 0,1\rangle\) (pointing up). At \((0,1)\): \(\mathbf{F} = \langle -1,0\rangle\) (pointing left). The vectors are tangent to circles centred at the origin — pure counterclockwise rotation.

docs.title: Example 4 — Gradient Field (sneak preview)
docs.text: $\(f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2 \implies \nabla f = \langle 2x, 2y \rangle\)$ This is the same as Example 2 scaled by 2. The gradient always points in the direction of steepest ascent of \(f\).

docs.title: Example 5 — Gravitational Field
docs.text: $\(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}) = -\frac{GM}{|\mathbf{r}|^3},\mathbf{r} \qquad \mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{R}^3 \setminus {\mathbf{0}}\)$ This points toward the origin (the mass), and its magnitude falls off as \(1/r^2\) — the inverse-square law.

docs.title: 4. Visualisation — How to Draw One
docs.text:
The standard way to sketch \(\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \langle P, Q\rangle\):

  1. Pick a grid of sample points \((x_i, y_j)\).
  2. At each sample point, draw an arrow in the direction \(\langle P(x_i,y_j), Q(x_i,y_j)\rangle\).
  3. Scale all arrows by the same factor so they don't overlap (the relative lengths still convey magnitude).

ASCII sketch of \(\mathbf{F} = \langle -y, x\rangle\) (counterclockwise rotation):

     ↑   ↑   ↑
← ←  +   +   +  → →
← ←  +   +   +  → →
     ↓   ↓   ↓

(Arrows form concentric circles; centre is a "vortex" or saddle point depending on the field.)

Key visual features to identify:

Feature What to look for Source Arrows diverging outward from a point Sink Arrows converging inward Vortex Arrows circling a point Saddle Arrows diverging in some directions, converging in others Uniform All arrows parallel and equal length

docs.title: 5.1 The Gradient (∇f)
docs.text:
The gradient converts a scalar field into a vector field: $\( abla f = \left\langle rac{\partial f}{\partial x},, rac{\partial f}{\partial y},, rac{\partial f}{\partial z} ight angle\)$

\( abla f(\mathbf{x}_0)\) points in the direction of steepest increase of \(f\) at \(\mathbf{x}_0\), with magnitude equal to the rate of increase in that direction.

Theorem (Gradient and Level Curves). \( abla f(\mathbf{x}_0)\) is perpendicular to the level curve (or level surface) of \(f\) passing through \(\mathbf{x}_0\).

docs.title: 5.2 The Divergence (∇ · F)
docs.text:
The divergence converts a vector field into a scalar field: $\(\operatorname{div}\mathbf{F} = abla \cdot \mathbf{F} = rac{\partial P}{\partial x} + rac{\partial Q}{\partial y} + rac{\partial R}{\partial z}\)$

Intuition. \(( abla \cdot \mathbf{F})(\mathbf{x}_0)\) measures how much the field is spreading out (acting as a source) or converging (acting as a sink) near \(\mathbf{x}_0\).

\[ abla \cdot \mathbf{F} > 0 \implies ext{source (fluid leaving a region)}$$ $$ abla \cdot \mathbf{F} < 0 \implies ext{sink (fluid entering a region)}$$ $$ abla \cdot \mathbf{F} = 0 \implies ext{incompressible / divergence-free}\]

Example. For the radial field \(\mathbf{F} = \langle x, y, z angle\) in \(\mathbb{R}^3\): $\( abla \cdot \mathbf{F} = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3\)$ Constant positive divergence: fluid is being created at every point at a uniform rate.

docs.title: 5.3 The Curl (∇ × F)
docs.text:
The curl converts a vector field in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) into another vector field: $\(\operatorname{curl}\mathbf{F} = abla imes \mathbf{F} = egin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \ \partial_x & \partial_y & \partial_z \ P & Q & R \end{vmatrix}\)$

\[= \left\langle rac{\partial R}{\partial y} - rac{\partial Q}{\partial z},; rac{\partial P}{\partial z} - rac{\partial R}{\partial x},; rac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - rac{\partial P}{\partial y} ight angle\]

Intuition. \(( abla imes \mathbf{F})(\mathbf{x}_0)\) measures the tendency of the field to rotate near \(\mathbf{x}_0\). The direction of the curl vector gives the axis of rotation (via the right-hand rule); the magnitude gives the angular speed of rotation.

Example. For the rotating field \(\mathbf{F} = \langle -y, x, 0 angle\): $\( abla imes \mathbf{F} = \left\langle 0,, 0,, rac{\partial x}{\partial x} - rac{\partial(-y)}{\partial y} ight angle = \langle 0, 0, 1+1 angle = \langle 0,0,2 angle\)$ Curl points in \(+z\) direction — counterclockwise rotation when viewed from above. Magnitude \(2\) gives the angular velocity.

In 2D, the curl reduces to the scalar quantity \(\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}\), sometimes called the scalar curl or 2D curl.

docs.title: 6. Conservative Vector Fields
docs.text:
Definition. \(\mathbf{F}\) is conservative on \(D\) if there exists a scalar function \(f : D \to \mathbb{R}\) such that \(\mathbf{F} = \nabla f\). The function \(f\) is called a potential function for \(\mathbf{F}\).

This is the vector field analogue of a function being an exact derivative.

Theorem (Curl Test). If \(\mathbf{F}\) is \(C^1\) on a simply connected domain \(D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3\), then: $\(\mathbf{F} \text{ is conservative on } D \iff \nabla \times \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{0} \text{ on } D\)$

Theorem (Path Independence). \(\mathbf{F}\) is conservative \(\iff\) \(\displaystyle\int_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}\) is path-independent (depends only on endpoints).

Theorem (Closed Curves). \(\mathbf{F}\) is conservative \(\iff\) \(\displaystyle\oint_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = 0\) for every closed curve \(C\) in \(D\).

To find the potential function \(f\) given conservative \(\mathbf{F} = \langle P, Q\rangle\):

  1. Integrate \(P\) with respect to \(x\): \(f(x,y) = \int P,dx + g(y)\).
  2. Differentiate with respect to \(y\) and set equal to \(Q\).
  3. Solve for \(g(y)\).

Example. \(\mathbf{F} = \langle 2xy,, x^2 + 1\rangle\). Check: \(\partial_y(2xy) = 2x\), \(\partial_x(x^2+1) = 2x\). ✓ Curl-free, so conservative. \(f = \int 2xy,dx = x^2 y + g(y)\). \(\partial_y f = x^2 + g'(y) = x^2 + 1 \implies g'(y) = 1 \implies g(y) = y\). Potential: \(f(x,y) = x^2 y + y\).

docs.title: 7. Line Integrals Over Vector Fields
docs.text:
Given a curve \(C\) parametrised by \(\mathbf{r}(t)\), \(t \in [a,b]\), and a vector field \(\mathbf{F}\):

\[\int_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t),dt\]

Physical meaning. This is the work done by \(\mathbf{F}\) on a particle travelling along \(C\).

Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals. If \(\mathbf{F} = \nabla f\) on an open set containing \(C\) from \(A\) to \(B\): $\(\int_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = f(B) - f(A)\)$ No need to parametrise the curve at all — only the endpoints matter.

Example. \(\mathbf{F} = \langle 2xy, x^2+1\rangle\), \(f = x^2y + y\). Compute the line integral from \((0,0)\) to \((1,2)\) along any path: $\(\int_C \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} = f(1,2) - f(0,0) = (1\cdot2 + 2) - 0 = 4\)$

docs.title: 8. Key Theorems (Big Picture)
docs.text:
These theorems are the profound culmination of the theory — each generalises the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus to higher dimensions.

Theorem Statement Dimension Green's Theorem \(\oint_{\partial D} \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)dA\) 2D Stokes' Theorem \(\oint_{\partial S} \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_S (\nabla\times\mathbf{F})\cdot d\mathbf{S}\) 3D, surface/curve Divergence Theorem \(\oiint_{\partial V} \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iiint_V (\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}),dV\) 3D, volume/surface

The pattern: integral of a derivative over a region = boundary integral of the original field. These are all special cases of the Generalised Stokes' Theorem in differential geometry.

docs.title: 9. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
docs.text: This is where vector fields are not just beautiful mathematics but working engineering.

docs.title: 9.1 The Loss Landscape is a Scalar Field
docs.text:
In training a neural network with parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) (where \(n\) might be billions), the loss function

\[\mathcal{L} : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\]

is a scalar field over parameter space. This is exactly the \(f\) you would compute the gradient of.

docs.title: 9.2 The Gradient is the Key Vector Field
docs.text:
\[\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}},\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \left\langle \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta_1}, \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta_2}, \ldots, \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta_n} \right\rangle\]

This is the gradient vector field of the loss, evaluated at the current parameter point \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\). Every iteration of training, you are:

  1. Evaluating this vector field at the current point.
  2. Taking a step in the negative gradient direction (steepest descent).
\[\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_t - \eta,\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)\]

Gradient descent is literally following a vector field.

docs.title: 9.3 Divergence and the Continuity of Probability Flow
docs.text:
In normalising flows and score-based generative models (e.g. diffusion models like DDPM, Stable Diffusion), the probability distribution \(p(\mathbf{x})\) evolves according to a Fokker-Planck equation, which involves the divergence:

\[\frac{\partial p}{\partial t} = -\nabla \cdot (p,\mathbf{v})\]

This is the continuity equation — conservation of probability mass. The divergence of the probability flux \(p,\mathbf{v}\) governs how the distribution spreads or concentrates over time.

docs.title: 9.4 Score Functions as Vector Fields
docs.text:
The score function used in score-based generative models is: $\(\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{x}) = \nabla_{\mathbf{x}} \log p(\mathbf{x})\)$

This is a vector field over data space \(\mathbb{R}^n\) that points in the direction of increasing probability density. Sampling algorithms (Langevin dynamics) follow this vector field, plus noise, to draw samples from \(p\).

The entire idea of diffusion models is: learn the score vector field from data, then integrate it backwards to generate new samples.

docs.title: 9.5 Conservative Fields and Energy Functions
docs.text:
Hopfield networks and energy-based models explicitly construct a scalar energy \(E(\mathbf{x})\) and update rules that follow \(-\nabla E\). The vector field \(-\nabla E\) is conservative by construction (it has a potential function \(E\)). This guarantees the dynamics converge to a local minimum — they cannot oscillate indefinitely.

Boltzmann Machines and RBMs are energy-based models where the equilibrium distribution is \(p \propto e^{-E(\mathbf{x})}\).

docs.title: 9.6 Curl in Neural ODE and Physics-Informed Networks
docs.text:
In Neural ODEs, the hidden state \(\mathbf{h}(t)\) evolves as: $\(\frac{d\mathbf{h}}{dt} = \mathbf{F}_\theta(\mathbf{h}(t), t)\)$

where \(\mathbf{F}_\theta\) is a learned vector field (parametrised by a neural network). The dynamics of the hidden state are literally integration along trajectories of a vector field.

Hamiltonian Neural Networks impose the constraint \(\nabla \times \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{0}\) (or its Hamiltonian equivalent) to ensure the learned dynamics conserve energy — a hard inductive bias from physics.

docs.title: 9.7 Summary Table
docs.text: ML Concept Vector Field Role Gradient descent Follow \(-\nabla\mathcal{L}\) vector field Adam, RMSProp Preconditioned vector fields (scaled gradients) Diffusion models Learn score \(\nabla\log p\) as a vector field Normalising flows Divergence-free or volume-preserving vector fields Energy-based models Conservative vector fields with potential \(E\) Neural ODEs Network parametrises an arbitrary vector field Hamiltonian NNs Constrain curl/divergence to preserve physics

docs.title: 10. References & Further Reading
docs.text:
Primary Sources:

  • Stewart, J. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. — Ch. 16 (Vector Calculus). This is the canonical undergraduate reference: clear proofs, good exercises, strong geometric intuition.
  • MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus (Auroux). Lecture notes and problem sets. Particularly strong on the divergence theorem and Stokes in coordinate-free form.

For the ML connections:

  • Song, Y. & Ermon, S. (2019). Generative Modeling by Estimating Gradients of the Data Distribution. NeurIPS. — Score-based generative models.
  • Chen, R.T.Q. et al. (2018). Neural Ordinary Differential Equations. NeurIPS. — Vector fields as learned dynamics.
  • Greydanus, S. et al. (2019). Hamiltonian Neural Networks. NeurIPS. — Conservative vector field constraints in deep learning.

docs.text: "The gradient is the single most important vector field in all of applied mathematics. Every time a system wants to improve itself, it follows one." — Personal note

docs.title: 1. Motivation
docs.text:
We already know the derivative of \(f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) captures the rate of change of \(f\) at a point. In higher dimensions, \(f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\), the question becomes richer:

"In which direction does \(f\) increase most rapidly, and at what rate?"

The gradient answers this — completely and canonically. It packages all partial derivatives into a single geometric object: a vector field that, at every point, aims uphill.

But there is a subtlety hiding here. The gradient is an operation on a scalar function. A gradient field is the resulting vector field \(\nabla f\). Not every vector field is a gradient field. The question of which ones are is one of the most beautiful problems in vector calculus, with deep topological content.

docs.title: 2. The Gradient of a Scalar Field
docs.text:
Definition. Let \(f : U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) be differentiable on the open set \(U\). The gradient of \(f\) at a point \(\mathbf{x} \in U\) is the vector $\( abla f(\mathbf{x}) = \left( rac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}(\mathbf{x}),; rac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}(\mathbf{x}),; \ldots,; rac{\partial f}{\partial x_n}(\mathbf{x}) ight) \in \mathbb{R}^n\)$

In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and \(\mathbb{R}^3\) respectively: $\( abla f(x,y) = rac{\partial f}{\partial x},\mathbf{i} + rac{\partial f}{\partial y},\mathbf{j}\)$

\[ abla f(x,y,z) = rac{\partial f}{\partial x},\mathbf{i} + rac{\partial f}{\partial y},\mathbf{j} + rac{\partial f}{\partial z},\mathbf{k}\]

The operator \( abla\) (nabla or del) is the vector differential operator: $\( abla = \left\langle rac{\partial}{\partial x_1}, rac{\partial}{\partial x_2}, \ldots, rac{\partial}{\partial x_n} ight angle\)$

Crucial point. \( abla f(\mathbf{x}_0)\) is a vector at a single point. The gradient field \( abla f : U o \mathbb{R}^n\) is the function that assigns this vector to every point in \(U\).

docs.title: 3. Gradient Fields — The Vector Field Perspective
docs.text:
Definition. A vector field \(\mathbf{F} : U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}^n\) is a gradient field (equivalently, a conservative field) if there exists a scalar function \(f : U o \mathbb{R}\) such that $\(\mathbf{F} = abla f\)$ The function \(f\) is called the potential function (or scalar potential) for \(\mathbf{F}\).

Terminology across disciplines:

Physics Mathematics ML/Optimisation Potential \(\phi\) Potential function \(f\) Loss / objective \(\mathcal{L}\) Conservative force \(\mathbf{F} = - abla\phi\) Gradient field \(\mathbf{F} = abla f\) Negative gradient \(- abla\mathcal{L}\) Energy conservation Path independence Convergence guarantees

Note the sign convention: in physics, forces are \(\mathbf{F} = - abla\phi\) (particle moves toward lower potential energy). In optimisation, we descend: \(- abla\mathcal{L}\). In pure mathematics we usually write \(\mathbf{F} = abla f\) without the sign.

docs.title: 4.1 Level Sets and Orthogonality
docs.text:
The level set of \(f\) at height \(c\) is: $\(L_c = {\mathbf{x} \in U : f(\mathbf{x}) = c}\)$

In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) these are level curves; in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) they are level surfaces.

Theorem. If \(f\) is \(C^1\) and \(\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_0) \neq \mathbf{0}\), then \(\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_0)\) is perpendicular to the level set \(L_{f(\mathbf{x}_0)}\) at \(\mathbf{x}_0\).

Proof sketch. Let \(\mathbf{r}(t)\) be any smooth curve on the level set \(L_c\), so \(f(\mathbf{r}(t)) = c\) for all \(t\). Differentiating: $\(\frac{d}{dt}f(\mathbf{r}(t)) = \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r}'(t) = 0\)$ So \(\nabla f\) is perpendicular to every tangent vector of \(L_c\) at \(\mathbf{x}_0\), hence perpendicular to the level set. \(\blacksquare\)

Visualisation for \(f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2\):

        ∇f points outward (radially)
        ↑
   _____|_____
  /  · ↗ · · \     ← level curve f = 4 (circle r=2)
 | · ↗   ↑ · |
 |↗    origin ↑|
 | · ↘   ↓ · |
  \  · ↘ · · /
   -----------
        ↓
  ∇f ⊥ level curves everywhere
  ∇f = ⟨2x, 2y⟩ — arrows point away from origin

docs.title: 4.2 Direction and Magnitude
docs.text:
Theorem. Among all unit vectors \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}\), the directional derivative \(D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}}f(\mathbf{x}_0) = abla f(\mathbf{x}_0) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}}\) is:

  • maximised when \(\hat{\mathbf{u}} = \dfrac{ abla f(\mathbf{x}_0)}{| abla f(\mathbf{x}_0)|}\) (direction of gradient), with maximum value \(| abla f(\mathbf{x}_0)|\)
  • minimised (steepest descent) when \(\hat{\mathbf{u}} = -\dfrac{ abla f(\mathbf{x}_0)}{| abla f(\mathbf{x}_0)|}\), with minimum value \(-| abla f(\mathbf{x}_0)|\)
  • zero when \(\hat{\mathbf{u}} \perp abla f(\mathbf{x}_0)\) (tangent to level set)

Proof. \(D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}}f = abla f \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}} = | abla f||\hat{\mathbf{u}}|\cos heta = | abla f|\cos heta\). This is maximised at \( heta = 0\) (same direction) and minimised at \( heta = \pi\) (opposite direction). \( lacksquare\)

The gradient is the compass of optimisation: at every point, it tells you exactly which direction to move to increase \(f\) most rapidly.

docs.title: 5. Directional Derivatives — The Gradient as a Linear Form
docs.text:
The total derivative (Fréchet derivative) of \(f\) at \(\mathbf{x}_0\) is the unique linear map \(Df(\mathbf{x}_0) : \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) such that: $\(f(\mathbf{x}_0 + \mathbf{h}) = f(\mathbf{x}_0) + Df(\mathbf{x}_0)\mathbf{h} + o(|\mathbf{h}|) \quad ext{as } \mathbf{h} o \mathbf{0}\)$

By the Riesz representation theorem on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with the standard inner product, every linear functional \(\mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) is represented by dot product with some fixed vector. That vector is precisely \( abla f(\mathbf{x}_0)\): $\(Df(\mathbf{x}_0)\mathbf{h} = abla f(\mathbf{x}_0) \cdot \mathbf{h}\)$

So: the gradient is the vector that represents the total derivative as a dot product. This is the coordinate-free definition — it explains why the gradient changes when you change the inner product (e.g., in Riemannian geometry).

Directional derivative (formal definition): $\(D_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}}f(\mathbf{x}_0) = \lim_{h o 0} rac{f(\mathbf{x}_0 + h\hat{\mathbf{u}}) - f(\mathbf{x}_0)}{h} = abla f(\mathbf{x}_0) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}}\)$

docs.title: 6. Critical Points and the Second Derivative Test
docs.text:
Definition. \(\mathbf{x}_0\) is a critical point of \(f\) if \(\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_0) = \mathbf{0}\).

Critical points are where the gradient field vanishes — where the "force" is zero. They are candidates for local minima, local maxima, or saddle points.

docs.title: The Hessian
docs.text:
The Hessian matrix of \(f\) at \(\mathbf{x}_0\) is: $\(H_f(\mathbf{x}_0) = \left[\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}(\mathbf{x}_0)\right]_{i,j=1}^n\)$

For \(f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\): $\(H_f = \begin{pmatrix} f_{xx} & f_{xy} \ f_{xy} & f_{yy} \end{pmatrix}\)$

(Symmetric by Clairaut's theorem if \(f \in C^2\).)

Second Derivative Test. At a critical point \(\mathbf{x}_0\) with \(\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_0) = \mathbf{0}\):

  • \(H_f(\mathbf{x}_0)\) positive definite \(\implies\) local minimum
  • \(H_f(\mathbf{x}_0)\) negative definite \(\implies\) local maximum
  • \(H_f(\mathbf{x}_0)\) indefinite \(\implies\) saddle point
  • \(H_f(\mathbf{x}_0)\) singular \(\implies\) test inconclusive

In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), let \(D = f_{xx}f_{yy} - f_{xy}^2 = \det H_f\):

\(D\) \(f_{xx}\) Type \(D > 0\) \(> 0\) Local minimum \(D > 0\) \(< 0\) Local maximum \(D < 0\) — Saddle point \(D = 0\) — Inconclusive

Example. \(f(x,y) = x^2 - y^2\) at \((0,0)\): \(\nabla f = \langle 2x, -2y\rangle = \mathbf{0}\) at origin. ✓ Critical point. \(H_f = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 0 \ 0 & -2\end{pmatrix}\), \(D = -4 < 0\) → saddle point. The gradient field flows outward along \(x\)-axis and inward along \(y\)-axis.

docs.title: Finding the Potential Function
docs.text:
Given \(\mathbf{F} = \langle P, Q, R\rangle\) known to be conservative, recover \(f\) such that \(\nabla f = \mathbf{F}\):

Method (integration and matching):

  1. Integrate \(P = \partial f/\partial x\) with respect to \(x\): $\(f(x,y,z) = \int P,dx + g(y,z)\)$
  2. Differentiate with respect to \(y\), set equal to \(Q\), solve for \(\partial g/\partial y\): $\(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = (\text{known}) + \frac{\partial g}{\partial y} = Q \implies \frac{\partial g}{\partial y} = Q - (\text{known})\)$
  3. Integrate to get \(g(y,z) = \int(\ldots),dy + h(z)\).
  4. Differentiate with respect to \(z\), set equal to \(R\), solve for \(h'(z)\), integrate.

Worked example. \(\mathbf{F} = \langle yz,; xz,; xy\rangle\).

Step 1. \(f = \int yz,dx = xyz + g(y,z)\).

Step 2. \(\partial f/\partial y = xz + \partial g/\partial y = xz \implies \partial g/\partial y = 0 \implies g = h(z)\).

Step 3. \(\partial f/\partial z = xy + h'(z) = xy \implies h'(z) = 0 \implies h = C\).

Potential: \(f(x,y,z) = xyz + C\). ✓ Check: \(\nabla(xyz) = \langle yz, xz, xy\rangle\). ✓

docs.title: Uniqueness
docs.text:
Proposition. If \(\mathbf{F} = abla f = abla g\) on a connected domain \(U\), then \(f - g = C\) (constant on \(U\)).

Proof. \( abla(f-g) = \mathbf{0}\) everywhere on \(U\). On a connected open set, a function with zero gradient is constant. \( lacksquare\)

So the potential is unique up to an additive constant — exactly like indefinite integrals in 1D.

docs.title: The Fundamental Theorem for Line Integrals
docs.text:
Theorem. Let \(\mathbf{F} = \nabla f\) on an open set \(U\) containing a smooth curve \(C\) from point \(A\) to point \(B\). Then: $\(\int_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = f(B) - f(A)\)$

Proof. Let \(\mathbf{r}(t)\), \(t \in [a,b]\), parametrise \(C\) with \(\mathbf{r}(a) = A\), \(\mathbf{r}(b) = B\). Then: $\(\int_C \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} = \int_a^b \nabla f(\mathbf{r}(t))\cdot\mathbf{r}'(t),dt = \int_a^b \frac{d}{dt}[f(\mathbf{r}(t))],dt = f(\mathbf{r}(b)) - f(\mathbf{r}(a)) = f(B) - f(A)\)$ by the chain rule and the 1D Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. \(\blacksquare\)

This is the n-dimensional generalisation of \(\int_a^b f'(x),dx = f(b) - f(a)\).

docs.title: 8. When is a Vector Field a Gradient Field?
docs.text: This is the central question of the theory. The answer has a beautiful topological flavour.

docs.title: Necessary Condition — Zero Curl
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(\mathbf{F} = abla f\) and \(f \in C^2\), then \( abla imes \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{0}\).

Proof. In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), the scalar curl is \(\partial Q/\partial x - \partial P/\partial y\). If \(P = f_x, Q = f_y\): $\( rac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - rac{\partial P}{\partial y} = f_{yx} - f_{xy} = 0\)$ by Clairaut's theorem (equality of mixed partials for \(C^2\) functions). In \(\mathbb{R}^3\) all three components of \( abla imes abla f\) vanish by the same argument. \( lacksquare\)

docs.title: Sufficient Condition — Simply Connected Domains
docs.text:
Theorem. Let \(\mathbf{F}\) be a \(C^1\) vector field on a simply connected open domain \(U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\). Then: $\(\mathbf{F} = abla f ext{ for some } f \iff abla imes \mathbf{F} = \mathbf{0} ext{ on } U\)$

Simply connected means \(U\) has no holes — every closed loop in \(U\) can be continuously shrunk to a point within \(U\).

The topological subtlety. On a domain with holes, zero curl does NOT imply conservative.

Standard counterexample. Let \(U = \mathbb{R}^2 \setminus {(0,0)}\) and: $\(\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \left\langle rac{-y}{x^2+y^2},; rac{x}{x^2+y^2} ight angle\)$

Check curl: \(\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}\). One computes this is \(= 0\) on all of \(U\).

But: integrate around the unit circle \(C: \mathbf{r}(t) = (\cos t, \sin t)\), \(t \in [0, 2\pi]\): $\(\oint_C \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} = \int_0^{2\pi}\left( rac{-\sin t}{\cos^2 t + \sin^2 t}\cdot(-\sin t) + rac{\cos t}{\cos^2 t + \sin^2 t}\cdot\cos t ight)dt = \int_0^{2\pi}1,dt = 2\pi eq 0\)$

Non-zero line integral around a closed loop \(\implies\) not conservative, despite zero curl. The hole at the origin makes \(U\) not simply connected, and the field "detects" the hole via its winding number.

(This \(\mathbf{F}\) is \( abla heta\) where \( heta = \arctan(y/x)\) is the polar angle — but \( heta\) is not well-defined as a single-valued function on all of \(U\).)

The full picture (first de Rham cohomology): The obstruction to a curl-free field being a gradient is measured by \(H^1_{ ext{dR}}(U)\). For simply connected \(U\), \(H^1 = 0\) and curl-free \(\implies\) exact. For \(U = \mathbb{R}^2 \setminus {0}\), \(H^1 \cong \mathbb{R}\) and there is one independent non-exact closed form — the one in the counterexample.

docs.title: 9. The Gradient in Curvilinear Coordinates
docs.text:
In coordinates other than Cartesian, the gradient takes a different form. This matters for numerical methods (especially on meshes) and physics.

Polar coordinates \((r, heta)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^2\): $\( abla f = rac{\partial f}{\partial r}\hat{\mathbf{r}} + rac{1}{r} rac{\partial f}{\partial heta}\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\)$

Spherical coordinates \((r, heta, \phi)\) in \(\mathbb{R}^3\): $\( abla f = rac{\partial f}{\partial r}\hat{\mathbf{r}} + rac{1}{r} rac{\partial f}{\partial heta}\hat{ oldsymbol{ heta}} + rac{1}{r\sin heta} rac{\partial f}{\partial \phi}\hat{ oldsymbol{\phi}}\)$

General orthogonal curvilinear coordinates \((u_1, u_2, u_3)\) with scale factors \(h_i = |\partial\mathbf{r}/\partial u_i|\): $\( abla f = \sum_{i=1}^3 rac{1}{h_i} rac{\partial f}{\partial u_i}\hat{\mathbf{e}}_i\)$

In Riemannian geometry with metric tensor \(g_{ij}\), the gradient is the vector field dual to \(df\) via \(g\): \(( abla f)^i = g^{ij}\partial_j f\). The Cartesian case is just \(g_{ij} = \delta_{ij}\).

docs.title: Example A — Full analysis of \(f(x,y) = x^2 y - y^3/3\)
docs.text:
Gradient field: $\(\nabla f = \langle 2xy,; x^2 - y^2 \rangle\)$

Critical points: Set \(\nabla f = \mathbf{0}\): $\(2xy = 0 \implies x = 0 \text{ or } y = 0\)$

  • If \(x = 0\): \(x^2 - y^2 = -y^2 = 0 \implies y = 0\). Point: \((0,0)\).
  • If \(y = 0\): \(x^2 - 0 = x^2 = 0 \implies x = 0\). Same point.

So the only critical point is \((0,0)\).

Hessian: $\(H_f = \begin{pmatrix} 2y & 2x \ 2x & -2y \end{pmatrix}, \quad H_f(0,0) = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 0 \ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}\)$

\(D = 0\): test inconclusive. Direct inspection: \(f(t,0) = 0\) for all \(t\), while \(f(0,t) = -t^3/3\) changes sign. So \((0,0)\) is neither a local min nor max — it is a degenerate saddle.

docs.title: Example B — Verify conservatism and find potential
docs.text:
\(\mathbf{F} = \langle 2xe^y + 1,; x^2 e^y - \sin y\rangle\)

Curl check: $\(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} = 2xe^y - 2xe^y = 0 \checkmark\)$

Find \(f\): $\(f = \int (2xe^y + 1),dx = x^2 e^y + x + g(y)\)$ $\(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = x^2 e^y + g'(y) = x^2 e^y - \sin y \implies g'(y) = -\sin y \implies g(y) = \cos y + C\)$

\[\boxed{f(x,y) = x^2 e^y + x + \cos y + C}\]

Line integral shortcut: Compute \(\int_C \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r}\) from \((0,0)\) to \((1, \pi)\) along any path: $\(f(1,\pi) - f(0,0) = (e^\pi + 1 + \cos\pi) - (0 + 0 + \cos 0) = e^\pi + 1 - 1 - 1 = e^\pi - 1\)$

docs.title: 11. Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
11.1 Gradient Descent — Following the Gradient Field
docs.text:
Every training algorithm in deep learning follows the gradient field of the loss. Gradient descent is: $\( oldsymbol{ heta}_{t+1} = oldsymbol{ heta}_t - \eta, abla_{ oldsymbol{ heta}}\mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{ heta}_t)\)$

This is discrete-time integration along the trajectory of the vector field \(- abla\mathcal{L}\). The continuous-time limit is the gradient flow ODE: $\(\dot{ oldsymbol{ heta}}(t) = - abla\mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{ heta}(t))\)$

This ODE drives \( oldsymbol{ heta}\) toward critical points of \(\mathcal{L}\). Because \(\mathcal{L}\) is a potential function, the flow is conservative — it always descends \(\mathcal{L}\) and cannot orbit indefinitely.

Fact. Along any gradient flow trajectory, \(\dfrac{d}{dt}\mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{ heta}(t)) = abla\mathcal{L}\cdot\dot{ oldsymbol{ heta}} = -| abla\mathcal{L}|^2 \leq 0\). The loss is non-increasing. Equality iff \( abla\mathcal{L} = 0\).

This is the energy dissipation property, directly from the theory of conservative fields.

docs.title: 11.2 The Loss Landscape as a Scalar Field
docs.text:
The loss \(\mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{ heta})\) for a neural network with \(n\) parameters lives in \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Its geometry:

Feature of \(\mathcal{L}\) Vector field language Local minimum \( abla\mathcal{L} = \mathbf{0}\), \(H_\mathcal{L}\) positive definite Saddle point \( abla\mathcal{L} = \mathbf{0}\), \(H_\mathcal{L}\) indefinite Flat region \( abla\mathcal{L} \approx \mathbf{0}\), slow gradient flow Sharp minimum Large curvature (large eigenvalues of \(H_\mathcal{L}\)) Wide minimum Small curvature (small eigenvalues) — generalises better

docs.title: 11.3 Variants of Gradient Descent — Preconditioned Gradient Fields
docs.text:
Modern optimisers do not follow \(- abla\mathcal{L}\) directly; they follow a preconditioned version:

\[ oldsymbol{ heta}_{t+1} = oldsymbol{ heta}_t - \eta, M_t^{-1} abla\mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{ heta}_t)\]

where \(M_t\) is a preconditioning matrix. This changes the effective vector field being followed.

Optimiser Preconditioner \(M_t\) SGD \(I\) (identity — plain gradient field) Momentum SGD Exponential moving average of \( abla\mathcal{L}\) AdaGrad \( ext{diag}(\sum_ au abla\mathcal{L}_ au \odot abla\mathcal{L}_ au)\) RMSProp \( ext{diag}(\mathbb{E}[ abla^2])\) — running average Adam \( ext{diag}(\hat{m}/\sqrt{\hat{v}})\) — bias-corrected moments Natural Gradient Fisher information matrix \(\mathcal{F}( oldsymbol{ heta})\)

Adam does not follow the gradient field of any potential. It is not a conservative vector field. This has deep implications: Adam can get stuck in places gradient descent would not, and vice versa.

docs.title: 11.4 Natural Gradient — The Riemannian Gradient
docs.text:
In information geometry, the parameter space of a probabilistic model carries a natural Riemannian metric — the Fisher information metric: $\(g_{ij}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathcal{F}_{ij}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial\log p_\theta}{\partial\theta_i}\frac{\partial\log p_\theta}{\partial\theta_j}\right]\)$

The natural gradient is the Riemannian gradient of \(\mathcal{L}\): $\(\tilde{\nabla}\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\nabla\mathcal{L}\)$

This is the correct gradient in the intrinsic geometry of the model manifold — it accounts for the fact that equal Euclidean steps in \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\)-space correspond to very unequal changes in the distribution \(p_\theta\). K-FAC and Shampoo are practical approximations.

docs.title: 11.5 Gradient Fields in Generative Models
docs.text:
Score matching. The score function of a distribution \(p(\mathbf{x})\) is: $\(\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{x}) = \nabla_\mathbf{x}\log p(\mathbf{x})\)$

This is a gradient field over data space \(\mathbb{R}^d\). It is the gradient of \(\log p\), so it is conservative by construction — it has \(\log p\) as its potential.

Denoising diffusion models (DDPM, Score SDE) learn an approximation \(\mathbf{s}_\theta(\mathbf{x}, t) \approx \nabla_\mathbf{x}\log p_t(\mathbf{x})\) at each noise level \(t\). Sampling is done via Langevin dynamics: $\(\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{x}_k + \epsilon,\mathbf{s}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_k) + \sqrt{2\epsilon},\boldsymbol{\xi}_k, \qquad \boldsymbol{\xi}_k \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, I)\)$

The deterministic part is gradient ascent on \(\log p\) (moving toward higher probability). The noise term prevents collapse to a mode.

Every image Stable Diffusion generates is obtained by integrating along a learned gradient field.

docs.title: 11.6 Energy-Based Models — Explicit Potential Functions
docs.text:
An energy-based model (EBM) directly parametrises a potential \(E_ heta(\mathbf{x})\) and defines: $\(p_ heta(\mathbf{x}) = rac{e^{-E_ heta(\mathbf{x})}}{Z_ heta}, \qquad Z_ heta = \int e^{-E_ heta(\mathbf{x})},d\mathbf{x}\)$

The gradient field is: $\( abla_\mathbf{x}\log p_ heta = - abla_\mathbf{x} E_ heta\)$

Inference dynamics follow \(- abla E_ heta\): particles roll downhill on the energy landscape to the most probable configurations. Hopfield networks are a classical special case with a quadratic energy.

docs.title: 11.7 Backpropagation is Gradient Computation
docs.text:
Backpropagation is the algorithm for computing \(\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}\) efficiently via the chain rule. For a network \(\mathbf{y} = f_L \circ f_{L-1} \circ \cdots \circ f_1(\mathbf{x})\) with loss \(\ell(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{y}^*)\):

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \boldsymbol{\theta}_l} = \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \mathbf{y}} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{y}}{\partial \mathbf{h}_L} \cdots \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_{l+1}}{\partial \mathbf{h}_l} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_l}{\partial \boldsymbol{\theta}_l}\]

Each factor is a Jacobian. The full backprop is computing one row of the gradient field of \(\mathcal{L}\) per parameter layer, propagated backwards. The gradient field is the reason backprop exists — you need the gradient to descend.

docs.title: 11.8 Second-Order Methods — Using the Hessian
docs.text:
Newton's method uses the Hessian of the loss: $\(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1} = \boldsymbol{\theta}_t - H_\mathcal{L}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t),\nabla\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)\)$

This is not following the gradient field of \(\mathcal{L}\), but the gradient field of the quadratic approximation to \(\mathcal{L}\) at \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t\). At a saddle point, Newton's method can move toward the saddle (it just finds critical points, not minima). Saddle-free Newton and trust-region methods fix this by using \(|H|\) instead.

docs.text:
Primary sources:

  • Stewart, J. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th ed. §14.5–14.6 (Gradient, directional derivatives), §16.3 (Conservative fields and potential functions). The worked examples in §16.3 are particularly clean.
  • MIT 18.02 (Auroux), Lectures 22–24. Rigorous treatment of exact differentials, the curl test, and the topological counterexample with \(d\theta\).

For the topological depth:

  • Munkres, J. Analysis on Manifolds, Ch. 6 — de Rham cohomology and what it measures about the domain.

For the ML connections:

  • Amari, S. (1998). Natural Gradient Works Efficiently in Learning. Neural Computation. — The Riemannian gradient in parameter space.
  • Song, Y. et al. (2021). Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations. ICLR. — Score functions as learned gradient fields.
  • LeCun, Y. et al. (2006). A Tutorial on Energy-Based Learning. — EBMs as explicit potential functions.

docs.title: Line Integrals
docs.text: "The ordinary integral asks: what is the total of \(f\) along an interval? The line integral asks: what is the total of \(f\) along a curve? The answer is the same machine — just bent into shape." — Personal note
