docs.title: Why the Formula Has \(\sqrt{1+(f')^2}\)
docs.text:
The arc length element ds:

   |         /|
   |        / |  <- f'(x) dx = vertical rise
   |       /  |
   |  ds  /   |
   |     /    |
   |____/_____|
       dx

   ds = √(dx² + (f'dx)²) = √(1 + f'²) dx

 Wrapping this strip around a circle of circumference 2πf(x):

   dA = 2πf(x) · ds = 2πf(x)√(1+f'²) dx

docs.title: §6. Pappus's Centroid Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem 6.1 (Pappus, ~320 CE). The area of a surface of revolution generated by rotating a curve \(\mathcal{C}\) (not crossing the axis) about an external axis equals

\[ A = 2\pi \bar{r} \cdot L, \]

where \(\bar{r}\) is the distance from the centroid of \(\mathcal{C}\) to the axis, and \(L\) is the arc length of \(\mathcal{C}\).

Proof from Theorem 3.1. The arc length of \(y = f(x)\) over \([a,b]\) is \(L = \int_a^b \sqrt{1+(f')^2},dx\). The centroid's \(y\)-coordinate (= distance to axis) is

\[ \bar{r} = \frac{1}{L}\int_a^b f(x)\sqrt{1+(f')^2}; dx. \]

Then \(2\pi\bar{r} L = 2\pi\int_a^b f(x)\sqrt{1+(f')^2},dx = A\). \(\blacksquare\)

Intuition. The surface area depends only on how far away the curve's center of mass is from the axis, not on any detailed shape. This is a deep theorem in the guise of a simple formula.

docs.title: §7. The Differential Geometric Perspective
docs.text:
A surface of revolution is a special Riemannian manifold with \(SO(2)\) symmetry. Let's see what this buys us.

The First Fundamental Form. With \(\mathbf{r}(x,\theta) = (x, f\cos\theta, f\sin\theta)\), compute the metric:

\[ g_{xx} = \mathbf{r}_x \cdot \mathbf{r}_x = 1 + (f')^2, \quad g_{x\theta} = \mathbf{r}_x \cdot \mathbf{r}_\theta = 0, \quad g_{\theta\theta} = \mathbf{r}_\theta \cdot \mathbf{r}_\theta = f^2. \]

So the metric tensor is:

\[ [g_{ij}] = \begin{pmatrix} 1 + (f')^2 & 0 \ 0 & f^2 \end{pmatrix}. \]

The area element \(dA = \sqrt{\det g}; dx, d\theta = f\sqrt{1+(f')^2}; dx, d\theta\), consistent with §2.

Principal Curvatures. Using the second fundamental form (computed from \(\hat{n} = \mathbf{r}_x \times \mathbf{r}_\theta / |\cdots|\)), the two principal curvatures of a surface of revolution are:

\[ \kappa_1 = \frac{-f''}{(1+(f')^2)^{3/2}} \quad \text{(meridional curvature)}, $$ $$ \kappa_2 = \frac{1}{f\sqrt{1+(f')^2}} \quad \text{(azimuthal curvature)}. \]

Minimal Surfaces. Mean curvature \(H = \frac{1}{2}(\kappa_1 + \kappa_2) = 0\) gives the ODE:

\[ \frac{-f''}{(1+(f')^2)^{3/2}} + \frac{1}{f(1+(f')^2)^{1/2}} = 0 \implies ff'' = 1 + (f')^2. \]

The solution is \(f(x) = c\cosh\left(\frac{x-x_0}{c}\right)\) — the catenoid, the only minimal surface of revolution.

The Catenoid: \(f(x) = a\cosh(x/a)\). This is the shape taken by a soap film stretched between two coaxial rings — nature minimizes surface area.

docs.title: §8. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: This section makes explicit the surprising appearances of surfaces of revolution and their closely related mathematics in modern AI.

docs.title: 8.1 Loss Landscapes and Radial Symmetry
docs.text:
In neural network training, the loss landscape \(\mathcal{L}: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) is a hypersurface in parameter space. For simple models (e.g., single-layer networks with weight matrix \(W\)), the loss often depends only on \(|W|\) or on singular values — creating approximate radial symmetry, which is exactly the symmetry principle behind surfaces of revolution.

More precisely: if \(\mathcal{L}(\theta) = h(|\theta|)\) for some \(h: \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} \to \mathbb{R}\), the level sets \({\mathcal{L} = c}\) are spheres — surfaces of revolution about any axis through the origin.

SGD on a rotationally symmetric loss follows the gradient radially: \(\dot{\theta} = -\nabla \mathcal{L} = -h'(|\theta|)\frac{\theta}{|\theta|}\). The trajectory lies on a ray — one-dimensional motion on a high-dimensional surface.

docs.title: 8.2 Radial Basis Functions (RBFs)
docs.text:
A radial basis function is any function of the form \(\phi(\mathbf{x}) = \phi(|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{c}|)\) — depending only on distance to a center \(\mathbf{c}\). Common examples:

Name Formula Gaussian \(\phi(r) = e^{-r^2/\sigma^2}\) Multiquadric \(\phi(r) = \sqrt{r^2 + c^2}\) Thin-plate spline \(\phi(r) = r^2 \log r\)

The graph of \(z = \phi(|\mathbf{x}|)\) over \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is literally a surface of revolution — it is the curve \(z = \phi(r)\) revolved about the \(z\)-axis. The Gaussian RBF produces a bell surface; the multiquadric produces a hyperboloid of revolution.

RBF networks approximate functions as \(\hat{f}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_i w_i \phi(|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{c}_i|)\). They are universal approximators and interpolate scattered data exactly.

docs.title: 8.3 Convolutional Neural Networks and Toroidal Topology
docs.text: The weight-sharing in CNNs can be understood through the topology of their parameter spaces. The space of circular convolution kernels is a torus \(T^n = (S^1)^n\) — a product of circles, each of which generates a surface of revolution. Analyzing CNN equivariance requires understanding this toroidal geometry.

docs.title: 8.4 Gaussian Processes and Stationary Kernels
docs.text: A kernel \(k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = k(|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}|)\) is called stationary and isotropic. In 2D, the level set \({(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}): k(|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}|) = c}\) is a circle; the graph of \(k\) over \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is a surface of revolution. The spectral density of such a kernel (its Fourier transform) also has rotational symmetry — this is Bochner's theorem and underlies the Matérn class of GP kernels widely used in Bayesian optimization (e.g., hyperparameter tuning in deep learning).

docs.title: 8.5 Manifold Hypothesis and Intrinsic Geometry
docs.text: The manifold hypothesis posits that high-dimensional data lies near a low-dimensional manifold. If this manifold has approximate rotational symmetry (common in image manifolds, e.g., rotated objects), one can model it as a surface of revolution plus small perturbations. The intrinsic geometry (metric, curvature) of a surface of revolution — computed via §7 — directly governs the quality of manifold learning algorithms like UMAP and t-SNE.

docs.title: 8.6 Normalizing Flows and Change of Variables
docs.text:
Normalizing flows transform a simple base distribution (often Gaussian, which is itself radially symmetric — a surface of revolution in density space) into a complex distribution via an invertible map \(T\). The change-of-variables formula

\[ p_X(\mathbf{x}) = p_Z(T^{-1}(\mathbf{x})) \left|\det \frac{\partial T^{-1}}{\partial \mathbf{x}}\right| \]

has direct parallels with our surface area computation: \(|\mathbf{r}_x \times \mathbf{r}_\theta|\) is precisely the Jacobian of the parameterization map \(\mathbf{r}: [a,b]\times[0,2\pi] \to S\). Training a normalizing flow is, in a precise sense, learning an optimal "reparameterization" of a manifold — the same problem as finding the best parameterization of a surface of revolution.

docs.title: §9. Exercises
docs.text:
9.1. [Stewart §8.2] Find the surface area of the surface obtained by revolving \(y = \sqrt[3]{x}\), \(1 \leq x \leq 8\), about the \(x\)-axis.

9.2. Verify that the catenoid \(f(x) = a\cosh(x/a)\) satisfies \(ff'' = 1+(f')^2\). Show that \(f' = \sinh(x/a)\) and compute \(\kappa_1 + \kappa_2\).

9.3. Use Pappus's theorem to find the surface area of a torus generated by revolving a circle of radius \(r\) about an axis at distance \(d > r\) from its center.

9.4. [MIT 18.02 flavor] Parameterize the surface of revolution generated by \(y = e^x\), \(0 \leq x \leq 1\), about the \(x\)-axis. Write the surface area as a definite integral and evaluate it numerically (you will not get a closed form).

9.5. [Deeper] Show that the Gaussian kernel \(k(r) = e^{-r^2/2}\) is a surface of revolution in \(\mathbb{R}^3\). Compute its Gaussian curvature \(K = \kappa_1\kappa_2\) as a function of \(r\). What does the sign of \(K\) tell you about the geometry of the kernel at its peak vs. tails?

docs.title: §10. Summary
docs.text:
Object Formula Source Parameterization \(\mathbf{r}(x,\theta) = (x, f\cos\theta, f\sin\theta)\) §2 Normal magnitude \(\|\mathbf{r}_x \times \mathbf{r}_\theta\| = f\sqrt{1+(f')^2}\) §2 Surface area \(A = 2\pi\int_a^b f(x)\sqrt{1+(f')^2},dx\) §3 Pappus \(A = 2\pi\bar{r}L\) §6 Metric \(ds^2 = (1+(f')^2)dx^2 + f^2,d\theta^2\) §7 Minimal SoR \(f(x) = a\cosh(x/a)\) (catenoid) §7

The deeper theme: rotational symmetry reduces a 2D problem to 1D. The cross-sectional structure collapses all \(\theta\)-dependence into the factor \(2\pi\), leaving a single integral over the profile curve. This is an instance of the far more general principle: symmetry reduces dimension, which appears everywhere from physics to representation theory to the architecture of neural networks.

docs.title: Tangent Planes
docs.text: "The derivative is the shadow of a function cast by a linear light."

docs.title: §0. Prefatory Remarks
docs.text:
The tangent line to a curve at a point is the best linear approximation to the curve near that point. The tangent plane is the direct generalization: the best linear approximation to a surface at a point.

This is not merely a geometric curiosity. The tangent plane is the foundation of:

  • Linearization and error estimation in multivariable calculus
  • Newton's method in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)
  • Backpropagation in deep learning (the gradient is the tangent hyperplane)
  • Differential geometry (the tangent space, the central object of manifold theory)
  • Optimization (first-order methods live entirely in tangent spaces)

The passage from "curve → tangent line" to "surface → tangent plane" is a passage from single-variable to multivariable thinking. Everything that follows is making that passage precise.

docs.title: §1. Motivation — From Tangent Lines to Tangent Planes
docs.text:
Recall: if \(y = f(x)\) and \(f\) is differentiable at \(x_0\), the tangent line at \((x_0, f(x_0))\) is

\[ y = f(x_0) + f'(x_0)(x - x_0). \]

This line is characterized by two properties:

  1. It passes through \((x_0, f(x_0))\).
  2. It has the same slope as \(f\) at \(x_0\).

Equivalently: the error \(f(x) - [f(x_0) + f'(x_0)(x-x_0)]\) is \(o(x - x_0)\) as \(x \to x_0\). The tangent line is the unique linear function making the error smaller than linear.

Now in two variables. Given a surface \(z = f(x,y)\), we want a plane through \((x_0, y_0, f(x_0,y_0))\) that best approximates \(f\) near \((x_0,y_0)\). A plane through this point has the form:

\[ z = f(x_0, y_0) + A(x - x_0) + B(y - y_0) \]

for some constants \(A, B\). The question is: what should \(A\) and \(B\) be?

Answer: \(A = f_x(x_0, y_0)\) and \(B = f_y(x_0, y_0)\).

Why? Restrict to the \(y = y_0\) slice: the surface becomes the curve \(z = f(x, y_0)\), and the plane becomes the line \(z = f(x_0,y_0) + A(x-x_0)\). For this to be the tangent line to the curve, we need \(A = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\big|_{(x_0,y_0)}\). Same argument in the \(x = x_0\) slice forces \(B = f_y\).

docs.title: §2. Definition and Existence
docs.text:
Definition 2.1 (Tangent Plane). Let \(f: U \subset \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\) be defined on an open set \(U\), and let \((x_0, y_0) \in U\). If the partial derivatives \(f_x\) and \(f_y\) exist at \((x_0, y_0)\), the tangent plane to the surface \(z = f(x,y)\) at the point \(P_0 = (x_0, y_0, f(x_0,y_0))\) is the plane

\[ \boxed{z = f(x_0, y_0) + f_x(x_0,y_0)(x - x_0) + f_y(x_0,y_0)(y - y_0).} \]

Critical Warning. The existence of \(f_x\) and \(f_y\) does not guarantee the tangent plane is a good approximation. We need differentiability.

Definition 2.2 (Differentiability). \(f\) is differentiable at \((x_0, y_0)\) if

\[ \lim_{(h,k)\to(0,0)} \frac{f(x_0+h, y_0+k) - f(x_0,y_0) - f_x(x_0,y_0)h - f_y(x_0,y_0)k}{\sqrt{h^2+k^2}} = 0. \]

In words: the error between \(f\) and its tangent plane is \(o(|(\Delta x, \Delta y)|)\) — it goes to zero faster than the distance to the point.

Theorem 2.3. If \(f_x\) and \(f_y\) exist and are continuous at \((x_0, y_0)\), then \(f\) is differentiable there.

Proof sketch. By the Mean Value Theorem applied twice: $$ f(x_0+h, y_0+k) - f(x_0,y_0) = f(x_0+h,y_0+k) - f(x_0,y_0+k) + f(x_0,y_0+k) - f(x_0,y_0) $$ $$ = f_x(x_0 + \xi_1 h, y_0+k)\cdot h + f_y(x_0, y_0 + \xi_2 k)\cdot k $$ for some \(\xi_1, \xi_2 \in (0,1)\). Since \(f_x\) and \(f_y\) are continuous: $$ f_x(x_0+\xi_1 h, y_0+k) \to f_x(x_0,y_0), \quad f_y(x_0, y_0+\xi_2 k) \to f_y(x_0,y_0). $$ So the error term \(\to 0\) faster than \(\sqrt{h^2+k^2}\). \(\blacksquare\)

Remark — The Pathological Case. Consider \(f(x,y) = \frac{xy}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\) at the origin (set \(f(0,0)=0\)). Both \(f_x(0,0) = 0\) and \(f_y(0,0) = 0\) exist, yet \(f\) is not differentiable at the origin — the "tangent plane" \(z=0\) is not a good approximation along the diagonal \(y=x\). Partial derivatives alone are insufficient.

docs.title: §3. The Normal Vector and Equation of the Plane
docs.text:
The tangent plane \(z - f(x_0,y_0) = f_x(x-x_0) + f_y(y-y_0)\) can be rewritten as

\[ f_x(x-x_0) + f_y(y-y_0) - (z - z_0) = 0, \]

which has the form \(\mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_0) = 0\) with

\[ \mathbf{n} = (f_x,; f_y,; -1). \]

This is the normal vector to the surface at \(P_0\). The minus sign in the \(z\)-component is not a sign error — it comes from rewriting the plane equation.

Equivalently, if the surface is presented as a level set \(F(x,y,z) = 0\) where \(F(x,y,z) = f(x,y) - z\), then

\[ abla F = (f_x, f_y, -1), \]

which is exactly \(\mathbf{n}\). This generalizes beautifully.

Theorem 3.1 (Tangent Plane to a Level Surface). If \(G: \mathbb{R}^3 o \mathbb{R}\) is \(C^1\) and \( abla G(P_0) eq \mathbf{0}\), the tangent plane to the level surface \(G(x,y,z) = c\) at \(P_0 = (x_0,y_0,z_0)\) is

\[ G_x(P_0)(x-x_0) + G_y(P_0)(y-y_0) + G_z(P_0)(z-z_0) = 0. \]

Proof. Any smooth curve \( oldsymbol{\gamma}(t)\) lying in the surface satisfies \(G( oldsymbol{\gamma}(t)) = c\). Differentiating: \( abla G \cdot oldsymbol{\gamma}'(t) = 0\). So \( abla G(P_0)\) is perpendicular to every tangent vector to every curve through \(P_0\) on the surface. The tangent plane is spanned by all such tangent vectors, and \( abla G(P_0)\) is its normal. \( lacksquare\)

docs.title: §4. Tangent Planes to Parametric Surfaces
docs.text:
For a parametric surface \(\mathbf{r}(u,v) = (x(u,v), y(u,v), z(u,v))\), the tangent vectors along the parameter curves are \(\mathbf{r}_u\) and \(\mathbf{r}_v\). The tangent plane at \(\mathbf{r}(u_0, v_0)\) is spanned by these two vectors, and the normal is their cross product.

Definition 4.1. The tangent plane to \(\mathbf{r}(u,v)\) at \((u_0,v_0)\) is the plane through \(\mathbf{r}(u_0,v_0)\) with normal

\[ \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{r}_u(u_0,v_0) \times \mathbf{r}_v(u_0,v_0), \]

provided \(\mathbf{n} \neq \mathbf{0}\) (the regular point condition).

Connection to surfaces of revolution. From our previous note, \(\mathbf{r}(x,\theta) = (x, f\cos\theta, f\sin\theta)\) gives

\[ \mathbf{r}_x = (1, f'\cos\theta, f'\sin\theta), \quad \mathbf{r}_\theta = (0, -f\sin\theta, f\cos\theta), \] \[ \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{r}_x \times \mathbf{r}_\theta = (f'f,; -f\cos\theta,; -f\sin\theta) = f\cdot(f', -\cos\theta, -\sin\theta). \]

So the unit normal is \(\hat{\mathbf{n}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+(f')^2}}(f', -\cos\theta, -\sin\theta)\). The tangent plane at any point on a surface of revolution is perpendicular to the \(r\theta\)-plane — as expected from the rotational symmetry.

docs.title: §5. Linearization — The Tangent Plane as Approximation
docs.text:
Definition 5.1 (Linear Approximation / Linearization). If \(f\) is differentiable at \((x_0,y_0)\), the linearization of \(f\) at \((x_0,y_0)\) is

\[ L(x,y) = f(x_0,y_0) + f_x(x_0,y_0)(x-x_0) + f_y(x_0,y_0)(y-y_0). \]

The total differential is $$ df = f_x, dx + f_y, dy. $$

Error Bound. If \(|f_{xx}|, |f_{xy}|, |f_{yy}| \leq M\) on a disk of radius \(d\) around \((x_0,y_0)\), then

\[ |f(x,y) - L(x,y)| \leq \frac{M}{2}\left(|x-x_0| + |y-y_0|\right)^2. \]

This is the multivariable Taylor remainder estimate — the tangent plane has second-order error.

docs.title: Example 6.2 — Sphere
docs.text:
Find the tangent plane to \(x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 14\) at \((1, 2, 3)\).

Let \(G(x,y,z) = x^2+y^2+z^2\). Then \(\nabla G = (2x, 2y, 2z)\), so \(\nabla G(1,2,3) = (2,4,6)\).

Tangent plane: \(2(x-1) + 4(y-2) + 6(z-3) = 0 \implies x + 2y + 3z = 14\).

Geometric sanity check: The normal to a sphere at any point is radial — pointing from the origin to the point. Indeed, \(\mathbf{n} = (1,2,3)\) is the position vector. ✓

docs.title: Example 6.3 — Implicit Surface
docs.text:
Find the tangent plane to \(xyz = 6\) at \((1, 2, 3)\).

\(G(x,y,z) = xyz\). \(\nabla G = (yz, xz, xy)\). At \((1,2,3)\): \(\nabla G = (6, 3, 2)\).

Tangent plane: \(6(x-1) + 3(y-2) + 2(z-3) = 0 \implies 6x + 3y + 2z = 18\).

docs.title: Example 6.4 — Parametric Surface (Torus)
docs.text:
The torus: \(\mathbf{r}(\phi, \theta) = ((R + r\cos\phi)\cos\theta,; (R+r\cos\phi)\sin\theta,; r\sin\phi)\).

\[ \mathbf{r}_\phi = (-r\sin\phi\cos\theta,; -r\sin\phi\sin\theta,; r\cos\phi), $$ $$ \mathbf{r}_\theta = (-(R+r\cos\phi)\sin\theta,; (R+r\cos\phi)\cos\theta,; 0). \]

The normal \(\mathbf{r}_\phi \times \mathbf{r}_\theta\) at any point gives the outward normal to the torus. At \(\phi=0, \theta=0\) (outermost point \((R+r, 0, 0)\)): \(\mathbf{r}_\phi = (0,0,r)\), \(\mathbf{r}_\theta = (0, R+r, 0)\), so \(\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{r}_\phi \times \mathbf{r}_\theta = (-r(R+r), 0, 0)\), pointing in the \(-x\) direction. Tangent plane is \(x = R+r\) — vertical, as expected.

docs.title: How the Partial Derivatives Determine the Plane
docs.text:
Fix y = y₀ (slice in xz-plane):          Fix x = x₀ (slice in yz-plane):

docs.title: §8. The Total Differential and Error Propagation
docs.text:
In applications, the total differential quantifies how errors in inputs propagate to outputs.

Setup. Suppose \(z = f(x,y)\) and we measure \(x, y\) with errors \(\Delta x, \Delta y\). The resulting error in \(z\) is approximately:

\[ \Delta z \approx dz = f_x, \Delta x + f_y, \Delta y. \]

Example 8.1. The period of a pendulum is \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}\). Suppose \(L\) is measured with \(1%\) error and \(g\) with \(0.5%\) error. What is the error in \(T\)?

\[ \frac{\partial T}{\partial L} = \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{Lg}}, \quad \frac{\partial T}{\partial g} = -\frac{\pi\sqrt{L}}{g^{3/2}}. \] \[ dT = \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{Lg}} dL - \frac{\pi\sqrt{L}}{g^{3/2}} dg = T\left(\frac{dL}{2L} - \frac{dg}{2g}\right). \]

Relative error: \(\frac{|dT|}{T} \leq \frac{1}{2}\cdot 1% + \frac{1}{2}\cdot 0.5% = 0.75%\).

docs.title: §9. Tangent Space — The Differential-Geometric View
docs.text:
In differential geometry, the tangent plane becomes the tangent space \(T_{P_0}S\) — a vector space of all tangent vectors to \(S\) at \(P_0\).

Definition 9.1. For a smooth surface \(S \subset \mathbb{R}^3\), the tangent space at \(P_0 \in S\) is

\[ T_{P_0}S = {\boldsymbol{\gamma}'(0) : \boldsymbol{\gamma}: (-\epsilon,\epsilon) \to S \text{ smooth}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}(0) = P_0}. \]

This is a 2-dimensional real vector space.

Why "tangent space" not "tangent plane"? The tangent space is a vector space anchored at the origin (it's been translated so \(P_0\) is the origin). The tangent plane in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) is the affine subspace \(P_0 + T_{P_0}S\).

For a manifold. On a smooth \(n\)-manifold \(M\), the tangent space \(T_pM\) at every point \(p\) is an \(n\)-dimensional vector space. This generalizes the tangent plane to arbitrary dimensions — the foundation for all of modern differential geometry and theoretical machine learning.

docs.title: §10. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
10.1 The Gradient as Normal to Level Sets
docs.text:
In optimization, we minimize \(\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) over parameters \(\boldsymbol{\theta} \in \mathbb{R}^n\). The key geometric fact: \(\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}\) is normal to the level set \({\boldsymbol{\theta}: \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = c}\) (the loss contour).

This is exactly Theorem 3.1. The level set is a hypersurface in parameter space; the gradient is its normal vector. Gradient descent steps in the normal direction to the current loss contour — the direction of steepest ascent/descent.

The tangent hyperplane to the loss landscape at \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0\) is:

\[ \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \approx \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0) + \nabla\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)^T (\boldsymbol{\theta} - \boldsymbol{\theta}_0). \]

This is exactly the linearization formula of §5, now in \(n\) dimensions. Every first-order optimizer (SGD, Adam, RMSProp) is doing tangent plane approximation.

docs.title: 10.2 Backpropagation is Iterated Chain Rule on Tangent Spaces
docs.text:
The chain rule for differentiation — the engine of backpropagation — is exactly the statement that the tangent map (derivative) of a composition is the composition of tangent maps:

\[ D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg(f(x)) \circ Df(x). \]

In coordinates: if \(\mathbf{z} = f(\mathbf{x})\) and \(L = g(\mathbf{z})\), then

\[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial x_i} = \sum_j \frac{\partial L}{\partial z_j}\frac{\partial z_j}{\partial x_i}. \]

Each \(\frac{\partial z_j}{\partial x_i}\) is an entry of the Jacobian matrix \(Df\) — the matrix representation of the tangent map. Backprop is the recursive computation of tangent maps through the network's computational graph.

docs.title: 10.3 Newton's Method and Second-Order Optimization
docs.text:
First-order (gradient) methods use the tangent plane. Second-order methods use the osculating paraboloid — the second-order Taylor approximation:

\[ \mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{ heta}) \approx \mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{ heta}_0) + abla\mathcal{L}^T \Delta oldsymbol{ heta} + rac{1}{2}\Delta oldsymbol{ heta}^T H \Delta oldsymbol{ heta}, \]

where \(H = abla^2\mathcal{L}\) is the Hessian. Newton's step minimizes this quadratic: \(\Delta oldsymbol{ heta} = -H^{-1} abla\mathcal{L}\).

The geometry: \(H\) measures how fast the tangent plane tilts as you move along the surface — it encodes curvature. K-FAC, Shampoo, and other second-order optimizers approximate \(H^{-1}\) efficiently to go beyond the tangent plane approximation.

docs.title: 10.4 Implicit Neural Representations (INRs)
docs.text:
A neural network \(F_\theta: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}\) can represent a surface implicitly as \({F_\theta(\mathbf{x}) = 0}\) (e.g., NeRF, DeepSDF, NeuralRBF). The tangent plane at a surface point \(\mathbf{x}_0\) is then

\[ \nabla_x F_\theta(\mathbf{x}_0) \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0) = 0, \]

exactly Theorem 3.1. The network's gradient with respect to input coordinates (not parameters) gives the surface normal — used for shading, collision detection, and physical simulation in neural rendering.

docs.title: 10.5 Tangent Spaces in Manifold Learning
docs.text:
The manifold hypothesis says data \({x_i} \subset \mathbb{R}^D\) lies near a \(d\)-dimensional manifold \(\mathcal{M}\) with \(d \ll D\). Methods like PCA (local), UMAP, and Isomap all estimate the tangent space \(T_{x_i}\mathcal{M}\) at each data point — the \(d\)-dimensional plane that best fits the data locally.

Local PCA at \(x_i\): compute the top-\(d\) eigenvectors of the local covariance matrix. These eigenvectors are a basis for the estimated tangent space. The tangent plane formula gives the first-order approximation to the manifold:

\[ \mathcal{M} \approx x_i + \text{span}(v_1, \ldots, v_d) \quad \text{near } x_i. \]

docs.title: 10.6 Riemannian Optimization
docs.text:
Modern ML encounters optimization on matrix manifolds: orthogonal matrices \(O(n)\), positive definite matrices \(\text{PD}(n)\), Grassmannians, Stiefel manifolds. Standard gradient descent ignores the manifold constraint and steps off the manifold.

Riemannian gradient descent projects the Euclidean gradient onto the tangent space at the current point, then uses a retraction (exponential map) to move along the manifold:

\[ \boldsymbol{\theta}_{t+1} = \text{Retr}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_t}!\left(-\eta, \text{grad}_R \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)\right), \]

where \(\text{grad}_R \mathcal{L} = P_{T_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_t}\mathcal{M}}(\nabla \mathcal{L})\) is the Riemannian gradient — the projection of \(\nabla\mathcal{L}\) onto the tangent plane. Without tangent planes, Riemannian optimization is impossible.

docs.title: §11. Exercises
docs.text:
11.1. Find the tangent plane to \(z = x^2 y + \sin(xy)\) at \((1, 0, 0)\).

11.2. Show that the tangent plane to the ellipsoid \(\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} + \frac{z^2}{c^2} = 1\) at \((x_0,y_0,z_0)\) is $$ \frac{x,x_0}{a^2} + \frac{y,y_0}{b^2} + \frac{z,z_0}{c^2} = 1. $$

11.3. [Pathological case] Let \(f(x,y) = \frac{x^2 y}{x^4 + y^2}\) for \((x,y)\neq(0,0)\), and \(f(0,0)=0\).

  • (a) Show \(f_x(0,0) = f_y(0,0) = 0\).
  • (b) Show \(f\) is not continuous at \((0,0)\) (approach along \(y = x^2\)).
  • © Conclude that the "tangent plane" \(z = 0\) is not a good approximation.

11.4. Two surfaces are said to be tangent at \(P_0\) if they share the same tangent plane there. Show that \(z = x^2 + y^2\) and \(z = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) are tangent at the origin. (Careful — neither is differentiable there in the classical sense. Interpret geometrically.)

11.5. [ML connection] Let \(\mathcal{L}(\theta_1, \theta_2) = \frac{1}{2}(\theta_1^2 + 4\theta_2^2)\) (an elongated paraboloid). Write the tangent plane at \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0 = (2, 1)\). In which direction does gradient descent step? Show this is the normal to the level curve \(\mathcal{L} = 4\).

11.6. [Riemannian] The sphere \(S^2 = {x^2+y^2+z^2=1}\). Find the tangent plane at \((\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})\). Show that the projected gradient of \(f(x,y,z) = z\) onto \(T_pS^2\) is \((−\frac{1}{3}, −\frac{1}{3}, \frac{2}{3})\) (up to normalization). This is the Riemannian gradient — the direction to maximize \(z\) while staying on the sphere.

docs.title: §12. Summary
docs.text:
Situation Tangent plane / normal \(z = f(x,y)\), explicit \(z = z_0 + f_x(x-x_0) + f_y(y-y_0)\); normal \((f_x, f_y, -1)\) \(G(x,y,z) = c\), level set \( abla G(P_0)\cdot(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_0) = 0\); normal \( abla G(P_0)\) \(\mathbf{r}(u,v)\), parametric spanned by \(\mathbf{r}_u, \mathbf{r}_v\); normal \(\mathbf{r}_u imes \mathbf{r}_v\) \(\mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{ heta})\), loss function linearization \(L( oldsymbol{ heta}) = \mathcal{L}( oldsymbol{ heta}_0) + abla\mathcal{L}^T\Delta oldsymbol{ heta}\); normal \( abla\mathcal{L}\)

The central theorem: For \(C^1\) functions, partial derivatives \(\Rightarrow\) differentiability \(\Rightarrow\) the tangent plane is a valid linear approximation with quadratic error. Partial derivatives alone are not enough.

The key principle: The tangent plane linearizes. Everything in first-order calculus — chain rule, gradient descent, backpropagation, linearization — is a version of the same idea: replace a nonlinear object locally by its tangent plane, work in the plane (where linear algebra applies), then return to the nonlinear world.

docs.title: Surface Area
docs.text: "To measure is to know." — Lord Kelvin

docs.title: §0. Prefatory Remarks
docs.text:
Surface area is one of those concepts that feels intuitively obvious — and is analytically subtle. The naive approach (approximate by rectangles, take a limit) fails catastrophically: there exist continuous surfaces whose "rectangular" approximations diverge to infinity while the true area is finite. This is the Schwarz lantern paradox, and it forces us to be precise about what "area" means.

The correct approach: approximate by flat triangular patches (tangent plane pieces), not by rectangles. This leads to the integral \(\iint |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|, du, dv\), which is the formula we derive and prove here.

Surface area appears throughout:

  • Physics: heat transfer, fluid drag, electrostatics (Gauss's law)
  • Differential geometry: minimal surfaces, isoperimetric inequalities
  • Computer graphics: texture mapping, mesh parameterization
  • Machine learning / deep learning: kernel methods, Gaussian process priors on manifolds, surface-loss functions in neural geometry processing

This note builds the theory from scratch, connects it to the previous notes on [[Surfaces_of_Revolution]] and [[Tangent_Planes]], and proves everything.

docs.title: 1.1 Arc Length as a Warm-Up
docs.text:
Recall how we measure arc length. For a curve \(\boldsymbol{\gamma}: [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^3\), we approximate by straight-line segments:

\[ L \approx \sum_{i} |\boldsymbol{\gamma}(t_{i+1}) - \boldsymbol{\gamma}(t_i)|. \]

As the partition refines, this converges to \(\int_a^b |\boldsymbol{\gamma}'(t)|,dt\). The key: we approximate by line segments tangent to the curve. This works.

docs.title: 1.2 The Schwarz Lantern Paradox
docs.text:
Inscribe a cylinder of radius \(1\) and height \(1\) with a triangular mesh: divide the height into \(n\) horizontal strips and rotate by \(\pi/m\) between strips, placing \(m\) triangles per strip. The true lateral area of the cylinder is \(2\pi\).

As \(n, m \to \infty\), what does the mesh area converge to?

If \(n = m\) (balanced refinement): the area converges to \(2\pi\). ✓

If \(n = m^2\) (height refined faster than circumference): the area diverges to \(\infty\). ✗

Moral. The limit depends on how you refine, not just that you refine. Rectangular subdivisions of a surface — unlike line-segment subdivisions of a curve — do not automatically converge to the correct area. We must use a definition that is independent of parameterization and robust to this issue.

The fix: use the tangent plane at each point. The correct area element is the area of the parallelogram spanned by the tangent vectors \(\mathbf{r}_u , du\) and \(\mathbf{r}_v , dv\).

docs.title: §2. The Setup — Parameterized Surfaces
docs.text:
Definition 2.1. A smooth parameterized surface is a map \(\mathbf{r}: D \subset \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^3\), \((u,v) \mapsto \mathbf{r}(u,v)\), where \(D\) is a bounded region, \(\mathbf{r} \in C^1(D)\), and the cross product \(\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v \neq \mathbf{0}\) everywhere on \(D\) (the regular condition).

The tangent vectors at \((u_0, v_0)\): $$ \mathbf{r}_u = \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial u}, \quad \mathbf{r}_v = \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial v}. $$

These span the tangent plane at \(\mathbf{r}(u_0,v_0)\) (as established in [[Tangent_Planes]], §4).

The area element. For a small rectangle \([u_0, u_0+\Delta u] \times [v_0, v_0+\Delta v]\) in parameter space, the image on the surface is approximated by the parallelogram with sides \(\mathbf{r}_u \Delta u\) and \(\mathbf{r}_v \Delta v\). The area of this parallelogram is

\[ |\mathbf{r}_u \Delta u \times \mathbf{r}_v \Delta v| = |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|, \Delta u, \Delta v. \]

Summing over all such patches and taking the limit gives the definition.

docs.title: §3. The Surface Area Formula
docs.text:
Definition / Theorem 3.1 (Surface Area). The surface area of a smooth parameterized surface \(\mathbf{r}: D \to \mathbb{R}^3\) is

\[ \boxed{A = \iint_D |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|, dA,} \]

where \(dA = du, dv\) is the area element in parameter space.

Proof (rigorous sketch). Partition \(D\) into small rectangles \(R_{ij} = [u_i, u_{i+1}] \times [v_j, v_{j+1}]\) with \(\Delta u = u_{i+1}-u_i\), \(\Delta v = v_{j+1}-v_j\). At each rectangle, approximate the surface patch \(\mathbf{r}(R_{ij})\) by the parallelogram with sides

\[ \mathbf{r}_u(u_i, v_j),\Delta u \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbf{r}_v(u_i,v_j),\Delta v. \]

The area of this parallelogram is \(|\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|(u_i,v_j),\Delta u,\Delta v\). Summing:

\[ A \approx \sum_{i,j} |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|(u_i,v_j),\Delta u,\Delta v. \]

This is a Riemann sum for \(\iint_D |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|,dA\). Since \(|\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|\) is continuous on the compact set \(D\) (as \(\mathbf{r} \in C^1\)), the Riemann sums converge as \(\Delta u, \Delta v \to 0\). This limit is the definition of surface area (independent of parameterization — proved in §5). \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: The Three Representations
docs.text:
Depending on how the surface is given, the formula takes three forms.

Case 1 — Explicit: \(z = f(x,y)\).

Parameterize by \((x,y)\) itself: \(\mathbf{r}(x,y) = (x, y, f(x,y))\).

\[ \mathbf{r}_x = (1, 0, f_x), \quad \mathbf{r}_y = (0, 1, f_y). \] \[ \mathbf{r}_x \times \mathbf{r}_y = \begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \ 1 & 0 & f_x \ 0 & 1 & f_y\end{vmatrix} = (-f_x,, -f_y,, 1). \] \[ |\mathbf{r}_x \times \mathbf{r}_y| = \sqrt{f_x^2 + f_y^2 + 1}. \] \[ \boxed{A = \iint_D \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right)^2}; dA.} \]

Case 2 — Parametric: \(\mathbf{r}(u,v)\).

\[ \boxed{A = \iint_D |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|; du, dv.} \]

Case 3 — Implicit: \(G(x,y,z) = 0\), solved as \(z = f(x,y)\).

Use Case 1 with \(f_x = -G_x/G_z\) and \(f_y = -G_y/G_z\):

\[ \sqrt{1 + f_x^2 + f_y^2} = \frac{\sqrt{G_x^2 + G_y^2 + G_z^2}}{|G_z|} = \frac{|\nabla G|}{|G_z|}. \] \[ \boxed{A = \iint_D \frac{|\nabla G|}{|G_z|}; dA.} \]

docs.title: §4. The First Fundamental Form
docs.text:
The quantity \(|\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|\) can be expressed in terms of the first fundamental form (metric tensor) of the surface. Define:

\[ E = \mathbf{r}_u \cdot \mathbf{r}_u, \quad F = \mathbf{r}_u \cdot \mathbf{r}_v, \quad G = \mathbf{r}_v \cdot \mathbf{r}_v. \]

These are the coefficients of the metric \(g_{ij}\), and we have the classical identity:

\[ |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|^2 = |\mathbf{r}_u|^2|\mathbf{r}_v|^2 - (\mathbf{r}_u \cdot \mathbf{r}_v)^2 = EG - F^2 = \det[g_{ij}]. \]

Proof of the identity. By the Lagrange identity: \(|\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}|^2 = |\mathbf{a}|^2|\mathbf{b}|^2 - (\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b})^2\). \(\blacksquare\)

So the area formula becomes:

\[ A = \iint_D \sqrt{EG - F^2}; du, dv. \]

This is the intrinsic formula — it depends only on the metric, not on the embedding in \(\mathbb{R}^3\). From the [[Tangent_Planes]] note, for a surface of revolution \(\mathbf{r}(x,\theta) = (x, f\cos\theta, f\sin\theta)\):

\[ E = 1+(f')^2, \quad F = 0, \quad G = f^2 \implies \sqrt{EG-F^2} = f\sqrt{1+(f')^2}, \]

recovering the formula from [[Surfaces_of_Revolution]], §3. ✓

docs.title: §5. Independence of Parameterization
docs.text:
A critical property: the area should not depend on how we parameterize the surface. This is non-obvious — the formula \(\iint |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|,du,dv\) explicitly involves \(u, v\).

Theorem 5.1 (Reparameterization Invariance). Let \(\mathbf{r}: D \to S\) and \(\tilde{\mathbf{r}}: \tilde{D} \to S\) be two regular parameterizations of the same surface, related by \(\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \tilde{\mathbf{r}}(\phi(u,v), \psi(u,v))\) where \((u,v) \mapsto (\phi,\psi)\) is a \(C^1\) diffeomorphism with Jacobian \(J\). Then

\[ \iint_D |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|,du,dv = \iint_{\tilde{D}} |\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\phi \times \tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\psi|,d\phi,d\psi. \]

Proof. By the chain rule: \(\mathbf{r}_u = \tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\phi \phi_u + \tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\psi \psi_u\) and \(\mathbf{r}_v = \tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\phi \phi_v + \tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\psi \psi_v\). The cross product:

\[ \mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v = (\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\phi \phi_u + \tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\psi\psi_u) \times (\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\phi\phi_v + \tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\psi\psi_v). \]

Expanding using bilinearity and \(\mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{0}\):

\[ = (\phi_u\psi_v - \phi_v\psi_u)(\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\phi \times \tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\psi) = J \cdot (\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\phi \times \tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\psi), \]

where \(J = \frac{\partial(\phi,\psi)}{\partial(u,v)}\) is the Jacobian determinant. So:

\[ \iint_D |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|,du,dv = \iint_D |\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\phi \times \tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\psi| \cdot |J|,du,dv = \iint_{\tilde{D}} |\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\phi \times \tilde{\mathbf{r}}_\psi|,d\phi,d\psi, \]

by the change-of-variables formula. \(\blacksquare\)

This is the multivariable analogue of the substitution rule for integrals. The Jacobian of the change of coordinates exactly cancels the change in \(|\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|\).

docs.title: Example 6.1 — Sphere of Radius \(R\)
docs.text:
Method 1: Explicit parameterization. Use \(\mathbf{r}(\phi,\theta) = (R\sin\phi\cos\theta, R\sin\phi\sin\theta, R\cos\phi)\) for \((\phi,\theta) \in [0,\pi]\times[0,2\pi]\).

\[ \mathbf{r}_\phi = R(\cos\phi\cos\theta, \cos\phi\sin\theta, -\sin\phi), $$ $$ \mathbf{r}_\theta = R(-\sin\phi\sin\theta, \sin\phi\cos\theta, 0). \]

Computing the cross product and its magnitude:

\[ E = R^2, \quad F = 0, \quad G = R^2\sin^2\phi, $$ $$ |\mathbf{r}_\phi \times \mathbf{r}_\theta| = R^2\sin\phi. \] \[ A = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi R^2\sin\phi, d\phi, d\theta = 2\pi R^2 \int_0^\pi \sin\phi, d\phi = 2\pi R^2 \cdot 2 = 4\pi R^2. \checkmark \]

Method 2: Explicit surface \(z = f(x,y)\). Use upper hemisphere \(z = \sqrt{R^2 - x^2 - y^2}\) over \(D: x^2+y^2 \leq R^2\) and double.

\[ f_x = \frac{-x}{\sqrt{R^2-x^2-y^2}}, \quad f_y = \frac{-y}{\sqrt{R^2-x^2-y^2}}. \] \[ 1 + f_x^2 + f_y^2 = 1 + \frac{x^2+y^2}{R^2-x^2-y^2} = \frac{R^2}{R^2-x^2-y^2}. \] \[ A = 2\iint_{x^2+y^2\leq R^2} \frac{R}{\sqrt{R^2-x^2-y^2}}, dA. \]

Switch to polar \(x = r\cos\theta\), \(y = r\sin\theta\):

\[ A = 2\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^R \frac{R}{\sqrt{R^2-r^2}}, r, dr, d\theta = 4\pi R \int_0^R \frac{r, dr}{\sqrt{R^2-r^2}}. \]

Let \(u = R^2 - r^2\), \(du = -2r,dr\):

\[ = 4\pi R \int_{R^2}^0 \frac{-du/2}{\sqrt{u}} = 2\pi R \int_0^{R^2} u^{-1/2},du = 2\pi R \cdot 2R = 4\pi R^2. \checkmark \]

docs.title: Example 6.2 — Paraboloid \(z = x^2 + y^2\) over \(x^2+y^2 \leq 1\)
docs.text:
\[ f_x = 2x, \quad f_y = 2y, \quad \sqrt{1 + 4x^2 + 4y^2} = \sqrt{1+4r^2}. \] \[ A = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 \sqrt{1+4r^2}, r, dr, d\theta = 2\pi \int_0^1 r\sqrt{1+4r^2}, dr. \]

Let \(u = 1 + 4r^2\), \(du = 8r,dr\):

\[ A = 2\pi \int_1^5 \sqrt{u}\cdot\frac{du}{8} = \frac{\pi}{4}\cdot\frac{2}{3}\left[u^{3/2}\right]_1^5 = \frac{\pi}{6}(5^{3/2} - 1) = \frac{\pi}{6}(5\sqrt{5}-1). \]

docs.title: Example 6.3 — Cone \(z = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) over \(x^2+y^2 \leq R^2\)
docs.text:
\[ f_x = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}, \quad f_y = \frac{y}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}, \quad 1+f_x^2+f_y^2 = 2. \] \[ A = \iint_{x^2+y^2\leq R^2} \sqrt{2}, dA = \sqrt{2}\cdot \pi R^2. \]

Sanity check: A cone of base radius \(R\) and height \(R\) (so \(z = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) has slope \(1\), height \(R\) at radius \(R\)) has slant height \(\ell = R\sqrt{2}\), lateral area \(\pi R\ell = \pi R^2\sqrt{2}\). ✓

docs.title: Example 6.4 — Torus
docs.text:
\(\mathbf{r}(\phi,\theta) = ((R+r\cos\phi)\cos\theta, (R+r\cos\phi)\sin\theta, r\sin\phi)\).

\[ E = r^2, \quad F = 0, \quad G = (R+r\cos\phi)^2, $$ $$ |\mathbf{r}_\phi \times \mathbf{r}_\theta| = r(R+r\cos\phi). \] \[ A = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} r(R+r\cos\phi), d\phi, d\theta = 2\pi r \int_0^{2\pi}(R + r\cos\phi), d\phi = 2\pi r \cdot 2\pi R = 4\pi^2 Rr. \]

(The \(\int_0^{2\pi}\cos\phi,d\phi = 0\) term vanishes.) This is Pappus's theorem: \(A = 2\pi R \cdot 2\pi r\). ✓

docs.title: The Area Element as a Parallelogram
docs.text:
Parameter space D:                 Surface in R³:

  v                                    z
  ^                                    ^
  |                                    |
  | v+dv *-------* (u+du, v+dv)        |          r_v·dv
  |      |       |                     |         /
  |      |  R_ij |          r(u,v) ----*---------
  |    v *-------* (u+du, v)           |\        |
  |      u      u+du                   | \       |
  +--------------------> u             |  r_u·du |
                                       |         |
  Area of R_ij = du·dv         Area of image patch 
                                ≈ |r_u × r_v| du dv
                                = area of parallelogram

docs.title: Why the Cross Product Gives Area
docs.text:
Two vectors a, b in R³:

         b
        /|
       / |
      /  | b·sin(θ)   <- height
     /θ  |
    *----+----------
         a

  Area of parallelogram = |a||b|sin(θ) = |a × b|

  Here: a = r_u·Δu,  b = r_v·Δv
  Area = |r_u·Δu × r_v·Δv| = |r_u × r_v| ΔuΔv

docs.title: Schwarz Lantern — Why Rectangles Fail
docs.text:
Correct triangulation (flat patches):      Schwarz's bad triangulation:
 triangles close to tangent plane            triangles skewed relative to surface

      /\   /\   /\                              /\   /\   /\
     /  \ /  \ /  \                            /||||\/||||\/||||\
    /    X    X    \                           /||||||||||||||||||\ 
   /    / \  / \    \                         each triangle nearly
  /__  /   \/   \  __\                        PERPENDICULAR to the
  area → correct as n→∞                      surface → area → ∞

docs.title: Computing \(|\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|\) — Summary
docs.text:
Surface type       |  Formula for dA = |r_u × r_v| du dv
 -------------------|---------------------------------------
 z = f(x,y)        |  √(1 + fx² + fy²) dx dy
 r(u,v) general    |  |r_u × r_v| du dv = √(EG-F²) du dv
 Sphere r(φ,θ)     |  R² sin(φ) dφ dθ
 Surface of rev     |  f(x)√(1+f'²) dx dθ → × 2π = area
 Cylinder r=R       |  R dθ dz

docs.title: §8. Surface Integrals — Integrating over the Surface
docs.text:
Once we have \(dA = |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|,du,dv\), we can integrate any function over the surface.

Definition 8.1 (Surface Integral of a Scalar). For a continuous function \(g: S \to \mathbb{R}\):

\[ \iint_S g, dA = \iint_D g(\mathbf{r}(u,v)), |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|, du, dv. \]

Setting \(g \equiv 1\) recovers surface area.

Example 8.2. Compute the average \(z\)-coordinate on the upper unit hemisphere \(z = \sqrt{1-x^2-y^2}\).

From Example 6.1 (with \(R=1\)): \(|\mathbf{r}_\phi \times \mathbf{r}_\theta| = \sin\phi\), and \(z = \cos\phi\) on the sphere.

\[ \bar{z} = \frac{1}{A}\iint_S z, dA = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos\phi\sin\phi,d\phi,d\theta = \frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot 2\pi\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos\phi\sin\phi,d\phi. \] \[ = \int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin 2\phi}{2},d\phi = \frac{1}{2}\left[-\frac{\cos 2\phi}{2}\right]_0^{\pi/2} = \frac{1}{2}\cdot 1 = \frac{1}{2}. \]

So the average height on the upper hemisphere is \(\frac{1}{2}\) — exactly halfway up. Geometric sanity check: the centroid of a hemisphere is at height \(R/2\). ✓

docs.title: 9.1 Surface Area of Revolution (Revisited)
docs.text:
From [[Surfaces_of_Revolution]], \(\mathbf{r}(x,\theta)\), \(|\mathbf{r}_x \times \mathbf{r}_\theta| = f(x)\sqrt{1+(f')^2}\):

\[ A = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_a^b f(x)\sqrt{1+(f')^2},dx,d\theta = 2\pi\int_a^b f(x)\sqrt{1+(f')^2},dx. \]

This is now seen as a special case of the general parametric formula.

docs.title: 9.2 Flat Surface (Plane)
docs.text:
Plane \(z = ax + by + c\) over domain \(D\):

\[ f_x = a, \quad f_y = b, \quad A = \sqrt{1+a^2+b^2}\cdot \text{Area}(D). \]

The factor \(\sqrt{1+a^2+b^2}\) is the secant of the angle between the plane and the horizontal — the area stretching factor.

docs.title: 9.3 Cylinder \(x^2 + y^2 = R^2\), \(0 \leq z \leq h\)
docs.text:
Parameterize: \(\mathbf{r}(\theta, z) = (R\cos\theta, R\sin\theta, z)\).

\[ \mathbf{r}_\theta = (-R\sin\theta, R\cos\theta, 0), \quad \mathbf{r}_z = (0,0,1). \] \[ \mathbf{r}_\theta \times \mathbf{r}_z = (R\cos\theta, R\sin\theta, 0), \quad |\cdot| = R. \] \[ A = \int_0^h\int_0^{2\pi} R,d\theta, dz = 2\pi R h. \checkmark \]

docs.title: §10. Minimal Surfaces
docs.text:
A minimal surface is one whose mean curvature \(H = \frac{1}{2}(\kappa_1+\kappa_2) = 0\) vanishes everywhere. Equivalently — and this is the variational characterization — minimal surfaces are critical points of the area functional.

Variational Setup. Fix the boundary \(\partial S\). Among all surfaces with this boundary, which has smallest area? The Euler-Lagrange equation for the area functional \(A[\mathbf{r}] = \iint |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|,du,dv\) is exactly \(H = 0\).

Theorem 10.1 (Euler-Lagrange for Area). A smooth surface is a critical point of \(A[\mathbf{r}]\) under fixed-boundary perturbations if and only if its mean curvature \(H = 0\) everywhere.

Proof sketch. Perturb: \(\mathbf{r}_\epsilon = \mathbf{r} + \epsilon\phi\hat{n}\) for a compactly supported function \(\phi\) and unit normal \(\hat{n}\). Compute \(\frac{d}{d\epsilon}A[\mathbf{r}_\epsilon]\big|_{\epsilon=0}\) and integrate by parts. The vanishing of this for all \(\phi\) forces \(H = 0\) (the first variation of area formula). \(\blacksquare\)

Examples of minimal surfaces:

Surface Description Plane \(H = 0\) trivially Catenoid \(f(x) = c\cosh(x/c)\); only minimal surface of revolution Helicoid \(\mathbf{r}(u,v) = (u\cos v, u\sin v, v)\); ruled minimal surface Enneper surface \(\mathbf{r}(u,v) = (u - u^3/3 + uv^2, -v + v^3/3 - vu^2, u^2 - v^2)\) Scherk surface \(e^z\cos y = \cos x\)

Plateau's problem (1760, solved 1930–31 by Douglas and Radó): Given any closed curve in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), does there exist a minimal surface bounded by it? Answer: yes (for rectifiable curves). Douglas won the first Fields Medal partly for this.

docs.title: §11. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
11.1 Surface Area as a Regularizer in Neural Geometry Processing
docs.text:
In neural implicit surface representations (NeRF, NeuralRBF, DeepSDF), a network \(F_\theta: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}\) defines a surface \(S = {F_\theta = 0}\). To prevent over-fitting and encourage smooth, minimal surfaces, practitioners add a surface area regularizer to the training loss:

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}} = \iint_S dA = \iint \frac{|\nabla F_\theta|}{|F_{\theta,z}|}, dA, \]

using the implicit surface formula of §3. Minimizing this term biases the learned surface toward smaller area — towards minimal surface solutions. This is Plateau's problem implemented as gradient descent.

docs.title: 11.2 Riemannian Metric Learning
docs.text: The surface area formula \(A = \iint \sqrt{EG-F^2},du,dv\) depends only on the first fundamental form \(g = {E, F, G}\) — the intrinsic metric. In metric learning, one directly learns a metric \(g\) on the data manifold \(\mathcal{M}\) such that geodesic distances reflect semantic similarity. The "volume" of data space (generalized area) is then \(\int \sqrt{\det g}, du, dv\) — exactly the Riemannian volume form. Controlling this volume controls the density of the learned representation.

docs.title: 11.3 Information Geometry and the Fisher Metric
docs.text:
In a statistical model \({p_\theta}\), the Fisher information metric

\[ g_{ij}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\partial \log p_\theta}{\partial\theta_i}\frac{\partial \log p_\theta}{\partial\theta_j}\right] \]

defines a Riemannian metric on the manifold of probability distributions. The volume of parameter space under this metric is \(\int\sqrt{\det g},d\theta\) — a generalized surface area. Natural gradient descent replaces the Euclidean gradient with the Riemannian gradient under \(g\) (exactly the Riemannian optimization from [[Tangent_Planes]], §10.6):

\[ \Delta\theta = -\eta, g^{-1}\nabla\mathcal{L}. \]

This is the mathematical foundation of K-FAC and other second-order optimizers. The Fisher metric quantifies how much the distribution changes per unit parameter change — it measures the "area" of the statistical manifold that a gradient step traverses.

docs.title: 11.4 Gaussian Processes on Manifolds
docs.text: A Gaussian process prior on a manifold \(\mathcal{M}\) requires a kernel \(k: \mathcal{M}\times\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{R}\). The heat kernel on a surface (the fundamental solution to the heat equation \(\partial_t u = \Delta_{\mathcal{M}} u\)) is intrinsic to the surface geometry and depends on the metric \(\sqrt{EG-F^2}\). Stationary kernels on surfaces generalize the RBF kernel, with the geodesic distance replacing Euclidean distance. Their spectral density (Mercer expansion via eigenfunctions of \(\Delta_\mathcal{M}\)) depends on the Riemannian volume form — our area element.

docs.title: 11.5 Score Matching and Diffusion on Surfaces
docs.text: Diffusion models (DDPM, score matching) are increasingly generalized to data on manifolds — e.g., proteins (data on \(SO(3)\)), molecular conformations (data on \(S^2\)), or any geometry-aware generative model. The score function \(\nabla_x \log p_t(x)\) on a manifold is the Riemannian gradient, and the forward/reverse diffusion processes use the Laplace-Beltrami operator \(\Delta_\mathcal{M}\) — which is defined via the metric \(\sqrt{EG-F^2}\). Without surface area theory, none of this makes sense.

docs.title: 11.6 Mesh-Based Deep Learning and Surface Discretization
docs.text: In graph neural networks on meshes (MeshCNN, DiffusionNet, PoinTr), the surface is discretized into triangles. Each triangle's area is \(\frac{1}{2}|\mathbf{e}_1 \times \mathbf{e}_2|\) where \(\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2\) are edge vectors — a discrete version of our cross-product formula. The cotangent Laplacian used in spectral mesh processing weights edges by \(\cot\alpha + \cot\beta\) (angles opposite the edge), which is exactly the discretization of \(\sqrt{EG-F^2}\). Every convolution on a mesh implicitly uses surface area.

docs.title: §12. Exercises
docs.text:
12.1. Compute the surface area of \(z = xy\) over the unit square \([0,1]^2\).

12.2. Find the area of the part of the plane \(x + 2y + 3z = 6\) that lies inside the cylinder \(x^2+y^2=4\).

12.3. [Implicit surface] Use the formula \(A = \iint |\nabla G|/|G_z|,dA\) to find the area of the ellipsoid \(\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}+\frac{z^2}{c^2}=1\) in the special case \(a=b\) (oblate spheroid). You should obtain an integral that can be evaluated by trigonometric substitution.

12.4. Show directly (by computing \(E, F, G\)) that a sphere of radius \(R\) in spherical coordinates has \(\sqrt{EG-F^2} = R^2\sin\phi\), and verify the area is \(4\pi R^2\).

12.5. [Pappus verification] A circle of radius \(r\) centered at \((R, 0, 0)\) (with \(R > r\)) is revolved about the \(z\)-axis. Use the parametric surface area formula to verify Pappus's theorem: \(A = 4\pi^2 Rr\).

12.6. [Minimal surfaces] Show that the helicoid \(\mathbf{r}(u,v) = (u\cos v, u\sin v, v)\) has \(E = 1+v^2\) — wait, recheck. Actually compute \(E, F, G\) for the helicoid and find \(H\).

12.7. [ML connection] A neural network defines a surface \(S = {F_\theta(\mathbf{x}) = 0}\) where \(F_\theta(x,y,z) = z - \sin(\pi x)\sin(\pi y)\). Write the surface area integral explicitly and discuss why adding \(\lambda A\) to the training loss encourages "flatter" surfaces.

docs.title: §13. Summary
docs.text:
| Surface | \(|\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|\) | Area | |---|---|---| | \(z = f(x,y)\) | \(\sqrt{1+f_x^2+f_y^2}\) | \(\iint_D \sqrt{1+f_x^2+f_y^2},dA\) | | General parametric | \(\sqrt{EG-F^2}\) | \(\iint_D \sqrt{EG-F^2},du,dv\) | | Surface of revolution | \(f(x)\sqrt{1+(f')^2}\) | \(2\pi\int_a^b f\sqrt{1+(f')^2},dx\) | | Sphere radius \(R\) | \(R^2\sin\phi\) | \(4\pi R^2\) | | Cylinder radius \(R\), height \(h\) | \(R\) | \(2\pi Rh\) | | Cone, base \(R\), slant \(\ell\) | \(\sqrt{2}R\) (for \(45°\) cone) | \(\pi R\ell\) | | Torus \((R,r)\) | \(r(R+r\cos\phi)\) | \(4\pi^2 Rr\) |

The conceptual hierarchy:

\[ \text{tangent vectors } \mathbf{r}_u, \mathbf{r}_v \xrightarrow{\text{cross product}} \text{area element } |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v| \xrightarrow{\text{integrate}} \text{surface area} \] \[ \text{metric tensor } g_{ij} \xrightarrow{\det} \sqrt{EG-F^2} \xrightarrow{\text{integrate}} \text{intrinsic area} \]

The deep point: both routes give the same answer, and neither depends on how you parameterize the surface. This invariance — under reparameterization — is the geometric content of the change-of-variables theorem.

docs.title: Surface Integrals
docs.text: "Integration is the act of adding up infinitely many infinitely small things. On a surface, each infinitely small thing is a tiny parallelogram."

docs.title: §0. Prefatory Remarks
docs.text:
A surface integral is the generalization of a line integral to two dimensions: instead of integrating along a curve, we integrate over a surface. There are two fundamentally different kinds:

  • Surface integrals of scalar fields \(\iint_S f, dS\) — integrate a function over the surface, weighted by area
  • Surface integrals of vector fields \(\iint_S \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}\) — integrate the flux of a vector field through the surface

The second type requires the surface to be oriented — it must have a consistent notion of "inside" and "outside," or "up" and "down." This orientation is the new conceptual ingredient.

These integrals are the backbone of:

  • Physics: Electric flux (Gauss's law), magnetic flux, fluid flow, heat transfer
  • Differential geometry: Integration of differential forms on manifolds
  • Deep learning: Information geometry, Fisher information matrix as a surface integral
  • PDEs: Green's theorem, divergence theorem, Stokes' theorem

Everything in this note builds from the parametric surface machinery developed in [[Surfaces_of_Revolution]] and [[Tangent_Planes]].

docs.title: §1. Parametric Surfaces — Recollection and Setup
docs.text:
Recall from [[Tangent_Planes]] §4: a parametric surface is a map

\[ \mathbf{r}: D \subset \mathbb{R}^2 \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^3, \quad \mathbf{r}(u,v) = \bigl(x(u,v),; y(u,v),; z(u,v)\bigr), \]

where \(D\) is a domain in the \(uv\)-plane (usually a rectangle or region with piecewise smooth boundary).

The tangent vectors: $$ \mathbf{r}_u = \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial u} = \left(\frac{\partial x}{\partial u}, \frac{\partial y}{\partial u}, \frac{\partial z}{\partial u}\right), \qquad \mathbf{r}_v = \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial v} = \left(\frac{\partial x}{\partial v}, \frac{\partial y}{\partial v}, \frac{\partial z}{\partial v}\right). $$

The surface element. At a point \((u_0, v_0)\), the small patch of surface corresponding to \([u_0, u_0+du] \times [v_0, v_0+dv]\) is approximated by the parallelogram spanned by \(\mathbf{r}_u, du\) and \(\mathbf{r}_v, dv\). Its area is:

\[ dS = |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|; du, dv. \]

Definition 1.1 (Regular Surface). The parametrization \(\mathbf{r}\) is regular at \((u_0,v_0)\) if

\[ \mathbf{r}_u(u_0,v_0) \times \mathbf{r}_v(u_0,v_0) \neq \mathbf{0}. \]

At regular points, the cross product gives a well-defined normal direction, and the tangent plane exists.

docs.title: Standard Examples of Parametric Surfaces
docs.text:
Sphere \(x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = a^2\): $$ \mathbf{r}(\phi,\theta) = (a\sin\phi\cos\theta,; a\sin\phi\sin\theta,; a\cos\phi), \quad \phi \in [0,\pi],; \theta \in [0,2\pi]. $$

Graph \(z = f(x,y)\) over region \(D\): $$ \mathbf{r}(x,y) = (x,; y,; f(x,y)), \quad (x,y) \in D. $$

Cylinder \(x^2 + y^2 = R^2\), \(0 \leq z \leq h\): $$ \mathbf{r}(\theta,z) = (R\cos\theta,; R\sin\theta,; z), \quad \theta \in [0,2\pi],; z \in [0,h]. $$

Surface of revolution (from [[Surfaces_of_Revolution]]): $$ \mathbf{r}(x,\theta) = (x,; f(x)\cos\theta,; f(x)\sin\theta), \quad x \in [a,b],; \theta \in [0,2\pi]. $$

docs.title: §2. Surface Integrals of Scalar Fields
docs.text:
Definition 2.1 (Surface Integral of a Scalar Field). Let \(f: S \subset \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}\) be continuous and \(\mathbf{r}: D \to S\) a regular parametrization. The surface integral of \(f\) over \(S\) is

\[ \boxed{\iint_S f, dS = \iint_D f(\mathbf{r}(u,v)), |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|; du, dv.} \]

Motivation. Partition \(D\) into small rectangles \(\Delta u_i \times \Delta v_j\). Each maps to a small surface patch of area \(\approx |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|,\Delta u_i,\Delta v_j\). The Riemann sum \(\sum_{i,j} f(\mathbf{r}(u_i,v_j)),|\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|,\Delta u_i,\Delta v_j\) converges to the integral in the limit.

Special case: \(f \equiv 1\). Then \(\iint_S 1, dS = \iint_D |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|, du, dv\) is the surface area — consistent with [[Surfaces_of_Revolution]] §3.

For a graph \(z = g(x,y)\): use \(\mathbf{r}(x,y) = (x,y,g(x,y))\).

\[ \mathbf{r}_x = (1, 0, g_x), \quad \mathbf{r}_y = (0, 1, g_y), \quad \mathbf{r}_x \times \mathbf{r}_y = (-g_x, -g_y, 1). \] \[ |\mathbf{r}_x \times \mathbf{r}_y| = \sqrt{1 + g_x^2 + g_y^2}. \]

So for a graph: $$ \iint_S f, dS = \iint_D f(x, y, g(x,y))\sqrt{1 + g_x^2 + g_y^2}; dx, dy. $$

docs.title: Example 2.1 — Mass of a Surface
docs.text:
A thin metallic sheet has the shape of the hemisphere \(x^2+y^2+z^2 = 1\), \(z \geq 0\), with surface density \(\rho(x,y,z) = z\). Find its total mass.

Parametrize: \(\mathbf{r}(\phi,\theta) = (\sin\phi\cos\theta, \sin\phi\sin\theta, \cos\phi)\), \(\phi \in [0,\pi/2]\), \(\theta \in [0,2\pi]\).

Compute cross product: $$ \mathbf{r}\phi = (\cos\phi\cos\theta, \cos\phi\sin\theta, -\sin\phi), \quad \mathbf{r}\theta = (-\sin\phi\sin\theta, \sin\phi\cos\theta, 0). $$

\[ \mathbf{r}_\phi \times \mathbf{r}_\theta = (\sin^2\phi\cos\theta,; \sin^2\phi\sin\theta,; \sin\phi\cos\phi). \] \[ |\mathbf{r}_\phi \times \mathbf{r}_\theta| = \sin\phi\sqrt{\sin^2\phi + \cos^2\phi} = \sin\phi. \]

Integrate: \(z = \cos\phi\) on the sphere, so

\[ M = \iint_S z, dS = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2} \cos\phi \cdot \sin\phi; d\phi, d\theta = 2\pi \int_0^{\pi/2} \sin\phi\cos\phi; d\phi = 2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2} = \pi. \quad \checkmark \]

docs.title: Example 2.2 — Surface Integral over a Graph
docs.text:
Compute \(\iint_S (x^2+y^2), dS\) where \(S\) is the surface \(z = 1 + 2x + 3y\) over \(D = [0,1]\times[0,1]\).

\[ g_x = 2, ; g_y = 3, \quad \sqrt{1+4+9} = \sqrt{14}. \] \[ \iint_S (x^2+y^2), dS = \sqrt{14}\int_0^1\int_0^1 (x^2+y^2), dx, dy = \sqrt{14} \cdot \frac{2}{3}. \]

docs.title: §3. Oriented Surfaces
docs.text:
This is where the new geometry enters. To integrate a vector field over a surface, we need to know which side is "positive" — i.e., which way the normal vector points.

Definition 3.1 (Orientation). An orientation of a smooth surface \(S\) is a continuous choice of unit normal vector \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}(P)\) at each regular point \(P \in S\).

A surface is orientable if such a continuous choice exists globally. Most familiar surfaces are orientable: spheres, planes, graphs \(z = f(x,y)\), cylinders (if we specify inner or outer). The famous exception is the Möbius band — it has only one side.

Two orientations always exist on an orientable connected surface: \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) and \(-\hat{\mathbf{n}}\). Choosing one is called orienting the surface.

Standard Conventions:

Surface Positive normal Closed surface (sphere, box) Outward-pointing Graph \(z = f(x,y)\) Upward: \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) has positive \(z\)-component Parametric surface $\hat{\mathbf{n}} = \frac{\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v}{

Reversing orientation: Swapping \(u \leftrightarrow v\) reverses the sign of \(\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v\), hence reverses the orientation. Swapping the parameters is how you change which side is "positive."

Definition 3.2 (Oriented Surface Element). Given orientation \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\), define the vector area element:

\[ d\mathbf{S} = \hat{\mathbf{n}}, dS = \frac{\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v}{|\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|} \cdot |\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|; du, dv = (\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v); du, dv. \]

The vector \(d\mathbf{S}\) encodes both the area element \(dS\) and the direction \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) simultaneously.

docs.title: §4. Surface Integrals of Vector Fields (Flux Integrals)
docs.text:
Definition 4.1 (Flux Integral). Let \(\mathbf{F}: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3\) be a continuous vector field and \(S\) an oriented surface with unit normal \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\). The flux of \(\mathbf{F}\) through \(S\) is

\[ \boxed{\iint_S \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iint_S (\mathbf{F} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}), dS.} \]

In terms of parametrization \(\mathbf{r}(u,v)\) with the induced orientation \(\hat{\mathbf{n}} = \frac{\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v}{|\mathbf{r}_u\times\mathbf{r}_v|}\):

\[ \iint_S \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iint_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v); du, dv. \]

Physical interpretation. \(\mathbf{F} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = |\mathbf{F}|\cos\theta\) where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\mathbf{F}\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\). This is the component of \(\mathbf{F}\) through the surface (not tangent to it).

  • If \(\mathbf{F}\) is a fluid velocity field: flux = net volume flow rate per unit time through \(S\)
  • If \(\mathbf{F}\) is electric field: flux = total electric charge enclosed (Gauss's law)
  • If \(\mathbf{F}\) is magnetic field: flux = magnetic flux (Faraday's law involves its time derivative)

For a graph \(z = g(x,y)\), \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) upward:

\[ \mathbf{r}_x \times \mathbf{r}_y = (-g_x, -g_y, 1), \quad d\mathbf{S} = (-g_x, -g_y, 1), dx, dy. \]

If \(\mathbf{F} = (P, Q, R)\):

\[ \iint_S \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iint_D \bigl(-Pg_x - Qg_y + R\bigr)\big|_{z=g(x,y)}; dx, dy. \]

docs.title: §5. Computing the Cross Product Systematically
docs.text:
Given \(\mathbf{r}(u,v)\), the key computational step is always \(\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v\). Here is the systematic approach:

\[ \mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \ \partial_u x & \partial_u y & \partial_u z \ \partial_v x & \partial_v y & \partial_v z \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} \partial_u y & \partial_u z \ \partial_v y & \partial_v z \end{vmatrix}\mathbf{i} - \begin{vmatrix} \partial_u x & \partial_u z \ \partial_v x & \partial_v z \end{vmatrix}\mathbf{j} + \begin{vmatrix} \partial_u x & \partial_u y \ \partial_v x & \partial_v y \end{vmatrix}\mathbf{k}. \]

In shorthand using the Jacobian notation:

\[ \mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v = \left(\frac{\partial(y,z)}{\partial(u,v)},; \frac{\partial(z,x)}{\partial(u,v)},; \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right), \]

where \(\frac{\partial(y,z)}{\partial(u,v)} = \begin{vmatrix} y_u & y_v \ z_u & z_v \end{vmatrix} = y_u z_v - y_v z_u\), etc.

This Jacobian notation reveals the deep structure: each component of \(\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v\) is the area of the projected parallelogram onto one coordinate plane. More on this in §8.

docs.title: Example 6.1 — Flux Through a Sphere
docs.text:
Let \(\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = (x, y, z)\) (radial field). Compute the flux outward through the sphere \(S: x^2+y^2+z^2 = a^2\).

Method 1 (geometric shortcut). On the sphere, \(\hat{\mathbf{n}} = \frac{(x,y,z)}{a}\) (outward unit normal). So

\[ \mathbf{F} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \frac{x^2+y^2+z^2}{a} = \frac{a^2}{a} = a. \]

The integrand is constant! So

\[ \iint_S \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = a \cdot \text{Area}(S) = a \cdot 4\pi a^2 = 4\pi a^3. \]

(Preview: by the Divergence Theorem, \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = 3\), and \(\iiint_{B} 3, dV = 3 \cdot \frac{4}{3}\pi a^3 = 4\pi a^3\). ✓)

docs.title: Example 6.2 — Flux Through a Cylinder (with caps)
docs.text:
Let \(\mathbf{F} = (x, y, 0)\). Compute the outward flux through the closed cylinder \(x^2+y^2 \leq 1\), \(0 \leq z \leq 1\).

The surface has three pieces: lateral side \(S_1\), top cap \(S_2\) (\(z=1\)), bottom cap \(S_3\) (\(z=0\)).

Lateral side \(S_1\): \(\mathbf{r}(\theta,z) = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta, z)\). $$ \mathbf{r}\theta = (-\sin\theta, \cos\theta, 0), \quad \mathbf{r}_z = (0,0,1). $$ $$ \mathbf{r}\theta \times \mathbf{r}z = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta, 0) \quad \text{(outward, since } x\text{-component positive when }\theta\in[0,\pi/2]\text{)}. $$ $$ \mathbf{F}\cdot(\mathbf{r}\theta \times \mathbf{r}z) = \cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1. $$ $$ \iint = \int_0} \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S{2\pi}\int_01 1; dz, d\theta = 2\pi. $$

Top cap \(S_2\) (\(z = 1\), upward normal \(\hat{\mathbf{n}} = \mathbf{k}\)): $$ \mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}} = (x,y,0)\cdot(0,0,1) = 0. \quad \iint_{S_2} = 0. $$

Bottom cap \(S_3\) (\(z = 0\), downward normal \(\hat{\mathbf{n}} = -\mathbf{k}\)): $$ \mathbf{F}\cdot(-\mathbf{k}) = 0. \quad \iint_{S_3} = 0. $$

Total flux: \(2\pi + 0 + 0 = 2\pi\).

(Check via Divergence Theorem: \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} = 2\), volume \(= \pi\). \(2\pi \cdot 1 = 2\pi\). ✓)

docs.title: Example 6.3 — Flux Through a Graph
docs.text:
Let \(\mathbf{F} = (0, 0, z)\) and \(S: z = x^2 + y^2\), \(0 \leq z \leq 1\) (paraboloid), upward orientation.

\[ \mathbf{r}(x,y) = (x, y, x^2+y^2), \quad D = {x^2+y^2 \leq 1}. $$ $$ g_x = 2x, \quad g_y = 2y, \quad d\mathbf{S} = (-2x, -2y, 1), dx, dy. $$ $$ \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = (0,0, x^2+y^2)\cdot(-2x,-2y,1) = x^2+y^2. $$ $$ \iint_S \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iint_D (x^2+y^2), dx, dy = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 r^2 \cdot r; dr, d\theta = 2\pi\cdot\frac{1}{4} = \frac{\pi}{2}. \]

docs.title: Example 6.4 — Flux Through the Torus (Conceptual)
docs.text: The torus has outward normal pointing away from the central circle (see [[Surfaces_of_Revolution]] §4 for parameterization). For a constant field \(\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{k}\), the flux through the torus is zero by symmetry: for every patch where \(\mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}} > 0\), there is a symmetric patch where \(\mathbf{F}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}} < 0\). This is an instance of the general principle: \(\iint_S \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = 0\) for any closed surface when \(\mathbf{F}\) is constant and the surface is closed (by the Divergence Theorem, \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} = 0\)).

docs.title: §8. The Differential Form Perspective
docs.text:
The surface integral of a vector field has a beautiful rewriting. If \(\mathbf{F} = (P, Q, R)\), then

\[ \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{F}\cdot(\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v), du, dv = P,\frac{\partial(y,z)}{\partial(u,v)} + Q,\frac{\partial(z,x)}{\partial(u,v)} + R,\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}; du, dv. \]

This is the 2-form: $$ \iint_S \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iint_S P, dy\wedge dz + Q, dz\wedge dx + R, dx\wedge dy. $$

This notation is not mere decoration — it is the language of differential geometry and Stokes' theorem on manifolds.

The exterior derivative of the 1-form \(\omega = P,dx + Q,dy + R,dz\) gives a 2-form \(d\omega\), and Stokes' theorem says \(\int_{\partial \Sigma} \omega = \iint_\Sigma d\omega\) for any oriented 2-manifold \(\Sigma\) with boundary \(\partial\Sigma\). This unifies:

Classical theorem Differential forms Fundamental theorem of calculus \(\int_a^b f',dx = f(b) - f(a)\) Green's theorem \(\oint_C P,dx + Q,dy = \iint_D (Q_x - P_y),dA\) Stokes' theorem \(\oint_C \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_S (\nabla\times\mathbf{F})\cdot d\mathbf{S}\) Divergence theorem \(\oiint_S \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iiint_V (\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}),dV\)

All are special cases of \(\int_{\partial M} \omega = \int_M d\omega\).

docs.title: §9. Stokes' Theorem and the Divergence Theorem — Statement
docs.text:
We state these without proof, as they deserve their own notes, but place them here for context.

Theorem 9.1 (Stokes' Theorem). Let \(S\) be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple closed curve \(\partial S\), oriented consistently (right-hand rule). Let \(\mathbf{F}\) be \(C^1\) on an open set containing \(S\). Then:

\[ \oint_{\partial S} \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_S (\nabla \times \mathbf{F})\cdot d\mathbf{S}. \]

Theorem 9.2 (Divergence Theorem / Gauss's Theorem). Let \(E\) be a simple solid region with outward-oriented boundary surface \(\partial E = S\). Let \(\mathbf{F}\) be \(C^1\) on an open set containing \(E\). Then:

\[ \oiint_S \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iiint_E (\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}), dV. \]

Mnemonic. Both theorems say: the integral of a derivative over a domain equals the integral of the original function over the boundary. Stokes: 2D → 1D. Divergence: 3D → 2D.

docs.title: §10. Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
10.1 Fisher Information Matrix as a Surface Integral
docs.text:
The Fisher information matrix \(I(\theta)\) for a statistical model \(p(x;\theta)\) is

\[ I(\theta)_{ij} = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(\cdot;\theta)}\left[\frac{\partial \log p}{\partial \theta_i}\frac{\partial \log p}{\partial \theta_j}\right]. \]

In geometric terms, \(I(\theta)\) is the Riemannian metric on the manifold of probability distributions (Fisher-Rao metric). For a continuous model with density \(p(x;\theta)\) over a domain \(\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2\):

\[ I(\theta)_{ij} = \iint_\Omega \frac{\partial \log p}{\partial \theta_i}\frac{\partial \log p}{\partial \theta_j}, p(x;\theta); dx_1, dx_2. \]

This is a surface integral of a scalar field — integrating \(\frac{\partial \log p}{\partial \theta_i}\frac{\partial \log p}{\partial \theta_j}\) weighted by the probability measure \(p,dA\). Natural gradient descent (used in KFAC, Shampoo, and other second-order optimizers) replaces the Euclidean gradient with the Riemannian gradient \(I(\theta)^{-1}\nabla\mathcal{L}\), which is coordinate-invariant.

docs.title: 10.2 Flux and Information Flow in Neural Networks
docs.text:
Consider a neural network layer as a map \(\mathbf{z} = \sigma(W\mathbf{x})\). The Jacobian \(J = \frac{\partial \mathbf{z}}{\partial \mathbf{x}}\) maps the input tangent space to the output tangent space. The singular values of \(J\) measure how much "information flux" passes through the layer.

For a 2D intermediate representation (e.g., a 2D convolutional feature map), the information flux through a surface \(S\) in feature space is:

\[ \Phi = \iint_S \mathbf{J}\cdot d\mathbf{S}, \]

where \(\mathbf{J}\) is the Jacobian field. Vanishing gradients correspond to \(\Phi \to 0\) — the "flux" of gradient information through the network collapses. Exploding gradients correspond to \(\Phi \to \infty\).

docs.title: 10.3 Gauss's Law and Implicit Neural Surfaces
docs.text:
Implicit neural representations (e.g., Neural Unsigned Distance Functions) represent surfaces as \({F_ heta(\mathbf{x}) = 0}\). Gauss's law applied to the learned signed distance function \(F_ heta\):

\[ \oiint_{\partial V} abla F_ heta \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iiint_V \Delta F_ heta; dV, \]

where \(\Delta = abla^2\) is the Laplacian. For a true signed distance function, \(| abla F| = 1\) everywhere (Eikonal equation), so $\Delta F = $ (mean curvature of level sets). Eikonal loss in training NeRF and NeuS models enforces this constraint:

\[ \mathcal{L}_ ext{eikonal} = \mathbb{E}_\mathbf{x}\left[(| abla F_ heta(\mathbf{x})| - 1)^2 ight]. \]

This is precisely requiring the flux of the gradient field through every surface to be controlled.

docs.title: 10.4 Normalizing Flows and Change of Variables on Surfaces
docs.text:
A normalizing flow \(T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n\) transforms a base density \(p_Z\) to a target density \(p_X\). The log-likelihood involves \(\log|\det J_T|\). Geometrically:

\[ \log|\det J_T(\mathbf{z})| = \log|\text{volume element distortion at } \mathbf{z}|. \]

For a 2D flow (e.g., a planar flow representing a 2D surface), \(|\det J_T|\) is the ratio of area elements — exactly the \(|\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v|\) factor in our surface integral formula! Training a normalizing flow to maximize likelihood is equivalent to learning a parametrization of a surface in probability space that minimizes area distortion.

docs.title: 10.5 Stokes' Theorem in Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs)
docs.text:
PINNs solve PDEs by minimizing residuals. For Maxwell's equations (governing electromagnetic fields in physics simulators and neural hardware models):

\[ abla imes \mathbf{B} = \mu_0 \mathbf{J} + \mu_0\epsilon_0 rac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t}. \]

Stokes' theorem converts this: \(\oint_C \mathbf{B}\cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_S ( abla imes\mathbf{B})\cdot d\mathbf{S}\). A PINN enforces this integral form as a loss:

\[ \mathcal{L}_ ext{Stokes} = \left|\oint_C \mathbf{B}_ heta \cdot d\mathbf{r} - \iint_S ( abla imes\mathbf{B}_ heta)\cdot d\mathbf{S} ight|^2. \]

The surface integral directly appears in the training objective.

docs.title: 10.6 Orientation and Signed vs. Unsigned Surfaces in 3D Deep Learning
docs.text:
In 3D point cloud networks (PointNet, PointNet++, DGCNN), surface orientation matters. A mesh-based network must consistently orient faces to define outward normals — exactly the orientation problem of §3. Learning orientation from unoriented point clouds is an active research area (2023–2025), and fails precisely on non-orientable surfaces — a topological obstruction, not a learning failure.

Watertight meshes (closed, orientable, consistently oriented) allow the Divergence Theorem to compute volumes from surface integrals:

\[ \text{Vol} = \frac{1}{3}\oiint_S \mathbf{r}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \frac{1}{3}\oiint_S (x,y,z)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}, dS. \]

This formula is used in computational geometry and 3D printing quality checks.

docs.title: §11. Exercises
docs.text:
11.1. Compute \(\iint_S z, dS\) where \(S\) is the cone \(z = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}\), \(0 \leq z \leq 1\).

11.2. Let \(\mathbf{F} = (y, -x, z^2)\). Compute the flux of \(\mathbf{F}\) upward through the paraboloid \(z = 4 - x^2 - y^2\), \(z \geq 0\).

11.3. Verify the Divergence Theorem for \(\mathbf{F} = (x^3, y^3, z^3)\) and the unit ball \(x^2+y^2+z^2 \leq 1\). Compute both sides.

11.4. Show that the Möbius band is non-orientable by explicit construction: parametrize it and show that \(\mathbf{r}_u \times \mathbf{r}_v\) cannot be made continuous and nonzero globally.

(Parametrization hint: \(\mathbf{r}(u,v) = \left((1 + v\cos\frac{u}{2})\cos u,; (1+v\cos\frac{u}{2})\sin u,; v\sin\frac{u}{2}\right)\), \(u \in [0,2\pi]\), \(v \in [-\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}]\).)

11.5. Let \(S\) be the surface of the unit cube \([0,1]^3\). Compute the outward flux of \(\mathbf{F} = (x^2, y^2, z^2)\) directly (six faces) and verify using the Divergence Theorem.

11.6. [Differential forms] Express the surface integral \(\iint_S xy, dz\wedge dx + z, dx\wedge dy\) in terms of a parametrization \(\mathbf{r}(u,v)\) and identify it as a flux integral of some \(\mathbf{F}\).

11.7. [Deep learning connection] For a 2-layer neural network with weight matrices \(W_1, W_2\) and scalar output \(y = \sigma(W_2\sigma(W_1\mathbf{x}))\), interpret the gradient \(\frac{\partial y}{\partial \mathbf{x}}\) as a flux through the "parameter surface" and explain what vanishing gradient means geometrically in terms of \(d\mathbf{S}\).

docs.title: §12. Summary
docs.text:
Object Formula Key point Scalar surface integral \(\iint_S f, dS = \iint_D f(\mathbf{r}),\|\mathbf{r}_u\times\mathbf{r}_v\|,du,dv\) Area-weighted Area element \(dS = \|\mathbf{r}_u\times\mathbf{r}_v\|,du,dv\) Jacobian of parametrization Orientation Continuous choice of \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) Required for flux integrals Vector area element \(d\mathbf{S} = (\mathbf{r}_u\times\mathbf{r}_v),du,dv\) Encodes area + direction Flux integral \(\iint_S \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iint_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r})\cdot(\mathbf{r}_u\times\mathbf{r}_v),du,dv\) Only normal component contributes Graph \(z=g(x,y)\) \(d\mathbf{S} = (-g_x, -g_y, 1),dx,dy\) (upward) Standard form Stokes' theorem \(\oint_{\partial S}\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_S(\nabla\times\mathbf{F})\cdot d\mathbf{S}\) Boundary ↔ interior Divergence theorem \(\oiint_{\partial E}\mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iiint_E(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}),dV\) Surface ↔ volume

The conceptual hierarchy:

\[ \underbrace{\int_a^b f,dx}_{\text{1D}} \longrightarrow \underbrace{\int_C \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{r}}_{\text{line integral}} \longrightarrow \underbrace{\iint_S f,dS}_{\text{scalar surface}} \longrightarrow \underbrace{\iint_S \mathbf{F}\cdot d\mathbf{S}}_{\text{flux / vector surface}} \]

Each arrow adds one dimension and one new idea: parameterization, area distortion, orientation. The flux integral is the culmination — it integrates a vector field's interaction with an oriented surface, and it is the object that Gauss, Stokes, and the entire theory of differential forms is built around.

  6. Wang et al. NeuS: Learning Neural Implicit Surfaces. NeurIPS 2021. For Eikonal loss and surface integrals in neural rendering.
