docs.title: Stokes' Theorem
docs.text: "In mathematics you don't understand things. You just get used to them." — von Neumann (But we're going to understand this one.)

docs.title: § 0 — The Philosophy Before the Formula
docs.text:
Before writing a single symbol, let me tell you what Stokes' theorem really is.

Every major theorem in vector calculus — Green's theorem, the Divergence theorem, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus — is secretly the same theorem. They all say:

\[\boxed{\int_{\partial \Omega} \omega = \int_{\Omega} d\omega}\]

The integral of a "derivative" over a region equals the integral of the original object over the boundary of that region. Stokes' theorem is the 3-dimensional surface version of this idea.

This is not just aesthetics. It is a profound structural fact about the universe. And it shows up everywhere — from fluid dynamics to Maxwell's equations to backpropagation.

docs.title: § 1 — Setting the Stage: What Are We Integrating Over?
1.1 Oriented Surfaces
docs.text:
Let \(S\) be a smooth, oriented surface in \(\mathbb{R}^3\). Oriented means we have chosen a consistent normal vector field \(\mathbf{n}\) on \(S\) — think of it as choosing which side of the surface is "up."

Examples of oriented surfaces:

  • The upper hemisphere \(z = \sqrt{1 - x^2 - y^2}\), with outward normal pointing up.
  • A saddle surface \(z = x^2 - y^2\) over some domain, with \(\mathbf{n}\) pointing upward.
  • Any graph \(z = f(x,y)\) over a region \(D\) in the \(xy\)-plane.

Personal note: The word "oriented" is doing enormous work here. The theorem is false without it. You must commit to a side.

docs.title: 1.2 The Boundary Curve and the Right-Hand Rule
docs.text:
The boundary \(\partial S\) of \(S\) is a closed curve (or a union of closed curves). The orientation of \(\partial S\) is determined by the right-hand rule:

If the thumb of your right hand points in the direction of \(\mathbf{n}\), your fingers curl in the positive direction of \(\partial S\).

Visualization:

        ↑ n (normal)
        |
    ____↑____
   /         \
  /     S     \
 /             \
 ←——— ∂S ———→   (boundary traversed counterclockwise when viewed from above)

This is not a convention chosen arbitrarily. It is the one that makes the algebra consistent.

docs.title: 2.1 Statement
docs.text:
Theorem (Stokes). Let \(S\) be an oriented, piecewise-smooth surface in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), bounded by a piecewise-smooth, positively oriented closed curve \(C = \partial S\). Let \(\mathbf{F} = \langle P, Q, R angle\) be a vector field whose components have continuous partial derivatives on an open region containing \(S\). Then:

\[\oint_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_S ( abla imes \mathbf{F}) \cdot d\mathbf{S}\]

Left side: A line integral of \(\mathbf{F}\) around the boundary curve \(C\).

Right side: A surface integral of the curl of \(\mathbf{F}\) over \(S\).

The curl is: $\( abla imes \mathbf{F} = egin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \ \partial_x & \partial_y & \partial_z \ P & Q & R \end{vmatrix} = \left\langle R_y - Q_z,\ P_z - R_x,\ Q_x - P_y ight angle\)$

And the surface integral is: $\(\iint_S ( abla imes \mathbf{F}) \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iint_S ( abla imes \mathbf{F}) \cdot \mathbf{n} , dS\)$

docs.title: § 3 — Proof (The Real Thing)
docs.text: We will prove Stokes' theorem for a surface that is a graph: \(S: z = g(x,y)\), \((x,y) \in D\), with upward normal.

docs.title: Step 1: Parameterize Everything
docs.text:
The surface is parameterized by \(\mathbf{r}(x, y) = \langle x, y, g(x,y) \rangle\).

The boundary \(C = \partial S\) is the image of \(\partial D\) under this parameterization.

docs.title: Step 2: Expand the Line Integral
docs.text:
\[\oint_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \oint_C P,dx + Q,dy + R,dz\]

On \(C\), we have \(z = g(x,y)\), so \(dz = g_x,dx + g_y,dy\). Substituting:

\[= \oint_{\partial D} (P + R g_x),dx + (Q + R g_y),dy\]

docs.title: Step 3: Apply Green's Theorem to the Plane
docs.text:
Green's theorem on \(D\) gives:

\[\oint_{\partial D} M,dx + N,dy = \iint_D \left(\frac{\partial N}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial M}{\partial y}\right) dA\]

with \(M = P + Rg_x\) and \(N = Q + Rg_y\). Computing \(\partial N/\partial x - \partial M/\partial y\) (using the chain rule carefully):

\[\frac{\partial N}{\partial x} = Q_x + Q_z g_x + R_x g_y + R g_{yx} + R_z g_x g_y\] \[\frac{\partial M}{\partial y} = P_y + P_z g_y + R_y g_x + R g_{xy} + R_z g_x g_y\]

Subtracting (and noting \(g_{xy} = g_{yx}\), \(R_z g_x g_y\) cancels):

\[\frac{\partial N}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial M}{\partial y} = (Q_x - P_y) + (R_y - Q_z)(-g_x)(-1)^{-1}\cdot(-g_x)\ \ldots\]

Let me collect terms cleanly:

\[= (R_y - Q_z)(-g_x) + (P_z - R_x)(-g_y) + (Q_x - P_y)\]

docs.title: Step 4: Recognize the Curl
docs.text:
The outward normal for \(z = g(x,y)\) with upward orientation is:

\[d\mathbf{S} = \langle -g_x, -g_y, 1 angle , dA\]

And \( abla imes \mathbf{F} = \langle R_y - Q_z,\ P_z - R_x,\ Q_x - P_y angle\).

So:

\[( abla imes \mathbf{F}) \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \left[(R_y - Q_z)(-g_x) + (P_z - R_x)(-g_y) + (Q_x - P_y) ight] dA\]

This is exactly what we computed in Step 3. Therefore:

\[\oint_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_D ( abla imes \mathbf{F}) \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iint_S ( abla imes \mathbf{F}) \cdot d\mathbf{S} \qquad lacksquare\]

Note: The general proof (for non-graph surfaces) follows by partitioning \(S\) into graph-like pieces and patching together. Interior boundary curves cancel in pairs because they are traversed in opposite directions — a beautiful combinatorial argument.

docs.title: What is the curl measuring?
docs.text:
\((\nabla \times \mathbf{F})(\mathbf{p}) \cdot \mathbf{n}\) measures the circulation density of \(\mathbf{F}\) at the point \(\mathbf{p}\) around the axis \(\mathbf{n}\).

More precisely: if you place a tiny paddle wheel at \(\mathbf{p}\) with axis \(\mathbf{n}\), the curl tells you how fast it spins and in which direction.

Stokes' theorem then says:

The total circulation around the boundary of \(S\) equals the sum of all the local spin contributions over the interior of \(S\).

This is the 3D version of how a river's global swirl is built up from local eddies.

docs.title: The "Telescope" Intuition
docs.text:
Divide \(S\) into infinitesimal parallelogram patches \(\delta S_i\). Around each patch, the circulation of \(\mathbf{F}\) is approximately \((\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) \cdot \mathbf{n} , \delta A_i\). When we sum all these tiny loops, the interior edges cancel (each shared edge is traversed once in each direction), leaving only the outer boundary \(C\). This is Stokes' theorem.

  +→→→→→→→→→→→+
  ↑  ↑→+  ↑→+ ↑
  ↑  ↑ ↓  ↑ ↓ ↑
  ↑  +-←+  +-←+↑
  ↑  ↑→+  ↑→+ ↑
  ↑  ↑ ↓  ↑ ↓ ↑
  +←←←←←←←←←←+
  (Interior arrows cancel; only the outer loop remains)

docs.title: Example 1: Verifying Stokes' theorem directly
docs.text:
Setup: Let \(\mathbf{F} = \langle -y, x, 0 \rangle\), and let \(S\) be the upper hemisphere \(x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1\), \(z \geq 0\), with upward normal. The boundary \(C\) is the unit circle \(x^2 + y^2 = 1\), \(z = 0\).

Left side (line integral):

Parameterize \(C\): \(\mathbf{r}(t) = \langle \cos t, \sin t, 0 \rangle\), \(t \in [0, 2\pi]\).

\[\oint_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \int_0^{2\pi} \langle -\sin t, \cos t, 0 \rangle \cdot \langle -\sin t, \cos t, 0 \rangle , dt = \int_0^{2\pi} (\sin^2 t + \cos^2 t) , dt = 2\pi\]

Right side (surface integral):

Compute the curl: $\(\nabla \times \mathbf{F} = \langle 0 - 0,\ 0 - 0,\ 1 - (-1) \rangle = \langle 0, 0, 2 \rangle\)$

On the hemisphere, \(d\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{n} , dS\) where \(\mathbf{n}\) is the outward unit normal. The curl dotted with \(\mathbf{n}\) integrates nicely:

\[\iint_S \langle 0, 0, 2 \rangle \cdot \mathbf{n} , dS = \iint_S 2 \cdot \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{n} , dS = 2 \iint_S \cos\phi , dS\]

where \(\phi\) is the polar angle. In spherical coordinates, \(dS = \sin\phi , d\phi , d\theta\):

\[= 2 \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2} \cos\phi \sin\phi , d\phi , d\theta = 2 \cdot 2\pi \cdot \left[\frac{\sin^2\phi}{2}\right]_0^{\pi/2} = 2 \cdot 2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{2} = 2\pi \checkmark\]

docs.title: Example 2: Choosing a Simpler Surface (The Key Trick)
docs.text:
Problem: Compute \(\oint_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}\) where \(\mathbf{F} = \langle y^2, z, x \rangle\) and \(C\) is the triangle with vertices \((1,0,0)\), \((0,1,0)\), \((0,0,1)\), traversed counterclockwise when viewed from above.

Key insight from Stokes: The surface integral depends only on \(\partial S = C\), not on which surface \(S\) we choose.

So we pick the flat triangular surface \(S\) lying in the plane \(x + y + z = 1\), \(x,y,z \geq 0\).

The normal to this plane (outward, consistent with the given orientation): \(\mathbf{n} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\langle 1, 1, 1 \rangle\), and \(dS = \sqrt{3} , dA\) where \(dA\) is the area element in the \(xy\)-plane projection.

Compute the curl:

\[\nabla \times \mathbf{F} = \langle R_y - Q_z, P_z - R_x, Q_x - P_y \rangle = \langle 0 - 1,\ 0 - 1,\ 0 - 2y \rangle = \langle -1, -1, -2y \rangle\]

Surface integral:

The projection of \(S\) onto the \(xy\)-plane is \(D: x \geq 0, y \geq 0, x + y \leq 1\).

\[\iint_S (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) \cdot \mathbf{n} , dS = \iint_D \langle -1,-1,-2y \rangle \cdot \langle 1, 1, 1 \rangle , dA = \iint_D (-2 - 2y) , dA\] \[= \int_0^1 \int_0^{1-x} (-2 - 2y) , dy , dx = \int_0^1 \left[-2y - y^2\right]_0^{1-x} dx\] \[= \int_0^1 \left[-2(1-x) - (1-x)^2\right] dx = \int_0^1 \left[-(1-x)(2 + 1 - x)\right] dx\] \[= \int_0^1 -(1-x)(3-x), dx = -\int_0^1 (3 - 4x + x^2), dx = -\left[3x - 2x^2 + \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = -\frac{4}{3}\]

docs.title: Example 3: When the Curl Vanishes — Conservative Fields
docs.text:
If \(\mathbf{F} = abla f\) for some scalar \(f\) (a conservative field), then:

\[ abla imes ( abla f) = \mathbf{0} \quad ext{(always)}\]

Stokes' theorem immediately gives:

\[\oint_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_S \mathbf{0} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = 0\]

for any closed curve \(C\). This is the vector calculus proof that conservative fields do zero work around closed loops — a fundamental law in physics and a building block for understanding energy conservation.

docs.title: 6.1 Green's Theorem as a Special Case
docs.text:
Take \(S\) to be a flat region \(D\) in the \(xy\)-plane, \(\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{k}\). Then:

\[\iint_S (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) \cdot \mathbf{k} , dA = \iint_D (Q_x - P_y) , dA\]

And \(\oint_C \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \oint_{\partial D} P,dx + Q,dy\).

This is exactly Green's theorem. So Green's theorem is Stokes' theorem for flat surfaces. The hierarchy:

\[\underbrace{\text{FTC}}_{\text{1D}} \subset \underbrace{\text{Green}}_{\text{2D, flat}} \subset \underbrace{\text{Stokes}}_{\text{2D, curved}} \subset \underbrace{\text{Generalized Stokes}}_{\text{any } n\text{-manifold}}\]

docs.title: 6.2 Stokes' Theorem in Physics: Maxwell's Equations
docs.text:
Maxwell's equations in integral form use Stokes' theorem directly.

Faraday's Law:

\[\oint_C \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = -\frac{d}{dt} \iint_S \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{S}\]

The left side is the EMF around a closed loop. The right side involves the flux of the magnetic field. The differential form \(\nabla \times \mathbf{E} = -\partial \mathbf{B}/\partial t\) is exactly Stokes applied locally.

Ampere's Law:

\[\oint_C \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \mu_0 \iint_S \mathbf{J} \cdot d\mathbf{S}\]

Without Stokes' theorem, these laws would be harder to state, let alone manipulate.

docs.title: § 7 — Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: This is where a lot of courses stop. We will not.

docs.title: 7.1 Geometry of Loss Landscapes
docs.text:
In deep learning, we optimize a loss function \(\mathcal{L}: \mathbb{R}^n o \mathbb{R}\) over parameter space (the weights \( heta\)). Stokes' theorem underpins several key ideas here:

Gradient flow as a vector field. The gradient \( abla_ heta \mathcal{L}\) is a vector field on parameter space. When we ask "does the optimizer get trapped in a loop?" — that is, can the gradient field have circulation? — the answer is: a pure gradient field is conservative, so \( abla imes ( abla \mathcal{L}) = 0\). This means gradient descent on a smooth loss cannot cycle: any closed path has zero net "work" done by the gradient.

But stochastic and adaptive optimizers (Adam, RMSProp) modify the effective gradient field, potentially introducing non-conservative components. The study of when these methods cycle or converge is partly a question about the curl of the effective update field.

docs.title: 7.2 Differential Geometry and Neural Manifolds
docs.text:
Modern deep learning theory models the data manifold — the submanifold of \(\mathbb{R}^d\) that the data lies on. When analyzing how neural networks learn or generalize, one asks:

  • What is the curvature of the data manifold?
  • How does a network's representation of the data change across layers?

Stokes' theorem (in its full generality on manifolds) is used in:

  • Topological Data Analysis (TDA): Persistent homology, which characterizes the topology of data (loops, voids, connected components), is built on the machinery of differential forms and their boundaries — the same framework as the generalized Stokes theorem.
  • Information geometry: The Fisher information metric makes parameter space into a Riemannian manifold. Curvature quantities (like the Riemann tensor) arise from the same algebraic structure as curl and circulation.

docs.title: 7.3 Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs)
docs.text:
PINNs train neural networks to satisfy PDEs (like Maxwell's equations or Navier–Stokes). Many of the PDEs they enforce are divergence/curl conditions:

\[\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0, \quad \nabla \times \mathbf{E} = -\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t}\]

Stokes' theorem is used to convert between the PDE (differential form) and its integral form when setting up training losses or evaluating conservation properties. A PINN that does not respect the Stokes structure will fail to conserve physical invariants.

docs.title: 7.4 Normalizing Flows and Generative Models
docs.text:
Normalizing flows are generative models that learn a diffeomorphism (a smooth, invertible map) \(f: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d\) transforming a simple distribution into a complex one. The change-of-variables formula involves the Jacobian determinant \(|\det Df|\).

Computing this determinant is expensive. One approach uses the instantaneous change of variables (continuous normalizing flows), where \(f\) is the flow of a vector field \(\mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}, t)\). The trace of the Jacobian \(\text{tr}(D\mathbf{v})\) is the divergence \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}\). Stokes / Divergence theorem guarantees that the integral of this divergence over a region equals the flux through the boundary — a key identity for deriving the log-likelihood update rule.

docs.title: 7.5 Equivariant Neural Networks and Symmetry
docs.text: Modern architectures (e.g., for molecular property prediction, physics simulation) enforce equivariance to rotation and reflection. The mathematical framework — group representations, differential forms on Lie groups — is the same framework that Stokes' theorem lives in. The general Stokes theorem on Lie groups is used to derive conservation laws that equivariant networks must respect by construction.

docs.title: § 8 — Common Mistakes and Pitfalls
docs.text: Mistake Why it's wrong Fix Ignoring orientation of \(C\) Stokes' theorem requires a specific orientation of \(C\) relative to \(\mathbf{n}\); reversing \(C\) negates the answer Apply the right-hand rule explicitly Using the wrong surface Any surface with \(\partial S = C\) works — but pick the simplest one Choose a flat disk or obvious surface Forgetting that \(\mathbf{F}\) must be \(C^1\) on an open set containing \(S\) If \(\mathbf{F}\) has a singularity inside \(S\), the theorem fails Check the domain of \(\mathbf{F}\) first Confusing Stokes with the Divergence theorem Stokes: curl integrated over a surface. Divergence: divergence over a volume Remember: Stokes = boundary is a curve, Divergence = boundary is a surface

docs.title: § 9 — Summary Card
docs.text:
\[\boxed{\oint_{\partial S} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} = \iint_S (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) \cdot d\mathbf{S}}\] Object What it is \(S\) Oriented, piecewise-smooth surface \(\partial S = C\) Boundary curve, positively oriented via right-hand rule \(\mathbf{F}\) \(C^1\) vector field on open set \(\supseteq S\) \(\nabla \times \mathbf{F}\) Curl: measures local rotation of \(\mathbf{F}\) \(d\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{n},dS\) Oriented surface area element

The theorem says: Global circulation around the boundary = Total local spin over the interior.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. James Stewart — Calculus: Early Transcendentals, §16.8 (Stokes' Theorem). The standard worked examples and computational techniques follow Stewart's treatment closely.

  2. MIT 18.02 Multivariable Calculus — Lecture notes and problem sets on vector calculus, surface integrals, and Stokes' theorem. The proof strategy via Green's theorem on the projected region follows the 18.02 approach.

  3. Spivak, M. — Calculus on Manifolds — For the generalized Stokes theorem in the language of differential forms (the \(\int_{\partial \Omega} \omega = \int_\Omega d\omega\) framework sketched in §0).

  4. Bronstein et al. — Geometric Deep Learning: Grids, Groups, Graphs, Geodesics, and Gauges (2021) — For the connection between differential geometry, Stokes' theorem, and equivariant neural networks.

docs.title: Divergence Theorem
docs.text: "The boundary knows everything about the interior — if you know how to listen."

docs.title: § 0 — The Philosophical Setup
docs.text:
We have now seen the pattern twice:

Theorem Integrates over Boundary is Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Interval \([a,b]\) Two points \({a, b}\) Green's Theorem Region \(D \subset \mathbb{R}^2\) Closed curve \(\partial D\) Stokes' Theorem Surface \(S \subset \mathbb{R}^3\) Closed curve \(\partial S\) Divergence Theorem Volume \(E \subset \mathbb{R}^3\) Closed surface \(\partial E\)

Each theorem moves one dimension up. Each says the same thing in a new costume: a derivative integrated over a region equals the original quantity on the boundary.

The Divergence theorem closes the trilogy in \(\mathbb{R}^3\). It relates the flux of a vector field through a closed surface to the divergence of that field inside the enclosed volume. It is the theorem behind fluid mechanics, electrostatics, heat flow, and a surprising amount of modern machine learning.

docs.title: § 1 — Divergence: What It Measures
docs.text: Before the theorem, we need to internalize what divergence actually is.

docs.title: 1.1 Definition
docs.text:
For \(\mathbf{F} = \langle P, Q, R \rangle\) with continuous partial derivatives:

\[\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = \frac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial R}{\partial z}\]

docs.title: 1.2 Physical Meaning
docs.text:
Place an infinitesimal volume element \(\delta V\) at a point \(\mathbf{p}\). The divergence \((\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F})(\mathbf{p})\) is the net rate of flux leaving that volume per unit volume:

\[(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F})(\mathbf{p}) = \lim_{\delta V \to 0} \frac{1}{|\delta V|} \oiint_{\partial(\delta V)} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}\]
  • \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} > 0\) at \(\mathbf{p}\): \(\mathbf{p}\) is a source — field lines emanate outward.
  • \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} < 0\) at \(\mathbf{p}\): \(\mathbf{p}\) is a sink — field lines flow inward.
  • \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = 0\) at \(\mathbf{p}\): incompressible at \(\mathbf{p}\) — no net creation or destruction.

Visualization:

  Source (div > 0)       Sink (div < 0)      Incompressible (div = 0)

   ↖  ↑  ↗               ↘  ↓  ↙               →  →  →
   ←  ·  →               →  ·  ←               →  →  →
   ↙  ↓  ↘               ↗  ↑  ↖               →  →  →

  (outward flow)         (inward flow)         (no net flux)

docs.title: 2.1 Setup
docs.text: Let \(E\) be a simple solid region in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) — meaning it is bounded, and its boundary \(\partial E = S\) is a piecewise-smooth closed surface. We orient \(S\) with the outward unit normal \(\mathbf{n}\) (pointing away from \(E\)).

docs.title: 2.2 Statement
docs.text:
Theorem (Gauss–Ostrogradsky, commonly "Divergence Theorem"). Let \(E\) be a simple solid region with outward-oriented boundary surface \(S = \partial E\). Let \(\mathbf{F} = \langle P, Q, R \rangle\) be a vector field with continuous partial derivatives on an open set containing \(E\). Then:

\[\oiint_S \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iiint_E (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}) , dV\]

Left side: The total flux of \(\mathbf{F}\) outward through the closed surface \(S\).

Right side: The total divergence — the sum of all sources and sinks — inside \(E\).

The \(\oiint\) notation emphasizes that \(S\) is a closed surface (no boundary of its own).

docs.title: 2.3 The Intuition in One Sentence
docs.text:
What flows out of the box must have been created inside it.

This is a conservation principle. If more field lines exit than enter, there must be sources inside. If more enter than exit, there are sinks inside. If the field is divergence-free, the flux in equals the flux out — exactly.

docs.title: § 3 — Proof
docs.text:
We prove the theorem for a simple solid region — one that is simultaneously type I, II, and III. The full proof decomposes into three separate equalities:

\[\oiint_S \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \oiint_S P,dydz + Q,dzdx + R,dxdy\]

and we prove each component separately. We demonstrate only the \(R\) component; the others are identical in structure.

Claim: $\(\oiint_S R,dxdy = \iiint_E \frac{\partial R}{\partial z},dV\)$

docs.title: Step 1: Write \(E\) as a Type I Region
docs.text:
\[E = {(x,y,z) : (x,y) \in D,\ \phi_1(x,y) \leq z \leq \phi_2(x,y)}\]

where \(D\) is the projection of \(E\) onto the \(xy\)-plane, and \(\phi_1, \phi_2\) are smooth functions with \(\phi_1 \leq \phi_2\).

docs.title: Step 2: Compute the triple integral
docs.text:
By Fubini:

\[\iiint_E \frac{\partial R}{\partial z},dV = \iint_D \left[\int_{\phi_1(x,y)}^{\phi_2(x,y)} \frac{\partial R}{\partial z},dz\right] dA\]

By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus in \(z\):

\[= \iint_D \left[R(x, y, \phi_2(x,y)) - R(x, y, \phi_1(x,y))\right] dA\]

docs.title: Step 3: Decompose the surface integral
docs.text:
The boundary \(S = \partial E\) consists of three parts:

  • \(S_2\): the top surface \(z = \phi_2(x,y)\), with upward outward normal.
  • \(S_1\): the bottom surface \(z = \phi_1(x,y)\), with downward outward normal.
  • \(S_3\): the lateral surface (if any), which is vertical: its outward normal is horizontal, so \(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{k} = 0\), contributing nothing to the \(R,dxdy\) component.

Top surface \(S_2\) (outward normal points up, \(dxdy > 0\)):

\[\iint_{S_2} R,dxdy = \iint_D R(x, y, \phi_2(x,y)),dA\]

Bottom surface \(S_1\) (outward normal points down, \(dxdy < 0\)):

\[\iint_{S_1} R,dxdy = -\iint_D R(x, y, \phi_1(x,y)),dA\]

docs.title: Step 4: Combine
docs.text:
\[\oiint_S R,dxdy = \iint_{S_2} + \iint_{S_1} + \underbrace{\iint_{S_3}}_{=0} = \iint_D \left[R(x,y,\phi_2) - R(x,y,\phi_1)\right] dA\]

This equals the triple integral from Step 2. The \(P\) and \(Q\) components follow by the same argument treating \(E\) as a type II and type III region. Adding all three:

\[\oiint_S \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iiint_E \left(\frac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial R}{\partial z}\right) dV = \iiint_E (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}),dV \qquad \blacksquare\]

Remark on the general case: For regions that are not simultaneously type I/II/III, we decompose \(E\) into finitely many such sub-regions. Interior boundary surfaces are shared between two adjacent regions with opposite outward normals, so their contributions to the surface integral cancel. Only the true outer boundary \(\partial E\) survives — the same telescoping argument as in Stokes.

docs.title: The "Box" Picture
docs.text:
Imagine a vector field \(\mathbf{F}\) representing fluid velocity. Enclose a region \(E\) in a box. The Divergence theorem says:

\[\text{Net fluid leaving through walls} = \int\int\int \text{(fluid being created inside)}\]

If the fluid is incompressible (\(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = 0\) everywhere in \(E\)), then the net outward flux through any closed surface enclosing a region with no singularities is zero. Every drop that flows out was already there.

docs.title: The Differential Version
docs.text:
The divergence theorem is the integral form of the divergence. The local statement is:

\[(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F})(\mathbf{p}) = \lim_{|E| \to 0,\ \mathbf{p} \in E} \frac{1}{|E|} \oiint_{\partial E} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}\]

This is the definition physicists often use for divergence, and the divergence theorem is what makes it consistent with the coordinate formula \(P_x + Q_y + R_z\).

docs.title: Example 1: Direct Verification
docs.text:
Setup: \(\mathbf{F} = \langle x, y, z \rangle\), \(E\) the unit ball \(x^2 + y^2 + z^2 \leq 1\).

Right side (triple integral):

\[\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3\] \[\iiint_E 3,dV = 3 \cdot \frac{4\pi}{3} = 4\pi\]

Left side (surface integral):

On the unit sphere \(S\), the outward unit normal is \(\mathbf{n} = \langle x, y, z \rangle\) (since \(|\mathbf{r}| = 1\)). So:

\[\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1 \quad \text{on } S\] \[\oiint_S \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \oiint_S 1,dS = \text{Area}(S) = 4\pi \checkmark\]

docs.title: Example 2: Avoiding a Nasty Surface Integral
docs.text:
Problem: Compute \(\oiint_S \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}\) where \(\mathbf{F} = \langle x^3, y^3, z^3 \rangle\) and \(S\) is the surface of the cylinder \(x^2 + y^2 \leq 4\), \(0 \leq z \leq 3\) (top, bottom, and lateral surface).

Why use the Divergence Theorem: Direct computation requires three separate surface integrals (top disk, bottom disk, curved lateral wall). The theorem replaces all three with one triple integral.

\[\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = 3x^2 + 3y^2 + 3z^2\]

In cylindrical coordinates \((r, \theta, z)\) with \(r \in [0,2]\), \(\theta \in [0, 2\pi]\), \(z \in [0,3]\):

\[\iiint_E (3x^2 + 3y^2 + 3z^2),dV = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2\int_0^3 3(r^2 + z^2),r,dz,dr,d\theta\] \[= 2\pi \int_0^2\int_0^3 3r(r^2 + z^2),dz,dr = 2\pi \int_0^2 \left[3r^3 z + r z^3\right]_0^3 dr\] \[= 2\pi \int_0^2 (9r^3 + 27r),dr = 2\pi \left[\frac{9r^4}{4} + \frac{27r^2}{2}\right]_0^2\] \[= 2\pi \left(36 + 54\right) = 180\pi\]

docs.title: Example 3: The Divergence Theorem with a Hole
docs.text:
Setup: Let \(\mathbf{F} = rac{\mathbf{r}}{|\mathbf{r}|^3} = rac{\langle x,y,z angle}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}}\). This is the electric field of a point charge at the origin.

Compute: \( abla \cdot \mathbf{F} = 0\) for all \((x,y,z) eq (0,0,0)\). But \(\mathbf{F}\) has a singularity at the origin — so the theorem does not apply directly to any region containing the origin.

Fix: Let \(E\) be the region between a small sphere \(S_\varepsilon\) of radius \(\varepsilon\) and a large sphere \(S_R\) of radius \(R\), both centered at the origin. The boundary of \(E\) is \(S_R\) (outward normal pointing out) and \(S_\varepsilon\) (outward normal pointing inward, i.e., toward origin).

Since \( abla \cdot \mathbf{F} = 0\) on \(E\):

\[0 = \iiint_E abla \cdot \mathbf{F},dV = \oiint_{S_R} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} - \oiint_{S_\varepsilon} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}\]

On \(S_\varepsilon\): \(\mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} = rac{1}{\varepsilon^2}\) and \( ext{Area}(S_\varepsilon) = 4\pi\varepsilon^2\), so:

\[\oiint_{S_\varepsilon} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = rac{1}{\varepsilon^2} \cdot 4\pi\varepsilon^2 = 4\pi\]

Therefore \(\oiint_{S_R} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = 4\pi\) for any \(R > 0\).

This is Gauss's Law in electrostatics. The total electric flux through any closed surface surrounding a point charge \(q\) is \(q/\varepsilon_0\) — independent of the surface's shape or size.

The singularity is captured by the Dirac delta distribution: \( abla \cdot \mathbf{F} = 4\pi \delta^{(3)}(\mathbf{r})\), which integrates to \(4\pi\) over any region containing the origin. This is the distributional version of the divergence theorem — the full story lives in functional analysis.

docs.title: Example 4: Computing Volume from a Surface Integral
docs.text:
An elegant corollary: since \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{r} = 3\) for \(\mathbf{r} = \langle x, y, z \rangle\):

\[\text{Vol}(E) = \frac{1}{3} \oiint_{\partial E} \mathbf{r} \cdot d\mathbf{S}\]

This lets us compute volumes purely from boundary data — useful in computer graphics and numerical simulation.

Similarly, with \(\mathbf{F} = \langle x, 0, 0 \rangle\): \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = 1\), so \(\text{Vol}(E) = \oiint_S x,dydz\). Different choices of \(\mathbf{F}\) give different but equivalent formulas.

docs.title: 6.1 Green's First and Second Identities
docs.text:
These are major consequences of the Divergence theorem, used throughout PDEs.

Green's First Identity: Take \(\mathbf{F} = f abla g\), so \( abla \cdot \mathbf{F} = abla f \cdot abla g + f abla^2 g\). Then:

\[\oiint_S f ( abla g \cdot \mathbf{n}),dS = \iiint_E ( abla f \cdot abla g + f abla^2 g),dV\]

Green's Second Identity: Subtract the same with \(f\) and \(g\) swapped:

\[\oiint_S (f abla g - g abla f) \cdot \mathbf{n},dS = \iiint_E (f abla^2 g - g abla^2 f),dV\]

These identities are foundational in the study of harmonic functions and are the integral backbone of the theory of elliptic PDEs — which includes the Laplace and Poisson equations everywhere in physics.

docs.title: 6.2 Integration by Parts in Higher Dimensions
docs.text:
Green's First Identity is the \(\mathbb{R}^3\) analogue of integration by parts. The surface integral term is the "boundary term." When \(f = 0\) on \(\partial E\) (Dirichlet boundary condition), the boundary term vanishes and we get:

\[\iiint_E f abla^2 g,dV = -\iiint_E abla f \cdot abla g,dV\]

This is used constantly in the weak formulation of PDEs — the foundation of the Finite Element Method.

docs.title: 6.3 Incompressible Flow
docs.text:
In fluid mechanics, a velocity field \(\mathbf{u}\) is incompressible (divergence-free) if \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0\). The Divergence theorem then says: for any control volume \(E\):

\[\oiint_{\partial E} \mathbf{u} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = 0\]

What flows in equals what flows out. Water, for practical purposes, is incompressible. So is the magnetic field (\(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0\) — one of Maxwell's equations). This is the fourth Maxwell equation in integral form:

\[\oiint_S \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = 0\]

There are no magnetic monopoles — no sources or sinks of magnetic field.

docs.title: § 7 — Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
7.1 Continuous Normalizing Flows and the Divergence
docs.text:
Normalizing flows learn a diffeomorphism \(\mathbf{x}(t)\) satisfying an ODE \(\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}, t)\), where \(\mathbf{v}\) is a neural network. The log-density evolves as:

\[ rac{d \log p(\mathbf{x}(t))}{dt} = - abla \cdot \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}(t), t)\]

The divergence of the neural velocity field is the core quantity. Computing \( abla \cdot \mathbf{v}\) exactly requires computing the full Jacobian (\(O(d^2)\) operations for dimension \(d\)) — expensive in high dimensions. This is why Hutchinson's trace estimator is used:

\[ abla \cdot \mathbf{v} = ext{tr}(J_{\mathbf{v}}) \approx \mathbb{E}_{ oldsymbol{\epsilon}}[ oldsymbol{\epsilon}^T J_{\mathbf{v}} oldsymbol{\epsilon}]\]

The divergence theorem guarantees the geometric meaning of this quantity: it is the infinitesimal flux per unit volume that determines how the probability density transforms. Getting this wrong — e.g., using a field with spurious divergence — will produce an incorrect generative model.

docs.title: 7.2 Score-Based Generative Models (Diffusion)
docs.text:
Score-based generative models (the backbone of modern image generation: Stable Diffusion, DALL-E, etc.) learn the score function \( abla_{\mathbf{x}} \log p(\mathbf{x})\) — the gradient of the log-density.

The score matching objective can be derived using integration by parts (i.e., Green's First Identity / Divergence theorem):

\[\mathbb{E}\left[|\mathbf{s}_ heta(\mathbf{x}) - abla_\mathbf{x} \log p(\mathbf{x})|^2 ight] = \mathbb{E}\left[|\mathbf{s}_ heta(\mathbf{x})|^2 + 2 abla \cdot \mathbf{s}_ heta(\mathbf{x}) ight] + ext{const}\]

The \(2 abla \cdot \mathbf{s}_ heta\) term comes directly from integration by parts, where the boundary term vanishes because \(p(\mathbf{x}) o 0\) at infinity. Without the Divergence theorem / Green's identity, this simplification — which makes score matching tractable — does not go through.

docs.title: 7.3 Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Enforcing Conservation Laws
docs.text:
PINNs embed physical constraints directly into the training loss. Conservation laws — mass, momentum, energy — are fundamentally divergence conditions:

  • Mass conservation: \( rac{\partial ho}{\partial t} + abla \cdot ( ho \mathbf{u}) = 0\)
  • Momentum conservation (Navier–Stokes): \( rac{\partial( ho\mathbf{u})}{\partial t} + abla \cdot ( ho \mathbf{u} \otimes \mathbf{u}) = - abla p + \mu abla^2 \mathbf{u}\)

The Divergence theorem converts these differential conservation laws to integral balance laws over control volumes. When training PINNs, enforcing the divergence condition on the velocity field (incompressibility) is one of the hardest constraints to satisfy — getting it wrong produces a field that "creates" or "destroys" fluid at random points, giving nonphysical results.

docs.title: 7.4 Graph Neural Networks and Discrete Divergence
docs.text:
The Divergence theorem has a discrete analogue on graphs. If \(G = (V, E)\) is a graph and \(f: E \to \mathbb{R}\) is an edge flow, the discrete divergence at a node \(v\) is:

\[(\text{div}, f)(v) = \sum_{e \ni v} \pm f(e)\]

summing over edges incident to \(v\) with sign depending on orientation. The discrete Divergence theorem says:

\[\sum_{v \in V} (\text{div}, f)(v) = \sum_{e \in \partial E_{\text{bdry}}} f(e)\]

Graph Neural Networks that enforce flow conservation (e.g., for traffic prediction, molecular dynamics, power grids) use exactly this structure. The design of "divergence-free" message passing — where no "information" is created or destroyed at nodes — mirrors the continuous incompressibility condition.

docs.title: 7.5 Variational Inference and the ELBO
docs.text:
The Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) in variational autoencoders involves:

\[\text{KL}[q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x}) | p(\mathbf{z})] = \int q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x}) \log \frac{q(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})}{p(\mathbf{z})},d\mathbf{z}\]

When \(q\) is parameterized as a flow (change of variables through a diffeomorphism), the Jacobian determinant appears, and computing it uses the divergence of the flow field. The Divergence theorem provides the geometric grounding: the change of density under a flow is governed by how much the flow "compresses" or "expands" volume elements locally, measured by the divergence.

docs.title: § 8 — Stokes vs. Divergence: The Complete Picture
docs.text:
This is the question that trips everyone up. Here is the definitive comparison:

Stokes' Theorem Divergence Theorem Integrates Curl over a surface Divergence over a volume Boundary is A closed curve A closed surface Orientation Right-hand rule (curve relative to surface normal) Outward normal on the surface Dimension \(\partial S\) is 1D, \(S\) is 2D \(\partial E\) is 2D, \(E\) is 3D Measures Circulation Net flux Key identity \( abla imes \mathbf{F}\) integrated over \(S\) \( abla \cdot \mathbf{F}\) integrated over \(E\) Green's theorem Special case (flat surface) Special case (2D, via \( abla \cdot\))

They are siblings in the generalized Stokes theorem \(\int_{\partial \Omega} \omega = \int_\Omega d\omega\):

  • Stokes: \(\omega\) is a 1-form, \(d\omega\) is a 2-form (the curl).
  • Divergence: \(\omega\) is a 2-form, \(d\omega\) is a 3-form (the divergence).

The unified framework: In the language of differential forms on an \(n\)-manifold:

\[\int_{\partial \Omega} \omega = \int_\Omega d\omega\]

Everything — FTC, Green, Stokes, Divergence — is this one equation.

docs.title: § 9 — Common Mistakes and Pitfalls
docs.text: Mistake Why it's wrong Fix Using inward normal instead of outward Flips the sign of the entire surface integral Outward normal is the convention — verify with a simple example Applying the theorem when \(\mathbf{F}\) has a singularity inside \(E\) The theorem requires \(\mathbf{F} \in C^1\) on an open set containing the closed region \(\overline{E}\) Remove the singularity with a small sphere; use the result from Example 3 Forgetting to include all pieces of \(\partial E\) A closed surface must enclose the region completely Check: top, bottom, lateral walls, or any missing caps Confusing \(\oiint\) (closed surface) with \(\iint\) (open surface) Stokes allows open surfaces; Divergence requires a closed one Divergence theorem always has the \(\oiint\) notation Computing \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}\) incorrectly Especially with products and compositions Write each component derivative carefully; check with simple test case

docs.title: § 10 — Summary Card
docs.text:
\[ oxed{\oiint_{\partial E} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \iiint_E ( abla \cdot \mathbf{F}),dV}\] Object What it is \(E\) Simple solid region, bounded, piecewise smooth boundary \(\partial E = S\) Closed surface, oriented with outward normal \(\mathbf{F}\) \(C^1\) vector field on open set \(\supseteq \overline{E}\) \( abla \cdot \mathbf{F}\) Divergence: local source/sink density \(\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}\) Outward flux through the surface

The theorem says: Total outward flux through the boundary = Total divergence (source strength) inside.

Special cases:

  • \( abla \cdot \mathbf{F} = 0\) everywhere in \(E\) \(\Rightarrow\) zero net flux through any enclosing surface.
  • \( abla \cdot \mathbf{r} = 3\) \(\Rightarrow\) \( ext{Vol}(E) = rac{1}{3}\oiint_{\partial E} \mathbf{r} \cdot d\mathbf{S}\).

docs.title: § 11 — The Three Theorems Together
docs.text:
\[\underbrace{\int_a^b f'(x),dx = f(b) - f(a)}_{\text{FTC}} \quad \longrightarrow \quad \underbrace{\iint_S (\nabla \times \mathbf{F}) \cdot d\mathbf{S} = \oint_{\partial S} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}}_{\text{Stokes}} \quad \longrightarrow \quad \underbrace{\iiint_E (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}),dV = \oiint_{\partial E} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{S}}_{\text{Divergence}}\]

Each one says: integrate a derivative over a region, get the original on the boundary. The deepest version of this statement — valid for differential forms on smooth manifolds of any dimension — is the Generalized Stokes Theorem. Everything in vector calculus is a shadow of that one truth.

docs.text:

docs.title: Second Order Linear DEs
docs.text: "The whole of mechanics — classical, quantum, and relativistic — is secretly a second order linear ODE wearing different clothes."

docs.title: § 0 — Why Second Order?
docs.text:
First order ODEs describe rates. Second order ODEs describe how rates change — and that is where physics lives.

Newton's second law: \(F = ma = m\ddot{x}\). Acceleration is a second derivative. The moment you write a physical law involving force, you get a second order ODE. The same is true for:

  • A mass on a spring: \(m\ddot{x} + c\dot{x} + kx = F(t)\)
  • An RLC electrical circuit: \(L\ddot{q} + R\dot{q} + \frac{1}{C}q = \mathcal{E}(t)\)
  • Heat conduction, wave propagation, quantum mechanics (\(\hat{H}\psi = E\psi\))
  • Beam deflection in structural engineering

The general theory of second order linear ODEs is not just a collection of techniques. It is a complete, elegant algebraic structure — and understanding it deeply unlocks everything above.

docs.title: 1.1 Standard Form
docs.text:
A second order linear ODE has the form:

\[P(x)y'' + Q(x)y' + R(x)y = G(x)\]

Dividing through by \(P(x)\) (assuming \(P(x) \neq 0\)), we get the standard form:

\[y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = g(x)\]

where \(p, q, g\) are continuous functions on some interval \(I\).

  • If \(g(x) = 0\): the equation is homogeneous.
  • If \(g(x) \neq 0\): the equation is nonhomogeneous.

Critical remark: The word "linear" refers to linearity in \(y\) and its derivatives — not in \(x\). The coefficients \(p(x), q(x)\) can be any functions of \(x\). The equation is linear because \(y\) appears only to the first power, with no products like \(yy'\).

docs.title: 1.2 The Operator Language
docs.text:
Define the linear differential operator:

\[L[y] = y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y\]

The equation becomes \(L[y] = g(x)\). The key property:

\[L[\alpha y_1 + \beta y_2] = \alpha L[y_1] + \beta L[y_2]\]

for any constants \(\alpha, \beta\). Linearity of \(L\) is the engine of the entire theory. Everything that follows — superposition, the structure of solution sets, variation of parameters — flows from this one property.

docs.title: § 2 — The Homogeneous Equation: Structure of Solutions
2.1 The Superposition Principle
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(y_1\) and \(y_2\) are both solutions of \(L[y] = 0\) on an interval \(I\), then so is any linear combination \(y = c_1 y_1 + c_2 y_2\) for constants \(c_1, c_2 \in \mathbb{R}\).

Proof. Direct computation:

\[L[c_1 y_1 + c_2 y_2] = c_1 L[y_1] + c_2 L[y_2] = c_1 \cdot 0 + c_2 \cdot 0 = 0 \qquad \blacksquare\]

The set of all solutions to \(L[y] = 0\) forms a vector space — specifically, a subspace of \(C^2(I)\).

docs.title: 2.2 The Wronskian
docs.text:
Given two solutions \(y_1, y_2\) of \(L[y] = 0\), the Wronskian is:

\[W(y_1, y_2)(x) = \begin{vmatrix} y_1 & y_2 \ y_1' & y_2' \end{vmatrix} = y_1 y_2' - y_1' y_2\]

Theorem (Abel). If \(y_1, y_2\) solve \(y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = 0\), then:

\[W(y_1, y_2)(x) = W(y_1, y_2)(x_0) \cdot e^{-\int_{x_0}^x p(t),dt}\]

Proof. Differentiate \(W\):

\[W' = y_1 y_2'' - y_1'' y_2\]

Since \(y_1'' = -p y_1' - q y_1\) and \(y_2'' = -p y_2' - q y_2\):

\[W' = y_1(-p y_2' - q y_2) - (-p y_1' - q y_1)y_2 = -p(y_1 y_2' - y_1' y_2) = -pW\]

So \(W' + p(x) W = 0\), a first order linear ODE. Solving: \(W(x) = Ce^{-\int p,dx}\). \(\blacksquare\)

Corollary (Abel): Either \(W(x) \neq 0\) for all \(x \in I\), or \(W(x) = 0\) for all \(x \in I\). There is no middle ground.

docs.title: 2.3 Fundamental Sets of Solutions
docs.text:
Definition. Two solutions \(y_1, y_2\) of \(L[y] = 0\) form a fundamental set of solutions if \(W(y_1, y_2)(x) eq 0\) on \(I\) — i.e., they are linearly independent.

Theorem (Existence of a Fundamental Set). If \(p, q\) are continuous on \(I\), then there exists a fundamental set of solutions \({y_1, y_2}\) for \(L[y] = 0\) on \(I\).

Theorem (General Solution). If \({y_1, y_2}\) is a fundamental set, then every solution of \(L[y] = 0\) can be written as:

\[y = c_1 y_1 + c_2 y_2\]

Proof sketch. Given any solution \(y\), pick \(x_0 \in I\) and consider the initial conditions \(y(x_0) = \alpha\), \(y'(x_0) = eta\). Since \(W(x_0) eq 0\), the linear system:

\[c_1 y_1(x_0) + c_2 y_2(x_0) = \alpha, \quad c_1 y_1'(x_0) + c_2 y_2'(x_0) = eta\]

has a unique solution \((c_1, c_2)\) (its determinant is \(W(x_0) eq 0\)). By the uniqueness theorem for ODEs, \(y \equiv c_1 y_1 + c_2 y_2\). \( lacksquare\)

The solution space of \(L[y] = 0\) is a 2-dimensional vector space over \(\mathbb{R}\). A fundamental set is a basis for this space.

This is the central structural fact. Everything else is about finding a good basis.

docs.title: 3.1 The Characteristic Equation
docs.text:
Consider:

\[ay'' + by' + cy = 0, \quad a, b, c \in \mathbb{R},\ a \neq 0\]

Guess: \(y = e^{rx}\) for some \(r\) to be determined. Then \(y' = re^{rx}\), \(y'' = r^2 e^{rx}\). Substituting:

\[e^{rx}(ar^2 + br + c) = 0\]

Since \(e^{rx} \neq 0\), we need:

\[\boxed{ar^2 + br + c = 0}\]

This is the characteristic equation. Its roots determine everything.

docs.title: 3.2 Case I: Two Distinct Real Roots (\(b^2 - 4ac > 0\))
docs.text:
Roots \(r_1 \neq r_2 \in \mathbb{R}\). Two solutions:

\[y_1 = e^{r_1 x}, \quad y_2 = e^{r_2 x}\]

Wronskian: \(W = (r_2 - r_1)e^{(r_1 + r_2)x} \neq 0\). Linearly independent. General solution:

\[y = c_1 e^{r_1 x} + c_2 e^{r_2 x}\]

Example: \(y'' - 5y' + 6y = 0\).

Characteristic equation: \(r^2 - 5r + 6 = (r-2)(r-3) = 0\), so \(r_1 = 2\), \(r_2 = 3\).

\[y = c_1 e^{2x} + c_2 e^{3x}\]

docs.title: 3.3 Case II: Repeated Real Root (\(b^2 - 4ac = 0\))
docs.text:
One root \(r_1 = r_2 = r = -b/(2a)\). We only get one solution \(y_1 = e^{rx}\) from the characteristic equation. We need a second, linearly independent solution.

Reduction of order: Assume \(y_2 = v(x) e^{rx}\). Substituting into \(ay'' + by' + cy = 0\) and using \(ar^2 + br + c = 0\) and \(2ar + b = 0\) (since \(r\) is a double root):

\[ae^{rx}(v'' + 2rv' + r^2 v) + be^{rx}(v' + rv) + ce^{rx}v = 0$$ $$e^{rx}\left[av'' + (2ar + b)v' + (ar^2 + br + c)v\right] = 0$$ $$e^{rx}\left[av'' + 0 \cdot v' + 0\right] = 0 \implies v'' = 0\]

So \(v(x) = c_1 + c_2 x\). Taking \(v = x\) gives the second solution:

\[y_2 = xe^{rx}\]

General solution:

\[y = (c_1 + c_2 x)e^{rx}\]

Example: \(y'' - 4y' + 4y = 0\).

\(r^2 - 4r + 4 = (r-2)^2 = 0\), so \(r = 2\).

\[y = (c_1 + c_2 x)e^{2x}\]

Why does \(xe^{rx}\) appear? This is the ODE analogue of a Jordan block in linear algebra. When an eigenvalue is repeated, the eigenspace is deficient; the generalized eigenvector contributes the factor of \(x\). The analogy is precise — the theory of constant-coefficient ODEs is linear algebra on the space of exponentials.

docs.title: 3.4 Case III: Complex Conjugate Roots (\(b^2 - 4ac < 0\))
docs.text:
Roots \(r_{1,2} = \alpha \pm i\beta\) where \(\alpha = -b/(2a)\), \(\beta = \sqrt{4ac - b^2}/(2a) > 0\).

Complex solutions: \(e^{(\alpha + i\beta)x}\) and \(e^{(\alpha - i\beta)x}\). By Euler's formula:

\[e^{(\alpha \pm i\beta)x} = e^{\alpha x}(\cos\beta x \pm i \sin\beta x)\]

Taking real and imaginary parts (both are real solutions by linearity):

\[y_1 = e^{\alpha x}\cos\beta x, \quad y_2 = e^{\alpha x}\sin\beta x\]

Wronskian: \(W = \beta e^{2\alpha x} \neq 0\). General solution:

\[y = e^{\alpha x}(c_1 \cos\beta x + c_2 \sin\beta x)\]

Example: \(y'' + 2y' + 5y = 0\).

\(r^2 + 2r + 5 = 0 \Rightarrow r = \frac{-2 \pm \sqrt{4 - 20}}{2} = -1 \pm 2i\).

So \(\alpha = -1\), \(\beta = 2\):

\[y = e^{-x}(c_1 \cos 2x + c_2 \sin 2x)\]

This is a damped oscillation: amplitude decays like \(e^{-x}\), oscillation frequency \(2\).

docs.title: 3.5 Summary: The Three Cases
docs.text:
Discriminant Δ = b² - 4ac

        Δ > 0                 Δ = 0                 Δ < 0
    (two real roots)      (repeated root)       (complex roots)
          |                      |                      |
  y = c₁eʳ¹ˣ + c₂eʳ²ˣ   y = (c₁+c₂x)eʳˣ    y = eᵅˣ(c₁cosβx + c₂sinβx)
          |                      |                      |
   exponential growth     polynomial × exp      damped oscillation

docs.title: 4.1 The Structure Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem. The general solution of \(L[y] = g(x)\) is:

\[y = y_p + y_h = y_p + c_1 y_1 + c_2 y_2\]

where \(y_p\) is any particular solution of \(L[y] = g\), and \(c_1 y_1 + c_2 y_2\) is the general solution of the homogeneous equation \(L[y] = 0\).

Proof. If \(y_p\) and \(y\) both solve \(L[y] = g\), then \(L[y - y_p] = L[y] - L[y_p] = g - g = 0\). So \(y - y_p\) solves the homogeneous equation, hence \(y - y_p = c_1 y_1 + c_2 y_2\). \(\blacksquare\)

The problem reduces to: (1) find a fundamental set for the homogeneous part, (2) find any one particular solution.

docs.title: 4.2 Method of Undetermined Coefficients
docs.text:
Valid when the equation has constant coefficients and \(g(x)\) is a simple function: polynomials, exponentials, sines, cosines, or products thereof.

The rule: Guess \(y_p\) in the same "family" as \(g(x)\).

\(g(x)\) Trial \(y_p\) \(P_n(x)\) (degree \(n\) polynomial) \(x^s(A_n x^n + \cdots + A_1 x + A_0)\) \(e^{\alpha x}\) \(x^s A e^{\alpha x}\) \(e^{\alpha x}\cos\beta x\) or \(e^{\alpha x}\sin\beta x\) \(x^s e^{\alpha x}(A\cos\beta x + B\sin\beta x)\) Sum of above Sum of corresponding trials

where \(s = 0\) if the trial function is not a solution of the homogeneous equation, \(s = 1\) if it is (simple resonance), \(s = 2\) if it is a double solution (double resonance).

Example 1 (no resonance): \(y'' - 3y' - 4y = 3e^{2x}\).

Characteristic roots: \(r^2 - 3r - 4 = (r-4)(r+1) = 0\), so \(r = 4, -1\).

\(e^{2x}\) is not a solution of the homogeneous (since \(2 \neq 4, -1\)). Try \(y_p = Ae^{2x}\):

\[4Ae^{2x} - 6Ae^{2x} - 4Ae^{2x} = 3e^{2x} \implies -6A = 3 \implies A = -\frac{1}{2}\] \[y = c_1 e^{4x} + c_2 e^{-x} - \frac{1}{2}e^{2x}\]

Example 2 (resonance): \(y'' - 4y = e^{2x}\).

Characteristic roots: \(r = \pm 2\). Since \(e^{2x}\) is a homogeneous solution (\(r = 2\)), multiply by \(x\). Try \(y_p = Axe^{2x}\):

\[y_p' = A(1 + 2x)e^{2x}, \quad y_p'' = A(4 + 4x)e^{2x}\] \[A(4 + 4x)e^{2x} - 4Axe^{2x} = 4Ae^{2x} = e^{2x} \implies A = \frac{1}{4}\] \[y = c_1 e^{2x} + c_2 e^{-2x} + \frac{x}{4}e^{2x}\]

Resonance — when the forcing term matches a natural frequency of the homogeneous equation — produces the \(xe^{rx}\) factor. In physical systems, this is resonance: forced oscillation at the natural frequency causes growing amplitude. Bridges collapse this way.

docs.title: 4.3 Variation of Parameters
docs.text:
This method works for any \(g(x)\), even when the coefficients are not constant (as long as we have a fundamental set \({y_1, y_2}\)).

Setup: Assume \(y_p = u_1(x) y_1(x) + u_2(x) y_2(x)\) where \(u_1, u_2\) are functions to be determined.

The system (derived by imposing \(u_1'y_1 + u_2'y_2 = 0\) and substituting):

\[\begin{pmatrix} y_1 & y_2 \ y_1' & y_2' \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} u_1' \ u_2' \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \ g(x) \end{pmatrix}\]

By Cramer's rule (denominator is the Wronskian \(W\)):

\[u_1' = -\frac{y_2 g}{W}, \qquad u_2' = \frac{y_1 g}{W}\]

Integrating:

\[u_1 = -\int \frac{y_2(x) g(x)}{W(x)},dx, \qquad u_2 = \int \frac{y_1(x) g(x)}{W(x)},dx\]

The particular solution:

\[\boxed{y_p = -y_1 \int \frac{y_2 g}{W},dx + y_2 \int \frac{y_1 g}{W},dx}\]

Why impose \(u_1'y_1 + u_2'y_2 = 0\)? We have two unknowns \(u_1, u_2\) and one equation (the ODE). This extra condition eliminates \(u_1''\) and \(u_2''\) from the second derivative of \(y_p\), making the algebra tractable.

Example: \(y'' + y = \sec x\), \(x \in (-\pi/2, \pi/2)\).

Homogeneous: \(r^2 + 1 = 0 \Rightarrow r = \pm i\). So \(y_1 = \cos x\), \(y_2 = \sin x\), \(W = 1\).

\[u_1' = -\frac{\sin x \cdot \sec x}{1} = -\tan x \implies u_1 = \ln|\cos x|\] \[u_2' = \frac{\cos x \cdot \sec x}{1} = 1 \implies u_2 = x\] \[y_p = \cos x \cdot \ln|\cos x| + x\sin x\] \[y = c_1 \cos x + c_2 \sin x + \cos x \ln|\cos x| + x\sin x\]

Undetermined coefficients could never handle \(\sec x\). Variation of parameters handles any \(g\).

docs.title: § 5 — Initial Value Problems and Existence/Uniqueness
docs.text:
Theorem (Existence and Uniqueness). Let \(p, q, g\) be continuous on an open interval \(I\) containing \(x_0\). Then the IVP:

\[y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = g(x), \quad y(x_0) = y_0,\ y'(x_0) = y_0'\]

has a unique solution on all of \(I\).

This is profound: continuity of coefficients alone guarantees both existence and uniqueness on the entire interval — no restriction on the size of \(y_0\) or \(y_0'\).

Example: \(y'' + (\tan x) y = 0\), \(y(0) = 1\), \(y'(0) = 0\).

Here \(p(x) = \tan x\) is continuous on \((-\pi/2, \pi/2)\). The theorem guarantees a unique solution on this entire interval, even though we may not be able to write it in closed form.

docs.title: § 6 — The Vibrating Spring: The Physical Archetype
docs.text:
The equation:

\[m\ddot{x} + c\dot{x} + kx = F(t)\]

is a second order linear ODE with constant coefficients. Here:

  • \(m > 0\): mass
  • \(c \geq 0\): damping coefficient
  • \(k > 0\): spring constant
  • \(F(t)\): external forcing

Divide by \(m\): \(\ddot{x} + \frac{c}{m}\dot{x} + \frac{k}{m}x = \frac{F(t)}{m}\).

Let \(\gamma = c/(2m)\) (damping), \(\omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m}\) (natural frequency). Characteristic roots:

\[r = -\gamma \pm \sqrt{\gamma^2 - \omega_0^2}\] Condition Name Behavior \(\gamma = 0\) Undamped Pure oscillation at \(\omega_0\): \(x = c_1\cos\omega_0 t + c_2\sin\omega_0 t\) \(0 < \gamma < \omega_0\) Underdamped Decaying oscillation: \(x = e^{-\gamma t}(c_1\cos\omega_d t + c_2\sin\omega_d t)\), \(\omega_d = \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - \gamma^2}\) \(\gamma = \omega_0\) Critically damped Fastest decay without oscillation: \(x = (c_1 + c_2 t)e^{-\gamma t}\) \(\gamma > \omega_0\) Overdamped Slow exponential decay, no oscillation 
  Amplitude
     |
     |  Underdamped         Critically damped     Overdamped
     |  /\/\/\__            /‾‾‾\_____            /‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾___
     | /        ‾‾‾---___  /            ‾---___  /
     |/                   /                     /
     +---------------------------------> time

Forced oscillation with \(F(t) = F_0 \cos\omega t\):

The particular solution when \(\omega \neq \omega_0\):

\[x_p = \frac{F_0/m}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2}\cos\omega t\]

As \(\omega \to \omega_0\), the amplitude \(\to \infty\). When \(\omega = \omega_0\) exactly (with no damping), the particular solution is:

\[x_p = \frac{F_0}{2m\omega_0} t\sin\omega_0 t\]

The factor of \(t\) causes unbounded growth — this is resonance. The Tacoma Narrows Bridge (1940) collapsed due to aeroelastic flutter near a resonant frequency.

docs.title: § 7 — Euler–Cauchy Equations
docs.text:
A special variable-coefficient equation that reduces to constant coefficients:

\[x^2 y'' + \alpha x y' + eta y = 0, \quad x > 0\]

Key substitution: \(x = e^t\), i.e., \(t = \ln x\). Then \(x rac{d}{dx} = rac{d}{dt}\), and:

\[x^2 y'' = rac{d^2 y}{dt^2} - rac{dy}{dt}\]

The equation becomes: \( rac{d^2y}{dt^2} + (\alpha - 1) rac{dy}{dt} + eta y = 0\) — constant coefficients in \(t\).

Alternatively, try \(y = x^m\) directly. Then \(y' = mx^{m-1}\), \(y'' = m(m-1)x^{m-2}\):

\[x^2 \cdot m(m-1)x^{m-2} + \alpha x \cdot mx^{m-1} + eta x^m = 0$$ $$x^m[m(m-1) + \alpha m + eta] = 0\]

The indicial equation: \(m^2 + (\alpha - 1)m + eta = 0\).

Three cases (mirroring the constant coefficient theory):

  • Two distinct real roots \(m_1 eq m_2\): \(y = c_1 x^{m_1} + c_2 x^{m_2}\)
  • Repeated root \(m_1 = m_2 = m\): \(y = x^m(c_1 + c_2 \ln x)\)
  • Complex roots \(m = \mu \pm i u\): \(y = x^\mu[c_1 \cos( u \ln x) + c_2 \sin( u \ln x)]\)

docs.title: § 8 — Series Solutions (Power Series Method)
docs.text: When coefficients are not constant and the equation is not Euler–Cauchy, we use power series.

docs.title: 8.1 Ordinary Points
docs.text:
\(x_0\) is an ordinary point of \(y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = 0\) if \(p\) and \(q\) are analytic at \(x_0\).

Theorem: Near an ordinary point \(x_0\), the equation has two linearly independent power series solutions:

\[y = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n (x - x_0)^n\]

converging in \(|x - x_0| < R\) where \(R\) is at least the distance from \(x_0\) to the nearest singular point in \(\mathbb{C}\).

Example: \(y'' + xy' + y = 0\) about \(x_0 = 0\).

Assume \(y = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n\). Then:

\[y'' = \sum_{n=2}^\infty n(n-1)a_n x^{n-2} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty (n+2)(n+1)a_{n+2}x^n\] \[xy' = \sum_{n=1}^\infty n a_n x^n = \sum_{n=0}^\infty n a_n x^n\]

Substituting and collecting powers of \(x^n\):

\[(n+2)(n+1)a_{n+2} + (n+1)a_n = 0 \implies a_{n+2} = -\frac{a_n}{n+2}\]

This recurrence relation gives all coefficients in terms of \(a_0\) and \(a_1\) (the two free parameters, corresponding to the two-dimensional solution space):

\[y = a_0\left(1 - \frac{x^2}{2} + \frac{x^4}{8} - \cdots\right) + a_1\left(x - \frac{x^3}{6} + \cdots\right)\]

docs.title: § 9 — Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: The reach of second order linear ODEs into modern AI is deeper than it first appears.

docs.title: 9.1 Neural ODEs and Second Order Dynamics
docs.text:
Neural ODEs (Chen et al., 2018) model continuous-depth networks as ODEs \(\dot{\mathbf{h}} = f_\theta(\mathbf{h}, t)\). First order — but limiting.

Second order Neural ODEs model acceleration, not just velocity:

\[\ddot{\mathbf{h}} + \gamma \dot{\mathbf{h}} + \omega^2 \mathbf{h} = f_\theta(\mathbf{h}, t)\]

This is precisely the damped oscillator equation with a neural forcing term. These models:

  • Better capture oscillatory dynamics in time series (physiological signals, physical simulations).
  • Have symplectic structure when undamped, conserving energy — crucial for Hamiltonian dynamics.
  • Are connected to momentum methods in optimization (see below).

docs.title: 9.2 Momentum-Based Optimizers: The ODE View
docs.text:
Heavy ball method (Polyak, 1964) and Nesterov momentum can be written as:

\[m\ddot{\theta} + c\dot{\theta} = -\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta)\]

This is a damped harmonic oscillator driven by the negative gradient. The gradient is the "force," inertia (\(m\)) resists rapid direction changes, and damping (\(c\)) prevents oscillation.

The continuous-time limit of Adam is more subtle but still maps to a second order system with adaptive damping. The connection is:

ODE Parameter Optimizer Analogue Mass \(m\) Momentum coefficient \(\beta_1\) Damping \(c\) Learning rate schedule, \(\beta_2\) \(-\nabla\mathcal{L}\) Gradient signal Natural frequency \(\omega_0\) Curvature of the loss landscape Resonance Learning rate too large → divergence Critical damping Optimal convergence rate

Critical damping in the ODE corresponds to the optimal momentum coefficient for a quadratic loss — the one that gives fastest convergence without oscillation. Sutskever et al. (2013) derived optimal Nesterov momentum via exactly this analogy.

The characteristic equation of the optimizer's ODE determines whether:

  • \(\Delta > 0\) (overdamped): slow convergence, no oscillation — too much damping.
  • \(\Delta = 0\) (critically damped): optimal convergence.
  • \(\Delta < 0\) (underdamped): oscillation around the minimum — can still converge but oscillates.

docs.title: 9.3 Attention and the Wave Equation
docs.text:
The wave equation \(u_{tt} = c^2 u_{xx}\) is a second order linear PDE. It factors as \((∂_t - c\partial_x)(\partial_t + c\partial_x)u = 0\) — two first order operators.

Transformer attention, when interpreted geometrically, can be seen as learning operators that propagate information along characteristic curves — the solution curves of the wave equation. Formally connecting attention to hyperbolic PDEs is an active research area (e.g., neural wave operators for physical simulation).

docs.title: 9.4 Recurrent Neural Networks: Characteristic Roots and Stability
docs.text:
A linear RNN is \(\mathbf{h}_t = A\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + B\mathbf{x}_t\). For a scalar second order linear recurrence:

\[h_t - b_1 h_{t-1} - b_2 h_{t-2} = x_t\]

This is the discrete analogue of a second order linear ODE. The characteristic equation is \(r^2 - b_1 r - b_2 = 0\), and:

  • If \(|r_i| < 1\) for all roots: stable (exponential decay of homogeneous response).
  • If \(|r_i| > 1\): unstable (exponential blow-up).
  • If \(|r_i| = 1\): marginally stable (oscillation without decay).

Vanishing and exploding gradients in RNNs are directly caused by the characteristic roots of the recurrence being too small or too large. This is why LSTMs and GRUs were designed: they implicitly modulate the characteristic roots to keep them near the unit circle. The HiPPO matrix (Gu et al., 2020) and S4 state space models explicitly parameterize the characteristic polynomial to achieve stable, long-range memory — the Euler–Cauchy equation and Legendre polynomials appear directly in the construction.

docs.title: 9.5 Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Solving Second Order ODEs
docs.text:
PINNs solve ODEs like:

\[y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = g(x), \quad y(x_0) = y_0,\ y'(x_0) = y_0'\]

by training a neural network \(y_\theta(x)\) to minimize:

\[\mathcal{L} = \underbrace{\int_I |y_\theta'' + p y_\theta' + q y_\theta - g|^2,dx}_{\text{PDE residual}} + \underbrace{|y_\theta(x_0) - y_0|^2 + |y_\theta'(x_0) - y_0'|^2}_{\text{IC residual}}\]

The theory guarantees a unique target solution exists (§5). The challenge is that neural networks must match second derivatives accurately — their approximation of \(y''\) is less stable than of \(y\) itself, and this is a core technical difficulty in PINN training.

docs.title: 9.6 Koopman Operator Theory and Linear Embeddings
docs.text:
The Koopman operator linearizes nonlinear dynamics. Given a nonlinear system \(\dot{\mathbf{x}} = f(\mathbf{x})\), Koopman theory lifts the state to a (possibly infinite-dimensional) function space where the dynamics become linear — governed by a linear operator, whose eigenfunctions satisfy second order linear ODEs (or systems thereof).

Deep learning is used to approximate the Koopman eigenfunctions directly. When the Koopman operator has purely imaginary eigenvalues \(\pm i\omega\), the eigenfunctions satisfy \(\phi'' + \omega^2 \phi = 0\) — the simple harmonic oscillator. The eigenvalue spectrum of the Koopman operator determines the intrinsic frequencies of the nonlinear system, discovered via neural network regression.

docs.title: § 10 — Common Mistakes and Pitfalls
docs.text: Mistake Why it's wrong Fix Not converting to standard form before applying theorems The theorems assume \(y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = g\) with leading coefficient 1 Always divide through by \(P(x)\) first Forgetting the \(x^s\) multiplier in undetermined coefficients when resonance occurs The trial function is a homogeneous solution, giving \(0 = g(x)\) upon substitution Check each piece of the trial against homogeneous solutions Claiming \(W \neq 0\) at one point implies independence everywhere True for ODEs (by Abel's theorem), not for arbitrary functions This is a special property of ODE solutions Taking \(c_1, c_2\) as functions in the general solution The general solution formula \(c_1 y_1 + c_2 y_2 + y_p\) has constant \(c_1, c_2\) Only variation of parameters uses functions \(u_1(x), u_2(x)\) Applying undetermined coefficients to variable-coefficient equations The method requires constant coefficients Use variation of parameters or series methods Ignoring the imaginary part in complex roots \(e^{(\alpha + i\beta)x}\) is a complex solution — the real solutions are \(e^{\alpha x}\cos\beta x\) and \(e^{\alpha x}\sin\beta x\) Always take real and imaginary parts separately

docs.title: The Homogeneous Equation \(L[y] = 0\):
docs.text:
• Solution space is a 2-dimensional vector space.
  • A fundamental set \({y_1, y_2}\) is any linearly independent pair of solutions (\(W \neq 0\)).
  • Abel's theorem: \(W(x) = W(x_0)e^{-\int p,dx}\) — either always zero or never zero.
  • General solution: \(y = c_1 y_1 + c_2 y_2\).

docs.title: Constant Coefficients — Characteristic Roots:
docs.text: \[\boxed{ar^2 + br + c = 0}\] \(\Delta = b^2 - 4ac\) Roots General Solution \(> 0\) \(r_1 \neq r_2 \in \mathbb{R}\) \(c_1e^{r_1 x} + c_2 e^{r_2 x}\) \(= 0\) \(r_1 = r_2 = r\) \((c_1 + c_2 x)e^{rx}\) \(< 0\) \(\alpha \pm i\beta\) \(e^{\alpha x}(c_1\cos\beta x + c_2\sin\beta x)\)

docs.title: The Nonhomogeneous Equation \(L[y] = g\):
docs.text:
\[y_{\text{general}} = \underbrace{y_p}_{\text{any particular solution}} + \underbrace{c_1 y_1 + c_2 y_2}_{\text{homogeneous general solution}}\]
  • Undetermined coefficients: constant coefficients, simple \(g(x)\). Fast but limited.
  • Variation of parameters: any \(g(x)\), any (solvable) homogeneous part. Always works.
\[y_p = -y_1 \int \frac{y_2 g}{W},dx + y_2 \int \frac{y_1 g}{W},dx\]

docs.text:

  2. MIT 18.02 / 18.03 — Differential Equations lecture notes. The operator formalism \(L[y]\), Abel's theorem proof, and the physical interpretation of damping follow the MIT 18.03 approach.

  3. Boyce & DiPrima — Elementary Differential Equations and Boundary Value Problems — The rigorous existence/uniqueness theorem and variation of parameters derivation.
