docs.title: IVP and BVP
docs.text: "An ODE without conditions is a family portrait. The conditions pick out one face from the crowd."

docs.title: § 0 — The Central Question
docs.text:
Solving a differential equation gives you a family of solutions — parameterized by arbitrary constants. For a second order ODE, two constants \(c_1, c_2\). The solution space is a plane.

Imposing conditions means picking a specific solution from this family. But conditions come in fundamentally different flavors, and the difference is not merely technical — it reflects a deep physical distinction about what kind of information we have.

docs.title: § 1 — Two Ways to Specify a Solution
1.1 Initial Value Problems (IVP)
docs.text:
An Initial Value Problem specifies the solution and its derivative at a single point \(x_0\):

\[y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = g(x), \qquad y(x_0) = y_0,\quad y'(x_0) = y_0'\]

Both conditions are imposed at the same location \(x_0\) — the "initial" point.

Physical meaning: You know the complete state of the system at time \(t_0\): position and velocity. From this, you predict the future (and past). This is the Cauchy problem — the formulation of classical mechanics.

docs.title: 1.2 Boundary Value Problems (BVP)
docs.text:
A Boundary Value Problem specifies conditions at two different points \(x = a\) and \(x = b\):

\[y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = g(x), \qquad \mathcal{B}_1[y](https://claude.ai/chat/a) = \alpha, \quad \mathcal{B}_2[y](https://claude.ai/chat/b) = \beta\]

where \(\mathcal{B}_1, \mathcal{B}_2\) are boundary operators (often evaluation of \(y\) or \(y'\)).

Physical meaning: You know something about the system at both ends of an interval, but nothing in between. This is the formulation of equilibrium problems — a beam deflecting between two supports, a wire with fixed endpoints, the temperature distribution in a rod with fixed endpoint temperatures.

docs.title: 1.3 The Fundamental Difference
docs.text:
IVP BVP Conditions at One point \(x_0\) Two points \(a\), \(b\) Information State at one moment Endpoint constraints Physical type Evolution in time Spatial equilibrium Existence/Uniqueness Always (if continuous coefficients) Not guaranteed Solution method Direct integration, characteristic eq. Shooting, finite difference, eigenfunction expansion

Key insight: For an IVP, existence and uniqueness are essentially free. For a BVP, they are delicate — a BVP may have no solution, exactly one, or infinitely many. This is the central surprise of the theory.

docs.title: § 2 — Initial Value Problems: The Complete Theory
2.1 Existence and Uniqueness
docs.text:
Theorem (Picard–Lindelöf for second order linear ODEs). Let \(p\), \(q\), \(g\) be continuous on an open interval \(I\) containing \(x_0\). Then the IVP:

\[y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = g(x), \quad y(x_0) = y_0, \quad y'(x_0) = y_0'\]

has a unique solution defined on all of \(I\).

Proof sketch. Write the IVP as a first order system by setting \(\mathbf{u} = \begin{pmatrix} y \ y' \end{pmatrix}\):

\[\mathbf{u}' = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ -q(x) & -p(x) \end{pmatrix} \mathbf{u} + \begin{pmatrix} 0 \ g(x) \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{u}(x_0) = \begin{pmatrix} y_0 \ y_0' \end{pmatrix}\]

The right-hand side is linear in \(\mathbf{u}\) with continuous coefficient matrix. A linear system with continuous coefficients satisfies a global Lipschitz condition, so Picard iteration converges on all of \(I\). Uniqueness follows from the Gronwall inequality. \(\blacksquare\)

What this theorem buys: Once you know \(y(x_0)\) and \(y'(x_0)\), the solution is completely and uniquely determined everywhere. No ambiguity whatsoever.

docs.title: 2.2 The Solution Algorithm
docs.text:
Step 1. Solve the homogeneous equation \(L[y] = 0\) to find a fundamental set \({y_1, y_2}\).

Step 2. Find a particular solution \(y_p\) (undetermined coefficients or variation of parameters).

Step 3. Write the general solution: \(y = c_1 y_1 + c_2 y_2 + y_p\).

Step 4. Apply initial conditions to determine \(c_1, c_2\):

\[\begin{cases} c_1 y_1(x_0) + c_2 y_2(x_0) = y_0 - y_p(x_0) \ c_1 y_1'(x_0) + c_2 y_2'(x_0) = y_0' - y_p'(x_0) \end{cases}\]

The coefficient matrix of this system is \(\begin{pmatrix} y_1(x_0) & y_2(x_0) \ y_1'(x_0) & y_2'(x_0) \end{pmatrix}\), whose determinant is \(W(x_0) \neq 0\) (since \({y_1, y_2}\) is a fundamental set). So the system always has a unique solution. This is exactly why IVPs always have unique solutions when the homogeneous equation is solved correctly.

docs.title: 2.3 Worked Example: Full IVP
docs.text:
Problem: Solve \(y'' - 3y' + 2y = e^{3x}\), \(y(0) = 1\), \(y'(0) = 0\).

Step 1: Characteristic equation: \(r^2 - 3r + 2 = (r-1)(r-2) = 0\). So \(y_1 = e^x\), \(y_2 = e^{2x}\).

Step 2: Since \(e^{3x}\) is not a homogeneous solution, try \(y_p = Ae^{3x}\): $\(9A - 9A + 2A = 1 \implies A = \frac{1}{2}\)$ So \(y_p = \frac{1}{2}e^{3x}\).

Step 3: General solution: \(y = c_1 e^x + c_2 e^{2x} + \frac{1}{2}e^{3x}\).

Step 4: Apply \(y(0) = 1\) and \(y'(0) = 0\): $\(c_1 + c_2 + \frac{1}{2} = 1 \implies c_1 + c_2 = \frac{1}{2}\)$ $\(c_1 + 2c_2 + \frac{3}{2} = 0 \implies c_1 + 2c_2 = -\frac{3}{2}\)$

Subtracting: \(c_2 = -2\). Then \(c_1 = \frac{5}{2}\).

\[\boxed{y = \frac{5}{2}e^x - 2e^{2x} + \frac{1}{2}e^{3x}}\]

docs.title: 2.4 Nonlinear IVPs: Local vs. Global Existence
docs.text:
For nonlinear IVPs \(y'' = f(x, y, y')\), the situation is more delicate.

Theorem (Local Existence). If \(f\), \(\partial f/\partial y\), \(\partial f/\partial y'\) are continuous near \((x_0, y_0, y_0')\), then the IVP has a unique solution on some interval \((x_0 - h, x_0 + h)\).

The solution may blow up in finite time. Example: \(y' = y^2\), \(y(0) = 1\) gives \(y = \frac{1}{1-x}\) — which blows up at \(x = 1\). Linearity is what prevents this from happening in the linear case.

docs.title: § 3 — Boundary Value Problems: Where Things Get Interesting
3.1 The Setup
docs.text:
Consider the second order linear BVP on \([a, b]\):

\[y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = g(x)\]

with boundary conditions (BCs) of one of these types:

Type Condition Name Dirichlet \(y(a) = \alpha\), \(y(b) = \beta\) Prescribed values Neumann \(y'(a) = \alpha\), \(y'(b) = \beta\) Prescribed derivatives (flux) Robin (Mixed) \(y'(a) - h_1 y(a) = \alpha\), \(y'(b) + h_2 y(b) = \beta\) Mixed value and flux Periodic \(y(a) = y(b)\), \(y'(a) = y'(b)\) Periodicity

The most common in practice (and in Stewart) are Dirichlet conditions.

docs.title: 3.2 The Shocking Difference from IVPs: Three Cases
docs.text:
Unlike IVPs, a BVP may have no solution, a unique solution, or infinitely many solutions. This is not a theorem — it is a fact you must check case by case. Here are three examples that make this vivid.

Example A: Unique Solution

\[y'' + y = x, \quad y(0) = 0, \quad y(\pi/2) = 0\]

Homogeneous solution: \(y_h = c_1 \cos x + c_2 \sin x\). Particular solution: \(y_p = x\).

General: \(y = c_1 \cos x + c_2 \sin x + x\).

Apply BCs:

  • \(y(0) = 0\): \(c_1 = 0\).
  • \(y(\pi/2) = 0\): \(c_2 + \pi/2 = 0 \implies c_2 = -\pi/2\).

Unique solution: \(y = -\frac{\pi}{2}\sin x + x\). ✓

Example B: No Solution

\[y'' + y = 0, \quad y(0) = 0, \quad y(\pi) = 1\]

Homogeneous solution: \(y = c_1 \cos x + c_2 \sin x\).

Apply BCs:

  • \(y(0) = 0\): \(c_1 = 0\). So \(y = c_2 \sin x\).
  • \(y(\pi) = 1\): \(c_2 \sin\pi = 0 \neq 1\). Contradiction.

No solution exists. ✗

Example C: Infinitely Many Solutions

\[y'' + y = 0, \quad y(0) = 0, \quad y(\pi) = 0\]

Apply BCs:

  • \(y(0) = 0\): \(c_1 = 0\). So \(y = c_2 \sin x\).
  • \(y(\pi) = 0\): \(c_2 \sin\pi = 0\), satisfied for any \(c_2\).

Solution: \(y = c_2 \sin x\) for any \(c_2 \in \mathbb{R}\). ✗ (infinitely many)

What just happened? The boundary condition \(y(\pi) = 0\) with \(y = c_2 \sin x\) is automatically satisfied because \(\sin\pi = 0\) regardless of \(c_2\). The boundary "accidentally" coincides with the structure of the homogeneous solution. This is not a coincidence — it is the phenomenon of eigenvalues, which is the heart of the BVP theory.

docs.title: 3.3 The Algebraic Reason: When Does Uniqueness Fail?
docs.text:
After applying the general solution \(y = c_1 y_1 + c_2 y_2 + y_p\) to Dirichlet BCs \(y(a) = \alpha\), \(y(b) = \beta\), we get the linear system:

\[\begin{pmatrix} y_1(a) & y_2(a) \ y_1(b) & y_2(b) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} c_1 \ c_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha - y_p(a) \ \beta - y_p(b) \end{pmatrix}\]

Let \(D = y_1(a)y_2(b) - y_1(b)y_2(a)\) (the determinant of the boundary matrix).

  • \(D \neq 0\): Unique solution always exists (for any \(\alpha, \beta, g\)).
  • \(D = 0\): Either no solution or infinitely many — depending on whether the right-hand side is consistent.

Note: \(D\) is not the Wronskian \(W(x)\) (which is never zero). \(D\) is the Wronskian-like expression evaluated at the two different boundary points \(a\) and \(b\). It can be zero even when \(W \neq 0\).

This is the fundamental obstacle in BVP theory, absent in IVP theory.

docs.title: 4.1 The Eigenvalue Problem
docs.text:
Consider the parameterized homogeneous BVP:

\[y'' + \lambda y = 0, \quad y(0) = 0, \quad y(L) = 0\]

For which values of \(\lambda\) does a nontrivial solution exist?

Case 1: \(\lambda < 0\). Write \(\lambda = -\mu^2\), \(\mu > 0\). General solution: \(y = c_1 e^{\mu x} + c_2 e^{-\mu x}\).

  • \(y(0) = 0\): \(c_1 + c_2 = 0\).
  • \(y(L) = 0\): \(c_1(e^{\mu L} - e^{-\mu L}) = 0 \implies c_1 = 0\) (since \(e^{\mu L} \neq e^{-\mu L}\)).
  • Only trivial solution \(y = 0\). No eigenvalue here.

Case 2: \(\lambda = 0\). \(y'' = 0 \Rightarrow y = c_1 + c_2 x\). BCs force \(c_1 = c_2 = 0\). No eigenvalue.

Case 3: \(\lambda > 0\). Write \(\lambda = \mu^2\), \(\mu > 0\). General solution: \(y = c_1 \cos\mu x + c_2 \sin\mu x\).

  • \(y(0) = 0\): \(c_1 = 0\). So \(y = c_2 \sin\mu x\).
  • \(y(L) = 0\): \(c_2 \sin\mu L = 0\). For nontrivial solution: \(\sin\mu L = 0 \Rightarrow \mu L = n\pi\) for \(n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)

Eigenvalues:

\[\lambda_n = \frac{n^2 \pi^2}{L^2}, \quad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\]

Eigenfunctions:

\[y_n(x) = \sin\left(\frac{n\pi x}{L}\right)\]

These eigenfunctions are the natural modes of the system. The BVP has nontrivial solutions if and only if \(\lambda\) is one of these eigenvalues.

docs.title: 4.2 Orthogonality of Eigenfunctions
docs.text:
The eigenfunctions \({y_n}\) satisfy a remarkable property:

\[\int_0^L \sin\frac{m\pi x}{L} \sin\frac{n\pi x}{L},dx = \begin{cases} 0 & m \neq n \ L/2 & m = n \end{cases}\]

The eigenfunctions are orthogonal in \(L^2([0,L])\). This is not a coincidence — it is a consequence of the Sturm–Liouville theorem.

docs.title: 4.3 Sturm–Liouville Theory
docs.text:
The general Sturm–Liouville problem is:

\[-\frac{d}{dx}\left[p(x)y'\right] + q(x)y = \lambda w(x) y, \quad a < x < b\]

with boundary conditions, where \(p > 0\), \(w > 0\) (weight function).

Theorem (Sturm–Liouville). Under appropriate conditions:

  1. All eigenvalues \(\lambda_n\) are real.
  2. The eigenvalues form an increasing sequence \(\lambda_1 < \lambda_2 < \lambda_3 < \cdots \to +\infty\).
  3. Each eigenvalue has exactly one linearly independent eigenfunction \(y_n\).
  4. The eigenfunctions \({y_n}\) are orthogonal with respect to the weight \(w\): $\(\int_a^b y_m(x) y_n(x) w(x),dx = 0, \quad m \neq n\)$
  5. The eigenfunctions form a complete orthogonal basis of \(L^2_w([a,b])\): any square-integrable function can be expanded as \(f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty c_n y_n(x)\).

This is why Fourier series exist. The sine and cosine functions are eigenfunctions of \(-d^2/dx^2\) with Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions respectively. Fourier series is Sturm–Liouville theory for the simplest operator.

More examples of Sturm–Liouville problems and their eigenfunctions:

Operator Domain BCs Eigenfunctions \(-d^2/dx^2\) \([0, L]\) \(y(0) = y(L) = 0\) \(\sin(n\pi x/L)\) \(-d^2/dx^2\) \([0, L]\) \(y'(0) = y'(L) = 0\) \(\cos(n\pi x/L)\) \(-\frac{1}{x}\frac{d}{dx}(x\frac{d}{dx})\) \([0,1]\) Regularity + \(y(1) = 0\) Bessel functions \(J_0(\lambda_n x)\) \(-(1-x^2)\frac{d^2}{dx^2} + 2x\frac{d}{dx}\) \([-1,1]\) Regularity Legendre polynomials \(P_n(x)\)

docs.title: § 5 — Shooting Method: Solving BVPs Numerically
docs.text: The shooting method converts a BVP into a sequence of IVPs — exploiting the clean existence/uniqueness theory of IVPs to handle the messy BVP.

docs.title: 5.1 The Idea
docs.text:
For the BVP \(y'' = f(x, y, y')\), \(y(a) = \alpha\), \(y(b) = \beta\):

We know \(y(a) = \alpha\) but don't know \(y'(a)\).

Guess \(y'(a) = s\) (the "shooting parameter"). Solve the IVP: $\(y'' = f(x, y, y'), \quad y(a) = \alpha, \quad y'(a) = s\)$

This gives a solution \(y(x; s)\). Define the residual: $\(F(s) = y(b; s) - \beta\)$

We want \(F(s) = 0\). Use root-finding (bisection, Newton's method) to find \(s^_\) such that \(F(s^_) = 0\).

  y
  |        β ------- target
  |       /
  |      /  ← too low (s too small)
  |   α /
  |    / ← correct s*
  |   /\  ← too high (s too large)
  +---+----------> x
      a          b

For a linear BVP, \(F(s)\) is linear in \(s\), so we only need two shots.

docs.title: 5.2 Linear Shooting Method
docs.text:
For the linear BVP \(y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = g(x)\), \(y(a) = \alpha\), \(y(b) = \beta\):

Solve two IVPs:

IVP 1: \(u'' + pu' + qu = g\), \(u(a) = \alpha\), \(u'(a) = 0\).

IVP 2: \(v'' + pv' + qv = 0\), \(v(a) = 0\), \(v'(a) = 1\).

By linearity, \(y = u + cv\) solves the ODE for any constant \(c\). Apply the boundary condition at \(b\):

\[y(b) = u(b) + cv(b) = \beta \implies c = \frac{\beta - u(b)}{v(b)}\]

provided \(v(b) \neq 0\) (which is exactly the condition \(D \neq 0\) from §3.3 — the unique solution condition).

The solution is \(y(x) = u(x) + \frac{\beta - u(b)}{v(b)} v(x)\).

docs.title: § 6 — Green's Functions: The BVP Analogue of Variation of Parameters
docs.text:
For the BVP: $\(L[y] = y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = g(x), \quad y(a) = 0, \quad y(b) = 0\)$

(homogeneous Dirichlet BCs), assuming unique solvability, there exists a Green's function \(G(x, t)\) such that:

\[y(x) = \int_a^b G(x, t) g(t),dt\]

docs.title: 6.1 Construction of \(G(x, t)\)
docs.text:
Let \({y_1, y_2}\) be the fundamental set of \(L[y] = 0\) with:

  • \(y_1\) satisfying the left BC: \(y_1(a) = 0\).
  • \(y_2\) satisfying the right BC: \(y_2(b) = 0\).

Then:

\[G(x, t) = \frac{1}{W(t)} \begin{cases} y_1(x)y_2(t) & a \leq x \leq t \ y_1(t)y_2(x) & t \leq x \leq b \end{cases}\]

where \(W(t) = W(y_1, y_2)(t)\) is the Wronskian.

docs.title: 6.2 Properties of the Green's Function
docs.text:
• \(G(x, t)\) is continuous at \(x = t\).
  • \(G_x(x, t)\) has a jump discontinuity at \(x = t\): \(G_x(t^+, t) - G_x(t^-, t) = \frac{1}{p(t)}\) (from the jump condition).
  • \(G(x, t) = G(t, x)\) when \(L\) is self-adjoint (Sturm–Liouville type) — symmetry of the Green's function.
  • \(L_x[G(x,t)] = \delta(x - t)\), where \(\delta\) is the Dirac delta — \(G\) is the "impulse response" of the operator \(L\).

The physical interpretation: \(G(x, t)\) is the displacement at position \(x\) of a string (or beam) due to a unit point load at position \(t\). The total displacement under a distributed load \(g(t)\) is the superposition integral \(\int G(x,t)g(t),dt\).

docs.title: 6.3 Worked Example: Green's Function for \(-y'' = g\), \(y(0) = y(1) = 0\)
docs.text:
This is the deflection of a string under load \(g(x)\).

Homogeneous equation \(-y'' = 0 \Rightarrow y'' = 0\): general solution \(y = Ax + B\).

  • \(y_1\) satisfies \(y_1(0) = 0\): take \(y_1 = x\).
  • \(y_2\) satisfies \(y_2(1) = 0\): take \(y_2 = 1 - x\).
  • Wronskian: \(W = y_1 y_2' - y_1' y_2 = x(-1) - 1(1-x) = -1\).
\[G(x, t) = \frac{1}{-1}\begin{cases} x(1-t) & 0 \leq x \leq t \ t(1-x) & t \leq x \leq 1 \end{cases} = \begin{cases} -x(1-t) & x \leq t \ -t(1-x) & x \geq t \end{cases}\]

Wait — let me recheck the sign. The equation is \(-y'' = g \Rightarrow L[y] = -y''\), so \(p = 0\), \(q = 0\), \(a = -1\) in \(L[y] = ay''\). The standard form \(y'' = -g\) gives the Green's function for \(y'' = \delta\):

\[G(x, t) = \begin{cases} -x(1-t) & x \leq t \ -t(1-x) & x \geq t \end{cases}\]

Note \(G \leq 0\) — deflection is downward under a downward load. Note also \(G(x,t) = G(t,x)\) — the symmetry of the self-adjoint operator. The solution:

\[y(x) = \int_0^1 G(x, t)(-g(t)),dt\]

For \(g = 1\) (uniform load): \(y(x) = \frac{x(1-x)}{2}\) — a parabola, as expected for a uniformly loaded string.

docs.title: § 7 — Finite Difference Methods for BVPs
docs.text: When analytic methods fail, we discretize. Replace the continuous BVP by a system of algebraic equations on a grid.

docs.title: 7.1 The Discretization
docs.text:
Divide \([a, b]\) into \(N+1\) equal subintervals: \(x_i = a + ih\), \(h = (b-a)/(N+1)\), \(i = 0, 1, \ldots, N+1\).

The second-order finite difference approximations:

\[y''(x_i) \approx \frac{y_{i-1} - 2y_i + y_{i+1}}{h^2}, \quad y'(x_i) \approx \frac{y_{i+1} - y_{i-1}}{2h}\]

docs.title: 7.2 The Linear System
docs.text:
For the BVP \(y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = g(x)\), \(y(a) = \alpha\), \(y(b) = \beta\), substituting the approximations at each interior node \(x_i\) (\(i = 1, \ldots, N\)):

\[\frac{y_{i-1} - 2y_i + y_{i+1}}{h^2} + p_i \frac{y_{i+1} - y_{i-1}}{2h} + q_i y_i = g_i\]

Multiplying through by \(h^2\):

\[\left(1 - \frac{h}{2}p_i\right)y_{i-1} + (-2 + h^2 q_i)y_i + \left(1 + \frac{h}{2}p_i\right)y_{i+1} = h^2 g_i\]

With \(y_0 = \alpha\) and \(y_{N+1} = \beta\) absorbed into the right-hand side, this is a tridiagonal linear system \(A\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{b}\) of size \(N \times N\):

\[A = \begin{pmatrix} -2 + h^2 q_1 & 1 + \frac{h}{2}p_1 & & \ 1 - \frac{h}{2}p_2 & -2 + h^2 q_2 & 1 + \frac{h}{2}p_2 & \ & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots \ & & 1 - \frac{h}{2}p_N & -2 + h^2 q_N \end{pmatrix}\]

Tridiagonal systems are solved in \(O(N)\) operations by the Thomas algorithm (tridiagonal LU factorization).

docs.title: Example 1: BVP with Unique Solution
docs.text:
Problem: \(y'' + 2y' + y = e^{-x}\), \(y(0) = 0\), \(y(1) = 1\).

Homogeneous: \(r^2 + 2r + 1 = (r+1)^2 = 0\). Repeated root \(r = -1\). $\(y_h = (c_1 + c_2 x)e^{-x}\)$

Particular: \(e^{-x}\) satisfies the homogeneous equation (double). Try \(y_p = Ax^2 e^{-x}\): $\(y_p' = A(2x - x^2)e^{-x}, \quad y_p'' = A(2 - 4x + x^2)e^{-x}\)$ $\(y_p'' + 2y_p' + y_p = A(2 - 4x + x^2 + 4x - 2x^2 + x^2)e^{-x} = 2Ae^{-x} = e^{-x}\)$ $\(\implies A = \frac{1}{2}\)$

General: \(y = \left(c_1 + c_2 x + \frac{x^2}{2}\right)e^{-x}\).

BCs:

  • \(y(0) = 0\): \(c_1 = 0\).
  • \(y(1) = 1\): \((c_2 + \frac{1}{2})e^{-1} = 1 \implies c_2 = e - \frac{1}{2}\).
\[y = \left[\left(e - \frac{1}{2}\right)x + \frac{x^2}{2}\right]e^{-x}\]

docs.title: Example 2: Checking for Nonexistence
docs.text:
Problem: \(y'' + \pi^2 y = \sin(\pi x)\), \(y(0) = 0\), \(y(1) = 0\).

Homogeneous: \(r^2 + \pi^2 = 0 \Rightarrow r = \pm i\pi\). So \(y_h = c_1\cos\pi x + c_2\sin\pi x\).

Particular: \(\sin(\pi x)\) is a homogeneous solution (resonance). Try \(y_p = x(A\cos\pi x + B\sin\pi x)\):

Computing: $\(y_p'' = \pi^2(-Ax\cos\pi x - Bx\sin\pi x) + 2\pi(-A\sin\pi x + B\cos\pi x)\)$ $\(y_p'' + \pi^2 y_p = 2\pi(-A\sin\pi x + B\cos\pi x) = \sin\pi x\)$

So \(-2\pi A = 1 \Rightarrow A = -\frac{1}{2\pi}\) and \(B = 0\).

\[y_p = -\frac{x}{2\pi}\cos\pi x\]

General: \(y = c_1\cos\pi x + c_2\sin\pi x - \frac{x}{2\pi}\cos\pi x\).

BCs:

  • \(y(0) = 0\): \(c_1 = 0\). So \(y = c_2\sin\pi x - \frac{x}{2\pi}\cos\pi x\).
  • \(y(1) = 0\): \(c_2 \cdot 0 - \frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot(-1) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \neq 0\).

No solution exists. ✗

The forcing \(\sin(\pi x)\) happens to be at the resonant eigenfrequency of the boundary problem, and the BCs cannot be simultaneously satisfied.

docs.title: § 9 — Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
9.1 Neural Networks as BVP Solvers: PINNs
docs.text:
Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) are trained to solve BVPs:

\[L[y] = g \text{ on } (a,b), \quad y(a) = \alpha, \quad y(b) = \beta\]

The network \(y_\theta(x)\) minimizes:

\[\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \underbrace{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N |L[y_\theta](https://claude.ai/chat/x_i) - g(x_i)|^2}_{\text{interior residual}} + \underbrace{|y_\theta(a) - \alpha|^2 + |y_\theta(b) - \beta|^2}_{\text{boundary residual}}\]

The IVP vs BVP distinction matters critically here:

  • IVP: Only the left boundary appears in the loss. Integration marches from left to right. This is numerically stable (Runge–Kutta).
  • BVP: Both boundaries constrain simultaneously. The optimizer must satisfy conditions on two sides at once. This is inherently harder — the loss landscape has ridges and saddle points that gradient descent struggles with near eigenvalues. When \(\lambda\) is close to an eigenvalue of \(L\), the problem is nearly singular, and the neural network must "learn" the shooting method implicitly.

docs.title: 9.2 Boundary Conditions in PDE-solving Networks
docs.text:
For higher-dimensional PDEs (the natural extension of BVPs), enforcing boundary conditions is an active research problem:

  • Soft enforcement (penalty): Add boundary residual to the loss. Simple but the boundary may not be exactly satisfied.
  • Hard enforcement: Parameterize the network as \(y_\theta(x) = A(x) + B(x)N_\theta(x)\), where \(A(x)\) satisfies the BCs exactly and \(B(x)\) vanishes on the boundary. Then \(N_\theta\) is unconstrained. This is analogous to the shooting method's linear decomposition \(y = u + cv\).

docs.title: 9.3 IVPs in Sequence Models: Autoregressive Generation
docs.text:
Autoregressive language models (GPT, etc.) solve a discrete IVP: given the "initial condition" (the prompt = \(y_0, y_0', \ldots\)), march forward in time to generate the sequence. The existence and uniqueness theorem for IVPs is mirrored in the fact that, given a prompt, the model deterministically (at temperature 0) generates a unique continuation — the discrete analog of the unique IVP solution.

The contrast with BVPs appears in constrained generation:

  • Generate text that starts with A (left BC) and ends with B (right BC).
  • This is a discrete BVP, and it may have no solution, one solution, or many.
  • Controlled generation methods (like FUDGE, PPLM, classifier guidance in diffusion) are essentially numerical BVP solvers operating in the space of text.

docs.title: 9.4 Diffusion Models as IVPs Running Backwards
docs.text:
Score-based diffusion models define a forward SDE (adding noise):

\[d\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}, t),dt + g(t),d\mathbf{W}\]

with initial condition \(\mathbf{x}(0) \sim p_{\text{data}}\). This is an IVP in distribution space.

The reverse (denoising) process is also an IVP, running backwards from \(t = T\) (pure noise as initial condition) to \(t = 0\) (generated sample):

\[d\mathbf{x} = \left[\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}, t) - g(t)^2 \nabla_\mathbf{x} \log p_t(\mathbf{x})\right]dt\]

The learned score \(\nabla_\mathbf{x} \log p_t(\mathbf{x})\) plays the role of \(p(x)\) in the ODE. The IVP structure guarantees that, given an initial noise vector, there is a unique denoising trajectory — which is why diffusion models are deterministic at inference given a seed.

docs.title: 9.5 Green's Functions and Attention
docs.text:
The output of self-attention in a transformer can be written as:

\[\text{Attention}(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V})_i = \sum_j A_{ij} \mathbf{V}_j\]

where \(A_{ij} = \text{softmax}(\mathbf{Q}_i \cdot \mathbf{K}_j / \sqrt{d})\).

This is a discrete integral operator with kernel \(A_{ij}\) — precisely the structure of a Green's function integral \(y(x) = \int G(x,t)g(t),dt\). The attention kernel \(A_{ij}\) plays the role of the Green's function \(G(x_i, t_j)\), and the values \(\mathbf{V}_j\) play the role of the forcing \(g(t_j)\).

More precisely: attention learns a data-dependent Green's function for the implicit operator that maps inputs to outputs. This connection is made rigorous in recent work on attention as integral operators and neural operators (Li et al., 2020 — Fourier Neural Operator), where the network directly parameterizes the Green's function of a PDE operator.

docs.title: 9.6 Eigenvalues, Stability, and the Spectrum of Neural Networks
docs.text:
The Sturm–Liouville eigenvalue theory has a direct analogue in deep learning:

  • The Hessian \(\nabla^2 \mathcal{L}\) of the loss function plays the role of \(L\) in \(L[y] = \lambda y\).
  • The eigenvalues of the Hessian determine convergence rate: directions with large \(\lambda\) (sharp curvature) are hard to optimize; directions with small \(\lambda\) are flat.
  • Batch normalization implicitly shifts the eigenvalue spectrum of layer-wise Jacobians — it is an attempt to solve a "spectral BVP" at each layer: keep the singular values of the weight Jacobian near 1.
  • Residual connections (ResNets) modify the spectrum: \(\mathbf{h}_{l+1} = \mathbf{h}_l + F(\mathbf{h}_l)\) shifts all eigenvalues by 1, preventing eigenvalues from being too close to 0 (vanishing gradients = small eigenvalues of the chain product Jacobian).

The S4 / Mamba state space models explicitly parameterize their recurrent matrices to have eigenvalues with negative real part — mirroring the Sturm–Liouville condition that eigenvalues are real and bounded below. This guarantees the IVP stability of the recurrence, preventing the exponential blow-up (exploding gradients) that plagues vanilla RNNs.

docs.title: IVP: \(y(x_0) = y_0\), \(y'(x_0) = y_0'\)
docs.text:
\[\boxed{\text{Always has a unique solution on } I \text{ if } p, q, g \in C(I)}\]
  • Two conditions at one point.
  • Solve: find general solution, apply ICs to get unique \(c_1, c_2\).
  • Nonlinear IVPs: may blow up in finite time.

docs.title: BVP: \(y(a) = \alpha\), \(y(b) = \beta\)
docs.text:
\[\boxed{\text{May have 0, 1, or } \infty \text{ solutions — check the boundary matrix determinant } D}\]
  • Two conditions at two different points.
  • Solve: shooting method, finite differences, eigenfunction expansion.
  • Eigenvalue problems: nontrivial solutions exist only for special \(\lambda\) — the eigenvalues.
  • Eigenfunctions form a complete orthogonal basis (Sturm–Liouville) — the foundation of Fourier series and spectral methods.

docs.title: Key Comparison
docs.text: IVP BVP Conditions Same point Boundary points Existence/Uniqueness Guaranteed Case-by-case Failure mode None (linear case) \(D = 0\) (resonance at eigenvalue) Numerical method Runge–Kutta Shooting, FD, spectral Green's function Variation of parameters Symmetric \(G(x,t) = G(t,x)\) AI analogue Autoregressive models, diffusion Constrained generation, PINNs

docs.text:

  2. MIT 18.02 / 18.03 — Lecture notes on IVPs, BVPs, and eigenvalue problems. The linear shooting method and Sturm–Liouville overview follow the 18.03 treatment.

  3. Boyce & DiPrima — Elementary Differential Equations and Boundary Value Problems, Ch. 10–11. The Sturm–Liouville theorem, Green's functions, and finite difference methods.

  4. Raissi, Perdikaris & Karniadakis (2019) — Physics-informed neural networks: A deep learning framework for solving forward and inverse problems involving nonlinear PDEs. The PINN formulation for BVPs.

  5. Li et al. (2020) — Fourier Neural Operator for Parametric Partial Differential Equations. The Green's function / attention kernel connection.

docs.title: Nonhomogeneous Equations
docs.text: "The homogeneous equation describes the soul of the system. The nonhomogeneous equation describes what happens when the world pushes back."

docs.title: § 0 — The Setup and the Question
docs.text:
We have spent considerable effort understanding the homogeneous equation \(L[y] = 0\). Now we turn on an external force. The nonhomogeneous second order linear ODE is:

\[\boxed{y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = g(x)}\]

where \(g(x) \not\equiv 0\) is the forcing function (also called the nonhomogeneous term, the input, or the driving term).

The fundamental question: Given that we understand \(L[y] = 0\) completely, how do we find all solutions to \(L[y] = g\)?

The answer has a breathtaking algebraic structure — one that appears in linear algebra, functional analysis, and throughout applied mathematics. Understanding it deeply means you will never need to memorize a method; you will derive every method from first principles.

docs.title: § 1 — The Structure Theorem
docs.text: This is the most important theorem of the subject. Everything else is a consequence.

docs.title: 1.1 Statement
docs.text:
Theorem (Structure of Solutions). Let \(p, q, g\) be continuous on an open interval \(I\). Let \({y_1, y_2}\) be a fundamental set of solutions of the homogeneous equation \(L[y] = 0\), and let \(y_p\) be any particular solution of \(L[y] = g\). Then every solution of \(L[y] = g\) on \(I\) has the form:

\[y = \underbrace{c_1 y_1 + c_2 y_2}_{y_h \text{ — homogeneous general solution}} + \underbrace{y_p}_{\text{particular solution}}\]

for some constants \(c_1, c_2 \in \mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: 1.2 Proof
docs.text:
Part 1 — \(y_h + y_p\) solves \(L[y] = g\):

\[L[y_h + y_p] = L[y_h] + L[y_p] = 0 + g = g \qquad \checkmark\]

Part 2 — Every solution has this form:

Let \(y\) be any solution of \(L[y] = g\). Consider \(z = y - y_p\). Then: $\(L[z] = L[y] - L[y_p] = g - g = 0\)$

So \(z\) solves the homogeneous equation. Since \({y_1, y_2}\) is a fundamental set, \(z = c_1 y_1 + c_2 y_2\) for some constants. Therefore: $\(y = y_p + z = y_p + c_1 y_1 + c_2 y_2 \qquad \blacksquare\)$

docs.title: 1.3 The Linear Algebra Interpretation
docs.text:
In linear algebra, if \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) has a solution \(\mathbf{x}_p\), then the general solution is:

\[\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_p + \mathbf{x}_{\text{null}}\]

where \(\mathbf{x}_{\text{null}} \in \ker(A)\). This is exactly the structure theorem above:

  • \(A \leftrightarrow L\) (the linear operator)
  • \(\mathbf{x}_p \leftrightarrow y_p\) (particular solution)
  • \(\ker(A) \leftrightarrow \text{span}{y_1, y_2}\) (null space, 2-dimensional)
  • \(\mathbf{b} \leftrightarrow g\) (the forcing)

The solution set of \(L[y] = g\) is a coset of the solution space of \(L[y] = 0\) — an affine subspace, not a vector space (it does not contain \(0\) unless \(y_p = 0\)).

The operational consequence: We need only find one particular solution. Any one will do — the constants \(c_1, c_2\) absorb the difference between different choices. This is the license to be clever about how we find \(y_p\).

docs.title: 2.1 The Idea
docs.text:
Valid for constant coefficient equations \(ay'' + by' + cy = g(x)\) when \(g(x)\) belongs to a special class of functions closed under differentiation: polynomials, exponentials, sines, cosines, and their products.

The principle: \(L[y_p]\) must equal \(g(x)\). If \(g\) is a sum of exponentials times polynomials times trig, then \(y_p\) should live in the same "family" — because differentiating such functions stays within the family. We guess the form, substitute, and solve for the unknown coefficients.

docs.title: 2.2 The Trial Function Table
docs.text:
For constant coefficient \(L = aD^2 + bD + c\) and the given \(g(x)\), the trial \(y_p\) is:

\(g(x)\) Trial \(y_p\) \(P_n(x) = a_n x^n + \cdots + a_0\) \(x^s(A_n x^n + \cdots + A_1 x + A_0)\) \(e^{\alpha x}\) \(x^s A e^{\alpha x}\) \(\cos(\beta x)\) or \(\sin(\beta x)\) \(x^s(A\cos\beta x + B\sin\beta x)\) \(e^{\alpha x}\cos(\beta x)\) or \(e^{\alpha x}\sin(\beta x)\) \(x^s e^{\alpha x}(A\cos\beta x + B\sin\beta x)\) \(P_n(x)e^{\alpha x}\) \(x^s(A_n x^n + \cdots + A_0)e^{\alpha x}\) Sum of above Sum of corresponding trials

The multiplicity rule for \(s\):

  • \(s = 0\) if no term in the trial is a solution of \(L[y] = 0\).
  • \(s = 1\) if some term in the trial is a solution of \(L[y] = 0\) (simple resonance).
  • \(s = 2\) if some term in the trial is a solution corresponding to a double root (double resonance).

Why does the multiplicity rule exist? If the trial \(y_p\) satisfies the homogeneous equation, then \(L[y_p] = 0 \neq g(x)\) — the substitution gives \(0 = g\) and no coefficient can be determined. Multiplying by \(x^s\) (with \(s\) chosen minimally) moves the trial out of the kernel of \(L\), making it possible to match \(g\).

docs.title: Example 1 — Polynomial Forcing
docs.text:
Problem: \(y'' - 2y' - 3y = 3x^2 + 4x\).

Homogeneous: \(r^2 - 2r - 3 = (r-3)(r+1) = 0\). Roots \(r = 3, -1\).

\(g(x) = 3x^2 + 4x\) is a polynomial of degree 2. Trial: \(y_p = Ax^2 + Bx + C\) (no resonance, \(s = 0\)).

\[y_p' = 2Ax + B, \quad y_p'' = 2A\]

Substituting: $\(2A - 2(2Ax + B) - 3(Ax^2 + Bx + C) = 3x^2 + 4x\)$ $\(-3Ax^2 + (-4A - 3B)x + (2A - 2B - 3C) = 3x^2 + 4x + 0\)$

Matching coefficients:

  • \(x^2\): \(-3A = 3 \implies A = -1\)
  • \(x^1\): \(-4A - 3B = 4 \implies 4 - 3B = 4 \implies B = 0\)
  • \(x^0\): \(2A - 2B - 3C = 0 \implies -2 - 3C = 0 \implies C = -\frac{2}{3}\)
\[y_p = -x^2 - \frac{2}{3}, \quad y = c_1 e^{3x} + c_2 e^{-x} - x^2 - \frac{2}{3}\]

docs.title: Example 2 — Exponential Forcing, No Resonance
docs.text:
Problem: \(y'' - 5y' + 6y = 2e^{4x}\).

Characteristic roots: \(r = 2, 3\). Since \(e^{4x}\) is not a homogeneous solution (\(4 \neq 2, 3\)), try \(y_p = Ae^{4x}\).

\[16Ae^{4x} - 20Ae^{4x} + 6Ae^{4x} = 2Ae^{4x} = 2e^{4x} \implies A = 1\] \[y = c_1 e^{2x} + c_2 e^{3x} + e^{4x}\]

docs.title: Example 3 — Resonance (\(s = 1\))
docs.text:
Problem: \(y'' - 5y' + 6y = 2e^{2x}\).

Roots \(r = 2, 3\). Now \(e^{2x}\) is a homogeneous solution (simple root \(r = 2\)). Multiply by \(x\): try \(y_p = Axe^{2x}\).

\[y_p' = A(1 + 2x)e^{2x}, \quad y_p'' = A(4 + 4x)e^{2x}\] \[A(4 + 4x)e^{2x} - 5A(1 + 2x)e^{2x} + 6Axe^{2x} = A(4 + 4x - 5 - 10x + 6x)e^{2x} = -Ae^{2x}\]

Setting \(-A = 2\): \(A = -2\).

\[y = c_1 e^{2x} + c_2 e^{3x} - 2xe^{2x}\]

docs.title: Example 4 — Double Resonance (\(s = 2\))
docs.text:
Problem: \(y'' - 4y' + 4y = e^{2x}\).

Characteristic: \((r-2)^2 = 0\). Double root \(r = 2\). Both \(e^{2x}\) and \(xe^{2x}\) are homogeneous solutions. Try \(y_p = Ax^2 e^{2x}\).

\[y_p' = A(2x + 2x^2)e^{2x}, \quad y_p'' = A(2 + 8x + 4x^2)e^{2x}\] \[A(2 + 8x + 4x^2)e^{2x} - 4A(2x + 2x^2)e^{2x} + 4Ax^2 e^{2x} = 2Ae^{2x} = e^{2x}\] \[A = \frac{1}{2}, \quad y = (c_1 + c_2 x)e^{2x} + \frac{x^2}{2}e^{2x}\]

docs.title: Example 5 — Trigonometric Forcing
docs.text:
Problem: \(y'' + 9y = 2\sin(3x)\).

Characteristic: \(r^2 + 9 = 0\), roots \(\pm 3i\). The homogeneous solution contains \(\sin 3x\) and \(\cos 3x\) — resonance! Try \(y_p = x(A\cos 3x + B\sin 3x)\).

\[y_p' = (A\cos 3x + B\sin 3x) + x(-3A\sin 3x + 3B\cos 3x)$$ $$y_p'' = (-3A\sin 3x + 3B\cos 3x) + (-3A\sin 3x + 3B\cos 3x) + x(-9A\cos 3x - 9B\sin 3x)$$ $$= 6B\cos 3x - 6A\sin 3x - 9x(A\cos 3x + B\sin 3x)\] \[y_p'' + 9y_p = 6B\cos 3x - 6A\sin 3x = 2\sin 3x\]

Matching: \(6B = 0 \Rightarrow B = 0\) and \(-6A = 2 \Rightarrow A = -\frac{1}{3}\).

\[y = c_1\cos 3x + c_2\sin 3x - \frac{x}{3}\cos 3x\]

Physical meaning of resonance: The forcing \(\sin(3x)\) is at exactly the natural frequency of the oscillator (\(\omega_0 = 3\)). The system has no way to "absorb" the energy — each cycle, the driving force is perfectly in phase with the response, pumping in more energy. The amplitude grows without bound as \(\frac{x}{3}\cos 3x\). In a physical system with no damping, this is catastrophic. Resonance is why bridges need careful engineering and why MRI machines have such tight frequency tolerances.

docs.title: Example 6 — Sum of Forcing Terms
docs.text:
Problem: \(y'' + 4y = x + e^x + \sin 2x\).

Roots: \(\pm 2i\). Homogeneous: \(c_1\cos 2x + c_2\sin 2x\).

Decompose \(g = g_1 + g_2 + g_3\) and find \(y_{p1}\), \(y_{p2}\), \(y_{p3}\) separately.

\(g_1 = x\): Trial \(Ax + B\) (no resonance). \(4(Ax + B) = x \Rightarrow A = 1/4\), \(B = 0\). So \(y_{p1} = x/4\).

\(g_2 = e^x\): Trial \(Ae^x\). \((1 + 4)Ae^x = e^x \Rightarrow A = 1/5\). So \(y_{p2} = e^x/5\).

\(g_3 = \sin 2x\): \(\sin 2x\) is a homogeneous solution (resonance, \(s = 1\)). Trial \(x(A\cos 2x + B\sin 2x)\).

\[y_{p3}'' + 4y_{p3} = -4B\cos 2x + 4A\sin 2x\cdot(-1) = \sin 2x\]

Wait — let me redo: working through as in Example 5 with \(\omega = 2\):

\[y_{p3}'' + 4y_{p3} = 4A\cos 2x + 4B\sin 2x \cdot (\ldots)\]

Differentiating \(y_{p3} = x(A\cos 2x + B\sin 2x)\): $\(y_{p3}'' = -4x(A\cos 2x + B\sin 2x) + (-4A\sin 2x + 4B\cos 2x)\)$ $\(y_{p3}'' + 4y_{p3} = 4B\cos 2x - 4A\sin 2x = \sin 2x\)$

So \(4B = 0\), \(-4A = 1 \Rightarrow A = -1/4\). Thus \(y_{p3} = -\frac{x}{4}\cos 2x\).

\[y = c_1\cos 2x + c_2\sin 2x + \frac{x}{4} + \frac{e^x}{5} - \frac{x}{4}\cos 2x\]

docs.title: 3.1 Motivation
docs.text:
Undetermined coefficients is fast but has two crippling restrictions:

  1. The equation must have constant coefficients.
  2. \(g(x)\) must belong to the "nice" family (polynomials \(\times\) exponentials \(\times\) trig).

Variation of parameters works for any \(g(x)\) and any equation where we can find a fundamental set — including variable-coefficient equations.

The price: we must compute two integrals, which may not have closed forms.

docs.title: 3.2 Derivation from First Principles
docs.text:
Given the fundamental set \({y_1, y_2}\) of \(L[y] = 0\), promote the constants to functions:

\[y_p = u_1(x)y_1(x) + u_2(x)y_2(x)\]

We have two unknowns \(u_1, u_2\) and one equation \(L[y_p] = g\). We impose a constraint to simplify — specifically, to eliminate second derivatives of \(u_1, u_2\):

\[\textbf{Constraint: } u_1'y_1 + u_2'y_2 = 0 \tag{C}\]

Under this constraint, differentiate \(y_p\):

\[y_p' = u_1'y_1 + u_1 y_1' + u_2'y_2 + u_2 y_2' = u_1 y_1' + u_2 y_2' \quad \text{(using C)}\] \[y_p'' = u_1'y_1' + u_1 y_1'' + u_2'y_2' + u_2 y_2''\]

Substitute into \(y_p'' + p y_p' + q y_p = g\):

\[u_1'y_1' + u_1 y_1'' + u_2'y_2' + u_2 y_2'' + p(u_1 y_1' + u_2 y_2') + q(u_1 y_1 + u_2 y_2) = g\] \[u_1'y_1' + u_2'y_2' + u_1(y_1'' + py_1' + qy_1) + u_2(y_2'' + py_2' + qy_2) = g\]

Since \(y_1, y_2\) solve \(L[y] = 0\), the bracketed terms vanish:

\[\textbf{ODE condition: } u_1'y_1' + u_2'y_2' = g \tag{ODE}\]

docs.title: 3.3 The System and Its Solution
docs.text:
Equations (C) and (ODE) form a \(2 \times 2\) linear system for \(u_1'\) and \(u_2'\):

\[\begin{pmatrix} y_1 & y_2 \ y_1' & y_2' \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} u_1' \ u_2' \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \ g \end{pmatrix}\]

The coefficient matrix has determinant \(W(x) = y_1 y_2' - y_1' y_2 \neq 0\). By Cramer's rule:

\[u_1' = -\frac{y_2 g}{W}, \qquad u_2' = \frac{y_1 g}{W}\]

Integrating:

\[u_1(x) = -\int \frac{y_2(x), g(x)}{W(x)},dx, \qquad u_2(x) = \int \frac{y_1(x), g(x)}{W(x)},dx\]

The particular solution:

\[\boxed{y_p(x) = -y_1(x)\int \frac{y_2(x), g(x)}{W(x)},dx + y_2(x)\int \frac{y_1(x), g(x)}{W(x)},dx}\]

docs.title: 3.4 The Formula as a Green's Function
docs.text:
Combining the integrals:

\[y_p(x) = \int_{x_0}^x \frac{y_1(t)y_2(x) - y_1(x)y_2(t)}{W(t)}, g(t),dt = \int_{x_0}^x G(x,t), g(t),dt\]

where \(G(x,t) = \frac{y_1(t)y_2(x) - y_1(x)y_2(t)}{W(t)}\) is the Green's function of the operator \(L\) (with initial conditions). The particular solution is the convolution of the Green's function with the forcing — every forcing value \(g(t)\) is weighted by how much influence it has at position \(x\), given by \(G(x,t)\).

docs.title: Example 7 — Variation of Parameters with Trig Denominator
docs.text:
Problem: \(y'' + y = \sec x\), \(x \in (-\pi/2, \pi/2)\).

Undetermined coefficients fails: \(\sec x\) is not in the "nice" family.

Homogeneous: \(r^2 + 1 = 0\), \(y_1 = \cos x\), \(y_2 = \sin x\).

Wronskian: \(W = \cos x \cos x - (-\sin x)\sin x = \cos^2 x + \sin^2 x = 1\).

\[u_1' = -\frac{\sin x \cdot \sec x}{1} = -\frac{\sin x}{\cos x} = -\tan x\] \[u_2' = \frac{\cos x \cdot \sec x}{1} = 1\]

Integrating:

\[u_1 = \int (-\tan x),dx = \ln|\cos x|, \qquad u_2 = x\] \[y_p = \cos x \cdot \ln|\cos x| + x\sin x\] \[y = c_1\cos x + c_2\sin x + \cos x\ln|\cos x| + x\sin x\]

docs.title: Example 8 — Variable Coefficient Equation
docs.text:
Problem: \(x^2 y'' - 2xy' + 2y = x^3\ln x\), \(x > 0\).

This is an Euler–Cauchy equation. The homogeneous equation \(x^2 y'' - 2xy' + 2y = 0\) has solutions found via \(y = x^m\):

\(m(m-1) - 2m + 2 = m^2 - 3m + 2 = (m-1)(m-2) = 0\), so \(y_1 = x\), \(y_2 = x^2\).

Wronskian: \(W = x \cdot 2x - 1 \cdot x^2 = x^2\).

Divide the ODE by \(x^2\) to get standard form: \(y'' - \frac{2}{x}y' + \frac{2}{x^2}y = x\ln x\).

So \(g(x) = x\ln x\).

\[u_1' = -\frac{x^2 \cdot x\ln x}{x^2} = -x\ln x\] \[u_2' = \frac{x \cdot x\ln x}{x^2} = \ln x\]

Integrating by parts:

\[u_1 = -\int x\ln x,dx = -\frac{x^2}{2}\ln x + \frac{x^2}{4}\] \[u_2 = \int \ln x,dx = x\ln x - x\] \[y_p = x\left(-\frac{x^2}{2}\ln x + \frac{x^2}{4}\right) + x^2(x\ln x - x) = -\frac{x^3}{2}\ln x + \frac{x^3}{4} + x^3\ln x - x^3\] \[y_p = \frac{x^3}{2}\ln x - \frac{3x^3}{4}\]

Since \(-\frac{3}{4}x^3\) looks like it could be absorbed (but \(x^3\) is not a homogeneous solution — check: \(y_1 = x\), \(y_2 = x^2\), so \(x^3\) is genuinely particular):

\[y = c_1 x + c_2 x^2 + \frac{x^3}{2}\ln x - \frac{3x^3}{4}\]

docs.title: Example 9 — When Integrals Don't Close
docs.text:
Problem: \(y'' + y = \frac{1}{1 + x^2}\).

Homogeneous: \(y_1 = \cos x\), \(y_2 = \sin x\), \(W = 1\).

\[u_1' = -\frac{\sin x}{1 + x^2}, \qquad u_2' = \frac{\cos x}{1 + x^2}\]

These integrals have no closed form in elementary functions. But the existence of the solution is guaranteed; we write:

\[y_p = -\cos x \int_0^x \frac{\sin t}{1 + t^2},dt + \sin x \int_0^x \frac{\cos t}{1 + t^2},dt\]

This is a perfectly valid, well-defined function — it just cannot be written in closed form. Numerically, it is computed as easily as any integral. This is why variation of parameters is the theoretically complete method: it always produces the answer, even when the answer is not "nice."

docs.title: § 4 — The Operator Method and Exponential Shift
4.1 The Annihilator Method
docs.text:
For constant coefficient equations, there is an elegant operator-theoretic method that systematizes undetermined coefficients.

The differential operator \(D = d/dx\) acts on functions. The ODE \(L[y] = ay'' + by' + cy = g\) is written as:

\[L(D)y = (aD^2 + bD + c)y = g\]

For the trial to work, we need \(L(D)[y_p] = g\). If we can find a differential operator \(A(D)\) — the annihilator — such that \(A(D)[g] = 0\), then applying \(A(D)\) to both sides:

\[A(D)L(D)[y] = 0\]

This is now a homogeneous equation with characteristic polynomial \(A(r)L(r) = 0\). Its general solution contains \(y_h\) (from \(L(r) = 0\)) plus extra terms from \(A(r) = 0\). These extra terms form the trial \(y_p\) — we substitute back into the original equation to find the coefficients.

Annihilators for common functions:

\(g(x)\) Annihilator \(A(D)\) \(x^n\) \(D^{n+1}\) \(e^{\alpha x}\) \(D - \alpha\) \(e^{\alpha x}x^n\) \((D - \alpha)^{n+1}\) \(\cos\beta x\) or \(\sin\beta x\) \(D^2 + \beta^2\) \(e^{\alpha x}\cos\beta x\) or \(e^{\alpha x}\sin\beta x\) \((D - \alpha)^2 + \beta^2\)

Example: \(y'' + 4y = x\cos 2x\).

Annihilator of \(x\cos 2x\): \((D^2 + 4)^2\) (since \(e^{0 \cdot x}\cos 2x\) has annihilator \((D^2 + 4)\), and the extra \(x\) requires squaring).

Apply \((D^2 + 4)^2\) to both sides: \((D^2 + 4)^3 y = 0\).

Characteristic roots of \((r^2 + 4)^3 = 0\): \(r = \pm 2i\) (each with multiplicity 3).

General solution of \((D^2 + 4)^3 y = 0\): $\(y = (c_1 + c_2 x + c_3 x^2)\cos 2x + (c_4 + c_5 x + c_6 x^2)\sin 2x\)$

The homogeneous part of the original (from \((D^2 + 4)y = 0\)): \(c_1\cos 2x + c_4\sin 2x\). The particular trial is the remaining part: \((c_2 x + c_3 x^2)\cos 2x + (c_5 x + c_6 x^2)\sin 2x\). Substitute into the original ODE to find the four free coefficients.

docs.title: 4.2 The Exponential Shift Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem. For any polynomial \(p(D)\) with constant coefficients: $\(p(D)[e^{\alpha x} f(x)] = e^{\alpha x} p(D + \alpha)[f(x)]\)$

Proof. By direct computation using the product rule and the fact that \(D[e^{\alpha x}] = \alpha e^{\alpha x}\): $\(D[e^{\alpha x} f] = e^{\alpha x}(\alpha f + f') = e^{\alpha x}(D + \alpha)[f]\)$

Iterating: \(D^n[e^{\alpha x}f] = e^{\alpha x}(D + \alpha)^n[f]\). Linearity extends to any polynomial. \(\blacksquare\)

Application: To find \(y_p\) for \(p(D)[y] = e^{\alpha x}g(x)\), write \(y_p = e^{\alpha x}v(x)\):

\[e^{\alpha x}p(D + \alpha)[v] = e^{\alpha x}g(x) \implies p(D + \alpha)[v] = g(x)\]

This replaces the original operator with a shifted operator — often simpler.

Example: \((D - 2)^2 y = e^{2x}\sin x\).

Try \(y_p = e^{2x}v\). Then \((D - 2)^2[e^{2x}v] = e^{2x}D^2[v] = e^{2x}\sin x\).

So \(v'' = \sin x \Rightarrow v = -\sin x\). Thus \(y_p = -e^{2x}\sin x\).

Check: \((D-2)^2[-e^{2x}\sin x] = e^{2x}D^2[-\sin x] = e^{2x}\sin x\). ✓

docs.title: § 5 — Superposition for Multiple Forcing Terms
docs.text:
A direct consequence of linearity:

Principle of Superposition. If \(y_{p_k}\) is a particular solution of \(L[y] = g_k(x)\) for \(k = 1, 2, \ldots, n\), then \(y_p = \sum_{k=1}^n c_k y_{p_k}\) is a particular solution of \(L[y] = \sum_{k=1}^n c_k g_k(x)\).

Proof: \(L\left[\sum c_k y_{p_k}\right] = \sum c_k L[y_{p_k}] = \sum c_k g_k\). \(\blacksquare\)

This is why, in Example 6, we found three separate \(y_p\)'s and added them. It is also why Fourier series is so powerful for PDEs: we can solve for each Fourier component separately, then superpose.

docs.title: § 6 — Choosing the Right Method
docs.text:
Condition Method to Use Why Constant coefficients, \(g\) is polynomial \(\times\) exp \(\times\) trig Undetermined coefficients Fast, systematic, no integration needed Constant coefficients, \(g\) is complex (e.g., \(\sec x\), \(\ln x\), \(1/(1+x^2)\)) Variation of parameters Handles any \(g\) Variable coefficients (non-Euler) with known \({y_1, y_2}\) Variation of parameters Only method that applies Euler–Cauchy equation Reduce to constant coefficients via \(x = e^t\), then either method Need explicit operator algebra, complex \(g\) decomposes nicely Annihilator method More systematic than guessing Many superposed forcing terms Superposition + undetermined coefficients One trial per term

Common mistake to avoid: Choosing undetermined coefficients when \(g\) has a resonant term, forgetting to multiply by \(x^s\). Always check whether each component of the trial solves the homogeneous equation.

docs.title: § 7 — The Full Solution Pipeline
docs.text:
For any nonhomogeneous linear second order ODE:

Step 1: Write in standard form y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = g(x)

Step 2: Solve L[y] = 0
        → Find characteristic roots (constant coeff)
        → Or use reduction of order, series, etc.
        → Get fundamental set {y₁, y₂}

Step 3: Find one particular solution yₚ
        → Undetermined coefficients (if applicable)
        → Variation of parameters (always works)

Step 4: Write y = c₁y₁ + c₂y₂ + yₚ

Step 5: If IVP/BVP given, apply conditions to find c₁, c₂

docs.title: § 8 — The RLC Circuit: The Canonical Physical Model
docs.text:
The equation:

\[L\ddot{q} + R\dot{q} + \frac{1}{C}q = \mathcal{E}(t)\]

where \(q(t)\) is charge, \(\mathcal{E}(t)\) is the EMF source, models an RLC circuit.

Rewriting: \(\ddot{q} + \frac{R}{L}\dot{q} + \frac{1}{LC}q = \frac{\mathcal{E}(t)}{L}\).

This is \(L[q] = g(t)\) with \(p = R/L\), \(q_{\text{coeff}} = 1/LC\), \(g = \mathcal{E}/L\).

Forced oscillations with \(\mathcal{E}(t) = E_0\cos\omega t\):

The particular solution represents the steady-state response: $\(q_p = \frac{E_0/L}{\sqrt{(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)^2 + (R\omega/L)^2}}\cos(\omega t - \delta)\)$

where \(\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}\) and \(\delta = \arctan\left(\frac{R\omega/L}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2}\right)\).

The homogeneous solution \(q_h\) (transient) decays to zero if \(R > 0\). The particular solution \(q_p\) (steady state) persists. In the long run, only \(y_p\) matters — the particular solution is the physically observable behavior.

  q(t)
   |     Transient (yₕ)        Total response (y = yₕ + yₚ)
   |   /\/\/\/\/\___            /\/\/\/\___________
   |  /               ‾‾‾---   /                  ~~~~~~~~~~
   |_/_________________________________> t
                              Steady state (yₚ) persists

docs.title: § 9 — Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
9.1 The Homogeneous/Particular Split in Representation Learning
docs.text:
The structure theorem says every solution is \(y = y_h + y_p\):

  • \(y_h\): lives in the null space of \(L\) — determined by initial conditions, independent of the forcing.
  • \(y_p\): the particular response to the forcing — depends entirely on \(g\), not on initial conditions.

In deep learning, this decomposition appears in the study of neural network representations:

  • The null space of the linear map at each layer corresponds to directions in weight space that do not affect the output. Training ignores these directions — they are the "homogeneous" part.
  • The particular solution corresponds to the minimum-norm solution found by gradient descent when the loss is underdetermined. The Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse gives this minimum-norm solution — the direct linear algebra analogue of variation of parameters.

docs.title: 9.2 Undetermined Coefficients and Basis Functions in ML
docs.text:
The idea of undetermined coefficients — guessing a function form and solving for coefficients — is the philosophy behind:

Basis function regression: Model \(f(x) = \sum_{k=1}^n w_k \phi_k(x)\) where \(\phi_k\) are fixed basis functions (polynomials, RBFs, Fourier modes). Fitting \(w_k\) to data is undetermined coefficients for the statistical operator \(\mathcal{L}[f] = f - \text{data}\).

Kernel methods (SVMs, Gaussian Processes): The kernel is a Green's function. The GP prediction \(\mu(x) = \int K(x, x') \alpha(x'),dx'\) is variation of parameters — the forcing \(g = \alpha(x')\) (the support vectors or posterior weights) is convolved with the Green's function \(K(x, x')\) of the kernel operator.

Neural tangent kernel (NTK): In the infinite-width limit, training a neural network is governed by the NTK, and the solution to the training dynamics is:

\[\mathbf{f}(t) = \mathbf{f}(\infty) + e^{-\Theta t}(\mathbf{f}(0) - \mathbf{f}(\infty))\]

This is exactly the structure theorem: \(\mathbf{f}(\infty)\) is the particular solution (the target), and \(e^{-\Theta t}(\mathbf{f}(0) - \mathbf{f}(\infty))\) is the homogeneous part (decaying transient from initial conditions). Training is convergence of the transient to zero.

docs.title: 9.3 Forcing and Fine-Tuning: Transfer Learning as Nonhomogeneous ODE
docs.text:
Pretrain a model on a large dataset (find \(y_h\) — the homogeneous solution, the "soul" of the model). Fine-tune on a small task-specific dataset (add \(y_p\) — the particular solution, the task-specific response to the "forcing" of the new data).

The total model \(= y_h + y_p\) (pretrained knowledge + task adaptation). The structure theorem says: \(y_p\) is not unique — any particular solution works, and the constants in \(y_h\) absorb the difference. In practice, different fine-tuning methods (LoRA, adapters, full fine-tuning) correspond to different choices of \(y_p\). LoRA, in particular, restricts \(y_p\) to be low-rank — a structured ansatz, analogous to undetermined coefficients (guess a restricted form, solve for coefficients).

docs.title: 9.4 Resonance and Adversarial Examples
docs.text:
Resonance in the ODE occurs when the forcing frequency matches a natural frequency of the homogeneous equation — the response grows without bound.

The analogue in neural networks is adversarial examples: inputs that are precisely tuned to match the "natural frequencies" of the network's decision boundary, producing catastrophically wrong outputs with imperceptible input changes. Just as resonance is not a bug in the ODE (it is mathematically correct behavior) but is catastrophic physically, adversarial sensitivity is a mathematically correct consequence of the network's geometry, but practically disastrous.

More formally: the Hessian of the loss \(\nabla^2 \mathcal{L}\) has eigenvectors — directions of sharp curvature. Perturbing inputs in these directions (the "resonant modes") causes the largest change in the output. Adversarial attacks are, in this sense, forcing at the resonant frequency of the network operator.

docs.title: 9.5 Variation of Parameters and Attention
docs.text:
Variation of parameters computes:

\[y_p(x) = \int G(x, t) g(t),dt\]

The Green's function \(G(x,t)\) weights the forcing at \(t\) by its influence at \(x\). Self-attention computes:

\[\text{Output}_i = \sum_j A_{ij} V_j\]

where \(A_{ij} = \text{softmax}(Q_i \cdot K_j^T / \sqrt{d})\) weights the values \(V_j\) by the relevance of position \(j\) to position \(i\). This is a discrete, learned variation of parameters: \(A_{ij}\) is a data-dependent Green's function, \(V_j\) is the "forcing" at position \(j\), and the output is the "particular solution" at position \(i\).

The key difference: in classical VoP, \(G(x,t)\) is determined by the differential operator. In attention, \(A_{ij}\) is learned from data — the network discovers its own Green's function.

docs.title: 9.6 Superposition and Ensemble Methods
docs.text:
The principle of superposition — \(L[y] = \sum g_k \Rightarrow y_p = \sum y_{p_k}\) — is the theoretical basis of ensemble methods in machine learning:

  • Gradient boosting: Sequentially solve for \(y_{p_k}\) where each \(g_k\) is the residual from the previous model. The total model \(\sum y_{p_k}\) is the superposition of particular solutions to residual forcing terms.
  • Mixture of Experts (MoE): Each expert handles a "component" of the forcing function (the input distribution). The gating network superimposes expert outputs — a learned superposition of particular solutions.
  • Random forests: Each tree is a particular solution to a noisy version of the forcing (bootstrap sample). The ensemble average superimposes, reducing variance while maintaining consistency.

docs.title: 9.7 Steady State, Transients, and Training Dynamics
docs.text:
The ODE decomposition \(y = y_h + y_p\) with \(y_h\) decaying (transient) and \(y_p\) persisting (steady state) is mirrored in neural network training:

  • Early training (transient phase): The network is far from the optimum. The homogeneous component (the response to initial conditions — random initialization) dominates. The loss decreases rapidly.
  • Late training (steady state): The transient has decayed. The network is near \(y_p\) — the particular solution corresponding to the data. The loss plateaus. Further training does not help.

Learning rate warmup delays the forcing ramp-up, letting the optimizer "find its feet" — analogous to turning on the forcing \(g(x)\) gradually to avoid resonant transients. Cosine annealing mirrors the smooth approach to steady state of a damped forced oscillator.

docs.title: § 10 — Common Mistakes and Pitfalls
docs.text: Mistake What goes wrong Fix Not checking for resonance in undetermined coefficients Substituting a homogeneous solution as trial gives \(0 = g\); coefficients are undetermined Check each component of the trial against every homogeneous solution; multiply by \(x^s\) Forgetting the constraint \(u_1'y_1 + u_2'y_2 = 0\) in VoP derivation Without the constraint, the system is underdetermined and the algebra doesn't simplify The constraint is a choice — it is the price for having only first derivatives of \(u_1, u_2\) in the equations Using the non-standard form in VoP VoP formula assumes the leading coefficient is 1 Always divide by \(P(x)\) first; \(g(x)\) in the formula is \(g/P\), not the original right-hand side Adding particular solutions that differ by a homogeneous solution This gives a "wrong" looking \(y_p\) but is actually fine Any particular solution works; the constants \(c_1, c_2\) absorb the difference Applying undetermined coefficients to variable-coefficient equations The method fails — differentiating \(p(x)y\) introduces new functions that cannot be matched Use variation of parameters or reduce to a solvable form Thinking the particular solution must satisfy any boundary/initial condition \(y_p\) is just one solution; \(c_1, c_2\) are determined by the conditions Apply BCs/ICs to the full solution \(y_h + y_p\), not to \(y_p\) alone

docs.title: The Master Formula
docs.text:
\[\boxed{y = \underbrace{c_1 y_1 + c_2 y_2}_{y_h} + \underbrace{y_p}_{\text{particular}}}\]

where \({y_1, y_2}\) is the fundamental set of \(L[y] = 0\) and \(y_p\) is any solution of \(L[y] = g\).

docs.title: Finding \(y_p\): Decision Tree
docs.text:
Is the equation constant-coefficient?
│
├─ YES: Is g(x) a polynomial × exponential × trig product?
│       │
│       ├─ YES: Undetermined Coefficients
│       │         → Identify trial form from table
│       │         → Check for resonance → multiply by xˢ
│       │         → Substitute and match coefficients
│       │
│       └─ NO:  Variation of Parameters
│
└─ NO:  Do you have the fundamental set {y₁, y₂}?
        │
        ├─ YES: Variation of Parameters
        │         u₁' = -y₂g/W,  u₂' = y₁g/W
        │         yₚ = u₁y₁ + u₂y₂
        │
        └─ NO:  Find {y₁, y₂} first (series, reduction of order, etc.)

docs.title: The Wronskian Reminder
docs.text: \[W(y_1, y_2)(x) = y_1 y_2' - y_1' y_2 \neq 0 \quad \text{(Abel: either always 0 or never 0)}\]

docs.title: Undetermined Coefficients
docs.text: "The beauty of this method is not that it always works — it is that when it works, it works with remarkable elegance."

docs.title: § 0 — Personal Preamble
docs.text:
This note lives at the intersection of structure and intuition. The method of undetermined coefficients is, at its heart, an educated guess made rigorous. We exploit the fact that certain families of functions are closed under differentiation — polynomials differentiate to polynomials, exponentials to exponentials, sinusoids to sinusoids. If the forcing function \(g(x)\) belongs to one of these families, we can guess the form of a particular solution, plug it in, and determine the coefficients algebraically.

It is not magic. It is pattern recognition elevated to theorem.

References consulted:

  • Stewart, James. Calculus, 8th ed. — §17.2
  • MIT OCW 18.02 Multivariable Calculus (Supplementary ODE notes)

docs.title: § 1 — The Setup: Second-Order Linear ODEs
docs.text:
We are working with equations of the form:

\[ay'' + by' + cy = g(x) \tag{1}\]

where \(a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}\), \(a \neq 0\), and \(g(x)\) is the forcing function (or nonhomogeneous term).

docs.title: The General Solution Decomposition
docs.text:
Theorem (Structure of the General Solution). Let \(y_c\) be the complementary solution — the general solution to the associated homogeneous equation \(ay'' + by' + cy = 0\) — and let \(y_p\) be any particular solution to \((1)\). Then every solution to \((1)\) is of the form: $\(y = y_c + y_p\)$

Proof sketch. If \(y\) solves \((1)\) and \(y_p\) solves \((1)\), then \(y - y_p\) satisfies the homogeneous equation (by linearity of \(L = aD^2 + bD + c\)). Hence \(y - y_p = y_c\) for some \(y_c \in \ker(L)\). \(\blacksquare\)

The method of undetermined coefficients is a systematic procedure for finding \(y_p\) when \(g(x)\) has a particular form.

docs.title: § 2 — The Admissible Forms of \(g(x)\)
docs.text:
The method applies when \(g(x)\) is a finite linear combination of functions from the following table:

Type of \(g(x)\) Trial Form \(y_p\) \(P_n(x)\) (polynomial of degree \(n\)) \(A_nx^n + A_{n-1}x^{n-1} + \cdots + A_0\) \(e^{\alpha x}\) \(Ae^{\alpha x}\) \(\cos(\beta x)\) or \(\sin(\beta x)\) \(A\cos(\beta x) + B\sin(\beta x)\) \(P_n(x)e^{\alpha x}\) \((A_nx^n + \cdots + A_0)e^{\alpha x}\) \(e^{\alpha x}\cos(\beta x)\) or \(e^{\alpha x}\sin(\beta x)\) \(e^{\alpha x}(A\cos(\beta x) + B\sin(\beta x))\) Products/sums of the above Products/sums of corresponding trial forms

Why these families? Because \(\frac{d}{dx}\) maps each family into itself. A polynomial differentiates to a polynomial. An exponential \(e^{\alpha x}\) differentiates to \(\alpha e^{\alpha x}\). A sinusoid differentiates to another sinusoid. This closure property guarantees that \(L[y_p]\) will have the same structural form as \(g(x)\), making coefficient matching possible.

docs.title: § 3 — The Algorithm
docs.text:
Step 1. Solve the homogeneous equation \(ay'' + by' + cy = 0\) to find \(y_c\).

Step 2. Identify the form of \(g(x)\) and write down the trial particular solution \(y_p\) with undetermined coefficients.

Step 3 (Modification Rule — Critical!). If any term in \(y_p\) duplicates a term in \(y_c\), multiply that term (or the entire trial solution if \(y_c\) has repeated roots matching the trial) by \(x^s\), where \(s\) is the smallest positive integer that eliminates the duplication.

Step 4. Substitute \(y_p\) into the ODE. Equate coefficients of like terms. Solve the resulting algebraic system.

Step 5. Write the general solution: \(y = y_c + y_p\).

docs.title: Example 1 — Polynomial Forcing
docs.text:
\[y'' - 3y' + 2y = 4x^2\]

Step 1: Homogeneous solution. Characteristic equation: \(r^2 - 3r + 2 = 0 \Rightarrow (r-1)(r-2) = 0\). $\(y_c = C_1 e^x + C_2 e^{2x}\)$

Step 2: Trial solution. \(g(x) = 4x^2\) is a degree-2 polynomial, so try: $\(y_p = Ax^2 + Bx + C\)$

Step 3: No overlap with \(y_c\) (which contains only exponentials). No modification needed.

Step 4: Substitute. $\(y_p'' - 3y_p' + 2y_p = 2A - 3(2Ax + B) + 2(Ax^2 + Bx + C)\)$ $\(= 2Ax^2 + (-6A + 2B)x + (2A - 3B + 2C) = 4x^2\)$

Matching coefficients:

  • \(x^2\): \(2A = 4 \Rightarrow A = 2\)
  • \(x^1\): \(-6A + 2B = 0 \Rightarrow B = 6\)
  • \(x^0\): \(2A - 3B + 2C = 0 \Rightarrow C = 7\)
\[y_p = 2x^2 + 6x + 7\]

General solution: $\(\boxed{y = C_1 e^x + C_2 e^{2x} + 2x^2 + 6x + 7}\)$

docs.title: Example 2 — Exponential Forcing (No Resonance)
docs.text:
\[y'' + y' - 2y = 3e^{4x}\]

Homogeneous: \(r^2 + r - 2 = (r+2)(r-1) = 0\), so \(y_c = C_1 e^{-2x} + C_2 e^x\).

Trial: \(y_p = Ae^{4x}\). No overlap with \(y_c\).

Substitute: \(16Ae^{4x} + 4Ae^{4x} - 2Ae^{4x} = 3e^{4x}\) $\(18A = 3 \Rightarrow A = \frac{1}{6}\)$

\[\boxed{y = C_1 e^{-2x} + C_2 e^x + \frac{1}{6}e^{4x}}\]

docs.title: Example 3 — Resonance (The Modification Rule in Action)
docs.text:
\[y'' - y' = 2e^x\]

Homogeneous: \(r^2 - r = r(r-1) = 0\), so \(y_c = C_1 + C_2 e^x\).

Trial attempt: \(y_p = Ae^x\). PROBLEM: \(e^x\) already appears in \(y_c\)!

Modification: Multiply by \(x\): \(y_p = Axe^x\).

Substitute: $\(y_p' = Ae^x + Axe^x, \quad y_p'' = 2Ae^x + Axe^x\)$ $\(y_p'' - y_p' = (2Ae^x + Axe^x) - (Ae^x + Axe^x) = Ae^x = 2e^x\)$ $\(A = 2\)$

\[\boxed{y = C_1 + C_2 e^x + 2xe^x}\]

Why does resonance require \(x\)-multiplication? Physically: when the natural frequency of the system matches the forcing frequency, energy accumulates — the response grows. Mathematically: \(e^x \in \ker(L)\), so \(L[Ae^x] = 0 \neq 2e^x\). The factor of \(x\) "shifts" the trial solution out of the kernel.

docs.title: Example 4 — Sinusoidal Forcing
docs.text:
\[y'' + 4y = \sin(3x)\]

Homogeneous: \(r^2 + 4 = 0 \Rightarrow r = \pm 2i\), so \(y_c = C_1\cos(2x) + C_2\sin(2x)\).

Trial: \(y_p = A\cos(3x) + B\sin(3x)\). No overlap (frequency 3 ≠ 2).

Substitute: $\(y_p'' + 4y_p = (-9A + 4A)\cos(3x) + (-9B + 4B)\sin(3x)\)$ $\(= -5A\cos(3x) - 5B\sin(3x) = \sin(3x)\)$

So \(A = 0\), \(B = -\frac{1}{5}\).

\[\boxed{y = C_1\cos(2x) + C_2\sin(2x) - \frac{1}{5}\sin(3x)}\]

Note on sinusoids: Always include both \(\cos\) and \(\sin\) in the trial, even if \(g(x)\) contains only one of them. Differentiation mixes them.

docs.title: Example 5 — Superposition of Forcing Terms
docs.text:
\[y'' - 2y' + y = xe^x + \cos x\]

Homogeneous: \((r-1)^2 = 0 \Rightarrow r = 1\) (repeated), so \(y_c = (C_1 + C_2 x)e^x\).

Use superposition: \(g(x) = g_1(x) + g_2(x)\) where \(g_1 = xe^x\) and \(g_2 = \cos x\).

For \(g_1 = xe^x\): Trial would be \((Ax + B)e^x\), but \(e^x\) and \(xe^x\) are both in \(y_c\) (repeated root!). Multiply by \(x^2\): $\(y_{p_1} = x^2(Ax + B)e^x = (Ax^3 + Bx^2)e^x\)$

After substitution: \(6Ax + 2B = x \Rightarrow A = \frac{1}{6},, B = 0\). $\(y_{p_1} = \frac{x^3}{6}e^x\)$

For \(g_2 = \cos x\): Trial \(y_{p_2} = A\cos x + B\sin x\) (no overlap).

After substitution: \(A = 0,, B = \frac{1}{2}\). $\(y_{p_2} = \frac{1}{2}\sin x\)$

General solution: $\(\boxed{y = (C_1 + C_2 x)e^x + \frac{x^3}{6}e^x + \frac{1}{2}\sin x}\)$

docs.title: § 5 — Visualization: The Anatomy of a Resonant Solution
docs.text:
Consider \(y'' + \omega_0^2 y = \cos(\omega_0 t)\) (pure resonance).

Amplitude
    ^
    |                           /\
    |                          /  \
    |                   /\    /    \
    |                  /  \  /      \
    |           /\    /    \/        \
    |          /  \  /               ------>  t
    |----/\---/    \/
    |   /  \/
    |--/

    y_c: bounded oscillation (dashed)
    y_p: t·sin(ω₀t) — GROWING envelope (solid)

    The amplitude grows linearly in time → unbounded

The particular solution under resonance is \(y_p = \frac{t}{2\omega_0}\sin(\omega_0 t)\). The factor of \(t\) is precisely the \(x\)-multiplication from the modification rule — it encodes the secular growth.

docs.title: § 6 — The Modification Rule: A Rigorous Justification
docs.text:
Theorem (Annihilator Interpretation). The trial solution must be chosen so that \(y_p otin \ker(L)\). If the natural guess \( ilde{y}_p \in \ker(L)\), then \(L[ ilde{y}_p] = 0\) identically, making it impossible to match the nonzero \(g(x)\). Multiplying by \(x^s\) uses the fact that if \(r_0\) is a root of the characteristic polynomial of multiplicity \(m\), then \(x^k e^{r_0 x}\) (for \(k < m\)) is in \(\ker(L)\), but \(x^m e^{r_0 x}\) is not.

More precisely: if \(r_0\) is a root of multiplicity \(m\), then: $\(\ker(L) i e^{r_0 x}, xe^{r_0 x}, \ldots, x^{m-1}e^{r_0 x}\)$ but \(x^m e^{r_0 x} otin \ker(L)\).

So \(s = m\) (the multiplicity of the overlap) is the correct shift.

docs.title: § 7 — When This Method Fails (And What To Do)
docs.text:
The method of undetermined coefficients is not universal. It fails when \(g(x)\) is:

  • \(\ln x\), \(x^{-1}\), \(\tan x\), \(\sec x\) — these are not closed under differentiation
  • Any function not expressible as a finite combination of the admissible types

In these cases, use: Variation of Parameters (Stewart §17.3), which works for any continuous \(g(x)\) and is more general but computationally heavier.

docs.title: § 8 — Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
docs.text: This is where classical analysis secretly lives inside modern learning systems.

docs.title: 8.1 — ODEs as Continuous-Time Dynamical Systems
docs.text:
Neural ODEs (Chen et al., 2018) replace discrete residual layers: $\(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} = \mathbf{h}_t + f(\mathbf{h}_t, \theta)\)$ with a continuous ODE: $\(\frac{d\mathbf{h}}{dt} = f(\mathbf{h}(t), t, \theta)\)$

Understanding particular solutions — how a system responds to forcing — is directly analogous to understanding how a network's hidden state evolves under the influence of input data.

docs.title: 8.2 — The Forcing Function as Input Signal
docs.text:
In a linear ODE model, \(g(x)\) is the input and \(y\) is the output. The particular solution \(y_p\) is the system's response to the input, while \(y_c\) encodes the intrinsic dynamics (how it behaves without input).

In signal processing and sequence modeling (RNNs, LSTMs, SSMs):

  • \(y_c\) ↔ hidden state dynamics (how the model evolves intrinsically)
  • \(y_p\) ↔ input-driven response (how the model reacts to data)

docs.title: 8.3 — State Space Models and Mamba
docs.text:
Modern State Space Models (e.g., Mamba, S4) are literally discretized versions of: $\(\mathbf{x}'(t) = A\mathbf{x}(t) + B\mathbf{u}(t)\)$ $\(\mathbf{y}(t) = C\mathbf{x}(t)\)$

This is a first-order linear ODE system with forcing \(B\mathbf{u}(t)\). The particular solution theory underpins the transfer function of these models — the frequency-domain characterization of how different inputs are amplified or suppressed.

docs.title: 8.4 — Resonance as Gradient Explosion / Instability
docs.text:
The resonance phenomenon (§4, §5) has a deep ML analogue: gradient explosion in RNNs. When the recurrent weight matrix has eigenvalues close to 1 (analogous to \(\omega_{\text{forcing}} \approx \omega_0\)), gradients grow without bound during backpropagation through time — mathematically the same secular growth as \(t\sin(\omega_0 t)\).

LSTM's gating mechanism and careful initialization (e.g., orthogonal initialization) are engineering solutions to this resonance problem.

docs.title: 8.5 — Fourier / Spectral Methods
docs.text:
The fact that \(\cos(\beta x)\) and \(\sin(\beta x)\) form closed families under \(L\) is the seed of spectral methods. In deep learning:

  • Attention mechanisms can be interpreted through the lens of kernel functions that decompose inputs spectrally
  • Positional encodings in Transformers use \(\sin\) and \(\cos\) precisely because they span a basis that is stable under linear operations — the same reason they work in undetermined coefficients

docs.title: 8.6 — Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs)
docs.text:
PINNs minimize: $\(\mathcal{L} = \underbrace{|L[u_\theta] - g|^2}_{\text{ODE residual}} + \underbrace{\text{boundary terms}}_{}\)$

Here \(u_\theta\) is a neural network approximating the solution. The particular solution \(y_p\) found by undetermined coefficients is the exact version of what a PINN tries to approximate. Understanding the analytic structure of \(y_p\) helps in initializing PINNs, choosing architectures, and diagnosing training failures.

docs.title: § 9 — Summary Table
docs.text: Situation Action \(g(x)\) is polynomial, exponential, sinusoid, or products/sums thereof Apply method of undetermined coefficients Trial \(y_p\) contains no term in \(y_c\) Use standard trial form Trial \(y_p\) overlaps with \(y_c\) Multiply by \(x^s\) where \(s\) = multiplicity of root \(g(x) = g_1 + g_2 + \cdots\) Use superposition: solve for each \(g_i\) separately, add results \(g(x)\) is a function not closed under differentiation Use Variation of Parameters

docs.title: § 10 — Exercises (Self-Diagnostics)
docs.text:
1. Find \(y_p\) for \(y'' + 2y' + y = e^{-x}\). (Hint: what is the multiplicity of \(r = -1\)?)

2. Find \(y_p\) for \(y'' - y = x^2 e^x\). (Modification rule applies.)

3. Verify that for \(y'' + \omega^2 y = \cos(\omega t)\), the particular solution is \(y_p = \frac{t}{2\omega}\sin(\omega t)\) by direct substitution.

4. (Theoretical) Show that if \(g(x) = e^{\alpha x}P_n(x)\cos(\beta x) + e^{\alpha x}Q_m(x)\sin(\beta x)\), the trial particular solution must include both cosine and sine terms with polynomials of degree \(\max(n,m)\).

5. (ML connection) Consider the linear RNN update \(h_{t+1} = ah_t + u_t\). Show that this is a discretization of \(h'(t) = (a-1)h(t) + u(t)\), and identify the conditions under which resonance (gradient explosion) occurs in terms of \(a\).

docs.title: § 11 — References
docs.text:
1. Stewart, James. Calculus: Early Transcendentals, 8th Edition. §17.2: Nonhomogeneous Linear Equations.
  2. MIT OpenCourseWare 18.02 — Supplementary ODE notes (Haynes Miller, Jeremy Orloff).
  3. Chen, R. T. Q. et al. (2018). Neural Ordinary Differential Equations. NeurIPS.
  4. Gu, A. et al. (2022). Efficiently Modeling Long Sequences with Structured State Spaces (S4).
  5. Raissi, M. et al. (2019). Physics-informed neural networks. Journal of Computational Physics.
