docs.title: Variation of Parameters
docs.text: "Where undetermined coefficients asks 'what shape should the answer be?', variation of parameters asks 'what if the constants were allowed to breathe?' — and in that breath, the entire method is born."

docs.title: § 0 — Personal Preamble
docs.text:
The method of undetermined coefficients is elegant but narrow — it demands that \(g(x)\) belong to a privileged family of functions closed under differentiation. The moment \(g(x) = \ln x\) or \(g(x) = \sec x\), the earlier method collapses.

Variation of parameters (due to Lagrange, 1774) is the universal answer. Its central idea is strikingly bold: take the complementary solution \(y_c = C_1 y_1 + C_2 y_2\) — which works because \(C_1, C_2\) are constants — and ask: what if they weren't? What if \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) were allowed to be functions of \(x\)?

This is not a trick. It is a systematic exploitation of the degrees of freedom that the homogeneous solution leaves behind.

References:

  • Stewart, James. Calculus, 8th ed. — §17.3
  • MIT OCW 18.02 — ODE supplementary notes (Haynes Miller)

docs.title: § 1 — The Setting
docs.text:
We work with the second-order linear ODE in standard form:

\[y'' + P(x)y' + Q(x)y = g(x) \tag{1}\]

Standard form is essential. If the equation is \(ay'' + by' + cy = g\), divide through by \(a\) first. The Wronskian formula below depends on the leading coefficient being 1.

Assume \(P, Q, g\) are continuous on an interval \(I\). Let \(y_1, y_2\) be two linearly independent solutions of the associated homogeneous equation:

\[y'' + P(x)y' + Q(x)y = 0 \tag{2}\]

So \(y_c = C_1 y_1 + C_2 y_2\).

docs.title: § 2 — The Core Idea: Letting the Constants Vary
docs.text:
Ansatz. Seek a particular solution of the form:

\[y_p = u_1(x), y_1(x) + u_2(x), y_2(x) \tag{3}\]

where \(u_1, u_2\) are unknown functions to be determined. This replaces the constants \(C_1, C_2\) with functions — hence the name.

We have two unknown functions but only one equation to satisfy. This gives us freedom to impose an additional constraint. We choose it to simplify the algebra.

docs.title: § 3 — Derivation (Full)
docs.text:
Differentiate \(y_p\):

\[y_p' = u_1' y_1 + u_1 y_1' + u_2' y_2 + u_2 y_2'\]

Impose the constraint:

\[\boxed{u_1' y_1 + u_2' y_2 = 0} \tag{I}\]

This eliminates the \(u_1', u_2'\) terms from \(y_p'\), giving:

\[y_p' = u_1 y_1' + u_2 y_2'\]

Differentiate again:

\[y_p'' = u_1' y_1' + u_1 y_1'' + u_2' y_2' + u_2 y_2''\]

Substitute \(y_p, y_p', y_p''\) into equation \((1)\):

\[\bigl(u_1' y_1' + u_1 y_1'' + u_2' y_2' + u_2 y_2''\bigr) + P(u_1 y_1' + u_2 y_2') + Q(u_1 y_1 + u_2 y_2) = g\]

Regroup by collecting \(u_1\) and \(u_2\) terms:

\[u_1\underbrace{(y_1'' + Py_1' + Qy_1)}_{=,0} + u_2\underbrace{(y_2'' + Py_2' + Qy_2)}_{=,0} + u_1'y_1' + u_2'y_2' = g\]

Since \(y_1, y_2\) solve the homogeneous equation, both bracketed expressions vanish. We are left with:

\[\boxed{u_1' y_1' + u_2' y_2' = g} \tag{II}\]

docs.title: § 4 — The Linear System and the Wronskian
docs.text:
Equations (I) and (II) form a \(2 \times 2\) linear system for the unknowns \(u_1'\) and \(u_2'\):

\[\begin{pmatrix} y_1 & y_2 \ y_1' & y_2' \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} u_1' \ u_2' \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \ g \end{pmatrix}\]

The coefficient matrix is exactly the Wronskian matrix, and its determinant is the Wronskian:

\[W = W(y_1, y_2)(x) = \begin{vmatrix} y_1 & y_2 \ y_1' & y_2' \end{vmatrix} = y_1 y_2' - y_2 y_1'\]

Abel's Theorem. If \(y_1, y_2\) are solutions of \((2)\), then: $\(W(x) = W(x_0), \exp!\left(-\int_{x_0}^x P(t), dt\right)\)$ In particular, \(W\) is either identically zero or never zero on \(I\). Since \(y_1, y_2\) are linearly independent, \(W \neq 0\) on \(I\). So the system is always uniquely solvable.

By Cramer's Rule:

\[u_1' = \frac{\begin{vmatrix} 0 & y_2 \ g & y_2' \end{vmatrix}}{W} = \frac{-y_2 g}{W} \tag{4}\] \[u_2' = \frac{\begin{vmatrix} y_1 & 0 \ y_1' & g \end{vmatrix}}{W} = \frac{y_1 g}{W} \tag{5}\]

Integrate to obtain \(u_1\) and \(u_2\) (no constants of integration — those belong to \(y_c\)):

\[u_1 = -\int \frac{y_2(x), g(x)}{W(x)}, dx, \qquad u_2 = \int \frac{y_1(x), g(x)}{W(x)}, dx \tag{6}\]

The particular solution is:

\[\boxed{y_p = -y_1 \int \frac{y_2, g}{W}, dx ;+; y_2 \int \frac{y_1, g}{W}, dx} \tag{7}\]

docs.title: § 5 — Existence and Uniqueness (Theoretical Note)
docs.text:
Theorem. Let \(P, Q, g\) be continuous on an open interval \(I\), and let \(y_1, y_2\) be linearly independent solutions of the homogeneous equation on \(I\). Then formula \((7)\) yields a particular solution \(y_p\) of \((1)\) defined on all of \(I\), and the general solution is \(y = C_1 y_1 + C_2 y_2 + y_p\).

This is a global existence result — not just local. The continuity of \(g\) (not a polynomial or exponential, but any continuous function) is all that is required.

This is the fundamental superiority of variation of parameters over undetermined coefficients.

docs.title: § 6 — Algorithm Summary
docs.text:
Step 1. Write the ODE in standard form: \(y'' + Py' + Qy = g\).

Step 2. Solve the homogeneous equation to find \(y_1, y_2\) (linearly independent).

Step 3. Compute the Wronskian: \(W = y_1 y_2' - y_2 y_1'\).

Step 4. Compute: $\(u_1 = -\int \frac{y_2 g}{W}, dx, \qquad u_2 = \int \frac{y_1 g}{W}, dx\)$

Step 5. Write \(y_p = u_1 y_1 + u_2 y_2\).

Step 6. General solution: \(y = C_1 y_1 + C_2 y_2 + y_p\).

Watch: Always divide by \(a\) before computing \(g\). If the original equation is \(2y'' + y' - y = e^x\ln x\), then \(g(x) = \frac{e^x \ln x}{2}\), not \(e^x \ln x\).

docs.title: Example 1 — The Classic: \(g(x) = \sec x\)
docs.text:
\[y'' + y = \sec x\]

This is impossible for undetermined coefficients. \(\sec x\) is not closed under differentiation.

Step 1. Already in standard form: \(P = 0\), \(Q = 1\), \(g = \sec x\).

Step 2. Homogeneous: \(r^2 + 1 = 0 \Rightarrow r = \pm i\). $\(y_1 = \cos x, \quad y_2 = \sin x\)$

Step 3. Wronskian: $\(W = \cos x \cdot \cos x - \sin x \cdot (-\sin x) = \cos^2 x + \sin^2 x = 1\)$

Step 4. $\(u_1 = -\int \frac{\sin x \cdot \sec x}{1}, dx = -\int \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}, dx = -\int \tan x, dx = \ln|\cos x|\)$

\[u_2 = \int \frac{\cos x \cdot \sec x}{1}, dx = \int 1, dx = x\]

Step 5. $\(y_p = \cos x \cdot \ln|\cos x| + x \sin x\)$

General solution: $\(\boxed{y = C_1 \cos x + C_2 \sin x + \cos x \ln|\cos x| + x \sin x}\)$

No undetermined coefficients method could produce this. The \(\ln|\cos x|\) is qualitatively different from any function in the admissible table.

docs.title: Example 2 — Polynomial Coefficient: \(g(x) = x^{-1}e^x\)
docs.text:
\[y'' - 2y' + y = \frac{e^x}{x}, \quad x > 0\]

Homogeneous: \((r-1)^2 = 0\), repeated root \(r = 1\). $\(y_1 = e^x, \quad y_2 = xe^x\)$

Wronskian: $\(W = e^x(e^x + xe^x) - xe^x \cdot e^x = e^{2x} + xe^{2x} - xe^{2x} = e^{2x}\)$

Compute \(u_1, u_2\): $\(u_1 = -\int \frac{xe^x \cdot \frac{e^x}{x}}{e^{2x}}, dx = -\int \frac{xe^{2x}}{xe^{2x}}, dx = -\int 1, dx = -x\)$

\[u_2 = \int \frac{e^x \cdot \frac{e^x}{x}}{e^{2x}}, dx = \int \frac{1}{x}, dx = \ln x\]

Particular solution: $\(y_p = (-x)e^x + (\ln x)(xe^x) = xe^x(\ln x - 1)\)$

General solution: $\(\boxed{y = C_1 e^x + C_2 xe^x + xe^x(\ln x - 1)}\)$

Observe: We can absorb the \(-xe^x\) term into \(C_2 xe^x\) by redefining \(C_2' = C_2 - 1\), so effectively \(y_p = xe^x \ln x\).

docs.title: Example 3 — Trigonometric Forcing with Non-Constant Coefficients
docs.text:
\[y'' + 4y = \csc(2x), \quad x \in (0, \pi/2)\]

Homogeneous: \(r^2 + 4 = 0 \Rightarrow r = \pm 2i\). $\(y_1 = \cos(2x), \quad y_2 = \sin(2x)\)$

Wronskian: $\(W = \cos(2x) \cdot 2\cos(2x) - \sin(2x) \cdot (-2\sin(2x)) = 2(\cos^2(2x) + \sin^2(2x)) = 2\)$

Compute \(u_1, u_2\): $\(u_1 = -\int \frac{\sin(2x)\csc(2x)}{2}, dx = -\int \frac{1}{2}, dx = -\frac{x}{2}\)$

\[u_2 = \int \frac{\cos(2x)\csc(2x)}{2}, dx = \int \frac{\cos(2x)}{2\sin(2x)}, dx = \frac{1}{4}\ln|\sin(2x)|\]

Particular solution: $\(y_p = -\frac{x}{2}\cos(2x) + \frac{1}{4}\sin(2x)\ln|\sin(2x)|\)$

General solution: $\(\boxed{y = C_1\cos(2x) + C_2\sin(2x) - \frac{x}{2}\cos(2x) + \frac{1}{4}\sin(2x)\ln|\sin(2x)|}\)$

docs.title: Example 4 — Verification that \(W\) Never Vanishes (Abel's Theorem Check)
docs.text:
For \(y'' - 2y' + y = 0\), \(P(x) = -2\). Abel says: $\(W(x) = W(0),e^{-\int_0^x (-2),dt} = W(0),e^{2x}\)$

With \(y_1 = e^x\), \(y_2 = xe^x\): \(W(0) = e^0(e^0 + 0) - 0 = 1\).

So \(W(x) = e^{2x}\) — consistent with our direct computation. Abel's theorem is not just theoretical; it is a computational shortcut.

docs.title: § 8 — Visualization: What "Variation" Really Means
docs.text:
Consider \(y_c = C_1\cos x + C_2\sin x\) — a family of circles in the phase plane \((y, y')\).

When we promote \(C_1 \to u_1(x)\) and \(C_2 \to u_2(x)\):

Phase Plane (y, y')
                    .  .  .
               .              .
           .      y_c circle      .
         .                          .
        .                            .
        .    y_p spirals outward     .  <-- u_1(x), u_2(x) changing
        .    as x increases          .
         .                          .
           .                      .
               .              .
                    .  .  .

The "constants" C_1, C_2 are now moving along the circle
as x changes — the solution point traces a DEFORMED path
that is no longer periodic, tracking g(x).

More precisely: at each \(x\), the point \((u_1(x), u_2(x))\) traces a curve in the \((u_1, u_2)\)-plane, driven by equations (4) and (5). The constraint (I) — \(u_1'y_1 + u_2'y_2 = 0\) — forces this motion to be perpendicular to \((y_1, y_2)^T\) at each step, keeping the first-derivative formula clean.

docs.title: § 9 — Green's Function Interpretation
docs.text:
The variation of parameters formula \((7)\) can be written as a convolution:

\[y_p(x) = \int_{x_0}^{x} G(x, t), g(t), dt\]

where the Green's function is:

\[G(x, t) = \frac{y_1(t)y_2(x) - y_2(t)y_1(x)}{W(t)}\]

Why this matters. \(G(x, t)\) is the response at position \(x\) due to a unit impulse at position \(t\). The particular solution is the superposition (integral) of all these impulse responses over the domain.

This is the ODE version of a fundamental principle: linear systems respond to general inputs by convolving with their impulse response. This connects directly to:

  • Fourier and Laplace transform methods
  • Signal processing (the ODE operator as a linear filter)
  • Deep learning (attention as learned kernel convolution)

docs.title: § 10 — Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
10.1 — Variation of Parameters as the Blueprint for Attention
docs.text:
The Green's function representation: $\(y_p(x) = \int G(x, t), g(t), dt\)$

is structurally identical to the attention mechanism in Transformers:

\[\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}!\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\]

In both cases:

  • A kernel (\(G(x,t)\) or the attention weight \(\text{softmax}(QK^T/\sqrt{d_k})\)) measures the "relevance" of source position \(t\) to target position \(x\)
  • The output is a weighted integral/sum over the source
  • The system is linear in the values (\(g(t)\) or \(V\))

The fundamental difference: \(G(x,t)\) is analytically derived from the ODE; the attention kernel is learned. Variation of parameters is the mathematical archetype of which attention is a learned, nonlinear generalization.

docs.title: 10.2 — Impulse Response and Convolutional Neural Networks
docs.text:
The Green's function is the impulse response of the differential operator \(L\). This maps directly to CNNs:

ODE / Variation of Parameters CNN Operator \(L\) (linear, shift-invariant if const. coeff.) Convolutional layer Green's function \(G(x,t)\) Learned kernel/filter Particular solution \(y_p = G * g\) Feature map = kernel \(*\) input Superposition principle Linearity of convolution

When \(P, Q\) are constants (constant-coefficient ODE), \(G(x, t) = G(x - t)\) — the Green's function depends only on the difference \(x - t\). This is shift invariance — the defining property of convolution and the motivation for weight sharing in CNNs.

docs.title: 10.3 — Neural ODEs and the Adjoint Method
docs.text:
In Neural ODEs, training requires computing gradients of a loss \(\mathcal{L}\) with respect to parameters \(\theta\). The adjoint method solves a backwards ODE:

\[\frac{d\mathbf{a}}{dt} = -\mathbf{a}(t)^T \frac{\partial f}{\partial \mathbf{h}}\]

where \(\mathbf{a}(t) = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{h}(t)}\) is the adjoint (co-state). This backward ODE is solved by variation of parameters: the adjoint is a particular solution with the "forcing" coming from the gradient of the loss.

Every time you train a Neural ODE, the backpropagation is variation of parameters applied to the adjoint system.

docs.title: 10.4 — Kernel Methods and Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces
docs.text:
The Green's function \(G(x, t)\) of a self-adjoint ODE operator \(L\) is a positive definite kernel — it satisfies: $\(\sum_{i,j} c_i c_j G(x_i, x_j) \geq 0\)$

This makes it a valid kernel for a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS). Kernel SVMs, Gaussian Processes, and kernel regression all operate in RKHSs. The "kernel trick" in ML — replacing dot products with kernel evaluations — is, for differential operators, exactly the Green's function.

Gaussian Process regression with a Matérn kernel is equivalent to Bayesian inference for a specific ODE with a stochastic forcing term — the posterior mean is the variation of parameters solution, and the posterior variance encodes uncertainty about \(g\).

docs.title: 10.5 — PINNs: Learning \(g\) When It's Unknown
docs.text:
In Physics-Informed Neural Networks, one scenario is inverse problems: \(g(x)\) is unknown and must be inferred from observations of \(y\). The forward map \(g \mapsto y_p\) is precisely variation of parameters (formula 7). Learning \(g\) from data is inverting this map — a deconvolution problem.

The neural network parametrizes \(g_\theta\), and the loss penalizes: $\(\left|y_{\text{observed}} - \left(y_c + \int G(x,t)g_\theta(t),dt\right)\right|^2\)$

The gradient of this loss with respect to \(\theta\) passes through the integral operator — it requires differentiating variation of parameters, which is again an ODE.

docs.title: 10.6 — Long-Range Dependencies: SSMs and the Green's Function
docs.text:
State Space Models (S4, Mamba) parametrize the Green's function directly:

\[y(t) = \int_0^t \underbrace{Ce^{A(t-s)}B}_{G(t,s)}, u(s), ds\]

This is variation of parameters for the first-order system \(\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x} + Bu\). The design of SSMs is the design of \(G\) — choosing \(A, B, C\) so that \(G(t,s)\) captures long-range dependencies efficiently. HiPPO theory (Gu et al., 2020) gives an optimal \(A\) matrix so that \(G\) best approximates function history in an \(L^2\) sense.

This is variation of parameters, elevated to a learned architectural principle.

docs.title: § 11 — Comparison: Undetermined Coefficients vs. Variation of Parameters
docs.text:
Feature Undetermined Coefficients Variation of Parameters Applicability Only for specific \(g(x)\) forms Any continuous \(g(x)\) Computation Algebraic (coefficient matching) Requires integration Integration needed? No Yes (can be hard) Modification rule? Yes (resonance case) Not needed — handles automatically Generalizes to variable-coefficient? No Yes Connection to Green's functions No Direct ML relevance Limited Deep (attention, kernels, SSMs)

In practice: Use undetermined coefficients when \(g(x)\) is in the admissible family (it's faster). Use variation of parameters when it isn't, or when you need the Green's function for theoretical analysis.

docs.title: § 12 — Extension to Higher Order
docs.text:
For \(n\)-th order equations \(y^{(n)} + p_{n-1}y^{(n-1)} + \cdots + p_0 y = g\), with \(n\) independent solutions \(y_1, \ldots, y_n\):

\[y_p = \sum_{k=1}^n u_k(x), y_k(x)\]

The system for \(u_k'\) becomes:

\[\begin{pmatrix} y_1 & y_2 & \cdots & y_n \ y_1' & y_2' & \cdots & y_n' \ \vdots & & & \vdots \ y_1^{(n-1)} & y_2^{(n-1)} & \cdots & y_n^{(n-1)} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} u_1' \ u_2' \ \vdots \ u_n' \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \ 0 \ \vdots \ g \end{pmatrix}\]

The coefficient matrix is the Wronskian matrix \(W[y_1, \ldots, y_n]\), and \(u_k' = W_k / W\) by Cramer's rule, where \(W_k\) is \(W\) with the \(k\)-th column replaced by \((0, \ldots, 0, g)^T\).

docs.title: § 13 — Exercises (Self-Diagnostics)
docs.text:
1. Solve \(y'' + y = \tan x\) using variation of parameters. (Recall \(\int \sec x, dx = \ln|\sec x + \tan x|\).)

2. Solve \(y'' - y = \frac{2}{1+e^x}\). Find \(y_1 = e^x\), \(y_2 = e^{-x}\) and compute the Wronskian.

3. (Verification) For Example 1, verify directly that \(y_p = \cos x\ln|\cos x| + x\sin x\) satisfies \(y'' + y = \sec x\) by differentiating twice.

4. (Abel's Theorem) For \(y'' + (\tan x)y' + y = \sec^2 x\), compute \(W(x)\) using Abel's theorem without finding \(y_1, y_2\) explicitly.

5. (Green's function) Write the Green's function for \(y'' + y = g(x)\) with initial conditions \(y(0) = y'(0) = 0\). Show it satisfies \(G(x, t) = 0\) for \(x < t\) (causality).

6. (ML connection) The attention weight \(\alpha(x, t) = \text{softmax}_t(q(x) \cdot k(t))\) plays the role of \(G(x,t)/|g|\) in the attention-as-variation-of-parameters analogy. What property of \(G\) does the softmax normalization enforce? What is lost?

docs.title: Applications
docs.text: "The same equation governs the spring in your mattress, the charge in your phone, and the gradient descent oscillations in a neural network. Mathematics does not care about the physical costume — only the underlying structure."

docs.title: § 0 — Personal Preamble
docs.text:
Second-order linear ODEs with constant coefficients:

\[ay'' + by' + cy = g(t) \tag{★}\]

are not merely a mathematical exercise. They are the universal language of oscillating systems — mechanical, electrical, biological, financial, and computational. The four applications in this note — free vibration, damped vibration, forced vibration, and RLC circuits — are all instances of \((★)\). The parameters \(a, b, c\) change interpretation (mass, resistance, capacitance), but the mathematics is identical.

This note builds each application from physical first principles, derives the ODE rigorously, and solves it completely. Every phenomenon — resonance, critical damping, beats — is a mathematical theorem wearing a physical disguise.

References:

  • Stewart, James. Calculus, 8th ed. — §17.3–17.4
  • MIT OCW 18.02 — ODE and Applications notes

docs.title: § 1 — The Undamped Vibrating Spring (Simple Harmonic Motion)
1.1 Physical Setup
docs.text:
A mass \(m\) (kg) hangs from a spring of natural length \(L\) with spring constant \(k\) (N/m). We measure displacement \(x(t)\) from the equilibrium position (where the spring force exactly balances gravity).

   __|__
  |     |   ← spring (constant k)
  |_____|
     |
    [m]     ← mass
     |
   x(t)     ← displacement from equilibrium (positive downward)

docs.title: 1.2 Derivation from Newton's Second Law
docs.text:
At equilibrium, the spring is stretched by \(\delta\) where \(k\delta = mg\).

When displaced by \(x(t)\) from equilibrium, the net forces on \(m\) are:

  • Gravity: \(+mg\) (downward)
  • Spring restoring force: \(-k(\delta + x)\) (upward; spring is further stretched by \(x\))

Newton's second law: \(m\ddot{x} = mg - k\delta - kx = -kx\) (since \(k\delta = mg\) cancels).

\[\boxed{m\ddot{x} + kx = 0} \tag{1.1}\]

Dividing by \(m\), let \(\omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m}\) (natural angular frequency, rad/s):

\[\ddot{x} + \omega_0^2 x = 0 \tag{1.2}\]

docs.title: 1.3 Solution
docs.text:
Characteristic equation: \(r^2 + \omega_0^2 = 0 \Rightarrow r = \pm i\omega_0\).

\[x(t) = C_1\cos(\omega_0 t) + C_2\sin(\omega_0 t) \tag{1.3}\]

Amplitude-phase form. Let \(A = \sqrt{C_1^2 + C_2^2}\) and \(\phi = \arctan(C_2/C_1)\):

\[\boxed{x(t) = A\cos(\omega_0 t - \phi)} \tag{1.4}\]

where:

  • \(A\) = amplitude (m)
  • \(\omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m}\) = natural frequency (rad/s)
  • \(T = 2\pi/\omega_0\) = period (s)
  • \(\phi\) = phase shift (rad), determined by initial conditions

Key fact: \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}\) is independent of amplitude \(A\). This isochrony (Galileo, 1602) is the foundation of mechanical timekeeping.

docs.title: 1.4 Example
docs.text:
A 0.5 kg mass stretches a spring 0.1 m at equilibrium.

\(k = mg/\delta = (0.5)(9.8)/0.1 = 49\) N/m. \(\omega_0 = \sqrt{49/0.5} = \sqrt{98} \approx 9.9\) rad/s. \(T = 2\pi/9.9 \approx 0.635\) s.

With initial conditions \(x(0) = 0.2\) m (pulled down 20 cm), \(\dot{x}(0) = 0\): $\(x(0) = C_1 = 0.2, \quad \dot{x}(0) = \omega_0 C_2 = 0 \Rightarrow C_2 = 0\)$ $\(x(t) = 0.2\cos(9.9t) \text{ m}\)$

docs.title: 1.5 Visualization
docs.text:
x(t) = A cos(ω₀t)

  A |     *           *
    |   *   *       *   *
    |  *     *     *     *
  0 |*---------*---------*------→ t
    |           *     *
    |            *   *
 -A |              *
    |
    |←—— T ——→|←—— T ——→|

No energy loss. Perpetual oscillation.
Amplitude A = constant for all t.

docs.title: 2.1 Physical Setup
docs.text:
Now introduce a damping force (dashpot/shock absorber) proportional to velocity:

\[F_{\text{damping}} = -c\dot{x}, \quad c > 0 \text{ (damping constant, N·s/m)}\]

The minus sign: damping opposes motion.

docs.title: 2.2 The ODE
docs.text:
Newton's second law with spring + damping:

\[m\ddot{x} = -kx - c\dot{x}\] \[\boxed{m\ddot{x} + c\dot{x} + kx = 0} \tag{2.1}\]

Dividing by \(m\), define:

  • \(2\gamma = c/m\) (damping coefficient, s⁻¹)
  • \(\omega_0^2 = k/m\) (natural frequency squared)
\[\ddot{x} + 2\gamma\dot{x} + \omega_0^2 x = 0 \tag{2.2}\]

Characteristic equation: \(r^2 + 2\gamma r + \omega_0^2 = 0\)

\[r = -\gamma \pm \sqrt{\gamma^2 - \omega_0^2} \tag{2.3}\]

The discriminant \(\Delta = \gamma^2 - \omega_0^2\) determines the regime.

docs.title: 2.3 Case I — Underdamped: \(\gamma < \omega_0\) (\(\Delta < 0\))
docs.text:
Define \(\omega_1 = \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - \gamma^2}\) (damped natural frequency).

Roots: \(r = -\gamma \pm i\omega_1\) (complex conjugate pair).

\[\boxed{x(t) = e^{-\gamma t}(C_1\cos(\omega_1 t) + C_2\sin(\omega_1 t)) = Ae^{-\gamma t}\cos(\omega_1 t - \phi)} \tag{2.4}\]

Interpretation: Oscillation with exponentially decaying envelope \(Ae^{-\gamma t}\). The system oscillates but energy leaks away.

x(t) — Underdamped

  A |   *
    |  * *          Ae^{-γt} envelope (dashed)
    | *   *       ·
    |*     *   · 
  0 |-------*·*--------*·------→ t
    |          ·  *   *  ·
    |           · * * ·
    |            ·*·
    |             ↑
    |         exponential decay

    Period T₁ = 2π/ω₁ > T₀ = 2π/ω₀
    (damping slows the oscillation)

docs.title: 2.4 Case II — Critically Damped: \(\gamma = \omega_0\) (\(\Delta = 0\))
docs.text:
Repeated root: \(r = -\gamma\) (multiplicity 2).

\[\boxed{x(t) = (C_1 + C_2 t)e^{-\gamma t}} \tag{2.5}\]

Interpretation: No oscillation. Returns to equilibrium as fast as possible without overshooting. This is the design goal for car suspensions and door closers.

x(t) — Three regimes compared

  A |·
    | ·    (A) Underdamped: oscillates, decays slowly
    |  ·     
    |   ·   (B) Critically damped: fastest return, no overshoot ←─ optimal
    |    ·
    |     ·  ·  ·  (C) Overdamped: slow return, no oscillation
    |      · ·· ···················
  0 |────────────────────────────────→ t

    (A) wiggles under 0
    (B) touches 0 exactly once
    (C) approaches 0 from above, very slowly

docs.title: 2.5 Case III — Overdamped: \(\gamma > \omega_0\) (\(\Delta > 0\))
docs.text:
Two distinct real negative roots: \(r_{1,2} = -\gamma \pm \sqrt{\gamma^2 - \omega_0^2} < 0\).

\[\boxed{x(t) = C_1 e^{r_1 t} + C_2 e^{r_2 t}} \tag{2.6}\]

Interpretation: Returns to equilibrium without oscillating, but slower than critical damping. Think: a door closer set too stiff.

docs.title: 2.6 The Damping Ratio \(\zeta\)
docs.text:
Engineers parametrize this with the damping ratio:

\[\zeta = \frac{\gamma}{\omega_0} = \frac{c}{2\sqrt{mk}}\] \(\zeta\) Regime Behavior \(0\) Undamped Perpetual oscillation \(0 < \zeta < 1\) Underdamped Decaying oscillation \(\zeta = 1\) Critically damped Fastest return, no overshoot \(\zeta > 1\) Overdamped Sluggish return, no oscillation

docs.title: 2.7 Example
docs.text:
\(m = 1\) kg, \(k = 25\) N/m (\(\omega_0 = 5\) rad/s), \(c = 6\) N·s/m (\(\gamma = 3\)).

\(\zeta = 3/5 = 0.6 < 1\) → underdamped.

\(\omega_1 = \sqrt{25 - 9} = 4\) rad/s.

With \(x(0) = 1\), \(\dot{x}(0) = 0\):

\(C_1 = 1\). \(\dot{x}(0) = -\gamma C_1 + \omega_1 C_2 = 0 \Rightarrow C_2 = \gamma/\omega_1 = 3/4\).

\[x(t) = e^{-3t}!\left(\cos 4t + \frac{3}{4}\sin 4t\right) = \frac{5}{4}e^{-3t}\cos(4t - \phi)\]

where \(\phi = \arctan(3/4) \approx 36.87°\).

docs.title: 3.1 Physical Setup
docs.text:
Now apply an external periodic force to the mass:

\[F_{\text{ext}}(t) = F_0\cos(\omega t)\]

where \(F_0\) = forcing amplitude (N) and \(\omega\) = forcing frequency (rad/s).

docs.title: 3.2 The ODE
docs.text:
\[m\ddot{x} + c\dot{x} + kx = F_0\cos(\omega t) \tag{3.1}\] \[\ddot{x} + 2\gamma\dot{x} + \omega_0^2 x = \frac{F_0}{m}\cos(\omega t) \tag{3.2}\]

The general solution splits: \(x(t) = x_c(t) + x_p(t)\) where \(x_c\) (the complementary/transient solution from §2) decays to zero, and \(x_p\) (the particular/steady-state solution) persists.

docs.title: 3.3 Steady-State Solution (Underdamped Case, \(\gamma > 0\))
docs.text:
Trial: \(x_p = A\cos(\omega t) + B\sin(\omega t)\).

After substitution and matching coefficients:

\[x_p(t) = \frac{F_0/m}{(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)^2 + 4\gamma^2\omega^2} \left[(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)\cos(\omega t) + 2\gamma\omega\sin(\omega t)\right]\]

In amplitude-phase form, define the steady-state amplitude:

\[\boxed{G(\omega) = \frac{F_0/m}{\sqrt{(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2)^2 + 4\gamma^2\omega^2}}} \tag{3.3}\]

So \(x_p(t) = G(\omega)\cos(\omega t - \delta)\) where \(\tan\delta = \frac{2\gamma\omega}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2}\).

docs.title: 3.4 Resonance: The Phenomenon and its Mathematics
docs.text:
Definition. The system is in resonance when \(G(\omega)\) is maximized over \(\omega\).

Differentiate \(G(\omega)^{-2}\) with respect to \(\omega^2\) and set to zero:

\[\omega_{\text{res}} = \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - 2\gamma^2} \tag{3.4}\]

The resonant amplitude is:

\[G(\omega_{\text{res}}) = \frac{F_0/m}{2\gamma\sqrt{\omega_0^2 - \gamma^2}} \tag{3.5}\]

Critical observation: As \(\gamma \to 0\), \(G(\omega_{\text{res}}) \to \infty\). In an undamped system forced at exactly \(\omega = \omega_0\), the amplitude grows without bound — the system tears itself apart. This is the Tacoma Narrows Bridge (1940).

docs.title: 3.5 The Frequency Response Curve
docs.text:
G(ω) — Amplitude vs. Forcing Frequency

      |
      |   ↑ ζ = 0.1 (nearly undamped) — TALL, sharp peak
      |   |
      |   |  ↑ ζ = 0.3
      |   | /|
      |   |/ | ↑ ζ = 0.7
G(ω) |   /  |/
      |  /   /
      | /  _/  ↑ ζ = 1.0 (critically damped) — flat, no peak
      |/__/____________________→ ω
      0      ω₀
             ↑
         ω_res (shifts left as ζ increases)

As ζ → 0: peak height → ∞, width → 0
As ζ → 1/√2 ≈ 0.707: peak disappears

docs.title: 3.6 The Undamped Resonance Case: Beats and Pure Resonance
docs.text:
Case A: \(\omega \neq \omega_0\), \(\gamma = 0\) (Beats)

\[\ddot{x} + \omega_0^2 x = \frac{F_0}{m}\cos(\omega t)\]

Particular solution (by undetermined coefficients, no resonance):

\[x_p = \frac{F_0/m}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2}\cos(\omega t)\]

With \(x(0) = \dot{x}(0) = 0\):

\[x(t) = \frac{F_0/m}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2}(\cos(\omega t) - \cos(\omega_0 t))\]

Using sum-to-product:

\[\boxed{x(t) = \frac{2F_0/m}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2}\sin!\left(\frac{\omega_0 - \omega}{2}t\right)\sin!\left(\frac{\omega_0 + \omega}{2}t\right)} \tag{3.6}\]

This is a high-frequency oscillation \(\sin!\left(\frac{\omega_0+\omega}{2}t\right)\) modulated by a slow amplitude envelope \(\sin!\left(\frac{\omega_0-\omega}{2}t\right)\). The result is beats — the periodic waxing and waning of amplitude heard when two tuning forks of nearly equal frequency are struck simultaneously.

x(t) — Beats (ω close to ω₀)

  A |   ***         ***
    |  *   *       *   *
    | *     *     *     *
  0 |*       *   *       *   *
    |         * *         * *
    |          *           *
 -A |
    |←beat period→|←beat period→|

    Fast oscillation at (ω₀+ω)/2
    Slow envelope at (ω₀-ω)/2

Case B: \(\omega = \omega_0\), \(\gamma = 0\) (Pure Resonance)

The trial \(x_p = A\cos(\omega_0 t)\) overlaps with \(x_c\) → modification rule: \(x_p = t(A\cos(\omega_0 t) + B\sin(\omega_0 t))\).

Substituting:

\[\boxed{x_p = \frac{F_0}{2m\omega_0}t\sin(\omega_0 t)} \tag{3.7}\]

The amplitude grows linearly: \(\frac{F_0}{2m\omega_0}t\). The system is not periodic — it is catastrophically unstable.

x(t) — Pure Resonance (ω = ω₀, no damping)

      |           /\            /\
      |          /  \          /  \
      |     /\  /    \    /\  /    \
      |    /  \/      \  /  \/      \
      |   /            \/            \
    0 |--/---------------------------→ t
      |                
      | Envelope: (F₀/2mω₀)t → ∞
      |
      Growing amplitude: UNBOUNDED

docs.title: 3.7 Example: Forced Underdamped Spring
docs.text:
\(m = 1\) kg, \(k = 9\) N/m (\(\omega_0 = 3\)), \(c = 2\) N·s/m (\(\gamma = 1\)), forced at \(\omega = 2\) rad/s with \(F_0 = 10\) N.

Steady-state amplitude: $\(G(2) = \frac{10}{\sqrt{(9-4)^2 + 4(1)^2(4)}} = \frac{10}{\sqrt{25 + 16}} = \frac{10}{\sqrt{41}} \approx 1.56 \text{ m}\)$

Phase lag: \(\tan\delta = \frac{2(1)(2)}{9-4} = \frac{4}{5}\), so \(\delta \approx 38.66°\).

The transient \(x_c = e^{-t}(C_1\cos(2\sqrt{2}t) + C_2\sin(2\sqrt{2}t))\) decays and after several time constants, only \(x_p\) remains.

docs.title: 4.1 The Physical Components
docs.text:
An RLC series circuit consists of:

  • Resistor \(R\) (ohms, Ω) — dissipates energy (analogous to damping)
  • Inductor \(L\) (henries, H) — stores energy in magnetic field (analogous to mass)
  • Capacitor \(C\) (farads, F) — stores energy in electric field (analogous to spring)
  • EMF source \(E(t)\) (volts) — external forcing
       R           L
  ┌───/\/\/───────UUUU───────┐
  │                          │
 E(t)                       ═╪═  C
  │                          │
  └──────────────────────────┘

  Charge on capacitor: Q(t)
  Current: I = dQ/dt

docs.title: 4.2 Derivation via Kirchhoff's Voltage Law
docs.text:
The voltage drops across each element:

  • Resistor: \(V_R = RI\) (Ohm's law)
  • Inductor: \(V_L = L\frac{dI}{dt} = L\ddot{Q}\)
  • Capacitor: \(V_C = Q/C\)

Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL): the sum of voltage drops equals the EMF:

\[L\ddot{Q} + R\dot{Q} + \frac{1}{C}Q = E(t) \tag{4.1}\]

This is identical in form to equation \((3.1)\). The analogy is exact:

Mechanical Electrical Mass \(m\) Inductance \(L\) Damping \(c\) Resistance \(R\) Spring constant \(k\) \(1/C\) (reciprocal capacitance) Displacement \(x\) Charge \(Q\) Velocity \(\dot{x}\) Current \(I = \dot{Q}\) External force \(F(t)\) EMF \(E(t)\) Natural frequency \(\sqrt{k/m}\) \(1/\sqrt{LC}\) Damping ratio \(c/2\sqrt{mk}\) \(R/2\sqrt{L/C} = R/(2Z_0)\)

docs.title: 4.3 Characteristic Impedance and \(Q\)-Factor
docs.text:
Define:

  • Resonant frequency: \(\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}\)
  • Characteristic impedance: \(Z_0 = \sqrt{L/C}\) (ohms)
  • Quality factor: \(Q_{\text{factor}} = Z_0/R = \frac{1}{R}\sqrt{L/C}\)

\(Q_{\text{factor}}\) is the electrical analogue of \(1/(2\zeta)\) in mechanics. High \(Q\) → sharp resonance → low damping.

docs.title: 4.4 Free Oscillations (\(E = 0\))
docs.text:
\[L\ddot{Q} + R\dot{Q} + \frac{Q}{C} = 0\]

Three cases mirror §2:

Underdamped (\(R < 2\sqrt{L/C}\)): $\(Q(t) = e^{-Rt/2L}(A\cos(\omega_1 t) + B\sin(\omega_1 t))\)$ where \(\omega_1 = \sqrt{1/LC - R^2/4L^2}\).

Circuit oscillates — energy sloshes between inductor (\(\frac{1}{2}LI^2\)) and capacitor (\(Q^2/2C\)) while resistor dissipates it.

Critically damped (\(R = 2\sqrt{L/C}\)): $\(Q(t) = (A + Bt)e^{-Rt/2L}\)$

Overdamped (\(R > 2\sqrt{L/C}\)): $\(Q(t) = Ae^{r_1 t} + Be^{r_2 t}\)$

docs.title: 4.5 Forced Oscillations: AC Circuit
docs.text:
Let \(E(t) = E_0\cos(\omega t)\) (AC source). The steady-state charge and current:

\[Q_p(t) = \frac{E_0}{\sqrt{(1/C - L\omega^2)^2 + R^2\omega^2}}\cos(\omega t - \delta)\]

The steady-state current \(I_p = \dot{Q}_p\) has amplitude:

\[I_0 = \frac{E_0\omega}{\sqrt{(1/C - L\omega^2)^2 + R^2\omega^2}} = \frac{E_0}{Z(\omega)} \tag{4.2}\]

where \(Z(\omega) = \sqrt{R^2 + (L\omega - 1/C\omega)^2}\) is the impedance of the circuit (the electrical analogue of steady-state amplitude denominator in §3.3).

Resonance occurs at \(\omega = \omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}\): $\(Z(\omega_0) = R \quad (\text{minimum impedance}) \Rightarrow I_0 = E_0/R \quad (\text{maximum current})\)$

The reactive terms \(L\omega\) and \(1/(C\omega)\) cancel at resonance — the circuit is purely resistive.

docs.title: 4.6 Example
docs.text:
\(L = 1\) H, \(R = 20\) Ω, \(C = 0.002\) F (2 mF), \(E(t) = 100\cos(10t)\) V.

\(\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{1 \times 0.002} = \sqrt{500} \approx 22.4\) rad/s.

Forcing \(\omega = 10\) rad/s ≠ \(\omega_0\).

Homogeneous: \(r = \frac{-20 \pm \sqrt{400 - 4/0.002}}{2} = \frac{-20 \pm \sqrt{400 - 2000}}{2}\).

\(\Delta = 400 - 2000 = -1600 < 0\): underdamped.

\(r = -10 \pm 20i\).

\(Q_c = e^{-10t}(A\cos(20t) + B\sin(20t))\) — transient, decays with time constant \(\tau = 1/10 = 0.1\) s.

Steady-state: \(Q_p(t) = A\cos(10t) + B\sin(10t)\).

Impedance at \(\omega = 10\): \(Z = \sqrt{400 + (10 - 50)^2} = \sqrt{400 + 1600} = \sqrt{2000} \approx 44.7\) Ω.

\(I_0 = E_0/Z = 100/44.7 \approx 2.24\) A.

Phase: \(\tan\delta = (L\omega - 1/C\omega)/R = (10 - 50)/20 = -2\), so \(\delta \approx -63.4°\) (current leads voltage since \(1/C\omega > L\omega\)).

docs.title: § 5 — The Unified Picture
docs.text:
All four applications are instances of:

\[\ddot{x} + 2\gamma\dot{x} + \omega_0^2 x = f(t)\]

with:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    UNIVERSAL OSCILLATOR                          │
│                                                                  │
│         ẍ  +  2γẋ  +  ω₀²x  =  f(t)                           │
│          ↑      ↑       ↑         ↑                              │
│       inertia damping stiffness forcing                          │
│                                                                  │
│  Spring:   m, c, k, F₀cos(ωt)                                   │
│  Circuit:  L, R, 1/C, E(t)                                      │
│  Pendulum: ml², b, mgl, τ(t)                                    │
│  Economy:  M, B, K, shock(t)   ← price oscillation models       │
│  Neuron:   membrane capacitance, leak, ..., stimulus             │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The solution structure is always:

\[x(t) = \underbrace{x_c(t)}_{\text{transient (dies)}} + \underbrace{x_p(t)}_{\text{steady-state (persists)}}\]

docs.title: 6.1 Spring Energy
docs.text:
The total mechanical energy is:

\[E(t) = \underbrace{\frac{1}{2}m\dot{x}^2}_{\text{kinetic}} + \underbrace{\frac{1}{2}kx^2}_{\text{potential}} \tag{6.1}\]

For undamped free vibration: \(\frac{dE}{dt} = m\dot{x}\ddot{x} + kx\dot{x} = \dot{x}(m\ddot{x} + kx) = \dot{x} \cdot 0 = 0\). Energy is conserved.

With damping: \(\frac{dE}{dt} = \dot{x}(m\ddot{x} + kx) = \dot{x}(-c\dot{x}) = -c\dot{x}^2 \leq 0\). Energy dissipates at rate \(c\dot{x}^2\).

docs.title: 6.2 Circuit Energy
docs.text:
\[E_{\text{circuit}} = \underbrace{\frac{1}{2}LI^2}_{\text{inductor}} + \underbrace{\frac{Q^2}{2C}}_{\text{capacitor}} \tag{6.2}\]

Rate of energy dissipation: \(-RI^2\) (Joule heating). This is the direct electrical analogue of \(-c\dot{x}^2\).

docs.title: § 7 — Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
7.1 Oscillations in Gradient Descent (Momentum and Damping)
docs.text:
The momentum update in SGD with momentum:

\[v_{t+1} = \beta v_t - \alpha \nabla \mathcal{L}(\theta_t)$$ $$\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t + v_{t+1}\]

can be written (near a minimum where \(\nabla \mathcal{L} \approx H\theta\), \(H\) = Hessian) as:

\[\theta_{t+1} - (1+\beta)\theta_t + \beta\theta_{t-1} = -\alpha H\theta_t\]

This is a discretized second-order ODE:

\[\ddot{\theta} + (1-\beta)\dot{\theta} + \alpha H \theta = 0\]

Compare to the damped spring! The momentum parameter \(\beta\) plays the role of the damping coefficient \(c\):

  • \(\beta = 0\): pure gradient descent (overdamped — slow)
  • \(\beta\) near 1: near-undamped — fast but may oscillate
  • Optimal \(\beta\): analogous to critical damping — fastest convergence without oscillation

The learning rate \(\alpha\) controls \(\omega_0^2 = \alpha\lambda\) (where \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of \(H\)). Choosing \(\alpha\) too large → resonance → divergence. Choosing \(\alpha\) optimally → critical damping → fastest convergence.

docs.title: 7.2 Resonance and Loss Landscape Instability
docs.text:
The condition for gradient explosion in SDG mirrors resonance:

\[\alpha \lambda_{\max} > 2(1+\beta)\]

(where \(\lambda_{\max}\) is the largest Hessian eigenvalue). This is the stability boundary — exactly the overdamped/underdamped phase boundary. Loss landscapes with sharp curvature (\(\lambda_{\max}\) large) → small learning rate required → slow training. This is why adaptive learning rates (Adam, RMSProp) are important: they effectively normalize by the curvature, maintaining consistent "damping" across parameter dimensions.

docs.title: 7.3 RNNs as Coupled Oscillators
docs.text:
A vanilla RNN: \(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} = \tanh(W_h\mathbf{h}_t + W_x\mathbf{x}_t)\).

Linearized near \(\mathbf{h} = 0\): \(\mathbf{h}_{t+1} \approx W_h\mathbf{h}_t + W_x\mathbf{x}_t\).

This is a system of first-order discrete ODEs — equivalent to a coupled system of second-order oscillators in the eigenspace of \(W_h\). Each eigenvalue \(\lambda_i\) of \(W_h\) controls:

  • \(|\lambda_i| < 1\): damped mode (information fades — vanishing gradients)
  • \(|\lambda_i| = 1\): undamped mode (information persists — LSTM/GRU are engineered to maintain this)
  • \(|\lambda_i| > 1\): resonant/growing mode (gradient explosion)

Orthogonal RNNs force \(|\lambda_i| = 1\) for all \(i\) — the electrical analogue of a lossless LC circuit.

docs.title: 7.4 Attention Resonance: Query-Key Alignment
docs.text: In self-attention, the softmax of \(QK^T/\sqrt{d}\) produces large weights when query \(q_i\) and key \(k_j\) are aligned. This is amplitude amplification — the same mechanism as resonance in forced vibration. When \(q_i \cdot k_j\) is large (resonant match), the attention "rings" — that position dominates the output. Transformers tune this through temperature scaling (\(\sqrt{d}\)), analogous to adding damping to prevent single-position dominance.

docs.title: 7.5 Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Oscillators
docs.text:
To solve the spring equation with a PINN, the network \(u_\theta(t)\) minimizes:

\[\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \underbrace{\int_0^T |m\ddot{u}_\theta + c\dot{u}_\theta + ku_\theta - F(t)|^2, dt}_{\text{ODE residual}} + \underbrace{|u_\theta(0) - x_0|^2 + |\dot{u}_\theta(0) - v_0|^2}_{\text{IC residual}}\]

The gradients \(\ddot{u}_\theta\) are computed by automatic differentiation through the network. The ODE residual enforces the physics; the IC residual pins the solution. Training converges to the true particular solution for any \(F(t)\), including forms that are analytically intractable.

Resonance near \(\omega \approx \omega_0\) creates stiff training dynamics — the PINN loss landscape itself becomes ill-conditioned, requiring careful learning rate scheduling. The physics of the problem bleeds into the mathematics of training.

docs.title: 7.6 Electrical Analogy for Neural Circuit Models
docs.text:
The Hodgkin-Huxley neuron model is a nonlinear RLC circuit:

\[C_m\dot{V} = -g_{Na}m^3h(V - E_{Na}) - g_K n^4(V - E_K) - g_L(V - E_L) + I_{\text{ext}}\]

The membrane capacitance \(C_m\) plays the role of capacitor \(C\); the ion conductances play the role of resistors; the Nernst potentials are EMF sources. Action potentials are the nonlinear analogue of resonance: a suprathreshold stimulus (forcing) drives the system past a bifurcation into a large-amplitude oscillation.

Deep learning models of neural circuits (spiking neural networks, neural field theories) are direct descendants of this RLC analogy.

docs.title: § 8 — Summary Table
docs.text: System ODE \(\omega_0\) Damping Resonance Condition Spring (free) \(m\ddot{x} + kx = 0\) \(\sqrt{k/m}\) None N/A Spring (damped) \(m\ddot{x} + c\dot{x} + kx = 0\) \(\sqrt{k/m}\) \(\zeta = c/2\sqrt{mk}\) N/A Spring (forced) \(m\ddot{x} + c\dot{x} + kx = F_0\cos\omega t\) \(\sqrt{k/m}\) \(\zeta = c/2\sqrt{mk}\) \(\omega = \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - 2\gamma^2}\) RLC circuit \(L\ddot{Q} + R\dot{Q} + Q/C = E(t)\) \(1/\sqrt{LC}\) \(R/2\sqrt{L/C}\) \(\omega = 1/\sqrt{LC}\)

docs.title: § 9 — Exercises
docs.text:
1. A 2 kg mass is attached to a spring with \(k = 32\) N/m. Find the period of oscillation, and write \(x(t)\) given \(x(0) = 0.5\) m and \(\dot{x}(0) = -1\) m/s.

2. For \(m = 1\), \(k = 16\), \(c = 10\): determine the regime and write the complete solution with \(x(0) = 1\), \(\dot{x}(0) = 0\).

3. Show that the maximum amplitude \(G(\omega_{\text{res}})\) in forced oscillations approaches \(\infty\) as \(\gamma \to 0\) and verify that \(\omega_{\text{res}} \to \omega_0\).

4. Derive the beat formula \((3.6)\) from scratch using the sum-to-product identity \(\cos A - \cos B = -2\sin!\left(\frac{A+B}{2}\right)\sin!\left(\frac{A-B}{2}\right)\).

5. An RLC circuit has \(L = 0.5\) H, \(R = 10\) Ω, \(C = 0.02\) F. Find the resonant frequency \(\omega_0\), classify the damping regime, and write \(Q(t)\) given \(Q(0) = 0.1\) C and \(I(0) = 0\).

6. (ML connection) Show that SGD with momentum \(\beta\) and learning rate \(\alpha\) near a quadratic minimum is equivalent to a damped harmonic oscillator. Derive the condition on \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) for critical damping.

docs.title: Series Solutions
docs.text: "When the equation resists closed form, we do not surrender — we expand. A power series is not an approximation. It is an exact representation, dressed in infinitely many terms."

docs.title: § 0 — Personal Preamble
docs.text:
Every ODE we have solved so far has yielded solutions expressible in terms of elementary functions: exponentials, sinusoids, polynomials. But nature is not obliged to produce equations with such convenient solutions.

The equation \(y'' - xy = 0\) (Airy's equation, governing light diffraction) has no solution in terms of elementary functions. Neither does \((1 - x^2)y'' - 2xy' + n(n+1)y = 0\) (Legendre's equation, governing gravitational and quantum potentials on spheres).

Series solutions are the systematic answer. We assume the solution is a power series, substitute into the ODE, and determine the coefficients recursively. The result is not an approximation — it is an exact representation of the solution as a convergent infinite series.

This method is the gateway to the special functions of mathematical physics — Legendre polynomials, Bessel functions, Hermite polynomials — which are the eigenfunctions of quantum mechanics, the basis of modern signal processing, and the activation-function cousins of deep learning.

References:

  • Stewart, James. Calculus, 8th ed. — §17.4 (Series Solutions)
  • MIT OCW 18.02 — Power Series and ODE notes (Haynes Miller)

docs.title: 1.1 Definition
docs.text:
A power series centered at \(x = a\) is:

\[\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n (x - a)^n = c_0 + c_1(x-a) + c_2(x-a)^2 + \cdots \tag{1.1}\]

We work almost exclusively with \(a = 0\) (series centered at the origin):

\[\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n x^n \tag{1.2}\]

docs.title: 1.2 Radius of Convergence
docs.text:
Every power series has a radius of convergence \(R \in [0, \infty]\) such that the series:

  • Converges absolutely for \(|x - a| < R\)
  • Diverges for \(|x - a| > R\)
  • May converge or diverge at the endpoints \(x = a \pm R\)

By the ratio test: \(R = \lim_{n\to\infty} \left|\frac{c_n}{c_{n+1}}\right|\) (when this limit exists).

docs.title: 1.3 Term-by-Term Differentiation
docs.text:
If \(y = \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n x^n\) converges on \(|x| < R\), then on the same interval:

\[y' = \sum_{n=1}^\infty n c_n x^{n-1} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty (n+1)c_{n+1} x^n \tag{1.3}\] \[y'' = \sum_{n=2}^\infty n(n-1)c_n x^{n-2} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty (n+2)(n+1)c_{n+2} x^n \tag{1.4}\]

The re-indexing trick — shifting the summation index so that all series start at \(x^n\) with the same power \(n\) — is the single most important algebraic manipulation in series solutions. Always re-index before matching coefficients.

docs.title: 1.4 Identity Principle
docs.text:
If \(\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n = 0\) for all \(x\) in an interval containing 0, then \(a_n = 0\) for all \(n\).

This is the key that unlocks series solutions: we force all coefficients to vanish, generating a recurrence relation.

docs.title: § 2 — Ordinary and Singular Points
docs.text:
The behavior of solutions near a point \(x_0\) depends critically on the structure of the ODE there.

Write the ODE in standard form:

\[y'' + P(x)y' + Q(x)y = 0 \tag{2.1}\]

Definition. \(x_0\) is an ordinary point of \((2.1)\) if \(P(x)\) and \(Q(x)\) are both analytic (representable as convergent power series) at \(x_0\).

Definition. \(x_0\) is a singular point if it is not an ordinary point — i.e., at least one of \(P, Q\) fails to be analytic at \(x_0\).

docs.title: 2.1 Regular vs. Irregular Singular Points
docs.text:
At a singular point \(x_0\), classify further:

Definition. \(x_0\) is a regular singular point if \((x - x_0)P(x)\) and \((x-x_0)^2 Q(x)\) are both analytic at \(x_0\).

Definition. \(x_0\) is an irregular singular point otherwise.

The Method of Frobenius (§4) applies at regular singular points. Irregular singular points require more advanced methods (asymptotic expansions) beyond this note.

docs.title: 2.3 Theorem: Radius of Convergence Guarantee
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(x_0\) is an ordinary point of \((2.1)\), and \(P(x), Q(x)\) have power series convergent for \(|x - x_0| < R\), then every solution of \((2.1)\) has a power series representation convergent in the same disk \(|x - x_0| < R\).

This theorem justifies the power series ansatz: we are guaranteed convergence at least up to the nearest singular point.

Practical corollary: The radius of convergence of the series solution is at least as large as the distance from \(x_0\) to the nearest singular point in the complex plane.

docs.title: § 3 — Power Series Method at Ordinary Points
3.1 The Algorithm
docs.text:
Step 1. Verify \(x_0 = 0\) is an ordinary point.

Step 2. Assume \(y = \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n x^n\).

Step 3. Compute \(y', y''\) and substitute into the ODE.

Step 4. Re-index all series so every term involves \(x^n\).

Step 5. Collect terms at each power of \(x^n\) and set the coefficient to zero (Identity Principle).

Step 6. Extract a recurrence relation giving \(c_{n+k}\) in terms of earlier \(c_j\).

Step 7. Determine \(c_0, c_1\) (free parameters — they become the two arbitrary constants of the general solution). Compute subsequent coefficients from the recurrence.

Step 8. Identify the two linearly independent solutions \(y_1, y_2\) (one involving \(c_0\), the other \(c_1\)).

docs.title: 3.2 Example 1 — Airy's Equation: \(y'' - xy = 0\)
docs.text:
This governs light near a caustic — the bright line on the bottom of a swimming pool. No elementary solution exists.

Step 1. \(P = 0\), \(Q = -x\): analytic everywhere. \(x = 0\) is ordinary.

Step 2. Let \(y = \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n x^n\).

Step 3. $\(y'' = \sum_{n=2}^\infty n(n-1)c_n x^{n-2}\)$ $\(xy = \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n x^{n+1}\)$

Step 4. Re-index \(y''\): let \(m = n-2\), so \(n = m+2\): $\(y'' = \sum_{m=0}^\infty (m+2)(m+1)c_{m+2} x^m\)$

Re-index \(xy\): let \(m = n+1\), so \(n = m-1\): $\(xy = \sum_{m=1}^\infty c_{m-1} x^m\)$

The ODE \(y'' - xy = 0\) becomes: $\(\sum_{m=0}^\infty (m+2)(m+1)c_{m+2} x^m - \sum_{m=1}^\infty c_{m-1}x^m = 0\)$

Step 5. Separate the \(m = 0\) term: $\(m = 0: \quad 2 \cdot 1 \cdot c_2 = 0 \Rightarrow c_2 = 0\)$

For \(m \geq 1\): $\((m+2)(m+1)c_{m+2} - c_{m-1} = 0\)$

Recurrence relation: $\(\boxed{c_{m+2} = \frac{c_{m-1}}{(m+2)(m+1)}, \quad m \geq 1} \tag{3.1}\)$

Step 6. This relates \(c_{n+3}\) to \(c_n\) (shift by 3). So \(c_0, c_1, c_2\) are the "seeds," but \(c_2 = 0\).

Free parameters: \(c_0\) and \(c_1\).

Coefficients from \(c_0\) (even-ish group):

\(m=1\): \(c_3 = \frac{c_0}{3 \cdot 2} = \frac{c_0}{6}\)

\(m=4\): \(c_6 = \frac{c_3}{6 \cdot 5} = \frac{c_0}{6 \cdot 30} = \frac{c_0}{180}\)

\(m=7\): \(c_9 = \frac{c_6}{9 \cdot 8} = \frac{c_0}{180 \cdot 72} = \frac{c_0}{12960}\)

Coefficients from \(c_1\):

\(m=2\): \(c_4 = \frac{c_1}{4 \cdot 3} = \frac{c_1}{12}\)

\(m=5\): \(c_7 = \frac{c_4}{7 \cdot 6} = \frac{c_1}{12 \cdot 42} = \frac{c_1}{504}\)

All \(c_n\) with \(n \equiv 2 \pmod{3}\): zero (since \(c_2 = 0\) and the recurrence propagates this).

Two linearly independent solutions:

\[y_1 = c_0!\left(1 + \frac{x^3}{6} + \frac{x^6}{180} + \frac{x^9}{12960} + \cdots\right)\] \[y_2 = c_1!\left(x + \frac{x^4}{12} + \frac{x^7}{504} + \frac{x^{10}}{45360} + \cdots\right)\]

General solution: \(y = c_0 y_1 + c_1 y_2\).

The functions \(\text{Ai}(x)\) and \(\text{Bi}(x)\) (Airy functions) are specific linear combinations of \(y_1, y_2\) normalized by convention.

Radius of convergence: \(R = \infty\) (no singular points anywhere).

For \(x < 0\): both \(\text{Ai}(x)\) and \(\text{Bi}(x)\) oscillate (the equation becomes \(y'' + |x|y = 0\), which is oscillatory).

For \(x > 0\): \(\text{Ai}(x)\) decays exponentially; \(\text{Bi}(x)\) grows exponentially.

This asymmetry — oscillatory on one side, exponential on the other — is the mathematical signature of a turning point in quantum mechanics (WKB approximation).

docs.title: 3.4 Example 2 — Hermite's Equation: \(y'' - 2xy' + 2ny = 0\)
docs.text:
This is the ODE of the quantum harmonic oscillator. When \(n \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\), the series solution terminates — giving a polynomial. These are the Hermite polynomials.

Let \(y = \sum_{k=0}^\infty c_k x^k\).

\[y' = \sum_{k=1}^\infty kc_k x^{k-1}, \quad y'' = \sum_{k=2}^\infty k(k-1)c_k x^{k-2}\]

Substituting and re-indexing:

\[\sum_{k=0}^\infty (k+2)(k+1)c_{k+2}x^k - \sum_{k=0}^\infty 2kc_k x^k + \sum_{k=0}^\infty 2nc_k x^k = 0\]

Collecting \(x^k\):

\[(k+2)(k+1)c_{k+2} + (2n - 2k)c_k = 0\]

Recurrence:

\[\boxed{c_{k+2} = \frac{2(k-n)}{(k+2)(k+1)}c_k} \tag{3.2}\]

Key observation: When \(n\) is a non-negative integer, \(c_{n+2} = \frac{2(n-n)}{(n+2)(n+1)} \cdot c_n = 0\).

And since \(c_{k+2}\) depends only on \(c_k\), this zero propagates: \(c_{n+4} = c_{n+6} = \cdots = 0\).

The series terminates at \(x^n\) — giving a polynomial of degree \(n\).

The Hermite polynomials (choosing \(c_0\) or \(c_1\) to give standard normalization):

\[H_0(x) = 1, \quad H_1(x) = 2x, \quad H_2(x) = 4x^2 - 2$$ $$H_3(x) = 8x^3 - 12x, \quad H_4(x) = 16x^4 - 48x^2 + 12\]

These are the wavefunctions of the quantum harmonic oscillator (up to a Gaussian factor \(e^{-x^2/2}\)).

docs.title: 3.5 Example 3 — A Simple Nonstandard Equation
docs.text:
\[y'' + xy' + y = 0, \quad y(0) = 1, ; y'(0) = 0\]

\(P = x\), \(Q = 1\): ordinary everywhere.

Let \(y = \sum c_n x^n\):

\[\sum_{n=0}^\infty (n+2)(n+1)c_{n+2}x^n + \sum_{n=0}^\infty nc_n x^n + \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n x^n = 0\] \[\sum_{n=0}^\infty \left[(n+2)(n+1)c_{n+2} + (n+1)c_n\right]x^n = 0\]

Recurrence:

\[c_{n+2} = \frac{-(n+1)c_n}{(n+2)(n+1)} = \frac{-c_n}{n+2} \tag{3.3}\]

ICs: \(c_0 = y(0) = 1\), \(c_1 = y'(0) = 0\).

Since \(c_1 = 0\): all odd coefficients vanish.

Even coefficients: $\(c_2 = -\frac{c_0}{2} = -\frac{1}{2}\)$ $\(c_4 = -\frac{c_2}{4} = \frac{1}{8}\)$ $\(c_6 = -\frac{c_4}{6} = -\frac{1}{48}\)$

\[y = 1 - \frac{x^2}{2} + \frac{x^4}{8} - \frac{x^6}{48} + \cdots = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n}{2^n \cdot n!}x^{2n}\]

Recognition: This is \(e^{-x^2/2}\) — check: \(\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(-x^2/2)^n}{n!} = \sum \frac{(-1)^n}{2^n n!}x^{2n}\). ✓

The series solution has recognized the Gaussian — a function whose series representation is more illuminating than its closed form.

docs.title: § 4 — The Method of Frobenius (Regular Singular Points)
docs.text:
At a regular singular point, the power series method fails because we cannot guarantee analytic solutions. Instead, we look for solutions of the form:

\[y = x^r \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n x^n = \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n x^{n+r}, \quad c_0 \neq 0 \tag{4.1}\]

where \(r\) is a (possibly non-integer, possibly complex) number to be determined. This is a Frobenius series or generalized power series.

docs.title: 4.1 The Indicial Equation
docs.text:
Consider \((2.1)\) with regular singular point at \(x = 0\). Multiply through by \(x^2\):

\[x^2 y'' + x\cdot[xP(x)]\cdot y' + [x^2 Q(x)]\cdot y = 0\]

Since \(xP(x)\) and \(x^2 Q(x)\) are analytic at 0:

\[xP(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty p_n x^n, \quad x^2 Q(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty q_n x^n\]

Substituting the Frobenius ansatz \(y = \sum c_n x^{n+r}\) and collecting the lowest power \(x^r\) (from \(n = 0\)):

\[c_0[r(r-1) + p_0 r + q_0] = 0\]

Since \(c_0 \neq 0\), we must have:

\[\boxed{r(r-1) + p_0 r + q_0 = 0} \tag{4.2}\]

This is the indicial equation — a quadratic in \(r\) whose roots \(r_1, r_2\) (with \(\text{Re}(r_1) \geq \text{Re}(r_2)\)) determine the form of the two linearly independent solutions.

docs.title: 4.2 Three Cases for the Solutions
docs.text:
Let \(\rho = r_1 - r_2\).

Case 1: \(\rho \notin \mathbb{Z}\) (roots do not differ by an integer)

Two independent Frobenius series: $\(y_1 = x^{r_1}\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n, \quad y_2 = x^{r_2}\sum_{n=0}^\infty b_n x^n\)$

Case 2: \(\rho = 0\) (repeated root \(r_1 = r_2 = r\))

\[y_1 = x^r \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n$$ $$y_2 = y_1 \ln x + x^r \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n x^n\]

The \(\ln x\) term is unavoidable — it is forced by the repeated root, analogous to repeated roots giving \(te^{rt}\) in constant-coefficient equations.

Case 3: \(\rho \in \mathbb{Z}^+\) (roots differ by a positive integer)

\[y_1 = x^{r_1}\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n$$ $$y_2 = cy_1\ln x + x^{r_2}\sum_{n=0}^\infty b_n x^n\]

The constant \(c\) may or may not be zero — it must be determined from the recurrence. If \(c = 0\), the second solution is also a pure Frobenius series.

docs.title: 4.3 Example — Bessel's Equation of Order \(\nu\)
docs.text:
\[x^2 y'' + xy' + (x^2 - u^2)y = 0, \quad u \geq 0 ag{4.3}\]

This governs vibrating circular membranes (drums), heat diffusion in cylinders, and wave propagation in cylindrical coordinates. It is arguably the most important ODE in classical physics.

Standard form: \(y'' + rac{1}{x}y' + \left(1 - rac{ u^2}{x^2} ight)y = 0\).

\(P = 1/x\), \(Q = 1 - u^2/x^2\): \(x = 0\) is a regular singular point.

\(xP(x) = 1 \Rightarrow p_0 = 1\), \(x^2 Q(x) = x^2 - u^2 \Rightarrow q_0 = - u^2\).

Indicial equation: \(r(r-1) + r - u^2 = 0 \Rightarrow r^2 - u^2 = 0 \Rightarrow r = \pm u\).

So \(r_1 = u\), \(r_2 = - u\), \( ho = 2 u\).

Case \( u otin \mathbb{Z}\) (non-integer order): Both Frobenius series work independently.

Let \(y = \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n x^{n+r}\) with \(r = u\). Substituting into \((4.3)\):

The recurrence (after careful computation) is:

\[c_n = rac{-c_{n-2}}{n(n + 2 u)}, \quad n \geq 2; \qquad c_1 = 0\]

All odd coefficients vanish. For even \(n = 2m\):

\[c_{2m} = rac{(-1)^m c_0}{m!,\Gamma( u + m + 1) \cdot 2^{2m}}\]

(using the Gamma function to handle non-integer \( u\)). Choosing \(c_0 = rac{1}{2^ u \Gamma( u+1)}\):

\[ oxed{J_ u(x) = \sum_{m=0}^\infty rac{(-1)^m}{m!,\Gamma( u + m + 1)}\left( rac{x}{2} ight)^{2m+ u}} ag{4.4}\]

This is the Bessel function of the first kind of order \( u\). It is one of the most important functions in all of applied mathematics.

For integer \( u = n \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\):

\[J_n(x) = \sum_{m=0}^\infty rac{(-1)^m}{m!,(m+n)!}\left( rac{x}{2} ight)^{2m+n} ag{4.5}\]

Special cases:

\[J_0(x) = 1 - rac{x^2}{4} + rac{x^4}{64} - rac{x^6}{2304} + \cdots\] \[J_1(x) = rac{x}{2} - rac{x^3}{16} + rac{x^5}{384} - \cdots\]

docs.title: 4.5 Example — Legendre's Equation: \((1-x^2)y'' - 2xy' + n(n+1)y = 0\)
docs.text:
In standard form: \(y'' - \frac{2x}{1-x^2}y' + \frac{n(n+1)}{1-x^2}y = 0\).

Singular points at \(x = \pm 1\). Point \(x = 0\) is ordinary.

Power series method (at \(x = 0\)) gives recurrence:

\[c_{k+2} = -\frac{(n-k)(n+k+1)}{(k+2)(k+1)}c_k \tag{4.6}\]

When \(n \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\): the series terminates at \(k = n\) (since \(c_{n+2} = 0\)), giving a polynomial.

The Legendre polynomials (normalized by \(P_n(1) = 1\)):

\[P_0(x) = 1, \quad P_1(x) = x, \quad P_2(x) = \frac{1}{2}(3x^2 - 1)$$ $$P_3(x) = \frac{1}{2}(5x^3 - 3x), \quad P_4(x) = \frac{1}{8}(35x^4 - 30x^2 + 3)\]

Orthogonality: $\(\int_{-1}^1 P_m(x)P_n(x),dx = \frac{2}{2n+1}\delta_{mn} \tag{4.7}\)$

The Legendre polynomials form an orthogonal basis for \(L^2[-1,1]\) — they are the analogue of Fourier modes for the interval \([-1,1]\).

They appear in the solution of Laplace's equation in spherical coordinates (gravitational and electric potentials), quantum mechanical angular momentum eigenfunctions (spherical harmonics), and approximation theory.

docs.title: § 5 — The Recurrence Relation as Algorithm
docs.text:
The recurrence relation is the heart of the method. It is always a linear relation, often of the form:

\[c_{n+k} = f(n), c_n \quad \text{or} \quad c_{n+k} = f(n), c_n + g(n), c_{n-j}\]

Generating coefficients systematically:

For the Airy equation recurrence \(c_{m+3} = \frac{c_m}{(m+3)(m+2)}\) (rewriting 3.1):

Dependency graph:

c₀ ──→ c₃ ──→ c₆ ──→ c₉ ──→ ...   (y₁ branch)
c₁ ──→ c₄ ──→ c₇ ──→ c₁₀ ──→ ...  (y₂ branch)
c₂ = 0 ──→ c₅=0 ──→ c₈=0 ──→ ...  (zero branch)

The three families are decoupled.
Two free parameters c₀, c₁ → two independent solutions.

This dependency graph structure is general: the recurrence has "step" \(k\) means indices split into \(k\) independent families, each seeded by a different \(c_j\) (\(0 \leq j < k\)).

docs.title: 6.1 The Key Theorem (Restated Sharply)
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(x_0\) is an ordinary point of \(y'' + P(x)y' + Q(x)y = 0\), then the general solution is: $\(y = c_0 y_1(x) + c_1 y_2(x)\)$ where \(y_1, y_2\) are power series centered at \(x_0\), convergent at least for \(|x - x_0| < R\), where \(R\) is the distance from \(x_0\) to the nearest singularity of \(P\) or \(Q\) in the complex plane.

Why the complex plane? The equation \(y'' + \frac{1}{1+x^2}y = 0\) has \(P = 0\), \(Q = (1+x^2)^{-1}\) — analytic on all of \(\mathbb{R}\). Yet the radius of convergence of the series solution at \(x_0 = 0\) is \(R = 1\), because the singular points \(x = \pm i\) (in \(\mathbb{C}\)) are distance 1 from the origin.

docs.title: 6.2 Ratio Test for Bessel Functions
docs.text:
For \(J_0(x) = \sum_{m=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^m}{(m!)^2}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)^{2m}\):

\[\left|\frac{a_{m+1}}{a_m}\right| = \frac{x^2}{4(m+1)^2} \to 0 \text{ as } m \to \infty\]

So \(R = \infty\) — \(J_0\) converges everywhere. This is expected: Bessel's equation has its only singular point at \(x = 0\), and \(J_0\) is the solution regular at \(x = 0\).

docs.title: Euler's Equation as a Test Case
docs.text:
\[x^2 y'' + \alpha xy' + \beta y = 0 \tag{7.1}\]

\(x = 0\) is a regular singular point. \(xP = \alpha\), \(x^2 Q = \beta\), so \(p_0 = \alpha\), \(q_0 = \beta\).

Indicial equation: \(r(r-1) + \alpha r + \beta = 0\).

With the Frobenius ansatz \(y = x^r \sum c_n x^n\):

Substituting, the \(n\)-th term gives: $\([(r+n)(r+n-1) + \alpha(r+n) + \beta],c_n = 0\)$

For \(n \geq 1\): the bracket is \((r+n)(r+n-1) + \alpha(r+n) + \beta\). This is the indicial polynomial evaluated at \(r + n\) — and since \(r\) is a root of the indicial equation, \(r + n\) (for \(n \geq 1\)) need not be a root, so the bracket \(\neq 0\), forcing \(c_n = 0\) for all \(n \geq 1\).

The Frobenius series collapses to a single term: \(y = c_0 x^r\).

This recovers the known result: Euler's equation always has solutions \(y = x^r\). The Frobenius method is consistent. \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: § 8 — Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
8.1 Hermite Polynomials and Probabilistic ML
docs.text:
The Hermite polynomials \(H_n(x)\) from §3.4 are orthogonal with respect to the Gaussian weight \(e^{-x^2}\): $\(\int_{-\infty}^\infty H_m(x)H_n(x)e^{-x^2},dx = \sqrt{\pi},2^n n!,\delta_{mn}\)$

In probabilistic machine learning:

  • Gaussian processes: the covariance functions of stationary GPs can be expanded in Hermite polynomials — this gives the connection between GP kernels and frequency-domain representations
  • Score-based generative models (diffusion models, DDPM): the score function \(\nabla_x \log p_t(x)\) for a Gaussian prior satisfies a Hermite-polynomial expansion
  • Gauss-Hermite quadrature: numerical integration of expectations under Gaussian distributions (used in variational inference, Laplace approximation) is based on the roots of \(H_n(x)\)

The quantum harmonic oscillator wavefunctions \(\psi_n(x) = H_n(x)e^{-x^2/2}\) are precisely the basis functions that diagonalize the quantum number operator — analogous to how Fourier modes diagonalize translation-invariant operators, and how eigenvectors diagonalize weight matrices in linear neural networks.

docs.title: 8.2 Bessel Functions and Graph Neural Networks
docs.text:
Bessel functions appear naturally on graphs and manifolds. The graph Laplacian \(\Delta_G\) has eigenfunctions that, on regular lattices, reduce to discrete Fourier modes. On radially symmetric graphs (like ego networks), the eigenfunctions of the Laplacian are discrete analogues of Bessel functions.

Spectral Graph Convolutional Networks (Kipf & Welling, 2017) use the eigenfunctions of the graph Laplacian as the basis for convolution. The "spectral" filters are essentially polynomial approximations to Bessel-type functions. The ChebNet approximation uses Chebyshev polynomials (themselves solutions to a Sturm-Liouville ODE) to avoid explicit eigendecomposition.

docs.title: 8.3 Legendre Polynomials and Positional Encoding
docs.text:
The HiPPO framework (Gu et al., 2020) for long-range sequence modeling — which underlies the S4 and Mamba architectures — computes online approximations to signal history using Legendre polynomial projections:

\[u(t) \approx \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} c_n(t) P_n(\tau)\]

where \(c_n(t)\) satisfies a linear ODE that can be updated in \(O(N)\) per step. The optimal \(A\) matrix in state-space models comes directly from the ODE recurrence \((4.6)\) for Legendre polynomials.

This is series solutions of ODEs embedded into the architecture of a language model.

docs.title: 8.4 The Neural ODE as a Series Solution
docs.text:
A Neural ODE \(\dot{\mathbf{h}} = f(\mathbf{h}, t, \theta)\) with small \(t\) can be expanded via the Picard iteration / Magnus expansion:

\[\mathbf{h}(t) = \mathbf{h}(0) + t f(\mathbf{h}(0), 0) + \frac{t^2}{2}\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} + f \cdot \nabla_h f\right) + \cdots\]

This is a Taylor series in \(t\) — exactly the power series method applied to a nonlinear ODE. The truncated Magnus expansion gives the ResNet (each term = one residual block). A full series solution = infinitely many layers = continuous depth.

docs.title: 8.5 Special Functions as Activation Functions
docs.text:
The standard neural network activation functions are non-analytic at most points. But polynomial network architectures use:

  • Hermite activations: \(\sigma(x) = H_n(x)e^{-x^2/2}\) — guaranteed orthogonal feature maps under Gaussian input distributions. This directly minimizes feature correlation in layers receiving Gaussian-distributed inputs.
  • Legendre activations on bounded domains: \(\sigma(x) = P_n(x)\) for \(x \in [-1,1]\) — used in FNO (Fourier Neural Operator) and related PDE-solving architectures.

The recurrence relations for these polynomials (e.g., \((n+1)P_{n+1} = (2n+1)xP_n - nP_{n-1}\)) allow efficient computation of all activation values up to order \(N\) in \(O(N)\) operations — making them computationally competitive with ReLU networks.

docs.title: 8.6 Airy Functions and Phase Transitions in Learning
docs.text:
The Airy function \(\text{Ai}(x)\) describes the edge of a semicircle law in random matrix theory. The empirical spectral distribution of a random weight matrix \(W/\sqrt{n}\) converges to the Marchenko-Pastur law, and fluctuations at the spectral edge are governed by the Tracy-Widom distribution — whose density involves \(\text{Ai}(x)\).

This matters for deep learning initialization theory: the distribution of singular values of weight matrices at initialization, and how these evolve during training, follows random matrix universality. The Airy-governed edge controls how information propagates through very deep networks — too close to the edge and gradients explode; too far and they vanish.

docs.title: § 9 — Summary: When to Use What
docs.text:
Given an ODE y'' + P(x)y' + Q(x)y = g(x)
                         │
              Is x₀ an ordinary point?
             /                         \
           YES                          NO
            │                           │
   Power series method          Is x₀ a REGULAR
   y = Σ cₙ(x-x₀)ⁿ            singular point?
   Recurrence relation         /              \
   Two free constants         YES              NO
                               │               │
                    Frobenius method     Irregular singular
                    y = |x-x₀|^r Σcₙxⁿ  point → asymptotic
                    Indicial equation     methods (beyond
                    Three sub-cases       this note)

docs.title: § 10 — Key Special Functions Reference
docs.text: Name ODE Series Orthogonality weight ML application Hermite \(H_n\) \(y''-2xy'+2ny=0\) Terminates (poly.) \(e^{-x^2}\) Gaussian quadrature, diffusion models Legendre \(P_n\) \((1-x^2)y''-2xy'+n(n+1)y=0\) Terminates (poly.) \(1\) on \([-1,1]\) HiPPO/S4, spherical harmonics Bessel \(J_\nu\) \(x^2y''+xy'+(x^2-\nu^2)y=0\) Non-terminating \(x\) on \([0,\infty)\) Graph NNs, cylindrical geometry Airy \(\text{Ai}\) \(y''-xy=0\) Non-terminating N/A (not \(L^2\)) Random matrix theory, initialization Chebyshev \(T_n\) \((1-x^2)y''-xy'+n^2y=0\) Terminates (poly.) \((1-x^2)^{-1/2}\) ChebNet, spectral GNNs

docs.title: § 11 — Exercises
docs.text:
1. Find the first four nonzero terms of a power series solution to \(y'' + x^2 y = 0\) about \(x_0 = 0\). What is the radius of convergence?

2. Apply the power series method to \(y'' - y = 0\). Show that the series solutions recover \(e^x\) and \(e^{-x}\).

3. Classify all singular points of \((x^2 - 4)y'' + 3xy' + y = 0\) as regular or irregular.

4. Find the indicial equation for \(2xy'' + y' + xy = 0\). Compute the roots and determine which Frobenius case applies.

5. Verify the recurrence \((4.6)\) for Legendre's equation and confirm that for \(n = 2\) (with \(c_1 = 0\), \(c_0 = -1/2\)), the series terminates at \(P_2(x) = \frac{1}{2}(3x^2 - 1)\).

6. (Theoretical) Show that \(J_0(x)\) and \(J_1(x)\) satisfy \(J_0'(x) = -J_1(x)\) using the series definition \((4.5)\).

7. (ML) The HiPPO-LegS matrix is defined via the recurrence for Legendre polynomials. Show that the \((n, k)\) entry of the optimal \(A\) matrix satisfies: $\(A_{nk} = \begin{cases}(2n+1)^{1/2}(2k+1)^{1/2} & k < n \ n+1 & k = n \ 0 & k > n\end{cases}\)$ by deriving it from the three-term Legendre recurrence.
