Since \(l > j\) and the matrix \(E_{kl}^{-1}\) operates on row \(k > l > j\), we have \(k \neq j\), so: \(\mathbf{e}_j^T \mathbf{e}_k = 0 \implies \text{cross term} = 0\) Again, the multipliers drop independently into their positions.

docs.title: Putting It Together:
docs.text: Applying both lemmas across all columns by induction: \(L = \prod_{\substack{i > j}} E_{ij}^{-1} = I + \sum_{\substack{i > j}} \ell_{ij}; \mathbf{e}_i \mathbf{e}_j^T\) The sum \(\sum_{i > j} \ell_{ij}; \mathbf{e}_i \mathbf{e}_j^T\) is a matrix whose \((i,j)\) entry (for \(i > j\)) equals \(\ell_{ij}\), and all other entries are zero. Adding the identity gives 1s on the diagonal. Therefore: $\(L = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \ell_{21} & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ \ell_{31} & \ell_{32} & 1 & 0 \\ \ell_{41} & \ell_{42} & \ell_{43} & 1 \end{pmatrix} \qquad \blacksquare\)$

docs.title: Example: Full 4×4 LU Decomposition
docs.text: Let:\(A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 3 & 3 & 1 \\ 8 & 7 & 9 & 5 \\ 6 & 7 & 9 & 8 \end{pmatrix}\)

docs.title: Step 1: Eliminate Column 1 (pivot = 2)
docs.text: Compute multipliers: \(\ell_{21} = \frac{4}{2} = 2, \qquad \ell_{31} = \frac{8}{2} = 4, \qquad \ell_{41} = \frac{6}{2} = 3\) Apply \(E_{41} E_{31} E_{21}\) to \(A\) (subtract \(\ell \times\) row 1 from each target row): $\(\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 4-2(2) & 3-2(1) & 3-2(1) & 1-2(0) \\ 8-4(2) & 7-4(1) & 9-4(1) & 5-4(0) \\ 6-3(2) & 7-3(1) & 9-3(1) & 8-3(0) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 3 & 5 & 5 \\ 0 & 4 & 6 & 8 \end{pmatrix}\)$

docs.title: Step 2: Eliminate Column 2 (pivot = 1)
docs.text: Compute multipliers from the updated matrix: \(\ell_{32} = \frac{3}{1} = 3, \qquad \ell_{42} = \frac{4}{1} = 4\) Apply \(E_{42} E_{32}\): $\(\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 3-3(1) & 5-3(1) & 5-3(1) \\ 0 & 4-4(1) & 6-4(1) & 8-4(1) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\)$

docs.title: Step 3: Eliminate Column 3 (pivot = 2)
docs.text: Compute multiplier: \(\ell_{43} = \frac{2}{2} = 1\) Apply \(E_{43}\): $\(\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2-1(2) & 4-1(2) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = U\)$

docs.title: Reading Off \(L\) and \(U\)
docs.text: The multipliers drop directly into \(L\) in their natural positions: $\(L = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 4 & 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad U = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\)$

docs.title: What Goes Wrong With Row Swaps
docs.text:
• \(P\) is the [[04.Permutation Matrices|Permutation Matrix]] recording all row swaps
  • \(L\) is unit lower triangular with multipliers sitting cleanly in their positions
  • \(U\) is upper triangular with the pivots on the diagonal \(PA = LU\) exists for any invertible \(A\). In practice, LAPACK and NumPy store \(P\) implicitly as a permutation vector (pivot indices).

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text: Suppose during column 2 elimination, the pivot \(a_{22}^{(2)} = 0\) — we must swap rows to continue. Apply the permutation matrix \(P_{23}\) that swaps rows 2 and 3.After swapping, the multiplier \(\ell_{31}\) — which was computed relative to the original row order — is now in row 2, not row 3. The subsequent column 2 elimination will modify entry \((2,1)\), contaminating the multiplier that was supposed to sit untouched in \(L\). The cross terms that vanished before now survive, because the permutation matrix moves entries around and breaks the condition \(k \neq j\).

docs.title: The Fix: \(PA = LU\)
docs.text: Permute \(A\) first (choosing all row interchanges in advance via partial pivoting), then factor: \(\boxed{PA = LU}\) where:

docs.title: Existence Without Row Swaps
docs.text: \(A = LU\) (without any permutation) exists if and only if all leading principal submatrices are invertible — equivalently, all pivots are nonzero during elimination. Leading principal submatrices are the upper-left \(k \times k\) corners: \(A_{1:k, 1:k}\) for \(k = 1, \ldots, n\).

docs.title: The Order of Multiplication — A Common Confusion
docs.text: The elimination operations are applied as: $\(\underbrace{E_{43}}_{\text{6th}} \underbrace{E_{42}}_{\text{5th}} \underbrace{E_{32}}_{\text{4th}} \underbrace{E_{41}}_{\text{3rd}} \underbrace{E_{31}}_{\text{2nd}} \underbrace{E_{21}}_{\text{1st}} A = U\)$ So \(E_{21}\) acts first (rightmost position), then \(E_{31}\), and so on. To recover \(A\), invert both sides and rearrange: $\(A = E_{21}^{-1} E_{31}^{-1} E_{41}^{-1} E_{32}^{-1} E_{42}^{-1} E_{43}^{-1} \cdot U = LU\)$ Note: the product \(E_{21}^{-1} E_{31}^{-1} \cdots\) is not the same as reversing the order \((E_{43} \cdots E_{21})^{-1}\). Inverting a product reverses the order: $\((E_{43} \cdots E_{21})^{-1} = E_{21}^{-1} \cdots E_{43}^{-1}\)$ This is the same order as what we wrote for \(L\)! The reversal happens automatically. And thanks to the vanishing cross terms, \(L\) is clean regardless of the direction.

docs.title: Using \(LU\) to Solve \(Ax = b\)
docs.text: Once \(A = LU\) is computed (cost \(O(n^3)\), computed once): - ### Forward Substitution: Solve \(Ly = b\) \(L\) is lower triangular, so solve from top to bottom: \(y_1 = b_1\) $\(y_i = b_i - \sum_{j=1}^{i-1} \ell_{ij}, y_j \quad \text{for } i = 2, \ldots, n\)$ - ### Backward Substitution: Solve \(Ux = y\) \(U\) is upper triangular, so solve from bottom to top: \(x_n = y_n / u_{nn}\) $\(x_i = \left(y_i - \sum_{j=i+1}^{n} u_{ij}, x_j\right) / u_{ii} \quad \text{for } i = n-1, \ldots, 1\)$ Cost: Each solve costs \(O(n^2)\). For \(k\) right-hand sides: total cost \(= O(n^3) + k \cdot O(n^2)\). Compare to: Computing \(A^{-1}\) explicitly costs \(O(n^3)\) and then each solve is \(A^{-1}b\) at \(O(n^2)\) — same asymptotic cost but LU has smaller constants and better numerical stability.

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text: Property \(L\) \(U\) Shape Lower triangular Upper triangular Diagonal All 1s (unit lower triangular) Pivots of elimination Off-diagonal below/above Elimination multipliers \(\ell_{ij}\) Entries computed during elimination Invertible iff Always (diagonal = 1) Pivots all nonzero Question Answer When does \(A = LU\) exist? All leading principal submatrices of \(A\) are invertible When does \(PA = LU\) exist? Always, for any invertible \(A\) Is \(A = LU\) unique? Yes, if it exists Cost of factorization \(O(n^3)\) — specifically \(\frac{2}{3}n^3\) flops Cost of each subsequent solve \(O(n^2)\)

docs.title: Common Mistakes and Misconceptions
docs.text:
• Mistake 1: Using original matrix entries for multipliers.

    • After column 1 elimination, the matrix entries change. Multiplier \(\ell_{32}\) uses \(a_{32}^{(2)}\) (the entry after column 1 is eliminated), not the original \(a_{32}\).

  • Mistake 2: Thinking \(L\) might be contaminated.

    • The vanishing cross terms guarantee that \(L\) stores the multipliers exactly as computed, with no modification during subsequent steps.

  • Mistake 3: Confusing \(E_{21}^{-1} E_{31}^{-1} \cdots\) with \((E_{21} E_{31} \cdots)^{-1}\).

    • These are different. The former is a product of individual inverses in the same order; the latter reverses the order. They both happen to give \(L\) only because of the structure above.

  • It fails if any pivot is zero and no row swap is available. Use \(PA = LU\) for robustness.

    • Mistake 4: Expecting \(A = LU\) to always exist.

  • Mistake 5: Computing \(A^{-1}\) explicitly to solve \(Ax = b\).

    • Never do this numerically. Use LU. Explicit inversion loses numerical precision and is slower.

docs.title: Key Formulas at a Glance
docs.text:
• \(E_{ij} = I - \ell_{ij}\mathbf{e}_i\mathbf{e}_j^T \qquad E_{ij}^{-1} = I + \ell_{ij}\mathbf{e}_i\mathbf{e}_j^T\)
  • \(\ell_{ij} = \frac{a_{ij}^{(j)}}{a_{jj}^{(j)}} \qquad \text{(ratio of entry to pivot, at current elimination stage)}\)
  • \(A = LU \quad \text{where} \quad L_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & i = j \ \ell_{ij} & i > j \ 0 & i < j \end{cases}\)
  • \(PA = LU \quad \text{(always exists for invertible } A\text{, used when pivoting is needed)}\)

docs.title: Vectors:
docs.text: A vector \(\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) is an ordered \(n\)-tuple of real numbers: $\(\mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \\ \vdots \\ v_n \end{pmatrix}\)$ I will always write vectors as column vectors. A row vector is \(\mathbf{v}^T\) There are two ways to think about \(\mathbf{v}\): 1) As a point. \(\mathbf{v}\) is a location in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), the point with coordinates \((v_1, \ldots, v_n)\). 2) As an arrow. \(\mathbf{v}\) is a displacement — a direction and a magnitude — rooted at the origin and ending at \((v_1, \ldots, v_n)\). Both pictures are useful. The arrow picture is better for understanding linear combinations geometrically. The point picture is better for probability (a random vector is a point in sample space). I will move between them freely.

docs.title: Vector Operations
docs.text:
1) Addition. For \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n\): \(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} u_1 + v_1 \ u_2 + v_2 \ \vdots \ u_n + v_n \end{pmatrix}\) Geometrically (arrow picture): place the tail of \(\mathbf{v}\) at the tip of \(\mathbf{u}\). The sum \(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}\) is the arrow from the origin to the new tip. This is the parallelogram law. ![[Pasted image 20260409145351.png]] 2) Scalar multiplication. For \(c \in \mathbb{R}\): \(c\mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} cv_1 \ cv_2 \ \vdots \ cv_n \end{pmatrix}\) Geometrically: stretch \(\mathbf{v}\) by factor \(|c|\), reversing direction if \(c < 0\). The set \({c\mathbf{v} : c \in \mathbb{R}}\) is the line through the origin in the direction of \(\mathbf{v}\) (and its negative). ![[Pasted image 20260409145614.png]]

These two operations are all that \(\mathbb{R}^n\) needs to be a vector space. Everything else — subspaces, bases, linear maps — is built on top of them.

docs.title: Linear Combinations:
docs.text: Given vectors \(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k \in \mathbb{R}^n\) and scalars \(c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_k \in \mathbb{R}\), the expression \(c_1 \mathbf{v}_1 + c_2 \mathbf{v}_2 + \cdots + c_k \mathbf{v}_k\) is called a linear combination of \(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k\) with coefficients \(c_1, \ldots, c_k\). This is the central operation of all of linear algebra. Everything — matrix-vector products, solutions to \(Ax = b\), projections, the entire subject — is a statement about which linear combinations are possible.

docs.title: The Column Picture of \(Ax\)
docs.text:
If \(A\) is \(m \times n\) with columns \(\mathbf{a}^{(1)}, \ldots, \mathbf{a}^{(n)}\), then for \(x = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)^T\): \(Ax = x_1 \mathbf{a}^{(1)} + x_2 \mathbf{a}^{(2)} + \cdots + x_n \mathbf{a}^{(n)}\) \(Ax\) is a linear combination of the columns of \(A\) with coefficients given by \(x\). This is the column picture of matrix-vector multiplication, and it reframes every question about \(Ax = b\):

Does there exist a linear combination of the columns of \(A\) that equals \(\mathbf{b}\)?

If yes, the coefficients are a solution \(x\). If the solution is unique, the representation is unique.

docs.title: Span of a Set of Vectors
docs.text:
The span of a set of vectors \(\{\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k\}\) is the set of all their linear combinations: \(\text{span}\{\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k\} = \left\{ \sum_{i=1}^{k} c_i \mathbf{v}_i \;:\; c_1, \ldots, c_k \in \mathbb{R} \right\}\) The span is always a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). It satisfies three closure properties: - Contains \(\mathbf{0}\) (set all \(c_i = 0\)) - Closed under addition - Closed under scalar multiplication

![[Pasted image 20260409151205.png]]

docs.title: Geometric Example:
docs.text:
• \(n = 2\), one nonzero vector \(\mathbf{v}\): \(\text{span}{\mathbf{v}} = {c\mathbf{v} : c \in \mathbb{R}}\) This is a line through the origin in direction \(\mathbf{v}\).
  • \(n = 2\), two vectors \(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2\) not parallel: \(\text{span}{\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2} = \mathbb{R}^2\) Any point in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) can be reached. The two vectors form a (possibly skewed) coordinate system.
  • \(n = 3\), two vectors not parallel: \(\text{span}{\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2} = \text{a plane through the origin}\)
  • \(n = 3\), three vectors: Either \(\text{span} = \mathbb{R}^3\) (if none lies in the plane spanned by the other two), or \(\text{span}\) is a plane or line (if they are redundant). The question of when adding a new vector actually enlarges the span is exactly the question of linear independence.

docs.title: Linear Independence:
docs.text:
Vectors \(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k\) are linearly independent if the only solution to \(c_1 \mathbf{v}_1 + c_2 \mathbf{v}_2 + \cdots + c_k \mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{0}\) is \(c_1 = c_2 = \cdots = c_k = 0\). They are linearly dependent if there exists a nontrivial solution (at least one \(c_i \neq 0\)).

Geometrically: if the vectors are dependent, at least one of them is redundant — it already lives in the span of the others. Dependence is the statement that the set of vectors has "more members than directions."

Restatement in terms of the matrix: \(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k\) are linearly independent iff the matrix \(V = [\mathbf{v}_1 \mid \cdots \mid \mathbf{v}_k]\) has \(\text{null}(V) = {\mathbf{0}}\), i.e., \(Vc = \mathbf{0}\) implies \(c = \mathbf{0}\).

docs.title: Important Points:
docs.text: 1) Any set containing the zero vector is linearly dependent. (Take \(c_i = 1\) for the zero vector's index, all others zero.) 2) A single nonzero vector is always linearly independent. 3) Two vectors are linearly dependent iff one is a scalar multiple of the other — i.e., they point in the same or opposite direction. 4) More than \(n\) vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) are always linearly dependent. You cannot have more independent directions than the dimension of the space. 5) Exactly \(n\) linearly independent vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) span all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) — they form a basis.

docs.title: Basis and Dimension:
docs.text:
A basis for a subspace \(V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) is a set of vectors that is: 1. linearly independent, and 2. spans \(V\). A basis is a minimal spanning set, or equivalently, a maximal independent set.

Theorem (Basis Theorem). Any two bases for the same subspace have the same number of vectors.This common number is the dimension of the subspace, \(\dim(V)\).

Proof sketch. Suppose \({\mathbf{u}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_p}\) and \({\mathbf{w}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{w}_q}\) are both bases for \(V\). Since \({\mathbf{u}_i}\) spans \(V\), each \(\mathbf{w}_j\) is a linear combination of the \(\mathbf{u}_i\)'s. By a replacement argument (Steinitz exchange lemma), this forces \(q \leq p\). By symmetry, \(p \leq q\). So \(p = q\). \(\blacksquare\)

The standard basis for \(\mathbb{R}^n\): \(\mathbf{e}_1 = \begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\\vdots\\0\end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{e}_2 = \begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\\vdots\\0\end{pmatrix}, \quad \ldots, \quad \mathbf{e}_n = \begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\\vdots\\1\end{pmatrix}\) Every \(\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) has a unique representation \(\mathbf{v} = \sum_{i=1}^n v_i \mathbf{e}_i\) — the coordinates \(v_i\) are exactly the coefficients in the standard basis expansion.

Uniqueness of representation. In any basis \({\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k}\) for \(V\), every vector \(\mathbf{w} \in V\) has a unique representation as a linear combination of the basis vectors.

Proof. Suppose \(\mathbf{w} = \sum c_i \mathbf{v}_i = \sum d_i \mathbf{v}_i\). Subtracting: \(\sum (c_i - d_i)\mathbf{v}_i = \mathbf{0}\). By independence, \(c_i = d_i\) for all \(i\). \(\blacksquare\) This uniqueness is what makes coordinates meaningful.

The Rank-Nullity Theorem: \(\dim(\text{col}(A)) + \dim(\text{null}(A)) = n\) \(\text{rank}(A) + \text{nullity}(A) = n\)

Proof. Let \(r = \text{rank}(A)\). Row reduce \(A\) to RREF. There are \(r\) pivot columns and \(n - r\) free columns. The \(n - r\) free variables parametrize \(\text{null}(A)\), giving a basis of \(n - r\) vectors. So \(\text{nullity}(A) = n - r\). \(\blacksquare\)

The orthogonality relations (Fundamental Theorem of Linear Algebra): \(\text{col}(A) \perp \text{null}(A^T), \qquad \text{row}(A) \perp \text{null}(A)\) So \(\mathbb{R}^m = \text{col}(A) \oplus \text{null}(A^T)\) and \(\mathbb{R}^n = \text{row}(A) \oplus \text{null}(A)\). Every vector in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) splits uniquely into a row-space component and a null-space component.

docs.title: The Four Fundamental Subspaces
docs.text: For \(A\) an \(m \times n\) matrix, the four subspaces associated to \(A\) are: 1) Column space \(\text{col}(A) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m\): the span of the columns of \(A\). This is the set of all \(\mathbf{b}\) for which \(Ax = \mathbf{b}\) has a solution. Dimension = \(\text{rank}(A)\). 2) Null space \(\text{null}(A) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\): the set of all \(x\) with \(Ax = \mathbf{0}\). Dimension = \(n - \text{rank}(A)\) (by rank-nullity). 3) Row space \(\text{row}(A) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\): the span of the rows of \(A\), equivalently \(\text{col}(A^T)\). Dimension = \(\text{rank}(A)\). 4) Left null space \(\text{null}(A^T) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m\): the set of all \(y\) with \(A^T y = \mathbf{0}\). Dimension = \(m - \text{rank}(A)\).

docs.title: Linear Combinations and Probability
docs.text:
This is the connection I keep thinking about when I study Stat 110.

If \(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n\) are random variables and \(\mathbf{a} = (a_1, \ldots, a_n)^T\) is a fixed vector, then:\(Y = \mathbf{a}^T \mathbf{X} = a_1 X_1 + a_2 X_2 + \cdots + a_n X_n\) is a linear combination of the \(X_i\)'s, and it is the most natural object in multivariate statistics. 1) [[02.Linearity of Expectation|Expectation]] is linear: \(E[Y] = \mathbf{a}^T E[\mathbf{X}] = \mathbf{a}^T \boldsymbol{\mu}\) 2) [[11.Variance|Variance]] of a linear combination: \(\text{Var}(Y) = \mathbf{a}^T \Sigma \mathbf{a}\) where \(\Sigma = \text{Cov}(\mathbf{X})\) is the \(n \times n\) covariance matrix. This is a quadratic form in \(\mathbf{a}\), and it is always \(\geq 0\) — which is exactly the statement that \(\Sigma\) is positive semidefinite. 3) Multivariate linear combination: if \(A\) is \(m \times n\) and \(\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^n\), then \(\mathbf{Y} = A\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^m\) is a vector of linear combinations: \(E[\mathbf{Y}] = A\boldsymbol{\mu}, \qquad \text{Cov}(\mathbf{Y}) = A \Sigma A^T\) This is the formula from the \(ABA^T\) [[05.Inverse of ABA^T]]note. Every column of \(A\mathbf{X}\) is a linear combination of the \(X_i\)'s, and the covariance structure transforms accordingly.

Why the span matters in probability: if \(\mathbf{X}\) has a singular covariance matrix \(\Sigma\) (i.e., \(\text{rank}(\Sigma) < n\)), then the distribution of \(\mathbf{X}\) is supported on a proper subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) — the column space of \(\Sigma\). The random vector \(\mathbf{X}\) lives in a lower-dimensional affine subspace with probability 1. This is a degenerate Gaussian, and it cannot have a density with respect to Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

docs.title: Things to Not Confuse
docs.text:
• Span vs. subspace. Every span is a subspace, but not every subspace is described as the span of a finite set. (In finite dimensions, every subspace is the span of finitely many vectors — just take a basis. But the description isn't unique.)
  • Linearly independent vs. orthogonal. Orthogonal vectors are always linearly independent, but independent vectors need not be orthogonal. Independence is purely about linear relations; orthogonality is a metric condition.
  • Basis vs. spanning set. A spanning set may be redundant. A basis is a spanning set with no redundancy. A linearly independent set may not span the whole space. A basis does both.
  • \(\text{rank}(A) = \dim(\text{col}(A)) = \dim(\text{row}(A))\). Column rank equals row rank. This is a theorem, not a definition, and it is genuinely surprising the first time.

docs.title: Vectors in 3D
docs.text:
A vector in \(\mathbb{R}^3\): \(\mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} v_1 \ v_2 \ v_3 \end{pmatrix} = v_1 \mathbf{e}_1 + v_2 \mathbf{e}_2 + v_3 \mathbf{e}_3\) where the standard basis vectors are:\(\mathbf{e}_1 = \begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{e}_2 = \begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{e}_3 = \begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}\) also written \(\hat{\mathbf{i}}, \hat{\mathbf{j}}, \hat{\mathbf{k}}\) in physics notation. I will use the column vector form throughout.

The length (Euclidean norm) of \(\mathbf{v}\): \(|\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2 + v_3^2}\) This is Pythagoras applied twice: first in the \(x\)-\(y\) plane to get \(\sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2}\), then in the vertical plane to get \(\sqrt{(\sqrt{v_1^2+v_2^2})^2 + v_3^2}\).

A unit vector has \(|\mathbf{v}| = 1\). The unit vector in the direction of \(\mathbf{v}\): \(\hat{\mathbf{v}} = \frac{\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|}\)

Proof. Place \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) tail-to-tail. The triangle with sides \(\mathbf{u}\), \(\mathbf{v}\), and \(\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{u}\) has: \(|\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{u}|^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2 + |\mathbf{v}|^2 - 2|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta \quad \text{(law of cosines)}\) But also:\(|\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{u}|^2 = (\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u})^T(\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}) = |\mathbf{v}|^2 - 2\mathbf{u}^T\mathbf{v} + |\mathbf{u}|^2\) Equating: \(\mathbf{u}^T\mathbf{v} = |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta\). \(\blacksquare\)

[!note] Consequences: \(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0 \iff \theta = 90° \iff \mathbf{u} \perp \mathbf{v}\). \(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} > 0 \iff \theta < 90°\) (vectors on the same side). \(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} < 0 \iff \theta > 90°\) (vectors on opposite sides). \(\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v} = |\mathbf{v}|^2\) always.

[!formula] Algebraic properties:

-Symmetry: \(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{u}\) -Linearity in each argument: \((c\mathbf{u}) \cdot \mathbf{v} = c(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v})\) and \((\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w}) \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{v}\) -Positive definiteness: \(\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v} \geq 0\), with equality iff \(\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}\)

These three properties make the dot product an inner product on \(\mathbb{R}^3\).

see more [[11.Length and dot product]]

Proof. From the geometric formula \(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta\) and \(|\cos\theta| \leq 1\). For a purely algebraic proof not relying on the angle interpretation: consider \(f(t) = |\mathbf{u} + t\mathbf{v}|^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2 + 2t(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}) + t^2|\mathbf{v}|^2 \geq 0\) for all \(t \in \mathbb{R}\). This quadratic in \(t\) is nonneg­ative everywhere, so its discriminant is \(\leq 0\): \(4(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})^2 - 4|\mathbf{u}|^2|\mathbf{v}|^2 \leq 0\). \(\blacksquare\)

Definition: For \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^3\): \(\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} u_2 v_3 - u_3 v_2 \ u_3 v_1 - u_1 v_3 \ u_1 v_2 - u_2 v_1 \end{pmatrix}\) The mnemonic: expand the determinant \(\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = \det \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{e}_1 & \mathbf{e}_2 & \mathbf{e}_3 \\ u_1 & u_2 & u_3 \\ v_1 & v_2 & v_3 \end{pmatrix}\) along the first row. Keep this formula — it is both the definition and the easiest way to compute. Geometric interpretation: 1. \(\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}\) is orthogonal to both \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\):

[!formula] $\((\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}) \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0, \qquad (\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}) \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0\)$

Proof of first. Direct computation: \((u_2v_3 - u_3v_2)u_1 + (u_3v_1 - u_1v_3)u_2 + (u_1v_2 - u_2v_1)u_3 = u_1u_2v_3 - u_1u_3v_2 + u_2u_3v_1 - u_1u_2v_3 + u_1u_3v_2 - u_2u_3v_1 = 0\). \(\blacksquare\)

  1. The magnitude:

    [!formula] $\(|\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}| = |\mathbf{u}| |\mathbf{v}| \sin\theta\)$ where \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\) is the angle between \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\). This equals the area of the parallelogram spanned by \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\). (Base \(|\mathbf{u}|\), height \(|\mathbf{v}|\sin\theta\).)

  2. The direction: \(\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}\) points in the direction given by the right-hand rule. Curl the fingers of the right hand from \(\mathbf{u}\) toward \(\mathbf{v}\); the thumb points in the direction of \(\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}\).

Algebraic properties:

  • Anti-symmetry: \(\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = -(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{u})\). Order matters.
  • Linearity in each argument: \((c\mathbf{u}) \times \mathbf{v} = c(\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v})\) and \((\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{w})\times\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w}\times\mathbf{v}\).
  • \(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}\) for any \(\mathbf{v}\).
  • \(\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0} \iff \mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) are parallel (or one is zero).
  • Not associative: \((\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}) \times \mathbf{w} \neq \mathbf{u} \times (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{w})\) in general.

Standard basis cross products:

\[\mathbf{e}_1 \times \mathbf{e}_2 = \mathbf{e}_3, \qquad \mathbf{e}_2 \times \mathbf{e}_3 = \mathbf{e}_1, \qquad \mathbf{e}_3 \times \mathbf{e}_1 = \mathbf{e}_2\]

and reversing each gives a minus sign. Think of the cycle \(1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 1\): going around the cycle forward gives \(+\), backward gives \(-\).

docs.title: The Dot Product
docs.text: For \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^3\): \(\boxed{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u}^T \mathbf{v} = u_1 v_1 + u_2 v_2 + u_3 v_3}\) ->This is a scalar. Geometric interpretation. :The dot product encodes the angle \(\theta\) between \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\): \(\bpxed{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = |\mathbf{u}| |\mathbf{v}| \cos\theta}\)

docs.title: [[14.The Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality|The Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality]]
docs.text: \(|\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}| \leq |\mathbf{u}| |\mathbf{v}|\) with equality iff \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) are parallel (one is a scalar multiple of the other).

docs.title: Projection
docs.text: The projection of \(\mathbf{u}\) onto \(\mathbf{v}\) is the component of \(\mathbf{u}\) in the direction of \(\mathbf{v}\): \(\boxed{\text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}} \mathbf{u} = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v}} \mathbf{v} = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|^2} \mathbf{v}}\) The scalar \(\dfrac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|}\) is the scalar projection (signed length of the shadow of \(\mathbf{u}\) onto \(\mathbf{v}\)). The rejection (component of \(\mathbf{u}\) perpendicular to \(\mathbf{v}\)): \(\mathbf{u} - \text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}} \mathbf{u}\) These two pieces are orthogonal and sum to \(\mathbf{u}\). This orthogonal decomposition is the seed of all of least squares theory.

docs.title: The Cross Product
docs.text: This is the operation that is genuinely new in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).

docs.title: Scalar Triple Product
docs.text:
\[\mathbf{u} \cdot (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{w}) = \det \begin{pmatrix} u_1 & u_2 & u_3 \\ v_1 & v_2 & v_3 \\ w_1 & w_2 & w_3 \end{pmatrix}\]

Geometric meaning: the signed volume of the parallelepiped spanned by \(\mathbf{u}\), \(\mathbf{v}\), \(\mathbf{w}\). The sign is positive if \((\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w})\) form a right-handed triple, negative if left-handed.

Key property: cyclic permutations preserve the value:

\[\mathbf{u} \cdot (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{v} \cdot (\mathbf{w} \times \mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{w} \cdot (\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v})\]

and swapping any two adjacent vectors flips the sign (since the determinant changes sign under row swap).

Consequence: \(\mathbf{u} \cdot (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{w}) = 0\) iff the three vectors are coplanar (the parallelepiped has zero volume, i.e., \(\mathbf{u}\) lives in the plane spanned by \(\mathbf{v}\) and \(\mathbf{w}\)).

docs.title: Vector Triple Product
docs.text:
\[\mathbf{u} \times (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{w}) = (\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{w})\mathbf{v} - (\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v})\mathbf{w}\]

This is the BAC-CAB rule: \(\mathbf{A} \times (\mathbf{B} \times \mathbf{C}) = \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{C}) - \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B})\).

Note that \(\mathbf{u} \times (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{w})\) lies in the plane spanned by \(\mathbf{v}\) and \(\mathbf{w}\) — it is a linear combination of \(\mathbf{v}\) and \(\mathbf{w}\), as the formula makes explicit.

A line is determined by a point \(\mathbf{p}\) on it and a direction vector \(\mathbf{d}\): \(\ell = {\mathbf{p} + t\mathbf{d} : t \in \mathbb{R}}\) This is a parametric description: varying \(t\) over \(\mathbb{R}\) traces out the entire line. Two lines in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) can be: - Intersecting: they meet at exactly one point. - Parallel: same direction, no intersection. - Skew: different directions, no intersection, not in the same plane. (This cannot happen in \(\mathbb{R}^2\).) The distance between two skew lines with directions \(\mathbf{d}_1\), \(\mathbf{d}_2\) passing through points \(\mathbf{p}_1\), \(\mathbf{p}_2\): $\(\text{dist} = \frac{|(\mathbf{p}_2 - \mathbf{p}_1) \cdot (\mathbf{d}_1 \times \mathbf{d}_2)|}{|\mathbf{d}_1 \times \mathbf{d}_2|}\)$

The numerator is the scalar triple product — the component of \(\mathbf{p}_2 - \mathbf{p}_1\) along the common perpendicular direction \(\mathbf{d}_1 \times \mathbf{d}_2\).

A plane is determined by a point \(\mathbf{p}_0\) on it and a normal vector \(\mathbf{n}\) perpendicular to it:

\[\mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}_0) = 0\]

Expanding: \(n_1 x_1 + n_2 x_2 + n_3 x_3 = n_1 p_{01} + n_2 p_{02} + n_3 p_{03} = d\), giving the standard form:

\[n_1 x_1 + n_2 x_2 + n_3 x_3 = d\]

The normal vector \(\mathbf{n} = (n_1, n_2, n_3)^T\) is read off directly from the coefficients.

Finding the normal from two vectors in the plane: if \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) lie in the plane, then \(\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}\) is normal to the plane. This is the main computational use of the cross product.

Distance from a point to a plane. Distance from \(\mathbf{q}\) to the plane \(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} = d\):

$\(\text{dist} = \frac{|\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{q} - d|}{|\mathbf{n}|}\)$ Derivation. The signed distance is the scalar projection of \(\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{p}_0\) onto \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\): $\(\frac{(\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{p}_0) \cdot \mathbf{n}}{|\mathbf{n}|} = \frac{\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{p}_0}{|\mathbf{n}|} = \frac{\mathbf{n}\cdot\mathbf{q} - d}{|\mathbf{n}|}\)$ Taking the absolute value gives the unsigned distance. \(\blacksquare\)

The determinant of a \(3 \times 3\) matrix \(A = [\mathbf{a}^{(1)} \mid \mathbf{a}^{(2)} \mid \mathbf{a}^{(3)}]\) is: \(\det(A) = \mathbf{a}^{(1)} \cdot (\mathbf{a}^{(2)} \times \mathbf{a}^{(3)})\) This is the signed volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the three columns. Three facts follow immediately: 1. \(\det(A) = 0\) iff the columns are linearly dependent (zero volume). 2. \(|\det(A)|\) is the volume scaling factor: if you apply \(A\) to the unit cube, you get a parallelepiped of volume \(|\det(A)|\). 3. \(\det(A) > 0\) iff \(A\) preserves orientation (right-handed to right-handed); \(\det(A) < 0\) iff \(A\) reverses orientation.

docs.title: Linear Independence in \(\mathbb{R}^3\)
docs.text: Three vectors \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^3\) are linearly independent if: \(\mathbf{u} \cdot (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{w}) \neq 0\) i.e., the scalar triple product is nonzero, i.e., the parallelepiped they span has nonzero volume. Equivalently, they are independent iff the \(3 \times 3\) matrix with these vectors as rows (or columns) has nonzero determinant. The span of three independent vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) is all of \(\mathbb{R}^3\) — they form a basis.The span of two independent vectors is a plane through the origin. The span of one nonzero vector is a line through the origin.

docs.title: Summary of the Two Products
docs.text: Property Dot product \(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}\) Cross product \(\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}\) Output type Scalar Vector in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) Symmetry \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{u}\) \(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v} = -\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{u}\) Zero condition \(\theta = 90°\) (perpendicular) \(\theta = 0°\) or \(180°\) (parallel) Magnitude \(\|\mathbf{u}\|\mathbf{v}\|\cos\theta\) \(\|\mathbf{u}\|\mathbf{v}\|\sin\theta\) Geometric meaning Projection / angle Area of parallelogram / normal direction Generalizes to \(\mathbb{R}^n\)? Yes (inner product) No (only \(\mathbb{R}^3\) and \(\mathbb{R}^7\))

docs.title: Things to Not Confuse
docs.text:
• \(\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}\) means \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) are parallel. \(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0\) means they are perpendicular. These are opposite extremes.
  • The cross product is not associative. Do not write \(\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{w}\) without parentheses — it is ambiguous.
  • The normal to a plane \(n_1x_1 + n_2x_2 + n_3x_3 = d\) is \((n_1, n_2, n_3)^T\). The plane itself is not through the origin unless \(d = 0\).
  • A line in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) cannot be described by a single linear equation. A single linear equation \(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} = d\) describes a plane. A line requires two such equations (intersection of two planes) or a parametric form.

docs.title: Length
docs.text:
The length (Euclidean norm) of a vector \(\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n\): \(|\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{v_1^2 + v_2^2 + \cdots + v_n^2} = \sqrt{\mathbf{v}^T \mathbf{v}}\) For \(n = 2\) this is Pythagoras. For \(n = 3\) it is Pythagoras applied twice. For general \(n\) it is the definition — we are extending the Euclidean notion of distance by declaring that the same formula holds in all dimensions.

Properties of the norm. For all \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) and \(c \in \mathbb{R}\): 1. \(|\mathbf{v}| \geq 0\), with \(|\mathbf{v}| = 0\) iff \(\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}\) — positive definiteness 2. \(|c\mathbf{v}| = |c| |\mathbf{v}|\) — homogeneity 3. \(|\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}| \leq |\mathbf{u}| + |\mathbf{v}|\) — triangle inequality Properties 1 and 2 are immediate from the definition. Property 3 requires Cauchy-Schwarz and is proved below.

Distance between two vectors: \(\text{dist}(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = |\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (u_i - v_i)^2}\) This makes \(\mathbb{R}^n\) a metric space.

docs.title: The Dot Product
docs.text:
Definition. For \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n\): \(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u}^T \mathbf{v} = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i v_i\) The dot product takes two vectors and returns a scalar. Observe : \(\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \sum_{i=1}^n v_i^2 = |\mathbf{v}|^2\) So the norm is recovered from the dot product: \(|\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}}\).

Algebraic properties. For all \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) and \(c \in \mathbb{R}\): 1. \(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{u}\) — symmetry 2. \((\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w}) \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{v}\) — additivity 3. \((c\mathbf{u}) \cdot \mathbf{v} = c(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})\) — homogeneity 4. \(\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v} \geq 0\), with equality iff \(\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}\) — positive definiteness

Properties 1–4 say the dot product is an inner product on \(\mathbb{R}^n\). This structure is what separates an inner product space from a mere vector space.

Properties 2 and 3 together say the dot product is bilinear: linear in each argument separately. This is the computation rule that makes everything tractable.

docs.title: The Geometric Formula
docs.text:
Theorem. For any \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) with \(\theta\) the angle between them: \(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta\)

Proof. Consider the triangle with vertices at \(\mathbf{0}\), \(\mathbf{u}\), and \(\mathbf{v}\). The side opposite \(\theta\) is \(\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{u}\). The law of cosines gives:$\(|\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{u}|^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2 + |\mathbf{v}|^2 - 2|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta\)\(Expand the left side using the algebraic properties:\)\(|\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{u}|^2 = (\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u})\cdot(\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}) = \mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v} - 2\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{u} = |\mathbf{v}|^2 - 2\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} + |\mathbf{u}|^2\)\(Equating the two expressions:\)\(|\mathbf{v}|^2 - 2\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} + |\mathbf{u}|^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2 + |\mathbf{v}|^2 - 2|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta\)$Cancel \(|\mathbf{u}|^2 + |\mathbf{v}|^2\) from both sides and divide by \(-2\):$\(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta \qquad \blacksquare\)$

This formula is how angle is defined in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) for \(n > 3\). In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and \(\mathbb{R}^3\) we already have geometric angles and can verify this formula. For \(n \geq 4\), we have no independent geometric notion of angle — we use this formula as the definition:$\(\cos\theta := \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|}\)$and Cauchy-Schwarz (proved below) guarantees \(|\cos\theta| \leq 1\) so this is always a valid angle.

docs.title: Orthogonality
docs.text:
\(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) are orthogonal (written \(\mathbf{u} \perp \mathbf{v}\)) if: \(\boxed{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0}\) From the geometric formula: \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0 \iff \cos\theta = 0 \iff \theta = 90°\). Convention: \(\mathbf{0}\) is orthogonal to every vector (since \(\mathbf{0}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0\) for all \(\mathbf{v}\)). This is purely algebraic — the zero vector has no direction, so "perpendicular" has no geometric meaning for it, but the algebraic definition still works.

The Pythagorean Theorem in \(\mathbb{R}^n\): if \(\mathbf{u} \perp \mathbf{v}\) then:$\(|\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}|^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2 + |\mathbf{v}|^2\)$ Proof.$\(|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}|^2 = (\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})\cdot(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}) = |\mathbf{u}|^2 + 2\underbrace{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}_{=0} + |\mathbf{v}|^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2 + |\mathbf{v}|^2 \qquad \blacksquare\)$This extends: if \(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k\) are mutually orthogonal then:$\(\left|\sum_{i=1}^k \mathbf{v}_i\right|^2 = \sum_{i=1}^k |\mathbf{v}_i|^2\)$

docs.title: [[14.The Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality]]
docs.text:
[!theorem] $\(|\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}| \leq |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\)$with equality if \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) are linearly dependent (one is a scalar multiple of the other, or one is zero).

Proof. If \(\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}\), both sides are zero and the inequality holds trivially. Assume \(\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}\). Consider \(f(t) = |\mathbf{u} - t\mathbf{v}|^2\) for \(t \in \mathbb{R}\). Since it is a squared norm, \(f(t) \geq 0\) for all \(t\). Expand: $\(f(t) = (\mathbf{u} - t\mathbf{v})\cdot(\mathbf{u}-t\mathbf{v}) = |\mathbf{u}|^2 - 2t(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}) + t^2|\mathbf{v}|^2\)$ This is a quadratic in \(t\) with positive leading coefficient \(|\mathbf{v}|^2 > 0\), and it is nonneg­ative for all \(t\). A nonneg­ative quadratic \(at^2 + bt + c \geq 0\) (with \(a > 0\)) has discriminant \(\leq 0\):\(b^2 - 4ac \leq 0\) Here \(a = |\mathbf{v}|^2\), \(b = -2(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})\), \(c = |\mathbf{u}|^2\). So: $\(4(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})^2 - 4|\mathbf{v}|^2|\mathbf{u}|^2 \leq 0\)$ $\((\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})^2 \leq |\mathbf{u}|^2|\mathbf{v}|^2\)$ $\(|\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}| \leq |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}| \qquad \blacksquare\)$

Equality holds if \(f(t) = 0\) for some \(t\), i.e., \(\mathbf{u} = t\mathbf{v}\) for some \(t\) — exactly when \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) are linearly dependent. Note: this proof works in any inner product space — Hilbert spaces, function spaces, \(L^2\), everything. The key was only that \(f(t) \geq 0\) for all \(t\), which follows from positive definiteness of the inner product._

docs.title: The Triangle Inequality
docs.text:
[!theorem] $\(|\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}| \leq |\mathbf{u}| + |\mathbf{v}|\)$

Proof. Square both sides (both sides are nonneg­ative, so squaring preserves the inequality): $\(|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}|^2 \leq (|\mathbf{u}|+|\mathbf{v}|)^2\)$

Left side: \(|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}|^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2 + 2\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} + |\mathbf{v}|^2\) Right side: \((|\mathbf{u}|+|\mathbf{v}|)^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2 + 2|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}| + |\mathbf{v}|^2\)

So the inequality reduces to: \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} \leq |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\) which follows from Cauchy-Schwarz (since \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} \leq |\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}| \leq |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\)). \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: The Parallelogram Law
docs.text:
[!formula] $\(|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}|^2 + |\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}|^2 = 2|\mathbf{u}|^2 + 2|\mathbf{v}|^2\)$

Proof. Direct expansion: $\(|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}|^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2 + 2\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} + |\mathbf{v}|^2\)$ $\(|\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}|^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2 - 2\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} + |\mathbf{v}|^2\)$

Add: the \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}\) terms cancel. \(\blacksquare\)

Geometric meaning: the sum of the squares of the diagonals of a parallelogram equals the sum of the squares of all four sides. This characterizes inner product spaces: a norm comes from an inner product iff it satisfies the parallelogram law. If a norm fails the parallelogram law (like the \(\ell^1\) norm), there is no inner product producing it.

Polarization identity. Rearranging, the dot product can be recovered from the norm alone:

\[\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = \frac{1}{4}\left(|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}|^2 - |\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}|^2\right)\]

This means inner product and norm carry identical information. You can work entirely with one and recover the other.

docs.title: Projection
docs.text:
The projection of \(\mathbf{u}\) onto \(\mathbf{v}\):

\[\text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}},\mathbf{u} = \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}},\mathbf{v} = \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|^2},\mathbf{v}\]

The scalar coefficient \(\dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|^2}\) is the coordinate of \(\mathbf{u}\) in the direction of \(\mathbf{v}\). Multiplying by \(\mathbf{v}\) gives the vector in that direction.

Decomposition. Every \(\mathbf{u}\) splits uniquely into:

\[\mathbf{u} = \underbrace{\frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|^2},\mathbf{v}}_{\parallel \text{ to } \mathbf{v}} + \underbrace{\mathbf{u} - \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|^2},\mathbf{v}}_{\perp \text{ to } \mathbf{v}}\]

Verification of orthogonality. Let \(\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{u} - \text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u}\). Then:

\[\mathbf{e}\cdot\mathbf{v} = \left(\mathbf{u} - \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|^2}\mathbf{v}\right)\cdot\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} - \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|^2}(\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0 \qquad \checkmark\]

Minimum distance interpretation. The projection \(\text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u}\) is the point on the line \({t\mathbf{v} : t \in \mathbb{R}}\) closest to \(\mathbf{u}\).

Proof. We want to minimise \(|\mathbf{u} - t\mathbf{v}|^2\) over \(t \in \mathbb{R}\). Expand:

\[|\mathbf{u} - t\mathbf{v}|^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2 - 2t(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}) + t^2|\mathbf{v}|^2\]

This is the same quadratic as in the Cauchy-Schwarz proof. Minimise over \(t\) by taking the derivative and setting to zero:

\[\frac{d}{dt}|\mathbf{u}-t\mathbf{v}|^2 = -2(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}) + 2t|\mathbf{v}|^2 = 0 \implies t^* = \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|^2}\]

So the closest point is \(t^*\mathbf{v} = \text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u}\). \(\blacksquare\)

This is the one-dimensional version of least squares. The higher-dimensional version — projecting onto a subspace — is exactly the same idea, just with a subspace replacing the line.

docs.title: [[13.Covariance and Correlation|Correlation]] as a Cosine
docs.text:
In statistics, the Pearson correlation coefficient between two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) is:

\[\rho(X,Y) = \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\text{Var}(X)\text{Var}(Y)}}\]

Now think of centred random variables \(X - E[X]\) and \(Y - E[Y]\) as vectors in the space of random variables with the inner product \(\langle X, Y\rangle = E[XY]\). Then: $\(\langle X - \mu_X,, Y - \mu_Y\rangle = E[(X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y)] = \text{Cov}(X,Y)\)$ $\(|X - \mu_X| = \sqrt{E[(X-\mu_X)^2]} = \sqrt{\text{Var}(X)} = \text{SD}(X)\)$ So: $\(\rho(X,Y) = \frac{\langle X-\mu_X,, Y-\mu_Y\rangle}{|X-\mu_X||Y-\mu_Y|} = \cos\theta\)$

where \(\theta\) is the angle between the centered random variables viewed as vectors.

Cauchy-Schwarz says \(|\rho| \leq 1\), which is the statement that correlation is always between \(-1\) and \(1\). This is not a separate fact — it is literally Cauchy-Schwarz applied to the inner product space of random variables.

\(\rho = 1\) if \(Y - \mu_Y = c(X-\mu_X)\) for some \(c > 0\): perfect positive linear relationship, angle \(= 0\).

\(\rho = -1\) if \(Y - \mu_Y = c(X-\mu_X)\) for some \(c < 0\): perfect negative linear relationship, angle \(= 180°\).

\(\rho = 0\) if the centered variables are orthogonal in this function space. Uncorrelated is the function-space version of perpendicular.

This is one of the most satisfying things I have learned: correlation is a cosine, Cauchy-Schwarz bounds it, and the geometry of the dot product completely explains why \(|\rho| \leq 1\).

docs.title: The Dot Product in Matrix Language
docs.text:
Everything above can be written cleanly using matrix multiplication. For column vectors \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n\): $\(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u}^T\mathbf{v} \quad (1\times n)(n\times 1) = 1\times 1 \text{ scalar}\)$ The outer product (rank-1 matrix): $\(\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^T \quad (n\times 1)(1\times n) = n\times n \text{ matrix}\)$ The projection formula in matrix form: $\(\text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u} = \frac{\mathbf{v}\mathbf{v}^T}{\mathbf{v}^T\mathbf{v}},\mathbf{u} = P\mathbf{u}\)$where \(P = \dfrac{\mathbf{v}\mathbf{v}^T}{\mathbf{v}^T\mathbf{v}}\) is the projection matrix onto the line spanned by \(\mathbf{v}\).

Properties of \(P\):

  • \(P^2 = P\) — idempotent (projecting twice gives the same result as projecting once)
  • \(P^T = P\) — symmetric
  • \(\text{rank}(P) = 1\)

These two properties (\(P^2 = P\) and \(P^T = P\)) characterise orthogonal projection matrices in general, not just rank-1 ones.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Concept Formula Geometric meaning Length \(\|\mathbf{v}\| = \sqrt{\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}}\) Distance from origin Dot product \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = \sum u_i v_i\) Scaled cosine of angle Angle \(\cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{u}\|\mathbf{v}\|}\) Defined by dot product in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) Orthogonality \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0\) \(\theta = 90°\) Cauchy-Schwarz \(\|\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}\| \leq \|\mathbf{u}\|\mathbf{v}\|\) $ Projection \(\frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|^2}\mathbf{v}\) Closest point on line, minimum distance Correlation \(\rho = \cos\theta\) Angle between centred random variables

docs.title: Things to Not Confuse
docs.text:
• \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}\) is a scalar. \(\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^T\) is an \(n\times n\) matrix. The order of transpose matters completely.
  • The projection of \(\mathbf{u}\) onto \(\mathbf{v}\) is not symmetric in \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\). \(\text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u} \neq \text{proj}_{\mathbf{u}}\mathbf{v}\) in general.
  • Cauchy-Schwarz gives \(|\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}| \leq |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\), not \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} \leq |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\). The absolute value matters when \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}\) is negative.
  • Orthogonal vectors are linearly independent (unless one is zero). Independent vectors need not be orthogonal. These are different conditions.

docs.title: Unit Vectors
docs.text:
A vector \(\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) is a unit vector if: \(|\mathbf{u}| = 1\) equivalently, \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{u} = 1\). Every nonzero vector \(\mathbf{v}\) can be normalized to a unit vector: \(\hat{\mathbf{v}} = \frac{\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|}\)

\(\hat{\mathbf{v}}\) points in the same direction as \(\mathbf{v}\) and has length exactly 1. The hat notation \(\hat{(\cdot)}\) signals "unit vector in this direction" and I will use it consistently.

Verification: $\(|\hat{\mathbf{v}}| = \left|\frac{\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|}\right| = \frac{|\mathbf{v}|}{|\mathbf{v}|} = 1 \qquad \checkmark\)$ using the homogeneity property \(|c\mathbf{v}| = |c||\mathbf{v}|\) with \(c = 1/|\mathbf{v}|\).

docs.title: The Standard Basis Vectors
docs.text: The most important unit vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) are the standard basis vectors: \(\mathbf{e}_1 = \begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\\\vdots\\0\end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{e}_2 = \begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\0\\\vdots\\0\end{pmatrix}, \quad \ldots, \quad \mathbf{e}_n = \begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\0\\\vdots\\1\end{pmatrix}\) Each \(\mathbf{e}_i\) has \(|\mathbf{e}_i| = 1\) and \(\mathbf{e}_i\cdot\mathbf{e}_j = \delta_{ij}\) (Kronecker delta: 1 if \(i=j\), 0 if \(i\neq j\)). They are an orthonormal set — mutually orthogonal unit vectors. In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and \(\mathbb{R}^3\), these are also written \(\hat{\mathbf{i}}, \hat{\mathbf{j}}, \hat{\mathbf{k}}\) in physics. I prefer the \(\mathbf{e}_i\) notation since it generalizes cleanly to \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

docs.title: Unit Vectors and the Dot Product
docs.text:
When \(\mathbf{u}\) is a unit vector, the dot product formula simplifies dramatically. For any \(\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) $\(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta = |\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta\)$ So \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}\) is exactly the signed length of the projection of \(\mathbf{v}\) onto \(\mathbf{u}\) — the scalar projection, with no division needed. More explicitly, the projection of \(\mathbf{v}\) onto the direction \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}\) $\(\text{proj}_{\hat{\mathbf{u}}},\mathbf{v} = \frac{\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}}{\hat{\mathbf{u}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}},\hat{\mathbf{u}} = \frac{\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}}{1},\hat{\mathbf{u}} = (\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}),\hat{\mathbf{u}}\)$ The denominator \(|\hat{\mathbf{u}}|^2 = 1\) disappears. Unit vectors make projection formulas clean.

Reading off coordinates. If \({\hat{\mathbf{u}}_1, \ldots, \hat{\mathbf{u}}_n}\) is an orthonormal basis (mutually orthogonal unit vectors), then any \(\mathbf{v}\) has the expansion: \(\mathbf{v} = \sum_{i=1}^n (\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i),\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i\) The \(i\)-th coordinate of \(\mathbf{v}\) in this basis is simply the dot product \(\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i\). No matrix inversion, no solving a linear system — just dot products. This is the defining advantage of orthonormal bases.

Proof. Write \(\mathbf{v} = \sum_j c_j \hat{\mathbf{u}}_j\). Take the dot product of both sides with \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i\): $\(\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i = \sum_j c_j (\hat{\mathbf{u}}_j\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i) = \sum_j c_j \delta_{ji} = c_i \qquad \blacksquare\)$

docs.title: Unit Vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^2\): Parameterisation
docs.text: Every unit vector in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) can be written as:\(\hat{\mathbf{u}}(\theta) = \begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta \ \sin\theta\end{pmatrix}\) for some angle \(\theta \in [0, 2\pi)\). The set of all unit vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is the unit circle \(S^1\). This parameterisation is worth internalising: \(\theta\) is measured counterclockwise from the positive \(x\)-axis. Two unit vectors \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}(\alpha)\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}(\beta)\) make an angle \(\beta - \alpha\) between them, and their dot product is: \(\boxed{\hat{\mathbf{u}}(\alpha)\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}(\beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta = \cos(\beta - \alpha)}\) This is the cosine addition formula, now understood as a dot product of unit vectors.

docs.title: Unit Vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^3\): Spherical Coordinates
docs.text:
Every unit vector in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) lives on the unit sphere \(S^2\). In spherical coordinates: \(\boxed{\hat{\mathbf{u}}(\phi, \theta) = \begin{pmatrix}\sin\phi\cos\theta \ \sin\phi\sin\theta \ \cos\phi\end{pmatrix}}\) where \(\phi \in [0,\pi]\) is the polar angle from the positive \(z\)-axis and \(\theta \in [0, 2\pi)\) is the azimuthal angle in the \(x\)-\(y\) plane.

Check: \(\sin^2\phi\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\phi\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\phi = \sin^2\phi(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta) + \cos^2\phi = \sin^2\phi + \cos^2\phi = 1\). \(\checkmark\)

docs.title: Orthonormal Sets and Matrices
docs.text:
A set of vectors \({\hat{\mathbf{u}}_1, \ldots, \hat{\mathbf{u}}_k}\) is orthonormal if: \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{u}}_j = \delta_{ij} = \begin{cases}1 & i = j \ 0 & i \neq j\end{cases}\) Every orthonormal set is automatically linearly independent.

Proof. Suppose \(\sum_i c_i \hat{\mathbf{u}}_i = \mathbf{0}\). Take the dot product of both sides with \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_j\): \(0 = \mathbf{0}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}_j = \sum_i c_i(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}_j) = \sum_i c_i \delta_{ij} = c_j\) So \(c_j = 0\) for every \(j\). \(\blacksquare\) When \(k = n\), an orthonormal set in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is an orthonormal basis.

docs.title: Orthogonal Matrices
docs.text:
If we pack an orthonormal basis \({\hat{\mathbf{u}}_1, \ldots, \hat{\mathbf{u}}_n}\) into the columns of a matrix \(Q\): \(Q = \begin{pmatrix} | & | & & | \\ \hat{\mathbf{u}}_1 & \hat{\mathbf{u}}_2 & \cdots & \hat{\mathbf{u}}_n \\ | & | & & | \end{pmatrix}\) then the orthonormality conditions \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}_j = \delta_{ij}\) are precisely the statement: $\(\boxed{Q^T Q = I}\)$ Check. The \((i,j)\) entry of \(Q^TQ\) is \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i^T\hat{\mathbf{u}}_j = \hat{\mathbf{u}}_i\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}_j = \delta_{ij}\). \(\checkmark\) Such a matrix is called orthogonal (a slight misnomer — the columns are orthonormal, not merely orthogonal). From \(Q^TQ = I\) we immediately get \(Q^{-1} = Q^T\): the inverse costs nothing to compute, it is just the transpose.

If the rows of \(Q\) are also orthonormal (which follows from \(Q^TQ = I\) when \(Q\) is square), then also \(QQ^T = I\).

Orthogonal matrices preserve lengths and dot products: $\(|Q\mathbf{v}| = |\mathbf{v}| \quad \text{for all } \mathbf{v}\)$

Proof. \(|Q\mathbf{v}|^2 = (Q\mathbf{v})^T(Q\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{v}^TQ^TQ\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}^TI\mathbf{v} = |\mathbf{v}|^2\). \(\blacksquare\)

And: \((Q\mathbf{u})\cdot(Q\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{u}^TQ^TQ\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u}^T\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}\) So an orthogonal matrix is a rigid motion (a rotation, or a rotation composed with a reflection). It moves vectors around without stretching or squishing anything.

\(\det(Q) = \pm 1\): \(+1\) for rotations, \(-1\) for rotations with a reflection.

docs.title: The Gram-Schmidt Process
docs.text: Given any linearly independent set \({\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k}\), Gram-Schmidt produces an orthonormal set \({\hat{\mathbf{u}}_1, \ldots, \hat{\mathbf{u}}_k}\) spanning the same subspace. This is how orthonormal bases are constructed in practice. 1. Step 1. Take the first vector and normalize: \(\mathbf{w}_1 = \mathbf{v}_1, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{u}}_1 = \frac{\mathbf{w}_1}{|\mathbf{w}_1|}\) 2. Step \(j\) (for \(j = 2, 3, \ldots, k\)). Subtract from \(\mathbf{v}_j\) its projections onto all previously found orthonormal vectors, then normalize: \(\mathbf{w}_j = \mathbf{v}_j - \sum_{i=1}^{j-1}(\mathbf{v}_j\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i),\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{u}}_j = \frac{\mathbf{w}_j}{|\mathbf{w}_j|}\) The key step is the subtraction: we remove every component of \(\mathbf{v}_j\) that lies in the span of \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_1, \ldots, \hat{\mathbf{u}}_{j-1}\). What remains, \(\mathbf{w}_j\), is orthogonal to all of them. Normalising then makes it a unit vector. \(\mathbf{w}_j \neq \mathbf{0}\) is guaranteed by linear independence: if \(\mathbf{w}_j = \mathbf{0}\), then \(\mathbf{v}_j\) would be in \(\text{span}{\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_{j-1}}\), contradicting independence. This is also QR decomposition. Writing out what Gram-Schmidt does in matrix language: \(A = QR\) where \(Q\) has orthonormal columns and \(R\) is upper triangular. \(R_{ij} = \mathbf{v}_j\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}_i\) (the projection coefficients) for \(i \leq j\).

docs.title: Example Gram-Schmidt in \(\mathbb{R}^3\)
docs.text:
Take: \(\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{v}_3 = \begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\)$

Step 1. \(\mathbf{w}_1 = \mathbf{v}_1 = (1,1,0)^T\). \(|\mathbf{w}_1| = \sqrt{2}\). \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\)

Step 2. Project \(\mathbf{v}_2\) onto \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_1\): $\(\mathbf{v}_2\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1\cdot1 + 0\cdot1 + 1\cdot0) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)$ Subtract: $\(\mathbf{w}_2 = \mathbf{v}_2 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\hat{\mathbf{u}}_1 = \begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix}1/2\\1/2\\0\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1/2\\-1/2\\1\end{pmatrix}\)$ \(|\mathbf{w}_2| = \sqrt{1/4 + 1/4 + 1} = \sqrt{3/2}\). $\(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_2 = \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\begin{pmatrix}1/2\\-1/2\\1\end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}\)$

Step 3. Project \(\mathbf{v}_3\) onto \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_1\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_2\): $\(\mathbf{v}_3\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(0+1+0) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\)$ $\(\mathbf{v}_3\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(0-1+2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\)$ Subtract: $\(\mathbf{w}_3 = \begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0\\1\\1\end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix}1/2\\1/2\\0\end{pmatrix} - \begin{pmatrix}1/6\\-1/6\\1/3\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}-2/3\\2/3\\2/3\end{pmatrix}\)$

\(|\mathbf{w}_3| = \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{3}\).

\[\hat{\mathbf{u}}_3 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}\]

Verify: \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_1\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}_3 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-1+1+0) = 0\). \(\hat{\mathbf{u}}_2\cdot\hat{\mathbf{u}}_3 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-1-1+2) = 0\). \(\checkmark\)

docs.title: Unit Vectors and the Normal Distribution
docs.text:
This connection surprised me when I first saw it.

Let \(\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, \ldots, Z_n)^T\) with \(Z_i \stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,1)\). The joint density is:

\[f(\mathbf{z}) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}} e^{-|\mathbf{z}|^2/2}\]

This density depends on \(\mathbf{z}\) only through \(|\mathbf{z}|\) — it is spherically symmetric. Every direction is equally likely. This means:

If \(Q\) is any orthogonal matrix, \(Q\mathbf{Z} \stackrel{d}{=} \mathbf{Z}\).

Proof. \(Q\mathbf{Z}\) is multivariate normal with mean \(\mathbf{0}\) and covariance \(QIQ^T = QQ^T = I\). So \(Q\mathbf{Z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, I) = \mathbf{Z}\) in distribution. \(\blacksquare\)

Decomposition into radius and direction. Write \(\mathbf{Z} = R\hat{\mathbf{U}}\) where:

\[R = |\mathbf{Z}|, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{U}} = \frac{\mathbf{Z}}{|\mathbf{Z}|}\]

\(R\) is the radial distance and \(\hat{\mathbf{U}}\) is the unit vector giving the direction. The spherical symmetry says \(\hat{\mathbf{U}}\) is uniformly distributed on the unit sphere \(S^{n-1}\), and \(R\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{U}}\) are independent. The radius \(R\) has distribution related to \(\chi_n\) (chi distribution with \(n\) degrees of freedom): \(R^2 = |\mathbf{Z}|^2 \sim \chi^2_n\).

This decomposition — separating length from direction — is the geometric heart of chi-squared distributions, \(t\)-distributions, and spherical symmetry arguments throughout probability.

docs.title: Things to Not Confuse
docs.text:
• Orthogonal vs. orthonormal. Orthogonal: \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0\). Orthonormal: \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 0\) AND \(|\mathbf{u}| = |\mathbf{v}| = 1\). An orthogonal set is not necessarily orthonormal. An orthonormal set is always orthogonal.
  • Orthogonal matrix. Despite the name, an orthogonal matrix has orthonormal columns. The naming is historical and unfortunate.
  • The formula \(\text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u} = \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|^2}\mathbf{v}\) simplifies to \((\mathbf{u}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{v}})\hat{\mathbf{v}}\) when \(\mathbf{v}\) is a unit vector. Always check whether the denominator is 1 before writing it out.
  • \(\hat{\mathbf{v}}\) and \(-\hat{\mathbf{v}}\) are both unit vectors in the direction of \(\mathbf{v}\) and \(-\mathbf{v}\) respectively. "The unit vector in the direction of \(\mathbf{v}\)" means \(+\hat{\mathbf{v}}\), not \(\pm\hat{\mathbf{v}}\).

docs.title: Angle Between Vectors
docs.text:
For nonzero vectors \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n\), the angle \(\theta \in [0, \pi]\) between them is defined by: $\(|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta = \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}\)$ equivalently: $\(\theta = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|}\right)\)$

Why this is well-defined. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality guarantees: \(|\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}| \leq |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\)

so \(-1 \leq \dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|} \leq 1\), which is exactly the range of \(\cos\). Without Cauchy-Schwarz this formula could produce a value outside \([-1,1]\) and \(\arccos\) would be undefined. Cauchy-Schwarz is not a consequence of this definition — it is the logical prerequisite.

In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and \(\mathbb{R}^3\) this definition agrees with the geometric angle you see. The formula is a theorem there, derived from the law of cosines (see the Length and Dot Product note). In \(\mathbb{R}^n\) for \(n \geq 4\), we have no independent visual notion of angle, so this formula is taken as the definition.

Convention: \(\theta \in [0,\pi]\). We always take the angle in the range \([0°, 180°]\), never reflex angles. This is because \(\cos\) is injective on \([0,\pi]\), so the angle is uniquely determined.

docs.title: Computing the Angle
docs.text:
From the definition, the computation is always the same three steps:

  1. Compute \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i v_i\)
  2. Compute \(|\mathbf{u}| = \sqrt{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{u}}\) and \(|\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}}\)
  3. Divide: \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|}\), then take \(\arccos\)

If only \(\cos\theta\) is needed (not \(\theta\) itself), stop at step 3.

docs.title: Example in \(\mathbb{R}^3\)
docs.text:
\[\mathbf{u} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\2\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}\]

Step 1. \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = (1)(2) + (2)(-1) + (2)(2) = 2 - 2 + 4 = 4\)

Step 2. \(|\mathbf{u}| = \sqrt{1 + 4 + 4} = \sqrt{9} = 3\), \(\quad |\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 4} = \sqrt{9} = 3\)

Step 3. \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{4}{3 \cdot 3} = \dfrac{4}{9}\), \(\quad \theta = \arccos!\left(\dfrac{4}{9}\right) \approx 63.6°\)

docs.title: Example in \(\mathbb{R}^4\)
docs.text:
\[\mathbf{u} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}\]

Step 1. \(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} = 2 + 0 - 1 + 0 = 1\)

Step 2. \(|\mathbf{u}| = \sqrt{1+0+1+1} = \sqrt{3}\), \(\quad |\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{4+1+1+0} = \sqrt{6}\)

Step 3. \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}\cdot\sqrt{6}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{18}} = \dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}\), \(\quad \theta = \arccos!\left(\dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}\right) \approx 76.4°\)

The procedure is identical regardless of dimension.

docs.title: Special Cases
docs.text:
\(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}\) \(\theta\) Relationship \(= \|\mathbf{u}\|\mathbf{v}\|\) \(= 0°\) Same direction, \(\mathbf{v} = c\mathbf{u}\), \(c > 0\) \(> 0\) \(\in (0°, 90°)\) Acute \(= 0\) \(= 90°\) Orthogonal \(< 0\) \(\in (90°, 180°)\) Obtuse \(= -\|\mathbf{u}\|\mathbf{v}\|\) \(= 180°\) Opposite directions, \(\mathbf{v} = c\mathbf{u}\), \(c < 0\)

The sign of the dot product alone tells you which side of \(90°\) you are on. That is often all you need.

docs.title: The Role of Direction: Normalised Form
docs.text: Since \(\cos\theta\) depends only on the directions of \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\), not their magnitudes, we can always reduce to unit vectors: $\(\cos\theta = \hat{\mathbf{u}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{v}}\)$ where \(\hat{\mathbf{u}} = \mathbf{u}/|\mathbf{u}|\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{v}} = \mathbf{v}/|\mathbf{v}|\). The angle is a property of directions, not lengths. This means: scaling \(\mathbf{u}\) or \(\mathbf{v}\) by any positive scalar does not change \(\theta\). Scaling by a negative scalar replaces \(\theta\) with \(\pi - \theta\).

docs.title: Angle and Cauchy-Schwarz: Two Sides of the Same Coin
docs.text:
Cauchy-Schwarz says \(|\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}| \leq |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\). Dividing both sides by \(|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\): $\(\left|\frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|}\right| \leq 1\)$ This is exactly \(|\cos\theta| \leq 1\). Without Cauchy-Schwarz the angle is not well-defined. In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and \(\mathbb{R}^3\) where angle is defined geometrically, \(|\cos\theta| \leq 1\) proves Cauchy-Schwarz. The two are logically equivalent, with causality depending on which direction you come from.

Equality. \(|\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}| = |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\) if \(|\cos\theta| = 1\) if \(\theta \in {0°, 180°}\) iff \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) are parallel. All the same statement.

docs.title: Angle in Terms of Projection
docs.text:
The scalar projection of \(\mathbf{u}\) onto \(\mathbf{v}\) is: $\(\frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|} = |\mathbf{u}|\cos\theta\)$

This is the signed length of the shadow of \(\mathbf{u}\) in the direction of \(\mathbf{v}\). Positive when \(\theta < 90°\), zero when \(\theta = 90°\), negative when \(\theta > 90°\).

The full vector projection: $\(\text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u} = \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|^2}\mathbf{v} = \frac{|\mathbf{u}|\cos\theta}{|\mathbf{v}|}\mathbf{v}\)$

And the Pythagorean decomposition confirms the geometry:

\[|\mathbf{u}|^2 = \underbrace{|\mathbf{u}|^2\cos^2\theta}_{|\text{proj}_\mathbf{v}\mathbf{u}|^2} + \underbrace{|\mathbf{u}|^2\sin^2\theta}_{|\mathbf{u} - \text{proj}_\mathbf{v}\mathbf{u}|^2}\]

which is just \(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1\).

docs.title: Connection to Correlation: Angle in \(L^2\)
docs.text:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be square-integrable random variables. Define the centred versions \(\tilde{X} = X - E[X]\) and \(\tilde{Y} = Y - E[Y]\), and regard them as vectors in \(L^2(\Omega, P)\) with inner product \(\langle \tilde{X}, \tilde{Y}\rangle = E[\tilde{X}\tilde{Y}] = \text{Cov}(X,Y)\) and norm \(|\tilde{X}| = \text{SD}(X)\).

The angle \(\theta\) between \(\tilde{X}\) and \(\tilde{Y}\) in this space:

\[\cos\theta = \frac{\langle\tilde{X},\tilde{Y}\rangle}{|\tilde{X}||\tilde{Y}|} = \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\text{SD}(X),\text{SD}(Y)} = \rho(X,Y)\]

The Pearson correlation coefficient is the cosine of the angle between the centred random variables. Every geometric fact about angles now has a statistical translation:

[!formula] \(|\rho| \leq 1\): Cauchy-Schwarz in \(L^2\). \(\rho = 1\): \(\theta = 0°\), \(\tilde{Y} = c\tilde{X}\) for \(c > 0\), perfect positive linear relationship. \(\rho = -1\): \(\theta = 180°\), \(\tilde{Y} = c\tilde{X}\) for \(c < 0\), perfect negative linear relationship. \(\rho = 0\): \(\theta = 90°\), uncorrelated = orthogonal in \(L^2\).

This is the same inner product space that Hilbert used to unify analysis and geometry. The fact that it applies here — to random variables — is not a metaphor. It is a theorem.

docs.title: The Angle Between a Vector and a Subspace
docs.text: The angle between a vector \(\mathbf{v}\) and a subspace \(\mathcal{W}\) is defined as: $\(\theta(\mathbf{v}, \mathcal{W}) = \min_{\mathbf{w} \in \mathcal{W},\ \mathbf{w} \neq \mathbf{0}} \theta(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w})\)$ the smallest angle between \(\mathbf{v}\) and any vector in \(\mathcal{W}\). The minimising vector \(\mathbf{w}^*\) is the projection \(\text{proj}_\mathcal{W}\mathbf{v}\), and the minimum angle satisfies: $\(\cos\theta(\mathbf{v}, \mathcal{W}) = \frac{|\text{proj}_\mathcal{W}\mathbf{v}|}{|\mathbf{v}|}\)$ The complementary angle (between \(\mathbf{v}\) and the orthogonal complement \(\mathcal{W}^\perp\)) is \(90° - \theta\). see more[[12.Four Fundamental Subspaces]]

docs.title: Things to Not Confuse
docs.text:
• \(\theta \in [0°, 180°]\) always. There is no notion of a signed or oriented angle between two vectors without additional structure.
  • \(\theta(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}) = \theta(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{u})\). The angle is symmetric — the formula is symmetric in \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\).
  • \(\theta = 0\) requires \(\mathbf{v} = c\mathbf{u}\) with \(c > 0\). The zero vector has no angle with anything — \(|\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}| = 0\) makes the formula undefined.
  • The angle between \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(-\mathbf{v}\) is \(\pi - \theta\) where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\). Flipping one vector reflects the angle around \(90°\).
  • Obtuse angle (\(\theta > 90°\)) does not mean the vectors are "going away from each other" in any absolute sense — it just means the dot product is negative, i.e., \(\mathbf{u}\) has a negative component in the direction of \(\mathbf{v}\).

docs.title: Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality
docs.text:
[!theorem] For any \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n\): $\(\boxed{|\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}| \leq |\mathbf{u}|,|\mathbf{v}|}\)$

with equality if and only if \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) are linearly dependent — that is, one is a scalar multiple of the other, or one is zero.

Squaring both sides (valid since both sides are nonnegative):

\[(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v})^2 \leq |\mathbf{u}|^2,|\mathbf{v}|^2 = (\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u})(\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v})\]

The squared form is cleaner to work with algebraically and is often what appears in proofs.

docs.title: What This Says Geometrically
docs.text:
Recall that the dot product satisfies \(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\cos\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between the two vectors. Cauchy–Schwarz is nothing more than the statement: \(|\cos\theta| \leq 1\)

Every form of this inequality in every setting is a version of this statement. The angle between two vectors is real, so its cosine cannot exceed 1 in absolute value. The rest is generalizations to infinite dimensions and abstract spaces. ![[Pasted image 20260409201422.png]]

docs.title: Proof 1:
docs.text:
This is the proof that generalizes furthest. It works in any inner product space, not just \(\mathbb{R}^n\). It requires only that the inner product is positive definite.

Setup. If \(\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}\), both sides are zero — trivial. Assume \(\mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}\).

Define \(f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) by: \(f(t) = |\mathbf{u} - t\mathbf{v}|^2\) -> This is the squared distance from \(\mathbf{u}\) to the vector \(t\mathbf{v}\) on the line through \(\mathbf{v}\).

Key observation. Since we are squaring a length: \(f(t) \geq 0 \quad \text{for all } t \in \mathbb{R}\) Expand. Using bi-linearity of the inner product: \(f(t) = (\mathbf{u} - t\mathbf{v}) \cdot (\mathbf{u} - t\mathbf{v}) = |\mathbf{u}|^2 - 2t(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}) + t^2|\mathbf{v}|^2\) Rewriting in standard form \(at^2 + bt + c\):\(f(t) = \underbrace{|\mathbf{v}|^2}_{a}, t^2 - \underbrace{2(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v})}_{-b}, t + \underbrace{|\mathbf{u}|^2}_{c}\) Apply the discriminant condition. This is a quadratic in \(t\) with positive leading coefficient \(a = |\mathbf{v}|^2 > 0\). A nonnegative quadratic with positive leading coefficient must have non-positive discriminant: \(b^2 - 4ac \leq 0\) ![[Pasted image 20260409202413.png]]

Substitute. With \(a = |\mathbf{v}|^2\), \(b = -2(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v})\), \(c = |\mathbf{u}|^2\): \((-2(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}))^2 - 4,|\mathbf{v}|^2,|\mathbf{u}|^2 \leq 0\) \(4(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v})^2 - 4|\mathbf{v}|^2|\mathbf{u}|^2 \leq 0\) \((\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v})^2 \leq |\mathbf{u}|^2,|\mathbf{v}|^2\)

Taking square roots of both sides (both sides nonnegative): $\(|\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}| \leq |\mathbf{u}|,|\mathbf{v}| \qquad \blacksquare\)$

docs.title: The Equality Conditio: Proof 1 in Detail
docs.text:
This deserves its own careful treatment.

  • Equality \(|\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}| = |\mathbf{u}||\mathbf{v}|\) occurs when \((\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v})^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2|\mathbf{v}|^2\), which means the discriminant is exactly zero. Discriminant \(= 0\) means the parabola \(f(t)\) touches the \(t\)-axis at exactly one point \(t^*\). That means: $\(f(t^*) = 0\)$$$ \implies |\mathbf{u} - t*\mathbf{v}|2 = 0$$ A squared norm is zero only for the zero vector:

$$\mathbf{u} - t^\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0} $$$\(\implies \mathbf{u} = t^*\mathbf{v}\)$ So \(\mathbf{u}\) is a scalar multiple of \(\mathbf{v}\). They are **linearly dependent*.

What is \(t^*\)? Minimise \(f(t)\) by differentiating: $$f'(t) = 2|\mathbf{v}|^2 t - 2(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}) = 0 $$$$ \implies t^* = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|^2}$$ This is exactly the scalar projection coefficient. The projection of \(\mathbf{u}\) onto \(\mathbf{v}\) is: \(\text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}},\mathbf{u} = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|^2},\mathbf{v} = t^*\mathbf{v}\) So \(t^*\) is asking: how much of \(\mathbf{v}\) do I need to best approximate \(\mathbf{u}\)? If the minimum distance is zero, \(\mathbf{u}\) lies exactly on the line spanned by \(\mathbf{v}\). ![[Pasted image 20260409203554.png]]

docs.title: Proof 2 — Lagrange's Identity (Algebraic, for \(\mathbb{R}^n\))
docs.text:
This proof gives more than just the inequality — it gives an identity that the inequality follows from.

Lagrange's Identity:

\[|\mathbf{u}|^2|\mathbf{v}|^2 - (\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v})^2 = \sum_{1 \leq i < j \leq n} (u_i v_j - u_j v_i)^2\]

Proof of the identity. Expand the left side:

\[\left(\sum_i u_i^2 ight)!\left(\sum_j v_j^2 ight) - \left(\sum_i u_i v_i ight)^2 = \sum_{i,j} u_i^2 v_j^2 - \sum_{i,j} u_i v_i u_j v_j$$ Separate the diagonal ($i = j$) terms, which cancel: $$= \sum_{i eq j} u_i^2 v_j^2 - \sum_{i eq j} u_i u_j v_i v_j$$ Use the symmetry $i \leftrightarrow j$ to write this as: $$= rac{1}{2}\sum_{i eq j}\left(u_i^2 v_j^2 + u_j^2 v_i^2 - 2u_i u_j v_i v_j ight) = rac{1}{2}\sum_{i eq j}(u_i v_j - u_j v_i)^2 = \sum_{i < j}(u_i v_j - u_j v_i)^2 \qquad lacksquare\]

Cauchy–Schwarz follows immediately. The right side is a sum of squares, hence \(\geq 0\): $\(|\mathbf{u}|^2|\mathbf{v}|^2 - (\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v})^2 \geq 0 \implies (\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v})^2 \leq |\mathbf{u}|^2|\mathbf{v}|^2\)$

Equality condition. Each term \((u_i v_j - u_j v_i)^2 = 0\), meaning \(u_i v_j = u_j v_i\) for all \(i,j\). This is precisely the condition for \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{v}\) to be proportional.

Special case in \(\mathbb{R}^2\). The sum has exactly one term (\(i=1, j=2\)):

\[|\mathbf{u}|^2|\mathbf{v}|^2 = (\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v})^2 + (u_1 v_2 - u_2 v_1)^2\]

The second term is \(|\mathbf{u} imes \mathbf{v}|^2\) (the square of the cross product magnitude). So this identity says:

\[|\mathbf{u}|^2|\mathbf{v}|^2 = |\mathbf{u}|^2|\mathbf{v}|^2\cos^2 heta + |\mathbf{u}|^2|\mathbf{v}|^2\sin^2 heta\]

which is just \(\cos^2 heta + \sin^2 heta = 1\). Cauchy–Schwarz in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is Pythagoras in disguise.

docs.title: Proof 3 — The Projection Argument (Most Geometric)
docs.text:
This is the proof that makes everything transparent.

Decompose \(\mathbf{u}\). Project \(\mathbf{u}\) onto \(\mathbf{v}\):

\[\mathbf{u} = \underbrace{\frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{|\mathbf{v}|^2}\mathbf{v}}_{\text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u}} + \underbrace{\mathbf{e}}_{\perp, \mathbf{v}}\]

where the error vector \(\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{u} - \text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u}\) satisfies \(\mathbf{e} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0\) (it is perpendicular to \(\mathbf{v}\)).

Apply Pythagoras. Since \(\text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u} \perp \mathbf{e}\):

\[|\mathbf{u}|^2 = |\text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u}|^2 + |\mathbf{e}|^2\]

Since \(|\mathbf{e}|^2 \geq 0\):

\[|\mathbf{u}|^2 \geq |\text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u}|^2 = \frac{(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v})^2}{|\mathbf{v}|^2}\]

Multiply both sides by \(|\mathbf{v}|^2\):

$\(|\mathbf{u}|^2|\mathbf{v}|^2 \geq (\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v})^2 \qquad \blacksquare\)$ ![[Pasted image 20260409203816.png]] Why this proof is the right one to understand. Cauchy–Schwarz says: the shadow of \(\mathbf{u}\) on \(\mathbf{v}\) is at most as long as \(\mathbf{u}\). The shadow is one component of \(\mathbf{u}\). A component cannot exceed the whole. This is visually obvious. The proof just makes it rigorous.

docs.title: Comparing the Three Proofs
docs.text:
All three proofs are the same idea in different clothing:

Proof Key quantity Why it's \(\geq 0\) Discriminant \(\|\mathbf{u} - t\mathbf{v}\|^2\) as a quadratic Squared norm Lagrange \(\sum_{i<j}(u_iv_j - u_jv_i)^2\) Sum of squares Projection \(\|\mathbf{e}\|^2 = \|\mathbf{u}\|^2 - \|\text{proj}\|^2\) Squared norm

In every case, the inequality comes from the nonnegativity of a squared quantity. That is the entire soul of Cauchy–Schwarz: something nonnegative forces the inequality.

docs.title: The Classical Form — Finite Sums
docs.text:
Before inner products existed as a concept, Cauchy (1821) proved the inequality for sums. For real numbers \(a_1, \ldots, a_n\) and \(b_1, \ldots, b_n\):

\[\left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i\right)^2 \leq \left(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2\right)\]

This is the vector form with \(\mathbf{u} = (a_1, \ldots, a_n)^T\) and \(\mathbf{v} = (b_1, \ldots, b_n)^T\). The sum \(\sum a_i b_i\) is the dot product.

docs.title: The Integral Form — \(L^2\) Functions
docs.text:
Schwarz (1885) extended the inequality to integrals. For square-integrable functions \(f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}\):

\[\left(\int_a^b f(x)g(x),dx\right)^2 \leq \left(\int_a^b f(x)^2,dx\right)\left(\int_a^b g(x)^2,dx\right)\]

This is Cauchy–Schwarz in \(L^2([a,b])\) with inner product \(\langle f, g \rangle = \int_a^b f(x)g(x),dx\).

The proof is identical. Define \(f(t) = \int_a^b (u(x) - t,v(x))^2,dx \geq 0\) for all \(t\). Expand, get a nonnegative quadratic, discriminant \(\leq 0\). Word-for-word the discriminant argument.

docs.title: The Probability Form — Random Variables
docs.text:
For square-integrable random variables \(X\) and \(Y\):

\[|E[XY]| \leq \sqrt{E[X^2]},\sqrt{E[Y^2]}\]

or in the centred form:

\[|\text{Cov}(X,Y)| \leq \text{SD}(X)\cdot\text{SD}(Y)\]

Proof. Define \(g(t) = E[(X - tY)^2] \geq 0\) (expectation of a nonnegative quantity). Expand: \(g(t) = E[X^2] - 2t,E[XY] + t^2 E[Y^2]\). Nonnegative quadratic, discriminant \(\leq 0\):

\[4(E[XY])^2 - 4,E[X^2],E[Y^2] \leq 0 \implies |E[XY]| \leq \sqrt{E[X^2],E[Y^2]} \qquad \blacksquare\]

The correlation bound. Applying to \(X - E[X]\) and \(Y - E[Y]\):
