Product of permutation matrices: The product of two permutation matrices is again a permutation matrix. The set of all \(n \times n\) permutation matrices forms a group under multiplication — isomorphic to \(S_n\), the symmetric group on \(n\) elements. For \(n = 3\), this is a group of order \(6\).

docs.title: The \(PA = LU\) Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem. For any invertible matrix \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\), there exists a permutation matrix \(P\), a unit lower triangular matrix \(L\), and an upper triangular matrix \(U\) with nonzero diagonal entries, such that

\[PA = LU\]

Equivalently, \(A = P^{-1} L U = P^T L U\).

docs.title: Why It Always Exists
docs.text:
The proof is constructive — it is Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting.

At each step \(k\) of elimination (choosing the pivot in column \(k\)), instead of taking whatever is currently in position \((k,k)\), we search rows \(k\) through \(n\) for the largest absolute value entry in column \(k\) (partial pivoting) or any nonzero entry (sufficient for existence). If the entire column below position \((k,k)\) is zero, then \(A\) is singular — but we assumed \(A\) is invertible, so this cannot happen. We swap the current row with the row containing the chosen pivot, record the swap in \(P\), then eliminate as usual.

The claim is that collecting all these row swaps into a single permutation matrix \(P\) applied at the start is equivalent to applying individual swap matrices throughout the process. More precisely:

Let \(P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_{n-1}\) be the individual permutation matrices applied at each step. Then \(P = P_{n-1} \cdots P_2 P_1\) (applied left to right in elimination order, but composed right to left as matrices). The full elimination gives

\[L_{n-1} P_{n-1} \cdots L_1 P_1 A = U\]

where each \(L_k\) is an elementary lower triangular matrix (one nonzero off-diagonal column). The key technical step — which I will not prove in full here — is that the individual \(P_k\) and \(L_k\) matrices can be rearranged so that all permutations accumulate into a single \(P\) on the left and all lower triangular factors accumulate into a single \(L\):

\[P_{n-1} \cdots P_1 A = LU \quad \Rightarrow \quad PA = LU \qquad \square\]

docs.title: A Full \(3 \times 3\) Example
docs.text:
Let

\[A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \ 3 & 2 & 1 \ 2 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\]

This has a nonzero \((1,1)\) entry, but I will force a row exchange anyway by using partial pivoting — choosing the largest pivot at each step — to illustrate the full machinery.

docs.title: Step 1: Choose the pivot in column 1.
docs.text:
Entries in column 1: \(|1|, |3|, |2|\). Largest is \(3\) in row 2. Swap rows 1 and 2.

\[P_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\] \[P_1 A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \ 3 & 2 & 1 \ 2 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2 & 1 \ 2 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\]

Eliminate column 1. Multipliers: \(\ell_{21} = 1/3\), \(\ell_{31} = 2/3\).

Row 2 \(\leftarrow\) Row 2 \(- \frac{1}{3}\) Row 1:

\[\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} - \frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \frac{4}{3} & \frac{2}{3} \end{bmatrix}\]

Row 3 \(\leftarrow\) Row 3 \(- \frac{2}{3}\) Row 1:

\[\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} - \frac{2}{3}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -\frac{1}{3} & \frac{7}{3} \end{bmatrix}\]

After step 1:

\[A^{(1)} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 1 \ 0 & \tfrac{4}{3} & \tfrac{2}{3} \ 0 & -\tfrac{1}{3} & \tfrac{7}{3} \end{bmatrix}\]

docs.title: Step 2: Choose the pivot in column 2 (rows 2 and 3 only).
docs.text:
Entries: \(|4/3|\) and \(|-1/3|\). Largest is \(4/3\) in row 2. No swap needed here.

\[P_2 = I\]

Multiplier: \(\ell_{32} = \frac{-1/3}{4/3} = -\frac{1}{4}\).

Row 3 \(\leftarrow\) Row 3 \(- (-\frac{1}{4})\) Row 2 = Row 3 \(+ \frac{1}{4}\) Row 2:

\[\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -\tfrac{1}{3} & \tfrac{7}{3} \end{bmatrix} + \frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & \tfrac{4}{3} & \tfrac{2}{3} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & \tfrac{7}{3} + \tfrac{1}{6} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & \tfrac{5}{2} \end{bmatrix}\]

After step 2:

\[U = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 1 \ 0 & \tfrac{4}{3} & \tfrac{2}{3} \ 0 & 0 & \tfrac{5}{2} \end{bmatrix}\]

docs.title: Assembling \(P\), \(L\), \(U\).
docs.text:
Only one row swap occurred (step 1), so

\[P = P_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

The multipliers go directly into \(L\):

\[L = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \ \ell_{21} & 1 & 0 \ \ell_{31} & \ell_{32} & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \ \tfrac{1}{3} & 1 & 0 \ \tfrac{2}{3} & -\tfrac{1}{4} & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

Important subtlety: The multipliers in \(L\) are the multipliers used after the row permutation at each step — they go into \(L\) without modification, in the positions determined by the reordered rows. This is the key thing that confused me initially: you do not permute the multipliers when you form \(L\). They just fill in below the diagonal in elimination order.

docs.title: Verification: \(PA = LU\).
docs.text:
\[PA = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \ 3 & 2 & 1 \ 2 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 1 \ 1 & 2 & 1 \ 2 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\] \[LU = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \ \tfrac{1}{3} & 1 & 0 \ \tfrac{2}{3} & -\tfrac{1}{4} & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 1 \ 0 & \tfrac{4}{3} & \tfrac{2}{3} \ 0 & 0 & \tfrac{5}{2} \end{bmatrix}\]

Row 1 of \(LU\): \(\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) \(\checkmark\)

Row 2 of \(LU\): \(\begin{bmatrix} \tfrac{1}{3}\cdot3 + 0 & \tfrac{1}{3}\cdot2 + \tfrac{4}{3} & \tfrac{1}{3}\cdot1 + \tfrac{2}{3} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \tfrac{2}{3}+\tfrac{4}{3} & \tfrac{1}{3}+\tfrac{2}{3} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) \(\checkmark\)

Row 3 of \(LU\): \(\begin{bmatrix} \tfrac{2}{3}\cdot3 + 0 & \tfrac{2}{3}\cdot2 + (-\tfrac{1}{4})\cdot\tfrac{4}{3} & \tfrac{2}{3}\cdot1 + (-\tfrac{1}{4})\cdot\tfrac{2}{3} + \tfrac{5}{2} \end{bmatrix}\)

\(= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & \tfrac{4}{3} - \tfrac{1}{3} & \tfrac{2}{3} - \tfrac{1}{6} + \tfrac{5}{2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & \tfrac{4}{6}-\tfrac{1}{6}+\tfrac{15}{6} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\) \(\checkmark\)

docs.title: Solving \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) Using \(PA = LU\)
docs.text:
Once we have \(PA = LU\), solving \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) proceeds in three steps.

Starting from \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\), multiply both sides on the left by \(P\):

\[PA\mathbf{x} = P\mathbf{b} \implies LU\mathbf{x} = P\mathbf{b}\]

Let \(\mathbf{c} = P\mathbf{b}\) (just permute the entries of \(\mathbf{b}\) — free), \(\mathbf{y} = U\mathbf{x}\). Then:

Step 1: Compute \(\mathbf{c} = P\mathbf{b}\) by permuting \(\mathbf{b}\).

Step 2: Solve \(L\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{c}\) by forward substitution (top to bottom, since \(L\) is lower triangular).

Step 3: Solve \(U\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y}\) by backward substitution (bottom to top, since \(U\) is upper triangular).

Each of steps 2 and 3 costs \(O(n^2)\). The expensive part — \(O(n^3)\) — was computing \(P\), \(L\), \(U\) in the first place. Once the factorization is done, each new right-hand side \(\mathbf{b}\) can be solved in \(O(n^2)\). This is the whole point of factorization when solving multiple systems with the same \(A\).

docs.title: Why Partial Pivoting Matters Numerically
docs.text:
The existence theorem says we need any nonzero pivot, not necessarily the largest one. But in practice, small pivots cause catastrophic cancellation in floating-point arithmetic. Dividing by a very small number amplifies rounding errors.

Partial pivoting (choosing the largest entry in the column at each step) is the standard numerical strategy. It bounds the growth of entries in \(U\) relative to \(A\), keeping the factorization numerically stable.

There is a quantity called the growth factor:

\[\rho = \frac{\max_{i,j} |u_{ij}|}{\max_{i,j} |a_{ij}|}\]

For partial pivoting, theory guarantees \(\rho \leq 2^{n-1}\). In practice, \(\rho\) is almost always much smaller — the worst case almost never occurs on real matrices. This empirical stability is why partial pivoting is the standard choice in LAPACK and virtually every numerical linear algebra library.

Complete pivoting (searching the entire remaining submatrix for the largest entry) gives a tighter theoretical bound but requires both row and column permutations, leading to \(PA Q = LU\). It is rarely used in practice because it is slower and partial pivoting is already excellent.

docs.title: The Deeper Structure — \(P\), \(L\), \(U\) as a Group Decomposition
docs.text:
There is a theorem in the theory of algebraic groups — the Bruhat decomposition — which says that for an invertible matrix, the factorization \(PA = LU\) is essentially unique up to a choice of \(P\). More precisely, for each permutation matrix \(P\), there is at most one pair \((L, U)\) such that \(PA = LU\) with \(L\) unit lower triangular and \(U\) upper triangular with nonzero diagonal.

I am not ready to prove this carefully. But it tells me that \(P\) is not just a computational convenience — it is a canonical invariant of the matrix \(A\). The choice of permutation is determined by the zero/nonzero structure of \(A\) in a precise way.

docs.title: The Subtlety I Always Get Wrong
docs.text:
When multiple row swaps happen at different stages of elimination, the question is: where do the multipliers go in \(L\)?

The rule: after a row swap at step \(k\), the multipliers computed in step \(k\) go into row positions as they are after the swap. The rows of \(L\) below the diagonal reflect the ordering of rows in the already-permuted matrix.

A common mistake is to compute the multipliers for the original row order, then try to "un-permute" them. That is wrong. The multipliers are always computed from the current state of the matrix — rows already permuted by all previous swaps. They go directly into \(L\) in the position they occupy at the time of computation.

I spent an embarrassing amount of time getting this wrong. The worked example above is clean because only one swap occurs. In practice, with two or more swaps, drawing the matrix at each step and tracking which row is which is the only reliable method.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
\[PA = LU\]

\(P\): permutation matrix (\(P^{-1} = P^T\), records all row swaps) \(A\): the original matrix \(L\): unit lower triangular (multipliers from elimination, in post-swap order) \(U\): upper triangular with nonzero diagonal (pivots on the diagonal)

Exists for every invertible \(A\). The factorization is the correct way to do Gaussian elimination — not \(A = LU\) with an asterisk for "assuming no zero pivots appear."

To solve \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\): permute \(\mathbf{b}\) to get \(P\mathbf{b}\), forward-substitute through \(L\), back-substitute through \(U\).

docs.title: DL^T Decomposition
docs.text:
You already know [[10. A = LU]]. For a symmetric matrix (\(A = A^T\)), there is hidden structure: \(U\) is not free — it is completely determined by \(L\) and the pivots. \(LDL^T\) makes this explicit.

Factorization Applies To Cost Requires \(LU\) Any square matrix \(n^3/3\) ops Non-singular leading submatrices \(LDL^T\) Symmetric \(n^3/6\) ops Same as LU Cholesky \(LL^T\) Symmetric Positive Definite \(n^3/6\) ops All pivots \(> 0\)

[!theorem] \(LDL^T\) Factorization If \(A\) is symmetric and all leading principal submatrices are non-singular (no row exchanges needed in Gaussian elimination), then: $\(A = LDL^T\)$ where \(L\) is unit lower triangular (1s on diagonal) and \(D\) is diagonal.

docs.title: Derivation from LU
docs.text:
Start from what you know: \(A = LU\). - Step 1: Use symmetry. \(LU = A = A^T = (LU)^T = U^T L^T\) - Step 2: Factor the diagonal out of \(U\). Let \(D = \text{diag}(u_{11}, u_{22}, \ldots, u_{nn})\), and write: \(U = D\tilde{U}\) where \(\tilde{U}\) is unit upper triangular (all diagonal entries = 1). - Step 3: Substitute back: \(A = LD\tilde{U}\) - Step 4: By the uniqueness of LU factorization, matching \(LD\tilde{U} = U^T L^T\) forces: \(\tilde{U} = L^T\)

Therefore: \(\boxed{A = LDL^T}\)

[!note] Key Insight The uniqueness of LU factorization does the heavy lifting. You don't need a separate proof — the algebra forces \(\tilde{U} = L^T\).

docs.title: 4. Example: \(3 \times 3\) Matrix
docs.text:
$\(A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 2 & -1 \\ -2 & -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\)$ Symmetry check: \(a_{12}=a_{21}=2\), \(a_{13}=a_{31}=-2\), \(a_{23}=a_{32}=-1\) ✓ - Step 1 : Eliminate Column 1 Pivot: \(a_{11} = 4\) Multipliers: \(\ell_{21} = \frac{2}{4} = \frac{1}{2}, \qquad \ell_{31} = \frac{-2}{4} = -\frac{1}{2}\) After row operations: \(\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\)

[!check] Symmetry at Work Notice: after eliminating column 1, the submatrix in rows/cols 2–3 is also symmetric. This is always true — eliminating from a symmetric matrix leaves a symmetric Schur complement.

  • Step 2: Eliminate Column 2 Pivot: \(a_{22}^{(2)} = 1\). Multiplier: \(\ell_{32} = 0/1 = 0\). No change. \(U = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\)

  • Step 3: Extract \(D\) and \(L^T\) \(D = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) \(L^T = D^{-1}U = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1/2 & -1/2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) \(L = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1/2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1/2 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)

[!tip] Shortcut The entries of \(L\) below the diagonal are exactly the Gaussian elimination multipliers \(\ell_{ij}\). You read them off automatically — no extra computation.

docs.title: Verification:
docs.text: \(LD = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) \((LD)L^T = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 2 & -1 \\ -2 & -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = A \checkmark\)

docs.title: 5. \(LDL^T\) and the Positive Definiteness Test:
docs.text:
\(A\) is positive definite (PD) if \(\mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x} > 0\) for all \(\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{0}\).

[!theorem] Pivot Test via \(LDL^T\) A symmetric matrix \(A\) is positive definite if and only if all diagonal entries of \(D\) are positive.

docs.title: Proof:
docs.text: \(\mathbf{x}^T A \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}^T L D L^T \mathbf{x} = \underbrace{(L^T\mathbf{x})^T}_{\mathbf{y}^T} D \underbrace{(L^T\mathbf{x})}_{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{y}^T D \mathbf{y}\) Let \(\mathbf{y} = L^T \mathbf{x}\). Since \(L^T\) is unit upper triangular, it is invertible, so as \(\mathbf{x}\) ranges over all nonzero vectors, so does \(\mathbf{y}\). \(\mathbf{y}^T D \mathbf{y} = \sum_{i=1}^n d_i y_i^2\) -> This is \(> 0\) for all \(\mathbf{y} \neq \mathbf{0}\) if and only if every \(d_i > 0\). $\(\boxed{A \text{ is PD} \iff d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_n > 0}\)$

docs.title: Applied to Our Example
docs.text:
\(D = \text{diag}(4, 1, 2)\) — all positive → \(A\) is positive definite ✓

![[Pasted image 20260417201901.png]]

![[Pasted image 20260417202651.png]]

Method Symmetric? PD Required? Conceptual Role \(LU\) No No General factorization \(LDL^T\) Yes No Symmetric factorization, pivot extraction Cholesky Yes Yes Numerically optimal for PD systems

[!note] Cholesky from \(LDL^T\) When all \(d_i > 0\), write \(D = D^{1/2} D^{1/2}\) and absorb: $\(A = L D L^T = (LD^{1/2})(D^{1/2}L^T) = \tilde{L}\tilde{L}^T\)$ The square roots \(\sqrt{d_i}\) require \(d_i > 0\), hence the PD requirement.

docs.title: Cholesky Decomposition
docs.text:
[!note] You already have \(LDL^T\). So why Cholesky?

Because it is the numerical workhorse for positive definite systems. It is: -Half the work of \(LU\) (\(n^3/6\) vs \(n^3/3\) operations) -Numerically the most stable factorization for PD matrices -The standard solver in statistics (covariance matrices), ML (Gaussian processes, Kalman filters), and physics simulations The one tradeoff: it requires positive definiteness. If any pivot is \(\leq 0\), the square root breaks.

docs.title: Derivation from \(LDL^T\)
docs.text:
Start from what you already know. - Step 1: For symmetric positive definite \(A\): \(A = LDL^T \quad \text{where all } d_i > 0\) - Step 2: Since all \(d_i > 0\), define the diagonal square root matrix: \(D^{1/2} = \text{diag}(\sqrt{d_1}, \sqrt{d_2}, \ldots, \sqrt{d_n})\) - Step 3: Factor \(D = D^{1/2} D^{1/2}\) and regroup: \(A = L \underbrace{D^{1/2} D^{1/2}}_D L^T = \underbrace{(LD^{1/2})}_{\tilde{L}} \underbrace{(D^{1/2}L^T)}_{\tilde{L}^T}\) - Step 4: Define \(\tilde{L} = LD^{1/2}\). Then: \(\boxed{A = \tilde{L}\tilde{L}^T}\) ->where \(\tilde{L}\) is lower triangular (not unit — diagonal entries are \(\sqrt{d_i}\), not 1).

[!note] What Changes vs \(LDL^T\) In \(LDL^T\): \(L\) has 1s on diagonal, \(D\) holds the pivot magnitudes separately. In Cholesky: \(\tilde{L}\) absorbs \(\sqrt{d_i}\) into its diagonal. The factorization collapses from three matrices to two.

[!theorem] Cholesky Factorization A symmetric matrix \(A\) is positive definite if and only if there exists a unique lower triangular matrix \(L\) with strictly positive diagonal entries such that: $\(A = LL^T\)$

The uniqueness is easy to verify: the diagonal of \(L\) is forced by \(d_i = \ell_{ii}^2 > 0\).

![[Pasted image 20260417203824.png]]

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
\(A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 2 & -1 \\ -2 & -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\) From [[15.Symmetric Matrices, Their Products, and LDLT|LDLT Decomposition]], we already know: \(D = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad L_{LDL} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1/2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1/2 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)

  • Step 1:Compute \(D^{1/2}\) \(D^{1/2} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix}\)

  • Step 2: Compute \(L = L_{LDL} \cdot D^{1/2}\) \(L = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1/2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1/2 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix}\)

docs.title: Verification: \(LL^T\)
docs.text: \(LL^T = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 & -2 \\ 2 & 2 & -1 \\ -2 & -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = A \checkmark\)

docs.title: Direct Algorithm (No \(LDL^T\) Intermediate)
docs.text:
You can compute \(L\) directly without first doing \(LDL^T\).

For \(j = 1, 2, \ldots, n\):

\[\ell_{jj} = \sqrt{a_{jj} - \sum_{k=1}^{j-1} \ell_{jk}^2}\]

For \(i > j\):

\[\ell_{ij} = \frac{1}{\ell_{jj}}\left(a_{ij} - \sum_{k=1}^{j-1} \ell_{ik}\ell_{jk}\right)\]

[!example] Trace Through for Our \(3 \times 3\)

\(\ell_{11} = \sqrt{4} = 2\)

\(\ell_{21} = (2)/2 = 1\), \(\quad \ell_{31} = (-2)/2 = -1\)

\(\ell_{22} = \sqrt{2 - 1^2} = \sqrt{1} = 1\)

\(\ell_{32} = (-1 - (-1)(1))/1 = 0\)

\(\ell_{33} = \sqrt{3 - (-1)^2 - 0^2} = \sqrt{2}\)

Result: \(L = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & \sqrt{2}\end{bmatrix}\) ✓

![[Pasted image 20260417204252.png]]

docs.title: Why Positive Definiteness is Required:
docs.text:
[!warning] The Square Root Requirement The formula \(\ell_{jj} = \sqrt{(\ldots)}\) requires the argument to be strictly positive at every step. If any pivot \(d_j \leq 0\), you get a complex or undefined \(\ell_{jj}\). This is not a computational failure — it is telling you that \(A\) is not positive definite.

Conversely, if the Cholesky algorithm runs to completion (all square roots of positive numbers), you have simultaneously proven that \(A\) is positive definite. Cholesky is therefore also the most efficient positive definiteness test: just attempt the factorization.

docs.title: Comparison Table — \(LU\) vs \(LDL^T\) vs Cholesky
docs.text:
Property \(LU\) \(LDL^T\) Cholesky \(LL^T\) Matrix type Any square Symmetric Symmetric positive definite Factors \(L\), \(U\) (unrelated) \(L\), \(D\), \(L^T\) \(L\), \(L^T\) Diagonal of \(L\) All 1s All 1s \(\sqrt{\text{pivots}}\) Operations \(n^3/3\) \(n^3/6\) \(n^3/6\) Storage Full \(L\) + \(U\) \(L\) + \(D\) vector \(L\) only Numerical stability Good Good Best for SPD PD test? Indirect Yes (check \(d_i > 0\)) Yes (attempt factorization)

[!tip] Decision Rule - Non-symmetric? → Use \(LU\) - Symmetric, PD uncertain? → Use \(LDL^T\) (no square roots, check sign of pivots) - Symmetric, know it's PD? → Use Cholesky (cleanest, fastest in practice)

docs.title: Numerical Stability: Why Cholesky Wins
docs.text:
Standard \(LU\) with partial pivoting is stable in practice but requires row interchanges, which destroys any structure. Cholesky for SPD matrices is unconditionally stable without any pivoting:

[!theorem] Stability of Cholesky For a symmetric positive definite matrix \(A\), the computed Cholesky factor \(\hat{L}\) satisfies: $\(\hat{L}\hat{L}^T = A + E, \quad |E|_2 \leq c_n \epsilon_{\text{machine}} |A|_2\)$ where \(c_n\) is a modest constant depending on \(n\).

No amplification of rounding errors. No need for pivoting. This is why numerical libraries (LAPACK's dpotrf, NumPy's linalg.cholesky, PyTorch's torch.linalg.cholesky) all default to Cholesky for positive definite systems.

docs.title: Why I'm Writing This
docs.text: I spent the first part of this course treating "vector space" as a synonym for \(\mathbb{R}^n\). That works for computation, but it obscures what is actually going on. The axioms of a vector space are an abstraction that captures exactly the structure needed for linear algebra to work — and once I see which axioms are load-bearing, the whole theory becomes more transparent. This note is about understanding the definition, not just using it.

docs.title: The Definition of a Vector Space
docs.text:
A vector space over \(\mathbb{R}\) is a set \(V\) together with two operations:

  • Addition: \(V \times V \to V\), written \(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}\)
  • Scalar multiplication: \(\mathbb{R} \times V \to V\), written \(c\mathbf{v}\)

satisfying the following eight axioms for all \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w} \in V\) and all \(c, d \in \mathbb{R}\):

(VS1) Commutativity of addition: $\(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u}\)$

(VS2) Associativity of addition: $\((\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) + \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{u} + (\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w})\)$

(VS3) Additive identity: There exists \(\mathbf{0} \in V\) such that $\(\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{v} \quad \text{for all } \mathbf{v} \in V\)$

(VS4) Additive inverse: For every \(\mathbf{v} \in V\), there exists \(-\mathbf{v} \in V\) such that $\(\mathbf{v} + (-\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{0}\)$

(VS5) Multiplicative identity: $\(1 \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}\)$

(VS6) Associativity of scalar multiplication: $\((cd)\mathbf{v} = c(d\mathbf{v})\)$

(VS7) Distributivity over vector addition: $\(c(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v}) = c\mathbf{u} + c\mathbf{v}\)$

(VS8) Distributivity over scalar addition: $\((c + d)\mathbf{v} = c\mathbf{v} + d\mathbf{v}\)$

The elements of \(V\) are called vectors — but that word now means any object satisfying these eight rules, not necessarily an arrow in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

Remark (personal). The first time I read these axioms I thought: this is just saying the obvious things about \(\mathbb{R}^n\). But the point is that other sets satisfy these axioms too — sets of functions, sets of matrices, sets of polynomials. The axioms are exactly what you need to do linear combinations. Nothing more, nothing less.

docs.title: \(\mathbb{R}^n\)
docs.text:
The standard example. Vectors are \(n\)-tuples of real numbers, addition and scalar multiplication are componentwise. All eight axioms hold by properties of \(\mathbb{R}\). The zero vector is \((0, 0, \ldots, 0)\).

Explicit for \(\mathbb{R}^3\): the vectors

\[\mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} u_1 \ u_2 \ u_3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} v_1 \ v_2 \ v_3 \end{bmatrix}\]

satisfy \(\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} u_1 + v_1 \ u_2 + v_2 \ u_3 + v_3 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(c\mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix} cu_1 \ cu_2 \ cu_3 \end{bmatrix}\). The axioms are immediate.

docs.title: \(M_{m \times n}\) — Matrices
docs.text:
The set of all \(m \times n\) real matrices is a vector space. Addition is matrix addition (componentwise), scalar multiplication scales every entry. The zero vector is the \(m \times n\) zero matrix.

For \(2 \times 2\) matrices:

\[\begin{bmatrix} a & b \ c & d \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} e & f \ g & h \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} a+e & b+f \ c+g & d+h \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \lambda \begin{bmatrix} a & b \ c & d \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \lambda a & \lambda b \ \lambda c & \lambda d \end{bmatrix}\]

This is a vector space of dimension \(mn\). Concretely, \(M_{2\times 2}\) has dimension 4 — four free entries, four basis "matrices."

docs.title: \(\mathcal{P}_n\) — Polynomials of Degree \(\leq n\)
docs.text:
The set of all polynomials of degree at most \(n\) with real coefficients:

\[\mathcal{P}_n = {a_0 + a_1 x + a_2 x^2 + \cdots + a_n x^n : a_i \in \mathbb{R}}\]

Addition: add coefficients of like terms. Scalar multiplication: scale all coefficients. The zero vector is the zero polynomial \(p(x) = 0\).

\(\mathcal{P}_n\) has dimension \(n+1\) with basis \({1, x, x^2, \ldots, x^n}\).

docs.title: \(C[a,b]\) — Continuous Functions
docs.text:
The set of all continuous functions \(f: [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}\). Addition: \((f+g)(x) = f(x) + g(x)\). Scalar multiplication: \((cf)(x) = c \cdot f(x)\). Zero vector: the constant function \(f(x) = 0\).

This is an infinite-dimensional vector space. No finite set of functions spans it. This is the setting where Fourier analysis lives — see [[Inner Products]].

docs.title: A Non-Example: The First Quadrant of \(\mathbb{R}^2\)
docs.text:
Let \(V = {(x, y) : x \geq 0, y \geq 0}\). Addition is fine. But scalar multiplication fails: take \(\mathbf{v} = (1, 1) \in V\) and \(c = -1\). Then \(c\mathbf{v} = (-1, -1) \notin V\).

Axiom (VS4) also fails: the additive inverse of \((1,1)\) is \((-1,-1)\), which is not in \(V\).

The first quadrant is closed under addition but not under scalar multiplication. It is not a vector space.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A nonempty subset \(W \subseteq V\) is a subspace of \(V\) if \(W\) is itself a vector space under the same addition and scalar multiplication inherited from \(V\).

Since \(W\) inherits its operations from \(V\), most axioms (commutativity, associativity, distributivity) are automatic. The only things that need to be checked are the closure conditions:

Theorem (Subspace Test). A nonempty subset \(W \subseteq V\) is a subspace of \(V\) if and only if:

(S1) Closed under addition: \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in W \Rightarrow \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \in W\)

(S2) Closed under scalar multiplication: \(\mathbf{v} \in W, c \in \mathbb{R} \Rightarrow c\mathbf{v} \in W\)

Proof. If \(W\) is a subspace, (S1) and (S2) hold by the vector space axioms applied in \(W\). Conversely, suppose (S1) and (S2) hold and \(W\) is nonempty. Pick any \(\mathbf{v} \in W\). By (S2), \(0 \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0} \in W\), so the zero vector is present. By (S2), \((-1)\mathbf{v} = -\mathbf{v} \in W\), so additive inverses exist. The remaining axioms (commutativity, associativity, distributivity) are inherited from \(V\). \(\square\)

Consequence: Conditions (S1) and (S2) can be combined into a single condition:

\[\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in W \text{ and } c, d \in \mathbb{R} \implies c\mathbf{u} + d\mathbf{v} \in W\]

i.e., \(W\) is closed under all linear combinations. This is equivalent to (S1) + (S2).

Every subspace must contain \(\mathbf{0}\). This is the fastest way to rule out a subset. If \(\mathbf{0} \notin W\), then \(W\) is not a subspace, full stop.

docs.title: The Four Fundamental Subspaces
docs.text: For a matrix \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\), there are four subspaces attached to it. These are the subspaces that actually appear in linear algebra — understanding them is the main goal of the first half of 18.06. I will define them here and develop them further in [[Column Space and Null Space]].

docs.title: Column Space \(C(A)\)
docs.text:
\[C(A) = {, A\mathbf{x} : \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n ,} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m\]

The set of all linear combinations of the columns of \(A\). It lives in \(\mathbb{R}^m\).

Example. Let

\[A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 2 & 1 \ 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

The columns of \(A\) are \(\mathbf{a}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \ 2 \ 3 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf{a}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \ 1 \ 0 \end{bmatrix}\).

\(C(A) = \left{ x_1 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \ 2 \ 3 \end{bmatrix} + x_2 \begin{bmatrix} 0 \ 1 \ 0 \end{bmatrix} : x_1, x_2 \in \mathbb{R} \right}\)

This is a 2-dimensional subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^3\) — a plane through the origin.

Why it is a subspace. Take \(\mathbf{b} = A\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{c} = A\mathbf{y}\) in \(C(A)\). Then \(\mathbf{b} + \mathbf{c} = A\mathbf{x} + A\mathbf{y} = A(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}) \in C(A)\). Similarly \(\lambda \mathbf{b} = A(\lambda \mathbf{x}) \in C(A)\). Closed under both operations. \(\checkmark\)

Connection to solvability. \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) has a solution if and only if \(\mathbf{b} \in C(A)\). The column space is exactly the set of right-hand sides for which the system is consistent.

docs.title: Null Space \(N(A)\)
docs.text:
\[N(A) = {, \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n : A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0} ,} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\]

The set of all solutions to the homogeneous equation. It lives in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

Example. Same \(A\) as above.

\(A\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 2 & 1 \ 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \ x_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 \ 2x_1 + x_2 \ 3x_1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \ 0 \ 0 \end{bmatrix}\)

From row 1: \(x_1 = 0\). From row 3: \(x_1 = 0\) (consistent). From row 2: \(2(0) + x_2 = 0 \Rightarrow x_2 = 0\).

So \(N(A) = {\mathbf{0}}\). The only solution to \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\) is the zero vector — \(A\) has trivial null space, meaning \(A\) has full column rank (\(r = n = 2\)).

Why it is a subspace. If \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\) and \(A\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{0}\), then \(A(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}) = A\mathbf{x} + A\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{0} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}\). Similarly \(A(c\mathbf{x}) = cA\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\). \(\checkmark\)

Remark (personal). The null space lives in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) (the domain), while the column space lives in \(\mathbb{R}^m\) (the codomain). They are subspaces of different spaces. This caused me genuine confusion early on — I kept thinking they should be comparable objects somehow. They are not. The rank-nullity theorem relates their dimensions, but the spaces themselves live in completely different ambient spaces.

docs.title: Row Space \(C(A^T)\)
docs.text:
\[C(A^T) = {, A^T \mathbf{y} : \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^m ,} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\]

The column space of \(A^T\), equivalently the span of the rows of \(A\). Lives in \(\mathbb{R}^n\).

docs.title: Left Null Space \(N(A^T)\)
docs.text:
\[N(A^T) = {, \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^m : A^T \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{0} ,} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m\]

The null space of \(A^T\). Lives in \(\mathbb{R}^m\).

docs.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Linear Algebra (Part 1)
docs.text:
If \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\) has rank \(r\), then:

\[\dim C(A) = r$$ $$\dim N(A) = n - r$$ $$\dim C(A^T) = r$$ $$\dim N(A^T) = m - r\]

These four numbers must add up correctly: \(r + (n-r) = n\) and \(r + (m-r) = m\).

The rank-nullity theorem is the \(n\)-side: \(\dim C(A) + \dim N(A) = n\).

The deeper Part 2 of the fundamental theorem — which says \(C(A)\) and \(N(A^T)\) are orthogonal complements in \(\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(C(A^T)\) and \(N(A)\) are orthogonal complements in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) — requires inner products and is developed in [[Projections and Orthogonality]].

docs.title: Subspace Arithmetic
docs.text:
Two operations on subspaces produce new subspaces:

Intersection: If \(W_1\) and \(W_2\) are subspaces of \(V\), then \(W_1 \cap W_2\) is a subspace.

Proof. If \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in W_1 \cap W_2\), then \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in W_1\) and \(\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in W_2\). By closure in each, \(c\mathbf{u} + d\mathbf{v} \in W_1\) and \(c\mathbf{u} + d\mathbf{v} \in W_2\), so \(c\mathbf{u} + d\mathbf{v} \in W_1 \cap W_2\). \(\square\)

Sum: The sum of two subspaces is defined as

\[W_1 + W_2 = {, \mathbf{w}_1 + \mathbf{w}_2 : \mathbf{w}_1 \in W_1, \mathbf{w}_2 \in W_2 ,}\]

This is also a subspace (the smallest subspace containing both \(W_1\) and \(W_2\)).

Union is not a subspace in general. \(W_1 \cup W_2\) fails closure under addition unless one contains the other. Standard example: in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), let \(W_1\) be the \(x\)-axis and \(W_2\) be the \(y\)-axis. Both are subspaces. But \((1, 0) \in W_1\) and \((0, 1) \in W_2\), while \((1,0) + (0,1) = (1,1) \notin W_1 \cup W_2\).

docs.title: Every Subspace Must Pass Through the Origin
docs.text:
This deserves emphasis. Let \(W\) be a subspace and pick any \(\mathbf{v} \in W\). By (S2), \(0 \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0} \in W\).

Consequence: Lines, planes, and hyperplanes that do not pass through the origin are not subspaces.

In \(\mathbb{R}^2\): the line \(x + y = 1\) is not a subspace — it does not contain \((0,0)\). The line \(x + y = 0\) is a subspace — it is the null space of the matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).

In \(\mathbb{R}^3\): the plane \(2x - y + 3z = 0\) is a subspace (null space of \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\)). The plane \(2x - y + 3z = 5\) is not — it misses the origin, and the sum of two points on it lies on \(2x - y + 3z = 10\), not on the original plane.

docs.title: Subspaces of \(\mathbb{R}^3\) — A Complete Classification
docs.text:
Every subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^3\) is one of exactly four types:

Dimension 0: \({\mathbf{0}}\). The trivial subspace.

Dimension 1: Any line through the origin. Parametrically, \({t\mathbf{v} : t \in \mathbb{R}}\) for some nonzero \(\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^3\).

Dimension 2: Any plane through the origin. The set of solutions to \(ax + by + cz = 0\) for some nonzero \((a,b,c)\). This is the null space of the \(1 \times 3\) matrix \(\begin{bmatrix} a & b & c \end{bmatrix}\).

Dimension 3: All of \(\mathbb{R}^3\) itself.

Nothing else exists. A subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^3\) cannot have dimension \(1.5\) or \(2.7\) — dimension is always a non-negative integer, and it is bounded above by \(3\).

This classification is worth internalizing. When I stare at a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^3\), I should immediately ask: what is its dimension? That single number tells me its geometric type.

docs.title: Span as the Smallest Subspace
docs.text:
Given vectors \(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k \in V\), the span is

\[\text{span}(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k) = \left{ \sum_{i=1}^k c_i \mathbf{v}_i : c_i \in \mathbb{R} \right}\]

Theorem. \(\text{span}(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k)\) is a subspace of \(V\).

Proof. Let \(\mathbf{u} = \sum c_i \mathbf{v}_i\) and \(\mathbf{w} = \sum d_i \mathbf{v}_i\) be two elements of the span. Then \(\alpha\mathbf{u} + \beta\mathbf{w} = \sum (\alpha c_i + \beta d_i)\mathbf{v}_i\) is again in the span. \(\square\)

Moreover, \(\text{span}(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k)\) is the smallest subspace containing all \(\mathbf{v}_i\): any subspace that contains all \(\mathbf{v}_i\) must contain all their linear combinations, hence must contain the span.

Connection to column space. \(C(A) = \text{span}(\mathbf{a}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n)\) where \(\mathbf{a}_j\) are the columns of \(A\). The column space is the span of the columns.

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
• The four fundamental subspaces satisfy orthogonality relations: \(C(A) \perp N(A^T)\) and \(C(A^T) \perp N(A)\). This requires the inner product machinery from [[Inner Products]] — specifically the fact that \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\) implies \(\mathbf{x} \perp\) every row of \(A\). I want to write this up carefully once I have projections down.
  • Direct sums: when \(V = W_1 \oplus W_2\) (direct sum), every \(\mathbf{v} \in V\) decomposes uniquely as \(\mathbf{w}_1 + \mathbf{w}_2\). The four fundamental subspaces split \(\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\mathbb{R}^m\) into direct sums in a specific way — this is the full content of the fundamental theorem. I am not ready to write that note yet.
  • Infinite-dimensional spaces: the subspace test and span definition work identically, but "dimension" is no longer a finite integer. \(C[a,b]\) has no finite basis. What replaces the rank-nullity theorem in that setting? This is functional analysis — far down the road, but I want to keep the question in view.

Last edited: today

docs.title: Why I'm Writing This
docs.text: Solving \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\) feels, at first, like a trivial problem — the answer is always \(\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\), right? It is not, unless \(A\) has full column rank. The null space is the entire solution set of the homogeneous equation, and understanding its structure — how many free variables there are, how to find a basis for it, why it is a subspace — is the foundation for understanding the solution set of \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) in general. You cannot understand the particular solution without first understanding the homogeneous one.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The null space of \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\) is

\[N(A) = {, \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n : A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0} ,}\]

It is a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) — the domain of \(A\), not the codomain. I established this in [[Vector Spaces and Subspaces]]. The proof is two lines: if \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\) and \(A\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{0}\), then \(A(c\mathbf{x} + d\mathbf{y}) = cA\mathbf{x} + dA\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{0}\).

What I want here is not the proof that \(N(A)\) is a subspace — that is done — but the algorithm for finding it, and the structural understanding of what it looks like.

docs.title: The Algorithm: Elimination to Reduced Row Echelon Form
docs.text:
The tool for finding \(N(A)\) is Gaussian elimination, carried all the way to reduced row echelon form (rref), not just row echelon form. Let me be precise about what these mean.

Row echelon form (ref): After forward elimination. Upper triangular structure. The first nonzero entry in each row (the pivot) is strictly to the right of the pivot in the row above. All zero rows are at the bottom.

Reduced row echelon form (rref): Row echelon form, plus:

  • Every pivot is \(1\) (scaled).
  • Every entry above a pivot is \(0\) (eliminated upward as well as downward).

The rref of a matrix is unique — there is only one rref for a given matrix, regardless of the order of elimination steps. That uniqueness is what makes rref the right canonical form for understanding the null space.

docs.title: Pivot Columns and Free Columns
docs.text:
After reduction to rref, columns of \(A\) fall into two categories:

Pivot columns: Columns that contain a leading \(1\) (a pivot). There are \(r\) of them, where \(r = \text{rank}(A)\).

Free columns: Columns with no pivot. There are \(n - r\) of them.

The variables \(x_j\) corresponding to free columns are called free variables. They can be set to any value. Once the free variables are chosen, the pivot variables are completely determined by back substitution.

This is the structural fact I want to internalize: \(N(A)\) has dimension \(n - r\), and I find a basis for it by setting each free variable to \(1\) (and all others to \(0\)) in turn, then solving for the pivot variables.

docs.title: A Full Example: \(3 \times 4\) Matrix
docs.text:
Let

\[A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 \ 2 & 4 & 6 & 8 \ 3 & 6 & 8 & 10 \end{bmatrix}\]

I want to find all \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^4\) with \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\).

docs.title: Step 1: Forward Elimination
docs.text:
Pivot in column 1: value \(1\), row 1.

Multipliers: \(\ell_{21} = 2\), \(\ell_{31} = 3\).

Row 2 \(\leftarrow\) Row 2 \(- 2 \cdot\) Row 1:

\[\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & 6 & 8 \end{bmatrix} - 2\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\]

Row 3 \(\leftarrow\) Row 3 \(- 3 \cdot\) Row 1:

\[\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 & 8 & 10 \end{bmatrix} - 3\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\]

After step 1:

\[\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 \ 0 & 0 & 2 & 4 \ 0 & 0 & 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\]

Column 2 has no pivot — it is all zeros below row 1 (and row 1's entry in column 2 is above the current elimination front). Column 2 is a free column.

Pivot in column 3: value \(2\), row 2.

Row 3 \(\leftarrow\) Row 3 \(- 1 \cdot\) Row 2:

\[\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

After forward elimination (row echelon form):

\[U = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 \ 0 & 0 & 2 & 4 \ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

Rank \(r = 2\). Pivots in columns 1 and 3. Free columns: 2 and 4. Free variables: \(x_2\) and \(x_4\).

docs.title: Step 2: Reduce to rref
docs.text:
Scale row 2 by \(1/2\):

\[\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 \ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

Eliminate above pivot in column 3: Row 1 \(\leftarrow\) Row 1 \(- 2 \cdot\) Row 2:

\[\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix} - 2\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\]

Reduced row echelon form:

\[R = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 & -2 \ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

docs.title: Step 3: Read Off the Solution
docs.text:
The system \(R\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\) is:

\[x_1 + 2x_2 - 2x_4 = 0$$ $$x_3 + 2x_4 = 0\]

Free variables: \(x_2\) and \(x_4\). Solve for the pivot variables \(x_1\) and \(x_3\):

\[x_1 = -2x_2 + 2x_4$$ $$x_3 = -2x_4\]

docs.title: Step 4: Find the Special Solutions (Basis for \(N(A)\))
docs.text:
Set \((x_2, x_4) = (1, 0)\): pivot variables give \(x_1 = -2\), \(x_3 = 0\).

\[\mathbf{s}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \ 1 \ 0 \ 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

Set \((x_2, x_4) = (0, 1)\): pivot variables give \(x_1 = 2\), \(x_3 = -2\).

\[\mathbf{s}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \ 0 \ -2 \ 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

The null space is

\[N(A) = \left{ x_2 \begin{bmatrix} -2 \ 1 \ 0 \ 0 \end{bmatrix} + x_4 \begin{bmatrix} 2 \ 0 \ -2 \ 1 \end{bmatrix} : x_2, x_4 \in \mathbb{R} \right} = \text{span}(\mathbf{s}_1, \mathbf{s}_2)\]

\(\dim N(A) = 2 = n - r = 4 - 2\). The rank-nullity theorem is satisfied.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
Check \(A\mathbf{s}_1 = \mathbf{0}\):

\[\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 \ 2 & 4 & 6 & 8 \ 3 & 6 & 8 & 10 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -2 \ 1 \ 0 \ 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 + 2 \ -4 + 4 \ -6 + 6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \ 0 \ 0 \end{bmatrix} \checkmark\]

Check \(A\mathbf{s}_2 = \mathbf{0}\):

\[\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 \ 2 & 4 & 6 & 8 \ 3 & 6 & 8 & 10 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \ 0 \ -2 \ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 + 0 - 4 + 2 \ 4 + 0 - 12 + 8 \ 6 + 0 - 16 + 10 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \ 0 \ 0 \end{bmatrix} \checkmark\]

docs.title: The rref and the Null Space: The General Pattern
docs.text:
Let me make the structure explicit for the general case. Suppose \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\) has rank \(r\). After reduction to rref, reorder the columns so that pivot columns come first. The rref looks like:

\[R = \begin{bmatrix} I_r & F \ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

where \(I_r\) is \(r \times r\) identity (in the pivot columns), \(F\) is \(r \times (n-r)\) (the free column entries in the pivot rows), and the zero blocks are padding.

Why this structure gives the null space immediately. The equation \(R\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\) with pivot variables \(\mathbf{x}_p \in \mathbb{R}^r\) and free variables \(\mathbf{x}_f \in \mathbb{R}^{n-r}\) reads:

\[I_r \mathbf{x}_p + F \mathbf{x}_f = \mathbf{0} \implies \mathbf{x}_p = -F \mathbf{x}_f\]

So the full solution is

\[\mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}_p \ \mathbf{x}_f \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -F \ I_{n-r} \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}_f\]

The null space matrix is

\[N = \begin{bmatrix} -F \ I_{n-r} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times (n-r)}\]

The columns of \(N\) are exactly the special solutions. The identity block \(I_{n-r}\) in the bottom half is what you get by setting each free variable to \(1\) and all others to \(0\) — which is exactly the procedure I followed above.

In the worked example: \(r = 2\), \(n - r = 2\). The free columns of \(R\) (columns 2 and 4) give

\[F = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\]

So \(-F = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 2 \ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\) and

\[N = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 2 \ 1 & 0 \ 0 & -2 \ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

Reading off the columns: \(\mathbf{s}_1 = (-2, 1, 0, 0)^T\) and \(\mathbf{s}_2 = (2, 0, -2, 1)^T\). Matches what I found above. \(\checkmark\)

docs.title: The Rank-Nullity Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem. For \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\):

\[\text{rank}(A) + \dim N(A) = n\]

equivalently \(r + (n - r) = n\).

Proof. The rref has \(r\) pivot columns and \(n - r\) free columns. Each free column produces exactly one special solution, and these solutions are linearly independent (the \(i\)-th special solution has a \(1\) in the \(i\)-th free variable position and \(0\) in all other free variable positions — the \(I_{n-r}\) block). So \(\dim N(A) = n - r\). \(\square\)

The proof is fully constructive: not only does it tell you the dimension, it gives you the basis explicitly.

docs.title: Distinct Cases by Rank
docs.text:
The structure of \(N(A)\) depends entirely on the rank \(r\) relative to \(n\).

\(r = n\) (full column rank): No free variables. The only solution to \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\) is \(\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\). \(N(A) = {\mathbf{0}}\), dimension \(0\).

This happens exactly when the columns of \(A\) are linearly independent. The map \(\mathbf{x} \mapsto A\mathbf{x}\) is injective — different inputs give different outputs.

\(r < n\) (rank deficient in columns): There are \(n - r \geq 1\) free variables. \(N(A)\) is nontrivial — it contains infinitely many vectors. \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\) has infinitely many solutions.

Square matrix, \(m = n\): \(A\) is invertible if and only if \(r = n\), i.e., \(N(A) = {\mathbf{0}}\). If \(A\) is singular, \(r < n\) and \(N(A)\) is nontrivial.

docs.title: What the Null Space Really Means
docs.text:
Let \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\) and think of \(A\) as a linear map \(T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m\), \(T(\mathbf{x}) = A\mathbf{x}\).

\(N(A)\) is the kernel of this map — the set of vectors that get sent to zero. The map collapses the entire subspace \(N(A)\) to the single point \(\mathbf{0}\).

Why this matters for \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\). Suppose \(\mathbf{x}_p\) is one particular solution to \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) (if one exists). Then the complete solution set is:

\[{\mathbf{x} : A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}} = \mathbf{x}_p + N(A) = {\mathbf{x}_p + \mathbf{v} : \mathbf{v} \in N(A)}\]

Proof. If \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\), then \(A(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_p) = A\mathbf{x} - A\mathbf{x}_p = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}\), so \(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_p \in N(A)\). Conversely, if \(\mathbf{v} \in N(A)\), then \(A(\mathbf{x}_p + \mathbf{v}) = A\mathbf{x}_p + A\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{b}\). \(\square\)

The solution set of \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) is a coset of \(N(A)\) — a translate of the null space by the particular solution. It is not a subspace (unless \(\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}\)), but it is a flat (an affine subspace) of dimension \(n - r\).

Remark (personal). This structure — particular solution plus null space — is the linear algebra analogue of the general solution to a linear ODE: \(y = y_{\text{particular}} + y_{\text{homogeneous}}\). The homogeneous solution is always present; the particular solution shifts you to the right affine flat. I find it genuinely helpful that both settings have identical structure.

docs.title: A Second Example: When There Are No Free Variables
docs.text:
Let

\[A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \ 2 & 7 \ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

This is \(3 \times 2\), so \(n = 2\). I expect at most \(2\) pivots.

Forward elimination. Multiplier \(\ell_{21} = 2\):

Row 2 \(\leftarrow\) Row 2 \(- 2 \cdot\) Row 1:

\[\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 7 \end{bmatrix} - 2\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

Row 3 has \(\ell_{31} = 0\), so no change. After step 1:

\[\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \ 0 & 1 \ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

Row 3 \(\leftarrow\) Row 3 \(- 1 \cdot\) Row 2:

\[\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

Reduce to rref: Row 1 \(\leftarrow\) Row 1 \(- 3 \cdot\) Row 2:

\[\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} - 3\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\] \[R = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 \ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

Rank \(r = 2 = n\). Both columns are pivot columns. No free variables.

\(R\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\) gives \(x_1 = 0\) and \(x_2 = 0\). So \(N(A) = {\mathbf{0}}\), dimension \(0 = n - r = 2 - 2\).

The columns of \(A\) are linearly independent.

docs.title: Linear Independence via the Null Space
docs.text:
This gives a clean definition:

The columns of \(A\) are linearly independent if and only if \(N(A) = {\mathbf{0}}\).

Proof. The columns are linearly independent iff the only solution to \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\) is \(\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\), by definition of linear independence (\(x_1\mathbf{a}_1 + \cdots + x_n\mathbf{a}_n = \mathbf{0}\) only when all \(x_i = 0\)). This is exactly the statement \(N(A) = {\mathbf{0}}\). \(\square\)

So computing the null space and testing linear independence are the same computation.

docs.title: Summary of the Algorithm
docs.text:
Given \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\), to find \(N(A)\):

  1. Row reduce \(A\) to rref \(R\).
  2. Identify pivot columns and free columns. Let \(r\) = number of pivots.
  3. For each free variable \(x_j\): set \(x_j = 1\), all other free variables \(= 0\), and solve \(R\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\) for the pivot variables.
  4. Each choice gives one special solution. Collect them: \({\mathbf{s}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{s}_{n-r}}\).
  5. \(N(A) = \text{span}(\mathbf{s}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{s}_{n-r})\), and \({\mathbf{s}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{s}_{n-r}}\) is a basis for \(N(A)\).

\(\dim N(A) = n - r\). Check: \(r + (n-r) = n\). ✓

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
• The rref is unique: the same matrix always produces the same rref regardless of the sequence of row operations. I have used this but not proved it. The proof goes through the uniqueness of pivot positions. Worth a short proof sketch.
  • The null space of \(A^T\) — the left null space \(N(A^T)\) — lives in \(\mathbb{R}^m\) and has dimension \(m - r\). The same rref algorithm applies to \(A^T\). The left null space is orthogonal to the column space: \(N(A^T) \perp C(A)\). I will establish this in [[Projections and Orthogonality]].
  • For the complete picture: once I have \(N(A)\) and a particular solution \(\mathbf{x}_p\), the full solution to \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) is \(\mathbf{x}_p + N(A)\). The question of when \(\mathbf{x}_p\) exists is the question of when \(\mathbf{b} \in C(A)\). These two questions — solvability and solution structure — are the subject of [[Complete Solution to Ax=b]].

Last edited: today

docs.title: Why I'm Writing This
docs.text: Row reduction is the computational engine behind almost everything in the first half of 18.06. I know how to do it mechanically. What I did not understand clearly until recently is what the rref is as a mathematical object — why it is unique, what information it compresses, and why going all the way to rref (rather than stopping at row echelon form) is the right canonical form for reading off the null space and the rank. This note is about understanding rref as a theorem, not just as an algorithm.

docs.title: The Three Forms: Triangular, Echelon, Reduced
docs.text:
There is a hierarchy of how far you can simplify a matrix by row operations.

Row echelon form (ref): The result of forward elimination only. The shape is staircase-upper-triangular:

  • All zero rows at the bottom.
  • In each nonzero row, the first nonzero entry (the leading entry or pivot) is strictly to the right of the pivot in the row above.

The pivots need not be \(1\), and there may be nonzero entries above the pivots.

Reduced row echelon form (rref): Row echelon form, plus:

  • Every pivot equals \(1\).
  • Every entry in a pivot column is \(0\) except the pivot itself — both above and below.

The rref goes further: it eliminates upward as well as downward, and scales pivots to \(1\). This extra work is what produces a unique canonical form.

Example: the same matrix at each stage.

Starting matrix:

\[A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 & 4 & 2 \ 2 & 4 & 10 & 8 \ 3 & 6 & 15 & 12 \end{bmatrix}\]

After forward elimination (ref):

\[\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & 10 & 8 \ 0 & 2 & 4 & 2 \ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

(I swapped rows 1 and 2 first since \((1,1)\) is zero.) The pivots are \(2\) and \(2\), not \(1\). Entries above the second pivot have not been cleared.

After rref (scale pivots to \(1\), clear above):

\[R = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 & 3 \ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

I will derive this step by step below.

docs.title: Row Operations and Row Equivalence
docs.text:
Three elementary row operations are allowed:

(R1) Row scaling: Multiply a row by a nonzero scalar \(c \neq 0\).

(R2) Row replacement: Replace row \(i\) by row \(i\) plus \(c\) times row \(j\) (for \(i \neq j\), any \(c\)).

(R3) Row swap: Exchange rows \(i\) and \(j\).

Each operation is invertible: scaling by \(c\) is undone by scaling by \(1/c\); row replacement by \(c\) is undone by replacement by \(-c\); a swap undoes itself. So row operations never change the solution set of \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) — they are equivalences.

Definition. Two matrices are row equivalent if one can be obtained from the other by a finite sequence of elementary row operations.

Row equivalence is an equivalence relation (reflexive, symmetric, transitive). The rref is the canonical representative of each equivalence class.

docs.title: Deriving the rref Step by Step
docs.text:
Return to the example. Starting matrix:

\[A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 & 4 & 2 \ 2 & 4 & 10 & 8 \ 3 & 6 & 15 & 12 \end{bmatrix}\]

Swap rows 1 and 2 (column 1, rows 1 and 3, have entries \(0, 2, 3\) — pick the nonzero entry in row 2):

\[\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & 10 & 8 \ 0 & 2 & 4 & 2 \ 3 & 6 & 15 & 12 \end{bmatrix}\]

Eliminate column 1 below pivot. Multiplier \(\ell_{31} = 3/2\).

Row 3 \(\leftarrow\) Row 3 \(- \frac{3}{2} \cdot\) Row 1:

\[\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 & 15 & 12 \end{bmatrix} - \frac{3}{2}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & 10 & 8 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\] \[\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & 10 & 8 \ 0 & 2 & 4 & 2 \ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

Column 2 has a nonzero entry in row 2. Pivot is \(2\). Nothing to eliminate below (row 3 is zero). This is ref.

Scale row 1 by \(1/2\):

\[\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 5 & 4 \ 0 & 2 & 4 & 2 \ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

Scale row 2 by \(1/2\):

\[\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 5 & 4 \ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

Eliminate above pivot in column 2. Row 1 \(\leftarrow\) Row 1 \(- 2 \cdot\) Row 2:

\[\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 5 & 4 \end{bmatrix} - 2\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\] \[R = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

This is the rref. (I get slightly different entries here than my initial claim — let me recheck from the start more carefully.)

Actually let me redo the original elimination cleanly.

Row 3 \(\leftarrow\) Row 3 \(- \frac{3}{2}\) Row 1:

\[\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 & 15 & 12 \end{bmatrix} - \frac{3}{2}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 & 10 & 8 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3-3 & 6-6 & 15-15 & 12-12 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

Good, row 3 is zero throughout. Scale rows: row 1 by \(1/2\), row 2 by \(1/2\):

\[\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 5 & 4 \ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

Upward elimination in column 2: Row 1 \(\leftarrow\) Row 1 \(- 2 \cdot\) Row 2:

\[\begin{bmatrix} 1-0 & 2-2 & 5-4 & 4-2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\] \[\boxed{R = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}}\]

Rank \(r = 2\). Pivot columns: 1 and 2. Free columns: 3 and 4. Free variables: \(x_3, x_4\).

docs.title: Reading Information Directly from the rref
docs.text: The rref is a data-compression device. Here is everything it tells you at a glance.

docs.title: The Rank
docs.text: $r = $ number of pivot rows = number of nonzero rows in \(R\). In the example: \(r = 2\).

docs.title: Pivot and Free Columns
docs.text:
Pivot columns are the columns containing leading \(1\)'s. Free columns are all others.

In the example:

  • Pivot columns: 1, 2
  • Free columns: 3, 4
  • Pivot variables: \(x_1, x_2\)
  • Free variables: \(x_3, x_4\)

docs.title: The Null Space
docs.text:
From the rref rows (nonzero rows only):

\[x_1 + x_3 + 2x_4 = 0 \implies x_1 = -x_3 - 2x_4$$ $$x_2 + 2x_3 + x_4 = 0 \implies x_2 = -2x_3 - x_4\]

Special solution 1: set \((x_3, x_4) = (1, 0)\):

\[\mathbf{s}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \ -2 \ 1 \ 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

Special solution 2: set \((x_3, x_4) = (0, 1)\):

\[\mathbf{s}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \ -1 \ 0 \ 1 \end{bmatrix}\] \[N(A) = \text{span}!\left(\begin{bmatrix} -1 \ -2 \ 1 \ 0 \end{bmatrix},\ \begin{bmatrix} -2 \ -1 \ 0 \ 1 \end{bmatrix}\right)\]

Dimension \(= n - r = 4 - 2 = 2\). ✓

docs.title: The Column Space (Which \(\mathbf{b}\) Make \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) Consistent)
docs.text:
The pivot columns of \(A\) (columns 1 and 2 of the original \(A\), not of \(R\)) form a basis for \(C(A)\). From \(A\):

\[A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 & 4 & 2 \ 2 & 4 & 10 & 8 \ 3 & 6 & 15 & 12 \end{bmatrix}\]

Pivot columns of \(A\) are columns 1 and 2:

\[\mathbf{a}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \ 2 \ 3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{a}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \ 4 \ 6 \end{bmatrix}\]

\(C(A) = \text{span}(\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2)\), a 2-dimensional subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^3\).

Warning. The pivot columns of \(R\) are the standard basis vectors \(\mathbf{e}_1, \mathbf{e}_2\) — they are not the same as the pivot columns of \(A\). The rref tells you which columns of \(A\) are pivot columns, but the actual basis vectors for \(C(A)\) must be taken from \(A\) itself, not from \(R\).

This is a point I got wrong more than once. Row operations change the column space. They preserve the row space and the null space, but not the column space.

docs.title: Uniqueness of the rref
docs.text:
Theorem. Every matrix has a unique reduced row echelon form.

I will not give the full proof (it requires induction on the number of pivot columns and careful case analysis), but the key idea is this: the pivot positions are determined by the matrix — specifically, the \(k\)-th pivot position is the leftmost column of \(A\) that is not in the span of the previous pivot columns. Once pivot positions are fixed, the rref entries are completely forced by the requirements that:

  • Each pivot is \(1\).
  • Each pivot column has zeros everywhere else.

Since there is no choice at any step, the result is unique.

Consequence. Two matrices have the same rref if and only if they are row equivalent. The rref is the canonical representative of a row equivalence class.

Contrast with \(LU\). The \(LU\) factorization is not unique in this sense — different orderings of row operations (with partial pivoting choices) give different \(L\) and \(U\) factors, and \(PA = LU\) depends on the chosen permutation. The rref, by contrast, is a property of the matrix itself, not of the algorithm used to compute it.

docs.title: The rref and Row Operations as Matrix Multiplication
docs.text:
Every elementary row operation is left-multiplication by an elementary matrix.

(R1) Scale row \(i\) by \(c\): Left-multiply by the matrix \(E\) which is \(I\) except with \(c\) in position \((i,i)\).

(R2) Add \(c\) times row \(j\) to row \(i\): Left-multiply by the matrix \(E\) which is \(I\) except with \(c\) in position \((i,j)\).

(R3) Swap rows \(i\) and \(j\): Left-multiply by the corresponding permutation matrix \(P_{ij}\).

Since each elementary matrix is invertible, the entire sequence of row operations corresponds to left-multiplication by an invertible matrix. Specifically:

\[R = E_k E_{k-1} \cdots E_2 E_1 A\]

for some sequence of elementary matrices \(E_1, \ldots, E_k\). Setting \(M = E_k \cdots E_1\) (invertible), we have

\[R = MA\]

This means \(R\) and \(A\) are related by an invertible left factor — they have the same row space and null space, but generally different column spaces.

Connecting rref to \(PA = LU\). Forward elimination corresponds to the \(E_i\)'s that do row replacements and swaps, producing \(U\). Going further to rref corresponds to additionally doing upward elimination (more row replacements) and row scaling. The rref is \(LU\) taken to completion.

docs.title: The \(\begin{bmatrix} I & F \end{bmatrix}\) Block Structure
docs.text:
When the matrix has full row rank (\(r = m\)) and the pivot columns are the first \(r\) columns (or after reordering columns so they are), the rref has the clean block form:

\[R = \begin{bmatrix} I_r & F \end{bmatrix}\]

where \(I_r\) is \(r \times r\) identity and \(F\) is \(r \times (n - r)\).

For a general \(m \times n\) matrix with rank \(r\):

\[R = \begin{bmatrix} I_r & F \ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

The \(F\) block encodes all the information about the free columns — how they are expressed as linear combinations of the pivot columns (after row reduction). The null space matrix is \(N = \begin{bmatrix} -F \ I_{n-r} \end{bmatrix}\), as I developed in [[Null Space of A — Solving Ax=0]].

In the worked example:

\[R = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 & 2 \ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

Here \(r = 2\), and in block form (pivot columns 1, 2; free columns 3, 4):

\[I_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad F = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

The null space matrix:

\[N = \begin{bmatrix} -F \ I_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -2 \ -2 & -1 \ 1 & 0 \ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

Columns are \(\mathbf{s}_1\) and \(\mathbf{s}_2\) from above. ✓

docs.title: What Row Reduction Preserves and What It Destroys
docs.text:
This deserves an explicit table, because getting it wrong is responsible for most errors at this stage.

Preserved by row operations:

  • The null space \(N(A)\). Since \(R = MA\) for invertible \(M\), \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0} \iff MA\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0} \iff R\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\).
  • The row space \(C(A^T)\). Row operations replace rows by linear combinations of rows — the span of the rows does not change.
  • The rank \(r\). Both row and column rank equal \(r\) and are invariant under row operations.
  • Linear (in)dependence relations among the columns. If columns \(j_1, \ldots, j_k\) of \(A\) are linearly dependent, the same columns of \(R\) are linearly dependent with the same coefficients.

Destroyed by row operations:

  • The column space \(C(A)\). The columns of \(R\) are generally different vectors than the columns of \(A\).
  • The eigenvalues (for square matrices). Row operations have no reason to preserve \(\det(\lambda I - A)\).
  • The left null space \(N(A^T)\). Since rows change, \(A^T\) changes, and its null space changes.

Remark (personal). The fact that the null space is preserved is what makes rref work for solving \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\) — solving \(R\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\) is the same problem. The fact that the column space is destroyed is why I must take basis vectors for \(C(A)\) from the original \(A\), not from \(R\). Both facts follow immediately from \(R = MA\).

docs.title: rref of a Square Invertible Matrix
docs.text:
If \(A\) is \(n \times n\) and invertible (rank \(r = n\)), then:

  • All \(n\) columns are pivot columns.
  • No free variables.
  • The rref is exactly \(I_n\).
\[R = I_n\]

Proof. An invertible matrix has \(n\) linearly independent columns, so all \(n\) columns become pivot columns after reduction. With \(r = n\) pivots and the rref conditions (each pivot is \(1\), each pivot column cleared), the only possibility is \(I_n\). \(\square\)

Consequence: the matrix inverse via rref. The augmented system \([A \mid I]\) reduced to rref gives \([I \mid A^{-1}]\). This is the Gauss-Jordan method for computing \(A^{-1}\): row-reduce \(A\) to \(I\), applying the same operations to \(I\), and \(I\) becomes \(A^{-1}\).

Why it works. The row operations applied to \([A \mid I]\) correspond to left-multiplication by \(M = E_k \cdots E_1\). On the left block: \(MA = I\), so \(M = A^{-1}\). On the right block: \(MI = M = A^{-1}\). So the right block of the reduced augmented matrix is \(A^{-1}\).

docs.title: A Note on Computation
docs.text:
In exact arithmetic (rational or symbolic), computing the rref is straightforward. In floating-point arithmetic, the situation is more delicate:

  • Small pivots cause large multipliers and amplify rounding errors.
  • The rref is theoretically unique but numerically unstable — small perturbations in \(A\) can change which columns are pivot columns (if a small pivot is barely nonzero vs. zero, numerical errors determine the answer).
  • For numerical computation, \(PA = LU\) with partial pivoting is preferred over rref. The rref is a theoretical tool; for actual computation with floating-point matrices, one uses rank-revealing \(QR\) decomposition or the SVD.

This does not diminish the theoretical importance of rref — it just means I should know when I am doing algebra and when I am doing numerics.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The rref of \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\) is the unique matrix \(R\) row equivalent to \(A\) satisfying:

  • Zero rows at the bottom.
  • Each nonzero row's first entry is \(1\) (the pivot).
  • Pivots strictly step right as rows go down.
  • Each pivot column has zeros everywhere except the pivot.

From \(R\) I read directly:

  • $r = $ rank = number of pivot rows.
  • Pivot and free columns, pivot and free variables.
  • Basis for \(N(A)\): one special solution per free variable.
  • Which columns of \(A\) form a basis for \(C(A)\): the pivot columns (taken from \(A\), not from \(R\)).

The rref is \(R = MA\) for some invertible \(M\). It preserves \(N(A)\) and \(C(A^T)\). It destroys \(C(A)\).

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
• The full proof of uniqueness of rref is worth writing out once. It is a clean induction argument — each pivot position is forced by the matrix's linear structure, and once all pivots are placed, all entries are forced.
  • The rref over fields other than \(\mathbb{R}\): the same definition and algorithm work for any field (rationals, complex numbers, \(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}\) for prime \(p\)). Linear algebra over finite fields is the foundation of coding theory. I want to come back to the \(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}\) case.
  • The Gauss-Jordan method for \(A^{-1}\) extends to solving \(AX = B\) for a matrix \(B\) by augmenting \([A \mid B]\). This is just simultaneous column-wise solution of multiple systems.
