docs.text:
• State the CLT precisely: i.i.d., finite positive variance, convergence in distribution of the standardized sum.
  • Prove it via MGF Taylor expansion, identifying exactly where independence, zero mean, and unit variance are each used.
  • Explain why the CLT fails for Cauchy-distributed variables.
  • State the Lindeberg condition and explain what it relaxes.
  • State the Berry-Esseen theorem and explain what it says about the rate of convergence.
  • Explain the continuity correction and when it matters.
  • State the LLN and distinguish it precisely from the CLT.
  • Derive the delta method from a first-order Taylor expansion.

docs.title: Why \(c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\)
docs.text: The Gaussian integral cannot be solved by any standard technique. It requires leaving the real line entirely, going to \(\mathbb{R}^2\), exploiting rotational symmetry, and coming back down. The fact that \(\pi\) appears in a probability distribution is a direct consequence of that geometry.

docs.title: The Setup
docs.text:
The standard Normal PDF is claimed to be:

\[f(z) = c \cdot e^{-z^2/2}, \quad z \in \mathbb{R}\]

for some constant \(c > 0\). For \(f\) to be a valid PDF, it must integrate to 1:

\[c \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-z^2/2}, dz = 1 \implies c = \frac{1}{\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-z^2/2}, dz}\]

So everything reduces to computing \(I = \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-z^2/2}, dz\).

docs.title: Why Direct Antidifferentiation Fails
docs.text:
The function \(e^{-z^2/2}\) has no elementary antiderivative. This is not a gap in technique — it is a theorem (Liouville's theorem on elementary integrals) that no composition of polynomials, exponentials, logarithms, and trigonometric functions equals \(\int e^{-z^2/2}, dz\). The antiderivative exists as a function (by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus) but cannot be written in closed form.

This means every standard single-variable technique — substitution, integration by parts, partial fractions — will fail. The definite integral over all of \(\mathbb{R}\) must be computed by a different route entirely.

docs.title: The Double Integral Trick
docs.text:
The key insight: if I cannot compute \(I\) directly, compute \(I^2\) instead and take a square root.

\[I^2 = \left(\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2/2}, dx\right)!\left(\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-y^2/2}, dy\right)\]

I have written the same integral twice, using different dummy variables \(x\) and \(y\). Since these are independent integrals, I can combine them into a double integral over \(\mathbb{R}^2\):

\[I^2 = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2/2} \cdot e^{-y^2/2}, dx, dy = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-(x^2 + y^2)/2}, dx, dy\]

The exponents add because the integrand factors. Now I have converted a one-dimensional problem I cannot solve into a two-dimensional problem I can — because \(x^2 + y^2\) is the squared distance from the origin in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), which is naturally expressed in polar coordinates.

docs.title: Polar Coordinate Transformation
docs.text:
Substitute \(x = r\cos\theta\), \(y = r\sin\theta\), where \(r \in [0, \infty)\) and \(\theta \in [0, 2\pi)\).

The key facts:

  • \(x^2 + y^2 = r^2\) (Pythagorean theorem)
  • The area element transforms as \(dx, dy = r, dr, d\theta\) (the factor \(r\) is the Jacobian of the polar coordinate transformation)

The Jacobian \(r\) is not optional — it accounts for the fact that at radius \(r\), a small angular slice \(d\theta\) sweeps out an arc of length \(r, d\theta\), so the area element grows with \(r\).

The integral becomes:

\[I^2 = \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^\infty e^{-r^2/2} \cdot r, dr, d\theta\]

The limits change: \(r\) runs from \(0\) to \(\infty\) (all distances from origin), \(\theta\) runs from \(0\) to \(2\pi\) (full rotation). Together these cover all of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) exactly once.

docs.title: Evaluating the Transformed Integral
docs.text:
The double integral separates into a product because the integrand factors as a function of \(r\) alone times a function of \(\theta\) alone:

\[I^2 = \left(\int_0^{2\pi} d\theta\right)!\left(\int_0^\infty r e^{-r^2/2}, dr\right)\]

Outer integral:

\[\int_0^{2\pi} d\theta = 2\pi\]

This is where \(\pi\) enters. The full rotation around the origin contributes exactly \(2\pi\).

Inner integral:

\[\int_0^\infty r e^{-r^2/2}, dr\]

Substitute \(u = r^2/2\), so \(du = r, dr\). When \(r = 0\), \(u = 0\); when \(r \to \infty\), \(u \to \infty\):

\[\int_0^\infty e^{-u}, du = \Big[-e^{-u}\Big]_0^\infty = 0 - (-1) = 1\]

The factor \(r\) in the integrand is precisely the \(du\) from the substitution. Without it — if the integrand were just \(e^{-r^2/2}\) — this substitution would not work. The Jacobian \(r\) is what makes the inner integral tractable.

docs.title: Final Result
docs.text:
\[I^2 = 2\pi \cdot 1 = 2\pi\] \[I = \sqrt{2\pi}\]

Therefore:

\[c = \frac{1}{I} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\]

And the standard Normal PDF is confirmed:

\[f(z) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-z^2/2}\]

docs.title: Why \(\pi\) Appears Here
docs.text:
This is worth pausing on. \(\pi\) appears in the Normal distribution not because of anything circular in the probability setup, but because:

  1. The trick requires going to \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
  2. In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), the natural coordinate system for \(e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2}\) is polar.
  3. The angular integration over a full rotation produces \(2\pi\).

The circle is hiding inside the Gaussian. The rotational symmetry of \(e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2}\) — it depends only on the distance \(r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) from the origin, not on the angle — is the property that makes the polar transformation so powerful. This same rotational symmetry is one of the characterizations of the Normal distribution: it is the only spherically symmetric distribution with independent components.

docs.title: Derivation of the Mean — \(E[Z] = 0\)
docs.text:
With the PDF established, compute the mean:

\[E[Z] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty z \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-z^2/2}, dz\]

By symmetry. The integrand is \(z \cdot f(z)\). Since \(f(z) = f(-z)\) (even function) and \(z\) is odd, the product \(z \cdot f(z)\) is an odd function. The integral of any odd function over a symmetric interval is zero:

\[\int_{-\infty}^\infty (\text{odd function}), dz = 0\]

provided the integral converges absolutely, which it does here since \(z \cdot e^{-z^2/2}\) decays faster than any polynomial.

Therefore \(E[Z] = 0\).

docs.title: Derivation of the Variance — \(\text{Var}(Z) = 1\)
docs.text:
Since \(E[Z] = 0\):

\[\text{Var}(Z) = E[Z^2] - (E[Z])^2 = E[Z^2]\]

By LOTUS:

\[E[Z^2] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty z^2 \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-z^2/2}, dz = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^\infty z^2 e^{-z^2/2}, dz\]

Integration by parts. Write \(z^2 e^{-z^2/2} = z \cdot \left(z e^{-z^2/2}\right)\) and set:

\[u = z \implies du = dz$$ $$dv = z e^{-z^2/2}, dz \implies v = -e^{-z^2/2}\]

where \(v\) is found by the substitution \(w = z^2/2\), \(dw = z, dz\), giving \(\int z e^{-z^2/2}, dz = -e^{-z^2/2}\).

Apply integration by parts \(\int u, dv = uv - \int v, du\):

\[\int_{-\infty}^\infty z^2 e^{-z^2/2}, dz = \Big[-z e^{-z^2/2}\Big]_{-\infty}^\infty + \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-z^2/2}, dz\]

Boundary term. Evaluate \(\lim_{z \to \pm\infty} z e^{-z^2/2}\). The exponential decay dominates the linear growth:

\[\lim_{z \to \infty} z e^{-z^2/2} = 0, \quad \lim_{z \to -\infty} z e^{-z^2/2} = 0\]

So the boundary term \(\Big[-z e^{-z^2/2}\Big]_{-\infty}^\infty = 0 - 0 = 0\).

Remaining integral. What is left is:

\[\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-z^2/2}, dz = I = \sqrt{2\pi}\]

exactly the Gaussian integral already computed.

Therefore:

\[E[Z^2] = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \cdot \sqrt{2\pi} = 1\] \[\text{Var}(Z) = 1 \quad \square\]

docs.title: The Structural Elegance
docs.text:
The variance derivation has a loop in it that is worth appreciating:

\[\int z^2 e^{-z^2/2}, dz \xrightarrow{\text{IBP}} \int e^{-z^2/2}, dz\]

Integration by parts converts the \(z^2\) moment integral back into the normalizing integral. The variance equals 1 because the normalizing integral equals \(\sqrt{2\pi}\), and the \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\) in front of the PDF cancels it exactly. The normalizing constant and the variance are not independent — the same integral \(I\) determines both.

This self-referential structure is not a coincidence. For any distribution in the exponential family, the moments are derivatives of the log-normalizing constant. For the Normal, this becomes the observation that differentiating \(\log Z(\theta)\) with respect to the natural parameter recovers the moments — and the variance being 1 for the standard Normal is the simplest instance of this.

docs.title: Summary of What Was Derived
docs.text: Quantity Method Result \(\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-z^2/2}, dz\) Square the integral, polar coordinates \(\sqrt{2\pi}\) Normalizing constant \(c\) Reciprocal of above \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\) \(E[Z]\) Odd function on symmetric domain \(0\) \(E[Z^2] = \text{Var}(Z)\) Integration by parts + normalizing integral \(1\)

docs.title: Standard Normal
docs.text: Everything about the Normal family reduces to the standard Normal. Not approximately — exactly. Once I understand \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) completely, I understand \(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) for free via a single linear transformation. The standard Normal is not a special case; it is the master copy.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
\(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\) has PDF:

\[\varphi(z) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-z^2/2}, \quad z \in \mathbb{R}\]

and CDF:

\[\Phi(z) = \int_{-\infty}^z \varphi(t), dt = \int_{-\infty}^z \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-t^2/2}, dt\]

\(\varphi\) is the PDF. \(\Phi\) is the CDF. These two letters are reserved for this distribution throughout all of statistics and I should never use them for anything else in a probability context.

Both have no closed form for arbitrary \(z\) — \(\Phi\) is a special function, evaluated numerically. But its properties are entirely derivable, and those properties are what I actually use.

docs.title: Properties of \(\varphi\)
docs.text:
Symmetry. \(\varphi(-z) = \varphi(z)\) for all \(z\). The PDF is an even function. This follows directly from the exponent: \((-z)^2 = z^2\).

Mode. \(\varphi\) is maximized at \(z = 0\), where \(\varphi(0) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \approx 0.3989\).

Inflection points. Compute \(\varphi''(z)\):

\[\varphi'(z) = -z \cdot \varphi(z)\] \[\varphi''(z) = -\varphi(z) - z \cdot \varphi'(z) = -\varphi(z) + z^2 \varphi(z) = (z^2 - 1)\varphi(z)\]

\(\varphi''(z) = 0\) when \(z^2 = 1\), i.e., \(z = \pm 1\). The PDF transitions from concave to convex (and vice versa) at \(z = \pm 1\). The inflection points are exactly one standard deviation from the mean.

Decay. For large \(|z|\):

\[\varphi(z) \sim \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-z^2/2}\]

The decay is super-exponential — faster than \(e^{-c|z|}\) for any \(c > 0\). This is why the Normal has light tails: moments of all orders are finite, and the MGF exists everywhere on \(\mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: Properties of \(\Phi\)
docs.text:
Symmetry. For all \(z\):

\[\Phi(-z) = 1 - \Phi(z)\]

Proof. By the symmetry of \(\varphi\):

\[\Phi(-z) = \int_{-\infty}^{-z} \varphi(t), dt\]

Substitute \(t = -s\), \(dt = -ds\). When \(t = -\infty\), \(s = \infty\); when \(t = -z\), \(s = z\):

\[= \int_{\infty}^{z} \varphi(-s)(-ds) = \int_z^{\infty} \varphi(s), ds = 1 - \Phi(z) \quad \square\]

This identity is used constantly. Whenever I need \(\Phi\) of a negative argument, I reflect:

\[\Phi(-z) = 1 - \Phi(z)\]

The CDF at zero. \(\Phi(0) = 1/2\). By symmetry, half the probability lies below 0 and half above.

Derivative. \(\Phi'(z) = \varphi(z)\). The PDF is the derivative of the CDF — this is the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, nothing more.

docs.title: Key Values of \(\Phi\) — Know These Cold
Standardization — How Everything Reduces to \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\)
docs.text:
If \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\), define:

\[Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma}\]

Then \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\).

Proof. The CDF of \(Z\):

\[P(Z \leq z) = P!\left(\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma} \leq z\right) = P(X \leq \mu + \sigma z) = F_X(\mu + \sigma z)\]

where \(F_X\) is the CDF of \(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\). By definition of the Normal CDF:

\[F_X(\mu + \sigma z) = \Phi!\left(\frac{(\mu + \sigma z) - \mu}{\sigma}\right) = \Phi(z) \quad \square\]

So any probability involving a general Normal reduces to \(\Phi\):

\[P(X \leq x) = \Phi!\left(\frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\right)\] \[P(a \leq X \leq b) = \Phi!\left(\frac{b-\mu}{\sigma}\right) - \Phi!\left(\frac{a-\mu}{\sigma}\right)\]

This is the computation I do every time I work with a Normal distribution.

docs.title: Moments of \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\)
docs.text:
The mean and variance were derived in [[08.The Normal Normalizing Constant]]]:

\[E[Z] = 0, \quad \text{Var}(Z) = 1\]

All odd moments are zero by symmetry: \(E[Z^{2k+1}] = 0\) for all \(k \geq 0\).

Even moments follow the pattern derived from the MGF:

\[E[Z^{2k}] = (2k-1)!! = 1 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdots (2k-1)\]

Derivation. From the MGF \(M_Z(t) = e^{t^2/2}\), expand:

\[e^{t^2/2} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{(t^2/2)^k}{k!} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{t^{2k}}{2^k k!}\]

The coefficient of \(t^{2k}\) is \(\frac{1}{2^k k!}\). Since \(M_Z(t) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{E[Z^n]}{n!} t^n\), the coefficient of \(t^{2k}\) is \(\frac{E[Z^{2k}]}{(2k)!}\). Equating:

\[\frac{E[Z^{2k}]}{(2k)!} = \frac{1}{2^k k!} \implies E[Z^{2k}] = \frac{(2k)!}{2^k k!}\]

Now verify this equals \((2k-1)!!\):

\[\frac{(2k)!}{2^k k!} = \frac{1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 \cdots (2k-1) \cdot 2k}{2^k \cdot k!} = \frac{(1 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdots (2k-1)) \cdot (2 \cdot 4 \cdots 2k)}{2^k \cdot k!} = \frac{(2k-1)!! \cdot 2^k k!}{2^k k!} = (2k-1)!!\]

So:

\[E[Z^2] = 1, \quad E[Z^4] = 3, \quad E[Z^6] = 15, \quad E[Z^8] = 105\]

The kurtosis \(E[Z^4] = 3\) is the baseline for excess kurtosis: any distribution with \(E[Z^4] > 3\) has heavier tails than the Normal (leptokurtic), and any with \(E[Z^4] < 3\) has lighter tails (platykurtic).

docs.title: The MGF
docs.text:
\[M_Z(t) = e^{t^2/2}, \quad t \in \mathbb{R}\]

The MGF exists for all \(t \in \mathbb{R}\) — a consequence of the super-exponential decay of \(\varphi\). This is not true for heavy-tailed distributions like the \(t\) or Cauchy, whose MGFs do not exist.

Derivation was done in [[06.Normal Distribution]] by completing the square. I record it here for completeness:

\[M_Z(t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{tz} e^{-z^2/2}, dz = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^\infty \exp!\left(-\frac{z^2 - 2tz}{2}\right) dz\]

Complete the square: \(z^2 - 2tz = (z-t)^2 - t^2\):

\[= \frac{e^{t^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-(z-t)^2/2}, dz = e^{t^2/2} \cdot 1\]

The integral is 1 because \(e^{-(z-t)^2/2} / \sqrt{2\pi}\) is the PDF of \(\mathcal{N}(t, 1)\), integrating to 1.

docs.title: The Quantile Function \(\Phi^{-1}\)
docs.text:
The quantile function (inverse CDF) \(\Phi^{-1}(p)\) gives the value \(z\) such that \(\Phi(z) = p\). It has no closed form.

Key quantiles:

\(p\) \(\Phi^{-1}(p)\) Common name \(0.500\) \(0\) Median \(0.841\) \(1\) One \(\sigma\) above mean \(0.950\) \(1.645\) 95th percentile \(0.975\) \(1.96\) Used in 95% CI \(0.990\) \(2.326\) 99th percentile \(0.995\) \(2.576\) Used in 99% CI

Symmetry of the quantile function. Since \(\Phi(-z) = 1 - \Phi(z)\):

\[\Phi^{-1}(1-p) = -\Phi^{-1}(p)\]

So I only need to know quantiles above the median — those below follow by negation.

docs.title: The Tail Probability and the Mill's Ratio
docs.text:
For large \(z > 0\), the tail probability \(P(Z > z) = 1 - \Phi(z)\) has the asymptotic bound:

\[\frac{\varphi(z)}{z}\left(1 - \frac{1}{z^2}\right) \leq 1 - \Phi(z) \leq \frac{\varphi(z)}{z}\]

Proof of the upper bound. For \(t > 0\), note \(1 < t/z\) when \(t > z\). So:

\[1 - \Phi(z) = \int_z^\infty \varphi(t), dt < \int_z^\infty \frac{t}{z} \varphi(t), dt = \frac{1}{z} \int_z^\infty t \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-t^2/2}, dt\]

The last integral is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \Big[-e^{-t^2/2}\Big]_z^\infty = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-z^2/2} = \varphi(z)\). So:

\[1 - \Phi(z) < \frac{\varphi(z)}{z} \quad \square\]

The practical implication: tail probabilities decay like \(\frac{e^{-z^2/2}}{z\sqrt{2\pi}}\), which is extremely fast. At \(z = 4\): \(P(Z > 4) \approx 3.2 \times 10^{-5}\). At \(z = 5\): \(P(Z > 5) \approx 2.9 \times 10^{-7}\).

This exponentially fast decay is what makes the Normal a "thin-tailed" distribution and distinguishes it sharply from power-law tails like the Cauchy or Pareto.

docs.title: \(Z^2 \sim \chi^2(1)\)
docs.text:
If \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\), then \(Z^2 \sim \chi^2(1)\).

Proof. Let \(Y = Z^2\). For \(y > 0\):

\[P(Y \leq y) = P(Z^2 \leq y) = P(-\sqrt{y} \leq Z \leq \sqrt{y}) = \Phi(\sqrt{y}) - \Phi(-\sqrt{y}) = 2\Phi(\sqrt{y}) - 1\]

Differentiate to get the PDF of \(Y\):

\[f_Y(y) = 2 \cdot \varphi(\sqrt{y}) \cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} = \frac{\varphi(\sqrt{y})}{\sqrt{y}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \cdot \frac{e^{-y/2}}{\sqrt{y}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} y^{-1/2} e^{-y/2}\]

Recognize this as \(\text{Gamma}(1/2, 1/2)\), using \(\Gamma(1/2) = \sqrt{\pi}\):

\[f_Y(y) = \frac{(1/2)^{1/2}}{\Gamma(1/2)} y^{1/2 - 1} e^{-y/2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} y^{-1/2} e^{-y/2} \quad \checkmark\]

This is the \(\chi^2(1)\) distribution by definition. It is also \(\text{Gamma}(1/2,, 1/2)\), confirming the Gamma–chi-squared connection in [[02.Formula Reference — All Distributions]]].

docs.title: The Half-Normal Distribution
docs.text:
The absolute value \(|Z|\) for \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\) has the half-Normal distribution.

For \(y > 0\):

\[P(|Z| \leq y) = P(-y \leq Z \leq y) = 2\Phi(y) - 1\]

PDF of \(|Z|\):

\[f_{|Z|}(y) = 2\varphi(y) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} e^{-y^2/2}, \quad y > 0\]

The factor of 2 comes from folding the symmetric distribution onto the positive half-line.

Mean of \(|Z|\):

\[E[|Z|] = \int_0^\infty y \cdot 2\varphi(y), dy = 2 \int_0^\infty \frac{y}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-y^2/2}, dy = \frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \Big[-e^{-y^2/2}\Big]_0^\infty = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\]

This value \(\sqrt{2/\pi} \approx 0.798\) comes up in the derivation of the mean of the Rayleigh distribution and in certain shrinkage estimators.

docs.title: The Standard Normal as a Building Block
docs.text:
The standard Normal generates several other distributions through simple operations:

Operation Result \(Z^2\) \(\chi^2(1) = \text{Gamma}(1/2, 1/2)\) \(Z_1^2 + \cdots + Z_k^2\), i.i.d. \(\chi^2(k) = \text{Gamma}(k/2, 1/2)\) \(Z / \sqrt{V/k}\), \(V \sim \chi^2(k)\) indep. \(t(k)\) (Student's \(t\)) \(Z_1 / Z_2\), i.i.d. \(\text{Cauchy}(0,1)\) \(e^{\mu + \sigma Z}\) \(\text{LogNormal}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) \(\mu + \sigma Z\) \(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\)

The last row is the standardization map in reverse — from \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) to any Normal. The others show the standard Normal sitting at the center of the named distribution families.

docs.title: The Gaussian Integral in Different Forms
docs.text:
Several equivalent forms come up in computations and it helps to have them all in one place:

\[\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-z^2/2}, dz = \sqrt{2\pi}\] \[\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-z^2}, dz = \sqrt{\pi}\] \[\int_0^\infty e^{-z^2}, dz = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}\] \[\int_0^\infty e^{-az^2}, dz = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{a}}, \quad a > 0\]

The second follows from the first by substituting \(z \mapsto z/\sqrt{2}\). The third is half the second by symmetry. The fourth generalizes the third. These show up when computing moments of the Normal, working with the Gamma function at half-integer arguments, and evaluating Gaussian integrals in other contexts.

The connection to the Gamma function: setting \(t = az^2\), \(dt = 2az, dz\) in the fourth form gives:

\[\int_0^\infty e^{-az^2}, dz = \frac{1}{2a^{1/2}} \int_0^\infty t^{-1/2} e^{-t}, dt = \frac{\Gamma(1/2)}{2\sqrt{a}} = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2\sqrt{a}}\]

confirming \(\Gamma(1/2) = \sqrt{\pi}\), which is the same \(\sqrt{\pi}\) that generates the \(\sqrt{2\pi}\) normalizing constant.

docs.title: What I Should Be Able to Do Without Notes
docs.text:
• Write down \(\varphi\) and \(\Phi\) and state the relationship \(\Phi' = \varphi\).
  • Derive \(\Phi(-z) = 1 - \Phi(z)\) from the symmetry of \(\varphi\).
  • State and use the standardization formula \(P(X \leq x) = \Phi!\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)\).
  • Derive all even moments \(E[Z^{2k}] = (2k-1)!!\) from the MGF series expansion.
  • Prove \(Z^2 \sim \chi^2(1)\) by computing the CDF of \(Z^2\) and differentiating.
  • Derive the PDF of \(|Z|\) and compute \(E[|Z|] = \sqrt{2/\pi}\).
  • State the Mill's ratio upper bound on the tail probability and prove it.
  • Recite the four equivalent Gaussian integral forms and the connection to \(\Gamma(1/2)\).

docs.title: 68-95-99.7 Rule
docs.text: This is one of those facts you memorize in week one and spend the rest of your degree actually understanding. Come back to this after MGFs, after CLT, after you've actually derived the normal PDF from scratch. It hits differently.

docs.title: The Statement
docs.text:
Let \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\). Then:

\[P(\mu - \sigma \leq X \leq \mu + \sigma) \approx 0.6827$$ $$P(\mu - 2\sigma \leq X \leq \mu + 2\sigma) \approx 0.9545$$ $$P(\mu - 3\sigma \leq X \leq \mu + 3\sigma) \approx 0.9973\]

Or in the standardized form — let \(Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\):

\[P(|Z| \leq 1) \approx 0.6827 \qquad P(|Z| \leq 2) \approx 0.9545 \qquad P(|Z| \leq 3) \approx 0.9973\]

These aren't definitions. They are computed facts about the normal distribution that follow from the shape of the Gaussian PDF.

docs.title: Where Does This Actually Come From?
docs.text:
The normal PDF is:

\[f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi},\sigma} \exp!\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\]

The rule is just evaluating:

\[P(\mu - k\sigma \leq X \leq \mu + k\sigma) = \int_{\mu - k\sigma}^{\mu + k\sigma} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi},\sigma} e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}, dx\]

Standardise with \(z = \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\), \(dz = \frac{dx}{\sigma}\):

\[= \int_{-k}^{k} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-z^2/2}, dz = 2,\Phi(k) - 1\]

where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal CDF. Now plug in:

\(k\) \(\Phi(k)\) \(2\Phi(k)-1\) 1 0.8413 0.6827 2 0.9772 0.9545 3 0.9987 0.9973

This integral has no closed form — \(\Phi\) is not elementary. That used to bother me. Now I think it's beautiful: the most important distribution in all of probability has a CDF you can't write in closed form. You have to respect it.

docs.title: The Proof That \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2/2},dx = \sqrt{2\pi}\)
docs.text:
This is the normalization constant and it's worth knowing cold. The trick is squaring the integral.

Claim: \(I = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2/2},dx = \sqrt{2\pi}\)

Proof.

\[I^2 = \left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2/2},dx\right)!!\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-y^2/2},dy\right) = \iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2},dx,dy\]

Convert to polar coordinates: \(x = r\cos\theta\), \(y = r\sin\theta\), \(dx,dy = r,dr,d\theta\):

\[I^2 = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\infty} e^{-r^2/2} \cdot r ,dr, d\theta = 2\pi \int_0^{\infty} r,e^{-r^2/2},dr\]

Substitute \(u = r^2/2\), \(du = r,dr\):

\[= 2\pi \int_0^{\infty} e^{-u},du = 2\pi \cdot 1 = 2\pi\]

So \(I = \sqrt{2\pi}\). \(\blacksquare\)

Every time I see this proof I'm briefly annoyed that the solution is "square it and use polar coordinates" — and then immediately grateful. It's one of the great tricks in analysis.

docs.title: Symmetry Makes It Cheap
docs.text:
Because the standard normal PDF \(\phi(z) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2}\) is even — i.e., \(\phi(-z) = \phi(z)\) — we get:

\[P(|Z| \leq k) = 2,\Phi(k) - 1\]

This symmetry isn't accidental. It reflects the fact that the normal is determined entirely by \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\), and the density depends only on \((x-\mu)^2\).

Concretely, this means:

\[P(Z > 1) = P(Z < -1) = \frac{1 - 0.6827}{2} \approx 0.1587\]

The tail probability at \(1\sigma\) is about \(15.87\) on each side. At \(3\sigma\), each tail is only \(0.135\) — this is the origin of the "\(3\sigma\) event" language in physics and finance.

docs.title: Why This Rule Matters Beyond Memorization
1. It Quantifies Rarity
docs.text: A "\(5\sigma\) event" (famously invoked in the Higgs boson discovery) corresponds to: $\(P(|Z| > 5) \approx 5.7 \times 10^{-7}\)$ That's about 1 in 1.7 million. The rule gives you the intuition for what sigma-multiples mean in terms of probability mass.

docs.title: 2. It's the Practical Output of the CLT
docs.text:
The [[07.The Central Limit Theorem]] says \(\bar{X}_n \approx \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2/n)\) for large \(n\). The 68-95-99.7 rule immediately tells you:

  • 95% confidence intervals are roughly \(\bar{X} \pm 2\cdot\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)
  • This is where the "2 standard errors" rule of thumb in statistics comes from.

docs.title: 3. Chebyshev vs. Empirical Rule
docs.text:
[[Chebyshev's Inequality]] gives a distribution-free bound: $\(P(|X - \mu| \geq k\sigma) \leq \frac{1}{k^2}\)$

At \(k=2\): Chebyshev says at most \(25\) of mass is outside \(2\sigma\). The empirical rule says only $4.55% for the normal. The normal is much better concentrated than Chebyshev guarantees — Chebyshev is tight for pathological distributions, not the bell curve.

I used to confuse these two. They answer the same question but from totally different angles. Chebyshev: any distribution, weak bound. Empirical rule: normal only, sharp fact.

docs.title: The Tail Behavior — Exponential Decay
docs.text:
For \(z\) large, the standard normal tail decays like:

\[P(Z > z) \approx \frac{\phi(z)}{z} = \frac{1}{z\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-z^2/2}\]

This is a sub-Gaussian tail — faster than any polynomial, but not as fast as a compactly supported distribution. This decay rate is what makes the normal so well-behaved in probability theory and why tools like MGFs and Hoeffding's inequality work cleanly for it.

docs.title: Personal Notes
docs.text:
• The numbers \(68, 95, 99.7\) are worth having in working memory — you'll use them constantly in applied settings, hypothesis testing, and when reading papers.
  • Don't just memorize the percentages. Know that they come from \(2\Phi(k)-1\) and know why the factor of 2 is there (symmetry of \(\phi\)).
  • The hardest part conceptually: the rule is only exactly true for the normal. For any other distribution, you need Chebyshev or distribution-specific bounds. The empirical rule is a normal-specific fact, not a universal law.
  • Joe Blitzstein in Stat 110 emphasizes the story behind distributions — the empirical rule is part of the normal's "story": it's the canonical unimodal symmetric distribution, and these percentages are the fingerprint of that shape.

docs.title: Folded Normal
docs.text: The folded normal is what happens when you care about magnitude but not sign. It sounds like a minor technicality — until you realize it's secretly the half-normal, the \(\chi\) distribution in disguise, and the reason \(|Z|\) behaves so cleanly. Don't sleep on it.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\). The folded normal is the distribution of:

\[Y = |X|\]

We are literally "folding" the real line at zero — the negative half folds onto the positive half. The name is geometric and exact.

Think of the PDF of \(X\) as a piece of paper. Folding it at zero means the left half flips onto the right half and the two layers add. That's it. That's the whole construction.

docs.title: PDF Derivation
docs.text:
This is a transformation of a random variable — one of the core techniques from Stat 110. Let's do it properly.

Step 1: CDF approach.

For \(y \geq 0\):

\[F_Y(y) = P(Y \leq y) = P(|X| \leq y) = P(-y \leq X \leq y)\] \[= \Phi!\left(\frac{y - \mu}{\sigma}\right) - \Phi!\left(\frac{-y - \mu}{\sigma}\right)\]

Step 2: Differentiate to get the PDF.

\[f_Y(y) = \frac{d}{dy} F_Y(y) = \frac{1}{\sigma}\phi!\left(\frac{y-\mu}{\sigma}\right) + \frac{1}{\sigma}\phi!\left(\frac{y+\mu}{\sigma}\right), \qquad y \geq 0\]

where \(\phi\) is the standard normal PDF. Expanding:

\[\boxed{f_Y(y) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\left[\exp!\left(-\frac{(y-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) + \exp!\left(-\frac{(y+\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\right], \quad y \geq 0}\]

and \(f_Y(y) = 0\) for \(y < 0\).

Two bumps, potentially. One centred at \(+\mu\), one at \(-\mu\) that got folded over to \(+\mu\) as well — except they don't generally land on top of each other unless \(\mu = 0\). This is why the shape depends heavily on \(\mu/\sigma\).

docs.title: The Special Case: \(\mu = 0\) (Half-Normal)
docs.text:
When \(\mu = 0\), the two exponential terms are equal and the PDF collapses to:

\[f_Y(y) = \frac{2}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp!\left(-\frac{y^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \cdot \frac{1}{\sigma} \exp!\left(-\frac{y^2}{2\sigma^2}\right), \quad y \geq 0\]

This is the half-normal distribution. It is the folded normal's cleanest avatar.

Why the factor of 2? Because all the probability mass that used to live on \((-\infty, 0)\) has been folded onto \((0, \infty)\), doubling the density there. Normalization is preserved:

\[\int_0^{\infty} \frac{2}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-y^2/2\sigma^2},dy = 2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} = 1 \checkmark\]

docs.title: General \(\mu\), \(\sigma\)
docs.text:
Let \(\lambda = \mu/\sigma\) (the signal-to-noise ratio, morally). Then:

Mean:

\[E[Y] = \sigma\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}},\exp!\left(-\frac{\mu^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) + \mu\left[1 - 2\Phi!\left(-\frac{\mu}{\sigma}\right)\right]\] \[= \sigma\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}},e^{-\lambda^2/2} + \mu\left(2\Phi(\lambda) - 1\right)\]

Second moment (this one's clean):

\[E[Y^2] = E[X^2] = \mu^2 + \sigma^2\]

Because \(Y^2 = X^2\), so \(E[Y^2] = E[X^2] = \text{Var}(X) + (E[X])^2 = \sigma^2 + \mu^2\). Elegant.

Variance:

\[\text{Var}(Y) = \mu^2 + \sigma^2 - (E[Y])^2\]

docs.title: Special case \(\mu = 0\):
docs.text:
\[E[Y] = \sigma\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}, \qquad E[Y^2] = \sigma^2, \qquad \text{Var}(Y) = \sigma^2!\left(1 - \frac{2}{\pi}\right)\]

The mean of the half-normal is \(\sigma\sqrt{2/\pi}\). That factor \(\sqrt{2/\pi}\) shows up constantly in truncated/folded normal calculations. It comes from \(E[Z \mid Z > 0] = \sqrt{2/\pi}\) for \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\), which is itself a nice exercise via the Gaussian integral.

Derivation of \(E[|Z|]\) for \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\):

\[E[|Z|] = 2\int_0^{\infty} z \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-z^2/2},dz\]

Let \(u = z^2/2\), \(du = z,dz\):

\[= \frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_0^{\infty} e^{-u},du = \frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi}} = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\]

docs.title: Connection to the \(\chi\) Distribution
docs.text:
Let \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\). Then \(|Z|\) is the half-normal, which is also the \(\chi\) distribution with 1 degree of freedom (\(\chi_1\)).

More generally: if \(Z_1, \ldots, Z_k \overset{iid}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,1)\), then:

\[\sqrt{Z_1^2 + \cdots + Z_k^2} \sim \chi_k\]

The folded normal (\(k=1\)) is the simplest case. The \(\chi_2\) distribution is the Rayleigh distribution. These are all "radial" distributions — they describe the distance from the origin in \(k\)-dimensional standard normal space.

\[|Z| \sim \chi_1 \qquad \longrightarrow \qquad Z^2 \sim \chi^2_1\]

So the folded normal sits right at the base of the \(\chi\) and \(\chi^2\) family trees. When you square it, you get the \(\chi^2_1\) distribution. When you generalize to \(k\) dimensions, you get \(\chi_k\).

docs.title: The Folding as a Change of Variables — Formally
docs.text:
The function \(g(x) = |x|\) is not monotone on all of \(\mathbb{R}\), so the standard one-to-one change-of-variables formula doesn't directly apply. You split the domain:

\[g^{-1}({y}) = {y, -y} \quad \text{for } y > 0\]

The correct formula for the density of \(Y = g(X)\) is:

\[f_Y(y) = \sum_{x : g(x) = y} \frac{f_X(x)}{|g'(x)|}\]

Here \(g'(x) = \text{sgn}(x)\), so \(|g'(x)| = 1\) everywhere except \(x = 0\). The two preimages are \(x = y\) and \(x = -y\):

\[f_Y(y) = f_X(y) \cdot 1 + f_X(-y) \cdot 1 = f_X(y) + f_X(-y)\]

which exactly recovers the PDF we derived via the CDF method. Good — the two approaches agree, as they must.

I always find it satisfying when the CDF method and the change-of-variables formula give the same answer. It's not obvious they should — one is analytic, one is geometric — but of course they do. The distribution of \(Y\) is unique.

docs.title: Shape Behaviour as \(\mu/\sigma\) Varies
docs.text:
The ratio \(\lambda = |\mu|/\sigma\) controls everything:

\(\lambda\) Shape of \(f_Y\) \(\lambda \approx 0\) Half-normal: unimodal, mode at 0, right-skewed \(\lambda \approx 1\) Slightly bimodal tendency; skewness decreasing \(\lambda \gg 1\) Approximately \(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) truncated to \((0,\infty)\); nearly symmetric

When \(\mu\) is very large relative to \(\sigma\), almost all the mass of \(X\) is already positive, so \(|X| \approx X\) and the folded normal looks like the original normal. The folding is asymptotically irrelevant.

When \(\mu = 0\), the distribution is maximally "folded" — equal mass on each side of zero, all of it collapsed to the right.

docs.title: Why This Comes Up
docs.text:
1. Absolute errors. In estimation, you often care about \(|X - \mu|\), not the signed error. Folded normal = distribution of absolute deviation when the error is Gaussian.

2. Signal processing / physics. When you measure an amplitude and lose phase information, you're folding. The Rician distribution (for instance) is a generalization.

3. The \(\chi\) family. As noted above — understanding the folded normal is the first step toward understanding \(\chi_k\), which underlies the \(t\)-distribution, \(F\)-distribution, and hence all of classical inference.

4. Simulation. If you generate \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\) and want a positive-valued standard-normal-shaped variable, \(|Z|\) is your cleanest option.

docs.title: Truncated vs. Folded — Don't Confuse These
docs.text:
This tripped me up early. They are not the same:

| | Folded Normal \(Y = |X|\) | Truncated Normal \(Y = X \mid X > 0\) | |---|---|---| | Construction | Reflect negative values | Throw away negative values | | Total probability | 1 (all mass kept) | 1 (renormalized) | | PDF at \(y > 0\) | \(f_X(y) + f_X(-y)\) | \(\frac{f_X(y)}{\Phi(\mu/\sigma)}\) (normalizing constant) | | Mass below 0 | 0 (by construction) | 0 (conditioned away) | | \(E[Y]\) | \(E[|X|]\) | \(E[X \mid X > 0]\) |

The truncated normal conditions on being positive and adjusts the density upward to compensate. The folded normal adds the density from \(-y\) to the density at \(+y\). Different objects, different applications.

docs.title: Personal Notes
docs.text:
• The second moment formula \(E[Y^2] = \mu^2 + \sigma^2\) is the one to tattoo on your brain. It falls out immediately because \(Y^2 = X^2\), and it means you can always get \(\text{Var}(Y)\) once you have \(E[Y]\).
  • The derivation via CDF is the right way to think about non-monotone transformations in general. Get comfortable with it — it reappears constantly (e.g., deriving the \(\chi^2\) density, the \(F\) density, etc.).
  • The \(\mu = 0\) case is so clean that it's worth solving everything for the half-normal first and then thinking about what breaks for \(\mu \neq 0\).
  • Blitzstein emphasizes the LOTUS and the CDF method as the two workhorses for distributions of transformations. This note is a good case study for the CDF method with a non-injective function.

docs.title: Exponential Distribution
docs.text: The exponential distribution is the continuous version of the geometric. Once you see that, everything else — memorylessness, the Poisson connection, the minimum of exponentials — falls into place. It's one of the most structurally rich distributions in all of probability, and it's built from a single parameter.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A random variable \(X\) has the exponential distribution with rate parameter \(\lambda > 0\), written \(X \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda)\), if its PDF is:

\[f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, \quad x > 0\]

and \(f(x) = 0\) for \(x \leq 0\).

The CDF is:

\[F(x) = P(X \leq x) = 1 - e^{-\lambda x}, \quad x \geq 0\]

Survival function (the complement, used constantly):

\[P(X > x) = e^{-\lambda x}\]

The survival function is the cleaner object here. Almost everything about the exponential is easier to see through \(P(X > x) = e^{-\lambda x}\) than through \(F(x)\). Train yourself to think in terms of survival probabilities.

docs.title: Normalization Check
docs.text: \[\int_0^{\infty} \lambda e^{-\lambda x},dx = \lambda \cdot \frac{1}{\lambda} = 1 \checkmark\]

docs.title: Parameters — Rate vs. Scale
docs.text:
There are two conventions. Know both:

Parametrization Parameter PDF Mean Rate (Stat 110 / this note) \(\lambda > 0\) \(\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\) \(1/\lambda\) Scale \(\beta = 1/\lambda > 0\) \(\frac{1}{\beta}e^{-x/\beta}\) \(\beta\)

Blitzstein uses rate. Much of engineering uses scale. When you read a paper, check which one they mean — getting this backwards doubles or halves everything.

docs.title: Mean
docs.text:
\[E[X] = \int_0^{\infty} x \lambda e^{-\lambda x},dx\]

Integrate by parts: \(u = x\), \(dv = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}dx\):

\[= \left[-x e^{-\lambda x}\right]_0^{\infty} + \int_0^{\infty} e^{-\lambda x},dx = 0 + \frac{1}{\lambda} = \frac{1}{\lambda}\]

Or more elegantly — use the survival function formula for non-negative random variables:

\[E[X] = \int_0^{\infty} P(X > x),dx = \int_0^{\infty} e^{-\lambda x},dx = \frac{1}{\lambda}\]

The survival function formula \(E[X] = \int_0^\infty P(X > t),dt\) is one of the most useful tools in Stat 110. Blitzstein loves it. Internalize it — it makes computing means of non-negative RVs trivial whenever the survival function is clean, and the exponential is the canonical example.

docs.title: Variance
docs.text:
First compute \(E[X^2]\) via integration by parts (or recognize the pattern):

\[E[X^n] = \frac{n!}{\lambda^n}\]

This follows from the fact that \(\int_0^\infty x^n \lambda e^{-\lambda x},dx = \frac{n!}{\lambda^n}\) — recognizable as the Gamma integral. So:

\[E[X^2] = \frac{2}{\lambda^2}\] \[\text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 = \frac{2}{\lambda^2} - \frac{1}{\lambda^2} = \frac{1}{\lambda^2}\] \[\text{SD}(X) = \frac{1}{\lambda}\]

The mean equals the standard deviation. This is a hallmark of the exponential — high variance relative to the mean. It's the distribution of "mostly short, occasionally very long" waiting times.

docs.title: MGF
docs.text:
\[M(t) = E[e^{tX}] = \int_0^{\infty} e^{tx} \lambda e^{-\lambda x},dx = \lambda \int_0^{\infty} e^{-(\lambda - t)x},dx = \frac{\lambda}{\lambda - t}, \quad t < \lambda\]

The MGF exists only for \(t < \lambda\) — it blows up at \(t = \lambda\) because the integral diverges. This is expected: the exponential has a heavy right tail (relative to Gaussian), and the MGF can't be defined everywhere.

You can recover moments: \(M'(0) = \frac{1}{\lambda}\), \(M''(0) = \frac{2}{\lambda^2}\), confirming the above.

docs.title: The Memoryless Property
docs.text:
This is the soul of the exponential distribution.

Theorem. \(X \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda)\) if and only if \(X\) is a non-negative continuous random variable satisfying:

\[P(X > s + t \mid X > s) = P(X > t) \quad \text{for all } s, t \geq 0\]

Proof (\(\Rightarrow\)): Direct computation.

\[P(X > s + t \mid X > s) = \frac{P(X > s + t)}{P(X > s)} = \frac{e^{-\lambda(s+t)}}{e^{-\lambda s}} = e^{-\lambda t} = P(X > t) \quad \blacksquare\]

Proof (\(\Leftarrow\), uniqueness): Suppose \(G(t) = P(X > t)\) satisfies \(G(s+t) = G(s)G(t)\) for all \(s,t \geq 0\) (this is what memorylessness says multiplicatively). With \(G\) right-continuous and \(G(0) = 1\), the only solution is \(G(t) = e^{-\lambda t}\) for some \(\lambda > 0\). This is a standard result about Cauchy's functional equation on \([0,\infty)\). \(\blacksquare\)

What it means: If you've been waiting \(s\) units of time and the event hasn't happened, the remaining waiting time has the same distribution as if you just started. The past is irrelevant. The process has no memory of how long you've waited.

This is the continuous analogue of the geometric distribution's memorylessness: \(P(X > m+n \mid X > m) = P(X > n)\) for \(X \sim \text{Geom}(p)\). The exponential is the geometric's continuous limit — and memorylessness is the property that pins down both uniquely.

Philosophical note. Memorylessness is extremely special. It characterizes exactly two distributions: Geometric (discrete) and Exponential (continuous). Every other distribution on \({0,1,2,\ldots}\) or \([0,\infty)\) has memory. If you're modelling a lightbulb that gets more likely to fail as it ages, the exponential is the wrong model.

docs.title: Connection to the Geometric: Taking the Limit
docs.text:
Let \(X_n \sim \text{Geom}(p)\) where \(p = \lambda/n\) (probability of success per trial). The number of failures before success, scaled by \(1/n\), converges in distribution to \(\text{Expo}(\lambda)\) as \(n \to \infty\).

Concretely: \(X_n/n \xrightarrow{d} \text{Expo}(\lambda)\).

Heuristic derivation. The survival function of \(\text{Geom}(\lambda/n)\) at \(k\) steps:

\[P(X_n > k) = (1 - \lambda/n)^k\]

Set \(k = \lfloor nt \rfloor\) for continuous time \(t\):

\[P(X_n/n > t) = \left(1 - \frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^{nt} \to e^{-\lambda t}\]

which is exactly the exponential survival function. The limit is clean because \((1 - \lambda/n)^n \to e^{-\lambda}\).

This is the prototype for the general "rare events in many trials" paradigm. Each trial has a tiny probability of success; the waiting time in continuous time is exponential. This is the foundation of the Poisson process.

docs.title: Connection to the Poisson Process
docs.text:
The exponential distribution and the Poisson distribution are two faces of the same coin.

Setup. A Poisson process with rate \(\lambda\) is a model for random arrivals in continuous time where:

  1. The number of arrivals in any interval of length \(t\) is \(\text{Pois}(\lambda t)\).
  2. Non-overlapping intervals are independent.

Key fact. The waiting time between consecutive arrivals in a Poisson process is \(\text{Expo}(\lambda)\).

Proof sketch. Let \(T_1\) = time of first arrival. Then:

\[P(T_1 > t) = P(\text{no arrivals in } [0,t]) = e^{-\lambda t}\]

which is the exponential survival function. The inter-arrival times \(T_1, T_2, T_3, \ldots\) are i.i.d. \(\text{Expo}(\lambda)\). Memorylessness ensures the process resets after each arrival.

So: Poisson counts, Exponential waiting times — same process, two views.

Question Distribution How many arrivals in \([0,t]\)? \(\text{Pois}(\lambda t)\) How long until the next arrival? \(\text{Expo}(\lambda)\) How long until the \(k\)-th arrival? \(\text{Gamma}(k, \lambda)\)

docs.title: Minimum of Independent Exponentials
docs.text:
This is one of the most important and beautiful facts about the exponential.

Theorem. Let \(X_1 \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda_1), \ldots, X_n \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda_n)\), all independent. Then:

\[M = \min(X_1, \ldots, X_n) \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda_1 + \cdots + \lambda_n)\]

Proof. Use the survival function and independence:

\[P(M > t) = P(X_1 > t, \ldots, X_n > t) = \prod_{i=1}^n P(X_i > t) = \prod_{i=1}^n e^{-\lambda_i t} = e^{-(\lambda_1 + \cdots + \lambda_n)t}\]

This is the survival function of \(\text{Expo}(\lambda_1 + \cdots + \lambda_n)\). \(\blacksquare\)

Furthermore: given that the minimum is \(X_j\) (i.e., \(X_j\) "wins"), we have:

\[P(X_j = M) = P(\min = X_j) = \frac{\lambda_j}{\lambda_1 + \cdots + \lambda_n}\]

Proof. By LOTP and the continuous analogue:

\[P(X_j < X_k) = \int_0^{\infty} P(X_k > x) \lambda_j e^{-\lambda_j x},dx = \int_0^{\infty} e^{-\lambda_k x} \lambda_j e^{-\lambda_j x},dx = \frac{\lambda_j}{\lambda_j + \lambda_k}\]

Generalizing: \(P(X_j = \min) = \frac{\lambda_j}{\sum_i \lambda_i}\).

This is the race interpretation. You have \(n\) independent exponential clocks ticking simultaneously. The first one to go off determines the winner. The winning probability is proportional to the rate — the faster clock wins more often. And the time until someone wins is itself exponential with the total rate. I find this almost unreasonably elegant.

Application. In a system with \(n\) components failing independently at rates \(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n\), the system fails at rate \(\sum \lambda_i\) (if it fails when any component fails — series system). This is the engineering reliability interpretation.

docs.title: Scaling Property
docs.text:
If \(X \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda)\) and \(c > 0\), then:

\[cX \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda/c)\]

Proof.

\[P(cX > t) = P!\left(X > \frac{t}{c}\right) = e^{-\lambda t/c}\]

which is the survival function of \(\text{Expo}(\lambda/c)\). \(\blacksquare\)

In particular, \(\lambda X \sim \text{Expo}(1)\). So every exponential is just a scaled \(\text{Expo}(1)\). This is the "standard exponential" — analogous to the standard normal \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\).

docs.title: Connection to the Gamma Distribution
docs.text:
The Gamma distribution \(\text{Gamma}(a, \lambda)\) generalizes the exponential. Specifically:

\[\text{Expo}(\lambda) = \text{Gamma}(1, \lambda)\]

Moreover, if \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{Expo}(\lambda)\), then:

\[X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_n \sim \text{Gamma}(n, \lambda)\]

This is the distribution of the waiting time until the \(n\)-th Poisson arrival.

Proof via MGFs. The MGF of a sum of independent RVs is the product of MGFs:

\[M_{X_1 + \cdots + X_n}(t) = \left(\frac{\lambda}{\lambda - t}\right)^n\]

which is precisely the MGF of \(\text{Gamma}(n, \lambda)\). \(\blacksquare\)

So exponential is to Gamma as Bernoulli is to Binomial. One trial vs. \(n\) trials. One arrival vs. \(n\) arrivals. The pattern is exact.

docs.title: Lack of Memory Makes It Markovian
docs.text:
The memoryless property is precisely what makes Poisson processes and continuous-time Markov chains tractable. In a CTMC, the time spent in each state is exponentially distributed — and memorylessness ensures the chain's future depends only on the current state, not the history. Without the exponential distribution, the theory of CTMCs would collapse.

This is deeper than it sounds: the exponential is special not just as a distribution, but as the only distribution that makes the Markov property work in continuous time.

docs.title: Summary of Key Facts
docs.text: Property Value PDF \(\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\), \(x > 0\) CDF \(1 - e^{-\lambda x}\) Survival \(e^{-\lambda x}\) Mean \(1/\lambda\) Variance \(1/\lambda^2\) MGF \(\lambda/(\lambda - t)\), \(t < \lambda\) Memoryless Yes — uniquely so among continuous distributions Min of \(n\) Expo(\(\lambda_i\)) \(\text{Expo}(\sum \lambda_i)\) Sum of \(n\) i.i.d. Expo(\(\lambda\)) \(\text{Gamma}(n, \lambda)\) Scaling: \(cX\) \(\text{Expo}(\lambda/c)\)

docs.title: Personal Notes
docs.text:
• Always use the survival function \(P(X > x) = e^{-\lambda x}\) as your primary object. The CDF is just \(1\) minus that and is uglier to work with algebraically.
  • The minimum-of-exponentials result is one of the first things I reach for in applied problems. Competing risks, first-passage times, reliability — they all reduce to this.
  • The \(E[X] = \int_0^\infty P(X > t),dt\) formula + exponential survival function = instant mean computation. Drill this until it's a reflex.
  • Memorylessness is an axiom in disguise. If your physical system has memory — aging components, queues with priority — the exponential is the wrong model and you need Weibull, Erlang, or something else. Always ask yourself: is memorylessness justified here?
  • The MGF blowing up at \(t = \lambda\) is a meaningful fact, not a technicality. It signals that the exponential has a genuinely heavy right tail — not heavy like Pareto, but heavy relative to the Gaussian. All the moments exist, but the tail is slow enough that the Laplace transform can't be extended to all of \(\mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: Poisson Process
docs.text: The Poisson process is the first serious stochastic process you meet, and it rewards the time you put into it. Everything connects: the Exponential inter-arrival times, the Poisson counts, the Gamma waiting times, the splitting and merging — they're not separate facts. They're the same object from different angles. Get the definition right first, then everything else is theorem.

docs.title: Definition (Axiomatic)
docs.text:
A Poisson process with rate \(\lambda > 0\) is a collection of random variables \({N(t) : t \geq 0}\) — where \(N(t)\) counts the number of arrivals in \([0, t]\) — satisfying:

  1. \(N(0) = 0\) — the process starts empty.

  2. Independent increments — for any \(0 \leq t_1 < t_2 \leq t_3 < t_4\), the increments \(N(t_2) - N(t_1)\) and \(N(t_4) - N(t_3)\) are independent. Non-overlapping intervals don't talk to each other.

  3. Stationary increments — \(N(t+s) - N(s) \overset{d}{=} N(t)\) for all \(s, t \geq 0\). The distribution of the count in an interval depends only on its length, not its position.

  4. Poisson counts — \(N(t) \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda t)\) for all \(t \geq 0\).

Some texts replace axiom 4 with the infinitesimal characterisation:

\[P(N(h) = 1) = \lambda h + o(h), \qquad P(N(h) \geq 2) = o(h)\]

as \(h \to 0\). This says: in a tiny interval, at most one arrival happens, and it happens with probability roughly \(\lambda h\). Axiom 4 is then a theorem derived from axioms 1–3 plus the infinitesimal condition. For us, taking axiom 4 as given is cleaner.

The two definitions are equivalent — the infinitesimal one is more physically intuitive ("rare events in tiny intervals"), the axiomatic one with Poisson counts is mathematically cleaner. Blitzstein uses the second. Know both exist.

docs.title: The Poisson Distribution Refresher
docs.text:
Since \(N(t) \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda t)\):

\[P(N(t) = k) = \frac{e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda t)^k}{k!}, \quad k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\] \[E[N(t)] = \lambda t, \qquad \text{Var}(N(t)) = \lambda t\]

The rate \(\lambda\) has units of arrivals per unit time. The expected count in \([0,t]\) is \(\lambda t\) — linear in \(t\), as it should be.

docs.title: Inter-Arrival Times Are Exponential
docs.text:
Let \(T_1\) be the time of the first arrival, \(T_2\) the time between the first and second arrival, and so on. Formally:

\[T_1 = \inf{t > 0 : N(t) = 1}$$ $$T_n = \text{time between }(n-1)\text{-th and }n\text{-th arrival}\]

Theorem. The inter-arrival times \(T_1, T_2, T_3, \ldots\) are i.i.d. \(\text{Expo}(\lambda)\).

Proof.

For \(T_1\): using the survival function,

\[P(T_1 > t) = P(N(t) = 0) = e^{-\lambda t}\]

So \(T_1 \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda)\).

For \(T_2\): given \(T_1 = s\), the time until the next arrival after \(s\) has the same distribution as \(T_1\), by stationary and independent increments — the process after time \(s\) is a fresh Poisson process with the same rate. So \(T_2 \mid T_1 = s \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda)\) for any \(s\), meaning \(T_2 \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda)\) and \(T_2 \perp T_1\).

By induction, all \(T_n\) are i.i.d. \(\text{Expo}(\lambda)\). \(\blacksquare\)

This is the Poisson process's memorylessness in disguise. The process doesn't remember how long it's been since the last arrival. It resets. This is exactly the Exponential's memoryless property at the process level.

docs.title: Arrival Times Are Gamma
docs.text:
Let \(S_n = T_1 + T_2 + \cdots + T_n\) be the time of the \(n\)-th arrival (the \(n\)-th order statistic of arrivals).

Theorem. \(S_n \sim \text{Gamma}(n, \lambda)\).

Proof. \(S_n\) is a sum of \(n\) i.i.d. \(\text{Expo}(\lambda)\) random variables. By the MGF:

\[M_{S_n}(t) = \left(\frac{\lambda}{\lambda - t}\right)^n\]

which is the MGF of \(\text{Gamma}(n, \lambda)\). \(\blacksquare\)

The PDF of \(S_n\) is:

\[f_{S_n}(t) = \frac{\lambda^n t^{n-1} e^{-\lambda t}}{(n-1)!}, \quad t > 0\]

Sanity check. \(P(S_n \leq t) = P(N(t) \geq n)\): the \(n\)-th arrival happens by time \(t\) if and only if there are at least \(n\) arrivals in \([0,t]\). This gives a beautiful identity between the Gamma CDF and the Poisson tail:

\[\sum_{k=n}^{\infty} \frac{e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda t)^k}{k!} = \int_0^t \frac{\lambda^n s^{n-1} e^{-\lambda s}}{(n-1)!},ds\]

This identity is non-obvious analytically but completely obvious probabilistically. Two different ways to ask "has the \(n\)-th arrival happened yet?" This is exactly the kind of thing Blitzstein means when he says to think about what events mean, not just what the formulas say.

docs.title: The Three Views of the Same Process
docs.text:
Question Answer Distribution How many arrivals in \([0,t]\)? \(N(t)\) \(\text{Pois}(\lambda t)\) How long between arrivals \(n-1\) and \(n\)? \(T_n\) \(\text{Expo}(\lambda)\) When does the \(n\)-th arrival happen? \(S_n\) \(\text{Gamma}(n, \lambda)\)

These are not three different processes. They are one process, described three ways. Any question about the Poisson process can be answered from any of these three angles — pick the cleanest one for the problem at hand.

docs.title: Merging Poisson Processes
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(N_1(t) \sim \text{PP}(\lambda_1)\) and \(N_2(t) \sim \text{PP}(\lambda_2)\) are independent Poisson processes, then their superposition \(N(t) = N_1(t) + N_2(t)\) is a Poisson process with rate \(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2\):

\[N(t) \sim \text{PP}(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)\]

Proof. For any interval of length \(t\), \(N_1(t) \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda_1 t)\) and \(N_2(t) \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda_2 t)\) independently. The sum of independent Poisson random variables is Poisson:

\[N(t) = N_1(t) + N_2(t) \sim \text{Pois}((\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)t)\]

Independent and stationary increments are preserved by superposition. \(\blacksquare\)

Merging is the Poisson process analogue of the minimum-of-exponentials result. Both say: combine independent Poisson/exponential objects and you stay in the same family, with rates adding. The two facts are related — the first arrival in the merged process is \(\min(T_1^{(1)}, T_1^{(2)}) \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)\), which is exactly the minimum-of-exponentials theorem.

docs.title: Splitting (Thinning) a Poisson Process
docs.text:
Theorem. Take a \(\text{PP}(\lambda)\) and independently mark each arrival as type 1 with probability \(p\) and type 2 with probability \(1-p\). Let \(N_1(t)\) and \(N_2(t)\) count type-1 and type-2 arrivals respectively. Then:

\[N_1(t) \sim \text{PP}(\lambda p), \quad N_2(t) \sim \text{PP}(\lambda(1-p)), \quad N_1 \perp N_2\]

Proof. Fix \(t\). We need to show \(N_1(t) \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda p t)\) and \(N_1(t) \perp N_2(t)\).

Condition on \(N(t) = n\): each of the \(n\) arrivals is independently type 1 with probability \(p\), so \(N_1(t) \mid N(t) = n \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)\).

By LOTP (law of total probability), using the Poisson PMF for \(N(t)\):

\[P(N_1(t) = k) = \sum_{n=k}^{\infty} \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k} \cdot \frac{e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda t)^n}{n!}\] \[= \frac{e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda p t)^k}{k!} \sum_{n=k}^{\infty} \frac{(\lambda(1-p)t)^{n-k}}{(n-k)!} = \frac{e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda p t)^k}{k!} \cdot e^{\lambda(1-p)t}\] \[= \frac{e^{-\lambda p t}(\lambda p t)^k}{k!}\]

So \(N_1(t) \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda p t)\). A symmetric argument gives \(N_2(t) \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda(1-p)t)\).

For independence: the joint PMF factors as the product of the marginals (verify by a similar calculation, or note that the conditional distribution \(N_1(t) \mid N(t) = n\) is Binomial, and the joint PMF of \((N_1(t), N_2(t))\) factors). \(\blacksquare\)

The independence of \(N_1\) and \(N_2\) is the surprising part. You'd think that knowing how many type-1 arrivals there are tells you something about type-2 arrivals — after all, they share the same parent process. But no. The Poisson structure absorbs the dependence. This is one of the Poisson process's truly remarkable properties.

docs.title: Conditioning on the Number of Arrivals: Uniform Order Statistics
docs.text:
Theorem. Given \(N(t) = n\), the \(n\) arrival times \(S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_n\) are distributed as the order statistics of \(n\) i.i.d. \(\text{Uniform}(0, t)\) random variables.

That is, conditional on \(n\) arrivals in \([0,t]\), the arrival times are uniformly and independently scattered over \([0,t]\) — we just sort them.

Proof sketch. The joint density of the ordered arrival times \(s_1 < s_2 < \cdots < s_n\) given \(N(t) = n\) is:

\[f(s_1, \ldots, s_n \mid N(t) = n) = \frac{n!}{t^n}, \quad 0 < s_1 < \cdots < s_n < t\]

which is exactly the joint density of the order statistics of \(n\) i.i.d. \(\text{Uniform}(0,t)\) random variables (\(n!/t^n\) on the ordered simplex). \(\blacksquare\)

This is the theorem that makes the Poisson process feel inevitable. If you're going to place \(n\) random points in \([0,t]\) with no memory and no preferred location, what else could they be but uniform? The Poisson process is the unique process consistent with this "complete randomness" — arrivals are as unsophisticated as possible.

Application. This theorem turns many Poisson process calculations into uniform distribution calculations, which are often much simpler. For example: given 10 arrivals in \([0,1]\), what is the expected time of the 3rd arrival? It's \(E[U_{(3)}]\) for \(U_{(3)}\) the 3rd order statistic of 10 i.i.d. Uniform\((0,1)\) variables, which is \(3/11\).

docs.title: The Poisson Process as a Limit of Bernoulli Processes
docs.text:
Consider \(n\) independent Bernoulli trials, each in a tiny interval of length \(h = t/n\), each with success probability \(p = \lambda h = \lambda t / n\). The total number of successes is:

\[\text{Bin}!\left(n, \frac{\lambda t}{n}\right) \xrightarrow{d} \text{Pois}(\lambda t) \quad \text{as } n \to \infty\]

This is the Poisson limit of the Binomial, applied continuously. The Poisson process is the continuous-time limit of a Bernoulli process where:

  • Time is divided into \(n\) tiny slots of length \(1/n\)
  • Each slot has an arrival with probability \(\lambda/n\)
  • Slots are independent

As \(n \to \infty\), discrete slots become continuous time, and Binomial counts become Poisson counts.

This is the "rare events" paradigm at the process level. The Poisson process is what you get when you take a Bernoulli process, let the time slots shrink to zero, and keep the rate fixed. The Binomial\(\to\)Poisson limit is a corollary.

docs.title: Why the Poisson Process Is Everywhere
docs.text:
The Poisson process is the canonical model for "arrivals occurring randomly in time" because it is the unique process satisfying:

  • Independent increments (the past doesn't affect the future)
  • Stationary increments (no preferred time)
  • Orderliness (at most one arrival at any instant)

These are minimal, natural conditions for "completely random" arrivals. Any process satisfying these axioms must be Poisson. This is a uniqueness theorem — the Poisson process is not just a model for random arrivals, it is the model.

Examples:

  • Radioactive decay events in a detector
  • Customer arrivals at a queue
  • Mutations along a DNA strand
  • Requests to a web server
  • Photon arrivals at a telescope sensor

In all of these: events arrive independently, at a roughly constant rate, with at most one per instant. Poisson process.

docs.title: The Non-Homogeneous Poisson Process
docs.text:
A mild but important generalisation: replace the constant rate \(\lambda\) with a rate function \(\lambda(t) \geq 0\) that varies over time.

Then \(N(t) \sim \text{Pois}(\Lambda(t))\) where \(\Lambda(t) = \int_0^t \lambda(s),ds\) is the cumulative intensity.

The axioms of independent and stationary increments still hold (for increments of \(\Lambda\), not \(t\)), but the Exponential inter-arrival time result fails — inter-arrival times are no longer i.i.d. Expo.

The non-homogeneous version is what you use when the rate changes over time: more customers at lunchtime, more server requests during business hours. The key object becomes \(\Lambda(t)\), not \(\lambda\).

docs.title: Personal Notes
docs.text:
• The three-views table is the most useful organising principle. Any Poisson process problem is asking you about counts (Poisson), inter-arrival times (Exponential), or arrival times (Gamma). Identify which view is cleanest before computing.
  • The splitting independence is always surprising to people. Burn this into memory: thinning a Poisson process gives two independent Poisson processes. This is used constantly in queueing theory, genetics, and network modelling.
  • The uniform order statistics theorem is the theorem I return to most often in applications. It reduces "where are the arrivals?" to a uniform distribution problem, which is almost always easier.
  • The merging + splitting theorems together say: the Poisson family is closed under both operations, with rates combining additively. This closure is what makes the Poisson process so analytically tractable.
  • The non-homogeneous process is more realistic in almost every application. The key insight: it's just a time-changed homogeneous process. If you set \(\tau = \Lambda(t)\), the process in \(\tau\)-time is homogeneous Poisson with rate 1.
