Value PDF ✓ \(\frac{1}{\pi(1+x^2)}\) CDF ✓ \(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\pi}\arctan(x)\) Median ✓ \(0\) Mode ✓ \(0\) Characteristic function ✓ \(e^{-\vert t \vert}\) Mean \(E[X]\) ✗ Undefined (principal value \(= 0\)) Variance ✗ Undefined \(E[X^k]\) for any \(k \geq 1\) ✗ \(+\infty\) MGF \(M_X(t)\) for \(t \neq 0\) ✗ \(+\infty\)

docs.title: Hybrid Distributions
docs.text: Reality does not respect the discrete/continuous divide. Insurance payouts, option prices, rainfall totals — these are neither purely discrete nor purely continuous. The hybrid is not a pathology. It is the generic case, and discrete and continuous are the special ones.

docs.title: The Problem with the Discrete/Continuous Dichotomy
docs.text:
Every introductory probability course splits random variables into discrete (PMF) and continuous (PDF). But what about:

  • Insurance: a payout that is exactly \(0\) with probability \(1/2\) (no accident), and otherwise exponentially distributed.
  • Censored data: a survival time that is observed exactly if death occurred, but recorded as \(T > C\) (a point mass at \(C\)) if the subject was censored.
  • Option pricing: a call option worth exactly \(0\) (with positive probability) if it expires out of the money, and continuously distributed otherwise.

These are hybrid (or mixed) random variables — they have both a discrete component (point masses) and a continuous component (a density). Neither a PMF alone nor a PDF alone describes them.

The CDF is the object that handles all cases uniformly.

docs.title: The CDF Is Always Well-Defined
docs.text:
For any random variable \(X\) — discrete, continuous, or hybrid — the CDF

\[F_X(x) = P(X \leq x)\]

is well-defined, right-continuous, nondecreasing, with \(F_X(-\infty) = 0\) and \(F_X(\infty) = 1\).

A hybrid \(X\) has a CDF that is:

  • Flat on intervals where there is no mass (neither discrete nor continuous),
  • Jumps at points with positive probability (the discrete atoms),
  • Rises smoothly on intervals where \(X\) has a density.

The Lebesgue decomposition theorem says every CDF decomposes uniquely into a discrete part, an absolutely continuous part, and a singular continuous part. For all distributions we encounter in probability courses, the singular part is zero — so every mixed distribution is a convex combination of a purely discrete and purely continuous distribution.

docs.title: The Decomposition
docs.text:
Write the CDF of a hybrid \(X\) as:

\[F_X(x) = p \cdot F_{\text{disc}}(x) + (1-p) \cdot F_{\text{cont}}(x), \quad p \in [0,1],\]

where:

  • \(F_{\text{disc}}\) is the CDF of a purely discrete distribution (a step function),
  • \(F_{\text{cont}}\) is the CDF of a purely continuous distribution (a continuous function),
  • \(p\) is the total probability mass sitting on discrete atoms.

Equivalently, there exist:

  • A set of atoms \({x_1, x_2, \ldots}\) with point masses \(p_i = P(X = x_i) > 0\) summing to \(p\),
  • A density \(f_{\text{cont}}(x)\) for the continuous part, integrating to \(1-p\).

The full "density" of \(X\) — in the sense of a measure — is:

\[\mu_X = p_{\text{disc}} + (1-p), f_{\text{cont}}(x), dx,\]

where \(p_{\text{disc}} = \sum_i p_i \delta_{x_i}\) is a sum of Dirac delta masses.

I won't use measure theory throughout — the CDF and the case-by-case approach is cleaner for computation.

docs.title: Computing Probabilities: Always Go Through the CDF
docs.text:
For a hybrid \(X\), probabilities of intervals are:

\[P(a < X \leq b) = F_X(b) - F_X(a).\] \[P(a \leq X \leq b) = F_X(b) - F_X(a^-) = F_X(b) - \lim_{x \nearrow a} F_X(x).\]

The distinction between \(F_X(a)\) and \(F_X(a^-)\) matters when \(a\) is an atom:

\[P(X = a) = F_X(a) - F_X(a^-).\]

For continuous points, \(F_X(a) = F_X(a^-)\) and \(P(X = a) = 0\).

docs.title: The Canonical Example: Zero-Inflated Exponential
docs.text:
\[X = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{with probability } p \ Y & \text{with probability } 1-p \end{cases}\]

where \(Y \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda)\), independent of the Bernoulli trial.

CDF:

\[F_X(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & x < 0 \ p + (1-p)(1 - e^{-\lambda x}) & x \geq 0. \end{cases}\]

At \(x = 0\): \(F_X(0) = p\). So there's a jump of size \(p\) at 0, corresponding to \(P(X = 0) = p\). For \(x > 0\), \(F_X\) rises smoothly.

Expected value:

\[E[X] = p \cdot 0 + (1-p) \cdot E[Y] = \frac{1-p}{\lambda}.\]

This is LOTP for expectations: \(E[X] = E[X \mid \text{atom}]\cdot p + E[X \mid \text{continuous}]\cdot (1-p)\).

General formula for \(E[X]\): For any hybrid $X = $ discrete atoms + continuous density:

\[E[X] = \sum_i x_i , p_i + \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x, f_{\text{cont}}(x), dx.\]

This is just linearity of expectation applied to the decomposition.

docs.title: Worked Example 1: Insurance Payout
docs.text:
A policy pays \(0\) if there is no claim (probability \(3/4\)), and pays an amount \(\text{Expo}(1/1000)\) (mean payout $1000) if there is a claim (probability \(1/4\)).

Let \(X\) be the payout.

CDF: For \(x < 0\): \(F_X(x) = 0\). For \(x \geq 0\):

\[F_X(x) = \frac{3}{4} + \frac{1}{4}(1 - e^{-x/1000}) = 1 - \frac{1}{4}e^{-x/1000}.\]

Jump of \(3/4\) at \(x = 0\). Smooth rise for \(x > 0\).

Mean payout:

\[E[X] = \frac{3}{4} \cdot 0 + \frac{1}{4} \cdot 1000 = 250.\]

\(P(X > 500)\):

\[P(X > 500) = 1 - F_X(500) = \frac{1}{4}e^{-1/2} \approx \frac{1}{4}(0.6065) \approx 0.1516.\]

docs.title: Worked Example 2: The Censored Random Variable
docs.text:
In survival analysis, a subject either dies (event time \(T \sim f_T\)) or is censored at time \(C\) (still alive at end of study). The observed time is:

\[X = \min(T, C), \quad \Delta = \mathbf{1}[T \leq C].\]

If \(T \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda)\) and \(C\) is a fixed constant:

\[P(X = C) = P(T > C) = e^{-\lambda C}.\] \[P(X \leq x) = P(T \leq x),\mathbf{1}[x < C] + 1 \cdot \mathbf{1}[x \geq C] = (1 - e^{-\lambda x}),\mathbf{1}[x < C] + \mathbf{1}[x \geq C].\]

So \(X\) has:

  • A continuous density \(\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\) on \([0, C)\),
  • A point mass \(e^{-\lambda C}\) at \(x = C\).

This is a hybrid distribution — it is impossible to describe \(X\) with either a PMF or a PDF alone.

docs.title: Worked Example 3: Mixed Bayes (The Key Probability Example)
docs.text:
This is the Stat 110 use case. A continuous prior, discrete likelihood — or vice versa.

Setup. A coin has bias \(p \sim \text{Beta}(1,1) = \text{Uniform}(0,1)\) (continuous prior). I flip it once and observe \(X \in {0,1}\) (discrete).

The joint distribution of \((p, X)\) is hybrid: \(p\) is continuous, \(X\) is discrete. The marginal of \(X\) is discrete; the marginal of \(p\) is continuous; the joint has no single representation as either a PMF or a PDF.

The joint "density" is:

\[f_{p, X}(p, x) = P(X = x \mid p), f_p(p) = p^x(1-p)^{1-x} \cdot 1, \quad p \in (0,1),; x \in {0,1}.\]

Marginal of \(X\):

\[P(X = 1) = \int_0^1 p \cdot 1, dp = \frac{1}{2}.\]

Posterior of \(p\) given \(X = 1\):

\[f_{p \mid X}(p \mid 1) = \frac{P(X=1 \mid p), f_p(p)}{P(X=1)} = \frac{p \cdot 1}{1/2} = 2p, \quad p \in (0,1).\]

So \(p \mid X = 1 \sim \text{Beta}(2,1)\). ✓

This is mixed Bayes: the prior is a continuous PDF, the likelihood is a discrete PMF, the posterior is a continuous PDF. The formula structure is identical to pure continuous Bayes — you just mix the object types appropriately.

docs.title: Expectation via LOTP: The General Tool
docs.text:
For a hybrid \(X\) and any event \(A\), LOTP gives:

\[E[X] = E[X \mid A], P(A) + E[X \mid A^c], P(A^c).\]

This always works regardless of whether \(X\) is discrete, continuous, or hybrid. The conditioning splits \(X\) into pieces that may each be easier to handle.

Example. \(X\) is zero-inflated Exponential as above. Let \(A = {X = 0}\).

\[E[X] = E[X \mid X = 0], P(X=0) + E[X \mid X > 0], P(X > 0) = 0 \cdot p + \frac{1}{\lambda}\cdot(1-p) = \frac{1-p}{\lambda}.\]

Here \(E[X \mid X > 0] = E[\text{Expo}(\lambda)] = 1/\lambda\) because given the continuous part is realised, \(X \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda)\).

docs.title: The CDF Characterises Everything
docs.text:
For a hybrid \(X\), the CDF \(F_X\) completely characterises the distribution. From \(F_X\):

  • Identify atoms: points where \(F_X\) jumps. The jump size at \(x_0\) is \(P(X = x_0) = F_X(x_0) - F_X(x_0^-)\).
  • Identify continuous density: wherever \(F_X\) is differentiable, \(f_{\text{cont}}(x) = F_X'(x)\).
  • Recover all probabilities: \(P(X \in B) = \int_B dF_X\) (Lebesgue-Stieltjes integral — the unified notation that handles both sums over atoms and integrals over densities).

The Lebesgue-Stieltjes integral \(\int g(x), dF_X(x)\) is the right way to write \(E[g(X)]\) for any distribution:

  • Discrete: \(\sum_i g(x_i), p_i\).
  • Continuous: \(\int g(x), f_X(x), dx\).
  • Hybrid: both terms summed.

This is the formalism that unifies everything. I don't need it for computation — LOTP does the work — but it's the reason there's no separate theory for each case.

docs.title: Common Mistake: Forgetting Point Masses in the CDF
docs.text:
For a hybrid \(X\) with an atom at \(x_0\):

\[P(X < x_0) = F_X(x_0^-) \neq F_X(x_0) = P(X \leq x_0).\]

The difference is \(P(X = x_0) > 0\).

When computing \(P(a \leq X \leq b)\), always be explicit about whether endpoints are included:

\[P(a \leq X \leq b) = F_X(b) - F_X(a^-).\]

If \(a\) is an atom and you write \(F_X(b) - F_X(a)\) instead, you lose the mass at \(a\). This is a silent error — the formula looks right and the answer is just slightly off.

docs.title: Why This Matters Beyond Probability Theory
docs.text:
The hybrid framework is not an abstract curiosity. It appears everywhere:

  • Econometrics: Tobit models — a continuous outcome censored at zero (wages, consumption). The observed variable is hybrid.
  • Biostatistics: Survival data with administrative censoring — the exact structure of Worked Example 2.
  • Finance: Digital options, barrier options — positive probability of ending at exactly zero or exactly at the barrier.
  • Mixture models: Latent variable models where a hidden discrete variable selects which continuous component generates the data. The marginal over the hidden variable is hybrid.
  • Renewal theory: The age of a renewal process at a fixed time has a point mass at zero (if a renewal just occurred) plus a continuous component.

In all these cases, the right tool is the CDF, LOTP conditioning on the discrete/continuous split, and the Lebesgue-Stieltjes expectation formula.

docs.title: 2D LOTUS
docs.text: [[07.LOTUS]]says you don't need to find the distribution of \(g(X,Y)\) to compute its expectation. You just integrate \(g\) against the joint density you already have. This sounds obvious — it is not. It is a theorem, and a useful one.

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
Suppose \((X, Y)\) has joint PDF \(f_{X,Y}\) and I want to compute \(E[g(X,Y)]\) for some function \(g : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\).

The naive approach: find the distribution of \(Z = g(X,Y)\) — its PDF or CDF — then compute \(E[Z] = \int z, f_Z(z), dz\).

The LOTUS approach: skip finding \(f_Z\) entirely and compute directly.

Finding the distribution of \(Z = g(X,Y)\) is often painful. It requires a change of variables, setting up inequalities, differentiating CDFs. LOTUS bypasses all of this.

docs.title: The Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem (2D LOTUS). Let \((X,Y)\) be a continuous random vector with joint PDF \(f_{X,Y}\), and let \(g : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\) be a measurable function. Then:

\[\boxed{E[g(X,Y)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x,y), f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx, dy,}\]

provided the integral converges absolutely (i.e., \(E[|g(X,Y)|] < \infty\)).

For the discrete case, with joint PMF \(p_{X,Y}\):

\[E[g(X,Y)] = \sum_x \sum_y g(x,y), p_{X,Y}(x,y).\]

What the theorem says: the expectation of a function of \((X,Y)\) is computed by integrating that function against the joint density. You do not need to know the distribution of \(g(X,Y)\).

docs.title: Why It's a Theorem, Not a Definition
docs.text:
\(E[Z]\) is defined as \(\int z, f_Z(z), dz\) for a random variable \(Z\) with PDF \(f_Z\). The statement that this equals \(\int!\int g(x,y) f_{X,Y}(x,y),dx,dy\) when \(Z = g(X,Y)\) is a genuine result — it requires proof.

Proof sketch (continuous case). By definition, \(E[g(X,Y)] = \int z, f_{g(X,Y)}(z), dz\). The PDF \(f_{g(X,Y)}\) is obtained by pushing forward the joint measure \((X,Y)\) through \(g\). The change-of-variables formula for measures gives exactly the right-hand side. More concretely, for \(g \geq 0\):

\[E[g(X,Y)] = \int_0^{\infty} P(g(X,Y) > t), dt = \int_0^{\infty} \iint_{{g(x,y)>t}} f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx, dy, dt.\]

Swapping the order of integration (Tonelli — all terms are nonneg):

\[= \iint \left(\int_0^{g(x,y)} dt\right) f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx, dy = \iint g(x,y), f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx, dy. \quad \square\]

For general \(g\): decompose \(g = g^+ - g^-\) and apply the nonneg result to each part, assuming absolute integrability.

docs.title: Special Cases Worth Naming
docs.text:
Linearity. \(E[aX + bY + c] = a,E[X] + b,E[Y] + c\).

Proof via 2D LOTUS with \(g(x,y) = ax+by+c\) and \(f_{X,Y}\) arbitrary:

\[E[aX+bY+c] = \iint (ax+by+c), f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx, dy$$ $$= a\iint x, f_{X,Y}, dx, dy + b\iint y, f_{X,Y}, dx, dy + c.\]

The first double integral equals \(\int x, f_X(x), dx = E[X]\) (marginalise out \(y\)). Similarly for \(E[Y]\). Linearity of expectation follows — and note it holds regardless of whether \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent.

Product of independent r.v.'s. If \(X \perp Y\), then \(f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_X(x) f_Y(y)\), so:

\[E[g(X)h(Y)] = \iint g(x)h(y), f_X(x), f_Y(y), dx, dy = \int g(x) f_X(x), dx \cdot \int h(y) f_Y(y), dy = E[g(X)], E[h(Y)].\]

This is the factorisation identity for independent r.v.'s, proved directly from 2D LOTUS + independence.

Covariance. \(\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E[(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y])]\). By 2D LOTUS:

\[\text{Cov}(X,Y) = \iint (x-\mu_X)(y-\mu_Y), f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx, dy.\]

Expanding and using linearity: \(\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X],E[Y]\), where \(E[XY] = \iint xy, f_{X,Y}(x,y), dx, dy\) by 2D LOTUS with \(g(x,y) = xy\).

docs.title: Worked Example 1: \(E[XY]\) for a Triangular Joint
docs.text:
\((X,Y)\) uniform on the triangle \({0 < x < y < 1}\), so \(f_{X,Y}(x,y) = 2\).

\[E[XY] = \int_0^1\int_0^y xy \cdot 2, dx, dy = \int_0^1 2y \cdot \frac{y^2}{2}, dy = \int_0^1 y^3, dy = \frac{1}{4}.\]

Compare: \(E[X] = \int_0^1 2x(1-x), dx = 2\left[\frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = \frac{1}{3}\).

\(E[Y] = \int_0^1 2y \cdot y, dy = \int_0^1 2y^2, dy = \frac{2}{3}\).

So \(\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y] = \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{2}{3} = \frac{1}{4} - \frac{2}{9} = \frac{9-8}{36} = \frac{1}{36} > 0\).

Positive covariance makes sense: large \(X\) forces large \(Y\) (since \(Y > X\)).

docs.title: Worked Example 2: \(E[X^2 + Y^2]\) for Uniform on the Disk
docs.text:
\((X,Y)\) uniform on the unit disk, \(f_{X,Y}(x,y) = 1/\pi\) for \(x^2 + y^2 < 1\).

\[E[X^2 + Y^2] = \iint_{x^2+y^2 < 1} \frac{x^2+y^2}{\pi}, dx, dy.\]

Switch to polar coordinates: \(x = r\cos\theta\), \(y = r\sin\theta\), Jacobian \(= r\).

\[= \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 r^2 \cdot r, dr, d\theta = \frac{1}{\pi} \cdot 2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{2}.\]

By symmetry \(E[X^2] = E[Y^2]\), so \(E[X^2] = \frac{1}{4}\).

Also \(E[X] = 0\) by symmetry, so \(\text{Var}(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 = \frac{1}{4}\).

docs.title: Worked Example 3: \(E[\max(X,Y)]\)
docs.text:
\((X,Y)\) i.i.d. \(\text{Uniform}(0,1)\), so \(f_{X,Y}(x,y) = 1\) on \([0,1]^2\). Let \(M = \max(X,Y)\).

Method 1 (LOTUS directly):

\[E[\max(X,Y)] = \int_0^1\int_0^1 \max(x,y), dx, dy.\]

Split the square into two triangles:

\[= \int_0^1\int_0^y y, dx, dy + \int_0^1\int_0^x x, dy, dx = \int_0^1 y^2, dy + \int_0^1 x^2, dx = \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{2}{3}.\]

Method 2 (via CDF of \(M\)): \(F_M(m) = P(X \leq m, Y \leq m) = m^2\), so \(f_M(m) = 2m\) and \(E[M] = \int_0^1 m \cdot 2m, dm = 2/3\). ✓

LOTUS gets there without ever computing \(f_M\). Both methods agree — the point of LOTUS is that Method 1 is often simpler to set up.

docs.title: Worked Example 4: \(E[e^{X+Y}]\) for Independent Exponentials
docs.text:
\(X, Y \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Expo}(1)\), \(f_{X,Y}(x,y) = e^{-x}e^{-y}\), \(x,y > 0\).

\[E[e^{X+Y}] = \int_0^{\infty}\int_0^{\infty} e^{x+y} \cdot e^{-x-y}, dx, dy = \int_0^{\infty}\int_0^{\infty} 1, dx, dy = \infty.\]

\(e^{X+Y}\) has infinite expectation — consistent with the MGF of \(\text{Expo}(1)\) being \(M_X(t) = 1/(1-t)\), which only exists for \(t < 1\), so \(t = 1\) gives \(\infty\).

But: \(E[e^{tX+sY}] = E[e^{tX}]E[e^{sY}] = \frac{1}{1-t}\cdot\frac{1}{1-s}\) for \(t, s < 1\).

This is the joint MGF of \((X,Y)\), computed via 2D LOTUS + independence.

docs.title: The Non-Rectangular Support Issue (Again)
docs.text:
When the support of \((X,Y)\) is not a rectangle, 2D LOTUS requires careful limit-setting — exactly the same issue as in marginalisation.

Rule: Always draw the support. For the inner integral, fix the outer variable and determine the range of the inner variable by intersecting with the support.

Example. \((X,Y)\) uniform on \({0 < x < y < 1}\), \(f_{X,Y}(x,y) = 2\). Compute \(E[Y - X]\).

\[E[Y-X] = \int_0^1\int_0^y (y-x)\cdot 2, dx, dy = \int_0^1 2\left[xy - \frac{x^2}{2}\right]_0^y dy = \int_0^1 2\left(y^2 - \frac{y^2}{2}\right) dy = \int_0^1 y^2, dy = \frac{1}{3}.\]

Sanity check: \(E[Y] = 2/3\), \(E[X] = 1/3\), so \(E[Y-X] = 1/3\). ✓ (Linearity of expectation gives the same answer with less work — useful check.)

docs.title: When 2D LOTUS Fails: Integrability
docs.text:
\(E[g(X,Y)]\) is only well-defined when \(E[|g(X,Y)|] < \infty\). If this fails, the expectation doesn't exist.

Example. \((X,Y)\) i.i.d. \(N(0,1)\), \(g(x,y) = x/y\). Then \(X/Y \sim \text{Cauchy}(0,1)\) (as we showed in [[09.Cauchy Distribution]]), which has no mean. Indeed:

\[E!\left[\frac{X}{Y}\right] = \iint \frac{x}{y} \cdot \frac{1}{2\pi}e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2}, dx, dy\]

does not converge absolutely — the integral of the absolute value is \(\infty\).

The practical check: before applying 2D LOTUS, verify (or at least expect) that \(\iint |g(x,y)| f_{X,Y}(x,y),dx,dy < \infty\). For \(g \geq 0\) this is automatic (Tonelli) — the expectation is either finite or \(+\infty\). For sign-changing \(g\), check absolute integrability first.

docs.title: The Discrete-Continuous Mixed Case
docs.text:
2D LOTUS extends immediately to hybrid distributions. If \(X\) is continuous with PDF \(f_X\) and \(Y\) is discrete with PMF \(p_Y\), and they are independent:

\[E[g(X,Y)] = \sum_y \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x,y), f_X(x), p_Y(y), dx = \sum_y p_Y(y) \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x,y), f_X(x), dx.\]

This is LOTUS for the mixed joint — sum over the discrete variable, integrate over the continuous one. Fubini/Tonelli justifies the interchange.

Example. \(N \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)\), \(X \mid N = n \sim \text{Binomial}(n, p)\). Find \(E[X]\).

\[E[X] = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} E[X \mid N=n], P(N=n) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} np \cdot \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n}{n!} = p\lambda \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{n-1}}{(n-1)!} = p\lambda.\]

(This is LOTP for expectations, which is itself a consequence of 2D LOTUS + the tower property.)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
2D LOTUS is the workhorse for computing expectations involving two random variables. The key points:

  • You do not need the distribution of \(g(X,Y)\). Integrate \(g\) against the joint density directly.
  • The hard part is the limits, not the theorem. Draw the support. Fix the outer variable, determine the inner limits.
  • Integrability matters. For \(g \geq 0\), Tonelli guarantees the integral is well-defined (possibly \(+\infty\)). For sign-changing \(g\), check \(E[|g|] < \infty\) before claiming \(E[g]\) exists.
  • Linearity of expectation and the independence factorisation are both special cases, derivable immediately from 2D LOTUS.

docs.title: Linearity via 2D LOTUS
docs.text: The standard proof of linearity goes: "use the definition, rearrange the sum." Fine. But it gives no intuition for why independence never enters. The 2D LOTUS proof does. Once you see this, linearity stops feeling like an algebraic accident and starts feeling geometrically inevitable.

docs.title: What We're Proving
docs.text: Theorem (Linearity of Expectation). For any two random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) defined on the same probability space (no independence required): $\(\mathbb{E}[X + Y] = \mathbb{E}[X] + \mathbb{E}[Y]\)$

docs.title: The Setup: Joint Distribution
docs.text:
\(X\) and \(Y\) have a joint distribution. Whether they're discrete, continuous, or mixed — there exists a joint PMF/PDF \(p(x, y)\) (or \(f(x,y)\)) over the sample space \(\mathbb{R}^2\).

The marginals recover from it: $\(p_X(x) = \sum_y p(x,y), \qquad p_Y(y) = \sum_x p(x,y)\)$

This is the key structural fact. The marginal is obtained by summing out (integrating out) the other variable. No independence. No factoring. Just the definition of a joint distribution.

docs.title: The 2D LOTUS Proof
docs.text:
LOTUS (Law Of The Unconscious Statistician) in 2D says: if \(g: \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\) is a function of two random variables, then: $\(\mathbb{E}[g(X,Y)] = \sum_x \sum_y g(x,y), p(x,y)\)$

We want \(\mathbb{E}[X + Y]\), so take \(g(x,y) = x + y\):

\[\mathbb{E}[X + Y] = \sum_x \sum_y (x + y), p(x,y)\]

Split the sum (linearity of finite summation — this is where we cash in):

\[= \sum_x \sum_y x, p(x,y) ;+; \sum_x \sum_y y, p(x,y)\]

First term: Factor out \(x\) from the inner sum over \(y\):

\[\sum_x \sum_y x, p(x,y) = \sum_x x \underbrace{\left(\sum_y p(x,y)\right)}_{= , p_X(x)} = \sum_x x, p_X(x) = \mathbb{E}[X]\]

Second term: Factor out \(y\) from the inner sum over \(x\):

\[\sum_x \sum_y y, p(x,y) = \sum_y y \underbrace{\left(\sum_x p(x,y)\right)}_{= , p_Y(y)} = \sum_y y, p_Y(y) = \mathbb{E}[Y]\]

Therefore: $\(\boxed{\mathbb{E}[X + Y] = \mathbb{E}[X] + \mathbb{E}[Y]}\)$

\(\square\)

docs.title: Why Independence Never Appears
docs.text:
Look carefully at where the proof uses the joint distribution \(p(x,y)\).

It uses it exactly once: to recover the marginals by summing out. The step \(\sum_y p(x,y) = p_X(x)\) is just the definition of the marginal — it holds for any joint distribution, dependent or not.

Independence would give us \(p(x,y) = p_X(x),p_Y(y)\). But we never needed to factor the joint. The proof works in the 2D grid of \((x,y)\) pairs and collapses each dimension separately. The dependence structure of \(X\) and \(Y\) determines which cells \((x,y)\) have probability mass and how much — but once you sum out a row or a column, the other variable's marginal is what's left. Every time. Regardless of correlation.

The intuition: \(\mathbb{E}[X]\) only cares about the marginal of \(X\). \(\mathbb{E}[Y]\) only cares about the marginal of \(Y\). And \(\mathbb{E}[X+Y]\) is just asking both questions simultaneously. The joint structure determines how \(X\) and \(Y\) co-vary, but marginals don't care about that — they've already forgotten it.

docs.title: The Continuous Version
docs.text:
Identical argument with integrals. By 2D LOTUS:

\[\mathbb{E}[X + Y] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (x + y), f(x,y), dx, dy\]

Split the integrand:

\[= \int!!\int x, f(x,y), dx, dy ;+; \int!!\int y, f(x,y), dx, dy\]

First integral: Integrate out \(y\) first:

\[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y),dy\right) dx = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x, f_X(x), dx = \mathbb{E}[X]\]

Second integral: Integrate out \(x\) first:

\[\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y \left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x,y), dx\right) dy = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} y, f_Y(y), dy = \mathbb{E}[Y]\]

Done. Same proof, same punchline. Fubini's theorem justifies swapping the order of integration (provided the integral converges absolutely, which \(\mathbb{E}[|X|] < \infty\) and \(\mathbb{E}[|Y|] < \infty\) guarantee).

docs.title: The Geometric Picture
docs.text:
Think of the joint PMF \(p(x,y)\) as a mass distribution over a 2D grid. Each lattice point \((x,y)\) carries weight \(p(x,y)\).

  • \(\mathbb{E}[X]\) is the \(x\)-coordinate of the centre of mass of this distribution.
  • \(\mathbb{E}[Y]\) is the \(y\)-coordinate of the centre of mass.
  • \(\mathbb{E}[X+Y]\) is the centre of mass projected onto the line \(x = y\), i.e. the expected value of the random variable that measures "diagonal distance."

The centre of mass of a 2D distribution decomposes into its coordinates. Of course it does — that's what centres of mass do. Independence has nothing to do with it. Whether the mass is smeared along the diagonal (positive correlation) or anti-diagonal (negative correlation), the \(x\)-coordinate of the centre is still \(\mathbb{E}[X]\) and the \(y\)-coordinate is still \(\mathbb{E}[Y]\).

This is the deepest version of the intuition. Linearity of expectation = linearity of centres of mass. And centres of mass are always linear in coordinates.

docs.title: Corollaries That Fall Out Immediately
docs.text:
Once you have \(\mathbb{E}[X+Y] = \mathbb{E}[X] + \mathbb{E}[Y]\), everything else is algebra:

Scaling: \(\mathbb{E}[cX] = c,\mathbb{E}[X]\) (trivial from the definition — multiply \(g(x) = cx\) through the PMF/PDF).

General linearity: For any \(a, b \in \mathbb{R}\): $\(\mathbb{E}[aX + bY] = a,\mathbb{E}[X] + b,\mathbb{E}[Y]\)$

Finite sums: By induction on \(n\): $\(\mathbb{E}!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right] = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}[X_i]\)$

No independence anywhere. This is why we can compute \(\mathbb{E}[\text{number of fixed points of a random permutation}]\) or \(\mathbb{E}[\text{number of matches in birthday problem}]\) so effortlessly — we write the count as a sum of indicator r.v.'s and linearity does the rest.

docs.title: The Indicator Trick (LOTUS + Linearity in Action)
docs.text:
If \(A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n\) are events (possibly dependent!), and \(X = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{1}_{A_i}\) counts how many occur, then:

\[\mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_{A_i}] = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{P}(A_i)\]

This works because \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{1}_A] = \mathbb{P}(A)\) (trivial from LOTUS) and linearity requires nothing from the \(A_i\)'s.

Example — matches in a hat-check problem (derangements): \(n\) people, hats returned randomly. \(X_i = \mathbf{1}[\text{person } i \text{ gets own hat}]\). The \(X_i\) are terribly dependent. But: $\(\mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{P}(X_i = 1) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{n} = 1\)$

Always 1, regardless of \(n\). Slick. And impossible to see without linearity.

docs.title: Technical Note: When Does This Fail?
docs.text:
The proof requires that the expectations exist (i.e. \(\mathbb{E}[|X|] < \infty\) and \(\mathbb{E}[|Y|] < \infty\)). If either expectation is infinite, the rearrangement of sums/integrals may not be valid (you'd be doing \(\infty - \infty\)). So technically:

\[\mathbb{E}[X + Y] = \mathbb{E}[X] + \mathbb{E}[Y] \quad \text{provided } \mathbb{E}[|X|] + \mathbb{E}[|Y|] < \infty\]

In practice this is always satisfied in the problems we work with, but worth knowing.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability — LOTUS (Ch. 4), linearity and indicators (Ch. 4–5)
  2. Harvard Stat 110 — Lecture 7–8 (LOTUS, linearity, indicator r.v.'s)
  3. The geometric "centre of mass" framing is mine — haven't seen it stated this cleanly elsewhere. Maybe worth expanding into a short write-up.

The proof is five lines. But what those five lines are saying is: we live in a 2D probability space, and collapsing to 1D separately in each direction gives you the marginals. Linearity is just that collapse, done twice.

docs.title: Covariance and Correlation
docs.text: These two are inseparable in my head. Covariance is the raw quantity — it measures joint variation but bleeds units. Correlation is covariance made dimensionless, which is why it's the one you can actually compare across problems. Know both cold.

docs.title: Covariance: The Definition
docs.text:
For random variables \(X\) and \(Y\): $\(\text{Cov}(X, Y) = \mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X])(Y - \mathbb{E}[Y])]\)$

This is the expected product of deviations. When \(X\) is above its mean at the same time \(Y\) is above its mean (or both below), the product is positive — they're moving together. When they move oppositely, the product is negative.

The computational formula — the one I actually use: $\(\text{Cov}(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}[XY] - \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y]\)$

Proof: Expand the definition directly: $\(\mathbb{E}[(X - \mu_X)(Y - \mu_Y)] = \mathbb{E}[XY - \mu_Y X - \mu_X Y + \mu_X\mu_Y]\)$ By linearity: $\(= \mathbb{E}[XY] - \mu_Y\mathbb{E}[X] - \mu_X\mathbb{E}[Y] + \mu_X\mu_Y = \mathbb{E}[XY] - \mu_X\mu_Y\)$

Memorise this: \(\text{Cov}(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}[XY] - \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y]\). It's the analogue of \(\text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2\), which is just \(\text{Cov}(X,X)\).

docs.title: Variance as a Special Case
docs.text:
\[\text{Cov}(X, X) = \mathbb{E}[(X - \mu_X)^2] = \text{Var}(X)\]

So variance is covariance with itself. Every variance identity is a covariance identity in disguise.

docs.title: Properties of Covariance
docs.text:
All of these follow from linearity of expectation. No independence needed unless stated.

Symmetry: $\(\text{Cov}(X, Y) = \text{Cov}(Y, X)\)$

Bilinearity — this is the big one: $\(\text{Cov}(aX + bY, Z) = a,\text{Cov}(X,Z) + b,\text{Cov}(Y,Z)\)$

And in both arguments: $\(\text{Cov}!\left(\sum_i a_i X_i,, \sum_j b_j Y_j\right) = \sum_i \sum_j a_i b_j, \text{Cov}(X_i, Y_j)\)$

Shift invariance: Adding a constant does nothing: $\(\text{Cov}(X + c, Y) = \text{Cov}(X, Y)\)$

because \(\mathbb{E}[X+c] = \mathbb{E}[X] + c\), so the constant cancels in the deviation.

Independence implies zero covariance: $\(X \perp Y \implies \text{Cov}(X,Y) = 0\)$

Proof: If \(X \perp Y\), then \(\mathbb{E}[XY] = \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y]\), so \(\text{Cov}(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}[XY] - \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y] = 0\).

The converse is FALSE. Zero covariance does not imply independence. Classic counterexample: \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\), \(Y = X^2\). Then \(\text{Cov}(X, Y) = \mathbb{E}[X^3] - \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[X^2] = 0 - 0 = 0\), but \(Y\) is completely determined by \(X\). Covariance only detects linear dependence.

docs.title: Variance of a Sum
docs.text:
The payoff of bilinearity. For any \(X, Y\): $\(\text{Var}(X + Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) + 2,\text{Cov}(X, Y)\)$

Proof: $\(\text{Var}(X+Y) = \text{Cov}(X+Y, X+Y) = \text{Cov}(X,X) + 2\text{Cov}(X,Y) + \text{Cov}(Y,Y)\)$

by bilinearity. Done.

For \(n\) variables, in full generality: $\(\text{Var}!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right) = \sum_{i=1}^n \text{Var}(X_i) + 2\sum_{i < j} \text{Cov}(X_i, X_j)\)$

If the \(X_i\) are pairwise uncorrelated (not necessarily independent — just \(\text{Cov}(X_i, X_j) = 0\) for \(i \neq j\)), then: $\(\text{Var}!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right) = \sum_{i=1}^n \text{Var}(X_i)\)$

This is the version that makes the CLT and sampling theory work.

docs.title: The Covariance Matrix
docs.text:
For a random vector \(\mathbf{X} = (X_1, \ldots, X_n)^\top\), the covariance matrix is: $\(\Sigma = \text{Cov}(\mathbf{X}) = \mathbb{E}[(\mathbf{X} - \boldsymbol{\mu})(\mathbf{X} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top]\)$

so \(\Sigma_{ij} = \text{Cov}(X_i, X_j)\) and \(\Sigma_{ii} = \text{Var}(X_i)\).

Key properties:

  • \(\Sigma\) is symmetric: \(\Sigma = \Sigma^\top\).
  • \(\Sigma\) is positive semi-definite: \(\mathbf{v}^\top \Sigma \mathbf{v} \geq 0\) for all \(\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n\).

Why PSD? Because \(\mathbf{v}^\top \Sigma \mathbf{v} = \text{Var}(\mathbf{v}^\top \mathbf{X}) \geq 0\) — variance is always non-negative.

This matrix is central to multivariate normals, PCA, and any multivariate inference.

docs.title: Correlation: Making It Dimensionless
docs.text:
Covariance has units of \((\text{units of } X) \times (\text{units of } Y)\). That makes it incomparable across problems. Fix it by normalising:

\[\text{Corr}(X,Y) = \rho_{XY} = \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\text{Var}(X),\text{Var}(Y)}} = \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\text{SD}(X),\text{SD}(Y)}\]

This is the Pearson correlation coefficient.

docs.title: The Crucial Bound: \(|\rho| \leq 1\)
docs.text:
Theorem. For any \(X, Y\) with finite variances: $\(-1 \leq \text{Corr}(X,Y) \leq 1\)$

Proof via the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. The probabilistic form of Cauchy-Schwarz states: $\((\mathbb{E}[UV])^2 \leq \mathbb{E}[U^2],\mathbb{E}[V^2]\)$

for any random variables \(U, V\). Apply with \(U = X - \mu_X\) and \(V = Y - \mu_Y\): $\(\text{Cov}(X,Y)^2 = (\mathbb{E}[UV])^2 \leq \mathbb{E}[U^2],\mathbb{E}[V^2] = \text{Var}(X),\text{Var}(Y)\)$

Divide both sides by \(\text{Var}(X),\text{Var}(Y)\): $\(\rho^2 \leq 1 \implies |\rho| \leq 1 \qquad \square\)$

When is \(|\rho| = 1\)? Cauchy-Schwarz is tight iff \(U = cV\) for some constant \(c\), i.e. \(X - \mu_X = c(Y - \mu_Y)\), i.e. \(X\) and \(Y\) are in an exact affine relationship \(X = aY + b\). Correlation \(\pm 1\) means perfectly linearly dependent.

Alternative proof via variance: Consider \(Z = \frac{X}{\sigma_X} \pm \frac{Y}{\sigma_Y}\). Then \(\text{Var}(Z) \geq 0\), expanding gives \(2 \pm 2\rho \geq 0\), so \(\rho \leq 1\) and \(\rho \geq -1\). Clean and self-contained.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
\(\rho\) Meaning \(+1\) Perfect positive linear relationship \((0, 1)\) Positive association (above average together) \(0\) No linear relationship (may still be dependent) \((-1, 0)\) Negative association \(-1\) Perfect negative linear relationship

What \(\rho\) does not capture:

  • Non-linear dependence (\(Y = X^2\) can have \(\rho = 0\))
  • The slope of the relationship (that's regression — \(\rho\) is scale-free)
  • Causation (obviously)

docs.title: Alternative Proof of the Bound: Completing the Square
docs.text:
This one is slick and elementary — no Cauchy-Schwarz needed.

For any \(t \in \mathbb{R}\), define \(Z = tX + Y\). Since variance is non-negative: $\(0 \leq \text{Var}(Z) = t^2\text{Var}(X) + 2t,\text{Cov}(X,Y) + \text{Var}(Y)\)$

This is a quadratic in \(t\) that is always \(\geq 0\), so its discriminant must be \(\leq 0\): $\(\Delta = 4,\text{Cov}(X,Y)^2 - 4,\text{Var}(X),\text{Var}(Y) \leq 0\)$ $\(\implies \text{Cov}(X,Y)^2 \leq \text{Var}(X),\text{Var}(Y) \implies |\rho| \leq 1\)$

I love this proof. It's pure algebra once you remember that variance \(\geq 0\). No linear algebra needed, no inner product spaces. Just: a quadratic in \(t\) that's always non-negative has non-positive discriminant.

docs.title: Connection to Regression
docs.text:
The slope in simple linear regression of \(Y\) on \(X\) is: $\(\hat{\beta} = \frac{\text{Cov}(X,Y)}{\text{Var}(X)}\)$

And correlation satisfies: $\(\rho = \hat{\beta} \cdot \frac{\text{SD}(X)}{\text{SD}(Y)}\)$

So \(\rho\) is the regression slope after standardising both variables to have unit variance. This is why \(\rho\) is scale-free and \(\hat{\beta}\) is not.

docs.title: Key Identities to Have Memorised
docs.text:
\[\text{Cov}(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}[XY] - \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y]$$ $$\text{Var}(X \pm Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) \pm 2,\text{Cov}(X,Y)$$ $$\text{Cov}(aX, bY) = ab,\text{Cov}(X,Y)$$ $$\rho(X,Y) = \rho!\left(\frac{X - \mu_X}{\sigma_X},, \frac{Y - \mu_Y}{\sigma_Y}\right)\]

The last one says: correlation is just the covariance of the standardised variables.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability — Ch. 7 (Joint distributions, covariance, correlation)
  2. Harvard Stat 110 — Lectures on covariance, Cauchy-Schwarz, and the correlation bound
  3. The "discriminant proof" of \(|\rho| \leq 1\) is my preferred elementary proof — cleaner than invoking Cauchy-Schwarz for students who haven't seen it.

The thing to keep straight: covariance is bilinear and symmetric — it's an inner product on the space of zero-mean finite-variance random variables. Correlation normalises it to live in \([-1,1]\). That's the whole story.

docs.title: Variance of Hypergeometric
docs.text: This is the computation I come back to whenever I need a reminder that indicator r.v.'s + covariance is the right tool. The variance formula has that haunting factor \((N-n)/(N-1)\) — the finite population correction — and deriving it cleanly via covariance of indicators is the only proof worth knowing.

docs.title: The Setup
docs.text:
You have an urn with \(N\) balls: \(K\) are white (successes), \(N-K\) are black (failures). Draw \(n\) balls without replacement. Let: $\(X = \text{number of white balls drawn}\)$

We want \(\text{Var}(X)\).

Indicator decomposition — the move that makes everything tractable: $\(X = X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_n, \qquad X_i = \mathbf{1}[\text{ball } i \text{ is white}]\)$

where "ball \(i\)" means the \(i\)-th ball drawn.

docs.title: Mean (Warm-Up)
docs.text:
By symmetry, every draw is equally likely to be any of the \(N\) balls, so: $\(\mathbb{E}[X_i] = \mathbb{P}(\text{draw } i \text{ is white}) = \frac{K}{N}\)$

By linearity: $\(\mathbb{E}[X] = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbb{E}[X_i] = n \cdot \frac{K}{N} = \frac{nK}{N}\)$

This is the expected number of white balls. Intuition: if you draw \(n\) from \(N\) balls of which \(K\) are white, you'd expect fraction \(K/N\) to be white. Perfect.

docs.title: Variance: The Covariance Decomposition
docs.text:
Since \(X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\), the variance formula for a sum gives:

\[\text{Var}(X) = \sum_{i=1}^n \text{Var}(X_i) + 2\sum_{i < j} \text{Cov}(X_i, X_j)\]

There are \(n\) diagonal terms and \(\binom{n}{2}\) off-diagonal covariance terms. By symmetry, all diagonal terms are equal and all off-diagonal terms are equal. So:

\[\text{Var}(X) = n,\text{Var}(X_1) + n(n-1),\text{Cov}(X_1, X_2)\]

(The factor \(2\binom{n}{2} = n(n-1)\) accounts for all ordered pairs \(i \neq j\), each contributing \(\text{Cov}(X_i, X_j)\) once.)

Now compute each piece.

docs.title: Computing \(\text{Var}(X_1)\)
docs.text: \(X_1 \sim \text{Bernoulli}(K/N)\), so: $\(\text{Var}(X_1) = \frac{K}{N}\left(1 - \frac{K}{N}\right) = \frac{K(N-K)}{N^2}\)$

docs.title: Computing \(\text{Cov}(X_1, X_2)\)
docs.text:
Use the computational formula: $\(\text{Cov}(X_1, X_2) = \mathbb{E}[X_1 X_2] - \mathbb{E}[X_1]\mathbb{E}[X_2]\)$

\(\mathbb{E}[X_1]\mathbb{E}[X_2]\): Both equal \(K/N\), so this is \(K^2/N^2\).

\(\mathbb{E}[X_1 X_2]\): Since \(X_1, X_2\) are indicators, \(X_1 X_2 = 1\) iff both draws are white: $\(\mathbb{E}[X_1 X_2] = \mathbb{P}(X_1 = 1 \text{ and } X_2 = 1)\)$

\[= \mathbb{P}(\text{draw 1 is white}) \cdot \mathbb{P}(\text{draw 2 is white} \mid \text{draw 1 is white})\] \[= \frac{K}{N} \cdot \frac{K-1}{N-1}\]

This is where without replacement bites: after drawing one white ball, there are \(K-1\) white balls left among \(N-1\) remaining.

Therefore: $\(\text{Cov}(X_1, X_2) = \frac{K}{N} \cdot \frac{K-1}{N-1} - \frac{K}{N} \cdot \frac{K}{N}\)$

\[= \frac{K}{N}\left(\frac{K-1}{N-1} - \frac{K}{N}\right)\] \[= \frac{K}{N} \cdot \frac{N(K-1) - K(N-1)}{N(N-1)}\]

Expand the numerator: $\(N(K-1) - K(N-1) = NK - N - KN + K = K - N = -(N-K)\)$

So: $\(\text{Cov}(X_1, X_2) = \frac{K}{N} \cdot \frac{-(N-K)}{N(N-1)} = -\frac{K(N-K)}{N^2(N-1)}\)$

The covariance is negative. This makes sense — drawing without replacement means seeing a white ball makes seeing another white ball slightly less likely. The balls are competing for the white "slots."

docs.title: Assembling the Variance
docs.text:
\[\text{Var}(X) = n \cdot \frac{K(N-K)}{N^2} + n(n-1) \cdot \left(-\frac{K(N-K)}{N^2(N-1)}\right)\]

Factor out \(\frac{nK(N-K)}{N^2}\):

\[= \frac{nK(N-K)}{N^2}\left(1 - \frac{n-1}{N-1}\right)\]

Simplify the bracket: $\(1 - \frac{n-1}{N-1} = \frac{N-1 - (n-1)}{N-1} = \frac{N-n}{N-1}\)$

Therefore:

\[\boxed{\text{Var}(X) = n \cdot \frac{K}{N} \cdot \frac{N-K}{N} \cdot \frac{N-n}{N-1}}\]

docs.title: The Finite Population Correction Factor
docs.text:
Write \(p = K/N\) (the proportion of white balls). Then:

\[\text{Var}(X) = np(1-p) \cdot \underbrace{\frac{N-n}{N-1}}_{\text{FPC}}\]

Compare to the Binomial\((n,p)\) variance: \(\text{Var}(X_{\text{bin}}) = np(1-p)\).

The hypergeometric variance is the binomial variance times the finite population correction (FPC): $\(\text{FPC} = \frac{N-n}{N-1} \in [0, 1]\)$

The FPC is always \(\leq 1\), so the hypergeometric variance is always less than or equal to the binomial variance. This is the mathematical expression of a fundamental truth:

Drawing without replacement reduces variance. Once you've seen some of the population, there's less uncertainty about the rest. Information accumulates faster without replacement.

Boundary cases:

  • \(n = 1\): FPC \(= 1\). A single draw is identical to Bernoulli sampling — with or without replacement makes no difference.
  • \(n = N\): FPC \(= 0\). You've drawn everyone. \(X = K\) with certainty. No randomness, zero variance. Correct.
  • \(N \to \infty\) with \(p = K/N\) fixed: FPC \(\to 1\). Sampling without replacement from a huge population is essentially the same as with replacement. Hypergeometric \(\to\) Binomial.

docs.title: Why Indicators + Covariance Is the Right Framework
docs.text:
You could also compute \(\text{Var}(X)\) directly from the PMF: $\(\mathbb{P}(X = k) = \frac{\binom{K}{k}\binom{N-K}{n-k}}{\binom{N}{n}}\)$

and grind through \(\mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2\) using combinatorial identities. It works, but it's brutal and opaque.

The indicator approach:

  1. Reduces everything to \(\text{Var}(X_i)\) and \(\text{Cov}(X_i, X_j)\) — two small, interpretable calculations.
  2. Makes the negative covariance visible — you see why without-replacement decreases variance.
  3. Generalises immediately. The same framework handles the variance of the number of matches in a random permutation, birthday coincidences, or any "sampling without replacement" problem.

The moral: whenever you have \(X = \sum X_i\) with indicator \(X_i\)'s, go straight to the covariance decomposition. The PMF is for computing probabilities. Indicators are for computing expectations and variances.

docs.title: Summary of the Key Numbers
docs.text:
Quantity Value \(\mathbb{E}[X_i]\) \(K/N\) \(\text{Var}(X_i)\) \(K(N-K)/N^2\) \(\text{Cov}(X_i, X_j)\), \(i \neq j\) \(-K(N-K)/[N^2(N-1)]\) \(\mathbb{E}[X]\) \(nK/N\) \(\text{Var}(X)\) \(np(1-p)(N-n)/(N-1)\)

Note that \(\text{Cov}(X_i, X_j) = -\text{Var}(X_i)/(N-1)\). This ratio is exact and beautiful — the covariance between any two indicators is exactly \(-1/(N-1)\) times the variance of each indicator. It falls out of the algebra but also has a direct combinatorial explanation.

docs.title: The \(-1/(N-1)\) Ratio, Explained
docs.text:
\[\frac{\text{Cov}(X_i, X_j)}{\text{Var}(X_i)} = \frac{-K(N-K)/[N^2(N-1)]}{K(N-K)/N^2} = -\frac{1}{N-1}\]

Why \(-1/(N-1)\)? Because the \(N\) indicators \(Y_1, \ldots, Y_N\) for the entire population (whether each ball is white) sum to exactly \(K\), a constant. So \(\text{Var}(\sum_{i=1}^N Y_i) = 0\), which forces:

\[N,\text{Var}(Y_1) + N(N-1),\text{Cov}(Y_1, Y_2) = 0\] \[\implies \text{Cov}(Y_1, Y_2) = -\frac{\text{Var}(Y_1)}{N-1}\]

The constraint that the population total is fixed forces all pairwise covariances to be exactly \(-\text{Var}/(N-1)\). This is the deep reason the FPC takes the form it does.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability — Ch. 4 (Hypergeometric), Ch. 7 (Covariance)
  2. Harvard Stat 110 — the indicator/covariance derivation of hypergeometric variance is done explicitly in lecture
  3. The \(-1/(N-1)\) constraint argument is the kind of thing Blitzstein would call a "story proof" — structural, not computational.

Every time I see the FPC I think: this is the reward for using covariance correctly. The formula \(np(1-p)(N-n)/(N-1)\) isn't magic — it's exactly what falls out when negative pairwise covariances partially cancel the diagonal variance terms. The structure of sampling without replacement is entirely encoded in that one negative covariance.

docs.title: Multinomial Distribution
docs.text: The multinomial is the natural generalisation of the binomial — instead of two outcomes per trial, you have \(k\) outcomes. Almost everything you know about the binomial lifts here, but the covariance structure is new and worth sitting with. The negative covariance between categories is not a coincidence — it's the same FPC story from hypergeometric, but now it's the constraint that all counts sum to \(n\).

docs.title: The Setup
docs.text:
\(n\) independent trials. Each trial results in exactly one of \(k\) categories, with probabilities: $\(p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_k, \qquad p_i > 0, \quad \sum_{i=1}^k p_i = 1\)$

Let \(X_i\) = number of trials falling in category \(i\). Then \((X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_k)\) follows the Multinomial\((n, p_1, \ldots, p_k)\) distribution.

Constraints baked in from the start: $\(X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_k = n \qquad \text{(always, with probability 1)}\)$ $\(X_i \in {0, 1, \ldots, n} \quad \text{for each } i\)$

The binomial is the special case \(k = 2\).

docs.title: The Joint PMF
docs.text:
\[\mathbb{P}(X_1 = n_1, X_2 = n_2, \ldots, X_k = n_k) = \frac{n!}{n_1!, n_2!, \cdots, n_k!}, p_1^{n_1} p_2^{n_2} \cdots p_k^{n_k}\]

for non-negative integers \(n_1, \ldots, n_k\) summing to \(n\).

Where this comes from. The multinomial coefficient \(\frac{n!}{n_1! \cdots n_k!}\) counts the number of ways to arrange \(n\) trials so that exactly \(n_i\) land in category \(i\) — it's the number of distinct orderings of a sequence with \(n_i\) copies of symbol \(i\). Each such ordering has probability \(p_1^{n_1} \cdots p_k^{n_k}\) (by independence). Multiply and you're done.

Sanity check: Sum over all valid \((n_1, \ldots, n_k)\): $\(\sum_{\substack{n_1+\cdots+n_k=n \ n_i \geq 0}} \frac{n!}{n_1!\cdots n_k!} p_1^{n_1}\cdots p_k^{n_k} = (p_1 + \cdots + p_k)^n = 1^n = 1\)$

by the multinomial theorem. The PMF is indeed a valid probability distribution.

docs.title: Marginals: Each \(X_i\) is Binomial
docs.text:
Theorem. \(X_i \sim \text{Binomial}(n, p_i)\).

Proof. Lump all categories except \(i\) into one "failure" category with probability \(1 - p_i\). Each trial is now a Bernoulli\((p_i)\). With \(n\) independent trials, \(X_i \sim \text{Bin}(n, p_i)\). \(\square\)

Formally: marginalise the joint PMF by summing over all valid \((n_1, \ldots, n_{i-1}, n_{i+1}, \ldots, n_k)\) given \(n_i = m\). What remains is \(\binom{n}{m} p_i^m (1-p_i)^{n-m}\). But the lumping argument is cleaner.

This immediately gives: $\(\mathbb{E}[X_i] = np_i, \qquad \text{Var}(X_i) = np_i(1-p_i)\)$

docs.title: Covariance Between Categories
docs.text:
For \(i eq j\): $\( ext{Cov}(X_i, X_j) = -np_ip_j\)$

Proof. Write each \(X_i = \sum_{\ell=1}^n \mathbf{1}[ ext{trial } \ell \in ext{category } i]\). Call these indicator r.v.'s \(I_{i\ell}\).

\[ ext{Cov}(X_i, X_j) = ext{Cov}!\left(\sum_\ell I_{i\ell},, \sum_\ell I_{j\ell} ight) = \sum_{\ell,m} ext{Cov}(I_{i\ell}, I_{jm})\]

Cross-trial terms (\(\ell eq m\)): Trials are independent, so \(I_{i\ell} \perp I_{jm}\), giving \( ext{Cov}(I_{i\ell}, I_{jm}) = 0\).

Same-trial terms (\(\ell = m\)): \(I_{i\ell}\) and \(I_{j\ell}\) are indicators for the same trial landing in categories \(i\) and \(j\) respectively. Since a trial can't be in both categories simultaneously: $\(\mathbb{P}(I_{i\ell} = 1,, I_{j\ell} = 1) = 0\)$

So \(\mathbb{E}[I_{i\ell} I_{j\ell}] = 0\), and: $\( ext{Cov}(I_{i\ell}, I_{j\ell}) = \mathbb{E}[I_{i\ell}I_{j\ell}] - \mathbb{E}[I_{i\ell}]\mathbb{E}[I_{j\ell}] = 0 - p_ip_j = -p_ip_j\)$

There are \(n\) same-trial terms, so: $\( ext{Cov}(X_i, X_j) = n \cdot (-p_ip_j) = -np_ip_j \qquad \square\)$

The covariance is negative for every pair \(i eq j\). The intuition is exactly the same as in the hypergeometric: the counts are competing. If more trials land in category \(i\), there are fewer left to land in category \(j\). The constraint \(\sum X_i = n\) forces this negative dependence. There is no way to have positive covariance between two categories in a multinomial.

docs.title: The Covariance Matrix
docs.text:
The full covariance matrix \(\Sigma\) of \((X_1, \ldots, X_k)\) has entries:

\[\Sigma_{ij} = \begin{cases} np_i(1-p_i) & i = j \ -np_ip_j & i \neq j \end{cases}\]

In matrix form, letting \(\mathbf{p} = (p_1, \ldots, p_k)^\top\): $\(\Sigma = n\left(\text{diag}(\mathbf{p}) - \mathbf{p}\mathbf{p}^\top\right)\)$

where \(\text{diag}(\mathbf{p})\) is the diagonal matrix with \(p_i\) on the diagonal.

This matrix is positive semi-definite but singular. Singular because \(\mathbf{1}^\top \mathbf{X} = n\) always — there's a linear constraint baked into the distribution. Any vector proportional to \(\mathbf{1} = (1,1,\ldots,1)^\top\) is in the null space of \(\Sigma\): $\(\Sigma \mathbf{1} = n(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}\mathbf{p}^\top\mathbf{1}) = n(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}) = \mathbf{0}\)$

So \(\Sigma\) has rank at most \(k-1\). The multinomial distribution is essentially \((k-1)\)-dimensional — once you know \(n_1, \ldots, n_{k-1}\), the last count \(n_k = n - \sum_{i<k} n_i\) is determined.

docs.title: The Constraint Forces Negative Covariance: A Formal Argument
docs.text:
Here's the clean argument that ties everything together. Since \(\sum_{j=1}^k X_j = n\) (constant), \(\text{Var}(\sum_j X_j) = 0\). Expand:

\[0 = \text{Var}!\left(\sum_{j=1}^k X_j\right) = \sum_{j=1}^k \text{Var}(X_j) + 2\sum_{i < j} \text{Cov}(X_i, X_j)\] \[= n\sum_{j=1}^k p_j(1-p_j) + 2\sum_{i<j}\text{Cov}(X_i, X_j)\]

We can verify our covariance formula by checking that it satisfies this:

\[2\sum_{i<j}(-np_ip_j) = -n\sum_{i \neq j} p_ip_j = -n\left[\left(\sum_i p_i\right)^2 - \sum_i p_i^2\right] = -n(1 - \sum_i p_i^2)\]

And:

\[n\sum_j p_j(1-p_j) = n\sum_j p_j - n\sum_j p_j^2 = n - n\sum_j p_j^2\]

Sum:

\[(n - n\sum p_j^2) + (-n + n\sum p_j^2) = 0 \checkmark\]

The constraint \(\sum X_i = n\) is exactly what makes the positive diagonal terms cancel with the negative off-diagonal covariances. The distribution is telling you: these \(k\) random variables are not free — they live in a \((k-1)\)-dimensional simplex.

docs.title: Lumping Property
docs.text:
If you merge categories \(i\) and \(j\) into one super-category with probability \(p_i + p_j\), the result is again multinomial. Formally:

\[(X_1, \ldots, X_{i-1}, X_i + X_j, X_{i+1}, \ldots, \hat{X}_j, \ldots, X_k) \sim \text{Multinomial}(n;, \ldots, p_i+p_j, \ldots)\]

This follows immediately from the definition — independence of trials plus the fact that probabilities sum correctly. It's why marginalising to \(X_i\) gives \(\text{Bin}(n, p_i)\): you've lumped all other categories into one.

docs.title: Conditional Distribution
docs.text:
Given \(X_1 = m\), the remaining counts \((X_2, \ldots, X_k)\) have conditional distribution:

\[(X_2, \ldots, X_k) \mid X_1 = m ;\sim; \text{Multinomial}!\left(n-m;; \frac{p_2}{1-p_1}, \ldots, \frac{p_k}{1-p_1}\right)\]

Proof sketch. Given that \(m\) trials landed in category 1, the remaining \(n - m\) trials are independent with each trial landing in category \(j \geq 2\) with conditional probability \(p_j/(1-p_1)\) (by Bayes and the law of total probability). These renormalised probabilities sum to 1. \(\square\)

This is the multinomial analogue of the memoryless / conditioning argument for the binomial.

docs.title: Connection to Binomial: The \(k=2\) Case
docs.text:
With \(k=2\), \(p_1 = p\), \(p_2 = 1-p = q\), \(X_1 = X\), \(X_2 = n - X\):

Multinomial formula Binomial formula \(\frac{n!}{n_1! n_2!} p^{n_1} q^{n_2}\) \(\binom{n}{k} p^k q^{n-k}\) \(\mathbb{E}[X_1] = np\) \(\mathbb{E}[X] = np\) \(\text{Var}(X_1) = npq\) \(\text{Var}(X) = npq\) \(\text{Cov}(X_1,X_2) = -np \cdot q\) \(\text{Cov}(X, n-X) = -\text{Var}(X) = -npq\)

The covariance check: \(\text{Cov}(X, n-X) = \text{Cov}(X,-X) = -\text{Var}(X) = -npq\). And indeed \(-np_1p_2 = -npq\). Consistent.

docs.title: Summary of Key Facts
docs.text: Quantity Formula PMF \(\frac{n!}{n_1!\cdots n_k!}p_1^{n_1}\cdots p_k^{n_k}\) Marginal \(X_i \sim \text{Bin}(n, p_i)\) \(\mathbb{E}[X_i]\) \(np_i\) \(\text{Var}(X_i)\) \(np_i(1-p_i)\) \(\text{Cov}(X_i, X_j)\), \(i\neq j\) \(-np_ip_j\) Covariance matrix \(n(\text{diag}(\mathbf{p}) - \mathbf{p}\mathbf{p}^\top)\) Rank of \(\Sigma\) \(k - 1\) Sum constraint \(\sum X_i = n\) always

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability — Ch. 7 (Joint distributions, multinomial)
  2. Harvard Stat 110 — Multinomial distribution, covariance structure, lumping
  3. The "constraint forces zero total variance" argument is a recurring theme: hypergeometric FPC, multinomial covariance, and exchangeability all use it. It's worth having as a general tool.

The thing I keep coming back to: the multinomial covariance matrix has a beautifully simple structure — \(n(\text{diag}(\mathbf{p}) - \mathbf{p}\mathbf{p}^\top)\). The outer product \(\mathbf{p}\mathbf{p}^\top\) is what kills the rank by one. Every pair of categories is negatively correlated, and the magnitude is determined entirely by \(p_i p_j\). Nothing else. That's elegant.

docs.title: Multivariate Normal
docs.text: This is the distribution. Everything in classical statistics — regression, PCA, hypothesis testing, Kalman filtering, Gaussian processes — lives here. The multivariate normal is not just "the normal but in higher dimensions." It has geometric structure that the univariate case hides from you. The elliptical level sets, the covariance matrix as a shape operator, the way conditioning collapses a joint into a lower-dimensional normal — all of this is worth understanding at a bone-deep level.

docs.title: Definition: Three Equivalent Ways
docs.text: There are three definitions, each illuminating a different aspect. Know all three.

docs.title: Definition 1 — via the PDF (when \(\Sigma\) is invertible)
docs.text:
A random vector \(\mathbf{X} = (X_1, \ldots, X_k)^\top\) has the Multivariate Normal distribution \(\mathcal{N}_k(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \Sigma)\) if its joint PDF is:

\[f(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{k/2}|\Sigma|^{1/2}} \exp!\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right)\]

where \(\boldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^k\) is the mean vector and \(\Sigma\) is a \(k \times k\) positive definite covariance matrix.

The exponent \((\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\) is the Mahalanobis distance squared from \(\mathbf{x}\) to \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\). It is a quadratic form in \(\mathbf{x}\), so the level sets \(f(\mathbf{x}) = c\) are ellipsoids centred at \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\), with axes determined by the eigenvectors of \(\Sigma\) and half-lengths proportional to the square roots of the eigenvalues.

docs.title: Definition 2 — via Linear Transformations (the constructive definition)
docs.text:
\(\mathbf{X} \sim \mathcal{N}_k(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \Sigma)\) if and only if: $\(\mathbf{X} = A\mathbf{Z} + \boldsymbol{\mu}\)$ where \(\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, \ldots, Z_m)^\top\) with \(Z_i \overset{i.i.d.}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,1)\), and \(A\) is a \(k \times m\) matrix satisfying \(AA^\top = \Sigma\).

Such an \(A\) always exists (e.g. the Cholesky factor of \(\Sigma\), or \(A = U\Lambda^{1/2}\) from the spectral decomposition \(\Sigma = U\Lambda U^\top\)). This definition works even when \(\Sigma\) is singular — the distribution is still well-defined, it just doesn't have a density with respect to Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb{R}^k\).

This is the definition that makes simulating multivariate normals trivial: generate i.i.d. standard normals, multiply by the Cholesky factor of \(\Sigma\), shift by \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\). Done.

docs.title: Definition 3 — via Univariate Marginals (the characterisation)
docs.text:
\(\mathbf{X}\) is multivariate normal if and only if every linear combination \(\mathbf{a}^\top \mathbf{X} = a_1 X_1 + \cdots + a_k X_k\) is (univariate) normal, for every \(\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^k\).

This is the most useful characterisation for proofs. To show something is MVN, show all its linear projections are normal. To disprove MVN, find one linear combination that isn't.

Warning. The converse of the marginal statement is FALSE: each \(X_i\) being marginally normal does NOT imply \(\mathbf{X}\) is jointly multivariate normal. There exist bivariate distributions with both marginals \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) that are not bivariate normal. Always need to check the joint structure.

docs.title: Mean and Covariance
docs.text:
\[\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}] = \boldsymbol{\mu}, \qquad \text{Cov}(\mathbf{X}) = \Sigma\]

Proof via Definition 2. \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{X}] = A\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{Z}] + \boldsymbol{\mu} = \boldsymbol{\mu}\). For the covariance: $\(\text{Cov}(\mathbf{X}) = \text{Cov}(A\mathbf{Z} + \boldsymbol{\mu}) = A,\text{Cov}(\mathbf{Z}),A^\top = A I_m A^\top = AA^\top = \Sigma\)$

where we used that \(Z_i\) are i.i.d. \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\), so \(\text{Cov}(\mathbf{Z}) = I_m\).

docs.title: Linear Transformations Close Under MVN
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(\mathbf{X} \sim \mathcal{N}_k(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \Sigma)\) and \(B\) is an \(m \times k\) matrix, \(\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^m\), then: $\(B\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{c} \sim \mathcal{N}_m(B\boldsymbol{\mu} + \mathbf{c},; B\Sigma B^\top)\)$

Proof. Write \(\mathbf{X} = A\mathbf{Z} + \boldsymbol{\mu}\). Then \(B\mathbf{X} + \mathbf{c} = BA\mathbf{Z} + (B\boldsymbol{\mu} + \mathbf{c})\), which has the form of Definition 2 with matrix \(BA\) and mean \(B\boldsymbol{\mu} + \mathbf{c}\). Covariance: \((BA)(BA)^\top = BAA^\top B^\top = B\Sigma B^\top\). \(\square\)

This is the property that makes the multivariate normal so powerful: any affine image of an MVN is MVN. Marginals, sums, projections — all normal.

Marginals: Taking \(B = e_i^\top\) (the \(i\)-th standard basis row vector) gives \(X_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_i, \Sigma_{ii})\).

Sums: \(\sum_i a_i X_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{a}^\top\boldsymbol{\mu},; \mathbf{a}^\top\Sigma\mathbf{a})\). (This is Definition 3, now as a theorem.)

docs.title: The Key Theorem: Zero Covariance \(\Leftrightarrow\) Independence
docs.text:
For jointly normal random variables, uncorrelatedness is equivalent to independence: $\(\mathbf{X}_1 \perp \mathbf{X}_2 \iff \text{Cov}(\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2) = 0\)$

Proof (\(\Rightarrow\)): Independence always implies zero covariance.

Proof (\(\Leftarrow\)): Partition \(\mathbf{X} = (\mathbf{X}_1^\top, \mathbf{X}_2^\top)^\top\) with \(\text{Cov}(\mathbf{X}_1, \mathbf{X}_2) = 0\). The joint PDF factors:

\[f(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2) \propto \exp!\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\right)\]

When \(\text{Cov}(\mathbf{X}_1,\mathbf{X}_2) = 0\), the covariance matrix is block-diagonal: $\(\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix}\Sigma_{11} & 0 \ 0 & \Sigma_{22}\end{pmatrix}, \quad \Sigma^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}\Sigma_{11}^{-1} & 0 \ 0 & \Sigma_{22}^{-1}\end{pmatrix}\)$

The exponent splits: $\((\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu}) = (\mathbf{x}_1-\boldsymbol{\mu}_1)^\top\Sigma_{11}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_1-\boldsymbol{\mu}_1) + (\mathbf{x}_2-\boldsymbol{\mu}_2)^\top\Sigma_{22}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_2-\boldsymbol{\mu}_2)\)$

So \(f(\mathbf{x}_1,\mathbf{x}_2) = f_1(\mathbf{x}_1)\cdot f_2(\mathbf{x}_2)\). Factoring of the joint density is exactly independence. \(\square\)

This is the one property of the multivariate normal that has no analogue in general. For arbitrary distributions, you can have zero covariance with strong dependence. In the Gaussian world, covariance structure IS the dependence structure — completely.

docs.title: Conditional Distribution
docs.text:
This is where MVN gets truly beautiful. Partition: $\(\mathbf{X} = \begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{X}_1 \ \mathbf{X}_2\end{pmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N}!\left(\begin{pmatrix}\boldsymbol{\mu}_1 \ \boldsymbol{\mu}_2\end{pmatrix},; \begin{pmatrix}\Sigma_{11} & \Sigma_{12} \ \Sigma_{21} & \Sigma_{22}\end{pmatrix}\right)\)$

where \(\mathbf{X}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^p\), \(\mathbf{X}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^q\).

Theorem (Conditional distribution). Assuming \(\Sigma_{22}\) is invertible: $\(\mathbf{X}_1 \mid \mathbf{X}_2 = \mathbf{x}_2 ;\sim; \mathcal{N}!\left(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{1|2},; \Sigma_{1|2}\right)\)$

where: $\(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{1|2} = \boldsymbol{\mu}_1 + \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_2 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_2)\)$ $\(\Sigma_{1|2} = \Sigma_{11} - \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}\Sigma_{21}\)$

Proof sketch. Write \(\mathbf{X}_1 = \boldsymbol{\mu}_1 + \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}(\mathbf{X}_2 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_2) + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\) where \(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} = \mathbf{X}_1 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_1 - \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}(\mathbf{X}_2 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_2)\). One can verify \(\text{Cov}(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}, \mathbf{X}_2) = 0\) (direct calculation), so by the key theorem, \(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon} \perp \mathbf{X}_2\). Given \(\mathbf{X}_2 = \mathbf{x}_2\), the expression for \(\mathbf{X}_1\) reduces to a fixed affine shift of \(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\), which is normal with mean \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{1|2}\) and covariance \(\Sigma_{1|2}\). \(\square\)

docs.title: Reading the Formulas
docs.text:
Conditional mean: \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{1|2} = \boldsymbol{\mu}_1 + \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}(\mathbf{x}_2 - \boldsymbol{\mu}_2)\)

This is a linear function of \(\mathbf{x}_2\). The matrix \(\Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}\) is exactly the matrix of regression coefficients when regressing \(\mathbf{X}_1\) on \(\mathbf{X}_2\). Conditioning in a Gaussian is the same thing as linear regression. This is not a coincidence — it is the theorem.

Conditional covariance: \(\Sigma_{1|2} = \Sigma_{11} - \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}\Sigma_{21}\)

This is the Schur complement of \(\Sigma_{22}\) in \(\Sigma\). Two remarkable facts:

  1. \(\Sigma_{1|2}\) does not depend on the observed value \(\mathbf{x}_2\). Conditioning always reduces variance by the same amount, regardless of what we observe. This is a purely Gaussian phenomenon.
  2. \(\Sigma_{1|2} \leq \Sigma_{11}\) (in the PSD sense) — conditioning can only reduce uncertainty. The reduction \(\Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}\Sigma_{21}\) is always PSD.

docs.title: The Geometry: Ellipsoids and Eigenstructure
docs.text:
The PDF's level sets are the ellipsoids: $\({(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}) = c^2}\)$

Spectral decompose \(\Sigma = U\Lambda U^\top\) where \(U\) is orthogonal (eigenvectors) and \(\Lambda = \text{diag}(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_k)\) (eigenvalues, all positive since \(\Sigma \succ 0\)).

In the coordinate system aligned with \(U\), the ellipsoid becomes a sphere rescaled by \(\sqrt{\lambda_i}\) in each direction. The eigenvectors of \(\Sigma\) are the principal axes of the ellipsoid; the eigenvalues determine the half-lengths \(c\sqrt{\lambda_i}\).

  • Large \(\lambda_i\) = high variance in that direction = elongated ellipsoid axis.
  • Small \(\lambda_i\) = low variance in that direction = compressed ellipsoid axis.
  • Equal \(\lambda_i\) = \(\Sigma = \sigma^2 I\) = spherical level sets = i.i.d. normal coordinates.

The Mahalanobis distance \(d_M(\mathbf{x}) = \sqrt{(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})}\) is Euclidean distance after the change of variables \(\tilde{\mathbf{x}} = \Lambda^{-1/2}U^\top(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\) — it whitens the distribution. In whitened coordinates, the MVN is exactly i.i.d. \(\mathcal{N}(0,1)\) and all level sets are spheres.

docs.title: The Moment Generating Function
docs.text:
\[M_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{t}) = \mathbb{E}[e^{\mathbf{t}^\top \mathbf{X}}] = \exp!\left(\boldsymbol{\mu}^\top\mathbf{t} + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{t}^\top\Sigma\mathbf{t}\right)\]

Proof. Reduce to the univariate case: \(\mathbf{t}^\top\mathbf{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{t}^\top\boldsymbol{\mu},, \mathbf{t}^\top\Sigma\mathbf{t})\) by Definition 3, so \(\mathbb{E}[e^{\mathbf{t}^\top\mathbf{X}}]\) is the MGF of a univariate normal evaluated at 1: $\(= \exp!\left(\mathbf{t}^\top\boldsymbol{\mu} + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{t}^\top\Sigma\mathbf{t}\right) \qquad \square\)$

The MGF uniquely characterises the distribution and is the fastest way to identify sums and linear transforms as normal.

docs.title: Bivariate Normal: The Special Case to Visualise
docs.text:
For \(k=2\), \(\boldsymbol{\mu} = (\mu_1, \mu_2)^\top\), \(\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix}\sigma_1^2 & \rho\sigma_1\sigma_2 \ \rho\sigma_1\sigma_2 & \sigma_2^2\end{pmatrix}\):

\[f(x_1,x_2) = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma_1\sigma_2\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}\exp!\left(-\frac{1}{2(1-\rho^2)}\left[\frac{(x_1-\mu_1)^2}{\sigma_1^2} - 2\rho\frac{(x_1-\mu_1)(x_2-\mu_2)}{\sigma_1\sigma_2} + \frac{(x_2-\mu_2)^2}{\sigma_2^2}\right]\right)\]

The conditional distribution \(X_1 \mid X_2 = x_2\): $\(X_1 \mid X_2 = x_2 ;\sim; \mathcal{N}!\left(\mu_1 + \rho\frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_2}(x_2-\mu_2),;; \sigma_1^2(1-\rho^2)\right)\)$

Reading this:

  • Conditional mean shifts by \(\rho\frac{\sigma_1}{\sigma_2}\) per unit deviation of \(x_2\) from \(\mu_2\). This is the regression coefficient.
  • Conditional variance is \(\sigma_1^2(1-\rho^2)\) — reduced from \(\sigma_1^2\) by factor \((1-\rho^2)\). At \(\rho = \pm 1\): zero conditional variance (exact linear relationship). At \(\rho = 0\): no reduction (\(X_1 \perp X_2\)).

docs.title: Summary of Key Properties
docs.text: Property Statement Closure under linear maps \(B\mathbf{X}+\mathbf{c} \sim \mathcal{N}(B\boldsymbol{\mu}+\mathbf{c}, B\Sigma B^\top)\) Marginals \(X_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_i, \Sigma_{ii})\) Uncorrelated \(\Leftrightarrow\) independent Only for jointly normal r.v.'s Conditional distribution Normal, mean linear in conditioning value Conditional variance Constant (doesn't depend on observed value) Level sets Ellipsoids aligned with eigenvectors of \(\Sigma\) MGF \(\exp(\boldsymbol{\mu}^\top\mathbf{t} + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{t}^\top\Sigma\mathbf{t})\)

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability — Ch. 7 (multivariate normal, conditional distributions)
  2. Harvard Stat 110 — BVN conditional distribution, the zero-covariance independence theorem
  3. Anderson, An Introduction to Multivariate Statistical Analysis — for the full conditional/marginal theory
  4. The Schur complement \(\Sigma_{11} - \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}\Sigma_{21}\) appears everywhere: block matrix inversion, partial correlations, Gaussian elimination. Worth having a note on it separately.

What I find most striking: the conditional covariance \(\Sigma_{1|2} = \Sigma_{11} - \Sigma_{12}\Sigma_{22}^{-1}\Sigma_{21}\) is the same for every value of \(\mathbf{x}_2\). In a non-Gaussian distribution, variance could depend on what you condition on. In a Gaussian, it never does. The uncertainty remaining after observation is fixed by the covariance structure alone — observation tells you where you are, but the shape of your residual uncertainty is predetermined.

docs.title: Independence of Sample Mean and Variance
docs.text:
Core Theorem: If \(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n \overset{iid}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\), then the sample mean \(\bar{X}_n\) and the sample variance \(S^2_n\) are independent.

This is a striking and non-obvious fact — \(\bar{X}\) and \(S^2\) are both computed from the same data, yet they carry zero information about each other. This independence is what underpins all of classical inference: t-tests, F-tests, confidence intervals.

Uniqueness Warning: This independence is special to the normal distribution. For non-normal populations, \(\bar{X}\) and \(S^2\) are generally not independent.

docs.title: Sample Mean
docs.text: \[\bar{X}_n = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\]

docs.title: Sample Variance (unbiased)
docs.text:
\[S^2_n = \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X}_n)^2\]

Why \(n-1\)? Using \(n-1\) (Bessel's correction) makes \(S^2\) an unbiased estimator of \(\sigma^2\): $\(\mathbb{E}[S^2] = \sigma^2\)$

Intuition: We lose one degree of freedom because \(S^2\) is computed relative to \(\bar{X}\), which itself was estimated from the data.

docs.title: The Theorem (Fisher, 1925)
docs.text:
Theorem (Independence of \(\bar{X}\) and \(S^2\)): Let \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \overset{iid}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\). Then:

  1. \(\bar{X}_n \sim \mathcal{N}!\left(\mu,, \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)\)
  2. \(\dfrac{(n-1)S^2_n}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-1}\)
  3. \(\bar{X}_n \perp!!!\perp S^2_n\)

All three conclusions hold jointly.

docs.title: Approach 1: Orthogonal Decomposition (Geometric / Most Elegant)
docs.text:
Key Idea: Decompose the data vector into two orthogonal components — one capturing the mean, one capturing the deviations.

Define the data vector \(\mathbf{X} = (X_1, \ldots, X_n)^T \in \mathbb{R}^n\).

Step 1 — Decompose the sum of squares: $\(\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \mu)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})^2 + n(\bar{X} - \mu)^2\)$

This is a Pythagorean decomposition in \(\mathbb{R}^n\):

  • The vector \((\bar{X}, \ldots, \bar{X})\) lies in the 1-dimensional subspace \(V_1 = \text{span}{\mathbf{1}}\)
  • The residual vector \((X_1 - \bar{X}, \ldots, X_n - \bar{X})\) lies in \(V_1^\perp\) (the \((n-1)\)-dimensional orthogonal complement)

Step 2 — Use rotational invariance of the normal: Since \(X_i \overset{iid}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\), the standardized vector \(\mathbf{Z} = (X_i - \mu)/\sigma\) is spherically symmetric. Any orthogonal rotation of \(\mathbf{Z}\) preserves the joint distribution.

Step 3 — Independence follows from orthogonality: \(\bar{X}\) is the projection of \(\mathbf{X}\) onto \(V_1\). \(S^2\) depends only on the projection onto \(V_1^\perp\). Since these subspaces are orthogonal and the distribution is rotationally symmetric (i.e., normal), the two projections are independent.

\[\boxed{\bar{X} \perp!!!\perp (X_1 - \bar{X}, \ldots, X_n - \bar{X})}\]

Since \(S^2\) is a function of only the residuals, independence follows.

docs.title: Approach 2: MGF / Direct Calculation
docs.text:
Step 1 — Rewrite \(X_i = \bar{X} + (X_i - \bar{X})\).

Step 2 — Show the cross term vanishes: $\(\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X}) = 0 \quad \text{(always, by definition of } \bar{X}\text{)}\)$

Step 3 — Joint MGF factorizes: For any linear combination \(a\bar{X} + b S^2\), if the joint MGF factors as \(M_{\bar{X}}(a) \cdot M_{S^2}(b)\), then \(\bar{X} \perp!!!\perp S^2\).

This works because for normal RVs, uncorrelated \(\Rightarrow\) independent (a property unique to the multivariate normal).

Key calculation: $\(\text{Cov}(\bar{X},, X_j - \bar{X}) = \text{Cov}!\left(\bar{X}, X_j\right) - \text{Var}(\bar{X}) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n} - \frac{\sigma^2}{n} = 0\)$

Since all \((X_j - \bar{X})\) are uncorrelated with \(\bar{X}\), and all are jointly normal, they are independent of \(\bar{X}\).

docs.title: Approach 3: Cochran's Theorem (Most General)
docs.text:
Cochran's Theorem: If \(\mathbf{Z} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, I_n)\) and \(|\mathbf{Z}|^2 = Q_1 + Q_2 + \cdots + Q_k\) where each \(Q_i\) is a quadratic form with rank \(r_i\), and \(\sum r_i = n\), then:

  • Each \(Q_i \sim \chi^2_{r_i}\)
  • \(Q_1, Q_2, \ldots, Q_k\) are mutually independent

Application: $\(\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^2 = n\bar{Z}^2 + \sum_{i=1}^n(Z_i - \bar{Z})^2\)$

where \(Z_i = (X_i - \mu)/\sigma\). The first term has rank 1, the second has rank \(n-1\), and \(1 + (n-1) = n\). By Cochran:

  • \(n\bar{Z}^2 \sim \chi^2_1\) (equivalently, \(\sqrt{n}\bar{Z} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\))
  • \(\sum(Z_i - \bar{Z})^2 \sim \chi^2_{n-1}\), which is \(\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\)
  • They are independent ✓

docs.title: The Chi-Squared Connection
docs.text:
The statement \(\dfrac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-1}\) deserves its own unpacking.

Definition: \(\chi^2_k = \sum_{i=1}^k Z_i^2\) where \(Z_i \overset{iid}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0,1)\).

Why \(n-1\) degrees of freedom? The \(n\) residuals \((X_i - \bar{X})\) satisfy the one linear constraint \(\sum(X_i - \bar{X}) = 0\), so they have only \(n-1\) free dimensions. Equivalently, estimating \(\mu\) by \(\bar{X}\) "uses up" 1 degree of freedom.

Source Distribution df \(\bar{X}\) (mean) \(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2/n)\) 1 \(S^2\) (variance) \(\chi^2_{n-1}\) (scaled) \(n-1\) Total \(\chi^2_n\) (scaled) \(n\)

docs.title: Why This Matters: The t-Distribution
docs.text:
The independence theorem is the exact reason the Student's t-statistic works.

\[T = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{S / \sqrt{n}}\]

Step 1: The numerator \(Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\).

Step 2: \(V = \frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2} \sim \chi^2_{n-1}\).

Step 3: \(Z \perp!!!\perp V\) (by the independence theorem).

Definition of t-distribution: \(T = \dfrac{Z}{\sqrt{V/(n-1)}}\) where \(Z \perp!!!\perp V\), \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\), \(V \sim \chi^2_{n-1}\).

Notice \(\sigma^2\) cancels: $\(T = \frac{(\bar{X} - \mu)/(\sigma/\sqrt{n})}{\sqrt{S^2/\sigma^2}} = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{S/\sqrt{n}} \sim t_{n-1}\)$

Without independence, this derivation collapses. The t-statistic would not have a known distribution.

docs.title: Key Formulas Summary
docs.text: Quantity Formula Distribution Sample mean \(\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n}\sum X_i\) \(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2/n)\) Sample variance \(S^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum(X_i-\bar{X})^2\) \(\frac{\sigma^2}{n-1}\chi^2_{n-1}\) Standardized variance \(\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\) \(\chi^2_{n-1}\) t-statistic \(\frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{S/\sqrt{n}}\) \(t_{n-1}\) Independence \(\bar{X} \perp!!!\perp S^2\) (Normal data only)

docs.title: Why Normality Is Essential
docs.text:
For non-normal distributions, \(\bar{X}\) and \(S^2\) are correlated in general. Concretely:

Counterexample (Exponential): Let \(X_i \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{Exp}(\lambda)\). Then:

  • \(\bar{X} = 1/\lambda\) estimates the mean
  • \(S^2\) estimates the variance \(1/\lambda^2\)

Both depend on \(\lambda\), so knowing \(\bar{X}\) gives information about \(S^2\). They are not independent.

The mechanism that breaks for non-normals: Orthogonality of projections (geometric proof) is always valid, but orthogonal normal vectors being independent is special to the multivariate normal (rotational symmetry). For non-normal distributions, \(\text{Cov} = 0\) does not imply independence.

Why is this theorem surprising? \(\bar{X}\) and \(S^2\) are both computed from the same \(n\) data points. You might expect that a large \(\bar{X}\) would somehow be associated with a particular behavior in \(S^2\). But for normals, the location of the data cloud (\(\bar{X}\)) and the spread of the data cloud (\(S^2\)) are completely decoupled.

Geometric intuition: Think of the data as a point in \(\mathbb{R}^n\). \(\bar{X}\) is its projection onto the "all-equal" axis (the 1-dimensional diagonal). \(S^2\) is determined by how far it is from that axis. These are orthogonal pieces of information.

docs.title: LOTUS and Transformations
docs.text: Two things that look like the same problem but are completely different operations. One is a theorem you should memorize and feel. The other is a procedure you reach for only when you actually need the full distribution — and that's rarer than you think.

docs.title: The Setup — Two Very Different Questions
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a random variable and \(g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) a measurable function. You might want either:

  1. Just the expectation \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)]\) — without ever finding the distribution of \(g(X)\)
  2. The full distribution of \(Y = g(X)\) — the PMF, PDF, or CDF of the new random variable

These are not the same task. And the first is answered by a theorem so clean it should feel like cheating.

docs.title: LOTUS — The Law of the Unconscious Statistician
Statement
docs.text:
Discrete case. If \(X\) is a discrete random variable with PMF \(p_X\), then for any function \(g\):

\[\mathbb{E}[g(X)] = \sum_x g(x), p_X(x)\]

Continuous case. If \(X\) is continuous with PDF \(f_X\), then:

\[\mathbb{E}[g(X)] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(x), f_X(x), dx\]

docs.title: The Punchline
docs.text:
You integrate (or sum) \(g(x)\) against the distribution of \(X\) — not against the distribution of \(g(X)\). The distribution of \(Y = g(X)\) never appears.

This is the theorem that lives in the name. The "unconscious statistician" computes \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)]\) without thinking — they just plug \(g\) into the integral over \(X\)'s distribution, as if by reflex. The name is a gentle joke: many people use this formula without realizing it even needs a proof.

docs.title: Why It Needs a Proof (It's Not Obvious)
docs.text:
The definition of expectation is: $\(\mathbb{E}[Y] = \sum_y y, p_Y(y) \quad \text{or} \quad \int y, f_Y(y), dy\)$

LOTUS claims this equals \(\sum_x g(x), p_X(x)\). These are different sums over different spaces. Why should they agree? The left side sums over values of \(Y\); the right side sums over values of \(X\). That they're equal is the content of the theorem.

docs.title: Proof of LOTUS (Discrete Case)
docs.text:
This is the version worth knowing cold. The continuous case follows from measure theory — the discrete case is where you see the idea.

Setup. \(X\) takes values in some countable set \(\mathcal{X}\). Let \(Y = g(X)\), taking values in \(\mathcal{Y} = g(\mathcal{X})\).

The PMF of \(Y\). For each \(y \in \mathcal{Y}\): $\(p_Y(y) = P(g(X) = y) = \sum_{\substack{x \in \mathcal{X} \ g(x) = y}} p_X(x)\)$

Start from the definition of \(\mathbb{E}[Y]\): $\(\mathbb{E}[Y] = \sum_{y \in \mathcal{Y}} y, p_Y(y)\)$

Substitute the expression for \(p_Y(y)\): $\(= \sum_{y \in \mathcal{Y}} y \sum_{\substack{x \in \mathcal{X} \ g(x) = y}} p_X(x)\)$

Since \(g(x) = y\) on the inner sum, replace \(y\) with \(g(x)\): $\(= \sum_{y \in \mathcal{Y}} \sum_{\substack{x \in \mathcal{X} \ g(x) = y}} g(x), p_X(x)\)$

The double sum partitions \(\mathcal{X}\) — every \(x\) appears in exactly one inner sum (the one where \(y = g(x)\)). So we can collapse: $\(= \sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} g(x), p_X(x) \qquad \square\)$

The move is: the partition \({g^{-1}(y) : y \in \mathcal{Y}}\) is a partition of \(\mathcal{X}\), so summing over \(y\) first and then over the fiber \(g^{-1}(y)\) is the same as summing directly over \(\mathcal{X}\). That's it. That's the whole proof.

The double sum collapsing to a single sum over \(\mathcal{X}\) is the "aha" — you're just reindexing, and LOTUS falls out.

docs.title: Why You Almost Never Need the Distribution of \(g(X)\)
docs.text:
The most common mistake early on: computing \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]\) by first finding the PMF of \(X^2\), then summing.

The wrong way (for \(X \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)\), find \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]\)):

\(X^2\) takes values \(0\) and \(1\). \(P(X^2 = 0) = 1-p\), \(P(X^2 = 1) = p\). So \(\mathbb{E}[X^2] = 0\cdot(1-p) + 1 \cdot p = p\).

That works, but it was unnecessary work. By LOTUS: $\(\mathbb{E}[X^2] = \sum_x x^2, p_X(x) = 0^2(1-p) + 1^2 \cdot p = p\)$

One line. And for harder problems, the distribution of \(g(X)\) might be a pain to derive — LOTUS lets you sidestep it entirely.

A case where the distribution really would be annoying. Let \(X \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\). Find \(\mathbb{E}[e^X]\).

Without LOTUS: find the density of \(Y = e^X\), then integrate \(y, f_Y(y)\).

  • \(Y\) takes values in \((1, e)\), CDF of \(Y\) is \(P(e^X \leq y) = P(X \leq \ln y) = \ln y\) for \(y \in (1,e)\)
  • \(f_Y(y) = 1/y\) on \((1,e)\)
  • \(\mathbb{E}[Y] = \int_1^e y \cdot \frac{1}{y}, dy = \int_1^e 1, dy = e - 1\)

With LOTUS: $\(\mathbb{E}[e^X] = \int_0^1 e^x \cdot 1, dx = e^x\Big|_0^1 = e - 1\)$

One line.

LOTUS is the answer to: "why would I ever bother finding the distribution of \(g(X)\)?" And the answer is: only when you need more than just the expectation — when you need quantiles, probabilities, or the full distributional shape.

docs.title: When You DO Need the Distribution of \(g(X)\)
docs.text:
The full distribution of \(Y = g(X)\) is necessary when:
