  • You need \(P(g(X) \leq t)\) for some specific \(t\) — a probability, not just an expectation
  • You need quantiles of \(Y\)
  • You need the variance or higher moments and the distribution simplifies the computation (though often LOTUS handles \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)^2]\) too)
  • You need to identify what named distribution \(g(X)\) follows — sometimes the distribution of a transformation is recognizable and useful

docs.title: The Three Methods for Finding the Distribution of \(Y = g(X)\)
Method 1 — CDF Method (Most General)
docs.text:
Find the CDF of \(Y\) directly: $\(F_Y(y) = P(Y \leq y) = P(g(X) \leq y)\)$ then differentiate to get \(f_Y\) if \(Y\) is continuous.

This always works. The challenge is solving \({x : g(x) \leq y}\) — which can be a union of intervals if \(g\) is not monotone.

Example. \(X \sim N(0,1)\), find the distribution of \(Y = X^2\).

\(P(Y \leq y) = P(X^2 \leq y) = P(-\sqrt{y} \leq X \leq \sqrt{y}) = \Phi(\sqrt{y}) - \Phi(-\sqrt{y}) = 2\Phi(\sqrt{y}) - 1\) for \(y > 0\).

Differentiate: \(f_Y(y) = \frac{d}{dy}[2\Phi(\sqrt{y}) - 1] = 2\phi(\sqrt{y}) \cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi y}}, e^{-y/2}\)

This is \(\chi^2_1\) — the chi-squared distribution with 1 degree of freedom. You'd never get that from LOTUS.

docs.title: Method 2 — Change of Variables / Jacobian (For Monotone, Smooth \(g\))
docs.text:
If \(g\) is strictly monotone and differentiable, and \(X\) has PDF \(f_X\):

\[f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y)) \cdot \left|\frac{d}{dy} g^{-1}(y)\right|\]

The \(|\text{Jacobian}|\) factor corrects for the stretching or compressing of probability mass under the map \(g\).

Intuition. Probability is preserved: \(f_X(x)|dx| = f_Y(y)|dy|\). Solving for \(f_Y(y)\): $\(f_Y(y) = f_X(x) \cdot \left|\frac{dx}{dy}\right| = f_X(g^{-1}(y)) \cdot |(g^{-1})'(y)|\)$

When \(g\) is not monotone — say \(g(x) = x^2\) — you need to sum over all branches: $\(f_Y(y) = \sum_{x_i : g(x_i) = y} f_X(x_i) \cdot \frac{1}{|g'(x_i)|}\)$

This is the multi-branch Jacobian formula. For \(Y = X^2\) with \(X\) symmetric, both \(x = \sqrt{y}\) and \(x = -\sqrt{y}\) contribute.

docs.title: Method 3 — MGF/Characteristic Function (When You Want to Identify the Distribution)
docs.text:
If \(g\) has nice enough structure, compute the MGF \(M_Y(t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{tY}] = \mathbb{E}[e^{t, g(X)}]\) — which is itself just LOTUS — and recognize the result.

This is especially powerful for sums: \(Y = X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_n\) with independent \(X_i\), because \(M_Y(t) = \prod M_{X_i}(t)\).

docs.title: The Comparison Table
docs.text: Task Tool When \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)]\) LOTUS Always — never find the distribution of \(g(X)\) just for this \(P(g(X) \leq t)\) CDF method Always works, messy if \(g\) not monotone \(f_Y\) from \(f_X\), \(g\) monotone Change of variables Fast and clean \(f_Y\) from \(f_X\), \(g\) not monotone CDF + differentiate or multi-branch Jacobian Need to identify all preimage branches Identify the distribution of \(Y\) MGFs or CDF method When you want to say "\(Y \sim\) [something named]"

docs.title: The Variance Formula — A LOTUS Application You'll Use Constantly
docs.text:
\[\text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - (\mathbb{E}[X])^2\]

The term \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]\) is LOTUS with \(g(x) = x^2\). You never need the distribution of \(X^2\).

Similarly, the second moment formula for any \(g\): $\(\mathbb{E}[g(X)^2] = \int g(x)^2, f_X(x), dx\)$

And more generally, for any two functions \(g, h\): $\(\mathbb{E}[g(X)h(X)] = \int g(x)h(x), f_X(x), dx\)$

docs.title: Example Collection
docs.text:
These are the ones to work through once by hand and then never forget.

1. \(X \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)\), find \(\mathbb{E}[X(X-1)]\).

By LOTUS: \(\mathbb{E}[X(X-1)] = \sum_{k=0}^\infty k(k-1) \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k}{k!} = \sum_{k=2}^\infty \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k}{(k-2)!} = \lambda^2 \sum_{j=0}^\infty \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^j}{j!} = \lambda^2\)

So \(\text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[X^2] - \lambda^2 = \mathbb{E}[X(X-1)] + \mathbb{E}[X] - \lambda^2 = \lambda^2 + \lambda - \lambda^2 = \lambda\).

The Poisson variance falls out cleanly via LOTUS + the falling factorial trick. Trying to compute \(\mathbb{E}[X^2]\) directly is messier.

2. \(X \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\), find \(\mathbb{E}[X^n]\).

\(\mathbb{E}[X^n] = \int_0^1 x^n \cdot 1, dx = \frac{1}{n+1}\)

The moments of the uniform are just \(\frac{1}{n+1}\). LOTUS makes this trivial.

3. \(X \sim \text{Exponential}(\lambda)\), find \(\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]\) for \(t < \lambda\).

\(\mathbb{E}[e^{tX}] = \int_0^\infty e^{tx} \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, dx = \lambda \int_0^\infty e^{-(λ-t)x}, dx = \frac{\lambda}{\lambda - t}\)

This is the MGF of the Exponential, derived in one line via LOTUS.

docs.title: A Note on Measure Theory (For Later)
docs.text:
In the full measure-theoretic framework, LOTUS is not actually a theorem with a special name — it's almost a definition. If \(Y = g(X)\), then for any measurable \(h\):

\[\mathbb{E}[h(Y)] = \mathbb{E}[h(g(X))]\]

because \(h(Y)\) and \(h(g(X))\) are literally the same random variable. LOTUS (with \(h = \text{id}\)) is then:

\[\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mathbb{E}[g(X)] = \int g, d\mu_X\]

where \(\mu_X\) is the pushforward measure of \(X\) — which is just a formal way of saying "integrate \(g\) against \(X\)'s distribution." The statement becomes transparent at this level, which is exactly why the name "unconscious statistician" exists: at the elementary level it requires thought; at the measure-theoretic level it's definitional.

docs.title: Pitfalls and Things Not to Mix Up
docs.text:
For the exam or any proof, keep these straight.

  1. LOTUS ≠ linearity of expectation. Linearity says \(\mathbb{E}[aX + b] = a\mathbb{E}[X] + b\). LOTUS is for general nonlinear \(g\). They're different tools. (Linearity doesn't require any computation; LOTUS does.)

  2. \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)] \neq g(\mathbb{E}[X])\) in general. Jensen's inequality quantifies the gap. LOTUS computes the left side correctly; the right side is a common error.

  3. Change of variables requires monotonicity or branch-counting. Don't apply the Jacobian formula to \(g(x) = x^2\) without accounting for both \(\pm\sqrt{y}\) branches.

  4. The CDF method works always; the Jacobian method is a shortcut. When in doubt, use CDF + differentiate. The Jacobian is faster when \(g\) is smooth and monotone.

  5. LOTUS needs absolute convergence. Formally, \(\mathbb{E}[g(X)]\) requires \(\mathbb{E}[|g(X)|] < \infty\) for the sum/integral to be well-defined. Don't apply it blindly to heavy-tailed distributions.

docs.title: Change of Variables
docs.text: The whole game is this: you know the distribution of \(X\), and you want the distribution of \(Y = g(X)\). Everything else is just technique.

docs.title: Why This Matters (To Me)
docs.text:
I keep running into this everywhere — mgfs, convolutions, order statistics, the whole works. The machinery here is the same machinery that underpins most of the slick derivations in Stat 110. So it's worth doing this properly, once, with full rigor, so I never have to fumble through it again.

The core tension: probability is fundamentally about sets (events), not values. When we change variables, we're really asking: what event in the new space corresponds to \({Y \leq y}\)? That's the whole conceptual heart of it.

docs.title: Part I — The Discrete Case (Warm-Up)
docs.text:
Let \(X\) be a discrete r.v. with PMF \(p_X\), and let \(Y = g(X)\) for some function \(g\).

\[p_Y(y) = P(Y = y) = \sum_{{x ,:, g(x) = y}} p_X(x)\]

Nothing surprising — you pool all the \(x\)-values that map to \(y\) under \(g\). If \(g\) is injective, there's at most one such \(x\) for each \(y\), and this simplifies cleanly.

Example I want to remember: If \(X \sim \text{Geom}(p)\) and \(Y = X^2\), then since \(X\) takes values in \({1, 2, 3, \ldots}\), squaring is injective here, so \(p_Y(k^2) = p_X(k)\) for each positive integer \(k\). Done.

docs.title: Part II — The Continuous Case via CDF
docs.text:
This is where the real action is.

Setup. Let \(X\) be a continuous r.v. with CDF \(F_X\) and PDF \(f_X\). Let \(Y = g(X)\).

The universal method: find \(F_Y\) first, then differentiate.

\[F_Y(y) = P(Y \leq y) = P(g(X) \leq y)\]

Now I have to think about what the set \({g(X) \leq y}\) looks like in terms of \(X\). This depends on \(g\).

Case 1: \(g\) strictly increasing.

\(g(X) \leq y \iff X \leq g^{-1}(y)\), so \(F_Y(y) = F_X(g^{-1}(y))\). Differentiating:

\[f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y)) \cdot \frac{d}{dy}, g^{-1}(y)\]

Case 2: \(g\) strictly decreasing.

\(g(X) \leq y \iff X \geq g^{-1}(y)\), so \(F_Y(y) = 1 - F_X(g^{-1}(y))\). Differentiating (noting \(\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y) < 0\) now):

\[f_Y(y) = -f_X(g^{-1}(y)) \cdot \frac{d}{dy}, g^{-1}(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y)) \cdot \left|\frac{d}{dy}, g^{-1}(y)\right|\]

docs.title: Part III — The Change of Variables Formula
docs.text:
Combining both cases into one clean theorem:

Theorem (Change of Variables, 1D). Let \(X\) be continuous with PDF \(f_X\), supported on interval \(I\). Let \(g: I \to \mathbb{R}\) be differentiable and strictly monotone. Let \(Y = g(X)\). Then:

\[\boxed{f_Y(y) = f_X!\left(g^{-1}(y)\right) \cdot \left|\frac{d}{dy}, g^{-1}(y)\right|}\]

Equivalently: \(f_Y(y) = f_X(x) \cdot \left|\dfrac{dx}{dy}\right|\) where \(x = g^{-1}(y)\).

Why the absolute value? The Jacobian factor \(|dx/dy|\) accounts for how \(g\) stretches or compresses probability mass. Think of it as conservation: \(f(x)|dx| = f(y)|dy|\) — probability in an infinitesimal interval is preserved under the transformation. If \(g\) expands a region of the \(x\)-axis, the density must fall proportionally so mass is conserved.

docs.title: Part IV — Worked Example: The Log-Normal
docs.text:
Let \(Z \sim N(0,1)\), and \(X = e^Z\). What's the distribution of \(X\)?

\(g(z) = e^z\) is strictly increasing. We have \(g^{-1}(x) = \ln x\) for \(x > 0\), and

\[\frac{d}{dx} \ln x = \frac{1}{x}\]

So by the formula:

\[f_X(x) = f_Z(\ln x) \cdot \frac{1}{x} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}, e^{-(\ln x)^2/2} \cdot \frac{1}{x}, \qquad x > 0\]

This is the Log-Normal distribution. Two lines. The machinery does the work.

It comes up everywhere — stock prices, income distributions, anything driven by multiplicative noise. The reason: if \(X\) is log-normal then \(\ln X\) is Gaussian, which happens when growth is proportional to current size (i.e., percentage changes are roughly iid).

docs.title: Part V — The Non-Monotone Case
docs.text:
What if \(g\) isn't monotone? Say \(Y = X^2\) with \(X\) continuous on all of \(\mathbb{R}\).

For \(y > 0\), both \(\sqrt{y}\) and \(-\sqrt{y}\) satisfy \(g(x) = y\), so \(g^{-1}\) is multi-valued. I can't apply the theorem directly.

Fix: work from the CDF, and break the domain into monotone pieces.

\[F_Y(y) = P(X^2 \leq y) = P(-\sqrt{y} \leq X \leq \sqrt{y}) = F_X(\sqrt{y}) - F_X(-\sqrt{y})\]

Differentiating:

\[f_Y(y) = f_X(\sqrt{y}) \cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} + f_X(-\sqrt{y}) \cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}, \qquad y > 0\]

General principle: if \(g\) is piecewise monotone with inverse branches \(h_1, \ldots, h_k\):

\[f_Y(y) = \sum_{i=1}^{k} f_X(h_i(y)) \cdot |h_i'(y)|\]

docs.title: Part VI — Chi-Squared as an Immediate Corollary
docs.text:
Let \(Z \sim N(0,1)\), \(Y = Z^2\). Using the formula above with symmetry \(\varphi(-t) = \varphi(t)\):

\[f_Y(y) = \frac{2}{2\sqrt{y}},\varphi(\sqrt{y}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}},e^{-y/2} = \frac{1}{2^{1/2},\Gamma(1/2)},y^{1/2 - 1},e^{-y/2}, \qquad y > 0\]

That's \(\text{Gamma}(1/2,, 1/2)\) — which is exactly \(\chi^2_1\) by definition. The chi-squared distribution just falls out of the machinery. I should remember this derivation cold.

docs.title: Part VII — Multivariable Change of Variables
docs.text:
Now the full story. Let \(\mathbf{X} = (X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) have joint PDF \(f_{\mathbf{X}}\), and let \(\mathbf{Y} = g(\mathbf{X})\) where \(g: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n\) is a diffeomorphism (smooth bijection with smooth inverse).

Theorem (Multivariate COV). Under the above:

\[f_{\mathbf{Y}}(\mathbf{y}) = f_{\mathbf{X}}!\left(g^{-1}(\mathbf{y})\right) \cdot \left|\det J_{g^{-1}}(\mathbf{y})\right|\]

where the Jacobian matrix of \(g^{-1}\) is:

\[\left(J_{g^{-1}}\right)_{ij} = \frac{\partial x_i}{\partial y_j}\]

Equivalently: \(f_{\mathbf{Y}}(\mathbf{y}),|d\mathbf{y}| = f_{\mathbf{X}}(\mathbf{x}),|d\mathbf{x}|\), since \(|d\mathbf{x}| = |\det J|,|d\mathbf{y}|\).

Why the determinant? Because \(|\det J|\) is the factor by which the linear approximation of \(g^{-1}\) scales \(n\)-dimensional volume. Probability is volume under the density, and the Jacobian determinant precisely captures how that volume is distorted. This is the \(n\)-dimensional version of \(|dx/dy|\).

docs.title: Part VIII — The Gaussian Miracle (Box-Muller)
docs.text:
Let \(X, Y \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0,1)\). Transform to polar coordinates:

\[R = \sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}, \qquad \Theta = \arctan(Y/X)\]

The joint PDF of \((X,Y)\) is:

\[f_{X,Y}(x,y) = \frac{1}{2\pi},e^{-(x^2+y^2)/2}\]

Inverse transform: \(x = r\cos\theta\), \(y = r\sin\theta\). Jacobian:

\[J = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -r\sin\theta \ \sin\theta & r\cos\theta \end{pmatrix}, \qquad |\det J| = r\]

So:

\[f_{R,\Theta}(r,\theta) = \frac{1}{2\pi},e^{-r^2/2} \cdot r = \underbrace{re^{-r^2/2}}_{\text{density of }R} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{1}{2\pi}}_{\text{density of }\Theta}\]

This factors, proving \(R \perp \Theta\), with \(\Theta \sim \text{Unif}(0, 2\pi)\) and \(R^2 \sim \text{Expo}(1/2)\) (i.e., \(R^2 \sim \chi^2_2\)). Beautiful.

Practical upshot — Box-Muller: To sample \(Z_1, Z_2 \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0,1)\), generate \(U_1, U_2 \sim \text{Unif}(0,1)\) and set:

\[Z_1 = \sqrt{-2\ln U_1}\cos(2\pi U_2), \qquad Z_2 = \sqrt{-2\ln U_1}\sin(2\pi U_2)\]

Exact, not approximate. The whole thing is just this theorem run backwards.

docs.title: Common Pitfalls I Keep Making
docs.text:
1. Forgetting to restrict the support. \(f_Y\) is only nonzero on the image of \(g\). Always figure out what values \(Y\) can take before writing down the formula.

  2. Forgetting the Jacobian. I've written \(f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y))\) without the derivative factor before. That's wrong and will never integrate to 1.

  3. Assuming monotonicity without checking. If \(g\) is not monotone on its full domain, the single-branch formula gives the wrong answer. Sketch the function.

  4. Getting the Jacobian direction wrong. It's \(|dx/dy| = |\frac{d}{dy} g^{-1}(y)|\), not \(|dy/dx|\). I differentiate the inverse map.

docs.title: The CDF Method vs. The Formula
docs.text:
I always have a choice:

Method When to use CDF method \(g\) non-monotone, domain issues, or I'm being careful Change of variables formula \(g\) is a smooth bijection on a clean domain

The formula is derived from the CDF method, so when in doubt, go back to basics. There's no shame in it.

docs.title: Bivariate Normal
docs.text: This one took me an embarrassingly long time to really sit with. The formula looks like a monster at first. But once you see it as a quadratic form inside an exponential — and you trace back where every piece comes from — it's actually quite beautiful. Don't memorize it. Derive it.

docs.title: Setup & Motivation
docs.text:
We want a joint distribution for \((X, Y)\) such that:

  • Every linear combination \(aX + bY\) is normal
  • Marginally, \(X \sim N(\mu_1, \sigma_1^2)\) and \(Y \sim N(\mu_2, \sigma_2^2)\)
  • The dependence is captured by a single parameter \(\rho = \text{Corr}(X, Y)\)

This is exactly what the Bivariate Normal (BVN) gives us. It is the "right" generalization of the univariate normal to two dimensions, and it will generalize further to the multivariate normal via the covariance matrix.

docs.title: The Joint PDF
docs.text:
Let \((X, Y)\) be Bivariate Normal with parameters \(\mu_1, \mu_2 \in \mathbb{R}\), \(\sigma_1, \sigma_2 > 0\), and \(\rho \in (-1, 1)\). Then the joint PDF is:

\[ f(x,y) = \frac{1}{2\pi \sigma_1 \sigma_2 \sqrt{1-\rho^2}} \exp!\left( -\frac{1}{2(1-\rho^2)} \left[ \frac{(x-\mu_1)^2}{\sigma_1^2} - \frac{2\rho(x-\mu_1)(y-\mu_2)}{\sigma_1 \sigma_2} + \frac{(y-\mu_2)^2}{\sigma_2^2} \right] \right) \]

The expression in the exponent is a quadratic form in \((x - \mu_1, y - \mu_2)\). This is the key structural insight — everything is governed by the inverse of the covariance matrix \(\Sigma\).

docs.title: Where This Comes From — The Derivation I Actually Like
docs.text: Don't just accept the formula. Here's the derivation via the conditional approach, which also gives you the conditional distribution for free.

docs.title: Step 1: Start with independent normals
docs.text:
Let \(Z_1, Z_2 \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0,1)\). Define:

\[ X = \mu_1 + \sigma_1 Z_1 $$ $$ Y = \mu_2 + \sigma_2(\rho Z_1 + \sqrt{1-\rho^2}, Z_2) \]

Check the marginals:

  • \(X \sim N(\mu_1, \sigma_1^2)\) ✓ (obvious)
  • \(Y \sim N(\mu_2, \sigma_2^2(\rho^2 + (1-\rho^2))) = N(\mu_2, \sigma_2^2)\) ✓

Check the correlation: $$ \text{Cov}(X, Y) = \text{Cov}(\sigma_1 Z_1, \sigma_2(\rho Z_1 + \sqrt{1-\rho^2}, Z_2)) = \sigma_1 \sigma_2 \rho \cdot \text{Var}(Z_1) = \sigma_1 \sigma_2 \rho $$ $$ \Rightarrow \text{Corr}(X, Y) = \frac{\sigma_1 \sigma_2 \rho}{\sigma_1 \sigma_2} = \rho \quad \checkmark $$

So the construction is consistent. Now derive the joint PDF by deriving the Jacobian of the inverse transformation from \((X, Y)\) to \((Z_1, Z_2)\), and multiplying by the joint PDF of \((Z_1, Z_2)\).

docs.title: Step 2: Invert the transformation
docs.text: \[ Z_1 = \frac{x - \mu_1}{\sigma_1}, \qquad Z_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\rho^2}}\left(\frac{y - \mu_2}{\sigma_2} - \rho \cdot \frac{x - \mu_1}{\sigma_1}\right) \]

docs.title: Step 3: Compute the Jacobian
docs.text:
The Jacobian of the map \((x,y) \mapsto (z_1, z_2)\) is:

\[ J = \begin{vmatrix} \partial z_1/\partial x & \partial z_1/\partial y \ \partial z_2/\partial x & \partial z_2/\partial y \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} 1/\sigma_1 & 0 \ -\rho/(\sigma_1\sqrt{1-\rho^2}) & 1/(\sigma_2\sqrt{1-\rho^2}) \end{vmatrix} = \frac{1}{\sigma_1 \sigma_2 \sqrt{1-\rho^2}} \]

docs.title: Step 4: Apply change of variables
docs.text:
\[ f_{X,Y}(x,y) = f_{Z_1,Z_2}(z_1, z_2) \cdot |J| \]

Since \(Z_1, Z_2\) are independent standard normals:

\[ f_{Z_1, Z_2}(z_1, z_2) = \frac{1}{2\pi} e^{-(z_1^2 + z_2^2)/2} \]

Now substitute \(z_1, z_2\) back in terms of \(x, y\). The exponent becomes:

\[ z_1^2 + z_2^2 = \frac{(x-\mu_1)^2}{\sigma_1^2} + \frac{1}{1-\rho^2}\left(\frac{y-\mu_2}{\sigma_2} - \rho \frac{x-\mu_1}{\sigma_1}\right)^2 \]

Expand the second term:

\[ = \frac{(x-\mu_1)^2}{\sigma_1^2} + \frac{1}{1-\rho^2}\left[\frac{(y-\mu_2)^2}{\sigma_2^2} - \frac{2\rho(x-\mu_1)(y-\mu_2)}{\sigma_1\sigma_2} + \frac{\rho^2(x-\mu_1)^2}{\sigma_1^2}\right] \] \[ = \frac{1}{1-\rho^2}\left[\frac{(x-\mu_1)^2}{\sigma_1^2}(1-\rho^2+\rho^2) - \frac{2\rho(x-\mu_1)(y-\mu_2)}{\sigma_1\sigma_2} + \frac{(y-\mu_2)^2}{\sigma_2^2}\right] \] \[ = \frac{1}{1-\rho^2}\left[\frac{(x-\mu_1)^2}{\sigma_1^2} - \frac{2\rho(x-\mu_1)(y-\mu_2)}{\sigma_1\sigma_2} + \frac{(y-\mu_2)^2}{\sigma_2^2}\right] \]

Multiply everything together, and you get exactly the joint PDF stated above. \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: The Matrix Form (Preview of Multivariate Normal)
docs.text:
Let \(\mathbf{x} = (x, y)^\top\), \(\boldsymbol{\mu} = (\mu_1, \mu_2)^\top\), and define the covariance matrix:

\[ \Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_1^2 & \rho \sigma_1 \sigma_2 \ \rho \sigma_1 \sigma_2 & \sigma_2^2 \end{pmatrix} \]

Then: $$ \det(\Sigma) = \sigma_1^2 \sigma_2^2 - \rho^2 \sigma_1^2 \sigma_2^2 = \sigma_1^2 \sigma_22(1-\rho2) $$

\[ \Sigma^{-1} = \frac{1}{\sigma_1^2\sigma_2^2(1-\rho^2)}\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_2^2 & -\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2 \ -\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2 & \sigma_1^2\end{pmatrix} \]

The exponent in the BVN PDF is precisely: $$ -\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}) $$

And the normalizing constant \(\frac{1}{2\pi\sigma_1\sigma_2\sqrt{1-\rho^2}} = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{2/2}\sqrt{\det(\Sigma)}} = \frac{1}{(2\pi)|\Sigma|^{1/2}}\).

So the BVN PDF in full matrix form is: $$ f(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)|\Sigma|^{½}} \exp!\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu})\top\Sigma)\right) $$}(\mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\mu

This is exactly the multivariate normal PDF. The BVN is just the \(n=2\) case. Every piece — the determinant, the inverse, the quadratic form — generalizes perfectly.

docs.title: 1. Marginals are Normal
docs.text:
\[ X \sim N(\mu_1, \sigma_1^2), \quad Y \sim N(\mu_2, \sigma_2^2) \]

Proof: Integrate out \(y\) from the joint PDF, or note it directly from the construction in Step 1.

⚠️ Converse fails. Marginals can each be normal without the joint being bivariate normal. You need to add the condition that every linear combination is normal (or equivalently, that the joint has the BVN form). This is a classic mistake — don't make it.

docs.title: 2. Conditional Distribution
docs.text:
\[ Y \mid X = x \sim N!\left(\mu_2 + \rho\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1}(x - \mu_1),\ \sigma_2^2(1-\rho^2)\right) \]

Proof: Write \(f(y \mid x) = f(x,y)/f_X(x)\). The calculation is just algebra with the exponent. The conditional mean is linear in \(x\) — this is the key fact underlying linear regression.

The conditional variance \(\sigma_2^2(1-\rho^2)\) is constant (doesn't depend on \(x\)). This is homoskedasticity built into the model.

The conditional mean \(E[Y | X=x] = \mu_2 + \rho\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1}(x - \mu_1)\) is exactly the linear regression line of \(Y\) on \(X\). This is not a coincidence — it's the reason why the bivariate normal is the natural probability model behind OLS.

docs.title: 3. Uncorrelated \(\Leftrightarrow\) Independent (BVN only!)
docs.text:
If \((X,Y)\) is BVN, then: $$ \rho = 0 \iff X \perp Y $$

Proof: If \(\rho = 0\), the joint PDF factors as \(f_X(x) \cdot f_Y(y)\). Independence implies uncorrelatedness always; the other direction holds only under joint normality.

docs.title: 4. Linear combinations are Normal
docs.text:
For any \(a, b \in \mathbb{R}\): $$ aX + bY \sim N(a\mu_1 + b\mu_2, a2\sigma_12 + 2ab\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2 + b2\sigma_22) $$

Proof: Use the construction from Step 1. \(aX + bY\) is a linear combination of \(Z_1, Z_2\), which are independent normals.

docs.title: The Shape: Level Sets
docs.text:
The set \({(x,y) : f(x,y) = c}\) for some constant \(c\) is given by:

\[ \frac{(x-\mu_1)^2}{\sigma_1^2} - \frac{2\rho(x-\mu_1)(y-\mu_2)}{\sigma_1\sigma_2} + \frac{(y-\mu_2)^2}{\sigma_2^2} = \text{const} \]

This is an ellipse centered at \((\mu_1, \mu_2)\), rotated when \(\rho \neq 0\). The axes of the ellipse are the eigenvectors of \(\Sigma\).

  • When \(\rho = 0\): the ellipse aligns with the coordinate axes (axes = \(x\)-axis and \(y\)-axis)
  • When \(\rho > 0\): the ellipse tilts toward the first/third quadrant
  • As \(\rho \to \pm 1\): the ellipse degenerates to a line — the distribution becomes singular

docs.title: Edge Cases and Warnings
docs.text:
Case What happens \(\rho = 0\) \(X, Y\) independent. PDF factors. \(\rho = \pm 1\) \(\det(\Sigma) = 0\). No density exists. \(Y = \mu_2 \pm \frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1}(X - \mu_1)\) a.s. — the distribution is supported on a line. \(\sigma_1 \to 0\) or \(\sigma_2 \to 0\) Same degeneracy as above.

When \(|\rho| = 1\), the BVN is degenerate — we need to work with the distribution purely through characteristic functions or the multivariate normal framework. The PDF doesn't exist in the classical sense.

docs.title: Convolutions
docs.text: Convolution is what happens when you add two independent random variables and ask for the resulting distribution. The operation looks intimidating in the continuous case — an integral of a product of two shifted functions — but it's the same idea as counting paths in the discrete case. Learn both. The discrete one builds the intuition.

docs.title: The Core Question
docs.text:
If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent random variables, what is the distribution of \(Z = X + Y\)?

This is one of the most fundamental questions in probability. The answer is the convolution of their distributions.

The independence assumption is load-bearing. Without it, you'd need the full joint distribution of \((X, Y)\), not just the marginals. Convolution is precisely what independence buys you.

docs.title: Discrete Case First
docs.text:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be independent, taking values in \(\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\). Then:

\[ P(Z = k) = P(X + Y = k) = \sum_{j=0}^{k} P(X = j), P(Y = k - j) \]

Why? Condition on \(X = j\). Given \(X = j\), we need \(Y = k - j\). Since \(X \perp Y\), this is \(P(X=j) P(Y = k-j)\). Sum over all valid \(j\). That's it.

This is literally polynomial multiplication. If you define generating functions \(G_X(s) = \sum_k P(X=k)s^k\) and \(G_Y(s) = \sum_k P(Y=k)s^k\), then:

\[ G_{X+Y}(s) = G_X(s) \cdot G_Y(s) \]

Convolution in PMF-space = multiplication in generating function space. This is why PGFs are so powerful for sums.

docs.title: Example: Sum of Two Dice
docs.text: Let \(X, Y \sim \text{Uniform}{1, \ldots, 6}\) independently. Then \(P(Z = k) = \sum_j P(X=j)P(Y=k-j)\). You're counting the number of ways to write \(k\) as an ordered pair \((j, k-j)\) with both in \({1,\ldots,6}\). The classic triangular histogram shape comes directly from this count.

docs.title: Continuous Case
docs.text:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be independent continuous RVs with PDFs \(f_X\) and \(f_Y\). The PDF of \(Z = X + Y\) is:

\[ f_Z(z) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_X(x), f_Y(z - x), dx = (f_X * f_Y)(z) \]

This is the convolution of \(f_X\) and \(f_Y\).

docs.title: Derivation from First Principles
docs.text:
Don't just accept this. Derive it via the CDF approach.

\[ F_Z(z) = P(X + Y \leq z) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} P(Y \leq z - x), f_X(x), dx = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} F_Y(z-x), f_X(x), dx \]

where we used independence to write \(P(X \in dx, Y \leq z - x) = f_X(x)dx \cdot F_Y(z-x)\).

Now differentiate with respect to \(z\) (under the integral, which is justified by dominated convergence in nice cases):

\[ f_Z(z) = \frac{d}{dz} F_Z(z) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_Y(z - x), f_X(x), dx \]

Done. \(\blacksquare\)

Geometric interpretation: \(f_Z(z)\) is the "overlap" between \(f_X\) and the reflected-and-shifted \(f_Y\). Fix \(z\). Flip \(f_Y\) around zero to get \(f_Y(-\cdot)\), then shift it right by \(z\) to get \(f_Y(z - \cdot)\). The integral is the inner product of \(f_X\) and this shifted-reflected \(f_Y\). As you slide \(z\), the overlap changes — that's the shape of the convolution.

docs.title: The MGF/CF Method (Almost Always Easier)
docs.text:
For independent \(X, Y\):

\[ M_{X+Y}(t) = E[e^{t(X+Y)}] = E[e^{tX}] E[e^{tY}] = M_X(t) \cdot M_Y(t) \]

So if you can identify the product of MGFs as the MGF of a known distribution, you're done — no integral needed.

This works with the characteristic function \(\phi(t) = E[e^{itX}]\) even when the MGF doesn't exist. The CF always exists.

Strategy: Always try the MGF method first. Only resort to the convolution integral when the MGF approach doesn't close nicely or you specifically need the PDF.

docs.title: 1. Poisson + Poisson
docs.text:
Let \(X \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda)\), \(Y \sim \text{Pois}(\mu)\), independent.

Via MGF: \(M_X(t) = e^{\lambda(e^t - 1)}\), \(M_Y(t) = e^{\mu(e^t - 1)}\).

\[ M_{X+Y}(t) = e^{(\lambda + \mu)(e^t - 1)} \]

This is the MGF of \(\text{Pois}(\lambda + \mu)\). So \(X + Y \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda + \mu)\). \(\square\)

Directly via PMF: $$ P(X + Y = k) = \sum_{j=0}^k \frac{e{-\lambda}\lambdaj}{j!} \cdot \frac{e{-\mu}\mu = \frac{e}}{(k-j)!} = \frac{e^{-(\lambda+\mu)}}{k!} \sum_{j=0}^k \binom{k}{j} \lambda^j \mu^{k-j{-(\lambda+\mu)}(\lambda+\mu)k}{k!} $$

Binomial theorem at the last step. Beautiful. This is the reproductive property of the Poisson.

docs.title: 2. Normal + Normal
docs.text:
Let \(X \sim N(\mu_1, \sigma_1^2)\), \(Y \sim N(\mu_2, \sigma_2^2)\), independent.

Via MGF: \(M_X(t) = e^{\mu_1 t + \frac{1}{2}\sigma_1^2 t^2}\), similarly for \(Y\).

\[ M_{X+Y}(t) = e^{(\mu_1+\mu_2)t + \frac{1}{2}(\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)t^2} \]

This is \(N(\mu_1 + \mu_2,\ \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2)\).

Note: variances add, not standard deviations. This is the fact that saves you from a lot of wrong answers. \(\text{SD}(X+Y) \neq \text{SD}(X) + \text{SD}(Y)\) in general.

docs.title: 3. Gamma + Gamma (same rate)
docs.text:
Let \(X \sim \text{Gamma}(a, \lambda)\), \(Y \sim \text{Gamma}(b, \lambda)\), independent. (Using shape-rate parameterization.)

Via MGF: \(M_X(t) = \left(\frac{\lambda}{\lambda - t}\right)^a\) for \(t < \lambda\).

\[ M_{X+Y}(t) = \left(\frac{\lambda}{\lambda - t}\right)^{a+b} \]

So \(X + Y \sim \text{Gamma}(a+b, \lambda)\). The rate must match for this to work.

Corollary: Since \(\text{Exp}(\lambda) = \text{Gamma}(1, \lambda)\), the sum of \(n\) i.i.d. \(\text{Exp}(\lambda)\) RVs is \(\text{Gamma}(n, \lambda)\). This is the waiting time for the \(n\)-th arrival in a Poisson process.

docs.title: 4. Uniform + Uniform (Convolution Integral Forced)
docs.text:
Let \(X, Y \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\) independently. Here the MGF method works but doesn't simplify to a named distribution, so let's do the integral.

\[ f_Z(z) = \int_0^1 f_X(x) \cdot f_Y(z-x), dx = \int_0^1 \mathbf{1}[0 \leq z-x \leq 1], dx = \int_0^1 \mathbf{1}[z-1 \leq x \leq z], dx \]

We need \(x \in [0,1]\) and \(x \in [z-1, z]\) simultaneously. There are two cases:

Case \(0 \leq z \leq 1\): The intersection is \([0, z]\), so \(f_Z(z) = z\).

Case \(1 < z \leq 2\): The intersection is \([z-1, 1]\), so \(f_Z(z) = 2 - z\).

Hence: $$ f_Z(z) = \begin{cases} z & 0 \leq z \leq 1 2 - z & 1 < z \leq 2 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$

This is the triangular distribution on \([0,2]\). Makes complete sense — the convolution of two box functions is a tent. By the CLT, summing more and more uniforms gives a shape that approaches Gaussian.

docs.title: Convolution and the Indicator-Function Trick
docs.text:
When the supports are bounded (like Uniform), you often end up integrating an indicator. The key skill is correctly intersecting the indicator constraints.

Template: $$ f_Z(z) = \int f_X(x) \cdot \mathbf{1}[z - x \in \text{supp}(Y)], f_Y(z-x), dx $$

The indicator carves out the valid range of \(x\). Always draw the constraints on a number line and find the intersection. This is where most errors happen — getting the cases wrong.

docs.title: \(n\)-fold Convolution
docs.text:
For i.i.d. \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) with PDF \(f\), the PDF of \(S_n = X_1 + \cdots + X_n\) is the \(n\)-fold convolution:

\[ f_{S_n} = f * f * \cdots * f \quad (n \text{ times}) \]

In Fourier/CF space, this is just \(\hat{f}(\xi)^n\) — exponentiation. This is exactly why the CLT is most naturally proved using characteristic functions.

docs.title: The Fourier Perspective
docs.text:
The Fourier transform of \(f_Z = f_X * f_Y\) is:

\[ \widehat{f_Z}(\xi) = \widehat{f_X}(\xi) \cdot \widehat{f_Y}(\xi) \]

Convolution in the original domain = pointwise multiplication in the Fourier domain. This is the fundamental theorem of convolution, and it's the reason CFs/MGFs are so effective.

The CF of \(X+Y\) (independent) is \(\phi_X(t) \cdot \phi_Y(t)\) — this is literally the above with \(\xi = t\), up to a sign convention. So the MGF factorization trick isn't a cute trick; it's an instance of a deep structural fact.

docs.title: When Convolution Fails (or Gets Complicated)
docs.text:
Situation Problem \(X, Y\) not independent Need the full joint distribution; can't just convolve marginals Distributions with different supports but weird overlap The indicator constraints get messy; just be careful Heavy-tailed distributions (Cauchy) MGF doesn't exist; must use CF \(X - Y\) instead of \(X + Y\) Convolve \(f_X\) with the reflection \(f_Y(-\cdot)\); i.e., \(f_Z(z) = \int f_X(x) f_Y(x-z) dx\)

For \(Z = X - Y\) where \(X, Y\) independent: this is the same as \(X + (-Y)\), and \(-Y\) has PDF \(f_{-Y}(y) = f_Y(-y)\). So \(f_Z(z) = (f_X * f_{-Y})(z) = \int f_X(x) f_Y(x-z) dx\). The cross-correlation rather than autocorrelation.

docs.title: Reproductive Properties Summary
docs.text:
These are worth memorizing not as facts but as corollaries of the MGF method:

Distribution Parameter Sum of independent copies \(\text{Pois}(\lambda_i)\) rate \(\text{Pois}(\sum \lambda_i)\) \(N(\mu_i, \sigma_i^2)\) mean, variance \(N(\sum \mu_i, \sum \sigma_i^2)\) \(\text{Gamma}(a_i, \lambda)\) shape (same rate!) \(\text{Gamma}(\sum a_i, \lambda)\) \(\text{Binomial}(n_i, p)\) trials (same \(p\)!) \(\text{Binomial}(\sum n_i, p)\) \(\chi^2(k_i)\) df \(\chi^2(\sum k_i)\) \(\text{Cauchy}\) location, scale Cauchy (use CF — MGF doesn't exist)

The constraint "same rate / same \(p\)" is essential. You can't add \(\text{Gamma}(2, 1)\) and \(\text{Gamma}(3, 5)\) and get a Gamma without doing real work.

docs.title: Beta Transformations
docs.text: "The Beta is not just a distribution — it's a mirror. It reflects the Uniform back at you, twisted by two shape parameters."

docs.title: Why I care about this
docs.text:
Before diving in: the Beta distribution lives on \((0,1)\), which makes it the natural home for probabilities, proportions, and anything that needs to be bounded. Every time I think "what's a prior over a probability?" — Beta. And the transformations here are what let me move between Beta, Gamma, and the Uniform in a principled way.

Blitzstein hammers this in Stat 110: know the stories, then the transformations follow.

docs.title: Setup: What is the Beta distribution?
docs.text:
\(X \sim \text{Beta}(a, b)\) means \(X\) has PDF

\[f(x) = \frac{1}{B(a,b)} x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}, \quad x \in (0,1)\]

where the Beta function is the normalizing constant:

\[B(a,b) = \int_0^1 x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1},dx\]

The key fact (proved via Gamma):

\[\boxed{B(a,b) = \frac{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)}}\]

I should know this identity cold. It comes up everywhere.

docs.title: The Fundamental Transformation: Beta from Gammas
docs.text:
Theorem. Let \(X \sim \text{Gamma}(a, 1)\) and \(Y \sim \text{Gamma}(b, 1)\) be independent. Then

\[W = \frac{X}{X+Y} \sim \text{Beta}(a, b)\]

and \(W\) is independent of \(X + Y \sim \text{Gamma}(a+b, 1)\).

docs.title: Proof (full, rigorous)
docs.text:
Let \(T = X + Y\). We want the joint distribution of \((W, T)\) via the change of variables

\[X = WT, \quad Y = (1-W)T\]

Step 1: Jacobian. The transformation \((x,y) \mapsto (w,t)\) is

\[x = wt, \quad y = (1-w)t\]

Compute the Jacobian \(\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(w,t)}\):

\[J = \begin{vmatrix} t & w \ -t & 1-w \end{vmatrix} = t(1-w) + wt = t\]

So \(|J| = t\).

Step 2: Joint PDF of \((X,Y)\). Since \(X, Y\) independent:

\[f_{X,Y}(x,y) = \frac{x^{a-1}e^{-x}}{\Gamma(a)} \cdot \frac{y^{b-1}e^{-y}}{\Gamma(b)}, \quad x,y > 0\]

Step 3: Substitute. With \(x = wt\), \(y = (1-w)t\), \(dx,dy = t,dw,dt\):

\[f_{W,T}(w,t) = \frac{(wt)^{a-1}e^{-wt}}{\Gamma(a)} \cdot \frac{((1-w)t)^{b-1}e^{-(1-w)t}}{\Gamma(b)} \cdot t\]

Collect terms:

\[= \frac{w^{a-1}(1-w)^{b-1} \cdot t^{a+b-1} e^{-t}}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}\]

Step 4: Factor. This factors as a product of a function of \(w\) alone and a function of \(t\) alone:

\[f_{W,T}(w,t) = \underbrace{\left[\frac{w^{a-1}(1-w)^{b-1}}{B(a,b)}\right]}_{\text{Beta}(a,b)\text{ PDF in }w} \cdot \underbrace{\left[\frac{t^{a+b-1}e^{-t}}{\Gamma(a+b)}\right]}_{\text{Gamma}(a+b,1)\text{ PDF in }t}\]

using \(B(a,b) = \frac{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)}\).

Conclusion. \(W \sim \text{Beta}(a,b)\), \(T \sim \text{Gamma}(a+b,1)\), and they are independent. \(\blacksquare\)

Personal note: The independence is the shocking part. I wouldn't have guessed that \(W = X/(X+Y)\) "forgets" the total \(X+Y\). This is the same flavor of miracle as the Gamma–Poisson relationship.

docs.title: Corollary: \(\text{Beta}(1,1) = \text{Uniform}(0,1)\)
docs.text:
Since \(\text{Gamma}(1,1) = \text{Expo}(1)\), if \(X, Y \sim \text{Expo}(1)\) independent, then

\[\frac{X}{X+Y} \sim \text{Beta}(1,1) = \text{Uniform}(0,1)\]

This is a great sanity check. The Beta interpolates between the Uniform (both shape params = 1) and more concentrated distributions.

docs.title: The Beta Function Identity (proved via the transformation)
docs.text:
Corollary. \(B(a,b) = \dfrac{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)}\)

Proof. We know \(W \sim \text{Beta}(a,b)\) must integrate to 1:

\[\int_0^1 \frac{w^{a-1}(1-w)^{b-1}}{B(a,b)},dw = 1\]

So \(\int_0^1 w^{a-1}(1-w)^{b-1},dw = B(a,b)\).

On the other hand, integrate the joint PDF over all \(w \in (0,1)\) and \(t > 0\):

\[\int_0^\infty \int_0^1 f_{W,T}(w,t),dw,dt = 1\]

Separating and using that each marginal integrates to 1 forces \(\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b) = B(a,b),\Gamma(a+b)\). \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: Order Statistics of the Uniform: Another Beta
docs.text:
Theorem. Let \(U_1, \ldots, U_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \text{Uniform}(0,1)\). The \(k\)-th order statistic \(U_{(k)}\) satisfies

\[U_{(k)} \sim \text{Beta}(k,, n-k+1)\]

docs.title: Proof
docs.text:
The PDF of \(U_{(k)}\) is derived by the "sandwich" argument: the probability that \(U_{(k)} \in (x, x+dx)\) is the probability that exactly \(k-1\) observations fall below \(x\), one falls in \((x,x+dx)\), and \(n-k\) fall above \(x+dx\). There are \(\binom{n}{1}\binom{n-1}{k-1}\) ways to assign roles:

\[f_{U_{(k)}}(x) = \frac{n!}{(k-1)!(n-k)!} x^{k-1}(1-x)^{n-k}, \quad x \in (0,1)\]

Recognizing the Beta PDF with \(a = k\), \(b = n-k+1\):

\[U_{(k)} \sim \text{Beta}(k, n-k+1) \qquad \blacksquare\]

Why I love this. It connects the abstract Gamma-construction Beta to something completely concrete: sorting uniforms. The median of \(n\) uniforms (when \(n\) is odd, \(k = (n+1)/2\)) is Beta-distributed. This is a great fact to keep in my back pocket.

docs.title: Symmetry of the Beta
docs.text:
Proposition. If \(X \sim \text{Beta}(a,b)\), then \(1 - X \sim \text{Beta}(b,a)\).

Proof. Let \(Y = 1 - X\). The PDF of \(Y\) at \(y \in (0,1)\):

\[f_Y(y) = f_X(1-y) \cdot 1 = \frac{(1-y)^{a-1} y^{b-1}}{B(a,b)} = \frac{y^{b-1}(1-y)^{a-1}}{B(b,a)}\]

using \(B(a,b) = B(b,a)\) (by symmetry of the definition). So \(Y \sim \text{Beta}(b,a)\). \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: Moments
docs.text:
For \(X \sim \text{Beta}(a,b)\):

\[E[X] = \frac{a}{a+b}\] \[E[X^2] = \frac{a(a+1)}{(a+b)(a+b+1)}\] \[\text{Var}(X) = \frac{ab}{(a+b)^2(a+b+1)}\]

Proof of the mean. Using the Beta function:

\[E[X] = \frac{1}{B(a,b)} \int_0^1 x \cdot x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1},dx = \frac{B(a+1,b)}{B(a,b)} = \frac{\Gamma(a+1)\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a+b+1)\Gamma(a)} = \frac{a}{a+b} \qquad \blacksquare\]

The mean is just the "weight" of \(a\) relative to \(a+b\). Makes intuitive sense when thinking about Beta as a prior: if I've seen \(a\) successes and \(b\) failures, my posterior mean for \(p\) is \(a/(a+b)\).

docs.title: Quick Summary Table
docs.text: Result Statement Beta from Gammas \(X \sim \Gamma(a,1), Y \sim \Gamma(b,1)\) indep. \(\Rightarrow X/(X+Y) \sim \text{Beta}(a,b)\) Independence \(X/(X+Y) \perp X+Y\) Beta(1,1) \(= \text{Unif}(0,1)\) Order stats \(U_{(k)} \sim \text{Beta}(k, n-k+1)\) Symmetry \(X \sim \text{Beta}(a,b) \Rightarrow 1-X \sim \text{Beta}(b,a)\) Mean \(a/(a+b)\)

docs.title: Bayes Billiards
docs.text: "Bayes' first proof of his own theorem was a billiards table. He didn't think in terms of priors and likelihoods — he thought geometrically. The abstraction came later."

docs.title: The Setup
docs.text:
This is one of the oldest problems in Bayesian inference, essentially the argument Thomas Bayes used in his posthumous 1763 paper. It's a beautiful way to see where the Beta distribution comes from before you even know what Bayesian inference is.

The story:

Throw a ball \(W\) onto a billiards table of length 1. It lands at some position \(p \sim \text{Unif}(0,1)\) — we don't observe \(p\). Now throw \(n\) more balls. Each lands to the left of \(p\) with probability \(p\), independently. We observe \(X =\) number of balls landing left of \(p\).

Question: Given \(X = k\), what do we know about \(p\)?

This is Bayesian inference before the formalism. The "prior" on \(p\) is \(\text{Unif}(0,1) = \text{Beta}(1,1)\). The "likelihood" is Binomial. And the posterior — this is the punchline — is Beta.

docs.title: The Formal Model
docs.text:
\[p \sim \text{Unif}(0,1) = \text{Beta}(1,1)\] \[X \mid p \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)\]

We want: \(f_{p \mid X}(p \mid X = k)\).

docs.title: The Posterior: Full Derivation
docs.text:
By Bayes' theorem for continuous-discrete mixtures:

\[f_{p \mid X}(p \mid X = k) = \frac{P(X = k \mid p) \cdot f_p(p)}{P(X = k)}\]

Numerator:

\[P(X = k \mid p) \cdot f_p(p) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k} \cdot 1\]

Denominator: Integrate over \(p\):

\[P(X = k) = \int_0^1 \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k},dp = \binom{n}{k} B(k+1,, n-k+1)\]

Using \(B(a,b) = \frac{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)}\) and \(\Gamma(m) = (m-1)!\) for integers:

\[B(k+1, n-k+1) = \frac{k!,(n-k)!}{(n+1)!} = \frac{1}{(n+1)\binom{n}{k}}\]

So:

\[P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} \cdot \frac{1}{(n+1)\binom{n}{k}} = \frac{1}{n+1}\]

Stop and stare at this. No matter what \(k\) is, \(P(X = k) = 1/(n+1)\). Each of the \(n+1\) possible values \(0, 1, \ldots, n\) is equally likely. This is not obvious at all from the setup — it's a consequence of the Uniform prior.

The posterior:

\[f_{p \mid X = k}(p) = \frac{\binom{n}{k} p^k(1-p)^{n-k}}{1/(n+1)} = (n+1)\binom{n}{k}, p^k (1-p)^{n-k}\]

Recognize this: it's proportional to \(p^k(1-p)^{n-k} = p^{(k+1)-1}(1-p)^{(n-k+1)-1}\), which is the kernel of a \(\text{Beta}(k+1, n-k+1)\) density.

\[\boxed{p \mid X = k ;\sim; \text{Beta}(k+1,; n-k+1)}\]

\(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: Why \(P(X = k) = \frac{1}{n+1}\): A Cleaner Argument
docs.text:
There's a slicker way to see this without integrating. Consider \(n+1\) balls thrown uniformly and independently onto \([0,1]\). Label one of them \(W\) (our "threshold") and the rest \(B_1, \ldots, B_n\). By symmetry, all \((n+1)!\) orderings of the \(n+1\) balls are equally likely.

The event \(X = k\) is the event that exactly \(k\) of the \(B_i\)'s land to the left of \(W\), which is the same as \(W\) being the \((k+1)\)-th smallest among all \(n+1\) balls. There are \(n+1\) ranks, each equally likely by symmetry.

\[P(X = k) = \frac{1}{n+1}, \quad k = 0, 1, \ldots, n \qquad \blacksquare\]

This is the argument I want to remember. No integration required — just symmetry. Blitzstein would approve.

docs.title: The Beta-Binomial Conjugacy (General Case)
docs.text:
The Billiards problem is a special case of a general conjugacy:

Theorem (Beta-Binomial Conjugacy). If

\[p \sim \text{Beta}(a, b), \qquad X \mid p \sim \text{Bin}(n, p)\]

then

\[p \mid X = k ;\sim; \text{Beta}(a + k,; b + n - k)\]

docs.title: Proof
docs.text:
\[f_{p \mid X=k}(p) \propto P(X=k \mid p) \cdot f_p(p) = \binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k} \cdot \frac{p^{a-1}(1-p)^{b-1}}{B(a,b)}\] \[\propto p^{a+k-1}(1-p)^{b+n-k-1}\]

This is the kernel of \(\text{Beta}(a+k, b+n-k)\). \(\blacksquare\)

Interpretation:

Quantity Meaning Prior \(\text{Beta}(a,b)\) \(a-1\) prior "successes", \(b-1\) prior "failures" Observe \(k\) successes in \(n\) trials Update counts Posterior \(\text{Beta}(a+k, b+n-k)\) \(a+k-1\) total successes, \(b+n-k-1\) failures

The Beta is the conjugate prior for the Binomial. The prior and posterior live in the same family — you just add the data counts to the shape parameters.

The Billiards problem is the case \(a = b = 1\) (Uniform prior).

docs.title: The Posterior Mean and Shrinkage
docs.text:
From [[Beta Transformations]], \(E[\text{Beta}(a,b)] = a/(a+b)\). So:

\[E[p \mid X = k] = \frac{a+k}{a+b+n}\]

In the Billiards case (\(a=b=1\)):

\[E[p \mid X = k] = \frac{k+1}{n+2}\]

Compare to the MLE \(\hat{p}_{\text{MLE}} = k/n\). The Bayesian estimate is shrunk toward \(1/2\) (the prior mean). As \(n \to \infty\), the posterior mean \(\to k/n\): the data dominates.

This is Laplace's rule of succession: having seen \(k\) successes in \(n\) trials, the probability the next trial succeeds is \((k+1)/(n+2)\).

Classic example: a coin has come up heads every time in \(n\) flips. The MLE says \(p = 1\). Laplace says \(p = (n+1)/(n+2) < 1\). The Bayesian hedge is never 100% certain.

docs.title: Connection to Order Statistics
docs.text:
From [[Beta Transformations]]: if \(U_1, \ldots, U_{n+1} \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \text{Unif}(0,1)\), then \(U_{(k+1)} \sim \text{Beta}(k+1, n-k+1)\).

The Billiards posterior is an order statistic. Given that \(W\) is the \((k+1)\)-th order statistic among \(n+1\) Uniform draws, its distribution is \(\text{Beta}(k+1, n-k+1)\). The two perspectives (Bayesian update and order statistic) are the same thing.

docs.title: Predictive Distribution
docs.text:
What is \(P(\text{next ball lands left of } p \mid X = k)\)?

Let \(Y = \mathbf{1}[\text{next ball left of } p]\). Then:

\[P(Y = 1 \mid X = k) = E[p \mid X = k] = \frac{k+1}{n+2}\]

This is the posterior predictive probability. It's also Laplace's rule again.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Object Expression Prior \(p \sim \text{Beta}(1,1) = \text{Unif}(0,1)\) Likelihood \(X \mid p \sim \text{Bin}(n,p)\) Marginal of \(X\) \(X \sim \text{Unif}{0,1,\ldots,n}\), i.e. \(P(X=k) = 1/(n+1)\) Posterior \(p \mid X=k \sim \text{Beta}(k+1, n-k+1)\) Posterior mean \((k+1)/(n+2)\) Predictive probability \((k+1)/(n+2)\)

docs.title: Things to not forget
docs.text:
• The marginal \(P(X=k) = 1/(n+1)\) is the cleanest result and best proved by symmetry, not integration.
  • The Beta-Binomial conjugacy is the engine. Billiards is just the \(a=b=1\) case.
  • Posterior = prior + data. Literally: shape params add.
  • As \(n \to \infty\), the posterior concentrates at the true \(p\) — Bayesian and frequentist estimates agree in the limit.

docs.title: Gamma Transformations
docs.text: "The Gamma is the distribution you get when you stop asking 'did it happen?' and start asking 'how long until it happens \(n\) times?' Everything flows from that story."

docs.title: Why this note exists
docs.text:
The Gamma distribution is the backbone of a surprising amount of probability. The Exponential is a special case. The Chi-squared is a special case. The Beta comes from two Gammas (see [[05.Beta Transformations]]). The Normal's square is a Gamma. Almost every distribution I care about either is a Gamma or is built from one.

The transformations here are what let me move between all of them. Know these cold.

docs.title: Definition and PDF
docs.text:
\(X \sim \text{Gamma}(a, \lambda)\) has PDF

\[f(x) = \frac{\lambda^a}{\Gamma(a)} x^{a-1} e^{-\lambda x}, \quad x > 0\]

where \(a > 0\) is the shape and \(\lambda > 0\) is the rate.

The normalizing constant uses the Gamma function:

\[\Gamma(a) = \int_0^\infty t^{a-1} e^{-t},dt\]

Key facts I must know:

  • \(\Gamma(n) = (n-1)!\) for positive integers \(n\)
  • \(\Gamma(1/2) = \sqrt{\pi}\)
  • \(\Gamma(a+1) = a,\Gamma(a)\) — the functional equation, proved by integration by parts

Special cases:

  • \(\text{Gamma}(1, \lambda) = \text{Expo}(\lambda)\)
  • \(\text{Gamma}(n/2, 1/2) = \chi^2_n\) (chi-squared with \(n\) degrees of freedom)

docs.title: The Gamma Function Identity: \(\Gamma(a+1) = a,\Gamma(a)\)
docs.text:
Proof. Integrate by parts with \(u = t^a\), \(dv = e^{-t}dt\):

\[\Gamma(a+1) = \int_0^\infty t^a e^{-t},dt = \Big[-t^a e^{-t}\Big]_0^\infty + \int_0^\infty a t^{a-1} e^{-t},dt = 0 + a,\Gamma(a) \qquad \blacksquare\]

The boundary term vanishes since \(e^{-t}\) dominates any polynomial.

docs.title: Transformation 1: Scaling
docs.text:
Proposition. If \(X \sim \text{Gamma}(a, \lambda)\), then \(cX \sim \text{Gamma}(a, \lambda/c)\) for \(c > 0\).

Proof. Let \(Y = cX\), so \(x = y/c\), \(dx = dy/c\):

\[f_Y(y) = f_X(y/c) \cdot \frac{1}{c} = \frac{\lambda^a}{\Gamma(a)} \left(\frac{y}{c}\right)^{a-1} e^{-\lambda y/c} \cdot \frac{1}{c} = \frac{(\lambda/c)^a}{\Gamma(a)} y^{a-1} e^{-(\lambda/c)y} \qquad \blacksquare\]

Consequence: If \(X \sim \text{Gamma}(a, \lambda)\), then \(\lambda X \sim \text{Gamma}(a, 1)\).

So WLOG I can always work with rate 1 and scale at the end. This is why all my Gamma computations use \(\text{Gamma}(a,1)\).

docs.title: Transformation 2: Summation (Additive Reproduction)
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) are independent with \(X_i \sim \text{Gamma}(a_i, \lambda)\), then

\[X_1 + \cdots + X_n \sim \text{Gamma}(a_1 + \cdots + a_n,; \lambda)\]

Proof via MGF. The MGF of \(X \sim \text{Gamma}(a, \lambda)\) for \(t < \lambda\):

\[M_X(t) = E[e^{tX}] = \int_0^\infty e^{tx} \frac{\lambda^a}{\Gamma(a)} x^{a-1} e^{-\lambda x},dx = \frac{\lambda^a}{\Gamma(a)} \int_0^\infty x^{a-1} e^{-(\lambda - t)x},dx\]

Substitute \(u = (\lambda - t)x\):

\[= \frac{\lambda^a}{\Gamma(a)} \cdot \frac{\Gamma(a)}{(\lambda-t)^a} = \left(\frac{\lambda}{\lambda - t}\right)^a\]

For the sum \(S = \sum X_i\), by independence:

\[M_S(t) = \prod_{i=1}^n M_{X_i}(t) = \prod_{i=1}^n \left(\frac{\lambda}{\lambda-t}\right)^{a_i} = \left(\frac{\lambda}{\lambda-t}\right)^{\sum a_i}\]

This is the MGF of \(\text{Gamma}(\sum a_i, \lambda)\). By uniqueness of MGFs, \(S \sim \text{Gamma}(\sum a_i, \lambda)\). \(\blacksquare\)

Special case: \(n\) independent \(\text{Expo}(\lambda)\) random variables sum to \(\text{Gamma}(n, \lambda)\).

This is the "waiting for the \(n\)-th event" story. If each inter-arrival is \(\text{Expo}(\lambda)\), the time until the \(n\)-th arrival is \(\text{Gamma}(n, \lambda)\). Poisson process waiting times.

docs.title: Transformation 3: The Gamma–Beta Relationship
docs.text:
This is the deepest transformation. Full proof is in [[05.Beta Transformations]], but I'll record the statement and the key idea here.

Theorem. Let \(X \sim \text{Gamma}(a, 1)\) and \(Y \sim \text{Gamma}(b, 1)\) be independent. Then:

\[W = \frac{X}{X+Y} \sim \text{Beta}(a, b), \qquad T = X+Y \sim \text{Gamma}(a+b, 1)\]

and \(W \perp T\).

Key step: The Jacobian of \((x,y) \mapsto (w,t)\) where \(x = wt\), \(y=(1-w)t\) is \(|J| = t\), and the joint PDF factors as \(f_W(w) \cdot f_T(t)\).

This is the construction that:

  1. Proves the Beta function identity \(B(a,b) = \Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)/\Gamma(a+b)\)
  2. Gives a way to simulate Beta random variables from Gammas
  3. Explains why the Beta lives on \((0,1)\) — it's a ratio normalized by the total

docs.title: Transformation 4: Gamma and the Chi-Squared
docs.text:
Definition. \(\chi^2_n = \text{Gamma}(n/2,, 1/2)\).

Theorem. If \(Z \sim N(0,1)\), then \(Z^2 \sim \chi^2_1 = \text{Gamma}(1/2, 1/2)\).

Proof. Let \(Y = Z^2\). For \(y > 0\):

\[F_Y(y) = P(Z^2 \leq y) = P(-\sqrt{y} \leq Z \leq \sqrt{y}) = 2\Phi(\sqrt{y}) - 1\]

Differentiate:

\[f_Y(y) = 2\phi(\sqrt{y}) \cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-y/2} = \frac{(1/2)^{1/2}}{\Gamma(1/2)} y^{1/2 - 1} e^{-y/2}\]

using \(\Gamma(1/2) = \sqrt{\pi}\). This is \(\text{Gamma}(1/2, 1/2) = \chi^2_1\). \(\blacksquare\)

Corollary. If \(Z_1, \ldots, Z_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0,1)\), then \(\sum Z_i^2 \sim \chi^2_n\) by the additive property.

docs.title: Transformation 5: The Poisson Connection
docs.text:
Theorem. Let \(T_n \sim \text{Gamma}(n, \lambda)\) be the waiting time for the \(n\)-th Poisson event. Then

\[P(T_n > t) = P(N(t) \leq n-1)\]

where \(N(t) \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda t)\).

Proof. The \(n\)-th event occurs after time \(t\) if and only if fewer than \(n\) events have occurred by time \(t\):

\[P(T_n > t) = P(N(t) < n) = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \frac{e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda t)^k}{k!} \qquad \blacksquare\]

This is the Gamma–Poisson relationship. It lets me convert between a CDF I can't compute in closed form (Gamma CDF) and one I can (Poisson PMF, summed).

In practice: if I need \(P(\text{Gamma}(n,\lambda) > t)\) and \(n\) is an integer, I compute a Poisson tail sum instead. Huge computational shortcut.

docs.title: Moments
docs.text:
For \(X \sim \text{Gamma}(a, \lambda)\):

\[E[X] = \frac{a}{\lambda}, \qquad \text{Var}(X) = \frac{a}{\lambda^2}\]

More generally, the \(r\)-th moment:

\[E[X^r] = \frac{\Gamma(a+r)}{\Gamma(a),\lambda^r}\]

Proof of mean. Raise and lower the shape parameter by 1:

\[E[X] = \int_0^\infty x \cdot \frac{\lambda^a}{\Gamma(a)} x^{a-1} e^{-\lambda x},dx = \frac{\lambda^a}{\Gamma(a)} \int_0^\infty x^a e^{-\lambda x},dx = \frac{\lambda^a}{\Gamma(a)} \cdot \frac{\Gamma(a+1)}{\lambda^{a+1}} = \frac{a}{\lambda} \qquad \blacksquare\]

docs.title: The Log-Gamma and Digamma (just a note to self)
docs.text:
The digamma function \(\psi(a) = \Gamma'(a)/\Gamma(a) = \frac{d}{da}\log\Gamma(a)\) comes up when computing \(E[\log X]\) for \(X \sim \text{Gamma}(a,\lambda)\):

\[E[\log X] = \psi(a) - \log\lambda\]

I don't need this right now but I'll need it when I hit exponential families and sufficient statistics. Flag for later.

docs.title: Simulation Takeaways
docs.text:
• To simulate \(\text{Gamma}(n, \lambda)\) for integer \(n\): sum \(n\) independent \(\text{Expo}(\lambda)\) samples
  • To simulate \(\text{Beta}(a,b)\): simulate \(X \sim \text{Gamma}(a,1)\), \(Y \sim \text{Gamma}(b,1)\), return \(X/(X+Y)\)
  • These aren't tricks — they're the distributional identities made algorithmic

docs.title: Summary of Key Transformations
docs.text: Transformation Input Output Scaling \(X \sim \text{Gamma}(a,\lambda)\) \(cX \sim \text{Gamma}(a, \lambda/c)\) Standardizing \(X \sim \text{Gamma}(a,\lambda)\) \(\lambda X \sim \text{Gamma}(a,1)\) Summation \(X_i \sim \text{Gamma}(a_i, \lambda)\) indep. \(\sum X_i \sim \text{Gamma}(\sum a_i, \lambda)\) Expo special case \(X_i \sim \text{Expo}(\lambda)\) indep. \(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i \sim \text{Gamma}(n,\lambda)\) Gamma → Beta \(X \sim \Gamma(a,1), Y \sim \Gamma(b,1)\) indep. \(X/(X+Y) \sim \text{Beta}(a,b)\) Normal → Chi-sq \(Z \sim N(0,1)\) \(Z^2 \sim \chi^2_1 = \text{Gamma}(1/2, 1/2)\) Gamma–Poisson \(T_n \sim \text{Gamma}(n,\lambda)\) \(P(T_n > t) = P(\text{Pois}(\lambda t) \leq n-1)\)

docs.title: Gamma-Poisson Conjugacy
docs.text: "The Beta-Binomial pair asks: what is the probability of success? The Gamma-Poisson pair asks: at what rate do events arrive? Same Bayesian skeleton, different story."

docs.title: The Setup
docs.text:
In [[Bayes Billiards]] we put a prior on a probability \(p \in (0,1)\). Here the unknown is a rate \(\lambda \in (0, \infty)\) — how fast a Poisson process is firing. We observe counts and update.

The model:

\[\lambda \sim \text{Gamma}(a, b) \qquad \text{(prior on the rate)}\] \[X \mid \lambda \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda) \qquad \text{(one observation)}\]

We want the posterior \(f_{\lambda \mid X}(\lambda \mid X = k)\).

This is the Poisson analogue of [[Bayes Billiards]]. The punchline: the posterior is again a Gamma — the Gamma is conjugate to the Poisson.

docs.title: Why Gamma as a Prior on \(\lambda\)?
docs.text:
Two reasons:

  1. Support. \(\lambda > 0\), and so does \(\text{Gamma}(a,b)\). The Uniform on \((0,1)\) won't do here — we need a distribution on the positive reals.

  2. Conjugacy. As we'll prove, the posterior lands back in the Gamma family. This is the algebraic miracle that makes the update clean.

The hyperparameters \(a, b\) have interpretations I'll make precise after the proof.

Convention note: I'm using \(\text{Gamma}(a,b)\) with \(b\) as the rate parameter throughout this note, so the PDF is \(f(\lambda) = \frac{b^a}{\Gamma(a)}\lambda^{a-1}e^{-b\lambda}\). This matches Blitzstein. Don't mix up rate vs. scale.

docs.title: The Posterior: Full Derivation
docs.text:
By Bayes' theorem:

\[f_{\lambda \mid X=k}(\lambda) \propto P(X = k \mid \lambda) \cdot f_\lambda(\lambda)\]

Likelihood:

\[P(X = k \mid \lambda) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k}{k!}\]

Prior:

\[f_\lambda(\lambda) = \frac{b^a}{\Gamma(a)}\lambda^{a-1}e^{-b\lambda}\]

Multiply and drop constants in \(\lambda\):

\[f_{\lambda \mid X=k}(\lambda) \propto e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k \cdot \lambda^{a-1}e^{-b\lambda} = \lambda^{a+k-1} e^{-(b+1)\lambda}\]

Recognize the kernel: \(\lambda^{(a+k)-1}e^{-(b+1)\lambda}\) is exactly the kernel of \(\text{Gamma}(a+k,; b+1)\).

\[\boxed{\lambda \mid X = k ;\sim; \text{Gamma}(a + k,; b + 1)}\]

\(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: The General Case: \(n\) Observations
docs.text:
Now suppose \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \text{Poisson}(\lambda)\) and let \(S = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\).

Since \(X_i \mid \lambda\) are independent Poissons, the joint likelihood factors:

\[P(X_1 = x_1,\ldots,X_n = x_n \mid \lambda) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{x_i}}{x_i!} \propto e^{-n\lambda}\lambda^S\]

Multiplying by the prior kernel \(\lambda^{a-1}e^{-b\lambda}\):

\[f_{\lambda \mid \mathbf{X}}(\lambda) \propto \lambda^{a+S-1}e^{-(b+n)\lambda}\] \[\boxed{\lambda \mid X_1,\ldots,X_n ;\sim; \text{Gamma}(a + S,; b + n)}\]

where \(S = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) is the total observed count. \(\blacksquare\)

The shape absorbs the total count. The rate absorbs the number of observations. Perfectly symmetric and clean.

docs.title: Interpreting the Hyperparameters
docs.text:
The posterior \(\text{Gamma}(a+S, b+n)\) reveals exactly what \(a\) and \(b\) mean in the prior \(\text{Gamma}(a,b)\):

Hyperparameter Interpretation \(a\) Prior pseudo-counts — equivalent to having seen \(a\) events already \(b\) Prior pseudo-time — equivalent to having watched for \(b\) time units \(a/b\) Prior mean of \(\lambda\)

After seeing \(S\) events in \(n\) observations, update: \(a \to a+S\), \(b \to b+n\).

This is Bayesian updating as bookkeeping: just add the observed counts and observations to the prior counts.

docs.title: Posterior Mean and Shrinkage
docs.text:
\[E[\lambda \mid X_1,\ldots,X_n] = \frac{a+S}{b+n}\]

The MLE of \(\lambda\) is \(\hat\lambda_{\text{MLE}} = S/n = \bar X\).

Rewrite the posterior mean as a convex combination:

\[\frac{a+S}{b+n} = \frac{b}{b+n} \cdot \frac{a}{b} + \frac{n}{b+n} \cdot \frac{S}{n}\] \[= \underbrace{\frac{b}{b+n}}_{\text{prior weight}} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{a}{b}}_{\text{prior mean}} ;+; \underbrace{\frac{n}{b+n}}_{\text{data weight}} \cdot \underbrace{\bar X}_{\text{MLE}}\]

The posterior mean is a convex combination of the prior mean and the MLE. As \(n \to \infty\), the data weight \(\to 1\) and the posterior mean \(\to \bar X\). The prior washes out.

This shrinkage formula appears in every conjugate family — Beta-Binomial, Gamma-Poisson, Normal-Normal. It's the mathematical expression of "data eventually dominates belief." Internalize the pattern, not just the formula.

docs.title: The Marginal Distribution of \(X\): Negative Binomial
docs.text:
What is \(P(X = k)\) unconditionally, integrating \(\lambda\) out entirely?

\[P(X = k) = \int_0^\infty P(X=k \mid \lambda), f_\lambda(\lambda),d\lambda = \int_0^\infty \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k}{k!} \cdot \frac{b^a}{\Gamma(a)}\lambda^{a-1}e^{-b\lambda},d\lambda\] \[= \frac{b^a}{k!,\Gamma(a)} \int_0^\infty \lambda^{a+k-1} e^{-(b+1)\lambda},d\lambda = \frac{b^a}{k!,\Gamma(a)} \cdot \frac{\Gamma(a+k)}{(b+1)^{a+k}}\] \[= \frac{\Gamma(a+k)}{\Gamma(a),k!} \cdot \left(\frac{b}{b+1}\right)^a \cdot \left(\frac{1}{b+1}\right)^k\]

Setting \(p = b/(b+1)\), so \(1-p = 1/(b+1)\):

\[\boxed{X ;\sim; \text{NegBin}!\left(a,; \frac{b}{b+1}\right)}\] \[P(X = k) = \binom{a+k-1}{k} p^a (1-p)^k, \quad k = 0,1,2,\ldots\]

The Negative Binomial is the Poisson with a Gamma-distributed rate. This is the canonical model for overdispersed count data — situations where the variance exceeds the mean, which is impossible under a Poisson but natural once you admit uncertainty in \(\lambda\).

Proof that \(\text{Var}(X) > E[X]\). By the law of total variance:

\[\text{Var}(X) = E[\text{Var}(X\mid\lambda)] + \text{Var}(E[X\mid\lambda]) = E[\lambda] + \text{Var}(\lambda) = \frac{a}{b} + \frac{a}{b^2} > \frac{a}{b} = E[X]\]

The extra variance is entirely from uncertainty about \(\lambda\). Lovely. \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: The Predictive Distribution
docs.text:
Given \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) with \(S = \sum X_i\), the posterior is \(\text{Gamma}(a+S, b+n)\). What does the next observation look like?

By the same Gamma-Poisson marginalization with updated hyperparameters:

\[X_{n+1} \mid X_1,\ldots,X_n ;\sim; \text{NegBin}!\left(a+S,; \frac{b+n}{b+n+1}\right)\]

The predictive mean:

\[E[X_{n+1} \mid X_1,\ldots,X_n] = E\left[E[X_{n+1}\mid\lambda] \mid X_1,\ldots,X_n\right] = E[\lambda \mid X_1,\ldots,X_n] = \frac{a+S}{b+n}\]

The predictive mean is the posterior mean of \(\lambda\). This is always true when \(E[X\mid\lambda] = \lambda\).

docs.title: Jeffreys Prior for the Poisson
docs.text:
What's the "least informative" prior for \(\lambda\)? The Jeffreys prior is \(\pi(\lambda) \propto \sqrt{I(\lambda)}\) where \(I(\lambda)\) is the Fisher information.

For \(X \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)\), compute the score:

\[\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda}\log P(X=k;\lambda) = \frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda}(k\log\lambda - \lambda) = \frac{k}{\lambda} - 1 = \frac{X}{\lambda} - 1\]

Fisher information:

\[I(\lambda) = E\left[\left(\frac{X}{\lambda}-1\right)^2\right] = \frac{\text{Var}(X)}{\lambda^2} = \frac{\lambda}{\lambda^2} = \frac{1}{\lambda}\]

So the Jeffreys prior is:

\[\pi(\lambda) \propto \sqrt{\frac{1}{\lambda}} = \lambda^{-1/2} = \lambda^{1/2 - 1}e^{-0\cdot\lambda}\]

This is the kernel of \(\text{Gamma}(1/2, 0)\) — an improper prior (doesn't integrate to a finite constant). But the posterior after observing \(S\) events in \(n\) trials is:

\[\lambda \mid \mathbf{X} \sim \text{Gamma}(S + 1/2,; n)\]

which is proper as long as \(n > 0\).

Improper priors make me a little uncomfortable, but they're standard. The rule to always check: even if the prior is improper, verify the posterior is proper. Here it is. Good.

docs.title: Comparison: Beta-Binomial vs Gamma-Poisson
docs.text:
Beta-Binomial Gamma-Poisson Unknown \(p \in (0,1)\) \(\lambda \in (0,\infty)\) Prior \(\text{Beta}(a,b)\) \(\text{Gamma}(a,b)\) Likelihood \(\text{Bin}(n,p)\) \(\text{Poisson}(\lambda)\) Sufficient statistic \(k = \sum x_i\) \(S = \sum x_i\) Posterior \(\text{Beta}(a+k,; b+n-k)\) \(\text{Gamma}(a+S,; b+n)\) Marginal of \(X\) \(\text{Unif}{0,\ldots,n}\) (when \(a=b=1\)) \(\text{NegBin}(a,; b/(b+1))\) Posterior mean \(\frac{a+k}{a+b+n}\) \(\frac{a+S}{b+n}\) Jeffreys prior \(\text{Beta}(1/2,1/2)\) \(\text{Gamma}(1/2, 0)\) — improper

Same skeleton throughout.

docs.title: The General Mechanism: Exponential Family Conjugacy
docs.text:
Both the Beta-Binomial and Gamma-Poisson are instances of a single theorem. For any exponential family likelihood:

\[f(x \mid \eta) = h(x)\exp!\left(\eta, T(x) - A(\eta) ight)\]

the conjugate prior is:

\[\pi(\eta \mid \chi, u) \propto \exp!\left(\eta, \chi - u, A(\eta) ight)\]

and the posterior after \(n\) observations with sufficient statistic sum \(\sum T(x_i)\) is:

\[\pi!\left(\eta ;\middle|; \chi + extstyle\sum T(x_i),; u + n ight)\]

The update rule: add the sufficient statistic to \(\chi\), add \(n\) to \( u\). That's it.

For Poisson: \(\eta = \log\lambda\), \(T(x) = x\), \(A(\eta) = e^\eta = \lambda\). For Binomial: \(\eta = \log(p/(1-p))\), \(T(x) = x\), \(A(\eta) = n\log(1+e^\eta)\).

Come back to this properly when doing exponential families. For now: the pattern is the whole point. Both conjugacies are the same theorem wearing different clothes.

docs.title: Beta-Gamma Connections
docs.text: The moment I first saw this identity it felt like a cheat code. Two distributions that look completely unrelated turn out to be inseparable siblings. Write this down carefully — it's one of those facts that unlocks a dozen other proofs.

docs.title: The Cast
docs.text:
Recall the key players before diving in.

Gamma function (the continuous factorial): $\(\Gamma(a) = \int_0^\infty t^{a-1} e^{-t}, dt, \quad a > 0\)$

This satisfies \(\Gamma(a+1) = a,\Gamma(a)\) and \(\Gamma(n) = (n-1)!\) for positive integers. Think of it as the analytic extension of factorial that makes everything below work.

Beta function: $\(B(a,b) = \int_0^1 t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}, dt, \quad a,b > 0\)$

Gamma distribution \(X \sim \text{Gamma}(a, 1)\): $\(f_X(x) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(a)} x^{a-1} e^{-x}, \quad x > 0\)$

Beta distribution \(W \sim \text{Beta}(a,b)\): $\(f_W(w) = \frac{1}{B(a,b)} w^{a-1}(1-w)^{b-1}, \quad 0 < w < 1\)$

The normalizing constant \(B(a,b)\) is exactly what we need to compute — and the Gamma distributions will hand it to us for free.

docs.title: 1. The Key Identity
docs.text:
\[\boxed{B(a,b) = \frac{\Gamma(a),\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)}}\]

This is the fact. Everything else is either a proof or a consequence.

docs.title: 2. Proof via Independent Gamma RVs
docs.text:
This is my favourite proof. It's a trick, but the trick is natural once you see it.

Let \(X \sim \text{Gamma}(a,1)\) and \(Y \sim \text{Gamma}(b,1)\) be independent. Define the transformation:

\[W = \frac{X}{X+Y}, \qquad T = X + Y\]

Claim: \(W \sim \text{Beta}(a,b)\), \(T \sim \text{Gamma}(a+b, 1)\), and \(W \perp T\).

docs.title: 2.1 Setting Up the Change of Variables
docs.text:
The map \((x,y) \mapsto (w,t)\) is: $\(x = wt, \qquad y = (1-w)t\)$

with domain \(x,y > 0\) mapping to \(0 < w < 1\), \(t > 0\).

Jacobian: $\(\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(w,t)} = \begin{vmatrix} t & w \ -t & 1-w \end{vmatrix} = t(1-w) + wt = t\)$

So \(|J| = t\).

docs.title: 2.2 Joint Density of \((X,Y)\)
docs.text: By independence: $\(f_{X,Y}(x,y) = \frac{x^{a-1}e^{-x}}{\Gamma(a)} \cdot \frac{y^{b-1}e^{-y}}{\Gamma(b)}\)$

docs.title: 2.3 Joint Density of \((W,T)\)
docs.text:
Substitute \(x = wt\), \(y=(1-w)t\) and multiply by \(|J|=t\):

\[f_{W,T}(w,t) = \frac{(wt)^{a-1}e^{-wt}}{\Gamma(a)} \cdot \frac{((1-w)t)^{b-1}e^{-(1-w)t}}{\Gamma(b)} \cdot t\] \[= \frac{1}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}, w^{a-1}(1-w)^{b-1}, t^{a+b-1} e^{-t}\]

This factors into a function of \(w\) alone times a function of \(t\) alone — so \(W \perp T\) immediately.

Reading off: $\(f_T(t) = \frac{t^{a+b-1}e^{-t}}{\Gamma(a+b)}, \quad t > 0 \implies T \sim \text{Gamma}(a+b,1)\)$

\[f_W(w) \propto w^{a-1}(1-w)^{b-1}, \quad 0 < w < 1 \implies W \sim \text{Beta}(a,b)\]

docs.title: 2.4 Extracting the Identity
docs.text:
Since \(f_{W,T}\) must integrate to 1:

\[\int_0^1\int_0^\infty \frac{w^{a-1}(1-w)^{b-1} t^{a+b-1}e^{-t}}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}, dt, dw = 1\] \[\frac{1}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)} \underbrace{\int_0^1 w^{a-1}(1-w)^{b-1},dw}_{B(a,b)} \cdot \underbrace{\int_0^\infty t^{a+b-1}e^{-t},dt}_{\Gamma(a+b)} = 1\]

Therefore: $\(B(a,b),\Gamma(a+b) = \Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)\)$

\[\therefore \quad B(a,b) = \frac{\Gamma(a),\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)} \qquad \blacksquare\]

Notice what happened: we never had to evaluate \(B(a,b)\) directly. The normalisation of two Gamma densities did all the work. This is the probabilistic method at its finest — embed your integral in a probability space and let normalisation finish the job.

docs.title: 3. Alternative Proof: Direct Convolution
docs.text:
A more analytic route, less elegant but worth knowing. Connects to Blitzstein & Hwang §8.2.

We know \(T = X+Y \sim \text{Gamma}(a+b,1)\) via convolution (the MGF argument, or direct computation). So:

\[f_T(t) = \int_0^t \frac{u^{a-1}e^{-u}}{\Gamma(a)}\cdot\frac{(t-u)^{b-1}e^{-(t-u)}}{\Gamma(b)},du = \frac{e^{-t}}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}\int_0^t u^{a-1}(t-u)^{b-1},du\]

Substitute \(u = tw\):

\[= \frac{e^{-t}t^{a+b-1}}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)} \int_0^1 w^{a-1}(1-w)^{b-1},dw = \frac{e^{-t}t^{a+b-1}}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}, B(a,b)\]

But we also know \(f_T(t) = \dfrac{t^{a+b-1}e^{-t}}{\Gamma(a+b)}\). Matching:

\[\frac{B(a,b)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)} = \frac{1}{\Gamma(a+b)} \implies B(a,b) = \frac{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)} \qquad \blacksquare\]

docs.title: 4.1 Beta Normalising Constant is Now Explicit
docs.text:
We can write down the Beta PDF with full confidence:

\[f_W(w) = \frac{\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}, w^{a-1}(1-w)^{b-1}\]

No more hand-wavy "proportional to." The constant is computed.

docs.title: 4.2 Integer Parameters: Clean Combinatorial Form
docs.text:
For positive integers \(a,b\):

\[B(a,b) = \frac{(a-1)!,(b-1)!}{(a+b-1)!} = \frac{1}{(a+b-1)\binom{a+b-2}{a-1}}\]

docs.title: 4.3 Order Statistics Connection
docs.text:
If \(U_{(k)}\) is the \(k\)-th order statistic of \(n\) i.i.d. \(\text{Uniform}(0,1)\) RVs, then:

\[U_{(k)} \sim \text{Beta}(k,, n-k+1)\]

The PDF is: $\(f_{U_{(k)}}(u) = \frac{n!}{(k-1)!(n-k)!}, u^{k-1}(1-u)^{n-k}\)$

The normalising constant checks out via: \(B(k, n-k+1) = \dfrac{(k-1)!(n-k)!}{n!}\). ✓

This is worth meditating on. The \(k\)-th order statistic "lives" at position \(k/(n+1)\) on average — and the Beta distribution captures the full uncertainty around that position. Beautiful.

docs.title: 4.4 Symmetry
docs.text:
\[B(a,b) = B(b,a)\]

Obvious from the Gamma formula (multiplication commutes). Also obvious geometrically: substitute \(t \mapsto 1-t\) in the integral definition.

docs.title: 5. The Aggregation Property (Bonus)
docs.text:
This fell out of the proof as a gift — don't skip it.

If \(X \sim \text{Gamma}(a,1)\), \(Y \sim \text{Gamma}(b,1)\) independent, then \(X + Y \sim \text{Gamma}(a+b,1)\).

Proof: We showed \(T \sim \text{Gamma}(a+b,1)\) above. This generalises: Gamma distributions with the same rate parameter are closed under addition. The shape parameters add. The rate stays fixed.

This is the Gamma analogue of "sum of Poissons is Poisson" — and there's a deep reason: Poisson processes.

docs.title: 6. Key Intuition to Carry Forward
docs.text:
The substitution \(W = X/(X+Y)\), \(T = X+Y\) is doing something profound:

  • \(T\) captures the total size (scale information)
  • \(W\) captures the proportion (shape/direction information)

The fact that \(W \perp T\) says: knowing the total tells you nothing about how it splits. This is a characterisation of the Gamma distribution — if \(W\) and \(T\) are independent under this split, then \(X\) and \(Y\) must be Gamma. (The Lukacs theorem.)

docs.title: 7. Connections Map
docs.text:
Gamma(a,1) + Gamma(b,1)
        |
        | (W = X/(X+Y), T = X+Y)
        |
   _____|_____
  |           |
Beta(a,b)   Gamma(a+b,1)
  |
  |--- Order statistics: U_(k) ~ Beta(k, n-k+1)
  |--- Bayesian conjugacy: Beta-Binomial model
  |--- Dirichlet generalisation (multivariate Beta)

docs.title: Beta Expectations
docs.text: Once you have \(B(a,b) = \Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)/\Gamma(a+b)\), computing moments of the Beta is almost embarrassingly easy. The whole game is recognising that the integral you're staring at is just another Beta function in disguise. This note is short because the proofs are short — and that's the point.

docs.title: 0. Setup
docs.text:
\(W \sim \text{Beta}(a,b)\), so: $\(f_W(w) = \frac{\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}, w^{a-1}(1-w)^{b-1}, \quad 0 < w < 1\)$

All moments live in \([0,1]\) — which should pass the sanity check immediately since \(W\) is supported on \((0,1)\).

docs.title: 1. The \(n\)-th Moment (Raw)
docs.text:
\[\mathbb{E}[W^n] = \int_0^1 w^n \cdot \frac{\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}, w^{a-1}(1-w)^{b-1}, dw\] \[= \frac{\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)} \int_0^1 w^{(a+n)-1}(1-w)^{b-1}, dw\]

The integral is exactly \(B(a+n,, b)\). So:

\[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[W^n] = \frac{\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)} \cdot \frac{\Gamma(a+n),\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b+n)}}\] \[= \frac{\Gamma(a+n)}{\Gamma(a)} \cdot \frac{\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a+b+n)}\]

The trick is always the same: absorb the extra \(w^n\) into the exponent, recognise a Beta integral, apply the identity. You will use this move constantly.

This has a clean form using the rising factorial (Pochhammer symbol) \(a^{(n)} = a(a+1)\cdots(a+n-1) = \Gamma(a+n)/\Gamma(a)\):

\[\mathbb{E}[W^n] = \frac{a^{(n)}}{(a+b)^{(n)}}\]

For \(n=1,2\) this gives everything we need below.

docs.title: 2. Mean
docs.text:
Set \(n=1\):

\[\mathbb{E}[W] = \frac{\Gamma(a+1)}{\Gamma(a)} \cdot \frac{\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a+b+1)} = a \cdot \frac{1}{a+b}\] \[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[W] = \frac{a}{a+b}}\]

Sanity checks:

  • \(a = b\): mean is \(1/2\) ✓ (symmetric distribution, symmetric mean)
  • \(a \gg b\): mean \(\to 1\) ✓ (weight pushed toward 1)
  • \(\text{Beta}(1,1) = \text{Uniform}(0,1)\): mean \(= 1/2\) ✓

Intuition from the Gamma construction. Recall \(W = X/(X+Y)\) where \(X \sim \text{Gamma}(a,1)\), \(Y \sim \text{Gamma}(b,1)\) independent. We know \(\mathbb{E}[X] = a\) and \(\mathbb{E}[Y] = b\). Naively you might guess \(\mathbb{E}[W] \approx a/(a+b)\) — and it's exactly right. (This is not obvious from Jensen since \(g(x,y) = x/(x+y)\) is nonlinear, but the Gamma structure makes it work out cleanly.)

docs.title: 3. Second Moment
docs.text:
Set \(n=2\):

\[\mathbb{E}[W^2] = \frac{\Gamma(a+2)}{\Gamma(a)} \cdot \frac{\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a+b+2)} = a(a+1) \cdot \frac{1}{(a+b)(a+b+1)}\] \[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[W^2] = \frac{a(a+1)}{(a+b)(a+b+1)}}\]

docs.title: 4. Variance
docs.text:
\[\text{Var}(W) = \mathbb{E}[W^2] - (\mathbb{E}[W])^2 = \frac{a(a+1)}{(a+b)(a+b+1)} - \frac{a^2}{(a+b)^2}\]

Let \(s = a+b\) for cleanliness. Then:

\[\text{Var}(W) = \frac{a(a+1)}{s(s+1)} - \frac{a^2}{s^2} = \frac{a}{s}\left[\frac{a+1}{s+1} - \frac{a}{s}\right]\] \[= \frac{a}{s} \cdot \frac{s(a+1) - a(s+1)}{s(s+1)} = \frac{a}{s} \cdot \frac{as + s - as - a}{s(s+1)} = \frac{a}{s} \cdot \frac{b}{s(s+1)}\] \[\boxed{\text{Var}(W) = \frac{ab}{(a+b)^2(a+b+1)}}\]

Reading the formula:

  • Numerator \(ab\): variance is maximised when \(a = b\) (most spread), killed when either parameter \(\to \infty\) relative to the other.
  • Denominator grows as \((a+b)^3\) for large \(a+b\): adding more "pseudodata" concentrates the distribution. This is the Bayesian intuition — more prior observations, tighter posterior.
  • For \(\text{Beta}(1,1)\): \(\text{Var} = 1/(4 \cdot 3) = 1/12\). Check: \(\text{Var}(\text{Uniform}(0,1)) = 1/12\) ✓

docs.title: 5. Summary Table
docs.text: Quantity Formula \(\mathbb{E}[W^n]\) \(\dfrac{a(a+1)\cdots(a+n-1)}{(a+b)(a+b+1)\cdots(a+b+n-1)}\) \(\mathbb{E}[W]\) \(\dfrac{a}{a+b}\) \(\mathbb{E}[W^2]\) \(\dfrac{a(a+1)}{(a+b)(a+b+1)}\) \(\text{Var}(W)\) \(\dfrac{ab}{(a+b)^2(a+b+1)}\)

docs.title: 6. Beta-Binomial: Where This Actually Lives
docs.text:
This is why I care about these moments.

Suppose \(W \sim \text{Beta}(a,b)\) and \(X \mid W \sim \text{Binomial}(n, W)\). This is the Beta-Binomial model — the Beta is a prior on the unknown probability \(p\).

By Adam's Law (LTE): $\(\mathbb{E}[X] = \mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[X \mid W]] = \mathbb{E}[nW] = n \cdot \frac{a}{a+b}\)$

By Eve's Law (LTVE): $\(\text{Var}(X) = \mathbb{E}[\text{Var}(X\mid W)] + \text{Var}(\mathbb{E}[X\mid W])\)$ $\(= \mathbb{E}[nW(1-W)] + \text{Var}(nW)\)$ $\(= n\left(\mathbb{E}[W] - \mathbb{E}[W^2]\right) + n^2,\text{Var}(W)\)$ $\(= n\left(\frac{a}{a+b} - \frac{a(a+1)}{(a+b)(a+b+1)}\right) + n^2 \cdot \frac{ab}{(a+b)^2(a+b+1)}\)$

The first term simplifies (factor out \(a/(a+b)\)):

\[\frac{a}{a+b}\left(1 - \frac{a+1}{a+b+1}\right) = \frac{a}{a+b}\cdot\frac{b}{a+b+1} = \frac{ab}{(a+b)(a+b+1)}\]

So: $\(\text{Var}(X) = \frac{nab}{(a+b)(a+b+1)} + \frac{n^2 ab}{(a+b)^2(a+b+1)} = \frac{nab}{(a+b)(a+b+1)}\left(1 + \frac{n}{a+b}\right) \cdot \frac{a+b}{a+b}\)$

Actually, let me write it cleanly. Set \(s = a+b\):

\[\boxed{\text{Var}(X) = \frac{nab(n+s)}{s^2(s+1)}}\]

Compare to \(\text{Binomial}(n,p)\) with fixed \(p = a/s\): that has variance \(np(1-p) = nab/s^2\). The Beta-Binomial variance has the extra factor \((n+s)/(s+1) > 1\) — it's overdispersed relative to the Binomial. The uncertainty in \(W\) inflates the variance. More prior "data" (large \(s\)) reduces this inflation.

docs.title: 7. The Bayesian Posterior Mean
docs.text:
One more thing worth recording here.

In the Beta-Binomial model: observe \(X = k\) successes in \(n\) trials. The posterior is:

\[W \mid X=k \sim \text{Beta}(a+k,, b+n-k)\]

Posterior mean: $\(\mathbb{E}[W \mid X=k] = \frac{a+k}{a+b+n}\)$

This is a weighted average of the prior mean \(a/(a+b)\) and the MLE \(k/n\):

\[\frac{a+k}{a+b+n} = \frac{a+b}{a+b+n}\cdot\frac{a}{a+b} + \frac{n}{a+b+n}\cdot\frac{k}{n}\]

As \(n \to \infty\), weight shifts entirely to the data. As \(a+b \to \infty\), the prior dominates. The moments of the Beta are doing Bayesian inference.

docs.title: Order Statistics
docs.text: Order statistics are one of those topics where the setup looks annoying — sorting random variables, tracking ranks — and then suddenly everything clicks and you realise the Beta distribution has been lurking here all along. The connection to Beta is not a coincidence; it's the whole story.

docs.title: 0. Setup
docs.text:
Let \(U_1, U_2, \ldots, U_n \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{Uniform}(0,1)\). Sort them:

\[U_{(1)} \leq U_{(2)} \leq \cdots \leq U_{(n)}\]

\(U_{(k)}\) is the \(k\)-th order statistic — the \(k\)-th smallest value. These are no longer independent (obviously: knowing \(U_{(1)}\) tells you something about \(U_{(2)}\)), and they are no longer Uniform.

We start with Uniforms because the CDF is trivial: \(F(u) = u\). Everything for general continuous RVs follows by the universality of the Uniform (probability integral transform). So Uniform is the right place to build the theory.

docs.title: 1. The CDF of \(U_{(k)}\)
docs.text:
Event: \({U_{(k)} \leq u}\) means at least \(k\) of the \(n\) variables fall in \([0,u]\).

Each \(U_i \leq u\) with probability \(u\), independently. So the count \(#{i : U_i \leq u} \sim \text{Binomial}(n, u)\).

\[\boxed{F_{U_{(k)}}(u) = P(U_{(k)} \leq u) = \sum_{j=k}^{n} \binom{n}{j} u^j (1-u)^{n-j}}\]

This is \(P(\text{Bin}(n,u) \geq k)\) — a tail probability of the Binomial. Useful for computation, but the PDF is cleaner.

docs.title: 2. The PDF of \(U_{(k)}\)
docs.text:
Differentiate the CDF. There's a slicker route: use a heuristic counting argument that gives the right answer and is perfectly rigorous in the limit.

Heuristic. For small \(du > 0\), \(P(U_{(k)} \in (u, u+du))\) is the probability that:

  • exactly \(k-1\) of the \(n\) variables fall in \([0,u]\),
  • exactly \(1\) falls in \((u, u+du)\),
  • the remaining \(n-k\) fall in \((u+du, 1]\).

Multinomial count times the probabilities:

\[\frac{n!}{(k-1)!,1!,(n-k)!} \cdot u^{k-1} \cdot du \cdot (1-u)^{n-k}\]

So:

\[\boxed{f_{U_{(k)}}(u) = \frac{n!}{(k-1)!(n-k)!}, u^{k-1}(1-u)^{n-k}, \quad 0 < u < 1}\]

Recognition: This is \(\text{Beta}(k,, n-k+1)\).

The normalising constant checks out via [[Beta-Gamma Connections]]:

\[B(k,, n-k+1) = \frac{\Gamma(k),\Gamma(n-k+1)}{\Gamma(n+1)} = \frac{(k-1)!,(n-k)!}{n!} \qquad \checkmark\]

So \(U_{(k)} \sim \text{Beta}(k, n-k+1)\). This is the theorem to remember. The multinomial argument is the proof. Everything else — mean, variance, joint density — flows from here.

docs.title: 3. Mean and Variance of \(U_{(k)}\)
docs.text:
Immediate from [[Beta Expectations]]:

\[\mathbb{E}[U_{(k)}] = \frac{k}{n+1}\] \[\text{Var}(U_{(k)}) = \frac{k(n-k+1)}{(n+1)^2(n+2)}\]

The mean formula \(k/(n+1)\) is beautiful. The \(n\) order statistics divide \([0,1]\) into \(n+1\) equal-length intervals on average. They are evenly spaced in expectation.

Intuition: by symmetry, the \(n+1\) gaps \(U_{(1)}, U_{(2)}-U_{(1)}, \ldots, 1-U_{(n)}\) are exchangeable (they are — this is the spacing result below), so each has mean \(1/(n+1)\), and \(\mathbb{E}[U_{(k)}] = k \cdot 1/(n+1)\).

Variance: peaks at \(k = (n+1)/2\) (middle order statistic is most uncertain), goes to 0 at the extremes as \(n \to \infty\) relative to fixed \(k\).

docs.title: 4. Joint Density of All Order Statistics
docs.text:
Theorem. The joint PDF of \((U_{(1)}, \ldots, U_{(n)})\) is:

\[f_{U_{(1)},\ldots,U_{(n)}}(u_1,\ldots,u_n) = n!, \quad 0 < u_1 < u_2 < \cdots < u_n < 1\]

Proof. There are \(n!\) orderings of \((U_1,\ldots,U_n)\). Each ordering is equally likely by symmetry (\(U_i\) are i.i.d.). Each ordering corresponds to exactly one point in the simplex \({0 < u_1 < \cdots < u_n < 1}\), which has volume \(1/n!\). So the joint density on this simplex must be \(n!\) (to integrate to 1). \(\blacksquare\)
