docs.title: N-step Transition
docs.text: "The \(n\)-step transition matrix is \(Q^n\). That's the whole story. Everything else in this note is just making sure I believe it and know how to use it."

docs.title: Why This Note Exists
docs.text:
The previous note ([[Markov Chains — Definitions and Transition Matrix]]) established the one-step transition matrix \(Q\). The entry \(q_{ij}\) tells me where the chain goes in a single step. But I immediately want to ask: what about \(n\) steps? If I'm at state \(i\) right now, where am I likely to be after \(n\) transitions?

The answer — that the \(n\)-step transition matrix is literally \(Q^n\), the matrix power — is one of those results that feels too clean to be true. This note is my attempt to be completely rigorous about why it's true, what it implies, and how I actually use it.

docs.title: Setup and Notation
docs.text:
\((X_n)_{n \geq 0}\) is a time-homogeneous Markov chain on a finite state space \(\mathcal{S} = {1, \ldots, M}\) with transition matrix \(Q\).

Definition. The \(n\)-step transition probability from state \(i\) to state \(j\) is:

\[q_{ij}^{(n)} := P(X_n = j \mid X_0 = i)\]

More generally, by time-homogeneity:

\[q_{ij}^{(n)} = P(X_{m+n} = j \mid X_m = i) \quad \text{for any } m \geq 0\]

The \(n\)-step transition matrix is \(Q^{(n)} = \bigl(q_{ij}^{(n)}\bigr)_{i,j \in \mathcal{S}}\).

Boundary case: \(Q^{(0)} = I\), the identity matrix — in zero steps, I stay where I am with probability 1.

Boundary case: \(Q^{(1)} = Q\) — this just recovers the original definition.

docs.title: The Chapman-Kolmogorov Equations
docs.text: This is the engine. Everything else follows from it.

docs.title: Theorem (Chapman-Kolmogorov)
docs.text:
For all \(m, n \geq 0\) and all states \(i, j \in \mathcal{S}\):

\[q_{ij}^{(m+n)} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{S}} q_{ik}^{(m)} , q_{kj}^{(n)}\]

In matrix form:

\[Q^{(m+n)} = Q^{(m)} , Q^{(n)}\]

docs.title: Proof
docs.text:
Condition on the intermediate state \(X_m\):

\[P(X_{m+n} = j \mid X_0 = i) = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{S}} P(X_{m+n} = j \mid X_m = k, X_0 = i) \cdot P(X_m = k \mid X_0 = i)\]

Now apply the Markov property: given \(X_m = k\), the future \(X_{m+n}\) is independent of the past \(X_0 = i\). So:

\[P(X_{m+n} = j \mid X_m = k, X_0 = i) = P(X_{m+n} = j \mid X_m = k) = q_{kj}^{(n)}\]

Substituting:

\[q_{ij}^{(m+n)} = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{S}} q_{ik}^{(m)} \cdot q_{kj}^{(n)}\]

The right-hand side is precisely the \((i,j)\) entry of the matrix product \(Q^{(m)} Q^{(n)}\). \(\blacksquare\)

The Markov property does exactly one thing in this proof: it collapses the three-event conditional into a two-event conditional. Without it, I'd be stuck — the past \(X_0 = i\) would pollute the future computation. With it, the sum over intermediate states \(k\) decomposes cleanly.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
The \(n\)-step transition matrix equals the \(n\)-th matrix power of \(Q\):

\[Q^{(n)} = Q^n\]

docs.title: Proof
docs.text:
By induction on \(n\).

Base cases: \(Q^{(0)} = I = Q^0\) and \(Q^{(1)} = Q = Q^1\). ✓

Inductive step: Suppose \(Q^{(n)} = Q^n\). Apply Chapman-Kolmogorov with \(m = n\), \(n = 1\):

\[Q^{(n+1)} = Q^{(n)} \cdot Q^{(1)} = Q^n \cdot Q = Q^{n+1}\]

\(\blacksquare\)

This is it. This is the theorem. To find the probability of going from state \(i\) to state \(j\) in exactly \(n\) steps, look at the \((i,j)\) entry of \(Q^n\).

I want to pause and appreciate this. The Chapman-Kolmogorov equations say that multi-step transitions compose like matrix multiplication. That's not a coincidence — it IS matrix multiplication. The entire spectral theory of matrices (eigendecompositions, diagonalization, Jordan forms) now applies to Markov chains. Linear algebra is not just a computational tool here; it's the right language.

docs.title: The Distribution at Time \(n\)
docs.text: Let \(\mathbf{t}^{(0)}\) be the initial distribution — a row vector with \(t^{(0)}_i = P(X_0 = i)\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
\[\mathbf{t}^{(n)} = \mathbf{t}^{(0)} Q^n\]

where \(t^{(n)}_j = P(X_n = j)\).

docs.title: Proof
docs.text:
By the Law of Total Probability (conditioning on \(X_0\)):

\[P(X_n = j) = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} P(X_n = j \mid X_0 = i) \cdot P(X_0 = i) = \sum_i t^{(0)}_i \cdot (Q^n)_{ij}\]

This is exactly the \(j\)-th entry of the row vector \(\mathbf{t}^{(0)} Q^n\). \(\blacksquare\)

One-step recursion: \(\mathbf{t}^{(n+1)} = \mathbf{t}^{(n)} Q\).

This recursion is useful for computation: if I know where the chain is at time \(n\), left-multiply by \(Q\) to get the distribution at time \(n+1\).

The row-vector convention: B&H and Stat 110 use row vectors left-multiplied by \(Q\). Some other texts use column vectors right-multiplied by \(Q^\top\). The math is identical; just be consistent. I'll always use the row convention.

docs.title: Computing \(Q^n\) in Practice
docs.text: For small matrices and small \(n\), just multiply. For large \(n\) or symbolic computation, diagonalization is the tool.

docs.title: Diagonalization (When Available)
docs.text:
Suppose \(Q\) is diagonalizable:

\[Q = P D P^{-1}\]

where \(D = \text{diag}(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_M)\) holds the eigenvalues and \(P\) holds the eigenvectors as columns. Then:

\[Q^n = P D^n P^{-1}, \qquad D^n = \text{diag}(\lambda_1^n, \ldots, \lambda_M^n)\]

Raising a diagonal matrix to a power is trivial — just raise each diagonal entry to the \(n\)-th power.

Explicit formula for two-state chain:

\[Q = \begin{pmatrix} 1-\alpha & \alpha \ \beta & 1-\beta \end{pmatrix}\]

The eigenvalues are \(\lambda_1 = 1\) and \(\lambda_2 = 1 - \alpha - \beta\) (I'll derive this below). The \(n\)-step matrix is:

\[Q^n = \frac{1}{\alpha+\beta}\begin{pmatrix} \beta & \alpha \ \beta & \alpha \end{pmatrix} + \frac{(1-\alpha-\beta)^n}{\alpha+\beta} \begin{pmatrix} \alpha & -\alpha \ -\beta & \beta \end{pmatrix}\]

As \(n \to \infty\), \((1-\alpha-\beta)^n \to 0\) (since \(|\lambda_2| < 1\) when \(\alpha, \beta \in (0,1)\)), and both rows converge to the stationary distribution \(\bigl(\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta}, \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}\bigr)\).

This is the convergence to stationarity in miniature. The second eigenvalue \(\lambda_2\) decays exponentially, and its rate of decay determines how quickly the rows of \(Q^n\) equalize. The spectral gap \(1 - |\lambda_2| = \alpha + \beta\) controls everything.

docs.title: Derivation of Eigenvalues for the Two-State Chain
docs.text:
\[\det(Q - \lambda I) = (1-\alpha-\lambda)(1-\beta-\lambda) - \alpha\beta = 0\]

Expand:

\[(1-\alpha-\lambda)(1-\beta-\lambda) - \alpha\beta = \lambda^2 - (2-\alpha-\beta)\lambda + (1-\alpha-\beta) = 0\]

Factor: \((\lambda - 1)(\lambda - (1-\alpha-\beta)) = 0\), giving \(\lambda_1 = 1\), \(\lambda_2 = 1 - \alpha - \beta\).

docs.title: The Spectral Picture of \(Q^n\)
docs.text:
For a general finite-state chain, if \(Q\) has eigenvalues \(1 = \lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots, \lambda_M\) and is diagonalizable with left eigenvectors \({\mathbf{v}_k}\) and right eigenvectors \({\mathbf{u}_k}\):

\[Q^n = \sum_{k=1}^{M} \lambda_k^n , \mathbf{u}_k \mathbf{v}_k^\top\]

Key facts about eigenvalues of a row-stochastic matrix:

  • \(\lambda_1 = 1\) always. (Since \(Q\mathbf{1} = \mathbf{1}\), the all-ones vector is a right eigenvector with eigenvalue 1. By Perron-Frobenius, this is the largest eigenvalue.)
  • All eigenvalues satisfy \(|\lambda_k| \leq 1\) — they lie in the closed unit disk.
  • For an irreducible aperiodic chain: \(\lambda_1 = 1\) is the unique eigenvalue with modulus 1. All others satisfy \(|\lambda_k| < 1\).

Long-run behavior: As \(n \to \infty\), all terms with \(|\lambda_k| < 1\) vanish:

\[Q^n \longrightarrow \mathbf{1} \mathbf{s}\]

where \(\mathbf{s}\) is the stationary distribution (the left eigenvector corresponding to \(\lambda_1 = 1\), normalized to sum to 1). The \((i,j)\) entry of \(Q^n\) converges to \(s_j\) — independent of the starting state \(i\).

Rate of convergence:

\[\bigl|Q^n - \mathbf{1}\mathbf{s}\bigr| \sim C \cdot |\lambda_2|^n\]

The spectral gap is \(\gamma = 1 - |\lambda_2|\). A large spectral gap \(\Rightarrow\) fast convergence. Maximizing the spectral gap is the core problem in the theory of mixing times, and it connects Markov chain theory to expander graphs, random walks on groups, and the analysis of MCMC algorithms.

I find the spectral picture genuinely beautiful. The eigenvalue \(\lambda_1 = 1\) is the "memory" that the chain retains forever — it's the stationary behavior. Every other eigenvalue is a "mode of forgetting" with timescale \(-1/\log|\lambda_k|\). The chain forgets its initial condition one mode at a time, fastest last.

docs.title: Worked Example: Three-State Chain
docs.text:
Let \(\mathcal{S} = {1, 2, 3}\) with transition matrix:

\[Q = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1/2 & 1/2 \ 1/3 & 1/3 & 1/3 \ 1/2 & 1/2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\]

What is \(P(X_2 = 3 \mid X_0 = 1)\)?

I need the \((1,3)\) entry of \(Q^2\). Compute \(Q^2 = Q \cdot Q\):

The \((1,3)\) entry of \(Q^2\):

\[q_{13}^{(2)} = q_{11} q_{13} + q_{12} q_{23} + q_{13} q_{33} = 0 \cdot \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{2} \cdot 0 = \frac{1}{6}\]

So \(P(X_2 = 3 \mid X_0 = 1) = \frac{1}{6}\).

Alternatively, by Chapman-Kolmogorov directly: sum over intermediate states at time 1:

\[P(X_2 = 3 \mid X_0 = 1) = \sum_{k=1}^{3} P(X_1 = k \mid X_0 = 1) \cdot P(X_2 = 3 \mid X_1 = k)$$ $$= \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{3} + ... \]

Wait — let me redo this carefully:

\[= P(X_1=1|X_0=1) \cdot q_{13} + P(X_1=2|X_0=1) \cdot q_{23} + P(X_1=3|X_0=1) \cdot q_{33}$$ $$= 0 \cdot \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{2} \cdot 0 = \frac{1}{6}\]

Both methods agree. ✓ The Chapman-Kolmogorov approach is just the matrix product written out explicitly.

docs.title: The \(n\)-Step Distribution is Still Row-Stochastic
docs.text:
Claim: For each \(n \geq 0\), the matrix \(Q^n\) is row-stochastic.

Proof: By induction. \(Q^0 = I\) is row-stochastic (trivially). If \(Q^n\) is row-stochastic, then:

\[\sum_j (Q^{n+1})_{ij} = \sum_j \sum_k (Q^n)_{ik} q_{kj} = \sum_k (Q^n)_{ik} \underbrace{\sum_j q_{kj}}_{=1} = \sum_k (Q^n)_{ik} = 1\]

where the last equality uses that \(Q^n\) is row-stochastic. \(\blacksquare\)

This is good to verify: every row of \(Q^n\) is a valid probability distribution, as it should be — it's the conditional distribution of \(X_n\) given \(X_0 = i\).

docs.title: Connection to the Stationary Distribution
docs.text:
A row vector \(\mathbf{s}\) is stationary if \(\mathbf{s} Q = \mathbf{s}\), equivalently \(\mathbf{s} Q^n = \mathbf{s}\) for all \(n\).

This follows immediately: if \(\mathbf{s} Q = \mathbf{s}\), then \(\mathbf{s} Q^2 = (\mathbf{s} Q) Q = \mathbf{s} Q = \mathbf{s}\), and by induction \(\mathbf{s} Q^n = \mathbf{s}\).

Conversely, the convergence \(Q^n \to \mathbf{1s}\) says: starting from any initial distribution \(\mathbf{t}^{(0)}\),

\[\mathbf{t}^{(n)} = \mathbf{t}^{(0)} Q^n \to \mathbf{t}^{(0)} \mathbf{1} \mathbf{s} = \mathbf{s}\]

since \(\mathbf{t}^{(0)} \mathbf{1} = \sum_i t^{(0)}_i = 1\). The chain converges in distribution to \(\mathbf{s}\) regardless of where it started. The \(n\)-step transition matrix is the bridge between the initial distribution and stationarity.

docs.title: Summary of Key Facts
docs.text: Object Formula Note \(n\)-step transition probability \(q_{ij}^{(n)} = (Q^n)_{ij}\) Central result Chapman-Kolmogorov \(Q^{(m+n)} = Q^m Q^n\) Proof via Markov property + LOTP Distribution at time \(n\) \(\mathbf{t}^{(n)} = \mathbf{t}^{(0)} Q^n\) Row vector, left-multiply Convergence (irred. aperiodic) \(Q^n \to \mathbf{1s}\) Rate $\sim Spectral gap \(\gamma = 1 - \|\lambda_2\|\) Controls mixing time

docs.title: Open Threads
docs.text:
• What happens when \(Q\) is not diagonalizable? Jordan form and the nilpotent part — does convergence still hold?
  • Aperiodicity: why does a periodic chain not converge? (Think of a two-state chain with \(\alpha = \beta = 1\) — it oscillates forever.) What does \(Q^n\) look like in that case?
  • Mixing times — formal definition as \(t_{\text{mix}}(\varepsilon) = \min{n : |Q^n - \mathbf{1s}|_{\text{TV}} \leq \varepsilon}\); how does the spectral gap give upper bounds?
  • Computing \(Q^n\) efficiently — matrix exponentiation by squaring takes \(O(M^3 \log n)\) multiplications instead of \(O(M^3 n)\)
  • Absorbing chains — if \(Q\) has absorbing states, \(Q^n\) doesn't converge to a stationary distribution in the usual sense; absorption probabilities come from the fundamental matrix \((I - R)^{-1}\)

docs.title: One-Line Summary for Future Me
docs.text:
The \(n\)-step transition matrix is \(Q^n\): Chapman-Kolmogorov shows that conditioning on the intermediate state at time \(m\) turns \(Q^{(m+n)} = Q^{(m)}Q^{(n)}\) into ordinary matrix multiplication, and induction gives \(Q^{(n)} = Q^n\). The distribution at time \(n\) is \(\mathbf{t}^{(0)}Q^n\), and for irreducible aperiodic chains this converges to the stationary distribution \(\mathbf{s}\) at rate \(|\lambda_2|^n\).

docs.title: Marginal Distribution
docs.text: " is the simplest question you can ask about a Markov chain after time zero. It's just LOTP, applied once. But the answer — \(\mathbf{t}^{(0)} Q^n\) — is the thread that connects initial conditions to long-run behavior."

docs.title: The Question
docs.text:
I have a Markov chain \((X_n)_{n \geq 0}\) with state space \(\mathcal{S} = {1, \ldots, M}\), transition matrix \(Q\), and some initial distribution \(\mathbf{t}^{(0)}\). I want to know:

\[\text{What is } P(X_n = j) \text{ for each state } j?\]

This is the marginal distribution of \(X_n\) — the unconditional distribution of where the chain is at time \(n\), averaging over all possible starting points.

Note the contrast with what I computed in [[n-Step Transition Probability]]: that was the conditional distribution \(P(X_n = j \mid X_0 = i)\). Now I'm asking for the unconditional \(P(X_n = j)\), which means I need to average over the randomness in \(X_0\) as well.

docs.title: Setup and Notation
docs.text:
Initial distribution: A row vector \(\mathbf{t}^{(0)}\) where:

\[t^{(0)}_i = P(X_0 = i), \qquad \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} t^{(0)}_i = 1, \qquad t^{(0)}_i \geq 0\]

Marginal distribution at time \(n\): A row vector \(\mathbf{t}^{(n)}\) where:

\[t^{(n)}_j = P(X_n = j)\]

The goal is to find \(\mathbf{t}^{(n)}\) in terms of \(\mathbf{t}^{(0)}\) and \(Q\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
\[\mathbf{t}^{(n)} = \mathbf{t}^{(0)} Q^n\]

Entrywise:

\[P(X_n = j) = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} P(X_0 = i) \cdot (Q^n)_{ij} = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} t^{(0)}_i \cdot q_{ij}^{(n)}\]

docs.title: Proof
docs.text:
Apply the Law of Total Probability, conditioning on \(X_0\):

\[P(X_n = j) = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} P(X_n = j \mid X_0 = i) \cdot P(X_0 = i)\]

From [[n-Step Transition Probability]], we know \(P(X_n = j \mid X_0 = i) = q_{ij}^{(n)} = (Q^n)_{ij}\). Substituting:

\[P(X_n = j) = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} t^{(0)}_i \cdot (Q^n)_{ij}\]

This is the \(j\)-th entry of the row vector \(\mathbf{t}^{(0)} Q^n\). \(\blacksquare\)

The proof is one line of real content: LOTP on \(X_0\), then plug in the \(n\)-step result. The conceptual content is that the marginal distribution is a mixture of the \(n\)-step conditional distributions, weighted by the initial distribution. The initial randomness and the transition randomness combine via matrix multiplication.

docs.title: The One-Step Recursion
docs.text:
A special case worth isolating:

\[\mathbf{t}^{(n+1)} = \mathbf{t}^{(n)} Q\]

Proof: \(\mathbf{t}^{(n+1)} = \mathbf{t}^{(0)} Q^{n+1} = (\mathbf{t}^{(0)} Q^n) Q = \mathbf{t}^{(n)} Q\). \(\blacksquare\)

Entrywise:

\[P(X_{n+1} = j) = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} P(X_n = i) \cdot q_{ij}\]

This is the most natural update rule: the distribution tomorrow is the distribution today, left-multiplied by \(Q\). Each step applies one copy of \(Q\) from the right.

I think of this as the "forward equation" for distributions. It's completely analogous to how transition matrices act on states — except instead of a state, I'm evolving an entire distribution. The chain on distributions is itself a linear dynamical system \(\mathbf{t} \mapsto \mathbf{t}Q\).

docs.title: Case 1: Deterministic Start at State \(i\)
docs.text:
If \(X_0 = i\) with certainty, then \(\mathbf{t}^{(0)} = \mathbf{e}_i\) (the \(i\)-th standard basis row vector). Then:

\[\mathbf{t}^{(n)} = \mathbf{e}_i Q^n = \text{row } i \text{ of } Q^n\]

So the \(n\)-step conditional distribution \(P(X_n = \cdot \mid X_0 = i)\) is just row \(i\) of \(Q^n\). The marginal distribution in this case is the same as the \(n\)-step transition distribution. No surprise — if the start is deterministic, there's nothing to average over.

docs.title: Case 2: Uniform Start
docs.text:
If \(X_0 \sim \text{Uniform}(\mathcal{S})\), then \(\mathbf{t}^{(0)} = \frac{1}{M} \mathbf{1}^\top\) (all entries \(\frac{1}{M}\)). Then:

\[\mathbf{t}^{(n)} = \frac{1}{M} \mathbf{1}^\top Q^n = \frac{1}{M} \mathbf{1}^\top\]

Wait — is that right? Only if \(\mathbf{1}^\top Q = \mathbf{1}^\top\), i.e., if the uniform distribution is stationary. That's not true in general. In general:

\[t^{(n)}_j = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{i} (Q^n)_{ij} = \frac{1}{M} (\text{column sum of column } j \text{ of } Q^n)\]

Column sums of \(Q^n\) are not 1 in general (only row sums are). The uniform distribution is stationary if and only if \(Q\) is doubly stochastic (both rows and columns sum to 1).

docs.title: Case 3: Stationary Start
docs.text:
If \(X_0 \sim \mathbf{s}\) where \(\mathbf{s} Q = \mathbf{s}\), then:

\[\mathbf{t}^{(n)} = \mathbf{s} Q^n = \mathbf{s}\]

The chain started in stationarity stays in stationarity for all time. This is the defining property of \(\mathbf{s}\), and \(\mathbf{t}^{(n)} = \mathbf{t}^{(0)} Q^n\) makes it transparent.

docs.title: As a Mixture
docs.text:
\[P(X_n = j) = \sum_i P(X_0 = i) \cdot P(X_n = j \mid X_0 = i)\]

The marginal distribution of \(X_n\) is a mixture of the conditional distributions \(P(X_n = \cdot \mid X_0 = i)\), with mixing weights given by the initial distribution \(\mathbf{t}^{(0)}\). This is LOTP in its purest form — there's no Markov property needed here, just conditioning.

docs.title: As a Linear Map
docs.text: The map \(\mathbf{t}^{(0)} \mapsto \mathbf{t}^{(n)} = \mathbf{t}^{(0)} Q^n\) is a linear map on the space of probability vectors (the \((M-1)\)-dimensional simplex). Different initial distributions evolve differently, but the evolution is linear — a key feature that makes Markov chains tractable.

docs.title: As Convergence
docs.text:
For an irreducible aperiodic chain with stationary distribution \(\mathbf{s}\), we know \(Q^n \to \mathbf{1s}\). Therefore:

\[\mathbf{t}^{(n)} = \mathbf{t}^{(0)} Q^n \to \mathbf{t}^{(0)} \cdot \mathbf{1s} = \left(\sum_i t^{(0)}_i\right) \mathbf{s} = \mathbf{s}\]

Every initial distribution converges to \(\mathbf{s}\). The marginal distribution of \(X_n\) approaches stationarity as \(n \to \infty\), regardless of \(\mathbf{t}^{(0)}\). The \(n\)-step marginal is the most direct way to see this: the initial distribution gets washed out.

This is the probabilistic content of the convergence theorem: I can start anywhere. If I wait long enough, I cannot distinguish the distribution of \(X_n\) from \(\mathbf{s}\). The initial condition becomes irrelevant. The chain "forgets" \(\mathbf{t}^{(0)}\) at rate \(|\lambda_2|^n\).

docs.title: Two-State Chain
docs.text:
\(\mathcal{S} = {1, 2}\), \(Q = \begin{pmatrix} 1-\alpha & \alpha \ \beta & 1-\beta \end{pmatrix}\), initial distribution \(\mathbf{t}^{(0)} = (p, 1-p)\).

From [[n-Step Transition Probability]], the \(n\)-step matrix is:

\[Q^n = \frac{1}{\alpha+\beta}\begin{pmatrix} \beta & \alpha \ \beta & \alpha \end{pmatrix} + \frac{(1-\alpha-\beta)^n}{\alpha+\beta} \begin{pmatrix} \alpha & -\alpha \ -\beta & \beta \end{pmatrix}\]

So:

\[P(X_n = 1) = \mathbf{t}^{(0)} Q^n \text{ entry 1} = \frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta} + \frac{(1-\alpha-\beta)^n}{\alpha+\beta}\bigl(p\alpha - (1-p)\beta\bigr)\] \[P(X_n = 2) = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta} - \frac{(1-\alpha-\beta)^n}{\alpha+\beta}\bigl(p\alpha - (1-p)\beta\bigr)\]

Check: \(P(X_n = 1) + P(X_n = 2) = 1\). ✓

As \(n \to \infty\): Both converge to \(\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta}\) and \(\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}\) respectively — the stationary distribution — regardless of \(p\). ✓

Special case \(p = \frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta}\): The correction term vanishes for all \(n\), confirming that starting in stationarity keeps you there.

docs.title: What \(\mathbf{t}^{(n)} = \mathbf{t}^{(0)} Q^n\) Does NOT Say
docs.text:
A point worth being careful about:

\(\mathbf{t}^{(n)} = \mathbf{t}^{(0)} Q^n\) gives the marginal distribution of \(X_n\) alone. It says nothing about the joint distribution of \((X_0, X_1, \ldots, X_n)\), or even the joint distribution of \((X_0, X_n)\).

For the joint distribution of a path, I need:

\[P(X_0 = i_0, \ldots, X_n = i_n) = t^{(0)}_{i_0} \cdot q_{i_0 i_1} \cdot q_{i_1 i_2} \cdots q_{i_{n-1} i_n}\]

The marginal at time \(n\) is obtained by summing this over all intermediate states \(i_1, \ldots, i_{n-1}\) — which is exactly what matrix multiplication computes.

This is the distinction I keep needing to remember: the marginal \(P(X_n = j)\) is a one-number summary of where the chain is at time \(n\). The full path distribution is a much richer object. The Markov property makes both tractable, but they're different things.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Object Formula How to compute Marginal at time \(n\) \(\mathbf{t}^{(n)} = \mathbf{t}^{(0)} Q^n\) Raise \(Q\) to the \(n\)-th power One-step update \(\mathbf{t}^{(n+1)} = \mathbf{t}^{(n)} Q\) Left-multiply current distribution by \(Q\) Deterministic start at \(i\) \(\mathbf{t}^{(n)} = \text{row } i \text{ of } Q^n\) Same as \(n\)-step conditional Stationary start \(\mathbf{t}^{(n)} = \mathbf{s}\) for all \(n\) By definition of stationarity Long-run limit \(\mathbf{t}^{(n)} \to \mathbf{s}\) Convergence theorem (irred. aperiodic)

docs.title: One-Line Summary for Future Me
docs.text:
\(P(X_n = j) = (\mathbf{t}^{(0)} Q^n)_j\): condition on \(X_0\) via LOTP, plug in the \(n\)-step transition probabilities \((Q^n)_{ij}\), and what comes out is a row-vector left-multiplication. Every initial distribution converges to the stationary distribution \(\mathbf{s}\) as \(n \to \infty\) for irreducible aperiodic chains.

docs.title: Classification of States
docs.text: "Before asking where a chain goes in the long run, I have to ask what kind of states it even has. Some states the chain visits forever. Some it eventually abandons and never returns to. The classification of states is the taxonomy that makes the convergence theory possible."

docs.title: Why Classify States?
docs.text:
The convergence theorem — that \(\mathbf{t}^{(n)} \to \mathbf{s}\) — doesn't hold for every Markov chain. It requires conditions: irreducibility and aperiodicity. Both of these are properties of the chain's states. Before I can state or prove the convergence theorem, I need a precise vocabulary for describing how states relate to each other and how the chain revisits them.

The classification of states answers two fundamental questions:

  1. Will the chain ever return to state \(i\)? (Recurrence vs. transience)
  2. How does the chain's graph structure look? (Communicating classes, irreducibility)
  3. Is the chain's return behavior periodic? (Aperiodicity)

docs.title: Definition: Accessibility
docs.text:
State \(j\) is accessible from state \(i\), written \(i \to j\), if:

\[q_{ij}^{(n)} = P(X_n = j \mid X_0 = i) > 0 \quad \text{for some } n \geq 0\]

There exists some \(n\) for which there is positive probability of reaching \(j\) starting from \(i\).

Convention: \(i \to i\) always, since \(q_{ii}^{(0)} = 1\).

docs.title: Definition: Communication
docs.text:
States \(i\) and \(j\) communicate, written \(i \leftrightarrow j\), if:

\[i \to j \quad \text{and} \quad j \to i\]

Both states are accessible from each other.

docs.title: Lemma: Communication is an Equivalence Relation
docs.text:
Communication satisfies:

  • Reflexivity: \(i \leftrightarrow i\) (trivially, \(i \to i\))
  • Symmetry: \(i \leftrightarrow j \Rightarrow j \leftrightarrow i\) (by definition)
  • Transitivity: \(i \leftrightarrow j\) and \(j \leftrightarrow k\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(i \leftrightarrow k\)

Proof of transitivity: If \(i \to j\) in \(m\) steps and \(j \to k\) in \(n\) steps, then by Chapman-Kolmogorov:

\[q_{ik}^{(m+n)} = \sum_{\ell} q_{i\ell}^{(m)} q_{\ell k}^{(n)} \geq q_{ij}^{(m)} q_{jk}^{(n)} > 0\]

So \(i \to k\). Similarly \(k \to i\). \(\blacksquare\)

Because communication is an equivalence relation, it partitions the state space \(\mathcal{S}\) into equivalence classes.

docs.title: Definition: Communicating Classes
docs.text:
The equivalence classes under \(\leftrightarrow\) are called communicating classes. Within a class, every state can reach every other. Between different classes, communication is broken in at least one direction.

I think of the communicating classes as the strongly connected components of the directed graph on \(\mathcal{S}\), where there's an edge \(i \to j\) whenever \(q_{ij} > 0\). The Chapman-Kolmogorov transitivity argument is exactly graph reachability — if I can get from \(i\) to \(j\) and from \(j\) to \(k\), I can get from \(i\) to \(k\) in the concatenated number of steps.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A Markov chain is irreducible if there is only one communicating class — i.e., every state communicates with every other state:

\[i \leftrightarrow j \quad \text{for all } i, j \in \mathcal{S}\]

Equivalently: from any state, every other state is reachable in some finite number of steps.

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
An irreducible chain cannot get "stuck" in a subset of states. The long-run behavior is not sensitive to which communicating class the chain is initialized in, because there's only one. This is the condition that guarantees the stationary distribution is unique.

Without irreducibility, different communicating classes might have different stationary distributions — or some classes might have none — and the long-run behavior depends entirely on which class the chain starts in.

The simplest failure of irreducibility: two absorbing states \(a\) and \(b\), with no way to move between them. If the chain starts near \(a\) it gets absorbed there; near \(b\) it gets absorbed there. There are two stationary distributions, \(\delta_a\) and \(\delta_b\), and every convex combination is also stationary. Irreducibility kills all of this pathology.

docs.title: Recurrence and Transience
docs.text: This is the deeper classification — not about the graph structure, but about whether the chain returns to each state.

docs.title: Definition: First Return Time
docs.text:
Define the first return time to state \(i\):

\[T_i = \min{n \geq 1 : X_n = i}\]

with the convention \(T_i = \infty\) if the chain never returns. Then:

\[f_{ii} = P(T_i < \infty \mid X_0 = i) = P(\text{chain ever returns to } i \mid \text{starts at } i)\]

docs.title: Definition: Recurrent and Transient States
docs.text:
• State \(i\) is recurrent if \(f_{ii} = 1\) — the chain returns to \(i\) with probability 1.
  • State \(i\) is transient if \(f_{ii} < 1\) — there is positive probability of never returning.

docs.title: The Canonical Theorem: Return Count Criterion
docs.text:
Let \(N_i = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mathbf{1}[X_n = i]\) be the total number of visits to state \(i\) after time 0.

Theorem.

\[i \text{ is recurrent} \iff E[N_i \mid X_0 = i] = \infty \iff \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} q_{ii}^{(n)} = \infty\] \[i \text{ is transient} \iff E[N_i \mid X_0 = i] < \infty \iff \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} q_{ii}^{(n)} < \infty\]

Proof.

Write \(N_i = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \mathbf{1}[X_n = i]\). By linearity of expectation:

\[E[N_i \mid X_0 = i] = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} P(X_n = i \mid X_0 = i) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} q_{ii}^{(n)}\]

Now I need to connect this to \(f_{ii}\).

Given \(X_0 = i\), the number of returns \(N_i\) is a geometric-type random variable. The chain returns to \(i\) for the first time with probability \(f_{ii}\). Each time it returns, the future is independent of the past (Markov property), so the chain again returns with probability \(f_{ii}\). Therefore \(N_i \mid X_0 = i\) has a Geometric distribution on \({0, 1, 2, \ldots}\) with success probability \(f_{ii}\):

\[P(N_i \geq k \mid X_0 = i) = f_{ii}^k\]

So:

\[E[N_i \mid X_0 = i] = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} P(N_i \geq k \mid X_0 = i) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} f_{ii}^k = \frac{f_{ii}}{1 - f_{ii}}\]

when \(f_{ii} < 1\) (transient), this is finite. When \(f_{ii} = 1\) (recurrent), this is \(\infty\). \(\blacksquare\)

The geometric structure here is the Markov property in action again. Each return to state \(i\) "resets" the chain — from \(i\)'s perspective, the chain has no memory of how many times it has been there before. So the number of visits is exactly geometric. This is the cleanest proof I know of the recurrence criterion.

docs.title: Corollary: Transient States Are Visited Finitely Often
docs.text:
If \(i\) is transient, then \(N_i < \infty\) almost surely — the chain visits \(i\) only finitely many times, and eventually leaves and never comes back.

If \(i\) is recurrent, then \(N_i = \infty\) almost surely — the chain returns to \(i\) infinitely often.

This is a 0-1 law: not "sometimes finite, sometimes infinite" — it's always one or the other, depending only on whether \(f_{ii} = 1\).

docs.title: Recurrence and Transience Are Class Properties
Theorem
docs.text:
If \(i \leftrightarrow j\) (they communicate), then \(i\) is recurrent if and only if \(j\) is recurrent.

Proof.

Suppose \(i \leftrightarrow j\). Then there exist \(m, n \geq 1\) such that \(q_{ij}^{(m)} > 0\) and \(q_{ji}^{(n)} > 0\). Let \(\alpha = q_{ij}^{(m)} q_{ji}^{(n)} > 0\).

For any \(k \geq 0\), by Chapman-Kolmogorov:

\[q_{ii}^{(m+k+n)} \geq q_{ij}^{(m)} \cdot q_{jj}^{(k)} \cdot q_{ji}^{(n)} = \alpha \cdot q_{jj}^{(k)}\]

Summing over \(k\):

\[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} q_{ii}^{(m+k+n)} \geq \alpha \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} q_{jj}^{(k)}\]

If \(j\) is recurrent, \(\sum_k q_{jj}^{(k)} = \infty\), so \(\sum_k q_{ii}^{(m+k+n)} = \infty\), hence \(\sum_k q_{ii}^{(k)} = \infty\), so \(i\) is recurrent. By symmetry, \(j\) recurrent \(\Rightarrow\) \(i\) recurrent. \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: Consequence
docs.text: Every state in a communicating class has the same recurrence/transience classification. So I can speak of recurrent classes and transient classes without ambiguity.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A communicating class \(C\) is closed if no state outside \(C\) is accessible from any state inside \(C\):

\[i \in C, , j \notin C \Rightarrow q_{ij}^{(n)} = 0 \text{ for all } n\]

A class that is not closed is open.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Every recurrent class is closed. Every finite closed class is recurrent.

Proof sketch (recurrent \(\Rightarrow\) closed): Suppose \(C\) is recurrent but not closed. Then some \(i \in C\) can reach \(j otin C\). Since \(j otin C\) and \(i \in C\), we have \(j ot o i\) (otherwise \(i \leftrightarrow j\), contradicting \(j otin C\)). So once the chain reaches \(j\), it never returns to \(i\) — contradicting recurrence of \(i\). \( lacksquare\)

Proof sketch (finite closed class \(\Rightarrow\) recurrent): In a finite closed class, the chain can never escape. It must visit some state infinitely often (by pigeonhole — finitely many states, infinite time). By the class property, all states in the class are visited infinitely often, so all are recurrent. \( lacksquare\)

The pigeonhole argument for finite closed classes is the reason finite irreducible chains are always recurrent — there's nowhere to escape to, and with finitely many states, the chain must keep coming back. This is why the theory simplifies so much in the finite case.

docs.title: Definition: Period
docs.text:
The period of state \(i\) is:

\[d(i) = \gcd{n \geq 1 : q_{ii}^{(n)} > 0}\]

the greatest common divisor of all return times. If \({n \geq 1 : q_{ii}^{(n)} > 0} = \emptyset\) (i.e., \(i\) is transient and never returns), set \(d(i) = \infty\) by convention.

State \(i\) is aperiodic if \(d(i) = 1\) and periodic with period \(d > 1\) if \(d(i) = d\).

docs.title: Lemma: Period Is a Class Property
docs.text:
If \(i \leftrightarrow j\), then \(d(i) = d(j)\).

Proof. Since \(i \leftrightarrow j\), there exist \(m, n\) with \(q_{ij}^{(m)} > 0\) and \(q_{ji}^{(n)} > 0\). Note \(q_{ii}^{(m+n)} \geq q_{ij}^{(m)} q_{ji}^{(n)} > 0\), so \(d(i)\) divides \(m + n\).

For any \(k\) with \(q_{jj}^{(k)} > 0\):

\[q_{ii}^{(m+k+n)} \geq q_{ij}^{(m)} q_{jj}^{(k)} q_{ji}^{(n)} > 0\]

so \(d(i)\) divides \(m + k + n\). Since \(d(i)\) divides \(m + n\), it divides \(k\). So \(d(i)\) divides every element of \({k : q_{jj}^{(k)} > 0}\), hence \(d(i) \leq d(j)\). By symmetry \(d(j) \leq d(i)\), so \(d(i) = d(j)\). \(\blacksquare\)

So I can speak of the period of a communicating class.

docs.title: What Periodicity Looks Like
docs.text:
A chain with period \(d > 1\) cycles through \(d\) groups of states in a fixed order. The canonical example:

Cycle graph on \({0, 1, \ldots, d-1}\): \(q_{i, i+1 \bmod d} = 1\). The chain moves deterministically around the cycle, returning to any state only at times \(d, 2d, 3d, \ldots\). Period = \(d\).

For such a chain, \(q_{ii}^{(n)} = 0\) whenever \(d \nmid n\), and the chain does not converge in distribution — it oscillates. This is why aperiodicity is a hypothesis in the convergence theorem.

docs.title: Sufficient Conditions for Aperiodicity
docs.text:
• If \(q_{ii} > 0\) for some \(i\) (self-loop), then \(d(i) = 1\), so \(i\) is aperiodic. If the chain is irreducible, the whole chain is aperiodic.
  • If the chain can return to \(i\) in both \(k\) and \(k+1\) steps (for some \(k\)), then \(\gcd(k, k+1) = 1\), so \(d(i) = 1\).

In practice, whenever I see a self-loop in the transition matrix, I immediately know the chain is aperiodic (if irreducible). Many applied chains — random walks with laziness, MCMC with rejection — are made aperiodic precisely by adding a self-loop: stay with probability \(1/2\), move with probability \(1/2\). This is a standard trick.

docs.title: The Full Picture: State Classification Tree
docs.text:
States of a Markov Chain
│
├── Recurrent (return with prob. 1; visited infinitely often)
│   │
│   ├── Positive recurrent: E[T_i | X_0 = i] < ∞
│   │   └── These states have a stationary distribution
│   │
│   └── Null recurrent: E[T_i | X_0 = i] = ∞
│       └── Return a.s., but expected return time is infinite
│           (occurs only in countably infinite state spaces)
│
└── Transient (positive prob. of never returning; visited finitely often)

For finite state spaces: Null recurrence cannot occur. Every recurrent state is positive recurrent. So the classification simplifies to just recurrent vs. transient.

For countably infinite state spaces (e.g., random walks on \(\mathbb{Z}\)): null recurrence is possible and important. The simple random walk on \(\mathbb{Z}\) is null recurrent — it returns to 0 with probability 1, but the expected return time is infinite.

Null recurrence is the strange middle ground: the chain keeps coming back, but it takes so long on average that there's no stationary distribution. I find this the most counterintuitive phenomenon in the classification — "recurrent but no stationary distribution" feels paradoxical. It only happens in infinite state spaces, which is why the finite theory is cleaner.

docs.title: Putting It Together: The Convergence Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem (Convergence to Stationarity). Let \((X_n)\) be an irreducible and aperiodic Markov chain on a finite state space. Then:

  1. There exists a unique stationary distribution \(\mathbf{s}\).
  2. For all \(i, j \in \mathcal{S}\):
\[q_{ij}^{(n)} \to s_j \quad \text{as } n \to \infty\]
  1. For any initial distribution \(\mathbf{t}^{(0)}\):
\[\mathbf{t}^{(n)} \to \mathbf{s} \quad \text{as } n \to \infty\]

The role of each condition:

  • Irreducibility: Ensures there is only one communicating class, so the stationary distribution is unique. Without it, the limit could depend on the starting class.
  • Aperiodicity: Ensures \(q_{ij}^{(n)}\) actually converges (doesn't oscillate). Without it, \(Q^n\) might not converge even if a stationary distribution exists.
  • Finite state space: Ensures positive recurrence (no null recurrence). In infinite state spaces, need to additionally assume positive recurrence.

This theorem is the payoff for all the classification work. Every condition in the hypothesis corresponds to exactly one pathology that it rules out. Irreducibility rules out multiple stationary distributions. Aperiodicity rules out oscillation. Finiteness rules out null recurrence. It's a beautifully tight set of hypotheses.

docs.title: Example 1: Irreducible and Aperiodic
docs.text:
\[Q = \begin{pmatrix} 1/2 & 1/2 \ 1/3 & 2/3 \end{pmatrix}\]

Both states communicate (\(q_{12}, q_{21} > 0\)), so irreducible. Self-loops (\(q_{11} = 1/2 > 0\)), so aperiodic. Convergence theorem applies. Unique stationary distribution: solve \(\mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}\), get \(\mathbf{s} = (2/5, 3/5)\).

docs.title: Example 2: Irreducible but Periodic
docs.text:
\[Q = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\]

States communicate, so irreducible. But \(q_{11}^{(n)} = 1\) if \(n\) even, \(0\) if \(n\) odd. Period \(d = 2\). The chain oscillates forever — \(Q^n\) does not converge. The stationary distribution \((1/2, 1/2)\) exists but \(\mathbf{t}^{(n)}\) oscillates around it rather than converging to it.

docs.title: Example 3: Reducible — Absorbing States
docs.text:
\[Q = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \ 1/2 & 0 & 1/2 \ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\]

States \({1}\) and \({3}\) are absorbing (closed recurrent classes). State \({2}\) is transient — it can reach 1 or 3 but neither can reach it back. The chain gets absorbed in 1 or 3; the long-run distribution depends on the starting state.

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text: Concept Definition Key consequence \(i \to j\) \((Q^n)_{ij} > 0\) for some \(n\) Reachability \(i \leftrightarrow j\) \(i \to j\) and \(j \to i\) Equivalence relation; partitions \(\mathcal{S}\) Irreducible One communicating class Unique stationary distribution Recurrent \(f_{ii} = 1\); \(\sum_n q_{ii}^{(n)} = \infty\) Visited infinitely often a.s. Transient \(f_{ii} < 1\); \(\sum_n q_{ii}^{(n)} < \infty\) Visited finitely often a.s. Closed class No escape to outside states Recurrent classes are always closed Period \(d(i)\) \(\gcd{n : q_{ii}^{(n)} > 0}\) Class property Aperiodic \(d(i) = 1\) \(Q^n\) converges Positive recurrent \(E[T_i \mid X_0 = i] < \infty\) Stationary distribution exists Null recurrent \(f_{ii} = 1\) but \(E[T_i] = \infty\) Recurrent, no stationary distribution

docs.title: One-Line Summary for Future Me
docs.text:
States are classified by two independent axes: recurrence (does the chain return?) and period (does the return time have a GCD \(> 1\)?). Both are class properties. An irreducible (one class), aperiodic (\(d = 1\)), positive recurrent chain on a finite state space is the "nice" case — unique stationary distribution, convergence from anywhere.

docs.title: Gambler's Ruin
docs.text: "The Gambler's Ruin is the first Markov chain where something genuinely hard happens — absorption. The chain doesn't converge to a stationary distribution. It terminates. The question is no longer 'where does it end up in the long run' but 'which absorbing state does it get trapped in, and how long does it take.' These are harder questions, and the answers are beautiful."

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
A gambler starts with \(k\) dollars. At each round, she wins 1 dollar with probability \(p\) and loses 1 dollar with probability \(q = 1 - p\). She stops when she is ruined (hits 0) or reaches her target fortune \(N\).

State space: \(\mathcal{S} = {0, 1, 2, \ldots, N}\)

Transition probabilities:

\[q_{i, i+1} = p, \quad q_{i, i-1} = q = 1-p \quad \text{for } i \in {1, \ldots, N-1}\] \[q_{00} = 1, \quad q_{NN} = 1 \quad \text{(absorbing boundaries)}\]

All other \(q_{ij} = 0\).

The transition matrix \(Q\) is tridiagonal with absorbing corners:

\[Q = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \ q & 0 & p & \cdots & 0 & 0 \ 0 & q & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \ \vdots & & \ddots & \ddots & & \vdots \ 0 & 0 & \cdots & q & 0 & p \ 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\]

docs.title: Classification of States
docs.text:
States \({0}\) and \({N}\): Absorbing states. Each is its own closed communicating class. Both are recurrent (trivially — once you're there, you stay).

States \({1, 2, \ldots, N-1}\): These form a single communicating class (any interior state can reach any other in finitely many steps). But this class is not closed — from any interior state, the chain can reach 0 or \(N\). By the theorem from [[Classification of States]], an open communicating class in a finite chain must be transient.

So the full classification:

States Class Type \({0}\) Singleton Absorbing / Recurrent \({1, \ldots, N-1}\) One open class Transient \({N}\) Singleton Absorbing / Recurrent

This is the structural fact that makes the problem tractable. The interior states are transient — the chain visits each one only finitely many times and eventually gets absorbed. The only question is: absorbed where, and after how long?

docs.title: The Two Questions
docs.text:
1. Absorption probabilities: Starting from state \(k\), what is the probability of being absorbed at \(N\) (winning) vs. at \(0\) (ruin)?

  2. Expected absorption time: Starting from state \(k\), how many steps until absorption?

Both are answered by setting up first-step equations — condition on the first transition, use the Markov property, solve the resulting system.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Let \(r_k = P(\text{absorbed at } N \mid X_0 = k)\) be the probability of winning starting from \(k\).

Boundary conditions (immediate from the absorbing state definitions):

\[r_0 = 0, \qquad r_N = 1\]

First-step equation for \(k \in {1, \ldots, N-1}\): condition on the first step:

\[r_k = p \cdot r_{k+1} + q \cdot r_{k-1}\]

This is a second-order linear recurrence relation with constant coefficients.

docs.title: Solving the Recurrence
docs.text:
Rearranged: \(p \cdot r_{k+1} - r_k + q \cdot r_{k-1} = 0\), or:

\[p \cdot r_{k+1} - (p+q) r_k + q \cdot r_{k-1} = 0\]

since \(p + q = 1\). The characteristic equation is:

\[p \lambda^2 - \lambda + q = 0 \implies \lambda = \frac{1 \pm \sqrt{1 - 4pq}}{2p}\]

Note that \(1 - 4pq = (p-q)^2\), so:

\[\lambda = \frac{1 \pm |p - q|}{2p}\]

The two roots are \(\lambda_1 = 1\) and \(\lambda_2 = q/p\).

docs.title: Case 1: \(p \neq q\) (biased walk)
docs.text:
Two distinct roots \(\lambda_1 = 1\), \(\lambda_2 = q/p\). General solution:

\[r_k = A \cdot 1^k + B \cdot \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^k = A + B\left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^k\]

Apply boundary conditions:

\[r_0 = 0: \quad A + B = 0 \implies B = -A\] \[r_N = 1: \quad A + B\left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^N = 1 \implies A\left(1 - \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^N\right) = 1 \implies A = \frac{1}{1-(q/p)^N}\]

Therefore:

\[\boxed{r_k = \frac{1 - (q/p)^k}{1 - (q/p)^N}}\]

docs.title: Case 2: \(p = q = 1/2\) (fair walk)
docs.text:
Repeated root \(\lambda = 1\). General solution:

\[r_k = A + Bk\]

Apply boundary conditions: \(r_0 = 0 \Rightarrow A = 0\); \(r_N = 1 \Rightarrow B = 1/N\). Therefore:

\[\boxed{r_k = \frac{k}{N}}\]

For a fair game, the probability of winning is simply the fraction of the way to the target you start at. The probability of ruin is \(1 - k/N = (N-k)/N\).

The fair game result \(r_k = k/N\) is elegant and somewhat intuitive — your winning probability is proportional to your current fortune. But the biased case reveals something darker. If \(p < q\) (unfavorable game), \((q/p)^k\) grows, and \(r_k \to 0\) as \(N \to \infty\) (infinite table). Even with a large starting fortune, playing against the house with a slight edge in their favor leads to certain ruin eventually. This is the mathematical foundation of why casinos win.

docs.title: The Ruin Probability
docs.text:
\(P(\text{ruined} \mid X_0 = k) = 1 - r_k\). For \(p \neq q\):

\[P(\text{ruined} \mid X_0 = k) = \frac{(q/p)^k - (q/p)^N}{1 - (q/p)^N}\]

docs.title: Limiting Case: \(N \to \infty\) (playing against an infinitely rich opponent)
docs.text:
For \(p < q\) (unfavorable): \((q/p) > 1\), so \((q/p)^N \to \infty\), and:

\[r_k \to \frac{1 - (q/p)^k}{\infty} = 0\]

Ruin is certain — you will be ruined with probability 1 regardless of your starting fortune.

For \(p > q\) (favorable): \((q/p) < 1\), so \((q/p)^N \to 0\), and:

\[r_k \to 1 - \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^k\]

There's a positive probability of never being ruined.

For \(p = q = 1/2\) (fair): \(r_k = k/N \to 0\) as \(N \to \infty\).

Ruin is also certain for the fair game against an infinitely rich opponent. This is the recurrence of the simple random walk on \(\mathbb{Z}\) — starting anywhere, the walk hits 0 almost surely (and also \(+\infty\)... from both directions). A famous result.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Let \(d_k = E[\text{absorption time} \mid X_0 = k]\).

Boundary conditions:

\[d_0 = 0, \qquad d_N = 0\]

First-step equation for \(k \in {1, \ldots, N-1}\):

\[d_k = 1 + p \cdot d_{k+1} + q \cdot d_{k-1}\]

The \(1\) accounts for the one step just taken. This is a non-homogeneous second-order linear recurrence.

docs.title: Solving the Recurrence
docs.text:
Rewrite: \(p \cdot d_{k+1} - d_k + q \cdot d_{k-1} = -1\).

The homogeneous solution is the same as before: \(d_k^{(h)} = A + B(q/p)^k\) (for \(p eq q\)).

For a particular solution, try \(d_k^{(p)} = Ck\):

\[pC(k+1) - Ck + qC(k-1) = -1$$ $$Ck(p - 1 + q) + C(p - q) = -1$$ $$C(p - q) = -1 \implies C = rac{1}{q - p}\]

So the general solution for \(p eq q\):

\[d_k = A + B\left( rac{q}{p} ight)^k + rac{k}{q-p}\]

Apply boundary conditions \(d_0 = d_N = 0\):

From \(d_0 = 0\): \(A + B = 0 \Rightarrow B = -A\).

From \(d_N = 0\):

\[A\left(1 - \left( rac{q}{p} ight)^N ight) + rac{N}{q-p} = 0 \implies A = rac{N}{(p-q)(1-(q/p)^N)}\]

Therefore:

\[ oxed{d_k = rac{1}{q-p}\left(k - N \cdot rac{1-(q/p)^k}{1-(q/p)^N} ight)} \quad (p eq q)\]

docs.title: Case \(p = q = 1/2\)
docs.text:
Particular solution: try \(d_k^{(p)} = Ck^2\):

\[\frac{1}{2}C(k+1)^2 - Ck^2 + \frac{1}{2}C(k-1)^2 = -1 \implies C = -1\]

General solution: \(d_k = A + Bk - k^2\). Boundary conditions give \(A = 0\), \(B = N\):

\[\boxed{d_k = k(N - k)} \quad (p = q = 1/2)\]

Starting from \(k\), the expected number of steps is \(k(N-k)\). Maximized at \(k = N/2\): starting in the middle, expected duration is \(N^2/4\).

The formula \(d_k = k(N-k)\) for the fair game is one of my favorite results in elementary probability. It says the expected game length is maximized when you start in the middle, and scales as \(N^2\). If \(N = 100\) and you start at 50, the expected game lasts 2500 rounds. If \(N = 1000\) and you start at 500, it lasts 250,000 rounds. The quadratic scaling makes long fair games very long indeed.

docs.title: The First-Step Equation as a Method
docs.text:
The technique used above — conditioning on the first step — is completely general and deserves to be called out explicitly.

Template: For any quantity \(h_k\) defined as an expectation or probability starting from state \(k\):

  1. Write the boundary conditions at absorbing states.
  2. For interior states, write \(h_k = (\text{immediate cost/contribution}) + \sum_j q_{kj} h_j\).
  3. Solve the resulting linear system (recurrence relation in 1D chains, linear system in general).

The Markov property is what licenses step 2 — the future expected cost from state \(j\) doesn't depend on how we got to \(j\).

For the Gambler's Ruin, the 1D structure turns the linear system into a second-order recurrence, which is exactly solvable. In a general Markov chain, step 2 gives a system of \(|\mathcal{S}|\) linear equations.

I think of first-step equations as the "dynamic programming" of Markov chain theory. The Markov property is the principle of optimality: given the current state, the future is independent of history. So I can recursively decompose any expectation or probability into a one-step look-ahead plus future. Every Markov chain problem I've seen in Stat 110 reduces to setting up and solving a first-step equation.

docs.title: Martingale Verification (Optional but Illuminating)
docs.text: There is a slicker way to derive the absorption probabilities that bypasses the recurrence entirely, using martingales. I'll sketch it because it reveals why the answer has the form it does.

docs.title: Fair Game (\(p = 1/2\))
docs.text:
\(X_n\) itself is a martingale: \(E[X_{n+1} \mid X_n] = \frac{1}{2}(X_n + 1) + \frac{1}{2}(X_n - 1) = X_n\).

By the Optional Stopping Theorem (under integrability conditions), \(E[X_T] = E[X_0] = k\), where \(T\) is the absorption time. But \(X_T \in {0, N}\), so:

\[E[X_T] = 0 \cdot P(\text{ruin}) + N \cdot r_k = N r_k = k \implies r_k = \frac{k}{N}\]

docs.title: Biased Game (\(p \neq q\))
docs.text:
\((q/p)^{X_n}\) is a martingale:

\[E\left[\left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{X_{n+1}} \Bigg| X_n\right] = p \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{X_n+1} + q\left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{X_n - 1} = \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{X_n}\left(q + q\right)\]

Wait, more carefully: \(= \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{X_n} \cdot \left(p \cdot \frac{q}{p} + q \cdot \frac{p}{q}\right)\)... let me redo:

\[= p \cdot \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{X_n} \cdot \frac{q}{p} + q \cdot \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{X_n} \cdot \frac{p}{q} = \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{X_n}(q + p) = \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{X_n}\]

Yes, it is a martingale. By Optional Stopping:

\[\left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^k = E\left[\left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^{X_T}\right] = \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^0 \cdot (1 - r_k) + \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)^N \cdot r_k\]

Solving for \(r_k\) gives exactly the formula above.

The martingale approach feels like magic the first time. The recurrence approach is more elementary but less illuminating — you solve a system of equations and the answer pops out. The martingale approach reveals why the answer involves \((q/p)^k\): because \((q/p)^{X_n}\) is the "right" function of the state to track, the one that is preserved on average. The answer is essentially forced by the structure of the martingale.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Fair (\(p = 1/2\)) Biased (\(p \neq q\)) \(P(\text{win} \mid X_0 = k)\) \(k/N\) \(\dfrac{1-(q/p)^k}{1-(q/p)^N}\) \(P(\text{ruin} \mid X_0 = k)\) \((N-k)/N\) \(\dfrac{(q/p)^k - (q/p)^N}{1-(q/p)^N}\) \(E[\text{duration} \mid X_0 = k]\) \(k(N-k)\) \(\dfrac{1}{q-p}!\left(k - N\cdot\dfrac{1-(q/p)^k}{1-(q/p)^N}\right)\) \(P(\text{ruin} \mid N \to \infty)\) \(1\) \(1\) if \(p < q\); \((q/p)^k\) if \(p > q\)

State classification: \({0}\) and \({N}\) are absorbing (recurrent). \({1, \ldots, N-1}\) are transient (open communicating class, finite chain).

Method: First-step equations — condition on the first transition, use the Markov property, solve the resulting recurrence with boundary conditions.

docs.title: One-Line Summary for Future Me
docs.text:
Gambler's Ruin is an absorbing Markov chain: interior states \({1,\ldots,N-1}\) are transient, boundaries \({0, N}\) are absorbing. Absorption probabilities and expected duration both satisfy first-step equations — second-order linear recurrences whose solutions are \(r_k = \frac{1-(q/p)^k}{1-(q/p)^N}\) (biased) or \(k/N\) (fair), and \(d_k = k(N-k)\) (fair) — derivable either by recurrence or by martingale optional stopping.

docs.title: Coupon Collector
docs.text: "The Coupon Collector is the Gambler's Ruin turned inside out. Instead of asking when the chain gets absorbed at a boundary, I'm asking when it climbs through every rung of a ladder. The first-step equation still does all the work — but the state space is cleverer, and the answer involves a harmonic sum that I should know by heart."

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
There are \(n\) distinct coupon types. Each box of cereal contains one coupon, chosen uniformly at random (with replacement) from the \(n\) types. I buy boxes one at a time.

Question: How many boxes do I expect to buy until I have collected at least one of every coupon type?

This is a classical problem, and the answer — \(n H_n = n\left(1 + \frac{1}{2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{n}\right)\) — is one of the results I want to know cold. But the goal here is to derive it rigorously as a Markov chain, with the full machinery of first-step equations.

docs.title: The Key Modeling Insight
docs.text:
The raw state "which coupons do I have?" is \(2^n\) states — exponential, intractable. But I don't actually care which coupons I have; I only care how many distinct coupons I have so far.

Why is this Markov? If I currently have \(k\) distinct coupons, the probability of getting a new one on the next draw is \(\frac{n-k}{n}\), and this depends only on \(k\) — not on which \(k\) coupons I have, nor on the order in which I collected them. The count \(k\) screens off all the history.

This is the Markov property in action as a modeling choice: I collapsed a \(2^n\)-state chain into an \((n+1)\)-state chain by identifying the right summary statistic.

This collapsing move — finding the right low-dimensional summary that is Markov — is one of the core skills in applied probability. The wrong state space makes a problem intractable. The right one makes it a two-line calculation. For the Coupon Collector, the count of distinct coupons is the right state.

docs.title: State Space and Transitions
docs.text:
State space: \(\mathcal{S} = {0, 1, 2, \ldots, n}\), where state \(k\) = "I currently have \(k\) distinct coupon types."

Transition probabilities: From state \(k \in {0, 1, \ldots, n-1}\):

\[q_{k, k+1} = \frac{n-k}{n} \qquad \text{(new coupon — probability of drawing one of the } n-k \text{ types I don't have)}\] \[q_{k, k} = \frac{k}{n} \qquad \text{(duplicate — probability of drawing one of the } k \text{ types I already have)}\] \[q_{kj} = 0 \quad \text{for all other } j\]

Boundary: State \(n\) is absorbing: \(q_{nn} = 1\). Once I have all \(n\) coupons, I'm done.

The transition matrix is upper bidiagonal (only diagonal and superdiagonal entries are nonzero for interior states):

\[Q = \begin{pmatrix} k/n & (n-k)/n & & & \ & \ddots & \ddots & & \ & & k/n & (n-k)/n & \ & & & 1 & \end{pmatrix}\]

with \(k\) running from \(0\) to \(n\) along the diagonal.

docs.title: Classification of States
docs.text:
State \(n\): Absorbing (recurrent). Once all coupons are collected, the chain stays.

States \({0, 1, \ldots, n-1}\): From any state \(k < n\), there is always positive probability of eventually reaching \(n\) (the chain can only move right or stay, so it must eventually hit \(n\)). But no state \(k < n\) can be reached from \(n\). So \({0, \ldots, n-1}\) is an open communicating class — actually, states \({0, \ldots, n-1}\) don't even communicate with each other in the usual sense, since the chain is monotone (it never goes left). Each state \(k < n\) can reach \(n\) but not vice versa.

More precisely: each state \(k \in {0, \ldots, n-1}\) is transient. The chain visits each one at most once before moving right — in fact, each state \(k\) is visited exactly once (the chain starts at 0, passes through \(1, 2, \ldots\) in order, and is absorbed at \(n\)).

The Gambler's Ruin chain could go left or right — it was a genuine random walk. The Coupon Collector chain only goes right or stays. It's monotone. This makes the classification trivial (all non-absorbing states are transient) and makes the first-step equations much simpler — there's no need to solve a coupled system, because from state \(k\) the chain never returns to states \(< k\).

docs.title: Expected Collection Time: First-Step Equations
docs.text:
Let \(d_k = E[\text{steps to reach state } n \mid X_0 = k]\) — the expected number of additional boxes given I currently have \(k\) distinct coupons.

Boundary condition:

\[d_n = 0\]

First-step equation for \(k \in {0, 1, \ldots, n-1}\): condition on the next draw:

\[d_k = 1 + \frac{k}{n} \cdot d_k + \frac{n-k}{n} \cdot d_{k+1}\]

The \(1\) is for the box I just opened. With probability \(k/n\) it's a duplicate and I'm still in state \(k\); with probability \((n-k)/n\) it's new and I move to state \(k+1\).

docs.title: Solving for \(d_k\)
docs.text:
Rearrange: subtract \(\frac{k}{n} d_k\) from both sides:

\[d_k\left(1 - \frac{k}{n}\right) = 1 + \frac{n-k}{n} \cdot d_{k+1}\] \[d_k \cdot \frac{n-k}{n} = 1 + \frac{n-k}{n} \cdot d_{k+1}\]

Divide both sides by \(\frac{n-k}{n}\):

\[d_k = \frac{n}{n-k} + d_{k+1}\]

This is a telescoping recurrence. No coupled system to solve — it unravels immediately.

docs.title: Telescoping to the Answer
docs.text:
Unroll from \(k\) to \(n\):

\[d_k = \frac{n}{n-k} + d_{k+1}$$ $$= \frac{n}{n-k} + \frac{n}{n-k-1} + d_{k+2}$$ $$= \frac{n}{n-k} + \frac{n}{n-k-1} + \cdots + \frac{n}{1} + d_n\]

Since \(d_n = 0\):

\[\boxed{d_k = n \sum_{j=1}^{n-k} \frac{1}{j} = n\left(\frac{1}{1} + \frac{1}{2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{n-k}\right)}\]

docs.title: The Answer: Starting from \(k = 0\)
docs.text:
\[d_0 = n \sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{j} = n H_n\]

where \(H_n = 1 + \frac{1}{2} + \cdots + \frac{1}{n}\) is the \(n\)-th harmonic number.

\[\boxed{E[\text{coupons to complete the set}] = n H_n}\]

docs.title: Decomposition: The Waiting Times Interpretation
docs.text:
The telescoping structure has a beautiful probabilistic interpretation that I want to make explicit.

Define the phases of the collection process:

  • Phase 1: Start with 0 coupons; wait for the 1st new coupon. This always happens on draw 1 — in state \(k=0\), any draw is new, so \(d_0 - d_1 = \frac{n}{n}= 1\).
  • Phase 2: Have 1 coupon; wait for the 2nd new one. \(d_1 - d_2 = \frac{n}{n-1}\).
  • Phase \(k+1\): Have \(k\) coupons; wait for the \((k+1)\)-th new one. \(d_k - d_{k+1} = \frac{n}{n-k}\).
  • Phase \(n\): Have \(n-1\) coupons; wait for the last new one. \(d_{n-1} = \frac{n}{1} = n\).

In state \(k\) (have \(k\) coupons), the next box is new with probability \(\frac{n-k}{n}\). So the number of boxes to get a new coupon is \(\text{Geom}!\left(\frac{n-k}{n}\right)\), with expectation \(\frac{n}{n-k}\).

The total collection time is:

\[T = T_1 + T_2 + \cdots + T_n\]

where \(T_{k+1} \sim \text{Geom}!\left(\frac{n-k}{n}\right)\) is the waiting time for the \((k+1)\)-th new coupon, and \(T_1, \ldots, T_n\) are independent (the phases are independent by the Markov property — once I enter state \(k\), the future depends only on \(k\)).

By linearity of expectation:

\[E[T] = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} E[T_{k+1}] = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \frac{n}{n-k} = n \sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{j} = nH_n\]

This decomposition is the cleanest proof — no recurrence to set up, just linearity of expectation applied to the sum of independent geometric random variables.

The Markov chain machinery gives the same answer as the direct decomposition, but through a different path. The first-step equations are the "correct" Markov chain approach. The phase decomposition is the "correct" probabilistic approach. They agree, as they must. I like having both — the first-step approach generalizes to questions beyond just the expectation (e.g., hitting time distributions), while the decomposition gives clearer intuition.

docs.title: Asymptotics: How Fast Does \(nH_n\) Grow?
docs.text:
Since \(H_n = \ln n + \gamma + O(1/n)\) where \(\gamma \approx 0.5772\) is the Euler-Mascheroni constant:

\[E[T] = n H_n \approx n \ln n + \gamma n + O(1)\]

The expected number of draws is \(\Theta(n \log n)\) — superlinear but subquadratic.

Numerical feel:

\(n\) \(nH_n\) Approx 10 29.3 \(\approx 10 \ln 10 \approx 23\) + correction 50 224.5 100 518.7 365 2364 (days to collect all birthdays)

For \(n = 50\) coupons, expect to buy about 225 boxes. The last few coupons dominate — phase \(n\) (waiting for the last coupon) alone takes \(n\) draws in expectation.

The last coupon is the killer. If I need 1 specific coupon out of \(n\), each draw hits it with probability \(1/n\), so I wait \(n\) draws on average. If \(n = 100\), I expect to spend 100 draws just for the last coupon — and the first 99 cost only \(100 H_{99} - 100 \approx 360\) draws total. The harmonic sum front-loads the easy coupons and back-loads the hard ones.

docs.title: Variance of the Collection Time
docs.text:
The first-step approach gives the expected value. For the variance, the phase decomposition is cleaner.

\[\text{Var}(T) = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \text{Var}(T_{k+1})\]

by independence of the phases. For \(T_{k+1} \sim \text{Geom}(p_k)\) with \(p_k = (n-k)/n\):

\[\text{Var}(T_{k+1}) = \frac{1 - p_k}{p_k^2} = \frac{k/n}{(n-k)^2/n^2} = \frac{kn}{(n-k)^2}\]

So:

\[\text{Var}(T) = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \frac{kn}{(n-k)^2} = n \sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{n-j}{j^2} = n\left(n\sum_{j=1}^n \frac{1}{j^2} - H_n\right)\]

Asymptotically, using \(\sum_{j=1}^n 1/j^2 \to \pi^2/6\):

\[\text{Var}(T) \approx \frac{\pi^2}{6} n^2 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty\]

The standard deviation is \(\sim \frac{\pi}{\sqrt{6}} n \approx 1.28n\) — so the collection time concentrates around \(nH_n\) with fluctuations of order \(n\). Since \(nH_n \sim n\ln n \gg n\), the relative fluctuation \(\text{SD}(T)/E[T] \to 0\) — the collection time concentrates around its mean.

docs.title: The Distribution of \(T\) via Inclusion-Exclusion
docs.text:
The Markov chain gives expectations and (via phase decomposition) variance. The full distribution of \(T\) can be obtained by inclusion-exclusion — this is the approach in B&H.

Let \(A_i\) = event "coupon type \(i\) never appears in the first \(t\) draws." Then \(P(T > t) = P(A_1 \cup \cdots \cup A_n)\).

By inclusion-exclusion:

\[P(T > t) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} (-1)^{k-1} \binom{n}{k} \left(\frac{n-k}{n}\right)^t\]

This is an exact formula for the CDF of \(T\), but it's not what Markov chains give directly — it comes from a different method. I record it here for completeness, but the Markov chain approach is the right one for expectations and first-step analysis.

docs.title: Non-Uniform Coupons
docs.text:
If coupon \(i\) appears with probability \(p_i\) (not necessarily \(1/n\)), the problem is no longer Markov with the "count" state, because the probability of getting a new coupon depends on which coupons I have, not just how many. The state space explodes back to \(2^n\).

This generalization is much harder. The expected collection time becomes:

\[E[T] = \sum_{\emptyset \neq S \subseteq [n]} \frac{(-1)^{|S|+1}}{1 - \sum_{i \in S} p_i}\]

by inclusion-exclusion. No clean closed form in general.

The uniform assumption is what collapses \(2^n\) states to \(n+1\). Non-uniform coupons break this symmetry entirely. This is a good reminder that the Markov property is a gift — it should never be taken for granted.

docs.title: Double Dixie Cup Problem
docs.text: How many draws to collect at least \(m\) copies of every coupon? The state becomes a vector in \({0, 1, \ldots, m}^n\) — large but still Markov. The expected collection time involves higher-order harmonic numbers. A much harder problem.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Object Formula State space \({0, 1, \ldots, n}\); state = number of distinct coupons Transition from \(k\) To \(k+1\) w.p. \((n-k)/n\); stay at \(k\) w.p. \(k/n\) State classification State \(n\) absorbing; all others transient First-step equation \(d_k = \frac{n}{n-k} + d_{k+1}\) Expected time from \(k\) \(d_k = n(H_{n} - H_{n-k}) = n\sum_{j=1}^{n-k} \frac{1}{j}\) Expected total time \(E[T] = nH_n \approx n\ln n\) Variance \(\text{Var}(T) \approx \frac{\pi^2}{6}n^2\) Phase decomposition \(T = T_1 + \cdots + T_n\), \(T_{k+1} \sim \text{Geom}!\left(\frac{n-k}{n}\right)\), independent

docs.title: One-Line Summary for Future Me
docs.text:
Model the Coupon Collector as a Markov chain on \({0, \ldots, n}\) where state $= $ number of distinct coupons; from state \(k\), move to \(k+1\) w.p. \((n-k)/n\). The first-step equation telescopes to \(d_k = n/(n-k) + d_{k+1}\), giving \(E[T] = nH_n\) — equivalently, the total time is the sum of \(n\) independent geometric waiting times with success probabilities \(n/n, (n-1)/n, \ldots, 1/n\).

docs.title: Stationary Distribution
docs.text: "A stationary distribution is a fixed point of the dynamics. Start there, and you never leave — not because you're frozen, but because the outflow from every state is exactly balanced by the inflow. It's equilibrium, not stasis. The chain is still moving; the distribution just doesn't notice."

docs.title: The Definition
docs.text:
Let \((X_n)_{n \geq 0}\) be a Markov chain on state space \(\mathcal{S}\) with transition matrix \(Q\).

Definition. A probability distribution \(\mathbf{s}\) (row vector, \(s_i \geq 0\), \(\sum_i s_i = 1\)) is a stationary distribution (also called steady-state, invariant, or equilibrium distribution) if:

\[\mathbf{s} Q = \mathbf{s}\]

Entrywise, for each \(j \in \mathcal{S}\):

\[\sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} s_i , q_{ij} = s_j\]

Equivalent characterization: If \(X_0 \sim \mathbf{s}\), then \(X_n \sim \mathbf{s}\) for all \(n \geq 1\).

Proof of equivalence: If \(\mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}\), then \(\mathbf{t}^{(1)} = \mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}\), and by induction \(\mathbf{t}^{(n)} = \mathbf{s}Q^n = \mathbf{s}\) for all \(n\). Conversely, if \(\mathbf{t}^{(1)} = \mathbf{s}\) whenever \(\mathbf{t}^{(0)} = \mathbf{s}\), then \(\mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}\). \(\blacksquare\)

The language of "stationary" can be misleading. The chain is not stationary in the sense of being stuck — it's still making random transitions at every step. What's stationary is the distribution: the probability mass on each state doesn't change over time. Think of it like a river at steady state: water flows, but the water level stays constant.

docs.title: The Balance Equation
docs.text:
Rewrite \(\sum_i s_i q_{ij} = s_j\) as:

\[s_j = \sum_{i eq j} s_i q_{ij} + s_j q_{jj}\] \[s_j(1 - q_{jj}) = \sum_{i eq j} s_i q_{ij}\] \[s_j \sum_{k eq j} q_{jk} = \sum_{i eq j} s_i q_{ij}\]

Left side: Total rate of flow out of state \(j\) (weighted by \(s_j\)). Right side: Total rate of flow into state \(j\) from all other states.

This is called the global balance equation: at stationarity, the flow out of every state equals the flow into it. It is the probabilistic version of conservation of mass.

docs.title: Theorem (Finite Irreducible Chains)
docs.text:
If \((X_n)\) is an irreducible Markov chain on a finite state space, then:

  1. A stationary distribution \(\mathbf{s}\) exists.
  2. It is unique.
  3. It is given by \(s_i = \frac{1}{E[T_i \mid X_0 = i]}\) — the reciprocal of the expected return time to state \(i\).

Proof of existence. Since \(\mathcal{S}\) is finite, every state in an irreducible chain is positive recurrent (no escape to infinity, pigeonhole forces infinitely many returns, and recurrence is a class property). For a positive recurrent state \(i\), define \(s_i = 1/m_i\) where \(m_i = E[T_i \mid X_0 = i] < \infty\). One can verify (via the renewal theory argument) that this defines a probability distribution satisfying \(\mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}\).

Proof of uniqueness. Suppose \(\mathbf{s}\) and \(\mathbf{s}'\) are both stationary. Then \(\mathbf{s}Q^n = \mathbf{s}\) and \(\mathbf{s}'Q^n = \mathbf{s}'\) for all \(n\). For an irreducible aperiodic chain, \(Q^n \to \mathbf{1s}\) (convergence theorem). Taking \(n \to \infty\): \(\mathbf{s}' = \mathbf{s}' \cdot \mathbf{1s} = \mathbf{s}\). \(\square\)

For an irreducible periodic chain, \(Q^n\) doesn't converge, but the uniqueness of \(\mathbf{s}\) still holds — periodicity only breaks convergence, not uniqueness.

The formula \(s_i = 1/m_i\) is one of the most useful things to know. It says: the fraction of time the chain spends in state \(i\) in the long run is the reciprocal of the average time between visits. This is exactly what you'd expect from the law of large numbers — if returns happen every \(m_i\) steps on average, the chain is in state \(i\) a fraction \(1/m_i\) of the time. The stationary distribution is the long-run time average.

docs.title: What Can Go Wrong Without Irreducibility
docs.text:
Multiple stationary distributions. If the chain has two closed communicating classes \(C_1\) and \(C_2\), each has its own stationary distribution \(\mathbf{s}_1\) and \(\mathbf{s}_2\), and every convex combination \(\alpha \mathbf{s}_1 + (1-\alpha)\mathbf{s}_2\) is also stationary. Infinitely many stationary distributions.

No stationary distribution. If all states are transient (e.g., a random walk on \(\mathbb{Z}\) with drift), there is no stationary distribution.

Null recurrence. On an infinite state space, an irreducible chain can be recurrent but null recurrent — every state is visited infinitely often, but \(m_i = \infty\) for all \(i\). Then \(s_i = 1/m_i = 0\) for all \(i\), which doesn't define a probability distribution. No stationary distribution exists.

docs.title: The System to Solve
docs.text:
Given transition matrix \(Q\), find \(\mathbf{s}\) satisfying:

\[\mathbf{s} Q = \mathbf{s} \qquad \text{(balance equations)}$$ $$\sum_{i} s_i = 1 \qquad \text{(normalization)}\]

The balance equations \(\mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}\) are equivalent to \(\mathbf{s}(Q - I) = \mathbf{0}\), i.e., \(\mathbf{s}\) is a left null vector of \(Q - I\).

Important: The system \(\mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}\) alone has rank \(M - 1\) (for an irreducible chain on \(M\) states) — one equation is redundant, since they all sum to the same thing. Always drop one equation and replace it with the normalization \(\sum_i s_i = 1\).

docs.title: General Procedure
docs.text:
1. Write out \(\mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}\) as \(M\) scalar equations.
  2. Drop any one equation (it's redundant).
  3. Add \(\sum_i s_i = 1\).
  4. Solve the resulting \(M \times M\) linear system.

docs.title: Two-State Example
docs.text:
\[Q = \begin{pmatrix} 1-\alpha & \alpha \ \beta & 1-\beta \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{s} = (s_1, s_2)\]

Balance equations: \(\mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}\):

\[s_1(1-\alpha) + s_2 \beta = s_1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad -\alpha s_1 + \beta s_2 = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad s_2 = \frac{\alpha}{\beta} s_1\]

Drop the second equation (redundant). Add normalization: \(s_1 + s_2 = 1\):

\[s_1 + \frac{\alpha}{\beta} s_1 = 1 \implies s_1 = \frac{\beta}{\alpha + \beta}, \quad s_2 = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha + \beta}\] \[\boxed{\mathbf{s} = \left(\frac{\beta}{\alpha+\beta},\ \frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}\right)}\]

Sanity check via \(s_i = 1/m_i\): the expected return time to state 1 should be \((\alpha+\beta)/\beta\). From state 1, the chain goes to state 2 with probability \(\alpha\), then returns to state 1 in a geometric number of steps. This is consistent. ✓

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The chain satisfies detailed balance with respect to distribution \(\mathbf{s}\) if for all \(i, j\):

\[s_i , q_{ij} = s_j , q_{ji}\]

Detailed balance says: the probability flux from \(i\) to \(j\) equals the flux from \(j\) to \(i\), at every pair of states individually.

This is stronger than global balance. Global balance requires total inflow = total outflow at each state. Detailed balance requires this pairwise, for every directed edge.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
If \(\mathbf{s}\) satisfies detailed balance with respect to \(Q\), then \(\mathbf{s}\) is stationary.

Proof. Sum the detailed balance condition over \(i\):

\[\sum_i s_i q_{ij} = \sum_i s_j q_{ji} = s_j \sum_i q_{ji} = s_j \cdot 1 = s_j\]

This is exactly \(\mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}\). \(\blacksquare\)

The converse is false: a chain can have a stationary distribution without satisfying detailed balance.

docs.title: Reversibility
docs.text:
A chain that satisfies detailed balance with respect to its stationary distribution is called reversible. The terminology comes from the following:

Proposition. If \((X_n)\) is a stationary reversible chain, then the time-reversed process \((X_{T-n})_{0 \leq n \leq T}\) has the same distribution as \((X_n)_{0 \leq n \leq T}\).

In other words, you cannot tell from the distribution whether the chain is running forward or backward in time.

Reversibility is a strong structural property. Physical systems in thermal equilibrium satisfy it (it's the content of the principle of detailed balance in statistical mechanics). In MCMC, the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm is specifically designed to satisfy detailed balance — that's how it guarantees the target distribution is stationary. So detailed balance is not just a mathematical curiosity; it's an algorithmic tool.

docs.title: Using Detailed Balance to Find \(\mathbf{s}\)
docs.text:
For reversible chains, detailed balance is often easier to solve than the global balance equations. The method:

  1. Write \(s_i q_{ij} = s_j q_{ji}\) for all pairs \((i,j)\) with \(q_{ij} > 0\).
  2. Express all \(s_i\) in terms of \(s_1\) (or any reference state) by multiplying ratios.
  3. Normalize.

Example — Birth-Death Chain:

States \({0, 1, \ldots, M}\), \(q_{k,k+1} = p_k\), \(q_{k,k-1} = r_k\), \(q_{kk} = 1 - p_k - r_k\). Detailed balance:

\[s_k p_k = s_{k+1} r_{k+1}\]

So \(s_{k+1} = s_k \cdot \frac{p_k}{r_{k+1}}\). Telescoping:

\[s_k = s_0 \cdot \frac{p_0 p_1 \cdots p_{k-1}}{r_1 r_2 \cdots r_k}\]

Normalize to find \(s_0\). Birth-death chains always satisfy detailed balance — they're always reversible.

Birth-death chains are the Coupon Collector and Gambler's Ruin in disguise. The Coupon Collector is a birth-death chain with \(p_k = (n-k)/n\) and \(r_k = 0\) (only births, no deaths — an absorbing chain). The two-state chain is the simplest birth-death chain. Detailed balance applies to all of them.

docs.title: The Stationary Distribution and Long-Run Behavior
Theorem (Ergodic Theorem for Markov Chains)
docs.text:
For an irreducible positive recurrent chain, for any bounded function \(f : \mathcal{S} \to \mathbb{R}\), almost surely:

\[\frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f(X_k) \longrightarrow \sum_{i \in \mathcal{S}} s_i f(i) = E_{\mathbf{s}}[f(X)]\]

In particular, taking \(f = \mathbf{1}_j\) (indicator of state \(j\)):

\[\frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \mathbf{1}[X_k = j] \longrightarrow s_j\]

The long-run fraction of time spent in state \(j\) is \(s_j\), regardless of the initial state.

This is the law of large numbers for Markov chains. It holds without any aperiodicity assumption — unlike the distributional convergence theorem (\(\mathbf{t}^{(n)} \to \mathbf{s}\)), which requires aperiodicity. The time-average always converges; the distribution at a fixed time might oscillate (if periodic).

This is why \(\mathbf{s}\) is called the stationary distribution and not the "limiting distribution." Limiting distribution requires aperiodicity. Stationary distribution just requires irreducibility and positive recurrence. The ergodic theorem is the more fundamental statement — it's about time averages, which always converge.

docs.title: Stationary Distribution Does Not Require Convergence
docs.text:
A periodic chain still has a unique stationary distribution — it just doesn't converge to it in the distributional sense.

Example: Two-state chain with \(\alpha = \beta = 1\) (deterministic alternation):

\[Q = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\]

The stationary distribution is \(\mathbf{s} = (1/2, 1/2)\) (solve \(\mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}\)). But starting from state 1: \(X_n = 1\) if \(n\) even, \(X_n = 2\) if \(n\) odd. The distribution of \(X_n\) oscillates between \(\delta_1\) and \(\delta_2\) — it never converges to \((1/2, 1/2)\).

However, the time average \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \mathbf{1}[X_k = 1] \to 1/2\) almost surely. The ergodic theorem holds; distributional convergence doesn't.

docs.title: Summary: Three Levels of "Convergence"
docs.text:
Statement Requires What it says \(\mathbf{s}\) exists and is unique Irreducible + positive recurrent (automatic for finite irreducible) There is a well-defined long-run distribution Time average \(\to s_j\) a.s. Irreducible + positive recurrent Fraction of visits to \(j\) converges to \(s_j\) \(\mathbf{t}^{(n)} \to \mathbf{s}\) Irreducible + aperiodic (+ positive recurrent) Distribution at time \(n\) converges to \(\mathbf{s}\)

Each level is strictly stronger than the one above.

docs.title: Key Facts at a Glance
docs.text: Fact Statement Definition \(\mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}\), \(s_i \geq 0\), \(\sum_i s_i = 1\) Existence + uniqueness Guaranteed for finite irreducible chains Formula \(s_i = 1/E[T_i \mid X_0 = i]\) How to compute Solve \(\mathbf{s}(Q-I) = 0\) with normalization; drop one balance equation Detailed balance \(s_i q_{ij} = s_j q_{ji}\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(\mathbf{s}\) stationary (sufficient, not necessary) Reversibility Detailed balance \(\Leftrightarrow\) chain is time-reversible Ergodic theorem Time average of \(f(X_k)\) \(\to\) \(E_\mathbf{s}[f]\) a.s. (no aperiodicity needed) Distributional convergence \(\mathbf{t}^{(n)} \to \mathbf{s}\) requires aperiodicity in addition

docs.title: One-Line Summary for Future Me
docs.text:
A stationary distribution \(\mathbf{s}\) satisfies \(\mathbf{s}Q = \mathbf{s}\); for finite irreducible chains it exists, is unique, and equals \(s_i = 1/m_i\) (reciprocal of mean return time). Find it by solving the balance equations with normalization. Detailed balance \(s_i q_{ij} = s_j q_{ji}\) is sufficient for stationarity and characterizes reversibility. The ergodic theorem says time averages converge to \(s_j\) always; distributional convergence \(\mathbf{t}^{(n)} \to \mathbf{s}\) additionally requires aperiodicity.
