docs.title: Code Breaking
docs.text: "Shannon's 1949 paper on secrecy systems is one of the most beautiful things I've ever read. He took a problem that had been purely combinatorial — how do you hide a message? — and recast it as a problem in probability theory. A cipher is a random variable. Security is a statement about conditional distributions. The perfect cipher is one where the ciphertext and plaintext are independent. And he proved, with elementary probability, exactly how much key you need to achieve this — and exactly how many ciphertext characters you need to read before the key is determined. The whole paper is just probability, applied with ruthless clarity."

docs.title: The Setup: A Probabilistic Model of Secrecy
docs.text:
Let me fix notation. A cryptosystem consists of:

  • \(\mathcal{M}\): the message space (plaintexts). Each message \(M \in \mathcal{M}\) is a random variable with some prior distribution \(P(M = m)\).
  • \(\mathcal{K}\): the key space. Key \(K \in \mathcal{K}\) drawn uniformly at random (or from some distribution), independent of \(M\).
  • \(\mathcal{C}\): the ciphertext space.
  • Encryption: \(C = E_K(M)\) — a deterministic function of \(M\) and \(K\).
  • Decryption: \(M = D_K(C)\) — the inverse: \(D_K(E_K(m)) = m\) for all \(m, k\).

The adversary observes \(C\) and wants to recover \(M\) (or learn something about it). The question: how much does \(C\) reveal about \(M\)?

This is a conditional distribution question:

\[P(M = m \mid C = c) = \frac{P(C = c \mid M = m) \cdot P(M = m)}{P(C = c)}\]

Security means the posterior \(P(M \mid C)\) is close to the prior \(P(M)\) — the ciphertext teaches the adversary nothing.

docs.title: The Caesar Cipher
docs.text:
Encryption: Shift each letter by a fixed key \(k \in {0, 1, \ldots, 25}\):

\[E_k(m_i) = (m_i + k) \bmod 26\]

Key space: \(|\mathcal{K}| = 26\).

Breaking it: Exhaustive search — try all 26 keys, find the one that produces readable English. Even by hand, this takes under a minute. Computationally, it's \(O(26 \cdot n)\) where \(n\) is the message length.

Probabilistically: If \(M\) is a single letter drawn from English letter frequencies, the posterior after observing one ciphertext letter \(C = c\) is:

\[P(K = k \mid C = c, M = m) = \mathbf{1}[c = (m + k) \bmod 26]\]

But I don't know \(M\). I know \(P(M = m)\) — the English letter frequencies. Bayes gives:

\[P(M = m \mid C = c) \propto P(C = c \mid M = m) P(M = m) = \mathbf{1}[E_k(m) = c] \cdot P(M = m)\]

For a fixed key \(k\), the cipher is a bijection on letters, so each ciphertext letter corresponds to exactly one plaintext letter under that key. There's no probabilistic uncertainty — if I know \(k\), I know \(m\) exactly. The uncertainty is purely about \(k\).

The Caesar cipher has essentially zero security: \(H(K) = \log_2 26 \approx 4.7\) bits of key entropy — trivially exhausted.

docs.title: The Vigenère Cipher
docs.text:
Encryption: Use a key \(\mathbf{k} = (k_1, \ldots, k_d) \in {0,\ldots,25}^d\) (period \(d\)). Encrypt the \(i\)-th letter by shifting by \(k_{i \bmod d}\):

\[E_{\mathbf{k}}(m_i) = (m_i + k_{i \bmod d}) \bmod 26\]

Key space: \(|\mathcal{K}| = 26^d\) — exponentially larger than Caesar.

Naive analysis: If the key length \(d\) is unknown, brute force is infeasible for large \(d\). Key entropy is \(H(\mathbf{K}) = d \log_2 26 \approx 4.7d\) bits.

But: The Vigenère is just \(d\) interleaved Caesar ciphers. Letters at positions \(1, d+1, 2d+1, \ldots\) are all encrypted with the same shift \(k_1\); letters at positions \(2, d+2, \ldots\) with shift \(k_2\); and so on.

Breaking it — two steps:

Step 1: Determine \(d\) (the key length).

Kasiski test: Look for repeated substrings in the ciphertext. If a plaintext substring appears at positions \(i\) and \(j\), and the key repeats with period \(d\), then the ciphertext will repeat iff \(d \mid (j - i)\). So: find all repeated trigrams in the ciphertext, compute the differences \(j - i\), take \(\gcd\) of all differences — that's likely \(d\) (or a multiple of it).

Index of Coincidence: More elegant. Define the index of coincidence of a text \(c_1, \ldots, c_n\) as:

\[\text{IC} = \sum_{l=0}^{25} \frac{f_l(f_l - 1)}{n(n-1)}\]

where \(f_l\) = frequency of letter \(l\) in the text. This is an estimate of \(P(\text{two random letters are equal}) = \sum_{l=0}^{25} p_l^2\), where \(p_l\) is the true frequency of letter \(l\).

For English text: \(\text{IC}_{\text{English}} \approx 0.065\) (because English is non-uniform — 'e' appears \(\sim 13%\) of the time, boosting \(\sum p_l^2\)).

For a uniformly random text: \(\text{IC}_{\text{uniform}} = \sum_{l=0}^{25} (1/26)^2 = 1/26 \approx 0.038\).

For a Vigenère-encrypted English text with key length \(d\): if I take every \(d\)-th character, I get a Caesar-shifted English text — IC \(\approx 0.065\). If I take every \(d'\)-th character for \(d' \neq d\), the letters mix like random — IC \(\approx 0.038\).

Algorithm: For \(d' = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\), compute IC of every \(d'\)-th subsequence. The true \(d\) is the smallest \(d'\) where IC jumps to \(\approx 0.065\).

Step 2: Break each Caesar cipher separately.

Once I know \(d\), split the ciphertext into \(d\) streams. Each stream is a Caesar cipher on English text. For each stream, compare the observed letter frequencies (shifted by \(k_j\)) to the English frequency distribution — find the shift that best aligns them.

Formally: Let \(\hat{p}_0, \ldots, \hat{p}_{25}\) be the observed letter frequencies in stream \(j\). The true frequencies are \(p_0, \ldots, p_{25}\) (English). The key \(k_j\) satisfies \(\hat{p}_{(l + k_j) \bmod 26} \approx p_l\) for all \(l\). Find \(k_j\) maximizing:

\[\sum_{l=0}^{25} \hat{p}_{(l+k_j) \bmod 26} \cdot p_l\]

(dot product of shifted observed with true frequencies — maximum at the correct shift). This is a maximum likelihood estimate under the assumption that letters are i.i.d. with English frequencies.

The IC is a beautiful object. It's just \(\sum p_l^2\) estimated from data — the probability that two randomly drawn letters match. The fact that this single number distinguishes "Caesar-shifted English" (IC \(\approx 0.065\)) from "random noise" (IC \(\approx 0.038\)) is what makes the Vigenère breakable. The non-uniformity of English letter frequencies is the lever. The more non-uniform the source, the easier the cipher is to break.

docs.title: Frequency Analysis as Maximum Likelihood
docs.text:
Let me be precise about what frequency analysis is doing probabilistically.

Model. Assume plaintext letters \(M_1, M_2, \ldots, M_n\) are i.i.d. with distribution \(\mathbf{p} = (p_0, \ldots, p_{25})\) (English frequencies). Ciphertext is \(C_i = (M_i + k) \bmod 26\) for unknown \(k\).

Likelihood of observing ciphertext counts \(\mathbf{f} = (f_0, \ldots, f_{25})\) given key \(k\):

\[L(k) = P(\mathbf{f} \mid k) = \prod_{l=0}^{25} p_{(l-k) \bmod 26}^{f_l}\]

(Letter \(l\) in the ciphertext came from plaintext letter \((l - k) \bmod 26\), which has probability \(p_{(l-k) \bmod 26}\).)

Log-likelihood:

\[\log L(k) = \sum_{l=0}^{25} f_l \log p_{(l-k) \bmod 26} = n \sum_{l=0}^{25} \hat{p}_l \log p_{(l-k) \bmod 26}\]

where \(\hat{p}_l = f_l / n\). Maximizing over \(k \in {0, \ldots, 25}\):

\[\hat{k}_{\text{MLE}} = \arg\max_k \sum_{l=0}^{25} \hat{p}_l \log p_{(l-k) \bmod 26}\]

This is the cross-entropy between \(\hat{\mathbf{p}}\) and the shifted English distribution — frequency analysis is maximum likelihood, nothing more.

Connection to KL divergence: Note \(\sum_l \hat{p}_l \log p_{(l-k)\bmod 26} = -H(\hat{\mathbf{p}}) - D_{\text{KL}}(\hat{\mathbf{p}} | \mathbf{p}_{-k})\) where \(\mathbf{p}_{-k}\) is \(\mathbf{p}\) shifted by \(-k\). Maximizing log-likelihood is equivalent to minimizing \(D_{\text{KL}}(\hat{\mathbf{p}} | \mathbf{p}_{-k})\) — finding the shift that makes the English frequencies closest to the observed frequencies, in KL-divergence.

docs.title: Perfect Secrecy: Shannon's Definition
docs.text:
Definition (Perfect Secrecy). A cryptosystem has perfect secrecy if for every message \(m \in \mathcal{M}\) and ciphertext \(c \in \mathcal{C}\):

\[P(M = m \mid C = c) = P(M = m)\]

Equivalently (by Bayes): \(P(C = c \mid M = m) = P(C = c)\) — \(C\) and \(M\) are independent. Observing the ciphertext gives zero information about the plaintext.

Equivalently (in terms of mutual information): \(I(M; C) = 0\).

Theorem (Shannon, 1949). A cryptosystem with \(|\mathcal{M}| = |\mathcal{C}| = |\mathcal{K}|\) achieves perfect secrecy if and only if:

  1. Every key is used with equal probability: \(K \sim \text{Uniform}(\mathcal{K})\).
  2. For every plaintext \(m\) and ciphertext \(c\), there exists exactly one key \(k\) such that \(E_k(m) = c\).

Proof.

(\(\Rightarrow\)) Assume perfect secrecy. Fix any ciphertext \(c\). For every \(m\):

\[P(C = c \mid M = m) = P(C = c)\]

Since \(P(C = c \mid M = m) = \sum_k P(K = k) \cdot \mathbf{1}[E_k(m) = c]\), summing over all messages:

\[P(C = c) = \sum_m P(M = m) P(C = c \mid M = m) = P(C = c) \cdot \sum_m P(M = m) = P(C = c)\]

This is tautological, but the constraint comes from fixing \(m\): for each \(m\), \(P(C = c \mid M = m) = P(C = c)\) must hold simultaneously for all \(m\). This forces the map \(k \mapsto E_k(m)\) to cover \(\mathcal{C}\) with the same distribution regardless of \(m\). Since \(|\mathcal{M}| = |\mathcal{K}| = |\mathcal{C}|\), the function \(k \mapsto E_k(m)\) is a bijection for each fixed \(m\), and uniform \(K\) gives uniform \(C\) for any \(m\). The key must be uniform, and the bijection must hold — conditions 1 and 2.

(\(\Leftarrow\)) Assume conditions 1 and 2. Then for any \(m, c\):

\[P(C = c \mid M = m) = P(E_K(m) = c) = P(K = \text{unique } k \text{ s.t. } E_k(m) = c) = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{K}|}\]

This is independent of \(m\), so \(C \perp M\). \(\blacksquare\)

Corollary (Key Length Lower Bound). For perfect secrecy: \(|\mathcal{K}| \geq |\mathcal{M}|\). Equivalently, \(H(K) \geq H(M)\). The key must be at least as long as the message.

Proof: From condition 2, for each \(c\), there are \(|\mathcal{K}|\) pairs \((m, k)\) with \(E_k(m) = c\) (one per key). These must cover all \(|\mathcal{M}|\) messages. So \(|\mathcal{K}| \geq |\mathcal{M}|\).

docs.title: The One-Time Pad: Perfect Secrecy Achieved
docs.text:
Construction. \(\mathcal{M} = \mathcal{K} = \mathcal{C} = {0,1}^n\) (bitstrings of length \(n\)). Key \(K \sim \text{Uniform}({0,1}^n)\). Encrypt:

\[C = M \oplus K \quad (\text{bitwise XOR})\]

Decrypt: \(M = C \oplus K\) (XOR is its own inverse).

Theorem. The one-time pad has perfect secrecy.

Proof. For any \(m, c \in {0,1}^n\):

\[P(C = c \mid M = m) = P(M \oplus K = c \mid M = m) = P(K = m \oplus c) = \frac{1}{2^n}\]

This is independent of \(m\). So \(C \perp M\). \(\blacksquare\)

The one-time pad is perfectly secure — and completely impractical. The key must be:

  1. As long as the message (\(n\) bits for \(n\) bits of plaintext).
  2. Truly random (not pseudorandom).
  3. Never reused. (Hence "one-time.")

Why no reuse? If \(C_1 = M_1 \oplus K\) and \(C_2 = M_2 \oplus K\), then \(C_1 \oplus C_2 = M_1 \oplus M_2\). The XOR of two ciphertexts equals the XOR of two plaintexts — and \(M_1 \oplus M_2\) leaks massive information about both \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) (especially for natural language, where many bits are redundant). This is the "two-time pad" attack, and it completely breaks one-time pad reuse.

The two-time pad attack is what broke the Venona project intercepts — Soviet intelligence reused one-time pad pages due to production pressure during WWII, and the NSA spent decades exploiting the resulting \(M_1 \oplus M_2\) relationships in intercepted cables. Perfect theoretical security, destroyed by a single implementation mistake.

docs.title: Unicity Distance: How Much Ciphertext Do I Need?
docs.text:
Shannon asked: given a ciphertext of length \(n\), how many keys are consistent with it producing meaningful (English) plaintext?

Definition. The unicity distance \(n_0\) is the minimum ciphertext length such that, in expectation, only one key is consistent with the ciphertext producing a valid plaintext. Formally, \(n_0\) is the smallest \(n\) such that the expected number of spurious keys — wrong keys that still decrypt to meaningful text — drops below 1.

Derivation. The number of meaningful \(n\)-letter English plaintexts is approximately \(2^{nH_{\text{English}}}\) where \(H_{\text{English}}\) is the per-letter entropy of English (empirically \(\approx 1.0\)–\(1.5\) bits per letter, accounting for all correlations; often approximated as \(1.0\) bits/letter for long texts).

The total number of \(n\)-letter strings is \(26^n = 2^{n \log_2 26} \approx 2^{4.7n}\).

The redundancy of English per letter: \(r = \log_2 26 - H_{\text{English}} \approx 4.7 - 1.5 = 3.2\) bits/letter.

For a key \(k\) chosen uniformly from \(|\mathcal{K}|\) keys, the expected number of spurious keys is:

\[\bar{s}(n) \approx |\mathcal{K}| \cdot \frac{2^{nH_{\text{English}}}}{26^n} = |\mathcal{K}| \cdot 2^{-nr}\]

Setting \(\bar{s}(n_0) = 1\):

\[|\mathcal{K}| \cdot 2^{-n_0 r} = 1 \implies n_0 = \frac{\log_2 |\mathcal{K}|}{r} = \frac{H(K)}{r}\]

For Caesar (\(|\mathcal{K}| = 26\), \(H(K) = \log_2 26 \approx 4.7\) bits):

\[n_0 = \frac{4.7}{3.2} \approx 1.5 \text{ letters}\]

With just 2 ciphertext letters, in expectation fewer than 1 spurious key — essentially unique decryption. (This matches intuition: even with 3-4 letters of Caesar, the correct key is usually obvious.)

For Vigenère with period \(d\) (\(|\mathcal{K}| = 26^d\), \(H(K) = d \log_2 26 \approx 4.7d\) bits):

\[n_0 = \frac{4.7d}{3.2} \approx 1.47d\]

With about \(1.5d\) letters of ciphertext, the key is essentially determined. Impressively small — a Vigenère cipher with 10-letter key is broken with about 15 letters of ciphertext (in principle; in practice you need more for the statistical estimates to be accurate).

For one-time pad (\(|\mathcal{K}| = 26^n\), \(H(K) = n \log_2 26\)):

\[n_0 = \frac{n \log_2 26}{r} = \frac{n \cdot 4.7}{3.2} > n\]

The unicity distance exceeds the message length — there are always multiple valid keys consistent with any ciphertext, so the key can never be uniquely determined from the ciphertext alone. This is perfect secrecy, recovered from the information-theoretic angle.

The unicity distance is the information-theoretic "point of no return" — below \(n_0\) characters, there isn't enough ciphertext to pin down the key; above \(n_0\), the key is essentially determined by the ciphertext (given a meaningful plaintext model). It's the boundary between "computationally hard to break" and "theoretically impossible to break." The OTP lives permanently below this boundary — by design.

docs.title: Entropy and the Security of Ciphers
docs.text:
Let me collect the information-theoretic picture.

Key equivocation \(H(K \mid C^n)\): the remaining entropy in the key after observing \(n\) ciphertext characters. As \(n\) increases:

  • For a finite-key cipher over redundant plaintext: \(H(K \mid C^n) \to 0\) as \(n \to \infty\). Eventually the key is determined.
  • For the one-time pad: \(H(K \mid C^n) = H(K)\) for all \(n\). Observing ciphertext gives zero information about the key (and hence about the plaintext).

Shannon showed:

\[H(K \mid C^n) = H(K) + H(M^n) - H(C^n)\]

(from the chain rule, since \(C^n\) is a deterministic function of \((M^n, K)\)). For a "good" cipher, \(H(C^n) \approx n \log_2 26\) (ciphertext looks uniform). So:

\[H(K \mid C^n) \approx H(K) + H(M^n) - n \log_2 26 = H(K) - n(\log_2 26 - H_{\text{English}}) = H(K) - nr\]

This decreases at rate \(r\) per ciphertext character. It hits zero at \(n = H(K)/r\) — the unicity distance.

Mutual information \(I(M^n; C^n)\): How much the ciphertext reveals about the plaintext.

\[I(M^n; C^n) = H(M^n) - H(M^n \mid C^n)\]

For perfect secrecy: \(I(M^n; C^n) = 0\) for all \(n\).

For a finite-key cipher: \(I(M^n; C^n) > 0\) and grows with \(n\) past the unicity distance — the ciphertext increasingly pins down the plaintext.

docs.title: Frequency Analysis in Code
docs.text:
Let me make this concrete with a Python implementation of the full Vigenère attack.

import numpy as np
from collections import Counter

# English letter frequencies (approximate)
ENGLISH_FREQ = np.array([
    0.0817, 0.0149, 0.0278, 0.0425, 0.1270, 0.0223, 0.0202,
    0.0609, 0.0697, 0.0015, 0.0077, 0.0402, 0.0241, 0.0675,
    0.0751, 0.0193, 0.0010, 0.0599, 0.0633, 0.0906, 0.0276,
    0.0098, 0.0236, 0.0015, 0.0197, 0.0007
])  # a=0, b=1, ..., z=25

def to_numbers(text):
    return [ord(c) - ord('a') for c in text.lower() if c.isalpha()]

def index_of_coincidence(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    if n < 2:
        return 0.0
    counts = np.bincount(nums, minlength=26)
    return np.sum(counts * (counts - 1)) / (n * (n - 1))

def find_key_length(ciphertext_nums, max_d=20):
    """Estimate key length via Index of Coincidence."""
    best_d, best_ic = 1, 0.0
    for d in range(1, max_d + 1):
        streams = [ciphertext_nums[i::d] for i in range(d)]
        avg_ic = np.mean([index_of_coincidence(s) for s in streams if len(s) >= 2])
        if avg_ic > best_ic:
            best_ic = avg_ic
            best_d = d
    return best_d

def break_caesar(stream):
    """MLE key for a Caesar-shifted stream."""
    counts = np.bincount(stream, minlength=26) / len(stream)
    scores = [np.dot(counts, np.roll(ENGLISH_FREQ, -k)) for k in range(26)]
    return np.argmax(scores)

def break_vigenere(ciphertext):
    nums = to_numbers(ciphertext)
    d    = find_key_length(nums)
    key  = [break_caesar(nums[i::d]) for i in range(d)]
    key_str = ''.join(chr(k + ord('a')) for k in key)
    plaintext = ''.join(
        chr((c - key[i % d]) % 26 + ord('a'))
        for i, c in enumerate(nums)
    )
    return key_str, plaintext

# --- Example ---
def vigenere_encrypt(plaintext, key):
    nums = to_numbers(plaintext)
    k    = to_numbers(key)
    return ''.join(
        chr((m + k[i % len(k)]) % 26 + ord('a'))
        for i, m in enumerate(nums)
    )

message    = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" * 10
key        = "secret"
ciphertext = vigenere_encrypt(message, key)

recovered_key, recovered_plaintext = break_vigenere(ciphertext)
print(f"Key found:  {recovered_key}")
print(f"Plaintext:  {recovered_plaintext[:50]}...")

What this does:

  1. index_of_coincidence estimates \(\sum p_l^2\) from data.
  2. find_key_length searches for the period \(d\) that maximizes average IC across streams — the true \(d\) makes each stream look like English.
  3. break_caesar solves the MLE problem \(\arg\max_k \sum_l \hat{p}_l \log p_{(l-k) \bmod 26}\) (equivalently, \(\arg\max_k \hat{\mathbf{p}} \cdot \mathbf{p}_{-k}\)).
  4. break_vigenere combines them.

For messages of length \(\geq 100\) characters, this recovers the key exactly. For shorter messages, the IC estimate is noisy and the key length detection can fail — consistent with the unicity distance analysis.

docs.title: The Redundancy of English: Why Ciphers Are Breakable
docs.text:
The entire analysis depends on English having \(H_{\text{English}} \ll \log_2 26\). Let me make this precise.

\(n\)-gram entropy. Model English text as a stationary stochastic process. The per-character entropy rate:

\[H_\infty = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{H(M_1, M_2, \ldots, M_n)}{n}\]

Empirical estimates (Shannon's original 1951 paper on entropy of English):

  • Unigram model (letters i.i.d. with English frequencies): \(H \approx 4.03\) bits/letter.
  • Bigram model: \(H \approx 3.32\) bits/letter.
  • Trigram model: \(H \approx 3.1\) bits/letter.
  • Full English (estimated via human prediction experiments): \(H_\infty \approx 1.0\)–\(1.5\) bits/letter.

Each model captures more structure. The first-order frequency analysis only uses the unigram approximation — it treats letters as i.i.d. with English frequencies. This already gives enough redundancy (\(r = 4.7 - 4.03 = 0.67\) bits/letter at the unigram level, or \(r \approx 3.2\) bits/letter using the true entropy rate) to break the Vigenère.

Higher-order attacks. If I model English as a bigram or trigram process, I can use the transition probabilities for frequency analysis — this works with shorter ciphertexts and handles more complex ciphers. The principle is identical: maximum likelihood over the key space, using a richer language model.

This is the moment where code-breaking and natural language processing meet. A better language model (lower \(H_\infty\) estimate, more accurate \(n\)-gram probabilities) gives a stronger attack. Modern cryptanalysis of classical ciphers often uses large \(n\)-gram frequency tables from billions of words of text. The math is the same as Shannon; the model is just better.

docs.title: Modern Implication: Why Modern Ciphers Are Different
docs.text:
Classical ciphers fail because:

  1. Short keys relative to message: \(H(K) < H(M)\), so unicity distance is finite.
  2. Structured operations (shifts, substitutions) that preserve statistical structure.

Modern symmetric ciphers (AES) avoid both:

  1. Long keys: AES-256 has \(H(K) = 256\) bits. At \(r \approx 1\) bit/bit for binary data, unicity distance \(\approx 256\) bits of ciphertext — a fraction of one block. But:
  2. Pseudorandomness: AES output is computationally indistinguishable from uniform random — not just statistically, but even for computationally bounded adversaries. Frequency analysis finds no structure because the cipher actively destroys it.

The distinction: Shannon's perfect secrecy is information-theoretic — even an adversary with unlimited computation can't break it. Modern cipher security is computational — an adversary with polynomial-time computation can't break it (under hardness assumptions like \(P \neq NP\)). The OTP is the only information-theoretically secure symmetric cipher. Everything else, including AES, is computationally secure.

docs.title: Things I Want to Come Back To
docs.text:
• Work through Shannon's 1949 paper directly — specifically the proof of the key equivocation formula \(H(K \mid C^n) = H(K) + H(M^n) - H(C^n)\).
  • Implement a bigram-based frequency analysis attack — does it crack shorter ciphertexts, as theory predicts?
  • The Enigma machine: it's a polyalphabetic substitution cipher with a much larger key space, but the reflector created a fatal flaw (no letter could encrypt to itself). How does this constraint reduce the effective key entropy? Write this up properly.
  • Kerckhoffs's principle: security should rest entirely on key secrecy, not algorithm secrecy. Formalize this in terms of the probabilistic model above.
  • Public-key cryptography as a completely different paradigm — RSA doesn't rely on \(H(K) \geq H(M)\) at all. The security is computational hardness of factoring. Write [[RSA and Computational Security]].

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Concept Details Perfect secrecy \(M \perp C\); equivalently \(I(M;C) = 0\) Shannon's theorem Perfect secrecy iff \(\|\mathcal{K}\| \geq \|\mathcal{M}\|\), uniform key, bijective encryption One-time pad \(C = M \oplus K\), \(K\) uniform and as long as \(M\); achieves perfect secrecy Caesar cipher Shift by \(k \in {0,\ldots,25}\); broken by exhaustive search or frequency analysis Vigenère cipher Period-\(d\) Caesar; broken by IC (find \(d\)) + MLE frequency analysis (find each \(k_j\)) Index of coincidence \(\text{IC} = \sum p_l^2\); English \(\approx 0.065\), uniform \(\approx 0.038\) Frequency analysis MLE: \(\hat{k} = \arg\max_k \hat{\mathbf{p}} \cdot \mathbf{p}_{-k}\); equivalent to minimizing KL divergence Unicity distance \(n_0 = H(K)/r\); ciphertext length needed to uniquely determine key Redundancy of English \(r = \log_2 26 - H_\infty \approx 3.2\) bits/letter; makes classical ciphers breakable Modern ciphers Computational security (AES); pseudorandom output destroys statistical structure

docs.title: One-Line Summary for Future Me
docs.text:
Code-breaking is Bayesian inference: the adversary updates \(P(K \mid C)\) using the prior \(P(M)\) (English language model); a cipher is broken when \(H(K \mid C^n) \approx 0\), which happens at the unicity distance \(n_0 = H(K)/r\); perfect secrecy (\(I(M;C) = 0\), achieved only by the one-time pad) places \(n_0 > \infty\) by making \(H(K) = \infty\) relative to any finite message.

docs.title: Knapsack Problem
docs.text: "The knapsack problem is one of the most honest problems in all of computer science. It looks trivial — I have items with weights and values, I want to fill a bag optimally — and yet it is NP-hard. Every approach I try turns out to either be exponential in the worst case, or only approximate, or pseudopolynomial (which sounds polynomial but isn't). And then, astonishingly, someone turned it into a public-key cryptosystem — and then someone else broke that cryptosystem using the very structure that was supposed to make it hard. The knapsack problem is where algorithms, complexity theory, and cryptography all collide."

docs.title: The Problem
docs.text:
0-1 Knapsack. Given \(n\) items, each with weight \(w_i > 0\) and value \(v_i > 0\), and a knapsack of capacity \(W\), find the subset \(S \subseteq {1, \ldots, n}\) that maximises total value subject to the weight constraint:

\[\max_{S \subseteq {1,\ldots,n}} \sum_{i \in S} v_i \qquad \text{subject to} \qquad \sum_{i \in S} w_i \leq W\]

The "0-1" means each item is either taken (\(x_i = 1\)) or not (\(x_i = 0\)) — no fractional items, no duplicates. In integer programming notation:

\[\max \sum_{i=1}^n v_i x_i \qquad \text{s.t.} \qquad \sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i \leq W, \quad x_i \in {0,1}\]

Variants:

  • Fractional knapsack: Items can be taken in fractions. Solvable in \(O(n \log n)\) by a greedy algorithm — take items in decreasing order of value density \(v_i/w_i\).
  • Unbounded knapsack: Each item can be taken any number of times.
  • Bounded knapsack: Item \(i\) can be taken at most \(c_i\) times.
  • Multi-dimensional knapsack: Multiple weight constraints (e.g., weight and volume).

The 0-1 version is the hard one. All complexity discussion below is about 0-1 knapsack unless stated.

docs.title: Brute Force: \(O(2^n)\)
docs.text:
The naive approach: enumerate all \(2^n\) subsets, compute total weight and value for each, return the feasible subset with maximum value.

Correctness: Trivially correct — we check every possibility.

Complexity: \(\Theta(2^n \cdot n)\) — one factor of \(n\) for computing the sum. For \(n = 30\), that's \(\approx 10^{10}\) operations. For \(n = 60\), \(\approx 10^{19}\). Completely impractical.

Meet-in-the-middle (slight improvement): Split items into two halves of size \(n/2\). Enumerate all \(2^{n/2}\) subsets of each half, storing (weight, value) pairs. For each subset of the left half, binary search the right half for the highest-value subset that fits in the remaining capacity. Total: \(O(2^{n/2} \cdot n)\). For \(n = 60\): \(\approx 10^{10}\) — still impractical but better. This is the best known exact algorithm in the exponential family.

docs.title: Dynamic Programming: \(O(nW)\)
docs.text:
The standard exact algorithm for small \(W\).

Recurrence. Define:

\[\text{dp}[i][w] = \text{maximum value using items } 1, \ldots, i \text{ with weight capacity } w\]

Base case: \(\text{dp}[0][w] = 0\) for all \(w\) (no items, no value).

Transition: For item \(i\) with weight \(w_i\) and value \(v_i\):

\[\text{dp}[i][w] = \begin{cases} \text{dp}[i-1][w] & \text{if } w_i > w \quad (\text{can't take item } i) \ \max!\big(\text{dp}[i-1][w],; v_i + \text{dp}[i-1][w - w_i]\big) & \text{if } w_i \leq w \end{cases}\]

The second case: either skip item \(i\) (value \(\text{dp}[i-1][w]\)) or take it (value \(v_i\) plus the best we can do with the remaining capacity \(w - w_i\), using items \(1, \ldots, i-1\)).

Correctness proof by induction.

Claim: \(\text{dp}[i][w]\) is the maximum value achievable using items \(1, \ldots, i\) with capacity \(w\).

Base case: \(\text{dp}[0][w] = 0\) — no items available, maximum value is 0. ✓

Inductive step: Assume \(\text{dp}[i-1][\cdot]\) is correct. In any optimal solution for items \(1,\ldots,i\) with capacity \(w\), either item \(i\) is included or not.

  • If not included: optimal value \(= \text{dp}[i-1][w]\) by the inductive hypothesis.
  • If included: \(w_i \leq w\) (feasibility), and the remaining items \(1,\ldots,i-1\) must be packed optimally in capacity \(w - w_i\), giving value \(v_i + \text{dp}[i-1][w - w_i]\) by the inductive hypothesis.

Taking the max of both cases gives \(\text{dp}[i][w]\). \(\blacksquare\)

Complexity: \(O(nW)\) time, \(O(W)\) space (maintain only the previous row — note that the transition only reads \(\text{dp}[i-1]\), so I can overwrite in place if I scan \(w\) from \(W\) down to \(w_i\)).

def knapsack_dp(weights, values, W):
    n = len(weights)
    dp = [0] * (W + 1)

    for i in range(n):
        # Scan backwards to avoid using item i twice
        for w in range(W, weights[i] - 1, -1):
            dp[w] = max(dp[w], values[i] + dp[w - weights[i]])

    return dp[W]

Reconstruction: To recover the optimal subset (not just the value), maintain a boolean table \(\text{keep}[i][w] = \mathbf{1}[\text{item } i \text{ is taken in the optimal solution for } (i,w)]\). Then backtrack from \((n, W)\).

docs.title: Why \(O(nW)\) is NOT Polynomial
docs.text:
Here is the subtlety that trips people up.

The complexity \(O(nW)\) looks polynomial. It is not. It is pseudopolynomial.

Why? The input size is \(O(n \log W + \sum_i \log w_i + \sum_i \log v_i)\) bits — to specify \(W\) requires \(\log_2 W\) bits, not \(W\) bits. If I double the number of bits used to represent \(W\) (i.e., replace \(W\) with \(W^2\)), the DP table size doubles exponentially in the input size.

Formally: Polynomial time means polynomial in the length of the input. The input length is \(L = O(n \log W)\). The DP runs in time \(O(nW) = O(n \cdot 2^{\log W}) = O(n \cdot 2^{L/n})\) — exponential in \(L/n\).

Intuition: \(W = 10^{18}\) can be written in 60 bits — a tiny input. But the DP table has \(10^{18}\) entries — completely infeasible. The DP is only practical when \(W\) is small (say, \(\leq 10^6\) or so).

This distinction — polynomial vs pseudopolynomial — is critical. The knapsack DP is not a polynomial-time algorithm. The knapsack problem remains NP-hard.

I remember being confused about this the first time I saw it. "\(O(nW)\) — that's linear in \(n\) and \(W\), which are the problem parameters!" But the problem parameters are not the input size. The input size is the number of bits needed to write down the problem. \(W\) contributes \(\log W\) bits, not \(W\) bits. Pseudopolynomial algorithms are fast when the parameter values are small but slow when the values are large — even if the values are written compactly.

docs.title: NP-Hardness
docs.text:
Theorem. 0-1 Knapsack is NP-hard.

Proof (reduction from Subset Sum).

Subset Sum: Given integers \(a_1, \ldots, a_n\) and target \(T\), does there exist \(S \subseteq {1,\ldots,n}\) with \(\sum_{i \in S} a_i = T\)?

Subset Sum is NP-complete (standard result — reduce from 3-SAT or from Partition).

Reduction: Given a Subset Sum instance \((a_1,\ldots,a_n, T)\), construct a Knapsack instance:

  • Set \(w_i = v_i = a_i\) for all \(i\).
  • Set \(W = T\).

Claim: The Subset Sum instance has a solution iff the Knapsack instance has optimal value \(\geq T\).

  • (\(\Rightarrow\)) If \(\sum_{i \in S} a_i = T\), then \(\sum_{i \in S} w_i = T \leq W\) (feasible) and \(\sum_{i \in S} v_i = T\).
  • (\(\Leftarrow\)) If the Knapsack has value \(\geq T\), then there exists \(S\) with \(\sum_{i \in S} v_i \geq T\) and \(\sum_{i \in S} w_i \leq T\). Since \(v_i = w_i = a_i > 0\) and \(\sum a_i \leq T\), combined with \(\sum a_i \geq T\), we get \(\sum_{i \in S} a_i = T\).

The reduction is polynomial (linear time). So Knapsack is NP-hard. \(\blacksquare\)

Knapsack is also in NP: Given a candidate subset \(S\), verify feasibility and value in \(O(n)\). So 0-1 Knapsack is NP-complete (as a decision problem: "is there a feasible subset with value \(\geq V\)?").

docs.title: Approximation: The FPTAS
docs.text:
Since exact solution is NP-hard (assuming \(P \neq NP\)), what can we approximate?

Definition. An algorithm is a \((1-\epsilon)\)-approximation for maximization if it returns a solution of value \(\geq (1-\epsilon) \cdot \text{OPT}\) for any \(\epsilon > 0\).

Definition. A Fully Polynomial-Time Approximation Scheme (FPTAS) is a \((1-\epsilon)\)-approximation algorithm that runs in time polynomial in both \(n\) and \(1/\epsilon\).

Theorem. 0-1 Knapsack has an FPTAS.

Construction.

  1. Let \(v_{\max} = \max_i v_i\). Set the scaling factor \(K = \lfloor \epsilon v_{\max} / n \rfloor\).
  2. Define scaled values \(v_i' = \lfloor v_i / K \rfloor\) (integer division).
  3. Run the DP on the scaled instance: the scaled optimal value is at most \(V' = \sum_i v_i' \leq \sum_i v_i/K \leq n \cdot v_{\max}/K \leq n^2/\epsilon\).
  4. DP runs in time \(O(n \cdot V') = O(n^3/\epsilon)\) — polynomial in \(n\) and \(1/\epsilon\).
  5. Return the optimal solution for the scaled instance.

Approximation guarantee. Let \(S^*\) be the true optimum and \(\hat{S}\) the FPTAS solution. For any item \(i\): \(v_i' = \lfloor v_i/K \rfloor \geq v_i/K - 1\), so:

\[\sum_{i \in S^_} v_i' \geq \sum_{i \in S^_} (v_i/K - 1) = \frac{\text{OPT}}{K} - |S^*| \geq \frac{\text{OPT}}{K} - n\]

Since \(\hat{S}\) is optimal in the scaled problem:

\[\sum_{i \in \hat{S}} v_i' \geq \sum_{i \in S^*} v_i' \geq \frac{\text{OPT}}{K} - n\]

So the unscaled value of \(\hat{S}\):

\[\sum_{i \in \hat{S}} v_i \geq K \sum_{i \in \hat{S}} v_i' \geq K!\left(\frac{\text{OPT}}{K} - n\right) = \text{OPT} - nK \geq \text{OPT} - \epsilon v_{\max} \geq \text{OPT}(1-\epsilon)\]

using \(nK \leq \epsilon v_{\max}\) and \(v_{\max} \leq \text{OPT}\) (the single best item is a lower bound on OPT). \(\blacksquare\)

The FPTAS is one of the most elegant tricks in approximation algorithms. The DP is pseudopolynomial because \(W\) and \(V\) can be large. The fix: scale down the values so that \(V'\) is bounded by a polynomial in \(n\) and \(1/\epsilon\). The scaling introduces a small additive error per item, which telescopes to a \((1-\epsilon)\) multiplicative bound. The insight is that if I only care about an \(\epsilon\)-approximation, I don't need the last few bits of precision in the values — rounding them loses at most \(\epsilon \cdot \text{OPT}\).

docs.title: Greedy and Its Failure
docs.text:
Fractional knapsack greedy: Sort items by value density \(v_i/w_i\) descending, take items greedily until the knapsack is full (take the last item fractionally if needed). This is optimal for the fractional variant — provably. Standard exchange argument proof.

0-1 knapsack greedy failure: The greedy fails for 0-1 knapsack. Counterexample:

Item Weight Value Density \(v/w\) 1 1 1 1.0 2 10 9 0.9

\(W = 10\). Greedy takes item 1 (highest density), then item 2 (fits, since \(1 + 10 > 10\)... wait, \(1 + 10 = 11 > 10\)). So greedy takes only item 1, value \(= 1\). Optimal: take item 2 alone, value \(= 9\).

How bad can greedy be? The greedy can be arbitrarily worse than optimal. In the example above, the ratio is \(1/9 \to 0\) as I scale the values. There is no constant approximation ratio for the greedy on 0-1 knapsack.

A \(1/2\)-approximation: Run the greedy on the fractional problem to get a fractional solution of value \(\text{OPT}_f \geq \text{OPT}\). The fractional solution uses at most one fractionally taken item (the "break" item). Compare: (value of all items except break item) vs (value of break item alone). Take the better. This gives value \(\geq \text{OPT}_f / 2 \geq \text{OPT}/2\). A ½-approximation in \(O(n \log n)\).

docs.title: Probabilistic Analysis: How Hard Is Knapsack on Average?
docs.text:
Worst-case NP-hardness doesn't mean every instance is hard. What does a "random" knapsack instance look like?

Model. Draw \(w_i \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)\) and \(v_i \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)\) i.i.d. Set \(W = n/2\) (half the total expected weight).

Expected total weight: \(E[\sum w_i] = n/2 = W\). So the capacity is exactly at the "interesting" point — not so loose that everything fits, not so tight that nothing fits.

Observation. For random instances with \(W = \Theta(n)\), the DP runs in \(O(nW) = O(n^2)\) — polynomial in \(n\). The pseudopolynomiality bites only when \(W\) is exponentially large relative to \(n\).

The continuous relaxation (fractional knapsack) is tight on average. For random instances:

\[\text{OPT}_{\text{integer}} / \text{OPT}_{\text{fractional}} \to 1 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty\]

Informal argument: In the fractional solution, the break item is taken fractionally. But as \(n \to \infty\), the break item's fractional part becomes a negligible fraction of the total value — \(O(v_{\max}/\text{OPT}) = O(1/n)\) contribution. So the integrality gap vanishes.

More precisely: By concentration inequalities (Chernoff/Hoeffding), the total value of items packed by the greedy concentrates sharply around its expectation. The fractional "wasted" portion of the break item has expected value \(E[v_{\text{break}}/2] = O(1/n \cdot \text{OPT})\) — vanishing relative to \(\text{OPT}\).

This is the usual phenomenon with NP-hard problems on random instances: the hard instances are rare, specially structured, and the typical case is much easier. The "hard" instances for knapsack are ones where many subsets have weights very close to \(W\) — an arithmetic coincidence that doesn't arise generically. Random instances with continuous weights are easy.

The hardest instances. The knapsack problem is hardest when:

  1. Many subsets have total weight exactly \(W\) — many feasible solutions to compare.
  2. Items have similar value densities \(v_i/w_i\) — hard to discriminate between items.
  3. \(W\) is large (making DP infeasible) but not so large that all items fit.

Instances with weights drawn from \({1, \ldots, \text{poly}(n)}\) uniformly are in the "easy" regime because \(W\) is polynomial and DP works. The hard regime is \(W = \Theta(2^n)\) — but then the weights themselves require \(\Omega(n)\) bits to specify, so the input is large anyway.

docs.title: Branch and Bound
docs.text:
In practice, exact knapsack solvers use branch and bound — an implicit enumeration of the \(2^n\) subsets, pruning branches that can't beat the current best solution.

Algorithm skeleton:

def branch_and_bound(items, W):
    best = greedy_solution(items, W)     # Initial lower bound

    def recurse(i, remaining_W, current_value):
        nonlocal best
        if i == n:
            best = max(best, current_value)
            return

        # Upper bound: fractional knapsack on remaining items
        ub = current_value + fractional_knapsack(items[i:], remaining_W)
        if ub <= best:
            return   # Prune: can't beat current best

        # Branch: include item i
        if items[i].weight <= remaining_W:
            recurse(i+1, remaining_W - items[i].weight,
                    current_value + items[i].value)

        # Branch: exclude item i
        recurse(i+1, remaining_W, current_value)

    recurse(0, W, 0)
    return best

The bounding function — fractional knapsack on remaining items — is an upper bound on what's achievable from state \((i, \text{remaining_W})\), because the fractional relaxation is always \(\geq\) the integer optimum.

Correctness: The tree enumerates all \(2^n\) subsets implicitly, but prunes branches where the upper bound can't improve the best known solution. Correctness follows from the validity of the upper bound.

Complexity: Worst case \(O(2^n)\) (no pruning, all branches explored). In practice, with good bounding and smart branching order (e.g., by value density), branch and bound solves instances with \(n = 100\)–\(1000\) in seconds — far better than the worst case.

LP relaxation as bound. An even tighter upper bound: solve the LP relaxation (allow \(x_i \in [0,1]\), not just \({0,1}\)). This requires solving an LP at each node — more expensive per node, but fewer nodes explored. This is the basis of modern mixed-integer programming (MIP) solvers.

docs.title: The Merkle-Hellman Knapsack Cryptosystem
docs.text: Here is where things get strange. In 1978, Merkle and Hellman proposed a public-key cryptosystem based on the knapsack problem. The idea: hiding a structured (easy) knapsack problem inside an apparently random (hard) one.

docs.title: Superincreasing Sequences
docs.text:
Definition. A sequence \(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n\) is superincreasing if each element exceeds the sum of all preceding elements:

\[a_k > \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} a_j \quad \text{for all } k = 2, \ldots, n\]

Example: \({1, 2, 4, 8, 16, \ldots}\) — powers of 2 are superincreasing.

Key property: A superincreasing knapsack is solvable in \(O(n)\) by a greedy algorithm.

Algorithm: Given target \(T\) and superincreasing \(a_1, \ldots, a_n\) (sorted descending for clarity: \(a_n > a_{n-1} > \cdots\)):

For i = n, n-1, ..., 1:
    if a_i <= T:
        include a_i  (set x_i = 1)
        T -= a_i

Correctness: Since \(a_n > \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} a_j\), if the target \(T \geq a_n\), then item \(n\) must be included in any solution — all other items combined are insufficient. So we greedily include or exclude the largest element, reduce the target, and recurse. Unique solution exists iff the target is achievable. \(\blacksquare\)

docs.title: Key Generation
docs.text:
1. Generate a superincreasing sequence \(\mathbf{a} = (a_1, \ldots, a_n)\) — the private key.
  2. Choose modulus \(m > \sum_i a_i\) and multiplier \(w\) with \(\gcd(w, m) = 1\) — so \(w\) has a multiplicative inverse \(w^{-1} \bmod m\).
  3. Compute the public key \(\mathbf{b} = (b_1, \ldots, b_n)\) where \(b_i = w \cdot a_i \bmod m\).

The public key \(\mathbf{b}\) looks like a random knapsack instance — hard to solve.

docs.title: Encryption and Decryption
docs.text:
Encryption (sender knows \(\mathbf{b}\), wants to send \(n\)-bit message \(\mathbf{x} \in {0,1}^n\)):

\[c = \sum_{i=1}^n b_i x_i = \sum_{i=1}^n (w a_i \bmod m) x_i\]

Send ciphertext \(c\).

Decryption (receiver knows \(\mathbf{a}, w, m\)):

  1. Compute \(c' = w^{-1} c \bmod m\).
  2. Note: \(c' = w^{-1} \sum_i (wa_i \bmod m) x_i \bmod m = \sum_i a_i x_i \bmod m\).
  3. Since \(m > \sum_i a_i \geq \sum_{i: x_i=1} a_i\), there is no wraparound — \(c' = \sum_i a_i x_i\) exactly.
  4. Solve the superincreasing knapsack \(\sum_i a_i x_i = c'\) in \(O(n)\).

Why it seems secure: An adversary sees \(\mathbf{b}\) and \(c\). To decrypt, they must solve \(\sum_i b_i x_i = c\) — an apparently random knapsack instance. NP-hard!

docs.title: Breaking It: The Shamir-Zippel Attack (1982)
docs.text:
Shamir (and independently others) broke the Merkle-Hellman system in 1982 using lattice reduction — specifically, the LLL algorithm.

The attack, intuitively. The public key \(\mathbf{b}\) is not a truly random knapsack. It is a modular transformation of a superincreasing sequence. The structure is hidden, but not destroyed — it lives in a lattice.

Setup. The attacker wants to find \(w^{-1} \bmod m\) (or equivalently, a pair \((w', m')\) that transforms \(\mathbf{b}\) back into a superincreasing sequence). This is a problem of finding a short vector in a lattice.

The lattice. Construct the \((n+1) \times (n+1)\) lattice basis matrix:

\[B = \begin{pmatrix} m & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \ b_1 & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \ b_2 & 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \ \vdots & & & \ddots & \vdots \ b_n & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 \end{pmatrix}\]

Any vector in the lattice \(\mathcal{L}(B)\) has the form \(Bz\) for integer \(z\). One particular short vector encodes \((w^{-1}, a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n)\) scaled appropriately — the private key.

LLL algorithm (Lenstra-Lenstra-Lovász, 1982): given a lattice basis, find a "reasonably short" vector in polynomial time. For the Merkle-Hellman lattice, this short vector recovers (or approximates) the private key.

Result: The Merkle-Hellman cryptosystem is completely broken in practice. Any ciphertext can be decrypted by an adversary using the LLL algorithm in polynomial time.

The Merkle-Hellman break is one of the most instructive failures in cryptography. The designers believed that modular transformation destroyed the superincreasing structure — and it does, in the sense that \(\mathbf{b}\) is indistinguishable from a random sequence by naive tests. But the structure is preserved in a higher-dimensional sense: the transformation \(b_i = wa_i \bmod m\) maps the private key to a specific short vector in a lattice, and lattice basis reduction finds short vectors efficiently. "Hiding" structure by modular arithmetic is not the same as destroying it. The lesson: security arguments must be rigorous, not intuitive.

docs.title: Connections to Other Topics
docs.text:
To [[Code-Breaking — Classical Ciphers & Information Theory]]: The Merkle-Hellman break uses the LLL algorithm, which is a polynomial-time algorithm for an apparently hard problem. Similarly, Vigenère seemed secure but had exploitable structure. The common theme: security must be proved against all polynomial-time algorithms, not just obvious ones.

To [[Dynamic Programming]]: The knapsack DP is the canonical example of DP over subsets, illustrating the principle of optimal substructure. The recurrence \(\text{dp}[i][w] = \max(\text{dp}[i-1][w], v_i + \text{dp}[i-1][w-w_i])\) is the template I reach for whenever I see a binary include/exclude decision.

To [[NP and Computational Complexity]]: The reduction from Subset Sum to Knapsack is a prototypical polynomial-time reduction. The FPTAS illustrates that NP-hardness doesn't preclude efficient approximation — a subtlety that distinguishes knapsack from problems like Max-Clique (which has no FPTAS unless \(P = NP\)).

To probability: The probabilistic analysis (random instances are easy) is an instance of a general phenomenon. Many NP-hard problems are easy on average. The theoretically hard instances are measure-zero in the space of all instances. This motivates the study of smoothed complexity (Spielman and Teng) — worst case over small random perturbations of instances — as a more realistic complexity measure than worst-case.

docs.title: Implementation: Full DP with Reconstruction
docs.text:
def knapsack_with_reconstruction(weights, values, W):
    n = len(weights)
    # dp[w] = max value with capacity w
    dp   = [0] * (W + 1)
    # keep[i][w] = True if item i is taken in optimal solution for capacity w
    keep = [[False] * (W + 1) for _ in range(n)]

    for i in range(n):
        # Scan backwards: ensures each item used at most once
        for w in range(W, weights[i] - 1, -1):
            if values[i] + dp[w - weights[i]] > dp[w]:
                dp[w] = values[i] + dp[w - weights[i]]
                keep[i][w] = True

    # Reconstruct optimal subset
    chosen = []
    w = W
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        if keep[i][w]:
            chosen.append(i)
            w -= weights[i]

    return dp[W], chosen

# Example
weights = [2, 3, 4, 5]
values  = [3, 4, 5, 6]
W       = 8
opt_val, opt_items = knapsack_with_reconstruction(weights, values, W)
print(f"Optimal value: {opt_val}")
print(f"Items taken:   {opt_items}")
# Expected: value = 10, items = [1, 3] (0-indexed: weights 3+5=8, values 4+6=10)

docs.title: Normal-Normal Conjugacy
docs.text: "Normal-Normal conjugacy is the result I reach for more than any other in Bayesian inference. It's clean, it's closed-form, and the posterior has a beautiful geometric interpretation: the posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the data mean. More information — higher precision — pulls the estimate closer to you. Less information — lower precision — lets the prior dominate. Every time I derive this I'm struck by how the algebra forces exactly the right answer. The math isn't just computing; it's explaining why Bayesian updating works the way it does."

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
I observe \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) where:

  • \(\sigma^2\) is known (the observation variance — I'll relax this later).
  • \(\mu\) is unknown — the parameter I want to infer.

I place a Normal prior on \(\mu\):

\[\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_0, \tau_0^2)\]

where \(\mu_0\) is my prior mean and \(\tau_0^2\) is my prior variance (how uncertain I am about \(\mu\) before seeing data).

Claim. The posterior is also Normal:

\[\mu \mid X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_n, \tau_n^2)\]

with parameters I will now derive.

docs.title: Step 1: Write the posterior kernel
docs.text:
By Bayes' theorem:

\[\pi(\mu \mid \mathbf{x}) \propto \underbrace{f(\mathbf{x} \mid \mu)}_{\text{likelihood}} \cdot \underbrace{\pi(\mu)}_{\text{prior}}\]

Likelihood (data \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\) given \(\mu\)):

\[f(\mathbf{x} \mid \mu) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp!\left(-\frac{(x_i - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \propto \exp!\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - \mu)^2\right)\]

Prior:

\[\pi(\mu) \propto \exp!\left(-\frac{(\mu - \mu_0)^2}{2\tau_0^2}\right)\]

Posterior kernel:

\[\pi(\mu \mid \mathbf{x}) \propto \exp!\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\mu)^2 - \frac{(\mu-\mu_0)^2}{2\tau_0^2}\right)\]

docs.title: Step 2: Complete the square in \(\mu\)
docs.text:
Expand the exponent. Collect all terms involving \(\mu\):

\[-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i - \mu)^2 - \frac{(\mu - \mu_0)^2}{2\tau_0^2}\] \[= -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\left(n\mu^2 - 2\mu\sum_i x_i + \sum_i x_i^2\right) - \frac{1}{2\tau_0^2}\left(\mu^2 - 2\mu\mu_0 + \mu_0^2\right)\]

Drop constants in \(\mu\) (they go into the normalizing constant):

\[\propto -\frac{\mu^2}{2}\left(\frac{n}{\sigma^2} + \frac{1}{\tau_0^2}\right) + \mu\left(\frac{\sum_i x_i}{\sigma^2} + \frac{\mu_0}{\tau_0^2}\right)\]

This is a quadratic in \(\mu\) of the form \(-\frac{A}{2}\mu^2 + B\mu\), which completes to:

\[-\frac{A}{2}\left(\mu - \frac{B}{A}\right)^2 + \text{const}\]

So the posterior is \(\mathcal{N}(B/A,; 1/A)\) with:

\[A = \frac{n}{\sigma^2} + \frac{1}{\tau_0^2}, \qquad B = \frac{n\bar{x}}{\sigma^2} + \frac{\mu_0}{\tau_0^2}\]

where \(\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i\) is the sample mean.

docs.title: Step 3: Read off the posterior parameters
docs.text:
Posterior precision (precision = reciprocal variance):

\[\boxed{\frac{1}{\tau_n^2} = \frac{n}{\sigma^2} + \frac{1}{\tau_0^2}}\]

Posterior mean:

\[\boxed{\mu_n = \tau_n^2!\left(\frac{n\bar{x}}{\sigma^2} + \frac{\mu_0}{\tau_0^2}\right)}\]

Posterior:

\[\mu \mid \mathbf{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_n,; \tau_n^2) \qquad \blacksquare\]

docs.title: The Precision Perspective
docs.text:
The cleanest way to remember this is in terms of precision \(\lambda = 1/\sigma^2\) (inverse variance).

Define:

  • \(\lambda_0 = 1/\tau_0^2\) — prior precision.
  • \(\lambda_{\text{data}} = n/\sigma^2\) — data precision (total information from \(n\) observations).
  • \(\lambda_n = \lambda_0 + \lambda_{\text{data}}\) — posterior precision.

Then:

\[\frac{1}{\tau_n^2} = \lambda_n = \lambda_0 + \frac{n}{\sigma^2}\] \[\mu_n = \frac{\lambda_0 \mu_0 + \lambda_{\text{data}} \bar{x}}{\lambda_n} = \frac{\lambda_0}{\lambda_n}\mu_0 + \frac{\lambda_{\text{data}}}{\lambda_n}\bar{x}\]

The posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the data mean. The weights sum to 1 and are proportional to how much information each source contributes.

Sequentially: If I observe one data point at a time, I can update iteratively:

\[\lambda_n = \lambda_{n-1} + \frac{1}{\sigma^2}, \qquad \mu_n = \frac{\lambda_{n-1}\mu_{n-1} + x_n/\sigma^2}{\lambda_n}\]

Each new observation adds precision \(1/\sigma^2\) and pulls the mean toward \(x_n\) with weight proportional to \(1/\sigma^2\). This is the Kalman filter in one dimension.

The precision perspective is the one I should tattoo on my brain. Precisions add. Variances don't. When I have two independent sources of information about the same quantity, the total precision is the sum of individual precisions. This is why Normal-Normal conjugacy is so tractable — the parameter space for precision is additive, and addition is the simplest operation. The moment I think in precisions instead of variances, every formula simplifies.

docs.title: As \(n \to \infty\) (infinite data):
docs.text:
\[\tau_n^2 = \frac{\tau_0^2 \sigma^2}{n\tau_0^2 + \sigma^2} \to 0, \qquad \mu_n \to \bar{x}\]

The posterior collapses to a point mass at the MLE \(\bar{x}\). The prior is overwhelmed by data — consistency.

docs.title: As \(\tau_0^2 \to \infty\) (flat/uninformative prior):
docs.text:
\[\mu_n \to \bar{x}, \qquad \tau_n^2 \to \sigma^2/n\]

The posterior becomes \(\mathcal{N}(\bar{x}, \sigma^2/n)\) — the sampling distribution of the MLE. Bayesian inference with an uninformative prior recovers the frequentist answer.

docs.title: As \(\tau_0^2 \to 0\) (infinitely informative prior):
docs.text:
\[\mu_n \to \mu_0, \qquad \tau_n^2 \to 0\]

The posterior collapses to the prior — the data can't move an infinitely confident prior. This is a pathology worth remembering: prior precision \(\to \infty\) means no amount of data updates the belief.

docs.title: Single observation (\(n = 1\)):
docs.text:
\[\mu_1 = \frac{\mu_0/\tau_0^2 + x_1/\sigma^2}{1/\tau_0^2 + 1/\sigma^2}\]

A precision-weighted average of \(\mu_0\) and \(x_1\). If \(\tau_0^2 = \sigma^2\) (prior as uncertain as one observation), \(\mu_1 = (\mu_0 + x_1)/2\) — equal weight. Perfect symmetry.

docs.title: The Posterior Predictive Distribution
docs.text:
Once I've updated my belief about \(\mu\), I often want to predict a new observation \(X_{n+1}\).

Theorem. The posterior predictive distribution is:

\[X_{n+1} \mid X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_n,; \sigma^2 + \tau_n^2)\]

Proof. By the law of total expectation and total variance:

\[X_{n+1} \mid \mathbf{x} = (X_{n+1} \mid \mu, \mathbf{x}) \text{ marginalized over } (\mu \mid \mathbf{x})\]

Since \(X_{n+1} \mid \mu \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) and \(\mu \mid \mathbf{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_n, \tau_n^2)\):

\[E[X_{n+1} \mid \mathbf{x}] = E[E[X_{n+1} \mid \mu, \mathbf{x}]] = E[\mu \mid \mathbf{x}] = \mu_n\] \[\text{Var}(X_{n+1} \mid \mathbf{x}) = E[\text{Var}(X_{n+1} \mid \mu)] + \text{Var}(E[X_{n+1} \mid \mu]) = \sigma^2 + \tau_n^2\]

Since the marginal of a joint Normal is Normal (and the sum of two independent Normals is Normal):

\[X_{n+1} \mid \mathbf{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_n,; \sigma^2 + \tau_n^2) \qquad \blacksquare\]

Interpretation: The predictive variance \(\sigma^2 + \tau_n^2\) has two parts:

  • \(\sigma^2\): irreducible observation noise — even if I knew \(\mu\) exactly, new observations still vary.
  • \(\tau_n^2\): parametric uncertainty — I don't know \(\mu\) exactly, which adds spread.

As \(n \to \infty\): \(\tau_n^2 \to 0\) and the predictive collapses to \(\mathcal{N}(\bar{x}, \sigma^2)\) — parametric uncertainty vanishes, only observation noise remains.

docs.title: Unknown Variance: The Normal-Inverse-Gamma Model
docs.text:
When \(\sigma^2\) is also unknown, the conjugate prior for \((\mu, \sigma^2)\) jointly is the Normal-Inverse-Gamma:

\[\sigma^2 \sim \text{Inv-Gamma}(\alpha_0, \beta_0), \qquad \mu \mid \sigma^2 \sim \mathcal{N}!\left(\mu_0, \frac{\sigma^2}{\kappa_0}\right)\]

The joint prior is \(\text{NIG}(\mu_0, \kappa_0, \alpha_0, \beta_0)\). After observing \(n\) data points:

\[\mu_n = \frac{\kappa_0 \mu_0 + n\bar{x}}{\kappa_0 + n}\] \[\kappa_n = \kappa_0 + n\] \[\alpha_n = \alpha_0 + \frac{n}{2}\] \[\beta_n = \beta_0 + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i - \bar{x})^2 + \frac{\kappa_0 n(\bar{x} - \mu_0)^2}{2(\kappa_0 + n)}\]

The marginal posterior of \(\mu\) (integrating out \(\sigma^2\)) is a Student-\(t\) distribution — heavier tails than Normal because \(\sigma^2\) is uncertain.

I won't derive the full NIG update here — it's a longer computation and belongs in [[Normal-Inverse-Gamma Model]]. But the key point: the four parameters \((\mu_0, \kappa_0, \alpha_0, \beta_0)\) each have clean interpretations as pseudo-data:

  • \(\mu_0\): prior mean of \(\mu\).
  • \(\kappa_0\): prior "sample size" — how many observations worth of confidence in \(\mu_0\).
  • \(\alpha_0, \beta_0\): prior shape and scale for \(\sigma^2\) — encodes prior belief about the noise level.

The NIG model is the honest version of Normal-Normal conjugacy. In practice, I almost never know \(\sigma^2\). The NIG gives me a tractable joint posterior at the cost of four hyperparameters instead of two. The Student-\(t\) marginal for \(\mu\) is the right answer when \(\sigma^2\) is uncertain — wider tails, more honest about what I don't know.

docs.title: Connection to the Kalman Filter
docs.text:
The Kalman filter is Normal-Normal conjugacy applied sequentially to a dynamic state.

Model:

\[X_t = \mu_t + \epsilon_t, \quad \epsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2) \quad \text{(observation)}$$ $$\mu_t = \mu_{t-1} + \eta_t, \quad \eta_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, Q) \quad \text{(state evolution)}\]

At each time step:

Predict: The prior on \(\mu_t\) given observations up to \(t-1\):

\[\mu_t \mid x_{1:t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_{t-1|t-1},; \tau_{t-1|t-1}^2 + Q)\]

The prediction step increases uncertainty by \(Q\) — the state has evolved randomly.

Update: After observing \(x_t\), apply Normal-Normal conjugacy:

\[\frac{1}{\tau_{t|t}^2} = \frac{1}{\tau_{t|t-1}^2} + \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\] \[\mu_{t|t} = \frac{\mu_{t|t-1}/\tau_{t|t-1}^2 + x_t/\sigma^2}{1/\tau_{t|t-1}^2 + 1/\sigma^2}\]

This is exactly the \(n=1\) Normal-Normal update, applied at each time step. The Kalman filter is nothing more than iterated Bayesian updating with Normal distributions — elegant in its simplicity, powerful in its generality.

The Kalman gain \(K_t = \tau_{t|t-1}^2 / (\tau_{t|t-1}^2 + \sigma^2) \in (0,1)\) controls how much the new observation moves the estimate:

\[\mu_{t|t} = \mu_{t|t-1} + K_t(x_t - \mu_{t|t-1})\]

High \(K_t\) (uncertain prior, precise observations): move a lot toward \(x_t\). Low \(K_t\) (precise prior, noisy observations): barely move.

docs.title: Simulation and Verification
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import norm

# --- Parameters ---
mu_true = 3.0       # true mean (unknown to the model)
sigma2  = 1.0       # known observation variance
mu0     = 0.0       # prior mean
tau0_sq = 2.0       # prior variance

n_obs   = 20
np.random.seed(42)
data = np.random.normal(mu_true, np.sqrt(sigma2), size=n_obs)

# --- Sequential Bayesian update ---
mu_post  = mu0
tau2_post = tau0_sq

mu_history  = [mu_post]
tau2_history = [tau2_post]

for x in data:
    # Precision update
    prec_post = 1/tau2_post + 1/sigma2
    tau2_post = 1/prec_post
    # Mean update
    mu_post   = tau2_post * (mu_history[-1]/tau2_history[-1] + x/sigma2)
    mu_history.append(mu_post)
    tau2_history.append(tau2_post)

# --- Batch formula (should match final sequential) ---
xbar     = data.mean()
tau2_n   = 1 / (1/tau0_sq + n_obs/sigma2)
mu_n     = tau2_n * (mu0/tau0_sq + n_obs*xbar/sigma2)

print(f"Sequential posterior: mean={mu_history[-1]:.6f}, var={tau2_history[-1]:.6f}")
print(f"Batch posterior:      mean={mu_n:.6f},            var={tau2_n:.6f}")
# Should be identical up to floating point

# --- Plot posterior evolution ---
mu_vals = np.linspace(-1, 6, 500)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4))
for i, step in enumerate([0, 1, 5, 10, 20]):
    lw = 2.5 if step == 20 else 1
    label = f'n={step}' + (' (posterior)' if step==20 else '')
    plt.plot(mu_vals,
             norm.pdf(mu_vals, mu_history[step], np.sqrt(tau2_history[step])),
             lw=lw, label=label)

plt.axvline(mu_true, color='k', ls='--', lw=1, label=f'True μ={mu_true}')
plt.xlabel('μ'); plt.ylabel('Density')
plt.title('Normal-Normal Posterior — Sequential Updates')
plt.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

What to look for:

  • The posterior at \(n=0\) is the prior — wide, centred at \(\mu_0 = 0\).
  • As \(n\) increases, the posterior narrows and shifts toward \(\mu_{\text{true}} = 3\).
  • Sequential and batch formulas give identical results (up to floating point).
  • The posterior mean is always between \(\mu_0\) and \(\bar{x}\) — the precision-weighted average.

docs.title: Why the Normal is Self-Conjugate: The MGF Argument
docs.text:
There's a deeper reason Normal-Normal conjugacy works: the Normal family is closed under multiplication of densities (up to normalization), because the product of two Gaussian kernels is another Gaussian kernel.

Lemma. For \(a, b > 0\) and \(\mu_1, \mu_2 \in \mathbb{R}\):

\[\exp!\left(-\frac{a(\mu - \mu_1)^2}{2}\right) \cdot \exp!\left(-\frac{b(\mu - \mu_2)^2}{2}\right) = C \cdot \exp!\left(-\frac{(a+b)(\mu - \mu^*)^2}{2}\right)\]

where \(\mu^* = (a\mu_1 + b\mu_2)/(a+b)\) and \(C\) is a constant in \(\mu\).

Proof. Expand both squares, collect \(\mu^2\) and \(\mu\) terms:

\[-\frac{a+b}{2}\mu^2 + (a\mu_1 + b\mu_2)\mu + \text{const} = -\frac{a+b}{2}\left(\mu - \frac{a\mu_1 + b\mu_2}{a+b}\right)^2 + \text{const}\]

This is completing the square. The result is a Gaussian in \(\mu\) with precision \(a+b\) and mean \(\mu^*\). \(\blacksquare\)

In the Normal-Normal update: the likelihood contributes precision \(n/\sigma^2\) and mean \(\bar{x}\); the prior contributes precision \(1/\tau_0^2\) and mean \(\mu_0\). The lemma gives the posterior directly — no integration required. The algebra is the proof.

docs.title: Connections to Other Topics
docs.text:
[[Beta Distribution & Simulation]]: Beta-Binomial is the discrete analogue. Beta is conjugate to Binomial; Normal is conjugate to Normal (known variance). Both update by adding pseudo-counts / pseudo-precision. Both have the posterior mean as a weighted average of prior and data.

[[Metropolis-Hastings Algorithm]]: When \(\sigma^2\) is unknown and the prior is non-conjugate, I can't get a closed-form posterior. MCMC (specifically Gibbs sampling on the NIG model, or MH for non-conjugate priors) is the fallback. Conjugacy is what makes closed-form inference possible — when it fails, I reach for [[Metropolis-Hastings Algorithm]].

[[Markov Chain Convergence Theorem]]: The Kalman filter is the Bayesian optimal estimator for a linear-Gaussian state space model. Its convergence (the steady-state Kalman gain) is related to the fixed point of the Riccati equation — an algebraic analogue of the chain's stationary distribution.

[[Central Limit Theorem]]: For large \(n\), the posterior \(\mathcal{N}(\mu_n, \tau_n^2)\) approximates the sampling distribution of the MLE \(\bar{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2/n)\). This is the Bernstein-von Mises theorem in this simple case: under mild conditions, the posterior converges to a Normal centred at the MLE as \(n \to \infty\), regardless of the prior.

docs.title: Things I Want to Come Back To
docs.text:
• Derive the Normal-Inverse-Gamma update in full — set up the joint likelihood, complete the square in \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\), verify the four update equations.
  • Bernstein-von Mises theorem: state precisely and prove for the Normal-Normal case. The posterior converges to \(\mathcal{N}(\hat{\mu}_{\text{MLE}}, I(\mu)^{-1}/n)\) as \(n \to \infty\) where \(I(\mu)\) is the Fisher information. Verify this matches \(\mathcal{N}(\bar{x}, \sigma^2/n)\).
  • Multivariate Normal-Normal: \(\mathbf{X} \mid \boldsymbol{\mu} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \Sigma)\), \(\boldsymbol{\mu} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_0, \Lambda_0^{-1})\). Precision matrices add: \(\Lambda_n = \Lambda_0 + n\Sigma^{-1}\). Same structure, matrix generalization.
  • The Kalman filter in full generality — multivariate state, non-identity observation matrix \(H\), time-varying noise. Understand the Riccati equation for the steady-state covariance.
  • Empirical Bayes: estimate \(\mu_0\) and \(\tau_0^2\) from the data (maximize marginal likelihood). This is the James-Stein shrinkage estimator. Surprising result: in \(d \geq 3\) dimensions, shrinking toward any fixed point dominates the MLE in MSE — the Stein paradox.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Concept Formula Model \(X_i \mid \mu \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\), \(\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_0, \tau_0^2)\) Posterior \(\mu \mid \mathbf{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_n, \tau_n^2)\) Posterior precision \(1/\tau_n^2 = 1/\tau_0^2 + n/\sigma^2\) (precisions add) Posterior mean \(\mu_n = \tau_n^2({\mu_0}/{\tau_0^2} + {n\bar{x}}/{\sigma^2})\) — precision-weighted average Sequential update Add \(1/\sigma^2\) to precision, update mean with each new \(x_i\) Limiting cases \(n\to\infty\): \(\mu_n \to \bar{x}\); \(\tau_0^2 \to \infty\): \(\mu_n \to \bar{x}\), \(\tau_n^2 \to \sigma^2/n\) Posterior predictive \(X_{n+1} \mid \mathbf{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_n, \sigma^2 + \tau_n^2)\) Unknown \(\sigma^2\) Conjugate prior is Normal-Inverse-Gamma; marginal posterior for \(\mu\) is Student-\(t\) Kalman filter Iterated Normal-Normal update with state evolution noise \(Q\) Why it works Product of Gaussian kernels is Gaussian; precisions add, means are precision-weighted

docs.title: One-Line Summary for Future Me
docs.text:
Normal-Normal conjugacy: prior \(\mathcal{N}(\mu_0, \tau_0^2)\) plus \(n\) observations with known variance \(\sigma^2\) gives posterior \(\mathcal{N}(\mu_n, \tau_n^2)\) where precisions add (\(1/\tau_n^2 = 1/\tau_0^2 + n/\sigma^2\)) and the posterior mean is the precision-weighted average of prior mean and sample mean — iterated one observation at a time, this is the Kalman filter.

docs.title: 1. The Core Problem It Solves
docs.text:
You want to sample from a joint distribution \(p(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n)\) that is:

  • Too complex to sample from directly (no closed form, high-dimensional), or
  • Only known up to a normalizing constant: \(p(\mathbf{x}) \propto \tilde{p}(\mathbf{x})\)

Gibbs Sampling sidesteps this by exploiting the fact that even when the joint is intractable, the full conditionals \(p(x_i \mid x_{\setminus i})\) are often tractable.

\[\text{Joint: intractable} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \text{Conditionals: tractable}\]

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Variables: \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_d)\)
  • Full conditional of variable \(i\): \(p(x_i \mid x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}, x_{i+1}, \ldots, x_d)\), written \(p(x_i \mid \mathbf{x}_{\setminus i})\)

docs.title: Pseudocode
docs.text:
Initialize: x^(0) = (x_1^(0), ..., x_d^(0))   ← random or prior draw

For t = 1, 2, ..., T:
    Sample x_1^(t)  ~ p(x_1  | x_2^(t-1), x_3^(t-1), ..., x_d^(t-1))
    Sample x_2^(t)  ~ p(x_2  | x_1^(t),   x_3^(t-1), ..., x_d^(t-1))
    Sample x_3^(t)  ~ p(x_3  | x_1^(t),   x_2^(t),   ..., x_d^(t-1))
    ...
    Sample x_d^(t)  ~ p(x_d  | x_1^(t),   x_2^(t),   ..., x_{d-1}^(t))

Return: {x^(t)} after burn-in B steps

Key: Each variable is updated one at a time, using the most recent values of all others (systematic scan).

docs.title: 3. Why It Works — The MCMC Lens
docs.text:
Gibbs sampling is a special case of Metropolis-Hastings with acceptance rate always = 1.

Each update step defines a Markov chain transition:

\[T(x_i^{new} \mid \mathbf{x}) = p(x_i^{new} \mid \mathbf{x}_{\setminus i})\]

This satisfies detailed balance with respect to the target joint \(p(\mathbf{x})\):

\[p(\mathbf{x}) \cdot T(\mathbf{x}' \mid \mathbf{x}) = p(\mathbf{x}') \cdot T(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{x}')\]

Proof sketch (2D case):

\[p(x_1, x_2) \cdot p(x_1' \mid x_2) = p(x_1, x_2) \cdot \frac{p(x_1', x_2)}{p(x_2)}$$ $$= p(x_1', x_2) \cdot \frac{p(x_1, x_2)}{p(x_2)} = p(x_1', x_2) \cdot p(x_1 \mid x_2) \checkmark\]

Therefore: the stationary distribution of the chain is the target joint \(p(\mathbf{x})\).

docs.title: 4. Concrete Example — Bivariate Gaussian
docs.text:
Target:

\[p(x_1, x_2) = \mathcal{N}\left(\begin{bmatrix}0\0\end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix}1 & \rho \ \rho & 1\end{bmatrix}\right)\]

Full conditionals (analytically tractable):

\[x_1 \mid x_2 \sim \mathcal{N}(\rho x_2,\ 1 - \rho^2)$$ $$x_2 \mid x_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(\rho x_1,\ 1 - \rho^2)\]

Python Implementation:

import numpy as np

def gibbs_bivariate_gaussian(rho=0.8, n_samples=5000, burn_in=500):
    samples = []
    x1, x2 = 0.0, 0.0  # initialization

    for t in range(n_samples + burn_in):
        # Sample x1 | x2
        x1 = np.random.normal(loc=rho * x2, scale=np.sqrt(1 - rho**2))
        # Sample x2 | x1
        x2 = np.random.normal(loc=rho * x1, scale=np.sqrt(1 - rho**2))

        if t >= burn_in:
            samples.append((x1, x2))

    return np.array(samples)

samples = gibbs_bivariate_gaussian(rho=0.9)
# samples[:, 0] ≈ N(0,1), samples[:, 1] ≈ N(0,1), corr ≈ 0.9

docs.title: 5. Bayesian Inference Use Case — LDA Flavor
docs.text:
In Latent Dirichlet Allocation and Bayesian models, you often need:

\[p(\theta, z \mid x) \propto p(x \mid z) \cdot p(z \mid \theta) \cdot p(\theta)\]

Gibbs cycles between:

  1. \(p(\theta \mid z, x)\) — often Dirichlet (conjugate)
  2. \(p(z \mid \theta, x)\) — often Categorical

This is collapsed Gibbs sampling when \(\theta\) is analytically integrated out, sampling only \(z\).

docs.title: 6. Convergence Diagnostics
docs.text:
Diagnostic What it checks Tool Trace plot Chain mixing visually matplotlib Autocorrelation Lag-k correlation of samples statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots Effective Sample Size (ESS) How many iid samples the chain is worth arviz.ess() R-hat (Gelman-Rubin) Convergence across multiple chains arviz.rhat() Burn-in removal Discard early non-stationary samples Manual / arviz

Rule of thumb: Run \(\geq 2\) chains. If \(\hat{R} < 1.01\) and ESS \(> 400\), trust your estimates.

docs.title: 7.1 Slow Mixing (High Correlation)
docs.text:
If \(\rho \approx 1\) in a Gaussian, the chain takes tiny correlated steps — ESS collapses.

Fix: Use reparameterization, or switch to Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC).

docs.title: 7.2 Multimodal Distributions
docs.text:
If \(p(\mathbf{x})\) has multiple modes separated by low-probability regions, the chain gets trapped in one mode.

Mode A ████████       ░░░░░░░░   Mode B ████████
          ↑ chain stuck here

Fix: Simulated Tempering, Parallel Tempering, or Normalizing Flows.

docs.title: 7.3 Deterministic Scan vs. Random Scan
docs.text:
• Systematic (deterministic) scan: Update \(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_d\) in fixed order. Simpler, commonly used.
  • Random scan: Pick \(x_i\) uniformly at random. Easier to prove detailed balance; preferred theoretically.

docs.title: 8. Gibbs vs. Metropolis-Hastings
docs.text:
Property Gibbs Metropolis-Hastings Acceptance step Always accept (rate = 1) Explicit accept/reject Proposal distribution Full conditional (exact) Arbitrary (Gaussian, etc.) Requires full conditional Yes (must be tractable) No Efficiency High when conditionals are easy Flexible but tuning-heavy Generalizes to HMC, Collapsed Gibbs NUTS, MALA

Insight: Gibbs = MH with a proposal of \(q(x_i' \mid \mathbf{x}) = p(x_i' \mid \mathbf{x}_{\setminus i})\). The acceptance ratio is always 1.

docs.text: \[\boxed{p(x_i^{(t)} \mid \mathbf{x}_{\setminus i}^{(t)}) = \frac{p(\mathbf{x})}{\int p(\mathbf{x}), dx_i}}\] \[\text{ESS} = \frac{T}{1 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \rho_k} \quad \text{(Geyer's formula)}\] \[\hat{R} = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{V}}{W}} \xrightarrow{T \to \infty} 1 \quad \text{(Gelman-Rubin)}\]

docs.title: 12. Mental Model / Intuition
docs.text: Think of Gibbs sampling as coordinate descent for distributions — instead of minimizing a loss function one variable at a time, you're sampling from the conditional distribution one variable at a time. The stationary point of descent becomes the stationary distribution of the Markov chain.

docs.title: 1D Poisson Process
docs.text: Type: Stochastic Process | Domain: Probability, Statistics, Stochastic Processes Prerequisite map: [[Exponential Distribution]] → [[Memoryless Property]] → [[Counting Processes]] → Poisson Process Relevant books: Introduction to Probability (Blitzstein), AIMA Ch.13 Relevant courses: Harvard Stat 110 (Lectures 13–14), MIT 18.650

docs.title: 1. The Core Intuition
docs.text:
A Poisson Process on the real line (time axis) models random arrivals — events that occur:

  • Independently of each other
  • At a constant average rate \(\lambda\) (events per unit time)
  • Such that no two events happen simultaneously

Physical picture: Buses arriving at a stop, photons hitting a detector, emails in your inbox, radioactive decay — all modeled as Poisson processes.

Time axis:
─────┼──────────┼────┼───────────────┼───┼──────────▶
     t₁         t₂   t₃              t₄  t₅

Interarrivals: X₁  X₂   X₃              X₄  X₅  ~ Exp(λ) iid

docs.title: 2. Three Equivalent Definitions
docs.text: These are not three different things — they are three lenses on the same object. Mastering all three = mastery of the Poisson process.

docs.title: Definition 1 — Counting Process Definition
docs.text:
A counting process \({N(t), t \geq 0}\) is a Poisson Process with rate \(\lambda > 0\) if:

  1. \(N(0) = 0\)
  2. Independent increments: For \(0 \leq s < t \leq u < v\): $\(N(t) - N(s) \perp N(v) - N(u)\)$
  3. Stationary increments: \(N(t+s) - N(s) \sim N(t) - N(0)\) (distribution depends only on length)
  4. Poisson counts: $\(N(t) - N(s) \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda(t-s))\)$

So the number of arrivals in any interval of length \(\ell\) is: $\(\boxed{N \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda \ell)}\)$

\[P(N(t) = k) = \frac{e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda t)^k}{k!}, \quad k = 0,1,2,\ldots\]

docs.title: Definition 2 — Interarrival Definition (Constructive)
docs.text:
Let \(X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots \overset{iid}{\sim} \text{Exp}(\lambda)\) be the waiting times between consecutive arrivals.

Define arrival times (partial sums): $\(T_n = X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_n \sim \text{Gamma}(n, \lambda)\)$

Then \(N(t) = \max{n : T_n \leq t}\) defines a Poisson process.

Why Exponential? The only memoryless continuous distribution. This is what makes the Poisson process "stationary" — the process has no memory of when the last event occurred.

\[\boxed{P(X > t + s \mid X > s) = P(X > t)}\]

docs.title: Definition 3 — Infinitesimal Definition
docs.text:
For a small interval \([t, t+dt]\):

\[P(N(t+dt) - N(t) = 1) = \lambda , dt + o(dt)$$ $$P(N(t+dt) - N(t) = 0) = 1 - \lambda , dt + o(dt)$$ $$P(N(t+dt) - N(t) \geq 2) = o(dt)\]

This says: in a tiny window, at most one event can occur, with probability proportional to \(\lambda , dt\).

This is the definition used to derive the Poisson PMF from first principles (Stat 110 style).

docs.title: 3.1 Number of Arrivals in \([0, t]\)
docs.text: \[N(t) \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda t)\] \[E[N(t)] = \lambda t, \qquad \text{Var}[N(t)] = \lambda t\]

docs.title: 3.2 Waiting Time to \(n\)-th Arrival
docs.text: \[T_n \sim \text{Gamma}(n, \lambda)\] \[f_{T_n}(t) = \frac{\lambda^n t^{n-1} e^{-\lambda t}}{(n-1)!}, \quad t > 0\] \[E[T_n] = \frac{n}{\lambda}, \qquad \text{Var}[T_n] = \frac{n}{\lambda^2}\]

docs.title: 3.3 Waiting Time to First Arrival
docs.text: \[T_1 \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda), \quad E[T_1] = \frac{1}{\lambda}\]

docs.title: 4. The Superposition and Thinning Theorems
docs.text: These are the power tools of Poisson processes.

docs.title: 4.1 Superposition (Merging)
docs.text:
If \(N_1(t) \sim \text{PP}(\lambda_1)\) and \(N_2(t) \sim \text{PP}(\lambda_2)\) are independent, then:

\[N_1(t) + N_2(t) \sim \text{PP}(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2)\]

Merging two independent Poisson streams gives a faster Poisson stream.

docs.title: 4.2 Thinning (Splitting)
docs.text:
Take a \(\text{PP}(\lambda)\). Independently mark each arrival as type A with probability \(p\), or type B with probability \(1-p\).

Then: $\(N_A(t) \sim \text{PP}(\lambda p), \qquad N_B(t) \sim \text{PP}(\lambda(1-p))\)$

And crucially: \(N_A \perp N_B\).

Intuition: Randomizing a Poisson process gives independent Poisson processes — the randomness "decomposes cleanly."

docs.title: 5. Conditioning — The Uniform Order Statistics Property
docs.text:
This is the deepest and most beautiful fact about the Poisson process.

Theorem: Given \(N(t) = n\), the \(n\) arrival times \(T_1, T_2, \ldots, T_n\) are distributed as the order statistics of \(n\) iid \(\text{Uniform}(0, t)\) random variables.

\[\boxed{(T_1, \ldots, T_n) \mid N(t) = n ;\overset{d}{=}; (U_{(1)}, \ldots, U_{(n)})}\]

where \(U_{(1)} < U_{(2)} < \cdots < U_{(n)}\) are sorted draws from \(\text{Uniform}(0, t)\).

Consequence: If you know exactly \(n\) events happened in \([0, t]\), each event's location is a uniform draw on \([0, t]\), independent of the others (before sorting).

Intuition: Conditioning on the count completely removes the "Poisson randomness" — all that remains is uniformly scattered points.

docs.title: Example 1 — No Arrivals
docs.text:
Buses arrive at rate \(\lambda = 3\)/hour. What is the probability of waiting more than 30 minutes for the first bus?

\[P(T_1 > 0.5) = e^{-\lambda \cdot 0.5} = e^{-1.5} \approx 0.223\]

docs.title: Example 2 — Counting Arrivals
docs.text:
Emails arrive at rate \(\lambda = 5\)/hour. What is the probability of receiving exactly 3 emails in the next 30 minutes?

\[\lambda t = 5 \times 0.5 = 2.5$$ $$P(N = 3) = \frac{e^{-2.5}(2.5)^3}{3!} = \frac{e^{-2.5} \cdot 15.625}{6} \approx 0.2138\]

docs.title: Example 3 — Thinning
docs.text:
Customers arrive at rate \(\lambda = 10\)/hour. Each is independently a "premium" customer with probability \(p = 0.2\).

  • Premium customers arrive as \(\text{PP}(2)\) per hour
  • Regular customers arrive as \(\text{PP}(8)\) per hour
  • These two streams are independent

docs.title: Example 4 — Uniform Order Statistics (Stat 110 Classic)
docs.text:
Given that exactly 1 person arrives between 12:00 and 13:00, what is the distribution of their arrival time?

\[T_1 \mid N(1) = 1 \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)\]

The arrival time is uniformly distributed across the hour — no "bunching" near start or end.

docs.title: 7. Derivation of Poisson PMF from Definition 3
docs.text:
Let \(p_k(t) = P(N(t) = k)\).

From the infinitesimal definition, write the forward Kolmogorov equations:

\[p_0'(t) = -\lambda p_0(t)$$ $$p_k'(t) = \lambda p_{k-1}(t) - \lambda p_k(t), \quad k \geq 1\]

Solve for \(p_0\): $\(p_0(t) = e^{-\lambda t}\)$

Solve recursively using integrating factor: $\(p_k(t) = \frac{(\lambda t)^k e^{-\lambda t}}{k!} \checkmark\)$

docs.title: 8. Poisson Process vs. Poisson Distribution
docs.text:
Poisson Distribution Poisson Process Type Discrete RV Stochastic process Input Fixed parameter \(\mu\) Rate \(\lambda\), time \(t\) Output Count \(N\) Count \(N(t)\) for all \(t\) Relationship \(N \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu)\) \(N(t) \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda t)\) Extra structure None Interarrivals, order statistics

The Poisson distribution is a snapshot. The Poisson process is the full movie.

docs.title: 9. Poisson Process on a Line vs. Time
docs.text:
The 1D Poisson process applies equally to:

  • Time axis: Events at random moments
  • Spatial axis: Points scattered on a line (e.g., defects on a wire, stars projected onto a line)

For spatial: replace \(t\) with length \(\ell\), and \(\lambda\) = events per unit length.

\[N(\ell) \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda \ell)\]
