docs.title: Core Idea
docs.text:
A return value is the output a function sends back to its caller. It is how a function communicates its result — the product of its computation — to the code that invoked it.

Every Python function returns something. If no return statement is reached, Python returns None implicitly. Understanding return values deeply means understanding what your functions produce, how callers use that output, and how to design clean function interfaces.

def add(a, b):
    return a + b      # explicit return

def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello, {name}")    # no return statement

result1 = add(3, 4)
print(result1)        # 7

result2 = greet("Alice")
print(result2)        # None — function printed but returned nothing

docs.title: Mechanics
docs.text:
return does two things simultaneously:

  1. Sends the specified value back to the caller
  2. Exits the function immediately — no further code in the function runs
def classify(x):
    if x > 0:
        return "positive"     # exits here when x > 0
    if x < 0:
        return "negative"     # exits here when x < 0
    return "zero"             # reached only when x == 0

print(classify(5))     # positive
print(classify(-3))    # negative
print(classify(0))     # zero

Code after a return in the same branch is unreachable:

def f(x):
    return x * 2
    print("this never runs")    # unreachable — not a SyntaxError but pointless

docs.title: Implicit None Return
docs.text:
A function with no return statement, or a return with no value, returns None.

def do_nothing():
    pass

def early_exit(x):
    if x < 0:
        return    # bare return — returns None
    return x * 2

print(do_nothing())        # None
print(early_exit(-1))      # None
print(early_exit(5))       # 10

Bare return is used as an early exit to stop execution when there is no meaningful value to return — equivalent to return None but more concise.

docs.title: Return Any Type
docs.text:
A function can return any Python object.

def return_int():        return 42
def return_float():      return 3.14
def return_str():        return "hello"
def return_bool():       return True
def return_none():       return None
def return_list():       return [1, 2, 3]
def return_dict():       return {"a": 1}
def return_tuple():      return (1, 2)
def return_function():   return lambda x: x ** 2
def return_class():      return list    # the list class itself

Functions are objects and can return functions, classes, or other callables. This is the foundation of closures and decorators.

docs.title: Returning Multiple Values
docs.text:
Python functions can return multiple values by packing them into a tuple. The parentheses are optional — the comma is what creates the tuple.

def min_max(data):
    return min(data), max(data)    # implicitly returns (min, max)

result = min_max([3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9])
print(result)           # (1, 9)
print(type(result))     # <class 'tuple'>

# Unpack immediately — preferred
lo, hi = min_max([3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9])
print(lo, hi)           # 1 9

def split_data(data, ratio=0.8):
    split = int(len(data) * ratio)
    return data[:split], data[split:]

train, test = split_data(list(range(100)))
print(len(train), len(test))    # 80 20

def compute_stats(data):
    n    = len(data)
    mean = sum(data) / n
    variance = sum((x - mean) ** 2 for x in data) / n
    return mean, variance, n

mean, var, count = compute_stats([2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9])
print(f"mean={mean}, var={var}, n={count}")

Unpack immediately at the call site. Carrying around a tuple and later accessing result[0] and result[1] loses all readability. Names matter.

docs.title: Named Return Values — namedtuple and dataclass
docs.text:
When a function returns several values, named tuples and dataclasses document what each value means.

from collections import namedtuple

Stats = namedtuple("Stats", ["mean", "variance", "count"])

def compute_stats(data):
    n    = len(data)
    mean = sum(data) / n
    var  = sum((x - mean) ** 2 for x in data) / n
    return Stats(mean=mean, variance=var, count=n)

result = compute_stats([2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9])
print(result.mean)       # 5.0
print(result.variance)   # 4.0
print(result.count)      # 8

# Still unpackable as a tuple
mean, var, count = result

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class TrainResult:
    train_loss: float
    val_loss:   float
    accuracy:   float
    epochs_run: int

def train(model, data):
    # ... training logic ...
    return TrainResult(
        train_loss = 0.342,
        val_loss   = 0.391,
        accuracy   = 0.873,
        epochs_run = 50,
    )

result = train(model, data)
print(result.accuracy)    # 0.873

Use named returns when:

  • Returning more than two or three values
  • The meaning of each value is not obvious from context
  • The return value will be passed around and accessed by field

docs.title: Return Value vs Side Effect
docs.text:
A function should either return a value or cause a side effect — ideally not both, and never confusingly mix the two.

# Pure — returns a value, no side effects
def double(x):
    return x * 2

# Side effect — modifies external state, returns None
def log(message):
    print(message)

# Mixed — modifies and returns — acceptable when mutation is the point
def append_and_return(lst, item):
    lst.append(item)
    return lst

The in-place vs return distinction is critical in Python:

# list.sort() — sorts in place, returns None
data = [3, 1, 2]
result = data.sort()
print(result)     # None  — common mistake
print(data)       # [1, 2, 3]  — data was mutated

# sorted() — returns new sorted list, original unchanged
data = [3, 1, 2]
result = sorted(data)
print(result)     # [1, 2, 3]
print(data)       # [3, 1, 2]  — unchanged

Python's built-in mutable methods (.sort(), .append(), .reverse(), .update(), .clear()) return None. They signal: "I mutated the object, there is no separate return value." sorted(), reversed(), dict.copy() return new objects and do not mutate.

Design your own functions the same way — be consistent. If a function mutates its argument, returning None signals that clearly. If it produces a new value, return it without mutating the input.

docs.title: Early Return — Guard Clause Pattern
docs.text:
Return early to handle special cases. Keep the happy path unindented and at the bottom.

# Deeply nested — hard to follow
def process(data, threshold):
    if data is not None:
        if len(data) > 0:
            if isinstance(data, list):
                result = [x for x in data if x > threshold]
                return result

# Flat — guard clauses up front
def process(data, threshold):
    if data is None:
        return None
    if len(data) == 0:
        return []
    if not isinstance(data, list):
        raise TypeError(f"expected list, got {type(data).__name__}")

    return [x for x in data if x > threshold]

Each guard clause handles one failure mode and exits. The main logic is reached only when all preconditions are met.

docs.title: Returning Functions — Closures and Factories
docs.text:
Functions can return other functions. The returned function captures variables from the enclosing scope — this is a closure.

def make_multiplier(factor):
    def multiply(x):
        return x * factor    # factor captured from enclosing scope
    return multiply           # return the function itself, not its result

double = make_multiplier(2)
triple = make_multiplier(3)

print(double(5))    # 10
print(triple(5))    # 15
print(double(triple(4)))    # double(12) = 24

def make_power(exponent):
    return lambda x: x ** exponent

square = make_power(2)
cube   = make_power(3)

print(square(4))    # 16
print(cube(3))      # 27

# Factory pattern — return configured function
def make_validator(min_val, max_val):
    def validate(x):
        return min_val <= x <= max_val
    return validate

is_valid_age    = make_validator(0, 150)
is_valid_score  = make_validator(0, 100)
is_valid_rating = make_validator(1, 5)

print(is_valid_age(25))       # True
print(is_valid_score(105))    # False
print(is_valid_rating(3))     # True

Returning functions is the mechanism behind decorators, callback patterns, and much of the functional programming style used in ML pipelines.

docs.title: Returning None Intentionally vs Accidentally
docs.text:
Returning None intentionally signals "no result" or "operation complete":

def find_first(data, predicate):
    for item in data:
        if predicate(item):
            return item
    return None    # explicit — nothing found

result = find_first([1, 2, 3, 4], lambda x: x > 10)
if result is None:
    print("not found")

Returning None accidentally is a bug:

def double_all(data):
    result = [x * 2 for x in data]
    # forgot return

doubled = double_all([1, 2, 3])
print(doubled)    # None — forgot return statement

Always check: does every code path that should produce a value actually hit a return statement?

docs.title: Type Hints for Return Values
docs.text:
Type hints document what a function returns. They are not enforced at runtime but are used by IDEs, type checkers (mypy), and documentation tools.

def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a + b

def greet(name: str) -> str:
    return f"Hello, {name}"

def process(data: list) -> None:
    for item in data:
        print(item)

def find(data: list, target) -> int | None:
    for i, item in enumerate(data):
        if item == target:
            return i
    return None

from typing import Optional, Tuple, List

def min_max(data: List[float]) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    return min(data), max(data)

def maybe_find(data: list, key: str) -> Optional[str]:
    return data.get(key)    # returns str or None

For ML code, type hints are especially useful on functions that transform tensors — documenting the expected shape and type prevents a class of bugs at design time.

docs.title: Common Patterns in ML
docs.text:
Returning train and validation split:

def train_val_split(dataset, val_ratio=0.2, seed=42):
    import random
    random.seed(seed)
    data = dataset.copy()
    random.shuffle(data)
    split = int(len(data) * (1 - val_ratio))
    return data[:split], data[split:]

train_data, val_data = train_val_split(full_dataset)

Returning loss and metrics from a training step:

def train_step(model, batch, optimizer, criterion):
    inputs, targets = batch
    outputs  = model(inputs)
    loss     = criterion(outputs, targets)
    accuracy = compute_accuracy(outputs, targets)

    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

    return loss.item(), accuracy    # return scalar values, not tensors

Returning model and tokenizer together:

def load_model(checkpoint_path):
    model     = build_model()
    tokenizer = build_tokenizer()
    state     = load_checkpoint(checkpoint_path)
    model.load_state_dict(state["model"])
    tokenizer.load_state(state["tokenizer"])
    return model, tokenizer

model, tokenizer = load_model("checkpoint_epoch_50.pt")

Returning early on invalid input:

def safe_divide(a, b):
    if b == 0:
        return None    # or raise ValueError — depends on your contract
    return a / b

result = safe_divide(10, 0)
if result is None:
    print("division by zero")

docs.text: Scenario Return behavior return value Sends value to caller, exits immediately return (bare) Returns None, exits immediately No return statement Returns None implicitly return a, b Returns tuple (a, b) — unpack at call site Mutable method (.sort()) Returns None — signals in-place mutation sorted() Returns new object — signals no mutation Returning a function Closure — function captures enclosing scope Type hint -> T Documents expected return type -> None Function is called for side effects -> T \| None Returns T on success, None on failure

docs.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
docs.text:
# Mistake 1: forgetting the return statement
def square(x):
    result = x ** 2    # computed but never returned

y = square(5)
print(y)    # None

# Mistake 2: using return value of in-place method
result = my_list.sort()    # None
result = sorted(my_list)   # correct

# Mistake 3: not unpacking multiple return values
result = min_max(data)
print(result[0])           # works but loses readability
lo, hi = min_max(data)     # correct — unpack immediately

# Mistake 4: checking returned None incorrectly
result = find(data, target)
if result:                  # wrong — 0 is falsy but a valid index
    use(result)
if result is not None:      # correct — explicit None check
    use(result)

# Mistake 5: returning inside a loop when you want all results
def get_evens(data):
    for x in data:
        if x % 2 == 0:
            return x        # returns first even only
    # correct:
    return [x for x in data if x % 2 == 0]

# Mistake 6: mixing mutation and return inconsistently
def process(lst):
    lst.append(0)
    return lst              # mutates AND returns — surprising
# either mutate (return None) or return new (don't mutate input)

docs.title: Core Idea
docs.text:
Scope determines where in your code a variable name is visible and accessible. Python enforces strict rules about which names are visible from which locations. Understanding scope prevents bugs caused by accidentally reading or modifying the wrong variable, and explains why code that looks correct sometimes raises NameError or produces unexpected values.

Every name in Python lives in exactly one scope at a time.

docs.title: The LEGB Rule
docs.text:
Python resolves names in this fixed order, stopping at the first match:

L — Local       — names defined inside the current function
E — Enclosing   — names defined in any enclosing function (for nested functions)
G — Global      — names defined at module level (the file)
B — Built-in    — names provided by Python itself (len, print, range, etc.)

x = "global"           # G — global scope

def outer():
    x = "enclosing"    # E — enclosing scope (relative to inner)

    def inner():
        x = "local"    # L — local scope
        print(x)       # local — found at L, stops here

    inner()
    print(x)           # enclosing — found at E

outer()
print(x)               # global — found at G

Python walks up the chain from L to B. The first match wins. If no match is found anywhere, NameError is raised.

docs.title: Local Scope
docs.text:
Variables assigned inside a function are local to that function. They exist only during the function's execution and are destroyed when the function returns.

def f():
    x = 10          # local variable — exists only inside f
    print(x)        # 10

f()
print(x)            # NameError: name 'x' is not defined

Parameters are also local:

def double(n):
    result = n * 2    # n and result are both local
    return result

double(5)
print(n)         # NameError — n is local to double
print(result)    # NameError — result is local to double

Local variables are completely isolated. Two different function calls each get their own independent copies of local variables.

def counter():
    count = 0
    count += 1
    return count

print(counter())    # 1
print(counter())    # 1  — fresh local variable each call, not shared

docs.title: Global Scope
docs.text:
Variables assigned at module level (outside any function) are global. They are visible anywhere in the module.

PI = 3.14159    # global

def circle_area(r):
    return PI * r ** 2    # reads PI from global scope — allowed

print(circle_area(5))    # 78.539...

Reading a global from inside a function works without any special syntax. Python follows LEGB — it does not find PI locally, so it looks in global scope and finds it there.

Assigning to a global from inside a function does NOT work without global.

count = 0

def increment():
    count += 1    # UnboundLocalError — Python sees assignment, treats count as local

increment()

When Python sees an assignment to count inside increment, it marks count as a local variable for that entire function — even if the assignment happens later. Reading count before the assignment (as in count += 1, which is count = count + 1) tries to read a local variable that does not exist yet.

docs.title: The global Keyword
docs.text:
Declares that a name refers to the global variable, not a new local one.

count = 0

def increment():
    global count      # tell Python: count refers to the global variable
    count += 1

increment()
increment()
print(count)    # 2

total = 0
items = []

def add(value):
    global total, items    # multiple names on one line
    total += value
    items.append(value)

add(10)
add(20)
print(total)    # 30
print(items)    # [10, 20]

docs.title: When to Use global — Rarely
docs.text:
global creates hidden coupling between a function and module-level state. The function is no longer self-contained — it depends on and modifies external state invisibly. This makes code harder to test, debug, and reason about.

# With global — hidden dependency, hard to test
count = 0

def increment():
    global count
    count += 1

# Without global — explicit, testable, pure
def increment(count):
    return count + 1

count = 0
count = increment(count)

Acceptable uses of global:

  • Module-level constants (but prefer reading, not writing)
  • Simple counters in scripts (not in production libraries)
  • Caches that need to persist across calls (but prefer a class or functools.lru_cache)

Avoid global in any function that is part of a reusable module or library.

docs.title: Enclosing Scope — Nested Functions
docs.text:
When a function is defined inside another function, it has access to the enclosing function's local variables. This is the E in LEGB.

def outer():
    message = "hello"       # enclosing scope variable

    def inner():
        print(message)      # reads from enclosing scope — works without nonlocal

    inner()

outer()    # hello

The inner function can read enclosing variables freely. It cannot assign to them without nonlocal.

def outer():
    count = 0

    def inner():
        count += 1    # UnboundLocalError — same problem as with global
        print(count)

    inner()

docs.title: The nonlocal Keyword
docs.text:
Declares that a name refers to a variable in the nearest enclosing (non-global) scope.

def outer():
    count = 0

    def inner():
        nonlocal count    # refer to outer's count, not a new local
        count += 1

    inner()
    inner()
    print(count)    # 2

outer()

docs.title: Closures — Capturing Enclosing State
docs.text:
A closure is a function that remembers variables from its enclosing scope even after the enclosing function has returned.

def make_counter():
    count = 0            # enclosing variable

    def increment():
        nonlocal count
        count += 1
        return count

    return increment     # return the inner function

c1 = make_counter()
c2 = make_counter()

print(c1())    # 1
print(c1())    # 2
print(c1())    # 3
print(c2())    # 1  — c2 has its own independent count

Each call to make_counter() creates a new enclosing scope with its own count. c1 and c2 are independent because they close over different count variables.

def make_multiplier(factor):
    def multiply(x):
        return x * factor    # factor captured from enclosing scope
    return multiply

double = make_multiplier(2)
triple = make_multiplier(3)

print(double(5))    # 10
print(triple(5))    # 15

Closures are the mechanism behind decorators, factory functions, and stateful callbacks. When you see a function that returns a function, it is almost always using closure to capture state.

docs.title: Built-in Scope
docs.text:
Python's built-in names — len, print, range, type, int, list, True, None, etc. — live in the built-in scope. They are always available as a last resort in LEGB lookup.

print(len([1, 2, 3]))    # len and print found in built-in scope

You can shadow built-in names — do not.

# This is valid Python but catastrophically wrong
list = [1, 2, 3]         # shadows the built-in list class
print(list([4, 5, 6]))   # TypeError — list is now [1, 2, 3], not the class

# Fix: delete the shadowing variable or rename it
del list
print(list([4, 5, 6]))   # works again

Common names accidentally shadowed: list, dict, set, tuple, id, type, input, len, min, max, sum, sorted, filter, map, zip, range, open, format, str, int, float.

In ML code, input is especially dangerous to shadow because it is a built-in function and also a common name for neural network inputs.

docs.title: Variable Lifetime
docs.text:
Scope Created Destroyed Local When function is called When function returns Enclosing When outer function is called When outer function returns (unless closure exists) Global When module is imported When program exits Built-in At Python startup At Python shutdown

When a closure captures an enclosing variable, that variable's lifetime is extended — it persists as long as the closure exists.

def make_counter():
    count = 0                    # normally destroyed when make_counter returns
    def increment():
        nonlocal count
        count += 1
        return count
    return increment

c = make_counter()               # make_counter returned, but count survives
print(c())                       # 1 — count still alive because c holds a reference

docs.title: Scope and Comprehensions
docs.text:
List, dict, and set comprehensions have their own scope in Python 3. The loop variable does not leak.

result = [x for x in range(5)]
print(x)    # NameError in Python 3 — x is local to the comprehension

Generator expressions also have their own scope:

gen = (x for x in range(5))
print(x)    # NameError — x is local to the generator

for loops do NOT create their own scope — the loop variable persists:

for i in range(5):
    pass
print(i)    # 4 — i persists after the loop

This is a source of subtle bugs when you use the same variable name in a loop and rely on it afterward thinking it holds the last value intentionally.

docs.title: Scope in Classes
docs.text:
Class bodies create a local namespace during class definition, but this namespace does not form part of the LEGB chain for methods inside the class.

class MyClass:
    class_var = 10

    def method(self):
        print(class_var)          # NameError — class scope not in LEGB for methods
        print(self.class_var)     # correct — access via self or MyClass
        print(MyClass.class_var)  # also correct

Methods look up names in local → enclosing → global → built-in. The class namespace is skipped. Always access class attributes explicitly via self.name or ClassName.name.

docs.title: Practical Rules
docs.text:
1. Keep functions pure — take inputs as parameters, return outputs.
   Avoid reading mutable globals inside functions.

2. Never write to a global from inside a function without global.
   If you think you need global, consider passing the value as a parameter
   and returning the modified value instead.

3. Never shadow built-in names.
   Do not use: list, dict, set, type, id, input, len, min, max, sum, etc.

4. Use nonlocal sparingly.
   If you find yourself using nonlocal often, consider whether a class
   with instance attributes would be cleaner.

5. Name enclosing scope variables clearly.
   When a closure captures a variable, its name should make its role obvious
   to anyone reading the inner function.

docs.title: LEGB Lookup — Full Example
docs.text:
x = "global_x"          # G

def outer():
    x = "enclosing_x"   # E (relative to inner)
    y = "enclosing_y"   # E

    def inner():
        x = "local_x"   # L — shadows enclosing x
        print(x)         # local_x    (L wins)
        print(y)         # enclosing_y (E — no local y)
        print(len)       # <built-in function len> (B — not in L, E, G)

    inner()
    print(x)             # enclosing_x (inner's local x does not affect this)

outer()
print(x)                 # global_x

docs.title: Common Patterns
docs.text:
Accumulator using return instead of global:

# Avoid — hidden global mutation
total = 0
def add(x):
    global total
    total += x

# Prefer — explicit, testable, composable
def add(total, x):
    return total + x

total = 0
total = add(total, 10)
total = add(total, 20)
print(total)    # 30

Persistent state using a class instead of global:

# Avoid — global state
call_count = 0
def process(x):
    global call_count
    call_count += 1
    return x * 2

# Prefer — encapsulated state
class Processor:
    def __init__(self):
        self.call_count = 0

    def process(self, x):
        self.call_count += 1
        return x * 2

p = Processor()
p.process(5)
print(p.call_count)    # 1

Module-level constants — the legitimate use of global names:

# Constants — global names that are only read, never written
MAX_RETRIES    = 5
DEFAULT_LR     = 0.001
VOCAB_SIZE     = 50000
PADDING_TOKEN  = "<PAD>"
DEVICE         = "cuda"

def train(model, data):
    for attempt in range(MAX_RETRIES):    # reading a constant — fine
        ...

Constants should be named in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE to signal that they are not meant to be reassigned.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Scope Keyword to modify Lifetime Accessible from Local (L) — (default assignment) Duration of function call Inside function only Enclosing (E) nonlocal Duration of outer function (or closure) Inner functions Global (G) global Duration of module Anywhere in module Built-in (B) N/A (cannot reassign) Duration of interpreter Everywhere

docs.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
docs.text:
# Mistake 1: expecting assignment inside function to affect global
x = 10
def f():
    x = 20    # creates a new local x — global x unchanged
f()
print(x)      # 10

# Mistake 2: UnboundLocalError from mixed read/write
count = 0
def increment():
    count += 1    # Python sees assignment -> count is local -> read before assign
# fix: global count, or pass count as argument and return new value

# Mistake 3: shadowing a built-in
list = [1, 2, 3]    # now list() is broken
del list            # fix: remove the shadowing name

# Mistake 4: assuming comprehension variable leaks (Python 3)
[x for x in range(5)]
print(x)    # NameError in Python 3 — x is local to comprehension

# Mistake 5: loop variable confusion
for i in range(5):
    pass
print(i)    # 4 — this DOES leak in a for loop (unlike comprehensions)

# Mistake 6: closure captures variable by reference, not by value
funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(5)]
print([f() for f in funcs])    # [4, 4, 4, 4, 4] — all see final value of i
# fix: capture by value using default argument
funcs = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(5)]
print([f() for f in funcs])    # [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]

docs.title: What is a Lambda Function
docs.text:
A lambda function is an anonymous function — a function defined without a name, in a single expression, using the lambda keyword. It is not a replacement for def; it is a tool for situations where defining a full function would be disproportionately verbose.

# Regular function
def square(x):
    return x ** 2

# Equivalent lambda
square = lambda x: x ** 2

print(square(5))   # 25

The name square here is just a variable binding — the lambda itself is nameless. Assigning a lambda to a variable and then calling it defeats most of the purpose; the real power is in passing lambdas inline.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
lambda <parameters> : <expression>
  • lambda — keyword
  • <parameters> — zero or more comma-separated inputs (same rules as def)
  • : — separator
  • <expression> — a single expression whose value is automatically returned
# Zero parameters
greet = lambda: "Hello"
print(greet())          # Hello

# One parameter
double = lambda x: x * 2
print(double(7))        # 14

# Multiple parameters
add = lambda x, y: x + y
print(add(3, 4))        # 7

# With default argument
power = lambda x, n=2: x ** n
print(power(3))         # 9
print(power(3, 3))      # 27

Critical constraint: A lambda body must be a single expression, not a statement. No if/else blocks, no for loops, no return, no assignments.

# Valid — ternary expression IS an expression
clamp = lambda x: x if x > 0 else 0

# Invalid — if/else block is a statement, not an expression
# lambda x: if x > 0: return x   ← SyntaxError

docs.title: 1. sorted() — Custom Sort Keys
docs.text:
The key parameter of sorted() accepts any callable. Lambdas are perfect here.

students = [("Alice", 88), ("Bob", 95), ("Carol", 72)]

# Sort by score (index 1)
by_score = sorted(students, key=lambda s: s[1])
print(by_score)
# [('Carol', 72), ('Alice', 88), ('Bob', 95)]

# Sort by name length
by_name_len = sorted(students, key=lambda s: len(s[0]))
print(by_name_len)
# [('Bob', 95), ('Alice', 88), ('Carol', 72)]

# Sort descending
by_score_desc = sorted(students, key=lambda s: s[1], reverse=True)
print(by_score_desc)
# [('Bob', 95), ('Alice', 88), ('Carol', 72)]

docs.title: 2. map() — Applying a Transformation
docs.text:
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

squared = list(map(lambda x: x ** 2, numbers))
print(squared)   # [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]

# With two iterables
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [10, 20, 30]
sums = list(map(lambda x, y: x + y, a, b))
print(sums)      # [11, 22, 33]

docs.title: 3. filter() — Selecting Elements
docs.text:
numbers = range(-5, 6)

positives = list(filter(lambda x: x > 0, numbers))
print(positives)   # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

evens = list(filter(lambda x: x % 2 == 0, numbers))
print(evens)       # [-4, -2, 0, 2, 4]

docs.title: 4. Immediately Invoked Lambda
docs.text:
Call the lambda right where it is defined. Rare in Python, but valid.

result = (lambda x, y: x * y)(6, 7)
print(result)   # 42

docs.title: 5. Inside min() / max()
docs.text:
data = [{"name": "Alice", "age": 30}, {"name": "Bob", "age": 25}]

youngest = min(data, key=lambda d: d["age"])
print(youngest)   # {'name': 'Bob', 'age': 25}

docs.title: Lambda vs def — When to Use Which
docs.text:
Situation Use Short throwaway key/callback, used once lambda Any logic requiring statements (for, if/else block, try) def Function you will call by name in multiple places def Needs a docstring def Needs more than one expression def

PEP 8 explicitly discourages assigning a lambda to a variable name:

# PEP 8 discourages this
double = lambda x: x * 2

# Prefer this
def double(x):
    return x * 2

The reason: def gives a function a proper __name__ attribute, which aids debugging and stack traces. A named lambda still shows as <lambda> in tracebacks.

docs.title: Lambdas and Closures
docs.text:
A lambda captures variables from its enclosing scope — it forms a closure, just like a nested def.

def make_multiplier(n):
    return lambda x: x * n

triple = make_multiplier(3)
print(triple(7))    # 21
print(triple(10))   # 30

Classic closure trap — late binding:

# Bug: all lambdas capture the same variable i
funcs = [lambda x: x * i for i in range(5)]
print(funcs[0](1))   # 4, not 0 — i is 4 when called
print(funcs[2](1))   # 4

# Fix: bind i at definition time with a default argument
funcs = [lambda x, i=i: x * i for i in range(5)]
print(funcs[0](1))   # 0
print(funcs[2](1))   # 2

This late-binding behavior is identical to closures formed with def. The default-argument fix works for both.

docs.title: Lambdas in ML/Data Code
docs.text:
You will encounter lambdas constantly in NumPy, Pandas, and PyTorch pipelines:

import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"score": [55, 78, 92, 41, 88]})

# Apply a transformation row-by-row
df["grade"] = df["score"].apply(lambda x: "pass" if x >= 60 else "fail")
print(df)
#    score grade
# 0     55  fail
# 1     78  pass
# 2     92  pass
# 3     41  fail
# 4     88  pass

In PyTorch, custom transforms for datasets are often lambdas:

from torchvision import transforms

transform = transforms.Lambda(lambda x: x / 255.0)

docs.title: Internal Model — What lambda Really Is
docs.text:
A lambda expression evaluates to a function object, exactly like def creates one. The difference is purely syntactic — lambda is limited to a single expression body.

f = lambda x: x + 1

print(type(f))        # <class 'function'>
print(f.__name__)     # <lambda>
print(f.__code__)     # <code object <lambda> at ...>

The interpreter compiles the lambda body into a code object at definition time. When called, it executes that code object and returns the expression's value.

docs.title: Common Errors
docs.text:
# SyntaxError: lambda body cannot contain assignment
bad = lambda x: (y = x + 1)   # ← invalid

# SyntaxError: no return statement allowed
bad = lambda x: return x       # ← invalid

# TypeError: calling with wrong number of args
f = lambda x, y: x + y
f(1)                            # TypeError: missing 1 required argument

# Silent bug: late binding in loops (see Closures section)
funcs = [lambda x: x * i for i in range(5)]   # all capture final i

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text: Feature Behavior Syntax lambda params: expression Return Implicit — the expression value Body Single expression only Parameters All types: positional, default, *args, **kwargs Name Always <lambda> in tracebacks Closure Yes — captures enclosing scope Type function — identical to def objects PEP 8 Do not assign to a variable name

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
E1. Write a lambda that takes three numbers and returns their average.

E2. Given this list:

words = ["banana", "fig", "apple", "kiwi", "cherry"]

Sort it first by length, then alphabetically for ties — using a single sorted() call with a lambda key that returns a tuple.

E3. Using map() and a lambda, convert a list of temperatures in Celsius to Fahrenheit. Formula: F = C * 9/5 + 32.

E4. Explain why the following produces unexpected output, and fix it:

actions = [lambda: i * 2 for i in range(4)]
print([f() for f in actions])   # Expected: [0, 2, 4, 6]

E5. Rewrite this using filter() and a lambda instead of a list comprehension:

result = [x for x in range(1, 101) if x % 3 == 0 and x % 5 == 0]

docs.title: What is Recursion
docs.text:
Recursion is a technique where a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem. The key insight is that many problems have a self-similar structure — the solution to the full problem can be expressed in terms of solutions to smaller instances of the same problem.

def countdown(n):
    if n == 0:
        print("Done")
        return
    print(n)
    countdown(n - 1)   # function calls itself with a smaller input

countdown(3)
# 3
# 2
# 1
# Done

This is not a trick or shortcut. Recursion is a fundamental computational model — it is how compilers think, how tree structures are traversed, how search algorithms explore spaces, and how mathematical induction maps to code.

docs.title: The Two Mandatory Parts
docs.text: Every correct recursive function has exactly two parts. Missing either one produces broken code.

docs.title: 1. Base Case — The Stopping Condition
docs.text:
The input so small that the answer is known directly, without recursion.

if n == 0:
    return 1

Without a base case, the function recurses forever until Python raises a RecursionError.

docs.title: 2. Recursive Case — The Self-Similar Step
docs.text:
The function calls itself with a strictly smaller input, moving toward the base case.

return n * factorial(n - 1)

The input must get smaller on every call. If it doesn't converge toward the base case, you have infinite recursion.

docs.title: Anatomy of a Recursive Call — The Call Stack
docs.text:
Understanding what Python actually does is non-negotiable. Each function call creates a stack frame — a block of memory holding that call's local variables and return address. Recursive calls stack these frames on top of each other.

def factorial(n):
    if n == 0:
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)

factorial(4)

Call stack — growing down, resolving upward:

factorial(4)  →  4 * factorial(3)
                     factorial(3)  →  3 * factorial(2)
                                          factorial(2)  →  2 * factorial(1)
                                                               factorial(1)  →  1 * factorial(0)
                                                                                    factorial(0)  →  1  ← BASE CASE

# Now unwinds:
factorial(1)  →  1 * 1  =  1
factorial(2)  →  2 * 1  =  2
factorial(3)  →  3 * 2  =  6
factorial(4)  →  4 * 6  =  24

Each frame is only resolved after all frames below it return. This is why recursive functions appear to "wait" — they are literally suspended mid-execution on the stack.

docs.title: Canonical Examples — From Simple to Deep
Factorial
docs.text:
def factorial(n):
    """n! = n * (n-1) * ... * 1.  Base case: 0! = 1"""
    if n == 0:          # base case
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)   # recursive case

print(factorial(5))    # 120
print(factorial(0))    # 1

Mathematical structure being expressed:

0! = 1
n! = n × (n-1)!

The code is a direct translation of the mathematical definition. This is the recursive mindset.

docs.title: Fibonacci
docs.text:
def fib(n):
    """fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1, fib(n)=fib(n-1)+fib(n-2)"""
    if n <= 1:              # two base cases
        return n
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)

print(fib(6))   # 8  (0,1,1,2,3,5,8)

This naive implementation has exponential time complexity O(2^n) — fib(50) takes minutes. Every subproblem is recomputed from scratch multiple times. This is the canonical example that motivates memoization.

from functools import lru_cache

@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def fib(n):
    if n <= 1:
        return n
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)

print(fib(50))   # 12586269025 — instant

lru_cache stores results of previous calls. The time complexity drops to O(n). This pattern — recursion + memoization — is dynamic programming.

docs.title: Sum of a List
docs.text:
def sum_list(lst):
    if not lst:           # base case: empty list
        return 0
    return lst[0] + sum_list(lst[1:])   # head + sum of tail

print(sum_list([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]))   # 15

Mental model: A list is either empty, or a head element followed by a smaller list. This head/tail decomposition is how functional languages think about all list operations.

docs.title: Binary Search
docs.text:
def binary_search(arr, target, lo, hi):
    if lo > hi:                     # base case: not found
        return -1

    mid = (lo + hi) // 2

    if arr[mid] == target:          # base case: found
        return mid
    elif arr[mid] < target:
        return binary_search(arr, target, mid + 1, hi)   # search right half
    else:
        return binary_search(arr, target, lo, mid - 1)   # search left half

arr = [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56]
print(binary_search(arr, 23, 0, len(arr) - 1))   # 5
print(binary_search(arr, 10, 0, len(arr) - 1))   # -1

Each recursive call eliminates half the search space. Time complexity: O(log n). The recursive structure mirrors the divide-and-conquer logic cleanly.

docs.title: Tree Traversal
docs.text:
Recursion's most natural domain. Trees are inherently recursive structures — a tree is either empty, or a node with subtrees that are themselves trees.

class Node:
    def __init__(self, val, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def inorder(node):
    """Left → Root → Right"""
    if node is None:       # base case
        return
    inorder(node.left)
    print(node.val)
    inorder(node.right)

#         4
#        / \
#       2   6
#      / \ / \
#     1  3 5  7

root = Node(4, Node(2, Node(1), Node(3)), Node(6, Node(5), Node(7)))
inorder(root)   # 1 2 3 4 5 6 7

No iterative solution can match this in clarity. The recursive call stack is the traversal algorithm.

docs.title: Power Function — Efficient Exponentiation
docs.text:
def power(base, exp):
    """Computes base^exp in O(log exp) instead of O(exp)"""
    if exp == 0:
        return 1
    if exp % 2 == 0:
        half = power(base, exp // 2)
        return half * half            # avoid calling twice
    return base * power(base, exp - 1)

print(power(2, 10))   # 1024
print(power(3, 5))    # 243

This is fast exponentiation — a divide-and-conquer strategy. It reduces O(n) multiplications to O(log n).

docs.title: Recursion vs Iteration — When to Use Which
docs.text:
Factor Recursion Iteration Problem structure Self-similar / tree / graph Linear / sequential Code clarity Often cleaner for divide-and-conquer Cleaner for simple loops Stack usage O(depth) stack frames O(1) Risk Stack overflow on deep input None Performance Function call overhead per frame Generally faster Tail call optimization Python does NOT optimize N/A

Use recursion when: the problem decomposes naturally into identical subproblems (trees, graphs, divide-and-conquer algorithms, mathematical induction). Use iteration when: the problem is a simple linear scan or accumulation.

Every recursive solution can be converted to iteration using an explicit stack. Python sometimes forces this due to recursion depth limits.

docs.title: Python's Recursion Limit
docs.text:
Python enforces a maximum call stack depth (default: 1000 frames) to prevent stack overflow from crashing the interpreter.

import sys

print(sys.getrecursionlimit())   # 1000

# You can raise it — but this is a workaround, not a fix
sys.setrecursionlimit(10000)

def infinite(n):
    return infinite(n + 1)

infinite(0)   # RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded

If you hit the recursion limit, the right fix is usually to convert to iteration or apply memoization — not to raise the limit.

docs.title: Tail Recursion — Why Python Doesn't Optimize It
docs.text:
In some languages (Scheme, Haskell, modern JavaScript), a recursive call in tail position (the very last operation before returning) is optimized: the compiler reuses the current stack frame instead of creating a new one, making it as efficient as a loop.

# Tail-recursive factorial (the recursive call is the LAST operation)
def factorial_tail(n, accumulator=1):
    if n == 0:
        return accumulator
    return factorial_tail(n - 1, accumulator * n)   # tail call

Python does not perform tail call optimization. Every call still creates a new frame. Guido van Rossum deliberately chose not to add this, arguing that stack traces become unreadable with TCO. Accept this and use iteration or lru_cache when depth is a concern.

docs.title: Memoization — Caching Recursive Results
docs.text:
When a recursive function recomputes the same subproblems repeatedly, cache the results.

# Manual memoization with a dictionary
def fib(n, memo={}):
    if n in memo:
        return memo[n]
    if n <= 1:
        return n
    memo[n] = fib(n - 1, memo) + fib(n - 2, memo)
    return memo[n]

Warning on mutable default arguments: Using memo={} as a default is a Python footgun — the dict persists across calls (it's created once at function definition, not per call). It works here intentionally, but is generally a bad pattern. Prefer lru_cache or pass the cache explicitly.

from functools import lru_cache

@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def fib(n):
    if n <= 1:
        return n
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)

docs.title: Designing a Recursive Solution — The 3-Step Method
docs.text:
When you encounter a problem, apply this process:

Step 1 — Identify the base case(s) What is the smallest input where the answer is trivially known?

Step 2 — Assume the recursive call works Pretend f(smaller_input) already returns the correct answer. What do you do with it to solve f(n)?

Step 3 — Ensure progress toward the base case Does every recursive call use a strictly smaller input? If not, you have infinite recursion.

Problem: Count occurrences of x in a list

Step 1: Base case → empty list → count is 0
Step 2: If head == x, count = 1 + count(tail). Else count = count(tail).
Step 3: Each call uses lst[1:], which is shorter. ✓

def count(lst, x):
    if not lst:
        return 0
    return (1 if lst[0] == x else 0) + count(lst[1:], x)

print(count([1, 2, 1, 3, 1], 1))   # 3

docs.title: Mutual Recursion
docs.text:
Two functions that call each other. Less common but valid.

def is_even(n):
    if n == 0:
        return True
    return is_odd(n - 1)

def is_odd(n):
    if n == 0:
        return False
    return is_even(n - 1)

print(is_even(4))   # True
print(is_odd(7))    # True

Both functions must be defined before either is called. The base case must still exist in the mutual chain.

docs.title: Common Errors
docs.text:
# 1. Missing base case → infinite recursion
def bad_factorial(n):
    return n * bad_factorial(n - 1)   # never stops
    # RecursionError

# 2. Base case never reached — wrong condition
def bad_sum(n):
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    return n + bad_sum(n + 1)   # n grows, never hits 0
    # RecursionError

# 3. Wrong return — forgetting to return the recursive call
def bad_search(lst, x):
    if not lst:
        return False
    if lst[0] == x:
        return True
    bad_search(lst[1:], x)   # ← missing return → always returns None

# Fix:
    return bad_search(lst[1:], x)

# 4. Off-by-one in base case
def bad_fib(n):
    if n == 0:       # missing n == 1 case
        return 0
    return bad_fib(n - 1) + bad_fib(n - 2)
    # bad_fib(1) → bad_fib(0) + bad_fib(-1) → infinite descent

docs.title: Recursion and the AI/CS Path
docs.text:
You will encounter recursion in nearly every domain of your reading list:

Course / Book Recursive concept Introduction to Algorithms Merge sort, quicksort, divide and conquer, dynamic programming AI: A Modern Approach Tree search (DFS, minimax, alpha-beta pruning) Discrete Mathematics Mathematical induction, recursive definitions, recurrence relations Deep Learning / PRML Computational graphs (backpropagation is recursive chain rule) CS:APP Recursive descent parsers, call stack mechanics OS Concepts Recursive file system traversal

Backpropagation — the algorithm that trains every neural network — is conceptually a recursive application of the chain rule through a computation graph. When you reach that point in your reading, the mental model you build here will make it click instantly.

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text: Concept Key Point Base case Mandatory — stops recursion Recursive case Must move strictly toward base case Call stack One frame per call — O(depth) memory Python limit 1000 frames default — use sys.getrecursionlimit() Tail recursion Python does NOT optimize — no benefit over regular recursion Memoization Cache subproblem results — converts O(2^n) to O(n) lru_cache Best way to memoize in Python Design method Base case → assume smaller works → ensure progress

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
E1. Write a recursive function power(base, exp) that computes base^exp without using **. No loops allowed.

E2. Write a recursive function that reverses a string. Do not use slicing [::-1] or reversed().

E3. Write a recursive function flatten(lst) that takes a nested list of arbitrary depth and returns a flat list:

flatten([1, [2, [3, [4]], 5], 6])   # → [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

E4. The number of ways to climb n stairs, taking 1 or 2 steps at a time, follows the Fibonacci pattern. Write a memoized recursive function climb(n) and verify climb(10) == 89.

E5. Write a recursive function binary_to_int(s) that converts a binary string like "1011" to its integer value 11. No int(s, 2) allowed. Hint: think about what "1011" means in terms of "101".

E6 (Hard). Implement merge sort recursively:

def merge_sort(lst):
    # split into halves, sort each recursively, merge
    ...

Verify on [38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10] → [3, 9, 10, 27, 38, 43, 82].

docs.title: Core Idea
docs.text:
A class is a blueprint for creating objects. An object is an instance of a class — a concrete entity that bundles together data (attributes) and behavior (methods) into a single unit.

This is the foundation of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP). The goal is not to write classes for everything — it is to recognize when grouping state and behavior together produces cleaner, more maintainable code than standalone functions and variables.

# Without a class — data and behavior are separate and unrelated
name   = "Alice"
age    = 30
salary = 75000

def give_raise(salary, amount):
    return salary + amount

# With a class — data and behavior are bundled into one coherent unit
class Employee:
    def __init__(self, name, age, salary):
        self.name   = name
        self.age    = age
        self.salary = salary

    def give_raise(self, amount):
        self.salary += amount

alice = Employee("Alice", 30, 75000)
alice.give_raise(5000)
print(alice.salary)    # 80000

docs.title: Defining a Class
docs.text:
class ClassName:
    """Docstring describing the class."""

    # class body — attributes and methods

By convention, class names use PascalCase (also called UpperCamelCase). Every word capitalized, no underscores.

class Dog:
    pass    # minimal valid class

docs.title: __init__ — The Constructor
docs.text:
__init__ is called automatically when an object is created. It initializes the instance's attributes.

class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, breed, age):
        self.name  = name     # instance attribute
        self.breed = breed
        self.age   = age

self is the first parameter of every instance method. It refers to the specific object being created or operated on. Python passes it automatically — you never supply it when calling.

rex = Dog("Rex", "German Shepherd", 3)
print(rex.name)     # Rex
print(rex.breed)    # German Shepherd
print(rex.age)      # 3

Dog("Rex", "German Shepherd", 3) calls Dog.__init__(rex, "Rex", "German Shepherd", 3) internally. Python handles the self binding.

docs.title: Instance Attributes
docs.text:
Attributes set on self inside __init__ (or any method) belong to the specific instance. Each object has its own copy.

class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

p1 = Point(1, 2)
p2 = Point(5, 7)

print(p1.x)    # 1
print(p2.x)    # 5  — p1 and p2 have independent x attributes

p1.x = 99     # modifies only p1
print(p1.x)   # 99
print(p2.x)   # 5  — unchanged

Attributes can also be added outside __init__, but this is generally avoided — it makes the object's structure unpredictable.

p1.z = 10    # valid but not recommended unless intentional

docs.title: Class Attributes
docs.text:
Defined directly in the class body, outside any method. Shared across all instances.

class Dog:
    species = "Canis lupus familiaris"    # class attribute — shared

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name                  # instance attribute — unique

rex  = Dog("Rex")
luna = Dog("Luna")

print(rex.species)     # Canis lupus familiaris
print(luna.species)    # Canis lupus familiaris
print(Dog.species)     # Canis lupus familiaris — access via class name

Dog.species = "Canis familiaris"    # modifying class attribute
print(rex.species)     # Canis familiaris — all instances see the change

Instance attribute shadows class attribute when names collide:

class Dog:
    legs = 4

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

rex = Dog("Rex")
print(rex.legs)    # 4 — reads class attribute (no instance attribute named legs)

rex.legs = 3       # creates an instance attribute that shadows the class attribute
print(rex.legs)    # 3 — reads instance attribute
print(Dog.legs)    # 4 — class attribute unchanged

Python looks up attributes in this order: instance __dict__ → class __dict__ → base classes.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
A method is a function defined inside a class. Instance methods automatically receive self as the first argument.

class Circle:
    PI = 3.14159265358979

    def __init__(self, radius):
        self.radius = radius

    def area(self):
        return Circle.PI * self.radius ** 2

    def perimeter(self):
        return 2 * Circle.PI * self.radius

    def scale(self, factor):
        self.radius *= factor    # modifies the instance's radius

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Circle(radius={self.radius})"


c = Circle(5)
print(c.area())         # 78.539...
print(c.perimeter())    # 31.415...
c.scale(2)
print(c.radius)         # 10
print(c)                # Circle(radius=10)

docs.title: Instance Methods
docs.text:
The default. Receive self — operate on the specific instance.

class Counter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.count = 0

    def increment(self):       # instance method
        self.count += 1

    def reset(self):
        self.count = 0

    def value(self):
        return self.count

c = Counter()
c.increment()
c.increment()
print(c.value())    # 2

docs.title: Class Methods — @classmethod
docs.text:
Receive cls (the class itself) instead of self. Operate on class-level state. Often used as alternative constructors.

class Date:
    def __init__(self, year, month, day):
        self.year  = year
        self.month = month
        self.day   = day

    @classmethod
    def from_string(cls, date_string):
        """Alternative constructor — create from 'YYYY-MM-DD' string."""
        year, month, day = map(int, date_string.split("-"))
        return cls(year, month, day)    # calls __init__

    @classmethod
    def today(cls):
        """Alternative constructor — create from current date."""
        import datetime
        d = datetime.date.today()
        return cls(d.year, d.month, d.day)

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Date({self.year}, {self.month}, {self.day})"


d1 = Date(2024, 1, 15)
d2 = Date.from_string("2024-06-20")
d3 = Date.today()
print(d2)    # Date(2024, 6, 20)

cls is used instead of Date directly so that subclasses can inherit the class method and return instances of themselves, not the base class.

docs.title: Static Methods — @staticmethod
docs.text:
Receive neither self nor cls. Just a regular function namespaced inside the class. Used for utility functions that logically belong to the class but do not need access to instance or class state.

class MathUtils:
    @staticmethod
    def is_prime(n):
        if n < 2:
            return False
        for i in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1):
            if n % i == 0:
                return False
        return True

    @staticmethod
    def clamp(value, lo, hi):
        return max(lo, min(value, hi))


print(MathUtils.is_prime(17))        # True
print(MathUtils.clamp(150, 0, 100))  # 100

Static methods can also be called on an instance (obj.static_method()) but calling via the class is clearer.

docs.title: Dunder (Magic) Methods
docs.text: Double-underscore methods that Python calls automatically in response to operators and built-in functions. They define how objects behave with standard Python syntax.

docs.title: __repr__ and __str__
docs.text:
class Vector:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

    def __repr__(self):
        """Unambiguous — for developers. Called by repr() and in REPL."""
        return f"Vector({self.x}, {self.y})"

    def __str__(self):
        """Human-readable — for end users. Called by print() and str()."""
        return f"({self.x}, {self.y})"


v = Vector(3, 4)
print(repr(v))    # Vector(3, 4)
print(str(v))     # (3, 4)
print(v)          # (3, 4)  — print() calls __str__

If only __repr__ is defined, it is used for both. Always define at minimum __repr__ — it makes debugging significantly easier.

docs.title: Arithmetic Operators
docs.text:
class Vector:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

    def __add__(self, other):
        return Vector(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y)

    def __sub__(self, other):
        return Vector(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y)

    def __mul__(self, scalar):
        return Vector(self.x * scalar, self.y * scalar)

    def __rmul__(self, scalar):
        """Called when scalar * vector (scalar on the left)."""
        return self.__mul__(scalar)

    def __neg__(self):
        return Vector(-self.x, -self.y)

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Vector({self.x}, {self.y})"


v1 = Vector(1, 2)
v2 = Vector(3, 4)

print(v1 + v2)     # Vector(4, 6)
print(v1 - v2)     # Vector(-2, -2)
print(v1 * 3)      # Vector(3, 6)
print(3 * v1)      # Vector(3, 6)  — uses __rmul__
print(-v1)         # Vector(-1, -2)

docs.title: Comparison Operators
docs.text:
class Temperature:
    def __init__(self, celsius):
        self.celsius = celsius

    def __eq__(self, other):
        return self.celsius == other.celsius

    def __lt__(self, other):
        return self.celsius < other.celsius

    def __le__(self, other):
        return self.celsius <= other.celsius

    def __gt__(self, other):
        return self.celsius > other.celsius

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Temperature({self.celsius}°C)"


t1 = Temperature(20)
t2 = Temperature(30)

print(t1 < t2)     # True
print(t1 == t2)    # False
print(sorted([t2, t1]))    # [Temperature(20°C), Temperature(30°C)]

Define __eq__ and __lt__ and Python can derive the rest (with @functools.total_ordering).

docs.title: Container Behavior
docs.text:
class Bag:
    def __init__(self):
        self.items = []

    def add(self, item):
        self.items.append(item)

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.items)

    def __contains__(self, item):
        return item in self.items

    def __getitem__(self, index):
        return self.items[index]

    def __iter__(self):
        return iter(self.items)

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Bag({self.items})"


bag = Bag()
bag.add("apple")
bag.add("banana")

print(len(bag))            # 2
print("apple" in bag)      # True
print(bag[0])              # apple
for item in bag:
    print(item)

docs.title: __call__ — Making Objects Callable
docs.text:
class Multiplier:
    def __init__(self, factor):
        self.factor = factor

    def __call__(self, x):
        return x * self.factor


double = Multiplier(2)
triple = Multiplier(3)

print(double(5))    # 10
print(triple(5))    # 15
print(callable(double))    # True

__call__ makes an object behave like a function. This is how PyTorch neural network modules work — model(input) calls model.__call__(input) which internally invokes model.forward(input).

docs.title: Object Identity and Equality
docs.text:
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

    def __eq__(self, other):
        return self.x == other.x and self.y == other.y

p1 = Point(1, 2)
p2 = Point(1, 2)
p3 = p1

print(p1 == p2)     # True  — __eq__ compares values
print(p1 is p2)     # False — different objects in memory
print(p1 is p3)     # True  — same object

Without __eq__, Python uses identity (is) for equality by default — two objects are equal only if they are the same object.

Defining __eq__ disables the default __hash__. If you define __eq__, also define __hash__ if you need the object to be hashable (usable in sets and as dict keys).

class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

    def __eq__(self, other):
        return self.x == other.x and self.y == other.y

    def __hash__(self):
        return hash((self.x, self.y))    # hash of the tuple of fields


p = Point(1, 2)
s = {p}                    # works — Point is hashable
d = {p: "origin-ish"}      # works as dict key

docs.title: Instance, Class, and Static — Decision Guide
docs.text:
Need Use Access or modify instance state (self.x) Instance method Access or modify class state, alternative constructor Class method Utility function logically grouped with class, no state needed Static method 
class Connection:
    max_connections = 100          # class attribute

    def __init__(self, host):
        self.host = host           # instance attribute
        self.active = False

    def connect(self):             # instance method — uses self
        self.active = True

    @classmethod
    def set_max(cls, n):           # class method — uses cls
        cls.max_connections = n

    @staticmethod
    def validate_host(host):       # static method — uses neither
        return isinstance(host, str) and len(host) > 0

docs.title: __dict__ — Inspecting Object State
docs.text:
Every instance has a __dict__ that stores its attributes as a dictionary.

class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age  = age

rex = Dog("Rex", 3)
print(rex.__dict__)    # {"name": "Rex", "age": 3}

This is how attribute access works under the hood. rex.name is effectively rex.__dict__["name"]. Useful for debugging and serialization.

docs.title: Dataclasses (Python 3.7+)
docs.text:
For classes that primarily hold data, @dataclass auto-generates __init__, __repr__, and __eq__.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Point:
    x: float
    y: float
    z: float = 0.0    # default value

@dataclass
class ModelConfig:
    lr:          float = 0.001
    epochs:      int   = 100
    batch_size:  int   = 32
    hidden_dims: list  = field(default_factory=list)
    # field(default_factory=list) — correct way to use mutable default

p = Point(1.0, 2.0)
print(p)                # Point(x=1.0, y=2.0, z=0.0)
print(p == Point(1.0, 2.0))    # True — __eq__ auto-generated

cfg = ModelConfig(lr=0.01, epochs=50)
print(cfg)    # ModelConfig(lr=0.01, epochs=50, batch_size=32, hidden_dims=[])

Use @dataclass for configuration objects, dataset records, and any class whose primary purpose is holding named fields. It eliminates boilerplate while keeping all the OOP benefits.

docs.title: Common Patterns in ML
docs.text:
Model configuration as a class:

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class TrainingConfig:
    model_name:    str   = "resnet50"
    learning_rate: float = 0.001
    batch_size:    int   = 32
    epochs:        int   = 100
    weight_decay:  float = 1e-4
    device:        str   = "cuda"

cfg = TrainingConfig(learning_rate=0.01, epochs=50)

Stateful metric tracker:

class AverageMeter:
    """Track running average of a metric."""

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name  = name
        self.reset()

    def reset(self):
        self.sum   = 0.0
        self.count = 0

    def update(self, value, n=1):
        self.sum   += value * n
        self.count += n

    @property
    def average(self):
        return self.sum / self.count if self.count > 0 else 0.0

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"AverageMeter({self.name}: {self.average:.4f})"


loss_meter = AverageMeter("loss")
for batch_loss in batch_losses:
    loss_meter.update(batch_loss)
print(loss_meter)    # AverageMeter(loss: 0.3421)

Custom dataset class (PyTorch pattern):

class ImageDataset:
    def __init__(self, image_paths, labels, transform=None):
        self.image_paths = image_paths
        self.labels      = labels
        self.transform   = transform

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.image_paths)

    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        image = load_image(self.image_paths[idx])
        label = self.labels[idx]
        if self.transform:
            image = self.transform(image)
        return image, label

This is exactly how torch.utils.data.Dataset works — you subclass it and implement __len__ and __getitem__. The DataLoader then uses these dunder methods to iterate batches. Understanding OOP at this level is what makes PyTorch feel natural rather than magical.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Concept Key Point Class Blueprint for objects — defined with class Object / Instance Concrete entity created from a class __init__ Constructor — called automatically on creation self Reference to the current instance — passed automatically Instance attribute Belongs to one object — set via self.name = ... Class attribute Shared across all instances — defined in class body Instance method Takes self — most common method type Class method Takes cls — @classmethod — alternative constructors Static method Takes neither — @staticmethod — utility functions Dunder methods __repr__, __add__, __len__ etc. — define operator behavior __repr__ Always define — makes debugging possible __eq__ Define when value equality matters — disables default __hash__ __call__ Makes object callable like a function @dataclass Auto-generates __init__, __repr__, __eq__ for data-holding classes

docs.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
docs.text:
# Mistake 1: forgetting self in method definition
class Dog:
    def bark():    # missing self — TypeError when called on instance
        print("Woof")

# Mistake 2: using class attribute for mutable shared state
class Team:
    members = []       # shared across ALL instances — almost always wrong

    def add(self, name):
        self.members.append(name)    # modifies class-level list

# fix: initialize in __init__
class Team:
    def __init__(self):
        self.members = []

# Mistake 3: mutable default in dataclass
from dataclasses import dataclass
@dataclass
class Config:
    items: list = []              # SyntaxError in dataclass
    items: list = field(default_factory=list)    # correct

# Mistake 4: defining __eq__ without __hash__
class Point:
    def __eq__(self, other): ...
    # __hash__ is now None — Point cannot be put in a set or used as dict key
    # fix: also define __hash__

# Mistake 5: accessing class attribute via instance when shadowing occurs
class Dog:
    legs = 4
rex = Dog()
rex.legs = 3            # creates instance attribute
print(Dog.legs)         # 4 — class attribute unchanged
print(rex.legs)         # 3 — reads instance attribute (shadows class)

# Mistake 6: calling self method without parentheses
class Counter:
    def value(self):
        return self.count

c = Counter()
print(c.value)      # <bound method ...> — forgot ()
print(c.value())    # correct

docs.title: The Problem They Solve
docs.text:
When you create multiple objects from the same class, each object needs its own private storage — its own data that doesn't bleed into other objects. self is the mechanism that gives each object its own namespace. __init__ is the function that initializes that namespace the moment the object is created.

Without understanding these two, OOP in Python is cargo-cult syntax. With them, everything else in OOP becomes obvious.

docs.title: self — What It Actually Is
docs.text:
self is a reference to the instance that called the method. It is not a keyword — it is a naming convention. Python passes it automatically as the first argument to every instance method.

class Dog:
    def bark(self):
        print(f"I am dog at memory address: {id(self)}")

d1 = Dog()
d2 = Dog()

d1.bark()   # I am dog at memory address: 140234567891234
d2.bark()   # I am dog at memory address: 140234567891456

d1.bark() is syntactic sugar for Dog.bark(d1). Python rewrites it that way internally. The instance is always passed as the first argument — self just gives it a name inside the method body.

# These two calls are identical
d1.bark()
Dog.bark(d1)

This is not magic. It is a deliberate design choice: methods are functions stored on the class, and the instance is threaded through explicitly. There is no hidden implicit this pointer like in C++ or Java — Python makes it visible.

docs.title: __init__ — The Initializer Method
docs.text:
__init__ is a dunder (double underscore) method that Python calls automatically immediately after creating a new object. Its job is to set up the object's initial state by assigning instance attributes via self.

class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, breed, age):
        self.name = name       # instance attribute
        self.breed = breed
        self.age = age

d = Dog("Rex", "Labrador", 3)
print(d.name)    # Rex
print(d.breed)   # Labrador
print(d.age)     # 3

What happens when Dog("Rex", "Labrador", 3) is called:

  1. Python calls Dog.__new__(Dog) — allocates memory for a new Dog object
  2. Python calls Dog.__init__(new_object, "Rex", "Labrador", 3) — initializes it
  3. The initialized object is returned and bound to d

You define __init__, Python handles __new__. In 99% of cases you never touch __new__.

docs.title: Instance Attributes — Stored on self
docs.text:
Every self.something = value inside __init__ creates an instance attribute — data that belongs to that specific object alone.

class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

p1 = Point(1, 2)
p2 = Point(10, 20)

print(p1.x)   # 1
print(p2.x)   # 10

# Each object has its own __dict__
print(p1.__dict__)   # {'x': 1, 'y': 2}
print(p2.__dict__)   # {'x': 10, 'y': 20}

__dict__ is the actual dictionary backing an object's attributes. Every instance has its own. Assigning to self.x in one instance has zero effect on any other instance.

docs.title: self in Methods Beyond __init__
docs.text:
self is available in every instance method, not just __init__. It's how methods access the object's own data and other methods.

class BankAccount:
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        self.balance += amount         # reads and writes self's data

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        if amount > self.balance:
            raise ValueError("Insufficient funds")
        self.balance -= amount

    def statement(self):
        return f"{self.owner}: ${self.balance:.2f}"

acc = BankAccount("Alice", 1000)
acc.deposit(500)
acc.withdraw(200)
print(acc.statement())   # Alice: $1300.00

Every method uses self to refer to the instance it was called on. There is no global state — each BankAccount object manages its own balance.

docs.title: What Happens Without self
docs.text:
A common mistake is forgetting self when assigning attributes, creating a local variable that dies when the method returns.

class Bad:
    def __init__(self, value):
        value = value   # ← assigns to a local variable, NOT the object
        # self.value never created

b = Bad(42)
print(b.value)   # AttributeError: 'Bad' object has no attribute 'value'

class Good:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value   # ← stored on the object

g = Good(42)
print(g.value)   # 42

The rule: if you want data to persist on the object, it must be assigned to self.something.

docs.title: __init__ with Default Arguments
docs.text:
class Vector:
    def __init__(self, x=0, y=0, z=0):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y
        self.z = z

    def magnitude(self):
        return (self.x**2 + self.y**2 + self.z**2) ** 0.5

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Vector({self.x}, {self.y}, {self.z})"

v1 = Vector(1, 2, 3)
v2 = Vector(x=4)        # y and z default to 0
v3 = Vector()           # all default to 0

print(v1)               # Vector(1, 2, 3)
print(v2)               # Vector(4, 0, 0)
print(v1.magnitude())   # 3.7416...

All default argument rules from [[20. Default and keyword arguments]] apply directly to __init__. The mutable default argument trap applies here too — never use [], {}, or set() as a default in __init__.

# Bug — all instances share the same list
class Bad:
    def __init__(self, items=[]):
        self.items = items   # ← mutable default shared across all instances

# Fix
class Good:
    def __init__(self, items=None):
        self.items = items if items is not None else []

docs.title: __init__ Does Not Return a Value
docs.text:
__init__ must return None. Returning anything else raises a TypeError.

class Wrong:
    def __init__(self, x):
        self.x = x
        return self   # TypeError: __init__() should return None

class Right:
    def __init__(self, x):
        self.x = x
        # implicit return None

If you want to control what is returned when constructing an object, that is the job of __new__, which is almost never overridden.

docs.title: Object Identity and self
docs.text:
self is always the same object as the variable you assigned the instance to.

class Tracker:
    def __init__(self):
        print(f"Inside __init__, id(self) = {id(self)}")

t = Tracker()
print(f"Outside, id(t) = {id(t)}")
# Both print the same memory address — they are the same object

This is important for understanding that mutations inside methods affect the original object, not a copy.

class Container:
    def __init__(self):
        self.data = []

    def add(self, item):
        self.data.append(item)   # mutates the list on self — permanent

c = Container()
c.add(1)
c.add(2)
print(c.data)   # [1, 2]

docs.title: Building a Real Example — Neural Network Layer
docs.text:
class LinearLayer:
    """A single fully-connected layer: output = W @ x + b"""

    def __init__(self, in_features, out_features):
        import random
        # Initialize weights as a 2D list (out x in)
        self.weights = [
            [random.gauss(0, 0.01) for _ in range(in_features)]
            for _ in range(out_features)
        ]
        # Initialize bias as a 1D list
        self.bias = [0.0] * out_features
        self.in_features = in_features
        self.out_features = out_features

    def info(self):
        return (f"LinearLayer({self.in_features} → {self.out_features}) | "
                f"params: {self.in_features * self.out_features + self.out_features}")

layer = LinearLayer(784, 128)
print(layer.info())
# LinearLayer(784 → 128) | params: 100480

This is structurally identical to how torch.nn.Linear.__init__ works — it stores weight tensors on self. When you eventually read PyTorch source code, you will see exactly this pattern.

docs.title: Introspection — Inspecting Objects
docs.text:
class Circle:
    def __init__(self, radius):
        self.radius = radius

    def area(self):
        import math
        return math.pi * self.radius ** 2

c = Circle(5)

# See all instance attributes
print(c.__dict__)           # {'radius': 5}

# See the class
print(type(c))              # <class '__main__.Circle'>
print(c.__class__.__name__) # Circle

# Check if attribute exists before accessing
print(hasattr(c, 'radius'))     # True
print(hasattr(c, 'diameter'))   # False

# Get attribute by name dynamically
print(getattr(c, 'radius'))     # 5
print(getattr(c, 'color', 'unknown'))  # 'unknown' — default if missing

# Set attribute dynamically
setattr(c, 'color', 'red')
print(c.color)   # red

hasattr, getattr, setattr are the programmatic interface to self.__dict__. You will use these in ML frameworks that dynamically configure layers.

docs.title: self is Just a Convention
docs.text:
The name self has no special meaning to Python. You could name it anything — but you never should.

class Point:
    def __init__(this, x, y):   # valid Python, terrible practice
        this.x = x
        this.y = y

    def distance(this):
        return (this.x**2 + this.y**2) ** 0.5

PEP 8 mandates self. Every Python programmer, every library, every framework uses it. Deviating breaks readability for no gain.

docs.title: Common Errors
docs.text:
# 1. Forgetting self as first parameter
class Bad:
    def __init__(name):       # TypeError when instantiating
        self.name = name

# 2. Typo in self — creates new attribute instead of setting intended one
class Typo:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.valeu = value    # typo — self.value never set

t = Typo(10)
print(t.value)   # AttributeError

# 3. Accessing attribute before it's set
class Order:
    def __init__(self, items):
        self.total = self.compute_total()   # Error — self.items doesn't exist yet
        self.items = items

    def compute_total(self):
        return sum(self.items)   # AttributeError: 'Order' has no attribute 'items'

# Fix — set attributes before using them
class Order:
    def __init__(self, items):
        self.items = items
        self.total = self.compute_total()   # now items exists

    def compute_total(self):
        return sum(self.items)

# 4. Mutable default argument
class Graph:
    def __init__(self, edges=[]):   # all Graph() instances share this list
        self.edges = edges

docs.text: Concept Key Point self Reference to the calling instance — passed automatically self name Convention only — could be anything, never change it d.method() Python rewrites as Dog.method(d) __init__ Called automatically after object creation — sets up state __init__ return Must be None — returning anything else raises TypeError Instance attributes Created via self.attr = value — stored in self.__dict__ No self. Assigns a local variable — dies when method returns Mutable defaults Never use [] or {} as __init__ defaults

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
E1. Create a Rectangle class with __init__ taking width and height. Add methods area(), perimeter(), and is_square(). Verify all three work correctly on instances.

E2. Create a Stack class backed by a list. Implement push(item), pop(), peek(), is_empty(), and size() — all using self.data. Make pop() and peek() raise IndexError on an empty stack.

E3. Demonstrate the mutable default argument bug:

  • Create a Bag class with __init__(self, items=[]) and an add(item) method.
  • Create two instances b1 = Bag() and b2 = Bag().
  • Add items to b1 only.
  • Print b2.items and explain why it is not empty.
  • Then fix the class.

E4. Use getattr and setattr to write a function copy_attrs(src, dst, attrs) that copies a list of named attributes from one object to another:

copy_attrs(p1, p2, ['x', 'y'])   # copies p1.x and p1.y onto p2

E5 (Design). Design a Neuron class that represents a single artificial neuron:

  • __init__ takes n_inputs — initialize self.weights as a list of n_inputs zeros and self.bias as 0.0
  • forward(inputs) — computes dot product of weights and inputs, adds bias, applies ReLU (max(0, x))
  • __repr__ — returns Neuron(n_inputs=N, bias=B)
