docs.title: 28. Instance vs Class vs Static Methods
The Core Question
docs.text:
A method is a function defined inside a class. But not all methods are the same — they differ in what they have access to and what Python automatically passes as the first argument.

There are exactly three kinds:

Method type Decorator First argument Has access to Instance method (none) self — the instance Instance state + class state Class method @classmethod cls — the class itself Class state only Static method @staticmethod (nothing) Neither instance nor class

The choice between them is not stylistic — it is a statement about what data the method needs to do its job.

docs.title: Instance Methods — The Default
docs.text:
An instance method receives the calling instance as self. It can read and write both instance attributes (self.x) and class attributes (self.__class__.x or ClassName.x).

This is the most common method type. If you are writing a method and it needs to access or modify the object's own data, it is an instance method.

class Circle:
    PI = 3.14159   # class attribute

    def __init__(self, radius):
        self.radius = radius   # instance attribute

    def area(self):                         # instance method
        return self.PI * self.radius ** 2

    def scale(self, factor):                # instance method
        self.radius *= factor               # modifies instance state

c = Circle(5)
print(c.area())    # 78.53975
c.scale(2)
print(c.radius)    # 10

self.PI works because Python looks up PI on the instance first, then on the class. Since PI is not on the instance, it finds it on the class.

docs.title: Class Methods — @classmethod
docs.text:
A class method receives the class itself as the first argument, named cls by convention. It has no access to instance data — there may not even be an instance.

Use a class method when the method logically belongs to the class but does not operate on any specific instance. The most important use case is alternative constructors.

class Date:
    def __init__(self, year, month, day):
        self.year = year
        self.month = month
        self.day = day

    @classmethod
    def from_string(cls, date_str):
        """Alternative constructor: Date.from_string('2024-03-15')"""
        year, month, day = map(int, date_str.split('-'))
        return cls(year, month, day)   # calls __init__ via cls()

    @classmethod
    def today(cls):
        """Alternative constructor using current date"""
        import datetime
        d = datetime.date.today()
        return cls(d.year, d.month, d.day)

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Date({self.year}, {self.month}, {self.day})"

d1 = Date(2024, 3, 15)
d2 = Date.from_string("2024-03-15")
d3 = Date.today()

print(d1)   # Date(2024, 3, 15)
print(d2)   # Date(2024, 3, 15)

Why cls instead of the class name directly?

Because cls refers to whatever class actually called the method — which matters for inheritance.

class Animal:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    @classmethod
    def create(cls, name):
        return cls(name)   # creates an instance of whatever class called this

class Dog(Animal):
    def speak(self):
        return "Woof"

d = Dog.create("Rex")
print(type(d))    # <class '__main__.Dog'> — not Animal
print(d.speak())  # Woof

If create used Animal(name) instead of cls(name), subclasses could never get instances of their own type. cls makes class methods inheritance-aware.

docs.title: Static Methods — @staticmethod
docs.text:
A static method receives nothing automatically — no self, no cls. It is a plain function that lives inside a class for organizational reasons only.

Use a static method when the logic is related to the class conceptually but does not need any class or instance data.

class MathUtils:
    @staticmethod
    def clamp(value, min_val, max_val):
        """Constrain value to [min_val, max_val]"""
        return max(min_val, min(value, max_val))

    @staticmethod
    def is_prime(n):
        if n < 2:
            return False
        for i in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1):
            if n % i == 0:
                return False
        return True

print(MathUtils.clamp(15, 0, 10))   # 10
print(MathUtils.is_prime(17))       # True

Static methods can also be called on instances, but calling them on the class is the cleaner pattern — it signals that no instance is involved.

m = MathUtils()
print(m.clamp(5, 0, 10))   # 10 — works, but misleading

Static methods vs module-level functions:

If a function genuinely has no relationship to a class, put it at module level. Use @staticmethod when the function is tightly coupled to the class's domain — it belongs there semantically, even if it doesn't need instance or class data.

docs.title: All Three Together — A Cohesive Example
docs.text:
class Temperature:
    ABSOLUTE_ZERO_C = -273.15   # class attribute — physical constant

    def __init__(self, celsius):
        if celsius < self.ABSOLUTE_ZERO_C:
            raise ValueError(f"Below absolute zero: {celsius}°C")
        self.celsius = celsius

    # --- Instance methods --- #
    def to_fahrenheit(self):
        return self.celsius * 9/5 + 32

    def to_kelvin(self):
        return self.celsius - self.ABSOLUTE_ZERO_C

    # --- Class methods (alternative constructors) --- #
    @classmethod
    def from_fahrenheit(cls, f):
        return cls((f - 32) * 5/9)

    @classmethod
    def from_kelvin(cls, k):
        return cls(k + cls.ABSOLUTE_ZERO_C)

    # --- Static methods (utilities) --- #
    @staticmethod
    def celsius_to_fahrenheit(c):
        return c * 9/5 + 32

    @staticmethod
    def is_valid_celsius(c):
        return c >= Temperature.ABSOLUTE_ZERO_C

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Temperature({self.celsius:.2f}°C)"


# Instance method — needs object state
t = Temperature(100)
print(t.to_fahrenheit())    # 212.0
print(t.to_kelvin())        # 373.15

# Class method — alternative constructor, no existing object needed
t2 = Temperature.from_fahrenheit(212)
print(t2)                   # Temperature(100.00°C)

t3 = Temperature.from_kelvin(0)
print(t3)                   # Temperature(-273.15°C)

# Static method — pure utility
print(Temperature.celsius_to_fahrenheit(0))    # 32.0
print(Temperature.is_valid_celsius(-300))      # False

docs.title: How Python Implements This — Descriptors
docs.text:
Under the hood, the three decorators produce different descriptor objects:

  • A plain function becomes a bound method when accessed via an instance — Python automatically prepends the instance as the first argument.
  • @classmethod wraps the function in a classmethod descriptor — Python prepends the class instead.
  • @staticmethod wraps the function in a staticmethod descriptor — Python prepends nothing.
class Demo:
    def instance_method(self): pass

    @classmethod
    def class_method(cls): pass

    @staticmethod
    def static_method(): pass

d = Demo()

# Type of each when accessed via instance
print(type(d.instance_method))   # <class 'method'>         — bound to instance
print(type(d.class_method))      # <class 'method'>         — bound to class
print(type(d.static_method))     # <class 'function'>       — no binding

# Type when accessed via class
print(type(Demo.instance_method))  # <class 'function'>     — unbound
print(type(Demo.class_method))     # <class 'method'>       — bound to class
print(type(Demo.static_method))    # <class 'function'>     — no binding

You do not need to implement descriptors — but knowing this model explains why the three method types behave differently and why calling an unbound instance method on the class requires manually passing an instance.

docs.title: Inheritance Behavior
docs.text:
This is where the distinction between instance and class methods becomes critical.

class Animal:
    category = "Animal"

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def describe(self):                    # instance method
        return f"{self.name} is a {self.__class__.category}"

    @classmethod
    def kingdom(cls):                      # class method
        return f"{cls.category} belongs to kingdom Animalia"

    @staticmethod
    def breathes():                        # static method
        return "Breathes oxygen"

class Dog(Animal):
    category = "Dog"

d = Dog("Rex")
print(d.describe())     # Rex is a Dog      — self.__class__ is Dog
print(Dog.kingdom())    # Dog belongs to kingdom Animalia — cls is Dog
print(Dog.breathes())   # Breathes oxygen  — no class reference at all
  • self.__class__ resolves to the actual runtime class of the instance — always Dog for Dog instances, even if the method is defined on Animal.
  • cls resolves to the class that received the call — Dog when called as Dog.kingdom().
  • Static methods inherit but carry no class information — they cannot be made polymorphic.

docs.title: Decision Guide — Which One Do You Need?
docs.text:
Work through these questions in order:

Does the method need to read or modify THIS object's data (self.x)?
    YES → instance method

Does the method need to create a new instance of THIS class (or a subclass)?
    YES → class method  (alternative constructor)

Does the method need to access class-level data (class attributes)?
    YES → class method  (or instance method, both work)

Is the method a utility that only processes its arguments, unrelated to
instance or class state?
    YES → static method

Would this function make equal sense as a module-level function?
    YES → consider making it a module-level function instead

docs.title: Real-World Pattern — ML Model Class
docs.text:
This pattern appears constantly in PyTorch, scikit-learn, and custom ML code:

class LinearRegression:
    learning_rate_default = 0.01   # class attribute

    def __init__(self, weights, bias=0.0, lr=None):
        self.weights = weights
        self.bias = bias
        self.lr = lr if lr is not None else self.__class__.learning_rate_default
        self.history = []

    # Instance method — operates on this model's weights
    def predict(self, x):
        return sum(w * xi for w, xi in zip(self.weights, x)) + self.bias

    def update(self, gradient):
        self.weights = [w - self.lr * g for w, g in zip(self.weights, gradient)]

    # Class method — alternative constructor: load from a config dict
    @classmethod
    def from_config(cls, config):
        return cls(
            weights=config["weights"],
            bias=config.get("bias", 0.0),
            lr=config.get("lr")
        )

    # Static method — pure math utility, no model state needed
    @staticmethod
    def mse_loss(predictions, targets):
        n = len(predictions)
        return sum((p - t) ** 2 for p, t in zip(predictions, targets)) / n

    @staticmethod
    def normalize(data):
        mean = sum(data) / len(data)
        std = (sum((x - mean)**2 for x in data) / len(data)) ** 0.5
        return [(x - mean) / std for x in data] if std != 0 else data


# Usage
model = LinearRegression(weights=[0.5, -0.3, 0.8])
print(model.predict([1, 2, 3]))   # 0.5*1 + (-0.3)*2 + 0.8*3 + 0 = 2.3

config = {"weights": [1.0, 2.0], "lr": 0.001}
model2 = LinearRegression.from_config(config)

preds = [2.1, 3.9, 5.2]
targets = [2.0, 4.0, 5.0]
print(LinearRegression.mse_loss(preds, targets))   # 0.02

docs.title: Common Errors
docs.text:
# 1. Calling instance method on class without passing instance
class Foo:
    def greet(self):
        return "hello"

Foo.greet()   # TypeError: greet() missing 1 required positional argument: 'self'
Foo.greet(Foo())   # Correct — manually pass an instance

# 2. Forgetting @classmethod — cls is treated as a regular parameter
class Bar:
    def make(cls):   # missing @classmethod — cls is just a name, not the class
        return cls()

Bar.make()   # TypeError: make() missing 1 required positional argument: 'cls'

# 3. Trying to access self inside a static method
class Baz:
    def __init__(self, x):
        self.x = x

    @staticmethod
    def show():
        print(self.x)   # NameError: name 'self' is not defined

# 4. Using class name instead of cls in a classmethod — breaks inheritance
class Parent:
    @classmethod
    def create(cls):
        return Parent()   # ← hardcoded — subclasses always get a Parent instance

class Child(Parent):
    pass

c = Child.create()
print(type(c))   # <class 'Parent'> — wrong, should be Child

# Fix: use cls()

docs.title: The Core Distinction
docs.text:
An attribute is any data stored on an object or a class. Python has two kinds:

  • Instance attributes — belong to one specific object. Each instance has its own copy, stored in self.__dict__. Changes to one instance never affect another.
  • Class attributes — belong to the class itself. Shared across every instance unless explicitly overridden on an instance. Stored in ClassName.__dict__.

The lookup rule determines which one you get when you access obj.attr. Understanding that rule is the entire topic.

docs.title: Declaring Each Type
docs.text:
class Dog:
    species = "Canis lupus familiaris"   # class attribute — shared by all dogs

    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name    # instance attribute — unique to this dog
        self.age = age      # instance attribute — unique to this dog

d1 = Dog("Rex", 3)
d2 = Dog("Bella", 5)

# Instance attributes — each dog has its own
print(d1.name)   # Rex
print(d2.name)   # Bella

# Class attribute — same for all
print(d1.species)   # Canis lupus familiaris
print(d2.species)   # Canis lupus familiaris
print(Dog.species)  # Canis lupus familiaris — accessible directly on class

docs.title: The Attribute Lookup Chain
docs.text:
When you write obj.attr, Python searches in this exact order:

1. obj.__dict__          (instance namespace)
2. type(obj).__dict__    (class namespace)
3. base classes          (MRO — method resolution order)
4. AttributeError        (if not found anywhere)

This is called the descriptor protocol / attribute lookup chain. The instance always wins over the class if the name exists in both.

class Config:
    debug = False    # class attribute

c1 = Config()
c2 = Config()

print(c1.debug)    # False — found on class, no instance attr exists yet
print(c2.debug)    # False

# Now shadow the class attribute on c1 only
c1.debug = True    # creates a NEW instance attribute on c1

print(c1.debug)    # True  — found on instance (shadows class attr)
print(c2.debug)    # False — still reads class attr (no instance attr on c2)
print(Config.debug) # False — class attribute unchanged

Assigning to obj.attr never modifies the class attribute. It always creates or updates an instance attribute. The class attribute is untouched and still visible on other instances.

docs.title: Modifying a Class Attribute
docs.text:
To actually change the class attribute — for all instances simultaneously — assign through the class, not through an instance.

class Config:
    debug = False

c1 = Config()
c2 = Config()

# Change via class — affects ALL instances that haven't shadowed it
Config.debug = True

print(c1.debug)    # True
print(c2.debug)    # True

# Now shadow on c1
c1.debug = False

Config.debug = True    # change class again
print(c1.debug)        # False — c1's instance attr shadows the class
print(c2.debug)        # True  — c2 still reads class attr

Mental model: Think of the class attribute as a default. The moment you do self.attr = value, you create a personal copy on the instance that permanently shadows the class default for that instance.

docs.title: Inspecting __dict__ Directly
docs.text:
The most direct way to see what's happening:

class Player:
    max_health = 100      # class attribute

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name       # instance attribute
        self.health = 100      # instance attribute

p = Player("Alice")

print(p.__dict__)          # {'name': 'Alice', 'health': 100}
print(Player.__dict__)     # {'max_health': 100, '__init__': ..., ...}

# max_health is NOT in p.__dict__ — it lives on the class
print('max_health' in p.__dict__)      # False
print('max_health' in Player.__dict__) # True

This is the ground truth. If it is not in p.__dict__, it is not an instance attribute — Python is finding it on the class.

docs.title: The Critical Trap — Mutable Class Attributes
docs.text:
Mutable class attributes (lists, dicts, sets) are shared across all instances. Mutating them (.append(), update(), etc.) modifies the shared object — it does not create an instance-level copy.

# Bug — all instances share the same list
class Bag:
    items = []    # class attribute — one list object shared by all

b1 = Bag()
b2 = Bag()

b1.items.append("apple")   # mutates the shared list — does NOT create instance attr
b1.items.append("bread")

print(b1.items)   # ['apple', 'bread']
print(b2.items)   # ['apple', 'bread']  ← b2 is affected!
print(id(b1.items) == id(b2.items))   # True — same object

Why does this happen? b1.items.append(...) does not assign to b1.items — it reads b1.items (finds the class attribute) and then mutates it in place. No instance attribute is ever created on b1.

# Contrast: assignment creates a new instance attribute
b1.items = ["apple"]   # NOW b1 gets its own list — class attr untouched
b2.items               # still the original shared [] — empty

The fix: always initialize mutable attributes in __init__:

class Bag:
    def __init__(self):
        self.items = []   # each instance gets its own fresh list

b1 = Bag()
b2 = Bag()

b1.items.append("apple")
print(b1.items)   # ['apple']
print(b2.items)   # []  — unaffected

This is one of the most common bugs in Python OOP. It also appears in __init__ with mutable defaults — see [[27. init, self]].

docs.title: When Class Attributes Are Intentional and Correct
docs.text: Not all class attributes are accidents. Some legitimate uses:

docs.title: Shared Constants
docs.text:
class Circle:
    PI = 3.14159265358979   # mathematical constant — should be shared

    def __init__(self, radius):
        self.radius = radius

    def area(self):
        return self.PI * self.radius ** 2

docs.title: Shared Configuration / Defaults
docs.text:
class NeuralLayer:
    activation = "relu"        # default activation for all layers
    weight_init = "xavier"     # default initialization strategy

    def __init__(self, units):
        self.units = units
        # Can override per-instance if needed
        # self.activation = "sigmoid"

docs.title: Instance Counter — Tracking All Instances
docs.text:
class Connection:
    count = 0   # tracks how many connections exist

    def __init__(self, host):
        self.host = host
        Connection.count += 1    # modify via class name — intentional

    def close(self):
        Connection.count -= 1

c1 = Connection("db1")
c2 = Connection("db2")
print(Connection.count)   # 2

c1.close()
print(Connection.count)   # 1

Notice: Connection.count += 1 is used, not self.count += 1. The latter would create an instance attribute on the first call and never modify the class attribute again.

docs.title: self.count += 1 vs ClassName.count += 1 — The Subtle Bug
docs.text:
class Counter:
    count = 0

    def increment_wrong(self):
        self.count += 1      # creates instance attr — class attr unchanged

    def increment_right(self):
        Counter.count += 1   # modifies class attr directly

c = Counter()
c.increment_wrong()
print(c.count)       # 1  — instance attr
print(Counter.count) # 0  — class attr untouched

c2 = Counter()
c2.increment_right()
print(Counter.count) # 1  — class attr updated
print(c2.count)      # 1  — reads class attr (no instance attr on c2)

self.count += 1 expands to self.count = self.count + 1. The right side reads the class attr (0), adds 1, and then assigns 1 to a new instance attribute. The class attribute stays at 0. Any other instance that calls increment_wrong() starts fresh from the class attr.

docs.title: Class Attributes and Inheritance
docs.text:
Class attributes are inherited by subclasses. Each subclass gets its own __dict__, but looks up the parent's class attributes through the MRO.

class Animal:
    kingdom = "Animalia"
    sound = "..."

class Dog(Animal):
    sound = "Woof"    # overrides class attr at the class level

class Cat(Animal):
    sound = "Meow"

print(Dog.kingdom)   # Animalia  — inherited from Animal
print(Dog.sound)     # Woof      — overridden on Dog
print(Cat.sound)     # Meow      — overridden on Cat
print(Animal.sound)  # ...       — parent unchanged

Changing Animal.kingdom after the fact propagates to all subclasses that haven't overridden it:

Animal.kingdom = "ANIMALIA"
print(Dog.kingdom)   # ANIMALIA — Dog has no own kingdom, reads Animal's

docs.title: vars() — Another Way to Inspect
docs.text:
class Rectangle:
    shape = "rectangle"

    def __init__(self, w, h):
        self.width = w
        self.height = h

r = Rectangle(4, 6)

print(vars(r))           # {'width': 4, 'height': 6}
print(vars(Rectangle))   # mappingproxy({'shape': 'rectangle', '__init__': ..., ...})

vars(obj) is equivalent to obj.__dict__. vars(ClassName) returns a mappingproxy — a read-only view of the class namespace.

docs.title: __slots__ — Restricting Attributes
docs.text:
By default, Python uses a __dict__ for every instance — flexible but memory-heavy. For classes with many instances and a fixed set of attributes, __slots__ replaces the per-instance dict with a compact structure.

class Point:
    __slots__ = ('x', 'y')   # only these attributes allowed

    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

p = Point(1, 2)
print(p.x)      # 1

p.z = 3         # AttributeError: 'Point' has no attribute 'z'
print(p.__dict__)   # AttributeError — no __dict__ with __slots__

Consequences of __slots__:

  • No __dict__ on instances — saves ~50 bytes per instance
  • Only the declared attributes can be set — stricter but cleaner
  • Class attributes still work normally
  • Inheritance with __slots__ requires care — every class in the chain should define __slots__

Use __slots__ when you have millions of lightweight instances (e.g., graph nodes, data records, particle simulations).

docs.title: Full Reference — Lookup Behavior
docs.text:
class Base:
    x = "class attr on Base"

class Child(Base):
    pass

obj = Child()

# Lookup order for obj.x:
# 1. obj.__dict__           → not found
# 2. Child.__dict__         → not found
# 3. Base.__dict__          → found: "class attr on Base"

print(obj.x)   # class attr on Base

# Shadow at instance level
obj.x = "instance attr"
print(obj.x)   # instance attr  — instance wins

# Shadow at subclass level
Child.x = "class attr on Child"
del obj.x                       # remove instance attr
print(obj.x)   # class attr on Child — Child wins over Base

docs.title: Side-by-Side Comparison
docs.text:
class Example:
    class_attr = "shared"      # in Example.__dict__

    def __init__(self):
        self.instance_attr = "mine"   # in self.__dict__

e1 = Example()
e2 = Example()

#                     e1          e2          Example
# class_attr        "shared"    "shared"    "shared"
# instance_attr     "mine"      "mine"      (not here)

e1.class_attr = "overridden"   # creates instance attr on e1

#                     e1              e2          Example
# class_attr        "overridden"    "shared"    "shared"
# instance_attr     "mine"          "mine"      (not here)

Example.class_attr = "new shared"   # changes class attr

#                     e1              e2              Example
# class_attr        "overridden"    "new shared"    "new shared"

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text: Instance attribute Class attribute Defined in __init__ via self.attr = val Class body, outside any method Stored in instance.__dict__ ClassName.__dict__ Unique per instance ✅ ❌ — shared unless shadowed Access via instance ✅ ✅ (via lookup chain) Access via class ❌ ✅ Mutable default danger Rare High — shared mutations affect all Memory One copy per instance One copy total Use case Object-specific state Shared constants, counters, defaults

E5 (Lookup Chain). Without running any code, predict the output of each print statement, then verify:

class B(A):
    pass

class C(A):
    x = 3

b = B()
c = C()

print(B.x)       # ?
print(C.x)       # ?
print(b.x)       # ?
b.x = 10
print(b.x)       # ?
print(B.x)       # ?
A.x = 99
print(b.x)       # ?
print(B.x)       # ?
print(c.x)       # ?

docs.title: What Inheritance Is
docs.text:
Inheritance is a mechanism where one class (the subclass or child) automatically receives all the attributes and methods of another class (the superclass or parent), without rewriting them. The subclass can then extend or replace any of that inherited behavior.

The fundamental purpose is code reuse with specialization. You define common behavior once on the parent, then build specialized variants as children.

class Animal:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def breathe(self):
        return f"{self.name} breathes oxygen"

    def speak(self):
        return "..."

class Dog(Animal):     # Dog inherits from Animal
    pass               # nothing added yet

d = Dog("Rex")
print(d.breathe())    # Rex breathes oxygen  — inherited from Animal
print(d.name)         # Rex                  — inherited __init__

Dog inherits everything. You wrote zero methods on it and it already works — because the lookup chain climbs to Animal when it cannot find the attribute on Dog.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
class Parent:
    pass

class Child(Parent):       # single inheritance
    pass

class Child(Parent1, Parent2):   # multiple inheritance
    pass

Every class in Python implicitly inherits from object if no parent is specified:

class Foo:
    pass

print(Foo.__bases__)    # (<class 'object'>,)
print(isinstance(Foo(), object))   # True

object is the root of all Python classes. It provides default implementations of __repr__, __str__, __eq__, __hash__, and others.

docs.title: Method Overriding
docs.text:
Overriding means defining a method in the subclass with the same name as a method in the parent. Python's lookup chain finds the subclass version first, so the parent's version is replaced for that class.

class Animal:
    def speak(self):
        return "..."

class Dog(Animal):
    def speak(self):         # overrides Animal.speak
        return "Woof"

class Cat(Animal):
    def speak(self):         # overrides Animal.speak
        return "Meow"

class Fish(Animal):
    pass                     # inherits Animal.speak unchanged

animals = [Dog("Rex"), Cat("Luna"), Fish("Nemo")]
for a in animals:
    print(a.speak())
# Woof
# Meow
# ...

Each subclass provides its own version of speak. The caller does not need to know which subclass it has — it just calls speak() and gets the right behavior. This is polymorphism.

docs.title: The Method Resolution Order (MRO)
docs.text:
When Python looks up an attribute, it follows a deterministic sequence called the MRO — the order in which it searches classes. For single inheritance it is linear. For multiple inheritance, Python uses the C3 linearization algorithm.

class A:
    def hello(self):
        return "A"

class B(A):
    def hello(self):
        return "B"

class C(A):
    def hello(self):
        return "C"

class D(B, C):
    pass

print(D.__mro__)
# (<class 'D'>, <class 'B'>, <class 'C'>, <class 'A'>, <class 'object'>)

print(D().hello())   # B — first class in MRO that defines hello

Inspect MRO at any time:

print(D.__mro__)        # tuple of classes in resolution order
print(D.mro())          # same, as a list

The rule: left to right, depth before breadth, no class appears twice.

docs.title: Extending the Parent — Calling super()
docs.text:
Often you want to extend the parent's method rather than completely replace it. You keep the parent's logic and add to it. super() gives you a proxy to the parent class in MRO order.

class Animal:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

    def describe(self):
        return f"{self.name}, age {self.age}"

class Dog(Animal):
    def __init__(self, name, age, breed):
        super().__init__(name, age)    # run Animal.__init__ first
        self.breed = breed             # then add Dog-specific attribute

    def describe(self):
        base = super().describe()      # get Animal's description
        return f"{base}, breed: {self.breed}"  # extend it

d = Dog("Rex", 3, "Labrador")
print(d.describe())   # Rex, age 3, breed: Labrador

Without super().__init__(), self.name and self.age would never be set — Dog's __init__ would need to duplicate that code. super() eliminates that duplication. See [[31. super()]] for the full treatment.

docs.title: 1. Full Replacement — Ignore the Parent Entirely
docs.text:
class Shape:
    def area(self):
        return 0

class Circle(Shape):
    def __init__(self, radius):
        self.radius = radius

    def area(self):
        import math
        return math.pi * self.radius ** 2   # completely replaces Shape.area

Use when the parent's implementation has nothing useful to offer.

docs.title: 2. Extension — Call Parent, Then Add
docs.text:
class Vehicle:
    def start(self):
        print("Engine on")

class ElectricVehicle(Vehicle):
    def start(self):
        super().start()             # parent runs first
        print("Battery check done")  # then child adds

ev = ElectricVehicle()
ev.start()
# Engine on
# Battery check done

Use when the parent's logic must still run — you are adding to it, not replacing it.

docs.title: 3. Pre-processing — Add First, Then Call Parent
docs.text:
class LoggedDict(dict):
    def __setitem__(self, key, value):
        print(f"Setting {key} = {value}")
        super().__setitem__(key, value)   # parent runs after logging

d = LoggedDict()
d["x"] = 10   # Setting x = 10
print(d["x"]) # 10

Use when you need to validate, transform, or log before delegating to the parent.

docs.title: isinstance() and issubclass()
docs.text:
These two functions expose the inheritance hierarchy at runtime.

class Animal: pass
class Dog(Animal): pass
class Cat(Animal): pass

d = Dog()

print(isinstance(d, Dog))     # True  — d is a Dog
print(isinstance(d, Animal))  # True  — Dog IS-A Animal
print(isinstance(d, Cat))     # False

print(issubclass(Dog, Animal))  # True
print(issubclass(Dog, object))  # True  — everything is a subclass of object
print(issubclass(Animal, Dog))  # False — not the other direction

isinstance is preferred over type(obj) == SomeClass because it respects the inheritance hierarchy. A Dog IS-A Animal — isinstance knows this, type() == does not.

docs.title: A Complete Hierarchy — The IS-A Test
docs.text:
Before creating an inheritance relationship, apply the IS-A test: does the child genuinely IS-A parent?

  • ✅ Dog IS-A Animal — valid
  • ✅ CheckingAccount IS-A BankAccount — valid
  • ✅ LinearLayer IS-A Module — valid (PyTorch's design)
  • ❌ Engine IS-A Car — wrong. Engine HAS-A relationship with Car (use composition instead)
class BankAccount:
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = balance

    def deposit(self, amount):
        if amount <= 0:
            raise ValueError("Deposit must be positive")
        self.balance += amount
        return self.balance

    def withdraw(self, amount):
        if amount > self.balance:
            raise ValueError("Insufficient funds")
        self.balance -= amount
        return self.balance

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"{self.__class__.__name__}(owner={self.owner}, balance={self.balance})"


class SavingsAccount(BankAccount):
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0, interest_rate=0.03):
        super().__init__(owner, balance)
        self.interest_rate = interest_rate

    def apply_interest(self):
        interest = self.balance * self.interest_rate
        self.balance += interest
        return interest


class CheckingAccount(BankAccount):
    def __init__(self, owner, balance=0, overdraft_limit=500):
        super().__init__(owner, balance)
        self.overdraft_limit = overdraft_limit

    def withdraw(self, amount):          # overrides — allows overdraft
        if amount > self.balance + self.overdraft_limit:
            raise ValueError("Exceeds overdraft limit")
        self.balance -= amount
        return self.balance


s = SavingsAccount("Alice", 1000, 0.05)
s.deposit(500)               # inherited from BankAccount
s.apply_interest()           # only on SavingsAccount
print(s)                     # SavingsAccount(owner=Alice, balance=1575.0)

c = CheckingAccount("Bob", 100, overdraft_limit=200)
c.withdraw(250)              # uses CheckingAccount.withdraw — overdraft allowed
print(c)                     # CheckingAccount(owner=Bob, balance=-150)

__repr__ uses self.__class__.__name__ — so it prints SavingsAccount for savings instances and CheckingAccount for checking instances, even though the method is defined only once on BankAccount.

docs.title: Multiple Inheritance
docs.text:
Python supports inheriting from more than one parent. The MRO resolves conflicts.

class Flyable:
    def move(self):
        return "flying"

    def describe(self):
        return "I can fly"

class Swimmable:
    def move(self):
        return "swimming"

    def describe(self):
        return "I can swim"

class Duck(Flyable, Swimmable):
    pass

d = Duck()
print(d.move())      # flying — Flyable is first in MRO
print(d.describe())  # I can fly

print(Duck.__mro__)
# (<class 'Duck'>, <class 'Flyable'>, <class 'Swimmable'>, <class 'object'>)

The diamond problem — when two parents share a grandparent, the MRO ensures the grandparent's method runs exactly once:

class A:
    def greet(self):
        return "A"

class B(A):
    def greet(self):
        return "B → " + super().greet()

class C(A):
    def greet(self):
        return "C → " + super().greet()

class D(B, C):
    def greet(self):
        return "D → " + super().greet()

print(D().greet())   # D → B → C → A
print(D.__mro__)     # D, B, C, A, object

super() in each class calls the next class in the MRO, not the literal parent. This ensures A.greet runs once, not twice. This cooperative super() pattern is the correct way to handle multiple inheritance.

docs.title: Inheritance in ML Frameworks — Why This Matters Now
docs.text:
PyTorch's entire model system is built on inheritance:

# Simplified version of how PyTorch nn.Module works

class Module:
    def __init__(self):
        self._parameters = {}
        self._modules = {}

    def forward(self, x):
        raise NotImplementedError

    def __call__(self, x):
        return self.forward(x)   # calls the subclass's forward


class Linear(Module):
    def __init__(self, in_features, out_features):
        super().__init__()       # sets up _parameters, _modules
        self.in_features = in_features
        self.out_features = out_features

    def forward(self, x):
        # matrix multiply x by weights
        return x   # simplified


class MyNetwork(Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.layer1 = Linear(784, 128)
        self.layer2 = Linear(128, 10)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.layer1(x)
        x = self.layer2(x)
        return x

When you write class MyNetwork(nn.Module) in real PyTorch, this is exactly what you are doing — inheriting from Module, calling super().__init__(), and overriding forward. The forward method is the prototypical override: nn.Module defines it as an abstract interface, and every model you write replaces it.

docs.title: Abstract Base Classes — Enforcing the Interface
docs.text:
Python's abc module lets you define methods that must be overridden by subclasses. If a subclass does not implement them, instantiation raises a TypeError.

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Shape(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def area(self):
        pass

    @abstractmethod
    def perimeter(self):
        pass

    def describe(self):
        return f"Area: {self.area():.2f}, Perimeter: {self.perimeter():.2f}"

class Circle(Shape):
    def __init__(self, radius):
        self.radius = radius

    def area(self):
        import math
        return math.pi * self.radius ** 2

    def perimeter(self):
        import math
        return 2 * math.pi * self.radius

class Square(Shape):
    def __init__(self, side):
        self.side = side

    def area(self):
        return self.side ** 2

    def perimeter(self):
        return 4 * self.side

# Shape()   ← TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class
c = Circle(5)
print(c.describe())   # Area: 78.54, Perimeter: 31.42

s = Square(4)
print(s.describe())   # Area: 16.00, Perimeter: 16.00

Abstract base classes are the Pythonic way to define an interface — a contract that subclasses must fulfill. PyTorch's nn.Module.forward is effectively abstract (raises NotImplementedError), following the same pattern.

docs.title: Common Errors
docs.text:
# 1. Forgetting super().__init__() — parent attributes never set
class Animal:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

class Dog(Animal):
    def __init__(self, name, breed):
        self.breed = breed   # forgot super().__init__(name)

d = Dog("Rex", "Lab")
print(d.breed)   # Lab
print(d.name)    # AttributeError: 'Dog' has no attribute 'name'

# 2. Overriding without calling super() when extension was intended
class Dog(Animal):
    def __init__(self, name, breed):
        super().__init__(name)   # correct
        self.breed = breed

# 3. IS-A violation — using inheritance when composition is correct
class Engine:
    def start(self):
        return "Vroom"

class Car(Engine):           # wrong — Car is not an Engine
    pass

# Should be:
class Car:
    def __init__(self):
        self.engine = Engine()   # Car HAS-A Engine (composition)

# 4. Shadowing a class attribute accidentally via inheritance
class Parent:
    data = [1, 2, 3]

class Child(Parent):
    pass

Child.data.append(4)   # mutates Parent.data — shared mutable class attr
print(Parent.data)     # [1, 2, 3, 4]  — unintended

docs.title: What super() Is
docs.text:
super() returns a proxy object that delegates method calls to the next class in the MRO (Method Resolution Order). It is the correct, robust way to call a parent class's method from a child class — without hardcoding the parent's name.

The naive alternative — calling ParentClass.method(self, ...) directly — works in simple single inheritance but silently breaks in multiple inheritance and during refactoring. super() is the general solution.

class Animal:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

class Dog(Animal):
    def __init__(self, name, breed):
        super().__init__(name)   # delegates to Animal.__init__
        self.breed = breed

d = Dog("Rex", "Labrador")
print(d.name)    # Rex    — set by Animal.__init__ via super()
print(d.breed)   # Labrador — set by Dog.__init__

docs.title: The Mechanical Reality — What super() Actually Does
docs.text:
super() does not simply call the parent class. It calls the next class in the MRO of the instance's actual class. These are different things in multiple inheritance.

super()
# is equivalent to:
super(__class__, self)

Two arguments:

  • __class__ — the class where this super() call is written (determined at compile time, not runtime)
  • self — the instance (determines which MRO to use)

Python finds __class__ in the MRO, then returns a proxy that starts searching one step after __class__ in that MRO.

class A:
    def greet(self):
        return "A"

class B(A):
    def greet(self):
        # __class__ is B, self is a D instance
        # MRO of D: D → B → C → A
        # super() starts after B → finds C.greet
        return "B + " + super().greet()

class C(A):
    def greet(self):
        return "C + " + super().greet()

class D(B, C):
    def greet(self):
        return "D + " + super().greet()

print(D().greet())      # D + B + C + A
print(D.__mro__)        # D, B, C, A, object

Each super() call hands off to the next class in the MRO — not to the literal parent. This is the cooperative multiple inheritance pattern.

docs.title: Why Not Just Hardcode the Parent Name
docs.text:
# Fragile — hardcodes the parent name
class Dog(Animal):
    def __init__(self, name, breed):
        Animal.__init__(self, name)   # works, but brittle
        self.breed = breed

Problem 1 — Refactoring breaks silently:

If you rename Animal to Creature, every hardcoded call breaks. super() is always correct regardless of class name.

Problem 2 — Multiple inheritance calls the grandparent twice:

class A:
    def __init__(self):
        print("A init")

class B(A):
    def __init__(self):
        A.__init__(self)   # hardcoded
        print("B init")

class C(A):
    def __init__(self):
        A.__init__(self)   # hardcoded
        print("C init")

class D(B, C):
    def __init__(self):
        B.__init__(self)
        C.__init__(self)
        print("D init")

D()
# A init   ← called by B
# B init
# A init   ← called again by C — wrong
# C init
# D init

A.__init__ runs twice. With super(), each class in the MRO runs exactly once:

class A:
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        print("A init")

class B(A):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        print("B init")

class C(A):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        print("C init")

class D(B, C):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        print("D init")

D()
# A init   ← called exactly once
# C init
# B init
# D init

MRO for D: D → B → C → A → object. Each super() hands off to the next — no class runs twice.

docs.title: super() in __init__ — The Most Common Use
docs.text:
The most frequent use of super() is in __init__ to ensure the parent sets up its attributes before the child adds its own.

class Shape:
    def __init__(self, color="black"):
        self.color = color
        self.visible = True

class Circle(Shape):
    def __init__(self, radius, color="black"):
        super().__init__(color)      # Shape sets self.color, self.visible
        self.radius = radius         # Circle adds self.radius

    def area(self):
        import math
        return math.pi * self.radius ** 2

class ColoredCircle(Circle):
    def __init__(self, radius, color, opacity=1.0):
        super().__init__(radius, color)   # Circle's __init__, which calls Shape's
        self.opacity = opacity

c = ColoredCircle(5, "red", 0.8)
print(c.color)    # red     — set by Shape.__init__
print(c.radius)   # 5       — set by Circle.__init__
print(c.opacity)  # 0.8     — set by ColoredCircle.__init__

The chain: ColoredCircle.__init__ → super() → Circle.__init__ → super() → Shape.__init__. Each level adds its own attributes. No duplication, no missed initialization.

docs.title: super() for Method Extension
docs.text:
Beyond __init__, super() is used to extend any method — run the parent's version, then add child behavior.

class Logger:
    def log(self, msg):
        print(f"[LOG] {msg}")

class TimestampLogger(Logger):
    def log(self, msg):
        import datetime
        timestamp = datetime.datetime.now().strftime("%H:%M:%S")
        super().log(f"{timestamp} — {msg}")   # extend, not replace

class PrefixLogger(TimestampLogger):
    def log(self, msg):
        super().log(f"[APP] {msg}")

p = PrefixLogger()
p.log("Server started")
# [LOG] 14:32:07 — [APP] Server started

The call chain: PrefixLogger.log → TimestampLogger.log → Logger.log. Each layer adds its transformation. The output is the composition of all three.

docs.title: super() with @classmethod
docs.text:
super() works inside class methods too. cls replaces self, and super() still uses the MRO correctly.

class Animal:
    @classmethod
    def create(cls, name):
        print(f"Animal.create called with cls={cls.__name__}")
        return cls(name)

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

class Dog(Animal):
    def __init__(self, name, breed="unknown"):
        super().__init__(name)
        self.breed = breed

    @classmethod
    def create_puppy(cls):
        instance = super().create("Puppy")   # calls Animal.create with cls=Dog
        instance.breed = "Mixed"
        return instance

d = Dog.create_puppy()
print(d.name)    # Puppy
print(d.breed)   # Mixed

docs.title: super() with @staticmethod
docs.text:
Static methods do not receive cls or self, so super() cannot be called inside them using the zero-argument form. You must use the explicit two-argument form or restructure as a class method.

class A:
    @staticmethod
    def helper():
        return "A helper"

class B(A):
    @staticmethod
    def helper():
        # super().helper()   ← NameError: super() without args needs __class__
        return A.helper() + " + B"   # only option for static methods

This is a known limitation. If you find yourself needing super() in a static method, that is a signal to reconsider whether it should be a class method instead.

docs.title: Explicit Two-Argument Form — super(Class, obj)
docs.text:
The zero-argument super() (Python 3) is shorthand for super(__class__, self). You can also call it explicitly, which is useful in some dynamic scenarios.

class A:
    def greet(self):
        return "A"

class B(A):
    def greet(self):
        return "B + " + super(B, self).greet()   # explicit form

class C(B):
    def greet(self):
        return "C + " + super(C, self).greet()

print(C().greet())   # C + B + A

The explicit form is occasionally needed when:

  • Working outside a method body (in a function, not a method)
  • Writing Python 2 compatible code (Python 2 requires the explicit form)
  • Deliberately skipping a class in the MRO (rare, usually a design smell)

In modern Python 3, always use super() with no arguments.

docs.title: super() and object
docs.text:
At the top of every MRO sits object. When super() reaches object, it calls object.__init__() — which accepts no arguments beyond self. This is usually harmless, but in cooperative multiple inheritance it requires care.

class A:
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)   # passes remaining kwargs up the chain

class B:
    def __init__(self, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)

class C(A, B):
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        super().__init__(x=x, y=y)   # all kwargs forwarded

# Eventually object.__init__() is called with no kwargs — fine if they're consumed

The pattern: use **kwargs to pass unhandled arguments up the MRO. Each class pops the arguments it knows about and passes the rest up. object.__init__ is called with an empty dict at the end.

docs.title: Full ML Example — Layer System
docs.text:
class Module:
    def __init__(self):
        self.training = True
        self._layers = []

    def forward(self, x):
        raise NotImplementedError

    def __call__(self, x):
        return self.forward(x)

    def parameters(self):
        return []


class TrainableModule(Module):
    def __init__(self, lr=0.01):
        super().__init__()           # Module sets training, _layers
        self.lr = lr
        self.grad = None

    def zero_grad(self):
        self.grad = None


class Linear(TrainableModule):
    def __init__(self, in_features, out_features, lr=0.01):
        super().__init__(lr=lr)      # TrainableModule sets lr, grad; Module sets training
        self.weights = [0.0] * in_features
        self.bias = 0.0
        self.in_features = in_features
        self.out_features = out_features

    def forward(self, x):
        return sum(w * xi for w, xi in zip(self.weights, x)) + self.bias

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Linear({self.in_features} → {self.out_features}, lr={self.lr})"


layer = Linear(4, 1, lr=0.001)
print(layer)            # Linear(4 → 1, lr=0.001)
print(layer.training)   # True    — from Module via super() chain
print(layer.lr)         # 0.001   — from TrainableModule
print(layer.weights)    # [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] — from Linear

The super() chain: Linear.__init__ → TrainableModule.__init__ → Module.__init__. Each level sets its own attributes. No duplication. No missed initialization.

docs.title: Common Errors
docs.text:
# 1. Forgetting super().__init__() entirely
class Dog(Animal):
    def __init__(self, name, breed):
        self.breed = breed    # Animal.__init__ never called
        # self.name never set — AttributeError later

# 2. Calling super() after setting attributes that depend on parent state
class Dog(Animal):
    def __init__(self, name, breed):
        self.full_info = f"{self.name} the {breed}"  # AttributeError — name not set yet
        super().__init__(name)   # too late

# Fix: super().__init__ first, always
class Dog(Animal):
    def __init__(self, name, breed):
        super().__init__(name)
        self.full_info = f"{self.name} the {breed}"   # fine now

# 3. super() outside a method — zero-arg form fails
def standalone():
    super()   # RuntimeError: super(): no arguments

# 4. Wrong argument count passed to super().__init__
class Animal:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

class Dog(Animal):
    def __init__(self, name, breed):
        super().__init__(name)    # TypeError: missing 'age'

# 5. Forgetting super() in cooperative multiple inheritance
class B(A):
    def __init__(self):
        # super().__init__() missing — C.__init__ never called in diamond
        print("B init")

docs.title: Decision Guide — When to Use super()
docs.text:
Are you overriding __init__ and the parent has state to set up?
    YES → call super().__init__() — always, as the first line

Are you overriding a method but want to keep the parent's behavior?
    YES → call super().method_name() — either before or after your additions

Are you completely replacing the parent's method?
    NO super() needed — you own the entire behavior

Are you using multiple inheritance?
    YES → every class in the chain should call super() — cooperative pattern

E1. Build a three-level chain Person → Employee → Manager. Each adds one attribute in __init__. Use super() at every level. Print all attributes on a Manager instance and verify none are missing.

E2. Create a diamond:

    A
   / \

    D

Give each class an __init__ that calls super().__init__() and prints its class name. Instantiate D and verify A.__init__ prints exactly once. Then replace super() with hardcoded parent calls and observe it prints twice.

E3. Write a ValidationMixin with a method validate(self, data) that checks data is not None. Write a LoggingMixin with validate(self, data) that prints "Validating..." then calls super().validate(data). ReLU(Module) implements forward(x) as max(0, x) elementwise. Sequential(Module) stores a list of modules, overrides parameters() to return combined parameters from all children via super(), and chains forward through all modules.

docs.title: What Dunder Methods Are
docs.text:
Dunder methods — short for double underscore methods — are special methods with names like __str__, __len__, __add__. Python calls them automatically in response to built-in operations. You never call them directly; you define them, and Python invokes them when the right operation is applied to your object.

x = [1, 2, 3]
len(x)        # Python calls x.__len__()
str(x)        # Python calls x.__str__()
x + [4]       # Python calls x.__add__([4])
x[0]          # Python calls x.__getitem__(0)

Every built-in operation in Python maps to a dunder method. By implementing these methods on your own classes, your objects integrate seamlessly with Python syntax — they can be printed, compared, added, iterated, indexed, and used in with statements, just like built-in types.

This is called the Python data model. It is one of the most powerful design decisions in the language.

docs.title: __repr__ and __str__ — String Representation
docs.text: These are the two most universally needed dunder methods.

docs.title: __repr__ — Unambiguous, Developer-Facing
docs.text:
__repr__ should return a string that could recreate the object. It is called by repr(obj), by the REPL when you evaluate an expression, and as the fallback when __str__ is not defined.

Rule: repr is for developers. It should be precise and unambiguous.

docs.title: __str__ — Readable, User-Facing
docs.text:
__str__ is called by str(obj) and print(obj). It should return a human-readable representation.

Rule: str is for end users. It should be clean and readable.

class Vector:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Vector({self.x!r}, {self.y!r})"   # unambiguous, could recreate

    def __str__(self):
        return f"({self.x}, {self.y})"              # clean, readable

v = Vector(3, 4)

print(repr(v))    # Vector(3, 4)       — calls __repr__
print(str(v))     # (3, 4)             — calls __str__
print(v)          # (3, 4)             — print calls __str__

# In a list, repr is used for each element
print([v])        # [Vector(3, 4)]     — list uses repr on elements

Fallback rule: If __str__ is not defined, Python falls back to __repr__. If neither is defined, Python uses object.__repr__ which gives <__main__.Vector object at 0x...>.

Minimum requirement: Always define __repr__. It is the one dunder method every class should have.

docs.title: __len__ — The len() Protocol
docs.text:
class Playlist:
    def __init__(self, songs):
        self.songs = songs

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.songs)

p = Playlist(["Song A", "Song B", "Song C"])
print(len(p))    # 3

# __len__ also enables truthiness evaluation
print(bool(Playlist([])))       # False — len is 0
print(bool(Playlist(["x"])))    # True  — len is non-zero

Any object with __len__ automatically participates in Python's truthiness protocol: bool(obj) returns False if len(obj) == 0, True otherwise — unless __bool__ is also defined (which takes precedence).

docs.title: __eq__, __lt__, __le__, __gt__, __ge__, __ne__ — Comparison
docs.text:
By default, == checks object identity (same as is). Defining __eq__ changes what equality means for your class.

class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

    def __eq__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, Point):
            return NotImplemented
        return self.x == other.x and self.y == other.y

    def __lt__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, Point):
            return NotImplemented
        return (self.x**2 + self.y**2) < (other.x**2 + other.y**2)

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Point({self.x}, {self.y})"

p1 = Point(1, 2)
p2 = Point(1, 2)
p3 = Point(3, 4)

print(p1 == p2)    # True   — value equality via __eq__
print(p1 is p2)    # False  — different objects
print(p1 < p3)     # True   — p1 is closer to origin

NotImplemented vs NotImplementedError:

Return NotImplemented (not raise) when the comparison is not supported. Python then tries the reflected operation on the other operand. Returning NotImplemented is part of the protocol — it tells Python to keep trying. Raising NotImplementedError would crash instead.

@functools.total_ordering — Define only __eq__ and one comparison:

from functools import total_ordering

@total_ordering
class Temperature:
    def __init__(self, degrees):
        self.degrees = degrees

    def __eq__(self, other):
        return self.degrees == other.degrees

    def __lt__(self, other):
        return self.degrees < other.degrees

    # total_ordering fills in __le__, __gt__, __ge__ automatically

t1 = Temperature(100)
t2 = Temperature(200)
print(t1 <= t2)   # True
print(t1 > t2)    # False

Warning: Defining __eq__ makes your class unhashable by default (Python sets __hash__ = None). If you need objects to be usable in sets or as dict keys, also define __hash__.

def __hash__(self):
    return hash((self.x, self.y))

docs.title: __add__, __sub__, __mul__ — Arithmetic Operators
docs.text:
class Vector:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

    def __add__(self, other):
        return Vector(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y)

    def __sub__(self, other):
        return Vector(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y)

    def __mul__(self, scalar):
        return Vector(self.x * scalar, self.y * scalar)

    def __rmul__(self, scalar):
        return self.__mul__(scalar)    # handles scalar * vector

    def __neg__(self):
        return Vector(-self.x, -self.y)   # unary negation

    def __abs__(self):
        return (self.x**2 + self.y**2) ** 0.5

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Vector({self.x}, {self.y})"

v1 = Vector(1, 2)
v2 = Vector(3, 4)

print(v1 + v2)    # Vector(4, 6)
print(v2 - v1)    # Vector(2, 2)
print(v1 * 3)     # Vector(3, 6)
print(3 * v1)     # Vector(3, 6)   — uses __rmul__
print(-v1)        # Vector(-1, -2)
print(abs(v2))    # 5.0

Reflected operations (__radd__, __rmul__, etc.):

When a + b is evaluated, Python first tries a.__add__(b). If that returns NotImplemented or is not defined, Python tries b.__radd__(a). Defining __rmul__ on Vector makes 3 * vector work even though int.__mul__ does not know about vectors.

Augmented assignment (__iadd__, __imul__, etc.):

def __iadd__(self, other):
    self.x += other.x
    self.y += other.y
    return self    # must return self for in-place operations

v1 += v2    # calls v1.__iadd__(v2)

If __iadd__ is not defined, v1 += v2 falls back to v1 = v1.__add__(v2) — creates a new object. Define __iadd__ for true in-place modification.

docs.title: __getitem__, __setitem__, __delitem__ — Indexing Protocol
docs.text:
class Grid:
    def __init__(self, rows, cols):
        self.data = [[0] * cols for _ in range(rows)]

    def __getitem__(self, pos):
        row, col = pos
        return self.data[row][col]

    def __setitem__(self, pos, value):
        row, col = pos
        self.data[row][col] = value

    def __delitem__(self, pos):
        row, col = pos
        self.data[row][col] = 0   # reset to zero on delete

g = Grid(3, 3)
g[1, 2] = 99       # calls __setitem__((1, 2), 99)
print(g[1, 2])     # 99   — calls __getitem__((1, 2))
del g[1, 2]        # calls __delitem__((1, 2))
print(g[1, 2])     # 0

NumPy arrays use exactly this mechanism — arr[0, 1] calls arr.__getitem__((0, 1)). Pandas DataFrames use __getitem__ for column access: df["col"] is df.__getitem__("col").

docs.title: __contains__ — The in Operator
docs.text:
class WordList:
    def __init__(self, words):
        self.words = set(words)

    def __contains__(self, word):
        return word.lower() in self.words

wl = WordList(["Python", "Java", "C++"])
print("python" in wl)    # True  — calls __contains__
print("Ruby" in wl)      # False

Without __contains__, in falls back to iterating via __iter__ (or __getitem__). Defining __contains__ lets you provide O(1) lookup.

docs.title: __iter__ and __next__ — Iteration Protocol
docs.text:
Making your object iterable so it works in for loops, list(), zip(), etc.

class CountDown:
    def __init__(self, start):
        self.start = start
        self.current = start

    def __iter__(self):
        self.current = self.start    # reset on each iteration
        return self                  # return self as the iterator

    def __next__(self):
        if self.current <= 0:
            raise StopIteration      # signal that iteration is done
        value = self.current
        self.current -= 1
        return value

cd = CountDown(3)
for n in cd:
    print(n)
# 3
# 2
# 1

print(list(CountDown(5)))   # [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]

Iterable vs Iterator:

  • Iterable: has __iter__ returning an iterator. Can be looped over multiple times.
  • Iterator: has both __iter__ and __next__. Maintains its own position. Exhausted after one pass.

Combining both on the same class (as above) is the simplest pattern but means only one active iteration at a time. For concurrent iterations, return a separate iterator object from __iter__.

docs.title: __call__ — Making Objects Callable
docs.text:
class Multiplier:
    def __init__(self, factor):
        self.factor = factor

    def __call__(self, x):
        return x * self.factor

double = Multiplier(2)
triple = Multiplier(3)

print(double(5))     # 10   — calls double.__call__(5)
print(triple(5))     # 15
print(callable(double))   # True

An object with __call__ is callable — it can be used anywhere a function is expected. This is how PyTorch's nn.Module works: model(x) calls model.__call__(x), which internally calls model.forward(x) plus hooks.

# Simplified PyTorch pattern
class Module:
    def __call__(self, x):
        # runs pre-hooks
        result = self.forward(x)
        # runs post-hooks
        return result

    def forward(self, x):
        raise NotImplementedError

docs.title: __enter__ and __exit__ — Context Manager Protocol
docs.text:
class ManagedFile:
    def __init__(self, path, mode='r'):
        self.path = path
        self.mode = mode
        self.file = None

    def __enter__(self):
        self.file = open(self.path, self.mode)
        return self.file      # value bound to 'as' variable

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb):
        if self.file:
            self.file.close()
        return False          # False = don't suppress exceptions

with ManagedFile("data.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("hello")
# file is closed automatically, even if an exception occurs

__exit__ receives exception info if one was raised inside the with block. Returning True suppresses the exception; returning False (or None) lets it propagate.

See [[60. Writing custom context managers]] for full treatment.

docs.title: __bool__ — Truthiness
docs.text:
class Budget:
    def __init__(self, amount):
        self.amount = amount

    def __bool__(self):
        return self.amount > 0

b1 = Budget(100)
b2 = Budget(0)
b3 = Budget(-50)

print(bool(b1))   # True
print(bool(b2))   # False
print(bool(b3))   # False

if b1:
    print("Budget available")    # prints

if not b2:
    print("No budget")           # prints

Priority: __bool__ takes precedence over __len__. If both are defined, Python uses __bool__ for truthiness evaluation.

docs.title: __hash__ — Hashability
docs.text:
Objects that define __eq__ become unhashable by default (Python sets __hash__ = None). To use them in sets or as dict keys, define __hash__.

class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

    def __eq__(self, other):
        return (self.x, self.y) == (other.x, other.y)

    def __hash__(self):
        return hash((self.x, self.y))   # must be consistent with __eq__

p1 = Point(1, 2)
p2 = Point(1, 2)

print(p1 == p2)         # True
print(hash(p1) == hash(p2))   # True — equal objects must have equal hashes

seen = {p1}
print(p2 in seen)       # True — hash lookup works

Rule: If a == b then hash(a) == hash(b) must hold. The reverse need not be true (hash collisions are allowed).

docs.title: __del__ — Destructor
docs.text:
Called when the object is about to be garbage collected. Use sparingly — the timing is not guaranteed.

class Resource:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        print(f"{name} acquired")

    def __del__(self):
        print(f"{self.name} released")

r = Resource("DB Connection")   # DB Connection acquired
del r                            # DB Connection released

Do not rely on __del__ for critical cleanup — use context managers (__enter__/__exit__) instead. __del__ is not guaranteed to run at a specific time, and in CPython it may not run at all in some circular reference scenarios.

docs.title: Complete Reference Table
docs.text: Dunder Triggered by Notes __repr__ repr(obj), REPL, fallback for str Always define this __str__ str(obj), print(obj) Falls back to __repr__ __len__ len(obj) Enables truthiness via length __bool__ bool(obj), if obj: Takes precedence over __len__ __eq__ obj == other Disables __hash__ by default __ne__ obj != other Auto-derived from __eq__ in Python 3 __lt__ obj < other Use @total_ordering for full set __hash__ hash(obj), sets, dict keys Must pair with __eq__ __add__ obj + other Return new object __radd__ other + obj Reflected — when left operand fails __iadd__ obj += other In-place — must return self __mul__ obj * other __rmul__ other * obj __neg__ -obj Unary negation __abs__ abs(obj) __getitem__ obj[key] Enables indexing __setitem__ obj[key] = val __delitem__ del obj[key] __contains__ item in obj Fallback: iterate __iter__ iter(obj), for x in obj: Return iterator __next__ next(obj) Raise StopIteration when done __call__ obj(args) Makes object callable __enter__ with obj as x: Return value bound to x __exit__ End of with block Return True to suppress exceptions __del__ Garbage collection Timing not guaranteed __len__ len(obj) __getattr__ Attribute not found normally Fallback attribute access __setattr__ obj.attr = val Intercepts all attribute setting

docs.title: A Complete Class Using Multiple Dunders
docs.text:
from functools import total_ordering

@total_ordering
class Matrix:
    """2x2 matrix with full operator support."""

    def __init__(self, data):
        # data is a 2x2 list: [[a, b], [c, d]]
        self.data = [row[:] for row in data]

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Matrix({self.data!r})"

    def __str__(self):
        rows = [f"  {row}" for row in self.data]
        return "[\n" + "\n".join(rows) + "\n]"

    def __eq__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, Matrix):
            return NotImplemented
        return self.data == other.data

    def __lt__(self, other):
        return self._det() < other._det()

    def __add__(self, other):
        return Matrix([
            [self.data[i][j] + other.data[i][j] for j in range(2)]
            for i in range(2)
        ])

    def __mul__(self, other):
        if isinstance(other, (int, float)):
            return Matrix([[v * other for v in row] for row in self.data])
        # Matrix multiplication
        result = [[0, 0], [0, 0]]
        for i in range(2):
            for j in range(2):
                for k in range(2):
                    result[i][j] += self.data[i][k] * other.data[k][j]
        return Matrix(result)

    def __rmul__(self, scalar):
        return self.__mul__(scalar)

    def __len__(self):
        return 2    # number of rows

    def __getitem__(self, pos):
        row, col = pos
        return self.data[row][col]

    def __setitem__(self, pos, value):
        row, col = pos
        self.data[row][col] = value

    def __contains__(self, value):
        return any(value in row for row in self.data)

    def __iter__(self):
        return iter(self.data)

    def _det(self):
        return self.data[0][0]*self.data[1][1] - self.data[0][1]*self.data[1][0]

    def __hash__(self):
        return hash(tuple(tuple(row) for row in self.data))


m1 = Matrix([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
m2 = Matrix([[5, 6], [7, 8]])

print(m1 + m2)          # Matrix addition
print(m1 * 2)           # Scalar multiply
print(2 * m1)           # __rmul__
print(m1 * m2)          # Matrix multiply
print(m1[0, 1])         # 2  — __getitem__
print(3 in m1)          # True — __contains__
print(m1 < m2)          # True — by determinant
print(len(m1))          # 2
for row in m1:
    print(row)          # iterates rows

docs.title: Common Errors
docs.text:
# 1. __str__ returns non-string — TypeError
class Bad:
    def __str__(self):
        return 42    # TypeError: __str__ returned non-string

# 2. __eq__ without __hash__ — object becomes unhashable
class Point:
    def __eq__(self, other):
        return True

p = Point()
{p}   # TypeError: unhashable type: 'Point'
# Fix: define __hash__ alongside __eq__

# 3. __iadd__ not returning self
class Vec:
    def __iadd__(self, other):
        self.x += other.x
        # forgot: return self
        # v += other now sets v to None

# 4. Raising NotImplementedError instead of returning NotImplemented
class Num:
    def __add__(self, other):
        if not isinstance(other, Num):
            raise NotImplementedError   # wrong — crashes instead of trying __radd__
            return NotImplemented       # correct — tells Python to try reflected op

# 5. __next__ without StopIteration — infinite loop
class Counter:
    def __next__(self):
        self.n += 1
        return self.n   # never raises StopIteration — for loop never ends

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
E1. Build a Polynomial class representing ax² + bx + c with:

  • __repr__ returning "Polynomial(a, b, c)"
  • __str__ returning a human-readable form like "3x² + 2x + 1"
  • __add__ combining two polynomials
  • __call__ evaluating the polynomial at a given x value
  • __eq__ comparing coefficients

E2. Build a SortedList class backed by a Python list that:

  • Maintains sorted order on every insertion via __setitem__ and an insert method
  • Implements __len__, __getitem__, __contains__, __iter__, __repr__
  • Verify that for x in SortedList([3,1,2]) yields 1, 2, 3

E3. Implement a Fraction class with full arithmetic:

  • __add__, __sub__, __mul__, __truediv__
  • __eq__, __lt__ (reduce to common denominator to compare)
  • __repr__ returning "3/4"
  • __float__ returning the decimal value
  • Use math.gcd to reduce fractions to lowest terms after each operation

E4. Create a CallCounter decorator class using __call__ and __init__:

@CallCounter
def add(x, y):
    return x + y

add(1, 2)
add(3, 4)
print(add.count)   # 2

E5 (ML). Implement a Tensor class (no NumPy) that supports:

  • __add__, __mul__ (elementwise, two tensors of same shape)
  • __rmul__ (scalar × tensor)
  • __getitem__ and __setitem__ (flat index)
  • __len__ (number of elements)
  • __repr__ showing shape and data
  • __iter__ yielding elements
