docs.title: 40. try / except / else / finally
docs.text: "An exception is not an error in the pejorative sense. It is a signal — a formal notification that the normal flow of execution cannot continue. The question is not whether to handle it, but where, and how precisely."

docs.title: The Core Idea
docs.text:
Python's exception handling is a structured control flow mechanism. When something goes wrong inside a try block, Python unwinds the call stack looking for a matching except clause. If it finds one, execution transfers there. If it doesn't, the program terminates with a traceback.

The full four-clause structure:

try:
    # code that might raise an exception
except SomeException:
    # runs if SomeException (or a subclass) was raised in try
else:
    # runs only if NO exception was raised in try
finally:
    # runs ALWAYS — exception or not, return or not

Each clause has a precise, non-overlapping role. The confusion comes from not understanding else and finally. We will fix that.

docs.title: How Python Raises and Propagates Exceptions
docs.text:
Before handling, understand the mechanism.

When an exception is raised:

  1. Python creates an exception object (an instance of some Exception subclass)
  2. Normal execution stops immediately at that line
  3. Python walks up the call stack frame by frame, looking for a matching except
  4. If found — execution transfers to that handler
  5. If not found — the exception is unhandled; Python prints a traceback and exits
def c():
    raise ValueError("something went wrong")

def b():
    c()           # exception propagates up from c()

def a():
    b()           # exception propagates up from b()

try:
    a()           # caught here
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"Caught: {e}")

The exception does not stop at c() — it bubbles up through b(), through a(), until a handler is found. This is stack unwinding.

docs.title: try / except — The Minimum
docs.text:
try:
    result = int("not a number")
except ValueError:
    print("conversion failed")

Catching the exception object:

try:
    result = int("abc")
except ValueError as e:
    print(type(e))    # <class 'ValueError'>
    print(e)          # invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'
    print(e.args)     # ('invalid literal for int() with base 10: \'abc\'',)

The as e binding gives you the exception instance. e.args is always a tuple of the arguments passed to the exception constructor.

docs.title: Catching Multiple Exception Types
docs.text:
Multiple except clauses — checked in order, first match wins:

try:
    value = data[key]
except KeyError:
    print("key not found")
except TypeError:
    print("data is not subscriptable")

Catching multiple types in one clause:

try:
    result = int(user_input) / divisor
except (ValueError, ZeroDivisionError) as e:
    print(f"Input error: {e}")

Catching any exception — use sparingly:

try:
    risky_operation()
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Unexpected error: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")

Do not write except: with no type. This catches everything including KeyboardInterrupt, SystemExit, and GeneratorExit — signals that are meant to propagate. Always catch at least Exception.

# BAD — swallows Ctrl+C, sys.exit(), everything
try:
    ...
except:
    pass

# CORRECT — lets system signals through
try:
    ...
except Exception:
    pass

docs.title: The Exception Hierarchy
docs.text:
The except clause matches the named type and all its subclasses. This is why catching order matters.

BaseException
├── SystemExit
├── KeyboardInterrupt
├── GeneratorExit
└── Exception
    ├── ArithmeticError
    │   ├── ZeroDivisionError
    │   ├── OverflowError
    │   └── FloatingPointError
    ├── LookupError
    │   ├── IndexError
    │   └── KeyError
    ├── ValueError
    ├── TypeError
    ├── AttributeError
    ├── NameError
    ├── OSError
    │   ├── FileNotFoundError
    │   ├── PermissionError
    │   └── TimeoutError
    ├── RuntimeError
    ├── StopIteration
    └── ... (many more)

Catch more specific exceptions first:

# BAD — LookupError catches both IndexError and KeyError
# The specific clauses below it are unreachable
try:
    ...
except LookupError:
    ...
except IndexError:   # DEAD CODE — never reached
    ...

# CORRECT — specific first, general last
try:
    ...
except IndexError:
    ...
except KeyError:
    ...
except LookupError:   # catches anything else in the LookupError family
    ...

docs.title: else — The Most Misunderstood Clause
docs.text:
The else clause runs only if the try block completed without raising any exception.

try:
    result = int(user_input)
except ValueError:
    print("Not a valid integer")
else:
    print(f"Got: {result}")   # only runs if int() succeeded

Why else exists — the precise semantic distinction:

# Without else — ambiguous
try:
    result = int(user_input)
    print(f"Got: {result}")   # did this fail, or did int() fail?
except ValueError:
    print("error")

# With else — unambiguous
try:
    result = int(user_input)  # only this is "protected"
except ValueError:
    print("error")
else:
    print(f"Got: {result}")   # this runs only on success

The else clause narrows the scope of what the except is guarding. Code in else is not protected by the except above it — if else raises, that exception propagates normally.

try:
    f = open("data.txt")
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("file missing")
else:
    data = f.read()   # if THIS raises, FileNotFoundError above does NOT catch it
    f.close()

This is the correct design — you only want FileNotFoundError to guard the open() call, not everything that follows.

docs.title: finally — The Guarantee
docs.text:
The finally clause runs unconditionally — whether an exception was raised or not, whether it was caught or not, even if there is a return statement inside try.

try:
    result = 10 / 0
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("division by zero")
finally:
    print("this always runs")

# Output:
# division by zero
# this always runs

finally runs even when an exception is NOT caught:

try:
    raise RuntimeError("uncaught")
finally:
    print("cleanup")   # prints before the program crashes

# Output:
# cleanup
# Traceback (most recent call last):
#   ...
# RuntimeError: uncaught

finally runs even through a return:

def f():
    try:
        return 1
    finally:
        print("finally runs")   # runs before the return

f()
# Output: finally runs
# Returns: 1

finally can override a return:

def f():
    try:
        return 1
    finally:
        return 2   # overrides the return 1

print(f())   # 2

This is almost always unintentional. Avoid return, break, or continue inside finally — they suppress exceptions silently.

docs.title: Full Four-Clause Flow — Execution Map
docs.text:
Enter try block
    │
    ├── No exception raised
    │       │
    │       ├── except: SKIPPED
    │       ├── else:   RUNS
    │       └── finally: RUNS
    │
    └── Exception raised
            │
            ├── Matching except found
            │       │
            │       ├── except: RUNS
            │       ├── else:   SKIPPED
            │       └── finally: RUNS
            │
            └── No matching except
                    │
                    ├── except: SKIPPED
                    ├── else:   SKIPPED
                    ├── finally: RUNS
                    └── Exception propagates up the call stack

docs.title: Resource Management — The Primary Use Case for finally
docs.text:
The canonical pattern: acquire a resource in try, release it in finally.

f = open("data.txt")
try:
    data = f.read()
    process(data)
except OSError as e:
    print(f"IO error: {e}")
finally:
    f.close()   # guaranteed to run even if process() raises

This pattern is so common that Python formalised it into the context manager protocol (with statement — see note [[46. Context manager]]). The with statement desugars to exactly this try/finally structure.

# This:
with open("data.txt") as f:
    data = f.read()

# Is equivalent to:
f = open("data.txt")
try:
    data = f.read()
finally:
    f.close()

Whenever you see a resource that must be released — file handles, database connections, network sockets, locks, GPU memory — finally is the mechanism. with is the ergonomic wrapper.

docs.title: Re-raising Exceptions
docs.text:
Sometimes you want to handle an exception partially and then let it continue propagating.

Bare raise — re-raises the current exception:

try:
    result = int(user_input)
except ValueError as e:
    log.error(f"Bad input: {e}")   # log it
    raise                           # re-raise unchanged

Raise a different exception — exception chaining:

try:
    data = json.loads(raw)
except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
    raise ValueError(f"Invalid config format") from e

The from e attaches the original exception as __cause__, preserving the full chain in tracebacks. Without from e, Python still chains automatically via __context__, but from makes it explicit and semantically intentional.

ValueError: Invalid config format

The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception:
  ...
json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: ...

Suppress the chain — from None:

try:
    value = d[key]
except KeyError:
    raise ValueError(f"Unknown key: {key}") from None
# Traceback shows only ValueError, not the KeyError

docs.title: Nested try Blocks
docs.text:
try blocks nest. Inner handlers get first chance; unhandled exceptions propagate to outer handlers.

try:
    try:
        result = int("abc")
    except ValueError:
        print("inner caught ValueError")
        raise RuntimeError("converted") from None
except RuntimeError as e:
    print(f"outer caught: {e}")

# Output:
# inner caught ValueError
# outer caught: converted

docs.title: Pattern 1 — Try/Except/Else for Clean Success Path
docs.text:
def load_config(path):
    try:
        f = open(path)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        return default_config()
    else:
        with f:
            return json.load(f)

docs.title: Pattern 2 — Retry Logic
docs.text:
import time

def fetch_with_retry(url, retries=3, delay=1.0):
    for attempt in range(retries):
        try:
            return requests.get(url, timeout=5)
        except requests.Timeout:
            if attempt == retries - 1:
                raise
            time.sleep(delay)

docs.title: Pattern 3 — Safe Conversion
docs.text:
def safe_int(value, default=None):
    try:
        return int(value)
    except (ValueError, TypeError):
        return default

safe_int("42")         # 42
safe_int("abc")        # None
safe_int(None, -1)     # -1

docs.title: Pattern 4 — Transaction-Style Commit/Rollback
docs.text:
def execute_transaction(conn, queries):
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    try:
        for q in queries:
            cursor.execute(q)
    except Exception:
        conn.rollback()
        raise
    else:
        conn.commit()   # only commit if everything succeeded
    finally:
        cursor.close()  # always release

This is the four-clause pattern at its most expressive:

  • try — attempt the work
  • except — rollback on failure
  • else — commit on success
  • finally — always release resources

docs.title: What Not to Do
docs.text:
Swallowing exceptions silently:

# BAD — you will never know why your program is wrong
try:
    train_model()
except Exception:
    pass

Using exceptions as control flow for predictable cases:

# BAD — LBYL (Look Before You Leap) is clearer here
try:
    value = d[key]
except KeyError:
    value = 0

# BETTER for this case
value = d.get(key, 0)

Python culture is EAFP (Easier to Ask Forgiveness than Permission) — use exceptions for exceptional situations, not as an if/else substitute for routine cases. However, EAFP is not a license to ignore exceptions. It means: try the operation, handle failure cleanly.

Catching too broadly:

# BAD — catches MemoryError, RecursionError, everything
try:
    complex_operation()
except Exception:
    print("something went wrong")   # useless diagnostic

# BETTER — catch what you can actually handle
try:
    complex_operation()
except (ValueError, KeyError) as e:
    handle_input_error(e)
except OSError as e:
    handle_io_error(e)

docs.title: Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: Exception handling is not boilerplate in ML — it is architecture. The difference between a research script and production ML code is largely in how exceptions are handled.

docs.title: 1. Training Loop Robustness
docs.text:
for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    for batch_idx, (X, y) in enumerate(dataloader):
        try:
            optimizer.zero_grad()
            outputs = model(X)
            loss = criterion(outputs, y)
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()
        except RuntimeError as e:
            if "out of memory" in str(e):
                # OOM — clear cache and skip this batch
                torch.cuda.empty_cache()
                print(f"OOM at batch {batch_idx}, skipping")
                continue
            raise   # re-raise anything else
        else:
            # Only log if no exception
            writer.add_scalar("loss", loss.item(), global_step)

torch.cuda.OutOfMemoryError (a subclass of RuntimeError) is one of the most common exceptions in deep learning. Catching it, clearing GPU memory, and continuing is standard practice.

docs.title: 2. Data Loading — Corrupt Samples
docs.text:
class RobustDataset(torch.utils.data.Dataset):
    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        try:
            return self.load_sample(idx)
        except (OSError, PIL.UnidentifiedImageError) as e:
            # Corrupt image — return a neighbouring sample
            print(f"Corrupt sample at {idx}: {e}")
            return self.__getitem__((idx + 1) % len(self))
        finally:
            self.access_log.append(idx)   # always log access

docs.title: 3. Model Serving — Never Crash on Bad Input
docs.text:
@app.route("/predict", methods=["POST"])
def predict():
    try:
        data = request.json
        tensor = preprocess(data)
    except (KeyError, TypeError) as e:
        return {"error": f"Invalid input: {e}"}, 400
    except ValueError as e:
        return {"error": f"Preprocessing failed: {e}"}, 422

    try:
        with torch.no_grad():
            output = model(tensor)
    except Exception as e:
        log.exception("Inference failed")
        return {"error": "Internal model error"}, 500

    else:
        return {"prediction": output.tolist()}, 200

The else clause here is exactly right: return the result only if no exception occurred at inference time. The two try blocks separate input validation errors (client's fault, 4xx) from inference errors (server's fault, 5xx).

docs.title: 4. Checkpoint Saving — finally as Guarantee
docs.text:
def train_with_checkpoint(model, config):
    checkpoint_saved = False
    try:
        train(model, config)
        checkpoint_saved = True
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        print("Training interrupted — saving checkpoint")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Training failed: {e}")
        raise
    finally:
        if not checkpoint_saved:
            # Attempt to save even on failure
            try:
                save_checkpoint(model, "emergency_checkpoint.pt")
            except Exception:
                print("Could not save emergency checkpoint")

This is a nested try/finally inside finally — valid and sometimes necessary when cleanup itself can fail.

docs.title: 5. NaN/Inf Detection During Training
docs.text:
def safe_loss_step(loss):
    try:
        if not torch.isfinite(loss):
            raise ValueError(f"Non-finite loss: {loss.item()}")
        loss.backward()
    except ValueError as e:
        print(f"Loss explosion detected: {e}")
        # Could trigger learning rate reduction, gradient clipping, etc.
        raise

docs.title: The else Clause — Why It Is Underused and Undervalued
docs.text:
A significant fraction of Python programmers never use else in try statements. The reason is that the following two patterns appear equivalent:

# Pattern A — no else
try:
    result = compute()
    use(result)
except SomeError:
    handle()

# Pattern B — with else
try:
    result = compute()
except SomeError:
    handle()
else:
    use(result)

They are not equivalent. In Pattern A, if use(result) raises SomeError, the except clause catches it — silently merging two different failure modes. In Pattern B, only compute() is guarded. A SomeError from use(result) propagates up.

The else clause is a precision tool. Use it whenever you want to narrowly scope what the except is guarding.

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text:
Clause When it runs Typical use try Always (it's the attempt) The code that might fail except Only if a matching exception was raised Handle the failure else Only if NO exception was raised Code that belongs after success finally Always, unconditionally Resource cleanup, logging

The four rules:

  1. except — catch the most specific exception you can actually handle
  2. else — use it to narrow the scope of what your except guards
  3. finally — the only place to put cleanup that must always run
  4. Never swallow exceptions silently — if you catch it, handle it or re-raise it

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1. Without running it, trace the output:

def f():
    try:
        return "try"
    except:
        return "except"
    else:
        return "else"
    finally:
        print("finally")

print(f())

Exercise 2. Why does the following code have a subtle bug? Fix it using else.

def parse_and_double(s):
    try:
        n = int(s)
        return n * 2
    except ValueError:
        return None

Hint: what if n * 2 raised something unexpected?

Exercise 3. Implement safe_divide(a, b) that returns a / b, returns 0 on ZeroDivisionError, and always prints "operation attempted" regardless of outcome.

Exercise 4. Write a function load_json_safe(path) that:

  • Returns the parsed JSON on success
  • Returns None if the file doesn't exist
  • Returns None if the content is not valid JSON
  • Always prints how many bytes were read (even on failure, print 0)
  • Uses all four clauses

Exercise 5 (theoretical). In the transaction pattern (commit/rollback), explain precisely why the else clause for commit and the except clause for rollback cannot be merged into a single try/except without the else.

docs.title: 41. Common Exceptions (ValueError, TypeError, IndexError, KeyError etc.)
docs.text: "An exception is not an error in the moral sense. It is the runtime asserting a mathematical precondition has been violated. Read it as a proof that your assumptions were wrong."

docs.title: The Exception Hierarchy — Read This First
docs.text:
Python exceptions are not a flat list. They form an inheritance tree. Understanding the tree tells you which except clauses catch which exceptions — and why catching Exception is almost always too broad.

BaseException
├── SystemExit              ← raised by sys.exit()
├── KeyboardInterrupt       ← Ctrl+C
├── GeneratorExit           ← generator .close() called
└── Exception               ← everything you normally handle
    ├── ArithmeticError
    │   ├── ZeroDivisionError
    │   ├── OverflowError
    │   └── FloatingPointError
    ├── LookupError         ← the "wrong key/index" superclass
    │   ├── IndexError
    │   └── KeyError
    ├── TypeError
    ├── ValueError
    │   └── UnicodeError
    │       ├── UnicodeDecodeError
    │       └── UnicodeEncodeError
    ├── AttributeError
    ├── NameError
    │   └── UnboundLocalError
    ├── OSError             ← also aliased as IOError, EnvironmentError
    │   ├── FileNotFoundError
    │   ├── PermissionError
    │   └── TimeoutError
    ├── RuntimeError
    │   └── RecursionError
    ├── StopIteration
    ├── MemoryError
    └── NotImplementedError

Critical design rule: except LookupError catches both IndexError and KeyError. except Exception catches almost everything. These are not equivalent choices — catch the most specific exception you can name.

docs.title: Reading an Exception
docs.text:
Before cataloguing individual exceptions, know how to read a traceback. Every piece of it is information.

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "train.py", line 47, in load_batch
    x = dataset[idx]
  File "dataset.py", line 23, in __getitem__
    return self.samples[idx]
IndexError: list index out of range

Reading order: bottom up. The last line is the actual error. The stack frames above it, from bottom to top, trace the call path from the site of the exception back to where your code entered. load_batch called __getitem__, which raised IndexError at self.samples[idx]. The bug is in load_batch passing an out-of-range idx.

docs.title: ValueError
docs.text:
Raised when: an operation receives an argument of the correct type but an invalid value for that type.

The type is right. The content is wrong.

int("hello")          # ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'hello'
int("3.14")           # ValueError — must do int(float("3.14"))
math.sqrt(-1)         # ValueError: math domain error
[1, 2, 3].index(99)   # ValueError: 99 is not in list
"abc".index("z")      # ValueError: substring not found

import numpy as np
np.array([1, 2, 3]).reshape(2, 2)   # ValueError: cannot reshape array of size 3 into shape (2,2)

The distinction — ValueError vs TypeError:

int(3.14)    # int — valid, truncates to 3. The type (float) is acceptable.
int("3.14")  # ValueError — the type (str) is acceptable for int(), but "3.14" is not a valid integer literal
int([1, 2])  # TypeError — the type (list) is not acceptable at all for int()

Where you will raise it yourself:

def set_learning_rate(lr):
    if lr <= 0 or lr >= 1:
        raise ValueError(f"Learning rate must be in (0, 1), got {lr}")
    self.lr = lr

docs.title: TypeError
docs.text:
Raised when: an operation is applied to an object of the wrong type entirely.

The operation does not know what to do with that type.

"hello" + 5           # TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
len(42)               # TypeError: object of type 'int' has no len()
1 + "1"               # TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'

def f(a, b): return a + b
f(1, 2, 3)            # TypeError: f() takes 2 positional arguments but 3 were given
f(1)                  # TypeError: f() missing 1 required positional argument: 'b'

None + 1              # TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'NoneType' and 'int'

Forgetting to call a function:

import math

math.sqrt            # This is the function object, not the result
type(math.sqrt)      # <class 'builtin_function_or_method'>

result = math.sqrt   # result is now the function itself, not a number
result + 1           # TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'builtin_function_or_method' and 'int'

# Correct:
result = math.sqrt(4)   # 2.0

This exact mistake appears when wiring up Keras/PyTorch callbacks — passing relu instead of relu().

docs.title: IndexError
docs.text:
Raised when: a sequence (list, tuple, string) is accessed with an index that is outside its valid range.

a = [10, 20, 30]

a[0]     # 10  — valid
a[2]     # 30  — valid
a[3]     # IndexError: list index out of range
a[-1]    # 30  — valid (negative indexing)
a[-4]    # IndexError: list index out of range

s = "hello"
s[10]    # IndexError: string index out of range

Off-by-one — the canonical source:

a = [10, 20, 30]    # length 3, valid indices: 0, 1, 2

for i in range(len(a) + 1):   # BUG: range goes 0, 1, 2, 3
    print(a[i])                # IndexError on i=3

Empty list — the silent ambush:

results = []
best = results[0]    # IndexError: list index out of range
# You assumed results was non-empty. It was not.

Slicing never raises IndexError:

a = [1, 2, 3]
a[10:20]    # []  — silently returns empty list
a[:100]     # [1, 2, 3]  — clamped to length

This asymmetry is intentional but trips people up. a[10] raises; a[10:11] returns [].

docs.title: KeyError
docs.text:
Raised when: a dictionary is accessed with a key that does not exist.

d = {"name": "Alice", "age": 30}

d["name"]     # "Alice"  — exists
d["email"]    # KeyError: 'email'
d[0]          # KeyError: 0  — 0 is not a key here

Safe alternatives:

d = {"name": "Alice"}

# .get() — returns None if key absent, or a default
d.get("email")             # None
d.get("email", "unknown")  # "unknown"

# Membership test before access
if "email" in d:
    print(d["email"])

# defaultdict — supplies a default on first access
from collections import defaultdict
counts = defaultdict(int)
counts["unseen_key"]    # 0, not KeyError
counts["unseen_key"] += 1

KeyError in ML — a common pattern:

# Vocabulary lookup — the unknown word problem
vocab = {"cat": 0, "dog": 1, "fish": 2}
token = "elephant"

vocab[token]              # KeyError: 'elephant'
vocab.get(token, vocab["<UNK>"])   # correct pattern with unknown token

docs.title: AttributeError
docs.text:
Raised when: you access an attribute or call a method that does not exist on an object.

x = 42
x.append(1)      # AttributeError: 'int' object has no attribute 'append'

import numpy as np
arr = np.array([1, 2, 3])
arr.push(4)      # AttributeError: 'numpy.ndarray' object has no attribute 'push'
                 # (NumPy uses np.append, not .push)

The None trap — the most common AttributeError in ML code:

def get_model():
    # forgot to return something
    model = build_model()
    train(model)
    # no return statement

model = get_model()   # model is None
model.predict(X)      # AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'predict'

Whenever you see AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute '...', the real question is: why did the variable get assigned None? A missing return in a function is the most common answer.

Typo in method name:

"hello".uper()    # AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'uper'
"hello".upper()   # 'HELLO'  — correct

docs.title: NameError
docs.text:
Raised when: a name (variable, function) is used before it has been defined in the current scope.

print(x)    # NameError: name 'x' is not defined

def f():
    return result    # NameError if result not defined in scope

# Common: running cells out of order in Jupyter
model.fit(X, y)   # NameError: name 'model' is not defined
                  # because the cell that defines model hasn't been run yet

UnboundLocalError — a subtle subcase:

Python determines at compile time whether a name is local or global. If you assign to a name anywhere in a function, it is local for the entire function — even before the assignment.

x = 10

def f():
    print(x)   # UnboundLocalError: local variable 'x' referenced before assignment
    x = 20     # this assignment makes x local for the whole function

f()

This is not a runtime check. Python's bytecode compiler sees the assignment on line 3 and marks x as a local variable for all of f. The print then tries to read an unbound local.

docs.title: ZeroDivisionError
docs.text:
Raised when: division or modulo by zero.

10 / 0      # ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
10 // 0     # ZeroDivisionError: integer division or modulo by zero
10 % 0      # ZeroDivisionError: integer division or modulo by zero

Float division by zero does not raise in NumPy:

import numpy as np
np.float64(1.0) / np.float64(0.0)   # inf, with RuntimeWarning
np.float64(0.0) / np.float64(0.0)   # nan, with RuntimeWarning

This is IEEE 754 behaviour. NumPy follows the standard; Python's built-in / does not. This matters when you are computing log-losses or normalisation factors.

The divide-by-zero in normalisation:

def softmax(x):
    exp_x = np.exp(x - x.max())
    return exp_x / exp_x.sum()    # fine as long as input is not all -inf

def normalize(x):
    norm = np.linalg.norm(x)
    if norm == 0:
        return x                  # or raise, depending on contract
    return x / norm

docs.title: StopIteration
docs.text:
Raised when: next() is called on an exhausted iterator.

it = iter([1, 2, 3])

next(it)    # 1
next(it)    # 2
next(it)    # 3
next(it)    # StopIteration

# Safe pattern — provide a default
next(it, None)   # None, not an exception

StopIteration is the protocol by which Python's for loop knows when to stop. The loop calls next() internally and catches StopIteration to exit cleanly. You will rarely see it in normal code; when you do, it almost always means you tried to advance an iterator manually beyond its end.

Inside generators — important subtlety:

In Python 3.7+, if StopIteration propagates out of a generator function, it becomes RuntimeError: generator raised StopIteration. This was a deliberate language change (PEP 479). If you are manually raising StopIteration inside a generator to signal completion, use return instead.

docs.title: FileNotFoundError
docs.text:
Raised when: a file or directory operation is attempted on a path that does not exist.

open("nonexistent.txt")    # FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'nonexistent.txt'

FileNotFoundError is a subclass of OSError. You can catch either, but catching the specific subclass is clearer intent.

try:
    with open("config.json") as f:
        config = json.load(f)
except FileNotFoundError:
    config = {}    # use defaults if config file is absent

docs.title: RecursionError
docs.text:
Raised when: the call stack exceeds Python's recursion limit (default: 1000 frames).

def f():
    return f()

f()    # RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded

The missing base case:

# BUG — base case never triggers for negative n
def factorial(n):
    if n == 0:
        return 1
    return n * factorial(n - 1)

factorial(-1)    # RecursionError — recurse forever toward -∞

Checking and adjusting the limit:

import sys
sys.getrecursionlimit()       # 1000
sys.setrecursionlimit(5000)   # increase — use with caution

In Python, deep recursion on large inputs is a design smell. For production ML code — traversing deep trees, processing large graphs — convert to explicit stack-based iteration.

docs.title: MemoryError
docs.text:
Raised when: an allocation fails because there is not enough memory.

x = [0] * (10 ** 12)    # MemoryError — allocating 8 TB is not going to work

In ML, this appears when:

  • Loading a dataset that does not fit in RAM
  • Allocating a full attention matrix for a very long sequence (\(O(n^2)\) space)
  • Creating an intermediate tensor that is larger than GPU VRAM
# Bad: materialises the entire N×N attention matrix in memory
scores = Q @ K.T          # shape (N, N)

# Better for long sequences: chunked or sparse attention

MemoryError is unrecoverable in most practical scenarios. The fix is architectural — use data generators, batching, memory-mapped files, or gradient checkpointing.

docs.title: NotImplementedError
docs.text:
Raised when: an abstract method or intentionally unfinished functionality is called.

class BaseModel:
    def forward(self, x):
        raise NotImplementedError("Subclasses must implement forward()")

class LinearModel(BaseModel):
    pass

m = LinearModel()
m.forward(x)    # NotImplementedError: Subclasses must implement forward()

This is not an error condition in the conventional sense — it is a design contract. In PyTorch, nn.Module uses exactly this pattern for forward(). In Python 3.4+, you can also use abc.abstractmethod which enforces the contract at instantiation time rather than at call time.

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class BaseModel(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def forward(self, x):
        pass

m = BaseModel()    # TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class — caught earlier

docs.title: Exception Relationships: A Decision Table
docs.text:
When you catch an exception, which class do you name?

What went wrong Exception to catch Wrong value for a valid type ValueError Wrong type entirely TypeError List/string index out of range IndexError Dict key does not exist KeyError Either index or key problem LookupError Attribute or method missing AttributeError Name not defined in scope NameError Division by zero ZeroDivisionError Iterator exhausted StopIteration File not found FileNotFoundError Any OS/file-system error OSError Recursion too deep RecursionError Out of memory MemoryError Abstract method not implemented NotImplementedError Anything (catch-all, use sparingly) Exception

docs.title: The Right Way to Catch Multiple Exceptions
docs.text:
# Catch multiple specific exceptions — different handlers
try:
    result = d[key] / count
except KeyError:
    print(f"Key {key!r} not in dict")
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("count is zero")

# Catch multiple exceptions — same handler
try:
    result = d[key] / count
except (KeyError, ZeroDivisionError) as e:
    print(f"Computation failed: {e}")

# DON'T catch Exception unless you have a very good reason
try:
    ...
except Exception:
    pass    # silently swallowing errors — this hides bugs

docs.title: The __class__.__mro__ Trap
docs.text:
Because exceptions inherit, you must order except clauses from most specific to most general. Python checks them in order and takes the first match.

# WRONG — IndexError will never be reached; LookupError catches it first
try:
    x = lst[10]
except LookupError:
    print("lookup failed")
except IndexError:            # dead code — IndexError is a LookupError
    print("index out of range")

# CORRECT
try:
    x = lst[10]
except IndexError:
    print("index out of range")
except LookupError:
    print("some other lookup error")

docs.title: Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: Exceptions in ML code are not edge cases — they are the primary debugging mechanism. Understanding which exception maps to which failure mode saves hours.

docs.title: ValueError in ML — shape mismatches
docs.text:
Shape errors in NumPy and PyTorch surface as ValueError. This is the single most common exception you will see when writing neural network code.

import numpy as np

A = np.ones((3, 4))
B = np.ones((5, 4))

A @ B              # ValueError: matmul: Input operand 1 has a mismatch in its core dimension 0
                   # Expected (4,), got (5,) — the inner dimensions do not match

# In PyTorch, the same operation raises RuntimeError with a shape message
# but the cause is identical: you are trying to multiply incompatible matrices

The weight matrix shape convention in ML:

Linear layer: \(y = Wx + b\) where \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{out} \times d_{in}}\), \(x \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{in}}\)

# If you get the shapes backwards:
W = np.random.randn(3, 5)   # 3 output features, 5 input features
x = np.random.randn(3)      # 3-dimensional input — should be 5-dimensional

W @ x    # ValueError — 5 ≠ 3

docs.title: KeyError — vocabulary and configuration
docs.text:
# Word embedding lookup
vocab = {"the": 0, "cat": 1, "sat": 2}
embedding_matrix = np.random.randn(3, 64)

def embed(word):
    return embedding_matrix[vocab[word]]    # KeyError if word not in vocab

embed("elephant")    # KeyError: 'elephant'

# Correct: handle unknown tokens
UNK_IDX = vocab.get("<UNK>", 0)
def embed_safe(word):
    return embedding_matrix[vocab.get(word, UNK_IDX)]

docs.title: IndexError — batch indexing and dataset access
docs.text:
class Dataset:
    def __init__(self, samples):
        self.samples = samples

    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        return self.samples[idx]    # IndexError if idx >= len(samples)

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.samples)

The DataLoader calls __getitem__ with indices from a sampler. If your sampler generates indices without respecting len(dataset), you get IndexError. This is a real failure mode in custom samplers.

docs.title: AttributeError — the unbuilt model
docs.text:
class Trainer:
    def __init__(self):
        self.model = None    # not yet built

    def train(self, X, y):
        self.model.fit(X, y)    # AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'fit'
                                # build() was never called

docs.title: RuntimeError in PyTorch — the GPU exception family
docs.text:
PyTorch uses RuntimeError for most of its internal errors, including:

RuntimeError: Expected all tensors to be on the same device
RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory
RuntimeError: Expected input batch_size (32) to match target batch_size (64)

These are not in Python's standard library, but they follow the same principle: a precondition was violated. Read the message, check the shapes and devices.

docs.title: Exceptions as a debugging strategy
docs.text:
In a training loop, wrapping the entire loop in a broad except catches everything but tells you nothing. The discipline is:

for epoch in range(epochs):
    for batch_idx, (X, y) in enumerate(dataloader):
        try:
            loss = train_step(X, y)
        except ValueError as e:
            print(f"Shape error at batch {batch_idx}: {e}")
            print(f"X shape: {X.shape}, y shape: {y.shape}")
            raise   # re-raise after logging — don't swallow

Catch specifically, log the context, then re-raise. Swallowing exceptions in ML training loops is how bugs become silent convergence failures that waste GPU hours.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1. Without running it, predict the exact exception and message:

d = {"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5]}
d["c"][0]

Then modify the line to return 0 instead of raising.

Exercise 2. This function has two bugs. Identify the exception each raises and fix both:

def normalise(v):
    total = sum(v)
    return [x / total for x in v]

normalise([])
normalise([0, 0, 0])

Exercise 3. Explain why this raises UnboundLocalError and not NameError, and fix it without using global:

count = 0
def increment():
    count += 1
    return count

Exercise 4. Write a safe_lookup(matrix, i, j) function that returns None instead of raising for both IndexError (row or column out of range) and TypeError (non-integer index). Handle both in a single except clause.

Exercise 5 (ML). A PyTorch training loop crashes with:

RuntimeError: Expected all tensors to be on the same device, but found at least two devices, cuda:0 and cpu!

This is not in Python's exception hierarchy, but the same diagnostic principle applies. What is the precondition that was violated? What two things do you check first?

docs.title: 42. Raising Exceptions (raise)
docs.text: "Raising an exception is an assertion. It says: this function's contract has been violated, and I refuse to proceed on false premises. A function that silently accepts bad input is not being kind — it is deferring a lie."

docs.title: The Core Idea
docs.text:
A raise statement does one thing: it interrupts normal control flow and hands a signal — an exception object — up the call stack until something catches it or the program terminates.

This is not error-handling. That is try/except. raise is the other side: deliberately signalling that a precondition has been violated.

The mental model: every function has an implicit contract.

precondition  →  function executes  →  postcondition

When the precondition is violated, the function should not silently proceed toward a wrong postcondition. It should raise — loudly, early, with a precise message — and let the caller decide what to do.

docs.title: Form 1 — Raise a new exception
docs.text:
raise ExceptionType("message")

This is the standard form. Instantiate an exception class with a message string and raise it.

def sqrt(x):
    if x < 0:
        raise ValueError(f"sqrt requires a non-negative argument, got {x}")
    return x ** 0.5

docs.title: Form 2 — Re-raise the current exception
docs.text:
raise

Used inside an except block. Re-raises the exception that is currently being handled, preserving its original traceback.

try:
    result = risky_operation()
except ValueError as e:
    log_error(e)    # do something — log, record, alert
    raise           # then let it propagate unchanged

docs.title: Form 3 — Raise with explicit cause (raise ... from)
docs.text:
raise NewException("message") from original_exception

Chains exceptions explicitly. The new exception carries a __cause__ attribute pointing to the original. The traceback displays both.

try:
    value = int(user_input)
except ValueError as e:
    raise TypeError(f"Expected an integer string, got {user_input!r}") from e

Output:

ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'hello'

The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception:

TypeError: Expected an integer string, got 'hello'

docs.title: Raise is Not return
docs.text:
A raised exception does not return a value. It unwinds the call stack frame by frame, looking for an except clause that matches. If none is found, the program terminates and prints the traceback.

f() calls g() calls h()
                  ↓
              h() raises ValueError
                  ↓
         g() has no matching except → unwinds
                  ↓
    f() has except ValueError → caught here

Every frame between the raise and the except is unwound. Local variables in those frames are lost. This is why re-raising with raise (not raise e) is important — it preserves the original traceback all the way down to the actual source.

docs.title: When to Raise: The Fail-Fast Principle
docs.text:
Raise early. Do not let bad data travel through your code until it produces a misleading error elsewhere.

Bad — silent propagation:

def train_step(model, X, y, lr):
    if lr <= 0:
        lr = 0.001    # silently "fix" the problem

    # 50 lines later... the model converges to a strange solution
    # and you have no idea why

Good — fail fast:

def train_step(model, X, y, lr):
    if lr <= 0:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Learning rate must be strictly positive, got {lr}. "
            f"Typical values are in [1e-5, 1e-1]."
        )

The rule: raise at the boundary where you first detect the violation, not deep inside where the consequence eventually surfaces.

docs.title: What to Raise: Choosing the Right Exception
docs.text:
Always raise the most semantically accurate exception from the standard hierarchy. Never raise Exception directly when a subclass fits.

Condition Raise Argument has the right type but wrong value ValueError Argument has the wrong type entirely TypeError A required dict key is absent KeyError An index is out of range IndexError An attribute or method does not exist AttributeError A file cannot be found FileNotFoundError An abstract method is not implemented NotImplementedError A general programming contract is violated RuntimeError Anything that does not fit above Custom exception (see [[43.Custom exception classes]]) 
def set_activation(name):
    valid = {"relu", "sigmoid", "tanh", "gelu"}
    if not isinstance(name, str):
        raise TypeError(f"Activation name must be a str, got {type(name).__name__!r}")
    if name not in valid:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown activation {name!r}. Valid options: {sorted(valid)}")

Two checks, two different exception types, for two different kinds of violation.

docs.title: Writing Good Exception Messages
docs.text:
An exception message is documentation that appears at the worst possible moment — when something is broken. Write it for the person debugging at 2am.

Minimum viable message:

raise ValueError("x must be positive")             # acceptable
raise ValueError(f"x must be positive, got {x}")   # better

Complete message — what, why, what to do:

raise ValueError(
    f"Learning rate {lr} is outside the valid range (0, 1). "
    f"Values above 0.1 often cause training instability. "
    f"Try lr=1e-3 as a starting point."
)

Always include the actual value. "x must be positive" without showing x = -7.3 forces the debugger to add a print statement and re-run. Show the value in the message.

# Bad
raise ValueError("Shape mismatch")

# Good
raise ValueError(
    f"Weight matrix shape {W.shape} is incompatible with input shape {x.shape}. "
    f"Expected W to have {x.shape[-1]} columns, got {W.shape[-1]}."
)

docs.title: raise Inside a Function: Guard Clauses
docs.text:
The guard clause pattern places all precondition checks at the top of the function before any work is done. The function's main logic is then written assuming all preconditions hold.

def matrix_multiply(A, B):
    # Guard clauses — all preconditions up front
    if not isinstance(A, list) or not isinstance(B, list):
        raise TypeError(f"Expected list inputs, got {type(A).__name__} and {type(B).__name__}")
    if len(A) == 0 or len(B) == 0:
        raise ValueError("Matrix arguments must be non-empty")
    if len(A[0]) != len(B):
        raise ValueError(
            f"Incompatible dimensions: A has {len(A[0])} columns "
            f"but B has {len(B)} rows"
        )

    # Main logic — written without defensive checks because guards already fired
    result = [[sum(A[i][k] * B[k][j] for k in range(len(B)))
               for j in range(len(B[0]))]
              for i in range(len(A))]
    return result

Contrast with the alternative: sprinkling if checks throughout the body. Guard clauses centralise all precondition logic, make the contract explicit, and keep the main logic clean.

docs.title: Re-Raising: Preserving the Original Traceback
docs.text:
Inside an except block, bare raise re-raises the caught exception with its full original traceback intact.

def load_config(path):
    try:
        with open(path) as f:
            return json.load(f)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        logger.error(f"Config file not found: {path}")
        raise    # caller sees the original FileNotFoundError with its traceback

The critical difference — raise vs raise e:

try:
    risky()
except ValueError as e:
    raise e    # BAD: traceback starts here — original location is lost
    raise      # GOOD: traceback preserved back to the original raise site

raise e creates a new traceback starting at the current line. raise continues the original traceback. Always use bare raise when re-raising.

docs.title: Exception Chaining: raise ... from
docs.text:
Python tracks two kinds of exception relationships:

Syntax Attribute set Meaning raise B from A B.__cause__ = A B was explicitly caused by A Exception during except A: B.__context__ = A B happened while handling A (implicit) raise B from None B.__cause__ = None, suppresses context B replaces A completely

docs.title: Explicit chaining — raise ... from
docs.text:
Use when a low-level exception should be re-expressed as a higher-level domain exception, but you want to preserve the original cause.

class ConfigError(Exception):
    pass

def load_config(path):
    try:
        with open(path) as f:
            return json.load(f)
    except FileNotFoundError as e:
        raise ConfigError(f"Configuration file missing: {path}") from e

The traceback shows:

FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'config.json'

The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception:

ConfigError: Configuration file missing: config.json

Both exceptions are visible. The caller sees ConfigError (the domain-level problem) and can trace it back to FileNotFoundError (the system-level cause).

docs.title: Suppressing context — raise ... from None
docs.text:
Use when the original exception is an implementation detail that should not appear in the user-facing traceback.

def get_user(user_id):
    try:
        return db_query(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE id={user_id}")
    except DatabaseConnectionError as e:
        raise RuntimeError("User lookup failed — service temporarily unavailable") from None

The from None suppresses the DatabaseConnectionError from the traceback. The caller sees only a clean RuntimeError. Use this when the original exception contains internal details (SQL queries, internal service names) you do not want exposed.

docs.title: Implicit Chaining — The Automatic Case
docs.text:
If an exception is raised while another is being handled, Python automatically sets __context__:

try:
    int("hello")
except ValueError:
    open("nonexistent.txt")    # raises FileNotFoundError

ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'hello'

During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred:

FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'nonexistent.txt'

Python shows both automatically. This is the "implicit chain" — no from keyword needed. It appears in tracebacks when your exception handler itself crashes.

docs.title: Raising in Abstract Base Classes
docs.text:
The canonical use of raise NotImplementedError is enforcing method contracts on subclasses.

class Optimizer:
    def step(self, gradients):
        raise NotImplementedError(
            f"{type(self).__name__} must implement step(). "
            f"See SGD or Adam for reference implementations."
        )

    def zero_grad(self):
        raise NotImplementedError(f"{type(self).__name__} must implement zero_grad()")


class SGD(Optimizer):
    def __init__(self, lr=0.01):
        self.lr = lr

    def step(self, params, gradients):
        for p, g in zip(params, gradients):
            p -= self.lr * g

    def zero_grad(self):
        pass    # stateless optimizer — nothing to zero

NotImplementedError (not NotImplemented, which is a special singleton for rich comparisons) signals an incomplete inheritance — a subclass that forgot to implement a required method.

docs.title: Raise in Assertions vs. Explicit Raise
docs.text:
Python has an assert statement:

assert x > 0, f"x must be positive, got {x}"

This raises AssertionError if the condition is false. It is not a substitute for raise.

assert raise Purpose Debugging, invariant checking Enforcing contracts, validating input Disabled by python -O (optimise flag) Never — always runs Exception type Always AssertionError Any exception you choose Use in production No Yes

assert is for invariants that should never fail if your code is correct — internal consistency checks during development. raise is for conditions that can fail depending on external input and must be handled in production.

# WRONG — assert for user input
def set_learning_rate(lr):
    assert lr > 0, "lr must be positive"   # disabled with -O; wrong exception type

# CORRECT — raise for user input
def set_learning_rate(lr):
    if lr <= 0:
        raise ValueError(f"lr must be positive, got {lr}")

# OK — assert for internal invariant
def _compute_gradient(loss, params):
    grad = autograd(loss, params)
    assert grad is not None, "autograd returned None — this is a bug in _compute_gradient"
    return grad

docs.title: Raise Inside Context Managers
docs.text:
Raising inside a with block triggers __exit__ on the context manager before the exception propagates. This ensures cleanup always runs.

with open("data.csv") as f:
    line = f.readline()
    if not line:
        raise ValueError("Data file is empty — cannot proceed with training")
# File is closed here even though an exception was raised

If __exit__ returns True, the exception is suppressed. If it returns False or None, the exception continues propagating. Standard context managers (open, Lock, etc.) do not suppress exceptions.

docs.title: Input validation at API boundaries
docs.text:
import numpy as np

def fit(X, y, epochs=10, lr=0.01):
    # Type checks
    if not isinstance(X, np.ndarray):
        raise TypeError(f"X must be a numpy array, got {type(X).__name__}")
    if not isinstance(y, np.ndarray):
        raise TypeError(f"y must be a numpy array, got {type(y).__name__}")

    # Shape checks
    if X.ndim != 2:
        raise ValueError(f"X must be 2-dimensional (n_samples, n_features), got shape {X.shape}")
    if y.ndim != 1:
        raise ValueError(f"y must be 1-dimensional (n_samples,), got shape {y.shape}")
    if X.shape[0] != y.shape[0]:
        raise ValueError(
            f"X and y must have the same number of samples. "
            f"Got X: {X.shape[0]}, y: {y.shape[0]}"
        )

    # Value checks
    if epochs <= 0:
        raise ValueError(f"epochs must be a positive integer, got {epochs}")
    if not (0 < lr < 1):
        raise ValueError(f"lr must be in (0, 1), got {lr}")

    # Main logic below — all preconditions guaranteed
    ...

docs.title: Re-raising with context in training loops
docs.text:
def train_epoch(model, dataloader, optimizer):
    for batch_idx, (X, y) in enumerate(dataloader):
        try:
            loss = train_step(model, X, y)
        except RuntimeError as e:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"Training failed at batch {batch_idx}. "
                f"Input shape: {X.shape}, Target shape: {y.shape}. "
                f"Original error: {e}"
            ) from e

docs.title: Signalling unimplemented features cleanly
docs.text:
class Model:
    def predict(self, X):
        raise NotImplementedError

    def predict_proba(self, X):
        raise NotImplementedError(
            f"{type(self).__name__} does not support probability estimates. "
            f"Use a probabilistic model such as LogisticRegression."
        )

    def save(self, path):
        raise NotImplementedError(
            f"Serialization not yet implemented. "
            f"Track progress at github.com/org/repo/issues/42."
        )

docs.title: The Full Raise Decision Tree
docs.text:
Something is wrong in my function.
           │
           ▼
Is this a violation of MY function's contract
(bad input, impossible state)?
    │                  │
   YES                 NO → handle it internally or let it propagate
    │
    ▼
Is there an accurate standard exception (ValueError,
TypeError, KeyError, etc.)?
    │                       │
   YES                      NO → raise a custom exception (note 43)
    │
    ▼
raise SpecificException(
    f"What was wrong: {actual_value}. "
    f"What was expected: <constraint>. "
    f"What to do: <hint>."
)

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
Raising the base Exception class:

raise Exception("something went wrong")    # too vague — use a specific subclass

Swallowing and re-raising incorrectly:

except ValueError as e:
    raise ValueError("wrapped") from e   # creates a chain — fine if intentional
    raise ValueError("wrapped")          # implicit chain — traceback looks odd
    raise e                              # loses original traceback location
    raise                                # correct bare re-raise

Raising a string instead of an exception:

raise "this is wrong"    # TypeError in Python 3 — must raise an exception instance

Using assert for user-facing validation:

assert lr > 0    # silently disabled with python -O; wrong exception type

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1. Write a function safe_divide(a, b) that raises TypeError if either argument is not a number, raises ValueError if b is zero with the message "Divisor must be non-zero", and returns a / b otherwise. Write three test calls that trigger each branch.

Exercise 2. What is the output of the following? Trace through it without running:

def f():
    try:
        raise ValueError("original")
    except ValueError as e:
        raise RuntimeError("wrapped") from e

try:
    f()
except RuntimeError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__)
    print(type(e.__cause__).__name__)
    print(e.__cause__)

Exercise 3. Explain the difference between:

raise RuntimeError("bad") from original_exception
raise RuntimeError("bad") from None
raise RuntimeError("bad")

What does each set on the new exception object? When would you use each?

Exercise 4. Write a Matrix class with a __getitem__ method that raises IndexError with a message that includes both the attempted index and the valid range. Then write a get(i, j, default=None) method that uses it internally but returns default instead of propagating the IndexError.

Exercise 5 (ML). You are writing a DataLoader class. Its __init__ takes a dataset, batch_size, and optional shuffle. Write the full set of guard clauses for __init__ using raise, covering: type of dataset, type and value of batch_size, type of shuffle, and the case where batch_size > len(dataset).

docs.title: 43. Custom Exception Classes
docs.text: "The standard exceptions are a vocabulary. Custom exceptions are the domain-specific dialect you invent when that vocabulary is not precise enough. A well-named exception is a compressed bug report — it tells you not just that something went wrong, but what kind of thing, in what layer, under what assumption."

docs.title: Why Custom Exceptions Exist
docs.text:
The standard library gives you ValueError, TypeError, KeyError, and a dozen others. These are sufficient for generic operations. They are not sufficient for domain reasoning.

Consider:

# Generic — tells you nothing about the domain
raise ValueError("invalid learning rate")

# Domain-specific — tells you exactly what failed and where
raise HyperparameterError("learning_rate", value=lr, constraint="must be in (0, 1)")

The second form lets you catch HyperparameterError specifically, write handlers only for configuration failures, and leave other ValueErrors to propagate. Without custom exceptions, every ValueError is the same — you cannot distinguish "bad user input" from "numerical domain error" from "malformed config file" without parsing the message string. That is fragile.

Custom exceptions give you:

  • Caller-side except clauses that match intent, not just type
  • Structured error data (not just a string message)
  • An exception hierarchy that mirrors your domain hierarchy
  • Self-documenting code — the exception name is part of the API

docs.title: The Minimal Custom Exception
docs.text:
class ValidationError(Exception):
    pass

That is a complete, usable custom exception. It inherits everything from Exception — the message, the traceback, __str__, __repr__. Raise it exactly like a standard exception:

raise ValidationError("Input failed schema check")

Catch it specifically:

try:
    validate(data)
except ValidationError:
    # only runs for ValidationError, not for TypeError or ValueError
    ...

The pass body is not laziness. For many exceptions, the name alone is the information. class DataPipelineError(Exception): pass is a complete design decision — you are saying the exception carries a string message and nothing else.

docs.title: The Exception Inheritance Contract
docs.text:
Every custom exception should inherit from Exception, not BaseException.

BaseException
└── Exception          ← inherit from here
    ├── ValueError
    ├── TypeError
    └── YourCustomError ← you are here

BaseException is the root of everything, including KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit. Code that does except Exception is a common pattern for "catch all application errors". If your exception inherits from BaseException directly, it escapes that net silently. Never do this unless you are building something that deliberately should not be catchable by normal except Exception blocks — which is almost never.

# WRONG
class MyError(BaseException):   # escapes except Exception — almost certainly wrong
    pass

# CORRECT
class MyError(Exception):
    pass

docs.title: Adding Structure: Custom __init__
docs.text:
When the exception needs to carry more than a string, define __init__.

class ShapeMismatchError(ValueError):
    def __init__(self, expected_shape, actual_shape, context=""):
        self.expected_shape = expected_shape
        self.actual_shape   = actual_shape
        self.context        = context
        message = (
            f"Shape mismatch: expected {expected_shape}, got {actual_shape}"
            + (f" ({context})" if context else "")
        )
        super().__init__(message)

Three things to notice:

  1. Inherit from ValueError, not Exception — because a shape mismatch is semantically a value error. Callers catching ValueError will still catch this.
  2. Store the structured data as attributes — the caller can access e.expected_shape and e.actual_shape programmatically, not by parsing a string.
  3. Call super().__init__(message) — this sets args[0], which is what str(e) and repr(e) display. Without it, the string representation is empty.
try:
    result = model(X)
except ShapeMismatchError as e:
    print(f"Expected: {e.expected_shape}")     # (32, 128)
    print(f"Got:      {e.actual_shape}")       # (32, 64)
    print(str(e))    # Shape mismatch: expected (32, 128), got (32, 64) (in linear layer 3)

docs.title: __str__ and __repr__
docs.text:
If the default message format from super().__init__ is insufficient, override __str__.

class ConfigError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, key, value, reason):
        self.key    = key
        self.value  = value
        self.reason = reason
        super().__init__(f"Invalid config: {key}={value!r} — {reason}")

    def __str__(self):
        return (
            f"ConfigError\n"
            f"  Key:    {self.key}\n"
            f"  Value:  {self.value!r}\n"
            f"  Reason: {self.reason}"
        )

Note: __repr__ on exceptions is handled by the base class and generally does not need overriding. Override __str__ when you want a formatted, multi-line display.

docs.title: Building a Domain Exception Hierarchy
docs.text:
For any non-trivial system, exceptions should form a tree that mirrors the domain structure. This lets callers choose how specific to be when catching.

# Root of the hierarchy — catch-all for the entire domain
class MLError(Exception):
    """Base exception for all errors in this ML library."""
    pass


# Second tier — broad categories
class DataError(MLError):
    """Errors in data loading, validation, or preprocessing."""
    pass

class ModelError(MLError):
    """Errors in model construction or configuration."""
    pass

class TrainingError(MLError):
    """Errors that occur during the training loop."""
    pass


# Third tier — specific conditions
class ShapeMismatchError(DataError):
    """Feature matrix shape does not match expected dimensions."""
    def __init__(self, expected, actual, location=""):
        self.expected = expected
        self.actual   = actual
        super().__init__(
            f"Shape mismatch at {location!r}: expected {expected}, got {actual}"
            if location else
            f"Shape mismatch: expected {expected}, got {actual}"
        )

class MissingFeatureError(DataError):
    """A required feature column is absent from the dataset."""
    def __init__(self, feature_name, available):
        self.feature_name = feature_name
        self.available    = available
        super().__init__(
            f"Required feature {feature_name!r} not found. "
            f"Available: {sorted(available)}"
        )

class InvalidActivationError(ModelError):
    """An unknown or unsupported activation function was requested."""
    VALID = {"relu", "sigmoid", "tanh", "gelu", "selu"}

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        super().__init__(
            f"Unknown activation {name!r}. "
            f"Supported activations: {sorted(self.VALID)}"
        )

class GradientExplosionError(TrainingError):
    """Gradient norm exceeded the threshold, indicating unstable training."""
    def __init__(self, norm, threshold, step):
        self.norm      = norm
        self.threshold = threshold
        self.step      = step
        super().__init__(
            f"Gradient explosion at step {step}: "
            f"norm={norm:.2f} exceeded threshold={threshold:.2f}"
        )

How callers use this hierarchy:

# Catch everything from the library
except MLError as e:
    log_and_abort(e)

# Catch only data-related problems
except DataError as e:
    request_new_data(e)

# Catch only this specific condition
except ShapeMismatchError as e:
    reshape_input(e.expected)

# Catch two unrelated specific exceptions
except (InvalidActivationError, MissingFeatureError) as e:
    fix_config(e)

This is the core payoff of the hierarchy. The caller controls granularity.

docs.title: Exceptions as Data Carriers
docs.text:
For failures in iterative processes — training loops, batch processing, pipeline stages — an exception that carries structured context is far more useful than a string.

class BatchProcessingError(TrainingError):
    """Raised when a specific batch causes a failure during training."""

    def __init__(self, batch_idx, epoch, cause, X_shape, y_shape):
        self.batch_idx = batch_idx
        self.epoch     = epoch
        self.cause     = cause     # the original exception
        self.X_shape   = X_shape
        self.y_shape   = y_shape

        super().__init__(
            f"Batch {batch_idx} in epoch {epoch} failed. "
            f"Input shape: {X_shape}, Target shape: {y_shape}. "
            f"Cause: {type(cause).__name__}: {cause}"
        )


# In the training loop:
for batch_idx, (X, y) in enumerate(dataloader):
    try:
        loss = train_step(model, X, y)
    except Exception as e:
        raise BatchProcessingError(
            batch_idx=batch_idx,
            epoch=current_epoch,
            cause=e,
            X_shape=X.shape,
            y_shape=y.shape,
        ) from e

The caller catching BatchProcessingError can log e.batch_idx, skip to the next epoch, or write the bad batch to disk for inspection — all without parsing a string.

docs.title: The __init_subclass__ Pattern: Self-Registering Exceptions
docs.text:
For large libraries, you can build a registry that maps exception names to classes automatically.

class MLError(Exception):
    _registry = {}

    def __init_subclass__(cls, **kwargs):
        super().__init_subclass__(**kwargs)
        MLError._registry[cls.__name__] = cls

class DataError(MLError): pass
class ModelError(MLError): pass
class TrainingError(MLError): pass

# After class definitions:
MLError._registry
# {'DataError': <class 'DataError'>,
#  'ModelError': <class 'ModelError'>,
#  'TrainingError': <class 'TrainingError'>}

This enables deserialising exceptions from logs or network messages by name, without a manual lookup table. It is an advanced pattern — note it for later.

docs.title: Organising Custom Exceptions in a Module
docs.text:
For any project beyond a single file, exceptions belong in their own module.

project/
├── exceptions.py       ← all custom exceptions live here
├── data/
│   ├── loader.py       ← from project.exceptions import DataError
│   └── pipeline.py
├── models/
│   └── base.py         ← from project.exceptions import ModelError
└── training/
    └── loop.py         ← from project.exceptions import TrainingError

exceptions.py:

"""
project.exceptions
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
All custom exceptions for the project, organised by domain layer.
Import from here, not from individual submodules.
"""

class MLError(Exception):
    """Base class for all project exceptions."""

class DataError(MLError):
    """Data loading, validation, and preprocessing failures."""

class ModelError(MLError):
    """Model construction and configuration failures."""

class TrainingError(MLError):
    """Training loop and optimisation failures."""

class ShapeMismatchError(DataError):
    def __init__(self, expected, actual, location=""):
        self.expected = expected
        self.actual   = actual
        super().__init__(
            f"Shape mismatch{f' at {location!r}' if location else ''}: "
            f"expected {expected}, got {actual}"
        )

# ... rest of hierarchy

This single-module pattern means any file in the project can do:

from project.exceptions import ShapeMismatchError, TrainingError

And users of the library see a clean, documented exception surface.

docs.title: __cause__, __context__, and Custom Exceptions
docs.text:
Custom exceptions participate in exception chaining exactly like standard ones.

class PipelineError(MLError):
    pass

# Translate a low-level OS error into a domain error
try:
    data = load_from_disk(path)
except OSError as e:
    raise PipelineError(f"Failed to load dataset from {path}") from e

OSError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'data/train.csv'

The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception:

PipelineError: Failed to load dataset from data/train.csv

The caller sees the domain-level PipelineError. The __cause__ attribute preserves the underlying OSError for debugging. The traceback shows both. This is the full exception chaining pattern from [[42.Raising Exceptions (raise)]] applied to your own hierarchy.

docs.title: Exceptions vs. Return Codes — The Design Choice
docs.text:
Some languages (C, Go) signal errors via return values. Python's idiomatic approach is exceptions. The practical question is: when does a condition merit a custom exception vs. returning None or a sentinel value?

Use a custom exception when:

  • The condition represents a violated contract — the caller passed something invalid
  • Recovery requires knowledge of the failure type (which except gives you)
  • The failure should propagate unless explicitly handled
  • The error occurs deep in a call stack and returning it would pollute every intermediate function

Return a sentinel value (None, empty list, False) when:

  • Absence is a normal, expected outcome — not a failure
  • The caller always handles the "nothing found" case immediately
  • The operation is a query: "does this exist?" — False is the right answer
# Exception — contract violation: the user explicitly asked for a key that must exist
def get_required_config(key):
    if key not in config:
        raise ConfigError(f"Required key {key!r} absent from configuration")
    return config[key]

# Return None — absence is normal: the user is probing, not asserting
def find_checkpoint(epoch):
    path = f"checkpoints/epoch_{epoch}.pt"
    return path if os.path.exists(path) else None

docs.title: Summary: The Design Checklist
docs.text:
When designing a custom exception:

  1. Where in the hierarchy? Inherit from the most specific standard exception that fits, or from your domain root. Never from BaseException.
  2. What does it carry? Decide what structured data the caller will need — beyond the string message. Add those as __init__ parameters stored as attributes.
  3. What is its name? The name should be a noun or noun-phrase describing the violated condition: ShapeMismatchError, MissingFeatureError, GradientExplosionError. Not BadInputError (too vague) or Error (meaningless).
  4. Does super().__init__(message) get called? It must. Otherwise str(e) is empty.
  5. Is it in exceptions.py? If the project has more than one file, yes.

docs.title: Full Working Example: A Mini ML Library
docs.text:
# exceptions.py

class MLError(Exception):
    """Base class for all library exceptions."""


class DataError(MLError):
    """Raised for data validation and preprocessing failures."""


class ModelError(MLError):
    """Raised for model construction and configuration failures."""


class TrainingError(MLError):
    """Raised during training loop execution."""


class ShapeMismatchError(DataError):
    def __init__(self, expected, actual, location=""):
        self.expected = expected
        self.actual   = actual
        self.location = location
        msg = f"Shape mismatch: expected {expected}, got {actual}"
        if location:
            msg += f" (at {location})"
        super().__init__(msg)


class NaNLossError(TrainingError):
    def __init__(self, step, loss_value):
        self.step       = step
        self.loss_value = loss_value
        super().__init__(
            f"Loss became NaN at step {step}. "
            f"Check learning rate, gradient clipping, and input normalisation."
        )


class InvalidArchitectureError(ModelError):
    def __init__(self, layer_name, reason):
        self.layer_name = layer_name
        self.reason     = reason
        super().__init__(f"Invalid layer {layer_name!r}: {reason}")


# ── model.py ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

from exceptions import ShapeMismatchError, NaNLossError, InvalidArchitectureError
import math

class LinearLayer:
    def __init__(self, in_features, out_features):
        if in_features <= 0:
            raise InvalidArchitectureError(
                "LinearLayer",
                f"in_features must be positive, got {in_features}"
            )
        if out_features <= 0:
            raise InvalidArchitectureError(
                "LinearLayer",
                f"out_features must be positive, got {out_features}"
            )
        self.W = [[0.0] * in_features for _ in range(out_features)]
        self.b = [0.0] * out_features
        self.in_features  = in_features
        self.out_features = out_features

    def forward(self, x):
        if len(x) != self.in_features:
            raise ShapeMismatchError(
                expected=(self.in_features,),
                actual=(len(x),),
                location=f"LinearLayer(in={self.in_features}, out={self.out_features})"
            )
        out = [
            sum(self.W[i][j] * x[j] for j in range(self.in_features)) + self.b[i]
            for i in range(self.out_features)
        ]
        if any(math.isnan(v) for v in out):
            raise NaNLossError(step=0, loss_value=float("nan"))
        return out


# ── Usage ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

layer = LinearLayer(4, 2)

try:
    output = layer.forward([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])  # only 3 values, expects 4
except ShapeMismatchError as e:
    print(f"Shape error caught. Expected: {e.expected}, Got: {e.actual}")
    # Shape error caught. Expected: (4,), Got: (3,)

try:
    bad_layer = LinearLayer(-1, 2)
except InvalidArchitectureError as e:
    print(f"Architecture error: {e}")
    # Architecture error: Invalid layer 'LinearLayer': in_features must be positive, got -1

docs.title: Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
docs.text: Custom exceptions in ML are not optional polish — they are architectural decisions that determine how debuggable your system is under real failure conditions.

docs.title: PyTorch's Own Exception Design
docs.text:
PyTorch uses RuntimeError for most of its own failures — shape mismatches, device mismatches, missing gradients. This is a design choice you can improve upon in your own code by wrapping PyTorch errors in domain exceptions:

import torch
from exceptions import ShapeMismatchError

def safe_matmul(A, B):
    try:
        return A @ B
    except RuntimeError as e:
        if "size mismatch" in str(e):
            raise ShapeMismatchError(
                expected=f"(..., {A.shape[-1]})",
                actual=str(B.shape),
                location="matmul"
            ) from e
        raise   # re-raise anything else unchanged

docs.title: Gradient Health Monitoring
docs.text:
class GradientError(TrainingError):
    pass

class VanishingGradientError(GradientError):
    def __init__(self, layer_name, norm, threshold=1e-7):
        self.layer_name = layer_name
        self.norm       = norm
        self.threshold  = threshold
        super().__init__(
            f"Vanishing gradient in {layer_name!r}: "
            f"norm={norm:.2e} < threshold={threshold:.2e}. "
            f"Consider skip connections, batch normalisation, or a different initialisation."
        )

class ExplodingGradientError(GradientError):
    def __init__(self, layer_name, norm, threshold=1e3):
        self.layer_name = layer_name
        self.norm       = norm
        self.threshold  = threshold
        super().__init__(
            f"Exploding gradient in {layer_name!r}: "
            f"norm={norm:.2e} > threshold={threshold:.2e}. "
            f"Apply gradient clipping: torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)"
        )

def check_gradients(model):
    for name, param in model.named_parameters():
        if param.grad is None:
            continue
        norm = param.grad.norm().item()
        if norm < 1e-7:
            raise VanishingGradientError(name, norm)
        if norm > 1e3:
            raise ExplodingGradientError(name, norm)

docs.title: Configuration Validation
docs.text:
Config validation at startup is cheaper than debugging a run that crashed 8 hours in.

class ConfigError(MLError):
    def __init__(self, field, value, constraint):
        self.field      = field
        self.value      = value
        self.constraint = constraint
        super().__init__(
            f"Invalid config field {field!r}={value!r}: {constraint}"
        )

def validate_config(cfg):
    validations = [
        ("learning_rate", cfg.get("learning_rate"),
         lambda v: 0 < v < 1,
         "must be in (0, 1)"),
        ("batch_size", cfg.get("batch_size"),
         lambda v: isinstance(v, int) and v > 0,
         "must be a positive integer"),
        ("optimizer", cfg.get("optimizer"),
         lambda v: v in {"sgd", "adam", "adamw", "rmsprop"},
         "must be one of sgd, adam, adamw, rmsprop"),
    ]
    for field, value, check, constraint in validations:
        if value is None:
            raise ConfigError(field, None, "is required but missing")
        if not check(value):
            raise ConfigError(field, value, constraint)

docs.title: The Exception Hierarchy as an API Contract
docs.text: When you publish a library, your exception hierarchy is part of the public API. Users write except YourLibrary.DataError in their code. If you rename or restructure exceptions in a patch release, you break their handlers silently. Treat exception class names with the same stability guarantees as function signatures.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1. Build a three-level exception hierarchy for a database access layer: a root DatabaseError, two second-tier classes ConnectionError and QueryError, and at least one specific third-tier class under each with a structured __init__. Write raise and catch examples for each level.

Exercise 2. What is wrong with the following, and what is the consequence?

class MyError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, code, message):
        self.code    = code
        self.message = message

e = MyError(404, "not found")
print(str(e))
print(e.args)

Fix it.

Exercise 3. Implement a BoundedFloat class whose __init__ accepts value, low, high and raises a custom BoundsViolationError (inheriting from ValueError) if value is outside [low, high]. The exception should carry value, low, and high as attributes and display a message showing all three.

Exercise 4 (hierarchy reasoning). Given this hierarchy:

MLError
├── DataError
│   └── ShapeMismatchError
└── TrainingError
    └── NaNLossError

For each except clause below, list all exceptions it would catch:

  • except MLError
  • except DataError
  • except ShapeMismatchError
  • except (DataError, NaNLossError)

Exercise 5 (ML). Write a Validator class for an ML dataset with three checks: all feature arrays must be 2D, all label arrays must be 1D, and the number of samples must match. Each violation should raise a different custom exception (all inheriting from a common DatasetError). Write a validate(X, y) method that runs all three checks.
