docs.title: 48. Importing Modules (import, from x import y, as)
docs.text: Tags: #python #modules #packages #namespace #ai-ml-relevance Prerequisites: [[47.Working with file paths]] · [[23.local vs global]] · [[26.Classes and objects]] Next: [[49.Writing your own modules]] · [[50.name == main pattern]] · [[51.Understanding init.py and package structure]] Phase: Phase 3 — Before writing ML code

docs.title: The Core Idea
docs.text:
A module is any .py file. A package is a directory of modules. The import system is how Python finds them, loads them into memory, executes them exactly once, and makes their names available in your namespace.

The word namespace is the key concept. Every import is fundamentally an answer to the question: which names become visible in my current scope, and under what label?

docs.title: What Actually Happens When You Import
docs.text:
This is not hand-waving — this is the exact sequence:

1. Python checks sys.modules (the import cache)
   → If found: return the cached module object. Done. No re-execution.
   → If not found: proceed.

2. Python locates the module file using sys.path
   (a list of directories searched in order)

3. Python creates a new module object

4. Python adds it to sys.modules immediately
   (before execution — handles circular imports)

5. Python executes the module's source code
   top-to-bottom, in the module's own namespace

6. The resulting module object is bound to a name in
   the importing scope

The critical invariant: a module's code runs exactly once, no matter how many files import it. All importers share the same module object.

import sys

import numpy as np
print(sys.modules["numpy"])   # <module 'numpy' from '...'>

import numpy as np2
print(np is np2)              # True — same object

docs.title: Form 1 — import module
docs.text:
import os
import math
import pathlib

This binds the top-level module name in your namespace. To access anything inside it, you use dot notation:

import os
import math

print(os.getcwd())
print(math.sqrt(2))
print(math.pi)

What goes into your namespace: one name — os, math, etc. Everything else is accessed through the module object.

Advantage: explicit origin. When you read os.path.join(...) three hundred lines into a file, you know exactly where join came from.

docs.title: Form 2 — from module import name
docs.text:
from math import sqrt, pi
from os.path import join, exists
from pathlib import Path

This executes the module (same as above) but only binds the specified names in your namespace:

from math import sqrt, pi

print(sqrt(2))    # no 'math.' prefix needed
print(pi)

What goes into your namespace: only the names you listed — sqrt, pi. The module object math is not bound.

Advantage: less typing, cleaner code for heavily-used names.

Danger: name collisions are invisible:

from math import sqrt
from cmath import sqrt   # silently overwrites the previous sqrt

Now sqrt refers to the complex version and you will not get an error — just wrong results.

docs.title: Form 3 — import module as alias
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import tensorflow as tf
import torch

This is identical to import module but binds the module to a different name. The aliases above are universal conventions in ML/data science — use them exactly as written.

import numpy as np

x = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(np.mean(x))

What goes into your namespace: one name — the alias.

Use it for: long module names, universal conventions, and avoiding collisions between two modules with the same short name.

docs.title: Form 4 — from module import name as alias
docs.text:
from datetime import datetime as dt
from collections import defaultdict as dd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression as LR

Imports one name and immediately renames it:

from datetime import datetime as dt

now = dt.now()

What goes into your namespace: one name — the alias.

Use it for: disambiguation when two modules export the same name, or shortening a frequently-typed name.

docs.title: The Wildcard Import — from module import *
docs.text:
from math import *      # imports everything not starting with _

This pulls every public name from the module into your namespace. It is almost always wrong:

  • You cannot tell where any name came from
  • It silently overwrites existing names
  • It makes static analysis and autocomplete unreliable
  • It pollutes your namespace with names you do not need

The one legitimate use: interactive REPL sessions and small scripts where you genuinely want everything from a specific module (e.g. from tkinter import * in a GUI tutorial). Never in production code.

A module can control what import * exports by defining __all__:

# inside mymodule.py
__all__ = ["PublicClass", "public_function"]
# private_helper will NOT be exported by import *

docs.title: The sys.path Search Order
docs.text:
When you write import foo, Python searches these locations in order:

1. sys.modules          — the import cache (already-loaded modules)
2. Built-in modules     — compiled into the interpreter (sys, builtins, etc.)
3. Frozen modules       — modules frozen into the interpreter
4. sys.path             — a list of directories, searched left to right:
   a. The directory of the script being run (or '' for interactive)
   b. PYTHONPATH environment variable entries
   c. Installation-dependent defaults (site-packages, stdlib)

import sys
for p in sys.path:
    print(p)

This is why import numpy works: numpy lives in site-packages, which is on sys.path.

You can add directories at runtime:

import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "/path/to/my/project")   # prepend — searched first

But in practice, the right solution is proper package structure (see [[51.Understanding init.py and package structure]]) or pip install -e . for editable installs.

docs.title: Importing Submodules and Nested Packages
docs.text:
# Import the submodule — os.path becomes available
import os.path
result = os.path.join("data", "train.csv")

# Import a name from a submodule
from os.path import join
result = join("data", "train.csv")

# Import a deeply nested name
from urllib.parse import urlparse, urlencode

# Import a submodule with an alias
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET
tree = ET.parse("config.xml")

When you write import os.path, Python imports os first (if not cached), then imports os.path as an attribute of os. Both os and os.path end up in sys.modules.

docs.title: Conditional import (compatibility)
docs.text:
try:
    import ujson as json        # fast C implementation
except ImportError:
    import json                 # fall back to stdlib

Use this when offering an optional faster backend without making it a hard dependency.

docs.title: Version-conditional import
docs.text:
import sys

if sys.version_info >= (3, 11):
    import tomllib              # built-in in 3.11+
else:
    import tomli as tomllib     # third-party backport

docs.title: Lazy import (defer until needed)
docs.text:
def load_model():
    import torch                # only imported when this function is called
    import torchvision
    model = torchvision.models.resnet50(pretrained=True)
    return model

Placing imports inside functions delays loading until the function is actually called. This is useful when:

  • A module is expensive to import (TensorFlow, PyTorch take seconds)
  • A module is only needed in one code path
  • You want to avoid circular imports (see below)

The module is still cached in sys.modules after the first call — subsequent calls pay no import cost.

docs.title: Circular Imports — The Trap
docs.text:
A circular import occurs when module A imports module B, and module B imports module A:

# a.py
from b import func_b

# b.py
from a import func_a     # a is partially initialised — func_a may not exist yet

Python handles this by inserting the partially-initialised module into sys.modules immediately (step 4 above). When B tries to import from A, it gets the half-built module — which may be missing names that haven't been defined yet.

Fix 1: restructure so the dependency is one-directional.

Fix 2: move the import inside the function that needs it:

# b.py
def func_b():
    from a import func_a    # imported at call time, not module load time
    return func_a()

Fix 3: import the module, not the name:

# b.py
import a                    # a may be incomplete, but the object exists
def func_b():
    return a.func_a()       # accessed at call time, when a is fully initialised

docs.title: Reloading a Module
docs.text:
In normal execution, each module runs once. In interactive development (REPL, Jupyter), you sometimes want to re-execute after editing:

import importlib
import mymodule

# After editing mymodule.py:
importlib.reload(mymodule)

This re-executes the module's code, but existing references to objects from the old module still point to the old objects. Use with caution. In Jupyter, %autoreload 2 is the practical solution.

docs.title: Visualisation — Namespace Effects of Each Form
docs.text:
Source: math module contains: {sqrt, pi, log, sin, cos, ...}

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Your namespace: { math → <module 'math'> }
Access via:     math.sqrt(2)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from math import sqrt, pi
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Your namespace: { sqrt → <function>, pi → 3.14159... }
Access via:     sqrt(2)
Note:           'math' is NOT in your namespace

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math as m
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Your namespace: { m → <module 'math'> }
Access via:     m.sqrt(2)
Note:           'math' is NOT in your namespace

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from math import sqrt as sq
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Your namespace: { sq → <function sqrt> }
Access via:     sq(2)
Note:           neither 'math' nor 'sqrt' in your namespace

docs.title: The Standard ML Import Block
docs.text:
Every ML script you write will begin with a block that looks approximately like this. Learn to read and write it fluently:

# ── Standard library ──────────────────────────────────────
import os
import sys
import json
import time
import random
import argparse
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Optional, List, Tuple, Dict

# ── Numerical computing ────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# ── Visualisation ──────────────────────────────────────────
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# ── Machine learning ───────────────────────────────────────
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, classification_report

# ── Deep learning ──────────────────────────────────────────
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader
import torchvision.transforms as transforms

# ── Experiment tracking ────────────────────────────────────
import mlflow
import mlflow.pytorch

The grouping and ordering is conventional (PEP 8): stdlib → third-party → local. Blank lines between groups. Alphabetical within groups is optional but common.

The aliases np, pd, plt, nn, F are not optional style choices — they are industry-wide conventions. Writing import numpy instead of import numpy as np will confuse every ML practitioner who reads your code.

docs.title: Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
Why torch.nn as nn and torch.nn.functional as F
docs.text:
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

torch.nn contains stateful building blocks — layers that hold parameters (weights and biases):

self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(3, 64, kernel_size=3)
self.bn1   = nn.BatchNorm2d(64)
self.fc    = nn.Linear(512, 10)

torch.nn.functional contains stateless functions — the same mathematical operations but without stored parameters:

x = F.relu(x)             # no parameters — just the function
x = F.dropout(x, p=0.5, training=self.training)
x = F.cross_entropy(logits, targets)

The convention is: use nn.X for layers you define in __init__, use F.X for operations you apply in forward. This distinction is architectural — blurring it leads to broken gradient flow or parameters that don't update.

docs.title: Selective imports reduce startup time
docs.text:
# Bad — imports all of sklearn (slow)
import sklearn

# Good — imports only what you need
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

TensorFlow is the extreme case — import tensorflow as tf takes 3–8 seconds on first import due to its enormous C++ backend. In a script that only uses one function, lazy imports or selective imports save meaningful time.

docs.title: __init__.py and what from torch import ... actually means
docs.text:
When you write:

from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader

Python is navigating a package hierarchy:

torch/
├── __init__.py
└── utils/
    ├── __init__.py
    └── data/
        ├── __init__.py      ← re-exports Dataset and DataLoader
        ├── dataset.py       ← defines Dataset
        └── dataloader.py    ← defines DataLoader

Dataset is not defined in __init__.py — it is defined in dataset.py and re-exported through data/__init__.py. The from ... import syntax lets you address the public API without knowing the internal file layout. This pattern (see [[51.Understanding init.py]]) is how every large Python library is organised.

docs.title: Namespace hygiene matters in Jupyter notebooks
docs.text:
Jupyter cells share a global namespace. Wildcard imports in one cell corrupt the namespace for all subsequent cells:

# Cell 1 — DON'T DO THIS
from numpy import *
from math import *     # 'log' now refers to math.log, not numpy.log
                       # numpy.log was silently overwritten

# Cell 1 — DO THIS
import numpy as np
import math
# now np.log and math.log are unambiguous

In long notebook sessions, restarting the kernel and re-running from the top is the only way to guarantee a clean namespace. Explicit imports make this reproducible.

docs.title: Common Mistakes and Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Naming your file after a standard library module

# You create a file called:
random.py

# Then in another file:
import random           # imports YOUR random.py, not the stdlib
random.randint(0, 10)  # AttributeError — your file has no randint

The current directory is first on sys.path. Never name your files os.py, math.py, random.py, json.py, etc. In ML projects, also avoid model.py and data.py if they shadow names you import elsewhere.

2. Mutating a module-level object and expecting isolation

import config
config.LEARNING_RATE = 0.01   # modifies the shared module object
                               # all other importers see this change

Modules are singletons. If module A modifies a mutable object in module B, module C sees the change. Use this intentionally (shared state) or avoid it (pass values explicitly).

3. from module import name does not stay in sync

from math import pi

# Later, if something reassigned math.pi (hypothetically):
# your local 'pi' still holds the original value
# 'import math; math.pi' would give the new value

# This is why mutable globals should be imported as the module, not the name:
import config             # if config.VALUE changes, you always get current
# not:
from config import VALUE  # a snapshot of VALUE at import time

4. Circular imports from poor project structure

The moment you have models.py importing from utils.py and utils.py importing from models.py, you have a design problem. The fix is almost always to extract shared definitions into a third module that neither imports from the other two.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Form Syntax Adds to namespace Access Module import import math math math.sqrt() Aliased import import numpy as np np np.array() Name import from math import sqrt sqrt sqrt() Aliased name from math import sqrt as sq sq sq() Wildcard from math import * everything public sqrt() — avoid

The invariant that governs everything: a module's code runs exactly once. All importers share one module object. import is a namespace operation — it controls which names are visible in your scope and under what label.

docs.title: The Core Idea
docs.text:
A module is any .py file. The moment you save a file called utils.py, it is a module. Any other Python file in the same directory can do import utils and access everything defined inside it.

That is the whole mechanism. What takes thought is not the syntax — it is the design: how to divide your code across files so that each module has a clear responsibility, a clean public interface, and no hidden dependencies that make it impossible to reuse or test in isolation.

This note covers both the mechanics and the design discipline.

docs.title: The Minimal Example
docs.text:
project/
├── geometry.py
└── main.py

# geometry.py

PI = 3.141592653589793

def circle_area(radius: float) -> float:
    """Return the area of a circle with the given radius."""
    return PI * radius ** 2

def circle_circumference(radius: float) -> float:
    """Return the circumference of a circle with the given radius."""
    return 2 * PI * radius

class Circle:
    def __init__(self, radius: float):
        self.radius = radius

    def area(self) -> float:
        return circle_area(self.radius)

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        return f"Circle(radius={self.radius})"

# main.py

import geometry

c = geometry.Circle(5.0)
print(c.area())                          # 78.539...
print(geometry.circle_circumference(5)) # 31.415...
print(geometry.PI)                       # 3.14159...

Or with selective imports:

from geometry import Circle, circle_area

c = Circle(5.0)
print(circle_area(3.0))

Every name defined at the top level of geometry.py — functions, classes, constants, even other imported names — is accessible as an attribute of the module object.

docs.title: What a Module's Namespace Contains
docs.text:
When Python executes geometry.py, it runs the file top-to-bottom in a fresh namespace. Everything that gets defined or imported at module level becomes an attribute of the resulting module object:

# geometry.py

import math                   # math is now an attribute of geometry
PI = math.pi                  # PI is an attribute
_TOLERANCE = 1e-9             # _TOLERANCE is an attribute (but private by convention)

def circle_area(r):           # circle_area is an attribute
    ...

class Circle:                 # Circle is an attribute
    ...

After import geometry:

geometry.math          # the math module — accessible but unintended
geometry.PI            # 3.14159...
geometry._TOLERANCE    # 1e-9 — accessible but signals "don't use this"
geometry.circle_area   # the function
geometry.Circle        # the class

The leading underscore on _TOLERANCE is a convention — it signals to readers (and to import *) that this name is an implementation detail, not part of the public interface. Python does not enforce it; discipline does.

docs.title: Controlling the Public Interface with __all__
docs.text:
__all__ is a list of strings that explicitly declares what your module exports. It has two effects:

  1. from geometry import * only imports names in __all__
  2. It serves as machine-readable documentation of your public API
# geometry.py

__all__ = ["Circle", "circle_area", "circle_circumference", "PI"]

PI = 3.141592653589793
_TOLERANCE = 1e-9          # not in __all__ — excluded from import *

def circle_area(radius):
    ...

def circle_circumference(radius):
    ...

def _validate_radius(r):   # not in __all__ — internal helper
    if r < 0:
        raise ValueError(f"Radius must be non-negative, got {r}")

class Circle:
    ...

When to define __all__: whenever your module is intended to be used by others — which means any module in an ML project that other files import. It forces you to think about what is public and prevents accidental exposure of internals.

docs.title: Module-Level Code — What Runs at Import Time
docs.text:
Every statement at the top level of a module runs when it is imported. This is both powerful and dangerous:

# constants.py — safe: only defines values
LEARNING_RATE = 1e-3
BATCH_SIZE = 256
MAX_EPOCHS = 100

# bad_module.py — dangerous: side effects at import time
import time

print("Loading model...")        # printed every import — annoying
model = load_huge_model()        # runs at import — slow, may fail
time.sleep(2)                    # blocks for 2 seconds at import

The rule: module-level code should only define things — functions, classes, constants. It should not do things — load files, make network requests, print output, or modify global state. Side effects belong inside functions that are called explicitly.

The one canonical exception is the if __name__ == "__main__": guard (see [[50.name == main pattern]]).

docs.title: Private vs. Public — The Convention System
docs.text:
Python has no access modifiers (private, protected). It has conventions:

Name pattern Meaning Effect on import * name Public — part of the interface Exported _name Internal — implementation detail Not exported __name Name-mangled — avoid accidental override in subclasses Not exported __name__ Dunder — Python's own special protocol names Not exported 
# metrics.py

def accuracy(y_true, y_pred):           # public — use this
    return _correct(y_true, y_pred) / len(y_true)

def _correct(y_true, y_pred):           # internal — don't depend on this
    return sum(a == b for a, b in zip(y_true, y_pred))

EPSILON = 1e-8                          # public constant
_CACHE = {}                             # internal cache — implementation detail

When you call from metrics import *, only accuracy and EPSILON come through (assuming no __all__ — underscore names are excluded). With import metrics, everything is accessible as metrics._correct, but the underscore is a social contract: "I might rename or remove this without warning."

docs.title: Docstrings at Module Level
docs.text:
The first string literal in a module, if it is a string expression (not assigned to anything), becomes the module's __doc__:

# metrics.py

"""
metrics.py
----------
Evaluation metrics for classification and regression tasks.

Public API:
    accuracy(y_true, y_pred)     — classification accuracy
    f1_score(y_true, y_pred)     — F1 score (binary)
    mean_squared_error(y, y_hat) — MSE for regression
"""

__all__ = ["accuracy", "f1_score", "mean_squared_error"]

...

import metrics
help(metrics)         # displays the docstring + all public names
print(metrics.__doc__)

Write a module docstring for any file that will be imported by others. It should state what the module contains and list the public API. This is the first thing a reader sees.

docs.title: A Real Example — A Metrics Module
docs.text:
This is what a well-structured module looks like in practice:

# metrics.py

"""
metrics.py
----------
Evaluation metrics for binary classification.

Public API:
    accuracy        — fraction of correct predictions
    precision       — TP / (TP + FP)
    recall          — TP / (TP + FN)
    f1_score        — harmonic mean of precision and recall
    confusion_matrix — 2x2 confusion matrix as a dict
"""

__all__ = [
    "accuracy",
    "precision",
    "recall",
    "f1_score",
    "confusion_matrix",
]

# ── Internal helpers ───────────────────────────────────────────────────

def _check_inputs(y_true: list, y_pred: list) -> None:
    if len(y_true) != len(y_pred):
        raise ValueError(
            f"Length mismatch: y_true has {len(y_true)} elements, "
            f"y_pred has {len(y_pred)}."
        )
    if not y_true:
        raise ValueError("Inputs must not be empty.")


def _counts(y_true: list, y_pred: list) -> tuple[int, int, int, int]:
    """Return (TP, FP, TN, FN) for binary labels."""
    _check_inputs(y_true, y_pred)
    tp = sum(t == 1 and p == 1 for t, p in zip(y_true, y_pred))
    fp = sum(t == 0 and p == 1 for t, p in zip(y_true, y_pred))
    tn = sum(t == 0 and p == 0 for t, p in zip(y_true, y_pred))
    fn = sum(t == 1 and p == 0 for t, p in zip(y_true, y_pred))
    return tp, fp, tn, fn


# ── Public API ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

def accuracy(y_true: list, y_pred: list) -> float:
    """Return the fraction of predictions that are correct."""
    _check_inputs(y_true, y_pred)
    return sum(t == p for t, p in zip(y_true, y_pred)) / len(y_true)


def precision(y_true: list, y_pred: list) -> float:
    """Return TP / (TP + FP). Returns 0.0 if no positive predictions."""
    tp, fp, _, _ = _counts(y_true, y_pred)
    return tp / (tp + fp) if (tp + fp) > 0 else 0.0


def recall(y_true: list, y_pred: list) -> float:
    """Return TP / (TP + FN). Returns 0.0 if no positive ground truths."""
    tp, _, _, fn = _counts(y_true, y_pred)
    return tp / (tp + fn) if (tp + fn) > 0 else 0.0


def f1_score(y_true: list, y_pred: list) -> float:
    """Return the harmonic mean of precision and recall."""
    p = precision(y_true, y_pred)
    r = recall(y_true, y_pred)
    return 2 * p * r / (p + r) if (p + r) > 0 else 0.0


def confusion_matrix(y_true: list, y_pred: list) -> dict:
    """Return a dict with keys TP, FP, TN, FN."""
    tp, fp, tn, fn = _counts(y_true, y_pred)
    return {"TP": tp, "FP": fp, "TN": tn, "FN": fn}

Notice the structure:

  • Module docstring first
  • __all__ immediately after — the public contract
  • Internal helpers in a clearly labelled section, all prefixed with _
  • Public functions in a clearly labelled section, all with docstrings
  • No side effects anywhere at module level

docs.title: Module Design Principles
docs.text:
These are not style preferences. They are engineering principles that determine whether your code survives contact with a real project.

1. Single responsibility. Each module should have one clear reason to exist. metrics.py computes metrics. data.py loads data. model.py defines the model architecture. If you cannot state a module's purpose in one sentence, it is doing too much.

2. Depend inward, not outward. Low-level utility modules (utils.py, metrics.py) should not import high-level modules (trainer.py, experiment.py). The dependency graph should be a DAG, not a cycle. If you find yourself needing a circular import, the design is wrong.

3. No side effects at import time. Module-level code defines, does not do. Loading data, initialising hardware, printing, sleeping — all of this goes inside functions.

4. Explicit public interface. Define __all__. Use _ prefixes for internals. A module with no explicit interface is one where every internal detail becomes a dependency others rely on, making refactoring impossible.

5. Keep modules importable in isolation. If importing model.py requires a GPU, a specific file to exist, and a database connection, you cannot test it, you cannot import it in a notebook, and you cannot use it anywhere that context is absent. Guard hardware and I/O behind functions.

docs.title: Visualisation — Module Structure
docs.text:
metrics.py
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  """Module docstring"""              ← __doc__          │
│                                                         │
│  __all__ = [...]                     ← public contract  │
│                                                         │
│  import math                         ← dependencies     │
│  from pathlib import Path                               │
│                                                         │
│  EPSILON = 1e-8                      ← public constant  │
│  _CACHE = {}                         ← internal state   │
│                                                         │
│  def _helper():   ...                ← internal         │
│  def _validate(): ...                ← internal         │
│                                                         │
│  def public_fn(): ...                ← public API       │
│  class PublicClass: ...              ← public API       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

When another file does:
    import metrics

    metrics.__doc__       → module docstring
    metrics.__all__       → ['accuracy', 'f1_score', ...]
    metrics.__file__      → '/path/to/metrics.py'
    metrics.__name__      → 'metrics'
    metrics.accuracy      → <function accuracy>
    metrics._helper       → <function _helper>  (accessible but private)
    metrics.EPSILON       → 1e-8

docs.title: Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
Every ML project is a collection of modules
docs.text:
A mature ML codebase splits naturally into modules by responsibility. Here is the canonical layout:

project/
├── data.py          # Dataset classes, data loading, transforms
├── model.py         # Network architecture definitions
├── train.py         # Training loop, optimiser step, gradient clipping
├── evaluate.py      # Metric computation, validation loop
├── utils.py         # Logging, checkpointing, reproducibility helpers
└── config.py        # Hyperparameters and paths as named constants

Each of these is a module you write. The discipline of [[49]] is what makes them composable — you can run evaluate.py standalone, import model.py into a notebook, and test data.py without a GPU.

docs.title: config.py — the module as a configuration object
docs.text:
Instead of scattering magic numbers through your code:

# config.py

"""
config.py
---------
All hyperparameters and paths in one place.
Change here; effects propagate everywhere.
"""

from pathlib import Path

__all__ = ["DATA", "TRAIN", "MODEL"]

# ── Paths ──────────────────────────────────
DATA_ROOT   = Path("data")
TRAIN_DIR   = DATA_ROOT / "train"
VAL_DIR     = DATA_ROOT / "val"
CKPT_DIR    = Path("checkpoints")

# ── Data ───────────────────────────────────
IMAGE_SIZE  = 224
BATCH_SIZE  = 256
NUM_WORKERS = 8

# ── Model ──────────────────────────────────
NUM_CLASSES = 1000
DROPOUT     = 0.2

# ── Training ───────────────────────────────
LEARNING_RATE = 1e-3
WEIGHT_DECAY  = 1e-4
MAX_EPOCHS    = 90
WARMUP_EPOCHS = 5

Every other module imports from config:

# train.py
from config import LEARNING_RATE, WEIGHT_DECAY, MAX_EPOCHS, CKPT_DIR

When you want to try LEARNING_RATE = 1e-4, you change one file. This is the modularity dividend.

docs.title: model.py — architecture as a module
docs.text:
# model.py

"""
model.py
--------
Neural network architecture definitions.

Public API:
    build_model(num_classes, dropout) — returns a compiled nn.Module
    ResNet                            — the base architecture class
"""

__all__ = ["build_model", "ResNet"]

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F


class _ResidualBlock(nn.Module):       # internal — not exported
    """A single residual block. Implementation detail of ResNet."""
    def __init__(self, channels: int):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, 3, padding=1, bias=False)
        self.bn1   = nn.BatchNorm2d(channels)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, 3, padding=1, bias=False)
        self.bn2   = nn.BatchNorm2d(channels)

    def forward(self, x):
        residual = x
        x = F.relu(self.bn1(self.conv1(x)))
        x = self.bn2(self.conv2(x))
        return F.relu(x + residual)


class ResNet(nn.Module):               # public — exported
    """A minimal ResNet-style classifier."""
    def __init__(self, num_classes: int = 10, dropout: float = 0.2):
        super().__init__()
        self.stem   = nn.Conv2d(3, 64, 7, stride=2, padding=3, bias=False)
        self.blocks = nn.Sequential(
            _ResidualBlock(64),
            _ResidualBlock(64),
        )
        self.pool   = nn.AdaptiveAvgPool2d(1)
        self.drop   = nn.Dropout(dropout)
        self.fc     = nn.Linear(64, num_classes)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = F.relu(self.stem(x))
        x = self.blocks(x)
        x = self.pool(x).flatten(1)
        x = self.drop(x)
        return self.fc(x)


def build_model(num_classes: int = 10, dropout: float = 0.2) -> ResNet:
    """Construct and return a ResNet classifier."""
    return ResNet(num_classes=num_classes, dropout=dropout)

_ResidualBlock is an internal implementation detail. Users of model.py import ResNet and build_model. If you later replace _ResidualBlock with a better implementation, the public interface is unchanged — all importing code continues to work without modification.

docs.title: Writing a reusable data.py
docs.text:
# data.py

"""
data.py
-------
Dataset and DataLoader construction for image classification.

Public API:
    ImageDataset          — torch Dataset for a directory of images
    build_dataloaders     — returns (train_loader, val_loader)
"""

__all__ = ["ImageDataset", "build_dataloaders"]

from pathlib import Path
from typing import Callable, Optional

import torch
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader
from PIL import Image
import torchvision.transforms as T


class ImageDataset(Dataset):
    """Load images from a directory. Each subdirectory is a class."""
    def __init__(self, root: Path, transform: Optional[Callable] = None):
        self.root      = Path(root)
        self.transform = transform
        self.samples   = sorted(self.root.rglob("*.jpg"))

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        return len(self.samples)

    def __getitem__(self, idx: int):
        path  = self.samples[idx]
        image = Image.open(path).convert("RGB")
        if self.transform:
            image = self.transform(image)
        return image


def _default_transform(image_size: int = 224) -> T.Compose:
    return T.Compose([
        T.Resize(image_size),
        T.CenterCrop(image_size),
        T.ToTensor(),
        T.Normalize(mean=[0.485, 0.456, 0.406],
                    std=[0.229, 0.224, 0.225]),
    ])


def build_dataloaders(
    train_dir: Path,
    val_dir:   Path,
    batch_size: int = 256,
    num_workers: int = 8,
    image_size: int = 224,
) -> tuple[DataLoader, DataLoader]:
    """Construct train and validation DataLoaders."""
    transform = _default_transform(image_size)
    train_ds  = ImageDataset(train_dir, transform=transform)
    val_ds    = ImageDataset(val_dir,   transform=transform)
    train_loader = DataLoader(train_ds, batch_size=batch_size,
                              shuffle=True,  num_workers=num_workers)
    val_loader   = DataLoader(val_ds,   batch_size=batch_size,
                              shuffle=False, num_workers=num_workers)
    return train_loader, val_loader

In train.py:

from data import build_dataloaders
from config import TRAIN_DIR, VAL_DIR, BATCH_SIZE, NUM_WORKERS

train_loader, val_loader = build_dataloaders(
    TRAIN_DIR, VAL_DIR, BATCH_SIZE, NUM_WORKERS
)

train.py does not need to know how images are loaded, how transforms are constructed, or what _default_transform does. It calls one function and gets two DataLoaders.

docs.title: Common Mistakes and Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Putting everything in one file

A single main.py with 800 lines containing model definition, data loading, training loop, evaluation, and visualisation is not a program — it is a script that cannot be reused, tested, or read. Split by responsibility from the start.

2. Making modules that import each other

model.py  → imports from  train.py
train.py  → imports from  model.py   ← circular import

The fix is always the same: extract the shared dependency into a third module that neither imports from the other two. Usually this is utils.py or config.py.

3. Module-level code with side effects

# bad_data.py

import pandas as pd

# This runs at import time — slow, may fail if file absent
df = pd.read_csv("data/train.csv")      # ← side effect at module level
print(f"Loaded {len(df)} rows")         # ← output at import time

Anyone who imports bad_data to use one of its functions pays the full cost of loading the CSV, even if they never use df. Wrap it in a function.

4. Importing everything into one namespace

# bad_utils.py — becomes a dumping ground
from model import *
from data import *
from metrics import *
from config import *

Now bad_utils has a namespace full of names from four other modules, none of them clearly attributed. Use explicit imports and explicit names.

5. Forgetting that imported names are module attributes

# a.py
VALUE = 10

# b.py
from a import VALUE

# elsewhere
import a
a.VALUE = 99    # modifies the module attribute

# back in b.py
print(VALUE)    # still 10 — b.py holds a reference to the original int
                # it does not hold a reference to a.VALUE

This is the mutable-vs-immutable import distinction. If VALUE were a list, a.VALUE.append(...) would be visible to b.py (same object). But reassigning a.VALUE = 99 is not visible to b.py's local binding VALUE. Import the module (not the name) when you need to see mutations.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Concept What to remember A module is Any .py file Module namespace Every top-level name: functions, classes, constants, imports __all__ Explicit public contract; controls import * _name convention Internal — implementation detail, may change Module-level code Should only define, never do Single responsibility One module, one clear purpose No circular imports Fix by restructuring, not by working around Module docstring First string literal; becomes __doc__

The central discipline: a module is a unit of encapsulation. Its public interface (what it exports) should be stable and intentional. Its internals (prefixed with _) should be free to change. Every file you write in an ML project that another file imports is a module, and it deserves the design care this implies.

docs.title: 50. The __name__ == "__main__" Pattern
docs.text: Tags: #python #modules #execution-model #scripting #ai-ml-relevance Prerequisites: [[48.Importing modules (import, from x import y, as)]] · [[49.Writing your own modules]] · [[23.local vs global]] · [[06.Comments and docstrings]] Next: [[51.Understanding init.py and package structure]] Phase: Phase 3 — Before writing ML code

docs.title: The One-Line Version
docs.text:
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

This block runs only when the file is executed directly — not when it is imported as a module. Understanding why requires understanding what __name__ is and how Python sets it.

docs.title: What Is __name__?
docs.text:
__name__ is a dunder attribute that Python sets automatically on every module before executing it. Its value depends on how the module is being run:

How the file is loaded __name__ value Run directly: python train.py "__main__" Imported: import train "train" Imported as: from train import X "train" Run as package: python -m train "__main__"

There is no magic here. Python simply sets __name__ = "__main__" before executing the entry-point file, and __name__ = "<module_name>" before executing any imported file. The if block is just a standard conditional — it checks which case applies.

docs.title: The Problem It Solves
docs.text:
Consider a file with no guard:

# utils.py — NO guard

def compute_loss(predictions, targets):
    return sum((p - t) ** 2 for p, t in zip(predictions, targets))

# "test" code written at the bottom during development
predictions = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
targets     = [1.1, 2.1, 2.9]
print("Loss:", compute_loss(predictions, targets))

When you run utils.py directly, this works fine. But the moment another file imports it:

# train.py
from utils import compute_loss   # importing triggers execution of utils.py

Python executes utils.py top to bottom. The test code at the bottom runs. You see:

Loss: 0.030000000000000013

printed in the middle of your training run — for no reason, with hardcoded dummy data. In a large project, this could mean:

  • Unwanted print output contaminating logs
  • Database connections being opened
  • Files being written
  • Slow initialisation code running unnecessarily
  • Tests failing because side effects fire on import

The guard prevents this entirely:

# utils.py — WITH guard

def compute_loss(predictions, targets):
    return sum((p - t) ** 2 for p, t in zip(predictions, targets))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    predictions = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]
    targets     = [1.1, 2.1, 2.9]
    print("Loss:", compute_loss(predictions, targets))

Now from utils import compute_loss is clean — the test block is skipped entirely.

docs.title: Anatomy of the Pattern — Three Roles in One File
docs.text:
The pattern enables a single .py file to serve three roles simultaneously:

# solver.py

# ── Role 1: Library ──────────────────────────────────────────
# Functions and classes importable by other modules
# These are always defined, regardless of how the file is loaded

def solve(matrix, vector):
    """Solve Ax = b via Gaussian elimination."""
    ...

class GradientDescent:
    def __init__(self, lr=0.01):
        self.lr = lr
    def step(self, params, grads):
        return [p - self.lr * g for p, g in zip(params, grads)]


# ── Role 2: Entry point ──────────────────────────────────────
# Executable behaviour when run as a script

def main():
    import argparse
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Run solver")
    parser.add_argument("--lr", type=float, default=0.01)
    parser.add_argument("--steps", type=int, default=100)
    args = parser.parse_args()

    optimizer = GradientDescent(lr=args.lr)
    # ... run the solver ...
    print(f"Solved in {args.steps} steps")


# ── Role 3: Guard ────────────────────────────────────────────
# The switch that activates Role 2 only when appropriate

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Usage:

# As a script — main() runs
python solver.py --lr 0.001 --steps 500

# As a module — main() does not run, only definitions are loaded
python -m pytest test_solver.py

docs.title: Why Define a main() Function?
docs.text:
You could put code directly in the guard:

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # 200 lines of training code here

This works but is worse for four reasons:

1. Scope: Variables defined directly in the if block are module-level globals. Variables inside main() are local — they do not persist in the module namespace and cannot accidentally shadow imports.

2. Testability: You cannot call if __name__ == "__main__": from a test. You can call main() — or better, the subfunctions that main() delegates to.

3. Readability: The function name documents intent. def main() signals "this is the entry point."

4. Profiling: python -m cProfile -s cumtime train.py profiles cleanly when main() is a real function — you can see main in the call graph.

The discipline is: keep the guard thin. The guard calls main(). main() orchestrates. Individual functions do the real work.

docs.title: __name__ Is a Module Attribute — Not Special Syntax
docs.text:
There is nothing syntactically special about __name__. It is an ordinary string attribute on the module object:

# In any file, you can inspect it:
print(__name__)        # "__main__" if run directly, module name if imported

# You can inspect other modules' __name__:
import math
print(math.__name__)   # "math"

import os.path
print(os.path.__name__) # "posixpath"  (the actual file behind os.path on Unix)

Every module has it. The if __name__ == "__main__": pattern is just a conditional that exploits the difference Python sets between these two cases.

docs.title: python -m — Running a Module as a Script
docs.text:
The -m flag tells Python to run a module from sys.path as a script, setting __name__ = "__main__":

python -m train          # runs train.py, __name__ == "__main__"
python -m pytest         # runs pytest as a module
python -m pip install X  # runs pip
python -m http.server    # starts a local HTTP server
python -m cProfile train.py  # profiles train.py

python -m module vs python module.py — the key difference is that -m imports the module through the normal import system, so relative imports work correctly. Running a file directly as python script.py does not go through the package system, which breaks relative imports inside packages.

Implication for ML projects: always run your training scripts with python -m src.train rather than python src/train.py. This ensures your package imports resolve correctly.

docs.title: The __spec__ Check — A Stricter Alternative
docs.text:
In some library code, you need to distinguish between three cases:

  1. Run directly: python script.py
  2. Run as module: python -m script
  3. Imported: import script

__name__ == "__main__" catches cases 1 and 2, but not 3. If you need to distinguish case 1 from case 2:

import sys

if __name__ == "__main__":
    if sys.argv[0].endswith("__main__.py"):
        # case 2: python -m package
        ...
    else:
        # case 1: python script.py
        ...

Or use __spec__:

if __name__ == "__main__" and __spec__ is None:
    # Run directly as a script — NOT via python -m
    ...

__spec__ is None when a file is run directly. It is a ModuleSpec object when run via -m. This distinction rarely matters in application code but appears in framework internals (pytest, multiprocessing).

docs.title: Multiprocessing — Where the Guard Is Not Optional
docs.text:
On Windows and macOS (with the spawn start method), the multiprocessing module starts new processes by importing the main module. If there is no guard, every child process re-executes the top-level code — spawning more children, which spawn more children, until the system runs out of resources.

# WRONG on Windows — infinite process explosion
import multiprocessing

def worker(x):
    return x ** 2

pool = multiprocessing.Pool(4)       # spawns 4 processes
results = pool.map(worker, range(10))  # each imports this file → spawns 4 more → ...
print(results)

# CORRECT — the guard prevents re-execution in child processes
import multiprocessing

def worker(x):
    return x ** 2

if __name__ == "__main__":
    pool = multiprocessing.Pool(4)
    results = pool.map(worker, range(10))
    print(results)

This is not a style issue. On Windows, the incorrect version crashes with a RuntimeError and a message telling you to use the guard. PyTorch's DataLoader with num_workers > 0 has the same requirement for the same reason.

docs.title: Visualisation — Execution Flow
docs.text:
python train.py
                         │
                   Is this the entry point?
                    Python sets __name__ = "__main__"
                         │
                    ┌────▼────────────────────────────┐
                    │  # train.py                     │
                    │                                 │
                    │  def build_model(): ...  ✓ runs │
                    │  def train_loop(): ...   ✓ runs │
                    │                                 │
                    │  if __name__ == "__main__":     │
                    │      ← "__main__" == "__main__" │
                    │      → True → block executes    │
                    │      main()              ✓ runs │
                    └─────────────────────────────────┘


                    from train import build_model
                         │
                   Is this an import?
                    Python sets __name__ = "train"
                         │
                    ┌────▼────────────────────────────┐
                    │  # train.py                     │
                    │                                 │
                    │  def build_model(): ...  ✓ runs │
                    │  def train_loop(): ...   ✓ runs │
                    │                                 │
                    │  if __name__ == "__main__":     │
                    │      ← "train" == "__main__"    │
                    │      → False → block skipped    │
                    │      main()              ✗ skip │
                    └─────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
Training scripts
docs.text:
Every real ML training script follows this structure:

# train.py
import argparse
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from pathlib import Path
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

from src.model import ResNet50
from src.data import ImageDataset
from src.utils import save_checkpoint, AverageMeter


def build_model(num_classes: int) -> nn.Module:
    model = ResNet50(num_classes=num_classes)
    return model


def train_one_epoch(model, loader, optimizer, criterion, device):
    model.train()
    loss_meter = AverageMeter()
    for images, labels in loader:
        images, labels = images.to(device), labels.to(device)
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        outputs = model(images)
        loss = criterion(outputs, labels)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        loss_meter.update(loss.item(), images.size(0))
    return loss_meter.avg


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--data-dir",    type=Path,  default=Path("data"))
    parser.add_argument("--epochs",      type=int,   default=90)
    parser.add_argument("--lr",          type=float, default=0.1)
    parser.add_argument("--batch-size",  type=int,   default=256)
    parser.add_argument("--num-classes", type=int,   default=1000)
    parser.add_argument("--checkpoint-dir", type=Path, default=Path("checkpoints"))
    args = parser.parse_args()

    device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

    model     = build_model(args.num_classes).to(device)
    optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=args.lr, momentum=0.9)
    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

    train_dataset = ImageDataset(args.data_dir / "train")
    train_loader  = DataLoader(train_dataset,
                               batch_size=args.batch_size,
                               num_workers=4,     # requires the guard on Windows
                               shuffle=True)

    for epoch in range(args.epochs):
        loss = train_one_epoch(model, train_loader, optimizer, criterion, device)
        print(f"Epoch {epoch+1}/{args.epochs}  loss={loss:.4f}")
        save_checkpoint(model, optimizer, epoch, loss, args.checkpoint_dir)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Note what this enables:

  • from train import build_model works cleanly in a test — no training loop fires
  • DataLoader(num_workers=4) works on Windows — the guard prevents subprocess explosion
  • python -m train --lr 0.01 --epochs 200 works from any directory via -m
  • argparse inside main() does not interfere with imports — sys.argv is not touched at import time

docs.title: Pytest and test discovery
docs.text:
# test_model.py
from train import build_model   # safe — guard prevents main() from running

def test_output_shape():
    model = build_model(num_classes=10)
    x = torch.randn(4, 3, 224, 224)
    y = model(x)
    assert y.shape == (4, 10)

Without the guard, import train would immediately start a training run whenever pytest collects the test file. With the guard, only the definitions are loaded — exactly what the test needs.

docs.title: Hugging Face training scripts
docs.text: The official Hugging Face example scripts (run_clm.py, run_glue.py, etc.) all use this exact structure: functions defined at module level, main() orchestrates, if __name__ == "__main__": main() at the bottom. They are designed to be both run directly and imported in notebooks or sweep scripts.

docs.title: torch.multiprocessing and DataLoader
docs.text:
# Required when num_workers > 0 on Windows/macOS with spawn
if __name__ == "__main__":
    loader = DataLoader(dataset, num_workers=8, batch_size=64)
    for batch in loader:
        ...

PyTorch's documentation explicitly states this requirement. The underlying reason is identical to the multiprocessing case above — the spawn start method re-imports the main module in each worker process.

docs.title: Common Mistakes and Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Putting imports inside the guard

# Wrong — torch is only importable when run directly
if __name__ == "__main__":
    import torch
    import numpy as np

    model = torch.nn.Linear(10, 1)

Imports belong at the top of the file. Other modules that import this file need those names too. Only execution logic belongs inside the guard.

2. Writing the guard without main()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # 300 lines of code
    data = load_data(...)
    model = build_model(...)
    for epoch in range(100):
        ...

Technically correct but untestable and unreadable. Extract into main() (and sub-functions). Keep the guard to one line.

3. Misspelling the dunder strings

if __name__ == "__main__":    # correct
if __name__ == '__main__':    # also correct — single quotes are fine
if __name__ == "__main_ _":   # wrong — space inside — always False, silently
if __Name__ == "__main__":    # wrong — capital N — NameError

Python will not warn you. The block simply never runs.

4. Expecting the guard to prevent execution in subprocesses on Unix

On Linux with the fork start method (the default), child processes are forked — they do not re-import the main module. The guard is not strictly required for multiprocessing on Linux. But write it anyway: your code should be platform-agnostic, and the guard is free.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Concept What to remember __name__ A string attribute Python sets on every module automatically When run directly __name__ == "__main__" → True → guard block executes When imported __name__ == "<module_name>" → False → guard block skipped python -m module Also sets __name__ = "__main__" — use for package entry points main() function Keep the guard thin — one line that calls main() Multiprocessing Guard is required on Windows with spawn; DataLoader(num_workers>0) same Core invariant Definitions always load. Side effects only fire when appropriate.

The pattern enforces one discipline that scales from a 50-line utility script to a 50,000-line ML framework: define behaviour in functions, trigger behaviour explicitly. Importability is not an afterthought — it is a design constraint. Every .py file you write should be safely importable, and the guard is the mechanism that guarantees it.

docs.title: The Core Distinction: Module vs. Package
docs.text:
A module is a single .py file. A package is a directory that Python treats as a namespace — a container for modules and sub-packages.

The mechanism that makes a directory a package is the presence of __init__.py. Without it, Python (in most contexts) treats the directory as just a directory, not an importable namespace.

my_project/
├── utils.py          ← module   (importable as 'utils')
└── models/
    ├── __init__.py   ← this file makes 'models' a package
    ├── resnet.py     ← module inside the package
    └── vgg.py        ← module inside the package

import utils                   # module — works
import models                  # package — works because __init__.py exists
from models import resnet      # submodule — works
from models.resnet import ResNet50  # name inside submodule — works

Remove __init__.py from models/ and import models raises ModuleNotFoundError in Python 3 (unless namespace packages are in play — see below).

docs.title: What __init__.py Actually Is
docs.text:
__init__.py is the initialisation code for the package. When Python imports a package, it executes __init__.py in that package's namespace. Everything defined or imported inside __init__.py becomes an attribute of the package object.

# models/__init__.py
print("models package initialised")    # runs once on first import
VERSION = "1.0.0"

import models
# prints: "models package initialised"
print(models.VERSION)    # "1.0.0"

__init__.py can be — and often is — completely empty. An empty __init__.py still makes the directory a package, but defines no attributes on the package object.

docs.title: The __init__.py as a Public API Controller
docs.text:
The most important use of __init__.py is controlling what the package exposes. A package's internal file layout is an implementation detail. The public API is what you define in __init__.py.

Consider this layout:

models/
├── __init__.py
├── _resnet.py      ← internal implementation
├── _vgg.py         ← internal implementation
└── _transformer.py ← internal implementation

Without any __init__.py wiring, users must know the internal structure:

from models._resnet import ResNet50        # exposes internal layout
from models._transformer import BertModel  # coupled to file names

With a well-designed __init__.py:

# models/__init__.py
from models._resnet import ResNet50
from models._vgg import VGG16
from models._transformer import BertModel

__all__ = ["ResNet50", "VGG16", "BertModel"]

Now users write:

from models import ResNet50    # clean — no internal paths exposed
import models
model = models.BertModel()     # works — BertModel is on the package object

You can reorganise the internal files completely — split _resnet.py into ten files, rename them, restructure — and the user-facing import from models import ResNet50 never changes. The __init__.py is the stable contract.

docs.title: __all__ — Controlling import *
docs.text:
__all__ is a list of strings that defines what from package import * exports. It also serves as explicit documentation of the public API:

# models/__init__.py
from models._resnet import ResNet50, ResNet101
from models._vgg import VGG16
from models._transformer import BertModel

__all__ = [
    "ResNet50",
    "ResNet101",
    "VGG16",
    "BertModel",
]

Without __all__, import * exports everything not prefixed with _. With __all__, it exports exactly the listed names — nothing more. Even names imported into __init__.py that are not in __all__ are excluded from wildcard imports.

__all__ does not prevent direct access — from models import ResNet50 works regardless. It only governs import * and signals intent to readers and static analysis tools.

docs.title: A Realistic ML Project Layout
docs.text:
This is the structure you should build and recognise in every serious ML project:

project/
│
├── src/                          ← source root (or project name)
│   ├── __init__.py
│   │
│   ├── data/                     ← data loading and preprocessing
│   │   ├── __init__.py
│   │   ├── dataset.py
│   │   ├── transforms.py
│   │   └── samplers.py
│   │
│   ├── models/                   ← model definitions
│   │   ├── __init__.py
│   │   ├── backbone.py
│   │   ├── heads.py
│   │   └── losses.py
│   │
│   ├── training/                 ← training logic
│   │   ├── __init__.py
│   │   ├── trainer.py
│   │   ├── optimizer.py
│   │   └── scheduler.py
│   │
│   └── utils/                    ← shared utilities
│       ├── __init__.py
│       ├── metrics.py
│       ├── logging.py
│       └── checkpointing.py
│
├── configs/                      ← configuration files (YAML/JSON)
│   ├── resnet50_baseline.yaml
│   └── transformer_large.yaml
│
├── tests/                        ← test suite
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── test_data.py
│   └── test_models.py
│
├── scripts/                      ← entry points
│   ├── train.py
│   ├── evaluate.py
│   └── export.py
│
├── notebooks/                    ← exploration (not imported)
│   └── eda.ipynb
│
├── setup.py  (or pyproject.toml) ← makes the package installable
└── README.md

Each __init__.py controls the public API of its sub-package. scripts/ contains entry points with if __name__ == "__main__" guards. notebooks/ is never imported. tests/ mirrors src/.

docs.title: Absolute vs. Relative Imports Inside a Package
docs.text: Once code lives inside a package, there are two ways to import between files within that package.

docs.title: Absolute imports (preferred)
docs.text:
# src/training/trainer.py

from src.models import ResNet50           # full path from project root
from src.data.dataset import ImageDataset
from src.utils.metrics import accuracy

Absolute imports work from any context — scripts, tests, notebooks, the REPL. They are always unambiguous. PEP 8 and most style guides prefer them.

docs.title: Relative imports
docs.text:
# src/training/trainer.py

from ..models import ResNet50             # go up one level, then into models
from ..data.dataset import ImageDataset   # go up one level, then into data
from .optimizer import build_optimizer    # same package (training/)

The dots encode directory traversal:

  • . → current package (src/training/)
  • .. → parent package (src/)
  • ... → grandparent package

Relative imports only work inside packages. If you run python src/training/trainer.py directly (not via -m), Python does not know the file is part of a package and raises ImportError: attempted relative import with no known parent package.

Fix: always run package code with python -m:

python -m src.training.trainer    # works — Python resolves the package context
python src/training/trainer.py    # breaks relative imports

docs.title: Namespace Packages — __init__.py-Free Packages (Python 3.3+)
docs.text:
PEP 420 introduced implicit namespace packages: directories without __init__.py can still be imported as packages in Python 3.3+. Python searches all entries on sys.path and assembles a namespace package from all matching directories.

site-packages/
├── mylib/          ← no __init__.py
│   ├── core.py
│   └── utils.py

import mylib.core    # works in Python 3.3+ even without __init__.py

When namespace packages are useful: splitting a single logical package across multiple directories or repositories (e.g., plugin systems, namespace packages like google.cloud, google.auth that ship separately but share the google namespace).

When to use explicit __init__.py: almost always. For application code, libraries, and ML projects, the explicit file gives you API control, initialisation logic, and unambiguous package identity. Use namespace packages only when you specifically need the split-directory behaviour.

The practical rule: if you intend to import it, give it an __init__.py.

docs.title: Making a Package Installable — setup.py and pyproject.toml
docs.text:
A package with __init__.py is importable only if its parent directory is on sys.path. For development, the cleanest solution is an editable install:

# pyproject.toml (modern — PEP 517/518)
[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools >= 61"]
build-backend = "setuptools.backends.legacy:build"

[project]
name = "my-ml-project"
version = "0.1.0"
dependencies = [
    "torch>=2.0",
    "numpy>=1.24",
]

pip install -e .     # editable install — src/ goes on sys.path permanently

After this, from src.models import ResNet50 works from anywhere — scripts, notebooks, test runners — without any sys.path manipulation. The -e flag means changes to your source files are reflected immediately without reinstalling.

Without an editable install, you would need:

import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "/path/to/project")   # fragile, machine-specific, wrong

Never do this in project code. Use editable installs instead.

docs.title: The __init__.py Execution Order
docs.text:
When Python imports a nested package, it executes __init__.py files from the outermost level inward:

from src.models.resnet import ResNet50

Execution order:

  1. src/__init__.py
  2. src/models/__init__.py
  3. src/models/resnet.py — then binds ResNet50 in the caller's namespace

Each __init__.py runs exactly once (cached in sys.modules as "src" and "src.models"). Subsequent imports of the same package skip re-execution.

import sys
import src.models

print("src" in sys.modules)         # True
print("src.models" in sys.modules)  # True
print("src.models.resnet" in sys.modules)  # False — not imported yet

docs.title: Visualisation — Import Resolution for a Nested Package
docs.text:
from src.models.resnet import ResNet50
         │       │       │
         │       │       └─ 3. Execute resnet.py
         │       │             Bind ResNet50 in caller namespace
         │       │
         │       └─ 2. Execute src/models/__init__.py
         │               Add to sys.modules as "src.models"
         │
         └─ 1. Execute src/__init__.py
                 Add to sys.modules as "src"


sys.modules after the import:
{
  "src":               <module 'src'>
  "src.models":        <module 'src.models'>
  "src.models.resnet": <module 'src.models.resnet'>
}

Caller's namespace:
{
  "ResNet50": <class 'src.models.resnet.ResNet50'>
}

docs.title: Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
How PyTorch is structured — reading framework source
docs.text:
PyTorch's package structure is the canonical example:

torch/
├── __init__.py          ← re-exports Tensor, nn, optim, etc.
├── nn/
│   ├── __init__.py      ← re-exports Module, Linear, Conv2d, etc.
│   ├── modules/
│   │   ├── __init__.py  ← re-exports all layer classes
│   │   ├── linear.py    ← defines Linear
│   │   ├── conv.py      ← defines Conv1d, Conv2d, Conv3d
│   │   └── ...
│   └── functional.py    ← stateless functions (relu, softmax, etc.)
├── optim/
│   ├── __init__.py      ← re-exports SGD, Adam, etc.
│   ├── sgd.py
│   ├── adam.py
│   └── ...
└── utils/
    └── data/
        ├── __init__.py  ← re-exports Dataset, DataLoader
        ├── dataset.py
        └── dataloader.py

When you write from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, you are not importing from torch/utils/data/__init__.py directly — DataLoader is defined in dataloader.py and re-exported through __init__.py. The __init__.py is the stable public API; the .py files inside are implementation details you can read but should not depend on.

This is why from torch.utils.data.dataloader import DataLoader also works but is considered bad practice — it couples you to the internal layout, which can change across versions.

docs.title: Building a training library as a package
docs.text:
# src/models/__init__.py

from src.models.backbone import ResNet50, ResNet101, EfficientNetB0
from src.models.heads import ClassificationHead, DetectionHead
from src.models.losses import FocalLoss, LabelSmoothingCrossEntropy

__all__ = [
    "ResNet50", "ResNet101", "EfficientNetB0",
    "ClassificationHead", "DetectionHead",
    "FocalLoss", "LabelSmoothingCrossEntropy",
]

# src/data/__init__.py

from src.data.dataset import ImageDataset, VideoDataset
from src.data.transforms import TrainTransform, ValTransform
from src.data.samplers import BalancedBatchSampler

__all__ = [
    "ImageDataset", "VideoDataset",
    "TrainTransform", "ValTransform",
    "BalancedBatchSampler",
]

Now your training script reads cleanly:

# scripts/train.py
from src.models import ResNet50, FocalLoss
from src.data import ImageDataset, TrainTransform
from src.training import Trainer
from src.utils import setup_logging, save_checkpoint

The imports read like English. The internal structure is invisible. This is what package design achieves.

docs.title: Hugging Face transformers — the registry pattern via __init__.py
docs.text:
HuggingFace uses __init__.py to implement a lazy loading registry — a sophisticated pattern where the __init__.py defines placeholder objects that only load the real module when accessed:

# Simplified sketch of transformers/__init__.py
from transformers.utils import _LazyModule

_import_structure = {
    "models.bert": ["BertModel", "BertTokenizer", "BertConfig"],
    "models.gpt2": ["GPT2Model", "GPT2Tokenizer"],
    # ... hundreds more
}

import sys
sys.modules[__name__] = _LazyModule(__name__, ..., _import_structure)

When you write from transformers import BertModel, the lazy module intercepts the attribute access and only then imports models/bert/modeling_bert.py. This makes import transformers instantaneous even though the library contains hundreds of models.

This is an advanced application of the same principle: __init__.py controls the public API and can interpose arbitrary logic between the caller and the underlying modules.

docs.title: pytest test discovery and __init__.py
docs.text:
pytest has two modes:

With __init__.py in tests/: pytest treats tests as part of a package. Imports are absolute and must be consistent with the installed package. This is the correct setup when you have a src/ layout with an editable install.

Without __init__.py in tests/: pytest uses its own import mechanism (rootdir insertion). This is simpler for small projects but can cause import conflicts when test files share names across directories.

The rule: if you have src/ with __init__.py, also put __init__.py in tests/ and use editable installs. Consistency throughout.

docs.title: Common Mistakes and Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Missing __init__.py and wondering why imports fail

src/
├── models/         ← NO __init__.py
│   └── resnet.py

from src.models import resnet   # ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'src.models'

Fix: add src/models/__init__.py (can be empty).

2. Circular imports through __init__.py

# src/models/__init__.py
from src.models.resnet import ResNet50   # imports resnet.py

# src/models/resnet.py
from src.models import ResNet101         # imports __init__.py again → circular

__init__.py imports resnet.py, which imports __init__.py, which is still being initialised. ResNet101 may not exist yet.

Fix: in resnet.py, import from the specific module, not from the package:

# src/models/resnet.py
from src.models.resnext import ResNet101   # direct — no circular path

3. Doing heavy work in __init__.py

# src/models/__init__.py — BAD
import torch
model_registry = {}
for name in ["resnet50", "vgg16", "bert"]:
    model_registry[name] = load_pretrained_weights(name)  # downloads 500MB each

__init__.py runs on every import src.models. If it does slow or stateful work, every test, every import, every subprocess pays that cost. Keep __init__.py to re-exports and minimal initialisation. Move expensive work into functions called explicitly.

4. Relative imports in scripts run directly

# src/models/resnet.py
from .backbone import ConvBlock   # relative import

# Then:
python src/models/resnet.py       # ImportError: attempted relative import
python -m src.models.resnet       # works — package context known

Always use python -m for files that use relative imports.

5. Shadowing package names with local files

project/
├── torch.py        ← YOUR file, named after a package
└── train.py

# train.py
import torch        # imports YOUR torch.py, not PyTorch

sys.path puts the current directory first. Your torch.py shadows PyTorch. This produces AttributeError: module 'torch' has no attribute 'nn' with no obvious cause. Never name files after packages you import.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Concept What to remember __init__.py Makes a directory a package; its code runs once on first import Empty __init__.py Valid — marks the directory as a package with no extra attributes API control Re-export names in __init__.py to define a stable public interface __all__ Controls import *; documents the public API for tools and readers Absolute imports Always unambiguous; preferred for application code Relative imports Package-internal shorthand; requires -m execution, breaks in scripts Namespace packages No __init__.py needed in Python 3.3+, but explicit is almost always better Editable install pip install -e . — the right way to make your package importable everywhere Execution order Outermost __init__.py first, inward; all cached in sys.modules

The __init__.py is the boundary surface of your package — the only thing the outside world should need to know about. Define it carefully, keep it thin, and the internal structure of your package becomes freely refactorable without breaking any caller.
