docs.title: 52. Mutability vs. Immutability in Depth
docs.text: Tags: #python #memory-model #execution-model #objects #ai-ml-relevance Prerequisites: [[01.Variables, data types]] · [[12.Lists]] · [[13.Tuples]] · [[26.Classes and objects]] · [[48.Importing modules]] Next: [[53.Shallow vs deep copy]] · [[54.How Python manages memory]] · [[55.Pass-by-object-reference behavior]] Phase: Phase 3 — Before writing ML code

docs.title: The Central Claim
docs.text:
In Python, every value is an object, and every object is either mutable or immutable. This is not a style preference or a performance hint — it is a fundamental property of the object that governs how assignment, function calls, container operations, and memory sharing behave.

Misunderstanding mutability is the source of an entire class of bugs that are silent, hard to reproduce, and devastating in ML pipelines where data flows through many transformations.

docs.title: What Mutability Means, Precisely
docs.text:
An object is immutable if its value cannot change after it is created. The bits that represent its content are fixed for its lifetime.

An object is mutable if its internal state can be modified in-place — without creating a new object, without changing the object's identity.

Python's identity operator is checks identity — whether two names point to the same object in memory, as measured by id():

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a              # b and a point to the same list object
b.append(4)

print(a)           # [1, 2, 3, 4] — a sees the change
print(a is b)      # True — same object
print(id(a) == id(b))  # True — same memory address

The list was mutated. Its identity (id) did not change. The object at that address now contains different data.

Compare with an immutable object:

x = "hello"
y = x
y = y + " world"   # creates a NEW string object

print(x)           # "hello" — unchanged
print(x is y)      # False — different objects

y + " world" did not modify the string at y's address. It created a fresh string and rebound the name y to it. The original "hello" object is untouched.

docs.title: The Complete Mutability Table
docs.text:
Type Mutable? Notes int No Rebinding creates a new object float No IEEE 754, fixed on creation complex No Fixed on creation bool No Subclass of int str No Unicode sequence, fixed on creation bytes No Immutable byte sequence tuple No* The tuple itself; contained mutables can change frozenset No Immutable version of set NoneType No Singleton list Yes Elements can be added, removed, changed dict Yes Keys/values can be added, removed, changed set Yes Elements can be added, removed bytearray Yes Mutable version of bytes array.array Yes Typed mutable array class instances Yes (default) Unless __setattr__ is overridden numpy.ndarray Yes In-place operations modify the buffer

*Tuples deserve special attention — see below.

docs.title: Identity, Equality, and the Integer Cache
docs.text:
Python caches small integers (typically −5 to 256) as singletons. This is a CPython implementation detail, not a language guarantee:

a = 256
b = 256
print(a is b)    # True  — same cached object

a = 257
b = 257
print(a is b)    # False — separate objects (outside cache range)
print(a == b)    # True  — same value

The rule this enforces: use == for value comparison, is for identity comparison. The only objects you should check identity for are None, True, and False (which are singletons):

if x is None:     # correct
if x == None:     # works but misleading — suggests value comparison

String interning is another caching mechanism — Python may intern string literals that look like identifiers:

a = "hello"
b = "hello"
print(a is b)     # True  — interned (CPython, compile-time constant)

a = "hello world"
b = "hello world"
print(a is b)     # False (usually) — spaces make interning less likely

Never rely on string interning for correctness. Use ==.

docs.title: The Aliasing Problem — Mutable Objects and Shared References
docs.text:
The most consequential consequence of mutability:

original = [1, 2, 3]
alias    = original      # both names point to the same list

alias.append(4)
print(original)          # [1, 2, 3, 4] — you modified 'original' via 'alias'

This is aliasing: two names bound to the same object. With immutable objects, aliasing is harmless — you cannot modify the shared object, so both names always see the same value. With mutable objects, aliasing means any modification through one name is visible through all others.

def add_element(lst):
    lst.append(99)        # modifies the object in place

data = [1, 2, 3]
add_element(data)
print(data)              # [1, 2, 3, 99] — the caller's list was modified

This is Python's pass-by-object-reference semantics (covered in depth in [[55.Pass-by-object-reference behavior]]). The function received the same list object — it did not receive a copy.

docs.title: Tuples — Immutability with a Caveat
docs.text:
A tuple is immutable: you cannot add, remove, or replace its elements. But if a tuple contains a mutable object, that object can still be mutated:

t = ([1, 2], [3, 4])

t[0].append(99)      # legal — we're mutating the list, not the tuple
print(t)             # ([1, 2, 99], [3, 4])

t[0] = [5, 6]        # TypeError — cannot rebind tuple element

The tuple guarantees that the references it holds do not change. It does not guarantee that the objects those references point to do not change. The tuple at a fixed memory address always contains the same two references — but the list at the other end of the first reference can be arbitrarily modified.

This distinction matters for hashing: tuples are hashable (usable as dict keys) only if all their contained objects are also hashable:

t1 = (1, 2, 3)
hash(t1)             # works — all ints are hashable

t2 = ([1, 2], 3)
hash(t2)             # TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'

docs.title: Immutability and Hashability
docs.text:
Only immutable objects can be used as dictionary keys or set members. The invariant: if an object's value could change, its hash could change, which would break the hash table's ability to find it.

d = {}
d[(1, 2)] = "a tuple key"      # works
d[[1, 2]] = "a list key"        # TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'

s = {1, "hello", (1, 2)}        # works — int, str, tuple are hashable
s = {1, [1, 2]}                 # TypeError

Custom class instances are hashable by default (using id() as the hash). If you override __eq__, you must also override __hash__ — or Python sets __hash__ = None, making your object unhashable. This is the correctness invariant: equal objects must have equal hashes.

docs.title: Rebinding vs. Mutating — The Critical Distinction
docs.text:
These two operations look similar but are fundamentally different:

# REBINDING — creates a new object, changes what the name points to
x = 5
x = x + 1          # x now points to the integer 6; the integer 5 still exists

lst = [1, 2, 3]
lst = lst + [4]     # creates a new list; the original [1, 2, 3] is unchanged


# MUTATING — modifies the existing object in place
lst = [1, 2, 3]
lst.append(4)       # same list object, now containing [1, 2, 3, 4]
lst += [5]          # += on lists calls __iadd__ → in-place mutation, NOT rebinding

The += behaviour is subtle and bites even experienced programmers:

# For immutable types: += rebinds
x = 5
print(id(x))        # some address
x += 1
print(id(x))        # different address — new int object

# For mutable types: += mutates in place
lst = [1, 2, 3]
print(id(lst))      # some address
lst += [4]          # calls lst.__iadd__([4]) → extends in place
print(id(lst))      # same address — same list object

This creates an asymmetry: lst += [4] and lst = lst + [4] both result in lst containing [1, 2, 3, 4], but:

  • lst += [4] mutates the original list (visible to all aliases)
  • lst = lst + [4] creates a new list (aliases still see the original)
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a

a += [4]            # mutates in place
print(b)            # [1, 2, 3, 4] — b sees it

a = a + [5]         # rebinds a to a new list
print(b)            # [1, 2, 3, 4] — b does NOT see this

docs.title: Mutable Default Arguments — The Classic Trap
docs.text:
This is one of the most notorious Python gotchas, rooted entirely in mutability:

def append_to(element, lst=[]):    # lst=[] created ONCE when function is defined
    lst.append(element)
    return lst

print(append_to(1))    # [1]
print(append_to(2))    # [2] — expected, but...
print(append_to(3))    # [3] — wait
# Actually:
# [1]
# [1, 2]
# [1, 2, 3]

The default value [] is a mutable object created once when the def statement executes. It persists as an attribute of the function object (append_to.__defaults__) and is shared across all calls that use the default. Every call that does not pass lst mutates the same list.

The fix: use None as the sentinel and create a fresh list inside the function:

def append_to(element, lst=None):
    if lst is None:
        lst = []
    lst.append(element)
    return lst

print(append_to(1))    # [1]
print(append_to(2))    # [2]
print(append_to(3))    # [3]

This applies to any mutable default: [], {}, set(), custom class instances. Immutable defaults (None, 0, "", ()) are safe because they cannot be modified.

docs.title: Immutability for Correctness — Using tuple and frozenset
docs.text:
When you want to guarantee data is not modified, reach for immutable types:

# Coordinates should not change — tuple over list
point = (3.14, 2.71)

# A fixed set of allowed labels — frozenset over set
VALID_LABELS = frozenset({"cat", "dog", "bird"})

# Config values that should not be mutated after setup
Config = collections.namedtuple("Config", ["lr", "epochs", "batch_size"])
cfg = Config(lr=0.001, epochs=90, batch_size=256)
cfg.lr = 0.01    # AttributeError — namedtuple is immutable

frozenset is hashable, so it can be used as a dict key or set member — useful for caching results keyed on sets of features.

docs.title: Visualisation — Object Model
docs.text:
Immutable (int, str, tuple, ...):

  name ──► [ object | value: fixed ]
              id: 0x7f1a

  rebinding:
  name ──► [ object | value: fixed ]   (new object, new id)
              id: 0x7f2b

  the old object at 0x7f1a is unchanged


Mutable (list, dict, set, ndarray, ...):

  name_a ──┐
            ├──► [ object | state: changeable ]
  name_b ──┘       id: 0x7f1a

  mutation:
  name_a ──┐
            ├──► [ object | state: CHANGED ]
  name_b ──┘       id: 0x7f1a  (same address — same object)

  name_a and name_b both see the change

docs.title: Connection to AI / Machine Learning / Deep Learning
docs.text: Mutability is not an abstract Python concern in ML — it is the mechanism behind how tensors work, why gradient computation is correct, and how data pipelines can silently corrupt themselves.

docs.title: NumPy — Views vs. Copies
docs.text:
NumPy arrays are mutable. More critically, many NumPy operations return views — objects that share the underlying memory buffer with the original array:

import numpy as np

a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
b = a[1:4]          # b is a VIEW of a, not a copy

b[0] = 99
print(a)            # [1, 99, 3, 4, 5] — a was modified through b
print(np.shares_memory(a, b))  # True

Slicing a NumPy array returns a view. Fancy indexing (boolean mask, integer array) returns a copy. This asymmetry is the source of countless ML bugs:

# Which one gives you a view?
b = a[1:3]          # view — slice notation
b = a[[1, 2]]       # copy — fancy indexing
b = a[a > 2]        # copy — boolean mask
b = a.reshape(1, -1)  # view (if possible)
b = a.T             # view — transpose shares memory

# To guarantee a copy:
b = a.copy()
b = a[1:3].copy()

In a preprocessing pipeline, if you slice a batch and then normalise the slice in-place, you normalise the original data too. This corrupts your dataset silently.

# Dangerous pattern in a data pipeline
def normalize(batch):
    batch -= batch.mean()      # in-place on the view
    batch /= batch.std()
    return batch

data = np.random.randn(1000, 128)
sample = data[:32]             # view
normalized = normalize(sample) # mutates data[:32] in place
# data is now partially normalised — the rest of it is not

Fix: either pass data[:32].copy() or use batch = batch - batch.mean() (rebinding, creates a new array).

docs.title: PyTorch — In-Place Operations and Autograd
docs.text:
PyTorch tensors are mutable, and in-place operations are marked with a trailing underscore by convention:

import torch

x = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])

x.add_(1)       # in-place — modifies x, same storage
x.mul_(2)       # in-place
x.zero_()       # in-place — zeros all elements
x.fill_(5.0)    # in-place

x = x + 1      # out-of-place — creates a new tensor, rebinds x
x = x * 2      # out-of-place

Critical: in-place operations on tensors that are part of the computation graph will raise a RuntimeError or silently corrupt gradients:

x = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0], requires_grad=True)
y = x * 2
x.add_(1)       # RuntimeError: a leaf Variable that requires grad
                # has been used in an in-place operation

PyTorch tracks the computation graph by recording operations. An in-place mutation changes the value that an earlier node in the graph depended on — making the stored value wrong for backward pass computation. PyTorch detects this and raises an error for leaf tensors, but not always for intermediate tensors, where silent gradient corruption is possible.

The rule: never mutate tensors in-place if they require gradients or if they are inputs to a computation you will differentiate through. Use out-of-place operations in forward() and reserve in-place for operations where you are certain no gradient flows through the mutated tensor (e.g., weight initialisation, zeroing gradients).

# Correct: zero gradients after stepping
optimizer.zero_grad()          # calls grad.zero_() — safe, no backward after this

# Correct: weight initialisation before any forward pass
with torch.no_grad():
    model.fc.weight.fill_(0.0) # in-place, no graph built

docs.title: PyTorch — Shared Memory in DataLoader
docs.text:
When num_workers > 0, PyTorch's DataLoader passes tensors between processes using shared memory. Tensors from the same batch may share an underlying storage buffer. If your collate_fn or dataset's __getitem__ mutates the tensor in-place:

def collate_fn(batch):
    images, labels = zip(*batch)
    images = torch.stack(images)
    images -= images.mean()    # in-place normalisation on shared memory
    return images, torch.tensor(labels)

The mutation may be visible in the worker process's memory and cause corrupted batches in subsequent iterations. Use out-of-place operations in data loading code.

docs.title: Immutable Configs — Protecting Hyperparameters
docs.text:
from typing import NamedTuple

class TrainConfig(NamedTuple):
    learning_rate: float = 1e-3
    batch_size:    int   = 256
    epochs:        int   = 90
    weight_decay:  float = 1e-4

cfg = TrainConfig(learning_rate=0.01, epochs=50)
cfg.learning_rate = 0.001    # AttributeError — immutable

# Dataclasses with frozen=True:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ModelConfig:
    num_layers:  int   = 12
    hidden_dim:  int   = 768
    dropout:     float = 0.1

mcfg = ModelConfig()
mcfg.num_layers = 24    # FrozenInstanceError — immutable

Experiment configs should be immutable after construction. If training code can mutate the config object, you cannot trust the config file to accurately record what a run actually used.

docs.title: Caching with Immutable Keys — functools.lru_cache
docs.text:
import functools
import numpy as np

@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=128)
def compute_kernel(sigma: float, size: int) -> tuple:
    # Returns a tuple (immutable) for safe caching
    x = np.arange(size) - size // 2
    kernel = np.exp(-x**2 / (2 * sigma**2))
    kernel /= kernel.sum()
    return tuple(kernel)    # convert to tuple — hashable and immutable

lru_cache requires hashable arguments. NumPy arrays are mutable and unhashable — you cannot cache on them directly. The pattern: convert to tuples or use the relevant immutable parameters as keys.

docs.title: Common Mistakes and Pitfalls
docs.text:
1. Confusing == and is

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [1, 2, 3]
print(a == b)    # True  — same value
print(a is b)    # False — different objects

2. Mutable default arguments (covered above — the canonical Python gotcha)

3. Assuming tuple prevents all mutation

t = ([1, 2], [3, 4])
t[0].append(99)   # legal — tuple's references are fixed, contents are not

4. NumPy slice is a view, not a copy

b = a[1:4]
b[0] = 99         # modifies a — use a[1:4].copy() if you need isolation

5. In-place PyTorch ops breaking autograd

x.add_(1)         # RuntimeError if x is a leaf with requires_grad=True

6. += on lists mutates; += on ints rebinds

a = b = [1, 2, 3]
a += [4]          # mutates — b sees it
a = a + [5]       # rebinds a — b does not see it

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Concept Rule Mutable objects list, dict, set, ndarray, class instances — modified in place Immutable objects int, float, str, tuple, frozenset, bytes — never modified Aliasing Two names → same mutable object → mutation visible through both Rebinding Name points to a new object — other names are unaffected += on mutables Calls __iadd__ → mutates in place → same id += on immutables Creates new object → rebinds name → new id Mutable defaults Use None sentinel — never [], {}, or other mutables Tuples References fixed; contained mutables can still change NumPy slices Views by default — use .copy() to guarantee isolation PyTorch in-place Trailing _ convention; illegal on graph-participating tensors

The governing principle: names are labels, not containers. Assignment always binds a label to an object. Whether that object can change is a property of the object, not the label. Understanding this — deeply, not superficially — is what separates programmers who debug mutability bugs in ten minutes from those who spend three days on them.

docs.title: 53. Shallow vs Deep Copy
docs.text: "Copying an object and copying what it points to are two entirely different operations. Most bugs in this space come from not knowing which one you did."

docs.title: The Core Problem
docs.text:
When you write b = a in Python, you are not creating a copy. You are creating a second label pointing to the same object in memory. This is assignment, not copying.

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a           # b and a point to the same list

b.append(4)
print(a)        # [1, 2, 3, 4]  ← a was "mutated" through b

This surprises people. The fix is to copy — but the word "copy" hides a crucial distinction.

docs.title: Mental Model: The Box-and-Arrow Diagram
docs.text:
Before any formal definition, draw this in your head.

Assignment (b = a):
    a ──────────────┐
                    ▼
                 [1, [2, 3], 4]
                    ▲
    b ──────────────┘

Shallow Copy (b = a.copy()):
    a ──────► [1,  ●──────────────► [2, 3],  4]
                   │
    b ──────► [1,  ●──────────────► [2, 3],  4]
                   │                   ▲
                   └───────────────────┘
              (outer lists differ, inner list is shared)

Deep Copy (b = copy.deepcopy(a)):
    a ──────► [1,  ●──────────────► [2, 3],  4]

    b ──────► [1,  ●──────────────► [2, 3],  4]
              (completely independent at every level)

The nested list [2, 3] is the trap. A shallow copy creates a new outer container but still shares the inner objects. A deep copy recursively copies everything.

docs.title: Shallow Copy
docs.text:
A shallow copy creates a new container object but fills it with references to the same child objects as the original.

import copy

original = [1, [2, 3], 4]
shallow  = copy.copy(original)        # or original.copy() or original[:]

print(original is shallow)            # False  ← different outer lists
print(original[1] is shallow[1])      # True   ← same inner list object

shallow[0] = 99
print(original[0])                    # 1  ← unaffected (int is immutable)

shallow[1].append(99)
print(original[1])                    # [2, 3, 99]  ← AFFECTED (shared mutable object)

Mutation of an immutable child (like int, str, tuple) is safe — those objects cannot be changed in place. Mutation of a mutable child (like list, dict, set) propagates back to the original.

docs.title: Deep Copy
docs.text:
A deep copy recursively creates new objects for every level of nesting. The result is fully independent of the original.

import copy

original = [1, [2, 3], 4]
deep     = copy.deepcopy(original)

print(original is deep)               # False
print(original[1] is deep[1])         # False  ← different inner list objects

deep[1].append(99)
print(original[1])                    # [2, 3]  ← completely unaffected

docs.title: Ways to Shallow Copy (and when each appears)
docs.text:
Method Works on Notes a.copy() list, dict, set The cleanest, most readable a[:] list, str, tuple Slice syntax; returns same type list(a) / dict(a) any iterable / mapping Constructor call copy.copy(a) any object General-purpose; works on custom classes 
lst  = [1, 2, 3]
d    = {"x": 1, "y": 2}
s    = {1, 2, 3}

lst_copy  = lst[:]          # shallow copy of list
dict_copy = d.copy()        # shallow copy of dict
set_copy  = s.copy()        # shallow copy of set

All four methods above are shallow. None of them protect nested mutable objects.

docs.title: Deep Copy: copy.deepcopy
docs.text:
import copy

data = {"users": ["alice", "bob"], "scores": [95, 87]}

snapshot = copy.deepcopy(data)
data["users"].append("charlie")

print(snapshot["users"])    # ["alice", "bob"]  ← untouched

deepcopy handles:

  • Arbitrary nesting depth
  • Circular references (via a memo dict — it tracks already-copied objects)
  • Custom classes (via __deepcopy__ if defined)

docs.title: The Numpy / PyTorch Connection (Critical for ML)
docs.text: This is not an academic exercise. Shallow-vs-deep copy is one of the most common sources of bugs in numerical computing and ML code.

docs.title: NumPy: Three Levels of "Copy"
docs.text:
import numpy as np

a = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])

# 1. No copy — same array, same data buffer
b = a
b[0] = 99
print(a[0])           # 99  — a is mutated

# 2. View (shallow) — same data buffer, different array object
v = a.view()
v[0] = 0
print(a[0])           # 0   — still shares underlying data

v = a[1:3]            # Slicing in NumPy returns a VIEW, not a copy
v[0] = -1
print(a)              # [ 0 -1  3  4]  ← a[1] changed

# 3. Deep copy — completely independent data buffer
c = a.copy()
c[0] = 999
print(a[0])           # 0   — a is unaffected

Key rule: NumPy slices are views, not copies. This is an intentional design for memory efficiency, but it means arr[start:end] is a live window into the original array.

# Dangerous pattern in data preprocessing:
train = X[:800]    # This is a VIEW of X
train -= train.mean()   # This modifies X in place too!

# Safe pattern:
train = X[:800].copy()
train -= train.mean()

docs.title: PyTorch: .detach(), .clone(), and the Computation Graph
docs.text:
In PyTorch, tensors carry a computation graph for automatic differentiation. Copy semantics interact with gradients.

import torch

x = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], requires_grad=True)

# view / slice: shares data AND stays in the computation graph
y = x[1:]

# detach: new tensor, shares data, severs from computation graph
z = x.detach()        # z will not receive gradients

# clone: new tensor, independent data, stays in computation graph
w = x.clone()         # safe copy for in-place operations in training loops

# clone().detach(): fully independent, no gradient tracking
snapshot = x.clone().detach()
Operation New Data Buffer In Computation Graph x[i:j] or x.view(...) No (shared) Yes x.detach() No (shared) No x.clone() Yes Yes x.clone().detach() Yes No

In training loops, failing to .clone() before in-place modification is a silent bug that corrupts gradients or tensors stored in a replay buffer.

docs.title: Custom Classes and __copy__ / __deepcopy__
docs.text:
import copy

class ModelConfig:
    def __init__(self, layers, hyperparams):
        self.layers      = layers         # mutable list
        self.hyperparams = hyperparams    # mutable dict

    def __copy__(self):
        # Shallow: new object, but same layers/hyperparams lists
        new = ModelConfig.__new__(ModelConfig)
        new.__dict__.update(self.__dict__)
        return new

    def __deepcopy__(self, memo):
        # Deep: new object with independently copied contents
        new = ModelConfig.__new__(ModelConfig)
        memo[id(self)] = new
        new.layers      = copy.deepcopy(self.layers, memo)
        new.hyperparams = copy.deepcopy(self.hyperparams, memo)
        return new

The memo dict in __deepcopy__ is passed by the deepcopy machinery to handle circular references — without it, an object that references itself would cause infinite recursion.

docs.title: Worked Example: Why This Destroys ML Experiments
docs.text:
# Bug: shallow copy of hyperparameter dicts in a sweep
base_config = {"lr": 0.01, "layers": [64, 128, 64]}

configs = []
for dropout in [0.1, 0.3, 0.5]:
    cfg = base_config.copy()        # SHALLOW COPY
    cfg["dropout"] = dropout
    cfg["layers"].append(32)        # Mutates base_config["layers"]!
    configs.append(cfg)

print(base_config["layers"])        # [64, 128, 64, 32, 32, 32]  ← corrupted

# Fix:
import copy
configs = []
for dropout in [0.1, 0.3, 0.5]:
    cfg = copy.deepcopy(base_config)
    cfg["dropout"] = dropout
    cfg["layers"].append(32)
    configs.append(cfg)

print(base_config["layers"])        # [64, 128, 64]  ← safe

docs.title: When to Use What
docs.text:
Object with no nested mutables (int, str, tuple of ints)
    → Assignment is safe. No copy needed.

Object with one level of nesting (list of ints, dict of strs)
    → Shallow copy is sufficient and faster.

Object with nested mutable containers (list of lists, dict of lists)
    → Use deepcopy.

NumPy array you're about to modify
    → arr.copy() before modification, especially after slicing.

PyTorch tensor for inference logging / replay buffer
    → tensor.clone().detach()

Custom class in a sweep or multi-trial experiment
    → deepcopy to guarantee independent state per trial.

docs.title: Performance Note
docs.text:
deepcopy is significantly slower than copy because it must traverse the entire object graph. For large nested structures in hot loops (e.g., batching training data), profile before defaulting to deepcopy. Often the right design is to restructure so that sharing is intentional and controlled, rather than copying everything defensively.

import copy, timeit

data = {"matrix": list(range(10000))}

t_shallow = timeit.timeit(lambda: copy.copy(data),     number=10000)
t_deep    = timeit.timeit(lambda: copy.deepcopy(data), number=10000)

print(f"Shallow: {t_shallow:.3f}s")
print(f"Deep:    {t_deep:.3f}s")
# Shallow: ~0.003s
# Deep:    ~2.1s   ← ~700x slower on this data

docs.title: Summary Table
docs.text: Operation New Object Nested Shared Use When b = a No Yes (everything shared) Intentional alias copy.copy(a) Yes Yes (nested shared) Flat container, or nested is immutable copy.deepcopy(a) Yes No (fully independent) Nested mutable, experiment configs np_arr.copy() Yes N/A (flat data buffer) NumPy in-place ops after slicing tensor.clone() Yes N/A PyTorch in-place ops, keep gradient tensor.clone().detach() Yes N/A PyTorch snapshot, no gradient

docs.title: 54. How Python Manages Memory (Reference Counting Basics)
docs.text: "Python does not give you manual control over memory — but if you do not understand what it is doing automatically, you will write code that is silently slower, leaks, or behaves in ways that seem like magic."

docs.title: The Central Idea
docs.text:
In C or C++, you call malloc to request memory and free to release it. You are the memory manager. In Python, you never call free. Instead, Python tracks how many names (references) point to each object. When that count hits zero, the object is destroyed and its memory is reclaimed automatically. This mechanism is called reference counting.

Everything else in this note is a consequence of that one design decision.

docs.title: Objects, Not Variables
docs.text:
First, the mental model must be right. Python does not store values inside variables. It stores values in objects, and variables are labels (references) that point to objects.

x = 300
y = x

Memory heap:

    int object (value=300, refcount=2)
         ▲       ▲
         │       │
         x       y

Both x and y point to the same integer object. The refcount is 2 because two names reference it.

x = "hello"   # x now points elsewhere

    int object (value=300, refcount=1)   ← refcount dropped to 1
         ▲
         │
         y

    str object (value="hello", refcount=1)
         ▲
         │
         x

When y also gets reassigned or goes out of scope, the int object's refcount drops to 0, and Python immediately deallocates it.

docs.title: The Reference Count in CPython
docs.text:
Every object in CPython (the standard Python interpreter) has a hidden integer field called ob_refcnt. Python's C API exposes this via sys.getrefcount:

import sys

a = [1, 2, 3]
print(sys.getrefcount(a))    # 2
#                              ^^
#  Why 2? Because passing `a` to getrefcount itself creates
#  a temporary reference inside the function call.

b = a
print(sys.getrefcount(a))    # 3  (a, b, and the getrefcount argument)

del b
print(sys.getrefcount(a))    # 2  (a and the getrefcount argument)

The count is always +1 higher than you expect because the function call holds a temporary reference. Subtract 1 to get the true count.

docs.title: What Increments the Reference Count
docs.text:
A reference is created whenever a new name binds to an existing object:

a = []          # refcount = 1  (name 'a')
b = a           # refcount = 2  (names 'a', 'b')
c = [a, a]      # refcount = 4  (names 'a', 'b', and two slots in c)

def f(x): pass
f(a)            # refcount temporarily +1 during the call, then back down

Every slot in a container (list element, dict value, object attribute) is also a reference:

lst = [None] * 3
lst[0] = a       # refcount +1 (the list slot holds a reference)

docs.title: What Decrements the Reference Count
docs.text:
Operation Effect del x Removes the name binding; refcount −1 Variable goes out of scope All its bindings are released lst.remove(obj) / lst.pop() Removes element reference; refcount −1 lst[i] = new_val Replaces slot; old object loses one reference Function returns Local variables are released 
def example():
    data = [1, 2, 3]    # refcount of list = 1
    return              # data goes out of scope, refcount → 0, list is destroyed

When the refcount hits zero, Python calls the object's destructor (__del__ if defined), frees the memory back to Python's internal allocator, and — when the allocator sees fit — returns it to the OS.

docs.title: Small Integer Caching and String Interning
docs.text:
Python pre-creates objects for integers −5 through 256 and reuses them. This is called the integer cache (or small int cache).

a = 100
b = 100
print(a is b)    # True  — same cached object

a = 300
b = 300
print(a is b)    # False — outside cache range, two separate objects

For 100:
    a ──────► int(100)  [cached singleton]
    b ──────► int(100)  [same object]

For 300:
    a ──────► int(300)  [object A]
    b ──────► int(300)  [object B, independent]

This is why you must never use is to compare integers (or strings). Use ==. The is operator tests object identity (same memory address), not equality.

# WRONG
if user_id is 200:
    ...

# CORRECT
if user_id == 200:
    ...

Python also interns short strings that look like identifiers (letters, digits, underscores). String literals in the same compilation unit may be deduplicated.

s1 = "hello"
s2 = "hello"
print(s1 is s2)     # True in CPython (interned)

s1 = "hello world"
s2 = "hello world"
print(s1 is s2)     # False in general (not guaranteed)

Rule: never rely on string identity. The interning behaviour is an implementation detail, not a language guarantee.

docs.title: The Garbage Collector: Handling Cycles
docs.text:
Reference counting has one fundamental weakness: circular references.

a = []
b = []
a.append(b)    # a references b
b.append(a)    # b references a

    list A  ──────────────────► list B
      ▲                            │
      └────────────────────────────┘

    refcount(A) = 1  (held by b's slot)
    refcount(B) = 1  (held by a's slot)

Now delete both names:

del a
del b

Both objects still have refcount 1 — they reference each other. Neither will ever reach refcount 0. This is a reference cycle, and pure reference counting cannot collect it.

Python solves this with a supplemental cyclic garbage collector (gc module) that runs periodically on top of reference counting. It identifies groups of objects that are only reachable from each other (not from any live root), and collects them.

import gc

# Trigger collection manually (normally automatic)
gc.collect()

# See current garbage
print(gc.garbage)

# Get collection stats
print(gc.get_count())   # (gen0, gen1, gen2) — three generational thresholds

The GC uses a generational strategy: most objects die young (short-lived temporaries), so it scans "generation 0" (recently allocated) frequently and older generations less often. This reduces overhead.

Generation 0 → collected most often   (new objects)
Generation 1 → collected occasionally  (survived gen 0)
Generation 2 → collected rarely        (long-lived objects)

Objects with __del__ methods were historically exempt from the cyclic GC (since Python couldn't safely decide destruction order). Since Python 3.4, this is no longer a restriction — __del__ cycles are handled correctly.

docs.title: __del__: The Finaliser
docs.text:
When a Python object's refcount drops to 0, Python calls __del__ if it exists, before freeing memory.

class Resource:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        print(f"{self.name} created")

    def __del__(self):
        print(f"{self.name} destroyed")

r = Resource("file_handle")    # prints: file_handle created
del r                           # prints: file_handle destroyed

__del__ is not a reliable destructor. You cannot count on when it runs (the GC may delay it), and it will not run at all if there is a reference cycle. Never rely on __del__ to release critical resources like file handles or network connections. Use context managers (with statement) instead — they are deterministic.

# WRONG: relying on __del__ for cleanup
class FileWrapper:
    def __init__(self, path):
        self.f = open(path)
    def __del__(self):
        self.f.close()   # Not guaranteed to run promptly

# CORRECT: context manager guarantees cleanup
with open("data.txt") as f:
    data = f.read()
# f is closed here, unconditionally

docs.title: Memory Arenas, Pools, and Blocks (CPython Internals)
docs.text:
Python does not call malloc for every object. That would be too slow. Instead, CPython has a three-level internal allocator sitting between your Python code and the OS:

Your Python code
        │
        ▼
  Object-specific allocators  (e.g., int freelist, list freelist)
        │
        ▼
  PyMalloc — Python's private heap
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Arena (256 KB)                                      │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  Pool (4 KB)  — fixed size class (e.g., 32B) │   │
  │  │  ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐        │   │
  │  │  │Block │ │Block │ │Block │ │ free │  ...    │   │
  │  │  └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘ └──────┘        │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────── ┐  │
  │  │  Pool (4 KB)  — different size class (e.g., 64B) │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        │
        ▼
  OS (malloc / mmap)
  • Block: smallest unit, holds one object of a given size class
  • Pool: 4 KB page of same-size blocks
  • Arena: 256 KB region of pools

PyMalloc handles allocations up to 512 bytes. Larger objects go directly to the OS malloc. This means Python processes often hold onto memory even after objects are deleted — the arena is returned to the OS only when it is entirely empty, which is rare for long-running processes.

This is why memory_profiler may show your Python process's RSS holding steady even after a large object is deleted: the memory is free from Python's perspective but has not been returned to the OS yet.

docs.title: NumPy Arrays Bypass PyMalloc
docs.text:
NumPy allocates array data buffers directly via malloc (not PyMalloc). The Python object wrapper has a refcount like any Python object, but the large memory block storing the actual numbers is managed by NumPy's own allocator.

import numpy as np, sys

a = np.zeros((10000, 10000))   # 800 MB data buffer — NOT in PyMalloc

# The Python wrapper object:
print(sys.getrefcount(a))      # 2 (a + getrefcount arg)

b = a                          # refcount → 3, but NO copy of the 800 MB buffer
del a                          # refcount → 2, buffer still alive via b
del b                          # refcount → 0, NumPy frees the 800 MB buffer

This is why b = a for a large NumPy array is not a 800 MB copy — it is a pointer. And it is why forgetting a reference (leaving b alive in a list somewhere) keeps that 800 MB buffer alive indefinitely.

docs.title: Views Keep the Base Array Alive
docs.text:
a = np.zeros((10000, 10000))   # 800 MB
b = a[:100, :]                 # b is a VIEW — it holds a reference to a's buffer

del a                          # a's Python wrapper refcount → 1 (b still holds it)
                               # the 800 MB buffer is NOT freed

print(b.base is not None)      # True — b knows its parent

This is a real memory management issue in data pipelines. If you slice a large array to extract a small subarray and discard the original name, the full buffer survives as long as the slice does. The fix:

b = a[:100, :].copy()   # independent buffer, only 100 rows
del a                   # now the 800 MB buffer is freed

docs.title: PyTorch and the Computation Graph
docs.text:
In PyTorch, tensors with requires_grad=True maintain a reference to their entire computation graph (the chain of operations that produced them). This graph holds references to intermediate tensors, which hold references to their data buffers.

import torch

x = torch.randn(1000, 1000, requires_grad=True)
y = (x * x).sum()              # y holds a graph that references x's data

del x                          # x's name is gone, but y's graph still holds a reference
                               # x's data is NOT freed yet

y.backward()
del y                          # now the graph is released, all intermediates freed

Forgetting to call .backward() or forgetting to del the loss in a loop accumulates graph memory across iterations — a common source of GPU OOM errors.

# Bug: memory grows every iteration
for batch in dataloader:
    loss = model(batch)
    losses.append(loss)         # appending the tensor keeps the graph alive!

# Fix: detach before storing
for batch in dataloader:
    loss = model(batch)
    loss.backward()
    losses.append(loss.item())  # .item() extracts a Python float, drops the graph

docs.title: Check refcount
docs.text:
import sys
print(sys.getrefcount(obj) - 1)   # subtract 1 for getrefcount's own arg

docs.title: Check if an object is still alive (weak references)
docs.text:
import weakref

class Expensive:
    pass

obj = Expensive()
ref = weakref.ref(obj)

print(ref())       # <__main__.Expensive object at 0x...>
del obj
print(ref())       # None  — object was collected

weakref lets you hold a reference that does not increment the refcount. When the object is collected, the weak reference returns None. This is used in caches — you want to keep an object around if something else needs it, but not keep it alive solely because of the cache.

docs.title: Profile memory usage
docs.text:
pip install memory-profiler

from memory_profiler import profile

@profile
def train_epoch(model, data):
    for batch in data:
        loss = model(batch)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad()

Run with python -m memory_profiler script.py to get line-by-line memory deltas.

docs.title: Summary: The Reference Counting Contract
docs.text:
1. Every object has a refcount.
2. Refcount increases when a new name/slot references the object.
3. Refcount decreases when a name is deleted, reassigned, or goes out of scope.
4. When refcount == 0, the object is immediately destroyed.
5. Circular references defeat pure refcounting → supplemental GC handles them.
6. Small integers (−5 to 256) and short identifier-like strings are cached singletons.
7. Never use `is` for value comparison. Use `==`.
8. NumPy and PyTorch have their own buffer management on top of this.
9. Slices and views keep the source buffer alive — use .copy() if you want independence.
10. For critical resources, use context managers, not __del__.

docs.title: 55. Pass-by-Object-Reference Behavior
docs.text: "Python is neither pass-by-value nor pass-by-reference. It is pass-by-object-reference — and the confusion between these three things is the source of an entire class of bugs that vanish the moment the model is clear."

docs.title: The Question That Causes All the Confusion
docs.text:
def double(x):
    x = x * 2

a = 5
double(a)
print(a)    # 5  ← unchanged. Why?

def append_one(lst):
    lst.append(1)

b = [10, 20]
append_one(b)
print(b)    # [10, 20, 1]  ← changed. Why?

Both functions receive one argument. Neither returns anything. Yet one modifies the caller's variable and the other does not. Understanding exactly why requires understanding what Python actually passes.

docs.title: The Three Models — and Which One Python Uses
Pass-by-Value (C, Java primitives)
docs.text:
A copy of the value is made. The function works on the copy. The caller's variable is never touched.

caller:  a = 5
         ┌───┐
         │ 5 │  ← copy made
         └───┘
              │
              ▼
function: x = 5  (independent copy)
          x = 10  (only local copy changes)

caller:  a = 5  (unchanged)

docs.title: Pass-by-Reference (C++ references, ref in C#)
docs.text:
The function receives the memory address of the caller's variable. Reassigning the parameter changes the caller's variable.

caller:  a = 5
         │
         ▼ (address passed)
function: x  →  same storage as a
          x = 10  →  a is now 10

caller:  a = 10  (changed by reassignment inside function)

Python does not work this way. Reassigning a parameter never changes the caller's variable.

docs.title: Pass-by-Object-Reference (Python)
docs.text:
Python passes a reference to the object — not a copy of the value, and not the address of the caller's variable. The parameter becomes a new label pointing to the same object.

caller:    a ──────────────► [10, 20]
                                ▲
function:  lst ─────────────────┘   (same object, new label)

The function can mutate the object through its label. But if it rebinds the label to a new object, the caller's label is unaffected.

docs.title: The Core Distinction: Mutation vs. Rebinding
docs.text:
This is the entire note in two lines:

  • Mutating the object → caller sees the change (same object in memory)
  • Rebinding the parameter → caller does not see the change (parameter now points elsewhere)
def mutate(lst):
    lst.append(99)      # MUTATION — modifies the object lst points to

def rebind(lst):
    lst = [1, 2, 3]     # REBINDING — lst now points to a new object
                        # the caller's list is completely unaffected

original = [10, 20]

mutate(original)
print(original)         # [10, 20, 99]  ← mutation visible

rebind(original)
print(original)         # [10, 20, 99]  ← rebinding invisible to caller

Draw it:

Before mutate():
    original ──────────────► [10, 20]
                                 ▲
    lst (inside mutate) ─────────┘

After lst.append(99):
    original ──────────────► [10, 20, 99]   ← same object, now modified
    lst ───────────────────────────────────► same

Inside rebind(), after lst = [1, 2, 3]:
    original ──────────────► [10, 20, 99]   ← unchanged
    lst ───────────────────► [1, 2, 3]      ← new object, local only

The caller's label original is never touched by rebinding. It still points where it always pointed.

docs.title: Immutable Objects: Why "Pass-by-Value" Feels True
docs.text:
For immutable types (int, float, str, tuple, frozenset), mutation is impossible by definition. Every operation that appears to modify the value actually produces a new object.

def increment(n):
    n = n + 1       # n + 1 creates a NEW int object
                    # n is rebound to it
                    # the original int is untouched

x = 10
increment(x)
print(x)            # 10  ← unchanged

Before:
    x ──────────────► int(10)  [refcount includes x and n]
    n ──────────────────────────────────► same int(10)

After n = n + 1:
    x ──────────────► int(10)  [untouched]
    n ──────────────────────────────────► int(11)  [new object]

It looks like pass-by-value, but it is not. The mechanism is identical to the mutable case — the parameter is a reference to the same object. It is just that you cannot mutate the object, so every "modification" is really a rebind, which the caller never sees.

docs.title: Mutable Objects: The Full Taxonomy of Operations
docs.text: For a mutable object, every operation falls into one of two categories:

docs.title: In-Place Mutations (caller sees these)
docs.text:
lst.append(x)
lst.extend(iterable)
lst.insert(i, x)
lst.remove(x)
lst.pop()
lst.sort()
lst.reverse()
lst[i] = x          # item assignment
lst[i:j] = [...]    # slice assignment

dct["key"] = value
dct.update(...)
dct.pop("key")

obj.attribute = value   # attribute assignment on any object

docs.title: Rebinding Operations (caller does NOT see these)
docs.text:
lst = new_list          # local rebind
lst = lst + [1, 2]      # + creates a NEW list, then rebinds lst
lst = sorted(lst)       # sorted() returns a new list
lst = lst[1:]           # slicing returns a new list

The + vs += distinction is subtle and important:

def f(lst):
    lst = lst + [99]    # creates new list, rebinds local lst
                        # caller unchanged

def g(lst):
    lst += [99]         # for lists, += calls __iadd__ which is lst.extend([99])
                        # in-place mutation — caller SEES this

original = [1, 2]
f(original);  print(original)   # [1, 2]    — unchanged
g(original);  print(original)   # [1, 2, 99] — changed

lst += x on a list calls list.__iadd__, which mutates in place and returns self. The label lst is rebound to the same object it already pointed to. The caller sees the mutation.

lst = lst + x creates a brand-new list object. lst is rebound to the new one. The caller's label never moves.

For immutable types like str and tuple, += also creates a new object (because mutation is impossible), so it behaves like = in this context.

docs.title: The Mutable Default Argument: Classic Python Trap
docs.text:
def append_to(element, target=[]):   # DEFAULT EVALUATED ONCE AT DEFINITION TIME
    target.append(element)
    return target

print(append_to(1))    # [1]
print(append_to(2))    # [1, 2]   ← NOT [2]. The list persists between calls.
print(append_to(3))    # [1, 2, 3]

Why? The default [] is a single list object created when the function is defined, not when it is called. Every call that uses the default is mutating the same object.

Function definition time:
    append_to.__defaults__ = ([],)   ← one list object, lives forever

Call 1: target ──────────────► []   → append(1) → [1]
Call 2: target ──────────────► [1]  → append(2) → [1, 2]  (same object)
Call 3: target ──────────────► [1, 2] → ...

The canonical fix: use None as the sentinel, create a fresh list inside the function body.

def append_to(element, target=None):
    if target is None:
        target = []         # new list created on each call
    target.append(element)
    return target

print(append_to(1))    # [1]
print(append_to(2))    # [2]   ← correct, independent lists

This pattern applies to all mutable defaults: dict, set, custom objects.

docs.title: Augmented Assignment on Immutables Inside a Function
docs.text:
A particular source of confusion with strings and tuples:

def try_to_modify(s):
    s += " world"       # str += creates a NEW str object, rebinds s
    print(s)            # "hello world"

msg = "hello"
try_to_modify(msg)
print(msg)              # "hello"  ← unchanged

The caller's msg is still pointing at "hello". The local s was rebound to a new string. This is immutability + rebinding working together.

docs.title: Functions That Return Modified Values — The Right Pattern
docs.text:
When you want a function to "modify" an immutable or produce a new version of something, return it explicitly:

# Pattern 1: return the new value
def prepend(element, lst):
    return [element] + lst

result = prepend(0, [1, 2, 3])
print(result)    # [0, 1, 2, 3]

# Pattern 2: modify in place (for mutables), return None implicitly
def normalize_inplace(arr):
    total = sum(arr)
    for i in range(len(arr)):
        arr[i] /= total

data = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]
normalize_inplace(data)
print(data)    # [0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4]

Design principle: a function should either mutate its argument OR return a new value — not both. Doing both (mutating and returning the mutated object) signals to the reader that a copy was made, when it was not.

# Confusing: appears to return a copy, actually mutates and returns same object
def bad_append(lst, x):
    lst.append(x)
    return lst          # returns the same list that was mutated

# This is why list.sort() returns None and sorted() returns a new list
# Python's stdlib follows the convention rigorously

docs.title: The ML Connection: Gradients, Optimisers, and In-Place Ops
In-Place Operations in PyTorch — When They Break the Graph
docs.text:
import torch

x = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], requires_grad=True)

# WRONG: in-place op on a tensor that requires grad
x += 1.0     # x.__iadd__(1.0) — modifies x's data in place
             # autograd cannot differentiate through this correctly
             # RuntimeError: a leaf Variable that requires grad has been used in an in-place operation

# CORRECT: rebind to a new tensor
x = x + 1.0  # creates a new tensor, registers the addition in the graph

This is exactly the mutation vs. rebinding distinction, applied to automatic differentiation. The computation graph needs to see an unmodified version of each tensor to compute gradients correctly. In-place mutation destroys that history.

docs.title: Optimiser Step is In-Place Mutation
docs.text:
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.01)

loss.backward()
optimizer.step()     # mutates model.parameters() IN PLACE
                     # (subtracts lr * grad from each weight tensor)
optimizer.zero_grad()

optimizer.step() is an in-place mutation of all parameter tensors. It does not return new parameter tensors. This is intentional — parameters are tracked by the model and the optimiser by reference. Rebinding would sever those connections.

docs.title: NumPy: In-Place Operations for Memory Efficiency
docs.text:
import numpy as np

X = np.random.randn(100000, 512)   # ~400 MB

# WRONG if memory is tight: creates a new 400 MB array
X = X - X.mean(axis=0)

# CORRECT: subtracts in place, no new allocation
X -= X.mean(axis=0)

-= on a NumPy array calls __isub__, which modifies the existing data buffer. No new array is allocated. For large arrays in preprocessing pipelines this is the difference between fitting in RAM and not.

docs.title: Function Arguments in Data Pipeline Functions
docs.text:
# Surprising bug: augmentation function mutates the input batch
def augment(batch):
    batch["image"] = random_flip(batch["image"])   # IN-PLACE dict mutation
    return batch

original = {"image": img_tensor, "label": 1}
augmented = augment(original)

print(original["image"] is augmented["image"])  # True  ← same tensor!
# original has been mutated silently

# Fix: copy the dict (shallow is sufficient if values are replaced, not mutated)
def augment(batch):
    batch = dict(batch)                            # new dict, same value refs
    batch["image"] = random_flip(batch["image"])   # rebind slot in new dict
    return batch

docs.title: id() as a Diagnostic Tool
docs.text:
id(obj) returns the memory address of the object in CPython. Use it to verify whether two names point to the same object.

def f(x):
    print(f"  inside f, id(x) = {id(x)}")
    x.append(99)
    print(f"  inside f after append, id(x) = {id(x)}")

lst = [1, 2, 3]
print(f"before call, id(lst) = {id(lst)}")
f(lst)
print(f"after call, id(lst) = {id(lst)}")
print(lst)

before call, id(lst) = 140234567890
  inside f, id(x) = 140234567890        ← same object
  inside f after append, id(x) = 140234567890  ← still same object
after call, id(lst) = 140234567890      ← unchanged address
[1, 2, 3, 99]

The address never changes. The object was mutated through two different labels pointing to the same address.

def g(x):
    print(f"  inside g, id(x) = {id(x)}")
    x = x + [99]
    print(f"  inside g after rebind, id(x) = {id(x)}")

lst = [1, 2, 3]
print(f"before call, id(lst) = {id(lst)}")
g(lst)
print(f"after call, id(lst) = {id(lst)}")
print(lst)

before call, id(lst) = 140234567890
  inside g, id(x) = 140234567890        ← same object at entry
  inside g after rebind, id(x) = 140234599999  ← NEW object
after call, id(lst) = 140234567890      ← caller unchanged
[1, 2, 3]

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Python passes a reference to the object — not the value, not the address of the variable.

The parameter is a new label pointing to the same object as the caller's argument.

MUTATION of the object through the parameter  →  caller sees the change.
REBINDING the parameter to a new object       →  caller is completely unaffected.

Immutable types (int, str, tuple) cannot be mutated.
Every apparent "modification" creates a new object and rebinds the local label.
This is why immutables appear to behave like pass-by-value — but the mechanism is identical.

The mutable default argument trap is this mechanism applied to function definition time.
Use None as sentinel; create fresh mutable objects inside the function body.

lst += x  on a list  →  in-place mutation (caller sees it)
lst = lst + x        →  new object, rebind (caller does not)

In ML code: PyTorch in-place ops break autograd; NumPy in-place ops save memory.
Know which operations mutate and which rebind — the distinction is load-bearing.

docs.title: 56. Variable Unpacking and Assignment Mechanics
docs.text: "Unpacking is not syntactic sugar. It is a window into how Python's assignment protocol works at the bytecode level — and once you see it clearly, you start using it everywhere, correctly."

docs.title: What Assignment Actually Does
docs.text:
Before unpacking makes sense, the assignment statement itself needs a precise definition.

x = expression

Python:

  1. Evaluates the right-hand side fully — produces an object
  2. Binds the name on the left to that object in the current namespace

The left-hand side is called a target. Targets can be:

  • A simple name: x
  • A subscript: lst[0], dct["key"]
  • An attribute: obj.attr
  • A tuple or list of targets — this is unpacking
# All of these are valid assignment targets:
x = 10
lst[0] = 10
obj.attr = 10
x, y = 1, 2       # tuple of targets
[a, b] = [1, 2]   # list of targets — identical semantics

docs.title: Basic Sequence Unpacking
docs.text:
The fundamental rule: the right-hand side is iterated, and its elements are bound to the left-hand side targets one-to-one.

a, b, c = [1, 2, 3]
a, b, c = (1, 2, 3)
a, b, c = "xyz"       # strings are iterable
a, b, c = range(3)    # any iterable works

print(a, b, c)        # 0 1 2  (for range case)

The count must match exactly. If not:

a, b = [1, 2, 3]   # ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)
a, b, c = [1, 2]   # ValueError: not enough values to unpack (expected 3, got 2)

The left-hand side tuple does not need parentheses — Python parses comma-separated names on the left of = as an implicit tuple of targets.

a, b = 1, 2       # equivalent to (a, b) = (1, 2)

docs.title: The Swap Idiom — Why It Works
docs.text:
a, b = b, a

This is not magic. Here is exactly what happens:

  1. Right-hand side b, a is evaluated fully — produces a tuple (old_b, old_a)
  2. The tuple is unpacked into a, b — a gets old_b, b gets old_a

The right-hand side is always evaluated completely before any binding occurs. This is what makes the swap safe without a temporary variable.

# In C you need a temp:
# int tmp = a; a = b; b = tmp;

# In Python the RHS evaluation IS the temp:
a, b = b, a    # clean, no temp, no risk of reading a partially-updated value

This generalises:

a, b, c = c, a, b    # cyclic rotation — all three evaluated first, then bound

docs.title: Extended Unpacking: The Star Expression
docs.text:
Python 3 introduced *name on the left-hand side. It captures all remaining elements as a list.

first, *rest = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print(first)    # 1
print(rest)     # [2, 3, 4, 5]

*init, last = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print(init)     # [1, 2, 3, 4]
print(last)     # 5

first, *middle, last = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print(first)    # 1
print(middle)   # [2, 3, 4]
print(last)     # 5

The starred variable always captures a list, even if zero or one elements remain:

first, *rest = [1]
print(rest)     # []   ← empty list, not an error

a, *b, c = [1, 2]
print(b)        # []   ← middle captured nothing

Only one star is allowed per unpacking expression — Python would have no way to resolve ambiguity with two.

*a, *b = [1, 2, 3]    # SyntaxError: two starred expressions in assignment

docs.title: Nested Unpacking
docs.text:
Targets can be nested to match the structure of nested iterables:

(a, b), c = (1, 2), 3
print(a, b, c)    # 1 2 3

(a, b), (c, d) = (1, 2), (3, 4)
print(a, b, c, d)    # 1 2 3 4

This is used constantly when iterating over structured data:

points = [(1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 6)]

for x, y in points:             # nested unpack per iteration
    print(f"x={x}, y={y}")

pairs = [((1, 2), "A"), ((3, 4), "B")]

for (x, y), label in pairs:    # doubly nested
    print(f"({x},{y}) → {label}")

docs.title: Unpacking in For Loops
docs.text:
The for loop's target is an assignment target — the same rules apply.

# Simple
for x in [1, 2, 3]:
    ...

# Tuple unpacking — extremely common with enumerate, zip, dict.items()
for i, val in enumerate(["a", "b", "c"]):
    print(i, val)

for key, value in {"x": 1, "y": 2}.items():
    print(key, value)

for (a, b), label in [((1, 2), "A"), ((3, 4), "B")]:
    print(a, b, label)

# Star unpacking in for loops
for first, *rest in [(1, 2, 3), (4, 5, 6, 7)]:
    print(first, rest)
# 1 [2, 3]
# 4 [5, 6, 7]

docs.title: Unpacking in Function Calls: * and **
docs.text:
This is the inverse operation: instead of unpacking an iterable into names, you unpack a container into function arguments.

def f(a, b, c):
    print(a, b, c)

args = [1, 2, 3]
f(*args)            # equivalent to f(1, 2, 3)

kwargs = {"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3}
f(**kwargs)         # equivalent to f(a=1, b=2, c=3)

# Both together:
positional = [1]
keyword    = {"b": 2, "c": 3}
f(*positional, **keyword)    # f(1, b=2, c=3)

docs.title: Merging Collections with Unpacking (Python 3.5+)
docs.text:
# Merge lists
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [4, 5, 6]
merged = [*a, *b]           # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

# Merge dicts (later keys win on conflict)
d1 = {"x": 1, "y": 2}
d2 = {"y": 99, "z": 3}
merged = {**d1, **d2}       # {"x": 1, "y": 99, "z": 3}

This is cleaner and faster than explicit list.extend or dict.update for constructing new collections inline.

docs.title: Ignoring Values with _
docs.text:
_ is a valid Python name. By convention it signals "I am intentionally discarding this value."

first, _, last = (1, 2, 3)    # discard middle value

for _ in range(5):             # loop body doesn't need the index
    print("hello")

_, (x, y) = "A", (3, 4)       # discard the string, keep the pair

_ is also used in the REPL to hold the result of the last expression. In real code it is purely a convention signal — Python treats it as a regular name.

For multiple discards, *_ absorbs everything unwanted:

first, *_, last = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
print(first, last)    # 1 6

docs.title: Augmented Assignment: +=, -=, etc.
docs.text:
Augmented assignment is not the same as assignment followed by an operation. It is a distinct protocol.

x += y

Python:

  1. Evaluates the target (x) to get the current object
  2. Calls type(x).__iadd__(x, y) — the in-place method
  3. Binds the result back to x

If __iadd__ is not defined, Python falls back to x = x + y.

For mutable objects that define __iadd__ (like list), step 2 mutates the object and returns self. The rebind in step 3 puts the same object back. Net effect: in-place mutation, no new object.

For immutable objects (like int, str, tuple), __iadd__ is not defined. Python falls back to x = x + y, which creates a new object. Net effect: rebind, identical to x = x + y.

# Mutable: list
a = [1, 2]
b = a
a += [3]          # __iadd__ → in-place mutation
print(b)          # [1, 2, 3]   ← b sees it (same object)
print(a is b)     # True        ← still same object

# Immutable: int
a = 10
b = a
a += 5            # no __iadd__ → a = a + 5 → new int
print(b)          # 10          ← b unchanged
print(a is b)     # False       ← different objects

This is the same mutation-vs-rebinding distinction from [[55. Pass-by-Object-Reference Behavior]], now visible at the assignment level.

docs.title: Chained Assignment
docs.text:
a = b = c = 0

Python evaluates 0 once, then binds all three names to the same object.

a ──────┐
b ──────┼──────► int(0)
c ──────┘

For immutables this is harmless — a += 1 rebinds a to a new int, leaving b and c pointing at 0.

For mutables this is a trap:

a = b = c = []      # ALL THREE point to the SAME list

a.append(1)
print(b)            # [1]   ← surprise
print(c)            # [1]   ← surprise

# Fix: create independent objects
a, b, c = [], [], []

The same trap appears in matrix initialisation:

# WRONG: all rows are the same list object
matrix = [[0] * 3] * 3
matrix[0][0] = 99
print(matrix)
# [[99, 0, 0], [99, 0, 0], [99, 0, 0]]  ← all rows changed

# CORRECT: list comprehension creates a new list per row
matrix = [[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)]
matrix[0][0] = 99
print(matrix)
# [[99, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]]   ← only first row changed

docs.title: Multiple Assignment Targets (Not the Same as Chained)
docs.text:
a = b = 0    # chained — one evaluation, binds both

a, b = 0, 0  # unpacking — two independent evaluations of literals
             # for literals, same effect; for complex expressions, different

import random

# Chained: random() called ONCE, both get same value
a = b = random.random()
print(a == b)    # True (always)

# Unpacking: random() called TWICE, independent values
a, b = random.random(), random.random()
print(a == b)    # False (almost certainly)

This distinction matters whenever the right-hand side has side effects or is non-deterministic.

docs.title: The Walrus Operator := (Assignment Expression)
docs.text:
Python 3.8 introduced :=, which assigns AND returns the value as an expression. It can appear inside conditions, comprehensions, and other expression contexts where = cannot.

# Without walrus: compute twice
if len(data) > 10:
    print(f"Long list: {len(data)} elements")

# With walrus: compute once, bind, use
if (n := len(data)) > 10:
    print(f"Long list: {n} elements")

# Useful in while loops reading input or processing chunks
while chunk := file.read(8192):
    process(chunk)

# Useful in comprehensions to avoid recomputing expensive expressions
results = [y for x in data if (y := expensive(x)) > threshold]
#          ↑ y is already computed, no need to call expensive(x) again in body

:= assigns to the enclosing scope — not the comprehension's local scope. This is a deliberate design choice so the value is accessible after the comprehension.

filtered = [y for x in range(10) if (y := x ** 2) < 50]
print(y)    # 49 — the last value assigned, accessible outside the comprehension

Use := when a value is computed in a condition and needed in the body. Do not use it gratuitously — it reduces readability when the value is only needed once inside a simple condition.

docs.title: Bytecode: What Python Actually Executes
docs.text:
For the rigorously curious — here is what a, b = 1, 2 compiles to:

import dis
dis.dis("a, b = 1, 2")

  1           0 LOAD_CONST               0 ((1, 2))   ← push tuple onto stack
              2 UNPACK_SEQUENCE          2            ← pop tuple, push elements right-to-left
              4 STORE_NAME               0 (a)        ← bind a
              6 STORE_NAME               1 (b)        ← bind b

UNPACK_SEQUENCE is the bytecode instruction for unpacking. It pops the iterable from the stack and pushes its elements in reverse order (so the first STORE_NAME picks up the first element). The extended star form uses UNPACK_EX instead.

dis.dis("a, *b, c = [1, 2, 3, 4]")

  1           0 LOAD_CONST               0 ([1, 2, 3, 4])
              2 UNPACK_EX                1 (1 before, 1 after)
              ...

Understanding this confirms that unpacking is a first-class language operation, not a macro or transform — it has dedicated bytecode with specific semantics.

docs.title: The ML Connection: Data Loading, Batches, and Tuple Returns
Unpacking Model Outputs
docs.text:
# Most PyTorch models return tuples or namedtuples
logits, hidden = model(x)           # unpack two outputs

# Transformers-style: many outputs, take only what you need
loss, logits, *_ = model(input_ids=ids, labels=labels)

docs.title: Unpacking DataLoader Batches
docs.text:
for images, labels in dataloader:       # standard supervised batch
    outputs = model(images)
    loss = criterion(outputs, labels)

for (images, masks), labels in loader:  # nested: (input pair, target)
    ...

# Ignoring labels for self-supervised training
for images, _ in dataloader:
    representations = encoder(images)

docs.title: Unpacking in Training Loops
docs.text:
# Enumerate gives (index, batch) — unpack naturally
for step, (x, y) in enumerate(dataloader):
    loss = model(x, y)
    if step % 100 == 0:
        print(f"Step {step}, loss {loss:.4f}")

docs.title: Returning Multiple Values from Training Functions
docs.text:
def train_epoch(model, loader, optimizer):
    total_loss, total_acc = 0.0, 0.0
    for x, y in loader:
        loss, acc = compute_loss_and_acc(model, x, y)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        total_loss += loss.item()
        total_acc  += acc.item()
    return total_loss / len(loader), total_acc / len(loader)

train_loss, train_acc = train_epoch(model, train_loader, optimizer)

Python functions return one object — but that object can be a tuple, and tuple unpacking makes multiple return values idiomatic and zero-cost.

docs.title: Star Unpacking for Flexible Architectures
docs.text:
# Unpack layer sizes from config
first, *hidden, last = [784, 256, 128, 64, 10]

layers = []
in_dim = first
for out_dim in hidden:
    layers += [nn.Linear(in_dim, out_dim), nn.ReLU()]
    in_dim = out_dim
layers.append(nn.Linear(in_dim, last))
model = nn.Sequential(*layers)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Assignment binds a name (or target) to an object. The RHS is always
evaluated completely before any binding begins.

Sequence unpacking: a, b, c = iterable
    → iterates the RHS, binds elements to targets one-to-one
    → count must match unless a star target is present

Extended unpacking: first, *rest = iterable
    → star target captures remaining elements as a list
    → exactly one star allowed per expression

Nested unpacking: (a, b), c = (1, 2), 3
    → matches structure of RHS recursively

Augmented assignment (+=, -=, ...):
    → calls __iadd__ (or equivalent) first
    → mutable objects with __iadd__: mutates in place, rebinds to same object
    → immutable objects: falls back to x = x + y, creates new object

Chained assignment (a = b = expr):
    → expr evaluated once, all targets bound to same object
    → safe for immutables, trap for mutables

Walrus operator (n := expr):
    → assigns and returns in expression context
    → assigns to enclosing scope, not local comprehension scope

  • [[54. How Python Manages Memory]] — refcount changes on every binding and unbinding
