docs.title: 01. The Learning Problem
docs.text:
"A computer program is said to learn from experience E with respect to some class of tasks T and performance measure P, if its performance at tasks in T, as measured by P, improves with experience E." — Tom Mitchell, Machine Learning, 1997

Part of: [[04.Machine Learning]] > Part 0 — Foundations Next: [[02. Statistical Learning Theory]]

docs.title: 1. What Is Learning?
docs.text:
Before writing a single line of code or touching a dataset, the question has to be asked precisely: what does it mean for a machine to learn?

The intuitive answer — "it gets better with experience" — is Mitchell's definition above. But intuition is not enough. To build algorithms, to prove guarantees, to know when things will fail, we need a mathematical formalisation.

The formalisation has three parts.

docs.title: 2. The Three Components of a Learning Problem
docs.text:
Every learning problem can be decomposed as a triple \((T, E, P)\).

Task \(T\) — what the system is trying to do. Examples: classify an email as spam or not spam; predict tomorrow's temperature; generate a caption for an image; recommend a product.

Experience \(E\) — what the system has access to during training. Examples: a dataset of labelled emails; historical temperature records; image-caption pairs; user click logs.

Performance measure \(P\) — how we evaluate whether the system is doing \(T\) well. Examples: classification accuracy; mean squared error; BLEU score; click-through rate.

The learning problem is then: given \(E\), improve performance on \(T\) as measured by \(P\).

This decomposition matters because it forces precision. "Build a model that predicts customer churn" is not a well-posed learning problem. "Train a binary classifier (\(T\)) on 12 months of transaction history (\(E\)) to maximise F1 score on a held-out test set (\(P\))" is.

docs.title: 3. The Formal Setup
docs.text:
Let the input space be \(\mathcal{X}\) (e.g., \(\mathbb{R}^d\), the space of all images, the space of all sentences) and the output space be \(\mathcal{Y}\) (e.g., \(\mathbb{R}\) for regression, \({0,1}\) for binary classification, \({1,\ldots,k}\) for multi-class).

We assume there exists an unknown target function:

\[f^* : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}\]

We do not know \(f^*\). If we did, the problem would be solved. Instead, we observe a training set:

\[\mathcal{D} = {(x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2), \ldots, (x_n, y_n)}\]

where each \((x_i, y_i)\) is drawn i.i.d. from some unknown joint distribution \(P_{\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}}\).

The goal of learning is to find a function \(h : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}\) that approximates \(f^*\) well — not just on the training data we have seen, but on new, unseen inputs drawn from the same distribution.

This last point is the entire difficulty. Fitting training data is easy. Generalising is hard.

docs.title: 3.1 The Hypothesis Class
docs.text:
We do not search over all possible functions \(h : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}\). The space of all such functions is astronomically large (uncountably infinite for continuous inputs). Instead, we restrict the search to a hypothesis class \(\mathcal{H}\):

\[\mathcal{H} = {h_\theta : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y} \mid \theta \in \Theta}\]

where \(\Theta\) is a parameter space. Learning then becomes: find the \(\theta \in \Theta\) such that \(h_\theta\) best approximates \(f^*\) on unseen data.

Examples of hypothesis classes:

Model Hypothesis class Linear regression \(\mathcal{H} = {x \mapsto w^Tx + b \mid w \in \mathbb{R}^d, b \in \mathbb{R}}\) Logistic regression \(\mathcal{H} = {x \mapsto \sigma(w^Tx + b) \mid w \in \mathbb{R}^d, b \in \mathbb{R}}\) Depth-\(k\) decision tree \(\mathcal{H} = {\text{all binary trees with depth} \leq k}\) 2-layer neural network \(\mathcal{H} = {x \mapsto W_2 \sigma(W_1 x + b_1) + b_2}\)

The choice of \(\mathcal{H}\) is arguably the most consequential modelling decision you make. It encodes what you believe about the structure of \(f^*\) before seeing any data. This belief is called inductive bias.

docs.title: 4. Inductive Bias
docs.text:
No algorithm can learn without assumptions. This is a theorem, not a matter of opinion. An algorithm with no inductive bias treats every unseen input as equally likely to have any output — which means it has learned nothing from the training data.

Definition. The inductive bias of a learning algorithm is the set of assumptions it makes about the target function \(f^*\), beyond what the training data alone can establish.

Examples:

  • Linear regression assumes \(f^*\) is a linear function of the inputs. It will fail systematically on data generated by a quadratic.
  • KNN with \(k=1\) assumes \(f^*\) is locally constant — nearby inputs have the same output. It makes no assumption about global structure.
  • A Gaussian Process with an RBF kernel assumes \(f^_\) is smooth — small changes in \(x\) produce small changes in \(f^_(x)\).
  • A convolutional neural network assumes \(f^*\) is translation-equivariant — the same pattern at different positions should be detected in the same way. This is why CNNs work on images.

The practical consequence: inductive bias is not a flaw to be minimised — it is a design choice to be made deliberately. Choosing a linear model for a nonlinear problem is not being rigorous; it is being wrong. Choosing a rich model for a simple problem invites overfitting.

The right inductive bias is the one that matches the structure of the actual problem.

docs.title: 5. The No Free Lunch Theorem
docs.text:
The No Free Lunch (NFL) theorem (Wolpert, 1996) formalises why inductive bias is unavoidable.

Theorem (informal). Averaged over all possible target functions \(f^* : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}\), every learning algorithm performs equally well.

More precisely: for any two algorithms \(A\) and \(B\), if you average their out-of-sample error over all possible data-generating distributions, they are equal.

What this means. There is no universally superior algorithm. An algorithm that outperforms all others on some problems must underperform on others. The gains are always elsewhere.

What this does not mean. The NFL theorem is not an argument for nihilism or for ignoring algorithm selection. It applies when averaged over all possible functions, including completely random and pathological ones. In practice, we are not interested in all possible functions — we are interested in the specific structure of the physical, biological, or social processes that generated our data. Those processes have regularity. Exploiting that regularity is what machine learning is.

The NFL theorem does not say: "don't bother choosing algorithms." It says: "your choice of algorithm embeds an assumption about the problem. Make that assumption explicit and make sure it's reasonable."

A linear model assumes the world is linear. If it is, the linear model wins. If it is not, the linear model loses, and something more flexible is needed. There is no free lunch. You pay with assumptions.

docs.title: 6. Types of Learning
docs.text: The taxonomy below is about the structure of experience \(E\) available to the learner.

docs.title: 6.1 Supervised Learning
docs.text:
The training set consists of input-output pairs:

\[\mathcal{D} = {(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^n\]

The labels \(y_i\) are provided by a supervisor (a human annotator, a measurement instrument, a simulation). The task is to learn a mapping from inputs to outputs.

Sub-cases:

  • Regression — \(\mathcal{Y} = \mathbb{R}\) or \(\mathbb{R}^k\). Predict a continuous quantity.
  • Classification — \(\mathcal{Y} = {1, \ldots, k}\). Predict a discrete category.
  • Structured prediction — \(\mathcal{Y}\) is a structured object (sequence, tree, graph). Examples: machine translation, dependency parsing.

The fundamental challenge: labels are expensive. Human annotation does not scale. This is why the field has invested heavily in the paradigms below.

docs.title: 6.2 Unsupervised Learning
docs.text:
The training set consists of inputs only:

\[\mathcal{D} = {x_i}_{i=1}^n\]

There are no labels. The task is to discover the underlying structure of the data distribution \(P(\mathcal{X})\).

Sub-tasks:

  • Clustering — partition inputs into coherent groups.
  • Dimensionality reduction — find a low-dimensional representation that preserves structure.
  • Density estimation — learn an explicit or implicit model of \(P(x)\).
  • Representation learning — learn features useful for downstream tasks.

Unsupervised learning is harder to evaluate (there is no ground truth) but scales to vast amounts of unlabelled data.

docs.title: 6.3 Semi-Supervised Learning
docs.text:
The training set contains a small number of labelled examples and a large number of unlabelled examples:

\[\mathcal{D} = {(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^m \cup {x_j}_{j=m+1}^n \quad \text{where } m \ll n\]

The key assumption: unlabelled data carries information about the structure of \(P(\mathcal{X})\), which can improve learning of the conditional \(P(\mathcal{Y} | \mathcal{X})\).

This is the most realistic setting for many practical problems, where labelling is expensive but raw data is abundant.

docs.title: 6.4 Self-Supervised Learning
docs.text:
A special case of unsupervised learning where the supervision signal is generated automatically from the data itself — no human annotation required.

Examples:

  • Masked language modelling (BERT): mask 15% of tokens, predict the masked tokens. The "labels" are the original tokens.
  • Next-token prediction (GPT): predict the next token given all previous tokens.
  • Contrastive learning (SimCLR): create two augmented views of the same image, train a network to represent them similarly and represent different images differently.

Self-supervised learning has become the dominant paradigm for pretraining large models. The pretrained representations are then fine-tuned on small labelled datasets — this is transfer learning.

docs.title: 6.5 Reinforcement Learning
docs.text:
There is no fixed dataset. An agent interacts with an environment, takes actions, and receives scalar reward signals. The task is to learn a policy \(\pi : \mathcal{S} \to \mathcal{A}\) (from states to actions) that maximises cumulative discounted reward:

\[G_t = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k r_{t+k}, \quad \gamma \in [0,1)\]

The challenge: the agent must explore to discover what actions are rewarding, but must also exploit what it already knows to collect reward. This exploration-exploitation tradeoff is fundamental.

RL differs from supervised learning in two crucial ways:

  1. There is no supervisor providing correct actions — only a reward signal that may be delayed and noisy.
  2. The data distribution depends on the agent's own behaviour — the agent influences what it sees.

docs.title: 7. The Generalisation Problem
docs.text:
Return to the core question: why is generalisation hard?

Suppose we have a training set \(\mathcal{D}\) of \(n\) examples. We can always find a hypothesis \(h \in \mathcal{H}\) that perfectly fits \(\mathcal{D}\) — just memorise the training set. But memorisation is not learning. A memorising model has zero training error and potentially very high test error.

This is overfitting: the model has learned the training data rather than the underlying pattern.

The opposite failure is underfitting: the hypothesis class \(\mathcal{H}\) is too restricted to capture the true pattern even with unlimited data. A linear model trying to fit a cubic relationship will underfit regardless of how much data it sees.

The tension between these two failures is the central problem of supervised learning. It is studied formally through:

  • Bias-variance decomposition — see [[02. Statistical Learning Theory]]
  • VC theory and PAC learning — see [[02. Statistical Learning Theory]]
  • Regularisation — see [[04.Bias Variance Tradeoff]]

For now, the key intuition: the size of the hypothesis class \(\mathcal{H}\) must be matched to the amount of data \(n\). Too small \(\mathcal{H}\) relative to the complexity of \(f^*\) → underfitting. Too large \(\mathcal{H}\) relative to \(n\) → overfitting.

More data always helps. More flexible models help only when data is sufficient to constrain them.

docs.text:
The table below is not exhaustive. It is a map for orientation.

Dimension Options Supervision Supervised, Unsupervised, Semi-supervised, Self-supervised, Reinforcement Output type Continuous (regression), Discrete (classification), Structured (sequence, graph, tree) Output cardinality Binary, Multi-class, Multi-label, Ordinal Data modality Tabular, Image, Text, Audio, Time series, Graph Online vs. batch Batch (fixed dataset), Online (stream of data, model updates incrementally) Stationary vs. non-stationary Stationary (\(P\) is fixed), Non-stationary (distribution shifts over time — concept drift) Single-task vs. multi-task Single task, Multi-task (shared representation across tasks), Transfer learning

Identifying where your problem sits in this taxonomy is the first step before choosing any algorithm.

Each stage is a note in this vault. This note is concerned only with the first stage: understanding what kind of problem you have and what the formal learning framework is.

docs.title: 10. Worked Example — Framing a Problem
docs.text:
Scenario. You work at a bank. The task is to detect fraudulent transactions.

Walk through the \((T, E, P)\) decomposition:

Task \(T\): Binary classification. Given a transaction \(x\) (amount, merchant category, location, time, account history, ...), predict \(y \in {0, 1}\) where \(y = 1\) means fraud.

Experience \(E\): Historical transaction records. Each record has been reviewed and labelled as fraudulent or legitimate by a human fraud team. Note: the dataset is severely class-imbalanced — fraud is rare, perhaps 0.1% of transactions.

Performance measure \(P\): Not accuracy. With 0.1% fraud rate, a classifier that always predicts "not fraud" achieves 99.9% accuracy while being completely useless. Better choices:

  • Precision — of the transactions flagged as fraud, how many are actually fraud? (Minimise false accusations)
  • Recall — of all actual fraud, how many did we catch? (Minimise missed fraud)
  • F1 score — harmonic mean of precision and recall
  • AUC-PR — area under the precision-recall curve — the right choice here
  • Business cost: false negatives (missed fraud) cost more than false positives (wrongly blocked transactions) — so weight recall higher

Hypothesis class \(\mathcal{H}\): Not yet determined. But the problem has structured tabular features, moderate \(n\) (millions of transactions), known class imbalance, and a need for some interpretability (for regulatory compliance). This points toward gradient boosting as a strong first candidate — see [[ML Algorithms Quick Reference]].

Inductive bias: Gradient boosting assumes the decision boundary is a piecewise-constant function that can be approximated by an additive combination of decision trees. For tabular fraud detection with threshold-based rules and interaction effects between features, this is a defensible assumption.

This is what proper problem framing looks like. The algorithm choice is almost a secondary concern once the framing is precise.

docs.title: 11. Exit Criteria
docs.text:
You know this note when you can do all of the following without looking anything up:

  1. State Mitchell's definition and explain why each of the three components is necessary.
  2. Define a hypothesis class formally and give three examples from different model families.
  3. Explain inductive bias with a concrete example — what does a linear model assume, and when does that assumption break?
  4. State the No Free Lunch theorem and explain what it means and what it does not mean.
  5. Distinguish supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised, self-supervised, and reinforcement learning by what structure of experience \(E\) each requires.
  6. Explain why a memorising model that achieves zero training error is not a good model.
  7. Given a new real-world problem, write out the \((T, E, P)\) decomposition with precision — specifying the output space, the data available, and a justified choice of performance measure.

docs.title: Statistical Learning Theory
docs.text:
"The question of what it means to learn, stated mathematically, turns out to be surprisingly subtle — and the answer is what separates algorithms that generalise from algorithms that merely memorise."

Part of: [[04.Machine Learning]] > Part 0 — Foundations Previous: [[01. The Learning Problem]] Next: [[03. Probability and Statistics Review]]

docs.title: 1. Why a Theory of Learning?
docs.text:
The previous note established the informal goal: find a hypothesis \(h \in \mathcal{H}\) that approximates the unknown target function \(f^*\) well on unseen data. But several questions remain unanswered:

  • How much training data is enough to guarantee good generalisation?
  • How do we quantify the complexity of a hypothesis class?
  • What is the precise relationship between training error and test error?
  • Can we prove that a learning algorithm will work, before seeing test data?

Statistical learning theory answers these questions formally. The framework developed here — risk minimisation, PAC learning, VC theory, and the bias-variance decomposition — underlies every algorithm in this vault, even when it operates silently in the background.

docs.title: 2.1 Setup
docs.text:
Let \(\mathcal{X}\) be the input space and \(\mathcal{Y}\) the output space. Assume all data is drawn i.i.d. from a fixed but unknown joint distribution:

\[P_{XY} \text{ over } \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}\]

The i.i.d. assumption is strong. It says:

  1. Every example is drawn from the same distribution (identically distributed).
  2. Examples are drawn independently — the \(i\)-th example gives no information about the \((i+1)\)-th.

In practice, this assumption is violated constantly — sequential data, selection bias, distribution shift over time. Knowing the assumption allows you to reason about when violations matter.

docs.title: 2.2 The Loss Function
docs.text:
A loss function \(\ell : \mathcal{Y} \times \mathcal{Y} \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\) quantifies the cost of predicting \(\hat{y}\) when the true label is \(y\).

\[\ell(\hat{y}, y) \geq 0, \quad \ell(\hat{y}, y) = 0 \text{ if and only if } \hat{y} = y \text{ (for most losses)}\]

Common examples:

Loss Formula Used for Squared loss \(\ell(\hat{y}, y) = (\hat{y} - y)^2\) Regression Absolute loss $\ell(\hat{y}, y) = \hat{y} - y 0-1 loss \(\ell(\hat{y}, y) = \mathbf{1}[\hat{y} \neq y]\) Classification Log loss \(\ell(\hat{p}, y) = -y \log \hat{p} - (1-y)\log(1-\hat{p})\) Probabilistic classifiers Hinge loss \(\ell(\hat{y}, y) = \max(0, 1 - y\hat{y})\) SVM

The choice of loss function is a modelling decision. It encodes what kinds of errors you care about and how much.

docs.title: 2.3 Population Risk
docs.text:
The population risk (or expected risk, or true risk) of a hypothesis \(h\) is:

\[R(h) = \mathbb{E}_{(x,y) \sim P_{XY}}\left[\ell(h(x), y)\right]\]

This is the average loss over the entire data-generating distribution. It is what we actually want to minimise. It is also what we can never compute directly, because \(P_{XY}\) is unknown.

The Bayes-optimal predictor is:

\[h^* = \underset{h}{\arg\min} \ R(h)\]

This is the best any model can do. For squared loss, the Bayes-optimal predictor is \(h^_(x) = \mathbb{E}[y \mid x]\) — the conditional expectation. The Bayes risk \(R(h^_)\) is the irreducible noise floor, determined entirely by the randomness in \(P_{XY}\).

docs.title: 2.4 Empirical Risk
docs.text:
Since \(P_{XY}\) is unknown, we cannot compute \(R(h)\). Instead, we approximate it using the training set \(\mathcal{D} = {(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^n\):

\[\hat{R}(h) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \ell(h(x_i), y_i)\]

This is the empirical risk — the average loss on training data. It is computable. It is also a biased estimate of \(R(h)\) when \(h\) is chosen using the same data.

The quantity we truly care about is \(R(h)\). The quantity we can measure is \(\hat{R}(h)\). The gap between them is the central object of study in learning theory.

docs.title: 3. Empirical Risk Minimisation
docs.text:
Empirical Risk Minimisation (ERM) is the learning principle: choose the hypothesis in \(\mathcal{H}\) that minimises empirical risk:

\[\hat{h} = \underset{h \in \mathcal{H}}{\arg\min} \ \hat{R}(h)\]

Almost every supervised learning algorithm is ERM in some form:

  • Linear regression: ERM with squared loss and linear \(\mathcal{H}\)
  • Logistic regression: ERM with log loss and sigmoid-linear \(\mathcal{H}\)
  • SVM: regularised ERM with hinge loss
  • Decision tree: approximate ERM with 0-1 loss (approximate because exact minimisation is NP-hard)

ERM is a reasonable principle. But it has a critical failure mode: if \(\mathcal{H}\) is too large, ERM can find a hypothesis that achieves zero training error while having arbitrarily bad test error. This is overfitting. The theory below characterises when ERM is safe.

docs.title: 4. The Generalisation Gap
docs.text:
Define the generalisation gap as:

\[\text{gen gap} = R(\hat{h}) - \hat{R}(\hat{h})\]

This is the difference between true error and training error for the learned hypothesis. It is always non-negative in expectation — training error is optimistically biased because \(\hat{h}\) was chosen to minimise it on the training data.

The fundamental question of learning theory: how large can the generalisation gap be, and what controls it?

The answer depends on two things:

  1. The complexity of \(\mathcal{H}\) — richer hypothesis classes can fit training data better, but they also have more room to overfit.
  2. The number of training examples \(n\) — more data shrinks the gap.

The theory below makes this precise.

docs.title: 5. PAC Learning
docs.text: Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning (Valiant, 1984) is the foundational framework for asking: when does learning provably work?

docs.title: 5.1 The Definition
docs.text:
A hypothesis class \(\mathcal{H}\) is PAC-learnable if there exists an algorithm \(\mathcal{A}\) and a function \(n_{\mathcal{H}}(\epsilon, \delta)\) such that: for any \(\epsilon > 0\) (accuracy parameter), any \(\delta > 0\) (confidence parameter), and any distribution \(P_{XY}\), when \(\mathcal{A}\) is run on \(n \geq n_{\mathcal{H}}(\epsilon, \delta)\) i.i.d. examples, it outputs \(\hat{h}\) satisfying:

\[P\left(R(\hat{h}) - R(h^*) \leq \epsilon\right) \geq 1 - \delta\]

Unpacking: with probability at least \(1 - \delta\) over the random draw of training data, the algorithm produces a hypothesis whose true risk is within \(\epsilon\) of the best possible.

The word "probably" refers to \(1 - \delta\). The word "approximately" refers to \(\epsilon\). Correct means we are close to the best hypothesis in \(\mathcal{H}\).

docs.title: 5.2 Sample Complexity
docs.text:
The function \(n_{\mathcal{H}}(\epsilon, \delta)\) is the sample complexity: the minimum number of training examples required to guarantee PAC learning.

For a finite hypothesis class \(|\mathcal{H}| < \infty\), a clean bound holds. With probability at least \(1 - \delta\), for all \(h \in \mathcal{H}\) simultaneously:

\[R(h) \leq \hat{R}(h) + \sqrt{\frac{\log|\mathcal{H}| + \log(1/\delta)}{2n}}\]

This is a uniform convergence bound — it holds for all \(h\) at once, not just for the particular \(\hat{h}\) chosen by ERM. The bound tells us:

  • More hypotheses (\(|\mathcal{H}|\) larger) → larger gap. Richer classes require more data.
  • More data (\(n\) larger) → smaller gap. At rate \(O(1/\sqrt{n})\).
  • Higher confidence required (\(\delta\) smaller) → slightly larger gap, only logarithmically.

The sample complexity for finite \(\mathcal{H}\) is:

\[n_{\mathcal{H}}(\epsilon, \delta) = O!\left(\frac{\log|\mathcal{H}| + \log(1/\delta)}{\epsilon^2}\right)\]

docs.title: 5.3 Proof Sketch (Finite \(\mathcal{H}\))
docs.text:
The proof uses two standard tools: Hoeffding's inequality and the union bound.

Hoeffding's inequality. If \(Z_1, \ldots, Z_n\) are i.i.d., bounded in \([a, b]\), with mean \(\mu\), then for any \(t > 0\):

\[P!\left(\bar{Z} - \mu \geq t\right) \leq \exp!\left(-\frac{2n^2 t^2}{\sum_i (b_i - a_i)^2}\right)\]

For a single hypothesis \(h\), each \(\ell(h(x_i), y_i)\) is a bounded random variable with mean \(R(h)\). Hoeffding gives:

\[P!\left(R(h) - \hat{R}(h) \geq \epsilon\right) \leq e^{-2n\epsilon^2}\]

Union bound. For \(|\mathcal{H}|\) hypotheses, taking a union over all of them:

\[P!\left(\exists h \in \mathcal{H}: R(h) - \hat{R}(h) \geq \epsilon\right) \leq |\mathcal{H}| \cdot e^{-2n\epsilon^2}\]

Setting the right side equal to \(\delta\) and solving for \(\epsilon\) gives the bound in Section 5.2. \(\square\)

docs.title: 5.4 The Problem with Infinite \(\mathcal{H}\)
docs.text: The bound in Section 5.2 requires \(|\mathcal{H}| < \infty\). But most useful hypothesis classes — linear classifiers, neural networks — are infinite. We need a different notion of complexity.

docs.title: 6. VC Dimension
docs.text: The Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) dimension (Vapnik & Chervonenkis, 1971) measures the complexity of an infinite hypothesis class by how many points it can classify in all possible ways.

docs.title: 6.1 Shattering
docs.text:
A hypothesis class \(\mathcal{H}\) shatters a set \({x_1, \ldots, x_m} \subset \mathcal{X}\) if for every possible binary labelling \(y \in {0,1}^m\) of those points, there exists \(h \in \mathcal{H}\) that achieves it:

\[\forall (y_1, \ldots, y_m) \in {0,1}^m, \exists h \in \mathcal{H}: h(x_i) = y_i \text{ for all } i\]

Shattering means \(\mathcal{H}\) is expressive enough to represent every possible dichotomy on that set.

docs.title: 6.2 VC Dimension Defined
docs.text:
\[\text{VC-dim}(\mathcal{H}) = \max{m : \exists {x_1,\ldots,x_m} \subseteq \mathcal{X} \text{ that } \mathcal{H} \text{ shatters}}\]

The VC dimension is the size of the largest set that \(\mathcal{H}\) can shatter.

docs.title: 6.3 Examples
docs.text:
Linear classifiers in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) (hyperplanes, i.e., \(h(x) = \text{sign}(w^Tx + b)\)):

\(\text{VC-dim} = d + 1\).

To see why: in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), any 3 non-collinear points can be shattered by lines — for any binary labelling of 3 points, a line exists separating the two classes. But no set of 4 points can always be shattered — the XOR labelling (alternating corners of a square) cannot be achieved by a single line.

In \(\mathbb{R}^d\): any \(d+1\) points in general position can be shattered, but no set of \(d+2\) points can always be shattered.

Intuition. A linear classifier in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) has \(d+1\) free parameters (\(d\) weights + 1 bias). The VC dimension matches the number of parameters for linear models — a useful rule of thumb, though not a theorem.

Intervals on \(\mathbb{R}\) (classify \(x\) as positive iff \(x \in [a, b]\)):

\(\text{VC-dim} = 2\).

Any two points \(x_1 < x_2\) can be shattered: choose \([x_1 - \epsilon, x_1 + \epsilon]\) for \({+, -}\), \([x_2 - \epsilon, x_2 + \epsilon]\) for \({-, +}\), \([x_1 - \epsilon, x_2 + \epsilon]\) for \({+, +}\), and \((-\infty, x_1 - \epsilon)\) for \({-, -}\). But 3 points \(x_1 < x_2 < x_3\) cannot be shattered — the labelling \({+, -, +}\) requires a union of two intervals, which a single interval cannot achieve.

Convex polygons in \(\mathbb{R}^2\):

\(\text{VC-dim} = \infty\).

For any \(n\), place \(n\) points on a circle. For any subset \(S\), the convex hull of \(S\) correctly classifies all points: those in \(S\) are inside (positive), those outside \(S\) are outside (negative). Since this works for any \(n\), the VC dimension is infinite.

Takeaway. Infinite VC dimension does not mean the class is unlearnable — it means PAC learning in the realizable setting requires additional assumptions. In practice, infinite VC dimension is a signal that the class can overfit badly with finite data.

docs.title: 6.4 The Fundamental Theorem of Statistical Learning
docs.text:
For binary classification with 0-1 loss, the following are equivalent:

  1. \(\mathcal{H}\) is PAC-learnable.
  2. \(\text{VC-dim}(\mathcal{H}) < \infty\).
  3. \(\mathcal{H}\) has the uniform convergence property.

This is the fundamental theorem. VC dimension fully characterises learnability for binary classification.

docs.title: 6.5 VC Generalisation Bound
docs.text:
For any \(\mathcal{H}\) with \(\text{VC-dim}(\mathcal{H}) = d < \infty\), with probability at least \(1 - \delta\):

\[R(\hat{h}) \leq \hat{R}(\hat{h}) + O!\left(\sqrt{\frac{d \log(n/d) + \log(1/\delta)}{n}}\right)\]

The sample complexity becomes:

\[n_{\mathcal{H}}(\epsilon, \delta) = O!\left(\frac{d \log(d/\epsilon) + \log(1/\delta)}{\epsilon^2}\right)\]

Key observations:

  • The rate is still \(O(1/\sqrt{n})\) in samples.
  • Complexity is controlled by \(d = \text{VC-dim}(\mathcal{H})\), not by \(|\mathcal{H}|\).
  • For linear classifiers in \(\mathbb{R}^d\): \(d+1\) dimensions of VC complexity → sample complexity scales linearly with the number of features.

docs.title: 7. The Bias-Variance Decomposition
docs.text: The VC bound is a worst-case result. It tells us when learning is possible. The bias-variance decomposition tells us what kind of error we are making and why.

docs.title: 7.1 Setup
docs.text:
Fix a point \(x \in \mathcal{X}\). Suppose we draw many training sets \(\mathcal{D}\) of size \(n\) from \(P_{XY}\), train a model \(\hat{h}_{\mathcal{D}}\) on each, and observe the resulting predictions \(\hat{h}_{\mathcal{D}}(x)\).

Define:

  • The expected prediction at \(x\): \(\bar{h}(x) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}[\hat{h}_{\mathcal{D}}(x)]\)
  • The true label generating process: \(y = f^*(x) + \epsilon\), where \(\epsilon \sim (0, \sigma^2)\) is noise with mean zero and variance \(\sigma^2\), independent of \(x\)

docs.title: 7.2 The Decomposition
docs.text:
For squared loss, the expected prediction error at a point \(x\) decomposes as:

\[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}, \epsilon}\left[(\hat{h}_{\mathcal{D}}(x) - y)^2\right] = \underbrace{\left(\bar{h}(x) - f^*(x)\right)^2}_{\text{Bias}^2} + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}\left[(\hat{h}_{\mathcal{D}}(x) - \bar{h}(x))^2\right]}_{\text{Variance}} + \underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{Irreducible noise}}\]

docs.title: 7.3 Full Derivation
docs.text:
Let \(\hat{h} = \hat{h}_{\mathcal{D}}(x)\), \(\bar{h} = \bar{h}(x)\), \(f = f^*(x)\), \(y = f + \epsilon\).

\[\mathbb{E}[(\hat{h} - y)^2] = \mathbb{E}[(\hat{h} - f - \epsilon)^2]\] \[= \mathbb{E}[(\hat{h} - f)^2] - 2\mathbb{E}[(\hat{h} - f)\epsilon] + \mathbb{E}[\epsilon^2]\]

Since \(\epsilon\) is independent of \(\hat{h}\) (which depends only on training data, not on the noise at test time), \(\mathbb{E}[(\hat{h} - f)\epsilon] = 0\). So:

\[= \mathbb{E}[(\hat{h} - f)^2] + \sigma^2\]

Now expand the first term by adding and subtracting \(\bar{h}\):

\[\mathbb{E}[(\hat{h} - f)^2] = \mathbb{E}[(\hat{h} - \bar{h} + \bar{h} - f)^2]\] \[= \mathbb{E}[(\hat{h} - \bar{h})^2] + 2\mathbb{E}[(\hat{h} - \bar{h})](\bar{h} - f) + (\bar{h} - f)^2\]

The cross-term vanishes: \(\mathbb{E}[\hat{h} - \bar{h}] = \mathbb{E}[\hat{h}] - \bar{h} = 0\) by definition of \(\bar{h}\).

Therefore:

\[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[(\hat{h} - y)^2] = \underbrace{(\bar{h} - f)^2}_{\text{Bias}^2} + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[(\hat{h} - \bar{h})^2]}_{\text{Variance}} + \underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{Irreducible}}}\]

\(\square\)

docs.title: 7.4 Interpreting Each Term
docs.text:
Bias\(^2\). The squared difference between the average prediction of the model (across all possible training sets) and the true function value. Bias measures systematic error — the error that persists even with infinite data. A linear model fitting a cubic function has high bias: no matter how much data you give it, it will never recover the cubic.

\[\text{Bias}^2 = (\bar{h}(x) - f^*(x))^2\]

High bias is caused by: too simple a hypothesis class \(\mathcal{H}\), wrong inductive bias, too much regularisation.

Variance. The expected squared deviation of the model's prediction from its own average across different training sets. Variance measures instability — sensitivity to the particular training set drawn. A depth-100 decision tree with 100 training points has high variance: swap a few training examples and the tree changes completely.

\[\text{Variance} = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}[(\hat{h}_{\mathcal{D}}(x) - \bar{h}(x))^2]\]

High variance is caused by: too complex a hypothesis class, too little data, too little regularisation.

Irreducible noise \(\sigma^2\). The variance of the label noise. This cannot be reduced by any model, regardless of its complexity or the amount of data. It reflects genuine randomness in \(P_{XY}\). The Bayes risk is exactly \(\sigma^2\).

docs.title: 7.5 The Bias-Variance Tradeoff
docs.text:
The total expected error is \(\text{Bias}^2 + \text{Variance} + \sigma^2\). Since \(\sigma^2\) is fixed, we want to minimise \(\text{Bias}^2 + \text{Variance}\).

These two terms pull in opposite directions as model complexity increases:

Error
  |
  |  \          Bias^2 + Variance
  |   \       /
  |    \     /
  |     \   /   Total error
  |      \ /
  |       X  <- optimal complexity
  |      / \
  |     /   \  Variance
  |    /     ---
  |---        Bias^2
  |_________________________ Model complexity

As complexity increases:

  • Bias decreases: richer \(\mathcal{H}\) can approximate \(f^*\) more closely.
  • Variance increases: richer \(\mathcal{H}\) is more sensitive to the particular training set.

The optimal model complexity sits at the bottom of the total error U-curve.

Important caveat — double descent. Modern deep learning has revealed that the classical U-curve is incomplete. For very large models (neural networks with millions of parameters trained on limited data), test error can decrease again after the classical overfitting peak. This "double descent" phenomenon occurs near the interpolation threshold where the model just fits the training data, and then continues to decrease as the model is made even larger. The bias-variance framework is still valid, but the relationship between model complexity and variance is more subtle than the classical picture suggests.

docs.title: 7.6 Implications for Regularisation
docs.text:
The bias-variance decomposition directly motivates regularisation:

  • L2 regularisation (Ridge): adds a penalty \(\lambda |w|_2^2\) to the loss. This constrains the hypothesis class, reducing variance at the cost of slightly increased bias. Equivalent to placing a Gaussian prior on weights.
  • L1 regularisation (Lasso): adds \(\lambda |w|_1\). Induces sparsity — drives some weights to exactly zero, effectively shrinking \(\mathcal{H}\) by removing features.
  • Early stopping: terminating gradient descent before convergence prevents the model from fully memorising the training set. Equivalent to L2 regularisation for gradient descent on convex losses.
  • Dropout: randomly zeroing activations during training. Equivalent to training an ensemble of thinned networks — reduces variance by averaging.

All regularisation is variance reduction at the cost of some bias. The hyperparameter (\(\lambda\), \(k\) in dropout, number of epochs) controls where on the bias-variance curve you sit.

docs.title: 8. Rademacher Complexity
docs.text: VC dimension is combinatorial and only applies to binary classification. A more general complexity measure is Rademacher complexity, which applies to any real-valued function class and any loss.

docs.title: 8.1 Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a class of functions \(f : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}\) and \(\mathcal{D} = {x_1, \ldots, x_n}\) a sample. The empirical Rademacher complexity is:

\[\hat{\mathcal{R}}_n(\mathcal{F}) = \mathbb{E}_\sigma!\left[\sup_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \sigma_i f(x_i)\right]\]

where \(\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_n \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \text{Uniform}({-1, +1})\) are Rademacher random variables.

The Rademacher complexity is \(\mathcal{R}_n(\mathcal{F}) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}[\hat{\mathcal{R}}_n(\mathcal{F})]\).

docs.title: 8.2 Intuition
docs.text:
The Rademacher variables \(\sigma_i\) are random \(\pm 1\) labels. The empirical Rademacher complexity asks: how well can functions in \(\mathcal{F}\) correlate with random noise?

A very rich function class can always find some \(f\) that correlates well with any random labelling. A simple class cannot. So \(\hat{\mathcal{R}}_n(\mathcal{F})\) measures the expressive power of \(\mathcal{F}\) — how much it can overfit noise.

docs.title: 8.3 Rademacher Generalisation Bound
docs.text:
With probability at least \(1 - \delta\) over a sample of size \(n\):

\[R(\hat{h}) \leq \hat{R}(\hat{h}) + 2\mathcal{R}_n(\mathcal{H}_\ell) + \sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{2n}}\]

where \(\mathcal{H}_\ell = {\ell(h(\cdot), \cdot) : h \in \mathcal{H}}\) is the loss class induced by \(\mathcal{H}\).

This bound is tighter than the VC bound in many cases and applies beyond binary classification to regression, multi-class, and structured prediction.

docs.title: 9. The Decomposition of Excess Risk
docs.text:
The total excess risk of a learned hypothesis \(\hat{h}\) over the Bayes-optimal \(h^*\) can be decomposed into two interpretable terms:

\[\underbrace{R(\hat{h}) - R(h^_)}_{\text{Excess risk}} = \underbrace{R(h^__{\mathcal{H}}) - R(h^*)}_{\text{Approximation error}} + \underbrace{R(\hat{h}) - R(h^*_{\mathcal{H}})}_{\text{Estimation error}}\]

where \(h^*_{\mathcal{H}} = \arg\min_{h \in \mathcal{H}} R(h)\) is the best hypothesis in the class.

Approximation error (bias term). How much worse is the best hypothesis in \(\mathcal{H}\) compared to the true Bayes-optimal? This is determined by the richness of \(\mathcal{H}\) and cannot be reduced by more data — only by a richer class.

Estimation error (variance term). How much worse is the learned \(\hat{h}\) compared to the best possible \(h^*_{\mathcal{H}}\)? This is due to finite samples and decreases as \(n \to \infty\).

The bias-variance tradeoff, VC theory, and Rademacher complexity all formalise different aspects of the same underlying tension: approximation error decreases as \(\mathcal{H}\) grows, estimation error increases as \(\mathcal{H}\) grows.

docs.title: 10. Occam's Razor as a Theorem
docs.text:
Occam's Razor — prefer simpler hypotheses — is not just philosophical wisdom. It follows from the PAC learning bound.

Recall from Section 5.2: with probability at least \(1 - \delta\), for all \(h \in \mathcal{H}\):

\[R(h) \leq \hat{R}(h) + \sqrt{\frac{\log|\mathcal{H}| + \log(1/\delta)}{2n}}\]

Suppose we can assign a prior complexity \(c(h) > 0\) to each hypothesis such that \(\sum_{h \in \mathcal{H}} e^{-c(h)} \leq 1\) (a valid probability distribution over hypotheses). Then a tighter bound holds:

\[R(h) \leq \hat{R}(h) + \sqrt{\frac{c(h) + \log(1/\delta)}{2n}}\]

A hypothesis with lower complexity \(c(h)\) gets a smaller generalisation penalty. The theorem says: if two hypotheses achieve the same training error, the simpler one (smaller \(c(h)\)) has a tighter bound on its true error.

This is Occam's Razor as a theorem. Simplicity is not an aesthetic preference — it is a statistical guarantee.

docs.title: 11. Structural Risk Minimisation
docs.text:
Structural Risk Minimisation (SRM) (Vapnik, 1982) uses the theory above to choose both a hypothesis and a hypothesis class simultaneously.

Suppose we have a nested sequence of hypothesis classes:

\[\mathcal{H}_1 \subset \mathcal{H}_2 \subset \cdots \subset \mathcal{H}_k\]

with increasing complexity \(d_1 \leq d_2 \leq \cdots \leq d_k\) (e.g., linear classifiers of increasing VC dimension, or polynomial regressors of increasing degree).

SRM selects:

\[\hat{k}, \hat{h} = \underset{k, h \in \mathcal{H}_k}{\arg\min} \left[\hat{R}(h) + \text{complexity penalty}(n, d_k, \delta)\right]\]

where the complexity penalty comes from the VC bound. SRM trades off training fit and model complexity in a principled way.

In practice, SRM motivates:

  • Cross-validation for model selection (empirically approximating the bound)
  • Regularisation paths in Lasso and Ridge (tracing \(\hat{h}\) as \(\lambda\) varies)
  • Bayesian model selection via marginal likelihood (integrating out parameters)

docs.title: 12. What This Theory Does and Does Not Say
What it says
docs.text:
• PAC learning gives sufficient conditions for generalisation: if \(\text{VC-dim}(\mathcal{H}) < \infty\) and \(n\) is large enough, ERM generalises.
  • The generalisation gap shrinks at rate \(O(1/\sqrt{n})\) in samples.
  • Model complexity must be matched to sample size.
  • Simpler models that fit the data well are preferable to complex ones that fit equally well.

docs.title: What it does not say
docs.text:
• The bounds are often very loose. A VC bound may say you need \(10^6\) samples; in practice \(10^3\) suffice. The bounds are informative about rates and dependencies, not about constants.
  • The theory assumes i.i.d. data. Distribution shift, covariate shift, and temporal dependence are not covered.
  • The theory does not explain the empirical success of modern deep learning, where models interpolate (zero training error) yet generalise. This is an active research area. The double descent phenomenon and implicit regularisation of SGD are partial explanations.
  • For neural networks, VC dimension is enormous (proportional to the number of parameters times the number of layers) — yet practical generalisation is far better than the bound predicts. The theory is necessary but not sufficient for understanding deep learning.

docs.title: 13. Exit Criteria
docs.text:
You know this note when you can do all of the following without reference:

  1. Define population risk, empirical risk, and the generalisation gap. Explain why the empirical risk of a learned hypothesis is a biased estimate of its true risk.

  2. State the ERM principle and identify it in three specific learning algorithms.

  3. Prove the finite hypothesis class generalisation bound using Hoeffding's inequality and the union bound.

  4. Define VC dimension precisely and compute it for (a) linear classifiers in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), (b) intervals on \(\mathbb{R}\).

  5. State the fundamental theorem of statistical learning: for binary classification, PAC-learnability is equivalent to finite VC dimension.

  6. Derive the bias-variance decomposition for squared loss from first principles. Identify what causes high bias and what causes high variance, and give one concrete example of each.

  7. Explain the excess risk decomposition into approximation error and estimation error. Relate these to the bias-variance tradeoff.

  8. State Occam's Razor as a formal theorem and explain what "complexity" means in that context.

  9. Explain one thing the theory correctly predicts about practical ML, and one thing where it fails to match empirical behaviour.
