docs.title: Performance Metrics
docs.text: "A metric is a compressed summary of model behaviour. Every compression loses information. The art is knowing which information you can afford to lose — and which losses will cost you in production."

docs.title: ✦ Why Metrics Matter More Than People Think
docs.text:
A metric does three things simultaneously:

  1. Defines what "better" means — it is the objective function of model selection
  2. Summarises a distribution of errors into a scalar — information is always lost
  3. Encodes a value judgement about which errors cost more

Choosing the wrong metric is not a technical mistake — it is a specification mistake. A model that perfectly optimises the wrong metric can be actively harmful. Classic examples:

  • Accuracy on imbalanced data: a cancer detector that predicts "no cancer" for everyone achieves 99.5% accuracy when prevalence is 0.5%. It has zero clinical utility.
  • MSE for demand forecasting: penalises overestimation and underestimation equally. If overstock costs $1/unit and stockout costs $10/unit, MSE optimises the wrong objective.
  • BLEU score for translation: maximises n-gram overlap. A model can score well by producing fluent but factually wrong translations.

The sections below derive each metric from first principles and make explicit what value judgement it encodes.

docs.title: ✦ Part I — Regression Metrics
docs.text: Setting: \(y \in \mathbb{R}\), predictions \(\hat{y}_i\), residuals \(e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i\).

docs.title: Mean Squared Error (MSE)
docs.text:
\[\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} e_i^2\]

What it encodes: squared error penalises large residuals quadratically. An error of 10 is penalised 100× more than an error of 1. MSE is the right metric when large errors are disproportionately costly.

Probabilistic derivation: MSE is the negative log-likelihood of a Gaussian noise model. If \(y_i = f(x_i) + \epsilon_i\) with \(\epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\):

\[-\log P(\mathcal{D}|\theta) = \frac{n}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^2) + \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i e_i^2\]

Minimising MSE is therefore equivalent to maximum likelihood estimation under Gaussian noise. This is the probabilistic justification for OLS.

Units: squared units of \(y\). Hard to interpret directly.

Sensitivity to outliers: extreme. A single outlier with \(|e_i| = 100\) contributes \(10^4\) to the sum. For robust regression, prefer MAE or Huber loss.

docs.title: Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)
docs.text:
\[\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\text{MSE}} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_i e_i^2}\]

Same units as \(y\). Directly interpretable as "typical error magnitude" — but still outlier-sensitive. Preferred over MSE for reporting because of interpretability.

RMSE vs. standard deviation of residuals:

\[s_e = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-p}\sum_i e_i^2}\]

RMSE divides by \(n\); \(s_e\) divides by \(n-p\) (degrees of freedom, \(p\) = number of parameters). For large \(n\), the difference is negligible. \(s_e\) is unbiased; RMSE is slightly biased downward.

docs.title: Mean Absolute Error (MAE)
docs.text:
\[\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} |y_i - \hat{y}_i| = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i |e_i|\]

What it encodes: all errors penalised linearly. Robust to outliers — a single large \(|e_i|\) contributes proportionally, not quadratically.

Probabilistic derivation: MAE is the negative log-likelihood under a Laplace noise model. If \(\epsilon_i \sim \text{Laplace}(0, b)\):

\[P(\epsilon_i) = \frac{1}{2b}\exp!\left(-\frac{|\epsilon_i|}{b}\right)\] \[-\log P(\mathcal{D}|\theta) \propto \sum_i |e_i|\]

Minimising MAE is MLE under Laplace noise. The optimal predictor under MAE is the conditional median \(\hat{y} = \text{median}(y|x)\); under MSE it is the conditional mean \(\hat{y} = \mathbb{E}[y|x]\).

Gradient: MAE is not differentiable at \(e_i = 0\). The subgradient is \(\text{sign}(e_i)\). In practice this causes instability near convergence for gradient-based optimisers — use Huber loss instead.

docs.title: Huber Loss
docs.text:
Combines MSE's smoothness near zero with MAE's robustness to outliers:

\[L_\delta(e) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2}e^2 & \text{if } |e| \leq \delta \ \delta|e| - \frac{1}{2}\delta^2 & \text{if } |e| > \delta \end{cases}\]

Quadratic for small residuals (smooth, fast convergence), linear for large residuals (robust to outliers). The hyperparameter \(\delta\) controls the transition point.

Why it matters in practice: Huber loss is the default in robust regression and is used as the regression head loss in many object detection networks (e.g., Faster R-CNN uses smooth L1, which is Huber with \(\delta=1\)).

docs.title: \(R^2\) (Coefficient of Determination)
docs.text:
\[R^2 = 1 - \frac{\text{SS}_{\text{res}}}{\text{SS}_{\text{tot}}} = 1 - \frac{\sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum_i (y_i - \bar{y})^2}\]

Interpretation: fraction of variance in \(y\) explained by the model. \(R^2 = 1\) means perfect prediction; \(R^2 = 0\) means the model does no better than predicting the mean \(\bar{y}\); \(R^2 < 0\) means the model is worse than the mean predictor.

Derivation of the decomposition. For OLS specifically (and OLS only, when an intercept is included):

\[\text{SS}_{\text{tot}} = \text{SS}_{\text{reg}} + \text{SS}_{\text{res}}\] \[\sum_i (y_i - \bar{y})^2 = \sum_i (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2 + \sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\]

This follows from \(\hat{\epsilon} \perp \hat{y}\) in OLS (the residuals are orthogonal to the fitted values — a consequence of the normal equations). This decomposition does not hold for arbitrary models or without an intercept.

Pitfalls:

  • \(R^2\) always increases as you add features (even noise features). Use adjusted \(R^2\): \(\bar{R}^2 = 1 - \frac{(1-R^2)(n-1)}{n-p-1}\), which penalises model complexity
  • \(R^2\) is not a measure of predictive accuracy for new data — a model can have high \(R^2\) in-sample and poor generalisation
  • For non-OLS models (random forests, NNs), \(R^2\) can be negative on the test set even if the model performs well

docs.title: Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE)
docs.text:
\[\text{MAPE} = \frac{100}{n}\sum_i \frac{|y_i - \hat{y}_i|}{|y_i|}\]

Scale-free: useful for comparing models across datasets with different units or magnitudes. Used heavily in forecasting (demand, finance).

Critical failure mode: undefined when \(y_i = 0\); heavily penalises underestimates relative to overestimates (asymmetric). Prefer sMAPE (symmetric MAPE) or MASE (mean absolute scaled error) for forecasting.

docs.title: The Confusion Matrix — The Foundation
docs.text:
For binary classification (\(y \in {0, 1}\), positive class = 1):

\[\begin{array}{c|cc} & \hat{y} = 1 & \hat{y} = 0 \ \hline y = 1 & \text{TP} & \text{FN} \ y = 0 & \text{FP} & \text{TN} \end{array}\]
  • TP (True Positive): correctly predicted positive
  • FP (False Positive): incorrectly predicted positive — Type I error
  • FN (False Negative): incorrectly predicted negative — Type II error
  • TN (True Negative): correctly predicted negative

Every binary classification metric is a function of these four numbers. Understanding the matrix is understanding all classification metrics.

docs.title: Accuracy
docs.text:
\[\text{Accuracy} = \frac{\text{TP} + \text{TN}}{\text{TP} + \text{TN} + \text{FP} + \text{FN}} = \frac{\text{correct predictions}}{n}\]

When it is meaningful: balanced classes, equal cost of FP and FN.

When it is misleading: class imbalance. If 95% of samples are negative, the trivial classifier \(\hat{y} = 0\) achieves 95% accuracy. This is the accuracy paradox.

The deeper problem: accuracy treats all errors equally. In most real problems, FP and FN have different costs. Accuracy ignores this.

docs.title: Precision and Recall — The Fundamental Tradeoff
docs.text:
\[\text{Precision} = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FP}} \qquad \text{Recall} = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FN}}\]

Precision answers: of all instances we predicted positive, what fraction actually are positive? It measures the quality of positive predictions. Low precision = many false alarms.

Recall (sensitivity, true positive rate) answers: of all actual positives, what fraction did we catch? It measures coverage of the positive class. Low recall = many missed positives.

The tradeoff is inherent and real. For any probabilistic classifier, predictions are \(\hat{p}(y=1|x)\), and a threshold \(\tau\) determines the decision: \(\hat{y} = \mathbf{1}[\hat{p} \geq \tau]\).

  • Increase \(\tau\): predict positive only when very confident → fewer FP (higher precision), more FN (lower recall)
  • Decrease \(\tau\): predict positive more liberally → more TP (higher recall), more FP (lower precision)

Domain determines which matters more:

Domain Costly Error Preferred Reasoning Cancer screening FN (missed cancer) High recall Missing cancer is catastrophic Spam filtering FP (lost legitimate email) High precision False alarms destroy user trust Information retrieval Depends on use case PR curve Plot the full tradeoff Fraud detection FN (missed fraud) High recall Financial losses from undetected fraud

docs.title: F1-Score — Harmonic Mean of Precision and Recall
docs.text:
\[F_1 = \frac{2 \cdot \text{Precision} \cdot \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}} = \frac{2\text{TP}}{2\text{TP} + \text{FP} + \text{FN}}\]

Why harmonic mean, not arithmetic? The harmonic mean penalises extreme imbalance between precision and recall. If precision = 1.0 and recall = 0.01:

\[\text{Arithmetic mean} = \frac{1.0 + 0.01}{2} = 0.505 \quad \text{(looks decent)}$$ $$F_1 = \frac{2 \times 1.0 \times 0.01}{1.0 + 0.01} = 0.020 \quad \text{(correctly poor)}\]

The harmonic mean is \(\leq\) the arithmetic mean, with equality only when both terms are equal. It rewards balanced precision and recall.

\(F_\beta\) generalisation: when FP and FN have different costs, weight recall \(\beta\) times more than precision:

\[F_\beta = (1 + \beta^2) \cdot \frac{\text{Precision} \cdot \text{Recall}}{\beta^2 \cdot \text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}\]
  • \(\beta = 0.5\): precision matters twice as much as recall
  • \(\beta = 1\): \(F_1\), equal weight
  • \(\beta = 2\): recall matters twice as much as precision (use for cancer detection)

docs.title: Specificity and False Positive Rate
docs.text:
\[\text{Specificity} = \frac{\text{TN}}{\text{TN} + \text{FP}} \qquad \text{FPR} = 1 - \text{Specificity} = \frac{\text{FP}}{\text{FP} + \text{TN}}\]

Specificity measures how well the classifier identifies negatives. FPR = probability of a false alarm given a truly negative instance. These appear on the x-axis of the ROC curve.

docs.title: ROC Curve and AUC
docs.text:
The Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve plots TPR (recall) vs. FPR at every possible threshold \(\tau \in [0, 1]\).

\[\text{ROC} = {(\text{FPR}(\tau), \text{TPR}(\tau)) : \tau \in [0,1]}\] 
TPR
1.0 |         ___________
    |       /            |
    |      /  Area = AUC |
    |     /              |
    |    /               |
    |   / (random)       |
0.0 |__/________________|
    0.0                 1.0  FPR

Key reference points:

  • \((0, 0)\): threshold = 1, predict everything negative
  • \((1, 1)\): threshold = 0, predict everything positive
  • \((0, 1)\): perfect classifier
  • Diagonal: random classifier

AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve):

\[\text{AUC} = \int_0^1 \text{TPR}(\text{FPR}), d(\text{FPR})\]

Probabilistic interpretation (Mann-Whitney U statistic): AUC equals the probability that the classifier assigns a higher score to a randomly chosen positive than to a randomly chosen negative:

\[\text{AUC} = P(\hat{p}(y=1|x^+) > \hat{p}(y=1|x^-))\]

where \(x^+\) is a random positive and \(x^-\) a random negative. This is a threshold-free measure of ranking quality.

Derivation. Let \(n_+, n_-\) be the number of positives and negatives. Order all \(n\) predictions by score. The Mann-Whitney U statistic counts concordant pairs:

\[U = \sum_{i: y_i=1} \sum_{j: y_j=0} \mathbf{1}[\hat{p}_i > \hat{p}_j]\]

Then \(\text{AUC} = U / (n_+ \cdot n_-)\). This gives an \(O(n \log n)\) algorithm for computing AUC exactly (sort by score, count inversions).

When AUC is appropriate: ranking quality matters, threshold is not fixed. AUC is threshold-invariant — good for comparing classifiers when the operating threshold will be chosen later.

When AUC is misleading: severe class imbalance. AUC can be high even when precision is catastrophically low. Consider a dataset with 1000 negatives and 10 positives. A classifier that ranks all positives above all negatives achieves AUC = 1.0, but at FPR = 1% it may have only 50% precision. Use the PR curve instead.

docs.title: Precision-Recall Curve
docs.text:
The PR curve plots Precision vs. Recall at every threshold \(\tau\).

\[\text{PR curve} = {(\text{Recall}(\tau), \text{Precision}(\tau)) : \tau \in [0,1]}\]

Average Precision (AP):

\[\text{AP} = \sum_k (\text{Recall}_k - \text{Recall}_{k-1}) \cdot \text{Precision}_k\]

This is the area under the PR curve, approximated by the step function of threshold-sorted predictions.

Why PR is preferred under class imbalance: Precision = TP/(TP+FP) — FP is in the denominator. When negatives are abundant, a classifier that generates many FP is correctly penalised by low precision. The ROC curve's FPR = FP/(FP+TN) — TN is in the denominator — so large TN dilutes the penalty for many FP. The ROC curve is "too forgiving" when negatives vastly outnumber positives.

Comparison:

Scenario Use Balanced classes, threshold flexibility ROC / AUC Imbalanced classes (fraud, disease, rare events) PR curve / AP Fixed operating point (specific threshold) Precision + Recall at that threshold Final report scalar F1 (balanced) or \(F_\beta\) (asymmetric costs)

docs.title: Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC)
docs.text:
\[\text{MCC} = \frac{\text{TP} \cdot \text{TN} - \text{FP} \cdot \text{FN}}{\sqrt{(\text{TP}+\text{FP})(\text{TP}+\text{FN})(\text{TN}+\text{FP})(\text{TN}+\text{FN})}}\]

MCC ranges from \(-1\) (perfect inverse prediction) to \(+1\) (perfect prediction). MCC \(= 0\) for a random predictor regardless of class balance.

Why MCC is more informative than \(F_1\):

\(F_1\) ignores TN entirely — it does not appear in the formula. This makes \(F_1\) insensitive to how well the classifier identifies negatives. MCC uses all four cells of the confusion matrix. For imbalanced binary classification, MCC is now the recommended metric in computational biology and is increasingly standard in ML (Chicco & Jurman, 2020).

Worked example: dataset with 90 negatives, 10 positives. Classifier predicts all negative:

\[\text{TP}=0,\ \text{FP}=0,\ \text{FN}=10,\ \text{TN}=90\] \[\text{Accuracy} = 90%$$ $$\text{Recall} = 0%,\quad \text{Precision} = \text{undefined (0/0)}$$ $$F_1 = 0%$$ $$\text{MCC} = \frac{0 - 0}{\sqrt{0 \cdot 10 \cdot 90 \cdot 90}} = 0\]

MCC = 0 correctly identifies this as a random-level classifier. Accuracy (90%) is wildly misleading.

docs.title: ✦ Part III — Multi-Class Classification
docs.text:
For \(C\) classes, extend the binary confusion matrix to a \(C \times C\) matrix where entry \((i,j)\) counts samples of true class \(i\) predicted as class \(j\).

Macro-averaging: compute the metric for each class independently, then take the unweighted mean. Treats all classes equally regardless of frequency. Sensitive to performance on rare classes.

Micro-averaging: aggregate TP, FP, FN across all classes first, then compute the metric once. Dominated by frequent classes. Equivalent to accuracy for F1.

Weighted averaging: weight each class by its support (number of true samples). Standard in sklearn's classification_report.

\[F_1^{\text{macro}} = \frac{1}{C}\sum_{c=1}^C F_1^{(c)} \qquad F_1^{\text{micro}} = \frac{2\sum_c \text{TP}_c}{2\sum_c \text{TP}_c + \sum_c \text{FP}_c + \sum_c \text{FN}_c}\]

When to use which:

  • Macro: when every class matters equally (e.g., multi-disease diagnosis)
  • Micro: when overall per-sample performance matters (e.g., tag prediction)
  • Weighted: when class frequency should inform the metric (standard reporting)

docs.title: ✦ Part IV — Probabilistic Classifiers
docs.text: Some classifiers output calibrated probabilities \(\hat{p}(y=1|x)\) rather than hard labels. Evaluating these requires metrics that account for the full probability output.

docs.title: Log-Loss (Binary Cross-Entropy)
docs.text:
\[\mathcal{L}_{\log} = -\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \left[y_i \log \hat{p}_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-\hat{p}_i)\right]\]

What it measures: the average negative log-likelihood of the true labels under the predicted distribution. A perfectly calibrated classifier achieves log-loss equal to the entropy of the label distribution. Lower is better.

Why it penalises overconfident wrong predictions so harshly: if the true label is \(y=1\) and the model predicts \(\hat{p} = 0.001\), the contribution is \(-\log(0.001) \approx 6.9\). A confident wrong prediction is catastrophically penalised. This incentivises calibration.

Log-loss is the training objective for logistic regression and the output layer of classification neural networks. Using it as the evaluation metric aligns training and evaluation objectives perfectly.

docs.title: Brier Score
docs.text:
\[\text{BS} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (\hat{p}_i - y_i)^2\]

MSE for probability predictions. Ranges from 0 (perfect) to 1 (maximally wrong). Less sensitive to extreme predictions than log-loss (quadratic vs. logarithmic penalty).

Brier score decomposition:

\[\text{BS} = \underbrace{\frac{1}{n}\sum_k n_k (\bar{p}_k - \bar{y}_k)^2}_{\text{Calibration}} - \underbrace{\frac{1}{n}\sum_k n_k \bar{y}_k(1-\bar{y}_k)}_{\text{Resolution}} + \underbrace{\bar{y}(1-\bar{y})}_{\text{Uncertainty}}\]

where bins \(k\) group predictions into intervals of \(\hat{p}\). Calibration measures whether predicted probabilities match empirical frequencies; Resolution measures how much predicted probabilities differ from the base rate (informative classifiers have high resolution); Uncertainty is a property of the data, not the model.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
A classifier is calibrated if among all instances where it predicts \(\hat{p} = 0.7\), approximately 70% are truly positive.

Calibration plot (reliability diagram): bin predictions by \(\hat{p}\), plot mean predicted probability vs. empirical positive rate per bin. A perfectly calibrated classifier lies on the diagonal \(y=x\).

Empirical
positive
rate
1.0 |                    /  ← over-confident
    |               /
0.7 |          / ← well calibrated
    |      /
    |  /
0.0 |/________________________
    0.0    0.5    1.0   Predicted probability

Common miscalibration patterns:

  • Sigmoid-shaped curve (over-confident): model predicts probabilities too close to 0 and 1. Common in SVMs and boosting
  • Inverse sigmoid (under-confident): probabilities too moderate. Common in Naive Bayes

Calibration methods:

  • Platt scaling: fit a logistic regression on top of the raw model scores. Works well for SVMs
  • Isotonic regression: non-parametric, more flexible. Risk of overfitting on small datasets

Calibration matters whenever probabilities are used downstream — risk stratification, decision thresholds based on cost-benefit analysis, ensembling.

docs.title: Full Pipeline in sklearn
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, StratifiedKFold, cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import (
    accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score,
    roc_auc_score, average_precision_score, matthews_corrcoef,
    log_loss, brier_score_loss, classification_report,
    confusion_matrix, RocCurveDisplay, PrecisionRecallDisplay
)
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=42
)

pipe = Pipeline([("sc", StandardScaler()), ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)

y_pred  = pipe.predict(X_test)
y_prob  = pipe.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

# ── Threshold-dependent metrics ──────────────────────────────────────
print("Accuracy:  ", accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred))
print("Precision: ", precision_score(y_test, y_pred))
print("Recall:    ", recall_score(y_test, y_pred))
print("F1:        ", f1_score(y_test, y_pred))
print("MCC:       ", matthews_corrcoef(y_test, y_pred))
print()
print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred, target_names=["malignant", "benign"]))
print("Confusion matrix:\n", confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred))

# ── Threshold-independent metrics ────────────────────────────────────
print("ROC-AUC:   ", roc_auc_score(y_test, y_prob))
print("Avg Prec:  ", average_precision_score(y_test, y_prob))

# ── Probabilistic metrics ─────────────────────────────────────────────
print("Log-loss:  ", log_loss(y_test, y_prob))
print("Brier:     ", brier_score_loss(y_test, y_prob))

# ── Curves ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))
RocCurveDisplay.from_estimator(pipe, X_test, y_test, ax=ax1)
ax1.plot([0,1],[0,1],'k--', label='Random'); ax1.legend()

PrecisionRecallDisplay.from_estimator(pipe, X_test, y_test, ax=ax2)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

docs.title: Computing AUC from Scratch (Mann-Whitney U)
docs.text:
def auc_from_scratch(y_true, y_score):
    """
    Exact AUC via Mann-Whitney U statistic.
    O(n_pos * n_neg) — use sort-based method for large n.
    """
    pos_scores = y_score[y_true == 1]
    neg_scores = y_score[y_true == 0]

    n_pos, n_neg = len(pos_scores), len(neg_scores)
    concordant = sum(
        1.0 if p > n else 0.5 if p == n else 0.0
        for p in pos_scores
        for n in neg_scores
    )
    return concordant / (n_pos * n_neg)

# Verify
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
auc_manual = auc_from_scratch(y_test, y_prob)
auc_sk     = roc_auc_score(y_test, y_prob)
print(f"Manual: {auc_manual:.6f}, sklearn: {auc_sk:.6f}")  # Should match

docs.title: Regression Metrics from Scratch
docs.text:
def regression_metrics(y_true, y_pred):
    y_true, y_pred = np.array(y_true), np.array(y_pred)
    e = y_true - y_pred
    n = len(y_true)

    mse  = np.mean(e**2)
    rmse = np.sqrt(mse)
    mae  = np.mean(np.abs(e))
    ss_res = np.sum(e**2)
    ss_tot = np.sum((y_true - y_true.mean())**2)
    r2   = 1 - ss_res / ss_tot
    mape = np.mean(np.abs(e) / (np.abs(y_true) + 1e-10)) * 100

    return {"MSE": mse, "RMSE": rmse, "MAE": mae, "R2": r2, "MAPE": mape}

docs.title: ✦ Metric Selection Guide
docs.text:
Is the output a probability?
├── Yes → Log-loss + Brier score + calibration plot
└── No (hard labels or rankings)
    │
    Is it regression?
    ├── Yes
    │   ├── Outliers present / asymmetric costs? → MAE or Huber
    │   ├── Gaussian errors / large errors costly? → MSE / RMSE
    │   └── Explainability needed? → R²  (with adjusted R²)
    │
    └── Classification
        │
        Is the data imbalanced?
        ├── Yes → PR curve / AP / F_β / MCC
        └── No
            │
            Do FP and FN have equal costs?
            ├── Yes → Accuracy / F1 / ROC-AUC
            └── No → F_β  (choose β based on relative cost)
                      or MCC (uses all confusion matrix cells)

docs.title: ✦ Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
Loss Functions as Training Metrics
docs.text:
The training loss and the evaluation metric should ideally be the same — or at least tightly aligned. When they diverge, optimising the training loss does not optimise the evaluation metric:

Evaluation Metric Matching Training Loss Notes Log-loss Binary cross-entropy Perfect alignment Brier score MSE on probabilities Good alignment AUC Surrogate losses (pairwise ranking losses, ListNet) AUC is non-differentiable; surrogates approximate it F1 Weighted cross-entropy / focal loss F1 is non-differentiable; focal loss addresses class imbalance BLEU (NLP) Cross-entropy on tokens Severe mismatch — active research in RLHF, minimum Bayes risk decoding

The mismatch between training loss and evaluation metric is a fundamental tension in applied ML. It motivates reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) in language models: the evaluation "metric" is human preference, which is non-differentiable, so a reward model is trained to approximate it, and policy gradient methods optimise the approximation.

docs.title: Focal Loss — Addressing Imbalance in Deep Learning
docs.text:
Lin et al. (2017, RetinaNet) introduced focal loss for object detection, where the class imbalance between background and objects is extreme (\(\sim\) 1000:1):

\[\text{FL}(p_t) = -\alpha_t (1 - p_t)^\gamma \log(p_t)\]

where \(p_t\) is the model's probability for the true class, \(\gamma > 0\) is the focusing parameter, and \(\alpha_t\) is a class weight.

The term \((1-p_t)^\gamma\) down-weights easy negatives (where \(p_t \approx 1\) for class 0, so the model is already confident). For \(\gamma = 0\), focal loss reduces to standard cross-entropy. For \(\gamma = 2\), a well-classified example with \(p_t = 0.9\) contributes only \((0.1)^2 = 0.01\times\) its cross-entropy loss — effectively, easy examples barely affect the gradient.

This is a direct consequence of the precision-recall tradeoff baked into the loss function.

docs.title: Metrics in LLM Evaluation
docs.text:
Evaluating large language models is an open research problem precisely because no single metric captures the relevant properties:

Property Metric Problem Fluency Perplexity Low perplexity ≠ useful output Translation quality BLEU Fails on paraphrases; doesn't measure factuality Summarisation ROUGE Recall-oriented; rewards copying source Factuality FactScore, SAFE Expensive; requires retrieval Human preference Win rate, Elo No ground truth; expensive; inconsistent Reasoning Accuracy on benchmarks Contamination, saturation issues

The impossibility of a single metric for language model quality is why RLHF was developed: learn a reward model from human comparisons, then optimise it. The reward model is itself a learned metric.

docs.title: ✦ Worked Example: The Full Picture on One Dataset
docs.text:
# Deliberately create imbalanced data to show metric divergence
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier

X, y = make_classification(
    n_samples=10000, n_features=20,
    weights=[0.95, 0.05],   # 95% negative, 5% positive
    random_state=42
)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, stratify=y)

# Model 1: trivial — predicts majority class always
dummy = DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent").fit(X_tr, y_tr)

# Model 2: logistic regression
pipe = Pipeline([("sc", StandardScaler()), ("clf", LogisticRegression())])
pipe.fit(X_tr, y_tr)

for name, model in [("Dummy", dummy), ("LogReg", pipe)]:
    y_pred = model.predict(X_te)
    print(f"\n── {name} ──")
    print(f"  Accuracy:  {accuracy_score(y_te, y_pred):.3f}")
    print(f"  F1:        {f1_score(y_te, y_pred, zero_division=0):.3f}")
    print(f"  MCC:       {matthews_corrcoef(y_te, y_pred):.3f}")
    if hasattr(model, "predict_proba"):
        y_prob = model.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
        print(f"  ROC-AUC:   {roc_auc_score(y_te, y_prob):.3f}")
        print(f"  Avg Prec:  {average_precision_score(y_te, y_prob):.3f}")

# Expected output (approximately):
# ── Dummy ──
#   Accuracy:  0.950   ← looks great, is useless
#   F1:        0.000   ← correctly zero
#   MCC:       0.000   ← correctly zero
#
# ── LogReg ──
#   Accuracy:  0.960   ← only slightly better than dummy by accuracy
#   F1:        0.700   ← clearly better
#   MCC:       0.680   ← clearly better
#   ROC-AUC:   0.970   ← strong ranking ability
#   Avg Prec:  0.750   ← strong precision at high recall thresholds

This example demonstrates the metric divergence concretely: accuracy flatters the dummy classifier; F1, MCC, AUC, and AP correctly identify it as useless.

docs.title: ✦ You Know This When...
docs.text:
• You can derive MSE as MLE under Gaussian noise and MAE as MLE under Laplace noise — from the likelihood function, not from memory
  • You can explain why the optimal predictor under MSE is the conditional mean and under MAE is the conditional median
  • You can derive the AUC as the Mann-Whitney U statistic and implement it in NumPy without sklearn
  • You can construct a dataset where accuracy is 95% and the model is completely useless — and explain which metrics correctly identify this
  • You can explain the precision-recall tradeoff mechanistically (in terms of the decision threshold) and choose the right operating point for a given cost structure
  • You can explain what calibration means, draw a reliability diagram, and name two calibration methods
  • You can explain focal loss as a direct response to the class-imbalance problem, and derive it from cross-entropy

docs.title: Bias-Variance Tradeoff
docs.text: "Every learning algorithm makes a bet on the shape of the world. Bias is what you lose when your bet is wrong. Variance is what you lose when you don't have enough data to be sure your bet was right. You cannot eliminate both simultaneously — you can only choose where to be wrong."

docs.title: ✦ The Setup
docs.text:
You want to learn \(f: \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}\) from noisy observations:

\[y = f(x) + \epsilon, \quad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2), \quad \mathbb{E}[\epsilon] = 0, \quad \epsilon \perp x\]

Given a training set \(\mathcal{D} = {(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^n\) drawn i.i.d. from \(\mathcal{P}\), your algorithm produces an estimate \(\hat{f}_\mathcal{D}\). At a new test point \(x\), the prediction is \(\hat{f}_\mathcal{D}(x)\).

The quantity of interest is the expected prediction error at \(x\), averaged over all possible training sets \(\mathcal{D}\) of size \(n\) drawn from \(\mathcal{P}\):

\[\text{EPE}(x) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}, \epsilon}\left[(y - \hat{f}_\mathcal{D}(x))^2\right]\]

The expectation is over both the randomness in \(\mathcal{D}\) (which determines \(\hat{f}_\mathcal{D}\)) and the noise \(\epsilon\) in the new observation \(y = f(x) + \epsilon\).

docs.title: ✦ The Full Derivation
docs.text:
This is the central derivation of statistical learning theory. Do it once, by hand, until it is automatic.

Let \(\bar{f}(x) = \mathbb{E}_\mathcal{D}[\hat{f}_\mathcal{D}(x)]\) denote the expected prediction at \(x\) over all training sets.

Step 1. Expand the squared error:

\[\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D},\epsilon}\left[(y - \hat{f}_\mathcal{D}(x))^2\right] = \mathbb{E}\left[(f(x) + \epsilon - \hat{f}_\mathcal{D}(x))^2\right]\]

Step 2. Add and subtract \(\bar{f}(x)\):

\[= \mathbb{E}\left[\left((f(x) - \bar{f}(x)) + (\bar{f}(x) - \hat{f}_\mathcal{D}(x)) + \epsilon\right)^2\right]\]

Step 3. Expand. The cross terms vanish:

  • \(\mathbb{E}[\epsilon] = 0\) eliminates all cross terms involving \(\epsilon\)
  • \(\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{D}[\bar{f}(x) - \hat{f}_\mathcal{D}(x)] = 0\) by definition of \(\bar{f}\)
  • \((f(x) - \bar{f}(x))\) is a constant with respect to both \(\mathcal{D}\) and \(\epsilon\)
\[= \underbrace{(f(x) - \bar{f}(x))^2}_{\text{Bias}^2} + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_\mathcal{D}\left[(\hat{f}_\mathcal{D}(x) - \bar{f}(x))^2\right]}_{\text{Variance}} + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\epsilon^2]}_{\text{Irreducible Noise}} \]

Therefore:

\[\boxed{\text{EPE}(x) = \text{Bias}^2[\hat{f}(x)] + \text{Var}[\hat{f}(x)] + \sigma^2}\]

This holds pointwise at every \(x\). Integrating over the data distribution gives the expected generalisation error:

\[\mathbb{E}_x[\text{EPE}(x)] = \mathbb{E}_x\left[\text{Bias}^2[\hat{f}(x)]\right] + \mathbb{E}_x\left[\text{Var}[\hat{f}(x)]\right] + \sigma^2\]

docs.title: What Each Term Means
docs.text:
Bias\(^2\) \(= (f(x) - \bar{f}(x))^2\)

The squared difference between the true function and the average prediction over all training sets. Bias measures systematic error — the error your algorithm makes even with infinite data. It captures the gap between the best function your hypothesis class can represent and the true \(f\).

A high-bias model has the wrong inductive bias: it cannot fit \(f\) no matter how much data you give it. A linear model applied to a quadratic \(f\) has irreducible bias.

Variance \(= \mathbb{E}_\mathcal{D}[(\hat{f}_\mathcal{D}(x) - \bar{f}(x))^2]\)

The expected squared deviation of \(\hat{f}_\mathcal{D}\) from its own mean. Variance measures sensitivity to the training set — how much the prediction at \(x\) changes when you train on a different draw of \(n\) samples. High variance means the model is fitting noise.

Irreducible noise \(= \sigma^2\)

The variance of \(\epsilon\) — noise in the labels that no model can remove. Even the perfect predictor \(\hat{f} = f\) incurs this error. It is a property of the data-generating process, not the model.

docs.title: The Key Insight
docs.text:
You cannot reduce \(\sigma^2\). You can only trade Bias against Variance.

Reducing bias (making the model more flexible — add features, increase depth, reduce regularisation) tends to increase variance.

Reducing variance (making the model less flexible — regularise, constrain, use simpler hypothesis class) tends to increase bias.

The optimal model sits at the minimum of \(\text{Bias}^2 + \text{Variance}\), not the minimum of either alone.

docs.title: Polynomial Regression
docs.text:
True function: \(f(x) = \sin(2\pi x)\) on \([0, 1]\). Noise: \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.1)\). Training set size: \(n = 15\).

Fit polynomials of degree \(d = 1, 3, 9\) to many training sets drawn from the same distribution. The figures below show the spread of fitted curves.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(0)
n_datasets = 50
n_train = 15
sigma = 0.3
x_test = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))

for ax, degree in zip(axes, [1, 3, 9]):
    predictions = []
    for _ in range(n_datasets):
        x_train = np.sort(np.random.uniform(0, 1, n_train))
        y_train = np.sin(2 * np.pi * x_train) + np.random.normal(0, sigma, n_train)

        coeffs = np.polyfit(x_train, y_train, degree)
        y_pred = np.polyval(coeffs, x_test)
        predictions.append(y_pred)
        ax.plot(x_test, y_pred, alpha=0.1, color='steelblue')

    predictions = np.array(predictions)
    mean_pred = predictions.mean(axis=0)
    y_true = np.sin(2 * np.pi * x_test)

    bias_sq  = np.mean((y_true - mean_pred) ** 2)
    variance = np.mean(predictions.var(axis=0))

    ax.plot(x_test, y_true, 'k-', lw=2, label='True f(x)')
    ax.plot(x_test, mean_pred, 'r-', lw=2, label=f'Mean prediction')
    ax.set_title(f'Degree {degree}\nBias²={bias_sq:.3f}  Var={variance:.3f}  '
                 f'Sum={bias_sq+variance:.3f}')
    ax.set_ylim(-2, 2); ax.legend()

plt.suptitle('Bias-Variance Tradeoff: Polynomial Regression', fontsize=14)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Typical output:

Degree Bias² Variance Bias² + Var 1 (line) 0.45 0.003 0.453 3 (cubic) 0.02 0.015 0.035 9 (overfit) 0.01 0.41 0.42

Degree 3 is the sweet spot. Degree 1 has high bias (can't fit the sine wave). Degree 9 has high variance (fits each training set perfectly but predicts wildly on new data). The optimal degree minimises the sum — this is the U-shaped generalisation error curve.

docs.title: The U-Curve
docs.text:
Error
  │
  │  \         Total = Bias² + Var + σ²
  │   \       /
  │    \     /
  │     \   /   ← Variance
  │      \_/
  │      Bias²
  │
  └─────────────────────────
      Simple         Complex
      (underfit)     (overfit)
         Model Complexity

The minimum of the U-curve is the optimal model complexity. To the left: underfitting (high bias dominates). To the right: overfitting (high variance dominates). The bottom of the curve shifts right as \(n\) increases — more data allows more complex models without variance exploding.

docs.title: ✦ Bias and Variance for Specific Models
\(k\)-Nearest Neighbours (Analytical)
docs.text:
For KNN regression with \(k\) neighbours, at a test point \(x\):

\[\hat{f}_k(x) = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{x_j \in \mathcal{N}_k(x)} y_j\]

Bias. As \(k\) increases, the neighbourhood expands and the average smooths over a larger region. For large \(k\), the local average approximates the global mean — unable to track the local structure of \(f\). Bias increases with \(k\).

Formally, assuming \(f\) is Lipschitz with constant \(L\): $\(\text{Bias}[\hat{f}_k(x)] \approx \frac{L \cdot r_k(x)}{d+2}\)$ where \(r_k(x)\) is the radius of the \(k\)-NN ball — which grows with \(k\).

Variance. Each \(y_j = f(x_j) + \epsilon_j\) with \(\text{Var}[y_j] = \sigma^2\). Averaging \(k\) i.i.d. noise terms:

\[\text{Var}[\hat{f}_k(x)] = \text{Var}!\left[\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^k y_j\right] = \frac{\sigma^2}{k}\]

Variance decreases as \(1/k\). Small \(k\) → high variance; large \(k\) → low variance.

The tradeoff: \(\text{EPE}(x) \approx \text{Bias}^2(k) + \frac{\sigma^2}{k} + \sigma^2\). The optimal \(k^* = \arg\min_k [\text{Bias}^2(k) + \sigma^2/k]\).

This is exactly the same tension as the polynomial degree example — just parameterised differently. See [[07.k-Nearest Neighbours|k-Nearest Neighbours]].

docs.title: Linear Models (OLS)
docs.text:
For OLS with model \(\hat{f}(x) = x^T\hat{w}\), \(\hat{w} = (X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty\):

\[\mathbb{E}[\hat{w}] = w^* \implies \text{Bias} = 0 \quad \text{(when the true model is linear)}\]

OLS is unbiased when the true function is linear in the features. The Gauss-Markov theorem says OLS is the **B**est **L**inear **U**nbiased **E**stimator (BLUE) — minimum variance among all linear unbiased estimators.

\[\text{Var}[\hat{w}] = \sigma^2 (X^TX)^{-1}\]

The variance is large when \((X^TX)^{-1}\) is large — i.e., when features are nearly collinear (multicollinearity) or when \(n\) is small relative to \(d\).

Ridge regression deliberately introduces bias to reduce variance:

\[\hat{w}_\lambda = (X^TX + \lambda I)^{-1}X^Ty\] \[\mathbb{E}[\hat{w}_\lambda] = (X^TX + \lambda I)^{-1}X^TX w^* \neq w^* \quad \text{for } \lambda > 0\]

The bias is \((X^TX + \lambda I)^{-1}X^TX w^* - w^* = -\lambda(X^TX + \lambda I)^{-1}w^*\) — nonzero but shrinking toward zero as \(\lambda \to 0\).

The variance:

\[\text{Var}[\hat{w}_\lambda] = \sigma^2 (X^TX + \lambda I)^{-1} X^TX (X^TX + \lambda I)^{-1}\]

The \((X^TX + \lambda I)^{-1}\) terms shrink the variance relative to OLS. For large enough \(\lambda\), the variance reduction outweighs the bias increase, and Ridge has lower MSE than OLS — the bias-variance tradeoff in its cleanest algebraic form.

docs.title: ✦ Diagnosing from Learning Curves
docs.text:
A learning curve plots training error and validation error as a function of training set size \(n\). It is the most useful diagnostic tool for bias vs. variance.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, Ridge
from sklearn.model_selection import learning_curve
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression

X, y = make_regression(n_samples=500, n_features=1, noise=30, random_state=0)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))

configs = [
    ("High Bias (degree=1)", Pipeline([
        ("poly", PolynomialFeatures(degree=1)),
        ("lr",   LinearRegression())
    ])),
    ("High Variance (degree=15)", Pipeline([
        ("poly", PolynomialFeatures(degree=15)),
        ("lr",   Ridge(alpha=0.0001))   # tiny regularisation
    ])),
]

train_sizes = np.linspace(0.1, 1.0, 10)

for ax, (title, model) in zip(axes, configs):
    sizes, train_scores, val_scores = learning_curve(
        model, X, y, train_sizes=train_sizes,
        cv=5, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error", n_jobs=-1
    )
    train_err = -train_scores.mean(axis=1)
    val_err   = -val_scores.mean(axis=1)

    ax.plot(sizes, train_err, 'o-', label='Train MSE',      color='steelblue')
    ax.plot(sizes, val_err,   's-', label='Validation MSE', color='darkorange')
    ax.set_xlabel('Training set size')
    ax.set_ylabel('MSE')
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.legend()
    ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

docs.title: Reading the Curves
docs.text:
High Bias (Underfitting):

MSE
 │  train ─────────────────  ← high and flat
 │  val   ─────────────────  ← high and flat, close to train
 │
 └──────────────────────────
       n (training set size)
  • Both train and validation error are high
  • They converge quickly and stay close together
  • Adding more data will not help — the model is fundamentally limited by its hypothesis class
  • Fix: increase model complexity, add features, reduce regularisation

High Variance (Overfitting):

MSE
 │  val   ╲___________________  ← starts high, slowly decreases
 │                              (large gap persists)
 │  train  ─────────────────── ← low, flat
 │
 └──────────────────────────────
        n (training set size)
  • Training error is low; validation error is much higher
  • Large, persistent gap between train and val
  • Validation error decreases as \(n\) increases (more data helps)
  • Fix: reduce model complexity, add regularisation, get more data, feature selection

Optimal Model:

MSE
 │  val   ╲_______  ← converges to near train error
 │  train  ───────
 │
 └──────────────────────────────
  • Small gap between train and val
  • Both errors are acceptably low
  • This is the target

docs.title: ✦ Regularisation as the Operational Solution
docs.text:
The bias-variance tradeoff is the diagnosis. Regularisation is the treatment.

Every regulariser constrains the hypothesis class, trading bias for variance.

docs.title: L2 Regularisation (Ridge / Weight Decay)
docs.text:
\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{Ridge}} = \underbrace{\frac{1}{n}\sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}_{\text{empirical risk}} + \underbrace{\lambda |w|_2^2}_{\text{regulariser}}\]

Bayesian interpretation: MAP estimation under a Gaussian prior \(w \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_w^2 I)\) with \(\lambda = \sigma^2 / \sigma_w^2\). Ridge shrinks all weights toward zero proportionally — never exactly zero.

Effect on the bias-variance tradeoff: increasing \(\lambda\) shrinks \(\hat{w}\) toward zero (increasing bias), while stabilising estimates across different training sets (decreasing variance).

In neural networks: L2 regularisation is called weight decay. In SGD:

\[w \leftarrow w - \alpha \nabla_w \mathcal{L} - 2\alpha\lambda w = (1 - 2\alpha\lambda) w - \alpha \nabla_w \mathcal{L}_{\text{data}}\]

The \((1 - 2\alpha\lambda)\) factor decays the weights at each step — hence the name.

docs.title: L1 Regularisation (Lasso)
docs.text:
\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{Lasso}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 + \lambda |w|_1\]

Bayesian interpretation: MAP under a Laplace prior \(w_j \sim \text{Laplace}(0, 1/\lambda)\).

Why L1 produces sparsity — geometric argument. The constraint region for L1 is a diamond (hypercube in \(\mathbb{R}^d\)) with corners on the axes. The loss function's level sets are ellipses (or hyperellipsoids). The intersection of an ellipse with a diamond tends to occur at a corner — where one or more \(w_j = 0\) exactly.

For L2, the constraint region is a sphere. The intersection with an ellipse rarely occurs at a point of zero curvature — weights are shrunk but not zeroed.

w₂                      w₂
 │    ╲  L1 constraint   │       L2 constraint
 │     ╲                 │      ╭─────╮
 │      ◇   ←sparse      │     │       │ ←dense
 │     ╱ ╲  solution     │      ╰─────╯  solution
 │    ╱   ╲             │
─┼──────────────         ─┼──────────────
             w₁                        w₁

Practical consequence: Lasso performs implicit feature selection. The number of nonzero weights is at most \(\min(n, d)\) — useful when you believe the true model is sparse.

docs.title: Elastic Net
docs.text:
\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{EN}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 + \lambda_1 |w|_1 + \lambda_2 |w|_2^2\]

Combines L1 sparsity with L2 stability. Preferred over Lasso when features are correlated (Lasso arbitrarily picks one among correlated features; Elastic Net tends to include all of them with shared weight).

docs.title: Early Stopping — Implicit L2 Regularisation
docs.text:
For gradient descent on the empirical risk, stop training before convergence. This is not ad hoc — for linear models with squared loss and gradient descent with learning rate \(\alpha\):

At step \(t\), the GD estimate satisfies:

\[\hat{w}^{(t)} = (I - (I - \alpha X^TX)^t) (X^TX)^{-1} X^T y\]

The eigenvalue decomposition of \(X^TX = V\Lambda V^T\) shows that component \(j\) of \(\hat{w}^{(t)}\) is multiplied by a factor \((1 - (1 - \alpha\lambda_j)^t)\). Small eigenvalues (corresponding to directions of low data variance) are suppressed more — exactly the behaviour of Ridge regression with \(\lambda \propto 1/t\).

Early stopping is therefore equivalent to Ridge regularisation with \(\lambda \approx 1/(\alpha t)\). More steps \(\leftrightarrow\) less regularisation \(\leftrightarrow\) higher variance.

docs.title: Dropout — Variance Reduction by Ensemble Approximation
docs.text:
Dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014) randomly sets each neuron's activation to zero with probability \(p\) during training. At test time, weights are scaled by \((1-p)\).

Bias-variance interpretation: each forward pass uses a different sub-network (a different random mask). Dropout training is approximately optimising an ensemble of \(2^d\) tied networks (where \(d\) is the number of neurons). Since ensemble averaging reduces variance (see [[01.Bagging and Random Forests|Bagging]]), dropout reduces the effective variance of the deep network.

More precisely, dropout acts as a regulariser equivalent to L2 on the pre-activation weights (Wager et al., 2013) — but adapted to the geometry of the network.

docs.title: Data Augmentation — Variance Reduction by Increasing Effective \(n\)
docs.text: By applying label-preserving transformations (flips, crops, colour jitter for images; back-translation for text), you effectively increase the training set size, pushing the U-curve's minimum rightward. More data reduces variance without increasing bias.

docs.title: ✦ The Double Descent Phenomenon
docs.text:
Classical statistical intuition says: increasing model complexity beyond the interpolation threshold (where training error = 0) increases variance and worsens generalisation. The U-curve ends there.

This turns out to be wrong for modern overparameterised models.

Belkin et al. (2019) showed that the risk curve has a second descent after the interpolation threshold:

Risk
  │
  │  \         Classical   │  Modern
  │   \          regime    │  regime
  │    \                   │
  │     \_____   ↑ peak    │ \___________
  │           ↑            │             (continues down)
  │   interpolation threshold
  └─────────────────────────────────────
              Model Parameters / n

The interpolation threshold (parameters \(=\) training samples) is where the model can exactly fit the training data. Classical theory predicts this is the worst point. In practice, for neural networks and other sufficiently structured models, going beyond the threshold produces models that interpolate the training data but still generalise — because among all interpolating solutions, the optimiser (SGD) finds the minimum-norm one, which has low effective complexity.

Why double descent occurs:

  1. Below interpolation: classical bias-variance tradeoff — complexity increases variance
  2. At interpolation: variance spikes — the model barely fits, and is extremely sensitive to training data
  3. Beyond interpolation: the model has excess capacity, finds a simple interpolating solution (minimum norm in the case of gradient descent + infinitely wide networks), variance decreases again

Implication for practice: for neural networks, adding more parameters (width, depth) past the interpolation point continues to improve generalisation, as long as you use appropriate regularisation (weight decay, dropout, early stopping). The "right" amount of regularisation shifts, but the direction of model scaling is reliably beneficial — this is the empirical foundation of modern large model scaling laws.

docs.title: ✦ Ensemble Methods — Explicitly Decomposing the Tradeoff
docs.text:
Ensemble methods are the practical engineering solution to the bias-variance tradeoff. They manipulate the two terms explicitly:

Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating):

If \(M\) base learners each have variance \(\sigma^2\) and pairwise correlation \(\rho\), the ensemble variance is:

\[\text{Var}!\left[\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^M \hat{f}_m(x)\right] = \rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{M}\sigma^2\]

As \(M \to \infty\): variance \(\to \rho\sigma^2\). The irreducible variance floor is \(\rho\sigma^2\) — determined entirely by the correlation between base learners. Decorrelation is the core goal of bagging. Random Forests achieve this by adding feature randomness at each split.

Bagging does not reduce bias — each learner is trained on roughly the same distribution, so the average has approximately the same bias as a single learner.

Boosting:

Fits models sequentially, each targeting the residuals of the previous. Boosting primarily reduces bias — it builds up an increasingly complex function that better approximates \(f\). It can increase variance if the boosted model overfits. Shrinkage (small learning rate) plus subsampling controls this.

See [[01.Bagging and Random Forests|Bagging and Random Forests]] and [[02.Boosting|Boosting]] for full derivations.

docs.title: ✦ Bias-Variance in Classification
docs.text:
The decomposition above is for squared loss. For 0-1 loss (classification), the decomposition is more complex and less clean.

Domingos (2000) extended the decomposition to classification:

\[\text{Error} = \text{Noise} + \text{Bias} + \text{Variance}\]

But the terms interact multiplicatively near the decision boundary in a way that has no clean closed form. The qualitative conclusions are the same:

  • Low-complexity classifiers (e.g., linear SVM, logistic regression): high bias if the true boundary is nonlinear
  • High-complexity classifiers (e.g., unpruned decision tree): high variance — decision boundary wiggles around training points
  • Ensembles of trees (Random Forest, XGBoost): reduce variance while controlling bias growth

In practice, even for classification, the MSE decomposition is used as a proxy and its intuitions transfer reliably.

docs.title: ✦ Connection to AI, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning
The Scaling Laws Perspective
docs.text:
Kaplan et al. (2020) showed that for language models, test loss follows a power law in model size \(N\), dataset size \(D\), and compute \(C\):

\[L(N, D, C) \approx \left(\frac{N_c}{N}\right)^{\alpha_N} + \left(\frac{D_c}{D}\right)^{\alpha_D} + L_\infty\]

where \(L_\infty\) is the irreducible loss (analogous to \(\sigma^2\)) and the power law terms are the reducible bias + variance.

This is the bias-variance tradeoff at the scale of frontier models:

  • Model size \(N\) controls expressivity → reducing bias
  • Dataset size \(D\) controls overfitting → reducing variance
  • Compute \(C\) determines where on the tradeoff you can afford to sit

The scaling laws tell you the optimal allocation of a compute budget between model size and data — the bias-variance tradeoff expressed as an engineering optimisation problem at scale.

docs.title: Underfitting and Overfitting in Practice — The Full Pipeline View
docs.text:
In a production ML pipeline, bias and variance do not only come from model complexity. They accumulate across the full system:

Source Bias Variance Label noise / annotation errors ✗ ✓ (irreducible, contributes to \(\sigma^2\)) Wrong features (missing signal) ✓ ✗ Too simple a model ✓ ✗ Too few training examples ✗ ✓ Too much regularisation ✓ ✗ Distribution shift (train ≠ test) ✓ ✗

Distribution shift is a form of bias that is invisible to the standard decomposition: the model's average prediction \(\bar{f}(x)\) is measured over training distributions, but the test distribution differs. The bias term explodes in ways that more data from the training distribution cannot fix. This is why domain adaptation and out-of-distribution generalisation are active research areas.

docs.title: ✦ Implementation: Full Bias-Variance Estimator
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingRegressor

def bias_variance_decomp(model_fn, X_train_sets, X_test, y_test_true):
    """
    Estimate bias² and variance of a model.

    model_fn:       callable, returns a fresh unfitted model
    X_train_sets:   list of training sets (each a tuple (X_train, y_train))
    X_test:         fixed test points
    y_test_true:    f(X_test) — noiseless true values
    """
    predictions = []
    for X_tr, y_tr in X_train_sets:
        model = model_fn()
        model.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
        predictions.append(model.predict(X_test))

    predictions = np.array(predictions)   # shape: (n_datasets, n_test)
    mean_pred = predictions.mean(axis=0)  # shape: (n_test,)

    bias_sq  = np.mean((y_test_true - mean_pred) ** 2)
    variance = np.mean(predictions.var(axis=0))

    return bias_sq, variance

# Demonstration: decision tree depth vs. bias-variance
np.random.seed(42)
n_datasets = 200
n_train = 50

def gen_data(n):
    x = np.sort(np.random.uniform(0, 1, n))
    y = np.sin(2 * np.pi * x) + np.random.normal(0, 0.3, n)
    return x.reshape(-1, 1), y

train_sets = [gen_data(n_train) for _ in range(n_datasets)]
x_test = np.linspace(0, 1, 100).reshape(-1, 1)
y_true = np.sin(2 * np.pi * x_test.ravel())

print(f"{'Depth':>6} {'Bias²':>8} {'Var':>8} {'Sum':>8}")
print("-" * 36)
for depth in [1, 2, 3, 5, 10, None]:
    fn = lambda d=depth: DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=d)
    b2, v = bias_variance_decomp(fn, train_sets, x_test, y_true)
    print(f"{str(depth):>6} {b2:>8.4f} {v:>8.4f} {b2+v:>8.4f}")

# Adding bagging to see variance reduction
print("\nWith Bagging (depth=10, n_estimators=50):")
fn_bag = lambda: BaggingRegressor(
    DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=10), n_estimators=50, random_state=0
)
b2, v = bias_variance_decomp(fn_bag, train_sets, x_test, y_true)
print(f"{'bag':>6} {b2:>8.4f} {v:>8.4f} {b2+v:>8.4f}")

Expected output pattern:

 Depth    Bias²      Var      Sum
------------------------------------
     1   0.4321   0.0051   0.4372  ← high bias, low variance
     2   0.1823   0.0089   0.1912
     3   0.0612   0.0183   0.0795
     5   0.0124   0.0521   0.0645  ← near optimal
    10   0.0021   0.1843   0.1864
  None   0.0008   0.3211   0.3219  ← low bias, high variance

With Bagging (depth=10, n_estimators=50):
   bag   0.0019   0.0312   0.0331  ← bagging collapses variance

Bagging a depth-10 tree reduces variance from 0.18 to 0.03 — an 83% reduction — without changing bias (both depth-10 variants have \(\text{Bias}^2 \approx 0.002\)). This is the mechanism of Random Forests in one table.

docs.title: ✦ You Know This When...
docs.text:
• You can derive the bias-variance-noise decomposition from \(\mathbb{E}[(y - \hat{f}(x))^2]\), showing all steps including why cross terms vanish — without looking it up
  • You can derive the variance of KNN regression as \(\sigma^2/k\) from the definition of variance
  • You can show algebraically that Ridge regression introduces bias and reduces variance relative to OLS — working from the closed-form estimators
  • You can read a learning curve and correctly diagnose high-bias vs. high-variance, and prescribe the right fix for each
  • You can derive the ensemble variance formula \(\rho\sigma^2 + (1-\rho)\sigma^2/M\) and explain why decorrelation (not just averaging) is the key to bagging's effectiveness
  • You can explain the double descent phenomenon and why it does not contradict the bias-variance tradeoff — it extends it
  • You can implement the bias-variance estimator in NumPy and verify that bagging reduces variance without reducing bias
