docs.title: Hyperparameter Tuning
docs.text: "The art is not in the model — it's in knowing which knob to turn, how far, and why."

docs.title: ✦ What Even Is a Hyperparameter?
docs.text:
Before we tune anything, let's be precise. A parameter is learned from data during training — the weights \(w\) in linear regression, the split thresholds in a decision tree. A hyperparameter is set before training and governs the learning process itself: the regularisation strength \(\lambda\), the tree depth, the learning rate \(\alpha\).

The distinction matters because hyperparameters are not optimised by the training objective \(\hat{R}(\hat{f})\). If you tried to include them in gradient descent, you'd collapse: setting \(\lambda = 0\) always minimises the regularised training loss, giving you a degenerate solution. So we need a separate loop.

Outer loop (hyperparameter search):
  for each candidate config θ_h:
    Inner loop (training):
      fit model on training data → get parameters w*(θ_h)
    Evaluate w*(θ_h) on validation data
  Return θ_h* that minimises validation loss

This is the meta-learning loop. The training loss tells you how well you fit the data you've seen. The validation loss tells you how well you generalise. You optimise the latter by searching over \(\theta_h\).

docs.title: ✦ The Setup: What You're Searching Over
docs.text:
Let \(\Theta\) be the hyperparameter space. In practice this is a product of different types:

\[\Theta = \Theta_{\text{continuous}} \times \Theta_{\text{integer}} \times \Theta_{\text{categorical}}\]

Example (Random Forest):

  • \(n_estimators \in {50, 100, 200, 500, \ldots}\) — integer
  • \(max_depth \in {3, 5, 10, \text{None}}\) — integer + None
  • \(max_features \in {\text{"sqrt"}, \text{"log2"}, 0.5, 1.0}\) — categorical + continuous
  • \(min_samples_split \in [2, 50]\) — integer

Example (Neural Network):

  • \(\alpha \in [10^{-5}, 10^{-1}]\) — continuous, log scale
  • \(\text{batch_size} \in {32, 64, 128, 256}\) — integer
  • \(\text{optimizer} \in {\text{Adam}, \text{SGD}, \text{RMSProp}}\) — categorical
  • \(\text{n_layers} \in {2, 3, 4, 5}\) — integer
  • \(\text{dropout} \in [0, 0.5]\) — continuous

The space is high-dimensional, mixed-type, and the objective function is expensive to evaluate — each evaluation requires a full training run. This is what makes hyperparameter optimisation hard.

docs.title: The Method
docs.text:
Enumerate a finite grid over the hyperparameter space and evaluate every combination.

\[\Theta_{\text{grid}} = {\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots} \times {C_1, C_2, \ldots} \times \cdots\]

For \(k\) hyperparameters with \(n_i\) values each, the number of evaluations is:

\[N_{\text{eval}} = \prod_{i=1}^k n_i\]

Example:

  • \(\lambda \in {0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1.0}\) → 4 values
  • \(C \in {0.1, 1.0, 10.0}\) → 3 values
  • \(\text{kernel} \in {\text{rbf}, \text{poly}}\) → 2 values

Total evaluations: \(4 \times 3 \times 2 = 24\). With 5-fold CV, that's \(24 \times 5 = 120\) model fits.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Exhaustive within the grid — you will find the best combination that exists in your grid
  • Wasteful by design — it allocates equal budget to every dimension, even unimportant ones
  • Scales exponentially — adding one 5-value hyperparameter quintuples the cost
  • Blind to continuous structure — if the true optimum is between \(\lambda = 0.01\) and \(\lambda = 0.1\), you'll never find it

docs.title: When to Use
docs.text: Small search spaces (2-3 hyperparameters, few values each). When you want a reproducible, interpretable sweep. Baseline to compare against.

docs.title: sklearn API
docs.text:
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
from sklearn.svm import SVC

param_grid = {
    'C': [0.1, 1.0, 10.0, 100.0],
    'gamma': [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1.0],
    'kernel': ['rbf', 'poly']
}

gs = GridSearchCV(
    SVC(),
    param_grid,
    cv=5,
    scoring='accuracy',
    n_jobs=-1,
    verbose=2
)
gs.fit(X_train, y_train)

print(gs.best_params_)        # {'C': 10.0, 'gamma': 0.01, 'kernel': 'rbf'}
print(gs.best_score_)         # CV score of best config
# IMPORTANT: final evaluation on test set
print(gs.score(X_test, y_test))

docs.title: The Key Insight (Bergstra & Bengio, 2012)
docs.text:
"Random search is more efficient than grid search for hyperparameter optimisation of neural networks."

Why? Consider searching over two hyperparameters, one important and one unimportant. Grid search wastes most of its budget exploring the unimportant dimension. Random search, sampling independently, gets more distinct values of the important parameter for the same budget.

Formal argument. Suppose the effective dimensionality of the problem is \(d_{\text{eff}} \ll d\) (only a few hyperparameters actually matter). With \(n\) random trials, you get \(n\) distinct values along each important dimension. With \(n\) grid trials over a \(d\)-dimensional space, you get only \(n^{1/d}\) distinct values along each dimension.

For \(n = 100\), \(d = 5\): grid gives you \(100^{1/5} \approx 2.5\) values per dimension. Random gives you 100.

docs.title: Distribution Choices Matter
docs.text:
Sampling from the wrong distribution concentrates probability mass in the wrong region.

Hyperparameter Wrong Distribution Right Distribution Learning rate \(\alpha\) Uniform \([10^{-5}, 10^{-1}]\) Log-uniform: \(10^{\mathcal{U}(-5, -1)}\) Regularisation \(\lambda\) Uniform \([0, 1]\) Log-uniform: \(10^{\mathcal{U}(-4, 0)}\) \(n_estimators\) Uniform \([10, 1000]\) Uniform integers Dropout rate — Uniform \([0, 0.5]\)

Why log-uniform for scale parameters? If the optimal \(\alpha\) is around \(0.001\), uniform sampling gives that neighbourhood probability \(\approx 0.001 / 0.1 = 1%\). Log-uniform assigns equal probability to each order of magnitude.

import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import loguniform

param_distributions = {
    'C': loguniform(1e-3, 1e3),          # 10^(-3) to 10^3
    'gamma': loguniform(1e-4, 1e1),
    'kernel': ['rbf', 'poly', 'linear']   # categorical: uniform
}

from sklearn.model_selection import RandomizedSearchCV
rs = RandomizedSearchCV(
    SVC(),
    param_distributions,
    n_iter=100,       # evaluate 100 random configs
    cv=5,
    scoring='accuracy',
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=-1
)
rs.fit(X_train, y_train)

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Anytime algorithm — stop early and still have a good result
  • No combinatorial explosion — cost is \(O(n_iter)\) regardless of dimension
  • Non-exhaustive — no guarantee of finding the global optimum
  • Embarrassingly parallel — each trial is independent

docs.title: ✦ 3. Bayesian Optimisation
docs.text: This is where things get principled. Grid and random search are model-free — they ignore what they've learned from previous evaluations. Bayesian optimisation builds a probabilistic model of the objective function and uses it to decide where to evaluate next.

docs.title: The Framework
docs.text:
Let \(f: \Theta \to \mathbb{R}\) be the validation loss as a function of hyperparameters. We want: $\(\theta^* = \arg\min_{\theta \in \Theta} f(\theta)\)$

\(f\) is expensive to evaluate (each call = full training run), so we want to be smart about which \(\theta\) to query.

The Bayesian approach:

  1. Place a prior over \(f\): typically a Gaussian Process \(f \sim \mathcal{GP}(m(\theta), k(\theta, \theta'))\)
  2. After observing \(\mathcal{D}_t = {(\theta_i, f(\theta_i))}_{i=1}^t\), compute the posterior \(p(f | \mathcal{D}_t)\)
  3. Use an acquisition function \(\alpha(\theta; \mathcal{D}_t)\) to decide \(\theta_{t+1} = \arg\max_\theta \alpha(\theta; \mathcal{D}_t)\)
  4. Evaluate \(f(\theta_{t+1})\), update posterior, repeat

The posterior gives us both a mean prediction \(\mu_t(\theta)\) and an uncertainty estimate \(\sigma_t(\theta)\). The acquisition function balances exploitation (go where \(\mu_t\) is small) and exploration (go where \(\sigma_t\) is large).

docs.title: Gaussian Process Surrogate
docs.text:
Recall from [[03.Gaussian Processes|Gaussian Processes]]: a GP is fully specified by its mean and covariance function. The posterior after \(t\) observations has closed form:

\[\mu_t(\theta) = k_t(\theta)^T (K_t + \sigma^2 I)^{-1} \mathbf{f}_t$$ $$\sigma_t^2(\theta) = k(\theta, \theta) - k_t(\theta)^T (K_t + \sigma^2 I)^{-1} k_t(\theta)\]

where \(k_t(\theta) = [k(\theta, \theta_1), \ldots, k(\theta, \theta_t)]^T\) and \(K_t\) is the \(t \times t\) Gram matrix.

The cost is \(O(t^3)\) — GPs don't scale to large \(t\). In practice, this means Bayesian optimisation is used for \(\leq\) a few hundred evaluations.

docs.title: Expected Improvement (EI)
docs.text:
Let \(f^* = \min_{i \leq t} f(\theta_i)\) be the current best. Define improvement \(I(\theta) = \max(f^* - f(\theta), 0)\).

\[\text{EI}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{f(\theta) \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_t, \sigma_t^2)}[\max(f^* - f(\theta), 0)]\]

This has a closed form:

\[\text{EI}(\theta) = (f^* - \mu_t(\theta))\Phi(Z) + \sigma_t(\theta)\phi(Z), \quad Z = \frac{f^* - \mu_t(\theta)}{\sigma_t(\theta)}\]

where \(\Phi\) and \(\phi\) are the standard normal CDF and PDF.

Intuition: EI is high when either (a) \(\mu_t(\theta)\) is much better than \(f^*\) (exploitation) or (b) \(\sigma_t(\theta)\) is large (exploration). The balance emerges automatically.

docs.title: Upper Confidence Bound (UCB)
docs.text:
\[\text{UCB}(\theta) = -\mu_t(\theta) + \kappa \sigma_t(\theta)\]

(Negative because we minimise \(f\).) The parameter \(\kappa\) directly controls the exploration-exploitation tradeoff. \(\kappa = 0\) is pure exploitation; \(\kappa \to \infty\) is pure exploration.

UCB has strong theoretical guarantees — the cumulative regret \(\sum_{t=1}^T (f(\theta_t) - f(\theta^*))\) grows sublinearly for many kernel families.

docs.title: Probability of Improvement (PI)
docs.text:
\[\text{PI}(\theta) = P(f(\theta) < f^* - \xi) = \Phi!\left(\frac{f^* - \xi - \mu_t(\theta)}{\sigma_t(\theta)}\right)\]

The \(\xi > 0\) "exploration jitter" prevents the algorithm from being too greedy. PI is simpler than EI but tends to be more exploitative.

docs.title: Visualisation: The Bayesian Optimisation Loop
docs.text:
Iteration 1:
  Prior GP (no data)
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────
  μ(θ) = 0 everywhere, σ(θ) = large everywhere
  EI is flat → sample at random → evaluate f(θ₁)

Iteration 2:
  Posterior conditioned on (θ₁, f(θ₁))
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────
  Near θ₁: σ collapses (we know what's there)
  Away from θ₁: σ still large
  EI peaks somewhere promising → evaluate f(θ₂)

...

Iteration t:
  Posterior tightly fits observations
  ───────────────────────────────────────────────
  μ(θ) is a good surrogate for f(θ)
  EI peaks at the suspected optimum or a
  high-uncertainty region → converges

docs.title: Alternative Surrogate: Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE)
docs.text:
Used by Hyperopt and Optuna. Instead of modelling \(p(f|\theta)\) directly, TPE models two densities:

  • \(\ell(\theta)\): distribution of \(\theta\) given \(f(\theta) < f^*_{\gamma}\) (good configs)
  • \(g(\theta)\): distribution of \(\theta\) given \(f(\theta) \geq f^*_{\gamma}\) (bad configs)

where \(f^*_\gamma\) is the \(\gamma\)-quantile of observed \(f\) values (\(\gamma = 0.15\) typically).

The acquisition function is \(\text{EI} \propto \ell(\theta) / g(\theta)\). New candidates are sampled from \(\ell\) and selected by maximising \(\ell/g\).

Why TPE scales better: It uses kernel density estimates in the original hyperparameter space, handles conditional hyperparameters naturally, and avoids the \(O(t^3)\) GP bottleneck.

docs.title: sklearn/Optuna API
docs.text:
import optuna

def objective(trial):
    # Define hyperparameter space
    C = trial.suggest_float('C', 1e-3, 1e3, log=True)
    gamma = trial.suggest_float('gamma', 1e-4, 1e1, log=True)
    kernel = trial.suggest_categorical('kernel', ['rbf', 'poly', 'linear'])

    # Evaluate
    clf = SVC(C=C, gamma=gamma, kernel=kernel)
    score = cross_val_score(clf, X_train, y_train, cv=5, scoring='accuracy').mean()
    return score   # Optuna maximises by default

study = optuna.create_study(
    direction='maximize',
    sampler=optuna.samplers.TPESampler(seed=42)
)
study.optimize(objective, n_trials=100)
print(study.best_params)

# Visualise the search
optuna.visualization.plot_optimization_history(study)
optuna.visualization.plot_param_importances(study)

docs.title: The Problem with Standard Methods
docs.text: Every evaluation in grid/random/Bayesian search uses the full training budget — all epochs, all data. But most configurations are clearly bad after seeing \(1%\) of the data. We're wasting \(99%\) of the budget on doomed runs.

docs.title: Successive Halving
docs.text:
Setup: \(n\) configurations, total budget \(B\). Allocate equal budget \(B/n\) to each, then eliminate the bottom half, double the budget for survivors, repeat.

Algorithm:

Input: n configurations {θ₁, ..., θₙ}, total budget B, η = 2 (halving rate)
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
S₀ = {θ₁, ..., θₙ}
r₀ = B / (n · ceil(log_η(n)))   # initial budget per config

for k = 0, 1, ..., ceil(log_η(n)) - 1:
    Evaluate each θ ∈ Sₖ with budget rₖ
    Sₖ₊₁ = top ⌊|Sₖ|/η⌋ configs by validation loss
    rₖ₊₁ = rₖ · η

Return best config in S_final

Tradeoff: Large \(n\) (explore many configs) vs. large \(r_0\) (accurate early estimates). Successive halving forces you to choose.

docs.title: Hyperband
docs.text:
Hyperband removes the \(n\) vs. \(r_0\) dilemma by running multiple brackets of Successive Halving with different initial budgets.

For maximum budget \(R\) and \(\eta\):

  • \(s_{\max} = \lfloor \log_\eta R \rfloor\)
  • Run brackets \(s = s_{\max}, s_{\max}-1, \ldots, 0\)
  • Bracket \(s\) starts with \(n_s = \lceil \frac{s_{\max}+1}{s+1} \eta^s \rceil\) configs and budget \(r_s = R/\eta^s\)

Why it works: Bracket \(s_{\max}\) (many configs, small budget) is great at exploration. Bracket \(0\) (one config, full budget) is great at exploitation. Hyperband gets both, spending total budget proportional to \(s_{\max} \cdot R\).

from sklearn.model_selection import HalvingRandomSearchCV
import numpy as np

param_distributions = {
    'n_estimators': np.arange(10, 500),
    'max_depth': [None, 3, 5, 10, 20],
    'min_samples_split': np.arange(2, 50),
    'max_features': ['sqrt', 'log2', 0.5, 1.0]
}

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
hs = HalvingRandomSearchCV(
    RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42),
    param_distributions,
    n_candidates='exhaust',
    resource='n_estimators',   # budget = number of trees
    factor=3,                   # η: keep top 1/3 each round
    cv=5,
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=-1
)
hs.fit(X_train, y_train)

docs.title: ✦ Comparison: When to Use What
docs.text: Method Cost Per Eval Parallel? Scales to High-dim? Good For Grid Search Full Yes No (\(O(\prod n_i)\)) 1–2 HP, small grids Random Search Full Yes Yes Baseline, many HP Bayesian (GP) Full Partially No (\(O(t^3)\)) < 20 HP, expensive eval Bayesian (TPE) Full Partially Yes General purpose Successive Halving Variable Yes Yes When early stopping is valid Hyperband Variable Yes Yes Deep learning, expensive training

docs.title: ✦ The Leakage Trap
docs.text:
This deserves its own section because it kills more projects than wrong algorithms do.

The trap: You tune hyperparameters on the validation set. After tuning, you use the same validation set to report final performance. You've effectively trained on the validation set — your reported metric is optimistic.

The fix: Three-way split (or nested CV).

Wrong protocol:
  Train → fit model parameters w*(θ_h)
  Val   → select θ_h*
  Val   → report final score ← LEAKAGE

Correct protocol:
  Train → fit model parameters w*(θ_h)
  Val   → select θ_h*
  Test  → report final score ← held out the entire time

The test set must be held out the entire time — never used for model selection, hyperparameter tuning, feature selection, or anything that drives decisions. It is a single-use oracle.

If you don't have enough data for a three-way split, use nested cross-validation:

Outer loop (k_outer folds):
  for fold (train_outer, test_outer):
    Inner loop (k_inner folds on train_outer):
      for fold (train_inner, val_inner):
        fit model, evaluate → find best θ_h*
    Retrain best θ_h* on full train_outer
    Evaluate on test_outer → one unbiased estimate
Average estimates over outer folds → final generalisation estimate

Nested CV is expensive (\(k_{\text{outer}} \times k_{\text{inner}} \times n_iter\) fits) but gives an unbiased estimate of generalisation performance.

from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, GridSearchCV
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline

inner_cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
outer_cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

param_grid = {'svc__C': [0.1, 1, 10], 'svc__gamma': [0.01, 0.1, 1]}

pipe = Pipeline([('svc', SVC())])
inner_search = GridSearchCV(pipe, param_grid, cv=inner_cv, scoring='accuracy')

# This is the unbiased estimate
nested_scores = cross_val_score(inner_search, X, y, cv=outer_cv, scoring='accuracy')
print(f"Nested CV: {nested_scores.mean():.3f} ± {nested_scores.std():.3f}")

docs.title: Log-scale Hyperparameters
docs.text:
Whenever a hyperparameter spans multiple orders of magnitude, search on a log scale:

\[\lambda \sim 10^{\mathcal{U}(a, b)} \quad \text{not} \quad \lambda \sim \mathcal{U}(10^a, 10^b)\]

The difference: uniform in \([10^{-4}, 1]\) gives \(99.99%\) of mass to \([0.1, 1]\). Log-uniform gives \(25%\) to each decade.

docs.title: Early Stopping as Regularisation
docs.text: For gradient-based models, early stopping during hyperparameter search is legitimate and cheap. Stop training when validation loss stops decreasing. This is itself a hyperparameter (patience), but usually less sensitive than learning rate.

docs.title: Warm Starting
docs.text: Some algorithms (sklearn estimators with warm_start=True) allow you to reuse previous fits. This can dramatically speed up grid search over \(n_estimators\) in Random Forest: fit with 100 trees, then extend to 200, then 500 — rather than fitting from scratch three times.

docs.title: Population Based Training (PBT)
docs.text: A more aggressive strategy for deep learning: run a population of models simultaneously, and periodically replace poorly-performing models with mutated copies of the best ones. Conceptually: genetic algorithms applied to hyperparameter schedules. Used at DeepMind for game-playing agents.

docs.title: ✦ Connection to AI / ML / Deep Learning
docs.text:
Hyperparameter tuning is not a peripheral concern — it is central to modern ML:

Deep Learning is especially sensitive. A neural network with \(\alpha = 0.1\) might diverge entirely. The same network with \(\alpha = 10^{-3}\) converges to 94% accuracy. With \(\alpha = 10^{-4}\), it converges to 96%. The difference between a useless and state-of-the-art model is often the hyperparameters, not the architecture.

AutoML automates this loop. Systems like Auto-sklearn, AutoKeras, and Google's AutoML pipeline use Bayesian optimisation + Hyperband + Neural Architecture Search (NAS) to automate the entire model selection and tuning process. The "learning" in AutoML is learning the hyperparameter objective.

Neural Architecture Search (NAS) treats the architecture itself as a hyperparameter. DARTS reformulates discrete architecture choices as continuous parameters and differentiates through them. This is hyperparameter optimisation taken to its logical conclusion.

Meta-learning ("learning to learn") goes further: train a model to predict good hyperparameters for a new task based on dataset meta-features. This is the same spirit as warm-starting Bayesian optimisation with knowledge from previous tasks. MAML (Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning) learns initial parameters that require minimal fine-tuning — another form of optimising across the outer loop.

Foundation Model Fine-Tuning. When fine-tuning BERT or GPT-style models, the learning rate schedule, warmup steps, and weight decay are the most critical hyperparameters. The LLM literature has accumulated strong defaults (e.g., linear warmup + cosine decay, \(\alpha \approx 2 \times 10^{-5}\) for BERT fine-tuning), but these are themselves the product of massive hyperparameter searches.

docs.title: ✦ Implementation From Scratch: Bayesian Optimisation (GP + EI)
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm
from scipy.optimize import minimize

class GaussianProcess:
    def __init__(self, length_scale=1.0, noise=1e-6):
        self.ls = length_scale
        self.noise = noise

    def rbf_kernel(self, X1, X2):
        # K[i,j] = exp(-||x_i - x_j||^2 / (2 * ls^2))
        diff = X1[:, None, :] - X2[None, :, :]
        return np.exp(-0.5 * np.sum(diff**2, axis=-1) / self.ls**2)

    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.X_train = X
        self.y_train = y
        self.K = self.rbf_kernel(X, X) + self.noise * np.eye(len(X))
        self.L = np.linalg.cholesky(self.K)
        self.alpha = np.linalg.solve(self.L.T, np.linalg.solve(self.L, y))

    def predict(self, X_test):
        k_star = self.rbf_kernel(self.X_train, X_test)
        mu = k_star.T @ self.alpha
        v = np.linalg.solve(self.L, k_star)
        sigma2 = self.rbf_kernel(X_test, X_test) - v.T @ v
        sigma = np.sqrt(np.maximum(np.diag(sigma2), 0))
        return mu, sigma


def expected_improvement(X, gp, f_best, xi=0.01):
    mu, sigma = gp.predict(X)
    Z = (f_best - mu - xi) / (sigma + 1e-9)
    ei = (f_best - mu - xi) * norm.cdf(Z) + sigma * norm.pdf(Z)
    ei[sigma < 1e-10] = 0.0
    return ei


def bayesian_optimisation(f, bounds, n_init=5, n_iter=25):
    """
    f: function to minimise (returns scalar)
    bounds: list of (low, high) per dimension
    """
    dim = len(bounds)

    # Random initialisation
    X = np.array([[np.random.uniform(lo, hi) for lo, hi in bounds]
                   for _ in range(n_init)])
    y = np.array([f(x) for x in X])

    for i in range(n_iter):
        gp = GaussianProcess(length_scale=1.0)
        gp.fit(X, y)
        f_best = y.min()

        # Maximise EI via random restarts
        best_ei, best_x = -np.inf, None
        for _ in range(100):
            x0 = np.array([np.random.uniform(lo, hi) for lo, hi in bounds])
            res = minimize(
                lambda x: -expected_improvement(x.reshape(1, -1), gp, f_best),
                x0,
                bounds=bounds,
                method='L-BFGS-B'
            )
            if -res.fun > best_ei:
                best_ei = -res.fun
                best_x = res.x

        # Evaluate
        y_new = f(best_x)
        X = np.vstack([X, best_x])
        y = np.append(y, y_new)

        print(f"Iter {i+1:3d}: f({best_x}) = {y_new:.4f}, best so far = {y.min():.4f}")

    return X[y.argmin()], y.min()


# Example: tune C and gamma for an SVC
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification

X_data, y_data = make_classification(n_samples=500, n_features=20, random_state=42)

def objective(theta):
    # theta = [log10(C), log10(gamma)]
    C = 10 ** theta[0]
    gamma = 10 ** theta[1]
    clf = SVC(C=C, gamma=gamma, kernel='rbf')
    score = cross_val_score(clf, X_data, y_data, cv=5, scoring='accuracy').mean()
    return 1 - score  # minimise 1 - accuracy

best_theta, best_val = bayesian_optimisation(
    objective,
    bounds=[(-3, 3), (-4, 1)],  # log-scale bounds
    n_init=5,
    n_iter=30
)
print(f"\nBest C = {10**best_theta[0]:.4f}, gamma = {10**best_theta[1]:.6f}")
print(f"Best validation accuracy = {1 - best_val:.4f}")

docs.title: Bagging and Random Forests
docs.text: "One tree is a guess. A thousand trees, each wrong in a different way, average out to something close to truth."

docs.title: ✦ The Problem: Why Trees Alone Fail
docs.text:
From [[05.Decision Trees|Decision Trees]], recall the fundamental tension: a fully grown tree has low bias (it can fit any training set perfectly) but high variance (small perturbations in the training data produce radically different trees). The tree is an unstable learner — it has memorised the data, not learned from it.

More precisely: decision trees are high-variance, low-bias estimators. The bias-variance decomposition tells us that expected test error decomposes as:

\[\mathbb{E}[(y - \hat{f}(x))^2] = \underbrace{\text{Bias}^2[\hat{f}(x)]}_{\text{stays low}} + \underbrace{\text{Var}[\hat{f}(x)]}_{\text{we need to kill this}} + \sigma^2\]

The question is: can we reduce variance without increasing bias? Yes. The answer is aggregation.

docs.title: The Core Idea
docs.text:
Bagging = B**ootstrap **Agg**regat**ing. Proposed by Leo Breiman (1996).

The variance of a random variable \(Z\) with variance \(\sigma^2\) satisfies:

\[\text{Var}!\left[\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B Z_b\right] = \frac{\sigma^2}{B} \quad \text{if the } Z_b \text{ are i.i.d.}\]

If we could train \(B\) independent models \(\hat{f}_1, \ldots, \hat{f}_B\) on \(B\) independent datasets and average their predictions, variance would shrink by a factor of \(B\). Bias is unchanged because averaging unbiased estimators is unbiased.

We don't have \(B\) independent datasets. We have one. But we can simulate independent datasets by resampling with replacement.

docs.title: Bootstrap Sampling
docs.text:
A bootstrap sample \(\mathcal{D}^*_b\) is constructed by drawing \(n\) samples with replacement from \(\mathcal{D} = {(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^n\).

Key facts about bootstrap samples:

  • Each \(\mathcal{D}^*_b\) has \(n\) points, same as \(\mathcal{D}\)
  • Each original point appears in \(\mathcal{D}^*_b\) with probability \(1 - (1 - 1/n)^n \approx 1 - e^{-1} \approx 0.632\)
  • Roughly 36.8% of original points are absent from each bootstrap sample — these are the out-of-bag (OOB) points

docs.title: The Bagging Algorithm
docs.text:
Input: training data 𝒟, base learner ℒ, number of bags B
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
for b = 1 to B:
    𝒟*_b ← bootstrap sample from 𝒟
    f̂_b ← ℒ(𝒟*_b)    ← train a fully grown tree (no pruning)

Aggregate:
    Regression:      f̂_bag(x) = (1/B) Σ_b f̂_b(x)
    Classification:  f̂_bag(x) = majority_vote{ f̂_b(x) }
                  or f̂_bag(x) = argmax_k (1/B) Σ_b P̂_b(y=k|x)  [soft voting]

docs.title: Variance Reduction: The Full Derivation
docs.text:
Suppose the \(B\) base learners each have variance \(\sigma^2\) and pairwise correlation \(\rho\) (they're not independent — they're all trained on draws from the same \(\mathcal{D}\)).

The variance of the average of \(B\) identically distributed random variables with pairwise correlation \(\rho\):

\[\text{Var}!\left[\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \hat{f}_b(x)\right] = \rho \sigma^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{B} \sigma^2\]

Proof. Let \(Z_b = \hat{f}_b(x)\), \(\text{Var}[Z_b] = \sigma^2\), \(\text{Cov}[Z_b, Z_{b'}] = \rho\sigma^2\) for \(b \neq b'\).

\[\text{Var}!\left[\frac{1}{B}\sum_b Z_b\right] = \frac{1}{B^2}\left(\sum_b \text{Var}[Z_b] + \sum_{b \neq b'}\text{Cov}[Z_b, Z_{b'}]\right)$$ $$= \frac{1}{B^2}\left(B\sigma^2 + B(B-1)\rho\sigma^2\right) = \frac{\sigma^2}{B} + \frac{(B-1)}{B}\rho\sigma^2$$ $$= \rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2\]

Interpretation:

\[\underbrace{\rho\sigma^2}_{\substack{\text{irreducible floor} \ \text{(correlation)}\vphantom{B}}} + \underbrace{\frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2}_{\substack{\text{vanishes as} \ B \to \infty}}\]

As \(B \to \infty\), the variance approaches \(\rho\sigma^2\), not zero. The correlation between trees is the bottleneck. The key to reducing ensemble variance is reducing \(\rho\), not increasing \(B\).

This is the central insight that motivates Random Forests.

docs.title: What Bagging Does to Bias
docs.text:
Averaging is a linear operation. If each \(\hat{f}_b\) is an unbiased estimator of \(f\), then the average is also unbiased. If each \(\hat{f}_b\) has bias \(b\) (e.g., from underfitting), the average also has bias \(b\).

Bagging reduces variance. It does not reduce bias.

This is why we use fully grown trees as base learners — they have low bias. Pruned trees would have higher bias that bagging cannot fix.

docs.title: Out-of-Bag (OOB) Evaluation
docs.text:
For each training point \((x_i, y_i)\), roughly \(B/e \approx 0.368B\) bootstrap samples did not include \((x_i, y_i)\). Call these the OOB samples for \(i\). The OOB prediction for \(x_i\) is:

\[\hat{f}_{\text{OOB}}(x_i) = \frac{1}{|{b : i \notin \mathcal{D}^__b}|} \sum_{b: i \notin \mathcal{D}^__b} \hat{f}_b(x_i)\]

The OOB error is the average loss of OOB predictions over the training set:

\[\text{OOB error} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \mathcal{L}(y_i, \hat{f}_{\text{OOB}}(x_i))\]

This is a nearly unbiased estimate of the test error — each prediction is made by models that never saw that point, exactly as in cross-validation, but at no extra computational cost. OOB evaluation comes for free.

from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingClassifier
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

bag = BaggingClassifier(
    estimator=DecisionTreeClassifier(),  # fully grown tree
    n_estimators=500,
    max_samples=1.0,           # bootstrap sample size = n
    bootstrap=True,
    oob_score=True,            # compute OOB score
    n_jobs=-1,
    random_state=42
)
bag.fit(X_train, y_train)

print(f"OOB Score:  {bag.oob_score_:.4f}")    # free validation
print(f"Test Score: {bag.score(X_test, y_test):.4f}")
# They should be close

docs.title: Reducing Correlation Between Trees
docs.text:
Bagging reduces variance, but trees grown on bootstrap samples of the same data are still highly correlated: if there's one very strong predictor \(x_j\), almost every tree will split on \(x_j\) near the root, making all trees look similar → \(\rho\) remains high → variance floor \(\rho\sigma^2\) remains high.

The Random Forest fix: At each node, before finding the best split, randomly sample \(m\) features and restrict the search to only those \(m\) features.

This injects randomness into each split decision:

  • Trees grown on different bootstrap samples will now make different choices at each node
  • The correlation \(\rho\) between any two trees decreases
  • The variance floor \(\rho\sigma^2\) decreases

The price: each individual tree is slightly worse (we might miss the best feature at some nodes). The gain: much lower inter-tree correlation. In practice the gain dominates.

docs.title: The Random Forest Algorithm
docs.text:
Input: training data 𝒟, number of trees B, feature subsample size m
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
for b = 1 to B:
    𝒟*_b ← bootstrap sample from 𝒟
    T_b ← grow_tree(𝒟*_b):
        At each node:
            Sample m features uniformly without replacement from all d features
            Find best split among only those m features
            Split node → recurse until stopping criterion
        Return fully grown tree T_b

Predict:
    Regression:      f̂_RF(x) = (1/B) Σ_b T_b(x)
    Classification:  f̂_RF(x) = majority_vote{ T_b(x) }

docs.title: Choosing \(m\): The Key Hyperparameter
docs.text:
Default recommendations (Breiman, 2001):

  • Classification: \(m = \lfloor\sqrt{d}\rfloor\)
  • Regression: \(m = \lfloor d/3 \rfloor\)

Intuition for why these work:

  • \(m = d\): standard bagging (all features at each split) — maximum individual tree quality, maximum correlation
  • \(m = 1\): random trees (one random feature per split) — minimum correlation, very poor individual trees
  • \(m = \sqrt{d}\): the empirical sweet spot — trees are decorrelated enough, quality is retained

As \(m\) decreases: \(\rho \downarrow\), \(\sigma^2 \uparrow\) (individual trees get worse). The tradeoff is nonlinear and the defaults work well in practice, but \(m\) should be tuned.

from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
import numpy as np

rf = RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators=500,
    max_features='sqrt',       # m = sqrt(d), default for classification
    max_depth=None,            # fully grown trees
    min_samples_leaf=1,
    bootstrap=True,
    oob_score=True,
    n_jobs=-1,
    random_state=42
)
rf.fit(X_train, y_train)

print(f"OOB Score:  {rf.oob_score_:.4f}")
print(f"Test Score: {rf.score(X_test, y_test):.4f}")

docs.title: The Effect of \(B\) (Number of Trees)
docs.text:
Unlike boosting, Random Forests do not overfit as \(B\) increases. Adding more trees only:

  1. Reduces the \(\frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2\) term → variance decreases
  2. Makes the average converge to the true ensemble prediction

The error curve is monotonically decreasing and levels off. The practical question is: when does it level off? Usually around \(B = 100\)–\(500\) for most datasets. Plot OOB error vs. \(B\) to find this:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Track OOB error as B increases
oob_errors = []
for n_est in range(1, 301, 5):
    rf_b = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=n_est, oob_score=True,
                                   max_features='sqrt', n_jobs=-1, random_state=42)
    rf_b.fit(X_train, y_train)
    oob_errors.append(1 - rf_b.oob_score_)

plt.plot(range(1, 301, 5), oob_errors)
plt.xlabel('Number of Trees'); plt.ylabel('OOB Error')
plt.title('OOB Error Converges as B Increases')

docs.title: ✦ Feature Importance
docs.text: Random Forests provide two distinct notions of feature importance. They measure different things and can disagree.

docs.title: 1. Mean Decrease in Impurity (MDI)
docs.text:
For each feature \(j\), sum the (weighted) impurity decrease over all splits on \(j\), averaged over all trees:

\[\text{MDI}(j) = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \sum_{\substack{t \in T_b \ \text{split on } j}} \frac{n_t}{n} \Delta I(t)\]

where \(\Delta I(t) = I(t) - \frac{n_{t_L}}{n_t}I(t_L) - \frac{n_{t_R}}{n_t}I(t_R)\) is the impurity decrease at node \(t\), weighted by the fraction of samples reaching \(t\).

Properties:

  • Computed for free during training
  • Fast, no retraining needed
  • Known bias: features with high cardinality (many unique values) or continuous features get artificially high importance, even if uninformative. This is because the tree has more opportunities to split on them.

docs.title: 2. Permutation Importance (MDA — Mean Decrease in Accuracy)
docs.text:
For each feature \(j\):

  1. Evaluate the trained forest on the validation set → baseline score \(s\)
  2. Randomly permute the values of feature \(j\) across all samples
  3. Re-evaluate → permuted score \(s_j^{\text{perm}}\)
  4. Importance of feature \(j\): \(\text{MDA}(j) = s - s_j^{\text{perm}}\)

Permuting feature \(j\) breaks its relationship with the target. If the score drops a lot, \(j\) was important. If the score barely changes, \(j\) was irrelevant or redundant.

Properties:

  • Model-agnostic: works for any fitted model
  • Unbiased with respect to feature cardinality
  • Accounts for the feature's actual predictive contribution, not just its role in the training splits
  • More reliable and preferred when cardinality varies across features
  • Caveat: can give low importance to features that are correlated with other informative features — their information is "shared" and permuting one doesn't hurt much if the other carries the same signal
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

# MDI (fast, potentially biased)
mdi = rf.feature_importances_

# Permutation importance (slower, more reliable)
result = permutation_importance(
    rf, X_val, y_val,
    n_repeats=30,           # permute each feature 30 times
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=-1
)
mda = result.importances_mean
mda_std = result.importances_std

# Compare
import pandas as pd
importance_df = pd.DataFrame({
    'feature': feature_names,
    'MDI': mdi,
    'MDA': mda,
    'MDA_std': mda_std
}).sort_values('MDA', ascending=False)
print(importance_df.head(10))

docs.title: When MDI and Permutation Importance Disagree
docs.text:
If a feature has high MDI but low permutation importance: it has many opportunities to split on (high cardinality / continuous) but its splits don't actually improve generalisation. Trust permutation importance.

If a feature has high permutation importance but low MDI: it's informative but competes with correlated features during training. Both measures can miss this.

docs.title: ✦ Extremely Randomised Trees (Extra-Trees)
docs.text:
Push the randomisation further: instead of finding the optimal threshold for each split among \(m\) random features, draw the threshold randomly as well.

At each node in Extra-Trees:
    Sample m features
    For each of those m features:
        Draw a random threshold uniformly in [min_val, max_val]
    Pick the (feature, threshold) pair with best impurity reduction

Effect:

  • Reduces variance further (more randomness → less correlation between trees)
  • Increases bias slightly (random thresholds are suboptimal)
  • Much faster to train: no sorting required to find optimal thresholds
  • Often competitive with or better than standard Random Forests on large datasets
from sklearn.ensemble import ExtraTreesClassifier

et = ExtraTreesClassifier(
    n_estimators=500,
    max_features='sqrt',
    n_jobs=-1,
    random_state=42
)
et.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(f"Extra-Trees Test Score: {et.score(X_test, y_test):.4f}")

docs.title: ✦ From Scratch: A Minimal Random Forest in NumPy
docs.text:
This implementation is intentionally minimal — the goal is to see the mechanics, not to reproduce sklearn. Assumes you have a DecisionTreeClassifier from [[05.Decision Trees|Decision Trees]].

import numpy as np
from collections import Counter

# Assumes: DecisionTree class with .fit(X, y) and .predict(X) methods
# from your decision tree implementation

class RandomForest:
    def __init__(self, n_estimators=100, max_features='sqrt',
                 max_depth=None, min_samples_split=2, random_state=None):
        self.n_estimators = n_estimators
        self.max_features = max_features
        self.max_depth = max_depth
        self.min_samples_split = min_samples_split
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(random_state)
        self.trees = []
        self.feature_indices = []   # which m features each tree sees at root?
        # (In a full impl, m features are sampled per node, not globally)

    def _bootstrap(self, X, y):
        n = len(X)
        idx = self.rng.choice(n, size=n, replace=True)
        oob_mask = np.ones(n, dtype=bool)
        oob_mask[idx] = False
        return X[idx], y[idx], oob_mask

    def _get_m(self, d):
        if self.max_features == 'sqrt':
            return max(1, int(np.sqrt(d)))
        elif self.max_features == 'log2':
            return max(1, int(np.log2(d)))
        elif isinstance(self.max_features, float):
            return max(1, int(self.max_features * d))
        elif isinstance(self.max_features, int):
            return self.max_features
        return d  # 'all'

    def fit(self, X, y):
        n, d = X.shape
        m = self._get_m(d)
        self.oob_predictions = np.full((n, len(np.unique(y))), 0.0)
        self.oob_counts = np.zeros(n)

        for b in range(self.n_estimators):
            X_boot, y_boot, oob_mask = self._bootstrap(X, y)

            # Feature subsampling: in a real impl this happens per node.
            # Here we simulate by training on a feature subset (simplified).
            feat_idx = self.rng.choice(d, size=m, replace=False)
            self.feature_indices.append(feat_idx)

            # Train a decision tree on the bootstrap sample
            tree = DecisionTree(
                max_depth=self.max_depth,
                min_samples_split=self.min_samples_split
            )
            tree.fit(X_boot[:, feat_idx], y_boot)
            self.trees.append(tree)

            # Accumulate OOB predictions
            if oob_mask.any():
                oob_proba = tree.predict_proba(X[oob_mask][:, feat_idx])
                self.oob_predictions[oob_mask] += oob_proba
                self.oob_counts[oob_mask] += 1

        # OOB score
        valid = self.oob_counts > 0
        oob_pred = self.oob_predictions[valid] / self.oob_counts[valid, None]
        oob_labels = oob_pred.argmax(axis=1)
        self.oob_score_ = (oob_labels == y[valid]).mean()
        return self

    def predict_proba(self, X):
        probas = np.zeros((len(X), len(self.trees[0].classes_)))
        for tree, feat_idx in zip(self.trees, self.feature_indices):
            probas += tree.predict_proba(X[:, feat_idx])
        return probas / self.n_estimators

    def predict(self, X):
        return self.predict_proba(X).argmax(axis=1)

    def score(self, X, y):
        return (self.predict(X) == y).mean()

Note: A production implementation samples \(m\) features per node, not globally per tree. The above simplification captures the spirit but not the full mechanics. In sklearn's C implementation, feature sampling happens inside _splitter.pyx at each node.

docs.title: ✦ Worked Example: Bias-Variance on a Toy Problem
docs.text:
Let's make the variance reduction concrete. Consider a 1D regression problem \(y = \sin(2\pi x) + \epsilon\), \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.1)\), with \(n = 50\) training points.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingRegressor, RandomForestRegressor

np.random.seed(42)
x_test = np.linspace(0, 1, 300).reshape(-1, 1)
true_f = np.sin(2 * np.pi * x_test.ravel())

n_simulations = 200
tree_preds = np.zeros((n_simulations, 300))
bag_preds  = np.zeros((n_simulations, 300))

for sim in range(n_simulations):
    # New training set each time
    X_train = np.random.rand(50, 1)
    y_train = np.sin(2 * np.pi * X_train.ravel()) + np.random.randn(50) * 0.1

    # Single tree
    tree = DecisionTreeRegressor()
    tree.fit(X_train, y_train)
    tree_preds[sim] = tree.predict(x_test)

    # Bagged forest
    bag = BaggingRegressor(DecisionTreeRegressor(), n_estimators=100, random_state=sim)
    bag.fit(X_train, y_train)
    bag_preds[sim] = bag.predict(x_test)

# Compute bias^2 and variance at each test point
tree_bias2 = (tree_preds.mean(0) - true_f)**2
tree_var   = tree_preds.var(0)
bag_bias2  = (bag_preds.mean(0) - true_f)**2
bag_var    = bag_preds.var(0)

print(f"Single Tree — Bias²: {tree_bias2.mean():.4f}, Variance: {tree_var.mean():.4f}")
print(f"Bagged Forest — Bias²: {bag_bias2.mean():.4f}, Variance: {bag_var.mean():.4f}")

# Expected output:
# Single Tree  — Bias²: ~0.012, Variance: ~0.080
# Bagged Forest — Bias²: ~0.012, Variance: ~0.008
# Variance drops ~10x. Bias is unchanged.

docs.title: ✦ Connection to AI / ML / Deep Learning
docs.text:
Random Forests as a foundation for modern ensemble methods. The feature-subsampling idea reappears in XGBoost (colsample_bytree, colsample_bylevel) and LightGBM (feature_fraction). These are not coincidental — Gradient Boosting with column subsampling is essentially applying the Random Forest decorrelation idea to the boosting framework.

The Bias-Variance Tradeoff, operationalised. Random Forests are perhaps the cleanest empirical demonstration that the bias-variance decomposition is not just theory — the formula \(\rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2\) is exactly what you observe when you vary \(m\) and \(B\). Deep learning has its own version: dropout (zero out random neurons during training) is analogous to Random Forest's feature subsampling, and ensemble training (training multiple neural networks and averaging) obeys the same \(1/B\) variance reduction.

Feature importance and model interpretability. MDI and permutation importance from Random Forests are the precursors to SHAP values (see [[03.Model Interpretability|Model Interpretability]]). SHAP's TreeExplainer is optimised specifically for tree ensembles and computes exact Shapley values in \(O(TLD^2)\) where \(T\) is trees, \(L\) leaves, \(D\) depth — much faster than model-agnostic SHAP.

Random Forests at scale. In production, Random Forests are often the baseline against which deep models are compared on tabular data. A 2022 study ("Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on tabular data?" — Grinsztajn et al.) showed that Random Forests and gradient-boosted trees consistently beat MLP-style deep models on tabular benchmarks, especially for datasets \(n < 10{,}000\). The inductive bias of axis-aligned splits is well-matched to tabular data with heterogeneous features.

Uncertainty quantification. The spread of predictions across trees in a Random Forest is a natural measure of uncertainty — akin to a Bayesian posterior. This is formalised in Mondrian Forests, which use a specific random splitting mechanism to provide valid confidence intervals. In deep learning, MC Dropout (Gal & Ghahramani, 2016) achieves a similar effect: dropout at test time produces an ensemble of subnetworks, analogous to the Random Forest ensemble.

docs.title: ✦ Common Pitfalls
docs.text:
Pitfall 1: Scaling features. Decision trees are scale-invariant — you don't need to standardise features. (Unlike SVMs or KNN which are distance-based.)

Pitfall 2: Trusting MDI on mixed-cardinality data. If you have a continuous feature and a binary feature, the continuous feature will almost always have higher MDI simply because there are more possible split points. Use permutation importance to verify.

Pitfall 3: Using OOB score as your test score. OOB gives an unbiased estimate, but it's still an estimate on training data. If you've already used OOB to tune hyperparameters, report the held-out test score, not OOB.

Pitfall 4: Stopping \(B\) too early. Plotting OOB error vs. \(B\) is cheap. Don't guess — verify convergence.

Pitfall 5: Ignoring class imbalance. Default Random Forests treat all samples equally. Use class_weight='balanced' or class_weight={0: w_0, 1: w_1} for imbalanced problems.

docs.title: ✦ Summary
docs.text:
Property Single Decision Tree Bagged Trees Random Forest Bias Low Low Slightly higher Variance High Moderate Low Interpretability High None None (but feature importances) Training cost \(O(nd \log n)\) \(B \times O(nd\log n)\) \(B \times O(nm\log n)\) Parallel? No Yes Yes Overfits as \(B \to \infty\)? — No No OOB evaluation No Yes Yes

The variance floor of a bagged ensemble is \(\rho\sigma^2\). The contribution of Random Forests is to drive \(\rho\) toward zero by randomising the feature selection at each split, without substantially increasing the bias \(\sigma^2\) of individual trees.

You know this when: you can derive the variance of the bagged ensemble from the definition of pairwise covariance, explain why increasing \(B\) eventually stops helping, implement a Random Forest in NumPy using your decision tree, and articulate when you'd trust permutation importance over MDI.

docs.title: Boosting
docs.text: "Bagging asks: can many independent weak learners agree? Boosting asks: can each new learner correct what the last one got wrong?"

docs.title: ✦ The Meta-Idea
docs.text:
Bagging reduces variance by averaging independent learners. The learners don't communicate — each one sees a different bootstrap sample and contributes an independent vote.

Boosting is fundamentally different. The learners are trained sequentially, and each new learner is explicitly shaped by the errors of all previous learners. The ensemble is built additively:

\[F_M(x) = \sum_{m=1}^M \alpha_m h_m(x)\]

where \(h_m\) are weak learners (typically shallow trees) and \(\alpha_m\) are their weights.

A weak learner is one that does only slightly better than random guessing — formally, its error rate \(\epsilon < 1/2\) for binary classification. The celebrated result of boosting theory (Schapire, 1990) is that any weak learner can be boosted into an arbitrarily accurate strong learner, provided the data is not noisy beyond a certain threshold.

docs.title: Motivation: Reweighting the Hard Examples
docs.text:
After the first classifier \(h_1\) makes predictions, some examples are correctly classified, others are not. The intuition: train \(h_2\) to focus on what \(h_1\) got wrong. Do this by upweighting misclassified examples and downweighting correctly classified ones.

The question AdaBoost answers rigorously: how much to reweight, and how much weight to give each classifier?

docs.title: The Algorithm
docs.text:
Setting: Binary classification, \(y_i \in {-1, +1}\), \(n\) training examples.

Initialise: w_i^(1) = 1/n for i = 1, ..., n

for m = 1, 2, ..., M:

    1. Train weak learner h_m on weighted dataset (X, y, w^(m))
       → h_m: X → {-1, +1}

    2. Compute weighted error:
       ε_m = Σᵢ wᵢ^(m) · 𝟙[h_m(xᵢ) ≠ yᵢ]

    3. Compute classifier weight:
       α_m = (1/2) ln((1 - ε_m) / ε_m)

    4. Update sample weights:
       w_i^(m+1) = w_i^(m) · exp(-α_m · y_i · h_m(x_i))
       Normalise: w_i^(m+1) ← w_i^(m+1) / Σⱼ wⱼ^(m+1)

Final classifier: F(x) = sign(Σ_m α_m h_m(x))

docs.title: Derivation of \(\alpha_m\): Where Does the Formula Come From?
docs.text:
We want \(\alpha_m\) such that the new ensemble \(F_m = F_{m-1} + \alpha_m h_m\) minimises the exponential loss:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\exp} = \sum_{i=1}^n \exp(-y_i F_m(x_i))\]

Substituting \(F_m = F_{m-1} + \alpha_m h_m\):

\[\mathcal{L}_{\exp} = \sum_i \exp(-y_i F_{m-1}(x_i)) \cdot \exp(-y_i \alpha_m h_m(x_i))\]

Let \(\tilde{w}_i = \exp(-y_i F_{m-1}(x_i))\) (the "unnormalised weight" — it's the current sample difficulty). Split the sum over correctly and incorrectly classified examples:

  • Correct: \(y_i h_m(x_i) = +1\), so \(\exp(-\alpha_m)\) factor
  • Incorrect: \(y_i h_m(x_i) = -1\), so \(\exp(+\alpha_m)\) factor
\[\mathcal{L}_{\exp} = e^{-\alpha_m} \sum_{y_i = h_m(x_i)} \tilde{w}_i + e^{\alpha_m} \sum_{y_i \neq h_m(x_i)} \tilde{w}_i\]

Let \(W_c = \sum_{y_i = h_m(x_i)} \tilde{w}_i\) (correct weight) and \(W_e = \sum_{y_i \neq h_m(x_i)} \tilde{w}_i\) (error weight), so \(W_c + W_e = W_{\text{total}}\).

\[\mathcal{L}_{\exp} = e^{-\alpha_m} W_c + e^{\alpha_m} W_e\]

Differentiate with respect to \(\alpha_m\) and set to zero:

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\exp}}{\partial \alpha_m} = -e^{-\alpha_m} W_c + e^{\alpha_m} W_e = 0\] \[e^{2\alpha_m} = \frac{W_c}{W_e} \implies \alpha_m = \frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{W_c}{W_e} = \frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{1 - \epsilon_m}{\epsilon_m}\]

where \(\epsilon_m = W_e / (W_c + W_e)\) is the normalised weighted error. \(\blacksquare\)

Interpretation of \(\alpha_m\):

\(\epsilon_m\) \(\alpha_m\) Meaning \(0\) \(+\infty\) Perfect — dominates the ensemble \(0.5\) \(0\) Random — contributes nothing \(> 0.5\) \(< 0\) Worse than random — negated

The weight update is then derived by substituting \(\alpha_m\) back and tracing how the unnormalised weights evolve:

\[\tilde{w}_i^{(m+1)} = \tilde{w}_i^{(m)} \cdot e^{-\alpha_m y_i h_m(x_i)}\]

which after normalisation gives the update rule in the algorithm above.

docs.title: Derivation: AdaBoost as Forward Stagewise Additive Modelling
docs.text:
The deeper result: AdaBoost is Forward Stagewise Additive Modelling (FSAM) with the exponential loss.

FSAM builds \(F_M = \sum_m \alpha_m h_m\) by solving at each step:

\[(\alpha_m, h_m) = \arg\min_{\alpha, h} \sum_i \mathcal{L}(y_i, F_{m-1}(x_i) + \alpha h(x_i))\]

For the exponential loss \(\mathcal{L}(y, F) = e^{-yF}\), solving this exactly gives the AdaBoost update. This is the Friedman-Hastie-Tibshirani (2000) characterisation — it reveals why exponential loss: it's the unique loss for which FSAM reduces to the elegant reweighting scheme.

Why exponential loss can be a problem: It is extremely sensitive to outliers and noisy labels. An example with \(y_i = +1\) that keeps being misclassified gets weight \(\propto e^{F_{m-1}(x_i)}\), which grows without bound. Gradient Boosting replaces exponential loss with something more robust.

docs.title: AdaBoost in Code
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

class AdaBoost:
    def __init__(self, n_estimators=50, learning_rate=1.0):
        self.M = n_estimators
        self.lr = learning_rate
        self.alphas = []
        self.clfs = []

    def fit(self, X, y):
        # y must be {-1, +1}
        n = len(y)
        w = np.ones(n) / n

        for m in range(self.M):
            # Train stump (depth-1 tree)
            clf = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=1)
            clf.fit(X, y, sample_weight=w)
            h = clf.predict(X)

            # Weighted error
            err = w @ (h != y)
            err = np.clip(err, 1e-10, 1 - 1e-10)  # numerical safety

            # Classifier weight
            alpha = 0.5 * np.log((1 - err) / err) * self.lr

            # Update weights
            w = w * np.exp(-alpha * y * h)
            w /= w.sum()

            self.alphas.append(alpha)
            self.clfs.append(clf)

        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        F = sum(a * clf.predict(X) for a, clf in zip(self.alphas, self.clfs))
        return np.sign(F)

    def score(self, X, y):
        return (self.predict(X) == y).mean()


# Usage
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=1000, n_features=20, random_state=42)
y = 2 * y - 1   # {0,1} → {-1, +1}

ada = AdaBoost(n_estimators=200)
ada.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(f"AdaBoost accuracy: {ada.score(X_test, y_test):.4f}")

docs.title: The Key Generalisation
docs.text:
AdaBoost is tied to exponential loss. What if we want to use:

  • Logistic loss (more robust classification)
  • Huber loss (robust regression)
  • Quantile loss (predicting percentiles)
  • Any differentiable loss

Friedman (2001) observed: the AdaBoost reweighting scheme can be interpreted as gradient descent in function space. This generalises to arbitrary differentiable losses.

docs.title: Gradient Descent in Function Space
docs.text:
Ordinary gradient descent optimises parameters \(\theta\):

\[\theta \leftarrow \theta - \alpha \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta)\]

Suppose instead we treat the prediction function \(F\) itself as the parameter. At each training point \((x_i, y_i)\), we want to move \(F(x_i)\) in the direction that most reduces the loss:

\[F(x_i) \leftarrow F(x_i) - \alpha \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}(y_i, F(x_i))}{\partial F(x_i)}\]

Define the pseudo-residual at step \(m\):

\[r_i^{(m)} = -\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}(y_i, F(x_i))}{\partial F(x_i)}\Bigg|_{F = F_{m-1}}\]

This is the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current prediction at \(x_i\). If we could update \(F\) directly at the training points, we'd just set \(F_m(x_i) = F_{m-1}(x_i) + \nu r_i^{(m)}\).

But we need \(F_m\) to generalise to new points. The trick: fit a weak learner \(h_m\) to the pseudo-residuals, then add it to the ensemble. \(h_m\) learns to approximate the negative gradient everywhere, not just at training points.

docs.title: The Gradient Boosting Algorithm
docs.text:
Input: training data {(xᵢ, yᵢ)}, loss L, M rounds, learning rate ν, weak learner ℒ
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Initialise: F₀(x) = argmin_γ Σᵢ L(yᵢ, γ)
               (the constant prediction that minimises average loss)

for m = 1, 2, ..., M:

    2. Compute pseudo-residuals:
       rᵢ^(m) = -∂L(yᵢ, F(xᵢ))/∂F(xᵢ) |_{F = F_{m-1}}

    3. Fit a regression tree h_m to {(xᵢ, rᵢ^(m))}
       (always regression, even for classification — fitting the gradient values)

    4. Find optimal leaf weights by line search:
       For each leaf j of h_m:
           γⱼ^(m) = argmin_γ Σᵢ∈leaf_j L(yᵢ, F_{m-1}(xᵢ) + γ)

    5. Update:
       F_m(x) = F_{m-1}(x) + ν · Σⱼ γⱼ^(m) · 𝟙[x ∈ leaf_j]

Return F_M

Step 1: For MSE loss, \(F_0 = \bar{y}\). For log-loss, \(F_0 = \log(\bar{p}/(1-\bar{p}))\).

Step 4: The line search adjusts each leaf's contribution to best reduce the loss. For MSE, this is trivially the mean of residuals in the leaf. For other losses it requires a 1D optimisation per leaf.

Step 5: \(\nu \in (0, 1]\) is the learning rate (also called shrinkage). Small \(\nu\) requires more trees but typically generalises better.

docs.title: Pseudo-Residuals for Common Losses
docs.text:
MSE Regression (\(\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{2}(y - F)^2\)):

\[r_i = -\frac{\partial}{\partial F}\frac{1}{2}(y_i - F)^2 = y_i - F_{m-1}(x_i)\]

The pseudo-residual is the actual residual. Gradient Boosting for MSE is exactly iterative residual fitting. Each tree fits the residuals left by the previous ensemble.

Binary Classification (\(\mathcal{L} = \log(1 + e^{-y_i F(x_i)})\), \(y_i \in {-1,+1}\)):

\[r_i = \frac{2y_i}{1 + e^{y_i F_{m-1}(x_i)}}\]

Binary Cross-Entropy (\(\mathcal{L} = -[y_i \log p_i + (1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)]\), \(F = \log\text{-odds}\), \(p_i = \sigma(F)\)):

\[r_i = y_i - p_i^{(m-1)}\]

The pseudo-residual is again the probability residual — how far the current predicted probability is from the true label. Intuitive: fit the next tree to how wrong our probabilities are.

MAE / \(L_1\) Regression (\(\mathcal{L} = |y - F|\)):

\[r_i = \text{sign}(y_i - F_{m-1}(x_i))\]

Each tree fits the signs of the residuals (not their magnitude). This makes gradient boosting with MAE robust to outliers.

docs.title: The Three Knobs
docs.text:
Gradient Boosting has three primary hyperparameters that govern the bias-variance tradeoff:

1. \(n_estimators\) (M): Number of trees. More trees → lower bias. But unlike Random Forests, GB can overfit as \(M\) increases — the model keeps fitting the training data harder. Use early stopping.

2. \(learning_rate\) (\( u\)): Shrinkage per step. Smaller \( u\) → each tree contributes less → need more trees for the same fit → better generalisation (with sufficient \(M\)). The Friedman shrinkage rule: decrease \( u\), increase \(M\) proportionally. Common range: \( u \in [0.01, 0.3]\).

3. \(max_depth\): Depth of individual trees. Depth-1 trees (stumps) = additive model (no interactions). Depth-2 = captures pairwise interactions. Depth 3–5 is typical. Unlike bagging, deep trees in boosting lead to overfitting.

Interaction between \( u\) and \(M\): they are not independent. A common pattern:

ν = 0.1, M = 100   →   same performance as   ν = 0.01, M = 1000

The smaller \( u\), the more trees you need. Tune \( u\) first (or use a fixed small \( u\)), then find \(M\) with early stopping.

docs.title: Gradient Boosting From Scratch (MSE)
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

class GradientBoostingMSE:
    """Gradient Boosting for regression with MSE loss."""

    def __init__(self, n_estimators=100, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=3):
        self.M = n_estimators
        self.nu = learning_rate
        self.max_depth = max_depth
        self.trees = []
        self.F0 = None

    def fit(self, X, y):
        # Step 1: Initialise with mean prediction
        self.F0 = y.mean()
        F = np.full(len(y), self.F0)

        for m in range(self.M):
            # Step 2: Pseudo-residuals (= actual residuals for MSE)
            r = y - F

            # Step 3: Fit regression tree to residuals
            tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=self.max_depth)
            tree.fit(X, r)

            # Step 4: Line search (trivial for MSE: mean of residuals per leaf)
            # DecisionTreeRegressor already does this internally
            update = tree.predict(X)

            # Step 5: Update ensemble
            F += self.nu * update
            self.trees.append(tree)

        return self

    def predict(self, X):
        F = np.full(len(X), self.F0)
        for tree in self.trees:
            F += self.nu * tree.predict(X)
        return F

    def mse(self, X, y):
        return np.mean((y - self.predict(X))**2)


# Demonstration: residuals shrink monotonically
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
X, y = make_regression(n_samples=500, n_features=10, noise=10, random_state=42)

gb = GradientBoostingMSE(n_estimators=200, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=3)
gb.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(f"Train MSE: {gb.mse(X_train, y_train):.2f}")
print(f"Test  MSE: {gb.mse(X_test, y_test):.2f}")

docs.title: Early Stopping
docs.text:
Since GB can overfit, use staged predictions to find the optimal \(M\):

from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor

gb = GradientBoostingRegressor(
    n_estimators=1000,
    learning_rate=0.05,
    max_depth=3,
    subsample=0.8,          # stochastic GB (see below)
    validation_fraction=0.1,
    n_iter_no_change=20,    # stop if val loss doesn't improve for 20 rounds
    tol=1e-4,
    random_state=42
)
gb.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(f"Best n_estimators: {gb.n_estimators_}")   # actual trees used

docs.title: ✦ Part 3 — Stochastic Gradient Boosting
docs.text:
Friedman (1999) observed that subsampling the training data at each boosting step (without replacement) both speeds up training and improves generalisation by adding variance to individual trees, reducing inter-tree correlation — the same intuition as Random Forests.

At each step \(m\), randomly sample a fraction \(0 < s \leq 1\) of training examples (without replacement). Fit \(h_m\) on this subsample only.

Effects:

  • Reduces overfitting (analogous to learning rate shrinkage)
  • Enables approximate computation on large datasets
  • subsample=0.5–0.8 is a common range; lower values = more regularisation

Combined with column subsampling (max_features), this is essentially a boosted random forest.

docs.title: ✦ Part 4 — XGBoost
docs.text: XGBoost (Chen & Guestrin, 2016) re-derives gradient boosting from first principles, adding three critical improvements: a regularised objective, second-order Taylor expansion, and algorithmic optimisations for scale.

docs.title: The Regularised Objective
docs.text:
Standard gradient boosting minimises only the loss. XGBoost adds explicit regularisation on the tree structure:

\[\mathcal{O}^{(m)} = \sum_{i=1}^n \mathcal{L}(y_i, F_{m-1}(x_i) + h_m(x_i)) + \Omega(h_m)\]

where the regularisation term is:

\[\Omega(h) = \gamma T + \frac{1}{2}\lambda \sum_{j=1}^T w_j^2\]
  • \(T\): number of leaves (penalises complexity)
  • \(w_j\): weight (prediction) in leaf \(j\)
  • \(\gamma\): minimum loss reduction required to make a split (structural regularisation)
  • \(\lambda\): L2 regularisation on leaf weights

This directly controls overfitting at the tree structure level.

docs.title: Second-Order Taylor Expansion
docs.text:
Approximate the loss using a second-order Taylor expansion around \(F_{m-1}(x_i)\):

\[\mathcal{L}(y_i, F_{m-1}(x_i) + h_m(x_i)) \approx \mathcal{L}(y_i, F_{m-1}(x_i)) + g_i h_m(x_i) + \frac{1}{2} h_i h_m(x_i)^2\]

where: $\(g_i = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}(y_i, \hat{y}_i)}{\partial \hat{y}_i}\Bigg|_{\hat{y}_i = F_{m-1}(x_i)}, \quad h_i = \frac{\partial^2 \mathcal{L}(y_i, \hat{y}_i)}{\partial \hat{y}_i^2}\Bigg|_{\hat{y}_i = F_{m-1}(x_i)}\)$

\(g_i\) is the gradient (same as the pseudo-residual, up to sign), \(h_i\) is the Hessian — the curvature of the loss at the current prediction.

Dropping constants and grouping by leaves, the objective for a fixed tree structure becomes:

\[\mathcal{O}^{(m)} \approx \sum_{j=1}^T \left[ \left(\sum_{i \in \text{leaf}_j} g_i\right) w_j + \frac{1}{2}\left(\sum_{i \in \text{leaf}_j} h_i + \lambda\right) w_j^2 \right] + \gamma T\]

This is a quadratic in \(w_j\) for each leaf. The optimal leaf weight is:

\[w_j^* = -\frac{G_j}{H_j + \lambda}, \quad G_j = \sum_{i \in \text{leaf}_j} g_i, \quad H_j = \sum_{i \in \text{leaf}_j} h_i\]

Substituting back gives the minimum objective value for a given tree structure:

\[\mathcal{O}^* = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^T \frac{G_j^2}{H_j + \lambda} + \gamma T\]

The gain from a split (used to greedily build the tree) is:

\[\text{Gain} = \frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{G_L^2}{H_L + \lambda} + \frac{G_R^2}{H_R + \lambda} - \frac{(G_L + G_R)^2}{H_L + H_R + \lambda}\right] - \gamma\]

This has an elegant interpretation: it measures how much the regularised objective improves by splitting a leaf into left and right children. If \(\text{Gain} < 0\) for all possible splits, the leaf is not split (the \(\gamma\) term enforces a minimum gain threshold).

Why does the Hessian matter? The Hessian \(h_i\) tells us the local curvature of the loss. Points with high \(h_i\) (near the decision boundary in classification, where the sigmoid is steep) receive more emphasis in the split search. This is a Newton step, not just a gradient step. Newton methods converge faster near the optimum.

For MSE: \(g_i = \hat{y}_i - y_i\), \(h_i = 1\). The Hessian is constant — Newton and gradient methods are identical. The benefit of second-order information is largest for asymmetric losses (logistic, Poisson, etc.).

docs.title: XGBoost in Practice
docs.text:
import xgboost as xgb

model = xgb.XGBClassifier(
    n_estimators=1000,
    learning_rate=0.05,
    max_depth=6,
    subsample=0.8,            # row subsampling
    colsample_bytree=0.8,     # column subsampling (per tree)
    colsample_bylevel=0.8,    # column subsampling (per level)
    reg_lambda=1.0,           # L2 on leaf weights
    reg_alpha=0.0,            # L1 on leaf weights
    gamma=0.1,                # min gain for split
    min_child_weight=1,       # min sum of hessians in a leaf
    early_stopping_rounds=50,
    eval_metric='logloss',
    random_state=42,
    n_jobs=-1
)

model.fit(
    X_train, y_train,
    eval_set=[(X_val, y_val)],
    verbose=100
)
print(f"Best iteration: {model.best_iteration}")
print(f"Test accuracy: {model.score(X_test, y_test):.4f}")

docs.title: Key XGBoost Hyperparameters
docs.text: Parameter Effect Typical Range n_estimators Number of trees 100–5000 (with early stopping) learning_rate Shrinkage \(\nu\) 0.01–0.3 max_depth Tree depth 3–10 subsample Row fraction per tree 0.5–1.0 colsample_bytree Column fraction per tree 0.5–1.0 reg_lambda (\(\lambda\)) L2 on leaf weights 0–10 reg_alpha L1 on leaf weights 0–10 gamma Min gain for split 0–5 min_child_weight Min sum-of-Hessians per leaf 1–10

docs.title: LightGBM
docs.text:
LightGBM (Ke et al., 2017) addresses XGBoost's two main bottlenecks: finding optimal splits (requires sorting all features for all data points) and memory for large datasets.

Key innovations:

1. Histogram-based splits. Instead of sorting continuous feature values to find all possible split points, bin each feature into \(B\) buckets (typically \(B = 256\)). Compute gradient/Hessian sums per bucket. Split search is \(O(Bd)\) instead of \(O(nd)\). Memory is \(O(Bd)\) instead of \(O(nd)\).

2. Leaf-wise tree growth. Standard gradient boosting grows trees level-wise (all leaves at the same depth). LightGBM grows leaf-wise: always split the leaf with the highest gain, regardless of depth. This grows asymmetric trees that can model complex patterns with fewer splits. Risk: can overfit on small datasets — control with min_data_in_leaf and max_depth.

3. GOSS (Gradient-based One-Side Sampling). Keep all instances with large gradients (high loss — these are the hard examples). Randomly subsample instances with small gradients. This maintains informativeness while reducing computation.

4. EFB (Exclusive Feature Bundling). Many features in high-dimensional data are mutually exclusive (rarely both nonzero). Bundle them into a single feature, reducing effective dimensionality.

import lightgbm as lgb

params = {
    'objective': 'binary',
    'metric': 'binary_logloss',
    'learning_rate': 0.05,
    'num_leaves': 63,           # LightGBM's primary complexity control (≤ 2^max_depth - 1)
    'max_depth': -1,            # -1 = no limit; use num_leaves instead
    'min_data_in_leaf': 20,     # prevents overfitting in leaf-wise growth
    'feature_fraction': 0.8,
    'bagging_fraction': 0.8,
    'bagging_freq': 5,
    'lambda_l1': 0.1,
    'lambda_l2': 0.1,
    'verbose': -1,
    'n_jobs': -1,
    'seed': 42
}

train_data = lgb.Dataset(X_train, label=y_train)
val_data   = lgb.Dataset(X_val,   label=y_val, reference=train_data)

callbacks = [lgb.early_stopping(50), lgb.log_evaluation(100)]
model = lgb.train(
    params,
    train_data,
    num_boost_round=2000,
    valid_sets=[val_data],
    callbacks=callbacks
)

docs.title: CatBoost
docs.text:
CatBoost (Prokhorenkova et al., 2018) focuses on categorical features and target leakage.

The target leakage problem in standard target encoding: When computing the target mean for a categorical value, you include the current sample's label — introducing leakage that overfits to the training distribution.

CatBoost fixes this with ordered target statistics: for sample \(i\), the target encoding for category \(c\) uses only samples \(j < i\) (earlier in a random permutation). This prevents leakage by construction.

Ordered boosting: Similarly, CatBoost builds each tree on a random permutation of the training data, using only preceding examples to compute gradients. This reduces prediction shift bias that arises in standard gradient boosting.

docs.title: ✦ Comparison: Bagging vs. Boosting
docs.text:
Property Bagging / Random Forest Boosting Trees trained In parallel (independent) Sequentially (dependent) Primary effect Reduces variance Reduces bias (and variance) Weak learner Deep trees (low bias) Shallow trees (stumps or depth 3–6) Overfitting Doesn't overfit as \(B \to \infty\) Can overfit; use early stopping Noisy labels Robust Sensitive (especially AdaBoost) Training cost Parallelisable Sequential (less parallelisable) Interpretability Feature importances Feature importances Typical performance Strong baseline Usually better on tabular data

The bias-variance lens:

  • Random Forests target the variance term — many decorrelated trees average out noise
  • Boosting targets the bias term — sequential correction drives residuals toward zero
  • Both benefit from regularisation to control the tradeoff

docs.title: ✦ Why Does Boosting Generalise?
docs.text:
The early theory suggested boosting should overfit badly — it's explicitly fitting the training data harder at each step. Empirically, it often didn't. Schapire et al. (1998) explained this through margin theory:

Define the margin of example \((x_i, y_i)\) as:

\[m(x_i, y_i) = y_i \cdot \frac{\sum_m \alpha_m h_m(x_i)}{\sum_m \alpha_m}\]

The margin is positive if correctly classified, and measures confidence. AdaBoost has been shown to increase margins even after training error reaches zero, which explains the observed generalisation. The ensemble keeps pushing confidently classified examples away from the decision boundary.

The modern understanding through statistical learning theory: boosting with a small learning rate is closely related to \(L_1\)-regularised regression in a very large feature space (one feature per weak learner). The implicit regularisation from many small steps + early stopping prevents overfitting.

docs.title: ✦ Connection to AI / ML / Deep Learning
docs.text:
Gradient Boosting ≡ Gradient Descent on Trees. The pseudo-residual derivation reveals that boosting is literally gradient descent — just in function space rather than parameter space. Every time you run model.fit() on a neural network, you're doing gradient descent in parameter space. Gradient boosting does the same thing, but represents the function as a sum of trees rather than as a neural network. The conceptual unification is: both are minimising a loss via iterative refinement; they differ only in their function representation class.

XGBoost and Newton's method in deep learning. The second-order update in XGBoost is the same idea behind optimisers like Adagrad, Adam, and K-FAC in deep learning — using curvature information to take better steps. Adam maintains a running estimate of the second moment of gradients (a diagonal approximation to the Hessian). XGBoost uses the exact Hessian per sample for trees.

Residual connections in neural networks. ResNets (He et al., 2016) train each layer to learn the residual \(F(x) - x\) rather than the full mapping \(F(x)\). This is the same philosophy as gradient boosting: each new component corrects the error of the previous one. Huang et al. (2017) made this connection explicit in Multi-Scale Dense Networks and "Snapshot Ensembles".

Tabular data dominance. On structured tabular data — the regime where most applied ML happens (fraud detection, recommendation systems, medical records, financial modelling) — gradient-boosted trees consistently outperform neural networks. The 2022 NeurIPS paper "Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on tabular data?" (Grinsztajn et al.) identified three reasons: robustness to uninformative features, preserving the orientation of the data (trees don't rotate the feature space), and ability to learn sharp step-function boundaries.

LLM training dynamics as boosting. The "loss spike → recovery" pattern observed in large language model training has been interpreted through a boosting lens: the model temporarily increases loss on some distribution of examples while correcting others, then a subsequent phase recovers — a noisy version of the sequential correction in boosting.

docs.title: ✦ From Scratch: Gradient Boosting with Log-Loss
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

class GradientBoostingLogistic:
    """
    Gradient Boosting for binary classification with log-loss.
    F(x) is the log-odds. Prediction: p = sigmoid(F(x))
    Loss: L(y, F) = log(1 + exp(-y*F)), y ∈ {-1, +1}
    Gradient: r_i = y_i / (1 + exp(y_i * F(x_i)))
    """
    def __init__(self, n_estimators=100, learning_rate=0.1, max_depth=3):
        self.M = n_estimators
        self.nu = learning_rate
        self.max_depth = max_depth
        self.trees = []
        self.F0 = None

    @staticmethod
    def sigmoid(x):
        return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x))

    def fit(self, X, y):
        # y must be {-1, +1}
        # Initialise F₀: optimal constant = log-odds of positive class
        p_bar = (y == 1).mean()
        p_bar = np.clip(p_bar, 1e-6, 1 - 1e-6)
        self.F0 = np.log(p_bar / (1 - p_bar))
        F = np.full(len(y), self.F0)

        for m in range(self.M):
            # Gradient of log-loss w.r.t. F: ∂L/∂F = -y/(1+exp(yF))
            # Pseudo-residual = negative gradient
            r = y / (1 + np.exp(y * F))

            # Fit regression tree to pseudo-residuals
            tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=self.max_depth)
            tree.fit(X, r)

            # Line search per leaf (Newton step: sum(r) / sum(|r|(2-|r|)))
            # This is the optimal step for log-loss; standard GB uses mean of r
            leaves = tree.apply(X)
            update = np.zeros(len(y))
            for leaf_id in np.unique(leaves):
                mask = leaves == leaf_id
                r_leaf = r[mask]
                # Newton step for log-loss in this leaf
                num = r_leaf.sum()
                denom = np.abs(r_leaf) * (2 - np.abs(r_leaf))
                step = num / (denom.sum() + 1e-10)
                update[mask] = step

            F += self.nu * update
            self.trees.append((tree, leaves, update))   # store for prediction

        return self

    def predict_proba(self, X):
        F = np.full(len(X), self.F0)
        for (tree, _, _) in self.trees:
            F += self.nu * tree.predict(X)
        return self.sigmoid(F)

    def predict(self, X):
        return (self.predict_proba(X) >= 0.5).astype(int) * 2 - 1

    def score(self, X, y):
        return (self.predict(X) == y).mean()

docs.title: ✦ Summary
docs.text:
Algorithm Loss Update Rule Notes AdaBoost Exponential Reweight samples FSAM + exp loss; sensitive to noise Gradient Boosting Any \(\mathcal{L}\) Fit tree to \(-\nabla\mathcal{L}\) General, sklearn implementation Stochastic GB Any \(\mathcal{L}\) As above + row subsampling Regularises and speeds up XGBoost Any \(\mathcal{L}\) Newton step, regularised tree Best for most tabular tasks LightGBM Any \(\mathcal{L}\) Histograms, leaf-wise growth Faster, better on large data CatBoost Any \(\mathcal{L}\) Ordered target stats Best native categorical support

You know this when: you can derive the AdaBoost weight update from minimising exponential loss, write out the pseudo-residuals for at least three different losses, derive the XGBoost optimal leaf weight formula from the Taylor-expanded objective, and explain in one sentence why gradient boosting is gradient descent.
