docs.title: Kernel PCA
docs.text:
"PCA finds the directions of maximum variance in the space you give it. Kernel PCA finds the directions of maximum variance in a space you never explicitly construct — and that is precisely what makes it powerful."

Part of: [[00.Dimensionality Reduction]] · [[04.Unsupervised Learning]] Requires: [[01.PCA]] (must be solid — Kernel PCA is PCA in a different space), [[04.Support Vector Machines]] (the kernel trick and Mercer's theorem), linear algebra (eigendecomposition, Gram matrices), [[03.Probability Review]] (inner products, feature maps) Connects to: [[03.t-SNE]] and [[04.Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP)]] (nonlinear DR alternatives), [[04.Support Vector Machines]] (shared kernel machinery), [[03.Gaussian Processes]] (RKHS is common ground)

docs.title: ✦ The Problem with Linear PCA
docs.text:
PCA finds principal axes by eigendecomposing the covariance matrix \(\Sigma = \frac{1}{n}X^TX\). It is a linear operation — it can only find structure that lives in a linear subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^d\).

Consider two concentric rings:

    ● ● ●                  The two rings are linearly inseparable.
  ●       ●                PCA projects onto a line or plane —
 ●  ○ ○ ○  ●               the two classes collapse onto each other.
 ●  ○   ○  ●               No linear projection separates them.
  ●  ○ ○  ●
    ● ● ●

Or the Swiss roll: a 2D surface rolled into a 3D ambient space. PCA in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) gives you a 2D projection that crushes the roll flat — destroying the intrinsic geometry. The true 2D coordinates (position along the roll, position across the roll) are nonlinearly embedded.

Linear PCA has no recourse. We need to operate in a richer space.

docs.title: ✦ The Core Idea: PCA in Feature Space
docs.text:
The kernel trick, which you have already seen in SVMs ([[04.Support Vector Machines]]), says: replace \(\langle x_i, x_j \rangle\) with \(k(x_i, x_j) = \langle \phi(x_i), \phi(x_j) \rangle_\mathcal{H}\) where \(\phi : \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{H}\) maps data into a (possibly infinite-dimensional) Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H}\).

The idea for Kernel PCA: run PCA in \(\mathcal{H}\), not in \(\mathbb{R}^d\).

The covariance matrix in \(\mathcal{H}\) is: $\(\tilde{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \phi(x_i)\phi(x_i)^T\)$

We want eigenvectors \(v \in \mathcal{H}\): \(\tilde{\Sigma} v = \lambda v\).

The crucial observation: every eigenvector of \(\tilde{\Sigma}\) lies in the span of \({\phi(x_1), \ldots, \phi(x_n)}\).

Proof. \(\tilde{\Sigma} v = \lambda v\) with \(\lambda > 0\) implies \(v = \frac{1}{\lambda}\tilde{\Sigma} v = \frac{1}{n\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^n \phi(x_i)\phi(x_i)^T v = \frac{1}{n\lambda}\sum_{i=1}^n \langle \phi(x_i), v\rangle_\mathcal{H} \cdot \phi(x_i)\). This is a linear combination of the \(\phi(x_i)\). \(\square\)

So we can write \(v = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i \phi(x_i)\) for some \(\alpha \in \mathbb{R}^n\). We never need to know \(\phi\) explicitly — we only need inner products \(\langle \phi(x_i), \phi(x_j)\rangle_\mathcal{H} = k(x_i, x_j)\).

docs.title: ✦ Derivation: From Covariance Eigenproblem to Kernel Eigenproblem
Step 1: The covariance eigenproblem in \(\mathcal{H}\)
docs.text:
We want \(v \in \mathcal{H}\) with \(|v| = 1\) satisfying: $\(\tilde{\Sigma} v = \lambda v\)$

Substituting \(\tilde{\Sigma} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \phi(x_i)\phi(x_i)^T\) and \(v = \sum_j \alpha_j \phi(x_j)\):

\[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \phi(x_i)\phi(x_i)^T \sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j \phi(x_j) = \lambda \sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j \phi(x_j)\] \[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \phi(x_i) \sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j k(x_i, x_j) = \lambda \sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j \phi(x_j)\] \[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \phi(x_i) (K\alpha)_i = \lambda \sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j \phi(x_j)\]

where \(K \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\) is the kernel (Gram) matrix with \(K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j)\).

docs.title: Step 2: Project onto \(\phi(x_l)\) for arbitrary \(l\)
docs.text:
Take inner product of both sides with \(\phi(x_l)\):

\[\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n k(x_l, x_i)(K\alpha)_i = \lambda \sum_{j=1}^n \alpha_j k(x_l, x_j)\] \[\frac{1}{n}(K^2 \alpha)_l = \lambda (K\alpha)_l\]

In matrix form: \(\frac{1}{n} K^2 \alpha = \lambda K \alpha\).

docs.title: Step 3: Simplify
docs.text:
Assuming \(K\) is invertible (or restricting to its range):

\[\frac{1}{n} K \alpha = \lambda \alpha \implies K\alpha = n\lambda \alpha\]

Renaming \(n\lambda \to \lambda'\): we need the eigenvectors of the kernel matrix \(K\).

\[K \alpha = \lambda' \alpha\]

This is the central result. The \(n \times n\) kernel matrix \(K\) plays the role of the \(d \times d\) covariance matrix \(\Sigma\). PCA in feature space reduces to eigendecomposing the Gram matrix.

docs.title: Step 4: Normalisation constraint
docs.text:
We need \(|v|_\mathcal{H} = 1\): $\(|v|^2 = \left|\sum_j \alpha_j \phi(x_j)\right|^2 = \sum_{i,j} \alpha_i \alpha_j k(x_i, x_j) = \alpha^T K \alpha = 1\)$

Since \(K\alpha = \lambda'\alpha\): \(\alpha^T K \alpha = \lambda' |\alpha|^2 = 1 \implies |\alpha|^2 = \frac{1}{\lambda'}\).

So after computing eigenvectors \(\alpha_l\) of \(K\) with eigenvalue \(\lambda_l'\), normalise by \(\hat{\alpha}_l = \frac{\alpha_l}{\sqrt{\lambda_l'}}\).

docs.title: ✦ Computing Kernel PCA Projections
docs.text:
The \(l\)-th kernel PC score for a training point \(x_i\) is:

\[z_{il} = \langle v_l, \phi(x_i)\rangle_\mathcal{H} = \sum_{j=1}^n \hat{\alpha}_{jl}, k(x_j, x_i) = \hat{\alpha}_l^T k_i\]

where \(k_i = (k(x_1, x_i), \ldots, k(x_n, x_i))^T \in \mathbb{R}^n\).

In matrix form, the full embedding of training data to \(p\) kernel PCs:

\[Z = K \hat{A} \quad \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}\]

where \(\hat{A} = [\hat{\alpha}_1 | \cdots | \hat{\alpha}_p] \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}\) (columns are normalised eigenvectors of \(K\)).

But since \(K\hat{\alpha}_l = \lambda_l' \hat{\alpha}_l\):

\[Z = K\hat{A} = \text{diag}(\lambda_1', \ldots, \lambda_p') \hat{A} \cdot \frac{\hat{A}}{\hat{A}} \cdot \hat{A}\]

More directly: \(Z_{il} = \lambda_l' \hat{\alpha}_{il}\) — the \(l\)-th kernel PC score for point \(x_i\) is \(\lambda_l' \hat{\alpha}_{il}\).

Wait — let us be careful. \(K\hat{\alpha}_l = \lambda_l' \hat{\alpha}_l\), so \((K\hat{A})_{il} = \lambda_l' \hat{\alpha}_{il}\). And \(\hat{\alpha}_{il} = \frac{\alpha_{il}}{\sqrt{\lambda_l'}}\), so:

\[Z_{il} = \lambda_l' \cdot \frac{\alpha_{il}}{\sqrt{\lambda_l'}} = \sqrt{\lambda_l'}, \alpha_{il}\]

where \(\alpha_l\) is the unit-norm eigenvector of \(K\) (before the \(\hat{\alpha}\) normalisation). This is the sklearn convention.

docs.title: ✦ Centring in Feature Space
docs.text:
The derivation above assumes \(\sum_i \phi(x_i) = 0\) — i.e., that the data is centred in feature space \(\mathcal{H}\). This is generally not true even if the original data \(X\) is centred, because \(\phi\) is nonlinear.

We must centre the kernel matrix. The centred kernel matrix is:

\[\tilde{K} = K - \mathbf{1}_n K - K \mathbf{1}_n + \mathbf{1}_n K \mathbf{1}_n\]

where \(\mathbf{1}_n = \frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^T \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\) (matrix of all \(1/n\)).

Entry-wise: $\(\tilde{K}_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j) - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{l=1}^n k(x_l, x_j) - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{l=1}^n k(x_i, x_l) + \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{l,m=1}^n k(x_l, x_m)\)$

This is the kernel-space analogue of subtracting the mean before computing PCA. Always centre the kernel matrix. Failing to do so is the most common implementation error in Kernel PCA.

Geometric interpretation: \(\tilde{K}_{ij} = \langle \phi(x_i) - \mu_\phi,, \phi(x_j) - \mu_\phi\rangle_\mathcal{H}\) where \(\mu_\phi = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \phi(x_i)\) is the mean in feature space. The centred kernel matrix is the covariance inner product matrix in \(\mathcal{H}\).

docs.title: Centring for out-of-sample points
docs.text:
For a new point \(x__\), its kernel vector is \(k__ = (k(x_1, x__), \ldots, k(x_n, x__))^T\). The centred version: $\(\tilde{k}_* = k_* - \frac{1}{n}K\mathbf{1} - \mathbf{1}_n k_* + \frac{1}{n^2}\mathbf{1}^T K \mathbf{1}\)$

where \(\mathbf{1} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) is the all-ones vector. In practice, store \(\frac{1}{n}K\mathbf{1}\) and \(\frac{1}{n^2}\mathbf{1}^T K\mathbf{1}\) from the training fit.

docs.title: ✦ Out-of-Sample Extension
docs.text:
A fundamental limitation of Kernel PCA (compared to linear PCA): the eigenvectors \(v_l\) live in \(\mathcal{H}\) and are expressed via the training data. Projecting a new point \(x_*\) requires:

\[z_{_l} = \langle v_l, \phi(x__)\rangle_\mathcal{H} = \sum_{j=1}^n \hat{\alpha}_{jl}, \tilde{k}(x_j, x_*)\]

where \(\tilde{k}(x_j, x__)\) is the centred kernel between training point \(x_j\) and the new point \(x__\).

This is \(O(n)\) per new point per component — and requires storing all \(n\) training points. Contrast with linear PCA: out-of-sample projection is \(O(d)\) and requires only the \(k \times d\) weight matrix.

Practical consequence: Kernel PCA does not scale to large \(n\). For \(n > 10^4\), it is typically replaced by:

  • Approximate methods: Nyström approximation (subsample \(m \ll n\) "landmark" points, build \(K_m\))
  • Sparse kernel PCA
  • UMAP (which also learns a nonlinear embedding but scales better)

docs.title: ✦ The Full Algorithm
docs.text:
Input:  X = {x₁,...,xₙ} ∈ ℝᵈ, kernel function k(·,·), n_components p
Output: Z ∈ ℝⁿˣᵖ (kernel PCA scores), stored training data for projection

--- TRAINING ---

1. Compute kernel matrix:
   K ∈ ℝⁿˣⁿ,  K[i,j] = k(xᵢ, xⱼ)

2. Centre the kernel matrix:
   row_means = K.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)      # (n,1)
   col_means = K.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True)       # (1,n)
   grand_mean = K.mean()
   K̃ = K - row_means - col_means + grand_mean

3. Eigendecompose K̃:
   eigenvalues λ', eigenvectors α  (K̃ α = λ'α)
   Sort descending by λ'

4. Keep top p eigenvectors: A = [α₁|...|αₚ]  (n×p)
   Normalise: Â[:,l] = A[:,l] / sqrt(λ'_l)

5. Scores: Z = K̃ Â   [equivalently Z[:,l] = sqrt(λ'_l) · α_l]

Store: {xᵢ}, K̃ row/col/grand means, Â, {λ'_l}

--- INFERENCE (new point x*) ---

6. Compute k* = (k(x₁,x*), ..., k(xₙ,x*))ᵀ

7. Centre k*:
   k̃*[i] = k*[i] - row_means[i] - mean(k*) + grand_mean

8. Project: z* = Âᵀ k̃*   (p-vector)

docs.title: ✦ Implementation from Scratch (NumPy)
docs.text:
import numpy as np

def rbf_kernel(X, Y, gamma):
    """K[i,j] = exp(-gamma ||xᵢ - yⱼ||²)"""
    # ||x - y||² = ||x||² + ||y||² - 2 x·y
    X_sq = np.sum(X**2, axis=1, keepdims=True)   # (n,1)
    Y_sq = np.sum(Y**2, axis=1, keepdims=True)   # (m,1)
    cross = X @ Y.T                               # (n,m)
    sq_dists = X_sq + Y_sq.T - 2 * cross
    return np.exp(-gamma * sq_dists)


class KernelPCA:
    def __init__(self, n_components, kernel='rbf', gamma=1.0, degree=3, coef0=1.0):
        self.p = n_components
        self.kernel_name = kernel
        self.gamma = gamma
        self.degree = degree
        self.coef0 = coef0

    def _kernel(self, X, Y):
        if self.kernel_name == 'rbf':
            return rbf_kernel(X, Y, self.gamma)
        elif self.kernel_name == 'poly':
            return (self.gamma * (X @ Y.T) + self.coef0) ** self.degree
        elif self.kernel_name == 'linear':
            return X @ Y.T
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"Unknown kernel: {self.kernel_name}")

    def fit(self, X):
        n = len(X)
        self.X_train_ = X.copy()

        # 1. Compute kernel matrix
        K = self._kernel(X, X)                      # (n,n)

        # 2. Centre: K̃ = K - 1ₙK - K1ₙ + 1ₙK1ₙ
        self.row_means_ = K.mean(axis=1)             # (n,)
        self.col_means_ = K.mean(axis=0)             # (n,)
        self.grand_mean_ = K.mean()

        K_centered = (K
                      - self.row_means_[:, None]
                      - self.col_means_[None, :]
                      + self.grand_mean_)

        # 3. Eigendecompose K̃
        eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(K_centered)
        # eigh returns ascending order; reverse
        idx = np.argsort(eigenvalues)[::-1]
        eigenvalues = eigenvalues[idx]
        eigenvectors = eigenvectors[:, idx]

        # 4. Keep top p, drop near-zero eigenvalues
        eigenvalues = eigenvalues[:self.p]
        eigenvectors = eigenvectors[:, :self.p]

        # Numerical safety: clip tiny negatives (rounding errors)
        eigenvalues = np.clip(eigenvalues, 1e-12, None)

        self.eigenvalues_ = eigenvalues
        # Normalised eigenvectors: α̂_l = α_l / sqrt(λ'_l)
        self.alphas_ = eigenvectors / np.sqrt(eigenvalues)[None, :]  # (n,p)

        return self

    def transform(self, X):
        # Compute kernel between new X and training data
        K = self._kernel(X, self.X_train_)           # (m,n)

        # Centre using stored training statistics
        # k̃[i,j] = k[i,j] - mean_row_train[j] - mean_col_new[i] + grand_mean
        K_centered = (K
                      - self.row_means_[None, :]     # subtract train row means
                      - K.mean(axis=1)[:, None]      # subtract new point col means
                      + self.grand_mean_)

        # Project: z = K̃ · Â  → (m,p)
        return K_centered @ self.alphas_

    def fit_transform(self, X):
        self.fit(X)
        # For training data, use training kernel directly (more stable)
        K = self._kernel(X, X)
        K_centered = (K
                      - self.row_means_[:, None]
                      - self.col_means_[None, :]
                      + self.grand_mean_)
        return K_centered @ self.alphas_


# --- Test on concentric rings ---
from sklearn.datasets import make_circles
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

X, y = make_circles(n_samples=400, factor=0.3, noise=0.05, random_state=42)

kpca = KernelPCA(n_components=2, kernel='rbf', gamma=10.0)
Z = kpca.fit_transform(X)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
axes[0].scatter(X[:,0], X[:,1], c=y, cmap='bwr', s=10)
axes[0].set_title('Original space')

axes[1].scatter(Z[:,0], Z[:,1], c=y, cmap='bwr', s=10)
axes[1].set_title('Kernel PCA (RBF, γ=10)')
plt.tight_layout()

Verify against sklearn:

from sklearn.decomposition import KernelPCA as skKernelPCA

kpca_sk = skKernelPCA(n_components=2, kernel='rbf', gamma=10.0)
Z_sk = kpca_sk.fit_transform(X)

# Subspaces should match (up to sign/rotation within 2D)
# Check that column spaces are the same
from numpy.linalg import svd
combined = np.hstack([Z / np.linalg.norm(Z, axis=0),
                      Z_sk / np.linalg.norm(Z_sk, axis=0)])
_, s, _ = svd(combined)
print(f"Singular values of combined: {s[:4]}")  # should be ~[√2, √2, 0, 0]

docs.title: ✦ Common Kernels and What They Do
Linear Kernel
docs.text:
\[k(x, y) = x^T y\]

Kernel PCA with the linear kernel is identical to standard PCA. This is the sanity check: if you implement Kernel PCA correctly and run it with a linear kernel, you recover PCA exactly (up to sign and scaling).

Why? The Gram matrix \(K_{ij} = x_i^T x_j = (XX^T)_{ij}\). The centred Gram matrix has the same eigenvectors as the centred covariance \(X^TX\) (up to the \(U\)-\(V\) duality in the SVD \(X = U\Sigma V^T\): \(XX^T = U\Sigma^2 U^T\) vs. \(X^TX = V\Sigma^2 V^T\)).

docs.title: Polynomial Kernel
docs.text:
\[k(x, y) = (\gamma x^T y + c_0)^d\]

Corresponds to a feature map \(\phi\) containing all monomials of degree \(\leq d\). Dimension of \(\phi\): \(\binom{d+\text{deg}}{\text{deg}}\) — exponential in degree.

For degree \(d=2\), \(\mathbb{R}^p\) input: \(\phi\) has \(1 + p + \binom{p}{2}\) features (constant, linear, and quadratic monomials). Kernel PCA in this space can separate data by quadratic boundaries.

docs.title: RBF (Gaussian) Kernel
docs.text:
\[k(x, y) = \exp!\left(-\gamma |x - y|^2\right) = \exp!\left(-\frac{|x-y|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\]

where \(\gamma = \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\).

Corresponds to an infinite-dimensional feature map. The feature space \(\mathcal{H}\) is the RKHS of the Gaussian kernel — functions that are smooth in proportion to \(\sigma\).

Proof of infinite dimensionality. Via Mercer's theorem and the Taylor expansion of the exponential: $\(\exp(-\gamma|x-y|^2) = \exp(-\gamma|x|^2)\exp(2\gamma x^Ty)\exp(-\gamma|y|^2)\)$ $\(= \exp(-\gamma|x|^2)\exp(-\gamma|y|^2)\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(2\gamma)^n}{n!}(x^Ty)^n\)$

Each term \((x^Ty)^n\) corresponds to degree-\(n\) polynomial features. Summing over all \(n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\) gives countably infinite features. The kernel evaluates all of them implicitly in \(O(d)\) via the exponential.

The \(\gamma\) hyperparameter:

  • Large \(\gamma\) (small \(\sigma\)): narrow kernel → points must be very close to have nonzero similarity → captures fine-grained local structure → risk of overfitting / fragmented clusters.
  • Small \(\gamma\) (large \(\sigma\)): broad kernel → all points are similar to all others → approaches linear PCA → loses nonlinear structure.

The RBF kernel is the default choice for Kernel PCA when the appropriate feature map is unknown.

docs.title: Choosing the Kernel
docs.text:
There is no universal best kernel — this is the No Free Lunch theorem applied to kernels. Guidelines:

  • Linear: baseline, interpretable, equivalent to PCA.
  • Polynomial: use when you have reason to believe the relevant structure is polynomial (e.g., interaction terms matter).
  • RBF: default for smooth, unknown manifolds. Tune \(\gamma\) via the explained variance of the kernel PCs or a downstream task.
  • Custom: domain-specific kernels encode prior knowledge (string kernels for text, graph kernels for molecular structures).

For Kernel PCA specifically, a useful heuristic for \(\gamma\) in RBF: set $\sigma = $ median pairwise distance of the training data (the "median heuristic"), i.e., \(\gamma = \frac{1}{2 \cdot \text{median}(|x_i - x_j|^2)}\).

docs.title: ✦ Mercer's Theorem: When Is \(k\) a Valid Kernel?
docs.text:
Not every function \(k : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}\) corresponds to a valid inner product. We need:

Mercer's Theorem. A continuous, symmetric function \(k : \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}\) is a valid kernel (i.e., \(\exists\) Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H}\) and map \(\phi\) s.t. \(k(x,y) = \langle\phi(x),\phi(y)\rangle_\mathcal{H}\)) if and only if the kernel matrix \(K \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\) is positive semi-definite for all finite sets of points \({x_1, \ldots, x_n} \subset \mathcal{X}\).

Equivalently: \(\sum_{i,j} c_i c_j k(x_i, x_j) \geq 0\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), all \({x_i}\), all \(c \in \mathbb{R}^n\).

Why this matters for Kernel PCA: If \(k\) is not a valid Mercer kernel, the Gram matrix \(K\) may have negative eigenvalues. These are not interpretable as variances. Centering can also introduce spurious negative eigenvalues for near-valid kernels. In the implementation, we clip eigenvalues at zero — but if many eigenvalues are substantially negative, the kernel is wrong for the data.

Constructing valid kernels: Valid kernels are closed under:

  • Positive scaling: \(c \cdot k\) for \(c > 0\)
  • Addition: \(k_1 + k_2\)
  • Multiplication: \(k_1 \cdot k_2\)
  • Composition: \(k(x,y) = k_0(f(x), f(y))\) for any \(f\)
  • Exponentiation: \(\exp(k_0)\)

This allows building complex kernels from simple ones: e.g., \(k(x,y) = \exp(-\gamma|x-y|^2) \cdot \cos(\omega^T(x-y))\) is valid (product of valid kernels).

docs.title: ✦ Geometric Interpretation: Unfolding Manifolds
docs.text:
The RBF kernel assigns high similarity to nearby points and near-zero similarity to distant ones. In the feature space \(\mathcal{H}\), all points are mapped to the unit sphere (since \(k(x,x) = 1\) for RBF): \(|\phi(x)|_\mathcal{H} = 1\) for all \(x\).

The Kernel PCA embedding then places similar points near each other on this hypersphere. The first kernel PC direction is the direction of maximum variance on this sphere — which corresponds to the principal direction of the manifold structure.

For the Swiss roll example: the RBF kernel in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) assigns high similarity to nearby points along the roll. PCA in this kernel space separates the "position along the roll" direction from the "position across the roll" direction — exactly the intrinsic 2D coordinates. Linear PCA cannot do this because the Swiss roll is not linear.

Swiss roll in ℝ³         RBF Kernel PCA embedding

   /────────/             ●●●●●●●●●●
  /  ● ● ● /    →        ●●●●●●●●●●●     (2D unfolding)
 / ●  ●  ● /             ●●●●●●●●●●
/──────────/

docs.title: ✦ Nyström Approximation: Scaling to Large \(n\)
docs.text:
The bottleneck of Kernel PCA is \(O(n^2)\) to form \(K\) and \(O(n^3)\) (or \(O(n^2 p)\) with partial eigendecomposition) to decompose it. For \(n = 10^5\), storing \(K\) alone requires 80 GB.

Nyström approximation (Williams & Seeger, 2001): subsample \(m \ll n\) "landmark" points \({x_{l_1}, \ldots, x_{l_m}}\) and approximate the full kernel matrix:

\[K \approx K_{nm} K_{mm}^{-1} K_{mn}\]

where \(K_{nm} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}\): kernel between all \(n\) points and the \(m\) landmarks, \(K_{mm} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times m}\): kernel among landmarks.

Approximate Kernel PCA via Nyström:

  1. Choose \(m\) landmark points (randomly, or by \(k\)-means).
  2. Compute \(K_{nm}\) and \(K_{mm}\).
  3. Eigendecompose \(K_{mm} = U_m \Lambda_m U_m^T\).
  4. Approximate eigenvectors of \(K\): \(\hat{U} = \sqrt{\frac{m}{n}} K_{nm} U_m \Lambda_m^{-1}\).
  5. Orthonormalise \(\hat{U}\) via QR decomposition.

Cost: \(O(m^2 n)\) instead of \(O(n^2 p)\). For \(m = 1000\), \(n = 10^6\): manageable.

The approximation error is controlled by how well \(K_{mm}\) "spans" the full kernel matrix — related to the spectral decay of \(K\).

docs.title: ✦ Kernel PCA vs. Other Nonlinear DR Methods
docs.text:
Kernel PCA t-SNE UMAP Isomap Objective Max variance in \(\mathcal{H}\) Preserve local prob. distributions Preserve fuzzy topology Preserve geodesic distances Global structure Yes (kernel-dependent) No Partially Yes Out-of-sample Yes (\(O(n)\) per point) No Yes (with extra fit) No Scalability \(O(n^2)\) / Nyström approx \(O(n \log n)\) approx \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(n^2)\) naive Interpretability Kernel eigenvalues None None Geodesic scale Cluster separation Good (right kernel) Excellent (visual) Good Moderate Noise sensitivity Depends on kernel High (perplexity) Moderate High (geodesic)

When to choose Kernel PCA over t-SNE/UMAP:

  • You need out-of-sample projection (new test points must be embedded).
  • You have a domain-informed kernel encoding structural similarity.
  • You want a method with a clear objective function (eigenvalue problem) rather than stochastic optimisation.
  • You care about explained variance (kernel eigenvalues are interpretable).

When to prefer UMAP:

  • \(n > 10^4\) and Nyström is insufficient.
  • You want a good 2D visualisation and don't need out-of-sample.
  • The manifold is locally uniform but globally complex.

docs.title: ✦ Connection to AI, ML, and Deep Learning
The Shared Foundation with SVMs
docs.text:
Kernel PCA and SVMs both rest on the same kernel trick and Mercer's theorem. In both cases:

  • The algorithm operates entirely through \(K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j)\).
  • The solution lives in the span of the training data (representer theorem).
  • The feature map \(\phi\) is implicit and potentially infinite-dimensional.

The mathematical machinery is identical; the objectives differ (unsupervised variance maximisation vs. supervised margin maximisation).

docs.title: The Kernel Trick and Neural Networks
docs.text:
Deep networks can be interpreted as learning the kernel. The Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK, Jacot et al., 2018) shows that infinitely wide neural networks trained with gradient descent are equivalent to kernel regression with a specific kernel determined by the architecture. The features learned by a neural network implicitly define a kernel — and the "kernel PCA" of those features is exactly the PCA of the network's learned representation.

This connection provides a theoretical foundation for understanding why deep networks generalise: they are learning good kernels.

docs.title: Gaussian Processes and the RKHS
docs.text:
Gaussian Processes ([[03.Gaussian Processes]]) also operate in the RKHS of a kernel \(k\). The GP posterior mean is the kernel regression estimate; kernel PCA extracts the principal directions of this space. Both methods share:

  • The same \(n \times n\) kernel matrix \(K\).
  • The same \(O(n^3)\) computational bottleneck.
  • The same Nyström / inducing point approximations for scaling.

The RKHS is the shared mathematical home of SVMs, Kernel PCA, and GPs.

docs.title: Kernel Methods and Pre-trained Embeddings
docs.text:
A modern workflow: use a pre-trained neural network (ResNet, BERT) as a fixed feature extractor \(\phi\), then run linear PCA on the embeddings \(\phi(x_i) \in \mathbb{R}^k\). This is equivalent to Kernel PCA with the kernel \(k(x_i, x_j) = \phi(x_i)^T\phi(x_j)\) — the linear kernel in embedding space. The pre-trained network has implicitly learned the right \(\phi\); linear PCA then extracts the principal structure.

This is a central pattern in modern ML: use deep networks to learn the feature map, then use classical kernel/linear methods on top.

docs.title: Spectral Clustering
docs.text:
Spectral clustering (a graph-based clustering method) is closely related to Kernel PCA. Both:

  1. Compute a \(n \times n\) affinity/kernel matrix.
  2. Eigendecompose it.
  3. Use the top eigenvectors as a new representation.

The difference: spectral clustering uses the graph Laplacian \(L = D - K\) (where \(D\) is the degree matrix) rather than the centred kernel matrix, and runs K-Means on the eigenvectors rather than using them directly as coordinates. Kernel PCA with subsequent K-Means is essentially spectral clustering with a different normalisation.

docs.title: ✦ Exit Criterion
docs.text: You know this when: you can derive the kernel eigenproblem from the covariance eigenproblem in feature space without notes; implement centring of the kernel matrix and explain why it is necessary; state Mercer's theorem precisely and give examples of valid and invalid kernels; derive the infinite-dimensional feature map of the RBF kernel via Taylor expansion; explain why Kernel PCA cannot scale to large \(n\) and how Nyström approximation fixes this; and connect the kernel trick here to the dual SVM formulation.

docs.title: t-SNE — t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbour Embedding
docs.text:
My note on the algorithm that made high-dimensional visualisation actually useful. The math is less clean than PCA, but the intuition is deep. Don't treat this as a black box.

Tags: #dimensionality-reduction #unsupervised #visualisation #nonlinear Part of: [[Dimensionality Reduction]] → [[04.Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP)|UMAP]] → [[04.Representation Learning|Representation Learning]] Prerequisites: [[01.PCA|PCA]], basic probability, KL divergence from [[03.Probability Review|Probability Review]]

docs.title: ✦ The Problem PCA Cannot Solve
docs.text:
PCA finds directions of maximum variance. It is a linear projection. That means it can only preserve structure that is linearly separable in the original space.

Consider the Swiss roll: a 2D manifold coiled in 3D. PCA projects it flat and destroys the manifold structure entirely. The distances that matter — distances along the manifold — get collapsed.

Swiss roll in 3D          PCA projection          t-SNE projection
     ╭──────╮               ████████               ·  ·  ·
    ╱  ····  ╲              ████████              ·      ·
   ╱  ·    ·  ╲   PCA→     ████████   t-SNE→    ·        ·
  ╱  ·      ·  ╲           ████████              ·      ·
 ╱  ············╲          ████████               ·  ·  ·
     (coiled)             (squashed)              (unrolled)

t-SNE's insight: forget global distances. Preserve local neighbourhoods. If \(x_i\) and \(x_j\) are close in high-dimensional space, their images \(y_i\) and \(y_j\) should be close in 2D. That's the whole game.

docs.title: Step 1 — High-Dimensional Similarities
docs.text:
For each pair \((i, j)\), define the conditional probability that point \(i\) would pick \(j\) as its neighbour, where the neighbourhood is defined by a Gaussian centred at \(x_i\):

\[p_{j|i} = rac{\exp!\left(-|x_i - x_j|^2 / 2\sigma_i^2 ight)}{\displaystyle\sum_{k eq i} \exp!\left(-|x_i - x_k|^2 / 2\sigma_i^2 ight)}\]

Note this is asymmetric: \(p_{j|i} eq p_{i|j}\) in general, because \(\sigma_i eq \sigma_j\).

To get a symmetric joint distribution (which is easier to optimise), symmetrise:

\[p_{ij} = rac{p_{j|i} + p_{i|j}}{2n}\]

This guarantees \(\sum_{i,j} p_{ij} = 1\) and \(p_{ij} = p_{ji}\).

Why symmetrise? The original asymmetric SNE (Hinton & Roweis 2002) used \(p_{j|i}\) directly and had a separate cost per point. The symmetric version gives a cleaner single KL divergence to minimise, and empirically works at least as well.

docs.title: Step 2 — The Perplexity Controls \(\sigma_i\)
docs.text:
The bandwidth \(\sigma_i\) is not a single global parameter — it is set per point, via a binary search that achieves a target perplexity:

\[\text{Perp}(P_i) = 2^{H(P_i)}, \qquad H(P_i) = -\sum_j p_{j|i} \log_2 p_{j|i}\]

Intuitively, perplexity ≈ the effective number of neighbours each point considers.

  • In dense regions, \(\sigma_i\) will be small (points are close; a narrow Gaussian suffices).
  • In sparse regions, \(\sigma_i\) will be large (need a wider Gaussian to include enough neighbours).

This adaptive bandwidth is what makes t-SNE robust to non-uniform density.

Typical values: \(\text{Perp} \in [5, 50]\). Van der Maaten recommends 30 as a default. For very large datasets (\(n > 10^4\)), larger perplexities (50–100) can be better.

docs.title: Step 3 — Low-Dimensional Similarities (The t-Distribution)
docs.text:
In the 2D embedding, we could use a Gaussian too. SNE does this. But there's a problem: the crowding problem.

The crowding problem: In \(d\) dimensions, the volume of a thin shell of radius \(r\) scales as \(r^{d-1}\). When you project to 2D, there simply isn't enough area to faithfully represent moderate distances — points at moderate distance in high-\(d\) get crushed against points that are truly close. The 2D Gaussian decays too fast at moderate distances; it can't push moderately-distant points far enough apart.

The fix: use a Student's t-distribution with 1 degree of freedom (the Cauchy distribution) in the low-dimensional space. Its heavier tails let moderately-distant clusters separate clearly:

\[q_{ij} = \frac{\left(1 + |y_i - y_j|^2\right)^{-1}}{\displaystyle\sum_{k \neq l} \left(1 + |y_k - y_l|^2\right)^{-1}}\]

The \((1 + |y_i - y_j|^2)^{-1}\) is exactly the unnormalised Cauchy kernel. The key property: it has much heavier tails than a Gaussian, so unlike the Gaussian, it assigns non-negligible probability to moderately large distances.

Probability (unnorm.)
   │
 1 ┤  ██                  ← Gaussian: decays fast
   │  █ █                   t (ν=1): decays slow
   │  █   █        ████████████████████████████
   │  █     ██████
   │  █
   └─────────────────────────────────────────── distance
     0    1    2    3    4    5

The mismatch is the key: high-dim uses Gaussian (\(p_{ij}\)), low-dim uses Student-t (\(q_{ij}\)). This mismatch is intentional — it's what creates the gap between clusters.

docs.title: Step 4 — The Objective: Minimise KL Divergence
docs.text:
The objective is to find a 2D configuration \({y_i}\) such that \(Q\) is as close to \(P\) as possible, in the sense of KL divergence:

\[\mathcal{L} = KL(P ,|, Q) = \sum_{i \neq j} p_{ij} \log \frac{p_{ij}}{q_{ij}}\]

Why KL divergence, not MSE? Because we're matching probability distributions, not raw distances. KL has an asymmetry that matters:

\[KL(P | Q) = \sum p_{ij} \log \frac{p_{ij}}{q_{ij}}\]
  • When \(p_{ij}\) is large (nearby in high-dim) and \(q_{ij}\) is small (far in low-dim): huge penalty. Nearby neighbours must stay nearby.
  • When \(p_{ij}\) is small (far in high-dim) and \(q_{ij}\) is large (close in low-dim): small penalty. The algorithm tolerates "false neighbours" more than it tolerates "torn neighbours".

This asymmetry is what gives t-SNE its character: it prioritises preserving tight local structure above everything else.

docs.title: Step 5 — Gradient and Optimisation
docs.text:
Taking \(\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial y_i\):

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial y_i} = 4 \sum_j (p_{ij} - q_{ij})(y_i - y_j)\left(1 + |y_i - y_j|^2\right)^{-1}\]

Interpretation: this is a force equation. Each pair \((i,j)\) exerts a force on \(y_i\):

  • If \(p_{ij} > q_{ij}\): they're closer in high-dim than in low-dim → attractive force, pulls \(y_i\) toward \(y_j\).
  • If \(p_{ij} < q_{ij}\): they're closer in low-dim than in high-dim → repulsive force, pushes \(y_i\) away from \(y_j\).

The \((1 + |y_i - y_j|^2)^{-1}\) term is the Cauchy weight — it amplifies attraction for nearby pairs and tapers repulsion at long range.

Optimisation uses gradient descent with momentum. The algorithm also uses early exaggeration: in the first ~250 iterations, multiply all \(p_{ij}\) by a factor (e.g. 4). This makes clusters form quickly before the repulsive forces spread them.

Computational complexity: Naïve: \(O(n^2)\) per iteration. Barnes-Hut t-SNE approximation: \(O(n \log n)\).

docs.title: ✦ Full Algorithm Summary
docs.text:
Input: high-dim data X = {x₁,...,xₙ}
       perplexity Perp, iterations T, learning rate η, momentum α

1. Compute pairwise p_{j|i} via Gaussian with σᵢ found by binary search on Perp
2. Symmetrise: p_{ij} = (p_{j|i} + p_{i|j}) / 2n
3. Initialise Y = {y₁,...,yₙ} ~ 𝒩(0, 10⁻⁴ · I)
4. Early exaggeration: multiply p_{ij} × 4 for first 250 iterations
5. For t = 1 to T:
     a. Compute q_{ij} using Student-t kernel on current Y
     b. Compute gradient ∂ℒ/∂yᵢ for all i
     c. Update: Y(t) = Y(t-1) + η · ∇ℒ + α(t)(Y(t-1) - Y(t-2))
6. Return Y

docs.title: ✦ A Worked Example
docs.text:
Suppose \(n = 4\) points in 2D (toy high-dim space), and we want a 1D embedding.

Points: \(x_1 = 0,\ x_2 = 1,\ x_3 = 5,\ x_4 = 6\)

Distances: \((1,2)\) are close. \((3,4)\) are close. \((1,3)\), etc., are far.

After computing \(p_{ij}\), the high similarities will be: \(p_{12}, p_{34}\) large; \(p_{13}, p_{14}, p_{23}, p_{24}\) small.

What t-SNE will do: push \(y_1, y_2\) close together; push \(y_3, y_4\) close together; push the two clusters apart. The gap between clusters will be amplified relative to the gap in the original data — that's the heavy-tailed \(q_{ij}\) at work. In 2D MNIST embeddings, you can see this: the 10 digit classes form well-separated blobs, with the within-cluster distances compressed.

High-dim:   ·· · · · ·····
            0 1       5 6

t-SNE 1D:   ··             ····
           y₁y₂           y₃y₄
           (gap amplified by heavy tail)

docs.title: ✦ What t-SNE Preserves vs. Destroys
docs.text:
Property Preserved? Notes Local neighbourhood structure ✅ Yes The whole point Cluster existence ✅ Yes (qualitatively) Clusters that exist will be visible Inter-cluster distances ❌ No Cannot compare distances between clusters Cluster sizes ❌ No Cluster area in plot is meaningless Global geometry ❌ No Far-apart points are unreliable Out-of-sample points ❌ No (standard) Must re-run entire algorithm

The most common misuse of t-SNE: "Cluster A is far from cluster B in the plot, so they are very different." This is wrong. The inter-cluster distances in a t-SNE plot encode almost nothing. The existence and cohesion of clusters is meaningful; the layout of clusters relative to each other is not.

docs.title: Perplexity
docs.text:
• Range: typically 5–50 (some recent work goes up to 100 for \(n > 10^5\))
  • Think of it as: how many effective neighbours does each point have?
  • Always run multiple perplexities. Different values reveal different structure.
  • If perplexity \(\geq n\): every point is a neighbour of every other — you get a blob.

docs.title: Number of iterations
docs.text:
• Minimum ~250 for early exaggeration, ~750+ total. For large data, 1000–5000.
  • Watch the KL divergence — it should decrease and plateau.

docs.title: Learning rate
docs.text:
• Default: 200 (scikit-learn). If the embedding looks like a ball, increase it. If it looks like many tiny clusters, decrease it.
  • Recent recommendation (Belkina et al. 2019): \(\eta = n/\text{early_exaggeration}\).

docs.title: Random seed
docs.text:
• t-SNE is non-convex. Always try multiple seeds before trusting a plot.
  • Two runs with different seeds can look qualitatively different.

docs.title: ✦ Connection to AI / ML / Deep Learning
1. Visualising Neural Network Representations
docs.text:
The canonical use: take a trained network (e.g., a CNN trained on MNIST or ImageNet), extract the penultimate layer activations for the test set, run t-SNE, and plot. If the network has learned good representations, the t-SNE plot will show semantically meaningful clusters.

Images → CNN → [h₁,...,h₅₁₂] → t-SNE → 2D plot
                  ↑
           high-dim feature space
           (not pixels — learned features)

This was how early deep learning papers demonstrated that CNNs learn semantic features rather than just memorising pixels (Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Maaten & Hinton, 2008).

docs.title: 2. Self-Supervised and Contrastive Learning
docs.text: In SimCLR and MoCo, the quality of learned representations is routinely assessed via t-SNE of the embedding space. A good contrastive model should push same-class examples together and different-class examples apart — exactly what t-SNE will make visible.

docs.title: 3. NLP: Word and Sentence Embeddings
docs.text: Word2Vec, GloVe, and transformer embeddings are typically 300–768 dimensional. t-SNE collapses these to 2D for inspection. The famous word embedding plots (king − man + woman ≈ queen) are often visualised via PCA first, then t-SNE for finer structure.

docs.title: 4. Single-Cell Biology / Genomics (ML application)
docs.text: One of the most successful ML applications of t-SNE outside CV/NLP: single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq). Each cell is a ~20,000-dimensional vector (gene expression). t-SNE reveals cell-type clusters that are impossible to see otherwise. This is now standard in computational biology.

docs.title: 5. Diagnosing Representation Collapse
docs.text: In representation learning, representation collapse = the encoder maps all inputs to nearly the same embedding. t-SNE immediately reveals this: instead of structured clusters, you see a single blob with no structure.

docs.title: 6. Limitations in Deep Learning Pipelines
docs.text: t-SNE's \(O(n^2)\) complexity (or \(O(n \log n)\) with Barnes-Hut) makes it impractical for full datasets. In practice: subsample \(n \leq 10^4\) points before running t-SNE. UMAP is now often preferred at scale (see [[04.Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP)]]).

docs.title: ✦ t-SNE vs. PCA vs. UMAP
docs.text:
Property PCA t-SNE UMAP Linear? Yes No No Preserves global structure Best Worst Middle Preserves local structure Poor Best Good Out-of-sample projection Yes No (standard) Yes Complexity \(O(nd^2 + d^3)\) \(O(n^2)\) or \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(n \log n)\) Deterministic? Yes No (random init) No (random init) General use Preprocessing, PCA whitening Visualisation only Visualisation + preprocessing Theoretical basis Linear algebra / variance KL divergence + t-kernel Riemannian geometry

Use PCA first to reduce to ~50 dims, then run t-SNE on the PCA output. This is standard practice (van der Maaten's original paper recommends it) — it removes noise while making t-SNE tractable.

docs.title: ✦ Implementation from Scratch (NumPy sketch)
docs.text:
import numpy as np

def pairwise_sq_dists(X):
    """||x_i - x_j||^2 for all pairs."""
    sum_sq = np.sum(X**2, axis=1)
    return sum_sq[:,None] + sum_sq[None,:] - 2 * X @ X.T

def compute_p_matrix(X, perplexity=30.0, tol=1e-5):
    n = X.shape[0]
    D = pairwise_sq_dists(X)
    P = np.zeros((n, n))
    log_perp = np.log(perplexity)

    for i in range(n):
        # Binary search for sigma_i
        beta = 1.0  # beta = 1 / (2 * sigma_i^2)
        lo, hi = -np.inf, np.inf
        Di = np.delete(D[i], i)

        for _ in range(50):  # max 50 binary search steps
            Pi = np.exp(-Di * beta)
            Pi /= Pi.sum()
            H = -np.sum(Pi * np.log(Pi + 1e-10))
            Hdiff = H - log_perp
            if np.abs(Hdiff) < tol:
                break
            if Hdiff > 0:
                lo = beta; beta = (beta + hi)/2 if hi != np.inf else beta*2
            else:
                hi = beta; beta = (beta + lo)/2 if lo != -np.inf else beta/2

        Pi_full = np.zeros(n)
        Pi_full[np.arange(n) != i] = Pi
        P[i] = Pi_full

    # Symmetrise
    P = (P + P.T) / (2 * n)
    P = np.maximum(P, 1e-12)
    return P

def tsne(X, n_iter=1000, perplexity=30, lr=200, early_exag=4):
    n = X.shape[0]
    P = compute_p_matrix(X, perplexity)
    P *= early_exag  # early exaggeration

    # Random initialisation
    Y = np.random.randn(n, 2) * 1e-4
    dY = np.zeros_like(Y)
    iY = np.zeros_like(Y)
    gains = np.ones_like(Y)

    for t in range(n_iter):
        if t == 250:
            P /= early_exag  # turn off early exaggeration

        # Compute Q
        D_low = pairwise_sq_dists(Y)
        Q_num = (1 + D_low) ** -1
        np.fill_diagonal(Q_num, 0)
        Q = Q_num / Q_num.sum()
        Q = np.maximum(Q, 1e-12)

        # Gradient
        PQ = P - Q
        grad = np.zeros_like(Y)
        for i in range(n):
            diff = Y[i] - Y  # (n, 2)
            grad[i] = 4 * np.sum((PQ[:,i] * Q_num[:,i])[:,None] * diff, axis=0)

        # Update with momentum
        momentum = 0.5 if t < 250 else 0.8
        gains = (gains + 0.2) * ((grad > 0) != (iY > 0)) + \
                (gains * 0.8) * ((grad > 0) == (iY > 0))
        gains = np.maximum(gains, 0.01)
        iY = momentum * iY - lr * gains * grad
        Y += iY
        Y -= Y.mean(axis=0)

        if t % 100 == 0:
            kl = np.sum(P * np.log(P / Q))
            print(f"Iter {t}: KL = {kl:.4f}")

    return Y

This is for understanding. In practice, use sklearn.manifold.TSNE or openTSNE (which supports out-of-sample and parallelism).

docs.title: ✦ Common Failure Modes and Diagnostics
docs.text:
Problem: All points collapse to one blob → Learning rate too low, or too few iterations. Increase lr and check KL divergence is decreasing.

Problem: Many tiny isolated clusters with no structure → Learning rate too high, or perplexity too low. Reduce lr or increase perplexity.

Problem: Different runs give completely different plots → This is expected for t-SNE. Average multiple runs or switch to UMAP for reproducibility.

Problem: "I can see 5 clear clusters, but the true number is 3" → t-SNE can split true clusters. Each cluster's internal structure can itself be projected as sub-clusters. Never use t-SNE for counting clusters — use silhouette analysis on the original space.

docs.title: ✦ Exit Criterion
docs.text: You know this when: you can derive the t-SNE gradient \(\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial y_i\) from the KL objective, explain precisely why the Student-t distribution is used instead of a Gaussian in the low-dimensional space, and state at least two structural properties of a dataset that a t-SNE plot cannot be used to infer.

docs.title: UMAP
docs.text:
The algorithm I reach for first now. Theoretically deeper than t-SNE — it takes topology seriously — but the intuition is honest once you unpack the construction. The math borrows from Riemannian geometry and category theory, which feels excessive until you see why it works.

Tags: #dimensionality-reduction #unsupervised #visualisation #nonlinear #manifold-learning Part of: [[Dimensionality Reduction]] → [[04.Representation Learning|Representation Learning]] Prerequisites: [[03.t-SNE|t-SNE]] (for contrast), [[01.PCA|PCA]], metric spaces, basic graph theory Authored: McInnes, Healy, Melville (2018) — arXiv:1802.03426

docs.title: ✦ Why Not Just Use t-SNE?
docs.text:
After building t-SNE from scratch in [[03.t-SNE]], the shortcomings are clear:

  1. No out-of-sample projection. Given a new point \(x_*\), t-SNE cannot embed it without re-running the entire algorithm. Useless in a pipeline.
  2. No global structure. Inter-cluster distances in a t-SNE plot are meaningless. The layout of clusters relative to each other is essentially noise.
  3. Slow. \(O(n \log n)\) with Barnes-Hut, but constants are large.
  4. Not a general-purpose preprocessing step. t-SNE outputs are not useful as features for downstream models — the optimisation is non-convex and unstable.

UMAP fixes all four. Same local-structure quality as t-SNE, but faster, with more honest global structure, out-of-sample projection, and stable enough to use as a preprocessing step for classifiers.

The cost: the theoretical justification is harder. UMAP's paper invokes Riemannian geometry, fuzzy topology, and category theory. I'll build up to it carefully.

docs.title: ✦ The Core Theoretical Claim
docs.text:
Claim: high-dimensional data lies on (or near) a low-dimensional Riemannian manifold embedded in \(\mathbb{R}^D\). The task of dimensionality reduction is to find a faithful low-dimensional representation of this manifold.

The key word is uniform. UMAP assumes the data is uniformly distributed on the manifold with respect to the manifold's intrinsic metric — not with respect to the Euclidean metric of the ambient space. This single assumption does most of the work.

Ambient space ℝ^D (Euclidean distances are misleading)
        ·  ·    ·  ·  · ← dense here (but just a curved region)
      ·              ·
    ·    MANIFOLD      ·
      ·              ·
        ·  ·    ·  ·  ·

Intrinsic distances (along manifold) are what UMAP uses.

docs.title: ✦ Step 1 — Building the Fuzzy Topological Representation
1a. The Local Metric
docs.text:
For each point \(x_i\), find its \(k\) nearest neighbours \({x_{i_1}, \ldots, x_{i_k}}\) and let \(\rho_i\) be the distance to the nearest neighbour:

\[\rho_i = \min_{j} |x_i - x_{i_j}|\]

This \(\rho_i\) is UMAP's analogue of t-SNE's adaptive bandwidth \(\sigma_i\). It normalises the local metric so that every point has at least one neighbour at distance zero on the manifold. In dense regions \(\rho_i\) is small; in sparse regions \(\rho_i\) is large.

Now define, for the \(k\)-nearest neighbours of \(x_i\), a local similarity:

\[v_{ij} = \exp!\left(-\frac{d(x_i, x_j) - \rho_i}{\sigma_i}\right)\]

where \(\sigma_i\) is a second bandwidth chosen (again by binary search) to achieve a target "effective number of neighbours" — UMAP's analogue of perplexity, called \(k\) (the n_neighbors parameter). The \(-\rho_i\) shift ensures the nearest neighbour always has similarity 1.

For points outside the \(k\)-neighbourhood, \(v_{ij} = 0\).

The picture to hold in mind: \(v_{ij}\) is 1 for the nearest neighbour, decays exponentially, and is 0 beyond the \(k\)-th neighbour. It encodes "how strongly does \(x_i\) consider \(x_j\) its local neighbour?"

docs.title: 1b. Symmetrisation via Fuzzy Union
docs.text:
\(v_{ij}\) is again asymmetric: \(v_{ij} \neq v_{ji}\). t-SNE symmetrised by averaging. UMAP uses a fuzzy union — the probabilistic OR:

\[w_{ij} = v_{ij} + v_{ji} - v_{ij} \cdot v_{ji}\]

This is exactly \(P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)\) for independent events. The interpretation: \(w_{ij}\) is the probability that the edge \((i,j)\) exists in the "fuzzy simplicial set" — the topological object UMAP constructs on top of the data.

If either \(x_i\) considers \(x_j\) a neighbour, or \(x_j\) considers \(x_i\) a neighbour, the edge is retained (with appropriate probability). This is less aggressive than averaging — edges are added, not washed out.

t-SNE vs. UMAP symmetrisation:

  • t-SNE: \(p_{ij} = \frac{p_{j|i} + p_{i|j}}{2}\) — arithmetic mean, shrinks both toward each other.
  • UMAP: \(w_{ij} = v_{ij} + v_{ji} - v_{ij}v_{ji}\) — fuzzy OR, strictly \(\geq \max(v_{ij}, v_{ji})\).

The OR operation preserves asymmetric local structure better. If \(x_i\) strongly pulls toward \(x_j\) but not vice versa, t-SNE halves the signal; UMAP keeps it.

The output of Step 1 is a weighted graph \(G = (V, E, w)\) on the \(n\) data points — a discrete approximation of the underlying topological space.

docs.title: ✦ Step 2 — Building the Low-Dimensional Representation
docs.text:
UMAP initialises the low-dimensional embedding \(Y = {y_1, \ldots, y_n} \subset \mathbb{R}^d\) (usually \(d = 2\)), typically via the spectral embedding of the graph Laplacian of \(G\) (much better than random init — it already roughly respects graph connectivity).

It then defines a low-dimensional similarity using a smooth approximation to a 1-simplex membership function:

\[\hat{w}_{ij} = \left(1 + a|y_i - y_j|^{2b}\right)^{-1}\]

The parameters \(a\) and \(b\) are fitted by a nonlinear least-squares procedure to approximate the family of curves:

\[\phi(r) = \begin{cases} 1 & r \leq \text{min_dist} \ \exp(-(r - \text{min_dist})) & r > \text{min_dist} \end{cases}\]

The min_dist hyperparameter controls how tightly points are clumped in the embedding. Small min_dist → tight clumps. Large min_dist → spread-out, preserves more topological spread.

When \(b = 1\), \(\hat{w}_{ij} = (1 + a|y_i - y_j|^2)^{-1}\), which is exactly the Student-t kernel from t-SNE (with \(a = 1\)). UMAP generalises t-SNE's low-dimensional kernel via the \(b\) parameter.

docs.title: ✦ Step 3 — The Objective: Cross-Entropy of Fuzzy Sets
docs.text:
t-SNE minimises \(KL(P | Q)\). UMAP minimises the binary cross-entropy between the high-dimensional and low-dimensional fuzzy set memberships:

\[\mathcal{L} = \sum_{(i,j) \in E} \left[ w_{ij} \log \frac{w_{ij}}{\hat{w}_{ij}} + (1 - w_{ij}) \log \frac{1 - w_{ij}}{1 - \hat{w}_{ij}} \right]\]

This is the cross-entropy \(H(w, \hat{w})\) over all edges (both present and absent).

Breaking it apart:

\[\mathcal{L} = \underbrace{\sum_{(i,j) \in E} w_{ij} \log \frac{w_{ij}}{\hat{w}_{ij}}}_{\text{attractive term}} + \underbrace{\sum_{(i,j) \in E} (1-w_{ij}) \log \frac{1-w_{ij}}{1-\hat{w}_{ij}}}_{\text{repulsive term}}\]
  • Attractive term: for edges that exist (\(w_{ij}\) large), penalises \(\hat{w}_{ij}\) being too small — pulls connected points together.
  • Repulsive term: for edges that don't exist (\(w_{ij} \approx 0\)), penalises \(\hat{w}_{ij}\) being too large — pushes disconnected points apart.

Why cross-entropy instead of KL? Because the \(w_{ij}\) are edge probabilities — binary (0 or 1) in the limit. Cross-entropy is the natural loss for a binary probability. KL divergence only applies to normalised probability distributions; \(w_{ij}\) doesn't sum to 1. UMAP's formulation is more honest about what \(w_{ij}\) actually represents.

docs.title: ✦ Step 4 — Stochastic Gradient Descent with Negative Sampling
docs.text:
The repulsive term in \(\mathcal{L}\) naïvely requires summing over all \(O(n^2)\) non-edges. UMAP approximates this via negative sampling — a technique from Word2Vec:

For each positive edge \((i,j)\), sample \(m\) negative examples \((i, k)\) where \(k\) is a random point. The gradient update becomes:

Attractive gradient (pull \(y_i\) toward \(y_j\)):

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{attr}}}{\partial y_i} = -\frac{2ab|y_i - y_j|^{2(b-1)}}{1 + a|y_i - y_j|^{2b}} \cdot w_{ij} \cdot (y_i - y_j)\]

Repulsive gradient (push \(y_i\) away from negative sample \(y_k\)):

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\text{rep}}}{\partial y_i} = \frac{2b}{(0.001 + |y_i - y_k|^2)(1 + a|y_i - y_k|^{2b})} \cdot (1 - \hat{w}_{ik}) \cdot (y_i - y_k)\]

(The \(0.001\) is a numerical stability epsilon.)

This gives \(O(n \cdot k \cdot m)\) per epoch, where \(k\) is n_neighbors and \(m\) is the number of negative samples (default 5). In practice, UMAP is significantly faster than t-SNE.

docs.title: ✦ Algorithm Summary
docs.text:
Input: high-dim data X = {x₁,...,xₙ}, n_neighbors k, n_components d,
       min_dist, n_epochs

1. For each xᵢ: find k-nearest neighbours, compute ρᵢ (dist to nearest)
2. Compute vᵢⱼ = exp(-(d(xᵢ,xⱼ) - ρᵢ) / σᵢ) for each neighbour xⱼ
   (σᵢ found by binary search to achieve effective cardinality = log₂(k))
3. Symmetrise: wᵢⱼ = vᵢⱼ + vⱼᵢ - vᵢⱼ·vⱼᵢ  (fuzzy union)
4. Fit parameters a, b to the min_dist profile via nonlinear least squares
5. Initialise Y using spectral embedding of graph Laplacian of (V, E, w)
6. For each epoch:
     For each edge (i,j) with probability ∝ wᵢⱼ:
       a. Compute attractive gradient; update yᵢ, yⱼ
       b. Sample m negative pairs (i,k); compute repulsive gradient; update yᵢ
7. Return Y

docs.title: ✦ Worked Example — Two Crescents
docs.text:
Consider the classic "two moons" dataset: 200 points on two interleaved crescents in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) (embedded in \(\mathbb{R}^{20}\) with noise).

What PCA does: projects onto variance axes → the two moons overlap completely. Indistinguishable.

What t-SNE does: preserves local neighbourhoods → separates the moons. But the shape of each moon is not preserved — it might look like two blobs.

What UMAP does: preserves local neighbourhoods and the topological structure (both moons are 1-dimensional loops). The resulting embedding looks like two actual crescents, with the global arrangement roughly faithful.

Original ℝ²⁰            t-SNE output           UMAP output

Points on two          Two separated           Two separated
interleaved            roughly circular        crescent shapes
crescents              blobs                   (topology preserved)

· · · · ·              ● ● ●   ○ ○ ○           ·····    ○○○○○
  ·····                  ● ●   ○ ○                ····    ○○○
○ ○ ○ ○ ○              ● ●●   ○ ○○             ·····      ○○○○
  ○○○○○                                                    ○○○○○

The shape is preserved in UMAP because the fuzzy simplicial set construction respects topology — the connectivity structure — not just pairwise distances.

docs.title: n_neighbors (default: 15)
docs.text:
Controls the balance between local and global structure.

  • Small (e.g., 5): only very local structure preserved. Tight local clusters, global layout unreliable.
  • Large (e.g., 200): more global structure. Clusters may merge; manifold layout more faithful.
  • Analogous to perplexity in t-SNE, but with a cleaner interpretation: literally the number of neighbours used to construct the graph.
n_neighbors = 5          n_neighbors = 15         n_neighbors = 50
  ·· ·   ·· ·            ···   ···               ··········
  ·· ·   ·· ·            ···   ···               ··········
  (tight clusters)        (balanced)              (global structure)

docs.title: min_dist (default: 0.1)
docs.text:
Controls how tightly points are packed in the embedding.

  • Small (e.g., 0.001): tight clumps — good for clustering tasks.
  • Large (e.g., 0.5): spread out — better for seeing the overall manifold topology.

docs.title: n_components (default: 2)
docs.text: The output dimensionality. Can be set to 10, 50, etc. for preprocessing — UMAP is not only a 2D visualisation tool.

docs.title: metric (default: 'euclidean')
docs.text: UMAP supports any metric: 'cosine', 'manhattan', 'correlation', custom. This is powerful for text embeddings (use cosine) or count data (use Hellinger).

docs.title: ✦ Out-of-Sample Projection
docs.text:
This is the capability t-SNE lacks entirely. After fitting UMAP on training data \(X_{\text{train}}\), new points \(x_*\) can be embedded without re-running the full algorithm:

\[y_* = \text{UMAP.transform}(x_*)\]

Mechanically: find \(x_*\)'s nearest neighbours in \(X_{\text{train}}\), compute the fuzzy set memberships, then use a few SGD steps to find the low-dimensional position that best satisfies those memberships given the already-fixed embedding.

This enables:

  • Embedding test data using a model fit on training data (no leakage)
  • Streaming inference: embed new points as they arrive
  • Using UMAP as a feature extractor in an ML pipeline
import umap

reducer = umap.UMAP(n_neighbors=15, min_dist=0.1, n_components=2)
reducer.fit(X_train)

Y_train = reducer.transform(X_train)
Y_test  = reducer.transform(X_test)   # ← t-SNE cannot do this

docs.title: ✦ UMAP as a Preprocessing Step
docs.text:
Because of out-of-sample projection and relative stability, UMAP can be used as a dimensionality reduction step before supervised learning — not just for visualisation.

Typical pipeline:

Raw features (D dims)
      ↓
   PCA (→ 50 dims, remove noise)
      ↓
   UMAP (→ 10–30 dims, nonlinear structure)
      ↓
   Classifier (Random Forest, SVM, etc.)

Studies (particularly in bioinformatics) show UMAP preprocessing can match or exceed PCA preprocessing on downstream classification, especially when the data has nonlinear manifold structure. See McInnes et al. (2018) and Becht et al. (2018, Nature Biotechnology).

Caution: UMAP's output is stochastic. If you use it in a pipeline, fix the random seed and document the hyperparameters — both affect the embedding, and therefore downstream model performance.

docs.title: ✦ The Riemannian Geometry Behind It
docs.text:
This section is for understanding why UMAP's theory is well-motivated. The algorithm works without this, but you asked for rigour.

The uniformity assumption, formalised:

Assume the data \({x_i}\) lies on a Riemannian manifold \((\mathcal{M}, g)\) and is uniformly distributed with respect to the Riemannian volume form \(\text{dvol}_g\). The metric \(g\) is unknown.

The geodesic distance problem: we observe Euclidean distances in \(\mathbb{R}^D\), but we want geodesic distances on \(\mathcal{M}\). These can differ dramatically (think: points on opposite sides of a fold that are Euclidean-close but geodesically far).

UMAP's construction: estimate the geodesic distance by noting that under the uniformity assumption, the distance to the \(k\)-th nearest neighbour in Euclidean space is proportional to the geodesic ball radius needed to contain \(k\) points. The \(\rho_i\) normalisation and \(\sigma_i\) adaptation are approximating this geodesic ball radius locally.

Concretely: the local connectivity condition (nearest neighbour at distance \(\rho_i\) has \(v_{ij} = 1\)) ensures every point has at least one geodesic neighbour at zero distance — i.e., the manifold is locally connected.

Fuzzy simplicial sets: the weighted graph \(G\) constructed in Step 1 is interpreted as a fuzzy simplicial set — a topological object that captures the manifold's shape (connected components, loops, voids) up to homotopy. The UMAP objective then finds a low-dimensional fuzzy simplicial set with the same topological structure.

The deep theoretical result (Theorem 1 in McInnes et al.) is:

Under the uniformity assumption and with sufficient data, the fuzzy simplicial set constructed by UMAP converges (in the sense of the Čech complex) to a topological representation of the underlying manifold.

In practice: UMAP is approximating manifold topology, not just pairwise distances. This is why it preserves structure that t-SNE discards.

docs.title: ✦ Connection to AI / ML / Deep Learning
1. Feature Space Analysis
docs.text: Same as t-SNE, but now usable in production. Extract activations from any layer of a neural network, run UMAP, and inspect. The improvement: because UMAP is faster and supports out-of-sample projection, you can do this continuously during training to watch representation learning unfold.

docs.title: 2. Preprocessing for Downstream Models
docs.text:
UMAP-reduced features fed into classifiers have shown competitive performance, particularly when:

  • The original feature space is very high-dimensional (\(D \gg 100\))
  • The manifold hypothesis holds (data lives on a lower-dimensional structure)
  • The downstream model is sensitive to curse of dimensionality (KNN, SVM with RBF kernel)

docs.title: 3. Self-Supervised / Contrastive Learning Evaluation
docs.text: In contrastive learning (SimCLR, MoCo, DINO), UMAP of the embedding space is the standard diagnostic. Good representations → well-separated, coherent clusters. The key advantage over t-SNE: UMAP embeddings of the training set generalise to the test set, so you can use the same projection to visualise both.

docs.title: 4. Large Language Models
docs.text: Sentence embeddings (from BERT, GPT, etc.) are 768–4096 dimensional. UMAP to 2–3D for visualisation reveals semantic clustering — similar topics cluster together. Used to diagnose dataset balance, discover topic drift, and identify outliers in fine-tuning datasets.

docs.title: 5. Anomaly Detection
docs.text: Because UMAP preserves density structure better than t-SNE, anomalous points (which have few true neighbours) tend to project to isolated positions in the embedding. A simple heuristic: fit UMAP on normal data, embed new points, flag those that fall far from any cluster.

docs.title: 6. Generative Models — Latent Space Visualisation
docs.text:
VAE and GAN latent spaces are typically 100–512 dimensional. UMAP to 2D lets you visually inspect:

  • Whether the latent space is well-organised
  • Whether interpolations between classes pass through sensible intermediate regions
  • Whether the encoder is collapsing (representation collapse → single blob)

docs.title: ✦ t-SNE vs. UMAP: Full Comparison
docs.text:
Property t-SNE UMAP Global structure preserved Poor Better (not perfect) Local structure preserved Excellent Excellent Out-of-sample projection No Yes Speed \(O(n \log n)\) \(O(n \log n)\), faster constants Deterministic No No (but more stable) Cluster sizes meaningful No Somewhat (not fully) Inter-cluster distances No Partially Can use as preprocessing No Yes Theoretical basis KL divergence + t-kernel Riemannian geometry + fuzzy topology Low-dim kernel Student-t (\(a=1, b=1\)) Generalised: \((1 + a\|y\|^{2b})^{-1}\) Symmetrisation Arithmetic mean Fuzzy union (probabilistic OR) Objective \(KL(P \| Q)\) Binary cross-entropy \(H(w, \hat{w})\) Initialisation Random (small noise) Spectral embedding of graph Laplacian Negative sampling No (Barnes-Hut for repulsion) Yes (Word2Vec-style)

The bottom line: UMAP is t-SNE with better theory, faster optimisation, honest global structure, and out-of-sample projection. Use UMAP unless you have a specific reason for t-SNE (e.g., existing pipeline, legacy code, paper comparison).

docs.title: ✦ What UMAP Still Cannot Tell You
docs.text:
Despite the improvements over t-SNE, these caveats remain:

Claim Valid? "These two clusters are far apart so they're very different" ⚠️ Partially — UMAP preserves more global structure than t-SNE but inter-cluster distances are still distorted "Cluster A is larger than cluster B so it has more points" ❌ No — min_dist controls visual cluster size, not point density "I see 7 clusters so there are 7 classes" ❌ No — UMAP can split or merge clusters depending on hyperparameters "These two points are close so they're similar" ✅ Yes (local structure is preserved) "The topology looks like a loop so the data has a cyclic structure" ✅ Yes (UMAP preserves topology)

docs.title: ✦ Implementation
docs.text:
# Standard usage
import umap
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# Always scale first — UMAP is distance-sensitive
X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)

# For visualisation
reducer_2d = umap.UMAP(
    n_neighbors=15,      # local/global balance
    min_dist=0.1,        # cluster tightness
    n_components=2,      # output dims
    metric='euclidean',  # or 'cosine' for text embeddings
    random_state=42      # reproducibility
)
Y_2d = reducer_2d.fit_transform(X_scaled)

plt.scatter(Y_2d[:, 0], Y_2d[:, 1], c=labels, cmap='tab10', s=5)
plt.title("UMAP projection")

# For preprocessing (higher-dim)
reducer_prep = umap.UMAP(n_components=20, n_neighbors=30)
reducer_prep.fit(X_train_scaled)
X_train_umap = reducer_prep.transform(X_train_scaled)
X_test_umap  = reducer_prep.transform(X_test_scaled)   # out-of-sample

# Then feed into classifier
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
clf = RandomForestClassifier()
clf.fit(X_train_umap, y_train)

For neural network activations:

# Get penultimate layer activations
activations = model.predict(X)  # shape (n, 512) for example

# PCA first to 50 dims (remove noise, speed up UMAP)
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
pca = PCA(n_components=50)
activations_pca = pca.fit_transform(activations)

# Then UMAP
reducer = umap.UMAP(n_neighbors=15, min_dist=0.05)
Y = reducer.fit_transform(activations_pca)

docs.title: ✦ A Note on Reproducibility
docs.text:
UMAP has two sources of randomness:

  1. Initialisation (spectral decomposition is deterministic, but numpy random state affects tie-breaking)
  2. Negative sampling in SGD

Fix random_state in the constructor. Even so, floating-point non-determinism across platforms means results may differ slightly between machines. For papers: always report n_neighbors, min_dist, metric, random_state, and the UMAP version.

docs.title: ✦ Exit Criterion
docs.text: You know this when: you can explain why UMAP uses a fuzzy union (not averaging) for symmetrisation and what topological object this constructs; derive the cross-entropy objective and explain why it differs from t-SNE's KL divergence; and explain what n_neighbors and min_dist control geometrically, not just empirically.
