docs.title: Autoencoders
docs.text:
The simplest possible self-supervised objective: predict the input from a compressed version of itself. Everything interesting in representation learning — VAEs, denoising, sparse coding, masked autoencoders — is a variation on this one idea.

Tags: #representation-learning #unsupervised #deep-learning #generative Part of: [[04.Representation Learning]] → [[Neural Networks & Deep Learning]] Prerequisites: [[01.Linear Regression]], [[02.Logistic Regression]], basic neural network forward/backward pass, [[03.Probability Review|MLE and KL divergence]]

docs.title: ✦ The Core Idea
docs.text:
An autoencoder is a neural network trained to reproduce its input at the output, subject to a bottleneck constraint. The network is split into two parts:

  • Encoder \(f_\phi: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Z}\) — compresses input \(x\) to a latent code \(z\)
  • Decoder \(g_\theta: \mathcal{Z} \to \mathcal{X}\) — reconstructs \(\hat{x}\) from \(z\)

The training objective is simply reconstruction:

\[\mathcal{L}(\phi, \theta) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \ell(x_i,, g_\theta(f_\phi(x_i)))\]

where \(\ell\) is a reconstruction loss — MSE for continuous data, binary cross-entropy for binary data.

Input x ──► [  Encoder f_φ  ] ──► z ──► [  Decoder g_θ  ] ──► x̂ ≈ x
  (high-dim)     (compress)      (low-dim)    (reconstruct)     (high-dim)
                                   ↑
                              bottleneck:
                              dim(z) << dim(x)

The bottleneck is the entire mechanism. If \(\dim(z) = \dim(x)\), nothing prevents the network from learning the identity map — trivially zero loss, zero useful structure learned. The bottleneck forces the encoder to learn a compressed representation that retains the information necessary for reconstruction.

Why is this useful? No labels needed. The supervision signal is the input itself. Given unlabelled data — which is the common case in practice — an autoencoder can learn structure for free.

docs.title: Undercomplete
docs.text:
\(\dim(z) < \dim(x)\). The bottleneck is the only regulariser. With a linear encoder and decoder, and MSE loss, the undercomplete autoencoder recovers exactly the PCA subspace — the \(k\) principal components. This is a theorem, not an accident.

Proof sketch: The MSE objective for a linear autoencoder is \(\min_{W_e, W_d} |X - X W_e W_d|_F^2\). The solution is \(W_e W_d = V_k V_k^T\), the projection onto the top-\(k\) PCA eigenvectors. With nonlinear activations, the autoencoder finds nonlinear generalisations of PCA — more expressive, but no longer has this clean characterisation.

docs.title: Overcomplete
docs.text: \(\dim(z) \geq \dim(x)\). Now the bottleneck alone does not prevent the identity. An overcomplete autoencoder must be regularised to learn useful features. This leads to sparse autoencoders, denoising autoencoders, and contractual autoencoders.

docs.title: Sparse Autoencoder
docs.text:
Add an L1 penalty on the activations of \(z\):

\[\mathcal{L} = |x - \hat{x}|^2 + \lambda |z|_1\]

This forces most hidden units to be inactive for any given input. The network learns dictionary-like features: each input is a sparse combination of basis elements. This is the deep learning analogue of sparse coding (Olshausen & Field, 1996).

A common alternative: penalise via KL divergence from a Bernoulli with small mean \(\rho\) (e.g. \(\rho = 0.05\)), interpreted as "5% of neurons should fire on average":

\[\Omega(z) = \sum_j \text{KL}(\rho | \hat{\rho}_j), \qquad \hat{\rho}_j = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i z_j^{(i)}\]

Connection to ML: Sparse representations have better sample efficiency for downstream tasks. Each learned feature has a specific, interpretable role. This is the intuition behind the current generation of sparse autoencoders used to interpret large language models (Anthropic's mechanistic interpretability work, 2023–2024).

docs.title: Denoising Autoencoder (DAE)
docs.text:
Instead of feeding clean \(x\), corrupt it first to \(\tilde{x}\), then train to reconstruct the original \(x\):

\[\mathcal{L} = |x - g_\theta(f_\phi(\tilde{x}))|^2, \qquad \tilde{x} = \text{corrupt}(x)\]

Common corruption: additive Gaussian noise \(\tilde{x} = x + \epsilon\), \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I)\); or masking noise (randomly zero out some dimensions).

x ──[corrupt]──► x̃ ──► [Encoder] ──► z ──► [Decoder] ──► x̂
↑                                                          │
└──────────────────── MSE(x, x̂) ◄─────────────────────────┘
     (target is *clean* x, not x̃)

Why this works: The denoising criterion forces the encoder to learn the data manifold. Specifically, the optimal DAE (in the limit of small Gaussian noise) learns to estimate the score function \(\nabla_x \log p(x)\) — the gradient of the log data density. This is a deep connection to diffusion models and score matching (Vincent, 2011).

Intuitively: a model that can denoise must understand the structure of the data distribution. Random noise takes you off the manifold; the denoiser learns to project back.

docs.title: Contractive Autoencoder (CAE)
docs.text:
Penalise the Frobenius norm of the Jacobian of the encoder with respect to the input:

\[\mathcal{L} = |x - \hat{x}|^2 + \lambda |J_{f_\phi}(x)|_F^2, \qquad J_{f_\phi}(x) = \frac{\partial f_\phi(x)}{\partial x}\]

This forces the learned representation to be insensitive to small perturbations in input space — the representation doesn't change much when the input changes a little. The encoder learns features that are invariant to nuisance variation.

Formally: DAE penalises sensitivity stochastically (via random corruption); CAE penalises it analytically (via the Jacobian). They are related — both push the representation onto a low-dimensional manifold.

docs.title: ✦ Variational Autoencoder (VAE)
docs.text: The VAE is not merely a regularised autoencoder — it is a latent variable generative model trained via approximate Bayesian inference. It earns its own detailed treatment but belongs here conceptually.

docs.title: The Generative Model
docs.text:
Assume data is generated by:

  1. Sample a latent vector: \(z \sim p(z) = \mathcal{N}(0, I)\)
  2. Sample the observation: \(x \sim p_\theta(x|z)\) (the decoder is the likelihood)

The marginal likelihood is:

\[p_\theta(x) = \int p_\theta(x|z), p(z), dz\]

This integral is intractable — we cannot compute it for general \(p_\theta\).

docs.title: The Inference Problem
docs.text:
We want the posterior \(p_\theta(z|x) = p_\theta(x|z) p(z) / p_\theta(x)\), but the denominator is the intractable marginal. The VAE's solution: amortised variational inference — approximate \(p_\theta(z|x)\) with a learned \(q_\phi(z|x) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_\phi(x), \text{diag}(\sigma^2_\phi(x)))\).

The encoder now outputs parameters of a distribution, not a single vector.

docs.title: The ELBO
docs.text:
Maximise the Evidence Lower BOund (ELBO) instead of the intractable log-likelihood:

\[\log p_\theta(x) \geq \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z|x)}[\log p_\theta(x|z)]}_{\text{reconstruction term}} - \underbrace{D_{KL}(q_\phi(z|x) ,|, p(z))}_{\text{regularisation term}}\]

Derivation: Start from \(\log p_\theta(x) = \log \int p_\theta(x|z)p(z) dz\). Introduce \(q_\phi\) via importance weighting, apply Jensen's inequality to the concave log:

\[\log p_\theta(x) = \log \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z|x)}!\left[\frac{p_\theta(x|z)p(z)}{q_\phi(z|x)}\right] \geq \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}!\left[\log \frac{p_\theta(x|z)p(z)}{q_\phi(z|x)}\right] = \text{ELBO}\]

Expanding the ELBO:

\[\text{ELBO} = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}[\log p_\theta(x|z)] - D_{KL}(q_\phi(z|x) | p(z))\]

The gap between \(\log p_\theta(x)\) and the ELBO is exactly \(D_{KL}(q_\phi(z|x) | p_\theta(z|x)) \geq 0\).

For Gaussian \(q_\phi\) and Gaussian prior \(p(z)\), the KL has a closed form:

\[D_{KL}(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) | \mathcal{N}(0,1)) = \frac{1}{2}\sum_j \left(\mu_j^2 + \sigma_j^2 - \log\sigma_j^2 - 1\right)\]

docs.title: The Reparameterisation Trick
docs.text:
Sampling \(z \sim q_\phi(z|x) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_\phi(x), \sigma^2_\phi(x))\) is non-differentiable — you cannot backpropagate through a sample. The fix:

\[z = \mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \odot \epsilon, \qquad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\]

Now the randomness is in \(\epsilon\), which does not depend on \(\phi\). The gradient flows through \(\mu_\phi\) and \(\sigma_\phi\) cleanly.

x ──► Encoder ──► μ_φ(x), σ_φ(x)
                       │
              z = μ + σ⊙ε,  ε ~ 𝒩(0,I)   ← randomness here, not in z
                       │
                    Decoder ──► x̂
                       │
              ℒ = -𝔼[log p(x|z)] + KL

docs.title: Interpretation of the Two Terms
docs.text:
Reconstruction term \(\mathbb{E}[\log p_\theta(x|z)]\): forces the decoder to reconstruct \(x\) faithfully from \(z\). For Gaussian \(p_\theta(x|z)\), this is exactly MSE. For Bernoulli, binary cross-entropy.

KL term \(D_{KL}(q_\phi | p)\): forces the posterior over \(z\) to stay close to the prior \(\mathcal{N}(0,I)\). This regularises the latent space — it prevents the encoder from mapping each \(x_i\) to a delta function at a distinct point (which would give perfect reconstruction but an unusable latent space).

The KL term creates a smooth, continuous latent space: nearby points in \(z\)-space decode to similar outputs. This is what makes VAE useful for generation — sample \(z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)\), decode, get a plausible \(x\).

docs.title: VAE vs. Standard Autoencoder
docs.text: Property Standard AE VAE Latent code Deterministic vector Distribution \(q_\phi(z\|x)\) Training objective Reconstruction only ELBO = reconstruction − KL Latent space structure Unstructured Regularised toward \(\mathcal{N}(0,I)\) Can generate new samples? No (no principled sampling) Yes — sample \(z \sim p(z)\), decode Theoretical basis Ad hoc Variational Bayes

docs.title: ✦ Masked Autoencoders (MAE)
docs.text:
The modern descendant of denoising autoencoders, scaled to vision transformers.

Idea: randomly mask a large fraction (e.g. 75%) of image patches, encode only the visible patches, then reconstruct the full image from the encoded representation.

\[\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{M}|} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{M}} |x_i - \hat{x}_i|^2\]

where \(\mathcal{M}\) is the set of masked patches.

This is a self-supervised objective — no labels. The model must learn rich semantic features to reconstruct masked regions from context. He et al. (2021) showed this produces representations competitive with supervised pretraining on ImageNet.

Why 75%? Unlike text (where masking 15% as in BERT is hard due to semantic density), images have high spatial redundancy — 75% masking is still a learnable task, and it forces the model to reason about global structure, not just local texture.

docs.title: ✦ Connection to the Broader ML/DL Landscape
1. Dimensionality Reduction
docs.text: An undercomplete deterministic autoencoder is a nonlinear generalisation of PCA. PCA is the special case with linear encoder/decoder. Both minimise reconstruction error; the autoencoder can capture curved manifolds that PCA cannot.

docs.title: 2. Generative Models
docs.text:
The VAE is one of three major frameworks for deep generative modelling:

  • VAEs: latent variable + variational inference
  • GANs: adversarial training, no explicit likelihood
  • Diffusion models: iterative denoising, connection to DAEs via score matching

VAEs produce blurry samples (the Gaussian likelihood averages over modes); GANs produce sharp samples but are harder to train; diffusion models currently dominate image quality.

docs.title: 3. Representation Learning and Transfer Learning
docs.text: A pre-trained encoder \(f_\phi\) can be used as a feature extractor: freeze \(\phi\), attach a small classifier on top, train on a small labelled dataset. This is transfer learning from self-supervised pretraining — the standard paradigm in NLP (BERT, GPT) and increasingly in vision (MAE, DINO).

docs.title: 4. Information-Theoretic View
docs.text:
The ELBO can be rewritten as:

\[\text{ELBO} = -\mathbb{E}[\text{reconstruction error}] - D_{KL}(q_\phi | p)\]

This is exactly the rate-distortion tradeoff from information theory:

  • Distortion = reconstruction error
  • Rate = bits needed to encode \(z\), upper bounded by \(D_{KL}\)

The \(\beta\)-VAE (Higgins et al., 2017) makes this tradeoff explicit by scaling the KL term: \(\mathcal{L} = \text{recon} - \beta \cdot D_{KL}\). High \(\beta\) → more compressed, more disentangled latent space; low \(\beta\) → better reconstruction.

docs.title: 5. Anomaly Detection
docs.text: A standard autoencoder trained on normal data will have low reconstruction error on normal inputs and high reconstruction error on anomalies (never seen during training, poorly represented). Threshold on reconstruction error → anomaly detector. Widely used in industrial fault detection, fraud detection, cybersecurity.

docs.title: 6. Mechanistic Interpretability (2023–present)
docs.text: Sparse autoencoders are now being applied to the residual stream of large language models. The idea: the superposition hypothesis states that LLMs pack many features into fewer neurons via superposition. A sparse autoencoder trained on LLM activations can decompose these superposed representations into sparse, interpretable features. This is an active research direction at Anthropic and DeepMind.

docs.title: ✦ Implementation Sketch (PyTorch)
docs.text:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

# --- Standard Autoencoder ---
class Autoencoder(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim=784, latent_dim=32):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(input_dim, 256), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(256, latent_dim)
        )
        self.decoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(latent_dim, 256), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(256, input_dim), nn.Sigmoid()
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        z = self.encoder(x)
        return self.decoder(z), z

# --- VAE ---
class VAE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim=784, latent_dim=32):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(input_dim, 256), nn.ReLU())
        self.fc_mu    = nn.Linear(256, latent_dim)
        self.fc_logvar = nn.Linear(256, latent_dim)
        self.decoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(latent_dim, 256), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(256, input_dim), nn.Sigmoid()
        )

    def encode(self, x):
        h = self.encoder(x)
        return self.fc_mu(h), self.fc_logvar(h)

    def reparameterise(self, mu, logvar):
        std = torch.exp(0.5 * logvar)
        eps = torch.randn_like(std)        # ε ~ N(0, I)
        return mu + eps * std              # z = μ + σ⊙ε

    def forward(self, x):
        mu, logvar = self.encode(x)
        z = self.reparameterise(mu, logvar)
        x_hat = self.decoder(z)
        return x_hat, mu, logvar

def vae_loss(x, x_hat, mu, logvar):
    recon = nn.functional.binary_cross_entropy(x_hat, x, reduction='sum')
    # KL divergence: -½ Σ(1 + log σ² - μ² - σ²)
    kl = -0.5 * torch.sum(1 + logvar - mu.pow(2) - logvar.exp())
    return recon + kl

Implementation notes:

  • Use logvar = log σ² not σ² directly — prevents numerical issues (log is unconstrained, σ² must be positive).
  • reduction='sum' for BCE — sum over pixels and batch, then divide by batch size outside. Using 'mean' implicitly scales the KL differently.
  • During inference/generation: pass \(z \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)\) directly to the decoder. No encoder needed.

docs.title: ✦ Failure Modes and Diagnostics
docs.text:
Posterior collapse (VAE): The encoder ignores the input and outputs \(q_\phi(z|x) \approx p(z) = \mathcal{N}(0,I)\) — the KL term goes to zero but reconstruction is poor. The decoder learns to ignore \(z\) and models \(p(x)\) by itself. Fixes: KL annealing (start with \(\beta=0\), slowly increase), free bits (allow a minimum KL per dimension), more expressive decoders.

Blurry reconstructions (VAE): The Gaussian reconstruction likelihood averages over modes. A pixel predicted as 0.5 is blurry. Fixes: use a learned variance for \(p_\theta(x|z)\), or switch to a discrete (categorical) likelihood, or use a flow-based decoder.

Trivial identity solution (standard AE): If the model is expressive enough and unconstrained, it learns identity. Ensure the bottleneck is genuinely narrow, or add explicit regularisation.

Overfitting the reconstruction (denoising AE): If corruption is too weak, the model just memorises. If too strong, the task is impossible. Tune noise level — typically validated via downstream task performance or KNN accuracy in \(z\)-space.

docs.title: ✦ Exit Criterion
docs.text: You know this when: you can derive the ELBO from first principles starting from \(\log p_\theta(x)\), explain why the reparameterisation trick is necessary for gradient-based training, implement a VAE in PyTorch from scratch including the KL closed-form term, and state the key difference between posterior collapse and underfitting.

docs.title: Bayesian Networks
docs.text:
A Bayesian network is a marriage of graph theory and probability theory. The graph encodes what is independent of what; the probability tables encode how much. Together they give you a compact, interpretable representation of a joint distribution over dozens or hundreds of variables — something a full joint table could never provide.

Tags: #probabilistic-graphical-models #bayesian #inference #directed-graphical-models Part of: Part 5 — Probabilistic Graphical Models Prerequisites: [[03.Probability Review|Bayes' theorem, conditional independence, chain rule of probability]], [[05.Decision Trees|DAGs conceptually]], basic graph theory

docs.title: ✦ The Problem Bayesian Networks Solve
docs.text:
Suppose you have \(d\) binary random variables \(X_1, \ldots, X_d\). A full joint distribution requires specifying \(2^d - 1\) numbers. For \(d = 30\): over a billion parameters. Storing, estimating, and querying this table is completely intractable.

Bayesian networks exploit conditional independence structure to represent the same joint distribution far more compactly. If variable \(X_i\) only directly depends on a small set of "parent" variables \(\text{Pa}(X_i)\), then specifying \(P(X_i \mid \text{Pa}(X_i))\) for each \(i\) suffices to reconstruct the full joint — and each conditional table is tiny.

The key insight: most variables in the world do not directly cause most other variables. Causal structure is sparse. A Bayesian network makes this sparsity explicit.

docs.title: ✦ Formal Definition
docs.text:
A Bayesian network (also: Bayes net, belief network, directed graphical model) is a pair \((\mathcal{G}, \mathcal{P})\) where:

  • \(\mathcal{G} = (V, E)\) is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) with one node per random variable
  • \(\mathcal{P} = {P(X_i \mid \text{Pa}_\mathcal{G}(X_i))}_{i=1}^d\) is a set of conditional probability distributions (CPDs), one per node

The joint distribution factorises as:

\[\boxed{P(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_d) = \prod_{i=1}^d P(X_i \mid \text{Pa}_\mathcal{G}(X_i))}\]

This is the chain rule of Bayesian networks — it follows from the chain rule of probability plus the conditional independence structure encoded in \(\mathcal{G}\).

Notation: \(\text{Pa}_\mathcal{G}(X_i)\) denotes the set of direct parents of \(X_i\) in \(\mathcal{G}\). If \(X_i\) has no parents, \(P(X_i \mid \text{Pa}(X_i)) = P(X_i)\), a marginal.

docs.title: Why Must \(\mathcal{G}\) Be Acyclic?
docs.text: A cycle \(X_i \to X_j \to X_i\) would require \(X_i\) to cause \(X_j\) and \(X_j\) to simultaneously cause \(X_i\). This makes the factorisation self-referential and undefined — there is no valid topological ordering in which to apply the chain rule. Acyclicity is not a modelling convenience; it is a logical requirement for the factorisation to define a valid distribution.

docs.title: ✦ A Canonical Example: The Student Network
docs.text:
A classic example (Koller & Friedman). Five variables:

  • \(D\): Difficulty of exam (easy/hard)
  • \(I\): Intelligence of student (low/high)
  • \(G\): Grade received (A/B/C)
  • \(S\): SAT score (high/low)
  • \(L\): Reference letter quality (strong/weak)
    D ──┐     I ──┐
        ▼         ▼
        G         S
        │
        ▼
        L

The factorisation:

\[P(D, I, G, S, L) = P(D), P(I), P(G \mid D, I), P(S \mid I), P(L \mid G)\]

Parameter count: \(D\): 1, \(I\): 1, \(G \mid D,I\): \(2 \times 2 \times 3 - 1 = 11\), \(S \mid I\): 2, \(L \mid G\): 6. Total: 21 parameters. The full joint has \(2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 2 \times 2 - 1 = 47\) parameters. The network is more than twice as compact — and more interpretable.

For a network with \(d\) nodes each with at most \(k\) parents over binary variables: at most \(d \cdot 2^k\) parameters, vs. \(2^d\) for the full joint. Exponential compression.

docs.title: Local Markov Property
docs.text:
The factorisation implies a fundamental independence statement: every variable is conditionally independent of its non-descendants given its parents:

\[X_i \perp !!! \perp \text{NonDesc}(X_i) \mid \text{Pa}(X_i)\]

This is the local Markov property. It is equivalent to the factorisation above.

docs.title: D-Separation
docs.text:
But the Bayesian network encodes more independences than just the local ones. The full set is read off the graph via d-separation (directional separation).

Definition: A path \(\pi\) between nodes \(X\) and \(Y\) is blocked by a set \(Z\) if there exists a node \(V\) on \(\pi\) such that one of:

  1. Chain: \(A o V o B\) and \(V \in Z\) — conditioning on \(V\) blocks the flow of information along the chain.
  2. Fork: \(A \leftarrow V o B\) and \(V \in Z\) — conditioning on the common cause \(V\) blocks the spurious correlation it induces.
  3. Collider: \(A o V \leftarrow B\) and \(V otin Z\) and no descendant of \(V\) is in \(Z\) — the collider is not conditioned on, so it blocks by default.

\(X\) and \(Y\) are d-separated by \(Z\) (written \(X \perp_\mathcal{G} Y \mid Z\)) if every path between \(X\) and \(Y\) is blocked by \(Z\).

The Soundness Theorem: If \(X \perp_\mathcal{G} Y \mid Z\), then \(X \perp!!!\perp Y \mid Z\) in every distribution \(P\) consistent with \(\mathcal{G}\).

The Faithfulness/Completeness Theorem: Conversely (under faithfulness), if \(X ot\perp_\mathcal{G} Y \mid Z\), then there exists a distribution \(P\) consistent with \(\mathcal{G}\) in which \(X ot\perp!!!\perp Y \mid Z\). The graph captures all and only the structural independences.

docs.title: The Three Fundamental Motifs
docs.text: These three patterns are the atoms of d-separation. Every complex network decomposes into combinations of them.

docs.title: 1. Chain (Serial Connection)
docs.text:
A ──► B ──► C

\(P(A, B, C) = P(A), P(B \mid A), P(C \mid B)\)

\[A \perp!!!\perp C \mid B, \qquad A \not\perp!!!\perp C\]

Intuition: \(B\) is the mediator. Conditioning on \(B\) blocks the information flow from \(A\) to \(C\). Example: Season → Sprinkler → Wet grass. Knowing the sprinkler state, the season tells you nothing about the grass.

docs.title: 2. Fork (Common Cause)
docs.text:
A ◄── B ──► C

\(P(A, B, C) = P(B), P(A \mid B), P(C \mid B)\)

\[A \perp!!!\perp C \mid B, \qquad A \not\perp!!!\perp C\]

Intuition: \(B\) is a common cause that induces a spurious correlation between \(A\) and \(C\). Conditioning on \(B\) removes the spurious dependence. Example: Season → Rain, Season → Sprinkler. Without knowing the season, rain and sprinkler are correlated. Knowing the season, they are independent.

docs.title: 3. Collider (Common Effect / v-Structure)
docs.text:
A ──► C ◄── B

\(P(A, B, C) = P(A), P(B), P(C \mid A, B)\)

\[A \perp!!!\perp B, \qquad A \not\perp!!!\perp B \mid C\]

Intuition: The collider \(C\) is blocked by default — \(A\) and \(B\) are marginally independent. But conditioning on \(C\) (or any descendant of \(C\)) opens the path — it creates a dependence. This is Berkson's paradox / explaining away.

Explaining away: Suppose \(C\) = "car won't start", \(A\) = "battery dead", \(B\) = "out of fuel". Marginally, battery state and fuel state are independent. But given that the car won't start, learning that the battery is fine makes "out of fuel" much more likely — the two causes compete to explain \(C\).

Collider example — selection bias:

A = Talent       B = Luck
        \         /
         ▼       ▼
          C = Famous

P(Talent ⊥ Luck) = True     (in the general population)
P(Talent ⊥ Luck | Famous) = False  (among famous people, high luck → lower talent, and vice versa)

This is one of the most common sources of spurious correlations in observational studies. Any time you condition on a collider — including by selecting a sample based on a collider — you induce spurious dependence between its parents.

docs.title: ✦ Worked D-Separation Examples
docs.text:
Using the Student network: \(D o G \leftarrow I o S\), \(G o L\).

Query 1: Is \(D \perp!!!\perp I\)? Path: \(D o G \leftarrow I\). This path has a collider at \(G\). \(G otin \emptyset\) and no descendant of \(G\) is in \(\emptyset\). Blocked. No other paths. \(\Rightarrow D \perp!!!\perp I\). ✓ (Difficulty and intelligence are marginally independent — sensible.)

Query 2: Is \(D \perp!!!\perp I \mid G\)? Path: \(D o G \leftarrow I\). Collider at \(G\); now \(G \in {G}\). Not blocked. \(\Rightarrow D ot\perp!!!\perp I \mid G\). ✓ (Given a student's grade, difficulty and intelligence become dependent — knowing the exam was hard makes low grade less informative about intelligence.)

Query 3: Is \(D \perp!!!\perp S \mid G\)? Paths from \(D\) to \(S\): only \(D o G \leftarrow I o S\).

  • At \(G\): collider, \(G \in {G}\) → open.
  • At \(I\): chain, \(I otin {G}\) → open. Path is not blocked. \(\Rightarrow D ot\perp!!!\perp S \mid G\).

Query 4: Is \(D \perp!!!\perp S \mid G, I\)? Path: \(D o G \leftarrow I o S\).

  • At \(G\): collider, \(G \in {G, I}\) → open.
  • At \(I\): chain, \(I \in {G, I}\) → blocked. All paths blocked. \(\Rightarrow D \perp!!!\perp S \mid G, I\). ✓ (Given both grade and intelligence, difficulty tells you nothing about SAT score.)

docs.title: ✦ Inference
docs.text:
Given a Bayesian network and some observed evidence \(\mathbf{e}\) (values of a subset of variables), compute the posterior over query variables \(\mathbf{Q}\):

\[P(\mathbf{Q} \mid \mathbf{e}) = \frac{P(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{e})}{P(\mathbf{e})} = \frac{\sum_{\mathbf{h}} P(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{e}, \mathbf{h})}{\sum_{\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{h}} P(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{e}, \mathbf{h})}\]

where \(\mathbf{h}\) are the hidden (unobserved) variables. Naïve computation sums over all configurations of \(\mathbf{h}\) — exponential in the number of hidden variables.

docs.title: Variable Elimination
docs.text:
The key insight: the factorisation of the joint distribution means many sum-product computations can be reordered and cached.

Factor: A factor \(\phi(X_{i_1}, \ldots, X_{i_k})\) is a non-negative function over a subset of variables. The joint distribution is a product of factors.

Variable elimination sums out one variable at a time in a chosen order, multiplying and marginalising factors:

\[P(Q \mid \mathbf{e}) \propto \sum_{X_1} \sum_{X_2} \cdots \prod_i \phi_i(\text{scope}_i)\]

The order of summation determines the computational cost. Finding the optimal elimination order is NP-hard in general, but good heuristics exist (min-fill, min-degree).

Example (using Student network, query \(P(L \mid D = d^0)\)):

\[P(L \mid d^0) \propto \sum_G P(L \mid G) \sum_I P(G \mid d^0, I), P(I) \sum_S P(S \mid I)\]

The inner sum \(\sum_S P(S \mid I) = 1\) (marginalising a complete CPD). This cancels \(S\) with zero cost. The remaining sums are over \(I\) and \(G\) — small tables.

Complexity: Exponential in the treewidth of the graph — a measure of how "tree-like" the graph is. For trees and polytrees, exact inference is polynomial. For general graphs, it is #P-hard.

docs.title: Belief Propagation (Sum-Product Algorithm)
docs.text:
For trees (no undirected cycles), exact inference runs in \(O(n \cdot k^2)\) time via message passing.

Each node sends messages to its neighbours. The message \(\mu_{X \to Y}(y)\) represents a summary of what \(X\) knows about \(Y\), based on \(X\)'s other neighbours:

\[\mu_{X \to Y}(y) = \sum_x \phi(x, y) \prod_{Z \in \text{Ne}(X) \setminus Y} \mu_{Z \to X}(x)\]

The marginal at each node is proportional to the product of all incoming messages:

\[P(X \mid \mathbf{e}) \propto \prod_{Y \in \text{Ne}(X)} \mu_{Y \to X}(x)\]

For directed trees, this decomposes into two passes: a forward (upward, leaves-to-root) pass and a backward (downward, root-to-leaves) pass.

Loopy belief propagation (LBP): Run the same message-passing algorithm on a graph with cycles. The algorithm is no longer exact — messages depend on each other cyclically — but it often converges and gives good approximations. LBP underlies modern LDPC error-correcting codes and is used in computer vision (stereo matching, image segmentation).

docs.title: Approximate Inference
docs.text: For graphs with high treewidth, exact inference is intractable. The two main approaches:

docs.title: Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)
docs.text:
Construct a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is \(P(\mathbf{X} \mid \mathbf{e})\). Sample from it.

Gibbs sampling (most common for Bayesian networks): repeatedly sample each variable from its Markov blanket — its parents, children, and children's other parents:

\[X_i^{(t+1)} \sim P(X_i \mid \text{Pa}(X_i), \text{Ch}(X_i), \text{Pa}(\text{Ch}(X_i)))\]

The Markov blanket is exactly the minimal set you need to condition on to make \(X_i\) independent of all other variables — a direct consequence of d-separation.

Convergence: guaranteed to the correct distribution asymptotically. Mixing time (how many samples you need) depends on the strength of correlations.

docs.title: Variational Inference
docs.text: Approximate \(P(\mathbf{X} \mid \mathbf{e})\) with a simpler distribution \(Q(\mathbf{X}; \lambda)\) by minimising \(D_{KL}(Q | P)\). The mean-field approximation assumes \(Q\) factorises fully: \(Q(\mathbf{X}) = \prod_i Q_i(X_i)\). Leads to a coordinate ascent algorithm — the ELBO you saw in [[05.Autoencoders|VAEs]] is exactly this.

docs.title: ✦ Learning Bayesian Networks
docs.text: Two sub-problems:

docs.title: Parameter Learning (Known Structure)
docs.text:
Given a fixed graph \(\mathcal{G}\) and i.i.d. data \(\mathcal{D} = {x^{(1)}, \ldots, x^{(n)}}\), estimate the CPDs.

With complete data (no missing values): MLE decomposes over CPDs. For a discrete variable \(X_i\) with parents \(\text{Pa}(X_i)\):

\[\hat{P}(X_i = k \mid \text{Pa}(X_i) = \pi) = \frac{#{X_i = k, \text{Pa}(X_i) = \pi}}{#{\text{Pa}(X_i) = \pi}}\]

Just count — each CPD is independent and estimated by its frequency table. MLE is the empirical conditional distribution.

With missing data: The log-likelihood no longer decomposes. Must use EM (Expectation-Maximisation):

  • E-step: Compute expected sufficient statistics using current parameters and BP for inference.
  • M-step: Update each CPD using the expected counts from the E-step.

Bayesian parameter estimation: Place a Dirichlet prior over each CPD (conjugate to the Categorical). Posterior is Dirichlet with counts augmented by pseudo-counts. MAP estimate = \(\frac{\text{count} + \alpha - 1}{\text{total count} + K(\alpha-1)}\). This is Laplace smoothing for discrete CPDs.

docs.title: Structure Learning (Unknown Structure)
docs.text:
Find the graph \(\mathcal{G}\) that best explains the data. Two approaches:

Score-based: Search over DAG space, score each candidate graph. Common scores:

  • BIC: \(\text{score}(G, \mathcal{D}) = \log P(\mathcal{D} \mid \hat{\theta}, G) - \frac{\log n}{2} |\theta_G|\) — penalises complexity.
  • BDe score: Bayesian Dirichlet equivalent — integrates out parameters, proper Bayesian score.

DAG space is super-exponential in \(d\) — exact search is impossible. Heuristics: greedy hill-climbing (add/remove/reverse one edge at a time), simulated annealing, genetic algorithms.

Constraint-based: Use conditional independence tests (\(\chi^2\) tests, mutual information tests) to determine which edges cannot be present. The PC algorithm (Peter-Clark) works by:

  1. Start with a complete undirected graph.
  2. Remove edge \((X, Y)\) if \(\exists, Z\) such that \(X \perp!!!\perp Y \mid Z\) in the data.
  3. Orient remaining edges using v-structure identification.

The PC algorithm recovers the correct skeleton and all v-structures consistently in the large-sample limit, under faithfulness. Output is a CPDAG (completed partially directed acyclic graph) — the equivalence class of all DAGs with the same skeleton and v-structures.

docs.title: ✦ Markov Equivalence
docs.text:
Two DAGs are Markov equivalent if they encode the same set of conditional independences (same d-separation statements). Markov equivalent DAGs have the same skeleton (same undirected edges) and the same v-structures (colliders).

Implication: From observational data alone, you cannot distinguish between Markov equivalent DAGs. To identify causal direction within an equivalence class, you need either:

  • Interventional data (do-calculus, randomised experiments)
  • Additional assumptions (e.g., non-Gaussianity, as in LiNGAM)
  • Temporal order constraints

This is why correlation does not imply causation — many causal structures are observationally equivalent.

docs.title: ✦ Connection to AI / ML / Deep Learning
1. Naive Bayes as a Bayesian Network
docs.text:
The Naive Bayes classifier (see [[06.Naive Bayes]]) is a Bayesian network with a specific structure: one class node \(Y\) pointing to all feature nodes \(X_1, \ldots, X_d\) with no edges among the \(X_i\). The conditional independence assumption \(X_i \perp!!!\perp X_j \mid Y\) is exactly the d-separation statement in this graph. Every Naive Bayes model is a Bayesian network; not every Bayesian network is Naive Bayes.

Naive Bayes BN:

        Y
      / | \
     ▼  ▼  ▼
    X₁ X₂ X₃   (no edges between Xᵢ)

docs.title: 2. Hidden Markov Models
docs.text:
An HMM (see [[02.Markov Models]]) is a Bayesian network on a chain:

Z₁ ──► Z₂ ──► Z₃ ──► Z₄    (hidden states)
│      │      │      │
▼      ▼      ▼      ▼
X₁     X₂     X₃     X₄    (observations)

The Viterbi algorithm is variable elimination on this chain. The forward-backward algorithm is belief propagation on this tree. Everything in sequential modelling — speech recognition, POS tagging, protein folding — is a Bayesian network with temporal structure.

docs.title: 3. Variational Autoencoders
docs.text:
The VAE's generative model \(z \to x\) is a two-node Bayesian network:

\[P(z), P_\theta(x \mid z) = P(x, z)\]

The inference network \(q_\phi(z \mid x)\) approximates the posterior \(P(z \mid x)\) — this is variational inference on a Bayesian network. The ELBO is exactly the variational lower bound used in general Bayesian network inference. The VAE is deep learning's answer to intractable Bayesian network inference.

docs.title: 4. Causal Inference and Do-Calculus
docs.text:
Judea Pearl's do-calculus (Pearl, 2000) extends Bayesian networks to reason about interventions. The do-operator \(do(X = x)\) removes all incoming edges to \(X\) in \(\mathcal{G}\), fixing its value. The interventional distribution \(P(Y \mid do(X = x))\) is generally different from the observational conditional \(P(Y \mid X = x)\) — this is the formal statement of why correlation \(\neq\) causation.

Modern causal ML (IRM, causal representation learning) builds on this foundation to train models that generalise across environments — a central problem in robust ML.

docs.title: 5. Probabilistic Programming
docs.text: PyMC, Stan, Pyro, and NumPyro all represent probabilistic models as Bayesian networks (or their continuous generalisations). Inference is automated — the user specifies structure and CPDs; the system runs MCMC or variational inference. The structure-inference separation in Bayesian networks is what makes this abstraction possible.

docs.title: 6. Graph Neural Networks
docs.text: A Bayesian network is a graph with a probability model. GNNs learn representations over graphs — they can be applied to Bayesian networks directly, learning to do amortised inference (predict posteriors for unseen evidence configurations without re-running BP). This is an active research area.

docs.title: ✦ Implementation Sketch
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from itertools import product

# --- Exact inference via Variable Elimination (discrete, small BN) ---

class Factor:
    """A factor over a subset of discrete variables."""
    def __init__(self, variables, cardinalities, values):
        self.variables = list(variables)
        self.cards = {v: c for v, c in zip(variables, cardinalities)}
        self.values = np.array(values).reshape(cardinalities)

    def marginalise(self, var):
        """Sum out a variable."""
        axis = self.variables.index(var)
        new_vals = self.values.sum(axis=axis)
        new_vars = [v for v in self.variables if v != var]
        new_cards = [self.cards[v] for v in new_vars]
        return Factor(new_vars, new_cards, new_vals)

    def product(self, other):
        """Multiply two factors, aligning shared variables."""
        all_vars = self.variables + [v for v in other.variables
                                     if v not in self.variables]
        all_cards = [self.cards.get(v, other.cards[v]) for v in all_vars]
        new_vals = np.zeros(all_cards)
        for idx in product(*[range(c) for c in all_cards]):
            assign = dict(zip(all_vars, idx))
            i1 = tuple(assign[v] for v in self.variables)
            i2 = tuple(assign[v] for v in other.variables)
            new_vals[idx] = self.values[i1] * other.values[i2]
        return Factor(all_vars, all_cards, new_vals)

    def condition(self, var, val):
        """Condition on var = val (set all other slices to 0 and fix axis)."""
        axis = self.variables.index(var)
        slices = [slice(None)] * len(self.variables)
        slices[axis] = val
        new_vals = self.values[tuple(slices)]
        new_vars = [v for v in self.variables if v != var]
        new_cards = [self.cards[v] for v in new_vars]
        return Factor(new_vars, new_cards, new_vals)

    def normalise(self):
        self.values = self.values / self.values.sum()
        return self

# --- Student network CPDs ---
# Variables: D (0=easy,1=hard), I (0=low,1=high),
#            G (0=A,1=B,2=C), S (0=low,1=high), L (0=weak,1=strong)

P_D = Factor(['D'], [2], [0.6, 0.4])
P_I = Factor(['I'], [2], [0.7, 0.3])

# P(G | D, I): shape (2, 2, 3) — D, I, G
P_G_DI = Factor(['D','I','G'], [2,2,3],
    [[[0.30, 0.40, 0.30],   # D=easy, I=low
      [0.05, 0.25, 0.70]],  # D=easy, I=high  (note: high I → worse grade is rare)
     [[0.90, 0.08, 0.02],   # D=hard, I=low
      [0.50, 0.30, 0.20]]]) # D=hard, I=high

P_S_I = Factor(['I','S'], [2,2], [[0.95, 0.05], [0.20, 0.80]])
P_L_G = Factor(['G','L'], [3,2], [[0.10, 0.90], [0.40, 0.60], [0.99, 0.01]])

# Query: P(L | D=hard) via variable elimination
# Order: S, I, G (eliminate hidden vars one at a time)
evidence = {'D': 1}  # D = hard

# Condition on evidence
f_D = P_D.condition('D', 1)
f_G = P_G_DI.condition('D', 1)  # Factor(['I','G'], ...)

# Eliminate S: marginalise out S from P_S_I
f_SI = P_S_I  # no evidence on S
f_S_marginalised = f_SI.marginalise('S')  # = Factor(['I'], ...) = [1, 1] (trivial)

# Eliminate I: multiply P(I), P(G|I, D=hard), P(S|I) and sum over I
f_combined = P_I.product(f_G).product(f_S_marginalised)
f_I_out = f_combined.marginalise('I')  # Factor over G

# Eliminate G: multiply P(L|G) and sum over G
f_LG = P_L_G.product(f_I_out)
f_L = f_LG.marginalise('G')
f_L.normalise()
print("P(L | D=hard):", f_L.values)
# → P(L=weak | D=hard), P(L=strong | D=hard)

docs.title: Markov Models
docs.text: "The future is independent of the past, given the present." — The Markov property, in plain English

docs.title: ✦ Why This Note Exists
docs.text:
Before we can talk about speech recognition, part-of-speech tagging, biological sequence alignment, or the underpinnings of modern reinforcement learning, we need a principled way to model sequences. The Markov model is that foundation.

This note builds the full machinery — from the basic chain to Hidden Markov Models and their three canonical algorithms — with every equation derived, every assumption named, and every connection to the broader ML map made explicit.

Prerequisites: [[03.Probability Review]] · [[01.The Learning Problem]] Feeds into: [[01.The RL Problem]] · [[01.Bayesian Networks]] · (eventually) Transformers and attention

docs.title: ✦ The Core Problem: Sequential Data
docs.text:
Most of classical ML assumes i.i.d. data: each \((x_i, y_i)\) is drawn independently from the same distribution. That assumption collapses the moment you have:

  • A sentence (each word depends on preceding words)
  • A time series (stock prices, sensor readings)
  • A DNA strand (nucleotide probabilities shift with context)
  • A trajectory in an RL environment

You need a model that respects temporal or positional structure. Markov models are the principled answer.

docs.title: 1.1 The Markov Property
docs.text:
Let \(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_T\) be a sequence of random variables taking values in a finite state space \(\mathcal{S} = {s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_N}\).

Definition (Markov Property, first-order): $$ P(X_t \mid X_{t-1}, X_{t-2}, \ldots, X_1) = P(X_t \mid X_{t-1}) $$

The present state \(X_{t-1}\) is a sufficient statistic for predicting the future. The entire history is irrelevant — all relevant information has already been "compressed" into the current state.

Notebook margin: The first-order assumption is a modelling choice, not a law of nature. You can always extend to \(k\)-th order: \(P(X_t \mid X_{t-k}, \ldots, X_{t-1})\). A \(k\)-th order chain over \(|\mathcal{S}|\) states is equivalent to a first-order chain over \(|\mathcal{S}|^k\) states, so we lose no generality by studying first-order chains.

docs.title: 1.2 The Transition Matrix
docs.text:
Assuming time homogeneity (transition probabilities don't change with \(t\)), we define: $$ A_{ij} = P(X_t = s_j \mid X_{t-1} = s_i), \quad A \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N} $$

Properties:

  • \(A_{ij} \geq 0\) for all \(i, j\)
  • \(\sum_j A_{ij} = 1\) for all \(i\) — each row is a probability distribution
  • \(A\) is called a stochastic matrix (or row-stochastic matrix)

The initial distribution \(\pi_0 \in \mathbb{R}^N\), where \((\pi_0)_i = P(X_1 = s_i)\), completes the model specification.

docs.title: 1.3 Computing Sequence Probabilities
docs.text:
The joint probability of a sequence \(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_T\) follows directly from the chain rule + Markov property: $$ P(X_1 = x_1, \ldots, X_T = x_T) = P(X_1 = x_1) \prod_{t=2}^T P(X_t = x_t \mid X_{t-1} = x_{t-1}) $$ $$ = (\pi_0){x_1} \prod $$}^T A_{x_{t-1}, x_t

This is a product of matrix entries — beautifully simple.

docs.title: 1.4 The Stationary Distribution
docs.text:
After many steps, does the chain "settle" into a stable distribution?

Definition: A distribution \(\pi^_\) is stationary (invariant) if: $$ \pi^_ = \pi^* A \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad (\pi_)T = A^T (\pi_)T $$ \(\pi^*\) is the left eigenvector of \(A\) corresponding to eigenvalue 1 (which always exists for stochastic matrices by the Perron-Frobenius theorem).

Convergence: If the chain is irreducible (every state reachable from every state) and aperiodic (no cycles), then for any initial distribution \(\pi_0\): $$ \lim_{t \to \infty} \pi_0 A^t = \pi^* $$

Example — A simple 2-state weather model: States: \({\)Sunny, Rainy\(}\), transition matrix: $\(A = \begin{pmatrix} 0.9 & 0.1 \ 0.5 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix}\)$ Row 1: if sunny today → 90% sunny tomorrow, 10% rainy. Stationary distribution: solve \(\pi^* A = \pi^_\), \(\pi^__S + \pi^__R = 1\): $\(\pi^__S = 0.833, \quad \pi^*_R = 0.167\)$ On a long enough timescale, ~83% of days are sunny regardless of today's weather.

docs.title: 2.1 Motivation: When the State Is Not Observed
docs.text:
In a plain Markov chain, the state \(X_t\) is directly observed. But in many real problems:

  • In speech recognition, the underlying phoneme is hidden; we observe an acoustic signal.
  • In POS tagging, the underlying grammar tag (noun, verb, ...) is hidden; we observe words.
  • In finance, "market regime" (bull/bear) is latent; we observe returns.

The Hidden Markov Model (HMM) separates the latent state sequence from the observed sequence.

docs.title: 2.2 Formal Definition
docs.text:
An HMM is a tuple \(\lambda = (A, B, \pi)\):

Symbol Name Definition \(\mathcal{S} = {s_1, \ldots, s_N}\) Hidden state space Latent states \(\mathcal{V} = {v_1, \ldots, v_M}\) Observation vocabulary Observable symbols \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}\) Transition matrix \(A_{ij} = P(z_t = s_j \mid z_{t-1} = s_i)\) \(B \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times M}\) Emission matrix \(B_{ik} = P(x_t = v_k \mid z_t = s_i)\) \(\pi \in \mathbb{R}^N\) Initial distribution \(\pi_i = P(z_1 = s_i)\)

The generative process:

  1. Sample initial state \(z_1 \sim \pi\)
  2. Emit observation \(x_t \sim B_{z_t}\) (the \(z_t\)-th row of \(B\))
  3. Transition to \(z_{t+1} \sim A_{z_t}\) (the \(z_t\)-th row of \(A\))
  4. Repeat from step 2

The joint distribution: $$ P(x_{1:T}, z_{1:T}) = \pi_{z_1} \prod_{t=1}^T B_{z_t, x_t} \prod_{t=2}^T A_{z_{t-1}, z_t} $$

Graphical structure:

  z_1  -->  z_2  -->  z_3  --> ... -->  z_T
   |          |          |                |
   v          v          v                v
  x_1        x_2        x_3             x_T

Hidden states form a Markov chain (top).
Each state independently emits an observation (bottom).

docs.title: 2.3 The Three Problems of HMMs
docs.text:
Rabiner (1989) identified three canonical problems that must be solved for HMMs to be useful in practice. Every algorithm below solves exactly one of them.

# Problem Question Algorithm 1 Evaluation Given \(\lambda\) and observations \(x_{1:T}\), what is \(P(x_{1:T} \mid \lambda)\)? Forward Algorithm 2 Decoding Given \(\lambda\) and \(x_{1:T}\), what is the most likely state sequence \(z_{1:T}^*\)? Viterbi Algorithm 3 Learning Given \(x_{1:T}\), find \(\lambda^* = \arg\max_\lambda P(x_{1:T} \mid \lambda)\) Baum-Welch (EM)

docs.title: 3.1 Why Naïve Computation Fails
docs.text:
The observation likelihood is: $$ P(x_{1:T} \mid \lambda) = \sum_{z_{1:T}} P(x_{1:T}, z_{1:T} \mid \lambda) $$

Summing over all \(N^T\) state sequences is \(O(N^T)\) — exponential in sequence length. For \(N = 10\), \(T = 100\): \(10^{100}\) terms. Completely intractable.

docs.title: 3.2 The Forward Variable
docs.text: Define the forward variable: $$ \alpha_t(i) := P(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_t, z_t = s_i \mid \lambda) $$ "The probability of seeing the partial observation sequence \(x_1, \ldots, x_t\) and being in state \(s_i\) at time \(t\)."

docs.title: 3.3 The Forward Recursion
docs.text:
Initialisation (\(t = 1\)): $$ \alpha_1(i) = \pi_i \cdot B_{i, x_1} $$

Recursion (\(t = 2, \ldots, T\)): $$ \boxed{\alpha_t(j) = \left[ \sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_{t-1}(i) \cdot A_{ij} \right] \cdot B_{j, x_t}} $$

The bracket sums over all ways to arrive in state \(j\) at time \(t\), then multiplies by the emission probability of \(x_t\) from state \(j\).

Termination: $$ P(x_{1:T} \mid \lambda) = \sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_T(i) $$

Complexity: \(O(N^2 T)\) — polynomial. We've converted exponential summation into dynamic programming.

Derivation sketch: $\(\alpha_t(j) = P(x_{1:t}, z_t = j) = \sum_i P(x_{1:t}, z_{t-1} = i, z_t = j)\)$ $\(= \sum_i P(x_t \mid z_t = j) \cdot P(z_t = j \mid z_{t-1} = i) \cdot P(x_{1:t-1}, z_{t-1} = i)\)$ $\(= B_{j,x_t} \sum_i A_{ij} \cdot \alpha_{t-1}(i) \qquad \square\)$

docs.title: 3.4 Numerical Issues: Log-Space Computation
docs.text:
Products of small probabilities underflow to zero rapidly. Standard fix: work in log-space using the log-sum-exp trick: $$ \log \sum_i e^{a_i} = a^* + \log \sum_i e^{a_i - a^}, \quad a^ = \max_i a_i $$

Notebook margin: This same trick appears in logistic regression (softmax), language model decoding, and variational inference. It's one of the half-dozen truly universal numerical tools in ML.

docs.title: 4.1 What We Want
docs.text:
Find the single most probable state sequence given the observations: $$ z^*{1:T} = \arg\max \mid \lambda) $$}} P(z_{1:T} \mid x_{1:T}, \lambda) = \arg\max_{z_{1:T}} P(z_{1:T}, x_{1:T

Note: This is the joint MAP over the entire sequence — it is not the sequence of individually most probable states \(\arg\max_{z_t} P(z_t \mid x_{1:T})\) at each time step (those are obtained by the backward algorithm and do not form a coherent sequence).

docs.title: 4.2 The Viterbi Variable
docs.text:
Define: $$ \delta_t(i) := \max_{z_{1:t-1}} P(z_1, \ldots, z_{t-1}, z_t = s_i, x_1, \ldots, x_t \mid \lambda) $$ "The probability of the most likely path ending in state \(s_i\) at time \(t\), given observations so far."

To recover the actual path, store the backpointer: $$ \psi_t(j) := \arg\max_i \left[ \delta_{t-1}(i) \cdot A_{ij} \right] $$

docs.title: 4.3 The Viterbi Recursion
docs.text:
Initialisation: $$ \delta_1(i) = \pi_i \cdot B_{i, x_1}, \quad \psi_1(i) = 0 $$

Recursion (\(t = 2, \ldots, T\)): $$ \boxed{\delta_t(j) = \max_i \left[ \delta_{t-1}(i) \cdot A_{ij} \right] \cdot B_{j, x_t}} $$ $$ \psi_t(j) = \arg\max_i \left[ \delta_{t-1}(i) \cdot A_{ij} \right] $$

Termination: $$ P^* = \max_i \delta_T(i), \quad z_T^* = \arg\max_i \delta_T(i) $$

Backtracking (\(t = T-1, \ldots, 1\)): $$ z_t^* = \psi_{t+1}(z_{t+1}^*) $$

Complexity: \(O(N^2 T)\) — identical to the forward algorithm, because we replaced \(\sum\) with \(\max\).

Insight: Viterbi is just the forward algorithm with \(\sum \to \max\). This swap is not cosmetic — it changes the semantics entirely from marginalisation to optimisation. The same substitution appears in belief propagation (sum-product vs. max-product) and in dynamic programming generally (shortest path vs. counting paths).

Example — POS Tagging: Sentence: "flies like arrows" States: \({\)NOUN, VERB, PREP\(}\) The word "flies" can be NOUN ("the flies") or VERB ("he flies"). "like" can be VERB or PREP. Viterbi finds the globally most coherent assignment — e.g., VERB-PREP-NOUN — using transition probabilities between POS tags (which encode grammar) and emission probabilities (which encode lexical likelihood).

docs.title: 5.1 The Problem Setup
docs.text:
Given: Observation sequences \(x_{1:T}\) (the state sequence \(z_{1:T}\) is latent). Find: \(\lambda^* = (A^_, B^_, \pi^*) = \arg\max_\lambda P(x_{1:T} \mid \lambda)\).

Direct MLE is intractable because the state sequence is hidden. This is exactly the structure EM was designed for.

Recall from [[03.Probability Review]]: EM maximises the ELBO (Evidence Lower Bound): $$ \log P(x \mid \lambda) \geq \mathbb{E}{q(z)}[\log P(x, z \mid \lambda)] - \mathbb{E}[\log q(z)] $$

In the E-step, set \(q(z) = P(z \mid x, \lambda_{\text{old}})\). In the M-step, maximise the expected complete-data log-likelihood.

docs.title: 5.2 The Backward Variable
docs.text:
To compute the posterior \(P(z_{1:T} \mid x_{1:T}, \lambda)\), we need both a forward and a backward pass.

Define the backward variable: $$ \beta_t(i) := P(x_{t+1}, x_{t+2}, \ldots, x_T \mid z_t = s_i, \lambda) $$ "The probability of the future observations \(x_{t+1:T}\), given that we're in state \(s_i\) at time \(t\)."

Initialisation: $$ \beta_T(i) = 1 \quad \text{for all } i $$

Recursion (\(t = T-1, \ldots, 1\)): $$ \boxed{\beta_t(i) = \sum_j A_{ij} \cdot B_{j, x_{t+1}} \cdot \beta_{t+1}(j)} $$

docs.title: 5.3 The Posterior Statistics
docs.text:
Using both \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), we can compute the two key posterior quantities:

State occupancy — probability of being in state \(i\) at time \(t\): $$ \gamma_t(i) := P(z_t = s_i \mid x_{1:T}, \lambda) = \frac{\alpha_t(i) \cdot \beta_t(i)}{\sum_k \alpha_t(k) \cdot \beta_t(k)} $$

Transition occupancy — probability of transitioning \(i \to j\) at time \(t\): $$ \xi_t(i,j) := P(z_t = s_i, z_{t+1} = s_j \mid x_{1:T}, \lambda) = \frac{\alpha_t(i) \cdot A_{ij} \cdot B_{j, x_{t+1}} \cdot \beta_{t+1}(j)}{\sum_{i'}\sum_{j'} \alpha_t(i') \cdot A_{i'j'} \cdot B_{j', x_{t+1}} \cdot \beta_{t+1}(j')} $$

docs.title: 5.4 The M-Step: Parameter Re-estimation
docs.text:
The Baum-Welch re-estimation equations are the M-step closed-form solutions (derivable by Lagrange multipliers subject to the stochastic constraints):

\[ \hat{\pi}_i = \gamma_1(i) \] \[ \hat{A}_{ij} = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \xi_t(i,j)}{\sum_{t=1}^{T-1} \gamma_t(i)} \quad = \frac{\text{expected number of } i \to j \text{ transitions}}{\text{expected time in state } i} \] \[ \hat{B}_{ik} = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^T \gamma_t(i) \cdot \mathbf{1}[x_t = v_k]}{\sum_{t=1}^T \gamma_t(i)} \quad = \frac{\text{expected time in state } i \text{ emitting } v_k}{\text{expected time in state } i} \]

docs.title: 5.5 Convergence Properties
docs.text:
• Guaranteed: Each EM iteration increases \(P(x_{1:T} \mid \lambda)\) (or leaves it unchanged).
  • Not guaranteed: Convergence to the global maximum. HMM likelihood surfaces are non-convex with multiple local optima.
  • Practical fix: Multiple random initialisations; choose the run with highest final likelihood.

The EM lens: Baum-Welch is EM with:

  • Latent variable: state sequence \(z_{1:T}\)
  • E-step: run Forward-Backward to compute \(\gamma_t, \xi_t\) (soft assignments)
  • M-step: plug into re-estimation formulas (weighted MLE with soft counts) Compare to K-Means (hard assignments) vs. GMM (soft assignments). Baum-Welch is the sequential analogue of GMM's EM.

docs.title: ✦ Part 6 — Continuous Observations
docs.text:
So far, \(x_t\) has been discrete (a vocabulary symbol). For real-valued observations (e.g., acoustic feature vectors in speech), replace the discrete emission matrix \(B\) with a continuous density:

\[ b_i(x_t) = \mathcal{N}(x_t \mid \mu_i, \Sigma_i) \quad \text{or} \quad b_i(x_t) = \sum_m c_{im} \mathcal{N}(x_t \mid \mu_{im}, \Sigma_{im}) \]

The Gaussian Mixture emission is standard in speech recognition. The M-step updates for \(\mu_i, \Sigma_i\) are just weighted MLE updates — same structure as GMM.

docs.title: ✦ Part 7 — Connection to AI and Deep Learning
7.1 Classical Applications
docs.text: Application Hidden States Observations Speech recognition Phoneme sequence Acoustic feature vectors (MFCCs) POS tagging Grammar tag sequence Word tokens Biological sequences Functional region (exon/intron) Nucleotides Gesture recognition Gesture phase Accelerometer readings Financial regime detection Market regime (bull/bear/volatile) Log-returns

docs.title: 7.2 HMMs as a Precursor to Deep Sequence Models
docs.text:
HMMs encode a specific inductive bias:

  • Markov assumption: only one step of memory
  • Parametric emissions: fixed functional form (Gaussian, multinomial)
  • Fixed state space: \(N\) states defined ahead of time

Modern sequence models relax all three assumptions:

Limitation How DL addressed it 1-step memory RNNs/LSTMs: learn arbitrary-length memory via gated hidden state \(h_t\) Parametric emission Neural language models: learn emission distribution from data Fixed discrete states Continuous latent spaces: VAEs, RNNs with dense hidden state \(h_t \in \mathbb{R}^d\) Markov property Transformers: full attention over all positions — explicitly non-Markovian

Yet HMMs remain the conceptual foundation. Understanding the three HMM problems — evaluation, decoding, learning — gives you the right vocabulary for understanding attention (soft assignment over positions), CTC decoding (sequence alignment), and the ELBO in VAEs (same EM structure, continuous latent variables).

docs.title: 7.3 HMMs in the Modern ML Stack
docs.text:
HMM (1960s–1990s)
  │
  ├── Recurrent Neural Networks (1986, Elman)
  │     └── LSTM (1997, Hochreiter & Schmidhuber)
  │           └── GRU (2014) → seq2seq → Attention → Transformer (2017)
  │
  ├── CRF (2001) → BiLSTM-CRF (still used in NER)
  │
  └── Structured State Spaces (S4, Mamba, 2021–2023)
        — HMM dynamics as a continuous-time model

Mamba (2023) explicitly revisits selective state-space models, a direct generalisation of HMMs, and achieves Transformer-level performance with linear complexity. HMMs are not historical curiosities — they are the theoretical backbone of an active research direction.

docs.title: 7.4 RL Connection
docs.text:
The HMM generative model \((A, B)\) is structurally identical to a Partially Observable MDP (POMDP):

  • Transition matrix \(A\) ↔ transition function \(P(s' \mid s, a)\)
  • Emission matrix \(B\) ↔ observation function \(P(o \mid s)\)

The Viterbi algorithm for decoding corresponds to finding the optimal policy in a degenerate POMDP. This connection deepens when we study RL with partial observability — the belief state maintained by the forward algorithm becomes the "sufficient statistic for planning."

docs.title: The Forward-Backward Lattice
docs.text:
Time:      t=1          t=2          t=3        ...   t=T
           ┌──────┐    ┌──────┐    ┌──────┐         ┌──────┐
State s_1  │α₁(1) │───▶│α₂(1) │───▶│α₃(1) │ ───▶   │αT(1) │
           └──────┘    └──────┘    └──────┘         └──────┘
                \    /        \    /
           ┌──────┐    ┌──────┐    ┌──────┐         ┌──────┐
State s_2  │α₁(2) │───▶│α₂(2) │───▶│α₃(2) │ ───▶   │αT(2) │
           └──────┘    └──────┘    └──────┘         └──────┘
                 ▲           ▲           ▲                 ▲
Observations:  x_1          x_2          x_3              x_T

Forward pass: → propagates probability left-to-right
Backward pass: ← propagates probability right-to-left
Both passes together: give full posterior γ_t(i) at every node

docs.title: The Three Algorithms at a Glance
docs.text:
Forward            Viterbi            Baum-Welch
           ───────            ───────            ──────────
Goal:    P(x_{1:T}|λ)      best z*_{1:T}       best λ*

How:     sum over paths    max over paths       EM: E=Forward-Backward
                                                    M=re-estimation

Replace: sum → sum         sum → max            iterate until convergence

Output:  scalar            sequence             new parameters (A,B,π)

Cost:    O(N²T)            O(N²T)              O(N²T) per iteration

docs.title: ✦ Complexity and Practical Notes
docs.text:
Operation Complexity Notes Forward algorithm \(O(N^2 T)\) Compute \(P(x_{1:T})\) Backward algorithm \(O(N^2 T)\) Needed for Baum-Welch E-step Viterbi decoding \(O(N^2 T)\) Path backtracking adds \(O(NT)\) memory Baum-Welch (per iteration) \(O(N^2 T)\) Often needs 50–200 iterations State space size \(N\) \(N^2\) in complexity \(N\) is a key hyperparameter; typically 5–100

Implementation notes for Python:

  • Work in log-space throughout; use scipy.special.logsumexp
  • Multiple restarts: train 10 random models, keep the best
  • hmmlearn is the standard Python library; understand it well enough to reimplement it
  • For large-scale applications (speech), deep learning replaced HMMs; but the decoding algorithms survive as postprocessing steps

docs.title: ✦ Exit Criterion
docs.text:
You know this when: you can derive the forward recursion from first principles (chain rule + Markov property), explain why Viterbi uses \(\max\) where forward uses \(\sum\) and what that changes semantically, implement Baum-Welch's E-step from scratch in NumPy, and describe exactly how HMMs connect to RNNs and POMDPs.

Concrete exercises:

  1. Implement the 3-state weather HMM from scratch: initialise \(A\), \(B\), \(\pi\) randomly; run Baum-Welch on a synthetic sequence; verify the learned parameters recover the ground truth.
  2. Implement Viterbi for POS tagging on a tiny corpus. Compare the Viterbi sequence to the sequence of per-step argmax posteriors \(\arg\max_i \gamma_t(i)\) — show they differ.
  3. Derive the M-step update for \(\hat{A}_{ij}\) using Lagrange multipliers on the constraint \(\sum_j A_{ij} = 1\).
