docs.title: Gaussian Processes
docs.text: "A Gaussian process is a probability distribution over functions, such that any finite collection of function values has a joint Gaussian distribution." — Rasmussen & Williams, 2006

docs.title: ✦ Why This Note Exists
docs.text:
Every model we've built so far has been parametric: fix a functional form, learn a finite-dimensional parameter vector \(\theta\). A Gaussian process takes a different path entirely — it places a prior directly over the space of functions, then conditions on data to obtain a posterior over functions.

This sounds abstract. It is not. The payoff is a model that:

  • makes predictions with calibrated uncertainty — the posterior variance tells you where it doesn't know
  • incorporates prior knowledge about function structure through kernel design
  • updates exactly via Bayes' theorem, no MCMC needed (for regression)
  • subsumes kernel ridge regression, spline smoothing, and RBF-kernel SVMs as special cases

GPs sit at the intersection of Bayesian inference, kernel methods, and functional analysis. Understanding them sharpens your intuition for everything that comes after — neural network weight-space vs. function-space perspectives, neural tangent kernels, and Bayesian deep learning.

Prerequisites: [[03.Probability Review]] · [[04.Support Vector Machines]] (kernel trick) · Linear Algebra (eigendecomposition, positive semi-definiteness) Feeds into: [[01.Kernel Methods]] · [[05.Hyperparameter Tuning]] (Bayesian optimisation) · Neural Tangent Kernel (advanced)

docs.title: 1.1 The Parametric Bottleneck
docs.text:
In Bayesian linear regression, we place a prior on the weight vector \(w \in \mathbb{R}^d\): $$ w \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \alpha^{-1} I), \quad y = w^T \phi(x) + \varepsilon, \quad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2) $$

This is expressive — but the function class is fixed by the choice of basis \(\phi(x)\). If you pick \(d = 10\) basis functions, you've committed to a 10-dimensional function space. You can extend \(\phi\) (polynomial, RBF, Fourier features...) but you're always choosing in advance.

The weight-space view: place a prior on \(w\), integrate out \(w\) to get a distribution over function values.

The function-space view: place the prior directly on \(f : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}\).

The key insight is that these are equivalent when the prior on \(w\) is Gaussian — and the function-space view generalises beyond finite-dimensional \(w\).

docs.title: 1.2 What Does a Prior Over Functions Mean?
docs.text:
A prior over functions seems infinite-dimensional and unwieldy. The Gaussian process sidesteps this through a consistency condition:

Definition (Gaussian Process): A Gaussian process is a collection of random variables \({f(x) : x \in \mathcal{X}}\) such that for any finite set of inputs \({x_1, \ldots, x_n} \subset \mathcal{X}\), the joint distribution: $$ \begin{pmatrix} f(x_1) \vdots f(x_n) \end{pmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{m}, K) $$ where \(m_i = m(x_i)\) and \(K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j)\).

We write: \(f \sim \mathcal{GP}(m(x),, k(x, x'))\)

The GP is completely specified by:

  • Mean function \(m(x) = \mathbb{E}[f(x)]\) — often set to zero a priori
  • Covariance function (kernel) \(k(x, x') = \text{Cov}(f(x), f(x'))\)

The key move: you never have to work with an infinite-dimensional object. Any computation with a GP reduces to a finite-dimensional multivariate Gaussian computation on the inputs you actually care about. The Kolmogorov extension theorem guarantees that a consistent family of finite-dimensional Gaussians uniquely defines a valid stochastic process.

docs.title: ✦ Part 2 — The Kernel: Encoding Prior Beliefs
2.1 The Kernel as a Similarity Measure
docs.text:
The kernel \(k(x, x')\) encodes our prior belief about how correlated \(f(x)\) and \(f(x')\) are. If \(k(x, x')\) is large, we believe \(f(x)\) and \(f(x')\) should take similar values.

This is precisely the kernel trick from SVMs — but now it has a direct probabilistic interpretation: \(k\) is the prior covariance between function values.

Validity condition (Mercer's theorem): \(k\) is a valid kernel iff the Gram matrix \(K\) with \(K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j)\) is positive semi-definite for all finite input sets. Equivalently, \(k(x, x') = \langle \phi(x), \phi(x') \rangle_\mathcal{H}\) for some (possibly infinite-dimensional) feature map \(\phi\) into a Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H}\).

docs.title: 2.2 Standard Kernels
docs.text: Each kernel encodes a different structural assumption about \(f\):

docs.title: Squared Exponential (RBF / Gaussian) Kernel
docs.text:
\[ k_{\text{SE}}(x, x') = \sigma_f^2 \exp!\left(-\frac{|x - x'|^2}{2\ell^2}\right) \]
  • Hyperparameters: \(\sigma_f^2\) (output scale), \(\ell\) (length-scale)
  • Encodes: infinitely differentiable, very smooth functions
  • Length-scale \(\ell\): controls how quickly the function varies. Small \(\ell\) → wiggly functions; large \(\ell\) → smooth, slowly varying functions
  • Feature map: corresponds to an infinite-dimensional feature space (Fourier features expansion)
  • Caution: too smooth for many real phenomena — geological, financial, biological data often has rougher structure

docs.title: Matérn Kernel
docs.text:
$$ k_{ u}(x, x') = rac{2^{1- u}}{\Gamma( u)} \left( rac{\sqrt{2 u} |x-x'|}{\ell} ight)^ u K_ u!\left( rac{\sqrt{2 u}|x-x'|}{\ell} ight) $$ where \(K_ u\) is a modified Bessel function.

  • Parameter \( u\): controls differentiability. \( u = 1/2\) → once-differentiable (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck); \( u = 3/2\) → twice; \( u = 5/2\) → three times; \( u o \infty\) → SE kernel
  • Why it matters: \( u = 5/2\) is the default recommendation in practice — smoother than OU, less pathologically smooth than SE
  • Special cases:
    • \( u = 1/2\): \(k(r) = \sigma^2 e^{-r/\ell}\) — exponential kernel, continuous but not differentiable
    • \( u = 3/2\): \(k(r) = \sigma^2(1 + rac{\sqrt{3}r}{\ell})\exp(- rac{\sqrt{3}r}{\ell})\)

docs.title: Periodic Kernel
docs.text: $$ k_{\text{per}}(x, x') = \sigma_f^2 \exp!\left(-\frac{2\sin2(\pi|x-x'|/p)}{\ell2}\right) $$ Encodes exactly periodic functions with period \(p\). Combine with SE kernel (multiply) to get functions that are approximately periodic with decaying coherence — standard for seasonal time series.

docs.title: Linear Kernel
docs.text: $$ k_{\text{lin}}(x, x') = \sigma_b^2 + \sigma_v^2 (x - c)(x' - c) $$ GP with this kernel is equivalent to Bayesian linear regression through the point \(c\). Useful as a component in additive kernel decompositions.

docs.title: Rational Quadratic Kernel
docs.text: $$ k_{\text{RQ}}(x, x') = \sigma_f^2\left(1 + \frac{|x-x'|2}{2\alpha\ell2}\right)^{-\alpha} $$ A scale mixture of SE kernels with different length-scales. As \(\alpha \to \infty\), recovers SE. Useful when the signal varies at multiple scales.

docs.title: 2.3 Kernel Engineering
docs.text:
Kernels compose:

  • Sum: \(k = k_1 + k_2\) → function is a sum of two independent GPs (additive structure)
  • Product: \(k = k_1 \cdot k_2\) → modulation; e.g., periodic \(\times\) SE = locally periodic
  • Composition: \(k_{\text{SE}}(g(x), g(x'))\) for learned feature maps \(g\) → deep kernels, connection to deep learning

Notebook margin — the kernel as a scientist's voice: When you choose a kernel, you are making a scientific claim about the structure of \(f\). SE says "I believe \(f\) is very smooth." Matérn-5/2 says "I believe \(f\) is three-times differentiable but not more." Periodic says "I believe there is a repeating structure with period \(p\)." The posterior will update these beliefs given data — but the kernel determines what it's even possible to learn.

docs.title: 3.1 The Setup
docs.text:
Observed data: \(\mathcal{D} = {(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^n\) where \(y_i = f(x_i) + \varepsilon_i\), \(\varepsilon_i \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_n^2)\)

Prior: \(f \sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k(x, x'))\) (zero mean WLOG)

Goal: compute the posterior \(p(f \mid \mathcal{D})\) and the predictive distribution \(p(f_* \mid x__, \mathcal{D})\) at new test points \(x__\).

docs.title: 3.2 The Joint Prior
docs.text:
Let \(\mathbf{f} = (f(x_1), \ldots, f(x_n))^T\) and \(f_* = f(x__)\). By the GP definition: $$ \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{y} f__ \end{pmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N}!\left(\mathbf{0},, \begin{pmatrix} K(X, X) + \sigma_n^2 I & K(X, x__) K(x__, X) & k(x__, x__) \end{pmatrix}\right) $$

where:

  • \(K(X, X) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\): Gram matrix, \(K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j)\)
  • \(K(X, x__) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 1}\): covariance between training inputs and test point, \([K(X, x__)]_i = k(x_i, x_*)\)
  • \(k(x__, x__)\): prior variance at test point

docs.title: 3.3 The Posterior Predictive Distribution
docs.text:
Using the Gaussian conditioning formula (the fundamental operation of all Gaussian inference):

Lemma (Conditional Gaussian): If \(\begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{a} \ \mathbf{b} \end{pmatrix} \sim \mathcal{N}!\left(\begin{pmatrix} \mu_a \ \mu_b \end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix} \Sigma_{aa} & \Sigma_{ab} \ \Sigma_{ba} & \Sigma_{bb} \end{pmatrix}\right)\) then: $\(\mathbf{a} \mid \mathbf{b} \sim \mathcal{N}!\left(\mu_a + \Sigma_{ab}\Sigma_{bb}^{-1}(\mathbf{b} - \mu_b),\ \Sigma_{aa} - \Sigma_{ab}\Sigma_{bb}^{-1}\Sigma_{ba}\right)\)$

Applying this with \(\mathbf{a} = f_*\), \(\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{y}\):

\[ \boxed{f_* \mid x__, X, \mathbf{y} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu__, \sigma_*^2)} \] \[ \mu_* = K(x_*, X),[K(X,X) + \sigma_n^2 I]^{-1},\mathbf{y} \] \[ \sigma__^2 = k(x__, x__) - K(x__, X),[K(X,X) + \sigma_n^2 I]^{-1},K(X, x_*) \]

This is the complete solution. No approximation. Exact Bayesian inference in closed form.

docs.title: 3.4 Interpretation — What These Equations Say
docs.text:
The mean \(\mu_*\): $$ \mu_* = K(x_*, X) \underbrace{[K(X,X) + \sigma_n^2 I]^{-1} \mathbf{y}}_{\alpha} $$

This is a linear combination of training outputs, weighted by the covariance between \(x__\) and each training input. Nearby training points (large \(k(x__, x_i)\)) contribute more. This is kernel regression — the GP mean is identical to kernel ridge regression with \(\lambda = \sigma_n^2 / \sigma_f^2\).

The variance \(\sigma_*^2\): $$ \sigma__^2 = \underbrace{k(x__, x__)}{\text{prior variance}} - \underbrace{K(x_, X)[K + \sigma_n^2 I]^{-1}K(X, x_*)}_{\text{variance reduction from data}} $$

The posterior variance is the prior variance minus what we learned from the data. The second term is always non-negative (positive semi-definiteness of \(K\)), so data never increases uncertainty. Crucially:

  • At a training input \(x_i\): \(\sigma_*^2 \to 0\) as \(\sigma_n^2 \to 0\) (exact fit)
  • Far from all training data: \(\sigma__^2 \approx k(x__, x_*)\) (reverts to prior)

Worked example — 1D regression: Prior: \(f \sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k_{\text{SE}})\) with \(\ell = 1\), \(\sigma_f^2 = 1\), \(\sigma_n^2 = 0.1\) Training data: 5 points sampled from \(\sin(x) + \mathcal{N}(0, 0.1)\)

The posterior mean threads through the data. The posterior variance (shaded region) is:

  • narrow near training points (we've observed \(f\) there)
  • wide in regions with no data (we genuinely don't know)
  • wider than the noise level even at training points (because we know \(y = f + \varepsilon\), not \(f\) directly)

This is calibrated uncertainty — the 95% confidence band actually contains 95% of future observations.

docs.title: 3.5 Predicting at Multiple Test Points
docs.text:
For a vector of test points \(X_* = (x_{_1}, \ldots, x_{_m})\): $$ \mathbf{f}__ \mid X__, X, \mathbf{y} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}*, \Sigma_) $$ $$ \boldsymbol{\mu}__ = K(X__, X)[K(X,X) + \sigma_n^2 I]^{-1}\mathbf{y} $$ $$ \Sigma__ = K(X__, X__) - K(X__, X)[K(X,X) + \sigma_n^2 I]^{-1}K(X, X__) $$

The full posterior covariance \(\Sigma_*\) captures correlation between predictions at different test points — this is something no other standard regression model directly provides.

docs.title: ✦ Part 4 — Computational Complexity and the \(O(n^3)\) Wall
4.1 The Bottleneck
docs.text:
The posterior requires computing \([K(X,X) + \sigma_n^2 I]^{-1}\). For \(n\) training points:

  • Matrix inversion: \(O(n^3)\) via Cholesky decomposition
  • Storage: \(O(n^2)\) for the kernel matrix
  • Prediction: \(O(n)\) per test point (after precomputing \(\alpha\)), \(O(n^2)\) for variance

For \(n = 10^3\): trivial. For \(n = 10^4\): feasible. For \(n = 10^5\): painful. For \(n = 10^6\): intractable.

In practice: use the Cholesky decomposition \(L L^T = K + \sigma_n^2 I\) (numerically stable, also gives \(O(n^3)\) but with a smaller constant than naive inversion).

docs.title: 4.2 Approximate GP Methods
docs.text:
Method Idea Complexity Sparse GPs (Inducing Points) Summarise \(n\) points with \(m \ll n\) inducing points \(Z\) \(O(nm^2)\) FITC / VFE Variational lower bound on the marginal likelihood \(O(nm^2)\) Random Fourier Features Approximate \(k(x, x') \approx \phi(x)^T\phi(x')\), finite \(D\) features \(O(nD)\) State-space GPs Convert GP to a linear dynamical system; Kalman filter \(O(n)\) for 1D inputs Structured kernel interpolation (SKI) Interpolate onto a grid; FFT-based matrix-vector products \(O(n \log n)\)

The inducing point / variational approach (Titsias 2009, Hensman et al. 2013) is the modern standard. The \(m\) inducing points \(Z\) are learnable — optimise them jointly with the hyperparameters.

Notebook margin — why Cholesky and not direct inversion? Numerically, \(K\) is often nearly singular (especially with the SE kernel and nearby points). Cholesky decomposition is numerically stable, reveals singularity, gives the log-determinant cheaply (sum of log diagonal), and allows efficient solves. Always use Cholesky for GP computations. Never call np.linalg.inv on a kernel matrix.

docs.title: 5.1 The Problem
docs.text:
The GP prior \(k(x, x'; \theta)\) has hyperparameters \(\theta\) — e.g., \(\theta = (\ell, \sigma_f^2, \sigma_n^2)\) for the SE kernel. How do we choose them?

Not cross-validation: too expensive (each CV fold requires an \(O(n^3)\) solve).

Bayesian answer: marginalise over the latent function \(f\) (already done in the posterior), then maximise the marginal likelihood \(p(\mathbf{y} \mid X, \theta)\) over \(\theta\).

docs.title: 5.2 The Log Marginal Likelihood
docs.text:
\[ \log p(\mathbf{y} \mid X, \theta) = -\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{y}^T (K_\theta + \sigma_n^2 I)^{-1}\mathbf{y} - \frac{1}{2}\log|K_\theta + \sigma_n^2 I| - \frac{n}{2}\log 2\pi \]

Three terms:

  1. \(-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{y}^T (K_\theta + \sigma_n^2 I)^{-1}\mathbf{y}\) — data fit: how well the model fits the observations
  2. \(-\frac{1}{2}\log|K_\theta + \sigma_n^2 I|\) — complexity penalty (Occam factor): penalises models that can explain too many datasets
  3. \(-\frac{n}{2}\log 2\pi\) — normalisation constant

The marginal likelihood automatically balances fit and complexity — models that overfit have high fit but are penalised by the log-determinant term. This is automatic Occam's razor.

docs.title: 5.3 Optimisation
docs.text:
Differentiate with respect to \(\theta\) and use gradient-based optimisation (L-BFGS or Adam): $$ \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta_j} \log p(\mathbf{y} \mid X, \theta) = \frac{1}{2} \text{tr}!\left[(K{-1}\mathbf{y}\mathbf{y}T K^{-1} - K^{-1})\frac{\partial K}{\partial \theta_j}\right] $$

where \(K = K_\theta + \sigma_n^2 I\).

Gradient cost: \(O(n^3)\) per evaluation — same as the posterior. Run from multiple random initialisations (marginal likelihood is non-convex in \(\theta\)).

What the marginal likelihood does to hyperparameters: If \(\ell\) is too small: the model is wiggly, many functions fit the data, large \(|K|\), large complexity penalty. If \(\ell\) is too large: the model is too smooth, fits the data poorly, large data-fit term. The marginal likelihood finds the length-scale where these forces balance — the one that best explains the data without overfitting. This is Bayesian model selection in action.

docs.title: ✦ Part 6 — GP Classification
docs.text:
For binary classification, \(y \in {0, 1}\) and we want: $$ p(y_* = 1 \mid x__, \mathcal{D}) = \int \sigma(f__), p(f_* \mid x__, \mathcal{D}), df__ $$

The GP prior is the same — but now the likelihood is Bernoulli, not Gaussian. The posterior \(p(f \mid X, \mathbf{y})\) is no longer Gaussian. Exact inference is intractable.

Approximate inference methods:

Method Idea Quality Laplace approximation Fit a Gaussian at the posterior mode Fast, good for unimodal posteriors Expectation Propagation (EP) Approximate each factor in the likelihood with a Gaussian More accurate than Laplace Variational inference (SVGP) Variational lower bound, scalable with inducing points Modern standard for large-scale GP classification

Multi-class: one GP per class (one-vs-rest) with softmax likelihood, or multi-output GP.

docs.title: 7.1 GP = Kernel Ridge Regression (in the noise-free limit)
docs.text: The GP posterior mean: $$ \mu_* = K(x_*, X)[K(X,X) + \sigma_n^2 I]^{-1}\mathbf{y} $$ is exactly the kernel ridge regression predictor with regularisation parameter \(\lambda = \sigma_n^2 / \sigma_f^2\). GPs give kernel ridge regression a Bayesian interpretation — and add uncertainty quantification for free.

docs.title: 7.2 GP = Infinite-Width Neural Networks
docs.text:
Neal (1994) showed: a single-hidden-layer neural network with i.i.d. priors on weights converges in distribution to a GP as the number of hidden units \(\to \infty\). The kernel is determined by the activation function.

More recently (Lee et al. 2018, Jacot et al. 2018): deep networks trained with gradient descent correspond (in the infinite-width limit) to kernel regression with the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK). This is a GP in function space. The NTK connection is an active research area linking GPs to deep learning theory.

docs.title: 7.3 GP Prior on the Parameters of a Deep Network
docs.text: In deep kernel learning, replace the hand-crafted feature map with a neural network: $$ k(x, x') = k_{\text{base}}(g_\theta(x), g_\theta(x')) $$ where \(g_\theta\) is a neural network. Jointly optimise \(\theta\) and GP hyperparameters via marginal likelihood. This combines the representational power of deep networks with GP uncertainty quantification — a practically important model class.

docs.title: 7.4 GP and SVMs
docs.text:
The SVM with RBF kernel and GP regression with SE kernel share the same kernel function. The difference:

  • SVM: finds a maximum-margin classifier; no probabilistic output; sparse (support vectors)
  • GP: full posterior distribution over \(f\); uncertainty quantification; not sparse

For classification: GP gives calibrated class probabilities; SVM gives a hard boundary. The GP is preferred when uncertainty matters (medical diagnosis, active learning, safety-critical systems).

docs.title: 7.5 GP in Bayesian Optimisation
docs.text:
This is the primary industrial application of GPs today — used inside every major AutoML system and neural architecture search tool.

Setup: You want to minimise \(f(x)\) where \(f\) is expensive to evaluate (e.g., training a neural network with hyperparameters \(x\)). You have a budget of \(T\) evaluations.

Algorithm:

  1. Place a GP prior on \(f\)
  2. Observe \(f(x_1), \ldots, f(x_t)\) — update GP posterior
  3. Choose next query \(x_{t+1}\) by maximising an acquisition function \(\alpha(x)\)
  4. Repeat

Acquisition functions:

Function Formula Behaviour Expected Improvement (EI) \(\mathbb{E}[\max(f^* - f(x), 0)]\) Balances exploration/exploitation; most popular Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) \(\mu(x) + \kappa \sigma(x)\) Explicit exploration parameter \(\kappa\) Probability of Improvement \(P(f(x) < f^* - \xi)\) Pure exploitation focus Thompson Sampling Sample \(\tilde{f} \sim p(f \mid \mathcal{D})\), maximise \(\tilde{f}\) Simple, strong theoretical guarantees

Why GPs specifically? The acquisition function requires both a prediction \(\mu(x)\) and an uncertainty \(\sigma(x)\) at every point in the input space — not just at training points. GPs provide exactly this, in closed form, for any \(x\).

Connection to hyperparameter tuning (Section 2.5 of the index): every time you use Optuna, Ray Tune, or a Gaussian Process optimiser to tune neural network hyperparameters, there is a GP computing posterior means and variances under the hood.

docs.title: ✦ Part 8 — Sampling from a GP
docs.text:
How do you actually draw a sample function \(f \sim \mathcal{GP}(0, k)\)?

  1. Choose a grid of points \(X = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)\)
  2. Compute the Gram matrix \(K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j)\)
  3. Add a small jitter for numerical stability: \(K \leftarrow K + 10^{-6} I\)
  4. Compute Cholesky: \(L = \text{chol}(K)\)
  5. Sample \(z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_n)\)
  6. Return \(f = Lz\)

This gives a draw from \(\mathcal{N}(0, K)\) — a finite-dimensional realisation of the GP prior.

import numpy as np

def sample_gp_prior(x_grid, kernel_fn, n_samples=5, jitter=1e-6):
    """
    Sample functions from a GP prior.
    x_grid: (n,) array of input points
    kernel_fn: callable, k(x, x') -> scalar
    """
    n = len(x_grid)
    K = np.array([[kernel_fn(x_grid[i], x_grid[j])
                   for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)])
    K += jitter * np.eye(n)  # numerical stability
    L = np.linalg.cholesky(K)
    z = np.random.randn(n, n_samples)
    return L @ z  # (n, n_samples): each column is a function sample

def se_kernel(x, xp, l=1.0, sf2=1.0):
    return sf2 * np.exp(-0.5 * (x - xp)**2 / l**2)

x = np.linspace(-5, 5, 200)
samples = sample_gp_prior(x, se_kernel, n_samples=5)
# samples[:, i] is the i-th function sample

Try this with different kernels (SE with varying \(\ell\), Matérn, periodic) — you will immediately develop intuition for what each kernel encodes.

docs.title: ✦ Part 9 — Full GP Regression Implementation
docs.text:
import numpy as np

class GaussianProcessRegressor:
    """
    Exact GP regression with SE kernel.
    Hyperparameters fixed (no marginal likelihood optimisation).
    """
    def __init__(self, length_scale=1.0, output_scale=1.0, noise_var=0.1):
        self.l   = length_scale
        self.sf2 = output_scale
        self.sn2 = noise_var
        self.L   = None  # Cholesky of (K + sn2*I)
        self.alpha = None  # (K + sn2*I)^{-1} y

    def _kernel(self, X1, X2):
        """SE kernel: (n1, d) x (n2, d) -> (n1, n2)"""
        diff = X1[:, None, :] - X2[None, :, :]   # (n1, n2, d)
        sq_dist = np.sum(diff**2, axis=-1)         # (n1, n2)
        return self.sf2 * np.exp(-0.5 * sq_dist / self.l**2)

    def fit(self, X_train, y_train):
        self.X_train = X_train
        n = len(X_train)
        K = self._kernel(X_train, X_train) + self.sn2 * np.eye(n)
        self.L = np.linalg.cholesky(K)                    # O(n^3)
        self.alpha = np.linalg.solve(
            self.L.T, np.linalg.solve(self.L, y_train))   # L L^T alpha = y

    def predict(self, X_test):
        K_star = self._kernel(X_test, self.X_train)        # (m, n)
        mu = K_star @ self.alpha                            # (m,)

        v = np.linalg.solve(self.L, K_star.T)              # (n, m)
        k_ss = self._kernel(X_test, X_test)                 # (m, m)
        cov = k_ss - v.T @ v                                # posterior covariance

        return mu, np.diag(cov)                             # mean, variance

    def log_marginal_likelihood(self, y_train):
        """Equation from Part 5. Useful for hyperparameter optimisation."""
        n = len(y_train)
        log_lik = (
            -0.5 * y_train @ self.alpha
            - np.sum(np.log(np.diag(self.L)))
            - 0.5 * n * np.log(2 * np.pi)
        )
        return log_lik

Usage: after gp.fit(X_train, y_train), call mu, var = gp.predict(X_test). The 95% confidence interval is \(\mu \pm 1.96\sqrt{\text{var}}\).

docs.title: 10.1 The Weight-Space / Function-Space Duality
docs.text:
Perspective Prior lives on Inference Predictions Bayesian NN (weight-space) \(p(w)\) Posterior \(p(w \mid \mathcal{D})\) — intractable \(\int p(y \mid x, w) p(w \mid \mathcal{D}) dw\) — approximate GP (function-space) \(p(f)\) — GP prior Posterior \(p(f \mid \mathcal{D})\) — exact Gaussian Exact predictive distribution

For finite-width networks, the weight-space prior induces a non-Gaussian process over functions. In the infinite-width limit, the central limit theorem makes it Gaussian — a GP. The kernel is determined by the network architecture and activation function.

docs.title: 10.2 Why This Matters for Modern DL
docs.text:
• Uncertainty quantification: GPs give exact posteriors. BNNs don't. The deep learning community's various approaches to UQ (MC Dropout, deep ensembles, SWAG) can often be understood as approximate GP inference.
  • Generalisation theory: NTK analysis (a GP analysis) is currently one of the main tools for understanding why overparameterised networks generalise — a central open question in deep learning theory.
  • Structured prediction: GP multi-output models, GP latent variable models, and deep GPs are active research directions that directly compete with (and complement) deep learning approaches.

docs.title: 10.3 Where GPs Are Preferred Over Neural Networks
docs.text: Scenario Reason Small data (\(n < 10^3\)) GPs are non-parametric; NNs overfit Calibrated uncertainty needed Exact GP posteriors vs. approximate NN uncertainty Scientific inference Kernel design encodes domain knowledge interpretably Optimisation (Bayesian opt.) Closed-form acquisition; cheap to evaluate Interpretability required Kernel hyperparameters have direct physical meaning

docs.title: ✦ Visualising the Posterior
docs.text:
Prior (no data):
f(x)
 │     ~~~~
 │   ~~    ~~
 │  ~        ~   (3 sample functions, all plausible)
 │~            ~~
 └──────────────── x
   wide shaded region = prior uncertainty

Posterior (5 training points observed, marked ×):
f(x)
 │          ×
 │    ×   ~~~~×~~~
 │  ~~× ~~       ~
 │~~                ~
 └──────────────────── x
   narrow band at × (data reduces uncertainty)
   wide band far from data (prior uncertainty returns)
   mean function threads through observations

This picture — posterior mean threading through data, variance collapsing at observations and widening in unobserved regions — is the visual essence of a Gaussian Process. Any model that behaves this way is doing Bayesian inference correctly.

docs.title: ✦ Exit Criterion
docs.text:
You know this when: you can derive the GP posterior mean and variance from the Gaussian conditioning lemma, explain why the posterior variance decreases monotonically with data, implement GP regression from scratch in NumPy using Cholesky, explain what the marginal likelihood is and what the three terms mean, and describe why GPs are \(O(n^3)\) and name at least two scalable alternatives.

Concrete exercises:

  1. Implement the full GP regressor above. Fit it to \(y = \sin(x) + \varepsilon\) on 10 training points. Plot the posterior mean and 95% confidence interval. Observe how the uncertainty widens between and beyond training points.
  2. Sample 5 functions from a GP prior with SE kernel, then with Matérn-½. Plot both. Write one sentence about what you observe.
  3. Implement the log marginal likelihood gradient with respect to \(\ell\) and \(\sigma_n^2\) using the formula in Part 5. Use scipy.optimize.minimize to learn the hyperparameters on a dataset with a known underlying length-scale. Verify recovery.
  4. Implement a one-dimensional Bayesian optimisation loop: GP posterior + EI acquisition + 15 iterations. Minimise \(f(x) = (x - 2)^2 + 0.1\sin(10x)\). Plot the acquisition function at each step.

docs.title: Kernel Methods
docs.text:
"The kernel trick is not a trick. It is a profound insight: similarity in a rich feature space can be computed cheaply in the original space."

Tags: #kernel-methods #SVM #RKHS #representer-theorem #deep-learning #machine-learning Status: 🟢 Core References: ESL Ch. 12 · PRML Ch. 6 · CS 229 Lecture 6–7 Prerequisites: [[04.Support Vector Machines]] · [[03.Probability Review]] · [[02.Statistical Learning Theory]]

docs.title: The Central Problem
docs.text:
Most machine learning algorithms assume a fixed, finite-dimensional feature representation. You hand the model a vector \(x \in \mathbb{R}^d\), and it does something with it. But what if the data is not linearly separable in \(\mathbb{R}^d\)? The naive solution: map to a higher-dimensional space where it is.

\[\phi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^D, \quad D \gg d \quad (\text{possibly } D = \infty)\]

The brutal fact: computing in \(\mathbb{R}^D\) is expensive. If \(D = d^2\) (all pairwise products), you're already in trouble for modest \(d\). If \(D = \infty\) — you literally cannot compute \(\phi(x)\) explicitly.

The kernel trick resolves this: you never need \(\phi(x)\) explicitly. You only ever need inner products \(\langle \phi(x_i), \phi(x_j) \rangle\), and a kernel function computes this cheaply.

\[k(x_i, x_j) \stackrel{\text{def}}{=} \langle \phi(x_i), \phi(x_j) \rangle_\mathcal{H}\]

docs.title: 1. Feature Maps and the Kernel Function
Setup
docs.text:
Let \(\mathcal{X}\) be the input space (e.g., \(\mathbb{R}^d\)). A feature map is \(\phi: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{H}\) where \(\mathcal{H}\) is a Hilbert space (a complete inner product space — possibly infinite dimensional).

A kernel function is any function \(k: \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}\) such that:

\[k(x, x') = \langle \phi(x), \phi(x') \rangle_\mathcal{H}\]

for some feature map \(\phi\). The point: we define \(k\) first, then the feature map \(\phi\) is implied by \(k\) — we may never need to construct it.

docs.title: Canonical Example: The Polynomial Kernel
docs.text:
Let \(x, x' \in \mathbb{R}^2\). Define:

\[k(x, x') = (x^\top x' + c)^2, \quad c \geq 0\]

Expand for \(x = (x_1, x_2)^\top\), \(x' = (x_1', x_2')^\top\), \(c = 1\):

\[k(x, x') = (x_1 x_1' + x_2 x_2' + 1)^2$$ $$= x_1^2 x_1'^2 + x_2^2 x_2'^2 + 1 + 2x_1 x_1' x_2 x_2' + 2x_1 x_1' + 2x_2 x_2'\]

This is precisely \(\langle \phi(x), \phi(x') \rangle\) where:

\[\phi(x) = (x_1^2,\ x_2^2,\ 1,\ \sqrt{2}x_1 x_2,\ \sqrt{2}x_1,\ \sqrt{2}x_2)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^6\]

Key observation: computing \(k(x, x')\) costs \(O(d)\) — one inner product and a squaring. Computing \(\langle \phi(x), \phi(x') \rangle\) directly costs \(O(D)\) where \(D = \binom{d+2}{2}\) grows quadratically in \(d\). The kernel saves us this cost.

docs.title: The RBF (Gaussian) Kernel — An Infinite-Dimensional Feature Map
docs.text:
\[k(x, x') = \exp!\left(-\frac{|x - x'|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\]

Claim: This corresponds to an infinite-dimensional feature map.

Proof sketch: Expand via the Taylor series of \(\exp\):

\[\exp!\left(-\frac{|x|^2 + |x'|^2 - 2x^\top x'}{2\sigma^2}\right) = e^{-|x|^2/2\sigma^2} \cdot e^{-|x'|^2/2\sigma^2} \cdot e^{x^\top x'/\sigma^2}\]

The last factor: \(e^{x^\top x'/\sigma^2} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(x^\top x')^n}{n! \sigma^{2n}}\). Each term \((x^\top x')^n\) corresponds to a degree-\(n\) polynomial kernel, which has its own feature map of dimension \(\binom{d+n}{n}\). Summing infinitely many such maps gives an infinite-dimensional \(\phi\). Yet \(k(x, x')\) is a single exponential — \(O(d)\) to evaluate. \(\square\)

This is the fundamental power: the feature space can be infinite-dimensional while the kernel evaluation remains cheap.

docs.title: 2. Mercer's Theorem — When is \(k\) a Valid Kernel?
docs.text: Not every function \(k: \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}\) corresponds to a valid inner product. We need a characterisation.

docs.title: Definition: Positive Semi-Definite Kernel
docs.text:
A symmetric function \(k\) is a positive semi-definite (PSD) kernel (also called a Mercer kernel) if for any finite set \({x_1, \ldots, x_n} \subset \mathcal{X}\) and any \(c \in \mathbb{R}^n\):

\[\sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n c_i c_j k(x_i, x_j) \geq 0\]

Equivalently, the Gram matrix \(K \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\) with \(K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j)\) is positive semi-definite for all choices of \({x_1, \ldots, x_n}\).

docs.title: Mercer's Theorem (Statement)
docs.text:
Let \(k: \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}\) be continuous and symmetric. Then \(k\) is a valid kernel (i.e., \(k(x, x') = \langle \phi(x), \phi(x') \rangle_\mathcal{H}\) for some Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H}\) and feature map \(\phi\)) if and only if \(k\) is positive semi-definite.

Proof direction (necessity): If \(k(x,x') = \langle \phi(x), \phi(x') \rangle\), then \(\sum_{i,j} c_i c_j k(x_i, x_j) = \left|\sum_i c_i \phi(x_i)\right|^2 \geq 0\). \(\square\)

The sufficiency direction is harder — it constructs the RKHS explicitly from \(k\). See Section 4.

docs.title: How to Check Validity
docs.text:
1. Directly verify PSD on the Gram matrix.
  2. Use closure properties (easier in practice):
    • If \(k_1, k_2\) are valid kernels, so are \(k_1 + k_2\), \(\alpha k_1\) (\(\alpha > 0\)), \(k_1 \cdot k_2\)
    • \(k(x, x') = f(x) k_1(x, x') f(x')\) for any function \(f\)
    • \(k(x, x') = \phi(x)^\top A \phi(x')\) where \(A \succeq 0\)

Common valid kernels:

Kernel Formula Hyperparameters Linear \(x^\top x'\) — Polynomial \((x^\top x' + c)^d\) \(c \geq 0\), \(d \in \mathbb{N}\) RBF (Gaussian) \(\exp(-\|x-x'\|^2 / 2\sigma^2)\) \(\sigma > 0\) Matérn (smoothness-controlled) \(\nu, \ell > 0\) Laplace \(\exp(-\|x-x'\| / \sigma)\) \(\sigma > 0\) Sigmoid \(\tanh(\alpha x^\top x' + c)\) only PSD for some \(\alpha, c\) — careful!

docs.title: 3. The Representer Theorem
docs.text: This is the theorem that justifies using kernels for learning. It says: when you minimise a regularised loss over a function space, the optimal solution lives in the span of the training data's feature maps.

docs.title: Theorem (Representer Theorem — Schölkopf, Herbrich, Smola, 2001)
docs.text:
Let \(\mathcal{H}\) be an RKHS with kernel \(k\). Consider the optimisation problem:

\[\hat{f} = \arg\min_{f \in \mathcal{H}} \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n L(y_i, f(x_i))}_{\text{empirical loss}} + \underbrace{\Omega(|f|_\mathcal{H})}_{\text{regularisation}}\]

where \(L\) is any loss function and \(\Omega: [0, \infty) \to \mathbb{R}\) is any strictly increasing function. Then the optimal \(\hat{f}\) has the form:

\[\hat{f}(\cdot) = \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i k(\cdot, x_i)\]

for some coefficients \(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n \in \mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: Proof
docs.text:
Decompose \(f \in \mathcal{H}\) into a component in the span of \({k(\cdot, x_i)}\) and its orthogonal complement:

\[f = \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i k(\cdot, x_i)}_{f_\parallel} + f_\perp\]

By the reproducing property of the RKHS (see Section 4):

\[f(x_j) = \langle f, k(\cdot, x_j) \rangle_\mathcal{H} = \langle f_\parallel, k(\cdot, x_j) \rangle_\mathcal{H} + \underbrace{\langle f_\perp, k(\cdot, x_j) \rangle_\mathcal{H}}_{= 0} = f_\parallel(x_j)\]

So adding \(f_\perp\) does not change any training prediction, but \(|f|^2_\mathcal{H} = |f_\parallel|^2 + |f_\perp|^2 \geq |f_\parallel|^2\), which means \(f_\perp\) only hurts the regularisation term. Therefore the optimal solution has \(f_\perp = 0\). \(\square\)

What this buys you: instead of optimising over an infinite-dimensional function space, you optimise over \(n\) real numbers \(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_n\). The learning problem reduces to finite-dimensional optimisation.

docs.title: 4. The Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS)
docs.text: This is the natural home for kernel methods. Understanding the RKHS is understanding why the whole framework is coherent.

docs.title: Construction
docs.text:
Given a PSD kernel \(k\), we construct the RKHS \(\mathcal{H}_k\) as follows:

Step 1. Start with the set of all "feature functions": for each \(x \in \mathcal{X}\), define \(k_x := k(\cdot, x)\) as a function \(\mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}\).

Step 2. Consider the linear span: \(\mathcal{F} = \left{ \sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i k_{x_i} \mid m \in \mathbb{N},\ \alpha_i \in \mathbb{R},\ x_i \in \mathcal{X} \right}\)

Step 3. Define an inner product on \(\mathcal{F}\):

\[\left\langle \sum_i \alpha_i k_{x_i},\ \sum_j \beta_j k_{x_j'} \right\rangle_\mathcal{H} := \sum_i \sum_j \alpha_i \beta_j k(x_i, x_j')\]

This is well-defined because \(k\) is PSD.

Step 4. Complete \(\mathcal{F}\) under the induced norm \(|f|_\mathcal{H} = \sqrt{\langle f, f \rangle_\mathcal{H}}\) to get the Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H}_k\).

docs.title: The Reproducing Property
docs.text:
The defining property of the RKHS, which gives it its name:

\[f(x) = \langle f, k(\cdot, x) \rangle_\mathcal{H} \quad \forall f \in \mathcal{H}_k,\ x \in \mathcal{X}\]

In other words: evaluating a function \(f\) at a point \(x\) is an inner product with the kernel function \(k(\cdot, x)\). This is the reason the representer theorem proof works.

Sanity check: Set \(f = k(\cdot, x')\). Then:

\[\langle k(\cdot, x'), k(\cdot, x) \rangle_\mathcal{H} = k(x', x) \checkmark\]

The RKHS norm \(|f|_\mathcal{H}\) has a concrete meaning: it measures the smoothness of \(f\) with respect to the kernel. The smoother the function, the smaller the norm. Regularisation with \(|f|_\mathcal{H}^2\) is literally a smoothness penalty.

docs.title: 5. Kernelised Algorithms
docs.text: The representer theorem + the kernel trick allows us to kernelise any algorithm that depends on the data only through inner products. We replace \(x_i^\top x_j \mapsto k(x_i, x_j)\) everywhere.

docs.title: Kernel Ridge Regression
docs.text:
Primal: \(\min_{w \in \mathcal{H}} |Xw - y|^2 + \lambda |w|^2\)

Primal solution: \(\hat{w} = (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1} X^\top y\) — works in \(\mathbb{R}^d\), breaks for infinite-dim \(\phi\).

Dual: By the representer theorem, \(\hat{f} = \sum_i \alpha_i k(\cdot, x_i)\). Substituting:

\[\hat{\alpha} = (K + \lambda I)^{-1} y\]

where \(K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j)\) is the \(n \times n\) Gram matrix. Prediction:

\[\hat{f}(x^_) = \sum_i \hat{\alpha}_i k(x^_, x_i) = k(x^*)^\top (K + \lambda I)^{-1} y\]

where \(k(x^_)_i = k(x^_, x_i)\).

Cost: \(O(n^3)\) to invert \((K + \lambda I)\) vs. \(O(d^3)\) for ridge regression. Kernel methods trade \(d\) for \(n\) in complexity — they scale with the number of samples, not the feature dimensionality.

Connection to Gaussian Processes: The kernel ridge regression predictor is identical to the GP posterior mean under an RBF prior. This is not a coincidence — they are the same model derived from different perspectives.

docs.title: Kernel SVM
docs.text:
Recall the SVM dual:

\[\max_\alpha \sum_i \alpha_i - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j} \alpha_i \alpha_j y_i y_j x_i^\top x_j \quad \text{s.t. } \sum_i \alpha_i y_i = 0,\ 0 \leq \alpha_i \leq C\]

Replace \(x_i^\top x_j \mapsto k(x_i, x_j)\):

\[\max_\alpha \sum_i \alpha_i - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j} \alpha_i \alpha_j y_i y_j k(x_i, x_j) \quad \text{s.t. } \sum_i \alpha_i y_i = 0,\ 0 \leq \alpha_i \leq C\]

Decision function:

\[\hat{y}(x) = \text{sign}!\left(\sum_{i \in \text{SV}} \alpha_i y_i k(x, x_i) + b\right)\]

We never need \(\phi\) explicitly. We never need to work in the feature space. Everything is mediated by \(k\).

docs.title: Kernel Logistic Regression
docs.text:
Replace the weight vector \(w\) with \(\sum_i \alpha_i k(\cdot, x_i)\) and optimise over \(\alpha\). The log-likelihood becomes:

\[\ell(\alpha) = \sum_i \log \sigma!\left(y_i \sum_j \alpha_j k(x_i, x_j)\right) - \lambda \alpha^\top K \alpha\]

The regularisation term \(\alpha^\top K \alpha = |f|^2_\mathcal{H}\) — this is the RKHS norm.

docs.title: Kernel PCA
docs.text:
Standard PCA: find eigenvectors of the covariance matrix \(C = \frac{1}{n} X^\top X\).

Kernel PCA: find principal components in the RKHS by computing the eigendecomposition of the centred Gram matrix \(\tilde{K}\):

\[\tilde{K} = K - \mathbf{1}_n K - K \mathbf{1}_n + \mathbf{1}_n K \mathbf{1}_n\]

where \((\mathbf{1}_n)_{ij} = 1/n\). This centres the data in feature space without constructing \(\phi(x)\) explicitly.

The projection of a new point \(x^*\) onto the \(j\)-th principal component:

\[z_j(x^_) = \sum_i \alpha_j^{(i)} k(x^_, x_i)\]

docs.title: 6. Kernel Design — Encoding Prior Knowledge
docs.text: The choice of kernel is a choice of inductive bias. When you pick the RBF kernel, you're saying: "I believe the function is smooth, and similar inputs should have similar outputs, where similarity decays exponentially with Euclidean distance." Different kernels encode different beliefs.

docs.title: Stationary Kernels
docs.text:
\(k(x, x') = k(x - x')\) — depends only on the difference between inputs. Implies translation invariance (stationarity).

  • RBF: \(k(r) = \exp(-r^2/2\sigma^2)\) — infinitely differentiable. Use when the target function is very smooth.
  • Laplace: \(k(r) = \exp(-|r|/\sigma)\) — only once-differentiable. Better for non-smooth functions.
  • Matérn-\( u\): interpolates between Laplace (\( u = 1/2\)) and RBF (\( u o \infty\)). The parameter \( u\) controls differentiability.

docs.title: Non-stationary Kernels
docs.text:
• Linear: \(k(x, x') = x^\top x'\) — equivalent to linear models. No nonlinearity.
  • Polynomial: encodes feature interactions up to degree \(d\).
  • Periodic: \(k(x, x') = \exp(-2\sin^2(\pi|x-x'|/p) / \ell^2)\) — for periodic functions (e.g., seasonal data).

docs.title: Kernels for Structured Data
docs.text:
The true power of kernels: they extend machine learning to non-Euclidean inputs by defining similarity directly.

  • String kernels: $k(s, s') = $ number of common substrings of length \(p\). Used in text classification and bioinformatics (protein sequences).
  • Graph kernels: $k(G, G') = $ a function of shared subgraph patterns. Used in chemoinformatics (molecular property prediction).
  • Tree kernels: for parse trees in NLP.

The definition of valid kernel is preserved: as long as the Gram matrix is PSD, any similarity function is a valid kernel — no matter how exotic the input space.

docs.title: The \(O(n^3)\) Problem
docs.text:
Kernel methods require computing and storing the \(n \times n\) Gram matrix \(K\). For large \(n\):

  • Storage: \(O(n^2)\) — infeasible at \(n = 10^6\)
  • Inversion (kernel ridge): \(O(n^3)\) — infeasible much earlier
  • This is why kernel methods fell out of favour when deep learning arrived

docs.title: Approximate Kernel Methods
docs.text:
Nyström approximation: approximate \(K\) using a low-rank factorisation:

\[K \approx K_{nm} K_{mm}^{-1} K_{nm}^\top\]

where \(m \ll n\) are randomly selected "landmark" points. Reduces to \(O(nm^2)\) computation.

Random Fourier Features (Rahimi & Recht, 2007): for shift-invariant kernels, Bochner's theorem guarantees:

\[k(x, x') = \mathbb{E}_\omega!\left[e^{i\omega^\top(x-x')}\right]\]

Sample \(D\) random frequencies \(\omega_1, \ldots, \omega_D \sim p(\omega)\) and construct:

\[z(x) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{D}}!\left(\cos(\omega_1^\top x + b_1), \ldots, \cos(\omega_D^\top x + b_D)\right)^\top\]

Then \(k(x, x') \approx z(x)^\top z(x')\). This reduces to a standard linear method in \(\mathbb{R}^D\), costing \(O(nD)\).

docs.title: 8. Connection to AI, Deep Learning, and Neural Networks
docs.text: Kernel methods and deep learning are more deeply connected than they might appear. Understanding this connection is important for a modern practitioner.

docs.title: Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK)
docs.text:
The central result (Jacot, Gabriel, Hongler, 2018): An infinitely wide neural network trained by gradient descent is equivalent to kernel regression with the Neural Tangent Kernel:

\[k_\text{NTK}(x, x') = \mathbb{E}_{\theta \sim \text{init}}!\left[\nabla_\theta f(x;\theta)^\top \nabla_\theta f(x';\theta)\right]\]

At infinite width:

  • The NTK stays constant throughout training (it doesn't change as weights update)
  • The network converges to a global minimum
  • The final predictor is a kernel regression predictor with kernel \(k_\text{NTK}\)

What this means practically: For very wide networks, the NTK regime predicts behaviour well. For finite-width networks (real practice), the NTK drifts during training — this is called feature learning and is what makes practical deep learning powerful beyond kernel methods. The kernel regime cannot learn new features; it is fixed by the initialisation.

docs.title: Deep Kernels
docs.text:
One response to the expressive power gap: learn the kernel. Define:

\[k(x, x') = k_\text{base}(\phi_\theta(x), \phi_\theta(x'))\]

where \(\phi_\theta\) is a neural network and \(k_\text{base}\) is a standard kernel (e.g., RBF). Train \(\theta\) jointly with the kernel machine. This is the basis of Deep Kernel Learning (Wilson et al., 2016) and gives a principled Bayesian uncertainty estimate from a deep model.

docs.title: SVMs vs. Neural Networks — Historical Perspective
docs.text:
In the 1990s, SVMs were the dominant large-margin classifier. The shift to neural networks was driven by:

  1. Scalability: Deep learning trains in \(O(n)\) per epoch via SGD; kernel SVMs scale as \(O(n^2)\)–\(O(n^3)\).
  2. Representation learning: CNNs learn the right features for images; SVMs with RBF kernels cannot exploit spatial structure as efficiently.
  3. Compositionality: Deep networks compose simple functions hierarchically; kernels are a single layer of feature mapping.

Yet SVMs with carefully designed kernels still dominate in domains with small \(n\) and structured data (e.g., genomics, cheminformatics). The choice is not doctrinal; it's empirical.

docs.title: Kernel Machines in Modern ML
docs.text:
• Gaussian Processes (used in hyperparameter optimisation via Bayesian optimisation, as uncertainty-aware surrogates in RL and AutoML) are fully defined by their kernel.
  • Graph Neural Networks can be understood as learnable graph kernels.
  • Attention in Transformers: the scaled dot-product attention \(\text{softmax}(QK^\top / \sqrt{d_k})V\) is a data-dependent kernel. \(Q^\top K / \sqrt{d_k}\) computes kernel similarities between query and key representations. This is the connection that has been formalised in kernel attention and Performer architectures.
  • Support Vector Regression (SVR) is still used as a strong baseline in time series and scientific ML.

docs.title: 9. Worked Example — Kernel SVM vs. Linear SVM
docs.text:
Consider the XOR problem: 4 points in \(\mathbb{R}^2\):

\[x_1 = (1,1),\ y_1 = +1 \quad x_2 = (-1,-1),\ y_2 = +1$$ $$x_3 = (1,-1),\ y_3 = -1 \quad x_4 = (-1,1),\ y_4 = -1\]

Linear SVM: not separable in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) — no hyperplane separates the classes.

Polynomial kernel of degree 2: \(k(x, x') = (x^\top x')^2\). The feature map is (for \(c=0\)):

\[\phi(x_1, x_2) = (x_1^2, x_2^2, \sqrt{2} x_1 x_2)\]

In this space:

  • \(\phi(1,1) = (1, 1, \sqrt{2})\), class \(+1\)
  • \(\phi(-1,-1) = (1, 1, \sqrt{2})\), class \(+1\)
  • \(\phi(1,-1) = (1, 1, -\sqrt{2})\), class \(-1\)
  • \(\phi(-1,1) = (1, 1, -\sqrt{2})\), class \(-1\)

Now the classes separate perfectly along the third coordinate \(\sqrt{2}x_1 x_2\): positive class has \(x_1 x_2 > 0\), negative has \(x_1 x_2 < 0\). The hyperplane is \(w_3 z_3 = 0\), i.e., the product \(x_1 x_2 = 0\).

docs.title: 10. Implementation from Scratch
docs.text:
import numpy as np

# ── Kernel functions ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def rbf_kernel(X1, X2, sigma=1.0):
    """
    Compute the RBF Gram matrix between rows of X1 and rows of X2.
    K[i,j] = exp(-||X1[i] - X2[j]||^2 / (2 * sigma^2))
    """
    # ||a - b||^2 = ||a||^2 + ||b||^2 - 2 a.b
    sq_dist = (np.sum(X1**2, axis=1, keepdims=True)
               + np.sum(X2**2, axis=1)
               - 2 * X1 @ X2.T)
    return np.exp(-sq_dist / (2 * sigma**2))

def polynomial_kernel(X1, X2, degree=2, c=1.0):
    return (X1 @ X2.T + c) ** degree

def linear_kernel(X1, X2):
    return X1 @ X2.T

# ── Kernel Ridge Regression ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
class KernelRidgeRegression:
    """
    Dual form: alpha = (K + lambda * I)^{-1} y
    Prediction: f(x*) = k(x*)^T alpha
    """
    def __init__(self, kernel=rbf_kernel, lam=1.0, **kernel_kwargs):
        self.kernel = kernel
        self.lam = lam
        self.kw = kernel_kwargs

    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.X_train = X
        n = X.shape[0]
        K = self.kernel(X, X, **self.kw)
        self.alpha = np.linalg.solve(K + self.lam * np.eye(n), y)
        return self

    def predict(self, X_test):
        K_star = self.kernel(X_test, self.X_train, **self.kw)
        return K_star @ self.alpha

# ── Kernel PCA ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
class KernelPCA:
    """
    1. Compute Gram matrix K
    2. Centre in feature space: K_tilde = K - 1_n K - K 1_n + 1_n K 1_n
    3. Eigendecompose K_tilde
    4. Project: Z = E_k Λ_k^{1/2}  (keep top k eigenvectors)
    """
    def __init__(self, n_components=2, kernel=rbf_kernel, **kernel_kwargs):
        self.n_components = n_components
        self.kernel = kernel
        self.kw = kernel_kwargs

    def fit_transform(self, X):
        self.X_train = X
        n = X.shape[0]
        K = self.kernel(X, X, **self.kw)

        # Centre the Gram matrix
        one_n = np.ones((n, n)) / n
        self.K_mean_rows = K.mean(axis=0)
        self.K_mean = K.mean()
        K_tilde = K - one_n @ K - K @ one_n + one_n @ K @ one_n

        # Eigendecomposition (K_tilde is symmetric PSD)
        eigvals, eigvecs = np.linalg.eigh(K_tilde)
        # Sort descending
        idx = np.argsort(eigvals)[::-1]
        eigvals, eigvecs = eigvals[idx], eigvecs[:, idx]

        self.eigvals = eigvals[:self.n_components]
        self.eigvecs = eigvecs[:, :self.n_components]

        return self.eigvecs * np.sqrt(np.maximum(self.eigvals, 0))

# ── Usage example ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
    n = 100
    # Two concentric circles — not linearly separable
    theta = rng.uniform(0, 2*np.pi, n)
    r = rng.choice([1.0, 2.5], n)
    X = np.column_stack([r * np.cos(theta), r * np.sin(theta)])
    y = (r > 1.5).astype(float) * 2 - 1   # +1 outer, -1 inner

    # Kernel ridge regression with RBF kernel
    model = KernelRidgeRegression(kernel=rbf_kernel, lam=0.1, sigma=1.0)
    model.fit(X, y)
    preds = np.sign(model.predict(X))
    print(f"Accuracy: {(preds == y).mean():.2%}")

    # Kernel PCA for visualisation
    kpca = KernelPCA(n_components=2, kernel=rbf_kernel, sigma=1.0)
    Z = kpca.fit_transform(X)
    print(f"Projected shape: {Z.shape}")

Original space ℝ²                   Feature space ℝ^D (or ∞-dim)
(not linearly separable)             (linearly separable)

    ●  ○                             ●  ●  ●

The kernel trick: we find this hyperplane WITHOUT ever moving to the
feature space. We work entirely with k(xᵢ, xⱼ) in the original space.

Decision boundary in ℝ² (from SVM dual):
  f(x) = Σᵢ αᵢ yᵢ k(x, xᵢ) + b = 0

This is a *nonlinear* curve in ℝ², induced by the kernel.
With RBF kernel, σ → 0: memorises every point (overfit)
With RBF kernel, σ → ∞: approaches linear classifier (underfit)

The bias-variance view of \(\sigma\) in the RBF kernel:

\(\sigma\) small \(\sigma\) large Narrow Gaussians Wide Gaussians High variance (overfitting) High bias (underfitting) Complex decision boundary Simple (near-linear) boundary Few effective support vectors Many support vectors

docs.title: 12. Summary and Exit Criteria
docs.text:
The logical chain:

\[\text{PSD kernel} \xrightarrow{\text{Mercer}} \text{valid inner product} \xrightarrow{\text{RKHS construction}} \text{Hilbert space } \mathcal{H}_k \xrightarrow{\text{Representer theorem}} \text{finite-dim optimisation over } \alpha \in \mathbb{R}^n\]

The kernel trick reduces any algorithm that uses data only through inner products to kernel evaluations. Kernelise the inner products, and the algorithm works in an implicit infinite-dimensional space at the cost of \(O(n^2)\) storage and \(O(n^3)\) computation.

You know this when you can:

  1. State Mercer's theorem and use it to verify or refute that a given function is a valid kernel.
  2. Derive the kernel ridge regression dual from the representer theorem — without looking it up.
  3. Prove the representer theorem using the orthogonal decomposition argument.
  4. Explain why the RBF kernel corresponds to an infinite-dimensional feature map (via Taylor expansion of \(\exp\)).
  5. Implement kernel ridge regression and kernel PCA in NumPy (~50 lines each).
  6. Explain the NTK connection and what it implies about the relationship between kernel methods and infinitely wide neural networks.
  7. Explain why Transformer attention is a form of data-dependent kernel.

docs.title: Structured Outputs
docs.text: "Most of what matters in the world has structure. A sentence is not a bag of words. A protein is not a bag of amino acids. The challenge is to make the model know this."

docs.title: ✦ Why This Note Exists in the Map
docs.text:
Standard supervised learning assumes \(\mathcal{Y}\) is simple: a scalar (regression) or a finite label (classification). But the real world rarely cooperates. Consider:

  • Sequence labelling: given a sentence, tag each word as NOUN, VERB, ADJ, ... — the output is a sequence of the same length as the input.
  • Parsing: given a sentence, produce a parse tree — the output is a variable-size tree.
  • Image segmentation: given an image, label each pixel — the output has \(H \times W\) interdependent labels.
  • Translation: given an English sentence, produce a German sentence of different length.

In all of these, the output components are not independent given the input. The label of word \(i\) depends on the label of word \(i-1\). Predicting each output independently (the "flat" approach) discards this structure and produces incoherent outputs.

This note builds the machinery to handle structured outputs properly, with rigour. Two major frameworks:

  1. Linear-Chain Conditional Random Fields (CRFs) — for sequence labelling.
  2. Structured SVMs — generalising the SVM margin to arbitrary output spaces.

docs.title: ✦ Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before reading this note you should be comfortable with:

  • [[04.Support Vector Machines]] — the margin, dual problem, KKT conditions
  • [[03.Probability Review]] — log-likelihood, conditional distributions
  • [[02.Statistical Learning Theory]] — ERM, structured loss functions
  • [[02.Logistic Regression]] — log-linear models, the softmax

docs.title: ✦ 1. The Structured Prediction Problem — Setting Up Formally
docs.text:
Setup. Let:

  • \(\mathcal{X}\) = input space (e.g., sequences of words)
  • \(\mathcal{Y}\) = structured output space (e.g., sequences of POS tags, trees, segmentation masks)
  • \((x_i, y_i)_{i=1}^n \sim \mathcal{D}\) — training data

The goal is to learn \(f: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}\) that minimises some task-specific loss \(\Delta(y, \hat{y})\) (e.g., Hamming loss on sequences, tree edit distance on parse trees).

The key difficulty. \(|\mathcal{Y}|\) is exponentially large. For a sequence of length \(T\) with \(K\) possible labels per position, \(|\mathcal{Y}| = K^T\). We cannot enumerate all outputs. Any tractable algorithm must exploit the structure of \(\mathcal{Y}\).

The key insight. We will define a scoring function \(s(x, y; \theta) \in \mathbb{R}\) and predict: $\(\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y \in \mathcal{Y}} s(x, y; \theta)\)$

If \(s\) decomposes over the structure of \(y\), then this maximisation — called inference or decoding — can be solved efficiently by dynamic programming.

docs.title: ✦ 2. Sequence Labelling — The Problem in Concrete Form
docs.text:
Running example throughout this note: Part-of-speech (POS) tagging.

Input: $x = [\text{The''}, \text{cat''}, \text{``sat''}]$ Output: \(y = [\text{DET}, \text{NOUN}, \text{VERB}]\)

The correct label of "sat" is VERB, and this is influenced by the fact that the previous tag is NOUN — the model should know NOUN → VERB is a common transition.

Why not just use a classifier at each position? We could train a multi-class classifier \(P(y_t | x)\) and apply it independently at each timestep. This ignores two critical signals:

  1. Transition patterns: DET → NOUN is far more common than DET → VERB.
  2. Long-range context: the label of position \(t\) may depend on positions far away.

A sequence model encodes both.

docs.title: 3.1 From Logistic Regression to CRF
docs.text:
Logistic regression for a single label: $\(P(y | x) = \frac{\exp(w^\top \phi(x, y))}{\sum_{y'} \exp(w^\top \phi(x, y'))}\)$

where \(\phi(x, y)\) is a feature vector. This is a log-linear model (also called a maximum entropy model).

The linear-chain CRF is exactly this — but the output \(y\) is now a sequence, and \(\phi(x, y)\) is defined to decompose over the sequence. Define:

\[P(y | x; w) = \frac{1}{Z(x, w)} \exp!\left(\sum_{t=1}^T w^\top \phi(x, y_t, y_{t-1}, t)\right)\]

where: $\(Z(x, w) = \sum_{y' \in \mathcal{Y}} \exp!\left(\sum_{t=1}^T w^\top \phi(x, y'_t, y'_{t-1}, t)\right)\)$

is the partition function (normalisation constant), and \(\phi(x, y_t, y_{t-1}, t)\) is a feature vector that can look at the entire input \(x\) at position \(t\), the current label \(y_t\), and the previous label \(y_{t-1}\).

Why "conditional"? A CRF models \(P(y | x)\) directly — it is discriminative. Compare to a Hidden Markov Model (HMM), which models \(P(x, y)\) jointly — it is generative. The CRF does not need to model the distribution of inputs; it only models the output given input.

docs.title: 3.2 The Feature Function — What Goes In \(\phi\)
docs.text:
The power of a CRF lies in the richness of the feature function \(\phi(x, y_t, y_{t-1}, t)\). Typical features:

Feature type Example feature Emission \(\mathbf{1}[\text{word}_t = \text{"sat"} \wedge y_t = \text{VERB}]\) Transition \(\mathbf{1}[y_{t-1} = \text{NOUN} \wedge y_t = \text{VERB}]\) Prefix/suffix \(\mathbf{1}[\text{word}_t \text{ ends in "-ing"} \wedge y_t = \text{VERB}]\) Context window \(\mathbf{1}[\text{word}_{t+1} = \text{"."} \wedge y_t = \text{NOUN}]\) Capitalisation \(\mathbf{1}[\text{word}_t \text{ is capitalised} \wedge y_t = \text{NOUN}]\)

Each feature is an indicator function (0 or 1). The weight vector \(w\) has one entry per feature. Training learns which features are informative.

Contrast with HMMs: An HMM must model \(P(\text{word}_t | y_t)\) as a probability distribution over all words — it cannot naturally use arbitrary features of the input. A CRF can.

docs.title: 3.3 Training — Maximum Conditional Log-Likelihood
docs.text:
Given training data \({(x_i, y_i)}_{i=1}^n\), we maximise: $\(\mathcal{L}(w) = \sum_{i=1}^n \log P(y_i | x_i; w) = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[\sum_{t=1}^{T_i} w^\top \phi(x_i, y_{it}, y_{i,t-1}, t) - \log Z(x_i, w)\right]\)$

Computing the gradient. Taking \(\nabla_w \mathcal{L}\): $\(\nabla_w \mathcal{L}(w) = \sum_{i=1}^n \left[\underbrace{\sum_t \phi(x_i, y_{it}, y_{i,t-1}, t)}_{\text{observed feature counts}} - \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{P(y|x_i;w)}!\left[\sum_t \phi(x_i, y_t, y_{t-1}, t)\right]}_{\text{expected feature counts}}\right]\)$

The gradient is: observed counts minus expected counts under the model. This is the standard result for log-linear models — the same structure appears in logistic regression.

The hard part: computing the expectation — i.e., the partition function \(Z(x, w)\) and the marginals \(P(y_t, y_{t-1} | x; w)\) — over all \(K^T\) possible sequences. We need dynamic programming.

docs.title: 3.4 The Forward-Backward Algorithm
docs.text:
Define the score of a partial sequence ending with label \(k\) at position \(t\): $\(\alpha_t(k) = \sum_{y_{1:t}: y_t = k} \exp!\left(\sum_{s=1}^t w^\top \phi(x, y_s, y_{s-1}, s)\right)\)$

Forward recursion: $\(\alpha_t(k) = \sum_{j=1}^K \alpha_{t-1}(j) \cdot \exp!\left(w^\top \phi(x, k, j, t)\right)\)$

with base case \(\alpha_1(k) = \exp(w^\top \phi(x, k, \text{START}, 1))\).

The partition function: \(Z(x, w) = \sum_k \alpha_T(k)\).

Backward recursion: similarly define \(\beta_t(k)\) summing over all extensions from position \(t\) to \(T\): $\(\beta_t(k) = \sum_{j=1}^K \exp!\left(w^\top \phi(x, j, k, t+1)\right) \cdot \beta_{t+1}(j)\)$

Marginals: $\(P(y_t = k, y_{t-1} = j | x; w) = \frac{\alpha_{t-1}(j) \cdot \exp(w^\top \phi(x, k, j, t)) \cdot \beta_t(k)}{Z(x, w)}\)$

Both forward and backward passes are \(O(K^2 T)\) — polynomial in sequence length, not exponential.

Complexity summary:

Operation Complexity Naïve (enumerate all \(y\)) \(O(K^T)\) Forward-backward (train) \(O(K^2 T)\) Viterbi (decode) \(O(K^2 T)\)

docs.title: 3.5 Decoding — The Viterbi Algorithm
docs.text:
At test time, we want: $\(\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y \in \mathcal{Y}} \sum_t w^\top \phi(x, y_t, y_{t-1}, t)\)$

This is the maximum weight path in a trellis — solved by the Viterbi algorithm, which replaces the \(\sum\) in the forward pass with \(\max\):

\[\delta_t(k) = \max_{y_{1:t-1}} \sum_{s=1}^t w^\top \phi(x, y_s, y_{s-1}, s) \Big|_{y_t = k}\]

Viterbi recursion: $\(\delta_t(k) = \max_j \left[\delta_{t-1}(j) + w^\top \phi(x, k, j, t)\right]\)$

Store the argmax at each step for backtracing.

Trellis diagram for POS tagging (T=3, K=3 tags: DET, NOUN, VERB):

t=1 (The)    t=2 (cat)    t=3 (sat)
  DET -------> DET -------> DET
    \         /|\          /|\
     \       / | \        / | \
  NOUN -----> NOUN -----> NOUN
     /       \ | /        \ | /
    /         \|/          \|/
  VERB -------> VERB -------> VERB

Each arrow = transition score + emission score.
Viterbi finds the maximum-weight path through this graph.
Optimal path here: DET → NOUN → VERB.

docs.title: 3.6 CRF vs. HMM — A Precise Comparison
docs.text:
Property HMM Linear-Chain CRF Model type Generative: \(P(x, y)\) Discriminative: \(P(y \| x)\) Emission model \(P(x_t \| y_t)\) — one word given tag \(\phi(x, y_t, t)\) — arbitrary features of entire \(x\) Transition \(P(y_t \| y_{t-1})\) — Markov \(\phi(y_t, y_{t-1})\) — same, but learned discriminatively Training EM (Baum-Welch) or MLE on counts Gradient ascent on conditional log-likelihood Decoding Viterbi Viterbi (identical structure) Performance on NLP Good baseline Typically stronger (richer features)

The key advantage of CRFs: you can add any features you want without worrying about whether they form a valid probability model. You cannot do this in an HMM.

docs.title: ✦ 4. Structured SVMs — Margin for Structured Outputs
4.1 Motivation
docs.text:
The CRF is a probabilistic model. The structured SVM is the large-margin alternative — it extends the binary SVM to arbitrary output spaces. This is sometimes called Structured Output Learning or the Max-Margin Markov Network (M³N).

Recall the binary SVM. We want: $\(w^\top \phi(x, y) - w^\top \phi(x, y') \geq 1 \quad \forall y' \neq y\)$

The left side is the score margin between the correct output and the best competitor. We want this margin to be at least 1.

docs.title: 4.2 The Structured SVM Objective
docs.text:
For structured outputs, we want the correct output \(y_i\) to score higher than every other output \(y' \in \mathcal{Y}\) by at least a task-specific margin \(\Delta(y_i, y')\):

\[w^\top \phi(x_i, y_i) \geq w^\top \phi(x_i, y') + \Delta(y_i, y') - \xi_i \quad \forall y' \neq y_i\]

where \(\xi_i \geq 0\) is a slack variable and \(\Delta(y_i, y')\) is the task loss (e.g., Hamming distance between two label sequences).

This gives the optimisation problem: $\(\min_{w, \xi} \frac{1}{2}|w|^2 + C\sum_i \xi_i\)$ $\(\text{s.t.} \quad w^\top [\phi(x_i, y_i) - \phi(x_i, y')] \geq \Delta(y_i, y') - \xi_i \quad \forall i, \forall y' \in \mathcal{Y}\)$

The problem: there are exponentially many constraints (one per output \(y'\) per training example). We cannot enumerate them.

The solution: Cutting-plane algorithms maintain a working set of active constraints and iterate:

  1. Solve the QP with the current working set.
  2. Find the most violated constraint for each training example — this is the key step.
  3. Add it to the working set.
  4. Repeat until convergence.

docs.title: 4.3 The Loss-Augmented Inference Step
docs.text:
Finding the most violated constraint for example \(i\) reduces to: $\(y_i^* = \arg\max_{y' \in \mathcal{Y}} \left[\Delta(y_i, y') + w^\top \phi(x_i, y') - w^\top \phi(x_i, y_i)\right]\)$

Dropping the constant \(-w^\top \phi(x_i, y_i)\): $\(y_i^* = \arg\max_{y' \in \mathcal{Y}} \left[\Delta(y_i, y') + w^\top \phi(x_i, y')\right]\)$

This is called loss-augmented inference — it is inference (finding the best output) but with the task loss \(\Delta\) added to the score. For Hamming loss on sequences, this decomposes position-by-position and can be solved with a modified Viterbi in \(O(K^2 T)\) — the same complexity as standard decoding.

docs.title: 4.4 The Structured Hinge Loss
docs.text:
We can write the Structured SVM objective as minimising a regularised structured hinge loss: $\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{struct}}(w) = \frac{1}{2}|w|^2 + C\sum_i \underbrace{\max_{y'} \left[\Delta(y_i, y') + w^\top \phi(x_i, y')\right] - w^\top \phi(x_i, y_i)}_{\text{structured hinge loss for example } i}\)$

The structured hinge loss is zero when the correct output scores higher than all others by the loss-weighted margin, and positive otherwise.

Comparison with binary SVM:

Binary SVM Structured SVM Output space \({-1, +1}\) Arbitrary \(\mathcal{Y}\) Margin 1 \(\Delta(y, y')\) (task-dependent) Inference at test time \(\text{sign}(w^\top x)\) \(\arg\max_{y} w^\top \phi(x, y)\) Training-time computation Solve a QP Solve a QP + loss-augmented inference Key algorithm SMO Cutting-plane + Viterbi (for sequences)

docs.title: 4.5 Connection: Structured SVM ↔ CRF
docs.text:
The structured SVM and the CRF are two approaches to the same problem. Their relationship:

  • CRF: log-linear model, trained with maximum likelihood. Produces probability estimates.
  • Structured SVM: margin-based model, trained with structured hinge loss. Does not produce probabilities.
  • Unifying perspective: both learn a scoring function \(s(x, y; w)\) of the form \(w^\top \phi(x, y)\). They differ only in the loss function used to train \(w\).

In practice, CRFs became the dominant approach in NLP because:

  1. Probabilistic outputs are useful downstream.
  2. Maximum likelihood has cleaner behaviour in the large-data regime.
  3. Deep learning made it natural to parameterise \(\phi(x, y_t, y_{t-1}, t)\) with a neural network — the BiLSTM-CRF and Transformer-CRF architectures.

docs.title: ✦ 5. Application: Named Entity Recognition (NER)
docs.text:
NER: tag each word in a sentence with its entity type — PER (person), ORG (organisation), LOC (location), O (other).

Input: ["Barack", "Obama", "visited", "Paris"] Output: [B-PER, I-PER, O, B-LOC]

(BIO tagging scheme: B- = beginning of entity, I- = inside, O = outside.)

Why a CRF? B-PER followed by I-ORG is illegal — the CRF's transition features learn to assign \(-\infty\) weight to such transitions. A flat classifier would not know this.

Features a linear-chain CRF might use:

  • Is the word capitalised? → strong signal for PER or ORG
  • Does the word appear in a gazetteer of known cities? → signal for LOC
  • Previous word is a title ("President", "Dr.")? → strong signal for B-PER
  • Transition: B-PER → I-PER vs. B-PER → O — the CRF learns this

Modern approach: Replace the hand-crafted \(\phi\) with a BiLSTM or Transformer to compute a contextual embedding at each position. The CRF layer sits on top:

Input:  [Barack,   Obama,    visited,  Paris  ]
         ↓         ↓         ↓         ↓
BiLSTM: [h_1,     h_2,      h_3,      h_4    ]  ← contextual embeddings
         ↓         ↓         ↓         ↓
Emit:   [e(h_1),  e(h_2),   e(h_3),   e(h_4) ]  ← emission scores (K-dim)
         ↓         ↓         ↓         ↓
CRF:    [B-PER,   I-PER,    O,        B-LOC  ]  ← globally optimal sequence

The CRF layer adds \(K \times K\) transition parameters on top of the neural emission scores. Viterbi decoding is applied at the output.

docs.title: 6.1 Sequence-to-Sequence (different input/output length)
docs.text:
For translation, summarisation, and similar tasks, the output sequence length differs from the input. The linear-chain CRF cannot handle this — the output structure no longer aligns position-by-position with the input.

Solutions:

  • Encoder-decoder with attention (the dominant approach): encode the input into a context vector, decode autoregressively. Not a CRF — instead uses a left-to-right language model.
  • CTC (Connectionist Temporal Classification): for speech recognition, where output phonemes don't align to input frames.

docs.title: 6.2 Structured Outputs Over Trees
docs.text:
For constituency parsing, the output is a parse tree. The structured SVM generalises — you need:

  • A feature function \(\phi(x, \text{tree})\) that decomposes over tree nodes.
  • An efficient inference algorithm — in this case, the CKY (Cocke-Kasami-Younger) algorithm for context-free grammars.

docs.title: 6.3 Image Segmentation
docs.text: Each pixel receives a label. The output space is a grid. A Markov Random Field (MRF) or CRF on a grid is the natural model — neighbouring pixels tend to have the same label. Inference on grids is harder than on chains (NP-hard in general) and requires approximate methods (graph cuts, mean field).

docs.title: ✦ 7. Connection to AI / ML / Deep Learning
7.1 The BiLSTM-CRF — State of the Art Before Transformers
docs.text:
The model of Lample et al. (2016) set the standard for NER:

  • BiLSTM encodes the sentence bidirectionally → contextual embeddings.
  • CRF decodes the label sequence respecting transition constraints.

This architecture is a structured prediction model where \(\phi(x, y_t, y_{t-1}, t)\) is parameterised by a neural network. The Viterbi and forward-backward algorithms run exactly as above — the only difference is that emission scores come from a BiLSTM rather than hand-crafted features.

docs.title: 7.2 Transformers and Structured Outputs
docs.text:
Modern approaches (BERT-based NER, T5, etc.) often drop the CRF layer entirely, relying on the Transformer's attention mechanism to model inter-label dependencies implicitly. But CRF layers are still used when:

  • Hard constraints matter (e.g., no I-PER without a preceding B-PER).
  • The training set is small (CRF transition constraints act as regularisation).
  • Calibrated probabilities are needed.

docs.title: 7.3 Structured Outputs in Reinforcement Learning
docs.text: The policy \(\pi(a|s)\) in RL is a structured output when the action space has structure. Sequence-to-sequence models trained with RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) generate tokens autoregressively — this is structured prediction with an RL objective.

docs.title: 7.4 The Argmax Bottleneck and Differentiable Structure
docs.text:
A core challenge: the \(\arg\max\) in structured prediction is not differentiable, which complicates end-to-end training with neural networks. Active research directions:

Method Idea STE (Straight-Through Estimator) Treat argmax as identity in backward pass Gumbel-Softmax Continuous relaxation of categorical sampling CRF with marginal inference Replace \(\arg\max\) with expected feature counts — differentiable SPIGOT Project gradient through argmax using polytope geometry

These are active research areas connecting structured prediction to deep learning.

docs.title: ✦ 8. Worked Example — CRF Forward Pass by Hand
docs.text:
Setup. 2 positions (\(T=2\)), 2 labels (\(K=2\): N=NOUN, V=VERB).

Define emission scores (already computed from \(w^\top \phi\)):

\(t=1\) (cat) \(t=2\) (sat) N 1.5 0.2 V 0.3 2.0

Transition scores (learned):

→ N → V START 0.8 0.1 N → 0.6 1.2 V → 0.4 0.9

Forward pass (\(\alpha_t(k)\) in log-space \(= \log \alpha\), actually in score space here for clarity):

\(t=1\): $\(\alpha_1(\text{N}) = \exp(0.8 + 1.5) = e^{2.3} \approx 9.97\)$ $\(\alpha_1(\text{V}) = \exp(0.1 + 0.3) = e^{0.4} \approx 1.49\)$

\(t=2\): $\(\alpha_2(\text{N}) = \alpha_1(\text{N}) \cdot e^{0.6 + 0.2} + \alpha_1(\text{V}) \cdot e^{0.4 + 0.2}\)$ $\(= 9.97 \cdot e^{0.8} + 1.49 \cdot e^{0.6} \approx 9.97 \cdot 2.23 + 1.49 \cdot 1.82 \approx 22.23 + 2.71 = 24.94\)$

\[\alpha_2(\text{V}) = \alpha_1(\text{N}) \cdot e^{1.2 + 2.0} + \alpha_1(\text{V}) \cdot e^{0.9 + 2.0}$$ $$= 9.97 \cdot e^{3.2} + 1.49 \cdot e^{2.9} \approx 9.97 \cdot 24.53 + 1.49 \cdot 18.17 \approx 244.6 + 27.1 = 271.7\]

Partition function: $\(Z = \alpha_2(\text{N}) + \alpha_2(\text{V}) \approx 24.94 + 271.7 = 296.64\)$

Posterior of N → V (the true sequence "cat sat" = NOUN VERB): $\(P(\text{N}, \text{V} | x) = \frac{\alpha_1(\text{N}) \cdot e^{1.2 + 2.0}}{Z} = \frac{9.97 \cdot 24.53}{296.64} \approx \frac{244.6}{296.64} \approx 0.824\)$

The model assigns 82.4% probability to the correct sequence — before any training.

Viterbi decoding would trace back the path through the trellis:

  • At \(t=2\): V wins (\(\alpha_2(\text{V}) = 271.7 \gg \alpha_2(\text{N}) = 24.94\))
  • Backtrack: best predecessor of V at \(t=2\) is N (score \(9.97 \cdot e^{3.2} = 244.6\) vs \(1.49 \cdot e^{2.9} = 27.1\))
  • Prediction: [N, V] = [NOUN, VERB] ✓

docs.title: 9.1 CRF Forward-Backward in NumPy
docs.text:
import numpy as np

def log_sum_exp(x):
    """Numerically stable log-sum-exp."""
    m = x.max()
    return m + np.log(np.sum(np.exp(x - m)))

def crf_forward(emission_scores, transition_scores):
    """
    emission_scores: (T, K) — score of each label at each position
    transition_scores: (K, K) — transition[i, j] = score of going from i to j

    Returns: log Z (partition function)
    """
    T, K = emission_scores.shape

    # alpha[k] = log sum of scores of all paths ending in label k at current t
    alpha = emission_scores[0]  # at t=0, no transition

    for t in range(1, T):
        # alpha_new[k] = log_sum_exp over j of (alpha[j] + trans[j,k] + emit[t,k])
        alpha_new = np.zeros(K)
        for k in range(K):
            scores = alpha + transition_scores[:, k] + emission_scores[t, k]
            alpha_new[k] = log_sum_exp(scores)
        alpha = alpha_new

    return log_sum_exp(alpha)  # log Z

def viterbi(emission_scores, transition_scores):
    """
    Returns: best label sequence (T,)
    """
    T, K = emission_scores.shape
    delta = emission_scores[0].copy()
    psi = np.zeros((T, K), dtype=int)  # backpointers

    for t in range(1, T):
        for k in range(K):
            scores = delta + transition_scores[:, k] + emission_scores[t, k]
            psi[t, k] = np.argmax(scores)
            delta[k] = scores[psi[t, k]]

    # Backtrace
    path = np.zeros(T, dtype=int)
    path[T-1] = np.argmax(delta)
    for t in range(T-2, -1, -1):
        path[t] = psi[t+1, path[t+1]]

    return path

# --- Example ---
T, K = 3, 3  # 3 positions, 3 labels
emission = np.random.randn(T, K)
transition = np.random.randn(K, K)

log_Z = crf_forward(emission, transition)
best_path = viterbi(emission, transition)
print(f"log Z = {log_Z:.3f}, best path = {best_path}")

docs.title: 9.2 Using sklearn-crfsuite or pytorch-crf
docs.text:
# PyTorch CRF (torchcrf library)
from torchcrf import CRF
import torch

num_tags = 5
crf = CRF(num_tags, batch_first=True)

# emissions: (batch, seq_len, num_tags) — from your BiLSTM/Transformer
emissions = torch.randn(2, 10, num_tags)
tags = torch.randint(num_tags, (2, 10))

# Training: maximise log-likelihood
loss = -crf(emissions, tags)

# Decoding: Viterbi
best_sequence = crf.decode(emissions)

docs.title: ✦ 10. Summary and Exit Criteria
docs.text:
You know this when you can:

  1. Derive the CRF partition function and explain why it requires the forward algorithm — not brute-force enumeration.
  2. State the complexity of the forward-backward and Viterbi algorithms and explain where the \(K^2\) factor comes from.
  3. Write the CRF gradient in terms of observed vs. expected feature counts and explain why this is the same structure as logistic regression.
  4. Explain why a CRF outperforms position-wise logistic regression for sequence labelling, with a concrete example.
  5. Formulate the Structured SVM as a QP, explain what loss-augmented inference is, and describe the cutting-plane algorithm at a high level.
  6. Compare CRF and Structured SVM on: model assumptions, training objective, output, and practical use cases.
  7. Implement the forward algorithm and Viterbi in NumPy without looking at references.
  8. Explain how the BiLSTM-CRF architecture uses these ideas, and why deep learning practitioners sometimes drop the CRF layer.
