docs.title: The RL Problem
docs.text:
\

"The agent does not know the rules of the game. It only knows what it did, and what happened next."

docs.title: ✦ Why RL Is Different
docs.text:
In supervised learning, someone hands you \((x_i, y_i)\) pairs. A teacher has already labelled the correct answer. In unsupervised learning, you have \(x_i\) alone and look for structure.

Reinforcement learning has neither. There is no teacher. There is only an agent living inside an environment, taking actions, and receiving rewards. The agent must figure out, entirely from this signal, what to do.

This changes everything:

- Supervised Unsupervised Reinforcement Feedback Correct label None Scalar reward (delayed, noisy) i.i.d. data? Yes Yes No — actions affect future observations Exploration needed? No No Yes — must try things to learn Credit assignment Immediate N/A Delayed — which action caused the reward?

The credit assignment problem is the central difficulty: the reward you receive now may be the consequence of an action you took ten steps ago. How do you know which action to credit?

docs.title: ✦ Prerequisites
docs.text:
• [[03.Probability Review]] — expectations, conditional distributions, Markov chains
  • [[04.Bias Variance Tradeoff]] — exploration vs. exploitation as a bias-variance analogue
  • [[02.Statistical Learning Theory]] — PAC learning, generalisation (for context)

docs.title: ✦ 1. The Markov Decision Process (MDP)
docs.text:
Every RL problem is formalised as a Markov Decision Process. An MDP is a tuple:

\[\mathcal{M} = \langle \mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, P, R, \gamma \rangle\] Symbol Name Meaning \(\mathcal{S}\) State space All possible situations the agent can be in \(\mathcal{A}\) Action space All possible actions the agent can take \(P(s' \| s, a)\) Transition kernel Probability of landing in \(s'\) after taking \(a\) in \(s\) \(R(s, a, s')\) Reward function Scalar feedback received after transition \(\gamma \in [0,1)\) Discount factor How much the agent cares about future rewards

The Markov property (the thing that makes MDPs tractable):

\[P(s_{t+1} | s_t, a_t, s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}, \ldots) = P(s_{t+1} | s_t, a_t)\]

The future depends on the present state and action only — not on the full history. This is the fundamental assumption. It is often violated in practice (partially observable environments), and we will note when this matters.

docs.title: 1.1 The Agent-Environment Loop
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
         │                                         │
         ▼                                         │
    ┌─────────┐   a_t    ┌─────────────┐           │
    │  Agent  │ ──────►  │ Environment │           │
    │         │          │             │           │
    │  π(a|s) │ ◄──────  │  P(s'|s,a)  │           │
    └─────────┘  s_{t+1} └─────────────┘           │
         │         r_{t+1}       │                 │
         │                       │                 │
         └───────────────────────┘─────────────────┘
                    one time step

At each time step \(t\):

  1. Agent observes state \(s_t \in \mathcal{S}\)
  2. Agent samples action \(a_t \sim \pi(\cdot | s_t)\)
  3. Environment transitions to \(s_{t+1} \sim P(\cdot | s_t, a_t)\)
  4. Agent receives reward \(r_{t+1} = R(s_t, a_t, s_{t+1})\)
  5. Repeat

The sequence \((s_0, a_0, r_1, s_1, a_1, r_2, s_2, \ldots)\) is called a trajectory or episode.

docs.title: 1.2 Concrete Examples
docs.text:
Domain \(\mathcal{S}\) \(\mathcal{A}\) \(R\) Chess Board position Legal moves \(+1\) win, \(-1\) loss, \(0\) otherwise CartPole \((x, \dot{x}, \theta, \dot{\theta})\) Left/Right \(+1\) per timestep upright Atari Breakout Raw pixels (screen) Joystick directions Score increment Robot arm Joint angles, velocities Torques Distance to target (negated) Recommender system User history Item to show Click, purchase, dwell time

Notice: in chess, reward is received only at the end of the game. In CartPole, reward is received at every step. The discount factor \(\gamma\) is the mechanism for handling both cases.

docs.title: ✦ 2. The Return
docs.text:
The agent's goal is not to maximise the immediate reward. It is to maximise the expected sum of future rewards. Define the return (or discounted cumulative reward) from time \(t\):

\[G_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma r_{t+2} + \gamma^2 r_{t+3} + \cdots = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k r_{t+k+1}\]

Why discount?

  1. Mathematical: ensures \(G_t\) is finite for bounded rewards. If \(|r| \leq R_{\max}\), then \(G_t \leq \frac{R_{\max}}{1 - \gamma}\).
  2. Economic: future rewards are uncertain; a reward now is worth more than a reward later.
  3. Practical: \(\gamma < 1\) allows the algorithm to converge. At \(\gamma = 1\), many algorithms diverge.

The recursive structure of the return — this is what makes dynamic programming possible: $\(G_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma G_{t+1}\)$

The return from \(t\) equals the immediate reward plus the discounted return from \(t+1\). This single equation is the seed from which Bellman equations grow.

docs.title: 2.1 Finite vs. Infinite Horizon
docs.text:
Horizon Setting Return Finite (\(T < \infty\)) Episodes end (chess, Atari) \(G_t = \sum_{k=0}^{T-t} r_{t+k+1}\), \(\gamma = 1\) possible Infinite (\(T = \infty\)) Continuing tasks (robot control) \(G_t = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k r_{t+k+1}\), requires \(\gamma < 1\)

For episodic tasks, it is common to define a terminal state \(s_{\text{terminal}}\) that absorbs all transitions with zero reward — this makes finite and infinite horizon mathematically equivalent.

docs.title: ✦ 3. The Policy
docs.text:
The policy \(\pi\) is the agent's behaviour — the mapping from states to actions.

Stochastic policy: \(\pi(a | s) = P(A_t = a | S_t = s)\) — a probability distribution over actions given state.

Deterministic policy: \(\pi(s) = a\) — a single action for each state.

Stochastic policies are more general and necessary for some environments (e.g., rock-paper-scissors — a deterministic policy is exploitable). Deterministic policies are a special case.

The goal of RL: find the optimal policy: $\(\pi^* = \arg\max_\pi \mathbb{E}_\pi[G_0]\)$

Everything in RL — value functions, Bellman equations, Q-learning, policy gradients — is a different approach to this optimisation.

docs.title: ✦ 4. Value Functions
docs.text: Value functions answer the question: "How good is it to be in state \(s\) (or to take action \(a\) in state \(s\)) when following policy \(\pi\)?"

docs.title: 4.1 The State-Value Function \(V^\pi\)
docs.text:
\[V^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_\pi\left[G_t ,\Big|, S_t = s\right] = \mathbb{E}_\pi\left[\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \gamma^k r_{t+k+1} ,\Big|, S_t = s\right]\]

This is the expected return starting from state \(s\), following policy \(\pi\) thereafter.

Intuition: \(V^\pi(s)\) is the "long-term value" of being in state \(s\) under policy \(\pi\). If \(V^\pi(s) = 100\), state \(s\) is great under \(\pi\). If \(V^\pi(s) = -50\), state \(s\) is terrible.

docs.title: 4.2 The Action-Value Function \(Q^\pi\)
docs.text:
\[Q^\pi(s, a) = \mathbb{E}_\pi\left[G_t ,\Big|, S_t = s, A_t = a\right]\]

This is the expected return starting from state \(s\), first taking action \(a\), then following policy \(\pi\) thereafter.

The relationship between \(V^\pi\) and \(Q^\pi\): $\(V^\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi(a|s) \cdot Q^\pi(s, a)\)$

\(V^\pi(s)\) is the \(\pi\)-weighted average of \(Q^\pi(s, a)\) over all actions — exactly what you'd expect. The value of a state is the expected value of the actions you'd take there.

Why \(Q^\pi\) is more useful for learning. If you know \(Q^\pi(s, a)\) for all \((s, a)\), you can improve the policy greedily: $\(\pi'(s) = \arg\max_a Q^\pi(s, a)\)$

without needing to know \(P(s'|s,a)\) — the transition dynamics. This is the key to model-free RL.

docs.title: 4.3 The Advantage Function
docs.text:
\[A^\pi(s, a) = Q^\pi(s, a) - V^\pi(s)\]

The advantage measures how much better action \(a\) is compared to the average action under \(\pi\) in state \(s\). If \(A^\pi(s, a) > 0\), action \(a\) is better than average. If \(A^\pi(s, a) < 0\), it's worse.

The advantage function appears naturally in policy gradient methods (Advantage Actor-Critic, PPO) because it reduces variance: instead of asking "is the total return good?", we ask "is this action better than expected?"

docs.title: ✦ 5. Bellman Equations — The Engine of RL
docs.text: The Bellman equations express a consistency condition: the value of a state must equal the immediate reward plus the discounted value of the next state. They are derived directly from the recursive structure of the return.

docs.title: 5.1 Bellman Expectation Equations
docs.text:
For \(V^\pi\): Start from the definition and expand using \(G_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma G_{t+1}\):

\[V^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[G_t | S_t = s]$$ $$= \mathbb{E}_\pi[r_{t+1} + \gamma G_{t+1} | S_t = s]$$ $$= \sum_a \pi(a|s) \sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a)\left[R(s,a,s') + \gamma \mathbb{E}_\pi[G_{t+1}|S_{t+1}=s']\right]\] \[\boxed{V^\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi(a|s) \sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a)\left[R(s,a,s') + \gamma V^\pi(s')\right]}\]

For \(Q^\pi\): Same derivation, conditioning on \((s, a)\):

\[\boxed{Q^\pi(s,a) = \sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a)\left[R(s,a,s') + \gamma \sum_{a'} \pi(a'|s') Q^\pi(s',a')\right]}\]

These are linear equations in \(V^\pi\) (or \(Q^\pi\)). Given \(\pi\) and the model \(P, R\), they can be solved exactly by linear algebra (for small state spaces) or by iterative methods.

docs.title: 5.2 The Backup Diagram
docs.text:
Bellman equation for V^π:

         s
        / \
       a₁  a₂        ← weighted by π(a|s)
      / \  / \
    s₁' s₂' s₃'      ← weighted by P(s'|s,a)

V^π(s) = Σ_a π(a|s) Σ_{s'} P(s'|s,a) [R + γ V^π(s')]

The value of s is computed by "backing up" from its successor states.

Bellman equation for Q^π:

        (s,a)
        /   \
      s₁'   s₂'       ← weighted by P(s'|s,a)
      / \   / \
    a₁' a₂' ...       ← weighted by π(a'|s')

Q^π(s,a) = Σ_{s'} P(s'|s,a) [R + γ Σ_{a'} π(a'|s') Q^π(s',a')]

docs.title: 5.3 Bellman Optimality Equations
docs.text:
The optimal value functions \(V^_\) and \(Q^_\) satisfy the Bellman optimality equations — the same structure, but with \(\max\) in place of \(\sum_a \pi(a|s)\):

\[\boxed{V^_(s) = \max_a \sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a)\left[R(s,a,s') + \gamma V^_(s')\right]}\] \[\boxed{Q^_(s,a) = \sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a)\left[R(s,a,s') + \gamma \max_{a'} Q^_(s',a')\right]}\]

Why the max? The optimal policy always takes the best action. So instead of averaging over \(\pi(a|s)\), we take the maximum.

The optimal policy from \(Q^*\): $\(\pi^_(s) = \arg\max_a Q^_(s,a)\)$

If you have \(Q^*\), the optimal policy is free — just act greedily. This is the core of Q-learning.

docs.title: 5.4 Bellman Equations Are Not Learning Algorithms
docs.text:
The Bellman equations are fixed-point conditions — they characterise what \(V^\pi\) or \(Q^*\) must look like. They are not algorithms by themselves. The algorithms (Value Iteration, Q-learning, TD learning) use these equations as update rules:

Algorithm Update rule Comes from Value Iteration \(V(s) \leftarrow \max_a \sum_{s'} P(s'\|s,a)[R + \gamma V(s')]\) Bellman optimality for \(V^*\) Policy Iteration Evaluate \(V^\pi\) exactly, then \(\pi \leftarrow \text{greedy}(V^\pi)\) Bellman expectation for \(V^\pi\) Q-learning \(Q(s,a) \leftarrow Q(s,a) + \alpha[r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s',a') - Q(s,a)]\) Bellman optimality for \(Q^*\) TD(0) \(V(s) \leftarrow V(s) + \alpha[r + \gamma V(s') - V(s)]\) Bellman expectation for \(V^\pi\)

docs.title: ✦ 6. The Optimal Policy Exists — And We Can Find It
docs.text:
Theorem (Existence of \(\pi^*\)). For any finite MDP, there exists at least one deterministic optimal policy \(\pi^_\) such that \(V^{\pi^_}(s) \geq V^\pi(s)\) for all \(s\) and all \(\pi\).

Proof sketch. Define \(V^_(s) = \max_\pi V^\pi(s)\) pointwise. One can show that the Bellman optimality equation has a unique fixed point \(V^_\) (by contraction mapping — the Bellman operator is a \(\gamma\)-contraction in the \(\ell^\infty\) norm). The greedy policy with respect to \(V^*\) is then optimal.

Theorem (Contraction of the Bellman operator). Define the Bellman optimality operator \(\mathcal{T}\): $\((\mathcal{T}V)(s) = \max_a \sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a)[R(s,a,s') + \gamma V(s')]\)$

Then \(|\mathcal{T}V - \mathcal{T}U|_\infty \leq \gamma |V - U|_\infty\) for all \(V, U\).

By Banach's fixed-point theorem, iterating \(\mathcal{T}\) converges to the unique fixed point \(V^*\). This is Value Iteration — and the contraction guarantees convergence at rate \(\gamma^k\) after \(k\) iterations.

docs.title: ✦ 7. Key Dichotomies in RL
docs.text: These distinctions determine which algorithm is appropriate for a given problem. Each is a design choice, not a fact about RL in general.

docs.title: 7.1 Model-Based vs. Model-Free
docs.text:
Model-Based Model-Free Uses \(P(s'\|s,a)\)? Yes (known or learned) No Planning Yes — can simulate trajectories No Sample efficiency High Low Computation High (planning) Low Examples Value Iteration, Dyna-Q, AlphaZero Q-learning, REINFORCE, PPO

Model-free is the dominant paradigm in deep RL because the transition model is often too complex to learn accurately (e.g., Atari pixels → next pixels). Model-based RL is preferred when the model is available (board games, physics simulators) or the sample budget is tiny (robotics).

docs.title: 7.2 On-Policy vs. Off-Policy
docs.text:
On-Policy Off-Policy What data is used? Data from the current policy \(\pi\) Data from any policy (including old ones) Sample efficiency Lower (must discard old data) Higher (can reuse data) Convergence Easier to guarantee Harder (deadly triad) Examples SARSA, REINFORCE, PPO Q-learning, DQN, SAC

Q-learning is off-policy because the update uses \(\max_{a'} Q(s', a')\) — the greedy action — regardless of what policy actually generated the data. This allows learning from a replay buffer of old experience.

docs.title: 7.3 Value-Based vs. Policy-Based vs. Actor-Critic
docs.text: Value-Based Policy-Based Actor-Critic What is learned? \(Q(s,a)\) or \(V(s)\) \(\pi_\theta(a\|s)\) directly Both \(\pi_\theta\) and \(V_\phi\) Policy Implicit: \(\pi = \arg\max_a Q\) Explicit Explicit Continuous actions? Hard (requires \(\arg\max\)) Natural Natural Variance Low (bootstrapping) High (Monte Carlo returns) Medium Examples Q-learning, DQN REINFORCE A2C, PPO, SAC

docs.title: 7.4 Tabular vs. Function Approximation
docs.text:
Tabular Function Approximation Represents \(Q(s,a)\) as a table \(Q(s,a;\theta)\) as a neural network State space Small, discrete Large, continuous, high-dimensional Convergence guarantees Strong Weaker (deadly triad) Expressiveness Limited High

The deadly triad (Sutton & Barto): combining function approximation + bootstrapping + off-policy learning can cause divergence. DQN carefully avoids this with experience replay and target networks — see [[02.Model-Free Methods]].

docs.title: ✦ 8. Exploration vs. Exploitation — The Fundamental Tension
docs.text:
The agent must explore (try new actions to gain information) and exploit (take the best known action to maximise reward). These are in direct conflict.

The multi-armed bandit is the pure form of this problem (no states, no transitions) — see [[03.Exploration vs Exploitation]].

In full MDPs, exploration is harder because:

  • The consequences of an action are delayed and entangled with future actions.
  • Some states are only reachable through specific action sequences.

Basic strategies:

Strategy Idea When to use \(\epsilon\)-greedy With prob \(\epsilon\), take random action Always a reasonable default Boltzmann / Softmax \(\pi(a\|s) \propto \exp(Q(s,a)/\tau)\) When you want graded exploration UCB (Upper Confidence Bound) Favour actions with high uncertainty Bandits, tabular RL Thompson Sampling Sample from posterior over \(Q\) values Bayesian RL Intrinsic motivation Reward for visiting novel states Sparse reward environments

docs.title: ✦ 9. Worked Example — GridWorld MDP
docs.text:
Setup. A \(4 \times 4\) grid. Agent starts at top-left. Goal state at bottom-right (reward \(+1\)). Cliff state at bottom-left (reward \(-1\), terminal). All other transitions: reward \(0\). Actions: \({\)N, S, E, W\(}\). \(\gamma = 0.9\).

┌─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┐
│  S  │     │     │     │
├─────┼─────┼─────┼─────┤
│     │     │     │     │
├─────┼─────┼─────┼─────┤
│     │     │     │     │
├─────┼─────┼─────┼─────┤
│  C  │     │     │  G  │
└─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┘
S = Start, G = Goal (+1), C = Cliff (-1)

MDP components:

  • \(\mathcal{S}\): 16 grid positions (plus 2 terminal states)
  • \(\mathcal{A}\): \({\)N, S, E, W\(}\)
  • \(P(s'|s,a)\): deterministic (actions succeed with prob 1, hit wall → stay)
  • \(R\): \(+1\) at \(G\), \(-1\) at \(C\), \(0\) elsewhere
  • \(\gamma = 0.9\)

Value Iteration (first two sweeps, for the state adjacent to G):

Let \(s_G^-\) denote the state immediately left of G.

Sweep 1: \(V(s_G^-) = \max_a \sum_{s'} P[R + \gamma V(s')] = \max(\ldots, 0 + 0.9 \cdot 0, \ldots, 1 + 0.9 \cdot 0) = 1\)

(Taking action East reaches G, reward \(+1\), \(V(G) = 0\) since terminal.)

Sweep 2: The state two steps left of G updates: \(V = 0 + 0.9 \cdot 1 = 0.9\)

After convergence, \(V^*(s)\) decreases with distance to G (and increases near C — the agent learns to avoid it). The optimal policy points toward G everywhere except near C, where it routes around.

docs.title: ✦ 10. Partial Observability — When the Markov Property Fails
docs.text:
The MDP assumes the agent observes the full state \(s_t\). Often it doesn't:

  • Poker: you cannot see opponents' cards.
  • Robot navigation: the robot sees only its camera, not the full map.
  • Medical treatment: the patient's true health state is hidden; only symptoms are observed.

The correct model is a Partially Observable MDP (POMDP): $\(\mathcal{M} = \langle \mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, \mathcal{O}, P, O, R, \gamma \rangle\)$

where \(\mathcal{O}\) is the observation space and \(O(o | s', a)\) is the observation model.

The agent maintains a belief state \(b_t = P(s_t | o_0, a_0, \ldots, o_t)\) — a probability distribution over states. The belief state is a sufficient statistic for the history, so \(b_t\) is itself Markovian. But \(|\mathcal{B}|\) (belief space) is infinite even if \(|\mathcal{S}|\) is finite.

Deep RL approximation: use an RNN (LSTM, GRU) to maintain a hidden state that approximates the belief state. This is why RNNs appear in RL for partially observable environments.

docs.title: ✦ 11. Connection to AI / ML / Deep Learning
11.1 Deep RL — Approximating Value Functions with Neural Networks
docs.text:
In the tabular setting, \(Q(s, a)\) is stored as a table. For large state spaces (Atari: \(210 \times 160 \times 3\) pixel screens), this is impossible. Deep Q-Networks (DQN) approximate: $\(Q(s, a) \approx Q(s, a; \theta)\)$

where \(\theta\) are the parameters of a convolutional neural network. The Bellman optimality equation becomes the training target: $\(\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\left[\left(r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a'; \theta^-) - Q(s, a; \theta)\right)^2\right]\)$

where \(\theta^-\) is a target network — a periodically frozen copy of \(\theta\) that stabilises training. See [[02.Model-Free Methods]].

docs.title: 11.2 RL as the Third Pillar of ML
docs.text:
Supervised learning: learn from labelled data. Unsupervised learning: find structure without labels. RL: learn to act from reward signals. These three are genuinely distinct and complementary:

  • A speech recogniser is trained with supervised learning.
  • A language model is pre-trained with self-supervised (unsupervised) learning.
  • A dialogue agent is fine-tuned with RL (RLHF — Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback).

RLHF is the mechanism behind GPT-4, Claude, and similar models — the MDP is: state = conversation history, action = next token, reward = human preference signal. The policy is the language model.

docs.title: 11.3 The Connection to Optimal Control
docs.text: RL is essentially optimal control without a known model. Classical optimal control (LQR, MPC) assumes \(P(s'|s,a)\) is known analytically. RL discovers the policy without knowing the model — making it applicable wherever simulation or interaction is possible but analytical models are not.

docs.title: 11.4 AlphaGo / AlphaZero
docs.text:
AlphaZero (Silver et al., 2017) is a model-based RL system for board games:

  • State: board position.
  • Action: legal moves.
  • Model: known (rules of chess/Go).
  • Value network: approximates \(V^*(s)\) — trained by self-play.
  • Policy network: approximates \(\pi^*(a|s)\) — guides Monte Carlo Tree Search.

The Bellman equations are the foundation; the neural networks are the approximation; Monte Carlo Tree Search is the planning algorithm. The MDP formalism unifies all of it.

docs.title: ✦ 12. Summary Table
docs.text: Concept Symbol Meaning State \(s \in \mathcal{S}\) Current situation Action \(a \in \mathcal{A}\) What the agent does Transition \(P(s'\|s,a)\) Where the agent ends up Reward \(R(s,a,s')\) Immediate feedback Return \(G_t = \sum_k \gamma^k r_{t+k+1}\) Long-term cumulative reward Policy \(\pi(a\|s)\) Agent's behaviour State-value \(V^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[G_t \| S_t=s]\) Expected return from \(s\) under \(\pi\) Action-value \(Q^\pi(s,a) = \mathbb{E}_\pi[G_t \| S_t=s, A_t=a]\) Expected return from \((s,a)\) under \(\pi\) Advantage \(A^\pi(s,a) = Q^\pi(s,a) - V^\pi(s)\) How much better \(a\) is vs. average Bellman (expectation) \(V^\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi \sum_{s'} P[R + \gamma V^\pi(s')]\) Consistency condition for \(V^\pi\) Bellman (optimality) \(V^_(s) = \max_a \sum_{s'} P[R + \gamma V^_(s')]\) Fixed point for optimal value Optimal policy \(\pi^* = \arg\max_\pi V^\pi\) The agent's goal

docs.title: ✦ Exit Criteria
docs.text:
You know this when you can:

  1. Write the MDP tuple \(\langle \mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, P, R, \gamma \rangle\) from scratch and define each component for a concrete domain (chess, CartPole, a recommendation system).
  2. Derive the Bellman expectation equation for \(V^\pi\) from \(G_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma G_{t+1}\), without looking at notes — two lines of algebra.
  3. State the Bellman optimality equations for both \(V^_\) and \(Q^_\), and explain the \(\max\) vs. \(\sum_a \pi\) distinction.
  4. Explain the contraction mapping argument: why does Value Iteration converge, and at what rate?
  5. Derive the relationship \(V^\pi(s) = \sum_a \pi(a|s) Q^\pi(s,a)\) from definitions.
  6. Define the advantage function \(A^\pi\) and explain why it appears in policy gradient methods.
  7. Classify any RL algorithm along the three dichotomies: model-based/free, on/off-policy, value/policy/actor-critic.
  8. Explain why \(Q^_\) is more useful than \(V^_\) for model-free RL.
  9. Explain what goes wrong when the Markov property fails, and how POMDPs handle it.
  10. Connect RLHF to the MDP formalism: what is the state, action, and reward in GPT fine-tuning?

docs.title: Model-Free Methods
docs.text: "Model-free methods are the empiricists of RL — they refuse to model the world, and instead learn entirely from what they experience."

docs.title: ✦ Where This Note Lives in the Map
docs.text:
[[01.The RL Problem]] established the MDP \(\langle \mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, P, R, \gamma \rangle\), the Bellman equations, and the goal: find \(\pi^*\).

Dynamic Programming (Value Iteration, Policy Iteration) solves this exactly — but requires knowing \(P(s'|s,a)\) and \(R(s,a,s')\) in closed form, and iterating over the entire state space. Neither assumption holds in most real problems.

Model-free methods discard both requirements. They learn directly from experience — sequences of \((s_t, a_t, r_{t+1}, s_{t+1})\) — without ever building a model of the environment. The price is sample efficiency. The payoff is generality.

This note covers the full hierarchy:

Model-Free RL
├── Dynamic Programming (model-based baseline — for contrast)
│   ├── Policy Evaluation
│   ├── Policy Iteration
│   └── Value Iteration
├── Monte Carlo Methods (learn from complete episodes)
│   ├── MC Prediction
│   └── MC Control (with ε-greedy)
├── Temporal Difference Learning (learn from incomplete episodes)
│   ├── TD(0) — Prediction
│   ├── SARSA — On-Policy Control
│   └── Q-Learning — Off-Policy Control
├── Deep Q-Networks (DQN)
│   ├── Experience Replay
│   └── Target Network
└── Policy Gradient Methods
    ├── REINFORCE
    ├── Actor-Critic (A2C)
    └── Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO)

docs.title: ✦ Prerequisites
docs.text:
• [[01.The RL Problem]] — MDP, Bellman equations, \(V^\pi\), \(Q^\pi\), \(A^\pi\) — all used immediately
  • [[01.Linear Regression]] — gradient descent mechanics
  • [[02.Logistic Regression]] — softmax, log-linear policy parameterisation
  • [[01.Bagging and Random Forests]] — intuition for variance reduction (relevant to policy gradients)

docs.title: ✦ Part I — Dynamic Programming (The Ideal Baseline)
docs.text: Dynamic Programming (DP) solves MDPs exactly when the model \(P, R\) is known. We cover it here to establish the benchmark that model-free methods approximate.

docs.title: 1.1 Policy Evaluation — Computing \(V^\pi\)
docs.text:
Given a fixed policy \(\pi\), compute \(V^\pi\) by iterating the Bellman expectation equation:

\[V_{k+1}(s) \leftarrow \sum_a \pi(a|s) \sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a)\left[R(s,a,s') + \gamma V_k(s')\right]\]

starting from \(V_0(s) = 0\) for all \(s\). This is a synchronous sweep — every state is updated using the values from the previous iteration.

Convergence: \(V_k \to V^\pi\) as \(k \to \infty\), at rate \(\gamma^k\) (from the contraction mapping theorem — see [[01.The RL Problem]] §6).

Complexity per sweep: \(O(|\mathcal{S}|^2 |\mathcal{A}|)\) — must loop over all states, actions, and next states.

docs.title: 1.2 Policy Iteration
docs.text:
Alternate between evaluation and improvement:

π₀ →[evaluate]→ V^{π₀} →[improve]→ π₁ →[evaluate]→ V^{π₁} →[improve]→ π₂ → ···

Policy Improvement step: given \(V^\pi\), construct a strictly better (or equal) policy: $\(\pi'(s) = \arg\max_a \sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a)\left[R(s,a,s') + \gamma V^\pi(s')\right]\)$

Policy Improvement Theorem. If \(\pi' \neq \pi\), then \(V^{\pi'}(s) \geq V^\pi(s)\) for all \(s\), with strict inequality for at least one \(s\).

Proof. Let \(s\) be any state. Since \(\pi'\) takes the greedy action: $\(V^\pi(s) \leq \max_a Q^\pi(s,a) = Q^\pi(s, \pi'(s)) = \mathbb{E}[r + \gamma V^\pi(s') | s, \pi'(s)]\)$ $\(\leq \mathbb{E}[r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q^\pi(s', a') | s, \pi'(s)] \leq \cdots \leq V^{\pi'}(s)\)$

Each step applies the greedy improvement and the Bellman equation. The chain terminates at \(V^{\pi'}(s)\). \(\square\)

Convergence: Policy Iteration converges in a finite number of iterations (at most \(|\mathcal{A}|^{|\mathcal{S}|}\) policies, but in practice much fewer).

docs.title: 1.3 Value Iteration
docs.text:
Collapse evaluation and improvement into a single sweep:

\[V_{k+1}(s) \leftarrow \max_a \sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a)\left[R(s,a,s') + \gamma V_k(s')\right]\]

This applies the Bellman optimality operator \(\mathcal{T}\) directly. Convergence follows from the \(\gamma\)-contraction: $\(|V_{k+1} - V^_|_\infty = |\mathcal{T}V_k - \mathcal{T}V^_|_\infty \leq \gamma |V_k - V^*|_\infty\)$

Value Iteration vs. Policy Iteration:

Policy Iteration Value Iteration Inner loop Full policy evaluation (many sweeps) Single sweep Outer loop Few iterations Many iterations When to prefer When evaluation is cheap When convergence speed matters Convergence Finite (in policy space) Asymptotic (in value space)

The fundamental limitation of DP: requires iterating over all \(s \in \mathcal{S}\) explicitly, and knowing \(P(s'|s,a)\). For Atari (screen pixels) or continuous state spaces, both are intractable. Model-free methods address this.

docs.title: ✦ Part II — Monte Carlo Methods
docs.text:
Monte Carlo (MC) methods learn from complete episodes — they wait until the end of an episode, compute the actual return \(G_t\), and use it as the target.

Key idea: the expected return \(\mathbb{E}[G_t | S_t = s]\) is exactly \(V^\pi(s)\). So average the actual returns observed after visiting \(s\).

docs.title: 2.1 MC Prediction — Estimating \(V^\pi\)
docs.text:
Algorithm: First-Visit MC Prediction
─────────────────────────────────────────────────
Input: policy π, number of episodes N
Initialise: V(s) = 0, Returns(s) = [] for all s

For episode = 1, ..., N:
    Generate trajectory: s₀,a₀,r₁,s₁,a₁,r₂,...,sT
    G ← 0
    For t = T-1, T-2, ..., 0:
        G ← γG + r_{t+1}
        If s_t not in {s₀,...,s_{t-1}}:        ← first-visit condition
            Append G to Returns(s_t)
            V(s_t) ← mean(Returns(s_t))
─────────────────────────────────────────────────

First-visit vs. every-visit: First-visit MC only averages returns from the first occurrence of \(s\) in each episode; every-visit MC averages all occurrences. Both converge to \(V^\pi\) by the law of large numbers.

The incremental update form. Instead of storing all returns: $\(V(s) \leftarrow V(s) + \frac{1}{N(s)}\left[G_t - V(s)\right]\)$

where \(N(s)\) is the visit count. With a fixed step size \(\alpha\) in place of \(\frac{1}{N(s)}\), this becomes: $\(V(s) \leftarrow V(s) + \alpha\left[G_t - V(s)\right]\)$

The term \([G_t - V(s)]\) is the prediction error — how wrong our estimate was. This is the prototype of the TD error we derive next.

Properties of MC:

  • Unbiased: \(G_t\) is the true return — no approximation.
  • High variance: \(G_t\) is one sample of a potentially long stochastic trajectory. Variance grows with episode length.
  • Non-bootstrapping: MC does not use estimates of \(V\) to update \(V\). It uses the actual return.
  • Requires complete episodes: cannot be used for continuing tasks.

docs.title: 2.2 MC Control — Finding \(\pi^*\)
docs.text:
For control, we need \(Q^\pi(s,a)\) (not \(V^\pi\)), because without the model we cannot do the greedy improvement step \(\arg\max_a \sum_{s'} P[R + \gamma V(s')]\) — we don't know \(P\).

With \(Q\), greedy improvement requires no model: \(\pi'(s) = \arg\max_a Q(s,a)\).

But greedy policies don't explore — they commit to the currently best-known action and never discover better ones. The standard fix: \(\epsilon\)-greedy policy:

\[\pi(a|s) = \begin{cases} 1 - \epsilon + \frac{\epsilon}{|\mathcal{A}|} & \text{if } a = \arg\max_{a'} Q(s,a') \ \frac{\epsilon}{|\mathcal{A}|} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\]

With probability \(1-\epsilon\), exploit; with probability \(\epsilon\), explore uniformly.

GLIE (Greedy in the Limit with Infinite Exploration): MC control converges to \(\pi^*\) if:

  1. Every \((s,a)\) pair is visited infinitely often.
  2. \(\pi \to \pi^*\) (greedy) in the limit.

This is achieved by decaying \(\epsilon \to 0\) as \(t \to \infty\).

docs.title: ✦ Part III — Temporal Difference Learning
docs.text:
Temporal Difference (TD) learning is the central idea in RL. It combines:

  • The sampling of Monte Carlo — learns from experience, no model needed.
  • The bootstrapping of Dynamic Programming — updates estimates using other estimates, without waiting for the end of the episode.

docs.title: 3.1 TD(0) — The Simplest TD Method
docs.text:
After each step \((s_t, a_t, r_{t+1}, s_{t+1})\), update:

\[\boxed{V(s_t) \leftarrow V(s_t) + \alpha\left[\underbrace{r_{t+1} + \gamma V(s_{t+1})}_{\text{TD target}} - V(s_t)\right]}\]

The term \(\delta_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)\) is the TD error — the difference between the Bellman-predicted value and the current estimate.

Why "temporal difference"? The update uses the difference between value estimates at two different times — \(V(s_t)\) and \(V(s_{t+1})\).

The bootstrapping insight: instead of waiting for the true return \(G_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma r_{t+2} + \cdots\), we substitute \(r_{t+1} + \gamma V(s_{t+1})\) — a one-step estimate that uses our current (imperfect) value function. This is called bootstrapping.

docs.title: 3.2 MC vs. TD — A Precise Comparison
docs.text:
Property Monte Carlo TD(0) Target \(G_t\) (actual return) \(r_{t+1} + \gamma V(s_{t+1})\) (bootstrap) Bias Zero (unbiased) Biased (uses approximate \(V\)) Variance High (long trajectory) Low (one-step transition) Requires episode end? Yes No — updates online Bootstrapping? No Yes Convergence To \(V^\pi\) To \(V^\pi\) (with appropriate \(\alpha\))

The bias-variance tradeoff of TD vs. MC is a direct analogue of the model complexity tradeoff. MC is unbiased but high-variance (like a flexible model with no regularisation). TD is biased but low-variance (like a regularised model). TD typically learns faster in practice.

docs.title: 3.3 The TD(\(\lambda\)) Spectrum
docs.text:
TD(0) uses a 1-step return. MC uses the full return. The \(n\)-step return interpolates:

\[G_t^{(n)} = r_{t+1} + \gamma r_{t+2} + \cdots + \gamma^{n-1} r_{t+n} + \gamma^n V(s_{t+n})\]

TD(\(\lambda\)) uses an exponentially weighted average of all \(n\)-step returns:

\[G_t^\lambda = (1-\lambda)\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \lambda^{n-1} G_t^{(n)}\]
  • \(\lambda = 0\): TD(0) — pure bootstrapping.
  • \(\lambda = 1\): Monte Carlo — no bootstrapping.
  • \(\lambda \in (0,1)\): intermediate — often best in practice.
         λ=0                              λ=1
         TD(0)                             MC
          |────────────────────────────────|
     low variance                    high variance
     high bias                        zero bias
     fast learning               slow/stable learning
          ↑
     often works well
     in deep RL (λ≈0)

Eligibility traces are the efficient implementation of TD(\(\lambda\)) — they maintain a decaying credit to each state, allowing multi-step updates in \(O(|\mathcal{S}|)\) per step.

docs.title: ✦ Part IV — TD Control: SARSA and Q-Learning
docs.text: For control, we extend TD to learn \(Q(s,a)\) and derive a policy from it.

docs.title: 4.1 SARSA — On-Policy TD Control
docs.text:
At each step, after taking action \(a_t\) and observing \(r_{t+1}, s_{t+1}\), sample next action \(a_{t+1} \sim \pi(\cdot|s_{t+1})\) and update:

\[Q(s_t, a_t) \leftarrow Q(s_t, a_t) + \alpha\left[r_{t+1} + \gamma Q(s_{t+1}, a_{t+1}) - Q(s_t, a_t)\right]\]

The name SARSA comes from the quintuple \((S_t, A_t, R_{t+1}, S_{t+1}, A_{t+1})\) used in the update.

On-policy: the target uses \(Q(s_{t+1}, a_{t+1})\) where \(a_{t+1}\) is drawn from the current policy \(\pi\) (e.g., \(\epsilon\)-greedy). SARSA learns the value of the policy it is actually following — including its exploratory actions.

SARSA converges to \(Q^{\pi^*}\) under GLIE conditions (all pairs visited, \(\epsilon \to 0\), \(\sum \alpha_t = \infty\), \(\sum \alpha_t^2 < \infty\)).

docs.title: 4.2 Q-Learning — Off-Policy TD Control
docs.text:
\[Q(s_t, a_t) \leftarrow Q(s_t, a_t) + \alpha\left[r_{t+1} + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s_{t+1}, a') - Q(s_t, a_t)\right]\]

One difference from SARSA: the target uses \(\max_{a'} Q(s_{t+1}, a')\) — the greedy action — regardless of what policy actually generated \(a_{t+1}\).

Off-policy: Q-learning learns \(Q^*\) directly, even while following an exploratory \(\epsilon\)-greedy policy. The behaviour policy (what generates data) and the target policy (what is being evaluated) are different. This is the defining property of off-policy learning.

Q-learning converges to \(Q^*\) with probability 1 under the same step-size conditions, for any behaviour policy that visits all \((s,a)\) pairs infinitely often.

docs.title: 4.3 SARSA vs. Q-Learning — The Cliff Walking Example
docs.text:
Consider a gridworld with a cliff along the bottom edge. The optimal path hugs the cliff. An \(\epsilon\)-greedy policy occasionally falls off.

┌────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  S                                     │
│                                        │
│                                        │
│  S ──[Q-learning]──────────────────► G │
│     ──[SARSA]─────────────────────► G  │
│  C  C  C  C  C  C  C  C  C  C  C  C  │
└────────────────────────────────────────┘
  • Q-learning learns the optimal (cliff-hugging) path, because its target is always \(\max_{a'} Q\). But during training, it occasionally falls off the cliff (due to \(\epsilon\)-greedy), incurring high reward penalties.
  • SARSA learns a safer path (away from the cliff), because it accounts for the exploratory policy's occasional falls. SARSA optimises the policy it is actually following.

The lesson: Q-learning optimises for the optimal policy. SARSA optimises for the current policy. In safety-critical settings, SARSA's conservative behaviour during training is preferable.

docs.title: 4.4 Tabular Q-Learning Algorithm
docs.text:
Algorithm: Q-Learning (Tabular)
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Initialise Q(s,a) = 0 for all s,a; Q(terminal,·) = 0

For each episode:
    s ← initial state
    While s is not terminal:
        a ← ε-greedy(Q, s)                 ← behaviour policy
        Take action a, observe r, s'
        Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α[r + γ max_{a'} Q(s',a') - Q(s,a)]
        s ← s'
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Convergence conditions (Robbins-Monro): $\(\sum_{t=0}^\infty \alpha_t = \infty \qquad \sum_{t=0}^\infty \alpha_t^2 < \infty\)$

e.g., \(\alpha_t = \frac{1}{t}\) satisfies both. A fixed \(\alpha\) (common in practice) does not guarantee convergence to \(Q^*\), but tracks non-stationarity.

docs.title: ✦ Part V — Deep Q-Networks (DQN)
docs.text:
Tabular Q-learning breaks when \(|\mathcal{S}|\) is large (continuous states, high-dimensional inputs like images). The fix: approximate \(Q(s,a) \approx Q(s,a;\theta)\) with a neural network.

Naïve function approximation fails. If we simply run Q-learning with a neural network, training is catastrophically unstable. Two reasons:

  1. Correlated updates: consecutive steps \((s_t, s_{t+1}, s_{t+2}, \ldots)\) are highly correlated. SGD assumes i.i.d. samples. Correlated gradients cause the network to overfit to recent experience and forget old experience.

  2. Moving targets: the target \(r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a'; \theta)\) changes every time \(\theta\) changes — we are chasing a moving goalpost. This creates instability analogous to trying to hit a target that moves whenever you shoot at it.

DQN (Mnih et al., 2015) fixes both with two mechanisms.

docs.title: 5.1 Experience Replay
docs.text:
Maintain a replay buffer \(\mathcal{D}\) of past transitions: $\(\mathcal{D} = {(s_t, a_t, r_{t+1}, s_{t+1})}_{t}\)$

At each training step, sample a random minibatch from \(\mathcal{D}\):

  1. Breaks temporal correlations — sampled transitions are approximately i.i.d.
  2. Allows each transition to be used for multiple gradient updates — improves data efficiency.
  3. Smooths the gradient signal over many past experiences.

Buffer size is a hyperparameter (typically \(10^5\)–\(10^6\) transitions). Old transitions are discarded when the buffer is full (FIFO).

docs.title: 5.2 Target Network
docs.text:
Maintain a target network \(Q(s, a; \theta^-)\) — a copy of the main network \(Q(s,a;\theta)\) whose parameters \(\theta^-\) are frozen for \(C\) steps (typically \(C = 10^4\)) before being updated to \(\theta\).

The loss is: $\(\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(s,a,r,s') \sim \mathcal{D}}\left[\left(r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a'; \theta^-) - Q(s, a; \theta)\right)^2\right]\)$

The target \(r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a'; \theta^-)\) is now stationary for \(C\) steps — the goalpost stops moving. Gradient descent on \(\theta\) has a stable target to chase.

Main network θ: updated every step via SGD
Target network θ⁻: frozen for C steps, then copied from θ

Step:  1  2  3  ...  C  |  C+1  C+2  ...  2C  |  2C+1  ...
θ:     updated at every step
θ⁻:   ───────────────────┤ copied ───────────────┤ copied

docs.title: 5.3 The DQN Algorithm
docs.text:
Algorithm: DQN
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Initialise Q(s,a;θ) with random weights θ
Initialise target network θ⁻ ← θ
Initialise replay buffer D with capacity N

For each episode:
    s ← initial state (preprocessed frames)
    While not terminal:
        a ← ε-greedy(Q(s,·;θ))
        Execute a, observe r, s'
        Store (s,a,r,s') in D

        Sample minibatch {(sⱼ,aⱼ,rⱼ,s'ⱼ)} from D

        yⱼ ← rⱼ                                   if s'ⱼ is terminal
        yⱼ ← rⱼ + γ max_{a'} Q(s'ⱼ,a';θ⁻)        otherwise

        Gradient step: θ ← θ - α ∇_θ (yⱼ - Q(sⱼ,aⱼ;θ))²

        Every C steps: θ⁻ ← θ
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

docs.title: 5.4 DQN Architecture for Atari
docs.text:
Input: 4 stacked 84×84 grayscale frames
       (stacking provides velocity information)
         ↓
Conv1: 32 filters, 8×8, stride 4, ReLU
         ↓
Conv2: 64 filters, 4×4, stride 2, ReLU
         ↓
Conv3: 64 filters, 3×3, stride 1, ReLU
         ↓
FC:    512 units, ReLU
         ↓
Output: |A| units (one Q-value per action, no activation)

Why no softmax on output? We want raw Q-values, not probabilities. The policy is \(\epsilon\)-greedy over these values.

docs.title: 5.5 DQN Variants
docs.text:
Variant Improvement Key idea Double DQN Reduces overestimation bias Use \(\theta\) to select action, \(\theta^-\) to evaluate it Dueling DQN Better value estimation Decompose \(Q(s,a) = V(s) + A(s,a)\) with two heads Prioritised Replay Better sample efficiency Sample transitions with high TD error more often Noisy Nets Better exploration Add learned noise to weights instead of \(\epsilon\)-greedy Rainbow All of the above Combines 6 improvements; current DQN SOTA

Double DQN deserves a derivation. Standard Q-learning overestimates \(Q^*\) because: $\(\mathbb{E}[\max_a Q(s,a)] \geq \max_a \mathbb{E}[Q(s,a)]\)$

(Jensen's inequality applied to a convex function of random variables — the max). Fix: decouple action selection from action evaluation:

\[y = r + \gamma Q!\left(s', \arg\max_{a'} Q(s',a';\theta);, \theta^-\right)\]

Use the online network \(\theta\) to select the action, but the target network \(\theta^-\) to evaluate it. This breaks the feedback loop that causes overestimation.

docs.title: ✦ Part VI — Policy Gradient Methods
docs.text:
All methods so far are value-based — they learn a value function and derive a policy implicitly (e.g., \(\pi(s) = \arg\max_a Q(s,a)\)). The \(\arg\max\) becomes problematic for:

  • Continuous action spaces: \(\arg\max_a Q(s,a)\) requires a continuous optimisation at every step.
  • Stochastic policies: value-based methods produce deterministic policies; some environments require randomness (e.g., card games, mixed-strategy Nash equilibria).

Policy gradient methods directly parameterise the policy \(\pi_\theta(a|s)\) and optimise the expected return:

\[J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi_\theta}[G_0] = \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi_\theta}\left[\sum_{t=0}^T r_{t+1}\right]\]

docs.title: 6.1 The Policy Gradient Theorem
docs.text:
Theorem. For any differentiable policy \(\pi_ heta\) and any start state distribution:

\[ abla_ heta J( heta) = \mathbb{E}_{ au \sim \pi_ heta}\left[\sum_{t=0}^T abla_ heta \log \pi_ heta(a_t | s_t) \cdot Q^{\pi_ heta}(s_t, a_t) ight]\]

Proof (finite horizon, no discount for clarity). Define trajectory \( au = (s_0, a_0, r_1, \ldots, s_T)\):

\[J( heta) = \sum_ au P( au; heta) R( au)\] \[ abla_ heta J( heta) = \sum_ au abla_ heta P( au; heta) R( au)\]

Apply the log-derivative trick: \( abla_ heta P( au; heta) = P( au; heta) abla_ heta \log P( au; heta)\):

\[= \sum_ au P( au; heta) abla_ heta \log P( au; heta) \cdot R( au)$$ $$= \mathbb{E}_{ au \sim \pi_ heta}\left[ abla_ heta \log P( au; heta) \cdot R( au) ight]\]

Now expand \(\log P( au; heta)\): $\(\log P( au; heta) = \log P(s_0) + \sum_t \log P(s_{t+1}|s_t,a_t) + \sum_t \log \pi_ heta(a_t|s_t)\)$

Taking gradient with respect to \( heta\): the first two terms vanish (they don't depend on \( heta\)): $\( abla_ heta \log P( au; heta) = \sum_t abla_ heta \log \pi_ heta(a_t|s_t)\)$

Therefore: $\( abla_ heta J( heta) = \mathbb{E}_{ au \sim \pi_ heta}\left[\sum_t abla_ heta \log \pi_ heta(a_t|s_t) \cdot R( au) ight]\)$

Replacing \(R( au)\) with the causally correct \(Q^{\pi_ heta}(s_t, a_t)\) (rewards after \(t\) only — past rewards don't depend on \(a_t\)):

\[ oxed{ abla_ heta J( heta) = \mathbb{E}_{ au \sim \pi_ heta}\left[\sum_t abla_ heta \log \pi_ heta(a_t|s_t) \cdot Q^{\pi_ heta}(s_t, a_t) ight]}\]

\(\square\)

Intuition. The gradient increases the log-probability of actions proportional to how good they were (\(Q\) value). If action \(a\) in state \(s\) led to high return, push \( heta\) to make \(a\) more likely in \(s\). If it led to low return, make it less likely. This is gradient ascent on \(J( heta)\).

The log-derivative trick is also called the REINFORCE trick or score function estimator. It appears throughout variational inference, generative models, and RL.

docs.title: 6.2 REINFORCE — Monte Carlo Policy Gradient
docs.text:
The simplest policy gradient algorithm: replace \(Q^{\pi_\theta}(s_t, a_t)\) with the Monte Carlo estimate \(G_t\) (actual return from \(t\)):

\[\theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha \sum_t \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t|s_t) \cdot G_t\] 
Algorithm: REINFORCE
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
For each episode:
    Generate trajectory τ = (s₀,a₀,r₁,...,sT) using π_θ
    For t = 0, ..., T-1:
        G_t ← Σ_{k=t}^{T-1} γ^{k-t} r_{k+1}    (actual return)
        θ ← θ + α G_t ∇_θ log π_θ(a_t|s_t)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────

The baseline trick — variance reduction. We can subtract any function \(b(s_t)\) from \(G_t\) without introducing bias:

\[\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_t \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t|s_t) \cdot (G_t - b(s_t))\right]\]

Proof that the baseline term vanishes in expectation: $\(\mathbb{E}\left[\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a|s) \cdot b(s)\right] = \sum_a \pi_\theta(a|s) \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a|s) \cdot b(s)\)$ $\(= b(s) \sum_a \pi_\theta(a|s) \frac{\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(a|s)}{\pi_\theta(a|s)} = b(s) \nabla_\theta \sum_a \pi_\theta(a|s) = b(s) \nabla_\theta 1 = 0\)$

The standard choice: \(b(s_t) = V^{\pi_\theta}(s_t)\). Then \(G_t - V^{\pi_\theta}(s_t)\) is an estimate of the advantage \(A^{\pi_\theta}(s_t, a_t)\). This dramatically reduces variance.

Problems with REINFORCE:

  • High variance: \(G_t\) is a full-trajectory Monte Carlo estimate.
  • Slow convergence: must complete episodes before updating.
  • On-policy: must generate new data with the current policy after every update.

docs.title: 6.3 Actor-Critic — Bootstrapped Policy Gradients
docs.text:
Replace the Monte Carlo return \(G_t\) in the policy gradient with a bootstrapped estimate from a learned value function (the critic):

\[\nabla_\theta J(\theta) \approx \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_t \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t|s_t) \cdot \delta_t\right]\]

where \(\delta_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma V_\phi(s_{t+1}) - V_\phi(s_t)\) is the TD error — an estimate of \(A^{\pi_\theta}(s_t, a_t)\).

Two networks:

  • Actor: \(\pi_\theta(a|s)\) — the policy being optimised.
  • Critic: \(V_\phi(s)\) — estimates the state-value function, trained by TD.
              ┌─────────────────┐
    s_t ─────►│   Actor  π_θ    │──── a_t ────► environment
              └─────────────────┘                  │
                       ↑                           │ r_{t+1}, s_{t+1}
              ∇_θ log π_θ · δ_t                    │
                       │                           ▼
              ┌─────────────────┐         δ_t = r+γV_φ(s')-V_φ(s)
    s_t ─────►│  Critic  V_φ    │◄──────────────────┘
              └─────────────────┘

Actor update: \(\theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha_\theta \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t|s_t) \cdot \delta_t\)

Critic update: \(\phi \leftarrow \phi + \alpha_\phi \delta_t \nabla_\phi V_\phi(s_t)\)

Why better than REINFORCE?

  • TD critic has much lower variance than MC return \(G_t\).
  • Can update online — no need to wait for episode end.

Why better than DQN?

  • Works naturally for continuous action spaces (no \(\arg\max\) needed).
  • Stochastic policy enables natural exploration.

A2C (Advantage Actor-Critic): synchronous version — multiple parallel workers generate experience, gradients are averaged, one synchronous update is performed. Stable and parallelisable.

A3C (Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic): asynchronous workers update a shared set of parameters independently. Faster wall-clock time, but noisier updates.

docs.title: 6.4 Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO)
docs.text:
A central problem with policy gradient methods: step size. If we take too large a step in \(\theta\)-space, the policy changes drastically — the new policy is so different from the old one that the old data is irrelevant, performance collapses, and recovery is difficult. If the step is too small, learning is slow.

Trust Region Policy Optimisation (TRPO) (Schulman et al., 2015) constrains updates to stay within a trust region: $\(\max_\theta \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\pi_\theta(a|s)}{\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}(a|s)} A^{\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}}(s,a)\right] \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \mathbb{E}[D_\text{KL}(\pi_\theta | \pi_{\theta_\text{old}})] \leq \delta\)$

The constraint is enforced via a conjugate gradient + line search — expensive and complex.

PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) achieves similar results with a simpler objective. Define the probability ratio: $\(r_t(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t|s_t)}{\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}(a_t|s_t)}\)$

PPO-Clip objective: $\(\mathcal{L}^\text{CLIP}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_t\left[\min\left(r_t(\theta) A_t,; \text{clip}(r_t(\theta), 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon) A_t\right)\right]\)$

The clip prevents \(r_t(\theta)\) from moving too far from 1 in either direction:

  • If \(A_t > 0\) (action was better than average): we want to increase \(\pi_\theta(a_t|s_t)\), so \(r_t > 1\). But we clip at \(1+\epsilon\) — don't increase probability too aggressively.
  • If \(A_t < 0\) (action was worse than average): we want to decrease \(\pi_\theta(a_t|s_t)\), so \(r_t < 1\). But we clip at \(1-\epsilon\) — don't decrease probability too aggressively.
   L^CLIP
    ↑
    │         clipped               unclipped
    │    ┌────────────┐           /
    │    │            │          /
    │    │            │         /
    │    │            │        /
    │────┼────────────┼───────/────────► r_t(θ)
    │  1-ε           1      1+ε
    │ (if A>0, clip here)

PPO training loop:

Algorithm: PPO
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
For each iteration:
    Collect N steps of data using π_{θ_old}
    Compute advantages Â_t using GAE (see below)

    For K epochs:
        For each minibatch:
            r_t(θ) ← π_θ(a_t|s_t) / π_{θ_old}(a_t|s_t)
            L_CLIP ← E[min(r_t·Â_t, clip(r_t,1-ε,1+ε)·Â_t)]
            L_VF ← E[(V_θ(s_t) - V_target_t)²]
            L_entropy ← E[H[π_θ(·|s_t)]]  ← exploration bonus

            L_total = L_CLIP - c₁·L_VF + c₂·L_entropy
            θ ← θ + α ∇_θ L_total

    θ_old ← θ
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

Generalised Advantage Estimation (GAE). The advantage \(A_t\) in PPO is estimated using GAE (Schulman et al., 2015b) — a \(\lambda\)-weighted blend of \(n\)-step TD errors:

\[\hat{A}_t = \sum_{l=0}^{\infty} (\gamma\lambda)^l \delta_{t+l}, \quad \delta_t = r_{t+1} + \gamma V_\phi(s_{t+1}) - V_\phi(s_t)\]
  • \(\lambda = 0\): one-step TD advantage — low variance, high bias.
  • \(\lambda = 1\): Monte Carlo advantage — high variance, low bias.
  • \(\lambda \approx 0.95\): typical in practice.

GAE with \((\gamma, \lambda) = (0.99, 0.95)\) is the standard configuration for PPO in continuous control tasks.

docs.title: ✦ Part VII — The Deadly Triad and When Things Diverge
docs.text:
The deadly triad (Sutton & Barto, Ch. 11): instability or divergence arises when all three of the following are combined:

  1. Function approximation (e.g., neural network for \(Q\))
  2. Bootstrapping (TD learning — using estimated values as targets)
  3. Off-policy learning (data not generated by the current policy)

Each pair is fine:

  • Function approx + bootstrapping + on-policy: stable (TD with linear function approx converges on-policy).
  • Function approx + MC + off-policy: stable (no bootstrapping, so no dangerous circularity).
  • Tabular + bootstrapping + off-policy: stable (tabular Q-learning provably converges).

All three together: can diverge. DQN manages this by:

  • Making it "approximately on-policy" via the target network (reduces the extent of off-policy-ness).
  • Using experience replay to stabilise gradients.

This is why deep RL is notoriously fragile — small hyperparameter changes can push a system into the deadly triad regime.

docs.title: ✦ Connection to AI / ML / Deep Learning
The RL Training Loop as Gradient Descent
docs.text: Value-based methods (Q-learning, DQN) minimise the Bellman residual — a regression loss. Policy gradient methods maximise \(J(\theta)\) — a non-convex objective. Both are stochastic gradient methods, connected to everything in [[01.Linear Regression]] through [[02.Boosting]].

docs.title: RLHF — Language Models as RL Policies
docs.text:
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (the training mechanism for GPT-4, Claude, Gemini):

  1. Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT): train a language model on high-quality demonstrations — supervised learning.
  2. Reward Model: train a model to predict human preferences between pairs of outputs.
  3. RL Fine-Tuning: treat the language model as a policy \(\pi_\theta\), the reward model as \(R\), and run PPO.

The MDP: state = prompt + generated tokens so far, action = next token, reward = reward model score at end of generation. PPO updates the language model policy to generate text that scores highly on human preference.

KL penalty in RLHF: the PPO objective includes a KL penalty \(-\beta D_\text{KL}(\pi_\theta | \pi_\text{SFT})\) to prevent the policy from drifting too far from the supervised baseline (which would cause incoherent text). This is analogous to the clip in PPO-Clip.

docs.title: AlphaGo / AlphaZero — Policy Gradients + MCTS
docs.text: AlphaZero's policy network is trained by a policy gradient update where the "policy" is the MCTS output distribution (not \(\pi_\theta\) directly). The value network is trained by TD-style updates. The combination — deep function approximation + planning — is more sample efficient than model-free RL alone.

docs.title: The Connection: Q-Learning = Gradient Descent on the Bellman Residual
docs.text:
Q-learning's update: $\(Q(s,a) \leftarrow Q(s,a) + \alpha[r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s',a') - Q(s,a)]\)$

is exactly a gradient descent step on the loss: $\(\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\left[\left(r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s',a';\theta^-) - Q(s,a;\theta)\right)^2\right]\)$

with the target held fixed (treating \(\theta^-\) as constant). This connects Q-learning to the linear regression framework — the Bellman target is the "label" and \(Q(s,a;\theta)\) is the "prediction."

docs.title: Q-Learning in NumPy (Tabular)
docs.text:
import numpy as np

class GridWorld:
    """4x4 grid, goal at (3,3), reward +1, else -0.01"""
    def __init__(self):
        self.n = 4
        self.goal = (3, 3)
        self.actions = [(0,1),(0,-1),(1,0),(-1,0)]  # E,W,S,N

    def step(self, s, a):
        r, c = s
        dr, dc = self.actions[a]
        nr, nc = max(0,min(self.n-1,r+dr)), max(0,min(self.n-1,c+dc))
        s_ = (nr, nc)
        reward = 1.0 if s_ == self.goal else -0.01
        done = (s_ == self.goal)
        return s_, reward, done

env = GridWorld()
n_states = env.n * env.n
n_actions = 4
Q = np.zeros((env.n, env.n, n_actions))

alpha, gamma, epsilon = 0.1, 0.9, 0.1

for episode in range(5000):
    s = (np.random.randint(4), np.random.randint(4))
    while True:
        r, c = s
        # ε-greedy
        if np.random.rand() < epsilon:
            a = np.random.randint(n_actions)
        else:
            a = np.argmax(Q[r, c])

        s_, reward, done = env.step(s, a)
        r_, c_ = s_

        # Q-learning update
        td_target = reward + gamma * np.max(Q[r_, c_]) * (1 - done)
        Q[r, c, a] += alpha * (td_target - Q[r, c, a])

        s = s_
        if done:
            break

# Extract greedy policy
policy_symbols = ['→','←','↓','↑']
for i in range(env.n):
    row = ''
    for j in range(env.n):
        if (i,j) == env.goal:
            row += ' G '
        else:
            row += f' {policy_symbols[np.argmax(Q[i,j])]} '
    print(row)

docs.title: PPO Skeleton (PyTorch)
docs.text:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class ActorCritic(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, obs_dim, act_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.shared = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(obs_dim, 64), nn.Tanh(),
            nn.Linear(64, 64), nn.Tanh()
        )
        self.actor = nn.Linear(64, act_dim)   # logits
        self.critic = nn.Linear(64, 1)         # V(s)

    def forward(self, x):
        h = self.shared(x)
        return self.actor(h), self.critic(h)

    def get_action(self, obs):
        logits, value = self(obs)
        dist = torch.distributions.Categorical(logits=logits)
        action = dist.sample()
        return action, dist.log_prob(action), value

def ppo_update(model, optimizer, obs, actions, old_log_probs,
               returns, advantages, clip_eps=0.2, n_epochs=4):
    for _ in range(n_epochs):
        logits, values = model(obs)
        dist = torch.distributions.Categorical(logits=logits)
        new_log_probs = dist.log_prob(actions)
        entropy = dist.entropy().mean()

        # PPO clip objective
        ratio = (new_log_probs - old_log_probs).exp()
        surr1 = ratio * advantages
        surr2 = ratio.clamp(1 - clip_eps, 1 + clip_eps) * advantages
        actor_loss = -torch.min(surr1, surr2).mean()

        # Critic loss
        critic_loss = (returns - values.squeeze()).pow(2).mean()

        loss = actor_loss + 0.5 * critic_loss - 0.01 * entropy
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 0.5)
        optimizer.step()

docs.title: ✦ Exit Criteria
docs.text:
You know this when you can:

  1. Derive the TD(0) update from the Bellman expectation equation and state exactly what "bootstrapping" means.
  2. Prove why SARSA is on-policy and Q-learning is off-policy — pointing to the specific term in each update rule that makes it so.
  3. Explain the cliff-walking example: why Q-learning finds the optimal path but SARSA finds a safer path during training.
  4. State the two problems of naïve deep Q-learning (correlated updates, moving targets) and explain precisely how experience replay and the target network fix each.
  5. Derive the policy gradient theorem using the log-derivative trick — from the definition of \(J(\theta)\) to the final expression in three steps.
  6. Prove that subtracting a baseline \(b(s_t)\) from \(G_t\) in REINFORCE does not introduce bias.
  7. State the PPO-Clip objective and explain geometrically what the clip does when \(A_t > 0\) vs. \(A_t < 0\).
  8. Name the three elements of the deadly triad and explain why DQN avoids divergence despite combining two of them.
  9. Implement tabular Q-learning in \(\sim\)30 lines of NumPy with no RL library.
  10. Map RLHF to the MDP formalism: identify state, action, reward, and the role of the KL penalty.
